# Anthropologia Sacra


## 1 Preface to the First Decade

To the most serene Elector of Saxony’s privy councillors, Lord Christoph von Loss in Schleiniz, Lord Marcus Gerstenberger in Schwerstadt, Trackendorff, and Schiebla, my most honorable lords and patrons,

Greetings. Most noble men, great patrons.

As there are two moments of nature, so there are of Scripture. There, the first is named by philosophers as form; the second as the property of form: here, the first can be called by theologians

Preface.

Faith, which is like a form; Charity, which is like a property, following the form. In the former the whole force of nature, in the latter the sum of Christianity consists. For Ignatius wrote most truly in Ep. 7. τὸ ὅλον πίσις ἡ εἰς θεὸν, καὶ ἀγάπη περὶ τὸν ὁμόφυλον, Our whole Christianity is nothing else than faith in God and charity toward one's neighbor. To faith pertains the knowledge of truth; to charity the practice of piety. There truth is apprehended, here piety is exercised. There God is known, here He is worshipped. The former is placed in sense, the latter in act. The former is of wisdom, the latter of religion. Lactantius writes briefly concerning both in book 4 of the Divine Institutes, chapter 4: It is the same God who must both be understood, which is of wisdom; and honored, which is of religion. But wisdom precedes, religion follows. Because it is first to know God, and consequently to worship Him. Thus therefore it remains certain that there are two general heads of Christianity, namely πίσις καὶ ἀγάπη, a true sense concerning God, and a right worship toward God: most briefly; true faith and a sincere life. And hence two parts of Theology arise, of which the one is περὶ τῶν πιστῶν, the other περὶ τῶν πρακτῶν. The former explains things to be believed, the latter things to be done. The former teaches Christians to believe rightly; the latter to live piously. Both are insinuated by the Apostle John, 1 Epist. 3. v. 23. This is the commandment of God, that we BELIEVE in the name of his Son Jesus Christ: and LOVE one another. By πιστεύειν he hints at the first part of Theology, by ἀγαπᾷν the second.

Furthermore, Faith and the knowledge of the truth is completed by two things: 1. The knowledge of God, 2. The knowledge of Ourselves. For as Augustine writes in his Manual, ch. 26: What is the knowledge of Truth? First to know Yourself: Then to know your Creator: both are highly necessary, and most fruitful. For if we do not know God, we are alienated from the highest Good, and cannot be saved. If we are ignorant of Ourselves, we neither recognize the disease of our nature, nor recover our health. Hence that γνῶθι σεαυτὸν, Know thyself, is deservedly said to have descended from heaven. And rightly does Bernard say, ch. 11 of the Meditations: The knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation. For when infirmity is known, both the Physician is sought more ardently, and the medicine is applied more willingly.

God indeed first created man upright, Eccles. 7:30, in His own image, Gen. 1:26, 27, in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. 4:24, so that he would not be ashamed, Gen. 1:last, nor be subject to death, Wisd. 2:23, Rom. 3:12, ch. 6:last. But the envious Devil, Wisd. 2:23, seduced the πρωτοπλάσους, Gen. 3, so that we are all conceived in iniquity, Ps. 51:5, are destitute of the glory of God, Rom. 3:23, and are born children of wrath, Eph. 2:3. O miserable lot of man, exclaims Augustine, ch. 31 of the Manual, when he lost that for which he was made! O dire and hard fall that! Alas, what did he lose, and what did he find? What departed, and what remained? He lost the blessedness for which he was made: and he found misery, for which he was not made. That departed, without which nothing is happy; and that remained, which by itself is nothing but miserable. God

Preface.

but He, who is rich in mercy, Ephes. 2. verf. 4. in turn loved the human race, Iohan. 3. verf. 16. and sent His Son, made of a woman, Galat. 4. verf. 4. that He might redeem those who were under the law, and we might receive the adoption of sons, verf. 5. For the Son of God was made the son of man, that man also might become the Son of God, Irenæus book 3. chap. 11. For God does not desire the death of the wicked, but that he should turn back and live, Ezech. 33. verse 11. and therefore He sent the Son as Savior of the world, 1. Iohan. 4. v. 14. who died for all, 2. Cor. 5. verf. 14. and 15. even for those who perish, Rom. 14. v. 16. 1. Cor. 8. v. 11. which word of grace is preached to all nations, Matth. 28. v. 19. that they may repent, Act. 17. v. 30. and be saved, 1. Tim 2. v. 4. But because many reject grace, and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, Act. 13. v. 46. hence on the last day certain ones will proceed to the resurrection of judgment. Ioh. 5. v. 29. For it stands, and will stand forever, that unshaken sentence of Christ the Savior: He who believes in

Preface.

the Son, has eternal life: but he who is unbelieving toward the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him, John 3, last verse. And these are those distinct states of human nature, which produce a sacred ἀνθρωπολογίαν, and without the knowledge of which no one can maintain the name of a Christian, much less of a Theologian.

Since, therefore, it was determined by me to prepare a Theological College, and to propose the principal controversies of the faith for disputation, these matters which concern the knowledge of Man and Christian ἀνθρωπολογίαν pleased me singularly above all the rest. For whether one looks at the necessity, or the utility, or the pleasantness, all things are excellently found in this Anthropological doctrine. I made, therefore, a beginning with God, and through his blessing I completed the first decade, in which the two first states are expounded, namely of Integrity and Corruption, of which the former is concerning the Bestowal of Grace through the κτίσιν of God, the latter concerning the loss of that which was bestowed through the πτῶσιν of Adam.

But to these first disputations, Men

Preface.

Most noble and supreme patrons, and eternally to be respected, I wished to prefix your most honorable name, so that these might have patrons who would go to defend them. For what can be said or written today that is immune from the bite of all rashly judging censors? But I will fear nothing, encouraged by your protection, but will rather proceed the more eagerly to the subsequent συζητήσεις, and will contribute to common use whatever the grace of the Most High has mercifully bestowed. Furthermore, the stimulus of gratitude has excited me to the same. For I have often experienced your clearly singular benevolence and kindness toward me, though undeserving, so that I frankly confess that I have long been bound to give a sign of a grateful mind. Finally, your zeal, with which you burn for religion, has moved me, as has your love of theological matters, with which you are accustomed to temper the most serious political cares and by the reading of which you are accustomed to refresh yourselves. That therefore you may receive these first fruits with a serene brow, against the malevolent

Preface.

that you may cherish, and furthermore favor my studies, in all ways that I can and ought, and with the greatest [earnestness] I pray. May God keep your Noble and Distinguished Lordships safe for a very long time, and may He command a most happy new year to dawn upon you. Given at Wittenberg, on the day before the Nativity of the Lord, in the year 1612.

Your Noble and Distinguished Lordships.

Most observant.

Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Theology.

S. P. D. Viri Nobilissimi, Mecœnates magni.

VTi Naturæ; ita Scripturæ duo sunt momenta. Ibi primum à Philosophis nominatur forma; secundum formæ proprium: Hic primum à Theologis vocari potest

Præfatio.

Fides, quæ instar formæ; secūdum Chasritas, quæ instar proprij, formam consequentis. In illis tota vis naturæ, in his summa Christianismi consistit. Nam verissimè scripsit Ignatius Ep. 7. τὸ ὅλον πίσις ἡ εἰς θεὸν, καὶ ἀγάπη περὶ τὸν ὁμόφυλον, Totus noster Christianismus nihil est aliud, quam fides in Deum & Charitas in proximum. Ad Fidem spectat γνῶσις ἀληθείας; ad Charitatem πρᾶξις εὐσεβείας. Ibi apprehenditur veritas, hîc exercetur Pietas. Ibi Deus noscitur, hîc colitur. Illud positum in sensu, hoc in actu. Illud sapientiæ, hoc Religionis est. De utroque breuiter Lactantius l. 4. Div. instit. cap. 4. Idem Deus est, qui & intelligi debet, quod est sapientiæ; & honorari, quod est religionis. Sed sapiētia præcedit, religio sequitur. Quia prius est Deum scire, consequens colere. Sic ergo certum manet, quòd duo sint Christianismi generalia capita, nēpè πίσις καὶ ἀγάπη, Verus de Deo sensus, & Rectus in Deū cultus: Breuissimè; Fides vera & vita sincera. Atque hinc duae partes Theologiae oriuntur, quarum altera est περὶ τῶν πιστῶν, altera περὶ τῶν πρακτῶν. Illa exponit credenda, haec facienda. Illa docet Christianos Rectè credere; Haec piè viuere. Vtrumque insinuatur ab A. Iohanne, 1. Epist. 3. v. 23. Hoc est mandatum Dei, vt CREDAMVS in nomine Filij eius Iesu Christi: & DILIGAMVS alij alios. Per πιστεύειν primam per ἀγαπᾷν secundam Theologiae partem innuit.

Porrò autem Fides & cognitio veritatis duobus absoluitur, 1. Notitiâ Dei, 2. Notitiâ Nostri. Nam vt Augustinus scribit in Manuali cap. 26. Quid est cognitio Veritatis? Primò cognoscere Teipsum: Deinde cognoscere Creatorem tuum: vtrumque est summè necesarium, & maximè fructuosum. Si enim Deum nescimus, à summo Bono alieni sumus, & saluari non possumus. Si Nosmetipsos ignoramus, morbum naturae nec agnoscimus, nec sanitatem recuperamus. Hinc meritò è caelo descendisse dicitur illud γνῶθι σεαυτὸν, Nosce teipsum. Et rectè Bern. c. 11. Medit. Notitia peccati initium est salutis. Cognitâ enim infirmitate, & Medicus quæritur ardentius, & medicamen adhibetur lubentius.

Hominem quidem Deus primum condidit rectum, Eccles. 7. v. 30. ad imaginem suam. Gen. 1. v. 26. 27. in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis, Ephes 4. v. 24. ut non erubesceret, Gen. 1. v. vlt. nec morti subiaceret, Sap. 2. v. 23. Rom. 3. v. 12. cap. 6. vers. vlt. Sed inuidus Diabolus, Sap. 2. v. 23. seduxit πρωτοπλάσους, Gen. 3. ut omnes concipiamur in iniquitate, Ps. 51. v. 6. destituamur gloriâ Dei, Rom. 3. v. 23. & nascamur iræ filij, Eph. 2. v. 5. O mifera sors hominis, exclamat August. cap. 31. Manu. cum hoc perdidit, ad quod factus est! O dirus ac durus casus ille! Heu quid perdidit, & quid inuenit? Quid abscessit, & quid remansit? Perdidit beatitudinem, ad quam factus est: & inuenit miseriam, ad quam factus non est. Abscessit, sine quo nihil felix est; & remansit, quod per se nõ nisi miserum est. Deus

Præfatio.

autem, qui diues est in misericordia, Ephes. 2. verf. 4. vicissim dilexit genus humanum, Iohan. 3. verf. 16. & misit Filium suum, factum ex muliere. Galat. 4. verf. 4. vt eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret, & adoptionem filiorum reciperemus, verf. 5. Filius enim Dei factus est filius hominis, vt & homo fieret Filius Dei, Irenæus libro 3. cap. 11. Nam Deus mortem impij non vult, sed vt reuertatur & viuat, Ezech. 33. versu 11. ideoque misit Filium Seruatorem mundi, 1. Iohan. 4. v. 14. qui mortuus est pro omnibus, 2. Cor. 5. verf. 14. & 15. etiam pro ijs qui pereunt, Rom. 14. v. 16. 1. Cor. 8. v. 11. quod verbum gratiæ prædicatur cunctis gentibus, Matth. 28. v. 19. vt resipiscãt, Act. 17. v. 30. & salui fiant, 1. Tim 2. v. 4. Quia verò multi gratiam repellũt, & semetipsos indignos iudicãt vitæ æternæ, Act. 13. v. 46. hinc in vltimo die cẽsor eo quidã procedẽt in resurrectionem iudicij. Ioh. 5. v. 29. Stat enim, & in æternum stabit incõcussa illa Christi seruatoris sententia: Qui credit in

Præfatio.

Filium, habet vitam æternam: qui autem incredulus est Filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum, Ioh. 3. v. vlt. Et hi sunt isti naturæ humanæ status distincti, qui sacram ἀνθρωπολογίαν pariunt, & sine quorũ notitia nemo Christiani, multò minùs Theologi nomen tueri potest.

Cùm ergo mihi constitutum esset, Collegium Theologicum adornare, & præcipuas fidei controuersias ad disputandum proponere, singulariter præ reliquis omnibus placuerunt ista, quæ Hominis cognitionem & Christianã ἀνθρωπολογίαν concernunt. Siuè enim spectetur necessitas, siuè vtilitas, siuè iucunditas, omnia in doctrina ista Anthropologica excellenter reperiuntur. Feci ergo cũ Deo initium, & per eius benedictionem primam decadem absolui, in qua duo primi status exponuntur, nempè Integritatis & Corruptionis, quorum ille est de Gratiæ Collatione per κτίσιν Dei, alter de collatæ amissione per πτῶσιν Adami.

His verò primis disputationibus, Viri

Præfatio.

Nobilissimi Mecœnates summi, & æternùm obseruandi, Honoratissimum Nomen Vestrū præscribere volui, vt Patronos haberēt, qui istas defensum irent. Quid enim hodiè dici scribiuè potest, quod ab omni censorum temerè iudicantium morsu immune sit? Verùm nihil timebo, Vestro animatus præsidio, sed pergam potiùs eò alacriùs ad subsequentes συζητήσεις, & in vsum communem conferam, quicquid Altissimi gratia clementer elargita fuerit. Porrò ad idem excitauit me gratitudinis stimulus.Vestram enim erga me immerentem beeuolentiam & humanitatem planè singularem expertus sum sæpius, vt ad grati animi signum edendum me iamdudum fuisse obstrictum ingenuè fatear. Tandem permouit me Zelus vester, quo in religionem feruetis, & amor rerum Theologicarum, quibus grauissimas curas politicas temperare, & quarum lectione vos recreare consueuistis. Vt igitur primitias has serenâ fronte accipiatis, contra maleuolos

Præfatio.

foueatis, meiq́; studijs porrò faueatis, modis quibus possum & debeo, omnibus, maximisq́; oro. Deus N N. V. V. diutissimè saluas conseruet, nouumq́; annum felicissimum illusescere iubeat. Dabam Witteb. die profesto Nativ. Domini, Anno 1612.

## 2 Disputation I. On the Image of God

Preface by Balthasar Meisner: Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Hieronymus Nymann; of Wittenberg, Saxon.

Prooemium. I.

The entire theological wisdom of man consists in two things: 1. In the knowledge of God. 2. In the knowledge of ourselves. Hence the daily prayer of Augustine: LORD, grant, grant me to know Thee, to know myself.

II. And from this also, sacred study can be divided into two members: 1. into Theology, 2. into Christian Anthropology.

III. Theology, taken specifically, is that part which treats of GOD and provides knowledge of Him. God, however, is to be known by reason of His 1. Being, 2. Will, 3. Working. The BEING OF GOD is such that He is one in essence, three in person. The WILL OF GOD is twofold: 1. legal, or of the law; 2. evangelical, or gracious. The former shows what GOD wishes to be done by us, the latter what He wishes to do for us. The WORKING OF GOD is either internal and hypostatic, or external, consisting in the creation of the world, the preservation of the created, governance, and other similar actions, about which it is disputed more prolixly elsewhere.

IV. By sacred or Christian Anthropology I mean that part which is occupied solely with the knowledge of man. Nothing is more useful than this, nothing more excellent after GOD.

O man, why do you concern yourself with the heights of the stars and the depths of the sea? Enter into the abyss of your own soul, and marvel, if you can, says Isidore, book 1, On the Highest Good.

V. The devout monk Bernard holds the same opinion, who says in chapter 65 of his Meditations: No knowledge is better than that by which you, O man, know yourself. Therefore leave other things, and examine yourself: run through yourself, and settle within yourself. Let your thought begin from yourself, and end in yourself: nor should you be stretched out in vain toward other things, while neglecting yourself.

VI. For the more we progress in the knowledge of ourselves, the closer we approach to the knowledge of God. The more deeply we look into ourselves, the more ardently we flee to Christ. He cannot be cast down into pride who always considers his own misery. He will not despair of guilt who thinks of grace. He will not be troubled by ignominy who weighs the future glory of man. Thus, therefore, the knowledge of oneself is the queen of all sciences, the workshop of all theological virtues.

VII. Considering this very thing, therefore, with other matters set aside and reserved for other times: it has pleased us to ventilate and propose as the subject of our disputations those things which lead to the knowledge of Man and thus to one's own knowledge, lest Bernard repeat his complaint from book 1 of On the Soul, chapter 1: Many know many things, and do not know themselves: they look at others, and desert themselves.

IIX. Man is known either according to his essence and parts or according to his diverse states. The former knowledge is more philosophical and constructs a physical anthropology: the latter is proper to theology, and therefore is not inappropriately called sacred or Christian anthropology.

IX. We send the former to the Lyceum: we shall provide the latter explained in a few dissertations. For as the former is more intricate, so the latter is more fruitful. As the former produces knowledge, so the latter shows the way to salvation.

X. For which reason Bernard, when of man had commended the knowledge, that the states of man must be known, he soon adds, when he writes further in the aforesaid Chapter 45: Examine what you are, what you have been, what you ought to have been, what you will be able to be. What you have been by nature; what you are now by fault; what you ought to have been by industry: what you may still be by grace.

XI. Following this salutary warning, therefore, which applies most aptly to the matter, we shall briefly repeat the purer doctrine CONCERNING THE STATES OF THE HUMAN RACE, and we shall present it enclosed in distinct questions, intending to make a beginning from the first state, which is commonly called that of Integrity or Innocence.

Latin:

Praef. Balth. Meisner: S S. Th. D. Resp. Hieronymo Nymanno; Witteberga Saxone.

Προοίμιον. Ι.

VNiuerfa hominis sapientia Theologica in duobus consistit: 1. In cognitione Dei. 2. In cognitione nostri. Hinc quotidiana Augustini precatio: DOMINE, da, da mihi nosse Te, nosse Me.

II. Atque hinc etiam studium sacrum in duo membra dispesci potest: 1. in Θεολογιαν 2. in Ανθρωπολογιαν Christianam.

III. Θεολογία specialiter accepta pars ea est, quae de DEO agit, eiusque cognitionem suppeditat. Cognoscendus autem est Deus ratione sui, 1. Esse 2 Velle 3 Operari. ESSE DEI tale est, vt sit vnus ουσία, trinus ὑπόστασει. VELLE DEI duplex est; 1. νομικόν seu legale. 2. ευαγγελικόν seu gratiosum. Illud ostendit, quid DEVS a nobis fieri velit, hoc quid de nobis facere velit. OPERARI DEI vel internum & hypostaticum est; vel externum, consistens in mundi creatione, creati conseruatione, gubernatione, alijsque similibus actionibus, de quibus alibi prolixiùs disputatur.

IV. Ανθρωπολογιαν sacram vel Christianam dico eam partem, quae in hominis cognitione occupata est vnice. Nihil hac vtilius, nihil post DEVM praestantius.

Q homo, quid curaris siderum altitudines & profunditatem maris? Animi tui abyssum intrà, & mirare, si potes, ait Isidorus lib. 1. de summo bono.

V. Idem censet devotus monachus Bernhardus, qui cap. 65. Meditationum: Nulla, inquit, scientia melior est illâ, quâ cognoscis homo seipsum. Relinque ergò cætera, & Teipsum discute: per Te curre, & in Te consiste. A Te incipiat cogitatio tua, & in Te finiatur: nec frustrà in alia distendaris, Te neglecto.

VI. Etenim quanto magis in cognitione nostri proficimus, tantò propiùs ad cognitionem Dei accedimus, Quò penitiùs nos introspicimus eo ardentiùs ad Christum confugimus. Non potest præcipitari in superbiam, qui suam semper considerat miseriam. Non desperabit de culpa, qui cogitabit de gratia. Non turbabitur ob ignominiam, qui futuram hominis perpendit gloriam. Ita igitur cognitio sui ipsius, omnium est scientiarum regina, omnium virtutum Theologicarum officina.

VII. Hoc ipsum ergo considerantes, sepositis alijs, alijşque tempori reservatis articulis: eos potissimùm ventilare, & pro materia disputationum proponere placuit; qui ad Hominis adeoque propriam cognitionem perducunt, ne Bernardus querelam suam repetat ex lib. de Anim. c. 1. Multi multa sciunt, & seipsos nesciunt: Alios inspiciunt, & seipsos deserunt.

IIX. Cognoscitur autem homo, vel secundum essentiam partesque vel secundum status diversos, Prior cognitio magis est Philosophica, & construit ἀνθρωπολογίαν Physicam: posterior Theologiæ est propria, ideoq; ἀνθρωπολογία sacra vel Christiana non incommode nuncupatur.

IX. Istam ad Lyceum remittimus: hanc nonnullis dissertationibus explicatam dabimus. Vt enim illa intricatior: ita hæc fructuosior. Vt illa scientiam parit, ità hæc viam ad salutem monstrat.

X. Quam ob causam Bernardus, cùm hominis notitiam commendâsset, status hominis cognoscendos esse, mox subiungit, cùm prædicto Cap. 45. porrò scribit: Discute quid sis quid fueris, quia esse debueris, quis a esse poteris. Quid fueris per naturam; quid modò sis per culpam; quid esse debueris per industriam: quid adhuc esse possis per gratiam.

XI. Hoc igitur salutare monitum sequentes, quod ad issimus veriat aptimè, puriorem DE STATIBVS HVMANI GENERIS doctrinam breuiter repetemus, eamque distinctis quæstionibus inclusam exhibebimus, initium facturi à statu primo qui Integritatis vel Innocentiæ vulgò appellatur.


### Question I. What are the states of the human race?

How many states of the human race are there?

I. The term state is here taken for the mode, condition, or disposition of some nature. Because, therefore, man has not always held himself, does not hold himself, and will not hold himself in one and the same way, hence theologians have named diverse states of human nature. But how many of them there are, not all agree.

II. Pererius, in book 5 on Genesis, concerning the true excellence of man, page 180, Cologne edition, in folio, year 1606, enumerates six states of human nature. The first is that of man constituted without the grace of God and without any sin, which they call in the Schools 'in pure naturals.' The second is that of man vitiated and corrupted on account of Adam's sin. The third is that of man possessing natural integrity, congruent with reason. The fourth is that of man endowed and adorned with original justice. The fifth is that of man liberated from the sin of Adam and healed of vices through the grace of Christ. The sixth is that of man advanced and led forward as far as heavenly glory and the sight of the divine nature.

III. But the first state is clearly fabricated,

For pure naturals are pure and simple Scholastic phantasies. There has never existed a man, and indeed cannot exist, with a simple negation of grace and sin. For it would be against God's providence if men themselves neither pleased nor displeased Him. Thus also the third state is nothing but a Papistic dream. For if by natural integrity is understood the concreated image, it is the state of innocence: if the ruins of the lost image, it pertains to the state of the fall and sin. Wherefore we conclude from this that Pererius's distinction is faulty, and that states are multiplied without necessity.

IV. The orthodox therefore count fewer, and indeed they agree on the thing itself, yet they differ in the manner of counting and expressing it, while some mention three, others four, others five.

V. Those who posit three express it thus: The first state was of nature infused in Adam before the fall: the second, of nature destitute in Adam after the fall: the third, of nature restored through Christ in the regenerate, which restoration is begun in this life, and is consummated in the other. Some designate the former as the state of Perfection; the latter of Defection; the third of Refection. The Hebrews say these three states are noted by three words by which man is signified in the Scriptures. For he is called 1. אָדָם that is, red, by reason of creation, because he was fashioned from the red soil and earth. 2. אֱנוֹשׁ that is, mortal or subject to all diseases and calamities. 3. אִישׁ that is, man, who excels in virtue and blessedness. The first word hints at the state of integrity; the second of mortality; the third of reparation.

VI. Those who recount four speak thus: The first state is of integrity before the fall. 2. The state of sin after the fall. 3. The state of restoration through Christ. 4. The state after death, which they in turn divide into the state of the blessed in heaven, and of the damned in hell. Others use these terms: The first state is of the bestowal of grace: the second, of the loss of that which was bestowed; the third, of that which was lost restoration; the fourth, concerning the consummation of the restored. Some express it thus: The first state was happy before sin; in which only Adam and Eve lived. The second, after sin without the grace of Christ, miserable and unhappy. The third, after sin under the grace of Christ, and that is partly happy, on account of the Spirit; partly unhappy, on account of the flesh. The fourth follows the elect after this life in eternal glory, most happy and most blessed: but the reprobate, in everlasting ignominy and punishments, most miserable.

VII. But to those whom the number five pleases, they say that one is the state of nature integral, another corrupt, another restored, another glorified, another damned. Which states some recount thus by dichotomies: The states of man are two, one in this life, while he is on the way, another after this life, when he arrives at the goal. The state in this life is in turn twofold: one of nature; the other of grace. The state of nature is likewise twofold, either integral, or corrupt. After this life there will be another state of the elect, namely the state of glory; another of the reprobate, namely of perpetual ignominy.

IIX. And from this it appears clearly enough that the discrepancy is not in the matter, but only in words and numbers. There are three states, namely if the discourse is about the pious and restoration is divided into begun and consummated. There are four, if the state after death is distinctly numbered, and not subjoined as a species to the state of restoration. But there are five, and they are most conveniently numbered thus, if all the conditions of men ought to be set forth separately.

IX. For man was once integral; now he is a son of either wrath, or grace; at some time he will be, either blessed, or damned. And from this flows. 1. The state of innocence, which was concreated in the first man. 2. The state of misery, into which we have fallen by the fault of the πρωτοπλάστων [first-formed]. 3. The state of grace, which the faithful obtain in Christ. 4. The state of glory, into which they are transferred on the last day. 5. The state of ignominy, with which the unfaithful and impenitent are affected by the just judgment of God. But the state of glory and ignominy has its own degrees. For both are begun before the final judgment as regards souls, the former of the pious, the latter of the impious; both will be consummated on the last day of judgment, when as regards body and soul the faithful will enjoy eternal joy, the unfaithful will be afflicted with eternal torments.

Latin:

Quot sint status humani generis?

I. Vocabulum status hic sumitur pro modo, conditione aut dispositione alicuius naturę. Quia igitur homo non vno semper eodemque modo sese habuit, habet & habebit, hinc diversos naturæ humanæ status Theologi nuncupârunt. Quot verò illorum sint, non omnes conueniunt.

II. Pererius l. 5. in Genesin, de verua excellentia hominis pag. 180. edit. Colon: in fol. anno 1606. sex naturę humanæ status enarrat. Primus, ipsi est homini sine gratia Dei, & sine vllo peccato constituti, quem in Scholis appellant in puris naturalibus. Secundus, est hominis propter Adami peccatum vitiati & corrupti. Tertius est hominis habentis naturalem integritatem, rationi congruentem. Quartus, est hominis iustitia originali præditi & ornati. Quintus, est hominis per gratiam Christi à peccato Adami liberati & à vitijs sanati. Sextus, est hominis vsque ad cœlestem gloriam, & diuinæ naturæ conspectum prouecti atque perducti.

III. Verùm primus status planè confictus est,

Pura enim naturalia sunt puræ putæ φαντασίαι Scholafticæ. Nunquam extitit homo, & ne quidem existere potest, cum simplici negatione gratiæ & peccati. Foret enim contra Dei prouidentiam, si homines ipsi nec placerent, nec displicerent. Ita & status tertius nil est, nisi somnium Papisticum. Si enim per naturalem integritatem intelligitur imago concreata, est status innocentiæ: si rudera imaginis amissæ, pertinet ad statum lapsus & peccati. Quare hinc concludimus, distinctionem Pererij vitiosam esse, statusque sine necessitate multiplicari.

IV. Orthodoxi ergo pauciores numerant, & quidem in re ipsa consentiunt, in modo tamen numerandi & exprimendi discrepant, dum nonnulli tres, alij quatuor alij quinque commemorant.

V. Qui tres ponunt, ita efferunt: Status primus fuit naturæ infuuæ in Adamo ante lapsum: fecundus, naturæ destitutæ in Adamo post Lapsum: tertius, naturæ restitutæ per Christum in renatis, quæ restitutio, in hoatur in hac vitâ, consùmatur in alterâ. Illum indigitant nonnulli statum Confectionis; istum Defectionis; hunc Refectionis. Hosce tres Status Hebræi dicunt notari tribus vocabulis, quibus homo significatur in Scripturis. Vocatur enim 1. אָדָם hoc est, russus, ratione creationis, quia ex humo & terra russa fuit conditus. 2. אֱנוֹשׁ id est, mortalis vel omnibus morbis & calamitatibus subiectus. 3. אִישׁ id est, vir, qui virtute & beatitudine præstat. Vox prima statum integritatis; secunda mortalitatis; tertia reparationis innuit.

VI. Qui quatuor recensent, sic loquuntur: Primus status est integritatis ante lapsum. 2. Status peccati post lapsum. 3. Status instaurationis per Christum. 4. Status post mortem, quem vicissim diuidunt in statum beatorum in cælo, & damnatorum in inferno. Alij his vtuntur terminis, Status primus est de gratiæ collatione: Secundus de collatæ amissione; tertius, de amissæ instauratione; quartus, de instauratæ consummatione. Quidam sic efferunt: Primus status fuit ante peccatum felix; in quo vixère Adam tantùm & Eua, Alter post peccatum sine gratia Christi, miser & infelix. Tertius, post peccatum sub gratia Christi, isque partim felix, propter Spiritum; partim infelix, propter carnem. Quartus electos sequitur post hanc vitam in gloria æterna felicissimus & beatissimus: reprobos verò, in sempiterna ignominia atque pœnis, miserrimus.

VII. Quibus verò placet quinarius, dicunt alium esse statum naturæ integræ, alium corruptæ, alium restauratæ, alium glorificatæ, alium damnatæ. Quos status nonnulli per dixotomías sic recensent: Status hominis duo sunt, vnus in hac vita, dum est in via, alter post hanc vitam, cùm peruenit ad metam. Status in hac vita vicissim duplex est: vnus naturæ; alter gratiæ Status naturæ itidem est duplex, vel integræ, vel corruptæ. Post hanc vitam alius erit status electorum, nempè status gloriæ; alius reprobatorum, videlicet ignominiæ perpetuæ.

IIX. Atque hinc satis luculenter apparet, non in re, sed verbis tantùm & numeris esse discrepantiam. Tres sunt status, nempè si de pijs sit sermo & reparatio in inchoatam & consummatam dispescatur. Quatuor sunt, si status post mortem distinctè numeretur, nec tanquam species statui restaurationis subiungatur. Quinque verò sunt, & commodissimè ita numerantur, si omnes hominum conditiones seorsim exponi debeant.

IX. Homo enim olim fuit integer; nunc est filius vel iræ, vel gratiæ; aliquando erit, vel beatus, vel damnatus. Atqui hinc fluit. 1. Status innocentiæ, quæ primo homini fuit concreata. 2. Status miseriæ, in quam πρωτοπλάστων culpâ prolapsi sumus. 3. Status gratiæ, quam fideles in Christo consequuntur. 4. Status gloriæ, in quam die vltimo transferuntur. 5. Status ignominiæ, quâ infideles & impœnitentes ex iusto Dei iudicio afficiuntur. Habet verò status gloriæ & ignominiæ suos gradus. Vtraque enim inchoatur antè extremum iudicium quoad animas, illa piorum, hæc impiorum; vtraque consunmabitur in vltimo die censoreo, vbi quoad corpus & animam fideles æternâ lætitiâ perfruentur, infideles æternis cruciatibus affligentur.


### Question II. How great was the excellence of the first state?

I. And this is described in diverse words, yet the thing itself always remains one. Some say that a triple grace had been bestowed upon the first man: 1. the grace of the soul, that is, original righteousness. 2. the grace of the body, that is, immortality. 3. the grace of place, that is, Paradise. See Bellarmine, On the grace of the first man, ch. 1. II. Pererius, book 5 on Genesis, in the preface, page 165, writes that the state of innocence had been adorned with seven things, of which three existed outside the man, such as the habitation of the earthly Paradise, the fruit of the tree of life, and the singular care of God, preserving man in that state. But four, he says, were in the man himself. There was, he says, in him a quadruple excellence: one of wisdom, another of grace making one acceptable, a third of original righteousness, a fourth of immortality and impassibility, which God had granted to his body.

III. But, as regards grace making one acceptable (by which they themselves understand some inherent quality, on account of which man was acceptable to God), it was not distinct from original righteousness. For man pleased God for no other reason than on account of the concreated perfection and rectitude, of which the primary part was original righteousness. For just as now after the fall the imputed righteousness of Christ renders us grateful and acceptable to God: so before the fall inherent righteousness and holiness rendered us so. Therefore, those things are distinguished by judgment which are in reality one. Bellarmine saw this, and therefore in chapter 3 he wished to refer grace that makes one pleasing to justice, as a part or root. We deservedly abstain from the term of grace that makes one pleasing; both because it is improper, and because it is stuffed with scholastic trifles.

IV. Our writers record that the happiness of man shines forth chiefly from four things: 1. From the condition of the soul, which was wise and holy. 2. From the condition of the body, which was beautiful, impassible, and immortal. 3. From the condition of life, which was happy and blessed. 4. From the condition of his dwelling, which was most pleasant, namely the garden of delight, which is called Paradise. See Rungius, public disputation 8, thesis 1.

V. But because there are few things that can be known about Paradise, therefore we shall contemplate further only the first three excellences; and because those are commonly expressed by the single term of the divine image, we shall therefore subjoin some questions concerning the image and likeness of God, to which the first man is read to have been created in Gen. 1, v. 26, 27, and c. 5, v. 1, from which the state of our first parents and their happiness may easily become known.

Latin:

I. Et hæc diuersis verbis describitur, res tamen semper vna permanet. Nonnulli dicunt triplicem primo homini gratiam fuisse collatam 1. gratiam animæ, id est, iustitiam originalem. 2. gratiam corporis, id est, immortalitatem. 3. gratiam loci, id est, Paradisi. Vide Bell. de grat. primi hom. c. 1. II. Pererius l. 5. in Genesin in præfat. pag. 165. scribit, statum innocentiæ septem rebus decoratum fuisse, quarum tres extra hominem, extiterint, velut habitatio Paradisi terrestris, fructus arboris vitæ, & singularis cura Dei, hominem in eo statu conseruantis. Quatuor autem in ipso homine fuisse, Erat, inquit, in eo quadruplex excellentia, vna sapientiæ, altera gratiæ gratum facientis, tertia iustitiæ originalis, quarta immortalitatis & impassibilitatis, quam corpori eius præstitisset Deus.

III. Verùm, quod spectat gratiam gratum facientem (per quam ipsi intelligunt qualitatem aliquam inhærentem, ob quam homo fuerit Deo acceptus,) à iustitia originali distincta non fuit. Ob nullam enim causam aliam homo placuit Deo, quàm ob concreatam perfectionem & rectitudinem, cuius primaria pars fuit iustitia originalis. Sicut enim nunc post lapsum iustitia Christi imputata, Deo nos gratos & acceptos reddit: sic ante lapsum reddidit iustitia & sanctitas inhærens. Arbitrò igitur distinguuntur, quæ realiter vnum sunt. vidit hoc Bellarm. ideoque C. 3. gratiam gratum facientem ad iustitiam, vt partem vel radicem referre voluit. Nos à termino gratiæ gratum facientis meritò abstinemus; tùm, quia improprius: tùm quia scholasticis nugis refertus est.

IV. Nostri felicitatem hominis ex quatuor potissimum rebus elucere scribunt, 1. Ex conditione animæ, quæ sapiens fuit & sancta. 2. Ex conditione corporis, quod pulchrum, impassibile immortale. 3. Ex conditione vitæ, quæ felix & beata. 4. Ex conditione domicilij, quod amœnissimum fuit, hortus nempè voluptatis, qui Paradisus dicitur. Vide Rungium disput. 8. publ. th. 1.

V. Quia verò pauca sunt, quæ de Paradiso sciri queunt, idcircò tres primas tantùm excellentias porrò contemplabimur; & quia illæ vno imaginis diuinæ vocabulo cōmuniter efferuntur, propterea quæstiones aliquot de imagine & similitudine Dei, ad quam homo primus creatus legitur Gen. 1, v. 26. 27, c 5. v. 1. subiungemus, ex quibus status primorum parentum, eorumque felicitas facilè innotescat.


### Question III

I. There have been and are various heresies and opinions concerning the image of God; the Manichaeans denied it entirely, and therefore rejected the whole Old Testament; Epiphanius judged that it is entirely unknown where and what the image of God is, book 3, heresy 30; the Jews place it in certain analogical likenesses with God; the Anthropomorphites in bodily structure and lineaments; the Origenians understood it as the humanity of Christ, to whose image we were created; Theodoret thought it consisted only in the soul and its faculties, quaest. 20. in Genesis. Chrysostom, in sovereignty and dominion, hom. 7 to the people, which the Photinians urge primarily today, Ostorod. in inst. c. 33. Catech. Racov. p. 23. Bernard, in freedom of will, counsel, and pleasure, serm. 80. on the Song of Songs. Other Fathers generally distinguish between image and likeness; by the latter, righteousness and holiness; by the former, however, the soul and its intelligent powers, whom Bellarmine cites and follows, de gratia prim. hom. c. 2. Eugubinus opined that God, when He wished to create man, assumed a form, and in this said 'let us make man in our image and likeness.' Others understand the idea of man conceived in the divine mind, according to which man was formed by God. The Flacians think it was the substance itself. The Papists, partly the soul, partly certain supernatural gifts, not connatural ones. The Calvinists seek it, both in the substance of man, and in the qualities, and in dignity or dominion, Bucan. loco 9. quæst. 8. Piscator in obseru. ad v. 26. cap. 1, Gen. & Perer. col. 279. Some of our own place it in the sole rectitude of the soul, some simultaneously in the dignity of the body and external dominion.

II. Since, therefore, differing opinions about the image of God are circulated, it will be worth the effort to prescribe certain marks or rules, by the help of which the precious may be easily distinguished from the vile, and the true from the false. We believe that six of these can primarily be held, which we will recount in order.

FIRST RULE.

III. The image of God must be placed in those things by reason of which some likeness exists between man and God.

For an image, unless it is similar to that which it ought to represent, is nothing less than an image. Hence Thomas Aquinas, p. 1. q. 93. art. 2, thought that it was called an image is, as if it were an imitation (which etymology, however, is sufficiently barbarous and remote) because it ought to imitate the prototype, or be fashioned according to the imitation of the prototype. And Augustine, book 83, question 73. Where there is, he says, an image, there is immediately a likeness. For that which is like something, and is expressed according to it, this is called an image: and so for any image whatsoever two things are required. 1. likeness. 2. expression according to the similar thing, whence an egg is said to be like an egg, but not an image of an egg, because it is not expressed according to it.

Let this canon be opposed to the Anthropomorphites, who place the reason for the divine image in the structure of the body, when nevertheless God is Spirit and without a body. How therefore will a body be the image of an incorporeal God?

SECOND RULE.

IV. The image of God is not to be placed in those things which remained intact in man after the fall.

The reason is at hand, because we lost the concreated image, which will be proved below. Whatever therefore is still intact after the fall was not of the essence of the image. They err, therefore, who think it was situated either in the soul or in the faculties of the soul.

THIRD RULE.

V. The image of God is not to be sought in one likeness of man with God, but in all.

Wherefore it ought not to be defined by dominion alone, not by holiness alone, not by immortality alone. These likenesses must be joined together, and a perfect definition will emerge.

FOURTH RULE.

VI. The image of God can be moderately known from the consideration of original sin.

For sin has succeeded to the place of the image. But contraries, when placed side by side, become more evident. concerning this, if we attend to wherein the nature of sin consists; from the contrary sense we shall easily be able to find the nature of the divine image, which is contrary to sin.

FIFTH RULE.

VII. The image of God can be best known if one attends to the renewal of man, which is done according to the lost image.

For that to which we are renewed, this we lost in Adam. But that which we lost pertained to the image of God. Wherefore, since we are renewed not to some substance, not to a rational soul, not to bodily features, it follows infallibly that none of these pertained to the image of God.

SIXTH RULE.

VIII. Consideration of the glorious state in the other life contributes not a little to the knowledge of the image.

For then first will the image of God be fully restored, and therefore what will be added to our souls and bodies in that state, that we had in some measure, if not in whole, yet in part, in our first parents. Therefore, because our future bodies are to be immortal and impassible, it is rightly inferred that they were such even in the state of innocence.

IX. And these are the primary rules leading to the knowledge of the divine image; which, that we may contract them, we include in this one aphorism: Whatever is similar to God; which we lost through the fall, the contrary of which we discover in unregenerate man; and which we know is to be restored in us; let us judge without doubt to have pertained to the image of God.

Latin:

I. Variæ fuerunt & sunt de Imagine Dei tùm hæreses, tùm sententię; Manichæi eam prorsus negârunt, ideoque totum V. T. reiecerunt; Epiphanius censuit, omninò incognitum esse, vbi & quid sit imago Dei, l. 3. hæres 30. Iudæi ponunt in quibusdam analogicis similitudinibus cum Deo; Antropomorphitæ in structura & lineamētis corporeis; Origeniani intellexerunt humanitatem Christi, ad cuius imaginem nos simus conditi; Theodoretus putauit tantùm consistere in anima eiusque facultatibus, quaest. 20. in Genesin. Chrysostomus, in principatu & dominio, hom 7 ad populum quod in primis hodiè vrgent Photiniani, Ostorod. in inst c. 33. Catech. Racov. p. 23. Bernardus, in libertate arbitrij, consilij & complaciti, serm. 80. super Cant Patres alij plerumque distinguunt inter imaginem & similitudinem; per hanc, iustitiam & sanctitatem; per illam verò, animam eiusque potentias intelligentes, quos citat & sequitur Bell. de gratia prim. hom. c. 2 Eugubinus opinatus est, Deum, cùm creare vellet hominem assumsisse formam, & in ista dixisse faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Alij intelligunt ideam hominis in mente diuina cõceptam, ad quam homo à Deo fuerit efformatus. Flaciani putant fuisse ipsam substantiam. Pontificij, partim animam, partim dona quædam supernaturalia, non connaturalia. Caluiniani quærunt, tum in substantia hominis; tum in qualitatibus, tum in dignitate vel dominio, Bucan. loco 9. quæst. 8. Piscator in obseru. ad v. 26. cap. 1, Gen & Perer col 279. Ex nostris quidam collocant in sola rectitudine animæ, quidam simul in corporis dignitate & externo dominio.

II. Cum igitur discrepantes de imagine Dei sententiæ circumferantur operæ pretium fuerit, quasdam siue notas, siue regulas præscribere, quarum ope, pretiosum a vili & verum à falso facilè discerni queat. Earum sex potissimùm haberi posse arbitramur, quas ordine commemorabimus.

PRIMA REGVLA.

III. Imago Dei ponenda est in ijs, quorum ratione homini cum Deo similitudo aliqua intercedit.

Imago enim nisi similis sit ei, quod repræsentare debet, nihil minus quam imago est. Hinc Thomas de Aquino, p. 1. q. 93. art. 2 imaginem dictam putur, quasi imitaginem, (quæ tamen etymologia satis barbara & remota est) quia prototypum imitari, vel ad prototypi imitationem agi debeat. Et Aug. l. 83 q. 73. Vbi est, inquit, imago, continuò est similitudo. Quod enim alicui simile, & ad illud expressum est, hoc imago dicitur: adeóq; ad quamuis imaginem duo requiruntur. 1. similitudo. 2 expressio ad rem similem, vnde ouum ouo simile dicitur, sed non imago oui, quia ad illud non expressum est.

Canon hic opponatur Antropomorphitis, qui in structura corporis rationem diuinæ imaginis ponunt, cùm tamen Deus sit Spiritus & absque corpore. Quomodo igitur corpus, Imago Dei erit incorporei?

SECVNDA REGVLA.

IV. Imago Dei non est collocanda in ijs, quæ post lapsum in homine manserunt integra.

Ratio in promptu est, quia imaginem concreatam amisimus, quod infrà probabitur. Quicquid ergò post lapsum adhuc integrum est, de ratione imaginis non fuit. Errant proinde, qui vel in anima, vel in facultatibus animæ sitam fuisse censent.

TERTIA REGVLA.

V. Imago Dei non in vna similitudine hominis cum Deo, sed in omnibus quæratur.

Quocirca non per solum Dominium, non per solam sanctitatem, nõ per solam immortalitatem definiri debet. Coniungendæ sunt hæ similitudines, & perfecta prodibit definitio.

QVARTA REGVLA.

VI. Imago Dei ex consideratione peccati originalis mediocriter innotescere potest.

Peccatum enim successit in locum imaginis. Contraria verò iuxta se posita elutescunt. circa, si attendamus in quo sita sit ratio peccati; è sensu contrario facilè poterimus invenire naturam diuinæ imaginis, quæ peccato est contraria.

QVINTA REGVLA.

VII. Imago Dei optimè potest cognosci, si attendatur renovatio hominis, quæ fit ad amissam imaginem.

Ad quod enim renouamur, hoc in Adamo perdidimus. Quod autem perdidimus, ad imaginem Dei pertinuit. Quare cùm renouemur non ad aliquam substantiam, non ad animam rationalem, non ad lineamenta corporea, sequitur infallibiliter, istorum nullum ad imaginem Dei pertinuisse.

SEXTA REGVLA.

IIX. Ad cognitionem imaginis non parum facit consideratio status gloriosi in vita altera.

Tunc n. primùm imago Dei plenariè restituetur, ideoque quod in isto statu nostris accedet animabus & corporibus, id quodammodo, etsi non ex toto, tamen ex parte, in primis parentibus habuimus. E. quia corpora nostra futura sunt immortalia & impassibilia, hinc in statu etiam innocentiæ talia fuisse, rectè colligitur.

IX. Et he sunt primariæ regulæ ad cognitionem imaginis diuinæ manuducẽtes; quas vt contrahamus, vni huic aphorismo includimus: Quodcunque Deo est simile; quod per lapsum perdidimus, cuius contrarium in homine non renato deprehendimus; & quod in nobis restaurandum nouimus; ad imaginem Dei pertinuisse sine dubio censeamus.


### Question IV. Whether image and likeness differ I. Moses joins both in describing the glorio

I. Moses joins both in describing by the counsel of the glorious Trinity, Jehovah said, (he says, c. 1 Gen. v. 26.) Let us make man in our image and likeness. The question therefore is, Do these words signify one thing, or indeed one thing and another? The Romanists maintain that by image is denoted the substance of the soul and its faculties; by likeness, the gifts and perfections of the faculties, namely the wisdom of the mind, the righteousness of the will, etc., as is evident from Bellarmine, chap. 2, from whom, however, Pererius dissents, book 4, on Genesis, pages 114, 115, and not without reasons, which our people have supplied.

II. Besides the fact that this distinction rests only on the conjectures of the Fathers; it can furthermore be most foully refuted by these arguments: 1. As the decree is, so is the execution of the decree. But in the decree both words are placed, Gen. 1. 26; in the execution, the word of likeness is omitted, verse 27, and yet in both places, because of the consonance of the decree with the execution, one and the same thing is said. Therefore, these words do not signify different things. 2. Scripture speaks promiscuously, and now places both names in the same case, as Gen. 1. v. 26, now in a different one, as Wis. 2. v. 23, now with the word of likeness omitted, it uses only the word of image, as Gen. 9. v. 6, which permutation is a certain indication of synonymy. 3. As in Gen. 1. v. 26, man is read to have been made to the image and likeness of God, so in Gen. 5. v. 3, Adam is said to have begotten Seth to his own image and likeness. But here no distinction has a place. Therefore, neither there. 4. The word of image in Scripture does not denote the substance of the soul but rather the gifts bestowed upon man, as is to be seen from 1 Cor. 15. v. 50 and Col. 3. v. 16.

III. Moved by these reasons, we conclude that these words do not differ, but that the word of likeness was added exegetically. For because not every image is exactly similar to its prototype, and various accounts of an image can be devised, Moses adds the name of likeness, so that he might show that the image was as similar as possible to God.

IV. Nor should it offend anyone that those words are distinguished in the Mosaic text. For the Hebrews often join two nouns as if they were entirely different things, when nevertheless one has the meaning of an adjective; as in Jer. 29, v. 11: I will give you an end and an expectation, that is, an expected end. Flacius noted more examples in part 2 of the Clavis, tract 3, on the construction of nouns, rule 23, page 153. So also it is said: To our image and likeness, where the noun is separated from its adjective, changed into the abstract by Hendiadys, so that the sense is: To an image that is as similar as possible.

V. As regards the authority of the Fathers, who interpreted the image as concerning the substance; I reply: 1. With Jerome on chapter 23 of Matthew: What is said without the authority of the Scriptures is rejected with the same ease with which it is asserted. 2. Not all the Fathers explain it thus: For it is evident from Lombard, book 2, dist. 16, letter C, that some understood the Son of God by image, and the Holy Spirit by likeness. 3. Pererius himself, moved by our arguments, does not heed the exposition of the Fathers. 4. The Fathers spoke popularly, not precisely. For one must distinguish between image spoken of properly and improperly; generally and specially; physically and theologically. The soul of man is indeed formed to the image of God, in so far as it is a spiritual, intelligent, and immortal substance. But this is only a general and physical congruence, and therefore an image spoken of improperly, about which we are not concerned. For if we wish to speak so broadly, every creature in a certain way reflects the image of God.

VI. The Scholastics acknowledged this very thing, among whom Bonaventure, question 2, disp. 16, art. 1, question 1, fol. 244 b, writes that a fourfold image or likeness is given. For 1. there is a certain likeness by way of complete agreement in nature, and thus the Son of God is to the Father similar. 2. Some things through the participation of some universal nature, just as man and brute are assimilated in animal. 3. Some things according to proportion, just as a sailor and a charioteer agree according to a comparison to those things which they govern. 4. Some things are through the agreement of order, since that which is expressed according to an exemplar is assimilated to the exemplar. In the first two ways no creature can be made similar to God; in the last two, everything is assimilated.

VII. Just as therefore any created being, especially animate ones, have a certain analogical congruence with God, yet are not said to be created to the image of God properly taken: so we do not deny with the Fathers that the substance of the rational soul is in a certain way similar to God; but that the reason of the image properly so called is situated in it, can be demonstrated neither by any argument nor even by a probable one.

Latin:

I. Moses vtrumque coniungit in describendo gloriosæ Trinitatis consilio, Dixit Iehouah, (inquit, c. 1 Gen. v. 26.) Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram. Quæritur ergò An vocabula hæc rem vnam, num verò aliam atque aliam significent? Romanenses statuunt per imaginem notari substantiam animæ, eiusq; facultates; per similitudinem, dona & perfectiones facultatum, nempè sapientiam mentis, iustitiam voluntatis &c. vti patet ex Bellar. cap. 2. à quo tamen dissentit Perer. l. 4. in Gen. pag. 114. 115 & non siue rationibus, quas nostri suppeditarunt.

II. Præterquam n. quòd distinctio ista tantùm coniecturis Patrum nitatur; his insuper argumentis foetissimè refutari potest, 1. Vt se habet decretum, ita decreti executio. Atqui in decreto vtraque vox ponitur, Genes 1. 26 in executione, vox similitudinis omittitur, vers. 27. & tamen vtrobique ob consonantiam decreti cum executione, vnum idemque dicitur. E. voces istæ res diuersas non significant. 2. Scriptura promiscuè loquitur, & nunc ponit vtrumque nomen in casu eodem, vt Gen. 1. v. 26. nunc in diuerso, vt Sap 2. v. 23. nunc omissâ voce similitudinis, tantùm vocem imaginis vsurpat, vt Gen. 9. v. 6. quæ permutatio certum Synonymias indicium est. 3. Vt Gen. 1. v. 26. homo legitur factus ad imaginem & similitudinem Dei, sic Gens 5 v. 3. Adam dicitur genuisse Seth ad imaginem & similitudinem suam. Ast nic nulla distinctio locum habet. Ergò nec ibi. 4. Vox imaginis in Scriptura non denotat substantiam animę sed potius dona homini collata quemadmodum videre est, ex 1. Cor. 15. v. 50. & Coloss. 3 v 16.

III. Hisce rationibus moti, vocabula ista non differre sed vocem similitudinis ἐξηγητικῶς adiectam esse concludimus. Quia enim non omnis imago exactè similis est prototypo, & varia imaginis ratio excogitari potest, addit Moses nomen similitudinis, vt imaginem Deo quam similimam fuisse ostenderet.

IV. Neque quenquam offendat, quod vocabula ista distinguantur in textu Mosaico. Hebręi enim sæpe duo Substantiua, tanquam res omninò diversas, conjungunt, cùm tamen alterum adiectiui significationem habeat; vt Ierem. 29. v. 11. Dabo vobis finem & expectationem, id est, finem expectatum. Plura exempla notauit Flacius par. 2. Clavis, tract. 3. de construct: nom. reg. 23. pag. 153. Sic etiam dicitur : Ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram, vbi separatur Substantiuum à suo Adiectiuo, in abstractum mutato per Hendiaden, vt sit sensus, Ad imaginem quam similimam.

V. Patrum authoritatem quod spectat, qui imaginem de Substantia interpretati sunt; Resp. 1. cum Hieronymo super c. 23. Matt. Quod sine Scripturarum authoritate dicitur, pari facilitate reijcitur, quâ asseritur. 2. Non omnes Patres ita exponunt: Constat enim ex Lombard. l. 2. dist. 16. lit. C. aliquos per imaginem Filium Dei; per similitudinem Spiritum Sanctum intellexisse. 3. Pererius ipse Patrum expositionem motus argumentis nostris, non attendit. 4. Patres populariter, non exquisitè locuti sunt. Distinguendum enim est inter imaginem propriè & abusiuè dictam; generalem & specialem; Physicam & Theologicam. Est sanè anima hominis ad imaginem Dei efformata, in quantum est substantia spiritualis, intelligens, immortalis. Sed hæc est tantùm generalis & Physica congruentia, ideoq; imago impropriè dicta, de qua soliciti non sumus. Si enim adeò πλατέως loqui velimus, omnis creatura imaginem Dei quodammodo refertet.

VI. Agnoverunt hoc ipsum Scholastici, quos inter Bonaventura, quæst. 2. disp. 16. art. 1 quæst. 1. fol. 244 b. quadruplicem scribit imaginem vel similitudinem dari. Nam 1. quædam est similitudo per conuenientiam omnimodam in natura, & sic Dei Filius Patri est similis. 2. Quædam per participationem alicuius naturæ universalis, sicut homo & brutum assimilantur in animali. 3. Quædam secundum proportionem, veluti nauta & auriga conueniunt secundum comparationem, ad illa quæ regunt. 4. Quædam est per conuenientiam ordinis, quoniam exemplari assimilatur id quod ad exemplar expressum est. Primis duobus modis nulla creatura potest Deo similis fieri; postremis duobus, omnis assimilatur.

VII. Sicut ergo quodvis ens creatum, inprimis animata quandam cum Deo analogicam habent congruentiam, non tamen ad Dei imaginem propriè sumtam, condita dicuntur: sic animæ rationalis substantiam Deo quodammodo esse similem cum Patribus non diffitemur; quòd autem in ea ratio imaginis κυρίως dictæ sita fuerit, neque ullo vel probabili tantùm argumento demonstrari potest.


### Question V. Whether the image of God was the very substance of man?

I. The terms having been explained, the very essence of the image remains to be investigated. We maintain, however, with the Orthodox, that it was not the very essence of man, or some essential image; but only mimetic or imitative; referring to God in some way, not completely equaling Him:

II. The contrary pleases the Flacians, who contend that the image of God was the very substance of man, and especially the rational soul. For thus writes Flacius, part 2, Clavis tract. 6, p. 370: I speak of that most noble form of substance, to which especially the heart itself, or rather the rational soul, was formed, so that ITS VERY ESSENCE was the image of God and represented Him. And conversely p. 375: God created man himself to His own image, not only his accidents. Therefore even THE VERY SUBSTANCE OF MAN is the image of God.

III. I do not inquire here. Whether Flacius thought as absurdly as he spoke? Since elsewhere he seems to admit a distinction between the substance of man and the image of God. For there are some who distinguish between the mind and the words of Flacius. Nor would I deny that the remaining Flacians were far more absurd and gross than Flacius himself in words and meaning. But, whatever the case may be, we pronounce it a dense error if the very substance of man is called the image of God. This could be proven by many things, but in a manifest matter why should a few not suffice?

IV. If, therefore, the image of God is established as the very substance of man, it follows: 1. When it is said, Man is created to the image of God, the meaning would be, Man is created to the substance of man, or man is created, which is absurd; since man is one thing and the image to which man is created is another. 2. No distinction would remain between the Son of God and man. For both would become ἰσιώσιος and a substantial image of God, which, however, is said only of the Son, Col. 1:15. He is the very image of the Father, but man is only created to the image. 3. Man would be made equal to God. For the image consists in righteousness and truth, Eph. 4:24. Therefore, if it were the very ἰσία of man, man would have been substantially righteous and holy, which is of God alone, Matt. 19:17. Wherefore the image of God must be described in such a way that assimilation remains, and equalization does not occur. 4. The image would not have been lost. For the very substance of Adam and his soul did not perish. Otherwise he would not have been man: And another would have sinned, another would have paid the penalty, which is against the letter of the history, Gen. 3. For God addresses and punishes that very Adam whom He had previously adorned, and to whom He had commanded not to eat from the tree. 5. We are not renewed to the image of God. For we are not regenerated to any ἰσία or substance, and nevertheless we are said to be renewed to the image of God, Col. 3:10. How, therefore, could this have been substance?

V. Nor does that little argument have any weight. The image of God gave being to the whole man, therefore it was a form and a substance. For Being is twofold, both absolute and modified. The former comes from Substance, the latter also from accidents. Whiteness gives being to a white man. Therefore is it a Substance? ἄτοπον. Thus the image of God gave being to man, not absolute, insofar as he was man; but modified, or such a Being, namely insofar as he was just and whole. Therefore, just as Being behaves, so does the form which gives it. But the Being which the image of God gave to man was accidental, therefore it itself was nothing but an accidental form. Let it be noted, therefore, that not all forms are Substantial; many accidental ones are also found, among which the image of God ought to be numbered.

VI. Others distinguish between form and formal reason. By form they understand the substantial part of a composite: by formal reason, certain respects and accidental modes, through which a Substance is called such and such. They deny, therefore, that the image of God was a form: but they concede that it was a formal reason, through which man was not man absolutely; but such a man; namely holy, and without sin. However, it does not follow: It is a formal reason. Therefore a Substance. For all the categories of accidents prove the contrary, which establish many formal reasons, but no substances of themselves.

Latin:

I. Explicatis vocibus, ipsa imaginis essentia restat indaganda. Statuimus verò cum Orthodoxis; eam fuisse non ipsam hominis οὐσίαν, vel imaginem aliquam ἰσιώδη; sed tantùm μιμητικὴν vel imitatiuam; Deum aliquo modo referētem, non penitùs exæquantem:

II. Contrarium placet Flacianis, qui contendunt. Imaginem Dei fuisse ipsam hominis substantiam, & præcipuè animam rationalem. Ita enim scribit Flacius, part. 2. Clavis tract. 6. p. 370. Loquor de ea nobilissima substantiatis forma, ad quam præcipuè ipsum cor, aut potiùs anima rationalis formata erat, ita vt IPSA SVA ESSENTIA esset Dei imago eumque repræsentaret. Et vicissim p. 375. Deus condidit ipsum hominē ad imaginem suam, non tantùm eius accidentia. Ergo etiam IPSA HOMINIS SVBSTANTIA est imago Dei.

III. Non a. hîc disquiro. An Flacius tam absurdè senserit, vt locutus est? cùm alibi videatur discrimen admittere inter Substantiam hominis, & imaginem Dei. Sunt enim nonnulli, qui inter mentem & verba Flacij distinguunt. Neque negauerim, Flacianos reliquos ipso Flacio lōgè absurdiores crassioresque fuisse in verbis & sensu, Verùm, quicquid horum sit, spissum errorem esse pronunciamus, si imago Dei dicetur ipsa hominis substantia. Multis euinci hoc posset, sed in re manifesta cur non pauca sufficerent?

IV. Quòd si igitur imago Dei statuatur ipsa hominis substantia, sequitur, 1. Cùm dicitur, Homo ad imaginem Dei est conditus, sensum esse, Homo ad substantiam hominis, vel homo est conditus, quod absurdum; cùm longè aliud sit homo & aliud imago, ad quam homo cōditus 2. Nullum manere discrimen inter Filium Dei & hominem. Vterque enim fieret ἰσιώσιος & substantialis imago Dei, quod tamen de solo Filio dicitur, Col. 1. v. 15. Hic ipsa imago Patris, homo autem tantùm ad imaginem conditus est. 3. Hominem adæquari Deo. Imago enim cōsistit in iustitia & veritate, Eph. 4. v. 24. Ergo, si fuit ipsa hominis ἰσία, homo substantialiter fuit iustus & sanctus, quod solius Dei Matth. 19 v. 1. Quare sic imago Dei describenda est, vt maneat assimilatio, non fiat exæquatio. 4. Imaginem non esse amissam. Ipsa enim Adami substantia, & anima non periit. Alias fuisset non homo: Et alius peccasset, alius pœnam dedisset, quod est contra literam historiæ, Gen. 3. Illum enim Adamum Deus alloquitur & punit, quem ante ornauerat, & cui præceperat, ne comederet de arbore. 5. Nos ad imaginem Dei non renouari. Ad nullam enim ἰσίαν vel Substantiam regeneramur, Et nihilominus ad imaginem Dei renouari dicuntur, Col. 3. v. 10. Qui ergò hæc substantia esse potuit?

V. Neque aliquid momenti habet ista ratiuncula. Imago Dei dedit esse homini integro, Ergo forma fuit & substantia. Nam Esse duplex est, tùm absolutum tùm modificatum. Istud a Substantia, hoc etiam ab accidentibus venit. Albedo dat Esse homini albo. Ergò ne Substantia? ἄτοπον. Sicimago Dei dedit homini esse, non absolutum, quatenus fuit homo; sed modificatum, vel Esse tale, nimirùm quatenus fuit iustus & integer. Prout igitur Esse se habet, sic & forma, quæ dat illud. Atqui Esse, quod homini dabat imago Dei fuit accidentale, E. & ipsa, nil nisi forma accidentalis fuit. Notetur proinde, quòd non omnes formę sint Substantiales, teperiuntur etiam multæ accidentales, quibus annumerari debet imago Dei.

VI. Alij distinguunt inter formam & formalem rationem. Per formam intelligunt partem substantialem compositi: performalem rationem, certos respectus ac modos accidentales, per quos Substantia talis vel talis dicitur. Negant ergo imaginem Dei fuïsse formam: concedunt autem fuisse formalem rationem, per quam homo non erat homo absolutè; sed homo talis; nempe sanctus, & absque peccato. Non sequitur autem: Est formalis ratio. Ergo Substantia. Contrarium enim euincūt omnes accidentium categoriæ, quæ multas formales rationes, nullas verò substantias ex se fundunt.


### Question VI. In what precisely was the reason of the divine Image situated?

I. We have said what it was not; it remains to be said what the image of God was. It was, however, nothing other than a certain excellent conformity with God, the πρωτοτύπῳ. For he is said to bear the image of someone, who is similar and conformable to him.

II. We say, however, that this conformity was twofold: the one we name πρωτεύουσαν or primary; the other, however, δευτερεύουσαν or less principal:

III. We judge the primary conformity of man with God to be situated in the soul, and indeed partly in the intellect of the soul, partly in the appetite.

In the intellect, there was a perfect knowledge of the divine will of God, and the highest science of all things, in which part man was conformable to the wisdom of God.

The appetite is twofold, rational and sensitive. In the rational or will there was: 1. A natural propensity toward the good. 2. A free and ready execution of the will. By the former, the holiness of God was represented; by the latter, His liberty.

In the sensitive appetite there was a conformity of both desires and affections with right reason, by which the αὐτάρκεια, chastity, purity, and integrity of God were figured.

These three dignities and excellencies are commonly expressed by the one name of original justice or innocence.

IV. We judge the less principal conformity of man with God to have been situated partly in the condition of the body, partly in external dominion. For although the body, as regards its stature and substance, cannot be similar to the incorporeal God, it was nevertheless so as regards some qualities. And thus both the whole man and the whole of man was the subject of the divine image, just as it is of sin and renewal.

Nor does it stand in the way that in Eph. 4, v. 24, the image of God is said to consist in righteousness and holiness of truth, since that is said κυριολεκτικῶς and concerning the principal reason of the image, and does not exclude the less principal conformity of man with God.

Nor does the image of God shine forth in the body only in a subtle and significant way, insofar as it is so formed that it evidently proves the soul which dwells within it to have been made in the image of God, as Pererius thinks, lib. 4. in Gen. quæst. 3. p. 120. For it also has in itself a certain likeness, on account of two most noble gifts, namely impassibility and immortality. For why should we exclude these from the image of God? By reason of them Adam was like to God: through the fall he lost these; contrary qualities succeeded, but in the other life these will be restored anew, all of which are most certain signs of the divine image.

Finally, that man might be like to God, He also granted him dominion and command over the animals; just as God was over man, so man was to be over all others. I refer, however, the dominion to the less principal reason of the image, both on account of the authority of the Apostle, Eph. 4. v. 24, and because through the fall it was not entirely lost

V. And this was that excellent conformity and likeness, by which man expressed most of the properties of God in his own way. For those things which are essential attributes in God, their images in man were accidental. Therefore, just as GOD is 1. infinitely, 2. immutably, and 3. by essence: so man in his first state was 1. finitely, 2. mutably, and 3. by grace wise, just, chaste, impassible, immortal, and powerful.

For the sake of memory, it is pleasing to include these endowments in a brief table

Which follows on the next page, since space did not permit it here.

WHENCE... which is twofold,

Of the body, which reflected God's impassibility and immortality

The image of GOD is the special conformity of man with GOD

But because it is not enough to have affirmed something, but reasons must also be added: therefore we shall furthermore confirm and explain these individual gifts in a few words.

Latin:

I. Diximus, quid nō fuerit; dicendum restat, quid fuerit imago Dei. Fuit autem nihil, quàm excellens quædam conformitas cum Deo, πρωτοτύπῳ. Is enim dicitur gerere imaginem alicujus, qui illi similis & conformis est.

II. Hanc verò conformitatem dicimus fuisse geminam: Vnam nominamus πρωτεύουσαν vel primariam; alteram verò δευτερεύουσαν seu minùs principalem:

III. Primariam hominis cum Deo conformitatem in anima sitam censemus, & quidem in animæ partim intellectu, partim appetitu.

In intellectu, erat perfecta Dei voluntatis diuinæ noticia, summaque rerum omnium scientia, qua in parte homo conformis fuit sapientiæ Dei.

Appetitus duplex, rationalis & sensitiuus. In rationali seu voluntate erat. 1. naturalis ad bonum propensio. 2. voliti libera & expedita executio. Isto Dei sanctitas, hoc libertas repræsentabatur.

In appetitu sensitiuo erat conformitas tùm cupiditatum, tùm affectuum cum recta ratione, quibus Dei αὐτάρκεια, castitas, puritas & integritas figurabatur.

Très verò hæ dignitates & excellentiæ vno iusticiæ vel innocentiæ originalis nomine communiter efferuntur.

IV. Minus principalem hominis cum Deo conformitatem partim in conditione corporis, partim in externo dominio positam fuisse arbitramur. Licèt n. corpus quoad staturam & substãtiam suam Deo incorporeo simile esse nequeat, fuit tamen quoad qualitates nonnullas. Atque ita subiectum imaginis diuinæ fuit & totus homo & totum hominis, non secus atque est peccati & renouationis.

Neque obstat, quòd Eph. 4. v. 24. Imago Dei in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis dicitur consistere, siquidem id κυριολεκτικῶς & de principali ratione imaginis dictum, non excludit minus principalem nominis cum Deo conformitatem.

Neque imago Dei relucet in corpore tantùm argutiuè & significatiuè, quatenus ita formatum est, vt euidenter arguat animam quæ in ipso habitat, ad imaginem Dei esse factam, vti censet Pererius l. 4. in Gen. quæst. 3. p. 120. Nam & in sese quandam habet similitudinem, ob duas dotes nobilissimas, impassibilitatem & immortalitatem. Cur enim has ab imagine Dei excluderemus? illarum ratione Adam fuit Deo similis: per lapsum istas amisit; contrariæ qualitates successêre, in altera verò vita istæ denuò restituentur, quæ omnia imaginis diuinæ sunt certissima signa.

Tandem, vt homo similis esset Deo, etiam dominium illi concessit & imperium super animalia; sicut veluti Deus homini, sic homo alijs omnibus præesset. Refero autem dominium ad minus principalem imaginis rationem, tùm ob authoritatem Apostoli, Eph. 4. v. 24. tùm quia per lapsum non planè fuit deperditum

V. Et hæc erat illa excellens conformitas & similitudo, qua homo plerasque Dei proprietates suo modo exprimebat. Quæ enim in Deo sunt attributa essentialia, illorum imagines in homine fuerunt accidentaliter, Sicut ergo DEVS 1. infinitè. 2. immutabiliter & 3. per essentiam : ita homo 1. finitè. 2. mutabiliter, & 3. per gratiam in primo statu fuit sapiens, iustus, castus, impassibilis, immortalis & potens.

Memoriæ verò causa dotes istas breui tabellæ placet includere

Quæ proximâ pagellâ sequitur, cùm hic spatium non permiserit.

...UNDEQ... quæ duplex,

Corporis, quod Dei impassibilitatem & immortalitatem referebat

Dominii, quo Dei potestas significabatur.

Imago DEI est specialis conformitas hominis cum DEO

1. Primitis, in anima

1. Intellectu, qui Dei sapientiam repræsentabat.

2. Appetitu

Propensione ad bonum, quo DEI sanctitas figurabatur.

Facili executione, quâ DEI libertas adumbrabatur

Cupiditatum.

αὐτάρκεια castitas Bonitas, Integritas.

Quia verò non sufficit, aliquid affirmâsse, sed rationes etiam addendæ : unt sidcircò dotes istas singulas paucis porrò confirmabim' & explicabimus.


### Question VI. In what precisely was the reason of the divine Image situated?: I. On the conformity of the Intellect with the Wisdom of God

I. On the conformity of the Intellect with the Wisdom of God.

VI. That an excellent knowledge of God and other things was concreated in the first man can be proved 1. by the sayings of Scripture. 2. by the deeds of Adam. 3. by firm reasons.

VII. SAYINGS are read, 1. Gen. 1. v. ult. God saw all things that He had made, and they were very good. For God created all animals, each perfect in its own kind, and therefore man also. This appears from the body, which was created perfect as to the integrity of age, the height of stature, and the firmness of strength. Therefore the soul also was created perfect, and consequently with cognition and science, since the perfection of the mind consists in this. For if Adam had been surrounded by such darkness and ignorance as his descendants are now; how, I ask, could it be said that all things were very good? Is gross ignorance also a good, and what is more, a very good thing?

2. Ecclesiastes 7. v. 30. God made man, ישר upright, namely in body and mind, in stature and wisdom. But now consider the extreme dimness of our intellect, the thick dullness, and the ease and inclination to err; certainly if you attribute this to Adam, he was not made upright, but altogether crooked and bent.

3. Ecclesiastes 17. v. 5. He filled them with the discipline of the intellect, namely the first men. For the verses immediately preceding prove that Ecclesiasticus is speaking principally about these. Moreover, He filled them not after creation, but in the very formation according to His image.

4 Colossians 3. v. 10. Put on the new man, him who is renewed in γνῶσιν, in knowledge, according to the image of him who created him. If we must be renewed in knowledge; therefore we once had it, [and] lost it. And if the image of God the creator consists in ἐπιγνώσει or knowledge, certainly Adam was created with this; since he was created in the image of God.

VIII. The DEEDS of Adam, arguments of his wisdom, are noted as two: 1. The imposition of names, Gen. 2. v. 19. If Adam had lacked knowledge of the animals, he could not have imposed names suitable to their natures. Whence Plato in the Cratylus concludes that he who first imposed names upon things was most wise. But Adam did not gather this knowledge through experience, since between his creation and the ὀνομαθεσίαν a very short time, and scarcely a few hours, as is commonly thought, intervened.

2. The recognition of Eve, Gen. 2. v. 23. He himself had been immersed in a deep sleep, and knew nothing of the formation of Eve: yet, as soon as he looked upon her, he recognized that she was his own flesh formed from his rib, and imposed upon her a most fitting name. These are most clear testimonies not of ordinary wisdom, but even of the gift of prophecy.

IX. Three REASONS are chiefly given. 1. From the contrary. For after the fall the human mind is blunted by incredible ignorance, whence it is everywhere compared to darkness; therefore before the fall it was illuminated by remarkable knowledge; since the attributes of contraries are contrary.

2. From the ruins. On account of certain small remnants of knowledge we are called the offspring of God, Acts 17. v. 29. With how much greater wisdom, therefore, shall we think Adam flourished, who was created wholly in the image of God as similar as possible?

3. From restoration. Through regeneration there is restored in us some ἐπίγνωσις, or knowledge of GOD. Therefore our first parents had this from creation. For what is restored to us, that was lost in Adam. But what he lost here, that he certainly had. For as there is no affection of a non-entity, so there is no loss of one.

X. Furthermore, that we may describe this wisdom concreated with Adam a little more fully; there are three things, as Augustine testifies, and Caelius Rhodiginus cites in book 2 of his Antiquities, chapter 2, which are known by the human intellect. 1. Some things are above it, such as GOD. 2. Some things are beside it, such as the Angels. 3. Some things are below it, such as the remaining creatures. The knowledge of all these was excellent and illustrious in Adam.

XI. For 1. HE KNEW GOD: inasmuch as he was created to this end, that he might celebrate his creator. But how could this have happened if he had been ignorant of God? For as there is no desire for the unknown, so there is no celebration of it. Without doubt, therefore, he knew the mystery of the Trinity; he knew God's will; he knew His goodness, wisdom, justice, and other attributes. He knew Him, however, not in a riddle, but in a way far clearer, although not with such fullness as will be given in the other life, where we shall see God face to face, 1 Cor. 13:12, as He is, 1 John 3:2. Hence some distinguish 1. Between the light of knowledge in Adam before the fall. 2. The light of faith. 3. The light of glory. The former was lower than the latter; the latter is higher than the former. Others say that there is a fourfold kind of knowing God: 1. Through faith. 2. Through illustrious contemplation. 3. Through sensible apparition. 4. Through open vision. The first mode belongs to the reborn, the last to the blessed, the two intermediate ones to Adam in the state of integrity.

XII 2. HE KNEW THE ANGELS, who ministered to him and whose company he enjoyed. To this point pertains that statement of Augustine, which is read in book 9 on Genesis, the last chapter: that ecstasy, he says, which GOD sent upon Adam, so that he might be lulled to sleep, is rightly understood to have been sent for this reason, that he might become a participant in it through ecstasy as if of the angelic court, and entering into the sanctuary of GOD, might understand the last things, etc. He also knew without doubt the horrible fall of the Angels, who were cast down from heaven on account of pride, which example ought deservedly to have kept him in humility and true obedience.

XIII. 3. HE KNEW THE NATURE OF ANIMALS, and of the remaining creatures, a fact which even the giving of names alone clearly proves, so that it is a wonder how Cajetan could have been so delirious as to deny that Adam had knowledge of the elements, the heavens, and the stars, whom Pererius himself refutes in book 5, disputation on the first excellence of man, question 2, p. 169.
