Adam indeed had regarding creatures not only 1. fullness but also 2. rectitude and 3. clarity of cognition, that is, he knew all things fully, rightly, and in an orderly manner.

Nor was the speculative intellect alone endowed with knowledge: but furthermore, in the practical intellect, regarding those things which were to be done by man, he had most exquisite prudence, and knowledge of those arts which have use, ingenuity, and honest delight, such as music, agriculture, architecture, etc. Meanwhile, however, his knowledge was finite; he did not know the number of atoms or stars; not future contingencies; because it was not expedient for him to know these, and the creator had reserved those for himself.

XIV. Several questions are raised here, but of little moment. 1. Whether the knowledge of Adam was innate, or acquired, or infused? Pererius names it infused, the Photinians acquired, we say innate, which will be demonstrated in its proper place. 2. Whether the knowledge of Adam could have grown with the passage of time? Certainly, partly through the observation of various vicissitudes in the elements; partly through further instruction from God, regarding even supernatural things. 3. Whether Adam was wiser than all mortals? If you except the one man Christ, we affirm it. Pererius indeed prefers the knowledge of the Apostles, book 5, p. 169, but falsely. For the Apostles also knew in part, 1 Cor. 13:9. And it would follow that in this life the image of God (regarding this part) was not only fully restored, but even more was granted. Although indeed Solomon is said to be wiser than all men 3. Kings 3:12, yet this is to be understood either of men after the fall; or of the kings of Israel prior to him, as he himself explains, Ecclesiastes 5, verse 10.

4. Would the descendants of Adam have been born with knowledge in the state of innocence? Entirely. For just as we are now born with ignorance, so then we would have been with knowledge. There would have been degrees, however, between Adam and his descendants, because he was to be the parent and common teacher of the human race.

Latin:

I De conformitate Intellectus cum Dei Sapientia.

VI. Homini primo excellentem Dei rerum que aliarum notitiam fuisse concretam, probari potest 1. dictis Scripturæ. 2 factis Adami. 3. firmis rationibus.

VII. DICTA leguntur, 1. Gen. 1. v. ult. Vidit Deus cuncta, quæ fecerat, & erant bona valdè. Deus enim omnia animalia creavit in suo quæque genere perfecta, ideoque & hominem. Apparet hoc ex corpore, quod creatum est perfectum, quantum ad integritatem ętatis, proceritatem staturę, & firmitatem virium. Ergo & anima perfecta fuit condita, ac per consequens cum cognitione & scientia, quippe in qua perfectio animi consistit. Si enim Adamus tenebris tantaque ignorantia fuisset septus, ut nunc eius posteri; quomodo quæso dici posset, omnia fuisse valdè bona? Num etiam crassa inscitia bonum, & quod maius, valdè bonum est?

2. Ecclesiastæ 7. v. 30. Fecit Deus hominem, ישר rectum, nempe corpore & mente, staturâ & sapientiâ. jam verò cogita summam intellectus nostri caliginem, spissam hebetudinem, errandique facilitatem & proclivitatem; certè si hanc Adamo tribuas, non rectus, sed obliquus & curvus omninò factus est.

3. Ecclesiast. 17. v. 5. Disciplinâ intellectus replevit illos, nempè primos homines. De his enim principaliter loqui Ecclesiasticum, versus proximè præcedentes evincunt. Replevit autem non post creationem, sed in ipsa ad imaginē suam efformatione.

4 Coloff. 3. v. 10. Induite novum hominem, eùm, qui renovatur in in' γνῶσιν, in agnitionem, secundum imaginem eius, qui creavit illum. Si renovari debemus in cognitionem; Ergo illam aliquando habuimus, amifimus. Et si imago Dei creatoris consistit in ἐπιγνώσει vel scientiâ, utique Adamus cum hac creatus fuit; quoniam ad Dei imaginem creatus est.

IIX FACTA Adami, sapientiæ argumēta, duo annotata sunt, 1. Nominum impositio, Gen. 2. v. 19. Si Adamᵘ scientiâ animaliũ caruisset, imponere nomina naturis convenientia non potuisset. Vnde Plato in Cratylo, Eum, qui primus nomina rebus imposuit, Sapientissimum fuisse concludit. Hanc verò notitiam Adamus non per experientiam collegit, cum inter eius creationem & ὀνομαθεσίαν brevissimum tempus, & vix aliquot horulæ, ut vulgò putatur, intercesserint.

2. Evæ agnitio, Gen. 2. v. 23. Ipse altissimo somno immersus fuerat, nihilque noverat de formatione Evæ: attamen, quàm primum aspexit, carnem esse suam ex costa formatam, agnovit, ipsique nomen aptissimum imposuit. Sunt hæc non vulgaris sapientiæ, imò etiam doni prophetiæ luculentissima testimonia.

IX. RATIONVM tres potissimùm dantur. 1. A contrario. Nam post lapsum mens humana incredibili ignorantiâ est obtusa, unde passim comparatur tenebris, Ergo ante lapsum insigni scientiâ fuit illustrata; quoniam contrariorum contraria sunt attributa.

2. A ruderibus. Ob exiguas quasdam reliquias scientiæ nominamur genus Dei, Act. 17. v 29. Quantò maiore igitur sapientia floruisse Adamum putabimus, qui totus ad imaginem Dei quàm similimam creatus fuit?

3 A restitutione. Per regenerationem in nobis restauratur nonnihil ἐπίγνωσις, vel cognitio DEI. Ergò primi parētes nostri, hanc ex creatione habuerunt. Quod enim nobis restituitur, id in Adamo amissum est. Quod verò hic amisit, id certé habuit. Non entis enim, ut nulla affectio; sic nulla amissio.

X. Porrò autem, vt hanc Adami concreatam sapientiam paulò pleniùs describamus; tria sunt, teste Augustino, & citante Caelio Rhodigino l. 2. Antiquit. c. 2. quæ ab intellectu humano cognoscuntur. 1. Quædam sunt supra ipsum, vt DEVS. 2. Quędam juxta ipsum, vt Angeli. 3. Quædam infra ipsum, vt creaturæ reliquæ. Horum omnium cognitio in Adamo excellens & illustris fuit.

XI. Nam 1. NOVIT DEVM: quippe ad hunc finẽ conditus, vt creatorem suum celebraret. Qui autem fieri hoc potuisset si Deum ignorasset? Nam ignoti vt nulla est cupido, sic nulla celebratio. Proculdubio igitur nouit mysterium Trinitatis; nouit Dei voluntatem; novit eius bonitatem, sapientiam, iustitiam & attributa cætera. Nouit autem non in ænigmate, sed modo longè clariori, quamuis non tantâ plenitudine, quanta dabitur in vita altera, vbi Deum videbimus à facie ad faciem, 1. Cor. 13. v. 12. ficuti est, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 2. Hinc quidam distinguunt 1. Inter lumen scientiæ, in Adamo ante lapsum. 2. lumen fidei. 3. lumen gloriæ. Illud hoc fuit inferius; isto superius. Alij dicunt, quadruplex dari genus cognoscendi Deum. 1. per fidem. 2. per illustrem contemplationem. 3. per sensibilem apparitionem. 4. per apertam visionem. Primus mod? competit renatis postremus beatis, duo intermedii Adamo in statu integritatis.

XII 2. NOVIT ANGELOS, qui ipsi ministrârunt & quorum consortio vsus est. Huc facit illud Augustini. quod legitur t 9. in Genes. c. vlt. illa, inquit, ecstasis, quam DEV S immisit in Adam, vt soporatus obdormiret, rectè intelligitur ob hoc immissa, vt & ipsius per ectasin particeps fieret tanquam Angelicæ curiæ, & intrans in sanctuarium DEI intelligeret nouissima, &c. Nouit etiam proculdubio horribilem Angelorum lapsum, propter superbiam cœlo deturbatorum, quod exemplum in humilitate & vera obedientia ipsum meritò continere debuisset.

XIII. 3. NOVIT NATVRAM ANIMALIVM, & reliquarum creaturarum, id quod vel sola νομοθεσία luculenter euincit, vt mirum sit, quomodo Caietanus adeò delirare potuerit, vt neget, Adamum habuisse scientiam elementorum, cœlorum & siderum, quem refutat ipse Pererius l. 5. disputat. de prima hominis excell quæst. 2. p. 169. Habuit verò Adamus quoad creaturas nõ modò 1. plenitudinem sed etiam 2. rectitudinem & 3. claritatem cognitionis, hoc est, omnia, plenè, rectè & ordinatè, cognouit.

Neque tantùm intellectus speculatiuus scientiâ præditus fuit: sed insuper in intellectu practico, circa ea, quæ homini agenda erant, exquisitissimam habuit prudentiam, & cognitionem artium earum, quæ habent vsum, ingenium, & honestam oblectationem, vt est musica, agricultura, architectura, &c. Interim tamen scientia eius finita fuit; non nouit numerum atomorum aut stellarum; non futura contingentia; quia hæc ipsum scire non expediebat, & creator illa sibi reseruauerat.

XIV. Mouentur hîc nonnullæ quæstiones, sed parui momenti. 1. Vtrum scientia Adami fuerit innata, vel acquisita, vel infusa? Pererius nominat infusam, Photiniani acquisitam, nos dicimus innatam, quod suo loco demonstrabitur. 2, An scientia Adami progressu temporis potuisset crescere? Vtique partim per obseruationẽ variarum vicissitudinum in elementis; partim per vlteriorem Dei, quoad res etiam supernaturales, institutionem. 3. An Adam sapientior fuerit cunctis mortalibus? Si vnicum hominẽ Christum excipias, affirmamus. Præfert quidem Pererius Apostolorum scientiam l. 5. p. 169. sed falsò Nam & Apostoli ex parte cognouerunt, 1. Cor. 13. v. 9 Et sequeretur in hac vita imaginem Dei (quoad hanc partem) non modò plenè restitutam, sed plus etiam concessum esse. Licèt verò Salomon dicatur sapientior omnibus hominibus 3. Reg. 3. v. 12. tamen hoc intelligendum est, vel de hominibus post lapsum; vel de Regibus Israëli priovibus, vt ipse exponit, Ecclesiast. 5. vers. 10.

4. An posteri Adam in statu innocentia cum scientia fuissent nasi? Omninò. Sicut enim nunc cū ignorantia nascimur, ita tunc cum scientia. Gradus tamē fuissent inter Adamum & posteros, quia ille parens & communis doctor humani generis esse debuit.


### Question VI. In what precisely was the reason of the divine Image situated?: II. Concerning the conformity of the will with the holiness and freedom of God

II. Concerning the conformity of the will with the holiness and freedom of God.

XV. This conformity includes two things: 1. an impulse and drive toward the good. 2. the prompt and easy execution of that impulse, which is called freedom. We prove it, 1. by sayings. 2. by reasons. 3. by testimonies.

XVI. Sayings. 1. We repeat that passage from Genesis 1, last verse. It is not said: What God had made; they were evil: for God is good: how then could He be the author of evil? Nor is it said: They were not good, that is, neither evil nor good or ἄλογα, for this neutral state lacks all testimony of Scripture and the Fathers, and all probable reason. And it is against the goodness and providence of God. What then is said? They were very good. Wherefore the will of man was also good, that is, upright, just, and holy. For as soon as you posit an obliquity or a propensity toward evil, or merely a neutral state, you contradict the very clear pronouncement of Moses concerning all things being very good.

2. We repeat also this from Ecclesiastes 7, verse 30. God made man upright. Conversely, τὸ ἀλογον is not hinted at here, but τὸ rectum is posited. But a will is not upright which is either unjust or not just.

3. We urge the saying from Eph. 4, v. 24. Be renewed, and put on the new man who according to God is created in righteousness and holiness of truth. Here by the Hebrew phrase, holiness of truth is put for true holiness and righteousness. I urge, however, both the word of renewal, which notes that we were once, namely in Adam, new, and therefore possessed the holiness in which that newness consists: then the word of justice, to which we are said to be renewed. It is certain that we are renewed to the image of God, from Col. 3, v. 10. But indeed we are renewed to justice, as the Apostle says here. Therefore the image of God was placed in justice. Wherefore when this new man is said to be created in justice and holiness, regard is had not only to the second creation, or our regeneration, but especially to the first creation, to the origin of Adam, who was created to the image of God, that is, as Paul interprets, in justice.

Some add a passage from Ecclesiasticus ch. 17, v. 3. God clothed man with virtue: but it is a fault of the translation. For in the Greek it is ἰσχὺς, strength; not ἀρετή or virtue.

XVII. REASONS. 1. From the remains. There are still innate in us certain stimuli of virtues and there remain in the will as it were little sparks of good from a huge flame. Much more therefore in the first state was the heart of Adam inclined to virtue, to the love of God and neighbor. 2. From the contrary. Now the hearts of men from early childhood are prone to evil. Gen. 8, v. 21. Wherefore by the force of contraries, before the fall they were prone to good.

XIIX. TESTIMONIES. 1. Gregory, book 2, on 1 Kings ch. 2. The image, he says, and likeness of God, is to hate evil with noble hatred, and to love good with perfect love. 2. Damascene, book 2, ch. 14, writes that Adam was created not only ἄκακον or not just, but also ἐνάρετον καὶ ἔνθυ, virtuous and upright, and πάσῃ ἀρετῇ κατηγλαϊσμένον, καὶ πᾶσιν ἀγαθοῖς κομῶντα, endowed with EVERY VIRTUE, and adorned with all good things.

XIX. Furthermore, that I may add something in particular concerning concreated holiness, it is known that that will of man is holy which agrees with the will of God, expressed by His law. There are, however, two principal members of the law. 1. To love God with all one's heart. 2. To love one's neighbor as oneself. Since, therefore, the will of Adam was holy by reason, he would have loved God with all his heart, and with all his strength, above all things and over all things, if he had remained in the state of integrity. Nothing would have been more pleasant to him, nothing more desired, than to execute the will of God.

For this most ardent love would have existed as the most pleasing food of the soul, just as Christ also says of himself in John 4:34: My food is that I may do the will of my Father. Just as, therefore, the Son of God by nature, so Adam, the son of God by grace, would have always had every delight of his soul placed in the love of God. And, just as now after the fall in the reborn, when the restoration of the divine image is begun, an ardent propensity is seen toward loving God, so indeed that they consider all their will to rest in this, and exclaim with the Psalmist: I was glad in those things which were said to me. We shall go into the house of the Lord. Psalm 122:1. So also then before the fall, the soul and heart of Adam would have naturally burned with the highest love toward God, which would not only have contained itself within the narrow boundaries of the heart, but would have been so ardent that it would have broken forth also to the outside, and Adam would have been entirely dissolved into the praises of God,

XX. Hence would have arisen the highest joy, hence perpetual doxology, by which he would have celebrated God his creator without end. For where there is more love, there is more praise and thanksgiving.

For there are three acts which follow one another in turn: 1. to see, 2. to love, 3. to praise. For he who sees God loves what he sees: he who loves, praises the one loved: and the more he sees, the more he loves, and the more he loves, the more he praises. Whence Augustine, in his book On Spirit and Soul, chapter 55, says of the blessed: They will praise as much as they will love, and they will love as much as they will know.

Because, therefore, Adam would have perpetually praised God in the state of innocence; therefore he would also have loved, and would have known set; from which it is sufficiently understood how great the rectitude and holiness of his will was.

XXI. But since he who perfectly keeps the first table of the law also fulfills the second, we therefore conclude without doubt that Adam, if he had had any neighbors, would have loved them just as ardently, would have done injury to no one, and would have been humane, just, placid, and beneficent toward all. In sum, no virtue can be given or imagined, whether it has God or anything else as its object, which would not have shone forth remarkably in Adam.

XXII. Moreover, he would have performed these very good works not under compulsion or necessity, but willingly and freely. τὸ γὰρ καλὸν πρέπει εἶναι ἀβίαστον, Good must not be violent, Damasc. bk. 4, O. F. ch. 20. That Adam possessed freedom of will, the very commandment or rather the prohibition of the Lord, Gen. 2:17, proves most clearly. Yet his will was free in such a way that it inclined toward the good, not otherwise than it is now, when turned away from the good, inclined toward evil. Thus, therefore, in the first state, piety toward God and charity toward one's neighbor flourished, and there was a far most beautiful harmony of all virtues, so that our parents led a life that was immaculate, just, and holy, in a word, blessed,

Latin:

II. De conformitate voluntatis cum Dei sanctitate & libertate.

XV. Duo comprehendithæc conformitas, 1. impetum & impulsum ad bonum. 2. expeditam facilemque istius impetus executionem, quæ libertas dicitur. Probamus eam, 1. dictis. 2. rationibus. 3. testimonijs.

XVI. Dicta. 1. Repetimus istud Genesis. 1. v. vlt. Non dicitur: Quæ Deus fecerat; Erant mala: Bonus enim est Dsvs: quî ergò malj author? Nec dicitur: Erant non bona, id est, nec mala nec bona vel ἄλογα, Status enim hic neutralis caret omni Scripturæ & Patrum testimonio, omni probabili ratione. Estque contra D e i bonitatem & prouidentiam. Quid ergo dicitur? Erant valde bona. Quare bona etiam fuit hominis voluntas, hoc est, recta, iusta & sancta. Quam primùm enim obliquitatem ponis vel propensionem ad malum, vel statum tantummodò neutrum, contradicis pronunciato Mosis clarissimo de cunctis valdè bonis.

2. Repetimus & hoc Ecclesiast. 7. vers. 30. Fecit Devs hominem rectum. Vicissim hîc non innuitur τὸ ἀλογον, sed ponitur τὸ rectum. Ast recta voluntas non est, quæ vel iniusta vel non iusta.

3. Vrgemus dictum ex Eph. 4. v. 24. Renouamini, & induite nouum hominem qui secundum Deum creatus est in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis Hic phrasi Hebræa sanctitas veritatis ponitur pro vera sanctitate & iustitia. Vrgeo autem, tum vocem renouationis, quæ notat nos aliquando, nimirum in Adamo novos fuisse, adeoque sanctitatem, in qua consistit illa novitas, habuisse: tum vocem iustitiæ, ad quam renovari dicimur. Certum est quòd ad imaginem Dei renodemur, ex Col. 3. v. 10. At verò renovamur ad iustitiam, dicente hîc Apostolo. Ergò imago Dei in iusticia fuit posita. Quare cùm hic novus homo dicitur creatus in iustitia & sanctitate, non respectus habetur ad secundam tantùm creationem, vel regenerationem nostram, sed potissimùm ad creationem primam, ad originem Adam, qui ad imaginem Dei, hoc est, interprete Paulo, in iustitia creatus est.

Addunt nonnulli locum ex Ecclesiastico c. 17. v. 3. Deus vestivit hominem virtute: sed vitium versionis est. In Græco enim habetur ἰσχὺς fortitudo; non ἀρετή vel virtus.

XVII. RATIONES. 1. A reliquijs. Sunt adhuc nobis innati quidam virtutum stimuli & in voluntate supersunt quasi scintillulæ boni ex ingenti flamma. Multò magis igitur in primo statu cor Adami ad virtutem, ad Dei & proximi dilectionem fuit inclinatum. 2. A contrario. Nunc corda hominum à prima pueritia prona sunt ad malum. Gen. 8. v. 21. Quare vi contrariorum, antè lapsum prona fuerunt ad bonum.

XIIX. TESTIMONIA. 1. Gregor. l. 2. in 1. reg. c. 2. Imago, inquit, & similitudo Dei, est inclyto odio malum odisse, & amore perfecto bonum diligere. 2. Damasc. l. 2. c. 14. scribit, Adamum conditum esse non tantùm ἄκακον vel non iustum, sed etiam ἐνάρετον καὶ ἔνθυ, virtuosen rectumque & πάσῃ ἀρετῇ κατηγλαϊσμένον, καὶ πάσιν ἀγαθοῖς κομῶντα, OMNI VIRTVTE præditum, & omnibus bonis ornatum.

XIX. Præterea verò vt in specie de sanctitate concreatâ quædam adjiciam, notum est, quòd illa voluntas hominis sit sancta, quæ consentit cum voluntate Dei, lege ipsius expressâ. Sunt autem duo principalia legis membra. 1. Diligere Deum ex toto corde. 2. Diligere proximum sicut seipsum. Quoniam igitur Adami voluntas erat sancta ex ratione, ideò ex toto corde, & omnibus viribus, præ omnibus & super omnia dilexisset Deum, si mansisset in statu integritatis. Nihil ipsi iucundius, nihil exoptatius fuisset, quàm voluntatem Dei exequi.

Hæc enim ardentissima dilectio extitisset gratissimum animę pabulū, sicut & Christus de se ait Joh. 4. v. 34. Meus cibus est, vt faciam voluntatem Patris mei. Quemadmodū igitur Filius Dei per naturam, ita Adam Filius Dei per gratiam, omnem animę delectationem in amore Dei positam semper habuisset. Et, sicuti nunc post lapsum in renatis, cum inchoatur restitutio imaginis diuinæ, ardens cernitur propensio ad diligendum Deum, ita quidem vt in hoc omnem suam voluntatem recumbere existiment, & cum Psalte exclament: Lætatus sum in his, quæ dicta sunt mihi. In domum Domini ibimus. Psal. 122. v. 1. Ita etiam tunc ante lapsum, anima & cor Adami naturaliter flagrâsset summo erga Deum amore, qui etiam sese non tantùm continuisset intra angusta cordis pomœria, sed adeò ardens fuisset, vt ad extra quoq; prorupisset, & Adam totus in laudes Dei dissolutus fuisset,

XX. Hinc extitisset summa lætitia, hinc perpetua δοξολογία, quà Deum creatorem suum sine fine celebrasset. Nam vbi plus amoris, ibi plus laudis & gratiarum actionis.

Tres enim actus sunt qui se in vicem consequũtur: 1. videre, 2. amare, 3. laudare. Qui enim Deum videt is visum amat: qui amat, is amatum laudat: & quò plus videt, eò plus amat, & quò plus amat, eò plus laudat. Vnde Augustinus l. de spiritu & anima c. 55. de beatis inquit: Tantum laudabunt, quantum amabunt & tantum amabunt, quantum cognoscent.

Quia ergò Adamus Deum perpetuò in statu innocentiæ laudasset; Ergò & amâsset, & cognouisset set; vnde quanta voluntatis rectitudo & sanctitas fuerit, satis intelligitur.

XXI. Quoniam verò is, qui primam legis tabulam perfectè servat, secundam quoq; implet, ideo indubitanter concludimus, Adamum suos si quos habuisset, proximos ardẽtissime itidem fuisse dilecturum, nemini facturum injuriam, erga omnes futurum humanum, justum, placidum & beneficum. In summa, dari vel excogitari nequit vlla virtus, siue pro objecto Deum, siue aliud quodcunq; habeat, quæ non in Adamo egregiè luxisset.

XXII. Hæc ipsa autem bona opera præstitisset non coactè aut necessariò, sed volenter & liberè. τὸ γὰρ καλὸν πρέπει εἶναι ἀβίαστον, Bonum non sit violentum, Damasc. l. 4. O. F c. 20. Habuisse verò Adamum libertatem arbitrij, vel solum pręceptum aut potius interdictũ Domini Gen. 2. v. 17, clarissimè probat. Sic autem libera erat voluntas, vt tamen propendere ad bonum, non sec9 atque nunc à bona aversa, in malium proclivis est. Sic ergò in primo statu viguit pietas in Deum, charitas in proximum, & fuit omnium virtutum concentus longè pulcherrimus, ita vt parentes nostri vitam duxerint immaculatam, justam & sanctam, vno verbo, beatam,


### Question VI. In what precisely was the reason of the divine Image situated?: III On the conformity of the Appetite with the chastity, purity, and integrity of GOD

III.

On the conformity of the Appetite with the chastity, purity, and integrity of GOD.

XXIII. There is no need for a lengthy proof here, since the arguments brought forward above confirm this very thing as well. Specifically, however, let two sayings and two reasons be noted.

XXIV. SAYINGS: 1. Gen. 2:25. They were naked, and were not ashamed. But what was the cause? None, other than chastity and the harmony of the faculties. For there were no inordinate motions in the members, but all things obeyed the judgment of reason. Thus Augustine explains it, bk. 14, De civ. Dei, ch.

17. They were naked, and were not ashamed; not that their nakedness was unknown to them: but shameful nakedness did not yet exist; because lust did not yet move those members against their will: the flesh did not yet in a certain way bear witness to its own disobedience to rebuke the disobedience of man. Therefore, it is an old woman's error of Josephus, book 1 of Antiquities, chapter 2, to maintain that that lack of shame came from the inexperience and childish simplicity of our first parents. For thus their state would have been made better by sin.

2. Gen. 3. v. 6. & 7. Their eyes were opened, and when they had known that they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together; here is not understood simple nakedness, but shameful and ignominious; not so much the nakedness of the body, as of the soul. Whence Augustine in the aforementioned place says: The eyes of both were opened, he says, not for seeing: for they saw even before; but for discerning between the good, which they had lost, and the evil, into which they had fallen. This knowledge of nakedness, therefore, after the fall, is an indication that our first parents lacked vicious affections before the fall. Otherwise, no reason can be given why their eyes are said to be opened.

XXV. REASONS 1. From concupiscence. The ἐπιθυμία of the flesh and of the members is sin, Rom. 7. v. 7. But in the state of integrity, sin had no place: For there would have been sin before sin, therefore neither concupiscence. Wherefore the harmony of appetite and reason was perfect.

2. From the absence of pain. Wherever there are inordinate affections, there pain and sadness arise in a pious soul, as is evident from the example of Paul from Rom. 7. But pain and cares were banished in the first state, for it was a state of joy, not of sadness, therefore the cause of pain, namely the inordination of affections, was also absent. Hence Augustine rightly exclaims in book 14 of The City of God, chapter 10: How happy were our first parents! They were agitated by no perturbations of the soul; they were harmed by no inconveniences of the body.

XXVI. Moreover, appetite is twofold. 1. Concupiscible, and 2. Irascible. The former is called ἐπιθυμία, the latter πάθος. To the former belongs the appetite for food, drink, and sexual matters: to the latter belong the affections, such as love and hatred. Both were ordered, and without sin. Man would have eaten and drunk, Gen. 1, v. 29, but without intemperance. He would have hungered and thirsted, but without discomfort. He would have begotten offspring, but without excessive lust. Hence Augustine, book 14, On the City of God, ch. 19: The movements of appetite before sin in Paradise, he says, were not vicious. The fact that we are moved in this way now is not health from nature, but weakness from guilt.

XXVII. In like manner the irascible appetite was ordered, and the affections were restrained, which we doubt not existed even in an uncorrupted nature. There was joy and gladness there, there was love of the good and hatred of evil: but there was no sadness, anger, fear, and other painful and disordered affections. For all were subject to the dictates of right reason. 1. As regards their excitation. For the appetite was not moved unless reason commanded. Indeed, it was more delightful for it to follow the precept of reason than to strive against it by clinging to its own pleasures and delights. 2. As regards their duration. For they did not last longer than it pleased man. 3. As regards their degrees. They were not more intense or more remiss than was just; but they always remained in equilibrium. In a word: There was supreme integrity, supreme rectitude, supreme harmony in all the faculties, without difficulty, without struggle, and without any rebellion.

Latin:

III.

De conformitate Appetitus cum DEI castitate, puritate & integritate.

XXIII. Prolixâ hîc probatione non est opus, cùm argumenta superiùs prolata, hoc ipsum quoq; cõfirment. In specie tamen notentur 1. duo dicta. 2 duę rationes.

XXIV. DICTA: 1. Gen. 2. v. 25. Erant nudi, & non erubescebant. Quæ verò causa? Nulla, quàm castitas & potentiarum harmonia. Motus enim inordinati in membris non erant, sed omnia rationis arbitrio obediebant. Ita exponit August. l. 14. de ciu. Dei c.

17. Nudi erant, & non confundebantur; non quod eis sua nuditas esset incognita: sed turpis nuditas nondum erat; quia nondum libido membra illa præter arbitrium commovebat: nondum ad hominis inobedientiam redarguendam sua inobedientia caro quodammodò testimonium perhibebat. Anilis proinde error est Iosephi l. 1. Antiquit. c. 2. statuentis, quòd inerubescentia illa ex imperitiâ venerit, & puerili simplicitate primorum parentum. Ita enim status eorum per peccatū melior fuisset effectus.

2. Gen. 3. v. 6. & 7. Aperti sunt oculi eorum, cumque cognovissent, se esse nudos, consuerunt folia ficus non hic intelligitur nuditas simplex, sed turpis & ignominiosa; non tàm nuditas corporis, quàm animi. Vnde Augustinus loco prædicto; Aperti sunt, inquit, oculi amborum, non ad videndum: nam & antea videbant; sed ad discernendum inter bonum, quod amiserant, & malum, in quod ceciderant. Hæc igitur nuditatis cognitio post lapsum, indicio est, parentes primos vitiosis adfectibus caruisse ante lapsum. Aliàs nulla poterit dari ratio, cur oculi eorum dicantur aperti.

XXV. RATIONES 1. A concupiscentia. Carnis & membrorum ἐπιθυμία peccatum est, Rom. 7. v. 7. In statu verò integritatis peccatum non habuit locum: Fuisset enim peccatum ante peccatum, Ergò nec cōcupiscentia. Quare optima fuit appetitus & rationis harmonia.

2. A doloris absentia. Vbicunque sunt inordinati adfectus, ibi dolor & tristitia in oritur animo pio, vt constat exemplo Pauli ex Rom. 7. At dolor & curæ in statu primo exulârunt, Fuit enim status lætitiæ, non tristitiæ, Ergò quoque abfuit doloris causa, nempè adfectuum inordinatio. Hinc August. meritò exclamat l. 14. de civit. Dei c. 10. Quam felices erant primi parentes! Nullis agitabantur perturbationibus animorum; nullis corporum lædebantur incommodis.

XXVI. Est autem appetitus duplex. 1. concupiscibilis. & 2. irascibilis. Ille dicitur ἐπιθυμία, hic πάθος. Ad illum spectat appetitus cibi, potus & rei venereæ: ad hunc adfectus, vt amor & odium. Vterq; fuit ordinatus, & absq; peccato. Comediffet homo & bibiffet, Gen. 1. v. 29. sed absq; intemperantia, Esuriiffet & sitiffet; sed absq; molestia. Generaffet prolem; sed absq; nimia libidine. Hinc August. l. 14. de civit. Dei c. 19. Motus, inquit, appetitus ante peccatum in Paradiso vitiosi non erant. Num quòd nunc itą movemur, non est sanitas ex natura, sed languor ex culpa.

XXVII. Pari modo ordinatus fuit apetitus irascibilis, & frænati adfectus, quos fuisse in natura etiam integra nulli dubitamus Fuit ibi gaudium & lætitia, fuit amor boni & odium mali: sed non fuit tristitia: ira, timor, aljique adfectus dolorosi & inordinati. Omnes enim erant dictamini rectæ rationis subiecti. 1. Quo ad ex citationem. Non enim moyebatur appetitus, nisi quando imperabat ratio. Imò delectabilius huic fuit, sequi rationis præceptum, quàm contrà niti, inhærendo proprijs voluptatibus & oblectationibus. 2 quoad durationem. Non enim diutius durabant, quam homini placebat. 3. Quoad gradus. Non erant justo intensiores, non remissiores; sed semper in æquilibrio confistebant. Vno verbo: Fuit summa integritas, summa rectitudo, summa harmonia in omnibus potentiÿs, sine difficultate, sine luctâ & sine omni rebellione.


### Question VI. In what precisely was the reason of the divine Image situated?: IV On the conformity of the body with the impassibility and immortality of God

IV.

On the conformity of the body with the impassibility and immortality of God.

XXVIII. As regards impassibility, it is sufficiently proved from nakedness. For if the bodies of our first parents had been passible, and exposed to cold or other injuries, they certainly could not have walked naked without pain.

XXIX. But immortality was denied of old by the Pelagians, asserting that man would have been mortal, even if he had not sinned, August. lib. de hær. C. 88. Today the Photinians, Catech. RACOV. pag. 21. Both falsely, because the death of the body is not a condition of φύσιας [nature], but a punishment of ἁμαρτίας [sin], which we give proof of in the following arguments:

XXX. 1. From the divine threat, Gen. 2. v. 17. In the day that you eat thereof, you shall surely die. These threats would have been a flash of lightning from a basin, if in the first state, and before sin, death had found a place. For the Lord wished to impose such a punishment as ought to follow the fault, not precede it. But it is not understood as only eternal death, but everything that comes under the name of death in Scripture. For which reason theologians rightly judge that this very thing was doubled, and said by the Lord as 'dying you shall die'.

Moreover, death is threefold: 1. The death of the body, which consists in the separation of the soul. 2. The death of the soul, which consists in the loss of grace. 3. The death of the whole man, which consists in the deprivation of eternal life, and the torments of hell. The former is commonly called the death of the body or of nature; the latter, the death of the soul or of grace; the last, the final death or of glory.

August. lib. 13. de ciuit. Dei cap. 12. makes four deaths: 1. Of the soul, when it is deprived of God. 2. Of the body, when it is deprived of the soul. 3. Again of the soul, when it is punished separated both from God and from the body. 4. The final one of the whole man, when the soul without God will suffer eternal punishments with the body. He says that the threat of the Lord embraces all these species of death, and Ambrose agrees, lib. de Paradiso, c. 9. But especially the execution teaches that this prohibition speaks of the death of the body itself, and it is evident from Gen. 3. v. 19. For here he is condemned to that punishment which the Lord had previously threatened: although Adam did not die immediately, yet the Lord inflicted death 1. as regards the guilt, 2. as regards the necessity of dying, 3. as regards the beginnings of bodily death, because the body immediately began to feel weariness, and gradually to be weakened.

XXXI. 2. From the testimony of the Wise Man, who in ch. 2, v. 23, expressly says that man was created ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, that is, in incorruption, or for immortality and an incorrupt state; the Vulgate renders it, 'inexterminabilem' [indestructible]. And, v. 24, he affirms that Death entered into the world through the envy of the devil. Wherefore before the sin, which was committed through the envy of Satan, death did not reign.

XXXII. 3. From the asseveration of the Apostle, Rom. 5, v. 12: 'By one man sin entered into this world, and by sin death.' If by sin. Therefore not by nature and creation. But what is understood by death? Not of the soul, since the Apostle places a real distinction between sin and death. But the death of the soul and sin do not differ in reality. Not eternal death only, since he writes that death reigns over men, even over infants themselves, who do not actually sin, nor do they perish eternally, before the last day, v. 14 and 17. Wherefore I conclude that the death of the body is denoted, yet in such a way that the guilt of eternal death is not excluded.

XXXIII. The following sayings prove the same, Rom. 6, v. 23, ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας, θάνατος [the wages of sin is death], Rom. 8, v. 10, THE BODY is dead (that is, subject to death) BECAUSE OF SIN. Where the word 'body' teaches that natural death is denoted, and the particle 'because of' proves that sin is established as its cause. Add 1 Cor. 15, v. 21: 'By man came death, and by man the resurrection of the dead,' v. 22: 'As in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive.' v. 55: 'The sting of death is sin': all of which clearly teach that death is the effect of guilt, not of the condition of nature.

XXXIV. 4. From the redemption of Christ. From whatever Christ has freed and redeemed us, this very thing, if not sin, is nevertheless the punishment of sin, and had no place in the first state before sin. But he redeemed us also from bodily death, otherwise we would not be recalled to life. Therefore, bodily death, since it is not a sin, was a punishment for sin, and in the first state before sin it had no place.

XXXV. 5. From the absence of cause. In the first state, every physical cause of death was absent, which is primarily fourfold: 1. External force, which at that time was none. 2. Hunger and thirst, which man could always appease and quench. 3. Diseases, to which he was not subject. 4. Old age and weakness, from which he was preserved by the fruit of the tree of life. But the cause being denied, the effect must also be denied. We conclude therefore with Augustine that death itself was also inflicted not by the law of nature, but by the merit of sin, from book 13 of The City of God, chapter 15.

XXXVI. It must be known here, however, that the immortality of the first man was not of the exact same nature as the glorious immortality of the blessed. For as it is one thing to be able not to sin, and another not to be able to sin; so it is one thing to be able not to die, and another not to be able to die. Or, it is one thing to have the power of not dying, and another to have the inability to die. The former immortality removes the act of dying, but does not exclude all power; the latter abolishes both. The former belongs to nature, the latter to glory. Therefore, just as by an innate power the will of Adam could be inclined in either direction, toward good and evil, so he could either retain life or bring death upon himself through sin. This statement of Lombard from book 2, distinction 19, letter A, pertains here: In the first state there was the ability not to die; in the second, the inability not to die; in the future, the inability to die. He took this from Augustine, book 3 of On Genesis, according to the letter, chapter 2, where he says: One thing, he says, is the immortality of the flesh which we received in Adam, another is that which we hope for in the resurrection through Christ. That man was made immortal so that he could not die if he did not sin, but he would die if he did sin. But the children of the resurrection will not be able to sin further, nor to die. Our flesh will not then need the refreshment of food, because there will be no possibility of decay.

XXXVII. Furthermore, it is asked here whether the immortality of Adam was a natural property, or indeed an extrinsic supernatural gift? Bellarmine affirms the latter in his book On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 9, but falsely. 1. If justice was natural to the first man: Therefore also immortality. For it cannot happen that one who is φύσει (by nature) holy, is φύσει (by nature) mortal, because death is the wages of sin. But that the former is true will be proved in the following disputation.

2. Supernatural and extrinsic gifts are not hereditary, nor are they propagated through generation. But Adam would have propagated his immortality to his descendants. Therefore it was not a supernatural or extrinsic gift.

2. The descendants of Adam after the fall are φύσει (by nature) children of wrath and death. Wherefore Adam before the fall was φύσει (by nature) a child of grace and life.

4. That which is the punishment of sin, and destroys nature in itself, its contrary was natural to man in his integrity. Death and mortality is the punishment of sin, and destroys nature in itself. Therefore, immortality, which is contrary to death, was natural to man in his integrity, which was to be demonstrated.

XXXVIII. Nor does the passage in 1 Cor. 15:47 stand in the way, where the first man is called earthly from the earth, and an animal body is attributed to him, v. 46. For the Apostle either speaks of Adam after the fall, when he became our common parent, and thus had a mortal body, and propagated it into us; or by an animal and earthly man he does not understand one who is φύσει (by nature) mortal, but one who lives an animal life; who needs food and drink, and generates one like himself. In this sense, the first man was earthly and animal, which itself will be abolished in the state of glorification, and thus we shall obtain a spiritual body.

But that the first man is said to be from the earth, this does not designate the quality of mortality, but his origin, because he was formed from the earth, which appears from the antithesis, where the Lord is said to be from heaven. 2. The place, because he was placed on the earth. 3. The end, because he was to till the earth. But what does this have to do with proving mortality? XXXIX. Furthermore, it is to be noted that in this question, the consideration of the whole is one thing, and that of the parts is another. As regards the whole man, he was by nature immortal, as we have just shown. As concerns the parts, there are two of them: 1. The soul. 2. The body. No Christian would deny that the soul, as a spirit devoid of matter, was and is by nature immortal. Regarding the body, however, opinions vary. Some think that even in the first state it was φθαρτὸν or mortal, others ἄφθαρτον or immortal. Both are not without their reasons.

XL. These arguments contend for the mortality of the body.

1. From its composition. The body was formed from corruptible matter, namely earth and the elements. Wherefore it itself was corruptible, because that which is originated follows the nature of its principles.

2. From the tree of life. What would have been the use and effect of the tree of life, if the body were immortal by nature? Was it called so only σικτικῶς, that is, significantly?

3. From hunger. Man needed food, therefore consumption preceded, and thus the mutual action of the elements. Therefore, there was not a perfect harmony of qualities, nor was man mortal by nature. For if he had fasted for a few weeks, the radical moisture would eventually have been completely consumed.

4. From the distinction of states. If the body is posited as ἄφθαρτον, the difference between the state of creation and glorification is removed: for in the latter, immortality will finally occur, according to that passage in Revelation 21:4, death shall be no more, nor mourning.

XLI. Arguments no less weighty can be brought forward for immortality.

1. From the harmony of qualities. That which consists of the most exact harmony of primary and secondary qualities is in itself and internally immortal. The body of Adam was of this kind, for it had an equal temperament. And, just as in the future state bodies will indeed be composed of elements, yet will be ἄφθαρτα: so what pro-

prevent, whereby it could not be established that the body of Adam was created ἀνενδεήτως

2. From the union with the soul: That which is essentially and by an indissoluble bond united to a soul created for immortality, that is certainly immortal. But the body of the first man was such, therefore it was immortal.

3. From the cause of death, which is sin, Rom. 5. v. 15. & c. 8. v. 10. But the cause of mortality being absent, mortality itself is also absent, and every inclination toward death. In the body of Adam that was absent, namely sin. Therefore this also.

4. From recovery. What we recover in Christ, that we had and lost in Adam. But we recover immortal bodies, 1. Cor. 15. v. 46. Therefore we had such in Adam.

5. From the absurd: For it would follow that man in his first state was by nature mortal. For whatever is said of the part is also predicated of the whole. Wherefore, if the body was by nature mortal, why not also the man? Especially since the denomination of mortality and immortality in man is always taken from the body.

XLII. And these are the principal arguments which can be brought forward for either side, and which render the question doubtful and intricate on every side. But that we may in some way extricate ourselves, we believe that an ambiguity lies in the word immortality and mortality, which, unless it is explained, makes a fall into error easy.

XLIII. Therefore, as concerns 1. Immortality; it is accepted in four principal ways.

1. For an absolute and total inability to die, in which sense God alone is said to be ἁπλῶς and by nature immortal, 1. Tim 6. v. 16.

2. For an inability to die by the grace of creation, and because of an essential separation from matter: in which way angels and our souls are immortal.

3. For an inability to die by gift and singular ordination tion of God. Thus the bodies of the blessed and the damned will be incorruptible, not by the property of nature, but by the grace and the peculiar disposition of God. 4. Propositions of not dying, in what sense that is immortal which does not actually die, yet can die, a certain condition being posited. And in this way the body of the first man was immortal. For there was not present an inability to die: (because this is proper to the state of glorification,) but yet a power of not dying, which would have reached even to us, had it not been converted into a necessity of dying.

XLIV. As regards mortality, something is said to be mortal by nature in two ways.

1. Properly, for that which inclines toward death that will certainly follow, and is naturally inclined to corruption through the successive consumption of parts. Thus the body of the first man was by no means mortal by nature, which the later arguments most clearly demonstrate. 2. Improperly and abusively, for any power of dying whatsoever, even the most remote, and such that, while nature stands and through nature, it is never brought into act. And in this improper and remote sense, the body of Adam was indeed mortal, no otherwise than as a tree is a bench by power: which is all that the reasons enumerated in the first place prove. For the body was not absolutely incorruptible, otherwise it would not have been subject to death: nor yet was it corruptible through power and near inclination, 1. because of the harmony of qualities. 2. because of the equality of temperament. 3. the indissoluble union of the soul. 4. because of the use of the most excellent fruits, especially of the tree of life: which if he had neglected, and had wished to fast for several weeks: by this very act he would have sinned against the order of God, who had commanded him to eat of the fruits, and so it would not have been a wonder if death had invaded him, namely not from the condition of nature, but from the transgression of the divine order.

XLV. That therefore we may finish, we say the body of Adam was immortal by nature; not because it was so by the act itself through natural causes, it would never have been corrupted before sin; then, because no proximate power or inclination to die had any place, just as in this state we carry bodies always subject to death. Meanwhile, it was not ἁπλῶς or absolutely immortal, through the exclusion of every power of dying; because this will properly be the dignity of the glorified: but only ὑποθετικῶς or conditionally, namely, if man had abstained from sins:

Latin:

IV.

De conformitate corporis cum Dei impassibilitate & immortalitate.

XXVIII. Quod spectat impassibilitatem, satis illa probatur ex nuditate. Si enim corpora primorum parentum fuissent passibilia, & frigori, alijs vè jujurijs exposita, certè nudi ambulare sine dolore non potuissent.

XXIX. Immortalitatem verò negârunt olim Pelagiani, statuentes hominem fuisse moriturum, etsi non peccasset, August. lib. de hær. C. 88. Hodiè Photiniani, Catech. RACOV. pag. 21 Vtrique falsò, quia mors corporis, non est conditio φύσιας, sed pœna ἁμαρτίας, quod sequentibus argumentis probatum damus:

XXX. 1. Ex cõminatione diuinâ, Gen. 2. v. 17. Quocunq; die comederis, morte morieris, Hæ minę fulgur ex pelvi fuissent, si in primo statu, & ante peccatũ mors locum inuenisset. Talem enim pœnam Dominus indicere volebat, quæ culpam sequi, non pręcedete debebat. Non autem intelligitur sola mors ẹterna, sed omne id, quod nomine mortis in Scriptura venit, Quám ob causam hoc ipsum duplicatum, & Morte morieris à Domino dictum esse, rectè existimant Theologi.

Est autem mors triplex: 1. Mors corporis, quæ consistit in separatione animæ. 2. Mors animæ, quę cosistit in amissione gratię. Mors totius hominis, quę consistit in priuatione vitæ æternæ, & cruciatibus inferni. Illa, mors corporalis vel naturæ: ista, mors spiritualis vel gratiæ; hæc, mors nouissima vel gloriæ communiter appellatur.

August. lib. 13. de ciuit. Dei cap. 12. facit quatuor mortes, 1. Animæ, cùm priuatur Deo. 2. Corporis, cùm priuatur anima. 3. Rursus Animæ, cùm & à Deo, & à corpore separata punitur. 4. Nouissimam totius hominis, cùm anima sine Deo cum corpore pœnas æternas luet. Omnes has mortis species, comminationẽ Domini complecti dicit, & adstipulatur Ambrosius l. de Paradiso, c. 9. Inprimis verò de ipsa corporis morte interdictũ istud loqui docet executio, & patet ex Gen. 3. v. 19. Hic enim ad illam pœnam damnatur, quam Dominus anteà minabatur: Licèt verò non statim mortuus fuerit Adam, mortem tamẽ Dominus inflixit 1. quoad reatum, 2. quoad moriendi necessitatem. 3. quoad initia mortis corporalis, quia corpus statim cœpit sentire, lassitudinem, & paulatim debilitari.

XXXI. 2. Ex testimonio Sapientis, qui c. 2. v. 23. expressè dicit, conditum esse hominem ἐν ἀφθαρσίᾳ, hoc est, in corruptione, vel ad immortalitatem & conditionem incorruptam; vulgata reddit, inexterminabilem. Et, vers. 24. affirmat, Mortem inuidiâ diaboli in mundum intrâsse. Quare ante peccatum, quod inuidia Satanæ comissum fuit, mors non regnauit.

XXXII. 3. Ab asseueratione Apostoli, Rom. 5. v. 12. Per vnam homine peccatum in hunc mundum intrauit, & per peccatum mors. Si per peccatum. Ergò non per naturam & creationem. Quid verò per mortem intelligitur? Non animæ, quoniam Apostolus inter peccatum & mortem reale discrimen ponit. Mors autem animæ & peccatum realiter non differunt. Non æterna tantùm, quoniam mortem eam in homines, in ipsos etiam infantes, qui actualiter non peccant, nec æternum pereunt, ante diem vltimum regnare scribit, v. 14. & 17. Quare concludo, mortem corporis notari, ita tamen, vt reatus mortis sempiternæ non excludatur.

XXXIII. Idem euincunt sequentia dicta, Rom. 6. v. 13. ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας, θάνατος, Rom. 8. vers. 10. CORPVS mortuum est, (hoc est, morti subiectum) PROPTER PECCATVM. Vbi mortem naturalem notari, docet vox corporis, eiusq́; causam constitui peccatum, particula propter euincit. Adde 1. Cor. 15. v. 21. Per hominem mors, & per hominem resurrectio mortuorum, v. 22. Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita in Christo omnes viuificantur. v. 55. Stimulus mortis peccatum est: quæ omnia luculenter docent esse mortem effectum culpæ, non conditione naturæ.

XXXIV. 4. A Christi redemptione. A quocunque nos Christus liberauit & redemit, hoc ipsum, si non, peccatum, peccati tamen supplicium est, & in primo statu ante peccatum locu non habuit, Atqui redemit nos etia a morte corporali. Alias in vitam non reuocaremur. Ergo mors corporalis, cum peccatum non sit, peccati supplicium fuit, & in primo statu ante peccatu locum non habuit.

XXXV. 5. A causa absentia. In statu primo aberat omnis Physica causa mortis, quæ potissimum quadruplex, 1. Externa vis, quæ tum nulla. 2. Fames & sitis, quam homo semper sedare & restinguere potuit. 3. Morbi, quibus subiectus non fuit. 4. Senium & debilitas, a qua per fructus arboris vitæ præseruatus fuit. Negata vero causa, negandus etiam est effectus, Concludimus ergo cum Augustino, ipsam quoque mortem, non lege naturæ, sed merito inflictam esse peccato, ex l. 13. de civit. Dei c. 15.

XXXVI. Sciendum vero hic est, immortalitatem primi hominis non plane eiusdem fuisse rationis, cum gloriosa beatorum immortalitate. Nam vt aliud est, posse non peccare, &c, non posse peccare: sic aliud est, posse no mori, &c, non posse mori. Vel, aliud est potentia non moriendi, & aliud impotentia moriendi. Prior immortalitas, moriendi actum tollit, potestatem omnem non excludit: Posterior vtrumque abolet. Illud est naturæ, hic gloriæ. Vt ergo ex insita vi, voluntas Adami in vtramque partem, ad bonum & malum flecti poterat, sic idem vel vitam retinere, vel mortem sibi per peccatum poterat accersere. Pertinet huc istud Lombardi ex l. 2. dist. 19. lit. A. In primo statu erat posse no mori, in secundo, non posse no mori, in futuro, non posse mori. Desumpsit hoc ex Augustino lib. 3. de Gen. c. ad lit. c. 2. vbi, alia, inquit, est immortalitas carnis, quam in Adamo accepimus alia, quam in resurrectione speramus per Christum. Ille factus est homo immortalis, vt posset non mori, si non peccaret moreretur autem si peccaret. Filij vero resurrectionis non poterunt vltro peccare, nec mori. Caro nostra non tunc egebit refectione ciborum, quia nulla poterit esse defectio.

XXXVII. Vlterius vero hic quæritur, Animmortalitas Adami fuerit naturalis proprietas, an vero donu supernaturale extrinsecum? Posterius adfirmat Bell. l. de gra. pri. hom. c. 9. sed falso. 1. Si iustitia primohomini fuit naturalis: Ergo & immortalitas. Fieri enim neqt, vt φύσει sanctus, sit φύσει mortalis, quia mors peccati est stipẽdium. Prius autem verum esse, sequenti disputatione probabitur.

2. Dona supernaturalia & extrinseca non sunt haereditaria, nec per generationem propagantur. Immortalitatem verò suam Adamus in posteros propagâsset. Non igitur donum supernaturale aut extrinsecum fuit.

2. Posteri Adae post lapsum sunt φύσει filij irę & mortis. Quare Adamus ante lapsum φύσει fuit filius gratiae & vitae.

4. Quod est poena peccati, & naturam per se destruit, eius contrarium homini integro fuit naturale. Mors & mortalitas poena peccati est, & naturam per se destruit. E. morti contraria immortalitas homini integro naturalis fuit, quod erat demonstrandum.

XXXVIII. Neque obstat locus 1. Cor. 15. v. 47. vbi, Primus homo terra terrenus dicitur, & corpus animale ipsi tribuitur, v. 46. Apostolus enim; vel loquitur de Adamo post lapsum, quando factus est communis noster parens, & sic corpus mortale habuit, inq́; nos propagauit; vel per hominem animalem & terrenum non intelligit eum, qui φύσει mortalis sit, sed qui vitam animalem vivat; qui cibo potuq́; egeat, &c sibi simile progeneret. Hoc sensu, primus homo fuit terrenus & animalis, quod ipsum in statu glorificationis abolebitur, adeoque corpus spirituale consequemur.

Quod autem primus homo dicitur de terra, hoc no mortalitatis qualitatem designat, sed originem, quia è terra format? est quod ex αντιθέσει apparet, vbi Dominus dicitur de coelo. 2. locum, quia in terra collocatus est. 3. finem, quia terram colere debuit. Quid autem hoc ad probandam mortalitatem? XXXIX. Porrò autem notandum, quòd in quæstione hac, alia sit consideratio totius, alia partium. Quod spectat totum hominem, fuit ille naturâ immortalis, vti modò ostendimus. Quod partes concernit, illarum duæ sunt: 1. Anima. 2. Corpus. Animam tanquam spiritum materiæ expertem, naturâ immortalem fuisse & esse, nemo Christianus negauerit. Quoad corpus verò variant sententiæ. Alij in primo etiam statu fuisse censent φθαρτὸν vel mortale, alij ἄφθαρτον vel immortalem. Vtrique suis rationibus non destituuntur.

XL. Pro mortalitate corporis hæc militant argumenta.

1. A compositione. Corpus inflatum erat ex materia corruptibili, nimirum terrâ & elementis. Quate & ipsum fuit corruptibile, quia principiatum sequitur naturam principiorum.

2. Ab arbore vitæ. Quis fuisset vsus & effectus arboris vitę, si corpus per naturam immortale? Num σικτικῶς tantùm, significatiuè sic dicta est?

3. A fame. Homo indigebat cibo, E. præcedebat absumtio, atque sic mutua elementorum actio. Non igitur summa fuit qualitatum harmonia, neque homo natura mortalis, Nam si ieiunasset per aliquot septimanas, humidum radicale tandem planè absumtum fuisset.

4. A discrimine statuum. Si corpus statuatur ἄφθαρτον, tollitur differentia inter statum creationis & glorificationis: In hoc enim continget demum immortalitas, juxta illud Apoc 21. v. 4. mors ampliùs non extabit, neque luctus.

XLI. Pro immortalitate non minus ponderosa proferri possunt argumenta.

1. A consonantia qualitatum. Quod exactissima primarum & secundarum qualitatum harmonia constat, perse & interius est immortale. Corpus Adami fuit huius modi, Habuit enim æquale temperamentum. Et, sicut in futuro statu corpora ex elementis quidem composita erunt, attamen ἄφθαρτα: ita quid pro-

hiberet, quò minus & Adami corpus ἀνενδεήτως creatum statui posset

2. Ab vnione cùm anima: Quod animæ ad immortalitatem conditæ essentialiter & indissolubili vinculo vnitum, illud vtique immortale est. Iam verò primi hominis corpus tale fuit, Immortale igitur.

3. A causa mortis, quæ peccatum est, Rom. 5. v. 15. & c. 8. v. 10. Absente verò mortalitatis causa, abest & ipsa mortalitas, omnisķue ad mortem inclinatio. In corpore Adami abfuit illa, nempe peccatum. Ergò & hæc.

4. A recuperatione. Quod in Christo recuperamus, id in Adamo habuimus & amisimus. Recuperamus verô corpora immortalia, 1. Cor. 15. v. 46. Ergò talia in Adamo habuimus.

5. Ab absurdo: Sequeretur enim hominem in primo statu fuisse naturâ mortalem. Nam quicquid de parte dicitur, de toto etiam prædicatur. Quare, si corpus naturâ mortale fuit, cur non & homo? præsertim, cùm mortalitatis & immortalitatis denominatio in homine à corpore semper sumatur.

XLII. Atque hæc sunt argumenta pręcipua, quæ pro vtraque parte proferri possunt, & quęstionem vndiquaque dubiam & intricatam reddunt. Vt verò nos quodammodò expediamus, in vocabulo immortalitatis & mortalitatis ambiguitatem lateré censemus, quæ nisi explicetur, facilis in errorem prolapsus est.

XLIII. Quod igitur concernit, 1. Immortalitatem; quatuor potissimùm modis accipitur.

1. Pro impotentia moriendi absoluta & omnimoda, quo sensu solus Deus ἁπλῶς & per naturam immortalis dicitur, 1. Tim 6. v. 16.

2. Pro impotentia moriendi ex gratia creationis, & propter essentialem à materia segregationem: quo pacto Angeli & animæ nostræ immortales sunt.

3. Pro impotentia moriendi ex dono & singulari ordinatione Dei. Sic corpora beatorum & damnatorum erunt incorruptibilia, non ex proprietate naturæ, sed Dei tum gratiâ, tum dispositione peculiari. 4. Propountia non moriendi, quo sensu istud immortale est, quod actu non moritur, mori tamen potest, certâ conditione positâ. Atque hoc modo corpus primi hominis immortale fuit. Non enim aderat impotentia moriendi: (quia hoc statu glorificationis proprium,) sed tamen potentia non moriendi, quæ ad nos etiam pervenisset, nisi innecessitatem moriendi conversa fuisset.

XLIV. Quod spectat th mortalitatem, dupliciter aliquid naturâ mortale dicitur.

1. Κυρίως pro eo, quod ad mortem certò secuturam propendet, & ad corruptionem naturaliter, per successivam partium absuntionem, inclinatur. Ita corpus primi hominis nequaquam naturâ fuit mortale, id quod argumenta posteriora clarissimè demonstrant. 2. άκυρως & abusivè, pro quacunque δυνάμει & potentiâ moriendi, etiam remotissima, & tali, quæ stante naturâ & per naturam in actum nunquam traductur. Atque hoc sanè sensu improprio remoteque corpus Adami mortale fuit, non secus atque arbor potentiâ est scamnum: id quod solùm probant rationes primo loco enumeratæ. Non enim erat corpus absolutè ἄφθαρτον, alias morti subjectum non fuisset: neque tamen erat φθαρτόν per potentiam & inclinationem propinquam, 1. ob qualitatum harmoniam. 2. ob temperamenti æqualitatem. 3. indissolubilem animæ vnionem. 4. ob vsum præstantissimorum fructuum, præsertim arboris vitæ: quos si neglexisset, & per septimanas aliquot jejunare voluisset: hoc ipso peccâsset contra ordinem Dei, qui ipsum de fructibus comedere jusserat adeoque mirum non fuisset, si ipsum mors invasisset, nimirum non ex conditione naturæ, sed ordinis diuini transgressione.

XLV. Vt ergò finiamus, corpus Adami naturâ immortale dicimus; non, quia ipso actu per naturales causas, ante peccatum nūquam fuisset corruptum; tum, quia nulla propinqua ad moriendum potentia vel inclinatio locum habuit, quemadmodum in hoc statu corpora gestamus morti semper obnoxia. Interim non fuit ἁπλῶς vel absolutè immortale, per exclusionem omnis potentiæ moriendi; quia hec propriè glorificatorum dignitas erit: sed tantùm ὑποθετικῶς seu conditionaliter, nimirum, si homo à peccatis abstinuisset:


### Question VI. In what precisely was the reason of the divine Image situated?: V. On the conformity of external dominion with the power of God

V. On the conformity of external dominion with the power of God.

XLVI. Just as God is King and Emperor of the whole world: so in the state of integrity he was prince and lord of all living creatures. For all things are for the sake of man, but man is for the sake of God, says Trismegistus. That this empire was indeed granted to man is clear from Gen. 1:26 and Eccles. 17:3-4. For it was fitting that he whom God had made similar to himself in dignity of nature, he should also make similar in the power of ruling: for dignity destitute of the protection of power is either as if unarmed, and gradually becomes worthless. And the rectitude of the natural order demands that the more imperfect be subjected to the more perfect, and the inferior be ruled by the superior.

XLVII. A twofold distinction, however, must be observed here:

1. Between absolute and direct dominion, which God reserved for himself alone, he is called Lord κατ' ἐξοχὴν in the Scriptures: and useful dominion, which denotes the inhabitation of the world with usufruct, and this alone was conferred upon man.

2. Between the κτῆσις of dominion or the concession, and the χρῆσις or the usurpation and execution of the concession. The κτῆσις was not lost, but still endures, and therefore it is permitted to capture and kill wild beasts, on account of the repeated concession of dominion, concerning which Genesis 9:2. The χρῆσις, however, is vehemently diminished,

It is filled with many difficulties. For before the fall, man had the living creatures naturally subject to him: after the fall, there is need of many bridles and great force. There they served of their own accord, here by compulsion. There all things could be easily tamed; here few, and with difficulty. There they did no harm at all; here he receives injury from many, and those of which man ought to be the master, these often lord it over man, by afflicting, wounding, and killing him.

XLVIII. Meanwhile, however, because some part of dominion has remained, let us live in such a way that we are not reduced to servitude: to which point Basil’s beautiful admonition looks, which is read in homily 10. Behold, he says, immediately as you were created, you were created a prince: the faculty of commanding was contributed to you. You are an imperial animal, O man: and why do you serve the passions? Why do you destroy your own dignity, and become a slave of sin? Why do you make yourself a captive of the Devil? etc.

XLIX. Finally, it is asked here, whether man would have been destined to rule only over brutes, or indeed also over man? Although nothing is read in the Scriptures concerning the order of man to man, but only concerning the order of man to brutes: it is nevertheless probable that there would have been some order of superiors and inferiors, lest confusion should arise.

L. It must be known, however, that dominion is twofold, one over slaves, the other over free men. The former is forced and harsh, the latter voluntary and pleasant. The former arises from the lust for dominating: the latter from the duty of providing. The former denotes servile subjection, the latter rather order or spontaneous submission. The former was contrary to the first state: the latter could have had a place, and indeed under a triple distinction. For there would have been dominion 1. paternal over children. 2. marital over a wife. 3. civil over seniors and inferiors. But why do we dispute about what could have been done; when that has been done by us, which ought not to have been done? Let us therefore rather acknowledge the fault, and pray to be spared the punishment; let us be renewed in spirit, that we may enjoy eternal joy.

LI. And these were those five conformities, in which the essence and formal reason of the divine image was placed. Where, however, this is to be noted by way of a conclusion, that this image of God, not otherwise than original sin, can be considered in two ways.

1. ἁπλῶς or absolutely, as it is in the Predicament of Quality, and is a concreated habit; and then it has as its formal aspect the native integrity of all the powers, which we have mentioned, namely the wisdom of the mind, the justice of the will, and the harmony of the appetite.

2. χετικῶς or relatively, as it is located in the Predicament of relation, in which way that integrity is the material, but the formal is the gracious indwelling of God, and the acceptance of the person, not otherwise than as the matter of sin, strictly taken, is the depravity of the faculties; but the form is the guilt and the divine aversion.

Latin:

V. De conformitate externi Dominii cum DEI Potestate.

XLVI. Quemadmodum Deus Rex & Imperator est totius mundi: Sic in statu integritatis princeps fuit & dominus cunctorum animantium. Omnia enim propter hominem, sed homo propter Deum, inquit Trismegistus. Imperium verò hoc concessum fuisse homini, patet ex Gen. 1. v. 26. & Eccles. 17. v. 3. 4. Conueniens enim erat, vt quem Deus fecerat sibi similem naturæ dignitate, assimilaret etiam dominandi potestate: Nam dignitas præsidio potentiæ destituta, vel vt inermis est, paulatimque vilescit. Et rectitudo naturalis ordinis postulat, vt imperfectiora perfectioribus subjiciantur, & inferiora per superiora regantur.

XLVII. Duplex autem distinctio hic venit observanda:

1. Inter dominium absolutum directumque, quod sibi soli Deus reservavit, κατ' ἐξοχὴν Dominus in Scripturis dicitur: & dominium vtile, quod notat incolatum orbis cum vsu-fructu, & hoc duntaxat homini collatum fuit.

2. Inter dominij κτῆσιν vel concessionem χρῆσιν vel concessi vsurpationem & executionem. Κτῆσις nō amissa est, sed etiamnum durat, ideoque licet feras capere & occidere, ob repetitam dominij concessionem, de qua Genes. 9. 2. Χρῆσιν autem vehementer imminuta,

multisq; difficultatib° referta est. Homo enim ante lapsum pronitè sibi subjecta habet animantia: post lapsum multis frænis, magnaque vi opus est. Illic sponte serviebant, hic coactè. Illic cuncta facilè domari poterant; hic pauca & difficulter. Illic minimè nocebant; hic à multis damnum accipit, & quorum homo debebat esse Dominus, ista sæpe dominantur homini, illum affligendo, vulnerando, occidendo.

XLVIII. Interim verò, quia dominij quædam pars remansit, ita vivamus, ne in servitutem redigamur: quò spectat pulcra Basilij admonitio, quæ legitur homil. 10. Ecce, inquit, statim vt conditus es, princeps es conditus: contributa est tibi imperandi facultas. Imperiale es animal ô homo: & quid seruis affectibus? Quid tuam ipsius dignitatem destruis, & servus fis pecati? Cur teipsum facis captiuum Diaboli? &c.

VLIX. Tandem hîc quæritur, An brutis duntaxat, an verò etiam homini homo dominaturus fuiffet? Quãvis verò in Scripturis nil legatur de ordine hominis ad hominem, sed tantùm de ordine hominis ad bruta: probabile tamen est, futurum fuisse aliquem superiorum & inferiorum ordinem, ne oriretur confusio.

L. Sciendum verò, quod dominium duplex sit, vnum in servos, alterum in liberos. Illud coactum est & acerbum, hoc voluntarium & jucundum. Illud sit libidine dominandi: hoc officio consulendi. Illud subiectionem servilem, hoc ordinem potius vel spontaneam submissionem denotat. Illud statui primo contrarium fuit: hoc locum habere potuit, & quidem sub triplici differentia. Fuisset n. dominium 1. patrium in liberos. 2 maritale in vxorem. 3. ciuile in seniores & inferiores. Sed cur disputamus de eo, quid fieri potuisset; cum à nobis factum sit, quod fieri non debuisset? Agnoscamus ergò potiùs culpam, & deprecemur pænam; renovemur animo, vt fruamur æterno gaudio.

LI. Et hæ fuerunt quinq; istæ conformitates, in quibus essentia & formalis ratio divinæ imaginis fuit posita. Vbi tamen illud colophonis loco notandum est, quòd imago hæc Dei, non secus atq; peccatum originale, duobus modis considerari queat.

1. ἁπλῶς vel absolutè, prout in Prædicamento Qualitatis, & habitus concreatus est; atque tum pro formali habet nativam, quam diximus, omnium potentiarum integritatem, nempè mentis sapientiam, voluntatis justitiam, & appetitus consonantiam.

2. χετικῶς vel relatiuè, prout locatur in Prædicamento relationis quo pacto integritas illa materiale est, formale autem inhabitatio Dei gratiosa, & personæ acceptatio, non secus atque peccati, restrictè sumti, materia, est facultatum deprauatio; forma verò, reatus & diuina auersatio.


### Question VII. Is woman created in the image of God?

I. We add this problem, as a corollary, on account of a twofold reason for doubting. 1. Eve did not have an exact knowledge of things. For she did not know that the Devil was speaking from the serpent. 2. Because 1 Cor. 11:7 it is said that the man is the glory and image of God, but the woman is the glory of the man.

II. But these reasons are not of such moment that we should therefore exclude the female sex from the image of God. For 1. when Moses had said in Gen. 1:27 that God created man in His own image; immediately explaining what he understands by man, he adds: Male and female He created them; 2. Because Eve confesses that the Lord's prohibition about not eating, with the threat of death, and thus the loss of the image, also pertains to her, Gen. 3:3; Because women, no less than men, are born with sin, and are renewed to the image of God. Wherefore they also lost it, and thus had it in their common parent. Hence Augustine writes in book 12 of the Trinity, chapter 7: Moses says that human nature was made to the image of God, which embraces both sexes, nor does it separate the woman from being understood as the image of God.

III. As regards the reasons for doubting, I respond to the first. 1. Some doubt whether Eve was ignorant that Satan was speaking through the serpent, since she could easily have known that speech is proper to man. 2. But let us posit this ἄγνοιαν (ignorance), but does the lack of the divine image immediately follow? We do not think so. For the first humans were wise in such a way that they nevertheless did not know certain things. Especially that Eve was endowed with such great knowledge of external things as Adam, is denied not without cause.

But the distinction of ἀγνοίας (ignorance) is to be noted, which is twofold. 1. κατ' ἀπόφασιν (by negation) or of pure negation. 2. κατὰ διάθεσιν (by disposition), or of depraved disposition, from 1 Posterior Analytics 13. The former denotes simple ignorance, the latter joined with error. The former could have had a place in the first state, the latter could not.

IV. To the second I respond: Paul is not speaking of intrinsic conformity, which consists in virtues, but extrinsic, which consists in dominion. There was parity, here a certain disparity. For the woman was not the head of the man, but the man was the head of the woman, and in this sense the man is called the glory of God, the woman of the man. For Adam was bound to obey no one except God: but Eve, both to God as creator, and to Adam as husband. That the Apostle looked to this is clear from verse 3, where it is said: The head of every man is Christ, but the head of the woman is the man. Therefore, we answer in one word: From the negation of marital dominion, the consequence to the negation of original justice is not valid.

Latin:

I. Addimus problema hoc, velut corollarium, ob rationem dubitandi geminam. 1. Eva non habebat exactam rerum cognitionem. Nesciebat enim Diabolum ex serpente loqui. 2. Quia 1. Cor. 11. v. 7. dicitur, quod vir gloria & imago Dei, mulier autem gloria viri.

II. Verùm, rationes hæ tanti non sunt momenti, vt propterea sexum fœmineum ab imagine Dei excludere debeamus. Nam 1. cùm Moses dixiffet Gen. 1. v. 27. Deum creasse hominem ad imaginem suam; mox quid per hominem intelligat, exponens addit: Masiculum & fœminam creavit illos; 2. Quia interdictum Domini de non comedendo, cum comminatione mortis, adeóque amiffione imaginis, se quoq; attinere fatetur Eva, Gen. 3 v. 3; Quia mulieres non secus atque viri cum peccato nascuntur, & ad imaginem Dei renouantur. Quare illam quoq; amiserunt, & ita in communi parente habuerunt. Hinc August. scribit l. 12. de Trin. c. 7. Ad imaginem naturam humanam factam dicit Moses, quæ sexum vtrumq; complectitur, nec ab intelligenda Dei imagine separat fœminam.

III. Quod spectat rationes dubitandi, Resp. ad primam. 1. Dubitant nonnulli, an Eva ignorauerit, Satanam loqui per serpentem, cùm facilè scire potuerit, loquelam homini esse propriam. 2. Sed ponamus hanc ἄγνοιαν, num verò statim sequitur divinæ imaginis carentia? Non censemus. Primi enim homines ita fuêre sapientes, ut tamen quædam nesciverint. Præsertim Evam tantâ rerum externarum notitiâ præditam fuisse, vt Adamum, non sine causa negatur.

Notanda verò est distinctio ἀγνοίας, quæ duplex. 1. κατ' ἀπόφασιν vel puræ negationis. 2. κατὰ διάθεσιν, vel pravæ dispositionis, ex 1. post. 13. Illa ignorantiam simplicem, hæc cum errore coniūctam denotat. Illa in statu primo locum habere potuit hæc non potuit.

IV. Ad secundam Resp. Paulus non loquitur de conformitate intrinseca, quę consistit in virtutibus, sed extrinseca, quæ consistit in dominio. Ibi fuit paritas, hic quædam disparitas. Non enim mulier viri sed vir mulieris caput fuit, & hoc sensu vir gloria Dei, Viri mulier dicitur. Adam enim nulli obedire debebat præter Deum: Eva verò, tùm Deo, ut creatori, tùm Adæ, vt marito. Huc respexisse Apostolum patet ex v. 3. ubi dicitur: Omnis viri caput Christus est, caput autem mulieris vir est. vno igitur verbo respondemus: A negatione dominij maritalis, ad negationem Iustitiæ originalis non valet consequentia.


## 3 Disputation II. On Original Justice

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Georgius Martini of Wroclaw, Silesia.

Πρόθυμον.

I. In the first disputation we contemplated the essence of the divine image, consisting partly in the principal conformity of the intellect with the wisdom of God, of the will with justice, and of the appetite with chastity and integrity; and partly in the less principal conformity of the body with immortality and of external dominion with the power of God. There remains to be considered a certain disputed affection of the image, namely, whether those gifts were natural,

II. And indeed, concerning external dominion no controversy is stirred; concerning immortality we have treated sufficiently in the preceding discussion; there remain the internal virtues and dignities of the soul, namely, the wisdom of the mind, the holiness of the heart, the integrity of the appetite, and the harmony of the other faculties.

III. All these excellences, however, are called by one name, original justice, which differs from the image of God as a part from the whole. For the image extends more broadly than justice, since it includes this.

IV. Justice is indeed (to describe it here briefly in the introduction) nothing other than the natural perfection of the whole man, and the rectitude and integrity of all his powers and faculties, both among themselves and in relation to their acts. For we are accustomed to call everything that is whole and perfect in its own nature just; and in that sense, the primary rectitude of the human soul has been called justice by theologians.

V. From which it becomes manifest that it is not taken here disjunctively, as if it were some particular virtue or a single habit: but conjunctively for universal justice, or the comprehension of all virtues, and the habitual perfection of all powers. For the soul was one thing, the faculties of the soul another, and the perfections of the faculties another. The former two remained, the latter was lost, and therefore this alone is to be understood by original justice.

VI. And from this, furthermore, the question can easily be settled: What was the true and genuine subject of justice? The Papists clearly disagree. Thomas 1.2. q. 83 and with him Gregorius de Valen. T. 1. disp. 7. q. 2. point 2. Col. 1488, [say it is] the essence of the soul; Scotus in book 2 of the Sentences, dist. 29, q. 1, [says it is] the will alone; Durandus in book 2, dist. 20, q. 5, contends that the sensitive appetite alone was the subject of justice; all of whom Pererius in Genesis, book 5, disputation on the third excellence, question 2, p. 184, refutes.

VII. We briefly distinguish between the subject of existence or inherence, and of completion or perfection. Justice did not inhere in the faculties of the soul: since an accident cannot inhere in an accident. However, it perfected primarily and proximately the faculties, and all of them, both the higher and the lower, from which we conclude that the subject of inherence of justice was the soul; but the subject of perfection was all the faculties of the soul.

VIII. It is not, however, called only justice, but for the sake of distinction the term original is added. For justice is manifold, since there is given: 1. Ethical. 2. Pharisaical. 3. Imputed. 4. Begun. 5. Consummated. In order to distinguish from all these the justice concreated in man, we therefore call it original; and indeed by reason of: 1. Itself, because it was the first of all in man, and therefore is rightly called original. 2. Man, because he had it from his origin. 3. Posterity, because it ought to have been propagated into them from Adam or their common parent and origin.

IX. Since therefore it is now established what original justice was, and whence it received its name: its affection, and the manner of its inhering, remains to be investigated, since concerning this there was a great controversy formerly, and one still exists even now in the Church of Christ: which one, unless it is rightly decided, the primary articles of our religion, such as those concerning original sin, free will, the grace of God, faith, and our justification, because of their coherence and mutual dependence, are most certainly corrupted.

X. This question is therefore a kind of theological crossroads, where the gate of truth and falsehood is opened, and from one side we are led to Lutheran ὀρθοδοξίαν (orthodoxy), from the other we are led away to Papistic ἑτεροδοξίαν (heterodoxy); for which very reason Bellarmine wished to place it first, so that, this foundation having been laid, he might more easily build upon it the remaining dogmas of Popery.

XI. But this is the question: Whether original justice was a supernatural gift, or whether it truly pertained to the condition of nature? To which question the Papists respond in one way, the Orthodox in another. Briefly concerning both.

XII. 1. Bellarmine explains the opinion of the Papists in his book on the grace of the first man, chapter five and the following. The sum is this. Man consists naturally of flesh and spirit, appetite and reason, and therefore of contrary propensities; whence arises a certain struggle, and from that struggle a huge difficulty in acting well, while one propensity hinders the other. If, therefore, from the very condition of matter a certain disease or languor flowed into human nature, to which divine providence applied a remedy immediately at the beginning of creation, it added a certain distinguished gift to man, namely original justice, which, as if by a certain golden bridle, the lower part to the higher part, and the higher part to God would be easily contained in subjection.

XIII. From which it furthermore follows that that righteousness was a supernatural gift, and added by God to nature itself for the curing of its languor: Wherefore, that being removed, human nature, left to itself, began to experience that struggle which was to have been natural, and would have followed from the condition of matter, had not God added the gift of righteousness to man. Wherefore, the state of man after the fall does not differ more from the state of the same in pure naturals than a despoiled person differs from a naked one. Nor is human nature worse, if you subtract original sin, nor does it labor more under ignorance and infirmity than it would be and would labor if created in pure naturals. Hence the corruption of nature flowed not from the lack of any natural gift, nor from the accession of any evil quality, but solely from the loss of the supernatural gift on account of Adam's sin.

XIV.
