And this is the almost common opinion of the Papists concerning original righteousness, excerpted from the leader of the Jesuit faction, Bellarmine; which, moreover, they are accustomed to declare by four similes. For they compare the concreated righteousness: 1. To a garland, which is placed upon the head of a virgin, and although it be taken away, she nevertheless remains a virgin. 2. To a garment, by the removal of which a man is indeed rendered naked, but his nature is not taken away. 3. To an antidote, which is outside the nature of the body, yet it represses poison, lest it break out into act and kill the man. 4. To Samson, who after his hair was cut off indeed lost that remarkable strength, received divinely, yet in such a way that nothing of his natural powers perished.

XV. These and other similes they bring forward, to this end only, that they may teach that original righteousness was an extrinsic gift of grace, not an intrinsic quality of nature.

XVI. This being presupposed, there soon follow other blossoms of Scholastic trifles, such as these: 1. That concupiscence is natural to man, not as some good, but as a vice of nature: resulting not from the intention of the creator, but from the condition of the matter. 2. That natural gifts remained intact in demons and man after the fall, and that nothing at all has been lost of them. 3. That death is the extreme of human defects by nature itself, but by guilt, as from a cause preventing its removal. 4. That concupiscence remaining in the regenerate is not sin. 5. That free will is given in spiritual matters; that the law can be fulfilled; and that good works are truly and properly meritorious of eternal life. These and similar ravings of an unhealthy mind Bellarmine has scattered throughout his book on the grace of the first man.

XVII. But Pererius defends the same error, lib. 5 in Gen. disp. on the third excellence, p. 180. In the same way, he says, man now stands in the state of fallen nature, as he would have stood if he had been created in pure naturals. For the sin of Adam neither lost nor diminished anything of those things which are natural to man. For just as after the sin of Adam the human body was made no more mortal or passible than it would have been if man were in pure naturals: so the human mind is not of itself weaker for doing good because of Adam's sin than it would have been if God had created him in pure naturals.

XIIX. It should be noted, however, that Jesu Wita here, with a few pages intervening, contradicts himself, while he concedes that the rebellion of the flesh against the spirit has arisen from the expected; and points to original righteousness as the natural perfection of man. Which very thing we also discover in the books of the Scholastics; who, although they argue most strongly for it as an extrinsic gift; sometimes, however, as if having obtained intervals of their madness, exclaim with Augustine: that through sin natural gifts in man were corrupted, and supernatural gifts were snatched away.

XIX. And thus far we have heard the Papist opinion, which we contract into a brief summary as follows: Adam's nature was created in itself with a rebellion arising from contrary propensities: in order that this might be restrained, God added the supernatural gift of justice, which having been lost through sin, nature was not corrupted, but only the rebellion co-created was brought into act.

XX. 2. As regards our opinion, it is directly opposed to the former, and therefore, since it is evident from the contrary, we can dispense with a lengthy commemoration of it. For we deny that the πρωτόπλαστον nature was created with any discord or dissension of powers. We deny that original justice was a supernatural gift, only extrinsically surrounding nature and not intrinsically perfecting it: and conversely we affirm that man was created so upright by God, that his mind was naturally full of the knowledge of the divine will, that all acts consented with the law of God impressed upon nature, and that all affections and motions existed holy, ordered, and integral. For just as now after the fall there is a natural ignorance of the mind, and a propensity of the will toward evil: so before the fall there naturally shone in the mind a light, by which it might distinguish the true from the false, the good from the evil; and with that shining before it, the will embraced the latter and turned away from the former: the lower faculties also were willingly compliant, and obeyed reason without any reluctance or repugnance.

XXI. From this comparison of opinions, therefore, it is clear that two things are especially in controversy; the one is the condition of nature; the other is the condition of justice. The former, created with a rebellion of powers, the Papists affirm; we deny. The latter, the Papists deny to have been natural; we affirm. The state of the question being thus established, we shall subjoin the problems themselves, intending to build up the truth and to destroy the falsehood to the best of our ability.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisner. S S. Th. D. Resp. Georgio Martini Vratislavia-Silesio.

Πρόθυμον.

I. DISputatione primâ contemplati sumus diuinæ imaginis ὀυσίαν, consistentem in conformitate partim principali, intellectus cum Dei sapientiâ, voluntatis cum iustitiâ; appetitus cum castitate & integritate; partim minùs principali, corporis cum immortalitate; & externi dominij cum potestate Dei: Restat consideranda quædam adfectio imaginis controuersa, nimirum, An dotes istæ naturales fuerint,

II. Et quidem de externo dominio nulla mouetur controuersia; de immortalite συζητήσει præcedente satis egimus, supersunt internæ virtutes & dignitates animi, nempè mentis sapientia, cordis sanctitas, appetitus integritas, & cæterarum virium consornantia.

III. Omnes autem istæ excellentiæ vno nomine dicuntur iustitia originalis, quæ ab imagine Dei differt, vt pars à toto. Imago enim latiùs patet, quàm iustitia, siquidem hanc includit.

IV. Est verò iustitia, (vt illam hîc in procœmio paucis describamus,) nihil aliud, quàm naturalis perfectio totius hominis, & omnium virium ac facultatum tùm inter se, tùm in ordine ad actus suos rectitudo & integritas. Omne enim integrum suâque naturâ perfectum solemus appellare iustum: eóque sensu primaria animæ humanæ rectitudo à Theologis dicta est iustitia.

V. Ex quo manifestum fit, illam hîc nõ sumi difjunctim, prout virtus aliqua particularis, aut habitus vnus est: sed coniunctim promflitia vniuersali, seu omnium virtutum comprehensione, omniumque virium perfectione habituali. Nam aliud fuit anima, aliud animæ facultates, aliud facultatum perfectiones. Priora duo mansêre, posterius amissum, ideoque hoc solum per iustitiam originalem intelligendum est.

VI. Atque hinc porrò facilè componi potest quæstio, Quodnam fuerit verum & genuinum iustitiæ subiectum? Pontificij planè dissentiunt. Thomas 1.2. q. 83 Et cum eo Gregorius de Valen. T. 1. disp. 7. q. 2. puncto 2. Col. 1488. animæ effentia; Scotus in l. 2. sent. dist. 29. q. vni. solam voluntatem; Durandus in l. 2. dist. 20. q. 5. solum appetitum sensitiuum iustitiæ subiectũ fuisse contẽdit quos omnes Pererius in Gen. l. 5. disput. de tertia excell. quæst. 2. m. p, 184, refutat,

VII. Nos breuiter distinguimus inter subiectum ὑπάρξεως vel inhæsionis, & τελειότητος vel perfectionis Animæ non facultatibus inhæsit iustitia: quoniam accidenti accidens inesse nequit: Perfecit autem πρώτως & proximè facultates, easque omnes, tàm superiores, quàm inferiores, ex quo cõcludimus, iustitiæ subiectum inhæsionis fuisse animam; perfectionis verò omnes animæ facultates.

VIII. Non autem iustitia tantùm dicitur, sed differentiæ causâ vocabulum originalis additur. Est enim iustitia multiplex, cùm detur, 1. Ethica. 2. Pharisæica 3. Imputata 4 Inchoata 5. Consummata. Ab his omnibus vt distinguamus institiam homini concreatam, idcirco originalẽ nuncupamus; & quidem ratione, 1. Sui, quia fuit omniũ prima in homine, adeoq́; rectè originalis dicitur 2. Hominis, quia eam ab origine sua habuit. 3. Posterorum, quia ab Adamo seu cõmuni parente & origine in illos propagari debuisset.

IX. Quoniam ergo nunc constat, quid originalis justitia fuerit, & vnde nomen acceperit: adfectio eius, modusque inhærendi indagandus superest, quoniam de hoc magna & olim fuit, & etiam num existit in Ecclesia Christi controversia: Quæ vna nisi rectè decidatur, primarij religionis nostræ articuli, quales sunt de peccato originis, libero arbitrio, Dei gratia, fide & justificatione nostra, ob cohærentiam & mutuam dependentiam, certissimè corrumpuntur.

X. Est igitur hæc quæstio quasi biuium quoddam Theologicum, vbi veri falsique porta panditur, & ex vna parte ad Lutheranicam ὀρθοδοξίαν ducimur ex altera ad Papisticam ἑτεροδοξίαν abducimur; quam ipsam ob causam Bellarminus eam præmittere voluit, vt, jacto hoc fundamento, reliqua Papismi dogmata faciliùs superstruere possit.

XI Hoc autem quæritur, An iustitia originalis donum supernaturale fuerit, an vero ad conditionem naturæ pertinuerit? Quam ad quæstionem aliter Pontificij, aliter Orthodoxi respondent. De vtriusque breuiter.

XII. 1. Pontificiorum opinionem exponit Bellarminus lib. de gratia primi hominis capite quinto & sequentibus. Summa hæc est. Constat homo naturaliter ex carne & spiritu, appetitu & ratione, adeoque contrarijs propensionibus; vnde oritur pugna quædam, & ex pugna ingens benè agendi difficultas, dum vna propensio alteram impedit, Si ergo ex ipsa conditione materiæ in naturam humanam morbus vel languor quidam dimanauit: cui & diuina prouidentia statim initiò creationis remedium adhiberet, donum quoddam insigne homini addidit, iustitiam videl. originalem, quæ velut aureo quodam fræno pars inferior parti superiori, & pars superior Deo subiecta facilè contineretur.

XIII. Ex quo porrò sequitur, rectitudinem illam fuisse donum supernaturale, & à Deo naturæ ipsi ad curandum languorem superadditum: Quapropter, eo remoto natura humana sibi relicta pugnam illam experiri cœpit, quæ naturalis futura erat, & ex conditione materiæ secutura, nisi Deus iustitiæ donum homini addidisset. Quare, non magis differt status hominis post lapsum à statu eiusdem in puris naturalibus, quam differt spoliatus à nudo. Neq; deterior est humana natura, si culpam originalem detrahas, neque magis ignorantiâ & infirmitate laborat, quàm esset & laboraret in puris naturalibus condita. Proinde corruptio naturæ, non ex alicuius doni naturalis carentia, neque ex alicuius malæ qualitatis accessu, sed ex solo doni supernaturalis, ob Adæ peccatum amissione profluxit.

XIV. Atque hæc communis ferè Papicolarum de justitia originali est sententia, ex Iesuiticæ factionis antesignano Bellarmino excerpta; quàm insuper quatuor similitudinibus declarare solent. Conferunt enim justitiam concreatam, 1. Serto, quod capiti virginis imponitur, & quamuis auferatur, ipsa tamen nihilominus virgo manet 2. Vesti, quâ exutâ homo quidem nudus redditur, sed natura non tollitur. 3. Antidoto, quod extra corporis naturam est, venenum tamen reprimit, ne in actum erumpat, & hominem interficiat, 4. Samsoni, qui post crines resectos amisit quidem insignem illam fortitudinem, diuinitùs acceptam, ita tamen, vt de naturalibus nihil perierit.

XV. Hæc & alias similitudines proferunt, eum duntaxat in finem, vt doceant, originalem iustitiam extrinsecum fuisse donum gratiæ, non intrinsecam qualitatem naturæ.

XVI. Quo praesupposito, mox sequuntur alii Scholasticarum nugarum flosculi, quales sunt: 1, Concupiscentiam esse homini naturalem, non vt bonum aliquod, sed yt vitium naturae: non ex intentione creatoris, sed ex conditione materiae consequens, 2. Naturalia in daemonibus & homine post lapsum mansisse integra, & nihil quiequam dejis esse deperditum 3. Mortem extremos defectus humanos esse a natura per se, a culpa vero, sicut a caussa remouere prohibens. 4. Concupiscentiam in renatis reliquam non esse peccatum. 5, Dari liberum in spiritualibus arbitrium; impleri posse legem; & opera bona vere proprieque meritoria esse vitae aeternae. Haec & similia animi male-sani deliria libro suo de gratia primi hominis passim inspersit Bellarminus.

XVII. Eundem vero errorem defendit. Pererius l. 5. in Gen. disp. de tertia excell. p. 180. Eodem inquit, modo se habet nunc homo in statu naturae lapsae, ac se habuisset sin puris naturalibus esset creatus. Peccatum enim Adami nihil de his, quae naturalia sunt homini, aut perdidit, aut diminuit. Quemadmodum enim post peccatum Adami corpus humanum nihilo magis factum est mortale aut passibile, quam fuisset, si homo esset in puris naturalibus: Ita humanus animus per se non est Adami peccato imbecillior ad bene agendum quam fuisset, si eum Deus in puris naturalibus creasset.

XIIX. Notandum vero, quod Iesu Wita hic, paucis paginis interjectis, sibi ipsi contradicat, dum rebellionem carnis aduersus spiritum expectato esse ortam concedit: & originalem justitiam, naturalem hominis perfectionem indigitat. Quod ipsum Scholasticorum quoque libris deprehendimus; qui, vt maxime pro extrinseco dono disputent; nonnunquam tamen, velut nacti furoris sui interualla cum Augustino exclamant: per peccatum naturalia in homine corrupta, supernaturalia erepta fuisse.

XIX. Et hactenus opinionem Papisticam audiuimus, quam in breue compendium ita contrahifmus : Adami natura in se condita fuit cum rebellione orta ex contrarijs propensionibus : quæ vt coerceretur, Deus addidit supernaturale donum iustitię, quo per pecatum amisso, natura non corrupta, sed tantùm rebellio concreata in actu perducta est.

XX. 2. Quod a nostram spectat sententiam, illa priori directè opposita est, ideoque cùm ex contrario pateat, prolixa ejus commemoratione supersedere possumus. Negamus, enim naturam πρωτόπλαστον cum terpore quodam aut dissensione virium esse conditam. Negamus, iustitiam originalem fuisse supernaturale donum, naturam extrinsecè tantùm circunstans non intrinsecè perficiens : & vice versâ adfirmamus, hominem ita rectum a Deo creatum esse, vt mens ipsius naturaliter plena fuerit noticiâ diuinæ voluntatis, vt omnes actus consenserint cum lege Dei naturæ impressâ, vt omnes adfectus motusque extiterint sancti, ordinati, integri. Sicut enim nunc post lapsum naturalis est ignorantia mentis, & propensio voluntatis in malum : sic ante lapsum naturaliter fulgebat in mente lux, quâ verum à falso, bonum à malo internosceret; eáque prælucente, voluntas illud amplectebatur, istud auersabatur : facultates quoque inferiores vltrò sequaces erant, & sine vlla morositate aut repugnantia rationi obtemperabant.

XXI. Ex hac igitur opinionum collatione patet, duo potissimùm controuerti; Alterum est, conditio naturæ; Alterum conditio iustitiæ, Illam cum rebellione virium creatam, Pontificij adfirmant; Nos negamus. Hanc Pontificij naturalem fuisse negant; Nos adfirmamus. Statu proindè ita constituto, ipsa problemata subnectemus, veritatem adstructuri, & falsitatem pro virili destructuri.


### Question I Whether the nature of the first man was created by God with a rebellion of powers?

QUESTION I.

Whether the nature of the first man was created by God with a rebellion of powers?

I. Our negative is this, the truth of which is demonstrated by all those testimonies of Scripture which we adduced in the preceding disputation concerning the justice and holiness of the will, Question 6, theses 16 and 24:

II. For 1. From Gen. 1, last verse. If all things were created very good, where then could the ἀταξία (disorder) of the powers and the inordinate ἐπιθυμία (desire) have had a place? Shall we call that also very good? It is inconsistent.

III. 2. From Gen. 2, v. 25. If our first parents were not ashamed when naked, certainly concupiscence and the disorder of the appetite were not created with them. For this is the cause of shame, as is evident from Gen. 3, v. 6, 7.

IV. 3. From Ecclesiastes 7, v. 30. If man was created upright; therefore without any crookedness, without rebellion of the powers, and without dissension of the faculties. For this is obliquity, it is not uprightness.

Nor is the exception valid, that Ecclesiastes speaks of natural, not moral, uprightness. For if by natural you understand the essence and powers of the soul, you depart from the purpose of Ecclesiastes. For he considers that which man lost through the fall, that is, that which was placed in holiness and in the harmony of all the powers. And this is not called moral, because it was not acquired through habituation; but natural, because it was implanted in nature at the first creation.

V. But we do not wish to recount and urge these things at greater length, but leave them to be repeated from the first discussion: we shall only briefly set forth the reasons drawn from the Scriptures, and not previously adduced by us, together with certain testimonies of the Fathers.

VI. REASON I. From the absurd. Our parents, having lost justice through an inordinate appetite of the senses, fell into the power of the Devil. Wherefore, if nature was created with such disorder, it follows that man, by creation, according to nature, apart from the superadded gift, was in like manner subject to the will of the Devil. For desire displeases God and pleases the Devil, and therefore leads man away from God and subjects him to the Devil. If therefore our first parents had this concreated, they could not but desire evil, and thus man, the workmanship of God, would have been in respect of creation, a slave of the Devil, in respect of rebellion, which is absurd and impious,

VII. REASON II. From Christ, in whom there is no rebellion. He was made like us in all things, and assumed an entire human nature, with all its consequences and essential properties. Wherefore, if the struggle of propensities were an immediate consequence of nature, he would not have been devoid of all sin. For the inordinate appetite of concupiscence is sin, Rom. 7. v. 7. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 16.

VIII. Nor should or can this agony of Christ be objected, in which it is said by some that the appetite, fleeing death, struggled with reason, which chose death. For it was not the human appetite and the human reason of Christ that struggled there; but rather, the whole man with God, the human will with the divine, as is evident from the very words, Not my will, but thine, be done, Luc: 22. v. 24. For it is natural for man to flee death, because it destroys nature, and thus is opposed to it. Wherefore it is not surprising that Christ also, as a true man, feared death, and asked of the Father, Let this cup pass from me. Especially, since he had to undergo not simple death, but a satisfactory one for the sins of men; all of which, together with the Father's wrath, the curse of the law, and the pains of hell, pressed upon him, and thus increased the flight and fear of death. Meanwhile, however, there was not an exact struggle there either, since the will of Christ was as it were wavering, and partly wished to die, on account of the misery of the human race; partly did not wish to, on account of the wrath of the Father, to whom, however, he finally submitted himself fully.

IX. REASON III. From the state of glorification. If that discord of propensities were a necessary effect of matter, and an affection of our nature, it would endure even in the state of glorification itself. For there nature will not be abolished, nor will appetite and reason be destroyed. Wherefore they will dissent even in eternal life: or, if the act be denied, yet the habitual torpor itself will remain, because by the condition of the matter, which as to ὑπόστασιν always necessarily follows according to the Papists. In what way, therefore, by this compact will that most blessed state be, and immune from every evil and vice.

X. REASON IV. From the extenuation of the first happiness, and original righteousness. If the nature of man was created with a torpor of powers, and a struggle of δυνάμεων, and this vice always remained fixed in nature, certainly the first state was not most happy, for ἐπιθυμία is such an evil, that Paul, even when reborn, because of its remnants, pronounces himself a ταλαίπωρον ἄνθρωπον, an unhappy man, Rom. 7. v. 24.

XI. Furthermore, original righteousness would not have been a gift so excellent, as it is everywhere proclaimed in the Scriptures. For it would have behaved only like a palliative medicine, which would not have purged nature, but merely covered the disease, so that it would not break out completely into act. Whence it follows that vicious motions also existed in the state of integrity, although they did not have dominion. For they compare it to a restraining bridle. But where there are no inordinate acts, there nothing can be checked or bridled. For where there is no rebellion, what need is there of a bridle? Where there is no disease, to what end is there a remedy?

XII. Wherefore, if they wish their hypotheses to be safe, they must confess that in the very state of integrity, the appetite sometimes, by the force of its nature, desired things contrary to reason, but was soon repressed and bridled by righteousness. Thus, therefore, with one effort they both take away the happiness of the first state, and detract not a little from original righteousness.

XIII. And truly the vertigo of the Papists is to be wondered at. For they altogether reject the Evangelical justification, by which we say that sin and concupiscence are cast away: yet here they themselves invent such an original righteousness, which would be anything other than a certain covering for a natural vice and innate concupiscence.

XIV. Furthermore, they fashion a sort of Telephus out of God, from whom the wound has proceeded no less than the remedy, just as if we were to say that it is the role of a surgeon to strike a man with blows of his own accord, so that he may have someone to cure with an application of panacea.

XV. REASON V. From the nature of concupiscence. This is nothing other than sin, Rom. 7:7, nor is it from the Father, but from the world, 1 John 2:16. Wherefore, if man received it from creation, 1. God will be the cause of the creator of sin, which is blasphemous; and 2. sin existed before the state of sin, which is absurd; and 3. the punishment preceded the fault, which is unjust.

XVI. To this reason Bellarmino objects in ch. 7, col. 28, with these words: The concupiscence of the flesh is indeed now a punishment for sin, yet had man been created in pure naturals, it would undoubtedly have been natural, not indeed as some good of nature, but as a defect and a sort of disease of nature, resulting from the condition of the matter. Wherefore it is most correctly said not to be from God; it is worthy of hatred, not love, evil, and contrary to nature, for two reasons. First, because it would not have existed in man from the intention of the author of nature, but contrary to his intention, if man had been created in pure naturals. Secondly, because God had removed it, and it has a place in us through the fault of man himself. He declared that former point in chapter 5 with a certain analogy taken from a smith, who, while he fashions a sword out of iron, is not the cause of the rust on the sword, which arises later from the condition of the matter.

XVII. We respond, however, that in this one exception not one, but quite a few falsehoods lie hidden, the principal ones of which we shall note in a few words.

XIIX. If that rebellion flows necessarily from the condition of the matter, God will not be freed from the fault. For he who is the author of the antecedent is also the author of the immediate consequent: or the cause of the cause is also the cause of the caused, in essentially subordinated things.

XIX. And who, pray, was the author of that evil, if God was not? Or the Devil? But he had no right over man before the sin. Or the Angels? But they, since they are ministers, labor rather to remove the evils of men, especially of the innocent, than to promote them. And what need is there of prolixity? Whatever began through creation has its origin from God, and must be attributed to God, whether this happens immediately or proximately, or mediately or remotely.

XX. 2. Everything natural is good, because it is created by God, whose works are all very good; Gen. 1, last verse; 1 Tim. 4, verse 4. Whence Augustine in Enchiridion, chapter 12, says: Every vicious nature, in so far as it is a nature, is good; in so far as it is vicious, it is evil. Hence, therefore, we conclude: Everything natural is good; and it pleases God, which is absurd and contrary to Bellarmine himself, who pronounces concupiscence to be evil and worthy of the hatred of God.

XXI. Nor can we inconveniently retort upon him his own argument, which he has in book 5, de amiss. grat. chapter 2, where he reasons thus against Flacius: John says: All things were made through him, and without him was made nothing. John 1, verse 3. But Saint Paul adds: Every creature is good. 1 Tim. 4, verse 4. From which he infers, if our substance is sin and evil, it is either not a creature, which would contradict the Gospel; or not every creature is good, which would contradict the Apostle: We argue against him by the same reasoning; If concupiscence is natural, it follows: either not everything created is good, which is opposed to the Apostle; or not everything natural before the fall was created by God, which is contrary to the Apostle.

XXII. 3. We ask, what matter does Bellarmine understand? The body? But the power of desiring is not proper to this. The soul? But this is inconveniently called matter. Furthermore, God immediately inspired it into Adam. Therefore, if the conflict of propensities naturally emanates from it, God [is] the very The primary cause of sin is established. For just as all the faculties of the soul are said to be from God, because they emanate by necessary birth from the soul which God inspired: so the ἀταξία (disorder) of the powers will be the offspring of the Best God, if it follows the soul in a similar way.

XXIII. 4. The Jesuits forget themselves. For they deny that concupiscence dwelling in the reborn is evil and worthy of God's hatred, as the Council of Trent, session 5, defined. Here, however, they concede that such ἀταξία (disorder) flowed from the nature of Adam, in whom, however, not the beginning, but the whole completion of the divine image existed.

XXIV. 5. They contradict themselves, while they call one and the same concupiscence both natural and contrary to nature. For everything φυσικὸν (natural), or which flows from natural principles, is agreeable to nature, not contrary. And conversely, what is contrary, this is not natural. How therefore can these contrary and ἀντιφατικὰ (contradictory) things be truly affirmed of one and the same thing.

XXV. 6. It is blasphemous that concupiscence proceeded from matter created by God, beyond the intention of the Creator. For thus God is accused of either ignorance or impotence. Of the former, because He did not foresee that such ἀταξία (disorder) would arise from such a condition of matter: Of the latter, because He could not [prevent] this stain and blemish. For we presuppose that God willed to create man in His own image, and therefore upright. Either therefore He could not, or He could. If not, He is impotent. If He could, He certainly did it. For where will and power are posited, the thing itself is posited. He has done whatever He willed, Psalm 113, verse 3. ὅσα τινα γίνηται (Whatever things happen), whatever He wills, come to pass, Damascene, book 2, Orthodox Faith, chapter 29.

XXVI. Furthermore, when something happens beyond the intention of the agent, then it deviates from its originally intended goal. The cause of which is either the lack of circumspection of the agent, or the multitude of obstacles, which he either did not foresee, or having foreseen, was not able to remove. But shall we say that the most wise God has strayed from his goal? Shall we attribute to providence itself a lack of circumspection, and to omnipotence itself a certain ἀμηχανίαν [helplessness]? Away with these blasphemies. God is all eye, he foresees all things, he provides for all things; how, therefore, could anything happen outside of his intention? It is not for a wise man to say, 'I had not thought.' Therefore, it will not be for a wise man, or indeed even for a Christian, to impute this to Wisdom itself.

XXVII. 7. It is false according to Papistic hypotheses that concupiscence was removed in the first state. For if it follows necessarily from the condition of the matter, and indeed the matter itself was not removed, how could concupiscence have been absent? Furthermore, since they say that original justice restrained the appetite; therefore, it was sometimes moved contrary to reason, otherwise there would have been no need for this compression. Finally, since they write that it is natural for the appetite to be always carried toward a sensible good, certainly it either desired this very thing, or it lacked it by its own nature. If the latter, natural things were not intact in the first state. If the former, concupiscence was present and therefore was not entirely removed. Which very thing, although the Papists deny it most strongly in words, they nevertheless do not think otherwise than that the appetite, according to its own disposition, desired any sensible good, and thus sometimes an evil; but was restrained by justice, as if by a guide, so that it would not overcome reason and obtain its own desire.

XXIIX. Finally 8. In the brought-forward analogy there is a great disparity. For 1. The smith does not forge the matter, as God does, and therefore he is not called the author of the rust arising from the matter. 2. Rust does not necessarily follow matter; nor is the matter itself the cause, but an external corrupting agent. 3. Rust is not in iron in act, nor is it its immediately efficient cause. 4. If the smith could, he would certainly forge such a sword that would not contract rust. But indeed, God created the very matter of man, and indeed, such according to

Papists, so that a certain ἀταξία [disorder] must necessarily follow from it, which was present in the very act; from which it follows that the fault resides solely in God, or that He Himself was so impotent that He could not purge the matter and remove the disorder that would follow, all of which are ἄτοπα καὶ βλάσφημα [absurd and blasphemous].

XXIIX. And thus far we have proposed our arguments: now we shall append one or two testimonies of orthodox antiquity. 1. Tertullian, On Patience: Man was innocent, most friendly to God, and a colonist of Paradise. 2. Augustine, book On Continence, ch. 7: Fault earned this infirmity, Nature did not have it. 3. The same, book On Correction and Grace, ch. 10: Man was certainly made upright without any vice. 4. Macarius, homily 12: Adam, having transgressed the commandment, lost the pure possession of his nature, which was beautiful and created according to the image and likeness of God. 5. Damascene, book 2, On the Orthodox Faith, ch. 12: God made man pure, and ἄπαντον [entirely] lacking in depravity,

XXIX. The adversaries have but one little argument, with which they are proud and promise themselves almost certain victory. Bellarmine places it in the first place in chapter 6, and this is the sum of it: 1. Man is carried toward a bodily good through the sensitive appetite, and toward a spiritual good through reason. From this, however, a struggle arises. Therefore, this is no less natural to man than appetite and reason themselves.

XXX. This argument has been answered at length in section 3, Phil. Sob. ch. 5, last question, p. 897. Let it be noted here in a few words that reason and appetite in the first state were not contrary, but subordinate. For the appetite did not precede reason, and it desired nothing without its persuasion. There was, therefore, a ἁρμονία [harmony] of inclinations, not a σύῤῥαξις [clash]: there was a friendly concord, not a hostile reluctance. For just as it is natural now after the fall to resist, so then before the fall it was natural to obey the appetite. For man, tempted and troubled by no such strife from himself against himself, enjoyed his own peace with himself in that place of blessedness, Augustine, On Correction and Grace, ch. 15. Wherefore, a distinction must entirely be made between appetite itself and the disorder of appetite: That is from God, and without sin. For even in Christ, the holiest of all men, there was an appetite for food, Matt. 4 v. 2, for drink, John 4 v. 7, and for sleep, Matt. 8 v. 24. This, however, did not flow from the very nature of man as it was created by God: but drew its origin from sin, which vitiates nature. In short: It is one thing to desire, another to desire wrongly. The former is of nature, the latter of guilt; the former is from God, the latter from the Devil: the former is concreated, the latter introduced: The former is contrary to reason, the latter is subordinate to it.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO I.

An natura primi hominis cum rebellione virium à Deo sit condita?

I. Negatiua nostra est, cuius veritas demonstratur omnibus istis Scripturæ testimonijs, quæ disput. præcedente pro iustitia & sanctitate voluntatis Quæst. 6. th. 16. & 24 adduximus:

II. Nam 1. Ex Gen. 1. v. vlt. Si omnia fuêre valdè bona condita qui ergo virium ἀταξία & inordinata ἐπιθυμία locum habere potuit? Num & illam valdè bonam appellabimus? ἀσύστατον.

III. 2. Ex Gen. 2 v 25. Si non erubuêre primi parentes nudi, vtiq; concupiscentia & appetitus inordinatio ijs concreata non fuit. Hæc enim pudoris causa, vti patet ex Gen. 3. v. 6. 7.

IV. 3. Ex Ecclesiaste 7. v. 30. Si homo rectus est creatus; Ergo sine omni curuitate, sine virium rebellione, & facultatum dissensione. Hæc enim obliquitas est, rectitudo non est.

Neque valet exceptio, Ecclesiasten loqui de rectitudine naturali, non morali. Si n. per naturalem intelligas animæ ὀυσίαν & δυνάμεις; à scopo Ecclesiastæ recedis. Nam illam attendit, quam homo per lapsum perdidit, hoc est, quę in sanctitate, & omnium δυνάμεων harmonia fuit posita. Et hæc non appellatur ἠθικὴ, quia per assuefactionem non est comparata; sed φυσικὴ, quia naturæ in prima creatione fuit implantata.

V. Verum prolixius hæc recensere, & vrgere nolumus, sed ex prima συζητήσει repetenda relinquimus: Rationes tantùm ex Scripturis petitas, & antè à nobis non adductas, breuiter, vnà cū quibusdam Patrum testimonijs apponemus.

VI. RATIO I. Ab absurdo. Parentes nostri ex inordinato sensilium appetitu amissâ justitiâ in Diaboli potestatem inciderunt. Quare, si natura cum tali ἀταξίᾳ est creata, sequitur hominem ex creatione, secundum naturam, extrà donum superadditum, pari modo fuisse Diaboli arbitrio obnoxium. Ἐπιθυμία enim Deo displicet, Diabolo placet, ideóque hominem à Deo abducit, Diabolo subjicit. Hanc ergo si concreatam habuerunt primi parentes, non potuere non male appetere, adeoque homo, Dei opificium, respectu creationis, fuisset vna Diaboli mancipium, respectu rebellionis, id quod absurdum & impium,

VII. RATIO II. A Christo, in quo nulla rebellio. Factus hic nobis est per omnia similis, & humanam naturam assumsit integram, cum omnibus consequentibus & proprijs essentialibus. Quare, si lucta propensionum foret immediatum naturæ consequens, non caruisset omni peccato. Concupiscentia enim appetitus inordinata est peccatum, Rom. 7. v. 7. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 16.

VIII. Neq; hic agon Christi debet aut potest obijci, in quo a nonnullis pugnasse dicitur appetitus, mortem fugiens, cum ratione mortem eligente. Non enim ibi luctabatur appetitus humanus, & ratio humana Christi; sed potius, totus homo cum Deo, voluntas humana cum diuina, vt patet ex ipsis verbis, Non sit mea, sed tua voluntas, Luc: 22. v. 24. Naturale enim est homini mortem fugere, quia naturam destruit, adeoque illi aduersatur. Quapropter mirum non est, quod & Christus tanquam verus homo, mortem timuerit, & à Patre petierit, Transeas à me calix iste. Præsertim, quoniam ipsi subeunda fuit non mors simplex, sed satisfactoria pro hominum peccatis; quæ omnia, vnà cum Patris ira, legis maledictione & doloribus inferni eum presserunt, adeoque mortis fugam & timorem adauxerunt. Interim tamen nec ibi fuit exacta pugna, quoniam voluntas Christi nutabat quasi, & mori partim volebat, ob miseriã humani generis; partim nolebat, ob iram Patris, cui tamen se plenè tandem subijciebat.

IX. RATIO III. A statu glorificationis. Si necessarius materiæ effectus, & naturæ nostrę adfectus esset, illa propensionum discordia, duraret in ipso etiam glorificationis statu. Ibi n. natura nõ abolebitur, nec appetitus & ratio destruetur. Quare dissentient in vita etiam æterna: aut, si actus negetur, tamen ipse habitualis torpor manebit, quia conditione materiæ, quæ quoad ὑπόστασιν semper vna necessario secundum Pontificios insequitur. Quo modo a. hoc pacto status iste beatissimus erit, & ab omni malo vitioque immunis.

X. RATIO IV. Ab extenuatione felicitatis primæ, & originalis iustitiæ. Si natura hominis cum torpore virium, & lucta δυνάμεων est condita, vitiumque hoc semper naturæ infixum hæsit, vtique primus status non fuit felicissimus, ἐπιθυμία enim tātum malum est, vt Paulus etiam renatus propter eius reliquias ταλαίπωρον ἄνθρωπον infelicem hominem se pronunciet, Rom. 7. v. 24.

XI. Deinde originalis iustitia non fuisset donum tum excellens, vt in Scripturis passim prædicatur. Habuisset enim se tantum instar medicinæ palliatiue, quæ naturam non purgauerit, sed morbum duntaxat contexerit, ne in actum penitus erumperet. Vnde sequitur, vitiosos etiam motus in statu integritatis fuisse, licet dominium non habuerint. Eam enim fræno compescenti comparant. Vbi autem nulli sunt inordinati actus, ibi nihil compesci aut refrænari potest. Vbi enim nulla rebellio, quid opus fræno? Vbi nullus morbus, quorsum remedium?

XII. Quare, si hypotheses suas saluas velint, fateantur oportet, in ipso integritatis statu appetitum mala nonnunquam, vi naturæ suæ, contra rationem appetiisse, sed per iustitiam mox repressum & refrænatum esse. Ita ergo vna opera tam felicitatem primi status tollunt, tam iustitiæ originali non parum detrahunt.

XIII. Et sane miranda est Papicolarum vertigo. Nam iustificationem Euangelicam, qua peccati & concupiscentiam rei dicimus omnino reijciunt: hic vero ipsi talem fingunt iustitiam originalem, quæ aliud fuerit, nisi tegmen quoddam naturalis vitij, & concupiscentiæ ingenitæ.

XIV. Ex Deo insuper quasi Telephum quendam effingunt, à quo non minus vulnus, quam remedium profectum sit, non secus ac si chirurgi partes esse dicamus, hominem vltrò ictibus contundere, vt habeat, quem Panaceæ epithemate curet.

XV. RATIO V. A concupiscentiæ natura. Nihil hæc est aliud, quàm peccatum, Rom. 7. v. 7. nec ex Patre est, sed mundo 1. Ioh. 2. v. 16. Quare, si homo illam ex creatione accepit, 1. Deus creator peccati causa erit, quod blasphemum; & 2. peccatum fuit ante statum peccati, quod absurdum; & 3. pœna pręcessit culpam, quod jniustum.

XVI. Ad rationem hanc excipit Bell. c. 7. Col. 28 his verbis: Concupiscentia carnis nunc quidem pœna peccati est, tamen homine condito in puris naturalibus fuisset sine dubio naturalis, non quidem, vt bonum aliquod naturæ, sed vt defectus & quasi morbus quidam naturæ, ex conditione materiæ consequens. Quare rectissimè dicitur, non esse ex Deo; odio, non amore dignam, malam, naturæq; contrariam, propter duas causas. Primùm, quia non ex intentione autoris naturæ, sed præter eius intentionem in homine extitisset, si in puris naturalibus homo creatus fuisset. Deinde, quia Deus illam sustulerat, & ex ipsius hominis culpa locum in nobis habet. Prius istud cap. 5. declarauit similitudine quadam à fabro desumtam, qui dum ex ferro gladium fabricat, non est causa rubiginis in gladio, quæ ex materiæ conditione postea oritur.

XVII. Respondemus autem, in vna hac exceptione non vnam, sed benè multas falsitates delitescere, quarum præcipuas paucis annotabimus.

XIIX. Si ex materiæ conditione necessariò fluit illa rebellio, Deus à culpa non liberabitur. Qui enim author est antecedentis, author etiam est immediati consequentis: vel causa causæ, est quoque causa causati, in essentialiter subordinatis.

XIX. Et quis tandem author fuit eius mali, si Deus non fuit? An Diabolus? Verùm hic ante peccatum nihil in hominem iuris habuit. Num Angeli? Verùm hi, cùm ministri sint, mala hominum, pręsertim innocentium, amouere potiùs, quàm promouere laborant. Et quid prolixitate opus est? Quicquid per creationem cœpit, à Deo ortum habet, Deoǻue acceptum ferri debet, siue ἀμέσως hoc fiat, vel proximè, siue ἐμμέσως vel remotè.

XX. 2. Omne naturale est bonum, quia à Deo creatum, cuius opera cuncta sunt valdè bona; Gen. 1. v. vlt. 1. Tim. 4. v. 4. Vnde August. in Enchir. cap. 12. Omnis, inquit, natura vitiosa, in quantum natura est, bona est; in quantum vitiosa, mala est. Hinc ergò concludimus: Omne naturale est bonum; Deoque placet, quod absurdum & ipsi Bellarmino contrarium, qui concupiscentiam malam, odioque Dei dignam pronunciat.

XXI. Nec incommodè ipsi reponere possumus argumentum proprium, quod habet lib. 5. de amiss. grā. cap. 2. vbi contra Flacium ita ratiocinatur: Iohannes dicit: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil. Iohannis 1. vers. 3. S. autem Paulus addit: Omnis creatura bona est. 1. Tim. 4. vers. 4. Ex quibus infert, si substantia nostra sit peccatum & malum, vel non esse creaturam, quod repugnaret Euangelio; vel non omnem creaturam esse bonam quod repugnaret Apostolo: Nos pari ratione contra ipsum argumentamur; Si concupiscentia est naturalis, sequitur; vel non omnē creatum esse bonum, quod aduersatur Apostolo; vel non omne naturale ante lapsum à Deo esse creatum, quod contrariatur Apostolo.

XXII. 3. Quærimus, quam Bellarminus intelligat materiam? Num corpus? Sed huic appetendi vis non est propria. Num animam? Ast hæc incommodè vocatur materia. Deinde Deus eam immediatè Adamo inspirauit. Ergò si ab illa naturaliter emanat propensionum pugna, Deus virissimpeccati causa prima constituitur. Sicut enim omnes facultates animae, à Deo esse dicuntur, quia ab anima, quam Deus inspirauit, necessario partu emanant: ita virium ἀταξία Optimi Dei soboles erit, si consimiliter animam insequatur.

XXIII. 4. Iesuitae sui obliuiscuntur. Negant enim concupiscentiam in renatis haerentem malam odiouè Dei dignam esse, vti Concil. Trident. sess. 5. definiuit. Hic verò concedunt, talem ἀταξίαν fluxisse ex natura Adami, in quo tamen non inchoamentum, sed totum complementum imaginis diuinae extitit.

XXIV. 5. Contradicunt sibi, dum vnam eandemq; concupiscentiam, & naturalem, & naturae contrariam dicunt. Omne enim φυσικὸν, vel quod fluit ex naturalibus principijs, naturae consentaneum est, non contrarium. Et vicissim, Quod contrarium, hoc naturale non est. Quomodo igitur haec contraria & ἀντιφατικὰ de vno & eodem verè affirmari possunt.

XXV. 6. Blasphemum est, concupiscentiam ex materia à Deo creata, praeter Creatoris intensionem prouenisse. Ita enim Deus accusatur, vel imperitiae, vel impotentiae. Illius, quia talem ἀταξίαν ex tali materiae conditione orituram non praeuiderit: Huius, quia labem labemque istam summoperè non potuerit. Praesupponimus enim, Deum voluisse hominem condere ad imaginem suam, adeoque rectum. Vel ergò non potuit, vel potuit. Si non; impotens est. Si potuit, vtique fecit. Vbi enim voluntas & potestas ponitur, res ipsa ponitur. Omnia, quaecunque voluit, fecit Psalm. 113. vers. 3. ὅσα τινα γίνηται, Quaecunq; vult, fiunt, Damasc. l. 2, O. F. c. 29.

XXVI. Porrò quando aliquid praeter intentionem agentis euenit, tùm à scopo suo primitus intento aberrat. Cuius causa est, vel agentis incircumspectio, vel obstaculorum multitudo, quae aut non præuidit, aut præuisa tollere nón ualuisti Num autem Deum sapientissimum à scopo suo aberrasse dicemus? Num ipsi prouidentiæ incircumspectionem, ipsi omnipotentiæ ἀμηχανίαν quandam attribuemus? Apage has blasphemias. Deus totus oculus est, omnia præuidet, omnibus prouidet; qui ergò præter eius intentionem aliquid eueniret? Non est sapientis dicere, non putâram. Ergo nec sapientis, imò nec Christiani erit, ipsi Sapientiæ hoc impingere.

XXVII. 7. Falsum est hypothesibus Papisticis concupijcentiam in primò statu sublatam esse. Si enim ex conditione materiæ necessariò sequitur, & verò materia ipsa sublata non fuit, qui concupiscentia abesse potuit? Præterea, cùm dicant, justitiam originalem compescuisse appetitum; Ergò hic contrà rationem quándoq́ue commotus est, aliàs compressione hâc opus non fuisset. Tandem cùm scribant, appetitui naturale esse, in bonum sensile semper ferri, vtique hoc ipsum aut appetijt, aut naturâ suâ caruit. Sihoc, naturalia in primo statu non fuêre integra. Sin istud, concupiscentia adfuit adeoque penitùs sublata non fuit. Quod ipsum, vt verbis maximè negant Papiscolæ, non tamen aliter sentiunt, quam appetitum pro indole suâ quoduis bonum sensile, & sic nonnunquàm malum appetiiffe; à iustitia verò, tanquam directrice, cohibitum esse ne rationem vinceret, suóque desiderio potiretur.

XXIIX. Denique 8. in allata similitudine maxima est disparitas. Nam 1. Faber materiam non cudit, vt Deus, ideoque rubiginis ex materia ortæ autor non dicitur 2. Rubigo materiam non necessariò insequitur; nec ipsa materia in causa est, sed externum corrumpens. 3. Rubigo in ferro non est actu, neque eius causa proxime efficiens. 4. Faber si posset talem vtique gladium fabricaret, qui rubiginem non contraheret. At verò, Deus ipsam hominis materiã condidit, & quidem, talem iuxta

Papicolas, vt eâ necessariò insequeretur quędam ἀταξία, quæ ipso actu adfuit; ex quo sequitur, culpam in Deo vnicè residere, vel ipsum adeò impotentem fuisse, vt materiam purgare & secuturam inordinationem tollere non potuerit, quę omnia sunt ἄτοπα καὶ βλάσφημα.

XXIIX. Et hactenus nostras rationes proposuimus: iam vnum atque alterum orthodoxæ antiquitatis testimonium subnectemus. 1. Tertull. de patien. Homo innocens erat, Deo maximè amicus, & Paradisi colonus. 2. August. l. de contin. cap. 7. Languorem istum culpa meruit, Natura non habuit. 3. Idem lib. de corrept. & gratiæ c. 10. Alatus certè sine vllo vitio factus est rectus. 4. Macarius homil. 12. Adam transgressus mandatum, perdidit possessionem puram naturæ suæ speciosam, & secundùm imaginem ac similitudinem Dei conditam. 5. Damasc. l. 2. O. F. cap. 12. Fecit Deus hominem purum, & ἄπαντον pravitate carentem,

XXIX. Vnicam vero aduersarij ratiunculam habent, quâ superbiunt & tantùm non certissimam sibi victoriam promittunt. Illam Bellarm. cap. 6. primo loco ponit, & hæc summa est. 1. Homo per appetitum sensitiuum fertur in bonum corporale, per rationem in spirituale. Hinc autem oritur lucta. Igitur hæc non minùs homini naturalis est, quàm ipse appetitus & ratio.

XXX. Ad argumentum hoc prolixè responsum est sect 3. Phil. Sob cap. 5 quæst. vlt. p. 897. Hic paucis notetur, quòd ratio & appetitus in statu primo non fuerint contraria, sed subordinata. Appetitus enim rationem non præcurrit, & sine eius suasu nihil appetijt. Fuit ergò propensionum ἁρμονία, non σύῤῥαξις: fuit amica concordantia, non hostilis reluctantia. Vtenim nunc post lapsum resistere: ita tunc ante lapsum obedire appetitui naturale fuit. Homo enim nulla tali rixâ à seipso aduersus seipsum tentatus atque turbatus in illo beatitudinis loco suâ secum pace fruebatur, August. de corrept. & gra. c. 15. Quare omnino distinguendum est inter appetitum ipsum & appetitus ἀταξίαν: Ille à Deo est, & absque peccato. Nam & in Christo omnium hominum sanctissimo fuit appetitus cibi, Matt. 4. v. 2. potus, Ioh. 4. v. 7. & somni Matth. 8. v. 24. Hæc autem nō ex ipsa hominis natura prout à Deo est cōdita, profluxit: sed ex peccato, naturam vitiante, originem sua traxit. Breuiter: Aliud est appetere, aliud male appetere. Illud naturæ, hoc culpæ; illud à Deo, hoc à Diabolo: illud concreatum, hoc introductum: Illud rationi contrarium, hoc subordinatum est.


### Question I. Was original justice a natural gift, or was it supernatural?

I. Before we proceed to the confirmation of our opinion, 1. we will refute two calumnies: and 2. we will explain the term (natural).

II. And indeed 1. Bellarmine, in chapters 1 and 6, slanders the Lutherans by saying they deny that there were supernatural gifts in the first man. But he is mistaken and is deceiving. We deny that righteousness was a supernatural gift, but we do not exclude others, the chief of which is the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. For if the whole Holy Trinity dwells in the regenerate, as is said in John 14 v. 13, 1 Cor. 3 v. 16, and 6 v. 19, how much more did it fix its tabernacle in the first man? That this indwelling, however, was not a part or property of nature, but a condition of grace, we readily admit.

Then he falsely attributes to us in chapter 5, column 16, C, that we call original righteousness natural in this sense, because it was a part of nature, or certainly flowed from the principles of nature. For that we think otherwise will be said in the second place, and will become manifest from the writings of our people.

III. Therefore, as regards the second point, the word Natural, it is taken 1. constitutively for that which is granted to nature itself to be. 2. Consecutively, for that which from the form essentially flows, as the faculties of the soul. 3. Subjectively, for that which adheres most deeply fixed to nature. 4. Perfectively, for that which adorns, aids, and perfects nature. 5. Transitively, that which is propagated naturally and through nature: We do not understand the first and second modes when we call justice natural; because it was neither a part nor a constitutive principle of man properly so called, nor any faculty of the soul: but we attend to all the latter modes, and thus we deny that infused original justice was a supernatural gift, because it did not adhere extrinsically, or consist of supernatural endowments or powers; but rather we call it connatural, both because it adhered to nature from creation by itself, and most closely as a natural property, and because it perfected the same, and thus contributed to its natural complement, and because it would have been propagated and naturally derived into descendants through carnal generation.

IV. Therefore, the opinion of our Churches having been explained, nothing else remains but that 1. we confirm it with invincible arguments. 2. We refute the Papal objections, both of which we shall provide briefly dispatched according to the plan of our undertaking.

I. Confirmation of our opinion.

V. It can be established by eight principal arguments, which we shall recount in order. 1. From the creation of man in the image of God. Whatever was concreated with man, and without which nature was not originally founded in its principles, this was a natural quality, not an adventitious or supernatural grace. For from what else shall we estimate the nature and natural things of man, if not from the first creation of nature? Whatever was concreated with other animals and bodies, we call all this natural; why then should we deny it of man alone? But justice was concreated with the first man; and it is evident from the Mosaic narrative, the image

of God, of which justice was a part, having pertained to the constitution and internal principles of man. For Jehovah said: Let us make man in our image and our likeness, namely as the ultimate perfection and complement of human nature, so much so that if only the production of the body and the inspiration of the soul were considered in man, without original justice, the creation of human nature would not yet be absolute: since it lacks its ultimate perfection. For just as animals are said to have been created according to their kind: so man in the image of God. Wherefore, just as for animals conformity with their kind was natural: so also for man was conformity with God, or concreated justice. And just as the nature of animals would not have been whole if it had lacked that conformity with its kind, so also, for a reason entirely similar, must one judge concerning human nature.

To this also pertains the passage in Ecclesiastes 7:30, where God is said to have made man upright. For if He made him upright immediately: therefore He did not first create man, and afterwards add uprightness as a supernatural gift.

VI. 2. From the end of man. Man was founded for the sake of God, that he might acknowledge Him, celebrate Him once acknowledged, and become a participant in eternal blessedness. For thus writes Lactantius in his book On the Anger of God, chapter 13: Man was created that he might know God; and through that knowledge attain immortality, which is the highest good. And conversely, in book 7 of the Institutes, chapter 6: Therefore the world was made, that we might be born; therefore we are born, that we might acknowledge God; therefore we acknowledge Him, that we might worship Him; therefore we worship Him, that we might obtain immortality as the reward for our labors. But he who is destined for an end proportionate to his nature, to him natural means are not denied. Therefore God also implanted in man natural powers, by which he could attain that end. For otherwise man would have been worse off than the brutes, which are equipped with the necessary means for attaining their end.

VII. 3. From the remnants of the divine image. Such as the remnants are, such is that of which they are the remnants. For when the whole and the parts are homogeneous, then they obtain the same condition and nature: But the remnants of the divine image or original righteousness, such as the κοιναι ἐννοιαι and the incentives of the virtues, are natural to man. For who in his right mind would call these a supernatural gift? Especially since the Apostle in Romans 1 affirms that the Gentiles by nature (φύσει) do the things of the law, verse 14, and have the work of the law written in their hearts, so that conscience itself bears witness concerning things done well or ill, verse 15. Wherefore we conclude that the whole image in the first state was much more natural. For if the remaining portion is natural, so that the work proceeding from it is said to be done by nature (φύσει) or by nature, how much more must the same be affirmed of the whole or entire thing?

VIII. 4. From natural propagation. The supernatural gifts of grace are not hereditary. For it would be as absurd for them to be propagated into individuals through generation as if one were to say that foals are born bridled, since the Papists compare original righteousness to a bridle, by which the impulses of the flesh were tamed and chastised. But original righteousness would have been hereditary, and propagated through carnal generation into all descendants, as the adversaries do not deny. Therefore it was not a supernatural gift, but rather a quality or property of nature itself. And let it be noted that Pererius, in his disputation on the third excellence, question 4, page 186, concedes that no other reason can be brought forward why Adam's sin harmed all his descendants, except that original righteousness was a gift, not of the person of Adam, but of the whole nature.

IX. 5. From the contrary. Contraries do not differ in their whole genus, but participate in the same reason: 'in the case of contraries, it is the same,' says the Philosopher, 6 Topics 9, § 4. But righteousness and original corruption are contraries. Therefore they do not differ in their whole genus. But original corruption is not something supernatural, but a natural quality, and one most deeply fixed in our nature, so much so that the Apostle affirms that we are by nature (φύσει) children of wrath, Eph. 2:3. Wherefore it follows that righteousness, being contrary to sin, was no less natural to the first man.

X. 6. From the state of glorification. It is sown a natural (ψυχικόν) or animal body, it will rise a spiritual (πνευματικόν) body, says the Apostle, 1 Cor. 15:45. Just as, therefore, animality is now a natural affection (πάθος) of the body, so in the future, spirituality, succeeding it, will not be something extrinsic or superadded, but likewise a natural quality and intrinsic to the glorified body. But since the state of integrity and the state of glorification correspond to each other by a certain analogy, inasmuch as in the latter is fully restored what was lost in the former, it follows in turn that the endowments of body and soul received through creation, and thus also original righteousness, were in the first state natural in the same way as the endowments to be conferred upon us in the resurrection will one day be.

XI. 7. From the testimonies of the Fathers. I shall not accumulate many here, but will set forth only one or two. 1. Augustine, in Enchiridion, ch. 11: Whatever vices of the soul there are, they are privations of NATURAL goods. 2. Leo, sermon 13 on the Passion of the Lord, calls the innocence of the first man natural. 3. Bernard, sermon 1 on the feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary: I consider it to be the divine image, which, being not ASSUMED, but INNATE, and impressed upon nature itself, cannot be divided or severed.

XII. 8. From the contradictions of the Papists. 1. The Council of Trent, session 5, teaches that on account of original sin we have fallen into the power of the devil, and that the whole man, according to body and soul, has been changed for the worse. That, however, is not merely to be deprived of a supernatural gift. 2. Furthermore, the Scholastics themselves often say that the natural faculties in man have been corrupted, as can be seen from Lombard, book 2, dist. 25, letter H. For as often as they read in the Scriptures how original sin is exaggerated; how foully and basely it has corrupted our nature in all its faculties; that it is not a mere privation, but at the same time the positing of a contrary vicious habit; then they could not conclude otherwise than that natural things had been depraved. But since this is so, how was justice a supernatural gift? For the removal of an extrinsic gift, such as a garland or a garment, cannot so horribly corrupt or contaminate nature itself. 3. Pererius, l. 4. on Genesis, in the digression on death, p. 122, writes openly: In order that it might be acknowledged that man is something proper and peculiar to God, He sealed him with the seal of His image, so deeply and tenaciously impressed that, WITHOUT PREJUDICE TO the NATURE of man, that seal could in no way be removed. Just as it has been handed down to memory that that most noble Phidias made the shield of Minerva, and included his own likeness in it with such art that it could not be taken out of the shield entirely. He is, however, as if forgetful of himself, l. 5. disp. on the third excellence. Qu. 3, p. 183, he affirms that justice, simply and absolutely, was a supernatural gift; yet, conversely, disagreeing with himself, he adds that it may in some sense be called a natural gift, because it did not properly and of itself perfect man in relation to a supernatural end, nor for supernatural acts, but supplied the defects of nature and provided man with NATURAL integrity, rectitude, and perfection. This fluctuation and contradiction, therefore, is the most certain indication of a bad cause. For just as in a sick body a bad humor is now carried into this part, so a weak mind imbued with error never stands still, wherever it inclines, always uncertain, says Arrian in Epict. bk. 2, diss. ch. 5.

Latin:

I. Antequam ad sententiæ nostræ confirmationem progrediamur, 1. duas calumnias refutabimus: & 2. vocabulum (naturale) explicabimus.

II. Et quidem 1. calumniatur Bellarminus cap. 1. & 6. Lutheranos negare, dona supernaturalia in primo homine fuisse. Sed fallit & fallitur. Iustitiam fuisse donum supernaturale negamus, cætera non excludimus, quorum præcipuum est inhabitatio sancti Spiritus. Si enim in renatis tota S S. Trinitas inhabitat, vt dicitur Ioh. 14 v. 13. 1. Cor. 3. v. 16. & 6. v. 19. quantò magis suum in primo homine tabernaculum fixit? Hanc verò ἐνοίκησιν non fuisse partem aut proprietatem naturæ, sed conditionem gratiæ, vltrò fatemur.

Deinde affingit nobis cap. 5 Col. 16. C. quòd iustitiam primæuam hoc sensu naturalem dicamus, quia fuerit pars naturæ, aut certè fluxerit à principijs naturæ. Aliter enim nos sentire, secundo iā loco dicetur, & ex Nostrarū scriptis manifestum euadet.

III. Quod igitur II. spectat vocem Naturalis, sumitur illa 1. constituiuè pro eo, quod ipsi naturæ largitur esse. 2. Consecutiuè, pro eo, quod à forma essentialiter fluit, vt facultates animæ. 3. Subiectiuè, pro eo quod naturæ penitissimè infixum hæret. 4. Perfectiuè pro eo, quod naturam exornat, iuuat, perficit. 5. Transitiuè, quod naturaliter & per naturam propagatur: Primum secundumque modum non intelligimus, cum iustitiam naturalem dicimus; quia nec pars aut principium hominis constitutiuum propriè dictum, nec aliqua facultas animæ fuit: postremos verò modos omnes attendimus, adeoque infusam primæuam donum supernaturale fuisse negamus, quia non extrinsecè adhæsit, aut supranaturales dotes aut vires fuit; sed potiùs connaturale dicimus, tùm, quia naturæ ex creatione per se, & arctissimè vt proprietas naturalis inhæsit, tùm quia eandem perfecit, adeoque ad eius complementum naturale concurrit, tùm quia per generationem carnalem in posteros fuisset propagata & naturaliter deriuata.

IV. Explicatâ igitur Nostrarum Ecclesiarum sententiâ, nihil restat aliud, quàm 1. inuictis eam argumentis confirmemus. 2. Papales obiectiunculas refutemus, quod vtrumque pro instituti ratione breuiter expeditum dabimus.

I. Confirmatio nostræ sententiæ.

V. Octo potissimùm argumentis illa stabiliri potest, quæ ordine recensebimus. 1. A creatione hominis ad imaginem Dei. Quicquid homini concreatum est, & sine quo natura in suis principijs non fuit primitus condita, hoc naturalis qualitas, non aduentitia vel supernaturalis gratia fuit. Vnde enim naturam & naturalia hominis æstimabimus, nisi ex prima creatione naturæ? Quicquid alijs animalibus & corporibus concreatum est, hoc omne naturale dicimus; De solo igitur homine cur negaremus. Atqui iustitia homini primo fuit concreata; & constat ex narratione Mosaica, imaginem

Dei, cuius pars erat iustitia ad constitutionem & principia interna hominis pertinuisse, Dixit enim Iehoua: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram, nempè velut vltimam perfectionem & complementum naturæ humanæ, adeò, vt si consideretur in homine tantùm productio corporis & inspiratio animæ, sine originali iustitia, nondum absoluta sit humanæ naturæ creatio: quoniam caret perfectione suâ vltimâ. Sicut enim animalia dicuntur creata esse secundum genus suum: sic homo ad imaginem Dei. Quapropter sicut animalibus conformitas cum genere suo fuit naturalis: ita & homini conformitas cum Deo, vel iustitia concreata. Et sicut animalium natura non fuisset integra, si caruisset illâ cum genere suo conformitate. Ita quoque, ob rationem prorsus similem, de humana natura iudicandum est.

Huc etiam pertinet locus Eccl. 7. v. 30. vbi Deus dicitur hominem fecisse, rectum. Etenim, si statim rectum fecit: Ergò nō primùm creauit hominem, post rectitudinem, veluti donum supernaturale adiecit.

VI. 2. A fine hominis. Conditus est homo propter Deum, vt illum agnosceret, agnitum celebraret, & æternæ beatitudinis particeps fieret. Ita enim scribit Lactantius l. de ira Dei c. 13 Homo creatus est, vt Deum cognoscat; & per illam cognitionem immortalitatem assequatur, quod est summum bonum. Et vicissim l. 7. inst. capite 6. Idcircò mundus factus est; vt nascamur, ideò nascimur, vt agnoscamus Deum; ideò agnoscimus; vt colamus ideò colimus, vt immortalitatem pro laborum mercede consequamur. Qui autem destinatur ad finem naturæ proportionatum, illi naturalia media non denegantur. Ergò & Deus naturales homini vires indidit, quibus finem illum consequi posset. Aliàs enim deterior fuisset homo brutis, quæ necessarijs ad finem suum adipiscendum medijs instructa sunt.

VII. 3. A reliquijs diuinæ imaginis. Quales sunt reliquiæ, tale id, cuius sunt reliquiæ. Quando enim homogenea sunt totum & partes, tum conditionem & naturam eandem obtinent: Atqui reliquiæ imaginis diuinæ vel iustitiæ originalis quales sunt κοιναι ἐννοιαι & stimuli virtutum, sunt homini naturales. Quis n. sanus ista donum supernaturale diceret? Præsertim cùm Apostolus Rom. 1. affirmet, gentes φύσει facere τὰ τοῦ νόμου, vers. 14. & opus legis in cordibus suis scriptum habere, adeò, vt ipsa conscientia reddat testimonium de bene aut malè factis v. 15. Quare concludimus, multò magis totam imaginem in primo statu fuisse naturalem. Si enim residua portio cùm naturalis est, vt opus ex illa prodiens φύσει vel naturâ dicatur fieri, quantò magis idipsum de integro vel toto affirmandum erit?

VIII. 4. A naturali propagatione. Dona supernaturalia gratiæ non sunt hæreditaria. Tàm enim absurdum foret, illa per generationem in singulos propagari, ac si quis diceret, pullos equinos nasci frænatos, quoniam Pontificij iustitiam originalem conferunt cum fræno, quo domati & castigati fuerint carnis impetus. Atqui iustitia originalis fuisset hæreditaria, & per carnalem generationem in omnes posteros propagata, non diffitentibus aduersarijs. Ergò donum supernaturale non fuit, sed potiùs qualitas vel proprietas ipsius naturæ. Et notetur, quòd Pererius disp. de tertia excellent. quæst. 4. pag. 186. concedat, nullam posse aliam adferri rationem, cur Adæ peccatum omnibus posteris nocuerit, nisi quia iustitia originalis donum fuit, non personæ Adami, sed totius naturæ.

IX. 5. A contrario. Toto genere non differunt contraria, sed eâdem ratione participant: ἐπὶ τῶν ἐναντίων ὡσαύτως, inquit Philosophus 6. Top. 9. §. 4. Atqui iustitia & labes originalis sunt contraria. Ergò toto genere non differunt. Est verò labes originalis non quiddam supernaturale, sed qualitas naturalis, nostraeque naturae quam altissimè infixa, adeò vt Apostolus adfirmet, nos φυση vel natura esse filios irae Eph. 2. v. 3. Quare sequitur peccato contrariam justitiam primo homini non minùs fuisse naturalem.

X. 6. A statu glorificatoris. Seminatur corpus ψυχικὸν vel animale resurget πνευματικὸν vel spirituale, inquit Apostolus 1. Cor. 15. v. 45. Sicut igitur animalitas nunc est naturale corporis πάθος: ita olim spiritualitas succedens, non erit quidda extrinsecū vel superadditum, sed consimiliter qualitas naturalis & corpori glorificato intrinseca. Cùm verò status integritatis & glorificationis certâ quâdam analogiâ sibi inuicē respondeant, siquidem in hoc plenè restituitur, quod ibi fuit deperditū, vicissim sequitur, dotes corporis animiq; per creationem acceptas, & sic etiam originalem justitiam, in primo statu pari modo fuisse naturales, sicut aliquando erunt dotes, in resurrectione nobis conferenda.

XI. 7. A testimonijs Patrum. Non multa hîc cumulabo, sed vnum duntaxat vel alterum adponam. 1. August. in Enchir. cap. 11. Quaecunque animorum vitia sunt, ea privationes NATVRALIVM bonorum sunt. 2. Leo serm. 13. de pass. Dom. vocat innocentiam primi hominis naturalem. 3. Bernhard. serm. 1. super festum Annunc. B. Mariae: Ego diuinam arbitror esse imaginem, quae nimirum non ASSVTA, sed INSITA, atque ipsi impressa natura diuidi scindique non potest.

XII. 8. A contradictionibus Pontificiorum. 1. Concil. Trid. sess. 5. docet, propter peccatum originis incurrisse nos in potestatem diaboli, totumq; hominem secundum corpus & animam in deterius mutatum. Id verò non est priuari solum dono supernaturali. 2. Praeterea ipsi Scholastici saepè dicunt, Naturalia in homine fuisse corrupta, vti videre est ex Lombardo l. 2. dist. 25. lit. H. Quoties enim in Scripturis legêre, quam exaggeretur peccatum originis; quàm foedè & turpiter corruperit naturam nostram in omnibus facultatibus; quòd non sit mera carentia, sed simul positio contrarij habitus vitiosi; tum aliter concludere non potuerunt, quàm naturalia fuisse deprauata. Hoc autem cùm sit, quomodo iustitia donum supernaturale fuit? Ablatio enim doni extrinseci, vt serti aut vestimenti, ipsam naturam tam horrendè corrumpere aut contaminarenequit. 3. Pererius l. 4. super Genes. in digress. mor p. 122. apertè scribit: Vt agnosceretur, hominem esse quid Dei proprium & peculiare, obsignauit eum sigillo suae imaginis, tam altè ac tenaciter impressae, vt SALVA hominis NATVRA signaculum illud auferri nullo modo posset. Quemadmodum memoriae proditum est, nobilissimum illum Phidiam fecisse clypeum Mineruae, atque in eum tanta arte effigiem suam inclusisse, vt ea integrè clypeo non posset eximi. Est tamen velut sibi oblitus, l. 5. disp. de tertia excell. qu. 3. pag. 183. iustitiam simpliciter & absolutè donum supernaturale fuisse adfirmat, Vicissim verò dissentiens à seipso subjicit, posse aliquâ ratione appellari donum naturale, quia propriè ac per se non perfecerit hominem, in ordine ad finem supernaturalem, neque ad actus supernaturales, sed suppleuerit defectus naturae, & NATVRALEM homini integritatem, rectitudinem & perfectionem prestiterit. Haec igitur fluctuatio & contradictio, certissimum malae caussae est indicium. Sicut enim in corpore aegro humor malus modò in illam fertur partem: sic animus imbecillis & errore imbutus, nunquam consistit, quouè inclinet, semper incertum, inquit Arianus apud Epict. l. 2. diss. c. 5.


### Question I. Was original justice a natural gift: II. Refutation of Papal Objections

II. Refutation of Papal Objections

XIII. Bellarmine collected all these in chapter 6 and divided them into three classes: 1. Into sayings of Scripture, 2. Testimonies of the Fathers, and 3. Reasons, all of which we shall consider briefly.

XIV. DICTA from the Holy Scriptures, he alleges four principally, 1. Gen 3. v. 19. Dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return. Whence he gathers, that man by nature was dust and fragile; and consequently that original righteousness could not have been natural.

Resp. I deny the consequence, because here we are disputing about the quality of the soul, the statement speaks of the origin of the human body. But what is the consequence: The body of Adam was formed from dust. Therefore, the righteousness of the soul was not natural? But the sense of the statement here is: As regards the origin of the body, you are earthly; but as regards the soul, you are endowed with natural righteousness and created for immortality. Now, however, because through the abuse of free will you have turned yourself to earthly things, this will be your punishment, that you shall return into the earth from which you were taken through death,

XV. 2. Psalm 8, v. 7. What is man, that you are mindful of him? You have crowned him with glory and honor. A similar passage exists in Psalm 49, v. 12. But because glory and honor are something extrinsic, he concludes from this that original righteousness, which is called glory here, was an extrinsic and supernatural gift.

I answer 1. Psalm 8 speaks of Christ, as is evident from the application in 1 Cor. 15, v. 27, Eph. 1, v. 22, Heb. 2, v. 9. 2. If it were twisted to apply to the human race, it would not, however, treat of the state before the fall, but rather after the fall, when man fell into misery, yet God mercifully looked upon him. 3. If it is applied most strongly to the state of integrity, there is still no consequence in the argument. For why must glory and honor be understood only as supernatural things? 4. Granted that supernatural gifts are noted, does it immediately follow that righteousness must be numbered among them? 5. Not all honor is external. For it is taken 1. For the foundation of honor, which is virtue. 2. For the internal reverence of the heart, by which we magnify someone. 3. For the external sign of this reverence. Since, therefore, the word is so ambiguous, nothing certain is concluded. For what would prevent this honor from being taken fundamentally for internal concreated righteousness, since in the first time there were no others who could honor the πρωτοπλάστος (first-formed one)? 6. Some distinguish glory and honor in such a way that the former signifies internal, the latter external dignity, so that the sense may be: You have crowned him with glory, within through natural wisdom and righteousness; with honor, without through authority over all creatures. Glory consists of virtue, an internal good; Honor of office, an external good.

XVI. 3. Ecclesiasticus 7, v. 2. God clothed man with power. He thinks righteousness is acquired by a garment, which is always something external.

Response. The word 'to clothe' is taken here metaphorically, in which sense it does not always denote something external. For Job was also clothed with flesh and skin, ch. 10, v. 11. God is clothed with light as with a garment, Psalm 104, v. 2. The grasses of the field are said to be clothed with beautiful colors, Matthew 6, v. 30. But are all these supernatural gifts? Absurd. 2. In the Greek it is, 'He clothed them with power' ἑαυτοὺς, according to themselves, by which words certainly an intrinsic, deeply implanted, and most natural rectitude is denoted.

XVII. 4. He cites the parable of Luke 10, v. 30, concerning the man stripped and wounded, who had lost only external goods.

Response. 1. Parabolic theology is not argumentative. 2. Arguments are effective only from the literal sense, not the mystical, says Bellarmine himself, book 3, on the Word of God, chapter 3.

2. Parables are not to be twisted to a purpose other than that for which they were brought forth; indeed, Christ's purpose here was by no means to shadow forth the state of the first man, but only to explain the doctrine concerning one's neighbor and the duty of charity.

3. Even if it is referred allegorically by some Fathers to the first state, it does not hinder our cause at all. For one can be stripped not only of supernatural, but also of natural gifts, such as sight, hearing, etc. And certainly that allegorical traveler did not retain his nature intact. For he was wounded lethally, and thus the continuity being broken, the integrity was harmed. Wherefore also the first man was wounded unto death by an intrinsic lesion of his very nature.

XIIX. Having said these things, he adds certain general testimonies of the Fathers, which, however, are all either corrupted, or the response to

falsely understood, or twisted elsewhere, or certainly doubtful, and therefore ineffective for proving. Having therefore dismissed these, we proceed to the arguments: we refuted the first at the end of question 1; we shall now add the rest in a slightly inverted order:

XIX. OBJECTION 1. No other cause of corruption can be given in nature, except the removal of a supernatural gift.

Resp. On the contrary, the seduction of the Devil, the consent of man, and the abuse of one's own liberty can be given, which were breaking up the harmony of nature and the concreated image, from which followed disorder and the corruption of all powers: For just as when a privation is placed in a capable subject, the contrary habit follows: so when integrity was lost, iniquity succeeded; when aversion from God was placed, conversion to the devil succeeded, just as he who loses health through intemperance certainly contracts disease and induces a vicious habit; for as virtue is lost through the multiplication of this act, and the habit of vice soon follows: so Adam, through his first evil action, which because of its remarkable deformity was far worse than many acts in corrupt nature, destroyed and expelled the habit of justice and, on the contrary, induced in himself the habit of injustice, so that there is no need to seek another efficient cause.

All these things can be explained by the example of the fallen Angels, in whom, from the condition of their nature, no rebellion can be imagined, so natural was holiness to them. Whatever proximate cause, therefore, shall be given for why they lost their natural justice and became lying spirits, that same cause can also be applied to the corruption of human nature.

XX. OBJECTION 2. By actual sins after the fall, only the gift of supernatural grace is lost, not any property or quality of nature, therefore also through Adam's sin natural things were not lost, and consequently the justice which we lost was supernatural.

Resp. I deny the consequence. 1. Because the effect of the Adamic sin is one thing, and the effect of other sins is another: That is natural, because it corrupted nature; and universal; with respect to men, all of whom it corrupted, as well as to vices, toward all of which it made us incline. These are personal, and therefore they do not take away a certain natural quality, but induce a personal guilt, and an inclination particular only to this or that vice.

2 Because the state of corrupted nature is one thing, that of integral nature another. To the latter the gift of justice is supernatural, but to the former it was natural, as we demonstrated above.

3 Because our justice ought to be compared with original holiness, not as it is begun in this life, but as it will be consummated in the other life. Where, in turn, it will not be an external gift, but an intrinsic one, and implanted in the nature of the blessed even more deeply than in Adam.

XXI. OBJECTION 3. If justice was natural, it follows that we too were natural sons of God. But only the λόγος is ὀσιώδως εἰκῶν of the Father.

Resp. An ambiguity lies in the term natural Son. For it either signifies him who by reason of ὀσία is the image of God; or him who from his first birth, and through a concreated quality of holiness, is a Son of God; just as nature also denotes either essence or first birth. In the former way, only the λόγος was a natural Son of God; in the latter, the first man was. The former, indeed, on account of identity of nature; the latter on account of concreated holiness. For just as now after the fall we are by nature or by birth sons of wrath: so before the fall we were by nature, that is, from our first creation, sons of God, and thus also in a certain way by grace, insofar as we did not have that ὑιοθεσία from ourselves from eternity, but received it in time from God.

Wherefore let it be noted that the title of Son of God is assigned to three. For 1. the λόγος is Son of God by nature only, or rather by ὀσία. 2. He is a Son of God partly by nature, partly by grace; as the first man, who was a Son of God by nature, with respect to natural justice, and yet at the same time by grace, with respect to a gracious creation. 3. He is a Son of God by grace only, such as the reborn are. Thus therefore briefly, λόγος is the Son of God by essence: Adam was by nature: the reborn are by rebirth. Or λόγος is by eternal generation: Adam was by temporal creation: the reborn are by gracious adoption.

Wherefore, since the term natural Son is so ambiguous, the argument concludes nothing. Theologians rightly warn, however, to avoid the suspicion of error, that only the λόγος should be called the natural Son of God, but Adam a Son by nature or by creation.

XXII. OBJECTION 4. If human nature could not be created by God without original righteousness; it follows that a dead man cannot be recalled to life by God unless endowed with original righteousness, although many have been resurrected without this.

Resp. 1. This argument is very twisted and has no strength: For what is the consequence: Adam's nature was adorned with original righteousness, Therefore God cannot resurrect anyone without this? Will you then force the power of God into the circle and straits of your reason?

2. It is clearly uncertain what the condition of those resurrected was. Therefore, they are absurd who presume to establish an article of Faith from such uncertain things and extraordinary miracles. But so that the uncertainty may appear, we shall annotate a few things about those resurrected, on the occasion of this argument, and as a finishing touch.
