XXIII. There are read, however, eight notable examples of those resurrected into this life. 1. The son of the woman of Zarephath, 1 Kings 17:22. 2. The son of the Shunammite, 2 Kings 4:33. 3. The one resurrected at the contact of the bones of Elisha, 2 Kings 13:21. 4. The daughter of Jairus, Matt. 9:25, Mark 5:42. 5. The son of the widow in Nain, Luke 7:15. 6. Lazarus, John 11:43-44. 7. Tabitha of Joppa raised by Peter, Acts 9:40. 8. Eutychus resurrected by Paul, Acts 20:10. But that we may say something about their condition, and collect various opinions, we institute such a discourse.

XXIV. Those men were either truly dead, or apparently so. If the latter, the authority of Scripture perishes; the truth of sacred history, the dignity of the miracles. For if the souls did not depart from the bodies, but lay hidden, as in those in an ecstatic state, then there was neither a true resuscitation, nor a true and divine miracle. Since all these things are impious, we affirm that they were truly dead, and that the souls were really released from the bodies.

XXV. From this, however, a question immediately arises, both concerning the body and the soul. So that this may be better understood, let us presuppose that regarding original sin three things are considered: 1. dominion, 2. sense, 3. the root. For in a carnal and unregenerate man, sin dominates, under which he is sold. In the regenerate, however, it is indeed present and felt, but it does not dominate, because it is repressed by the spirit. The root, however, is called that very vicious and habitual quality, infecting and depraving both the soul and the body. This root, according to the theologians, is removed by reduction into ashes, just as sense is removed by death, and dominion by renewal.

XXVI. These things being thus presupposed, the first difficulty exists concerning the body. For this was resuscitated either without the root of sin in glory, or with the root of sin in misery. If you affirm the former: 1. Weighty reasons must be brought forward, such as perhaps will scarcely be found. 2. It will conflict with the arrangement of the root to be purged. This consists in total destruction and reduction to ashes. But those bodies were not yet reduced to ashes. 3. It is contrary to the condition of glorified bodies, which are said to be invisible, impassible, agile, and subtle. But those were gross, always seen, they ate, they drank; and this not from a special dispensation, but from the condition of their nature and bodies. Although indeed it is not perpetual or long-lasting: but they were always seen, and therefore resuscitated, especially the children, so that they might live on an animal life (for this the parents sought) just like other men.

And certainly it is foreign to the state of glorification and eternal blessedness, where there are only angels and those equal to angels, to live among miserable men, corrupted by sin in this world, and to associate with them for so long: Nor should we think that they were translated into heaven shortly after the resurrection, since this would not have lessened, but rather increased, the grief of the parents, for whose comfort those miracles occurred.

XXVII. Since therefore the former opinion is improbable, must it be said that those bodies were recalled to life together with the root of sin? So indeed it seems, 1. On account of the denial of incineration. 2. The condition of the bodies. 3. The nature of the actions, which were animal and physical, not spiritual or angelic. And 4. on account of the lack of any certain or even probable argument by which the contrary might be proved.

XXIIX. There is, however, one thing which they object, that a stain is cast upon God if it is said that he resurrected bodies with sin. But we do not think that this certainly follows. For if God is not defiled when he preserves the most wicked sinners, neither will he be defiled when he resurrects sinners: For why should we not pass the same judgment on similar cases? And shall we think that in the resurrection the bodies of the wicked, and their souls, will be purged of sin? Nay, rather it will remain in them, so that they may perpetually feel the gnawing worm: There will be reproaches, blasphemies, despairs, all of which are proofs of present and unremoved crime. And how could they be resurrected without sin, when they never obtained forgiveness of sins in this life on account of impenitence?

Wherefore, since on the last day of judgment, the wicked are to resurrect with sin without any fault or stain of God: why could not the bodies of the pious also have been recalled to life by God with the root of sin? For the body itself was only resurrected, and that the root of sin adhered to it is not to be ascribed to God who resurrected it, but to the gravity of the corruption, which does not expire in the pious except through the total destruction of the body.

XXIX. And these things concerning the body of the resurrected: there remains a difficulty regarding the soul. For since it is the danger of sin, and therefore this is deeply rooted in it, one not undeservedly inquires about purgation. The Papists kindle a purgatorial fire: but this has long since been extinguished by waters drawn from the fountains of Israel.

How then shall it be purged? Concerning this briefly, that a pious and faithful soul, as soon as it is released from the body, is at the same time released from sin; but how or by what means or in what manner this happens, is known only to Him in whose hand are the souls of the pious, Wisd. 3:1, and in whom the dead are blessed henceforth, Rev. 14:13. Thus, therefore, we know the fact, we do not know the manner and the means.

XXX. Now, and let us apply these things to our purpose, a question arises, whether the souls of those who were resurrected had been purged from sin, or otherwise? If you affirm the former, you will be entangled in many and great difficulties: For every faithful soul released from the body and purged from sin is received into Paradise, and is joined to the fellowship of the blessed, by the example of the thief, Luke 23:43. For there are only two habitations, one in eternal fire, the other in the eternal kingdom. Augustine, on the words of the Apostle, sermon 18. Therefore, just as impenitent souls are immediately thrust down into hell; so penitent ones are immediately transported into heaven, by the example of the rich glutton and the poor Lazarus, Luke 16:22-23. Whence it follows, if the souls of the resurrected are said to have been purged, that they were immediately translated from a state of misery into a state of glory, and therefore were received into Paradise.

XXXI. With this presupposed, three huge difficulties arise, from which we not undeservedly doubt whether anyone can extricate himself: 1. It would follow that God is unjust, because He thrusts a soul purged from sin again into a body infected with sin: and again, that He casts down a soul from a state of glory, without any fault of its own, into a state of misery. Elsewhere we say that God would be unjust if He were to join a pure soul with an impure body: But would not that very thing follow much more, if He were to unite a soul already existing in a state of blessedness to a mortal body corrupted by sins?

2. It would follow that one and the same man was at one and the same time in a state of glory, and without sin, namely as regards the purified soul; and then in a state of misery and sins, namely as regards the body still depraved; which certainly anyone understands to be inconsistent and absurd.

3. If the soul was glorious, how could it concur with the body for animal actions, such as eating, nutrition, augmentation, and the like: For all these have a place only in the state of mortality, from which when the soul has been exempted, how does it perform or could it perform those operations in a state of integrity?

XXXII. Since it can hardly be answered sufficiently to all these things, it seems more probable that the souls of those resurrected were not freed from the root of sin.

But this also is not asserted without difficulties. For 1. since the souls of the pious, departing from their bodies, are immediately purified, what cause will be given for which purification in those souls was hindered or delayed. 2. After the release from their bodies, where did they exist? In hell? But we presuppose they were faithful. In heaven? But nothing defiled or corrupted by sin can arrive there, 1 Cor. 15 v. 58. In some intermediate place? But there is no middle place, so that it is only with the devil, who is not with Christ. August. lib. 1 de remiss. pecc. cap. 28.

Wherefore, unless we take refuge here in a singular ordinance of God, by which, on account of the miracle that was to follow, the souls were neither freed from sin, nor taken up into heaven, but were kept elsewhere; we shall hardly be able to extricate ourselves from these thorns and difficulties.

XXXIII. If, therefore, anyone strictly demands of us what the condition of those resurrected was, we judge it most common to suspend judgment (ἐπέχειν), and we repeat that of Augustine: It is not clear. Meanwhile, privately, it seems more probable to us that those men were not without sin, lived an animal life, and died again. We do not condemn the contrary, nor do we affirm that as apodictic, but rather we leave both in doubt and therefore deservedly censure the audacity of the Papists who do not blush to build articles of faith upon uncertain and doubtful matters.

XXXIV. Briefly therefore, this we know from Scripture, that Christ truly recalled the dead to life. But where their souls were in the meantime, whether their bodies were resurrected without or with the root of sin, whether they died a second time? We cannot know certainly and infallibly, nay, nor ought we. For what is not handed down in the Scriptures is ignored without crime, not investigated without danger. For which reason we are content to be ignorant of what we can neither know nor ought to know. Let us not seek to have known what God has willed to be secret, with which admonition of St. Ambrose, taken from the book on the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 8, we wish this our disputation to be concluded and as it were sealed.

Latin:

II. Refutatio Obiectionum Papalium

XIII. Collegit istas omnes Bellarminus c. 6. & in tres classes diuisit 1. In dicta Scripturae. 2 Testimonia Patrum, & 3. Rationes, quae omnia paucis considerabimus.

XIV. DICTA ex sacris literis, quatuor praecipuè allegat, 1. Gen 3. v. 19. Puluis es, & in puluerem reuerteris. Vnde colligit, hominem naturâ fuisse puluerê & fragile; ac per consequens iustitiam originalem non potuisse naturalem esse.

Resp. N. C. quia hîc disputamus de qualitate animæ, dictum loquitur de corporis humani origine. Quæ autem sequela: Corpus Adami ex puluere formatum est. E. iustitia animæ naturalis non fuit? Sensus autem dicti hic est: Quoad originē corporis tuis terrenus es; sed quoad animam naturali iustitiâ præditus, & ad immortalitatem conditus. Nunc verò, quia per abusum liberi arbitrij ad terrena te conuertisti, hæc erit pœna tua, vt in terram, de qua sumptus es per mortem reuertaris,

XV. 2. Psal. 8. v. 7. Quid est homo, quòd memor es eius? Gloriâ & honore coronâsti eum. Similis locus extat Psal. 49. v. 12. Quia verò gloria & honor sunt quiddam extrinsecum, hinc rectitudinem originalem, quæ gloria hic vocatur, fuisse donum extrinsecum & supernaturale concludit.

Respondeo 1. Psalm. 8 de Christo loquitur, vti patet ex applicatione, 1. Cor. 15. v. 27. Eph. 1. v. 22. Heb. 2. v. 9. 2. Ad genus humanum si torqueretur non tamen ageret de statu ante lapsum, sed potiùs post lapsum vbi homo in miseriam incidit, Deus tamen clementer eum respexit. 3. Si maximè applicetur ad statum integritatis, nulla tamen argumento inest consequentia. Per gloriam enim & honorem, cur tantùm supernaturalia sunt intelligenda? 4. Posito, notari dona supernaturalia, num autem protinus sequitur, iustitiam illis annumerari debere? 5. Non omnis honor externus est. Sumitur enim 1. Pro fundamento honoris, quod virtus. 2. Pro interna cordis reuerentia, quâ aliquem magnificamus 3. Pro externo huius reuerentiæ signo, Cùm ergò vox sit tàm ambigua, nihil certi concluditur. Quid enim impediret, quò minùs honor hic fundamentaliter accipi posset, pro interna concreata rectitudine, cùm primo tempore non fuerint alij, qui πρωτοπλάστος honorarent? 6. Nonnulli gloriam & honorem ita distinguunt, vt illa internam, hic externam dignitatem significet, vt sit sensus: Coronâsti illum gloriâ, intus per naturalem sapientiam & iustitiam; honore foris, per imperium in omnes creaturas. Gloria inest ex virtute bono interno; Honor ex officio, bono externo.

XVI. 3. Ecclesiastici. 7. v. 2. Deus hominem vestivit virtute. Hic justitiam putat comparari indumento, quod semper est quiddam extrinsecum.

Resp. Vox vestiendi sumitur hic metaphoricè, quo sensu non semper aliquid externum notat, Nam Iobus etiam carne & cute vestitus, c. 10. v. 11. Deus lumine velut vestimento amictus, Psal. 104. v. 2. Gramina agri pulchris coloribus vestita dicuntur, Matth. 6 v. 30. Num autem hæc omnia dona sunt supernaturalia ? Absurdum. 2. In Græco est, Vestivit eos virtute ἑαυτοὺς, secundum seipsos, quibus certè verbis rectitudo intrinseca, altè implantata & naturæ convenientissima denotatur.

XVII. 4. Allegat parabolam Luc. 10 v. 30. de homine spoliato & sauciato, qui tantùm extrinseca bona amiserit.

Resp. 1. Theologia parabolica non est argumentativa, 2. Ex solo sensu literali, non mystico argumenta sunt efficacia, inquit Bell. ipse. l. 3. de V. D. cap. 3.

2. Parabolæ extra scopum, quo prolatæ non sunt aliò detorquendæ, Christi verò scopus hîc nequaquam fuit, statum primi hominis adumbrare, sed tantùm doctrinam de proximo & charitatis officio explicare.

3. Si maximè cum nonnullis Patribus allegoricè ad primum statum referatur, causæ tamen nostræ nihil officit. Spoliari enim quis potest non tantum supernaturalibus, sed etiam naturalibus donis, vt visu, auditu &c. Et certè viator iste allegoricus naturam non retinuit integram. Vulneratus enim est lethaliter, atque sic continuū solutum, integrum fuit læsum. Quare & homo primus, intrinsecâ ipsius naturæ læsione ad mortem fuit vulneratus.

XIIX. Dictis his subjungit quædam testimonia Generalia Patrum, quæ tamen omnia, vel sunt depravata, vel responsio ad-

falso intellecta, vel aliò detorta, aut certè dubia, ideoque ad probandum inefficacia. Missis ergò istis, ad rationes progredimur: Primam in fine quæst. 1. confutauimus reliquas inuerso paulùm ordine nunc addemus:

XIX. OBIECTIO 1. Nulla potest alia dari causa corruptionis in natura, nisi remotio doni supernaturalis.

Resp. Imò verò dari potest Diaboli seductio, hominis consensio, & propriæ libertatis abusio, quæ distribuebant harmoniam naturæ & imaginem concreatam, vnde sequebatur inordinatio, & omnium virium corruptio: Vt enim posita priuatione in subiecto habili, sequitur habitus contrarij: sic amissa integritate, successit iniquitas; posita auersione à Deo, successit conuersio ad diabolum, sicut qui intemperantia sanitatem perdit, morbum certè contrahit, & habitum vitiosum inducit; Vt enim hunc per multiplicationem actum virtus deperditur, vitijque habitus mox sequitur: sic Adamus per primam actionem malam, quæ ob insignem deformitatem longè deterior erat, quam multi actus in natura corrupta, destruxit & expulit habitum justitiæ & è contrario jniustitiæ habitum sibi ipsi induxit, vt aliam causam immittentem quærere nihil sit opus.

Declarari hæc omnia possunt exemplo Angelorum lapsorum, in quibus ex conditione naturæ nulla potest fingi rebellio, adeò sanctitas ijs naturalis fuit. Quæcunque ergo causa propinqua dabitur, quod illi naturalem suam iustitiam perdiderint. & spirituum mendaces facti sint, illa ipsa etiam corruptioni naturæ humanæ accommodari poterit.

XX. OBIECTIO 2. Peccatis actualibus post lapsum perditur tantum donum supernaturalis gratiæ, non aliqua proprietas aut qualitas naturæ, E. etiam per Adami peccatum naturalia non fuêre deperdita, & per consequens iustitia quam amisimus, fuit supernaturalis.

Resp. N. C. 1. Quia alius est effectus peccati Adamitici, & alius peccatorum cæterorum: Illud est natùrale, quia naturam deprauauit; & vniuersale; respectu hominum, quos omnes corrupit, tum vitiorum, ad quæ omnia nos propendere fecit. Hæc sunt personalia, ideoque naturalem quandam qualitatem non adimunt, personalem reatum, & particularem tantùm ad hoc vel illud vitium inclinationem inducunt.

2 Quia alius est status naturæ corruptæ, alius integræ. Illi donum justitiæ est supernaturale, huic verò fuit naturale, vti suprà demõstravimus.

3 Quia cum sanctitate originali justitia nostra comparari debet, non vt inchoata est in hac vita, sed qualis erit consummata in vita altera. Vbi vicissim non donum externum erit, sed intrinsecum, naturǽque beatorum, profundiùs etiam quàm Adamo implantatum.

XXI. OBJECTIO 3. Si iustitia fuit naturalis, sequitur & nos fuisse naturales Dei filios. At solus λόγος est ὀσιώδως εἰκῶν Patris.

Resp. Ambiguitas latet in vocabulo Filij naturalis. Vel enim significat eum, qui ratione ὀσίας est imago Dei; vel qui ex prima natiuitate, & per concreatam sanctitatis qualitatem Dei Filius est; sicut etiam natura vel essentiam, vel primam natiuitatem notat. Priori modo, solus λόγος, posteriori primus homo fuit naturalis Dei Filius. Ille nimirum, ob naturæ identitatem; hic ob concreatam sanctitatē, Sicut enim nunc pòst lapsum natura vel ex natiuitate sumus filij iræ: sic ànte lapsum naturâ, id est ex prima creatione fuimus Filij Dei, atque sic etiam quodammodo per gratiam quacenus illam, ὑιοθεσίαν non ab æterno à nobismetipsis habuimus; sed in tempore à Deo accèpimus.

Quare notetur, quod titulus Filij Dei tribus assignetur Nam 1. est Filius Dei per naturã tantùm vel potius per ὀσίαν ὁ λόγος 2. est Filius Dei partim per naturam, partim per gratiam; vt primus homo, qui natura fuit Dei Filius, respectu naturalis justitię, & tamē simul gratiæ, respectu creationis gratiosę. 3. Est Filius Dei per gratiam tiam tantùm quales sunt renati Sic ergò breviter, λόγος est Filius Dei per essentiam: Adamus fuit per naturam: renati sunt per renascentiam. Vel λόγος est per æternam generationem: Adamus fuit per temporalem creationem: renati sunt per gratiosam adoptionem.

Quapropter, cùm vocabulum naturalis Filij tàm sit ambiguum, nihil concludit argumentum. Rectè autem monent Theologi, ad vitandam erroris suspicionem, solum λόγον dicendum esse Filium Dei naturalem, Adamum verò Filium φύσει seu ex creatione.

XXII. OBJECTIO 4. Sinatura humana non potuit à Deo creari sine originali justitia; sequitur, non posse hominem mortuum à Deo revocari in vitam nisi præditum originali justitiâ, cùm tamē multi absq́, hac resuscitati fuerint.

Resp. 1. Argumentum hoc valdè contortum est, & nervos non habet: Quæ enim sequela: Adami natura fuit ornata originali justitiâ, Ergo Deus sine hac neminem resuscitare potest? Tune ergò Dei potentiam in gyrum & angustias rationis tuæ coges?

2. Incertum planè est, qualis resuscitatorum fuerit conditio, Absurdi proinde sunt, qui ex hujusmodi rebus incertis, & miraculis extraordinarijs articulum Fidei stabilire præsumunt. Vt autem incertitudo appareat, de resuscitatis istis, occasione hujus argumenti, & velut colophonis loco, pauca annotabimus,

XXIII. Leguntur autem octo insignia resuscitatorum in hanc vitam exempla. 1. Filius Sareptanę, 1. Reg. 17. v. 22. 2. Filius Sunamitidis, 1. Reg. 4. v. 33. 3. Resuscitatus ad contactum ossium Eliæ, 2. Reg. 11. v. 21. 4. Filia Iairi, Matth. 9. vers. 25. Marc. 5. vers 42. 5. Filius viduæ in Nain, Luc. 7. vers. 15. 6. Lazarus. Ioh. 11. v. 43. 44. 7. Tabita Ioppensis à Petro excitata, Act. 9. v. 40. 8. Eutychus à Paulo resuscitatus, Act 20. vers. 10. Vt verò de horum conditione aliquid dicamus, & varias opiniones colligamus, talem discursum instituimus.

XXIV. Homines illi aut verè fuerunt mortui, aut apparenter. Si hoc, perit Scripturæ authoritas; historiæ sacræ veritas, miraculorum dignitas. Si enim animæ non excesserunt è corporibus, sed latuerunt, vt in ecstaticis, tum neque vera resuscitatio, neque verum & diuinum miraculum fuit. Quæ omnia cùm sint impia, verè illos mortuos, & animas à corporibus realiter fuisse solutas affirmamus.

XXV. Hinc autem statim oritur quæst. tum dè corpore, tum de anima. Quod vt magis intelligatur; præsupponamus, circa peccatum originale tria considerari, 1. dominium 2. sensum, 3. radicem. In homine n. carnali & non renato, dominatur peccatum, sub quo est venundatus. In renato autem adest quidem & sentitur, sed non dominatur, quia per spiritum reprimitur. Radix verò appellatur ipsa vitiosa & habitualis qualitas, tum animam, tum corpus inficiens & deprauans. Hæc a. radix secundum Theologos tollitur per reductionem in cineres, vt sensus per mortem, & dominum per renouationem.

XXVI. His ita præsuppositis, prima difficultas existit de corpore. Hoc enim resuscitatum est, aut sine peccati radice in gloria, aut cùm peccati radice in miseria. Si prius affirmes, 1: Ponderosas rationes adduci oportet, quales fortassis vix reperientur. 2. Repugnabit ordinatio purgandæ radicis modò. Hic consistit in totali destructione & cinefactione. Ista verò corpora in cineres nondum fuère redacta. 3. Aduersatur conditioni corporum glorificatorum, quæ dicuntur inuisibilia, impassibilia, agilia, subtilia. Ast illa fuêre crassa, semper visa, comederunt, biberunt; & hoc non ex peculiari dispensatione, sed suæ naturæ & corporum conditione. Quanquam enim non est perpetua aut diuturna: Illi verò semper visi sunt, & ideò resuscitati, præsertim filij, vt vitam animalem (hanc enim parentes petiêré) velut alij homines porro viuerent.

Et certè alienum est à statu glorificationis & beatitudidis æternæ, vbi tantùm sunt ἄγγελοι & ἰσάγγελοι, inter homines miseros, peccatoque corruptos in hoc mundo viuere, & cum illis tàm diu conuersari: Neque putemus, eos paulò post resuscitationem fuisse in cœlum translatos, siquidem hoc parentibus, in quorum solatium miracula ista contigêre dolorem nõ minuisset, sed de nouo auxisset.

XXVII. Cum ergo prior opinio sit improbabilis, dicendūnē est, corpora ista vna cūm peccati radice in vitam esse reuocata? Ita quidem videtur, 1. Ob cinefactionis negationem. 2 Corporum conditionem 3. Actionum rationem, quæ fuêre animales & Physicæ, non spirituales vel angelicæ. Et 4. ob certi aut probabilis tantùm argumenti, quò contrarium probetur defectum.

XXIIX. Vnum verò est, quod obijciunt, Deo impingi maculam, si corpora cū peccato resuscitasse dicantur. At verò illud certò sequi non arbitramur. Si enim Deus non inquinatur, cùm peccatores scelestissimos conseruat; neque inquinabitur, cùm peccatores resuscitat: De similibus enim idem iudicium cur non feramus? Et num in resurrectione corpora impiorum, animasque à peccato purgatum iri existimabimus? Imò verò manebit in ijs, vt perpetuo rodenten vermem sentiant: Erunt ibi exprobrationes, blasphemationes, desperationes, quæ omnia præsentis, & non sublati criminis documenta sunt. Et quomodo absque peccato resuscitari possent, cûm peccatorum veniam in hac vita nunquam consecuti sint ob impœnitentiam?

Quapropter, cùm in vltimo die censoréo, impij cum peccato resurrecturi sint sine culpa aut macula Dei: cur non & piorum corpora cùm peccati radice à Deo in vitam reuocari potuissent? Ipsum n. corpus tantùm resuscitatum est, cui quòd radix peccati adhæsit, non Deo resuscitanti adscribendum est, sed labis grauitati, quæ nisi per totalem corporis destructionem in pijs non expirat.

XXIX. Ethæ de corpore resuscitatorum: restat difficultas quoad animam. Cùm enim d'επικινόν sit peccati, adeoque hoc alte in illa radicetur, de purgatione non immeritò quæritur. Pontificij succendunt ignem purgatorium: sed hic vndis ex Israelis fontibus haustis jamdudum extinctus est.

Quî ergò purgabitnr? De eo breuiter, animam piam & fidelem, quam primùm corpore soluitur, simul sol ui à peccato; quomodo autem quouè medio vel num ἀνόσως fiat, illi soli notum est, in cuius manu sunt animæ piorum, Sap. 3. v. 1. & in quo mortui sunt beati amodo, Apoc. 14. 13. Ita E. rem scimus, modum mediumque nescimus.

XXX. Nunc, et hæc ad institutum applicemus, quæstio exoritur, An animæ resuscitatorum à peccato fuerint purgatæ, vel secus? Si primum affirmes, multis magnisque difficultatibus implicaberis: Nam omnis anima fidelis à corpore soluta, & à peccato purgata in Paradisum recipitur, & beatorum consortio adiungitur, exemplo latronis, Luc. 23 45. Duę enim tantùm habitationes sunt, vna in igne æterno, altera in regno æterno. Augustinus de verb. Apostol. serm. 18. Sicut ergò animæ impœnitentes mox detruduntur in infernum; sic pœnitentes mox transportantur in cælum, exemplo diuitis lurconis, & pauperis Lazari, Luc. 16. v. 22. 23. Vnde sequitur, si resuscitatorum animæ purgatæ dicantur, illas protinus ex statu miseriæ in statum gloriæ translatas, adeoque in Paradisum receptas fuisse.

XXXI. Quo præsupposito, tres ingentes difficultates exsurgunt, ex quibus, an quis se expedire queat, nõ immeritò dubitamus, 1. Sequeretur Deum esse iniustum, quòd animam à peccato purgatam denuò intrudat in corpus peccato infectum: & rursus, quod animam ex statu gloriæ, sine omni culpa sua, deijciat in statum miseriæ. Alibi dicimus, Deum iniustum fore, si animam puram cum corpore impuro coniungeret: Annón verò multò magis illud ipsum sequeretur, si animam in statu beatitudinis jam existentem, mortale & peccatis corrupto corpori aduniret?

2. Sequeretur unum eundemque hominem simul & semel fuisse in statu gloriae, & absq; peccato, nempè quoad animam purgatam; tùm in statu miseriae & peccatorum nempe quoad corpus adhuc depravatum; quod sanè inconueniens, & absurdum esse quiuis intelligit.

3. Si anima fuit gloriosa, quomodo potuit cum corpore ad actiones animales concurrere, vt ad comestionem, nutritionem, augmentationem, & similes: Hæc enim omnia tantùm in statu mortalitatis locum habent, à quo cùm exemta fuerit anima, quomodo istas operationes in statu integritatis peragit aut peragere potuit?

XXXII. Ad quæ omnia cùm sufficienter responderi vix queat, videtur probabilius, animas resuscitatorum à radice peccati liberatas non fuisse.

Verùm & hoc sine difficultatib. non asseritur. Nam 1. cùm animæ piorum è corporibus secedentes, statim purgentur, quæ causa dabitur, ob quam purgatio in istis animab. impedita aut dilata fuerit. 2. Post solutionem à corporibus vbi extiterunt? Num in inferno? Ast fideles fuisse præsupponimus. Num in cælo? Ast eò nil coinquinati peccatóue corrupti pervenire potest, 1, Cor. 15. v. 58. Num in loco quodam intermedio? At non est locus medius, vt sit nisi cum diabolo, qui non est cum Christo. August. l. 1. de remiss. pecc. c. 28.

Quapropter nisi hîc ad singularem Dei ordinationem confugiamus, quâ, ob secuturum miraculum, animæ à peccato nec liberatæ, nec in cælum, assumtæ, sed alibi asservatæ sint; ex istis spinis & difficultatibus expedire nos vix poterimus.

XXXIII. Quòd si ergo aliquis rigorosè à nobis exquirat, qualis resuscitatorum fuerit conditio, ἐπέχειν censemus tritissimum, & istud Augustini repetimus; Non liquet. Interim priuatim videturnobis probabilius, istos peccato non caruisse, vitam animalē vixisse iterumq́; mortuos esse. Contrā riū non damnamus, neq; istud vt apodicticū adfirmamus, sed vtrumq; potius in dubio relinquimus adeoque, Papicolarum audaciam meritò taxamus qui rebus incertis dubijsque articulos fidei superstruere non erubescunt.

XXXIV. Breuiter ergò, Hoc ex Scriptura scimus, Christum verè in vitam reuocasse mortuos. Vbi verò interim fuerint ipsorum animæ, num corpora sine vel cum radice peccati resuscitati sint, num secundâ vice mortui fuerint? certò & infallibiliter scire non possumus, imò nec debemus. Quod enim in scripturis non est traditum, sine crimine ignoratur, non sine discrimine indagatur. Quam ob causam lubenter nesciamus, quæ scire nec possumus, nec debemus. Non appetamus habere cognitum, quod Deus voluit esse secretum, quâ B. Ambrosij admonitione, ex lib. de Vocat. gent. c. 8. desumpta disputationem hanc nostram conclusam & velut obsignatam volumus.


## 4 Disputation III. On Sin in General

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Master Moses Hermann, of Langfeld in the Palatinate.

Προοίμιον. I.

Original righteousness, which we received in our first parents through creation in the image of God, we lost in the same through the violation of the divine precept, being cast down from the most happy state of integrity, and into the most miserable slavery of sin thrust by our own fault, the memory of which, as often as we recall it, makes our hair stand on end, our mind shudder, our cheek weep, and our right hand grow stiff.

II. Since, therefore, the bestowal of grace and the state of righteousness have been treated, order now demands that we proceed to discuss the loss of what was bestowed, which occurred through sin, and consequently the second state of human nature, which is called the state of the fall or corruption.

III. But just as sin is most harmful, so the knowledge of sin is most beneficial. Hence Bernard rightly says in his book On the Soul, ch. 11: 'The knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation.' And a little before: 'Perhaps the very knowledge of guilt will be, before God, the pious judge, the obtaining of pardon.' For the more the gravity of the disease becomes known, the more vehement the desire to seek the Physician flourishes. And the more ardently the sick man sighs with desire, the more ready is the help of the compassionate Physician.

IV. But just as everywhere, so here also, the greater the utility, the greater the difficulty is seen to be. 'Nothing is more known than sin; yet for understanding it, nothing is more secret,' says Augustine in his book On the Morals of the Church, ch. 22. For that it exists, we know and experience daily more than enough; but what it is and of what kind it is, whence it is and how manifold it is, how few are they who accurately understand or weigh it?

V. The doctrine concerning sin and the state of the fall can be conveniently included in three chapters, namely, if we speak 1. of sin in general, 2. of original sin, and 3. of actual sins. We shall settle the first in this disputation, and the remaining two in the following ones.

VI. Conversely, regarding the generic consideration of sin, four things are to be observed, which are especially controversial in our time, namely: 1. its essence, 2. its quality, 3. its alleged necessity, 4. the cause of sin. Concerning these four, therefore, we shall form distinct questions and briefly set forth our opinion on them.

QUESTION I.

What is sin in general?

I. The nature and quiddity of things is not better known than through a definition. For it is ὁρισμὸς τῆς οὐσίας γνωρισμὸς, as the Philosopher says in 2. post 3. §. 7. Commonly, however, a twofold definition is established: the one ὀνοματώδης or nominal: the other πραγματώδης or real. The former declares the name of the thing defined; the latter its nature and essence. If, therefore, we wish to perceive fully the quiddity of sin, both the nominal and the real definition must be attended to, concerning each of which we shall speak briefly.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisner. SS. Th. D. Resp. M. Mose Hermanno, Langfeldensi Palatino.

Προοίμιον. I.

IVstitiam originalem, quam in πρωτοπλάστοις per creationem ad Dei imaginē accepimus, in ijsdem per præcepti diuini violationem amisimus, deturbati è felicissimo integritatis statu, & in miserrimam peccati seruitutem propriâ culpâ detrusı, cujus quoties recordamur. Stat coma, mens horret, flet gena, dextera riget

II. Quoniam ergò de collatione gratiæ, statuque justitiæ actum est, ordo nunc postulat, vt de collata amissione, per peccatum facta, adeóque secundo humanæ naturæ statu, qui lapsus vel corruptionis vocatur, porrò differamus.

III. Vt autem peccatum maxime obest: sic cognitio peccati maximè prodest. Hinc rectè Bernhardus l. de anima c. 11. Notitia peccati initium est salutis Et paulo antè: Erit fortasse apud Deum, pium iudicem, ipsa cognitio culpæ impetratio veniæ. Quò enim magis morbi grauitas innotescit, eò vehementior ad quærendum Medicum cupiditas efflorescit. Quò verò ardentius ægrotisuspirantis desiderium, eò paratius Medici miserantis est auxilium.

IV. Sicut autem vbique, ita hic etiam quo vtilitas, eò & difficultas major conspicitur. Nihil est notius quàm peccatum; ad intelligendum vero nihil secretius, inquit August. l. 1. de moribus Ecclesiæ c. 22. Quod enim sit, hoc scimus & experimur quotidiè plus quàm satis est; quid verò & quale sit, vnde & quotuplex sit, quotus est, qui accuratè intelligat aut perpendat?

V. Tribus verò capitulis doctrina de peccato, statuque lapsus non incommodè potest includi, nempè si dicatur 1. de peccato in genere, 2. de peccato originali, & 3. de peccatis actualibus. Primum hac disputatione, reliqua duo sequentibus expediemus.

VI. Vicissim autem quoad genericam peccati considerationem quatuor obseruanda, & nostro inprimis tempore controuersa occurrunt, nimirum 1. quidditas 2. qualitas 3. ficta necessitas. 4. causa peccati. De his ergò quatuor distinctas quęstiones formabimus, nostramque de jis sententiam breuiter exponemus.

QVAESTIO I.

Quid sit peccatum in genere?

I. Rerum natura & quidditas melius, quam per definitionem non cognoscitur. Est enim ὁρισμὸς τῆς οὐσίας γνωρισμὸς, dicente Philosopho 2. post 3. §. 7. Vulgò autem duplex Definitio constituitur: Altera ὀνοματώδης vel nominalis: Altera πραγματώδης vel realis. Illa definiti nomen; hæc naturam & essentiam declarat. Quòd si ergò peccati quidditatem plenè percipere voluerimus, & nominalis & realis definitio attendenda est, de qua vtraque paucis.


### I. Concerning the nominal definition of sin

I. Concerning the nominal definition of sin.

II. Three things come to be explained here: 1. ἐτυμολογία or the notation of the name. 2. ὁμωνυμία or various acceptation. 3. συνωνυμία or equivalent terms.

III. As regards 1. the ἐτυμολογία of sin, there is no doubt that peccatum is derived from the verb peccandi. But from whence pecco is said to be derived, I find noted by almost no one, so that most consider that word to be primitive. Some, however, say that among the ancients peccare signified only to commit adultery, and therefore pecco is the same as to cohabit with a mistress. Isidore looked to this when, in book 10 of the Etymologies under the letter P, he writes thus: Peccator is said to be called from pellice, that is, a harlot, as if pellicator, which name among the ancients signified only a shameful act, but afterwards passed into a designation for all wicked people. He also adds another notation when he says: Peccator is likewise named from the crowd of the breast, because the hidden things of transgressions are stored therein. But this is an allusive rather than a true etymology.

IV. As concerns II. the ὁμωνυμία, it must be known that sin is accepted in one way in the forum or polity, and in another way in the choir or Church. For Papinian teaches one thing, and Paul another, as Jerome writes in his epitaph

Fabiolae Epist. 30. ch. 1. For politicians and jurists, sin is nothing other than an action committed knowingly and willingly against right reason and positive law. Philosophers approach somewhat closer, and they blame even the interior affections themselves, and count them among vices; whence arose the ethical precepts concerning the moderation of the affections. But in theology, the acceptance of sin is broader. For here it denotes everything that is against the law of God, whether it be voluntary or involuntary, and committed either by one who knows or one who is ignorant; whether it be a defect or a habit, and whether it be innate or acquired, as will be indicated more fully presently.

V. That, moreover, can be observed here as if ἐν παρόδῳ, that the doctrine of the Church concerning sin differs from the doctrine of the philosophers concerning vices in regard to all kinds of causes. For the philosophers and pagan politicians err. 1. Regarding the efficient cause of sin. For they sought this either in Stoic fate, or in the inconstancy of matter, or elsewhere. For what could they know about this matter, who neither knew nor read that: 'Through one man sin entered into the world'? says Augustine somewhere. 2. Regarding the matter, because they thought that only external acts or grosser affections are in vice: but that naked thoughts, and those which are had from birth, are free from all guilt. 3. Regarding the form, because they thought that sins are aberrations only from human laws or right reason. But that most exact norm of works, the divine law, as it has been revealed and explained in the Word, they were ignorant of. 4. Regarding the end and effect, for they philosophized only about civil punishments and the stings of conscience: but that sins merit eternal damnation, and corporal and spiritual punishments, about this there was deep silence in paganism.

VI. Furthermore, in the Scriptures, sin not only signifies an aberration from the law, but also, 1. guilt alone, as in Gen. 43, v. 9. 'I will be a sinner against thee all the days,' that is, I shall be guilty of sin throughout my whole life, 2. a sacrifice or victim for sin, in which sense it is often taken in Leviticus; and in Hosea 4 verse 8 it is said, The sins of my people they eat, that is, the sacrifices, as Augustine explains it in book 3 against the two epistles of the Pelagians, chapter 6. And some think this meaning holds in the passage 2 Cor. 5 verse 21, God made Christ sin for us, that is, a victim for sin, although others judge that it can be more conveniently explained concerning the imputation of sin.

VIII. As regards finally III. synonymy, it is manifold. For synonyms are found 1. Latin. 2. Greek. 3. Hebrew. IIX. LATIN. Of these there are very many, but the principal ones are these, that 1. it is called delictum, as if derelictum [abandoned]. For he who commits a fault, what does he abandon except the good? says Augustine, book 3 of questions on Leviticus, chapter 20. Others think it is so called from liquidum, because it flows away from the stability of the law. 2. crimen, scelus, or flagitium, which all denote the same thing as sin, but yet a gross and enormous one. 3. error, because it is an aberration from the law. 4. vitium, because the soul is vitiated and corrupted by sins. 5. culpa, because he who sins always contracts guilt. 6. prævaricatio, because it is a transgression of the law: which word Isidore derives from varus, that is, oblique, perverse, whose legs are turned inward. 7. debitum, both because it is an undue neglect of the obedience due to God; and because it has the guilt of the due punishment attached to it.

IX. And all these words are used indiscriminately, and generally signify lawlessness or illegality or something contrary to the law. The Scholastics indeed distinguish between vice and sin, and affirm that the former is the name of a habit, the latter of an evil operation. Bellarmine, book 1 on the loss of grace, chapter 2, says, commission is usually called sin, omission is usually called a fault properly. And in the same place, he posits this distinction between crime and sin, that the former denotes a mortal, the latter a venial wickedness. Besides the fact that it is imagined that a sin is venial in itself, these differences are not always observed, as is evident from sacred and ecclesiastical books. Meanwhile, however, we do not deny that a certain distinction can be given between these terms, if we pursue ἀκρίβειαν. For sin in general signifies any evil act committed; a fault, however, a good act omitted; a crime and a wickedness, a gross sin; an error, a sin of ignorance; a vice, an evil habit; a fault and a debt, guilt: but as I said, these distinctions are not perpetual.

X. 2. GREEK [terms], of which in turn these are the primary ones: ἁμαρτία, which word is derived from ἁμαρτάνειν, which is ἄσκοπα τοξεύειν, or τῶ σκόπῳ ἀποτυχάνειν, to miss the mark, whence Suidas defines ἁμαρτία as τὴν τῶ ἀγαθῶ ἀποτυχίαν, a deflection from the good. Some derive ἁμαρτία from the privative particle α and the verb μάρπτειν, which is to attain or apprehend, so that ἁμαρτία is an aberration, or a privation of attainment. Others derive it from μὴ and ἀρτέω, that is, I fit or accommodate, because sin is something inept and incongruous. Iniquity or injustice, 2. ἀδικία, is thus said to be from the privation τῆς δίκης. Some distinguish ἁμαρτία and ἀδικία thus, that the former denotes an involuntary, the latter a voluntary sin, to which pertains that of Demosthenes in the oration περὶ στεφάνου: ἀδικεῖ τις ἄκων, ἠξήμαρτε τις ἑκών. But in the Scriptures this distinction is not held. 3. παράπτωμα, a slip or transgression, from παραπίπτειν, to fall beside, or from παράπτεσθαι, which is to touch something rashly and with an erring hand. Jerome in chapter 2 to the Ephesians says that παραπτώματα are the beginnings of sins; ἁμαρτίας, when something completed by action arrives at the end. But that this distinction is not observed in turn is evident from Rom. 5, verse 18, and 7, verse 5. 4. παρακοή, or disobedience, which word for the most part denotes actual and voluntary sins. 5. κακία and πονηρία, malice, by which are denoted mortal sins. 6. πλημμέλεια a fault or error, from πλὴν or πάλιν, and μέλειν, because it ought to be repaired by later care, which is always better. It therefore properly denotes an omission, just as ἁμαρτία denotes a commission.

XII. HEBREW. Commonly among the Hebrews sin is called חטאה from the root חטא to stray from the mark, to deflect from the way, or rather from the norm of divine law. By another name it is called עון iniquity or perversity: they say that by the former original sin is denoted, by the latter actual sin, but Scripture attributes both to each. See more synonyms, both Greek and Hebrew, in Chemnitz in Loci Communes, part 1, in the section on sin, chapter 2; Flacius, part 1 of the Clavis, columns 850, 851; and Mr. Dr. Gerhard, Volume 2, on actual sin, sections 8 and 9.

Latin:

I. De peccati definitione nominali.

II. Tria hîc exponenda veniunt, 1. ἐτυμολογία vel nominis notatio. 2. ὁμωνυμία seu varia acceptio. 3. συνωνυμία seu vocabula æquipollentia.

III. Quod spectat 1. ἐτυμολογία peccati, dubium non est, quin peccatum à verbo peccandi deriuetur. Vnde autem pecco dictum sit, à nemine fermè annotatum inuenio, ita vt plerique censeant, vocem istam esse primitiuam. Nonnulli tamen dicunt, quòd veteribus peccare tantùm signârit adulterium committere, ideoque pecco sit idem, quod cum pellice coëo. Huc respexit Isidorus, quando l. 10. Etymolog. in lit. P. ita scribit: Peccator dicitur à pellice, id est, meretrice vocatus quasi pellicator, quod nomē apud antiquos tantùm flagitiosum sign ficabat, postea transiit in appellationem omnium iniquorum. Subiungit quoque aliam notationem, cùm ait: Peccator item à pectoris caterua cognominatus est, pro eo, quod inibi occulta delictorum conduntur. Sed hæc magis allusiua, quàm vera etymologia est.

IV. Quod concernit II. ὁμωνυμίαν, sciendum, quòd peccatum aliter accipiatur in foro seu politia, aliter in choro seu Ecclesia. Aliud enim Papinianus, aliud Paulus docet, vt scribit Hieronymus in epitaphio

Fabiolae Epist. 30. ca. 1. Politicis & Iureconsultis peccatum nihil aliud est, quam actio a sciente & volente contra rectam rationem, & legem positiuam commissa. Philosophi nonnihil propius accedunt, & ipsos etiam interiores adfectus culpant, & vitijs annumerant; vnde orta sunt praecepta Ethica de adfectuum moderamine. Sed in Theologia latior est acceptio peccati. Hic enim notat omne id, quod contra legem Dei est, siue voluntarium sit, siue involuntarium, & vel a sciente vel ignorante commissum; siue sit defectus, siue habitus, & vel connatus, vel acquisitus, vti mox fusius indicabitur.

V. Illud praeterea hic velut ἐν παρόδῳ obseruari potest, doctrinam Ecclesiae de peccato a doctrina Philosophorum de vitijs, quoad omnia causaru genera differre. Errant enim Philosophi & politici gentiles. 1. Quoad efficientem peccati. Hanc enim vel in fato Stoico; vel in materiae inconstantia, vel alibi quaesierunt. Quid enim illi de hac re sapere potuerunt, qui nec sciuerunt, nec legerunt illud; Per vnum hominem peccatum intrauit in mundum? inquit alicubi Augustinus. 2. Quoad materiam, quia rati sunt, externos tantum actus vel crassiores affectus in vitio esse: nudas vero cogitationes, & quae ex natiuitate habentur, omni culpa vacare. 3. Quoad formam, quia putarunt, peccata esse aberrationes ab humanis duntaxat legibus vel recta ratione. Illam vero exactissimam operum normam, legem diuinam, prout patefacta & in verbo explicata est, ignorarunt. 4. Quoad finem & effectum, Philosophati enim sunt tantum de poenis ciuilibus, & conscientiae morsibus: quod autem promereantur peccata damnationem aeternam, poenasque corporales & spirituales, de hoc altum in gentilismo fuit silentium.

VI. Porro in Scripturis peccatum non modo significat aberrationem a lege, sed etiam, 1. solum reatum, vt Gen. 43, v. 9. Tibi peccabo omnibus diebus, hoc est, peccati reus ero per omnem vitam, 2. sacrificium vel victimam pro peccato, quo sensu sæpè accipitur in Leuitico; & Oseæ 4 vers. 8. dicitur, Peccata populi mei comedunt, id est, sacrificia sic exponente August. l. 3. contra duas epistolas Pelag. cap. 6. Et hunc significatum putant nōnulli obtinere in loco. 2. Cor. 5. vers. 21. Deus Christum pro nobis fecit peccatum, hoc est, victimam pro peccato, quamvis alij commodiùs de imputatione peccati posse exponi censeant.

VIII. Quod tandem III. συνωνυμίαν attinet, multiplex ea est. Inueniuntur enim Synonyma 1. Latina. 2. Græca. 3. Hebraica. IIX. LATINA. Horum benè multa, sed præcipua sunt ista, quòd 1. vocatur, delictum quasi derelictum. Qui enim delinquit, quid relinquit nisi bonum? inquit August. l. 3. qq. supra Leuit. c. 20. Alij sic dictum putant à liquido, quia defluat à stabilitate legis. 2. crimen scelus aut flagitium, quæ omnia idem notant, quod peccatum, sed tamen crassum & enorme. 3. error, quia est aberratio à lege. 4. vitium, quia peccatis vitiatur & corrumpitur animus. 5. culpa, quia semper reatum contrahit, qui peccat. 6. prævaricatio, quia est legis tansgressio: quam vocem Isidorus deducit à varo, id est, obliquo, perverso, cui crura sunt introrsum obtorta. 7. debitum, tum, quia est indebita obedientiæ Deo debitæ neglectio; tùm quia reatum pœnæ debitæ adiunctum habet.

IX. Atque hæc vocabula omnia indiscretè vsurpantur, & generaliter ἀνομίαν vel illegalitatem aut quiddam legi contrarium significant. Scholastici quidem distinguunt inter vitium & peccatum, illudque habitus, hoc operationis malæ nomē esse adfirmant. Bellarm l. 1. de amiss. grat. cap. 2. commissio, inquit, peccatum, omissio delictum propriè dici solet. Et ibidem, inter crimen & peccatum hanc distinctionem ponit, quòd illud mortale, hoc veniale scelus denotet. præterquam quòd fingatur peccatum ex se veniale esse non semper obseruantur istæ differentiæ, vti patet ex libris sacris & Ecclesiasticis. Interim tamen non negamus quandam posse distinctionem inter ista vocabula dari, si ἀκρίβειαν sectemur. Peccatum enim in genere significat quemlibet malum actũ commissum; delictum verò bonum actum omissum; crimen & scelus, peccatum crassum; error peccatum ignorantiæ; vitium, malum habitum; culpa & debitum, reatum: sed vt dixi, discrimina ista non sunt perpetua.

X. 2. GRÆCA, ex quibus vicissim hæc sunt primaria, ἁμαρτία, quæ vox deducitur ab ἁμαρτάνειν, quod est ἄσκοπα τοξεύειν, seu τῶ σκόπῳ ἀποτυχάνειν à scopo aberrare, vnde Suidas ἁμαρτίαν definit, τὴν τῶ ἀγαθῶ ἀποτυχίαν, deflexionem à bono. Nonnulli ἁμαρτίαν ab α priuatiua particula & verbo μάρπτειν, quod esse assequi aut apprehendere, vt sit ἁμαρτία sit aberratio, vel assecutionis priuatio. Alij deriuant à μὴ & ἀρτέω, id est, apto, accommodo, quia peccatum est quiddam ineptum & incongruum. quitas vel iniustitia, 2. ἀδικία, iniquæ sic dicitur à priuatione τῆς δίκης, Quidam ἁμαρτίαν & ἀδικίαν sic distinguunt, quòd illa notet in voluntarium, hæc voluntarium peccatum, quo pertinet illud Demosthenis in oratione περὶ στεφάνου: ἀδικεῖ τις ἄκων, ἠξήμαρτε τις ἑκών. Sed in Scripturis hoc discrimen non habetur. 3. παράπτωμα lapsus vel transgressio, à παραπίπτειν, prætercadere vel à παράπτεσθαι, quod est temerè & aberrante manu aliquid tangere. Hieronym. in cap. 2. ad Ephes. ait; παραπτώματα esse initia peccatorum; ἁμαρτίας, cùm quid opere consummatum peruenit ad finem. Sed vicissim non obseruari hanc distinctionem patet ex Rom. 5. vers. 18. & 7. vers. 5. 4. παρακοή, vel inobedientia, quæ vox plerunque notat peccata actualia & voluntaria. 5. κακία & πονηρία malitia, quibus notantur peccata mortalia. 6. πλημμέλεια delictum vel error, à πλὴν vel πάλιν, & μέλειν, quòd posteriore curâ; quæ semper melior, sarciri dedebeat. Notat ergò propriè omissum, sicut ἁμαρτία commissum.

XII. HEBRAICA. Communiter Hebræis peccatum dicitur חטאה à radice חטא aberrare à scopo, deflectere à via, vel potiùs norma diuinæ legis. Alio nomine vocatur עון iniquitas vel perversitas: illo originale, hoc actuale peccatum notari dicunt, sed Scriptura vtrique attribuit. Plura Synonyma tùm Græca, tùm Hebræa vide apud Chemnitium in l. Com. par, 1, loco de pecc. cap. 2. Flacium parte 1. Clauis col. 850. 851. Dn. D. Gerhardum Tom. 2. de pecc. actual, sect. 8. & 9.


### II. On the real definition of sin

II. On the real definition of sin.

XIII. Sin in general is nothing other than an aberration from a mark, norm, or rule, as appears from the comparison of all the words. Whence to sin, for Cicero in book 3 of the Paradoxa, is to cross over the lines set before one. Hence it is taken not only for moral evil, or the transgression of divine law, but for any deviation whatsoever from a mark: in which sense it is said of the Benjamites in Judges 20, verse 16, that they were the best slingers, so that they did not sin, that is, they never strayed from the target. To this some refer that passage of Job 5, verse 24, "You shall visit your tabernacle and shall not sin," that is, you shall not stray from it, but will easily find it. Whoever, therefore, declines from the mark set before him, at which he was aiming, and deflects from the norm which he ought to have attained, whether it happens in corporal or spiritual matters, this person is said to sin in that regard.

XIIII. But since the norm of natural acts is one thing, that of artificial acts another, and that of moral acts another, hence a threefold aberration from a norm, or a threefold sin, is commonly established: 1. natural, 2. artificial, 3. moral or theological, concerning which alone we are concerned here.

XIV. The norm or rule, indeed, from which theological sin deviates, is solely the will and justice of God. For just as that alone is good which agrees with the divine will, so that alone is evil which departs from the divine will.

XV. There is indeed no other σύμβολον or sign of the divine good pleasure than the law: and that is both ἔμφυτος or inscribed upon hearts, and θεόσδοτος or prescribed through Moses; the former of which we commonly call Nature, the latter Scripture.

XVI. And hence it happens that this symbol of the norm is very often taken for the norm itself, and it is the same thing to deviate from the law as to depart from the divine will and justice, since the former is, as I have said, an expression of the latter.

XVII. And upon these foundations John built his definition of sin, when in 1 Epist. ch. 3, verse 4, he says, ἁμαρτία, ἐστὶν ἀνομία, sin is lawlessness. We judge this definition to be not perfunctory and halved, but full and altogether accurate: so that this may be shown, those things which are included in the single word ἀνομίας must be unfolded.

XVIII. But before this is done, it must be known that there is a twofold acceptance of sin; the one absolute, as it is in the category of quality or action: the other respective, as it inhabits the category of relation. For according to this diverse acceptance, it obtains one material and another formal aspect. For if it is taken respectively, its material is a vicious act or habit; but its formal is guilt or obligation to punishment, in which sense theologians say that the formal of sin is taken away through Baptism, but the material remains. However, sin is not defined here according to the respective acceptance, because it is not related according to being, but according to saying, nor does its whole essence consist in πρός τι: but according to absolute consideration, as for things are, so they are defined. Three things, however, are to be noted concerning the absolute nature of sin, which are made known by the one word ἀνομίας, namely 1. Material, 2. Formal, 3. Guilt or obligation to punishment, concerning which briefly.

XIX. 1. The material holds the place of the genus, and is that everything whatever is comprehended by divine law, whatever it may be, or is so constituted, that it has a certain reason or a certain respect to the law; in one word, it is that very thing which receives ἀταξίαν, illegality; for as matter is the δοχεῖον of all forms: so the material of sin is nothing other than the subject of viciousness and ἀνομαλία.

XX. 2. The formal or specific difference is the very declination or deviation from the law, which is denoted by τὸ μόριον στερητικὸν. For because the νόμος θεῦ is the norm of every good; certainly whatever is alien from this norm, or whatever is ἀνομία, that is, illegality, all this will be evil or sin. And conversely, whatever it is fitting to be numbered among sins, it must be ἀνομία or an exorbitance from the law.

XXI. 3. Because God himself proclaimed through Moses: Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all things which are written in the book of this law, Deut 27, last verse, hence it follows spontaneously that by the name of ἀνομίας the guilt of sin is simultaneously involved, which is nothing other than an obligation to punishment, in respect of which sin is said to be forgiven. For what has been done cannot be made undone, and therefore when God forgives sins already committed, this is understood only as that He releases the guilt, and no longer imputes the misdeeds to us.

XXII. Thus therefore the Apostle John briefly expressed whatever pertains to the essence of sin; which if anyone desires to be proposed more distinctly and by a definition a little more diffuse, he will be able to learn that of Philip Melanchthon in the Worms Colloquy, opposed to Eck, and approved by Luther, which is as follows: Sin is either a defect, or an inclination, or an action fighting against the law of God; offending GOD, condemned by

God, and making not guilty of the eternal wrath of God and of present and eternal punishments, unless remission is made on account of the Son the mediator. Or more briefly: sin is whatever deviates from the norm of the divine law, gravely offending God, and provoking to severe vengeance.

XXIII. From what has been said thus far, we further deduce that not only evil actions, but even the inclinations themselves, and vicious qualities, and indeed even defects, are deservedly numbered among sins. For all these things deviate and dissent from the law, inasmuch as it requires internal holiness of mind and total justice of heart, and therefore works of this kind, which proceed from a nature that is whole and holy in every respect. Hence Flacius rightly warned in part 1 of the Clavis, q. 848, that the word יחם in the first conjugation signifies not only an action, but also an inherent quality or the condition or lot of a man, as in Psalm 51, verse 7: In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother conceived me. Where David does not speak of actual sins, nor does he accuse his mother, but himself, because he was conceived and brought into the light in manifold uncleanness, guilt, and crime. Thus, when the Jews say to the man born blind and healed by Christ, John 9, v. 34: You were born entirely in sins, and do you teach us? they do not indeed strictly refer to the original sin of all men, but they do wish to intimate that he was of such a distorted and perverse nature from the womb that it was not without cause that mother nature marked him with blindness, so that she might testify to all that this man was of a malicious disposition and depraved character.

XXIV. Hence, therefore, it is certain that it is repugnant to the divine law, and therefore is sin, not only a depraved action, but also the natural propensity itself from which the action arises, and the lack of good. For these things follow one another: 1. defect, 2. the affection contrary to the defect, 3. the evil and perverse act flowing from the affection; all of which deviate from the law, and therefore are deservedly numbered among sins. For ἀνομία and ἁμαρτία are ἀντίστροφα, like a definition and the thing defined, since every ἀνομία is at the same time ἁμαρτία and vice versa.

XXV. Wherefore Andradius is very absurd, who in book 3 of the defense of the Council of Trent denies that every ἀνομία is a sin. And the Rheims translators in their annotations on 1 John 3 most ineptly maintain that, while every sin is a deviation from the rule of the law, it is not the converse, that whatever deviates from the law is a sin, so that they may thus exempt the concupiscence adhering to the regenerate from the census of sins. This is, of course, to concede the definition and deny the thing defined; to posit the form and deny the formed. For if something is ἀνομία, why would it not be ἁμαρτία? For I ask, is that ἄνομον either good or evil? Not good, because it is an aberration. If it is evil, then it is either of punishment or of fault. Not of punishment, because this is from God, and therefore does not oppose His will. Therefore, it is an evil of fault, or in one word, a sin.

XXVI. And certainly it is not without malice that the Papists call whatever is repugnant to the constitutions and decrees of the Popes a notable sin, but assert that what deviates from the law of God Himself is indeed ἀνομία, but not ἁμαρτία. This error is as malicious as it is most gross. For in evaluating all things, whether they are good or evil, we observe this order, that we compare them with their norm and measure. If we discover agreement, we designate them as good; if discrepancy, as evil. What arrogance, therefore, it is to be unwilling to evaluate actions that are pleasing or displeasing to God according to the will of God, and the law which is the symbol of His will, which is the sole rule and norm of all actions.

XXVII. Therefore a certain and immovable conclusion stands: Every deviation from the law is by this very fact evil and a sin properly so called, whether it be a moral act or a natural affection, such as concupiscence. This is what the Fathers wished to intimate when they defined sin in the manner of John of the Apostle have defined. For thus Ambrose, book on Paradise, ch. 8: Sin is a transgression of the divine law, and disobedience to heavenly precepts. Chrysostom on ch. 18 of Matthew: Sin is not to obey GOD. Damascene, book 4, On the Orthodox Faith, ch. 23: τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ παράβασις ἁμαρτία ἐστί. Transgression of a precept is sin. And Anselm on Hebrews 2: Sin is either to do things forbidden, or not to do things commanded. XXIIX. The same, as if forgetful of themselves and contrary to themselves, the Scholastics and Papists confess; for Thomas, 1, question 71, article 9, concedes that sin is nothing else than an aberration from the rule and the goal; following whom, Stapleton constitutes the formal nature of sin in that deviation. Both are supported by Bellarmine, book on the loss of grace, ch. 1, where he writes: Sin is to decline and recede from the rule. Now indeed we subsume; that vicious qualities always inherent in our nature decline from the rule of the law, which they themselves in turn do not deny: who therefore will go on to deny what follows from that, namely, that those vicious qualities are sin properly so called? It is the mark of a sophist, not a good disputant, to concede the premises and deny the conclusion that follows immediately.

XXIX. And thus far we have sufficiently explained the definition of sin proposed by the Apostle John: but because some objections are moved against it, therefore the solution or discussion of them, for a better and fuller understanding, remains to be subjoined in a few words.

Latin:

II. De Peccati definitione reali.

XIII. Peccatum in genere nihil aliud est quàm aberratio à scopo, norma aut regula, quemadmodum ex omnium vocabulorum collatione apparet. Vnde peccare Ciceroni libro 3. Parad. est præfixas lineas transilire. Hinc non tantùm pro malo morali, seu transgressione legis diuinæ, sed pro quacunque deuiatione à scopo accipitur: quo sensu de Benjamitis dicitur Iud. 20. v. 16. Illos fuisse optimos fundibularios, ita vt non peccarent, id est, nunquam à meta aberrarent. Hûc referunt nonnulli istud Iohannis 5. vers. 24. Visitabis tabernaculum tuum & non peccabis, hoc est non aberrabis ab eo, sed facilè inuenies; Quicunque igitur declinat à scopo sibi præfixo, in quem collimabat, & deflectit à norma, quam assequi debebat, siue in corporalibus fiat, siue spiritualibus, hic in care peccare dicitur.

XIIII. Quoniam verò alia est norma actuum naturalium, alia artificialium, alia moralium, hinc triplex aberratio à norma, vel triplex peccatum vulgò constituitur, 1. naturale. 2. artificiale. 3. morale seuTheologicum de quo solo hic soliciti sumus.

XIV. Norma vero vel regula, a qua peccatum Theologicum deflectit, est sola Dei voluntas & justitia. Sicut enim id tantum est bonum, quod cum voluntate diuina congruit: ita id tantum malum, quod a voluntate diuina recedit.

XV. Est vero beneplaciti diuini nullum aliud σύμβολον vel signum, quam lex: eaque tum ἔμφυτος vel cordibus inscripta: tum θεόσδοτος, vel per Mosen praescripta; quarum illam Naturae, hanc Scripturae vulgo nuncupamus.

XVI. Atque hinc fit, vt istud normae symbolum saepissime sumatur pro ipsa norma, idemque sit aberrare a lege, atque discedere a voluntate & justitia diuina, quoniam ista hujus, vt dixi, est expressio.

XVII. Et hisce fundamentis suam peccati definitionem superstruxit A Iohannes, quando 1. Epist. c. 3. vers. 4. ἁμαρτία, inquit, ἐστὶν ἀνομία, Peccatum est illegalitas. Quam definitionem non perfunctoriam & dimidiatam sed plenam & omnino accuratam esse judicamus: quod vt ostendatur, evoluenda sunt ea, quae vnico ἀνομίας vocabulo sunt inclusa.

XVIII. Hoc autem antequam fiat, sciendum, quod duplex sit peccati acceptio; altera absoluta, prout est in praedicamento qualitatis, vel actionis: altera respectiua, prout relationis categoriam incolit, Pro diuersa enim hac acceptione, aliud materiale, & aliud formale nanciscitur. Nam si respective sumatur, materiale ejus est vitiosus actus habitusve; formale autem reatus seu obligatio ad poenam, quo sensu dicunt Theologi, quod formale peccati per Baptismum tollatur, materiale vero remaneat, Non autem definitur hic peccatum iuxta respectiuam acceptionem, quia no est relatum secundum esse, sed dici, nec omnis essentia eius in πρός τι consistit: verum juxta considerationem absolutam, prout enim res sunt, ita definiuntur. Tria verô circa absolutum peccati esse notanda sunt, quæ vno ἀνομίας vocabulo innotantur, nempè 1. Materiale 2. Formale, 3. Reatus vel obligatio ad pœnam, de quibus breviter.

XIX. 1. Materiale locum generis habet, & est istud omne quicquid diuinâ lege comprehēditur, quicquid sit, vel ita comparatum est, vt quandam rationem siue respectū quendam ad legem habeat vno verbo, est illud ipsum, quod ἀταξίαν illegalitatem recipit 1. vt enim materia est δοχεῖον omnium formarum: ita materiale peccati nil aliud est, quam subiectum vitiositatis & ἀνομαλία.

XX. 2. Formale seu differentia specifica est ipsa declinatio vel â lege aberrogatio, quæ per τὸ μόριον στερητικὸν denotatur Quia enim νόμος θεῦ omnis boni norma est; Vtiq; quicquid ab hac norma alienum, vel quicquid ἀνομία est sine illegalitas, hoc omne malum erit vel peccatum. Et vicissim, quicquid peccatis annumerari decet, ἀνομία vel exorbitatio à lege sit oportet.

XXI. 3. Quia Deus ipse per Mosen edixit: Maledictus omnis, qui non manserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis huius Deut 27. v. vltimo, hinc spontè sequitur, nomine ἀνομίας simul involui reatum peccati, qui nihil est aliud, quâm obligatio ad pœnam cuius respectu peccatū dicitur remitti. Quod enim factum est, infectum fieri nequit, ideoŕ cùm Deus condonat peccata jam ante commissa, hoc tantum intelligitur, quod soluat reatum, & malefacta non amplius nobis imputet.

XXII. Sic ergo Apostolus Iohannes breviter expsessit, quicquid ad peccati essentiam pertinet; quæ siquis distinctiùs & definitione paulò fusiore proponi cupiat, illam Philippi Melanthonis in Colloquio Wormatiensi Eccio oppositam, & à Luthero approbatam ediscere poterit, quæ sic habet: Peccatum vel est defectus, vel inclinatio, vel actio pugnans cum lege Dei; offendens DEVM, damnata à

Deo, & faciens non reos aterna ira Dei & pœnarum præsentium ac æternarum, nisi fiat remissio propter Filium mediatorū. Vel breuius: peccatum est quicquid à norma legis diuinæ aberrat, grauiter offendens Deum, & ad seueram vindictam prouocans.

XXIII. Ex hactenus verò dictis porrò deducimus, non tantùm actiones malas, sed ipsas etiam inclinationes, & vitiosas qualitates, imo & defectus inter peccata merito numerari. Nam hæc omnia deflectunt & dissentiunt à lege, quippe quæ requirit internam mentis sanctitatem & omnimodam cordis justitiam, adeoque; opera huius modi, quæ à natura integra & vndiquaque sancta proueniant, Hinc rectè monuit Flacius par. 1. Clauis q. 848. quòd verbum יחם in prima Conjugatione non modò actionem, sed qualitatem quoque inhærentem seu conditionem sortemue hominis significet, vt Psal. 51. vers. 7. In iniquitatibus conceptus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Vbi Dauid non loquitur de peccatis actualibus, neque matrem sed semetipsům accusat quòd in multiplici immundicie, reatu & crimine conceptus, atque in lucem sit editus. Sic, cum Iudæi ad cæcum natum, & à Christo sanatum inquiunt, Iohan. 9. v. 43. In peccatis natus est totus, & vis nos docere? non illi quidem propriè in originale peccatum omnium hominum respiciunt, sed tamen innuere, volunt, eum ex vtero ita distortæ & peruerfæ naturæ esse, vt non sinè causa ipsum mater natura cæcitate signauerit, vt omnibus testaretur, hunc hominem esse malitiosi ingenij & deprauatæ indolis.

XXIV. Hinc igitur certum est, diuinæ legi repugnare, ideoque peccatum esse non prauam modò actionem, sed ipsam quoque, à qua oritur actio, naturalem propensionem, bonique carentiam. Hæc enim se inuicem consequuntur 1. defectus a. defectui contrarius adfectus 3. ex adfectu fluens malus & peruersus actus; quæ omnia deflectunt à lege, ideoq; peccatis meritò annumeratur. A'νομία enim & ἁμαρτία sunt ἀντίστροφα, ceu definitio & definitum, siquidem omnis ἀνομία est simul ἁμαρτία & vicissim.

XXV. Quapropter valdè absurdus est Andradius, qui lib. 3. defens. Concil. Trid. negat, quamuis ἀνομίαν peccatum esse. Et Rhemenses in annotationibus super 1. Iohan. 3. ineptissimè statuunt, . omne quidem peccatum esse declinationem à regula legis, sed non contra, peccatum esse, quicquid à lege deflectit, vt ita concupiscentia renatis adhærentem è censu peccatorum eximere possint. Hoc nimirum est definitionem concedere, & definitum negare; formam ponere, & formatum inficiari. Si enim aliquid ἀνομία est, cur ἁμαρτία non foret? Quæro enim, istud ἄνομον aut bonum sit, vel malum? Non bonum, quia est aberratio. Si malum. E. vel pœnæ, vel culpæ. Non pœnę, quia hęc à Deo est, ideoque voluntati eius non aduersatur. E. malū culpæ est, vel vno verbo, pecatū.

XXVI. Et certè malitia non caret, quòd Papicolę appellant insigne peccatum, quicquid constitutionibus & decretis Pontificum repugnat: quod verò ab ipsius Dei lege deflectit, ἀνομίαν quidem, sed non ἁμαρτίαν esse asserunt. Qui error vt malitiosus, ita crassissimus est. In omnibus enim rebus æstimandis an bonæ sint vel malæ, hunc obseruamus ordinem, vt illas conferamus cum sua norma & mensura. Si deprehendimus conuenientiam, bonas; si discrepantiam, malas indigitamus. Quæ igitur petulantia est, actiones Deo placentes, vel displicentes æstimare nolle, secundum voluntatem Dei, voluntatisque σύμβολον legem, quæ actionum omnium regula & norma est vnica.

XXVII. Stat ergo certa & immota conclusio: Omnem à lege deflexionem, hoc ipso malum & peccatum propriè dictum esse, siue actus sit moralis, siue affectus naturalis, vt concupiscentia. Quod ipsum Patres innuere voluerunt, quando peccatum ad modum Iohannis Apostoli definiërunt. Ita enim Ambrosius l. de Parad. c. 8. Peccatum est legis divinæ prævaricatio, & cælestium inobedientia præceptorum. Chrysost. in cap. 18. Matth. Peccatum est DEO non obedire. Damasc. l. 4. O F. c. 23. τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ παράβασις ἁμαρτία ἐστί. Transgressio precepti est peccatum. Et Anshelmus super 2. Hebr. Peccatum est vel facere vetita, vel non facere iussa. XXIIX. Idem, velut sui obliti, sibique contrarij fatētur Scholastici & Pontificij Thomas enim 1. quæst. 7. 1. art. 9. cōcedit, peccatū nihil esse aliud, quàm aberrationem à regula & scopo; quem sequens Stapletonus formalem peccati rationem in ista deuiatione constituit. Vtrique adstipulatur Bell. l. de amiss. gra. c. 1. vbi scribit: Peccatum esse à regulà declinare & recedere. Iam verò subsumim⁹; Qualitates vitiosas naturæ nostræ semper inhærētes à regulà legis declinare, quod ipsum vicissim non diffitentur: Qui ergò negatum ibunt, quod inde sequitur, nimirum, qualitates istas vitiosas peccatum esse propriè dictum? Sophistæ est, non boni disputatoris, præmissas concedere, & conclusionem immediatè sequentem inficiari.

XXIX. Et hactenus definitionem peccati, ab A. Iohanne propositam satis explicuimus: quia verò nonnullæ obiectiones contrà mouentur, idcirco λύσις illarum vel discussio, ad meliorem plenioremque intelligentiam, paucis subiungenda restat.


### Objection I

OBJECTION I.

XXX. In every true definition two distinct concepts are to be posited, one is called of agreement and material; the other of difference and formal, from 2 Posterior Analytics 13, § 2. But the Apostle John posited one word, anomia: who therefore will note such distinct concepts? For a word is the index and parent of only one concept. Response: In any word two things are observed, both the material, which are the letters and syllables; and the formal, which is the meaning. With this presupposed, we say that the term ἀνομία is indeed one materially, because it is one word: yet not formally or in meaning, because it involves many things. For when illegality is named, there is immediately posited: 1. aberration in general: 2. aberration from the law in species: 3. the essential consequence of aberration, or guilt: the former implies the genus, the latter the difference, and this the effect of sin. Wherefore, if those things which the one word ἀνομίας includes are recounted distinctly, a full definition consisting of distinct terms will emerge, namely such: Sin is an aberration from the divine law, drawing eternal damnation.

OBJECTION II.

XXXI: Error concerning the doctrine of the Gospel is a sin, and yet it is not ἀνομία. Wherefore the definition will be too narrow: since it does not comprehend all species of sin.

Response 1. There are those who distinguish between unbelief and lawlessness, in this sense, that the former signifies errors of doctrine, the latter sins of conduct. For just as faith in Christ is one thing, and works commanded by the law are another: so they judge that their contraries, namely infidelity and impiety, also differ in genus. And thus they deny the antecedent, namely, that an error against the Gospel is a sin properly so called.

2. Just as sin, so lawlessness is taken in two ways. For sin is used: 1. generally, for everything that is contrary to either the law or the Gospel. 2. specifically, for that which is only opposed to the law. Similarly, lawlessness is taken in a double sense: 1. generally, for everything that deviates from the will of God, whether you understand it as legal or evangelical. For since law in general is nothing other than the expression of the divine will, and this has truly been revealed not only through the doctrine of Moses, which is the law of works, but also through the doctrine of the Gospel, which is called the law of faith by the Apostle, it certainly follows that it denotes also ἀνομία itself or illegality in general, as any disobedience, fighting against the justice and will of God. 2. Specifically for that which transgresses the moral law or the law of works. With this distinction presupposed, we say that the term ἀνομία in the Johannine definition can be correctly accepted the law of works, and in that sense infidelity or error concerning the Gospel is correctly called both ἀνομία and ἁμαρτία.

3. Even if the word ἀνομία is taken only specifically, we can nevertheless not inconveniently refer ἀπιστία to it. For does not the first table, and its first commandment, since it requires faith and obedience toward God in general, consequently punish and condemn all ἀπιστία and disobedience, and therefore also that by which someone is incredulous toward the Gospel, the very word of God? For where the whole genus is prohibited, it is beyond doubt that all species of the genus are prohibited at the same time.

Therefore, to conclude, Error against the Gospel is most truly called sin and illegality, both in a general sense, because it deviates from the Evangelical will of God or the law of faith, and especially in a specific sense, because it violates the first commandment of the moral law concerning obedience toward GOD.

Latin:

OBIECTIO I.

XXX. In omni verá definitione duo distincti conceptus sunt ponendi, alter conuenientiæ & materiale; alter differentiæ & formale dicitur, ex 2. post. 13. §. 2. Apostolus verò Iohannes vnum ἀνομίας vocabulum posuit: Qui ergò tam distinctos conceptus notabit? Vox enim vnà non nisi vnius conceptus index & parens est. Resp. In quauis voce spectantur duo, tum materiale, quod sunt literæ & syllabæ: tum formale, quod est significatio. Quo præsupposito dicimus ἀνομίαν vocabulum esse quidem vnum materialiter, quia est vna dictio: non tamen formaliter vel significatione, quia multa inuoluit. Nominatâ enim illegalitate, statim ponitur, 1. aberratio ingenere: 2. aberratio à lege in specie: 3. aberrationis essentiale consequens, vel reatus: illud genus, illud differentiam, hoc effectum peccati subinnuit. Quare, si distinctim recenseantur, quæ vnum ἀνομίας vocabulum includit, plena distinctisque terminis constans prodibit definitio, nempè talis: Peccatum est aberratio à lege diuina, damnationem æternam attrahens.

OBIECTIO. II.

XXXI: Error circa doctrinam Euangelij peccatum est, & tamen ἀνομία non est. Quare definitio nimis erit angusta: cùm omnes peccati species non comprehendat:

Respond. 1. Sunt qui distinguant inter ἀπιστίαν & ἀνομίαν, hoc sensu, quòd illa errores doctrinæ, hæc peccata morum significet. Vt enim aliud est fides in Christu; & aliud sunt opera lege præcepta: sic etiam genere differre censent eorum contraria, nempè infidelitatem & impietatem. Atque ita negant Antecedens, nimirum, quòd error contra Euangelium sit peccatum propriè dictum.

2. Quemadmodum ἁμαρτία, sic ἀνομία dupliciter accipitur, Peccatum enim vsurpatur. 1. γενικῶς, pro omni eo, quod contrariatur vel legi vel Euangelio. 2. εἰδικῶς pro eo, quod tantùm aduersatur legi. Similiter ἀνομία duplici sensu sumitur, 1. generaliter, pro omni eo quod à Dei voluntate deflectit, siue legalem vel Euangelicam intelligas. Cùm enim lex in genere nihil sit aliud, quàm diuinæ voluntatis expressio, & verè hæc non tantùm per doctrinam Mosis, quæ lex factorum, sed etiam per doctrinam Euangelij, quæ lex fidei nuncupatur ab Apostolo, patefacta sit, consequitur certè, ipfam quóque ἀνομίαν vel illegalitatem in genere quamuis inobedientiam, cum Dei iustitia & voluntate pugnantem denotare. 2. Specialiter pro eo, quòd legem moralem vel legem factorum tranfgreditur. Quâ distinctione præsupposita, dicimus vocabulum ἀνομίας in definitione Iohannæa rectè accipi posse generaliter, pro illegalitate quauis, & contra legem fidei, & contra legem factorum, eoque sensu infidelitas erroruè circà Euangelium & ἀνομία & ἁμαρτία rectè dicitur.

3. Si maximè tantùm specialiter vox ἀνομίας sumatur, tamen eò ἀπιστίαν non incommode referre possumus. Prima enim tabula, primumque eius præceptum, cum fidem & obedientiam erga Deum requirit in genere, annon consequenter omnem ἀπιστίαν & inobedientiam, adeoque illam etiam, quâ quis Euangelio, ipsius Dei verbo, sit incredulus castigat & condemnat? Nam vbi totum genus prohibetur, omnes simul generis species prohiberi extra dubium est.

Proinde, vt concludamus, Error contra Euangelium verissimè peccatum & illegalitas dicitur, tùm sensu generali, quia deflectit à voluntate Dei Euangelica vel lege fidei, tũ imprimis speciali quia violat primum legis moralis præceptum de obedientia erga DEVM.


### Objection III

OBJECTION III.

XXXII. If everything that is repugnant to the law is sin, it follows that devils and wicked men also, on account of that repugnance, are sin, which is absurd.

Resp. This is a puerile sophism of Andradius; because it plays on the ambiguity of the phrase, To be repugnant to the law.

For 1. it is taken either formally and abstractly, for ἀνομία itself; or materially and concretely, for the subject of ἀνομία; in the former sense whatever is repugnant to the law, this is sin; but not in the latter.

Therefore the deception of the argument will soon appear, if the Greek terms are substituted, as Every ἀνομία is ἁμαρτία: Now let it be subsumed, Devils & men are: what? surely ἀνομία itself? false. What then? ἄνομοι. From this however it by no means follows, that they are ἁμαρτία itself or sin, since ἀνομία and ἄνομον, sin and the subject of sin, an inherent accident and a receiving substance, are far different things.

2. Something is repugnant to the law either καθ' αὑτὸ, by itself, or δι' ἄλλο, by another. The former is sin, the latter is not. Now indeed devils and impious men are repugnant to the law not ὀσιωδῶς, by essence, but δι' ἄλλο, by and because of another, namely inherent malice. As therefore the impious are indeed repugnant, but are not repugnance itself: ἄνομοι, not ἀνομία, lawless, not lawlessness: so they are rightly called sinners, but not sin itself.

This can be declared by a similar argument, as, It does not follow, Whatever is conformable to the law, is a good work. The nature of angels is conformable to the law. Therefore a good work. Likewise, To give each his own is justice, Aristides gave each his own. Therefore he was justice. There is, I say, no consequence here, because the abstract and the concrete, τὸ καθ' αὑτὸ and δι' ἄλλο, are always confused.

OBJECTION IV.

XXXIII. Finally, the Papists oppose the authority of Blessed Augustine, who in book 22 against Faustus, chapter 27, defines it by a word, deed, or desire against the eternal law, from which they conclude that vicious qualities adhering to nature are not properly sins, because they are not words or deeds or desires.

Resp. Augustine there defines actual sin, nor does he wish this to be opposed to original sin, for which he fights most vehemently elsewhere, and proves by many arguments that it is contrary to the divine law. Wherefore they pervert his mind, whoever hawk that definition as general and oppose it to the sin of nature. Bellarmine himself saw this, and therefore in book 4, chapter 10, column 276. lit. D. admits that Augustine there defined not every sin, but only actual sin.
