And before him Bonaventure, following the opinion of the Master on book 2 of the Sentences, dist. 35, art. 1, 1, fol. 529. b., did not hesitate to write: The aforesaid definition (he understands Augustine's) is of actual and mortal sin.

XXXIV. Since therefore the objections heard thus far have been of no weight or moment, we deservedly retain that definition of John as most accurate, because it clearly expresses the very nature of sin and sufficiently includes all species, namely anomian, both original and actual; which is either inurion in internal motions, which Augustine calls to covet against the law; or paraphainousa, situated in external utterances and acts, which Augustine calls a word or deed against the law: Wherefore it can not inappropriately be attributed to this definition what Scaliger writes concerning the word autarkes coined by himself in Ex. 365, sect. 2, that it expresses its defined object with an admirable scope of meaning and comprehends all species of the defined.

Latin:

OBIECTIO III.

XXXII. Si omne, quòd repugnat legi peccatum est, sequitur, Diabolos etiam hominesque sceleratos, ob istam repugnantiam peccatum esse, quod absurdum.

Resp. Puerile hoc Andradij sophisma est; quia ludit ambigitate phraseos, Repugnare legi.

Nam 1. accipitur vel formaliter & abstractè, pro ipsa ἀνομίᾳ; vel materialiter & concretè, pro subiecto ἀνομίᾳ; Priori sensu quicquid legi repugnat, hoc peccatum est; sed non posteriori.

Mox ergo fucus argumenti apparebit, si Græci termini substituuntur, vt Omnis ἀνομία est ἁμαρτία: Iam subsumatur, Diaboli & homines sunt: quidnam? num ἀνομία ipsa? falsum. Quid ergo? ἄνομοι. Hinc autem minimè sequitur, esse ipsam ἁμαρτίαν vel peccatum, cùm longe aliud sit ἀνομία & ἄνομον, peccatum & peccati subiectum, accidens inhærens, & substantia recipiens.

2. Repugnat aliquid legi vel καθ' αὑτὸ, per se, vel δι' ἄλλο per aliud. Illud peccatum est, hoc non est. Iam verò diaboli & homines impij repugnant legi non ὀσιωδῶς, καθ' αὑτὸ, & per essentiam, sed δι' ἄλλο per & propter aliud, nempè inhærentem malitiam. Vt ergò impij repugnant quidem, sed non sunt ipsa repugnantia: ἄνομοι, non ἀνομία, illegales, non illegalitas: ita peccatores rectè dicuntur, sed non peccatum ipsum.

Declarari hoc potest simili argumento, vt, Non sequitur, Quicquid legi conforme est, bonum opus est. Angelorum natura est legi conformis. Ergo bonum opus. Item, Suum cuique tribuere est iustitia, Aristides suum cuique tribuit. Ergo iustitia fuit. Nulla, inquam, hic sequela est, quia semper confunditur abstractum & concretum, τὸ καθ' αὑτὸ & δι' ἄλλο.

OBIECTIO IV.

XXXIII. Tandem opponunt Papicolæ authoritatem B. Augustini, qui l. 22. contra Faustum. cap. 27. definit per dictum, factum, vel concupitum contra legem æternam, ex quo concludunt, vitiosas qualitates naturæ adhærentes propriè peccata non esse, quia non sint dicta vel facta, vel concupita.

Resp. Augustinus ibi definit peccatum actuale, nec hoc opponi vult peccato originali, quippè pro quo alibi vehementissimè pugnat, & legi diuinæ adversari multis argumentis probat. Quare mentem eius peruertunt, quicunq; definitionem istam pro generali venditant & peccato naturæ opponunt. Vidit hoc ipse Bell. ideoque l. 4. c. 10. col. 276. lit. D. fatetur, Augustinum ibi non omne, sed duntaxat actuale peccatum definiuisse. Et ante eum Bonaventura ex sententia Magistri super l. 2. sent. dist. 35. art. 1. 1. fol. 529. b. scribere no dubitavit: Praedicta definitio (Augustini intelligit) est peccati actualis & mortalis.

XXXIV. Cum igitur obiectiones hactenus auditae, nullius fuerint ponderis aut momenti; merito definitione illam Iohannis vt accuratissimam retinemus, quia ipsam peccati naturam luculenter exprimit, omnesque species sufficienter includit, nempe anomian tum originalem, tum actualem; quae vel est inurion in internis motibus, quos Augustinus nominat concupiscere contra legem; vel paraphainousa, in externis locutionibus & actibus sita, quos Augustinus dictum vel factum contra legem appellat: Quocirca definitioni huic, non incommode tribui potest, quod de voce autarkes a se excogitata scribit Scaliger Ex 365. sect. 2. eam admirabili ambitu significatus definitum suum exprimere, omnesque definiti species comprehendere.


### Question II Is every sin voluntary?

QUESTION II.

Is every sin voluntary?

1. The Papists affirm, having abused the saying of Augustine which is read in the book On True Religion, chapter 14: Sin is a voluntary evil to such an extent that it is in no way a sin if it is not voluntary. Hence those Papistic flowers: It is not properly against the law unless it is voluntary. For the law is not properly given except to those who have the use of free will, Bellarm. book 1 On the Loss of Grace, chapter 1, col. 594. D. Sin intrinsically requires a free will, nor can it be understood how something is properly a sin if it is not properly free, book 2 On Grace, chapter 7, col. 774. C: Sin in itself cannot be distinct unless it has been willed and intended in itself. Col. 575. A. But they dispute these things to this end, that they might be able to maintain that concupiscence in the regenerate is not sin, and that therefore the law can be perfectly fulfilled by them.

II. We indeed hold the negative, and against the Papists who affirm it, we oppose this truly theological rule: For the definition of sin, it is sufficient that there be τὸ ἄνομον [lawlessness] or that τὸ ἑκούσιον [voluntariness] be absent. In order that the truth of this rule may be demonstrated, certain arguments must be noted by which it is firmly proven that the voluntary is not of the essence of sin. There are, in fact, four principal ones of these, of which we shall speak in order.

III. 1. From the silence of John. If τὸ ἑκούσιον [the voluntary] were of the essence of sin, John's definition, since he defines it by ἀνομία [lawlessness] alone, would be imperfect. But this is absurd, and not to be attributed to such an Apostle; for all the pious, and not a few from among the Papists, receive it as full and accurate with thanksgiving. Because, therefore, the Apostle makes no mention at all of the voluntary, we rightly conclude that it does not enter into the ὑσίαν [essence] of sin.

IV. 2. From the testimony of Paul, which is twofold. For 1. Rom. 7:15, he affirms concerning himself: 'Not what I will, the good, this I do, but what I hate, that I do,' v. 16: 'If, however, what I do not will, this evil I do.' Now, indeed, the evil that we do is fault; the evil that we suffer is punishment. Wherefore, that evil also which Paul did was an evil of fault, and therefore sin; whence he says that he was sold under sin, verse 14. From which we now infer thus: What Paul did, this he did not will, but hated. What Paul did, this was sin. Therefore, a certain sin is not voluntary, but joined with the detestation of the will. 2. Gal. 5:17: 'The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things that you will.' Here I ask in turn, what was that which the Galatians are said to do against their will? It certainly was not good, because the will desires this, it does not flee from it. Therefore it was evil: And because it was not punishment, it was an evil of fault, or sin. Whence we again conclude: If a certain sin can be committed by one who is unwilling, then certainly it will not be voluntary by the reason and definition of sin; otherwise there would follow an ἀντίφασις or contradiction.

V. 3. Concerning sins of ignorance and infirmity. For all sins are of one genus, but some are of infirmity, others of lack of skill, others of malice, as Augustine himself testifies in his 83 Questions, question 26. And yet all are truly and properly called sins, from which it follows that not all are voluntary, nor always committed by one who knows and wills. Moses speaks of sins of ignorance, Num. 15, verse 27: If a soul shall sin through imprudence. Verse 28: The priest shall reconcile it for its sin, which the LXX call ἁμαρτίαν ἀκούσιον, an involuntary sin; and David, Psalm 19, verse 13: Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from my hidden ones. Nor are other examples lacking in the Scriptures. For Genesis 12, verse 17: Pharaoh, out of ignorance of Abraham, asked for his wife as a spouse, and yet for that reason God punished him. Genesis 20, verse 2. Abimelech takes Sarah, vers. 6. The Lord says: I know that you have done this with a simple heart, and I therefore prevented you from sinning against me. Acts 3. vers. 20. You did it in ignorance. 1. Tim. 1 v. 13. I did it in ignorance. Gal. 6. v. 1 If a man be overtaken in any fault &c. And Bellarmine himself in l. 1. c. 3. concedes that certain sins are committed out of infirmity and ignorance, and he opposes these to sins of malice. From all of which we argue: Whatever is committed out of ignorance and infirmity is not voluntary. For otherwise the distinction between sins of infirmity and of malice would be removed; since they are distinguished in this, that the latter are voluntary, the former involuntary; the latter with assent, the former without assent. For the will is suddenly snatched away by the former, and is led, as it were, off course. But certain sins are committed out of ignorance and infirmity, as we have proved. Therefore, certain sins are not voluntary, which was to be demonstrated.

To this pertains that statement of Augustine, book 2 against Julian, chapter 15: Even he who has sinned unknowingly is not inappropriately said to sin UNWILLINGLY. Even the sounder philosophers do not exempt from blame those things which are done ἀκουσίως (involuntarily) and through ignorance, as is evident from Ethics 3.1. And that statement from Ethics 3.5 is well known: ὀὐδεὶς ἑκὼν πονηρὸς ἐδ' ἄκων μάκαρ, No one is wicked willingly, nor happy unwillingly.

VI. 4. From original sin. If nothing is properly a sin unless it is a voluntary act and committed by one's own will, original sin will be denied. For this is propagated before any use of the will into us while we are clearly unaware, to such an extent that infants themselves are called sinners, Rom. 3:9, 23; 5:12, and by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:3. And certainly the Papists will never be able to demonstrate the sin of nature against the Pelagians as long as they hold to this hypothesis concerning the voluntary. For in his book On the Loss of Grace, chapter 8, column 91 D, Bellarmine writes: Sins that are entirely involuntary, among those who can judge correctly, are not venial, but are nothing. I subsume: The sin of origin in infants is entirely involuntary. For they lack every exercise of the will. Therefore the Pelagian conclusion follows, that the sin of origin is nothing. Conversely, book 2 on grace, chapter 7, column 594, book [?]. It cannot be understood how something is properly a sin if it is not properly free. Therefore, an action which is not free in itself does not have a malice distinct from the malice of its cause. I subsume again: Original sin in us, and therefore that which in itself, insofar as it inheres in us, is not properly free. Therefore, because involuntary malice is not distinct from the malice of the cause, it follows that the malice of original sin is none other than the malice of actual sin, once committed by Adam, which was the impious and profane opinion of Pighius.

VII. However, we do not deny that Augustine also said that the sin of origin, as it is naturally propagated, is voluntary, namely by a will not one's own but another's. For in book 1 On Marriage and Concupiscence, chapter 28, he calls that voluntary by the will of the first parent, in whom all have sinned; following whom Bonaventure in [book] 2.

dist. 1, quest. 3. He says that original sin is voluntary, not by the will of him in whom it is, but by the will of him from whom it is. But we judge with Chemnitz (part 1, Exam. page 89) that this answer of Augustine, given to the Pelagians, is more subtle and ingenious than true and accurate. For it follows that original sin, because it is properly voluntary not in us but only in Adam, is not sin properly so called in us, but only in Adam.

VIII. Wherefore we maintain that this stain of sin, ingenerated and inherent in us, is most rightly called involuntary: 1. because it is hereditary and natural. But voluntary things are not natural, since they are opposites; for the latter are contingent, the former necessary. 2. Because the motions of sin are involuntary, so much so that for this reason Paul often affirms that he does what he does not want to do. If therefore the motions of sin are such, how much more must the thing itself be involuntary? 3. Because in more mature age we do not consent, but rather are saddened on account of it, and are indignant at our first parents because by their fall they drew such corruption upon us.

IX. Therefore, when the Jesuits object with the statement of Augustine concerning the voluntary, let them hear Augustine himself, book 1 against Julian, chapter 5, explaining his mind thus: You think in vain that there is no sin in infants because there is no will in them; it cannot be. For these things are rightly said OF THE PROPER SIN OF EACH ONE, not of the contagion of original sin, which nevertheless itself also took its beginning from the first evil will of man. You hear here the opposition between original sin and personal or actual sins, and that his opinion concerning the voluntary is not to be expounded universally, but restricted to proper and mortal sins. For Augustine accepted the word 'sin' in the same sense, when he requires the voluntary, as the Apostle James does, when in chapter 1 of his epistle, verse 15, he says: Lust, when it has conceived, brings forth sin, namely, reigning and mortal. Hence in book 1 of the Retractations, chapter 13, he writes expressly that the doctrine concerning original sin does not prejudice that political opinion: that nothing is a sin unless it is done by one who knows and wills it.

Latin:

QVAESTIO II.

An omne peccatum sit voluntarium?

1. Pontificij adfirmant, abusi dicto Augustini, quod legitur l. de vera religione. cap. 14. Vsque adeo peccatum voluntarium est malum, vt nullo modo sit peccatum, si non sit voluntarium. Hinc illi Flosculi Papistici. Non est proprie contra legem, nisi id, quod est voluntarium. Neque enim lex proprie datur, nisi ijs, qui habent vsum liberi arbitrij, Bellarm. lib. 1. de amiss. gra. cap. 1. coll. 594. D. Peccatum intrinsece requirit liberam voluntatem, nec potest intelligi, quomodo aliquid sit proprie peccatum, si non sit proprie liberum, libro 2. de gra. cap. 7. coll. 774. C: Peccatum in se dssinctum non potest esse, nisi fuerit Volitum & intentum in se. Coll. 575. A. Haecautem eo fine disputant, vt cōcupiscentiam in renatis peccatum non esse ideoque legem perfecte ab ijs impleri posse, obtinere queant.

II. Negatiuam vero nos tenemus, & Papicolis affirmantibus regulam hanc vere Theologicam opponimus Ad peccati rationem satis est, τὸ ἄνομον siue absit τὸ ἑκούσιον. Cuius regulā veritas vt demonstretur annotanda sunt quædam argumenta, quibus voluntarium de ratione peccati non esse, firmiter euincatur. Sunt verò illorum potissimum quatuor, de quibus ordine dicemus.

III. 1. Iohannis silentio. Si τὸ ἑκούσιον foret de peccati essentia, Iohannis definitio, cùm per solam ἀνομίαν definit, imperfecta esset. Hoc verò absurdum, & tanto Apostolo non tribuendum, Omnes enim pij, & ex Pontificijs non pauci, eam, vt plenam & accuratam, cum gratiarum actione recipiunt. Quia igitur voluntarij planè non meminit Apostolus, peccati ὑσίαν illud non ingredi rectè concludimus.

IV. 2. A pauli testimonio, quod geminum, Nam. 1. Rom. 7. v. 15. de seipso adfirmat; Non, quod volo, bonum, hoc, ago, ἀλλ’ ὅ μισῶ quod Opi, illud facio, v. 16. Si autem ὃ ὐ θέλω quod No LO, malum hoc ago. Iam verò malum, quod agimus culpa; malum, quod patimur, pœna est. Quapropter & malum illud, quod Paulus egit, malum culpæ, adeoq; peccatum fuit; vnde Propter hoc sese sub peccato venundatum dicit, vers. 14. Ex quo nunc ita inferimus: Quod Paulus egit, hoc non voluit, sed odit. Quod Paulus egit, hoc peccatum fuit. Ergo quoddam peccatum est non voluntarium, sed cum detestatione voluntatis coniunctum. 2 Gal. 5. vers. 17. Caro concupiscit aduersus Spiritum, Spiritus aduersus carnem, vt non quæ vultis, illa faciatis. Hic vicissim quæro quid fuerit istud quod nolentes facere dicuntur Galatæ? Bonum certè non fuit, quia hoc voluntas appetit, non fugit. Ergo malum: Et quia non pœna, fuit malum culpæ, vel peccatum. Vnde rursus colligimus: Si quoddam peccatum à nolente potest fieri, tum vtique voluntarium non erit de ratione & definitione peccati: aliàs enim fequeretur ἀντίφασις vel contradictio.

V. 3. A peccatis ignorantiae & infirmitatis. Nam omnia peccata sunt vnius generis, sed aliqua sunt infirmitatis, alia imperitiae, alia malitiae, teste ipso Augustino qq. lib. 83. quaest. 26. Et tamen omnia sunt verè proprieque dicta peccata, ex quo sequitur, non omnia esse voluntaria nec semper à sciente & volente commissa. De peccatis autem ignorantiae loquitur Moses, Num. 15. vers. 27. Si anima per imprudentiam peccauerit. vers. 28. Sacerdos reconciliabit eam pro peccato suo, quod LXX. vocant ἁμαρτίαν ἀκούσιον, peccatum inuoluntarium; Et Dauid Psalm. 19. vers. 13. Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me. Nec desunt alia in Scripturis exempla. Nam Genes. 12. vers. 17. Pharao ex ignorantia Abrahae vxorem in coniugem postulauit, & tamen ob id Deus illum puniuit. Genesis 20. vers. 2. Abimelech accipit Saram, vers. 6. dicit Dominus: Noui quod simplici corde fecisti hoc, prohibui itaque ne peccares mihi. Act. 3. vers. 20. Per ignorantiam fecistis. 1. Tim. 1 v. 13. Ignorans feci. Gal. 6. v. 1 Si praeoccupatus fuerit homo delicto aliquo &c. Et Bell ipse l. 1. c. 3. concedit, quaedam peccata committi ex infirmitate & ignorantia eaque opponit peccatis ex malitia. Ex quibus omnibus argumentamur: Quicquid ex ignorantia & infirmitate committitur, voluntarium non est. Aliàs enim tolleretur discrimen inter peccata infirmitatis & malitiae; Siquidem in eo distinguuntur, quod hae sint voluntaria, illae involuntaria; hae cum assensu, illae sine assensu. Voluntas enim per illa subitò abripitur, & quasi transuersa ducitur. Atqui peccata quaedam ex ignorantia & infirmitate committuntur, vti probauimus, Ergo peccata quaedam non sunt voluntaria, quod erat demonstrandum.

Ethuc pertinet illud Aug l. 2. contra Iul. cap. 15, Etiam qui nesciens peccauit, non incongruenter NOLENS peccare dicitur. Ipsi etiam saniores Philosophi, ea quæ ἀκουσίως & per ignorantiam fiunt, à culpâ non eximunt, vti patet ex 3 Ethic. 1. Et notum est illud ex 3. Eth. 5. ὀὐδεὶς ἑκὼν πονηρὸς ἐδ' ἄκων μάκαρ, Nemo volens malus, nec inuitus felix.

VI. 4. A peccato originali Si nihil est propriè peccatum, nisi quod actum voluntarium, propriâque voluntate commissum est, negabitur peccatum originale. Hoc n. ante omnem voluntatis vsum in nos planè inscios propagatur, adeò vt infantes ipsi dicantur peccatores, Rom. 3. v. 9. 23. c. 5. v. 12. naturâq; filij ὀργ., Eph. 2. v. 3. Et certè nunquam poterunt Pontificij peccatum naturæ contra Pelagianos demonstrare, quamdiu hâc de voluntario hypothesin tenuerint. Nam l. de Amiss gra. ca. 8. col. 91. D. scribit Bell. Peccata prorsus involūtaria apud eos qui rectè iudicare possunt, non venalia, sed nulla sunt. Subsumo: Peccatum originis in infantibus est prorsus inuoluntarium. Carent enim omni voluntatis exercitio, Sequitur ergo cōclusio Pelagiana, quòd peccatum originis nullum sit. Vicissim l. 2. de gratia c. 7. col. 594. lib. c. Non potest intelligi, quomodo aliquid sit propriè peccatum, si non sit propriè liberum. Proinde actio, quæ non est libera in se non habet malitiam distinctam à malitia causæ suæ. Subsumo iterum: Originale peccatum in nobis, adeòq; quæ in se quatenus nobis inhæret, non est propriè liberum. Ergo quia malitia inuoluntary n n est distincta à malitia causæ, sequitur, quòd malitia peccati originalis nulla sit alia, quàm malitia peccati actualis, ab Adamo quondam commissi, quæ Pighij fuit impia & profana sententia.

VII. Non autem diffitemur Augustinum originis quoq; peccatum prout naturaliter propagatur, dixisse voluntarium nempè voluntate non propriâ sed aliená. Nam l. 1. de nupt. & concupisc. c 28. appellat istud voluntarium voluntate primi parentis, in quo omnes peccârunt; quem sequens Bonauentura in 2.

dist 1. quæst. 3. peccatum originale voluntarium esse ait, non voluntate ejus, in quo est, sed voluntate ejus, à quo est. Verùm censemus cum Chemnicio (part. 1, Exam. pagina. 89. ) hanc Augustini responsionem, Pelagianis datam, magis subtilem & argutam, quam veram & accuratam esse. Sequitur enim, quòd originis peccatum, quia non in nobis, sed in Adamo tantùm propriè est voluntarium, non etiam in nobis sit, sed in Adamo tantùm peccatum propriè dictum.

IIX. Quocirca statuimus, labem istam peccati nobis ingeneratam & inhærentem rectissimè involuntariam dici, 1. quia est hæreditaria & naturalis. Voluntaria autem non sunt naturalia, quippe opposita, ista enim sunt contingentia hæc necessaria. quia motiones peccati sunt involuntariæ, adeò, vt propterea Paulus sēpè se, quod nolit, facere adfirmet. Si ergo tales sunt peccati motus, quantò magis ipsumerit involuntarium? quia in ætate adultiori non consentimus, sed ob id potiùs tristamur, primisŃue parentibus indignamur, quod tantam nobis corruptionem lapsu suo attraxerint.

IX. Proinde cùm Iesuitæ dictum Augustini de voluntario obijciunt; audiant ipsum Augustinum l.contra Iulianum c 5. mentem suam ita explicantem: Frustrà putas, ideo in paruulis nullum esse delictum, quia in eis nulla est; esse non potest. Hæc enim rectè dicuntur DE PROPRIO CVI VSQVE PECCATO, non de originalis peccati contagio, quod tamen & ipsum à prima hominis mala voluntate sumsit exordium, Audis hîc oppositionem inter peccatum originale, & peccata personalia vel actualia, illamŃue de voluntario sententiam non vniuersaliter exponi, sed ad peccata propria & mortalia restringi. Eodem enim sensu vocem peccati accepit Augustinus, quando requirit voluntarium, quo postolus Iacobus, cùm cap. 1. suæ epistolæ v. 15. Concupiscensia, inquit, si conceperit, parit peccatum, videlicet regnans & mortale. Hinc l. 1. Retract. c. 13. expressê scribit, dotrinâ de peccato originali non praeiudicare politicam istam sententiam. Nihil esse peccatum, nisi fiat à sciente & volente.


### Question VI. Was sin absolutely necessary?

QUESTION VI. Was sin absolutely necessary?

I. There were formerly, and there still are, those who dream that sin was introduced by inevitable necessity. Partly because God could not have manifested His glory without sin; partly because, given one of two contraries, the other must also be posited. We shall treat of the former in the following disputation; concerning the latter, we shall now add a few words.

II. Thus, therefore, they philosophize: A contrary not only does not exist in the nature of things without its contrary, but it cannot even be understood or conceived by the mind. With one of them removed, the other is immediately removed; wherefore, with one posited, the other is immediately posited. And the reason is at hand, because the same thing is not opposed to itself, but every contrariety exists between two; and therefore, if one contrary is given, the other must necessarily be conceded. Now, indeed, good and evil, justice and sin, are contraries. Therefore, if good had to exist in nature, it was also simply necessary for evil to exist.

III. Truly, this argument is weak and lacks strength. Contraries, indeed, when placed next to each other, shine more brightly; but by what firm reason will it be demonstrated that one cannot simply exist or be known without the other?

IV. Our God, the Best and Greatest, that supreme and infinite good, existed from eternity in Himself; shall we therefore conclude from this that there was some infinite evil from eternity? This would be impious, and the heretical delirium of the Manichaeans, long since proscribed and condemned in the divine code by the holy Fathers, and indeed by right reason itself.

V. Thus in the first creation and state of integrity before the fall of the first-formed, no evil, no sin found a place: but did good, the contrary to evil, not exist on that account? But indeed Moses contradicts this in express words, who in Gen. 1, last verse, after the narration of the six days of creation, adds this clause and commendation: God saw what he had made, BEHOLD THEY WERE VERY GOOD. If therefore there was a time when all things were very good, without any evil, then evil is by no means absolutely necessary for the existence of good.

VI. Add that it is the common voice of the sounder-minded that an opposite does not depend upon its opposite. For the one does not include, but excludes the other: and contraries do not posit, but repel each other. There is therefore no necessity that, one being given, the other is immediately given. And therefore it was not necessary that evil be posited so that good might exist.

VII. And the Aristotelian canon looks to this, which he left written in the book of Categories, ch. 11, in these words: It is not necessary, if one contrary exists, that the other also exists. For if all are in good health, there will be health, not disease, and if all things are white, there will be white, not black. If the Calvinists would thoroughly consider this one maxim of the Philosopher, they would not defend the absolute necessity of evil on account of the nature of contrariety.

IIV. Contrariety is indeed always between two things, but it is not required that both actually exist in nature: for in opposition we look not so much at the existence of particulars as at the essence of universals. Winter cold is certainly contrary to summer heat, as regards its ὑπόστασιν [substance]; yet both are not posited at the same time, nor is it necessary that they be posited, unless we wish to confuse summer with winter, and winter with summer, and thereby overturn the whole nature of things. In a similar way, it is rightly said that good is opposed to evil, namely with respect to its οὐσίας [essence], even though evil does not exist, but its quiddity is conceived by the mind only through the privation of good.

Latin:

QVAESTIO VI. An peccatum absolutè fuerit necessarium?

I. Et fuerunt olim, & sunt etiamnum, qui peccatum ineuitabili necessitate introductum somniant. Partim, quia Deus gloriam suam absque peccato manifestare non potuisset: partim quia posito contrariorum vno ponendum quoque sit alterum. De priori sequente disputatione agemus : de posteriori jam pauca addemus.

II. Sic ergô philosophantur: Contrarium sine contrario in natura rerum non solùm non est, sed nec intelligi quidem animôque concipi potest. Vno eorum sublato, alterum mox tollitur : Quare vno posito, statim alterum ponitur. Et ratio est in promptu, quia idem sibi ipsi non aduersatur, sed omnis contrarietas inter duo existit: ideoque si datur contrarium vnum, necessariô concedendum est alterum. Iam vero bonum & malum, justitia, & peccatum sunt contraria. Ergo si bonum in natura existere debuit, malum etiam esse simpliciter necessum fuit.

III. Verum, elumbis haec est ratio & neruis caret. Contraria quidem juxta se posita, magis elucescunt: quòd verò alterum sine altero simpliciter nec esse, nec cognosci queat, quâ ratione firmâ demonstrabitur?

IV. Deus noster optimus Max. summum illud & infinitum bonum, ab aeterno extitit in seipso: vnum verò hinc ab aeterno infinitum quoddam fuisse malum colligemus; Impium hoc foret, & haereticum Manichaeorum delirium, in diuino codice à sanctis Patribus, imô ab ipsâ ratione rectâ jamdudum proscriptum & condemnatum.

V. Sic in prima creatione & statu integritatis ante lapsum πρωτοπλάστων, nullum malum, nullum peccatum inuenit locum: num autem propterea bonum malo contrarium non extitit? At verò disertis verbis contradicit Moses, qui Gen. 1. vers. vlt. post narrationem hexaëmeri hanc clausulam & commendationem adjicit: Vidit Deus quæ fecerat, ECCE ERANT VALDE BONA. Si ergo tempus fuit, vbi omnia erant valdè bona, sine vllo malo, vtique malum ad boni existentiam non est absolutè necessarium.

VI. Adde, quod communis saniorum vox sit, Oppositum ab opposito non dependere. Alterum enim non includit, sed excludit alterum: Et, contraria se non ponunt, sed pellunt. Nulla igitur necessitas, vt vno dato, protinus detur alterum. Ideoque nec necessum fuit, poni malum, vt existeret bonum.

VII. Et huc spectat canon Aristotelicus, quem in libro Categoriarum c. 11. his verbis scriptum reliquit: Non necesse est, si contrarium alterum sit, etiam reliquum esse. Nam omnibus benè valentibus sanitas erit, non morbus, & omnibus albis existentibus, album erit, non nigrum. Quam vnam Philosophi maximam, si Caluiniani penitus considerarent, absolutam mali necessitatem ob contrarietatis naturam non propugnarent.

IIV. Contrarietas quidem semper est inter duo, sed non requiritur, vt vtrumque realiter in natura existat: in oppositione enim non tam existentiam singularium, quàm essentiam vniuersalium spectamus. Frigus hyemale contrarium certè est calori æstiuo, quoad ὑπόστασιν suam; non tamen vtrumque simul ponitur, aut poni necessarium est, nisi æstatem cum hyeme, & hyemem cum æstate confundere, adeoque totam rerum naturam peruertere velimus. Pari modo, rectè dicitur bonum malo aduersari, nempe respectu οὐσίας suæ, quatumuis malum non existat, sed eius quidditas mente tantùm per priuationem boni concipiatur.


### Question IV What is the cause of sin?

I. Augustine, book 3 of Free Choice, chapter 2, rightly pronounced: We are swifter to excuse than to acknowledge sins. This is true above all when an inquiry is instituted concerning the cause of evils. For there the status of transference will perpetually be employed; and sins are not acknowledged, but rather excused, and all blame is attributed to some other principle established outside of us. And hence so many false opinions concerning the cause of sin have arisen, that in such great variety many fluctuate as to what should be determined, and do not find where to plant their foot. However, it is not our purpose here to propose that doctrine fully, since that has been done elsewhere, and we shall treat of the cause of the first fall, as well as of hardening, in what follows: we shall say only a few things in general, 1. concerning the false and fabricated causes of sins. 2. concerning the true ones, which are not alien to the analogy of faith; but we shall reserve more specific matters for the disputations that follow.

I. Concerning the false causes of sin.

II. A twofold faction of those who err occurs here; 1. Philosophers outside the Church, 2. Heretics within the Church. There were formerly three sects of philosophers in particular, 1. Stoics, 2. Epicureans, 3. Peripatetics. The former accused fate, the latter fortune, the latter matter. For the Stoics maintained that all things happen by inevitable necessity according to the immutable laws of the Fates, and therefore that all sins depend upon and proceed from fate, defined by the necessary connection of primary and secondary causes. The Epicureans went in entirely opposite directions, judging that all things happen by chance and the blind guidance of fortune, and therefore that one should not labor much concerning a certain cause of evils. The Peripatetics wished to walk a middle path, thinking that not all things happen by chance, nor all things by necessity, but that contingency and liberty are indeed granted, yet that we are inclined toward sins by matter. For since that is mutable, fluid, and inconstant, they judged that all evils, whether found in natural or voluntary agents, draw their origin from matter, and that man is carried into sins because and insofar as he has much φαύλης τῆς ὕλης admixed.

III. But all these opinions collapse of their own vanity, and to have recited them is to have refuted them. For the Stoic Fate takes away justice from God and liberty from men: the Epicurean Fortune removes the providence of God and leads men into security: the Peripatetic Matter accuses the Creator, by whom such matter was founded, and does not explain the cause of sins, but involves it. Wherefore, dismissing these as unworthy of refutation, we shall subjoin the opinions of the heretics.

IV. They are indeed in a twofold distinction: 1. Certain older ones. 2. Certain more recent ones. Among the older ones were: 1. The Messalians, who contended that Satan is the president of our life and actions, by whom men are ruled and drawn throughout their whole life even against their will, whence they were called by another name, Sataniani, as reported by D. Pappus in Epit. Hist. Eccles. m. p. 313. But this is not an error here, but manifest impiety: for the Devil can indeed suggest evils, but he cannot bend wills, much less draw them against their will.

V. 2 The Luciferian Marcionites, who referred every cause of sin to God, nay, blasphemed that He Himself is guilty of sin—the former because He cast Lucifer out of heaven, the latter because He hardened Pharaoh and drowned the Egyptians in the Red Sea: which horrendous blasphemies we leave to be avenged by God the just judge.

VI. 3. The Manichaeans, who, knowing that nothing but good can proceed from a good God, [held that] another God must be added they thought, and therefore they imagined two infinite and eternal principles, namely the highest good and the highest evil; of which the former is the cause of good things in the world, the latter of evil things. Which heresy of theirs they wished to persuade by five reasons, which, since they contribute not a little to a better understanding of this doctrine, we shall examine in a few words:

VII. 1. Given contrary effects, such as good and evil, contrary causes must also be posited, in which one must finally arrive at some first cause:

But concerning particulars that may indeed be conceded, yet to wish to invent as many first causes as there are special effects is most absurd. Add that evil is opposed to good not so much contrarily as privatively, and is a defect rather than an effect, and consequently has a cause not efficient, but deficient; not per se but per accidens.

IIX. 2. As good and better are spoken of with respect to the highest good, so evil and worse will require some highest evil.

But the consequence is null, since from one Best [Being] good and evil can have a relation, namely good by approach; but evil by recession from good and not by any new approach to a highest evil.

IX. 3. That which is by participation is reduced to that which is such by essence: But sins are evils by participation. Therefore there will be given a highest evil by essence.

But in truth sins are not evils by participation, but rather by the privation of participation, and therefore it is not necessary that a reduction be made to something which is evil by essence. For nothing can be evil in itself, since every being, as such, is good. And evil, insofar as it is evil, does not exist per se, but is always in good as in a subject; and from good as a cause per accidens. For it cannot exist from itself and in itself, because it is a privation, which always requires another principle and subject. X. 4 A bad effect is reduced to a bad cause, and therefore, lest there be an infinite regress, it must be posited that there is a certain supreme evil, which is the principle and cause of all other evils. But in the causes of evil, it is not necessary to proceed either to infinity or to one first and supreme evil, but all evils can be reduced to some good thing, from which evil flows per accidens. For a good thing is not the cause of evil per se, since opposites do not beget, but rather destroy, one another. However, it becomes a cause per accidens when it deviates and, contrary to intention, turns aside from a suitable order, if indeed you take evil as evil. It happens to a good thing that, while it chooses or does something good (whether it be true or apparent), it chooses or does some evil that is conjoined to the good that is being sought. XI 5. Everything that is by accident is reduced to something that is by itself: and therefore if a cause of evil by accident is granted, the supreme evil must also be granted, which is the cause of evil by itself.

But that axiom concerning the reduction of the per accidens to that which is per se is valid indeed for entities that are truly positive, but not for privative ones; as regards effects, not defects; which can be illustrated by the example of monsters in nature. For of these there is given only a cause per accidens. In like manner, we do not reduce sins to a cause per se, nor can we reduce them, but we rest at last in a cause per accidens, namely, in the good deviating. For they come to pass, as we conclude, by an equivocal production, not a univocal one, which always presupposes a cause similar in species, or rather the same.

XII. Furthermore, from the more recent heretics, in turn, three orders or classes emerge. 1. The Libertines, who raved that all things which are seen to be done by men, even if they be evil, proceed from the one Spirit of God, who works all things in all, and that therefore sin is a mere opinion, since it comes from God, who does nothing but good. But this dogma is so monstrous that it destroys all truth.

Scripture, which everywhere reproves sins and sinners; let it take away the merit of Christ, who if sin is an opinion, died in vain; let it take away the word and the Sacraments, which were instituted for the remission of sins; let it finally take away the future judgment and hell, into which men will be unjustly thrust on account of a mere opinion.

XIII. 2. The Jesuits, with whom they do not fear to write, since they follow from the condition of the matter the rebellion of vices in man, and the struggle of appetite and reason; do they not consequently ascribe to God the creator the cause of all sins, flowing from that concreated ἐπιθυμίᾳ? For in things subordinate and immediately connected, he who is the cause of the cause is also the cause of the caused. But this has been treated quite prolixly in the preceding disputation.

XIV. 3. The Calvinists, although they no longer pronounce God to be the cause of sin in words and directly, (which nevertheless some did not hesitate to assert at the first, before they learned to speak more cautiously,) yet indirectly and by their hypotheses they blasphemously transfer all blame for evil onto Him.

XV. For they write 1. That God works all things without distinction. 2. That He willed and decreed the fall of Adam. 3. That He impelled the πρωτοπλάστῳ from within to sin. 4. That He imposes necessity upon other sins by His foreknowledge. 5. That He seriously wills them. 6. That He reprobates the greatest part of mankind by an absolute decree. 7. And therefore creates them for damnation and the causes of damnation. 8. That He casts occasions of sin in their way. 9. That He commands the Devil to seduce. 10. That He instigates to evil. 11. That He cooperates by a hidden power, and finally 12. That He uses Satan and the impious, as they are such, as instruments, by which He may more easily arrive at the execution of His proposed end. All these hypotheses are found in the writings of the Calvinists, as has been proven elsewhere; and they are such that it is easy to gather from them that the primary principle and supreme cause of all sin is placed in the eternal decree of God, in temporal impulse, and in hidden cooperation, not without blasphemy of the divine name.

XVI. Although a more prolix ἔλεγχος (refutation) is not necessary, since the absurdity is evident at first glance, it is nevertheless pleasing to add certain arguments out of abundance, and to refute the Calvinistic opinion 1. from Scripture, 2. by reasons, and 3. by testimonies:

XVII. Therefore, as far as SCRIPTURE is concerned, it removes every suspicion of guilt from God in many ways and by many assertions. Five of these pertain especially to the general consideration of sin, which we shall recount in order:

XVIII. THE FIRST assertion OF SCRIPTURE; God does not will sins; but He forbids them before they are committed. Psalm 5, verse 5: You are not a God WILLING iniquity. Psalm 30, verse 7: YOU HATED those who observe empty vanities. Psalm 44, verse 8: You have loved righteousness, and HATED impiety. Isaiah 61, verse 12: You did evil in my eyes, and you chose what I DID NOT WILL. Add Zechariah 8, verse 17; Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 22; Wisdom 14, verse 20.

Latin:

I. August. l. 3. lib. arbit. c. 2. rectè pronunciauit: Velociores sumus ad excusanda quàm agnoscenda peccata. Imprimis hoc verum est, cùm decausa malorum disquisitio instituitur. Ibi enim translationis status perpetuò adhibebitur; & peccata non agnoscuntur, sed potius excusantur, omniśque culpa alij principio, extra nos constituto, accepta fertur. Atque hinc tot falsæ opiniones de causa peccati sunt exortæ, vt in tanta varietate quid statuendum sit, multi fluctuent, & quò pedem figant, haud in veniat. Non autem hic instituti nostri est, doctrinam illam plenè proponere, cùm istud alibi factum, & de primi lapsus, tum etiam indurationis causa in sequentibus acturi simus: In genere tantùm pauca dicemus, 1 de causis peccatorum falsis & confictis. 2. de veris & ab analogia fidei non alienis; specialiora vero disputationibus secuturis reservabimus.

I. De falsis peccati causis.

II. Duplex errantium factio hic occurrit; 1. Philosophorum extra Ecclesiam, 2. Hæreticorum in Ecclesia. Philosophorum fuere olim tres in primis sectæ, 1. Stoici. 2. Epicurei, 3. Peripatetici. Illi fatum, isti fortunam, hi materiam accusarunt Stoici enim statuebant, omnia ineuitabili necessitate secundum immotas Parcarum leges contingere adeoque omnia peccata à fato, necessaria connexione primarum & secundarum causarum definito, pendere & prouenire. Epicurei in contrarias planè partes abibant, censentes omnia casu cæcoque fortunæ ductu euenire, ac proinde de certa malorum causa non admodum laborandum esse. Peripatetici viâ mediâ incedere volebãt, existimantes nec omnia fortuito, neque omnia necessario fieri, sed contingentiam quidem & libertatem dari, ad peccata tamen per materiam nos inclinari. Cùm enim illa sit mutabilis, fluxa & inconstans, hinc omnia mala, siue in agentibus naturalibus, siue voluntarijs reperiantur, à materia ortum trahere, hominemque in peccata ferri censebant, quia & quatenus multum φαύλης τῆς ὕλης admixtum haberet.

III. Verùm opiniones hæ omnes vanitate suâ vltrò corruunt, easque recitâsse est refutâsse. Fatum enim Stoicum adimit Deo justitiam, hominibus libertatem: Fortuna Epicurea tollit Dei prouidentiam, homines abducit in securitatem: Materia Peripatetica creatorem, à quo illa talis condita, incusat, causamque peccatorum non exponit, sed involvit. Quocirca missis ijs, vt refutatione indignis, hæreticorum opiniones subiungemus.

IV. Sunt verò illi in duplici differentia 1. Quidam Antiquiores. 2. Quidam recentiores. Ex antiquioribus fuerunt. 1. Messaliani, qui Satanam vitæ actionumque nostrarum præsidem esse contenderunt, à quo totâ vitâ inuiti etiam homines regantur & trahantur, vnde alio nomine Sataniani dicti sunt, referente D. Pappo in Epit. Hist. Eccles. m. p. 313. Verum non hîc error, sed manifesta impietas est: Diabolus enim mala quidem suggerere potest, voluntates autem flectere non potest, multò minus inuitas trahere.

V. 2 Luciferani Marcionitæ qui omnem peccati causam in Deum retulerunt, imò ipsum peccati reum esse blasphemârunt, ille quidem, quòd Luciferum è cœlo eiecerint, hic verò, quòd Pharaonem indurauerit, & Ægyptios in mari rubro submerserit: quas horrendas blasphemias Deo justo judici vindicandas relinquimus.

VI. 3. Manichæi, qui scientes, à Deo bono non nisi bona proficisci, alium Deum esse adiungendum censebant, ideoque duo principia infinita & æterna fingebant, nempe summum bonum & summum malum; quorum illud bonorum, hoc malorum in mundo causa sit. Quam hæresin suam quinque rationibus persuadere voluerunt, quias cum ad meliorem huius doctrinæ intelligentiam non parum faciant, paucis examinabimus:

VII. 1. Contrarijs effectibus positis, vt boni & malè poni quoque debent contrariæ causæ, in quibus tandem perveniendum ad aliquam primam:

Verum de particularibus illud quidem concedi potest, velle autem tot causas primas confingere, quot sunt affectus speciales, absurdissimum est. Adde, quod malum non tam contrariè, quam priuatiue bono opponatur, potiusque defectuss quam effectus sit, & per consequens causam habeat non efficientem, sed deficientem; non per se sed per accidens.

IIX. 2. Vt bonum & melius dicitur respectu ad summum bonum, sic malum & peius requirent aliquod summum malum.

Sed sequela nulla est, cum ab vno Optimo bonum malumque respectum habere possit, nempe bonum, per accessum; malum vero per recessum a bono & non per aliquem novum ad summum malum accessum.

IX. 3. Quod est per participationem, reducitur ad id quod est per essentiam tale: Peccata vero sunt mala participatione. Dabitur igitur malum summum per essentiam.

At vero peccata non sunt mala per participationem, sed potius per priuationem participationis, ideoque non est necesse, fieri reductionem ad aliquid, quod per essentiam malum sit. Nihil enim secundum malum esse potest, cum omnis ens, qua talis, bona sit. Et malum quatenus malum, per se non existit, sed semper est in bono, vt subiecto; & a bono, vt causa per accidens. A seipso enim & in seipso esse nequit, quia privatio est, quæ aliud semper principium & subiectum requirit. X. 4 Malus effectus reducitur ad malam causam, ideoque ne progressus fiat in infinutū, poni oportet quoddā summum malum, quod principium & causa sit omniū aliorū malorū. Ast in causis mali neque in infinitum, neque ad vnum primum summumque malum opus est procedere, sed omnia mala in aliquā rem bonam reduci possunt, ex qua malum per accidens profluxit. Per se enim bonum causa mali non est, cùm opposita sese non gignant; sed tollant. Fit autem causa per accidens, quando deuiat, & ab ordine conuenienti, præter intentionē, si nempè malum, quâ malum accipias, declinat. Accidit rei bonæ, vt dum aliquid boni (seu verum sit, seu apparens) eligit vel agit, aliquod malum, bono, quod spectatur, adiunctum eligat vel agat. XI 5. Omne per accidens reducitur ad aliquid, quod est per se: ideoque si datur causa mali per accidens, dandum quoque summum malum, quod sit mali causa per se.

Verùm sóyxiov istud de reductione τō̄ per accidēs ad id, quod per se est, valet quidem quod entia verè positiua, sed non priuatiua; quoad effectus, non defectus; id quod exemplo monstrorum in natura declarari potest. Horum enim non nisi causa per accidens datur. Pari modo, peccata ad causam per se non reducimus, nec reducere possumus, sed tandem in causa per accidens, bono nimirum deviante acquiefcimus. Fiunt enim, vt concludamus æquiuocâ productione, non vniuoca, quæ semper pręsupaponit causam specie similem, vel potius eandem.

XII. Porrò ex recentioribus hæreticis vicissim tres ordines vel classes prodeunt. 1. Libertini, qui delirâ- runt, omnia, quæ fieri videntur ab hominibus siue mala sint, ab vno Dei Spiritu prouenire, qui omnia in omnibus operetur, propterea peccatum meram esse opinionem, quippe, cùm à Deo sit, qui nil nisi bonum faciat. Sed tam monstrosusm sit hoc dogma, ut tollat omnem veritatem

Scripturæ, quæ peccata & peccatores passim reprehendit; tollat meritum Christi, qui si peccatum opinio sit, vtque frustrà mortuus est; tollat verbum & Sacramenta, quæ in remissionem peccatorum instituta; tollat denique futurum iudicium & gehennam, in quam ob meram opinionem jniustè homines detrudentur.

XIII. 2. Iesuitæ, quiscum scribere non vereantur, ex conditione materiæ sequi rebellionem vitium in homine, pugnamque appetitus & rationis; annón omnium peccatorum, ex illa concreata ἐπιθυμίᾳ fluentium causam Deo creatori consequenter adscribunt? In subordinatis enim & immediatè connexis, qui causa est causæ, causa etiam est causati. Sed de hoc præcedente disp. satis prolixè actum est.

XIV. 3. Caluiniani, licet verbis & directè Deum peccati causam non amplius pronuncient, (quod tamen primo tempore antequam cautiùs loqui discerent, nonnulli asserere non dubitârunt,) indirectè tamen & hypothesibus suis omnem mali culpam in ipsum blasphemè transferunt.

XV. Scribunt enim 1. Deum sine distinctione omnia operari. 2. Lapsum Adę voluisse & decrevisse. 3. πρωτοπλάσῳ ad peccandum intus impulisse. 4. peccatis cæteris prævisione sua necessitatem imponere. 5. illa serio velle. 6 Maximam partem hominum ex absoluto decreto reprobare. 7. ideoque ad damnationem & damnationis causas creare 8. occasiones peccandi obijcere. 9. Diabolo seductionem imperare. 10. ad malum instigare. 11. Occultâ vi cooperari, & tandem 12. Satanâ impiisque, vt tales sint, velut instrumentis vti, quo ad propositi finis executionem faciliùs peruenire queat. Omnes hæ hypotheses in scriptis Caluinianorum reperiuntur, vt alibi probatum; & tales sunt vt collectu indè sit facile, primū omnis peccati principium summamque causam in ęterno Dei decreto, temporali impulsu, occulta que cooperatione, non sine blasphemiadiuini nominis reponi.

XVI. Quamvis E. prolixius ἔλεγχος non sit necessarius, cùm primo aspectu pateat absurditas placet tamen ex abundanti argumenta quaedam addere, & opinionem Calvinisticam refutare 1. ex Scriptura, 2. rationibus, & 3. testimoniis:

XVII. Quod ergo SCRIPTURAM concernit, multis illa modis & assertionibus EMNEM à Deo suspicionem culpae removet. Harum quinque potissimum ad generalem peccati considerationem faciunt, quas ordine recensebimus:

XVIII. PRIMA SCRIPTURAE assertio; Deus peccata non vult; sed prohibet, antequàm fiant. Psalm: 5. vers. 5. Non Deus VOLENS iniquitatem tu es. Psalm: 30. vers. 7. ODISTI observantes vanitates supervacaneas. Psalm 44. v. 8. Dilexisti iustitiam, & ODISTI impietatem. Esai: 61. v. 12. Faciebatis malum in oculis meis, & quod NON VOLVI, elegistis. Adde Zach 8. v. 17. Eccl. 15. v. 22. Sap. 14. v. 20.


### Question IV What is the cause of sin?: XIX. A threefold distinction, however, must be observed here

XIX. A threefold distinction, however, must be observed here: 1. Between To will, not to will, and to be unwilling: To will is to approve of something and to choose it from an internal principle of the will: Not to will is a simple negation of volition, without an effort to prevent: To be unwilling is not merely a bare aversion, but at the same time a serious attempt to prevent: We say, therefore, that sins happen, not with God willing them, nor simply against His will, or resisting, but not willing them; for the former would be against God's goodness; the latter against His power, both are impious and blasphemous.

XX. 2. Between the προηγουμένην (antecedent) or antecedent will of God, and the ἑπομένην (consequent) or consequent will, from Damascene, book 2, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 19. The former regards men as men: the latter as they are such and such. The former gives ἄνοιαν (counsel), the latter concerns the πρᾶξιν (action) of men. The former is universal, the latter particular. The former is of mercy, the latter of judgment: When therefore God is sometimes said to will evil, as in Matthew 11: verse 29, 1 Peter 2: verse 8, it is concerning the consequent will of God, and God punishing sins with sins, that it must be understood where, however, in turn He wills the sin not by reason of the term from which, as it is an undue action; but only by reason of the term to which; as it is a due passion, in which sense Prosper says concerning the crucifixion of Christ: The action displeased, the passion was pleasing

XXI. Between the evil of fault and the evil of punishment, Tertullian in book 2 against Marcion calls it the evil of transgression and the evil of torment. Augustine, Vol. 6, against Fortunatus the Manichaean, in 'On the Conflict', ch. 1, calls it sin and the punishment of sin. Against Adimantus, ch. 26, he names it the evil which man does, and the evil which man suffers. Basil in his sermon that God is not the author of evils, and Damascene, book 4, 'On the Orthodox Faith', ch. 20, distinguishes between τὸ φύσει κακὸν (evil by nature) and τὸ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν αἴσθησιν κακὸν (that which is evil to our sense and troublesome to us). Thus these evils differ: 1. that the subject of fault is man's action, of punishment man's very substance; 2. that fault comes from the will, punishment against the will; 3. that fault is properly situated in acting, punishment in suffering. As often, therefore, as Scripture affirms that evil happens by God willing and ordaining it, as in Amos 3:6, Lamentations 3:37-38, let us consider that it speaks of the evil of punishment or torment, not of fault or transgression. And yet God does not properly effect the punishments themselves, as He does other beings, but is said to send them by justly withdrawing a good, not by doing any evil. Thus He punishes with sterility and diseases by taking away the blessing of the earth and the health of the body. For every punishment by its own nature is nothing other than the privation of some good, and therefore it is not properly effected, as a being and a good, but follows the subtraction of a good, just as every privation follows its habit.

XXII SECOND: God does not instigate to sins, so that they may happen. To this pertain: In general, all the sayings commending God's goodness and justice, both by reason of Himself and by reason of His works, such as are read in Genesis 1:31, Deuteronomy 32:4, Psalm 33:4, Psalm 111:7, Zephaniah 3:5, Matthew 19:17, Mark 10:18, Luke 11:13, John 1:5.

For from this it follows most firmly that God is not the author of sin. For how would He who is absolutely good, nay, who is infinite goodness itself, incite men to sins? For this impulse is evil, proper to the Devil, contrary to the law, and therefore to be removed as far as possible from a good and just God. 2. In particular, let the following be noted. Jer. 33:23. They have seduced my people with their lies, when I HAD NOT SENT THEM, NOR COMMANDED them. James 1:13. Let no man say when he is tempted, that he is tempted of God, for God TEMPTETH NO MAN. Ecclus. 15:12. Say not, he hath caused me to err.

XXII. THIRD: God does not command the Devil to seduce. For 1. He punishes for seduction, Gen. 3:14, 15; Rev. 20:9, 10. But it would be unjust to punish a minister who is so faithfully executing his commanded duties. 2. He commands that the Devil be resisted, Eph. 4:27; James 4:7; 1 Pet. 5:9. But no one wishes his own minister to be resisted, unless he is contrary to himself. 3. Satan seeks leave and permission from God, and therefore does not have a command to seduce, as is evident from the history of Job, chapters 1 and 2.

Nor does the passage 1 Kings 22:27 stand in the way, where a deception seems to be enjoined upon the spirit of lies. For imperative verbs in the Scriptures do not always signify a command, but sometimes a permission, as appears from 2 Kings 2:17, where Elisha says: Send, and yet he did not wish them to be sent, but only permitted it, and likewise from a comparison of Matt. 8:32 and Luke 8:32.

XXIV. FOURTH: God does not approve of sins when they are committed. For just as He did not decree them from eternity before they were committed, so He does not approve of them in time when they are committed; He does not promote them, but hinders them; He does not compensate for them, but punishes them: that which Scripture cries out everywhere and innumerable examples testify. Hence every cause and occasion of damnation is removed from God and ascribed to man. Ezek. 33:12; Hos. 13:9; 1 Tim. 2:4; 2 Pet. 3:9. XXV. FIFTH. God does not cooperate with sinners regarding the sin itself by a hidden action. For what participation has justice with iniquity? 2 Cor. 6:14. The wicked are not useful to God, Ecclesiasticus 15:12. To God, both the wicked and his wickedness are hateful, Wisdom 14:10. All his works are perfect, Deut. 32:4. Sins are not from the Father, but from the world, 1 John 2:16. Why then does a man murmur against God? Let each one murmur against his own sins. Lamentations 3:39. And is it a small thing for you, Calvinist men, to be troublesome to men, unless you are also troublesome to our God? Isaiah 7:13.

XXVI. And thus far we have shown from the Scriptures that God is not the author of sin; now in the second place, REASONS must be added, which, however, we shall not enumerate all of, but only the principal ones, and indeed only five of them.

XXVII. 1. From the nature of sin. Every sin is committed because there is a withdrawal from the order which is in God as the end. For it is an aberration from the ultimate goal, which is God. If, therefore, He instigates to sins, He is the cause of a withdrawal from Himself, and thus He would be contrary to Himself. For whoever impels to evil makes men withdraw from God. God impels men to evil. Therefore, God makes men withdraw from God. That which is absurd and contradictory.

XXVIII. 2. From the manner of causing sin. Evil cannot be committed, nor can anyone be instigated to sin, except through defect and exorbitance. For that does not have an efficient cause, but only a deficient one. But God cannot fail or be exorbitant, because He is the highest goodness, and the most absolute measure and rule of all that is right. Therefore, He cannot be the cause or author of sin either.

XXIX. 3. From the will of God. The more perfect the will, the more it is carried toward the good and detests evil. But the will of God is most perfect, nay, it is itself perfection. Therefore it is carried only toward the good, and consequently it is not the cause of evils. For otherwise sin would be a mere opinion, just as the Libertines contended. For that will of man is good which wills what God wills it to will, but that is evil which wills something other than what God wills it to will. Wherefore no man's will is evil. For by doing that which God wills, it does not depart from the will of God, and therefore it does not perform evil.

XXX. 4. From the prohibitions, threats, and complaints of God. Whoever forbids a thing before it is done, and threatens punishments if it is done, and complains after it has been done, this person certainly cannot be said to be established as its cause. For to forbid, to threaten, and to complain are proofs of a mind that is opposing, not willing. But God forbids sins in the law; He threatens temporal and eternal punishments, indeed He complains most gravely about the misdeeds of men, as the entire Biblical codex testifies. Therefore He cannot in any way be said to be established as the cause of sins.

XXXI. 5. From repentance. If we are incited to sins by God Himself, what need is there for repentance and the petitioning of pardon? For a servant, when he has executed the will of his master, is filled with joy, not tormented by grief, much less is he anxious for pardon for the deed. Thus, who will repent of crimes if they are committed while God wills it; or, what is more, if God exists as the cause of them by His hidden operation? But we are prolix in vain regarding a matter so manifest: we shall only append certain testimonies of the Fathers and of the sounder pagans, who, by the guidance of reason, recognized that sins are by no means to be ascribed to God.

XXXII. 1. Augustine to the 13th article of the false [teaching]. It is a sin to ascribe the fall to God. NOTHING there the Father, NOTHING the Son, NOTHING the Holy Spirit. Nor does anything of the divine will intervene in such a business, by whose aid we know that many were held back lest they fall, but none were impelled to fall. The same in bk. 3 of De libero arbitrio, ch. 19: I find absolutely no way, and I confirm that it is impossible to find, and that there is entirely none, how our sins can be attributed to our Creator GOD. And conversely de gra. c. 2, Let no one blame God in his heart, but let each one blame himself when he sins. 2. Fulgent. l. 1. ad Mon. p. 12. If sin is not in God, then sin is not from Him; and what is not from Him is certainly not His work. And again p. 46. Far be this from us, and from all Christians, that anyone should dare to attribute the cause of any sin whatsoever to divine justice: 3. Nazianzenus Orat. 1. in Iul. God is in no way the cause of evil, being by nature good, and the vice is his who chooses it. 4. Chrysost. homil. 23, in Act. Apost. Let no one say, GOD is the author of evils for us: And below: It would be better to be buried six hundred times than to hear such perverse things about God. 5. Ambrosius l. 1. Hexam. cap. 8. God wills that malice be eradicated from the souls of individuals. How, therefore, do we attribute the beginning of it to the Lord? But this is the late opinion of those who thought the Church ought to be disturbed. 6. Gregory on c. 45 of Isaiah. Let those be confounded who consider God the author of evils. 7. Damascenus l. 2. O. F. c. 29. He does not will evils, and truly evil things, either antecedently or consequently, yet He allows the will to be free toward them. 8. Mercurius Trismeg. in Timan. From God the creator nothing base, nothing evil can proceed. 9. Plato, dial. 2. de Repub. God is indeed the sole cause of good things, but it is fitting to seek the cause of evil things anywhere other than in God. For that God is the cause of evil to anyone must be refuted entirely, nor should anyone be permitted to say this in his city, if the city is to be governed by good laws. 10. Euripides; εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσι φαῦλον, οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί, that is, Gods cease to be Gods, if they commit any evil.

XXXIII. However much God may not efficiently concur in sins, as has been proven thus far, it by no means follows from this that He is an idle spectator. For in any sin whatsoever there are two things: 1. the action, 2. the ἀταξία of the action. Concerning both God operates, but in a different manner regarding the action itself, which he effects as the first cause. For in any human work these three principles concur: 1. universal, which is God. 2. Common, which is nature. 3. particular, which is the will. But as regards disorder, he neither approves nor assists it; yet he does not watch it idly, but 1. prohibits it before the act. 2. restrains it in the act. 3. punishes it and directs it toward good after the act. For the good God would not allow evil to be done, unless he were omnipotent enough to be able to make good out of evil, as Augustine speaks in the Enchiridion, ch. 100.

Latin:

XIX. Triplex autem distinctio hîc observanda venit: 1. Inter Velle, non velle, & nolle: Velle est aliquid approbare, & ex interno voluntatis principio eligere: Non velle, est simplex volitionis negatio, absque impediendi studio: Nolle, non est nuda duntaxat aversatio, sed simul serius impediendi conatus: Dicimus ergò peccata fieri, non Deo volente, nec simpliciter invito, aut repugnante, sed non volente; Illud enim foret contra Dei bonitatem; istud potestatem, utrumque impium & blasphemum.

XX. 2. Inter voluntatem Dei προηγουμένην vel antecedentem, & ἑπομένην vel consequentem, ex Damasc. l. 2. O. F. c 19. Illa respicit homines, in quantum homines: haec in quantum tales vel tales sunt. Illa ἄνοιαν Dat, haec πρᾶξιν hominum concernit. Illa universalis haec particularis. Illa misericordiae, haec judicii est: Cùm igitur quandoque Deus malum velle dicitur, ut Matth. 11: v: 29. 1. Petri 2. v. 8. de voluntate Dei consequente, & peccata peccatis puniente intelligendum est vbi tamen vicissim peccatum vult non ratione termini à quo, vt est actio indebita; sed tantùm ratione termini ad quem; vt est passio debita, quo sensu Prosper de crucifixione Christi ait: Actio displicuit, passio grata fuit

XXI. Inter malum culpæ, & malum pœnæ Tertull. lib. 2. contra Marcionem vocat malum delicti, & malum supplicij. August. T. 6. contra Fortun. Manichei. de Agon: c. 1. appellat peccatum & pœnam peccati. Contra Adimantum c. 26. nominat malum, quod fecit homo; & malum, quod patitur homo. Basilius in concione, quòd Deus non est autor malorum, & Damasc. l. 4. OF. c. 20. distinguit inter τὸ φύσει κακὸν naturâ malum, & τὸ πρὸς τὴν ἡμετέραν αἴσθησιν κακὸν quod sensu nostro malum nobisque molestum est. Sic a. mala hæc differunt. 1. quòd culpæ subiectum sit hominis actio, pœnæ ipsa hominis substantia; 2. quod culpæ fit ex voluntate, pœnæ contra voluntatem. 3. quòd culpæ propriè sita sit in agendo, pœnæ in patiendo. Quotiescunque igitur Scriptura affirmat, quòd malum Deo volente & ordinante contingat, vt Amos 3. v. 6: Thren. 3. v. 37 38. de malo pœnæ vel supplicij, non culpæ vel delicti illam loqui existimemus. Et tamen nec ipsas pœnas propriè Deus efficit, vt reliqua entia, sed dicitur illas immittere, justè subtrahendo bonum, non faciendo aliquod malum. Sic sterilitate morbisque punit, auferendo benedictionem terræ, & sanitatem corporis. Omnis enim pœna suâ naturâ nihil aliud est, quàm priuatio alicuius boni, ideoque non efficitur propriè, vt ens & bonum, sed sequitur subtractionem boni, sicut omnis priuatio suum habitum.

XXII SECVNDA: Deus ad peccata non instigat, ut fians. Huc pertinent: In genere, omnia dicta, Dei bonitatem & justitiam, tum ratione sui, tum ratione operum commendantia, qualia leguntur Gen. 1. vers 31. Deut 32. vers. 4. Psal. 33. vers. 4. Psal. 111, v. 7. Sophon. 3. v. 5. Ma. 19. v. 17. M. 10. v 18. Luc. 11 v. 13. Ioh. 1. v.

Hinc enim firmissimè sequitur, Deum peccati authorem non esse. Qui enim absolutè bonus, imò qui ipsa infinita bonitas est, ad peccata homines quomodo instigabit? Hic enim impulsus malus est, Diabolo proprius, legi contrarius, ideoque à bono & justo Deo longissimè remouendus. 2. In specie notentur sequentia. Ierem. 33. v. 23. Seduxerunt populum meum in mendacio, cùm ego NON MISISSEM EOS, NEC MANDASSEM eis Iac. 1. v. 13. Nemo cùm tentatur, dicat se à Deo tentari quoniam Deus NEMINEM TENTAT. Eccles. 15. v. 12. Non dicas, ille me implanauit.

XXII. TERTIA: Deus non imperat Diabolo, vt seducat. Nam 1. Punit ob seductionem, Gen. 3. v. 14. 15. Apoc. 20. v. 9. 10. Iniustum autem foret punire ministrum, mandata munia tàm fideliter exsequentem. 2. Iubet resisti Diabolo, Ephes. 4. v. 27. Iacob. 4. v. 7. 1. Pet. 5. v. 9. At nemo vult resisti ministro suo, nisi qui sibi ipsi contrarius. 3. Satanas veniam & permissionem petit à Deo, ideoque mandatum seducendi non habet, vt patet ex historia Iobi, cap. 1, & 2.

Neque obstat locus 1. Reg. 22. v. 27. vbi spiritui mendaciorum videtur deceptio iniungi. Nam verba imperatiua in Scripturis non semper præceptionem, quandoque permissionem significant, vt apparet ex. 4. Reg. 2. v. 17. vbi Elisæus dicit: Mittite, & tamen nolebat mitti, sed tantùm permittebat, itemque ex collatione Matth. 8. v. 32. Luc. 8. v. 32.

XXIV. QVARTA: Deus peccata non adprobat, cùm fiunt. Sicut enim illa ab æterno non decreuit, antequam fierent; ita non adprobat in tempore, cùm fiunt; non promouet, sed impedit; non compensat, sed punit: id quod & Scriptura passim clamat & exempla innumera testantur. Hinc damnationis causa & occasio omnis à Deo remouetur, homini adscribitur. Ezech. 33. v. 12. Oseæ 13. v. 9. 1. Tim. 2, v. 4. 2. Pet. 3 v. 9. XXV. QVINTA. Deus peccatoribus quantum ad ipsum peccatum, occulta actione non cooperatur. Nam quæ participatio justitię cum iniquitate. 2. Cor. 6. v. 14. non Deo nō sunt vtiles inipij, Ecclesiastici 15. v. 12. Odio sunt ipsi impius & impietas eius, Sap. 14. v. 10. Omnia opera eius perfecta, Deut. 32. v. 4. Peccata non sunt ex Patre, sed ex mundo, 1. Iohan. 2. v. 16. Quid ergo murmurat homo contra Deum? Murmuret vnusquisque contra peccata sua. Thren. 3. v. 39. Et nunquid vobis, viri Caluiniani, parum est, molestos esse hominibus, nisi molesti etiam sitis Deo nostro. Esai. 7. v. 13.

XXVI. Et hactenus ex Scripturis, Deum peccati autorem non esse ostendimus: jam secundo loco RATIONES addendæ sunt quas tamen non omnes, sed tantùm præcipuas, & quidem earum quinque duntaxat enumerabimus.

XXVII. 1. A natura peccati. Omne peccatum admittitur, quia receditur ab ordine, qui est in Deum sicut in finem. Est enim abberratio à scopo vltimo, qui est Deus. Hic ergo si ad peccata instigat, causa est recessus à seipso, adeòque sibi sit contrarius. Nam quicunque ad malum impellit, homines à Deo recedere facit. Deus homines ad malum impellit. E. Deus homines à Deo recedere facit. id quod absurdum & ἀντιφαλικόν.

XXVIII. 2. A modo caussandi peccatum. Non potest malum committi, aut aliquis ad peccatum instigari, nisi per defectum & exorbitationem. Non enim habet istud causam efficientem, sed tantùm deficientem. Atqui Deus deficere vel exorbitare nequit, quia est summa bonitas, omnisque recti mensura & regula absolutissima. Ergo etiam peccati causa, vel author esse nequit.

XXIX. 3 A Dei voluntate. Voluntas, quò perfectior, eò magis fertur in bonum, & detestatur malum. Dei autem voluntas perfectissima, imò ipsa perfectio est. Ergo tantum fertur in bonum, & per consequens malorum causa non est. Alias enim peccatum foret mera opinio, quemadmodum Libertini contenderunt. Nam ea hominis voluntas bona est, quae id vult, quod Deus eam velle vult, mala autem, quae aliud vult, quam quod Deus eam velle vult. Quare, si Deus vtrumque & malum, & bonum decernit atque approbat, sequitur nullius hominis voluntatem esse malam. Faciendo enim id, quod Deus vult, a voluntate Dei non recedit, ideoque malum non operatur.

XXX. 4. A Prohibitionibus, minis & querelis Dei Quicunque remprohibet antequam fiat, & minatur poenas, si fiat; & conqueritur, postquam facta est, hic certe causa eius nequaquam statui diciue potest. Prohibere enim, minari & conqueri documenta sunt aduersantis, non volentis animi. Deus autem peccata prohibet in lege; poenas temporales & aeternas minatur, immo de malefactis hominum grauissime conqueritur, vti testatur vniversus codex Biblicus. Ergo peccatorum causa nequaquam statui diciue potest.

XXXI. 5. A poenitentia. Si ab ipso Deo irritamur ad peccata, quid opus est poenitentia & petitione veniae? Minister enim, cum executus est voluntatem heri sui, gaudio perfunditur, dolore non maceratur, multo minus de facti venia solicitus est. Ita quem poenitebit scelerum, si Deo volete committuntur; aut, quod magis est, si Deus eorum occulta operatione in nobis causa existit? Sed frustra prolixi sumus in re adeo manifesta: subjungemus tantum Testimonia quaedam Patrum & saniorum gentilium, qui rationis ductu peccata Deo minime adscribenda esse cognouerunt.

XXXII. 1. Augustinus ad 13. art. falsi. Nefas est, Deo lapsum adscribere causas NIHIL ibi Pater NIHIL Filius NIHIL Spiritus sanctus Nec in tali negotio quicquam diuina voluntatis interuenit, cuius ope scimus, multosne laberentur, retentos: nullos autem vt laberentur, impulsos. Idem l 3. de lib. arb. c. 19. Omninò non inuenio, non invenire posse, & prorsus non esse confirmo, quomodo tribuantur peccata nostra Creatori nostro DEO. Et vicissim de gra. c. 2, Ne quis Deum causetur in corde suo, Sed sibi quisque imputet cùm peccat. 2. Fulgent. l. 1. ad Mon. p. 12. Si. us peccatum in Deo non est, ita peccatum ex eo non est; quod autem ex eo non est, opus eius vtique non est. Et rursus p. 46. Absit hoc à nobis, atque ab omnibus Christianis, vt causam cuiuslibet peccati quisquam deputare diuinæ audeat æquitati: 3. Nazianzenus Orat. 1. in Iul. Deus nullomodo causa est mali, quippe naturâ bonus, vitiúmque eius est qui eligit. 4. Chrysost. homil. 23, in Act Apost. Nullus dicas, DEVS nobis author malorum est: Et infrà: Satiùs fuerit, sexcenties defodi quam Deum audire talia pervers. 5. Ambrosius l. 1. Hexam. cap. 8. Eradicari Deus malitiam vult ex animis singulorum. Quomodo ergò ei initium à Domino damus? Sed hæc opinio seralis eorum, qui perturbandam Ecclesiam putauerunt. 6. Gregorius supra c. 45. Esai. Confundantur, qui Deum malorum authorem arbitrantur. 7. Damascenus l. 2. O. F. c. 29. Mala, & reuera mala, neque præcendenter, neque consequenter vult, sinit tamen arbitrium ad illa liberum. 8. Mercurius Trismeg. in Timan. A Deo factore nihil turpe, nihil malum prodire potest. 9. Plato, dial. 2. de Repub. Bonorum quidem solus DEVS causa est, malorum autem quamlibet etiam præter Deum causam quærere decet. Nam malorum alicui causam esse Deum, refellendum est omnino, nec permittendum hoc quenquam dicere in sua ciuitate, si bonis in]. rut ciuitas legibus decet. 10 Euripides; εἰ θεοί τι δρῶσι φαῦλον, οὐκ εἰσὶν θεοί, hoc est, Dij esse Dei cessant, mali si quid patrant.

XXXIII. Quantumuis autem Deus ad peccata efficienter non concurrat, vt hactenus euictum, hinc tamen otiosum esse eum spectatorem, minimè sequitur. In peccato enim quouis duo sunt, 1. actio, 2. actionis ἀταξία. Circa vtrumque Deus operatur, sed dispari modo Actionem ipsam, vt causâ prima, simul efficit. Nam in quouis opere humano concurrunt hæc tria principia, 1. vniuersale, quod Deus. 2. Commune, quod natura. 3 particulare, quod voluntas. Αταξίαν vero quod attinet, illam quidem nec approbat, nec adiuuat; non tamen otiosè spectat, sed 1. prohibet ante actum. 2. cohibet in actu. 3. punit & ad bonum dirigit post actum. Non enim sineret bonus fieri malè, nisi omnipotens de malo posset facere benè, vti loquitur Augustinus in Enchiridio, c. 100.


### Question IV What is the cause of sin?: II. Concerning the true causes of sin

II. Concerning the true causes of sin.

XXXIV. Nazianzenus advises: δεῖ πρὸς τῶ εἰπεῖν ὃ μὴ ἔστι καὶ ὃ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, after it has been said what it is not, it is necessary to say what it is. Since, therefore, we have removed the false causes of sin, it is required that we further indicate the true ones. Where, however, we premise this, that the name of cause is taken here in a broad sense, for everything that in any way concurs to the effecting of sin. For if we wish to speak accurately and properly, it must be established with Dionysius from the book on the Divine Names: that evil lacks essence, end, and efficient cause: And with Augustine from book 12 of the City of God, ch. 7: that the cause of evil is to be sought not so much as an efficient, but as a deficient cause. Meanwhile, however, since philosophical accuracy does not always find a place in the articles of faith, nothing will prevent us from being able to assign to sin, along with the theologians, certain causes also in a broad sense and in a more general meaning.

XXXV. But because in the following disputation we are going to treat of the fall of the first man, therefore we shall here investigate primarily the causes of the sins which are committed after the fall. Now those are of a twofold distinction; some are external, or outside us: some are internal, or within us. Of the external there are four, of which some are causes by accident, others in themselves, concerning each of which we shall add a few words.

XXXVI. External causes accidentally are two, objects running into the sense, and provoking the appetite. For it is certain that objects move much, as the example of Eve alone teaches. She saw that the tree was good for food, and fair to the eyes, and she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, Gen. 3 v. 6. The appetite of Eve was therefore irritated by the beauty of the object; and thus even now many are moved to sin by external things. But all this happens accidentally, not by the fault of the objects, but by our own vice, and the instinct of the devil, who abuses external things, as if they were instruments, to stir up the appetite.

XXXVII. 2. The other accidental cause is the law of GOD, which is indeed good in itself; yet the stricter it is, the more contumacious it renders men. For forbidden things excite a desire for themselves more than those which are prohibited by no laws, according to that of the Poet: We always strive for what is forbidden, and desire what is denied. Hence the Apostle Rom. 7 v. 8. Sin Διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς by the commandment wrought in me all manner of concupiscence. Not that the law or commandment did this of itself, but because it accidentally moved the vicious nature more to the contrary. For thus the Apostle explains it, when in v. 11 he adds: Sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me.

XXXIIX. External causes of themselves, in turn, are two. Perverse men, seducing others. For these by their persuasions precipitate many into sins, which they would otherwise never have attempted. Thus Eve moved Adam to eat of the forbidden fruit, whence the beginning of sin is said to be from the woman, Syrac. 25 v. 33. Thus women turned away the heart of Solomon, 1 Kings 11 v. 3. And Jeroboam made Israel to sin, 1 Kings 15 v. 26. Moreover, man is a cause of sin to man, 1. by words, or counsel. 2. by deeds, or example. 3. by threats or punishment, which last is proper to tyrants, and especially to the Antichrist.

XXXIX. 2. The spirit of darkness or Satan, who did not stand in the truth and is the father of lies. John 8. v. 44. For here it is said throughout the Scriptures that he blinds the minds, 2. Cor. 4. v. 4. works in the children of disobedience, Ephes. 2. v. 2. fills the heart with malice, Acts 5. v. 3. holds men captive, 2. Tim. 2. v. 26. and sows tares, Matth. 13. v. 28.

XL. It is to be noted, however, that men and the devil are not sufficient causes of sins. For we can, and indeed we ought to, resist, according to the admonitions. James 4. v. 7. 1. Pet. 5. v. 9. Wherefore they cause sins, not by compelling the will, but 1. by proposing objects. 2. by persuading from without, and 3. by stirring up the imagination from within, and suggesting depraved thoughts, which last is nevertheless the property of the Devil alone. Since, therefore, it is placed in our power either to consent to Satan or to resist, therefore sinners are not immune from guilt, although they wish to transfer it all onto the Devil.

XLI. The causes of sins within us, in turn, are of two kinds. For 1. there are those that incline, 2. there is that which is truly and directly efficient.

XLII. There are chiefly four of those that incline. 1. Ignorance of the mind: For often the intellect judges things to be good which are nevertheless evil in themselves, from which sin subsequently arises. Hence Socrates said that all sins proceed from ignorance. And Aristotle, book 3 of the Ethics, 1. that every evil man is ignorant. Induced by this cause, the Apostle Paul persecuted the Church in the early time. For thus he writes 1 Tim. 1. v. 13. I was a blasphemer and a persecutor, but I did it in ignorance.

XLIII. 2. Infirmity of the flesh. For many know what is good, and are at first drawn to it, yet afterwards, carried away by the weakness of the flesh, they contaminate themselves with sins. For the spirit is indeed willing, but the flesh is weak, Matth. 26. v. 41. Thus the Apostles denied Christ, not out of deliberate malice, not out of any ignorance, but only out of the infirmity of the flesh.

XLIV. 3. Concupiscence, appetite. How much this can do in causing sins is both testified by experience and indicated by the Apostle James in his epistle, ch. 1, v. 14, when he writes: Every man is tempted by his own concupiscence, being drawn away and enticed. This very thing precipitated Eve into the first fall, David into adultery, Ammon into incest. It, as it were, captivates reason, so that it either does not see the good, or at least does not follow it. For it is so arranged with the faculties of the soul that when one is intensified, the other is relaxed. Indeed, even the intellect, if it is too occupied in studies, the vegetative faculty languishes. Hence, learned men are for the most part κακόσιτοι; but country folk are ἰσόσιτοι. Therefore, when concupiscence and the affections are intensified, they impede reason, so that it can neither judge accurately nor advise so promptly, whence the fall into sins is most easy.

XLV. 4. Evil habits.
