For when these have been contracted through the multiplication of acts, man proceeds daily in evils, since that which is fixed by perpetual use passes into nature, as Erasmus speaks in Meth. Theol. p. 201. And to overcome custom is a hard fight, says Augustine on Psalm 30. When, therefore, to natural corruption is added habitual vice, then man is continuously impelled toward perverse acts, as is evident from the example of drunkards.

XLVI. Finally, however, to all these causes is added the last, which alone is proximate and sufficient, namely οἰκεία ἑκούσιος προαίρεσις, the proper will and choice of each person, as Damascenus names it, l. 4, O. F. c. 20. For this is the proximate principle of all actions, and therefore unless its consent were added, neither external causes nor internal ones could carry man away and precipitate him into sins. And hence arise those just accusations of men in the Scriptures that they have spontaneously abandoned the precepts of the Lord, that they have walked in their own inventions, and have done those things which the Lord did not will. Concerning this see Proverbs 1, verse 24. Isaiah 65, verse 2. Jeremiah 61, verses 16, 17. Luke 14, verse 24. Acts 13, verses 44, 46. Romans 11, verse 2. § 2. 2 Thessalonians 2, verse 20.

Latin:

II. De veris peccati causis.

XXXIV. Nazianzenus monet: δεῖ πρὸς τῶ εἰπεῖν ὃ μὴ ἔστι καὶ ὃ ἔστιν εἰπεῖν, postquam dictum est, quid non sit, oportet dici, quid sit. Cum ergo falsas peccati causas remouerimus, vt veras porrò indicemus, requiritur. Vbi tamen istud præmittimus, causæ nomen hic sumi ἐν πλάτει, pro omni eo, quod ad peccatum efficiendum quoquo modo concurrit. Ακριβῶς enim & propriè si loqui velimus, statuendum est cum Dionysio ex l. de diui. nomin. Malum carere tum essentiâ, tum fine, tum efficiente: Et cum Augustino ex l 12. de C.D. c. 7. Mali causam non tam efficientem, quàm deficientem quærendam esse. Interim tamen, cum ἀκρίβεια Philosophica in articulis fidei locum non semper inueniat, nihil impediet, quò minus cum Theologis peccato etiam causas quasdam ἐν πλάτει & sensu generaliori assignare queamus.

XXXV. Quia verò sequente disputatione de lapsu primi hominis acturi sumus, ideò hic peccatorum, quæ post lapsum committuntur, causas potissimùm inuestigabimus. Sunt autem illæ in duplici differentia; quædam externæ, vel extra nos: quædam internæ, vel intra nos. Externarum sunt quatuor, quarum aliæ sunt causæ per accidens, aliæ perse, de quibus singulis pauca adponemus.

XXXVI. Causæ externæ per accidens sunt duæ, Obiecta in sensum incurrentia, & appetitum prouocantia. Certum enim est, obiecta multum mouere, vt vel solum Evæ exemplum docet. Vidit illa, quòd bonum esset lignum ad vescendum, & pulcrum oculis, & tulit de fructu illius, & comedit, Gen. 3 v. 6. Irritabatur ergò appetitus Evæ à pulchritudine obiecti; & sic etiamnum multi ad peccatum per exteriora commouentur. Sed hoc omne fit ex accidenti, non obiectorum, sed nostro vitio, & diaboli instinctu, qui rebus externis, velut instrumentis, ad ciendum appetitum abutitur.

XXXVII. 2. Altera causa per accidens, est lex DEI, quæ quidem in se bona; attamen quò seuerior, eò contumaciores reddit homines. Res enim vetitę sui desiderium magis excitant, quam quæ nullis legibus sunt prohibitæ, secundum illud Poëtæ: Nitimur in vetitum semper, cupimusque negata. Hinc Apostolus Rom. 7. v. 8. Peccatum Δια τῆς ἐντολῆς per mandatum operatum est in me omnem concupiscentiam. Non, quod lex seu mandatum per se hoc fecerit, sed quia naturam vitiosam per accidens in contrarium magis commouit. Ita enim exponit Apostolus, cùm v. 11. addit: Peccatum occasione accepta per mandatum seduxit me.

XXXIIX. Causæ externæ per se, vicissim duæ sunt. P. rversi h mines, alios seducentes. Hi enim persuasonibus suis multos in peccata præcipitant, quæ alias nunquam tentassent Sic Eva mouit Adamum ad comedendum de fructu vetito vnde à muliere Initium peccati factum dicitur Syrac. 25. v. 33. Sic mulieres auerterunt cor Salomonis, 1. Reg. 11. v. 3. Et Ieroboam peccare fecit Israël, 1. Reg. 15. v. 26. Est autem homo homini causa peccati, 1. dictis, vel consilio. 2. factis, vel exemplo. 3. minis vel supplicio, quod postremum tyrannorum, & inprimis Antichristi est proprium.

XXXIX. 2. Spiritus tenebrarũ vel Satanas, qui in veritate non stetit & pater est mendacij. Iohan 8. v. 44. Hîc enim passim in Scripturis dicitur excœcare mentes, 2. Cor. 4. v. 4. operari in filijs diffidentiæ, Ephes. 2. v. 2. implere cor malitiâ, Act. 5. v. 3. captiuos tenere homines, 2. Tim. 2. v. 29. & seminare Zizania, Matth. 13. v. 28.

XL. Notandum verò, quòd homines & diabolus non sint causæ peccatorum sufficientes. Resistere enim possumus, imó & debemus, juxta commonitiones. Iacob. 4. v. 7. 1. Pet. 5. v. 9. Quare peccata causant, non cogendo voluntatem, sed 1. obiecta proponendo. 2 foris persuadendo, & 3. intus phantasian commouendo, prauasque cogitationes suggerendo, quod posterius tamen solius Diaboli proprium, Cùm igitur in nostra potestate situm sit, vel consentire Satanæ, vel resistere, idcircò peccatores à culpa immunes non sunt, licèt eam omnem in Diabolum translatam velint.

XLI. Causæ peccatorum intra nos vicissim in duplici sunt differentia. Nam 1. dantur inclinantes 2. datur verè directéque efficiens.

XLII. Inclinantium sunt potissimum quatuor. 1. Ignorantia mentis: Sæpè enim intellectus censet bona esse, quæ tamèn in sè mala sunt, vnde postmodum oritur peccatum. Hinc Socrates dixit, omnia peccata proficisci ex ignorantia. Et Aristoteles l. 3. Ethic. 1. Omnem malum esse ignorantem. Hac causâ inductus fuit Apostolus Paulus, vt primo tempore persequeretur Ecclesiam. Ita enim scribit 1 Tim. 1. v. 13. Fui blasphemus & persequutor, sed ignorans feci.

XLIII. 2. Infirmitas carnis. Multi enim nouerunt bona, & ad illa primùm feruntur, pòst tamen imbecillitate carnis abrepti, peccatis se contaminant. Spiritus enim promptus quidem, sed caro infirma, Matth. 26. vers. 69. Sic Apostoli Christum negârunt non ex distinatâ malitia, non ex quadam ignorantia, sed tantùm ex carnis infirmitate.

XLIV. 3. Concupiscentia, appetitus. Quantum hæc possit in peccatis causandis & testatur experientia, & indicat Apostolus Iacobus in epistola sua, c. 1. v. 14. cùm scribit: Vnusquisque tentatur à concupiscentia sua abstractus & illectus. Hæc ipsa Evam in primum lapsum, Davidem in adulterium, Ammonem incestum præcipitavit. Hæc rationem quasi captivat, vt bonum vel non videat, vel tamen non sequatur. Sic enim comparatum est cum facultatibus animæ, vt quando vna intenditur, altera remittitur. Quin & intelligens in studijs si nimium occupetur, facultas vegetans languescit. Hinc literati plerunque sunt κακόσιτοι; sed rustici ἰσόσιτοι. Quando igitur concupiscentia & affectus intenduntur, rationem impediūt, vt nec exactè iudicare, nec tàm promptè queat consulere, unde prolapsus in peccata est facillimus.

XLV. 4. Mali habitus. Cùm n. hi per multiplicationem actuum contracti sunt, homo in malis quotidiè pergit, siquidem in naturam abit, quod vsu perpetuo est infixum, uti loquitur Erasmus in meth. Theol. p. 201. Et vincere consuetudinem, dura est pugna, inquit Augustinus supra Psal. 30. Quando ergo ad corruptionem naturale accedit vitium habituale, tum ad perversos actus continuè impellitur homo, quemadmodum patet exemplo ebriosorū.

XLVI. Tandem verò ad causas has omnes accedit vltima, quæ sola propinqua & sufficiens est, nimirum οἰκεία ἑκούσιος προαίρεσις, propria cujusque voluntas & electio, uti Damascenus nominat. l. 4. O. F. c. 20. Hæc enim omnium actionum principium est proximum, ideoque nisi ejus consensus accederet, neque externæ causæ, neque internæ inclinantes hominem abripere, & in peccata præcipitem dare possent. Atque hinc oriuntur justæ illæ hominum accusationes in Scripturis quòd sponte dereliquerint præcepta Domini, quòd ambulaverint in proprijs adinventionibus, & bus & fecerint ea, quæ noluerit Dominus. De hoc vide Prouerb. 1. vers 24. Esai. 65. v. 2. Ierem. 61. v. 16. 17. Luc. 14. vers. 24. Actor. 13. vers. 44. 46. Rom. 11. vers. 2. § 2. 2. Thess. 2. v 20.


## 5 Disputation IV. On the Fall of the First Man


### Proem

Prooimion. I.

After the general theory of sin, there follows a consideration of its species, and indeed first of Original Sin. For this, as it precedes the others in origin, so it does also in knowledge.

II. Original sin is taken in a twofold sense: 1. For the evil act which man committed in Paradise by violating the law of the Lord. 2. For the evil habit which man contracted by acting evilly and perfidiously. Our theologians designate the former as the fall of the first man; the latter, specifically, as original or natural sin.

III. The Scholastics use clearly barbaric and non-Latin terms when they call that original sin active or original originating; and this one, passive original or original originated. More tolerable is that distinction of Bonaventure, which he set forth in the second book of his Sentences, distinction 21, folio 398. The sin of man, he says, is threefold. 1. A certain one in which the person corrupted the nature, and this was the sin of the first man. 2. A certain one in which the nature corrupts the person, and this is original actively so called 3. A certain one, in which the person corrupts himself, and this is actual, of which in turn there are many species.

IV. We, setting aside for the present the doctrine of natural and actual sin, will dispute concerning the first Fall of man, which was nothing other than the first actual sin of Adam, or the transgression of the law concerning not eating from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This was the first cause of our corruption and misery, by which also the stain of nature was contracted. For thus our evils follow: 1. Adam began to sin in Paradise. 2. Hence nature was depraved, and with such corruption was propagated into us. 3. From which we are daily incited to various actual sins. Therefore an evil act preceded in Adam, which produced an evil habit in nature; from which vicious actions follow in our person.

V. Many idle questions, however, are moved by the Scholastics concerning the fall of the first man: which, as fruitless, we cutting away, will be content with four principal ζητήμασι (inquiries), which we shall expound. 1. Who sinned? 2. What was the cause of that first sin? 3. What was it? and 4. What kind of sin was it? For if 1. the agent, 2. the moving cause, 3. the quiddity, and 4. the quality are known; hardly anything further can be desired concerning the knowledge of any act.

Latin:

Προόιμιον. I.

POst θεωρίαν peccati generalem, sequitur consideratio specierum, & quidem primò Peccati originalis. Hoc enim vt cætera præcedit origine; ita & cognitione.

II. Sumitur autem originis Peccatum dupliciter 1. pro Malo actu, quem commisit homo in Paradiso, legem Domini violando. 2. Pro Malo Habitu, quem contraxit homo, malè & perfidè agendo. Illud Theologi nostri lapsum primi hominis; hoc in specie peccatum originale vel naturale indigitant.

III. Scholastici planè barbaris & illatinis vtuntur terminis, cùm istud peccatum originale activè vel originale originans; hoc originale passiuum vel originale originatum nuncupant. Tolerabilior est illa Bonauenturæ distinctio, quam posuit in libro secundo sentent. dist. 21. fol. 398. Hominis, inquit, peccatum triplex est. 1. Quoddam in quo persona corrupit naturam, & hoc fuit peccatum primi hominis. 2. Quoddam in quo natura corrumpit personam, & hoc est originale actiue sic dictum 3. Quoddam, in quo persona corrumpit seipsam, & hoc est actuale, cuius vicissim multæ sunt species.

I V. Nos impræsentiarum seponentes doctrinam peccati naturalis & actualis, disputabimus de primo hominis Lapsu, qui nihil aliud fuit, quam primum Adami peccatum actuale, seu transgressio legis, de non comedendo ex arbore scientiæ boni & mali. Hæc prima corruptionis miseriæque nostræ causa fuit, quâ & labes naturæ contracta est. Ita enim consequuntur mala nostra 1. Adamus peccare cœpit in Paradiso. 2. Hinc natura deprauata, & cum tali corruptione in nos propagata est. 3. Ex quo ad varia peccata actualia quotidiè incitamur. Præcessit ergò malus actus in Adamo, qui produxit malum habitum in natura; vnde sequuntur vitiosæ actiones in persona nostra.

V. Multæ autem otiosæ quæstiones circa lapsum primi hominis mouentur à Scholasticis: quas, vt infructuosas resecantes, quatuor ζητήμασι principalibus contenti erimus, exposituri. 1. Quis peccauit? 2. Quæ istius primi peccati causa? 3. Quodnam? & 4. Quale peccatum fuerit? Si enim cognoscitur, 1. agens, 2, causa mouens, 3. quidditas, 4. qualitas; vix vltrà aliquid circa notitiam alicuius actus desiderari poterit.


### Question I. Who sinned in Paradise?

I. This question seems superfluous, since we have a manifest decision in Genesis 3:6, where we read that both Adam and Eve violated the command of the Lord. Because, however, two other texts are found in the Scriptures which seem contrary to the cited passage, therefore it must be indicated in a few words and as if in the vestibule, how that φαινομένη ἀντίφασις (apparent contradiction) ought to be reconciled.

II. The PRIOR text, seemingly contrary, is found in Rom. 5. 12. δἰ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου, through ONE man sin entered into the world. From which it follows: If through one; therefore not through two; and therefore Adam and Eve were not jointly the causes of original sin.

III. However, this apparent conflict is usually reconciled in two ways: 1. That by one man both Adam and Eve are understood together. For in Genesis also, chapter 1, verse 26, where the decree of the Trinity is recited, 'Let us make man,' mention is made of one man in the singular, and yet the male and female are understood, as the execution of that decree shows, concerning which verse 27 says: 'And God created man; male and female He created them.' Thus, therefore, Scripture explains itself, what it wishes to be understood by 'man,' namely, male and female: and therefore the Apostolic phrase concerning one man sinning does not exclude the female, but rather includes her. But if it is asked why the male and female are called one man, when they were two persons? It is answered that this is done not indeed because of unity of number or sex, but because of unity 1. of nature or species, 2. of marriage or association, since spouses in the Scriptures are also called one flesh, as in Matt. 19. 6.

IV. 2. That Paul by one man understands primarily Adam, yet in such a way that Eve is not entirely excluded. And this reconciliation seems better than the preceding one. For 1. all men are indeed one in species; but not one man. 2. The Apostle compares the second Adam, who is Christ, with the first Adam. For he always joins these: 'As by the offense of one many died; so the grace of one abounded,' verse 15. 'By the offense of one came condemnation; by the righteousness of one came justification,' verse 18. Therefore, just as he understands numerical unity in the apodosis, so also in the protasis. And just as by 'one man' in the apodosis he implies only Christ or the second Adam:

thus in the πρωτόκῳ it directly refers only to the first Adam.

V. But sin is said to have entered through one Adam for a twofold reason.

1. Because men are the heads of women, 1 Cor. 11:3, and therefore these are not numbered separately, but are always numbered with the men, which can be proven by many examples from the Old Testament. And hence a male is called in Hebrew זָכָר from the root זָכַר which is, to remember, because in genealogies mention or record is made only of males, στῦλοι γὰρ οἴκων παῖδές εἰσιν ἄῤῥενες, for males are the foundation of the family, according to Euripides.

2. Because the Apostle is speaking not of sin itself, but of the propagation of sin. Now generation, and everything that is transferred through generation, is usually ascribed to men as the agents. Just as therefore in Gen. 46:26, because of the primary reason of generation, 66 souls are said to have come out of the thigh of Jacob alone, so sin is rightly said to have entered through one and only Adam: that is, to have been propagated, yet in such a way that neither there nor here are women entirely excluded.

VI. A later text that is apparently contrary is read in 1 Tim. 2:14, Ἀδὰμ οὐκ ἠπατήθη, Adam was not seduced, but the woman being seduced was in the transgression. Why therefore is it said in Gen. 3:6 that Adam gave place to the persuasion of the woman, and ate together with her? Why does the Apostle write that sin entered through Adam, if he was not seduced into the transgression?

VII. A fourfold reconciliation is usually brought forward for this passage.

For 1. One seduction is diabolical; another is human, which indeed has its origin from the Devil, but in such a way that man intervenes as a kind of medium and instrument. The Apostle Paul speaks of the former, the Prophet Moses of the latter, for Adam was not seduced by the serpent or the Devil alone ἀμέσως, but through the mediation of the woman's persuasion.

2. Seduction is either external, from without through the address of the serpent; or internal, from within through the suggestion of Satan. In the former sense Adam was not seduced, because Satan only attacked and addressed Eve from without in the serpent.

3. External seduction is taken either strictly, where it not only posits the deception of the one seduced, but also presupposes the fraud of the one seducing; or somewhat more broadly, in which sense it denotes simple deception, without the presupposed fraudulent intent of the persuader. In the former way only Eve, not Adam, in the latter Adam, not Eve, was seduced. The Apostle speaks of the former, Moses of the latter, as Augustine explains in book 11 of De Genesi ad litteram, last chapter.

4 Seduction is one thing, the order of seduction is another. The Apostle attends not to the former, but to the latter; as appears from the text itself. For the words cohere thus: Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not seduced, namely first, just as he was created first. For Satan knew that the order of destruction is contrary to the order of construction. For those things which are last in composing are for the most part first in resolving. Since therefore the woman was made last, hence the Devil wished to attack her first, concluding that if he seduced her, she would not rest until she had also deceived Adam. Therefore, to collect our responses, we say with the Apostle that Adam was not seduced, namely by a seduction that was 1. immediate, 2. external, 3. taken strictly, and 4. first.

VIII. But if anyone should further object that by this arrangement sin did not enter through Adam, because he was not seduced first, and therefore did not sin first: then we distinguish between the beginning of sin and the propagation of the sin that has begun. Eve indeed sinned first or began to sin, whence it is said in Sirach 25:33: From the woman was the beginning of sin: yet she did not primarily propagate the sin, because propagation is ascribed to the father who begets. Thus, therefore, we refer the beginning of sin with the son of Sirach to the woman, but the transmission of sin with the Apostle to the man.

Latin:

I. Videtur hæc quæstio superuacanea, cùm decisionem habeamus manifestam Genes. 3. 6. vbi & Adamum & Euam mandatum Domini violasse legimus. Quia tamen in Scripturis alij duo textus reperiūtur qui loco allegato vidētur contrarij: idcircò paucis & velut in vestibulo indicandum est, quomodo ista φαινομένη ἀντίφασις conciliari debeat.

II. PRIOR textus, in specie contrarius, habetur Rom. 5. 12. δἰ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπου per VNYM hominem peccatum intrauit in mundum, Ex quo sequitur, Si per vnum; Ergo non per duos; ideoque Adam & Eua coniunctim peccati originalis causæ non fuerunt.

III. Duobus autem modis apparens hæc pugna componi solet 1. Quòd per vnum hominem & Adam & Eua simul intelligantur Nam in Genesi etiam cap. 1. v. 26. vbi recitatur decretum Trinitatis, Faciamus hominem, vnius hominis in singulari fit mentio, & tamen intelligitur masculus & fœmina, vti ostendit decreti istius executio, de qua v 27. Et creauit, Deus hominem; masculum & fœminam creauit eos. Ita ergo Scriptura semetipsam explicat, quid per hominem intellectum velit, nempè masculum & fœminam: ideoq; phrasis Apostolica de vno homine peccante, fœminam non excludit, sed potius includit. Si autem quæratur, cur mas & fœmina dicantur vnus homo, cùm duæ fuerint personæ? Respondetur, fieri hoc non quidem ob vnitatem numeri vel sexus, sed ob vnitatem 1. naturæ vel speciei, 2. Coniugij vel consôciationis, quoniam coniuges in Scripturis etiam dicuntur vna caro, vt Matth. 19. 6.

IV. 2. Quòd Paulus per vnum hominem præcipuè Adamum intelligat, ita tamen, vt Eua non penitus excludatur. Et hæc conciliatio præcedente melior videtur. Nam 1. omnes homines sunt quidem vnum specie; sed non vnus homo. 2. Apostolus comparat cum Adamo primo Adamum secundum, qui est Christus, Semper enim hæc coniungit; Vt vnius delicto multi mortui sunt; ita vnius gratia abundauit, vers. 15. Per vnius delictum condemnatio per vnius iustitiam iustificatio, vers. 18. Sicut ergo numericam vnitatem intelligit in ἀποδόσει sic etiam in προτάσει. Et velut per vnum hominem in ἀποδόσει tantùm innuit Christum vel Adamum secundum:

sic in πρωτόκῳ directè tantùm respicit Adamum primum.

V. Dicitur autem peccatum intrasse per vnum Adamum duplici de causa.

1. Quia viri sunt capita mulierum, 1. Cor. 11. 3. ideoque seorsum istæ non numerantur, sed semper viris annumerantur, id quod multis ex V. Testam. exemplis probari potest. Et hinc masculus Hæbræis dicitur זָכָר à radice זָכַר quod est, recordari, quia in genealogijs masculorum duntaxat fit recordatio vel mentio, στῦλοι γὰρ οἴκων παῖδές εἰσιν ἄῤῥενες, Fundamentum enim familiæ sunt masculi, iuxta Euripidem.

2. Quia loquitur Apostolus non de peccato ipso, sed peccati propagatione. Generatio autem, & omne id, quod per generationem transfertur, viris vt agentibus adscribi solet. Sicut igitur Gen. 46. v. 26. propter primariam generationis rationem de femore solum Iacobi egressæ dicũtur animæ 66. Ita peccatum rectè per solum & vnum Adamum intrâsse: hoc est, propagatum esse dicitur, ita tamen vt nec ibi, neque hic omninò excludantur mulieres.

VI. Posterior textus apparenter contrarius legitur 1. Tim. 2. v. 14. Ἀδὰμ ἠπατήθη, Adam non est seductus, sed mulier seducta in præuaricatione fuit. Cur ergo Gen. 3. 6 dicitur, quòd Adam persuasioni mulieris locum dederit, & vnâ comederit? Cur Apostolus per Adamum intrâsse peccatum scribit, si in præuaricationem seductus non fuit?

VII. Quadruplex autem conciliatio ad hunc locum adferri solet.

Nam 1. Seductio alia est Diabolica; alia humana, quæ à Diabolo quidem suum quoq; ortum habet, sed ita vt homo quasi medium & instrumentum interueniat. De illa loquitur Apostolus Paulus, de hac Propheta Moses, Adam enim non est seductus à solo serpente vel Diabolo ἀμέσως, sed mediante mulieris persuasione.

2. Seductio vel est exterior, foris per alloquium serpentis; vel interior, intus per suggestionen Satanae. Priori sensu Adam non fuit seductus, quia Euam tantùm foris aggressus & allocutus est in serpente Satanas.

3. Seductio externa sumitur vel strictè, vbi non tantum ponit deceptionem seducti, verùm etiam praesupponit fraudem seducentis; vel nonnihil latius, quo sensu notat simplicem deceptionem, sine praesupposito persuadentis animo fraudulento. Illo modo sola Eua, non Adam, hoc Adam, non Eua seducta fuit, De illo Apostolus, de hoc Moses loquitur, explicante August. l. 11. de Gen. ad lit. cap. vlt.

4 Aliud est seductio, aliud seductionis ordo. Non illam, sed hunc attendit Apostolus; quemadmodum ex ipso textu apparet. Ita enim verba cohaerent: Adam primus formatus est, deinde Eua. Et Adam non est seductus, nempè primùm, sicuti creatus erat primùm. Nouit enim Satanas, ordinem destructionis contrarium esse ordini constructionis. Nam quae sunt vltima in componendo plerumque prima sunt in resoluendo. Quoniam ergo mulier vltimô est facta, hinc primò eam aggredi voluit Diabolus, conijciens, si illam seduxerit, quieturam non esse, donec Adamum quoque deceperit. Vt igitur colligamus responsiones, dicimus cum Apostolo Adamum non fuisse seductum, nempè seductione. 1. Immediata, 2. externa. 3. strictè sumpta & 4. primâ.

VIII. Si verò quis porrò obijciat, hoc pacto per Adamum non intrâsse peccatum, quia non est seductus primùm, ideoque nec peccasse primùm: tum distinguimus inter peccati inchoationem, & inchoati propagationem. Eua quidem primum peccauit vel peccare coepit, vnde dicitur Syr. 25. 33. A muliere initium factum est peccati: non tamen illa primariò peccatum propagauit, quia propagatio patri generanti adscribitur. Ita igitur initium peccati cum Syracide ad mulierem, sed traductionem peccati cum Apostolo ad virum referimus.


### Question II

What was the cause of the first fall or sin?

I. Regarding this question, the Calvinists teach one thing, the orthodox another. The former propose a false cause, the latter a true one. A few words on both:

I. Concerning the false cause of the fall, devised by the Calvinists.

II. Since the Scholastics extolled the freedom of the will too much, saying that man is free in good actions as well as in bad ones; Calvin, contradicting them, fell into the opposite error by destroying freedom and introducing necessity.

III. Moreover, he established the primary cause of this necessity as the immutable will of God, by whose decree all things happen, and they could not happen otherwise. From which he concluded that the first man also necessarily fell; because God had decreed from eternity that it should happen so. In order that this might be executed in time, he had created man fallible, had prescribed a law, had instigated the devil, had withdrawn what was good, and had impelled him toward evil, so that He might manifest His glory regarding the human race, namely, mercy toward those to be saved, and justice toward those to be damned.

IV. For thus writes Calvin, Inst. book 3, ch. 23, § 7: I confess the decree is indeed horrible, yet no one will be able to deny that God foresaw what end man would have before He created him, and He foresaw it for this reason, because He had so ordained it by His own decree. Theodore Beza explained these things more fully in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, where on p. 428 he reasons thus: If man had remained in the state of integrity, there would have been no place for the declaration of either justice or mercy in that very day: therefore one way had to be found by which man was prepared and disposed for both. Hence he concludes on page 429. Man, established in an upright state, did not fall rashly. If not rashly, certainly by the providence of God. Because it HAD TO come to pass, which God decreed; who by the fall of man sought for himself a way and method, so that the declaration of his glory might be manifested in his mercy and justice. Conversely, p. 431. It WAS NECESSARY for man to sin: IT WAS NECESSARY, therefore, that the first men also fell, GOD SO ORDAINING, that some might be damned. And part 2. Response to the Acts, p. 177. Neither unwillingly, nor unknowingly, nor idly foreknowing, and therefore in truth: I said that the first men fell BECAUSE GOD SO WILLED AND DECREED, etc.

V. The opinion, therefore, of the Calvinists, in brief, is this: that God, the Best and Greatest, is the primary and supreme cause of the human fall, since he concurred in it by many ways and actions, as a means of declaring his glory: Therefore, it must now be examined, can any act be found in God which caused the sin of Adam, even in some slightly lighter way? The Calvinists indeed count a great many, yet all can be divided into two kinds: the former of which contains acts falsely ascribed to God by the Calvinists: the latter, true ones, but which contribute nothing at all to the efficiency of sin. We shall briefly consider both kinds.

VI. Therefore, to begin with the ACTIONS FALSELY ASCRIBED TO GOD, the Calvinists count three of them primarily, namely: 1. The eternal and decretory will of God, 2. The temporal provocation of the devil to seduce, and 3. The internal impulse of man to consent. That all these acts are falsely and blasphemously attributed to God, must now be proven and demonstrated in order.

VII. I. As regards the ETERNAL DECREE OF GOD, the Calvinists declaim about it as prolixly and exactly as if they had been present in the secret council of the Holy Trinity, and as if they had been his counselors, as Jacob Andreae rightly objected to Theodore Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 438. But the sum is touched upon in thesis 4 and in a few words is this: God from all eternity made a decree concerning the manifestation of his glory, which consists chiefly in justice and mercy. But because the manifestation of glory is impossible unless there be someone to whom it may be manifested: therefore he made a second decree concerning the creation of the human race, and indeed in his own image in justice and holiness, by which the display of his glory might afterwards become more evident. Furthermore, because mercy has no place unless misery precedes it, nor justice where there is no fault, therefore from eternity he willed and decreed that man should fall into sin, by which he might thus manifest his justice in fallen men as regards those to be damned, and his mercy as regards those to be saved. Since God therefore willed this end, he also willed the means, namely the sin of man, and thus the πρωτοπλάστοι, with God decreeing and ordaining it, violated the law that had been laid down and fell. This is the epitome of the whole Calvinistic mystery, a wider deduction of which you will find in Calvin, Institutes, book 3, chapter 13; Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard and part 2 of his Responses; Zanchius in his Miscellanies; and Rennecher in his Golden Chain of Salvation.

VIII. But in order that this blasphemous opinion may be refuted, two things especially must be attended to: 1. Whether God willed and from eternity decreed the fall of man? 2. Whether for the sake of that end, namely the manifestation of his glory, he willed or could have willed it? We deny both, and we present this denial included in our genuine thesis.

IX. FIRST Thesis: God did not decree, nor did he will, that the first man should fall, but rather that he should stand and persist in good.

This thesis comprises two members; for it treats 1. of the will of God denied, regarding the fall, 2. of the will affirmed, regarding perseverance in good. We shall confirm and defend both.

X. 1. That God did not will the fall of Adam, we prove 1. By the passage of Psalm 5, verse 5: 'You are not a God who wills iniquity.' If God wills iniquity in no way, therefore he neither willed nor could have willed the first one.

2. The interdiction of the fruit, Genesis 2, verse 17: 'Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat.' A commandment is an index of the will. God commanded, however, that man should not eat. Therefore He willed that he should not eat. Furthermore, the first sin consisted in the forbidden eating. And God willed this sin according to the Calvinists. Therefore He willed that man should eat. Behold, therefore, God is contrary to Himself! Calvin affirms the former, Moses the latter. But the former mendaciously, the latter truthfully. Furthermore, it follows from this that Adam sinned and did not sin by one and the same act. For insofar as he was fulfilling the secret will of God, he was not sinning, since it is ἄτοπον [absurd] for someone to sin in that in which he is executing the will of God. But insofar as he was not doing the will of God comprised in the commandment, he was sinning; since all ἀνομία [lawlessness] is ἁμαρτία [sin], 1 John 5 v. 4. Wherefore Adam ought also to have been punished and not punished, to lose the concreated image and not to lose it, all of which things are κατάφασικά [affirmative] and most absurd.

3. By the testimony of Ecclesiasticus, from c. 15. v. 14. & 15. God from the beginning created man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. But if he sinned by an inevitable decree of God, how was he left to himself, how was his salvation in his own will? For the will of God is the necessity of things, says Calvin, l. 3. Inst. c. 23. §. 6.

4. By the hatred of God. The Lord was most gravely indignant at the πρωτοπλάστοις [first-formed] after the fall, Gen. 3. Wherefore He did not decree this, He did not will it. For of that of which God is the author, He is not the hater; because He hates nothing of those things which He has made. Wis. 11. v. 25.

5. By the punishment of the πρωτοπλάστων [first-formed], which is described in Gen. 3. God, however, is not the author of that of which He is the avenger; Fulg. l. 1. ad Mon. p. 41. And He punishes no one who does His will, John 14. v. 21. But He punished Adam on account of the fall. Therefore, by falling, he did not do His will. Wherefore God did not will that man should fall, and therefore He did not exist as the cause of the first sin.

6. By the authority of the Fathers. Clement, l. 4. Strom: That man chose, and indeed chose that which was forbidden, The fault is not to be transferred to God, Chrysostom in Homily on the interdiction of the tree. It is manifest that God did not wish Adam to sin; who wished to fortify him before the fall. He could have obeyed God, because he did not wish to, because he preferred to listen to the devil.

XI. Nor indeed do the Calvinistic arguments have any weight, of which there are principally four. 1. God decreed the mission of the Son and the redemption of the human race. Wherefore he also decreed the fall, and it was necessary for Adam to sin, since otherwise men could not have been redeemed.

Resp. 1 God did not decree redemption because he had previously decreed, but because he had previously foreseen the fall. 2. The Scholastics distinguish between the decree of 1. commanding, 2. effecting, 3. permitting; and they say that God decreed the fall, but by a decree of permitting. But it is safer to distinguish between the fall itself and the permission of the fall. The decree of God ought to be referred to the latter alone, but not to the former, as such. 3. Adam fell necessarily, but by a necessity of the consequent, not of the consequence; hypothetically, not absolutely; in respect to God foreseeing, not decreeing or impelling.

2. Adam's fall was either with God willing it, or not willing it. Not the latter, because nothing happens against God's will, since he is omnipotent; therefore the former.

Resp. Evils happen not with God willing, or not willing, but not willing, just as Lombard concludes from the writings of the Fathers, book 1, Sentences, distinction 49, letter F. Therefore the enumeration of parts in the antecedent is insufficient. For the Philosopher himself, book 3, Ethics, chapter 1, places mixed or intermediate actions between ἑκούσιον and ἀκούσιον. Therefore we say that the fall of Adam happened not with God willing, nor not willing, or resisting, but not willing, not approving.

3. If a little sparrow does not fall without the will of God, Matthew 10, verse 29, much less a man. Therefore the decree of God ought not to be excluded from the chance or fall of the first-formed.

Resp. We distinguish between a physical and a theological fall, or natural and moral. The latter is vicious; the former is not. This God disapproves and does not will: that he approves and wills. Of the latter the fifth Psalm, of the former

The Apostle Matthew speaks: There are therefore four terms, because the collection is made from a natural fall to a moral one, from a fall of the body to a fall of the soul. 4. He who wills the end, or also the means. God willed the end of the fall, as of the means, namely the redemption of certain men, and the manifestation of His glory: Therefore He also willed the fall itself. Resp. The major premise is not universal. For a magistrate wills the end of evil customs, namely the promulgation of good laws, yet he does not will the evil customs themselves. A gardener wills the end of a withered tree, namely the heating of his dwelling, or its sale, yet he did not will the withering itself of the fruit-bearing tree. Therefore 2. we distinguish between a means per se, and a means per accidens, or between a means φύσει and a means ἰδίᾳ. Of the former, not of the latter, the major premise is true: but of the latter, and not the former, the minor premise speaks. For sin is not per se, and φύσει a means to useful ends, (since from evil, as evil, good does not follow) but it becomes a means per accidens, namely through the wisdom of God, directing and accommodating every evil to good ends.

XII. II. That God willed that man should persist in good, we prove, 1. From the image of God, according to which man was created Gen. 1. v. 27. & 2. v. 7. Wis. 2. v. 23. That image consisted, however, in righteousness and holiness of truth, Eph. 4. v. 23. If therefore man was created by God, so that he might be righteous and holy, certainly he was not created so that he might sin; but rather, so that he might stand and persist.

2. From the renewal to the lost image, Eph. 4. v. 23. Col. 3. v. 9. If those who wish to be righteous, and partakers of eternal life, must be renewed to the image of the first man, and be made conformable to him, certainly he was not created to sin, but to stand, and to act righteously. Otherwise, it would be commanded that we also should not be constant in newness.

3. From the precept of multiplication, Gen. 1. v. 28. God willed that man should increase, and indeed in such a state in which He had created him, that is, He wished that he should propagate this image of his also to his descendants, since by divine ordination like must always beget like. Therefore, He wished that he should persist. For how could he have derived that image into his descendants according to the will of the Lord, if he had not persisted in good

5. From Wisdom 2, verse 7. God created man in ἀφθαρσία. The Vulgate has 'Inexterminabilem' [Incorruptible]; most interpreters explain it as 'For incorruptibility.' If, therefore, man was created for this, God certainly wished that he should stand. For otherwise He would not have created him for corruptibility.

XIII. The Calvinists, however, bring forward three objections to the contrary. 1. Man did not stand. Therefore, he was not created so that he might stand, since otherwise God would have been frustrated in His end of creation.

Response: I deny the consequence, because many instances can be given. No one can keep the law of God: was it therefore not given so that it might be kept? Not all obey the Holy Spirit: was He therefore not speaking to us for this end, that we might obey Him? Why then are men said to resist and contradict Him? Acts 7, verse 51. Not all students turn out learned in the Academies. Were they therefore not sent there for this end? We distinguish, therefore, between ends: 1. Some are absolute and independent, which always follow. 2. Some are conditional and dependent upon a certain condition, which if it is absent, the end does not follow, although it ought to follow. And in such a way perseverance was the end of creation, namely, not absolute but conditional, if man himself should wish, and not spontaneously precipitate himself into evil. Although, therefore, man did not stand, God wished him to stand; but under a condition, unless he himself should have resisted.

2. What God has willed, He has done, Psalm 113, verse 3, and Isaiah 46, verse 10. ὅσα θέλῃ γίνεται, Damascene, book 2, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 29. Therefore, what does not happen, God does not will. But it did not happen that Adam stood; rather he fell: therefore God did not will that, but this.

Resp. The major premise is not universal, because many things happen which God does not will, and vice versa. We have examples, Prov. 1. v. 28. chap. 19. v. 3. Isa. 65. v. 12. ch. 66. v. 4. Ezek. 33. v. 11. Matt. 23. v. 37. Luke 7. v. 30. Acts 7. v. 51. 1. Timothy 2. v. 3, 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. God wills that we keep his law, and yet it is not done: He wills that we love one another, and do penance, and yet we do not do it. Therefore, one must distinguish between the absolute and conditional θέλημα of God: the former is always efficacious; the latter, because it depends on a certain condition, is therefore sometimes inefficacious, namely when that condition is absent. In such a conditional manner, however, God willed the perseverance of man.

3. If God had willed man to stand, He would not have created him mutable. Resp. N. C. [Non Consequens] because of the fallacy of the cause, because He did not create Adam mutable so that he might stand, but because 1. He willed him to be a man, not a brute; therefore it was necessary that he be of free will. 2. He willed a spontaneous worship; ἀβίαστον δὲ πρᾶγμα εἶναι τὸ καλὸν, writes Damasc. b. 4. ch. 20.

Latin:

Quaenam fuerit primi lapsus vel peccati causa?

I. Quoad hanc quaestionem aliter Caluiniani, aliter orthodoxi docent. Illi falsam, hi vera causam proponunt. De vtraque paucis:

I. De falsa lapsus causa, à Caluinianis excogitata.

II. Cùm Scholastici libertatem arbitrij nimium extollerent, dicentes hominem tàm in bonis, quam malis actionibus esse liberum; Caluinus ijs contradicens, in contrarium errorem incidit, libertatem destruendo, & necessitatem invehendo.

III. Huius autem necessitatis causam primariam statuit immutabilem Dei voluntatem, cuius decreto omnia fiunt, nec aliter euenire queant. Ex quo conclusit hominem quoque primum necessariò fuisse lapsum; quia Deus ab æterno ita fieri decreuerit. Quod vt exequeretur in tempore, hominem condidisse labilem, prescripsisse legem, instigâsse diabolum, deseruijsse quod bonum & impulisse ad malum, quò gloriam suam circa genus humanum manifestare posset, nempè misericordiâ circa saluandos, & iustitiam circa damnandos.

IV. Ita n. scribit Caluinus l. 3. Inst. c. 23. §. 7. Decretum quidem horribile fateor, inficiari tamen nemo poterit, quin præsciuerit Deus, quem exitum esset habiturus homo, antequam conderet, & ideò præsciuerit, quia DECRETO SVO sic ordinauerat. Fusiùs hæc exposuit Theod. Beza in Colloq. Momp. vbi p. 428. ita ratiocinatur. Si in statu integritatis homo permansisset, neque iustitiæ, neque misericordiæ in die ipso declarandæ locus fuisset: Vna ergò invenienda fuit, quà homo ad vtrumque paratus & dispofisus esset. Hinc concludit pag. 429. Non temere cecidit homo, in integro statu constitutus. Si non temere, certe ex providentia Dei. Quia venire OPORTVIT, quod Deus decrevit; qui hominis lapsu sibi viam & rationem quæsivit, ut gloria eius declarationem misericordiæ & iustitiæ suæ manifestaretur. Vicissim p. 431. OPORTVIT hominem peccare: NECESSE ERAT, ideo lapsos quoque esse homines primos, DEO SIC ORDINANTE, vt quide damnentur. Et par. 2. Resp. ad Acta. p. 177. Neque invito, neque ignorante, neque otiose præsciente, ac proinde revera: SIC VOLENTE ET DECERNENTE DEO primos homines esse lapsos dixi, &c.

V. Sententia ergo Caluinianorum συντόμως, hæc est, quod Deus Opt. Max. sit prima & suprema lapsus humani causa, quandoquidem multis modis & actionibus ad illum concurrerit, veluti medium declarandæ suæ gloriæ: Proinde iam dispiciendum est, An ullus in Deo reperiri queat actus, qui peccatum Adami vel aliquo saltem leviusculo modo causarit? Caluiniani quidem bene multos numerant, omnes tamen in duo genera dispesci possunt: quorum prius continet actus a Caluinianis falso adscriptos Deo: posterius veros, sed ad peccati efficientiam nihil omnino cōducentes. Vtrumque genus breuiter considerabimus.

VI. Vt ergo ab ACTIONIBVS FALSO ADSCRIPTIS DEO incipiamus, earum tres potissimum numerant Caluiniani nimirum: 1. Æternam & decretoriam Dei voluntatem, 2. Temporalem diaboli ad seducendum provocationem, & 3. Internam hominis ad consentiendum impulsionem, Actus hos omnes falso & & blaspheme Deo attribui, ordine iam probandum & demonstrandum est.

VII. I. Quod ÆTERNUM DEI DECRETVM spectat, de illo tam prolixe & exacte rhetoricantur Caluiniani, ac si coram affediffent in arcano SS. Trinitatis consilio, & quasi consiliarij illius fuissent, vti Theod. Bezæ recte obiecit Iacobus Andr. in Coll. Mompelg p. 438. Summa vero th. 4. tacta & paucis paucis hæc est: Deus ab omni æternitate decretum fecit de manifestanda sua gloria, quæ potissimum in iustitia & misericordia consistit. Quia vero manifestatio gloriæ impossibilis, nisi sit aliquis, cui ea manifestetur: propterea fecit decretum alterum de creatione generis humani, & quidem ad imaginem suam in iustitia & sanctitate, quo postmodum gloriæ ostensio evaderet evidentior. Porro autem, quia locum non habet misericordia, nisi ubi præcedit miseria, nec iustitia, ubi nulla est culpa, idcirco ab æterno voluit & decrevit, ut homo laberetur in peccatum, quo sic in lapsis hominibus suam manifestaret iustitiam quoad dammandos, & misericordiam, quoad salvandos. Hunc ergo finem cum Deus voluerit, ideo & medium voluit, nempe peccatum hominis, adeoque πρωτοπλάστοι decernente & ordinante Deo legem latam violarunt & lapsi sunt. Hæc ἐπιτομή est totius mysterij Caluinistici, cuius latiorem deductionem invenies apud Calvinum l. institut. c. 13. Bezam in Colloq Mompelg. & par. 2. Resp. Zanchium Miscell. & Rennecherum in aurea salutis catena.

IIX. Vt verò blasphema hæc opinio refutetur, duo potissimum attendenda sunt: 1. An Deus voluerit, & ab æterno decreverit lapsum hominis? 2. An propter istum finem, nempè gloriæ suæ manifestationem voluerit, vel velle potuerit? Vtrúmq; nos negamus, & hanc negationem genuinæ thesi inclusam exhibemus.

IX. PRIOR Thesis: Deus non decrevit, nec voluit, ut primus homo laberetur, sed potius ut staret, inque bono persisteret.

Thesis hæc duo membra complectitur; siquidem agit 1. de voluntate Dei negata, quoad lapsum, 2. de voluntate affirmata, quoad perseverantiam in bono. Vtrumque confirmabimus & defendemus.

X. 1. Deum non voluisse lapsum Adæ, probamus 1. Dicto Psalmi 5 vers. 5. Non Deus volens iniquitatem tu es, Si Deus nullâ vult iniquitatem, Ergo nec primam voluit, aut velle potuit.

2. Interdictio pomi, Genes. 2. vers. 17. De ligno scientiæ boni & mali ne comedas. Præceptum est index voluntatis. Præcepit autem Deus, nè homo comederet. Ergo voluit, nè comederet. Porrò, peccatum primum consistebat in comestione vetita. Et peccatum hoc voluit Deus iuxta Caluinianos. Ergo voluit, vt homo comederet. Ecce igitur Deum sibi ipsi contrarium! Illud Caluinus, hoc Moses affirmat. Sed ille mendaciter, hic veraciter. Præterea èxinde sequitur. Adamũ vno eodemque actu peccásse, & non peccasse. Quatenus enim implebat arcanam Dei voluntatem, non peccabat, cùm ἄτοπον sit, peccare aliquem in eo quo Dei voluntatem exèquitur. Quatenus verò non faciebat voluntatem Dei præcepto comprehensam, peccabat; cùm omnis ἀνομία sit ἁμαρτία, 1. Iohan. 5 v. 4. Quare debuit Adamus etiam puniri, & non puniri, imaginem concreatam amittere & non amittere, quæ omnia sunt κατάφασικά & absurdissima.

3. Testimonio Ecclesiastici, ex c. 15. v. 14. & 15. Deus ab initio constituit hominem, & reliquit illum in manu consilij sui, At si ineuitabili decreto Dei peccauit, quomodo sibi relictus, quomodo salus eius in propria voluntate sua fuit? Dei enim voluntas est rerum necessitas, inquit Caluinus l. 3. Inst. c. 23. §. 6.

4. Odio Dei. Grauissimè indignabatur Dominus πρωτοπλάστοις post lapsum, Gen. 3. Quare hunc non decreuit, non voluit. Cuius enim Deus author est, eius osor non est; quia nihil odit eorum quæ fecit. Sap. 11. v. 25.

5. Supplicio πρωτοπλάστων, quod describitur Gen. 3. Deus autem non est author, cuius est vltor; Fulg. l. 1. ad Mon. p. 41. Et neminem punit, qui facit voluntatem eius, Ioha. 14. v. 21. Adamum verò puniuit ob lapsum. Ergo labendo, voluntatem eius non fecit, Quare Deus hominem labi non voluit, ideoque peccati primi causa non extitit.

6. Authoritate Patrum. Clemens l. 4. Strom: Quod homo elegerit, atque adeo id quod erat vetitum, elegerit, Non est culpain Deum transferenda, Chrisost. in Homil. de interdict. arboris? Manifestū est, Deum noluisse Adam peccare; qui voluit eum ante deictū præstruere, Potuit Adā leo parere, quia noluit, quia õsentire diabolo maluit.

XI. Neq; verò momenti aliquid habent ratiunculæ Caluinisticæ, quarum præcipuè sunt quatuor. 1. Deus decreuit missionem Filij & redemptionem generis humani. Quare decreuit etiam lapsum, & oportuit Adamam peccare, cùm alias homines redimi non potuissent.

Resp. 1 Non Deus decreuit redemptionem quia prius decreuerat, sed quia pri° præuiderat lapsum. 2. Scholastici distinguunt inter decretum, 1. præcipientis, 2. efficientis, 3. permittentis; & dicunt, Deum decreuisse lapsum, sed decreto permittentis. Verùm tutius est distinguere inter lapsum ipsum, & lapsus permissionem. Ad hanc solam, non vero ad illum, quà talis, decretum Dei referri debet. 3. Necessariò lapsus est Adam, sed necessitate consequentis, non consequentis; hypotheticâ, non absolutâ; respectu Dei prævidentis, non decernentis aut impellentis.

2. Lapsus est Adam aut Deo volente, aut nolente. Non hoc, quia Deo inuito nihil fit, cùm sit omnipotens; E. illud.

Resp. Non Deo volente; vel nolente, sed non volente fiunt mala, quemadmodum ex Patrum scriptis concludit Lombardus l. 1. sent. dist. 49. lit. F. Est ergo insufficiens enumeratio partium in antecedente. Nam & Philosophus ipse l. 3. Ethic. c. 1. inter ἑκούσιον & ἀκούσιον ponit actiones μικτàς vel intermedias. Proinde dicimus lapsum Adami non Deo volente, neque nolente, aut reluctante, sed non volente, non approbante contigisse.

3. Si passerculus non cadit sine Dei voluntate, Matth. 10. v. 29. multò minus homo. Non igitur debet decretum Dei à casu vel lapsu πρωτοπλάστων excludi.

Resp. Distinguimus inter lapsum Physicum & Theologicum, vel naturalē & moralem. Hic vitiosus est; ille non est. Hanc Deus improbat & non vult: illum adprobat & vult. De hoc Psalmus quintus, de illo

Apostolus Matthæus loquitur: Sunt ergo quatuor termini, quia collectio fit à lapsu naturali ad moralem, à lapsu corporis ad lapsum animæ. 4. Qui vult finem, vel etiam media. Deus voluit finem lapsus, vt medij, nempe redemptionem quorundam hominum, & gloriæ suæ manifestationem: Ergo ipsum quoque lapsum voluit. Resp. Maior non est vniuersalis Nam Magistratus vult finem malorum, nempè promulgationem bonarum legum, nec tamen vult ipsos malos mores. Hortulanus vult finem arefactæ arboris nempe calefactionem contubernij, vel venditionem, nec tamen voluit ipsam arefactionem arboris frugiferæ. Igitur 2. distinguimus inter medium per se, & medium per accidens, vel inter medium φύσει & medium ἰδίᾳ. De illo, non de hec vera est maior: de hoc autem, & non illo loquitur minor. Peccatum enim non est per se, & φύσει medium ad fines vtiles, (cum ex malo, quà malum, non sequatur bonum) sed per accidens fit medium, nempè per sapientiam Dei, malum omne ad fines bonos dirigentis & accommodantis.

XII. II. Deum voluisse vt homo persisteret in bono, probamus, 1. Ab imagine Dei, ad quam homo conditus Genes. 1. v. 27. & 2. v. 7. Sap. 2. v. 23. Consistebat autem illa in iusticia & sanctitate veritatis, Eph. 4. v. 23. Si ergo conditus est homo à Deo, vt iustus esset & sanctus, vtique non fuit conditus, vt peccaret; sed potius, vt staret & persisteret.

2. A renouatione ad imaginem amissam, Ephes. 4. v. 23. Coloss. 3. v. 9. Si ij, qui volunt esse iusti, & participes vitæ æternæ, renouari debent ad imaginem primi hominis, illique conformes fieri, vtique iste non fuit conditus ad peccandum, sed ad standum, & iustè agendũ, Aliàs præciperetur, vt & nos in nouitate constantes haut fimus.

3. Ex præcepto multiplicationis, Gen. 1. v. 28. Volebat Deus, vt homo cresceret, & quidem in tali statu, quo eum creauerat, hoc est, volebat vt istam imaginem suam ad posteros quoque propagaret, cum simile sibi semper simile ex ordinatione diuina generare debeat. E. voluit, vt persisteret. Quomodo enim imaginem istam potuisset in posteros secundum Domini voluntatem deriuare, si in bono non perstitisset, sed lapsus fuisset?

5. Ex Sap. 2. v. 7. Creauit Deus hominem in' ἀφθαρσία. vulgata habet Inexterminabilem, Interpretes plerique exponunt, Ad incorruptibilitatem. Si igitur ad hanc conditus fuit homo, vtique voluit Deus, vt staret. Aliàs enim ad corruptibilitatem non creasset.

XIII. Tres verò in contrarium obiectiunculas Caluinistæ proferunt. 1. Homo non stetit. E. conditus non fuit, vt staret, cùm Deus aliàs, suo creationis fine frustratus esset.

Resp. N. C quia multæ dari possunt instantiæ. Nemo potest legem Dei seruare: Ergóne data non fuit, vt seruaretur? Non omnes obtemperant Spiritui sancto: Ergóne hoc fine non loquitur ad nos, vt illi obtemperemus? Cur igitur homines ei dicuntur resistere & contradicere? Act. 7. v. 51. Non omnes studiosi euadūt docti in Academijs. Ergóne hoc fine nō eò mittuntur? Distinguimus igitur inter fines: 1. Quidam sunt absoluti & independentes, qui semper sequuntur. 2. Quidam conditionati & à certa quadam conditione dependentes, quæ si abfuerit, finis non sequitur, licèt sequi deberet. Et tali modo perseuerantia erat finis creationis, nempè non absolutus sed conditionatus, si homo ipse vellet, & non spontè in malum se præcipitaret. Licèt igitur homo non steterit, eum stare Deus voluit; verùm sub conditio ne, nisi ipse reluctatus fuerit.

2. Quæ Deus voluit, fecit, Psal. 113. v. 3. & Esa. 46. vers. 10. ὅσα θέλῃ γίνεται, Damasc. lib. 2. OF cap. 29. E. quæ non fiunt, ea non vult. Non autem fiebat huc, vt Adam staret; sed labebatur: Ergo Deus non illud, sed hoc voluit.

Resp. Maior non est vniuersalis, quia multa fiunt, quæ Deus non vult, & contra. Habemus exempla, Prov. 1. v. 28. cap. 19. v. 3. Esa. 65. v. 12. c. 66. v. 4. Ezech. 33. v. 11. Matth. 23. v. 37. Luc. 7. v. 30. Act. 7. v. 51. 1. Timoth. 2. v. 3, 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. Vult Deus, vt legi eius seruemus, nec tamen fit: Vult vt nos inuicem diligamus, & pœnitentiam agamus, nec tamen facimus. Distinguendum igitur est inter θέλημα Dei absolutum & conditionatum: illud semper est efficax; hoc quia à conditione certa depēdet, propterea quandoque sit inefficax, nimirum quando illa conditio abest, Tali autem modo conditionato volebat Deus hominis perseuerantiam.

3. Si Deus voluisset hominē stare, non condidisset labilem. Resp. N. C. propter fallaciam causæ, quia non condidit labilem Adamum, vt staret, sed quia 1. hominem eum esse volebat, non brutum; liberi ergo vt esset arbitrij necesse erat. 2. Volebat cultum spontaneum; ἀβίαστον δὲ πρᾶγμα εἶναι τὸ καλὸν, scribit Damasc. l. 4. c. 20.


### Question II: XIV. Subsequent Thesis; The manifestation of glory did not move God, nor could it move Him, to make a decree concerning the fall of man

XIV. SUBSEQUENT Thesis; The manifestation of glory did not move God, nor could it move Him, to make a decree concerning the fall of man.

For whence will the Calvinists provide proof of this? There is a threefold method of knowing the decrees of princes. 1. If someone has been present at the council of the prince. 2. If he has heard it from those who were present. 3. If the decree has been publicly posted or promulgated. By which of these methods, however, have the decrees of God and their reasons become known to Calvin? For they have not been publicly posted and promulgated in the Holy Scriptures, as he admits in b. 1. Instit. ch. 17. §. 2. Nor indeed did he himself, or others, take part, since from eternity nothing existed besides God. Wherefore, whatever the Calvinists blather about the decree of God and the end of the decree is a figment and the dream of a poorly sleeping mind.

XV. But in order that we may more firmly establish our thesis, and press our adversaries more strongly, the following aphorisms we propose. 1. The manifestation of divine justice and mercy was not of simple necessity. The glory of God through the creation and preservation of the universe had already been sufficiently made known before: nor does Scripture teach anywhere that it was simply necessary that individual ἰδιώματα [idioms/properties] be made conspicuous by an external work. Many theologians affirm that not a few of God's attributes still lie hidden from us, of which both the name and the reason are unknown. Whence we conclude that the revelation of individual properties is not ἁπλῶς [simply] necessary.

XVI. 2. The manifestation of divine idioms is given as twofold: we call one real, the other verbal. The former consists in an external work: the latter occurs through the word and revelation. Even if, therefore, God had not declared either his mercy or his justice by an external work, he could nevertheless have done this by words, just as he notified his eternity, infinity, and other idioms.

XVII. 3 Real manifestation can in turn be divided into ἔμμεσον [indirect] or mediate, and ἄμεσον [direct] or immediate. We name the former when a certain idiom is known by means of the work of another idiom, but the latter when it is shown through itself and its own proper ἐνέργημα [energy/operation].

As far as mediate φανέρωσιν [manifestation] is concerned, we say that in this way both God's justice and his mercy had been sufficiently manifested. For because he had created the world, and by so creating had declared his supreme goodness, therefore from that work it was very easy to infer that God is also just and merciful. For he who is supremely good is not unjust and [is] merciful.

But as regards immediate φανέρωσιν [manifestation], it also had a place before sin, as far as God's justice is concerned. For this had been sufficiently declared, partly through the creation of a just man, who by his natural rectitude and justice represented the very justice of God, to whose image he had been created: partly through the confirmation of the good Angels in good, which was an act of justice rewarding good deeds: partly through the punishment of the fallen Angels and their thrusting down to the underworld, which likewise was an act of divine justice punishing evil deeds. But from where will it be proven that there was need for another manifestation of justice besides? It was likewise not necessary that mercy also be made known by a singular external work. Indeed, even if it had been, God could nevertheless without doubt have found another way according to His infinite wisdom, even if sin and evil had not entered into the world, Θεὸς γὰρ ὀυκ ἔχηι χρείαν ἁμαρτωλῶ ἀνδρὸς, God has no need of a sinful man, Eccl. 15. verse 12. But He would have had the greatest need, if He could have manifested His mercy through no one except a sinning man.

XIIX. 4. Finally, even if it be posited that God willed sin for the sake of that Calvinistic end, yet He would not have attained it if the opinion of Calvin is held. For justice will not be just if anyone is said not to have found a guilty person to punish, but to have made one, according to Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, page 7: a prince would not be just if he compelled a certain subject to commit homicide, in order that he might afterwards behead him, and thus be able to declare himself just. Likewise, God would have manifested anything but justice if He had cast a just man into sin and injustice, and had wished to demand punishment from him for that, of which He Himself was the author and instigator.

In like manner, benevolence is malevolent if anyone wishes someone to be miserable so that he may pity him, by the testimony of Augustine: book 3 of the Confessions, chapter 1. He is not merciful who casts his neighbor into a pit so that he may afterwards pull him out and by pulling him out manifest mercy. He is not benevolent because he wounds another so that he may heal him, or despoils him so that he may in turn clothe him: thus also God would by no means have shown His mercy if He had made a blessed man miserable in order that he might afterwards have mercy on him.

XIX. From these things, therefore, it is evidently clear that all those things which the Calvinists are accustomed to urge with prolix declamations concerning the good end which God regarded in the decree of the fall are vain and profane.

Nor does their little argument have any weight, that God would have immediately destroyed our first parents if He had not intended that end. For we say with Augustine from book 11 of De Genesi ad litteram, chapter 10: God could have turned the will of our first parents to good, since He is omnipotent, or completely changed their nature. He could have indeed. Why then did He not do it? BECAUSE HE DID NOT WILL IT. Why He did not will it rests with Him. We ought not to be wiser than it behooves us to be. 1 Corinthians 4:6. Meanwhile, however, we judge with the theologians that sufficiently probable reasons for this divine sustenance can be given.

1. Because this would have been against God's wisdom and providence. For He had created species so that they might remain, not so that they might immediately perish. Hence He rested on the seventh day, that is, He ceased from the new creation of species, especially the principal ones. 2. Because God had devised a saving means of redemption through the mission of His Son, and therefore there was no need for the creation of new men so that they might be saved. 3. If He had been obliged to create a new man, He would have created either the same one or one different in species. If the same one, he too could have fallen, and thus the danger of the fall would not have been removed. If a different one, He would not have founded a true man, and consequently one species would have perished, which is absurd.

And let these things suffice concerning the first act falsely ascribed.

XX. II. The second act falsely ascribed to God is temporal, and they name it THE PROVOCATION OF THE DEVIL TO SEDUCE. For thus writes Zanchius, book 5, De Natura Dei, chapter 2, part 4, page 736a: God created the serpent and the devil, who would tempt Eve. But we prove that this is most false.

1. By the silence of Scripture. It is the saying of Theodoret, dialogue 2.

I am not so perfidiously confident that I dare to affirm anything which Scripture passes over in silence. But where is anything read concerning this provocation of the devil to tempt? In Gen. 3 the fall of man is described accurately according to all circumstances; that provocation is not expressed by even a little word. Indeed, the serpent approached of its own accord, not by the command of the Lord, as is gathered from the first verse.

2. The punishment of the serpent, which exists in Gen. 3, v. 14 & 15. From this we infer: He who does the command and will of God is loved and affected with rewards by God, John 14, v. 21. The serpent seducing the first-formed is not loved, nor is it affected with rewards, but with punishments by God, on account of that seduction. Therefore, it did not do the command of God by seducing Eve. Wherefore it was not provoked by God to tempt, unless you wish to say blasphemously that the serpent was unjustly punished for that which God wanted and commanded it to do.

XXI. III. The last act is falsely ascribed, THE INTERNAL IMPULSION OF MAN TO SIN. Concerning this, Calvin says in book 1 of the Institutes, ch. 18, section 4: Man does by the just impulsion of God what is not permitted to him. Beza writes similar things in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 429, 431. Rennacher in the catena, p. 29. But in turn, against this impious opinion, we urge: 1. The silence of Scripture. 2. The punishment of the first-formed. 3. The interdict of God. For how could He have justly impelled man to do that which He had forbidden him to do, Gen. 2, v. 17? 4. Free will, which must be entirely denied if the impulsion of God is to be granted. For he who acts with another impelling him does not act freely and with a plain will. Why, therefore, is it said in Ecclesiastes 7, v. 30, that man has entangled himself in infinite questions? How was he left in the hand of his own counsel, Ecclesiasticus 16, v. 14? Wherefore we conclude with Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, p. 36: the malice of the will itself was not from God. For man would not have this, if he did not depart from God.

XXII. And thus far we have removed from God the false, or rather falsely ascribed, acts concerning the first sin of Adam; there follow now TRUE & REAL ACTS, which, however, in no way whatsoever inclined the mind of Adam to that sin as such, much less impelled it. Moreover, these are in turn twofold: 1. some GENERAL, 2. some SPECIAL.

XXIII. We call those GENERAL which concur with every action, or even accompanied the fall, in so far as it was an action. Of these there are chiefly two, of which one is eternal, the other temporal.

XXIV. 1. The eternal act is πρόγνωσις or foreknowledge. For because God beholds all things with a most present eye (Dan. 13:42, Hos. 5:3, Sir. 23:27 & 29), there is no doubt that from all eternity He also foresaw, or rather saw, the fall of Adam. But that this πρόγνωσις is the cause of the fall, or imported a necessity of falling, as the Calvinists think, that is most false. For if foreknowledge were the cause of things, it would follow: 1. That all things had existed from eternity, because the foreknowledge of things existed from eternity. 2. That God Himself does not act freely, but necessarily, because He also foresees His own actions. 3. That all things which God knows happen certainly, when nevertheless the contrary is evident from 1 Sam. 23:12, Matt. 11:21, 26:53. Wherefore, just as an astrologer is not the cause of a foreseen and predicted eclipse, nor a physician of a disease, nor a shipmaster of a storm: so neither is God foreseeing, nor the foreknowledge of God, the cause of things. For 1. it is an internal act of the divine intellect, denoting simple fore-notice, not an efficacious will of producing. Therefore, of itself it causes or effects nothing. 2. An act is never the cause of its object, but on the contrary. Foreknowledge is indeed an act, whose objects are the things foreknown. Therefore, the former is not the cause of the latter, but on the contrary. Hence theologians have the rule: A thing does not depend on knowledge, but knowledge on things. Origen explains the cause in his commentary on chapter 8 of the Epistle to the Romans with these words: For something will not be because God knows it will happen, but because it is going to happen, it is therefore known by God before it happens.

XXV. Although the foreknowledge of God is infallible, and things in relation to it are necessary by hypothesis, this is not, however, a simple necessity, nor does it remove the contingency of things. For just as all events, when they are and insofar as they are, are necessary, they are nevertheless called contingent by reason of their causes, because before they happened, they could have happened or not happened: So all things, by reason of divine foreknowledge, are indeed necessary by hypothesis, because they are subject to it, not as future acts, but as most present; yet in themselves they are contingent, since by reason of their causes they could have been produced or not produced.

XXVI. 2. The temporal act is the cooperation of the action itself. Where, however, one must immediately distinguish between the action and the disorder of the action in the act. The latter is to be ascribed to man alone; the former to God also, as the primary cause. For the determination of an act depends on a particular principle, not a universal one. For that which is good, not only in kind according to God (insofar as it is a being), but also good in species according to nature (insofar as it is a physical motion), may be evil in the individual, according to the reason of the proximate singular principle. Wherefore, just as monsters are not attributed to universal and common causes, but to proper and particular ones, since error falls neither upon God nor upon common nature: so it is also with the monsters of the soul or sins.

XXVII. Therefore, for this very thing to be applied to the fall of Adam, the eating itself, as such, or insofar as it was a physical act, was from God cooperating, but insofar as it was the eating of the forbidden fruit, insofar as it was an inordinate eating, it was from the will of man alone, desiring wickedly. Nor is it absurd that something should concur toward an action, and yet not toward the disorder of the action, since we have an example 1. in limping. 2. in the δυσφωνίᾳ of a lyre. 3. in clocks. The motion itself is from the locomotive power, but not the limping: the sound is from the lyre-player, but not the defect of the sound: the rotation of the smaller wheels is from the larger wheel, but not simply the disorder. You may think the same concerning God concurring toward an action, yet not causing nor approving the defect.

XXVII. Therefore that principle, A secondary cause effects nothing without the first, is true if it is understood concerning the action, but false if it is understood concerning the defect of the action. For the effect is one thing, the defect is another. A secondary cause cannot effect anything without the first. Let the Theological rule therefore be noted: When several causes concur toward some action in which there is a defect, all are indeed causes of the action, but not of the defect, only that one which errs and fails in acting.

XXIX. We call those the SPECIAL acts of God which do not occur in all works, but only in evil ones, and especially concerning the first sin of Adam. We divide them in turn 1. into antecedent; 2. into concomitant; 3. into consequent.

XXX. 1. We count two of the antecedent [acts]. 1. The creation of man as liable to fall. For unless God had created him liable to fall, he could not have fallen. But this itself was not the cause of sin. He created him liable to fall, however, not so that he might fall, but so that he might obey freely, not ἀλόγως. 2. The promulgation of the law. God gave it, however, not as an occasion for falling, but for the exercise of obedience. But when the Calvinists ask, Why did He not prescribe another law, which he could have kept?

We answer. 1. God owes nothing to anyone: He can therefore justly prescribe any law whatsoever. 2. He could hardly have given a law easier to observe. For in such a variety of fruits, in such perfection of nature, it would have been very easy to abstain. 3. If God [had given] such a-

had imposed, its object would have been in itself undesirable, man would not have rendered obedience properly so called. 4. Finally, whatever law God had imposed, nevertheless man could have transgressed even that, if he had made bad use of free will:

XXXI. II. We assign in turn two concomitants: 1. It is desertion, that is, the denial of singular grace. From this, however, the efficiency of the fall cannot be gathered, since to desert and to work efficiently do not posit one another, but rather exclude one another. Furthermore, God did not withdraw the grace of creation, although he did not bestow special grace, to the bestowing of which he was bound by no right: 2. It is permission, while God allowed man then to be tempted by Satan, then to feel of his own accord. This permission is not the cause of the fall, since permitted acts are performed not by the one permitting but by the agent, as Fr. Junius admits in quest. 2 on the first sin, ch. 2, and permission is nothing other than a remission of the will, as Scaliger says in Ex. 307, sect. 23. Who therefore, by permitting, will be the cause of the permitted crime? Although indeed guilt sometimes redounds, yet in the one permitting that is accustomed to happen only when 1. the one falling is not instructed with sufficiently adequate safeguards for standing. 2. If the one permitting is bound by right to preserve the one about to fall, and 3. if he is destitute of a just cause for permission, all of which were absent in the Adamic fall. For man had been created in righteousness. God did not owe special grace, but he had just causes for permission, namely 1. that he might test man, 2. that he might show his omnipotence, 3. providence, 4. mercy, 5. justice.

XXXII. III. We likewise posit two consequent acts: 1. It is the determination of the fall to a useful end: which does not make God the author of sin; just as neither is the craftsman's elaboration, or accommodation to a certain end, the cause of the breaking or ruining of a vessel by an unskilled apprentice. 2. The tolerance and sustenance of fallen men. He did not tolerate [it], as if he were delighted by their fall: but 1. because he did not wish to annihilate immediately that which had just been created, 2. because he is good, and had from eternity devised a means for restoring man.

XXXIII. And thus far we have abundantly considered all the divine acts which occurred regarding the first sin of Adam: And because none of them cooperated efficiently to produce the fall itself, as such, hence we conclude that the Calvinistic opinion concerning God as the author of the fall is impious and blasphemous.

Latin:

XIV. POSTERIOR Thesis; Manifestatio gloriæ Deum non mouit, nec mouere potuit ad decretum de lapsu hominis faciendum.

Vnde enim hoc probatum dabunt Caluiniani? Triplex est modus cognoscēdi decreta principum. 1. Siquis interfuerit consilio principis. 2. Si ab ijs, qui interfuerunt, audiuerit 3. Si decretum publicè affixum aut promulgatum fuerit. Quo autem ex his modo decreta Dei, & eorum rationes Caluino innotuêre? Publicè enim affixa, & in sacris literis promulgata non sunt, vti fatetur l. 1. Instit. c. 17. §. 2. Neque verò vel ipse, vel alij interfuerunt, cùm ab æterno præter Deū nihil extiterit. Quare figmentum est, & animi malè dormientis somnium, quicquid de decreto Dei, decretique fine Caluiniani blaterant.

XV. Vt verò thesin nostram magis stabiliamus, & aduersarios fortiùs premamus, sequentes aphorismos proponimus. 1. Iustitiæ & misericordiæ diuinæ manifestatio non fuit de simplici necessitate. Glorian. Dei per creationem & conseruationem vniuersi iam antè satis innotuerat: neque Scriptura vllibidoce. simpliciter opus fuisse, vt singula ἰδιώματα externo opere redderentur conspicua. Multi Theologorum affirmant, non pauca Dei attributa nos adhuc latere, quorum & appellatio & ratio sit incognita. Vnde singularum proprietatum patefactionem ἁπλῶς non necessariam concludimus.

XVI. 2. Manifestatio idiomatum diuinorum duplex datur: alteram realem, alteram verbalem dicimus. Illa consistit in externo opere: hæc per verbum & reuelationem contingit. Etiamsi igitur Deus opere externo suam nō declarasset vel misericordiam, vel iustitiā, potuisset tamen hoc verbis facere, sicut æternitatem, infinitatē & alia idiomata notificauit.

XVII. 3 Realis manifestatio vicissim dispesci potest in ἔμμεσον vel mediatam, & ἄμεσον vel immediatam. Illam nominamus, quando idioma quoddam mediante alterius idiomatis opere cognoscitur, hanc autem, quando per se suumque proprium ἐνέργημα ostenditur.

Quod mediatam φανέρωσιν attinet, dicimus hoc modo satis fuisse manifestatam Dei tùm iustitiam, tum misericordiam. Quia enim creauerat mundum, & sic creando summam bonitatem suam declarauerat, idcò ex illo opere facillimum erat colligere, Deum quoq; iustum esse & misericordem. Qui enim summè bonus, is non est iniustus & misericors.

Immediatam verò φανέρωσιν quod spectat, habuit & illa locum ante peccatum, quoad Dei iustitiam. Hæc enim satis erat declarata, partim per creationem hominis iusti, qui naturali suâ rectitudine & iustitia repræsentabat ipsam Dei iustitiam, ad cuius imaginem erat conditus: partim per bonorum Angelorum confirmationem in bono, quæ actus fuit justitiæ remunerantis benefacta: partim per lapforum Angelorum pœnam & ad inferos detrusîonem, quæ itidem actus fuit justitiæ diuinæ malefacta punientis. Alia autem præterea justitiæ manifestatione opus fuisse vnde probabitur? Misericordiam quoque externo opere singulari notificari, pariter non erat necessarium. Imò etsi fuisset, alium tamen dubio procul modum pro infinita sua sapientia inuenire potuisset Deus, licèt peccatum malumque in mundum non introiisset, Θεὸς γὰρ ὀυκ ἔχηι χρείαν ἁμαρτωλῶ ἀνδρὸς, Non opus habet Deus viro peccatore, Ecclef. 15. vers. 12. Opus autem quàm maximè habuisset, si misericordiam suam nullo, nisi peccante homine manifestare potuisset.

XIIX. 4. Denique etiamsi ponatur, Deum voluisse peccatum, propter finem istum Caluinisticum, tamen consecutus eum non fuiffet, si sententia Caluini teneatur. Etenim iustitia iusta non erit, si quis puniendum reum non inuenisse, sed fecisse dicatur, juxta Fulgentium l. 1. ad Monim. pag. 7. justus non foret princeps, si subditum quendam ad homicidium cogeret, quo postea eum decollare, & ita justum se esse declarare posset. Ita; Deus nihil minus quam justiciam patefecisset, si justum hominem in peccatum & injustitiam præcipitasset, & ab eo propter illam, cujus tamen ipse author & suasor, pœnam poscere voluisset.

Pari modo, maleuola est beneuolentia, siquis miserum aliquem esse velit, vt eius misereatur, testimonio Augustini: l. 3. Confess. cap. 1. Misericors non est, qui proximum deijcit in puteum, vt ipsum postea extrahat & extrahendo misericordiam manifestet. Beneuolus haut est, quia alium vulnerat, vt sanet, vel spoliat vt vicissim vestiat: Ita & Deus suam minimè ostendisset misericordiam, si hominem beatum fecisset miserum, vt eius postmodum misereretur.

XIX. Ex his ergò euidenter patet, vana & profana esse omnia ea, quæcunque de bono fine, quem Deus in decreto lapsus respexit prolixis declamationibus vrgere solent Calviniani.

Neque ipsorum ratiuncula acı̀pos habet, Deus primos parentes statim aboleuiffet, nisi finem istum intendiffet. Dicimus enim cum Augustino ex lib. 11. de Gen. ad lit. c. 10, Potuisset DEVS voluntatem primorum parentum in bonum conuertere, quoniam omnipotens est, vel naturam ipsorum planè immutare. Potuisset vtique. Cur ergo non fecit? QVIA NOLVIT. Cur noluerit penes ipsum est. Debemus nos non plus sapere, quam oportet. 1. Corinth. 4. v. 6. Interim tamentres istius sustentationis diuinæ causas sat probabiles dari posse, cum Theologis censemus.

I Quia fuisset hoc contra Dei sapientiam & prouidentiam. Nam creauerat species, vt manerent, non vt statim interirent. Hinc quieuit die septimo, hoc est, specierum, præsertim principalium, creationem nouam intermisit. 2. Quia Deus salutare medium redemtionis per missionem Filij sui excogitauerat, ideoque nouorum hominum, vt saluarentur, creatione opus non erat. 3. Si nouum hominem creare debuisset, vel eundem, vel diuersum specie creasset. Si eundem, & ipse labi potuisset, adeoq; periculum lapsus non fuisset amotum. Si diuersum non condidisset verum hominem, & per consequens vna species periisset, quod absurdum.

Et hæc de primo actu falso adscripto sufficiant.

XX. II. Secundus actus falso adscriptus Deo, est temporalis, eumque nominant DIABOLI AD SEDUCENDUM PROVOCATIONEM. Ita enim scribit Zanchius l. 5. de N. D. c. 2 par. 4. p. 736. a. Creauit, Deus serpentem & diabolum, qui Euam tentaret. At verò hoc falsissimum esse probamus.

1. Scripturæ silentio. Theodoreti dictum est, dial. 2.

Ego non adeò perfide confidens sum, vt audeam aliquid affirmare, quòd Scriptura silentio præterit. Vbi autem quicquam de ista diaboli ad tentandum provocatione legitur? Gen. 3. accuratè secundum omnes circumstantias, lapsus hominis describitur, provocatio ista ne verbulo exprimitur. Imò serpens spontè, non jussu Domini accessit, vti colligitur ex versiculo primo.

2. Serpentis suppliciū, quod extat Gen. 3. v. 14 & 15. Hinc inferimus: Faciens mandatum & voluntatem Dei, diligitur & præmijs à Deo afficitur, Iohan. 14. v. 21. Serpens seducens πρωτοπλάστους non diligitur, nec præmijs, sed pœnis à Deo, ob seductionem istam. Ergò non fecit mandatum Dei seducendo Evam.
