Quare à Deo non fuit provocatus ad tentandum, nisi blasphemè dicere velis, injustè punitum esse serpentem ob id, quod eum Deus facere volebat, & imperabat.

XXI. III. Vltimus actus falsò adscriptus est, INTERNA HOMINIS AD PECCANDVM IMPVLSIO. De hoc ait Calvinus l. 1. Instit, c. 18. sectione. 4. Homo iusto Dei impulsu agit, quod sibi nõ licet, Similia scribit Beza in Colloquio Mompelg. m. p. 429. 431. Rennacherus in catena. p. 29. Vicissim autem contra hanc opinionem impiam urgemus. 1, Scripturæ silentium. 2. πρωτοπλάστων supplicium. 3. Dei interdictum. Quomodo enim justè impulisset hominem ad faciendum id quod facere prohibuerat, Gen. 2, v. 17.? 4. Liberum arbitrium, quod omninò negandum, si impulsus Dei concedendus. Qui enim alio impellente agit, hic liberè & planâ voluntate non agit. Cur ergò dicitur Ecclesiastæ 7. v. 30. quod homo semetipsum. infinitis miscuerit quæstionibus? Quomodo relictus erat in manu Consilij sui Ecclesiastici 16. v. 14? Quare cōcludimus cum Fulgentio lib. 1. ad Monim. p 36. ipsa malitia voluntatis à Deo non fuit. Hanc enim, si homo à Deo non discederet, non haberet.

XXII. Et hactenus falsos, vel potius falso adscriptos actus circa primum Adæ peccatum, à Deo remouimus, sequuntur nunc ACTVS VERI & REALES qui tame[n] ad ipsum peccatum, quà tale nullo prorsus modo inclinarunt animum Adæ, multominus impulerunt. Sunt autem illi vicissim duplices, 1. quidam GENERALES, 2. quidam SPECIALES,

XXIII. GENERALES dicimus, qui concurrunt cum omni actione, siue mala sit, adeoque lapsum etiam, in quantum actio erat, comitabantur, Horum potissimum duo sunt, quorum alter æternus est, alter temporalis.

XXIV. 1. Actus æternus est πρόγνωσις vel præscientia. Quia enim Deus omnia præsentissimo oculo aspicit Dan. 13. v. 42. Os. 5. v. 3. Syr. 23. v. 27. & 29. propterea ab omni æternitate lapsum quoque Adami præuidisse vel potius vidisse, nullum est dubium. Quod autem ista πρόγνωσις lapsus causa sit, vel necessitatem labendi importauerit, vt Caluiniani existimant, id falsissimum est. Si enim præscientia rerum causa foret, sequeretur 1. omnes res fuisse ab æterno, quia præscientia rerum fuit ab æterno. 2. Deum ipsum non liberè, sed necessariò agere, quia & suas actiones præuidet. 3. Omnia certò euenire, quę Deus nouit, cum tamen contrarium pateat ex. 1. Reg. 23. v. 12. Matth. 11. v. 21. 26. v. 53 Quapropter, sicut Astrologus non est causa præuisæ & prædictæ ecclipseos, neque medicus morbi, neque nauclerus tempestatis: Ita nec Deus præuidens, vel Dei præscientia rerum causa est. Etenim 1. interna intellectus est diuini actio, notans simplicem prænotitiam, non efficacem producendi voluntatem. Per se igitur nil causat vel efficit. 2. Actus nunquam est causa sui objecti, sed contra. Præscientia vero actus est, cuius obiectum sunt res præscitæ. Ergo illa harum causa non est, sed contrà. Hinc Theologi habent regulam: Res non pendens à scientia, sed scientiaArebus Causam exponit Origenes super c. 8. epist. ad Rom. his verbis: Non enim propterea aliquid erit, quia id scit Deus futurum, sed quia futurum est ideò scitur a Deo, antequam fiat.

XXV. Quamvis autem praescientia Dei infallibilis, & res quoad illam ex hypothesi sint necessariae, non tamen simplex haec est necessitas, nec contingentiam rerum tollit. Etenim sicut omnes eventus, quando sunt & quatenus sunt, necessarii sunt, dicuntur tamen contingentes ratione causarum, quia antequam fierent, fieri & non fieri poterant: Ita res omnes ratione praescientiae diuinae ex ὑποθέσεως quidem sunt necessariae, quia isti subjacent, non vt actus futuri, sed vt praesentissimi in se tamen sunt contingentes, quoniam ratione causarum produci & non produci poterant

XXVI. 2. Actus temporalis est ipsius actionis coefficientia. Vbi tamen statim distinguendum inter actionem & actionis ἀταξίαν inhypio. Haec soli homini: illa Deo quoque, tanquam causae primae adscribenda est. Nam determinatio actus pendet à principio particulari, non vniuersali. Quod enim bonum est, non modo genere secundum Deum, (quatenus ens) sed etiam bonum specie secundum naturam, (quatenus est motus physicus) malum sit in indiuiduo, secundum rationem principij proximi singularis. Quapropter, sicuti monstra non causis vniuersalibus & communibus, sed propriis & particularibus tribuuntur, quandoquidem error neque in Deum, neque in naturam communem cadit: ita quoque cum monstris animorum vel peccatis comparatum est.

XXVII. Hoc ipsum ergo vt ad lapsum Adae applicetur, ipsa comestio, quà talis, vel in quantum actus Physicus, à Deo cooperante erat, sed qua pomi vetiti erat comestio, in quantum inordinata erat manducatio, à sola erat voluntate hominis prauè appetentis. Neque verò absurdum est, concurrere aliquid ad actionem, nec tamen actionis inordinationem, cùm exemplum habeamus 1. in claudicatione. 2. in δυσφωνίᾳ cytharæ. 3. in horologijs. Motio ipsa à locomotiva, sed non claudicatio : sonus à cytharœdo, sed non soni vitium : minorum rotularum circumagitatio à rota maiori, sed non simpliciter inordinatio. Idem de Deo ad actionem concurrerent, vitium tamen non causante nec probante cogites.

XXVII. Proinde istud principium, Causa secunda nihil efficit sine prima, verùm est si de actione, falsum, si de actionis vitio intelligatur. Aliud enim est effectus, aliud defectus. Non potest causa secunda sine prima aliquid efficere. Notetur ergo regula Theo logica : Quando plures causæ concurrunt ad actionem aliquam, in qua est vitium, omnes quidem sunt causæ actionis, non tamen vitij, sed illa tantùm, quæ in agendo errat & deficit.

XXIX. SPECIALES actus Dei illos nuncupamus, qui non in omnibus operibus, sed tantùm malis, & præsertim circa primum Adami peccatum occurrunt. Eos vicissim dividimus 1. in antecedentes. 2. in concomitantes; 3: in consequentes.

XXX. 1. Antecedentium duos numeramus. 1. Est hominis labilis creatio. Nisi enim Deus labilem condidisset, labi non potuisset. Hoc verò ipsum peccati causa non erat. Condidit autem labilem, non ut laberetur, sed ut liberè, nõ ἀλόγως obsequeretur. 2. Legis promulgatio. Eam verò dabat Deus non in occasionem labendi, sed in exercitium obediendi. Cùm autem Calviniani quærunt, Cur non aliam legem præscripserit, quàm servare potuisset?

Respondemus. 1. Deus nemini quicquam debet: justè igitur quamvis legem præscribere potest 2. Vix observatu faciliorem legem dare potuisset. In tanta enim varietate fructuum, in tanta naturæ perfectione, facillimum fuisset abstinere. 3. Si Deus talem-

tulisset, eius obiectum per se fuisset inappetibile, obedientiam propriè dictam non praestitisset homo. 4. Denique quamcunque legem Deus tulisset, tamen & illam potuisset homo transgredi, si libero arbitrio malè fuisset vsus:

XXXI. II. Concomitantium vicissim duos assignamus, 1. Est desertio, hoc est, singularis gratiae denegatio. Hinc autem colligi nequit efficientia lapsûs, siquidem deserere & efficienter operari non se ponunt mutuò, sed potius tollunt. Praeterea Deus non subtraxit gratiam creationis, licet specialem non erogauerit, ad quam etiam erogandam jure nullo obstrictus fuit: 2. Est permissio, dum Deus sinebat hominem tum à Satana tentari, tum sponte sentiri. Haec a permissio causa lapsus nõ est, quoniam actus permissi non à permittente sed ab agente perficiuntur, vti fatetur Fr. Iunius quaest. 2. de pri. pecc. c 2. & permissio nihil est aliud, quam voluntatis remissio, dicente Scaligero Ex 307. sect. 23. Qui ergo permittens causa erit permissi criminis? Licet verò culpa quadoq; redundet, in permittente tamen id tum demum fieri consueuit, quando 1. labens non satis sufficientibus ad standum praesidijs instructus est. 2. Si permittens jure obligatus sit ad seruandum ruiturum, & 3. si iusta permissionis causa destituatur, quę omnia in lapsu Adamitico aberant. Homo enim creatus erat in justitia. Deus specialem gratiam non debebat, sed justas permissionis causas habebat, nimirum 1. vt probaret hominem 2. vt ostenderet suam omnipotentiam. 3. prouidentiam. 4. misericordiam. 5. justitiam.

XXXII. III. Actuum Consequentium itidem duos ponimus 1. Est lapsus ad finem vtilem determinatio: quae Deum peccati authorem non facit; veluti nec artificis elaboratio, vel ad finem certum accommodatio, quoad vas à rudi discipulo confractum aut perditum, causa est ipsius confractionis. 2. Lapsorum hominum tolerantia & sustentatio. Non tutem tolerauit, ac si ipsorum lapsu delectaretur: sed 1. quia speciem modò creatam nolebat statim annihilare, 2. quia bonus est, & salutare de repa rando homine medium ab æterno excogitauerat.

XXXIII. Atque hactenus omnes actus diuinos, qui circa primum Adami peccatum occurrerunt, abundè considerauimus: Et quia nullus eorum ad ipsum lapsum, quà talis, producendum efficienter cooperatus est, hinc opinionem Caluinisticam de Deo lapsus authore, impiam & blasphemam esse concludimus.


### Question II: II. Concerning the true cause of the fall assigned in the Scriptures

II. Concerning the true cause of the fall assigned in the Scriptures.

XXXIV. It is twofold, 1. We name the one extrinsic and inciting, 2. The other intrinsic and efficient.

XL. THE EXTRINSIC [cause], or that which is constituted outside of man and is inciting, was the Devil. For he, partly πρωτοπαθως invisibly and by internal suggestions; partly visibly and under the form of a serpent, solicited Eve to the violation of the divine law. For that serpent in Gen. 3 was neither naked and merely natural, as Josephus contends in book 1 of Antiquities, ch. 3, nor merely allegorical, as pleased Philo in 'On the Creation of the World' and Origen in homily 13 on Exodus, but it was the devil, having entered a true serpent, and through it having attacked the first mother.

XXXVI. For that it was the Devil who tempted Eve is evident 1. From the conversation, which belongs to no brute, but only to a rational substance, which either forms itself into a voice, like a man, or [speaks] in an assumed body, like a Spirit: 2. From the deed itself. That serpent perverted the command of God and seduced man, which was a very grave crime, which in turn does not fall upon a brute animal, and ought not to be attributed to a good creature, as it was created by God. 3. From the supposition, of which indeed some part concerns the natural serpent, but the principal part, which is about the crushing of the head, concerns the devil. For the seed of the woman is Christ, who crushed the head not of a physical serpent, but of an infernal one. Otherwise the first Evangelical promise would expire, and the passages referring this struggle to Christ would fall, as Ps. 91:13, Matt. 4:3 and following, 1 John 3:8, Rev. 12:17. 4 From other testimonies of Scripture, by which the origin of sin and death is ascribed to the devil, Wis. 2:23, and to the father of lies, John 8:44, who is therefore called the tortuous serpent, Isa. 27:1. The serpent corrupting thoughts, 2 Cor. 11:3, the great dragon and ancient serpent deceiving the whole world, Rev. 12:7, 9, ch. 20:2.

XXXVII. II. That it was a real serpent through which Satan spoke to Eve. 1. It is clear from the plain letter, Gen. 3:1, where that serpent is expressly numbered among the living creatures and is celebrated for its craftiness, and therefore the devil judged it would be the most convenient instrument for temptation. 2. From the punishment: Gen. 3:14. That triple [punishment], namely the change of 1. form, 2. gait, 3. food, which does not befit the devil, as he is a Spirit. 3. From the lack of a firm reason. We have a rule: one should not rashly depart from the literal and historical sense of Moses. But indeed no evident or compelling reason can be brought forward why we should not understand the real serpent which the letter denotes. Wherefore let us not suffer ourselves to be driven from the proper sense to an allegorical one without reason.

XXXIIX. THE INTRINSIC and efficient [cause] was the own will of man, spontaneously assenting to the Devil. Gen. 3, Rom. 5:12. For this, although it was created by God with a natural inclination toward the good, was nevertheless free and had the faculty of turning itself away from the good. Therefore, no other cause of the fall or of the vicious assent in man can be given that is superior or prior to the freedom of the will. For just as God introduced a state of life for man: thus man drew upon himself the state of death. Tertull. lib. 2 adv. Mar. It is to be noted, however, that the will was the cause of the vicious assent, not as will, or as good, but as vicious, or insofar as it itself was deviating from the law. Whence, however, that vice in the will? From itself, yet not per se, but per accidens: for the cause of evil is good, but not per se, and insofar as it is good, but per accidens, and insofar as it is deficient.

XXIX. Since, however, the will desires nothing unless reason persuades that it should be desired, for that reason in the first fall also the intellect erred, thinking that to be good which was not good at all: but this false judgment arose from the devil's persuasion, so much so that such a process was observed in the fall of the first man. First the devil persuaded, (both by disparaging the commandment of God and by promising wisdom) that it was good to eat from the forbidden tree, at once the intellect of man was corrupted, so that it judged to be good that which was in itself evil, and therefore under the appearance of good it was proposed to the will, which, acquiescing in the judgment of the intellect, with the appetite approaching, moved by the beautiful external appearance, chose that which the intellect said was to be chosen and was good, and which the appetite desired, which election was followed by the ὁρμὴ of the whole body, which excited τὸ κινητικὸν, so that man extended his hand, plucked the fruit, opened his mouth, and filled his greedy jaws with the deadly fruit, and thus, the commandment of God having been violated, he lost the concreated image to the great detriment of his descendants, alas! Briefly therefore 1. The devil persuaded. 2. The intellect believed the persuader: 3. It proposed it to the will under the appearance of good. 4. The latter assented, and 5. It excited the appetite 6. This [excited] the locomotive ὁρμὴ. Whence followed the external act, from which [came] the corruption of nature, which we all draw from our parents through carnal generation.

Latin:

II. De vera lapsus causa in Scripturis assignata.

XXXIV. Duplex ea est, 1. Alteram extrinsecam & irritantem, 2. Alteram intrinsecam & efficientem nominamus.

XL. EXTRINSECA vel extra hominem constituta & irritans erat Diabolus. Hic n. partim πρωτοπαθως inuisibiliter & internis suggestionibus; partim Euam visibiliter & sub forma serpentis ad violationem legis diuinæ solicitauit. Neque enim serpens ille Gen 3. fuit nudus & tantùm naturalis, vti contendit Iosephus l. 1. Antiq. c. 3. neque merè allegoricus, vt placuit Philoni περι κοσμοποιϊας, & Origeni homil. 13. in Exod. sed fuit diabolus, verum serpentem ingressus, & per illum primam matrem aggressus.

XXXVI. Nam Diabolum fuisse, qui Euam tentauit, patet 1. Ex colloquio, id quod nulli bruto competit, sed tantùm rationali substantiæ, quæ vel se in vocem format, vt homo, vel in assumto corpore, vt Spiritus: 2. Ex ipso facto. Serpens iste mandatum Dei peruertit, & hominem seduxit, id quod crimen fuit longè grauissimum, quod vicissim in animal brutum non cadit, & creaturæ bonę, prout à Deo condita est, tribui non debet. 3, Ex supposito, cuius pars quidem aliqua serpentem naturalem, præcipua verò quæ est de conculcatione capitis, diabolum spectat. Semen n. mulieris Christus, non serpentis physici, sed infernalis caput contrivit. Aliàs expiraret prima promissio Evangelica, & caderent dicta certamen istud ad Christum referentia, vt Psal. 91. v. 13. Matth. 4. v. 3. & seqq. 1. Ioh. 3 v. 8. Apoc. 12. v. 17. 4 Ex alijs Scripturæ testimonijs, quibus peccati & mortis origo adscribitur diabolo, Sap. 2. v. 23. & patri mendaciorum, Ioh. 8: v. 44, qui propterea vocatur serpens tortuosus Esa. 27. v. 1. Serpens cogitationes corrumpens, 2. Cor. 11. v. 3. draco magnus & serpens antiquus seducens vniversum orbem, Apoc. 12. v. 7. 9. c. 20, v. 2.

XXXVII. II. Verum serpentem fuisse, per quem Satanas Evam allocutus est 1. Ex clara litera, Gen. 3. v. 1. patet: vbi serpes iste animatibus disertè annumeratur, & ob calliditatem, celebratur, ideoq; diabolus commodissimum tentationis organum fore arbitratus est. 2 Ex pœna: Gen. 3. v. 14. Triplex illa, nempe mutatio, 1. formæ, 2. gressus 3. victus, quæ diabolo, vt pote Spiritui, non conueniunt. 3. Ex defectu firmæ rationis. Regulam habemus: à literali & historico sensu Mosis temerè non est recedendum. At verò nulla euidens cogensue causa proferri potest, cur no verum serpentem, quem litera notat, intelligere debeamus. Quapropter à sensu proprio ad allegoricum sine ratione nos detrudi non patiamur.

XXXIIX. INTRINSECA & efficiens erat propria voluntas hominis Diabolo spontè assentientis. Gen. 3. Rom. 5. v. 12. Hæc enim quamuis à Deo esset creata cum naturali ad bonum propensione, attamen libera erat, & facultatem habebat à bono sese auertendi, Alia igitur causa lapsus vel vitiosi assensus in homine nulla potest dari superior aut prior, quam voluntatis libertas. Sicut enim Deus hominis vita statum induxit: ita sibi homo mortis statum attraxit. Tertull. l. 2. adv: Mar: Notandum autem, quod voluntas assensus vitiosi causa fuerit, non qua voluntas, aut qua bona, sed qua vi iosa, vel quatenus ipse a lege deflectebat. Vnde autem illud in voluntate vitium? Ab ipsa, non tamen perse, sed per accidens: Mali enim causa bonu est, verum non per se, & quatenus bonum, sed per accidens, & quatenus deficit.

XXIX. Quoniam vero voluntas nihil appetit, nisi quod appetendum ratio suadet, propterea in primo etiam lapsu intellectus erravit, ratus bonum esse, quod bonum minime fuit: Iudicium autem istud falsum ex diaboli persuasione oriebatur, adeo vt talis processus in lapsu primi hominis observatus fuerit. Primum diabolus persuadebat, (tum præceptum Dei elevando, tum sapientiam promittendo) bonum esse de arbore vetita vesci, vna de corrumpebatur intellectus hominis, vt judicaret bonum esse, quod in se malum erat, ideoque sub specie boni eius iste proponebatur voluntati, quæ intellectus judicio acquiescens, accedente appetitu, externa specie pulcra commoto eligebat id, quod intellectus eligendum bonumque, esse dicebat, & quod appetitus cupiebat, quam electionem consequebatur ὁρμὴ totius corporis, quæ excitabat τὸ κινητικὸν, ita ut homo manum extenderet, pomum defringeret, os aperiret, & funesto fructu cupitas fauces expleret, atque sic violato Dei mandato concreatam imaginem cum summo posteriorum damno, eheu! amitteret. Breviter ergo 1. Diabolus persuadebat. 2. persuadenti intellectus credebat: 3. Sub specie boni voluntati proponebat. 4. Hæc assentiebat, & 5. Excitabat appetitum 6. Hic locomotivam ὁρVnde sequebatur actus externus, ex quo naturæ corruptio, quam omnes ex parentibus per generationem carnalem trahimus.


### Question III. What was the first sin?

What was the first sin?

I. Two things come to be noted here: 1. The sin itself or the vicious act, 2. The order of the sin or acts, concerning both of which [I shall speak] in a few words.

I. Concerning the sin itself.

II. There are some who opine that the first sin was nothing other than the external eating of the forbidden fruit, arising from intemperance and the desire of gluttony. But these think too thinly of the sin, and therefore it must be known that far more vicious motions and acts concurred there, which cannot be better known than if they are examined according to the Mosaic law, since our first parents violated not just one particle of it, but all the precepts and interdictions entirely; and especially Eve, who was seduced by the serpent.

II. For there was 1. in their heart doubt and infidelity. 2. In their mouth a depravation of the divine command, Gen. 3. v. 3. and a blasphemous translation of the guilt onto God, v. 12, 13. 3. In their work contempt and actual disobedience, by which they transgressed the three precepts of the first table. In like manner also the second table of the law was shaken, and indeed its fourth precept by ἀχαρισίᾳ and impiety toward the heavenly Father; the fifth by homicide, by which they precipitated themselves and their descendants into the death of 1. nature, 2. grace, and 3. glory; the sixth, by perfidy toward the husband, to whom the eating was persuaded, and by immoderate love toward the wife who was persuading; the seventh by theft and the handling of another's property, against the will of the Lord; the eighth by false testimony and assent to false testimony; finally the ninth and tenth by the depraved concupiscence of a higher status and greater knowledge. So many and such great flagitious acts lay hidden in that single fall of the πρωτοπλάςων [first-formed ones], from which it is very easy to judge partly of its gravity, partly of its just punishment is. Leo, however, expressed most of these acts in epistle 86 to Nic. Aquil. The sin, he says, of the first man was pride, because man preferred to be in his own power rather than in God's: and sacrilege, because he did not believe in God, and homicide, because he cast himself into death: and spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by serpentine persuasion: and theft, because the forbidden food was usurped, and avarice, because he desired more than ought to have sufficed for him:

II. Concerning the order of sin.

VI. Although all these vicious acts were committed at almost one and the same time, nevertheless a certain order can and ought to be given among them, so that one stood out as the first of all, and the rest followed. Concerning this first vicious act of all, however, the opinion of authors is not one. The old Scholastics and the modern Jesuits fight for pride, for thus wrote Biel in 2. dist. 22. qu. 2. the sin of the woman was begun in pride, had its progress in avarice, but its consummation in gluttony. Bellarmine defends the same, book 3 de statu pecc. ch. 4 and 5. Pererius, book 9 in Gen. disp. de pecc. Evæ quest. 1. Luther assumes the contrary in his Commentary on chapter 3. Gen., establishing that the first sin of all was doubt concerning the divine command, or in one word, infidelity: Although this question is not about faith, but only about faith, the matter having been such that perhaps it is safer to leave it in doubt than to discuss it scrupulously: it pleases me, however, to note one or another argument for Luther's opinion against the Papists:

V. 1. From the order of temptation, the Devil solicited Eve to infidelity before pride: Therefore Eve was unfaithful before she was proud. For if she had been proud first, this would not have been done through the seduction of Satan, since the first degree of temptation was to infidelity, which is evident from v. 2

Gen. 3. where in v. 3. it is recounted how Eve was immediately moved to doubt and infidelity, while she corrupted the commandment of God, partly by addition (lest we touch it), partly by diminution (lest perhaps we die); but afterwards when the serpent saw Eve doubting, and as it were indignant at the rigor of the commandment, having become bolder, he denies that which God had affirmed, about which the woman had doubted, v. 4. You shall not die. And that he might persuade this more easily, he adds the cause in v. 5. taken from the promise of singular knowledge, which was the second temptation, namely to pride. From this order of seduction, therefore, we see that doubt or infidelity preceded, and elation or pride followed.

VI. 2. From the saying of Ecclesiasticus, ch. 10. v. 14. The beginning of pride is to apostatize from God; but apostasy is unbelief, or certainly a part of unbelief. Wherefore infidelity always precedes pride, as the cause the effect, and the mother her offspring. From which it follows of its own accord that our first parents were first unfaithful, and from this infidelity took the beginning of pride.

VII. 3. From the nature of faith. It is impossible for a man, as long as he retains trust in God, to be proud against God. Therefore the first-formed also, before they were proud, were unfaithful. For they would not have despised the threat of death, unless, with the light of faith extinguished, they had thought that they could escape the former and obtain the latter. For they desired divine knowledge for this reason, because they did not believe that death would follow from the eating of the fruit, but rather that this knowledge would follow. But they could not have intended this end, if they had not first doubted the truth of the divine threat.

IIX. But that the opinion of our Luther may be better understood, we shall examine in a few words the principal arguments of Bellarmine, by which he wished to refute it.

IX. 1 Ecclesiasticus 10. verse 15. it is said the beginning of sin is pride; therefore it was also the beginning of the first sin.

Resp. 1. This statement does not speak of the first and original pride, but of that which has arisen from the first and is actual, which Ecclesiasticus says incites men to other sins as well, whence Luther rightly translates, Hoffart treibet zu allen Sünden. We therefore willingly concede that many other flagrant sins sprout from pride after the fall, but it does not follow from this that pride was the first transgression of all in sin. 2. I oppose v. 14, where the beginning of pride is called ἀποστασία or ἀπισία. But the same thing is not the beginning of its own beginning. Therefore, ἡ ἀπισία is the beginning of ὑπερηφανίας, which is said in v. 14; certainly, this will not be the beginning of that. Ecclesiasticus therefore wishes to except ἀποστασία when he calls pride the beginning of every sin. The sense, therefore, is that infidelity is the mother of pride, from which many other sins subsequently follow.

X. 2. Tobit 4:14. In pride every destruction had its beginning. That, however, in which destruction had its beginning, was the first vicious act.

Resp. 1. It is a fault of the Vulgate version. For the words in Greek are thus: ἐν τῇ ὑπερηφανίᾳ ἀπώλεια, καὶ ἐν καταστροφᾷ πολλή. (Luther translates, Sie ist ein Anfang alles Verderbens.) But what is the consequence: From pride is perdition. Therefore was it the first sin of all? 2. The discourse is not of original, but of actual pride. The order of the first acts is therefore not indicated here. 3. And although it were speaking of the pride of Eve, yet nothing would follow from this: because not the order of acts, but only the effect of pride is indicated; which, however, is not to be understood exclusively, since they can likewise say, from intemperance, from ἀπισίᾳ, from contempt is perdition, and yet these acts were not all first in order; since the effect which is inherent in all these vicious acts is one thing, and the primacy of order, which is proper to one alone, is another: of the former, not the latter, the present text speaks, if it is to be understood of the first pride.

XL 3. Rom. 5. v. 19. By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners. Disobedience, however, is the first degree of pride, namely, to be unwilling to be subjected to the authority and precepts of another.

Resp. 1. By disobedience is not understood the first act in the sin of Adam, but rather the whole sin. Absurdly, therefore, and aimlessly is this saying applied to the order of acts. 2. What Bellarmine calls the first degree of pride, that is of infidelity. For we cannot describe ἀπείθειαν otherwise than by not doing, or being unwilling to do, the command and will of God.

XII. 4. Many sayings and testimonies of the fathers are brought forward.

Resp. 1. The aim of the fathers was not always to speak accurately about the order of vicious acts. 2. By pride they often understand ἀπιστίαν or a proud contempt of divine precepts, in which sense Bede writes: Everyone who sins is proud, in that by doing forbidden things, he holds divine precepts in contempt. And hence it appears that for the fathers pride is often the same as infidelity, or contempt of the law. 3. They posit pride as an effect, and yet they presuppose ἀπιστίαν as a cause; that is, they designate the cause by the effect.

XIII. 5. An act concerning the end is prior to one concerning the means: but pride was the end, neglect of the command was the means. Therefore, the former is prior, the latter posterior.

Resp. 1. We distinguish between election and seduction. When someone chooses something spontaneously, then indeed he thinks of the end first, afterwards of the means. In seduction, however, the contrary often happens. Thus one can immediately recruit another for his journey, and only afterwards indicate the end. Thus Gen. 23, Isaac was ignorant of the end of the journey, and therefore the means was there prior to the end.

2. We distinguish between the end of the seducer and the seduced. The end of the seducer was the violation of the divine command; to this, therefore, he was soliciting first: And the means was the promise of wisdom, which he added. The end of man, however, was indeed a greater excellence; and the means, the neglect of the word: but in the order of acts, it is not considered what man intended primarily, but what he did first. That, however, he did first, to which he was first tempted, which was doubt and infidelity, as the end of the serpentine temptation. The devil therefore made his own end the beginning of seducing; and man the beginning of sinning, when he assented and began to doubt.

Latin:

Quodnam fuerit peccatum primum?

I. Duo hic notanda veniunt, 1. Ipsum peccatum vel vitiosi actus, 2. Peccati vel actuum ordo, de quo vtroque paucis.

I. Depeccato ipso.

II. Sunt nonnulli, qui opinantur peccatum primum nil fuisse aliud, quam externam fructus vetiti comestionem, ex intemperantia, gulaeqve cupidine ortam. Sed hi nimis tenuiter de peccato sentiunt, ideoque sciendum, quod longe plures vitiosi motus & actus ibi concurrerint, qui melius non poterunt cognosci, quam si ad legem Mosaicam examinentur, quippe cuius non unam duntaxat particulam sed omnia omnino praecepta & interdicta violaverunt parentes primi; & praesertim Eva, quae a serpente fuit seducta.

II. Nam erat 1. in corde ipsorum dubitatio & Infidelitas. 2. In ore mandati divini depravatio, Gen. 3. v. 3. & blasphema culpae in Deum translatio v. 12. 13. 3 In pere contemtus & actualis inobedientia, quibus tria primae tabulae praecepta trangressi sunt. Pari etiam modo secundae legis tabula fuit excussa, & quidem praeceptum eius quartum ἀχαρισίᾳ & impietate in Patrem coelestem; quintum homicidio, quo se ac posteros in mortem. 1. naturae, 2. gratiae ac 3. gloriae praecipitarunt, sextum, perfidia erga maritum, cui esus persuadebatur, & immoderato amore erga vxorem persuadentem; septimum furto & contrectatione rei alienae, invito Domino; octavum falso testimonio, falsique testimonij assensu; nonum denique decimumque prava altioris status & maioris scientiae concupiscentia. Tot & tanta flagitia in vnico isto πρωτοπλάςων lapsu delitescebant, ex quibus partim de gravitate, partim de iusto illius suplicio judicare facillimum est. Actus autem istos plerosquè expressit Leo epist. 86. ad Nic. Aquil. Peccatum, inquit, primi hominis superbia fuit, quia in sua homo potius esse, quàm in Dei potestate dilexit: & sacrilegium quia in Deum non credidit, & homicidium, quia se præcipitauit in mortem: & fornicatio spiritualis, quia integritas mentis humanæ serpentina suasione corrupta est: & furtum, quia prohibitus vsurpatus est cibus, & avaritia, quia plus quàm sufficere illi debuit, appetiuit:

II. De peccati ordine.

VI Qvantumuis vno fermè tempore omnes isti actus vitiosi fuerint commissi, attamen ordo quidam inter illos dari potest & debet, ita vt vnus omnium primus extiterit, & reliqui consecuti fuerint. De isto autem primò omnium actu vitioso non vna est auctorum sententia. Scholastici veteres ac hodierni Iesuitæ pugnant pro superbia, ita enim scripsit Biel. in 2. dist. 22. qu. 2. peccatum mulieris inchoatum fuit in superbia, progressum habuit in avaritia, consummationem verò in gula. Idem defendit Bell. l. 3. de statu pecc. c. 4. & 5. Pererius l. 9. in Gen. disp. de pecc. Evæ quæst. 1. Contrarium assumit Lutherus in Comment. super c. 3. Gen. statuens primum omnium peccatum fuisse dubitationem de mandato diuino, vel vno verbo, infidelitatem: Licet a: hæc wæstio non sit de fide, sed duntaxat circa fidem, rem fuisse ita vt fortassè tutius sit, eam in dubio relinquere; quàm scrupulosè discutere: placet tamen pro Lu theri sententia contra Pontificios, vnum vel alterum argumentum annotare:

V. 1. Ab ordine tentationis, Diabolus Evam prius solicitavit, ad infidelitatem, quàm ad superbiam: Ergo Eva prius fuit infidelis, quàm superba. Si enim prius superbiisset, non per seductionem Satanæ hoc factum fuisset, cùm primus tentationis gradus fuerit, ad infidelitatem id quod patet ex i. 2

Gen. 3. vbi v. 3. recensetur, quomodo Eva statim ad dubitationem & infidelitatem fuerit permota, dum mandatum Dei corrupit, partim additione, (ne tangeremus,) partim diminutione (ne fortè moriamur) póst autem cum serpens Evam videret dubitantem, & quasi indignantem ob rigorem mandati factus audacior, id quod Deus affirmaverat, de quo mulier dubitaverat, ipse pernegat, v. 4. Nequaquam moriemini. Et vt hoc facilius persuaderet, addit causam v. 5. petitam à promifsione singularis scientiæ, quæ secunda erat tentatio, nimirum ad superbiam. Ex hoc igitur seductionis ordine videmus, quòd præcesserit dubitatio vel infidelitas, & secuta fuerit elatio vel superbia.

VI. 2. A dicto Ecclesiastici, c. 10. v. 14. Initium superbiæ est, apostatare à Deo ἀποστασία autem est ἀπισία, vel certè pars ἀπισίας. Quare infidelitas semper præcedit superbiam, sicut causa effectum, & mater sobolem. Ex quo vltrò sequitur, primos parentes primùm fuisse infideles, & ex hac infidelitate initium sumpsisse superbiam.

VII. 3. A natura fidei. Impossibile est hominem, quàm diu fiduciam in Deum retinet, adversus Deum superbite. Igitur protoplastæ etiám, antequam superbirent, infideles fuêre. Neque enim interminationem mortis spreuissent, nisi extincto fidei lumine illam effugere, hanc adipisci se posse cogitassent. Nam ideò appetebant scientiam divinam, quia non credebant ex esu pomi mortem, sed istam potius scientiam secuturam. Finem verò hunc intendere non potuissent, si non prius de veritate comminationis divinæ dubitassent.

IIX. Vt autem Lutheri nostri sententia melius intelligatur, præcipua Bellarmini argumenta, quibus illam refutare voluit, paucis examinabimus.

IX. 1 Ecclesiastici 10. versus 15. dicitur ἀρχὴ ἁμαρτίας ὑπερηφανία; initium omnis peccati est superbia. Ergò fuit etiam initium peccati primi.

Resp. 1. Dictum hoc non loquitur de prima & originali, sed ex prima orta & actuali superbia, quam ad alia quoque peccata homines irritare dicit Ecclesiasticus, vnde Lutherus recte vertit, Hoffart treibet zu allen Sůnden. Hoc ergo libenter concedimus, quod ex superbia post lapsum multa pullulent flagitia alia, non autem exinde sequitur, quod superbia in peccato primi omnium prima fuerit transgressio. 2. Oppono v. 14. vbi initium superbiæ dicitur ἀποστασία vel ἀπισία. Idem vero non est initium sui initij. E. ἡ ἀπισία est initium ὑπερηφανίας, quod dicitur v. 14. vtique, hæc non erit initium illius. Exceptam igitur vult Ecclesiasticus ἀποστασίαν, quando superbiam omnis peccati initium appellat. Sensus proinde est, quod infidelitas sit mater superbiæ, ex qua postmodum multa alia sequantur peccata.

X. 2. Tobiæ 4. v. 14. In superbia initium sumpsit omnis perditio. Id autem, in quo perditio sumpsit initium, fuit primus actus vitiosus.

Resp. 1. Est vitium vulgatæ versionis. Verba enim in Græco sic habent: ἐν τῇ ὑπερηφανίᾳ ἀπώλεια, καὶ ἐν καταστροφᾷ πολλή. (Lutherus vertit, Sie ist ein Anfang alles Verderbens.) Quæ autem consequentia: Ex superbia est perditio. Ergo fuit omnium primum peccatum? 2. sermo est non de originali, sed actuali superbia. Ordo igitur actuum primorum hîc non indicatur. 3. Et licèt de superbia Euæ loqueretur, nihil tamen hinc sequeretur: quia non ordo actuum, sed effectus tantùm superbiæ indicatur; qui tamem non exclusiuè intelligendus, quandoquidem pariter dicere possunt, ex intemperantia, ex ἀπισίᾳ, ex contemtu est perditio, nec tamen actus hi omnes primi fuerunt in ordine; quoniam aliud est effectus, qui omnibus istis vitiosis actibus inest, aliud primitas ordinis, quæ vni duntaxat propria: de illo, non hac loquitur præsens textus, si de prima superbia sit intelligendus.

XL 3. Rom. 5. v. 19. Per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi. Inobedientia autem est primus gradus superbiæ, videlicet nolle subijci imperio, & præceptis alterius.

Resp. 1. Per inobedientiam non intelligitur actus primus in peccato Adami, sed totum potius peccatum. Ἀτόπως igitur καὶ ἀσκόπως ad ordinem actuum applicatur hoc dictum. 2. Quod Bellarminus vocat primum gradum superbiæ, id infidelitatis est. Non enim describere possumus ἀπείθειαν aliter, quàm per non facere, vel nolle facere mandatum & voluntatem Dei.

XII. 4. Profertmulsa patrum dicta & testimonia.

Resp. 1. Patrum scopus non semper fuit accurate loqui de ordine actuum vitiosorum. 2. Per superbiam sæpè intelligunt ἀπιστίαν vel superbum præceptorum diuinorum contemtum, quo sensu scribit Beda: Omnis peccans superbus est, eò quod faciendo vetita, contemtum habet præcepta diuina. Atque hinc apparet, Patribus superbiam sæpè idem esse, quod infidelitatem, seu contemtum legis. 3. Ponunt superbiam tanquam effectum, & tamen presupponunt ἀπιστίαν, veluti causam, hoc est, designant causam per effectum.

XIII. 5. Prior est actus circa finem, quàm circa media: sed superbia erat finis, neglectus mandati, erat medium. E. illa prior hic posterior.

Resp. 1. Distinguimus inter electionem & seductionem. Cùm aliquis spontè quid eligit, tum quidem de fine primùm cogitat, pòst de medijs. In seductione autem sæpè fit contrarium. Ita potest alter alterum ad iter suum statim adsciscere, & pòst demum finem indicare. Sic Gen. 23. Isaac ignorabat finem profectionis, ideoque medium ibi prius erat, quàm finis.

2. Distinguimus inter finem seducentis & seducti. Finis seducentis erat violatio mandati diuini, ad hanc igitur primùm solicitabat: Et medium erat promissio sapientiæ, quam subjungebat. Finis autem hominis erat quidem excellentia maior; & medium, neglectus verbi: sed in ordine actuum non consideratur, quid homo intenderit principaliter, sed quid primùm egerit. Id autem primùm egit, ad quod primùm tentatus est, quod fuit dubitatio & infidelitas, tanquam finis serpentinæ tentationis. Fecit ergo diabolus à suo fine initium seducendi; & homo initium peccandi, cùm assentiretur & dubitare inciperet.


### Question IV

I. Bellarmine, book 3, chapter 10, denies that the first sin was absolutely the most grievous. Bonaventure, in book 2, distinction 21, last article, last question, folio 320, distinguishes between intensive and extensive gravity; and says that the first sin was indeed extensively the most grievous, because it contaminated the whole human race, yet not intensively, and by reason of the act; because there are found sins in which there is greater malignity, such as direct hatred of God, sin against the Holy Spirit, and blasphemy of the divine name.

II. But since these things make for the extenuation of the first sin, for that reason we judge the contrary opinion to be true, and that it may be proved, we premise this theological aphorism: The gravity of sins and sinners is to be estimated from five things. 1. From the object. 2. The law. 3. The will. 4. The work. 5. The punishment. In these five respects we say that the first sin was more grievous than other actual ones and those following the first, which we shall now prove in order.

III. And indeed it was greater and more grievous, with respect to 1. The object. There are three objects of sins. 1: God. 2. One's neighbor, and 3. That very person who sins. Against all these the protoplasts were injurious and contumelious. 1. By sinning against God, because they detracted from His truth, not holding the commandment as true, and turned themselves away from Him. Moreover, the gravity of the sin is intensified if one considers that supreme grace which God had granted to the first man. For the more benefits one receives, and the more ungrateful one is toward the benefactor, the more gravely one sins. 2. Against their neighbor, and against all their descendants, whom they cast down together with themselves into eternal destruction. But no one by other sins brings damnation upon others also, but only upon himself. 3. Against themselves, because they contaminated themselves with their own and most wicked homicide, which is the more grave because by it they deprived themselves not only of the life of nature, but also of grace, or of that first created integrity.

IV. 2. Of the law. A sin is the graver, the lighter and easier to observe the law is that is violated. Such, however, was that one concerning not eating: for how easily could they have abstained in such a variety and abundance of fruits? No law has been enacted since the fall that is so easy, and therefore the first sin was most grave in this respect also: which is furthermore intensified if one considers that all the commandments of the decalogue were violated, nor can a sin almost be named that did not concur there, so much so that the first fall may not undeservedly be called a farrago and a sink of all sins.

V. 3. Of the will. The holier the will that deviates, and the more voluntary the sin, the graver and more deformed it becomes. And the first sin was in the highest degree voluntary. For no sinner has such freedom of will as the first man had: moreover, there was a supreme perfection of will, such as is found in no man after the fall. Nature inclined toward the good, and he could observe the law not only without difficulty, but even with a natural propensity. When, therefore, he was carried against this φυσικὴν δύναμιν, and the law which he could so easily keep, when he violated it, how great a malignity shall we think there was? For one must estimate how great the iniquity was in sinning, where there was such facility for not sinning. August. lib. 14. de Civ. Dei c. 15.

VI. 4. Works, whose extreme deformity in turn appears quite evidently from the violation of the whole law. Man was ungrateful and blasphemous toward God, an enemy to his neighbor and to himself. He insinuated a lie against God, and wished to transfer the blame onto Him: he depraved the whole human nature, and cast himself headlong into eternal punishments. He sinned in heart, mouth, work, and hand: he offended in effect, affection, and speech: In sum, a certain vicious work can hardly be imagined that was not present; whence the gravity of the fall is intensified, especially if the perfection and beauty of nature, and afterward the deformity of sin, are considered together.

VIII. 5. Punishment. A crime is the more grave, the more gravely it is punished by a just judge. But the first sin was most gravely punished. Therefore it was the most grave. For man lost not only life and the divine image, but also attracted death, and that threefold: 1. of nature, 2. of grace, and 3. of glory. Because of that fall, the Lord cursed both the serpent and the earth, indeed almost the whole of nature; and not only his own person, as happens in other sins, which are hence called personal, but also the whole human nature and all the posterity of the first-formed were miserably corrupted and depraved, whence it has been accustomed to be designated as natural sin.

IIX. Since all these things are so, we conclude that the first sin was not only extensively, but also intensively, not just in some way, but absolutely the far greatest and most grave of all sins.

IX. But one thing seems to stand in the way, namely, the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is said to be irremissible. Adam's sin, however, was remissible.

and is, and therefore inferior to it; since that which is always remissible is lighter than that which is irremissible.

Response. 1 The gravity of a sin is to be considered by reason of its own being, not by reason of something extrinsic, that is, with respect to what it is, not with respect to what is about it, or is done. However, to be remitted or not to be remitted is not of the sin, but about the sin, and therefore one cannot judge from that alone concerning the quiddity or gravity of the sin,

2. A fallacy of cause is committed. The sin against the Holy Spirit is not irremissible as if it were graver, but accidentally, because it is joined with the contempt of the means.

3. It may in a certain way be conceded that with respect to an extrinsic factor, namely irremissibility, the sin against the Holy Spirit is graver. Nor do we deny that there can be sins that are graver regarding one or another condition and circumstance, but not absolutely graver.

4. It is one thing to be irremissible ἁπλῶς, καὶ καθ' ἁυτὸ, another to be so κατάτι & συμβεβηκότως. If the sin against the Holy Spirit were irremissible in itself, then it would be graver. But since that cannot be affirmed, as will be explained more fully below, we still pronounce that the first fall was absolutely the gravest and most foul.

To God alone be glory.

Latin:

I. Bellarm. l. 3. c. 10. negat peccatum primum fuisse absolutè gravissimum. Bonavent. in l. 2. dist. 21. art. vlt, quæst vlt. f. 320 distinguit inter gravitatem intensivam & extensivam; dicitque peccatum primum extensiuè quidem fuisse gravissimum, quia totum genus humanum contaminauerit, non tamen intensivè, & ratione actus; quia reperiantur peccata, in quibus major sit malignitas, vt directum Dei odium, peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, & blasphemia nominis diuini.

II. Sed cùm hæc faciant ad extenuationem peccati primi, propterea contrariam sententiam veram esse judicamus, quæ vt probetur, præmittimus aphorismum hunc Theologicum; Peccata & peccatorum gravitas ex quinque rebus æstimanda est. 1. ex obiecto. 2 lege. 3. voluntate. 4. opere. 5 pœna. Hic quinque respectibus omnibus peccatum primum dicimus fuisse gravius alijs actualib⁹ & primum sequentibus, id quod nunc ordine probabimus.

III. Et quidem maius graviusque fuit, respectu 1. Objecti. Tria sunt peccatorum objecta. 1: Deus. 2. proximus, & 3. ille ipse, qui peccat. In omnia hæc iniurij & contumeliosi erant protoplastæ. 1. peccancdo in Deum, quia veritati eius detrahebant, mandatum pro vero non habentes, sefeque ab illo avertebant. Intenditur autem peccati gravitas, si consideretur summa illa gratia, quam Deus homini primo concesserat. Eò enim gravius quis peccat, quò plura accipit beneficia, & quò magis erga benefactorem est ingratus. 2. In proximum, & in omnes posteros suos, quos vnà secum in æternam perniciem præcipitabant. Nemo autem per cætera peccata alijs quoque, sed sibi soli damnationem attrahit. 3. In teipsos, quia proprio eoque scelestissimo homicidio sese contaminabant, quod eò gravius, quia per istud non tantùm vitâ naturæ, verùm etiam gratiæ, vel prima istâ concreatâ integritate sese privabant.

IV. 2. Legis. Eò peccatum est gravius, quò lex, quæ violatur, est leuior & observatu facilior. Talis autem erat illa de non comedendo: quàm facilè enim potuissent abstinere in tanta fructuum varietate & vbertate? Non est post lapsum lex vlla tam facilis lata, ideoque peccatum primum & hoc respectu fuit gravissimum: quod præterea intenditur, si cogitetur, quod omnia omnino decalogi præcepta fuerint violata, neq; possit fermè nominari peccatum, quod ibi non concurrerit, ita quidem vt primus lapsus non immeritò farrago & colluuies omnium peccatorum queat appellari.

V. 3. Voluntatis. Quò sanctior est voluntas exorbitans, & quò peccatum magis voluntarium, eò fit gravius & deformius. Atque peccatum primum fummè erat voluntarium. Nullus n. peccator tantam habet voluntatis libertatem ac primus habuit: summa insuper erat voluntatis perfectio, qualis in nullo homine post lapsum reperitur. Propendebat natura ad bonum, & non modò sine difficultate, sed etiam naturali propensione legem observare poterat. Contra hanc ergo φυσικὴν δύναμιν cū ferretur, legemq; quam adeò facilè seruare poterat, cùm violaret, quantam putabimus malignitatem fuisse? Existimare enim oportet, quanta fuerit iniquitas in peccando, vbi tanta erat non peccandi facilitas. August. lib. 14. de Civ. Dei c. 15.

VI. 4. Opera, Cuius deformitas summa vicissim ex violatione totius legis satis evidenter apparet. Erat homo ingratus & blasphemius in Deum, inimicus in proximum & seipsum. Mendacij insinuabat Deum, & culpam in ipsum transferre volebat: Naturam humanam totam depravabat, & semetipsum in æternas pœnas præcipitem dabat. Peccabat corde, ore, opere & manu: delinquebat effectu, affectu, affatu: In summa, vix potest opus quoddam vitiosum excogitari, quod non fuerit; vnde gravitas lapsus intenditur, præsertim si naturæ perfectio & venustas, pòst peccati deformitas coniunctim considerentur.

VIII. 5. Pœna. Eò est gravius delictum, quò à justo judice gravijùs punitur. Primum autem peccatum fuit gravissimè punitum. Ergo fuit gravissimum. Etenim amisit homo non tantùm vitam & imaginem diuinam, sed etiam attraxit mortem, eámque tergeminam 1. naturæ. 2. gratiæ, & 3. gloriæ. Propter istum lapsum & serpenti & terræ, imò toti quasi naturæ maledixit Dominus; nec persona duntaxat propria, vt fit in alijs peccatis, quæ hinc personalia nominantur, sed etiam tota humana natura, omnisq́ue protoplastarum posteritas miserabiliter corrupta & depravata fuit, vnde peccatum naturale indigitari consueuit.

IIX. Quæ omnia cùm ita sese habeant, peccatum primum non modò extensiuè, verùm & intensiue non duntaxat aliquo modo, sed absolutè peccatum omnium fuisse longè maximum & gravissimum, concludimus.

IX. Vnicum verò videtur obstare, videlicet, peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, quod irremissibile dicitur. Adami autem peccatum remissibile fuit

& est, ideoque illo inferius; cum remissibile semper sit leuius irremissibili.

Respond. 1 Grauitas peccati consideranda est, ratione sui esse, non ratione alicuius extrinseci, id est, respectu eius, quod est, non respectu eius, quod dirca illud est, aut fit. Remitti autem, vel non remitti non est de peccato, sed circa peccatum, ideoque exinde tantùm de peccati quidditate aut grauitate iudicare nequit,

2. Committitur fallacia causæ. Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum non est irremissibile, ac si foret grauius, sed per accidens, quia coniunctum est cum contemptu mediorum.

3. Potest quodammodo concedi, quòd respectu extrinseco, nimirum irremissibilitatis, peccatũ in Spiritum Sanctum grauius sit. Neq; hoc negamus posse dari peccata, quoad vnam vel alteram conditionem & circumstantiam, verùm non absolutè grauiora.

4. Aliud est irremissibile ἁπλῶς, καὶ καθ' ἁυτὸ, aliud κατάτι & συμβεβηκότως. Si per se irremissibile foret peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum, tunc grauius esset. Illud verò cuni affirmari nequeat, quemadinfrà fusius exponetur, lapsum primum absolutè grauissimum & fœdissimum fuisse, etiamnùm pronunciamus.

Soli Deo Gloria.


## 6 Disputation V. On the Existence and Propagation of Original Sin

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Master Paulus Röber of Wurzen, Alumnus of the Elector of Saxony.

Προόιμιον.

I.

FROM the first fall of the first-formed, or Pandora's box, evils of every kind have erupted into the world. For Adam was, and in him we all were, we all perished. From a corrupt root a praiseworthy sap is not drawn: thus the nature of man, being vitiated, has produced none but vicious offspring, infected with the plague of sin.

II. For original integrity was granted under condition, namely, that if man were to obey, it would come to pass that he would both retain it for himself and propagate it to his descendants; but if not, that the image being lost, nature would immediately be corrupted, with the greatest destruction of all his posterity.

III. Since therefore Adam was disobedient, he was justly deprived of his innate perfection, and there followed a depravation of all his powers, which all his descendants draw from him as from an unhappy fountain, and thus, being turned away from the good and prone to evil, in a word, they are born children of wrath.

IV. And this is that original evil, which is neither κτιστόν or concreated, nor ἀγένητον or uncreated, but supervening, but was introduced, namely through the fall of Adam, as the Greek Fathers speak. Concerning which corruption all the sounder philosophers indeed complained, but from where it flowed, they were ignorant. That it is not from God, right reason indeed dictated, whence Gellius, book 6, Attic Nights, chapter 1, reports that Chrysippus said that nature was not created with evils but that these things exist by consequence; but the cause itself and the antecedent, that was clearly unknown to the nations, but was revealed in the Scriptures alone.

V. This article concerning original sin has its ordinary seat in the Epistle to the Romans: where the Apostle treats of it in two ways. 1. Absolutely and commonly. 2. Restrictively and specially, insofar as it is still remaining in the reborn after regeneration. There it dominates; here it is chastised by the Spirit. There guilt is present; here it is absent. There the person displeases God; here he pleases. Concerning the former, the Apostle speaks in chapters 3 and 5; concerning the latter, in chapter 6 and especially 7.

VI. Although the whole doctrine of original sin can be included in these two chapters, for the sake of a better distinction we shall divide it into four members, intending to treat 1. of the existence and propagation of sin. 2. of its essence and definition. 3. of its punishment and burning. 4. of its pardon and liberation. In the first we shall hear that there is some sin of nature, and how it is derived to us; in the second, what it is, and in what it is formally situated; in the third, what calamities it has introduced, and how we are fully liberated from it.

VII. We shall assign individual disputations to individual members, intending to make a beginning from that primary controversy: Whether there is and exists some sin which is inherent from the first origin of man, and infects and corrupts the whole nature? Which very thing, so that it may be distinctly taught and demonstrated, we shall form certain questions according to our custom and explain the purer opinion of our Churches in a few words.

QUESTION I. What are the appellations of original sin?

I. The sin in which, and with which all men are born, was not called by any peculiar and significant term before Augustine. Irenaeus called it the ancient wound of the serpent. Tertullian, the transmission of evil. Cyprian, another's sin and the contagion of ancient death. Chrysostom, πρώτην ἁμαρτίαν. Ambrose, hereditary bond, and defilements of nature.

II. These terms, however, are so constituted that they could all be eluded by Pelagius, and in fact were eluded. For he willingly confessed that sin is the ancient wound of the serpent, but inflicted upon our first parents: that it is a transmission of evil, but by example: that it is another's, but not our own by birth: that it is the first, yet not derived into posterity: that it is a hereditary bond and defilements, not by propagation, but by imitation.

III. Nor indeed did Augustine dare to name it φυσικὸν or natural, on account of the suspicion of Manichaeism. For Pelagius could easily have interpreted this through calumny, as if it were being taught that sin was concreated with nature itself, or that nature was substantially evil, which is Manichaean. Wherefore, that every suspicion of error might be removed, and that the equivocations and tricks of Pelagius might be more easily averted, he wished to designate it sin of origin or original, for the sake of distinction from actual sins.

IV. But here is not intended 1. The origin of creation, as if this evil had also taken its origin together with the rest of the creatures, since all things, originally created, were very good. 2. Nor the origin of human nature, since this was first founded without any sin. 3. Nor the origin of the world only, under the beginning of which it was committed: but for three other respects this name was imposed, and is still retained by us.

V. 1. It is called original. By reason of the principle, which was Adam. For he first sinned and drew in evil, and from him as from a common trunk and origin, it is derived into all descendants by hereditary right, and creeps like a contagion. 2. By reason of the effect, which are actual sins. For these flow forth from this first one and draw their origin from it. Flacius strongly urges and inculcates this notation taken from a transitive sense in part 2 of the Clavis, tract 6, on original sin, p. 370, for which reason on p. 371 he calls it radical and fountain-head sin. 3. By reason of the subject, or of each person, since we are both conceived and born in this and with this sin, and thus it takes its origin in man immediately with the origin of any man, and hence it is principally called original: For as the scholastics speak barbarously, As soon as a man is originated, sin is indeed originated in the man. For it does not arrive from elsewhere after birth, but arises in the very birth of man, and therefore Anselm rightly wrote that it is called original from the origin of each person, treatise on the conception of the virgin, chapter 1.

VI. Luther, part 3 of the Smalcald articles, article 1, calls it capital and principal sin. Commonly, natural or congenital, because it is born in us or born with us, whence it is also called innate or connate. This appellation seems to be taken from Ephesians 2:3: We were φύσει or by nature children of wrath. For if the guilt is natural, the sin itself, which for that reason is rightly called φυσικὸν or natural, is also, not because it is nature itself, nor because it is from God the creator of nature, as the Manichaeans contended, but because it adheres in nature and arises with nature. Augustine explained it thus long ago when he writes in book 4 of the Hypognosticon: We say and believe that lust is not a natural good, but a natural evil. We call it a natural evil thus, not because it is congenital to nature from God the creator, but because it is transferred from a sinning nature into a sinful nature, that is, because it is a defect of the sinful nature, not nature itself. Thus also Anselm explained, writing, that sin, which in Adam was personal, is in us of nature, not because it is from the essence of nature but because the corruption is assumed with nature itself.

VII. It is also commonly called hereditary, since it is as it were the first inheritance which we receive from our parents. For because it arises in nature and with human nature, certainly he who generates nature simultaneously propagates the vice of nature, and thus this original malice is derived into us as if by natural inheritance.

IIX. It is not rarely called militant sin, from its impetus or perpetual motion. For although it is in a way mortified in the saints, nevertheless it continually, powerfully, and furiously wars against the new man. But this appellation is somewhat more restricted, since it especially regards sin as it inheres in the regenerate and is opposed to the spirit.

IX. The Scholastics recount eight principal names. For it is called 1. the law of the flesh, 2. the law of the members, 3. the law of nature, 4. original sin, 5. the fuel (fomes), 6. the tyrant, 7. concupiscence, 8. concupiscibility. He who desires more synonyms, and especially the appellations of Scripture, can consult Chemnitz, part 1, book on original sin, chapter 1, and Mr. Gerhard, Vol. 2, on original sin, sections 67 and 68.

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisner. S S. Th. D.

Resp. M. Paulo Röbero Wurzensi, Alumn. Elect. Saxon.

Προόιμιον.

I.

EX primo πρωτοπλάστων lapsu, seu Pandorae pyxide, omnis generis mala in mundum eruperunt. Fuit enim Adam, & in illo fuimus omnes, perijmus omnes. Ex corrupta radice laudabilis succus non trahitur: sic natura hominis vitiata, non nisi vitiosos, & peccati tabe infectos progenuit.

II. Nam integritas originalis sub conditione fuit concessa, nimirum, si obediret homo, fore, vt & sibi eam retineret, & in posteros propagaret; sin minus, amissa imagine protinus corruptam iri naturam, cum summo totius posteritatis exitio.

III. Quoniam ergo Adamus inobediens fuit, iustè orbatus est perfectione congenita, & successit omnium virium deprauatio, quam ex ipso, velut infelici fonte omnes posteri hauriunt, adeoque auersi à bono, proni ad malum, vno verbo, filij irae nascuntur.

IV. Atque hoc est illud originale malum, quod neque κτιστόν vel concreatum, neque ἀγένητον vel increatum, ἀλλὰ ἐπιγινόμενον, sed intro ductum est, nempe per lapsum Adæ, vti Patres græci loquuntur, De qua corruptione omnes quidem saniores Philosophi conquesti sunt, vnde verò fluxerit, ignorarunt. A Deo non esse, recta quidem ratio dictauit, vnde Gellius l. 6. N. A. c. 1. Chrysippum dixisse refert, quòd natura non sit creata cum malis sed esse hæc κατά παρακολόυθησιν per consequentiam: causam verò ipsam & antecedentis, istud gentibus planè ignotum, in solis verò Scripturis patefactum est.

V. Habet autem articulus hic de Originali peccato sedem suam ordinaria in epist. ad Romanos: vbi duobus modis Apostolus de illo agit. 1. Absolutè & communiter. 2. restrictè & specialiter, quatenus in renatis post παλιγγενεσίαν adhuc est reliquum. Ibi dominatur; hic per Spiritum castigatur. Ibi reatus adest; hic abest. Ibi persona Deo displicet; hic placet. De priori Apostolus verba facit c. 3. & 5. de posteriori cap. 6. & inprimis 7.

VI. Quamuis autem duobus hisce capitulis includi possit tota peccati originalis doctrina, melioris tamen distinctionis gratia in quatuor membra dispescemus, acturi 1. de peccati existentia & propagatione. 2. de essentia & definitione 3. de pœna & vstione. 4. de venia & liberatione. In primo audiemus, quod sit peccatum aliquod naturæ, & quomodo ad nos deriuetur; in secundo, quid sit, & in quo formaliter situm sit; in tertio, quas calamitates induxerit, & quomodo ab illo plenè liberemur.

VII. Singulis autem membris singulas disputationes tribuemus, initium facturi à controuersia illa primaria. An sit & detur aliquod peccatum, quod à prima hominis origine insit, totámque naturam inficiat & corrumpat? Quod ipsum, vt distinctè doceatur & demonstretur, pro more nostro ζητήματα quædam formabimus & puriorem nostrarum Ecclesiarum sententiam paucis explicabimus.

QVAESTIO I. Quae sint peccati originalis appellationes?

I. Peccatum in quo, & cum quo omnes homines nascuntur, ante Augustinum peculiari & significante aliquo vocabulo non appellabatur. Irenaeus vocauit antiquam serpentis plagam. Tertullianus traducem mali. Cyprianus, peccatum alienum & contagium mortis antiquae. Chrysostomus πρώτην ἁμαρτίαν. Ambrosius vinculum haereditarium, & inquinamenta naturae.

II. Haec autem vocabula taliter sunt comparata, vt à Pelagio omnia potuerint eludi, req; ipsa fuerint elusa. Nam lubenter fatebatur, peccatum esse antiquam serpentis plagam, sed primis parentibus infictam: Esse traducem mali, sed per exemplum: Esse alienum, sed nobis ex natiuitate non proprium: Esse primum, non tamen in posteros deriuatum: Esse vinculum haereditarium & inquinamenta, non propagatione, sed imitatione.

III. Neque vero audebat Augustinus nominare φυσικὸν vel naturale, ob suspicionem Manicheismi. Potuisset enim Pelagius per calumniam hoc facilè interpretari, ac si doceretur, peccatum naturae ipsi concreatum, vel naturam substantialiter malam esse, quod Manicheum. Quocirca, vt omnis supicio erroris tolleretur, vt aequiuocationes & Pelagij strophae faciliùs auerterentur, peccatum originis vel originale, ad differentiam actualium indigitare voluit.

IV. Non autem hic attenditur 1. Origo creationis, quasi vnà cum reliquis creaturis malū istud suam quoq; sumpsisset originem, cùm omnia, primitus creata, valdè fuerint bona. 2. Nec origo humanae naturae, cùm haec primùm absque omni peccato fuerit condita. 3. Nec origo mundi tantùm, sub cuius initium fuit commissum: sed alijs tribus respectibus nomen istud impositum est, & à nobis etiamnùm retinetur.

V. 1. Dicitur originale. Ratione principij, quod fuit Adam. Hic enim primus peccauit, malumque attraxit, & ab hoc tanquam communi stipite & origine, in omnes posteros hæreditario jure deriuatur, & ceu contagium serpit. 2. Ratione effecti, quod sunt peccata actualia Hẹc enim ex isto primò profluunt, suamque originem trahunt. Hanc notationem à sensu transitiuo desumtam maximè vrget & inculcat Flacius part. 2. Clauis tract. 6. de pecc. orig. p. 370. quam ob causam P. 371. vocat peccatum radicale, & scaturiginale. 3. Ratione subiecti, vel cuiusque personæ, quoniam in hoc & cum hoc peccato tum concipimur, tum nascimur, atque sic cum origine cuiusuis hominis suam mox in homine sumit originem, & hinc principaliter originale dicitur: Nam vt scholastici barbarè loquuntur, Quam primum originatur homo, originatur žuidem in homine peccatum. Non enim post ortum aliundè aduenit, sed in ipso statim ortu hominis oritur, ideoque Anshelmus rectè scripsit, Originale dici ab origine cuiusque personæ, tr. de concept. virg. cap. 1.

VI. Lutherus part. 3. artic. Smalcald. artic. 1. vocat capitale & principale peccatum. Communiter, naturale vel congenitum, quia nobis annascitur vel connascitur, vnde & annatum connatumuè dicitur. Appellatio hæc videtur desumta ex Ephes. 2. v. 3. Eramus φύσει vel naturâ filij iræ. Si enim reatus est naturalis, ipsum quoque peccatum, quod illius causa rectè φυσικὸν vel naturale dicitur, non quòd sit ipsa natura, nec quòd sit ab opifice naturæ Deo, ut Manichæi contendebant, sed quoniam in natura hæret, & cum naturæ oritur. Ita explicauit olim Augustinus cum l. 4. ὑπογνωστικῶν scribit: Nos libidinem non naturale bonum, sed naturale malum esse dicimus credimusque. Naturale malum sic dicimus, non quia sit naturæ Deo opifici congenitum, sed quod à peccante naturâ transfertur in peccatricem naturam, id est, quod sit naturæ peccatricis vitium, non ipsa natura. Sic etiam exposuit Anshelmus, scribens, peccatum; quod in Adamo fuit persona e, in nobis esse naturæ, no quod sit ab essentia naturæ sed qui corruptio cum ipsa natura assumitur.

VII. Vulgo etiam nuncupatur hæreditarium, quoniam est veluti prima hæreditas, quam a parentibus accipimus. Quia enim in natura, & cum natura humana oritur, vtique qui generat naturam, simul propagat naturæ vitium, & sic quasi per naturalem hæreditate in nos deriuatur malitia hec originalis.

IIX. Non raro appellatur peccatum militans, ab impetu seu perpetuo motu. Licet enim in sanctis quodammodo mortificetur, tamen continue, potenter & furenter militat aduersus nouum hominem. Sed appellatio hæc nonnihil restrictior est, cum potissimum respiciat peccatum, prout in renatis hæret, & spiritui opponitur.

IX Scholastici octo potissimum nomina recensent. Nam dicitur 1. lex carnis 2. lex membrorum. 3. lex naturæ. 4. Peccatum originale. 5. fomes. 6. Tyrannus 7. concupiscentia 8. concupiscibilitas. Plura Synonyma, & præsertim appellationes Scripturæ qui desiderat, is consulere potest Chemnitium, part. 1. l. de pecc. orig. cap. 1. & Dn. Gerhardum. Tom. 2. de pecc. orig. sect. 67. & 68.


### Question II. How various have been and are the opinions concerning original sin?

How various have been and are the opinions concerning original sin?

I. It is superfluous to say much about the ancient philosophers. For what could they know about this matter, who neither knew nor read that: By one man sin entered into the world? August. book 4 against Julian, chapter 15. They have indeed often complained about the obliquity and depravity of nature. Plato, book 2 of the Republic, says: Men are by their own nature evil, and cannot be induced to practice justice, but only lest they suffer injustice. Cic. l. 3. Tuscul. As soon as we are brought into the light and accepted, we are immediately involved in every depravity and in the greatest perversity of opinions, so that we seem to have sucked in error almost with our nurse's milk. The same author, in his book on the Republic, as cited by Augustine in book 4 against Julian, writes that man is brought into the light by a stepmother nature, with a body naked, fragile, and infirm, with a mind anxious for troubles, humble for fears, weak for labors, prone to lusts, in which the divine fire is buried, [as well as] talent and character. However much, as I have said, they acknowledged the corruption of nature, they nevertheless denied that it was sin in the stricter sense. Hence Aristotle argues that neither virtue nor vice comes about by nature (φύσει γίγνεται). Hence Seneca, epistle 96, concludes: You are mistaken if you think that vices are born with us: they have supervened, they have been introduced.

II. These speculations, however, did not keep themselves within the Lyceum, but breaking forth, they crept into the Church as well. The voice of Scripture concerning congenital sin is indeed clear; but that light and clarity is not perceived by all, due to the vice of a darkened mind. The number of those who err is not small, yet they can all be divided into two ranks. The former includes the older ones, the latter the more recent ones. In the rank of the Ancients we place 1. The Pelagians. 2. The Armenians. 3. The Scholastics, of whom [we shall speak] in order.

III. 1. The Pelagians were named after Pelagius the Briton, who lived around the year of our Lord 420, first a monk at Rome, later a presbyter, and finally a heresiarch. He was the first to openly attack the sin of origin in the Church, and he taught that to infants, before the action of their own will, no vicious affections and no depravity adhere, and therefore that death is not a punishment for sin, but a natural condition of human nature, which is composed of the warring qualities of the elements. And at first he indeed affirmed that the sin of Adam had harmed his descendants not at all; but later, in the Palestinian Synod, he revoked this error, but fraudulently. For he explained it thus: that it had indeed harmed his descendants, but not by propagation, but rather only by bad example, occasion, or imitation, in that children learned to sin by the example of their parents, just as the younger ox learns to plow from the older one:

IV. There were, therefore, four primary members of the Pelagian opinion. 1. That no sin passes from Adam into men through generation, and therefore there is nothing vicious in children. As we are born without virtue, they said, so we are procreated without vice, as Augustine reports in book 2 de pecc. orig. c. 6. 13. 15. 2. That no one is damned on account of Adam's sin. 3. That it does not pass into men by any other reason than by example: nor does it harm us otherwise than because we make it our own by imitation. 4. That by Baptism no sins are remitted to little ones, since they have none; but only that the kingdom of heaven is opened to them: For if they die without Baptism, although they are not damned, they are nevertheless not received into heaven, because of the assertion of Christ in John 3, v. 5: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven.

V. The Armenians followed the Pelagians after the year 700, who indeed denied original sin, yet established that guilt was contracted from the first disobedience of Adam: And indeed they fostered three main errors. 1. That no sin is actually derived into men from Adam, in which they agreed with Pelagius. 2. That all, however, are held guilty of eternal damnation on account of the first fall, unless they are freed through Christ, in which they disagreed with Pelagius: 3. That all who lived before the coming of Christ were actually damned.

VI. 3. Many among the Scholastics also approved and interpolated the long-since condemned dogma of Pelagius. Lombard himself reports in book 2, dist. 30, letter E, that certain Scholastic Doctors held that original sin is not the guilt of punishment for the sin of the first man, that is, a debt or liability by which we are liable and addicted to temporal and eternal punishment for the actual sin of the first man. Although the Master disapproves of this opinion, he could not persuade his disciples not to encrust the same absurdity. For

Scotus in 4. d. 14 q. 1. art. 1. And Biel on the same distinction, question 1, note 2, expressly affirm that after any sin, and therefore also that of Adam, nothing remains but the liability to punishment. Durandus in 2. dist. 30. q. 2. & 3. denies that original sin must be called a fault. William, Bishop of Paris, on vices and sins, chapter 7, proceeded so far as to determine that this natural vice is worthy of no punishment. Alexander of Hales, when he had Bonaventure as a boy under his discipline, was accustomed to say: In this Adam did not sin. Occam in 2. at the end of the book confesses that he, if he were not hindered by the authority of the Fathers, would say that original sin is only the liability for another's sin, without any vice inherent in us. Others have determined that it is indeed a vice, but only in the sensitive appetite, not in the higher faculties. Some [say] that it is indeed a disease and a vice corrupting the whole nature, but not a sin properly so called. Certain others [say] that it is a sin and a fault, but that it is a mere lack of the justice that is due, and includes no positive quality. And this opinion is the most common, which Bellarmine also defends in book 5, chapter 15.

VII. These were the ancient errors concerning original sin, which follow one another, and are so arranged that one always surpasses the other in absurdity. The crassest ones absolutely denied that the fall of Adam harmed his descendants. Others [said] that it harmed them, but only by example. Others [said] that it is a fault, but an alien one, only imputed to us: not inherent. Others [said] that something is propagated, but only the liability. Others [said] that a vice is propagated, but that it adheres only in the appetite. Others [said] that it is in all the faculties, but is not a fault properly so called. Others [said] that it is a fault, but a mere privation, [containing] no positive quality. This latter [view], however, the orthodox Fathers assumed, and always defended strongly against any heretics whatsoever.

VIII. As regards the more recent ones, some [say] that the evil of origin they directly, some indirectly impugn, or at least excessively diminish.

Those who do this directly are 1. Anabaptists. 2. Photinians. 3. Certain Calvinists. 4. Certain Papists.

IX. 1. The Anabaptists affirm that Christ by his death so completely removed that sin from human nature that infants are born entirely innocent and immune from vice, indeed so that they do not need the washing of Baptism in infancy. Hence they slanderously call our doctrine an invention of Augustine, similar to the eccentrics and epicycles of the mathematicians. See the Colloquium of Frankenthal, art. 4, act. 11, p. 198, 245, 248.

X. 2. The Photinians assume and defend the same error. For thus writes Ostorodt in his German Institution, ch. 35: We do not concede that nature is corrupted on account of the first sin of man. And in the Racovian Catechism, p. 285, they assert that neither Adam's [nature] could be corrupted by sin, much less that of his descendants. For which reason they call it a fable of the Manichaeans, born from a perverse understanding of Scripture, and devised to defend the superstition of infant baptism.

XI. Certain Calvinists have similarly raved, among whose number is especially Huldrych Zwingli, who in the Confession published in the year [15]30 and offered to Emperor Charles, art. 4, writes: Whether we like it or not, we are forced to admit that original sin, as it is in the children of Adam, is not properly a sin. For it is not a crime against the law. It is therefore properly a disease and a condition, which he declares by the example of stammering and hereditary stone. He delivers the same more extensively in his commentary on chapter 5 to the Romans and in his epistle to Urbanus Rhegius. Whitaker indeed tries to excuse him in book 1, On Original Sin, ch. 9, but the letter is clear, which admits of no cloak. For either Zwingli contradicted himself, or he revoked his earlier writings and changed his opinion.

XII. 4. Certain Papists, among whom is Albertus Pighius in his first controversy on original sin, establishing that there is nothing in infants which has the true nature of sin, but that the stain of origin is one in number, in the first man in reality, in the others by imputation, not otherwise than as from slaves, who lost their liberty by their own fault, slaves are born not by their own but by their parents' fault, and just as the son of a harlot sustains the infamy of his mother without any fault of his own adhering to him, which comparisons Chemnitz reports Pigichus to have used in part 1 of his Examination, p. 88.

2. Ambrosius Catharinus in his Opusculum on the fall of man, ch. 6, and on ch. 5 of Romans, where he teaches that by the very fact that we are children of a transgressor, who promised that he would retain the received gifts for himself and his children, and did not retain them, we are constituted sinners and worthy of hatred, not otherwise than sometimes the children of wicked parents, who nevertheless do not commit the same sins as their parents, are deprived of paternal goods and are forced to be exiled forever according to the justice of the court: Bellarmine wished to refute both in book 5, chapter 16, who nevertheless sticks in the same mud, as will be indicated a little later.

3. Dominicus Scotus the Spaniard, intimate in councils to the Council of Trent, who dreams that concupiscence, that primary part of sin, was concreated in us, and therefore lacks sin properly so called. For thus he says in book 1 on gifts and grace, ch. 3: From these things it is clear that that struggle, of which the Apostle makes mention to the Galatians, that the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh, is innate to man by nature.

Latin:

Quam varia fuerint & sint de originis peccato sententiæ?

I. De antiquis Philosophis multa dicere supersuacaneum est. Quid enim illi de hac re sapere poterunt, qui nec scierunt, nec legerunt illud; Per vnum hominem peccatum intrauit in mundum? August. l. 4. contra Iul: c. 15. Sæpius quide conquesti sunt de naturæ obliquitate & deprauatione. Plato 2. de Repub. ait: Homines sua natura sunt mali, & induci non possunt, vt iustiam colant, sed tantùm, ne iniuriam patiantur. Cic. l. 3. Tuscul. Simul atque editi sumus in lucem & suscepti, in omni continuò prauitate, & in summa opinionum peruersitate versamur, vt penè cum lacte nutricis errorem suxisse videamur. Idem l. de Repub. vti citatur ab Augustino l. 4. contra Iul. Hominem, scribit, à natura noverca in lucem edi, corpore nudo, fragili atque infirmo, animo anxio ad molestias, humili ad timores, debili ad labores, procliui ad libidines, in quo diuinus ignis sit obrutus, ingenium & mores. Quantumuis autem, ut dixi, corruptionem naturae agnouerint, eam tamen peccatum propius dictum esse negârunt. Hinc disputat Aristoteles, quòd nec virtus nec vitium φύσει γίγνεται. Hinc Seneca epist. 96. concludit: Erras, si existimas nobiscum nasci vitia: Superuenerunt, ingesta sunt.

II. Non autem intra Lyceum continuerunt sese speculationes istae: sed prorumpentes in Ecclesiam quoque irrepserunt. Clara quidem de peccato congenito Scripturae est vox; verùm lux & claritas illa non ab omnibus conspicitur, mentis obtenebratae vitio.
