Est verò errantium numerus non exiguus, qui tamen omnes in duo agmina queunt diuidi. Prius antiquiores, posterius recentiores complectitur. In Antiquorum agmine locamus 1. Pelagianos. 2. Armenios. 3. Scholasticos, de quibus ordine.

III. 1. Pelagiani dicti sunt à Pelagio Britanno, qui vixit circa annum Domini 420. primum Monachus Romae post Presbyter, tandem haeresiarcha. Hic eum primus peccatum originis in Ecclesia manifeste oppugnauit, docuitque Infantibus ante actionem propriae voluntatis, nihil vitiosorum affectuum, nihil deprauationis adhaerere, ideoque mortem non esse poenam peccati, sed naturalem humanae naturae, expugnantibus elementorum qualitatibus compositae, conditionem. Et initiò quidem affirmauit, peccatum Adae posteris omnino nihil nocuisse; post autem in Synodo Palaestina errorem hunc reuocauit, sed fraudulenter. Ita enimExposuit, nocuisse quidem posteris, sed non propagatione, verum malo duntaxat exemplo, occasione, seu imitatione, eo quod liberi exemplo parentum peccare didicerint, sicut a boue maiori discit arare minor:

IV. Quatuor ergo primaria opinionis Pelagianae membra fuerunt. 1. Nullum ex Adamo peccatum in homines per generationem transire, eoq; nihil in pueris esse vitiosum. Vtine virtute, dicebant, ita sine vitio procreamur, referente Augustino l 2. de pecc. orig. c. 6. 13. 15. 2. Neminem propter peccatum Adae damnari, 3. Illud in homines non alia ratione transire, quam exemplo: neque nobis aliter obesse, quam quia imitatione nostrum efficimus. 4. Per Baptismum nulla remitti paruulis peccata, cum nulla habeant; sed tantum aperiri illis regnum caelorum: Si enim moriantur absque Baptismo, licet non damnentur, in coelum tamen non recipi, ob assertionem Christi Iohan. 3. v. 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest introire in regnum caelorum.

V. Armenij Pelagianos secuti sunt, post annum 700. qui peccatum originis quidem negarunt, reatum tamen ex prima Adami inobedientia contractum esse statuerunt: Et quidem tres potissimum errores fouere. 1. Nullum reipsa in homines deriuari peccatum ab Adamo, in quo consentiebant Pelagio. 2. Omnes tamen damnationis aeterne ob lapsum primum reos teneri, nisi liberentur per Christum, in quo dissentiebant a Pelagio: 3. Omnes, qui vixerunt ante Christi aduentum, reipsa damnatos esse.

VI. 3. Ex Scholasticis etiam multi dogma Pelagij iampridem damnatum adprobarunt & interpolarunt. Refert Lombardus ipse l. 2. dist 30. lit. E: quosdam Doctores Scholasticos sensisse, peccatum originis non esse reatum pana pro peccato primi hominis, id est, debitum vel obnoxietatem, quo obnoxij & addicti simus pana temporali & aeterne pro primi hominis actuali peccato. Quam opinionem licet improbet Magister, non tamen persuadere potuit discipulis suis, quo minus eandem absurditatem incrustarent. Nam

Scotus in 4. d. 14 q. 1. art. 1. Et Biel in eandem distinctionem quaest. 1. not. 2. diserte affirmant post quodvis peccatum, ideoque Adami etiam, nihil remanere quam reatum poenae. Durandus in 2. dist. 30. q. 2. & 3. negat peccatum originis oportere dici culpam. VVilhelmus Episcopus Parisiorum, de vit, & peccat. cap. 7. co processit, vt naturale hoc vitium nullo supplicio dignum esse statuerit. Alexander Alensis, cum Bonauenturam puerum sub disciplina haberet, solitus est dicere: In hoc Adam non peccauit. Occam. in 2. in fine libri fatetur; Se, si non impediretur authoritate Patrum, disturum esse, peccatum originis tantum esse reatum alieni peccati, sine aliquo vitio haerente in nobis. Alij statuerunt, vitium quidem esse, sed tantum in appetitu sensutiuo, non in superioribus facultatibus. Nonnulli, esse quidem morbum & vitium totam naturam corrumpens, non autem peccatum proprie dictum. Quidam, peccatum & culpam esse, sed meram iustitiae inesse debitae carentiam, nullamque qualitatem positiuam includere. Et haec sententia est communissima, quam defendit etiam Bellarm. lib. 5. cap. 15.

VII. Hi fuere antiqui de peccato originali errores, qui se inuicem consequuntur, & ita comparati sunt, vt semper alter alterum absurditate vincat. Crasissimi, prorsus negarunt, lapsum Adae nocuisse posteris. Alij, nocuisse, sed exemplo tantum. Alij, culpam esse, sed alienam, nobis tantum imputatam: non inhaerentem. Alij, propagari aliquid, sed tantum reatum. Alij, propagari vitium, sed duntaxat in appetitu haerere. Alij, inesse omnibus facultatibus, sed non esse culpam proprie dictam. Alij, culpam esse, sed meram priuationem, nullam qualitatem positiuam. Hoc autem posterius orthodoxi Patres assumserunt, semperque contra haereticos quosuis fortiter defenderunt.

IIX. Recensiores quod attinet, nonnulli malum originis directè, quidam indirectè impugnant, vel certè nimium extenuant.

Qui directè hoc faciunt, sunt 1. Anabaptistæ. 2. Photiniani 3. Quidam Caluiniani. 4. Quidam Pontificij.

IX. 1. Anabaptistæ adfirmant, Christum morte sua peccatum illud sic planè sustulisse ex natura humana, vt infantes nascantur prorsus innocentes, & à vitio immunes, ita quidem vt non indigeat in infantia Baptismatis lavacro. Hinc doctrinam nostram per calumniam appellant Augustini figmentum, simile Mathematicorum Eccentricis & Epicyclis. Vide Colloquium Franc. art. 4. act. 11. p. 198. 245. 248.

X. 2, Photiniani eundem errorem assumunt & propugnant, Ita enim scribit Ostorodus in Instit. German. c. 35. Non concedimus, quòd propter primum hominis peccatum natura sit corrupta. Et in Catech. Racov. p. 285. asserunt, ne Adami, qui dona naturalia per peccatum corrumpi potuisse, nedum posteriorum. Qua de causa fabulam Manichæorum vocant, natam ex pravo intellectu Scripturæ, & excogitatam ad defendendam Pædobaptismi superstitionem.

XI. Quidam Caluiniani similiter delirarunt, ex quorum numero potissimum est Huldric. Zwinglius, qui in Confessione anno 30. edita, & Carolo Imperatori oblata art. 4. scribit: Velimus, nolimus, cogimur admittere, peccatum originale, vt est in filijs Adæ, non propriè peccatum esse. Non enim est facinus contra legem. Morbus igitur est propriè, & conditio, quod declarat exemplo balbutientium & calculi hæreditarij. Idem fusius tradit in comment. super capite. 5. ad Rom. & in epist. ad Vrban. Regium. Excusare quidem eum conatur Whitak. l. 1. de pecc. orig. c. 9. sed clara est litera, quæ nullum pallium admittit. Aut enim Zwinglius sibi contradixit, aut prius scripta reuocauit, & sententiam mutauit.

XII. 4. Quidam Pontificij, ex quibus est Albertus Pigichus controu. prima de pec. orig. statuens nihil ineffe paruulis, quòd veram peccati rationem habeat, sed originis labem numero effe vnam, in primo homine reipsâ, in cæteris per imputationem, non aliter atque ex feruis, qui proprio vitio libertatem amiserunt, náscantur serui nön suo sed parentum vitio, & sicut filius scorti sustineat infamiam matris sine proprio aliquo in se hærente vitio, quibus similibus vsum esse Pigichum refert Chemnitius par. 1. Exam. p. 88.

2. Ambrosius Catharinus in Opusc. de lapsu hominis c. 6. & super c. 5. Rom. vbi eo ipso, quòd filij simus præuaricatoris, qui promisit se retenturum accepta dona pro se & filijs suis, nec retinuit, nos peccatores & dignos odio constitutos esse tradit, non secus atque nonnunquam scelerosorum parentum filij, qui tamen non eadem cum parentibus peccata perpetrant, paternis bonis priuatur, & æternùm exulare coguntur secundum iustitiam fori: Vtrumque refutare voluit Bellar. l. 5. cap. 16. qui tamen in eodem luto hæret, vti paulò pòst indicabitur.

3. Dominicus Scotus Hispanus, Concilio Tridentino intimus à consilijs, qui concupiscentiam, illam peccati primariam partem, nobis concreatam esse, adeoque culpâ propriè dicta carere somniat. Itá enim ait l. 1. donat. & grat. c. 3. Ex his palàm sit, luctam illam, cuius meminit Apostolus ad Galatas, vt caro concupiscat aduersus Spiritum, & Spiritus aduersus carnem, esse homini à natura ingenitum.


### Question II. How various have been and are the opinions concerning original sin?: Ruardus Tapperus in his article on original sin, writing

4. Ruardus Tapperus in his article on original sin, writing: In a newborn infant nothing is found which truly and properly has the nature of sin.

5. Franciscus de Mayro, who argues thus: Something has as much of the nature of sin as it has of the nature of the voluntary. But original sin was voluntary only in the particular, namely in the πρωτοπλάστοις, but in the universal, that is, in us, it is entirely involuntary: Therefore it has no character of sin at all. Chemnitius noted this argument in part 1 of the Examination, p. 89.

XIII. Furthermore, both the Calvinists and the Papists attack original sin obliquely or indirectly in turn.

XIV. 1. The Calvinists, while they affirm that the infants of the faithful are born holy and in the covenant. For thus Beza in Creoph. fol. 167: The children of the faithful are holy before God from the womb by the formula of the covenant. And Hemmingius in Syntag. p. 23: In infants born of Christian parents there is no formal sin. See Calvin saying this very thing in book 4 of the Institutes, ch. 15, 16; Beza in qq. 124, 126, and part 2 of the Response to the Acts of the Colloquy of Montbéliard, pages 101, 102, 106; Martyr on Genesis, p. 69, and on 1 Corinthians. To this must also be referred that less correct, to speak most mildly, opinion of Keckermann, book 2 of the System of Theology, ch. 5, p. 257, 258, writing thus: I think that sin, properly so called, cannot be said to be propagated from parent to offspring in itself, I say, and considered according to itself, as if the sin itself already constituted proceeds from the parents and infects the offspring, but a certain principle of this sin; that is, that from which this sin can arise descends from the parents into the offspring, namely, a disposition to such a depraved temperament of man, such as is adjacent to original sin, is propagated through the seed. But if only a disposition and a principle from which sin can arise is propagated, certainly the sin itself will not be propagated. Why therefore does David affirm that he was conceived in sin? Psalm 51, v. 7. And what will change that disposition so that it becomes a habit and a sin properly so called?

XV. 2. The Papists cherish such hypotheses that, while they stand, the evil of origin cannot stand. There are, however, eleven of them primarily. 1. That original sin is less than any venial sin, Thomas in 2, distinct. 23, question 1, article 2. But since eternal death is not due to a venial sin by its own nature, as the Papists believe, it will be much less owed to original sin, and thus its formal element will be removed, namely the guilt of death and eternal damnation. Conversely, since venial sins are the least of all, how can anything less than them be imagined? Certainly, whatever is less than a venial sin is not a sin, which, however, since the Papists assert this of original [sin], it follows undoubtedly that it is removed from the number of sins. Moreover, original sin is so much the greater, the less it is believed to be, Δια το͂το μέ- γα ἐςὶ κακὸν, λᾳδο͂υ ὀὐδέν ἐῖναι δοκε͂ι, therefore it is a great evil, because it is thought to be nothing, says Chrysostom in chapter 1 to the Romans. And the author of the Ascetica says, What kind of sin, he says, is it, which you will dare to call light? Jerome, Epistle 14. I do not know whether we can call any sin light, which is committed in contempt of GOD.

2. That original sin does not merit eternal death and the punishments of hell, Bellarmine, book 6 on the Grace of the First Man, chapter 5 and following. But that which does not incur the curse of the law, nor is worthy of death, this very thing also is not lawlessness, and therefore not sin.

3. That hereditary malice is a punishment, not a fault, unless we obey it with free will, Bellarmine, book 5 on free choice, chapter 20. But indeed infants, since they lack the use of reason, cannot yet freely obey. Therefore, in infants it has nothing of the nature of a fault or sin.

4. That natural faculties remained intact after the fall, which is the common voice of the Papists. If they remained intact, nature is certainly not corrupted. Therefore, natural sin falls, and the Pelagians have won.

5. That actual sin cannot corrupt the natural gifts of man, Bellarmine, on the grace of the first man, chapter 6. But indeed original justice was a natural gift: the sin of Adam was actual. Therefore, it has not yet been taken away, wherefore we are still born righteous, not unrighteous or children of wrath.

6. That concupiscence in itself and without consent is not a sin, but is called so only analogically and by a trope, which

and let the cause of sin be named sin. Ruardus Tapperus, art. 2. Bellarmine, book 2, on the Loss of Grace, ch. 2, book 5, ch. 9. But concupiscence is the primary and formal part of sin. Wherefore, if that is only a punishment, not a fault, it follows conversely that no sin adheres to infants.

7. That the rational soul is not propagated by generation. Bellarmine, book 4, on the Loss of Grace, ch. 11, where he calls the contrary opinion a proven error, nay, a heresy, from Thomas, part 1, question 118, art. 2. But truly this is the πρω̂τον ψευ̂δος of sin, as Thomas admits, 1. 2. q. 83. art. 2. Therefore, if that is not propagated, neither will this be derived into it.

8. That in regeneration sin is entirely taken away, and that the reborn are innocent and immaculate, Council of Trent, Session 5. Since, therefore, Adam undoubtedly performed penance, and thus was reborn, certainly nothing remained in his nature that had the character of sin. Who, therefore, could propagate original stain? Or is there even a propagation of a non-entity?

9. That a law is not properly given except to those who have the use of free will, Bellarmine, book 1, on the Loss of Grace, ch. 1. But truly infants lack the use of free will. Therefore they are not capable of law, and thus no sin, which is ἀνομία, will fall upon them.

10. That nothing has the character of sin unless it is voluntary, Bellarmine, book 1, on the Loss of Grace, ch. 1, and book 2, on grace, ch. 7. But original sin, as it adheres in us, or with respect to us, is entirely involuntary. Therefore, it is also entirely nothing.

11. That we have free will in spiritual matters, and that we can prepare ourselves for grace without grace, Thomas in 2, dist. 28, art. 4; that we can act well, avoid sins, and fulfill commandments from natural powers alone, Biel in 2, dist. 28; that the unregenerate can obtain justification through works of penance, Bellarmine, book 5, on grace, ch. 12. But if the powers of nature are so great, sin infecting nature will be none, or certainly very slight.

XVI. And thus far the various opinions of those who err We have seen, which all tend at last to the denial of the existence of sin: than which error nothing is more dangerous. For thus the stain and wasting disease of souls is hidden, man is rendered secure, Pharisaical swelling is induced, Christ the Physician is not sought, because no disease is presumed. Rightly Hippocrates in his aphorisms: Those who in a serious disease do not feel pain, are in a very bad way, and the hope of life is small, almost none.

XVII. Attending to which, our Churches, all those errors having been rejected, teach, believe, and confess. That our nature is most gravely corrupted, and polluted by a most foul sin drawn from our parents, so much so that we are able to will or effect nothing good, as far as our conversion is concerned. For thus it stands in art. 2. A. C. They teach that after the fall of Adam all men propagated according to nature are born with sin, that is, without fear of God, without trust toward God, and with concupiscence, and that this disease or vice of origin is truly sin, condemning and bringing even now eternal death to those who are not reborn through Baptism and the Holy Spirit. Which orthodox opinion, although our people have hitherto explained it in many and those most clear writings, the Papists nevertheless do not cease to slander, and, themselves entirely immersed in errors, they object three errors to us.

XIIX. 1. That we remove Adam's sin from his descendants. For thus Bellarmine slanders in book 5, chapter 16: The Lutherans contend that the depravity of human nature is properly sin, even without relation to the sin of Adam. But where has this been said or written by our people in that sense? We indeed deny that the act of Adam passed into his descendants, yet we affirm that it is imputed to us: and thus we all sinned in Adam as in a common root, and so the First fall is ours, not indeed by propagation, yet by imputation; not actually, but originally. Hence we are all said to have sinned in Adam, Rom 5. v. 12. and by the disobedience of one to be sinners v. 19. Nor could guilt be propagated into us, unless the imputation of the act had preceded, since indeed it is the foundation of that. For which reason Bernard, Sermon 1 on the 1st Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany, rightly wrote concerning original sin: It is another's because we all sinned descending in Adam: it is ours, because although in another, we nevertheless sinned, and it was imputed to us by the just judgment of God, although hidden. For in every body, whether it be physical, or political, or mystical, that which the head does, insofar as it is the head, this is by right imputed to the whole body. The will, which is as it were the head and queen in man, when it has sinned, the whole body is punished. The deeds of a magistrate are imputed to the whole Republic, the deeds of a father of a family to the whole family, so much so that even children, on account of the crime of rebellion or high treason, although it may have been committed by the father alone, are by right despoiled of all things by the Prince. Since therefore Adam was the head of the whole human race, and we all are his members: he the Father, we the sons: deservedly the sin, which he as head committed, is imputed to us, and as regards guilt is propagated into us.

XIX. 2. That we deny original sin. Bellarmine attributes this to us, book 4, chapter 2, at the end. The Lutherans, he says, just as they do not at all acknowledge the gift of original righteousness as something superadded and habitual to nature, so they cannot acknowledge its privation; and therefore they are compelled to constitute and place original sin in concupiscence itself: From which it follows that the Lutherans themselves also deny original sin, although they fight fiercely for asserting it. For that concupiscence is not sin, except metonymically. A bold and impudent statement indeed. For we are so far from denying original righteousness that we defend that it was natural to Adam. Why therefore should we not acknowledge its privation? Nay, it has been written by us more than a thousand times, and everywhere inculcated, that the evil of origin is both a ςέρησιν ἐμφύτου καλõ and a θέσιν ἐπεισάκτου κακõ, that is, the lack of righteousness and the position of concupiscence; which will be proved below to be sin not metonymically, but properly.

XX. 3 That we confuse original sin with actual sins. Bellarmine attributes this to us in book 5, chapter 4, although all methodical textbooks proclaim and urge the contrary. He presumes, however, to prove this calumny: 1. By the testimonies of Luther and Philipp, who write that the fuel of sin is not without actual sin, nay rather that it is actual sin. Response: To Luther and Philipp, actual and active are the same. For they wish to show against the Scholastics that sin is not a mere δύναμιν, but is present in act; that it is not a dead or idle thing, but living and busy. Hence they call it actual sin, not because it is committed by one who knows, but because it is sin in the very act, or is most active, so much so that it does not rest even in infants, but excites vicious motions, especially in the sensitive part. But if this acceptance of the word actual stirs up a dispute, Bellarmine, we recall this of Durand to memory: Verbose, contentious, calumnious, malicious men dispute about names. 2. By the authority of the Augustan Confession, which describes the sin of origin through words actively. Response: This calumny has long since been refuted in the Apology itself. For by those active words, through a Hebrew idiom, we denote not actions, but rather a habit and depraved inclinations: in which we follow the custom of Scripture, which likewise often employs active words, as in Romans 3, verse 12: There is none that understandeth; there is none that seeketh after God; they are all gone out of the way, etc. Therefore, to conclude, the Augustan Confession used active words: 1, for the example of Scripture; 2, to indicate the activity of sin; 3, to more strongly chastise those who extenuate it.

XXI. From these things, therefore, I reckon it is now sufficiently clear what our opinion is concerning original sin. Briefly: We establish and teach that, on account of the disobedience of Adam imputed to his descendants, we are all not only born without righteousness and holiness, but also with the most profound of all virium corruption, with ignorance of the mind, malice of the will, stubbornness of the heart, and the repugnance of the other δυνάμεων, so that man by nature is a child of wrath, and from natural powers alone cannot prepare himself for grace, much less convert. This thesis, which we judge to be true in all respects, conformable to the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, and approved by the perpetual consent of the Church, is what must now be demonstrated a little more fully.

Latin:

4. Ruardus Tapperus in artic. de pec. orig. scribens, In paruulo recens nato nihil inueniri, quod verè & propriè peccati rationem habeat.

5. Franciscus de Mayro, qui sic argumentatur: Tantum habet aliquid de ratione peccati, quantum habet de ratione voluntarij. Atqui peccatum originale in particulari, nempe πρωτοπλάστοις solummodò fuit voluntarium, sed in vniuersali, hoc est, in nobis, omninò est inuoluntarium: Ergò nullam omnino habet rationem peccati. Annotauit hoc argumentum Chemn. parte 1. Exam. p. 89.

XIII. Porrò obliquè vel indirectè peccatum originis impugnant vicissim tum Caluiniani , tum Pontificij.

XIV. 1. Caluiniani, dum infantes fidelium sanctos & in fœdere nasci adfirmant. Ita enim Beza in Creoph. fol. 167. Fidelium pueri ex fœderis formula ab vtero coram Deo sancti sunt. Et Hemming. in syntag. p. 23. In infantibus ex Christianis parentibus natis non est formale peccati. Vide hoc ipsum dicentem Caluinum libro 4. Institut. cap. 15. 16. Bezam in qq. 124. 126. & part. 2. Responf. ad Acta Colloq. Mompelg. pag. 101. 102. 106. Martyrem super Genes. p. 69. & super 1. ad Corinth. Huc etiam referri debet illa minùs recta, vt mollissimè dicam, Keckerm. sententia l. 2. syst. Theolog. c. 5. p. 257. 258. ita scribentis: Existimo, peccatum propriè dici nõ posse propagari à parente in sobolem per se, inquam, & secundum se consideratum, quasi ipsum iam peccatum constitutum à parentibus proueniat, & sobolem inficiat, sed principium quoddam peccati huius; hoc est, id, à quo hoc peccatum oriri possit, è parentibus in prolem descendit, nimirum dispositio ad prauam eiusmodi hominis temperiem, qualis peccato originis adiacet, per semen propagatur. Quòd si autem dispositio tantùm & principium, à quo peccatum oriri potest, propagatur, certè non ipsum peccatũ propagabitur. Cur ergò Dauid in peccato se conceptum adfirmat? Psalm. 51. v. 7. Et quid illam dispositionem mutabit, vt fiat habitus, & peccatum propriè dictum?

XV. 2. Pontificij tales fouent hypotheses, vt ijs stantibus, originis malum stare nequeat. Sunt autem illarum vndecim potissimùm. 1. Peccatum originale quouis veniali minus esse, Thomas in 2. distinct. 23. quæst. 1. art. 2. Cùm autem veniali mors æterna non debeatur ex natura sua, vti censent Pontificij, multò minùs debebitur originali, adeoque tolletur ejus formale, nimirum reatus mortis & damnationis æternæ. Vicissim, cùm venialia peccata sint omnium minima, quomodo ijs aliquid minus fingi poterit? Peccatum certè non est, quicquid veniali minus est, quod ipsum tamen cùm de originali asserant Pontificij, è peccatorum numero istud eximi, indubitatò sequitur. Est autem peccatum originis in sic antò maius, quãtò minus creditur, Δια το͂το μέ- γα ἐςὶ κακὸν, λᾳδο͂υ ὀὐδέν ἐῖναι δοκε͂ι, propterea grãde malum est, quia nullum esse putatur, ait Chrysost. in c. 1. ad Rom. Et author Asceticorum, Quale, inquit peccatum est, quos quid audebis patuum dicere? Hieron. Epist. 14. Nescio, an possimus leue aliquod peccatum dicere, quod in DEI contemtum admittitur.

2. Peccatum originis non mereri mortem æternam, & pœnas inferni, Bell. l. 6 de A. G. 5. & seqq. At quod legis maledictionem non incurrit, nec morte dignum est, hoc ipsum quoque ἀνομία non est, ideoque nec ἁμαρτία.

3. Malitiam hæreditariam pœnam esse non culpam, nisi liberâ voluntate ei obediamus, Bell. l. 5. de lib. art. c. 20. At verò infantes, cùm vsu rationis careant, nondum liberè odedire possunt. Ergo in infantibus nihil habet rationem culpæ, vel peccati.

4. Naturalia post lapsum mansisse integra, quæ communis Papicolarum vox est. Si integra mansêre, natura vtique corrupta non est. Cadit igitur peccatum naturale, & vicerunt Pelagiani.

5. Peccatum actuale non posse corrumpere dona hominis naturalia, Bell. de gra. pri. hom. c. 6. At verò justitia originalis fuit donum naturale: peccatum Adami fuit actuale. Ergò illa nondum sublata est quare iusti etiamnum nascemur, non iniusti vel filij iræ.

6. Concupiscentiam per se & sine consensu non esse peccatum, sed dici tantùm analogicè & secundum Tropum, quæ

pentus & causa peccati nominetur peccatum. Ruardus Tapperus art. 2. Bell. l. 2. de A. G. c. 2. l. 5. c. 9. At concupiscentia est primaria & formalis pars peccati. Quare, si illa tantū poena sit, non culpa, vicissim infantibus nullum peccatū adhaerere sequitur.

7. Animan rationalem non propagari per generationem. Bell. l. 4. de A. G. c. 11. ubi contrariam sententiam vocat exploratum errorem, imò haeresin ex Thoma part. 1. quaest. 118. art. 2. At verò haec est πρω̂τον ψευ̂δος peccati, fatente Thoma 1. 2. q. 83. art 2. Ergo si illa non propagatur, neque hoc in illam derivabitur.

8. In regeneratione peccatum penitùs tolli, renatosque innocentes & immaculatos esse, Concil. Trid. Sess. 5. Cùm ergò Adamus procul dubio poenitentiam egerit, adeoque renatus fuerit, vtique in ejus natura nihil ampliùs haesit, quod rationem peccati habuit. Qui ergo labem originalem propagare potuit? An etiam non entis datur propagatio;

9. Legem propriè non dari, nisi iis, qui habent vsum liberi arbitrij, Bell. l. 1. de A. G. c. 1. At verò infantes carent vsu liberi arbitrii. Ergo legis capaces non sunt, ideoque in eos nullum cadet peccatum quod est ἀνομία.

10. Nihil habere rationem peccati, nisi quod sit voluntarium, Bell. l. 1. de A G. c. 1. & l. 2. de gra. c. 7. Atqui peccatum originis, prout in nobis haeret, vel respectu nostri, prorsus involuntarium est. Igitur & prorsus nullum.

11. Liberum in spiritualibus nos habere arbitrium, & posse nos sine gratia praeparare ad gratiam, Thomas in 2. dist. 28. art. 4. posse ex solis naturalibus benè agere, peccata cavere, & praecepta implere. Biel in 2. dist. 28. posse non renatos per opera poenitentiae impetrare justificationem, Bell. l. 5. de gra: c. 12. At si tantae sunt vires naturae, peccatum vtique naturam inficiens nullum, vel certè perexiguum erit.

XVI. Et hactenus varias errantium opiniones vidimus, quæ omnes tandem ad peccati existentiam negandam tendunt: quo errore nihil est periculosius. Ita enim labes & tabes animarum occultatur, homo securus redditur, Pharisaicus tumor inducitur, Christus Medicus non quæritur, quia nullus morbus præsumitur. Rectè Hippocrates in aphorismis: Qui in gravi morbo dolorem non sentiunt, malè omninò se habent, & vitæ spes exigua est, propè nulla.

XVII. Quod attendentes Ecclesiæ nostræ, omnibus istis erroribus rejectis, docent, credunt, & confitentur. Naturam nostram gravissimè corruptam, & fœdissimo peccato ex parentibus tracto pollutam esse, adeò ut nihil boni, quoad conversionem nostram, velle aut efficere valeamus. Ita enim habet art. 2. A. C. Docent, quòd post lapsum Adæ omnes homines secundum naturam propagati, nascantur cum peccato, hoc est, sine metu Dei, sine fiducia erga Deum, & cum concupiscentia, quodque hic morbus seu vitium originis sit verè peccatum damnans & afferens nunc quoque æternam mortem his, qui non renascuntur per Baptismum & Spiritum sanctum. Quam orthodoxam sententiam, licèt multis ijsque clarissimis scriptis nostri hactenus explicuerint, Papicolæ tamen calumniari non desistunt, & tres errores, ipsi toti erroribus immersi, nobis objiciunt.

XIIX. 1. Nos Adami peccatum à posteris removere. Ita enim calumniatur Bell. l. 5. c. 16. Lutherani depravationem naturæ humanæ propriè peccatum esse contendunt, etiam sine relatione ad peccatum Adami. Vbinam verò hoc à nostris eo sensu dictum, scriptum? Actum quidem Adami in posteros transiisse negamus, illum tamen nobis imputari adfirmamus: atque sic omnes in Adamo tanquam communi stipite peccavimus, adeoque Primus lapsus est noster, non quidem propagatione, tamen imputatione; non actualiter, sed originaliter. Hinc omnes dicimur in Adamo deliquisse, Rom 5. v. 12. & per unius inobedientiam peccatores esse v. 19. Neque in nos propagari posset reatus, nisi præcessisset imputatio actus, quippè quæ illius fundamentum est. Quam ob causam Bernhardus Serm. 1. super Dom. 1. post 8. Epih. de culpa originali rectè scripsit: Aliena est quia in Adam omnes descientes peccavimus: nostra, quia etsi in alio, nos tamen peccavimus, & nobis justo Dei judicio imputabatur, licèt occulto. In vnoquoque enim corpore, siue sit physicum, siue politicum, siue mysticum, id quod facit caput, quatenus caput, hoc toti corpori jure imputatur. Voluntas, quæ quasi caput & regina est in homine, cùm peccavit, totum corpus plectitur. Facta magistratûs toti Reipubl. facta, patrisfamiliâs toti familiæ imputantur, adeò vt & liberi ob cirmen rebellionis, vel læsæ maiestatis, licèt à solo patre commissum sit omnibus jure spolientur à Principe. Cùm igitur Adamus fuerit caput totius humani generis, & nos omnes illius membra: ille Pater, nos filij: meritò peccatum, quod ille vt caput admisit, nobis imputatur, & quoad reatum in nos propagatur.

XIX. 2. Nos peccatum originis negare. Affingit hoc nobis Bell. l. 4. c. 2. in fine. Lutherani, inquit, vt donum istitiæ originalis naturæ supperadditum atque habituale minimè agnoscunt, ita nec ejus privationem agnoscere possunt; & ideo peccatum originis in ipsa concupiscentia constituere & collocare coguntur: Ex quo sequitur, vt ipsi etiam Lutherani peccatum originis negent, quamvis acriter pro eo asserendo pugnent. Nam concupiscentia illa non est peccatum, nisi metonymicè. Audax certè & impudens effatum. Iustitiam enim originalem adeò non negamus, vt Adamo naturalem fuisse defendamus. Cur ergò privationem ejus non agnosceremus? Imò plus quàm millies à nobis scriptum, & vbique inculcatum, originis malum tùm ςέρησιν ἐμφύτου καλõ esse, tum θέσιν ἐπεισάκτου κακõ, hoc est carentiam iustitiæ, & positionem concupiscentiæ; quam non metonymicè, sed propriè peccatum esse infrà probabitur.

XX. 3 Nos confundere peccatum originale cum actualibus. Tribuit hoc nobis Bell. l. 5. c. 4. cum tamen contrarium omnes libelli methodici clament & vrgeant. Probare tamen præsumit istam calumniã, 1. Testimonijs Lutheri & Philippi, scribentium, fomitem peccati non esse absque actuali peccato, imò verò esse actu-ale peccatum. Resp. Actuale Luthero & Philippo idem sunt, quòd actuosum & operosum. Volunt enim contra Scholasticos ostendere, peccatum nõ esse nudam δύναμιν, sed adesse actu; non esse rem mortuam vel otiosam, sed viuam & negotiosam. Hinc nuncupant Actuale peccatum, non quòd à sciente committatur, sed quia ipso actu peccatum, vel maximè actuosum est, adeò vt nè in parvulis quidem quiescat, sed vitiosos motus, in sensitiua præsertim excitet. Quòd si verò hæc vocabuli actualis acceptio litem moueat Bell, istud Durandi reuocamus in memoriam: Verbosi, contentiosi, calumniosi, malitiosi homines disputant de nominibus. 2. Authoritate Confess. A. quæ peccatum originis per verba actiuè describit. Resp. Calumnia hæc jamdudum in ipsa Apologia est refutata. Nam verbis istis actiuis per idiotismum Hebraicum non actiones, sed habitum potiùs & prauas inclinationes denotamus: in quo sequimur morem Scripturæ, quæ itidem verba actiua sæpè adhibet, vt Rom, 3. v. 12. Non est, qui intelligat; Non est, qui requirat; Omnes defecerunt &c. Vt ergò concludamus, vsa est Augustana Confessio verbis actiuis. 1, ob exemplum Scripturæ 2. ad indicandum peccati actuositatem. 3. ad fortius castigandos eius extenuatores.

XXI. Ex his igitur jam satis constare autumo, quæ nostra sit de peccato originis sententia. Breuiter: Statuimus & docemus, ob inobedientiam Adæ posteris imputatam, nos omnes non tantùm nasci sine iustitia & sanctitate, sed etiam cùm profundissima omnium virium corruptione, cum ignorantia mentis, malitia voluntatis, contumacia cordis, & cæterarum δυνάμεων repugnantia, adeò vt homo naturâ sit filius iræ, & ex solis naturalibus ad gratiam se præparare nequeat, multo minus conuersere. Quam thesin per omnia veram, Scripturis & analogiæ fidei conformem, perpetuoque Ecclesiæ consensu comprobatam esse censemus, id quod nunc paulò fusiùs demonstrandum erit.


### Question III By what arguments is the corruption of human nature, or original sin, demonstrated?

I. We shall divide these arguments into three classes, of which 1. Testimonies of the Old and New Testament. 2. Reasons drawn from the analogy of faith. 3. Authorities of the ancient Fathers will be briefly set forth according to the plan of the institution.

The first class containing the sayings of Scripture.

II. Both the Old and New Testament graphically describe the depravity of our nature. The Old is divided by Christ himself into Moses, the Psalms, and the Prophets, Luke 24, v. 44. In each, testimonies concerning original sin are found, of which we shall speak in order.

III. From Moses, 1. Gen. 5, v. 3. Adam lived one hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in HIS OWN image and likeness. The Fathers wish to be noted here especially that opposition between the image of God, to which man is said to have been created in v. 1, and the image of Adam, to which he begat a Son. For hence we conclude thus: The nature of opposites is opposite. But by the image of God is denoted the integrity, justice, and holiness of nature, as we demonstrated in the first disputation. Therefore, by the image of Adam, which is opposite to the former, is understood the corruption of nature, injustice, and sin.

They err therefore 1. Who explain the generation of Seth according to the image of Adam, concerning the tenor of nature and species. For man is one thing, the image to which he was begotten is another. Adam begat a man, where you see an identity of nature, but to what? Not to the image of God, because he had lost this. 2. Who interpret these words concerning the piety of Seth, by which he was similar to Adam, as Chrysostom judged, saying that those were not added in the birth of Cain because he had basely departed from the character of his father. Now indeed it has been proven that not Adam's piety but natural corruption is denoted by that phrase. Therefore, Hugo expressed the sense of this saying best when he writes: Just as Adam was made by God innocent and immortal, innocent and immortal: so he himself, having been made a sinner and mortal, begat a sinner and a mortal.

VI. Gen. 6. v. 5. The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and every imagination of the thoughts of his heart only evil all the days. We acknowledge, however, that this text speaks of the actual sins of the antediluvian world, just as also v. 11, 12, 13, yet in such a way that regard is had in a certain manner at the same time to the very root of all crimes. For.

1. It is a universal sentence, including a triple katholikon: 1. of the subject, Every imagination of the heart, 2. of the act, Only evil, 3. of the time, all the days. Nor is it said restrictively: Every imagination of the heart of those men, but absolutely, Every imagination of the human heart. Why therefore do we limit, where Scripture itself has added no limitation?

2. The cause of actual evil is brought forward here. For just as the Savior testifies in Matt. 15 v. 16, Evil thoughts proceed from the heart; so here it is hinted that wickedness has arisen from the depraved imagination of the heart. Therefore, the second act is not to be opposed to the first act, the stream to the source, the effect to the cause. For the Lord sees both, both the great wickedness and the imagination of the heart evil at all times. That signifies actual sin, this original: that signifies evil fruits, this an evil tree: that signifies the proximate cause of the flood, this the cause of the cause.

3. Since the cause of the flood is rendered, therefore the words must be explained thus; so that infants are not excluded, since even they perished in the flood. But indeed, if by the evil figment of the heart you understand only actual iniquity, what is this to infants? It follows therefore that either a common cause, and thus natural corruption, is involved at the same time, or that infants were punished without any fault, which is impious: Therefore we conclude thus: The cause of the flood was sin. Infants perished in the flood, therefore on account of sin. But not actual sin. For they could not commit such a thing on account of the denied use of reason. Therefore something else besides, namely original sin, must be conceded.

4. Other testimonies are added, where the very tinder of sins is indicated by similar words, as Gen. 8:21. In which place the Lord does not speak of men already destroyed, but henceforth pronounces anew and universally concerning the very depraved nature of man: The thought of the human heart is evil from his youth. Both texts respond to each other. The latter, however, speaks of original sin. Therefore the former does too. Add Job 14, Psalm 5, Rom. 2, concerning which places we shall speak presently.

5. The Papists, playing the plagiarist, attempt to weaken this text thoroughly; Bellarmine, book 5 de A. G. ch. 3, writes that it is a hyperbole when all the thoughts of men are said to be evil, since Noah was just and perfect in his generations. Pererius urges the same in book 8 on Genesis, disp. 5, p. 284, namely that the speech of Moses is hyperbolic.

Resp. 1. Every hyperbole exceeds the truth of a thing and has the appearance of a lie. Therefore, let those who ascribe hyperbolic speech to GOD see to it that they do not make Him a liar and blaspheme:

2. By what sufficiently firm argument will they prove this hyperbole? The Holy Spirit does not play there, but speaks emphatically, and from the truth of the matter, to express the supreme malice and corruption of men. 3. Noah was indeed righteous by grace, yet a sinner by nature, so that if his flesh and natural constitution be considered, it may be said of him no less than of others, Every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was evil every day.

VI. 3. Gen. 8. v. 22. The sense and thought of the human heart are prone to evil from their youth. So indeed the Vulgate reads, but faultily. For in the Hebrew 1. there is not 'sense', through which the motions of the appetite; nor 'thought', through which the counsels of reason, as Pererius understands in lib. 3. in Genes. disp. 14. pag. 365. But יֵצֶר לֵב is thought, or the imagination of the heart in general. 2. It is not said to be prone to evil, but רַע absolutely evil, so that the Lord speaks not so much of a propensity as of habitual and natural malice. 3. Nor is it held 'from youth', that is, when reason begins to exert itself and actually to sin, but מִנְּעֻרָיו from the first man's childhood and infancy.

Let it therefore be noted. 1. That God speaks of the whole human race, and its natural constitution. 2. That at that time no other men lived on the earth than Noah the righteous with his own, so that it is said of these also, The imagination of the heart is evil. 3. That the discourse is not of the sudden motions of the sensitive appetite, but of the heart itself forming thoughts, of the very imagination of reason which the Apostle in Rom. 8. verse 6. calls φρόνημα σαρκός, the mind of the flesh. 4. That this imagination is not said to incline toward evil, but in reality to be evil. 5. And indeed not through habituation or examples, but from earliest infancy, and thus through generation, and the natural corruption of the heart. 6. That this malice is alleged as a cause provoking divine mercy, not because it is so light and unworthy of punishment, but truly, because it is not contracted voluntarily, but by nature immediately in the very conception is engendered in us. From which we conclude thus: If the human heart is universally corrupt, to such an extent that its imagination is not only inclined to evil, but is itself evil from earliest infancy, and thus moves GOD to have mercy, as if it were a misery not voluntarily contracted, but implanted in us without our knowledge, it follows that besides actual and voluntary sins, something else inheres in us and is drawn from birth.

For otherwise there would be no truth or logical consistency in the argument of Jehovah. But the former is undoubtedly true, on account of the infallible account of Moses. Wherefore the latter also must be conceded, not denied.

VII. From the Psalms. 1. Psalm 14, v. 2. 3. The Lord looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there were any that did understand, or seek God. They are all gone aside, they are all together become filthy: there is none that doeth good, no, not one. Which words are found in Psalm 53, v. 3. 4. The Prophet here accuses the malice of men: the question is, what kind? Whether only actual, or only original? We say both, which we prove,

1. From the declaration for the exclusive: For our adversaries bring forward nothing else than that the Psalmist is speaking about the actual sins of men. But we willingly concede this: and it does not hinder our cause at all. For what kind of consequence is it: It is a matter of actual sin, therefore not original? A logician says, the consequence from an inclusive to an exclusive does not hold, especially when no absurdity follows from the inclusion of both members. Therefore, it must be proven by firm reasoning that the discourse is only and uniquely about grosser crimes. They can indeed easily prove that David is speaking about actual sins, and especially in verses 4, 5, 6; but that it is only so, and in verses 2 and 3 as well, they will never be able to prove.

2. From the scope of the Prophet, which is to argue against the vice and impiety of the human race: For although he speaks primarily about the enemies of Israel in verses 6 and 7, nevertheless the universal particles in verses 2 and 3 show that he is simultaneously looking at the common corruption of men, and nothing absurd follows from this interpretation; for it holds men guilty of sin. 1. From works, both internal, or unbelief, and external, or unrighteousness, in the first verse. 2. From the testimony of God, looking down from heaven upon all the children of men, v. 2, and yet finding no one just or good. 3. From universal good, but ready for evil. 4. From the testimony of their own conscience, v. 4, that they themselves have known this, and are well aware of such great deformity in themselves. If all these things are diligently weighed, it is easily understood that the very vice of origin is here viewed by David at the same time. 3. From the universality repeated several times, we have a rule: one must not depart from the clear letter, unless an evident reason and the analogy of faith compel it. But here is the clear letter concerning the universal turning aside or declination of men, and their uselessness. For 1. it is said that God looked down: upon whom? Upon the enemies of Israel? Or the Gentiles ignorant of God? Or the Jews going astray? Or upon one city, or nation? Nothing of these is held in the text. Upon whom then? על־בני אדם upon the children of men in general, that is, upon the whole human race, with absolutely no one excepted: since an indefinite statement is equivalent to a universal one. 2. The purpose of the looking down is added, namely, whether there is even one among the children of men who is understanding and seeking God, and thus the statement is conversely universal. 3. Now follows the outcome; and how it is with the children of men. כל סר Everyone has turned aside; all, and indeed equally, have become corrupt and useless: there is no one doing good, there is not even one. Who does not see here that the universal, and indeed thrice-repeated, corruption of the human race is noted? And what reason will be given why we ought to restrict and limit that universality? For as the looking down of God is general, upon all the children of men, (for this phrase, placed absolutely and indefinitely, does not admit particularity) so also the corruption, which he saw in the children of men, is universal.

4. From the absurd. Either original malice must be understood, or the Prophet's opinion is absurd, nay false. For if you understand actual declination and ἀχρειότητα [uselessness], it certainly cannot be said of all that they have declined. For there are some among the children of men who, imbued with ethical precepts, guard themselves against external vices. There are boys, there are infants, who do not actually sin, and yet are numbered among the declining children of men. Conversely, if you understand moral good, how can it be said that there is not even one among the children of men who does good? For from the midst of paganism contrary examples can be brought forward. Wherefore ἔκκλισις [declination] and ἀχρεία [uselessness] regarding the good must be explained in such a way that it applies to all, with none excepted, which cannot be done unless you understand the very corruption of nature and original decay.

5. From the Apostolic application, which exists in Rom. 3, v. 9. We have previously charged, says the Apostle, that Jews and Greeks are all under sin, AS IT IS WRITTEN, namely in Ps. 14 and 53. There is no one righteous, etc. Here we have an infallible interpreter, who are those whom the Psalmist affirms to have declined and become useless? Namely, that they are not only Gentile Epicureans, but all, even those devoted to the pursuit of virtues; not only some Jews, but all, with not even one excepted: which the Apostle demonstrates with this end, that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God, v. 19. But he would not obtain his purpose if the Psalm which he cites were to be explained as concerning only the extremely impious and gross sinners. For the Apostle wishes to demonstrate that the world, all men, not even excluding infants, are immersed in sin and guilty of damnation, and therefore are not justified before God except through the mercy of the Father and the merit of Christ, just as he finally infers in v. 23. All have sinned, and lack the glory of God, etc. 11, v. 32. He has concluded God has shut up all under unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all. To prove this universality of sinners, he cites Psalm 14, in which there is a universal, that all have turned aside, and an exclusive, that not one remains who does good. Now if you interpret these words particularly, the whole force of the argument perishes, because the consequence from a particular to a universal, from some evil men to all evil men, is not valid. For the Apostle would have concluded just as if someone were to infer thus: Some are learned. Therefore all are learned. For according to the adversaries, the Psalm only affirms this: Some are evil and sinners; but Paul gathers from it: Therefore all are evil and sinners. What is the strength here, what is the reason for the consequence? Wherefore, to conclude, that particular exposition of the Psalm can be defended; unless the Apostle, or rather the Holy Spirit himself, be accused of ἀπαιδευσίας (lack of instruction) in inciting, and of ἀσυλλογισίας (lack of syllogistic reasoning) in arguing, both of which are impious and blasphemous.

Latin:

I. Argumenta ista in tres classes dispescemus, quarum 1. Testimonia veteris & noui Testamenti. 2. Rationes ex analogia fidei petitas. 3. Autoritates antiquorum Patrum pro ratione instituti breviter exponet.

Classis prima continens dicta Scripturæ.

II. Deprauationem naturæ nostræ & Vetus & Novum Testamentum graphicè describit. Vetus ab ipso Christo diuiditur in Mosen, Psalmos & Prophetas, Luc. 24. v. 44. In singulis testimonia de peccato originali reperiuntur, de quibus ordine.

III. Ex Mose, 1. Gen. 5. v. 3. vixit Adam centum triginta annis, & genuit filium ad imaginem & similitudinē SVAM. Patres hic inprimis notari volunt illam oppositionem inter imaginem Dei, ad quam homo creatus dicitur v. 1. & imaginem Adami, ad quam genuit Filium. Hinc enim ita concludimus: Oppositorum opposita est ratio, Atqui per imaginem Dei notatur naturæ integritas, iustitia, & sanctitas, vt disput. primâ demonstravimus. Ergo per Adami imaginem priori oppositam, intelligitur naturæ corruptio, iniustitia & peccatum.

Errant ergò 1. Qui generationem Sethi ad imaginem Adami, de naturæ & fpecieis tenore exponunt. Aliud enim est homo, aliud imago, ad quam genitus. Adam genuit hominem, vbi vides identitatem naturæ, Sed ad quid? Non ad imaginem Dei, quia hanc amiferat. 2. Qui verba hæc de pietate Sethi, qua fimilis fuerit Adamo, interpretantur, vti censuit Chryfostomus, dicens illa in Caini natiuitate non fuiffe adjecta eò, quod turpitèr ab ingenio Patris defciuerit. Iam verò probatum est, non Adami pietatem sed natiuan corruptionem phrasi illâ denotari, Senfum proinde dicti huius optimè expreffit Hugo, cùm scribit: Sicut Adam factus fuit a Deo innocente & immortali, innocens & immortalis: ita ipse factus peccator & mortalis, genuit peccatorem & mortalem.

VI. Gen. 6. v. 5. Vidit Dominus, quod multa effet malitia hominis in terra, & omne figmentum cogitationum cordis eius tantum malum omnibus diebus. Fatemur autem hunc textum loqui de peccatis actualibus mundi antediluuiani, quemadmodum etiam v. 11. 12. 13. ita tamen, vt ad ipsam simul omnium scelerum radicem quodammodo respectus habeatur. Nam.

1. Est sententia vniuersalis, includens triplex καθολικον 1. fubiecti, Omne figmentum cordis, 2. Actus Tantùm malum, 3. Temporis, omnibus diebus. Neque dicitur restrictè; Omne figmentum cordis hominum istorum sed absolutè, Omne figmentum cordis humani. Cur ergo nos limitamus, vbi Scriptura ipsa limitationem non addidit?

2. Adfertur hîc Causa maliua actualis. Sicut enim Saluator Matth 15 v. 16. testatur, Ex corde egredi cogitationes malas; Ita hîc malitiam ex deprauato cordis figmento ortam esse innuitur, Actus ergo secundus actui primo, riuus fonti, effectus causæ non est opponendus. Vtrumque enim videt Dominus, & multam malitiam, & figmentum cordis omni tempore malum. Istud peccatum actuale, hoc originale: Istud malos fructus, hoc malam arborem : Istud diluvij causam proximam, hoc causam causae significat.

3. Quoniam causa diluvij redditur, idcircò verba sic exponenda erunt; vt infantes non excludantur, quandoquidem & hi diluvio periêre At verò, si per figmentum cordis malum, actualem tantùm iniquitatem intelligas, quid hoc ad infantes? Sequitur ergò vel causam communem, adeoque naturalem labem simul inuolui, vel infantes absque omni culpa punitos esse, quod impium: Proinde sic concludimus: Diluvij causa fuit peccatum. Infantes periere diluuio, Ergò propter peccatum. Non autem actuale. Nam tale quid ob negatum rationis vsum committere non potuerunt. Aliud ergò praeterea, nimirum originale, concedendum erit.

4. Accedunt alia testimonia, vbi similibus verbis ipse peccatorum fomes indicatur, vt Gen. 8. v: 21. Quo in loco Dominus non de hominibus jam deletis, sed deinceps de ipsa hominis natura praua denuo & vniuersaliter pronunciat: Cogitatio cordis humani mala est a pueritia sua. Vterque textus sibi inuicem respondet. Posterior autem de malo originali loquitur. Ergò & prior. Adde Iob. 14. Psal. 5. Rom: 2. de quibus locis mox dicemus.

5. Pontificij πλαγιανίζοντες textum hunc penitùs eneruare conantur, Bell. l. 5. de A. G. c. 3. scribit hyperbolen, cùm omnes cogitationes hominum dicuntur malae, siquidem Noë justus & perfectus fuerit in generationibus suis. Idem vrget Pererius l. 8. in Gen. disp. 5. p. 284 nimirum orationem Mosis esse hyperbolicam.

Resp. 1. Omnis hyperbole rei veritatem excedit, & habet speciem mendacij. Qui ergò hyperbolicam orationem DEO adscribunt, viderint, ne ipsum mendacem faciant, & blasphement:

2. Quo argumento satis firmo hyperbolem istam probabunt? Spiritus sanctus ibi non ludit, sed emphatice loquitur, & ex rei veritate, ad exprimendam summam hominum, malitiam & corruptionem. 3. Noe quidem iustus fuit per gratiam, peccator tamen per naturam, adeo, vt si caro eius & constitutio naturalis attendatur, non minus de ipso, quam alijs dici queat, Omne figmentum cogitationum cordis eius malum fuit omni die.

VI. 3. Gen. 8. v. 22. Sensus & cogitatio humani cordis in malum prona sunt ab adolescentia sua. Ita quidem legit vulgata, sed vitiose. Nam in Hebræo 1. non est sensus, per quem motiones appetitus; nec cogitatio, per quam consilia rationis P. rerius intelligit l. 3. in Genes. disp. 14. pag. 365. Sed יֵצֶר לֵב cogitatio, vel figmentum cordis in genere. 2. Non dicitur esse pronum ad malum, sed רַע absolute malum, vt non tam de propensione, quam habituali & naturali malitia loquatur Dominus. 3. Nec habetur ab adolescentia nimirum cum ratio se exerere & actualiter peccare incipit, sed מִנְּעֻרָיו a primi hominis pueritia & infantia.

Notetur proinde. 1. Quod Deus loquatur de toto genere humano, & naturali eius constitutione. 2. Quod tum temporis nulli vixerint in terra homines alij, quam Noe iustus cum suis, vt ita de his etiam dictum sit, Figmentum cordis malum est. 3. Quod sermo sit non de motibus subitaneis appetitus sensitiui, sed de ipso corde cogitationes formante, de ipso figmento rationis quod Apostolus Rom. 8. vers. 6. appellat φρόνημα σαρκός, prudentiam carnis. 4. Quod figmentum istud non dicatur propendere ad malum, sed reipsa esse malum. 5. Et quidem non per assuefactionem vel exempla, sed a prima infantia, adeoque per generationem, & naturalem cordis corruptionem. 6. Quod malitia ista allegetur, vt causa irritans misericordiam diuinam, non quod adeo leuis & supplicio indigna sit, verum, quia non sponte contrahitur, sed per naturam statim in ipsa conceptione nobis ingeneratur. Ex quibus ita concludimus: Si cor humanum vniuersaliter corruptum est, adeò vt figmentum eius non modò ad malum inclinatur, sed teipsà malum sit à prima infantia, adeoque DEVM moueat ad miserendum, tanquam miseria sponte non contracta, sed nobis nescientibus implantata, sequitur præter actualia & voluntaria peccata aliud quoddam nobis inhærere, & ex natiuitate trahi.

Aliàs enim nulla argumento Iehouæ veritas aut consequentiæ ratio inesset. Prius autē indubitato verum est, ob infallibilem Mosis relationem. Quare & posterius concedi debet, non negari.

VII. Ex Psalmis. 1. Psal. 14. v. 2. 3. Dominus de cælo prospexit super filios hominum, vt videat, si est intelligens aut requirens Deum. Omnes declinauerunt, simul inutiles facti sunt: Non est qui faciat bonum, non est vsq; ad vnum. Quæ verba reperiuntur Psalm. 53. v. 3. 4. Accusat hîc Propheta malitiam hominum: quæritur, qualem? an tantùm actualem, an tantùm originalem? Dicimus vtramque quod probamus,

1. A declarationis pro exclusiua: Aduersarij enim nihil aliud proferunt, quàm Psaltem loqui de peccatis actualibus hominum. At verò lubenter hoc concedimus: neque causæ nostræ quicquam officit. Quæ enim sequela: Agitur de peccato actuali, Ergò non originali? Logicus, inquit, Ab inclusiua ad exclusiuam non valet consequentia, præsertim quando nullum ex vtriusq; membri inclusione absurdum sequitur. Hoc ergo ratione firma est euincendum, quod tantùm & vnicè de crassioribus sceleribus sermo sit. Illi quidem probare possunt facilè, Dauidem loqui de actualibus, & pręsertim vers. 4. 5. 6. quòd verò tantùm & versiculo etiam 2. 3. probare nunquam poterunt.

2. A Prophetæ scopo, qui est humani generis vitium & impietatem arguere: Quamuis enim de hostibus Israelis potissimùm loquatur vers. 6. & 7. tamen simul ad communem hominum corruptionem respicere vers. 2, 3. vniuersales particulæ euincunt, & nihil absurdi ex ex hac interpretatione sequitur; Hominis enim peccati reos agit. 1. Ab operibus, tum internis, vel ἀπισίᾳ, tùm externis, vel ἀδικίᾳ, versiculo primo. 2. à testimonio Dei, è cælo prospicientis super omnes filios hominum, v. 2. & tamen neminem justum aut bonum inuenientis. 3. Ab vniuersali corruptione, v. 3. quia omnes simul, nè vno quidem excepto, sunt inutiles ad bonum, promti verò ad malum. 4. A proprio conscientiæ testimonio, v. 4. quod ipsi hoc cognouerint, & tantæ deformitatis sibi benè conscij sint. Quæ omnia si diligenter ponderantur, ipsum originis vitium à Dauide simul hic spectari, facilè intelligitur. 3. Ab vniuersalitate aliquoties repetita, Regulam habemus: A clarâ litera discedēdum non esse, nisi euidens ratio cogat & analogia fidei. At verò hic estc̀ ara litera de vniuersali hominū cùm ἐκκλίσῃ vel declinatione, tùm ἀχρειόᾳ vel inutilitate, Nam 1. dicitur Deus prospexisse: super quos? An hostes Israëlis? Vel Ethnicos Dei ignaros? Vel Iudæos exorbitantes? Vel super vnam vrbem, aut nationem? Nihil horum in textu habetur. Super quos ergò? על־בני אדם super filios hominum in genere, hoc est, super totum genus humanum, nullo prorsus excepto: siquidem indefinita æquipollet vniuersali. 2. Additur finis prospectionis nimirum, an vel aliquis tantum inter filios hominum sit intelligens & quærens Deum, àdeoque vicissim vniuersalis est locutio. 3. Iam sequitur euentus; & quomodo cùm filijs hominum sit comparatum. כל סר Omnis recessit; Omnes, & quidem pariter rancidi & inutiles facti sunt: Non est faciens bonum, non est etiam vnus. Quis hic non videt, vniuersalem & quidem ter repetitam humani generis corruptionem notari? Et quę dabitur ratio cur vniuersalitatem istam restringere & limitare debeamus Vt enim prospectus Dei est generalis, super omnes filios hominum, (phrasis enim hæc absolutè & indefinitè posita, particularitatem non admittit) ita etiam corruptio, quam vidit in filiis hominum, vniversalis est.

4. Ab absurdo. Aut intelligenda est originalis malitia, aut absurda, imò falsa est Prophetæ sententia. Si enim declinationem & ἀχρειότητα actualem intelligas, dici certè nequit de omnibus, quòd declinauerint. Sunt enim aliqui inter filios hominum, qui præceptis Ethicis imbuti, à vitiis externis sibi cavent. Sunt pueri, sunt infantes, qui actualiter non peccant, & tamen filiis hominum declinantibus annumerantur. Vicissim, si bonum morale intelligas, quî dici poterit, ne vnum quidem esse inter filios hominum, qui faciat bonum? Nam ex medio gentilismi contraria exempla proferri possunt. Quare ἔκκλισις & ἀχρεία ad bonum sic exponenda est, vt omnibus, nullo excepto, conveniat, quod fieri nequit, nisi ipsam naturæ corruptionem, & tabem originalem intelligas.

5. Ab applicatione Apostolica, quæ extat Rom. 3. v. 9. Præcausati sumus, inquit Apostolus, Iudæos & Græcos omnes sub peccato esse, SICVT SCRIPTVM est, nimirùm Psal. 14. & 53. Non est iustus quisquam &c. Hic habemus interpretem infallibilem, quisnam sint ij, quos Psaltes declinasse & inutiles factos affirmat? nimirum non esse gentiles tantùm Epicureos, sed omnes, etiã virtutũ studiis deditos; non Iudæos modò aliquos, sed omnes nè vno quidem excepto: quod hoc fine demonstrat Apost. vt omne os obfirmetur, & reus fiat omnis mundus Deo, vers. 19. Non autem obtineret propositum suum, si Psal. quem citat, de solis extremè impijs & crassis peccatoribus foret exponendus. Nam Apostolus vult demonstrare, mundum, omnes homines, ne quidem infantibus seclusis, peccato immersos, & damnationis reos esse, ideóque non nisi per misericordiam Patris, & meritum Christi coram Deo iustificari, veluti tandem infert v. 23. Omnes, peccaverunt, & egent gloria Dei & c. 11. v. 32. Conclusit c. 11. v. 32. Conclusit Deus omnia sub incredulitatem, ut omnium misereretur. Ad hanc peccatorum vniuersalitatem probandam citat Psalmum 14. in quo habetur vniuersalis, omnes declinasse, & exclusiua, ne vnum supersse qui faciat bonum. Iam si particulariter verba hæc interpreteris, perit tota vis argumenti, eò quòd à particulari ad vniuersale, à quibusdam malis ad omnes malos non valeat consequentia. Perinde enim conclusisset Apostolus, ac si quis ita inferret: Quidam sunt docti. Ergo omnes sunt docti. Nam secundum adversarios, Psalmus hoc tantùm adfirmat: Quidam sunt mali & peccatores; Paulus verò inde colligit: Ergo omnes sunt mali & peccatores. Quis hic neruus, quæ ratio sequelæ? Quocirca, vt finiam, potest illa particularis Psalmi expositio defendi; nisi Apostolus, vel ipse potiùs Spiritus S. cum incitando ἀπαιδευσίας, tum in argumentando ἀσυλλογισίας insimuletur, quod vtrumque impium & blasphemum.


### Question III By what arguments is the corruption of human nature: VIII. But the things which are opposed to the contrary are light, and easy of solution

VIII. But the things which are opposed to the contrary are light, and easy of solution.

1. V. 1. The summary of the Psalm is proposed. The prophet, however, speaks only of gross sinners, who are called fools, and deny that there is a God. Wherefore the following verses also are to be explained concerning these alone.

Resp. This conclusion is opposed to the Apostolic citation. Therefore there will be a flaw in the argument. We say, therefore, that the summary of v. 1 is not always prefixed, nor do all the verses of one Psalm always speak of the same object. Granted, therefore, that David argues first against the actual and desperate malice of some, it does not follow from this, however, that original sin is not described in the following verses. For we repeat that logical principle: It is not permitted to argue from an inclusive to an exclusive. 2. Some rightly accommodate v. 1 to the vice of origin: For we are all by nature Nabals, which is the word in Hebrew; or fools, blind, stupid and having an intellect darkened by darkness, Eph 4. v. 18, while all naturally left to themselves deny God, or say there is no God, if not with their mouth, yet by their work, if not by words, yet by deeds: if not outwardly through open denial, yet inwardly through hidden doubt concerning God's providence, They profess that they know God, but in works they deny him.

2 David uses mere active verbs, to corrupt his way, to do an abominable work, not to seek, not to understand, not to do good. Wherefore he speaks only of actual sins.

Resp 1. And Paul uses active verbs: yet he does not wish actual and particular malice to be understood, but original and universal ἐπίκλισιν. 2. A Hebraism is known and frequent in the Scriptures, that by active verbs not only acts, but also habits and inherent qualities are denoted. The Prophet followed the same mode of speaking in describing the natural corruption of men:

3. V. 7. The restoration of the Jews from captivity is sought. Therefore in the preceding verses David spoke of the enemies of Israel. Resp. 1. Be it so: but does it immediately follow that he spoke only of enemies? The Apostle writes the contrary, the arguments placed above prove it, S. Gesn. in Psal 19. p. 140. does not interpret that petition corporally, but spiritually, namely concerning the mission of the Son, who is the salvation of Israel out of Zion, concerning liberation from the tyranny of the Devil and the servitude of sin, the gravity of which the Prophet had described a little before.

IV. 2. Psal. 19. v. 13. Who understands his faults? Cleanse me from my hidden ones. The LXX have: παραπτώματα τίς συνήσει, ἐκ τῶν κρυφίων μὲ καθάρισόν με. In the Hebrew it is מנסתרות, from hidden things, from the root סתר, he hid, he concealed, he covered: From which we infer thus, Actual sins are not hidden, nor every escape the understanding. David, however, speaks of a certain hidden sin: therefore this is not actual, but rather original, fixed in nature itself and so clandestine that it suggests depraved things to us even when we are unwilling and unaware. These are those hidden things, for the pardon and remission of which all the reborn are compelled to ask. You object that venial sins are noted. But all these are not hidden: And whence those in the reborn, if there is no beginning of origin? Not from the devil alone, because David calls them HIS hidden things. Not from one's own will, because the reborn does not want them, but hates them. Not from the indwelling Spirit, because He is the author of nothing but good things. It is necessary, therefore, that the corruption of nature itself be acknowledged, and the secret decay of powers, from which these hidden sins arise. Original sin is rightly called hidden, 1. because it is always troublesome to us by hidden habits and suggestions: 2. because it is not acknowledged by many, 3. because it inheres intimately, although it is not felt. For just as ferocity is innate to lion cubs, although it lies hidden: so is malice to infants, although it does not betray itself by manifest acts: And just as a youth in the Sacred language is called עָלֶם hidden, because he does not yet exercise any public administration: so sin inheres hiddenly in all, although neither they themselves, nor others, have noticed this. The simile of Augustine also pertains here: In the eye of a blind man, even at night, there is the defect of blindness, even if it does not appear; nor is there a distinction between the one seeing and the blind, unless light comes: so in a boy the defect does not appear to be present, until the time of more advanced age occurs.

X. 3. Psal. 51. v. 7. Behold I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins did my mother conceive me. In the Hebrew there exist two words, the former of which is חול, which signifies to be affected by the pains of childbirth, in the passive voice of the 2nd conjugation, to be begotten and formed: The latter is יחם which is very emphatic, and signifies to be heated or to grow warm, for which reason Arias Montanus translates, Behold I was formed in iniquity and in sin my mother warmed me, Tremellius has cherished me. The LXX rendered it thus: ἰδ’ ἐν ἀνομίαις συνειλήφθην, καὶ ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ἐκίσσησέ με ἡ μήτηρ με. Now κισσᾶν is the same as to suffer from pica, the disease of pregnant women, whence afterwards it is used for the very act of conceiving and bearing. noted here: 1. Of whom the Prophet speaks. 2. What he speaks.

As regards the first, there are those who think he is speaking not of his own sins, but of his parents', and of the excessive heat of lust, but falsely, which is proved 1. From the purpose of David, which was to confess his own guilt. Now it would not have been the act of a penitent and confessor, but rather of an ungrateful cuckoo, to accuse his parents by way of shifting the blame, and to prove himself innocent. 2. From the mode of concluding, He was imploring the mercy of God and seeking forgiveness of sin, as is evident from v. 1, 2. Among other arguments he also brings this one forward, because he was conceived and born in iniquity. The nerve of it is, Behold my God, sin was engendered in me while I was still an embryo without my consent, and since I have been carried away by its force, I pray that you forgive me the more readily. But if you interpret it concerning his parents, the whole force of the argument perishes. For what is the consequence: My parents sinned in my generation, but I did not draw sin from them. Therefore, forgive me my adultery and homicide? 3. From the emphasis of the words. For the word חוללתי I was formed, denotes not an active will to sin, but a passive act of being born; not the parents' intercourse, but the son's formation. So also the other word יחמתני regards not so much the mother warming, as the very warming of the embryo.

Now furthermore let us see what he speaks and confesses about himself? I was formed and born, he says, But how? In holiness, and with justice? By no means, but בְּעָוֹן in iniquity, so that in his first formation he drew sin from his parents, and although not yet were all the organs of mind and will fully developed, he himself was nevertheless infected and contaminated by iniquity. Then he says he cherished and warmed his mother: but how in sin, that is, when the mass of my nature first began to be cherished by the heat of the womb, even then I was in sins, even then that very mass was defiled by sin. For he does not wish to make the vegetative power of the mother, and the very power of warming, guilty of actual sins, since that is irrational and destitute of all intellect as well as assent: but he attends to the most profound corruption of origin, which he confesses he drew from a corrupt mother, and therefore expects a more ready pardon. Hence Ambrose in Apology of David, ch. 11: Rightly did David tearfully lament in himself the defilements of nature, because the stain began in man before life.

Thus therefore we conclude: by the sin in which he says he was conceived, David understands either actual or original sin. But not actual, 1. because by the act itself he could not yet sin in his mother's womb. 2. because it cannot be proven that the Prophet's mother always sinned as long as she cherished and warmed him. 3. because sin cannot properly be ascribed to the power of cherishing, of which he speaks, since it is irrational. 4. because he speaks in the singular of a certain sin, not in the plural of many actual ones. 5. what is this to David's person, even if the mother had sinned actually, if he himself had been conceived and born without sin? It follows therefore that original sin is understood, which was to be demonstrated.

I add a crowning argument taken from the contrary: John the Baptist had parents who were just and irreproachable, Luke 1, v. 6. Can I therefore say: John was conceived in justice, and his mother warmed him in irreproachable holiness? By no means, because everyone understands that this phrase denotes the holiness of the son, not of the parents, and therefore implies as if John were born just and holy in himself, which is fal-

stara. Now since the principle of contraries is the same, it follows that the phrase applied, to be conceived in sin, signifies not the actual transgressions of parents, but the innate corruption of children, and implies this, that all are born unjust and sinners.

XI. 4. Psalm 116, v. 11. I said in my excess. In Hebrew it is בְּחָפְזִי in my haste, Arias: or rather consternation, as Gesner explains. But what did the Prophet say? כָּל־הָאָדָם כֹּזֵב πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ψεύστης. Every man is a liar, which is repeated in Rom. 3, v. 4. The Prophet and the Apostle speak here universally of all men, not particularly of some. Jerome indeed restricts the universal, so that 'every' is the same as 'the greatest part,' but this is against the scope of the Apostle, who concludes from this that the whole world is subject to sin, v. 12 and following. But what is understood by 'liar'? Either the moral act of lying, or the physical proclivity to lie and deceive. Not the former, because not all men lie in act, Apoc. 14, v. 5. Therefore the latter. From which it follows that every man draws a corrupt nature from his parents, and consequently a proclivity to deceive and lie. For unless this is conceded, it will never be possible to demonstrate how every man is truly called a liar.

Jerome raises a scruple in his commentary on Ephesians 5:1. If every man is a liar, then so is he who says this. Wherefore when he says that every man is a liar, by that very fact he will be lying, and consequently the contrary will be true, that every man is truthful.

Latin:

VIII. Quæ verò in contrarium opponuntur; leuia sunt, & solutione facilia.

1. V. 1. Proponitur summa Psalmi. Loquitur autem propheta tantùm de crassis peccatoribus, qui vocantur insipientes, & negant esse Deum. Quare de his solis sequentes etiam versiculi exponendi.

Resp. Hæc conclusio aduersatur citationi Apostolicæ. Igitur vitiùm erit in argumento. Dicimus ergò, non semper summam v. 1. præmitti, nec semper de eodem objecto omnes vnius Psalmi versiculos loqui. Concesso igitur, Dauidem arguere primùm actualem nonnullorum & desperatam malitiam, hinc tamen versiculis sequentibus originalem haut describi nequaquam sequitur. Repetimus enim istud soixêον Logicum: Ab inclusiua ab exclusiuam non licet argumentari. 2. Nonnulli & vers. 1. ad originis vitium rectè accommodant: Omnes enim naturâ sumus Nabales, quæ vox est in Hebræo; vel insipientes, cæci, stupidi & habentes intellectum, tenebrib. obscuratum, Eph 4. v. 18 dum omnes naturaliter sibi relictinegant Deum, vel dicunt non esse Deum, si non ore, tamen opere, si non dictis, tamen factis: si non foris per apertam inficiationem, tamen intus per occultam dubitationem de Dei prouidentia, visione, gratia & similibus. Quo spectat illud Apostoli ad Tit. 2. v. ult. Confitentur se nosse Deum, factis autem negant.

2 Dauid meris vtitur verbis actiuis, corrumpere viam suam, facere opus abominandum, non quaerere, non intelligere, non facere bonum. Quare non nisi de peccatis actualibus sermonem facit.

Resp 1. Et Paulus verbis actiuis vtitur: neque tamen actualem & particularem malitiam, sed originalem & vniuersalem ἐπίκλισιν vult intellectam. 2. Notus & frequens est Hebraismus in Scripturis, , verbis actiuis non actus modo, sed habitus etiam & qualitates inhaerentes notari. Eundem loquendi modum secutus est Propheta in describenda naturali hominum corruptione:

3. V. 7. Petitur reductio Iudaeorum ex captiuitate. Ergo in praecedentibus Dauid de Israelis hostibus locutus est. Resp. 1. Sit ita: num autem mox sequitur, de solis hostibus locutum esse? Contrarium scribit Apostolus, euincunt argumenta superius posita, S. Gesn.in Psal 19. p. 140. petitionem istam non corporaliter interpretatur, sed spiritualiter, nimirum de missione Filij, qui est salus Israelis ex Sion, de liberatione a tyrannide Diaboli & seruitute peccati, cuius grauitatem Propheta paulo ante descripserat.

IV. 2. Psal. 19. v. 13. Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me. LXX. habent: παραπτώματα τίς συνήσει, ἐκ τῶν κρυφίων μὲ καθάρισόν με. In Hebraeo est מנסתרות, ab absconditis, a radice סתר, occuluit, occultavit, abscondit: Ex quo ita inferimus, Peccata actualia non sunt occulta, nec omnem intellectum subterfugiunt. David autem loquitur de peccato quodam occulto: igitur hoc actuale non est, sed potius originale, ipsi naturæ infixum & tam clancularium vt nobis nolentibus & nescientibus prava suggerat. Hæc sunt illa occulta, quorum veniam & remissionem omnes renati petere coguntur. Excipis, notari peccata venialia. Ast hæc omnia non sunt occulta: Et vnde illa in renato, si nullum originis initium? Non à solo diabolo, quia David occulta SVA nominat. Non à voluntate propria, quia renatus illa non vult, sed odit. Non à Spiritu inhabitante, quia hic non nisi bonorum author. Necesse igitur est, vt ipsius naturæ corruptio agnoscatur, & arcana virium tabes, vnde abscondita ista peccata oriantur. Rectè autem peccatum originis vocatur occultum, 1. quia occultis moribus & suggestionibus nobis semper molestum est: 2. quoniam à multis non agnoscitur, 3. quia intimè inhæret, quamvis non sentiatur. Sicut enim catulis leonum ferocia annata est, quamvis lateat: sic infantibus malitia, licèt manifestis actibus se non prodat: Et sicut iuvenis in Sacra lingua dicitur עָלֶם absconditus, quia publicam quandam administrationem nondum exercet: ita peccatum occultè omnibus inhæret, quanquam nec ipsi, nec alij hoc animadverterint. Huc quoque pertinet similitudo Augustini: In oculo cæci etiam de nocte cæcitatis vitium est, etsi non apparet; nec discernitur inter videntem & cæcum, nisi veniente luce: sic in puero vitium esse non apparet, donec ætatis provectioris tempus occurrat.

X. 3. Psal. 51. v. 7. Ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. In Hebræo extant duo vocabula, quorum prius est חול, quod significat doloribus partus affici, voce passivâ coniug. 2. genitum & formatum esse: Posterius est יחם quod valdè emphaticum, & significat, calefieri vel incalescere, quam ob causam Ariæmontanus vertit, Ecce in iniquitate formatus sum & in peccato calefecit, Tremellius habet fouit me mater mea. LXX. sic reddiderunt ἰδ’ ἐν ἀνομίαις συνειλήφθην, καὶ ἐν ἁμαρτίαις ἐκίσσησέ με ἡ μήτηρ με. Est autem κισσᾶν idem quod laborare picâ, morbo prægnantium, vnde post modum pro ipso concipiendi & pariendi actu ponitur. Sunt autem duo potissimùm hîc notanda: 1. De quo loquatur Propheta. 2. Quid loquatur.

Primum quod spectat, sunt, qui ipsum non de proprijs, sed parentum peccatis, & nimio libidinis æstu verba facere existimant, sed falsò, quo probatur 1. A scopo Dauidis qui erat culpam propriam confiteri. Iam verò non fuisset pœnitentis & confitentis, sed potiùs ingrati cuculi, per μετάςασιν accusare parentes, atque se insontem probare. 2. A modo concludendi, Implorabat misericordiam Dei & petebat veniam peccati, vti patet ex v. 1. 2. Inter argumenta alia & hoc adducit, quia in iniquitate sit conceptus & genitus. Neruus est, Ecce mi Deus, peccatum mihi adhuc embryoni sine consensu meo ingeneratum est, à cuius impetu cum abreptus fuerim, eo promptiùs condones oro. Sin autem de parentibus interpreteris, vis argumenti tota perit. Quæ enim consequentia: Parentes peccauerunt in mei generatione, ego autem ex ijs peccatum non traxi. Ergo adulterium & homicidium mihi remittas? 3. Ab emphasi vocabulorum. Nam vox חוללתי formatus sum, non ἐνεργητικὴν peccandi voluntatem, sed παθητικὴν nascendi actum; non parentum concubitum, sed filij efformationem denotat. Sic etiam alterum verbum יחמתני non tam matrem calefacientem, quam ipsam embryonis calefactionem respicit.

Nunc porrò videamus quid de seipso loquatur & fateatur? Formatus & natus sum, inquit, Quomodo autem? Num in sanctitate, & cum justitia? Neutiquam, sed בְּעָוֹן in iniquitate adeo vt in prima formatione peccatum ex parentibus hauserit, & licet nondum planè omnia mentis & voluntatis organa fuerint elaborata, ipse tamen iniquitate infectus & contaminatus fuerit. Deinde ait, matrem se fouisse & calefecisse: ast quomodo בחטא in peccato i. e. cum massa meæ naturæ primùm inciperet foveri calore matricis, jam tùm eram in peccatis, jam tùm illa ipsa massa peccato erat inquinata. Non n. τὸ φυτικὸν matris, & ipsam calefaciendi δυναμιν peccatorum actualium vult ream agere, cum illa sit ἄλογος, omnique vt intellectu sic assensu destituta: sed profundissimam originis corruptionem attendit quam se ex corrupta matre traxisse fatetur, ideoque veniam promtiorem expectat. Hinc Ambr. in Apol. Dauid c. 11. Meritò Dauid flebiliter deplorauit in seipso inquinamenta naturæ, quod prius inciperet in homine macula, quàm vita.

Sic ergo concludimus: Dauid per peccatum, in quo se conceptum ait, aut actuale intelligit, aut originale. Atqui non actuale, 1. quia ipso actu nondum peccare potuit in vtero matris. 2. quia probari nequit, matrem Prophetæ semper peccasse, quamdiu ipsum fouit & calefecit. 3. quia potentiæ fouendi, de qua loquitur, cùm irrationalis sit, peccatum propriè adscribi nequit. 4. quia loquitur in singulari de peccato certo, non in plurali de multis actualibus. 5. quid hoc ad Dauidis personam, vt maximè mater peccâsset actualiter, si ipse fuisset sine peccato conceptus & editus? Sequitur ergò, originale intelligi, id quod fuit demonstrandum,
