Colophonis locorationem addo ex contrario, desumtam: Iohannes Baptista parentes habuit justos & irreprehensibiles, Luc. 1. v. 6. Num a. propterea possum dicere; Iohannes conceptus est in justitia, & mater calefecit eum in sanctitate irreprehensibili? Neutiquam, quia quiuis intelligit phrasin istam sanctitatem filij, non parentum notare, adeoque hoc importare, ac si Iohannes in se justus & sanctus esset genitus, quod fal-

stara. Iam cum contrariorum eadem sit ratio, sequitur & phrasin appositam, concipi in peccato, non actualia parentum delicta, sed natiuum filiorum corruptionem significare, & hoc innuere, quòd omnes iniusti & peccatores nascantur.

XI. 4. Psalm. 116. v. 11. Ego dixi in excessu meo. In Hebr. est בְּחָפְזִי in festinatione meâ, Ariæm: vel potiùs consternatione, vt exponit Gesnerus. Quid verò dixit Propheta? כָּל־הָאָדָם כֹּזֵב πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ψεύστης. Omnis homo mendax, quod repetitur Rom, 3. v. 4. Loquitur hic Propheta & Apostolus vniuersaliter de omnibus hominibus, non particulariter de aliquibus. Hieronymus quidem restringit vniuersalens, vt omnis idem sit, quòd maxima pars, verùm est hoc contra scopum Apostoli, qui totum mundum peccato subiacere hinc concludit, v. 12. & sequentibus. Quid autem intelligitur per mendacem? Aut Fihicus mentiendi actus, aut Physica mentiendi & fallendi procliuïtas. Non ille, quia non omnes homines mentiuntur actu, Apoc. 14. v. 5. Ergò hæc. Ex quo sequitur, omnem hominem ex parentibus trahere naturam corruptam, adeoque procliuitatem ad fallendum & mentiendum. Nisi enim hoc concedatur, nunquam demonstrari poterit, quomodo omnis homo verè dicatur mendax.

Hieronymus objicit scrupulum in comm. super 5. 1. ad Ephes. Si omnis homo mendax est, igitur & ille, qui hoc loquitur. Quare cùm ait, omnem hominem esse mendacem, eo ipso mentietur, & per consequens verum erit contrarium, omnem hominem esse veracem.


### Question III By what arguments is the corruption of human nature: But we answer 1. That every man is a liar, but does not always lie

But we answer 1. That every man is a liar, but does not always lie. The former denotes the depravation and propensity of nature, the latter denotes the act. 2. These are not the words of a man, but rather of the Holy Spirit speaking through a man. They are not brought forth from the suggestion of the flesh, but from the revelation of God, not by an ordinary man, but by a Prophet of God and an Apostle of Christ.

XII. From the Prophets 1. Job 14. vers. 4. Who can make clean from an unclean seed conceived? Is it not thou, who alone art? So indeed the Vulgate version reads, but corruptly. In the Hebrew it is: Who shall give clean from unclean? Not one. Whence Luther: Who will find a clean one among those where no one is clean? The LXX are a little different: For who shall be clean from filth, but no one, even if his life upon the earth is but one day, which Augustine rendered thus: No one is clean from filth, not even the infant whose life is one day upon the earth. Which passage describes original sin and the vice of nature so clearly that the adversaries find nothing solid that they can object. For thus we conclude: Job understands filth either external to the body or internal to the soul. Not of the body, 1. because he speaks of a singular and certain hidden uncleanness, but that our bodies are contaminated is nothing singular. 2. because he notes such filth from which no man can be purged and freed by man in this life. Hence he says: Who shall give clean? Not one. But indeed the filth of the body can be washed and cleaned. 3. because the discourse is about such impurity on account of which we are brought into the judgment of God. For thus he says in verse 3: And dost thou open thine eyes upon such a one? And wilt thou bring me into judgment with thee? From these therefore we conclude that the internal filth of the soul is understood by Job. But what kind? Only actual ones? By no means. For 1. He speaks so universally that he does not except even one man, and thus not even an infant of one day, as the LXX have it, upon whom, however, actual sins do not fall. And it is certain from the preceding verses that Job here expresses and deplores the universal weakness of the whole human race, belonging to all, with not one excepted. 2. He treats of filth perpetually adhering. But this cannot be said of actual sins. For not all adults always sin actually, and after those have been committed, they pass away, nor does a certain absolute uncleanness remain from them, but only guilt or obligation to punishment. 3. He speaks of filth not contracted by our own fault but derived to us from our parents. For thus the words hold: Who will give a clean מטמא from an unclean or from an unclean one? Where the expression is elliptical, because טמא is a participial noun and adjective, requiring some substantive next to it. The first origin of man is noted, and therefore there must be understood either the seed, from which we are begotten, or the parent, from whom we are begotten, so that the sense may be: Not even one can be given clean from sin. What is the reason? Because all are born from an unclean and sin-infected seed or parent. From which it is most manifest that Job does not refer to personal or actual sins, but to the original stain of nature, which is propagated in a continuous tract to descendants from unclean parents. 4. He speaks of incurable impurity. For he brings this forward in place of an excuse and argument, that God ought not to contend with him in judgment nor demand supreme purity, since no mortal can avoid the filth of the soul, inasmuch as all are born unclean from the unclean. But this is false regarding personal and merely actual sins, since everyone, not abusing free will, can avoid those, as the adversaries do not deny. Since all these things are so, we conclude that Job is speaking not of the impurity of the body, but of souls, and that not actual, but original and innate.

XIII. 2. Isaiah 48. v. 8. I know that dealing treacherously you will deal treacherously and I have called you a transgressor from the WOMB. Hence the orthodox Fathers argue thus for the natural stain: If the people of Israel were truly called and were a transgressor immediately in the womb, and as soon as they proceeded from the womb, it follows that not all sins are actual, but a certain natural vice must be conceded, in which we are conceived, with which we are born, and on account of which we can be truly and in reality called transgressors from the womb. But the former is certain, by the words of the passage cited. Therefore the latter is also.

XIV. 3. Jeremiah 17. v. 9. The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable, who shall know it? In the Hebrew it is עקב הלב מלב ואנש Arias Montanus translates, supplanting heart above all things, and itself anxious. Tremellius: The heart itself is deceitful above all things, and deadly, Luth. It is the heart a defiant and desperate thing. Two things, however, are to be noted here: 1. Of whom the Prophet speaks. 2. What he speaks.

I. He does not speak of hypocrites alone or the manifestly wicked, but indefinitely of the human heart and therefore of all men. For he had commanded in verse 5 and following that one must trust in God alone, and in no man. Soon in verse 9 he adds the reason, because the heart of man is depraved and supplanting. Hence I infer: A universal consequent presupposes a universal antecedent. But the Prophet concludes universally, that no man is to be trusted. Therefore, both the medium and the antecedent must be universal, namely, because the heart of all men, with none excepted, is depraved. And Jeremiah speaks so generally that he does not even except himself from that depravity, and therefore in verse 14 he prays: Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed.

II. He says three things about the human heart; 1. that it is עקב deceitful and perverse, from the root עקב which signifies to supplant, to tread with the soles of the feet, and to deceive. Chemnitius in Locis, m. p. 253, notes that just as a path that is trodden has two disadvantages, since first it loses its smoothness, and afterwards becomes callous and rough; so by that word it is indicated that the heart of man is deprived of its original rectitude, and in its place depravity and hardness have succeeded. 2. that it is אנש miserable, vehemently diseased and incurable. For in this sense that word is taken in Jer. 15 v. 18, Mic. 1 v. 9. Therefore that most unhappy and indelible depravity of the human heart is noted. 3. He adds the word מכל above all; by which the highest and extreme corruption is indicated, so that the human heart, left to itself, is naturally depraved, at all times, in every business, and above all things, so that no one can sufficiently perceive or understand it, except God alone, the καρδιογνώστης. Thus, therefore, all the words by nature regarding vice, and exaggerate the depravity of the human mind. Nor indeed can it be excepted that only actual malice is being noted. For 1. The Prophet speaks of a common and universal evil, whereas actual and personal sins are not equally common to all. 2. He speaks of a malice that is inevitable and indelible in this mortality, which cannot be said of personal ones. 3. The force of the argument would perish. For although the heart of some may be small, yet if that φαυλότης is not bitter, and some are found whose heart also is not perverse, it cannot be concluded from this means to remove all confidence universally.

XV. And these were the principal testimonies of the Old Testament concerning original sin: now we shall also run through the New, and we shall bring forward a few things from the writings of the Evangelists and a few from the epistles that pertain to our purpose.

XVI. From the Evangelists, 1. Matt. 7. verse 18. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit, neither can a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. The Savior warns there about avoiding false prophets, and prescribes a rule by which they are to be known, namely from their fruits. He adds the cause, taken from a general axiom, because a corrupt tree cannot bring forth good fruits. Which saying the Fathers not inappropriately applied to original sin. For this is that vicious root, from which actual sins as poisonous branches are born. Therefore, just as effects testify of the cause, so do actual vices testify of original sin. From which we conclude thus: Where there are evil fruits, there a corrupt tree precedes. In men there are perpetually evil fruits, such as the vicious suggestions of the heart and depraved actions, so much so that it is sometimes observed even in little children, since they are always carried toward what is forbidden and do not wish to obey. Therefore a corrupt tree precedes, which can be nothing other than original corruption and the sin of nature.

To this may be referred also that of the Saviour in Matt. 12, v. 34: How can you speak good things, when you are evil? For there is nothing absurd in explaining this of original and actual malice at the same time. Thus in Matt. 15, v. 19 it is said: Out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, certainly not as it is a substance, but as it is corrupted and depraved by nature and habits.

XVII. John 1, v. 29. Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου, that sin of the world. The Baptist speaks not in the plural of many sins, but in the singular of a certain sin, which he names the sin of the world, from which it follows that he is looking at that common vice of nature which entered into this world through Adam and passed through the whole of posterity. For if it is the sin of the world, infants will not lack it either, since they too are unclean, and it is for the sake of redeeming them from sin that the Saviour came.

XIIX. John 3, v. 5, 6. Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven, because that which is born of the flesh is flesh. Two arguments lie hidden here. 1. From the necessity of παλιγγενεσίας or renewal. If all men born must be renewed, and are not saved unless they are renewed, then certainly all are born with sin, since this alone excludes one from the kingdom of heaven. 2. From the word σαρκὸς or flesh. He does not here denote the bare substance of man, but at the same time connotes the natural corruption of the substance. For the Saviour gives the reason why all need renewal, namely because they are born flesh of flesh, where if you exclude the sin of nature and attend only to nature, there is no force in the argument. For even in the state of integrity man would have been born of man, but he would not have had need of ἀνακαινώσεως, nor would it be said correctly that flesh born of flesh was then begotten: from which it appears that by the name of σαρκὸς, not only is substance denoted, but the sin of origin is simultaneously involved, which in John 1, v. 13 is

Latin:

Sed respondemus 1. Omnem hominem esse mendacem, non verò semper mentiri. Illud naturæ deprauationem & propensionem, hoc actum denotat. 2. Non sunt ea verba hominis, sed potius Spiritus sancti per hominem loquentis. Non proferuntur ex carnis suggestione, sed Dei reuelatione, non ab homine vulgari, sed Propheta Dei & Apostolo Christi.

XII. Ex Prophetis 1. Iob. 14. vers. 4. Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? nonnè tu, qui solus es? Ita quidem legit vulgata versio, sed vitiosè. In Heb. est; Quis dabit mundum de inmundo? Ne vnus. Vnde Lutherus: Wer wil einen reinen finden/bey denen/da keiner rein ist? Paulò aliter LXX. Τίς γὰρ καθαρὸς ἔσται ἀπὸ ῥύπε, ἀλλ’ ὀὐδεὶς, ἐὰν καὶ μία ἡμέρα ὁ βίος αὐτῶ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, quod Augustinus ita reddidit; Nemo mundus à sorde, nec infans cuius est vnius diei vita super terram. Qui locus tàm clarè peccatum originis & naturæ vitium describit, vt nihil solidi inueniant aduersarij, quod excipere queant. Sic enim colligimus: Intelligit Iobus sordes vel externas corporis vel internas animi. Non corporis, 1. quia de singulari & occultâ quâdam immundicie loquitur, Corpora verò nostra contaminari, nihil singulare est. 2. quia tales sordes notat, à quibus nemo hominum ab homine in hac vitâ purgari & liberari potest. Hinc ait: Quis dabit mundum? Ne vnus. At verò sordes corporis ablui & mundari possunt. 3. quia sermo est de tali impuritate, ob quam in iudicium Dei adducimur. Ita enim inquit vers. 3. Etiam super hunc aperuisti oculos tuos? Et me adduces in iudicium tecum? Ex his ergò concludimus, interiores animi sordes à Iobo intelligi. At quales? Num tantùm actuales? Neutiquam. Nam 1. Adeò vniuersaliter loquitur, vt nè vnum quidem hominem, adeoque nec infantem vnius diei excipiat, vt habent LXX. in quos tamen actualia peccata non cadunt. Et certum est ex versiculis præcedentibus, Iobum hî̂c vniuersalem totius generis humani imbecillitatem omnibus, ne vno excepto, competentem exprimere & deplorare. 2. Agit de sordibus perpetuò adhærentibus. Ast hoc de actualibus peccatis dici nequit. Non enim omnes adulti semper peccant actualiter, & postquam illa commissa sunt, transeunt, neque immundicies quædam absoluta de ijs manet reliqua, sed tantùm reatus vel obligatio ad pœnam. 3. Loquitur de sordibus, non propriâ culpâ contractis sed ex parentibus in nos deriuatis. Sic enim habent verba: Quis dabit mundum מטמא de immundo vel ex immundo? Vbi elliptica est locutio, quia טמא est participiale nomen & adiectiuum, requirens iuxta se aliquod substantiuum, Notatur autem prima hominis origo, adeóq; subintelligi debet vel semen, ex quo gignimur, vel parens, à quo gignimur, vt sit sensus: Non potest vel vnus dari à peccato mundus. Quæ ratio? Quia omnes ex immundo & peccatis infecto semine aut parente nascuntur, Ex quo manifestissimum est, Iobum non respicere peccata personalia vel actualia, sed originalem naturæ labem, quæ in posteros continuato tractu à parentibus immundis propagatur. 4. Loquitur de impuritate incurabili. Nam hoc excusationis & argumenti loco profert, quòd Deus secum adeò non debeat contendere in iudicio nec puritatem summam exigere, cùm nemo mortalium sordes animæ queat euitare, siquidem omnes nascantur immundi ex immundis. Falsum verò hoc est de peccatis personalibus & merè actualibus, cùm illa, non diffitentibus aduersarijs, vnusquisque libero arbitrio, non abutens, euitare possit. Quæ omnia cùm ita se habeant Iobum non de corporis, sed animarum immundicie, illaque non actuali, sed originali & ingenirata loqui concludimus.

XIII. 2. Esai. 48. v. 8. Scio quia præuaricans præuaricaberis & transgressorem ex VTERO vocauite. Hinc pro naturali tabe sic argumentantur orthodoxi Patres: Si populus Israël statim in vtero, & quam primùm progrediebatur ex vtero, transgressor verè vocatus est & fuit, sequitur, non omnia peccata esse actualia, sed concedendum naturale quoddam vitium, in quo concipiamur, cum quo nascamur, & propter quod transgressores ex vtero verè & reipsâ vocari possimus. Atqui prius est certum, vĥ dicti allegati. Ergò & posterius.

XIV. 3. Ierem. 17. v. 9. Prauum est cor hominis & inscrutabile, quis cognoscet illud? In Hebræo est עקב הלב מלב ואנש Arias montanus vertit, supplantauum cor pre omnibus, & anxium ipsum. Tremellius: Fraudulentum cor ipsum super omnia, & mortiferum est, Luth. Es ist das Hertz ein trotzig vnnd verzagt ding. Duo autem & hic notanda: 1. De quo loquatur Propheta. 2. Quid loquatur.

I. Non agit de solis hypocritis aut manifeste sceleratis, sed indefinite de corde humano adeoque omnibus hominibus Praeceperat enim vers. 5. & seqq. soli Deo, nulli homini confidendum esse, Mox vers. 9. subijcit causam, quia cor hominis sit prauum & supplantatiuum. Hinc infero: Vniuersale consequens praesupponit vniuersale antecedens. Concludit autem Propheta vniuersaliter, Nulli homini fidendum esse. Ergo & medium & antecedens vniuersale sit oportet, nempe, quia cor omnium hominum, nullo excepto sit prauum. Adeo vero generaliter loquitur Ieremias, vt ne seipsum quidem ab illa prauitate excipiat, ideoque vers. 14. orat. Sana me Domine, & sanabor.

II. Tria vero de corde humano dicit; 1. quod sit עקב fraudulentum & peruersum, a rad. עקב quae significat supplantare, plantis pedum calcare & decipere. Chemnitius in Locis, m. p. 253. annotat, quod sicut via quae calcatur duo habet incommoda, siquidem primum planiciem amittit, & post callosa fit & aspera; sic voce illa innuatur, cor hominis prima rectitudine priuatum esse, & in eius locum prauitate & duritiem successisse. 2. quod sit אנש miserum, vehementer morbidum & insanabile. Hoc enim sensu vox illa sumitur Ier. 15 v. 18. Mich. 1. v. 9. Notatur ergo illa infelicissima & indelebilis humani cordis deprauatio. 3. Addit vocabulum מכל super omnia; quo summa & extrema labes indicatur, adeo, vt cor humanum sibi relictum, naturaliter prauum sit, omni tempore, in omni negotio, & super omnia, vt nemo satis percipere aut intelligere possit, nisi solus καρδιογνώστης Deus, Sic igitur omnia vocabula nature vitium, & humanæ mentis prauitatem exaggerant. Neque verò excipi potest, actualem tantùm malitiam notari. Nam 1. Propheta loquitur de malo communi & vniuersali, Actualia verò & personalia peccata non sunt ex æquo omnibus communia. 2. Loquitur de malitia ineuitabili & indelebili in hac mortalitate, id quod de personalibus dici nequit. 3. Periret vis argumenti. Licèt enim quorundam cor paruum sit, tamen si φαυλότης ista non sit amara, & reperiantur aliqui, quorum cor quóq non sit peruersum, vniuersaliter ad remouendam omnem fiduciam, ex isto medio concludi non potest.

XV. Et hæc fuerunt præcipua Testamenti Veteris de malo originali testimonia: nunc etiã Nov v m percurremus & parum ex Euangelistarum scriptis parum ex epistolis dicta quædam ad institutum facientia proferemus.

XVI. Ex Evangelistis, 1. Matth. 7. vers. 18. Non potest arbor bona malos fructus facere, neque arbor mala bonos fructus facere. Monet ibi Saluator de cauendis Pseudo prophetis, & præscribit regulam, vnde sint cognoscendi, nimirum ex fructibus. Addit causam à generali axiomate petitam, quia arbor mala nequeat proferre fructus bonos. Quod dictum non incommodè Patres applicuerunt ad peccatum originis. Hæc enim est illa vitiosa radix, ex qua peccata actualia ceu venenati rami enascuntur. Vt ergò effectus de causa, sic actualia vitia de originali testantur. Ex quo ita concludimus: Vbi sunt mali fructus, ibi præcedit mala arbor. In hominibus perpetuò sunt mali fructus, vt vitiosæ cordis suggestiones, & prauæ actiones, adeò vt in puerulis etiam quandoque conspiciatur, siquidem in vetitum semper feruntur, & obedire nolunt. Ergo præcedit mala arbor, quæ esse alia non potest, quàm originalis corruptio & peccatum naturæ.

Huic referri potest & illud Saluatoris Matth. 12. v. 34. Quomodo potestis bona loqui, cùm sitis mali? Nihil enim absurdi est, de originali & actuali malitia simul hoc exponere. Sic Matth. 15. v. 19. dicitur: Ex corde exeunt cogitationes malæ, non certè quâ substantia est sed qua per naturam & mores corruptum atque deprauatum est.

XVII. 2. Ioh. 1. v. 29. Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου, peccatum illud mundi. Loquitur Baptista non in plurali de peccatis multis, sed in singulari de peccato certo, quod nominat peccatum mundi, ex quo sequitur, illum respicere ad istud commune vitium naturæ, quod per Adamum intrauit in hunc mundum, & pertransijt totam posteritatem. Si enim peccatum mundi est, nec infantes eo carebunt, quoniam & hi immundi sunt, & propter hos â peccato redimendos venit Saluator.

XIIX. 3. Ioh. 3. v. 5. 6. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non intrabit in regnum cælorum, quia quod natum est ex carne, caro est. Duo hîc argumenta latent. 1. A necessitate παλιγγενεσίας vel renouationis. Si omnes nati hominum renouari debent, nec saluantur nisi renouentur, tunc vtique omnes nascentur cum peccato, siquidem hoc vnum à regno cælorum excludit. 2. A vocabulo σαρκὸς vel carnis. Non hic notat nudam hominis substantiam, sed vnâ connotat naturalem substantiæ corruptionem. Reddit n. Saluator causam, cur omnes egeant renouatione, nimirum quia nascantur caro de carne, vbi si naturæ peccatum secludas & naturam solam attendas, nulla vis argumento inest. Nam & in statu integritatis homo de homine natus fuisset, sed ἀνακαινώσεως opus non habuisset, neque diceretur rectè carnem de carne tum prognatam fuisse: Ex quo apparet, σαρκὸς nomine, non substantiam modò notari, sed simul inuolui peccatum originis, quòd Iohan. 1. v. 13. nomi-


### Question III By what arguments is the corruption of human nature: called θέλημα σαρκὸς [the will of the flesh], which by nature hinders us from…

called θέλημα σαρκὸς [the will of the flesh], which by nature hinders us from being procreated as children of God by our parents. Rom 8. v. 6. φρόνημα σαρκὸς [mind of the flesh], which wages an implacable war against the φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος [mind of the Spirit]. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit. Galat. 5. v. 17.

From the same chapter 3, Augustine cites verse 36: 'He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him.' Observe, indeed, that it is not said, 'The wrath of God will come,' but 'remains upon him,' because it is already there beforehand, and remains in all the children of Adam, unless it is taken away through Christ.

XIX. FROM THE APOSTLE PAUL 1. Rom. 5. v. 12. Through one man sin entered into the world and death through sin, and so death passed into all men, in whom all have sinned; for the fuller understanding of which passage six things come to be explained.

1. What is understood by sin, whether actual and original? We say both: Actual, as the cause; original, as the effect. For three things concur in the Adamic sin: 1. Actual guilt. 2. Legal liability. 3. Natural depravity. These all entered into the world at once, and into all of Adam's descendants, who are therefore miserable for a threefold reason: 1. By participation in actual guilt. For they sinned in Adam, because they were in his loins. 2. By imputation of legal liability, because the first man stood and fell with the condition of imputing it to his children. 3. By propagation of natural depravity, which diffuses itself into all and each, with no one excepted. These are those three misfortunes which are denoted by sin entering.

2. How did sin enter? The Apostle indicates this with the Greek word εἰσῆλθε: for this denotes either a clandestine creeping in or an impetuous breaking in. Therefore, when sin is said to have entered, both modes can be understood; the former, however, is more appropriate, because sin crept in through the deceits of the Devil.

3. Into whom did it enter? Into the world, says the Apostle. Where is not understood the machine of the world, which is inanimate and in itself incapable of sin, but man the μικρόκοσμος, and thus all the descendants of Adam, such as they are born by nature, who are called the world on account of worldly and malignant pursuits.

4. What is the death that passes through? Ambrose understands only bodily death; Socinus only spiritual; We understand all that which God had threatened in Gen. 2. v. 12, namely 1. bodily death or death of nature. 2. spiritual death or death of grace. 3. eternal death or death of glory. 4. the forerunners of death, such as diseases, and the consequences, such as putrefaction and corruption. This death therefore entered through sin, as an effect with its cause, and a shadow with its body, and that 1. because of the truth of the threat. 2. because of the infinite justice of God. 3. because of the law and natural equity.

5. What do the particles ἐφ᾽ ᾧ denote? The Vulgate has 'in quo' (in whom), so that it may refer to Adam, in whom the descendants sinned, and Augustine defends this in book 6 against Julian, chapter 12. For Pelagius explained it causally, so that it is used for 'because' or 'since'. However, it is the same, and the matter comes to the same result, whether the relative or the causal interpretation is assumed: For in both cases it is implied that all have sinned, because all are subject to death. Nor are there lacking examples where ἐφ᾽ ᾧ signifies the rendering of a cause. Hence Luther translates: Death has passed through to all men, because they have all sinned.

6. What does it mean to sin? The Pelagians, since it is an active verb, think that only actual sins are denoted, but falsely. For in general it signifies any ἁμαρτίαν (sin), whether it be an act or a habit: Indeed, the Apostle himself in verse 19 explains it by 'being constituted a sinner', when he says: By the disobedience of one man many were constituted sinners. To sin here, therefore, is nothing other than to become and to be a sinner.

XX. Now these things being presupposed, we shall extract arguments from the text for original sin, and we shall show against the Pelagians that the Apostle is speaking not of the imitation of sin, but of its propagation.

1. If to sin in Adam were to imitate Adam, it could not be said that sin entered through Adam. For those who sin do not always sin because of Adam's example, since many have heard nothing of Adam. Who, therefore, will imitate a thing that is clearly unknown? Who will snatch an occasion for sinning from a transgression that is entirely unknown?

2. The Apostle speaks in the singular number: Sin entered, Sin passed through, etc. But if he had wished to denote actual sins, he would have used the plural number. For there are many of those, especially when the whole world is being discussed. But since he uses the singular, it is concluded that he is speaking of one certain and natural vice, of course. The rule of the theologians points to this: Sin in the singular number, especially with the article, and in the Pauline writings, signifies that root and head of sin, namely original corruption,

3. The limit of sin is the world, from which it follows that all men, with no one excepted, have been contaminated by sin. For the world is used synecdochically for all who live in the world: and although in verse 19 it is said that many were constituted sinners, the particle of multitude is nevertheless equivalent to a universal, as is evident from the ὑποδόχη, and from verses 12 and 13, where all are expressly named.

4. Where death passed, there also sin passed; because death entered through sin. But death passed into all of Adam's descendants, even into infants themselves, who die no less than adults. Therefore, sin also did. But infants do not sin actually. Wherefore, besides actual sins, it must be granted that there is original sin, which little ones draw from their parents, and on account of which they are subject to death. Nor is the exception valid that the death of the body is drawn, not that of the soul, that is, sin. For the Lord threatened this also, and the death of the body is the death of sin (of which it is the wages, Rom. 6, last verse)

presupposes: For if we had no sin, we would not die. Whence Augustine, book 13 of The City of God, chapter 15, says: It is agreed among Christians holding the Catholic faith, that even this death of the body was inflicted upon us not by the law of nature, but by the merit of sin.

5. Actual sins, especially προαιρετικὰ (voluntary), are not hereditary, nor do they pass through to all men, nor are they common. But the sin of which Paul speaks here is hereditary and common, which together with death passed through to all. Therefore it is not actual, but rather natural and original.

6. Just as death entered into the world, so also did sin, because the Apostle joins both. But death or the guilt of death did not enter through imitation, but through propagation. Therefore, so also did sin.

7. As sin is the cause of death, so Adam is the cause of sin entering into this world. For in turn both are coupled in the text in an equal manner. But sin is the cause of death not through imitation, but through generation, James 1; v. 15. Therefore Adam is also the cause of sin not through imitation, but through generation.

8. In v. 14 it is said that death reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression: but this was actual. Therefore the sin dissimilar to this is not actual. There are, however, those who think that that dissimilarity is situated not in the species, but in the mode of sin, and that it is noted that those also died to whom, as to Adam, the law was not proposed until Moses the νομοθέτης (lawgiver) came, which we leave in doubt.

9. Adam is called the type of the one to come, that is, of Christ, v. 14. Wherefore, just as Christ diffuses the lost righteousness not by imitation, but by regeneration, so Adam transmitted sin not by imitation, but by generation. Here is the μόλυσις (defilement) of disobedience from man to man by means of natural γενέσει (generation): there is the μετάδοσις (communication) of righteousness from Christ into men, by means of παλιγγενεσίᾳ [regeneration] from water and Spirit: 10. August. l. 1. de pec. mer & remiss. concludes thus: If it had been proposed by the Apostle that sin was brought in by the first sinner or by the imitation of sin, then he would rather have said by the example of Christ, John 8. v. 41. 42. that sin entered into the world through an Angel; since he was the first to sin. 11. Unless this passage is explained concerning propagation; no reason can be given why it is said that sin entered through one man, namely Adam, and not rather through Eve, seeing that she sinned before Adam, and with her sinning, sin began to be in the world: Therefore, it is not understood as actual sin, which began through Eve, but original [sin], which was propagated through Adam:

XXI. 2. 2. Cor. 5. v. 15. If one died for all, then all are dead, and Christ died for all. Hence the cause of the Lord's death is established as the death of all which preceded it. For Christ died for all for this reason, because all were previously dead. But by what death? It cannot be understood as bodily [death] alone, because Christ does not redeem us from this alone: nor did that precede in act. Therefore, the death of the soul or rather sin is noted, just as life, which is opposed to this death in the same verse, signifies not life for the body, but especially for the soul:

XXII. 3. Eph. 2. v. 5. We were by nature children of wrath, even as others. Hence we gather: If we are children of wrath φύσει or by nature, then not μιμήσει or by imitation: Therefore we do not contract sins and guilt first ourselves, but we draw them from our parents and through birth. For the word (φύσει) usually signifies those things which are naturally inherent, and belong to us by nature, since it is opposed to τῷ ἔθει [to custom] or imitation, in which sense it is taken, Rom. 2. v. 14. Gal. 2. v. 15. Nor can it be said that Paul speaks only of the Gentiles, since he includes himself and other Jews, and speaks universally of all, as to what kind they were φύσει;

doubtless children of wrath, although now through renewal they have been made children of grace. And certainly this passage is so clear that the adversaries can oppose nothing to it except rotten cavils.

XXIII. And up to this point I have reviewed the testimonies of the Scriptures, and indeed somewhat at length, lest these be immediately rejected as if weak on account of any small exception, or lest arguments brought forth by the Elders with such great consensus be rashly and without any reason abandoned; however, all these can be included in certain orders or classes. For 1. some speak of the loss of the image by creation, as Gen. 5, v. 3. 2. some describe this evil privatively, as Psalm 14, v. 2 and following. 3. some positively, as Gen. 6, v. 5, ch. 8, v. 22. 4. some speak of natural guilt, as Ephes. 2, verse 3. 5. some of sin in the regenerate, as Rom. 7. 6. some of the will as clearly enslaved in spiritual matters, and the depravation of all faculties, such as will be proposed below where the powers of the will will be disputed expressly.

Latin:

statur θέλημα σαρκὸς, quod natura nobis obstat, quò minùs à parentibus filij Dei procreemur. Rom 8. v. 6. φρόνημα σαρκὸς, quod bellum gerit ἄσπονδον aduersus φρόνημα τοῦ πνεύματος. Caro enim concupiscit aduersus Spiritum. Galat. 5. v. 17.

Ex eodem c 3. allegat Augustinus v. vlt Qui non credit in Filium, ira Dei manet super eum, Obseruate enim, non esse dictum, Ira Dei veniet, sed manet super eum, quia iam antea est, & manet in omnibus filijs Adæ, nisi per Christum tollatur.

XIX. EX APOSTOLO PAVLO 1. Rom. 5. v. 12. Per vnum hominem peccatum in mundum intrauit & per peccatum mors, & ita in omnes homines mors pertransijt, in quo omnes peccauerūt ad cujus loci pleniorem intelligentiam sex veniunt exponenda.

1. Quid per peccatum intelligatur, num actuale & originale? Dicimus vtrumque: Actuale, vt causa, originale, vt effectus. Nam tria in peccato Adamitico concurrunt; 1. Culpa actualis. 2. Reatus legalis. 3. Prauitas naturalis. Hæc omniâ simul intrarunt in mundum, & in omnes Adæ posteros, qui propterea triplici ratione sunt miseri 1. Participatione culpæ actualis. In Adamo enim peccâruit, quia in ejus lumbis fuerunt, 2. Imputatione reatus legalis, quia primus homo stabat & cadebat cum conditione imputandi liberis. 3. Propagatione prauitatis naturalis, quæ in vniuersos & singulos, nullo excepto se diffundit. Hæc sunt tria ista infortunia, quæ per peccatum introiens denotantur.

2. Quomodo peccatum intrauerit? Hoc Apostolus voce Græcâ εἰσῆλθε inuuit: Hæc enim notat vel clandestinam irreptionem, vel impetuosam irruptionem. Cùm ergò peccatum intrasse dicitur, vterque modus intelligi potest, Prior tamen magis conuenit, quia peccatum per fraudes Diaboli irrepsit.

3. In quos intrauit? In mundum, inquit Apostolus? Vbi non intelligitur machina mundi, quæ inanimata & in se peccati capax nõ est, sed homo μικρόκοσμος, adeoque omnes Adæ posteri, quales nascuntur naturâ, qui mundus vocantur propter mundana & maligna studia.

4. Quid sit mors pertransiens? Ambrosius intelligit tantùm mortem corporalem; Socinus tantùm spiritualem; Nos omne illud quod Deus Gen. 2. v. 12. comminatus fuerat, nempè 1. mortem corporalem vel naturæ. 2. spiritualem vel gratiæ. 3 perennem vel gloriæ 4. mortis anteambulones; vt morbos, & subseqvas, vt putredinem & corruptionem. Hæc igitur mors intrauit per peccatum, vt effectus cum causa, & vmbra cum corpore suo, idque. 1. ob interminationis veritatem. 2. ob iustitiam Dei infinitam. 3. ob legem & æquitatem naturalem.

5. Quid notent particulæ ἐφ᾽ ᾧ? Vulgata habet, in quo vt referatur ad Adamum, in quo peccârunt posteri, & propugnat hoc Augustinus lib. 6. cont. Iul. cap: 12 Pelagius enim exposuit causaliter, vt sit positum pro quoniam aut quandoquidem. Perinde autem est, & res eodem recidit, siue relatiua, siue causalis interpretatio assumatur: Nam vtrobique innuitur, omnes peccasse, quia omnes morti sunt obnoxii. Nec desunt exempla, vbi ἐφ᾽ ᾧ redditionem causæ significat. Hinc Lutherus vertit: Der Tod ist zu allen Menschen durchgedrungen/ dieweil sie alle gesündiget haben.

6. Quid peccare significet? Pelagiani, cùm sit verbum actiuum, non nisi peccata actualia notari existimant, sed falsò. Nam in genere significat quamuis ἁμαρτίαν, siue actus sit, siuè habitus: Imò Apostolus ipse v. 19. per τὸ peccatorem constitui exponit, cùm inquit: Per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi. Peccare igitur hic nihil aliud est, quàm fieri & esse peccatorem.

XX. Nunc istis præsuppositis, argumenta ex textu pro peccato originis eruemus, & non depeccati imitatione, sed propagatione Apostolum verba facere, contra Pelagianos ostendemus.

1. Si in Adamo peccare, esset Adamum imitari, dici non posset, per Adamum intrasse peccatum. Qui enim peccant, non semper peccant, ob Adami exemplum, cùm multi de Adamo nihil audierint. Qui ergo imitabuntur rem planè incognitam? qui ex delicto prorsus ignoto occasionem peccandi abripient?

2. Loquitur Apostolus in singulari numero: Peccatum intrauit, Peccatum pertransiit, &c. Si verò peccata actualia voluisset notata, pluralem numerum adhibuisset. Eorum enim multa sunt, præsertim cùm de toto mundo agitur. Cùm autem singulari vtitur, de vno certoque nimirum naturali vitio, ipsum loqui concluditur. Huc spectat regula Theologorum: Peccatum in singulari numero; præsertim cum articulo; Paulopterumque, illam radicem, & caput peccati, nempè originalem corruptionem significat,

3. Terminus peccati est mundus, vnde sequitur, omnes homines, nullo excepto, contaminatos esse peccato. Nam mundus Synecdochicè ponitur pro omnibus in mundo viuentibus: Et licèt vers: 19. dicatur, multos esse constitutos peccatores, æquipollet tamen multitudinis particula vniuersali, vt patet ex ὑποδόχη, & v: 12. 13. vbi omnes expressè nominantur.

4. Quò mors transiit, eò & peccatum transijt; quia mors per peccatum intráuit. Atqui transijt mors in omnes Adæ posteros in ipsos etiam infantes qui non minus moriuntur, quàm adulti. Ergò etiam peccatum. At verò infantes non peccant actualiter. Quare preter actualia concedendum est originale, quod paruuli trahant ex parentibus, & propter quod morti subiaceant. Neque valet exceptio, mortem corporis trahi, non animæ, id est, peccatum. Nam & hanc Dominus minatus est, & mors corporis, peccatum (cuius est stipendium Rom. 6. vers. vlt.)

præsupponit: Si enim peccatum non haberemus non moreremur. vnde August. l. 13. de C. D. c. 15. ait: Constat inter Christianos Catholicam tenentes fidem, etiam ipsam nobis corporis mortem non lege naturæ, sed meritò inflictam esse peccati.

5. Peccata actualia, præsertim προαιρετικὰ non sunt hæreditaria, nec in omnes homines pertranseunt, aut communia sunt. Atqui peccatum, de quo hîc Paulus loquitur, est hæreditarium & commune, quod vnà cum morte in omnes pertransiit. Ergò actuale non est, sed potiùs naturale & originale.

6. Sicut mors intravit in mundum, ita & peccatum, quia vtrumque coniungit Apostolus. Mors vero vel mortis reatus non intravit per imitationem, sed propagationem. Ergò & peccatum.

7. Vt peccatum est causa mortis, sic Adam est causa peccati, in hunc mundum intrantis. Nam vicissim vtrumque pari modo copulatur in textu. Atqui peccatum est causa mortis non per imitationem, sed generationem, Iac. 1; v. 15. Ergo & Adamus causa est peccati non per imitationem, sed generationem.

8. V. 14. dicitur mors regnasse etiam in eos, qui non peccaverunt in similitudinem prævaricationis Adæ: Hæc autem fuit actualis. Ergò peccatum huic dissimile non est actuale. Sunt tamen qui illam dissimilitudinem, non in specie, sed modo peccati sitam arbitrantur, & notari, istos quoque mortuos esse, quibus, vt Adamo lex non fuit proposita, donec Moses νομοθέτης veniret, id quod in dubio relinquimus.

9. Adam dicitur forma futuri, hoc est, Christi v. 14. Quare vt Christus justitiam amissam non imitatione, sed regeneratione diffundit, sic Adam peccatum non imitatione, sed generatione transmisit. Hic μόλυσις est inobedientiæ ex homine in hominem mediante naturali γενέσει: illic μετάδοσιςiustitiæ ex Christo in homines, mediante παλιγγενεσίᾳ ex aqua & Spiritu: 10. August. l. 1. de pec. mer & remiss. ita concludit. Side primo peccante vel imitatione peccati a gere apostolo propositum foret, tum potiùs exemplo Christi Ioh. 8. v. 41. 42. dixiffet per Angelum peccatum intrâsse in mundum; siquidem is primus peccavit. 11. Nisi de propagatione exponatur hic locus; causa dari non poterit, cur per vnum hominem, nempe Adamum, dicatur intrâsse peccatum, & non potiùs per Euam, quippe quæ priùs peccauit, quàm Adam, & quâ peccante, cœpit esse peccatum in mundo: Non ergo intelligitur peccatum actuale, quod cœpit per Euam, sed originale, quod propagatum est per Adamum:

XXI. 2. 2. Cor. 5. v. 15. Si vnus pro omnibus mortuus est, ergò omnes mortui sunt, & pro omnibus mortuus est Christus. Hinc causa mortis Dominicæ statuitur mors omnium quæ præcessit. Ideò enim Christus est mortuus pro omnibus, quia priùs omnes erant mortui. Quâ autem morte? Sola corporalis intelligi nequit, quia ab hac sola nos Christus non redemit: nec illa præcessit actu. Ergò mors animæ vel peccatum potiùs notatur, sicut & vita, quę huic morti in eodem versiculo opponitur, non vitam corpori, sed animæ potissimùm significat:

XXII. 3. Eph. 2. v. 5. Eramus naturâ filij iræ, sicut & cæteri. Hinc colligimus: Si φύσει vel naturâ sumus filij iræ, ergo non μιμήσει vel imitatione: Ergò peccata & reatum non ipsi primùm contrahimus, sed ex parentibus & per natiuitatem attrahimus. Vocabulum enim (φύσει) vsitatè significat ea, quæ naturaliter insunt, & per naturam nobis conueniunt, siquidem opponitur τῷ ἔθει assuefactioni vel imitationi, quo sensu sumitur, Rom. 2. v. 14. Gal. 2. v. 15. Neque dici potest; Paulus de gentilibus tantùm loqui, quoniam semetipsum aliosque Iudæos includit, & vniuersaliter loquitur de omnibus, quales nam φύσει fuerint;

nimirum filij iræ, licet nunc per renouationem facti sint filij gratię. Et certè locus hic tã perspicuus est, vt pręter putida cauilla nihil opponerè queant aduersarij.

XXIII. Et huc vsque Scripturarum testimonia recensui, & quidem nonnihil prolixiùs, ne ista ob quamuis exceptiunculam velut infirma protinus reijciantur, neuè argumenta à Maioribus tāto consensu prolata temèrè & absque omni ratione deserantur, possunt autem ista omnia certis siuè ordinibus siue classibus includi, Nam 1. quædam loquuntur de concread imaginis amissione, vt Gen. 5. v. 32. 2. quædam malū istud describunt primatiuè, vt Psalm. 14. v. 2. & seqq. 3. quædam positiuè, vt Gen. 6. v. 5. c. 8. v. 22. 4. quædam loquuntur de reatu naturali, vt Ephes. 2. vers. 3. 5. quædam de peccato in renatis, vt Rom. 7. 6. quædam de arbitrio in spiritualibus planè seruo, omniúmque facultatum deprauatione, qualia proponentur infrà vbi èx professo de viribus arbitrij disputabitur.


### Question III By what arguments is the corruption of human nature: The second class, containing arguments taken from the analogy of faith

The second class, containing arguments taken from the analogy of faith.

XXIV. 1. From circumcision. This was no obscure indication of native corruption, since it was instituted to the end that males might by this means be purged from sin, and therefore it was commanded to be done in that member in which the effect of sin is more evidently shown, and through which the human race is carnally propagated, and by propagating is contaminated.

XXV. 2. From the purification of women. For in the O.T. they were considered unclean from childbirth, and therefore stood in need of cleansing and their own sanctification. No probable reason for this matter can be brought forward if original sin, or natural corruption, which is wont to exercise itself most of all in the act of generation, is denied. For childbirth itself, as such, is not unclean since it is a work of nature commanded by God himself: Gen. 1. ver. 28. and originated from divine blessing.

XXVI. 3. From baptism. Whoever is baptized has sin. For baptism is conferred for the remission of sins; Acts 2. v. 37. whence it is called a washing, Eph. 5. v. 26. And indeed a washing of regeneration, Tit. 3. v. 5. washing away the filth not of the flesh, but of the conscience, 1 Pet. 3. v. 21. But infants are baptized, and indeed necessarily, and because of need: For unless they were washed by this saving water, they would not enter into the kingdom of heaven, John 3. v. 5. Therefore infants have sin, and are by nature children of wrath. Hence rightly Fulgentius, De incarn. Dom. c. 15. p. 744: The Sacrament of Baptism is therefore uniformly conferred upon infants and adults alike, so that the stain of original sin may be recognized as existing in all.

XXVII. 4. From concupiscence in the regenerate. For since in those also who commit many voluntary offenses, a true and properly so-called sin lies hidden, it follows that besides actual sin there is another, an original one, most deeply fixed in nature itself. And this very thing, Rom. 7. v. 19 & 20, is called indwelling sin, because it does not pass away, but has a fixed seat in the flesh, v. 21: evil that is present, v. 23: the law of sin existing in the members. Heb. 12. verse 1, it is called εὐπερίστατος ἁμαρτία, sin that surrounds on all sides, or tenaciously adheres, and occupies all members and powers, all of which cannot be said or affirmed of actual sins.

XXVIII 5. From common death. All children of Adam are subject to this, so that not even infants just born are excepted. Now truly death is the punishment of sin, Gen. 2. v. 17, and the wages, Rom. 6. v. last, and that soul alone dies which has itself sinned, Ezek. 18. v. 20. Therefore, since infants sustain the punishment of sin, they will not be immune from sin. For every punishment, if it is just, is a punishment of sin; and it is called judgment, says Augustine, book 1, Retractations, chapter 9. Hence Fulgentius rightly concluded in his book on the Incarnation, chapter 14, page 739: By what justice is a little one subjected to the wages of sin, if there is no pollution of sin in him? Or how do we see him pricked by death, if he has not felt the sting?

XXIX. 6. From the kingdom of heaven. This includes the remission of sins, as is well known. But Christ affirms that the kingdom of heaven belongs also to children and infants, Matthew 19, verse 14. Therefore they are not devoid of sins. For where there is no guilt, there is no need for pardon or remission.

XXX. 7. From παλιγγενεσίᾳ (regeneration). For as often as spiritual generation is commended in Scripture, so often is carnal generation condemned. Therefore, just as the former implies a gratuitous liberation from sin, so the latter implies natural pollution of sin.

XXXI. 8. From the flesh of sin. Our nature is so named, Romans 3, verse 3, from which Fulgentius, in his book on the Incarnation, chapter 15, page 741, concludes thus: If it is not falsely called the flesh of sin, the flesh itself has sin in it; but if it does not have sin, it bears the name of flesh falsely. But Paul, the truthful disciple of truth, calls it the flesh of sin, of which he speaks. It remains, therefore, that just as it is truly flesh when it is called flesh, so it truly has sin in it when it is called the flesh of sin by the Apostolic mouth.

XXXII. 9. From the incarnation of Christ. God came in the likeness of the flesh of sin, Romans 8, verse 3. If, therefore, infants do not have sin, it follows either that Christ was not made in the likeness of the flesh of sin, or if he was, that he did not assume human nature, because through the assumption of the flesh of sin, he was not assimilated to the flesh of infants, which is truly human nature. Whence Fulgentius, in the aforementioned book, concludes in turn: Either let them not say that the flesh of Christ is human, or let them judge that the flesh of all men, in whose likeness God sent his Son, is the flesh of sin.

XXXIII. 10. From the assimilation of Christ, it is said that he was made like us in all things, yet excepting sin. But, if the flesh of infants is without sin, this will differ in nothing from the flesh of Christ, and therefore sin is wrongly excepted. For if we also are born without sin, as Christ, what need is there for that exception?

XXXIV. 11. From the redemption of Christ. Whoever are born without sin do not need a Redeemer. Wherefore Christ did not die for the whole world. Therefore, neither are all who are saved, saved through and because of the merit of Christ. Since this, however, is absurd, we invert the argument: Infants are saved because of the merit of Christ. Therefore He died for them, just as it is expressly said that He died for all, 2 Cor. 5:14. And yet He died for sinners, Rom. 5:6. For those who lack sin do not need the price of redemption. From which it follows in turn that infants are born corrupt and sinners.

XXXV. 12. From one's own sense and the testimony of conscience. It is not without reason to be wondered at that such profane men are found as to dare to deny original sin and the corruption of nature, when nevertheless anyone in himself experiences it sufficiently, and more than sufficiently. For whence comes this ignorance and blindness of mind, whence this proclivity to err, this difficulty in what is good and depravity of appetite, if nature is intact? Why are those who strive to devote themselves to virtue nevertheless snatched away sideways? Why do those who wish to do good not have the power, but perpetrate the evil which they hate? Why do the saints themselves complain and exclaim, 'Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death?' Rom. 7:24. Indeed, why in any good work do we fear for ourselves, and if we think of the divine tribunal, do we immediately turn pale and tremble? These are certainly all clear testimonies of inherent sin, and of the highest corruption, on account of which we cannot stand in the judgment of God, and all our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth, Isaiah 64:6. Wherefore they declare war both upon their own sense and upon conscience itself, whoever deny original sin, and consequently as foolish disputants, according to the Philosopher's warning, are to be sharply rebuked and chided.

Latin:

Classis secunda, continens argumenta ab analogia fidei petita.

XXIV. 1. A circumcisione. Fuit hoc non obscurum natiuæ corruptionis indicium, quandoquidem eum in finem instituta est, vt masculi hoc medio purgarentur à peccato, ideoq; in eo membro fieri iussa est, in quo peccati effectus euidentiùs ostenditur, & per quod genus humanum carnaliter propagatur, ac propagando contaminatur.

XXV. 2. A purgatione mulierum. Nam in V. T. immundæ censebantur à partu, & propterea mundatione suíque sanctificatione indigebant. Cuius rei nulla poterit probabilis ratio afferri, si peccatum originis, vel corruptio naturalis, quæ in actu generationis sese quàm maximè solet exercere negetur. Non enim ipse partus, quà talis, immundus est; cùm sit opus naturæ ab ipso Deo: Genes. 1. ver. 28. præceptum, & ex divina benedictione ortum.

XXVI. 3. A baptismo. Quicunque baptizantur, peccatum habent. Baptismus enim confertur in remissionem peccatorum; Act. 2. v. 37. vnde lavacrum dicitur Eph. 5. v. 26. Et quidem lavacrum regenerationis. Tit: 3. v. 5. abluens sordes non carnis, sed conscientiæ. 1. Pet. 3. v. 21. Atqui infantes baptizantur, & quidem necessariò, & propter indigentiam: Nisi enim aqua hac salutari abluerentur, non intrarent in regnum cælorum, Ioh. 3. v. 5. Ergo infantes peccatum habent, & iræ filij sunt naturâ. Hinc rectè Fulgentius de incarn. Dom. c. 15. p. 744. Baptismatis Sacramentum ideò vniformiter infantibus maioribusque confertur, vt omnibus originalis in-esse peccati macula cognoscatur.

XXVII. 4. Aconcupiscentia in renatis. Cùm enim in his etiám, qui multa committunt delicta voluntaria, verum proprieque dictum peccatum delitescat, sequitur quòd præter actuale sit aliud quoddam originale, ipsi naturæ penitissimè infixum. Et hoc ipsum, Rom. 7. v. 19 & 20. nuncupatur peccatum inhabitans, quia non transit, sed fixam in carne sedem habet, v. 21: malum adiacens, v 23. lex peccati in membris existens Hebr. 12. vers. 1. appellatur εὐπερίστατος ἁμαρτία, peccatum vndique circumstans, seu tenaciter inhærens, & cuncta membra viresque. occupans, quæ omnia de peccatis actualibus dici aut adfirmari nequeunt.

XXVIII 5. A communi morte. Subjacent huic omnes filij Adæ adeò vt nec infantes modò nati excipiantur. Iam verò mors est pœna peccati, Gen. 2. v. 17. & stipendium, Rom 6. v. ult. moriturque illa tantùm anima, quæ ipsa peccavit, Ezech. 18. v. 20. Ergò, cùm infantes pœnam peccati sustineant, à peccato immunes non erunt, Omnis enim Pœna, si iusta est, pœna peccati est; & iudicium nominatur inquit August. l. 1. Retr. c 9. Hinc rectè conclusit Fulgentius l. de incarnat. c. 14. p. 739. Quâ iustitiâ parvulus subycitur peccati stipendio, si nulla est in eo peccati pollutio? vel quomodo videmus morte punctum, si non sensit aculeum?

XXIX. 6. Aregno cœlorum. Complectitur hoc remissionem peccatorum, vti notum est. At verò Christus adfirmat, puerorum quoque & infantum esse regnum cœlorum, Matth. 19. v. 14. Ergò peccatis non destituuntur. Vbi enim nulla culpa, ibi non opus est veniâ aut remissione.

XXX. 7. A παλιγγενεσίᾳ Quoties enim in Scriptura commendatur generatio spiritualis, toties condemnatur generatio carnalis. Sicut ergò illa gratuitam liberationem à peccato, ita hæc naturalem pollutionem peccatum importat.

XXXI. 8. A carne peccati. Sic nuncupatur natura nostra, Rom. 3. v. 3. ex quo Fulgentius l. de Incarnat c. 15. p. 741. ita colligit. Si caro peccati non mendaciter dicitur, habet in se caro ipsa peccatum: si verò peccatum non habet, falsum portat carnis vocabulum. Sed eam, dequa loquitur, carnem peccati; verax discipulus veritatis Paulus appellat. Restat igitur, vt sicut verè caro est, cùm caro dicitur; ita verè in se peccatum habeat, cùm caro peccati ore Apostolico nuncupatur.

XXXII. 9. Ab incarnatione Christi. Deus venit in similitudinem carnis peccati. Rom. 8. v. 3. Quòd si ergò infantes peccatum non habent, sequitur; aut Christum non esse factum similem carni peccati; aut si hoc, non assumsisse humanam naturam quia per assumtionem carnis peccati, infantum carni, quæ verè est humana natura; non fuit assimilatus. Vnde vicissim Fulgentius d: l. concludit: Aut carnem Christi humanam esse non dicant, aut omnium hominum carnem, in cuius similitudinem Deus Filium suum misit, carnem peccati esse censentiant.

XXXIII. 10. Ab assimilatione Christi, Dicitur nobis per omnia factus similis excepto tamen peccato. At, si caro infantum est sine peccato, nihil hæc distabit à carne Christi, ideoque peccatum malè excipitur. Si enim & nos sine peccato nascimur, vt Christus quid illa exceptione opus?

XXXIV. 11. A redemptione Christi. Quicunque nascuntur sine peccato Redemtore non egent. Quare nec Christus prototo mundo est mortuus. Ergo nec omnes qui saluantur, per & propter meritum Christi saluantur. Hoc autem cùm sit absurdum, invertimus argumentum: Infantes saluantur propter meritum Christi. Ergo pro ijs mortuus est, sicut expressè pro omnibus dicitur esse mortuus, 2. Cor. 5. v. 14. Atqui pro peccatoribus est mortuus, Rom. 5. v. 6. Qui enim peccato carent, redemtionis precio non egent. Ex quo vicissim sequitur infantes nasci corruptos & peccatores.

XXXV. 12. A proprio sensu & conscientiæ testimonio. Non immeritò mirandum est, tàm profanos reperiri homines, vt peccatum originis & naturæ corruptionem inficiari audeant, cùm tamen quiuis in semetipso eam satis, & plus quàm satis experiatur. Vnde enim ista mentis ignorantia & cæcitas, vnde ista errandi procliuitas, ista in bono difficultas & appetitus prauitas, si natura sit integra? Cur, qui virtuti operam dare student intransuersum tamen abripiuntur? Cur, qui bonum volunt facere, non possunt, sed malum, quod oderunt, perpetrant? Cur ipsi sancti quiritantur & exclamant, Infelix ego homo quis me liberabit à corpore mortis huius? Rom. 7. v 24. Imo cur in quouis bono opere nobis timemus, & si tribunal diuinum cogitamus, mox expallescimus, trepidamus? Hæc certò omnia luculenta sunt testimonia inhærentis peccati, & summæ corruptionis, ob quam in judicio Dei consistere non possumus, & omnes iustitiæ nostræ sunt sicut pannus menstruatæ, Esai. 64. v. 6. Quocirca & sensui proprio, & ipsi conscientiæ bellum indicunt, quicunque peccatum originis negatum indicunt, quicunque peccatum originis negaturi sunt, ac proinde tanquam insulsi disputatores, juxta Philosophi monitum, acriter increpandi & obiurgandi sunt.


### Question III By what arguments is the corruption of human nature: The third class, containing certain testimonies of the Fathers

The third class, containing certain testimonies of the Fathers.

XXXVI. Many things could be noted, but let a few, and those the principal ones, suffice. 1. Irenaeus, book 5, chapter 17. Christ wiped out the handwriting, our debts, fastening it to the cross, so that since we were made debtors to God through a tree, we might receive the remission of the debt through a tree.

Tertullian, book on the soul, chapter 40. Every soul is reckoned in Adam until it is reckoned anew in Christ: it is unclean as long as it is not reckoned anew. Moreover, it is a sinner, because it is unclean.

3. Origen, homily on Leviticus. Whatever soul is born in the flesh is polluted by the filth of iniquity and sin, on account of which it is said, No one is clean from filth, not even an infant whose life is one day upon the earth.

4. Ambrose in Apology of David, chapter 11. Before we are born, we are stained by contagion; before we enjoy the light, we receive the injury of our origin itself, we are conceived in iniquity. And on the Ark of Noah, chapter 22. There is no one without sin, not even an infant of one day.

5. Augustine, book 2 against Pelagius, chapter 25. Whoever contends that human nature at any age does not need the physician, the second Adam, because it was not corrupted in the first Adam, is convicted as an enemy of the grace of God, not in any question in which one can doubt and err without prejudice to the faith, but in the very rule of faith by which we are Christians. The same author, book 2 against Julian, at the end, appeals to the authority of the ancient Fathers with these words. For the sake of which Catholic truth, the holy and blessed priests, most illustrious in the treatment of divine utterances, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Innocent, John, Basil: to whom I add, whether you like it or not, the presbyter Jerome, to omit those who have not yet fallen asleep, bring forth against you the judgment concerning the original sinful succession of all men: from where could it arise, except him whom without the law of sin fighting against the law of the mind the Virgin conceived. 6. Fulgentius, book on the Incarnation, ch. 14. If they do not wish to be engaged in death-bearing impiety to the insult of God himself, let them confess that sin first passed into all men with death through man. 7.

Prosper on the ungrateful, ch. 27. For the poisonous drunkenness of sin runs through all, and persists in the womb of the corrupt heart; the carbuncle keeps the raw food, hence the vigor of the soul is overwhelmed.

8. Bede on ch. 21 of Leviticus. Every man who enters this world is contaminated in father and mother, from whom he draws original sin. 9. Bernard, treatise on the degrees of humility. We are born, we die, and therefore we are born about to die, because we die first about to be born. But by death, through which we die about to be born, he understands nothing other than sin, which includes the guilt of death, and separates us from true life, God being indeed blessed and glorious.

XXXVII. And thus far indeed we have brought forward our arguments for the existence of original sin. It remains that we run through the principal objections of the adversaries for a better understanding of the truth, and a fuller demonstration of the falsehood. There are six of them chiefly, concerning which in order.

XXXVIII. 1. The voice is Jehovah's, Ezekiel 18, v. 20. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. Wherefore, because of the fall of Adam alone, the whole nature is not corrupted, nor is the entire posterity contaminated by sin.

Response 1. The Prophet speaks not of guilt, but of punishment; not of vice, but of penalty. For thus the words hold: The soul that shall have sinned, it shall die. The son shall not bear (namely, the punishment) in the iniquity, or on account of the iniquity of the father. For in the preceding words the Prophet had said that God does not punish the offenses of parents in obedient and upright children. The Jews object in verse 19 that this is a protestation contrary to the fact. For they themselves pay the penalty, although they are without guilt, but only for this reason that the children's teeth were set on edge, because the fathers had eaten sour grapes. Here the Lord answers: that no one is punished who has not sinned: for that soul alone dies which itself transgresses, nor does the son bear the penalty for the father's iniquity alone. But what of this against original sin? So little, that the argument can rather be inverted into this sense: Whoever is punished, he has sinned. For where guilt does not precede, there punishment has no place. Every punishment, if it is just, is a punishment of sin, says Augustine, book 1, Retractations, chapter 9. But all the descendants of Adam are punished in their own person. Therefore they have sinned not only in Adam, but also have guilt adhering to themselves. Hence rightly Anselm, On the Conception of the Virgin, chapter 16: An infant who is damned for original sin is not damned for the sin of Adam, but for his own. For if he did not have his own sin, he would not be damned. And Augustine, book 6, against Julian, chapter 4: The sins of parents are in a certain way called foreign, and yet in a certain way they are found to be our own. Foreign, indeed, by the property of the action, and our own by the contagion of propagation. If this were false, surely the heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam from the day of their coming forth from their mother's womb would in no way be just.

2. If the guilt itself is understood, and not only the penalty of guilt, so that the sense may be: The sins of parents are not propagated into the children. Then a distinction must be made between natural and personal sin, or between universal and singular. The Prophet is not speaking of natural sin, which pertains to the whole species; but of singular sin, which pertains only to certain persons. This is not ordinarily propagated through generation, but that other is justly derived into descendants. For Adam was representatively the whole human race, and he received gifts both for himself and for his descendants, so that if he retained them he would propagate them to his descendants, but if he lost them, they would be lost for his descendants as well. For just as Levi was tithed in the loins of Abraham, Hebrews 7, verses 9 and 10, so in Adam the whole human race both ought to have stood, and could have fallen. But he violated the law of the Lord, and therefore lost the gifts granted not only for himself, but for all his descendants, upon whose expulsion there succeeded not in Adam alone, but in the whole species, a horrible corruption and depravity of nature. 3. Augustine, considering the statement of Jer. 31. 31. concerning the grace of the New Testament, expounded it and rendered this meaning: In the New Testament the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, because then it will have been remitted: but when it has not yet been remitted, then the son is compelled to bear the iniquity of the father. But this response does not seem to suffice, and therefore we acquiesce in the former ones just given.

XXXIX. 2. Infants are called innocent. Ps. 106. v. 38. nor to have done anything good or evil: Rom. 9. v. 11. Wherefore they are not infected with sin.

Response. In turn, a distinction must be made between natural and personal sin, between the matter and the ingenerate corruption. In the former respect they are called innocent, but not in the latter. They do not indeed do evil, yet they have it fixed in their nature. For they are so innocent that they are nevertheless called unclean, Job 14. conceived in sins, Psalm 51. 7. by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2. 3. To this point refers that of Augustine, book 2, Confessions, ch. 7: The weakness of infant limbs is innocent, not the mind of infants.

XXXX. 3. For sin two things are required. 1. Knowledge of the law. 2. Transgression of what is known. For where there is no law, there is no transgression, Rom. 4. 15. But to infants no law is given, for if it were given they would be able to know it. Therefore they do not transgress, and consequently they do not sin.

Response. The Pelagians presuppose two false things: 1. That there is no transgression unless knowledge of the law precedes it. For that this is false, sins of ignorance show. And the Apostle says in Rom. 2. 12, those who sinned without the law of Moses will perish without the law. And Rom. 5. v. 14 it is said that death, as the penalty of sin, reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, that is, who had not transgressed a certain known law. For there was sin in the world even before Moses. v. 13. Therefore Christ also John 15:22 names the transgression of a known law a special sin; "If I had not come," he says, "and spoken to them, they would not have sin," namely, such a sin as takes away all excuse, so that their conscience convicts them. For shall we think that the Pharisees would have sinned not at all if Christ had not spoken to them? ἄτοπον. 2. It is false what they say, that there is no law which the descendants of Adam have violated. For 1. In Adam we violated that law of Gen. 2:17, "In the day that you eat," etc. For Adam was the stock and root of the whole human race. Therefore, just as if Adam had stood, we also would have stood, so when Adam fell, we also fell, and transgressed the law of the Lord. Hence Ambrose says in lib. 7 in Luc.: "Adam existed, and in him we all existed; Adam perished, and in him all perished." Nor did Prosper sing ill concerning our evil nature: "The once inviolate and sublime image of God, after," etc. In the first [man] we all existed, while he dwelt in the deep grove and fell, and as the parent fell, we all fell together in him, and by the decree the parent warns us against the tree from which we fell.

And Augustine, book 16, De Civitate Dei, chapter 27, writes: Even infants, not according to the particularity of their own life, but according to the common origin of the human race, all broke the covenant of God in that one man, in whom all sinned. 2. We also violate the law in our own person, and indeed not one, but both tables, and therefore the whole decalogue. For it must be known that the law is violated both actually and habitually, that is, partly by an evil act, partly by an evil habit. For both he who acts evilly, and he who is prone to evil by nature, is against the law of sin. Furthermore, the law is violated either privatively or positively, by sins either of omission or of commission. These things being established, we affirm that the whole Decalogue is violated by us 1. on account of a lack of righteousness, and thus because of sins of omission. The law requires such integrity, that we love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength, without any hesitation, without any contempt. This integrity, because it is not found in us, therefore we violate the law, by which also on account of that defect we are accused and condemned. 2. On account of the sin of omission, not indeed actual, but habitual, while in our members from our very birth a bad habit adheres, which is entirely contrary to the law and to all the precepts of the law. For just as original justice was the observance of the whole Decalogue: so injustice, which expelled this, is the transgression of the whole Decalogue.

XL. 4. Every sin is voluntary. The evil of origin is not voluntary. Therefore it is not sin properly so called.

Resp. There are those who say that the sin of origin, as it also inheres in us, can be called voluntary. 1. Effectively, because it has its origin from the evil will of the first man, in whom all our wills were. 2. Subjectively, because it inheres in the will. 3. Conjecturally, because when a man reaches age, he in a certain way consents to the sin: nevertheless, speaking simply and properly, it should rather be called involuntary; both because it is natural and hereditary, and because its motions in the regenerate are involuntary, nor does consent always follow in more mature age. Therefore we deny the major premise in theology, and we affirm that it is inconveniently transferred from philosophy to impugn the sin of origin. In a forensic judgment, indeed, nothing is held to be a sin unless it is voluntary. But in the divine judgment every ἄνομον is sin, whether it be otherwise ἑκόυsιον or ἀκόυsιον, as we demonstrated above in s. 3, quest. 2.

XLI. 5. If sin is remitted to pious parents in Baptism and repentance, why therefore is it propagated in their children? For what someone does not have, he cannot transfer to another.

Resp. 1. Augustine gives an instance from the foreskin and the chaff, for thus he writes in book 3 de peccat. meri. c. 8. In turn I also ask, how does the foreskin, which is taken away through circumcision, remain in those whom the circumcised have begotten? How also does the chaff, which is separated by human labor with such diligence, remain in the fruit which is born from the cleansed wheat?

2. Generation does not occur according to grace, but nature; not according to the Spirit, but the flesh. Therefore, such as the parents were φύσῃ [by nature], such children they beget from themselves. To this pertains that statement of Augustine, Serm. 34 de ver. Apost.: 'It is born of the baptized, because he does not beget him from whence he was regenerated, but from whence he was generated; that which is born of the flesh is flesh.' 3. We deny that the pious are entirely without sin after Baptism. For a distinction must be made between sin itself and the guilt of sin: the latter is taken away through Baptism; the former, however, is left behind, and therefore is drawn along by descendants. For sin always adheres to the reborn, although it is not imputed. But from the denial of imputation to the denial of the corruption itself, the consequence does not hold.

XLII. 6. If sin is propagated through generation, marriages would have to be condemned. Resp. I deny the consequence, because marriage is an institution of God Himself, never to be condemned, always to be approved. It happens only accidentally that sin is propagated in marriage, and from this accidental vice it is not permitted to argue for the destruction of the divine order. For the vices of nature do not take away the benefits and the order instituted by God, the Creator of nature.

Latin:

Classis tertia, continens quædam testimonia Patrum.

XXXVI. Multa possent annotari, sed pauca, eaque præcipua sufficiant. 1. Irenæus lib. 5. cap. 17. Delenit Christus chirographum, debita nostra, affigens illud cruci, vt quoniam per lignum facti sumus debitores Deo, per lignum accipiamus debiti remissionem.

Tertul. l. de ani. c. 40. Omnis anima eò vsque in Adam censetur, donec in Christo recenseatur: tam diu immunda, quàm diu recenseatur. Peccatrix autem, quia immunda.

3. Origines homil. in Leuit. Quæcunq; anima in carne nascitur, iniquitatis, & peccati sorde polluitur, propter quod dictum est, Nemo mñdus à sorde, nec infans, cuius est vnius diei vita super terram.

4 Ambrosius in Apol. Dauid. c. 11. Antequam nascamur, maculamur contagio; antequam vsuram lucis, originis ipsius excipimus iniuriam, in iniquitate concipimur. Et de arca Nohæ, c. 22. Non est sine peccato, nec vnius diei infans,

5. August. l. 2. contra Pelag. cap. 25. Quisquis humanam contendit in qualibet ætate naturam non indigere medico secundo Adam, quia non est vitiata in primo Adam, non in aliqua quæstione, in qua dubitari &c errari salua fide potest, sed in ipsa fidei regula, quà Christiani sumus gratiæ Dei conuincitur inimicus Idem l. 2. contra Iulianum in fine prouocat ad antiquorum Patrum authoritatem his verbis. Propter quam Catholicam veritatem sancti ac beati in diuinoru eloquiorum pertractatione clarissimi sacerdotes Irenæus, Cyprianus, Reticius, Olympius, Hilarius, Ambrosius, Gregorius, Innocentius, Iohannes Basilius: quibus addo presbyterum velis nolis, Hieronymum, vt omittam eos, qui nondum dormierunt, aduersum vos proferunt, de omnium hominum pecca o originali obnoxia successione sententiam: vnden maocrit, nisi quem sinelege peccati repugnante legi mentis virgo concepit. 6. Fulgent l. de Incarnat. c. 14. Si nolunt in ipsius Dei contameliam morifera impietate versari, fateantur homine primum in omnes homines cum morte transmisisse peccatum. 7.

Prosper de ingratis c. 27. Transcurrit enim virosa per omnes Peccati ebrietas corrupti & cordis in aluo Persistit, cruda seruet carbunculus esca, Hinc animi vigor obrutus.

8. Beda in cap. 21. Leuit. Omnis homo, qui hunc mundum ingreditur, in patre & matre contaminatur, ex quibus originale trahit peccatum. 9. Bernh. tractat. de grad. humil. Nascimur, morimur, ideoque nascimur morituri, quia prius morimur nascituri. Per mortem vero, qua nascituri morimur, nihil aliud intelligit, quam peccatum, quod mortis reatum includit, & nos a vera vita separat, Deo nimirum benedicto & glorioso.

XXXVII. Et hactenus quidem argumenta nostra pro peccati originalis existentia retulimus. restat, vt praecipuas aduersariorum obiectiones percurramus ad meliorem veritatis intellectum, & pleniorem falsitatis demonstrationem. Sunt illarum sex potissimum de quibus ordine.

XXXVIII. 1. Iehouah vox est Ezech. 18. v. 20. Filius non portabit iniquitatem Patris, Quare ob lapsum solius Adae non corrupta est tota natura, nec peccato contaminata vniuersa posteritas.

Resp. 1. Non de culpa, sed pœna, non de vitio, sed supplicio loquitur Propheta. Sic enim habent verba: Anima quae peccauerit, ipsa morietur. Filius non feret (nempe pœnam) in iniquitate, vel propter iniquitatem Patris. In praecedentibus enim verbis dixerat Propheta, Deum non punire delicta parentum in filijs morigeris & probis. Excipiunt Iudaei vers. 19. Esse protestationem facto contrariam. Se enim luere pœnam, cum tamen sint absq; culpa, sed duntaxat ideò dentes filiorum obstupuisse, quia Patres comederint uyam acerbam. Hîc respondet Dominus: Nem nem puniri, qui non peccauerit: illam enim duntaxat animam mori, quæ ipsa præuaricetur, nec filium pœnam ferre ob solam patris iniquitatem. Quid verò hinc contra peccatum originis? Adeò nihil, vt potiùs inuerti queat argumentum in hunc sensum: Quicunque punitur, is peccauit. Vbi enim non præcedit culpa, ibi locum non habet pœna. Omnis pœna, si iusta est, pœna peccati est, inquit August. l. 1. Retract. c. 9. Atqui omnes posteri Adæ in propria persona puniuntur. Ergò peccauerunt non in Adamo tantùm, sed culpam sibiipsis quoque adhærentem habent. Hinc rectè Anshelmus de part. virg. c. 16. Infans qui damnatur pro peccato originali, non damnatur pro peccato Adæ, sed pro suo. Nam si ipse non haberet suum peccatum non damnaretur. Et August. libro 6. contra Iulia. c. 4. Parentũ peccata modo quodã dicuntur aliena & rursus modo quodam reperiuntur & nostra. Aliena quippè proprietate sunt actionis, & nostra sunt contagione propaginis. Quod si falsum esset, profectò graue iugũ super filios Adami à die exitˡ de ventre matris eorum nullo modo iustũ esset.

2. Si culpa ipsa intelligatur, & non sola culpæ pœna, vt sensus sit. Peccata parentum in filios non propagari. tum distinguendum est inter peccatum naturale & personale, vel inter vniuersale & singulare. Loquitur Propheta nō de peccato naturali, totam speciem attinente; sed singulari, certis tantùm personis competente. Hoc per generationem ordinariè non propagatur, illud autem in posteros iustè deriuatur. Adam enim repræsentatiuè fuit totum genus humanum, & accepit dona tum pro se, tum pro suis posteris, vt si ea retineret in posteros propagaret, sin amitteret, etiam posteris amissa essent. Sicut enim Leui decimatus est in lumbis Abrahæ. Hebr. 7. v. 9. 10. Sic in Adamo totum genus humanum & stare debebat, & cadere poterat. Ille autem legem Domini violauit, ideoque dona concessa non sibi modò, sed omnibus posteris amisit, quibus expulsis successit non in solo Adamo, sed tota specie horribilis naturę corruptio & deprauatio, 3. Augustinus considerans dictum Ier. 31. 31. de gratia N. T. exposuit, & hunc sensum reddidit: In N. T. filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, quia tunc erit remissa: quando autem nondum remissa est, tunc filius iniquitatem Patris portare cogitur. Sed responsio hæc non videtur satis facere, ideoque in prioribus modò datis acquiescimus.

XXXIX. 2. Infantes dicuntur innocentes. Psal. 106. vers. 38. nec fecisse aliquid boni aut mali: Rom. 8. v. 12. Quare peccato non sunt infecti.

Respond. Vicissim distinguendum est inter peccatum naturale & personale, inter matiam & corruptionem ingeneratam. Priori respectu dicuntur innocentes, sed non posteriori. Malum quidem non faciunt, iuæ tamen naturę infixum habent. Ita n. sunt innocentes, vt tamen dicantur immundi, Iob. 14. in peccatis concepti. Psalm 51. 7. naturâ filij iræ Eph. 2. 3. Huc spectat illud August. l. 2. Confess c. 7. Imbecillitas meinbrorum infantilium innocens est, non animus infantum.

XXXX. 3. Ad peccatum duo requiruntur. 1. legis cognitio. 2. cognita præuaricatio. Nam vbi nulla lex, ibi nulla præuaricatio, Rom. 4 15. Infantibus verò lex nulla datur, si enim daretur eam cognoscere possent. Ergo nec præuaricantur, & per consequens non peccant.

Resp. Duo falsa præsupponunt Pelagiani, 1. quod nulla sit præuaricatio, nisi vbi præcedit legis cognitio. Hoc enim falsum esse, ostendunt peccata ignorantiæ. Et Apostolus ait Rom 2. 12. qui sine lege Mosis peccau runt, sine lege peribunt Et Rom. 5. v. 14 dicitur, quòd mors tanquam pœna peccati, etiam in eos regnauerit, qui non peccauerunt in similitudinem pręuaricationis Adæ, id est, qui non legem quandam cognitam fuerunt transgressi. Erat enim peccatum in mundo etiam ante Mosen. v. 31. Idcirco Christus quoq; Ioh: 15. 22. transgressionem legis scitæ peculiare peccatum nominat, Si non venissem, ait, & dixissem illis peccatum non haberent, videlicet peccatum tale, quo tollitur omnis excusatio, vt conscientia ipsos conuincat. Num n. putabimus Pharisæos planè non peccasse, si Christus ipsis non dixisset? ἄτοπον. 2. Falsum est, quod aiunt nullam legem esse, quam posteri Adami violarint. Etenim 1. In Adamo violavimus istam legem Gen. 4. 17. Quâ die comederis &c. Adam n. stirps erat & radix totius generis humani.
