Vt ergo si Adam stetisset, & nos stetissemus, ita cùm Adam caderet, & nos cadebamus, legemq; Domini transgrediebamur. Hinc Ambros. ait l. 7. in Luc. Fuit Adam, & in illo fuimus omnes: perijt Adam & in illo perierunt omnes. Nec malè Prosper de mala natura cecinit; Inviolata Dei quondam & sublimis imago st postquam, &c. In primo cuncti fuimus Patre, dum nemore alto Corruit & cunctis simul in genitore cadente Degit, & edicto parens cauet arbore ab ima Corruimus.

Et August. l. 16. C. D. c. 27. scribit: Etiam paruuli non secundum vitæ suæ proprietatem, sed secundum communem generis humani originem omnes in illo vno Testamentum Dei dissipauerunt, in quo omnes peccauerunt. 2. In propria etiam persona violamus legem, & quidem non vnam, sed vtramque tabulam, adeóq; totum decalogum, Sciendum enim, quod lex violetur tum actualiter tum habitualiter, h. e. Partim per malum actum, partim per malum habitum. Etenim & qui male agit, & qui ad mala per naturam pronus est, est contra legem peccati. Deinde lex violatur vel priuatiuè vel positiuè, per peccata vel omissionis vel commissionis. His positis, affirmamus à nobis violari totum Decalogum 1. propter defectum justitiæ, & sic ob peccata omissionis. Lex n. requirit integritatem talem, vt Deum diligamus ex toto corde, ex tota anima, & ex omnibus viribus, sine vlla dubitatione, sine omni comtemptu. Hæcintegritas, quia in nobis nō reperitur, ideò legem violamus, à quâ etiam ob illum defectum arguimur & condemnamur. 2. Propter peccatum omissionis, nō quidem ætuale, sed habituale, dum in membris nostris à prima vsque natiuitate malus hæret habitus, qui prorsus legi, omnibusque præceptis legis est contrarius. Sicut enim justitia originalis fuit obseruatio totius Decalogi: ita jnjustitia, quæ hanc expulit, est transgressio totius Decalogi.

XL. 4. Omne peccatum est voluntarium. Malum originis non est voluntarium. Ergo non est peccatum propriè dictum.

Resp. Sunt qui dicant, peccatum originis, prout nobis etiam inhæret, nuncupari posse voluntarium. 1. Effectiuè, quia ex mala voluntate primi hominis, in quo nostræ voluntates fuere omnes, originem habet. 2. Subiectiuè, quia voluntati inhæret. 3. Coniectiuè, quia cùm homo ad ætatem peruenit, peccato quodammodo consentit: attamen ἁπλῶς & propriè loquendo involuntarium potius dicendum est; tùm quia naturale & hæreditarium, tùm quia motus ejus in renatis sunt involuntarij, neque semper in adultiore ætate consensus accedit. Proinde maiorem in Theologia negamus, & illam incommodè ex Philosophia ad impugnandum originis peccatum transferri adfirmamus. In judicio quidem forensi pro peccato nihil habetur, nisi quod est voluntarium. Ast in judicio diuino omne ἄνομον peccatum est, siue aliàs sit ἑκόυsιον siue ἀκόυsιον, ut supra s. 3. quæst. 2. demonstrauimus.

XLI. 5. Si peccatum pijs parentibus in Baptismo & pœnitentia remittitur, cur ergo in liberis propagatur? Quod enim aliquis non habet, in alium transferre nequit.

Resp. 1. Augustinus dat instantiam à præputio & palea, lta n. scribit l. 3. de peccat. meri. c. 8. Vicissim & ego rogo, quomodo præputium, quod per circumcisionem aufertur, maneat in ijs, quos genuerint circumcisi? Quomodo & palea, quæ opere humano tantâ diligentiâ separatur, maneat in fructu, qui de purgata tritico nascitur?

2. Generatio non fit secundum gratiam, sed naturam non secundum Spiritum, sed carnem Quales ergo parentes fuere φύσῃ, tales ex se gignunt liberos. Huc pertinet illud Augustini Serm. 34. de ver. Apost. De baptizatorum usibu nascitur, quia non eum generat, vnde regeneratus, sed vnde generatus est, quod nascitur de carne, caro est. 3. negamus pios post Baptismum peccato penitus carere. Nam distinguendum est inter peccatum ipsum, et peccati reatum: Hic per Baptismum tollitur; illud tamen relinquitur. ideoque à posteris attrahitur. Semper enim renatis peccatum adhæret, licet non imputetur. A negata verò imputatione ad uegationem ipsius corruptionis non valet consequentia.

XLII. 6. Si per generationem peccatum propagatur, damnanda erant coniugia. Resp. Nego consequentiam, quia conjugium est ipsius Dei institutum, nunquam damnandum, semper adprobandum. Per accidens autem tantùm fit, quod propagatur in coniugio peccatum, à quo accidentali vitio ad destructionem ordinis diuini non licet argumentari. Vitia enim naturæ non tollunt beneficia & ordinem, à Deo naturæ opifice institutum.


### Question III. How does original sin pass into us?

I. Pelagius indeed once raved that it passes only by example and imitation; we, however, establish that it passes by carnal generation. Hence Adam is said to have begotten a son in his own image, Gen. 5:3. Hence we are all unclean from an unclean seed, Job 14:4. Conceived in sins, Ps. 51:7; flesh from flesh, John 3:6; by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2:3.

II. Here, however, the Pelagians immediately objected: If propagation occurs through generation, it follows that the rational soul also, as the πρωτον δεκτικὸν [first recipient] of sin, is generated, which Since the latter seems absurd, the former will not have to be brought forward either. And from this has now arisen that most noble question, sufficiently sung in the Lyceum and the Church, concerning the origin of rational souls: whether, indeed, they are created immediately by God, or whether they are generated by parents?

III. Augustine seized upon τὸ ἐπέχειν [suspension of judgment] as the safest course: For there is no danger if the origin of the soul remains hidden, provided that its redemption is clear, he says in Epist. 157, adapted: And since the assertion of Scripture is evident, that we are all conceived in sins, let us therefore hold this thesis, even if we do not know the origin of the soul. For it is certain that sin is propagated, although the mode of propagation regarding the soul is uncertain. Let us acknowledge here the custom of Scripture, for which it is solemn to state the fact, but to withhold the mode.

IV. If, however, something must be said out of abundance, we hold with the blessed Luther the opinion of traducianism, and indeed for this reason primarily, because the transmission of original sin cannot otherwise be proven. For neither by reading, nor by praying, nor by reasoning can it be found how original sin is defended along with the creation of souls, a fact which Augustine ingenuously confesses he has experienced in Epist. 27 and 157. Since this argument has been treated at length in Sect. 0. 3. Phil. Sob. c. 6. q. 1., and the whole of this question is discussed there, I do not wish to do what has already been done, but I refer the reader there, especially since this dispute would otherwise grow beyond expectation.

Latin:

I. Pelagius quidem olim delirauit, transire tantùm exemplo & imitatione, nos 1. statuimus, carnali generatione. Hinc Adam dicitur filium generasse ad imaginem suam, Gen. 5. 3. Hinc omnes immundi sumus de immundo semine, Iob. 14. 4. Concepti in peccatis, Psal. 51. 7. caro ex carne, Ioh. 3. 6. naturâ filij iræ, Ephes. 2. 3.

II. Hic verò protinus obiecerunt Pelagiani: Si propagatio fit per generationem, sequitur & animam rationalem, tanquam peccati πρωτον δεκτικὸν generari, quod posterius cùm absurdum videatur, neque prius afferendum erit. Atque hinc jam orta est quæstio illa nobilissima, in Lyceo & Ecclesia satis decantata de origine animarum rationalium, an nimirùm à Deo immediatè creentur, an verò à parentibus ingenerentur?

III. Augustinus τὸ ἐπέχειν tanquam tutissimum arripuit: Non enim periculum est si origo animi lateat, dummodo redemtio clareat, inquit Epist. 157. adaptatum: Et cum evidens sit Scripturæ assertio, nos omnes in peccatis concipi, propterea thesin hanc teneamus, licet animę ortum nesciamus. Peccatum etenim propagari certum est, quamvis modus propagationis quo ad animam sit incertus. Agnoscamus hic Scripturæ morem, cui solenne est rem dicere, modum retinere.

IV. Si tamen ex abundanti aliquid dicendum sit, tenemus cum B. Luthero sententiam de traduce, & quidem ob hanc imprimis causam, quia peccati originalis traductio aliàs nequit probari. Neque enim legendo, neque orando, neque ratiocinando inueniri potest, quo modo cùm animarum creatione peccatum originis defendatur, in quod se expertum esse ingenuè confitetur August. Epist. 27. & 157. Quod argumentum cùm prolixè sit pertractatum. Sect. 0. 3. Phil. Sob. c. 6. q. 1. ibiqué tota hæc quæstio discussa habeatur, actum agere nolo, sed lectorem eò remitto, præsertim cum aliàs disputatio hæc præter opinionem excreuerit.


### Question V. If Eve alone had sinned, would she have propagated original sin to her descendants?

I. The Scholastics raise this question, but idly. For it is already established that Adam sinned together with her; who without a doubt would not have known Eve if she alone had violated the law of the Lord. What good, therefore, will it do to dispute about that which did not exist before, and of whom Scripture has made no mention at all?

II. Meanwhile, however, it is likely that sin would not have been transmitted to descendants if Adam had remained in a state of integrity. For the man is the active principle of generation, and therefore also of those things which are propagated through generation. From a just parent, therefore, injustice could not have proceeded. And to this point looks that statement of Augustine, book 12 on the Trinity, chapter 12: In those two first humans, each bore their own person, and therefore if the woman alone had eaten the forbidden food, she alone would certainly have been punished with the penalty of death. But whether God would have added a spouse to him as well is uncertain, nor is it for us to inquire into that.

III. By way of a finishing touch, let two Scholastic errors be noted here. 1. Some write, as Bellarmine reports in book 4 on the Loss of Grace, chapter 13, that the necessity of dying and the other inconveniences which mortality brings with it would have flowed down to the children from the sin of Eve alone, but without sin: But how could a penalty without fault, the wages of sin without the sin itself, have been propagated? 2. Scotus in book 2, distinction 32, affirms that even if Adam had not sinned, nevertheless, if Cain had sinned, the guilt would have been derived to his descendants. But indeed, Cain was not the head and root of the entire human race, and therefore, if he had sinned, he could not on that account have infected the whole nature.

Latin:

I. Mouent hanc quæstionem Scholastici, sed otiosè. Iam enim constat Adamum vnà peccâsse; qui procul dubio Evam non cognouisset, si sola legem Domini violasset. Quid igitur proderit, de non ante, & cuius Scriptura nullam planè mentionem fecit multis altercari?

II. Interim tamen vero simile est, peccatum non fuisse traducēdum in posteros, si Adam in statu integritatis permansisset. Vir enim est principium actiuum generationis, ideoque & eorum, quæ per generationem propagantur. A parente igitur justo jniustitia non potuisset proficisci. Et huc spectat illud August. l. 12 de Trin. c. 12. In illis duobus primis hominibus personam suam quisque portabat, & ideò si sola mulier cibum edisset illicitum, sola vtique mortis supplicio plecteretur. Num autem Deus etiam ipsi additurus fuisset coniugem, incertum est neque nostrum in ea inquirere.

III. Colophonis loco annotentur hic duo errores Scholastici. 1. Scribunt nonnulli, referente Bellarm. l. 4. de A. G. c. 13. ex peccato solius Euæ dimanaturam in filios moriendi necessitatem, & cætera incommoda, quæ mortalitas secum trahit, sed absque peccato: Verùm quomodo pœna sine culpa, stipendium peccati sine ipso peccato potuisset propagari? 2. Scotus in 2. dist. 32. adfirmat, si maximè Adam non peccâsset, attamen peccante Caino culpam in posteros fuisse deriuatam. At verò Cain non fuit caput & radix totius generis humani ideoque si peccasset, ob id totam naturam inficere non potuisset.


### Quaestio VI. And the last. Do the sins of immediate parents pass over to their children?

The Papists deny this universally, as can be seen from Lombard, book 2, distinction 33, letter E, and Bellarmine, book 4 on the Loss of Grace, chapter 18. We, however, although not always and ordinarily, yet sometimes assert that those things are propagated. For 1. Exodus 20:5, God threatens that He will visit the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation

And this could not happen, unless sins or the seeds of sins were propagated together. For otherwise the Son would bear the iniquity of the Father, if he were entirely immune from guilt. God therefore permits that wicked parents beget such children, whom for that reason he affects with the same punishment, and thus visits the sins unto the third and fourth generation. 2. Experience itself testifies to this, while from the avaricious the avaricious, from the lustful the lustful, are for the most part begotten, not otherwise than from the stone-afflicted the stone-afflicted. Meanwhile, however, we maintain that the habits of vices themselves are not transfused, but only the seeds, and a greater propensity than in others is engendered, which itself, however, is not perpetual, since the best Kings, Hezekiah and Josiah, were born from the worst parents.

Latin:

Vniuersaliter hoc negant Pontificij, vti videre est ex Lomb. l. 2. dist 33. lit. E. & Bell. 4. de A. G. c. 18. Nos autem, licèt non semper & ordinariè; quandoque tamen illa propagari asserimus, Nam 1. Exod. 20. 5. minatur Deus, se visitaturum iniquitatem Patrum in filios, in tertiam & quartam generationem

Ac fieri hoc non posset, nisi peccata vel peccatotum semina vnà propagarentur. Aliàs enim Filius portaret iniquitatem Patris, si à culpa planè foret immunis. Permittit ergo Deus, vt scelerati parentes tales progeneret filios, quos ob id eodem supplicio afficit, & ita in tertiam & quartam generationem peccata visitat. 2. Testatur hoc ipsum experientia, dum ex auaris auari, ex libidinosis libidinosi, non secus atque ex calculosis calculosi plerunq̄ue gignuntur. Interim v. non ipsos vitiorum habitus transfundi, sed tantùm semina, maiorem præ alijs pronitatem ingenerari statuimus, quod ipsum tamen non est perpetuum, siquidem Reges Optimi, Ezechias & Iosias ex pessimis parentibus fuere prognati.


## 7 Disputation VI. On the Essence and Definition of Original Sin

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Augustinus Pauspertel of Iglau, Moravia.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisner. S S. Th. D.

Resp. Augustino Pauspertel Iglaniâ-Morano.


### Problem I

After it has been proven in the preceding discussion that there exists a certain sin of origin, most foully corrupting human nature; it is necessary to investigate what that thing is in which it formally consists, and what definition it has.

II. Before Augustine, however, with the Pelagians not yet litigating, no accurate resolution of this controversy is read: but the faithful in pious simplicity, and simple piety, were content with the explanation of these three problems. 1. Whether there is any original sin? 2. Whence it is? What its effects were. III. Pelagius seized upon this, because he saw that his own error could be covered under that generality, and therefore he rebuked Augustine, because he dared to define sin with such vehemence, which nevertheless the whole of Antiquity had not been the cause of. Hence he contended that the knowledge of those three was sufficient; the rest, which are wont to be moved; Whether it is contracted by imitation or propagation? Whether it is guilt, or some inherent depravity? are matters OF QUESTION NOT OF FAITH.

IV. Pighius reheated this gross Pelagianism in our century, greatly accusing the rashness of those (as he himself indeed rashly called it) who did not blush to define original sin, and on that account he agitated not a little against the Augsburg Confession.

V. But the Council of Trent, although at first glance it seems to posit something certain, and to bring forward something concerning sin; is nevertheless mere fraud, if we believe Andradius; since, as he himself reports, the Fathers deliberately wrapped the proper definition of sin in silence and left it free for everyone to opine, with the exception only of the Protestants.

VI. But in truth, because we have Scripture shining before us, and the examples of Augustine and other Fathers who established something certain; therefore, so that that native stain may be thoroughly known, and the tricks of heretics may be more easily guarded against, it pleases us to inquire somewhat more diligently into its nature: to which end we shall propose and briefly discuss five distinct ζητήματα. 1. Whether original sin is a substance? 2. Whether it is a total privation of the divine image? 3. Whether besides στέρησιν it is at the same time a positive quality? 4. What subject it has? And finally 5. How it may be accurately defined:

QUESTION I. Whether original sin is a substance?

I. The Manichaeans formerly imagined certain evil substances sprung from an evil god, which essentially and by their own nature are sin itself, which error has long since been proscribed from the Church. It is said, however, to have been renewed by Matthias Flacius Illyricus, a distinguished theologian, whence a distinction is commonly made between ancient and recent Manichaeism, and between the older and more recent Manichaeans.

II. This controversy began in the year 1561 in the Weimar disputation, which Flacius held with Victorinus Strigelius the Synergist. Since the latter too much extenuated original sin, calling it a slight accident which could not corrupt the substance; Flacius, in the heat of the disputation, leaning to the other extreme, called sin the very substance of man, which thesis he afterwards wished to defend by all means.

III. But because that error is too gross and monstrous, so that it is hardly probable that so great a theologian would have completely removed every distinction between the substance of man and inherent sin, hence some distinguish between the words and the mind of Flacius and think that he spoke badly, but did not think so badly.

IV. And indeed very harsh words are found in the writings of Flacius, while he calls original sin the very substantial form of man, the heart itself, nay, the rational soul itself in the highest degree, and with its best powers, and there are many more expressions similar to those; The whole man, he says, part 2, Clavis tract. 6, on original sin, p. 368, as much as he is, whether in substance or in accidents, insofar as he is such, is a mere abomination and sin. And on the same page: We were formerly in the first creation something very good, both in accidents and in substance, afterwards we have been changed essentially into a thing very evil in its substance, as if the best wine were changed into the most bitter vinegar. P. 370. In this way I feel and assert that the primary original sin is substance, because the rational soul, and especially its most noble and substantial powers, namely the intellect and will, which before were so excellently formed that they were the true image of God, are now by the fraud of Satan so completely inverted that they are the true and living image of Satan.

V. Although these words are sufficiently crude and foreign to the ὑποτυπώσει ὑγιαινόντων λόγων: yet they judge that it does not follow from there that Flacius denied every difference between accident and substance. For in that very treatise, he concedes that something of good remained in man after the fall. As much as possible, he says, p. 370, there still remains in man something created by God which is properly and PER SE GOOD, just as in the devils there still survives some excellent creature of God: yet that very thing is like that more ignoble matter, and like clay from a pot. p. 369 he distinguishes between material and formal substance. For he says, the substance of some earthen or glass or silver vessel can be considered, both insofar as it is from such matter, and insofar as that vessel is thus formed beautifully or uglily, brought into an honest or foul form. He applies this distinction thus p. 370: in this dispute concerning the corruption of man, I do not deny that that viler matter or mass of man founded in the beginning has still somehow REMAINED, even though greatly vitiated, just as in wine or spices, with the airy and fiery substance expiring, there would remain only the earthy and watery: but I feel that the substantial form, or formal substance, has perished, nay, and has been changed into the contrary. I speak however NOT OF THAT EXTERNAL AND CRUDE FORM as that man consists of body and soul, has an erect stature, two feet, hands, eyes, ears and the like, and is a laughing, counting, reasoning animal, etc. but I speak of that most noble substantial form, to which especially the heart itself, or rather the rational soul, was formed. This substantial strength most especially, and this Theology properly then regards and considers; and from it judges him, not whether an animal is risible, as that risible Philosophy does (in this forum, indeed): In turn a little later: Just as a vessel of dishonor is judged not by its matter, but by its substantial form and use: so man is estimated by that highest degree of most noble form, and is either a holy and just image of God: or on the contrary, an image and mask of Satan and sin, in truth, judged hostile and abominable to God, and is so called by God and Scripture. And soon he adds: Nor do I deny that some part of original sin is ACCIDENTS. Sin has so pervaded the whole man, and also the whole world, that it can be found in the whole man and in all categories; and it is almost a certain transcendent. For some sin is substance, namely the flesh itself, the old Adam, the heart of stone or the sense of the flesh, some is accident, such as vain and worst inclinations born with us, etc. Again p. 378. Before men and Philosophy perhaps it is still the same species of man that was before, but God and Theology will by no means concede that the sons of God and the sons of the devil, angels of light and angels of darkness, are the same species: new and old men: having the image of God, or formed to the image of God, and transformed into the image of Satan. And finally p. 379 Some may object that it is nevertheless necessary to distinguish the creature of God from sin, which is not from God. I respond: separate for me now the devil from his inherent malice. We cannot therefore distinguish these things for another except by saying that man, by reason of his first creation and also his present preservation, is from God, just as the devil himself is: but by reason of that horrible metamorphosis he is from the devil, who, by the vigor of the effective sentence and punishment of an angry God, 'You shall die the death,' not only snatched us for himself into most vile slaves: but also refounded, remade, and changed, or if I may so say, metamorphosed us into another man (as Scripture speaks), just as he himself is inverted.

VI. From these and similar explanations of Flacius they gather that he himself acknowledged a certain distinction between sin and the substance of man, and thus had only spoken poorly: which they judge to be even more clearly evident from this, if the sources from which he derived his dogma, and the respects in which he defended it, are considered a little more exactly. And of these, five in particular can be counted.

VII. 1. He saw that Scripture for the most part uses concrete and substantial words, not abstract ones; so that it accuses the man himself, the soul itself, and the heart, by calling it iron, stone, adamant, etc. But because sin is accused: hence he concluded that the very substance of man is sin, when nevertheless he ought to have distinguished between that which is accused and condemned in itself, and that which is accused and condemned on account of something else. The man himself indeed is accused in his entirety, but not in himself, as man, but on account of something else, namely sin, which he has in himself or commits. And indeed every error of Flacius flowed from this source, or among the first, that he never wished to speak of sin itself in the abstract, but always in the concrete, by joining man and the corruption of man, and therefore he said that sin, taken in that copulative and concrete sense, is the very corrupted substance of man. Hence on page 368 he writes: God does not contend with abstracts or ideas (which in reality are nothing in the nature of things but only for the sake of a certain convenience in thinking, not otherwise than as circles of the heavens are imagined in a sphere by astronomers) but with the concretes themselves, and their subjects, authors, and sources.

IIX. 2. He did not consider man physically, but theologically, not as he has a soul and body, but rather as he has such a soul and such a body, whence he always distinguished between the physical and the theological man: For theology considers man in his states; not as he is a rational animal, but as he is either a Son of God or a son of the devil, that is, as he is whole or corrupted. That integrity and this corruption Flacius called substantial form and formal substance, because that gave to

Latin:

POsteaquàm præcedente συζητήσει euictum est; dari quoddam originis peccatum, naturam humanam fœdissimè corrumpens; indagandum testat, quidnam illud sit, in quo formaliter consistat, & quam definitionem habeat?

II. Ante Augustinum verò, Pelagianis nondum litigantibus non legitur accurata aliqua controversiæ huius enodatio: sed fideles in pia simplicitate, & simplici pietate contenti erant trium horum problematum explicatione. 1. An sit aliquod malum originale? 2. Vnde sit? Quæ eius fuerint effectus. III. Arripuit hoc Pelagius, quia vidit sub ista generalitate suum tegi posse errorem, ideoque corripuit Augustinum, quod tanta vehementia peccatum definire auderet, quod tamen vniuersa Antiquitas causæ non fuerit. Proinde notitiam trium istorum sufficere contendit; reliqua, quæ moueri soleant; Vtrum imitatione vel propagatione contrahatur? An reatus sit, vel inhærens aliqua prauitas? esse res QVAESTIONIS NON FIDEI.

IV. Crassum hunc Pelagianismum nostro seculo recoxit Pighius, valdè accusans eorum temeritatem, (vt ipse quidem temerè nuncupauit) qui originale peccatum definire non erubescerent, eoque nomine Augustanam Confessionem non parum exagitanit.

V. Concilium verò Tridentinum, quamuis primâ fronte videatur certi aliquid ponere, & de peccato afferrere; mera tamen, si Andradio credimus, fraus est; cùm ipso referente propriam peccati rationem consulto silentio Patres inuoluerint & cuique opinari liberum reliquerint exceptis solis Protestantibus.

VI. Verum enimverò, quia Scripturam prælucentem, & Augustini Patrumque aliorum certi aliquid statuentium exempla habemus; propterea, vt natiua labes illa penitùs cognoscatur, & hæreticorum strophæ faciliùs præcaueantur, in naturam eius nonnihil diligentius placet inquirere: quem in finem quinque distincta ζητήματα proponemus & breuiter discutiemus. 1. An peccatum originis sit substantia? 2. An omnimoda sit diuinæ imaginis priuatio? 3. An præter στέρησιν simul positiua sit qualitas? 4. Quod subiectum habeat? Et denique 5. Quomodo accuratè definiri queat:

QVAESTIO I. An peccatum originis sit Substantia?

I. Manichæi olim quasdam Substantias malas à Deo malo ortas finxerunt, quæ ὑσιωδῶς & per naturam suam sint ipsum peccatum, qui error jam dudum ex Ecclesia proscriptus fuit. Renovatus autem dicitur à Matthia Flacio Illyrico, Theologo insigni, vnde vulgò distinguitur inter Manichæismum veterem & recentem, interque Manichæos antiquiores & recentiores.

II. Cœpit autem hæc controuersia anno 1561. in disputatione Vinariensi, quam Flacius habuit cum Victorino Strigelio Synergista. Hic cùm nimis extenuaret peccatum originis, nominando illud leviculum accidens, quod substantiam corrumpere haud queat; Flacius in feruore disputationis ad extremum alterum declinans, peccatum ipsam hominis substantiam appellauit, quam θέσιν postea omnibus modis φυλάττειν voluit.

III. Quia verò error iste nimis crassus & monstrosus est, vt vix probabile sit, tantum Theologum, omnem penitus distinctionem inter hominis substantiam & peccatum inhærens sustulisse, hinc nonnulli inter verba & mentem Flacij distingunt eumque malè locutum esse, sed non ita malè sensisse arbitrantur.

IV. Et sane durissima verba in scriptis Flacij reperiuntur, dum peccatum originis vocat ipsam substantiælem hominis formam, ipsum cor, imò ipsam rationalem animam in summo gradu, optimisque potentiis suis & quæ locutiones sunt plures illis similes; Totus homo inquit, par. 2. Clavis tract. 6. de pecc. orig. p. 368. quantus tam est siue in substantia, siue in accidentibus quatenus talis est, mera abominatio ac peccatum est. Et ead. pag. Nos olim fuimus in prima creatione quiddam valde bonum, tam in accidentibus, tum in substantia, postea mutati sumus essentialiter in rem valde malam substantia sua, vt si vinum optimum esset mutatum in acetu acerbissimum. P. 370. Hoc modo sentio & assero, primarium peccatum originale esse substantiam, quia anima rationalis, & praesertim eius nobilissimae substantialesque potentiae, nempe intellectus & voluntas, quae antea ita erant praeclare formatae, vt essent vera imago Dei, nunc sunt fraude Satanae adeo prorsus inuersae, vt sint vera ac viua imago Satanae.

V. Quamuis autem haec verba satis crassa sunt, & ab ὑποτυπώσει ὑγιαινόντων λόγων aliena: tamen inde non sequi censent, Flacium omnem accidentis & substantiae differentiam negasse, Nam in illo ipso tractatu, concedit, aliquid boni post lapsum remansisse in homine. Vt maxime, inquit, p. 370. remaneat adhuc aliquid in homine à Deo creatu quod propriè ac PER SE BONVM est, sicut & in diabolis adhuc aliqua praestans Dei creatura superest: tamen illud ipsum est velut illa ignobilior materia, ac veluti lutum de testa. p. 369 distinguit inter substantiam materialem & formalem. Potest enim inquit, considerari substantia alicuius testacei aut vitrei, aut argentei vasis, tùm quatenus ex tali materia est, tum quatenus vas illud sic formatum est pulcrè aut turpiter, in formam honestam aut foedam perductum. Hanc distinctionem ita applicat p. 370: in hac disputatione de corruptione hominis, non nego illam viliorem materiam aut massam hominis initio conditam adhuc vtcunque REMANSISSE, tametsi valde vitiatam, sicut in vino aut aromatibus, expirante aëreà & igneà substantia remaneret tantùm in terrena & aquea: sed formam substantialem, aut substantiam formalem deperijsse, imò & in contrariam esse mutatam sentio. Loquor autem NON DE ISTA EXTERNA ET CRASSA FORMA vt quod homo constet corpore & animà, habet staturam erectam, duos pedes, manus, oculos aures & similia, sitque animal ridens, numerans, ratiocinans, &c. sed loquor de ea nobilissima substantiali forma, ad quam praecipuè ipsum cor, aut potius anima rationalis formata erat. Hanc fortudinem substantialem potissimàm, & hoc propriè tum respicit & considerat Theologia; & ex eo eum censet, non an sit animalis risibile, vt facit ista, (in hoc quidem foro) risibilis Philosophia: Vicissim paulo pòst: Sicut vas ignominiae non ex materia, sed ex forma substantiali ac vsu censetur:ita homo ex illo summo gradu nobiliss. formae æstimatur, & vel imago Dei sancta & iusta: vel contra, imago ac larua Satanae & peccatum, reuera, Deo inimica & abominabilis censetur, ac à Deo Scripturaque vocatur. Et mox addit: Neque nego aliquam partem peccati originalis esse ACCIDENTIA Scion. peccatum ita peruafisse totum hominem, ac etiam totum mundum, vt possit in toto homine & in omnibus prædicamentis reperiri; ac sit ferme transcendens quoddam. Aliquod enim peccatum est substantia, nempe ipsa caro, vetus Adam, cor lapideum aut sensus carnis, aliquod est accidens, vt vanæ & pessimæ inclinationes nobiscum natæ, &c. Rursus P. 378. Coram hominibus & Philosophia forte est adhuc eadem species hominis, quæ fuit antea, sed Deus ac Theologia nequaquam concedent, eandem speciem esse filios Dei, & filios diaboli, angelos lucis, & angelos tenebrarum: nouos & veteres homines: habentes imaginem Dei, aut formatos ad imaginem Dei, & transformatos in imaginem Satanæ. Et tandem p. 379 Opponant aliqui, oportere tamen distingui creaturam Dei à peccato, quod non est à Deo. Respond. separato tu mihi jam diabolum à sua inhærente malitia. Non ergo alteri possumus ista distinguere quàm dicendo, hominem ratione primæ creationis & præsentis etiam conseruationis esse à Deo, sicut & ipsum diabolum: sed ratione istius horrendæ metamorphoseos esse à diabolo, qui nos vigore efficacis sententiæ ac pœnæ irati Dei; Morte morieris, non solùm sibi in vilissima mancipia rapuit: sed etiam refudit, recoxit, & commutauit, aut vt ità dicam, metamorphizauit in virum alium, (vt Scriptura loquitur) sicut ipsemet inuersus est.

VI. Ex hisce & similibus Flacij explicationibus colligunt, ipsum quoddam inter peccatum & hominis substantiam discrimen agnouisse, adeoque tantum malè locutum esse: quod muper ex eo evidentiùs patere censent, si fontes, ex quibus dogma suum deduxit, & respectus, quibus illud defendit, paulo exactiùs considerentur. Illorunique quinque potissimum numerari possunt.

VII. 1. Vidit Scripturam plerumque concretiuis & substantialibus, non abstractiuis vti vocibus; ita vt ipsum hominem, ipsam animam & cor accuset, vocando illud ferreum, lapidem, adamantinum, &c. Quia verò peccatum accusatur: hinc ipsam hominis substantiam peccatum esse conclusit, cùm tamen distinguere debuisset, inter id quod per se, & inter id quod propter aliud accusatur & damnatur. Ipse quidem homo totus accusatur, sed non per se, quâ homo, verùm ob aliud nempe peccatum, quod in se habet, aut committit. Et sanè omnis error Flacij ex hoc fonte vel in primis fluxit, quod nunquam in abstracto de peccato ipso loqui voluit, sed semper in concreto, conjungendo hominem, & hominis corruptionem, ideoque peccatum illo sensu copulatiuo & concretiuo sumtum, dixit esse ipsam hominis substantiam corruptam. Hinc P. 368. scribit: Deus non contendit cum abstractis aut ideis, (quae reuerâ nihil in rerum natura sunt sed tantùm commoditatis cuiusdam in cogitando causa non aliter ac apud Astronomos cœlorum circuli in sphæra finguntur) sed cum ipsis cõcretis, & eorũ subiectis, authoribus ac fontibus.

IIX. 2. Non physicè considerauit hominem, sed Theologicè, non prout habet animam & corpus, sed potius prout talem animam, tale corpus habet, vnde semper distinxit inter hominem Physicum & Theologicum: Nam Theologia hominem in statibus suis considerat; non prout est animal rationale, sed prout est vel Filius Dei, vel filius diaboli, hoc est, prout integer aut corruptus est. Illam integritatem, & hanc corruptionem vocauit Flacius formam substantialem, & substantiam formalem quia ista dedit ho-


### Problem I: man being, so that he may be whole, these, so that he may be a corrupt man

man being, so that he may be whole, these, so that he may be a corrupt man: And from this he deduced that sin itself is a substantial form, because it gave being to the corrupt man, when nevertheless this being was rather accidental than substantial, and therefore he again played with terms and perverted words. For what we call a quality, that Flacius called a substantial form. For he judged that the soul and body are merely the matter of the Theological man, but that integrity or corruption is the form, and consequently the substance. When therefore from a whole man he becomes corrupt, then he says the form of the Theological man is lost, that is, his integrity and substance (not Physical, but Theological) are changed; while another form is introduced into this matter, namely corruption. From which it appears how inconveniently he spoke, while he named the quality itself and the mode of considering it a formal substance. It must rather be said that the substance, both in the state of integrity and in the state of the fall, always is and remains the same in itself, and that only the states are varied, on account of the diverse qualities, which are inconveniently called substantial forms. Nevertheless, they argue that it is evident from this that Flacius never thought that the physical substance of man had been changed, that man had lost his soul and body itself, but that he meant this: In Theology the form of man is not the soul, but either sin or righteousness: But because every form is οὐσία or substance, therefore sin also is a substance, because it is the form of the Theological man. Thus his mind would have been sound, and his tongue only culpable.

IX. 3. He estimated man from his end, which he declared with this simile: Just as a hand, when it is in a corpse, and cannot exercise its duties, is not called the same hand as it was before except equivocally, so man, because after the fall he cannot do that which God willed him to do, and for the doing of which He created him, therefore he is not called the former man in Theology except equivocally: He adds another simile p.

§ 77. Just as a cook does not consider a pot a pot when it is unfit for cooking, and just as salt is not salt when it does not have the power to salt, so man, created in the image of God, did not retain his form when he was depraved through sin. Hence, some think it follows in turn that Flacius held that the very physical substance of man was changed. For the substance of salt and of the pot remains, even if the salt loses the power of salting and the pot the power of cooking. Thus, the physical substance of man remains; yet because it has lost that power of acting which it ought to have acted, he therefore says that man has been entirely changed into another substance, considered, of course, theologically. But he spoke inconveniently again, when he called the power of acting well a certain substance.

X. 4. He saw and knew well that, just as the image of God, so also sin does not adhere extrinsically, but adheres intrinsically and most deeply to man, indeed in such a way that it cannot be separated from the body except through total destruction. Therefore, in order to exaggerate this deformity, on account of which it is natural for man to sin, against the Synergists, he pronounced it not an accident, which is said to be present beyond the corruption of the subject, but the very nature and substance of man. But again, wrongly: for false things must not be assumed so that true things may be defended. Original sin can be exaggerated in other words; there is no need for it to be called a substance. And although sin is natural to us, it is nevertheless not nature itself.

XI. 5. He observed certain similar expressions in the writings of Luther, which he himself cites on pages 372 and 373. Such as, that sin is of the essence of man, that reason is the most stubborn enemy and foe of God; that it is the fountain of all fountains of evils, etc. But all these things were said by Luther about reason and the soul not absolutely, but relatively, on account of the sin with which the soul is infected and contaminated, and therefore it ought not to have been absolutely designated as a substance.

XII. And these were the sources of the Flacian phrase: and as for the respects in which he called sin a substance, whether they free him entirely from error, let the judgment be with others. For he was heard in the presence of many and excellent theologians, whom it is not likely never to have understood the mind of Flacius, and to have condemned him undeservedly.

On the other hand, when the words of Flacius are accurately weighed, he does not seem to have abolished every distinction between accident and substance, unless we wish to say that he contradicted himself, or did not write those things seriously. Wherefore we leave this very thing in doubt, and we affirm neither rashly, preferring to follow the censure and judgment of others in all things: This is what had to be noted, lest anyone calumniate. We add this, however, that Flacius was deservedly and by every right refuted by our people. For even if he had not erred in matters, he nevertheless stubbornly and contentiously defended that most absurd phrase, and one entirely contrary to the analogy of faith, which was in no way to be tolerated in him.

XIII. Furthermore, whatever may be the case regarding the mind of Flacius, his followers nevertheless cannot be excused in the least. For these spoke far more crudely, and thought more absurdly, inasmuch as they were so importunate that they affirmed the nature and soul of man to be simply nothing else than sin, and thus they abolished every distinction whatsoever between substance and the vice of substance. Against these unlearned and importunate Flacians, therefore, our people chiefly opposed themselves, and first established an article concerning this question in the Formula of Concord.

XIV. But because they always calumniate that original sin is too much extenuated by us, for that reason, before we come to the proof of the truth, we shall premise three theses or maxims, from which both the nature of sin and our opinion will become more clearly known.

XV. Thesis 1. Original sin is not a trivial accident.

For He did not leave nature uncorrupted, but so deeply infected all the powers and faculties of man, that the mind is blind in spiritual matters, the will is turned away, and every thought by nature inclines only toward evil. We therefore condemn all who minimize sin, and we both desire and allow it to be exaggerated in every way, provided that such exaggeration does not clash with the analogy of faith or remove the form of sound words.

XVI. II. Sin is not a temporal or passing accident; but fixed, permanent, and clinging most tenaciously throughout the whole time of life,

There are certain accidents that corrupt their subject, but only for a time, and therefore they can be separated by external care, such as some diseases of the body. Lest anyone think, therefore, that sin is considered by us as only a passing and temporal evil, we say expressly that it is not only a corrupting accident, but also a perpetual one, always remaining in the nature of man. For just as innate heat can never be separated from the body, so neither can sin from the nature of man. For sin is ἁμαρτία εὐπερίσατος, as it is called in Heb. 12, verse 7, that is, a depravity tenaciously clinging to the whole human substance and all its parts.

XVII. Thesis III. Sin and the substance of man are not to be torn apart, or placed separately and apart.

This Thesis contributes greatly to the exaggeration of sin against the Synergists, since they distinguish sin and the subject of sin—namely, the substance of man—so far apart that they pronounce sin indeed to be evil, but the very substance of man to be pure, whole, and unharmed. It must by no means be established in this way, but it must be most firmly believed that sin has so invaded the whole nature, and is so deeply fixed in it, that for this reason the whole man is corrupted, and all his substance is most basely depraved, for which reason he can think and do nothing but evil from himself and his own powers.

XVIII. These things therefore being now presupposed, for the exaggeration of sin and the refutation of calumnies, we further teach: That nevertheless there is a great distinction between the substance of man and his inherent sin, so that sin is not precisely the man himself, nor is the man the sin itself, but rather sin adheres in man, as an accident in a subject, and the man is one thing, and the man's sin is another. For in both the substance of man and in sin, two things can be considered: 1. their ὕπαρξις and existence. 2. their ἰδία or essence. As far as their existence is concerned: they are most closely joined, so that you can or should think of neither man without sin, nor sin without man. Therefore, in this respect, he who distinguishes sin and places the substance of man separately and sin separately, or thinks that it at least adheres to him extrinsically, that man Pelagianizes. But as regards their essence; there certainly, unless you overturn all the foundations of the Christian faith, it must be confessed that the very τὸ εἶναι of man is not the τὸ εἶναι of sin, or vice versa; but that the essence of man, because he is man, is one thing, and the essence of sin, as it is sin, is and remains another. And in this respect we say that the nature of man, as created by God, is good; but sin itself, as introduced by the Devil, is evil and vicious.

XIX. Do not, however, infer from this: If nature is good, why is it vicious, and said to do only evil? For we consider man in two ways. 1. abstractly, as regards his simple τὸ εἶναι, and this we call good, because it has God as its author, from whom come only good things. 2. concretely, not only as regards his τὸ εἶναι or by reason of his definition, but also as regards his τὸ ὑπάρχειν and existence, insofar as that original vice adheres in him and always exists together with him. And in this concrete and existential sense, if I may so speak, the pronouncements of the theologians are to be understood when they call man evil, corrupt, and vicious: he is evil, to be sure, not essentially, as if his essence were nothing other than malice; but he is evil accidentally, insofar as the original disease perpetually exists in him and with him, and while it is dominant and not yet repressed, it is impossible for him to act well (I mean spiritual and truly theological goodness), although nature itself as regards τὸ ἄνω is good, since nature does not act immediately, but always through the mediation of accidents and faculties, which, since they are most corrupt through sin, it follows that man, both from nature and by nature, is inclined to nothing but evil.

XX. Briefly, therefore, we include our opinion in this aphorism: human substance and the sin of the substance are to be distinguished, but not torn apart; they are to be distinguished so that Flacianism may be avoided, and not torn apart so that Pelagianism may be avoided. We add, for the sake of illustration, a simile taken from bodily leprosy.

For just as leprosy infects and depraves the whole body and even the most minute particles of the body, so that no health at all remains, nor can a small portion be shown that is not vitiated and foul: so spiritual leprosy, namely original sin, has corrupted the whole substance of man, so that in spiritual matters he is no longer able or capable of anything. Furthermore, just as leprosy and the body are indeed most closely joined as regards existence, and in no way separated, yet the essence of leprosy is not the essence of the human body itself, or vice versa; but the body is one thing, in which the leprosy adheres, and the leprosy itself is another, which infects the body as an accident: so we do not disguise that sin is by no means separated from the substance of man, nor is there anything found in man that is not defiled and depraved by that stain and corruption: similarly the εἶναι of man is not, nor can it be, the εἶναι of sin itself, but these two are most distinct, although they cohere and coalesce in one subject. XXI. And this was the explanation of our opinion, to the confirmation of which we now proceed, intending to bring forward: 1. Sayings of Scripture and consequences derived from them.

Latin:

mini esse, vt sit integer, hæc, vt sit homo corruptus: Atque hinc deduxit, ipsum peccatum esse formam substantialem, quia homini corrupto dedit esse, cùm tamen hoc esse potius accidentale fuerit quàm substantiale, ideoque rursus terminis lusit & vocabula peruertit. Quod enim nos qualitatem, id Flacius formam dixit substantialem. Censuit enim, animam & corpus esse duntaxat materiam hominis Theologici, integritatem verò vel corruptionem esse formam, & per consequens substantiam. Quando igitur ex homine integro fit corruptus, tunc perdi ait formam hominis Theologici, id est, integritatem & substantiam eius (non Physicam, sed Theologicam) immutari; dum alia forma in istam materiam introducitur, videlicet corruptio. Ex quibus apparet, quàm incommodè locutus sit, dúm substantiam formalem nominauit ipsam qualitatem & modum considerandi. Dicendum potius est, substantiam tum in statu integritatis, tum in statu lapsus semper esse & manere in sese eandem, variari tantùm status, propter diuersas qualitates, quæ incommodè dicuntur formę substantiales. Nihilominis autem hinc patere autument, Flacium nunquam sensisse, quod physica hominis Substantia fuerit immutata, quod homo ipsam animam & corpus amiserit, sed hoc voluisse, In Theologia formam hominis non esse animam, sed vel peccatum, vel iustitiam: Quia verò forma omnis sit ὑσία vel substantia, ideò & peccatum esse substantiam, quia forma sit hominis Theologici. Sic mens eius fuisset sana, & lingua tantùm culpabilis.

IX. 3. Æstimauit hominem a fine, quod declarauit hac similitudine: Sicut manus, quando est in cadave re, & non potest exercere sua munia, non nisi æquiuocè dicitur manus eadem, quæ fuit antea, ita homo, quia post lapsum non potest id facere, quod eum facere voluit, & ad quod faciendum creauit Deus, ideò non nisi æquiuocè in Theologia dicitur prior homo: Addit aliud simile p.

§ 77. Sicut coquus ollam pro olla non habet, quando ad coquendum est inepta, & sicut sal non est sal, quando non est saliens, ita homo ad imaginem Dei creatus, formam suam non retinuit, cùm per peccatum depravatus est. Hinc a. vicissim sequi existimant, quod Flacius senserit, ipsam Physicam hominis substantiam esse immutatam. Salis n. & ollæ substantia manet, etiamsi sal saljendi, olla coquendi vim amittat. Ita manet hominis substantia physica; attamen quia vim illam agendi, quod agere debebat, amisit; ideo dicit hominem prorsus fuisse immutatum in substantiam aliam, Theologicè nimirum consideratam. Sed rursus incommodè est locutus, dum vim benè agendi substantiam quandam nominavit.

X. 4. Vidit & bene novit, quod, ut imago Dei, sic & peccatum non extrinsece adhæreat, sed intrinsece & altissime inhæreat homini, ita quidem, ut nequeat sequestrari a corpore, nisi per totalem destructionem. Hanc ergo deformitatem, propter quam homini naturale est peccare, vt contra Synergistas exaggeraret, ideò non accidens, quod præter sub ecti corruptionem adesse dicitur, sed ipsam hominis naturam & substantiam esse pronunciavit, Sed iterum malè: Non enim assumenda sunt falsa, vt defendantur vera. Potest aliis verbis peccatum originis exaggerari; Non opus est, vt nuncupetur substantia. Et quâvis peccatū nobis naturale sit, ipsa tamē natura nõ est.

XI. 5. Observavit in scriptis Lutheri similes quasdam locutiones; quas ipse citat pag. 372. 373. Vt, quod peccatum sit de essentia hominis, quod ratio sit pertinacissima hostis & inimica Dei; quòd sit fons fontium omnium malorum, &c. Sed hæc omnia de ratione & anima dicta sunt à Luthero non absolutè, sed relatè, propter peccatū quo anima infecta & contaminata est, ideoque illud non debuisset absolutè substantia indigitari.

XII. Et hi fuerunt fontes Phraseos Flacianæ: & respectus quibus peccatum dixit substantiam, qui nùm eum ab errore penitus liberent, apud alios esto judicium. Auditus enim coràm est à multis & præstantibus Theologis, quos mentem Flacij nunquam percepisse, eumque immeritò condemnasse non sit vero simile.

Versa autem vice, cùm verba Flacij accuratè perpenduntur, non omnem distinctionem accidentis & substantiæ videtur sustulisse, nisi velimus dicere illum sibi contradixisse, vel illa seriò non scripsisse. Quapropter hoc ipsum in dubio relinquimus, & neutrum temerè ad firmamus, aliorum potiùs censuram & judicium in omnibus secuturi: Id quod monendum fuit, ne quis calumnietur. Hoc tamen addimus, meritò omnique iure Flacium à nostris esse refutatum. Nam si maximè non errâsset in rebus, phrasin tamen istam absurdissimam, & analogiæ fidei prorsùs contrariam, pertinaciter & contentiose defendit, quod in ipso minimè tolerandum fuit.

XIII. Porrò autem quicquid sit de mente Flacij, sectatores tamen eius minimè excusari possunt. Hi enim longè crassiùs locuti sunt, & absurdiùs senserunt, siquidem tàm fuêre importuni, vt naturam animamque hominis simpliciter nil esse aliud affirmauerint, quàm peccatum, adeóque omnem omninò inter substantiam & substantiæ vitium discriminationē sustulerin, His ergò indoctis & importunis Flacianis Nostri potissimùm sese opposuerunt, primumque de quæstione hac articulum in Formula Concordiæ constituerunt.

XIV. Quia verò semper calumniantur, malum originale nimiùm à nobis extenuari, ea de causa, priusquam ad veritatis probationem veniamus, tres sive theses siue maximas præmittemus, ex quibus tùm peccati natura, tùm nostra sententia clariùs innotescet.

XV. Thesis 1. Peccatū originale non est accidens leuiculum.

Non enim incorruptam reliquit naturam, sed omnes penitus vires & Facultates hominis adeò infecit, vt mens in spiritualibus cæca sit, voluntas auersa, omnisq́ue cogitatio tantùm ad malum propendeat ex natura. Damnamus proindè omnes peccati extenuatores, modisq́ue omnibus illud exaggerari, & volumus & patimur, modò exaggeratio ista in analogiam fidei non impingat, aut formam ὑγιαινόντων λόγων tollat.

XVI. II. Peccatum non est accidens temporale aut transiens; sed fixum, permanens, & omni vitæ tempore tenacissimè inhærens,

Sunt quædam accidentia subjectum suum corrumpentia, sed duntaxat ad tempus, ideoque per extrinsecam curam separari queunt, quales sunt nonnulli corporis morbi. Ne igitur quis putet, à nobis peccatum pro transeunte & temporali tantùm malo haberi, idcircò expressè dicimus, quòd non modò corruptiuum sit accidens, sed etiam perpetuum, semperque in natura hominis permanens. Sicut enim calor natiuus nunquam separari potest à corpore, ita nec peccatum ab hominis natura. Est enim ἁμαρτία εὐπερίσατος, vti vocatur Heb. 12. vers 7. id est, prauitas tenaciter inhærens toti substantiæ humanæ omnibusque ipsius partibus.

XVII. Thesis III. Peccatum & substantia hominis non sunt diuellenda, aut seorsim & separatìm ponenda.

Plurimum facit hæc Thesis ad exaggerationem peccati contra Synergistas, quandoquidem isti peccatum, peccatique subjectum, hominis nempè substantiam, adeò longè discernunt, vt peccatum quidem malum esse pronuncient, ipsam verò hominis substantiam puram, integram & illæsam. Neutiquam ita statuendum, sed firmissimè credendum est, peccatum naturam omnem ita inuasisse, & tàm altè in ea defixum esse, vt propterea totus homo corruptus, omnisq́; eius substantia turpissimè deprauata sit, quàm ob causam ex se suisq́; viribus non nisi mala cogitare & operari potest.

XIIX. His ergò iam præsuppositis, ad exaggerationem peccati, & retorsionem calumniarum facientibus, porrò docemus : Quod nihilominus inter inter hominis substantiam, & eius peccatum inhærens magnum sit discrimen, ita vt peccatum non sit præcisè ipse homo, nec homo sit ipsum peccatum, verùm in homine peccatum hæreat, velut accidens in subiecto, aliudque homo, & aliud hominis peccatum sit. Possunt enim & in hominis substantia, & in peccato duo considerari, 1. eorum ὕπαρξις & existentia. 2. eorum ἰδία vel essentia. Quod existentiam eorum attinet: coniunctissima sunt, ita, vt nec sine peccato hominem, nec sine homine peccatum cogitare possis aut debeas. Hoc igitur respectu qui peccatum distinguit, & seorsum substantiam hominis, seorsum peccatum ponit, vel hoc illi saltem extrinsecè adhærescere existimat, ille Pelagianizat. Quod verò eorum essentiam spectat; ibi certè, nisi omnia fidei Christianæ fundamenta euertas, fatendum est, quòd ipsum τὸ εἶναι hominis, non sit τὸ εἶναι peccati, aut contra; sed quòd alia hominis, quia homo, alia peccati, vt peccatum est, sit & maneat essentia. Et hoc respectu hominis naturam, tanquam à Deo creatam, dicimus bonam; ipsum verò peccatum, tanquam à Diabolo introductum, malum & vitiosum.

XIX. Non tamen hinc inferas: Si natura bona est, cur eog vitiosa, & tantum mala agere perhibetur? Nam consideramus hominem dupliciter. 1. abstractè, quoad simplex εἶναι, & hoc bonum dicimus, quo niam Deum habet authorem, à quo non nisi bona. 2. concretè nō modò quoad τὸ εἶναι vel ratione ὁρίας, sed etiam quoad τὸ ὑπάρχειν & existere, quatenus in eo hæret, & vnà cum eo semper existit illud originale vitium. Atque hoc concretiuo & existentiali, vt ita loquar, sensu intelligenda sunt Theologorum pronunciata, cùm hominem malum corruptum & vitiosum dicunt: malus nimirum est non essentialiter, ac si eius essentia nihil aliud sit, quàm malitia; sed malus est accidentaliter, quatenus in eo & cum eo perpetuò existit originalis morbus, quo dominante & nondum represso impossibile est vt benè agat (bonitatem spiritualem & verè Theologicam intelligo) licèt ipsa natura quoad τὸ ἄνω sit bona, quandoquidem natura non agit immediatè, sed semper mediantibus accidentibus & facultatibus, quæ cum per peccatum sint corruptissimæ, hinc adeò sit, vt homo & ex natura per naturam non nisi ad malum proclivis sit.

XX. Breviter ergò opinionem nostram huic aphorismo includimus, Humana substantia, & substantiæ peccatum sunt distinguenda, sed non divellenda; distinguenda, vt Flacianismus; non divellenda, vt Pelagianismus evitetur. Addimus illustrationis gratia similitudinem à lepra corporali desumtam.

Sicutenim lepra omne corpus, corporísque, etiam minutissimas particulas inficit & depravat, ita vt nihil omninò sanitatis maneat reliquum, neque possit ostendi portiuncula, quæ non sit vitiata & fœtida: sic lepra spiritualis, nempe peccatum originale totam hominis substantiam corrupit, vt in spiritualibus nihil ampliùs valeat aut possit. Porrò quemadmodum lepra & corpus, quoad existentiam quidem sunt coniunctissima: nulloque modo divulsa, attamen lepræ essentia non est ipsa corporis humani essentia, aut contrà; sed aliud est corpus; in quo hæret lepra, & aliud est ipsa lepra, quæ corpus velut accidens inficit: ita non dissimulamus, peccatum à substantia hominis nequaquam esse separatum, neque reperiri quicquam in homine, quod non sit inquinatum & labe tabeque ista depravatum: consimiliter tamen hominis εἶναι non est, nec esse potest ipsùm τὸ peccati εἶναι, sed hæc duo sunt distinctissima, licèt in vno subjecto cohæreant & coalescant. XXI. Et hæc fuit sententiæ nostræ explicatio, ad cuius confirmationem nunc progredimur, allaturi. 1. Dicta Scripturæ & consequentias inde petitas. 2. Testimonia Patrum


### Problem I: Class 1, containing arguments from the Scriptures and the analogy of faith

Class 1, containing arguments from the Scriptures and the analogy of faith.

XXII. 1. From the saying of John 1, v. 3, and 1 Tim. 4, v. 4. John the Evangelist, chapter 1, v. 3, says: All things were made by him, and without him was not any thing made that was made; from which saying it evidently appears that every substance subsisting by itself was made and created by God. Again, however, it is written in 1 Timothy 4, verse 4, Every creature of God is good, since the good is the author of nothing but the good. For God saw what he had made, and behold! they were very good, Gen. 1, last verse. From these sayings we now infer as follows: Every substance is a creature of God, John 1, verse 3. Original sin is a substance, according to the Flacian statement. Therefore, original sin is a creature of God, which is the first absurdity. Furthermore, Every creature of God is good, 1 Tim. 4, v. 4. Original sin is a creature of God, which has now been proven. Therefore, original sin is good, which is unspeakable. For thus we prove that contradiction: No sin is good, which has now been concluded. Therefore, original sin is not sin. You see here a contradiction, which you will not be able to avoid, unless you deny either that every substance is from God, which is against John; or that every creature is good, which is against the Apostle Paul.

XXIII. 2. From Rom. 7, verse 18, and following, where these words are read: I know that there dwelleth in me, that is, in my flesh good. For I do not do the good that I want; but I do the evil that I do not want. If, however, I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me. From this passage we deduce two very strong and completely invincible arguments. First: The inhabitant and that in which it inhabits are not not inhabit itself. But sin and man stand in relation as the inhabitant and that in which it inhabits, because sin is that which inhabits, and man is that in which it inhabits, as Paul says. Therefore sin and man are not one and the same, but differ really. Second: Whatever things are one without distinction, the same things can also be predicated of them. But the same things cannot be predicated of man and original sin. Therefore man and original sin are not one and the same without any distinction. We prove the minor premise, because the Apostle says of sin that it works evil, or that it is the cause of evil: but he denies that this very thing can be said of himself as a man. For the words are clear: It is not I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me. Therefore the sin working evil was one thing, and the Apostle, not working that evil, was another. For to work and not to work cannot be attributed to one and the same thing in the same respect.

XXIV. 3. From Psalm 51, verse 7. Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me. From this we conclude: The one conceived and that in which, or with which, he is conceived, are not one and the same. Otherwise David or anyone else could be said to be conceived in himself, which is absurd. But David was conceived in sins. Psalm 51. Therefore David and the sin in which he was conceived, that is, original sin, are not one and the same.

XXV. From Hebrews 12, verse 1. Where the evil of origin is called εὐπερίστατος ἁμαρτία, the sin surrounding us on all sides and as it were besieging us. It is therefore something distinct from the substance of man, whom it surrounds and besieges. For nothing surrounds itself, or adheres to itself.

XXVI. 5. From the article of creation. Whatever is from God is not evil and sin. But the substance of man, even after the fall, is from God. Therefore, it is not itself evil and sin: We prove the minor premise from Deut. 32, verse 6. It is God who made and created you. Isaiah 45, verse 9. Woe to him who contradicts his maker. Similar things are held in Isaiah 54, verse 5, chapter 64, verse 8. Job 10, verse 10, and following. Psalm 100, verse 3, 139, verses 14 and 15. Ecclesiasticus 19, verse 12. Hebrews 3, verse 4. Thus in Revelation 4, verse 11, it is said: You, Lord, have created all things, and because of your will they are and were created. We add this reason besides: The substance of man is either created or uncreated: For a third option regarding substances is not given. If uncreated, it will be God himself; if created, it will be from God. How therefore could it be sin itself? Shall we manifestly constitute God as the author of sin? But if the Flacians should say that human substance, since it is sin itself, is not from God but from the Devil; another absurdity would follow, namely that the Devil is a creator, and indeed of such an excellent substance, which is against all Scripture and the first article of the Apostolic Creed, where God alone is believed to be the creator of all things.

XXVII. 6. From the article of the divine image. Contraries are in the same genus or predicament; the concreated image of God and the succeeding sin are contraries. Therefore they are in the same genus or predicament. But the divine image was not a substance, but an accident. Therefore, sin also is not a substance, but an accident. The last antecedent was demonstrated in the first disputation, and can be easily proved. Because if that image and concreated justice had been the very essence of man, it would follow: 1. That Adam was God, because whatever is essentially or by essence just and good, is God. 2. That the form of man and his soul had been lost, because the image was lost. 2. That the image of God was created to the image of God, which is absurd: For man was created to the image as regards essence, it follows certainly, that absurdity, that the image was created to the image, itself to itself.

XXIIX. 7. From the article of preservation. Whatever is sustained, moved, and exists in God, that cannot be evil, since in the good there are and can be only good things. But the substance of man even after the fall is sustained, moved, and exists in God. Therefore the substance of man even after the fall cannot be evil and sin itself. The minor premise is proved by that classic text Acts 17:28. In God we live, and move, and have our being.

XXIX. 8. From the article of incarnation. Christ did not assume sin, Christ assumed our nature. Therefore our nature is not sin itself. The major premise is proved by that saying Heb. 2:17 and 4:15. He was made like us in all things, sin excepted, whence it is evidently clear that sin in us is one thing, and we ourselves are another, since Christ was not made like unto sin, yet He was made like unto us and our nature in all things. For as the Greeks said τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον, that which is not assumed is not healed. Unless therefore Christ had assumed our nature, or the same nature with our species, we would not yet be redeemed. And yet He assumed no sin, from which it is invincibly gathered that our nature is not sin itself, and vice versa. From these two absurdities, therefore, it is necessary that the Flacians defend one, namely that Christ either assumed sin, or did not assume our nature. Both are against the faith, and the alleged Apostolic saying.

The adversaries object that Christ is a man of the same genus and species if considered physically, but not if considered theologically

Resp. The distinction between the Physical and the Theological man is indeed frequent among the Flacians; but it is nevertheless vain, and helps them not at all, which we show thus: The Physical man differs from the Theological either in essence, or only in qualities. If he differs in essence, it follows 1. that one man has two essences, Physical and Theological, and thus he will be a double man, that is, a monster. 2. That Christ is nevertheless not assimilated to us in all things; because according to the Flacians he assumed only our Physical, but not our Theological essence; the former argument therefore still holds. But if the Physical and Theological man differ only in qualities and accidents, the Flacians will have no support from this distinction. For we concede that there were other qualities in the nature of Christ than in ours, yet we urge in turn that the essence of both was one and the same; for since the humanity of Christ was not sin itself, neither will ours be, since Christ's and ours do not differ in species and οὐσίᾳ. Therefore that distinction was fabricated by the Flacians: and it viciously accomplished what it ought to have brought forth. It should rather be spoken of thus: Let man first be considered in himself, insofar as he is man, and has a human essence, and thus we, and the man Christ, have the same nature in species; this consideration of essence the Flacians call the physical man. Then he is considered not in himself, as he is a just or unjust man, born in sin or without sin: And in this respect Christ is not like us, since he was conceived without it, we with sin. And this consideration, they name the Theological man, but altogether wrongly. For there are not two men, or two species and essences of humanity, but one only in both cases: through the same essence man is man in Physics, and through the same in Theology: there are only two considerations of the same man, the one of essence, which can be called Physical, for the sake of teaching; the other of qualities, which is Theological. Different ways of considering, however, do not immediately produce different species of the thing considered, as the Flacians wrongly opine.

XXX. 9. From the article of sanctification. Man is sanctified. Sin is not sanctified. Therefore sin is not the man himself. The major premise is certain from many sayings of Scripture, especially from Eph. 5:26 ff. The minor premise cannot be denied from this, because to be sanctified is the same as to be made holy and righteous. But every sin is evil in its essence; how therefore will sin become holy? It would certainly be an ἀντίφασις ἐν προσκείμῳ, if you were to call sin sanctified or holy. Since therefore evil itself can never become holy, but man both is made and can be made holy or sanctified; hence it follows again invincibly that the man who is sanctified is one thing, and the sin which is not sanctified is another.

XXXI. 10. From the article of regeneration. Man is regenerated. Sin is not regenerated. Therefore sin is not the man himself. Regarding the major premise, there can be no doubt. As for the minor, let it be noted that some establish that the regeneration of man denotes two things: 1. the remission of sin, or the absolution of guilt, and 2. the renewal and the bestowing of new virtues. But indeed neither suits sin itself, but only man.

Not the first; because sin is not that to which remission is made, but that of which remission is made. For what is remitted in regeneration? Sin: to whom? To man. But sin is not remitted to sin. Therefore from this we gather that the man to whom it is remitted is one thing, and the sin which is remitted is another. Not the second; because not sin, but man is renewed; for an opposite never becomes its other opposite. But sin and renewal, or the old and the new man, are opposites. Therefore sin cannot become the new man, that is, it cannot be renewed.

XXXII. From the article of the resurrection. That very man who has died will rise again. Sin will not rise again. Therefore, sin is not the man himself. The major premise is proven, because the resurrection is of him who fell. If at the final judgment another substance, different in species, were to be produced from our ashes, then it would not be the resurrection of the dead, but the new creation or production of a new man. The same is proven more evidently from Job 19, verse 26, where he says that he will rise again in that very flesh and will see the Lord. The minor premise is also certain, since the just will rise to eternal life: for who would believe that sin is going to enter and possess that blessed life, which no one unclean and defiled will see? Shall we think that sin will be glorified, which is, however, nothing other than stench and uncleanness?

Some object that the same individual will rise again, but with the substantial form changed. But in what way will it be the same individual if it does not have the same substantial form? For the unity of an individual depends entirely upon the numerical unity of the form.

XXXIII. 12. From the article of eternal life. In eternal life, those who have struggled here will be crowned. But sin will not be crowned. Therefore, sin is not that which struggled here, that is, it is not the man himself. The major premise is certain, since eternal life will be the reward of the labors endured here, which is gathered especially from Matthew 25 and other places. It is necessary, therefore, that that very thing which struggled here and sustained labors should enter eternal life. For how would the labors be compensated for that which will clearly not exist, nor will the same return? The minor premise can be established by the preceding argument and very many sayings, which unanimously testify that in eternal life nothing unclean, nothing defiled will have a place.

XXXIV. 13. From the mixture of flesh and Spirit in the regenerate. One man cannot have two contrary essences. But whoever is reborn is one man. Therefore he cannot have two contrary essences. He would have them, however, if sin were an essence itself. For in every reborn person there are two, flesh and Spirit, the old man and the new man. But for Flacius both are something substantial. Therefore in one man there are two contrary essences. He is not therefore one simple man. Wherefore he is manifold, and consequently a monster.

XXXV. 14. From the unity of Adam and other men. If a man, as often as he is changed theologically, were to acquire a new essence or substance, as the Flacians wish, it would follow that there are four essentially distinct Adams. The first would have been before the fall, created in the image of God; the second after the fall, corrupted by original sin; the third in regeneration, renewed in part to the lost image; and the fourth would be in the resurrection and eternal life. And thus the corruption of the second Adam would pertain nothing to the first, nor would the first have been punished, nor could God have truly said, Because you have eaten of the tree, etc. Gen. 3. v. 17. For he to whom He was speaking was not the first Adam, but a completely new substance. So also regarding other men, regeneration would not pertain to him who is generated by parents, nor would resurrection to the reborn; all of which are most absurd.

XXXVI. Finally 15. from Manichaeism. Every Manichaean opinion is condemned and contrary to the Scriptures. But the opinion of Flacius is Manichaean. Therefore it is condemned and contrary to the Scriptures. The minor premise is proven because there are three things in the writings of the Flacians which they have in common with the Manichaeans: 1. That some substance is evil essentially, and not created by God, but by the devil. 2. That the cause of actual sins is not free will, but that evil substance. 3. That there are two substances in man, the one good, the other evil, especially in the regenerate.

Latin:

Classis 1. continens argumenta ex Scripturis & analogia fidei.

XXII. 1. Ex dicto Iohan. 1. v. 3 & 1. Tim. 4. v. 4. Iohannes Euangelista cap. 1. v. 3. dicit: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt, & sine ipso factum est nihil, quod factum est; ex quo dicto euidenter apparet, omnem substantiam per se subsistentem à Deo factam & creatam esse. Rursus autem scribitur 1. Timoth. 4. vers. 4, Omnis creatura Dei bona est, quoniam bonus non nisi boni author est. Vidit enim Deus quæ fecerat, & ecce! erant valdè bona, Gen. 1. v. vlt. Ex his dictis iàm ita inferimus: Omnis substantia est creatura Dei, Iohan. 1. vers. 3. Peccatum originis est substantia, dicente Flaciano. Ergo peccatum originis est creatura Dei, quòd primum absurdum. Porrò, Omnis creatura Dei est bona. 1. Tim. 4. v. 4. Peccatum originis est creatura Dei, quod iam probatum, Ergo peccatum originis est bonum. quod ἀνεκφώνητον. Sic enim probamus istam illam ἀντίφασιν: Nullum peccatum est bonum, quod iam conclusum Ergo peccatum originis non est peccatum. Vides hîc contradictionem, quam euitare non poteris, nisi neges, vel omnem substantiam à Deo esse, quod contra Iohannem; vel omnem creaturam bonam esse, quod contra Apostolum Paulum.

XXIII. 2. Ex Rom. 7. vers. 18. & seqq. vbi hæc leguntur verba: Scio quia non habitat in me, hoc est, in carne mea bonum. Non enim, quod volo bonum, hec facio; sed quod nolo malum, hoc ago. Si aute quod nolo, illud facio, jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum. Ex quo loco duo deducimus argumenta fortissima, & prorsus invicta Primum: Inhabitas, & illud, in quo habitat, non sunt vnum & idem, sed semper differunt realiter, quia idem in seipso non habitat. Peccatum autem & homo habent sese, vt inhabitans, & illud in quo habitat, quia peccatum est id, quod habitat, & homo id, inquo habitat, dicente Paulo. Ergo peccatum & homo non sunt vnum & idem, sed differunt realiter. Secundum: Quæcunque sine discrimine vnum sunt, de ijs etiam eadem prædicari possunt. Sed de homine & peccato originali eadem prædicari non possunt. Ergo homo & peccatum originis non sunt vnum idemque sine omni discrimine. Minorem probamus, quia Apostolus dicit de peccato, quod operetur malum, vel quod sit causa malis: hoc autem ipsum de se vt homine, dici posse negat. Sunt enim verba clara: Non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum. Aliud ergo erat peccatum operans malum, & aliud erat Apostolus, malum illud non operans. Operari enim & non operari vni eidemque & eodem respectu attribui nequeunt.

XXIV. 3. Ex Psal. 51. v. 7. Ecce in iniquitatibus conceptus sum, & in peccatis concepit me mater mea. Hinc concludimus: Conceptus & id, in quo, vel cum quo concipitur, non sunt vnum & idem. Alias Dauid vel alius quispiam in seipso conceptus dici posset, quod absurdum. Dauid autem fuit conceptus in peccatis. Psal. 51. Ergo Dauid, & peccatum, in quo fuit conceptus, id est, peccatum originis non sunt idem & vnum.

XXV. Ex Hebr. 12. v 1. Vbi malum originis vocatur εὐπερίστατος ἁμαρτία peccatum circunstas nos vndique & quasi obsidens. Est igitur quiddam distinctum à substantia hominis, quem circumstat & obsidet. Nihil enim seipsum cingit, aut sibi ipsi inhæret.

XXVI. 5. Ex articulo creationis. Quodcunque à Deo est, malum & peccatum non est. Sed substantia hominis etiam post lapsum à Deo est. Ergò malum & peccatum ipsum non est: Minorem probamus ex Deut. 32. vers. 6. Deus est qui fecit & creauit te. Esai. 45. vers. 9. Væ, qui contradicit factori suo. Similia habentur, Esai 54. vers. 5. cap. 64. v. 8. Iob. 10. v. 10. & seqq. Psalm. 100 v. 3. 139 v. 14. & 15. Eccles. 19 v. 12. Hebr. 3. v. 4. Sic Apocal 4 v. 11. dicitur: Tu Domine creasti omnia & propter voluntatem tuam sunt, & creata sunt. Addimus hanc insuper rationem: Substantia hominis vel creata est, vel increata: Tertium enim quoad substantias non datur. Si increata, erit ipse Deus; si creata erit à Deo. Quomodo igitur esse poterit peccatum ipsum? Num peccati authorem Deum manifestè constituemus? Quod si autem Flaciani dixerint, substantiam humanam, quoniam ipsum peccatum sit, à Deo non esse, sed à Diabolo; Sequeretur aliud absurdum, nempe Diabolum esse creatorem, & quidem substantiæ tam excellentis, id quod contra omnem Scripturam, & primum Symboli Apostolici articulum, vbi solus Deus omnium rerum creator creditur.

XXVII. 6. Ex articulo imaginis diuinæ. Contraria sunt in eodem genere vel prædicamento, Imago Dei concreata & peccatum succedens sunt contraria. Ergo sunt in eodem genere vel prædicamento. Ast imago diuina non fuit substantia, sed accidens, Ergo & peccatum non est substantia, sed accidens. Antecedens vltimum disputatione primâ demonstratum est, & facilè probari potest. Quia si imago ista & iustitia concreata fuiffet ipsa essentia hominis, sequeretur 1. Adam fuiffe Deum, quia quicquid essentialiter vel per essentiam est iustum bonumque, Deus est. 2. Formam hominis animamque esse amissam, quia imago fuitamissa, 2. Imaginem Dei ad imaginem Dei esse creatam, quod absurdum: Homo enim creatus est ad imaginem quoad essentiam, sequitur certè, absurdum istud, imaginem ad imaginem, ipsum ad seipsum esse creatum.

XXIIX. 7. Ex articulo conservationis. Quicquid in Deo sustentatur, mouetur & est, illud malum esse nequit, cùm in bono non nisi bona sint, & esse possint. At substantia hominis etiam post lapsum in Deo sustentatur, mouetur & est. Ergò substantia hominis etiam post lapsum, ipsum malum & peccatum esse nequit. Minor probatur classico isto textu Actor. 17. v. 18. In Deo viuimus, mouemur & sumus.

XXIX. 8. Ex articulo incarnationis. Christus non assumsit peccatum, Christus assumsit naturam nostram. Ergo natura nostra non est ipsum peccatum. Maior probatur dicto isto Hebr: 2. v. 17 & 4. v. 15. Factus est nobis per omnia similis, excepto peccato, vnde patet evidenter aliud esse peccatum in nobis, & aliud esse nos ipsos, quoniam peccato Christus non est factus similis, nobis tamen nostræque naturæ in omnibus similis est factus. Nam vt Græci dixerunt τὸ ἀπρόσληπτον ἀθεράπευτον, Inassumtum incuratum est. Nisi igitur Nostram, vel cum Nostra specie eandem naturam assumsisset Christus, redempti nondum essemus. Et tamen peccatum nullum assumsit, ex quo inuictè colligitur, naturam nostram nō esse ipsum peccatum, & contrà.
