Ex his ergò absurdis duobus vnum vt defendant Flaciani necessum est, nempe Christum aut assumsisse peccatum; aut non assumsisse naturam nostram. Vtrumque est contra fidem, & allegatum dictum Apostolicum.

Excipiunt aduersarij Christum hominem esse naturam eiusdem generis & speciei si Physicè, non verò si Theologicè consideretur

Resp. Crebra quidem est distinctio apud Flacianos inter hominem Physicum & Theologicum; sed tamen vana, & ipsos nihil iuuat quod sic ostendimus: Homo Physicus à Theologico vel differt essentia, vel tantùm qualitatibus. Si differt essentia, sequitur 1. vnum hominem duas habere essentias, Physicam & Theologicam, atque sic duplex erit homo, id est, monstrum. 2. Christum nihilominus nobis per omnia non esse assimilatum; quia duntaxat Physicam nostram, non autem Theologicam essentiam iuxta Flacianos assumsit; Viget igitur adhuc prius argumentum. Quod si autem homo Physicus & Theologicus tantùm qualitatibus differunt & accidentibus, nihil inde patrocinij ex hac distinctione habebunt Flaciani. Etenim concedimus, in Christi natura alias fuisse qualitates, ac in nostra, hoc tamen vrgemus vlicissim, quòd vtriusque vna & eadem fuerit essentia; quia verò Christi humanitas non fuit ipsum peccatum, nec nostra erit, cùm Christi & nostra specie & οὐσίᾳ non differant. Distinctio proinde ista à Flacianis conficta est: & vitiosè effecit, quod efferre debebat. Potiùs ita loquendum: Homo primùm consideretur in se, quatenus est homo, & essentiam humanam habet, atque ita nos, & homo Christus eandem specie habemus naturam; Hanc considerationem essentiæ vocant Flaciani hominem physicum. Deinde consideratur non in se, vt est homo iustus aut iniustus, in peccato vel sine peccato natus: Et hoc respectu Christus nobis non est similis, quoniam illo sine nos cum peccato concipimur. Et hanc considerationem, nominant isti hominẽ Theologicum, sed malè omninò. Non enim duo sunt homines, vel duæ humanitatis species & essentiæ, sed vnica vtrobique: per eandem essentiam homo in Physica, & per eandem in Theologia homo est: tantùm duæ sunt eiusdem hominis considerationes, altera essentia, quæ Physica vocaripotest, docendi ergò; altera qualitatum, quæ Theologica. Diuersi autem modi considerandi non statim diuersas rei consideratę species producunt, vt malè opinantur Flaciani.

XXX. 9. Ex articulo sanctificationis. Homo sanctificatur. Peccatum non sanctificatur. Ergò peccatum non est ipse homo, Major certa est ex multis Scripturæ dictis, præsertim ex Ephes. 5. v. 26. seqq. Minor negari nequit ex eo, quia sanctificari idem est, quod sanctum justumque fieri. Omne autem peccatum essentiâ est malum; quomodo igitur peccatū fiet sanctum? Esset certè ἀντίφασις ἐν προσκείμῳ, si peccatum sanctificatum vel sanctum diceres. Quoniani ergò malum ipsum nunquam fieri potest sanctum, homo autem & fit & fieri potest sanctus vel sanctificatus; hinc rursùs inuictè sequitur, aliud esse hominem, qui sanctificatur, & aliud esse peccatum, quod non sanctificatur.

XXXI. 10. Ex articulo regenerationis. Homo regeneratur. Peccatum non regeneratur. Ergò peccatum non est ipse homo. De maiore dubium esse potest nullum. Quoad minorem notetur quosdam statuere, quod regeneratio hominis duo notet, 1. remissionem peccati, vel absolutionem reatús, & 2. renouationem, nouarumque virtutum elargitionem. At verò neutrum convenit ipsi peccato, sed tantùm homini.

Non primum; quia peccatum non est id cui fit remissio, sed id, cuius fit remissio. Remittitur enim in regeneratione, quid? peccatum: cui? homini. Non autem peccatum peccato remittitur. Ergo hinc colligimus, aliud esse hominem, cui remittitur, & aliud esse peccatum, quod remittitur. Non secundum; quia non peccatum, sed homo renouatur; Oppositum enim nunquam fit oppositum alterum. Peccatum autem & renouatio, seu vetus & novus homo sunt opposita. Ergò peccatum non potest fieri novus homo, id est, nequit renouari.

XXXII. Ex articulo resurrectionis. Ille ipse homo, qui mortuus est, resurget. Peccatum non resurget. Ergo peccatum non est ipse homo. Maior probatur, quia resurrectio est eius, qui cecidit. Si in extremo iudicio alia & specie diuersa ex cineribus nostris substantia produceretur, tum non esset resurrectio mortui, sed noua noui hominis creatio aut productio. Probatur idem euidentius ex Iob. 19. vers. 26. vbi ait, se in illa ipsa carne resurrecturum, & visurum Dominum. Minor etiam certa est quoniam iusti resurgent ad vitam æternam: Quis autem crederet, peccatum esse ingressurum & possessurum beatam istam vitam, quam nemo immundus & coinquinatus videbit? Num putabimus peccatum iri clarificatum, quod tamen nihil aliud est, quàm fœtor & immundicies?

Excipiunt nonnulli, esse idem indiuiduum resurrecturum, sed formâ substantiali mutatâ. Verùm quo pacto idem erit indiuiduum, si non habebit eandem formā substantialem? Vnitas enim indiuidui ex numerica formæ vnitate in totum dependet.

XXXIII. 12. Ex articulo vitæ æternæ. In vita æterna illi, qui certarunt hîc, coronabuntur. At peccatum non coronabitur. Ergo peccatum non est id, quod hic certauit, id est, non est ipse homo. Maior certa, quandoquidem vita æterna pręmium erit laborum hic exantlatorum, quod præcipuè ex Matth. 25. alijsqûe locis colligitur. Necessum igitur est, vt illud ipsum vitam æternam intret, quod hic certauit & labores sustinuit. Quomodo enim labores compensarentur illi, qui planè non erit, nec redibit idem? Minor per præcedens Argumentum & dicta quàm plurima stabiliri potest, vnanimiter testantia, in vita æterna nihil immundum, nihil coinquinatum locum esse habiturum.

XXXIV. 13. Ex mixtura carnis & Spiritus in renatis. Vnus homo duas contrarias essentias habere nequit. Quiuis autem renatus est vnus homo. Ergo duas contrarias essentias habere nequit. Haberet autem, si peccatum esset ipsa essentia, Nam in quouis renato sunt duo, caro & Spiritus, homo vetus & homo nouus. Ast vtrumque Flacio est aliquid substantiale. Ergo in vno homine duæ sunt contrariæ essentiæ. Non igitur est vnus simplex homo. Quare multiplex, & per consequens monstrum.

XXXV. 14. Ab vnitate Adami aliorumq; hominum. Si homo quoties Theologicè mutatur, nouam, vt volunt Flaciani, acquireret essentiam vel substantiam, sequeretur, quatuor essentialiter distinctos esse Adamos. Primus fuisset ante lapsum, ad imaginem Dei creatus; Secundus post lapsum, peccato originali corruptus; Tertius in regeneratione, ad imaginem amissam ex parte renouatus; & Quartus esset futurus in resurrectione & vita æterna, Atque sic corruptio secundi Adami nihil pertineret ad primum, neque primus fuisset punitus, neque potuisset Deus verè dicere, Quia comedisti de ligno &c. Gen. 3. v. 17. Non enim ille, cui loquebatur, primus erat Adam, sed noua planè substantia. Sic etiam quoad alios homines regeneratio non pertineret ad eum, qui à parentibus est generatus, nec resurrectio ad regeneratum; quæ omnia sunt absurdissima.

XXXVI. Tandem 15. à Manichæismo. Omnis opinio Manichæa est damnata & Scripturis contraria. Sed opinio Flacij Manichæa est. Ergo damnata & scripturis contraria. Minor probatur quia tria sunt in Flacianorum scriptis, quæ cum Manichæis habent communia, 1. Quòd aliqua substantia sit mala ἐοιωδῶς, & non à Deo, sed diabolo procreata. 2. Quòd peccatorum actualium causa non sit liberum arbitrium, sed substantia illa mala. 3. Quòd duæ sint in homine homine substantiæ, altera bona, altera mala, præsertim in renatis.


### Problem I: Class II. containing the testimonies of the Fathers

Class II. containing the testimonies of the Fathers.

XXXVII. Many of these could well be brought forward, but since that very thing has been done here and there by other theologians, we shall therefore append only a few, and those only from Augustine and Luther. Thus, therefore, writes Augustine, lib. 5. hypognost. That men themselves are is the work of God, but that which is in them, sin, is the work of the Devil. L. 2. When man sinned, nature sinned: and nature became now sinful, that is, having the vice of sin, but it was not itself made vice or sin. The same, lib. 7. cap. 12. That evil, which I was seeking, whence it was, is not a substance; because if it were a substance, it would be good. The same, lib. 2. de grat. & peccat. cap. 33. Both are propagated at the same time, both nature and the vice of nature, of which one is good: the other evil. The former is taken from the bounty of the Creator, the latter is drawn from the condemnation of origin. The same, l. 1. contra Iul. cap. 3. No nature, in so far as it is nature, is evil, but because it falls short of that nature which is the supreme and unchangeable good. In the same place he says. We do not sufficiently resist the Manichaeans unless we maintain that evils have not arisen except from goods, and that those evils are not substances, but vices of created substances; by which they fall short of the good. This is the soundness of Catholic doctrine, by which the virus of the Manichaean pestilence is expelled. The same in Enchirid: cap. 13. Every nature, even if it is vicious, in so far as it is nature, is good; in so far as it is vicious, it is evil. The Augsburg Confession has the same, articles 2 & 19. The Smalcald Articles, part 3, art. 1. Both Catechisms of Luther in the explanation of the first article. Luther, in cap. 3 & 4 Gen., in cap. 25, writes openly, This deformity is to be distinguished from the creature, which God wills to be glorious and magnified.

XXXIIX. And up to this point we have reviewed the arguments confirming our thesis. It remains that we examine the objections of the Flacians. They are of those

the goddess especially, concerning which in order.

Objections of the Flacians.

XXXIX. 1. Whatever conflicts with the law of God, that is sin, 1 John 3:4. The whole nature of man conflicts with the law of God. Therefore, the whole nature of man is sin. Response: 1. There are four terms, because the major premise is taken in an abstract sense, but the minor in a concrete sense. That is: these words, 'whatever conflicts with the law of God,' denote in the abstract the ἀνομία itself, but not in the concrete the τὸ ἄνομον. For if the sinning subject were included in the major premise, and not only sin in the abstract were understood, then it is false. In the minor premise, however, the nature of man is said to conflict with the law only in the concrete, insofar as that ἀνομία and sin adheres in it. The phrase 'to conflict with the law of God' is therefore ambiguous. For it is taken either formally and abstractly for the ἀνομία itself, or materially and concretely for the ἀνόμῳ subject. In the former sense the major is true, in the latter it is false. But in the minor premise, not the former, but the latter sense is assumed; whence four terms emerge.

2. We distinguish the major premise in this way. Whatever conflicts with the law of God ὀσιωδῶς καὶ καθ' ἀυτὸ; essentially and per se, that is sin. But the whole nature of man conflicts with the law of God, not ὀσιωδῶς καὶ καθ' ἀυτὸ, but δι' ἄλλο, through and because of something else; namely, because of innate malice.

3. We add an instance, arguing thus: Whatever is agreeable to the divine law is a good work or a virtuous action, generally speaking. But the whole nature of glorified men in the other life will be agreeable to the divine law. For nothing unclean shall enter into the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, the nature of glorified men will be nothing but a good work or a virtuous action: wherefore it will not be a substance, which is absurd. Consequently, there is no validity in the argument, since abstract and concrete, the τὸ καθ' ἀυτὸ and the δι' ἄλλο, are confused.

Whatever, therefore, the Flacians may reply to this, that also can be similarly applied to their own argument.

XL. 2. Scripture in describing sin uses substantial words. Therefore, sin is a substance and not an accident. The antecedent is proved from Genesis 8, verse 21, where the figment of the human heart is called evil: likewise from Romans 8, verse 6, where it is named the old man and the body of sin. But every body is a substance.

Response. 1. Generally. Sin is considered in two ways. 1. Regarding its ὀυσίαν [essence] and in the abstract, and thus it is never expressed by substantial words, but always by accidental ones, denoting a vicious quality or action. 2. Regarding its ὕπαρξιν [existence] or its existence and in the concrete, insofar as not only it itself is expressed, but the subject is connoted along with it. And in this latter respect the substantial words of Scripture are to be understood, with this distinction observed, that the substance itself is understood of the man, and the limitation added to the substance is understood of the sin, as when it is said, John 3, verse 6: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh; a concrete term is held, namely of flesh, denoting both the substance and the oldness of the substance, denoting both the subject and the vice adhering to the subject.

2. Specifically. Regarding Gen. 8, by 'figment' is not understood the substance itself, but the motion of the heart, which is certainly an accident. Regarding Rom. 6, by 'body of sin' it can be understood through a certain trope as a multitude and, as it were, a heap of vices which we have contracted by living badly. Others think that by 'body' is understood strength and dominion, by a Hebrew phrase, so that the sense is that the strength and dominion of sin must be destroyed and taken away, which explanation is sufficiently conformable to the text itself.

XLI. 3. Whatever produces all other sins, that is original sin. But the heart itself produces all other actual sins, Matthew 15, verse 19. Therefore, the heart itself is original sin.

Response. 1. To the major premise, which can be understood both of the principal and primary efficient cause, and of the impelling and inciting cause. If it is of the primary efficient cause, then it is false. For man himself is the principal efficient cause of all actual sins, and if they call original sin the principle, they are begging the question. If it is of the inciting principle, and not the primary agent, then it is granted by us, and is answered.

2. To the minor premise, that this is true and speaks of the primary agent, but not of the inciting principle, just as the major premise speaks; whence four terms arise, since the minor can and ought to be understood of the primary causing agent, the major only of the inciting principle.

3. We limit the major premise thus: Whatever ὀσιωδῶς and of itself effects other sins, that is original sin. But the heart does not produce actual sins ὀσιωδῶς and of itself, but accidentally and δι' ἄλλο, insofar as it is corrupt. Therefore, it cannot be called sin by its very essence, but only corrupted and defiled by sin. Therefore, as great a distinction as there is between φθορὰν and φθαρτὸν, so great a distinction still remains between the substance of the heart and original sin; the latter is φθορὰ, the former is not φθορὰ itself but only φθαρτὸν.

4. We add this instance: Whatever is the cause of all reasonings and discourses, that is the intellect, or the faculty of understanding, implanted in the soul. But man is the cause of all discourses. Therefore, man is the faculty of understanding itself, and thus an accident. In order for this to be answered, it must be said that the major premise speaks of the formal principle or instrument; the minor of the principally efficient cause, and thus there are four terms. Therefore, let the Flacians take the same answer for their own objection.

XLII. 4. Justification is the creation of a new heart, whence it is said, Psalm 51, v. 12: Create in me a clean heart, O Lord.

And Ezek. 36. v. 26. I will take away from you the heart of stone, and I will give you a heart of flesh. It follows therefore that sin is a substance, both because it is called a heart of flesh, and because justification from sin is the creation of a new substance, of a new heart. If therefore the term to which in justification is a substance, certainly the term from which will be such also.

Response. The whole flaw of the argument arises from the confusion of abstract and concrete terms. For regeneration is the creation of a new heart, not as if another substance of the heart were formed, but because newness, or new qualities of the heart, are produced, on account of which the heart itself and the subject is called new and of flesh. The Flacians therefore beg the question when they say that the term to which of renewal is a substance, when it is only the production of new virtues and qualities, and thus of accidents. Creation, however, is spoken of in a broad sense, insofar as everything that is made and formed by God, whether it be an accident or a substance, is called creation. Otherwise, speaking strictly, we do not deny that creation is the production of a substance, whence theologians say: Only substances are created, accidents are co-created. But there is one proper, and another broad and somewhat improper, acceptance of creation.

XLIII. 5. Men are called by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2, v. 3, and their malice is natural, Wis. 12, v. 10. Therefore sin pertains to the very nature and essence of man.

Response. We deny the consequence, and so that the reason for this denial may be clear, it must be known that natural is said in three ways. 1. It denotes τά ὑσιώδη, and the essential principles of a thing itself: thus the form of any body is called natural or even nature itself. 2. τὰ ἑπουσιώδη and co-essential or consequent to the essence itself, and produced from it by emanation, such as are all proper accidents. Thus risibility and docility are said to be natural to man. Both these kinds of natural are good, and have their origin from God, because nature, insofar as it is nature, is not vicious, according to the dictum of Augustine cited above. For this double reason, therefore, it cannot be called a natural sin, unless we posit God as the author of sin, through manifest blasphemy. 3. He notes τὰ συμβεβηκότα or τὰ συνέμφυτα, that is, those things which are neither the essence of the thing itself, nor sprout from the essence, yet surround the essence, and cohere with it, and are produced at the same time. Thus, he who is blind from birth, his blindness is said to be natural, yet it is not the essence of the blind man itself, nor an essential consequence; but merely an accident, which nevertheless, because it began with the nature of that man, and he was born such, is rightly named natural blindness. In the same sense that original malice in which all are born is often designated as natural, both in Scripture and among orthodox theologians, only because it draws its origin with the nature and essence of man, so that as soon as a man begins to be formed in the womb, it is also present. But if the Flacians have called that malice natural in another respect, then they are begging the question, and to prove this, they must be pressed.

XLIV. 6. That which is baptized and sanctified is nothing other than sin. The whole man or the repugnant nature of the whole man is baptized. Therefore, the whole man is original sin.

Response. The minor premise is false. For it is not sin itself, but the sinful man that is baptized and sanctified. Hence Christ in Matthew 28:19 commands not to baptize sin, but sinful nations. Sin is indeed that from which a man is washed in Baptism, yet it is not that very thing which is washed. Just as therefore in every action and motion, the subject of the motion is one thing, and the terms of the motion are another, both that from which and that to which: so also in this spiritual change and washing, the subject is one thing, namely the man who is baptized, and the term from which is another, namely sin, from which man is purged and washed in Baptism.

XLV. 7. The flesh is baptized. The flesh is original sin.

Therefore original sin is baptized; and consequently it is the same thing as man or the very substance of man.

Response. There are four terms which derive their origin from the ambiguity of the word flesh: For it is taken in two ways: ἰδίως and properly, insofar as it denotes the nature and human mass itself, and in this respect alone the major premise is true. 2. μετωνυμικῶς for the vice and corruption inherent in the substance, and thus it is always opposed to the spirit, in which sense it is taken in that Gal. 5. v. 17. The flesh lusts against the spirit. In this respect the minor premise is true, on account of which πληθυσία of terms there is no consequence in the argument.

XLVI. 8. From the authority of Luther. They always urge this, that Luther called original sin natural (a nature-sin), likewise, that the nature of man, the essence (being) is sin, that the nature of man after the fall is changed, that original sin is the very thing which is born from father and mother, that man is sin itself, etc.

Response. We cannot deny that Luther used these and similar phrases to exaggerate the deformity of sin against the Papist and Synergist extenuators, yet he by no means used them in the Flacian sense, which removes every distinction between substance and sin. In order that this may be understood, the individual words and phrases of Luther must be explained.

1. As far as the word natural is concerned, it has just been said of it that it is called natural sin, not as if it were οὐσιῶδες or ἐπουσιῶδες, but because it is σύμφυτον, and adheres in nature, and arises with nature, not otherwise than as blindness or another disease of the body is called natural.

2. As regards the phrase, The nature of man is sin, it must be known that this word also is ambiguous. For it is either taken substantially, for the very essence and οὐσία of man, or accidentally for the disposition, condition, or inclination, as when I say, It is the nature of a fox to lie in wait for other small animals, it is the nature of wild beasts to be cruel. Luther said this also, and in no other sense, that it is of man to sin, that is, his nature, his inclination naturally leans toward sins. In like manner, the word essence sometimes denotes the substance itself considered in itself, but sometimes the pursuits and actions of men; which ambiguity has a place especially in the German word Wesen, which is most common to Luther.

3. As regards the change of man, it is to be noted that it is twofold: the one substantial, which is from being to non-being, or conversely; the other accidental, which is from such to such a being, when only new accidents are introduced. And this accidental, not that substantial, is understood when a man is said to be changed, since he has not lost his former essence, but has only been affected by a new quality.

4. Concerning the remaining and similar phrases, it is to be observed: 1. That most of them are uttered αὐξητικῶς and in the sense of the rhetoricians. For when they wish to describe a man as remarkably happy or calamitous, they then speak in the abstract: he is happiness itself, calamity itself. Thus Luther, wishing to exaggerate that native evil, called man not only a sinner, but often sin itself. 2. Because original sin is not a certain transient act, but adheres most deeply and inseparably in the nature of man, therefore Luther often used words connoting the very substance of man. 3. That Luther disputed against the sophists, the extenuators of sin, and therefore all his sayings should be judged as opposed only to the Pelagians, not to the orthodox.

XLVII. 9. The corruption of one thing is the generation of another. But the substance of man is corrupted through the fall. Therefore a new one was generated. But that cannot be other than sin. This therefore is Substance.

Resp. There are four terms, since the major premise speaks of corruption and substantial φθορᾷ, but the minor of accidental, the alteration of qualities. The substance is corrupted, as regards vicious qualities, but it has not been substantially corrupted, as if it had been plainly annihilated and reduced to nothing, which experience itself has taught.

XLVIII. 10. That by which a man is what he is, that is his form and essence. But through sin a man is corrupted in what he is. Therefore sin is the form and essence of man.

Response: In the minor premise a concrete term is placed, involving two things, from which ambiguity arises; for man is considered either in himself, as he is a substance, and then his form is not sin, but the rational soul, or in respect to another, insofar as he is corrupted, and this is from sin. From this, however, it does not follow that sin is the very substantial form of man. Indeed, sin gives to man that he is corrupted; but it is not given that he is a man. This can be proven by the examples of all other accidents. Because of whiteness a man is white, because of wisdom he is wise, yet the substance of man itself is not therefore anything other than whiteness and wisdom.

XXXIX. 11 An accident is that which can be present and absent without the corruption of the subject. Sin is not present without the corruption of the subject. Therefore it is not an accident.

Response: 1. We provide an instance from bodily diseases. These are not present without the corruption of the subject and of health; shall they therefore be substances, not accidents?

2. That definition is only superficial, not accurate: of a common accident, not of every one. In general it is defined thus: An accident is a being which does not subsist by itself, but inheres in a subject: which definition can be very well applied to original sin.

3. By corruption Porphyry does not understand physical corruption, which consists in the depravation and evil affection of the subject, but logical, which brings about the destruction of the essence and a contradictory repugnance. For whatever is present or absent without the essence of the thing being immediately destroyed or denied, that is an accident for Porphyry. This very thing can indeed be applied to sin. For even if sin is separated (as it will be separated on the last day), the subject is not corrupted, the essence is not is destroyed or denied, but man will be and will remain a true man. For just as a disease indeed harms the human body, yet does not take away its essence, since a sick man is still a true man: So sin indeed harmed and contaminated nature, yet it did not substantially corrupt it, or take away its entire essence, since a sinful man is just as much a man as he who lacks sin.

Latin:

Classis II. continens testimonia Patrum.

XXXVII. Horum benè multa proferri possent sed quoniam id ipsum à Theologis alijs hinc inde factum est, propterea pauca duntaxat apponemus, eaque tantùm ex Augustino & Luthero. Sic ergo scribit Augustin. lib. 5. hypognost. Ipsi homines quòd sunt opus Dei est, quod vero in ipsis est peccatum, est opus Diaboli. L. 2. Cùm peccauit homo, natura peccauit: & facta est natura iam peccatrix, hoc est, vitium habens peccati, non verò ipsa facta est vitium vel peccatum. Idem lib. 7. cap. 12. Malum illud, quod quærebam, vnde esset, non est substantia; quia si substantia esset, bonum esset. Idem lib. 2. de grat. & peccat. cap. 33. Simul vtrumque propagatur, & natura, & naturæ vitium, quorum vnum est bonum: alterum malum. Illud de conditoris largitate sumitur, hoc de originis damnatione attrahitur. Idem l. 1. contra Iul. cap. 3. Nulla natura in quantum natura est, malum est, sed quia deficit ab illa natura, quæ summum & incommutabile bonum est. Ibidem ait. Non satis resistimus Manichæis, nisi obtineamus, non esse mala orta, nisi ex bonis, nec ea mala substantias esse, sed substantiarum vitia creatarum; quibus deficiunt à bono. Hæc est doctrinæ Catholicæ sanitas, quâ Manichææ pestilentiæ virus expellitur. Idem in Enchirid: cap. 13. Omnis natura etiamsi vitiosa est, in quantum natura est, bona est; in quantum vitiosa est, mala est. Idem habet Augustana Confessio artic. 2. & 19. Articuli Schmalcaldici part. 3. art. 1. Cathechismus vterque Lutheri in explicatione primi articuli. Luth. in cap. 3. & 4. Gen. in cap. 25. scribit apertè, Discernenda est deformitas ista à creatura, quàm vult Deus gloriosam & magnificari.

XXXIIX. Et huc vsque argumenta thesin nostram confirmantia recensuimus. Restat, vt Flacianorum obiectiones examinemus. Sunt illarum ma-

deam potissimum, de quibus ordine.

Obiectiones Flacianorum.

XXXIX. 1. Quicquid pugnat cum lege Dei, illud est peccatum, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 4. Tota hominis Natura pugnat cum lege Dei. Ergo tota hominis natura est peccatum. Respond. 1. Sunt quatuor termini, quia maior sumitur in sensu abstractiuo, minor autem concretiuo. hoc est. Verba ista, quicquid pugnat cum lege Dei, notant in abstracto ipsam ἀνομίαν, non autem in concreto τὸ ἄνομον Sienim subiectum peccans vnâ includatur in maiore, & non solùm peccatum in abstracto intelligatur, tunc falsa est. In minore a. hominis natura cum lege pugnari dicitur tantùm in concreto, quatenus in ea hæret ἀνομία ista & peccatum. Ambigua igitur est phrasis, pugnare cum lege Dei. Vel enim formaliter & abstractè pro ipsa ἀνομίᾳ vel materialiter & concretè, pro subiecto ἀνόμῳ sumitur. Priori sensu maior vera est, posteriori falsa est. At verò in minore non prior, sed posterior sensus assumitur; vnde quatuor emergunt termini.

2. Distinguimus maiorem hoc modo. Quicquid pugnat cum lege Dei ὀσιωδῶς καὶ καθ' ἀυτὸ; essentialiter & per se, illud est peccatum. Tota verò hominis natura pugnat cum lege Dei, nón ὀσιωδῶς καὶ καθ' ἀυτὸ, sed δι' ἄλλο per & propter aliud; nempè propter annatam malitiam.

3. Addimus instantiam, ita argumentando: Quicquid legi diuinæ consentaneum est, bonum opus vel virtuosa actio est, generaliter loquendo. Atqui tota hominum glorificatorum natura in alterâ vitâ legi diuinæ erit consentanea. Nihil enim immundum ingredietur in regnum cælorum. Ergo hominum glorificatorum natura nil erit nisi bonum opus vel virtuosa actio: Quare non erit substantia, quod absurdum. Nulla proinde argumento inest consequentia, quoniam confunduntur abstracta & concreta, τὸ καθ' ἀυτὸ & δι' ἄλλο.

Quicquid igitur Flaciani ad hoc respõderint, illud quoque ad ipsorum argumentum similiter applicari poterit.

XL. 2. Scriptura in describendo peccato vtitur verbis substantialibus. Ergo peccatum est substantia, & non accidens. Probatur antecedens ex Genes 8. vers. 22. vbi figmentum cordis humani malum dicitur: Item ex Rom. 8. vers. 6. vbi vetus homo & corpus peccati nominatur. Omne autem corpus est substantia.

Respond. 1 Generaliter. Peccatum dupliciter consideratur. 1. quoad ὀυσίαν suam & in abstracto, at que sic nunquam verbis substantialibus, sed semper accidentalibus, vitiosam qualitatem aut actionem notantibus effertur. 2. quoad ὕπαρξιν vel existentiam suam & in concreto, quatenus non ipsum solum effertur, sed vnâ subiectum connotatur. Atque hoc posteriori respectu intelligenda sunt verba Scripturæ substantialia, hoc obseruato discrimine, vt ipsa substantia de homine intelligatur substantiæ addita limitatio de peccato, yt cùm dicitur, Iohan 3. vers.6. Quicquid ex carne natum est, caro est; habetur vox concreta, nimirum carnis notans tum substantiam tum substantię vetustatem, notans & subiectum & subiecto adhærens vitium.

2. Specialiter. Ad Gen. 8. per figmentum non intelligitur substãtia ipsa, sed motio cordis quæ certè accidens est. Ad Rom. 6. per corpus peccati per tropum quendam intelligi potest multitudo & quasi congeries vitiorum, quam malè viuendo contraximus. Alij putant per corpus intelligi robur & dominium phrasi hebraica, vt sit sensus, destruendum & auferendum esse peccato suum robur & dominium, quæ explicatio ipsi textui satis est conformis.

XLI. 3. Quicquid efficit omnia alia peccata illud est peccatum originis. Sed ipsum cor efficit omnia alia peccata actualia, Matth. 15. vers. 19. Ergo ipsum cor est peccatum originis.

Respond. 1. ad maiorem, quæ intelligi potest tum de efficiente principali & primario, tum de impellente & irritante. Si de efficiente primario, tunc falsa est. Ipse enim homo est causa efficiens omnium peccatorum actualium principalis, quem si originale peccatum dixerint principium petunt. Si de principio irritante, & non primario agente, tunc conceditur à nobis, atque respondetur.

2. Ad minorem, hanc veram esse & loqui de primario agente, non autem de principio irritante, quemadmodum maior loquitur; vnde oriuntur termini quatuor, quandoquidem de primario causante minor, de principio tantum irritante maior intelligi potest & debet.

3. Maiorem sic limitamus: Quicquid ὀσιωδῶς & per se efficit peccata alia istud originale peccatum est. Cor autem non ὀσιωδῶς & per se, sed accidentaliter & δι' ἄλλο, quatenus corruptum est, peccata actualia producit. Ergo non potest per essentiam ipsam dici peccatum, sed tantùm peccato corruptum & inquinatum. Quantum igitur discrimen inter φθορὰν & φθαρτὸν, tantum adhuc manet inter cordis substantiam & peccatum originale; hoc φθορὰ, illud non φθορὰ ipsa sed duntaxat φθαρτὸν est.

4. Instantiam hanc adijcimus: Quicquid est causa omnium ratiocinationum & discursuum, istud est intellectus, vel intelligendi facultas, animæ insita. Sed homo est causa omnium discursuum. Ergo homo est ipsa intelligendi facultas, idenque accidens. Hic vt respondeatur, dicendum maiorem loqui de principio formali vel instrumento; minorem de causa principaliter efficiente, atque sic quatuor esse terminos, Idem igitur ad suam obiectionem responsum capiant Flaciani.

XLII. 4. Iustificatio est creatio noui cordis, vnde dicitur, Psalm. 51. v. 12. Cor mundum crea in me Domine.

Et Ezech. 36. v. 26. Auferam à vobis cor lapideum, & dabo vobis cor carneum. Sequitur ergo, peccatum esse substantiam, tùm quia vocatur cor carneum, tùm quia iustificatio à peccato est, nouæ substantiæ, noui cordis creatio. Si igitur terminus ad quem in iustificatione est substantia, vtique & terminus à quo talis erit.

Respond. Totum argumenti vitium oritur ex confusione vocum abstractarum & concretiuarum. Nam regeneratio est creatio cordis noui, non ac si alia substantia cordis formaretur, sed quia nouitas, vel nouæ cordis qualitates producuntur, propter quas ipsum cor & subiectum vocatur nouum & carneum. Petunt igitur Flaciani principium, quando dicunt, renouationis terminum ad quem esse substantiam, cùm nouarum duntaxat virtutum & qualitatum, adeóque accidentium productio sit. Dicitur autem creatio sensu lato, quatenus omne id, quod à Deo fit & formatur, siue accidens sit, siue substantia, creatio appellatur. Aliàs strictè loquendo creationem esse substantiæ productionem non negamus, vnde Theologi dicunt: Solæ substantiæ creantur, accidentia concreantur. Sed alia est propria, alia verò lata & nonnihil impropria creationis acceptio.

XLIII. 5. Homines dicuntur naturâ filij iræ, Eph. 2, v. 3. & malitia eorum naturalis, Sap. 12. v. 10. Ergo peccatum ad naturam ipsam & essentiam hominis pertinet.

Respond. Negamus consequentiam, cuius negationis ratio vt pateat, sciendum, quòd naturale tribus dicatur modis. 1. notat τά ὑσιώδη, & ipsa essentialia rei principia: sic forma cuiuslibet corporis dicitur naturalis vel etiam natura ipsa. 2. τὰ ἑπουσιώδη & coessentialia seu consequentia ipsam essentiam, ex eaque per emanationem producta, qualia sunt omnia accidentia propria. Sic risibilitas & docilitas homini naturalis esse dicitur. Vtraque hæc est naturalis species bona est, & à Deo ortum habet, quia natura, in quantum natura, vitiosa non est, juxta dictum Augustini suprà allegatum. Hoc igitur duplici respectu peccatum naturale dici nequit, nisi peccati authorem statuamus Deum, per manifestam blasphemiam. 3. notat τὰ συμβεβηκότα vel τὰ συνέμφυτα, hoc est, ea, quae neque sunt ipsa essentia rei, neque ex essentia pullulant, essentiam tamen circumstant, & cum ea cohaerent, simulque producuntur. Sic qui ex nativitate caecus est, illi caecitas naturalis esse dicitur, non tamen est ipsa caeci essentia, vel essentiale consequens; sed duntaxat accidens, quod tamen, quia cum natura hominis istius coepit, & ille talis natus fuit, rectè caecitas naturalis nominatur. Eodem sensu originalis illa malitia in qua omnes nascuntur, saepe naturalis, & in Scriptura & apud orthodoxos Theologos indigitatur, tantùm quia cum natura & essentia hominis ortum trahit, ita ut quamprimum homo incipiat formari in utero, illa etiam adsit. Quod si alio respectu istam malitiam naturalem dixerint Flaciani, tunc principium petunt, & hoc ut probent, urgendi sunt.

XLIV. 6. Quod baptizatur & sanctificatur, id nihil est aliud, quàm peccatum. Totus homo vel totius hominis repugnans natura baptizatur. Ergo totus homo est peccatum originis.

Respond. minor falsa est. Non enim peccatum ipsum, sed homo peccator baptizatur & sanctificatur. Hinc Christus Matth. 28. v. 19 jubet non peccatum, sed gentes peccatores baptizare. Est quidem peccatum id, à quo abluitur homo in Baptismo, non tamen est illud ipsum, quod abluitur. Sicut igitur in omni actione & motu, aliud est subiectum motus, & aliud sunt termini motus, tùm a quo, tùm ad quem: Ita etiam in ista spirituali mutatione & ablutione, aliud est subjectum, nempe homo, qui baptizatur, & aliud est terminus á quo, nempe peccatum, à quo homo in Baptis. purgatur & abluitur.

XLV. 7. Caro baptizatur. Caro est peccatum originis.

Ergo peccatum originis baptizatur; & per consequens idem est, quod homo vel ipsa hominis substantia.

Respond. Sunt quatuor termini, qui trahunt ortum ex ambiguitate vocabuli carnis: Sumitur enim dupliciter: idiōs & propriè, quatenus ipsam notat naturam massaḿque humanam & hoctantùm respectu maior vera est. 2. μετωνυμικῶς pro substantiae vitio & corruptione inhaerente, atque ita semper opponitur spiritui quo sensu accipitur in isto Gal. 5. v. 17. Caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum. Hoc respectu minor vera est, ob quam terminorum πληθυσιαν nulla in argumento est consequentia.

XLVI. 8. Ab authoritate Lutheri Semper hoc vrgent, quòd Lutherus peccatum originis dixit Naturale (ein Natur suͤnde) item, naturam hominis, essentiam (Wesen) esse peccatum, hominis naturam post lapsum esse mutatam, peccatum originis esse idipsum quod nascitur ex patre & matre, hominem esse ipsum peccatum &c.

Respond. Diffiteri non possumus, Lutherum istis & similibus phrasibus vsum esse, ad exaggerandam peccati deformitatem contra extenuatores Pontificios & Synergistas, minimè tamen vsus fuit sensu Flaciano, omnem distinctionem inter substantiam & peccatum tollente. Hoc vt intelligatur, singulae voces phraseśque Lutheri erunt explicandae.

1. Quod igitur vocem naturalis attinet, de ea modò dictum est, quod peccatum naturale dicatur, non ac si esset οὐσιῶδες, vel ἐπουσιῶδες, sed quia est σύμφυτον, & in natura haeret, & cum natura oritur, non secus, ac caecitas, aliusvè morbus corporis, naturalis vocatur.

2. Quod spectat phrasin, Natura hominis est peccatum, sciendum quòd & ista vox sit ambigua. Vel enim sumitur substantialiter, pro ipsa hominis essentia & οὐσια, vel accidentaliter pro ingenio, conditione aut inclinatione, vt cùm dico, Vulpis natura est, aliis animalculis insidiari, ferarum natura est immites esse. Hoc etiam, & nullo alio sensu dixit Lutherus, hominis esse peccare, id est, ejus ingenium, ejus inclinatio ad peccata naturaliter propendet. Pari modo vox essentiæ interdum notat ipsam substantiam in se consideratam, interdum verò studia & actiones hominum; quæ æquivocatio in germanico vocabulo Wesen/ Luthero usitatissimo potissimum locum habet.

3. Quod attinet mutationem hominis, notandum, quòd ea duplex sit, altera substantialis, quæ est ab esse ad non esse, vel contrà altera accidentalis quæ est à tali ad tale esse, quando noua tantùm accidentia introducuntur. Et hæc accidentalis, non illa substantialis intelligitur, cùm homo mutatus dicitur, quoniam priorē essentiam non perdidit, sed nova duntaxat qualitate affectus est.

4. De reliquis & similibus phrasibus obseruandum 1. quòd pleræque αὐξητικῶς & rhetorum sensu sint prolatæ. Hi enim quando hominem insigniter felicem vel calamitosum describere volunt, tunc in abstracto dicunt, est ipsa felicitas, ipsa calamitas. Sic Lutherus volens exaggerare malum istud nativum, hominem non peccatorem tantùm, sed sæpè ipsum peccatum nominauit. 2. quia peccatum originale non est actus quidam transiens, sed profundissimè & inseparabiliter hæret in natura hominis, ideò Lutherus sæpè usus est vocabulis ipsam vnâ substantiam hominis connotātibus 3. Quòd Lutherus cōtra sophistas, extenuatores peccati disputaverit, ideoque omnia ejus dicta Pelagianis modò, non orthodoxis opposita censeantur.

XLVII. 9. Corruptio unius est generatio alterius. Substantia verò hominis est corrupta per lapsum. Ergò generata fuit noua. Illa verò nequit esse alia, quàm peccatum Hoc igitur est Substantia.

Resp. Sunt quatuor termini, quandoquidem major loquitur de corruptione & φθορᾷ substantiali, minor autem de accidentali, qualitatum alteratione. Corrupta est substantia, quoad vitiosas qualitates, non autem corrupta est substantialiter, ac si planè annihilata & in nihilum redacta fuisset, quod ipsa docuit experientia.

XLVIII. 10. Per quod homo est id quod est, id forma & essentia eius est, Sed per peccatum homo corruptus est id quod est. Ergo peccatum hominis forma & essentia est.

Resp. in minore ponitur vocabulum concretum, involvens duo, vnde oritur ambiguitas; Homo enim consideratur, vel in se, vt est substantia, & tunc eius forma non est peccatum, sed anima rationalis, vel respectu alterius, prout est corruptus, & hoc à peccato est. Hinc autem non sequitur, peccatum ipsam hominis substantialem formã esse. Equidem peccatum dat homini, vt sit corruptus; sed non datur, vt sit homo. Potest hoc probari per exempla omnium aliorum accidentium. Propter albedinem homo est albus, sapientiâ sapiens, non tamen ideo ipsa substantia hominis nil al iud est quã albedo & sapiẽtia.

XXXIX. 11 Accidens est, quod potest adesse & abesse præter subiecti corruptionem. Peccatum non adest præter subiecti corruptionem. Ergo non est accidens.

Respond. 1. Damus instantiam à morbis corporalibus. Hi non adsunt præter subiecti & sanitatis corruptionem, Ergonè propterea erunt substantiæ, non accidentia?

2. Definitio illa tantùm est superficialis, non accurata: accidentis communis, non omnis. In genere sic definitur: Accidens est ens, quod non per se subsistit, sed subiecto inhæret: qui ὁρισμὸς ad peccatum originis optimè accommodari potest.

3. Per corruptionem Porphyrius non Physicam intelligit quæ in depravatione & mala subjecti affectione consistit, sed Logicam, quæ essentiæ destructionem & repugnantiam contradictoriam infert. Nam quocunque vel præsente vel absente rei essentia non statim destruitur aut negatur, illud Porphyr. o accidens est. Hoc verò ipsum ad peccatum applicari potest. Nam etiamsi separetur peccatum (ut separabitur in extrèmo die) non tamen corrumpitur subjectum, essentia non destruitur aut negatur, sed homo erit & manebit verus homo. Sicut enim morbus lædit quidem corpus humanum, eius essentiam tamen non tollit, cùm homo ægrotus etiam verus sit homo: Ita peccatum læsit quidem & contaminauit naturam, non tamen substantialiter corrupit, vel sustulit eius essentiam omnem, cùm homo peccator tam sit homo, quam is qui peccato caret.


### Problem I: Question II. Whether original sin is a full and total privation of the divine image?

QUESTION II. Whether original sin is a full and total privation of the divine image?

I. Origen, in chapter 26 of Genesis, Homily 14, maintains that the image of God is indeed obscured but not entirely obliterated. The Son of God, he says, is the painter of this image. And because such and so great a painter he is, his image can be obscured through carelessness, but it cannot be erased through malice. For the image of God always remains in you, even if you superimpose upon yourself the image of the earthly. Epiphanius, in heresy 64 and in his epistle to John, Bishop of Jerusalem, contends that it has remained entirely intact. Bellarmine, having become bolder from this, brands with the mark of heresy all who say that the image of God has been lost, in book 4 of the Church Militant, chapter 9. The more recent Photinians argue similarly that the image of God in man has by no means been lost, Catechism of Raców, p. 22.

II. Now all these pronouncements tend either toward the denial, or certainly the extenuation, of original sin. For if the image of God is not lost, then neither was the grace of God, nor natural justice, forfeited. If the privation of good did not precede, corruption could not follow: For as long as a clear light shines, there is no place for darkness: And where there is firm health, there is no infirmity. It is therefore the same whether one denies original sin or the loss of the divine image. For they are so connected that if one is taken away, the other is immediately taken away along with it. The Papists, however, deny the loss of the concreated image, insofar as natural things have remained intact and the image They affirm that [the image] of God has neither been lost, nor made worse in any part of itself. Wherefore they deny original sin itself, and serve in the condemned camp of Pelagius.

III. But that these things may be better perceived, the ambiguity which lies hidden in the word 'image' must be unfolded. 1. Some Fathers distinguish it from likeness, in such a way that they judge the former to denote substance, and the latter the gifts and virtues of the soul. And in this sense, indeed, the image has not been lost. For man, in and after the fall, retained his soul, nor was he made irrational from being rational. 2. Sometimes it is taken for a certain general congruence and ἀναλογίᾳ (analogy), by which man expresses certain θεῖα (divine things), especially regarding the soul, whose three faculties are an εἰκών (image) of the Trinity. And not even regarding this γενικὴν (general) conformity has the image been lost. 3. It is taken by some only for the image of dominion, externally over living creatures, the χρῆσις (use) of which was indeed weakened, yet not entirely lost, but the κτῆσις (possession) itself remained in its entirety. And in this way Epiphanius defined the image, and therefore denied its loss.

IV. But we do not attend here to those general acceptations, but we understand the image of God properly and according to the phrase of Scripture, as it is defined in the disputation, and signifies the wisdom of the mind, the holiness of the heart, the harmony of the appetite, and the innate perfection of all faculties and powers. Concerning which this is our opinion briefly: The image of God was entirely lost through the fall, yet in such a way that certain ruins, as it were, of a great building, and as it were faint little sparks of a huge flame, have remained.

This thesis embraces two things: 1. The total destruction of the image. 2. The remaining of some ruins. Concerning both, in a few words;

Latin:

QVÆSTIO II. An peccatum originale sit plena & omnimoda imaginis diuinæ priuatio?

I. Origenes in c. 26. Gen. Hom. 14. imaginem Dei obscuratam quidem sed non penitus obliteratam esse autumat. Filius Dei, ait, pictor est huius imaginis. Et quia talis ac tantus pictor est, imago eius obscurari per incuriam potest, deleri per malitiam non potest. Manet enim semper imago Dei in te, licèt tu tibi ipsi superinduas imaginem terreni. Epiphanius hæresi 64. & in epist. ad Ioh. Episc. Hierosolim. prorsus integram permansisse contendit. Bellarminus inde audacior factus, hæreseos notam impingit omnibus, imaginem Dei amissam esse dicentibus, l. 4 de milit. Eccl. ca. 9. Recentiores Photiniani similiter disputant, imaginem Dei in homine neutiquam amissam esse Catech. Racov. p. 22.

II. Tendunt autem hæc effata omnia vel ad negationem, vel certè extenuationem mali originalis. Si enim imago Dei non est amissa, tum neque Dei gratia, neque naturalis justitia fuit deperdita. Si non præcessit boni priuatio, succedere non potuit corruptio: Quàmdiu enim clara lux micat, tenebris locus non est: Et vbi sanitas firma, ibi infirmitas nulla. Perinde igitur est, siue quis peccatum originis, siue amifsionem diuinæ imaginis neget. Ita enim cohærent vt vno sublato, mox vnâ tollatur alterum. Pontificii autem amissionem imaginis concreatę negant, siquidem naturalia mansisse integra & imagi- [nem] Dei nec perditam, nec vllâ sui parte deteriorem factam esse adfirmãt. Quare ipsum originis peccatum negãt, & in damnatis Pelagij castris militant.

III. Vt verò hæc melius percipiantur, evolvenda est ambiguitas, quæ latet in voce imaginis. 1. Patres nonnulli distinguunt eam à similitudine, sic vt ista substantiam, hac dotes & virtutes animæ notari censeant. Et hoc sanè sensu imago non est amissa. Homo enim in & post lapsum retinuit animam, nec ex rationali factus est irrationalis. 2. Nonnullquam sumitur pro generali quadam congruentia & ἀναλογίᾳ, quâ homo quædam θεῖα exprimit, præsertim quoad animam, cuius tres facultates sunt εἰκών Trinitatis. Et neque quoad hanc γενικὴν conformitatem imago est deperdita. 3. Accipitur à quibusdam tantùm pro imagine dominij externinè super animantia imperij, cuius χρῆσις quidem labefactata est, non tamen prorsus amissa, ipsa verò κτῆσις in totum remansit. Et hoc modo Epiphanius imaginem definiuit, ideoque eius amissionem negauit.

IV. Nos verò generales istas acceptiones hîc non attendimus, sed imaginem Dei propriè & secundum Scripturæ phrasin intelligimus, prout ea difput. 1. definita est, & significat mentis Sapientiam, cordis sanctitatem, appetitus harmoniam & omnium facultatum viriumque congenitam perfectionem. De qua hæc nostra breuiter est sententia: Imago Dei per lapsum penitus est amissa, sic tamen, vt quædam quasi rudera de magno ædificio, & velut tenues scintillulæ de igenti flamma remanserint.

Thesis hæc duo complectitur: 1. Totalem imaginis destructionem. 2. Aliqualem ruderum remansionem. De vtroque paucis;


### Problem I: I. Concerning the total destruction of the image

I. Concerning the total destruction of the image.

V. The formal aspect of the image of God had a twofold nature: 1. Relative ness, which was the gracious presence of God dwelling in man. This is utterly lost, to such an extent that we are born no longer children of grace, but of wrath, Eph. 2. v. 3. For sin separates us from God, Isa. 50. v. 2. not as regards His universal presence, but His special and gracious one. For God hates those who observe vain superstitions, Ps. 31. v. 6 [30. v. 7], He loved righteousness and hated wickedness, Ps. 45. v. 8 [44. v. 8], and therefore He does not enter an unfaithful soul. Hence Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus: he is justly deserted by God who deserts God. And because man, deserting God, sins, God, deserting the sinner, preserves justice. Wherever I go, says Augustine, ch. 14 of the Soliloquies: You, O Lord, do not desert me, unless I first desert You. Since, therefore, the protoplastoi by sinning deserted God, they were in turn deserted by God through the withdrawal of grace; and thus they completely lost the image of God as regards the formal relative aspect.

VI. 2. The other formal aspect was absolute, which in one word we call original justice or integrity; related to knowing and desiring spiritual things. We prove that this has been totally destroyed and completely lost: 1. From the ignorance of the mind. For in the place of wisdom and innate light, darkness has succeeded. Hence Christ is called the light in darkness, John 1. v. 5 [v. 8], we are said to be turned from darkness, Acts 26. v. 18. We have an intellect darkened by darkness, Eph. 4. v. 18. We are by nature darkness, Eph. 5. v. 8. We lived in times of ignorance, Acts 17. v. 30. We sit in darkness and the shadow of death, Isa. 9. v. 1, Luke 1. v. 79 [v. 39]. The phronema sarkos is enmity against God, Rom. 8. 7. The natural man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit, 1 Cor. 2. v. 14. We are not sufficient to think anything of ourselves, as from ourselves, 2 Cor. 3. v. 5, and therefore every thought must be taken captive under the obedience of Christ, 2 Cor. 10. v. 5. Such great blindness and ignorance, therefore, being engendered in us, the primeval wisdom cannot but be lost and destroyed:

VII. 2. From the depravity of the will. In the first state the heart

ours was upright, holy, conformed to the law of God, turned away from evil, and inclined toward good: but alas! what a transformation has now been made! Where is that righteousness and holiness of truth? We are by nature dead in sins. Job 5:15. Col. 2:13. Eph. 2:1. We are slaves of sin, John 8:34. Every imagination of our heart is only evil every day, Gen. 6:5, from early childhood, Gen. 8:21. We are conceived in sins, Ps. 51. Unclean from the unclean, Job 14:4. Flesh from flesh, John 3:6. We have a heart of stone, Ezek. 36:26: and deceitful, Jer. 17:9: and vain, Ps. 5:9: and slow, Luke 24:25. and hardened, Rom. 2:15, so that we are not able to do the good that we wish to do, Rom. 7:15, but are called captives by the law of the members, warring against the law of our mind, v. 23, all of which provide most clear testimony concerning the loss of holiness and the succession of depravity.

VIII. 3. From a clear description of the deprivation, to which Psalm 14 and Romans 3 especially point. For there is not anyone righteous, v. 10. There is none who understands, there is none who seeks God, v. 11. All together have become ἄχρειοι (useless), there is none who does good, there is not even one, v. 12. They have not known the way of peace, v. 17. There is no fear of God before their eyes, v. 18. All lack the glory of God, v. 23, etc. In these verses that horrible πτωσις (fall) and deprivation of the divine image is clearly depicted, while the mind is said to be most miserably bereft of knowledge, the members of uprightness, the heart of fear, and the whole man of the glory of God.

IX. 4. From a comparison of both states. If we compare the happiness of our first parents before the fall with the misery of their descendants after the fall, as both are described in Scripture and confirmed by experience, it will appear most evidently that man has been changed from wise to ignorant, from pious to impious, from just to unjust, from rich to poor, from healthy to sick, from upright to crooked, from immortal to mortal, from free a captive, from living a dead man, from a friend of God an enemy, from a son of grace a son of wrath, from an heir of eternal life, made a slave of Gehenna, and thus the image of God having been lost, transformed into the image of Satan; for which reason we are said to bear the image of the earthly Adam, 1 Cor. 15, ver. 49, who is turned away from God and destitute of holiness, and liable to death and eternal damnation, unless reconciliation be made through Christ.

X 5. From the comparison of Adam and Christ. This exists in Rom. 5, v. 12 et seqq., where it is shown what goods we have received from our first parent by hereditary right, namely not the image of God distinguished by justice and life, but sin and death, and thus the likeness of the Devil rather than of God.

XI. 6. From restoration and ἀνακαινώσει [renewal]. Whatever is restored to us, and is restored in us through a new creation, that certainly was previously lost and perished: for that which is always retained is not said to be restored. But the image of God is restored to us while we are renewed to it through the Holy Spirit. Therefore, it was previously lost in Adam through the fall. The following confirm the minor premise: 1. 2 Cor. 3, v. 18. We are transformed into the same image from glory to glory as by the Spirit of the Lord. Where note the word μεταμορφώσεως [transformation]. For if we are renewed to the image through the transmutation of the former form, it follows certainly that we were first destitute of that image. 2. Eph. 4, v. 23. Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who according to God is created in justice and holiness. If we must be renewed, therefore we naturally lack that newness of Spirit, which is justice and holiness, and consequently the image of God. 3. Col. 3, v. 10. Put off the old man and put on the new, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him. If the newness of man consists in the knowledge of God, it follows that this is not present in us. For what need would there be of renewal for that which we already possess beforehand.

XII. 7. From the testimonies of the Fathers 1. Origen, homily 1 on Genesis: Man brought in the image of the evil one through sin: therefore Christ came, made in the likeness of men, that we might be reformed to His image. 2. Basil on Psalm 48: After man lost the image of the supercelestial Creator, he assumed the likeness of the earthly. 3. Nyssen, book on the life of Macrina: The integrity of nature is crushed. 4. Damascene, book 4, Orthodox Faith, chapter 4: God had made man in incorruption for the sake of communion with Himself. But through the transgression of the commandment we have obliterated the characters of the divine image, and now, established in malice, we are justly deprived of divine communion.

XIII. Finally 8. From the confession of adversaries. 1. Alphonsus de Castro, book 2 against heresies, title Adam, writes: Origen understood by the image either the native or original substance; or he signified the likeness or quality of the soul. But if Origen used it in this way, who does not see that there is no suspicion of heresy there; from which it follows, since we also accept it in this sense, that the mark of heresy is unjustly branded by Bellarmine. 2. Pererius, book 4 on Genesis, question 7, page 121, number 5, expressly affirms that the image of God has not indeed been lost, if it is explained as the rational nature; but if it is considered according to the beauty and perfection of nature, which is the natural completion and consummation of the image, then such likeness and image of God is entirely blotted out and destroyed by sinning.

XIV. And thus far we have given a sufficiently proven loss of the divine image, from which furthermore the solution to this question is easy, whether natural qualities have remained intact in man. For because in disputation 2 we proved that original righteousness and therefore the image of God itself was natural to man; and indeed we now show that it has been lost, it follows certainly that we have lost certain natural qualities, and therefore have not retained all things intact and unharmed. For we do not wonder without cause why the Papists fight so much for the integrity of natural things in man, since they say that they did not remain intact in the serpent, which nevertheless neither sinned, nor persuaded sin, but was only the instrument of the one persuading. For the same serpent, to whom it was previously natural to walk upright and feed on herbs, having lost these natural things, moves upon its breast and feeds on earth, as Bellarmine concedes, book 3, On the Grace of the First Man, chapter 11. Although Pererius disagrees, book 6, on Genesis, question 4, page 260. If, however, the natural things of the serpent did not remain intact, much less did those of man.

XV. There remains now one or another small objection, to which we shall respond in a few words. 1. Genesis 9, verse 6. Even after the fall, man is said to be created in the image of God, and therefore the shedding of blood is forbidden. And James 3, verse 9, men are said to be made καθ' ὁμοίωσιν Θεῦ, according to the likeness of God. That image and likeness, therefore, is not entirely lost.

Response. There are various expositions of those texts, which, if they are all joined together, a full response will emerge. 1. By image, a certain general conformity and congruence of man with God can be understood, such as that he consists of a spiritual, rational, immortal soul, etc. For some of the Fathers accepted this in a broad sense. From this, however, it does not follow that because the general image remained, the special one defined by justice also remained. For from the position of one to the position of the other, the consequence is not valid. 2. If the special and properly so-called image is understood, it can be explained concerning the first formation of man. For just as in Adam, as the head, we all sinned, so in him we are all said to have been created in the image of God. Now, however, we are no longer created, but begotten. Therefore, since those texts speak of the immediate creation of man in the image of God, they ought to be explained concerning the first condition of Adam and the whole human race in Adam, not concerning the subsequent generation of anyone in particular. 3. If individual men are considered in their own person, even these can be said to have been produced in the image of God, not as to its total fullness, but as to slight particles that after the fall still remain, which are the φυσικαὶ notions of honorable and base things, which ought deservedly to recall a killer from human slaughter. 4. Finally, the image can be understood; not that which is now present, but that which ought to or can be for the sake of being, or that which is indeed present, but not from natural generation, but rather from spiritual regeneration, just as the preposition not per but propter may denote, and thus the sense may be, Let not man be killed, because for the sake of the image of God, namely in him through Christ, he was created either restored or to be restored. These are the primary expositions of those texts; the sum of which is this: Man after the fall is said to be created to the image of God either general, which always remains; or special and properly so called, which indeed has been lost, nevertheless we are called holy according to it; either in Adam, as head, or in his own person; as regards the remnants; or in Christ through restitution. In brief: We were made to the image of God, both taken broadly, and properly so called, and indeed partly bestowed in Adam; partly remaining as regards the ruins; partly restored through Christ and to be repaired in us, here incipiently, there consummately.

XVI. 2. If certain ruins remain of the first image; Therefore it is not totally lost.

Response. There is no consequence in the argument; for although certain small portions have remained, it is nevertheless rightly said to be destroyed in its entirety, 1. Because the whole formal σχετικὸν has perished, namely the grace of God, 2. and the whole formal absolute, namely the full integrity of all faculties. 3. and the whole free will, namely as regards divine and spiritual things, which are the primary object of the image of God. But whatever remains, this only regards external discipline, it pertains to the lower hemisphere, which concerns worldly things; it is in itself very languid and imperfect, and ought rather to be referred to the material than the formal. Just as therefore the whole building is said to be utterly destroyed, when it has lost its form, and has been leveled to the ground; although stones and certain material ruins remain

ends: thus when we have lost the whole form of the image, for that reason we are rightly said to have lost it entirely, although certain small particles have remained behind.

Latin:

I. De totali imaginis destructione.

V. Imago Dei formale duplex habuit: 1. Relatis rum, quod fuit gratiosa Dei in homine habitantis praesentia. Hoc penitus deperditum est adeo, vt non amplius gratiae, sed irae filij nascamur, Eph. 2. v. 3. Peccatum enim separat nos a Deo, Esa. 50. v. 2. non quoad praesentiam vniuersalem, sed specialem & gratiosam. Deus enim odit obseruantes vanitates superuacaneas, Psal. 30. v. 7. dilexit justitiam & odit impietatem, Psal. 44. v. 8. ideoque non ingreditur animam infidelem. Hinc Fulgentius l. 1. ad Mon. juste deseritur a Deo, qui deserit Deum. Et quia homo deserens Deum peccat, deserens peccatorum Deus iustitiam seruat. Quocunque iero, inquit August c. 14. Soliloqui: Tu me Domine non deseris, nisi prior ego te deseram. Cum igitur πρωτοπλάτοι peccando deseruerint Deum, vicissim deserti sunt a Deo per subtractionem gratiae; adeoque imaginem Dei quoad σχετικὸν formale prorsus amiserunt.

VI. 2. Alterum formale fuit absolutum, quod vno verbo justitiam vel integritatem originalem dicimus; relatam ad res spirituales cognoscendas & appetendas. Hanc totaliter destructam & penitus amissam esse probamus: 1. Ab ignorantia mentis In locum enim sapientiae & lucis concreitae successerunt tenebrae, Hinc Christus dicitur lux in tenebris Ioh. 1. v. 8, dicimur conuerti a tenebris, Act. 26. v. 18. Habemus intellectum obscuratum tenebris. Eph. 4. v. 18. Sumus natura tenebre Eph. 5. v. 8. Viuimus in temporibus ignorantiae Act. 17 v. 30 Sedemus in tenebris & vmbra mortis Esa. 9. v. 1. Luc. 1. v. 39. φρόνημα σαρκὸς est inimicitia aduersus Deum, Rom. 8. 7. animalis homo non percipit ea quae sunt Spiritus, 1. Cor. 2 v. 14. Non sumus idonei cogitare aliquid ex nobis, quasi ex nobis, 2. Cor. 3. v. 5. ideoque πᾶν νόημα captiuendum est sub Christi obsequiu, 2. Cor. 10. v. 5. Tanta igitur caecitas & ignorantia cum nobis ingeneretur, non potest non amissa & deperdita esse primeua sapientia:

VII. 2. A prauitate voluntatis. In primo statu cor

nostrum erat rectum, sanctum, conforme cum lege Dei, auersum à malo, & oclive ad bonum: sed eà heu! quantà nunc facta μεταμόρφωσις? Vbi massia sit illa iustitia & sanctitas veritatis? Sumus naturâ mortui in peccatis. Iob. 5. v. 15. Col. 2. v. 13. Eph. 2. v. 1. Sumus serui peccati, Iob. 8. v. 34. Omne figmentum cordis nostri tantùm malum est omni die, Gen. 6. v. 5. à primà pueritia, Gen. 8. 12. Sumus in pecatis concepti, Psal. 51. Immundi de immundis, Iob. 14. v. 4. Caro de carne. Ioh. 3. v. 6. Habemus cor lapideum, Ezech 36. v. 20: & fraudulentum, Ier. 17. v. 9: & vanum, Psal. 5. v. 10 & tardum, Lu. 24. v. 24. & dutum, Rom. 2. vers. 15. adeò vt bonum, quod volumus facere non valeamus, Rom. 7. v 15. sed captiui dicamur à lege membrorum, repugnante legi mentis nostræ, v 32. quæ omnia de sanctitatis amissione, & prauitatis successione luculentissimum præbent testimonium.

VIII. 3. Aclara scriptione depriuationis, quò potissimùm spectat Psal. 14: & c 3. ad Rom. Non enim est iustus quisquam v. 10. Non est intelligens non est requirens Deum, v. 11. Omnes simul ἄχρειοι inutiles facti sunt, non est, qui faciat bonum, non est vsque ad vnum. v. 12. viam pacis non cognouerunt v. 17. non est timor Dei ante oculos eorum. v. 18. Omnes egent gloriâ Dei, v. 23. & c. Hisce versiculis horrenda illa πτωσις & priuatio diuinæ imaginis luculenter depingitur, dum mens scientiâ, membra rectitudine, cor timore, totus homo gloriâ Dei miserrimè orbatus dicitur.

IX. 4. À collatione vtriusque statûs. Si comparemus felicitatem primorum parētum ante lapsum, cum miseriâ posterorum post lapsum, qualis vtraque & in Scripturà describitur, & experientiâ confirmatur, apparebit evidentissimè, hominem ex sapiente ignorantem, ex pio impium ex iusto jniustum ex diuite pauperem, ex sano ęgrum, ex recto obliquum, ex immortali mortalessi ex libero captivum, ex vivente mortuum, ex amico Dei hostem, ex filio gratiae filium irae, ex hærede vitae æternæ, mancipium gehennæ factum, adeoque amissa imagine Dei, in Satanæ imaginem transformatum esse quam ob causam portare dicimur imaginem terrestris Adæ, 1. Cor. 15. ver. 49. qui aversus est a Deo & destitutus sanctitate, & obnoxius morti, æternæque damnationi nisi per Christum fiat reconciliatio.

X 5. A collatione Adami & Christi. Extat hæc Rom. 5. v. 12 seqq. vbi ostenditur, quæ bona a primo parente hæreditario jure acceperimus, nempe non imaginem Dei justitia & vita insignem, sed peccatum & mortem, adeoque Diaboli potius, quam Dei similitudinem

XI. 6. A restauratione & ἀνακαινώσει, Quicquid nobis restituitur, & per novam creationem in nobis restauratur, illud vtique prius amissum & deperditum fuit: Nam quod semper retinetur, restitui non dicitur. Atqui imago Dei nobis restituitur, dum per Spiritum S. ad illam renouamur. E. prius in Adamo per lapsum amissa fuit. Minorem confirmant sequentia: 1. 2. Cor. 3. v. 18. Transformamur ad eandem imaginem a claritate in claritatem tanquam a Domini Spiritu. Vbi nota vocabulum μεταμορφώσεως. Si enim renouamur ad imaginem per prioris formę transmutationem, sequitur vtique nos destitutos primum fuisse illa imagine. 2. Eph. 4. v. 23. Renouamini Spiritu mentis vestræ, & induite novum hominem, qui secundum Deum creatus est in justitia & sanctitate. Si renouari debemus, ergo ista novitate Spiritus, quæ est justitia & sanctitas, & per consequens imagine Dei naturaliter caremus. 3. Col. 3. v. 10. Exuite hominem veterem & induite nouum, qui renovatur in agnitionem secundum imaginem ejus, qui creavit illum. Si novitas hominis confistit in agnitione Dei, sequitur hanc nobis quod non inesse. Quid enim opus foret renouatione ad id, quod jam ante possidemus.

XII. 7. A testimonijs Patrum 1. Origenes homil. 1. in Gen. Homo maligni imaginem adduxit per peccatum: ideo Christus venit in similitudine hominum factus, vt nos ad eius imaginem reformemur. 2. Basilius in Psal. 48: Homo postquam supercoelestis opificis imaginem amisit, terreni similitudinem assumsit. 3. Nyssenus l. de vita Mar. Natura integritas est contrita 4. Damasc. l. 4. O. F. c. 4. In incorruptione fecerat Deus hominem propter sui ipsius communionem. At per trangressionem præcepti divinæ imaginis characteres obliteravimus, & nunc in malitia constituti diuinâ communione iustè sumus privati.

XIII. Tandem 8. A confessione aduersariorum. 1. Alphonsus deCastro l. 2. adversus hæreses, tit. Adam scribit: Origines per imaginem intelligebat, vel natiuum seu substantiam originalem; vel significabat similitudinem seu animi qualitatem. Quòd si Origines secundum hunc modum usurpauerit, quis non videt, ibi nullam esse hæreseos suspicionem; Ex quo sequitur, cùm & nos isto sensu accipiamus, iniquè à Bellarmino hæreseos notam inpingi. 2. Pererius l. 4. in Genel. quæst. 7. p. 121. num. 5, disertè adfirmat, imaginem Dei non quidem amissjam esse, si exponatur de naturâ rationali; quòd si verò consideretur secundum pulcritudinem & perfectionem naturæ, quæ sit naturalis imaginis absolutio & consummatio, tum huiusmodi similitudinem & imaginem Dei peccandi penitus deleri atque destrui.

XIV. Et hactenus satis probatam dedimus diuinæ imaginis amissionem, vnde porrò facilis est solutio & istius quæstionis, Vnum naturalia in homine permanserint integra. Quia enim disput 2. evicimus; iustitiam originalem adeoque & ipsam imaginem Dei fuisse homini naturalem; & verò nunc ostendimus, eam esse amissam, sequitur vtique, nos quædam naturalia perdidisset, ideoque nō omnia integra & illæsa retinuisse. Non a. immeritò miramur, cur Pontificij adeò pugnent pro integritate naturalium in homine, cum ea non integra mansisse dicant in serpente, qui tamen nec peccauit, nec peccatum persuasit, sed suadentis tantum instrumentum fuit. Cui enim antea naturale erat rectum incedere & herbis vesci, idem serpens, amissis his naturalibus super pectus graditur, & terra vescitur, vti concedit Bell. l. 3. de A. G. c. 11. Quamuis dissentiat Pererius l. 6. in G. q. 4. p. 260. Si autem serpentis naturalia non manserunt integra, multo minus hominis.

XV. Superest nunc vna vel altera obiectiuncula, ad quam paucis respondebimus. 1. Gen. 9. v. 6. Etiam post lapsum dicitur homo ad imaginem Dei conditus, ideoque prohibetur sanguinis effusio. Et Iacob. 3. v. 9. homines καθ' ὁμοίωσιν Θεῦ secundum similitudinem Dei facti dicuntur. Illa igitur imago & similitudo non est penitus amissa.

Resp. Textuum istorum variæ sunt expositiones, quæ si jungantur omnes, prodibit plena responsio, 1. Per imaginem intelligi potest generalis quædam conformitas & congruentia hominis cum Deo, vt quod constat animâ spirituali, rationali, immortali, &c. Hoc enim lato sensu nonnulli ex Patribus acceperunt. Hinc vero non sequitur, quia mansit generalis imago, specialem quoque definitam justitiâ permansisse. Nam à positione vnius ad positionem alterius non valet consequentia. 2. Si imago specialis & propriè dicta intelligatur, exponi potest de prima hominis formatione. Sicut enim in Adamo, vt capite omnes peccavimus, ita in illo ad imaginem Dei omnes creati dicimur. Iam verò non ampliùs creamur, sed generamur. Proinde cùm textus isti de immediata creatione hominis ad imaginem Dei loquantur, de primâ Adami totiufque humani generis in Adamo conditione, non de subsequente quorumuis in indiuiduo generatione exponi debent. 3. Si maximè singuli homines in propria persona attendantur, tame & hi dici possunt ad imaginem Dei producti, non quoad ei' totam plenitudinem, sed quoad tenues particulas post lapsum adhuc reliquas, quæ sunt notitiæ φυσικαὶ, honestorum & turpium, quæ interfectorem à cæde humana meritò reuocare deberent. 4. Tandem intelligi potest imago; non quæ jam adsit, sed quæ ad esse debeat aut possit, vel quæ adsit quidem, sed non ex generatione naturali, verùm regeneratione spirituali, sicut præpositio non per sed propter notet, adeoque sensus sit, Non interficiatur homo, quia propter imaginem Dei, in ipso nimirum per Christum, vel reparatam vel reparandam creatus est. Hæ sunt primariæ istorum textuum expositiones; quarum hæc summa: Homo post lapsum creatus dicitur ad imaginem Dei vel generalem, quæ semper manet; vel specialem & propriè dictam, quæ quidem amissa est, nihilominus ad illam sancti dicimur; vel in Adamo, tanquam capite, vel in propria persona; quoad reliquias; vel in Christo per restitutionem. Breuissimè: Facti sumus ad imaginem Dei, tum latè sumtam, tum propriè dictam & quidem partim in Adamo collatam; partim quoad rudera residuam; partim per Christum restitutam & in nobis reparandam, hic inchoatè, illic consummatè.

XVI. 2. Si rudera quædam supersunt de imagine prima; Ergo totaliter non est amissa.

Respond. Nulla inest argumento consequentia; Licet enim portiunculæ quædam remanserint, rectè tamen dicitur in totum destructa, 1. Quia totum formale σχετικὸν periit, nempe gratia Dei, 2. & totum formale absolutum, nempe plena omnium facultatum integritas. 3. & totum liberum arbitrium, nempè quoad res diuinas & spirituales, quæ sunt primarium imaginis Dei obiectum. Quicquid verò superest, hoc tantùm externam disciplinam respicit, ad hemisphærium inferius, quod concernit res mundanas, pertinet; in se valdè languidum & imperfectum est, potiusque ad materiale, quàm formale referri debet. Sicut ergò totum ædificium penitus destructum dicitur, cùm formam suam amisit, & solo adæquatum est; licet lapides & rudera quædam materialia super-

finit: ita cùm totã imaginis formam perdiderimus, idcircò illam totam amisisse rectè dicimur quamvis exiguæ quædam particulæ manserint residuæ.


### Problem I: II. Concerning the remains of the destroyed image

II. Concerning the remains of the destroyed image.

XVII. As the remains are not to be opposed to the total loss of the image, which the Papists do, so they are not to be entirely removed, which the Photinians do. For thus we have lost grace, yet we have retained nature, and in nature certain notions of God and Good, indicators of just and unjust, base and honest. The Apostle speaks of these in Rom. 1. v. 18. 19. etc., and especially in ch. 2. v. 14. 15., where he affirms that τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου, the work of the law itself, is written in the hearts of the Gentiles, so much so that φύσει, or by nature, they do the things that are of the law. The same is proven by conscience and synderesis, which is like a law obliging to good, and an indicator testifying of the deed, and a judge accusing evil works. For unless the distinction between honest and base things were innate to man, the wicked would not tremble so much, or accuse themselves. But this has been treated and disputed by us elsewhere at sufficient length.

XVIII. The use, however, of these remains is primarily fivefold. For they have remained 1. That they may be testimonies of the first happiness. For if the ruins and ἐρείπια are so excellent, what shall we think of the whole building? If the little sparks shine so much, what shall we judge of the whole fullness of light? Moreover, let this consideration lead us by the hand to the acknowledgment of the divine goodness, by which we were created in the image of God. For we are born in such a way that our parents make us condemned before we are born, Bernh. c. 2. Meditat. And although this image is restored here, yet this is done imperfectly, so that just as the elders of Israel lamented the destruction of the first temple when they saw that the second did not correspond to it, so not undeservedly do we owe tears, as often as we recall our first happiness, and observe that the temple of our heart, because of innate concupiscence, differs greatly from the dignity of the πρωτοπλάσων, who were the most beautiful dwelling-place of the Trinity. Meanwhile, however, just as this second temple was at length remarkably adorned, so that its glory was greater than the first, so let us not despair, but humbly seek and firmly expect the perfection of our souls, and a fuller grace and beauty.

XIX. 2. That external discipline and public peace may be preserved. For these remnants are as it were certain little sparks of virtues, stimulating us, lest we live an altogether barbarous and beastly life. They are like torches, which in such great darkness of errors lead Princes so that they may follow what is right; and subjects, so that they may imitate princes. They teach the latter to live in peace without injury: the former, to offer violence to no one, and to repel injury from those upon whom it is inflicted.

XX. 3. That God may be sought, and the true worship of God may be investigated. For lest the Gentiles, established outside the Church, be able to plead a total lack of means, God has caused these remnants to survive, so that they may be like a pedagogue, leading to the Church, and consequently to the restoration of the divine image. For since we know that there is a God, and the remnants of the image suggest that He must be worshipped, they simultaneously exhort us to investigate the true method of worship. Whence the Apostle in Acts 17, v. 27, says that God created men, and determined appointed times ζητεῖν τὸν κύριον, that they should seek the Lord, namely, who He is, or in what manner He wishes and ought to be honored?

XXI. 4. That He who is sought and found may be glorified. Every creature is dissolved into the praises of its maker, inasmuch as the heavens also declare the glory of God, Psalm 19, v. 1. But since man is the most excellent creature, therefore, so that he may glorify God more, the remnants of the image and natural knowledge have been impressed upon him. But here we must exclaim with the Poet: Alas, why are so many accustomed to extinguish the remnants of divine light, forgetting both themselves and God!

For when they know God, they do not glorify Him as God, nor give thanks, but they become vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart is darkened, Rom. 1. v. 21.

XXII. 5. So that, if men neglect these things, they may become inexcusable. The preceding uses were primary and essential, but this last one is secondary and accidental, not arising from the intention of God who imprints it, but from the malice of sinning men; for when the law of nature rightly persuades, yet they do evil, they become ἀναπολόγητοι [inexcusable], Rom. 1. v. 20. For just as the Jews have no excuse for their sin, because Christ announced the truth to them, John 15. v. 28, so the Gentiles can pretend nothing against the just judgment of God, because the law of nature and the remnants of the image urged them to the flight of crimes and the search for true worship.

Latin:

II. De imaginis destructæ reliquiis.

XVII. Vthæ non sunt opponendæ totali amissioni imaginis quod faciunt Pontificij, ita non sunt penitùs tollendæ, quod faciunt Photiniani.
