Sic enim perdidimus gratiam, vt tamen retinuerimus naturam, & in natura quasdã noticias de Deo & Bono, justi & injusti, turpis & honesti indices. De his verba facit Apostolus Rom. 1. v. 18. 19. &c. in primis. c. 2. v. 14. 15. vbi τὸ ἔργον τοῦ νόμου ipsum opus legis in cordibus gentilium scriptum esse affirmat, adeò quidem vt φύσει vel naturâ faciant ea, quæ sunt legis. Idem evincit conscientia & synteresis, quæ est instar legis obligantis ad bonum, & indicis testificantis de facto, & judicis accusantis mala opera. Nisi enim homini discrimen honestorum & turpium innatum esset, sceloresi non adeò trepidarent, aut semetipsos accusarent. Verùm de hoc alibi satis prolixè à nobis actum & disputatum est.

XVIII. Vsus verò istarum reliquiarum est potissimùm quintuplex. Remanserunt enim 1. Vt sint testimonia primæ felicitatis. Si enim rudera & ἐρείπια tàm sunt præstantia, quid de toto ędificio censebimus? scintillulæ adeò micant, quid de tota lucis plenitudine judicabimus? Hæc autem consideratio nos manu ducat ad agnitionem bonitatis divinæ, quâ ad imaginem Dei creati sumus. Sic enim jam nascimur, vt parentes nos priùs faciant damnatos, quàm natos, Bernh. c. 2. Meditat. Et licet imago ista hic restituatur, fit tamẽ hoc imperfectè, adeò vt sicut seniores Israelis deplorarunt destructionem primi templi, cùm viderent secundum illi non respondere, ita non immeritò lacrymas erumpere debeamus, quoties felicitatem primam recolimus, & templum cordis nostri ob annatam concupiscentiam à πρωτοπλάσων dignitate, qui pulcherrimum Trinitatis habitaculum erant, plurimum discrepare animaduertimus. Interim tamen sicuti templum istud secundum insigniter tandem exornatum est, vt gloria eius maior fuerit, quàm primi, ita non desperemus, sed perfectionem animarum, & pleniorem gratiam ac pulchritudinem humiliter petamus, & firmiter expectemus.

XIX. 2. Vt externa disciplina & pax publica conseruetur Sunt enim istæ reliquiæ quasi quidam igniculi virtutum, nos stimulantes, ne planè barbaram & beluinam vitam viuamus. Sunt facis instar, quæ in tantis errorum tenebris Principes ducunt vt rectum sequantur; subditos, vt principes imitentur. Docent hos vt sine iniuria in pace viuant: illos, vt nemini vim inferant, & ab his quibus infertur, iniuriam propulsent.

XX. 3. Vt Deus quæratur, verusque cultus Dei indagetur. Ne enim gentiles extra Ecclesiam constituti omnem defectum mediorum queant prætendere, Deus reliquias istas superesse fecit, vt sint instar Pædagogi, ducentis ad Ecclesiam, & consequenter ad instaurationem diuinę imaginis. Cùm enim sciamus esse Deum, illumque colendum esse imaginis reliquiæ suggerant, simul & hortantur, vt veram cultus rationem inuestigemus. Vnde Apostolus Act. 17. v. 27. ait Deum creasse homines, & definijsse statuta tempora ζητεῖν τὸν κύριον, vt quærant Dominum, nempe quis sit? quove modo honorari velit & debeat?

XXI. 4. Vt quæsitus & inuentus glorificetur. Omnis creatura in laudes opificis sui soluitur, siquidem & cœli enarrant gloriam Dei, Psal. 19. v. 1. Homo autem cum creatura sit præstantissima, idcircò vt Deum magis glorificare, reliquiæ imaginis & noticiæ naturales impressæ sunt. Verùm hîc cum Poëta exclamandum: Heu cur relliquias divinæ extinguere lucis Tàm multi obliti seq́ue Deuḿque solent!

Cùm enim Deum cognoscant, non sicut Deum glorificant, aut gratias agunt, sed evanescunt in cogitationibus suis, obscuratum est insipiens cor eorum, Rom 1. v. 21.

XXII. 5. Vt, si homines ista negligant, inexcusabiles fiant. Præcedentes vsus fuêre primarij & essentiales, hic autem vltimus est secundarius & accidentalis, non ex Dei imprimentis intentione; sed hominum peccantium malitia ortus, cùm enim lex naturæ recta suadet, illi tamen mala faciunt, ἀναπολόγητοι fiunt, Rom. 1. v. 20. Sicut enim Iudæi excusationem non habent de peccato, quia Christus veritatem ijs annunciauit, Ioh. 15. v. 28. Ita gentiles nihil prætendere possunt contra justum Dei judicium, quia lex naturæ & reliquiæ imaginis ad fugam scelerum, verique cultus inquisitionem eos solicitarunt.


### Problem I: Question III. Whether original sin includes any positive quality besides the privation of the divine image?

QUESTION III. Whether original sin includes any positive quality besides the privation of the divine image?

I. Bellarmine reports (lib. 5 de A. G. cap. 15) that certain Catholics maintain that original sin is not a bare privation, but furthermore a depraved concupiscence, and therefore a morbid quality in the soul perpetually exciting depraved desires. He himself, however, declares for the contrary opinion, moved by arguments that are trivial and not at all weighty, which we shall briefly examine.

II. First, he brings forward certain testimonies of Augustine, whom he says maintains that concupiscence is the sensitive appetite itself, such as is also found in brutes; and therefore [it is] no corrupted or vicious quality, except insofar as it is destitute of the bridle of original justice.

But this is attributed to Augustine, nor can it be firmly proven from his writings, since in book 1 of On Marriage, chapter 25, he expressly calls concupiscence a certain affection of an evil quality, and elsewhere a morbid affection of the flesh, and here and there in other places, a disease and a languor.

III. Next, he brings forward some little arguments, but very weak ones.

1. If concupiscence were a positive quality, it ought to have a positive cause. But no such cause can be named.

Response. Nay, indeed, we expressly give and name it, namely, the malicious suggestion of the Devil and the voluntary assent of man, in one word, the first disobedience.

For just as now the habit of some vice is acquired through the frequent repetition of evil acts, so then, through a single evil action, which because of its remarkable enormity was far more laborious than the frequent multiplication of acts, the habit of original concupiscence was contracted. And just as elsewhere a contrary habit immediately succeeds a privation, since the στέρησις (privation) of virtue is followed by vice, and the στέρησις (privation) of health is followed by disease: so, with the image of God destroyed by the fall, what else could follow but the disorder and horrendous corruption of all powers? Why then do you seek a hidden crack for the introduced evil, when you have a most open door? From Augustine, book 2 of On Marriage, chapter 28.

IV. 2. It could not be said how this sin is transmitted to descendants, since acquired habits are not passed on.

Response. A distinction must be made between habits that are ἐμφύτους (innate) or natural, and ἐπικτήτους (acquired) or personal and acquired. We willingly concede that the latter are not propagated; but it is not permitted to argue from the latter to the former because of their disparate nature. Thus, original justice was a habit in Adam, and yet he would have propagated it to his descendants. How so? Because the habit was not acquired, but concreated. In like manner, since sin, the contrary of justice, is a ἕξις φρονικὴ (a habitual disposition), and adheres most deeply and inseparably to nature itself, hence it follows that this is always derived into children along with nature.

V. 3. It would follow either that God is the cause of that habit, or that not all things were made through Him, which is against the Evangelist John 1. v. 3.

Resp. All things that were made were made through God. But sin was not made, but introduced. Hence the Fathers: τὸ κακὸν ὐδὲ γενητὸν ὐδὲ ἀγέννητον ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιγινόμενον. And to this pertains the distinction of beings, usually handed down by some, as that a being is either created, like the works of the six days; or generated, like the remaining succeeding individuals; or made, like artificial things; or restored, like heaven and hell; or introduced, like sin. Thus, therefore, both remain true: both that all things which were made or created are from God; and that God is not the cause of sin, because that was not made, but introduced through the envy of Satan and the disobedience of man.

VI. 4. It could not be understood how infected flesh would infect the soul.

Resp. This argument does not militate against us, because we do not maintain that souls are created, but propagated, and therefore they are not infected by the body, but are transmitted already infected. For such as is the propagating soul of the father, such also is the soul of the son, which is propagated.

VII. 5. Since that quality is adventitious, it would have long since been extinguished or changed.

Respond. I deny the consequence, because sin is not some extrinsic and trivial accident, which can be easily separated or extinguished, but it pervades nature most deeply, so that it cannot be abolished except through the total resolution of the body. Hence it is called κακὸν παρακείμενον, the evil that most tenaciously lies near, Rom. 7. v. 21. And ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος, the sin that always surrounds us, Hebr. 12 v. 1.

VIII. 6. No positive quality is necessary for the flesh to lust against the Spirit, since the sensitive appetite, deprived of the bridle of original righteousness, is sufficient.

Resp. It is not indeed absolutely necessary, but by hypothesis. For by the lapse of the harmony and rectitude of all the powers, a collapse and corruption of nature necessarily followed. 2. The appetite in itself and by itself, as it was created by God, does not lust against the Spirit. Nor can a mere privation incite it to lust after evil. Wherefore a vicious quality must necessarily be conceded, which both corrupts the appetite itself and thus moves it to rebellion.

XI. 7. It would follow that original sin is not taken away by Baptism, since that depraved concupiscence remains in the baptized.

Resp. Sin is not taken away in its entirety, but only to an extent, not simply but in a certain respect. For the formal debt is taken away, but the absolute remains. The punishment is taken away, the vice is left. For Baptism causes, not that sin does not exist, but that it is not imputed. August. book 1 de nuptiis ch. 25.

X. Thus far we have responded to the little arguments of Bellarmine: now we shall submit our arguments for a positive quality, of which there are five principal ones. 1. From the description of sin. For Scripture depicts it in such a way as to indicate that, besides the privation of the image, the whole nature and all its faculties are most foully depraved. Hence the figment of the human heart is said to be only evil, Gen. 6 v. 5, ch. 8 v. 22, and fraudulent, Jer. 17 v. 9, and the mind of the flesh is enmity against God, Rom. 8 v. 7, and there are other sayings describing sin positively. From which we conclude thus: Whatever is designated by habitual vices of the soul, that is not merely privative, since a habit and a privation are opposed. But original sin is designated in the Scriptures by habitual vices of the soul, namely the foolishness of the mind, the malice of the heart, the contumacy of the appetite, and the enmity of the whole man against God. Therefore it is not a merely privative entity,

XI 2. From inherence. Whatever is adjacent to and constantly inheres in the soul of man, this is something positive. For privations are not properly said to inhere or be adjacent. Original sin, however, in Rom. 7:21 is called an adjacent evil, v. 23 the law of sin existing in the members, v. 17 & 20 sin dwelling therein, because it does not pass away but has a fixed seat in the flesh; in Heb. 12:1 it is called ἀπειρίστατος ἁμαρτία, sin surrounding on all sides. Wherefore it is rightly concluded to be something positive.

XII. 3. From the effect. From whatever source positive acts and effects flow, that very thing itself must also be a positive being, since cause and effect do not differ in their entire genus. But from original sin arise positive acts and effects, namely actual sins. Wherefore it follows that it itself is also a positive being.

XIII. 4. From contrariety. Every contrariety is between positive beings. Natural sin and original justice are opposed not only privatively, but also contrarily. Therefore they are also positive beings.

XIV. 5. From authority. Augustine, book 1 de nupt. & concupisc. ch. 25, and book 6 cont. Iulian ch. 7, expressly calls sin an evil quality and compares it to a languor, whence Luther rightly pronounced that sin has most wretchedly corrupted and wasted our whole nature like leprosy or a pestilential plague. Thomas Aquinas, 2, question 28, article 1, names it a corrupt habit. For he speaks thus: Just as bodily sickness has something of privation, in that the equality of temperament and health is removed, and something positive, such as the humors themselves being inordinately disposed: So original sin IS NOT A PURE PRIVATION, but a certain corrupt HABIT. Upon which passage Cajetan comments thus: Corruption is distinguished from pure privation. For privation gives a negation in a subject apt by nature: but corruption adds a positive contrary, founding that negation. And to this also pertains that

Gerson, that original sin is an inability for good, and an ability for evil. Which confessions of the adversaries are to be noted, especially Thomas's, so that the Papists' position regarding the primary head of faith may appear, and how in many things the Jesuits depart from the ancient Papistic religion.

XV. Furthermore, it is to be observed that our theologians do not teach that sin is, strictly and in all respects, a positive quality, but that they use this term πλάτει, or in a certain latitude, just as that ἁμαρτία συνεισέρχεται is called a positive entity, chiefly because of its constant adherence and the profound corruption of nature, not otherwise than as a disease of the body is not only a privation of health, but at the same time the position of a depraved disposition, and the vices of the soul are opposed to virtues not only privatively, but also contrarily. For because the Papists argue that sin is merely a privation of a supernatural gift, of original righteousness, and that nature itself has remained in itself such as it was created from the beginning: hence it happened that, in order to refute this scholastic error more strongly, our theologians assumed the term of a positive [quality], and thus by it they indicate only this: that sin not only took away righteousness, but at the same time corrupted nature, so that the τὰ φυσικὰ have not remained whole and unharmed. This corruption and depravation of nature, therefore, distinct from the substance, we wish to be marked solely by the term of a positive quality.

XVI. To this, moreover, can be referred that distinction of privation, that one is simple, denoting a mere lack, as darkness; another is habitual, which is joined with a contrary form, as diseases. The Papists refer original sin to the former species, our theologians to the latter. For thus it is a ςέρησις of righteousness so that it simultaneously includes an ἕξιν of unrighteousness and of depraved concupiscence.

XVII. Nor let that metaphysical argument trouble us: Every positive being is good. Sin is a positive being. Therefore it is good. For the major premise proposes concerning created being, and exquisitely positive. The minor premise subsumes concerning being introduced and ἐν πλάτει positive, whence four terms arise, and the consequence of the argument perishes.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO III. An peccatum originis præter priuationem divinæ imaginis qualitatem aliquam positiuam includat?

I. Refert Bell. l. 5. de A. G. c. 15 quosdam Catholicos statuere, peccatum originis non esse nudam priuationem, sed insuper pravam concupiscentiam, adeóque qualitatem mor bidam in anima perpetuò prava desideria excitantem. Ipse verò in contrariam aijt sententiam, motus argumentis leuiculis & minimè ponderosis, quæ breuiter examinabimus.

II. Primùm profert quædam Augustini testimonia, quem statuere ait, concupiscentiam esse ipsum appetitum sensitiuum, qualis etiam in brutis reperitur; ideoque nullam qualitatem corruptam aut vitiosam, nisi quatenus fræno originalis iustitiæ destituatur.

Verum affingitur hoc Augustino, neque ex scriptis eius firmiter probari potest, siquidem l. 1. de nuptijs c. 25. concupiscentiam disertè vocat affectionem quandam malæ qualitatis, & c. morbidum carnis affectum, alibíque passim, morbum & languorem.

III. Deinde profert nonnullas ratiunculas, sed valdè debiles.

1. Si concupiscentia qualitas esset positiva positinam causam habere deberet. Sed nulla talis nominari potest.

Respond. Imò verò expressè damus & nominamus eam nempè malitiosam Diaboli suggestione m, & voluntariam hominis assensionem, vno verbo primam inobedientiam.

Sicut enim nunc habitus alicuius vitij per crebram malorum actuum iterationem acquiritur: ita nunc per vnicam actionem malam, quæ ob insignem enormitatem suam longè operosiór erat, quàm crebra actuum multiplicatio, contrahebatur habitus originalis cōcupiscentię. Et sicut aliàs privationi statim succedit contrarius habitus, siquidem στέρησις virtutis vitium, στέρησις sanitatis morbus sequitur: sic deletâ imagine Dei per lapsum, quid aliud sequi poterat, quàm omnium virium inordinatio & horrenda corruptio? Quid ergo quæris latentem introducti mali rimam, cùm habeas apertissimam ianuam? ex August. l. 2. de nuptijs c. 28.

IV. 2. Non posset esse di, quomodo peccatum istud transmittatur in posteros, cùm habitus adquisiti non trajiciantur.

Respond. Distinguendum est inter habitus ἐμφύτους vel naturales, & ἐπικτήτους vel personales & acquisitos. Hos non propagari lubenter concedimus; ab his verò ad illos argumentari non licet ob naturam disparem. Sic justitia originalis fuit in Adamo habitus, & tamen propagasset eam in posteros. Qui sic? Quoniam habitus fuit non acquisitus, sed concreatus. Pari modo, cùm peccatum, justitiæ contrarium, ἕξις φρονικὴ sit, ipsíque naturæ profundissimè & inseparabiliter inhæreat, hinc illud in liberos vnàcum natura semper deriuari sequitur.

V. 3. Sequeretur, aut Deum esse causam istius habitus, aut non omnia per ipsum facta esse, quod contra Euangelistam Ioh. 1. v. 3.

Resp. Omnia, quæ facta per Deum facta sunt. Peccatum verò non est factum, sed introductum. Hinc Patres : τὸ κακὸν ὐδὲ γενητὸν ὐδὲ ἀγέννητον ἀλλ᾽ ἐπιγινόμενον. Et huc pertinet entium distinctio, à non nullis tradi solita, vt quòd ens sit vel creatum, vt opera sex dierum; vel generatum, vt reliqua supposita succedentia; vel factum, vt artificialia; vel reparatum, vt cœlum & infernus; vel introductum, vt peccatum. Sic ergo vtrumque verum permanet, tum omnia, quæ facta vel creata sunt, à Deo esse; tum Deum peccati causam non esse, quia illud non factum, sed per invidiam Satanæ, & inobedientiam hominis introductum est.

VI. 4. Intelligi non posset, quomodo caro infecta animam inficeret.

Resp. Argumentum hoc contra nos non militat, quia non statuimus animas creari, sed propagari, ideoque à corpore non infici, sed infectas transmitti. Qualis enim est propagans anima Patris, talis est etiam anima filij, quæ propagatur.

VII. 5. Cum qualitas illa sit aduentitia, iam dudum extincta vel immutata esset.

Respond. N. C. quia peccatum non est extrinsecum quiddam & leuiculum accidens, quod facilè separari extinguiuè queat, sed altissimè peruadit naturam adeò vt non nisi per totalem corporis resolutionem aboleri queat. Hinc nominatur κακὸν παρακείμενον, malum quod tenacissimè adjacet, Rom. 7. v. 21. Et ἁμαρτία εὐπερίστατος, peccatum nos semper circumstans, Hebr. 12 v. 1.

VIII. 6. Nulla qualitas positiua est necessaria, vt caro concupiscat aduersus Spiritum, cùm sufficiat appetitus sensitiuus, fræno originalis iustitiæ destitutus.

Resp. Non quidem est necessaria absolutè, sed ex ὑποθέσει. Distincta enim per lapsum omnium virium ἁρμονίᾳ & rectitudine, necessariò secuta est σύρῥαξις & naturæ corruptio. 2. Appetitus in se & per se prout à Deo conditus, non concupiscit adversus Spiritum. Neque nuda priuatio illum incitare potest ad malè concupiscendum. Quare necessariò concedenda est vitiosa qualitas, quæ & appetitum ipsum corrumpat, adeóque ad rebellionem commoveat.

XI. 7. Sequeretur peccatum originis non tolli per Baptismum, cùm praua illa concupiscentia in baptizatis maneat.

Resp. Peccatum tollitur non in totum, sed in tantùm, non ἁπλῶς sed κατά τι. Tollitur enim formale χρετικόν, sed remanet absolutum. Tollitur supplicium relinquitur vitium. Baptismus enim facit, non vt peccatum non sit, sed vt non imputetur. August. l. 1. de nuptijs c. 25.

X. Hactenus ad ratiunculas Bellarmini respondimus: nũc argumenta nostra pro qualitate positiua subjiciemus, quorum quinque sunt præcipua. 1. A descriptione peccati. Sic enim illud depingit Scriptura, vt præter στέρησιν imaginis simul totam naturam, omnesque ejus facultates fœdissimè deprauatas esse indicet. Hinc figmentum cordis humani tantùm malum esse dicitur, Genes. 6. v. 5. c. 8. v. 22. & fraudulentum Ierem. 17. v. 9. & τὸ φρόνημα σαρκὸς inimicitia aduersus Deum, Rom. 8. v. 7. & quæ sunt alia dicta peccatum politiuè describentia. Ex quibus ita concludimus: Quicquia per habitualia animi vitia designatur, illud non est merè priuatiuum, cùm habitus & priuatio opponantur. Atqui peccatum originis designatur in Scripturis per habitualia animi vitia, nempe mentis stultitiam; cordis malitiam, appetitus contumaciam, & totius hominis aduersus Deum inimicitiam. Non igitur est ens merè priuatiuum,

XI 2. Ab inhaesione. Quicquid adiacet & animae hominis constanter inhaeret, hoc aliquid positiui est. Priuationes enim propriè non dicuntur inherere vel adiacere. Peccatum autem originis Rom. 7. v. 21. nominatur malum adiacens, v. 23. Lex peccati in membris existens. v. 17. & 20 Peccatum inhabitans eò, quia nõ transit sed fixam in carne sedein habet, Hebr. 12. v. 1. appellatur ἀπειρίστατος ἁμαρτία peccatum vndique circumstans. Quare quiddam positiui esse rectè concluditur.

XII. 3. Ab effectu. A quocunque promanant actus & effectu positiui, illud ipsum quoque ens positiyum esse oportet, quandoquidẽ causa & effectus toto genere non differunt. Ast à peccato originali oriuntur actus & effectus positiui, nimirum peccata actualia. Quapropter & ipsum esse ens positiuum consequitur.

XIII. 4. A contrarietate. Omnis contrarietas est inter entia positiua. Peccatum naturale & iustitia originalis opponuntur non modò priuatiuè, sed & contrariè. Igitur entia quoque positiua sunt.

XIV. 5. Ab authoritate. August. l. 1. de nupt. & concupisc. c. 25. & l 6. cont. Iulian cap. 7. peccatum disertè appellat malam qualitatem, & languori comparat, vnde Lutherus rectè pronunciauit, quòd peccatum totam naturam nostram leprae aut luis pestiferae instar pessimè corruperit, & tabificauerit. Thomas de Aquino 2. quaest. 28. artic. 1. nominat corruptum habitum. Ita enim loquitur. Sicut aegritudo corporalis habet aliquid de priuatione, in quantum tollitur aequalitas temperamenti & sanitatis, & aliquid positiuum, vt ipsos humores inordinatè dispositos: Ita peccatum originale NON EST PVRA PRIVATIO, sed corruptus quidam HABITVS. Super quem locum Caietanus ita commentatur: Corruptio contra puram priuationem distinguitur. Priuatio enim dat negationem in subiecto apto nato: Corruptio verò addit positiuum contrarium, fundans illam negationem. Et huc spectat etiam illud

Gersonis, vitium originale esse impotentiam ad bonum, & potentiam ad malum. Quæ confessiones aduersariorum notandæ sunt, inprimis Thomæ, vt Papicolarum circa primariū fidei caput appareat, & quam in multis Iesu Witæ ab antiqua religione Papistica discedant.

XV. Porrò autem obseruandum est, quòd nostri Theologi non doceant peccatum, exquisitè & per omnia esse qualitatem positiuam sed termihum istum vsurpantiν πλάτει, vel in quadam latitudine sicut ἁμαρτία illa συνεισέρχε ens positiuum dicatur, potissimùm ob constantem adhærentiam & profundam naturæ corruptionem, non secus atq; morbus corporis non modò priuatio sanitatis est, sed vnà positio prauæ dispositionis, & vitia animi virtutibus opponuntur non priuatiuè tantùm, verum etiam contrariè. Quia enim Pontificij disputant, peccatum meram esse doni supernaturalis, iustitiæ originalis priuationem, ipsamque naturam in se talem permansisse, qualis ab initio fuit condita: hinc factum, vt ad errorem istum scholasticum fortiùs refutandum Theologi nostri terminum positiui assumserint, adeoque per istum hoc duntaxat indicant peccatum non modo abstulisse iustitiam, sed simul corrupisse naturam, adeò vt τὰ φυσικὰ non permanserint integra & illesa. Hanc igitur corruptionē & deprauationem naturæ à susoq distinctam, termino positiuæ qualitatis vnicè notatam volumus.

XVI. Huc insuper referri potest illa priuationis distinctio, quòd alia sit simplex, notans meram carentiam, vt tenebræ; alia habitualis quæ conjuncta est cum contraria forma, vt morbi. Ad priorem speciem Pontificij, ad posteriorem Nostri peccatum originale referūt. Sic enim est ςέρησις iustitię vt simul includat ἕξιν iniustitiæ, præuæque concupiscentiæ.

XVII. Neque nos turbet argumētum istud Metaphysicum: Omne ens positium est bonum. Peccatum est en: positinum. Ergo bonum. Maior enim proponit de ente creato, & exquisitè positiuo. Minor subfumit de ente introducto & ἐν πλάτει positiuo, vnde oriuntur quatuor termini, & perit consequentia argumenti.


### Question IV. What subject does original sin have?

I. The subject of sin is twofold. One is of category or predication, and it is every man, or the whole human species, except Christ. The other is of existence or inherence, and it is the whole man, and the whole of man. Concerning both, in a few words.

II. CONCERNING THE SUBJECT OF PREDICATION. This is every man, and the whole human race, with the Savior alone excepted. For Scripture speaks universally, that every imagination of the heart is evil, Gen. 6. v. 5. ch. 8, 21. nor is one given as clean, because all are from an unclean seed, Job 14. v. 4. nor is one given who does good, but all have turned aside, Psalm 14. v. 23. that every man is a liar, Psalm 116, v. 11. and the heart of man is deceitful, Jer. 17. v. 9. all are born flesh of flesh John 3, v. 5. all lack the glory of God. Rom. 3. v. 27. all have sinned, Rom. 5. v. 12. and are by nature children of wrath, Eph. 2, v. 3.

III. From this universality, however, Scripture itself excepts Christ the Mediator. For He is the holy of holies, Dan. 9. v. 24. He was conceived by the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, Luke 1. v. 35. not from the polluted, but from the chaste and most pure blood of Mary, as Damascenus speaks, b. 3. c. 2. whence the holy thing is called τὸ ἅγιον, Luke 1. v. the same, and was made like us except for sin. Heb. 4. v. 15. and therefore separated from sinners. Heb. 7. v. 26. But besides Him, since Scripture excepts no other man, we ought not rashly to depart from that universality.

IV. And from this we deduce that they err. 1. The Papists, who maintain that the Blessed Virgin Mary was immune from every defilement of sin. For Costerus did not hesitate to write thus in book 5 of his Christian Institutions, addressed to Mary: You never had even a blemish of sin, whether that which was propagated by the first parents of the human race, or that which might have been committed by any fault of your own; even the slightest and easily worthy of pardon; you never admitted, either by deed, or word, or thought, anything that was not in every way most pleasing to God. See similar things in Gabriel Biel in 3. dist. q. 1. art. 2. and Bellarmine, book 4, on the Grace of Christ, chapter 5. To this opinion we oppose: 1. The express universality, of which we have just spoken. 2. The silence of Scripture, which nowhere mentions such a privilege. But in questions of faith, this must hold: ἰδ' ὧν ἄτερ γραφῆς. 3. Mary's sinfulness, in which she persevered with the Apostles, Acts 1, v. 14, the primary part of which was undoubtedly the Lord's Prayer, in which, among other things, the remission of sins is requested. 4. Mary's redemption and justification. For Christ redeemed her also, and therefore she was justified in the same way as other men, namely, not by the non-imputation, but by the remission of sins, Rom. 4, v. 7, 8, 9. 5. Mary's actual sins, such as that she did not guard Christ with the care that was fitting, Luke 2, verse 43; that she is not rebuked for prescribing to him in matters that did not pertain to maternal care, Luke 2, v. 49, John 2, v. 4; that she even doubted the kingdom of the Messiah, and his resurrection, etc. 6. Mary's calamities and death, to which she would not have been subject if she had been devoid of all sin. But what is said about the assumption of Mary lacks a foundation and is a fable of the monks. The testimony of Augustine, book 5 against Julian, writing thus: If without doubt the flesh of Christ is not flesh of sin, but similar to the flesh of sin, what remains for us to understand, except that, with that exception, ALL THE REST of human flesh is flesh of sin? And whoever denies this is found to be a detestable HERETIC.

V. 2. The Calvinists, who [maintain that] the children of the faithful are holy, and born in the covenant, whose testimonies we have alleged in disp. 5. quest. 2. th. 14. To which we in turn oppose, 1. the universal sentence of Scripture, 2. The example of Job, ch. 14. v. 4. & of David, Psal. 51. v. 7, 3. The assertion of Christ, John 3. vers. 5. seqq. 4. The testimony of Paul, Ephes. 2. vers. 3. N Wherefore we are not born holy, or in the covenant. 5. The necessity of Baptism, Mark 16. v. 16. 6. The end of Baptism, which is sanctification, Eph. 5. v. 27. Whence it follows, that holiness does not precede Baptism, but follows as an effect, 7. The testimonies of the fathers. Tertull. in Apolog. cap. 17. Christians are made, not born. August. l. 3. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 9. What will you answer, why one is born of Christians, unless because generation does not make Christians, but regeneration? But this error will be treated more fully in the disputation on Baptism.

VI. 2. ON THE SUBJECT OF INHERENCE: When original sin is considered, not with respect to the whole species, of which it is predicated, but of the individual, to whom it is born, and in whom it inheres, then it has for its object not only the body of man, nor the soul alone, but body and soul together, and thus the whole man. Hence the whole is said to be unclean, Job 14. v. 4. Conceived in sins. Psal. 51. v. 7. & born of flesh, flesh. Job 3. v. 5. Hence it is described by the blindness of the mind 1. Cor. 2. v. 4. Eph. 4. v. 18. by the malice of the heart. Gen. 6. v. 5. c. 8. v. 21. Jerem. 17. v. 9. by the ἀχρησίαν of the body and of all the members, Psal. 14. v. 2. 3. Rom. 3. v. 12. by the uncleanness and corruption of the seed itself, Job 14. v. 5. Psalm 5. v. 7.

VII. From these things, moreover, it follows that those Papists err, who place sin and concupiscence only in the lower part of the soul, namely the sensitive appetite, but deem the higher powers to be immune from it. For 1. Scripture describes it through the universal depravity and ἀταξίαν of all the powers, especially of the mind and will. 2. Gal. 5. v. 20. Among the lusts of the flesh are also reckoned idolatries and heresies, which certainly arise not from the corruption of the lower faculties, but rather of the higher. For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, not only with sensual pleasures, but also with doubt of the mind, depraved choice of the will, and the like.

3. The subject of original righteousness was not the appetite alone, but especially the mind and will, Eph. 4:24. The same, therefore, will be the subject of original sin, in that habits and privations revolve around the same. 4. The same is proven by the renewal of man, which concerns the whole man and all his faculties, especially the higher ones: For we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, Eph. 4:23, and are transformed by the newness of our mind, Rom. 12:2, that we may set our minds on things that are above, Col. 3:2. But that which is renewed, that was previously corrupted by oldness, and thus was the subject of sin.

5. Some of the adversaries themselves agree. Thomas writes somewhere: As the act of virtue is not perfected by that which is of the sensuality alone, but rather by that which is of the reason and will, so sin is much more effected by that which is of the reason and will than that which is of the sensuality. Bellarmine, lib. 7 de A. G. cap. 15, says: It must not be denied that a similar vice is found even in the higher part of the soul. For that part of the soul also is prone to covet honors, vain glory, and other vanities, and even if we are unwilling, it sometimes brings forth such desires. Which confession of Bellarmine is to be studiously noted and opposed to them. For if such a vice adheres to the intellect itself, then certainly concupiscence did not take its origin from the condition of matter.

Latin:

I. Subiectum peccati duplex est, Aliud κατηγορίας vel prædicationis, & est omnis homo, vel tota species humana, excepto Christo. Aliud ὑπάρξεως vel inhæsionis, & est totus homo, & totum hominis. De vtroque paucis.

II. DE SVBIECTO PRAEDICATIONIS. Hoc est omnis homo, & totum genus humanum, solo Saluatore excepto. Scriptura enim vniuersaliter loquitur, Omne figmentum cordis malum esse, Genes. 6. vers. 5. cap. 8, 21. nec vnum dari mundum, quia omnes sint de immundo semine, Iob 14. v. 4. nec vnū dari facere bonum, sed omnes declinasse, Psal. 14. v. 23. Omnem hominem esse mendacem, Psalm. 116, v. 11. & cor hominis fraudulentum, Ierem. 17. v. 9. omnes nasci carnem de carne Ioh. 3, vers. 5. omnes egere gloriâ Dei. Rom. 3. vers 27. omnes peccâsse, Rom. 5. v. 12. & naturâ esse filios iræ, Eph. 2, v. 3.

III. Ab hac tamen vniuersalitate Scriptura ipsa Christum Mediatorem excipit. Hic enim est sanctus sanctorum, Dan. 9. v. 24. hic obumbratione Spiritus sancti conceptus est, Luc. 1. v. 35. non ex pollutis, sed castis & purissimis Mariæ sanguinibus vti loquitur Damascenus, l. 3. c. 2. vnde τὸ ἅγιον sanctum dicitur, Luc. 1. v. eodem, & nobis similis factus excepto peccato. Hebr. 4. v. 15. & propterea separatus à peccatoribus. Hebr. 7. v. 26. Præter hunc verò cùm Scriptura nullum alium hominem excipiat, ab vniuersalitate ista temerè discedere non debemus.

IV. Atque hinc errare deducimus. 1. Pontificios, qui B. virginem Mariam ab omni inquinamento peccati immunem fuisse statuunt. Ita enim scribere non dubitavit Costerus l. 5. Christ. Institut. ad Mariam. Nunquam vel nævum habuisti peccati, siue quod à primi humani generis parentibus propagatum, siue quod aliqua tua culpa commissum esset; etiam leuissimum & venia facilè dignum; nhu;iquam, vel opere, vel verbo, vel cogitato admisisti, quod non vsquequaque Deo gratissimum. Similia vide apud Gabrielem Biel in 3. dist. q. 1. art. 2. & Bell. lib. 4: de A: G. c. 5. Cui sententiæ nos opponimns. 1. expressam vniuersalitatem, de qua modò dictum. 2. Scripturæ silentium, quæ talis priuilegij nuspiam meminit. In quæstionibus autem fidei istud valere debet: ἰδ' ὧν ἄτερ γραφῆς. 3. Mariæ peccationem, in qua perseuerauit cum Apostolis Act. 1. v. 14. cuius primaria pars proculdubio fuit Oratio Dominica, in qua inter alia petitur remissio peccatorum. 4. Mariæ redemptionem & iustificationem. Nam & illam Christus redemit, ideoque eodem modo iustificata est, quo alij homines, nempè per non imputationem, sed remissionem peccatorum, Rom. 4. v. 7. 8. 9. 5. Mariæ peccata actualia, vt quòd non eâ, quâ par erat, cura custodiuit Christum Luc. 2. vers. 43. quòd ei in his, quæ ad maternam curam non pertinebant, præscriptum non reprehenditur, Luc. 2. v. 49. Ioh. 2. v. 4. quòd etiam dubitauit de regno Messiæ, eiusque resurrectione, &c. 6. Mariæ calamitates & mortem, quibus nō fuisset subiecta, si omni peccato caruisset. Quod verò dicitur de assumptione Mariæ, id Fundamento caret, & Fabula Monachorum est. Testimonium Augustini l. 5. contra Iulian. ita scri entis: Si absque dubio caro Christi non est caro peccati, sed similis carni peccati, quid restat, vt intelligamus, nisi ea exceptâ, OMNEM RELIQVAM humana carnem, carnem esse peccati? Et quisquis hoc negat, detestandus HAERETICVS inuenitur.

V. 2. Caluinianos, qui liberos fidelium sanctos, & in fœdere nasci adfirmans, quorum testimonia allegauimus disp. 5. quæst. 2. th. 14. Quibus vicissim opponimus, 1. vniuersalem Scripturæ sententiam, 2. Exemplum Iobi, c. 14. v. 4. & Dauidis, Psal. 51. v. 7, 3. Christi asseuerationem, Iohan. 3. vers. 5. seqq. 4. Pauli testificationem Ephes. 2. vers. 3. Nam si naturá sumus filij iræ : Ergo non gratiæ. Quare nec sancti nascimur, aut in fœdere. 5. Baptismi necessitatem, Marc. 16. v. 16. 6. Baptismi finem, qui est sanctificatio, Eph. 5. v. 27. Vnde sequitur, sanctitatem non præcedere Baptismum, sed sequi vt effectum, 7. Testimonia patrum. Tertull. in Apolog. cap. 17. Fiunt non nascuntur Christiani. August. l. 3. de peccat. merit. & remiss. cap. 9. Quid respondebitis, quare de Christianis nascatur, nisi quia non facit generatio, sed regeneratio christianos? Verùm de hoc errore pluribus agetur in disputat. de Baptismo.

VI. 2. DE SVBIECTO INHAESIONIS: Quando peccatum originis consideratur, non respectu totius speciei, de qua prædicatur, sed indiuidui, cui adnascitur, & inhæret, tum pro obiecto habet non solum hominis corpus, neq; solam animam, sed corpus & animam simul, adeoque totum hominem. Hinc totus dicitur immundus, Iob. 14. v. 4. In peccatis conceptus. Psal. 51. v. 7. & ex carne caro natus. Iob. 3. v. 5. Hinc describitur per cœcitatem mentis 1. Cor. 2. v. 4. Eph. 4. v. 18. per malitiam cordis. Gen. 6. v. 5. c. 8. v. 21. Ierem. 17. v. 9. per ἀχρησίαν corporis & omnium membrorum, Psal. 14. v. 2. 3. Rom. 3. v. 12. per ipsius feminis immundiciem & corruptionem, Iob. 14. v. 5. Psalm 5. v. 7.

VII. Ex his autem porrò sequitur, errare Pontificios istos, qui peccatum & concupiscentiam in inferiore tantùm animæ parte, nimirum appetitu sensitiuo collocant, superiores autē vires ab eo immunes esse autumant. Nam 1. Scriptura per vniuersalem omnium virium, præsertim mentis & voluntatis deprauationum & ἀταξίαν describit. 2. Gal. 5. v. 20. Inter concupifcentias carnis recensentur etiam idolatriae & haereses, quae certè non ex corruptione virium inferiorum, sed potius superiorum oriuntur. Caro enim concupiscit aduersus Spiritum, non tantùm sensualibus voluptatibus, sed etiam dubitatione mentis, prauâ electione voluntatis, & similibus.

3. Subiectum originalis iustitiae non fuit solus appetitus, sed potissimùm mens & voluntas, Ephes. 4. v. 24. Idem igitur subiectum erit peccati originalis, eò quod habitus & priuationes circà idem versentur. 4. Idē euincit hominis renouatio, quae spectat totum hominem, omneśque facultates, praesertim superiores : Renouamur enim spiritu mentis. Ephes. 4 v. 23. & reformamur nouitate mentis. Rom. 12. v. 7. vt sapiamus, quae sursum sunt, Col. 3. vers. 2. Quod autem renouatur, istud prius vetustastate corruptum, adeòque peccati subiectum fuit.

5. Consentiunt quidam ex ipsis aduersarijs Thomas alicubi scribit; Vt actus virtutis non perficitur per id, quod sensualitatis tantùm est, sed magis per id, quod est rationis & voluntatis, ita peccatū multò magis per id, quod rationis & valūtatis, quam quod sensualitatis est, efficitur. Bellarminus l. 7. de A. G. c. 15. Negandum, ait, non est, etiam in parte animae superiore simile vitium inueniri. Nam ea quoque animi pars prona est ad concupiscendos honores, inanem gloriam, & alias vanitates, & etiamsi nolimus, interdum eiusmodi parit desideria. Quæ Bellarmini confessio studiosè notanda & ipsi opponēda est. Si enim tale vitium adhaeret ipsi intellectui, vtique concupiscentia non traxit ortum ex conditione materiae.


### Question V: And the last

1. Various descriptions of sin are read among the ancients. Augustine: It is a fault which we all, conceived concupiscentially, draw. Gerson: It is a certain habitual aversion from God, by which the soul is affected with a propensity, not to render the justice which it owes. Hugo: It is a vice which we contract by being born, through ignorance in the mind, and concupiscence in the flesh. See more in Chemnitius in the Commonplace on original sin, ch. 3.

II. But because these are descriptions rather than absolute definitions: it must be known that five things are chiefly to be considered regarding the nature of sin, and to be expressed in its definition. 1. It is a privation or the loss of good granted. For sin expelled original justice and took us captive. 2. A habit or the succession of the contrary evil: But this evil is called by one name desire or concupiscence, which embraces all evil habits succeeding original justice, such as blindness of mind, aversion of the will, stubbornness of the heart, and the repugnance of all powers. 3. Guilt or obligation to punishment. For because of sin we are subject to the wrath of God and the tyranny of Satan, we are guilty of all the curses of the law, and of eternal damnation: Hugo briefly recounts these three when he says: Original disease comprises ignorance of good, concupiscence of evil, and the punishment from both. 4. The subject, which is every man, except Christ, and also the whole man, as regards body and soul, as regards higher and lower powers. 5. The mode of transmission, which is carnal generation.

III. From these five members, therefore, we construct a full definition of sin, namely such as this: Original sin is a horrible corruption of the whole human nature, except however Christ, and of all its powers, with a defect of original justice, propagated from the first parents into all descendants through carnal generation, and subjecting all to eternal and temporal punishments, unless they are reborn of water and the Spirit, and thus obtain remission. Or more briefly: Sin is the corruption of the whole nature destitute of justice, on account of which death passed into all.

To God alone be glory.

Latin:

1. Variae leguntur peccati descriptiones apud Veteres. Augustinus: Est culpa, quã omnes concupiscentialiter concepti trahimus. Gerson: Est auersio quaedam habitualis à Deo, quâ anima prona affecta est, non reddere iustitiam, quam debet. Hugo: Est vitium, quod nascendo contrahimus, per ignorantiam in mente, & concupiscentiam in carne. Plures vide apud Chemnitiuni in Loco de peccat. orig. c. 3.

II. Quia verò istæ descriptiones potius sunt, quàm absolutæ definitiones: sciendum, quinq; potissimum circa peccati naturam consideranda, inque eius ὁρισμῷ esse exprimenda. 1. est στέρησις vel boni concessi amissio. Peccatum enim iustitiam originalem expulit, & nos captivavit. 2. ἕξις seu mali contrarij successio: Vno autem nomine malum istud vocatut ἐπιθυμία vel concupiscentia, quæ complectitur omnes habitus nialos, iustitiæ originali succedentes, vt sunt cæcitas mentis, aversio voluntatis, contumacia cordis, & repugnantia omnium virium. 3. Reatus seu ad pœnam obligatio. Propter peccatum enim subjacentus iræ Dei & tyrannidi Satanæ, rei sumus omnium maledictionum legis, & æternæ damnationis: Tria hæc breuiter recenset Hugo, cum inquit: Morbus originalis complectitur ignorantiam boni, concupiscentiam mali, & supplicium de vtroque. 4. Subiectum, quod est omnis homo, excepto Christo, etiam totus homo, quoad corpus & animams quoad vires superiores & inferiores. 5. Modus traductionis, quæ est carnalis generatio.

III. Ex hisce igitur quinque membris plenam peccati definitionem extruimus, nimirum talem: Peccatum originis est horrenda corruptio totius naturæ humanæ, excepto tamen Christo, & omnium virium, cum defectu originalis iustitiæ, ex primis parentibus in omnes posteros per carnalem generationem propagata, omnesq; æternis & temporalibus pœnis subjiciens, nisi renascantur ex aqua & Spiritu, adeoque remissionem consequantur. Vel breuius: Peccatum est corruptio totius naturæ iustitiâ destitutæ, ob quam mors in omnes pertransiit.

Soli Deo Gloria.


## 8 Disputation VII. On the Punishment of Original Sin

Prefaced by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Georg Ludwig, of Stettin in Pomerania:

Problem I.

After the existence and the essence of sin have been understood, there follows the third chapter of this doctrine, which is concerning guilt and punishment. For vice and punishment, fault and penalty, offense and vengeance accompany one another; because the former is the preceding cause, the latter the certainly following effect.

II. The Papists commonly enumerate four punishments of original sin: 1. Ignorance in the mind. 2. Malice in the will. 3. Concupiscence in the appetitive faculty, and 4. Infirmity in the irascible faculty.

III. Bellarmine, book 6, on the Grace of Adam, chapter 8 and following, commemorates more punishments and miseries of this kind. In chapter 9, he recounts the wounds or diseases of the human mind; which are: 1. Ignorance of necessary things in infants, so great that it is not even seen in beasts. 2. Fatuity, with which some are born. 3. Difficulty of learning. 4. Ignorance of the ultimate end. 5. Ignorance of the means to the end. 6. Difficulty of understanding the natures of things. 7. Ignorance of one's own mind. 8. The impediment which the body opposes in understanding. 9. A certain almost natural curiosity. 10. That we desire many vain, light, and inept things in our mind, even against our will, and also other at the most [blank] time. c. 10. treats of the wounds of the will, which are 1. φιλαυτία or self-love 2. The difficulty which we experience in overcoming vices and cultivating virtues. 3. A certain incredible negligence in those things which pertain to living happily, both in this life and also after death. 4. Immoderate will, which is most slow to worship the true God, but most prompt to worship false gods. 6. Inconstancy, instability, a certain struggle and contention of the human will. 7. Disgust with one's own state. 8. That no one, unless he be renewed, can avoid all mortal sins, but venial ones can indeed be renewed, chapter 11 treats of the wounds of the lower part of the soul, of which he notes five: 1. That many are born blind, or deaf, or mute, or lame, or in another way harmed in this part. 2. The illusion of dreams, which is effected through the interior senses. 3. That the interior sense often in a wondrous way hinders and confuses the understanding. 4. Infirmity in the irascible appetite: 5. Concupiscence, which after original justice was lost, being unrestrained, fights against the Spirit.

IV. We willingly confess, however, that all those evils, and even far more, were introduced into the world through the sin of Adam; nevertheless, we cannot approve of this Jesuitical discourse. For 1. He errs if he thinks that these vices, and the very ἀταξίαν of the mind, will, and appetite, are punishments of original sin properly so called. For they do not follow sin, but constitute it; they are not the punishment, but the very form of sin. For what else is that vice of nature than ignorance of the mind and depravity of all the faculties? 2. He is ignorant of the elenchus if he understands by sin the actual disobedience of Adam. For these evils indeed followed this; but here the question is not about the punishment of the first evil act, but of the natural vice, which alone is properly called original sin, where its form and punishment ought not to be confused. 3. Par- For just as sin, so also the punishment of sin properly so-called is common to all the posterity of Adam; and on the contrary, what is not common ought not to be reckoned among the punishments of sin. But indeed stupidity, blindness, lameness and the like are only particular defects, not common to the whole human race, and therefore they are wrongly enumerated among the universal and properly so-called punishments of sin. We indeed admit that these evils draw their origin from original sin, yet in such a way that they are not general punishments, but are sometimes sent by God for special reasons:

V. Wherefore, that we may express the common and properly so-called punishment of original sin, we describe it by one name, and we call it DEATH. For the Lord threatened this in place of punishment, Gen. 2. v. 17, this entered through sin, Rom. 5. v. 12, and it is named the wages of sin, Rom. 6. v. ult.

VI. But this one word death includes four general punishments of sin. 1 The manifold miseries and hardships of this life, by which we are daily worn down, and are as it were prepared for death: Such are the pains of women, Gen. 3. v. 16, the labors of men, v. 17, 18. and sweats, v. 19, various diseases, unexpected accidents, the disobedience of brute animals, the cruelty of men toward men, and six hundred other similar things; where it is to be noted, however, that these evils are indeed punishments with respect to the impenitent; but as regards the faithful, they are chastisements, not punishments; both by reason of the principle, because they do not proceed from an angry GOD, but from a benign Father, and are as it were bitter arrows from a sweet hand; and by reason of the end, because they tend to the testing and improvement of the good, since they are μεταμέλεια of the fall, ὄργανα of mortification, προφυλακτικά from sins; παιδευτήρια of hope, patience, and repentance and the like; and by reason of the correlate, because punishment has no place when all guilt has been remitted. For these are relative, and they posit and remove each other. Hence Chrysostom aptly says in 1 Cor. hom. 28: When we are rebuked by the Lord, it is more of an admonition than a condemnation; of medicine than of punishment; of correction than of penalty.

VII. 2. The death of grace, or the wrath of God. For He hates all who work iniquity, Ps. 5, v. 7. He loves righteousness and hates wickedness, Ps. 44, v. 8, and therefore His wrath remains upon the unbelievers, John 3, v. last; nor does God dwell in an unfaithful soul, since sins separate men from God, Isa. 59, v. 2. But with the gracious indwelling of God removed, man is immediately subjected to the tyranny of Satan. For whom God deserts, the demons take up, says Gregory the Great, lib. 25 Moral. cap. 9. Hence by nature we are slaves of sin, John 8, v. 34; 2 Pet. 2, v. 19; under the power of darkness, Col. 1, v. 13; bound by the snares of the Devil to do his will, 2 Tim. 2, v. last; who is effective in the children of disobedience, Eph. 2, v. 2, and makes them fall from sin into sin, Ps. 69, v. 28.

VIII. 3. The death of nature or bodily death, which the Lord denounced for sin to Adam, Gen. 3, v. 19, from whom it passed to all, Rom. 5, v. 12, and therefore all die, 1 Cor. 15, v. 21, and it is appointed for men to die once, but after this the judgment: Heb. 9, v. 27. It is to be noted here also that death is a penalty regarding the impious, but with respect to the pious it is: 1. gain, Phil. 1, v. 21; 2. sleep, Deut. 31, v. 16; John 11, v. 11; Acts 7, v. 60; 3. a release from prison, Phil. 1, v. 23; 4. a liberation from the sense of sin and the miseries of life, 1 Cor. 15, v. 36; and finally, 5. a passage to the Father: John 14, v. 28; ch. 13, v. 1; and a migration to a house not made with hands, but eternal in the heavens, 2 Cor. 5, v. 1.

IX. 4. The death of glory, or everlasting death: which will be the perpetual unhappiness of the whole man, when according to body and soul he is separated from the blessed vision of God: to eternal death and damnation after the resurwill be delivered over to correction. It is commonly accustomed to be called the final death; Apoc. 20. v. 14 it is called the second death, concerning which it is written in Psalm 34. v. 22. The death of sinners is most evil. For the quantity and quality of it hardly any thought of mortals attains, so far is it from expressing it, speech, as witnessed by Augustine, serm. 51. de tempore. For there will be trembling and fear of anguish and confusion, the pain of a horrendous vision, the trembling of a horrendous dwelling. There will be a lake of those weeping, gnashing of teeth, the biting of worms, the clamor of those suffering, the mourning of those groaning, the voice of crying sinners saying, Woe to us, woe to us children of Eve! Augustine cap. 3 Speculi peccatorum.

X. These are the four common punishments of original sin, concerning the first three of which we shall add nothing further, since the statements of the Scriptures concerning them are most manifest. But as regards the last, namely eternal death, there is great controversy among theologians. Indeed, that adults dying in unbelief and contaminated by gross sins will certainly be the brands of Gehenna on account of actual disobedience and final impenitence, there is no one who doubts. But concerning infants not baptized, or dying before the reception of Baptism, an arduous question is raised: Is God, the most just judge, on account of original sin alone, which they seem to draw from their parents without their own fault, going to exclude them eternally from the fellowship of the blessed in heaven, and on the contrary subject them to perpetual damnation in hell?

XI. We confess, however, that this problem is sufficiently intricate and most difficult of decision, which nevertheless ought to offend no one. For although we do not know the solution, our salvation will in no way be endangered by this, since that question is rather about the faith than of the faith; nor is it asked about our own, but another's salvation, which although it remains in doubt, nevertheless nothing will be lost to us, because the just man lives and is saved by his own, not another's, faith, Hab. 2. v. 4. Rom. 1. vers. 17. Indeed, if that knowledge had been so necessary, Scripture would certainly have explained clearly what ought to be thought, since all things necessary for salvation by knowledge are contained in it. XII. Nor, however, should it be inferred from this that one ought rather to be silent about such abstruse matters than to speak, since those things which Scripture has not expressed are ignored without crime, but are not investigated without danger. For although this question is not decided in the sacred code in its entirety, yet it is in part; although not αὐτολεξεὶ, yet κατὰ διάνοιαν and by consequence. Added to this is the audacity of the Papists, who not only define something as certain, but also insinuate that our own opinion is an error, as can be seen in Bellarm. l. 6. de A. G. 1. & seqq., where this question is discussed at length. XIII. Therefore we shall not entirely waste our effort, nor can it be held against us as a fault, if we run through those things which can be gathered from the Scriptures concerning this controversy, and which have been noted by our Theologians, by repeating them in a few words. So that this may be done distinctly, we shall present the whole matter expedited by three ζητήμασι: 1. Are the unbaptized infants of Christians damned on account of original sin? 2. Are the children of infidels damned? 3. What punishment do they sustain in damnation, whether only of loss and not of sense, as the Papists affirm?

Latin:

Præf. Balth. Meisner: SS: Th. D.

Refp: Georgio Ludovico, Stetinenfi Pomerano:

Προβληματιον: I.

POst cognitam peccati tùm existentiam, tùm essentiam, sequitur caput huius doctrinæ tertium, quod est de reatu & pœnâ. Comitantur enim se inuicem, vitium & supplicium, culpa & pœna, offensa & vindicta; eò quòd illud sit causa præcedens, hœc effectus certò consequens.

II. Quatuor autem pœnas, peccati originis vulgò numerant Pontificij: 1. Ignorantiam in mente. 2. Malitiam in voluntate. 3. Concupiscentiam in appetitu ἐπιθυμητικῷ, & 4. Infirmitatem in θυμικῷ.

III. Bellar. l. 6. de A. Gr. c. 8. & seqq. plures huiusmodi pœnas & miserias commemorat. c. 9. humanæ mentis vulnera siue morbos recenset; qui sint 1. Ignorantia rerũ necessariarum in infantibus tanta, quanta nec in bestijs quidem cernitur. 2. Fatuitas, cum qua nōnulli nascuntur. 3. Difficultas discendi. 4. Ignoratio vltimi finis. 5. Ignoratio mediorum ad finem. 6. Difficultas intelligendi naturas rerum. 7. Ignoratio propriæ mentis. 8. Impedimentum, quod corpus in intelligendo obijcit. 9. Curiositas quędam propemodum naturalis. 10. Quòd multa inania, leuia, inepta volumus animo, vel inuiti, etiam alięs niffimo tempore. c. 10. agit de vulneribus voluntatis, quae sint 1. φιλαυτία vel amor sui 2. Difficultas, quam experimur in vitjis superandis & virtutibus excolendis. 3. Incredibilis quaedam negligentia injiis, quae ad beate vivendum, tum in hac vita tum etiam post mortem pertinent. 4. Immoderata sollicitudo in temporalibus lucris captandis. 5. Mira quaedam diversitas volutatis humanae, quae ad verum Deum colendum tardissima est, ad colendos autem Deos falsos promtissima. 6. Inconstantia, instabilitas, pugna quaedam & contentio voluntatis humanae. 7. Fastidium proprii status. 8. Quod nullus, nisi renovetur, peccata omnia mortalia vitare possit, venialia vero renovari quidem possint, cap. 11. pertractat vulnera partis animae inferioris, quorum quinque notat: 1. Quod multi nascantur caeci, aut surdi, aut muti, aut claudi, aut alio modo in hac parte laesi. 2. Illusio somniorum, quae per sensus interiores efficitur. 3. Quod interior sensus saepe mirum in modum intelligentiam impedit & confundit. 4. Infirmitas in appetitu irascibili: 5. Concupiscentia, quae post amissam originalem justitiam soluta contra Spiritum pugnat.

IV. Fatemur autem lubenter, mala ista omnia, & longe plura etiam per peccatum Adae in mundum introducta esse, discursum tamen istum JesuWiticum adprobare non possumus. Nam 1. Errat, si vitia ista, & ipsam mentis, voluntatis, appetitus ἀταξίαν poenas esse peccati originalis proprie dictas existimat. Non enim consequuntur peccatum, sed constituunt; non poena, sed ipsa forma peccati sunt. Quid enim aliud est illud naturae vitium, quam ignorantia mentis & depravatio omnium virium? 2. Elenchum ignorat, si per peccatum actualem Adae inobedientiam intelligit. Hanc enim mala ista quidem insecuta sunt; verum hic non quaeritur de suplicio primi actus mali, sed naturalis vitii, quod solum originale peccatum proprie appellatur, ubi forma eius & pœna confundi non debent. 3. ParVt enim peccatum, ita & peccati supplicium propriè dictum toti Adæ posteritati commune est; & contrà, quod commune non est, inter peccati pœnas recenseri non debet. At verò fatuitas, cœcitas, claudicatio & similia sunt defectus tantùm particulares, non toti humano generi communes, ideoą; pœnis peccati vniuersalibus & propriè dictis malè annumerantur. Fatemur quidem mala ista ex peccato originis ortum trahere, ita tamë, vt non sint pœnæ generales, sed à Deo specialibus de causis nonnunquam immittantur:

V. Quocirca vt communem & propriè dictam peccati originalis pœnam exprimamus, vno illam nomine describimus, & M O R T E M dicimus. Hanc enim Dominus pœnę loco minatus est. Gen. 2. v. 17. hæc per peccatum intrauit, Rom. 5. vers. 12. & peccati stipendium nominatur, Rom. 6. v. vlt.

VI. Vnum verò istud mortis vocabulum quatuor generales peccati pœnas includit. 1 Multiplices huius vitæ miserias & ærumnas, quibus quotidiè maceramur, & ad mortem quasi præparamur: Tales sunt mulierum dolores, Genes. 3. vers. 16. virorum labores, v. 17. 18. & sudores, v. 19. varij morbi casus inopinati, brutorum inobedientia, hominum in homines sæuitia, & sexcenta alia similia; vbi tamen notandum, quòd mala hæc pœnæ quidem sint respectu impœnitentium; quoad fideles autem castigationes, non pœnæ; tum ratione principij, quià non proueniunt ab irato DEO, sed à Patre benigno, & sunt quasi amaræ sagittæ ex dulci manu; tum ratione finis, quia tendunt ad bonorum probationem & emendationem, siquidem sunt μεταμέλεια lapsus ὄργανα mortificationis, προφυλακτικά à peccatis; παιδευτήρια spei patientiæ & pœnitentiæ & similium; tum ratione correlati, quia non habet locum pœna, quando remissa est omnis culpa. Sunt enim hæc relata, & se inuicem ponunt, tolluntque. Hinc scitè Chrysostomus in 1. Cor. hom. 28: Cùm corripimur à Domino, magis est admonitionis, quàm damnationis; medicinæ, quàm supplicij, correctionis, quàm pœnæ.

VII. 2. Mortem gratiæ, vel iram Dei. Odio enim habet omnes, qui operantur iniquitatem, Psal. 5. v. 7. Diligit iustitiam, & odit impietatem, Psal. 44. v. 8. ideoque ira eius manet super incredulos. Ioh. 3. v. ult. nec habitat Deus in anima infideli, quoniam peccata separant homines à Deo. Esai. 59. v. 2. Sublatâ verò gratiosâ inhabitatione Dei, homo protinus subijcitur Satanæ tyrannidi. Quem enim Deus deserit, dæmones suscipiunt, inquit Gregorius M. l. 25. Moral. cap. 9. Hinc naturâ sumus serui peccati, Iohan. 8. v. 34. 2. Pet. 2. vers. 19. sub potestate tenebrarum. Coloss. 1. vers. 13. constricti laqueis Diaboli ad voluntatem eius, 2. Tim. 2. vers. ult. qui efficax est in filijs diffidentiæ, Ephes. 2. v. 2. eosque facit ruere de peccato in peccatum, Psal 69. v. 28.

VIII. 3. Mortem naturæ vel corporalem, quam Dominus ob peccatum denunciauit, Adamo Gen. 3 v. 19. à quo in omnes pertransijt, Rom. 5. vers. 12. ideoque omnes moriuntur, 1. Cor. 15. v. 21. & statutum est hominibus semel mori, post hoc autem iudicium: Hebr. 7. v. 27. Notandum verò & hîc est, quòd mors, pœna sit quoad impios, sed respectu piorum est, 1. lucrum, Philip. 1. v. 21. 2. somnus. Deuter. 31. v. 16. Iohan. 11. v. 11. Actor. 7. vers. 60. 3. dissolutio ex carcere, Philip. 1. v. 23. 4. liberatio à sensu peccati, vitæque miserijs, 1. Cor. 15. v 36. & tandem. 5. transitus ad Patrem: Ioh 5. v. 34. c. 13. vers. 1. & migratio ad domum non manu factam, sed æternam in cœlis, 2. Cor. 5. vers. 1.

IX. 4. Mortem gloriæ, vel sempiternam: quæ erit perpetua totius hominis infelicitas, quando secundum corpus & animam à beata Dei visione separatus: æternæ morti & damnationi post resurrectionem mancipabitur. Vulgò mors nouissima nominari solet; Apoc. 20. v. 14. dicitur mors secunda, de qua scriptum Psalm. 34. v. 22. Mors peccatorum pessima. Eius enim quantitatem & qualitatem vix vlla mortalium assequitur cogitatio, tantum abest exprimat, oratio teste Augustino, serm. 51. de tempore. Erit enim ibi tremor ac timor angustiæ ac confusionis, dolor horrendæ visionis, tremor horrendæ mansionis. Erit lacus flentium, stridor dentium, morsus vermium, clamor dolentium, luctus gementium, vox clamantium peccatorum & dicentium, Væ nobis, væ nobis filijs Hevæ! August cap. 3 Speculi peccatorum.

X. Ethæ sunt quatuor communes pœne peccati originalis, de quarum prioribus tribus nihil addemus vltrà, cùm dicta Scripturarum de ijs sint manifestissima. Vltimam verò quod spectat, nimirum mortem æternam, de hac magna inter Theologos est controuersia. Equidem adultos in incredulitate decedentes crassísque peccatis contaminatos, propter inobedientiam actualem, & impœnitentiam finalem gehennæ titiones certò fore nemo est, qui dubitet. De infantibus autem non baptizatis, vel ante Baptismi susceptionem morientibus ardua mouetur quæstio, An eos Deus, iudex iustissimus, propter solum originis peccatum, quod ex parentibus sine propriâ culpâ trahere videntur, æternùm sit exclusurus à beatorum consortio in cælo, & contrà subiecturus perpetuæ damnationi in inferno?

XI. Fatemur autem problema hoc satis intricatum & decisione difficillimum esse, quod tamen ipsum neminem offendere debet. Quamuis enim solutionem nesciamus, hinc tamen salus nostra minimè periclitabitur, siquidem quæstio illa potiùs circa fidem est quam de fide; nec quæritur de propria, sed alienâ salute, quæ licet in dubio maneat, nobis tamen nihil decedet, quia iustus sua non alienâ fide viuit & saluatus, Hab. 2. v. 4. Rom. 1. vers. 17. Imo si scitu istud adeò fuiffet necessarium, Scriptura vtique, quid sentiendum sit, disertè exposuisset, cùm omnia scitu ad salutem necessaria in ea contineantur. XII. Neque tamen hinc inferri debet, de talibus abstrusis silendum potius esse, quàm loquendum, cùm ista, quae Scriptura non expressit, sine crimine ignorentur, verùm non sine discrimine indagentur. Nam licèt ista quaestio in sacro codice non decisa habeatur ex toto, tamẽ ex parte; licèt non αὐτολεξεὶ, tamen κατὰ διάνοιαν & per consequentiam. Accedit Pontificiorum audacia, qui non modò certi quid definiunt, sed nostram quoque sententiam erroris insinuant, vt videre est apud Bellarm. l. 6. de A. G. 1. & seqq. vbi quaestio haec fusè disceptata habetur. XIII. Proinde non omninò perdemus operam, neque vitio verti nobis poterit, si ea, quae circa controuersiam istam ex Scripturis colligi queunt, & à nostris Theologis annotata sunt paucis repetendo percurramus Quod vt distinctè fiat, tribus ζητήμασι rem omnem expeditã dabimus, 1. An Christianorum infantes non baptizati propter originis peccatum damnentur? 2. An infidelium liberi damnetur? 3. Quam in damnatione paenam sustineant, an damni tantùm non sensus, vt adfirmant Pontificij?


### Question I. Are the unbaptized infants of Christians damned on account of original sin?

QUESTION I. Are the unbaptized infants of Christians damned on account of original sin?

I. The Papists universally exclude all infants, as uncircumcised, so also unbaptized, from the kingdom of heaven. Lombard, book 4, Distinction 1, letter L, m. p. 294, writes: If it is asked about little ones who died before the eighth day, before circumcision was made by the Law, whether they were saved or not? The same can be answered as is felt concerning infants who have died before Baptism, whom it is certain PERISH. Thomas, part 3, question 65, article 4, writes that Baptism is necessary for salvation by a simple and absolute necessity. Dominicus à Soto, 2 de nat. & grat. c. 10, says: It is most firmly established in the Roman Church that no infant without Baptism in reality (which he cannot have in desire) enters the kingdom of heaven. Bellarmine, book 6 de A G. c. 2, proves with many arguments and testimonies that infants dying without Baptism are to be condemned with the penalty of eternal death.

II. We, however, with the orthodox Theologians, affirm that this Papistic opinion is both too harsh and less probable, and therefore we adopt the contrary. For although in John 3:5 Christ himself affirms: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God: yet that this is to be understood not universally, but limitedly 1. under the condition of possibility, and 2. outside the case of necessity, and thus 3. in the ordinary way, can be demonstrated by two undoubted examples.

III. The other is of the thief, crucified with Christ, and converted only on the cross. For here, by the force of Christ's promise, Today you will be with me in Paradise, Luke 23:43, he was certainly saved, and yet he is not read to have been baptized on the cross, but all maintain that he died without Baptism: whence it is gathered that the saying of Christ is not to be understood ἁπλῶς or universally, or without the exception of necessity.

IV. The other is of the Catechumens, of whom there were very many in the first centuries of the Church. They were instructed in Christian doctrine and thus truly believed in Christ: yet many were killed in times of persecution before the reception of Baptism. But shall we think these were damned because they were not baptized? By no means, since they were martyrs and had true faith.

For he who believes in Christ is not judged. John 3, v. 18. He who believes in the Son has eternal life, v. 36. The example of Cornelius also pertains here, Acts 10, v. 1, and Lydia, Acts 16, v. 4. For Luke records that both that man and that woman believed: but if they had died before Baptism, shall we therefore think that these believers were excluded from the kingdom of heaven?

V. But they object that the case of adults and infants is different, since the former supply the lack of Baptism with faith; but infants, if they are not baptized, do not have faith, and therefore are necessarily damned. Truly, we entirely deny the hypothesis that they posit. Indeed, if infants did not believe at all, who would be so absurd as to think that they are saved? Therefore, both the faith and the salvation of infants are equally in dispute. However, the orthodox maintain: that just as God endowed John the Baptist with faith in his mother's womb, so He confers the same upon other children of Christians, excluded from Baptism by a case of necessity, and thus, on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, He remits original sin and saves them eternally.

VI. In order to prove this, we propose for consideration the analogy of circumcision and Baptism, for each is a sacrament of initiation, by which, as an ordinary means, infants were once inserted into the Church, and are still inserted today: The great necessity of both on the part of men was indicated; of Baptism indeed in John 3, v. 5. Of circumcision, however, in Gen. 17, v. 14. The male, whose flesh of his foreskin shall not be circumcised, that soul shall be cut off from his people, because he has made my covenant void. From this, therefore, we conclude thus: If the uncircumcised sons of the Jews, notwithstanding that threat in Gen. 17, were saved, then certainly the unbaptized infants of Christians will also be able to be saved. The consequence is firm, since the reason and necessity of both sacraments is equal, in both cases also the condition both of the infants and of the parents is the same. But the uncircumcised sons of the Jews were saved. Therefore, the unbaptized children of Christians will also be saved. We prove the minor premise with the following examples.

VII. 1. We bring forward the males in Egypt, who as soon as they were born were snatched away by the ministers of Pharaoh, and were thrown uncircumcised into the river, Exod. 1. v. ult. Certainly no one will be able to condemn these, since they were martyrs, and were killed for this very reason, that they were descended from the people of the Lord.

IIX. 2. We allege the example of the infants in the desert, during the time of the Israelite pilgrimage. For these were not circumcised, either because of the continuous departures and long journeys, or even because of a certain negligence of the parents, Jos. 8. v. 7. But shall we judge that all these, who died before circumcision, perished eternally? If Moses had thought so, then he would have ordered them to be circumcised in the midst of the pilgrimage, even at the risk of their temporal life, rather than have allowed them to be left uncircumcised with the certain outcome of damnation.

IX. 3. We wish the example of the little son of David, conceived by Bathsheba, to be considered. That child died on the seventh day and thus before circumcision, as is read in 2. Sam. 12. v. 18. And nevertheless King David says, v. 23, I shall go to him, but he will not return to me. But how could David have said that he would go to him, if he had thought that he was going to be eternally damned on account of the deprivation of circumcision? Therefore we argue: David says he will go to his uncircumcised little son. Therefore, where David wished to go, there his son was. But he did not wish to go to the damned in hell, but to the blessed in heaven. Therefore his son was also in heaven.

X 4. In the time of the Antiochene persecution (concerning which 1. Macc. 1. & 2. Macc. 6.), very many Jewish infants were most miserably slaughtered, nor were they admitted to circumcision. Yet all these, as being martyrs of the Most High, the most excellent theologians all maintain are not damned, but saved.

XI. From all these examples, therefore, it is gathered quite evidently that just as the uncircumcised children of the Jews, so also the unbaptized children of Christians are immediately endowed with faith by the Lord, and through it are eternally saved, and therefore parents should by no means despair of their salvation and glorification.

XII. But because distressed parents consider an argument from examples to be weak, since they are accustomed to doubt, 'Does God also wish to kindle faith immediately in their children in a similar way?' therefore, for their consolation, immovable foundations must be noted, from which they can be rendered certain of the life and eternal salvation not only of their own, but of all infants whatsoever born to faithful parents, even if they were conceived in sins and died without Baptism in a case of necessity. Now those foundations are threefold: 1. some on the part of God, 2. some on the part of the infants, and 3. some on the part of the parents themselves.

XIII. 1. ON THE PART OF GOD two things should be considered: 1. His infinite power, on account of which it is very easy for Him to infuse faith into infants immediately, and thus to save them through faith. For that which seems difficult in our eyes is not difficult in the eyes of the Lord, Zech. 8:6. He is powerful to do all things superabundantly, above what we ask or understand, Eph. 3:20. A pagan poet acknowledged this when he sang thus in Metamorphoses 8: 'Immense is the power of heaven, and it has no end: and whatever the gods above have willed, it is accomplished.' Let us not, therefore, think that God is bound to the Sacraments, as if He could confer salvation upon no one without them. Two thousand and forty-eight years passed from the creation of the world until the 99th year of Abraham's age, during which time all the faithful were saved without circumcision and Baptism: so also all females without an external means or Sacrament of initiation (for Scripture expresses none) are thought to be saved. From which it is firmly inferred that the grace of God is not simply and absolutely bound to the Sacraments, as if He could not work and save outside of them. For He did not prescribe those laws and that order for Himself, but for us. He can therefore work beyond and outside of that in infinite ways. Therefore, just as He gifted females, because they were incapable of circumcision, with faith immediately by His infinite power and clemency, so let us not doubt that He can do, and indeed actually does, the same regarding the infants of the faithful who are excluded from Baptism due to grave necessity.

XIV. 2. His beneficent will. God can do many things which He does not will, and therefore does not do: for which reason the power of God is not sufficient; the will must also be proven regarding the salvation of infants. This very thing, therefore, we demonstrate.

XV. 1. From the federal promise. I will be your God and that of your seed after you. Gen. 17. v. 7. Which promise, although spoken to Abraham alone, was not however made to him alone, but pertains equally to all Christians and their children, as the Apostle explains, Rom. 4. v. 17, and Peter affirms, Acts 2. v. 38. Hence, therefore, we conclude thus: Whoever does not actually resist, God wills to be their God, by virtue of the federal promise. But infants of the faithful do not actually resist. Therefore, God wills to be their God. Furthermore, those whose God is God, they live, nor can they die eternally, as Christ Himself argued against the Sadducees. But God is the God of all infants born of the faithful. Therefore, all infants of the faithful live, nor can they die eternally, and by consequence, this applies also to those who are excluded from Baptism due to necessity.

If they should object that this promise is not absolute, but limited and conditional, namely, if the use of the means ordained by God has been added. We reply that they are begging the question, and are attacking the universality of the promise against the clear letter. Then the very

Latin:

QVAESTIO I. An Christianorum infantes non baptizati propter peccatum originis damnentur?

I. Pontificij vniuersaliter omnes infantes, vt incircumcisos, sic non baptizatos è regno caelorum excludunt. Lombardus l. 4. Distinct. 1. lit. L. m. p. 294. scribit: Si quaeritur de paruulis, qui ante diem octavum moriebantur, antequam fieret circumcisio ex Lege, vvtrum saluarentur vel non? Idem potest responderi, quod sentitur de paruulis ante Baptismum defunctis, quos PERIRE constat. Thomas parte 3. quæst. 65. art. 4. scribit, Baptismum ad salutem esse necessarium, necessitate simplici & absolutâ. Dominicus à Soto. 2. de nat. & grat. c. 10. ait: In Ecclesia Romana constitutissimum est, nullum paruulum absque Baptismo in re(quam in voto habere non potest)intrare regnum cælorum. Bellarminus l. 6 de A G. c. 2. multis argumentis & testimonijs probat, paruulos sine Baptismo decedentes, mortis æternæ pœnâ esse damnandos.

II. Nos autem cum orthodoxis Theologis sententiam hanc Papisticam & nimis duram & minùs probabilem esse adfirmamus, ideoque contrariam assumimus. Licèt enim Ioh. 3. v. 5. Christus ipse adfirmet; Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu, non potest intrare in regnũ Dei: tamen istud non vniuersaliter, sed limitatè 1. sub conditione possibilitatis, & 2. extra casum necessitatis, adeoque 3. modo ordinario esse intelligendum, duobus indubitatis exemplis potest demonstrari.

III. Alterum latronis est, cum Christo crucifixi, & in cruce demum conuersi. Hîc enim vi promissionis Christi, Hodie mecum eris in Paradiso, Luc. 23. vers. 43. certò saluatus fuit, neque tamen in cruce baptizatus esse legitur, sed sine Baptismo decessisse omnes statuunt: vnde colligitur, dictum Christi, non ἁπλῶς vel vniuersaliter, aut sine necessitatis exceptione intelligendum esse.

IV. Alterum Catechumenorum est, quorum benè multi primis Ecclesiæ seculis fuerunt. Illi in doctrina Christiana instituebantur & sic verè credebant in Christum: multi tamen tempore persecutionum ante Baptismi susceptionem necabantur. Hos autem nùm damnatos putabimus, quia baptizati non fuerunt? Neutiquam, cùm martyres extiterint, fidemque veram habuerint.

Qui enim credit in Christum, non judicatur. Ioh. 3. v. 18. qui credit in filium habet vitam æternam v. 36. Huc etiam pertinet exemplum Cornelij Act. 10. v. 1. & Lydiæ Act. 16. v. 4. Nam & illum & istam credidisse commemorat Lucas: quòd si autem ante Baptismum mortui fuissent, num propterea fideles istos à regno cælorum exclusos fuisse arbitrabimur?

V. Sed excipiunt, diversam esse rationem adultorum & infantum, quoniam isti defectum Baptismi fide suppleant; Infantes autem si non baptizentur, fidem non habere, ideoque necessario damnari. Verùm, quam isti ponunt hypothesin eam nos omninò negamus. Equidem si infantes planè non crederent, quis tàm absurdus foret, vt eos saluari putaret? Vtrumquè igitur, tàm fides, quàm salus infantum æque controvertitur. Statuunt autem orthodoxi: quòd sicuti Deus Iohannem Baptistam in vtero materno fide donauit, ita eandem alijs Christianorum liberis, à Baptismo ob necessitatis casum exclusis conferat, & sic ob meritum Christi fide apprehensum peccatum originale remittat, eosque æternum salvet.

VI. Quod vt evincatur considerandam proponimus analogiam circumcisionis & Baptismi, vtrumque enim Sacramentum initationis est, quo tanquam medio ordinario & olim inserti sunt Ecclesiæ infantes, & etiamnùm hodiè inseruntur: Vtriusque summa necessitas ex parte hominum fuit indicata; Baptismi quidem d l. Iohan. 3. v. 5. Circumcisionis autem Gen. 7. v. 14. Masculus, cuius præputij caro circumcisa non fuerit, delebitur anima illa de populo suo, quia pactum meum irritum fecit. Hinc igitur ita colligimus: Si incircumcisi Iudæorum filij non obstante istâ comminatione Gen. 17. fuerunt saluati, tum vtique nõ baptizati Christianorum infantes etiam saluari poterunt. Consequentia est firma, quoniam vtriusque Sacramenti par est ratio & necessitas, vtrobique etiam eadem tū infantum, tum parentum est conditio Atqui incircumcisi Iudæorum filij sunt saluati. Ergo & Christianorum liberi non baptizati saluabuntur. Minorem probamus sequentibus exemplis.

VII. 1. Producimus masculos in Ægypto, qui statim ac nati fuerant, à ministris Pharaonis abripiebantur, & incircumcisi in fluentem proijciebantur, Exod. 1. v. ult. Hos certè damnare nemo poterit, cùm martyres fuerint, & propter hoc ipsum interfecti, quod ex populo Domini essent oriundi.

IIX. 2. Allegamus exemplum infantum in deserto, tempore peregrinationis Israëliticæ.
