Etenim isti non sunt circumcisi, vel propter continuas profectiones, & longinqua itinera, vel etiam propter quandam parentum incuriam, Ios. 8. v. 7. Num autem omnes istos, ante circumcisionem mortuos, æternùm perijsse iudicabimus? Si Moses ita censuisset, tum potiùs cum temporalis vitæ periculo in media peregrinatione eos circumcidi iussisset, quàm vt incircumcisos cum certo damnationis exitio relinqui permisisset.

IX. 3. Considerari volumus exemplum filioli Dauidis, ex Bethsaba suscepti. Mortuus ille fuit die septimâ & sic ante circumcisionem, vt legitur. 2. Sam. 12. v. 18. Et nihilominus Rex David ait, v. 23. Ego vadam ad eum, ille verò non reuertetur ad me. Quomodo autem potuisset David dicere, se ad illum abiturum, si eum ob priuationem circumcisionis, æternùm iri damnatum existimasset? Proinde argumentamur: David se abiturum dicit ad filiolum suum incircumcisum. Ergo quò abire voluit David, ibi filius ejus fuit. Abire autem voluit non ad damnatos in inferno, sed ad beatos in cœlo. Ergo & filius eius fuit in cœlo.

X 4. Tempore persecutionis Antiochenæ, (de qua 1. Macc. 1. & 2. Macc. 6. ) Iudæorum infantes plurimi miserrimè trucidabantur, nec ad circumcionem admittebantur. Hos tamen omnes, vt pote martyres Altissimi, non damnatos, sed saluatos esse præstantissimi quique Theol. statuunt.

XI. Ex his ergo exemplis omnibus satis evidenter colligitur, quòd sicut Iudæorum incircumcisi, ita & Christianorum non baptizati filij immediatè donentur fide à Domino, & per eam æternùm salventur, ideoque parentibus de ipsorum salute & glorificatione nequaquam sit desperandum.

XII. Quia verò consternati parentes argumentum ab exemplis pro infirmo habēt, siquidem dubitate solent, Num & Deus consimiliter in suis liberis fidem velit immediatè accendere? propterea ad consolationem eorum immota sunt annotanda fundamenta, exquibus certi queant reddi de vita & salute æterna, nō tantùm suorum sed omnium omninò infantum, & fidelibus parentibus natorum, licèt in peccatis concepti sint & sine Baptismo in casu necessitatis decesserint. Sunt autem illa fundamenta triplicia: 1 quædam ex parte Dei 2. quædam ex parte infantum, & 3. quædam ex parte ipsorum parentum.

XIII. 1. EX PARTE DEI duo considerentur, 1. Infinita eius potestas, ob quam ipsi facillimum est, infantibus immediatè fidem infundere, & sic per fidem eos saluare. Non enim quod difficile videtur in oculis nostris, difficile est in oculis Domini Zach 8. v. 6. Potens hic est omnia facere superabundanter, suprà quam petimus aut intelligimus, Eph. 3. v. 20. Agnovit hoc gentilis Poeta, cùm 8. Metamorph. ita cecinit. Immensa est, finemque potentia cæli Non habet: Et quicquid superi voluēre, peractum est. Non igitur putemus, quòd alligatus sit Deus ad Sacramenta, acsi absque ijs salutem conferre nemini possit. Abierunt à condito Mundo bis mille quadraginta octo anni, vsq; ad 99. ætatis Abrahami, quo tēpore omnes fideles sine circumcisione & Baptismo salvati sunt: Ita etiam fœmellæ omnes sine externo medio vel Sacramento initiationis (nullum enim Scriptura exprimit) faluatæ putantur. Ex quibus firmiter infertur, gratiam Dei non esse simpliciter & absolute alligatam ad Sacramenta, ac si extra ea operari & saluare non posset. Non enim sibi, sed nobis leges eas ordinemq́; præscripsit. Potest igitur præter & extra illum infinitis modis operari Propterea, quemadmodum fœmellas, quia incapaces erant circumcisionis, infinita suâ potestate & clementiâ ἀμέσως fide donauit, sic idem adhuc circa infantes fidelium, à Baptismo ob grauem necessitatem exclusos facere posse, imò actu facere nulli dubitemus.

XIV. 2. Be efica eius voluntas. Multa potest Deus, quæ non vult, ideoque nec facit: quam ob cau sam non sufficit Dei potestas; probanda etiam est voluntas, quoad saluationem infantum Hanc ipsam igitur demonstramus.

XV. 1. A fœderali præmissione. Ero Deus tuus & seminis tui post te. Gen. 17. v 7. quę promissio soli quidem Abrahamo dicta, non tamen soli facta est, sed æquè ad omnes Christianos, eorumque liberos pertinet, explicante Apostolo, Rom. 4. v. 17. & affirmate Petro, Act. 2. v. 38 Hinc igitur sic colligimus: Quicunq; non resistunt actualiter, illarum Deus vult esse Deus, vi promissionis fœderalis. At verò infantes fideliūm actualiter non resistunt. Ergo illorum Deus vult esse Deus Porrò Quorum Deus est Deus, illi viuunt, nec æternum mori possunt. vti Christus ipse contra Sadducæos argumentabatur. Omnium autem infantum ex fidelibus natorum Deus est Deus. Ergò omnes infantes fidelium viuunt, nec æternùm mori possunt, & per consequentiam illis etiam, qui ob causam necessitatis à Baptismo excluduntur.

Si exceperint, promissionem istam non esse absolutam, sed limitatam & conditionatam, nempè, si vsus mediorū à Deo ordinatorum accesserit. Resp. quòd principium petant, & vniuersalitatem promissionis contra claram literam impugnent. Deindè ip-


### promise itself is the reason that infants are admitted to the reception of the…

promise itself is the reason that infants are admitted to the reception of the means. They could not or should not be baptized in infancy, unless the federal promise pertained to them: for no other reason can be given why the children of unbelievers are excluded from Baptism in infancy than this, because the federal promise does not directly reach them. Since, therefore, an immediate approach to Baptism is open to all children of the faithful, we infer from this that this federal promise reaches all, with none excepted, yet with this distinction, that the application of the promise and the bestowal of the promised good is only mediate with regard to those who can be participants of the Sacraments, but immediate with regard to the rest who are excluded from the Sacraments by a case of necessity. We confirm this clearly by the example of females in the O.T. dying in infancy, and yet saved. For these were not capable of the ordinary means, namely circumcision, and there exists nothing in the whole Scripture concerning another Sacrament proper to females. Therefore, it must be concluded that they were saved immediately. We ask, however, about the cause: whence could the parents be certain of their salvation? A special promise made to females is nowhere read. Therefore, it must be said that they were saved by virtue of the general and federal promise itself. Hence, therefore, we conclude: Just as in the O.T., because of the promise of the covenant, God saved immediately both females and all those who could not become participants of the ordinary means, so also in the N.T., where the same promise exists, He certainly wills to save all children of the faithful who likewise cannot be made partakers of the ordinary means on account of a case of necessity.

XVI. 2. From a special calling which exists in Matt. 19, v. 14: Suffer the little children to come unto me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven. This calling is found in Mark 10, v. 13 and Luke 18, v. 16. Although it is probable that most of those infants offered to Christ had been circumcised and inserted into the Church, yet because Luke uses this word τὰ βρέφη v. 15, which denotes the most tender and infants just born, hence it can probably be said that even uncircumcised boys not yet eight days old, at the very least uncircumcised females, were offered together and that concerning them also it was pronounced by Christ that the kingdom of God is theirs. Indeed, however the matter may stand, let the universal statement of God remain; Sinite τὰ παιδία to come to me, τῶν γὰρ τοιότων ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῦ θεῦ. This indeed ought to be understood not of all absolutely, but nevertheless of all the children of the faithful (such as were then being offered). Hence by a most firm consequence we conclude again: Whose the kingdom of heaven is, those God wishes to save immediately, and saves by the very act, if they are deprived of the ordinary means. Of all infants born of Christian progenitors is the kingdom of God, Christ saying so. Therefore all infants of Christians God wishes to save immediately, and saves by the very act, if they are deprived of the ordinary means.

XVII. 3. From the clear assertion of the Lord, which exists in Isaiah 48, v. 18 & 19, where the Lord says that He would not have destroyed the seed of the Israelites, unless they had fallen away from the Lord. Therefore, the parents of whatever infants are faithful and Christian, they are not excluded, nor destroyed, and therefore if they lack the means, they are saved immediately by God. Some also refer to this that passage of Isaiah 49, v. 25: I WILL SAVE your children. We acknowledge, however, that this last argument, taken from Isaiah 49, is only probable, not apodictic.

XIIX. 2. FROM THE PART OF THE INFANTS likewise two things are to be considered: 1. Birth in the Church. There is altogether a great distinction between those who are born in the Church to Christian parents, and those who are born outside the Church to pagan parents. For on this account Peter distinguishes so accurately between the children of the covenant and outsiders, Acts 3, verse 25; Paul between the circumcised and the uncircumcised, Rom. 2, verse [26], and also between those who are within and those who are without, 1 Cor. 5, v. 12. And 1 Cor. 7, v. 14, those born in the Church he calls holy, but outsiders unclean. By which holiness, however, is not to be understood the interior and spiritual purity of the soul, but only the Ecclesiastical, as they call it, dignity. Of this, moreover, there are two primary privileges. 1. that the federal promise pertains to all born in the Church. 2. that they are immediately admitted to the Sacraments and goods of the Church. Of the former we have just spoken: from the latter we conclude thus: Whomever God wills to be admitted immediately to Baptism, those He also wills to be entirely saved in their infant age. For they are baptized for this reason, that sins may be remitted to them and thus they may be saved. But He wills that all children of Christians be admitted immediately to Baptism, and He commands it, for which reason they are called holy, 1 Cor. 7 v. 14. Therefore He wills them to be entirely saved in their infant age as well. We argue further thus: Those whom God wills to be entirely saved on account of the federal promise and birth in the Church, He saves immediately if they are necessarily excluded from the ordinary means. Such, however, are the infants of Christians who have died before Baptism. Therefore He saves them immediately. We prove the major premise, because the grace of God is not bound to the means. Those, therefore, whom God seriously wills to be members of His Church and to be saved, He also makes members, and actually saves.

XIX. Nor is there any reason for anyone to object that God wills the salvation of all, 1 Tim. 2 v. 9, and yet does not actually save all. For as far as adults are concerned, the fault is not in God, but in themselves, who resist the Holy Spirit and place an obstacle. But since this contumacy is absent in infants, therefore God executes His work in them without impediment, and works salvation. Furthermore, let that distinction between the children of the covenant and outsiders be diligently considered, Acts 3 v. 25. For if the children of Christians are to be damned, what will that distinction be? What kind of children of the covenant or testament will they be? Wherefore from this we infer thus: To every child of the covenant the bequeathed inheritance is due. All children of Christians, as being born in the Church, are children of the covenant, such as outsiders are not. To them the inheritance is owed, and consequently it is given by God, since they do not render this covenant void, as adults do, due to the lack of actual sins. Now, in a case of necessity, the inheritance cannot be given and conferred mediately. Therefore, it is given immediately, and thus all infants of the faithful are saved: they are not damned.

XX. 2. The simple lack of Sacraments. Theologians have a rule: It is not the deprivation, but the contempt of the Sacraments that damns. Where, therefore, there is a bare and simple deprivation of Baptism, there damnation has no place. But in the infants of Christians dying prematurely, there is a bare and simple deprivation of Baptism, not one that is malicious or joined with contempt. Therefore, no damnation has place there. And certainly, if the threats of Gen. 17 and John 3 are diligently considered, it will appear most manifestly that in both places the discourse is not so much about deprivation as about contempt. There, because these words are added: because he has made my covenant void. But one does not make it void, except through contempt. In Hebrew the root פרר, which signifies to violate, to despise, to neglect, to break. Here, because he is speaking with the adult Nicodemus, who held rebirth to be inconvenient and impossible. To him, therefore, Christ said that if anyone despises and neglects Baptism, and is not reborn of water, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God. But since this contempt is very far removed from the infants of Christians, we conclude that the punishment is also absent from them. For where guilt has not preceded, there the punishment of guilt has no place. Moreover, to be blotted out from the people of the Lord, and not to enter into the kingdom of God, is the punishment of a despised Sacrament. But the infants of Christians do not despise it. Wherefore they ought not to be held as damned. And thus that saying was explained by Lombard himself, Book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 4, letter E, when he writes expressly: it is to be understood of those who can be baptized and despise it. Which passage of the Master we deservedly oppose to the other Papists.

XXI. 3. ON THE PART OF THE PARENTS, let their ardent prayer be considered, which they are accustomed to pour out with the whole Church to God for the salvation of their children, even while they are still lying in the mother's womb. But that it is ineffective, and not heard, why should we believe, when the words of the promise are clear: Amen, Amen I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Matt. 7. v. 7, c. 21. v. 22, Mark 11. v. 24, Luke 11. v. 29, John 14. v. 13, c. 16. v. 23, James 1. v. 6. For because it is not the will of God that one of these little ones should perish, Matt. 18. v. 14, therefore let parents not doubt, both to commend their children to God with pious prayers, and that these very prayers are mercifully heard:

For God does not cast out the little children who are offered to him. Now this offering is twofold; the one is made through Baptism, the other through prayers. Therefore, just as God adopts as sons all those who are offered to him through Baptism, so also those who are offered through prayers. For the efficacy of these is so great that they are profitable not only to the person of the one praying but also to others, and thus also to infants, for whom the prayer is undertaken, and they obtain for them both faith and consequently eternal salvation.

XXII. We do not indeed say this, that infants are saved by the faith of their parents, but rather by their own proper faith, Habakkuk 2. v. 4, Romans 1. v. 17. Now this faith, which others receive only through Baptism, infants dying prematurely obtain by the benefit of the prayers poured out by their parents. For that the prayer of the pious obtains faith and help from God for those lacking faith is testified by the servant of the centurion, Matt. 8. v. 6, the daughter of the Canaanite woman, Matt. 15. v. 22, the daughter of Jairus, Luke 8. v. 41, the lunatic son, Luke 9. v. 39, and the son of the nobleman, John 4. v. 47.

XXIII. If they object that by this reasoning all infants of Christians believe before they are baptized, we answer that prayers are and ought to be conditional, if indeed the infants cannot be made partakers of the Sacrament. Those, therefore, whom God foreknows will live until the time of Baptism, to them He neither confers faith immediately before Baptism, nor is there access so that He might confer it.

XXIV. And these were those principal foundations upon which the salvation of unbaptized infants, yet born in the Church, rests; by the diligent consideration of which, pious parents can have firm consolation in every temptation:

XXV. But if it be further asked: What is to be determined concerning those infants whose parents, although they live in the Church, are nevertheless impious and hypocrites, and have no care for their children, but neglect their Baptism, let alone pray for their salvation? We answer briefly that they do not bear the iniquity of their parents, Ezek. 18 v. 19, especially since all the foundations of salvation hitherto recounted are common to them equally with the infants of the former. For although the prayers of the parents are lacking regarding these, yet the Church supplies that defect, which in its Litanies faithfully commends to God embryos and all infants, which prayers must be determined to be entirely valid and firm. However, that parents of such a kind will not only render an account to God for their impiety and despised Baptism, but will also pay the penalty unless they repent, is placed beyond all hazard of doubt:

XXVI. In place of a colophon, let these testimonies of the Fathers be noted: 1. August. b. 4 against the Donatists, ch. 23. Just as in the thief Baptism was lacking corporally through necessity, salvation was perfect because it was present spiritually through piety: So also when it itself is at hand, if it is lacking through necessity, that which was lacking to the thief, salvation is perfected: 2. The same, b. 1 on Baptism, ch. 22 & 24. Then the Sacrament of Baptism is fulfilled visibly, when that same thing, not by contempt of religion, but by the point of necessity excludes 3. Bern. epist. 77. The will is imputed for the deed, where necessity excludes the deed.

Latin:

sa promissio est causa, quòd infantes ad susceptionem mediorum admittãtur. Non baptizari possent aut deberent in infantili ætate, nisi promissio fœderalis eos attineret: Alia enim causa dari nequit, cur infideliũ liberi secludantur à Baptismo in infantia, quàm hæc, quia promissio fœderalis eos directè non attingit. Quia igitur omnibus fidelium liberis ad Baptismum aditus patet immediatus, hinc inferimus, promissionem istam fœderalem omnes, nullo excepto, attinere, hoc tamen discrimine, yt promissionis applicatio, bonique promissi collatio non nisi mediata sit quoad eos, qui Sacramentorum possunt esse participes, immediata autē quoad reliquos, qui necessitatis casu à Sacramentis excluduntur. Confirmamus hoc luculenter exemplo fœmellarum in V. T. in infantia morientium, & tamen saluatarum. Etenim ordinarij medij, nempe circumcisionis capaces hæ non erant, de alio autem & fœmellis proprio Sacramento nihil extat in vniuersa Scriptura. Igitur immediatè saluatas fuisse concludendum est. Quærimus autem de causa, vnde certi potuerint esse parentes de ipsarum salute? Specialis promissio fœmellis facta nullibi legitur. Ergo dicendum quòd vi generalis ipsius & fœderalis promissionis saluatę sint. Hinc ergo concludimus, Sicut in V, T. propter promissionem fœderis immediatè saluauit Deus & fœmellas, & omnes eos, qui ordinarij medij part cipes fieri non poterant, ita etiam in N T., vbi eadem promissio, certò saluare vult omnes fidelium liberos, qui itidem ordinarij medij ob necessitatis casum compotes reddi nequeunt.

XVI. 2. A speciali vocatione quæ extat Matth, 19. v. 14. Sinite parvulos ad me venire, Talium enim est regnum cœlorum. Reperitur hæc vocatio Marc. 10. v. 13. & Luc. 18. v. 16. Quã vis verò probabile sit, pleros - que istos Christo oblatos infantes fuisse circumcisos & Ecclesiæ insertos, attamen quia Luc. vtitur vocabulo hoc τὰ βρέφη v. 15 quod tenerrimos & modò natos infantes denotat, hinc probabiliter dici potest, quòd etiam incircumcisi & nondum octo dies nati pueri, ad minimum incircumcisæ fœmellæ, vnà fuerint oblatæ deque ijs quoque à Christo pronunciatum, quòd regnum Dei illorum sit. Imò vtut sese res habeat, maneat tamen vniuersalis Dei locutio; Sinite τὰ παιδία ad me venire, τῶν γὰρ τοιότων ἐστιν ἡ βασιλεία τῦ θεῦ. Id quod quidem non de omnibus absolutè, attamen de omnibus fidelium, (quales tum offerebantur) liberis intelligi debet. Hinc firmissima sequela iterum concludimus: Quorum est regnum cœlorum, illos Deus immediatè saluare vult, ipsóque actu saluat, si ordinario medio priuentur. Omnium infantum, ex Christianis progeneratorum, est regnum Dei, dicente Christo. Ergo omnes Christianorum infantes Deus immediatè saluare vult, actúque ipso saluat, si ordinario medio priuentur.

XVII. 3. A luculenta Domini asseueratione, quæ extat Eja. 48. v. 18. & 19. vbi Dominus ait, se non deleturum fuisse semen Israelitarum, nisi à Domino desciuissent Igitur quorumcunque infantum parentes sunt fideles & Christiani, ij non excluduntur, nec delentur, ideoque si medio careant immediatè à Deo seruantur. Nonnulli etiam huc referunt illud Esa 49. v. 25. Filios tuos ego SALVABO. Agnoscimus verò argumentum hoc vltimum ex Eja. 49. petitum, duntaxat esse probabile non apodicticum.

XIIX. 2. EX PARTE INFANTVM itidem duo considerentur 1. Natiuitas in Ecclesia. Magnum omninò discrimē est inter eos, qui in Ecclesia à Christianis, & eos, qui extra Ecclesiam à paganis nati sunt parentibus. Propterea enim tam accuratè distinguit Petrus inter filios pacti & exteros, Act. 3. vers. 25. Paulus inter circumcisos & præputiatos. Rom. 2. vers. vult & inter eos, qui intus sunt & qui foris. 1. Cor. 5. v. 12. Et 1. Cor: 7. v. 14. in Ecclesia natos appellat sanctos, exteros autem immundos. Per quam tamen sanctitatem non interior & spiritualis animæ puritas intelligenda est, sed Ecclesiastica tantùm, vti vocant, dignitas. Huius autem duo sunt primaria priuilegia. 1. quòd omnes in Ecclesia natos attineat promissio fœderalis. 2. quòd immediatè ad Sacramenta & bona Ecclesiæ admittantur. De priori modò dictum: ex posteriori sic colligimus: Quoscunq; Deus immediatè ad Baptismum admitti vult, illos quoque in ætate infantili omninò saluatos vult. Ideò enim baptizantur, vt ijs peccata remittantur & sic saluentur. Atqui omnes Christianorum liberos immediatè ad Baptismum admitti vult, & præcipit, qua de causa dicuntur sancti, 1. Cor. 7. v. 14. Ergo eos in infantili quoque ætate omninò saluatos vult. Vlterius sic argumentamur: Quos Deus omninò saluatos vult ob fœderalem promissionem & natiuitatem in Ecclesia, eos, si necessariò excludantur ab ordinarijs medijs immediatè saluat. Tales autem sunt infantes Christianorum, ante Baptismum extincti. Ergo eos immediatè saluat. Majorem probamus, quia gratia Dei non est alligata ad media. Quos igitur Deus seriò vult Ecclesiæ suæ membra esse & saluari, illos etiam membra facit, actuque saluat.

XIX. Neque est, vt excipiat quis; Deum velle omnium salutem, 1. Tim. 2. v. 9. nec tamen omnes actu saluare. Etenim quod adultos attinet, culpa non est in Deo, sed in ipsis, qui Spiritui S. resistunt, & objicem ponunt Hæc autem contumacia cùm absit in infantibus, propterea Deus absque impedimento opus suum in ijs exequitur, & salutem operatur. Præterea diligenter consideretur illa distinctio inter filios pacti & exteros, Act. 3. ver25. Etenim si Christianorum filij sunt damnandi quale erit discrimen istud? Quales erunt filij pacti vel testamenti? Qua propter ex eo sic inferimus: Omni filio pacti debetur hæreditas legata. Omnes Christianorum liberi, vt pote in Ecclesia nati, sunt filij pacti, quales non sunt exteri. E illis debetur hæreditas, & per consequens datur à Deo, cum ipsi pactum istud non reddant iritum, vt adulti, ob carentiam peccatorum actualium. Iam verò in casu necessitatis mediatè dari & conferri hæreditas nequit. Ergo datur immediatè, atque sic omnes fidelium infantes saluantur: non damnantur.

XX. 2. Simplex Sacramentorum carentia. Habent Theologi regulam: Non priuatio, sed contemtus Sacramentorum damnat. Vbi igitur nuda simplex est Baptismi priuatio, ibi locum non habet damnatio. Atqui in infantibus Christianorum immaturè morientibus nuda simplexque non malitio sa aut cum contentu coniuncta Baptismi priuatio est. Ergo nulla ibi locum habet damnatio. Et certè, si diligenter considerentur comminationes Gen. 17. & Ioh. 3. vtrobique non tam de priuatione, quam contemtu sermonem esse, apparebit manifestissimè. Ibi, quoniam adduntur hæc verba: quia irritum fecit pactum meum. Irritum autem non facit, nisi per contemtum. In Hebræo radix פרר, quæ significat, violare, contemnere, negligere, frangere. Hic, quia loquitur cum adulto Nicodemo, qui renascentiam habebat pro inconueniente & impossibili. Huic ergò Christus dixit, quòd si quis contemnat negligatque Baptismum, nec renascatur ex aqua, introire in regnum Dei non possit. Hic autem contemtus cum longissimè absit ab infantibus Christianorum, & pœnam ab ijs ab esse concludimus. Vbi enim non præcessit culpa, ibi nec locum habet culpæ pœna, Deleri autem è populo Domini, & non introire in regnum Dei, est pœna spreti Sacramenti. Infantes autem Christianorum, illud non spernunt. Quare pro damnatis haberi non debent. Atque ita dictum istud exposuit ipseLombardus l. 4. Sent. dist. 4. lit E. cùm expresse scribit: intelligendum est de ijs, qui possunt & contemnunt baptizari. Quem locum Magistri cæteris Papicolis meritò opponimus.

XXI. 3. EX PARTE PARENTVM consideretur ardens ipsorum precatio, quam ad Deum pro salute suorum liberorum, etiam in vtero matris adhuè jacentium, cum tota Ecclesia fundere consueuerunt. Eam verò inefficacem esse, nec exaudiri, quâ crederemus, cùm clara sint promissionis verba: Amen, Amen dico vobis, si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo dabit vobis. Matth. 7. v. 7. c. 21. v. 22. Mar. 11. v. 24. Luc. 11. v 29. Ioh. 14 v. 13. c. 16. v. 23. Iacobi 1. v. 6. Quia enim non est voluntas Dei, vt pereat vnus de pusillis istis. Matth. 18. v. 14 propterea non dubitent parentes, tùm liberos suos precibus pijs Deo commendare, tùm has ipsas clementer exaudiri:

Etenim non eijcit Deus infantulos, qui ipsi offeruntur. Hæc autem oblatio duplex; altera fit per Baptismum, altera per preces. Sicut igitur Deus in filios adoptat omnes eos, qui ipsi per Baptismum offeruntur, ita etiam qui per precès, Tanta enim harum est efficacia vt non tantùm ipsi personæ petentis sed & aliis, atque sic etiam infantibus, pro quibus oratio suscipitur conducant, eisque & fidem, & consequenter salutem æternam impetrent.

XXII. Non quidem hoc dicimus, quòd fide parentum saluentur infantes, sed fide potius sua propriaque Habac. 2. v. 34. Rom 1. v. 17. Hanc autem fidem quam alij ex Baptismo demum percipiunt; infantes immaturè morientes beneficio precum à parentibus fusarum adipiscuntur. Quòd enim piorum oratio fide carentibus fidem & auxilium à Deo impetret, testatur famulus centurionis, Matth. 8. v. 6. filia mulieris Chananææ, Matth. 15. v. 22. filia Iairi, Luc 8. v. 38. filius Lunaticus, Luc. 9. v. 39. & filius reguli, Ioh. 4. v. 47.

XXIII. Si objecerint, hac ratione omnes infantes Christianorum credere antequam baptizentur, respondemus, quòd preces sint & esse debeant conditionatæ, si nimirum infantes non possint fieri participes Sacramenti. Quos igitur Deus præscit vsque ad tempus Baptismi victuros; ijs fidem immediatè antè Baptismum nec confert nec vt conferat accessum est.

XXIV. Et hæc fuerunt ista principalia fundamenta, quibus salus infantum non baptizatorum; in Ecclesia tamen natorum innititur ; quorum consideratione sedulâ parentes pij firmam in omni tentatione consolationem habere possunt:

XXV. Quòd si autem vlterius quæratur: Quid sit statuendum de ijs infantibus quorum parentes; licet in Ecclesia viuant; impij tamen sunt & hypocritæ ; nullamque liberorum curam habent , sed ipsorum Baptismum negligunt; ne dum vt pro ipsorum salute orent? Resp: breuiter, quòd non portent iniquitatem parentum Ezech. 18 v. 19. præsertim cùm omnia salutis fundamenta hactenus recensita ijs ex æquo cum priorum infantibus sint communia: Licet enim preces parentum quoad istos desint, tamen defectum eum supplet Ecclesia quæ in Litaniis suis Deo embryones; omnesq; infantes fideliter commendat, quas preces ratas firmasq; esse omninò statuendum est. Parentes autem eiusmodi grauem suæ impietatis & spreti Baptismi non tantùm rationem Deo reddituros, sed etiam pœnam; ni resipiscant, daturos esse, extra omnem dubitationis aleam est positũ:

XXVI. Colophonis loco notentur hæc Patrum testimonia, 1. August. l. 4. contra Donat: c. 23. Sicut in latrone per necessitatem corporaliter Baptismus defuit, perfecta salus est, quia per pietatem spiritualiter adfuit: Sic & cùm ipsa præsto est, si per necessitatem desit; quod latroni defuit perficitur salus: 2. Idem l. 1. de Baptismo c. 22. & 24. Tunc Sacramentum Baptismi impletur visibiliter, cùm idipsum non contemptus religionis, sed necessitatis articulus excludit 3. Bern. epist. 77. Voluntas pro facto imputatur, vbi factum excludit necessitas.


### Question II. Are the children of infidels born outside the Church damned?

QUESTION II. Are the children of infidels born outside the Church damned?

I. This problem is debated on both sides, to such an extent that many hesitate, and hardly find what should be determined. Some think that although the infants of infidels are infected with original sin, and by the nature of the matter are subject to eternal damnation, nevertheless on account of the supreme φιλανθρωπίαν of Jehovah they are gifted with faith extraordinarily, and thus are eternally saved. Which opinion of theirs relies chiefly on the following arguments.

II. They urge the infinite mercy of God toward the human race. For concerning this, He willed to show mercy rather than justice, and therefore to punish is called a strange and foreign work. Isa. 28. v. 13. Whoever, however, is supremely merciful: he, if especially he can easily do so, does not allow him to perish in misery who cannot free himself from it, and has fallen into that misery not so much by his own fault as by the fault of others. For it is the nature of mercy that the heart be moved by misery. But where there is a moving of the heart; there immediately arises an inclination to help: which cannot but be followed by the actual help itself, if the supreme power over all things is present.

III. 2. They propose sayings speaking of the universal will of God, such as are 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. Ezech. 33. v. 11. John 3. v. 16. 17. and especially that one Rom. 11. verse 32. He has concluded all, that He might have mercy on all, and Matt. 18. v. 14. It is not the will before your Father, who is in heaven, that one of these little ones should perish. This very will of the eternal Father concerning the salvation of all, and thus of infants also, has not been changed, but is most serious: Wherefore that which He wills, He certainly brings into act, either through certain means as in adults, or immediately in those who by reason of age are not capable of means, such as infants. For whoever wills anything seriously, He always executes what He wills, unless He is resisted. God therefore, since He seriously wills be eternally saved, will certainly free them, since they, unlike adults, do not resist. If any prince were to boast with many words that he would free his subjects who perhaps are held captive in Turkey, and yet remained idle in his citadel, and did not procure their liberation by all means and powers, then he would deservedly be thought to have feigned and mocked his subjects: in like manner, that universal and serious will of God can hardly be defended against the Calvinists if we posit that he indeed wills to save infants, yet undertakes nothing that contributes to promoting their salvation by the act itself.

IV. 3. To prove the same, they produce sayings concerning the universal merit and redemption of Christ, such as are: John 1:29, ch. 3:16, 17, ch. 4:43, ch. 6:51, ch. 12:47, Rom. 5:18, 19, 1 Cor. 15:22, 2 Cor. 5:14, 15, 1 John 2:2, from which they infer thus: If Christ redeemed all, and truly acquired eternal life for all, then if the redemption is not to be empty and in vain, it is necessary that the acquired good be offered and conferred upon all who do not resist, such as infants. For would it not be considered a mockery if someone were to boast at length that he had redeemed all captives and had procured true liberty for all, and yet did not provide the means for exiting the prison to all, or did not immediately lead out and free those who are not capable of the means? In like manner, either the merit of Christ will not be universal, or it will not be true and serious, unless he either offers the means of salvation to infants, or, if he is unwilling to give the means, confers salvation by the act itself.

V. 4. Against the Calvinists we fight manfully for the universality of the calling and the sufficiency of grace, teaching tes, that God truly and really calls all to salvation, and actually bestows sufficient grace for obtaining salvation: but, unless we say that all infants are saved, it hardly appears how that can be defended. For the infants of unbelievers cannot be called by the word, because they cannot hear it: they are not called by Baptism, because this is conferred only upon the children of the faithful. Besides these modes of mediate calling, however, no third can be given. Therefore it must be said that those infants are either not called at all, which is Calvinistic; or they are called immediately and thus saved, since they do not resist God who calls. For calling is nothing else than the offer of grace. But to whomever grace is offered, if he does not resist, it is also conferred, as our theologians teach. Infants, however, do not resist, nor can they resist, because they do not yet use reason. Wherefore if they are called; if grace is offered to them, they will certainly be saved. But that they are called, and that sufficient grace is offered to them, must be defended against the Calvinists. It seems therefore to follow necessarily that they are saved. And certainly if we acknowledge no immediate action of God concerning infants, it will hardly be possible to show how they have sufficient grace. For they are entirely deprived of the ordinary means. Wherefore if God neither offers immediately, nor works extraordinarily in infants, they will be destitute of all aids for obtaining salvation. But is this to have sufficient grace, and an aid efficient for salvation?

VI. 5. They consider the solicitous care of God regarding the salvation of adults. He proposes the word to them, sends his ministers, offers the Sacraments, stretches out his arms, waits all day, calls, cries out, shows wonders, casts them into calamities, exhorts, threatens, promises, and attempts with the greatest zeal all things which seem to contribute to their conversion. Shall we think that God has such care for them, that he completely forgets infants, who nevertheless neither actually sin nor resist? Shall we think that he pours out all grace upon adults, and completely neglects miserable infants? Since therefore this is absurd and contrary to the benevolent will of God, it is necessary that we say that he works in infants immediately, just as he works mediately in adults, and therefore saves them, since they do not resist, by the very act.

VII. 6. They urge the universality of the promises, since they are read to have been made to all without exception, not only to those born in the Church, but also outside the Church, especially Acts 2:39. To you, the text says, the promise is made, and to your children, and to all who are far off, as many as the Lord shall call. Therefore, just as the infants of the faithful are thought to be saved by virtue of the divine promises, so also the children of unbelievers will be saved, since, as Peter says, even though they are still far off, the promise has been made to them.

IIX. 7. They further say that regarding the infants of pagans, all the foundations are found which have been brought forward for the salvation of Christians. On the part of God, both the power and the will are given, which consist both of the promises of salvation and of the universal calling. On the part of the infants, there is given a mere and simple privation, without any contempt. On the part of the Church, there is given an ardent prayer for the salvation of all who do not contumaciously resist. Only one thing is lacking, that they were not born in the Church, which itself, however, seems to hinder their salvation in no way, just as the contrary does not benefit others. For wherever anyone is born, he is nevertheless a child of wrath, and needs the grace of God who regenerates. Heretics are in the Church; yet this helps them nothing: Indeed, even the children of the faithful seem to be outside the Church, insofar as they have not yet been inserted by Baptism, and yet God has mercy on them. Therefore, the external circumstance of place will not hinder the salvation of the infants of unbelievers.

IX. 8. Finally, theologians teach that no sin, but only unbelief, formally condemns, which they define by the contempt of offered grace, and the neglected use of the means. It is not merely a negation of faith, but at the same time a contrary vice; namely, contempt of what is offered, since it is opposed to faith not only privatively but also contrarily, and thus presupposes the offering of grace and merit, then posits the contempt and neglect of what is offered. But such unbelief they cannot be damned either. They prove the minor premise, because if God does not immediately offer grace to them, then it is offered in no way, since they lack both Baptism and the hearing of the word. But if nothing is offered, how can they despise any offered good? Indeed, how can contempt fall upon those who understand nothing, nor can use reason? Therefore, with the cause of damnation absent and denied, how can damnation be affirmed?

X. And these are the arguments for the common salvation of infants, even those born of pagan parents, certainly not light, but very difficult and weighty, so that they may sufficiently exercise anyone: it is now pleasing to propose the reasons of those who deny this, and who hold the children of unbelievers to be damned.

XI. 1. They think this is the mind of the Augsburg Confession, when in the second article it says, Sin damns and brings death to those who are not reborn through Baptism and the Holy Spirit; the Apology also, art. 9, p. 156, clearly affirms: that the promise of salvation pertains indeed to little children, but not to those who are outside the Church of Christ, where there is neither word nor Sacraments, etc. Hence they infer: To whom the promise of salvation does not pertain, they are not saved. But since the Apology says the promise of salvation does not pertain to those born outside the Church, therefore they are not saved.

XII. 2. They urge that Theological element: Outside the Church there is no salvation. He does not have God as Father in Heaven, who does not have the Church as mother. Hence Augustine, quest. 65, writes to Orosius: Just as no one in the ark of Noah was freed from the flood except he who was in it, so no one, unless he has been a member of the Church, will be saved. But this principle, hitherto chanted for so many centuries in the Theological Schools, will have to be entirely denied if the salvation of infidel infants is certainly established.

XIII. 3. They propose the examples of adults outside the Church. For there are many to whom the word of God and the Sacraments are clearly not offered, but they live entirely ignorant of all these. Concerning these, therefore, it cannot be said that they reject offered grace, since it is by no means offered. But shall we think the mercy of God to be so great, or the power of the merit of Christ so great, that they are immediately and extraordinarily converted and saved? All theologians hold the negative. Just as, therefore, neither the mercy of God, nor the universal will, redemption, calling, and promise are weakened, although adult gentiles, to whom however the means of salvation have never been brought, are damned. So concerning infants, why should we not judge the same? And, just as they are rightly said to be damned on account of unbelief, although they reject no means, since they were not offered, so also infants will be able to be justly damned on account of their original unbelief.

XIV. 4. They wish the lack of a promise, especially a federal one, to be considered. Concerning the infants of the faithful, there indeed exists a clear promise, Is. 49. v. 25: I will save your children. And Gen. 17. v. 7: I will be your God, and of your seed after you. But concerning infidels, no such thing is read anywhere, but rather God threatens, Ex. 20. v. 5, that He will visit the iniquity of the parents upon the third and fourth generation. Since, therefore, He also punishes infants with the deprivation of the word and the Sacraments, on account of the preceding sins of the parents, hence it is evident that God ordinarily wills that all of them be damned and perish in their unbelief. For if He absolutely willed them to be saved, He would certainly grant the word and the Sacraments, since it is most easy for Him to raise up ministers and send them there. But whence do we prove that God saves them extraordinarily, when He is accustomed rather to work salvation through means and ordinarily? Nor can the cause of necessity be pretended from the part of the infidels; since God has denied to them all and entirely the ordinary means, and not just a few, and sometimes they are excluded from them. Which are certainly all manifest signs of divine wrath, on account of which those infidels with all their seed will perish eternally. For God has not entered into a covenant with them. Therefore they do not enjoy the federal promise, and therefore they cannot be saved, as believers and the children of believers are.

XV. 5. They inculcate the Apostolic distinction between the holy and the unclean, 1 Cor. 7:14, and between those who are within and those who are without, 1 Cor. 6:12, or between the children of the covenant and outsiders, Acts 3:25. For if the condition of all infants were equal, if all were equally saved, and if the promises of God equally pertained to anyone, how would that distinction stand? Therefore we argue thus: He who is without and entirely unclean, who is a stranger and not a child of the covenant, he cannot be saved equally with the holy and those who are within and the children of the covenant. But all the children of infidels are and are called such. Therefore they cannot be saved equally. For how does it happen that the children of infidels are not immediately admitted to Baptism? Certainly this ought to be done if the kingdom of God and eternal inheritance were equally promised to them. From which in turn it can be inferred. Those to whom eternal life is thought to be so promised that they are saved extraordinarily, if they cannot be made capable of the ordinary means, they are to be admitted immediately to Baptism as the first means of salvation. But the infants of infidels, because they are born outside the Church, are not immediately admitted to Baptism. Therefore eternal salvation is not so promised to them that they are saved immediately.

XVI. 6. They propose two theological hypotheses, one from the mercy, the other from the omniscience of God. God is supremely merciful and at the same time also omniscient. If therefore He had foreseen that the infants of infidels, when they had grown up, would perform repentance, He would certainly have preserved them to that time, because He is supremely merciful. But because He allows them to perish in infancy, from this they conclude that He foresaw their future impenitence, because He is omniscient; and thus condemned them, because He is just. For whoever are always going to remain impenitent and disobedient are justly condemned. But the infants of the faithful are always going to remain impenitent and disobedient, just like their parents. For if the contrary were going to happen, God would have foreseen this, and thus would have preserved them in life out of His mercy. Therefore, they are justly condemned even in infancy. They declare this with a comparison taken from the whelps of wolves. For just as these, even at a young age, before they can grow up and ravage sheepfolds, are accustomed to be killed, because we know that rapacity is implanted in them by nature, which they would certainly exercise if they grew up: So God can justly summon and condemn the children of unbelievers, since He knows and sees that the same unbelief and obstinacy is ingrained in them, which they would also never lay aside, even if they reached a late age.

XVII. 7. They bring forward some testimonies from the Fathers, especially from Augustine. For he writes in Book 1 of Faith to Peter, chapter 27: Hold most firmly, and doubt in no way, that not only men already using reason, but also little ones, who either begin to live in their mothers' wombs and die there, or when they pass from this world born of their mothers without the Sacrament of holy Baptism (which is given in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit), are to be punished with the everlasting torment of eternal fire. Because, even if they had no sin of their own action, they nevertheless drew the condemnation of original sin by carnal conception and birth. These things are there in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 92. The mildest punishment indeed will be for all those who, besides original sin, which they drew, have added nothing further. He says the same in the book On Nature and Grace, chapter 9. Indeed, Augustine thought that unbaptized infants of the Gentiles were so far from being saved that he even shut off salvation from unbaptized children.

XVIII. And thus far various arguments we have reviewed those things which on one side assert the salvation, and on the other the damnation of the infants of pagans, and thus render this question doubtful on every side, and sufficiently intricate. Wherefore we think that τὸ ἐπέχειν [suspension of judgment] is safest here, and with Augustine we say: It is not clear. The great Apostle of the Gentiles, Saint Paul, whom we deservedly imitate, did the same. He was caught up into the third heaven, and instructed in the most accurate knowledge of theological matters, yet he wished to determine nothing concerning the death or salvation of those born outside the Church, but humbly said 1 Cor. 12. v. 13. τί γάρ μοι τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν; What have I to do to judge them that are without? For them that are without God judgeth. Rom. 11. when he had entered into the consideration of the works and judgments of God, seeing that he could not sufficiently perceive that depth, v. 33. he exclaims: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways! For which reason we also commit the judgment concerning the infants of infidels solely to God. We confess that He can save them, since He is omnipotent. Who shall take away from τῷ πατρὶ τῶν ὀικτιρμῶν [the Father of mercies] the right of doing good? Moreover, we know from the Scriptures that they are not ordinarily saved, since they are destitute of the usual means. But whether God wishes to convert them extraordinarily and immediately, it is nowhere written nor revealed to us, nor can we demonstrate it either a priori or a posteriori. Let us not therefore desire to have known what God has willed to be secret, as Ambrose warns in his book De Vocat. gent. c. 8. For however the matter may stand, nothing is taken away from our salvation, nor from God's justice or mercy. We can be saved, however much they may be damned. God remains just and merciful even if He saves the infants of the faithful, and casts those of the infidels into hell. For He does not lose the severity of judgment in the goodness of mercy, nor in judging with severity does He lose the goodness of mercy, as Augustine skillfully writes on Psalm 100. For God is good and God is just: He can save without good merits, because He is good: He cannot condemn without evil merits, because He is just, as the same author writes in book 1 against Julian, chapter 8.

XIX. To speak briefly, therefore: Either the question is asked, what do the infants of pagans deserve on account of sin? Or what their future lot will be in the other life? Regarding the former, we affirm that they are deserving, on account of the corruption of nature, of both eternal exile from heaven and destruction in hell, because nothing unclean is admitted into the kingdom of heaven, Apoc. 21, v. 25. Regarding the latter, we leave them to the judgment of God. This is, however, either ordinary and universal, the sum of which is John 3, last verse: He who is unbelieving toward the Son of God shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him; by which agreement we cannot promise salvation to the infants of pagans; or it is extraordinary and particular, the reason for which is unknown to us, which not having been revealed, we therefore presume to affirm nothing here absolutely and rashly.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO II. An liberi infidelium extra Ecclesiam nati damnentur?

I. Problema hoc in vtramque partem disceptatur, adeò, vt multi hæreant, & quid statuendum sit, vix inueniant. Nonnulli censent, quòd licet infantes infidelium peccato originali sint infecti, & per naturam rei damnationis æternæ, attamen ob summam Iehovæ φιλανθρωπίαν fide donentur extraordinarè, atque sic æternùm saluentur. Quæ ipsorum sententia sequentibus potissimum argumentis nititur.

II. Vrgent infinitam Dei misericordiam erga genus humanum. Circa hoc enim illam potius, quam justitiam ostendere voluit, ideoque punire opus alienum & peregrinum vocatur. Esa. 28. v. 13. Quicunque autem summè est misericors: ille, si præsertim facilè possit, non sinit in miseria perire eum qui seipsum inde liberare nequit, & non tàm propria, quàm aliorum culpâ in miseriam istam deuenit. Natura enim misericordiæ est, vt cor miseriâ commoueatur. Vbi verò cordis est commotio; ibi statim ad auxiliandum oritur inclinatio: quam non potest non sequi ipsum actuale auxilium, si summa omnium rerum potestas adfuerit.

III. 2. Proponunt dicta, de vniuersali voluntate Dei loquentia, qualia sunt. 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. Ezech. 33. v. 11. Ioh. 3. v. 16. 17. & præsertim istud Rom. 11. vers. 32. Conclusit omnia, vt omnium misereatur, & Matt. 18. v. 14. Non est voluntas ante Patrem vestrum, qui in cælis est, vt pereat vnus de pusillis istis. Hęc ipsa autem voluntas æterni Patris de salute omnium, & sic infantum quoque non simutata est, sed maximè feria: Quapropter istud etiam quod vult, certo in actum deducit, aut per certa media ut in adultis, aut immediatè in ijs qui mediorum per ætatem capaces non sunt, vt infantes. Etenim, quicunque aliquid feriò vult, ille, quod vult, exequitur semper, nisi resistatur ipsi. Deus igitur, cùm feriò infantes liberatos velit à reatu peccati, vt æternùm saluos, vtique & liberabit eos, quoniam vt adulti, non reluctantur. Si princeps quispiam multis verbis gloriaretur, se liberaturum subditos suos, qui fortè in Turcia captiui detinentur, & tamen in arce maneret otiosus, nec omnibus modis viribusque liberationem procuraret, tum ille simulasse, & subditis illusisse meritò putabitur: pari modo vniuersalis eaque seria voluntas Dei contra Calvinianos defendi vix poterit, si statuamus, ipsum infantes quidem saluare velle, nihil tamen suscipere, quod ad salutem ipsorum actu ipso promovendam, faciat.

IV. 3. Producunt ad idem evincendum dicta de vniuersali Christi merito & redemtione, qualia sunt. Ioh: 1. 29. c. 3. 16, 17. c. 4. 43. c. 6. 51. c. 12. 47. Rom. 5. vers. 18. 19. 1. Cor. 15 22. 2. Cor. 5. 14. 15. 1. Ioh. 2. 2. ex quibus ita inferunt: Si Christus omnes redemit, omnibusque vitam æternam verè acquisi vit, tum si non inanis & frustranea debet esse redemtio, necessum est, vt bonum acquisitum offeratur & conferatur omnibus non resistentibus, quales sunt infantes. Annon enim pro lusu haberetur, si quis prolixè jactitaret, se omnes captiuos redemisse, omnibusque libertatem veram conciliaffe, & tamen non omnibus media è carcere exeundi suppeditaret, aut non immediatè, qui mediorum capaces non sunt, educeret & liberaret? Pari modo aut meritum Christi non erit vniuersale, aut non verum serúmque, nisi infantibus vel salutis media offerat, vel si media dare nolit, salutem actu ipso conferat.

V. 4. Contra Calvinianos masculè pugnamus pro vniuersalitate vocationis & sufficientia gratiæ, docentes, Deum ad salutem omnes verè & realiter vocare, actuque sufficientem gratiam ad consequendam salutem elargiri: verùm, nisi infantes omnes salvari dicamus, quomodo istud defendi possit, vix apparet. Etenim infantes infidelium non vocari possunt per verbum, quia istud audire nequeunt: non vocantur per Baptismum, quia hic duntaxat fidelium liberis confertur. Praeter hos autem vocationis mediatae modos tertius nullus dari potest. Ergo dicendum infantes istos vel omninò non vocari, quod Calvinisticum; aut immediatè vocari & sic salvari, quoniam vocanti Deo non resistunt. Vocatio enim nihil est aliud, quàm gratiae oblatio. Cuicunque autem gratia offertur, illi, si non resistat, etiam confertur, vti docent nostri Theologi. Infantes autem non resistunt, nec resistere possunt, quia ratione nondum vtuntur. Quare si vocantur; si illis gratia offertur, certò salvabuntur. Atqui eos vocari, & sufficientem gratiam offerri, defendendum est contra Calvinianos. Sequi ergò videtur necessariò, quòd saluentur. Et certè si nullam immediatam Dei circa infantes actionem agnoscamus, ostendi vix poterit, quomodo sufficientem gratiam habeant Ordinarijs enim medijs omninò sunt priuati. Quocirca si nec Deus immediatè offerat, & in infantibus extraordinariè operetur, adminiculis omnibus salutem consequendi destituentur. Hoccine autem est sufficientem gratiam, & efficiens ad salutem auxilium habere.

VI. 5. Considerant solicitantem Dei curam, quoad salutem adultorum. Proponit ijs verbum, mittit ministros suos, offert Sacramenta, expandit vlnas, expectat totâ die, vocat, clamat, ostendit prodigia, conijcit in calamitates, hortatur, minatur, pollicetur, omniaque summo tentat studio, quae ad ipsorum conversionem videntur facere. Numà putabimus Deum ita horum curam habere, vt infantum planè obliviscatur, qui tamen actualiter nec peccant nec resistunt? Num existimabimus, omnem gratiam in adultos effundere, & miseros infantes planè negligere? Cū igitur hoc absurdum & beneficę voluntati Dei contrarium, necesse est, vt dicamus, eum sicut in adultis mediatè, sic in infantibus immediatè operari, ideoque illos cum non reluctentur, actu ipso saluare.

VII. 6. Vrgent vniversalitatem promissionum, quippè quæ omnibus omninò, non tantùm in Ecclesia, sed etiam extra Ecclesiam natis factæ legūtur, præsertim Act 2. v. 39. Vobis, habet text⁹, facta est promissio & filijs vestris, & omnibus, qui longe sunt, quoscunq; advocaverit Dominus. Sicut igitur infantes fidelium putātur saluari, vi promissionum divinarum ita & infideliū liberi saluabuntur, cū, dicente Petro ipsi quoq; licet adhuc lōge sint, facta fuerit pmissio.

IIX. 7. Vlteriùs dicunt, quoad paganos etiam infantes omnia reperiri fundamenta, quæ pro salute Christianorum sunt allata. Ex parte Dei datur & potestas & voluntas, quæ constat tūm ex promissionibus salutis tùm ex vocatione vniuersali. Ex parte Infantum, datur mera simplexq́; priuatio, sine vllo contemtu. Ex parte Ecclesiæ datur ardens precatio pro salute omnium, qui non contumaciter resistunt. Vnum duntaxat deest, quod nati non sint in Ecclesia, quod ipsum tamen saluti ipsorum nil videtur officere, sicuti nec contrarium alijs prodesse. Etenim vbicunque aliquis nascatur, tamen est filius iræ, & eget gratiā Dei regenerantis. Hæretici sunt in Ecclesia; nil tamen hoc ipsos juvat: Imò & fideliū liberi extra ecclesiam videntur esse, quatenus illi per Baptismum nondum sunt inserti & tamen De⁹ illorū miseretur. Externa igitur loci circūstantia salutē infantum infideliū non impediet.

IX. 8. Denique tradunt Theologi nullum peccatum, sed solam incredulitatem damnare formaliter, quam definiūt per contemtum oblatæ gratiæ, & neglectam medioru usurpationem. Nonn. est mera negatio fidei, sed simul contrarium vitjum;nempe contemtus oblati, cum fidei opponatur non privative tantum sed etiam contrarie, atque sic presupponat gratiae & meriti oblationem,deinde ponat oblati contemtum & neglectionem. Talis autem incredulitas non cadit in infantes infidelium. Ergo nec damnari poterunt. Minorem probant, quia si immediate Deus gratiam iis non offerat, tum nullo modo offertur, cum & Baptismo, & verbi auditu careant. Si autem nil offeratur quomodo aliquod oblatum bonum contemnere possunt? Imo quomodo contemtus cadet in eos, qui nil intelligunt, nec ratione vti queunt? Absente igitur & negata damnationis causa, quomodo affirmari poterit damnatio?

X. Et haec sunt argumenta pro communi salute infantium, etiam ex paganis parentibus natorum, non certe levia, sed valde ardua & ponderosa, vt vnumquemque satis exercere possint: placet nunc proponere rationes negantium, liberofque infidelium pro damnatis habentium.

XI. 1. Putant hanc esse mentem Augustanae Confessionis, quando articulo secundo inquit, Peccatum damnare & mortem afferre his, qui non renascuntur per Baptismum & Spiritum sanctum, Apologia etiam art. 9. m. p. 156. clare affirmat: quod promissio salutis pertineat quidem ad parvulos, sed non ad illos, qui sunt extra Ecclesiam Christi, vbi nec verbum, nec Sacramenta sunt, &c. Hinc inferunt: Ad quos non pertinet promissio salutis, ij non saluantur. Atqui dicente Apologia, promissio salutis non pertinet ad natos extra Ecclesiam Ergo non saluantur

XII. 2. Vrgent Theologicum istud στοιχεῖον: Extra Ecclesiam non est salus. Non Pater in Coelis, cui non Ecclesia mater. Hinc August. quaest. 65. ad Orosium scribit: Sicut in arca Noah nemo, nisi qui in ea erat, a diluuio liberabatur: Ita nullus, nisi Eccl. membrum fuerit, saluabitur. Principium autē istud hactenus per tot secula in Scholis Theologicis decantatum, omninò erit negandum, si infantum infidelium salus certò statuatur.

XIII. 3. Proponunt exempla adultorum extra Ecclesiam. Multi enim sunt, quibus verbum Dei & Sacramenta planè non offeruntur, sed horum omnium prorsus ignari viuunt. De his igitur dici nequit, quòd rejiciant oblatam gratiam, cum nequaquam offeratur. Num verò putabimus misericordiam Dei tantam esse, aut tantam vim meriti Christi, vt illi ἀμέσως & extraordinariè convertantur & saluentur? Negatiuam tenent omnes Theologi. Sicut ergò nec misericordia Dei, nec vniuersalis voluntas, redemtio, vocatio & promissio labefactantur, licèt adulti gentiles, quibus tamen media salutis nunquam sunt collata, damnentur. Ita de infantibus, cur non idem censeamus? Et, velut ij ob incredulitatem damnari rectè dicuntur, quamuis media nulla, cùm oblata non sint, rejiciant, sicetiam infantes justè ob incredulitatem suam originalem damnari poterunt.

XIV. 4. Considerari volunt defectum promissionis, præsertim fœderalis. De infantibus fidelium quidem clara extat promissio Es. 49. v. 25. Filios tuos saluabo. Et Gen 17. v. 7. Ero Deus tuus, & seminis tui post te. De infidelibus autē tale quid nullibi legitur, sed Deus potius comminatur, Ex. 20. v. 5 se visiturum iniquitatē parentū in tertiam & quartam generationē. Cùm igitur & infantes puniat priuatione verbi & Sacramentorum, ob præcedentia parentū delicta, hinc patet, Deum ordinariè velle, omnes eos damnari & in incredulitate sua perire. Nā si saluatos omnino vellet, verbū vtiq; & Sacramēta cōcederet, cùm facilimū ipsi sit ministros excitare, eóque mittere. Vnde verò probamus, Deum extraordinariè eos saluare, cū potiùs soleat per media & ordinariè salutē operari? Neq; necessitatis caůs prętēdi potest ex parte infidelium; cùm Deus ipsis omnibus & omninò negauerit media ordinaria, neque pauci duntaxat, & quandoque ab ijs excludantur. Quæ certè omnia sunt manifesta indicia irę diuinæ, ob quã infidelibus istis cum omni semine æternùm erit pereundum. Non enim cum ijs foedus inijt Deus. Ergo nec gaudent promissione foederali, ideoq; nec saluari possunt, vti fideles, fideliumq; liberi.

XV. 5. Inculcant discrimen Apostolicum inter sanctos & immundos. 1. Cor. 7. v. 14. & inter eos, qui intus sunt, & qui foris. 1. Cor. 6. v. 12. vel inter filios pacti, & exteros, Act. 3. v 25. Etenim, si omnium infantum par esset ratio, si omnes æquè saluarentur, Deíq; promissiones pariter attinerent quosuis, quomodo consisteret discrimen illud? Proinde ita argumentamur: Qui foris est & omninò immundus, qui extraneus est, nec filius pacti, ille cum sanctis & qui intus sunt, cumque filijs pacti, pariter saluari nequit. At qui tales sunt & dicuntur omnes infidelium liberi. Ergo pariter saluari nequeunt. Quî enim fit, quod infidelium liberi ad Baptismum immediatè non admittantur? Certè fieri hoc deberet, si regnum Dei & hereditas æterna ijs pariter promissa foret. Ex quo vicissim inferri potest. Quibus vita æterna sic promissa putatur, vt saluentur extraordinariè, si mediorum ordinariorum capaces fieri nequeant, ij ad Baptismum tanquam primum salutis medium, sunt admittendi immediatè. Infantes autem infidelium, quia extra Ecclesiam nati sunt, immediatè non admittuntur ad Baptismum. Ergò nec salus æterna iis sic promissa est, vt saluentur immediatè.

XVI. 6. Duas hypotheses Theologicas proponunt, alteram à misericordia, alteram ab omniscentia Dei. Summè misericors, & simul etiam omniscius est Deus. Si igitur præuidisset infantes infidelium, cùm adoleuerint, pœnitentiam acturos, vtiq; conseruasset ad id tempus, quia summè misericors est. Quia verò in infantia perire sinit, hinc colligunt, illum futuram eorum impoenitentiam præuidisse, quia omnisciùs; & sic damnasse, quia iustus est. Quicunque enim semper mansuri sunt impoenitentes & immorigesi, iustè damnantur. Ast infantes fidelium semper mansuri sunt impoenitentes & immorigesi, sicut ipsorum parentes. Si enim contrarium fuisset euenturum, Deus hoc præuidisset, & sic in vita ob misericordiam suam conseruasset. E. in infantia etiam iustè damnantur. Declarant hoc similitudine, à luporum catulis desumta. Sicut enim hi primâ etiam ætate, antequàm adolescant, & ouilia deuastare queant, necari solent, propterea quòd sciamus, rapacitatem naturâ ijs esse inditam, quàm certò exercerent, si adolescerent: Ita Deus iustè potest euocare & damnare infidelium liberos, quoniam scit & videt, eandem ijs incredulitatem & pertinaciam esse ingeneratam, quam quoque deponerent nunquam, licèt ad seram ætatem peruenirent.

XVII. 7. Ex Patribus nonnulla testimonia afferunt, præsertim ex Augusti, Hic enim l. 1. de Fide ad Petr. c. 27. scribit: Firmissimè tene, & nullatenus dubites, non solum homines iam ratione vtentes, verùm etiam paruulos, qui siue in vteris matrum viuere incipiunt, & ibi moriuntur, siue cùm de matribus nati sine Sacramento sancti Baptismatis (quod datur in nomine Patris & Filij, & Spir. S.) de hoc seculo transeunt, ignis æterni sempiterno supplicio puniendos. Quia, etsi propria actionis peccatum nullum habuerunt, originalis tamen peccati damnationem carnali conceptione & natiuitate traxerunt. Hæc ibi in Enchir. ad Laur c. 92. Mitissima sanè pœna erit omnium eorum, qui præter peccatum originale, quod traxerunt nullum insuper addiderunt. Idem dicit l. de Natura & grat. c. 9. Imò August. infantes non baptizatos gentilium adeo non saluari existimauit, vt etiam non baptizatis liberis salutem præcluserit.

XIIX. Atque hactenus varia argumenta reconrecensuimus, quæ ex vna parte salutem, ex altera damnationem infantum paganorum adstruunt, adeoque quæstionem hanc vndiquaque dubiam, & satis intricatam reddunt. Quocirca existimamus τὸ ἐπέχειν hic esse tutissimũ, & cum Augustino dicimus. Non liquet. Idem fecit magnus ille gentium Apostolus Diuus Paulus, quem nos meritò imitamur. Raptus hic fuit in tertium cœlum, rerumque Theologicarum accuratissimâ scientia instructus, nihil tamen vel de morte vel salute extra Ecclesiam natorum determinare voluit, sed humiliter dixit 1. Cor. 12. v. 13. τί γάρ μοι τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν; Quid mihi de ijs, qui foris sunt, iudicare? Nam eos, qui foris sunt Deus iudicat. Rom. 11. cùm ingressus esset considerationem operum & iudiciorum divinorum, videns nõ satis se percipere posse istam profunditatem v. 33. exclamat: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ & scientiæ Dei! Quàm incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia eius, & quàm impervestigabiles viæ eius! Quâ de causa & nos judicium de infantibus infidelium Deo vnicè committimus, Fatemur hunc posse eos salvare, cùm omnipotens sit. Quis τῷ πατρὶ τῶν ὀικτιρμῶν benefaciendi jus eripiet? Ex Scripturis insuper scimus, ordinarie illos non salvari, cùm vsitatis medijs destituantur. Extraordinariè autem & immediatè an Deus illos velit conuertere, nullibi scriptum neque nobis reuelatum est, neque vel à priori, vel à posteriori demonstrare possumus. Non igitur appetamus habere cognitum, quod Deus voluit esse secretum, monente Ambrosio lib. de Vocat. gent. c. 8. Quomodocunq́; enim se res habeat, nec nostræ saluti, nec Dei iustitiæ aut misericordiæ aliquid decedit. Salvari nos possumus, quantum vis illi damnentur. Iustus manet Deus & misericors etiã si fidelium infantes saluet, infidelium in gehennam detrudat. Nec enim in bonitate misericordiæ perdit iudij severitatem, nec in iudicando cum severitate, amittit misericordiæ bonitatem, quemadmodum scitè scribit Augustin Psalm 100. Nam bonus est Deus & justus est Deus: potest sine bonis meritis salvare, quia bonus est: Non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est, vti scribit idem l. 1. contra Iul. c. 8.

XIX. Summatim igitur dicendo: Aut quæritur, quid infantes paganorum ob peccatum mereantur? Aut quæ ipsorum sors futura sit in altera vita? Quoad prius, adfirmamus, eos esse meritos ob vitium naturę sempiternum tum exilium à cœlo, tum exitium in inferno, quia nihil immundum intromittitur in regnum cœlorum, Apoc. 21. v. 25. Quoad posterius Dei iudicio illos relinquimus. Est autem hoc, vel ordinarium & vniuersale cuius summa Ioh. 3. vers. vlt. Qui incredulus est Filio Dei, non videbit vitam sed ira Dei manet super eum; quo pacto salutem infantibus paganorum promittere non possumus; vel extraordinarium & particulare, cuius ratio nobis incognita est, qua non reuelata, ideoque nihil hîc absolutè temereque adfirmare præsumimus.


### Question III. If unbaptized infants are damned, are they to suffer only the punishment of loss and not also of sense?

QUESTION III. If unbaptized infants are damned, are they to suffer only the punishment of loss and not also of sense?

I. The Scholastics, and especially Durandus, book 3, dist. 22, question 4, whom even modern Jesuits follow, distinguish the whole edifice of hell, fabricated and devised by them, into four cells or stories. The first, according to them, is of the damned, and is called hell, in which there is both perpetual exile and destruction: they call the former the punishment of loss, which is the deprivation of blessedness, and the latter the punishment of sense, because it is the suffering of infernal torments. The second is of unbaptized infants, although born in the Church, which for that reason they call the limbo of children, where on account of original sin there is perpetual punishment of loss, but not of sense, that is, where infants are indeed excluded from the joys of eternal life, yet feel no pain. The third is of those to be purged, called for that reason purgatory, in which there is punishment of both loss and sense, but only temporal who died before the coming of Christ, which they call the limbo of the Fathers, in which there was punishment of loss only, and that indeed not perpetual, but temporal. From this, however, we prove by the following arguments that their opinion, especially regarding the second chamber and the punishment of unbaptized infants, is false and improbable.

II. 1. Nothing is to be rashly asserted outside of Scripture. But it is entirely ignorant of such dining rooms and chambers in hell. Therefore, they are mere figments of the Scholastics. This indeed we know, that there are two receptacles for souls, one of glory, the other of misery; the former we call heaven, the latter hell. For there are two dwellings, one in eternal fire, the other in the eternal kingdom. Aug. de ver. Apo. Ser. 18. But we have no third or fourth place expressed besides. Therefore, we maintain that the souls of infants, if they are not saved and are not received into heaven, are infallibly damned and cast into hell, and not into some peculiar limbo. For there is no middle place for anyone, so that he who is not with Christ is with the devil, writes Augustine: lib. 1 de remiss. peccat. cap. 28.

III. 2. The sin of unbaptized infants is either remitted and not imputed, or it is not remitted and is imputed. If the former, they will not be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, but will be blessed, Psalm 32 v. 1. If the latter, they will certainly be damned and cast into hell because they are children of wrath, Eph. 2 v. 3, and are subject to the curse of the law, Deut. 27 v. 26, Galat. 3 v. 10, which includes eternal damnation.

IV. 3. Rev. 20. v. 15: Whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire. Unbaptized infants, according to the Papists, are not written in the book of life, because they are not saved. Therefore they will be cast into the lake of fire: Wherefore they will sustain the punishment of loss and of sense, and consequently, the limbo of children is nothing.

V. 4. Rom. 8. v. 1. There is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, whence we infer from the contrary sense: Those who are not in Christ are certainly condemned. But unbaptized infants, according to the Papists, are not in Christ, nor in his body the Church; because they deny that they are immediately gifted with faith. Therefore they will certainly be condemned, and thus they will also suffer the punishment of sense:

VI. 5. These unbaptized infants either believe, or they do not believe. If they believe, they will be saved, John 3. v. 18 and 36. If they do not believe, they will be condemned, because he who has not believed will be condemned, Mark 16, verse 16. He who does not believe is already judged, he will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. v. last: where expressly to all unbelievers not only the punishment of loss, but also of sense is denounced.

VII. That distinction between the punishment of loss and of sense is inept, nay, it is null. For either infants are devoid of all sense, or they are possessed of it: If the former, they will not be properly punished, because no one sustains punishment unless he feels the punishment. If the latter, it will not be merely a punishment of loss, but also of sense: Others gather it thus. Infants either know themselves to be excluded from God, or they do not know. If they know, they cannot but grieve and thus they will also sustain the punishment of sense. If they do not know, this punishment will be nothing, because those who are knowing, not those who are ignorant, are properly punished.

IIX. 7. These infants will either be completely idle in their limbo, and as it were perpetually oppressed by sleep, or they will do and feel something. The former is inconvenient and absurd. Therefore they will do or feel something: Wherefore they will either delight and rejoice, or they will suffer and grieve. They cannot rejoice, because they are excluded from heaven, and the wrath of God remains upon them. Therefore they will grieve. Not therefore only the punishment of loss, but of sense also they will sustain. And these two latter arguments so moved Bell. vol. 6. de A. G. c. 6. that he confesses, unbaptized infants will suffer pain, not indeed the external pain of fire, but the internal pain of the mind, although most mild. But there is no need to refute this opinion with new reasons, since the arguments enumerated thus far are sufficiently effective for attacking it as well. We add only, by way of a finishing touch, the testimony of Augustine, which is read in book 1 de orig. anim. ch. 9. Let no one promise to unbaptized infants any place of rest or happiness whatsoever and wheresoever between damnation and the kingdom of heaven, as if it were a middle place.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO III. Si non baptizati infantes damnantur, an duntaxat damni & non vnà sensus pœnam sint perpessuri?

I. Scholastici & præsertim Durandus l. 3. dist. 22. quæst. 4. quem sequuntur etiam hodierni IesuWitæ totum inferni ædificium, ab ipsis fabricatum & excogitatum, in quatuor siue cellas, siue contignationes distinguunt. Prima secundum istos damnatorum est, & infernus dicitur, in quo perpetuum sit & exilium & exitium: istud pœnam damni, quopiam priuatio est beatitudinis, hoc pœnam sensus, quia perpessio est tormentorum infernalium, appellant. Secunda est infantum non baptizatorum, licèt in Ecclesia natorum, quam propterea vocant limbum puerorum, vbi propter peccatum originale sit perpetua pœna damni, sed non sensus, hoc est, vbi infantes exclusi quidem sint à gaudiis vitæ æternæ, nullum tamen dolorem persentiscant. Tertia purgandorum est, dicta ob id purgatorium, in quo & damni & sensus pœna, sed duntaxat temporalis. Et vltima Patrum fuit in V. T. ante adventum Christi mortuorum, quam limbum Patrum vocant, in quo si pœna damni duntaxat, & ea quidem non perpetua, sed temporalis. Hinc verò ipsorum opinionem, præsertim quoad cellam alteram, pœnamque non baptizatorum infantum falsam esse & improbabilem sequentibus probamus argumentis.

II. 1. Extra Scripturam temerè nihil est affirmandum. Illa autem huiusmodi triclinia & cameras in inferno distinctas omninò ignorat. Mera igitur figmenta sunt Scholasticorum. Hoc quidem scimus, quod duo sint animarum receptacula, alterum gloriæ, alterum miseriæ, illud cœlum, hoc infernum dicimus. Duæ quippe habitationes sunt, vna in igne æterno, alia in regno æterno. Aug. de ver. Apo. Ser. 18. Tertium verò, vel quartum præterea locum nullam habemus expressum. Proinde statuimus animas infantum, si non saluantur, nec in cœlum recipiuntur, infallibiliter damnari & in infernum, non autem peculiarem quendam limbum detrudi, Non enim vlli vllus est locus medius, vt sit nisi cum diabolo, qui non est cum Christo. scribit August: l. 1 de remiss. peccat. c. 28.

III. 2. Peccatum infantum non baptizatorum aut remittitur, & non imputatur; aut non remittitur & imputatur. Si illud, non excludentur è regno cœlorum, sed beati erunt, Psal. 32 v. 1. Si hoc, certò damnabuntur, & in infernum conjicientur quia sunt filii iræ, Eph. 2. v. 3. & subiacent maledictioni legis Deut. 27 vers 6. Galat. 3. v. 10. quæ includit damnationem æternam.

IV. 3. Apoc. 20. v. 15: Qui non inuentus est in libro vitæ scriptus, missus est in stagnum ignis. Infantes non baptizati iuxta Pontificios non sunt scripti in libro vitæ, quia non saluantur. Ergo mittentur in stagnum ignis: Quare sustinebunt pœnam damni & sensus, & per consequens, limbus puerorum nullus est.

V. 4. Rom. 8. v. 1. Nihil est damnationis his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, vnde inferimus à contrario sensu; Eos, qui non sunt in Christo certò damnari. Infantes autem non baptizati iuxta Pontificios non sunt in Christo, nec eius corpore Ecclesiâ; quia negant eos immediatè donari fide. Ergò certò damnabuntur, & sic pœnam sensus quoq; perpetientur:

VI. 5. Infantes isti non baptizati, aut credunt; aut non credunt. Si credunt saluabuntur, Ioh. 3. v. 18: & 36. Si non credunt, damnabuntur, quia qui non crediderit, condemnabitur, Marc. 16, vers. 16. Qui non credit, iam iudicatus est, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. v. ult: vbi expresse incredulis omnibus non modò pœna damni, sed sensus etiam denunciatur.

VII. Distinctio ista inter pœnam damni & sensus inepta, imò nulla est. Aut enim infantes sensus omnis sunt expertes, aut eius sunt compotes: Si illud, propriè non punientur, quia pœnam non sustinet, nisi qui pœnam sentit. Si hoc, non erit merà damni pœna, sed vnà sensus: Alij sic colligunt. Infantes aut sciunt se exclusos à Deo, aut nesciunt. Si sciunt, non possunt non dolere &, sic quoque pœnam sensus sustinebunt. Si nesciunt, pœna hæc nulla erit, quia scientes, non ignorantes propriè puniuntur.

IIX. 7. Infantes isti aut planè otiosi erunt in suo limbo, & quasi perpetim somno oppressi, aut aliquid agent sentientque. Illud inconueniens & absurdum. Ergò aliquid agent vel sentient: Quare vel delitiabuntur, & gaudebunt, vel patiētur & dolebunt. Gaudere nequeunt, quia sunt exclusi è coelo, & ira Dei manet super eos. Ergò dolebunt. Non igitur solùm damni, sed sensus quoque poenam sustinebunt. Et haec duo posteriora argumenta ita mouerunt Bell. vel. 6. de A. G. c. 6. fateatur, paruulos non baptizatos passuros esse dolorem, non quidem externum ignis, sed internum animi, quamuis mitissimum. Verùm non opus est hanc sententiam nouis refutare rationibus, cùm argumenta hactenus enumerata, ad eam quoque impugnadam satis sint efficacia. Addimus tantùm colophonis loco Augustini testimonium, quod legitur l. 1. de orig. anim. ca. 9. Paruulis non baptizatis nemo promittat quietis aut felicitatis cuuflibet atque vbilibet inter damnationem regnumẽ, coelorum quasi medium locum.


### To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 9 Disputation VIII. On the Remission and Removal of Original Sin


### Proem I

Presiding: Balth. Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Master Iohan. Georg Brunner of Regensburg.

Προόιμιον.

I. Augustine rightly teaches in his book de peccat. orig. ch. 24, that the Christian faith consists properly in the case of two men, by one of whom we were sold under sin, and by the other we are redeemed from sins. The Apostle makes mention of both men, Rom. 5, v. 19. As he says, by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also by the obedience of one many will be made righteous. He explains this more clearly in 1 Cor. 15, v. 21, 22. By a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead

to the studious. For as in Adam all die, and so in Christ shall all be made alive.

II. Thus far we have dealt sufficiently at length with the disobedience and vice of the first Adam, indicating what it was; how horribly it corrupted nature; and what great miseries and punishments it brought upon the whole human race: now we shall add a few things concerning the obedience and benefit of the second Adam, intending to show how we are purged from that stain, and what the condition of sin is after it has been forgiven in Baptism and through repentance.

III. However much this dissertation may seem to pertain properly to the state of grace and restoration, since a man reborn and having obtained forgiveness of sin is no longer a child of wrath, but has passed from darkness into light, from death into life: nevertheless, it is not inappropriately referred by our theologians to the topic of sin, since there is no full knowledge of it unless it is considered at the same time as it remains in the reborn, and it is taught what motions it excites there, in what way it lusts against the Spirit, and that it cannot be completely removed except through the total destruction of the body. For all these things contribute to a better understanding and a more forceful exaggeration of the corruption of nature, and render us more eager for the pursuit of mortification and a pious desire for dissolution.

IV. There are indeed four things in sin from which we must be delivered: 1. Guilt, 2. Dominion, 3. Sense, 4. Root. We are delivered from guilt through regeneration, from dominion through renewal; from sense through death; from the root, through glorification.
