Regarding the latter two, there is not so great a controversy: for although the Papists maintain that the soul must first be purged by flames after separation from the body, and is not immediately freed from sin: yet that question is neither primarily of this place, nor does it have difficulty. For the perpetual silence of Scripture, the sufficient merit of Christ, and the immediate passage of the souls of the faithful into heaven,

Apoc. 14. v. 13. Sap. 3. v. 1. That papal purgatory is not an Apostolic dogma, but a monastic fiction, they prove quite clearly.

V. But as concerns the first two members of liberation, many seek many things; we shall present the whole matter enclosed in a twofold problem: For with the orthodox we affirm that through Baptism, which is the washing of regeneration, Tit. 3. v. 5, and repentance, which is a turning back to God, we are indeed perfectly freed from the guilt of sin, but not from sin itself. For as long as you live, it is necessary that sin be in your members, at least that its kingdom be taken away, that it may not be done, which it commands, as Augustine writes in tract 42 on John. And although not only the guilt is removed, but we are furthermore renewed and thus the flesh is mortified, that renewal is nevertheless imperfect, and only begun: For it does not happen at once, but little by little: it is not a total liberation but a partial one, which has its own degrees; indeed, so that from day to day, we are to be renewed more and more as long as we live, 2. Cor. 4. v. 16: There is indeed no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8. v. 1; nevertheless, sin dwells perpetually in them, Rom. 7. v. 12, whose deeds they ought to mortify daily, Rom. 8. v. 13, until they are restored into the full liberty of eternal life, v. 21. And this is what our Theologians say briefly and clearly: The regenerate in this life are freed from punishment totally, from vice partially: The remission is perfect, but the renewal is imperfect. Augustine expressed this very thing most briefly, writing in book 2 against Julian: God heals the corrupted in the state of guilt, from infirmity little by little.

VI. But from this thesis of ours, two rather doubtful questions arise. 1. Whether after regeneration or the remission of guilt, sin properly so-called remains in the regenerate? Or which is the same thing, Whether concupiscence remaining after Baptism is truly sin, hostile and hateful to God? 2. Whether renewal, that other part of liberation, consists only in the removal of dominion, or the suppression of the flesh, or indeed furthermore in the partial destruction and annihilation of the sin itself? Regarding the former problem, the decision is straightforward and certain: regarding the latter, however, it is somewhat doubtful and uncertain; there, therefore, we shall dispute demonstratively, here topically: there we shall state an opinion, here we shall leave it in doubt, because it is better to doubt about hidden things than to litigate about uncertain ones, August. lib. 8 de Gen. ad lit. cap. 5. But to the matter.

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisner. SS. Th. D.

Resp. M. Iohan. Georgio Brunnero Ratisbonensi.

Προόιμιον.

I. REctè Augustin. docet in lib. de peccat. orig. c. 24. quòd in causa duorum hominum, quorum per vnum venundati sumus sub peccato, per alterum redimimur a peccatis, propriè fides Christiana consistat. Vtriusque hominis meminit Apostolus, Rom. 5. v. 19. Sicut inquit, per inobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita & per vnius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi. Clariùs hoc exponit. 1. Cor. 15. v. 21. 22. Per hominem mors, & per hominem resurrectio mor-

studiossis. Nam sicut in Adamo omnes moriuntur, & ita in Christo omnes viuificabuntur.

II. Hactenus autem de Adami primi inobedientia & vitio prolixè satis egimus, indicando quid fuerit; quàm horrendè naturam corruperit; & quantas miserias pœnasque super vniuersum genus humanum induxerit:nunc de Adami secundi obedientia & beneficio pauca subiungemus, ostensuri, quomodo ab ista labe purgemur, & quænam ratio sit peccati posteaquam in Baptismo, & per pœnitentiam remissum est.

III. Quantumuis autem hæc dissertatio ad statum gratiæ & restaurationis propriè spectare videatur, siquidem homo renatus & peccati veniam consecutus, non ampliùs iræ filius est, sed à tenebris in lucem,à morte in vitam transijt: attamen à Theologis nostris non incommodè ad locum de peccato refertur, cùm huius plena non sit cognitio, nisi consideretur simul, prout in renatis est reliquum, & doceatur, quos ibi motus excitet, quos modo contra Spiritum concupiscat, & non nisi per totalem corporis destructionem penitus tolli queat. Hæc enim omnia ad naturæ corruptionem rectius intelligendam, fortiusque exaggerandam faciunt & nos ad mortificationis studium, piumque dissolutionis desiderium alacriores reddunt.

IV. Quatuor verò sunt in peccato; à quibus liberari debemus; 1. Reatus, 2. Dominium. 3. Sensus. 4. Radix. A reatu liberamur per regenerationem, à dominio per renouationem; à sensu par mortem;à radice, per ti factionem. Quoad posteriora duo non adeò magna est controuersia: Licet enim pontificij statuant, animam post separationem à corpore flammis prius purgandam esse, nec à peccato protinus liberari: ea tamen quæstio nec huius loci primò est, nec difficultatē habet. Nam perpetuum Scripturæ silentium, sufficiens Christi meritum, & immediatus animarum fidelium transitus in cœlum,

Apoc. 14. v. 13. Sap. 3. v. 1. Papale purgatorium non esse dogma Apostolicum, sed figmentum monasticum, satis luculenter euincunt.

V. Quod autem priora duo liberationis membra concernit, multi multa quærunt, nos rem omnem gemino problemati inclusam exhibebimus: Cum orthodoxis enim adfirmamus, per Baptismum quod est lauacrum regenerationis, Tit. 3. v. 5. & pœnitentiam, quæ est reuersio ad Deum, à peccati quidem reatu nos perfectè liberari, sed non à peccato ipso. Quamdiu enim viuis, necesse est, peccatum esse in membris tuis, saltem illi regnum auferatur, non fiat, quod iubet, vt August. scribit tract 42. in Iohan. Et quamuis non tantùm reatus tollatur, sed insuper renouemur adeoque caro mortificetur, ista tamen renouatio imperfecta, & tantùm inchoata est: Non enim contingit statim, sed paulatim: non est liberatio ὁλικὴ sed μερικὴ, quæ suos gradus habet; ita quidem, vt de die in diem, magis magisque quamdiu viuimus renouandi simus, 2. Cor. 4. v. 16: Nihil quidem damnationis est his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom. 8. v. 1. peccatum tamen in ijs perpetuò habitat, Rom. 7. vers. 12. cuius facta quotidiè mortificare debent, Rom. 8. v. 13. donec in plenam libertatem vitæ æternæ restituantur. v. 21. Atque hoc est, quod nostri Theologi breuiter & διλικῶς dicunt: Renati in hac vita liberantur a supplicio ὁλικῶς, à vitio μερικῶς: Perfecta est remissio, sed imperfecta renouatio. Hoc ipsum breuissimè expressit Augustinus l. 2. contra Iulianum scribens: Deus, vitiatum sanat in reatis statum, ab infirmitate paulatim.

VI. Ex hac verò thesi nostra duo ζητήματα satis dubia oriuntur. 1. An post regenerationem vel remissionem culpæ, in renatis peccatum propriè dictum remaneat? Vel quod idem est, An concupiscentia post Baptismum residua vere peccatum sit, Deo inimicum & odiosum? 2. An renouatio altera illa liberationis pars in sola dominij sublatione, carnisue suppressione, an verò insuper in partiali ipsius fius peccati destructione & annihilatione consistat? Quoad prius problema, decisio est expedita & certa: quoad posterius verò nonnihil dubia & incerta; Ibi ergo disputabimus Apodicticè, hic Topicè: ibi sententiam dicemus, hic in dubio relinquemus, quia melius est dubitare de occultis, quam litigare de incertis, August. l. 8. de Gen. ad lit. c. 5. Sed ad rem.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and repentance is truly and properly sin?

Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and repentance is truly and properly sin?

I. The word concupiscence is ambiguous. For some is good, some is evil. The good is in turn either φυσικὴ or natural, or πνευματικὴ or spiritual. Natural concupiscence denotes either the δύναμιν of concupiscing or the appetitive faculty, or the ἐνέργειαν and the act itself. Neither concupiscence is a vice. For God created the former, the latter follows what was created, and is in itself indifferent, as the appetite for food, drink, sleep. Therefore, neither comes into question: Spiritual concupiscence is proper to the reborn, as when they cry out to the Lord with David, and desire Him; Psalm 42, verse 1, or when the Spirit lusts against the flesh, Gal. 5, v. 17. Furthermore, however, evil concupiscence, by which illicit things prohibited by the law of God are sought, is either actual or original. Actual is in turn either mortal, which is joined with consent, delight, and the pursuit of that thing to which the flesh stimulates us; or venial, which denotes depraved inclinations and the first motions of the mind soliciting toward vices, yet suppressed by the Spirit and not brought into the act itself. But original concupiscence is the very vice of nature, drawn from parents, the vicious root itself, and habitual corruption, [affecting] the intellect, the will, and most foully depraving all the remaining powers. And we understand this concupiscence and its first impulses and stimuli to be the matter in question. For both are found in the regenerate, both original vice and the titillations of the flesh bubbling up from it: it is asked concerning both, whether it is sin truly and properly so called? But concerning the remaining species of concupiscence, there is no controversy between us and the Papists.

II. Thus, however, the Fathers gathered in the Council of Trent set forth their mind regarding this problem in session 5. The holy Synod declares that the Catholic Church has never understood that concupiscence, which the Apostle sometimes calls sin, is called sin because it is truly and properly sin in the regenerate; but because it is from sin, and inclines to sin. If anyone, however, thinks the contrary, let him be anathema. The Jesuits defend this decree of the conventicle in every way, especially Bellarmine, book 5, on the loss of grace, who in chapter 7 writes thus: We assert that the corruption of nature or concupiscence, such as it remains after Baptism in the regenerate, is not original sin, not only because it is not imputed, but also because it cannot be imputed, since it is not sin in itself or by its own nature. And Gregory of Valencia, Vol. 2, Commentary on Thomas, disp. 6, question 12, point 1, § 5, Col. 755. It must be established, he says, by firm faith; that concupiscence, and indeed the remaining powers of the soul, as they are destitute of the gift of original justice in the regenerate, do not have the true nature of sin.

III. We, however, say that this opinion is contrary to the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles, and therefore we maintain that original sin, remaining in the regenerate, is sin truly and properly so called, or an evil of guilt, fighting against the divine law, although accidentally, on account of the merit of Christ, it is not imputed to the faithful, nor does it constitute them guilty, nor subject them to eternal death.

VI. But let it not be thought that this controversy is trivial, or an empty logomachy, about which it is free for anyone to have an opinion. Indeed, on this depends the glory of Christ, the doctrine concerning our justification through faith. For if it is shown that sin always clings to the reborn, it immediately follows of its own accord that the law is not perfectly fulfilled, and therefore that no one can be justified by works. Because the Papists notice this, they labor with such great effort and preparation to remove concupiscence from of sins: for which reason, if both the glory of Christ the Savior and our own salvation and righteousness are dear to us, we must not believe here, but by all means impugn, nay, utterly storm that Papal opinion. That this may be done, we shall produce: 1. Arguments from the Epistle to the Romans. 2. Reasons taken from other sayings and the analogy of faith. 3. Testimonies of the Fathers, and 4. we shall briefly examine the principal objections of the Romanists.

Latin:

An concupiscentia post Baptismum & poenitentiam in renatis reliqua; verè propriéque peccatum sit?

I. Concupiscentiæ vox est ambigua. Quædam enim bona, quædam mala est. Bona vicissim vel φυσικὴ seu naturalis, vel πνευματικὴ seu spiritualis. Concupiscentia naturalis, vel notat, δύναμιν concupiscendi siue facultatem appetentem, vel ἐνέργειαν & ipsum actum. Neutra concupiscentia in vitio est. Illam enim Deus concreauit, hæc concreatam sequitur, & per se indifferens est, vt appetitus cibis potus, somni Nulla igitur in quæstionem venit: Concupiscentia spiritualis est renatorum propria, vt quando cum Dauide ad Dominum clamant, eumque desiderant; Psalm. 42. vers: 1. vel quando Spiritus concupiscit aduersus carnem, Gal. 5. v. 17. Porrò autem concupiscentia mala quâ appetuntur illicita, & lege Dei prohibita, vel actualis est, vel originalis. Actualis vicissim aut mortalis, quæ coniuncta cum consensu, delectatione & prosecutione eius rei, ad quam caro nos exstimulat; aut venialis, quæ notat prauas inclinationes, primosque animi motus ad vitia solicitantes, per Spiritum tamen suppressos, neque in actum ipsum perductos. Concupiscentia verò originalis est ipsum naturæ vitium, ex parentibus tractum, ipsa radix vitiosa, & habitualis corruptio, intellectum, voluntatem, omnésque vires reliquas quàm fœdissimè deprauans. Et hanc concupiscentiam ejusœ; primos impetus & stimulos in quæstione posita intelligimus. Vtrúmque enim in renatis reperitur, & originale vitium, & hinc ebullientes carnis titillationes: de vtroque quæritur, An peccatum sit verè propriéque ita nuncupatum? De reliquis verò concupiscentiæ speciebus nulla inter nos & Pontificios est controuersia.

II. Sic autem Paterculi in Tridentino Concilio congregati mentem suam quoad problema istud exposuerunt sess. 5. Concupiscentiam illam, quam aliquando Apostolus peccatum vocat, sancta Synodus declarat, Ecclesiam Catholicam nunquam intellexisse peccatum appellari, quod verè & propriè in renatis peccatum sit; sed quia ex peccato est, & ad peccatum inclinat. Si quis autem contrarium senserit, anathema sit. Hoc Conciliabuli decretum modis omnibus propugnant Iesuwitæ, imprimis Bell. l. 5. de A. G. qui c. 7: ita scribit: Asserimus naturæ corruptionem siue concupiscentiam qualem remanet post Baptismum in regeneratis, non esse peccatum originis non solùm, quia non imputatur, sed etiam, quia imputari non potest, cùm nullum sit ex se; vel sua natura peccatum. Et Gregor. de Val. T. 2. Comm. in Thomam disp. 6. quæst. 12 pun. 1. §. 5. Col. 755. De firma, inquit, fide statuendum est; concupiscentiam, atq; adeò reliquas animæ vires, vt in renatis dono iustitiæ integræ destitutæ sunt, veram rationem peccati non habere.

III. Nos verò hanc sententiam Christi & Apostolorum doctrinæ aduersari dicimus ideoque induuias originalem, in renatis reliquam, statuimus esse peccatum verè propriéœ dictum, seu malum culpæ, pugnans cum lege diuina, licet ex accidenti propter Christi meritum, fidelibus non imputetur, nec reos cōstituat, mortiuè sẽpiternę subjiciat.

VI. Non autem existimetur, controuersiam hanc esse leuiculam, aut inanem λογομαχίαν, de qua opinari cuiuis sit liberum. Imò verò hinc dependet gloria Christi, doctrina de nostri iustificatione per fidem. Si enim ostendatur, renatis semper adhærere peccatum, mox vltrò sequitur, legem perfectè non impleri, adeoque per opera neminem iustificari posse. Quod eum Papicolæ animaduertant, hinc tanto conatu & apparatu concupiscentiam è peccatorum numero eximere laborant: Quam ob causam si nobis cordi est, tum Christi Saluatoris gloria, tum nostra salus & iustitia, non debemus hic credere, sed modis omnibus Papalem illam sententiam impugnare, imò prorsus expugnare. Quod vt fiat producemus. 1. Argumenta ex epistola ad Rom. 2. Rationes ex alijs dictis & analogia fidei desumptas, 3 Testimonia Patrum, & 4. præcipuas Romanensium obiectiones paucis examinabimus.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: I. Arguments from the Epistle to the Romans

I. Arguments from the Epistle to the Romans:

V. The proper seat of this doctrine is the sixth and seventh chapters of the Epistle to the Romans, which the adversaries therefore labor strenuously to obscure in many ways and to pervert its genuine sense: before, therefore, we extract the arguments themselves, three questions in particular, for a fuller understanding of the text and to forestall the exceptions of the Papists, come to be discussed as if in the place of a προγνώσεως.

VI. 1. Of what person does the Apostle speak in chapter 7?

Formerly, when Augustine was a young man, he judged that Paul was not speaking of himself as reborn, but had assumed the person of another, namely of a man not reborn and profane, or if he spoke of himself, he understood the time before his conversion. The Photinians seize upon this interpretation today, and strive to persuade [others] with many arguments, as appears from the writing of a certain Prosper Dysidaeus (whom they suppose to be Socinus) to a certain most noble man.

VII. But Augustine, after he had weighed that Apostolic text more diligently, saw that such an interpretation could not stand, and therefore he retracted his opinion, l. 1. Retract. c. 32. & l. 2. c. 1. Furthermore, l. 5. contra Iul. Pelag. c. 11. he writes expressly: I had previously understood that passage otherwise, or rather I had not understood it, which my own writings of that time also testify. For it did not seem to me that the Apostle could have said of himself, 'But I am carnal,' when he was spiritual. But afterwards I yielded to better and more intelligent men, or rather to the truth itself, which must be confessed, so that I might see that in those words of the Apostle there is the groaning of the saints struggling against carnal concupiscences.

VIII. But in order that this very truth may be demonstrated, we urge three arguments above all. 1. From the clear letter. The Apostle speaks always in the first person, and thus of himself: 'I am carnal,' v. 14. 'What I hate, I do,' v. 15. 'I consent to the law,' v. 16, and so consequently up to the end. Although elsewhere speech is made under another person, this is nevertheless easily apparent from the text. Here, however, the Apostle does not hint by even one iota that he is speaking about someone else. Therefore, that gloss directly contradicts the text. For when Paul says, 'I am carnal,' they interpret this as if it had been said: 'It is not I, but some other person who is not regenerate.'

IX. 2. From the notation of time. He does not speak in the past tense, but always in the present. He does not say: 'Therefore I was carnal: I once did evil,' as he had said in verse 9: But, 'I am carnal,' v. 14. 'Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me?' v. 24. Yet truly, when he was writing these things, he was no longer a child of wrath, but of grace and regenerate, and therefore he wrote and confessed these things about himself as a regenerate man.

X. 3. From the properties of the regenerate. He of whom the properties of the regenerate are predicated is regenerate. But the properties of the regenerate are predicated of the man whom Paul describes here. Therefore he is regenerate. There are indeed ten of these, primarily, which are recited in order. 1. To will and approve the good, to not will and to disapprove the evil. 'For what I will, that I do not, but what I hate, that I do,' v. 15. And it is repeated v. 19. 20. Although the ungodly indeed sometimes approve and desire what is good, nevertheless that will is not constant; nor does it arise from a love of virtue and reverence for the law of God, but from fear of punishments, nor does it regard every good, much less spiritual and theological, but only either natural or moral. The Apostle, however, attends to every good, and especially the spiritual, which is evident from verses 14, 21, 22, 25. Add this: Every unregenerate person does evil knowingly and willingly. But Paul testifies that he hates that and does it unwillingly. Therefore, he is not speaking under the persona of an unregenerate person.

2. To consent to the law, and to be delighted by it. If I do what I do not want, I consent to the law that it is good, v. 16. I delight in the law of God according to the inner man, v. 22. But indeed this is fitting only for the regenerate, as is evident from the example of David, Psalm 1, verse 2; Psalm 119, verses 77, 103. For the unregenerate either do not know the law of God, or they violate it voluntarily, which they would not do if they were delighted by obedience to the law; since consent to the law includes an unwillingness to transgress. For whoever is seriously delighted by the law, and desires to lead a life conformable to it, does not knowingly and willingly prevaricate against the law, which, however, all unregenerate people do, whether they be pagans, or Epicureans, or hypocrites. Knowledge indeed and a general assent to the law can fall to the ungodly, but not delight, or a serious zeal for obeying; for this belongs uniquely to the regenerate.

3. Not to work evil. Now I do not work that, but the sin that dwells in me, v. 17. 19. Conversely, this cannot be affirmed of the unregenerate. For no such distinction has a place there, since the sins of the ungodly are voluntary and deliberate. Who would say of a fornicator: He did not work the evil, but the sin that dwells in him? Nay, indeed, he himself worked it, because he consented freely; otherwise the secondary act could not have been posited, since it always presupposes consent.

4. To will every good, but to be unable to perform it, 'To will is present with me, but to perform I find not,' ver. 18. If this did not apply to the regenerate, they would never sin mortally. For to avoid mortal and gross crimes, they can both have the will and perform it. For an adulterer cannot say: I had the will but could not perform it. Indeed, unless he had consented willingly, he could have performed, that is, abstained from adultery.

5. He has an inner man. 'I delight in the law of God κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, according to the inner man,' ver. 22. Here, however, by the phrase of Scripture he signifies the renewal of the heart. For he who has not been begotten does not have an inner man, inasmuch as he is from the Spirit, and is strengthened through the Spirit, Eph. 3:16, which single statement sufficiently refutes the frivolous objection of the Photinians, that by τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον is understood the mind and intellect, not the newness of the heart. Add that the Apostle here opposes the inner man to the members and the flesh, that is, to the corruption of nature, not to the body itself.

-6. To feel the struggle of the flesh and the Spirit. 'I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,' ver. 23. But truly this is proper to the regenerate, Gal. 5:17, who alone have the Spirit of God, Rom. 8:14, whom the world cannot receive, John 14:17. The ungodly, however, and the unregenerate, who are held in the snares of Satan, 2 Tim. 2:26, do not experience such a struggle, but knowingly and willingly rush into sins.

7. To be led captive by the law of sin, which is in the members, in the same, ver. 23. Captivity, however, presupposes a will against the prison. Therefore, he who is led captive by the flesh and carnal thoughts, he by no means consents, which in turn cannot be affirmed of the unregenerate.

8. To acknowledge depravity and seek liberation. 'O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?' ver. 25. The unregenerate, however, do neither. For they neither acknowledge the gravity of the fall because this is for the penitent: nor do they seriously implore God, because this is for believers. Since, therefore, they interpret this exclamation as being about one not reborn, they must most absurdly concede that repentance and faith can fall to those not reborn.

9. To give thanks for redemption and justification. The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, v. 25. Here the Apostle acknowledges that, although he cannot be completely purged from sin, he is nevertheless redeemed by Christ and reconciled to God the Father, for which reason he gives thanks, which is entirely false concerning the ungodly and the not-reborn.

10. To serve God in the Spirit. I myself with the mind serve the law of God: but with the flesh the law of sin, verse 15. To serve the law is: to exhibit spiritual worship to God in the newness of the Spirit. Hence in verse 6 he said: Now we are delivered from the law of death, in which we were held, so that we serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter. Since the not-reborn does not perform this in the least, we rightly conclude again that the Apostle is not speaking about him.

XI. But they object, that one reborn cannot be understood here, because he is said to be carnal, and sold under sin, verse 16. Captive to the law of sin, verse 23. serving sin with the flesh, v. 25. etc.

But I respond. Our renewal is begun here, not consummated; it happens in part, not in whole, and therefore in every reborn man two contrary principles concur, flesh and Spirit, the old man and the new, the outer man and the inner, the law of the members and of the mind, the law of the flesh and of the Spirit, the oldness mortified and the newness begun, just as the Apostle most openly teaches by his own example. And hence it happens that the reborn are called both spiritual and carnal. They are spiritual as regards the newness begun, insofar as they have an enlightened mind, a converted will, and a restrained appetite. They are carnal as regards the remaining oldness, insofar as doubts and ignorances adhere to the mind, and to the depraved will inclinations, and carnal desires to the appetite. For although the flesh is mortified to the greatest extent, it is not yet entirely rooted out; although it is not obeyed, it does not cease to incite to evil, whence it happens that contrary things are said of one and the same person: namely, to be carnal and spiritual, to will the good and to do the evil, to consent to the law but not be able to perform it, to serve the law of God with the mind, but with the flesh the law of sin. The former are said with regard to the firstfruits of newness; the latter with regard to the remnants of the oldness, both truly, which the example of Paul teaches, and any pious person experiences in himself.

Nor is it absurd to say that one and the same man is new and old, regenerate and not regenerate. For similar things occur in nature. The sickly are partly healthy insofar as they are freed from disease; partly not healthy, insofar as they still have certain remnants of infirmity. Thus, before sunrise at dawn, our hemisphere is said to be partly bright, partly dark, because it is neither entirely occupied by darkness nor suffused with full light. In like manner, renewal is imperfect, while natural darkness is partly driven away, partly remains, and we live here as if in the twilight of the Spirit. For heavenly light partly occupies our minds, and partly does not occupy them, and therefore we are partly light, partly darkness; partly flesh, partly spirit, partly ψυχικοί or animal, partly πνευματικοί or spiritual. Thus also wine diluted with water is said to be partly water, partly wine, not because some part is diluted with water and another is not diluted, and therefore one part is pure and another is not; but because a total mixture has been made, and so that whole thing is in part wine. By similar reasoning, let us not think that in the regenerate one part of him, namely the soul, is regenerated and has become entirely Spirit, while the other, namely the body, is flesh: but because the regeneration of both soul and body is imperfect, hence the same man, both with regard to the soul and as regards the body, is partly flesh, partly Spirit. And for this reason the Apostle declares contrary things about himself alone, and teaches that in him, that is, in his flesh or corrupted nature, nothing good dwells; yet in him, insofar as he was Spirit, or reborn from the Spirit, something good dwells. We therefore deny that the phrase, to be carnal, and to be held captive by sin, denotes a man who is absolutely not reborn. It indeed denotes the depravity of nature, and the evil of origin, but it does not infer the absence of renewal: it implies that this is imperfect, but not that it is entirely null. For both, as we have said, can consist together, and meet in one subject, namely the corruption of the flesh, and the renewal of the mind. Otherwise, in the same man, the flesh would not lust against the Spirit, nor the Spirit against the flesh, which is nevertheless affirmed, Gal. 5. v. 17. He who does not feel this struggle of opposing tenants either falsely arrogates to himself angelic perfection, or does not yet have the Spirit of Christ. For the flesh does not lust against the flesh, but against the Spirit. Hence, therefore, he who receives [the Spirit] immediately feels the flesh opposing, and therefore if he does not feel it, he has not yet received the Spirit of God. But that, moreover, is to be noted here, that men are called carnal in Scripture in a double sense.

1. Some are carnal purely and entirely, in whom the flesh uniquely dominates, as in the unregenerate,

2. some are carnal restrictedly and in part, in whom the flesh is indeed present, but is suppressed by the Spirit, and does not dominate, as in the regenerate. Briefly: Some are carnal by reason of servitude; some only in the sense of the flesh. The former consent to sin, the latter merely feel it. The former [sin] mortally, the latter venially. The former are totally and absolutely flesh, the latter are only called carnal. Since the Photinians confuse these diverse significations, it is no wonder that they err so shamefully.

Latin:

I. Argumenta ex epist. ad Romanos:

V. Propria sedes huius doctrinæ est caput Episstolæ ad Romanos sextum & septimum, quæ propterea multis modis obscurare, sensumque genuinum peruertere strenuè laborant aduersarij: Priusquam ergo ipsa argumenta excerpamus, quæstiones imprimis tres, ad pleniorem textus intelligentiam, & præcauendas Papicolarum exceptiones, veluti προγνώσεως loco discutiendæ veniunt.

VI. 1. De qua persona cap. 7. loquatur Apostolus?

Olim, cum iuuenis esset Augustinus, Paulum non de seipso renato loqui, sed alienam personam, nempe hominis non renati & prophani induisse, aut si de seipso loquatur, tempus ante conuersionem suam intelligere censuit. Hanc expositionem arripiunt hodie Photiniani, multisque argumentis persuadere satagunt, vt apparet ex Scripto cuiusdam Prosperi Dysidæi, (quem Socinum esse autumant) ad virum quendam nobilissimum.

VII. Augustinus verò postquam textum istum Apostolicum diligentius perpendit, interpretationem talem consistere non posse vidit, ideoque sententiam suam retractavit, l. 1. Retract. c. 32. & l. 2. c. 1. Praeterea l. 5. contra Iul. Pelag. c. 11. expresse scribit: Ego prius locū eum aliter intellexeram, vel potius non intellexeram, quod mea quidem illius temporis etiam Scripta testantur. Non mihi enim videbatur Apostolus & de seipso dicere potuisse, Ego autem carnalis sum, cùm esset spiritualis. Sed postea melioribus & intelligentioribus cessi, vel potius ipsi, quod fatendum est, veritati, ut viderem, in illis Apostoli gemitum esse sanctorum contra carnales concupiscentias dimicantium.

IIX. Vt autem haec ipsa veritas demonstretur, tria potissimùm argumenta urgemus. 1. A clara litera. Loquitur Apostolus semper in persona prima, adeoque de seipso, Ego carnalis sum, v. 14. Ego, quod odi, facio. v. 15. Ego consentio legi. v. 16. & sic consequenter usque ad finem. Quamvis autem alibi sub alia persona fiat sermo, hoc tamen ex textu facilè patet. Hic autem ne uno quidem apiculo innuit, Apostolus, se de alio quodam verba facere. Glossa igitur ista textui directè contradicit. Quando enim Paulus inquit, carnalis sum, hoc interpretantur, ac si dictum esset. Non ego sum, sed alius quispiam non renatus.

IX. 2. A notatione temporis. Non loquitur in praeterito, sed semper in praesenti. Non ait. Ergo carnalis eram: Ego aliquando malum faciebam, ut vers. 9. dixerat: Verùm, Ego carnalis sum, v. 14. Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit? v. 14. Tum verò, cum hęc scriberet, non amplius irae, sed gratiae filius & regeneratus fuit, ideoque ista de se renato scripsit, & confessus est.

X. 3. Ex proprietatibus renatorum. De quo praedicantur renati propria ille renatus est, Atqui de homine, quem Paulus hic describit praedicantur renati propria. Ergo renatus est. Sunt verò illorum decem potissimùm quę ordine recitantur. 1. Velle & adprobare bonum, nolle & improbate malum. Non quod volo bonum, hoc ago, sed quod odi, illud facio, v. 15. & repetitur v. 19. 20. Licèt verò & impii bonum quandoque probent & velint, tamen voluntas ea non est constans; nec oritur ex amore virtutis, & reverentia legis Dei, sed metu pœnarum, nec respicit bonum omne, multò minus spirituale & Theologum, sed tantùm vel naturale vel morale. Apostolus autem & omne bonum, & imprimis spirituale attendit, quod patet ex vers. 14. 21. 22. 25. Adde hoc, Omnis non renatus scenter & volenter facit malum. Paulus autem se istud odisse & nolenter facere testatur. Ergo sub persona non renati non loquitur.

2. Consentire legi, & hac delectari. Si quod nolo, illud facio, consentio legi quoniam bona est, v. 16. Condelector legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem, v. 22. At verò hoc solis renatis convenit, vt patet exemplo Dauidis Psal. 1. vers. 2. Psal. 119. vers. 77. 103. Non renati enim vel nesciunt legem Dei, vel tamen voluntariè violant, quod non facerent, si lege legisœ; obedientiâ delectarentur: siquidem legis consensio includit noluntatem trangressionis. Quisquis enim seriò delectatur lege, vitamœ; illi conformē agere desiderat, is sciēter & volenter legem non pręuaricatur, quod tamen faciunt omnes non renati, siue pagani sint, siue Epicurei, siue hypocritæ. Notitia quidē & generalis assensus legis cadere potest in impios, sed non delectatio, vel serium obediendi studium; hoc enim vnicè renatis competit.

3. Non operari malum. Iam ego non operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum, v. 17. 19. Vicissim hoc de non-renato affirmari nequit. Nulla enim ibi distincto talis locum habet, cùm peccata impiorum sint voluntaria & deliberata. Quis de fornicatore diceret: Non ille malum operatus est, sed peccatũ quod in ipso habitat? Imò verò licet ipse operatus est, quia liberè consensit, aliàs actus secundus poni non potuisset, quoniam consensum semper præsupponit.

4. Velle omne bonum, sed perficere non posse, Velle adiacet mihi, perficere autem non inuenio, ver. 18. Hoc si non renatis conueniret, nunquam mortaliter peccarent. Ad euitanda enim scelera mortalia & crassa habere possunt & velle & perficere. Nam adulter dicere nequit: Velle habui sed perficere non potui. Imo nisi sponte consensisset, perficere, hoc est, ab adulterio, abstinere potuisset.

5. Habet interiorem hominem. Condelector legi Dei κατὰ τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, secundum interiorem hominem, vers. 22. Hic autem phrasi Scripturae renouationem cordis significat. Qui enim generatus non est, interiorem hominem non habet, quippe qui est a Spiritu, & corroboratur per Spiritum, Ephes. 3. v. 16. quod vnicum dictum satis refutat friuolam Photinjanoru exceptionem, per τὸν ἔσω ἄνθρωπον, intelligi mentem & intellectum, non cordis nouitatem. Adde, quod Apostolus interiorem hominem hic opponat membris & carni, hoc est, corruptioni naturae, non ipsi corpori

-6. Sentire luctam carnis & Spiritus. Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meae. v. 23. At vero hoc renatorum est proprium, Gal. 5. v. 17. qui soli habent Spiritum Dei, Rom. 8. v. 14 quem mundus accipere nequit, Iohan. 14. vers. 17. Impij vero & non renati, qui tenentur laqueis Satanae. 2. Thess. 2. vers. 26. talem luctam non experiuntur, sed scienter & volenter in peccata ruunt.

7. Captiuari lege peccati, quae est in membris, eodem, v. 23. Captiuitas autem praesupponit voluntatem carceris. Qui ergo captiuatur per carnem & carnales cogitationes, ille nequaquam consentit, quod vicissim de non renato affirmari nequit.

8. Agnoscere deprauationem & petere liberationem. Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit de corpore mortis huius? vers. 25. Non renati vero neutrum faciunt. Neque enim agnoscunt grauitatem lapsus, quia hoc est pœnitentium: nec Deum seriò implorant, quia hoc est credentium. Quia ergò istam exclamationem de nõ renato interpretantur, hi pœnitẽtiam & fidem in non renatos cadere posse absurdissimè cõcedant oportet.

9. Gratias agere pro redemtione & iustificatione. Gratia Dei per Iesvm Christvm Dominum nostrum, v. 25. Hic Apostolus agnoscit, quamuis à peccato penitus purgari nequeat, se tamen à Christo redemtum, & Deo Patri reconciliatumm esse, quo nomine εὐχαριστῶ vel gratias agit, quod omne de impijs & non-renatis falsum est.

10. Spiritu seruire Deo. Ego ipse mente seruio legi Dei: carne autem legi peccati, vers. 15. Seruire legi, est: spiritualem cultum Deo exhibere in nouitate Spiritus. Hinc vers. 6. dixit: Nunc soluti sumus à lege mortis, in qua detinebamur, ita vt seruiamus in nouitate Spiritus & non in vetustate literæ. Hoc autem cùm non renatus minimè præstet, iterum de illo Apostolum non loqui rectè concludimus.

XI. Obijciunt verò, Non posse hîc renatum intelligi, quia dicatur carnalis, & venundatus sub peccatum, vers. 16. Captiuus lege peccati, vers. 23. carne seruiens peccato, v. 25. &c.

Sed Respond. Renouatio nostra hîc inchoatur non consummatur, ex semisse fit, non ex asse, ideoque in quouis homine renato duo cõtraria principia concurrunt, caro & Spiritus, homo vetus & nouus homo exterior & interior, lex membrorum & mentis, lex carnis & Spiritus, vetustas mortificata & nouitas inchoata, quemadmodum Apostolus exemplo suo apertissimè docet. Atque hinc fit, vt renati dicantur, & spirituales & carnales. Spirituales sunt, quoad nouitatem inchoatàm, quatenus habent mentem illustratam, voluntatem conuersam, & appetitum refrenatum. Carnales sunt, quoad vetustatem residuam, quatenus menti adhærent dubitationes & ignorantiæ, voluntati prauæ inclinationes, & appetitui carnalia desideria. Vt enim maxime caro mortificetur, non tamen penitus euellitur; licet ei non obediatur, ad malum tamen instigare non desistit, vnde fit, vt contraria de vno & eodem dicantur: nimirum carnalem & spiritualem esse, velle bonum, & facere malum, consentire legi, sed perficere non posse, mente seruire legi Dei, carne autem legi peccati. Priora dicuntur, quoad primitias novitatis; posteriora, quoad reliquias vetustatis, vtraq; verè, quod exemplum Pauli docet, & quiuis pius in semetipso experitur.

Neque absurdum dictu est, vnum eundemque hominem nouum & veterem esse, renatum & non renatum. Similia enim occurrunt in natura. Valetudinarij partim valent quatenus liberati sunt à morbo; partim non valent, quatenus adhuc quasdam infirmitatis reliquias habent. Sic ante solis ortum sub auroram hemisphærium nostrum dicitur partim lucidum, partim tenebricosum, quia neque penitus à tenebris est occupatum, neque plenâ luce perfusum. Pari modo imperfecta est renouatio, dum tenebrę naturales partim pelluntur, partim manent, & nos velut in crepusculo Spiritus hîc viuimus. Lux enim cœlestis mentes nostras partim occupat, partim non occupat, ideoque sumus partim lux, partim tenebræ; partim caro, partim spiritus, partim ψυχικοί vel animales, partim πνευματικοί vel spirituales. Sic etiam vinum aqua dilutum, dicitur esse partim aqua, partim vinum, non quòd aliqua pars aquâ sit diluta, alia non diluta, eóque vna pars sit merum, alia non item; sed quia totalis facta est commixtio, adeoque totum illud ex parte vinum est. Simili ratione non putemus, in renato vnam ipsius partem, nempe animam esse regeneratam, & totam Spiritum factam, alteram verò, nempe corpus, esse carnem: sed quia regeneratio tùm animi, tùm corporis imperfecta est, hinc idem homo, & quoad animam, & quoad corpus partim caro est, partim Spiritus. Et hanc ob causam Apostolus de se vno contraria enunciat, & docet, in se, hoc est, in carne vel natura sua corrupta nihil boni habitare; in se tamen quatenus Spiritus, vel ex Spiritu renatus erat, aliquid boni habitare. Negamus proinde phrasin, carnalem esse, & captiuum teneri à peccato, notare hominem absolutè non renatum. Notat quidem naturæ deprauationem, & malum originis, non autem infert absentiam renouationis: innuit, hanc esse imperfectam, non verò esse penitus nullam. Vtrumque enim, vt diximus, simul potest consistere, & in vno subjecto conuenire, nimirum carnis corruptio, & mentis renouatio. Alias in eodem homine caro non concupisceret ad versus Spiritum, nec Spiritus aduersus carnem, quod tamen affirmatur, Gal. 5. v. 17. Quam aduersantium inquilinorum luctam qui non sentit, aut Angelicam perfectionem falsò sibi arrogat, aut Spiritum Christi nondum habet. Caro enim non aduersus carnem, sed aduersus Spiritū concupiscit. Hinc ergo qui accipit, carnem aduersantem protinus sentit, ideoque si non sentiat, Spiritum Dei nondum accepit. Illud verò hĩc insuper notandum, quod homines in Scripturis duplici sensu carnales dicantur.

1. Quidam sunt carnales purè & ex toto, in quibus caro vnicè dominatur, vt in non renatis,

2. quidam sunt carnales restrictè & ex parte, in quibus caro quidem adest, sed per Spiritum supprimitur, non dominatur, vt in renatis. Breuiter: Quidam sunt carnales ob seruitutem; quidam tantùm in sensum carnis. Illi peccato consentiunt, hi duntaxat sentiunt. Illi peccatum mortaliter, hi venialiter. Illi totaliter & absolutè caro, hi tantùm carnales dicuntur. Quas significationes diuersas cùm confundant Photiniani, mirum non est, illos tam turpiter errare.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: XII. II. Of which concupiscence Paul speaks

XII. II. Of which concupiscence Paul speaks.

The Papists foster two errors here. 1. That the Apostle speaks of concupiscence by a voluntary act, especially in v. 7 and 8. For thus writes Bellarmine, lib. 5, de A. G., c. 10, Col. 392. B. I answer that concupiscence is not taken for the seed, but for the voluntary act of desiring, which is prohibited by the law: Thou shalt not covet. This will the Scholastics call formed ἐπιθυμίαν; but they call the involuntary and original [concupiscence] unformed, because it lacks the assent of the deliberate will. They think, therefore, that the formed is sin, and the unformed is not. 2. That the discourse is made concerning the concupiscence of the flesh, or of the sensitive appetite, not of the heart or of the superior powers. Both are most false, which must be demonstrated in a few words.

XIII. 1. That the Apostle, by the concupiscence prohibited by the law, does not understand only the voluntary, but rather original [concupiscence] itself, and its first involuntary motions, we prove.

1. From the ignorance of sin; I did not know sin, except through the law, says the Apostle, v. 7. For I did not know concupiscence, unless the law said: Thou shalt not covet. Interpreters note here that he speaks in the singular; τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔγνων, I did not know sin. He understands, therefore, not many actual [sins], but one singular sin, namely original [sin], the gravity and deformity of which he had not sufficiently known before his conversion in Pharisaism. For the Pharisees did not hold involuntary suggestions and vicious qualities of nature to be sins, as is known from the sermon of Christ, Matt. 5. The Apostle therefore hints that he had recognized the sin of origin through the law, namely as explained and more rightly understood by Christ. Hence, therefore, we conclude thus: Of that concupiscence whose depravity is most recent, and known even to the Pharisees themselves and the sounder Heathens, the Apostle does not speak. For he understands that which is recognized with difficulty, and not except through an accurate consideration of the law. But the depravity of voluntary concupiscence is most known from the light of nature without the illumination of the law, nor [is there] anyone of sound one can doubt concerning that, which is manifest. Nor was Paul so dull that, before his conversion, he was ignorant that voluntary concupiscence of evil is a sin, since he was most studious of an honest life, Acts 23:1, Phil. 3:6, 2 Tim. 1:3. Therefore the Apostle is not speaking of that, but rather of another, which is original and connate.

2. From the perpetual cohesion of the text. It is certain that the Apostle is speaking of the same corruption, of one and the same sin, since all things cohere in a right order and immediately: he asserts, therefore, that that concupiscence is forbidden by the law which he deplores, and on account of which he affirms himself to be held captive. For he speaks of himself, of his own sin, of his own concupiscence. But this is not voluntary, because such does not fall upon the regenerate, but is involuntary and original. Therefore he asserts that this very thing is forbidden by the law. Or, the Apostle understands that concupiscence which he confesses he feels and which dwells in his flesh. But this is not voluntary, but original. For he says openly that he did not will it, that he hated it, and that he resisted it, and even now resists it. Who, therefore, would understand ἐπιθυμίαν as voluntary and joined with consent?

3. From the properties of original concupiscence. Whatever corrupts nature, is opposed to the law of God, hinders the saints from fulfilling the law, and against which the regenerate perpetually fight, that the Apostle understands by concupiscence forbidden by the law, as the letter of the clear text and the Pauline description evince. But these properties agree not so much with voluntary as with original and venial concupiscence, which is again manifest in itself. Wherefore the Apostle, by ἐπιθυμίαν forbidden by the law, intended not so much the voluntary as the original to be understood.

4. From the lesser to the greater. When the effect is condemned, much more so is the cause itself. If it is forbidden to act greedily, why not also greed? If to live incontinently, much more so incontinence itself. Wherefore, if the Apostle condemns the act of concupiscence, and affirms it to be forbidden by the law, he certainly at the same time includes concupiscence itself, that vicious root. We willingly concede indeed that by the law Thou shalt not covet the voluntary act of coveting is forbidden, but we deny that it is only that which is forbidden, and therefore it is not permitted for Papists to argue from an inclusive to an exclusive For every vicious ἐπιθυμία, and one displeasing to God, is interdicted there, namely 1. original. 2. involuntary actual. 3. voluntary actual. For these three are involved in the one term of concupiscence taken generically.

Hence it is compared to a kindled furnace, which if it does not breathe out the greatest flames, yet it continually breathes out sparks; the kindled furnace denotes the very root of concupiscence, the sparks the first involuntary motions, the flames the appetite as if raging and joined with full consent and the ὁρμῇ of the whole body. The Apostle Paul, however, here adapts this general interdict chiefly to the first two species of concupiscence.

XIV. 2. That the Apostle by concupiscence understands not only the appetite, but of the heart, not only of the senses, but of the mind, and thus the depravation of all the powers, we show in what follows.

1. From the prohibition of concupiscence. That ἐπιθυμία which is forbidden by the law, and without the law is recognized with difficulty, is that which is chiefly understood by Paul. But such is the involuntary ἐπιθυμία of the mind and the superior powers. For he who asserts that only gross desires are interdicted raves with the Pharisees, and concedes nothing more than what was known to the Gentiles even from the light of nature. Wherefore not only the ἐπιθυμία of the flesh, but chiefly the more subtle ἐπιθυμία of the heart and mind is understood by the Apostle.

2. From the subject of concupiscence before regeneration. Where there is concupiscence before regeneration, there it also remains after regeneration. For only the guilt passes away, but the act remains, or the vicious habit: And yet depraved concupiscence not only infects the body or the appetite before regeneration, but is diffused throughout the whole man, and resides especially in the higher powers of the soul; which not even the Papists can deny. Therefore, it remains in the same seat after regeneration.

3. From renovation. Whatever is renewed from day to day, that is contaminated by concupiscence: for the term from which renovation proceeds is the ἀνδιμία itself, since after the remission of sin nothing else remains. But indeed, not only the lower powers are renewed, but the heart itself, the reason itself, and the higher faculties of the mind: Hence the Apostle says in Rom. 12:2: Be transformed in the newness τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, of your mind. And Eph. 4:23: Be renewed τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, in the spirit of your mind. Therefore, the mind and reason itself is contaminated by concupiscence.

4. From rebellion. Whatever in the regenerate person opposes the Spirit, all that pertains to concupiscence. For this is that law of the members warring against the law of the mind, Rom. 7:23; this is that stubborn beast which always makes the flesh lust against the Spirit, Gal. 5:19. Hence, whoever are tempted, which also happens to the saints, are said to be tempted by nothing other than their own concupiscence, Jas. 1:14. Now, indeed, not only bodily desires, but also the vices of the mind and the inclinations of a depraved will oppose the Spirit; the regenerate are not tempted only through anomalies of the appetite, but also through doubts of the mind, through the desires of man, through errors, through ignorance, through distrust, and the like. From which it follows in turn that concupiscence is diffused through all the powers of man.

5. From prayers: Wherever the Apostle prays to God that He may renew our minds and incline the will toward God, which he does in Eph. 1:16, 17, 18 and elsewhere throughout, there he simultaneously implies that the minds, through original desire, even after rebirth are corrupted, and for that reason always need the help of God, lest they be overcome by depraved suggestions. Moreover, all these things provide clear testimony concerning the total corruption always adhering to us, and thus concerning concupiscence, residing in body and soul, and in all their faculties.

6. From experience. We appeal here to the consciences of all who seem to themselves most holy. Who is there who does not feel many shadows in his intellect, a huge φιλαυτία (self-love) in his will, and distrust in his heart? Who is there who does not experience all the faculties of his mind sometimes straying from the true, the just, and the good? Who is there who does not sometimes loathe the word of God, who does not hear it with difficulty, or at least understand it with difficulty? Who is there who does not continually feel vicious impulses toward sensible objects in all his faculties? If you see gold, are you not immediately tempted by πλεονεξία (covetousness)? If pleasures are offered, are you not affected by φιληδονία (love of pleasure)? If there is any hope of glory, behold φιλοδοξία (love of glory) is present, which inflames one to seek it. If there is any opportunity for ruling: behold φιλαρχία (love of power), which stimulates one to aspire to a kingdom. In sum: There is no one among the most holy whose mind is not surrounded by errors, whose will is not surrounded by depraved suggestions; whose heart and all his faculties are not surrounded by vicious desires: and whoever denies this, I shall pronounce him a great hypocrite and remarkably foolish. For Cyprian says most truly in his Sermon on Almsgiving: Whoever calls himself blameless is either proud or foolish. Since, therefore, in the regenerate all faculties, and especially the higher δυνάμεις (powers), are and always remain corrupt, and indeed that corruption is comprehended by the Apostle under the single name of ἐπιθυμία (desire), we conclude that by it not only the appetite but also the concupiscence of the mind; not only of the senses, but also of the reason, is noted and understood:

XV. They object, however: 1. That it is commonly called the concupiscence of the flesh, and therefore resides only in the sensitive appetite.

Resp. Flesh, when it is opposed to the Spirit, in Scripture's phrase denotes the total corruption of man, which adheres both to reason and to appetite. For whatever lusts against the Spirit is called flesh by this one name: Gal. 5 v. 17. For not only the senses lust, but reason itself, the heart itself, insofar as it is corrupted. Wherefore all these things are understood by Paul under the term of flesh. For which reason, enmities, idolatries, emulations, contentions, dissensions, heresies, and the like are numbered among the works of the flesh in v. 20, which are not motions of vicious appetite, but actions of the mind and heart itself. Indeed, the Apostle expressly attributes to the flesh τὸν νοῦς φρόνημα. Rom. 8 v. 7. Coloss. 2 v. 18. The Savior himself calls the whole man, with all his powers, flesh, John 3 v. 6: namely, insofar as one who is unclean is born from the unclean. [3] Whence it appears that by the term flesh, Scripture does not denote only sensuality, as those people speak, or only the ἀταξίαν and repugnance of the sensitive appetite, but rather the depravation of the whole man and of all his δυνάμεων. Let it be noted, however, that the word flesh, when it is opposed to the Spirit, is taken in two ways. 1. Concretely and materially, or conjunctively, for the substance of man and the vice of the substance; in which sense it is said in John 3 v. 6: Whatever is born of the flesh is flesh. 2. Abstractly and formally, or distinctly, for the vice and corruption of nature alone; in which sense it is said in Gal. 5 v. 17: The flesh lusts against the spirit. For hence the formal principle, existing in man and resisting the spirit, is denoted: XVI. Rom. 7 v. 18: I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, there dwells no good. Hence Andradius concludes in his defense of the Council of Trent, book 5. [4] that concupiscence dwells in the flesh as in a military tabernacle, and from there makes an assault upon the mind. For the Apostle denies that it dwells in him as a whole, and affirms that it dwells only in the flesh.

Latin:

XII. II. De qua concupiscentia Paulus verba faciat.

Pontificij duos hîc errores fouent. 1. Apostolum loqui de concupiscentia actu voluntariô, præsertim v. 7. & 8. Ità enim scribit Bellarm. lib. 5. de A. G. c. 10. Col. 392. B. Respondeo concupiscentiam non accipi pro semite, sed pro actu voluntario cõcupiscente, qui prohibitus est lege: Non concupisces. Hanc voluntatem ἐπιθυμίαν Scholastici vocant formatam; involuntariam verô & originalem dicunt informem, quia careat deliberatæ voluntatis assensu. Putant ergo, formatam peccatum esse, informem non esse, 2. Sermonem fieri de concupiscentia carnis, vel appetitus sensitivi, non cordis, vel superiorum virium. Vtrumque est falsissimum, quod paucis demonstrandum.

XIII. 1. Quòd Apost. per concupiscentiam lege prohibitã, non intelligat solam voluntariam, sed ipsam potius originalem, eius que primos motus involuntarios, probamus.

1. Ab ignorantia peccati; Peccatum non cognovi, nisi per legem inquit Apostolus v. 7. Nam concupiscentiam nesciebam, nisi lex diceret: Non concupisces. Notât hîc interpretes, quòd loquatur in singulari; τὴν ἁμαρτίαν οὐκ ἔγνων, Peccatum non cognoui, Intelligit ergo non multa actualia, sed vnum singulare peccatum nimirum originale, cuius grauitatem & deformitatem non satis cognoverat ante suam conversionem in Pharisaismo. Involuntarias enim suggestiones, & vitiosas naturæ qualitates pro peccatis non habebant Pharisæi, vti notum est ex concione Christi Math. 5. Innuit ergo Apostolus, se agnovisse peccatum originis per legem, nimirum à Christo explicatam & rectiùs intellectam. Hinc igitur ita concludimus. Cuius concupiscentiæ pravitas est novissima, ipsis que Pharisæis & sanioribus Ethnicis cognita, de illa non loquitur Apostolus. Eam enim intelligit, quæ difficulter, & non nisi per accuratam legis considerationem agnoscitur. Atqui concupiscentiæ voluntariæ pravitas ex naturæ lumine absque collustratione legis est notissima, nec quisquam sanæ de illa dubitare potest, quod manifestum. Neque Paulus adeò crassus fuit, vt ante cōuersionem ignoraverit, voluntariam mali concupiscentiam esse peccatum, siquidem honestæ conuersationis fuit studiosissimus, Act. 23. vers. 1. Phil. 3. vers. 6. 2, Tim. 1. v. 3. Ergo de illa non loquitur Apostolus, sed potius de alia, quæ est originalis & connata.

2. A Perpetua textus cohæsione. Certum est, de eadem corruptione, de vno eodemque peccato Apostolum loqui, cum omnia recto ordine & immediatè cohærent: Illam ergo concupiscentiam lege prohibitam asserit, quam deplorat, & ob quam se captivum teneri adfirmat. Loquitur enim de seipso, de suo peccato, de sua concupiscentia. Ast hæc non est voluntaria, quia talis non cadit in renatos, sed involuntaria & originalis. Ergo hanc ipsam lege prohibitam esse asserit. Velita Eam concupiscentiam intelligit Apostolus, quam se sentire, & in carne sua fatetur habitare. Hæc verò non est voluntaria, sed originalis. Dicit enim aperte, se illam noluisse, odisse, ipsique repugnasse, ac etiam num repugnat. Qui ergo ἐπιθυμίαν voluntariam & cū consensu coniunctam intelligeret?

3. Ab originalis concupiscentiæ proprijs. Quicquid naturam corrumpit, legi Dei adversatur, sanctos impedıt, ne legem perficiant, & contra quod renati perpetuò pugnant, illud Apostolus per concupiscentiam lege prohibitam intelligit, vti clari textus litera, & descriptio Paulina euincit. At verò hæc propria non tàm voluntariæ, quàm originali & veniali concupiscentiæ conueniunt, quod iterum per se manifestum. Quare Apostolus per ἐπιθυμίαν lege prohibitam, non tàm voluntariam quàm originalem intellectam voluit.

4. A minori ad maius. Cùm damnatur effectus, multò magis causa ipsa. Si prohibetur avarè agere quidni & avaritia? Si incontinenter viuere, multo magis ipsa in continentia. Quare, si Apostolûs actum concupiscentiæ damnat, & lege prohibitum adfirmat, vtique ipsam simul concupiscentiam, radicem illam vitiosam includit. Lubenter quidem concedimus, lege Non concupisces actum concupiscendi voluntarium prohiberi, negamus autem tantum prohiberi, ideoque ab inclusiuą ad exclusiuam non licet Papicolis argumentari. Omnis enim ἐπιθυμία vitiosa, Deoq; displicens ibi interdicitur, nimirũ 1. originalis. 2. actualis inuoluntaria. 3. actualis voluntaria. Hæc enim tria vnum concupiscentiæ vocablum γενικῶς sumtum involuit.

Hinc comparatur illa fornaci accensæ, quæ si non maximas flammas, attamẽ scintillas continenter efflat, Fornax accensa notat ipsam concupiscentiæ radicem, scintillæ primos motus inuoluntarios, flammæ appetitum quasi furentem & cum pleno consensu totiusque corporis ὁρμῇ coniunctum. Apostolus autem Paulus generale istud interdictum præcipuè ad priores duas concupiscentiæ species hic accommodat.

XIV. 2. Quòd Apostolus per concupiscentiam non tantùm appetitus, sed cordis, non tantùm sensus, sed mentis, adeoque omnium virium deprauationem intelligat sequentibus monstratum damus.

1. A prohibitione concupiscentiæ. Quæ ἐπιθυμία lege prohibita est, & sine lege difficulter agnoscitur, ea potissimùm à Paulo intelligitur. At vero talis est inuoluntaria mentis & superiorum virium ἐπιθυμία. Qui enim crassas tantùm cupiditates interdictas autumat, cum Pharisæis delirat, & nihilo plus concedit quam quod gentilibus etiam ex lumine naturæ innotuit Quare non sola carnis, sed potissimùm subtilior cordis & mentis ἐπιθυμία ab Apostolo intelligitur.

2. A subiecto concupiscentiæ ante παλιγγενεσίαν. Vbi est concupiscentia ante regenerationem, ibi quoque manet post regenerationem. Tantùm enim transit reatus, manet autem actus, vel vitiosus habitus: Atqui praua concupiscentia non solum corpus aut appetitum inficit ante regenerationem, sed in toto homine diffusa est, & in superioribus animæ potentijs maximè residet; quod nè Pontificij quidem inficiari possunt. Ergo in eadem sede manet post regenerationem.

3. A renouatione. Quicquid renouatur de die in diem; istud concupiscentia est contaminatum: Renouationis enim terminus à quo, est ipsa ἀνδιμία, cum post remissionem peccati nihil aliud sit reliquum. At verò renouantur non tantùm inferiores potentiæ, sed ipsorum cor, ipsa ratio, & superiores animi facultates: Hinc Apostolus Rom: 12. 2. ait: Reformamini in nouitate τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν, mentis vestræ. Et Eph. 4. 23. Renouamini τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ νοὸς ὑμῶν. Spiritu mentis vestræ. Ergo ipsa mens & ratio concupiscentia est contaminata.

4 A rebellione. Quicquid in renato aduersatur Spiritui, istud omne ad concupiscentiam pertinet. Hęc enim est ista lex membrorum repugnans legi mentis, Rom. 7. 23. hæc est illa contumax bestia, quæ carnem semper facit concupiscere aduersus Spiritum, Gal. 5. 19. Hinc quicunque tentantur, quod sanctis etiam contingit, non nisi à concupiscentia sua tentari dicuntur, Iac. 1. 14. Iam verò non tantum corporalia desideria, sed animi etiam vitia, & pravæ voluntatis inclinationes aduersantur Spiritui; Non tentantur renati solùm per appetitus anomalias, sed etiam per mentis dubitationes, per desideria hominis, per errores, per ignorantiam, per diffidentiam & similia. Ex quo vicissim sequitur, concupiscentiam per omnes hominis vires esse diffusam.

5. A precationibus: Vbicunque Apostolus precatur Deum, vt renouet mentes nostras, & voluntatem ad Deum inclinet, quod facit Eph. 1. v. 16. 17. 18. & alibi passim, ibi simul innuit, mentes per ἐπιθυμίαν originalem post renascentiam quoque corruptas esse, eaque de causa auxilio Dei semper indigere, ne a prauis suggestionibus vincantur. Haec autem omnia luculentum praebent testimonium de totali corruptione nobis semper adhaerente, adeoque de concupiscentia, in corpore & anima, omnibusque potentijs residente.

6. Ab experientia. Appellamus hic omnium, qui sibi videntur sanctissimi, conscientias. Quis est, qui non in intellectu suo multas sentiat tenebras, in voluntate ingentem φιλαυτίαν, in corde diffidentiam? Quis est, qui non omnes animi sui facultates nonnunquam a vero, iusto & bono aberrare experiatur? Quis est, qui non aliquando fastidiat verbum Dei, qui non aegre istud audiat, vel certe difficulter intelligat? Quis est, qui non ad obiecta sensibilia vitiosos motus in omnibus potentijs continuo sentiat? Si aurum vides, an non statim a πλεονεξία solicitaris? Si voluptates offeruntur annon a φιληδονία afficeris: Si qua gloriae spes, En φιλοδοξία adest, quae ad illam expetendaminflammat. Si qua regnandi occasio: En φιλαρχία, quae ad regnum affectandum exstimulat. In summa: Nemo est ex sanctissimis, cuius mens non sit circumsepta erroribus, voluntas prauis suggestionibus; cor & omnes potentiae vitiosis desiderijs: quod qui negaverit, hunc magnum hypocritam, & insigniter stultum pronuntiauero. Nam verissime Cyprianus Serm. de Eleemos. Quisquis se inculpatum dixerit; aut superbus, aut stultus est. Cum igitur in renatis corruptae sint semperque maneant omnes, & praesertim superiores δυνάμεις, & vero illa corruptio vno ἐπιθυμίας nomine ab Apostolo comprehendatur, idcirco per illam non modo appetitus, sed mentis; non sensus, sed rationis quoque concupiscentiam notari & intelligi concludimus:

XV. Objiciunt autem 1. Communiter vocari concupiscentia carnis, ideoque in appetitu tantu sensitiuo haerere.

Resp. Caro, cum Spiritui opponitur, Scripturaephrasi notat totalem hominis corruptionem, tum quæ rationi, tum quæ appetitui adhæret Quicquidenim aduersus Spiritum concupiscit, hoc vno nomine caro dicitur: Gal. 5. v. 17. Concupiscit vero no sensus modo, sed ipsa ratio, ipsum cor, prout corruptum est. Quare hæc omnia carnis vocabulo apud Paulum intelliguntur. Qua de causa operibus carnis v. 20. annumerantur inimicitiæ, idololatriæ, æmulationes, contentiones, dissidia, hæreses, & similia, quæ non vitiosæ appetitus motiones, sed ipsius mentis & cordis actiones sunt. Imo Apostolus carni expresse tribuit τὸν νοῦς φρόνημα. Rom. 8. v. 7. Coloss. 2. v. 18 Saluator ipse hominem totum, cum omnibus potentijs vocat carnem, Ioh. 3. v. 6: nempè quatenus ex immundis immundus nascitur. Vnde apparet, carnis vocabulo Scripturam non denotare solam sensualitatem, vti loquuntur isti, vel solam appetitus sensitiui ἀταξίαν & repugnantiam, sed potiustotius, hominis, omniumque δυνάμεων deprauationem. Notetur autem, quòd carnis vox, cum Spiritui opponitur, dupliciter sumatur. 1. Concretè & materialiter, vel coniunctim pro substantia hominis, & substantiæ vitio; quo sensu dicitur Ioh. 3. v. 6. Quicquid excarne natum est, caro est. 2. Abstracte & formaliter, vel distinctim, pro solo vitio & naturæ corruptione; quo sensu dicitur. Gal. 5. v. 17. Caro concupiscit aduersus spiritum. Hinc enim formale principium, in homine existens, & spiritui resistens donotatur: XVI. Rom. 7. v: 18. Scio quod in me, hoc est, in carne mea, non habitat bonum. Hinc concludit Andradius in defens. Concil. Trid. l. 5. concupiscentiam in carne, tanquam in tabernaculo militari versari, atque inde in mentem impetum facere. Negat enim Apostolus, eum in se toto, & affirmat, tantùm in carne habitare.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: Resp. By flesh he does not understand either the substance of the body or the…

Resp. By flesh he does not understand either the substance of the body or the faculty of desiring itself. For he says that no good resides in his flesh. But indeed in the body

& with all his soul, with all his strength the Holy Spirit dwelt in Paul. For the reborn are temples of Him, 1 Cor. 6 v. 19. Wherefore by the flesh, in which nothing good dwells, he understands himself entirely, insofar as he was carnal or still contaminated by sin.

You ask: Why therefore does he distinguish himself from his flesh, by saying, I know that in me, that is in my flesh, etc.

We say that this was done on account of the gracious indwelling (κατοίκησιν) of the Holy Spirit, who was not a part of the corrupt nature. Therefore, lest anyone think that the Apostle excludes the grace of the Spirit when he says that nothing good dwells in him, he added for the sake of explanation, in the flesh, so that we might understand that he is not speaking of himself absolutely, but relatively, insofar as he has flesh or a corrupt nature.

XVII. 3. Rom. 6 v. 12 it is said: Let not sin reign in your mortal body. Therefore concupiscence does not cling to the soul, but only to the body,

We respond. Just as the soul is sometimes, so also the body is used in the Scriptures synecdochically (συνεκδοχικῶς) for the whole man, in which sense it is also taken here: for that the Apostle does not exclude the soul is evident from the fact that he immediately adds, To obey its concupiscences. But these solicit not only the members of the body, but rather the soul itself and its highest faculties.

And yet sin is said to rule in the body; when the intellect is obscured by darkness, when the will and appetite, and the whole man with all his faculties rushes into evil, and commits whatever sins. Interpreters of the Apostles note that he mentions the body for this reason: 1. because sin is propagated through the corporeal seed. 2. because it exerts itself chiefly through corporeal actions. 3. because it cares only for corporeal or earthly things, and 4. because it is most deeply rooted in the body, so that it cannot be expelled and moved from its seat except through total destruction.

XIIX. III. What is understood by the law of the members and the law of the mind?

The Apostle describes in v. 23 a grave struggle, when he says: I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind. There are therefore two athletes struggling and warring, the law of the members and the law of the mind, by which terms what is denoted is in doubt. The Scholastics have expounded this Apostolic doctrine according to Aristotelian Ethics. By the law of the members they understand sensuality; by the law of the mind, reason and natural judgment, the discriminator of the true and the good, not otherwise than as Aristotle in book 1 of the Ethics, ch. 13, makes two parts of the soul: one λογικὴν, which is reason; the other ἄλογον, which is appetite. Reason, according to him, inclines toward the best things, but appetite often rebels and draws in the contrary direction: hence he compares it to a paralytic limb, which when it is moved to the right, falls to the left and in the opposite direction. In a similar way they thought that the Apostle is here describing an ἀκρατῆ or incontinent man, who, while he is carried by reason toward the good, is snatched away by desires toward evil, not otherwise than the Ovidian Medea, who confessed concerning herself: I see the better things and approve them, I follow the worse.

XIX. But we have shown before that the Apostle is by no means speaking of the unregenerate, but of himself and therefore of the regenerate. He does not therefore attend to the struggle of reason and appetite concerning moral good before regeneration; but of flesh and Spirit concerning spiritual good after regeneration. He does not speak of the warring faculties of the soul; but of two contrary principles existing in his whole self. He does not understand by the law of the members the ἀταξίαν of appetite alone, but original concupiscence, corrupting all powers. Thus Augustine expounded it in book 6 against Julian, ch. 11. In these words, he says, are the groans of the saints struggling against carnal concupiscences.

XX. The Pauline scope therefore being known, the true sense of the phrase appears of its own accord. For that by the law of the members he wishes to be noted, which lusts against the Spirit. This, however, is the flesh, Gal. 5. v. 17. or sin dwelling in the flesh, Rom. 7. v. 18. in one word, innate concupiscence. For he deplores the captivity of this, that he indeed wills the good, but does not find how to perform it. This concupiscence is called a law, in that it binds a man like a law, and teaches, persuades, and prescribes nothing but evil: but by the members, in which this law is said to exist, the same thing is noted as was written before by the flesh in which evil dwells v. 18. For the members are opposed to the inner man and the mind, and therefore they signify man, insofar as he still has the vice of origin adhering to him, in one word, they signify the whole corrupt nature. For sin does not occupy only the external members, but pervades the whole man, and primarily dwells in the soul: yet it is said to exist in the members, for the same reasons which we brought forward in thesis 17.

XXI. Now indeed, because contrary things placed next to each other easily shine forth, there will no longer be any doubt what ought to be understood by the law of the mind. For this is opposed to the law of the members, that is, to the old man. Wherefore it will not denote the mind taken physically, that is, the superior part of the soul, or reason, but rather the mind accepted theologically, that is, the new man, or the gift of renewal, in one word, the Spirit, to whom the flesh is repugnant, and against whom it lusts. For these are those two athletes, two contrary principles always struggling in the children of God. For the law of the mind leads to holiness and life: the law of the members draws to unrighteousness and death: the former must increase, the latter must be diminished; the former must conquer, the latter must be suppressed. And if this happens, it will suffice in this life, for the regenerate cannot be wholly mind, nor wholly flesh, but partly mind, partly flesh, they serve both the law of God in the mind, and the law of sin in the flesh. The former, that they may not despair on account of misery; the latter, that they may not be proud on account of grace. Hence Augustine, Sermon 43 on the season, writes: In this war is the whole life of the saints, and in this war man is always in danger until he dies.

XXII. And thus far we have discussed those three questions necessary for a true understanding of the Pauline disputation: now we shall set forth in order the arguments flowing from the sixth [chapter], by which it is proved that concupiscence is sin. There are seven of them primarily.

XXIII. 1. From the explicit designation of sin.

Whatever Scripture calls sin in the proper seat of the article, that is truly and properly called sin. But Scripture calls concupiscence sin in the proper seat of this article, namely Rom. 6: 2, 6, 7, 11, 12, 13, 14, 16, 17, 18, 19; Rom. 7: 7, 8, 9, 12, 13, 14, 17, 20, 23, 24; Rom. 8: 5, 10. Therefore concupiscence is truly and properly called sin.

XXIV. The Papists object: Concupiscence is called sin, not properly, because this is not added, but figuratively, primarily because it is from sin and inclines to sin, as the Council of Trent, Session 5, holds; and Bellarmine says in book 5 of 'De Amissione Gratiae', chapter 10, that it is called sin improperly by the figure of metonymy, because it is the cause of sin if it is obeyed. Pererius in his disputation on the Epistle to the Romans, disp. 10, no. 61, writes that it is called sin: 1. because it is a defect of nature, like deafness or blindness; 2. because it is an effect of sin; 3. because it is the instrument by which original sin is propagated through the act of generation.

Response. We urge a double rule of Biblical interpretation: First: Scripture in the articles of faith in their proper seat does not speak tropically, or at least it itself indicates and declares the trope and figure. Second: The words of Scripture are always to be taken properly, unless either the coherence of the text or the analogy of faith requires a tropical exposition. Both rules are inculcated by the Fathers and are urged by the Papists when they dispute against the Calvinists concerning the Supper. For thus Bellarmine, book on the Eucharist, chapter 9: 'Principal dogmas are not accustomed to be handed down in divine letters except in proper words.' And conversely: 'This is the common rule for explaining Scripture, that we should never abandon the proper' sense of the words, unless we are compelled by some other Scripture, or by some article of faith, or certainly by the common explanation of the whole Church. For otherwise faith will perish, and only an opinion about divine things will remain, and a door will be opened to infinite errors. Therefore, however much it is not added by the Apostle that ἐπιθυμία is sin properly so called, it is nevertheless understood by the force of the rules just set forth. For the native and proper meaning always prevails in the sayings of Scripture, unless the text itself hints at the contrary. Otherwise all sayings could be explained figuratively, because it is not added that they are spoken properly: therefore all faith will perish, and any heresy could be defended, if no text is to be understood properly, unless when a term of proper diction is found attached. And why, I ask, do they explain it metonymically, when this is not added either, that the word sin ought to be understood metonymically? Nor is it sufficient to have shown that sin is spoken of ambiguously, namely either of guilt, or of the cause of sin, or of a sacrifice, which is the expiation of sin: but it is required that it be proven by firm reasons that the same metonymical meaning, and not the proper one, has a place in this text also, which they will never be able to demonstrate.

Latin:

Resp. Per carnem non intelligit vel substantiam corporis, vel ipsam facultatem appetendi. Ait enim in carne sua nil boni residere. At vero in corpore

& totâ animâ, omnibusœ; viribus Pauli habitabat Spiritus S. Huius enim templa sunt renati, 1. Cor. 6. v. 19. Quare per carnem, in quâ nil boni habitat, se totum, quatenus erat carnalis vel peccato adhuc contaminatus, intelligit.

Inquis : Cur igitur se à carne sua distinguit, dicendo, Scio, quod in me, hoc est in carne mea. &c.

Dicimus, hoc factum esse ob gratiosam Spiritûs Sancti κατοίκησιν, qui non erat pars corruptæ naturæ. Ne ergo quis putet, Apostolum excludere gratiam Spiritus, cùm dicit, in se nil boni habitare, propterea explicationis ergò adjecit, in carne, vt intelligeremus, ipsum de se non loqui absolutè, sed respectivè, quatenus carnem vel corruptam natutam habeat.

XVII. 3. Rom. 6. v. 12. dicitur: Non regnet peccatum in vestro mortali corpore. Non igitur in anima, sed in corpore tantùm haret concupiscentia,

Respond. Vt anima nonnunquàm, ita & corpus in Scripturis συνεκδοχικῶς ponitur pro toto homine, quo etiam sensu hîc accipitur: Apostolum enim non excludere animam, vel inde patet, quòd statim addit, Ad obediendum concupiscentijs eius. Hæ autem non tantùm membra corporis, sed ipsam potius animam, summasque eius potentias solicitant.

Et tamen dicitur peccatum in corpore dominari; quando intellectus tenebris obscuratus est, cùm voluntas & appetitus, totusque homo cum omnibus facultatibus in malum ruit, & quævis peccata perpetrat. Annotant verô interpretes Apostolorum ideò corporis meminisse, 1. quia peccatum per semen corporeum propagatur. 2. quia per actiones corporeas se potissimum exerit. 3. quia tantùm corporea vel terrena curat, & 4. quia in corpore profundissimè radicatur, vt nisi per totalem destructionem expelli suaque sede moueri nequeant.

XIIX. III. Quid per legem membrorum & legem mentis intelligatur?

Describit Apostolus v. 23. grauem luctam, cùm inquit: Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, Duo igitur athletæ luctantes & repugnantes, sunt lex membrorum, & lex mentis, quibus vocabulis quid notetur in dubio est. Scholastici doctrinam hanc Apostolicam exposuerunt secundum Ethicam Aristotelicam. Per legem etiam membrorum intelligunt sensualitatem per legem mentis-, rationem & naturale iudicium, veri bonique discretivum, non secus atque Aristoteles lib. 1. Eth. 13. duas facit animi partes vnam λογικὴν quæ sit ratio; alteram ἄλογον, quæ sit appetitus Ratio juxta ipsum inclinat ad optima, sed appetitus sæpè rebellat, & trahit in contrarium: Hinc comparat membro paralytico, quod cùm mouetur dextrorsum, cadit sinistrorsum & in oppositum. Pari modo putarunt illi, ab Apostolo hic describi hominem ἀκρατῆ vel incontinentem, qui cùm ratione feratur ad bonum, cupiditatibus abripiatur ad malum, non secus ac Medea Ovidiana, quæ fatebatur de seipsa: Video meliora proboqué Deteriora sequor.

XIX. Verum antè ostendimus, Apostolum nequaquam de non renato, sed de seipso adeoque renato loqui. Non igitur attendit pugnam rationis & appetitus circa bonum morale, ante regenerationem; sed carnis & Spiritus circa bonum spirituale post regenerationem. Non loquitur de pugnantibus facultatibus animæ; sed de duobus contrarijs principijs in se toto existentibus. Non intelligit per legem membrorum ἀταξίαν solius appetitus, sed originalem concupiscentiam, omnes vires corrumpentem. Ita exposuit Augusti 6. contra Iul. c. 11. In istis inquit, vocibus sunt gemitus sanctorum contra carnales concupiscentias dimicantium.

XX. Scopo igitur Paulino cognito, verus phraseos sensus vltrò apparet. Istud enim per legem membrorum notatum vult, quod concupiscit adversus Spiritum.
