Hoc autem est caro, Gal. 5. v. 17. vel peccatum in carne habitans, Rom. 7. v. 18. vno verbo, auita concupiscentia. Huius enim captiuationem deplorat, quòd bonum quidem velit, sed perficere non inveniat. Dicitur autem ista concupiscentia lex, eo quod hominem instar legis obstringat, & non nisi mala doceat, suadeat, prescribat: per membra verò, in quibus lex ista dicitur existere, idem notatur, quod antè per carnem in qua malum habitare scribit v. 18. Opponuntur enim membra interiori homini & menti, ideaque significant hominem, quatenus adhuc adhærens habet originis vitium, vno verbo, significant totam naturam corruptam. Neque enim peccatum externa tantum membra occupat, sed totum hominem pervadit, & in anima primariò habitat: in membris tamen existere dicitur, ob easdem causas, quas thes. 17. adduximus.

XXI. Iam verò, quia contraria juxta se posita facilè elucescunt, dubium amplius nullum erit, quid per legem mentis intelligi debeat. Hæc enim opponitur legi membrorum, hoc est, homini veteri. Quare non notabit mentem physicè sumtam, hoc est, partem animæ superiorem, vel rationem, sed potius mentem Theologicè acceptam, hoc est, hominem novum, vel donum renouationis, vno verbo, Spiritum, cui caro repugnat, & aduersus quem concupiscit. Hi enim sunt duo illi athletæ, duo contraria principia in filijs Dei semper reluctantia. Lex enim mentis ducit ad sanctimoniam & vitam: lex membrorum trahit iniustitiam & mortem: Illam oportet crescere, hanc minui; illam vincere, hanc supprimi. Quod si fiat, in hac vita sufficiet, Renati enim non possunt esse toti mens, neque toti caro, sed partim mens, partim caro, seruiunt tum legi Dei mente, tum legi peccati carne. Illud, ne desperent propter miseriam; hoc, ne superbiant propter gratiam. Hinc Augustin. Serm. 43. de tempore scribit : In isto bello est tota vita sanctorum, & in hoc bello semper homo periclitatur, quousque moriatur.

XXII. Et hactenus tres istas quæstiones ad verum disputationis Paulinæ intellectum necessarias discussimus: nunc argumenta ex sextu fluentia, quibus probatur, concupiscentiam esse peccatum ordine adponemus. Sunt illorum septem potissimum.

XXIII. 1. A diserta peccati appellatione.

Quicquid Scriptura in propria sede articuli, peccatum appellat, istud est verè & propriè dictum peccatũ. Atqui Scriptura concupiscentiam in propria sede huius articuli vocat peccatum, nempè Rom. 6. v. 2 6. 7. 11. 12. 13 14 16. 17. 18. 19. Rom. 7. v. 7. 8. 9. 12. 13. 14, 17. 20. 23. 24. Rom. 8. v. 5. 10. Ergo concupiscentia est verè & proprie dictum peccatum.

XXIV. Excipiunt Pontificij: Concupiscentiam vocari peccatum, non proprie, quia hoc non addatur, sed figurate, primitùm quia ex peccato est, & ad peccatum inclinat, vti habet Concil. Trid. Sess. 5. et Bell. ait l. 5. de A. G. c. 10. vocari peccatum improprie per figuram metonymiæ, quòd sit causa peccati si ei obediatur. Pererius in epist. ad Rom. disp. 10. num. 61. scribit. peccatum dici, 1. quia sit vitium naturæ, vt surditas, cæcitas. 2. quia sit peccati effectus. 3. quia sit instrumentum, quo per actum generationis peccatum originis propagetur.

Respond. Vrgenius duplicem regulam interpretationis Biblicæ: Prima: Scriptura ac articulis fidei in sede propria non loquitur tropice, aut certe tropum & figuram ipsa innuit & declarat Secunda: Verba Scripturæ semper sunt accipienda proprie; nisi vel textus cohærentia, vel fidei analogia tropicam expositionem requirat. Vtraque regula inculcatur à Patribus, & vrgetur è Pontificijs, quando disputant contra Calvinianos de Cœna. Ita enim Bell. lib. de Euch. c. 9. Dogmata præcipua non nisi Propriis verbis tradi solent in diuinis literis. Et vicissim: Communis regula explicandæ Scripturæ hæc est, vt Nunquã dimittamus propriam verborum sensum, Nisi cogamur ab alia aliqua Scriptura, vel ab aliquo articulo fidei, aut certè à communi totius Ecclesiæ explicatione. Alioqui enim peribit fides, & remanebit sola opinio de rebus diuinis, & aperietur porta infinitis erroribus. Quantumvis ergo ab Apostolo non addatur, ἐπιθυμίαν peccatum esse propriè dictum, vi tamen regularum modo expositarum subintelligitur. Natiua enim & propria significatio in dictis Scripturæ semper obtinet, nisi textus ipse contrarium subinnuat. Aliàs omnia dicta figuratè possent exponi, quia non adjicitur, dici propriè: Omnis igitur fides peribit, & quævis hæresis defendi poterit, si nullus textus propriè sit intelligendus, nisi cùm terminus propriæ dictionis adiunctus reperitur. Et cur quæso metonymicè exponunt; cùm nec hoc additum sit, vocem peccati metonymicè intelligi debere? Neque sufficit ostendisse; peccatum ambiguè dici, nimirum vel de culpa, vel de causa peccati, vel de sacrificio, qd est peccati expiatio: Verùm requiritur, vt firmis rationibus euincatur, eandem significationem metonymicam; & non propriam in hoc etiam textu locum habere, quod nunquã demonstrare poterūt.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: XXV. II. From illegality

XXV. II. From illegality.

Whatever is repugnant to divine law, that is sin properly so called. Concupiscence in the regenerate remains repugnant to divine law. Therefore it is sin properly so called. The major premise is certain from the definition of sin in 1 John 3, ἁμαρτία ἐστιν ἀνομία. The minor is proven by the assertion of the Apostle, Rom. 7:7, 'I did not know concupiscence, unless the law said: Thou shalt not covet.' By which prohibition we have proven above in thesis 13 that every ἐπιθυμίαν, both original and actual, is forbidden. Therefore the conclusion of our argument stands firm. For the defined cannot be removed from that to which the definition truly applies.

XXVI.

But the Papists have devised various exceptions to this most firm argument, for whose cause they easily understand that their own throat is being sought. There are four of them primarily, which we shall see in order.

XXVII. 1. Bellarmine, book 5, on the Grace of the First Man, chapter 10, distinguishes between precepts. Some, he says, command only the manner, as fighting against enemies; some the means and the end, as conquering enemies. The former bind, the latter do not. But he says the precept about not coveting is of such a kind. The means of salvation, according to him, is not to resist concupiscences. The end and perfection is not to covet at all. He maintains that we are bound by the law to the former only, not to the latter. The same is the exception of Stapleton in his Antidotes, when he wrote: The first motion of concupiscence is prohibited by the law not by way of obligation, under penalty of mortal or venial sin, but by way of doctrine, concerning the disease of nature and seeking a physician, because the end of the law here is that we should be free from all depraved concupiscence.

I respond 1. Concupiscence is either a good thing, or a bad thing, or indifferent. It is not good nor indifferent, since the Apostle expressly calls it evil in verse 21, nor do the Papists dissent from this. If therefore it is evil, it will be contrary to the law. For as every practical good formally consists in εὐνομίᾳ, or conformity with the law: so every evil consists in ἀνομίᾳ or departure from the law. Therefore they must concede one or the other, either that concupiscence is not evil, or that it is truly repugnant to the law. The former is against the Apostle. Wherefore the latter is true; from which it follows that concupiscence is prohibited not by way of doctrine only, but by way of obligation. For if this were not so, how would ἐπιθυμία be repugnant to the law?

2. The mind of the Apostle, reborn through the Spirit, and the law of God wanted the same thing, as is gathered from verse 16, where he affirms that he consents to the law of God. But the mind of the Apostle did not want to feel concupiscence. Therefore this also is repugnant to the law of God, and therefore it is prohibited by way of obligation. To this point looks that statement of Augustine, Sermon 5 on the words of the Apostle: You who say, O law! You shall not covet, and I do not want to covet. My infirmity does not fulfill the law, but my will praises the law.

3. The Apostle in verse 14 says of himself: The law is spiritual, I am carnal, sold under sin. Note here the opposition between the spiritual law and carnal concupiscence, under which Paul was sold. For whatever departs from the spiritual law and causes the reborn to be carnal, that is ἀνομία and is repugnant to the law, and consequently is prohibited by way of obligation.

4. The law of God and the law of sin are opposites, as is clear from v. 25. Therefore, whatever approaches the law of sin, that departs from the law of God. But the flesh, to which concupiscence pertains, approaches the law of sin, because the Apostle confesses that he serves the law of sin with the flesh. Therefore it departs from the law of God; indeed, it is said to be repugnant to the law of the mind, v. 29. From which it follows in turn that concupiscence, being repugnant to the law of the mind and of God, is prohibited not by way of doctrine, but of obligation.

5. This distinction is fabricated and lacks any foundation. For this is the form of law, that it obligates one to perform what it prescribes. For if it only teaches, it is not a law, but a moral rule; not a precept, but a counsel. Nor can a prohibition even be conceived without obligation. For to prohibit a thing legally is not to warn someone, but rather to obligate them not to do it, and to impose penalties if they do. Either, therefore, ἐπιθυμία is prohibited by the law of the Lord, or it is not. If the latter, how is it said to be repugnant to the law of the mind, which includes the law of God? If the former, how are we not obligated by that law?

6. The law of God obligates us not only to the means, but to the end itself. Its end is twofold: 1. Internal, which consists in perfect integrity and the love of God in every way, without any concupiscence. 1 Tim. 1 v. 5. But the law requires this very thing from us and binds us to it, as interpreted by Christ in Matt. 22 v. 37, 38, 39, Luke 10 v. 28, and by the Apostle, Rom. 13 v. 8, 9. if the law did not oblige to this end, it would oblige in no way at all, because all the remaining precepts tend to that. 2. external, which is the attainment of eternal life. He who desires this is obliged to the full fulfillment of the law by the law itself. Matt. 19. v. 17. Luke 10. v. 18. Whoever therefore shall have violated even the least precept, is the least, that is, is nothing in the kingdom of heaven, Matt. 5. v. 29. and consequently, we are obliged by the law regarding all precepts, and all particles of the precepts under penalty of eternal damnation.

7. It is false that not to covet does not pertain to the external end, nor to the means of the law. For it is a part of perfect justice, which is the means of obtaining salvation from the law. For he who covets does not keep the law: and therefore is not saved by the law. Furthermore, the falsity of the Jesuit statement is evident from the fact that in Rom. 13. v. 9. the law concerning not coveting is joined with the law concerning not killing and not committing adultery, and is held in the same estimation. As therefore we are obliged not to commit adultery, so we are obliged not to covet. But indeed we are obliged not to commit adultery as a means of obtaining salvation. Therefore by equal reasoning we are obliged not to covet.

8. From the violation of which law follows a curse, that is proposed by way of obligation. But from the violation of the law concerning not coveting follows a curse. Therefore it is proposed by way of obligation. The minor is proved from Deut. 27. v. 26. Gal. 3. v. 10. Cursed is he who shall not have remained in ALL things which are written in the book of the law. Therefore he also is cursed who covets evil things. For he does not keep the law concerning not coveting.

9. These similarities have no force of proof. For either it is in the strength of the soldiers to win, and then they are truly obliged if the leader obtains victory: or it is not in their own strength, and then a precept of this kind is not accustomed to be given, nor ought it to be. Now indeed the law concerning not coveting was enacted and imprinted on nature before the fall and therefore at that time, when not to covet was in our power. Wherefore it truly and properly obliged. Nay, it even now obliges, for God does not change His will, although we have been changed by the fall. He rightly demands His due, although we are unable to pay.

XXIIX. 2. Stapleton objects that concupiscence is prohibited by the law, not as a sin, but as an evil and a disease of nature; not so that we are bound to punishment, but so that we are driven to seek a Physician.

Response. 1. It is an ἀντίφασις ἐν προσκειμένῳ [contradiction in terms], to be prohibited not as a sin. For whatever is prohibited by the moral law is by that very fact a sin. For it is prohibited because it is contrary to the divine will. Whatever departs from this cannot but be a sin. For to sin in general is to cross the rule. Therefore, when something is done which is prohibited by law, by that very fact it deviates from the rule and is a sin.

2. That evil which is called a disease of nature is either an evil of fault or an evil of punishment. A third [category] regarding the evil of man will not be given. And yet, formally, it is not an evil of punishment: for thus it would be from God, and in itself good. It is indeed sometimes called the punishment of the first fall, but this ought to be understood not of the disease itself, as it is a disease of nature, but only of the divine permission and the withdrawal of grace. For God punished Adam, not by efficiently sending in the corruption itself, but by withdrawing grace, from which that spontaneously followed. Since, therefore, the disease of nature formally, as it is a disease, does not have God as its author, we conclude that it is an evil not of punishment but of fault, and consequently a sin properly so called.

3. That every law, if it is violated, binds to punishment is manifest from Deut. 27. v. 26. But that it simultaneously impels one to seek a physician, this is accidental.

4. That exception is against the scope and mind

of the Apostle. For from the fact that the law says, Thou shalt not covet, he himself concludes that concupiscence clinging in his members is sin. How so? Because the law forbids it. It is not, therefore, a disease without sin, but a disease with sin, or rather sin itself. For every disease or corruption of the soul, as such, is truly sin.

5. Concupiscence is considered in two ways, either before or after regeneration. There, guilt and act are present: here, the guilt passes away, yet the act, or the very οὐσία of concupiscence, remains. Now I ask, why is ἐπιθυμία before regeneration sin? And nothing else can be answered than because it is such in itself and by itself that it departs from the divine law. Furthermore, because this very ἐπιθυμία remains after regeneration, and indeed in such a way that its essence is not changed, why then is it determined not to depart from the law? For either the sense of the law or the nature of concupiscence will be changed. Not the sense of the law, since this, no less than the will of God, of which it is an icon, is immutable. Therefore, what the law forbids, and in what sense it forbids it once, it forbids always in that same sense. But the law forbids this disease of nature, as they call it, or the root of concupiscence, before παλιγγενεσίαν, as properly called sin, deviating from its rule.

Therefore it also forbids it after παλιγγενεσίαν. Nor is the οὐσία of ἐπιθυμία changed. For it does not happen that concupiscence becomes non-concupiscence, or disease becomes non-disease: but that very vice remains which was present before, and was concreated with nature. Why then after regeneration is it not numbered among sins properly so called? Why does that which retains the same essence change its genus? Why is that which is evil and sin in itself, intrinsically, and ἑαυτῶς, pronounced not evil and not sin on account of an accidental respect, namely remission? Either, therefore, let them say that concupiscence does not remain in the reborn, but is utterly destroyed, or if its essence remains, let them admit that it is properly sin, since in itself and essentially it is nothing other than evil and sin prohibited by law.

XXIX. 3. Others object, if that commandment, Thou shalt not covet, forbids original concupiscence, it will follow that the law was given to brute flesh, in which that concupiscence resides, and not to man, endowed with reason and will, in whose power it is not.

Response. There is no consequence, since the Apostle affirms both, that concupiscence is prohibited by the law, and that the law was given to rational man.

2. Concupiscence does not adhere to brute flesh, or to the sensitive appetite alone; but it has pervaded and corrupted the whole man and all his faculties, as we demonstrated above.

3. A false hypothesis is presupposed, that the law does not oblige unless it is possible and can be kept. For, because we cannot love God with our whole heart, does God therefore not require full love from us? Thus, although we are never free from concupiscence, God nevertheless justly demands and commands that we do not covet, of which more will be treated at length in the place concerning free will.

XXX. 4. Finally, some object that not everything which is repugnant to the law is ἁμαρτίαν [sin], since both the devil and the whole nature of man are rebellious to the law. Therefore, these things are ἀντιστρέφοντα [convertible], but not ἀντίστροφα [reciprocal].

Response. It is perpetually and reciprocally true: that every ἀνομίαν [lawlessness] is ἁμαρτίαν [sin], and vice versa. However, the ἀνομία [lawlessness] itself ought not to be confused with the ἀνόμῳ [lawless] subject, which is not sin itself, but is corrupted by sin. But we have responded to this at length in disp. 3, quest. 1, th. 32.

XXXI. 3. From the Apostolic description. Paul depicts the concupiscence inherent in himself and all the regenerate in such a way that no doubt can arise that it is truly and properly sin. For 1. he says it is not good, but evil. v. 18, 21, 2. he describes the privatively v. 15. 16. 18. 19. 3. positively v. 15, 23. 4. He calls it sin, under which he is sold, and on account of which he is carnal v. 14. 5. he says it fights against the commandment of the Lord, Thou shalt not covet, verse 7. 6. to fight against the law of the mind and the Spirit v. 23. 7. To take captive into the law of sin v. the same. 8. To be an evil to be crucified, Rom. 6. v. 6. and to be mortified Rom. 8. 13. 9. and so much so, that all the pious must exclaim, Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death? verse 24. From which ὑποτύπωσις it appears most clearly that concupiscence is a thing neither indifferent, nor good, but rather a certain evil, and indeed an evil not of punishment, but of fault, and of such a fault that it fights against the law of the Lord, both privatively and positively, and therefore is sin most properly so called, not indeed reigning, because he says he serves the law of God with his mind verse 25. nor condemning, because there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus Rom. 8. v. 1. nor mortal, because if we mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, we shall have life, Rom. 8. v. 13. but of such a kind that, considered in itself, it is indeed contrary to the law and hateful to God, yet when it is mortified by the Spirit, it does not bind the regenerate with the guilt of condemnation. That therefore it is not imputed, this is from the grace of God, but that it fights against the law, this is from the nature of sin. But every thing ought to be judged from itself and its own nature, not from that which happens extrinsically. For accidental respects do not abolish the essences of things. Wherefore neither does the dismissal of guilt take away the nature of ἐπιθυμία. It indeed makes a mortal sin not mortal, a reigning one not reigning, and thus changes the qualities but does not make a sin not a sin, because thus it would change its nature, nay, would clearly take it away, which is against Scripture and experience.

XXXII. 4. From the hindered fulfillment of the law. Whatever hinders and excludes the perfect fulfillment of the law, this is ἀνομία, and consequently is properly sin. But concupiscence hinders perfect fulfillment of the law. For this is the reason that the reborn remain carnal, sold under sin, Rom. 7. v. 14. and when they wish to do good, evil lies close to them, v. 21. Therefore ἀνομία and consequently it is properly sin. XXXIII. Scotus objects that what is called evil, or inclines toward sin, and hinders perfection, is not immediately sin. For even a bodily disease is accustomed to be the cause of anger, impatience, etc., and yet they are not therefore sins. Response. There is a great dissimilarity between diseases and concupiscence. The former are not in all, nor always, nor of themselves, but accidentally; the latter is in all and always, and of itself is the cause of sin, and hinders perfection. The former have no dissonance with the law, the latter perpetually struggles against the law. Whence it follows that concupiscence (because it is the cause of sins, hindering the saints from observing the law as they wish) is condemned by the law, and therefore is rightly numbered among sins properly so called.

XXXIV. V. From the merit of eternal damnation. Whatever merits everlasting damnation is sin. But concupiscence in itself and of itself merits everlasting damnation. Therefore it is sin. The minor is proved from Rom. 8. v. 13. If you live according to the flesh, you will die. But if by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, you will live; from which text it is evident that unless the flesh and concupiscence are tamed in the reborn, it makes the person himself guilty of hell. Therefore, in itself and δι᾽ ἑαυτῶς it is evil, and thus sin, which in itself merits the curse of the law, yet, when it is suppressed, it is not imputed to the person.

XXXV. VI. From misery. Whatever renders men miserable in the spiritual life before God, and from which they are not liberated except through Christ, that is to be held in the place of sin. But indeed these things agree with concupiscence. For on account of this the Apostle exclaims v. 24. ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, Wretched man that I am! who will deliver me? And he adds v. 25. The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord: Nor does the Apostle speak of the misery of punishment, since the regenerate are not subject to punishments properly so called, and in tribulations rather exult with the Apostle, Rom. 5. verse 3. but of the misery of guilt, on account of which evil lies near to him, he does not find how to perform good, but perpetually feels the law of the members resisting the law of the mind.

Latin:

XXV. II. Ab illegalitate.

Quicquid repugnat legi divinæ, illud peccatum est propriè dictum Concupiscentia in renatis reliqua repugnat legi diuinæ. Ergo est peccatum propriè dictum. Maior certa est ex definitione peccati 1. Ioh. 3. ἁμαρτία ἐστιν ἀνομία Minor probatur ab asseveratione Apostoli, Rom. 7. v 7. Concupiscentiam nesciebam, nisi lex diceret: Non concupisces. Quo interdicto omnem ἐπιθυμίαν tàm originalem quàm actualem prohiberi supra thes. 13. probatum dedimus. Firma igitur perstat argumenti nostri conclusio. Neq; enim definitum removeri potest ab eo, cui verè competit definitio.

XXVI.

Varias verò exceptiones commienti sunt Papicolæ ad rationē hanc firmissimam, quæ causæ suæ jugulum peti facilè intelligunt. Sunt earum quatuor potissimum, quas ordine videbimus.

XXVII. 1. Bell. l. 5. de A. G. c. 10. distinguit inter præcepta. Quædam ait, imperare solùm modò, vt pugna contra hostes; quædam medium & finem, vt vincere hostes. Illa obligare, hæc non item. Tale verò esse præceptum de non concupiscendo. Medium salutis iuxta ipsum est, concupiscentiis non resistere. Finis & perfectio est, plane non concupiscere. Ad illud tantùm; non ad hoc per legem nos obstringi statuit, Eadem est exceptio Stapletoni in Antidotis, cùm scripsit, Primum concupiscentiæ motum lege prohiberi non per modum obligationis, sub pœna peccati mortalis aut venialis, sed per modū doctrinæ, de naturæ morbo & quærendo medico, quia legis hic sit finis, ut omni concupiscentiâ prauâ careamus.

Respond 1. Concupiscentia vel res bona est, vel mala, vel indifferens. Non bona est nec indifferens, quoniam Apostolus disertè voçat malum v. 21. neque hoc dissitentur Pontificij. Si ergo mala, erit legi contraria. Vt enim omne bonum πρακτικὸν formaliter consistit in ἐυνομίᾳ; vel conformitate cum lege: sic omne malum in ἀνομίᾳ vel recessu à lege. Alterutrum igitur concedant oportet, aut concupiscentiam malã non esse, aut legi verè repugnare. Illud cõtra Apostolum. Quare hoc verum; vnde sequitur, concupiscentiã non per modum doctrinæ tãtùm, sed per modū obligationis prohiberi Hoc enim ni esset, quomodo Ἐπιθυμίαν legi repugnaret?

2. Mens Apostoli per Spiritum renata, & lex Dei volebant idem, vti colligitur ex v. 16. vbi se legi Dei consentire adfirmat. Atqui mens Apostoli nolebat sentire concupiscentiam. Ergo hoc etiam legi Dei repugnat, ideoque per modum obligationis prohibetur. Huc spectat istud August. Serm. 5. de verbis Apost. qui dicis, ô lex! Non concupisces, & ego nolo concupiscere. Non implet legem infirmitas mea, sed legem laudat voluntas mea.

3. Apostolus v 14. de se ait: Lex spiritualis est, Ego gem carnalis sum venundatus sub peccato. Nota hic oppositionem inter legem spiritualem, & concupiscentiam carnalem, sub qua Paulus erat venundatus. Quicquid enim recedit à lege spirituali, & facit, vt renati sint carnales, istud ἀνομία est legíque repugnat, & per consequens prohibetur per modum obligationis. Talis verò cùm esse asseratur concupiscentia: erit etiam ἀνομία per modum obligationis interdicta.

4. Lex dei & lex peccati sunt opposita, vt patet ex v. 25. Quod igitur accedit ad legem peccati, illud recedit à lege Dei. At vero caro, ad quam pertinet concupiscentia, accedit ad legem peccati, quia fatetur Apostolus, se carne seruire legi peccati. Ergo recedit à lege Dei, Imò repugnare dicitur legi mentis. v. 29. Ex quo vicissim sequitur, concupiscentiam legi mentis & Dei repugnantem per modum non doctrinae, sed obligationis prohiberi.

5 Distinctio ista est conficta, & caret omni fundamento. Haec enim est forma legis, vt obliget ad praestandum id, quod praescribit. Si enim tantùm doceat, non lex est, sed regula moralis, non praeceptum, sed consilium. Neque vel concipi tantùm potest prohibitio sine obligatione. Rem enim legaliter prohibere, non est monere aliquem, sed potius obligare, ne faciat, & poenas indicere, si faciat. Aut igitur ἐπιθυμία lege Domini prohibita est, aut non est. Si hoc, quomodo legi mentis, quae includit legem Dei, repugnare dicitur? Sin illud, quomodo per istam legem non obligamur?

6. Non solùm ad media, sed ad ipsum finem lex Dei nos obligat. Finis ejus duplex est, 1. Internus, qui consistit in perfecta integritate, & omnimoda Dei dilectione, sine omni concupiscentia. 1. Tim. 1. v. 5. Hoc ipsum verò lex à nobis requirit, & ad istud nos obstringit, interprete Christo Matth. 22. v. 37. 38. 39. Luc. 10. v. 28. & Apostolo, Rom. 13. v. 89. Si enim ad hunc finẽ lex non obligaret, nullo prorsus modo obligaret, quia omnia præcepta reliqua eò tẽdunt. 2. externus, qui est consecutio vitæ æternæ Hâc qui desiderat, ad plenam legis impletionẽ per ipsam legem obligatur. Matth. 19. v. 17. Luc. 10. v. 18. Quisquis igitur vel minimum præceptum violauerit, minimus, hoc est, nullus est in regno cœlorum, Matth. 5. v. 29. & per consequens, à lege quoad omnia pręcepta, & omnes pręceptorũ particulas sub pœna æternæ damnationis obligamur.

7. Falsum est, non concupiscere ad finem externum, non media legis pertinere. Est enim pars justitiæ perfectæ, quæ medium est consequendæ salutis ex lege. Qui enim concupiscit, legem non seruat: ideoque per legem non saluatur. Patet insuper falsitas effati IesuVVitici ex eo, quòd Rom. 13. v. 9. lex de non concupiscendo cum lege de non occidendo, & non mœchando conjungitur, eodemque censu habetur. Vt igitur obligamur ad non mœchandum, sic ad non concupiscendum At verò obligamur ad non mœchandum tanquam ad medium consequendi salutem. Ergo pari ratione obligamur ad non concupiscendum.

8. Ex cuius legis violatione sequitur maledictio, illa proponitur per modum obligationis. Atqui ex violatione legis de nõ concupiscendo sequitur maledictio. Ergo proposita est per modum obligationis. Minor probatur ex Deut. 27. v. 26. Gal. 3. v. 10. Maledictus qui non permăserit in OMNIBVS quæ scripta sunt in libro legis. Igitur & iste maledictus est qui concupiscit mala. Non enim seruat legem de non concupiscendo.

9. Similia ista nullam probationis vim habent. Aut enim in militum viribus est vincere, & tùm verè obligantur, si dux victoriam percipiat: aut non est in ipsorum viribus, & tunc præceptum huiusmodi dari non solet, nec debet. Iam verò lex de non concupiscendo, lata est & naturæ impressa antè lapsum adeoque isto tempore, vbi non concupiscere in nostra erat potestate. Quapropter verè & propriè obligauit. Imò etiamnum obligat, Deus enim voluntatem suam non mutat, licet nos per lapsum mutati simus. Iure poscit debitum suum, licèt nos soluere nequeamus.

XXIIX. 2. Stapletonus excipit, concupiscentiam lege prohiberi, non vt peccatum, sed vt malum & morbum naturæ; non vt obligemur ad supplicium, sed vt adigamur ad quærendum Medicum.

Respond. 1. Est ἀντίφασις ἐν προσκειμένῳ, prohiberi non ut peccatum. Quicquid enim lege morali prohibetur, hoc ipso peccatum est. Nam ideo prohibetur, quia voluntati diuinæ contrariatur. Ab hac quicquid recedit, non potest non peccatum esse. Peccare enim in genere, est regulam transire. Quando igitur aliquid fit, quod lege prohibitum est, hoc ipso à regula declinat, & peccatum est.

2. Malum istud, quod vocatur morbus naturæ aut malum culpæ est, aut malum pœnæ. Tertium in circa malum hominis non dabitur. Atqui formaliter non est malum pœnæ: sic enim à Deo foret, & in sese bonum. Dicitur quidem nonnunquam pœna primi lapsus, sed hoc intelligi debet non de morbo ipso, quâ est naturæ morbus, sed tantùm de diuinæ permissione & subtractione gratiæ, Puniuit enim Deus Adamum, non efficienter immittendo ipsam corruptionem, sed subtrahendo gratiam, vnde illa spontè sequebatur. Cum igitur morbus naturæ formaliter, vt morbus est, Deum authorem non habeat, concludimus, esse malum non pœnæ sed culpæ, & per consequens peccatum propriè dictum.

3. Quòd omnis lex, si violetur, ad pœnam obliget, manifestum est ex Deut. 27. v. 36 Quod autem ad medicum quærendum simul impellat, hoc est per accidens.

4. Exceptio ista est contra scopum & mentem

Apostoli. Ex eo enim quod lex dicit, Non concupisces ipse concludit, concupiscentiam in membris suis hærentem esse peccatum. Qui ita? Quia lex illam prohibet. Non igitur morbus est sine peccato, sed morbus cum peccato, vel potius ipsum peccatum. Omnis enim animi morbus vel corruptio, quà talis, verè peccatum est.

5. Concupiscentia consideratur dupliciter, vel ante, vel post regenerationem. Ibi adest reatus & actus: Hic transit reatus, manet tamen actus, vel ipsa concupiscentiæ ὀσία. Iam quæro, cur ἐπιθυμία ante regenerationem peccatum sit? Et nihil aliud responderi poterit, quàm quia in se & per se talis est, ut recedat à lege divina. Porrò, quia hæc ipsa ἐπιθυμία manet post regenerationem, & quidem ita ut ejus essentia non immutetur, cur ergo tum à lege non recedere statuitur? Aut enim legis sensus, aut concupiscentiæ natura mutabitur. Non sensus legis, cùm hæc non minùs ut Dei voluntas, cuius est icon, sit immutabilis. Quod ergò lex & quo sensu semel prohibet, istud eoque sensu semper prohibet. Atqui morbum istum naturæ, ut vocant, vel radicem concupiscentiæ lex prohibet ante παλιγγενεσίαν, tanquam propriè dictum peccatum, à sua regula deflectens.

Ergo etiam prohibet post παλιγγενεσίαν Neque mutatur ἐπιθυμίας ἐσία. Non enim ex concupiscentia fit non concupiscentia, aut ex morbo fit non morbus: sed illud ipsum remanet vitium, quod anteadfuit, & naturæ concreatum est. Cur ergo post regenerationem peccatis propriè dictis non annumeratur? Cur quod eandem essentiam retinet, genus suum mutat? Cur id, quod per se, intrinsecè & ἑαυτῶς malum & peccatum est, ob accidentalem respectum, nempè remissionem, non malum, non peccatum esse pronunciatur? Aut ergo dicant, concupiscentiam non manere in renatis, sed penitus deleri, aut si essentia eius remanet, fateantur oportet, propriè peccatum esse, cum per se & essentialiter nil aliud sit, quàm malum & peccatum lege prohibitum.

XXIX. 3. Alij excipiunt, si, præceptum istud, Non concupisces, vetat concupiscentiam originalem, efficietur legem datam esse brutæ carni, in qua inest concupiscentia ista, non autem homini, ratione & voluntate prædito, in cujus potestate non est.

Respond. Nulla est consequentia, quoniam Apostolus vtrumque adfirmat, tum concupiscentiam lege prohibitam, tum legem homini rationali datam esse.

2. Concupiscentia non hæret in bruta carne, vel solo appetitu sensitiuo; sed pervasit & corrupit totum hominem omnesque facultates, vt suprà demonstrauimus.

3. Præsupponitur falsa hypothesis, legem non obligare, nisi possibilis sit & seruari queat. Num enim, quia Deum toto corde diligere non possumus, Deus propterea plenam dilectionem à nobis non requirit? Ita, licet concupiscentia nunquam careamus, iuste tamen Deus exigit & præcepit, ne concupiscamus, de quo fusius agetur in loco de lib. arbitrio.

XXX. 4. Tandem excipiunt nonnulli, Non omne quod legi repugnat, esse ἁμαρτίαν cùm & diaboli & tota hominis natura legi rebelles. Esse igitur ista ἀντιστρέφοντα, sed non ἀντίστροφα.

Respond. Perpetuò & reciprocè verum: omnem ἀνομίαν esse ἁμαρτίαν, & contra. Non autem confundi debet ἀνομία ipsa, cum subjecto ἀνόμῳ quod non ipsum peccatum, sed peccato corruptum est. Verùm ad hoc prolixè respondimus disp 3. quæst. 1. th. 32.

XXXI. 3. A descriptione Apostolica. Concupiscentiam sibi cunctisque renatis inhærentem ita depingit Paulus, vt nullum oriri queat dubium, illam verò proprièq; peccatum esse. Nam 1. dicit esse non bonum, sed malum. v. 18. 21, 2. describit priuatiuè v. 15. 16. 18. 19. 3. positiuè v. 15, 23. 4. Vocat peccatum, sub quo venundatus, & propter quod carnalis sit v. 14. 5. ait pugnare cum præcepto Domini, Non concupisces, vers. 7. 6. repugnare legi mentis & Spiritus v. 23. 7. Captiuare in lege peccati v. eodem. 8. Esse malum crucifigendum, Rom. 6. v. 6. & mortificandum Rom. 8. 13. 9. adeoque tantùm, vt omnibus pijs exclamandum sit, Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit à corpore mortis huius? vers. 24. Ex qua ὑποτυπώσει luculētissimè apparet, concupiscentiam esse rem nec indifferentem, nec bonam, sed potius malum quid, & quidem malum non pœnæ, sed culpæ, & talis culpæ, quæ repugnet legi Domini, tum priuatiuè, tum positiuè, adeoq́; peccatum esse propriissimè dictum, non quidem regnans, quia dicit se mente seruire legi Dei vers. 25. nec damnans, quia nihil damnationis his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu Rom. 8. v. 1. nec mortale, quia si Spiritu facta carnis mortificemus, vitam habebimus, Rom. 8. v. 13. sed huiusmodi, quod in se cōsideratum, legi quidem contrarium & Deo exosum est, attamen cum Spiritu mortificatur, renatos damnationis reatu non obstringit. Quòd ergò non imputatur, hoc est à gratia Dei, quod verò legi repugnat, hoc est à natura peccati. Vnaquæqué autem res debet ex seie & sua natura iudicari, nō ab eo, quod extrinsecus accidit. Nam respectus accidentales non abolent rerum essentias. Quare nec dimissio reatus, tollet naturam ἐπιθυμίας. Facit quidem ex peccato mortali non mortale, ex regnante non regnans, adeoque mutat qualitates sed non facit ex peccato non peccatum, quia sic naturam eius mutaret, imò planè tolleret, quod contra Scripturam & experientiam.

XXXII. 4. Ab impedita legis impletione. Quicquid perfectam legis impletionem impedit, & excludit, hoc ἀνομία, & per consequens propriè peccatum est. Atqui concupiscentia impedit perfectam legis impletionem. Haec enim in causa est, vt renati maneāt carnales, venundati sub peccato, Rom. 7. v. 14. & cùm facere volunt bonum, malum ijs adjaceat, v. 21. Ergò ἀνομία & per consequēs propriè peccatum est. XXXIII. Scotus excipit, non statim peccatum esse quod malum dicitur, vel ad peccatum inclinat, & profectionem impedit. Nam & morbus corporis solere causam esse iracundiae, impatientiae, &c. nec tamen ideò peccata esse. Respond. Magna est dissimilitudo inter morbos & concupiscentiam. Illi non in omnibus, nec semper, nec per se, sed ex accidenti; haec in omnibus & semper, & per se causa peccati est, & perfectionem impedit. Illi nullam cum lege dissonantiam habent, haec legi perpetuò reluctatur. Vnde sequitur, concupiscentiam (quia peccatorum causa est, sanctos impediens, ne legem, vt volunt, obseruent) lege damnari, ideoque peccatis propriè dictis rectè annumerari.

XXXIV. V. A merito æternæ damnationis. Quicquid meretur damnationem sempiternam, peccatum est. Atqui concupiscentia in se & per se meretur damnationem sempiternam. Ergo peccatum est. Minor probatur ex Rom. 8. v. 13. Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Si autem Spiritu facta carnis mortificaueritis, viuetis; ex quo textu patet euidenter quod nisi caro & concupiscentia in renatis dometur, ipsam personam gehennæ ream faciat. Per se igitur & δι᾽ ἑαυτῶς mala est, adeoque peccatum, quod in se legis maledictionem meretur, attamen, cùm supprimitur, personæ non imputatur.

XXXV. VI. A miseria. Quicquid homines in vita spirituali coram Deo miseros reddit, & à quo non nisi per Christum liberantur, illud peccati loco habendum. At verò ista conueniunt concupiscentiæ. Ob hanc enim exclamat Apostolus v. 24. ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit: Et subdit v. 25. Gratia Dei per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum: Nequè loquitur Apostolus de miseria pœnæ, cùm renati pœnis propriè dictis non subiaceant, & in tribulationibus cum Apostolo potius exultent, Rom. 5. verj 3. sed de miseria culpæ, propter quam sibi malum adiaceat, bonum perficere non inueniat, sed legem membrorum repugnantem legi mentis perpetuò sentiat.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: II. Reasons taken from other sayings and the analogy of faith

II. Reasons taken from other sayings and the analogy of faith.

XXXVI. 1. From all the testimonies of Scripture establishing original sin, such as Gen. 6. v. 5. c. 8. v. 21. Job 14. v. 4. Psalm 14. verses 2. 3. Psalm 19: v. 13. Psalm 51 v. 7. 12. Jerem. 17. verse 9. and similar ones, from which we gather: If every imagination of the human heart is evil, and all are conceived from unclean seed in sin properly so called, then true sin will also adhere to the regenerate, which is concupiscence. We give this reason for the consequence, because the evil of origin is not entirely removed from our mortal body in this life. This argument is therefore most firm: That which we are conceived and born in always adheres to us as regards its own ἰδίαν. But indeed we are born and conceived in sin properly so called, which the alleged testimonies prove. Therefore sin properly so called always adheres to us as regards its own ἰδίαν. We say as regards its own ἰδίαν, because we willingly concede that guilt and accidental respects are removed through renewal. Either therefore let them confess that the sin of origin expires entirely, or is transformed into another nature, or remains the same as regards its essence. The first is contrary to experience. The second incurs the same absurdity: For if the remaining evil is clearly not sin, then not only has it been changed accidentally, but rather the very essence of the evil has been entirely removed, and therefore it is not the sin of origin that remains, but that it has been totally destroyed. For that which in no way has the nature of sin, how will that be original sin? By denying the whole genus, all the species are immediately denied at the same time. Wherefore if no sin remains in the reborn, neither will original sin remain, which is absurd.

XXXVII. 2. From Galatians 5, verse 17. The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. The attributes of contraries are contrary. But indeed the concupiscence of the flesh, which is in the reborn, is contrary to the concupiscence of the Spirit. This, however, is a good work, and conformable to the law. Therefore that is an evil work and disconformable to the law, in one word, sin. For between immediate opposites, such as good and evil, έννομία and ἀνομία, holiness and sin, no third thing can be given or imagined.

XXXIIX. 3. From Hebrews 12, verse 1. It is commanded there to the reborn that they lay aside ἁμαρτίαν εὐπερίσατον, the sin which doth so easily beset. By this, however, nothing else is understood than concupiscence, which is called εὐπερίσατος according to Chrysostom, either because it easily besets us, or because it itself can be easily beset and overcome. But the active sense approaches more closely to the Apostolic scope, which is accustomed to exaggerate sin, not to extenuate it; and he warns, not that we should eradicate concupiscence entirely, because this is not placed within our powers, but that we should suppress it and take away its kingdom, lest it ensnare us with its snares. Because therefore the Apostle expressly calls it sin, and indeed such a one that always adheres, we conclude in turn that we are not without sin.

XXXIX. From 1 John 1, verse 7. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. The Apostle speaks here of the reborn, and includes himself, and pronounces universally that it is a deception and a lie if anyone pronounces himself immune from all sin. Nor can it be excepted that he understands only actual sins. For he distinguishes clearly between having sin and committing sin. And this indeed he commands to be far from all the reborn, c. 3. v. 4. 89. but that he declares to be common to himself and to all in the aforementioned text. He is not therefore speaking of sins of deed, but primarily of habitual sin innate in individuals, which is concupiscence itself, remaining after Baptism.

XL. 5. From the daily petition for remission. Those who daily seek forgiveness of sin are not immune from all sin. The reborn seek it. Therefore they are not immune from all sin. We prove the minor premise both from Psalm 32, v. 56: You have forgiven the impiety of my sin. For this every saint will pray to you at an opportune time: and from the Lord's Prayer, in which the Savior himself taught and commanded us to pray daily for the remission of debts.

XLI. 6. From common death; when the cause is removed, the effect is removed, and conversely, the true cause of death is sin, Rom. 5, v. 12; c. 6, v. last. If, therefore, through Baptism everything that has the true nature of sin is removed from the reborn, why are the reborn, nay, why are infants themselves, who are alien to all actual sins, nevertheless subject to death?

XLII. 7. From the lack of the divine image. The Papists themselves think this is so truly sin that they place the formal nature of original evil in it. But in truth, the reborn are destitute of that image, such as it was when created. For although they are in a certain way renewed, they are never brought to that fullness of the created image in this life. Wherefore the reborn are not immune from all sin properly so called. And because concupiscence includes that ἄγνοιαν, and at the same time posits a vicious quality and iniquity, hence it follows much more that it is sin. And to this point serves that statement of Augustine, book 6 against Julian, chapter 8: Concupiscence in the reborn is iniquity. For it is iniquitous that a man should be depraved from that justice in which he had been created. For it is not the case that there is no iniquity, when In a living man, either the higher parts basely serve the lower; or the lower parts stubbornly resist the higher, even if they are not allowed to win.

XLIII. 8. From the Hatred of God. Whatever God pursues with hatred is sin: For He hates nothing of those things which are from Him. But God pursues concupiscence with hatred. For it is an evil thing, and contrary to the law. Indeed, the regenerate themselves hate it, how much more therefore does God? Nor does He hate it as an evil of punishment, because this is inflicted by God Himself. He hates it therefore as an evil of fault, or as sin properly so called, which was to be demonstrated.

Latin:

II. Rationes ex aliis dictis & analogiâ fidei desumtæ.

XXXVI. 1. Ab omnibus Scripturæ testimonijs, peccatum originale adstruentibus, qualia sunt Genes. 6. v. 5. c. 8. v. 21. Iob. 14. v. 4. Psalm. 14. vers. 2. 3. Psa m. 19: v. 13. Psalm 51 v. 7. 12. Ierem. 18. vers. 9. & similia, ex quibus colligimus: Si omne figmentum cordis humani malum est, & omnes de immundo semine in peccato propriè dicto concipiuntur, tùm & renatis verum peccatum adhærebit, quod est concupiscentia. Rationem sequelæ damus istam, quia malum originis in hac vita non penitus tollitur ex nostro mortali corpore. Firmissimum igitur est hoc argumentum: Istud nobis quoad ἰδίαν suam semper adhæret, in quo concipimur & nascimur. At verò in peccato propriè dicto nascimur & concipimur, quod allegata testimonia euincunt. Ergo peccatum propriè dictum quoad ἰδίαν suam nobis semper adhæret. Quoad ἰδίαν dicimus, quia reatum & respectus accidentales per renouationem tolli lubenter concedimus. Aut ergò fateantur, peccatum originis prorsus expirare, aut in aliam naturam transformari, aut idem quoad essentiam semper remanere, Primum est contrá experientiam. Secundum incurrit eandem absurditatem: Si enim malum remanens planè non est peccatum, tùm non tantùm accidentaliter mutatum, sed ipsa potius essentia mali penitus sublata est, ideoque non peccatum originis remanet, sed illud totaliter destructum est. Quod enim nullo modo peccati rationem habet, istud peccatum originis qui erit? Negato toto genere, mox simul omnes negantur species. Quare si nullum in renatis peccatum est reliquum, nec originale remanebit, quod absurdum.

XXXVII. 2. Ex Galat. 5. v. 17. Caro concupiscit aduersus Spiritum, & Spiritus aduersus carnem. Contrariorum contraria sunt attributa. At vero concupiscentia carnis, quæ est in renatis, contrariatur concupiscentiæ Spiritus. Hæc autem est opus bonum, legique conforme. Ergo illa opus malum legique difforme, vno verbo, peccatum. Inter opposita enim immediata, qualia sunt bonum & malum, έννομία, & ἀνομία, sanctitas & peccatum, nullum dari vel excogitari potest tertium.

XXXIIX. 3. Ex Hebr. 12. v. 1. Præcipitur ibi renatis, vt deponant ἁμαρτίαν εὐπερίσατον peccatum circumstans. Per hoc vero nil intelligitur aliud, quàm concupiscentia, quæ dicitur εὐπερίσατος secundum Chrysostomum, vel quod nos facilè circumueniat, vel quòd ipsa circumueniri & vinci facilè possit. Sed actiuus sensus magis accedit ad scopum Apostolicum, qui peccatum exaggerare, non extenuare solet; & monet, non vt concupiscentiam prorsus eradicemus, quia hoc in viribus nostris non est positum, sed vt deprimamus, & regnū ipsi auferamus, ne suis insidijs nos irretiat. Quia ergo Apostolus peccatū disertè vocat, & quidem tale, quod semper adhæreat, & peccato non carere vicissim concludimus.

XXXIX. Ex 1. Ioh. 1. v. 7. Si dixerimus, quòd peccatum non habemus, ipsi nos seducimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Loquitur Apostolus hìc de renatis, seq; ipsum includit, & vniuersaliter pronunciat, seductionem & mendacium esse, si quis ab omni peccato se immunem pronunciet. Neque potest excipi quòd peccata tantùm actualia intelligat. Distinguit enim luculenter tum inter peccatum habere, tum inter peccatum facere. Et hoc quidem jubet alienum esse ab omnibus renatis, c. 3. v. 4. 89. illud autem sibi omnibusque commune esse praeallegato textu pronunciat. Nō igitur verba facit de peccatis facti, sed imprimis de peccato habituali singulis innato, quod est ipsa cōcupiscentia, post Baptismū residua.

XL. 5. A quotidiana remissionis petitione. Qui quotidiē peccati veniam petunt, ab omni peccato immunes non sunt. Renati petunt. Igitur ab omni peccato immunes non sunt. Minorem probamus tum ex Psal. 32. v. 56. Remisisti impietatem peccati mei. Pro hac orabit ad te omnis sanctus in tempore oportuno: tum ex oratione Dominica, in qua pro debitorum remissione nos quotidiē orare Saluator ipse docuit & praecepit.

XLI. 6. A communi morte; Ablata causa tollitur effectus, & contra jam verō mortis causa est peccatum Rom. 5. v. 12. c. 6. v. ult. Si ergo per Baptismū è renatis tollitur omne id, quod veram peccati rationem habet, cur renati, imò cur infantes ipsi, ob omnibus peccatis actualibus alieni, nihilominus morti subjecti sunt?

XLII. 7. A carentia imaginis divinae. Hanc ipsi Papicolae tām verē peccatum essen autumant, vt formale originalis mali in ea collocent. At verō imagine illa, qualis quidē concreata fuit, destituuntur renati. Licetenim quodammodo renoventur, ad istam tamen imaginis concreatae plenitudinem in hac vita nunquā perducuntur. Quare ab omni peccato ppriè dicto renati haut sūt immunes. Et quia concupiscentia istam ἄγνοιαν includit, simulque vitiosam qualitatem & iniquitatem ponit, hinc etiam multò magis peccatum esse consequitur. Et huc facit istud Augustini. libro 6. contra Iulian: caput 8. Concupiscentia in renatis iniquitas. Est enim iniquum, quod homo depravatus sit ab ea iustitia, in quā creatus fuerat. Neque enim nulla iniquitas, conin viuo homine, vel superiora inferioribus turpiter seruiunt; vel inferiora superioribus contumaciter reluctantur, etsi vincere non sinantur.

XLIII. 8. Ab Odio Dei. Quicquid Deus odio prosequitur, peccatum est: Nihil enim odit eorum, quae sunt ab ipso, Atqui Deus concupiscentiam prosequitur odio. Est enim res mala, legique contraria. Imo ipsi renati illam oderunt, quanto magis igitur Deus? Neque odit vt malum poenae, quia hoc ab ipso Deo infligitur. Odit ergo vt malu culpae, vel vt peccatum proprie dictum, quod fuit demonstrandum.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: III. Testimonies of the Fathers

III. Testimonies of the Fathers.

XLIV. 1. Cyprian on the Lord's Prayer: Lest anyone should please himself as if innocent, and by exalting himself perish all the more: he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is taught to pray daily for sins. Thus finally also John in his Epistle, setting it down, said: if we say, etc.

2. Gregory Nazianzen in his Apologetic: Within ourselves we are attacked by our own vices and passions; and day and night we are pressed by the fiery goads of this humility of the body, and of the body of death.

3. Hilary in his exposition of Psalm 1 says, Our nature carries us to sin. And in Psalm 58: Who shall boast that he has a chaste heart before God? Not even if he has been an infant of one day, with the origin and law of sin remaining in us also according to the Apostle. And in a certain homily on the book of Job: We possess nothing clean in us, nothing innocent.

4. Ambrose: On the Sacraments. Concupiscence is taken away in Baptism, not so that it does not exist, but so that it does not harm.

5. Augustine, Book 5 against Julian, chapter 3. Concupiscence, against which the Spirit lusts, is both a sin, because there is in it disobedience against the dominion of the mind, and it is the punishment of sin, because it was rendered as a reward for disobedience, and it is the cause of sin, through the failure of the one consenting or the contagion of the one being born. The same author, On the Perfection of Righteousness. Sin is indeed in the members, but it does not reign, because its desire is not obeyed. From Epistle 29. As long as charity can be increased, that which is less than it ought to be is certainly from vice, from which vice there is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin. And tract. 41 on John: However much you may examine a just man in this life; although he may already be worthy of the name of just, he is nevertheless not without sin.

IV. Objections of the Papists.

XLV. 1. From perfect redemption. Christ is a perfect Savior and Redeemer. Hence he is said to take away all offenses. Ex. 34. verse 7. Isaiah 27 v. 9, to blot out, to take away. Psalm 51 v. 11, to make white. Isaiah 1 v. 8, to cleanse; Ezekiel 36. verse 25. Titus 2. 24, to cast into the depths of the sea. Micah 7. v. 19, to take away, John 1 v. 29. Therefore nothing remains in the reborn which has the nature of sin: otherwise it would follow that Christ is not a full Savior: and his works, such as renewal, would be argued of imperfection, when nevertheless a perfect cause does not act except perfectly.

Response 1. The words to take away, to blot out, to remove, do not denote the total absence of sin, but either perfect satisfaction or full remission. The former concerns all men, the latter all believers. We prove this both from the fact that the sins of the world are said to be taken away, John 1 v. 29, where if you understand the total expulsion of sin and not satisfaction, it would follow that the whole world is without sin; because the ἁμαρτία of the whole world has been taken away by the Lamb of God: and also from this, that in the cited sayings the discourse is primarily about actual sins: But how are these taken away or blotted out? Certainly not that they lose the nature of sin: For what is done cannot be made undone, but only because they are not imputed through justice, but are truly remitted through grace. For David's adultery did not cease to be adultery after his conversion: and yet it is said to be blotted out in Psalm 51. In what sense? In no other than that it was remitted and pardoned.

Hence therefore we conclude that the words to take away and to blot out, when they are said concerning sins, in the phrase of Scripture, [denote] either the universal satisfaction of Christ, or the particular and denotes the remission bestowed upon believers, but not the annihilation of sins, or their expulsion from the subjects, a fact which both the coherence of the statements and the analogy of faith most clearly confirm. For when sin is said to be blotted out in one place, then this is explained in another by being pardoned and remitted.

2. This in no way detracts from the perfection of the Redeemer; for although Christ does not renew us perfectly in this life, he nevertheless remains a perfect Savior. 1. Because of his perfect satisfaction. For he took all our sins upon himself, and both by acting and by suffering he made most full satisfaction for them. 2. Because of his perfect remission. For he pardons all iniquities for his faithful ones, and totally frees them from guilt. 3. Because of his continued renewal. For although he allows concupiscence to remain, he nevertheless mortifies it more and more day by day by the power of his Spirit, nor does he in any way impute it to us for condemnation. 4. Because of his full removal, which however does not happen in this life, but partly in death, regarding the soul, which is immediately purified; partly in the resurrection, regarding the body especially, which will then be glorified, and will be joined most purely with a most pure soul. If, therefore, all these benefits are joined together, it will no longer be possible to doubt in any way concerning the perfect redemption and salvation of Christ.

3. Divine works concerning the faithful are considered in two ways, both with respect to the agent and with respect to the patient. The agent is God and Christ the Savior, who acts perfectly in whatever he does. The patient are carnal men and those sold under sin, to whom evil, existing in the flesh, always adheres. Now, there is a common rule: Whatever is received is received according to the mode of the receiver. Because, therefore, men who are being renewed are imperfect, and as long as they live are infected with original sin, hence it happens that the renewal itself occurs according to the mode of the receiver, and thus remains imperfect. Therefore, the cause is not to be sought in God acting, or his weakness, but in the receiving subject, and his total depravity. The summer sun acts and shines perfectly upon the earth: yet not all fruits become perfect, not by the fault of the Sun, but of the earth. Thus, that our hearts are not fully illuminated by the rays of divine light, the cause is the native thickness of our minds, not the infirmity of the light itself. To this point looks their distinction, that some works of Christ are solitary, which proceed from him alone and by himself, such as redemption, satisfaction, remission, which are always perfect: some are joined, which he works in us and with us, such as the mortification of the flesh, the observance of the law, and the like. These, however, are imperfect not by Christ's fault, but our own; not because of the infirmity of the agent, but of the recipient.

4. This distinction also ought to be observed, that the works of God may be considered in two ways in another sense, 1. as they are in the making. 2. as they are in absolute being, and have their dἱow. When in the making, it is no wonder that they are imperfect. For every work, insofar as it is still to be completed and not yet completed, has an attached imperfection. Thus the mass created on the first day was indeed a work of God, yet imperfect: How so? Because it was not yet completed, but was in the making. But when God had finished the work of creation, then he saw what he had made, and Behold, All things were very good Gen. 1. v. last. In a similar way it is compared with our renovation. This does not reach its absolute being as long as we live; but is only in the making: For we are not in the fatherland, but on the way; we do not stand but run; and therefore we are renewed from day to day. What wonder is it, therefore, that this ἀνακαίνωσις is imperfect? Contemplate it as it will be, when after the making it shall be brought to absolute being in the other life: and then you will discover no imperfection any longer, but will cry out with Moses from Deut. 32. v. 4: All the works of God are perfect.

5. We confess furthermore most willingly, that God can indeed in this life perfectly renew us; for who will set limits to His infinite power? But that He wills to do this itself, whence will it be proved? Scripture affirms the contrary; experience confirms it. We urge, therefore, this truly theological Canon: What the grace of God and the merit of Christ work in the regenerate, how and in what order, must be determined from the Word of God, not from arguments based on what is possible.

Nor indeed are there no reasons why God willed to begin our renewal here, but not to complete it. He did this for our sake and for our benefit. For thus we must not be proud because of grace, nor despair because of misery. Thus we always have that in which we may exercise ourselves. Thence arises humility, while we acknowledge our own infirmity: arises faithful prayer, while we sigh daily for the forgiveness of hidden things; arises true hope and confidence, while we flee to God alone. Thence arises filial fear, constant patience under the cross, daily repentance; contempt for worldly pleasures, ardor for hearing the Word of God, a serious desire for death and eternal life; so that daily we may groan with Paul: Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? Rom. 7. v. 24. The ancients here use the example of the Canaanites, whose yoke and empire God had taken away from the necks of the Israelites, yet He had not completely destroyed all their remnants, but had left them surviving as material for continuous exercise to prevent security. Therefore, let us not stubbornly expostulate with God, but let us humbly give thanks, let us bravely mortify the flesh, and let us patiently await the future consummation in heaven: For He who willed that the flesh should remain in us does not desert us with His grace, but urges us to subdue it and makes us eager. I can explain this in two ways especially. For when we wish to tame and conquer enemies, we approach the matter both by starvation, by prohibiting supplies and necessities, and by arms, manfully fighting and laying low enemies. Thus, if we wish to break and storm sin dwelling in us, which has occupied not only the suburbs and members of the body, but our very citadel, namely the heart and reason; let us also attempt the matter. 1. By fasting, and let us cut off all supply of sin, by which our enemy is nourished, i.e., let us flee carnal desires, and let us not walk in the counsel of the ungodly. 2. By spiritual weapons, and let our delight be in the law of the Lord, and in his law let us meditate day and night, Psal. 1. v. 1-3. If Adam had done both, i.e., if he had abstained from illicit desire, and had recalled the commandment of the Lord, neither he nor his descendants would have been immersed in such great miseries. Therefore, when the flesh meditates war within us, let us withdraw all nourishment; when it attempts to break out, let us immediately resist with contrary weapons. When it wishes to break out through depraved conversations, let us struggle against it through holy ones; when it attacks the matter through suggestions of pleasures, let us fight back through pious meditations on the will of God, on the merit of Christ, on our misery, on the four last things: death, judgment, heaven, and hell. For he who thinks on these things does not sin forever. Syr. 7. v. ult. St. Peter briefly shows both this means, 1. Epist. 5. v. 8, when he says: Be sober and watch. For he wishes the enemy 1. to be finished by fasting, that we may live soberly. 2. By vigilance, that we may repress it when it attempts to break out, and resist it strong in the faith: which if we do, we shall certainly carry away the crown of righteousness. 2. Tim. 4. v. 8.

XLVI. 2. From the removal of damnation. Rom. 8. v. 1. There is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. Hence they infer that in the reborn there is nothing worthy of damnation, so that even if the Lord were to enter into judgment with them, with the shelter of the Lord's merit removed as much as possible, yet nothing could be found that would keep them from the entrance of heaven.

Response. Why therefore does the Apostle pronounce that sin adheres to him, why does he pronounce that the law of the members fights against the law of the mind? Does not sin, and the law fighting against the Spirit, deserve condemnation? Wherefore they confuse condemnation itself with damnable sin. This indeed the Apostle affirms, that there is οὐδὲν κατάκριμα for the reborn, that they are not condemned, nor should they fear condemnation on account of adhering vice, because they are in Christ, and apprehend his merit with firm faith: but he by no means says that no sin, nothing damnable, or hostile to God adheres in them, because thus he would directly contradict himself. It suffices, however, for our consolation, that we know the remnants of sins, although they are present, are nevertheless not lethal. For where there is no condemnation, there is also no wrath; where there is no wrath, there is grace, where there is grace; there is also no death; where there is no death, there is mere salvation and life. Sin after regeneration is therefore like wasps, which, having lost their sting, cannot sting, even if they make much noise.

XLVII. 3. From the washing of Baptism 1 Cor. 6 v. 11. Such indeed you were, but you were washed, you were sanctified and justified. Eph. 5 v. 26. Christ presents to himself a glorious Church by the washing of water, not having spot or wrinkle. And Tit. 3 v. 5. Baptism is called the washing of regeneration and renewal. From which they infer that Baptism is a full washing away of all sins, and therefore that no spot and nothing that has the nature of sin remains in the baptized.

In general Baptism confers two distinct gifts. Resp. The remission of sins. The renewal of the sinner. 2. Remission is consummated and perfect, taking away the guilt of all sins. Renewal is begun and imperfect, indeed mortifying the flesh, but not thoroughly expelling it. Hence the Apostle himself complains of sin adhering to him, and the law of the members resisting, Rom. 7 v. 22. Hence we are commanded to destroy the old man, Rom. 6 verse 6, to mortify the deeds of the flesh Rom. 8 v. 13, and to purge out the old leaven. 1 Cor. 5 v. 7. Hence we are said to be renewed from day to day, 2 Cor. 4 v. 16. Attending to which place Augustine, book 2 on the merit and remission of sin, chapter 7, writes: If in the very soul perfect, which is the inner man, were made known in Baptism, the Apostle would not say, Even if our outer man is being corrupted, yet the inner is being renewed day by day. For indeed he who is renewed day by day is not yet entirely renewed, and in so far as he is not yet renewed, in that measure he is still under the oldness. We say briefly, therefore, that the consequence does not hold from perfect remission to perfect renewal. Baptism indeed cleanses us fully from sin or guilt: but it does not destroy the whole body of sin, but leaves it for us to be destroyed by daily mortification. Baptism removes the vice of origin, not as a medicine which expels the disease entirely; but as a Sacrament, which confers full remission and begins renewal. For we are so washed and sanctified by Baptism, that we are nevertheless commanded to cleanse ourselves from all defilement of the flesh and Spirit, and to perfect sanctification. 2. 2 Cor. 7, v. 1.

2. Specifically. Regarding Eph. 5, v. 26. This saying can be explained either of the Church militant or of the triumphant. 1. If of the militant, the imputed holiness of Christ is to be understood. For this alone makes us immaculate and irreprehensible; Christ alone has been made for us righteousness and sanctification, 1 Cor. 1, v. last. But if it is extended to the gift of renewal, we cannot interpret it as complete and perfect holiness, unless we contradict the Apostle and the sense. For the Church is so without spot that it nevertheless groans daily, Forgive us our debts. It is called all fair, Cant. 4, v. 1, yet it is sometimes struck by the guards because of sloth, Cant. 5:7, that is, it is stirred to contrition by pastors through sermons of the law. It is all fair, if not because of the purity of life, then because of the sincerity of doctrine, as some explain. If of the triumphant, inherent holiness can be understood. For in the other life concupiscence will no longer have a place, no imperfections will be present, but the Church will be without any wrinkle and spot adhering. To this pertains the rule of Augustine, which he set down in book against the Donatists, chapter 7. Whatever testimonies of the divine Scriptures can be cited, by which the Church is foretold as pure from all mixture of evil: it is not as it now is that it is foretold by those testimonies, but as it is to be after that mortality in eternal life. Therefore the state of the blessed and the reborn ought not to be confused: the state of those attaining and those running: the state of victory and of warfare. There we shall be immune from sin, but here, as long as we live, we feel the goads of sin. For there are three kinds of men. 1. Some are only Spirit, without the struggle of the flesh. 2. Some are only flesh, without the struggle of the Spirit. 3. Some are partly flesh, partly Spirit, with the struggle of both. The first kind we call the blessed and inhabitants of heaven, the second the wicked and sons of the world; the third the reborn and disciples of Christ. Let us associate ourselves with these, let us avoid those, so that we may triumph with the former in heaven.

Latin:

III. Testimonia Patrum.

XLIV. 1. Cyprianus de orat. Domini; Ne quis sibi quasi innocens placeat, & se extollendo plus pereat: instruitur & docetur, se peccare quotidie, cum quotidie pro peccatis docetur orare. Sic denique & Iohannes in Epistola sua ponens dixit: si dixerimus &c.

2. Gregorius Nazianzenus in Apologetico: Intranosmetipsos proprijs vitijs ac passionibus impugnamur; & die noctuque ignitis stimulis corporis humilitatis huius, & corporis mortis vrgemur.

3. Hilarius in exposit. Psal. 1. dicit, Vitam natura nostrae nos ferre ad peccatum. Et in Psalmo 58. Quis gloriabitur, castum se habere cor coram Deo? nec si vnius diei fuerit infans, manente in nobis etiam secundum Apostolum & origine & lege peccati. Et in homilia quadam de libro Iobi: Nihil in nobis mundum, nihil innocens obtinemus.

4. Ambr: de Sacram. Tollitur in Baptismo concupiscentia, non vt non sit, sed ne obsit

5. Aug. 5. cont. Iul. c. 3. Concupiscentia, aduersus quam concupiscit Spiritus & peccatum est, quia inest illi obedientia aduersus dominatum mentis, & poena peccati est, quia reddita est merito inobedientiae, & causa peccati, defectione consentientis, vel contagione nascentis. Idem de perfect. iustit. Inest quide peccatum in membris, sed no regnat, quia non obeditur desiderio eius. Ex Epist. 29. Quamdiu caritas augeri potest, profecto illud, quod minus est, quam debet, ex vitio est, ex quo vitiō non est iustus in terra; qui faciat bonum & non peccet Et tract. 41. in Iohan. Quamlibet valdè iustum discutias in hac vita; quamuis iam sit dignus iusti vocabulo, non est tamen sine peccato.

IV. Obiectiones Papicolarum.

XLV. 1. A perfecta redemptione. Christus est perfectus Saluator & Redemptor. Hinc dicitur omna delicta auferre. Ex. 34. vers. 7. Esai. 27 v. 9, delere, tollere. Pfal. 51. v. 11. dealbare. Isai. 1 v. 8. mundare; Ezech. 36. vers. 25. Tit. 2. 24. proijcere in profunduni maris. Mich. 7. v. 19. tollere, Io. 1 v. 29. Nihil ergo remanet in renatis, quod rationem peccati habeat: Aliàs enim sequeretur, Christum non esse plenum Saluatorem: eiusq́; opera, qualis est renouatio, arguerentur imperfectionis cùm tamen causa perfecta non agat nisi perfectè.

Respond. 1. Verba tollendi, delendi, auferendi, non notant omnimodam peccati absentiam, sed vel perfectam satisfactionem, vel plenam remissionem. Illud omnes homines, hoc omnes credentes concernit. Probamus tum ex eo, quia dicuntur tolli peccata mundi, Ioh. 1. v. 29. vbi si totalem peccati expulsionem, & non satisfactionem intelligas, sequetur, totum mundum carere peccato; quia ἁμαρτία totius mundi per agnū Dei est sublata: tum ex hoc, quia in allegatis dictis potissimum de actualibus peccatis sermo est: Quomodò verò hæc tolluntur vel delentur? Non certè quòd peccati rationem amittant: Ex facto enim infectum fieri nequit, sed tantum, quia non imputantur per iustitiam, verùm remittuntur per gratiam. Dauidis enim adulterium non desijt esse adulterium post conuersionem: & tamen illud deletum dicitur Psa. 51. quo sensu? Non alio, quàm quia remissum & condonatum fuit.

Hinc ergo colligimus, verba tollendi & delendi, cùm de peccatis dicuntur, Scripturæ Phrasi, vel vniuersalē Christi satisfactionem, vel particularem & credentibus collatam remissionem, non autem peccatorum annihilationem, vel e subiectis expulsionem denotare, id quod & cohærentia dictoru & analogia fidei clarissimè confirmat. Quando enim peccatum in aliquo loco deleri dicitur, tum hoc in alio per condonari & remitti explicatur.

2. Nihil hoc derogat perfectioni Redemptoris; Christus enim licet non perfectè in hac vita nos renouet, perfectus tamen Saluator permanet. 1. Ob perfectam satisfactionem. Omnia n. peccata nostra in se recepit, & tum agendo, tum patiendo pro ijs plenissimè satisfecit. 2. Ob perfectam remissionem. Nam fidelibus suis omnes iniquitates condonat, & a reatu totaliter liberat. 3. Ob continuatam renovationem. Licet enim concupiscentiam remanere sinat, eam tamen vi Spiritus sui indies magis magisque mortificat, nec ullo modo eam ad condemnationem nobis imputat. 4. Ob plenam sublationem, quæ tamen non contingit in hac vita, sed partim in morte, quoad animam, quæ statim purgatur; partim in resurrectione, quoad corpus potissimum, quod tum clarificabitur, & purissimum cum purissima anima copulabitur. Hæc ergò beneficia omnia si coniungatur, de perfecta Christi redemtione & saluatione nullo amplius modo dubitari poterit.

3. Opera diuina circa fideles considerantur dupliciter, tum respectu agentis, tum respectu patientis. Agens est Deus & Saluator Christus, qui perfectè agit, quicquid agit. Patiens, sunt homines carnales & sub peccato venundati, quibus semper adhæret malum in carne existens. Iam verò habet communis regula: Quicquid recipitur secundum recipientis modum recipitur. Quia ergò homines, qui renouantur sunt imperfecti, & quamdiu viuunt peccato originis infecti, hinc fit, vt & ipsa renouatio iuxta modum recipientis contingat, adeòque imperfecta maneat. Causa igitur non est quærenda in Deo agente, vel eius imbecillitate, sed in subiecto recipiente, & eius summa deprauatione. Sol æstiuus perfectè agit & influit in terram: haud tamen omnes fructus perfecti fiunt, non Solis, sed terræ vitio. Sic quòd corda nostra non illuminantur plenè à radijs diuinæ lucis, causa est natiua nostrarum mentium crassities, non lucis ipsius infirmitas. Huc spectat illorum distinctio, quòd quædam opera Christi sint solitaria, quæ ab ipso solo & per se proueniunt, vt redemtio, satisfactio, remifsio, quæ semper perfecta: quædam sunt coniuncta, quæ operatur in nobis & cum nobis, vt sunt mortificatio carnis, obseruatio legis & similia. Hæc autem imperfecta sunt non Christi, sed nostro vitio; non ob agentis, sed recipientis infirmitatem.

4. Obseruari debet & hæc distinctio, quòd opera Dei alio sensu dupliciter considerentur, 1. vt sunt in fieri. 2. vt sunt in esse absoluto, & dἱow habent. Cùm in fieri mirum non est, quòd imperfecta sint. Omne enim opus quatenus adhuc absoluendum & nondum absolutum, coniunctam habet imperfectionem. Sic moles primo die condita opus quidem Dei erat, attamẽ imperfectum: Qui ita? Quoniam nondum absolutum, sed in fieri erat. Cùm autem finiisset Deus creationis opus, tum vidit, quæ fecerat, & Ecce, Omnia erant valdè bona Gen. 1. v. vlt. Pari modo comparatum est cum nostra renouatione. Non hæc attingit suum esse absolutum quamdiu viuimus; sed tantùm est in fieri: Non n. in patria sumus, sed via; non stamus sed currimus; ideóque de die in diem renouamur. Quid ergò mirum quòd ἀνακαίνωσις ista sit imperfecta? Contemplare ipsam, qualis erit, cùm post fieri ad esse absolutum perducetur in vita altera: & tum nullam amplius imperfectionẽ deprehendes, sed clamabis cum Mose ex Deut. 32. v. 4: Omnia opera Dei sunt perfecta.

5. Fatemur præterea perlubenter, quòd Deus possit quidem in hac vita perfectè norenouare; quis n. infinitae eius potentiae terminos ponet; Velle autem hoc ipsum facere, vnde probabitur? Contrarium adfirmat Scriptura; confirmat experientia. Vrgemus ergo Canonem hunc vere Theologicum: Quid gratia Dei & meritum Christi in renatis operetur, quomodo & quo ordine statuendum est ex Verbo Dei non ex argumentationibus a possibili.

Neque vero nullae sunt causae ob quas Deus renouationem nostram hic inchoare, non consummare voluit. Nostri causa & propter nostram vtilitatem hoc fecit. Ita enim nobis non est superbiendum ob gratiam, nec desperandum ob miseriam. Ita semper habemus, in quo nos exerceamus. Oritur inde humilitas, dum infirmitatem propriam agnoscimus: oritur fidelis deprecatio, dum provenia occultorum quotidie suspiramus; oritur vera spes & fiducia, dum ad solum Deum confugimus. Oritur inde filialis timor, constans sub cruce patientia, quotidiana poenitentia; voluptatum mundanarum contemtus, ardor ad audiendum verbum Dei, serium mortis vitaeque aeternae desiderium; vt quotidie cum Paulo ingemiscamus: Infelix ego homo, quis me liberabit a corpore mortis huius Rom.7.v.24. Veteres hic vtuntur exemplo Cananaeorum, quorum iugum & imperium abstulerat Deus a ceruicibus Israëlitarum, nec tamen reliquias eorum vniuersas penitus deleuerat, sed in materiam continui exercitij ad securitatem praecauendam eos superstites reliquerat. Non igitur cum Deo contumaciter expostulemus, sed gratias humiliter agamus, carnem fortiter mortificemus, & futuram in coelo consummationem patienter expectemus: Qui n. carnem in nobis superesse voluit, sua nos gratia non deserit, sed ad illam subigendam instigat, & alacres reddit. Expedire hoc possum9 modis potissimum duobus. Cum n. hostes domare & expugnare volumus, rem aggredimur tum inedia, prohibendo commeatum & necessaria, tum armis masculè pugnando & hostes prosternendo. Ita si peccatum in nobis habitans, quod nō tantùm suburbia & membra corporis, sed ipsam arcem nostram, nimirum cor & rationem occupauit, frangere & expugnare velimus;rem quoque tentemus 1. Inediâ, & præcludamus omnem peccati commeatum, quō hostis noster fouetur,h. e. fugiamus carnalia desideria, & non abeamus in consilia impiorum. 2. Spiritualibus armis, & sit voluptas nostra in lege Domini, & in lege eius meditemur die & nocte, Psal.1.v. 13. Vtrumque si fecisset Adamus, h. e. si à desiderio illicito abstinuisset, & mandatum Domini recoluisset, tantis miserijs nec ipse, nec posteri eius immersi fuissent. Cùm igitur caro in nobis pugnam meditatur, omnem alimoniam subtrahamus, cum erumpere tentat mox contrarijs armis resistamus. Cum vult erumpere per colloquia praua, reluctemur per sancta; cum rem aggreditur per suggestiones voluptatum, repugnemus per pias meditationes de Dei voluntate, de Christi merito, de nostra miseria, de quatuor nouissimis, morte, iudicio, cœlo & inferno. Hæc n. qui cogitat, in æternum non peccat. Syr. 7.v. vlt. Vtrumque hoc medium breuiter ostendit A. Petrus. 1.Epist. 5.v.8. cum inquit: Sobrij estote & vigilate. Vult enim hostem 1. confici inediâ vt sobriè viuamus. 2. Vigilantiâ, vt erumpere conantem reprimamus, & in fide fortes resistamus: quod si fecerimus, coronam iustitiæ certe reportabimus. 2. Tim. 4. v. 8.

XLVI. 2. A damnationis remotione. Rom. 8. v. 1. Nihil damnationis est ijs, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. Hinc colligunt, in renatis nil esse damnatione dignum, vt si maximè remoto meriti Dominici vmbraculo in iudicium cum intret Dominus, nihil tamen reperiri possit, quod ipsos ab ingressu cœli remoretur.

Respond. Cur ergo Apostolus peccatū sibi adhærere, cur legem membrorum legi mentis repugnare pronunciat? An peccatum, & lex Spiritui repugnans condemnationem non meretur? Quare confundunt damnationem ipsam cùm peccato damnabili. Hoc quidem adfirmat Apostolus, quod ὀδὲν κατάκριμα sit renatis, quod non damnentur, nec damnationem ob adhærens vitium metuere debeant, quia sint in Christo, eiusque meritum firma fide apprehendant: nequaquam verò ait, nullum peccatum, nihil damnabile, Deòve inimicum in jis hærere, quia sic directè sibi ipsi contradiceret. Sufficit autem ad consolationem nostram, quòd sciamus reliquias peccatorum, licèt insint, non tamen lethales esse. Vbi enim nulla condemnatio, ibi nec ira; vbi non ira, ibi gratia, vbi gratia; ibi nec mors; vbi nulla mors, ibi mera salus & vita. Est igitur peccatum post regenerationem instar vesparum, quæ amisso aculeo pungere non possunt, etiam si multùm obstrepant.

XLVII. 3. A Baptismi ablutione 1. Cor. 6. v. 11. Hæc quidem fuistis, sed abluti estis, sanctificati estis & iustificati. Eph. 5. v. 26. Christus lauacro aquæ sistit sibi Ecclesiam gloriosam, non habentem maculam aut rugam. Et Tit. 3. v. 5. Baptismus vocatur lauacrum regenerationis ac renouationis. Ex quibus inferunt, Baptismum esse plenam ablutionem omnium peccatorum, ideoq; nullam maculam & nihil, quod peccati rationem habeat, in baptizatis superesse.
