In genere Baptismus duo dona distincta confert. Resp. Remissionẽ peccatorum. Renouationem peccatoris. 2. Remissio est consummata & perfecta, tollens reatum omnium peccatorum. Renouatio est inchoata & imperfecta, mortificans quidem carnem, sed non penitus expellens Hinc Apost. ipse de peccato sibi adhærente, & lege membrorum repugnante conqueritur Rom. 7. v. 22. Hinc veterem hominem jubemur destruere, Rom. 6. vers. 6. facta carnis mortificare Rom. 8. v. 13. & vetus fermentum expurgare. 1. Cor. 5. v. 7. Hinc de die in diem renouari dicimur, 2. Cor. 4. v. 16 Quem locum attendens August. l. 2. de peccato: mer. & remiss. cap. 7. scribit. Si in ipsa animo perfecta, qui est homo interior, in Baptismo notas fieret, non diceret Apostolus, Etsi exterior homo noster corrumpitur, tamen interior renouatur de die in diem. Profectò enim qui de die in diem renouatur, adhuc nondum totus est renouatus, & in quantum nondum renouatus, in tantum adhuc sub vetustate est. Breuiter ergo dicimus, A perfecta remissione ad perfectam renouationem non valere consequentiam. Baptismus quidem à peccato vel reatu plenè nos abluit: sed non totum peccati corpus destruit, verùm quotidianâ mortificatione destruendum nobis relinquit. Tollit Baptismus originis vitium, non vt pharmacum, quod prorsus expellit morbum; sed vt Sacramentum, quod remissionem plenam confert, renouationem inchoat. Sic enim Baptismo abluimur & sanctificamur, vt nihilominus mundare nos iubeamur ab omni inquinamento carnis & Spiritus, ac sanctificationem perficere. 2. Cor 7. v. 1.

2. In specie. Ad Eph, 5. v. 26. Dictum istud exponi potest vel de Ecclesia militante, vel de triumphante. 1. Si de militante, intelligenda est sanctitas Christi imputata. Hæc enim sola nos immaculatos facit & irreprehensibiles, solus Christus nobis factus est iustitia & sanctificatio, 1. Cor. 1. v. vlt. Quòd si ad renouationis donum extendatur, de cōpleta & perfecta sanctitate interpretari non possumus, nisi Apostolo & sensui contradicamus. Sic enim Ecclesia est sine macula, vt tamen quotidiè ingemiscat, Dimitte nobis debita. Sic tota pulchra dicitur, Cant. 4. vers. 1. vt tamen ob segnitiem à custodibus nonnunquam percutiatur, Cant. 5. 7. id est, ad contritionem à pastoribus per conciones legis excitetur. Tota pulchra est, si non ob puritatem vitæ, tamen ob sinceritatem doctrinæ, vt nonnulli explicant. Si de triumphante, intelligi potest sanctitas inhęrens. In vita enim altera non amplius locum habebit concupiscentia, nullæ aderunt imperfectiones, sed Ecclesia erit sine omni ruga & macula inhærēte. Huc pertinet regula Augustini, quam posuit lib. contra Donat. cap. 7. Quæcunque testimonia diuinarum Scripturarum commemorari potuerint, quibus ab omni malorum permixtione pura prænunciatur Ecclesia: non qualis nunc est, illis testimonijs prænunciatur, sed qualis post illam mortalitatem in vita æterna futura est. Non ergò confundi debet status beatorum & renatorum: Status attingentium & currentium: Status victoriæ & militiæ. Ibi à peccato erimus immunes, hic autem, quamdiu viuimus, peccati stimulos sentimus. Sunt enim tria hominum genera. 1. Quidam sunt tantùm Spiritus, sine pugna carnis. 2. Quidam sunt tantùm caro, sine pugna Spiritus. 3. Quidam sunt partim caro, partim Spiritus, cùm pugna vtriusque, Primi generis nuncupamus beatos & cœli incolas, secundi sceleratos, & seculi filios; tertij renatos, & Christi discipulos. His nos associemus, istos vitemus, vt cum illis in cœlo triumphemus.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: XLVIII. 4. From concupiscence bringing forth sin

XLVIII. 4. From concupiscence bringing forth sin.

James 1:15, Concupiscence when it has conceived, brings forth sin: and sin when it is finished brings forth death. Therefore simple concupiscence is not sin, because it only brings forth sin.

I respond. 1. Nay rather, it is for that very reason sin, because it is the mother of sin. For as is the effect, such is the cause. Is a father therefore not a man, because he begets a man? Nay rather the contrary. Wherefore as good comes from good: so evil from evil, sin from sin. Concupiscence is therefore sin, not indeed begotten, but begetting; not actual, but original: of the former the Apostle speaks, but he does not deny the latter. For it is just as if I were to say; In the sons of the world original concupiscence brings forth sin, and instigates to many flagrant acts. But does it follow here that concupiscence is not even in the sons of the world sin? It does not follow at all, because from the affirmation of actual sin, to the negation of original sin; from the inclusion of one thing, it is not permitted to argue for the exclusion of another.

XLIX. 5. From the removal of the formal element. When the formal element is removed, the thing itself is removed. In Baptism, the formal element of sin is taken away. Therefore, at the same time, the thing itself or the sin itself is removed.

Response. 1. The formal element of sin is twofold: 1. Relative, when sin is considered as condemning, and then it has guilt as its formal element. 2. Absolute, when we consider it in itself, as it is sin, or a vicious quality, and then it has ἀνομίαν (lawlessness), or a departure from the law, as its formal element. We say, therefore, that in Baptism the formal element is removed, but not all of it, only the relative; the absolute, however, remains. For Baptism does not cause sin to no longer exist, or to be changed into a good or indifferent thing, but [causes it] not to harm or condemn. This logical canon points to this: Foundations can remain when relations are extinguished. For a stone is a stone, and does not lose its form, even if the boundary does not remain, but ceases to be a boundary. Thus, original sin after Baptism is and remains sin, although it does not remain mortal, but ceases to condemn. A magnet is always a magnet, and always by its nature has the power to attract iron to itself; if, however, it is rubbed with garlic, it cannot actually attract [it]: thus sin is always sin, and has the power of condemning, but if it is covered by the merit of Christ, it can no longer actually and in effect condemn.

2. The guilt of concupiscence is one thing, the guilt of the person is another. The former denotes damnableness, the latter condemnation itself. The former remains after Baptism, although the latter is removed. For by the sacred washing, concupiscence is neither taken away nor changed into another nature; it does not become a thing worthy of God's love or eternal life, since every evil in itself and always displeases God. Psalm 5:5. But the guilt is removed from the baptized person only, because concupiscence is not imputed for condemnation, not because it is not worthy of death, but because God, on account of the merit of Christ, forgives it out of grace.

Hence Augustine, book 6, against Julian, chapter 6: The guilt of sin is taken away in Baptism, not the guilt of that by which it itself was guilty. Others use these terms, that the guilt of sin is either actual, binding the person by the very act to damnation, or potential, when it could indeed make the person guilty if God wished to enter into judgment, yet it does not make them guilty in act, not indeed by its own nature, but solely by the mercy of God, and therefore the cause of the impeded guilt must be sought not in it, but outside of it. The former guilt is removed through Baptism, the latter is left behind, and consequently concupiscence is deservedly numbered among sins properly so called. To this refers that saying of Bernard, sermon on the Supper: Although Christ has taken away the damnation, yet he still allows sin to remain in us and to afflict us grievously, so that we may feel what grace provides for us, and may always have recourse to the help of that grace.

L. 6. From the absurd and contradiction: God either hates the remaining sin, or he does not hate it. If the latter, it is not sin. If the former, it is not forgiven. Response: It will be granted that God hates the remaining concupiscence, but it does not follow that it is therefore not forgiven, but still condemns. For those things are not ἀντικειμενὰ, but can stand together, yet in a different respect. God hates sin on account of its ἀνομίαν: he does not hate the person on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. Concupiscence could condemn, but it does not condemn, because God does not impute it. Thus a vice in a friend displeases us, yet the person of the friend pleases and is loved. Thus a father hates the vices in his son, but does not hate the son himself. He could sometimes disinherit him on account of the gravity of his crimes, but he does not do so on account of his στοργὴν and charity. It is compared in a similar way with the reborn. A double merit concurs regarding them: 1. Intrinsic, which is of the sin dwelling in them. 2. Extrinsic, which is of Christ, making satisfaction for sin. Sin of itself deserves death: but Christ by his merit has acquired life. Now since Christ's merit is far stronger than the merit of sin, hence it happens that when one believes in Christ, the virtue of the Lord's merit is conferred upon him, and so the merit of sin is suppressed, and the sinner is freed from damnation. Because, however, sin is not entirely taken away, hence it is indeed held in hatred by God, yet the person is loved out of grace and on account of Christ's merit. From which it furthermore appears that a distinction must necessarily be made between legal and Evangelical syllogisms. Legally, a universal conclusion from sin to curse is valid. For in whomever the law finds sin, it condemns him. Evangelically, however, it is not permitted to argue universally, but only particularly. For from sin dominating in an unbelieving person, the consequence to damnation is indeed valid, but not from sin suppressed in a believing person. For this is the sum of the Gospel. He who believes in the Son has eternal life, but he who is unbelieving toward the Son of God shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. John 3, last verse. Therefore, although sin is present in the regenerate to the greatest degree, yet there is nothing of damnation in it, because they believe in Christ. Therefore, sin being posited, the curse immediately follows, whatever the person may be, as in a legal syllogism. But sin being posited, yet with faith and the merit of Christ interposed, the curse does not follow, as in an Evangelical syllogism. Although, therefore, sin dwells in us, it does not, however, separate us from the favor of God. It has that whereby it can condemn us, but our Christ has more, whereby He can save us. That indeed fights against the law of our mind: but in all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us. Therefore let there be thanks to God, who has given us the victory through Jesus Christ our Lord. 1 Cor. 15, v. 26.

Latin:

XLVIII. 4. A concupiscentia peccatum pariente.

Iac. 1. v. 15, Concupiscentia postquam concepit, parit peccatum: Peccatum verò peractum gignit mortem. Ergò concupiscentia simplex non est peccatum, quia demum gignit peccatum.

Respond. 1. Imò verò ideò peccatum est, quia peccati mater est. Qualis enim effectus, talis causa. Num pater ideò non est homo, quia gignit hominem? Imò verò contrà. Quare vt bonum à bono: sic malum à malo, peccatum à peccato. Est igitur concupiscentia peccatum non quidem genitum, sed gignens; non actuale, sed originale: De illo Apostolus loquitur, hoc autem non inficiatur. Perinde enim est, ac si dicerem; In filijs seculi concupiscentia originalis parit peccatum, & instigat ad multa flagitia. Num autem hic sequitur, concupifcentiam ne quidem in filijs seculi peccatum esse? Nequaquam sequitur, quia ab affirmatione peccati actualis, ad negationem peccati originalis; ab vnius inclusione ad alterius exclusionem non licet argumentari.

XLIX. 5. A formalis sublatione. Formali sublato, res ipsa tollitur. In Baptismo formale peccati aufertur. Ergò vnà res ipsa vel peccatum ipsum tollitur.

Respond. 1. Formale peccati duplex est 1. Relatum quando peccatum consideratur, vt damnans, & tum pro formali habet reatum. 2. absolutum quando consideramus in se, vt est peccatum, vel vitiosa qualitas & tum pro formali habet ἀνομίαν, seu recessum à lege. Dicimus ergo in Baptismo tolli formale, ast non omne, sed tantùm relatum, manet verò absolutum, Baptismus enim facit, non vt peccatum non amplius sit, aut immutetur in rem bonam vel indifferentem, sed ne obsit, vel damnet. Huc spectat Canon iste logicus: Fundamenta relinqui possunt relationibus extinctis. Nam lapis est, & formam suam non perdit, licèt limes non permaneat, sed limitare desinat. Sic peccatum originis post Baptismum est & manet peccatum, quamuis mortale non maneat, sed damnare desinat. Magnes semper est magnes, & semper suâ naturâ vim habet ad se ferrum trahendi; sitamen vngatur allio, re ipsâ non potest trahere: sic peccatum semper est peccatum, & vim habet condemnandi, quòd si tamen tegatur merito Christi, reipsâ & actu condemnare non amplius potest.

2. Alium est reatus concupiscentiæ, alium personæ. Ille notat damnabilitatem, hic ipsam damnationem. Ille post Baptismum manet, licèt hic tollatur. Non enim per sacram lotionem concupiscentia vel aufertur vel in aliam naturam mutatur; non fit res digna Dei amore vel vita æternâ siquidem omne malum per se & semper Deo displicet. Psal. 5 v. 5. sed demitur reatus à baptizato tantùm, quia concupiscentia non imputatur ad damnationem, non quòd morte digna non sit, sed quia Deus ob Christi meritum ex gratia condonat.

Hinc August. l. 6. cont. Iul. c. 6. Tollitur in Baptismo reatus peccati, non reatus eius, quo ipsa rea erat. Alii hos terminos usurpant, quod reatus peccati sit vel actualis, personam obstringens actu ipso ad damnationem, vel potentialis, quando ream quidem personam facere posset, si Deus in iudicium intrare vellet, haud tamen actu rem facit, non quidem ex natura sua, sed ex sola Dei misericordia, ideoque causa reatus impediti non in ipsa, sed extra ipsam quaeri debet. prior reatus per Baptismum adimitur, posterior relinquitur, & per consequens concupiscentia peccatis proprie dictis merito annumeratur. Quo spectat illud Bern. serm. de Coena: Licet damnationem abstulerit Christus, tamen adhunctiandos nos peccatum adhuc patitur in nobis & graviter nos affligere, vt sentiamus, quid gratia nobis praestet, & semper ad illius gratiae auxilium reccurramus.

L. 6. Ab absurdo & contradictione, Deus peccatum residuum vel odit, vel non odit. Si hoc, peccatum non est, Si illud, remissum non est. Resp. Deum odisse concupiscentiam residuam concedetur, propterea vero remissam non esse, sed etiamnum damnare, non sequitur. Illa n. haut sunt ἀντικειμενὰ, sed simul stare possunt, diuerso tamen respectu, Odit Deus peccatum, ob suam ἀνομίαν: non odit personam ob meritum Christi fide apprehensum. Damnare posset cōcupiscentia, sed non damnat, quia Deus non imputat. Sic vitium in amico nobis displicet, amici tamen persona placet & diligitur. Sic pater vitia odit in filio, sed non odit ipsum filium. Posset nonnunquam exhaereditare ob scelerum grauitatem, sed non facit ob στοργὴν & charitatem. Pari modo comparatum est cum renatis. Concurrit quoad eos duplex meritum, 1. Intrinfocum, quod est peccati in ipsis habitantis. 2. Extrinsecum, quod est Christi, pro peccato satis facientis. Peccatum per se meretur mortem : Christus autem suo merito acquisiuit vitam. Iam cum Christi maritũ longè sit forti⁹ peccati merito, hinc fit, vt cum in Christũ creditur, virtus meriti Domini ei conferatur, adeóq; peccati meritum supprimatur, & peccator à dãnatione liberetur. Quia tamen peccatum nõ prorsus tollitur, hinc ipsum quidem odio à Deo habetur, persona tamen ex gratia, & ob Christi meritum diligitur. Ex quibus porrò apparet, quod necessariò distinguendum sit inter syllogismos legales & Evangelicos. Legaliter valet vniuersalis conclusio à peccato ad maledictionem. In quocunque enim lex peccatum reperit, eum condemnat. Euangelicè a. non licet vniuersaliter argumentari: sed tantum particulariter. A peccato n. dominante in persona infideli valet quidem consequentia ad dãnationem: sed non à peccato suppresso in persona credẽte. Sũma. n. Euangelij hæc est. Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam, qui autem incredulus est Filio Dei, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum Ioh. 3. v. vlt. Quare vt maximè peccatum adsit in renatis, nihil tamen in est damnatonis, quia credunt in Christum. Posito igitur peccato, mox sequitur maledictio, qualiscunque sit persona, vt syllogismi legalis, Posito autem peccato, sed interposita fide & Christi merito, non sequitur maledictio, vt syllogismi Evangelici. Licèt ergo peccatum in nobis habitet, non tamen à fauore Dei separat. Habet illud, vnde nos damnare possit, sed plus habet Christus noster, vnde nos salvare possit. Illud quidem repugnat legi mentis nostræ: sed in his omnibus superamus propter eum, qui dilexit nos. Sit ergò gratia Deo, qui dedit nobis victoriam per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum. 1. Cor. 15. v 26.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: Question II Does renewal consist solely in the removal of dominion and the suppression of the flesh?

QUESTION II.

Does renewal consist solely in the removal of dominion and the suppression of the flesh?

I. Lombard, book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 32, maintains that renewal consists simultaneously in the extenuation and diminution of sin. For he writes thus at letter A: Although concupiscence remains after Baptism, it does not, however, dominate and reign as it did before; rather, through the grace of Baptism it is mitigated and DIMINISHED; so that it cannot dominate afterwards, unless one restores strength to the enemy by following after concupiscences; And soon he adds at letter B: Therefore, original sin is said to be remitted in Baptism for a twofold reason, because through the grace of Baptism the vice of concupiscence IS WEAKENED and EXTENUATED.

II. This opinion of Lombard does not lack its patrons, nor is it destitute of reasons. For 1. those testimonies of Scripture which speak of the crucifixion, corruption, and destruction of the flesh seem to assert the same thing. Rom. 6 it is expressly said, Our old man is crucified together, that the body of sin might be destroyed; 2 Cor. 4 v. 16, He who is our outward man is corrupted; Gal. 5 v. 24, They who are Christ's have crucified their flesh. Now indeed the words to be corrupted, to be destroyed, to be crucified, certainly do not seem to denote only the suppression of the flesh and concupiscence, but rather a diminution, extenuation, and partial annihilation. 2. This very thing can be proved from ignorance and blindness, which is a part of original sin. For not only is its kingdom taken away, but rather, as regards its ἕξιν, if not in whole, yet at least as regards its parts, it is expelled. For when our mind is illuminated by the word and learns the saving knowledge of God, native ignorance certainly departs, and γνῶσις is introduced. For the knowledge of God, which we draw from the Scriptures, and the ignorance of God, which we draw from our parents, cannot exist together. For just as when light comes, darkness is driven away in reality: so when the mind is illuminated by the Spirit, the ἄγνοια of origin is put to flight. 3. Our people seem to imply the same thing when they maintain that mortification is begun, for dominion over the flesh in in the regenerate, as such, it is fully taken away, not begun. Otherwise, it would have to be completed in the other life. Wherefore we would also have flesh then, which is absurd. Therefore, they understand the diminution of sin itself when they write about begun mortification.

4. The opposition of the old and new man also pertains to this. The former is said to be corrupted and destroyed: the latter to be renewed and increased from day to day. Therefore, just as the new man is made through the accession of new powers, so the old man is destroyed through the partial subtraction of old powers. For oldness and newness are opposed. The alteration of both is begun here and continued daily. Therefore, just as some particles are added to newness from time to time, so some are subtracted from oldness from time to time.

III. Now, on the other hand, there are not lacking reasons for doubting.

For 1. If a particular abolition and diminution of sin occurs in renewal, how will the whole sin be propagated by regenerate parents? For parents transmit what they have when they beget. But then they no longer have the whole sin, but an attenuated one, and one diminished as to certain parts. Therefore, they do not propagate the whole. For how can one propagate to others what one does not have? Nor do the likenesses of Augustine suffice here, that from cleaned wheat an impure one is nonetheless generated, or that from those once circumcised, uncircumcised ones were born: for in these examples, the cause of production is nature, which always acts in one and the same way, unless it is hindered. Hence it happened that the circumcised nonetheless begat uncircumcised ones, because nature forms man according to the common idea of the species, if I may so speak, not according to the particular reason of this or that individual. But all this expires because thus the origin and propagation of sin would at the same time be reduced to God, the nature the author, which is impious. I ask therefore, by what principle, or by what cause, does the portion of sin, which has been abolished in the parents, arrive anew and become implanted in the children? Certainly nothing can be named; whence it follows that neither less nor more of sin is transmitted than what adheres in the nature of the parents. For otherwise that new particle, and one pertaining to the fullness of sin, would not be propagated: for the propagation of a thing always presupposes its presence in the propagator. Therefore, if parents do not have the whole sin, they will not propagate the whole either, but a part. But whence, I ask, will that other part arrive which was lost in the parents? And how can it be said of this that it was propagated by the father? The children of the reborn will therefore have opposing parts of sin, of which one will have been propagated by the parents, the other not propagated, but introduced from elsewhere, which is absurd. Nor can it be said that the sin remaining in the parents, when it is transmitted, simultaneously brings forth in the children that part which had departed through παλιγγενεσίαν. For whence will this be proven? A minute part of sin can indeed infect the whole nature, just as a little leaven infects the whole lump: but that one part should as it were beget another part, or that diminished sin, when it is derived into the children, should as it were attract the abolished portion, is not without reason doubted to be either aptly said or sufficiently demonstrable. Add that the same doubt recurs; namely, that the whole sin is not propagated, but only a part which afterwards is most laborious; and in turn brings sin to its ἀκμὴν and fullness.

2. The cited sayings of Scripture do not seem to imply a diminution or a particular abolition, but only the subjection and restraint of sin, so that it may not rule. For when the Apostle says, Rom. 6. v. 6. that the body of sin is to be destroyed, he explains this in Rom. 8. v. thirteen, by mortifying the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit. Indeed, in the same place he adds an ἐξηγησιν [exegesis]. For the words cohere thus: that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth I should not serve sin. Then, therefore, sin is destroyed, when it is not served, but its dominion is taken away.

3. We might seem to be gradually leaning toward the Papists. For they, in order to obtain more easily their dogma that the regenerate can fulfill the law of God, maintain that sin is diminished, broken, and attenuated. For when sin is said to be diminished and, as it were, broken in certain parts, the holiness of works can be obtained more easily than if it were asserted that nothing at all had departed from the ἕξει [habit/disposition] of sin.

4. If in renewal some part departs, then, with renewal lost and the Holy Spirit shaken off, it will return. But from where and by what principle? Does the same part that departed return, or is a new one introduced? Nothing can be said here without absurdity. Perpetual departures and returns of sin will have to be posited, because the regenerate do not always remain in a state of grace, but sometimes shake off the Spirit. Let even just the example of David be considered from infancy to old age. How many times, I ask, in this one subject would one and the same sin have been now in part abolished, now in turn restored, soon again abolished, and so on, all of which certainly seem incongruous and absurd.

IV. And these are the principal arguments of both sides, certainly such and so great that they render the mind doubtful on every side. For whatever we may say, we discover that difficulties are prepared for us. That, however, we may add something as if ἐν παρόδῳ [in passing].

1. It is certain that the powers of sin are diminished in renewal, and that its power is not such and so great as it was before renewal. For the Apostle says expressly in Rom. 6:14: Sin shall not have dominion over you [ὑπερισχύσει]. For you are not under law, but under grace.

2. In sin there are two things, privation and vicious quality,

which is called concupiscence. As regards privation, such as is primarily the ignorance of the mind and the utmost blindness in spiritual matters, we do not deny that this is abolished in part, on account of the testimony of experience itself. For when our mind is illuminated by the Spirit, those thick natural shadows of agnoias are certainly put to flight, although not entirely, yet in part. This ignorance, however, although it may be diminished in the regenerate, can nevertheless be propagated in its entirety, because it is not a positive entity, but a privation, which follows of its own accord when the light of the mind, which is a personal gift of the regenerate, is not transmitted. For just as when light is withdrawn, darkness follows spontaneously: so since parents propagate the soul without the gift of illumination, which they themselves have obtained; hence it follows of its own accord that ignorance is immediately placed in the son.

3. As regards the positive aspect of sin, and therefore concupiscence itself, how this is propagated in its entirety if it is not present in its entirety in the one propagating? It hardly appears. Indeed, if the particular abolition of sin were proven, then we would not be so anxious about its propagation: for we experience more than enough that it is truly transmitted. We would therefore say that both stand, the diminution of sin and yet the propagation of the whole; although we cannot understand that, nor in any way express it; but because that is in doubt, therefore this answer does not yet suffice:

V. What then, finally, is to be determined, you ask? I hardly find it, and I prefer to hear others here than to speak. For if anywhere, here certainly that saying of Augustine is most true: Truth is safer heard than taught. Out of an abundance, however, and so that I may supply material for others to think about, I add this: When the particular abolition of sin is spoken of, it is presupposed to have parts. But what kind? It is not an essential whole; because it is not a substance: nor an integral whole, because it is not something corporeal: nor a universal whole, because it is not a genus, but a species of sin. What kind, therefore? Metaphysicians enumerate a certain kind of whole, which they call a potential whole, and that is what does not have true and properly so-called parts, yet its powers are called parts in a broad sense. And although they wish for substance, which is distinguished by various faculties, to be noted especially by this name, yet analogically accidents, which include various powers and different degrees of powers, can be so called. If, therefore, any sin ought to be called a whole, it will certainly be none other than a potential one. With this presupposed, what kind of parts it has will be easier to understand and explain. It does not have integral parts, just as a body is distinguished into its integrated members, because it is not an integral whole divisible in such a way that one part can be removed while another remains; it does not admit of this. For I do not see how an immaterial quality can be called divisible in itself, since every partition arises from matter, which is absent there. Therefore, such as the whole is, such are the parts of sin. But the whole is potential. Therefore, the parts will also be spoken of in the same sense. From which we conclude that the parts of concupiscence are spoken of with respect to operation, and thus it is nothing other than powers of acting and different degrees of activity. For then sin is greater when it operates more; then it is less when it has a lesser force of acting. In this sense, therefore, we willingly concede that sin is diminished in renewal, and that certain parts are abolished, that is, the powers of operating are broken and the highest degrees of activity are removed, so that there is not as much after as there was before the παλιγγενεσίαν. But whoever, beyond this abolition of powers and potential parts, thinks that certain parts are as it were cut off from the very essence of sin, let him 1. consider that the ἄτομον of sin is indivisible. 2. that it does not have essential or integral parts, but is one impartible quality. 3. how he can satisfy the arguments set forth in thesis 3, which we judge will be most difficult for him. They seem indeed our theologians sometimes speak as if certain parts of the substance of sin were departing in daily renewal: yet without doubt they understand nothing but the breaking and diminution of its powers. For thus writes Dr. Arcularius, tom. 2, disp. Marp., disp. 8, th. 70: Corruption, the mother of guilt, is abolished in the regenerate either PARTICULARLY through regeneration and the mortification of the flesh, or totally through death and resurrection. Conversely, th. 37: That abolition, as it is imperfect, so it has its degrees and increments. Similar things are read in Dr. Rungius in his disp. on the epistle to the Romans, disp. 8, on the old and new man, th. 15. & 16, whose words are these: Such as is the destruction, such also must the body to be destroyed be understood in this place: But the destruction of the old Adam is an alteration of our nature, by which the body of sin, a servitude deeply inherent in nature, is gradually abolished, and the gift of renewal succeeds, bestowed by the Holy Spirit, by which in the place of spiritual weakness, new powers of acknowledging and invoking God are divinely kindled in us, and with spiritual vices expelled, the heart is purged, and is illuminated and sanctified with new light, intelligence, and good motions. Paul calls this alteration crucifixion and destruction, so that he may show that this change is ungrateful and troublesome to our flesh, that is, to our reason, affections, and all our powers; and at the same time teach that the darkness of the mind must be fully dispelled, and the depraved affections of the heart must be entirely extirpated, if the whole renewal of man is to be carried out, which, however, cannot be perfectly performed in this life on account of the weakness of nature. In these and similar locutions, theologians indeed make mention of particular abolition, but as I have said, they undoubtedly mean not substantial or quantitative parts, which concupiscence lacks, but only analogical and potential ones, which are degrees and powers of operating.

VI. And these things indeed I wished to dispute on the occasion of this question, not out of rash curiosity or untimely scrutiny of sublime matters, but as useful for better understanding the nature of our renewal, and for more strongly refuting the errors of the Papists. For as things abstruse are not to be investigated too scrupulously, so those things which can be known are not to be entirely neglected. For both are a vice, both curious rashness and idle security. Ambrose dissuades from both in book 1, de vocat. gent. c. 7, when he says: Things which God willed to be hidden are not to be searched out; but those which He has made manifest are not to be denied; lest in the former we be found illicitly curious, and in the latter damnably ungrateful.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO II.

An renovatio in sola dominij sublatione carnisque suppressione consistat?

I. Lombardus l. 2. Sent. dist. 32. statuit, renovationem simul consistere in peccati extenuatione & imminutione. Ita enim scribit lit. A. Licèt remaneat concupiscentia post Baptismum, non tamen dominatur & regnat, sicut antè; Imò per gratiam Baptismi mitigatur & MINVITVR; vt pòst dominari non valeat, nisi quis reddat vires hosti, eundo post concupiscentias; Et mox subjungit lit. B. Duplici ergò ratione peccatum originale dicitur dimitti in Baptismo, quia per gratiam Baptismi vitium concupiscentia DEBILITATVR atque EXTENVATVR.

II. Hæc Lombardi sententia suis non caret patronis, nec destituitur rationibus. Nam 1. videntur idem adstruere illa Scripturæ testimonia, quæ loquuntur de carnis crucifixione, corruptione & destructione, Rom. 5. disertè dicitur, Vetus noster homo simul crucifixus est, vt destruatur corpus peccati, 2. Cor. 4 v. 16. Is qui foris est, noster homo corrumpitur, Gal. 5. v. 24. Qui sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt. Iam verò vocabula corrumpi, destrui crucifigi, non certè videntur notare solam suppressionem carnis & concupiscentiæ, sed potius imminutionem, extenuationem, & partialem annihilationem. 2. Probari hoc ipsum potest ab ignorantia & cæcitate, quæ pars est peccati originalis. Illi enim non tantùm regnum aufertur, sed potius quoad ἕξιν suum, si non ex toto, attamen quoad partes expellitur. Nam cùm mens nostra per verbum illuminatur, & salutarem Dei notitiam addiscit, natiua certè ignorantia abit, & γνῶσις introducitur. Nequeunt enim simul consistere cognitio Dei, quam haurimus ex Scripturis, & ignorantia, Dei, quam trahimus ex parentibus. Nam veluti luce veniente, pelluntur tenebræ reipsâ: sic mente per Spiritum collustratâ fugatur originis ἄγνοια. 3. Idem videntur innuere nostri, cùm statuunt, mortificationem inchoari, Dominium enim carni in renatis, quà tales, plenè adimitur, non inchoatur. Alias enim consummandum foret in uita altera Quare & tum carnem haberemus, quod absurdum. Ipsam igitur peccati diminutionem intelligunt, cum de inchoata mortificatione scribunt.

4. Huc etiam pertinet Veteris & noui hominis oppositio. Ille dicitur corrumpi & destrui: Hic de die in diem renouari & augeri. Sicut ergo nouus homo fit, per nouarum virium accessionem: ita vetus homo destruitur, per antiquarum virium subtractionem partialem. Opponuntur enim vetustas & nouitas, Vtriusque alteratio hîc inchoatur, & quotidiè continuatur. Sicut ergo nouitati subinde accedunt, ita vetustati subinde decedunt aliquæ particulæ.

III. Iam verò ex altera parte iterum non desunt rationes dubitandi.

Nam 1. Si particularis abolitio & diminutio peccati contingit in renouatione, quomodo peccatum totum à parentibus renatis propagabitur? Istud enim transmittunt parentes, quod habent, cùm generant. At verò tum non amplius peccatum habent totum, sed extenuatum, & quoad certas partes diminutum. Ergo nec propagant totum. Quod enim quis non habet; quomodo in alios propagare potest? Neque sufficiunt hic similitudines Augustini, quòd ex tritico purgato nihilominus generetur impurum, ex circumcisis olim nati sint incircumcisi: In his enim exemplis, causa productionis est natura, quæ vno semper eodemque modo agit, nisi impediatur. Hinc factum, vt circumcisi nihilominus genuerint incircumcisos, quia natura format hominem secundum communem speciei ideam, vt sic loquar, non secundùm particularem huius vel illius indiuidui rationem. Hoc omne autem expirat quia sic peccati origo & propagatio simul reduceretur in Deum, naturæ authorem, quod impium. Quæro igitur, per quod principium, vel per quam causam peccati portio, quæ abolita est in parentibus, denuò adueniat & implantetur liberis? Nihil certe nominari poterit; vnde sequitur, nec minus, nec plus de peccato transmitti, quàm quantum hæret in natura parentum. Alias enim particula ista noua; & ad peccati plenitudinem pertinens non propagaretur: Nam propagatio rei semper præsupponit præsentiam eius in propagante. Ergo, si parentes peccatum totum non habent, neque totum propagabunt, sed partem. Vnde autem quæso adueniet pars illa altera in parentibus deperdita? Et quomodo de hac dici poterit, quod à patre propagata sit? Habebunt igitur renatorum liberi partes peccati oppositas, quarum altera erit à parentibus propagata, altera non propagata, sed aliunde inducta, quod abfurdum. Neque dici potest, peccatum in parentibus residuum, cùm transmittitur, simul progignere in filiis partem illam, quæ per παλιγγενεσίαν decessisit. Vnde enim hoc probabitur? Potest quidem minuta etiam peccati pars totam naturam inficere, sicuti parum fermenti totam massam: quòd autem pars vna gignat quasi partem alteram, quod peccatum diminutum, cùm in liberos derivatur, velut attrahat portionem abolitam vel congruè dici, vel satis demonstrari posse non immeritò dubitatur. Adde, quod recurrat idem dubium; nempe peccatum totum non propagari, sed tantùm partem quæ post maximè sit operosa; & peccatum vicissim ad ἀκμὴν & plenitudinem suam perducat.

2. Allegata Scripturæ dicta non videntur importare diminutionem vel particularem abolitionem, sed tantum peccati subactionem & franationem, ne dominetur. Quando enim Apostolus dicit, Rom. 6. v. 6. corpus peccati destruendum esse, hoc R. 8. v. decimo tertio, exponit per mortificate facta carnis Spiritu. Imo ibidem addit ἐξηγησιν. Verba enim sic cohærent: vt destruatur corpus peccati, vt vltra non seruiam peccato. Tum ergo peccatum destruitur, quando illi non seruitur, sed dominium adimitur.

3. Videri possemus ad Pontificios paulatim declinare. Isti enim vt eò facilius obtineant dogma suum, quòd renati legem Dei implere possint, peccatum minui, frangi & extenuari statuunt. Cùm enim peccatum imminutum, & quibusdam partibus quasi fractum dicitur, sanctitas operum obtineri facilius potest, quàm si de peccati ἕξει nihil omninò decessisse asseratur.

4. Si in renouatione pars aliqua recedit, ergo perdita renouatione, & excusso Spiritu S. redibit. Vnde verò & per q principium? An redit eadem pars quę abijt, an inducitur noua? Nihil hîc sine absurditate dici poterit. Statuendę erunt perpetuæ abitiones & reditiones peccati, quia renati non semper manent in statu gratiæ, sed nonnunquã excutiunt Spiritum. Consideretur vel solum Dauidis exemplum ab infantia vsque ad senectam. Quot quæso vicibus in hoc vno subjecto peccatum vnum & jdem fuisset jam ex parte abolitum jam vicissim redintegratum, mox iterum abolitum, & sic consequenter, quæ omnia certè videntur incongrua, & absurda.

IV. Et hæc sunt vtriusque partis argumenta præcipua talia certè & tanta, vt animum vndiquaque dubium reddant. Quicquid enim dixerimus, difficultates nobis paratas esse deprehendimus. Vt tamen velut ἐν παρόδῳ aliquid addamus.

1. Certum est peccati vires in renouatione minui, nec talem & tantam eius esse vim, qualis & quanta fuit ante renouationem. Disertè enim inquit Apostolus Rom. 6. v. 14. Peccatum vobis ὑπερισχύσει non dominabitur. Non enim estis sub lege, sed sub gratia.

2. In Peccato duo sunt, priuatio & vitiosa qualitas,

quae vocatur concupiscentia. Priuationem quod spectat, qualis est inprimis ignorantia mentis & summa caecitas in spiritualibus, hanc ex parte aboleri non inficiamur, ob ipsius experientiae testimonium. Cùm enim mens nostra per Spiritum illuminatur, certè fugantur spissae istae agnoias naturalis tenebrae, quamuis non ex toto tamen ex parte. Haec autem ignorantia, licèt in renato imminuta sit, tamen tota propagari potest, quia non est ens positium, sed priuatio, quae vltro sequitur, cùm lux mentis, quae est personale donum renatorum, non transmittitur. Sicut enim luce subtracta sponte sequuntur tenebrae: Ita quoniam parentes propagant animam sine dono illuminationis, quod ipsi consecuti sunt; hinc ignorantiam in filio mox poni, vltrò sequitur.

3. Quòd spectat positivum peccati, adeóque ipsam concupiscentiam, quî haec tota propagetur, si non adsit tota in propagante? vix apparet. Equidem si probata foret particularis peccati abolitio, tum adeò soliciti non essemus de propagatione: Nam verè traduci plus quàm satis experimur. Diceremus ergo vtrumque stare, peccati diminutionem, & tamen totius propagationem; licèt nos illud haut intelligere, nulloque modo exprimere valeamus; Quia verò istud in dubio est, propterea haec responsio nondum sufficit:

V. Quid ergo tandem statuendum, inquis? Vix invenio, & hic alios audite, quam dicere malo. Si enim alibi, hîc certè verissimum & illud Augustini: Tutius auditur, quàm docetur veritas. Ex abundanti tamen, & vt aliis cogitandi materiam suppeditem, hoc addo: Cùm particularis peccati abolitio dicitur, partes habere praesupponitur. At quales? Totum essentiale non est; quia non substantia: nec totum integrale, quia non est corporeum quid: nec totum vniuersale, quia non genus, sed species peccati est. Quale igitur? Metaphysici numerant quandam totius speciem, quam dicunt totum potestatiuum, & illud est, quod partes veras propriéque dictas non habet, eius tamen vires sensu lato partes dicuntur. Et quamuis hoc nomine potissimum notatam velint substantiam, quæ variis potentiis distinguitur, tamen analogicè & accidentia, quæ varias vires viriúmque gradus diuersos includunt, ita appellari possunt. Quod si ergo peccatum aliquod totum dici debeat, nullum certè aliud erit, quam potestatiuum. Quo præsupposito, quales partes habeat, intellectu & explicatu erit facilius. Integrales non habet, veluti corpus in sua membra integrata distinguitur, quia non est totum integrale diuisibile, sed vna demi, altera manere possit, non admittit. Non enim video, quomodo qualitas immaterialis in sese queat ita partibilis vocari, cum omnis partitio ex materia oriatur, quæ ibi exulat. Quale igitur totum est peccatum, tales sunt partes. Atqui totum est potestatiuum. Ergò & partes eodem sensu dicentur. Ex quo concludimus, concupiscentię partes dici respectu ad operationem, adeoqué nihil est aliud, quam vires agendi, & diuersos actiuitatis gradus. Tum enim peccatum maius est, cùm magis operatur; tum minus, cum minorem agendi vim habet. Hoc igitur sensu lubenter concedimus, peccatum in renouatione minui, partesque quasdam aboleri, hoc est, vires operandi, frangi, & summos actiuitatis gradus demi, vt non sit tantum post, quantum fuit ante παλιγγενεσίαν. Qui verò præter hanc virium partiumque potestatiuarum abolitionem, existimat de ipsa peccati essentia partes quasdam quasi præscindi, ille 1. cogitet, quod ἄτομον peccati sit indiuisibile. 2. quod partes essentiales aut integrales non habeat, sed vna impartibilis qualitas sit. 3. quomodo argumentis th. 3. positis satis facere queat, id quod ipsi fore difficillimum arbitramur. Videntur quidem nostri quandoque Theologi sic loqui, ac si de peccati substantia partes quedam decederent in renovatione quotidiana: procul tamen dubio non nisi virium fractionem & imminutionem intelligunt. Ita enim scribit D. Arcularius tom. 2. disp. Marp. disp. 8. th. 70. Corruptio, reatus genitrix in renatis aboletur vel PARTICVLARITER per regenerationem & mortificationem carnis, vel totaliter per mortem & resurrectionem. Vicissim th. 37. Abolitio illa vt imperfecta est, ita suos habet gradus & incrementa. Similia leguntur apud D: Rungiu in epist. ad Rom. disp. 8. de vet: & nov. hom. th. 15. & 16. cuius hæc verba: Qualis est destructio, tale etiam corpus destruendum hoc loco intelligi oportet: Destructio v. veteris Adami est naturæ nostræ alteratio, quâ corpus peccati seruitium altè inhærens naturæ paulatim aboletur & succedit donum renovationis, collatum à Spiritu S. quâ in locum âduvantas spiritualis novæ vires agnoscendi & invocandi Deum diuinitus in nobis accendantur, & expulsis vitiis spiritualibus, cor purgatur, & noua luce, intelligentia & bonis motibus illustratur & sanctificatur. Hanc alterationem vocat Paulus crucifixionem & destructionem, vt ostendat, hanc mutationem carni nostræ, hoc est rationi, affectibus, & omnibus viribus ingratam & molestam esse; & simul doceat tenebras mentis plenè discutiendas, & pravos affectus cordis omnino extirpandos esse, si tota hominis renouatio geri debeat, quod tamen in hac vita propter naturæ imbecillitatem perfectè præstari nequit. In his & similibus locutionibus Theologi quidem mentionem faciunt abolitionis particularis, sed vt dixi, proculdubio notatas volunt partes non substantiales aut quantitatiuas, quibus concupiscentia caret, sed tantùm analogicas & potestatiuas, quæ sunt gradus & vires operandi.

VI. Et hæc quidem occasione huius quæstionis disputare volui, non ex temeraria curiositate, aut intempestiuo rerum sublimium scrutinio, sed vtilê ad naturam renovationis nostræ melius intelligendam, & Pontificiorum errores fortiùs redarguendos. Vt enim abstrufa, non sunt scrupulosiùs indaganda:sic,quæ cognosci queunt,non sunt penitus negligenda. Vtrumque enimin vitio, & curiosa temeritas, & otiosa securitas. Ab utroque dehortatur Ambrosius l. 1. de vocat. gent. c. 7. cùm inquit: Quæ Deus occulta esse voluit non sunt scrutanda: quæ autem manifesta fecit, non sunt neganda; ne in illis illicitè curiosi, & in istis damnabiliter inueniamur ingrati.


### Question I. Whether concupiscence remaining in the reborn after Baptism and…: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 10 Disputation IX. On Mortal Sin, Venial Sin; and Induration


### Proem

Presiding: Balth. Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Master Michael Hermann of Wrocław:

Προοίμιον. I.

Thus far we have discoursed concerning sin in general, and its first species, namely original sin; there follows now the third chapter of this doctrine, which is concerning actual sins. For the vice born in us is never idle, but always industrious and busy. It is moved, it does not rest; it solicits the regenerate to evils: it precipitates the unregenerate into whatever crimes. For it is like a poisoned fountain, Jer. 6:7, and an evil tree, Matt. 7:17. As from the former nothing but poisoned waters gush forth; as from the latter nothing but evil fruits are brought forth: so the stain of origin, like a fertile mother, perpetually produces an innumerable offspring of actual sins.

II. Actual sin is so called from the act, which it always has conjoined to it. For two things concur in any actual sin. 1. The act itself. 2. The ἀταξία of the act. The former is material, the latter is formal.

Some doubt concerning the sin of omission, how it can be called actual, since there nothing is done, but only that which ought to be done is omitted? Although indeed omission formally is nothing but the negation of a due act, nevertheless it usually has conjoined with it undue acts, either interior, such as willing to omit, or exterior, such as the occasions and causes of omitting. Add that omission is called an actual sin in a somewhat broader sense, insofar as everything is called actual which is distinguished against original sin.

III. By Augustine, however, in book 22 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 27, actual sin is defined as a deed or word or desire against the law of God. In place of the genus he placed the material, which is threefold, for every act either inheres in the heart, or is done by the mouth, or is perfected by an external work. The former is called by Augustine desired, the latter spoken, the last done. He took the difference from ἀνομία, or illegality. For by that very fact some act is a sin, because it departs from the law.

IV. It can be defined somewhat more perfectly thus: Actual sin is ἀνομία, by which human acts proceeding from the flesh transgress the law of God, with the guilt of eternal and temporal punishments. The genus is ἀνομία, because this is rightly divided into original and actual; the matter is human acts. The efficient cause is the flesh or concupiscence. The norm by which it is prohibited is the law of God. The form is the particular deflection of the act itself from the law. The effect is the guilt of punishments, which are justly inflicted upon the impenitent, and gratuitously remitted to the penitent. Such punishments are 1. The wrath of God, 2. The pain of conscience: 3. The corruption of the soul. 4. Temporal miseries, and finally 5. Eternal damnation.

V. How various indeed the species of actual sins are, can hardly be told.

1. Regarding the efficient cause, some sins are voluntary, some involuntary; and these in turn are either of ignorance, or of infirmity.

2. Regarding the acting persons, some are mortal, some venial. The former are called sins of the impious, the latter sins of the saints.

3. Regarding the matter about which or the object, some are committed against God, some against one's neighbor, some against one's own person.

4. Regarding the matter in which or the subject, some are concerned primarily with the soul, such as heresies, some go forth outwardly, and infect the body more, such as gluttony, lasciviousness. Hence the former are called spiritual, the latter carnal; the former interior, the latter exterior; the former of the heart, the latter of the work.

5. Regarding the matter from which, spoken analogically, or by reason of the act, some are of omission, some of commission; and either desired, or spoken, or done, which consist either in aversion from God, or in conversion to creatures,

6. Regarding the form, or by reason of the law, some are against the first, some against the second table of the moral law.

7. Regarding the effect and guilt, some are sins crying out to God, some not crying out; some capital, some arising from those; some graver, some lighter; some remissible, some irremissible, such as the sin against the Holy Spirit.

8. Regarding the cause and effect together, some are sins only; others are sins and at the same time causes, but punishments of sins.

9. Regarding the adjuncts, some sins are hidden, some manifest; and others are without induration, some joined with induration.

10. Regarding the mode of attribution, some are our own, some another's.

Finally 11. by accident, some are sins in themselves; some on account of another, one is living, one kind dead, another remaining, and another remitted. VI. These are the principal species of actual sins, which if anyone wishes to join and connect together, he will be able to combine them thus: Sins are either others' or our own. Our own are either irremissible and with induration, or remissible and without induration. Those which are only sins are either venial and involuntary, or mortal and voluntary. Of mortal ones, some are of omission, some of commission. These are committed either against God, or against a neighbor, or against one's own person; and they are either interior and hidden, or exterior and manifest; against the table of the Decalogue, either the first or the second; yet in such a way that some always exist as graver or lighter than others.

VII. However, it is not our intention to laboriously describe and explain the individual species. This has been done by Flacius, p. 1 of the Clavis under the word 'peccatum': by Chemnitz, part 1 of the Loci Communes. Recently by Mr. Dr. Gerhard, Vol. 2, p. 704 and following. We shall only run through those divisions which are doubtful and are called into controversy. Of these there are chiefly three: 1. When one sin is called mortal, another venial. 2. When it is established that one kind is without induration, another joined with induration. 3. When it is divided into remissible and irremissible. Therefore, we shall have to deal with the three principal controversies hereafter: 1. Concerning the distinction between mortal and venial sin. 2. Concerning induration. 3. Concerning the irremissible sin, or the sin against the Holy Spirit. We shall expound the first two chapters in this disputation, but we wish the third and last to be reserved for the following one.

QUESTION I.

Are certain sins rightly called mortal, and others venial?

I. TaxanI. These terms are criticized by certain Calvinists, while they assert that they can be used less conveniently. For thus Ursinus, part 1, Explanations of the Catechism, in the place concerning sin, question 3, middle of page 64: 'For mortal and venial sin, I would prefer to say reigning sin.' 1. Because Scripture uses these designations. 2. Because those words of mortal and venial sin are ambiguous and obscure. 3. On account of the Papists.

II. Although, however, when the matter is rightly understood, we would not easily stir up a dispute with anyone over words, it is nevertheless false that the terms mortal and venial sin ought not to be used at all. For 1. This distinction was used by the Fathers before the corruptions of the Papists. For Tertullian, in his book On Modesty, says: 'Some sins are capital or mortal, some are of daily occurrence.' 2. In the Scriptures, the term mortal sin is not obscurely insinuated. Rom. 1, v. 32: 'Those who do such things are worthy of death'; chap. 6, v. 5: 'The passions of sins bring forth fruit unto death'; chap. 8, v. 13: 'If you live according to the flesh, you shall die.' James 1, v. 15: 'Sin, when it is finished, brings forth death.' 3. The matter is expressed more clearly by these terms. For this is what is sought: Whether all sins bind a person to the guilt of death? Since this must be denied, therefore it is rightly distinguished between mortal and venial, which are so called, not because they are worthy of pardon in themselves, but because God deems the person sinning in such a way worthy of pardon. 4. The use of a thing is not to be rejected on account of the abuse of others. Although, therefore, the Papists abuse these words, nevertheless they can be retained in a sound sense and use without danger. 5. Speaking properly, the distinction of sin into reigning and not reigning is not a distinction of actual sin, but of original sin. For this has a double condition: it either dominates or is mortified; that which cannot be said of actual sin. For it belongs to original sin alone, either to reign in the body, or not to reign, but to be suppressed. Moreover, the whole coherence of the text proves that the Apostle, chapter 6 to the Romans by sin, which is said to be restrained, to understand not actual sins, but rather original sin, and therefore the terms of reigning and non-reigning sin are used against the mind of the Apostle, if they are applied to actual transgressions. III. Meanwhile, however, we do not deny that more convenient terms can be substituted, lest anyone think that either mortal sins indeed deserve death but do not bring it, or that venial sins by their own nature are so light and trivial that they are unworthy of eternal damnation. For which reason some say deadly instead of mortal, and sin of infirmity instead of venial. We, however, retain those terms, because they have been used by the Fathers and are customary in the schools, and can be explained quite conveniently.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisner: S S. Th. D. Resp. M. Michaele Hermanno Vratislauiensi:

Προοίμιον. I.

HActenus de peccato in genere, primâq; eiùs specie, videlicet peccato originali disseruimus; sequitur iam doctrinæ huius caput tertium quod est de peccatis actualibus. Vitium enim nobis annatum nunquam otiosum, sed semper operosum, & negotiosum est. Mouetur, non quiescit; ad mala solicitat renatos: In quæuis scelera præcipitat non renatos. Est enim instar venenati fontis Ier. 6. v. 7. & malæ arboris. Matth. 7. v. 17. Vt ex illo non nisi venenatæ aquæ scaturiunt; vt ab hac non nisi fructus mali proferuntur: ita labes originis innumeram peccatorum actualium sobolem ceu fœcunda mater, perpetuo producit.

II. Dicitur autem peccatum actuale ab actu, quem semper adjunctum habet. Duo n. concurrunt in quouis actuali. 1. Actus ipse. 2. ἀταξία actus. Illud materiale, hoc formale est.

De peccato a. omissionis nonnulli dubitant, qui actuale dici queat, cum ibi non aliquid fiat; sed tantum omittatur, quod fieri debebat? Licet vero omissio formaliter nil sit nisi negatio actus debiti, attamen plerumque coniunctos habet actus indebitos, vel interiores, vt velle omittere, vel exteriores, vt occasiones & causas omittendi. Adde, quod omissio peccatum actuale dicatur sensu nonnihil latiore, quatenus omne id actuale vocatur, quod peccato originis contra distinguitur.

III. Ab Augustino autem l. 22. contra Faustum Manich. c. 27. peccatum actuale definitur factum vel dictum vel concupitum contra legem Dei. Generis loco posuit materiale, quod est triplex, Omnis enim actus vel haeret in corde, vel fit ore, vel perficitur externo opere. Illud ab Augustino concupitum, istud dictum, hoc factum appellatur. Differentiam desumsit ab ἀνομίᾳ, vel illegalitate. Eo enim ipso actus aliquis peccatum est, quoniam a lege recedit.

IV. Paulo perfectius ita definiri potest: Peccatum actuale est ἀνομία, qua actus humani a carne profecti legem Dei transiliunt, cum reatu aeternarum & temporalium poenarum. Genus ἀνομία, quia haec recte in originalem & actualem dispescitur; Materia sunt actus humani. Causa efficiens, est caro vel concupiscentia. Norma, qua prohibetur, est lex Dei. Forma est ipsius actus a lege deflexio particularis. Effectus est reatus poenarum, quae impoenitentibus iuste infliguntur, poenitentibus gratuito remittuntur. Tales poenae sunt 1. Ira Dei, 2. Dolor conscientiae: 3. Corruptio animae. 4. Temporales miseriae, & tandem 5. aeterna damnatio.

V. Quam variae vero sint peccatorum actualium species, dici vix potest.

1. Quoad causam efficientem, peccata quædam sunt voluntaria, quædam involuntaria; & hęc vicissim vel vel ignorantiæ, vel infirmitatis.

2. Quoad personas agentes, quædam sunt mortalia, quædam venialia. Illa impiorum, hæc sanctorum peccata nuncupantur.

3. Quoad materiam circa quam vel obiectum, quædam committuntur in Deum, quædam in proximum quædam in propriam personam.

4. Quoad materiam in qua vel subiectum, quædam versantur in anima potissimum, vt hæreses, quædam foràs exeunt, & magis corpus inficiunt, vt gula, lascivia. Hinc illa spiritualia, hæc dicuntur carnalia, illa interiora, hæc exteriora: illa cordis, hæc operis.

5. Quoad materiam ex qua, analogicè dictam, vel ratione actus, quædam sunt omissionis, quædam commissionis; & vel concupita, vel dicta, vel facta, quæ consistunt vel in auersione à Deo, vel in conuersione ad creaturas,

6. Quoad formam, vel ratione legis, alia sunt contra primam, alia contra secundam legis moralis tabulam.

7. Quoad effectum & reatum, alia sunt peccata ad Deum clamantia, alia non clamantia; quædam capitalia, quædam ex illis orta; quædam grauiora quædam leuiora; quædam remissibilia, quædam irremissibilia, vt peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum.

8. Quoad causam & effectum simul, alia sunt peccata tantùm; alia sunt peccata & simul causæ, at panę peccatorum.

9. Quoad adiuncta, quædam sunt peccata occulta, quædam manifesta; & alia sunt sine induratione, quædam cum induratione coniuncta.

10. Quoad modum attributionis, quædam sunt nostra, quædam aliena.

Tandem 11. ex accidenti, quædam sunt per se peccata; quædam propter aliud, quoddam est viuens quoddam mortuum, aliud manens, & aliud remissum. VI. Hæ sunt pręcipuæ peccatorum actualium species, quas si quis copulatas & inuicem connexas velit, ita combinare poterit, Peccata vel aliena, vel nostra sunt. Nostra vel irremissibilia sunt & cum induratione, vel remissibilia, & sine induratione. Remissibilia, vel tantùm peccata sunt, vel simul causæ peccatorum & pœnæ. Quæ tantùm peccata, vel sunt venialia, & involuntaria, vel mortalia & voluntaria. Mortalium quædam sunt omissionis, quædam commissionis. Hæc vel in Deum, vel in proximum; vel in propriam personam committuntur; & sunt vel interiora & occulta, vel exteriora & manifesta; contra Decalogi tabulam, vel primam, vel secundam; ita tamen, vt alia alijs semper graviora vel leuiora existant.

VII. Non autem instituti nostri est singulas species operosè describere & explicare. Factum hoc à Flacio, p. 1. Clavis in voce peccati: à Chemnitio part. 1. Locor. Com. Recenter â Dn. D. Gerharde, Tom. 2. p. 704. & seqq. Illas tantùm diuisiones percurremus, quæ dubiæ sunt, & in controuersia vocantur. Harum tres sunt potissimùm, 1. Cùm peccatum aliud mortale, aliud veniale dicitur. 2. Cùm quoddam sine induratione esse, quodã cum induratione coniunctum statuitur. 3. Cùm in remissibile & irremissibile dispescitur. De tribus ergo principalibus controuersijs agendum nobis erit in posterum 1. De discrimine peccati mortalis & venialis. 2. De induratione. 3. De peccato irremissibili, vel in Spiritum Sanctum. Priora duo capita exponemus hac disputatione, tertium verò & vltimum sequenti reseruatum volumus.

QVÆSTIO I.

An rectè peccata quædam mortalia, quædam venialia nuncupentur?

I. TaxanI. Taxantur hi termini à quibusdam Caluinianis, dum illos minus commodè adhiberi posse autumant. Ita enim Vrsinus part. 1. Explic. Catech. loco de peccat, quęst 3. m. p. 64. Ego pro peccato mortali & veniali malim dicere peccatum regnans. 1. Quia Scriptura his appellationibus vtitur. 2. Quia vocabula illa mortalis & venialis peccati ambigua sunt & obscura 3. Propter Pontificios.

II. Quamuis verò re dextrè intellectâ, nemini litem facilè moueamus ob vocabula, falsum tamen & illud est quod termini mortalis & venialis peccati prorsus non debeant adhiberi. Nam 1. A patribus ante Pontificiorum corruptelas fuit hæc distinctio vsurpata. Nam Tertullianus in lib. de Pudicitia, Quædam, inquit, peccata sunt capitalia seu mortalia, quædam quotidianæ incursationis. 2. In Scripturis vox peccati mortalis haud obscurè insinuatur. Rom. 1. v. 32, Qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte, cap. 6. v. 5. Peccatorum passiones fructificant morti, cap. 8. v. 13. Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Iacob. 1. v. 15. Peccatum cùm consummatum fuerit, generat mortem 3. Magis exprimitur res hisce terminis. Hoc enim quæritur. Vtrum omnia peccata personam mortis reatu obstringant? Quòd cùm negandum, idcircò rectè distinguitur inter mortalia & venialia, quæ taliter dicuntur, non quod per se veniâ sint digna, sed quia Deus personam taliter peccantem veniâ dignatur, 4. Vsus rei non est abjiciendus propter aliorū abusum, Licèt ergò Pontificij his vocabulis abutantur, attamen in sano sensu & vsu absque periculo retineri possunt. 5. Propriè loquendo peccati distinctio in regnans & noh regnans non est distinctio peccati actualis, sed peccati originalis. 'Hoc enim duplicem habet conditionem, vel dominatur, vel mortificatur: id quod de actuali peccato dici nequit. Originali enim soli competit, vel regnare in corpore, vel non regnare, sed supprimi. Tota insuper cohærentia textus evincit, Apostolum c. 6. ad Romanos per peccatum, quod compesci dicitur, non actualia, sed originale potius intelligere, ideoque termini regnantis & non regnantis peccati contramentem Apostoli usurpantur, si ad actualia delicta accommodentur. III. Interim tamen non diffitemur, commodiores substitui posse terminos, ne quis existimet vel mortalia peccata, mortem quidem mereri, sed non adferre; vel venialia per naturam suam esse adeò leuia & exigua, vt æternâ damnatione sint indigna. Quam ob causam pro mortali quidam dicunt mortiferum, & pro veniali peccatum infirmitatis. Nos tamen illos terminos retinemus, quia à Patribus adhibiti, & in scholis vsitati sunt, satisq; commodè exponi possunt.


### Question II Are all sins by their own nature mortal, or are some indeed venial?

I. The Pharisees formerly affirmed the latter, establishing that there are given certain transgressions that are clearly trivial, and such light little sins, as it were, that although they are indeed against the law, nevertheless they only overstep the smallest, not the great precepts of the law, and therefore can by no means bring about the guilt of death.

II. The Scholastics and Papists are almost worse than the Pharisees, while they think that certain sins by their own nature and in themselves deserve pardon, because they are not against the law, but only beside the law. Such they say are all involuntary sins, and hence Bellarmine, book 5 on the Grace of Christ, chapter 10, writes that these involuntary sins are repugnant to the law only materially. And so that venial sins may be more easily distinguished from mortal ones, they therefore narrow this down, and establish only seven of them, namely Pride, Avarice, Lust, Anger, Gluttony, Envy, Sloth, all of which include their initial letters in the single word SALIGIA for the sake of memory. Therefore, they hold that all other sins, which are not included in that septenary, are venial and do not deserve death.

III. Let us hear their own words, so that what they understand by venial sins, and how they judge them to be remitted, may be more thoroughly known. Thus, therefore, Lombard, book 2, Sentences, dist. 42, B: If a sin is mortal, it binds us to eternal punishment; if it is venial, it binds us to temporal punishment. For there are two kinds of sins, namely mortal and venial. Mortal is that by which a man deserves eternal death. For a crime, as Augustine says, is that which is worthy of accusation and condemnation. Venial, however, is that which does not burden a man to the point of the guilt of perpetual death, yet it deserves punishment, but is easily pardoned. Thomas philosophizes even more crudely about this distinction: For he writes thus in 1. 2, question 77, Art. 8, ad 1: Venial is spoken of in three ways. In one way, from the cause, because it has some cause of pardon, which diminishes the sin: and thus a sin from infirmity or ignorance is called venial. In another way, from the outcome, just as every sin, through penance, becomes venial, that is, obtains pardon. In a third way, it is called venial by its kind, such as an idle word. And this alone is the venial that is opposed to mortal. Conversely, question 88, article 1, ad 1: A venial sin is called a sin according to an imperfect definition, and in relation to mortal sin; just as an accident is called a being in relation to substance, according to an imperfect definition of being, for it is not against the law because one sinning venially does not do what the law prohibits, nor does he omit what the law obligates by precept, but he acts beside the law; because he does not observe the measure of reason which the law intends. And art. 2: A venial sin is so called from pardon (venia). Therefore, some sin can be called venial in one way, because it has obtained pardon, and thus Ambrose says that every sin becomes venial through penance: and this is called venial from the outcome. In another way it is called venial, because it does not have in itself that from which pardon does not follow, either totally or in part: in part indeed, as when it has in itself something diminishing the guilt; as when it happens from infirmity or ignorance, and this is called venial by cause. In whole, however, from the fact that it does not remove the order to the ultimate end, whence it does not merit eternal punishment, but temporal, and of this venial [sin] we intend for the present. For when the will is carried by sins into that which in itself contains a certain inordinateness, yet does not contradict the love of God and neighbor: if it is an idle word, superfluous laughter, and other things of this kind, such are venial sins by their own genus.

Bonaventura in 2. sent. dist. 42. art. 2. quæst. 3. fol. 630. If aversion is properly understood, the venial [sin] and the mortal [sin] do not at all agree in aversion. Since the venial, as it is not in contempt of God, does not turn one away from Him at all, as the mortal does. And quæst. 2. fol. 632. Since a venial sin neither separates a man forever from life because it excludes grace, nor holds a man forever separated from life: hence it is that a venial sin neither of itself obligates to eternal punishment, nor is eternal punishment rendered to it in itself.

Durandus in lib. 2. Sent. dist. 42. quæst. 7. To a mortal sin is owed eternal punishment, but not to a venial one. Which is evident, because as it is in worldly civility, so in its own way it ought to be in divine civility, but in worldly civility it is so, that he who by his own fault totally subverts, as much as is in him, the peace and friendship of citizens toward one another, or obedience to the prince, deserves to be totally extirpated from the civility by death, exile, or perpetual imprisonment. In the same way it ought to be in divine civility, in which men are gathered by the law of faith and charity, that he who subverts, as much as is in him, the order of charity toward neighbor, or of subjection to God, deserves to be totally extirpated from the civility by death, exile, or imprisonment. But by mortal sin alone does such subversion occur in divine civility, wherefore to mortal sin alone is eternal punishment owed.

IV. Bellarmine repeats these discourses of the scholastics in lib. 1. de A. G. c. 3. when he says, venial sins are so called either from the cause, or from the outcome, or from the nature and reason of sin, concerning which alone there is controversy. These he in turn divides into venial by their kind, and venial by the imperfection of the work. The former are, he says, those which have an evil and inordinate object, but which are not repugnant to the charity of God or neighbor, such as an idle word, excessive laughter, and others of that kind. The latter are those which, although they could be mortal by their kind, are nevertheless rendered venial on account of the imperfection of the work: He thinks that that imperfection consists, both in subreption, when sins are not perfectly voluntary, such as sudden motions of desire, anger, envy, and others similar: and in the smallness of the matter when a sin is committed in a small and light thing, such as would be the theft of one obol. Gregorius de Valentia has similar things in Tom. 2. disput. 6. quæst. 2. puncto 2. quæst. 18. punct 1.

V. As regards the remission of venial sin, they judge that penance is not necessary for this, since it can be easily expiated. For thus Biel in 4. sent. dist. 16. q. 5. art. 2. For the remission of venial sin, penance properly accepted is not required, neither actual, nor habitual, nor sacramental, because one remaining in venial sin until death is not damned, but will eventually be saved. Since therefore there is no need for penance, and yet venial sins must be expiated, hence they establish that satisfaction is made for them by any meritorious work whatsoever, and thus they are remitted. In particular, however, they recount certain works of this kind as expiatory, yet they do not agree as to the number. Others commemorate only six, and include them in this verse: 1. Praying, 2. sprinkled, 3. eating, 4. confessing, 5. giving, 6. blessing.

They understand, however, 1. the recitation of the Lord's Prayer. 2. The sprinkling of holy water. 3. The communion of the Lord's body. 4. General confession. 5. The bestowing of alms, and 6. Episcopal blessing. Others enumerate eight expiatory works and remedies for venial sins, comprised in these two verses, 1. I confess, 2. I strike my breast, 3. I am sprinkled, 4. I am crushed, 5. I pray, 6. I am signed, 7. I eat, 8. I give, by which I put away venial sins. Others multiply remedies and recount twelve ways of expiating, namely 1. worthy communion, 2. the sprinkling of holy water, 3. the bestowing of alms, 4. the remission of injuries, 5. prayer, especially the Lord's Prayer, 6. general confession, 7. Episcopal, Priestly, and Monastic blessing, 8. devout striking of the breast, 9. contrition of heart, 10. Extreme unction, 11. patience under scourges, 12. any good work whatsoever.

VI. And thus far we have abundantly perceived what the opinion of the Papists is concerning venial sin: but we on the contrary establish: that there is no sin which, by its own kind or by the imperfection of the work, is venial or worthy of pardon; but that all are mortal by their own nature and deserve eternal damnation. Meanwhile, however, we also assert this, that involuntary sins and sins of infirmity do not subject believers to eternal death, nor are they imputed unto death, not because of any slightness of their own, but solely because of the merit of Christ, by which they are covered. And this is what we commonly say, that sins are considered either νομικῶς and according to the Law, or εὐαγγελικῶς and according to the Gospel. If they are judged legally, all are mortal. For cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things which are written in the book of the Law to do them, Deut. 27. v. last, Gal. 3. v. 10. If they are considered evangelically, they are indeed mortal in themselves, yet not actually deadly, but because they are not imputed, they become venial. For there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8. v. 1.

VII. Nor yet by this do we abolish the distinction of sins, or pronounce all to be equal, as the Papists falsely allege. For we willingly concede that some sins are graver than others, indeed we even prove it from Num. 15. v. 22, 30, Matt. 5. v. 22, ch. 11. v. 24, Luke 12. v. 47, 48, John 19. v. 11.

Nor do we deny that mortal sins are also called venial by their outcome, since they are remitted to those who repent, in which sense the author of 'On True and False Repentance' in Augustine, ch. 18, says: there are certain sins which are mortal and become venial in repentance. But this is what we deny: that there are certain sins so light that they are worthy of pardon by their own nature, or, as Lindanus speaks, that there are certain slight little vices and sprinklings which cannot contaminate the works of the reborn. We say that this dogma of the Papists is Pharisaical, devised to destroy the righteousness of faith and to introduce that of works, and is therefore injurious to the blood of Christ: so that this may be evidently demonstrated, 1. We shall bring forward arguments for the confirmation of our thesis, and 2. We shall briefly discuss the objections of the Romanists, especially those of Bellarmine.

Latin:

I. Pharisæi olim adfirmabant posterius, statuentes dari præuaricationes quasdam planè exiguas, & tàm leuia quasi peccatilla, vt quidem contra legem sint, attamen tantùm minima, non magna legis præcepta transiliant, adeoque reatum mortis nequaquam superinducere queant.

II. Scholastici & Pontificij Pharisæis fermè deteriores sunt, dum peccata quædam ex natura sua & per se veniam mereri existimant, quia non sint contra legem, sed dūtaxat præter legem. Talia dicunt esse omnia inuolūtaria, & hinc Bell. l. 5 de A. G. c. 10. scribit, eædem inuoluntariani nõ nisi materialiter legi repugnare. Vtq́; venialia faciliùs discerni possint à mortalibus, idcircò hoc contrahunt, & eorum tantùmmodò septem statuunt, nempè Superbiam, Auaritiam, Luxuriam, Iram, Gulam, Inuidiam, Acediam, quæ omnia p initiales literas vni voci SALIGIA memoriæ causâ includunt. Cætera ergò peccata omnia, quæ isto septenario non funt comprehensa, venialia esse, nec mortem promereri sentiunt.

III. Audiamus verò propria ipsorům verba, vt quid per venialia intelligant, & quomodo ea remitti censeant, penitius innotescat. Ita ergo Lombardus l. 2. sent. dist. 42. B, Si peccatum mortale est, obligat nos pœnæ æternæ; si veniale obligat nos pœnæ temporali. Duo enim funt genera peccatorum, mortalium scilicet & venialium. Mortale est, per quod homo mortem æternam meretur. Crimen enim, vt ait Augustinus, est, quod est dignum accusatione & damnatione, Veniale autem quod hominem vsque in reatum perpetuæ mortis non grauat, veruntamen pœnam meretur, sed facilè indulgetur. Thomas de hoc discrimine adhuc crassius philosophatur: Ita enim scribit 1. 2. quæst. 77. Art. 8. ad 1, Veniale dicitur tripliciter. Vno modo, ex causa, quia scilicet habet aliquam causam veniæ, quæ diminuit peccatum: & sic peccatum ex infirmitate vel ignorâtia dicitur veniale. Alio modo, ex euentu, sicut omne peccatum, per pœnitentiam fie veniale, id est, veniam consequitur. Tertio modo, dicitur veniale ex genere, sicut verbum otiosum. Et hoc folùm veniale opponitur mortali. Vicissim quæst. 88 artic. 1. ad 1. Peccatum veniale dicitur peccatum secundum rationem imperfectam, & in ordine ad peccatum mortale; sicut accidens dicitur ens in ordine ad substantiam, secundum imperfectam rationem entis, non n. est contra legem quia venialiter peccans non facit quod lex prohibet, nec prætermittit s!, quod lex per præceptum obligat sed facit præter legem; quia non obseruat modum rationis, quem lex intendit. Et art. 2. Peccatum veniale à venia dicitur. Potest igitur aliquod peccatum dici veniale vno modo, quia est veniam consecutum, & sic dicit Ambros. quod omne peccatum per pœnitentiam fit veniale: & hoc dicitur veniale ex euentu. Alio modo dicitur veniale, quia non habet in se, vnde veniam non consequatur, vel totaliter, vel in parte: in parte quidem, ficut cùm habet in se aliquid diminuens culpam; vt cùm fit ex infirmitate, vel ignorantia, & hac dicitur veniale ex causa. In toto autem ex eo, quod non tollit ordinem ad vltimum finem, vnde non meretur pœnam æternam, sed temporalem, & de hoc veniali ad præsens intendimus. Quando enim voluntas peccatis fertur in id quod in se continet quandam inordinationem, non tamen contrariatur dilectioni Dei & proximi: si utiverbum otiosum risus superfluus, & alia huiusmodi, talia sunt peccata venialia ex suo genere.

Bonaventura in 2. sent. dist. 42. art. 2. quæst. 3. fol. 630. Si auersio proprie intelligatur, veniale cum mortali minimè in auersione conueniunt. Siquidem veniale, cum non sit in contemtum Dei, ab illo prorsus non auertit, ficut mortale facit. Et quæst. 2. fol. 632. Quoniam veniale peccatum nec separat hominem in perpetuum separatum à vita quia excludit gratiam, nec tenet hominem in perpetuum separatum à vita: hinc est, quod peccatum veniale, nec de se obligat ad pœnam æternam, nec ei secundum se redditur pœna æterna.

Durandus in lib. 2. Sent. dist. 42. quæst. 7. Peccato mortali debetur pœna æterna, non autem veniale. Quod patet, quia sicut est in ciuilitate mundana, sic suo modo debet esse in ciuilitate diuina, sed in ciuilitate mundana sic est, quòd ille qui ex culpa sua totaliter subvertit, quantum in se est, pacem & amicitiam ciuum ad inuicem, vel obedientiam ad principem, meretur exstirpari totaliter a ciuilitate per mortem, exilium vel perpetuum carcerem. Eodem modo debet esse in ciuilitate diuina, in qua congregantur homines lege fidei & charitatis, quòd ille qui subvertit, quantum in se est, ordinem charitatis ad proximum, vel subiectionis ad Deum, meretur exstirpari totaliter à ciuilitate per mortem, exilium, vel carcerem. Per solum autē peccatum mortale sit talis subuersio in ciuilitate diuina, quare soli peccato mortali debetur pœna æterna.

IV. Hos scholasticorum discursus repetit Bell. l. 1. de A. G. c. 3. quando inquit, peccata venialia sic dici vel à causa, vel ab euentu, vel ex natura & ratione peccati, de quibus solis sit controuersia. Hæc vicissim diuidit in venialia ex genere suo, & venialia ex imperfectione operis. Illa sunt, inquit, quæ habent pro obiectorem malam & inordinatam, sed quæ charitati Dei vel proximi non repugnet, quale est verbum otiosum, risus nimius, & alia id genus.
