Hæc sunt, quæ tamesfi ex genere suo mortalia esse possent, tamen ob imperfectionem operis venialia efficiuntur: Illam verò imperfectionem consistere putat, tum in subreptione, quando peccata non sunt perfecte voluntaria, quales sunt subiti motus cupiditatis, iræ, inuidentiæ, & alij similes: tum in materiæ paruitate quando peccatuin in re parua & leui cominittitur, quale esset furtum vnius oboli. Similia habet Gregoriuus de Valentia Tom. 2. disput. 6. quæst. 2. puncto 2. quæst. 18. punct 1.

V. Quod spectat remissionem peccati venialis, ad hoc pœnitentiam non esse necessariam censent, cùm facilè expiari possit. Sic emm Biel in 4. sent. dist. 16. q. 5. art. 2. Ad remissionem peccati venialis non requiritur pœnitentia propriè accepta, nec actualis, nec habitualis, nec Sacramentalis, quia manens in veniali vfque ad mortem non damnatur, sed tandem saluabitur. Cùm ergò pœnitentiâ non sit opus, & tamen venialia expiari debeant, hinc statuunt, per quodlibet opus meritorium pro illis satis fieri, adeó que remitti. In specie verò quædam huius modi opera expiatoria recensent, quoad numerum tamen non conueniunt. Alij tantùm sex commemorant, & huic versiculo includunt: 1. Orans, 2. tinctus, 3. edens, 4. confess° 5. dans, 6 benedices.

Intelligunt autem 1. recitationem Orationis Dominicæ. 2. Aspersionem aquæ benedictæ. 3. Communionem corporis Dominici. 4. Confessionem generalem. 5. Largitionem eleemosynarum, & 6. Benedictionem episcopalem. Alij octo opera expiatoria & remedia peccatorum venialium enumerant, his duobus versiculis comprehensa, 1. Confiteor, 2. tundo, 3. conspergor, 4. conteror, 5 oro, 6. Signor, 7. edo, 8. dono, per quæ venialia pono. Alij remedia multiplicant & duodecim modos expiandi enarrant, nimirum 1. dignam communionem. 2. aquæ benedictæ aspersionem, 3. eleemosynarum largitionem, 4. injuriarum remissionem, 5. precationem, inprimis Dominicam, 6. confessionem generalem, 7. benedictionem Episcopalem, Sacerdotalem & Monialem, 8. deuotam pectoris tunsionem, 9. cordis contritionem. 10. Extremam vnctionem, 11. patientiam flagellorum 12. quodlibet opus bonum.

VI. Et hactenus, quæ Pontificiorum sit sententia de peccato veniali, abundè percepimus : Nos autem contra statuimus: nullum esse peccatum, quod ex suo genere, vel ex operis imperfectione veniale aut veniâ dignum sit; sed omnia ex natura sua esse mortalia, & æternam damnationem promereri. Interim tamen & hoc asserimus, quòd peccata inuoluntaria & infirmitatis credentes morti æternæ non subjiciant, nec ad mortem imputentur, non ob aliquam exilitatem suam, sed vnicè ob Christi meritum, quoteguntur. Et hoc est, quod vulgo dicimus peccata considerari vel νομικῶς & secundum legem, vel εὐαγγελικκῶς & secundum Euangelium. Legaliter si æstimentur, omnia sunt mortalia. Maledictus enim est omnis, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis ut faciat ea, Deut. 27. v. ult Gal. 3. v. 10. Euangelicè si considerentur, sunt quidem in se mortalia, non tamen actu mortifera, verùm quia non imputantur, fiunt venialia. Nihil enim damnationis his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom. 8. v. 1.

VII. Neque tamen hoc ipso peccatorum difcrimen tollimus, aut omnia esse paria pronunciamus, velut adfingunt Pontificij. Lubenter enim concedimus, peccatorum alia alijs grauiora esse, imò etiam probamus ex Num. 15. v. 22. 30. Matth. 5. v. 22. c. 11. v. 24. Luc. 12. v. 47. 48. Ioh. 19. v. 11.

Neque inficiamur, mortalia quoq; ab eventu dici venialia, quandoquidem pœnitentibus remittuntur, quo sensu Author de vera & falsu pœnitentia apud August. c. 18. ait, quædam peccata sunt, quæ sunt mortalia & in pœnitentia fiunt venialia. Hoc verò est, quod negamus, dari peccata quædam tàm levia, vt per se veniâ sint digna, vel vt Lindanus loquitur, esse quædam leuicula vitiola & aspergines, quæ non possunt contaminare renatorum opera. Dicimus hoc Papicolarum dogma esse Pharisaïcum ad justitiam fidei destruendam, & operum inducendam excogitatum, adeóque in Christi sanguinem injurium: quod vt evidenter demonstretur, 1. Argumenta pro theseos nostræ confirmatione adducemus, & 2. Romanensium, præsertim Bellarmini, objectiones paucis discutiemus.


### Question II Are all sins by their own nature mortal: I. Arguments that all sins are mortal by their own nature

I. Arguments that all sins are mortal by their own nature.

VIII. Our thesis can be proved and confirmed 1. By sayings of Scripture, 2. By reasons from the analogy of faith, 3. By testimonies of the Fathers and of adversaries, concerning which in order. IX. SAYINGS. 1. James 2, v. 10. 'Whoever shall offend in ONE, is made guilty of all.' This is a most clear saying, from which it follows of its own accord that whoever commits even one single sin is guilty of the whole law, and indeed for this reason, because one and the same is the author of all the commandments, namely God. For He who said, 'Do not commit adultery,' said also, 'Do not kill,' v. 11. But Bellarmine is absurd, who in book 1, chapter 12, thinks that James is speaking only of a criminal offense, not a venial one, when he is speaking generally about any sin whatsoever. For his reason is taken from the author, GOD: God enacted all the commandments. Therefore, he who violates one single commandment sins against GOD just as much as he who violates them all. And in chapter 3 it is said: 'In many things we all offend.'

From which it is clear how the term 'to offend' is to be understood, namely not only concerning crimes and flagrant acts, but also concerning sins of infirmity:

2. Deut. 27. v. last. Galat. 3. v. 10. Cursed is everyone who does not continue in ALL things which are written in the book of the Law. Ezech. 18. v. 4. The soul that sins, it shall die. Rom 6. v. last. The wages of sin is death. Hence arises the argument: Every sin is mortal, and incurs the curse of the Law, since these sayings speak generally of every sin, of every ἀνομίᾳ, and admit no exception. A venial sin is a sin. Therefore it is mortal, and incurs the curse of the Law. Bellarmine excepts, that these ought to be understood only of crimes, otherwise those sinning venially would not only be able to die eternally, but would actually die. I answer, this would indeed follow, if this appendix were not to be understood, unless remission is immediately made in the very act through Christ.

3. Matth. 5. v. 19. Whoever shall break one of these least commandments, shall be called least in the kingdom of God. But Ελάχιστος or least in the kingdom of heaven is here put for nothing. For in heaven there will be nothing except what is great, says Augustine. But Christ speaks thus in the likeness of the Pharisaic phrase. For just as they called commandments 'least' which they held for nothing, and thought did not bind: So Christ calls him 'least' in the kingdom of heaven who was to be absolutely nothing in it, which Bellarmine also concedes, column 165. If therefore the transgression of even the least commandments excludes one from the kingdom of God, it is rightly gathered that all sins are of themselves mortal. Which is clear all the more brightly if the scope of Christ is considered, which was to correct the Pharisaic doctrine, not to condemn lighter sins. The Savior taught the contrary, and therefore by the force of that opposition it follows in turn, that those sins that we may speak thus, are even the most minute things mortal,

4. John 13. v. 8. If I do not wash you, you will have no part with me. The Savior said this not only because of the stubbornness and disobedience of Peter, by which he did not want his feet washed by Christ, as a punishment, but because the washing and cleansing of the feet, by which spiritual cleansing from sins was denoted, was altogether necessary on account of the venial sins by which the disciples were still defiled. For if the disciples could have had a part with the Lord without that washing, Christ would certainly have omitted it, and that especially because he says afterwards to Peter, He who is washed does not need except to wash his feet, showing that the disciples were already washed and cleansed from more serious sins: but that in the meantime it is necessary, if they wish to have a part with Christ and not be damned, that they also wash their feet and take care that lighter and daily sins are purged. For Bellarmine admits himself, that it is impossible for anyone to enter the kingdom of heaven with such filth, yet he does not exclude them absolutely from the kingdom but only for a time, until they have been purged. From this, however, we firmly conclude that such sins, considered in themselves without purgation, simply exclude one from the kingdom of heaven. For if they are able to exclude for a time, they are certainly mortal by nature: but that they do not always do so, this happens not because of their lightness, but because of purgation: on which account Bellarmine is contrary to himself.

X. REASONS. Every ἀνομία deserves death: for the wages of sin is death. But truly involuntary sins, which adhere to the reborn, are also called sins; Rom. 6. v. 7. and 1 John 1. v. 8. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves. Refer here the following, Exod. 34. v. 7. 2 Chron. 6. v. 36. Job 15. v. 14. ch. 25. v. 4. Proverbs 20. v. 9. Eccles. 7. v. 21.

2. Those sins for which that remission must be sought bind one to the guilt of eternal punishment. For nothing else is remitted than the guilt. And yet the remission of venial sins must be sought. For this reason the Saints pray, Forgive us our debts, and for this every Saint will pray, Psalm 32, v. 6.

3. Whatever is remitted by grace is not remitted because of its lightness. And yet all sins, even the most minute, are remitted by grace alone. For if you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand? Psalm 129, verse 3. Psalm 142, v. 2. Ezra 9, v. 15.

4. Whoever does not perfectly fulfill the Law is condemned by the Law because of the absence of perfect fulfillment. But not even the most holy person in this life fulfills the law perfectly, because charity with the whole heart, with the whole soul, that is, the total integrity of all powers, is required. Therefore, even the most holy person is condemned according to the Law, and consequently, all sins are mortal and damning. Hence it is said in Luke 17, v. 10: Even if you have done all things, yet say, we are unprofitable servants: we have done what we ought to have done. Whoever, therefore, does not do what he ought to do, certainly incurs the annexed curse.

5. Whatever injures the infinite justice of GOD, to which the definition of sin applies, and for which an account must be rendered to God on the day of judgment, all this deserves eternal death: But such are even venial sins, so that the Savior forewarns that an account must be rendered for every idle word, Matthew 12, v. 35. Wherefore it deserves eternal death by its own nature, which was to be demonstrated.

XI. TESTIMONIES 1. August. Epist. 108. There is a daily penance of good and humble believers, in which we beat our breasts, saying: Forgive us our debts. For we do not wish to be forgiven those things which we do not doubt were forgiven in Baptism, but rather those which, however small, yet frequently creep into human frailty, which if they are gathered against us, will weigh us down and overwhelm us just as one great sin. For what difference does it make for a shipwreck whether a ship is covered and overwhelmed by one great wave, or whether water creeping in little by little into the bilge, and neglected and despised through negligence, fills the ship and sinks

stand? And in book 2 on the merit of sins, ch. 3. Who would depart from this life with any hope of attaining eternal salvation, if that sentence remained that whoever has kept the whole Law, but offends in one, has become guilty of all, unless a little later it followed, but mercy triumphs over judgment? And in book 9 of the Confessions, last chapter. Woe even to the praiseworthy life of men, if you examine it with mercy removed. 2. Nazianzen, oration 31. Every sin is the death of the soul. 3. Jerome, Epistle 14. I do not know if we can call any sin light, which is committed in contempt of God. And Dialogue 2 against the Pelagians. If anger and injury of speech and sometimes a joke are consigned to judgment and council and the fires of hell, what will the desire for base things and avarice deserve? 4. Gregory in Ezekiel, book 1, homily 2. Every sin is grave, because it does not permit the mind to be raised to sublime things. 5. Theodoret in Dialogue. The devil is the father of sin, and sin is the mother of death. 6. Bede in Samuel, book 1, chapter 10. Not only the capital conflagrations of crimes, in which the open work of the devil is clear, but also every small thing, and those which to men seem perhaps extreme or light sins, the sentence of the strict judge reprovingly condemns. 7. Bernard in meditations or book on the soul, chapter 11. It does not differ much, whatever substance, vile or precious, is sought, provided the affection is equally corrected: For it is not the knife that is in use, but the desire for the knife: nor is gold in the vice, but the greed for gold. 8. Gerson on spiritual reading, 1. Every sin, in so far as it is an offense against God and against His eternal Law, is by its condition and indignity mortal according to the rigor of justice, and a separator from the life of glory. Again: No offense against God is venial in itself, except only by respect to divine mercy. 9. Michael Baius, Professor of Louvain: It is not, he says, to be disapproved, the opinion by which it is said that even light sins, with the blood of Christ set aside, by their own nature exclude one from the kingdom of God.

Latin:

I. Argumenta, quòd omnia peccata ex sua natura sint mortalia.

VIII. Probari & confirmari potest thesis nostra 1. Dictis Scripturæ, 2. Rationibus ab analogia fidei, 3. Testimonijs Patrum & adversariorũ, de quibus ordine. IX. DICTA. 1. Iacobi 2. v. 10. Qui offenderit in UNO, factus est omnium reus, Apertissimum hoc dictum est, ex quo vltrò sequitur, quòd vel vnum duntaxat peccatum commitens, reus sit totius legis, & quidem ideó, quia vnus idemque est omnium præceptorum author, nempè Deus. Nam qui dixit, ne mæchaberis, dixit etiam, ne occidas, v. 11. Absurdus autem est Bellarminus, qui l. 1. cap. 12. censet Iacobum loqui tantùm de offensione criminali, non veniali, cùm generatim de quouis peccato verba faciat. Ratio enim ejus desumta est ab authore DEO: Deus omnia præcepia tulit. Ergo tàm peccat contra DEUM, qui vnum aliquod, quàm qui omnia violat. Et c. 3. dicitur; In multis offendimus omnes

Ex quo patet, quomodo vocabulum offendendi sit accipiendum, videlicet non tantum de criminibus & flagitiis, sed etiam de peccatis infirmitatis:

2. Deut. 27. v. ult. Galat. 3. v. 10. Maledictus omnis, qui non permanserit in OMNIBVS, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis. Ezech. 18. v. 4. Anima, quæ peccaverit, ipsa morietur. Rom 6. v. ult. Stipendium peccati mors est. Hinc oritur argumentum: Omne peccatum est mortale, & incurrit maledictionem Legis, quoniam dicta ista generaliter loquuntur de omni peccato, de omni ἀνομίᾳ, & nullam exceptionem admittunt. Peccatum veniale est peccatum. Ergo mortale est, & incurrit maledictionem Legis. Excipit Bellarminus, hæc tantum de criminibus debere intelligi, alias venialiter peccantes non solum possent æternum mori, sed actu morerentur. Respondeo, sequeretur hoc vtique, si non subintelligenda esset ista appendix, nisi statim & in ipso actu fiat remissio per Christum.

3. Matth. 5. v. 19. Quisquis solverit vnum ex mandatis hisce minimis, minimus vocabitur in regno Dei. Ελάχιστος autem vel minimus in regno cœlorum hic pro nullo ponitur. In cœlo enim nil erit nisi magnum, inquit August. Christus autem ita loquitur ad similitudinem phraseos Pharisaicæ. Sicut enim hi vocabant præcepta minima, quæ habebant pro nullis, & putabant non obligare: Sic Christus vocat minimum in regno cælorum qui plane nullus in eo futurus erat, quod etiam concedit Bellarminus column. 165. Si ergo transgressio minimorum quoque præceptorum, excludit e regno Dei, vtique peccata omnia ex se mortalia esse, recte colligitur. Quod eo patet luculentius, si consideretur scopus Christi, qui erat corrigere doctrinam Pharisaicam, peccata leuiora non damnare. Contrarium docebat Saluator, ideoque vi oppositionis istius vicissim sequitur, peccata illas vt fic loquamur, etiam minutissima esse mortalia,

4. Iohan. 13. v. 8. Si non lauero te, non habebis partem mecum. Hoc non tantum propter pertinaciam & in-obedientiam Petri, qua nolebat a Christo pedes sibi lauari, poenae loco Seruator dicebat, sed quia omnino necessaria erat propter peccata venialia, quibus adhuc polluti erant discipuli, lotio ac mun-datio pedum, qua spiritualis a peccatis emunda-tio denotabatur. Si enim discipuli absque illa lotione partem cum Domino potuissent habe-re, vtique Christus eam intermisisset, idque ma-xime, quia postea ad Petrum dicit, Qui lotus est, non indiget, nisi vt pedes lauet, ostendens; quod discipuli iam antea loti ac mundi sint a peccatis grauiori-bus: at interim necessarium esse, si partem cum Christo velint habere, & non damnari, vt etiam pedes lauent, & peccata leuiora atque quotidia-na purgari curent. Nam fatetur Bellarm. ipse, fieri non posse, vt quis regnum coelorum ingrediatur cum talibus sordibus, excludere tamen non abso-lute a regno sed tantum ad tempus, donec purga-ta fuerint. Inde autem talia peccata ex se conside-rata sine purgatione, simpliciter excludere a re-gno coelorum firmiter concludimus. Si enim ad tempus excludere queunt, vtique per naturam sunt mortalia: quod autem non semper id faciant, hoc non propter leuitatem, sed propter purgatio-nem fit: quo nomine Bellarminus sibiipsi est con-trarius.

X. RATIONES. Omnis ἀνομία meretur mortem: sti-pendium enim peccati est mors. At vero peccata in-uoluntaria, quae renatis adhaerent, etiam dicuntur pec-cata; Rom. 6. v. 7. & 1. Iohan. 1. v. 8. Si dixerimus, quo-niam peccatum non habemus, ipsi nos seducimus. Refer huc sequentia, Exod. 34. v. 7. 2. Paral. 6. v. 36. Iob. 15. v. 14. c. 25. v. 4. Prouerb. 20. v. 9. Eccles. 7. v. 21.

2. Quorum peccatorum petenda est remissio ista obligant reatu poenae aeternae. Nihil enim aliud remittitur, quàm reatus. Atqui peccatorum venialium remissio est petenda. Ideò enim orant Sancti, Remitte nobis debita nostra, & pro hoc orabit omnis Sanctus Psalm. 32. v. 6.

3. Quodcunque remittitur ex gratia, id non remittitur ob leuitatem. Atqui omnia peccata etiam minutissima remittuntur ex sola gratia. Si enim iniquitates obseruaueris Domine, quis sustinebit? Psal. 129 versus 3. Psal. 142 v. 2 Esdræ 9. v. 15.

4. Quicunque perfectè Legem non implet, damnatur à Lege ob impletionis perfectæ absentiam. Sed neque sanctissimus in hac vita legem perfecte implet, quia charitas ex toto corde, totâ animâ, id est, summa omnium virium integritas requiritur. Ergò sanctissimus etiam secundum Legem damnatur, & per consequens, omnia peccata sunt mortalia & damnantia. Hinc dicitur Luc. 17. v. 10. Etiam si omnia feceritis; tamen dicite, serui inutiles sumus: quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Quisquis igitur non facit, quod facere debet, annexam maledictionem certò incurrit.

5. Quæcunque infinitam DEI iustitiam lædit, cui definitio peccati competit, & propter quod Deo est reddenda ratio in die iudicij, hoc omne promeretur mortem æternam: At talia sunt peccata etiam venialia, sic vt de quouis verbo otioso rationem reddendam esse, Saluator prænunciet, Matth. 12. v. 35. Quare mortem æternam ex natura sua promeretur, id quod fuit demonstrandum.

XI. TESTIMONIA 1. August. Epist. 108. Est pænitentia bonorum & humilium fidelium quotidiana, in qua pectora tundimus, dicentes: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Neque enim à nobis dimitti volumus, quæ dimissa non dubitamus in Baptismo, sed illa vtique quæ humanæ fragilitati quamvis parua; tamen crebra subrepunt, quæ si collecta contra nos fuerint, ita nos grauabunt & oppriment, ficuti vnum aliquod grande peccatum. Quid enim interest ad naufragiū, vtrù vno grãdi fluctu nauis operiatur & obruatur, an paulatim subrepens aqua insentinam, & per negligentia derelicta atq; contempta impleat nauem atq; submer-

stat? Et lib. 2. de peccat. mer. c. 3. Quis cum spe aliqua adipiscendae salutis aeternae de hac vita migraret, manente illa sententia quod quicunque totam Legem servaverit, offendas autem in vno, reus factus sit omnium, nisi post paululum sequeretur, misericordia autem superexultat iudicio? Et lib. 9. Confess. c. vlt. Vae etiam laudabili hominum vitae, si remota misericordia discutias eam. 2. Nazianzenus orat. 31. Omne peccatum animae mors est. 3. Hierony mus Epist. 14. Nescio an possimus leue aliquod peccatum dicere, quod in Dei contemptum admittitur. Et Dial. 2. aduers. Pelag. Si ira & sermonis iniuria atque interdum iocus iudicio concilioque & gehennae ignibus delegantur, quid merebitur turpium rerum appetitio & avaritia? 4. Gregor. in Ezech. lib. 1. homil. 2. Omne peccatum graue, quia non permittit animum ad sublimia eleuari. 5. Theod. in Dial. Peccati pater Diabolus, & peccatum mortis mater. 6. Beda in Sam. l. 1. cap. 10. Non tantum capitalia incendia criminum, in quibus apertum opus Diaboli claret, sed & parua quaeque, & quae hominibus extrema vel leuia fortè peccata videntur, districti iudicis sententia reprobans damnat. 7. Bernhardus in meditat. vel lib. de anima cap. 11. Non multum distat, quacunque substantia vilis vel pretiosa requiratur dum aequaliter sit correptus affectus: Non enim cultellus in vsum est, sed cultelli appetitus: neque aurum in vitium est, sed auri cupiditas. 8. Gerson de spirit. lect. 1. Omne peccatum, pro quanto est offensa Dei & contra Legem eius aeternam, est de sua conditione & indignitate mortiferum secundum rigorem iustitiae, & à vita gloriae separatiuum. Rursus: Nulla offensa Dei est venialis de se, nisi tantummodo per respectum ad diuinam misericordiam. 9. Michael Baius Professor Louaniensis: Non est, ait, improbanda opinio quâ dicitur, quòd etiam leuia peccata secluso Christi sanguine, ex natura sua secludunt à regno Dei.


### Question II Are all sins by their own nature mortal: II. Objections of the Romanists

II. Objections of the Romanists.

XII. 1. Only a manifest insult deserves the hell of fire. Therefore, hidden anger is venial by its own kind. The antecedent is proven from Matt. 5: v. 22. Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever says to his brother, Racha, will be liable to the Council; and whoever says, you fool, will be liable to the hell of fire.

Response. A fallacy of φράσεως is committed in this argument because of a false interpretation of the words, which is repugnant to the whole of Scripture. For it is repugnant to all those Scriptures which say that anger is a damnable thing and a work of the flesh—Eccles. 7: v. 10, Coloss. 3: v. 8, 1 Tim. 2: v. 8, James 1: v. 19 & 20—that only manifest abuse makes one liable to eternal damnation, but not hidden anger. But in order that the true meaning of these words may be held, the following things must be well noted. 1. The scope of CHRIST: Since He did not come here to destroy, but to fulfill the moral Law, verse 17, and this fulfillment consists in: 1. satisfaction, 2. explanation, 3. imputation, and 4. the beginning of renewal; hence, in chapter 5 of Matthew, He proposes the second mode of fulfillment, consisting in the true and genuine explanation of the Law, to the undertaking of which He was moved by various and most serious corruptions of the Pharisees. For Christ says that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven through the righteousness of the Pharisees, verse 20, because it is not abundant and sufficient, since the least commandments are being loosened, verse 19.

From this it is gathered what the opinion of the Pharisees was concerning the Law and salvation from the Law. They knew that the fulfillment of the Law was necessary for obtaining eternal life. But because they saw that the very smallest things in the Law, especially concerning the integrity and rectitude of the interior faculties, could not be observed in this deformity of nature, they therefore invented such a distinction: that some commandments of the Law are least, and some are great. And [they held] the observation of these alone [was sufficient] for eternal life. they thought the consequence was necessary, but that the fulfillment of those least ones, since it concerns minute matters, was not strictly required. That he therefore is righteous before God, who has observed the great commandments, as they are concerning not killing, not committing adultery, stealing, &c., with which opinion this puffed-up Pharisee came into the temple, Luke 18. Christ opposes himself to these Pharisaic inventions, showing that that distinction between great and least sins, taken in the Pharisaic sense, is null, and that no one can enter into the kingdom of heaven, unless his righteousness has abounded more than that of the Pharisees. For he who has broken one of these least ones, will be the least in the kingdom of heaven, that is, an outcast entirely, and not only not righteous, but even worthy of the punishment of eternal damnation. And thus, by the transgression of the least commandments, he denounces both the punishment of loss or privative, and the punishment of sense or positive, which sentence of Christ was clearly contrary to the doctrine of the Pharisees. For they had handed down from antiquity that he who keeps the great commandments, although he has broken the least, will not be guilty of eternal damnation, but will be great in eternal life; Christ, however, says that such a one will be nothing, nay, will be liable to damnation in hell, since such perfection is required by the law, that heaven and earth shall sooner pass away than a minute apex, nay, even the smallest iota of one apex in the law can be violated without punishment. And this was the scope of Christ, from which it appears that he was speaking not of political and temporal punishments and rewards, but rather of eternal ones. But what he said first in general about all the commandments, he declares afterwards in particular through some precepts, and indeed he begins from the fifth, v. 21. and 22. where it is to be observed.

11. Mode of speaking. First, v. 21. he proposes the opinion of the Pharisees: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, Thou shalt not kill, and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment. By that which was said to the ancients, He understands not the law itself, but the Pharisaical interpretations and corruptions. Not all those things which Christ adds are found in the law and the Prophets themselves. Nor does He say, You read in Moses, but you have heard, and therefore He refers to unwritten traditions. The Pharisees thought, however, that the fifth commandment was perfectly fulfilled if one killed no one by hand: and that only he was guilty by the force of the fifth commandment (which is signified by the word judgment) who had killed his brother. To this Pharisaical commentary Christ opposes His own true opinion; I, He says, say to you: Whosoever is angry, etc. In which saying are to be observed both the degrees of sins and the degrees of punishments, of which three are counted on each side.

The first degree of sin against the fifth commandment is hidden anger: Whosoever is angry with his brother. In the Greek the particle εἰκῇ, rashly, is added: Therefore not every anger is understood here (for public persons justly become angry out of righteous zeal on account of vices, Psalm 139:22, which the examples of Moses, Christ, and Paul testify), but only that which is rash, proceeding from a mind malevolent on account of an offense, and desiring its own revenge. The second degree is the sign and gesture of an angry and malevolent mind, which are noted by the word רקא, about which many feel many things, but the opinion of Chemnitz is the simplest, that this word in itself signifies nothing certain, but is an interjection of a moved mind; and it is the same as when the Germans say, Pfun dich an: for רק signifies to spit or to spit upon to the Chaldeans. However it may be explained, provided this is observed, that the degrees of sins are not confused. For by this word such a sin is noted, which is intermediate between hidden anger and open insult. The third degree is manifest reviling. If anyone shall say, thou fool. But that which is lightest in revilings is named is, so that from there the remaining more serious insults may be estimated from the lesser. And here in turn it is to be noted, that not all angry words, but those that are rash, proceeding from an irascible mind, are condemned. For Christ also spoke somewhat harshly to his disciples, but not from a malevolent heart, but rather a paternal one, Matt. 16 v. 33. he calls Peter Satan, Luke 24 v. 25. he names the Emmaus disciples foolish, slow, Gal. 3 v. 1. the Galatians are called senseless by Paul.

And these three degrees of sins the Pharisees clearly neglected, and counted among the lesser sins, which are neither against the law, nor cared for by God, nor worthy of eternal damnation. But Christ affirms the contrary, while he says the first degree is worthy of judgment, the second of the council, the third of the hell of fire. Which terms Bellarmine interprets thus, Col. 93. lit. c. He is called guilty of judgment, who has done something whereby he may be called into judgment, so that his case may be discussed. He is called guilty of the council, whose fault is certain, but it is ambiguous how great it is, and what punishment it deserves, and therefore the judges come together into a Council, so that they may define the measure of the punishment. He is called guilty of the hell of fire, whose fault and the measure of the fault and by this also the gravity of the punishment is certain. Moreover, by hell is signified eternal death in the underworld. By judgment and council, however, he thinks is signified not eternal punishment, but a lighter one, and a temporal one, which interpretation we prove to be false and contrary to the text by three arguments.

1. In the same sense that the word judgment is taken in v. 21. it is also taken in v. 22. For the Pharisees assigned the punishment of judgment only to manifest homicide: but Christ assigns the punishment of judgment to the one who is angry. In both places, therefore, it is taken in the same way. But indeed in v. 21. the word judgment denotes eternal punishment. For a homicide does not sin venially, but mortally, and is worthy of eternal damnation. Therefore the same meaning also has a place in verse 22.

Whence it follows that by the judgment penalty due to an angry heart is understood not temporal chastisement, but eternal damnation.

2. From the opposition of opinions between Christ and the Pharisees. They thought that those least sins did not exclude anyone from the kingdom of heaven, nor oblige one to the penalty of eternal damnation: but Christ affirms the contrary: He who shall break one of the least commandments, he shall be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Therefore, if the opposition of opinions is to be true, it follows that Christ intended the terms of judgment and council to denote eternal damnation. For what other opposition would there be? Least sins are not worthy of eternal death, which was the opinion of the Pharisees: And least sins are not worthy of eternal death, yet they deserve a temporal penalty, which would be, according to Bellarmine, Christ's opinion, not opposed to the former. For the question between Christ and the Pharisees was not, Whether those least sins deserve some penalty, whatever it may be? but this, Whether he who shall have broken one of the least commandments, such as those who are rashly angry, can enter the kingdom of God, or whether they deserve eternal damnation? Here the Pharisees held the affirmative: but Christ the negative. Now if the terms of judgment and council are not explained as referring to eternal penalties, certainly Christ did not hold the negative, and therefore his opinion was clearly the same as that of the Pharisees; which is absurd.

3. Those terms were political, taken from the distinct orders of courts in the Jewish polity. 1. There was the court of the triumvirs, who pronounced on cases of manifest law, such as the penalty for homicide. 2. In every city there was a small sanhedrin, consisting of 23 judges, who judged on more serious cases which had some element of controversy. 3. In Jerusalem sat 72 judges, who took cognizance of the highest cases, and it was called the great συνέδριον or Council. Whoever, therefore, was condemned for sinning against the fifth commandment, either in the court, or in the small, or in the great Sanhedrin, was always punished with death; meanwhile, a more severe penalty was pronounced in the Council than in the court, although in both cases a capital penalty was decreed. Therefore, just as one sinning against the fifth commandment was punished capitally according to the judgment of the court; so he who is angry with his brother gives a capital penalty to God, that is, he is punished with eternal death. And conversely, just as a more severe mode of capital punishment was decreed in the Council: so he who says Raca to his brother will be more severely punished in eternal damnation. By the hell of fire, however, an even more intense penalty is designated. For this kind of punishment was very atrocious, when the bodies of evildoers were cast unburied into the valley of Ben-Hinnom or of the sons of Hinnom, which place was abominable to the Jews, and called Tophet: whence it came about that hell is also called Tophet, Isaiah 30, verse 33. Gehenna, by a certain inflection. Therefore, just as the greatest degree of punishment in the Jewish polity was if anyone were cast into the valley of Ben-Hinnom, so also will he be afflicted with a greater degree of punishment in hell if anyone has called his brother a fool. By all these terms, therefore, of judgment, council, and Gehenna, eternal damnation is noted, and at the same time certain degrees of damnation according to the custom of the Jewish polity.

Latin:

II. Obiectiones Romanensium.

XII. 1. Manifestum duntaxat conuitium mereturgehennam ignis. Ergo occulta ira ex suo genere venialis est. Antecedens probatur ex Matth. 5: v. 22. Omnis, qui irascitur fratri suo, reus erit iudicio: qui autem dixerit fratri suo Racha, reus erit Concilio: qui autem dixerit, fatue, reus erit gehennæ ignis.

Respond. Committitur in hoc argumento fallacia φράσεως ob falsam verborum interpretationem, quæ toti repugnat Scripturæ Nam manifestum duntaxat conuitium reum esse æternâ damnatione, non autem iram occultam, repugnat omnibus ijs Scripturis, quæ iram dicunt esse rem damnabilem & opus carnis, Eccles. 7. v. 10. Coloss 3. v. 8. 1. T:m. 2. v. 8. Iacobi 1. v. 19. & 20. Vt autem vera istorum verborum teneatur sententia, sequentia probè sunt notanda. 1. Scopus CHRISTI: Quoniam hic non venit ad destruendam, sed implendam Legem moralem, vers. 17. impletio autem ista sita est. 1. in satisfactione, 2. explicatione, 3. imputatione, & 4. inchoat one renouationis; hinc cap. 5. Matth. secundum impletionis modum proponit, consistentem in vera & genuina Legis explicatione, ad quam suscipiendam mouebatur à varijs ijsque grauissimis Pharisæorum corruptelis. Dicit enim Christus, quòd nemo per iustitiam Pharisæorum possit intrare in regnum cælorum, vers. 20. quia non sit abundans & sufficiens, cùm soluantur mandata minima, vers. 19.

Hinc colligitur, quæ fuerit Pharisæorum sententia de Lege & salute ex Lege. Sciuerunt, opus esse impletione Legis ad vitam æternam consequendam. Quoniam verò viderunt, non posse minutissima quæque in Lege, præsertim de integritate & rectitudine interiorum virium præcipientia, in hac naturæ deformitate obseruari, ideò finxerunt talem distinctionem, quædam mandata Legis esse minima, quædam magna. Et horum duntaxat obseruationem ad vitæ æternæ consecutionem putabant esse necessariam, istorum verò minimorum impletionem, quippe quæ circa res minutulas versetur non exigi strictè. Iustuin igitur esse coram Deo omnem illum, qui mandata magna, vt sunt de nõ occidendo, de non mœchando, furando, &c. obseruauerit, quâ opinione turgidus Pharisæus iste venit in templum, Luc. 18. Hiice Pharisæicis commentis sese opponit Christus, ostendens distinctionem illam inter peccata magna & minima sensu Pharisæico sumtam, nullam esse, nec posse quemquam intrare in regnum cœlorum, nisi cuius iustitia abundauerit plus quam Pharisæorum. Illum enim, qui soluerit vnum ex minimis istis, minimum fore in regno cœlorum, id est, extorrem omninò, & non modò non iustum, sed etiam dignum pœnâ damnationis æternæ. Atque sic transgressione mandatorum minimorum, & pœnam damni seu priuatiuam & pœnam sensus seu positiuam denunciat, quæ sententia Christi planè erat contraria doctrinæ Pharisæorum. Nam hi antiquitùs tradiderant, eum, qui seruat mandata magna, licèt soluerit minimas non fore reum æternæ damnationis, sed iri magnum in vita æterna, Christus verò ait, talem fore nullum, imò iri obnoxium damnationi in inferno, quandoquidem talis requiratur à lege perfectio, vt cœlum & terra prius transeant, quàm minutus apex, imò vel minutulum vnius apiculi iota in lege violari sine pœnâ possit. Atque hic fuit scopus Christi, ex quo apparet, quòd non de pœnis & præmijs politicis ac temporalibus, sed potiùs æternis verba fecerit. Quòd autem primùm in genere de omnibus mandatis dixit, illud postmodùm in specie per aliquot præcepta declarat, & quidem à quinto orditur, v. 21. & 22. vbi obseruandus est.

11. Modus loquendi. Primùm vers. 21. proponit sententiam Pharisæorum: Audistis quæ diEtum est antiquis, Non occides, qui autem occiderit, reus erit iudicio. Per id quod antiquis dictum est non ipsam legem, sed Pharisaicas interpretationes & corruptelas intelligit. Non omnia ea, quæ Christus addit, in ipsa lege & Prophetis reperiuntur. Neque dicit, Vos in Mose legitis, sed audistis, ideoque ad traditiones non scriptas respicit. Putabant autem Pharisæi, perfectè impletum esse preceptum quintum, si quis neminem manu occiderit: Et eum tantùm æterna damnatione (quæ per iudicij vocem significatur) reum esse vi quinti præcepti, qui occiderit fratrem. Huic commento Pharisaico Christus opponit suam veramque sententiam; Ego, inquit, dico vobis: Qui irascitur, &c. In quo dicto obseruandi sunt tum gradus peccatorum, tum gradus pœnarum, quorum vtrinque numerantur tres.

Primus gradus peccati contra quintum præceptum est ira occulta: Qui irascitur fratri suo. In Græco addita est particula εἰκῇ temerè: Non ergò omnis ita hic intelligitur (personæ enim publicæ ex iusto zelo iustè irascuntur ob vitia Psalm. 139. v. 22. quod testantur exempla Mosis, Christi, Pauli) sed tantùm temeraria, profecta ex animo propter offensionem maleuolo, & vltionem propriam appetere. Secundus gradus, est signum gestusque irati ac maleuoli animi, qui notantur voce רקא, de qua multi multa sentiunt, sed simplicissima est Chemnitij sententia, quòd ista vox per se nihil certi significet, sed sit interiectio animi commoti; & idem sit, ac quando Germani dicunt, Pfun dich an: רק enim Chaldæis significat spuere, vel conspuere. Vtcunque verò exponatur, modò hoc obseruetur, ne gradus peccatorum confundantur. Est enim hoc vocabulo tale peccatum notatum, quod sit intermedium inter iram occultam & apertam contumeliam. Tertius gradus, est manifestum conuitium. Si quis dixerit fatue. Nominatur autem id, quod in conuitijs leuissimum est, vt inde à minori reliqua grauiora conuitia æstimentur. Et hîc vicissim notandum, quòd non omnes voces stomachosiores, sed eæq́ seu temerariæ, ex animo iracundo profectæ damnentur. Nam & Christus nonnihil durius allocutus est suos discipulos, sed non ex corde malevolo, sed potiùs paterno, Matth. 16 v. 33. vocat Petrum Satanam Luc. 24. v 25. nominat Emaunticos stultos, tardos Gal. 3. v. 1. Gal. à Paulo vocātur insensati.

Et hos tres peccatorum gradus Pharisaei planè negligebant, & inter peccata minora recensebant, quæ nec sint contra legem, nec à Deo curentur, nec digna sint æternâ damnatione. Verùm Christus contrarium adfirmat, dum primum gradum dignum esse dicit iudicio, secundum concilio, tertium gehenna ignis. Quæ vocabula Bellarmin. ita interpretatur Col. 93. lit. c. Reus iudicij dicitur, qui aliquid fecit, vnde in iudicium vocari possit, vt causa eius discutiatur. Reus concilij dicitur, cuius culpa certa est, sed ambiguum quanta sit, & quam pœnam mereatur, & ideò iudices inter se conueniunt in Concilium, vt definiant pœnæ mensuram. Reus gehennæ ignis dicitur, cuius culpa & mensura culpæ ac per hoc etiam pœnæ grauitas certa est. Significatur autem per gehennam mors æterna apud inferos. Per judicium autem & concilium putat significari non pœnam æternam, sed leuïorem, eaḿque temporalem, quam interpretationem falsam & textui contrariam esse tribus argumentis evincimus.

1. Quo sensu vocabulum judicij sumitur v. 21. eodem etiam sumitur v. 22. Nam Pharisæi pœnam judicii assignabant tantùm manifesto homicidio: Christus vero pœnam judicii irascenti assignat. Vtrobique igitur eodem modo sumitur. At verò v. 21. vocabulum judicii denotat pœnam æternam. Homicida enim non peccat venialiter, sed mortaliter, & dignus est damnatione æternâ. Ergò eadem significatio etiam locum habet versu 22.

Vnde sequitur, quòd per pœnam judicij debitam cordi irato, intelligatur non temporalis castigatio, sed æterna damnatio.

2. Ex oppositione sententiarum inter Christum & Pharisæos. Hi putabant, peccata illa minima non excludere aliquem è regno cœlorum, nec obligare ad pœnam æternæ damnationis: Christus autem contrarium affirmat: Qui solverit vnum ex mandatis minimis, ille minimus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Ergò si vera debet esse oppositio sententiarum, sequitur, quòd Christus per vocabula judicij & concilij æternam damnationem denotatam voluerit. Quæ enim aliàs foret oppositio? Peccata minima non sunt digna morte æternâ, quæ erat sententia Phàrisæorum: Et peccata minima non sunt digna morte æternâ, pœnam tamen promerentur temporalem, quæ esset juxta Bellar. Christi sententia, priori non opposita. Non enim quærebatur inter Christum & Pharisæos, Vtrum aliquam pœnam mereantur peccata ista minima, qualiscunque etiam sit? sed hoc, Vtrum is, qui solverit unum ex mandatis minimis, quales sunt temerè irascentes, possit intrare regnum Dei, ne promerentur æternam damnationem? Hîc Pharisæi affirmatiuam tenuerunt: Christus autem negatiuam. Iam si vocabula judicij & concilij non explicantur de pœnis æternis, certè Christus non tenuit negatiuam, ideoque ejusdem planè cum Pharisæis fuit sententiæ; ἄτοπον.

3. Vocabula ista erant politica, desumta à distinctis ordinibus judiciorum in politia judaici. 1. Erat iudicium triumuirorum, qui pronunciabant de causis manifesti juris, vt de pœna homicidij. 2. In qualibet ciuitate erat paruum synedrium, constans ex 23. judicibus, qui judicabant de causis grauioribus, quæ habebant aliquid controuersiæ. 3. Hierosolymis sedebant. 72. Iudices, qui de summis causis cognoscebant, & vocabatur συνέδριον magnum seu Consilium. Quicunq; igitur contra præceptum quintum peccans vel in iudicio, vel in parvo, vel in magno fynedrio damnabatur, semper capite plectebatur, interim in Concilio gravior dictabatur pœna, quàm in iudicio, licet vtrobique capitalis pœna decerneretur. Sicut ergò peccans contra quintum præceptum, secundum sententiam iudicij capitaliter puniebatur; ita irascens fratri capitalem Deo dat pœnam, id est, morte æternâ punitur. Et vicissim, sicut in Concilio gravior modus capitalis pœnæ decernebatur : ita dicens fratri suo Raca, in æterna damnatione graviùs punietur. Per gehennam ignis autem ferverior adhuc pœna designatur. Erat enim hoc supplicij genus valdè atrox, quando corpora maleficorum inhumata abjiciebantur in vallem Benhinnon vel filiorum Hinnon, qui locus abominabilis erat Iudæis, & Thophet dictus : vnde factum, vt infernus dicatur etiam Thophet, Esai. 30. versu. 33. Gehenna, per quandam inflexionem. Sicut ergò maximus erat pœnæ gradus in politia Iudaica, si quis in vallem Benhinnon abijciebatur, ita & maiori pœnæ gradu in inferno affligetur, si quis fratrem suum stultum dixerit. Omnibus igitur his vocabulis, judicij, concilij & gehennæ notatur æterna damnatio, simulque certi damnationis gradus secundum consuetudinem politiæ Iudaicæ.


### Question II Are all sins by their own nature mortal: XIII. 2. Matt. 23. v

XIII. 2. Matt. 23. v. 24. Certain sins are compared to a gnat, certain ones to a camel; Luke 6. v. 24. conversely, certain ones are compared to a splinter, certain ones to beams. Whence they gather that there are given certain very light offenses, which by their own nature are venial.

I respond: Not so. For nothing else can be proved from thence, than that there are given certain degrees of sins, according to which some are more severe and lighter than others. Meanwhile, that certain ones are by themselves, and according to their own nature, worthy of pardon is said neither explicitly nor implicitly. But especially in the former passage, nothing of this is hinted. For Christ there deals with the nature of hypocrites, who, anxious about minute things, neglect the principal things expressly, nor do they distinguish those things which are necessary in themselves and always, from those whose privation does not make us guilty, but contempt does.

XIV. 3. Luke 12. v. 59. You shall not depart thence until you pay even the last mite, by which mite they understand venial sins, which indeed do not condemn, yet for which satisfaction must be made in the prison of purgatory.

Response. Christ speaks there of reconciliation, and therefore of enmities with one's neighbor, which are a mortal sin, as is evident in Gal. 5. v. 20. The works of the flesh are enmities, strife, emulations. And 1 John 3. v. 15. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. He describes, therefore, the most exquisite exaction of debt, that no liberation is to be hoped for from prison, unless the whole debt, and indeed the last mite, is paid, which is impossible to do. But that Bellarmine seeks a loophole for escape in the particle Until, it is known that it does not always signify a limit, but more often perpetuity and continuation, as 2 Sam. 6. v. last. Ps. 110. v. 1. Isa. 22. v. 14. c. 42. v. 4. Matt. 5. v. 25. c. 28. v. 20. 1 Cor. 15. v. 25. For he who is once cast into hell is never liberated from there: for from hell there is no redemption. That, however, it is not a fabricated purgatory that is to be understood here, but hell, is evident from Matt. 5. v. 25, where it is called a prison, into which one is sent by an angry judge, and is delivered to the exactor, that is, the devil. But these things do not befit purgatory. For there is no exactor or torturer there, since thus hell and purgatory would be confounded; nor are souls delivered into purgatory by an angry God, since they always retain the grace of God, according to the Papists.

XV. 4. 1 Cor. 3. v. 12. For other foundation no man can lay, but that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if any man build upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble, every man's work shall be made manifest: For the day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire, etc. By hay and stubble they understand venial sins, which are not punished by the flames of hell, but are expiated by the punishments of purgatory. I respond. 1. An article of faith cannot be proven from obscure and ambiguous passages. But how ambiguous this passage is, see in Bellarmine, book 1, chapter on purgatory. And Augustine testifies to its obscurity in his book on faith and works, chapter 15. 2. He does not speak of all Christians and hearers, but only of teachers (as is clear from verses 8, 9, 12) who, while keeping the foundation, cherish certain stubble or erroneous opinions in their doctrine, which, because they have proceeded from the infirmity of the flesh and do not fight against the foundation of faith, therefore do not make the person guilty of death. 3. By the foundation is understood Christ, as is clear from verse 11. and Bellarmine concedes. 4. By gold we understand sound doctrine and the true explanation of Scripture, by wood and stubble, human opinions and curious questions. Works cannot be understood (unless clearly secondarily) because all saints have the stubble of works, and thus there would be no distinction, and the saints also would have to be purged by fire. 5. By the day manifesting it is not understood the last day (because the word κυρίε is not found in the Greek) but either indefinitely time, as it is said, die zeit wirds bringen, or definitely the day of probation. 6. By fire revealing is noted probation, either by the cross or by Scripture. For both are compared to fire. The sense therefore is: They will recognize their stubble either at the time of the cross or through diligent collation and meditation of Scripture. 7. By detriment is understood the bite of conscience, the disapproval and rejection of empty dogmas. 8. The sense of the phrase as if through fire is this: He will be saved, not otherwise than through the fire of probation, with those false opinions having been burned away first; or not without difficulty and danger. The Papists, however, deduce a triple fire from this: 1. of the conflagration of the world, 2. of the universal judgment, 3. of purgation. But of one word in one place there is one meaning: which is otherwise συνíχα.

XVI. 5 James 1. v. 15. When concupiscence has conceived, it brings forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, brings forth death. Therefore, sin that is not finished does not bring forth death.

Response. There is an equivocation in the phrase 'to bring forth death,' which is to be understood not so much of the sin itself as of the person sinning, in such a way that it is the same as to bind the person with the guilt of death, in which sense it is said in Rom. 8. v. 13: If you live according to the flesh, you shall die. And Rom. 7. v. 5: The passions of sins were working in our members to bring forth fruit unto death. For to bring forth death and to bring forth fruit unto death are the same thing. Since, however, there is no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, Rom. 8. v. 1, it follows that sin, which by its nature was mortal, does not hasten death for the person himself. For James counts in this place three degrees, as it were, of sin: the viciousness itself, the motion of the viciousness, and the action of the motion: all of which are worthy of death, but not all bring forth death: for the former two can exist in a regenerate person, in whom there is no condemnation: but the latter cannot.

XVII. 9. Venial sins in the regenerate are only venial. Therefore, in the unregenerate they are mortal. But the consequent is false, which is proved from the fact that in the same kind of sin a believer offends God more grievously than an unbeliever, Luke 12. v. 47, 48,

Response 1. A false hypothesis is presupposed, namely, that a believer offends God more in every sin than an unbeliever. For here not the sins themselves, but rather the persons sinning are to be considered. For the distinction between mortal and venial sin is not taken from the substance of the sin, but from the person of the agent, just as our Luther speaks. Sins indeed in one kind, considered in themselves, are equal. For example: An ambitious thought is lawlessness contrary to the divine will both in the believer and in the unbeliever; nevertheless, this lawlessness does not condemn the believer, because it displeases him, which displeasure is as it were an extemporaneous repentance, on account of which that lawlessness is not imputed: In the unbeliever, however, there is no repentance and faith, and therefore the person is condemned on account of the same sin. Thus a father does not punish a beloved son as severely as a contumacious one, although both may be caught in the same offense.

3. The saying alleged from Luke does not speak of venial sins or sins of infirmity, but of gross and mortal ones, committed against conscience, where we willingly concede that the regenerate sin more grievously in the same kind of offense than unbelievers, in that the former willingly cast off the benefits of grace, and thus offend God doubly, partly through ingratitude for the benefits, and partly through the malice of the act itself.

XVIII. 7. A sin is not called venial because it is not imputed unto death, but it is not imputed because it is venial. For it is called venial because it is worthy of pardon.

Resp. The notation is fallacious. For a sin is not called venial because it is worthy of pardon, but because God deems the sinner worthy of pardon. Why this? Because it is done by him to whom such a sin is displeasing, which displeasure is repentance. On account of this extemporaneous μετάνοια, therefore, joined with the sin of infirmity, God does not impute the sin, but grants pardon.

XIX. 8. Not every slight offense dissolves human friendship. Therefore, neither does it dissolve divine friendship.

Respond. 1. Similitudes do not prove a doubtful point, but only illustrate what has been proven. 2. Sins are not to be judged by our reason, but by the divine law. Whatever departs from this incurs its curse. 3. The judgment of God is one thing, the judgment of man is another. For as much higher are the heavens than the earth, so much higher are the ways of God than our ways, Isaiah 59:9. 4. In human affairs also, an offended friend could break off a friendship, but the fact that this is not broken off is due to the kindness and placability of the offended party. Thus, any sin, offending God, deserves death by its nature but does not

XX. 9, Sin is not predicated univocally of mortal and venial, but by a certain analogy; and therefore a venial sin is not perfectly a sin: both because it is not perfectly voluntary, and because it is not against the law.

Response 1. Bellarmine contradicts himself. For in chapter 3 he says that a venial sin is simply and absolutely opposed to a mortal one. Here, however, he attributes to both a genus that is not univocal, but merely analogical. But things cannot be absolutely contrary unless they are under one genus univocally. Therefore, if the genus is analogical, there is no proper and absolute contrariety, but only an analogical one.

2. τὸ ἑκούσιον (the voluntary) is not required for the form of sin: τὸ ἄνομον (the lawless) suffices, and whoever denies that this is present in a venial sin states an opposite in the subject.

3. That Bellarminian κρησφύγετον (refuge/excuse) is absurd, that venial sins are not against, but beside the law. For in book 5 of De Amissione Gratiae, chapter 1, he says: Every sin is repugnant to the law. If every, then also venial. But that which is repugnant to the law is not beside, but against the law. Furthermore, will not that 'beside the law' provide a middle ground between conformity and difformity, just and unjust, oblique and straight? ἄτοπον (absurd).

XXI. 10. Whatever sins have need of a petition for forgiveness, those are imputed. Venial sins have need of a petition. Therefore, they are imputed.

Response 1. It does not follow; This must be prayed for from God. Therefore, it will not happen by itself. We pray that the name of the Lord may be hallowed, and his will be done, which both, although some may not pray for them, will nevertheless come to pass by virtue of the promises. Thus Daniel, chapter 9, verse 3, prays that the Lord may lead out the people from captivity, which nevertheless was otherwise promised, and therefore Jerome comments thus upon this passage: Jeremiah had indeed predicted 70 years of the desolation of the temple, after which the people would return to Judea, and the temple and Jerusalem would be built: which matter does not make Daniel negligent, but rather provokes him to pray, that what God promised through his clemency, he might fulfill through their prayers, lest negligence and pride beget offense. 2. It is an ignorance of the refutation. For it is not asked here, Whether these venial sins are in themselves such that they cannot or ought not to be imputed? But rather, Whether these sins, at the very time they are committed, are so imputed to the sinning person that he falls from the grace of God? Here we hold the negative, the cause however is, because repentance has a place simultaneously in the very act of sin, for it is committed with the displeasure of the person, which is repentance itself. But mortal sins are so constituted that, in the very act, they cannot have such displeasure and repentance joined to them, since they presuppose the plenary consent of the will. Wherefore, as mortal sins are imputed in act when they are committed; so venial sins are not indeed imputed at the very time they are committed, yet they could be imputed, if God wished to deal rigidly with the regenerate. And for that reason the petition for remission is necessary, and thus a venial sin does not exclude the conditions by reason of which it becomes venial, but rather includes them.

XXII. 11. If sins are therefore venial because they consist simultaneously with faith, it follows that even mortal sins, as much in doctrine as in morals, are venial, because one committing such things can believe that GOD is propitious to him on account of Christ.

I respond. It is a mere begging of the question: For faith is a trustful apprehension of the grace of God through Christ the redeemer in the promise of the Gospel, which to be able to stand simultaneously with a purpose of sinning, or with sins themselves reigning, is simply false. Every one who abides in God does not sin 1 John 3:6. And those who reject a good conscience make shipwreck concerning the faith 1 Tim. 1:19. This does not depend on our own powers, but is a gift of God: it is given to no one who has the intention of sinning. For this excludes the intention of new obedience. And therefore also true repentance. Wherefore all the things that Bellarmine trifles about the Lutheran faculty of believing proceed from the Pelagian principle that faith is placed in the powers of our own free will. Because this is false, it follows that he who sins against conscience, or presumes to sin, is not gifted with faith by God and consequently does not truly believe in Christ. Chemnitz explains these things piously and learnedly in Tom. 3, L. C., in the place concerning the distinction of mortal and venial sins, ch. 3. and venial sins, ch. 3, where these words are: If anyone in sins against conscience induces that persuasion, I know indeed that God does not approve of this, but yet because He is merciful, I believe He will be merciful to me even while I continue in sins. Such a persuasion is not true faith. For the property of true faith is not to seek a privilege for baseness, but with a contrite heart to seek the remission of sins. And furthermore, the tree is rightly judged by its fruits. The fruits of true faith are not to seek an occasion for sinning, not to remain in sins, but to mortify the flesh. And therefore Luther says in the Smalcald Articles: When sin is admitted against conscience, faith is lost. To this also pertains the saying of Tertullian: What is, he says, this persuasion, to feign for oneself a license to sin, and to say in one's heart, It will not harm me, provided you say you repent? This is a phantom of faith, not true faith.

Latin:

XIII. 2. Matth. 23. v. 24. Peccata quædam culici, quædam camelo; Lucæ 6. v. 24. vicissim quædam festucæ, quædam trabibus comparantur. Vnde colligunt, dari delicta quædam leuissima, quæ ex natura sua sint venialia.

Respond. N. C. Nam nihil aliud inde probari potest, quàm dari certos peccatorum gradus, secundum quos alia alijs graviora & leuiora sint. Interim quædam perse, & secundum naturam suam veniâ esse digna nec explicitè, nec implicitè dicitur. Inprimis verò in priori loco nihil huius innuitur. Nam Christus ibi ágit de natura hypocritarum, qui in minutis anxij præcipua ex professo negligunt, nec distinguunt ea, quæ per se & semper sunt necessaria, ab iis, quorum non priuatio, sed contemtus nos reos facit.

XIV. 3. Luc. 12. v. 59. Non exies inde donec etiam nouissimum minutum reddas, per quod minutum intelligunt delicta venialia, quæ quidem non damnent, esse tamen pro ijs satisfaciendum in carcere purgatorij.

Respond. Loquitur ibi Christus de reconciliatione, adeoque de inimicitiis cum proximo, quas esse peccatum mortale, patet Gal. 5. v. 20. Opera carnis sunt inimicitiæ, lis, æmulationes. Et 1. Ioh. 3. v. 5. Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Describit ergò exquisitissimam debiti exactionem, quòd nulla excarcere sit sperada liberatio, nisi omne debitum, & quidem extremū minutum sit persolutum, id quod factu impossibile. Quòd verò in particula Donec elabendi rimam quærit Bellarminus, notum est, quòd ea nō semper terminum, sed sæpius perpetuitatem & continuationem significet, vt 2. Sam. 6. v. ult. Psal. 110. v. 1. Esa. 22 v. 14. c. 42. v. 4. Matth. v. 25. c. 28. v. 20. 2. Cor. 15. v. 25. Qui enim semel in infernum conjicitur, nunquam inde liberatur: Ex inferno enim nulla redemtio. Quod autem hîc non confictum purgatorium, sed infernus sit intelligendus, patet ex Matt 5. vers. 25. vbivocatur carcer, in quem quis mittitur ab irato judice, traditur exactori, id est, diabolo. Ast hæc non competunt purgatorio. Non enim ibi exactor vel tortor est, cùm ita infernus & purgatorium confunderentur; nec ab irato Deo in purgatorium animæ traduntur, cùm Dei gratiam semper retineant, secundum Pontificios.

XV. 4. 1 Cor. 3. v. 12. Fundamentum aliud nemo potest ponere, præter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Si quis autē superædificauerit aurum, argentum, lapides pretiosos, ligna, fænum, stipulam, vniuscuiusque opus manifestum erit: Dies enim Domini declarabit, quia in igne reuelabitur, &c. Per foenum & stipulas intelligunt peccata venialia, quæ non puniantur flammis inferni, sed expientur pœnis purgatorij. Respond. 1. Ex locis obscuris & ambiguis nequit probari articulus fidei. Quàm autem ambiguus sit hic locus, vide apud Bellar. lib. 1 c. de purg. Et de obscuritate testatur. August. l. de fide & operibus c. 15. 2. Non de omnibus Christianis, & auditoribus loquitur, sed tantùm de doctoribus (vt patet ex v. 8. 9. 12.) qui saluo fundamento, quasdam in doctrina stipulas seu erroneas opiniones fouent, quæ quia ex infirmitate carnis sunt profectæ, nec pugnant cum fundamento fidei, ideo personam non faciunt ream mortis. 3. Per fundamentum intelligitur Christus, vt patet ex vers. 11. & concedit Bellar. 4. aurum intelligimus sanam doctrinam veramque explicationem scripturæ, per lignum & stipulas, opiniones humanas & quæstiones curiosas Opera a. intelligi nequeunt (nisi planè secundariò) quia omnes sancti stipulas operum habent, adeoque nullum foret discrimen, & sancti quoque essent igne purgandi. 5. Per diem manifestantem non intelligitur dies vltimus (quia vox κυρίε in Gręco non reperitur (sed vel indefinitè tempus, sicut dicitur, die zeit wirds bringen, vel definitè dies probationis. 6. Per ignem reuelantem notatur probatio, vel per crucem, vel per Scripturam. Vtrumque enim igni comparatur, Sensus ergo est: Cognofcent stipulas suas vel tempore crucis, vel per diligentem Scripturæ collationem & meditationem. 7. Per detrimentum intelligitur morsus conscientiæ, improbatio & abjectio dogmatum inanium. 8. Phraseos quasi per ignem hic sensus: Saluabitur, non nisi per ignem probationis, exustis priùs istis opinionibus falsis; vel non absque difficultate & periculo. Pontificij verò triplicem ignem hinc deducunt, 1. conflagrationis mundi, 2. vniuersalis iudicij, 3. purgationis. Sed vnius vocis in vno loco vna est significatio: quæ aliàs συνíχα.

XVI. 5 Iacob. 1. v. 15. Concupiscentia cum conceperit, parit peccatum: peccatum autem cùm consummatum fuerit, generat mortem. Ergò peccatum non consummatum non generat mortem.

Respond. est æquiuocatio in phrasi generare mortem, quæ non tàm de peccato ipso, quàm persona peccante intelligenda est, ita, vt idem sit, atque personam reatu mortis obligare, quo sensu Rom. 8. v. 13. dicitur: Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Et Rom 7. v. 5. Passiones peccatorum operabantur in membris nostris, vt fructificarent morti. Idem enim est generare mortem, & fructificare morti. Quoniam autem nulla est condemnatio his qui sunt in Christo Iesu, Rom 8. v. 1. hinc fit, vt peccatum, quod naturâ suâ erat mortale, ipsi personæ mortem non acceleret. Numerat enim hoc loco Iacobus tres quasi gradus peccati ipsam vitiositatem, vitiositatis motionem, motionis actionem: qui omnes digni sunt morte, sed non omnes generant mortem: priores enim duo esse possunt in persona renata, in qua nulla condemnatio: posterior autem non item.

XVII. 9. Venialia peccata in renatis tantùm sunt venialia. Ergò in non renatis mortalia. Consequens autem falsum, quod probatur inde, quia in eodem genere peccati grauius Deum fidelis quam infidelis offendit, Luc. 12. v. 47. 48,

Resp. 1. Præsupponitur hypothesis falsa, nimirum, quòd fidelis in omni peccato magis offendat Deum, quàm infidelis. Etenim hîc non ipsa peccata; sed personæ potius peccantes sunt attendendæ. Discrimen enim peccati mortalis & venialis non desumitur à substantia peccati, sed à persona agentis, quemadmodum Lutherus noster loquitur. Peccata quidem in vno genere quoad se considerata sunt æqualia. Exempligratia: Ambitiosa cogitatio & in fideli, & in infideli ἀνομία est repugnans voluntati divinæ, attamen hæc ἀνομία fidelem non damnat, quia ipsi displicet, quæ displicentia est quasi extemporalis pœnitentia, ob quam ista ἀνομία non imputatur: In infideli autem non est pœnitentia & fides, ideoque persona ob idem peccatum condemnatur. Sic pater non tàm graviter punit filium dilectum, quàm contumacem, licèt in eodem delicto uterque deprehendatur.

3. Dictum ex Luca allegatum non loquitur de peccatis venialibus vel infirmitatis, sed de crassis & mortalibus, contra conscientiam commissis, ubi lubentur concedimus, in eodem delicti genere graviùs peccare renatos, quàm infideles eò quòd illi beneficia gratiæ volenter excutiant, adeoque dupliciter Deum offendant, partim per ingratitudinem pro beneficiis, partim per ipsam actus malitiam.

XVIII. 7. Non ideò peccatum aliquod veniale dicitur, quia ad mortem non imputatur sed non imputatur quia veniale est. Nam veniale dicitur, quia est veniâ dignum.

Resp. Fallax est notatio. Non enim ideò peccatum veniale dicitur quia veniâ est dignum, sed, quia Deus peccatorem veniâ dignatur. Cur hoc? quia fit ab eo, cui peccatum tale displicet, quæ displicentia est pœnitentia. Ob hanc ergò extemporalem μετάνοιαν, cum peccato infirmitatis conjunctam, Deus peccatum non imputat, sed veniam concedit.

XIX. 8. Non quævis offensiuncula amicitiam dissoluit humanam. Ergò nec divinam.

Respond. 1. Similitudines non probant dubium, sed tantùm illustrant probatum. 2. De peccatis non est judicandum ex ratione nostra, sed ex lege divinâ. Quicquid ab hac recedit, eius maledictionem incurrit. 3. Aliud est iudicium Dei, aliud hominis. Nam quantò altiores sunt cœli, quàm terra, tantò altiores sunt viæ Dei, quàm viæ nostræ, Esai 59. v. 9. 4. In humanis etiam offensi amici rumpere posset amicitiam, quòd verò hæc non rumpitur, in causa est offensi benignitas & placabilitas, Sic quoduis peccatum, offendens Deum, mortem meretur per suam naturam sed non infert, , ob Dei gratiam,

XX. 9, Peccatum non vniuoce dicitur de mortali & veniali, sed per analogiam quandam; ideoque veniale non est perfectè peccatum: tum quia non est perfecte voluntarium, tum, quia non est contra legem.

Respond 1. Contradicit sibi Bellarminus. Nam cap 3. ait, Veniale peccatum simpliciter & absolute opponi mortali. Hic autem vtrique genus non vniuocum, sed duntaxat analogicum attribuit. Ast absolutè contraria esse non possunt, nisi sub vno genere vniuoce. Ergò si genus est analogicum non est contrarietas propria & absoluta, sed tantùm analogica.

2. τὸ ἑκούσιον non requiritur ad formam peccati: sufficit τὸ ἄνομον, quod adesse in peccato veniali qui negat, oppositum in apposito dicit.

3. Absurdum est κρησφύγετον illud Bellarminianum, peccata venialia non esse contra, sed præter legem. Nam l. 5. de A. G. c. 1. dicit. Omne peccatum legi repugnare, Si omne, ergò & ueniale. Quod autem legi repugnat, non præter sed contra legem est. Deinde, an non per illud præter legem dabitur medium inter conformitatem & difformitatem, iustum & injustum, obliquum & rectum? ἄτοπον.

XXI. 10. Quæcunque peccata opus habent petitione remissionis, ea imputantur. Venialia opus habent petitione. Ergò imputantur.

Resp. 1. Non sequitur; Hoc orandum'est à Deo. Ergò per se non eueniet. Oramus, vt sanctificetur nomen Domini, & fiat voluntas eius, quod vtrumque licet nonnulli haud orent, nihilominus vi promissionum euenturum est. Sic Daniel. c. 9. v. 3 precatur, vt Dominus educat popustum ex captivitate, quod tamen aliàs erat promissum, ideoque Hieron. super istum locum ita commentatur: Prædixerat quidem Ieremias 70. annos desolationis templi, post quos rursus veniret populus in Iudæam, & ædificaretur templum & Hierusalem: quæ res Danielem non facit negligentem, sed magis provocat ad rogandum, ut quod Deus per suam promisit clementiam, per horum impleat preces, ne negligentia & superbia pariat offensam. 2. Est ignorantia Elenchi. Non enim hic quæritur, Vtrum peccata ista venialia per se talia sint, ut non imputari possint aut debeant? Verùm, An peccata ista eo ipso, quo committuntur tempore, ita personæ peccanti imputentur, ut excidat gratia Dei? Hic nos negativam tenemus, Causa autem est, quia pœnitentia simul locum habet in ipso peccati actu, Committitur enim cum personæ displicentia, quæ est ipsa pœnitentia. Peccata autem mortalia taliter sunt comparata, ut in ipso actu, huiusmodi displicentiam & pœnitentiam non possint adiunctam habere, quandoquidem plenarium voluntatis consensum præsupponunt. Quare ut mortalia actu imputantur, quando fiunt; sic venialia non quidem imputantur eo ipso, quo fiunt tempore, imputari tamen possent, si Deus rigidè cum renatis agere vellet. Atque eam ob causam petitio remissionis necessaria est, adeoque peccatum veniale non excludit conditiones, quarum ratione fit veniale, sed potiùs includit.

XXII. 11. Si peccata ideò venialia sunt, quia simul consistunt cum fide, sequitur peccata etiam mortalia, tam in doctrina, quam in moribus esse venialia, quia talia committens potest credere, DEVM sibi propter Christum esse propitium.

Respond. Est mera petitio principij: Etenim fides est gratiæ Dei per Christum redemtorem in promissione Euangelij fiducialis apprehensio, quam simul stare posse cum peccandi proposito, vel ipsis peccatis regnantibus simpliciter falsum est. Omnis est. Omnis enim, qui in Deo manet, non pececat 1. Ioh. 3. v. 6. Et qui bonam conscientiam repellunt, naufragium faciunt circa fidem 1. Tim. 1. v. 19. Non pendet hec ex nostris viribus, sed est donum Dei: nemini datur, qui habet propositum peccandi. Hoc enim excludit propositum nouae obedientiae. Ergo & veram poenitentiam. Quapropter omnia, que Bellarminus nugatur de facultate credendi Lutherana, proueniunt ex principio Pelagiano quod fides in viribus nostri arbitrij sit posita. Hoc quia falsum, sequitur eum, qui contra conscientiam peccat, vel peccare praesumit, a Deo fide non donari ac proinde in Christum vere non credere. Pie & erudite haec exponit Chemnitius Tom. 3. L. C. loco de discr. peccat. mort. & ven. c. 3. vbi haec verba: Si quis in peccatis contra conscientiam inducat illam persuasionem, Scio quidem, Deum hoc non probare, sed tamen quia est misericors, credo eum mihi etiam in peccatis pergenti fore misericordem. Talis persuasio non est vera fides. Nam proprietas vere fidei non est, quaerere turpitudinis priuilegium, sed corde contrito quaerere peccatorum remissionem. Et praeterea ex fructibus recte statuitur de arbore. Fructus vera fidei sunt, non quaerere occasionem peccandi, non permanere in peccatis, sed mortificare carnem. Et ideo Lutherus inquit in art. Smalcald. Quando admittitur peccatum contra conscientiam, amissa est fides. Huc etiam spectat dictum Tertulliani: Quid est inquit, ista persuasio, sibi fingere licentiam peccandi, & in corde suo dicere, Non nocebit, duntaxat dic te punitere? Spectrum hic fidei est non fides vera.


### Question III. In what does the formal notion of venial sin consist?

I. Thus far we have demonstrated that all sins are by their nature mortal, offend God, and draw upon themselves the guilt of eternal damnation. Now, indeed, it is read everywhere in the Scriptures that sins adhere even to the saints. For all pray for forgiveness, Ps. 32, v. 6. Who can say, My heart is clean, I am pure from sin? Prov. 20, v. 9. I am carnal, sold under sin, Rom. 7, v. 14. Sin dwells in me, v. 17. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, 1 John 1, v. 8. Since, therefore, sins are found even in the regenerate, it is not without reason asked what it is that the effect of sin is suspended there, which is the casting off of the Holy Spirit and the indignation of God? For all those sins which adhere to the saints and are daily perpetrated by them are called venial, because God deems such a sinner worthy of forgiveness, nor does He immediately abandon him with His grace.

II. But before we recount the causes of forgiveness, it must be known which evil motions in man are called venial sins; which will be able to be known if the distinct degrees of sins are observed, which the blessed Chemnitius enumerates thus from James 1, v. 14, 15. 1. There is ἰδία ἐπιθυμία, concupiscence itself, which is nothing else than that original stain, which can be called πάθος, from which follow παθήματα or evil acts. And this tinder is always remaining in the regenerate, because renewal in this life is imperfect. 2. Tò πειράζειν of that concupiscence, which is the first beginning of temptation, when it begins to solicit us to evil and casts evil thoughts before us. 3. Ἐξελκέαθαι, which are the enticements inviting, which the flesh casts before us, so that it may the more successfully persuade the reason to evil. 4. τὸ ἐξέλκειν, when the will is as it were captured and carried off sideways. 5. τὸ συλλαμβάνειν concipere, which is an evil purpose or a plotting toward evil. 6. Τὸ τίκτειν, when the deed itself follows, by the perpetration of which sin brings forth death. Of these steps, the first pertains to original sin, the companion and the third to actual venial sin, the last three to actual mortal sin. Lombard, following Augustine, enumerates them thus: 1. is the tinder, 2. suggestion, 3. delectation, 4. consent, 5. machination, 6. the operation itself. From an evil operation, however, arises the habit of sinning, from the habit of sin, the excuse, hence the defense, afterwards obstinacy, thence exultation and boasting in sins, then a reprobate sense, and finally induration or the sin against the Holy Spirit. As regards the tinder, it is remitted in Baptism and can no longer bind the reborn. But it is chiefly concerning evil suggestion that the question is raised here: for all the following degrees are referred to mortal sins, which wound and devastate the conscience. Concerning those vicious internal motions of original sin, therefore, and those that are involuntary, the controversy is raised: for what reason do they not drive out the Holy Spirit, nor deprive man of the grace of God, nor condemn him? But that a distinct answer may be given, we note these causes.

III. The 1st cause is the intercession of Christ, according to that in Rom. 8:34: Who is he that shall condemn? Christ Jesus, who died, yea, who also rose again, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. This intercession causes these sudden sins and sins of infirmity, which arise in us against our will, not to be imputed by the heavenly Father, and therefore He does not desert us with His gracious presence. The forgiveness of sins is through Christ the intercessor, says Tertullian, book on modesty.

2. The mercy of the Father. For God exercises mercy toward man more than justice. Although, therefore, He could by His right reject man, yet when he sins out of infirmity, out of mere mercy, moved by the intercession of His Son, He pardons these offenses for them.

3. The petition for remission. For the saints, because they know well that they are surrounded on all sides by such infirmities, therefore sigh anxiously with Paul, and are greatly moved, because they are compelled in their body to carry around so restless an evil, and therefore with David they pray perpetually, Cleanse me from my secret faults, O Lord, forgive us our debts. On account of this daily prayer, God deigns to grant pardon for those sins which are mortal in themselves, according to the promise: Whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, he will give you.

4. Extemporaneous repentance. For as soon as an evil thought creeps in, so that the regenerate feel it, then immediately they turn away from it and grieve that they cannot be immune from such vicious impulses.

This displeasure, however, is sorrow and contrition, and a kind of extemporaneous repentance; on account of which those sins that are mortal in themselves become venial. For, as Augustine says in his Soliloquies: That which was criminal in the act becomes venial through confession. And this is what Luther says on Galatians ch. 5: The distinction between mortal and venial sin is not taken from the substance of the sin, but from the person of the agent.

IV. Therefore, to summarize what has been said so far, we include the orthodox opinion concerning venial sin in one aphorism, which is as follows: A venial sin is such and is so called, not because it is worthy of pardon on account of its smallness, but 1. because of the intercession of Christ, 2. the mercy of the Father, 3. the petition for remission, 4. and extemporaneous repentance. This aphorism our blessed Luther inculcates and declares everywhere. For thus he writes on Galatians 5: mortal and venial sin is distinguished not by the substance, or according to the difference of the sins committed, but by the person, or because of the difference of those committing the sins. And in Volume 1 of the Latin works, fol. 305a: No sin is venial by its own nature, but all are damnable: that they are venial is to be attributed to the grace of God. Volume 4, fol. 172a: it is a pernicious error of the Sophists, who distinguish sins by the substance of the deed, not by the person. He who believes has the same and equally great sin as the unbeliever; yet to the believer it is pardoned and not imputed; to the unbeliever it is retained and imputed: to the one it is venial, to the other mortal. Not because of a difference in the sins, that the sin of the believer is less and that of the unbeliever greater, but because of the person. Cassian explains this very briefly in Collation 22. Venial sins, he says, are such to the righteous.

V. A twofold doubt occurs here, which we shall briefly discuss by way of a conclusion. 1. Mortal and venial sins are distinguished in this, that the latter are involuntary, but the former voluntary; the latter are only internal, but the former, for the most part, are external. The question therefore is concerning involuntary homicide, which Bellarmine, book 5, De Amissione Gratiae, chapter 10, denies to be against the law and a sin; ought it to be numbered among venial or mortal sins? If among mortal, it follows that such a person immediately loses the Holy Spirit, which does not seem probable. If among venial, it follows that external and gross sins can also be venial.

Response.
