It cannot be denied that involuntary homicide is a sin and against the law: but it cannot be called mortal, but rather venial, because mortal sins are committed against conscience by deliberate consent. But involuntary homicide is not such. Nor do we call it venial because of its slightness or its nature, as if it could not make a man an enemy of God, but because of extemporaneous repentance. For a truly regenerate person, killing someone by accident, immediately grieves in the very act, which grief is true contrition and repentance, on account of which God does not impute the sin: And those committing such things immediately sigh, O God, do not impute it, I did it imprudently, etc.

VI. 2. Concerning non-fundamental error in doctrine, there is a very great doubt. We consider it placed beyond controversy that such an error is a sin. No one doubts that it is likewise venial if pertinacity is not added. However, the primary condition and cause of a venial sin seems to be lacking: because it is not involuntary. For it is not committed with a certain struggle of the flesh and the Spirit. For the Apostle Peter knowingly and willingly was compelling the Gentiles to Judaize, Gal. 2. v. 14. Nor does it have an extemporaneous repentance attached to it. For such an error does not immediately displease, but often delights and is defended for a time.

It is answered. 1. Some doubt whether such an error in a circumstance of faith can properly be called a sin and ἀνομία; for it does not seem to oppose the will of God precisely. E.g., Peter did not know, nor had it been revealed by any law, that God did not want the Gentiles to Judaize, and therefore he does not seem to have sinned properly.

2. But let it be so, and let it be called a sin: yet nevertheless it will be venial. For the three former causes mentioned above are all present in this sin. You will say: But it is not involuntary. Indeed, it is in a certain way. For, to persist in the alleged example; if Peter had known that he was erring (just as he knew those concupiscences to be evil), he would have immediately cast off that error. And what τὸ nolle is in sins of morals, that is τὸ nescire in a circumstantial error. For there are certain sins of the will, and certain of the intellect. Both are mortal, the former if they proceed from malice, the latter if they proceed from knowledge. Both are venial; the former if they are joined with malice, the latter if they are joined with the will, the latter if they are joined with the infirmity or ignorance of the sinner.

Latin:

I. Hactenus demonstrauimus, omnia peccata per naturam suam esse mortalia, Deum offendere, & damnationis æternæ reatum attrahere. Iam verò passim in Scripturis legitur, quòd peccata sanctis etiam adhæreant Omnes enim pro venia orant, Psal. 32. v. 6. Quis potest dicere, Mundū est cor meum, purus sum à peccato? Prov. 20. vers. 9. Ego carnalis sum, venundatus sub peccato, Rom. 7. v 14. Habitat in me peccatum v. 17. Si dixerimus, quoniam peccatum non habemus, ipsi nos seducimus, 1. Iohan. 1. v. 8. Cùm ergo peccata in renatis quoque inueniantur, non immeritò quæritur, quis sit, quod ibi effeclus peccati suspendatur, quæ est excussio Spiritus sancti, & indignatio DEI? Omnia enim ista peccata, quæ hærent in sanctis, & ab iis quoudiè perpetrantur, dicuntur venialia, quia veniâ dignatur Deus taliter peccantem, nec eum statim gratiâ suâ derelinquit.

II. Priusquam verò causas veniæ recenseamus, sciendum, quinam motus mali in homine dicantur pecvata venialia? quod innotescere poterit, si obseruentur distincti gradus peccatorum, quos ita enumerat B. Chemnicius ex Iacobi 1. v. 14. 15. 1. Est ἰδία ἐπιθυμία ipsa concupiscentia, quæ nihil est aliud, quàm ista labes originalis, quæ vocari potest πάθος, ex quo sequuntur παθήματα seu mali actus. Atque hic fomes semper residuus est in renatis, quia renouatio in hac vita est imperfecta. 2. Tò πειράζειν illius concupiscentiæ, quod est primum inchoamentum tentationis, quando incipit nos solicitare ad malum & malas cogitationes obiicit. 3. Ἐξελκέαθαι quod sunt illecebræ inuitantes, quas caro obijcit, vt eò felicius persuadeat rationi malum. 4. τὸ ἐξέλκη, quando voluntas quasi captiuatur, & in transuersum rapitur. 5. τὸ συλλαμβάνειν concipere, quod est malum propositum, seu machinatio ad malum. 6. Τὸ τίκτειν, quando ipsum opus sequitur, quo perpetrato peccatum generat mortem. Ex his gradibus primus pertinet ad peccatum originale, socius dus & tertius ad peccatum actuale veniale, postremi tres ad peccatum actuale mortale. Lombardus ex Augustino ita numerat, 1. est fomes, 2. suggestio, 3. delectatio, 4. consensio, 5. machinatio, 6. ipsa operatio. Ex operatione autem mala oritur peccandi consuetudo, ex consuetudine peccati excusatio, hinc defensio, pòst obstinatio, inde in peccatis exultatio & gloriatio, tum sensus reprobus, & demum induratio seu peccatum in Spiritum sanctum. Fomitem quod attinet, ille in Baptismo remittitur, & renatos amplius obligare nequit. De mala autem suggestione potissimum hic quæritur: sequentes enim gradus omnes ad peccata mortalia, sauciantia & vastantia conscientiam referuntur. De illis igitur vitiosis peccati originalis motibus internis, ijsque inuoluntariis controuertitur, quâ de causa non excutiant Spiritum sanctum, nec hominem priuent gratia Dei, vel condemnent? Vt autem distinctè respondeatur, has causas annotamus.

III. Causa 1. est intercessio Christi, juxta illud Rom. 8. v. 34. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus Iesus, qui mortuus est, imo qui & resurrexit, qui & est ad dextram Dei, qui & interpellat pro nobis. Hæc interpellatio facit vt peccata ista subitanea & infirmitatum, quæ nobis inuitis suboriuntur, â Patre cœlesti non imputentur, ideoque nec gratiosâ suâ præsentiâ nos deserat. Venia peccatorum est per exoratorem Christum, inquit Tertull. l. de pudicit.

2. Misericordia Patris. Deus enim magis exercet circa hominem misericordiam, quàm iustitiam. Licèt igitur posset pro iure suo hominem reijcere, tamen quando ex infirmitate peccat, ex merâ misericordia, motus intercessione Filij sui, hæc eis delicta condonat.

3. Petitio remissionis. Sancti enim, quia probe nôrunt, se talibus infirmitatibus vndiquaque circũdatos, propterea cum Paulo anxiè suspirant, & valdè aguntur, quòd in corpore suo cogantur circumferre tam irrequietum malum, ideoque cum Dauide perpetuo orant, Ab occultis meis munda me, Domine dimitte nobis debita nostra. Ob hanc quotidianam precationem, peccata illa per se mortalia, Deus dignatur venia, iuxta promissionem: Quæcunque petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. Iohan 16. v 23.

4. Extemporalis pœnitentia. Quamprimùm enim subrepit mala cogitatio, ita vt eam sentiant renati, tùm statim auersantur illam & dolent, quòd à talibus vitiosis motibus immunes esse nequeant.

Hæc autem displicentia est dolor & contritio, & quasi extemporalis pœnitentia; ob quam peccata illa per se mortalia, fiunt venialia. Nam, vt Augustinus inquit in Soliloquiis: Fit per confessionem veniale, quod criminale erat in operatione. Atque hoc est, quod Lutherus dicit ad Galat. c. 5. Discrimen peccati mortalis & venialis non sumitur à substantia peccati, sed à persona agentis.

IV. Vt ergo in summam hactenus dicta contrahamus, vni aphorismo orthodoxam de peccato veniali sententiam includimus, qui talis: Peccatum veniale, tale est & dicitur, non quoad ob exilitatem suam venia dignum sit, sed 1. propter intercessionem Christi, 2. Misericordiam patris, 3. petitionem remissionis, 4. & pœnitentiam extemporalem. Quem aphorismum passim inculcat & declarat B. noster Lutherus. Sic enim scribit super Gal. 5. peccatum mortale & veniale distinguitur non penes Substantiam, seu iuxta differentiam peccatorum admissorum, sed penes personam, seu propter differentiam peccata admittentium. Et Tomo 1. lat. fol 305. a. Nullum peccatum sua natura veniale est, sed omnia damnablia: quod autem venialia sunt, hoc gratiæ Dei tribuendum est. Tomo 4. fol 172. a. pernitiosus error Sophistarum est, qui peccata distinguunt penes substantiam facti, non penes personam. Qui credit, idem & æquè magnum peccatum habet, vt incredulus: credenti tamen condonatur & non imputatur; incredulo retinetur & imputatur: illi veniale, huic mortale est. Non propter differentiam peccatorum quod credentis peccatum minus, increduli majus sit, sed personam. Hoc breuissimè exponit Cassianus collat. 22. Venialia inquit, talia sunt iusto.

V. Geminum verò dubium hic occurrit quod colophonis loco breuiter discutiemus. 1. Peccata mortalia & venialia in eo distinguuntur, quòd hæc sint inuoluntaria, ista verò voluntaria, hæc tantùm interna, ista verò quoad potissimam partem externa. Quæritur ergò de cæde inuoluntaria, quam Bell. l 5. de A. G. c. 10. negat esse contra legem & peccatum, num venialibus, an mortalibus annumerari debeat? Si mortalibus, sequitur, quòd talis continuò amittat Spiritū sanctum quod non videtur probabile. Si venialibus, sequitur, externa & crassa peccata etiam esse posse venialia.

Respond. Cædem involuntariam peccatum esse & contra legem, negari nequit: non autem dici potest mortale, sed potiùs veniale, quia mortalia fiunt contra conscientiam à deliberato consensu. Cædes autem inuoluntaria talis non est. Neque tamen veniale nuncupamus propter exilitatem aut naturam suam, ac si non possit hominem Deo facere inimicum, sed propter extemporalem pœnitentiam. Verè enim renatus fortuitò quendam interficiens, continuò dolet in ipso facto, qui dolor est vera contritio & pœnitentia, ob quam Deus peccatum non imputat: Et talia committentes statim suspirant, O Deus imputare noli, imprudens feci, &c.

VI. 2. De errore non fundamentali in doctrinâ maximum est dubium. Errorem talem peccatum esse, extra controuersiam positum censemus. Esse itidem veniale si non accedat pertinacia, nemo dubitat. Videtur autem deficere primaria conditio, & causa venialis peccati: quia non est involuntarium. Non enim committitur cum luctâ quadam carnis & Spiritus. Nam Apostolus Petrus scienter & volenter cogebat gentes judaizare, Gal. 2. v. 14. Nec adjunctam habet extemporalem pœnitentiam. Non enim statim displicet, sed sæpè oblectat & ad tempus defenditur talis error.

Respondetur. 1. Ambigunt quidam, an error talis in circumstantia fidei possit propriè peccatum & ἀνομία appellari; Non enim videtur precisè voluntatem Dei oppugnare. E. g. Petrus nescicbat nec quâdam lege revelatum erat, Deum nolle gentiles Iudaizare, ideoque non videtur propriè peccâsse.

2. Verùm sit ita, & nominetur peccatum: attamen nihilominus veniale erit. Priores enim tres suprà dictæ causæ omnes dâtur in hoc peccato. Inquis: At non est involuntarium. Imò vero est quodammodò. Nam vt in allegato exemplo persistamus; Si scivisset Petrus se errare (quemadmodum sciebat concupiscentias illas esse malas) continuò errorem istum abjecisset. Et quod est τὸ nolle in peccatis morum, hoc est τὸ nescire in errore circumstantiali. Sunt enim peccata quædam voluntatis, quædam intellectus. Vtraque sunt mortalia, illa, si ex malitia, hæc, si ex scientia procedant, Vtraque sunt venialia; illa si ex malitia, hæc, si cum voluntate, hæc si cum infirmitate vel ignorantiâ peccantis conjuncta sint.


### Question III. In what does the formal notion of venial sin consist?: Question IV. Whether the good works of the reborn are also mortal sins

QUESTION IV. Whether the good works of the reborn are also mortal sins.

I. Luther, Tom. 1. lat. fol. 11. a, says: Every work of the law without the grace of God appears good, but within it is sin. Fol. 26. No man knows how often he sins mortally even in good works, on account of vainglory. Therefore, despairing of himself, he ought to cast himself with confidence into the abyss of the divine mercy of Him who faithfully promises. Fol. 29.

The works of the righteous would be mortal, were they not feared by the righteous themselves, as mortal, out of a pious fear of God. Fol 489. a. Even our good works, if God should judge by rigor, and not forgive by forgiving mercy, are damnable and mortal.

II. The Papists seize upon this, and perpetually object it to us, as if Luther had abolished the distinction between honorable and base, good and evil works. But they deceive and are deceived. For neither did Luther say, nor do we teach, that all the good works of the reborn are formally sins, as if there were nothing in them of good that might please God. But we maintain that there is sin in good works in another, and indeed a threefold, respect.

III. 1. Insofar as they are done under the opinion of perfection and merit. For even if you distribute all your goods among the poor, and continually afflict your flesh: yet if you seek the praise of perfection in them and presume to merit salvation, you displease God, and in those very works, which outwardly seem good, you sin most gravely. Thus the works of the Essenes and Pharisees were in themselves praiseworthy, but because they sought righteousness and the glory of perfection in them, they are for that reason most often rebuked by Christ. This, therefore, is the first respect in which it happens that there is sin in good works, which Augustine also hints at, book 4 against Julian, chapter 3, in these words: When a man does something, where he does not seem to sin, if he does not do it for the sake of that for which he ought to do it, he is convicted of sinning. And therefore he warns in his commentary on the thirty-first psalm, Do not pay much attention to what a man does, but to what he looks to when he does it.

IV. 2. Insofar as they are considered without faith, apprehending the merit of Christ. For faith is the form and, as it were, the soul of good works, because without faith it is impossible to please God, Heb. 11. v. 5. Faith is the vestibule through which the soul is lifted up to the height of good acts, Gregory, homily 19 on Ezekiel. ὅτι ἐστὶ χωρὶς πίστεως πρᾶξις ἵππευτῷ Nazianzen, in the oration of those returned from the field.

are without faith, even those which seem to be good works, are turned into sin, August. lib. 3 ad Bonif. Whence Prosper rightly sang in his poems: For every work of piety, unless it arises from the seed of true faith, is sin, and is turned into guilt, and sterile glory heaps up punishment for itself.

And the reason is manifest, because no work is so good that it does not have a certain imperfection annexed to it. Therefore, unless this is covered by the merit of Christ, it defiles the work itself, so that it does not specially please God. But it cannot be covered if faith is absent. For this alone apprehends the merit of Christ, by which the imperfection joined to the work is to be veiled. Wherefore no work is truly good if it is considered without regard to faith and the apprehended righteousness of Christ. And Luther always looked to this hypothesis when he called works sins. For he did not understand that ἁπλῶς (simply), but ὑποθετικῶς (hypothetically), insofar as they are estimated in themselves and without faith, without which the added blemishes are not remitted.

V. 3. Insofar as all good works are imperfect. For because our renewal is only begun here, not consummated, therefore in every good work two things concur: 1. ἐννομία (conformity to law), or a certain conformity with the law; 2. ἀνομία (lawlessness), or a certain disconformity from the law. For we do something, but not everything, nor with due perfection. For the law requires such works as proceed from a most integral nature, without any repugnances and imperfections. But because this is impossible for us in such great corruption of the flesh, therefore every good work is at once both good and evil, yet in a different respect; good, insofar as it consents with the law; evil, insofar as it dissents from the law.

VI. That this may be declared by a certain example; the love of God considered in itself agrees with the

Latin:

QVÆSTIO. IV. Num etiam bona renatorum opera sint peccata mortalia.

I. Lutherus Tom. 1. lat. fol. 11. a inquit: Omne opus legis sine gratia Dei apparet bonum, sed intus est peccatum. Fol. 26. Nullus hominum nouit, quoties peccet mortaliter etiam in bonis operibus, propter vanam gloriam. Ideò de se desperando cum fiducia in abyssum misericordiæ diuinæ fideliter promittentis debet sese proijcere. Fol. 29.

Iustorũ opera essent mortalia, nisi pio Dei timore ab ipsismet iustis, vt mortalia timerentur. Fol 489. a. Etiam bona opera nostra, si Deus per rigorem iudicet, & non misericordiâ ignoscente ignoscat, sunt damnabila & mortalia.

II. Arripiunt hoc Pontificij, & perpetuò nobis objiciunt, ac si Lutherus sustulisset discrimen honostorum & turpium, bonorum & malorum operum. Verùm fallunt & falluntur. Non enim vel Lutherus dixit, vel nos docemus, omnia renatorum bo na opera formaliter esse peccata, ac si nihil in ijs sit boni, quod Deo placeat. Sed alio, eóque tergemino respectu in operibus bonis peccari statuimus.

III. 1. Quatenus fiunt sub opinione perfectionis & meriti. Etiam si enim omnia bona tua dístribuas inter pauperes, & carnem tuam continuè affligas: attamen si ijs laudem perfectionis captes & salutem mereri præsumas, Deo displices, & in illis ipsis operibus, quæ exteriùs videntur bona, grauissimè peccas. Sic opera Essenorum & Pharisæorum in sese erant laudabilia, quia verò in illis quærebant iustitiam & perfectionis gloriam, propterea sæpissimè à Christo vituperantur. Hic ergò primus respectus est, quo in operibus bonis peccari contingit, quem Augustinus etiam innuit, l. 4. cont. Iul. c. 3. his verbis: Cùm facit homo aliquid, vbi peccare non videtur, si non propter hoc facit, propter quod facere debet, peccare conuincitur. Et idcircò monet in comment. super psalmum tricesimum primum, Non valdè attendas, quid homo faciat, sed quid, cùm facit, aspiciat.

IV. 2. Quatenus considerantur absque fide, meritum Christi apprehendente. Forma enim & velut anima bonorum fides est, quia sine fide Deo quicquam placere impossibile, Heb. 11. v. 5. Fides est vestibulum, per quod anima ad bonorum actuum altitudinem subleuatur, Gregor homil. 19. in Ezech. ὅτι ἐστὶ χωρὶς πίστεως πρᾶξις ἵππευτῷ Nazianzen. in orat. reuersi ex agro.

sint fide, etiam quæ videntur bona opera, in peccatum vertuntur, August. l. 3. ad Bonif. Vnde Prosper recte cecinit in suis carminibus: Omne etenim pietatis opus, nisi semine veræ Exoritur fidei, peccatum est, inq; reatum Vertitur, & sterilis cumulat sibi gloria pœnam.

Et ratio est in aprico, quia nullum opus adeò bonum, quin annexam habeat quandam imperfectionem. Hæc igitur nisi merito Christi contegatur, ipsum opus coinquinat, vt Deo specialiter non placeat. Contegi autem nequit, si fides absit. Hæc enim sola apprehendit meritum Christi, quo adjuncta operis imperfectio est obvelanda. Quare nullum opus est vere bonum, si citra respectum fidei, & apprehensæ justitiæ Christi consideretur. Et ad hanc hypothesin semper respexit Lutherus, quando opera appellauit peccata. Non enim ἁπλῶς istud intellexit, sed ὑποθετικῶς, quatenus nimirum æstimantur ex se & absque fide, sine qua additi næui non remittuntur.

V. 3. Quatenus omnia opera bona sunt imperfecta. Quia enim renouatio nostra hic tantùm inchoatur, non consummatur, ideò in omni opere bono duo concurrunt, 1. ἐννομία, vel quædam cum lege conformitas, 2. ἀνομία vel quædam à lege disformitas. Nam facimus aliquid, sed non omne, nec cum debita perfectione. Lex enim talia requirit opera, quæ proueniant â natura integerrima, sine vllis repugnantiis & imperfectionibus. Hoc autem quia in tanta carnis corruptione nobis impossibile est, idcircò omne opus bonum simul & malum est, diuerso tamen respectu; bonum, quà consentit cum lege; malum, quà dissentit à lege.

VI. Vt hoc declaretur exemplo quodam; Dilectio Dei in se considerata conuenit cum primo


### Question

commandment of the first table. But because the regenerate do not love God with their whole heart and above all things, nor can they love Him, on account of inherent sin; hence it comes about that that very love does not accord with this commandment of the first table, by which it is commanded that God is not only to be loved, but to be loved above all things and in all things, and with all one's strength. Thus, therefore, our love is a good work, in so far as God is loved: it is an evil work, or rather has an evil work conjoined to it, in so far as God is not loved above all things and perfectly.

VII. And this very thing happens also in all other actions. For because in every regenerate person the old man and the new man concur, therefore the old man always sprinkles the works of the new man with certain stains, on account of which they become evil and can be called sins. For as soon as we think of something good, the old man resists: if we bring it into act, he is indignant and angry. And on account of this resistance and indignation of the flesh, it comes about that a good work can rightly be called evil, in that the good works of the law ought to be totally and fully good, and to proceed from a most integral nature. For in so far as it is not ἁπλῶς and in every respect good, to that extent it is non-conforming to the law, and consequently is evil.

VIII. This was the mind and opinion of Luther, when he asserted that man sins in all his works, which doctrine so far from hindering holiness and Christian virtues, rather excites and inflames us toward it. For from thence there is kindled in the mind of the regenerate true humility, ardent prayer, hope and charity, and other exercises of good works.

QUESTION V. What is hardening?

I. Induration, when taken generally for hardness of heart, is divided into original and actual. The former is ἔμφυτος or connate: the latter ἐπίκτητος or acquired. The former is drawn from parents by birth: the latter is contracted through a continued zeal for sinning. Of the former, mention is made in Ezek. 36. v. 26. and Mark 16. v. 14. Concerning the latter, our question is primarily instituted.

II. Furthermore, actual induration is concerned with a twofold object; 1. with doctrine. 2. with morals and life. For those are said to be indurated who contumaciously resist the truth; and those who pertinaciously persevere in sins against conscience. We speak, however, primarily of induration concerning the faith, which in the Scriptures is attributed to diverse men, 1. primarily to those to whom the will of God has been revealed through the word, and who either were never reborn, as Pharaoh and his servants; or at some time became partakers of παλιγγενεσίας, as Judas and the Jews who mocked the miracles of Christ. 2. secondarily to infidels and Gentiles, to whom the word of God and the will revealed by the word never became known, in which sense the Apostle ascribes induration to the nations, Rom. 1. v. 24. and Eph. 4. v. 19. We look here, however, primarily at the primary attribution of induration, the character and nature of which we cannot better understand than if we run through in a few words the principal terms and the proper ones by which it is described, which we shall provide briefly explained.

III. 1. The Hebrews for the most part use the verb קשה which signifies to harden, so that it cannot be bent or handled. For it denotes that natural malice and hardness of heart is increased by new increments: whence its signification is twofold, either when from soft (reborn) one becomes hard, or when from hard (not reborn) one becomes harder, as Pharaoh. In Exod. 7. verse 3. this verb is found, when God is said אַקְשֶׁה I will harden the heart of Pharaoh,

ואני אקשה את לב פרעה, Adjacent to this is the word כבד: which signifies to aggravate, and denotes the heart as if hindered by a mass of greater weight, so that it cannot raise itself to God. Scripture also uses the word חזק, which signifies to prevail, to strengthen, to consolidate, Exod. 4. verse 21. אחזק I will harden the heart of Pharaoh.

IV. The Greeks for the most part use the word σκληρυνειν. For σκληρὸς signifies hard from dryness, and is opposed to soft and loose. Grammarians derive it from σκέλλειν, which is to dry up or desiccate. It is transferred to the heart of man, when it, with the juice of divine grace exhausted, dries up and hardens like clay. The word κατισχύειν is also used, which otherwise neutrally signifies to prevail, but here it is taken transitively for strength, when someone confirms and hardens his heart to resist. John 12. 40. Eph. 4. verse 18. Hardening is called πώρωσις or callus. For when soft parts induce a callus, then they harden. - Thus also the heart is said to have become callous, when it hardens. Heb. 3. v. 15. it is called παραπικρασμὸς, exacerbation. For those who are hardened, their hearts are as it were exacerbated toward God.

V. The Latins use the word for hardening, aggravating, blinding, stopping, fattening, according to the distinct members to which hardening is attributed in the Scriptures. For there are seven principal members which impious men are said to harden, or by the abuse of which the hardening of man is circumscribed. 1. Heart. 2. Eyes. 3. Ears. 4. Neck. 5. Forehead. 6. Face and 7. Back.

VI. 1. The heart of extremely impious men is sometimes said to be hardened, confirmed, consolidated, as Ps. 95. v. 8. Do not harden your hearts. Sometimes fattened or made fat from the root שמן, because evidently the hearts, as if thickened by fat, become stupid and inept for understanding. For according to those skilled in physiognomy, a fat and large heart denotes a mind dull and stupid. The Greeks use the verbs παχύνειν and λιπαίνειν. In this sense it is said in Is. 6.10, השמן 'Make fat the heart of this people,' and Deut. 32. v. 15, 'The upright one grew fat and kicked, he grew fat, he grew thick, he grew sleek, he forsook God his maker.' And Matt. 13. v. 15, 'is grown fat.' Sometimes 'hardened.' 1 Sam. 6. v. 9, 'Why do you harden your hearts, as Egypt?' Ps. 4. v. 3, 'O sons of men, how long will you be of heavy heart?' Sometimes 'blinded,' Deut. 28. 28, 'May God strike you with blindness of mind,' Is. 6. 10, 'Blind the heart of the people.' Sometimes 'sawn through,' Acts 7. 54, 'Hearing these things διεπρίοντο ταῖς καρδίαις they were sawn through in their hearts.' Sometimes 'set into adamant,' as Zech. 7. 12. And this σκληροκαρδίαν or hardness of heart is usually followed by ἀπαλγησία, insensibility, because they lose every sense of a conscience stinging with pain, whence they are called ἀπηλγηκότες, those who are insensible or despairing. Eph. 4. v. 19.

VII. II. EYES are said to be darkened, Ps. 69. 24, 'Let their eyes be darkened, that they may not see': and closed, Is. 6. 10, 'Shut their eyes, cover them, lest perhaps they see': and Matt. 13. 15, it is said, ἐκάμμυσαν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῶν, 'They closed their eyes.' Moreover, μύειν signifies to close, and is properly used of the mouth and lips; but when it is attributed to the eyes, it signifies to blink. And the spontaneous malice of the wicked who close their eyes is noted, and the blindness which follows this, which John calls τύφλωσιν, chap. 12. 40.

IIX. III. THE EARS of the hardened are sometimes said to be 'hardened' [aggravated], as Zech. 7. v. 11, 'They hardened their ears, that they might not hear,' from the word כבד which signifies to make heavy by imposing a weight; and it denotes such an obstruction of the ears, when as if by design the ears are closed from the outside by something thrown over them, so that they either do not perceive the offered sound at all, or do so with difficulty. It is repeated in Is. 6. 10. Sometimes 'hearing heavily.' Matt. 13. 15, τοῖς ὠσὶ βαρέως ἤκουσαν, 'they heard heavily with their ears,' which defect is called by the Greeks βαρύτης, torpor or heaviness: whence βαρύηκοοι, the hard of hearing, who partly do not want to hear, partly are unable to hear. Sometimes stopped up, as Ps. 58. 5. like as the deaf adders that stop their ears. Sometimes also uncircumcised, Acts 7. v. 51.

IX. IV. The NECK of the wicked is called stiff, as Acts 7. 51. Stiffnecked &c. Hardened, Deut. 10. 16. Be ye no more stiffnecked, Iron, Is. 48. 4. See FOREHEAD is called brazen Is. 48. 4. and hard, Ezek. 2. 4. VI. The FACE of the profane is named hardened upon the earth, or rendered more stubborn than a rock Jer. 5. 3. VII. The BACK or shoulders are said to be turned away, Zech. 7. 11. They turned the back to one giving good counsel.

X. As the hardening is described by the external parts of the body: so also by the internal corruption of the senses and conscience. For the sense of the hardened is called reprobate, Rom. 1. 28. And their conscience is named cauterized, 1 Tim. 4. 2. κεκαυτηριασμένων τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν. For just as we mark some malicious person with a cautery, so that he may be recognized by all and held as infamous, or just as the limbs of animals are seared with a cautery and as it were hardened, so that they lack all sense, nay even sometimes are cut off; so a cauterized conscience is either the same as perverse, or the same as stopped up, without any sense of pain, and therefore completely cut off. Which cautery of the conscience is otherwise called πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, the spirit of compunction, Rom. 11. 8, which phrase is taken from Is. 29. 10, where the LXX translated תרדמה as the spirit of compunction. The Hebrew phrase signifies a heavy stupor completely depriving one of all sense, and denotes the sloth and incorrigible ἀναισθησία (insensibility) of the wicked in matters concerning salvation. But when κατάνυξις is transferred to the mind, it signifies the pain by which it is pierced, and by this phrase the Spirit of God wished to denote that the reprobate completely suppress the goads and evidence or κατάνυξις of the conscience, not that they feel no goads of conscience, but that they make nothing of them, whence they are called αὐτοκατάκριτοι (self-condemned). Tit. 3. v. 11. Others by this

By κατάνυξιν they understand the mutual conflict of thoughts accusing and defending themselves, Rom. 2. 15.

XI. From what has been said thus far, therefore, it appears that the synonyms of hardening are 1. fattening, thickening, aggravation of the heart. 2. closing, darkening, blinding of the eyes. 3. aggravation, torpor, and stopping of the ears. 4. Iron hardness of the neck. 5. brazen forehead. 6. face more hardened than a rock. 7. turning away of the shoulders or back. 8. reprobate sense, and 9. cauterized conscience. Whence we conclude that hardening is nothing other than a work by which the back is turned, the eyes are closed, the ears are stopped, the neck is hardened like iron, the forehead like brass, the face is rendered more hardened than a rock, the conscience is marked with a cautery, every sense becomes reprobate, and the heart, to which Scripture attributes the power of understanding and will, is thickened, fattened, aggravated, and placed into an adamant, and is as if covered with a callus so that it may not understand, nor embrace the things shown by the word of God, and that it may care for them not at all, or wish to care for them, whence they are called ἀπηλγηκότες καὶ αὐτοκατάκριτοι.

XII. And from this it is easy to gather what are the προσκείμενα or rather the properties of the hardened. For such are they who

1. turn their back or rebellious shoulders to one who advises well, Zech. 7. 11.

2. who suffer from the τυφλώσει of the eyes, John 12. v. 40.

3. whose ears hear βαρέως, Matt. 13 v. 15.

4. who are of a stiff and iron neck, Acts 7. v. 50. Isa. 48. verse 4.

5. who have a brazen forehead, knowing not how to blush, ibid.

6. who have made their faces harder than a rock. Jer. 5 v. 3.

7. whose mind is ἀδόκιμος reprobate, Rom. 1. v. 28.

8. who are κεκαυτηριαμένοι τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν (seared in their own conscience), 1. Tim. 4. vers. 2.

9. Having a πνεῦμα κατανύξεως (spirit of stupor). Rom. 11. v. 8.

10. And πώρωσιν καὶ παραπικρασμὸν τῆς καρδίας (blindness and provocation of the heart) or σκληρότητα (hardness). Rom 11. v. 7. & καρδίαν ἀμετανόητον (impenitent heart), Rom. 2. v. 5.

11. Whence follows ἀπαλγησία (insensibility) Eph. 4 v. 19.

12. And αὐτοκατάκρισις (self-condemnation), Tit. 3. v. 11. XIII. From these conditions of the hardened, however, it appears that not all the reprobate are hardened, although all the hardened are at the same time reprobate. For many die in infidelity before they reach the years of discretion: many sin in their morals, although they do not err in doctrine: some err concerning this, but ignorantly, certain ones knowingly, but not pertinaciously, but they yield at length to those teaching better things. And all these are not hardened.

XIV. Therefore, before anyone is hardened, it is necessary that many sins have preceded, all of which can be conveniently distinguished into five degrees, from Acts 13:45 & 46, where the Jews, filled with the zeal of envy against the Apostles, become ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ βλασφημοῦντες, ἀπωθοῦντες τὸν λόγον θεῦ καὶ ἑαυτὸς τῆς αἰωνίε ζωῆς ἐκ ἀξίες κρίνοντες, that is, they contradict, blaspheme, repel the word of God, and judge themselves unworthy of eternal life.

The first degree is παρακοὴ, disobedience against the Gospel. The second is ζῆλος ὁ κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν, the zeal of envy or internal malevolence against the doctrine and the teachers. The third is βλασφημία ἢ κακολογία, blasphemy, when speech follows disobedience and unholy zeal, corresponding to the internal affection, namely, railing and blasphemous. The fourth is ἄπωσις, the repelling of the sermon, when they violently repel the word of God from themselves. The fifth is αὐτοκατάκρισις or ἀπαλγησία, when men judge themselves unworthy of eternal life, and are condemned by their own judgment. These are called in Romans 9:22 σκευῆ τῆς ὀργῆς, vessels of wrath, both by reason of merit, because they merit divine wrath; and by reason of effect, because a living example of divine wrath is seen in them.

XV. A most illustrious example of this kind was Pharaoh, King of Egypt, who through many preceding sins contracted a clearly incorrigible and desperate σκληροκαρδίαν (hardness of heart). Seven of them are commonly numbered. 1. τεκνοφονία (infanticide), Exod. 1:16 & 22. 2. The monstrous persecution of the Israelites, Exod. 1:23, ch. 2:32, ch. 15:6. 3. απισία (unbelief) and contumacy, Exod. 7:23, ch. 9:34.

4. Blasphemy against God, Exod. 5. v. 2. 5.

The zeal of the Magicians, Exod. 7. v. 11. 22. ch. 10. v. 10. 6.

Impenitence & hypocrisy, Exod. 8. v. 15. 32. ch. 9. v. 34: ch. 10. v. 10. 7. contempt of the ministry, Exod. 5. v. 4. ch. 10. v. 28.

XVI. And from this example and the preceding description of both the hardened and of hardening, it becomes manifest that hardening is the most horrible and most grievous sin of all, and indeed that very thing which is called in Matt. 12. ver. 32. blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. 1

John 5. ver. 16.

A sin unto death, which is not forgiven in eternity, Mark 3. v. 30. for which there remains no more sacrifice. Heb. 10. v. 16.

Latin:

primæ tabulæ præcepto. Quia verò renati Deúm ex toto corde & super omnia non diligunt, nec diligere possunt, ob inhærens peccatum; hinc adeò fit, vt illa ipsa dilectio non conueniat cum isto primæ tabulæ præcepto, quo Deus non solum diligendus, sed super omnia & in omnibus, & ex omnibus viribus diligendus præcipitur. Sic ergò nostra dilectio est bonum opus, in quantum Deus diligitur: est malum opus, vel potius habet adjunctum malũ opus, in quantum Deus super omnia & perfectè non diligitur.

VII. Atque hoc ipsũm contingit etiam in omnibus alijs actionibus. Quia enim in omni renato uetus nouusᾱ; homo concurrunt, ideò vetus noui hominis operibus semper adspergit quasdam maculas, ob quas mala fiunt, & peccata dici possunt. Nam quam primùm aliquid boni cogitamus, renititur vetus homo: si in actum deducimus, indignatur & succenset. Atque ob hanc resistentiam & indignationem carnis fit, vt opus bonum rectè queat appellari malum eò, quòd opera legis bona, totaliter & plénè bona esse, atque à natura integerrima prouenire debeant. Quatenus enim non est ἁπλῶς & undiquaque bonum, eatenus legi inconforme, & per consequens malum est.

VIII. Hæc Lutheri mens fuit & sententia, quando hominem in omnibus suis operibus peccare asseruit, quæ doctrina sanctitatem & virtutes Christianas adeò non impedit, vt potius ad illam nos excitet & inflammet. Inde enim in animo renati accenditur vera humilitas, ardens precatio, spes & charitas, aliaque operum bonorum exercitia.

QVÆSTIO V. Quid sit induratio?

I. Induratio, cum generaliter pro duritie cordis sumitur, in originalem & actualem dispescitur. Illa est ἔμφυτος vel connata: hæc ἐπίκτητος vel acquisita. Illa à parentibus ex natiuitate trahitur: hæc per continuatum peccandi studium contrahitur. De illa sermo fit. Ezech. 36. v, 26. & Marci 16. v. 14. De hac quæstio nostra potissimùm instituta est.

II. Porrò autem induratio actualis circa geminum versatur objectum; 1. circa doctrinam. 2. circa mores & vitam. Nam indurari dicuntur & illi, qui contumaciter veritati resistunt; & isti, qui pertinaciter in peccatis contra conscientiam perseuerant. Loquimur autem primariò de induratione circa fidem, quæ in Scripturis diuersis hominibus tribuitur, 1. πρώτως his, quibus Dei voluntas per verbum est patefacta, & vel nunquam renati fuerunt, vt Pharao & serui ejus; vel aliquando παλιγγενεσίας facti sunt compotes, vt Iudas & Iudæi miraculorum Christi irrisores. 2. δευτέρως infidelibus & Ethnicis, quibus verbum Dei, & voluntas verbo reuelata nunquam innotuit quo sensu Apostolus indurationem adscribit gentibus, Rom. 1. v. 24. & Ephes. 4 v. 19. Spectamus autem hic potissimùm primariam indurationis attributionem, cuius indolem & naturam meliùs intelligere non possumus quàm si præcipua vocabula, & propria quibus describitur: paucis percurramus, id quod breuiter expeditum dabimus.

III. 1. Hebræi plerumque vtuntur verbo קשה quod significat indurescere, vt flecti tractariue nequeat. Notat enim naturalem malitiam ac duritiem cordis nouis augeri incrementis: vnde duplex eius est significatio, vel quando ex molli (renato) fit durus, vel quando ex duro (non renato) fit durior, ut Pharao. Exod. 7. vers 3. reperitur hoc verbum, quando Deus dicitur אַקְשֶׁה ego indurabo cor Pharaonis,

ואני אקשה את לב פרעה, Confine huic est verbum כבד: quod significat aggrauare, & notat cor quasi maioris ponderis mole impediri, ne se ad Deum erigere queat. Vtitur etiam Scriptura verbo חזק, quod significat præualere, roborare, consolidare, Exod. 4. vers. 2. אחזק Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis.

IV. Græci plerumque vtuntur voce σκληρυνειν. Nam σκληρὸς significat durum ex ariditate, opponiturq́; molli & laxo. Grammatici deriuant à σκέλλειν, quod est arefacere vel exiccare. Transfertur ad cor hominis, quando id succo diuinæ gratiæ exhausto arescit & obduresseit instar luti. Vsurpatur etiam verbum κατισχύειν, quod aliàs neutraliter præualere significat, hic autem transitiuè sumitur pro robore, quando quis cor suum confirmat & obfirmat ad resistendum. Ioh. 12. 40. Eph. 4. vers. 18. Induratio vocatur πώρωσις vel callus. Quando n. partes molles callum inducunt, tunc obdurescant. - Ita etiam cor dicitur occaluisse, quando indurescit. Heb. 3. v. 15. dicitur παραπικρασμὸς exacerbatio. Qui n. sunt indurati, eorum corda sunt quasi exacerbata erga Deum.

V. Latini vtuntur vocabulo indurandi, aggrauandi, excæcandi, obturandi, impingandi, pro ratione distinctorum membrorum, quibus induratio in Scripturis attribuitur. Septem enim sunt membra præcipua, quæ homines impij dicuntur indurare, vel quorum abusu hominis induratio circumscribitur. 1. Cor. 2. Oculi. 3. Aures, 4 Ceruix. 5. Frons, 6. Facies & 7. Tergum.

VI. 1. Cor hominum extremè impiorum dicitur interdum induratum, obfirmatum, consolidatum, vt Ps. 95. v. 8. Ne induretis corda vestra. Nonnunquam incrasiatū vel impingnatum à rad. שמן quòd videlicet corda quasi pinguedine incrassata, stupida fiant, & inepta ad intelligēdum. Nam testib. Pysiognonię peritis cor obesum & magnum denotat ingeniumhebes & stolidum. Græci verbo παχύνειν & λιπαίνειν vtuntur. Hoc sensu dicitur Es. 6.10. השמן Impingua cor populi huius, Et Deut. 32. v. 15. Incrassatus est rectus & recalcitravit, incrassatus, impinguatus, dilatatus dereliquit, Deum factorem suum. Et Matth, 13. v. 15, incrassas tum est cor. Nonnunquam aggrauatum. 1 Sam. 6. v. 9. Quare aggrauatis corda vestra, sicut Ægyptus. Ps. 4. vers. 3. Filij hominum vsque quò graui corde? Nonnunquam excæcatum Deut. 18 28. Percutiat te Deus cæcitate mentis, Es. 6. 10. Excæca cor populi. Nonnunquam dissectum Act. 7, 54. Audientes hæc διεπρίοντο ταῖς καρδίαις dissecabantur corde. Nonnunquam positum in adamantem, vt Zach. 7, 12. Et hanc σκληροκαρδίαν vel cordis indurationem plerunque sequitur ἀπαλγησία dedolentia, quòd sensum omnem doloris pungentis conscientiam amittant, vnde ἀπηλγηκότες dedolentes vel desperantes dicuntur. Eph. 4. v. 15.

VII. II. OCVLI dicuntur obscurati ψ 69. 24. Obscurentur oculi eorum, ne videas: Et clausi, Es. 6. 10. Oculos eorum claude, perstringe, ne fortè videat: & Matth. 13. 15. dicitur, ἐκάμμυσαν τὂς ὀφθαλμὂς αὐτῶν, Occluserunt oculos eorum. Significat autem μύειν claudere, ac propriè vsurpatur de ore & labijs: cùm verò oculis tribuitur significat côniuere. Ac notatur spontanea impiorum oculos claudentium malitia, & quæ hanc sequitur cæcitas, quam Iohannes vocat τύφλωσιν, cap. 12. 49.

IIX. III. AVRES induratorum dicuntur nonnunquam aggrauata, vt Zach, 7. v. 11. Aures suas aggrauauerunt, ne audirent, à verbo כבד quod significat, pondere imposito aggrauare; talemque aurium obstructionem notat, quando quasi de industria aures forinsecus realiquâ superiniectâ occluduntur, vt oblatum sonum vel omninò nõ percipiant, vel ægrè. Repetitur Es. 6. 10. Nonnunquam graviter audentes. Matth. 13. 16. τοῖς ὠσὶ βαρέως ἤκουσαν, auribus grauiter audierunt, quod vitium dicitur græcis βαρύτης, torpor vel gravitas: vnde βαρύηκοοι surdastri, qui partim audire nolunt, partim audire nequeunt. Nonnunquam obturatae, vt Pf. 58. 5. sicut aspides obturauerunt aures suas. Aliquando etiam incircumcisae, Act. 7. v. 51.

IX. IV. CERVIX impiorum dicitur dura, vt Act. 7. 51. Dura ceruice &c. Indurata, Deut 10. 16. Ceruicem vestram ne induretis amplius, Ferrea, Ef. 48. 4. v. FRONS vocatur aenea Ef. 48. 4. & dura, Ezech. 2. 4. VI. FACIES prophanorum nominatur indurata super terram, vel obfirmatior petrâ reddita Ier. 5. 3. VII. TERGVM vel scapulae dicuntur obuersae, Zach. 7. 11. Obuerterunt tergum benè monenti.

X. Vti v. induratio describitur per externam membrorum: ita & p internam sensuū & conscientiae corruptionem. Nam sensus induratorū dicitur reprobus, Rom. 1. 28 Et conscientia eorum nominatur cauteriata, 1. Tim. 4, 2. κεκαυτηριασμένων τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν. Sicut n. cauterio aliquem malitiosum signamus, vt ab omnibus agnoscatur, & pro infami habeatur, vel sicut cauterio mēbra animaliū aduruntur, & quasi indurantur, vt omni sensu careant, imò etiam quandoq́; abscinduntur; ita conscientia cauteriata vel idem est, quod peruersa, vel idem, quod obturata, sine omni sensu doloris, adeoque planè resecta. Quod conscientiae cauterjum aliâs πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, spiritus compunctionis dicitur. Rom. 11. 8 quae phrasis ex Ef 29.9, est desumta, vbi תרדמה verterunt LXX. Spiritum compunctionis. Hebraea phrasis significat soporem grauem omni sensu penitus priuantē, & notat improborū in rebus salutem concernentibus ignaviam & ἀναισθησίαν incorrigibilem. Κατάνυξις verò cùm ad animū transfertur, significat dolorem, quo is lancinatur, & hac phrasi id notare voluit Spiritus S quod reprobi stimulos ac indicium vel κατάνυξιν conscientiae penitus prosternant, non quòd nullos conscientiae stimulos sentiant, sed quod eosdem nihili faciant, vnde, αὐτοκατάκριτοι dicuntur. Tit. 3. v. 11. Alij p istam

κατάνυξιν intelligunt mutuum conflictum cogitationum sese accusantium & defendentium, Rom. 2. 15.

XI. Ex hactenus ergò dictis apparet, quod Synonyma indurationis sint 1. impingatio, incrasfatio, aggrauatio cordis. 2. occlusio, obscuratio, excæcatio oculorum. 3. aggrauatio, torpor & obtururatio aurium. 4. Ferrea durities ceruicis. 5. frons ænea. 6. facies petrâ obfirmatior. 7. scapularum vel tergi obuersiō. 8. sensus reprobus, & 9 conscientia cauteriata. Vnde concludimus, quòd induratio nihil sit aliud quàm opus, quo tergum obuertitur, oculi clauduntur, aures obsturantur, ceruix ferri, frons æris instar induratur, facies petrâ obfirmatior redditur, conscientia cauterio notatur, sensus omnis fit reprobus, & cor, cui Scriptura intelligentiæ & voluntatis vim tribuit, incrassatur, impinguatur, aggrauatur, atq; in adamātem ponitur, & quasi callo obducitur ne intelligat, neuè amplectatur res verbo Dei monstratas, easque planè nihil curet, vel curare velit, vnde ἀπηλγηκότες καὶ αὐτοκατάκριτοι dicuntur.

XII. Atque hinc facilè licet colligere, quæ sint προσκείμενα vel potiùs propria induratorum. Tales enim sunt, qui

1. Tergum benè monenti vel scapulas aversatrices obuertunt, Zach. 7. 11.

2. qui τυφλώσει oculorum laborant, Ioh. 12. v. 40.

3. quorum aures βαρέως audiunt, Matth. 13 v. 15.

4. qui ceruicis sunt duræ & ferreæ, Act. 7. v. 50. Esa. 48. vers. 4.

5. qui frontē habent æneam, erubescere nescientem, ibid.

6. qui facie suā petrâ obfirmatiorē reddiderūt. Ier. 5 v. 3.

7. quorum nūs est ἀδόκιμος reprobus, Rom. 1. v. 28.

8. qui sunt κεκαυτηριαμένοι τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν, 1. Tim. 4. vers. 2.

9. Habentes πνεῦμα κατανύξεως. Rom. 11. v. 8.

10. Et πώρωσιν καὶ παραπικρασμὸν τῆς καρδίας vel σκληρότητα. Rom 11. v. 7. & καρδίαν ἀμετανόητον, Rom. 2. v. 5.

11. Vnde sequitur ἀπαλγησία Eph. 4 v. 19.

12. Et αὐτοκατάκρισις, Tit. 3. v. 11. XIII. Ex his verò induratorum conditionibus apparet, non omnes reprobos esse induratos, quamvis omnes indurati simul sint reprobi. Multi enim moriuntur in infidelitate, antequam ad annos discretionis perueniant: multi peccant in moribus, quamuis non errant in doctrina: nonnulli errant circa hanc, sed ignoranter, quidam scienter, sed non pertinaciter, verùm cedunt tandem meliora docentibus. Et hi omnes non sunt indurati.

XIV. Proinde antequam induretur aliquis, necessum est, vt multa præcesserint peccata, quæ omnia in quinque gradus commodè possunt distingui, ex Act. 13. v. 45. & 46. vbi Iudæi repleti zelo inuidiæ adversus Apostolos fiũt ἀντιλέγοντες καὶ βλασφημοῦντες, ἀπωθοῦντες τὸν λόγον θεῦ καὶ ἑαυτὸς τῆς αἰωνίε ζωῆς ἐκ ἀξίες κρίνοντες hoc est, contradicunt, blasphemant, repellunt verbum Dei & indignos iudicant semetipsos æternæ vitæ.

Primus gradus est, παρακοὴ, inobedientia aduersus Euangelium. Secundus ζῆλος ὁ κατ’ ἐπίγνωσιν, zelus inuidiæ seu maleuolentiæ internus aduersus doctrinam & docentes. Tertius est βλασφημία ἢ κακολογία blasphemia, quando inobedientiam ac Zelum ἄζηλον sequitur oratio; interno affectui respondens, nimirum maledica & blasphema. Quartus est ἄπωσις repulsio sermonis, cum violenter sermonem Dei à se repellunt. Quintus est αὐτοκατάκρισις vel ἀπαλγησία, quando homines seipsos iudicant indignos vitâ æternâ, & suopte iudicio sunt condemnati. Hi dicuntur Rom. 9. v. 22. σκευῆ τῆς ὀργῆς vasa iræ, tum ratione meriti, quia merentur iram diuinam; tum ratione effectus; quia in iis viuum iræ diuinum exemplum cernitur.

XV. Huiusmodi exemplum in primis illustre fuit Pharao, Rex Ægypti, qui per multa peccata præcedentia incorrigibilem planè & desperatam contraxit σκληροκαρδίαν. Illorum septem numerantur communiter. 1. τεκνοφονία, Exod. 1. v. 16. & 22. 2. Israëlitarum immanis persecutio, Exod. 1. v. 23. c. 2. v. 32. ca. 15. v 6. 3. απισία & contumacia, Ex. 7. v. 23. c. 9. vers. 34.

4. βλασφημία in Deum, Exod. 5. v. 2. 5. Sudium Magis, Exod. 7. v. 11. 22. c. 10. v. 10. 6. Impoenitentia & hypocrisis, Exod. 8. v. 15. 32. cap. 9. v. 34: c. 10. v. 10. 7. contemptus ministerii, Exod. 5. v. 4. c. 10. v. 28.

XVI. Atque ex hoc exemplo & praecedente tum induratorum tum indurationis descriptione manifestum evadit, omnium horrendissimum & gravissimum peccatum esse indurationem, & quidem illud ipsum, quod Matth. 12. ver. 32. dicitur blasphemia in Spiritum sanctum. 1. Ioh. 5. ver. 16. Peccatum ad mortem, quod in aeternum non remittitur, Marc. 3. v. 30. pro quo nulla amplius restat hostia. Heb. 10. v. 16.


### Question: Question VI

QUESTION VI.

What are the causes of hardening? I. Hardening is attributed in the Scriptures to four things, as to acting principles. 1. To the Devil. 2. To Man. 3. To God. 4. To the ministers and Prophets of God. But in what sense God is said to harden, we shall explain in the last question. It is ascribed to the ministers of God in Isa. 6. 10. where the Prophet is commanded to make fat the heart of the people and to aggravate their ears, and to close their eyes, lest perhaps they see, hear, understand, and be converted. But this happens plainly by accident: since the heralds of the word do not instill hardness (σκληρότητα) into the hearers, but these very people from their own malice take occasion from it to resist more and more and to aggravate their heart against God. However, this accidental mode of hardening properly belongs to God himself, whose word it is that is preached: but to the ministers by communication. For God is accustomed to communicate the effect with his servants, so that what he himself does, he ascribes to them, and thus the ministers of the word are said to blind the disobedient, Isa. 6. v. 11, to convert their hearers, and to lay a foundation, 1 Cor. 3:10; to bind and loose sins, Matt. 18:18, John 20:24; to justify others, Dan. 12:3; to save, 1 Tim. 4:6, all of which are otherwise proper to God. II. The last two principles being therefore removed, there remain two true and properly so-called causes of hardening, namely the Devil suggesting and man consenting, and hardening himself out of spontaneous malice. We do not, however, exclude other causes, both external, of which it was spoken in disputation 3, last question: but here we are concerned only with the primary and proximate causes.

III. This is expressly ascribed to the Devil. 2 Cor. 4: The god of this world HAS BLINDED the minds of the unbelieving, that the illumination of the gospel of the glory of Christ might not shine upon them. Hence he is said to fill the heart with malice, Acts 5:3; to work in the children of disobedience, Eph. 2:2; and to hold men captive, 2 Tim. 2:26. However much the Devil may otherwise be able to suggest evils, he cannot incline the wills: yet in the hardened his power is far greater: since by the just judgment of God they are so permitted to Satan that he holds them as if bound in snares, and precipitates them into any crimes and outrages whatsoever. For he disturbs all the senses, blinds the intellect entirely, sears the conscience as if with a cauterizing iron, so that they care for neither God nor men, and forget themselves and their own, and thus, as if driven by madness, they dare anything, and rush with great impetus and incited course into the most present danger.

IV. 2. It is attributed primarily to the man himself, as the principal and direct cause, as is evident from the following testimonies. Exod. 7:13, 22, ch. 8:19: The heart of Pharaoh hardened itself, and he did not listen to them; ch. 9:35: Pharaoh added to sin and hardened his heart, he and his servants; ch. 13:15: It came to pass, when Pharaoh had hardened himself; Deut. 10:16: Do not harden your neck any more; 2 Kings 17:14: They hardened their neck; 2 Chron. 30:8: Do not harden your necks:

your fathers, 2 Chron. 36. 13. Zedekiah stiffened his neck, Neh. 9. v. 16. They stiffened their necks and did not listen to your commandments. Ps. 95. 8. Do not harden your hearts. Jer. 5. 3 They hardened their faces like rock. Similar things are read in ch. 7. v. 26, ch. 17. v. 24, ch. 19. v. 15. Zech. 7. v. 12. Heb. 3 v. 8.

V. From these statements it is evidently clear that the first and principal cause, as of other sins, so also of hardening, is the men themselves, who of their own accord do not wish to hear the word of God, or after they have heard it, refuse to obey. To this pertains that statement of Augustine, Sermon 88 de tempore: It must be believed most certainly that it was not the violence of God, but his own iniquity and indomitable pride that caused Pharaoh to be hardened so many times against the commandments of God. And Prosper, in his book on predestination and grace, chapter 15, writes thus concerning the two kings, Pharaoh and Nebuchadnezzar: As far as nature is concerned, both were men; as far as dignity, both were kings; as far as the cause, both were possessing the captive people of God; as far as the punishment, both were warned by scourges. What, therefore, made their ends different, except that one, feeling the hand of God, groaned in the remembrance of his own iniquity, while the other fought with free will against the most merciful truth of God.

Latin:

QUAESTIO VI.

Quanam indurationis causae sint? I. Induratio quatuor rebus, tanquam principiis agentibus in Scripturis attribuitur. 1. Diabolo 2. Homini. 3. Deo. 4. Dei ministris & Prophetis. Quo sensu autem Deus dicatur indurare, quaestione ultima exponemus. Dei ministris adscribitur Es. 6. 10. ubi praecipitur Prophetae, ut incrasset cor populi & aures eius aggrauet, & oculos claudat, ne forte videant, audiant, intelligant & conuertantur. Fit autem hoc plane per accidens: quandoquidem praecones verbi σκληρότητα non immittunt auditoribus, sed hi ipsi ex propria malitia occasionem inde sumunt magis magisque resistendi & cor aduersus Deum aggrauandi. Hic autem indurationis modus accidentalis proprie ipsi Deo competit, cuius est verbum, quod praedicatur: ministris autem per communicationem. Solet enim Deus cum seruis suis effectum communicare, vt, quod ipse agit, eis adscribat, adeoque ministri verbi dicantur inobedientes excaecare, Es. 6. v. 11, auditores suos conuertere, uertere, & fundamentum ponere, 1. Cor. 3. 10. peccata ligare & soluere, Matth. 18. v. 18. Iohan. 20. v. 24. alios iustificare, Dan. 12. v. 3. saluos facere, 1. Tim. 4 v. 6. quæ omnia Dei aliàs sunt propria. II. Remotis ergo postremis duobus principijs, remanent duæ indurationis causæ veræ & proprie dictæ, nimirum Diabolus suggerens & homo consentiens, seque ipsum ex spontanea malitia indurans. Non autem excludimus causas alias, tùm externas, de quibus disput. 3. quæst. vlt. dictum: sed hîc tantùm de primarijs, proximisque causis soliciti sumus.

III. Diabolo hoc expressè adscribitur. 2. Cor. 4. Deus huius seculi EXCXCAVIT mentes infidelium, vt non fulgeat eis illuminatio Euangelij gloriæ Christi. Hinc dicitur cor implere malitiâ Act. 5. v. 3. operari in filijs diffidentiæ, Eph. 2. v. 2. & captiuos tenere homines, 2. Tim. 2 6. Quantumuis autem aliàs Diabolus mala quidem suggerere possit, voluntates inclinare non possit: in induratis tamen longè maior est potestas eius: siquidem ex iusto Dei iudicio ita permittuntur Satanæ, vt quasi laqueis alligatos teneat, & in quęuis scelera & flagitia præcipitet. Nam omnes sensus perturbat, intellectum prorsus excæcat, conscientiam velut cauterio abscindit, vt nec Deum nec homines curent, & sui & suorum obliuiscantur, adeoque velut furore perciti quiduis audeant, & magno impetu cursuque incitato in præsentissimum periculum ruant.

IV. 2. Ipsi verò homini, tanquam causæ principali & directæ inprimis attribuitur, vt patet ex sequentib. testimonijs. Exod. 7. 13. 22. c. 8. 19. Roborauis se cor Pharaonis, & non audiuit eos cap. 9. 35. Addidit Pharao ad peccandum & aggrauauit cor suum ipse & serui eius. c. 13. 15 Factum est, cùm indurasset se Pharao, Deut. 10. 16. Ceruicem vestram ne indurate amplius. 2 Reg. 17. 14. Indurauerunt ceruicem suam 2. Paral. 30 v. ert. 8. Nolite indurare ceruices vestras:

tut Patres vestri, 2. Paral. 36. 13. Sedechias indurauit ceruicem suam, Neh. 9. v. 16. Indurauerunt ceruices suas & non audierunt ma:da:a tua. Pf. 95. 8. Nolite obturare corda vestra. Ier. 5. 3 Indurauerunt facies suas sicut petram. Similia leguntur c. 7. v. 26 c. 17. v. 24 c. 19. v. 15. Zach. 7. v. 12. Heb. 3 v. 8.

V. Ex hisce dictis euidenter patet, primam & principalem causam, vt aliorum peccatorum, ita & indurationis, ipsos esse homines, qui sponte verbum Dei audire nolunt, vel postquam audierunt, obedire renuunt. Quo pertinet illud August. Serm. 88. de tempore: Certissimè credendum, quod Pharaonem non Dei violentia, sed propria iniquitas & indomabilis superbia contra Dei præcepta toties fecerit indurari. Et visitissim l. de prædest. & grat. cap. 15. de duobus Regibus, Pharaone & Nebucadnezare ita scribit: Quantùm ad naturam, ambo homines erant; quantùm ad dignitatem; ambo reges; quantùm ad causam; ambo captiuum Dei populum possidentes, quantùm ad pœnam, ambo flagellis admoniti. Quid ergò fines eorum fecit esse diuersos, nisi quòd vnus manum Dei sentiens, in recordatione proprię iniquitatis ingemuit, alter libero contra Dei misericordissimam veritatem pugnauit arbitrio.


### Question VII. and last. In what sense is God said to harden?

In what sense is God said to harden?

I. Not once, but several times, hardening is found ascribed to God himself in the Scriptures, as Exod. 4. 21. I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, ch. 7. 3. I will make the heart of Pharaoh harden, ch. 9. 12. The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, which is repeated in verses 33, 34, ch. 10. 27, ch. 11. 10, ch. 14. 8. Josh. 11. 20. It was from the Lord that their hearts should be hardened. Isa. 63. 17. You have hardened our heart, so that we do not fear You. Rom. 9. 18. The Lord hardens whom He wills. Hence, therefore, it is not without cause asked, Why and in what sense is God said to harden? II. Moreover, there have been in the past, and still are, various opinions concerning this question. The Manichaeans understood it as referring to the efficacious operation of malice. Some of them, as Augustine testifies in Sermon 88 de tempore, dared with sacrilegious fury to criticize the Old Testament because of these and similar sayings of the Scriptures. In our century, the Calvinists have not hesitated to assert from the same sayings that God is the impelling cause of evil wills to sin. On the other side, the Pelagians, Papists, and Synergists interpret these sayings about hardening as referring to the bare and idle permission and tolerance of God, which explanations are taken from the Fathers, especially Origen, Jerome, and Augustine, book 2 de Praedestinat. et grat. c. 4. §. 6. book 1, question to Simplicianus, question 2, from Psalm 77, and other places. And although they are true in a certain respect, nevertheless they are extensively criticized by the blessed Luther against Erasmus, because they do not sufficiently express the force of the scriptural phrase in this matter. For that Luther does not simply reject divine permission is clear from his own words in volume 3 of the Jena Latin edition, page 206: God hardened Pharaoh while He invaded him through the word of Moses as if to take away his kingdom, and He did not give the Spirit within, but permitted his own impious corruption to grow and proceed with a certain fervor and contempt, with Satan reigning.

III. To state our opinion briefly, it should be noted that there is a threefold consideration of hardening: 1. Insofar as it is a sin. 2. Insofar as it is a cause of sins. 3. Insofar as it is a punishment for preceding crimes. In this last respect, it is nothing other than the just judgment of God, following from His consequent will, by which the preceding contumacy of men is punished through the withdrawal of grace and full delivery into the power of Satan, who is the executor of the divine judgment, and by whom men, with God permitting, are effectively hardened and precipitated into various crimes. In this judicial respect, hardening is rightly attributed to God, even as the principal agent. For every punishment, if it is just, has God as its author, since there is no evil in the city which the Lord has not done, Amos 3. v. 6. Lam. 3. v. 27. 28.

It must be known, however, when hardening is called a punishment, that the sin itself and the hardness of heart are not formally understood. For God does not effect this, nor does He send it in, when He punishes with hardening. What then? Nothing is understood but the judicial acts of God, upon which being posited, the sin of hardening follows of its own accord. Such are the desertion of man, the handing over into the power of Satan, the permission that a man be carried away into any crimes, and similar things, about which more will be said: Briefly, therefore, God punishes by hardening, not by efficiently sending in hardness, but by deserting, permitting, and handing over to Satan.

IV. Furthermore, as regards the first two considerations of hardening, insofar as it is sin and the cause of sin, in this sense it can in no way befit or be attributed to God as the acting principle: For the whole Scripture and the entire analogy of faith cries out that God the Best, that supreme and greatest Good, is in no way the author of sin. By this very thesis is removed from God 1 ἐνταλμά or commandment: For He does not command, but prohibits sins; as is evident from the Decalogue. They built high places, which I did not command, Jer. 19, v. 5. The prophets seduced the people, when I had not commanded them, c. 23, v. 32. 2 ἰυδοκία or good pleasure. He does not approve; He does not will, but hates sins. For God is not one who wills iniquity, Ps. 5. v. 5. You chose what I did not will, He says in Is. 65: v. 12. Do not think evil, and do not love a lying oath. For all these are things that I hate, says the Lord, Zech. 8. v. 17. Hence rightly Fulgentius 1. 1. ad Mon. p 43. From the will of God the origin of sinning never proceeds. 3. ἐνέργεια, or effective concurrence: For He does not instigate men to sins, but calls them away, He does not together effect evil, but either permits or hinders it, for all the works of God are perfect; Deut. 32: v. 4: The just Lord will not do iniquity, Eph. 3. v. 5. Hence again Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, p. 12: Just as sin is not in God, so sin is not from Him. But that which is not from Him is certainly not His work.

V. Since therefore God is neither the cause nor the author of any sin, how, I ask, does He efficiently concur in hardening, that sin which is by far the most grave and atrocious? For if that which seems more to be present is not present, neither will that which seems less to be present be present. Add 1. God's interdict, that men should not harden their hearts, Psalm 95, v. 8. But would He not be contrary to Himself if He were to prohibit the hardening which He willed and produced? 2. God's complaint that men have hardened themselves, Exodus 10, v. 3, 4, and throughout the Prophets. But how could He complain if He Himself had mitigated men and had efficiently caused the hardening in them? 3. God's punishment, with which He affects the hardened. But a judge justly punishes for whatever deed; this displeases Him, and therefore it does not draw its origin from Him. Wherefore, since God severely avenges hardening, we conclude most firmly from this that it does not have God as its author: for the universal maxim is: Of those things of which God is the avenger, He is not the author.

VI. And thus the holy Fathers also taught in times past, especially Augustine, who writes in his book on Exodus, question 83: Regarding Pharaoh, it is easily answered that by his former merits, by which he afflicted strangers in his kingdom, he was made worthy that his heart should be hardened, so that he would not believe even the most manifest signs of God commanding. And in the book On Nature and Grace, ch. 2: God sometimes punishes sins, and from that punishment more and graver sins always arise. And yet concerning hardening and blinding, that is, concerning sins which are the punishment of sins, Paul says in Romans 11, v. 11: Have they stumbled that they should fall? God forbid. So truly God is not a God who wills iniquity, Psalm 5:5. Otherwise, how shall He judge the world? Romans 3:6.

VII. Although, however, God does not efficiently concur in the sin of hardening, as such; yet He is not a completely idle spectator but

He operates through many acts concerning that very thing, which, so that we may recount them distinctly, we divide into general and special.

VIII. Of the general [acts], which concur with any action whatsoever, whether it be good or evil, there are chiefly two.

1. Foreknowledge, by which God from eternity foresees, and sometimes in time predicts, the malice of men who spontaneously harden themselves, just as He announced beforehand the hardening of Pharaoh, Exod. 3. verse 19. Concerning which Augustine, in his book on predestination and grace, chapter 6, writes thus: He who desires to know the cause of Pharaoh's hardening, let him re-read that place of Scripture where God first appeared to Moses in the burning bush, and so inflamed his heart with the ardor of divine brightness that he might speak testimonies in the sight of kings without confusion; there he will find that all this, which is said to be God hardening the heart of Pharaoh, pertains not to the operation of God, but to His foreknowledge.

2. The co-efficiency of the action itself. For in God we are, we live, we move, Acts 17. v. 28. Wherefore we cannot move even a hand without His help, nay, we can think or do absolutely nothing. God, therefore, as the primary cause, produces all the actions of man, but only insofar as they are physical actions and motions: but not insofar as they decline from the good and are sins. And to this point tend certain harsher sayings of Luther in his book on the enslaved will, as when he says that God drives and snatches the tongue and will of Pharaoh; that the will cannot in any way be moved or impelled except by God. All of which must be understood only concerning the general motion of the members, and not concerning the vice or ἀταξίᾳ of the motion. For he himself writes thus, Tom. 3. Ien. fol. 200. He speaks simply, I will cause the heart of Pharaoh to be hardened, that is, that it be hardened while I am operating and acting. How this is done, we have heard; namely, by an internal general motion I will move the evil will itself, so that it may proceed with its own impetus and course of willing, nor shall I cease to move it, nor can I do otherwise.

IX. We call those special acts, which occur not in all, but only in evil actions, and especially in the sin of hardening. We divide these: 1. Into antecedent. 2. Into concomitant. 3. Into consequent. For hardening can be considered either before it happens, or when it happens, or after it has been done: In each individual case, certain acts of God are conspicuous.

X. We count four antecedent ones:

1. It is the prohibition of sin with an attached threat. For in general God prohibits all sins, and thus also hardening, and at the same time adds the most serious punishments, which He threatens to those who offend, from which it is clearly evident that hardening is thoroughly displeasing to God:

2. The offering of the Word, or the calling to repentance: For God is so good that He not only prohibits evils, but also offers the means by which they can easily be prevented; He sends out His ministers so that they may instruct men, call them to repentance, and lead them to eternal salvation. Which in turn is an indication of a benevolent will and one that does not take pleasure in the sin or the destruction of men:

3. Desertion: For when the fatherly admonitions of God, the prohibitions, and the threats avail nothing; His just judgment begins and not undeservedly deserts such stubborn men. For just as God in His fatherly governance is said to guard His own, lest they sin, Gen. 20 v. 6, so He withdraws His grace from a man who stubbornly resists, and leaves him to himself, as is evident from 1 Samuel 16 v. 14. How easy, moreover, is the fall into sin when God deserts, Scripture shows by the example of Hezekiah, 2 Chron. 32 v. 31, and Saul; 1 Sam. 16 v. 14, therefore the pious in the Psalms pray against this punishment, My God, do not desert me. This desertion, however, is not the cause of the sin itself, just as a physician is not the cause of a disease when he deserts a sick man, but one who is intemperate and rejects sounder advice: but rather, just as a physician does not insert vicious humors into a sick man but

Latin:

Quo sensu Deus dicatur indurare?

I. Non semel, sed aliquoties induratio in Scripturis ipsi Deo adscripta reperitur, vt Exod 4. 2. Ego indurabo cor Pharaonis c. 7; 3. Ego faciam indurefcere cor Pharaonis, cap. 9. 12. Indurauit Dominus cor Pharaonis, quod repetitur vers: 33. 34. cap: 10: 27. cap. 11. 10. c. 14. 8. Ios. 11. 20. A Domino fuerat, vt indurarentur corda eorum. Esa. 63. 17. Indurasti cor nostrum, ne timeamus Te. Rom. 9. 29. Dominus quem vult, indurat. Hinc ergò non immeritò quæritur, Cur & quo sensu Deus dicatur indurare? II. Variæ autem de quæstione hac & olim fuerunt, & etiamnum sunt sententiæ. Manichæi intellexerunt de efficaci malitiæ operatione. Nonnulli eorum, teste Augustino Serm. 88. de temp. ob hæc & similia scripturarum dicta V. T. sacrilego furore ausi sunt reprehendere. Nostro seculo ex iijsdem dictis Caluiniani non dubitarunt asserere, Deum esse causam impellentem malas voluntates ad peccandum. Ab altera parte Pelagiani, Papistæ & Synergistæ dicta hæc de induratione interpretantur de nuda ac otiosa permissione ac tolerantia Dei, quæ explicationes ex Patribus, præsertim Origene, Hieronymo & Augustino lib. 2. de Prædestinat, & grat. c. 4. §. 6. l. 7. b. 1. quæst. ad Simplic. quæst 2. ex Psal. 77. alijsque locis sunt desumtæ. Etsi autem veræ sunt secundum quid, tamen prolixè exagitantur à B. Luthero, contra Erasmum, eò quòd vim phrasews Scripturæ in hoc negotio sufficienter non exprimant. Quòd enim Lutherus non simpliciter rejiciat permissionem diuinam, patet ex ipsius verbis tomo 3. Ien. lat. pagina 206. Deus Pharaonem indurauit, dum illum per verbum Mosis velut regnum ablaturus inuasit, & intus Spirituum non dedit, sed ipsius impiam corruptionem permisit, regnante Satana, succrescere, & procedere cum ferueritate quadam & contemtu.

III. Vt nostram breuiter dicamus sententiam, notandum, quòd triplex indurationis consideratio. 1. Quatenus est peccatum. 2. Quatenus est causa peccatorum. 3. Quatenus est pæna præcedentium scelerum, Hoc vltimo respectu nihil est aliud, quàm iustum Dei iudicium, ex voluntate consequente eorum, quo vindicatur præcedens hominum contumacia per subtractionem gratiæ, & plenam traditionem in potestatem Satanæ, qui judicij diuini executor est, & à quo homines, permittente Deo, efficaciter indurantur, & in varia scelera præcipitantur. Hoc respectu judiciali induratio rectè attribuitur Deo, etiam vt prinsipiô agenti. Omnis enim pœna si iusta est, Deum aucthorem habet, siquidem non est malum in ciuitate, quod non fecerit Dominus, Amos 3. v. 6. Thren. 3. v. 27. 28.

Sciendum verò, cùm induratio pœna dicitur, quòd non ipsum peccatum & durities cordis formaliter intelligatur. Hâc enim Deus non efficit, non im mittit, quando induratione punit. Quid ergò? Non nisi actus Dei iudiciales intelliguntur, quibus positis, vltro sequitur peccatum indurationis. Tales sunt desertio hominis, traditio in potestatē Satanæ, permissio vt in quæuis scelera homo abripiatur, & similes, de quibus plura dicentur: Breuiter Ergòs Punit Deus induratione, non duriciem efficienter immittendo, sed deserendo, permittendo & Satanæ tradendo.

IV. Porrò autem qẽ spectat priores duâs indurationis cosiderationes, prout peccatum & causa peccati est, hoc sensu Deo: vt agenti principio nequaţ vel conuenire potest, vel attribui debet: Vniuersa enim enim Scriptura & tota fidei analogiä clamat, quòd Deus Optimus, Bonum illud summũ & maximũ, nullo modo peccati author sit. Quâ ipsâ thesi remouetur à Deo 1 ἐνταλμά vel mandatum: Non enim præcipit, sed prohibet peccata; vt patet ex Decalogo. Edificarunt excelsa, quæ non præcepi, Ierem. 19, v. 5. Prophetæ seduxerunt populum, cùm non mandissem eis, c. 23, v. 32. 2 ἰυδοκία vel beneplacitũ. Non adprobat; non vult, sed odit peccata. Non enim Deus volens iniquitatem est, Psal. 5. v. 5. Quod non volui, elegistis, inquit apud Es. 65: v. 12. Malum ne cogitetis, & iuramentum mendax ne diligatis. Omnia enim hæc sunt, quæ odi, dicit Dominus, Zach. 8. v. 17. Hinc rectè Fulgentius 1. 1. ad Mon. p 43. Ex voluntate Dei nunquam procedit origo peccandi. 3. ἐνέργεια, vel concursus effectiuus: Non enim homines ad peccata instigat, sed auocat, non vnà malum efficit, sed vel permittit, vel impedit, Omnia enim opera Dei sunt perfecta; Deut. 32: v. 4: Dominus iustus non faciet iniquitatem, Eph. 3. v. 5. Hinc iterum Fulgentius l. 1. ad Mon. p. 12. Sicut peccatum in Deo non est, ita peccatum ex eo non est. Quod autem ex eo non est opus eius vtique non est.

V. Cùm igitur nullius peccati causa vel author existat Deus, quî quæso ad indurationem, peccatum istud longè grauissimum & atrocissimum efficienter concurrit? Si enim id non inest, quod magis inesse videtur, nec illud inerit, quod minus inesse videtur. Adde 1. Dei interdictum, ne homines obturent corda, Psalm. 95. v. 8. Annòn autem sibi ipsi foret contrarius si indurationem, quam vellet & produceret, simul prohiberet? 2. Dei querelam, quòd homines sese indurauerint, Exod. 10. v. 3. 4. & in Prophetis passim. Quî autem conqueri posset, si ipsemet homines mitigasset, & indurationem in ijs efficiēter causâsset? 3. Dei pœnam, quâ induratos afficit. Iudex autem, ob quodcunq; factum iustè punit, hoc ipsi displicet, ideoque abillo originem non trahit. Quare cùm Deus indurationē seuerè vlciscatur, hinc illam Deum authorem non habere, firmissimè concludimus: Vniuersalis enim est Maxima: Quorum Deus vltor est, eorum author non est.

VI. Atque ita sancti etiam Patres olim docuerunt, inprimis Augustinus, qui in lib. super Exod. quæst 83. scribit: De Pharaone facilè respondetur, prioribus meritis quibus afflixit in regno suo peregrinos, dignum effectum, cui obduretur cor, vt nec manifestissimis signis iubentis Dei crederet. Et l. de nat. & grat. c. 2. Deus aliquaties vindicat peccata & ex illâ vindicta semper plura & grauiora peccata consurgunt. Et tamen de induratione, excæcatione, id est, de peccatis, quæ sunt pœna peccatorū; dicit Paulus Rom. 11. v. 11. Nunquid impegerunt, vt caderent? Absit. Adeò nimirū Deus non est Deus, volens iniquitatem, Psal. 5. 5. Aliàs quomodo iudicabit mundum? Rom: 3. v. 6.

VII. Quamuis autem Deus ad peccatum indurationis, quà tale, non concurrat efficienter; attamen non est otiosus planè spectator sed

Multis actibus circa illud ipsum operatur, quos vt recenfeamus distincte, in generales & spe iales dispescimus.

VIII. GENERALIVM, qui ad quamuis actionem, siue bona sit, siue mala concurrunt, potissimum duo sunt.

1. Præscientia, quà Deus malitiam hominum spontè semetipsos indurantium ab æterno pręuidet & nonnunquam in tempore prædicit, quemadmodum Pharaonis indurationem prænunciauit, Exod. 3. vers. 19. de quo August. l. de prædest. & grat. c. 6. ita scribit: Qui causam indurati Pharaonis scire desiderat, illum Scripturæ locum relegat, vbi primùm Deus Mosi in rubo ignis apparuit, atque ita cor eius ardore claritatis diuinæ igniuit, vt in conspectu regum testimonia sine confusione loqueretur; ibi inueniet totum hoc, quod indurasse Deus cor Pharaonis dicitur, non ad operationem Dei, sed ad præscientiam pertinere.

2. Ipsius actionis coefficientia. In Deo enim sumus, viuimus, movemur, Act. 17. v. 28. Quare nec manum quidem sine ipsius ope mouere, imò nihil prorsus cogitare vel operari possumus. Deus igitur omnes actiones hominis, vt causa prima, simul producit, verùm duntaxat quatenus actiones & motus Physici sunt: non autem, quatenus à bono declinant, & peccata sunt. Et huc tendunt dicta quædam duriora Lutheri in libro de seruo arbitrio, vt quàdo ait, Deum pellere & rapere linguã & voluntatem Pharaonis; non posse vllo modo voluntatem moueri aut impelli, nisi à Deo. Quæ omnia tantùm de generali membrorũ motu, non autem motus vitio vel ἀταξίᾳ intelligi debent. Ita enim scribit ipse Tom. 3. Ien. fol. 200. Simpliciter loquitur, Ego faciam vt cor Pharaonis induretur, hoc est, vt me operante & faciente induretur. Quod quomodo fiat, audiuimus; scilicet intus generale motu ipsam mouebo voluntatem malam, vt suo impetu & cursis volendi pergat, nec cessabo mouere, nec possum aliter.

IX. SPECIALES actus vocamus illos, qui non in omnibus sed tantum malis actionibus, & praesertim in peccato indurationis occurrunt. Hos diuidimus 1. In antecedentes. 2. In concomitantes. 3. In consequentes. Potest enim induratio considerari vel antequam fiat, vel cùm fit, vel postquam facta est: Citra singula certi actus Dei sunt conspicui.

X. ANTECEDENTIVM quatuor numeramus:

1. Est peccati prohibitio cum adiuncta comminatione. In genere enim omnia peccata Deus prohibet, & sic quoque indurationem, simulque addit grauissimas poenas, quas minatur delinquentibus vnde Deo indurationem penitùs displicere luculenter patet:

2. Verbi oblatio, vel ad poenitentiam vocatio: Ita enim bonus est Deus, vt non tantùm prohibeat mala, sed etiam offerat media, quibus illa praecauerifacilè possint; emittit ministros suos, vt erudiant homines, ad poenitentiam vocent, & ad salutem aeternam perducant. Quod vicissim est indicium voluntatis beneuolae & non delectantis hominum vel peccato vel interitu:

3. Desertio: Cùm enim nihil proficiunt paternae Dei admonitiones, nihil interdicta & minae; iudicium ejus justum incipit & tàm praefractos homines non immeritò deserit. Quemadmodum enim Deus in paterna gubernatione suos custodire dicitur, ne peccent, Gen. 20 v. 6. ita homini contumaciter resistenti suam subtrahit gratiam, & ipsum sibi relinquit, vt patet ex 1. Samuel 16. v. 14. Quàm a. sit facilis lapsus in peccatum, deserente Deo, ostendit Scriptura exemplo Ezechiae, 2. Paral. 32. v. 3. & Saulis; 1. Sam. 16. v. 14. ideò pij in Psalmis deprecantur hanc poenam, Deus meus ne deseras me. Haec autem desertio non est causa ipsius peccati, sicut nec medicus morbi quando hominem aegrum, sed intemperantem, & consilia saniora respuentem deserit: sed potiùs, vti medicus aegro vitiosos humores non inserit sed jam infusos


### Question VII. and last. In what sense is God said to harden?: leaves those already infused, so God by His desertion does not infuse malice…

leaves those already infused, so God by His desertion does not infuse malice into sinners, but rather permits it, inasmuch as it is incorrigible, to remain by a just judgment. Hence, speaking of the fall of Adam, Augustine writes: The desertion of God was not the cause of the Adamic fall, but this very fall was the cause of the desertion. For God did not withdraw His grace from man before the fall, but man himself through and because of the fall lost it. Moreover, desertion is twofold: privative, regarding the reborn, and negative, regarding the not reborn. The former are deserted when prior grace is withdrawn; the latter, however, when none is imparted.

4. Delivery into the power of Satan. For whom God deserts, demons immediately take up. Gregory, book 25 of Morals, ch. 9: When we are deserted by God, we are delivered to the devil, and having been brought into his power, we are afflicted with countless evils, Chrysostom on the 12th chapter of John, homily 68. Concerning this act, there is discourse in Psalm 53, verse 5. From this, however, various sins indeed follow, yet the blame is not to be ascribed to God. For He does not inject malice, but only permits it by delivering man to Satan, which He does not do out of absolute hatred, but out of a just judgment by which He rightfully avenges the contumacy of men. Unless these had resisted God with spontaneous malice and had previously rejected all means of salvation, God would never desert them or permit them to the will of Satan. These, therefore, are those four antecedent acts, of which the first two pertain to the antecedent will, which is of mercy, the latter to the consequent, which is of justice.
