XI. We count, in turn, four CONCOMITANT acts.

1. It is permission. For if God wished to work extraordinarily, He could indeed bend the wills of men and in one moment change them completely, just as He miraculously converted Paul while he was in the midst of his fury: but because He owes nothing to anyone, and denies to no one the ordinary means which suffice for salvation; hence if these are rejected, by a just judgment He permits men to fall, harden themselves, and by the devil to be taken captive. Concerning which speak the following sayings: Ps. 81, verse 13; Hosea 4, v. 14; Zech. 8, v. 10; Acts 14, verse 16. This permission, however, is not altogether simple, but joined, 1. with divine omnipotence. For God could prevent it if He wished: by which reason divine permission differs much from human, which, on account of impotence and violence, is often more coercion than permission. 2. with the will of God, not indeed of effecting, but of permitting, and thus, not willing the sin, He nevertheless wills to permit it. It is to be noted, moreover, that there is a twofold permission; one, by which God permits a man to sin, the other, which permits him to persevere in sin: the former is called simple permission, the latter is called hardening, blinding. Therefore, just as God is said to cause to err, when nevertheless He only permits it by simple permission; so He is said to harden, when He permits men to persevere in sin.

2. Detestation of sin. For although God permits hardening, He does not, however, approve of it, but in the very act He hates and detests it, as a most grave sin, contrary to His will and law. He wills it indeed, in so far as it is a punishment, or in so far as He makes the sinner more and more guilty of eternal damnation on account of preceding offenses; but He does not will it absolutely, and as it is a fault, prohibited by law, because thus God would contradict Himself.

3. Tolerance of the sinner. He does not immediately drag the hardened one to punishment, nor does He forthwith call him away from here, which nevertheless would be very easy for Him: but He tolerates him with great patience. Rom. 9, v. 22, because He does not wish anyone to perish, but all to return to repentance, 2 Pet. 3, v. 9. For this is that kindness and long-suffering of God, by which He leads to μετάνοιαν [repentance], Rom. 3, v. 4, which when the hardened neglect, they treasure up for themselves wrath in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, v. 5. And to this the Apostle looked, Rom. 8, v. 17, when he says that Scripture affirms concerning Pharaoh, εἰς αὐτὸ τῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε: For this very thing I have raised thee up, or rather preserved thee, that I may show my power. For those words are taken from chapter 9 of Exodus, verse 16, where it is read thus: And indeed for this העמדתיך that I might make you see my patience. Arias Montanus, however, translates this, I made you remain. The 70 διετηρήθης ἕνεκα τού- του, You have been preserved until this time. Tremellius & Junius, I made you remain. Therefore, no cooperation of God toward hardening, as it is a sin, is denoted, but only the preservation of the sinner, so that the sense may be: When you had deserved that you should immediately either be swallowed by the earth, or be consumed by fire from heaven, your animals killed, I truly made you subsist, and with great leniency I bore your tyranny, not because I approved of your crimes, but since you were incurable, that I might show in your case and destruction my wrath and power.

2. Restraint, or the prescription of boundaries. For God does not allow the devil and wicked men to run wild freely, but sets certain limits beyond which they cannot wander. This appears again from the history of Pharaoh. He had been afflicted with so many plagues by Moses and Aaron, yet he did not remove them from the midst, a thing which must be held in the place of a great miracle. He himself was fierce and cruel: Moses and Aaron were under his power: He thought of nothing but the destruction of the Israelites: He had experienced so many misfortunes which the Lord had sent through Moses, and yet it is not read that he laid hands on these legates of God, or cast them into prison, or attempted anything similar. Whence, however, this? It was done by the Lord, who restrained Pharaoh in the midst of his fury, lest he rage against his servants. God put a ring in his nostrils, and a bridle in his lips, just as is read concerning Sennacherib, Isaiah 37, v. 29. And so it always happens, that God is not an idle spectator, but prescribes boundaries, restrains the hardened, and casts a halter upon tyrants, lest they completely destroy or devastate the Church.

XII. Of the CONSEQUENCES there are only two.

2. The end is governance. For there is nothing so evil that God, according to His infinite wisdom and power, is not accustomed to direct toward good, which is partly for the benefit of the Church, and partly for the illustration of His own glory. For the good One would not allow evil to be done, unless the omnipotent One could bring good out of evil, Augustine in Enchiridion, chapter 100. Although God is not the author of evil thoughts, He is nevertheless the ordainer of evil wills, and He does not cease to work good from the evil work of anyone; Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, p. 55.

2. Actual punishment, by which He punishes the hardened. For after He has tolerated them for long enough, and no hope of repentance remains, at length by a just judgment He calls them to punishment, and partly punishes them with a horrendous kind of death as regards the body, and partly condemns them to infernal flames as regards the soul, just as the example of Pharaoh, drowned in the Red Sea, confirms quite clearly in turn.

XIII. And these are those twelve acts of God, conspicuous regarding the sin of hardening, from which two πορίσματα flow. 1. That God is not an idle spectator. 2. Nor is He the author of hardening itself. For all these acts are so constituted that they indicate no efficiency on the part of God, but rather the displeasure and hatred with which He pursues both the sin and the sinner.

XIV. But this one thing now remains to be explained: Why does Scripture use active verbs, and why is God said to harden and to blind, if He does not harden by act Himself, nor cooperate efficiently toward hardening? Here that rule of the grammarians, deduced from the perpetual usage of Scripture, comes to mind: that active verbs do not always signify an efficacious operation, but rather permission, or occasion, or declaration, or some other respect and concurrence. We have produced many good examples in Phil. Sob. Grammatical Question 4, p. 397 and 398, where they may be seen.

XV. Since, therefore, the whole analogy of faith is undermined, if God is established as efficiently working hardening, hence we conclude that the words of hardening must be explained not actively, but in another way. There are, however, six principal ways or respects in which God is said to harden.

For 1. He hardens apophatically or negatively, when He does not remove. For often affirmative verbs and nouns are placed for their negative opposites. Thus, to hate is sometimes the same as not to approve, not to embrace. To love life, that is, not to expose it to dangers for the Gospel. In this sense God is said to harden and blind, when the opposite is denied, that is, when He neither softens nor illuminates. Augustine hints at this in Epist. 105: God does not harden by imparting malice, but by not imparting grace. And in the book De praedest. Sanc. cap. 4: God is said to harden when He does not soften, to blind when He does not illuminate. For as the absence of the sun, not its energy, causes darkness, so the desertion of God, not His operation, hardens.

2. aphaireticos or privatively, when He takes away whatever softness of heart was previously granted. For when one does not have, even that which he has is taken away, Matt. 13, verse 12; ch. 25, verse 29. For as blindness follows when sight is taken away, so hardness of heart follows when the grace of God is withdrawn: for which reason God is said to harden, not by unjustly injecting hardness, but by justly taking away grace, to which hardening soon succeeds.

3. parachoreticos or permissively. For action in the Scriptures is often attributed to the one who permits. Thus, those are said to give life who permit men to live, when they could kill. In a similar way, God hardens, that is, He permits hardening. Hence Theodoret says Pharaoh was hardened not by divine power, but by divine patience. Augustine, sermon 88, declares this with the example of servants, which permission and indulgence are said to have corrupted. Thus God hardens by indulging, by doing good, and by deferring punishments. Luther indeed rejects this interpretation against Erasmus, namely if we say that a man is hardened by the mere tolerance of God, with the remaining judgments omitted. But we ourselves do not understand such permission and tolerance, but we join with it the remaining actions of God.

4. Materially or objectively, when God offers the word, shows wonders, and thus calls to repentance. For hence the impious are hardened more and more, by their own fault, not God's. Meanwhile, however, for this reason God himself is said to harden, but clearly by accident, not otherwise than as the law is said to work sin, Rom. 7, verse 8. Thus gifts subvert the just, Exod. 23, verse 8, and the sun blinds those with sore eyes, and external cold by antiperistasis intensifies heat. To this refers that Prov. 25, verse 20: Vinegar upon nitre, is he that singeth songs to a heavy heart. And Luther especially attends to this accidental mode of hardening in his book against Erasmus when he writes everywhere that God offered the word so that Pharaoh might be hardened. All this was done by accident, no otherwise than as the Gospel is said to be the odor of death, 2 Cor. 2, verse 16. But that this happens only by accident is evident from the fact that by that very word, by which some are blinded, others are converted, as is evident from the example of the Egyptians and the Jews, of whom the former were hardened by the sermons of Moses, the latter were edified.

5. Metonymically or declaratively. For active verbs frequently indicate not the bringing about of a thing, but the showing of a thing brought about. Thus Jeremiah ch. 1, verse 10, destroys nations when he announces that they are to be destroyed: thus we are justified by works, James 2, verse 24, that is, we are declared justified. In a similar way God hardened Pharaoh, that is, by many wonders he showed that his heart was extremely impious and thoroughly hardened.

6. Διατακτικῶς or directively. For although God neither wills nor effects hardening, yet because He works concerning it by prescribing limits and directing it to the advantage of the Church and the manifestation of His own glory, for that reason the hardening itself is attributed to God. But I have discussed all these things at length in the Phil. Sob. in the stated questions, and in the Academic schools in disputation 3, thesis 69 up to thesis 108, to which we remit the reader for the sake of brevity, lest we idly and tediously repeat here what has been done elsewhere.

Latin:

relinquit, ita Deus desertione sua peccatoribus malitiam non infundit, sed eam potius, quippe incorrigibilem iusto iudicio remanere permittit. Hinc de lapsu Adami verba faciens Augustinus scribit: Non desertio Dei fuit causa lapsus Adamitici, sed hic ipse lapsus causa desertionis extitit. Neque enim Deus gratiam suam homini ante lapsum subtraxit sed homo ipse per & propter lapsum eam deperdidit. Est autem desertio duplex, tum priuatiua, quoad renatos, tum negatiua, quoad non renatos. Illi deseruntur, cùm prior gratia subtrahitur; hi verò, cùm nulla impertitur.

4. In potestatem Satanæ traditio. Nam quem Deus deserit, dæmones mox suscipiunt. Gregor. l. 25 Moral. c. 9. Cùm deserimur à Deo, tradimur diabolo in cuius potestatem redacti, innumeris malis afficimur, Chrys. in 12. caput Iohan. homil. 68. De hoc actu sermo est Psalmo 53. vers. 5. Hinc autem sequuntur quidem varia peccata, non tamē culpa Deo est ascribenda. Hic enim malitiam non immittit, sed tantùm permittit, hominem tradendo Satanæ, quod ipsum non facit ex absoluto odio, sed ex justo iudicio quo contumaciam hominum iure ulciscitur. Nisi isti spontanea malitia Deo repugnassent, omniaque salutis media prius reiecissent, nunquam eos desereret Deus aut Satanæ arbitrio permitteret. Hi ergò sunt quatuor illi actus antecedentes, quorum duo priores spectāt ad voluntatem antecedentem, quæ est misericordiæ, posteriores ad consequentem, quæ est iustitiæ.

XI. CONCOMITANTIVM vicissim quatuor numeramus.

1. Est permissio. Nam si Deus extraordinariè operari vellet, hominum quidem voluntates inflectere vnoque momento penitùs immutare posset, veluti Paulum in medio furore existentem miraculosè conuertit: sed quia nemini quicquam debet, & nulli denegat ordinaria media, quæ ad salutein sufficiunt; hinc si ista respuantur, iusto iudicio homines labi, semetipsos indurare & à diabolo captiuari permittit. De quo loquuntur sequentia dicta Ps. 81. vers. 13. Osee 4. v. 14. Zach 8. v. 10. Act. 14. vers. 16 Hæc autem permissio non omninò simplex est, sed coniuncta, 1 cùm omnipotentia diuina. Posset n. Deus impedire si vellet: quâ ratione permissio diuina multum differt ab humana, quę propter impotentiam & violentiam sæpè coactio magis est quàm permissio. 2. cum voluntate Dei, non quidem efficiendi, sed permittendi, atque sic non volens peccatum, volens tamẽ permittit. Notandum insuper, quòd duplex sit permissio; vna, quâ Deus hominem permittit peccare, altera, quæ permittit in peccato perseuerare: illa permissio simplex, hæc induratio, excæcatio nominatur. Sicut ergò Deus dicit facere errare, cùm tamen id solùm simplice permissione permittat; ita dicitur, indurare, quando homines in peccato perseuerare permittit.

2. Peccati detestatio. Quamuis enim Deus indurationem permittat, non tamen adprobat. sed in ipso actu odit & detestatur, tanquam peccatum grauissimum, voluntati legique suę contrarium. Vult quidem, in quantum pœna est, seu quatenus peccatorem ob præcedentia delicta, magis magisque reum facit æternæ damnationis; non autem vult absolutè, & prout culpa est, lege prohibita, quia sic Deus sibi contradiceret.

3. Tolerantia peccatoris. Non statim ad pœnam trahit induratum: nec protinus hinc auocat. quod tamen ipsi facillimum esset: sed tolerat magna patientiâ. Rom. 9. v. 22. quia non vult aliquem perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reuerti, 2. Petr. 3. v. 9. Hæc enim est illa Dei benignitas & longanimitas, quâ ad μετάνοιαν addūcit, Rom. 3. v. 4. quam cùm indurati negligunt, thesaurizant sibi iram in die iræ & reuelationis iusti iudicij Dei. v. 5. Atque huc respexit Apostolus Rom. 8. v. 17. cùm Scripturam de Pharaone adfirmare dicit, εἰς αὐτὸ τῦτο ἐξήγειρά σε: In hoc ipsum excitaui, vel potiùs seruaui te, vt ostendam virtutem meam. Nam verba illa de sumpta sunt ex cap. 9. Exod. vers. 16. vbi sic legitur: Et profectò propter hoc העמדתיך vt videre te faciâ patientiâ meam. Ariæ mont. autem istud vertit, Feci restare. 70 διετηρήθης ἕνεκα τού- του, Conservatus es vsque ad hoc tempus. Tremel. & Iunius, Feci vt restares. Non ergò denotatur cooperatio aliqua Dei ad indurationem, vt peccatum est, sed tantùm conservatio peccatoris, vt sensus sit: Cùm meritus fuisses, vt statim vel terrâ absorbereris, vel igne cælitus consumereris, animalia tua occidi, te verò feci subsistere, magnaq; lenitate tuam tyrannidem tuli, non quòd scelera tua adprobarem, sed cùm insanabilis esses, vt ostenderem in tuo casu & exitio iram atque potentiam meam.

2. Cohibitio, vel metarum præscriptio. Non enim sinit Deus diabolum & malos homines liberè grassari, sed certos ponit limites extra quos vagari nequeunt. Apparet hoc iterum ex historia Pharaonis. Tot plagis adfectus erat à Mose & Aarone, non tamen illos è medio sustulit, id quod maximi miraculi loco habendum. Erat ipse atrox & crudelis: Erant Moses & Aaron sub eius potestate: Nil cogitabat, quàm Israëlitarum perniciem: videbat hos viros eductionem populi meditari: Expertus erat tot infortunia, quæ Dominus per Mosen immiserat, neque tamen legitur, quòd istis Dei legatis manus intulerit, aut in carcerem abiecerit, vel simile quicquâ tentauerit. Vnde verò hoc? A Domino factum est, qui Pharaonem in medio furore cohibuit, ne sæuiret in seruos suos. Deus posuit circulum in naribus eius, & frænum in labijs, sicuti legitur de Sennacherib. Esai. 37. v. 29. Atque ita semper contingit, vt Deus non sit otiosus spectator, sed metas præscribat, induratos cohibeat, & tyrannis capistrum inijciat, ne Ecclesiam planè diruant aut deuastent.

XII. CONSEQUENTIVM tantùm duo sunt.

2. Finis gubernatio. Nihil enim tàm malum, q̄ Deus pro infinita sua sapientia & potentia non soleat dirigere ad bonum, quod & partim Ecclesiæ commodum; partim gloriæ suæ illustratio. Non enim sineret bonus fieri malè, nisi omnipotens de malo possit facere benè, August. in Enchir. cap. 100. Deus licet author non sit malarum cogitationum, ordinator tamen est malarum voluntatum, & de malo opere, cuiuslibet non desinit ipse bonum operari; Fulgentius libro 1. ad Mon. p. 55.

2. Actualis pœna, quâ punit induratos. Posteaquam enim sat diu illos tolerauit, nec vlla resipiscentiæ spes est reliqua : tandem ex iusto iudicio ad pœnam vocat, & partim horrendo mortis genere punit quoad corpus, partim infernalibus flammis addicit, quoad animam, vti vicissim Pharaonis in mari rubro submersi exemplum satis luculenter confirmat.

XIII. Et hi sunt isti duodecim actus Dei, circa indurationis peccatum conspicui, ex quibus duo πορίσματα fluunt. 1. Deum non esse otiosum spectatorem. 2. Nec esse ipsius indurationis autorem. Omnes enim isti etiã actus taliter sunt comparati, vt nullam efficientiam ex parte Dei indicent, sed potiùs displicentiam & odium, quo tum peccatum, tum peccatorem prosequitur.

XIV. Hoc verò vnum nunc expediendum restat; Cur Scriptura verbis actiuis vtatur, Deusque indurare & excæcare dicatur, si non actu ipse indurat, nec efficienter ad indurationem cooperatur? Hîc succurrit illa Grammaticorum regula ex perpetuo Scripturæ vsu deducta, quòd verba actiua non semper efficacem operationem, sed vel permissionem, vel occasionem, vel declarationem, vel alium quendam respectum & concursum significent. Exempla benè multa produximus in Phil. Sob. quæst. Gram. 4. p. 397. & 398. vbi videantur.

XV. Quoniam ergo tota fidei analogia labefactatur, si Deus indurationem efficienter oparari statuatur, hinc verba indurandi non actiuè, sed alio modo exponenda esse concludimus. Sunt autem istorum siue modorum siue respectuum, quibus Deus indurare dicitur, sex potissimum.

Nam 1. indurat ἀποφατικῶς vel negatiuè, quando non tollit. Sæpè enim verba & nomina affirmantia ponuntur pro contrarijs negatis. Sic odisse nonnunquam idem est, quod non adprobare, non amplecti. Amare vitam, id est, eam non exponere periculis pro Evangelio. Hoc sensu Deus indurare & excæcare dicitur, quando contrarium negatur, hoc est, quando nec emollit, nec illuminat. Innuit hoc Augustin. Epist. 105. Non obdurat Deus impertiendo malitiam, sed non impertiendo gratiam, Et lib. de prædest. Sanc. cap. 4. Deus dicitur indurare, quando non mollit, excæcare, quando non illuminat. Vt enim solis ἀπυγία non ἐνέργεια tenebras efficit, sic Dei desertio, non operatio indurat.

2. ἀφαιρετικῶς vel priuatiuè, quando qualemcunque cordis mollitiem antea concessam auffert. Nam quando quis non habet, etiam illo quod habet, priuatur, Matth. 13, vers. 12. c. 25. vers. 29. Vt enim ablato visu, sequitur cæcitas, ita subtractâ Dei gratiâ, sequitur cordis durities: quam ob causam Deus indurare dicitur, non σκληρότητα iniquè immitendo, sed gratiam iustè auferendo cui sigich mox succedit induratio.

3. παραχωρητικῶς vel permissiuè. Actio enim in Scripturis permittenti sæpè attribuitur. Sic viuificare dicuntur, qui homines viuere permittunt, cùm interficere possent. Pari modo Deus indurat hoc est, indurationem permittit. Hinc Theodoretus Pharaonem non diuinâ potentiâ, sed diuinâ patientiâ obdurauit. Aug. serm. 88. declarat exemplo seruorum, quos fieri permissio & indulgentia dicitur corrupisse. Sic Deus indurat indulgendo, benefaciendo & pœnas differendo. Rejicit quidem Lutherus contra Erasmum hanc interpretationem, videlicet si sola Dei tolerantia hominem indurari dicimus, omissis reliquis iudicijs. Talem vero permissionem & tolerantiam nos ipsi non intelligimus, sed cum ea coniungimus reliquas Dei actiones.

4. ὑλικῶς vel obiectiue, quando Deus verbum offert, prodigia ostendit, & sic ad poenitentiam vocat. Hinc enim impij magis magisque indurantur, suo non Dei vitio. Interim tamen ob hoc ipse Deus dicitur indurare, sed planè per accidens, non secus atque lex dicitur operari peccatum, Rom. 7. vers. 8. Sic munera subuertunt justos, Exod. 2 v. 8. & Sol excœcat lippientes, & externum frigus per ἀντιπερίστασιν calorem intendit. Huc spectat illud Pro. 5. vers. 20. Acetum in nitro, qui cantat carmina cordi pessimo. Et hunc indurationis modum accidentalem præcipuè attendit Lutherus in libro contra Erasmum cùm passim scribit, Deum obtulisse verbum, vt Pharao induraretur. Factum hoc omne per accidens, non aliter ac Euangelium dicitur odor mortis. 2. Cor. 6. vers. 16. Quod verò hoc non nisi per accidens fiat, patet inde, quia per illud ipsum verbum, quo nonnulli excœcantur, alij conuertuntur, vti constat exemplo Ægyptiorum & Iudæorum, quorum illi per conciones Mosis indurabantur, hi ædificabantur.

5. Μετωνυμικῶς vel declaratiuè. Verba enim Actiua crebrò non rei effectionem, sed effectæ ostensionem indicant. Sic Ieremias c. 1. vers 10. gentes dissipat, quando dissipandas esse prænunciat: Sic ex operibus justificamur, Iac. 2. vers. 24. hoc est justificati declaramur. Pari modo Deus indurauit Pharaonem, id est multis prodigijs ostendit, cor eius extremè impium & penitus induratum esse.

6. Διατακτικῶς vel directiuè. Quamuis enim Deus indurationem nec velit, nec efficiat, quia tamen circa illam operatur, metas præscribendo, & ad commodum Ecclesiæ, suæque glorię ostensionem dirigendo, eam ob causam ipsa induratio Deo attribuitur. Sed de his omnibus fusè disserui in Phil. Sob. quæst. dicta, & in scholis Academicis disput. 3. th. 69. vsque ad thesin 108. quò lectorem breuitatis causà remittimus, ne alibi actum hîc otiosè & tædiosè iterùm agamus.


### Question VII. and last. In what sense is God said to harden?: To God Alone Glory

To God Alone Glory

Latin:

Soli Deo Gloria


## 11 Disputation X. On the Sin Against the Holy Spirit


### Proem

Presiding: Balth. Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Michaël Czayka of Nová Lhota, Pannonian.

Prooemium. I.

After the primary questions which are accustomed to be raised concerning the state of corruption have been dispatched, there remains the final one concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is the most grievous of all actual sins, and is not forgiven in eternity, whence it is called irremissible.

II. Many, however, think that one ought not to speak or dispute at all about this sin, for the reason that a cause for despair can easily be taken from it. for when the infirm hear that it is altogether irremissible, and that it is forgiven neither in this world nor in the world to come, then they are tempted by the Devil, and as if they themselves had committed such a thing, they could, if not altogether despair of their salvation and all hope of pardon, at least doubt it very much. It seems better, therefore, if it be wrapped in perpetual silence, than that many things be said and written about it.

III. But by this reasoning it is written to the Holy Spirit himself. For if every mention of that sin were harmful, God would certainly have ill-advised his faithful when he mentions in the Scriptures several times the blasphemy that is not to be forgiven. But because all Scripture is useful, 2 Tim. 3. 16, and what is written is written for our instruction, Rom. 15. verse 4, therefore this very article about the sin against the Holy Spirit will also be useful and not alien to doctrine, since it is written and proposed by Christ himself and the Apostles. Matt. 12, Mark 3, Luke 12, Tit. 3, Heb. 6 & 10, John 5. Since therefore the command is universal, Search the Scriptures, John 5. v. 39, for that reason those things also which speak of this special sin ought to be considered. For as hidden things ought not to be searched out, so things made manifest ought not to be altogether ignored.

IV. But if some are offended, it is necessary to distinguish between scandal given and taken, between that which happens per se and that which happens per accidens. For the stumbling block is not given, but taken from this; it does not follow per se from the doctrine itself, but is introduced per accidens by the malice of the devil. Therefore, in order that we may firmly resist this, and powerfully snatch ourselves away, it is necessary to know accurately and have a clear understanding of the nature of that sin. For thus we shall see that its essential requirements are lacking as far as we are concerned, we shall be able to conclude invincibly that we are not guilty of it, and therefore why should we despair of pardon and our salvation? But he who is ignorant of the nature of this crime can easily be deceived, and cast by the devil into despair.

V. Four problems concerning this head of doctrine are usually moved most especially: 1. Whether there is a certain sin against the Holy Spirit? 2. What it is? 3. What kind it is? & 4. How many-fold it is, or what species it has? Concerning all of which, according to the reason of our institution, we shall treat briefly.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisner. S S. Th. D.

Resp. Michaële Czayka Novilihoteno Pannonio.

Προοίμιον. I.

POst expeditas quæstiones primarias, quæ circa statum corruptionis moueri solent, restat vltima de peccato in Spiritum sanctum, quod omnium actualium est grauissimum, & in æternum non remittitur, vnde irremissibile vocatur.

II. Multi verò existimant, omninò non esse loquendū aut disputandum de hoc peccato, eò quòd exinde desperationis causa facilè sumi possit. Quādo n. audiut infirmi, illud esse prorsus irremissibile, & nec in hoc, nec in futuro seculo dimitti, tum tententur à Diabolo, ac si & ipsi tale quid commisissent, de salute sua, omnique spe veniae si non omninò desperent, attamen plurimùm dubitare possent. Videri proinde melius, si silentio perpetuo inuoluatur, quàm vt multa de eo dicantur & scribantur.

III. Verùm hac ratione dica scribitur ipsi Spiritui sancto. Si enim noxia foret omnis peccati istius mentio, Deus vtique malè consuluisset fidelibus suis dum in Scripturis aliquoties blasphemiae non remittendae meminit. Quia verò omnis Scriptura est vtilis, 2 Tim. 3. 16. & quod scriptum ad nostram doctrinam scriptum est, Rom. 15. vers. 4. ergò vtilis quoque nec à doctrina alienus erit hic ipse de peccato in Spiritum sanctum articulus quoniam scriptus est, & ab ipso Christo, Apostolisque propositus. Matth 12. Marc. 3. Luc. 12. Tit. 3. Hebr. 6 & 10 Ioh 5. Cùm igitur vniuersale sit mandatum, Scrutamini Scripturas, Ioh. 5. v. 39. propterea & ista, quae de speciali hoc peccato loquuntur considerari debent. Vt n. abscondita non oportet scrutari, sic patefacta non oportet omninò ignorare.

IV. Quòd si autem quidam offendantur, distingui oportet inter scandalum datum & acceptum, inter id quod perse, & quod per accidens obtingit. Non enim datur, sed sumitur hinc offendiculum; non perse ex ipsa doctrina sequitur, sed per accidens malitiâ diaboli introducitur. Huic ergo vt resistamus firmiter, & nosmet ipsos eripiamus potenter, necessarium est, accuratè naturam istius peccati cognoscere & perspectam habere. Sic enim viderimus deficere quoad nos essentialia eius requisita, inuictè poterimus inferre reos nos illius haut esse, ideoque de venia & salute nostra cur desperemus? Qui verò ignorat flagitij huius naturam, is facilè potest decipi, à diabolo in desperationem conjici.

V. Quatuor autem problemata circa hoc doctrinæ caput potissimum moueri solent, 1. An sit quoddam peccatum in Spiritum sanctum? 2 Quid sit? 3. Quale sit? & 4. Quotruplex sit, vel quas species habeat? De quibus omnibus; pro ratione instituti nostri, breuiter agemus.


### Question I. Whether there is and exists a certain special sin against the Holy Spirit?

Whether there is and exists a certain special sin against the Holy Spirit?

I. It is beyond controversy that, in a general way, all sins are in or against the Holy Spirit. For whose commandment is violated, against him is the sin committed. Now, indeed, transgressors violate the law prescribed by the whole Trinity. Therefore they sin against the whole Trinity, and thus also against the third person of the Trinity, namely the Holy Spirit: But that which is called into doubt is this. Whether in some special way there is and exists some sin directed uniquely in or against the Holy Spirit?

II. It is indeed a rule of theologians: That the works of the Trinity ad extra are common: & whatever is said of one person; the same also ought to be said of another person; whence some conclude that there cannot exist a sin which is only against the Holy Spirit, and not at the same time against the Father and the Son, since in this way the unity and identity of actions in the Trinity would be undermined.

III. But here it must be known that the order between the persons of the Trinity is preserved, and that they are distinguished not only by internal characters, but also by certain external marks & actions, so that although for a certain work all persons concur, yet it is not predicated of all of them equally, but only of one, which manifested itself most especially in that work. As for example, the whole Trinity created the world, the whole redeemed the human race, the whole gathers and sanctifies the Church: Nevertheless, such an order and distinction is observed among the persons in the Apostolic Creed, that the Father is said to be most especially the creator, the Son the redeemer, and the Holy Spirit the teacher, leader, and sanctifier of the Church. In like manner, this special blasphemy indeed harms the whole Trinity, yet it is said to be directed most especially against the Holy Spirit, because it is primarily directed against his sanctification, which is ascribed to him as his proper work.

IV. That such a sin specially opposed to the Holy Spirit is given, must furthermore be proved from the Scriptures. Wherefore we shall collect all the testimonies whatsoever that are found in the sacred writings concerning this sin. These are the principal ones of them.

V. 1: Matt. 12, v. 30 & 31. Every sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men, ἡ δὲ τῦ πνεύματος βλασφη- μία shall not be forgiven. And whosoever shall speak a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ἔιπη κατὰ τῶ πνεύμα- τος τῷ ἁγίε, ὀκ ἀφεθήσεται αὐτῷ neither in this world, nor in the world to come. From this saying it appears manifestly that there is given a certain sin specially harming and offending the Holy Spirit, on account of a triple opposition.

VI. For 1. it opposes common blasphemy and βλασφημίαν τῶ πνεύματος, which opposition and distinction would not have a place, unless a special sin against the Holy Spirit were given. For just as common βλασ- φημία is said to be against the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, so βλασφημίαν τῶ πνεύματος is to be thought to be directed not otherwise than primarily against the Holy Spirit. For how else would it be called the βλασφημία of the τῶ πνεύματος alone?

VII. 2. He makes a distinction between sins κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου and sins κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου. Just as, therefore, a sin against the Son is not immediately a sin against the Holy Spirit: so also a sin against the Spirit will not at the same time be against the Son. There is, therefore, a blasphemy which is not brought and directed against the Father and the Son, but in a special way against the Holy Spirit alone.

IIX. Moreover, the reason for the distinction between sins against the Son and the Holy Spirit is to be noted here, which consists chiefly in this, that he is said to sin against the Son who indeed blasphemes and persecutes the saving doctrine concerning Christ, either regarding his person or his office, but out of ignorance and preposterous zeal, and therefore is said to offend against the Son, but not against the Spirit, because he does not entirely reject the means of salvation and conversion, but if he is instructed, he allows himself to be led and converted by the Holy Spirit, and does not resist; and therefore he can obtain the remission of sins.

IX. An example of one sinning against the Son is Paul, who before his conversion attacked the Gospel concerning Christ in all ways and quite hostilely: yet when afterwards the Gospel was preached to him, both by God and by Ananias, a minister of the Holy Spirit, he did not resist, but received it, and was converted: and therefore he is said to have sinned before not against the Spirit and out of malice, but against the Son and out of ignorance, as he writes about himself, 1 Tim. 1, verse 13.

X. There are therefore two principal conditions of sin against the Son. 1. It is blasphemy and hostile attack on the doctrine concerning Christ, and 2. It proceeds from ignorance and zeal without knowledge, but not from malice, nor does it presuppose the acknowledgment of the truth. The former is common to sins against the Son with the sin against the Spirit: the latter with sins arising from infirmity. By reason of the latter, therefore, it differs from other sins, and agrees with the sin against Spirit: by reason of this, it differs from blasphemy against the Spirit, and agrees with other sins. For that βλασφημία is indeed likewise an opposition to the doctrine concerning Christ, but one that is acknowledged, and of whose truth someone is convinced in his own conscience, which he also blasphemes not out of ignorance but with full knowledge of the mind; not out of infirmity, but with contumacious malice of the will, as will be declared more fully in question 2.

XI. 3. The Savior established such a difference, that other sins are forgiven, but this one will not be forgiven: whence an invincible argument arises, and it is indeed such: An irremissible sin is something else and must necessarily be distinguished from remissible sins. But the sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible, while all others, as Christ says, are remissible: Therefore the sin against the Spirit is something else and must necessarily be distinguished from remissible sins, ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι.

XII. II. Mark 3. v. 30. 31: Truly I say to you that all sins will be forgiven to the sons of men, and blasphemies, with which they have blasphemed. He who has blasphemed against the Holy Spirit has no forgiveness forever; but will be guilty of eternal judgment. Here in turn a distinction is made between the general βλασφημία of the whole Trinity, and the special βλασφημία of the Holy Spirit; or against the Holy Spirit.

XIII. III. Luke 12. v. 10. Everyone who speaks a word against the Son of man, it will be forgiven him: but he who has blasphemed the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven. From this saying the same arguments are deduced which we have just now mentioned from Matt. 12.

XIV. IV. Heb. 6. v. 4. 5. 6. It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted also the heavenly gift; and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit; and have tasted the good word of God, and the mighty works of the world to come, and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance, again crucifying to themselves the Son of God; and putting him to an open shame. From this text the Novatians took the occasion of their error, teaching that all those who, for fear of persecutions, especially after having received Baptism, have denied the doctrine concerning Christ, can no longer obtain any pardon or remission for their sin, even if they seriously lament it and desire to perform true repentance.

XV. But if the individual circumstances are weighed more diligently, it will be clearly evident that the Apostle is not speaking of any denial whatsoever, but of a malicious and blasphemous one, joined with final impenitence, that is, of the very and sole sin against the Holy Spirit.

For 1. from the beginning of the chapter he speaks about the principal articles of faith and warns the Hebrews to persevere firmly in them; since he explains this admonition by its contrary in the following verses, it is gathered from this that he is speaking of a true and interior apostasy from the faith: but those who merely deny the faith out of fear of dangers, such as persecution, do not immediately fall away from the faith, because they can retain it in their heart, even if they deny it with their mouth.

2. He says that they were previously enlightened, and tasted the heavenly gift, and were thus truly renewed, and afterwards fall away, that is, become blind and contumacious: for he opposes falling away to enlightenment and tasting. But this cannot be said of those who deny the faith in a time of persecution, since they do not fall away in such a way that they lose all faith entirely and become completely blind.

3: He says it is impossible for them to be renewed to repentance. But many who have denied the faith have been renewed, as the example of Peter and others teaches. From all of which it is concluded that the Apostle is speaking of a special sin, namely, of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

XVI. V. Heb. 10. v. 26. ἑκουσίως ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν μετὰ τὸ λαβεῖν τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας ὀυκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρ- τιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία: If we sin willfully after having received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,

And v. 29. He deserves worse punishments who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, and has considered the blood of the Testament unclean, in which he was sanctified, and has done despite to the Spirit of grace. That this passage also is to be understood only of the sin against the Holy Spirit is proven by: 1. The scope of the Apostle, since he is entirely concerned with dissuading the Hebrews from apostasy from the truth. 2. Because he speaks of a voluntary abnegation of the doctrine previously acknowledged, and not one done out of fear. 3. He distinguishes it from all other sins by singular marks, while he opposes it to the law of Moses, while he calls it a trampling of the Son, a profanation of the blood of the Testament, a despite to the Holy Spirit, from all of which it is gathered most clearly that there is talk here of a peculiar sin, since these marks and προσκείμενα are found neither in fearful abnegation nor in other crimes.

XVII. VI. 1 John 5. v. 16. ἔστιν ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, ὀυ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ, There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should pray for that. By this saying, a distinction of sins is indicated, while some are said to be not unto death, but a certain one in particular is said to be a sin unto death. Then he says that for some who are sinning one should pray, but for others not likewise, from which it is firmly gathered that there is given a certain special ἁμαρτία, which κατ' ἐξοχήν is mortal, deadly, and therefore irremissible, which we say is the βλασφημία of the Holy Spirit.

XIX. And these are the principal sayings speaking of this sin: Two others can be added. 1. From Acts 7. v. 51. Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart, you always resist the Holy Spirit. Here is noted the rejection of means, and resistance against the Spirit, which likewise is not repeated except in this special sin. 2. From Titus 3. v. 10, 11. Avoid a heretical man after one or two admonitions, knowing that he is αυτοκατάκριτος. To this also pertains that 1 Timothy 4. verse 2. In the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to spirits of error and doctrines of devils speaking in hypocrisy of liars, and having their own conscience seared. By the cauterizing of the conscience is denoted either the hardening of the heart, because flesh marked with a cautery is hardened; or perversity and malice, because those upon whom a stigma is branded are held as infamous. All the sayings which speak of the hardened may also be referred here: Isa. 48. ver. 4, Jer. 5. ver. 3, Zech. 7. ver. 11, Matt. 13. v. 15, John 12. v. 40, Rom. 1. v. 25, ch. 2. v. 5, ch. 11. v. 8, Eph. 4. v. 19, etc.

XIX. From these testimonies of Scripture, however, such a most firm argument can be woven: Whatever Scripture specifically names as a sin, or blasphemy of the Spirit, in such a way that it circumscribes it with singular marks, that is a peculiar species, and ought to be distinguished from all others. But such is the sin against the Holy Spirit, as has been proven thus far. Therefore it is a peculiar species of sin, and ought to be distinguished from all others, which was to be demonstrated.

Latin:

An sit & detur quoddam speciale peccatum in Spiritum sanctum?

I. Extrà controuersiam est, generali modo omnia peccata esse in vel contra Spiritum sanctum. Cujus enim mandatum violatur, in illum peccatur. Iam verò delinquentes violant legem, à tota Trinitate præscriptam. Ergo peccant in totam Trinitatem, atque sic quoque in tertiam Trinitatis personam, nempè Spiritum sanctum: Istud vero est, quod in dubium vocatur. Num speciali quadam ratione sit & detur peccatum aliquod; vnice in vel contra Spiritum sanctum directum?

II. Theologorum quidem regula est: Quòd ope ra Trinitatis ad extra sint communia: & quicquid dicatur de persona vna; idem quoque dici debere de persona altera; vnde concludunt nonnulli, dari non posse peccatum, quod tantùm sit in Spiritum sanctum, & non vnà in Patrem & Filium, quoniam hoc modo vnitas & identitas actionum in Trinitate labefactetur.

III. Verùm hic sciendum est seruari ordinem inter personas Trinitatis, easq́; non tantum internis characteribus, sed etiam externis quibusdam notis & actionibus distingui, ita vt licet ad opus quoddam omnespersonæ concurrant, non tamen de omnibus ex æquo istud prædicetur, sed duntaxat de vnâ, quæ potissimum opere isto sese manifestauit. Vt exempli causâ, Tota Trinitas creauit mundum, tota redemit genus humanum, tota colligit & sanctificat Ecclesiam: Nihilominus tamen talis ordo & distinctio obseruatur inter personas in symbolo Apostolico, vt Pater potissimùm creator, Filius redemptor, & Spiritus Sanctus, Ecclesiæ doctor, ductor & sanctificator dicatur. Pari modo blasphemia ista specialis totam quidem lædit Trinitatem, attamen in Spiritum Sanctum potissimum ferri dicitur, quoniam contra sanctificationem eius, quæ illi vt proprium opus adscribitur, primariò dirigitur.

IV. Tale ergo Spiritui sancto specialiter oppositum peccatum dari, ex Scripturis porrò probandum est. Quare omnia testimonia colligemus, quæcunq́; in sacris literis hoc de peccato reperiuntur. Illorum hæc sunt præcipua.

V. 1: Matth. 12. v. 30. & 31. Omne peccatum & blasphemia remittetur hominibus ἡ δὲ τῦ πνεύματος βλασφημία non remittetur. Et quicunq́ue dixerit verbum contrà Filium hominis, remittetur ei: ὃς δ᾽ ἂν ἔιπη κατὰ τῶ πνεύματος τῷ ἁγίε, ὀκ ἀφεθήσεται αὐτῷ neque in hoc seculo, neque in futuro. Ex hoc dicto apparet manifestè, dari quoddam peccatum specialiter Spiritum Sanctum lædens & offendens, ob triplicem oppositionem.

VI. Nam 1. opponit blasphemiam communem & βλασφημίαν τῶ πνεύματος, quæ oppositio & distinctio locum non haberet, nisi speciale contra Spiritum sanctum daretur peccatum. Sicut enim βλασφημία communis esse dicitur in Patrem, Filium, sanctumque Spiritum, ita βλασφημίαν τῶ πνεύματος non nisi in Spiritum sanctum πρώτως ferri putandum est. Quomodo enim aliàs solius τῶ πνεύματος βλασφημία diceretur?

VII. 2. Discrimen facit inter peccata κατὰ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου & peccata κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ ἁγίου. Sicut ergo peccatum in Filium non statim est peccatum in Spiritum sanctum: sic quoque peccatum in Spiritum, non vnà erit in Filium. Datur igitur blasphemia, quæ non in Patrem Filiumque sed speciali ratione in solum Spiritum sanctum adfertur & dirigitur.

IIX. Notanda autem hîc est ratio discriminis inter peccata in Filium & Spiritum sanctum, quæ in eo potissimùm consistit, quòd in Filium peccare dicatur, qui quidem salutificam de Christo doctrinam, vel quoad personam, vel quoad officiū eius blasphemat, & persequitur, sed ex ignorantia & zelo præpostero, ideoque in Filium delinquere dicitur, sed non in Spiritum, quia media salutis & conuersionis prorsus non abijcit, sed si erudiatur, à Spiritu sancto seduci & conuerti sinit, nec reluctatur; ideoque remissionem peccatorum consequi potest.

IX. Exemplum peccantis in Filium Paulus est, qui ante conuersionem modis quidem omnibus & planè hostiliter impugnabat Euangelium de Christo: cùm tamen postmodum ipsi, & à Deo & ab Anania Spiritus Sancti ministro, prædicaretur Euangelium, non resistebat, sed suscipiebat illud, & conuertebatur: ideoque antè non in Spiritum & ex malitia sed in Filium, & ex ignorantia peccâsse dicitur, vti de se metipso scribit, 1. Tim. 1. vers. 13.

X. Duo igitur sunt principalia peccati in Filium προσκείμενα. 1. Est blasphemia & hostilis impugnatio doctrinæ de Christo, & 2. Proficiscitur ex ignorantia, & zelo sine scientia, non autem ex malitia, nec præsupponit veritatis agnitionem. Illud peccatis in Filium commune est cum peccato in Spiritum: hoc cum peccatis ex infirmitate subortis. Ratione igitur istius differt ab alijs peccatis, & conuenit cum peccato in Spiritum: ratione huius, differt a blasphemia in Spiritum, & conuenit cum peccatis alijs. Illa enim βλασφημία similiter quidem oppugnatio est doctrihæ de Christo, sed agnitæ, & de cuius veritate aliquis in conscientia sua conuictus est, quam etiam blasphemat non ex ignorantia sed plena scientia mentis; non ex infirmitate, sed contumaci malitia voluntatis, vti quæst. 2. fusius declarabitur.

XI. 3. Saluator eiusmodi differentiam constituit, quod alia peccata remittantur, hoc autem non remittetur: vnde argumentum inuictum oritur & is stud quidem tale: Peccatum irremissibile, aliud est & necessario distinguendu a remissibilibus peccatis. Atqui peccatum in Spiritum sanctum est irremissibile, cætera omnia dicente Christo, sunt remissibilia: Ergo peccatum in Spiritum aliud est & necessario distinguendum a peccatis remissibilibus, ὅπερ ἔδει δεῖξαι.

XII. II. Marci 3. v. 30. 31: Amen dico vobis quoniam omnia dimittentur filijs hominum peccata, & blasphemiæ, quibus blasphemauerint. Qui blasphemauerit in spiritSpiritum sanctum, non habet remissionem in æternum; sed reus erit æterni iudicij. Hic vicissim fit discrimen inter βλασφημίαν generalem totius Trinitatis, & βλασφημίαν specialem Spiritus sancti; vel in Spiritum sanctum.

XIII. III. Luc. 12. v. 10. Omnis, qui dicit verbum in Filium hominis, remittetur ei: qui autem Spiritum sanctum blasphemauerit, non remittetur. Ex hoc dicto eadem deducuntur argumenta, quæ ex Matth. 12. iam modo commemorauimus.

XIV. IV. Hebr. 6. v. 4 5. 6. Impossibile est eos, qui semel sunt illuminati, & gustauerunt etiam donum cœleste; & participes facti sunt Spiritus sancti; & gustauerunt bonum Dei verbum, virtutesque venturi seculi, & prolapsi sunt, rursus renouari ad pœnitentiam, rursum crucifigentes sibimetipsis Filium Dei; & ostentui habentes. Ex hoc textu erroris sui occasionem sumpserunt Nouasiani; docentes, omnes eos, qui doctrinam de Christo, metu persecutionum, præsertim post acceptum Baptisma abnegarunt, peccati sui nullam amplius veniam aut remissionem consequi posse, etiam si seriò istud deplorent, veramque poenitentiam agere desiderent.

XV. Verùm si singulæ diligentiùs expendantur circumstantiæ, patebit luculenter Apostolum non de quavis abnegatione, sed de malitiosa blasphemâque, cùm impoenitentia finali coniuncta, hoc est, de ipso & solo peccato in Spiritum sanctum loqui.

Etenim 1. ab initio capitis verba facit de præcipuis fidei articulis monetque Hebræos, vt in ijs firmiter perseuerent, quam admonitionem cùm contrario declaret in sequentibus, colligitur exinde, ipsum de vera & interiore Apostasia à fide verba facere: Qui autem duntaxat metu periculorum vt persecutione fidem abnegant, non statim resiliunt à fide, quia corde eam possunt retinere, licet ore diffiteantur.

2. Dicit, quòd priùs fuerint illuminati, & gustauerint donum cœleste, adeoque verè renouati fuerint, & postmodum prolabantur, id est, fiant cæci & contumaces: Prolapsionem enim opponit illuminationi & gustui. Hoc autem dici nequit de abnegatoribus, tempore persecutionis, quandoquidem illi non ita prolabuntur, vt omnem omninò fidem amittant, & prorsus cæci fiant.

3: Ait impossibile esse eos renouari ad pœnitentiam. At verò multi abnegatores sunt renouati, quod exemplũ docet Petri & aliorum. Ex quibus omnibus concluditur, quòd de speciali peccato loquatur Apostolº, nempè de blasphemia in Spiritũ sanctum.

XVI. V. Hebr. 10. v. 26. ἑκουσίως ἁμαρτανόντων ἡμῶν μετὰ τὸ λαβεῖν τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας ὀυκ ἔτι περὶ ἁμαρτιῶν ἀπολείπεται θυσία: Voluntariè peccantibus post acceptam notitiam veritatis, iam non relinquitur pro peccatis hostia,

Et v. 29. Deteriora meretur suppl cia qui Filium Dei conculcauerit, & sanguinem Testamenti pollutum duxerit in quo sanctificatus est, & Spiritui gratiae contumeliam fecerit. Quem etiam locum de solo in Spiritum sanctum peccato intelligendum esse, euincit 1. Scopus Apostoli, quandoquidem totus in eo est, vt ab apostasia veritatis dehortetur Hebraeos. 2: quia loquitur de voluntaria, & no ex metu facta doctrinae prius agnitae abnegatione. 3. singularibus notis secernit ab omnibus alijs peccatis, dum legi Mosis opponit, dum vocat conculcationem Filij, profanationem sanguinis Testamenti, contumeliam Spiritus sancti, ex quibus omnibus colligitur apertissime, de peculiari peccato hic sermonem fieri, quoniam istae notae & προσκείμενα nec in abnegatione meticulosa, nec in alijs criminibus reperiuntur.

XVII. VI. 1. Ioh. 5. v. 16. ἔστιν ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, ὀυ περὶ ἐκείνης λέγω ἵνα ἐρωτήσῃ, Est peccatum ad mortem; Non pro illo dico, vt roget quis. Duplex hoc di- &to discrimen peccatorum indicatur, dum alia dicuntur esse non ad mortem, quoddam autem in specie dicitur esse peccatum ad mortem. Deinde ait, quod pro nonnullis peccantibus sit orandum; pro nonnullis autem non item, vnde firmiter colligitur, dari quandam ἁμαρτίαν specialem, quae κατ' ἐξοχήν sit mortalis, lethifera, ideoq; irremissibile qua nos dicim' esse βλασφημίαν Spiritus sancti.

XIX. Et haec sunt principalia dicta, de peccato isto loquentia: Addi possunt alia duo. 1. Ex Act. 7. v. 50. Dura ceruice & incircumcisis cordibus, Vos semper resistitis Spiritui sancto. Hic notatur abiectio mediorum, & resistentia aduersus Spiritum, quae itidem no nisi in hoc speciali peccato repetitur. 2: Ex Tit. 3. v. 10. 11. Haereticum hominem post vnam atque alteram admonitionem deuita, sciens quod sit αυτοκατάκριτος. Pertinet huc etiam illud 1. Timot. 4. vers. 2. Nouissimis temporibus discedent quida a fide, attendentes spiritibus errois & doctrinis daemoniorum in hypocrisi loquentium mordacium, & κεκαυτηριασμένων τὴν ἰδίαν συνείδησιν. Per cauterium verò conscientiæ notatur vel induratio cordis, quia caro cauterio notata, est obdurata; vel perversitas & malitia, quia quibus stigma inuritur, ij pro infamibus habentur. Possunt huc etiam referri omnia dicta, quæ loquuntur de induratis Esa. 48. vers. 4 Ierem. 5. vers. 3 Zach. 7. vers. 11. Matth. 13. v. 15. Ioh. 12. v. 40. Rom. 1. v. 25. c. 2. v. 5. c. 11. v. 8. Eph 4. v. 19. &c.

XIX. Ex hisce verò Scripturæ testimonijs tale argumentum necti potest firmissimum: Quodcunque Scriptura specialiter nominat peccatum, vel blasphemiam Spiritus, ita vt singularibus notis circumscribat, id peculiaris species est, & ab alijs omnibus distingui debet. At verò tale est peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, vti hactenus probatum. Ergò peculiaris peccati species est, & ab alijs omnibus distingui debet, id quod fuit demonstrandum.


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is

What the sin against the Holy Spirit is.

I. The knowledge and description of this sin is difficult. Augustine, in sermon 11 on the words of the Lord, pronounces that God wished to exercise us with the difficulty of the question concerning this sin, since perhaps in all the Scriptures no greater, no more difficult one is found: We judge, however, that its nature will be perceived in some way if one observes 1. its names, 2. its examples, 3. its essential requirements, of which we are now about to speak in order:

I. Concerning the names of this sin.

II. There are four primary appellations of this sin, the reason for which, if it is explained, the nature of the sin itself is in some measure declared, since we are very often led from the use of a word into the perception of the thing.

III. It is named, moreover, 1. commonly from its object.

sin against the Holy Spirit. Not that it is directed against Him by reason of essence, because this is common to the whole Trinity, or by reason of person, since one person of the Trinity cannot be offended without the injury of the sin immediately redounding to the one Deity; but 1. By reason of office. For the Holy Spirit is to illuminate and convert the hearts of men through the Word and Sacraments, which office He even attempts to carry out among these hardened men. But because they spurn, reject, blaspheme, and in all ways resist His grace, they are therefore said to sin against the Spirit who attempts to execute His office of illumination in them. 2. By reason of testimony. The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth and bears witness concerning it through the Word and miracles; indeed, in such a way that even the conscience itself of hardened men is convinced; and they know that the doctrine which they deny, blaspheme, and oppose is most true: Because, therefore, they speak against and resist this testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning the truth of the faith against their own conscience, hence in turn they are not undeservedly said to sin and offend against the Spirit Himself. Briefly, therefore, these men are directed against the Holy Spirit's 1. illumination, by resisting; 2. testimony, by denying. There they oppose His office, here His testimony; in both cases they sin gravely against Him.

IV. 2. It is named blasphemy of the Spirit from the act itself, just as it is called in Matthew 12: verse 32, λόγος κατὰ τῦ πνεύματος τῦ ἁγίε, a word against the Holy Spirit. For whoever are liable to this sin do not cease to curse the Spirit and to affect Him with insults insofar as they impugn His doctrine and defame it as a lie. And this is to blaspheme, because that word signifies nothing else than either to detract from God the things that are His and pertain to His glory, or to attribute to Him the things that make for His ignominy.

V. 3. It is called the irremissible sin from its adjunct.

For such is the nature of this sin, that it always has joined to it the hardening and blinding of the heart, and thus also the rejection of all means of salvation, and a perpetual resistance toward the Holy Spirit, on account of which it is impossible that such men be converted and return to repentance, since God does not thrust His grace upon the unwilling and resisting.

VI. 4. From the consequent punishment, namely death and eternal damnation, it is called the sin unto death, ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, 1 John 5:16. For although all sins by their own nature are mortal and lethal, this one is nevertheless said to be specially unto death because not only is the guilt of death found in it, as in all other sins, but also the act itself, the very eternal damnation, follows infallibly. Wherefore it is called the sin unto death not so much by reason of the guilt, as with respect to the infallible damnation. And these have been the Biblical appellations of this sin: I do not append the ecclesiastical ones, since they are few, and if there were any, they could be understood most easily from the notation of the former.

Latin:

Quid sit peccatum in Spiritum sanctum.

I. Difficilis est huius peccati cognitio & descriptio. Augustinus serm. 11. de verbis Domini pronunciat, quòd Deus exercere nos voluerit difficultate quæstionis de hoc peccato, cùm in omnibus Scripturis fortè nulla maior, nulla difficilior inueniatur: Censemus tamen qualitercunq́; perspectā iri eius naturam, si obseruentur 1 illius nomina, 2. Exempla. 3. Essentialia requisita, de quib. nunc ordine dicturi sumus:

I. De nominibus huius peccati.

II. Quatuor sunt primariæ huius peccati appellationes, quarum ratio si exponatur, ipsa peccati natura, quodammodo declaratur, cùm sæpenumero; ex vsu vocis prouehamur in rei perceptionem.

III. Nominatur autē 1. communiter ab obiecto.

peccatu in Spiritum S. Non quod feratur in ipsum ratione essentiæ, quia hæc toti Trinitati communis aut ratione personæ, cùm offendi nequeat vna Trinitatis persona, quin peccati injuria in ipsam vnicam Deitatem statim redundet; sed 1. Ratione officij. Etenim Spiritus. S. est illuminare & conuertere corda hominum per verbum & Sacramenta, quod ipsum etiam officium expedire tentat apud istos induratos homines. Hi autem quia gratiam eius spernunt, abjiciunt; blasphemant, illique modis omnibus resistunt; ideo in Spiritum qui suum illuminationis officium in ijs exequi conatur, peccare dicuntur. 2. Ratione testimonij. Spiritur Sanctus est Spiritus veritatis & de ea testimonium perhibet per verbum & miracula; ita quidem, vt etiam conscientia ipsa induratorum hominum conuincatur; sciantque verissimam esse doctrinam eam, quam abnegant, blasphemant & oppugnant: Quia igitur huic Spiritus sancti de veritate fidei testimonio contra conscientiam propriam obloquuntur & resistunt, hinc vicissim non immerito in ipsum Spiritum peccare & delinquere dicuntur. Breuiter ergò, homines isti feruntur contra Spiritus sancti. 1. illuminationem, resistendo; 2. testificationem, negando. Ibi officium, hîc testimonium eius oppugnant; vtrobique in ipsum grauiter peccant.

IV. 2. Ab ipso actu nominatur βλασφημία Spiritus, velut dicitur Matth: 12: vers: 32. λόγος κατὰ τῦ πνεύματος τῦ ἁγίε. Sermo contra Spiritum sanctum. Quicunqs enim huic peccato sunt obnoxij, nō cessant Spiritui maledicere, & contumelijs afficere quatenus doctrinam ejus impugant, & tanquam mendacium diffamant. Atque hoc est blasphemare, quia vox ista nil significat aliud, quàm Deo vel detrahere, quæ ipsius sunt, & ad eius gloriam spectant; vel attribuere, quæ ad eius ignominiā faciunt.

V. 3. Ab adjuncto appellatur peccatum irremissibile.

Ea enim peccati huius natura est, vt coniunctam semper habeat indurationem & excœcationem cordis, atque sic etiam abiectionem omnium mediorum salutis, & perpetuam erga Spiritum sanctum resistentiam, ob quam impossibile est, vt tales homines conuertantur & ad pœnitentiam redeant, cùm Deus inuitis & repugnantibus suam non obtrudat gratiam.

VI. 4. A consequente pœna certissima, nimirum morte & damnatione æterna vocatur peccatum ad mortem, ἁμαρτία πρὸς θάνατον, 1. Ioh. 5. v. 26. Quamuis enim omnia peccata φύσει suâ sint mortalia & lethifera, hoc tamen specialiter ad mortem esse dicitur quia non tantùm reatus mortis in eo, vt in alijs peccatis omnibus reperitur, verùm etiam actus ipse, ipsa damnatio æterna infallibiliter sequitur Quare non tàm ratione reatus, quàm respectu infallibilis damnationis peccatũ ad mortem nuncupatur. Ethæ fuerunt Biblicæ appellationes huius peccati: Ecclesiasticas non appono, cùm carum sint paucæ, & si quæ fuerint, illæ ex superiorũ notatione intelligi possint quâ facillimè


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is: II. Concerning the examples of this sin

II. Concerning the examples of this sin.

VII. Our theologians warn that one should not rashly pronounce judgment concerning this sin and its examples, and therefore no one ought easily to be accused and charged with it, especially if he is still among the living, since it is not sufficiently certain whether all the requirements for it coincide. Indeed, we ought not to judge even the dead thoughtlessly, since we are ignorant of whether he might have been converted in his death throes and returned to repentance. For which reason we shall not enumerate doubtful and uncertain examples, but only those which are indubitably true and are found in the very sacrosanct code of Scripture. The chief and primary of those are these following.

VIII. I. We bring forward the example of Pharaoh. For although it is not certain that he was devoted to the true worship of God, but rather, as history testifies, an idolater and a gentile, yet with all respect to the judgments of others, he is said not inappropriately to have sinned against the Holy Spirit. For 1. he resisted God not out of infirmity or ignorance, but with full will and out of mere malice, saying, Exod. 5. v. 2. Who is the Lord, that I should obey (that is, I care nothing for, I do not fear. For it must be understood as a practical 'not knowing') I will not let Israel go. 2. He slandered and mocked the miracles of the Lord, while having summoned his sorcerers, Ex. 7. v. 11. he produced things similar in appearance. For by this he wished to show that the God of Israel was not so great, since He could perform no more than his own magicians and enchanters. 3. He knew and was convinced in his conscience that those miracles could not come from any source but God and divine power, since the enchanters themselves said, Exod. 8. v. 19. This is the finger of God. Pharaoh himself also wished that they should pray to the Lord for him, and thus he acknowledged that the punishments had been inflicted by Him, and therefore that He alone could remove them. Exod. 10. v. 16. & 17. he himself says: I have sinned against the Lord your God, and against you; but now forgive my sin to me this once, and pray to the Lord your God, that he may take away. Thus therefore we conclude. Whoever against knowledge and conscience denies an article of faith, sins against the Holy Spirit. Pharaoh did this, because he knew the God of Israel to be the true God from the miracles, and yet maliciously, that is, in words and deeds, he denied it. For the confirmation of the minor premise we add this. He who acknowledges the God of Israel alone to be omnipotent, he acknowledges Him alone to be the true God. But Pharaoh did indeed acknowledge that. Exod. 10. v. 16. 17. For he believed that no one could remove those plagues, and therefore he solicited Moses to intercede with God for him. Although indeed no mention is made that he blasphemed the doctrine of the Israelites, nevertheless there is no doubt about it. For they wished to go out because of the worship of their God. But he knew that this very one was the true God from miracles, and nevertheless he hindered his worship, and without a doubt blasphemed. Furthermore, miracles are appendices of doctrine; therefore, he who blasphemes the miracles of God, he consequently attacks both his word and his doctrine.

And what need is there of many words? He certainly sinned against the Spirit 1. by reason of his office, because he resisted the Spirit wishing to convert him through the word of Moses. 2. by reason of testimony, while he denied the truth of the miracles which he acknowledged against his conscience. For the truth of God is twofold, one of word and doctrine, the other of deed and miracles. Whether one knowingly and willingly blasphemes both or either one, he sins against the Holy Spirit.

IX. 2. The hearers of the Prophet Jeremiah. Concerning these he says in ch. 5, v. 12: They have denied the Lord, and said: It is not he, neither shall evil come upon us. Chapter 7, v. 16: And they said: We have not walked, v. 17: We will not hear. Chapter 7, verse 16, Jeremiah is forbidden to pray for them. Whence we gather that they committed a sin unto death. The words have it thus: Therefore do not pray for this people, nor take up for them supplication and prayer, and do not resist me, for I will not hear you. Chapter 44, verse 16, they say: The word which you have spoken to us in the name of the Lord, we will not hear from you, but we will certainly do every word that shall go out of our mouth, to sacrifice to the queen of heaven. What are all these things other than most certain proofs of sin against the Holy Spirit? They knew that only the worship prescribed by Moses was true; they were convinced in their conscience that Jeremiah was speaking to them in the name of the Lord; and nevertheless they directly resist the Holy Spirit, and with a clear voice say that they do not wish to obey the Lord, and do not wish to follow his doctrine. Therefore they were sinning unto death, and hence the Lord did not wish for them to be prayed for.

X. 3. The Pharisees in the time of Christ, concerning whom Matt. 12, Mark 3, Luke 12. For they not only knew that Christ was from God, as Nicodemus confesses, John 3, v. 2, but also who he was, And you know me, and you know whence I am, he says

Christ, John 7, v. 24. Matthew 22, v. 16, they say: Master, we know that you are truthful, and teach the way of God in truth. And nevertheless, against their conscience and the internal testimony of the Spirit, they did not cease to disparage his divine works, to blaspheme his doctrine, to curse his miracles, and to slander him, saying that he has an unclean spirit and casts out demons by the power of Beelzebub. All of which are infallible signs of the sin against the Holy Spirit, of which matter they are also accused by Christ himself in the aforementioned places of the Gospel history.

XI. 4. The Pharisees and Jews in the time of the Apostles, especially of Stephen, Acts 6, v. 10, it is reported of them that they could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit that was speaking, and thus they acknowledged that the Apostolic doctrine proceeded from God himself; nevertheless, they resisted them, blasphemed, and hostilely persecuted them against their conscience, and therefore Stephen, Acts 7, v. 51, says: You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears: you always resist the Holy Spirit; verse 54 it is said of them that, hearing these things, διεπρίοντο they were cut to the heart, and gnashed their teeth at Stephen.

XII. 5. The apostates of the last time, concerning whom the Apostle Paul prophesied in 2 Timothy 4, 1, following. For it is said of them that 1. they shall depart from the faith. 2. They shall follow the spirit of error and doctrines of demons. 3. They shall speak lies in hypocrisy, and thus against their conscience.

XIII. Others add to these the example of Saul and Judas: but since neither opposed the doctrine or denied it once acknowledged, they do not seem to have sinned against the Holy Spirit. The example of the Emperor Julian is more appropriate. For he was duly instructed in the Christian religion, he knew the truth of the Gospel, which he also publicly professed, having received Baptism; but afterwards, by the persuasion of certain ill-philosophizing men, namely Libanius, Iamblichus, and the like, he defected from Christ and blasphemed the sound doctrine of the Gospel, and persecuted it in every way. XIV. Regarding Francesco Spiera, there is doubt among some: but the answer is straightforward, that he should by no means be considered a sinner against the Holy Spirit, because 1. he fell away to the Papacy not out of malice, but out of infirmity; not of his own accord, but persuaded by friends. 2. He did not attack or blaspheme the doctrine of the Gospel, but grieved deeply that he had fallen away from the truth. His sin was therefore indeed despair, but not blasphemy against the Spirit, since he did not deny the orthodox faith, but always bore witness to the truth of it until his death.

Latin:

II. De Exemplis huius peccati.

VII. Monent nostri Theologi, haut temere esse pronunciandum de hoc peccato, eiusque exemplis, & propterea nemo facilè illius accusari & insimulari debet, præsertim si in viuis adhuc sit, cùm satis non constet, an omnia requisita in eo conueniant. Imò nec post mortem incogitantes iudicare debemus, cùm ignari simus, annon in agone fuerit conuersus, & ad pœnitentiã redierit. Quam ob causam non enumerabimus exempla dubia & incerta, sed ea tantùm, quæ indubitanter vera sunt & in ipso sacrosancto Scripturam codice reperiuntus. Illorum verò præcipua & primaria sunt hæc sequentia.

IIX. I. Proferimus exemplum Pharaonis. Quamvis enim non constet, illum fuisse vero Dei cultui addictum, sed potius, vt historia testatur, idololatram & gentilem, attamen saluis aliorū iudiciis in Spiritū sanctum nō incommodè peccasse dicitur, Nam 1. non ex infirmitate aut ignorantia, sed plena voluntate & ex mera malitia resistebat Deo dicens, Exod. 5. v. 2. Quis est Dominus, vt audiam vocem eius, & dimittam Israel; Nescio Dominum (id est, nihil curo, non timeo. Intelligendum enim est τό nescire practicum) Israel non dimittam. 2. Miracula Domini calūniabatur & irridebat, dum conuocatis maleficis suis Ex. 7. v. 11. quoad speciē similia edidit. Hinc enim volebat ostēdere, Deum Israelis non adeò magnum esse cùm plus præstare nequeat, quàm Magi sui & incantatores. 3. Sciebat & in conscientia conuictus erat, non nisi à Deo & potentiâ diuina prouenire ista miracula, quoniam ipsi incantatores dicebant, Exod. 8. v. 19. Digitus Dei est hic. Ipse quoque Pharao voluit, vt pro se orarent Dominum, atque sic agnouit, ab eo pœnas esse illatas, ideoque & ipsum solum eas tollere posse. Exod. 19. v. 16. & 17. ait ipse: Peccaui in dominum Deum vestrum, & in vos sed nunc dimittite peccatum meum mihi & hac vice, & rogate Dominum Deum vestrum, vt auferat. Sic ergo concludidimus. Quisquis contra scientiam & conscientiam negat articulum fidei, peccat in Spiritum S. Pharao hoc fecit, quia nouit, Deum Israelis esse verum Deum ex miraculis, & tamen malitiosè hoc est verbis & factis negauit pro con confirmatione minoris addimus hoc. Qui agnoscit Deum Israelis solum esse omnipotentem, is agnoscit, eum solum esse verum Deum. At verò illud agnoscebat Pharao. Exod. 10. v. 16. 17. Credidit enim, neminem posse istas plagas auferre, ideoque solicitauit Mosen, vt apud Deum pro se incederet. Quamvis verò non fiat mentio, quòd doctrinam Israëlitarum blasphemauerit, attamen de eo nullum est dubium. Volebant enim exire propter cultum Dei sui. Hunc autem ipsum verum esse Deum ex miraculis sciebat, & nihilominus cultum ejus impediebat, & procul dubio blasphemabat, Præterea miracula sunt appendices doctrinæ, qui igitur miracula Dei blasphemat, ille & verbum ejus & doctrinam consequenter impugnat.

Et quid multis opus? Peccabat certè in Spiritum 1.ratione officij, quia Spiritui per verbum Mosis ipsum conuertere volenti resistebat. 2. ratione testimonij dum veritatem miraculorum agnitam contra conscientiam negabat. Est enim veritas Dei duplex, altera verbi & doctrinæ, altera facti & miraculorum. Siue quis vtramq; siue alterutram scienter & volenter blasphemet, in Sp. S. peccat.

IX. 2. Auditores Prophetæ Ieremiæ. De his dicit c. 5. v. 12. Negauerunt Dominum, & dixerunt: Non est ipse, neque veniet super nos malum cap. 7. v. 16. Et dixerunt: Non ambulauimus, v. 17. Non audiemus. Cap. 7. ver. 16 prohibetur Ieremias pro ijs orare. Vnde colligimus, illos commisisse peccatum ad mortem. Verba sic habēt: Tu ergo noli orare pro populo hoc, nec assumas pro eis deprecationem & orationem & non obsistas mihi, quia non exaudiam te cap. 44. ver. 16. ajunt Sermonem quem locutus es ad nos in nomine Domini, non audiemus ex te sed facientes faciemus omne verbum quod egredietur de ore nostro, vt sacrificemus reginæ cæli. Hæc omnia quid sunt aliud, quam certissima peccati in Spiritum sanctum τεκμήρια? Nouerant, solū cultum à Mose præscriptum esse verum, erant conuicti in conscientia, quòd in nomine Domini ad eos loquatur Ieremias; & nihilominus directè resistunt Spiritui sancto, claraque voce dicunt, Se nolle Domino obedire, nolle eius doctrinā sequi. Ad mortē igitur peccabāt, & hinc p ijs orari nolebat Dominˠ

X. 3. Pharisæi tempore Christi, de quibus Matth. 12. Marc. 3. Luc. 12. Illi enim non modo nôrant Christum esse à Deo, fatente Nicodemo, Ioh. 3. v. 2. Sed etiam quis esset, Et me nostis, & vnde sim nostis inquit

Christus Ioh. 7. v. 24. Matth. 22. v. 16. dicunt: Magister scimus, quia verax es, & viam Dei in veritate doces. Et nihilominus contra conscientiam suam, internumque Spiritus testimonium, non desistebant operibus illius diuinis detrahere, eius doctrinam blasphemare, miraculis maledicere & calumniari, quòd Spiritum habeat immundum, & ope Beelzebub eijciat demonia. Quæ omnia sunt infallibiles notæ peccati in Spiritum sanctum, cuius etiam rei aguntur ab ipso Christo, prædictis Euangelicæ historiæ locis.

XI. 4. Pharisæi & Iudæi tempore Apostolorum, præsertim Stephani, Actor. 6. v. 10. refertur de ijs, quod non potuerint resistere sapientiæ & Spiritui, qui loquebatur, adeoque agnouerint, Apostolicam doctrinam ab ipso Deo prouenire, nihilominus ijs resistebant, camblasphemabant, & hostiliter contra conscientiam persequebantur, ideoq; Stephanus Act. 7. v. 10. ait: Duræ ceruice & incircumcisis auribus: Vos semper Spiritui sancto resistitis, vers. 54. dicitur de ijs, quòd hæc audientes διεπρίοντο dissecabantur cordibus suis, & stridebant dentibus in Stephanum.

XII. 5. Apostatæ ultimi temporis, de quibus vaticinatus est Apostolus Paulus 2. Tim. 4. 1. seqquent. Dicitur enim de illis, quod 1. discessuri sint à fide. 2. secuturi Spiritum erroris, & doctrinas dæmoniorum. 3. locuturi mendacium in hypocrisi, atque ita contra conscientiam.

XIII. His adjungunt alij exemplum Saulis & Iudæ: sed cùm neuter doctrinam oppugnauerit, aut agnitam abnegauerit, in Spirit. S. peccasse non videntur. Iuliani Imperatoris exemplum conuenientius est Hic n. ritè institutus fuit in religione Christiana, cognouit veritatem Euangelij, quam & publice professus est, suscepto Baptismo; Postea autem suasu quorundam malè philosophantium, nempè Libanij, Iamblichi & similium, defecit à Christo, sanamque Euanglij doctrinam blasphemauit, & modis omnibus persecutus est. XIV. De Francisco Spiera a nonnullis dubitatur: sed expedita est responsio, eum pro peccatore in Spiritum sanctum minime habendum esse, quia 1. non ex malitia, sed infirmitate; non sponte sed persuasus ab amicis defecit ad Papatum. 2. non impugnauit aut blasphemauit doctrinam Evangelij, sed summe doluit, quod a veritate defecisset. Fuit ergo peccatum ejus desperatio quidem, sed non blasphemia in Spiritum, cum fidem orthodoxam non negauerit, sed isti semper vsque ad mortem testimonium veritatis perhibuerit.


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is: III On the essential requirements of the sin against the Holy Spirit

III On the essential requirements of the sin against the Holy Spirit,

XV. From the examples enumerated thus far, and the testimonies of Scripture placed above, we shall now gather the γνωρίσματα and essential requirements or properties of this sin, of which some count seven, others eight, some ten or even more. But we shall divide all those into three general classes, the first of which will be taken from the object, the second from the principle, the third from the work and act itself of this sin.

1. Requirements on the part of the object.

XVI. The object of sin is twofold: 1. that against which it is directed, 2. that about which it is concerned. The former is threefold: God, one's neighbor, and the one who sins himself. For by sinning we harm either God or our neighbor or ourselves. As for blasphemy against the Spirit: it is indeed harmful both to one's neighbor, on account of the bad example, and to the sinner himself, on account of the great punishment, and it harms the whole Trinity; yet on account of its supreme viciousness it is directed πρώτως and primarily against the Holy Spirit, and is contrary both to his office and to his testimony, as we said in the preceding question. But we are not concerned here with the object into which or against which it is directed; rather, the object about which it is concerned must be considered, by reason of which we posit two requirements, included in two theses.

XVII. 1. The sin against the Holy Spirit does not concern morals and life, but the word of God, and faith and the appendages of faith, miracles.

For although everyone contaminated by this sin also leads a vicious and perverse life, and is of most wicked morals; nevertheless the formal aspect and the τὸ ἐν ὧ εἶναι (that in which it consists) of this crime does not consist in sins of morals, but rather concerns faith and doctrine, concerns the word and miracles of God, which is demonstrated by the following reasons.

XIIX. 1. All sins of morals are forgiven, which can be proven by examples through individual species of sins. The sin against the Holy Spirit, however, is not forgiven: 2. The Apostle teaches this in Hebrews 6, who describes this sin through ἀποστασίαν or defection from the faith. 3. The same is expressed in Hebrews 10 where there is a distinction between sins of morals, by which the law is violated, and this sin, when it is said in v. 28: 'Anyone who has set aside the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses: how much worse punishment will he be thought to deserve, who has trampled the Son of God underfoot?' From this therefore we deduce that this sin is not in morals or against the law primarily, insofar as it is a norm of works, but against the Gospel and the doctrine of truth. 4. By induction of individuals the same is proven. Pharaoh attacked the word and worship of God, and his miracles: the hearers of Jeremiah opposed themselves to the doctrine, and so did the Pharisees: Thus 1. Timothy 4, express mention is made of apostasy from the faith, and doctrines of demons.

XIX. From all these things, therefore, it is most firmly gathered that the object of this sin is not morals and life, but faith and doctrine, or in one word, the word and truth of God. This truth, however, 1. either consists in deeds and miracles, and therefore he who maliciously blasphemes them, and against his conscience assigns them to the Devil, when he knows they proceeded from God, is not undeservedly thought to sin against the Holy Spirit. 2. or in words and the doctrine itself, which is divided into law and Gospel. Theologians, however, commonly establish that this sin is concerned primarily with the doctrine of the Gospel: yet it cannot be denied that it is also directed against the law

XX. It must be known, however, that the law is considered in two ways: 1. insofar as it is a norm and rule of actions. 2. insofar as it is doctrine and the word of God. In the former way, one sins against the law who does not observe it: in the latter, one who denies it and does not hold it for the word or truth of God. When, therefore, theologians say that the sin against the Holy Spirit is not concerned with the law, they are considering it as it is a norm of works. And thus, whoever violates and transgresses it sins against the law, in which sense every moral sin is against the law. But when it is considered as it is the word of God, as a part of faith and doctrine, then someone can also sin against the Holy Spirit regarding the law, namely by blaspheming it and by not acknowledging it as the doctrine of God. As if someone were to say that the law of Moses is diabolical doctrine, and were to defend this maliciously against his conscience, then he would certainly sin against the Holy Spirit.

XXI. Someone might object: To attack the law is against the law itself, insofar as it is a norm of actions. For it is against the first commandment, where all unbelief is prohibited.
