But a certain sinning against the Holy Spirit is to attack the law. Therefore, this also will be against the law, insofar as it is a norm of works. Blasphemy, therefore, against the Spirit will be a mortal sin.

I respond: I distinguish between genus and species, or between a general and a special act. The genus of the sin itself is indeed prohibited in the law, namely unbelief, yet its species or special act is not expressed. We concede, therefore, that just as unbelief, so also blasphemy against the Spirit in a general sense, or by reason of its genus, is against the law; yet its special act is not expressed by the law, and therefore it is called ἀνομία rather than ἁμαρτία. It must be known that this blasphemy is estimated in two ways: 1. insofar as it is a sin, and thus it is called ἀνομία, and is directed against the law as it is a norm; 2. insofar as it is a sin against the Holy Spirit, and thus it has as its formal element ἀπιστίαν or the voluntary denial of the acknowledged truth.

Furthermore, it is to be noted that it does not pertain to, nor is it necessary for the constituting of a sin against the Holy Spirit, that one should deny every doctrine and truth of God and the whole Gospel, but it suffices that one should impugn either the more important part or only some part, as the example of the Pharisees and Jews teaches. Provided that this is held, that this sin, taken formally, is occupied only with the truth of God and denotes a voluntary opposition to it while the conscience protests.

XXII. From which emerges this corollary: 1. that those who sin against the Holy Spirit are not easily laymen, but learned and erudite men who have read the Bible and know what is true, and therefore heretics or heresiarchs are especially contaminated by this sin. For whoever maliciously impugns a certain article of faith against his conscience, he sins against the Holy Spirit. Such, however, are heretics. From which it is concluded: 2. that sinners against the Holy Spirit live especially in the Church, not outside it; they are Christians, not pagans. Meanwhile, however, although as regards the greater part the matter is so, it cannot be denied that even 1. infidels can sin against the Holy Spirit, since we have the manifest example of Pharaoh. 2. Laymen and commoners, especially those who are dazzled by the external brilliance of miracles. For these can be convinced that they are the miracles of God, and nevertheless they can blaspheme. For without doubt among the courtiers of Pharaoh and the Egyptians there were many such: why should there not be such today as well: meanwhile, however, if doctrine and sincere faith are considered, the learned especially and those who read Scripture and abuse their reason sin against the Holy Spirit, and defile themselves with blasphemy.

XXIII. II. The doctrine, concerning which the sin against the Holy Spirit revolves, must first be acknowledged.

This requirement can be confirmed by many reasons. 1. Because unless this is said, every distinction between sins against the Son and against the Holy Spirit is removed. For we have hitherto distinguished them thus, that he sins against the Spirit who opposes and blasphemes acknowledged doctrine; he who opposes and blasphemes doctrine not acknowledged, against the Son. 2. The example of Paul himself proves this. He opposed the truth, and yet he did not sin against the Holy Spirit, because he obtained mercy. And he himself names ignorance as the cause of the mercy. 1 Tim. 1. verse 13. 3. The statements in Heb. 6 and 10 mean the same. For it is said there that they were enlightened and had tasted the good word of God. 4. The individual examples alleged above demonstrate the same, from the induction of which it is clearly gathered that this sin presupposes an acknowledgment of the truth. For Pharaoh, the hearers of Jeremiah, the Pharisees, etc., acknowledged it. Whence we infer that everyone sinning against the Holy Spirit acknowledges the truth.

XXIV. But here it must further be known that the acknowledgment of the truth is twofold: one γραμματική and merely literal, such as even the devils have; the other πνευματικὴ and gracious, where the truth is not only known and acknowledged, but at the same time is graciously sealed by the Holy Spirit in the heart of man. That acknowledgment is always required for the sin against the Holy Spirit, but this one is not always; as the example of Pharaoh and the Pharisees shows, who indeed were convinced in their conscience of the truth of the miracles and the doctrine of Christ, meanwhile they were not truly reborn, nor was this doctrine confirmed in all by a gracious κατοίκησιν by the Holy Spirit:

XXV. And hence theologians establish two species of blasphemy against the Spirit. The one is, when the sinner was previously reborn, and illuminated by the Holy Spirit through grace, or as the epistle to the Hebrews 6 speaks, who has tasted the heavenly gift, and has been made a partaker of the Holy Spirit. The other, however, is when the truth is known and acknowledged nakedly and literally, without the preceding gracious illumination and indwelling of the Holy Spirit. And this is to be added, so that this sin may not be too strictly circumscribed, and all those who were not previously reborn and truly faithful may not be excluded from it: the acknowledgment of the truth is sufficient, a gracious sealing in the souls is not required.

Latin:

III De essentialibus peccati in Spiritum sanctum requisitis,

XV. Ex enumeratis hactenus exemplis, & supra positis Scripturae testimonijs, colligemus nunc γνωρίσματα & essentialia huius peccati requisita vel propria, quorum nonnulli septem, alij octo, quidam decem vel etiam plura recensent. Verum omnia illa diuidemus in tres generales classes, quarum prima erit desumta ab obiecto, altera a principio, tertia ab ipso opere & actu huius peccati.

1. Requisita ex parte obiecti.

XVI. Objectum peccati duplex est, 1. contra quod fertur, 2. circa quod versatur. Illud triplex est, Deus, pro ximus, & ille ipse qui peccat. Etenim Deum vel proximum, vel nos ipsos peccando laedimus. Quod jam spectat blasphemiam in Spiritum: illa quidem noxia est tum proximo, ob malum exemplum tum ipsi peccanti, ob grande supplicium, laeditque totam Trinitatem; ob summam vitiositatem πρώτως tamen & primario in Spiritum Sanctum fertur, contrariatur ejus tum officio, tum testimonio, vti praecedente quaestione diximus. Verum de obiecto in quod vel contra quod, hic non sumus soliciti; objectum potius circa quod versatur considerandum venit, ratione cuius duo requisita, duabus thesibus inclusa ponimus.

XVII. 1. Peccatum in Spiritum S non versatur circa mores & vitam, sed circa verbum Dei, & fidem fideique appendices, miracula.

Quamuis enim omnis hoc peccato contaminatus vitiosam quoque & peruersam ducat vitam, moribusque sit scelestissimis; attamen formale & τὸ ἐν ὧ εἶναι huius sceleris, non in peccatis morum consistit, sed potius circa fidem & doctrinam, circa verbum & miracula Dei versatur, id quod sequentibus rationibus demonstratur.

XIIX. 1. Omnia peccata morum remittuntur, id quod exemplis per singulas peccatorum species probari potest. Peccatum autem in Spiritum sanctum non remittitur: 2. Docet hoc Apostolus Hebr. 6. qui describit peccatum istud per ἀποστασίαν wel defectionem à fide. 3. Idem exprimitur Hebr. 10 vbi sit discrimen inter peccata morum, quibus lex violatur, & hoc peccatum, cùm dicitur v. 28. Irritam faciens legem Mosis, duobus vel tribus testibus moritur: quantò magis putabis deteriora mereri supplicia, qui Filium Dei conculcauerit? Hinc igitur deducimus, quòd peccatum hoc non sit in moribus vel contra legem primò, quatenus est norma operum, sed contra Euangelium & doctrinā veritatis. 4. Ex inductione singulorum idem probatur. Pharao impugnabat verbum cultumque Dei, & miracula eius: Ieremiæ auditores opponebant sese doctrinę, sic & Pharisæi: Ita 1. Timot 4. expressè fit mentio apostasias à fide, & doctrinæ dæmoniorum.

XIX. Ex his ergo omnibus colligitur firmissimè, peccati huius obiectum non esse mores & vitam, sed fidem & doctrinam, vel vno verbo, verbum & veritatem Dei. Hæc autem veritas 1. vel consistit in factis & miraculis, ideoque qui malitiosè illa blasphemat, & contra conscientiam Diabolo assignat, cùm à Deo profecta sciat, in Spiritum sanctum peccare non immeritò putatur. 2. vel in verbis & ipsa doctrinâ, quæ dispescitur in legē & Euangelium. Statuunt verò Theologi communiter, quod peccatum hoc circa Euangelii doctrinam potissimum versetur: attamen negari nequit quod contra legem etiam feratur

XX. Sciendum autem, quod lex dupliciter consideretur, 1. quatenus est norma & regula actionum. 2. quatenus est doctrina & verbum Dei. Illo modo peccat in legem non obseruat eam: hoc, qui negat eam nec pro verbo aut veritate Dei habet. Quando ergo Theologi dicunt, quòd peccatum in Spiritum sanctum non versetur circa legem, considerant eam, prout est norma operum. Et sic aduersus legem peccat, quicunq; eam violat & transgreditur, quo sensu omne peccatum morale est contra legem. Quando autem consideratur, vt est verbum Dei, vt pars fidei & doctrinæ, tunc etiam aliquis circa legem peccare potest in Spiritum sanctum, eam nimirum blasphemando; & pro doctrina Dei non agnoscendo. Vt si quis diceret, legem Mosis doctrinam diabolicam, & malitiosè contra conscientiam hoc defenderet, tum vtiq; in Spiritum sanctum peccaret.

XXI. Obijcere aliquis posset: Impugnare legem est contra ipsam legem, prout est norma actionum. Etenim contra primum præceptum, vbi omnis prohibetur incredulitas. Sed quoddam peccare in Spiritum sanctum est impugnare legem. Ergo & hoc erit contra legem, prout est norma operum. Blasphemia igitur in Spiritum erit peccatum mortale.

Respond. distinguo inter genus & speciem, vel inter actum generalem & specialem. Ipsum genus peccati quidem est prohibitum in lege, nimirum infidelitas, species tamen eius vel actus specialis non est expressus. Concedimus ergo, sicut incredulitatem, ita & blasphemiã in Spiritum generali sensu, vel ratione generis sui, contra legem esse, specialis tamen eius actus lege non est expressus, ideoq; potius ἀνομία, quam ἁμαρτία dicitur, Sciendum enim, quòd hæc blasphemia dupliciter æstimetur, 1. quatenus peccatum est, & sic ἀνομία dicitur, & contra legem, vt norma est, fertur, 2. quatenus peccatum in Spiritum sanctum est, & sic pro formali habet ἀπιστίαν vel abnegationem voluntariam veritatis agnitæ.

Porrò autem notandum, quòd non pertineat vel opus sit ad peccatum in Spiritum sanctum constituendum, vt quis omnem Dei doctrinam & veritatem, totumque Euangelium abneget, sed sufficit, vt vel potiorem, vel aliquam tantum partem impugnet, vti docet exemplum Pharisæorum & Iudæorum. Modò istud teneatur, quod peccatum hoc formaliter sumtum non nisi circa veritatem Dei occupetur, & denotet voluntariam ejus oppugnationem reclamante conscientiâ.

XXII. Ex quo emergit πόρισμα hoc 1. quod in Spiritum sanctum peccantes non facilè sint Lajci, sed viri docti & eruditi, qui legerunt Biblia, & sciunt quid verum sit, ideoque hoc peccato potissimum contaminantur hæretici vel hæresiarchæ. Quicunque enim articulum quendam fidei contra conscientiam malitiosè impugnat, ille in Spiritum sanctum peccat. Tales autem sunt hæretici. Ex quo concluditur 2. quòd peccatores in Spiritum sanctum potissimum viuant in Ecclesia, non extra; Christiani sint, non pagani. Interim tamen, licèt quoad potiorem partem res ita sese habeat, negari tamen nequit, quòd etiam 1. infideles in Spiritum sanctum peccare queant, quoniam habemus manifestum exemplum Pharaonis. 2. Laici & Plebeij, præsertim qui miraculorum externo fulgore perstringuntur. Hi enim conuinci possunt, Dei esse miracula, & nihilominus blasphemare queunt. Nam procul dubio inter aulicos Pharaonis & Ægyptios tales multi erant: quidni & hodiè tales esse possent: interim tamen, si doctrina consideretur & fides sincera, docti potissimum & Scripturam legentes rationéque abutentes in Spiritum sanctum peccant, & blasphemia sese contaminant.

XXIII. II. Doctrina, circa quam versatur peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, prius debet esse agnita.

Requisitum hoc confirmari potest multis rationibus. 1. Quia nisi hoc dicatur, omne discrimen inter peccata in Filium & in Spiritum sanctum tollitur. Ita enim hactenus ea distinximus, quod in Spiritum peccet, qui agnitam; in Filium, qui non agnitam doctrinam oppugnat & blasphemat. 2. Evincit hoc ipsum Pauli exemplum. Oppugnavit hic veritatem, & tamen in Spiritum sanctum non peccavit, quia veniam consecutus est. Et ignorantiam veniæ causam ipse nominat. 1. Tim. 1. vers. 13. 3. Idem volunt dicta Heb. 6. & 10. Nam ibi dicitur, quòd sint illuminati & gustaverint bonum Dei verbum. 4: Idem demonstrant exempla singula suprà allegata, ex quorum inductione colligitur cuisdenter, peccatum hoc agnitionem veritatis præsupponere. Etenim agnovit eam Pharao, Ieremiæ auditores, Pharisæi & c. Vnde inferimus, omnem in Spiritum sanctum peccantem agnoscere veritatem.

XXIV. Hic autem porrò sciendum, quod veritatis agnitio sit duplex, altera γραμματική & mere literalis, qualem habent etiam diaboli, altera πνευματικὴ & gratiosa, vbi veritas non modò scitur & agnoscitur, sed simul gratiosè à Spiritu sancto in corde hominis obsignatur, Illa agnitio semper requiritur ad peccatum in Spiritum sanctum, hæc autem non semper; vt ostendit exemplum Pharaonis & Pharisæorum, qui quidem in conscientia sua erant convicti de veritate miraculorũ & doctrinæ Christi, interim verè renati non erant, nec à Spiritu sancto hæc doctrina in omnibus per gratiosam κατοίκησιν erat confirmata:

XXV. Atque hinc Theologi duas blasphemiæ in Spiritum species constituunt. Altera est, quando peccans ante renatus fuit, & a Spiritu S. per gratiam illuminatus, vel vt loquitur epist. Hebr. 6. qui gustauit donum coeleste, & particeps factus est Spiritus S. Altera autem, quando veritas nude & literaliter scitur atque agnoscitur, sine praecedente gratiosa Spiritus sancti illuminatione & inhabitatione. Et hoc ideo addendum, ne nimis stricte circumscribatur peccatum hoc, & ab eo excludantur omnes, qui ante renati non fuerunt & vere fideles: Sufficit veritatis agnitio, non requiritur agnitio gratiosa in animis obsignatio.


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is: 2. Requirements on the part of the principle

2. Requirements on the part of the principle.

XXVI. There are two intrinsic principles of human acts, the one is the intellect, the other is the will: The intellect considers, judges, and proposes what is to be done. The will, however, afterwards follows the judgment of the intellect, and by the act itself chooses what reason has persuaded is to be chosen, and commands the locomotive and other faculties to execute and bring into act that which is willed.

XXVII. Each faculty, however, can behave in two ways in the production of acts. For as regards the intellect; it either clearly knows and acknowledges its object, or it knows it imperfectly, and is ignorant of most things, whence two kinds of actions arise; some are said to proceed from full knowledge, others from ignorance of the mind. The will likewise behaves in two ways. It either applies and moves itself alone to act, or it is moved and as it were drawn by another principle, namely either through the weakness of the flesh, or through fear of danger, or through things persuaded by others, etc. Whence in turn a double kind of actions emerges, so that some are called voluntary, others involuntary, of which the former proceed from the full and deliberate counsel of the will; these latter, however, are indeed joined with the will (for they are not entirely against one's will), yet in such a way that the will is led as if captive, and does not follow its own, but follows the guidance and inclination of another principle, whence they are held as acts committed not out of full will, but out of infirmity.

XXIIX. Now therefore it is asked, What kind of act is the sin against the Holy Spirit? We say briefly that it proceeds from knowledge, not ignorance, from full will, not infirmity. Therefore, we posit two things required in turn for this blasphemy on the part of the principle.

XXIX. 1. The sin against the Holy Spirit is committed not out of ignorance, but out of the full knowledge of the agent.

The reason for this requirement is sought in turn. 1. From the example of Paul. For he, because he attacked the truth ignorantly, therefore obtained pardon, and did not sin against the Holy Spirit, 1 Tim. 1 v. 13. 2. From the induction of individual examples which are contained in the Scriptures. For we see that all of them attacked the truth knowingly and not ignorantly. 3. From the statement in 1 Tim. 4 that they would speak a lie in hypocrisy against their own knowledge, and it is immediately added that they have a seared conscience, which they could not have unless they sinned knowingly: The words of Heb. 6 are also clear, where they are said to be enlightened, especially Heb. 10 v. 26, where they are said ἁμαρτάνειν μετὰ τὸ λαβεῖν τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας. Since, however, he has knowledge of the ἀληθείας, he certainly denies it knowingly, not ignorantly.

XXX. Therefore, there can be no doubt any longer that he who sins against the Holy Spirit, and cannot return to repentance, sins knowingly in this sense, that he is convicted in his own conscience, and most certainly knows that the doctrine which he maliciously attacks and blasphemes is the word of God, is the truth itself, and is saving faith. As when the Pharisees said that Christ cast out demons by the works of Beelzebub, they were convicted in their hearts, and were compelled to believe inwardly because of the testimony of conscience, that that miracle was truly divine, and they knew that Christ's doctrine was most firmly founded in the Prophetic Scriptures. This, therefore, was to oppose and blaspheme the truth knowingly and with full knowledge of the mind.

XXXI. Here then arises the question, How can full knowledge of the mind consist with blindness? For it was predicted of the Pharisees that they were to be blinded, Isa. 6. v. 9: And this very thing is clearly said of them in John 12. verse 40. But what else is blindness and the blinding of the mind than ignorance? For it is described by darkness, Eph. 5. verse 8. He, therefore, who acts out of blindness and ignorance does not oppose the truth out of full knowledge of the mind.

XXXII. Response. That blinding does not take away the simple, bare, and literal knowledge of the doctrine: For they are not said to be blinded as if they knew nothing at all about the faith, like the Gentiles and pagans, but in another and indeed twofold respect:

1. By reason of spiritual ignorance, insofar as they do not apprehend the acknowledged truth with faithful assent, that is, insofar as they are destitute of spiritual and πνευματικῇ [spiritual] knowledge. They know the truth as to the letter, they do not know it and are blind as to the Spirit and faithful assent. Knowledge and blindness, therefore, because they are taken in a different respect, can hence very well concur together in the same subject. And this both the Prophet Isaiah in chapter 6 and the Savior himself in John 12 indicated, when both say that they are blinded, so that seeing they do not see and understanding they do not understand. For here both are joined, to see and not to see, to know and not to know, of which the former is to be understood of literal, the latter of spiritual and faithful γνώσει [knowledge] of the truth. For it is evident from John 3. verse 2 that very many Pharisees knew and were convinced in their conscience of the truth, who nevertheless are themselves said to be blinded, whence we conversely gather that blinding does not take away but rather presupposes that literal knowledge of the truth.

2. By reason of negligence. For it is a sign of the highest madness and extreme blindness that these men know what they ought to do, how they might be able to escape eternal damnation; and nevertheless are so unmindful of their own salvation that they neglect it entirely, nor ever apply their mind to those things which make for the attainment of salvation and eternal happiness: If any sick person knew that by the use of a certain medicine his lost health would be restored to him, and saw the physician standing by, offering the medicine and urging its use by all means, but he nevertheless wished to blaspheme the physician and cast away the medicine and trample it underfoot, who would not think him a madman and insane? In like manner, those sinning against the Holy Spirit, because they know the truth and know the way of escaping damnation, nevertheless blaspheme the Spirit and deny the truth, are not undeservedly called blinded and mad. Conversely, therefore, literal knowledge does not remove, but aggravates blindness: For a person is said to be the more blinded, the more he casts away those things which he knows more distinctly and fully are going to be of benefit to him.

Latin:

2. Requisita ex parte principii.

XXVI. Duo sunt principia actuum humanorum intrinseca, alterum intellectus, alterum voluntas est: Intellectus considerat, judicat & proponit, quid agendum sit. Voluntas autem postea intellectus judicium sequitur, & actu ipso eligit, quod eligendum ratio suasit, imperatque locomotiuae & caeteris facultatibus, vt exequantur & in actum deducant istud volitum.

XXVII. Vtraque autem facultas duobus modis se habere potest in productione actuum. Nam quod attinet intellectum; ille objectum suum vel plane scit & agnoscit, vel imperfecte scit, & pleraque ignorat, vnde actiones oriuntur duplices; quaedam ex plena scientia, quaedam ex ignorantia mentis profectae dicuntur. Voluntas itidem dupliciter se habet. Vel semetipsam sola ad agendum applicat, & commouet, vel ab alio principio mouetur & quasi trahitur, nempe vel per infirmitatem carnis, vel per metum periculi, vel per persuasas ab alijs, &c. Vnde vicissim duplex actionum genus emergit, vt quadam dicantur voluntariae, quaedam inuoluntariae, quarum istae ex pleno & deliberato voluntatis consilio prodeunt; hae autem cum voluntate quidem conjunctae sunt, (non enim inuitae prorsus) ita tamen, vt illa quasi captiua ducatur, & non suum, sed alterius principij ductum & ingenium sequatur, vnde habentur pro actibus, non ex plana voluntate, sed infirmitate commissis.

XXIIX. Nunc ergò quæritur, Qualis actus sit peccatum in Spiritum sanctum? Dicimus breuite quòd ex scientia, non ignorātitia, ex plana voluntate, non infirmitate procedat. Blasphemiæ igitur hujus ex parte principij duo vicissim requisita ponimus.

XXIX. 1. Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum non ex ignorantia, sed plena agentis scientia committitur.

Requisiti huius ratio uicissim petitur. 1. Ab exemplo Pauli. Hic enim quia veritatem ignoranter oppugnauit, propterea veniam consecutus est, & in Spiritum sanctum non peccauit, 1. Tim. 1. v. 13. 2. Ab inductione singulorum exemplorum, quæ continentur in Scripturis. Videmus enim omnes eos sciente & non ignoranter veritatem oppugnasse. 3. Ex dicto 1. Tim. 4. quòd in hypocrisi sint locuturi mendacium contra scientiam suam, & statim subditur, quòd cauteriatam habeant conscientiam, quam habere non possent, nisi scienter peccarent: Clara etiam sunt verba Hebr. 6. vbi illuminati dicuntur, præsertim Hebr. 10. v. 26. vbi dicuntur ἁμαρτάνειν μετὰ τὸ λαβεῖν τὴν ἐπίγνωσιν τῆς ἀληθείας. Quia autem notitiam habet ἀληθείας, ille certè scienter, non ignoranter eam abnegat.

XXX. Nullum proinde dubium amplius esse potest, eum qui in Spiritum S. peccat, & ad pœnitentiam redire nequit, scienter peccare hoc sensu, quod in conscientia sua conuictus sit, & certissime sciat esse verbum Dei, esse ipsam veritatem fidemque saluificam eam doctrinam, quam malitiosè oppugnat & blasphemat. Vt cum Pharisęi dicerent, Christum opera Beelzebub ejicere dæmonia conuicti erant in cordibus suis, & intus credere cogebantur ob testimonium conscientiæ, miraculum istud, verè diuinum fuisse, sciebantqué Christi doctrinam in Scripturis Propheticis esse fundatissimam. Hoc igitur erat veritatem scienter, plenaque mentis notitiâ oppugnare & blasphemare.

XXXI. Hic auë oritur quęstio, Quomodo plena mentis notitia cum cœcitate possit consistere? Nam prædictum erat de Pharisæis, quòd essent excæcandi Ejas. 6. v. 9: Et hoc ipsum de ijs clarè dicitur Iohan. 2. vers. 40. Cæcitas autem & excœcatio mentis quid aliud est, quàm ignorantia? Per tenebras enim ista describitur, Eph. 5. vers. 8. Qui ergo ex cœcitate & ignorantia, is non ex plena mentis notitia veritatem oppugnat.

XXXII. Respond. Excœcatio ista non tollit scientiam doctrinæ simplicem, nudã & literalem: Etenim non dicūtur excœcati, ac si planè nihil scirent de fide, vt gentiles & pagani, sed alio eoque gemino respectu:

1. Ratione ignorantiæ spiritualis, quatenus fideli assensu non apprehendunt veritatem agnitam, id est, in quantum Spirituali & πνευματικῇ notitiâ destituuntur. Sciunt veritatẽ quoad literam, nesciunt & cœci sunt quoad Spiritum & fidelem assensum. Scientia igitur & excœcatio, quia diuerso respectu sumuntur, hinc in eodem subiecto simul optimè possunt concurrere. Et hoc cum Propheta Esaias c. 6. tum ipse Saluator Iohan. 12. indicauit, quando vterque dicit, excæcatos illos esse, vt videntes non videant & intelligentes non intelligant. Hic enim coniungitur vtrumque, videre & non videre, scire & non scire, quorum illud de literali, hoc de spirituali & fideli veritatis γνώσει intelligendum est. Etenim Pharisæos plurimos sciuisse, & in conscientia conuictos fuisse de veritate, constat ex Iohan. 3. vers. 2. qui tamen ipsi dicuntur, excœcati, vnde vicissim colligimus excœcationem non tollere sed potius pręsupponere literalem istam veritatis scientiam.

2. Ratione negligentia. Nam summæ dementiæ & cæcitatis extremæ signum est, quod isti homines sciant, quid agere debeant, quomodo æternam damnationem effugere queant; & nihilominus propriæ salutis adeò sint immemores, vt ipsam prorsus negligant, nec vnquam animum adjiciant ad ea, quæ ad salutem & æternam beatitudinem consequendam faciunt: Si ægrotus quispiam sciret, certi medicaminis vsurpatione restitutam sibi iri sanitatem perditam, & astantem videret medicum, medicamen proponentem, & ad vsurpationem modis omnibus solicitantem, ille verò nihilominus blasphemare vellet Medicum & medicinã abijceret, pedibusque conculcaret, quis non pro demēte & insano eum putaret? Pari modo peccantes in Spiritum sanctum, quia sciunt veritatem & nouerunt modum effugiendi damnationem, nihilominus tamen blasphemant Spiritum, & veritatem abnegant, non immeritò excœcati & dementes appellantur. Vicissim igitur scientia literalis non tollit, sed adgrauat excœcationem: Eò enim magis dicitur quis excœcatus, quò magis projicit ea quæ sibi profutura esse, distinctiùs & plenius cognoscit.


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is: XXXIII. II. Sin against the Holy Spirit is perpetrated not out of infirmity, but out of full and malicious will

XXXIII. II. Sin against the Holy Spirit is perpetrated not out of infirmity, but out of full and malicious will.

For a completely deliberate counsel and purpose is required if anyone is to be held guilty and accused of this sin: and therefore those who, whether circumvented by heretics, or terrified by the fear of dangers, or overcome by the severity of torments, deny the truth, these (unless they afterwards voluntarily persevere in blasphemy) are not considered to have sinned against the Holy Spirit. For every cause moving the will and carrying it, as it were, sideways, must be absent. But we understand an extrinsic cause, and one that carries away the will, for an intrinsic cause can be conceded, because a deliberate purpose of the will does not remove it. But those sinners can be moved either by ambition, or by a desire for glory, because they are unwilling to retract what has once been said; or by an appetite for riches and earthly pleasures, which are more conveniently enjoyed among the enemies of the truth. And these causes do not excuse, or absolve from blasphemy against the Spirit; because they are intended by the agent himself, they do not arise from an external principle, nor do they capture his will, or carry it off in a transverse direction. But if external moving causes are present, and the will is carried off by them, there the Holy Spirit is not blasphemed.

XXXIV. This can be proven. 1. From the examples of those who denied the truth in persecutions, and yet were afterwards converted in turn. Thus the example of Peter is most clear, who indeed denied Christ; but out of fear of death and danger; and therefore he obtained forgiveness. 2. From the induction of examples, for whoever are said in the Scriptures to have sinned against the Holy Spirit, they all blasphemed willingly, not out of infirmity, as the example of Pharaoh, the Pharisees, and the hearers of Jeremiah teaches in particular. 3. From evident sayings, especially Heb. 10:26, Ἐκουσίως, for us sinning voluntarily. Thus 1 Tim. 4, they are said to apostatize from the faith against their conscience. Whatever, however, is committed against conscience, that proceeds from malice and full will.

XXXV. Here a certain doubt arises, whether it is possible for anyone to be found so desperately impious that he can deny the acknowledged truth against his conscience out of sole and mere malice? For this seems to be repugnant to the natural inclination of both the human intellect and will. The intellect of man naturally desires to know the truth. Therefore, it cannot be averse to and deny the truth. The will naturally desires the good, and everyone flees his own destruction and loss. But if, therefore, they knew, and seriously believed that they were denying the truth, they would certainly also know that the punishments of eternal damnation must certainly be undergone by them. But everyone turns away from this. Wherefore also that immediate antecedent, namely the voluntary denial of the truth.

XXXVI. Response 1. There is no consequence in the argument, on account of contrary examples. Even the miser, the drunkard, and the fornicator know that damnation is certainly prepared for them: nevertheless, such is the perversity of the human heart that, as if it knew nothing of hell, it continues in sins against its own knowledge and conscience. Nor are examples lacking, but we cite both Pharaoh, who had endured several plagues and knew very well that Moses was powerful in miracles, and yet, unmindful of himself and his whole kingdom, resisted God, and thus willingly cast himself into everlasting damnation; and the hearers of Jeremiah, who knew that Jeremiah was a Prophet of the Most High, knew that all the disobedient incur the eternal curse of the law, yet willingly out of mere malice said: The word which you have announced to us in the name of the Lord, we will not do; and the Pharisees, who knew that the miracles of Christ were divine? and that destruction was prepared for them, and yet they willingly blasphemed. And to this we refer in turn the sayings in 1 Tim. 4 and Heb. 10, in which a voluntary denial of the truth is proposed. On account of these examples, therefore, we conclude that there is no consequence in the argument:

2. As regards natural inclination, both the examples provided prove that man often acts contrary to it, and Medea testifies to this when she said, I see and approve the better things, I follow the worse. For her appetite was carried toward the good, and nevertheless she followed the evil. Hence it is that theologians say that some sins are against nature, when someone does that from which his nature recoils, such as incest and commingling with blood relatives. Just as, therefore, in that case, against nature and natural propensity, man works, so it is no wonder that sometimes he knowingly denies and blasphemes the truth.

3. It is not contradictory to know the truth inwardly and to be unwilling to confess it outwardly. For there is nothing more common among men than to lie and to dissemble the truth that is known. Therefore, every lie would be impossible if this argument held.

4. Man does not desire damnation, but flees from it: yet, because of perversity, he can desire that which causes damnation. Thus, no one wants to be hanged, yet one can desire theft, although this is the most certain cause of hanging. So no one wants to be damned; yet one can desire any sins whatsoever under the appearance of good, even though they infallibly damn. Since all these things are so, one must certainly distinguish between man considered by reason of his natural propensity, or the remnants of the image of God, and by reason of his hardening and blindness. In the former respect, he cannot deny the truth; but when he is hardened and delivered into the power of Satan, there, against his own nature, through the leading of the devil and the dominion of the flesh, he can not only be carried into any most inhuman crimes whatsoever, but is actually carried and swept away into them.

Latin:

XXXIII. II. Peccatum in Spiritum sanctum non ex infirmitate, sed plena & malitiosa voluntate perpetratur.

Etenim deliberatū omninò consilium & propositum requiritur, si quis huius peccati reus fieri & insimulari debeat: ídeoque qui vel hæreticis circumuenti, vel metu periculorum territi, vel grauitate tormentorum victi veritatem abnegant, isti (nisi postmodum voluntariè in blasphemia perseverent) in Spiritum sanctum peccasse non statuuntur. Omnis enim causa voluntatem permouens & velut in transuersum rapiens abesse debet. Causam verò intelligimus extrinsecam, & voluntatem abripientem, intrinseca enim causa concedi potest, quia deliberatum voluntatis propositum non tollit. Sed moueri possunt peccatores isti vel ambitione, vel cupiditate gloriæ, quod semel dicta reuocare nolint; vel appetitu diuitiarum & terrenarum voluptatum, quibus inter veritatis hostes commodius datur perfrui. Et hæ causæ non excusant, vel absoluunt à blasphemia in Spiritum; quia ab agente ipso intenduntur, non ab externo principio oriuntur, nec voluntatem eius captiuant, vel in transuersum rapiunt. Quòd si autem externæ causæ motrices adfuerint, ijsque voluntas abripiatur, ibi Spiritus sanctus non blasphematur.

XXXIV. Probari hoc potest. 1. Ab exemplis illorum, qui in persecutionibus veritatem abnegarunt, & tamen postea vicissim conuersi sunt. Sic clarissimum est exemplum Petri, qui Christum quidem negabat; sed ex metu mortis & periculi; ideoque veniam consecutus est. 2. Ab exemptorum inductione quicunque enim in Scripturis in Spiritum sanctum peccasse dicuntur ij omnes volenter, non ex infirmitate blasphemârunt, vti docet imprimis exemplum Pharaonis, Pharisæorum & auditorum Ieremiæ. 3. Ab euidentibus dictis præsertim Hebr. 10. v. 26. Ἐκουσίως voluntariè nobis peccantibus. Sic 1. Tim. 4. dicuntur contra conscientiam à fide apostatare. Quicquid autem contra conscientiam committitur, istud ex malitia & plena voluntate proficiscitur.

XXXV. Hic dubium quoddam exoritur, An sit mirum possibile sit, reperiri quempiam, adeò desperatè impium, vt contra conscientiam possit veritatem agnitam ex solâ meraque malitia abnegare? Etenim videtur hoc repugnare naturali inclinationi cùm intellectus, tùm voluntatis humanæ. Intellectus hominis naturaliter verum scire desiderat. Ergo veritatem non potest auersari & abnegare. Voluntas naturaliter appetit bonum, & quiuis suum fugit interitum damnumque. Quòd si igitur isti scirent, & seriò crederent, se veritatem abnegare, vtique & hoc scirent, æternæ damnationis pœnas sibi certò subeundas esse. Has autem quiuis auersatur. Quare & istud immediatum antecedens, nempè voluntariam veritatis abnegationem.

XXXVI. Respond. 1. Nulla inest argumento consequentiá, ob exempla contraria. Etiam auarus, ebrius & scortator scit, certò sibi paratam damnationem: nihilominus tanta est cordis humani peruersitas, vt quasi nihil sciret de inferno contra scientiam & conscientiam propriam in peccatis pergat. Neque desunt exempla, sed allegamus tùm Pharaonem, qui aliquot plagas sustinuerat, optimeque nouerat, potentem in miraculis Mosen esse, & tamen immemor sui totiusque regni resistebat Deo, & sic in sempiternam damnationem volenter sese præcipitabat: tùm auditores Ieremiæ, qui sciebant Ieremiam esse Prophetam Altissimi, sciebant quosuis inobedientes æternam legis maledictionem incurrere, volenter tamen ex merâ malitiâ dicebant: Verbum quod annunciâsti nobis in nomine Domini, non faciemus; tùm Pharisæos, quid faciebat Christi miracula diuina esse sciebat? & sibi paratum exitium, & tamen volenter blasphemabant. Et huc vicissim referimus dicta 1. Tim 4. Hebr. 10 in quibus voluntaria veritatis abnegatio proponitur, Ob hæc igitur exempla nullam argumento consequentiam inesse concludimus:

2. Quod spectat naturalem inclinationem, illi hominem sæpè contrariari & posita exempla euincunt, & Medea testatur, quando dicebat, Video meliora proboque, Deteriora sequor. Huius enim appetitus in bonum ferebatur, & nihilominus malum sequebatur Hinc est quod Theologi dicunt, peccata nonnulla esse contra naturam, quando aliquis id facit, à quo eius natura abhorret, vt incestus & commixtio cùm consanguineis. Sicut igitur ibi cōtra naturam naturalemq; propensionem homo operatur, ita non mirum est, quòd quandoque veritatem scienter abneget & blasphemet.

3. Non sunt contraria, veritatem interius scire, & exterius diffiteri nolle. Nihil enim est familiarius apud homines, quàm vt mentiantur, & veritatem scitam dissimulent. Omne igitur mendacium esset impossibile, si argumentum istud procederet.

4. Homo non appetit damnationem, sed fugit: ob peruersitatem tamen appetere potest illud, quod causat damnationem. Ita suspendi nemo vult, furtum tamen velle potest, licèt hoc certissima suspendij causa sit. Sic nemo damnari vult; velle tamen potest sub specie boni peccata quæuis, licet illa infallibiliter damnent. Quæ omnia cùm ita se habeant, distinguendum vtique est inter hominem ratione naturalis propensionis, vel reliquiarum imaginis & ratione indurationis atąue excæcationis consideratum. Illo quidem respectu veritatem abnegare nequit; quando autem induratus est & in potestatem Satanæ traditur, ibi contra naturam suam per diaboli ductum & carnis dominium in quæuis etiam inimanissima scelera non modo ferri potest, sed actu etiam ipso fertur & abripitur.


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is: 3. Requisites on the part of the act itself

3. Requisites on the part of the act itself.

XXXVII. We count here four essential προσκείμενα, or requisites, of the sin against the Holy Spirit, since four primary special acts are conspicuous in it.

XXXIIX. 1. It is the denial of the truth acknowledged. For those who are contaminated by this sin deny the truth which they know in their heart, and are unwilling to confess it outwardly with their mouth, but deny it, and defame it as false before everyone at all times: which, in turn, can be evidently proven and demonstrated to be evil by the sayings and examples of Scripture cited.

XXXIX. 2. Denied blasphemy. Hence it is called the blasphemy of the Spirit, Matt. 12, Mark 3, Luke 12. And this is what the epistle to the Hebrews says, ch. 6, v. 6, that these men crucify the Son of God again, and put him to an open shame, that is, slander and blaspheme. Heb. 10, v. 29, it is said that they do despite unto the Spirit of grace. An essential requirement therefore of this sin is the blasphemy of the doctrine: which, although it may not always be uttered in manifest words, yet it is certain that such men in their heart blaspheme and execrate the acknowledged truth, as the example of the Pharisees teaches.

XL. 3. Blasphemed opposition. For they are not content with private blasphemy of the truth, but they also attempt to suppress and oppose it publicly and by all means, by voice, by pen, by sword, and by force: just as the example of Pharaoh, the Pharisees, and certain Jesuits proves, to whom nothing is more delightful than to labor for this, that the truth may be eradicated, and all its defenders be killed. And this is to oppose the acknowledged truth maliciously, and thus with the Pharisees to sin against the Holy Spirit.

XLI. 4. The effect of the opposed truth is the rejection of all means of salvation. This, besides examples, is confirmed in turn by the epistle to the Hebrews, when in chapter 6 it says such men crucify Christ again, and in chapter 10 count the Son of God as trodden under foot and count the blood of the covenant an unholy thing. But because there is no other means of salvation than the word and blood of Christ, Acts 4, v. 12, and ch. 10, v. 43, we gather from this that all means are despised by such wicked men and as it were trampled underfoot. For they blaspheme the word of truth, in which grace is offered; they cast away the Sacraments, through which it is accustomed to be conferred; they treat with despite the Holy Spirit, who wishes to work in their hearts, and they resist him in all ways.

XII. And these were those eight principal requirements of the sin against the Spirit, which we briefly recount, so that individually and collectively they may be obvious at a single glance. 1. It concerns doctrine. 2. And that which is acknowledged. 3. And it proceeds from the full knowledge of the one bestowing. 4. Extreme malice of the will. 5. And it denies the acknowledged truth. 6. It blasphemes what it has denied. 7. It attacks what it has blasphemed, and 8. with what is attacked it prostrates and tramples upon all means of salvation. From the collection of these requirements, however, such a definition can be formed: The sin against the Holy Spirit is the malicious and voluntary denial, blasphemy, and attacking of acknowledged truth, and the rejection of all means of salvation.

XIII. And thus from what has been said so far, the nature of this sin has been moderately understood, from which it further appears that neither unbelief alone, nor contumacy alone, nor any other sin should be held as blasphemy against the Spirit, if the voluntary and blasphemous denial of the truth is lacking. No one, therefore, who remains in the Church and retains the faith can or ought to be troubled by those dangerous thoughts, as if he himself had sinned against the Spirit. For when he knows that he has not denied that doctrine, nor blasphemed, he can be certain that he will obtain forgiveness for all his offenses, however many and great and of whatever kind they may be, since the words of Christ are most clear, Matt. 12, where all sins are said to be forgiven, except only blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. As often, therefore, as we must console one who is tempted on account of this sin, the individual requirements must be proposed to him, and it must be shown that they are not found in him, and therefore the conclusion is ready, that he has not sinned against the Holy Spirit, and consequently he ought not to despair of the forgiveness and pardon of his offenses.

Latin:

3. Requisita ex parte ipsius actus.

XXXVII. Quatuor hîc peccati in Spiritum S. essentialia προσκείμενα, vel requisita numeramus, quoniam quatuor primarij actus speciales in eo sunt conspicui.

XXXIIX. 1. Est veritatis agnitæ abnegatio. Hoc enim peccato qui contaminati sunt, ij veritatem, quam in corde suo sciunt diffitentur, & exterius ore fateri nolunt, sed abnegant, & tanquam falsam apud omnes omni tempore diffamant: id quod vicissim allegatis Scripturæ tum dictis, tum exemplis euidenter ad malum probari & demonstrari potest.

XXXIX. 2. Abnegata blasphematio. Hinc enim vocatur blasphemia Spiritus, Matth. 12. Marc. 3. Luc. 12. Et hoc est, quod epistola ad Hebræos dicit. c. 6. vers. 6. homines istos rursum crucifigere Filium Dei, & ostentui habere, id est, calumniari & blasphemare. Hebr. 10. v. 29. dicitur, quòd contumeliam faciant Spiritui gratiæ. Essentiale igitur requisitum peccati huius est blasphematio doctrinæ: quæ ipsa licèt non semper manifestis verbis proferatur, tamen certum est, eiusmodi homines in corde suo blasphemare & execrari veritatem agnitam, vti docet exemplum Pharisæorũ.

XL. 3. Blasphemata oppugnatio. Non enim contenti sunt priuatâ veritatis blasphemiâ, sed publicè etiam modisque omnibus, voce, calamo, ferro, & vi eam supprimere & oppugnare conantur: quemadmodum euincit exemplum Pharaonis, Pharisæorum & quorundam Iesuitarum, quibus nihil magis volupe est, quàm in id elaborare, vt veritas eradicetur, omnesque eius defensores interficiantur. Et hoc est veritatem agnitam malitiosè oppugnare, atque sic cùm Pharisæis in Spiritum sanctum peccare.

XLI. 4. Efficium oppugnatæ veritate omnium salutis mediorum abiectio. Hoc præter exempla vicissim confirmat epistola ad Hebræos, dùm cap. 6. dicit tales homines denuò crucifigere Christum, c. 10. conculcare Filium Dei & sanguinem testamenti pollutum ducere. Quia verò nullum aliud salutis medium est, quàm verbum & sanguis Christi, Act. 4. vers. 12. & c. 10. vers. 43. colligimus inde, omnia media ab eiusmodi sceleratis hominibus contemni & quasi pedibus proculcari, Etenim verbum veritatis, in quo gratia offertur, blasphemant; Sacramenta, per quæ illa conferri solet, abiiciunt; Spiritum. S. qui in ipsorum cordibus operari vult, contumelia afficiunt, illique modis omnibus reluctantur.

XII. Et haec fuerunt ista octo requisita principalia peccati in Spiritum, quae breviter recensemus, vt vno aspectu singula & vniuersa sint obvia. 1. versatur circa doctrinam. 2. eamque agnitam. 3. & procedit ex plena donantis scientia. 4. extrema voluntatis malitia. 5. agnitamque veritatem abnegat. 6. abnegatam blasphemat. 7. blasphematam oppugnat, & 8. cum oppugnata omnia salutis media prosternit & conculcat. Ex horum verò requisitorum collectione talis formari potest definitio: Peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum est veritatis agnitae malitiosa & voluntaria abnegatio, blasphematio & oppugnatio, omniumque salutis mediarum abiectio.

XIII. Atque ita ex hactenus dictis, natura hujus peccati mediocriter fuit cognita, vnde porrò patet, quòd nec sola incredulitas, nec sola contumacia, nec quoduis aliud peccatum pro blasphemia in Spiritum habendū sit, si voluntaria & blasphemia veritatis abnegatio desit. Nemo igitur qui in Ecclesia manet & fidem retinet, turbari potest aut debet periculosis istis cogitationibus, ac si & ipse in Spiritum peccasset. Quando enim scit, se doctrinam istam non abnegasse, nec blasphemasse, certus esse potest se consecuturum esse veniam delictorum suorum omnium, quot & quanta & qualia etiam sint, quandoquidem clarissima sunt verba Christi, Matth. 12. vbi omnia peccata dicuntur remitti, exceptâ solâ in Spiritum sanctum blasphemia. Quotiescunque ergo tentatum ob peccatum hoc consolari debemus, requisita singula isti sunt proponenda, & ostendendum, quòd in ipso non inueniantur, ideoq; paratam esse conclusionem, quòd in Spiritum sanctum non peccauerit, & per consequens de venia & condonatione delictorum suorum desperare non debeat.


### Question II. What the sin against the Holy Spirit is: Question III. What kind is it?

QUESTION III. What kind is it?

I. If we wish to know what kind this sin is, it is necessary that we attend to its adjuncts, which accompany and surround it. For just as form and quiddity grant being simple, so adjuncts grant being such. We establish, however, five primary adjuncts of the sin against the Spirit, which we shall review briefly and concisely.

II. 1. It is of utmost gravity. For indeed this sin is commonly accustomed to be called the most grave, on account of its greatest deformity and malignity. However, a distinction must be made between the first sin of Adam and sins committed after the fall. The blasphemy of the Spirit is called the most grave sin, not absolutely, as if it were also graver than the first sin of Adam; but limitedly, or with respect to the sins which are committed after the fall. The gravity of this sin appears most especially from a diligent consideration of examples and a careful inspection of the individual requirements: especially from the fact that it is never forgiven, which follows as an adjunct already.

III. 2. Irremissibility. The Savior says that all sins are forgiven, but this one is not forgiven either in the present or in the future age, whence theologians gather that the blasphemy of the Spirit is irremissible. It must be noted, however, that Christ indeed employs words signifying the act, yet understands the very power of forgiving. For He said, All sins are forgiven; but this one will not be forgiven. If you understand the act of forgiveness itself here according to the letter, it will follow that all sins are actually forgiven, which is false. Therefore, only the power of forgiving is noted, so that the sense is, All sins can be forgiven, or any other sinner can obtain forgiveness and repent: only the sinner against the Holy Spirit cannot repent, nor obtain remission. Or certainly those words, Every sin shall be remitted, are to be explained thus: that it speaks of the kinds of individual sins, not the individuals of the kinds, and it is indicated that there is no kind of sin that is not remitted (although the individuals of that kind may not be remitted), but only that the sin against the Spirit is never remitted, and is never remitted.

IV. Furthermore, the irremissibility of this offense is confirmed from Heb. 6. v. 4, where it is expressly said that it is impossible for such sinners to return and be renewed to repentance. There is therefore no doubt that this sin is truly called and is irremissible, and by this is distinguished from all other sins. For it alone is irremissible; all other things, as Christ says, are remissible. Hence Athanasius in the disputation against Arius: ὁ εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον βλασφημήσας, ὑπεύθυνός γίνεται αἰωνίꙋ ἁμαρτίας, μὴ συγχωρꙋμένης τῷ σφάλματι, He who speaks blasphemies against the Holy Spirit shall be guilty of an eternal sin, with the lapse of this kind placed beyond pardon. And in the book on the common essence of the Father and the Son: ἀπαραίτητος δίκη τοῖς βλασφημᾶσι τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, An inescapable punishment, he says, for those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit.

V. But some object, Just as this sin by itself and its own nature is not simply irremissible, but is called such by the event: so what would prevent the remaining crimes from also being called irremissible, if the person's repentance is absent? For no sin is absolutely irremissible, on account of the universal grace of God and the redemption of Christ: but it is called irremissible only relatively, insofar as the repentance of man is absent and it is not actually remitted. In this sense and respect, however, all things can be called irremissible. Therefore there will be no distinction between a remissible and an irremissible sin.

VI. I answer, That it is called remissible in a twofold manner, either by reason of the act or by reason of the power, and therefore a distinction must be made between non-remission and irremissibility, and thus also between a sin that is not remitted and one that is irremissible. All other things, when repentance is absent, can be called not remitted, yet not properly irremissible, because it is not impossible for them to be remitted. Concerning this sin, however, it is clearly said, 1 John 5, that it is unto death. Therefore, this alone, by itself and by reason of its quiddity, is conjoined with the impossibility of remission.

VII. But if it be asked further, Whence is this impossibility? We answer in no way from an absolute decree, or a defect of grace, or the particularity of the merit of Christ, or a lack of the Word and Sacraments, because all these are present, and so on the part of God it is not simply impossible that this sin be remitted, since the grace of God abounds over every sin, Rom. 5, v. 20, but this impossibility arises solely from the impossibility of repentance. For it is said expressly, Heb. 6, that it is impossible for such men to return to repentance. Hence, therefore, we argue: Whatever by its own nature is so constituted that it shuts off every approach to repentance, that by its own nature is irremissible, and in this it can well be distinguished from other sins. Such, however, is the sin against the Holy Spirit. Wherefore by its own nature it is irremissible.

IIX. When therefore it is asked, Why is blasphemy against the Spirit called irremissible, and all other sins remissible? We answer briefly that this happens not on the part of God, but only of man, because it is impossible that such a man should perform repentance and apply to himself the grace of God and the merit of Christ. In other sins, however, this is not impossible: Therefore in that respect they are not irremissible.

IX. But if it be asked further, Why is repentance impossible in this sin, and possible in others? The answer will be ready, that for these two reasons

1. It is hardening, and the delivery of man into the power of Satan. For whoever are polluted by this sin, they are hardened, forsaken by God, and delivered to Satan: on account of which hardening it comes to pass that they can never be softened and perform repentance: 2. It is the rejection of all means. For because repentance and conversion occur only through the Word and the Sacraments, hence it is impossible that anyone who always despises and rejects these means should return to repentance. He can never be healed who rejects all medicine: thus he can never be converted who spurns the means divinely ordained. Since, therefore, the nature of this sin consists in this, that the blood of the Testament is polluted, the Word is blasphemed, and thus all means are always rejected, hence arises the impossibility of repentance, and consequently the impossibility of remission, and therefore this sin is called irremissible, while others are remissible, because they are not joined with hardening and the perpetual rejection of means. * 3. Hugo Cardinalis enumerates eight reasons why this sin is irremissible: 1. because it is opposed to the source of remission. 2. because it has no color of excuse. 3. because such a person can scarcely humble himself to seek pardon or to do good. 4. because it is remitted to few and rarely. 5. because it is never read to have been remitted. 6. because it is punished more severely, as if nothing of the due penalty is remitted. 7. because such a person deserves not to repent, 8. because it remains even after death as to the act.

XI. 3. It is hardening. For this is an infallible and most certain consequence of this sin, as all examples show. For when a man blasphemously resists God, he is justly forsaken by God. A spirit of giddiness is sent in, and he is delivered into a reprobate mind. For God always observes this, that He hardens those who are unwilling to believe and yield to the truth. And hence it is that theologians say that the blasphemy of the Spirit is not only a sin, but also a penalty and a cause of sin. It is a punishment, by reason of hardening and desertion: but a cause, by reason of other vices which sprout from it. Therefore, everyone who sins against the Holy Spirit is hardened, yet not conversely, because there is a twofold hardening, one in sins of morals, another in error of faith. He who is hardened in the latter way always sins against the Holy Spirit, but not he who is hardened in the former, since this sin is concerned with doctrine, not with morals.

XII. Final impenitence. For this follows hardening like an inseparable companion. Therefore, everyone who sins against the Spirit is finally impenitent, but not conversely, because many also persevere in sins of morals, and thus are finally impenitent. Hence, final impenitence cannot be the form of this sin, because it is not reciprocal with it, as we have said. But every form is said to be reciprocal with that which it informs. Wherefore it is more conveniently established that final impenitence is not an essential requisite or form, but merely a common, yet inseparable, accident, because this sin is never found unless joined with final impenitence. The reason is that it is never forgiven. If, however, someone were to do penance, it would certainly be forgiven. And what need is there for a lengthy proof, when it is clearly asserted in Heb. 6 that it is utterly impossible for such men to return to repentance?

XIII. 5. Denial of prayer. For the Lord forbade that we should pray for those who blaspheme against the Holy Spirit, Jer. 7 and 1 John 5. But since Augustine warns in Sermon 11 on the words of the Lord that one should not judge concerning this sin except a posteriori and after death and the declaration of divine judgment, to what purpose did it pertain that no one should pray for such a sinner? Ambrose, in book 1 of On Penance, ch. 9, answers from the name 'Who': I do not say that no one should pray for him, namely, someone from the common people, because a sin of this kind needs a perfect intercessor. Jerome, in book 2 against Jovinian, interprets it μετανοητῶς, as if prayer were placed for the pardon which is prayed for. As in Jer. 6. v. 10. Do not pray for this people, that is, you will pray in vain. Others seem to themselves very subtle, when they distinguish between the sin itself and the sinner, and say that one must not indeed pray for the sin, but yet for the sinners. But we ask of them, What is it to pray for sin, or not to pray? Do we not then not pray, when we do not ask for its remission? Therefore the sinner himself is included at the same time, to whom it ought to be remitted, and so all that distinction collapses, because to pray for sin is nothing other than to ask that the sin not be imputed for punishment. And hence we infer that prayer is prohibited both for the sin and the sinner, since the one includes the other.

XIV. But it is to be noted that some are indeed sinners against the Spirit, some seem to be; of the former we know for certain, of the latter we conjecture probably. For these one ought to pray, under this condition of course, if they are not altogether hardened. But when we know from infallible signs that they are truly hardened, and have already for many years maliciously resisted the Spirit, then certainly one ought not to pray for them, by virtue of the divine command. But one must not rashly pronounce and judge concerning such a man, because we can often be deceived, and the judgment of truth is one thing, the judgment of probability another: one is επιστημη, another is δοξα. In the primitive Church indeed there was the gift of the discernment of spirits, 1 Cor. 12. verse 10, which since it has now ceased, for that reason let us not suspend our prayers, but let us include in them even persecutors and blaspheming apostates, unless it is certain and indubitable concerning their malicious hardening.

XII. They object: Christ nevertheless prayed on the cross for the hardened Pharisees, whom He knew had sinned against the Holy Spirit.

I respond 1. Christ did not pray for those sinning maliciously, but ignorantly. For He says: Forgive them Father, for they know not what they do. The prayer of Christ

Latin:

QVÆSTIO III. Quale sit?

I. Si scire voluerimus, quale sit hoc peccatum, necessum est, vt attendamus eius adiuncta, quæ istud comitantur & circumstant. Vt enim forma & quidditas esse simplex, sic adiuncta esse tale largiuntur. Quinque autem primaria peccati in Spiritum adiuncta constituimus, quæ breuiter & strictim recensebimus.

II. 1. Est summagrauitas. Etenim communiter hoc peccatum solet appellari grauissimum, ob maximam deformitatem & malignitatem suam. Distinguendum autem est inter peccatum Adami primum, & peccata exprimootia, vel peccata post lapsum commissa. Blasphemia Spiritus dicitur peccatum grauissimum, non absolutè, ac si grauius quoque foret primo Adami peccato; sed limitatè vel respectu peccatorum, quæ post lapsum committuntur. Grauitas autem huius peccati apparet potissimum ex diligenti exemplorum consideratione, & sedula singulorum requisitorum inspectione: præsertim ex eo, quod nunquam remittatur, quod adiunctam jam sequitur.

III. 2. Irremissibilitas. Dicit Saluator, quod omnia peccata remittantur, hoc autem nec in præsenti, nec in futuro seculo dimittatur, vnde colligunt Theologi, blasphemiam Spiritus esse irremissibilem. Notandum autem, quòd Christus quidem adhibeat verba actum significantia, ipsam tamen remittendi dynamin intelligat. Dixit enim, Omnia peccata remittuntur; hoc autem non remittetur. Si hîc ipsum remissionis actum juxta literam intellexeris, sequetur omnia peccata actu remitti, quod falsum. Sola igitur potentia remittendi notatur, vt sensus sit, Omnia peccata remitti possunt, vel quiuis alius peccator remissionem consequi potest, & pœnitere: sofus autem peccator in Spiritum S. non potest pœnitere, nec remissionem consequi. Aut certè verba ista, Omne peccatum remittetur sic sunt exponenda: quod loquatur de generibus singulorum peccatorum, non singulis generum, & indicetur, non esse vllum genus peccati, quod non remittatur (licèt non singula istius generis remittantur) solùm autem peccatum in Spiritum nunquam remissum esse, & nunquam remitti.

IV. Vlterius autem irremissibilitas hujus delicti confirmatur ex Heb. 6. v. 4. vbi expressè dicitur, quòd sit impossibile tales peccatores vicissim redire & renovari ad pœnitentiam. Nullum igitur est dubium, peccatum hoc verè dici & esse irremissibile, & per hoc ab alijs peccatis omnibus distingui. Ipsum enim solùm est irremissibile, cætera, dicente Christo, omnia sunt remissibilia. Hinc Athanasius in disp. contra Arium: ὁ εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον βλασφημήσας, ὑπεύθυνός γίνεται αἰωνίꙋ ἁμαρτίας, μὴ συγχωρꙋμένης τῷ σφάλματι, Qui in Spiritũ sanctum blasphemias dicit, reus erit æterni peccati lapsu huiusmodi extra veniam constituto. Et in libro de communi essentia Patris & Filij: ἀπαραίτητος δίκη τοῖς βλασφημᾶσι τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον, Indetrectabilis, inquit, pœna blasphemantibus Spiritum sanctum.

V. Objiciunt autem nonnulli, Sicut hoc peccatum per se & suam naturam non simpliciter est irremissibile, sed ab eventu tale dicitur: ita quid prohiberet, quo minùs & reliqua scelera dicantur irremissibilia, si absit personæ pœnitentia? Nullum enim peccatum absolutè est irremissibile, ob vniuersalem Dei gratiam & Christi redemptionem: dicitur autem irremissibile tantùm respectiuè, quatenus abest hominis pœnitentia & actu non remittitur. Hoc verò sensu & respectu omnia nuncupari possunt irremissibilia. Nulla igitur erit distinctio inter pecatum remissibile & irremissibile.

VI. Respondeo, Quòd remissibile dicatur dupliciter vel ratione actus vel ratione potentiæ, ideóq; distinguendum est inter irremissionem & irremissibilitatem, atque sic etiam inter peccatum irremissum & inremissibile. Cætera omnia quando abest pœnitentia, dici possunt irremissa, non tamen propriè irremissibilia, quia non est impossibile illa remitti. De hoc autem peccato clarè dicitur, 1. Ioh. 5. quòd sit ad mortem. Solum ergo hoc per se & ratione quidditatis suæ conjunctum est cum impossibilitate remissionis.

VII. Quod si autem quæratur ulterius, Vnde sit hæc impossibilitas? Respondemus nullo modo ex absoluto decreto, aut defectu gratiæ, aut particularitate meriti Christi, aut carentiâ verbi & Sacramentorum, quia hæc omnia adsunt, adeoque ex parte Dei non est simpliciter impossibile, vt remittatur hoc peccatum, quandoquidem gratia Dei exuberat omne peccatum, Rom. 5. v. 20. sed impossibilitas ista vnicè prouenit ex impossibilitate pœnitentiæ. Dicitur enim expressè, Heb. 6. quòd impossibile sit, eiusmodi homines redire ad pœnitentiam. Hinc igitur argumentamur: Quicquid per suam naturam taliter est comparatum, vt intercludat omnem pœnitentię aditum, istud per suam naturam est irremissibile, & in eo benè distingui potest à peccatis alijs. Tale autem est peccatum in Spiritum sanctū. Quare per suam naturam est irremissibile.

IIX. Cum ergo quæritur, Cur blasphemia in Spiritum dicatur irremissibilis, & reliqua peccata omnia remissibilia? Respondemus breuiter id fieri non ex parte Dei, sed tantum hominis, quia impossibile est, vt talis homo agat pœnitentiam, & gratiam Dei, meritumque Christi sibi applicet. In cæteris autem peccatis hoc non est impossibile: Igitur eo respectu non sunt irremissibilia.

IX. Quòd si autem porrò quæratur, Quare impossibilis sit pœnitentia in hoc peccato, & in cæteris possibilis? Parata erit responsio, quòd ob duas istud rationes

1. Est induratio, & hominis in potestatem Satanæ traditio, Quicunque enim hoc peccato polluti sunt, illi indurantur, a Deo deseruntur, & Satanæ traduntur: ob quam indurationem fit, vt nunquam emolliri & pœnitentiam agere possint: 2. Est omnium mediorum abiectio. Quia enim pœnitentia & conuersio non nisi per verbum fit & Sacramenta, hinc impossibile est, vt aliquis ad pœnitentiam redeat, qui ista media semper contemnit & abijcit. Nunquam sanari potest, qui omnem medicinam respuit: sic nunquam conuerti, qui media diuinitus ordinata spernit. Cùm igitur natura huius peccati in eo consistat, vt sanguis Testamenti polluatur verbum blasphemetur, & ita omnia media semper abijciantur, hinc oritur impossibilitas pœnitentię, & per consequens impossibilitas remissionis, ideoque peccatum hoc dicitur irremissibile, cætera autem remissibilia, quia cum induratione, & perpetua mediorum abiectione nō sunt cōuncta. * 3. Hugo Cardinalis enumerat octo causas, cur peccatum hoc sit irremissibile: 1. quia aduersatur fonti remissionis. 2. quia non habet colorem excusationis. 3. quia talis vix se potest humiliare ad petendam veniam vel ad bonum. 4. quia paucis & rarò remittit.. 5. quia nunquam legitur remissum. 6. quia grauius punitur, quasi nihil de pœna debita dimittatur. 7. quia meretur talis non pœnitere, 8. quia etiam post mortem remanet quoad actum.

XI. 3. Est induratio. Hæc enim infallibile & certissimum huius peccati consequens est, vti ostendunt omnia exempla. Nam cùm homo blasphemè Deo reluctatur iustè à Deo deseritur. Spiritus vertiginis immittitur, & in reprobum sensum traditur. Semper enim hoc Deus obseruat, vt induret, qui veritati credere & cedere nolūt. Aq; hinc est, quod Theologi dicunt, blasphemiā Spiritus non modo peccatum esse, sed & pœną & causam peccati. Pœna est, ratione indurationis & desertionis: Causa verò, ratione aliorum, quæ inde pullulascunt, vitiorum. Omnis ergo peccans in Spiritum sanctum est induratus, non tamen contrà, quia duplex est induratio, quædam in peccatis morum, quædam in errore fidei. Posteriori modo qui induratus est, semper peccat in Spiritum sanctum, non autem qui priori, quoniam peccatum hoc circa doctrinam, non circa mores versatur.

XII. Finalis impœnitentia. Hæc enim indurationem velut individuus comes sequitur. Omnis igitur peccans in Spiritum, est finaliter impœnitens, sed non contra, quia multi etiam in peccatis morum perseverant, & sic finaliter impœnitentes sunt. Proindè impœnitentia finalis nequit esse forma huius peccati, quia non reciprocatur cum eo, vt diximus. Omnis autem forma cum suo formato reciprocè dicitur. Quare convenientius statuitur, finalem impœnitentiam, non esse essentiale requisitum aut formam, sed duntaxat accidens commune, attamen inseparabile, quia nunquam datur istud peccatum nisi conjunctum cum impœnitentia finali. Ratio, quia nunquam remittitur. Si autem pœnitentiam quis ageret, vtique remitteretur. Et quid opus est prolixa probatione, cum clarè asseratur. Hebr. 6. tales homines redire ad pœnitentiam prorsus esse impossibile?

XIII. 5. precationis negatio. Prohibuit enim Dominus, ne pro blasphemis in Spiritum S. oremus, Ier. 7. & 1. Ioh. 5. Cùm autem August. moneat ferm. 11 de verb. Dom. non nisi à posteriori & post mortem, divinique judicij declarationem judicandum esse de hoc peccato, quorsum attinebat, ne quis pro tali peccato oret? Ambr. l. 1. de pœn. c. 9. ex pro nomine Quis respondet; Non dico, vt pro eo quis oret, scili: de plebe aliquis, quia huiusmodi peccatum indiget perfecto deprecatore. Hieron. l. 2. ad v. Iovin. interpretatur μετανοητῶς, quasi oratio posita sit pro venia, quae oratur. sicut Ier. 6. v. 10. Noli orare pro isto populo, hoc est, frustra orabis, Alij videntur sibi valde subtiles, du distinguunt inter peccatum ipsum & peccatorem, dicuntque pro peccato quidem orandum non esse, attamen pro peccatoribus. Verum quaerimus ex ijs, Quid sit pro peccato orare, vel non orare? An non tum non oramus, quando eius remissionem non petimus? Includitur ergo ipse simul peccator, cui debebat remitti, adeoque corruit omnis illa distinctio, quia pro peccato orare, nihil aliud est, quam petere, ne peccatum imputetur ad poenam. Atque hinc inferimus, prohibitam esse precationem & pro peccato & peccatore, quoniam vnum includit alterum.

XIV. Notandum vero est, quod peccatores in Spiritum quidem sint, quidam videantur, De illis certo scimus, de his probabiliter conjicimus. Pro his orari debet, sub hac nimirum conditione, si omnino non sunt indurati. Quando autem ex infallibilibus indicijs cognoscimus, illos vere induratos esse, & iam per multos annos malitiose resistere Spiritui, tum certe pro ijs, vi mandati diuini orari non debet. Non autem temere pronunciandum & iudicandum est de homine tali, quia saepe possumus falli & aliud veritatis, aliud probabilitatis est iudicium: aliud επιστημη aliud δοξα. In primitiua quidem Ecclesia signif. donum Διακρίσεως πνευμάτων, 1. Cor. 12. vers. 10. quod cum iam cesset, idcirco preces nostras non supendamus, sed ijs persecutores etiam & blasphemos Apostatas comprehendamus, nisi certo & indubitanter de malitiosa illorum induratione constat.

XII. Obijciunt: Christus tamen orauit in cruce pro Pharisaeis induratis, quos sciebat peccasse in Spiritum sanctum.

Respond 1. Christus non orauit pro peccantibus malitiose, sed ignoranter. Dicit enim: Remitte ijs Pater, quia nesciunt, quid faciant. Precatio Christi


## 12 Preface to the Second Decade

A twofold knowledge of God is commonly established: the one they call intuitive, the other indeed enigmatic. According to the former, the essence of God is known fully and in itself: according to the latter, it is described obscurely only through works and ἰδιώματα (idioms/properties). The former is a priori, the latter a posteriori. The former belongs to Christians who are triumphant, the latter to those who are militant. For we are here on the way, not yet in the fatherland; we are still running in the stadium, we have not yet received the full βραβεῖον (prize). Wherefore we see God only through a glass in a riddle, 1 Cor. 13, v. 12, not yet of

Preface.

face to face, as he is, 1 John 3:2. We can see his back parts with Moses, we cannot see his face and live. Exod. 33:23.

There are indeed many idioms by which God is proposed to us to be known only a posteriori, among which three excel above all. 1. Inexhaustible goodness. 2. Immutable justice. 3. Ineffable mercy. Concerning goodness it is read in Matt. 19:17. No one is good, except one God. Concerning justice. Ps. 119:137. Righteous are you, O Lord, and upright is your judgment. Concerning mercy Luke 6:36. Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful.

God is good both essentially, because he is goodness and charity itself in the abstract 1 John 4:16, and efficiently, because he derives into creatures the fountains of his goodness, with which the earth is full, Ps. 33:5, and finally, because he is the end of ends, and the greatest good of all goods, indeed he himself is all things, and in all, 1 Cor. 15:28, Coloss. 3:11.

God manifested vindictive justice both by words, Deut. 4:24, Job 9:13, Isa. 30:27, ch. 34:2, Nahum 1:25, Heb. 10:31, and by threats, Levit. 26:14, Deut. 28:15, Ps. 11:6, Prov. 1:24, and by examples, such as the damnation of demons, Epistle of Ju de, v. 6. The universal flood, Gen. 7. v. 20. 21. 22. The conflagration of Sodom, Gen. 19. v. 24. The drowning of Pharaoh, Ex. 14. v. 27. The expulsion of the Canaanites, Ios. 6. v. 10. The passion of Christ, and the final devastation of Jerusalem.

The mercy of God is when His heart is moved by the misery of another, and is inclined to bring aid. This is so great that we can more easily marvel at it than express it in words. For the Lord is good to all, and His mercies are over all His works, Ps. 145. v. 9.

And these are those three primary properties, indices of the divine θείας: which, although they are exerted regarding various objects, were nevertheless made conspicuous primarily through works concerning man. For just as all things were created for the sake of man, and man alone for the sake of God: so also God takes care of man above all, and in this very care He has manifested Himself in various ways.

There are three principal states of human nature in this life. 1. Of innocence or integrity. 2. Of misery or the fall. 3. Of grace or reparation. In each state a peculiar ἰδίωμα and ἰσχὺς of God is shown. Goodness shines forth from the state of innocence: Justice from the state of the fall: Mercy from the state of reparation.

Consider, O man, how great was the goodness of God,

who, when you were nothing, brought it about that you were something? He formed the body distinguished by various members: He breathed in a rational soul, so that you might be named the Horizon of corporeal and spiritual nature. Nor was that enough: We were created in the image of God himself, Gen. 1. v. 26, and our intellect was conformed to Him through Wisdom, Coloss. 3. v. 10, the will through justice, Eph. 4. v. 24, the appetite through rectitude, Ecclesiastes 7. v. 30, the whole man through immortality, Wis. 2. v. 23, and power over the other creatures, Gen. 1. v. 26. Behold, as soon as you were founded, you were founded a prince: You are an imperial animal, O man! says Basil, homily 10. Who from this would not recognize the goodness of the Creator? Who would not exclaim with the Psalmist: Taste and see how sweet the Lord is? Ps. 34. v. 9. Furthermore, just as goodness shone forth in creation, so justice shone forth in the fall, alas, a pitiable one, the memory of which makes my hair stand on end, my mind shudder, my cheek weep, my right hand stiffen. We were cast out of the garden into death, from roses into thorns, from blessing into anxiety and a curse. The Lord arose there to judge a just judgment. He inflicted punishments upon the Serpent, Gen. 3. v. 14, who only was the instrument of Satan. Punishments for the seducer, v. 15, whose head was to be crushed. Punishments for the woman, v. 16, whose sorrows were multiplied. Punishments for the earth itself, v. 17, which incurred a curse. Punishments for Adam, v. 19, because he must eat his bread in the sweat of his brow. But the wrath of the Lord has not yet been appeased: He has afflicted the whole human race on account of the one transgression of the πρωτοπλάςων with most just punishments. If you look at life, what else is it but pain and labor? Psalm 90, v. 10. If the body, it is born subject to various diseases and finally to death: If the soul, it is, alas, deprived of the image of God. We are born slaves of sin, John 8, v. 32, and children of wrath, Ephesians 2, v. 3, under the power of darkness, Colossians 1, v. 13, bound by the snares of the Devil to do his will, 2 Timothy 2, v. last. Four horrendous wounds have been inflicted upon the soul, with God permitting and the Devil as the author. Ignorance clings to the mind, malice to the will, concupiscence to the ἐπιθυμητικῷ [appetitive part], and finally infirmity to the θυμικῷ [irascible part], on account of perverse and vehement affections. In so many ways and examples, indeed, has God made his justice manifest regarding the fall of men.

But I have narrated and explained all these things more fully in the first decade of the Anthropological disputations. For it has been spoken concerning the state of integrity of the fall and corruption. There we saw the goodness of GOD, that we might worship: here [we see] his justice, that we might fear, and acknowledge the deformity of sin.

As concerns the third principal ἰδίωμα of GOD, namely Mercy, a living delineation and picture of this is proposed in the state of Restoration. Man had been cast into misery: but the Most High has had mercy upon us. He took counsel concerning the liberating of the human race: He ordained the Means, by which those who use them, obtain the inheritance of eternal salvation.

And here that abyss of divine gifts and counsels is opened, so that one must exclaim in the manner of the Apostle: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and mercy of God! How incomprehensible are his benefits! Here one must speak of divine grace, and the eternal predestination of believers to salvation: one must speak of the execution of this decree in time: one must speak of the universal means necessary for obtaining salvation, of the Redemption made through Christ; of the calling through the Word and Sacraments; of faith apprehending the merit of Christ; of justification, Renewal, Preservation, and similar most brilliant arguments of divine grace. Who here would not see the most wide-spread field of discourse being opened, the beginning of which you will find easily, but the end with difficulty?

I have entered this field with God, and I began some contemplation of divine φιλανθρωπίας, and I was detained at the very threshold for so long that an entire decade of disputations had to be composed concerning the first and principal charisma, which is eternal predestination, the foundation and anchor of our salvation. For so many most serious questions occurred that, unless I wished the σκέψιν I had begun to be incomplete and half-full, I could not have contracted the disputations any further.

But because the entry was so laborious, and the consideration of one χαρίσματος demanded such a long time, I almost cast aside all hope and thought of progress and continuation. For the account of my office does not promise that I should grant much time to meditations of this kind, even if I wished to most of all. Nevertheless, I wished these preliminary little dissertations, collected into one bundle, to go forth, so that all the pious might admire with me the depth of divine Mercy, and rejoice in the abundance of heavenly blessing. Confess therefore to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever. Let Israel now say, For he is good, for his mercy is forever.

Latin:

DVplex cognitio Dei vulgò conftituitur: Alteram intuitiuam vocant, alteram verò ænigmaticam. Secundum Illam effentia Dei plenè & in fe cognofcitur: Secundum hanc per opera tantum & ἰδιώματα obfcurè defcribitur. Illa eft à priori, hæc à pofteriori. Illa triumphantibus, hæc militantibus Chriftianis competit. Sumus n. hîc in via, nondum in patria; Adhuc currimus in stadio, nondum βραβεῖον plenum accipimus. Quare Deum videmus non nifi per fpeculum in ænigmate, 1. Cor. 13. v. 12. nondum de

Præfatio.

facie ad faciem, sicuti est, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 2. Posteriora eius videre possumus cum Mose, faciem videre & viuere non possumus. Exod. 33. v. 23.

Sunt vero multa idiomata, quibus Dei sola nobis à posteriori proponitur cognoscenda, inter quæ tria potissimûm excellunt. 1. Inexhausta bonitas. 2. Immutabilis iustitia. 3. Ineffabilis misericordia. De bonitate legitur Mat. 19. ver. 17. Nemo est bonus, nisi unus Deus. De iustitia. Pf. 119. v. 137. Iustus es Domine, & rectum iudicium tuum. De misericordia Luc. 6. v. 36. Estote misericordes, sicut & Pater vester misericors est.

Bonus est Deus tùm essentialiter, quia est ipsa in abstracto bonitas & charitas 1. Ioh. 4. v. 16. tùm efficienter, quia in creaturas, derivat fontes bonitatis suæ, quâ plena est terra, Pf. 33. v. 5. tùm finaliter, quia est finium finis, & bonorum omnium bonum maximum, imò ipse est omnia, & in omnibus, 1. Cor. 15. v. 28. Coloss. 3. v. 11.

Iustitiam vindicatricem manifestauit Deus tùm dictis. Deut. 4. v. 24. Iob. 9. v. 13. Esa: 30. v. 27. c. 34. v. 2. Nahum. 1. v. 25. Hebr. 10. v. 31. tùm minis, Leuit. 26. v. 14. Deut. 28. v. 15.
