Pf. 11. v. 6. Prou. 1. v. 24. tùm exemplis, qualia sunt damnatio dæmonum, Epist. Iuda. v. 6. Vniuersale diluuium, Gen. 7. v. 20. 21. 22. Sodomæ deflagratio, Gen. 19. v. 24. Pharaonis submersio, Ex. 14. v. 27. Cananæorum expulsio, Ios. 6. v. 10. Christi passio, & vltima Hierosolymæ vastatio.

Misericordia Dei est, cum alienâ miseriâ cor ipsius mouetur, & ad opem ferendam flectitur. Hæc tanta est, vt facilius eam mirari, quàm verbis effari possimus. Bonus enim est Dominus vniuersis, & miserationes eius supra omnia opera eius Ps. 145. v. 9.

Et hæ sunt tres illæ proprietates primariæ, θείας diuinæ indices: quæ licèt circa varia obiecta exerantur, inprimis tamen per opera circa hominem maximè facta sunt conspicua. Vt enim omnia propter hominem, solus homo propter Deum est conditus: sic & Deus hominis potissimùm curam gerit, & in cura hac ipsa semetipsum variis modis manifestauit.

Tres sunt naturæ humanæ status in hac vita principales. 1. Innocentiæ vel integritatis. 2. Miseriæ vel lapsus. 3. Gratiæ vel reparationis. In quolibet statu peculiare ἰδίωμα Dei καὶ ἰσχὺς ostensum est. Bonitas elucet ex statu innocentiæ: Iustitia ex statu lapsus: Misericordia ex statu reparationis.

Cogites, ô homo, quanta fuerit Dei boni-

tas, qui cùm nihil esses, effecit, vt aliquid esses? Formauit corpus variis membris distinctum: inspirauit animam rationalem, vt nominari possis Horizon corporalis & spiritualis naturæ. Nec satis fuit: Ad imaginem ipsius Dei creati sumus, Gen 1.v. 26.& conformatus ipsi est intellectus noster per Sapientiam, Coloss. 3. v. 10. voluntas per iustitiam, Eph. 4. v. 24. appetitus per rectitudinem, Ecclesiastæ.7.v.30. totus homo per immortalitatem, Sap. 2. v. 23. & potestatem super creaturas cæteras, Gen. 1.v. 26. Ecce Statim vt conditus es, princeps es conditus: Imperiale es animal, ô homo! inquit Basilius homil. 10. Quis inde non agnoscat bonitatem creatoris? Quis non cum Psalte exclamet: Gustate & videte, quàm suauis sit Dominus? Psal. 34.v.9. Porrò vt bonitas in creatione, sic iustitia emicuit in lapsu, proh dolor, miserando, cujus dum recordor, Stat coma, mens horret, flet gena, dextra riget. Coniecti sumus ex horto in mortem, ex rosis in spinas, ex benedictione in anxietatem & maledictionem. Surrexit ibi Dominus ad iudicandum iustum iudicium. Pœnas inflixit Serpenti, Gen. 3. v. 14. qui duntaxat ὄργανον fuit Satanæ. Pœnas seductori. v. 15, cuius caput conterendum fuit. Pœnas mulieri. v. 16. cujus ærumnæ multiplicatæ sunt, Pœnas ipsi terræ v. 17, quæ maledictionem incurrit. Pœnas Adamo v. 19. quòd in sudore vultus pane suo vesci debeat. Sed nondum acquieuit ira Domini: Totum genus humanum ob vnam πρωτοπλάςων præuaricationem justissimis pœnis adfecit. Si vitam adspicis, quid aliud est, quàm dolor & labor? Psalm. 90. v. 10. Si corpus, variis morbis, mortique tandem obnoxium nascitur: Si animam, priuata, eheu, est imagine Dei. Nascimur serui peccati, Ioh. 8. v. 32. & iræ filii, Ephes. 2. v. 3. sub potestate tenebrarum, Coloss. 1. v. 13. constricti laqueis Diaboli ad voluntatem eius, 2. Tim. 2. v. ultim. Inflicta sunt animæ, permittente DEO, authore Diabolo, quatuor horrenda vulnera. Hæret in mente ignorantia, in voluntate malitia, in appetitu ἐπιθυμητικῷ Concupiscentia, in θυμικῷ denique infirmitas, ob proteruos & vehementes adfectus. Tot nimirum modis & exemplis suam Deus iustitiam circa hominum lapsum testatam fecit.

Hæc omnia verò primâ disputationum Anthropologicarum decade fusius enaraui & explicui. Dictum enim est de statu integritatis; disputatum est de statu lapsus & corruptionis. Ibi bonitatem DEI vidimus, vt colamus: hîc iustitiam, vt timeamus, & peccati deformitatem agnoscamus.

Tertium principale ἰδίωμα DEI quod attinet, nempè Misericordiam, huius viua delineatio & pictura in statu Reparationis proponitur. Coniectus erat homo in miseriam: sed misertus nostri est Altissimus. Consilium cepit de liberando genere humano: Media ordinauit, quibus qui vtuntur, aeternae salutis haereditatem adipiscuntur.

Atque hîc abyssus illa panditur diuinorum charismatum & consiliorum, vt exclamandum sit ad Apostoli morem: O altitudo diuitiarum sapientiae & misericordiae Dei! Quàm incomprehensibilia sunt eius beneficia! Dicendum hîc est de gratia diuina, & aeterna praedestinatione credentium ad salutem: dicendum est de decreti huius executione in tempore: dicendum est de mediis vniuerfalibus ad salutem consequendam necessariis, de Redemtione per Christum facta; de vocatione per Verbum & Sacramenta; de fide meritum Christi apprehendente; de iustificatione, Renouatione, Conseruatione, & similibus diuinae gratiae argumentis luculentissimis. Quis hî non videat latissimum difserendi campum aperiri, cuius exordium facilè, difficulter finem inueneris?

Ingressus ego sum cum Deo hunc campum, & incepi φιλανθρωπίας diuinæ contemplationem aliquam, inque primo limine tamdiu detentus sum, vt integra disputationum decas conficienda fuerit de primo & principali charismate, quod est æterna prædestinatio, salutis nostræ fundamen & anchora. Tot enim quæstiones grauissimæ occurrerunt, vt nisi σκέψιν inceptam voluerim mancam esse & semiplenam, disputationes magis contrahere nequiuerim.

Quia vero ingressus tàm fuit laboriosus, & vnius χαρίσματος consideratio tàm diuturnum tempus postulauit, de progressu & continuatione spem ferè & cogitationem omnem abieci. Nec enim promittit officii ratio, vt multum temporis tribuam huiusmodi meditationibus, si maximè vellem. Has tamen præliminares dissertatiunculas in vnum fasciculum collectas prodire volui, vt pii omnes profunditatem Misericordiæ diuinæ mecum admirarentur, & vbertate cœlestis benedictionis lætarentur. Confitemini ergo Domino, quoniam bonus, quoniam in seculum misericordia eius. Dicat nunc Israel, Quoniam bonus, quoniam in seculum miseri-


### Preface

Preface.

his mercy. Let the house of Aaron now say, That his mercy endureth for ever. Let all the godly now say, who fear the Lord, That his mercy endureth for ever, from Ps. 118, v. 1 & following.

This second Decade of Christian ἀνθρωπολογίας (anthropology), I wish to be sacred and dedicated to Your Name, most Reverend and Magnificent Man, Lord and Brother in Christ to be honored forever. In it is discussed an arduous controversy of the greatest importance, which I willingly submit to the judgment of excellent Theologians. Among these, I count Your R. T. M. (Reverend and Magnificent Excellency) in the first place, because of your merits toward the Church, which are great, and because of your most learned writings, of which there are many. I will not recount them individually. Even your single most vigorous Commentary on the divine ἀποκάλυψιν (revelation) testifies most clearly to your hidden Theological erudition and dexterity in interpretation. May our God preserve You, and grant you enough leisure so that you may be able to continue these holy labors and happily complete them. It will then have been enough accomplished, enough labored: the ἀποκάλυψις (revelation) will no longer be able to be obscure to anyone, but full, open, perspicuous: for which name posterity, if there is to be any, will give thanks to You, and will decorate you with the most deserved right with the encomium of a Great Theologian and Faithful interpreter.

Preface.

If, therefore, your suffrage should be added to these little lucubrations of mine, it will be like that of many, nor shall I care so much if Momus finds fault with them, nor that everything be touched to the quick. As is our renewal, so is our knowledge imperfect: but it can grow from day to day. We live there, where the perfect perfection of divine gifts is not yet, inasmuch as where every perfect person is unworthy of perfection, as Fulgentius says, lib. 1 ad Mon. p. 31. Whoever, therefore, says he is blameless, is either proud or foolish, by the judgment of Cyprian, Serm. de Eleemos. I therefore willingly acknowledge my infirmity: if there be any error anywhere, I wish to be admonished in a friendly manner, and I ask to be benevolently forgiven. Unless someone brings this spirit, let him leave these things untouched, and let him assume they were not written for him. This suffices for me, that I know nothing alien to the analogy of Faith and the Symbolic books is defended here. Therefore, also in this name, R. T. M. I consecrate these things, that they may be a testimony of our consensus in faith, and of our most intimate union in Christ.

But above all, let this inscription be a certain argument of my observance and gratitude. For that you pursue me, undeserving as I am, with a sincere and not at all feigned spirit, I have perceived and am most certain. Therefore, in whatever way I may declare a grateful spirit

Latin:

Præfatio.

cordia eius. Dicat nunc domus Aaren, Quoniam in seculum misericordia eius. Dicant nunc omnes pij, qui timent Dominum, Quoniam in seculum misericordia eius ex Pf. 118. v. 1. & sequentibus.

Hanc verò secundam ἀνθρωπολογίας Christianæ Decadem Nomini Tuo, Vir admodum Reuerende & Magnifice, Domine & in Christo Frater æternùm honorande, sacram dicatamque volo. Disputatur in ea de ardua, maximique momenti controuersia, quam excellentium Theologorum censuræ lubens subiicio. His R. T. M. inprimis annumero, propter merita in Ecclesiam, quæ magna, & propter scripta eruditissima, quorum multa sunt. Non recensebo singula. Vel solus in divinam ἀποκάλυψιν Commentarius nervosissimus, de recondita eruditione Theologica, & interpretandi dexteritate Vestra luculentissimè testatur. Seruet Te Deus noster, & tantum otii concedat, vt sanctos hos labores cõtinuare, & feliciter possis absoluere. Satis tùm erit præstitum, satis laboratum: Nulli amplius obscura esse poterit ἀποκάλυψις, sed plena, aperta, perspicua: quo nomine posteritas, si qua futura est, Tibi gratias aget, encomio Theologi Magni, Fidelisque interpretis iure meritissimo decorabit.

Præfatio.

Quod si ergo vestrum accedat suffragium ad has lucubratiunculas meas, instar multorum istud erit, nec curabo adeò, si Momus illas reprehendat, nec omnia sint acu tacta. Vt renovatio, sic cognitio nostra imperfecta est: De die autem in diem crescere potest. Ibi viuimus, vbi diuinorum munerum nondum est perfecta perfectio, vtpote vbi omnis perfectus perfectionis est indignus, dicente Fulgentio l. 1. ad Mon. pag. 31. Quisquis ergo se inculpatum dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est, Cypriani iudicio, Serm. de Eleemos. Meam proinde infirmitatem lubens agnosco: Sicubi erratum sit, amicè moneri volo, & benevolè ignosci peto. Quem animum nisi quis adferat, hæc intacta linquat, & sibi scripta non esse autumet. Mihi hoc sufficit, quod ab analogia Fidei & libris Symbolicis nihil alienum hîc defendi sciam. Proinde & hoc nomine R. T. M. ista consecro, vt testimonium sint nostri consensus in fide, & coniunctionis in Christo arctissimæ.

Inprimis autem hæc inscriptio certum sit argumentum observantiæ & gratitudinis meæ. Quod enim sincero minimeque fucato animo immerentem me prosequaris, perspectum habeo & compertissimum. Quocunque igitur pacto animum gratum decla-


### Preface

Preface.

I am rarely able, I confess myself bound to that; hence I honor You and will honor You as long as I shall live: for my mind is on my forehead; as I feel, so I speak; I honor, I say, You and will honor You, because I am not able to compensate for your merits in any other way. For that purpose, therefore, I offer these disputations to Your Reverend Magnificence, and I ask that they be looked upon with favorable eyes, of which I have no doubt. May GOD from on high mercifully bless You, and preserve You safe for a very long time for the benefit of the Church and of many good people, Amen. Thus I was vowing. Wittenberg, the 24th day of February, 1614.

To Your Reverend Magnificence.

Most devoted Brother in Christ

BALTHASAR MEISNER, D.

BALTHASAR MEISNERVS D,


## 13 Disputation I. On the Grace of God

Preface by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Wilhelm Nigrinus, a Bohemian from Kadaň.

Προοίμιον. I.

In the first decade of our disputations, we considered both the state of innocence, which was created by God, and the state of misery, which was introduced through the fall; there follows a third state, which is called that of Grace or Restoration. For once misery is known, the next step is to seek a remedy. Therefore, just as the first decade was for the most part παθολογικὴ (pathological), so this second one will be θεραπευτικὴ (therapeutic). There we recognized the evil, here we shall seek the remedy: there we were saddened on account of guilt, here we shall exult on account of grace: there with trembling we saw the punishing justice of God: here with joy we shall perceive the justifying mercy of God.

II. Moreover, this state is most extensive on account of the abundance of its subject matter. For all the benefits of God flow together and concur here in abundance, such as eternal predestination, temporal redemption, the calling of the redeemed, the justification of the called, the renewal of the justified; and the preservation of the renewed until the end of life, which will finally be followed by everlasting glorification. Whence it happens that the principal articles of our religion must be explained here, such as those concerning the grace of God, concerning Election and Redemption, concerning the Christ the person and office of the Redeemer. Concerning the nature and powers of our free will before conversion. Concerning the means of conversion, namely concerning the Law and the Gospel, concerning the Sacraments, concerning Baptism and the Supper of the Lord, concerning the application of grace itself, which occurs through justification and repentance, concerning the fruits of justice or good works, concerning the Church, concerning the cross, concerning prayers, and concerning the different orders of life.

III. But because it would be too long if all and each of these heads of doctrine were to be discussed, for that reason we shall set aside certain controversies, and we shall ventilate only those which Bellarmine cast into his last volume: for we treated of Christ in the Academic Schools in disputations 1 and 2. The doctrine concerning the Sacraments, which Bellarmine treats in the third volume, we shall reserve for a special course, if the Lord wills. The article concerning the Church, and those things which pertain to this, we have explained sufficiently at length both in the Academic schools in disputation 4, and in the Catholic Consultation opposed to Leonard Lessius. Since, therefore, we do not wish to do what has already been done, we shall only follow the footsteps of Bellarmine at this time, and just as in the preceding decade we dispatched the first two general controversies of the last volume, namely concerning the grace of the first man, and concerning the loss of grace, and the state of sin: so now we shall examine the last one with God, which he inscribed concerning the reparation of grace through Jesus Christ our Lord.

IV. He divided, however, this last controversy into three other principal ones. 1. It is concerning grace and free will, where he also examined the topic of predestination. 2. Concerning justification and good works in general, where the article concerning the Law and the Gospel is also held. 3. Concerning good works in particular, namely prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. These controversial articles, therefore, we shall primarily explain, and so in the future we shall dispute. 1. Concerning the grace of God, which is the source of our reparation. 2. Concerning predestination, by which we were chosen from eternity to life. 3. Concerning free will, in what manner that behave before justification. 4. Of the Law and the Gospel, which are the means of conversion. 5. Of justification, in which the benefits of redemption are applied. 6. Of good works, which follow justification.

V. But in this συν' συζητήσει [joint discussion] we shall make a beginning from the eternal grace of God, through which we are all that we are, 1 Cor. 15:10. For He, when we were not, gave out of grace that we might be; and when it was ill with us, out of grace He brought it about that it could be well. He works, beginning, that we may will, and He cooperates, perfecting, with those who will, August. de grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 17. We implore His grace, that we may say and do things pleasing to Him and salutary to the Church, Amen.

VI. But three questions especially come to be considered here. 1. In how many ways is the word Grace accepted in the Scriptures? 2. What does Grace especially denote in the article of both Election and justification? 3. How many species or divisions of Grace are there? Therefore, we shall set forth our mind on each of these in order.

Latin:

Præf. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Wilhelmo Nigrino, Cadanensi Bohemo.

Προοίμιον. I.

PRimâ disputationum nostrum Decade considerauimus, tùm statum Innocentiæ, quæ à Deo concteata; tùm statum miseriæ, quæ per lapsum introducta est, sequitur status tertius qui vocatur Gratiæ vel Reparationis. Cognita enim miseriâ, proximum est, vt quæratur medicina. Vt ergò Decas prima quoad maximam partem fuit παθολογικὴ: ita hæc secunda erit θεραπευτικὴ. Ibi cognouimus malum, hic quæremus remedium: Ibi tristati sumus ob culpam, hic exultabimus ob gratiam: Ibi cum tremore vidimus iustitiam Dei punientem: hic cum gaudio sentiemus misericordiam Dei iustificantem.

II. Est autem status hic ob rerum copiam diffusissimus. Omnia enim Dei beneficia vbertim hûc confluunt & concurrunt, qualia sunt æterna prædestinatio, temporalis redemptio, redemptorum vocatio, vocatorum iustificatio, iustificatorum renovatio; & renouatorum vsq; ad finem vitæ conseruatio, quam tandem excipiet perennis glorificatio. Vnde fit, vt præcipui nostræ religionis articuli hîc explicandi veniant, quales sunt de gratia Dei, de Electione & Redemptione, de Christi demptoris persona & officio. De natura & viribus nostri arbitrij ante conuersionem. De medijs conuersionis, nimirum de lege & Euangelio, de Sacramentis, de Baptismo & Cœna Domini, de ipsa gratiæ applicatione, quæ fit per iustificationẽ & pœnitentiam, de fructibus iustitiæ vel bonis operibus, de Ecclesia, De cruce, de precibus, & de diuerfis vitæ ordinibus.

III. Quia verò nimis prolixum esset futurum, si hæc doctrinæ capita vniuersa & singula deberent discuti, ob id controuersias quasdam seponemus, & eas tantùm ventilabimus, quas Bellarminus in tomum vltimum coniecit: De Christo enim egimus in Scholis Academicis disp. 1. & 2. Doctrina de Sacramentis, quam tertio tomo pertractat Bellarminus, peculiari collegio, si Dominus voluerit, reseruabimus. Articulum de Ecclesia, & quæ hûc spectant, fusè satis exposuimus tum in scholis Acad. disp. 4. tûm in Consult. Cathol. Leonhardo Lessio opposita. Cùm ergò actum agere nolimus Bellarmini tantùm vestigia hoc tempore prememus, & sicut præced. decade duas primas Tomi vltimi controuersias generales expediuimus, nimirum de gratia primi hominis, & de amissione gratiæ, statuque Peccati: sic nunc postremam cum Deo excutiemus, quam inscripsit de Reparatione gratiæ per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum.

IV. Dispescuit autem hanc vltimam controuersiam in tres alias principales. 1. Est de gratia & libero arbitrio, vbi simul inspexit locu de prædestinatione. 2. De iustificatione & bonis operibus generatim, vbi habetur etia articulus de lege & Euangelio. 3. De bonis operibus in specie, nimirū oratione, ieiunio & eleemosyna. Hos igitur controuersos articulos potissimùm exponemus, adeóq; in posterū disputabimus. 1. De gratia Dei, quæ fons est reparationis nostræ. 2. De prædestinatione, quâ ab æterno electi sumus ad vitam. 3. De libero arbitrio, quo modo istud se habeat ante iustificationem. 4. De lege & Evangelio, quæ sunt media conversionis. 5. De iustificatione, in qua beneficia redemptionis applicantur. 6. De bonis operibus, quæ iustificationem sequuntur.

V. Hæc autem συν' συζητήσει faciemus initium ab Æternæ Dei gratia, per quam sumus omne quod sumus, 1. Cor. 15. v. 10. Is enim, cum non essemus, ex gratia dedit, vt essemus; cumque nobis malè esset; ex gratia effecit, vt benè esse posset. Ipse vt velimus, operatur incipiens, & volentibus cooperatur perficiens, August. de grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 17. Ipsius gratiam imploramus. vt grata ipsi, Ecclesiæque salutaria dicamus & faciamus, Amen.

VI. Tres verò quæstiones potissimùm hîc consideranda veniunt. 1. Quot modis vocabulum Gratiæ in Scripturis accipiatur? 2. Quid Gratia in articulo tùm Electionis tùm iustificationis præcipuè denotet. 3. Quot sint species vel divisiones Gratiæ? De his ergo singulis mentem nostram ordine exponemus.


### Question I. What are the principal meanings of Grace in the Scriptures?

I. The Jesuits wish grace to be called from 'giving freely' (gratis dando). For thus Bellarmine writes, l. 1. de grat. cap. 1: grace received its name from Grace, because it is given freely. He proves it from August. tract. in Ps. 44, who says: It is deservedly named Grace, because it is given freely. And Gregorius de Valent. tom. 2. disp. 8. quæst. 1: punct. 1, cites the saying of August. in Ps. 49: If it is called grace, it is given freely. And to this they refer that passage in Rom. 4:4: To him who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace, but according to debt.

II. Hence also it is that grace properly signifies to them a gift, given freely by God, and especially that gift which they say is conferred in the justification of man. For thus Becanus explains it, disp. On the aids of grace, part 2, chapter 1. Grace, properly speaking, is a gratuitous and supernatural gift of God, which is conferred upon us through the merits of Christ for the sake of obtaining eternal life.

III. However, although we do not deny that 'grace' sometimes denotes gratuitous gifts in the Scriptures, yet we deny that it is properly and principally called grace from 'giving freely' (gratis dando). For this derivation of the name is too narrow, and it does not suit every grace, but only that which is 'freely given,' as they say, that is, gratuitous gifts. For which reason, some derive it rather from 'grateful' (grato), which denotes a thing accepted, loved, and desired.

IV. But, setting aside the etymology of the name, we judge it to be more fruitful if the principal significations are noted, of which there are primarily three, though in such a way that not all are equally principal and common.

V. 1. The most common and most principal signification of Grace is this: that it denotes the favor and mercy, or rather the merciful and clement will of God, by which He is affected toward us humans. Flacius, in his Clavis Scripturae, calls this signification 'Active,' because God acts toward us through it. The Hebrew word is חָנַן, 'he has affected with grace' or 'deemed worthy of favor.' Hence, as the inspection of the letters themselves teaches, the German 'gönnen/gunst.' The LXX mostly rendered it by 'to have mercy,' 'to spare,' 'to show grace to someone,' 'to be gracious and merciful,' 'to be favorable and well-disposed toward someone.' Thus it is used in Exodus 33, verse 19: 'I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy.' In the Hebrew it is וְחַנּוֹתִי, which the Apostle in Romans 9, verse 15, explains by 'to have mercy'; ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω. In this signification it is taken in Deuteronomy 28, verse 50; Numbers 6, verse 25; Judges 21, verse 22; Amos 5:15. Thus it is said of Noah that he found grace in the eyes of the Lord, Genesis 6, verse 8, 'that he found grace/favor/and mercy with God'; as the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11, verse 7, explains. Refer here to Genesis 39, verse 21; Joshua 11, verse 20; Jeremiah 16, verse 16. VI. It is used in the same sense among Latin writers. Plutarch says in Cato Uticensis, 'If I wished to save my life, χάριτι τῆ καίσαρ@', that is, by the grace, favor, and clemency of Caesar. We are accustomed to say commonly, to obtain, to enter into, to reconcile to oneself grace, that is, favor, clemency, and mercy. In the New Testament, the word χαρίζομαι and χαριτόω is in use, which properly signifies to confer gifts, to love, to favor, to embrace with grace. Luke 1, v. 28; 2 Cor. 2, verse 10; Acts 27, v. 24; Eph. 1, v. 6.

VII. And this is, as I have said, the principal and most common meaning of this word in the sacred scriptures, upon which all the others depend, and to which they relate analogically.

IIX. 2. It is taken for gratuitous gifts or those conferred out of grace, by a metonymy of the effect for the cause, because the principle of donation, which is grace, is put for the gift. This meaning can be called passive, because it is the reception of a gift. For every reception is a certain passion, as the philosophers say. Suidas and Varinus show with certain examples from Sophocles that χάριν signifies both the gift and the return of a favor, and they describe it thus: χάρις ἐςὶ πράγματος ὠφελίμου δόσις. In this sense the Latins say, 'Grace begets grace.' Thus חנן sometimes signifies to donate, as when Jacob says to Esau concerning his children, Gen. 33, v. 5: 'These are the boys whom God חנן, has gratified, or bestowed out of gratuitous favor.' Acts 11, v. 23, it is said of Barnabas: 'Who when he had seen τὴν χάριν τῦ Θεῦ,' that is, the gift poured out upon the believers, as some explain it, 'he rejoiced.' To this also can be referred that from Acts 6, verse 8. where Stephen is said to be full of grace; in the Greek is the word πίσεως καὶ δυνάμεως: Eph. 4, v. 7: 'To each one of you grace has been given, according to the measure of the gift of Christ.' 1 Pet. 4, v. 10: 'As each has received grace, administering it to one another.' Rom. 6, v. 23: 'Eternal life is χάρισμα Θεῦ,' that is, the gift of God.

IX. 3. For graciousness, or for that gentleness and affability by which one makes oneself lovable and acceptable to all good men. Luke 1, v. 26. Mary is called full of grace, holdselig [gracious]. Luke 2, v. 25. He increased in grace and wisdom before men. The Greeks say χάρις λόγων, acceptable and pleasing words, χάρις τῆς ἀρετῆς, gracious virtue. Whence the poet: And the grace of diffusion, which delay retards, is absent.

X. Flacius, part 1, Clav. under the word grace, enumerates many significations, but they can almost all be reduced to these, which most Scholastics also admit. For thus writes Thomas, 1. 2. q. 110. art. 1: According to the common way of speaking, grace is accustomed to be accepted in three ways. In one way, for the love of someone: just as we are accustomed to say that this soldier has the grace of the king, that is, the king holds him dear. Secondly, it is taken for some gift given freely: just as we are accustomed to say, I do this favor [grace] for you. In the third way, it is taken for the recompense of a benefit freely given, according to which we are said to give thanks for benefits. The second of these three depends on the first: for from the love by which someone holds another dear, it proceeds that he bestows something upon him freely. From the second, however, proceeds the third: because from benefits freely exhibited, the giving of thanks arises. Thus, therefore, regarding the significations of the word, we and the Papists agree in a certain way.

XI. Bellarmine, indeed, in his books on grace, makes no mention of that principal signification by which it is taken for favor, but asserts that grace in Scripture always denotes a gift freely given. But Gregory of Valencia is somewhat sounder, since he admits this signification and says that grace is sometimes taken for divine benevolence, which is communicated to us as a free gift, Tom. 1, disp. 8, q. 1, punct. 1. To this he adapts that passage in Rom. 4, verse 5: To him who believes, faith is imputed for righteousness according to the purpose of the grace of God.

XII. That, however, is most controversial: What exactly the Apostle Paul intended to be denoted by this word when he says we are justified by the grace of God, through the grace of God he asserts that one is saved? For there we understand by gifts his favor. It is not therefore without cause that it is asked what the sense of this word is in those places? concerning which it will now be necessary to proceed.

Latin:

I. IesuWitæ gratiam à gratis dando dictam volunt. Ita enim scribit Bellarminus l. 1. de grat. cap, 1. gratiam à Gratia inde nomen accepit, quod gratis detur. Probat ex August. tract. in Ps. 44. qui, Gratia, inquit, meritò nominatur, quia gratis datur. Et Gregorius de Valent. tom. 2. disp. 8. quæst. 1: punct. 1. dictum August. in Ps. 49. citat: Si gratia vocatur, gratis datur. Atque hûc referunt illud Rom. 4. v. 4. Ei qui operatur, merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum.

II. Hinc etiam est, quod gratia illis propriè donum significet, gratis datum à Deo, & præcipuè donum istud, quod conferri dicunt in iustificatione hominis. Ita enim exponit Becanus disp. de auxilijs grat. par. 2. cap. thom. 1. Gratia proprie est gratuitum & supernaturale Dei donum, quod per Christi merita nobis confertur ad vitam æternam consequendam.

III. Quantumuis autem non negemus, gratiam quandoque in Scripturis gratuita denotare dona, attamen propriè & principaliter gratiam à gratis dando dictam esse inficiamur. Hæc enim nominis notatio nimis stricta est, nec omni gratiæ, sed tantùm gratis datæ, vt loquuntur, h. e. gratuitis donis conuenit. Quam ob causam nonnulli à grato potius deriuant, quod rem acceptam, amitam & exoptatam denotat.

IV. Verùm missâ nominis Etymologiâ, fructuosius esse censemus, si præcipuæ significationes annotentur, quarum inprimis sunt tres, ita tamen, vt non omnes æquè sint principales & vsitatæ,

V. 1. Vsitatissima & maximè principalis Gratiæ significatio hæc est, quòd denotat fauorem & misericordiam, vel potiùs misericordem & clementem voluntatem Dei, quâ erga nos homines affectus est. Quam significationem vocat Flacius in Claue Scripturæ Actiuam, quia Deus por eam erga nos agit. Hebræa vox est חָנַן gratiâ affecit vel fauore dignatus est. Hinc, vt ipsarum literarum inspectio docet, Germanicum gönnen/gunst. LXX. plerumque reddiderunt, per misereri, parcere, einem gnad erzeigen/ gnedig vnd barmhertzig sein / einem günstig vnnd wol gewogen sein. Sic vsurpatur Exod. 33. vers. 19. Miserebor cui voluero. In Hebræo est וְחַנּוֹתִי quod Apostolus Rom. 9. v. 15. per misereri exponit; ἐλεήσω ὃν ἂν ἐλεῶ, καὶ οἰκτειρήσω ὃν ἂν οἰκτείρω. In hac significatione sumitur Deut. 28. v. 50. Num 6. v. 25. Iud. 21. v. 22. Amos 5. 15. Sic de Noah dicitur, quòd gratiam inuenerit in oculis Domini Gen. 6. v. 8 das er gnad/huld/vnd barmhertzigkeit bey Gott funden habe; vt exponit Epistola ad Hebr. c. 11. v. 7. Huc refer Gen. 39. v. 21. Ios. 11. v. 20. Ierem. 16. v. 16. VI. Eodem sensu apud Latinos Scriptores in vsu est. Plutarchus inquit in Catone Vticensi, Si vellem vitam seruare, χάριτι τῆ καίσαρ@ id est, gratiâ fauore & clementiâ Cæsaris. Vulgò dicere solemus, consequi, inire, conciliare sibi gratiam, id est, fauorem, clementiam & misericordiam. In nouo Test. verbum χαρίζομαι & χαριτόω in vsu est, quod propriè significat dona conferre, diligere, fauere, gratia complecti. Luc. 1. v. 28. 2. Cor. 2 vers. 10. Act. 27. v. 24. Eph 1. v. 6.

VII. Atque hæc est, vt dixi, principalis & vsitatissima huius vocabuli in sacris literis significatio, à quâ reliquæ omnes dependent, & ad quam sese analogicè habent.

IIX. 2. Sumitur pro donis gratuitis vel ex gratia collatis, per metonymiam effecti pro causa, quia pro dono ponitur principium donationis, quod est gratia: Potest hæc significatio vocari Passiua, quia est receptio doni. Omnis a. receptio est quædam passio, vt loquuntur Philosophi. Suidas, & Varinus exemplis quibusdam ex Sophocle ostendunt, χάριν significare, καὶ τὴν δωρεὰν καὶ ἀντίχαριν, &c sic describunt, χάρις ἐςὶ πράγματος ὠφελίμου δόσις. Hoc sensu Latini dicunt, Gratia gratiam parit: Sic חנן significat quandoque donare, vt cùm Iacob ad Esavum dicit de suis liberis Gen. 33. v. 5. isti pueri sunt, quos Deus חנן gratificatus, seu ex gratuito fauore largitus est. Act. 11. v. 23. dicitur de Barnaba: Qui cùm vidisset τὴν χάριν τῦ Θεῦ, id est, donum in credentes effusum, vt quidam exponunt, gauisus est. Hûc & illud referri potest ex Act. 6. vers. 8. vbi Stephanus dicitur plenus gratiâ, In Græco est vocabulum πίσεως καὶ δυνάμεως: Eph 4. v. 7. Vnucuique vestrûm donata est gratia, secundum mensuram doni Christi. 1. Petr. 4: v. 10. Gratiam, vt quisque accepit, in alterum administrantes. Rom. 6. v. 23. Vita æterna χάρισμα Θεῦ, id est, donum Dei.

IX. 3. Pro gratiositate, seu pro illa mansuetudine & comitate, quâ quis se omnibus bonis amabilem reddit & gratum. Luc. 1. v. 26. Maria dicitur gratia plena holdselig Luc. 2. v. 25. Proficiebat gratia & sapientia coram hominibus. Græci dicunt χάρις λόγων, accepti & grati sermones, χάρις τῆς ἀρετῆς, gratiosa virtus Vnde poëta : Gratiaque offusio, quod mora tardat, abest.

X. Flacius part. 1. Clav. sub voce gratiæ plures enumerat significationes, sed ad has ferè omnes possunt redigi, quas etiām plerique admittunt Scholastici. Ita n. scribit Thom. 1. 2. q 110. art. 1; Secundum communem modum loquendi, Tripliciter gratia accipi consueuit, Vno modo pro dilectione alicuius : sicut consueuimus dicere, quòd iste miles habet gratiam regis, id est, rex habet eum gratum. Secundò sumitur pro aliquo dono gratis dato : sicut consueuimus dicere, Hanc gratiam facio tibi. Tertio modo sumitur pro recompensatione beneficij gratis dati secundum quod dicimur agere gratias beneficiorum. Quorum trium secundum dependet ex primo: ex amore enim, quo aliquis habet alium gratum procedit, quòd aliquid ei gratis impendat: Ex secundo autem procedit tertium : quia ex beneficijs gratis exhibitis gratiarum actio consurgit. Sic ergo quoad significationes vocabuli quodam modo inter nos & Pontificios conuenit.

XI. Bellarminus quidem in libris suis de gratia non facit mentionem principalis illius significationis, quâ pro fauore sumitur, sed gratiam semper in Scriptura notare autumat, donum gratis datum. Ast Gregorius de Valentia nonnihil sanior est, quoniam admittit hanc significationem, & ait gratiam quandoque sumi pro diuina beneuolentia, quæ nobis donum gratis communicatur, Tom: 1. disp: 8. q. 1. punct. 1. Hûc accommodat illud Rom. 4. versu 5. Credenti fides imputatur ad iustitiam secundum propositum gratiæ Dei:

XII. Illud verò maximè controuersum est, Quid propriè per hanc vocem notatum voluerit A. Paulus, quando nos gratâ Dei justificari, per gratiam Dei saluari asserit? Ibi n. illi dona nos fauorem intelligimus. Non igitur immeritò quæritur quisnam sit in istis locis huius vocis sensus? de quo jam porrò agendum erit.


### Question II: What the word grace properly signifies in the article of justification

I. The genuine meaning of this word is not only corrupted today by the Jesuits, but was also in times past in a wonderful manner depraved and obscured by the Pelagians.

II. Pelagius at the beginning of the struggle contended that Paul by grace understands the grace of creation, or the gifts of human nature bestowed in generation: for we could not have merited, either that we should be, or that we should be such, and therefore those gifts are deservedly called grace. Thus also Erasmus in the Hyperaspistes says; That this also redounds to the praise and glory of God, if something is attributed to the powers of the unregenerate free will in actions; because they themselves also, since they are gifts of God, are comprehended under grace. But by this reasoning Christ would have died in vain. For if we could be justified by the gifts of nature, to what purpose would the passion of Christ have been useful or necessary?

III. When therefore Pelagius saw that this interpretation was not proceeding, he devised another, and when we are said to be justified by grace, he understood the grace of vocation, and that it consists in this; that God has revealed to us in the word his decree and counsel, and also his will, but as soon as man hears this manifestation, then it is in his powers to assent to them, and to do what God commands. But because we did not merit that manifestation, for that reason it is called grace.

For this reason also Christ would have died in vain, because God had already sufficiently revealed His will to the human race, partly by living voice, partly in the Mosaic and prophetic writings, already before in the Old Testament.

IV. But setting aside the Pelagians, today we must contend primarily with the Jesuits, who for the most part understand by grace infused qualities, so that for them to be justified by grace is to be justified by infused qualities or good works. For in this article they do not follow Paul, but Aristotle, thinking that the reason for justification and righteousness is the same in Theology as it is in Philosophy. For just as he is ethically just whose intellect is endowed with the habit of justice, so they think that he is properly just and accepted before God to whom a habit of justice has been divinely infused, which, since it is given freely by God, is therefore called grace, and is understood by Paul when he writes that we are justified by grace. Whence the Council of Trent, sess. 6, cap. 11, strikes with an anathema all those who assert that the grace by which we are justified is only the favor of God. For the sake of distinction, however, they call this grace 'gratum facientem' [grace making one pleasing] from its office, because it makes us pleasing and accepted to God. If you wish to see the mind of the Papists explained at greater length, see Bellarmine, lib. 1, de Gr. c. 3, and Gregor. de Valent., tomo 2, disp. 8, quaestio 1, punct. 1, and Becanus, disp. de auxilijs gratiae.

V. We, however, maintain that in the Pauline epistles the grace of God, by which we are said to be justified and saved, denotes nothing other than the gratuitous favor, the clement and merciful will of God, by which He both embraces the whole human race and specially loves and accepts all who believe in Christ: For just as love, so also grace, which is twofold because of love. One is general, which has appeared and shone upon all men, Tit. 2, verse 11: The other special, with which God deems only believers worthy, Rom. 3. v. 24. Eph. 2. v. 5. & 8. And this special [grace] is noted in particular, which we shall now prove with the following arguments.

VI. 1. From Rom. 3. v. 24. Justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Here 1. by justification is noted not an infusion of righteousness, but an imputation, as is declared from Ps. 32. Rom. 4. v. 6. 7. 8. 2. It is said χάριτι τῇ αὐτοῦ, by which we are taught that we are justified by the grace of God, not insofar as it has its effects in us, but insofar as it is in God. For the words τῇ αὐτοῦ signify grace, not that which is from him, but rather that which is of him, and is in him. 3. The particle freely is added, so that it may be denoted that we are not justified by the grace of God insofar as it is some gift in us. For the word freely is opposed to our works and qualities. 4. He mentions faith; Justified through faith in his blood. Therefore we are not justified by something inherent in us, since it is the nature of faith to apprehend those things which are outside of us. And when we are said to be justified by faith, faith is not taken as a work but is rather opposed to works. For so it is said in Rom. 4. v. 5. To him who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is imputed for righteousness. Where you see that τὸ operari (working) and τὸ credere (believing) are expressly opposed.

VII. From the opposition of grace and good works. Grace is opposed to infused qualities and good works. Therefore grace does not denote good works. I prove the antecedent from Rom. 4. v. 4. To him that worketh is the reward not reckoned of grace. Rom. 11. v. 6. And if by grace, then it is no more of works: otherwise grace is no more grace. The Papists invert this: If by grace, then certainly by works. Tit. 3. v. 5. Not by works ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ (in righteousness) which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us. Here the Papists cannot object that only the works of the unregenerate are understood, since it treats of those things which were done ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ (in righteousness). Eph. 2. v. 8. by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves, (that is, not from anything that inheres in you: it is the gift of God, not from works. 2 Tim. 1:9. He saved us, not according to our works, but according to his own πρόθεσιν [purpose] and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time. Here neither an infused habit, nor an action flowing from a habit can be understood, since both are given in time: but the grace of which Paul speaks here was given before the ages of time. Thus, conversely, Rom. 4, Abraham is said to be justified, not from works, but from the mere grace of God. But the works of Abraham were not the works of an unregenerate man, but of a faithful one, nevertheless even those are excluded from the business of justification, which comes about by grace: not otherwise than as Christ said in Luke 17:10, Even if you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants, i.e. even if you have done all things which the law requires, yet you are unworthy of grace, since you have done only those things which you ought to have done. And so there is a perpetual opposition in the Scriptures between grace and our qualities and actions, when the business of salvation is discussed.

VIII. 3. From the superabundance of grace and sin. Rom. 5:20. Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. If here the word grace is taken for an infused habit of justice, then this absurdity follows, that where a habit of injustice abounds, there a habit of justice must simultaneously abound, and thus where one contrary is, there the other is found and immediately joined, which is ἄτοπον [absurd]. And this statement is indeed so evident that the Jesuits have nothing they can object, if indeed in that passage grace is opposed not only to good works, but also to a habit. For according to the opinion of the Papists, one would have to speak thus: Where a habit of injustice is and abounds, there a habit of justice cannot be. But the Apostle inverts this, and says that grace is there where injustice abounds. Wherefore we conclude that by grace one must understand not an infused quality, but rather the mercy of God, by which He embraces sinners.

IX. 4. From the objection of the Pseudo-Apostles. If Paul had understood by grace inherent qualities, why had it been objected to him that by preaching grace he destroys the pursuit of good works, which objection is read in Rom. 6, v. 1, 14, 15? Namely, this happened because some thought that if we are justified by the grace or mercy of God, an opportunity is provided for security. From which it is manifest that the Apostle Paul understood by grace not some inherent qualities, but rather the gratuitous mercy of God.

X. 5. From the effects of that grace. Vocation flows from the grace of God, Gal. 1, v. 15: God called me by his grace. But if grace always signified a gift and a habit of justice, how could that have been said? For justice and the gift of renewal is not the cause of vocation, but rather the latter precedes it. Wherefore by grace, by which we are called, the mercy of God is understood. For this alone, and not some inherent quality, is the cause of our election, our vocation, and our justification, according to the statements in Rom. 8, v. 29, 30, and Eph. 1, v. 4, 5, and 11.

XI. 6. From the opposition of law and grace, Gal. 5, v. 4: You have fallen from grace, as many of you as are justified by the law. By the name of law, however, he understands everything that the law commands, such as not only external deeds, but primarily the internal renewal of the heart. When therefore Scripture says that we are justified by the grace of God, and not by the law, it excludes every renewal and every internal and external good action from the office of justifying, and ascribes it solely to the gratuitous favor of God. Renewal is indeed not separated from the justified person, but it is separated from the office of justifying. For it is one thing for a man to be justified without works, and another thing to be justified without works and without renewal. For although those things are distinct, they nevertheless exist together, so much so that justification is indeed done without works, but it is not without works.

XII. 7. From Eph. 2, v. 8: By grace you are saved through faith, and this not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast. If to be saved by grace signifies by infused to be saved by qualities, then they can boast of being justified. For although these qualities are gifts of God, nothing, however, stands in the way of boasting because of this. For wisdom, and all the gifts of the mind, are gifts of God, and yet that men can boast in them, Jeremiah ch. 9, v. 23 shows: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom. Thus everything that we have, and therefore also our good works, are from the Father of lights; nevertheless, Paul affirms that if justification is by works, a wide door is opened to boasting. In the same way, if we were justified by infused qualities, we would have something in which we could boast, which is ἀτόλογον.

Latin:

I. Genuina huius vocabuli significatio non hodie solùm à IesuVvitis corrumpitur, sed olim etiam à Pelagianis mirum in modum deprauata & obfuscata fuit.

II. Pelagius in principio certaminis contendit, Paulum per gratiam intelligere gratiam creationis, vel dona naturæ humanæ in generatione collata: Nos n. non potuisse mereri, vel vt essemus, vel vt tales essemus, ideoque ista dona meritò vocari gratiam. Sic & Erasmus in Hyperaspiste dicit; Redundare & hoc in laudem & gloriam Dei, si viribus liberi arbitrij non renati aliquid tribuatur in actionibus; quia & ipsæ, cùm sint dona Dei, comprehendantur sub gratia. Verùm hac ratione Christus frustrà fuisset mortuus. Si enim per dona naturæ iustificari possemus, ad quid prodesset vel necessaria fuisset Christi passio?

III. Cùm ergo Pelagius videret, non procedete hanc interpretationem, aliam excogitauit, & quando gratia justificari dicimur, gratiam vocationis intellexit, eamque in hoc consistere; quòd Deus in verbo suum nobis decretum & consilium, suam quoque voluntatem reuelauerit, quàm primùm autem homo hanc patefactionem audiat, tunc in eius viribus esse, illis assentiri, & quæ Deus præcipit facere. Quia verò illam patefactionem non meruimus, ob id vocari gratiam.

hac etiam ratione Christus frustrà fuisset mortuus, quia Deus voluntatem suam, humano generi, partim viva voce, partim in Mosaici & propheticis scriptis jam antè satis revelauerat in V. T.

IV. At missis Pelagianis, hodiè cum JesuWitis potissimùm nobis certandum est, qui plerumque per gratiam intelligunt infusas qualitates, ita vt gratiâ justificari ipsis sit infusis qualitatibus vel bonis operibus justificari. Non a. in hoc articulo Paulum, sed Aristotele sequuntur, arbitrantes, eande esse justificationis iustitiaeque rationem in Theologia, quae est in Philosophia. Nam quemadmodum is demum Ethicè justus est, cuius intellectus habitu justitiae praeditus: Ita putant illum propriè coram Deo justum & acceptum esse, cui diuinitus insusus sit justitiae habitus, qui cùm à Deo gratis detur, hinc gratiam appellari, & eum ipsum à Paulo intelligi, quando nos Gratiâ justificari scribit. Vnde Concil. Trid. sess. 6. cap. c. 11. anathemate ferit omnes eos, qui asserunt, gratiam, quâ iustificamur, esse tantùm fauorem Dei. Distinctionis autem causâ, gratiam hanc ab officio suo vocant gratum facientem, quia nos Deo gratos faciat & acceptos. Pluribus Pontificiorum mentem si velis explicatam, vidè Bellarminum lib: 1: de Gr. c. 3. & Gregor: de Valent: tomo 2. disp. 8: quaestio. 1. punct. 1. & Becanum disp. de auxilijs gratiae.

V. Nos autem statuimus, in Paulinis epistolis gratiam Dei, quâ iustificari & saluari dicimur, nihil denotare aliud, quàm gratuitum favorem, clementem & misericordem Dei voluntatem, quâ tum genus humanum totum complectitur, tum omnes in Christum credentes specialiter diligit, & acceptat: Sicut enim dilectio, ita & gratia, quae dilectionis causa duplex est. Vna generalis quae omnibus hominibus apparuit & illuxit, Tit. 2. versu 11: Altera specialis, qua solos credentes dignatur Deus, Rom. 3. v. 24. Eph. 2. v. 5. & 8. Et hæc specialis notatur inprimis, id quod nunc sequentibus argumentis evictum dabimus.

VI. 1. Ex Rom. 3. v. 24. Iustificati gratis per gratiam ipsius, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo Iesu. Hîc 1. per justificationem non infusio justitiæ, sed imputatio notatur, vti ex Ps. 32. Rom. 4. v. 6. 7. 8. declaratur, 2. Dicitur χάριτι τῇ αὐτοῦ, quo docemur, nos justificari gratiâ Dei, non quatenus in nobis sua habet officia, sed quatenus in Deo est. Verba enim τῇ αὐτοῦ gratiam significant, non quæ ab ipso, sed potius quæ ipsius, & in ipso est. 3. Additur particula gratis, vt denotetur, nos non justificari gratiâ Dei, quatenus donum aliquod in nobis est. Opponitur enim vox gratis operibus & qualitatibus nostris. 4. Meminit fidei; Iustificati per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Non ergò justificamur per aliquod nobis inhærens, cum fidei sit, ea quæ extra nos sunt, apprehedere. Et quando fide iustificari dicimur, fides non pro opere sumitur sed potius opponitur operibus. Ita enim dicitur Rom. 4. v. 5. Ei qui non operatur, credit autem in eum, qui iustificat impium, fides eius imputatur ad iustitiam. Vbi vides, expressè opponi τὸ operari & τὸ credere.

VII. Ab oppositione gratiæ & bonorum operum. Gratia opponitur infusis qualitatibus & bonis operibus. Ergò gratia non denotat bona opera. Antecedens probo, ex Rom 4. v. 4. Operanti merces non imputatur secundum gratiam. Rom. 11. v. 6. Quòd si per gratiã, iam non ex operibus, alioquin gratia iam non esset gratia. Invertunt Pontificii: Si ex gratia, vtique ex operibus. Tit. 3. vers. 5. Non ex operibus ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ quæ fecimus nos, sed secundum misericordiam suam saluos nos fecit Hîc non possunt Pontificij excipere, intelligi tantùm opera non renatorum, siquidem de ijs agit, quæ ἐν τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ, facta sunt. Eph. 2. v. 8. gratiâ saluati estis per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, (id est, non ex aliquo quod vobis inhaereat:) Dei donum est, non ex operibus. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. Salvos nos fecit, non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum idiam πρόθεσιν & gratiam, quae data est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora saecularia. Hic nec infusus habitus, nec ex habitu promanans actio potest intelligi, cum utrunque in tempore detur: gratia autem, de qua hic loquitur Paulus data est ante tempora secularia. Sic vicissim Rom. 4. Abraham dicitur iustificatus, non ex operibus, sed ex mera Dei gratia. Opera autem Abrahami non erant opera hominis non renati, sed fidelis, nihilominus tamen & illa excluduntur e negotio justificationis, quae gratia contingit: non secus atque Christus dixit Luc. 17. v. 10. Etiamsi omnia feceritis, dicite, servi inutiles sumus, h. e. etiamsi omnia feceritis, quae lex requirit, tame indigni estis gratia, quoniam ea tantum, quae debuistis facere, fecistis. Vtque adeo perpetua in Scripturis est oppositio inter gratiam & nostras qualitates & actiones, cum de negotio salutis disseritur.

IIX. 3. A superabundantia gratiae & peccati. Rom. 5. v. 20. Vbi abundavit delictum, superabundavit & gratia. Si hic gratiae vox pro infuso iustitiae habitu sumitur, tum absurdum hoc sequitur, quod vbi abundat habitus iniustitiae, ibi simul abundet habitus iustitiae, & sic vbi est vnum contrarium, ibi simul reperiatur statimque conjungatur alterum, quod ἄτοπον. Et hoc quidem dictum adeo evidens est, ut nihil habeant, quod excipere possint JesuWitae, si quidem in illo gratia non solum bonis operibus, sed & habitui opponitur. Ex sententia enim Pontificiorum ita foret loquendum: Vbi est & abundat habitus iniustitiae, ibi esse nequit habitus iustitiae. Sed invertit hoc Apostolus, aitque ibi gratiam esse, vbi abundat iniustitia. Quare per gratiam non qualitatem infusam, sed potius misericordiam Dei, qua peccatores complectitur, intelligendam esse concludimus.

IX. 4. Ab objectione Pseudo-Apostolorum. §§ per gratiam Paulus intellexisset inhærentes qualitates votas, cur ipsi obiectum fuisset, quòd prædicando gratiam, destruat studium bonorum operum, quæ obiectio legitur Rom. 6. v. 1. 14. 15? Nempè factum hoc inde; quod nonnulli arbitrabantur, si gratiâ vel misericordiâ Dei justificemur, præberi ansam securitati. Ex quo manifestum sit, Apostolum Paulum per gratiam intellexisse non aliquas inhęrentes qualitates, sed potius misericordiam Dei gratuitam.

X. 5. Ab effectis istius gratię. Vocatio ex gratiâ Dei profluit, Gal. 1. v. 15. Deus vocavit me per suam gratiam. At si gratia donum semper significaret & habitum justitiæ, quî istud dici potuisset? Non enim iustitia & donum renouationis causa est vocationis, sed hæc potius pręcedit. Quare per gratiam, quâ vocamur, Dei misericordia intelligitur. Hęc enim sola, & non inhærens quędam qualitas, causa est tùm electionis, tùm vocationis, tùm justificationis nostræ, juxta dicta Rom 8. v. 29 30. & Eph. 1. v. 4. 5. & 11.

XI. 6. Ab oppositione legis & gratiæ Gal 5. v. 4. A gratia excidistis, quotquot in lege iustificamini. Legis autem nomine intelligit omnia, quæ lex præcipit, qualia sunt non externa tantùm facta, sed inprimis interna cordis renouatio. Cum igitur Scriptura dicit, per gratiam Dei nos iustificari, & non per legem, omnem renouationem, omnemque internam & externam actionem bonam ab officio iustificandi excludit, solique gratuito Dei fauori adscribit. Non quidem separatur renouatio à iustificato, sed ab officio iustificandi. Aliud enim est, Iustificari hominem sine operibus, Et aliud, Iustificatum esse sine operibus & sine renovatione. Nam quamvis ea distincta sint, simul tamen consistunt, adeo vt iustificatio fiat quidem sine operibus, sed non sit sine operibus.

XII. 7. Ex Eph. 2. v. 8. Gratiâ estis saluati per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, Dei enim donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur. Si gratia saluari significat infusis qualitatibus saluari, tunc possunt justificati gloriari. Nam licet qualitates istae sint dona Dei, nil tamen hoc obstat gloriationi. Nam & sapientia, omnesque animi dotes sunt dona Dei, & tamen posse in jis homines gloriari, ostendit Ierem. c. 9. v. 22. Non glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua. Sic omne, quod habemus, adeoque & opera nostra bona, sunt a Patre luminum, nihilominus adfirmat Paulus, si ex operibus fit justitia, patentem gloriationi portam esse apertam. Pari modo, justificaremur qualitatibus infusis, haberemus aliquid, in quo gloriari possemus, quod ἀτόλογον.


### Question II: XIII. 8. From imputation

XIII. 8. From imputation. Paul always describes our righteousness through imputation and never makes mention of any inherent habit. Since, therefore, we are justified by something imputed, it will certainly be outside of us, and consequently, we will not be justified by any inherent quality. Whence it follows in turn that the grace of God, through which righteousness is imputed, does not signify something inherent.

XIV. 9. From election. Whatever grace denotes in the article of Predestination, it denotes the same in the article of Justification. For by the same grace we are elected from eternity and justified in time, since election and justification stand as the decree and the execution of the decree. But this grace, by which we are elected, does not denote inherent qualities (for we are not elected because of good works, Rom. 9, v. 11), but only favor and mercy, or the merciful will of God. Therefore, it will retain the same meaning when we are said to be justified by grace. Hence, 2 Tim. 1, v. 9, the Apostle says: He saved us, not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace (note that the eternal purpose of God and grace are joined here), which was given to us in Christ Jesus before the secular times.

XV. 10. From the permutation of Scripture. Justification, which in Rom. 3, v. 24 and Eph. 2, v. 8 is ascribed to the grace of God, is attributed to the mercy of God, Psalm 51.

ver. 3. Matt. 15. v. 26. ch. 18. v. 35. Rom. 9. v. 18. likewise to the Benignity & humanity of God, Tit. 3. v. 4 & 5. whence it follows, that all these are Synonyms.

XVI. 11. By paraphrastic locutions. Often this word of grace is rendered παραφρασικῶς & ἐξηγητικῶς [paraphrastically & exegetically] by mercy, as Heb. 4. v. last. Let us approach the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help. Where by grace new qualities are not implied. For 1. these are not, nor can they be called, the throne of grace, to which the reborn approach, 2. to receive mercy and to find grace are said ἐξηγητικῶς [exegetically]. 3. Mention is made of timely help. Now indeed our help is from a merciful and benign God, not from our renovation, Ps. 123. 124. 125. Thus 1 Tim. 1. v. 2. grace and mercy are likewise conjoined. And Eph. 2. v. 7. we read: That he might show the abundant riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus, see ibid. v. 4. & 5.

XVII. 12. From the absurd. This statement, we are justified by grace, would be tautological if grace denoted infused qualities. For the Papists understand by to be justified the infusion of qualities. Therefore the sense would be, by infused qualities are infused qualities infused. For according to them, as Gregor de Valentia defines, justification is the infusion of qualities, or the eduction of justice from the passive power of the soul. For they distinguish between active justification. Active justification is that by which men are just, passive, that by which they are made just: actively they call them just through an infused habit, passively just, through the infusion of a habit. Because therefore the locution here is passive, We are justified by grace, it follows that to be justified here is nothing other than for qualities to be infused. Now if by grace they likewise understand qualities, this absurd locution will emerge: by infused qualities are qualities infused.

XVIII. In place of a colophon to indicate the agreement of the adversaries, we add the confession of Pighius, who in book 5 on free will writes thus: Grace we seek the various acceptation not from the schools, but from the divine Scriptures. Since in those [schools] they almost imagine that the grace of God is some quality uncreated in our soul by God, either the same as the habit of charity, or distinct from the same. All of which I consider to be fictitious, and to have no authority from the Scriptures. These are his words.

XIX. But they have nothing solid to oppose to the contrary. They especially urge certain testimonies of the Fathers, because they seem to have explained the term of grace concerning infused qualities. To which we respond in a few words.

1. That the style of the Fathers neither ought to, nor can, prejudice the phrase of the Holy Spirit.

2. That the argument proceeds from a particular. For we confess that sometimes the word of grace was understood by the Fathers in that sense, but not always, which was what needed to be demonstrated.

3. Many testimonies of the Fathers conclude nothing for the Papists. For most of them indicate only this, that the grace of renewal has been given to the reborn, namely faith, hope, charity, and other virtues, but they do not say that our justification is placed in those virtues, nor do they exclude the other signification of grace, as the Papists think.

4. The occasion of such interpretations must be considered, which was this: Pelagius, driven from his defenses which he had first opposed to grace, finally said that it was only valid for this, that past sins might be forgiven us. But for exercising virtues, for mortifying the flesh, there is no need for the peculiar grace of the Holy Spirit; but all these things can be accomplished by the powers of free will. Which dogma, since it mutilated the benefit of Christ, the Fathers rightly contended that the grace of God and the merit of Christ do not consist only in this, that sins are forgiven, but also that the flesh is mortified, that the law is obeyed. Hence it happened that, because the Fathers were contending with Pelagius not about the grace of remission, but of renewal, for the most part the word received grace for gifts, without mention being made of the other meaning, since that was not in dispute. If this occasion is attended to, the harsher sayings of the Fathers can easily be both understood and excused, although meanwhile we must needs confess that Augustine and the rest did not accurately weigh in which places of Scripture grace is taken for the favor of God, and in which for the gifts of renewal. For they were too intent upon the Pelagian struggle. And so it happened that many sayings speaking of the favor of God under the word grace were interpreted as referring to the gifts of renewal. In this, therefore, they are not to be imitated, but it must be carefully seen where grace is taken actively and where passively, lest we rashly confuse the article of Justification and Renewal.

XX. Finally, a certain scruple remains from Rom. 5, where the Apostle, speaking of justification, seems to take grace for a gift. For in verses 15, 16, and 17, it is noted by those three words, always in the same sense. V. 15 it is called χάρισμα. But not as the trespass, so also the χάρισμα, the interpreter rendered it 'gift'. Luth.: 'Aber nicht helt sichs mit der Gaben/wie mit der Sünde.' Here χάρισμα is opposed to τῷ παραπτώματι, the gift to the offense. Therefore, nothing else is understood by the gift than the grace of God and the merit of Christ, as is indicated in the same verse. For what he just named χάρισμα, that he calls in the following words χάριν τῆ Θεῆ καὶ δωρεάν ἐν χάριτι τῆ χριστῆ. Wherefore, since the comparison is the same, these two words χάρισμα and χάρις, gift and grace, must necessarily be equivalent. 'Gabe vnnd Gnade', so that the gift here is the same as gratuitous favor and goodness, which our interpreters do not deny, as can be seen in Hunnius, Rungius, Balduinus, V. 16. it is called δώρημα, and soon again χάρισμα, by which word it cannot be doubted that the favor of God is understood, since it is said τὸ χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων εἰς δικαίωμα. If here χάρισμα denoted the grace of renewal, not the favor and mercy of God, it would follow that in renewal, and thus in infused qualities our justification is placed. For thus Luther translates, The gift helps from many sins to righteousness. v. 17. δικαιοσύνη is called δωρεὰ and δώρημα; that which makes for justification is named χάρις. From all of which it seems to be able to be gathered, that χάρις also in the article of Justification signifies a δώρημα or a certain gift, since these words χάρισμα, δώρημα, δώρεα are so frequently interchanged among themselves.

XXI. We answer, however, that an ignorance of the Elenchus is committed in this argument. For it is not asked whether the grace of God and the righteousness of Christ imputed to us can be called a gift in the sense that it is given freely; but whether by that gift a certain inherent quality is signified? That which can in no way be proved from this text. For we argue thus: Whatever is described by the favor, grace, and mercy of God, that does not denote a certain inherent quality. But this gift, by which we are said to be justified, is described by love v. 5, 8, and by the grace of God, v. 15. Therefore, the gift by which we are said to be justified does not denote a certain inherent quality. Furthermore, it is not the reborn man who is compared here with Adam, but Adam and Christ. From the former is sin, from the latter is grace, and thus are opposed the χάρις or παράπτωμα of Adam and the χάρις or χάρισμα of Christ. Whence it follows in turn that the χάρισμα, of which there is speech here, does not signify a good quality inherent in the reborn. For as all are infected by sin, so all would have infused good qualities; and where there is much injustice, there would be much justice; because this χάρισμα superabounds where sin abounds, verse 20. Finally, this grace is the cause of liberation from sin. For verse 16 it is hinted that just as through one transgression all are constituted sinners, so from all transgressions we are liberated through this one χάρισμα. Therefore, that which does not liberate us rauit from all sins, that is not denoted by this χάρισμα. But an inherent quality did not free us from sin, but the grace of God and the merit of Christ. Therefore these are understood only

XXII. Although this χάρις is at the same time named χάρισμα, δώρημα, δωρεά; it should not, however, be gathered from this that a certain inherent habit is denoted by this gift, since a gift has its name not from inherentness, but from giving. Therefore, the righteousness of Christ, which is not infused into us but imputed, is called a gift, because it is given and freely conferred, not otherwise than as eternal life (which certainly is not a certain accident inherent in us) is called a gift. For thus it is read in Rom. 6:23 [v. 24], χάρισμα θεῦ eternal life. And Eph. 2:8, By the grace of God you have been saved, not of yourselves, it is the δῶρόν of God.

XXIII. Finally, this may still be asked: in what way is v. 15 distinguished, χάρις τῦ θεῦ καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι τῇ τῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπε Ἰησῦ χρισῦ; and v. 17, χάρις καὶ δωρεὰ τῆς δικαιοσύνης? We answer that in v. 15, by χάριν θεῦ is understood the favor and mercy of God the Father, which in v. 5 is called ἀγάπη, which is likewise called δωρεὰ, because it is entirely gratuitous. By χάριν τῦ χρισῦ, however, is understood the righteousness and merit of Christ. Therefore, Luther rendered the sense very well in his German version: So ist viel mehr GOttes Gnade vnnd Gabe vielen reichlich widerfahren/durch die Gnade des einigen Menschen Jesu Christi: v. 17, likewise by χάριν is denoted the favor of God, by δικαιοσύνης δωρεὰν the gifted righteousness of Christ (for it is a Hebraism), or the merit of Christ which He freely performed and paid for us.

XXIV. The sum, therefore, of what has been said thus far is: That by gift and χάρισμα is understood both the grace of God and the merit of Christ, which two benefits are called a gift because they came to us freely without our merits, and consequently nothing is treated here concerning habitual grace or inherent righteousness, which was to be demonstrated.

Latin:

XIII. 8. Ab imputatione. Paulus per imputationem semper describit nostram iustitiam & nunquam facit mentionem alicuius habitus inhaerentis. Cum ergo iustificemur per aliquod imputatum, vtique id extra nos erit, & per consequens, non justificabimur inhærente aliquâ qualitate. Vnde vicissim sequitur, quòd gratia Dei, per quam iustitia imputatur, quiddam inhærens non significet.

XIV. 9. Ab electione. Quicquid denotat gratia in articulo Praedestinationis, idem denotat in articulo Iustificationis. Eadem enim gratiâ ab ęterno electi sumus, & in tempore iustificamur, cum electio & iustificatio se habeant vt decretum & decreti executio, Atqui gratia ista, quâ electi sumus, non denotat inhærentes qualitates, (non enim propter bona opera electi sumus, Rom. 9. v. 11.) sed solum fauorem & misericordiam, vel misericordem Dei voluntatem. Ergo eandem significationem retinebit, cùm gratiâ iustificari dicimur. Hinc 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. inquit Apostolus: Saluos nos fecit, non secundum, opera nostra; sed secundum suum propositum & gratiam, (nota, conjungi hîc æternum Dei propositum & gratiam) quae data est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia.

XV. 10. A permutatione Scripturæ. Iustificatio, quæ Rom 3. v. 24 & Eph. 2. v. 8. gratiæ Dei adscribitur, misericordiæ Dei accepta fertur, Psal. 51.

vers. 3. Matth. 15. v. 26. c. 18. v. 35. Rom. 9. v. 18. item Benignitati & humanitati Dei, Tit. 3. v. 4 & 5. vnde sequitur, ista omnia esse Synonyma.

XVI. 11. A locutionibus paraphrasticis. Sæpè παραφρασικῶς & ἐξηγητικῶς redditur hoc gratiæ vocabulum per misericordiam, vt Hebr. 4. v. vlt. Accedamus ad thronum gratiæ, vt accipiamus misericordiam & inueniamus gratiam ad auxilium opportunum. Vbi per gratiam non innuuntur nouæ qualitates. Nam 1. hæ non sunt, nec dici possunt thronus gratiæ, ad quem renati accedant, 2. accipere misericordiam & inuenire gratiam ἐξηγητικῶς dicuntur. 3. Fit mentio auxilij opportuni. Iam verò auxilium nostrum à Deo est misericorde & benigno, non ex nostra renouatione, Psal. 123. 124. 125. Sic 1. Tim 1. v. 2. coniungitur itidem gratia & misericordia. Et Eph. 2. v. 7. legimus: Vt ostenderet abundantes diuitias gratiæ suæ in bonitate erga nos in Christo Iesu, vide ib. v. 4. & 5.

XVII. 12. Ab absurdo. Tautologica esset hæc oratio, gratia iustificamur, si gratia denotaret infusas qualitates. Etenim pontificij per justificari intelligunt qualitatum infusionem. Foret ergò sensus, per infusas qualitates infunduntur infusæ qualitates. Nam secundum ipsos, vti definit Gregor. de Valentia, iustificatio est infusio qualitatum, vel eductio iustitiæ è potentia passiua animi. Distinguunt enim inter iustificationem actiuam. Iustificatio actiua est, quâ homines justi sunt, passiua, qua iusti fiunt: actiuè justos dicunt per infusum habitum, passiuè iustos, per infusionem habitus. Quia igitur hic passiua est locutio, Gratia iustificamur, sequitur, quòd iustificari hic nihil sit aliud, quàm qualitates infundi. Nunc si per gratiam itidem qualitates intelligant, hæc emerget absurda locutio: per infusas qualitates infunduntur qualitates.

XIIX. Colophonis loco ad indicandam aduersariorum concordiam, addimus confessionem Pighij, qui l. 5. de libero arbitr. ita scribit: Gratia acceptionem variam non ex scholis, sed ex diuinis Scripturis petimus. Quandoquidem in illis ferè imaginantur, gratiam Dei qualitatem aliquam esse increatã animæ nostræ à Deo, vel eandem cum charitatis habitu, vel distinctam ab eodem. Quæ commentitia vniuersa existimo, nec ex Scripturis vllam auctoritatem habere. Hæc ille.

XIX. In contrarium verò nil solidi habent, quod opponant. Potissimùm vrgent testimonia quædam Patrum, quia gratiæ vocabulum de qualitatibus infusis exposuisse videntur. Ad quod paucis respondemus.

1. Quòd stylus Patrum neque debeat, neq; possit præiudicare phrasi Spiritus sancti.

2. Quod argumentum à particulari procedat Fatemur enim, nonnunquam à Patribus isto sensu intellectam fuisse vocem gratiæ, sed non semper, id quod erat demonstrandum.

3. Multa Patrũ testimonia nihil concludunt pro Pontificijs. Pleraq; enim hoc duntaxat indicant, renatis donatam esse gratiam renouationis, nempè fidem, spem, charitatem & alias virtutes, non autem dicunt, in illis virtutibus positam esse nostram iustificationem, nec excludunt alteram gratiæ significationem, vti censent Papicolæ.

4. Consideranda est occasio talium interpretationum, quæ hæc fuit: Pelagius depulsus à suis præsidijs, quę gratiæ primùm opposuerat, tandẽ dixit, illam ad hoc vnicè valere, vt præterita peccata nobis remittantur. Ad excercendas verò virtutes, ad mortificandam carnem, non esse peculiari gratiâ Spiritus sancti opus; sed hæc omnia posse perfici viribus liberi arbitrij. Quod dogma, cùm beneficiũ Christi mutilaret, rectè contenderunt Patres, gratiã Dei & meritũ Christi non in hoc tantùm consistere, vt dimittantur peccata, sed etiã vt mortificetur caro, vt legi obediatur. Hinc factũ, vt quia Patres cü Pelagio contendebant non de gratia remissionis, sed renouationis, plerumq; vocabulum gratiæ pro donis acciperent, non factâ mentione alterius significationis, quippe quæ non erat controuersa. Hæc occasio si attēdatur, facilè duriora Patrum dicta tùm intelligi, tùm excusari possunt, quāuis interea fateri necessum habeamus, Augustinū & reliquos nō accuratè perpēdisse, in quibus Scripturę locis gratia pro fauore Dei, in quibus p donis renouationis accipiatur. Erant. n. nimis intenti in certamen Pelagianum. Atq; ita contigit, vt multa dicta de fauore Dei sub vocabulo gratiæ loquētia, de donis renouationis intērptati fuerint. In hoc ergo nō sunt imitādi, sed probè vidēdū, vbi gratia actiuè vbi passiuè sumatur, ne articulū Iustificationis & Renouationis temerè confundamus.

XX. Tandem scrupulus quidam restat ex Rom. 5. vbi Apostolus de iustificatione loquens, gratiam pro dono accipere videtur. Nam v. 15. 16 17. tribus illis notatur vocabulis, eodem semper sensu. V. 15. dicitur χάρισμα Sed non sicut debitum, ita & χάρισμα, interpres reddidit donum. Luth. Aber nicht helt sichs mit der Gaben/wie mit der Sünde. Opponitur hic χάρισμα τῷ παραπτώματι, donum delicto. Nihil ergo aliud per donum intelligitur, quàm gratia Dei & meritum Christi, sicut in eodem versu indicatur. Quod enim modò nominauit χάρισμα, id verbis sequentibus vocat χάριν τῆ Θεῆ καὶ δωρεάν ἐν χάριτι τῆ χριστῆ. Quare cùm eadem sit comparatio, æquipolleant necessum est hæc duo vocabula χάρισμα & χάρις, donum & gratia. Gabe vnnd Gnade/vt ita donum hîc idem sit, quod gratuitus fauor & bonitas, id quod non inficiantur nostri Interpretes, vti videre est apud Hunnium, Rungium, Balduinū, V. 16. vocatur δώρημα, & mox rursum χάρισμα, per quam vocem intelligi fauorem Dei, dubium esse nequit, cùm dicatur τὸ χάρισμα ἐκ πολλῶν παραπτωμάτων εἰς δικαίωμα. Si hîc χάρισμα gratiam renouationis, non fauorem & misericordiam Dei denotaret, sequeretur, quòd in renouatione, & sic in infusis qualitatibus nostra iustificatio sit posita. Ita enim vertit Lutherus, Die gabe hilfft auß vielen sünden zur Gerechtigkeit. v 17. δικαιοσύνη vocatur δωρεὰ & δώρημα; istud, quod facit ad iustificationem, nominatur χάρις. Ex quibus omnibus colligi posse videtur, quod χάρις etiam in articulo Iustificationis δώρημα vel donum quoddam significet, cùm vocabula hæc χάρισμα, δώρημα δώρεα inter se tàm crebrò permutentur.

XXI. Respondemus autem, quòd committatur in hoc argumento ignoratio Elenchi. Non enim quęritur, an gratia Dei, & iustitia Christi nobis imputata, donum vocari possit eo sensu, quia gratis donatur; sed, an per istud donum inhærens quædam qualitas significetur? Id quod ex hoc textu probari nullo modo potest. Ita enim argumentamur: Quodcunque describitur fauore, gratia & misericordia Dei, id non inhærentem quandam qualitatem denotat. Atqui donum istud, quo iustificari dicimur. describitur per dilectionem v. 5. 8. & per gratiam Dei, v. 15. Ergo donum, quo iustificari dicimur, non inhærentem quandam qualitatem denotat. Porrò confertur hic non homo renatus cum Adamo, sed Adam & Christus. Ab illo est peccatum, ab hoc gratia, atque sic opponuntur χάρις, vel παράπτωμα Adami & χάρις vel χάρισμα Christi. Vnde vicissim sequitur, quòd χάρισμα, de quo hic sermo, non significet qualitatem bonam renatis inhærentem. Vt enim omnes peccato sunt infecti, ita omnes haberent infusas qualitates bonas; & vbi multum iniustitiæ, ibi multum foret iustitiæ; quia χάρισμα hoc superabundat, vbi peccatum abundat, vers. 20, Tandem hæc gratia est causa liberationis à peccato. Nam vers. 16. innuitur, quòd sicut per vnum delictum omnes sunt constituti peccatores, ita ab omnibus delictis per vnum hoc χάρισμα simus liberati. Quod ergo nos non liberauit à peccatis omnibus, id non notatur per hoc χάρισμα. Inhærens verò qualitas non liberauit nos à peccato, sed gratia Dei & meritum Christi. Ergo hæc tantùm intelliguntur

XXII. Licèt autem χάρις ista simul nominetur χάρισμα, δώρημα, δωρεά; non tamen hinc colligi debet, quod inhærens quidam habitus per donum istud notetur, cùm donum non ab inhærendo, sed à donando nomen habeat. Iustitia ergo Christi, quæ nobis non infunditur, sed imputatur; donum dicitur, quia donatur & gratis confertur, non secus, atque vita æterna, (quæ certè nō est accidens quöddam nobis inhærens) donum vocatur. Ita enim legitur Rom. 6. v. 24 χάρισμα θεῦ vita æterna. Et Eph. 2. v. 8. Gratiâ Dei saluati estis, non ex vobis Dei δῶρόν est.

XXIII. Denique istud adhuc quæri potest, quâ ratione distinguatur v. 15. χάρις τῦ θεῦ καὶ ἡ δωρεὰ ἐν χάριτι τῇ τῦ ἑνὸς ἀνθρώπε Ἰησῦ χρισῦ; & vers. 17. χάρις καὶ δωρεὰ τῆς δικαιοσύνης? Respondemus v. 15. per χάριν θεῦ intelligitur fauor & misericordia Dei patris, quæ v. 5. ἀγάπη dicitur, quæ itidem δωρεὰ nuncupatur, quia prorsus gratuita est. Per χάριν τῦ χρισῦ autem intelligitur iustitia & meritum Christi. Sensum ergo Lutherus optimè reddidit in versione Germanica: So ist viel mehr GOttes Gnade vnnd Gabe vielen reichlich widerfahren/durch die Gnade des einigen Menschen Jesu Christi: v. 17. itidem per χάριν notatur fauor Dei, per δικαιοσύνης δωρεὰν donata Christi iustitia, (est enim Hebraismus) seu meritum Christi quod gratis pro nobis præstitit & persoluit.

XXIV. Summa igitur hactenus dictorum est, Quod per donū & χάρισμα intelligatur tùm gratia Dei, tùm meritum Christi, quę duo beneficia dicuntur donū, quia nobis sine nostris meritis gratis obtigerūt, & p consequens nihil hîc agitur de gratia habituali vel iustitia inhæsiua, id q fuit demonstrandum.


### Question III. How many species or divisions of grace are there?

I. The Jesuits, following the Scholastics, put forward many divisions of grace, some of which we admit, and some we reject. We shall therefore review them one by one, and briefly indicate which are to be accepted and which are to be rejected.

The first division, into eternal and temporal grace.

II. Bellarmine proposes this division in book 1, chapter 2. He writes: Eternal grace is that love with which God loved us before the foundation of the world, from eternity itself, to the praise and glory of which grace the Apostle testifies that we were predestined by God and chosen for the adoption of sons, Ephesians 1, verse 6. Temporal grace is the name given to the benefits of vocation and justification, which are derived from eternal grace as effects from a cause.

III. In these words of Bellarmine there are three things less to be approved; 1. That by temporal grace he seems to understand not the favor and mercy of God, but some inherent gifts: which could be conceded if the discussion were only about the gifts of renewal; but because he speaks primarily of vocation and justification, we deny that by that grace, by which we are called and justified, anything inherent in us is to be understood:

IV. 2. He seems to make a real distinction between eternal and temporal grace, which we do not concede in any way. For the distinction of times does not apply to God: therefore, His grace, by which He loved us both from eternity and in time, is one and perpetual. One must, however, distinguish between grace itself and the manifestation of grace. God loved us from eternity, but He did not manifest that love from eternity, but in time, by sending His Son. More correctly thence a distinction is made between grace and the work of grace. Grace was from eternity, and now also is one and the same: for by the same grace, and not by another different one, with which God loved the human race from eternity, he now loves it. The works of grace, however, were not from eternity, but finally took their beginning in time: If, therefore, by eternal grace the grace and mercy of God itself, which perpetually remains one, is understood, and by temporary grace the manifestation or works of grace, such as redemption and vocation, are understood, this distinction can be conceded. But if grace is doubled, as if we were chosen by one grace from eternity, but loved by another in time, in this sense we do not concede it.

V. 3. He confuses general grace with special, because he thinks that men are called at the same time by the grace by which we are elected, when nevertheless these are most distinct.
