For from eternity, by reason of the object, the grace and love of God was twofold: The one general, by which he loved the whole human race, and this grace is manifested in time through the mission of the Son and the announcement of the word; The other special, which is called love in the beloved, by which he chose us from eternity: which is manifested in time through justification, renewal, and preservation in holiness: Therefore, one must speak distinctly and cautiously here; lest we confuse either general grace with special, and vice versa, or the manifestation of general grace with the special works of grace, from which many errors and greatest perplexities are accustomed to arise in this article:

Latin:

I. Iesuwitae ex Scholasticis multas proferunt diuisiones gratiae, quarum aliquas admittimus, nonnullas reijcimus. Singulas igitur recensebimus, & quae recipiendae, quae rejiciendae sint breuiter indicabimus.

Prima diuisio, in gratiam aeternam & temporariam.

II. Bellarminus hanc diuisionem proponit l. 1. c. 2. scribit: Gratia aeterna est ille amor, quo nos Deus ante mundi constitutionem ab ipsa aeternitate dilexit, in cuius gratiae laudem & gloriam nos a Deo praedestinatos esse usque electos in adoptionem filiorum testatur Apostolus Ephes. 1. v. 6. Gratia temporaria dicuntur beneficia vocationis & iustificationis, quae ex aeterna gratia, vt effectus ex causa deriuantur.

III. In quibus Bellarmini verbis tria sunt minus approbanda; 1. Quod per gratiam temporariam non fauorem & misericordiam Dei, sed inhaerentia aliqua dona videtur intelligere: quod concedi posset, si tantum de donis renouationis sermo foret: verum quia de vocatione & justificatione potissimum loquitur; negamus quod per istam gratiam, qua vocamur & justificamur, aliquid nobis inhaerens sit intelligendum:

IV. 2. Videtur reale discrimen facere inter gratiam aeternam & temporariam, quod nullo modo concedimus. In Deum enim non cadit distinctio temporum: Vna ergo perpetuo est ejus gratia, qua & ab aeterno, & in tempore nos dilexit. Distinguendum vero inter ipsam gratiam & gratiae manifestationem. Ab aeterno nos Deus dilexit, verum non ab aeterno dilectionem manifestauit, sed in tempore, mittendo suum filium. Rectius proinde distinguitur inter gratiam & gratiæ opus. Gratia ab æterno fuit, & nunc etiam est vna & eadem: quâ enim gratia genus humanum Deus ab æterno amauit, eâdem & non alia diuersâ nunc diligit. Opera verò gratiæ non fuerunt ab æterno, sed demum initium sumserunt in tempore: Quod si ergò per gratiam æternam ipsa gratia Dei & misericordia, quæ perpetuò vna manet: per gratiam temporariam manifestatio vel opera gratiæ, vt redemptio, vocatio, intelligantur, concedi potest hæc distinctio. Sin verò gratia duplicetur, ac si aliâ ab æterno sumus electi, aliâ verò in tempore diligamur hoc eam sensu non concedimus.

V. 3. Confundit gratiam generalem cum speciali, quia per gratiam, qua sumus electi, simul vocari censet homines, cùm tamen hæc maximè sint distincta. Nam ab æterno ratione objecti, duplex fuit Dei gratia & dilectio: Altera generalis qua diligebat totum genus humanum, & hæc gratia manifestatur in tempore per missionem Filij, & annunciationem verbi; Altera specialis, quæ dicitur dilectio in dilecto; quâ nos ab æterno elegit: quæ in tempore manifestatur per justificationem, renouationem & conseruationem in sanctitate: Distinctè igitur hic & cautè loquendum; nè vel gratiam generalem cum speciali, & contra, vel gratiæ generalis manifestationem cum operibus specialibus gratiæ confundamus, vnde multi errores, & maximæ perplexitates in hoc articulo suboriri solent:


### Question III. How many species or divisions of grace are there?: The second division, of temporary grace into general and special

The second division, of temporary grace into general and special.

VI. Bellarmine also makes mention of this division in chapter 2, book 1, who by general grace understands that concurrence of the first cause with secondary causes, as much for evil actions as for good ones, while by special grace he denotes that which was inserted only for producing good acts.

VII. But that division does not fit here. For we are not disputing about the grace of God the Creator, which is common to all creatures whatsoever, but rather about the grace of God the Redeemer, which uniquely concerns man, whose works are the mission of the Son, calling, justification, and the like. Furthermore, the grace of God the Redeemer in its own sense can be called either general or special: the former, as has just been said, pertains to all men; the latter pertains only to believers.

The third division, of special grace into grace freely given, and grace making one pleasing.

VIII. This is a division proper to the Scholastics, who were the first of all to devise it, which even the modern Jesuits keenly defend, although meanwhile they do not all agree in defining these species of grace: Lombard, book 2, distinction 37, letter D, understands by grace freely given that which precedes the will of man. For he says thus: 'Since therefore good merits are said to be from grace and to begin, either grace freely giving is understood, that is God; or rather grace freely given precedes the will of man.' Bonaventure, cited by Flacius, part 1, Clavis, defines his graces in this way: 'Grace is generally called divine aid, liberally and freely bestowed upon a creature, for any act whatsoever indifferently. Grace freely given is aid given divinely, so that one may prepare oneself to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, which arrives at the state of merit:' Grace making one pleasing is aid given divinely for meriting.

IX. But the modern Jesuits agree in this, that grace freely given denotes particular gifts of God, which are conferred upon someone for the sake of more successfully converting others; but grace making one pleasing is the infused habit of justice itself, because by it one is formally just and accepted before God: For thus says Becanus in disput. de Auxilijs grat. c. 1. th: 2. Grace is divided into grace freely given and grace making one pleasing. The former is conferred upon man for the utility of others, the latter for his own salvation and justification: Likewise Bellarmine defines these graces in l. 1. de grat: c. 2: Greg. de Val. tom 2. disput. 8. quæst. 7. pun. 1.

X. Graces freely given acknowledge nine principal kinds, from 1. Cor: 12. v. 8: 1. Wisdom, 2. knowledge, 3. faith, 4. the gift of healings, 5. the working of miracles, 6. prophecy, 7. the discerning of spirits, 8. kinds of tongues, & 9. the interpretation of speeches, which gifts, all and singular, just as many others, we do not deny are given freely by God, and principally for converting one's neighbor.

XI. That, however, is manifestly false, which they suppose, that grace freely given can sometimes be found in an unregenerate man, when nevertheless faith, the discerning of spirits, the interpretation of speeches, are included in grace freely given, which gifts anyone understands cannot exist in one who is unregenerate and not converted.

XII. Nor is there any reason why they should urge that 1. Cor. 13. v. 1, 2, & 3: If I should have all knowledge and all faith, but have not charity, it profits me nothing: whence Bellarmine concludes, c. 10. that knowledge and faith can exist without charity. For there is no consequence in this argument, since the Apostle speaks ὑποθετικῶς (hypothetically). But even beginners in Logic know that a conditional statement posits nothing: For it is just as if someone were to argue thus: If an ass flies, it has wings; Therefore an ass can fly.

XIII. But as regards the gift of Prophecy, we do not deny that it is sometimes given to impious men. For we have an express example in Balaam, an impious man, Num. 22 & 23, to whom God spoke secretly. And Num. 24. v: 2 it is said: the Spirit of God rushing upon him, etc. Upon which text Osiander noted these words: This pertains to the gifts of God, by which men are indeed excellently adorned, but not sanctified and thence regenerated. In the New Testament we have the example of Caiaphas prophesying, John 11, v. 51.

XIV. Furthermore, we utterly reject grace making pleasing in the Popish sense. For how could grace making pleasing be in us, when it is said in Luke 17, v. 10: When you have done all things, say, we are unprofitable servants. And whatever of good qualities or virtues is in us, that is a gift of God, and pertains to grace freely given, not grace making pleasing. For that we are rendered pleasing to God not through some inherent habit of justice, but through the sole imputed justice of Christ, will be proved below in the Article of Justification.

XV. Therefore, most absurd is Gregor. de Val. in the said book, who interprets these passages of inherent grace: Rom. 3, v. 24, Justified freely, by his grace. And Eph. 2, v. 6, He predestined us to the praise of the glory of his grace, which text, however, Bellarmine explains as the favor of God, ch. 2.

XVI. But as for what is further disputed here, whether grace making pleasing inheres in the essence of the soul, which Bellarmine denies in chapter 6, Becanus affirms in ch. 1, thesis 4, and Valent. in quest. 2, point 3. Whether in the powers of the soul? which Bellarmine affirms, they deny. Likewise, whether grace making pleasing is really distinguished from charity? which the said book denies, Bellarmine affirms, Valent. in quest. 2, point 2; all these things we dismiss, and reject as useless. For once it is proved that grace denotes the favor of God, not an inherent quality, there is no need to inquire at length what kind of habit that is, what its subject might be, etc. For of a non-entity there are no affections.

Latin:

Secunda diuisio, gratiæ temporariæ in generalem & specialem.

VI. Facit huius quoque diuisionis mentionem Bellarminus c. 2. l. 1. qui per generalem gratiam intelligit illum concursum causæ primæ cum secundis, tam ad malas, quàm bonas actiones, per gratia verò specialem notat eam, quæ tantùm ad actus bonos producendos inseruit.

VII. Verùm diuisio ista hûc non quadrat. Non enim disputamus de gratia Dei creatoris, quæ omnibus omninò creaturis communis est, sed potius de gratia Dei Redemptoris, quæ vnicè concernit hominem, cuius opera sunt missio Filij, vocatio, iustificatio & similia. Cæterùm gratia Dei redemptoris suo sensu potest dici vel generalis, vel specialis: illa, vti modò dictum, omnes homines: hæc solos attinet credentes.

Tertia diuisio, gratiæ specialis in gratiam gratis datam, & gratiam gratum facientem.

IIX. Propria hæc Scholasticorum est diuisio, qui omnium primi eam excogitârunt, quam hodierni etiam IesuWitæ acriter defendūt, quamuis interea non omnes consentiant, in definiendis istis gratię speciebus: Lombardus l. 2. dist. 37. lit. D. per gratiam gratis datam intelligit eam, quæ voluntatem hominis præuenit. Ita enim inquit Cum ergò ex gratia dicuntur esse bona merita & incipere, aut inucligitur gratia gratis dans, id est Deus; vel potius gratia gratis data voluntatem hominis præuenit. Bonaventura, citante Flacio; par. 1. Cla. hoc modò suas gratias definit: Gratia generaliter dicitur adiutorium diuinum, creaturæ liberaliter & gratis impensum, ad quemcunque actum indifferenter. Gratia gratis data est adiuiorium diuinitus datum, vt quis præparet se ad suscipiendum Spiritus sancti donū quòd peruenit ad statum meriti: Gratia gratum faciens, est adiutorium diuinitus datum ad merendum.

IX. Hodierni verò IesuWitæ conueniunt in eo, quòd gratia gratis data, peculiaria notet dona Dei; quæ alicui conferantur, ad felicius convertendos alios; gratia verò gratum faciens sit ipse infusus iustitiæ habitus, quòd quis formalitèr coram Deo justus sit & acceptus: Ita enim ait Becanus in disput. de Auxilijs grat. c. 1. th: 2. Gratia diuiditur in gratiam gratis datam & gratiam gratum facientem. Illa confertur homini ad vtilitatem aliorum, hæc ad propriam salutem & iustificationem: Pariter has gratias definit Bellarminus l. 1. de grat: c. 2: Greg. de Val.tom 2.disput.8.quæst.7.pun.1.

X. Gratiæ gratis datæ novem præcipua agnoscunt genera, ex 1. Cor:12.v.8: 1.Sapientiam 2 scientiam, 3.fidem, 4.gratiam sanitatum, 5. operationem virtutum,6: prophetiam.7. discretionem Spirituum; 8. Genera linguarum; & 9. interpretationem sermonum, quæ dona omnia & singula, sicut & alia multò plura gratis à Deo dari, & præcipuè ad conuertendum proximum, non inficiamur:

XI. Illud vero manifestè falsum est, quod arbitrantur, gratiam gratis datam quandoque reperiri posse in homine non renato, cùm tamen fides, discretio spirituum, interpretatio sermonum, inclusa sit gratiæ gratis datæ, quæ dona omnia in non renato, & non conuerso non esse posse quiuis intelligit.

XII. Nec est, quòd vrgeant illud 1.Cor. 13.v. 1: 2.& 3: Si habuero omnem scientiam & omnem fidem, charitatem autem non habeam,nihil mihi prodest: vnde concludit Bellarminus, c. 10. quòd scientia & fides esse possit absque charitate. Nulla enim inest huic argumento consequentia, quoniam Apostolus ὑποθετικῶς loquitur. Conditionalem verò nihil ponere, norunt etiam tyrones Logicæ: Perindè enim est,ac si quis ita argumentaretur:Si asinus volat, habet pennas; Ergo asinus potest volare.

XIII. Donum Prophetiæ autem quod attinet, non negamus illud quandoque hominibus dari impijs. Habemus enim expressum Exemplum in Balaam homine impio, Num 22. & 23 cui Deus secretò loquebatur. Et Num.24. v:2 dicitur: Irruente in se Spiritus Dei, &c. Ad quemtextum hæc verba annotauit Osiander: Pertinet hoc ad dona Dei, quib.egregiè quidem exornantur, non autem sanctificantur homines & inde regenerantur. In No. T. habemus Exemplum Caiphæ Prophetantis, Iohan. 11. v. 51.

XIV. Porrò Gratiam gratum facientem sensu Papistico prorsus rejicimus. Quomodo enim esset in nobis gratia gratum faciens, cùm Luc. 17. v. 10. dicatur: Si omnia feceritis, dicite, serui inutiles sumus Et quidquid in nobis est bonarū qualitatū vel virtutum, id donum Dei est, & ad gratiam gratis datam, non gratum facientem pertinet. Non enim per inhærentem quendam iustitiæ habitum, sed per solam Christi justitiam imputatam nos Deo gratos reddi infra in Artic. Iustificationis probabitur

XV. Proinde quam maximè absurdus est Gregor. de. Val. d. L. qui de gratia inhærente interpretatur loca hæc Rom. 3. v. 24. Iustificati gratis, per gratiam ipsius. Et Eph. 2. v. 6. Prædestinauit nos in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ suæ, quem tamen textum de fauore Dei exponit Bellarminus c. 2.

XVI. Quæ verò porrò hic disputantur, Vtrum gratia gratum faciens hæreat in essentia animæ, quòd negat Bellarminus cap. 6. affirmat Becanus c. 1. thesi 4. & Valent. quæst. 2. pun. 3. An in potentiis animæ? quod affirmat Bellarminus, negant illi. Item, An gratia gratum faciens realiter distinguatur à charitate? quod d. l. negat Bellarminus, affirmat Valent. quæst. 2. pun. 2. ea omnia nos missa facimus, & tanquam inutilia rejicimus. Probato enim, quòd gratia fauorem Dei, non inhærentem qualitatem denotet, opus non est prolixè disquirere, qualis sit iste habitus, quodnam eius subiectum detur? &c. Non entis enim nullæ sunt affectiones.


### Question III. How many species or divisions of grace are there?: Fourth division, of grace making pleasing into habitual and actual

Fourth division, of grace making pleasing into habitual and actual.

XVII. Bellarmine, in chapter 2, calls habitual grace permanent grace, and says it is the infused habits of faith, hope, and charity. He writes that actual grace, however, is a motion of God by which man is aided toward operations that in some way surpass his nature; Valentia, question 3, part 2, defines it thus: We call habitual grace a gratuitous gift, which is given to man durably, and which therefore can remain in him continuously. But we call actual grace a motion, divinely excited in the mind, whether it be cognition, or desire, or operation.

XIIX. And we do not entirely reject this distinction. For it cannot be denied that the reborn become habitually good through the daily exercises of good works and the continued mortification of the flesh. But if by habitual grace they understand justifying grace, or think that those perfect habits of charity, hope, and the remaining theological virtues are infused at the first moment of conversion, then in this sense we do not admit that distinction. For it is not conceded by our people that we love God from a habit at the first moment of regeneration, but rather they affirm that the principle of that love is the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, illuminating and moving the hearts of men: but when a converted man daily mortifies his flesh by the work of the Spirit, and exercises himself in good works, then he begins to love God as if from a habit of charity, indeed in such a way that, just as at the beginning of conversion the Holy Spirit was the sole and immediate principle of love, so after continued exercises of good works, He is no longer the principle of love ἀμέσως, but ἔμεσως, namely through the mediation of the habit of charity.

XIX. This is evident 1. From the restoration of the divine image. For through renewal the lost image of God is gradually restored. But just as this consisted not only in good works, but rather in the most praiseworthy of the habits of nature, so when it is separated, certain habits are restored, namely justice and holiness. 2. From the opposition of the old and new man. As it gives being to the old, not only actual, but rather habitual justice. When therefore the remission of sins has been made, then at the same time renewal begins to be made, there follows the mortification of the old Adam, and the production of the new man, that is, step by step and day by day through good works the old man is more and more mortified, and the new man rises again, who according to God is created in justice and holiness of truth, Eph. 4. v. 23. Hence Gal. 6. v. 15. the reborn are called a new creature, in that their nature is clothed with new qualities.

XX. We do not therefore simply deny all habitual grace, since the reborn not only work justly, but also are just, for which an inherent habit of justice is required; which we do not deny to true and constant reborn persons, although it is only begun, not consummated, nor does it enter into the act of our justification.

XXI. Here, however, we further note the error of Valentianus, that he distinguishes habitual gifts by reason of their subjects; that some perfect the essence of the soul, and some perfect the powers of the soul; such as are the habits of the theological virtues. By a habitual gift, however, perfecting the essence of the soul, he understands inherent grace, by which we are justified: But because the whole Scripture is entirely ignorant of this, therefore this distinction of habitual gifts is null, and there remain only the habits of the theological virtues, which are in that subject which they perfect. Since therefore some direct the intellect, some the will, hence some are said to be in the intellect, as faith, insofar as it is knowledge and assent, some in the will, as faith, insofar as it is trust, hope, charity, etc.

Latin:

Quarta diuisio, gratiæ gratum facientis in habitualem & actualem.

XVII. Gratiam habitualem vocat Bellarminus c. 2. gratiam permanentem, & dicit esse habitus infusos, fidei, spei, & charitatis. Gratiam verò actualem scribit esse motionem Dei, quâ homo ad operationes, quæ naturam suam aliquomodo superant, adiuvatur, Valent. quæst. 3. p. 2. ita definit: Gratiam habitualem vocamus gratuitum donum, quæd datur homini durabiliter, quodque proinde in eo manere continenter potest. Actualem autem gratiam vocamus motum, in mente diuinitus exsitatum, siue ille sit cognitio, siue appetitio, siue operatio.

XIIX. Et hanc distinctionem non omninò reijcimus. Etenim per quotidiana bonorum operum exercitia, & continuatam carnis mortificationem renatos habitualiter bonos fieri, negari nequit. Sin verò per gratiam habitualem intelligant gratiam iustificantem, vel putent, primo conuersionis tempore infundi perfectos illos habitus charitatis, spei & reliquarum virtutum Theologicarum, tum hoc sensu istam distinctionem non admittimus. Non enim conceditur à Nostratibus, quòd primo regenerationis tempore ex habitu diligamus Deum, sed potius adfirmant, quòd principium istius dilectionis sit gratiosa Spiritus sancti inhabitatio, corda hominum illustrantis & mouentis: quando autem homo conuersus, ope Spiritus carnem suam quotidiè mortificat, & sese in bonis operibus exercet, ibi tum quasi ex habitu charitatis Deum diligere incipit, ita quidem, vt sicut in primordio conuersionis Spiritus sanctus vnicum & immediatum erant dilectionis principium, ita post continuata bonorum operum exercitia non amplius sit dilectionis principium ἀμέσως, sed ἔμεσως, mediante videlicet habitu charitatis.

XIX. Patet hoc 1. Ex restitutione imaginis diuinæ. Per renouationē enim paulatim restituitur amissa imago Dei. Sicut autẽ hæc consistebat non tantùm in bonis operibus, sed potius in laudatissimis naturæ habitibus, ita cùm feparatur, quidam habitus restituuntur, iustitia nimirum & sanctitas. 2. Ex oppositione veteris & noui hominis. Vt veteri esse dat, nō modò actualis, sed habitualis potiùs iustitia. Quando igitur facta est remissio peccatorum, tūc simul incipit fieri renouatio, sequitur veteris Adami mortificatio, & noui hominis productio, hoc est pedetentim propedie per bona opera magis magisǫ; mortificatur vetus, & resurgit nouus Homo, qui secundù Deum creatus est in justitia & sanctitate veritatis, Eph. 4. v. 23. Hinc Gal 6. v. 15. dicuntur renati noua creatura, eà quòd ipsorum natura nouis qualitatibus induatur.

XX. Non ergo simpliciter inficiamur omnem gratiam habitualem, cùm renati non solùm justè operentur, sed & justi sint, ad quod requiritur inhærens justitiæ habitus; quem veris & constantibus renatis non denegamus, licèt is duntaxat sit inchoatus, non consummatus, neque actum iustificationis nostræ ingrediatur.

XXI. Hic verò insuper notamus errorem Valentiani, quod dona habitualia ratione subiectorum ita distinguit; quòd aliquod perficiat essentiam animæ, & quædam perficiant potentias animæ; quales sint virtutum Theologicarum habitus. Per donum autem habituale, essentiam animæ perficiens; intelligit gratiam inhærentem, quâ justificemur: Hanc verò quia vniuersa Scriptura prorsus ignorat, ideò hæc donorum habitualium distinctio nulla est, remanentque soli habitus virtutum Theologicarū, quæ in có sunt subjecto, quòd perficiunt. Cùm igitur quædam intellectum, quędam voluntatē dirigant, hinc aliquæ dicuntur esse in intellectu, vt fides, put est notitia & assens, aliquæ in voluntate, vt fides, prout est fiducia, spes, charitas, &c.


### Question III. How many species or divisions of grace are there?: The fifth division, of actual grace into operating and cooperating

The fifth division, of actual grace into operating and cooperating.

XXII. This division of grace was first handed down by Augustine himself. For thus he says in lib. de grat. & lib. arbit. c. 17: 'He works so that we may will, beginning [the work] in those who are willing, and perfecting it by cooperating with those who will.' On account of which the Apostle says, 'I am confident that he who works a good work in you will perfect it, even unto the day of Christ Jesus.' Therefore, so that we may will, he works without us; but when we will, and so will that we may act, he works with us. And below: 'Without him, either working so that we may will, or cooperating when we will, we are able to do nothing for the good works of piety.'

XXIII. Operating grace is that which works upon the will not yet converted, and moves and excites and prepares it for conversion, and converts it once prepared. Cooperating grace, however, is that which, after conversion, cooperates with man for the production of good works, and causes man to persevere in the good he has begun. The effects of operating grace, therefore, are the illumination of the mind and the conversion of the will; those of cooperating [grace], however, are good works and perseverance in faith.

XXIV. Bellarmine in c. 14 and Becanus in c. 2 ask here how operating grace works in us without us, and is the cause of conversion? They distinguish, however, between an ethical and a physical cause. An ethical cause of conversion is for them nothing other than persuasion and exhortation to perform penance. A physical cause, however, is that which effects and produces penance. They say, therefore, that operating grace works in us without us ethically indeed, but not physically; that is, that grace alone persuades us and exhorts us to perform penance (for we do not exhort ourselves), yet that operating grace alone does not actually excite conversion; but rather our will also wills and produces it together with it.

XXV. But because by this arrangement something is ascribed to free will, as if two partial causes concur in effecting our conversion, the grace of God and our will, therefore we attribute the entire efficiency of conversion to grace alone, and clearly affirm that it is only the grace of God that both knocks at our heart and, once knocked upon, converts it, but not that the heart either prepares or converts itself by its own powers,

XXVI. But if it be asked, not about conversion, but about the willing of conversion, we say that it cannot properly be ascribed to grace as to a subject (although it is ascribed to it as a cause), but only to the human will. For God does not stand in need of conversion. Therefore, He cannot will His own conversion, but rather man, hearing the word, begins to will to be converted, but this willing does not proceed from the nature of the will, but from the grace of God itself.

XXVII. A distinction must therefore be made between τὸ velle and the cause of τẽ velle: The human will alone is that which wills to be converted (for this alone is the convenient subject). But it is asked, what does it that the will should will this? There it is answered, that the sole and unique grace of God does this.

XXIIX. Furthermore, it is also customary to dispute here whether there is one grace that is operating, and another that is cooperating; we maintain, however, that just as there is one God, who gives both to will and to perform, so there is one grace, which operates in us without us, and which operates in us with us. And thus that grace is distinguished not by itself, but because of its effects. For insofar as it converts us without us, it is called operating grace; but insofar as it makes us persevere in conversion and piety with us, it is termed cooperating grace.

XXIX. Moreover, these species of grace are also accustomed to be designated by other names. For operating grace is also named prevenient, and cooperating is named subsequent, not by reason of their nature, but by reason of their acts and offices. For the act of operating grace is prior to the act of cooperating grace (for we are converted before we are confirmed in conversion), and therefore the former is named prevenient, the latter subsequent.

XXX. Regarding these names of grace, Augustine speaks thus in his book De natura et gratia, ch. 32: God precedes, so that we may be healed; He follows, so that, being healed, we may be invigorated. He precedes, so that we may be called; He follows, so that we may be glorified. He precedes, so that we may live piously; He follows, so that we may live with Him forever, because without Him we can do nothing. And in Enchiridion 32, he says: He precedes the unwilling, so that he may will; He follows the willing, so that he may not will in vain. And Gregory, homily 9 on Ezekiel: He precedes us, so that we may will; and He follows us, who are willing, so that we may not will emptily. Hence the Church sings: Precede our actions by inspiring them, and follow them by assisting them. Fulgentius also, in book 1 to Monimus, p. 13, says: He Himself freely grants grace to the unworthy, by which the impious man, having been justified, may be illuminated by the gift of good will and the faculty of good operation, so that by preceding mercy he may begin to will the good, and by following mercy he may be able to do the good that he wills. P. 21. He precedes the impious, so that he may become just; He follows the just, so that he may not become impious. He precedes the blind, so that He may grant the light which he does not find; He follows the seeing, so that he may preserve the light which He bestowed. He precedes the fallen, so that he may rise; He follows the raised, so that he may not fall. He precedes by granting man a good will; He follows the one who wills well, by working in him the faculty of a good work.

XXXI. Finally, operating grace is also called exciting, because it first excites us and renews our will: but cooperating grace is named assisting, because it assists the will once excited and renewed, so that it may be able to do the good which it wills, and may remain in the good. Hence Augustine, l. 2 de peccat. meritis & remiss., writes: That we are turned to God, we cannot do unless He excites and assists us. And Bern. lib. de grat. & lib. arbitr.: Our efforts are both vain if they are not assisted, and null if they are not excited.

Latin:

Quinta diuisio, gratiæ actualis in operantem & cooperantem.

XXII. Diuisio hæc gratiæ primùm ab ipso Augustino fuit tradita. Ita enim inquit l. de grat. & l. arbitr. c. 17. Ipse vt velimus, operatur incipiens qui volentibus cooperatur perficiens. Propter quod ait Apostolus, Certus sum, quoniam qui operatur in vobis opus bonum perficiet, vsque in diem Christi Iesu Vt ergò velimus, sine nobis operatur, cum autem volumus, & sic volumus, vt faciamus, nobiscum operatur. Et infrà: Sine illo, vel operante, vt velimus, vel cooperante cum volumus, ad bona pietatis opera nihil valemus.

XXIII. Est autem gratia operans ea, quæ in voluntatem nondum conuersam operatur, illamque mouet & excitat præparatq́; ad conuersionem, & præparatam conuertit, Gratia verò cooperans est, quæ post conuersionem, homini cooperatur ad productionem bonorum operum, facitq́; vt homo in incepto bono perseueret. Operantis igitur gratiæ effectus sunt, illuminatio mentis & conuersio voluntatis: cooperantis autem, bona opera & perseuerantia in fide.

XXIV. Quærit hîc Bellarminus c. 14. & Becanus c. 2. quomodo gratia operans in nobis sine nobis operetur, & conuersionis causa sit? Distinguunt yerò inter causam Ethicam & Physicam. Causa conuersionis Ethica nihil est ipsis aliud, quàm suasio & adhortatio ad agendam pœnitentiam. Physica verò causa est ea, quæ efficit & producit pœnitentiam. Dicunt ergò gratiam operantem sine nobis operari in nobis, Ethicè quidem, non autem Physicè; hoc est solam gratiam nobis persuadere & hortari nos ad agendam pœnitentiam, (neque enim nos ipsos exhortamur, ) attamen non solam gratiam operantem actu excitare conuersionem; sed potius nostram voluntatem vnâ quoque eam velle & producere.

XXV. Quia vero hoc pacto, libero arbitrio aliquid adscribitur, ac si in efficienda nostri conuersione duæ concurrant partiales causæ, gratia Dei & nostra voluntas, ideo soli gratiæ omnem conuersionis efficientiam tribuimus, clarèque adfirmamus, quòd duntaxat gratia Dei cor nostrum & pulset, & pulsatum conuertat, non autem quod cor semetipsu ex suis virib. vel præparet vel cõuertat,

XXVI. Quòd si autem quæratur, non de conuersione, sed de velle conuersionis, dicimus illud non posse propriè asscribi gratiæ tanquam subjecto, (licet asscribatur veluti causę) sed soli voluntati humanæ. Deus enim conuersione non indiget. Ergo sui conuersionem velle nequit, sed potius homo audiens verbum, incipit velle se conuerti, sed hoc velle non prouenit ex natura voluntatis, sed ipsa Dei gratia.

XXVII. Distinguendum igitur est inter τὸ velle & inter causam τẽ velle: Sola voluntas humana est quæ vult conuerti, (hæc enim sola commodum est subiectum.) Quæritur autem, quid faciat, vt voluntas hoc velit? Ibi respondetur, solam & vnicam Dei gratiam hoc facere.

XXIIX. Porrò hîc & istud disceptari solet, Vtrum alia sit gratia operans, & alia cooperans; Statuimus verò, sicut vnus est Deus, qui & velle dat & perficere, ita vnam esse gratiam, quæ in nobis sine nobis operatur, & quæ in nobis cum nobis operatur Atque sic gratia ista distinguitur non ex se, sed propter effectus. Quatenus enim nos sine nobis conuertit, gratia operans dicitur; quatenus verò nos cum nobis conuersione & pietate perseuerare facit, gratia cooperans nuncupatur.

XXIX. Cæterùm & aliis nominibus hæ gratiæ species indigitari consueuerunt. Gratia enim operans nominatur quoque præueniens, & cooperans subsequens, non ratione suæ naturæ, sed ratione suorum actuum, & officiorum. Actus enim gratiæ operantis, prior est actu gratiæ cooperantis (pri⁹ enim cõuertimur, quã in cõuersione cõfirme mur) ideoq; illa præueniẽs, hęc nominatur subsequẽs.

XXX. De his nominibus gratiæ ita loquitur Augustinus l. de nat. & grat. c. 32. Deus præuenit, vt fanemur, subsequitur, vt fanati vegetemur. Præuenit, vt vocemur; subsequitur, vt glorificemur. Præuenit, vt piè viuamus; subsequitur, vt cum illo femper viuamus, quia sine illo nihil possumus facere. Et in Enchirid. 32. ait: Nolentem præuenit, vt velit; volentem subsequitur, ne frustrà velit Et Gregor. homil. 9. in Ezech. Nos præuenit, vt velimus; & volentes subsequitur, ne inaniter velimus. Hinc canit Ecclesia Actiones nostras adspirando præueni, & adiuuando profequere. Fulgentius etiam l. 1. ad Monimum p. 13. ait: Ipse donat gratis indigno gratiam, quà iustificatus impius illuminetur munere bonæ voluntatis, & facultate bonæ operationis, vt præueniente misericordiâ bonum velle incipiat, & subsequente misericordiâ bonum, quod vult, facere valeat. P. 21. præuenit impium, vt fiat iustus, subsequitur iustum, ne fiat impius. Præuenit cæcum, vt lumen, quod non inuenit, donet: subsequitur videntem, vt lumen quod contulit, feruet. Præuenit elisum, vt surgat: subsequitur eleuatum, ne cadat. Præuenit donans homini bonam voluntatem: subsequitur benè volentem, operando in illo boni operis facultatem.

XXXI. Tandem gratia operans vocatur etiam excitans, quia nos excitat primùm, & voluntatem nostram renouat: gratia verò cooperans nominatur adiuuans, quia voluntatem excitatam & renouatam iuuat, vt bonum quod vult, facere valeat, & in bono permaneat. Hinc Augustinus l. 2 de peccat, meritis & remiss. scribit. Quòd ad Deum nos conuertimur, nisi ipso excitante & adiuuante, non possumus. Et Bern. lib. de grat. & lib. arbitr. Conatus nostri & cassi sunt, si non adiuuentur, & nulli, si non excitentur.


### Question III. How many species or divisions of grace are there?: The sixth and final division, of operating grace into sufficient and efficacious

The sixth and final division, of operating grace into sufficient and efficacious.

XXXII. Theologians call sufficient grace that, says Gregorius de Valentia, quest. 3, point 4, through which a man can procure his own salvation by pious actions and attain it. But efficacious grace is that through which the thing itself does this. Bell. l. 1. c. 2. defines it thus: Sufficient aid is said to be that by which God so calls and excites a man and is prepared to help by directing, protecting, and cooperating, that he who is thus excited and called can in reality will to believe, will to cooperate, will to that by which God so calls and excites a man, and is prepared to help by directing, cooperating, and protecting, that he infallibly in reality believes, is converted, and does good. Becanus c. 3. th. 1. writes: Efficacious grace is that which has an effect in us; sufficient is that which can indeed have an effect, yet in reality does not have it. Others call it efficacious and inefficacious, others congruent and incongruent.

XXXIII. We do not entirely disapprove of that distinction, and so that it may be understood, we distinguish between the ordinary and the extraordinary or miraculous conversion of man.

XXXIV. As regards this, we say that it happens through efficacious grace infallibly and always: for this grace so calls a man that he is converted by a will that is as it were necessary and a necessity that is voluntary. We have examples in Abraham and Paul, who were called extraordinarily to faith and the Church. Where it is asked, whether this grace was such that it could have been rejected either by Abraham or by Paul? And theologians judge that it must be answered in the negative. This extraordinary grace, therefore, if it is compared with the ordinary, can be called efficacious of itself and always, because all who are called by this grace are always converted. And all the benefits which God has bestowed upon this or that person beyond the hearing of the word can be referred to this: just as it was an extraordinary grace that greater miracles were performed in Chorazin than in Tyre and Sidon. Matt. 11. v. 20.

XXXV. But no cause for this grace can be given beyond the will of God. All men are indeed ordinarily called by one and the same grace: but extraordinarily God often calls this person by a peculiar grace before that one, the cause of which thing is known to Him who searches the reins and hearts of men.

XXXVI. But as regards ordinary grace, this cannot be called efficacious in the stated sense, and therefore, for the sake of distinction, it is called sufficient. The cause is taken from the twofold will of God, namely, simple and conditional. Extraordinary grace proceeds from the simple and absolute will, ordinary from the conditional will. Just as, therefore, the absolute will cannot be hindered, so also extraordinary grace, which is its effect, can never be interrupted, whence it happens that it is always efficacious. But just as not all things which God wills by a conditional will come to pass, so neither is that ordinary grace always efficacious.

XXXVII. Therefore these two graces are not one and the same grace, which is distinguished at least by the outcome, but rather they are distinct, and are separated from one another not because of an unequal outcome, but rather because of an unequal nature and power, which inequality of nature is the cause of the unequal outcome. For just as extraordinary grace proceeds from the absolute will of God, so it has joined to it the absolute power of God, which is always most efficacious: but ordinary grace, just as it draws its origin from the conditional will of God, so it has annexed to it only the limited and conditioned power of God, which is not efficacious unless the conditions are present; and since these can sometimes be absent, it happens that this grace is not always efficacious, although it is always sufficient.

XXXIIX. Furthermore, as regards ordinary grace, which is given equally to all, we say that it too can be distinguished in such a way that, by reason of different men, who are either converted by it or are not converted, it can be called either efficacious or only sufficient; efficacious by reason of the converted, sufficient by reason of the unconverted.

XXXIX. It must be noted, however, that this distinction is not to be taken from the essence of grace itself, as if efficacious grace were of itself of greater ἐνεργείας, but sufficient grace of lesser. For each in itself is one and the same, bound to one and the same word of God, which all hear at the same time. For when many hear the word at one and the same time, then one does not hear one word and another another, but all hear one and the same: all therefore, together with the one and same word, ordinarily receive one and the same grace. For the word is the δοχεῖον, the vehicle and receptacle of that grace, since it is called the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Rom. 1. v. 16. Hence I infer: Where there is one and the same vehicle, there is also one and the same power and grace, which is conveyed by that vehicle. But one and the same vehicle of grace reaches many hearers, namely, the preached word. Therefore, the grace also is one and the same.

XL. Since these things are so, we conclude that grace, of itself and by its own nature, cannot be so distinguished that it is called efficacious by reason of this hearer, and sufficient by reason of that one, because thus it would not be one in number; and therefore that division is sought rather from the outcome, so that the same grace is termed efficacious and inefficacious or sufficient. It is called efficacious when it obtains its outcome; inefficacious, when, although it could obtain the same by its innate power and ἐνεργείᾳ, it nevertheless does not obtain it in actual fact. And thus the diversity of effect, which shines forth in different subjects, makes the ordinary grace, which is one in itself, diverse respectively. Briefly, efficacious grace is that which persuades in such a way that it does persuade; but inefficacious grace is that which persuades in such a way that, although it could persuade, it nevertheless does not actually persuade.

XLI. Here, however, a most difficult question arises: From what does this diversity of outcomes depend? How does it happen that, while one and the same grace is ordinarily offered to all through one and the same word, not all are converted by it? What, therefore, makes that one grace efficacious in this hearer and inefficacious in that one? This question the human mind scarcely grasps, and therefore perhaps to one seeking such things it should be answered, restrain your lip with your finger. Nevertheless, because something can be said from the Scriptures to the proposed πρόβλημα, and because heretics go off into contrary opinions, it will be useful to note a few things here.

XLII. The Calvinists answer this question in one way, the Papists in another, and the Orthodox in another. The Calvinists in turn disagree among themselves. For some think that the preached word is not universally joined with a certain efficacious power (as Piscator writes in his theses on the ministry of the word), and therefore that grace is not offered to all through the preached word, but only to the predestined. Others concede that grace is offered to individuals through the word, but that the power of it is intercepted not by the resistance of men, but by the will of God and the absolute decree of reprobation, which errors of the Calvinists will be refuted in the section on predestination. Here we are concerned primarily with the Papists, who fight among themselves like the Cadmean brothers.

XLIII. Gregory of Valentia, quest. 3, point 4, maintains that efficacious grace is so called not from the event, but rather from its own nature, and is distinct from sufficient grace, in this sense: that the former is always efficacious, while the latter can sometimes be hindered; and therefore he writes that it cannot happen that two hearers receive this grace, and yet one is converted and the other is not converted; if he understands this of extraordinary grace, he speaks the truth; but if of ordinary grace, it is false, as we have just proved.

XLIV. But if you should further ask him the reason why those who are ordinarily called by the same grace are not converted at the same time, he answers in these words, col. 3. 226: Because since this one was free, so that with God effectively helping he might be converted, and he had received that very grace, being helped by the same, through his own conversion as if through something prior in another genus (namely, of natural cause), thus clearly he was converted, and accepted that grace, namely, being helped by the same. The other, however, although he was also free to do that, did not do it. Wherefore he who did not do it must ascribe it to his own will alone, that he did not do it. He, however, who did it, must not ascribe it to his own will alone, that he did it, but primarily to the efficacious grace of God and at the same time also to his own will, as helped by that grace. And thus he can boast, not indeed in himself alone, but then in the Lord, and then subsequently in himself, when he has consented to the help of grace and has cooperated with the Lord. These are his words.

XLV. Becanus, chapter 3, thesis 5, judges that grace is efficacious in this, not because of the diversity of the grace itself, but because of the diversity of the manner of offering, because to this one it was offered in such a place, and time, and with such circumstances, that he both wills and is able to consent freely, but to the other it was not so. In thesis 6 and 7, he places the cause in the free will of man. For it is in human powers to either assent to grace or not; therefore, he who by the power of free will accepts that grace is converted, but he who does not accept that same grace is not converted. For thus he says in thesis 7: If, therefore, the first root is sought, why this grace is efficacious and that one inefficacious, one must have recourse to the free cooperation of the will, and not to the foreknowledge of God, by which He foresaw that this or that grace would be congruent. He affirms the same in chapter 7, thesis 1.

XLVI. Bellarmine, however, is completely doubtful and slippery on this question, as can be seen in book 1 de Grat. chapters 12 and 13. Chapter 12: he brings forward this reason, column 559, C. If it is asked, why two who are called by the same grace are not converted at the same time? He replies: because God, according to His free will, suspends the act of grace in this one, but not in the other. And thus he refers the cause to the secret decree of the divine will, and thus far he is a Calvinist. Chapter 13, column 566, letter B, he seeks the cause in the diversity of the manner, grace being offered to this one in a way convenient to place and time, but not so to the other, and thus far he agrees with Becanus. Chapter 12, column 559, letter C, and column 560, letters A and B; section 13, column 567, letter B, column 568, letter C, he dissents from Gregory and Becanus, omAnd he refutes those who think that grace obtains its effect because the human will cooperates. He brings forward an insoluble reason, because thus the believer would be distinguished from the unbeliever by free will, and the believer could boast before the unbeliever, which is contrary to Phil. 2:13, 1 Cor. 4:7. The words are so manifest that they cannot be eluded by any cavil. Soon, forgetful of himself, c. 13, fol. 568, lit. C, he receives that opinion which he had rejected, and brings forward a twofold cause of this inequality: one primary, the will of God; the other secondary, free will, in which, however, he again disagrees with Betanus and Valentianus. For these think the primary root and cause of that inequality is placed in the free operation of man. And this is that egregious Papistic consensus. XLVII. But that we may extricate ourselves from that thicket of opinions, we posit the following conclusions. 1. 1. The cause of this diverse outcome is not to be placed in the diversity of grace. For we are inquiring here about ordinary grace, which is offered to all as one and the same, and not extraordinary grace, by which sometimes one here, in preference to another, can rejoice according to the sole and unique good pleasure of God. 2. The cause of this diverse outcome is not to be placed in a certain absolute decree of GOD, suspending the efficacy and act of grace. For this Calvinistic opinion will be sufficiently refuted in the place concerning predestination. 3. The cause of this diverse outcome is not to be placed on both sides in the cooperation of free will. For grace does not become effective because man received it by the power of free will. For that such free will is nothing will be proven in its own time. 4. The true cause of this diverse outcome is to be placed solely in the contumacy of man freely resisting. For Prosper said most correctly, l. 2: de Vocat: gentium c. 28. It is manifest that God wills all men to be saved in diverse and innumerable ways, but those who come are directed by the help of God, those who do not come resist by their own pertinacity. Habet, for man has the freedom of resisting, but he does not have the freedom of assenting to grace. Our will is free toward evil, but truly a slave toward good.

XLIIX. If therefore you ask: Why is one and the same grace effective in this listener, but ineffective in that one? I answer, because this one resisted, that one did not resist. For it is in the power of man to resist and not to resist. However, it is not in the power of man to assent or not to assent at will. This one, therefore, is converted, not because he willed to be converted (for he cannot will the good), but because he did not resist; the other is not converted, not because he did not will to assent (for this is not in his power), but because he resisted.

XLIX. And by this reasoning we escape those two most dangerous rocks, namely the Calvinian decree of reprobation, besides the same, and Pelagianism, which extols human powers, and we defend the grace of God in such a way that His justice is not endangered, and thus [we defend] justice, so that grace is not diminished.

L. That this opinion is founded in the Scriptures can be easily proven. For first, that those who are converted are not converted on account of the free cooperation of the will is evident from all those sayings which show that man cannot even think anything good: likewise, that it is God alone who works in us both to will and to perform, which sayings will be reviewed in the treatment of the article on free will. Then, however, that those who are not converted are not converted on account of their own will and resistance alone is evident both from manifest sayings, Prov. 1:24, 'I have stretched out my hand, and you refused,' Matt. 23:38, 'I would have gathered you, but you would not,' Acts 7:51, 'You always resist the Holy Spirit'; and also from all those [passages] which prove that God does not delight in the perdition of men. For from this it follows that the cause of the ineffectiveness of grace cannot be sought in the will and counsel of God.

LI. From this, therefore, we conclude: Man can render grace ineffective, but not effective: for he has free will only in evil, not in good. The effectiveness of grace, therefore, depends solely on God, its ineffectiveness solely on man. Man is converted by God, but he does not convert himself, for this he cannot do: man is not converted because he resists God who wills to convert him. Therefore, that grace which was most effective for converting becomes ineffective by the will of the resisting man, but it is and becomes effective not by the will of man, but by the power of God. And thus, to speak summarily, effectiveness is ascribed solely to God who works, ineffectiveness solely to man who resists.

LII. To this resistance, indeed, can be reduced the diversity of manner, of which Bellarmine speaks, because, namely, grace is offered to this person at this time, when it has more obstacles than at another, whence it happens that he is converted either with more difficulty or not at all. For he who has many obstacles resists the Holy Spirit more strongly than he who has few, and few impediments are removed more easily than many. Thus, in our time, the Jews are converted with difficulty because they are of an obstinate heart, and furthermore many sects are found, all of which were absent in the time of the Messiah coming in the flesh. If, therefore, a modern Jew had lived in the time of the birth of the Messiah, perhaps he would not have resisted the Holy Spirit so much. And thus the diversity of circumstances also makes the same grace unequal. The primary cause, however, is the repugnance of men, to which we refer the circumstances that render it either greater or lesser.

LIII. Someone might object here: 1. If man has τὸ nolle [the will not to], therefore also τὸ velle [the will to]. If he can resist grace: therefore also assent. Resp. N. C. [I deny the consequence]. For if our will were still sound and uncorrupted, then the argument would proceed; but because our will is immersed in sin, hence it happens that it wills nothing but evil, when it wills. Meanwhile, it is in the power of man to posit or to omit that act of willing. In civil matters, indeed, it holds: He has τὸ nolle [the not-willing]. Therefore, also τὸ velle [the willing], but not in spiritual matters. LIV. 2. It would follow that man could boast, for he himself is the cause that he is converted: For if he had resisted, he would not have been converted: Resp. There is no consequence in return. For Scripture affirms both: that man cannot boast, and yet that man can resist the Holy Spirit. For even if man can hinder his own conversion, he cannot, however, effect it. Therefore, he cannot reason thus: I have not struggled against the Holy Spirit: Therefore, my conversion depends on my own powers and on my free will: For just as he who does not hinder a motion, which he can hinder, is not the cause of the motion: so man, not struggling against the Holy Spirit, is not the cause of that work. For if I ask, who converted you? You cannot answer, I and the Holy Spirit; but He alone is the one who converts you. Meanwhile, man can hinder that solitary action of the cause, and yet he in no way concurs in producing that effect, whence also he can in no way ascribe it to himself. If, therefore, one distinguishes between the cause removing the obstacle and the efficient cause, the answer will be straightforward. The will cannot act so that it obeys, but it can act so that it does not obey. For as in the former it is idle and ἄεργος [inactive], so in the latter it is very busy and ἐνεργὴς [active].

Latin:

Sexta & vltima diuisio, gratiæ operantis in sufficientem & efficacem.

XXXII. Gratiam sufficientem appellant Theologi eam, inquit Gregor. de Valent. quæst. 3. pun. 4. per quam homo potest piis actionibⁿ salutem suam procurare & consequi. Gratiam autem efficacem eam, per quam res ipsa hoc facit. Bell. l. 1. c. 2. ita definit: Auxilium sufficiens dicitur, quo Deus ita hominem vocat & excitat & iuuare dirigendo, protegendo, cooperando paratus est, ut reuera possit ille sic excitatus & vocatus velle credere, velle cooperari, velle bonum aliquod facere: Auxilium efficax dicitur, quo Deus hominem ita vocat & excitat, & iuvare diligendo, cooperando, protegendo paratus est, vt infallibiliter reipsa credat, conuertatur, bonum faciat. Becanus c. 3. th. 1. scribit: Gratia efficax est, quæ effectum habet in nobis; sufficiens, quæ potest quidem habere effectum, re ipsa tamen non habet. Alij voçant efficacem & inefficacem, alij congruam & non congruam.

XXXIII. Distinctionem verò istam non omninò improbamus, quod vt intelligatur, distinguimus inter conuersionem hominis ordinariam & extraordinariam vel miraculosam.

XXXIV. Hanc quod attinet, dicimus eam fieri per gratiam efficacem infallibiliter & semper: Hæc enim gratia hominem ita vocat, vt quasi necessariâ voluntate & voluntariâ necessitate convertatur. Exempla habemus in Abrahamo & Paulo, qui extraordinariè vocabantur ad fidem & Ecclesiam. Vbi quæritur, An hæc gratia talis fuerit, vt potuisset vel ab Abrahamo, vel à Paulo rejici? Et negatiuè respondendum esse censent Theologi. Hæc igitur gratia extraordinaria, si conferatur cum ordinaria, potest vocari efficax ex se & semper, quia omnes, qui hâc vocantur gratiâ, semper conuertuntur. Et huc referri possunt omnia beneficia, quæ præter auditum verbi Deus vel huic vel illi largitus est: vt gratia extraordinaria erat, quòd in Chorazin majores sunt factæ virtutes, quàm in Tyro & Sidone. Matth. 11. v. 20.

XXXV. Gratiæ verò huius præter voluntatem Dei causa dari nulla potest. Omnes quidem homines ordinariè vna eademque gratia vocantur: extraordinariè autem Deus sæpè hunc peculiari gratia vocat præillo, cuius rei causam nouit is, qui scrutatur renes & corda hominum.

XXXVI. Quod verò spectat gratiam ordinariam, hæc dicto sensu efficax vocari nequit, ideoque distinctionis ergò appellatur sufficiens. Causa sumitur à duplici voluntate Dei, nimirum simplici & conditionali. Gratia extraordinaria prouenit à simplici & absoluta, ordinaria à conditionali voluntate. Sicut ergo voluntas absoluta impediri nequit, ita & gratia extraordinaria, quæ eius effectum, nunquam potest interuerti, vnde fit, vt semper sit efficax. Sicuti verò non omnia, quæ vult Deus voluntate conditionali fiunt, ita nec gratia ista ordinaria semper est efficax.

XXXVII. Non igitur hæ duæ gratiæ sunt vna ac eadem gratia, quæ per euentum saltem distinguatur, verum potiùs sunt distinctæ, & à se invicem non ob inæqualem eventum, sed potius ob inæqualem naturam & potentiam disterminatæ, quæ inæqualitas naturæ causa est inæqualis euentus. Gratia enim extraordinaria quemadmodum provenit à voluntate Dei absoluta, ita coniunctam habet potentiam Dei absolutam, quæ semper est efficacissima: Ordinaria autem gratia vti à voluntate Dei conditionali ortum trahit, ita annexam habet non nisi potentiam Dei limitatam & conditionatam quæ efficax non est, nisi præsentibus conditionibus; quæ cùm quandoque abesse possint, fit, vt gratia ista non semper sit efficax, quamvis semper sit sufficiens.

XXXIIX. Cæterùm quod attinet gratiam ordinariam, quæ omnibus æqualiter datur, dicimus eam quoque ita distingui posse, vt ratione diversorum hominum, qui vel per eam conuertuntur, vel non conuertuntur, dici queat vel efficax vel sufficiens tantum; Efficax ratione conuersorum, sufficiens ratione non conuersorum.

XXXIX. Notandum autem, quod hoc discrimen non sumatur ab ipsa gratiarum essentia, ac si efficax gratia ex se maioris sit ἐνεργείας gratia verò sufficiens minoris. Nam vtraque in se vna est ac eadem deuincta vni & eidem verbo Dei, quod omnes simul audiunt. Quando enim vno & eodem tempore multi audiunt verbum, tunc non vnus aliud, & alter aliud verbum audit, sed omnes vnum idemque: omnes igitur vna cum verbo vno & eodem, vnam & eandem gratiam ordinariè accipiunt. Verbum enim est δοχεῖον vehiculum & receptaculum istius gratiæ, siquidem potentia Dei dicitur ad salutem omni credenti, Rom. 1. v. 16. Hinc infero; Vbi vnum & idem vehiculum, ibi est etiam vna eademque potentia, & gratia, quæ isto vehiculo aduehitur. Atqui ad multos auditores vnum & idem peruenit gratiæ vehiculum, nempè verbum prædicatum. Ergo etiam vna est eademque gratia.

XL. Quæ cum ita sint, concludimus, quòd gratia ex se & sua natura nequeat ita distingui, vt ratione huius auditoris dicatur efficax, ratione illius sufficiens, quia sic numero vna non esset, ideoque ab euentu potius petita est illa diuisio, vt eadem gratia nuncupetur efficax & inefficax seu suficiens. Efficax dicitur, quando suum sortitur euentum, inefficax, quando, cùm sortitur eundem posset pro innata vi & ἐνεργείᾳ non tamen actu ipso sortitur, Atque sic diuersitas effectus, quæ in diuersis subjectis elucet, gratiam ordinariam, in se vna, respectiuè diuersam efficit, Breuiter Gratia efficax est quæ ita suadet, vt persuadeat; Inefficax verò ita suadet, vt cùm persuadere possit, non tamē actu persuadeat.

XLI. Hîc autem difficilima oritur quæstio: Vndè nam dependeat ista euentuum diuersitas? qui fiat, quòd dum omnibus per vnum & idem verbum vna eademque gratia ordinariè offertur, non tamen omnes per istam convertantur; Quid ergo gratiam illam vnam in hoc auditore faciat efficacem in illo inefficacem; Quæstionem hanc vix capit captus humanus, ideoque forsitan talia quærenti respondendum foret, digito compesce labellum. Attamen, quia ex Scripturis aliquid ad propositum πρόβλημα dici potest, & quia hæretici in contrarias abeunt sententias, pauca hîc adnotare profuerit.

XLII. Aliter vero ad hanc quæstionem respondent Caluiniani, aliter Pontificij, aliter Orthodoxi. Caluiniani vicissim à seipsis dissentiunt. Nonnulli enim censent, verbum prædicatum vniuersaliter non esse conjunctum cum efficaci quadam potentia (vti scribit Piscator in thes. de ministerio verbi) ideoque gratiam non omnibus per prædicatum verbum offerri, sed duntaxat prædestinatis. Alij concedunt, singulis per verbum offerri gratiam, vim verò illius interuerti non per repugnantiam hominum, sed voluntatem Dei, & absolutum reprobationis decretum, qui Caluinianorum errores in loco de prædestinatione refutabuntur. Hic cum Pontificiis potissimùm nobis res est, qui vt Cadmei fratres inuicem digladiantur.

XLIII. Gregorius de Valentia quæst. 3. pun. 4. gratiam efficacem non ab eventu, sed potius ex natura sua ita dictam, & à sufficiente distinctam vult, hoc sensu, quòd illa semper sit efficax. hæc nonnunquam impediri queat, ideoque non posse fieri scribit, vt duo auditores gratiam percipiant hanc, & tamen vnus conuertatur, alter non convertatur; quod ipsum si de gratia extraordinaria intelligat, verum dicit; sin de ordinaria, falsum, vti modò probauimus.

XLIV. Quòd si autem ab eo præterea quæras causam, cur qui ordinariè eâdem gratiâ vocantur non simul conuertantur? respondet his verbis. col. 3. 226. Quia cum hic esset liber, vt Deo efficaciter adjuvante conuerteretur, eamque ipsam gratiam ab eodem adiutus per conuersionem suam tanquam per aliquid prius in alio genere (scilicet causæ naturalis) acceperat, ita planè conuersus est, & eam gratiam acceptauit, scilicet ab eodem adutus. Alter autem cùm ad id faciendum liber quoque esset, id non fecit. Quapropter is, qui id non fecit, soli suæ voluntati debet adscribere, quod non fecit. Is autem, qui fecit, non soli suæ voluntati debet adscribere, quod fecit, sed inprimis gratiæ efficaci Dei & simul etiam suæ voluntati, vt adiutæ per eam gratiam. Atque ita gloriari potest, non quidem in se solo, sed tum in Domino, tum deinde in se, cùm adiutorio gratiæ consenserit, & cooperatus fuerit Domino. Hæc ille.

XLV. Becanus cap. 3. thesi. 5. censet gratiam in hoc esse efficacem, non ob diuersitatem ipsius gratiæ, sed ob diuersitatem modi offerendi, quia huic tali loco, & tempore, & cum talibus circumstantijs oblata est, vt & velit & possit liberè consentire, alteri verò non item. Th. 6. & 7. causam ponit in libero hominis arbitrio. Esse enim in viribus humanis gratiæ vel assentiri, vel non, qui ergò vi liberi arbitrij illam gratiam acceptat, conuertitur, qui verò non acceptat illam ipsam, non conuertitur. Itą enim dicit th. 7. Si ergò quæratur prima radix, quare hæc gratia sit efficax, illa inefficax, recurrendum est ad liberam cooperationem voluntatis, non autē ad præscientiā Dei, quâ præuidit hanc aut illam gratiā fore congruam. Idem affirmat c. 7. th. 1.

XLVI. Bellarminus verò prorsus dubius est & lubricus in hac quæstione, vti videre est lib. 1. de Grat. c 12. & 13. C. 12: hanc affert rationem, colum. 559. C. Si quæratur, cur duo, qui eâdem gratiâ vocantur, non simul conuertuntur? Resp. quòd Deus pro liberâ voluntate actum gratiæ in hoc suspendat, in altero non item. Et sic causam refert ad arcanum diuinæ voluntatis decretū, atq; hactenus Caluinianus est. C. 13. column. 566. lit. B. causam quærit in diuersitate mod, huic loco & tempore conueniente, illi non itē gratia est oblata, atque hactenus cōsentit cum Becano. C. 12. col. 559. lit. C. & col. 560. lit. A. & B.§. 13. col. 567. lit. B. col. 568. lit. C. dissentit à Gregorio & Becano, omdiesq́; eos refutat, qui cesent, gratiam ideò sortiri effectum, quia voluntas humana cooperetur. Rationem affert insolubilem, quia sic fidelis ab infideli per liberum arbitrium discerneretur, & fidelis coram infideli gloriari posset, quod est contrà Phil. 2. v. 13. 1. Cor. 4. v. 7. Verba adeò manifesta sunt, vt nullo cauillo eludi queant. Mox sui oblitus c. 13. tol. 568. lit. C. illam opinionem, quam reiecerat, recipit, duplicemœue causam inæqualitatis huius affert, vnam primariam, voluntatem Dei; alteram secundariam, liberum arbitrium, in quo tamen rursum dissentit a Betano & Valentiano. Hi enim primam istius inæqualitatis radicem & causam in libera hominis operatione collocatam arbitrantur. Atque hic est egregius ille consensus Papisticus. XLVII. Sed vt nos ex illo opinionum senticeto extricemus, sequentes ponimus conclusiones. 1. Causa diuersi istius euentus non est ponenda in diuersitate gratiæ. Quærimus enim hîc de gratia ordinaria, quæ omnibus vna & eadem offertur, non autem extraordinaria, quâ nonnunquam hic prę alio secundum solum & vnicum Dei beneplacitum, gaudere potest. 2. Cauja istius diuersi euentus non est ponenda in absoluto quodam DEI decreto, efficaciâ & actum gratiæ suspendente. Hæc enim Caluinistica opinio satis consutabitur in loco de prædestinatione. 3. Causa istius diuersi euentus non est ponenda vtrinque in liberi arbitrij cooperatione. Non enim gratia ideò efficax fit, quia eam homo ex vi liberi arbitrij recepit. Tale enim arbitrium nullum esse, suo tempore probabitur. 4. Vera istius diuersi euentus causa vnicè ponenda est in hominis liberè repugnantis contumacia. Rectissimè enim dixit Prosper. l. 2: de Vocat: gentium c. 28. Manifestum sit, quod diuersis atque innumeris modis omnes homines vult Deus saluos fieri, sed qui veniunt Dei auxilio diriguntur, qui non veniunt, suâ pertinacia reluctantur. Habet enim homo libertatem reluctandi, sed non habet libertatem assentiendi gratiæ. Ad malum liberum est, ad bonum verò seruum est nostrum arbitrium.

XLIIX. Si ergò quæras. Cur vna & eadem gratia in hoc auditore sit efficax, in illo inefficax? Respondeo, quia hic repugnauit, ille non repugnauit. In hominis enim potestate est, τὸ repugnare, & τὸ nõ repugnare. In hominis autem potestate non est, pro lubitu assentiri vel non assentiri. Hic ergo conuertitur, non quia voluit conuerti (bonum enim non potest velle) sed quia non repugnauit; alter non conuertitur, nõ quia non voluit assentiri, (hoc enim in ei⁹ potestate non est) sed quia repugnauit.

XLIX. Atque hac ratione periculosissimos istos duos scopulos, Caluinianismũ nempè reprobationis decretũ, pręter eundem, & Pelagianismum, vires humanas extollentem effugimus, Deique gratiam ita defendimus, ne eius periclitetur iustitia, & sic iustitiam, ne extenuetur gratia.

L. Hanc verò sententiam in Scripturis fundatam esse facilè probari potest. Primò enim eos, qui conuertuntur, non conuerti ob liberam voluntatis cooperationem, ex omnibus illis dictis patet, quibus ostenditur, hominem ne quidem aliquid boni cogitare posse: item, quòd solus Deus sit, qui & velle & perficere in nobis operetur, quæ dicta recensebuntur in tractatione articuli de libero arbitrio. Deinde verò eos, qui non conuertuntur, propter solam propriam voluntatem & repugnantiam non conuerti, patet tùm ex manifestis dictis, Prov. 1. v. 24. Extendi manum meam, & vos renujstis, Matth. 23. v. 38. Volui vos congregare, sed noluistis, Act. 7. v. 51. Semper Spiritui sancto resistitis; tùm ex illis omnibus, quæ probant, Deum non delectari perditione hominum, Hinc enim sequitur, quod in Dei voluntate & consilio causa inefficacitatis gratiæ quæri non possit,

LI. Hinc ergò concludimus: Inefficacem potest homo gratiam reddere, sed non efficacem: habet enim liberum arbitrium in malo tantum non in bono. Efficacitas igitur gratiæ à Deo tantùm, inefficacitas ab homine tantùm dependet. Conuertitur homo à Deo, non autem conuertit seipsum, hoc enim nec potest: non conuertitur homo, quia Deo eũ conuortere volenti reluctatur. Ea ergo gratia, quæ ad conuertendum erat efficacissima, fit inefficax voluntate hominis repugnantis, efficax autem est & fit non voluntate hominis, sed potestate Dei. Atque sic, summatim dicendo, efficacia soli Deo operanti, inefficacia soli homini reluctanti adscribitur.

LII. Ad hanc verò reluctantiam reduci potest diuersitas modi, de quo Bellarminus, quia videlicet gratia hoc tempore, huic offertur, quo plura habet obstacula, quàm alio, vnde fit, vt vel difficilius, vel planè non conuertatur. Fortius enim resistit Spiritui sancto, qui multa habet obstacula, quàm qui pauca, & facilius remouentur impedimenta pauca, quàm multa. Sic nostro tempore Iudæi difficilè cõuertuntur, quia obstinato sunt corde, multæque insuper sectæ inueniuntur, quæ omnia tempore Messiæ in carnem venientis aberant. Si Iudæus igitur hodiernus vixisset tempore nati Messiæ, forsitan non tàm reluctatus fuisset Spiritui sancto. Et ita diuersitas circumstantiarum eandem quoq; gratiã facit inæqualem. Prima tamen causa est repugnantia hominum, ad quam referimus circumstantias, quæ illam vel maiorem vel minorem reddunt.

LIII. Obijcere hîc aliquis posset, 1. Si homo habet τὸ nolle, Ergo etiam τὸ velle. Si potest repugnare gratiæ: Ergo etiam assentiri. Resp. N. C. Si enim voluntas nostra adhuc sana esset, & incorrupta, tum procederet argumentum; quia verò voluntas nostra peccato est immersa, hinc fit, vt non nisi mala velit, quando vult. Interim in potestate hominis est, illum nolendi actum ponere vel intermittere. In ciuilibus quidem negotijs valet: Habet τὸ nolle. Ergo etiam τὸ velle, sed non in spiritualibus. LIV. 2. Sequeretur, hominem posse gloriari, ipse enim est causa, quod sit conuersus: Si enim repugnasset, non fuisses conuersus: Resp. Nulla vicissim est consequentia. Vtrumque enim affirmat Scriptura, hominem non posse gloriari, & tamen hominem posse Spiritui sancto resistere. Etiamsi enim homo queat impedire sui conuersionem, non tamen eam potest efficere. Nequit ergo ita ratiocinari; Ego non reluctatus sum Spiritui sancto: Quare a meis viribus, & a meo libero arbitrio pendet mei conuersio: Nam sicuti qui non impedit motum, quem impedire potest, non est causa motus: ita homo non reluctans Spiritui sancto, non est causa istius operis. Si enim quaero, quis te conuertit? Non potes respondere, Ego & Spiritus Sanctus; sed hic solus est, qui te conuertit. Interim illam solitaria causae actionem potest homo impedire, & tamen nullo modo cōcurrit ad producendum istum effectum, vnde etiam nullo modo sibi illum potest asscribere. Si ergo distinguatur inter causam remouentem prohibens, & causam efficientem, responsio erit expedita. Non potest voluntas agere, vt obediat, potest autem agere, ne obediat. Vt enim in illo est otiosa & ἄεργος, ita in hoc admodum est negotiosa, & ἐνεργὴς.


### Question III. How many species or divisions of grace are there?: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 14 Disputation II. On the Universal Will and Love of God

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent, Michael Mönchmeier, of Salza in Saxony.

Προοίμιον. Whether the doctrine of predestination should be proposed to the common people; and what rules are to be observed here?

I.

With the article on the Grace of God explained, there follows the topic of Predestination, by which God has most clearly declared His beneficent will. This head of doctrine, the more useful it is, the more intricate it is, indeed so much so that that saying of Augustine, which he spoke concerning the mystery of the Trinity, may not inappropriately be applied here: Nothing is sought with more labor than the article of predestination, and nowhere is it more dangerous to err, and nothing is found more fruitfully.

II.

Therefore, so that we may consider this doctrine accurately, three things come to be set forth by way of a preface. 1. Whether one should dispute about Predestination, or speak to the people from the pulpit? 2. What rules are to be observed here? And finally, 3. Into what chapters may this article be conveniently divided?

III. ON THE FIRST.

In the times of Augustine, there were found in Gaul men, for that reason called the brothers of Gaul, who judged that the definition of predestination was contrary to the utility of preaching: Against whom Augustine wrote in his book On the Predestination of Saints, ch. 14; the book On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 14, 15, 16; the book On Rebuke and Grace, ch. 5, 14.

16. & l. 6. ὑπογνωστικῶν. Certain of the Calvinists are of the same opinion, especially Theodore Beza, who in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 308, Wittenberg edition, 1605, proposed these words: Nor is it advisable to confer about this article before everyone, lest perhaps more be offended than instructed, who cannot grasp those things. And page 316: This dispute cannot be held in a public assembly without grave offense to those who are not capable of such a mystery, whether they assent to our opinion or the contrary one. Whence a new seedbed of dissension might arise, so that this dispute should be debated in schools, among trained theologians, rather than in a public gathering of the common people.

IV. We, however, maintain that such dangerous concealment of the truth is pernicious and highly suspect, and therefore we intend to demonstrate by the following arguments that this doctrine ought to be treated and explained not only in schools by the learned, but also in churches by pastors to the unlearned.

V. 1. From the general command of Christ, which is contained in Mark 16:15, the force and sum of which is that the Gospel must be preached, and indeed whole and entire, not only to some, but to all, not only privately, but also publicly, not only in schools, but also in temples and churches. But indeed the doctrine of predestination, no less than other articles, is a part of the Gospel concerning Christ. Why, therefore, would it not be advisable to dispute and converse about it?

VI. 2. From the example of the Prophets, Christ, and the Apostles. That which they delivered and inculcated to everyone can and ought to be proposed to everyone, both in schools and in churches. For they were written to that end, that they might be read by all and explained to all. For why would they have been committed to writing if they could not be delivered in public without grave offense? Shall we brand the Spirit with the mark of imprudence? instituted as holy, that in that book, which he wished to be τῆς ψυχῆς φάρμακον, he caused scandalous dogmas to be annotated: And yet Christ and the Apostles delivered the doctrine of predestination and reprobation to the Prophets and to all people born, as is evident from Isa. 6. ver. 9. Malach. 1. ver. 1. 2. Matth. 11. v. 21. chap. 13. v. 13. John 10. ver. 27. chap. 12. ver. 39. Rom. 9. Eph. 1. etc. Therefore, it can and ought to be proposed to all people, both in schools and in temples.

VII. 3. From utility. All scripture is useful, 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. And whatever things were written before, were written for our learning, Rom. 15. v. 4. How, therefore, could the topic of predestination, which is written in the sacred code, not be proposed without offense? On the contrary, it truly illustrates the glory of God, teaches the intimate causes of salvation, refutes the Pelagians, instructs the elect in all parts of holiness, consoles the infirm, and corrects those who, having abused this doctrine, either pour themselves into a supine license for sinning or cast themselves into despair of salvation. On the contrary, however, if anyone is ignorant of this article of faith, a scruple can easily arise for him concerning his own eternal reprobation; from which he cannot extricate himself due to ignorance. And how will all be able to beware of heretics and false brothers, according to the warning of Christ in Matt. 7. v. 15, if this doctrine ought not to be delivered or proposed to all?

VIII. From the authority of the orthodox fathers. For these were not afraid to treat and explain the mystery of predestination in their writings, and indeed in their homilies. Why, therefore, should we not imitate their laudable example? Augustine expressly censures such untimely fear in his book On the Gift of Perseverance, ch. 14. Why, he says, do we consider the definition of Predestination, which the same divine Scripture commends, useless for preaching, precept, exhortation, and correction, all of which divine Scripture frequents? Furthermore, the saying of Theodoret from his dialogues is known: ἐδᾶ τὰ κεκρυμμένα

ζητᾶν, ὅδὲ τὰ δεδηλωμένα παντελῶς ἀγνοεῖν; It is not fitting to scrutinize hidden things, nor to be entirely ignorant of things made manifest. In which sense also Ambrose, book 1, de Vocat. gent. ch. 7: Things which God willed to be hidden are not to be scrutinized, but things which He made manifest are not to be denied, lest in the former we be found illicitly curious, and in the latter damnably ungrateful.

IX. 5. From the confession of recent Calvinists. For most make a divorce from Beza, and not obscurely disapprove of his opinion concerning the hiding of this article. For thus writes Sohnius in Volume 2, p. 994: It cannot be denied WITHOUT manifest BLASPHEMY against the Spirit of God that this doctrine is useful to the Church of God and necessary to be known and preached. Polanus in didasc. page 1: To deny that what GOD Himself has handed down ought to be taught in the Church is sacrilegious impiety and wicked madness. Hubertus Sturmius in Diatribe de prædest. th. 1, p. 18, 19: Those who judge that this doctrine should be suppressed, do they not interpolate and dig up the wicked Pelagius, ungrateful to God, Christ, and the Church: for whom a certain cross is fixed. Zanchius has similar things in book 5, de natura Dei, chapter 2, p. 752, and in part 1 of Miscell. p. 411.

X. The things which are brought forward to the contrary are light and easy to solve. They object: 1. If it is preached that the elect are not damned, and the reprobate are not saved, then the effort to rise again will be taken away from those who have fallen, and torpor and sloth in not progressing will be added to those who are standing. Resp. 1. Those who are offended in such a way are either weak or contumacious. If they are weak, let them be instructed; if they are contumacious, let them be abandoned. 2. Because of the abuse and mockery of the wicked, the elect are not to be defrauded of this doctrine. For Augustine rightly says: It is not to be feared, because the Heretic does not keep silent, that he might be offended by our speaking, he who cannot or will not grasp the truth, so that by our keeping silent, he who can grasp the truth might be captured by falsehood. 3. This objection is opposed to the Holy Spirit Himself. For if these stumbling blocks accompany the doctrine of election by their very nature, why has it been recorded in the scriptures and commended to us?

4. Those things which are subordinate are held to be opposites. For election does not take away the pursuit of good works and perseverance in faith, but promotes it, since they relate to each other as an end and the means which are subordinated, not opposed. For those who are elected from eternity, they perform repentance in time, believe in Christ, and persevere in piety: if it happens otherwise, election is falsely presumed. Wherefore this reasoning is impious: If I am elected, I shall attain life even without piety: For the argument must be inverted: If I am elected, I ought to renounce worldly pursuits. For God chose us, that we should be holy and blameless, Eph. 1. v. 4. Therefore, this must always be inculcated to the hearers, that God in eternal election had regard for faith, and therefore it is necessary that the elect believe in time, and make their faith attested by good works. But those who do not believe, and do not wish to believe, their faith could not be foreseen from eternity, and consequently they are not predestined. In this way, the pursuit of repentance and good works will not languish, but rather will grow, and will take on greater increases day by day.

XI. They object 2. The mystery of election is too deep to be grasped by the common people. For who has known the mind of the Lord, Rom. 11. verse 33? Therefore, it should rather be kept silent about than spoken of. Resp. 1. Although it cannot be known in its entirety, yet it can be known to an extent, and therefore Christ inculcated it even before the common people. Augustine wisely says in his book on the gift of perseverance, ch. 15: Must that which is open be denied because that which is hidden cannot be comprehended? 2.
