Election is considered with respect to either causes or special cases. Those can be known, although a reason cannot be given for all of these. 3. This doctrine is obscure to the slow and to those who are perishing, 2. Cor. 4. v. 3, but not to pious and devout investigators, for whom light shines out of darkness, v. 6. 4. The heralds of the word ought to apply effort, so that Let them treat this article both soberly and prudently. Soberly, so that they may explain it from the Word of God alone, not from the judgment of reason. Prudently, so that they may apply sound words to sound doctrine, and direct the matter to this end, that every occasion may be snatched away both from Pharisaical presumption and from Judaic despair, so that the pious may be preserved in humility, and the impious may be thrust down from security. If this is done, this doctrine will be appropriately proposed, usefully heard, and clearly understood.

XII. CONCERNING THE SECOND. Since the mystery of predestination is arduous and sublime, theologians prescribe certain rules which we must always observe if we wish to proceed here without stumbling. Selneccer, in part 2 of the Paedagogus, p. 606, recounts seven such rules or axioms, and includes them in these verses:

1. The Word: 2. the promise: 3. the person equal: 4. the one will of God: 5. goodness greater than sin: 6. the Fall of Adam destroying us: 7. God is the life and salvation.

The sum of these rules is indeed this: 1. Nothing is to be said about the will of God outside of the Word of God. 2. The promise of God concerning the grace of God is universal, and pertains to all. 3. With God there is no προσωποληψία or respect of persons. 4. In God there are no contradictory wills. 5. The grace of God surpasses every sin. 6. Just as in Adam all fell, so in Christ all rise again. 7. God created no creature either for sin or for destruction.

XIII. Aegidius Hunnius, in his tract on predestination, p. 95, inculcates four principal rules: 1. Predestination is not to be considered a priori, but only a posteriori, according to the prescription of the revealed Word. 2. One is not to judge concerning predestination from the doctrine of the Law, but of the Gospel. 3. The eternal decree of election must be diligently compared with the execution of the decree which takes place in time. 4. In

Contradictory wills do not fall upon God.

XIV. More recent authors enumerate a few more, which, however, we believe can all be reduced to the following seven.

XV. FIRST. One must not dispute or judge concerning predestination except from the Word of God.

For our reason is otherwise blind in divine matters: how then will it be able to soar into the very penetralia of divine counsels, so that it might know them a priori and without the revealed Word?

And to this point pertains that distinction of Luther between God absolute and relative, or what is the same, hidden and revealed. Let us direct our thoughts to the latter only, not to the former. For to deal with the hidden God, according to Luther, is that apple in which our first parents devoured death, because they wanted to know those things which they ought not to have known. Let us therefore always be mindful of that golden aphorism, which Hilary, book 5 de Trin., prescribed in these words: One must not judge concerning divine predestination by human judgments. For our nature is not such that it can raise itself into heavenly knowledge by its own powers. We must learn from God what is to be understood concerning God and the will of God. Because God is not known except with God as the author. Since, therefore, it was impossible to learn God without God, He teaches men to know God through the Word. Wherefore let a limit be placed upon human curiosity, lest we desire to have known what God willed to be secret, Ambrose, book 1 de Vocat. gent, chapter 8. For those who go after their own thoughts and speak of the deep things of God are submerged into the deep, Augustine, sermon 7 de verbis Apost.

XVI. SECOND. Predestination is not to be known from the doctrine of the Law, but of the Gospel. For the Law convicts of sins, it does not remit them; it accuses, it does not pardon, John 5, verse 45. From the Law comes a curse, not salvation, Deuteronomy 27, verse 16; Galatians 3, verse 10. How, therefore, can the decree of salvation be known from the Law? The Gospel is rather to be consulted, inasmuch as in it Only through the Son who declares Him, John 1:18, is the will of God the Father manifested. Hence it is called the revelation of the mystery, kept secret for eternal times, Rom. 16:25. Therefore, those who define the secret of election either according to the works of the law, as the Papists do, or without respect to the Evangelical promises concerning the universal grace of God and the merit of Christ, as the Calvinists do, are in error.

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Michaele Mönchmeiero, SaltzaSaxone.

Προοίμιον. Num doctrina praedestinationis vulgo proponenda; Et quaenam hîc regulae obseruandae sint?

I.

EXplicato articulo de Gratia Dei, succedit locus de Praedestinatione, quâ Deus voluntatem suam beneficam luculentissimè declarauit. Quod doctrinae caput, quò est vtilius, eò intricatius, ita quidem, vt istud Augustini, quod de mysterio Trinitatis dixit, nõ incommodè huc applicari queat, Nihil praedestinationis articulo laboriosius quaeri & nullibi periculosius errari, & nihil fructuosius inueniri.

II.

Proinde vt doctrinam hanc accuratè consideremus, tria proœmij loco exponẽda veniunt. 1. Num de Praedestinatione disputandum sit, vel ad populum è suggesto loquendum? 2. Quaenam regulae hîc obseruandae? Et tandem. 3. In quae capita articulus hic commodè diffesci queat?

III. DE PRIMO.

Temporibus Augustini repertisunt in Gallia viri, ob id fratres Galliae nominati, qui iudicârunt prędestinationis definitionem esse aduerfam vtilitati praedicationis: Contra quos scripsit Augustinus l. de Praedest, ca. 14. L. de bono perseuerantiae, cap. 14. 15. 16. L. de corrupt. & gras. cap. 5. 14.

16. & l. 6. ὑπογνωστικῶν. Eiusdem opinionis sunt quidam ex Caluinianis, præsertim Theodorus Beza, qui in Colloquio Mompelg. m. p. 308. edit. Witteb. Anno 1605. hæc verba proposuit: Neque consultum est coram omnibus de hoc articulo conferre, ne fortè plures offendantur, quàm erudiantur, qui illa capere non possunt. Et pag. 316. In publico cœtu haberi hæc disputatio non potest sine graui eorum offendiculo, qui tanti mysterij capaces non sunt, sine nostra siue contrariæ sententiæ assentiantur. Vnde nouum exoriri dissensionis seminarium possit, vt hæc disputatio potiùs in scholis, inter exercitatos Theologos, quàm in publico quoruncatu disceptanda sit.

IV. Nos autem statuimus, pernitiosam & maximè suspectam esse illam periculosam veritatis occultationem, ideoq; non solùm in scholis a literatis, sed in templis etiam à Pastoribus ad idiotas tractari, atque explicari hanc doctrinam debere sequentibus argumentis demonstraturi damus.

V. 1. à Generali mandato Christi, quod continetur Marc. 16. v. 15. cuius hæc vis & summa est, quòd Euangelium prædicandum sit, & quidem totum ac integrum, non tantum quibusdam, sed omnibus, non tantùm priuátim, sed quoque publicè, non modò in scholis, sed etiam in templis & Ecclesiis. At verò doctrina prædestinationis, non minùs atque alij articuli, pars est Euangelii de Christo. Cur ergò de illa disputare & colloqui consultum non foret?

VI. 2. Ab Exemplo Prophetarum Christi & Apostolorum. Quòd hi quibusuis tradiderunt, & inculcarunt, id etiam quibusuis tùm in scholis tùm in templis proponi potest & debet. Eo enim fine scripta sunt, vt ab omnibus legantur, & omnibus exponantur. Cur enim literis consignata essent, si absque graui offendiculo tradi in publico non possent? Num imprudentiæ notam inuremus Spistitui sancto, quod in illo libro, quem τῆς ψυχῆς φάρμακον esse voluit, dogmata scandalosa annotari fecerit: Atqui Prophetæ Christus & Apostoli doctrinam prædestinationis & reprobationis, prote nata quibusuis tradiderunt, vt patet ex Eja. 6. vers. 9. Malach. 1. vers. 1. 2. Matth. 11. v. 21. cap. 13. v. 13. Ioh. 10. vers. 27. cap. 12. vers. 39. Rom. 9. Eph. 1. &c. Ergò eà ipsa quibusuis tùm in scholis, tùm in templis proponi potest & debet.

VII. 3. Ab vtili. Omnis scriptura vtilis est, 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. Et quæcunque præscripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam pręscripta sunt, Rom. 15. v. 4. Quî ergò locus de prædestinatione, qui in sacro codice pręscriptus est, sine offendiculo proponi non posset? Imo verò illustrat gloriam Dei, docet intimas salutis causas, arguit Pelagianos, instituit electos ad omnes sanctitatis partes, consolatur infirmos, & corrigit eos, qui hac doctrinâ abusi semet vel in supinam peccandi licentiam effundunt, vel in de sperationem salutis abijciunt. Cont rà verò, si quis ignoret hunc fidei articulum, facilè illi suboriri potest scrupulus, de æterna sui reprobatione; ex quo sese ob ignoratiam expedire nequit. Et quo modo hæreticis falsique fratribus, iuxta Christi monitum Matt. 7. v. 15. cauere sibi poterunt omnes, si non omnibus hæc doctrina tradi proponiuè debeat?

VIII. Ab authoritate orthodoxorum patrum. Hi e him nō sunt veriti in scriptis, quin & homilijs suis mysterium prædestinationis tractare & explicare. Cur ergo illorum laudabile exemplum non imi taremur. Augustinus expressè taxatistam intempestiuam formidinem l. de bono perseuer. ca. 14. Cur, inquit, prædicationi, pręceptioni, exhortationi, corrptionique quæ omnia frequentat Scriptura diuina, existimamus inutilem diffinitionem Prædestinationis, quam com mendat eadem Scriptura diuina? Notum insuper est Theodoreti dictum ex dialogis: ἐδᾶ τὰ κεκρυμμένα

ζητᾶν, ὅδὲ τὰ δεδηλωμένα παντελῶς ἀγνοεῖν; Non oportet scrutari abscondita, nec omninò ignorare patefacta. In quem etiam sensum Ambrosius l. 1. de Vocat. gent. c. 7. Quæ Deus occulta esse voluit, non sunt scrutanda, quæ autem manifesta fecit, non sunt neganda, ne in illis illicitè curiosi, & in istis damnabiliter inveniamur ingrati.

IX. 5. A confessione recentium Calvinianorum. Plerique enim à Beza divortium faciunt, eiusque opinionem de occultando hoc articulo haud obscurè improbant. Ita enim scribit Sohnius Tomo 2. p. 994. Non potest SINE manifesta in Spiritum Dei BLASPHEMIA negari, hanc doctrinam Ecclesiæ Dei vtilem esse & necessariam scitu & prædicatu. Polanus in didasc. pag. 1. Negare illud esse in Ecclesia docendum, quod DEUS ipse tradidit, est sacrilega impietas, & improba vesania. Hubertus Sturmius in Diatribe de prædest. th. 1. p. 18. 19. Qui hanc doctrinam obruendam censent, ne illi Pelagium nefarium interpolant ac refodiunt, ingrati in Deum, Christum & Ecclesiam: quibus crux certa fixa. Similia habet Zanchius l: 5. de natura Dei cap. 2. p. 752. & in part. 1 Miscell. p. 411.

X. Quæ in contrarium afferunt, leuia sunt, & solutu facilia. Objiciunt. 1. Si prædicatur, electos nō damnari, reprobatos non saluari, tùm prostratis adimetur conatus resurgendi, stantibus addetur torpor & segnities nòn progrediendi. Resp. 1. Qui taliter offendūtur, aut sunt infirmi, aut contumaces. Si infirmi, erudiantur, sin contumaces, deserantur. 2. Propter improborum abusum & irrisionem non sunt hâc doctrinâ defraudandi electi, Nam rectè Augustinus: Non est timendum, quia Hæreticus non tacet, vt nobis loquentibus offendatur, qui veritatem nō potest, vel non vult capere, vt nobis tacentibus, qui veritatem capere potest falsitate capiatur. 3. Hæc obiectio ipsi Spiritui sancto opponitur. Si enim offendicula ista per se doctrinam electionis comitantur, cur in scripturis relata & nobis commendata est?

4. Pro oppositis habentur, quæ subordinata sunt. Electio enim studium bonorum operum & perseverantiam in fide non tollit, sed promouet, siquidem habent se, vt finis, & media, quæ subordinantur, non contrariantur. Nam qui ab æterno electi sunt, illi in tempore pœnitentiam agunt, in Christum credunt, & in pietate perseuerant: secus si fiat, electio falsò præsumitur. Quare impia est hæc ratiocinatio: Si electus sum, etiam sine pietate vitam consequar: Inuērtendum enim est argumētum: Si electus sum, secularibus studijs renunciare debeo. Elegit enim nos Deus, vt essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles, Eph. 1. v. 4. Hœc igitur semper inculcandum est auditoribus, quòd Deus in æterna electione ad fidem respexerit, ideoque electos in tempore credere, & fidem bonis operibus testatam facere oportet, Qui verò non credunt, & credere nolunt, eorum fides ab æterno præuideri non potuit, & per consequens prædestinati non sunt. Hoc pacto studium pœnitentiæ, bonorum operum non languescet, sed potiùs crescet, & maiora indies incrementa sumet.

XI. Obijciunt 2. Electionis mysterium altius est, quàm vt a vulgo capi possit. Quis enim cognouit mentem Domini, Rom. 11. vers. 33? Ergò potiùs silendum de illo, quam loquendum. Resp. 1. Etsi non in totum, tamen in tantum cognosci potest, ideoque Christus coram vulgo etiam illud inculcauit. Scitè Augustinus lib. de bono persev. c. 15. Numquid ideo negandum est, quod apertum est, quia comprehendi non potest, quod occultum est? 2. Electio consideratur respectu, vel causarum, vel specialiū casuum. Illæ cognosci possunt, quamuis de his omnibus ratio reddi nequeat. 3. Doctrina hæc obscura est tardis & pereuntibus, 2. Cor. 4. v. 3. non autē piis & devotis indagatoribus, quibus lux è tenebris exfplendescit, v. 6. 4. Operam adhibere debent præcones verbi, vt hunc articulum tractent tùm sobriè tùm prudenter, Sobriè, vt ex solo Dei verbo, non rationis iudicio, illum explicent. Prudenter, vt ad sanam doctrinam sana verba adhibeant, eoqué rem dirigant, vt omnis occasio præripiatur tùm Pharisaicæ præsumptioni, tùm Iudaicæ desperationi, vt in humilitate conseruentur pij, à securitate detrudantur impij. Quod si fiat; doctrina hæc conuenienter proponetur, vtiliter audietur, luculenter intelligetur.

XII. DE SECVNDO. Cùm arduum & sublime sit prædestinationis mysterium, regulas quasdam præscribunt Theologi, quas semper obseruare debemus, si in offenso pede hic procedere voluerimus. Selneccerus par. 2. Pædag. p. 606. septem huiusmodi siue regulas siue axiomata recenset, & his versibus includit:

1. Verbum: 2. promissum: 3. persona æqualis: 4. voluntas Vna Dei 5. bonitas peccato maior: 6. Adami Lapsus nos perdens: 7. Vita Deus atque salutis.

Summa verò istarum regularum hæc est: 1. Extra verbum Dei nihil dicendum est de voluntate Dei. 2. Promissio Dei de gratia Dei vniuersalis est, & ad omnes pertinet. 3. Apud Deum non est προσωποληψία vel respectus personarum. 4. In Deo non sunt contradictoriæ voluntates. 5. Gratia Dei exsuperat supra omne peccatum, 5. Quemadmodum in Adam omnes ceciderunt, ita in Christo omnes resurgunt. 7. Deus nullam creaturam vel ad pecca tum, vel ad exitium creauit.

XIII. Ægidius Hunnius in tract. de prædest. p. 95. quatuor potissimum regulas inculcat, 1. Prædestinatio non à priori, sed tantùm à posteriori consideranda est; secundum verbi reuelati præscriptum. 2. De prædestinatione non est iudicandum ex doctrina legis, sed Euangelij. 3. Æternum electionis decretum, diligenter est cum executione decreti quæ sit in tempore, conferendum. 4. In

Deum non cadunt contradictoriæ voluntates.

XIV. Recentiores paulò plures enumerant, quas tamẽ omnes ad sequentes septem reduci posse arbitramur.

XV. PRIMA. De prædestinatione non nisi ex verbo Dei disputandum & iudicandum est.

Ratio enim nostra in diuinis aliàs cæca est: quî ergo subvolare poterit in ipsa consiliorum diuinorum penetralia, vt illa à priori & sine verbo reuelato cognoscat?

Atque huc pertinet illa Lutheri distinctio inter Deum absolutum & relatum, vel quod idem est, absconditum & reuelatum. Ad hunc vnicè, non ad illum cogitationes dirigamus. Cùm Deo enim abscondito his agere, iuxta Lutherum, pomum illud est in quo primi parentes nostri mortẽ vorârunt, quòd scire voluerunt ea, quæ scire non debuerunt. Semper ergo memores simus aureoli istius aphorismi, quem Hilarus lib. 5. de Trin. his verbis præscripsit: Non est de diuina prædestinatione humanis iudicijs sentiendum. Neque enim nobis ea natura est, vt sein cælestem cognitionem suis viribus efferat. A Deo discendum est, quid de Deo Deique voluntate intelligendum sit. Quia Deus non nisi Deo authore cognoscitur. Quoniam igitur impossibile erat sine Deo discere Deum, per verbum homines docet scire Deum. Quocirca modus ponatur humanæ curiositati, ne appetamus habere cognitum, quod Deus voluit esse secretum, Ambrosius libro. 1. de Vocat. gent, cap. 8. Qui enim eunt post cogitationes suas & loquuntur de Dei profundo, merguntur in profundum, August. serm. 7. de verbis Apost.

XVI. SECVNDA. Non ex doctrina legis, sed Euangelij cognoscenda est prædestinatio. Lex enim peccata arguit, non remittit; accusat, non condonat, Iohan. 5. vers. 45. Ex lege maledictio venit, non salus, Deuter. 27. vers. 16. Gal. 3. v. 10. Salutis ergò decretum ex lege quî cognosci poterit? Euangelium potius consulendum est, quippe in quo solo per Filium enarrantem Ioh. 1. v. 18. voluntas Dei patris manifestatur. Hinc nominatur releuatio mysterij, temporibus æternis taciti, Rom. 16. v. 45. Errant igitur quicunque electionis arcanum, vel secundum opera legis, vt pontificii, vel sine respectu ad Euangelicas promissiones de vniuersali gratia Dei & merito Christi, vt Caluiniani, definiunt.


### XVII. Third. The temporal execution must be diligently compared with the eternal predestination

XVII. THIRD. The temporal execution must be diligently compared with the eternal predestination.

For it cannot be better known what God has decreed to do concerning the salvation of the human race than by attending to what He does in time: for His will is immutable. Therefore, what He willed to do and how He willed to do it from eternity, that He does and in that way He does it in time. Hence Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, p. 12: 'What is never in the work of God was never in the predestination of God.' He adds the reason a little later: 'For His predestination is nothing other than the eternal preparation of future works.' Therefore, a comparison of temporal deeds with eternal decrees, and of eternal decrees with temporal deeds, must always be established. From which it follows that we are elected from eternity in the same way and for the same reasons as we are justified and saved in time. The Apostle hints at this harmony of decree and execution in Eph. 1:4: 'He has blessed us with spiritual blessings, καθώς AS He chose us.' Whence the axiom was born in Theological schools: The reason and the cause are the same for both election and justification. Since, therefore, God in time justifies no one without the intuition of faith, it follows from this that God from eternity made a decree to save no one without faith, which is Election. And since in time no one is damned absolutely, but because of his own unbelief, it follows conversely from this that God from eternity made a decree that no one is to be damned absolutely, but all because of unbelief, which is Reprobation. To this point refers that statement of Bernard, epistle 107 to Thomas. Proposition: Acknowledge the counsel of God in your justification. For your present justification is both a revelation of the divine counsel and a certain preparation for future glory.

XVIII. FOURTH. With God there is no προσωποληψία or respect of persons.

Since, therefore, the whole human race has fallen in Adam, hence the whole was also liable to eternal damnation. But God, who is rich in mercy, when neither the wisdom of angels nor of men could find a remedy for that evil, made and manifested a decree of reparation, Gen. 3. verse 15. The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent. Since He offers this promise to all without προσωποληψία, and inasmuch as the Son has died for all, it cannot happen that, out of an absolute good pleasure without any regard for faith or infidelity, the greatest part of men were destined for death, and very few for eternal life.

XIX. FIFTH. In God there are no contradictory wills.

For He is eternal truth, knowing not how to lie. As He does not change His essence, so He does not change His essence, Ψευδὴς ἐν λόγῳ, as Plato said. In the promises of God there is no falsehood, writes Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus. Therefore, since He declares Himself in the Word in such a way that He wills all to be saved, it is not to be thought that there is given in Him a certain secret will contrary to the revealed one. For God is not a hypocrite, but an invariable truth, perpetually consistent with Himself. Therefore, what He says He wills, this very thing, and not another, He wills: as He professes outwardly, so He feels and decrees inwardly. Wherefore, since He sent Christ to the whole world, and calls all to repentance, it cannot conversely happen that by an absolute and hidden decree He has passed over most men, and has not willed them to be eternally saved.

Latin:

XVII. TERTIA. Cum æterna prædestinatione temporalis executio diligenter est conferenda.

Non enim melius sciri potest quid Deus circa salutem generis humani facere decreuerit, quàm si attendatur, quid in tempore faciat: Ejus enim voluntas est immutabilis. Quod ergò & quomodo facere ab æterno voluit, istud eoque modo in tempore facit. Hinc Fulgentius l. 1. ab Monimum. p. 12. Quod nunquam est in opere Dei, nunquam fuit in prædestinatione Dei. Rationem paulò pòst addit: Neque enim alia est eius prædestinatio, quam futurorum operum æterna præparatio. Proinde semper instituenda est collatio factorum temporalium cum decretis æternis, & decretorum æternorum cum factis temporalibus. Vnde sequitur, quod eo modo & ob istas causas electi ab æterno simus, quomodo & propter quas causas in tempore justificamur & saluamur. Quam decreti & executionis consonantiam innuit Apostolus Eph. 1. v. 4. Benedixit nos in benedictionibus spiritualibus, καθώς SICVT elegit. Vnde natum axioma in scholis Theologicis: Eadem ratio, & eadem causa sunt cum electionis, tum iustificationis. Cum igitur Deus in tempore sine intuitu fidei neminem justificet, hinc sequitur, quòd Deus ab æterno fecerit decretum de nemine absque fide saluando, quòd est Electio. Et cùm in tempore nemo damnetur absolutè, sed propter incredulitatem suam, hinc vicissim sequitur, quòd Deus ab æterno decretum fecerit, neminem absolutè, sed omnes propter incredulitatem damnandos esse, quod est Reprobatio. Huc spectat illud Bernardi epist. 107. ad Thomam propositum: Agnosce consilium Dei in Iustificatione tui. Præsens namq; iustificatio tui, & diuini est consilij reuelatio, & quædam ad futuram gloriam præparatio.

XVIII. QVARTA. Apud Deum non est προσωποληψια vel respectus personarum.

Quia igitur totum genus humanum in Adamo est lapsum, hinc & totum æternæ damnationi fuit obnoxium. Deus autem qui diues in misericordia, cùm malo illi nec angelorum nec hominum sapientia remedium inuenire posset, decretum reparationis fecit & manifestauit, Gen. 3. vers. 15. Semen mulieris conteret caput serpentis. Hanc promissionem cùm sine προσωποληψίᾳ omnibus offerat, adeoque Filius pro omnibus sit mortuus, hinc fieri nequit, vt ex absoluto beneplacito sine omni fidei aut infidelitatis intuitu maxima pars hominum ad mortem, paucissimi ad vitam æterno destinati fuerint.

XIX. QVINTA. In Deo non sunt contradictoriæ voluntates.

Est enim æterna veritas, mentiri nesciens. Vt non essentiam, sic neque mutat essentiam, Ψευδὴς ἐν λόγῳ, vti Plato dixit. In promissis Dei nulla inest falsitas, scribit Fulgentius, l. 1. ad Monim. Proinde cùm in verbo se ita declaret, quòd omnes saluos velit, non cogitandum est, dari in ipso quandam voluntatem arcanam reuelatæ contrariam. Non enim Deus est hypocrita, sed inuariabilis, sibique perpetuò constans veritas. Quod igitur se velle dicit, hoc ipsum, & non aliud vult: vti foris profitetur, ita intus sentit & decernit. Quare, cùm Christum miserit toti mundo, & omnes vocet ad pœnitentiam, vicissim fieri nequit, vt ex absoluto & abscondito decreto plerosque homines præterierit, & æternùm saluos noluerit.


### XX. Sixth. Outside of Christ, one must not think about predestination

XX. SIXTH. Outside of Christ, one must not think about predestination.

For the grace of God has no place, unless satisfaction is made to justice. For He is merciful in such a way that He does not cease to be just. When, therefore, the satisfaction of Christ is excluded, gratuitous election ought not to be presumed. Hence Scripture, as often as it describes that mystery, leads us straight to Christ, as the throne of grace. The Apostle explains this explicitly. Eph. 1. 4. He chose us IN CHRIST laid. And to this pertains that well-known saying, that the decree of election is the circumference, of which Christ is the center. If we apprehend Him with true faith, with a constant purpose of persevering, then we rightly conclude that we are included in the circumference of predestination. Thus, therefore, Christ will be the daily mirror of our heart, and a sufficiently firm antidote against any temptations whatsoever.

XXI. SEVENTH. Concerning Predestination, it is to be taught in such a way that the weak may be raised up, and the stubborn corrected.

For since there are two primary vices of the human mind, namely 1. μεγαλαυχία or overconfidence, 2. μικροθυμία or diffidence, Jerem. 7. v. 9, the dogmas of Scripture heal both vices. For if the mind is secure and too confident, they rebuke it and call it back to the path; if it is anxious and too diffident, they raise it up and suffuse it with consolation, which uses are noted, Rom. 15. v. 4. 2. Tim. 3. v. 16. seqq. Therefore, whatever dogma does not produce these uses, but hinders them, ought to be held as suspect, nay, even false. If the Calvinistic doctrine is examined according to this rule, it can easily be convicted of falsehood. For if the decree of election is absolute, neither can secure minds be corrected by solid νοθεσίας, nor can anxious ones be sustained by true παρακλήσει, which will be proven more fully in its proper place. The Formula of Concord, art. 11, p. 521, especially commends this rule, the words of which are as follows; We believe and hold that when the doctrine concerning the election of God to eternal life is proposed in such a way that troubled pious minds can derive no consolation from it, but rather through it are led into anxieties of mind or may be cast into despair, or the impenitent may be confirmed in their dissolute life: because this article is treated badly and wrongly, not according to the norm of the Word and will of God, but according to the judgment of human reason and indeed by the impulse of Satan.

XXII. On the Third. Concerning Predestination many have written many things, both from our side and from our adversaries, and each follows his own peculiar method. We believe, however, that all things which look to this matter and must be said can be included in four principal chapters, about which we shall treat in order hereafter. Chapter I will be about the three hypotheses, or sources, of gratuitous election, namely, the universal will of God the Father, the merit of Christ, and the calling of the Holy Spirit. II. Concerning predestination itself, what it is, upon what causes it depends, how firm and immutable it is, and whatever other things shall seem to pertain to it. III. Concerning the Predestined, who and how many are the elect? whether few, or all? whether their number is fatal? in what way they attain the certainty of election? whether they can totally lose grace for a time? etc. Finally IV. concerning Reprobation, which is the decree contrary to election.

XXIII. Therefore, with this disputation we shall make a beginning from the first chapter, which comprises three hypotheses preceding the decree of election, for God from eternity willed all men to be saved, His Son to suffer for all, and this His counsel to be announced to all. But because not all in time recognize these benefits, nor apply them to themselves, hence was made the decree concerning those to be saved, not all, but only those perseveringly believing. Thus, therefore, we see how these three hypotheses precede predestination in order. And these are as it were three θεμέλια or fulcrums, by which standing, the absolute Calvinistic decree immediately collapses. For it cannot happen that by mere good pleasure the greatest part of men is destined for destruction, if God wills all to be saved, if Christ for all has suffered and died, if finally all are seriously called to repentance through the preaching of the word.

XXIV. But because it would be too prolix to run through all these hypotheses in one disputation, therefore we shall divide the tasks, and this time we shall consider only the first source or fulcrum of election, namely the universal and merciful will of God, by which He embraces the whole human race. Two primary questions occur here to be ventilated. I. How manifold is the will of God? Where some distinctions, familiar in this controversy, are brought forward. II. Whether the will of God is universal, that is, whether He seriously wills all to be saved and to arrive at the knowledge of the truth? Concerning these two problems, therefore, some things must be brought forward.

Latin:

XX. SEXTA. Extra Christum de prædestinatione non est cogitandum.

Non enim locum habet Dei gratia, nisi satisfiat justitiæ. Nam ita est misericors, ne desinat esse justus. Cùm ergò excluditur Christi satisfactio, non præsumi debet gratuita electio. Hinc Scriptura, quoties mysterium illud describit, ad Christum, ceu thronum gratiæ protinus nos deducit. Disertè hoc exponit Apostolus. Eph. 1. 4. Elegit nos IN CHRISTO, ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Et huc pertinet scitum illud, Electionis decretum peripheriam esse, cujus centrum sit Christus. Hunc si vera fide apprehendamus, cum constanti proposito perseverandi, tum peripheriæ prædestinationis nos inclusos esse, rectè concludimus. Sic ergò Christus quotidianum, cordis nostri speculum, & satis firmum contra quasvis tentationes erit antidotum.

XXI. SEPTIMA. De Prædestinatione sic est docendum, ut erigantur infirmi, & corrigantur præfracti.

Cùm enim duo sint animi humani vitia primaria, nempè nimia 1. μεγαλαυχία vel confidentia, 2 μικροθυμία vel diffidentia, Ierem. 7. v. 9, utrique vitio medentur Scripturæ dogmata. Si enim mens sit secura, & nimium confidens, corripiunt eam & in viam reuocant; si sit anxia & nimium diffidens, erigunt & solatio perfundunt, qui usus notantur, Rom, 15. v. 4. 2, Tim. 3. v. 16. seqq. Quodcunque igitur dogma usus hos non parit, sed impedit suspectum, imò falsum haberi debet. Secundum quam regulam si examinetur doctrina Calvinistica, falsitatis facilè conuinci potest. Si enim decretum electionis absolutum sit, neque securæ mentes solida νοθεσίας corripi, nec anxię verâ παρακλήσει sustentari queunt, id quod suo loco fusiùs probabitur. Regulam verò istam imprimis commendat Formula Concordiæ art. 11. m. p. 521. cujus verba sic habent; Credimus & sentimus, quando doctrina de electione Dei ad vitam æternam, eo modo proponitur ut perturbatæ piæ mentes ex ea consolationem nullam capere queant, sed potius per eam in animi angustias aut desperationem conÿciantur, aut impœnitentes in dissoluta sua vita confirmentur: quòd articulus hic non ad normam verbi & voluntatis Dei, sed iuxta humanæ rationis iudicium & quidem impulsu Sathanæ malè & perperàm tractetur.

XXII. De Tertio. De Prædestinatione multi multa scripserunt, tùm ex nostris, tùm ex aduersarijs, & suam quisque methodum peculiarem sequitur. Censemus autem omnia, quę hûc spectant, & dicenda sunt, quatuor præcipuè capitibus includi posse, de quibus in posterum ordine agemus. Caput I. erit de tribus siue hypothesibus, siue fontibus gratuitæ electionis, nimirum de vniuersali voluntate Dei Patris, merito Christi, & vocatione Spiritus sancti. II. De ipsa prædestinatione, quid sit, ex quibus causis pendeat, quàm firma sit & immutabilis, quæque alia eò pertinere videbuntur. III. De Prædestinatis, quinam & quot sint electi? num pauci, an omnes? num fatalis eorum sit numerus? quo pacto electionis certitudinem consequantur? num gratiam totaliter ad tempus possint amittere? &c. Tandem Iv. de Reprobatione, quæ decretum est electioni contrarium.

XXIII. Hâc igitur disputatione faciemus initium à capite primo, quod comprehendit tres hypotheses, electionis decretum præcedentes, Deus enim ab æterno voluit, omnes homines saluos fieri, Filium suum pro omnibus pati, & hoc suum consilium omnibus annunciari. Quia verò non omnes in tempore beneficia hæc agnoscunt, nec sibi applicant, hinc factum est decretum de saluandis non omnibus sed tantùm perseueranter credentibus. Ita ergo videmus, quomodo tres istæ hypotheses prædestinationem ordine antecedant. Et sunt istæ quasi tria θεμέλια vel fulcra, quibus stantibus mox corruit absolutum decretum Caluinisticum. Fieri enim nequit, vt ex mero beneplacito maxima hominū pars sit destinata exitio, si Deus omnes vult saluos, si Christus pro omnibus est passus & mortuus, si denique omnes per prædicationem verbi seriò ad pœnitentiam vocantur.

XXIV. Quia verò prolixum nimis foret, vnâ disputatione omnes istas hypotheses percurrere, idcircò partiemur operas, & hac vice primum duntaxat fontem vel fulcrum electionis considerabimus, nempe vniuersalem & misericordem Dei voluntatem, quâ totum genus hominum complectitur. Duæ autem primarię quæstiones hic ventilandæ occurrunt. I. Quotuplex sit Dei voluntas? Vbi afferuntur distinctiones aliquot, in hac controuersia familiares, I I. An voluntas Dei sit vniuersalis, hoc est, num omnes seriò velit saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire? De his ergo duobus problematibus porrò quædam in medium afferenda sunt.


### Question I How manifold is the will of God?

QUESTION I.

How manifold is the will of God?

I. As is the essence of God, so also His will is one and individual in number. For essence and will are not one thing in God and another, but they are one ταυτὸ. Meanwhile, although in God Himself the will is most simply one, yet when it proceeds outwardly, it admits a certain distinction, not by reason of itself, but on account of various objects and the diverse mode of willing. For He wills some things absolutely, others conditionally: some antecedently, some consequently. Whence have flowed several distinctions of the divine will, which are frequently used in this article. There are four principal ones of these, concerning which in order.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO I.

Quotuplex sit voluntas Dei?

I. Vt Dei essentia, sic & voluntas numero vna est & indiuidua. Neque enim aliud est in Deo essentia & voluntas, sed sunt vnum ταυτὸ. Interim, licèt in ipso Deo voluntas sit simplicissimè vna, tamen cùm ad extra progreditur, distinctionem quandam admittit, non ratione sui, sed propter obiecta varia, & diuersum volendi actum modumque. Nonnulla enim vult absolutè, alia conditionatè : quædam antecedenter, quædam consequenter. vnde promanarunt nonnullæ distinctiones voluntatis diuinæ, quæ in hoc articulo frequenter vsurpantur. Quatuor earum sunt præcipuæ, de quibus ordine.


### Question I. First distinction. Into absolute and conditional will

Into absolute and conditional will.

II. We read in Psalm 113: Our God is in heaven; he hath done all things whatsoever he would: whence that saying of Damascenus is taken, l. 2. de F. O. c. 29, ὅσα ἤθελε γίνεται, whatsoever he wills, come to pass. Experience nevertheless testifies that many things happen which God does not will; and that he wills many things which do not happen, whence he himself complains in Isaiah c. 66. v. 4: They have chosen those things in which I delighted not. The question is therefore, How is this apparent ἀντιλογία (contradiction) to be reconciled? This can be done most conveniently through the distinction just insinuated.

III. For just as a twofold power falls upon God, namely 1. absolute, 2. ordinary: so also a twofold will of God must be established. One is absolute, the other conditional, or ordinary. The former has no condition added, the latter has some condition added, in the absence of which, that which God otherwise wills to happen does not happen. For which reason the former is in itself and always θέλημα ἐνεργητικὸν (active will) or efficacious: but the latter, because of the absence of the condition, sometimes becomes θέλημα ἀνενεργητόν (inactive will) or inefficacious, as Augustine speaks in Enchirid. c. 102. & 103. Others designate the former as the will of effectuation, the latter as the will of approbation.

IV. Moreover, many examples can be brought forward of those things which God wills to happen, and yet they do not happen. 1. You have chosen those things in which I delighted not, Isa. 65. v. 12. Here God willed that the Jews should not choose evil things, which nevertheless did not happen. 2. I will that the wicked turn, Ezech. 33. v. 11. And yet not all are converted. A similar saying is read in 2. Pet. 3. v. 9: God wills all to return to repentance: yet they do not return. 3. I would have gathered you, as a hen gathers her chickens, Matth. 23. v. 37. But were all gathered? By no means. Why so? Because you would not. 4. The Pharisees rejected the counsel of God, Luke 7. verse 30. It is read that what God willed to be done by the Pharisees was not done. For otherwise they would not have rejected his counsel. 5. You resist the Holy Spirit, Acts 7. verse 51. But the Holy Spirit could not will that he be resisted. For then they would not have resisted: For he who does what the Holy Spirit wishes him to do, does not resist the Spirit. 6. God wills that all should satisfy the law perfectly, which, however, does not happen, and indeed cannot happen in this infirmity of nature. 7. Finally, God willed and commanded that Adam should not eat from the forbidden tree; yet he ate.

Wherefore from all these things we conclude that what God wills to happen does not always happen, not because of an inefficacy of the will in itself, but because of the absence of a condition which prevents that from happening which otherwise would happen.

V. And by this conditional or ordered will, God also wills all men to be saved, namely if they believe the Gospel and walk worthily according to it. For if He willed it absolutely, all would be saved. But because this does not happen, we gather from that that God wills the salvation of men not ἁπλῶς or simply, but ὑποθετικῶς or conditionally, namely if they have not neglected the means necessary for obtaining salvation:

VI. These things can be explained by the example of some Prince who can enrich his subjects and seriously wills them to become rich, and yet we do not see it happen that way. What is the cause? Because he does not will it absolutely and immediately through the distribution of his goods among them, but conditionally, so that, namely, they themselves may labor and trade, and thus acquire riches by legitimate means. Unless they do this, then they do not become rich, even if the Prince both wills them to become rich and can enrich them. Therefore, from 'to be able' and 'to will' to 'the thing itself being done,' the consequence is not valid, unless the 'willing' is absolute and free from every condition.

Latin:

In voluntatem absolutam & conditionatam.

II. Legimus Psal. 113. Deus noster in cœlo, omnia, quæcunque voluit fecit: vnde desumtum illud Damasceni. l. 2. de F. O. c. 29. ὅσα ἤθελε γίνεται, quæcunque vult, fiunt. Testatur nihilominus experientia, multa fieri, quæ Deus non vult; & multa velle, quæ non fiunt, vnde conqueritur ipse apud Esaiam c. 66. v. 4. Elegerunt, quæ nolui. Quæritur ergo, Quomodo hæc apparens ἀντιλογία sit concilianda? Fieri hoc commodissimè potest per distinctionem modò insinuatam.

III. Nam sicuti duplex potestas in Deum cadit, nempe 1. absoluta 2. ordinaria: sic & voluntas Dei duplex statuenda est. Alia absoluta, alia conditionata, vel ordinaria. Ista nullam, hæc aliquam conditionem habet additam, quâ absente, non fit, quod Deus alioquin fieri vult. Quam ob causam illa perse & semper est θέλημα ἐνεργητικὸν vel efficax: hæc autem, ob absentiam conditionis, nonnunquam fit θέλημα ἀνενεργητόν vel inefficax, vti loquitur Augustinus in Enchirid. c. 102. & 103. Alij illam effectionis, hanc approbationis voluntatem indigitant.

IV. Exempla autem eorum, quæ Deus fieri, vult, nec tamen fiunt, multa proferri possunt. 1. Elegistis, quæ nolui, Esa. 65. v. 12. Hic Deus volebat nè Iudæi mala eligerent, quod tamē non fiebat. 2. Volo, vt conuertatur impius, Ezech. 33. v. 11. Nec tamen omnes conuertuntur. Simile dictum legitur 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. Deus vult omnes ad pœnitentiam reuerti: neque tamen reuertuntur. 3. Ego volui vos congregare, sicut gallina congregat pullos suos, Matth. 23. v. 37. Num autem omnes congregati sunt? Neutiquam. Qui sic? Quia noluistis. 4. Pharisæi consilium Dei spreuerunt. Luc. 7. versu 30. legitur id quod Deus à Pharisæis fieri volebat, factum non est. Aliàs enim consilium eius non spreuissent. 5. Spiritui sancto resistitis, Act. 7. versu. 51. Resisti autem sibi, non poterat velle Spiritus sanctus. Nam tum non restitissent : Qui enim facit, quod eum Spiritus Sanctus facere vult, non resistit Spiritui. 6. Vult Deus, vt omnes satisfaciant legi perfecte quod tamen non fit, & ne quidem fieri potest in hac infirmitate naturae. 7. Tandem volebat & praecipiebat Deus, ne Adam comederet de arbore vetita; tamen comedit.

Quare ex his omnibus concludimus, non fieri semper, quod Deus vult fieri, non ob inefficacitatem voluntatis per se, sed ob absentiam conditionis, quae impedit, quo minus fiat, quod alias fieret.

V. Atque hac etiam conditionali vel ordinata voluntate Deus omnes homines vult saluos fieri, nempe si Euangelio credant, & digne secundum illud ambulent. Si enim absolute vellet, omnes saluarentur. Quia vero hoc non fit, ex eo colligimus, Deum velle salutem hominum non apws vel simpliciter; sed vpotheos vel conditionaliter, nimirum si media ad salutem consequendam necessaria non neglexerint:

VI. Declarari haec possunt exemplo alicuius Principis, qui subditos suos ditare potest, & eos etiam ditescere serio vult, nec tamen ita evenire videmus. Quae causa? Quia non vult absolute & immediate, per suorum bonorum inter illos distributione sed conditionate, vt nimiru ipsi laboret & negotietur, atqs ita diuitias legitimis modis acquirant. Hoc nisi faciant; tum non ditescunt etiam si Princeps eos & ditescere velit, & ditare possit. Quocirca a posse & velle ad ipsum fieri nou valet consequentia, nisi to velle absolutum & ab omni conditione sit liberum.


### Question I. First distinction. Into absolute and conditional will: Second distinction: Into antecedent and consequent will

Second distinction: Into antecedent and consequent will.

VII. This distinction is taken from the Greek Fathers who said that the θέλημα θεοῦ is either προηγούμενον The antecedent, or ἑπομένην, the consequent. The antecedent, according to the definition of Damascenus, book 2, chapter 29, is that which exists from Him Himself; the consequent is that which exists from our cause. The former regards men insofar as they are men; the latter insofar as they are such and such: the former concerns the φύσιν of God, the latter the τᾶξιν of men: the former is universal, the latter is particular; the former precedes, the latter follows; the former is called of mercy, the latter of justice or judgment. Both involve not a priority or posteriority of time, but only of order.

VIII. Others express it thus: That the will in God has a double respect, one simple, insofar as the merciful will of God is considered in itself; and another relative, insofar as the faith or infidelity of men is attended to. Regarding the former respect, it is called antecedent; regarding the latter, consequent. In the antecedent, regard is had to the means of salvation, as they are ordained on the part of God and offered to all: in the consequent, regard is had to the same means, but as they are accepted or neglected by men. The antecedent will is so called because it precedes the consideration of the obedience or disobedience of men, and consists in a simple respect, by which that beneficial will of God holds itself equally toward all. It is therefore called consequent because it follows the consideration of the obedience or disobedience of men; and consists in a determined respect, as the same will holds itself toward men, either following or neglecting that τάξιν of means by their own act. In the antecedent will, only one decree of universal love occurs, which nevertheless includes both the end and the means at once: As I live, says God, I will and decree that no mortal should perish, but that all should come to the knowledge of the truth, and be saved through faith, Ezek. 18, v. 23, ch. 33, v. 11, 2 Pet. 3, v. 9. But joined with the consequent will is the special πρόγνωσις of God, by which men are considered, which ones believe, or do not remain obedient? Whence two distinct and opposite decrees arise. The one is of Election: As I live, says God, I will and decree that everyone who perseveringly believes in Christ shall not perish, but have eternal life. Matt. 10 v. 22. John 3 v. 36. 1 Cor. 1 v. 21. The other of Reprobation: As I live, says God, I will and decree that whoever does not believe in Christ, but dies in infidelity, shall not for this reason have life, but shall perish eternally. Mark 16 verse 12. John 3 verse 18.

IX. Tertullian expressed both briefly in his book On the Resurrection of the Flesh, when he writes: God is best from His own nature, just from ours. For in the antecedent will, God proposed to us His own, that is, His kindness, according to which He is best. In the consequent will, He regards ours, that is, our acceptance or rejection of His grace, in which respect He is just, when, of course, He executes what He has decreed, by saving the faithful and damning the unfaithful.

X. The Scholastics express it thus, that one will is primary, another secondary. By the primary will, God wills every man to be saved, but by the secondary will, He does not will the reprobate as such to be saved. They also add this, that by this distinction the simplicity of the divine will is not taken away, insofar as it is the same as God Himself, but this distinction only denotes different acts of willing, arising from the distinct condition and consideration of the objects, and therefore they say: The distinction of the will into antecedent and consequent is to be taken not on the part of the divine will itself, in which there is nothing prior and posterior, but on the part of the things willed.

XI. This distinction is indeed very useful for reconciling ἐναντιοφανῆ (seemingly contradictory) passages of Scripture. For sometimes it is said that God wills all men to be saved, 1 Tim. 2 v. 4, and that none should perish, 2 Pet. 3 v. 9, but that all should be converted, Ezek. 33 v. 11. Elsewhere, however, it is said that He laughs at the destruction of the wicked, Prov. 1 v. 25, that He wills to harden some, and to have mercy only on some, Rom. 9 v. 18, etc. Unless, therefore, it should be thought contrary to Scripture, the former statements are to be explained regarding the antecedent will of goodness, the latter regarding the consequent will of judgment.

XII. This distinction is, however, vehemently hated by the Calvinists, because by means of it most arguments appearing to fight for an absolute decree can be skillfully and successfully refuted. Hence they clamor that it is fictitious and absurd, and that it is not at all consistent with itself; so that this calumny may be blunted and overthrown, some common examples can not uselessly be noted here, from which it is evidently demonstrated that this distinction is true, necessary, and by no means absurd.

XIII. Indeed, seven of them can be brought forward. 1. It is taken from a physician. He requests convalescence from the sick person, seriously desires it for him, and therefore prescribes salutary medicines so that he may be restored to his former health. But if the sick person rejects them and casts them away from himself, then the physician has a just cause for abandoning him, so that by a consequent will he does not wish to heal him whom by an antecedent will he wished to heal. 2. From a magistrate. He, if he is good, desires and wishes from his heart for the safety and longevity of his subjects, provided they live peacefully and according to the prescribed law. But if they stir up rebellion and refuse to obey any longer, he is kindled with just anger and wishes the rebellious subjects to be cast out from his empire and utterly extirpated. 3. From a head of a household. He, by an antecedent will, wishes his son to be the heir of all his paternal goods; the same son, if he is enormously disobedient, he excludes by a consequent will and strikes out from the number of heirs. 4. From a teacher who desires to faithfully instruct all the students committed to his trust. But if anyone is perpetually disobedient and admits no scholastic discipline and refuses to attend lectures, finally the teacher rejects him by just judgment, and deservedly excludes him from the number of his disciples. 5. From a gardener, who antecedently wishes not only to tolerate all the trees in his garden, but also to take care of them. But if, through their own fault, they bring forth no fruits at all, then consequently he wishes those trees to be cut down and utterly eradicated. 6. From a Christian Prince. If anyone were to have many provinces, but destitute of colonists, and therefore were to redeem Christian captives from the Turkish Emperor through the intervention of a certain sum of money, then he would seriously wish all of them to be restored to liberty, especially if he were to send thither either his only-begotten son or some intimate friend, who would pay the ransom for all, and make this known publicly and town by town to each and every one. But if there are some among them who would rather remain in Turkey than emigrate from there, perhaps because they shrink from the hardships of the journey or look to their private comforts, then the Christian Prince deservedly leaves such contemners of his grace in captivity; and by a consequent will, he laughs at their destruction and exile. 7. From a king inviting guests to the wedding of his Son, which parable Christ himself proposed, Matt. 22 and Luke 14. For that king seriously invited all to the wedding, but they were unwilling to obey the calling, to such an extent that they even killed the servants inviting them. Wherefore, the king being afterwards angered, all those whom by an antecedent will he desired to be present at the wedding, by a consequent will he excluded from the wedding and punished most severely.

XIV. From all which examples it is evident to the eye that these two wills are not ἀντιφατικὰς (contradictory), but ὑπαλλήλως (subordinately) subordinated, and therefore there is no absurdity or contradiction if we say alike that God wills προηγυμένως (antecedently) the salvation of all men, if they have not despised the means of grace, the word, and the Sacraments; or rather, the iniquity of the wicked brings destruction and damnation, when they resist the Holy Spirit and spurn the counsel of God against themselves. The Savior himself clearly hints at this in Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34, where he reproaches the Jewish people for their incredulity and exclaims with a complaining voice: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her brood, and you would not? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate. Here both are joined, the gathering of the Jews and the desertion of the same. Christ willed both, but with a different will: the gathering antecedently, the desertion consequently; which distinction, unless it is accepted, it will not be possible to explain how Christ seriously willed acts so contrary.

XV. Wherefore the Calvinists expend vain labor when they anxiously seek out many sayings of Scripture in which God is said to will the destruction of the impious, so that they may thus prove that He does not will the salvation of all. For these are not opposed, but subordinated, and are to be understood concerning different wills. Therefore, by way of a conclusion, let this Theological Canon be noted: Just as the consequent will does not take away the antecedent will, so the sayings of Scripture speaking of the consequent will are not to be opposed to those testimonies which establish the antecedent will of God.

Latin:

Secunda distinctio: In voluntatem antecedentem & consequentem.

VII. Distinctio haec ex Patribus graecis desumta est qui o panon Ois dixerunt esse vel proegumenen Antecedentem, vel ἑπομένην consequentem. Antedens definitore Damasceno l 2. c. 29. est quæ ex ipso exstitit Consequens, quæ ex nostra causa existit. Illa respicit homines, in quantum homines; hæc in quantum tales vel tales sunt : Illa φύσιν Dei hæc τᾶξιν hominum concernit : illa vniuersalis, hæc particularis est, illa præcedit, hæc sequitur, illa misericordiæ, hæc justitiæ vel judicij dicitur. Vtraque non prioritatem aut posteritatem temporis, sed tantum ordinis inuoluit.

VIII. Alij sic efferunt: Voluntatem in Deo duplicem habere respectum, vnum simplicem, quatenus voluntas Dei misericors in sese consideratur; & alterum relatum, quatenus attenditur hominum vel fides vel infidelitas. Quoad priorem respectum vocatur antecedens, quoad posteriorem consequens. In antecedente respectus habetur mediorum ad salutem, prout ex parte Dei ordinata sunt, & omnibus offeruntur : In consequente respectus habetur eorundem mediorum, sed prout ab hominibus acceptantur vel negliguntur. Antecedens voluntas sic appellatur, quia considerationem obedientiæ vel inobedientiæ hominum præcedit, & respectu constat simplici, quo beneficialla Dei voluntas æqualiter se habet erga omnes. Consequens ideò sic dicitur, quia considerationem obedientiæ vel inobedientiæ hominum subsequitur; & respectu constat determinato, prout eadem voluntas se habet ad homines, τάξιν illam mediorum ipso actu vel sequentes, vel negligentes. In voluntate antecedente vnum tantùm vniuersalis dilectionis decretum, quod tamen simul includit & finem & media, occurrit : Viuo ego Deus, volo & decerno, vt nemo mortalium pereat, sed omnes ad agnitionem veritatis perueniat, & per fide salui fiant, Ezech. 18. v. 23. c. 33. v. 11. 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. Cum voluntate autē consequente coniuncta est specialis πρόγνωσις Dei, quâ considerantur homines, quinam credant, vel inobedientes maneat? Vnde duo distincta & opposita decreta oriuntur. Alterum est Electionis: Viuo ego Deus, volo & decerno, vt omnis, qui perseueranter credit in Christum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam aeternam. Math. 10. v. 22. Ioh. 3. v. 36. 1. Cor. 1. v. 21. Alterum Reprobationis: Viuo ego Deus, volo & decerno, vt qui in Christum non credit, sed in infidelitate decedit, propter hoc non vitias, sed aeternum pereat. Marci 16. versu 12. Ioh. 3. vers. 18.

IX. Tertullianus vtramque breuiter expressit. l. de resurrect. carnis, cum scribit: Deus de suo optimus, de nostro iustus. In voluntate enim antecedente Deus proposuit nobis suam, h. est, benignitatem suam, secundum quam est optimus. In consequente respicit nostram, hoc est, nostram gratiae suae vel acceptationem vel rejectionem, quo respectu iustus est, quando nimirum exequitur quod decreuit, fideles saluando, & infideles damnando.

X. Scholastici ita efferunt, quod voluntas alia sit prima alia secunda. Voluntate prima velle Deum omnem hominem salvum fieri, sed voluntate secunda reprobum qua talem, non velle salvum. Addunt & hoc, quod distinctione ista non tollatur simplicitas voluntatis diuinae, prout idem est, quod ipse Deus, sed discrimen hoc tantum denotet diuersos volendi actus, ex distincta obiectorum habitudine & consideratione ortos, ideoq; dicunt, Distinctionem voluntatis in antecedentem & consequentem, accipi non ex parte ipsius voluntatis diuinae, in qua nihil est prius & posterius, sed ex parte volitorum.

XI. Permultum vero facit haec distinctio ad loca Scripturae ἐναντιοφανῆ concilianda. Nonnunquam enim dicitur, Deum velle omnes homines saluos fieri, 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. nec vllum perire. 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. sed omnes conuerti, Ezech. 33. v. 11. Alibi vero dicitur, ridere in interitu impiorum, Prouerb. 1. v. 25. velle quosdam indurare, & nonnullorum tantum misereri Rom. 9. v. 18. &c. Ni igiturScripturæ opposita existimetur, priora dicta de antecedente bonitatis, posteriora de consequente iudicij voluntate exponenda sunt.

XII. Vehementer autem exosa est hæc distinctio Caluinianis, quia per illam pleraque argumenta pro absoluto decreto in speciem pugnantia, dextrè & feliciter confutari possunt. Hinc eam esse fictam & absurdam, sibique ipsi minimè constare clamitant; quæ calumnia vt retundatur & prosternatur, non inutiliter hic notari possunt exempla quædam vulgaria, exquibus distinctionem istam esse veram, necessariam & minus absurdam, euidenter demonstratur.

XIII. Illorum verò septem proferti possunt. 1. Desumitur à Medico. Hic postulat ab ægroto, convalescentiam ipsius seriò optat, ideoque salutaria 'medicamina præscribit, vt sanitati pristinæ restitui possit. Quod si verò ægrotus illa respuat, & à se projiciat, tunc justam deserendi causam habet Medicus, ita vt consequente voluntate eum sanare nolit, quem antecedente sanare voluit. 2. A Magistratu. Hic, si bonus sit, subditorum incolumitatem & longæuitatem ex animo cupit & desiderat, modò ipsi tranquillè, & secundum præscriptam legem viuant. Sin autem rebellionem excitent, & parere amplius recusent, justâ irâ accenditur, rebellesque subditos ex imperio suo ejectos vult & penitus extirpatos. 3. A Patrefamiliâs. Hic filium suum antecedente voluntate hæredem esse vult omnium paternorum bonorum, eundem, si enormiter inobediens sit, consequente voluntate excludit, & ex numero hæredum expungit. 4. A Præceptore qui omnes discipulos fidei suæ commissos, fideliter cupit informare. Si verò aliquis perpetuò sit inobediens, nullamque disciplinam scholasticam admittat, & lectiones frequentare renuat, tandem Præceptor ipsum justo judicio rejicit, & e numero suorum discipulorum meritò excludit. 5. Ab hortulano, qui antecedenter omnes arbores in horto suo non tantum vult tolerare, sed etiam curam earum gerere. Quòd si autem proprio vitio nullos omninò fructus proferant, tum consequenter arbores istas vult excisas, & prorsus eradicatas. 6. A Principe Christiano. Si quispiam multas haberet prouincias; sed colonis destitutas, ideoque ab Imperatore Turcico captiuos Christianos, certæ pecuniæ interventu, redimeret, tum ille omnes libertati restitutos seriò vellet, præsertim si eò vel vnigenitum filium suum, vel amicum quendam intimum ablegaret, qui lytrum pro omnibus persolueret, & singulis ac vniuersis publicè oppidatimque hoc notum faceret. Quòd si autem ex ijs aliqui sint qui lubentius in Turcia manere, quàm exinde emigrare velint, fortè quia molestias itineris detrectant, aut priuata commoda spectant, tùm Princeps Christianus ejusmodi gratiæ suæ contemtores meritò in captiuitate relinquit; & voluntate consequente in interitu & exilio ipsorum ridet. 7. A rege hospites inuitante ad nuptias Filij sui, quam parabolam ipse Christus proposuit, Matth. 22. & Luc 14. Rex enim iste omnes seriò inuitabat ad nuptias, illi autem vocationi obtēperate nolebant, adeò, vt etiam seruos inuitantes occiderent. Quare postmodum iratus rex, omnes eos, quos voluntate antecedente nuptijs interesse desiderabat, consequente à nuptijs excludebat, & seuerissimè puniebat.

XIV. Ex quibus exemplis omuibus ad oculum patet, duas istas voluntates non esse ἀντιφατικὰς, sed ὑπαλλήλως subordinatas ideoque nulla est vel absurditas, vel contradictio, si pariter dicamus, Deum velle προηγυμένως omniū hominum salutem, si media gratiæ verbum & Sacramenta, non contemserint; vel autem iniquitas piorum perniciem & damnationem, quando Spiritui sancto resistunt, & consilium Dei aduersus semetipsos spernunt. Hoc ipse Saluator manifestè innuit Matth. 23. v. 37. & Luc. 13. v. 34. vbi incredulitatem populo Iudaico exprobrat, & querulâ voce exclamat: Ierusalem; Ierusalem, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, sicut gallina congregat pullos, & noluisti? Ecce relinquetur domus vestra deserta. Hic coniungitur vtrumque, Iudæorum congregatio, & eorundem desertio. Vtrumque Christus voluit, sed voluntate diuersâ: Congregationem antecedent;, desertionem consequente: quæ distinctio nisi recipiatur, explicari non poterit, quo pacto Christus seriò voluerit actus adeo contrarios.

XV. Quocirca vanum laborem insumunt Calviniani, quando anxiè multa Scripturæ dicta conquirunt, in quibus Deus interitum impiorum velle dicitur, vt ita probent, non velle omnium salutem. Hæc enim non sunt opposita, sed subordinata, & de diuersis voluntatibus intelligenda. Igitur Colophonis loco notetur hic Canon Theologicus: Quemadmodum voluntas consequens non tollit voluntatem antecedentem; ita Scripturæ dicta, de voluntate consequente loquentia, non sunt opponenda ijs testimonijs, quæ voluntatem Dei antecedentem adstruunt.


### Question I. First distinction. Into absolute and conditional will: Third distinction. Into hidden and revealed will

Third distinction. Into hidden and revealed will.

XVI. Both our people and the Calvinists use this distinction, but in a different sense. By the hidden will, our people understand both the mystery of the Gospel before universal preaching, inasmuch as it is called the mystery kept secret for eternal times, Rom. 16:25, hidden from ages and generations, Col. 1:26, and especially particular

God's judgments, and special cases, of which a reason cannot be rendered, as why so many miracles were not performed in Tyre and Sidon as in Chorazin? Why does God preserve his Church among these, and not others? etc. These and similar things pertain to the hidden will of God, at the consideration of which the Apostle exclaims, Rom. 11. v. 33. O the depth of the riches, of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how incomprehensible are his judgments and his ways past finding out! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? But by the revealed [will] they understand the very doctrine of the Gospel, comprised in the sacred code, announced by the prophets and Apostles, which embraces all things necessary for the attainment of salvation. For whatever it is necessary for us to know, and whatever concerns both our election and our salvation, all this has been revealed and in writings consigned, for which reason we acknowledge no hidden or secret will concerning the business of salvation. Hence Luther rightly warned that the hidden God is to be left alone, and the revealed one is to be looked to solely. For even if his particular counsel is most hidden, yet his universal good pleasure concerning the love of the whole human race, the satisfaction of the Son, the election of all who perseveringly believe, and other things of this kind, is revealed. Thus, therefore, briefly, the hidden will denotes the wonderful government of God over all things, especially the Church: but the revealed [will denotes] his counsel concerning the salvation of the human race, which he has made manifest through the Scriptures.

XVII. But the Calvinists explain these terms in a far different sense. For they do not attribute different objects to the hidden and revealed will, as we do, but one and the same, namely the business of salvation and election. They say, therefore, that the revealed will is the universal promises of God, which are indeed offered outwardly to all, and by which God declares that he wills the salvation of all and conversion, but meanwhile cherishing a different opinion within, which they call hidden, by reason of which he never willed that all men should be converted and be saved. Thus, therefore, according to the Calvinists, the revealed will is the exterior voice of God, which is sweet, but the arcane is the interior sense, which is horrendous and terrible. There he says he loves all, here he hates most; there he calls all, here he reprobates the greatest part, and destines them to eternal destruction.

XVIII. It is not, however, without reason asked, whether these things are so, and whether those things which concern our salvation and that manner of attaining it are hidden, or rather fully revealed? We affirm the latter, and we shall provide it demonstrated by three arguments, but weighty ones.

XIX. 1. The Apostle says in Acts 20:27: I testify this day, that I have not shrunk from declaring unto you all the counsel of God, which certainly concerns the salvation of men, and which it is fruitful and necessary for us to know. Thus 1 Cor. 2:7 he writes, we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, even the hidden wisdom, which God ordained before the world. Now if all the counsel of God has been declared, if that wisdom hidden before the ages has been made manifest through the sermon of the Apostle, there will certainly be no will hidden in God concerning the election and salvation of men. For whatever has been revealed by the Apostles cannot be arcane, since the opposite members of a division exclude, they do not include, one another.

XX. 2. If there were a certain arcane will of God concerning the predestination and salvation of men, it would certainly be expedient for us to know it. But the Calvinists must admit that everything which is necessary for us for salvation is revealed in the Scriptures, unless it pleases them to Papize. Now, if it has been revealed through the Scriptures, it will no longer be a hidden will. Or if it has not been revealed, then there will be no need for us to know it. Why, therefore, do they stir up a dispute about such a matter which is not necessary? & whose knowledge we can most easily do without? XXI. 3. If the will of God, by which He has decreed what He wishes to be done concerning each individual man, is hidden, and not revealed in the Scriptures, from where have the Calvinists known it? For according to all parts they describe it so clearly that it is no longer, nor does it remain, hidden. There are, however, three ways, and no more, by which men have known the secret counsels of princes. 1. If they themselves were present at those counsels and deliberations. 2. If they heard it from those who were present. 3. If the sum of the decree is publicly posted. By which of these, then, have the Calvinists known the decree of the supreme King and Prince, our blessed and glorious God? They were not present at them; for who has been present in the counsels of the Lord and has seen and heard His words? Jeremiah 23, v. 18. They have not heard it from others who were present: nor has it been publicly posted, that is, revealed in the Scriptures. By what way, then, at last, have they perceived that will of God? Nor is it for them to object that they have known from the Scriptures only τò ὅτι, but not τò διότι of the secrets of His will. For besides the fact that not even τò ὅτι can be proven, they furthermore depict it according to all circumstances in such a way that nothing more could be desired, since they do not rest in the question of whether it is, but they even touch upon the question of what it is and how it is, and explain it at length, as can be seen from the Colloquy of Mömpelgard. From this emerges a notable contradiction, while those men call the will hidden, and nevertheless declaim many things about it. But that which is hidden is not revealed: that which is not revealed is not known; that which is not known cannot be truly or soundly disputed. Thus, therefore, the will of God is one, and is both hidden and revealed according to the Calvinists: As for words, they say it is hidden, but in reality they consider it made manifest; indeed, they themselves reveal and make it manifest everywhere. But let us remember that while they openly confess that the will, by which God does not will the destruction of men, is that which has been revealed in the Scriptures, by this very fact they show that the other will, by which God would will destruction, has not been revealed in the Scriptures, and thus remains a pure and simple Calvinistic fiction.

XXII. But in order to cast some color over their will of the hidden revealed and the revealed hidden, they take refuge in certain sayings, in which the ways of the Lord are called unsearchable, such as exist in Job 41:5, Isa. 40:13, Rom. 11:33, 1 Cor. 2:11.

But we respond, 1. These sayings do not speak of the will of God regarding the election and salvation of men, but only of the admirable and unsearchable counsels of God in governing the world and ruling the Church.

2. We ourselves concede that we cannot in this darkness search out everything entirely, but that there are some things, concerning the consideration of which we must exclaim with the Apostle: O the depth! Meanwhile, however, those things which are necessary for salvation, even if they concern the election of men, are not secret, but revealed.

3. They contradict themselves. For if that will is hidden, why do they manifest and reveal it?

4. Ex abundanti, if it were even proven (which, however, will never be proven) that there is some hidden will of God concerning the salvation of men, yet it would remain to be demonstrated first that it is contrary to the revealed will, and diametrically opposed as it were, as the Calvinists imagine.

Latin:

Tertia distinctio. In voluntatem absconditam & reuelatam.

XVI. Distinctione hac vtuntur tùm Nostri, tùm Caluiniani, sed diuerso sensu. Nostri per voluntatem absconditam intelligunt, tum mysterium Euangelij ante vniuersalem prædicationem, quippe quòd vocatur mysterium æternis temporibus tacitum, Rom. 16. vers. 25. à seculis & generationibus absconditum, Col. 2. v. 26. tum inprimis particularia

Dei judicia, & speciales casus, quorum reddi nequit ratio, vt cur in Tyro & Sidone tot miracula non fuerint edita, quot in Chorazin? Cur Deus inter hos, non alios Ecclesiam suam conseruet? &c. Haec & similia pertinent ad voluntatem Dei absconditam, quorum consideratione exclamat Apostolus, Rom. 11. v. 33. O altitudo diuitiarum, sapientiae & scientiae Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt iudicia eius & imperuestigabiles viae eius! Quis enim cognouit sensum Domini? Aut quis consiliarius eius fuit? Per reuelatam verò intelligunt ipsam doctrinam Euangelij, in sacro codice comprehensam, per prophetas & Apostolos annunciatam, quae complectitur omnia ad salutis adeptionem necessaria. Quicquid enim scire nobis opus est, & quicquid spectat tum electionem, tum saluationem nostram, hoc omne reuelatum scriptisq; consignatum est, qua de causa nullam absconditam vel arcanam voluntatem circa negotium salutis agnoscimus. Hinc Lutherus rectè monuit, Deum absconditum esse deserendum, & reuelatum vnicè adspiciendum. Si enim maximè absconditum sit particulare consilium eius, reuelatum tamen est vniuersale beneplacitum de dilectione totius generis humani, de satisfactione Filij, de Electione omnium perseueranter credentium, & quae huius generis sunt alia. Sic ergo breuiter voluntas abscondita notat mirandam Dei gubernationem omnium, inprimis Ecclesiae : reuelata verò, consilium eius de salute generis humani, quod patefecit per Scripturas.

XVII. Longè autem alio sensu Caluiniani terminos istos exponunt. Nam illi absconditae & revelatae voluntati non diuersa objecta, vti nos sed vnum idemque attribuunt, nempe salutis & electionis negotium. Dicunt ergo, voluntatem reuelatam esse vniuersales Dei promissiones, quae exterius quidem offerantur omnibus, & quibus declaret se Deus, quòd velit omnium salutem & conversionem, interim verò intus diuersam fouere sententiam, quam vocant absconditam, ratione cuius nunquam voluerit, vt omnes homines conuertantur & salui fiant. Sic igitur juxta Caluinianos voluntas reuelata est exterior vox Dei, quæ suauis, sed arcana est interior sensus, qui horrendus & terribilis. Ibi se omnes amare dicit, hic plerosque odit: ibi vocat omnes, hic maximam partem reprobat, æternoque exitio destinat.

XVIII. Non autem immeritò quæritur, Num hæc ita se habeant, & Vtrum ea, quæ salutem nostram modumque illum adipiscendi spectant, sint abscondita, vel potius plenè reuelata? Posterius affirmamus, tribúsque argumentis, sed ponderosis demonstratum dabimus.

XIX. 1. Apostolus inquit Act. 20. v. 27. Contestor hodiernâ die, quòd nihil subtraxerim, sed annunciauerim vobis omne consilium Dei, quòd nimirum spectat salutem hominum, & quod scire nobis fructuosum est & necessarium. Sic 1. Cor. 2. v. 7. scribit, seloqui sapientiam Dei in mysterio occultatam, quam præfinierat Deus ante secula. Iam si annunciatum est omne consilium Dei, si sapientia illa ante secula abscondita per sermonem Apostoli patefacta est, nulla certè erit in Deo abscondita de electione & salute hominum voluntas, Quicquid enim reuelatum ab Apostolis, hoc arcanum esse nequit, cùm opposita diuisionis membra se inuicem excludant, non includant,

XX. 2. Si arcana quædam voluntas Dei esset de prædestinatione & salute hominum, certè nos eam scire expediret. Omne autem quod nobis ad salutem necessarium, in Scripturis reuelatum esse fateantur oportet Caluiniani, nisi Papizare illis placuerit. Iam verò si per Scripturas reuelata est, non amplius erit voluntas occulta. Aut si reuelata non est, nec eam scire nobis opus erit. Quid igitur litem mouent de tali re quæ necessaria non est & cuius noticia facilimè carere possumus? XXI. 3. Si abscondita est voluntas Dei, quâ decreuit, quid de vno quoque homine fieri velit, nec in Scripturis reuelata, vnde eam cognouerunt Caluiniani? Nam secundùm omnes partes ita luculenter eam describunt, vt non amplius sit, maneatve abscondita. Sunt autem tres modi non plures, quibus arcana principum consilia nouerunt homines. 1. Si ipsi interfuerint istis consilijs & deliberationibus. 2. Si ab iis, qui intersuerunt, audiuerint. 3. Si publicè decreti summa affigatur. Quo autem ex his cognouerunt Caluiniani decretum summi regis & principis, Dei nostri benedicti & gloriosi? Non interfuerunt ipsis; Quis enim affuit in confilia Domini & vidit & audiuit sermones eius? Ieremiæ 23. v. 18. Non audiuerunt ab alijs, qui interfuerint: neque etiam publicè affixum, hoc est, in Scripturis reuelatum est. Quo ergo tandem modo illam Dei voluntatem perceperunt? Nec est vt excipiant, se tantùm τò ὅτι, non autem τò διότι arcana illius voluntatis ex Scripturis cognosse. Nam præterquã quòd nec τò ὅτι probari queat, sic insuper eam depingunt secundum omnes circumstantias, vt nihil amplius desiderari queat, siquidem in quæstione an sit non acquiescunt, verùm etiam quæstionem quid sit, & quomodo sit attingunt fusèque explicant, vti videre est ex Colloquio Mompelg. Vnde emergit contradictio insignis, dum illi homines voluntatem absconditam appellant, & nihilominus plurima de illa rhetoricantur. Quod autem absconditum est, id reuelatum non est: quod non reuelatum, illud nescitur; quod nescitur, de eo verè solidèue disputari nequit. Sic ergo voluntas Dei vna, tum abscondita est, tum reuelata secundum Caluinianos: Quoad verba dicunt eam absconditam, reipsa vero patefactam censent, imò ipsi vbique reuelant & patefaciunt. Nos verò meminerimus, quòd dum apertè fatentur voluntatem, quâ Deus non vult perniciem hominum, eã esse, quæ in Scripturis patefacta sit, hoc ipso ostendunt, voluntatem alteram, quâ Deus velit perniciē in Scripturis patefactam nō esse, atque sic manere purum putum commentum Caluinisticum.

XXII. Vt verò aliquem colorem obducant voluntati suæ abscondito reuelatæ & reuelato ab sconditæ, ad dicta quædam confugiunt, in quibus viæ Domini imperuestigabiles dicuntur, qualia extant. Iobi 41. v 5 Eja. 40. v. 13. Rom. 11. v. 33. 1. 1. Cor. 2. v. 11.

Sed respondemus, 1. Hæc dicta non loqui de voluntate Dei, quoad electionem & salutem hominum, sed duntaxat, de admirandis & imperuestigabilibus consilijs Dei in gubernando mundo, & regenda Ecclesia.

2. Ipsi concedimus, non posse nos in hac caligine omnia omninò perscrutari, sed aliqua esse, circa quorum considerationem nobis exclamandum sit cum Apostolo; O Altitudo! Interim tamen ea, quæ ad salutem necessaria sunt, & si electionem hominum concernunt, non arcana, sed patefacta sunt.

3. Sibijpsis contradicunt. Si enim voluntas ista occulta est, cur eam manifestant & patefaciunt.

4. Ex abundanti, si maximè probaretur, (quod tamen in æternum non probabitur,) esse quandam de salute hominum voluntatem Dei absconditam, tamen hoc in primis demōstrandum restaret, quòd sit voluntati reuelatæ contraria, & è diametro quasi opposita vti fingunt Caluiniani.


### Question I. First distinction. Into absolute and conditional will: Fourth distinction Into the will of sign and of good pleasure

Fourth distinction.

Into the will of sign and of good pleasure.

XXIII. This distinction is found among the Scholastics, our own, and the Calvinists, but in turn in a different sense.

XXIV. I. The Scholastics say that the will of God is taken in two ways, or properly in itself, as it is a disposition and good pleasure notified externally, as is evident from Lombard, Book 1, Sentences, dist. 45, letter f, and following. And hence arose the distinction between the will of sign and of good pleasure, which Thomas Aquinas posits, Part 1, Summa, q. 19, art. 11, and explains thus: The will properly so-called is called the will of good pleasure. The will metaphorically so-called is the will of sign, in that the sign itself of the will is called the will. Gregory of Valencia, Vol. 1, disp. 1, quest. 19, point 2, Col. 422, describes it thus: The will of good pleasure is called the very inclination or propensity of God toward an object known by Himself, which inclination is properly named the divine will. The will of sign, however, is named that which is accustomed to be among us a sign of will toward something, and which therefore by its own nature is accustomed to be, or certainly can be, a sign of the divine will as well. From which it is understood that in the scholastic sense the will of good pleasure is the internal counsel of God itself, but the will of sign is either a word or some act by which He manifests His internal counsel. Because this is done in various ways, hence they constitute a fivefold will of sign: 1. precept, 2. prohibition, 3. counsel, 4. permission, 5. operation, as recounted by Gregory of Valencia in the said place and Fr. Suarez on the first of Thomas, Book 3, on divine attributes, ch. 2, p. 1, 48, which species Durandus mentions as comprised in this verse in 1, dist. 45, qu. 5: 1. You command and 2. you prohibit, 3. you permit, 4. you counsel, 5. you fulfill.

XXV. II. Our people explain that distinction in four principal ways. 1. Some understand by the will of sign the legal will, and by the will of good pleasure the Evangelical will. For in the Law God indicates and requires our duty; in the Gospel He announces His good pleasure and counsel concerning the redemption of the human race. For εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe, 1 Cor. 1 v. 21. Where in the Law God teaches what He wills to be done by us out of duty: here in the Gospel what He wills to do concerning us out of grace, and therefore that is called the will of sign, this of good pleasure.

2. For others, the will of sign is the same as conditional will; and of good pleasure, as absolute, whence they say that the good pleasure of God always attains its end, according to Isa. 14 v. 24, 27, ch. 25 v. 1, ch. 26 v. 3, ch. 40, Jer. 1 v. 12. Since therefore that which God wills to be done does not happen, they explain this concerning the will of sign, which nevertheless is no less serious than the will of good pleasure, although it does not always attain its effect. But because those terms are obscure, and are perverted by the Calvinists, it is safer that the terms of conditional and absolute will be retained.

3.
