Some interpret the will of sign as the revealed will, inasmuch as through it God notifies or signifies what things are to be believed and what are to be done: but the will of good pleasure as the hidden [will], which concerns not the business of salvation, but certain special cases and the admirable economy of the world. Luther accepts it in this sense in ch. 6 of Genesis, where he refers the secret counsels of God to the will of good pleasure, such as: Why God wills to exhibit the Body and Blood of His Son through bread and wine, and not through other nobler means in the Sacrament; Why He willed to choose the Israelite people for Himself as a peculiar possession in times past, having passed over other nations; Why here at Wittenberg, and not at Rome or Constantinople, and why through the wretched monk Luther, and not through Emperors or other Monarchs, He willed to undertake that divine work of the Evangelical Reformation? If therefore by the will of sign is understood that which is proposed in the revealed word concerning things pertaining to our salvation: but by the will of good pleasure that which embraces the wonderful judgments of God and His ways ἀνεξιχνιάστους [unsearchable], Rom. 11 v. 33, in this sense it can certainly be tolerated: although it must be confessed that the revelation of the Gospel itself is εὐδοκίαν or the good pleasure of God, as is hinted at 1 Cor. 1 v. 21. Hence Luther said, that the will of good pleasure is rightly called that which the Gospel shows.

If, however, it is retained under the former sense, then let us note that rule of Luther: We must only rest in the will of the sign: But concerning the will of good pleasure, nothing must be scrutinized, but one must simply abstain.

4. Some of the Scholastics approve the exposition, and call everything the will of the sign through which God manifests His counsel, in which way the whole Scripture, which is a sign διάλυμα τῶ divine, can be called the will of the sign; but by the will of good pleasure they understand the internal counsel or decree of God.

And these are those four expositions concerning the will of the sign and of good pleasure, with respect to which that distinction can be tolerated, although on account of Calvinistic frauds and sophistications it is more advisable to abstain from it entirely, and to use other more convenient terms.

XXVI. III. But the Calvinists have twisted these words into a foreign and completely different meaning. For by the will of good pleasure they understand a certain absolute decree, preceding all causes, by which God has ordained from eternity what He wills to be done concerning each and every man, and according to which He has created a few for salvation, and all the rest for eternal damnation: i.e., and has absolutely predestined them. But they call the will of the sign that by which God makes known in the Scriptures, and according to which He declares outwardly indeed that He is delighted by the salvation of all, but inwardly in His secret counsel has a far different decree.

XXVII. But this Calvinistic Theology is too crude, nay, blasphemous, which can be refuted by three principal, but most powerful, arguments.

XXVIII. 1. From the truth and holiness of God. Our God is not a hypocrite or a simulator, He is not a liar and mutable, Num. 23. v. 10. But all His works are his in truth, Ps. 33:4. As therefore he speaks outwardly, so he feels inwardly: those things which he says he wills, those he most truly wills, and those which he says displease him, those also seriously displease him. But if the Calvinistic distinction were to stand, he would be a most wicked simulator and hypocrite, inasmuch as he would openly testify that he delights in the salvation of men, but at home and secretly would feel far otherwise. Christ says in Matt. 5:37: Let your speech be yea, yea; nay, nay: whatever is more than these is from EVIL. If the speech of men ought to be such, how much more will that be fitting? It is therefore from evil that Calvinists change the most true words of God into mere ὑποκρίσεις and simulations. Human justice and veracity are only traces of divine perfection. Moreover, it is repugnant to human veracity to profess one thing openly and to will another secretly. Much more, therefore, will it be repugnant to divine perfection, and therefore, since God in his revealed word wills the salvation of all, the contrary was certainly never decreed by him.

XXIX. 2. From the unity of the divine will. Above we noted that contradictory or contrary wills do not fall upon God. Wherefore, one must not invent some δίαταγμα of good pleasure, which would abolish the will revealed in the word, which they call the will of sign, or argue it of lying. But would not the wills be contrary if GOD were to command all to repent, to believe in Christ, and to love their neighbor, and yet by a secret good pleasure did not will those things to be done by the reprobate or those rejected? For these things fight against each other: God seriously wills all to believe and be saved; And, God does not seriously will all to believe and be saved. Which ἀντιλογίαν the Calvinists can reconcile by no other reason than by saying that God wills those things openly and outwardly, but does not will them secretly and at home, which itself is to invent contrary wills for God and with a wicked daring to brand the most holy one with the mark of hypocrisy.

XXX. 3. From the nature of the sign and the signified. Never are these opposed to one another, but rather are referred to one another. Therefore, the will of the sign will not be opposed to the will of good pleasure as to the thing signified. Whatever, therefore, is notified through the will of the sign, this very thing, and not its contrary, is established within. For that is nothing other than an external sign of the internal will. distinction of the Scholastics, which the Calvinists basely abuse, in his commentary on 1 Thomas, volume 3, on the divine attributes, chapter 3, rightly writes: The will of the sign, or the sign of the will, must always indicate in God some true will, otherwise it would not be a true sign, nor would it deserve the name of will; just as a painted man, unless he represented a true man, could not even analogically be called a man. In these signs, therefore, it must be attentively considered what true will they indicate in God. Just as, therefore, a sign is false which signifies something other than that of which it is said to be a sign: so the will of the sign is nothing if it does not express that very thing which is decreed within. Consequently, it is so far from the case that the will of the sign can be different from the will of good pleasure, that it must rather be entirely similar to it, noting the same object and the same action. Wherefore, if the sayings of Scripture about God willing the salvation of all denote the will of the sign, it is necessary that such a willing and good pleasure also be found in God, according to which He desires all to be saved. For such clearly is the χέσις between the will of the sign and the will of good pleasure, as that between words and concepts. For just as words are signs of concepts, so the will of the sign is nothing but a sign of the will of good pleasure. Just as, therefore, words cease to be true signs when something else is signified by them than what is conceived in the mind: so the will of the sign is not what it ought to be, as soon as it is imagined to differ from the internal good pleasure of God, from which it is rightly concluded that this Calvinistic distinction is false and self-contradictory.

Latin:

Quarta distinctio.

In voluntatem signi & beneplaciti.

XXIII. Distinctio hæc reperitur apud Scholasticos, Nostros, & Caluinianos, sed vicissim diuerso sensu.

XXIV. I. Scholastici dicunt, voluntatem Dei dupliciter capi vel propriè in se, vt est dispositio & beneplacitum exterius notificatur, vti patet ex Lomb. l. 1. Sent. dist. 45. lit. f. & seqq. Atque hinc orta distinctio inter voluntatem signi & beneplaciti, quam ponit Thomas de Aquino, par. 1. summæ, qu. 19. art. 11. & sic explicat. Voluntas propriè dicta vocatur voluntas beneplaciti. Voluntas autem metaphoricè dicta est voluntas signi, eò quòd ipsum signum voluntatis voluntas dicitur. Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 1. disp. 1. quæst. 19. pun. 2. Col. 422. ita describit: Voluntas beneplaciti appellatur ipsa inclinatio seu propensio Dei in obiectum à se cognitum, quæ inclinatio propriè voluntas diuina nominatur. Voluntas autem signi nominatur id, quod solet esse apud nos signum voluntatis erga aliquid quodque idcircò ex ratione quidem sua solet esse, aut certè potest esse signum voluntatis etiam diuinæ. Ex quibus intelligitur quod sensu scholastico voluntas beneplaciti sit ipsum internum Dei consilium, voluntas signi autem vel verbum, vel actus aliquis, quo interius suum consilium manifestat. Quòd cum varijs modis fiat, hinc quintuplicem signi voluntatem constituunt. 1. præceptum, 2. prohibitionem, 3. consilium 4. permissionem, 5. operationem, recensente Gregorio de Valent. l. d. & Fr. Suarez super primam Thomæ l. 3. de attrib. div. c. 2. p. 1. 48 quas species hoc versiculo comprehensas memorat Durandus in 1. dist 45. qu. 5. 1. Præcipis ac 2. prohibes. 3. permittis, 4. consulis, 5. imples.

XXV. II. Nostri distinctionem istam quatuor potissimùm modis exponunt. 1. Quidam per voluntatem signi intelligunt legalem, per beneplaciti Euangelicam voluntatem. In lege enim Deus debitum nostrum indicat, & requirit; In Euangelio beneplacitum & consilium suum de redemtione generis humani annunciat. Nam εὐδόκησεν ὁ θεὸς beneplacuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis salvos facere credentes, 1. Cor. 1. v. 21. vbi in lege docet Deus, quid velit à nobis ex debito fieri: hic in Euangelio quod velit de nobis ex gratia facere, ideoque servua illud signi, hoc beneplaciti appellatur.

2. Alijs voluntas signi idem est, quod voluntas conditionata; & beneplaciti, quod absoluta, vnde beneplacitum Dei finem suum semper assequi dicunt, juxta Esa. 14. v. 24 27. c. 25. v. 1. c. 26: v. 3. c. 40. Ierem. 1. v. 12. Cum ergo non sit, quod tamen fieri Deus vult, de signi voluntate hoc exponunt, quæ tamen non minus seria est atque voluntas beneplaciti, licèt effectum suum non semper consequatur. Quia verò termini isti sunt obscuri, & à Caluinianis peruertuntur, tutiùs est, vt conditionatæ & absolutæ voluntatis termini retineantur.

3. Nonnulli voluntatem signi interpretantur de voluntate revelata, quippe per quam Deus notificet vel significet, quæ tum credenda, tum facienda sint: voluntatem beneplaciti verò de abscondita, quæ non negotium salutis, sed speciales quosdam casus, & admirandam mundi œconomiam concernit. Hœc sensu eam accipit Lutherus in. c. 6. Genes. vbi ad voluntatem beneplaciti arcana Dei consilia refert, vt, Cur Deus per panem & vinum Corpus & sanguinem Filii sui, nō verò per alia media nobiliorem Sacramento exhibere velit; Cur populum Israeliticum post habitis cæteris gentibus olim in peculium sibi eligere voluerit; Cur hic Wittebergæ, non verò Romæ aut Constantinopoli, & Cur per misellum monachum Lutherum, non per Imperatorum, aut pœt alios Monarchas diuinum illud Reformationis Evangelicæ opus moliri voluerit ? Si ergò per voluntatem signi intelligatur ea, quæ de rebus ad salutem nostram pertinentibus in verbo reuelato proponitur: per voluntatem beneplaciti autem ea, quæ miranda Dei judicia & vias ejus ἀνεξιχνιάστς imperuestigabiles, Rom. 11. v. 33. complectitur hoc sanè-sensu tolerari potest: quamuis confitendum sit ipsam Euangelij reuelationem esse εὐδοκίαν vel beneplacitum Dei, vt innuitur 1. Cor. 1 v. 21. Hinc Lutherus dixit, recte voluntatem beneplaciti illam vocari, quam Euangelium ostendit.

Si tamen sub priori sensu retineatur, tum illam Lutheri regulam notemus: Nobis tantum requiescendum est in voluntate figni: De voluntate autem beneplaciti nihil scrutandum, sed simpliciter abstinendum est.

4. Quidam Scholasticorum expositionem adprobant, & id omne voluntatem figni dicunt, per quod Deus consilium suum manifestat, quo pacto tota Scriptura, quæ est signum διάλυμα τῶ diuini, voluntas figni nuncupari potest; per voluntatem verò beneplaciti internum Dei consilium vel decretum intelligunt.

Et hæ sunt illæ quatuor expositiones de voluntate figni & beneplaciti, quarum respectu distinctio ista tolerari potest, licèt ob fraudes & Sophisticationes Caluinisticas consultius sit, ab ea prorsus abstinere, aliosque commodiores terminos vsurpare.

XXVI. III. Caluiniani verò in alienam penitufque diuersam significationem vocabula ista detorserunt. Nam per voluntatem beneplaciti intelligunt absolutum quoddam, omnesque causas antegressum decretum, quo sanciuerit Deus ab æterno, quid de vno quoque homine fieri velit, & secundum quod paucos ad salutem, reliquos omnes ad æternam damnationem creauit: i. & absolutè prædestinauerit. Voluntatem verò signi eam vocant, quà Deus in Scripturis patefaciat, & iuxta quam omnium salute delectari seje exterius quidem declaret, intus autem in arcano consilio suo longè aliud decretum habeat.

XXVII. Nimis verò cruda, imò blasphema est hæc Theologia Caluinistica, quæ tribus potissimum argumentis, sed fortissimis refutari potest.

XXVIII. 1. A Dei veritate & sanctitate. Non est Deus noster hypocrita vel simulator, nō est mendex & mutabilis, Num. 23. vers. 10. Sed omnia opera eius sunt inveritate, Pf. 33. v. 4. Vt ergo foris loquitur, sic intus sentit: quæ se velle dicit, ea verissimè vult, & quę sibi displicere ait, illa seriò quoque displicent. At si stare debeat distinctio Caluiniftica, pessimus foret simulator & hypocrita, quippe qui palam testaretur, se delectari hominum salute, domi verò & clàm longè aliter sentiret. Christus inquit Matth. 5. v. 37 Sermo vester sit stà, ita, non, non: quicquid præterea est, ex MALO est. Si hominum sermo talis esse debet, quantò magis istud conueniet? Ex malo igitur est quòd Caluinistæ Dei verissîmi sermones in meras ὑποκρίσεις & simulationes commutant. Iustitia & veracitas humana sunt tantùm vestigia diuinæ perfectionis. Humanæ autem veracitati repugnat, aliud palam profiteri, & aliud clàm velle, Multò igitur magis diuinæ perfectioni repugnabit, ideoque, cum Deus in verbo reuelato velit omnium salutem, vtique contrarium ab ipso nunquam fuit definitum.

XXIX. 2. A diuinæ voluntatis vnitate. Suprà notauimus, in Deum non cadere voluntates contradictorias vel contrarias. Quare non est fingendum aliquod δίαταγμα beneplaciti, quod voluntatem in verbo patefactam, quam signi dicunt, tollat, vel mendacij arguat. Annon autem forent contrarię voluntates, si DEVS præciperet omnibus pœnitentiam agere, in Christum credere, proximumque diligere, & tamen arcano beneplacito nollet ea fieri à reprobis vel reprobatis? Hæc enim pugnant inuicem: Deus seriò vult omnes credere & saluos fieri; Et, Deus non vult seriò omnes credere, & saluos fieri. Quam ἀντιλογίαν Caluiniani nullâ ratione aliâ conciliare possunt, quàm dicendo, Deum illa velle palàm & foris, sed nolle clàm & domi, quod ipsum est contrarias voluntates fingere Deoŕ sanctissimo hypocriseos notam nefario ausu inurere.

XXX. 3. À natura signi & signati. Nunquam hæc sibi opponuntur, sed potius ad inuicem referuntur. Ergo & signi voluntas, voluntati beneplaciti tanquam signato, non erit opposita. Quicquid ergo per voluntatem signi notificatur, hoc ipsum, & non contrarium intus statuitur. Est enim illa nihil aliud, quàm signum externum voluntatis internæ. Hinc Suaresz distinctionem illam Scholastirorum, quâ Caluiniani turpiter abutuntur, exponens in comm. super 1. Thomæ t. 3. de attr. div. c. 3. rectè scribit: Voluntas gni, vel signum voluntatis, semper debet indicare in Deo aliquam veram voluntatem, aliàs non esset verum signum, neque nomen voluntatis mereretur; sicut homo pictus, nisi verum hominem repræsentaret, nec analogicè hominem repræsentaret, nec analogicè homo dici posset. In his ergo signis attentè considerandum est, quàm veram voluntatem in Deo indicent. Quemadmodum igitur falsum est signum, quod aliud significat, præter id, cuius signum esse dicitur: Itą voluntas signi nulla est, si non illud ipsum, quod intus decretum est, exprimit. Proinde, tantum abest, vt signi voluntas à voluntate beneplaciti alia esse possit, vt potius huic omninò simils esse debeat, notans idem obiectum & eandem actionem. Quare, si dicta scripturæ de Deo omnium salutem volente, notant voluntatem signi, necesse est, vt & in Deo reperiatur husinodi velle & beneplacitum, secūdum quod omnes saluos fieri desideret. Nam talis planè χέσις est inter signi & beneplaciti voluntatem, qualis inter verba & conceptus. Sicut enim verba sunt signa conceptuum, ita voluntas signi nil est, nisi signum voluntatis beneplaciti. Quemadmodum ergo verba desinunt esse vera signa, quando ijs aliud significatur, & aliud mente concipitur: ita voluntas signi non est, quod esse debet; quam primum ab interno Dei beneplacito discrepare fingitur, ex quo Caluinisticam istam distinctionem falsam & sibi ipsi contrariam esse, rectè concluditur.


### Question I. First distinction. Into absolute and conditional will: XXXI. And these were our arguments, to which the Calvinists oppose three small…

XXXI. And these were our arguments, to which the Calvinists oppose three small exceptions, which we shall briefly discuss.

XXXII. 1. Zanchius, book 3, on the nature of God, chapter 4, question 10, in order to remove the contrariety of the divine will, institutes a lengthy discourse, the sum of which is this: Although God commands certain things to all, which He does not wish to be done by the reprobate and those created for damnation, nevertheless there are no contrary wills in God on that account. The reason is that God, although He proposes His law to all, does not properly wish it to be kept by all, but only by the elect: For those things which He properly wills, they come to pass. Therefore, with respect to the damned, this is properly the will of God, that they sin and persevere in sins: but it is not properly His will that they keep the proposed precepts and commands. Thus, therefore, only one will of God, properly so called, remains perpetually.

Response 1. It is an impious statement that God does not wish His commands to be observed by all. For did He not propose the law equally to all, as much to the impious as to the pious? Did He not seriously wish that the Kings of Israel should walk in the precepts of the Lord? Why, therefore, did He punish them? Why, when they followed the law of God, did His grace flow to them mercifully? Therefore we reason thus: Whoever does nothing against the will of God properly so called does not sin, because sin is nothing other than the transgression of the law or of the divine will properly so called. But the impious do nothing against the will of God properly so called, as Zanchius asserts. Therefore the impious do not properly sin, and thus no sin properly so called will exist.

2. The reason which he brings forward is null, since he does not distinguish between the absolute and the conditioned will of God: For not only the former, but the latter also is a proper will. Although, therefore, the precepts of the Lord are not always observed by all, He nevertheless seriously wishes them to be observed. For He truly and from the heart wished that David should obey the sixth commandment, and not commit adultery, and yet this did not happen. He seriously wished to gather the Jews, just as a hen gathers her chicks, yet they themselves did not wish it, Matt. 25. v. 37. And, if nothing exists except by the will of God, why are many things said to have been done against the will of the Lord? Proverbs 19. v. 3. Why are the Pharisees said to have rejected the COUNSEL of God? Luke 7. v. 30. Why does Stephen say in Acts 7. v. 51 that the Israelites resist the Holy Spirit, that is, that they did something other than what the Holy Spirit wished them to do? In Ezech. 33. v. 11, Jehovah cries out from heaven, I live, I do not wish the death of the sinner, but I wish that he be converted. But does God not truly wish for conversion here? Why then does He repeat it in the same place? Be converted, be converted; From all of which the absurdity of the Zanchian dictum clearly appears: God does not properly wish that His precepts be kept by the impious, since they are not kept: why do we oppose this orthodox view? Whatever God seriously commands to be done, He also seriously wishes to be done by all those to whom He proposes His precepts. For every command presupposes the will of the one commanding: For what one commands to be done, that he wishes to be done. Thus, when God commands good works, He certainly wishes (and indeed properly, just as He properly commands) them to be done by all, because the command of God is nothing other than an index and sign of His will.

XXXIII. 2. There are given in the Scriptures examples in which God, by the will of the sign, commanded and wished something, which, however, by the will of His good pleasure He did not wish, as when He commanded Abraham to kill his son, Gen. 22. v. 12, or Pharaoh to release the people, Exod. 5. v. 1, when nevertheless He did not wish the killing of the son and the release of the people. For He wished to harden Pharaoh, Exod. 7. v. 3. Thus toward the Canaanite woman, by the will of the sign or outwardly, He showed Himself angry and severe, when nevertheless by the hidden will of His good pleasure the paternal affection of divine clemency lay hidden, Matt. 15. v. 23. R. These examples are distinct, and therefore we shall respond distinctly. 1. Regarding the command given to Pharaoh concerning the release of the Israelite people, we say that it was most serious. For God willed from the heart that Pharaoh should let the people go: but because he resisted the divine will by his own spontaneous malice. Hence God, in punishment for his preceding sins, hardened and blinded him by a just judgment. Whom, therefore, He willed to be saved by His antecedent will, and obedient to His precepts, him He willed to be hardened by His consequent will. Therefore, the Calvinists beg the question with this example, and they must first prove that God did not will that Pharaoh should let the people go. We urge the passage in Exodus 10, verses 3 and 4, where it is read thus: 'Thus says the Lord: How long do you refuse to submit to me? Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me: but if you resist, etc.' But how could he resist God, if it was not the will of God that he should let the people go? For when two people will and do the same thing, then certainly one cannot resist the other.

2. As regards the command concerning the sacrificing of Isaac, that was not serious, and thus an ignorance of the Elenchus is committed. For the question is: Whether that which God openly wills and proclaims to be done by all, He can secretly oppose and will that it not be done. But that that command was not serious is evident from Genesis chapter 22, verse 2, where it is said: 'After these things were done, God tempted Abraham': by which word 'tempting' it is indicated that the command of the Lord was not given seriously, but only for the purpose that Abraham's faith and obedience might be tested. Let the Calvinists demonstrate, therefore, that God also gave His law not seriously, but only for the sake of tempting and testing.

3. As regards the story of the Canaanite woman, it is to be noted that there is a twofold simulation: 1. Illicit, which deceives and harms. 2. Licit, which benefits and teaches. Illicit is that which is repugnant to the will of God and the charity of one's neighbor: but licit is that which does not oppose the law, and therefore can fall upon a good man. Such a licit simulation it was, when God, in the presence of Abraham, simu lated that He willed the immolation of His son Isaac: this at first glance seemed evil on the part of Abraham, who would have been so miserably despoiled of his son, yet God directed it toward good, so that the faith of Abraham might be rendered conspicuous. There was a similar reason for the simulation of Christ toward the Canaanite woman. It was not hypocrisy, but a testing, directed not to the destruction, but to the salvation of the Canaanite woman. But if we truly consider that simulation which the Calvinists attribute to God, saying that He indeed professes universal love in word, but feels otherwise in His heart, it can be proven with little effort that it is utterly illicit and iniquitous. For 1. the promises of God would be mere mockeries of men. 2. The bland words of God would have a hidden poison, if, of course, the Evangelical promises were offered to the reprobate for no other end than that their damnation might be aggravated. 3. Evil simulations are those which promise good things by an external appearance, but involve hidden evils. 4. If we wish to attach any simulation to the promises of God, what then will be the πληροφορία of our faith, what certainty of Scripture?

From all these things, therefore, it appears that the examples brought forward and the Calvinistic thesis differ in many ways: 1. By reason of the object, because there it is a matter of bodily benefits, here of eternal salvation, concerning which certainty and solidity are required. 2. By reason of the end, because there a fatherly affection of God lay hidden under the will of the sign, here a hostile hatred, which is altogether illicit. 3. By reason of the persons, because there God acts by a singular dispensation with one person, here with the whole human race, which He does not deceive in the business of salvation. 4. By reason of the duration, because there He soon revealed His serious will, but here He perseveres and allows His grace to be inculcated daily, nor has He manifested by any signs since the foundation of the world that He secretly cherishes anything else in His heart concerning the redemption of the human race. Let this impious and crude theology of the Calvinists therefore be of no value, which feigns contradictory wills; it removes all certainty and, with a most wicked attempt, fashions the best God into a hypocrite and a deceiver.

XXXIV. 3. Num. 22. v. 20. & 35. God commands Balaam to go to King Balak. This was the will of sign, but not of good pleasure, because He did not want him to go. And it seems that this simulation was a trap, because it tended toward Balaam's destruction. Thus, therefore, a clear example of that distinction between the will of sign and of good pleasure is held.

Resp. There are various expositions of this passage: I. Some think that God's command regarding the departure was not simulated, but serious. For although He first prohibited it, v. 12, yet He later granted it, v. 20. Especially v. 35, where Balaam says: I have sinned, not knowing that you stood against me, and now if it displeases you that I go, I will return, and the Angel answered: Go with them and take care that you speak nothing other than what I have commanded you. Which command certainly could not have been simulated, since Balaam wanted to return. Meanwhile, however, that this departure displeased God is clear from v. 22: God was angry that he went. How, therefore, will they be reconciled: in verse 20 the Lord says: Arise and go. In verse 22 it is said: He was angry that he went. Why, therefore, was He angry, if He seriously wanted him to go and commanded it? We will therefore add other interpretations.

II. Some say that the Lord's response was ironic, by which Balaam was deluded, because he did not want to be content with God's first and clear response, but sought and expected another different from the former. Which εἰρωνεία, even if it might find a place regarding v. 20, nevertheless seems to expire regarding v. 35. For there Balaam was promising a return and seeking God's response, and yet the departure is commanded, which to be said through irony and done simulatedly appears too harsh and alien to the truth of God.

III. There are therefore others who call the distinction of antecedent and consequent will to their aid, saying that God, indeed, antecedently did not will the departure of Balaam; consequently, however, because he was obstinate and disobedient to the first command, He willed the departure as a punishment for his contumacy, as a means, making it serve for the illustration of His glory, the blessing of the people of Israel, and the delusion of Balaam. Therefore, it was a serious command, not ironic, but it proceeded not from His antecedent will, by which He did not will the departure, but from His consequent will, which they call [the will] of judgment, and according to which He commanded the departure: if this answer does not yet satisfy, we add.

IV. That another opinion appears in v. 20 and 35. There, indeed, an imperative is held, but it denotes only permission. For it happens quite often that words of command are to be explained permissively. A most clear example is held in 4 Kings 2:16, where Elisha did not want to send certain men to seek Elijah; at length, however, they compelled him to acquiesce and say: Send, that is, I will indeed permit that some be sent; but it will be in vain. Thus, the command of Christ, Go, made to the demons about to enter the swine of the Gergesenes, Matt. 8:32, is explained permissively in Luke 8:32, And He permitted them. In a similar way, when the Lord said to Balaam, Arise and go, not so much a will as a permission is to be understood, so that the sense may be: Because you do not wish to acquiesce in my response, go indeed, but at your own peril: I will permit it to be done so, but it will result in your detriment. But as regards v. 35, nothing prevents a serious command from being admitted there. Because Balaam had also once entered upon that journey, God did not want him to turn back, but wanted him to proceed, so that from this He might seize the occasion to illustrate His glory. Thus, therefore, God nowhere dissembled: Not in v. 20, because there only παραχώρησις is held, joined with displeasure and anger, of which [we read] in v. 22. Not in v. 35, because there the Lord seriously willed that Balaam should proceed, although He did not approve of the beginning of the journey.

Finally, however, in whatever way that of Balaam

Latin:

XXXI. Et hæc fuerunt argumenta nostra, quibus tres exceptiunculas opponunt Caluiniani, quas breuiter discutiemus.

XXXII. 1. Zanchius l. 3. de natura Dei, c. 4. quæst. 10. vt contrarietatem voluntatis diuinæ amoliatur, prolixum instituit discursum, cuius hæc est summa: Etsi Deus quædam omnibus præcipiat, quæ à reprobis, & ad damnationem creatis fieri nolit, propterea tamen in Deo non sunt contrariæ voluntates. Ratio, quia Deus, licet omnibus legem suam proponat, non tamen ab omnibus eam seruari propriè vult, sed tantùm ab electis: Nam quæ propriè vult, ea fiunt. Respectu ergo damnatorum, hæc est propriè voluntas Dei, vt peccent, & in peccatis perseuerent: propriè autem voluntas eius non est, vt seruent præcepta & mandata proposita. Sic ergo vna tantùm voluntas Dei propriè dicta perpetuò manet.

Respon. 1. Impiè dictum est, Deum non velle, vt ab omnibus mandata eius obseruentur. Annón enim omnibus æquè proposuit legem, tàm impijs, quàm pijs? Annón serio voluit, vt Reges Israelitici ambulārēt in pręceptis Domini? Cur igitur eos puniuit? Cur, quando legē Dei secuti sunt, ijs gratia sua clementer affluit? Quare sic ratiocinamur: Quicunque nihil facit contra voluntatem Dei propriè non peccat, quia peccatum nihil est aliud, quàm transgressio legis seu voluntatis diuinæ propriè sic dictæ. Atqui impij nihil faciunt contra voluntatem Dei propriè sic dictam, asserente Zanchio. Ergo impij propriè non peccant, adeoque nullum dabitur peccatum propriè sic dictum.

2. Ratio, quam affert, nulla est, siquidem non distinguit inter voluntatem Dei absolutam & conditionatam: Non enim illa tantùm, sed hæc etiam propriè voluntas est. Licet igitur non semper ab omnibus obseruentur præcepta Domini, seriò tamen vult illa obseruari. Nam verè & ex animo voluit, vt Dauid obtemperaret præcepto sexto, nec committeret adulterium, neque tamen hoc factum est. Seriò voluit Iudæos congregare, sicut gallina congregat pullos suos, ipsi tamen noluerunt, Matth. 25. v. 37. Et, si nihil sit nisi volente Deo, cur multa dicuntur esse facta fieri contra voluntatem Domini? Proverb. 19. v. 3. Cur Pharisæi dicuntur sprevisse CONSILIVM Dei? Luc. 7. vers: 30. Cur Stephanus ait Act. 7. v. 5. Israëlitas resistere Spiritui sancto, id est, eos aliud fecisse, quàm quod eos facere volebat Spiritus sanctus, Ezech. 33. v. 11. è cælo clamat Iehovah, Vivo ego, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed volo, ut convertatur. An verò hîc Deus non vult propriè conversionem? Cur ergo ibidem ingeminat? Convertimini, Convertimini; Ex quibus omnibus luculenter patet absurditas Zanchiani effati: Deus non vult propriè, vt ab impijs serventur eius præcepta, quoniam non servantur: cur nos opponimus hoc orthodoxum? Quæcunque Deus serio præcipit fieri, illa & fieri seriò vult ab omnibus ijs, quibus præcepta sua proponit. Nam omne mandatum præsupponit voluntatem mandantis: Quod enim quis mandat fieri, illud vult fieri. Sic cùm Deus mandat bona opera, certè vult (& quidem propriè, sicut propriè mandat) ea fieri ab omnibus, quia mandatum Dei nihil est aliud, quàm index & signum voluntatis.

XXXIII. 2. Dantur in Scripturis exempla, in quibus Deus voluntate signi aliquid præcepit & voluit, quod tamen voluntate beneplaciti noluit, vt, quando Abrahæ mandavit, vt occideret filium. Gen. 22. v. 12. Pharaoni, vt dimitteret populum, Exod 5. v. 1. cùm tamen occisionem filij, & dimissionem populi nollet. Pharaonem enim volebat indurare, Exod. 7. v. 3. Sic erga mulierem Chananæam, voluntate signi seù forinsecus se iratum atq; severum ostendit, cùm tamen dycanâ voluntate beneplaciti paternus divinæ clementiæ affectus occultatus latuerit, Matth. 15. v. 23. R. Exempla ista distincta sunt, ideoque distinctè respondebimus. 1. Quod attinet præceptum Pharaoni datum, de dimittendo populo Israëlitico, dicimus illud fuisse maximè serium. Ex animo n. volebat Deus, vt Pharao dimitteret populum : Quia verò spontaneâ malitiâ voluntati diuinæ reluctabatur. Hinc Deus in pœnam præcedentium delictorum illum iusto iudicio indurauit & excœcauit. Quem igitur voluntate antecedente saluatum, & suis pręceptis obsequentem, hanc voluntate consequente induratum volebat. Proinde Caluiniani exemplo isto principium petunt, & prius probare debent, noluisse Deum, vt Pharao dimitteret populum. Nos vrgemus locum Exod. 10. v. 3. & 4. vbi sic legitur. Hæc dicit Dominus : vsque quò non vis subyci mihi? dimitte populum meum, vt sacrificet mihi: sin autem resistis, &c. Quomodo verò poterat Deo resistere, si voluntas Dei non erat, vt dimitteret populum ? Cùm enim duo idem volunt & faciunt, tùm certè alter nequit alteri resistere.

2. Quod spectat pręceptum de immolando Isaaco, illud non fuit serium, adeóque committitur ignoratio Elenchi. Quæritur enim, Vtrum id, quod Deus seriò ab omnibus fieri palàm vult, & edicit, clàm possit auersari & velle nè fiat. Quod autem serium non fuerit illud præceptum, patet ex ca. 22. Gen. v. 2. vbi dicitur : Quæ postquam gesta sunt, tentauit Deus Abrahamum : quo tentandi vocabulo indicatur, mandatum Domini non seriò, sed tantùm idcircò datum fuisse Abrahamo, vt fides eius & obedientia probaretur. Demonstrent igitur Caluiniani, Deum quoq; legē suam tulisse non seriò, sed duntaxat tentandi & probandi gratiâ.

3. Quod attinet historiam de muliere Chananæa, notandum, quod duplex sit simulatio, 1. Illicita, quæ fallit & nocet. 2. Licita quæ prodest & docet. Illicita est, quæ Dei voluntati, proximíque charitati repugnat: Licita verò, quæ non aduersatur legi, ideoque in bonum virum cadere potest. Talis licita simulatio erat, cùm Deus coram Abrahamo simulabat, se velle immolationem filij Isaici: hoc primâ fronte videbatur malum ex parte Abrahæ, qui ita filio suo miserè spoliatus fuisset, Deus tamen id in bonũ dirigebat, vt fides Abrahę redderetur conspicua. Par ratio fuit simulationis Christi erga Chananæam. Non erat hypocrisis, sed probatio, non in perniciem, sed salutê Chananææ directa. Quod si verò consideremus simulationem illam, quam Deo Caluiniani tribuunt, dicentes, ipsum in verbo quidem amorem vniuersalem profiteri, sed in corde diuersum sentire, eam prorsus esse illicitam & iniquam, facili negotio probari potest. Nam 1 promissiones Dei mera essent hominum ludibria. 2. blanda Dei verba haberent occultatum virus, si nimirum promissiones Euangelicæ altum in finem reprobis non offerrentur, quàm vt damnatio illorum aggrauaretur. 3. Malæ simulationes sunt, quæ externâ specie bona promittunt, sed occultis malis implicant. 4. Si promissionibus Dei aliquam simulationem affingere volumus, quę tandem erit πληροφορία fidei nostrę, quæ certitudo Scripturæ?

Ex his ergò omnibˢ apparet, exempla prolata, & thesin Caluinisticã multis modis discrepare, 1. Ratione obiecti, quia ibi agitur de beneficijs corporalibus, hic de salute æterna, circa quã certitudo & soliditas requiritur. 2. Ratione finis, quia ibi sub volutate signi latuit paternus Dei affectˢ, hic hostile odium, quod omninò illicitum. 3. Ratione personarum, quia ibi Deus agit ex dispensatione singulari cum vna persona, hic cum toto genere humano, quod in negotio salutis non decipit. 4. Ratione durationis, quia ibi voluntatem suam seriam mox patefecit, hic autem perseuerat suamque gratiam quotidiè inculcare sinit, nec vllis indicijs à condito mundo manifestauit, se circa generis humani redemptionem aliud sub corde clam fouere. Valeat ergò impia ista & cruda Caluinistarum Theologia, quę voluntates contradictorias fingit; omnem certitudinem tollit & ex Deo optimo hypocritam & illusorem conatu scelestissimo efformat.

XXXIV. 3. Num. 22. v. 20. & 35. Deus præcipit Balaamo, vt abeat ad Regem Balac. Hæc erat voluntas signi, sed non beneplaciti, quia ipsum abire nolebat. Et videtur, simulationem istam fuisse thalam, quia tendebat ad Balaami perniciem. Ita ergo luculentum habetur exemplum distinctionis istius inter voluntatem signi & beneplaciti.

Resp. Loci istius variæ sunt expositiones: I. Nonnulli putant, mandatum Dei de abitu non simulatum, sed serium fuisse. Licet enim primùm istud prohibuerit. v. 12. Tamen pòst concessisse, vers. 20. Inprimis vers. 36. vbi Balaam dicit; Peccavi nesciens, quod tu stares contra me, & nunc si displicet tibi, vt vadam revertar, & respondit Angelus: Vade cum istis & caveto nè aliud quàm præcepero tibi, loquaris. Quod certè præceptum non potuit esse simulatum, cùm Balaam redire voluerit, Interim tamen istum abitu displicuisse Deo, patet ex 22. Iratus est Deus, quòd abiret ipse. Quomodo igitur concillabuntur: versu 20: ait Dominus: Surge & abi. vers. 22. dicitur: Iratus est, quod abiret. Cùr ergò iratus est, si ipsum abire seriò voluit, & præcepit? Addemus proinde alias interpretationes.

II. Quidam dicunt, responsum Domini fuisse ironicum quo Balaam delusus sit, eò quòd contentus esse noluerit primo & perspicuo Dei responso, sed petierit & expectaverit aliud à priori diuersum. Quæ εἰρωνεία si maximè locum inueniat quoad v. 20. tamen expirare videtur quoad v. 35. Ibi enim Balaam promittebat reditum, petebátque Dei responsum, & tamẽ præcipitur abitus, quod per ironiam dictum, & simulatè factum esse nimis durum apparet, & à veritate Dei alienum.

III. Sunt ergò alij qui distinctionem voluntatis antecedentis & consequentis in subsidium vocant, dicentes, Deum antecedentes quidem noluisse abitum Balaami; consequenter tamen, quia pertinax fuit, & primo mandato inobediens, in pœnam contumaciæ abitum voluisse, tanquam medium, faciens ad gloriæ suæ illustrationem, populi Israelitici benedictionem, & Balaami illusionem. Serium ergò præceptum fuit, non ironicum, profectum verò non ex antecedente voluntate, quâ abitum nolebat, sed consequente, quam judicij appellant, & secundum quam abitum mandabat: quæ responsio si nondum satisfaciat, addimus.

IV. Aliam videri sententiam v. 20. & 35. Ibi quidem Imperativus habetur, sed tantùm notatur permissio. Fit enim sæpius, vt verba mandati exponenda sint permissivè. Exemplum clarissimum habetur. 4. Reg. 2. v. 16. vbi Elisæus nolebat mitti quosdam ad quærendum Eliam: tandem tamen coegerunt eum, vt acquiesceret, & diceret: Mittite, h. e. Permittam sanè, vt quidam mittantur; sed frustrà erit. Sic Christi mandatum, Ite, factum ad Dæmones, porcos Gergesenorum ingressuros, Matth. 8. v. 32. permissivè exponitur Luc. 8. v. 32. Et Permisit illis. Pari modo, cùm Dominus ad Balaamum dixit. Surge & vade, non tam voluntas, quàm permissio intelligenda est vt sensus sit. Quia non vis acquiescere in responso meo, vadas sanè, sed suo periculo: Ego permittam ita fieri, sed cedes in tuum detrimentum. Quod verò spectat v. 35. nihil impedit, quo minus ibi serium mandatum admitti queat. Quia etiam Balaam semel ingressus erat iter istud, noluit Deus eum reuerti, sed volebat pergere, vt hinc occasionem captaret illustrandæ suæ gloriæ. Ita ergò nullibi simulauit Deus: Non v. 20. quia ibi tantùm παραχώρησις habetur, coniuncta cum displicentia & ira, de qua v. 22. Non v. 35. quia ibi Dominus seriò voluit, vt pergeret Balaamus, licet initium itineris non adprobauerit.

### Question II. Sayings of Scripture

history may be, nothing will be taken away from our own, nothing will be added to the Calvinistic opinion. For that example is 1. singular. 2. entirely irrelevant, since we are inquiring about the salvation of men and the promises of God. 3. uncertain and subject to various interpretations, from which a doubtful thesis, and especially an article of faith, neither ought to nor can be demonstrated.

QUESTION II. Does GOD seriously and by an internal good pleasure wish all men to be saved?

I. The Calvinists hold the negative, of whom these are the choice flowers: I say this, that there never was, is, or will be a time when God has wished, wishes, or will wish to have mercy on individuals, Beza, part 2, Resp. ad colloq. p. 194. Those who imagine to themselves that God has mercy on all and wishes individuals to be saved, err by a whole heaven and commit a great sin, Rennech. de praedest. p. 114. God likewise absolutely wishes the elect to be saved, and likewise absolutely wishes the reprobate not to be saved, Zanchius in Miscell. p. 302.

II. We, however, believe, teach, and profess that God with great desire has so loved the whole human race seriously and ardently, that He wishes and desires all and singular, with none excepted, to repent and be saved eternally; and that He never made any secret or absolute decree, either from eternity or in time, by which He either created many, or few, or even one alone for damnation, or, having created them, destined them without any regard for unbelief to eternal destruction out of mere hatred. Which hypothesis must be clearly proven against the Calvinists, and once proven, must be firmly held. We shall confirm it, however, by 1. Sayings of Scripture: 2. Reasons. 3. Testimonies.

III. SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE. 1. From Ezech: 33. verse 11. As I live, says the Lord God, I do not desire the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live. Similar things exist in ch. 18, v. 32 & 33. Why will you die, O house of Israel? I desire not the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord God. Return ye and live. Moreover, we read in Heb. 6:17 et seqq. that men swear by a greater, and an oath for confirmation is to them an end of all strife. Therefore, when God wished to show us in an exceptional way oath, so that by two immutable things (namely, the promise and the oath) in which it is impossible for God to lie, we might have strong consolation. This most religious oath of God, therefore, ought by right to have ended every controversy between us and the Calvinists. For He swears for this reason, that if we do not believe God promising, we might at least believe Him swearing for our salvation, writes Jerome, tom. 2, epist. 46. For what is the swearing of the true and truthful God, if not a confirmation of the promise and a certain rebuke of the faithless? as Augustine says, lib. 16 de civ. Dei, cap. 32. O happy men, exclaims one of the Fathers, for whose sake God swears, but more unhappy are those who do not have faith even in God swearing!

But, even if God testifies by a most holy oath that He does not from His heart desire the death of the wicked and of him that dieth, nevertheless the Calvinists withhold their faith, objecting: 1. In the Hebrew it is not 'to will,' but 'to take pleasure.' 2. That this saying speaks not of all men, but only of the Jews. 3. That the discourse is not about every wicked person, but only about him who is converted. 4. That it must be understood of temporal death, not eternal.

Response to 1. In the Hebrew text is found the root חפץ, which in general signifies, as the lexicographers note, 'to have pleasure'; 'to be agreeable'; 'to will,' and it is read in Psalm 5:5, 'God not willing iniquity.' Psalm 113:3, 'He hath done whatsoever He willed,' from which appears the vanity of the Calvinistic objection. Furthermore, even if the Prophet had set down these words, 'God does not take pleasure in the death of the wicked,' it would still have been enough to blunt the Calvinists. For their pleasure is that which they will. we are, and conversely: If therefore God does not delight in the death of the wicked, certainly He does not will it, for if He were to will it, He would certainly delight in it.

To 2. Even if this address was proposed properly and primarily to the Jews, this nevertheless does nothing for the Calvinistic opinion, since they say that God willed the destruction and eternal damnation of many of the Jews: which blasphemous dogma is clearly refuted by the present testimony.

To 3. An injury is done to the text. For it is not said: God does not will the death of the wicked, who is converted, but God does not will the death of the wicked, but (He wills, one must understand) that he be converted. Furthermore, this little exception is thoroughly routed from chapter 18, where the Lord says, I do not will the death of the one who dies.

To 4. Again they do violence to the text. For that the Prophet speaks of death and eternal damnation is clear, 1. because that death is opposed to eternal life. I do not will the death of the wicked, but that he be converted and live, where to understand temporal life, since it is absurd, certainly the death opposed to this life will also not be temporal, but eternal. For even if the wicked were not converted, he could still live a temporal life. 2. because the death of the body was common to all the Jews, both those repenting and the impenitent. Here, however, he speaks of such a death by which only the wicked die: in which sense it is said to the impenitent David, 2 Sam. 12. verse 13. You shall not die, that is, you shall not be damned. 2. And let us grant in meipoiar, that God speaks of temporal death, yet no support will accrue to the Calvinists from that. For we shall argue from the lesser to the greater: If God does not will the temporal death of the wicked, much less will He will eternal death. If an earthly father cannot will that his son be beaten, much less will he be able to will that he be punished with the death penalty.

Latin:

laami Historia nil tamen decedet nostrae, nil accedet Caluinisticae opinioni. Nam exemplumistud 1. singulare est. 2. prorsus alienum, cùm nos de salute hominum & promissionibus Dei quaeramus. 3. incertum & varijs expositionibus obnoxium, ex quo thesis dubia, inprimis verò articulus fidei neque debet neque potest demonstrari.

QVAESTIO II. Num DEVS omnes homines seriò internoque beneplacito velit saluos fieri?

I. Negatiuam tenent Caluiniani, quorum hi sunt flosculi: Hoc dico, nunquam tempus fuisse, vel esse, vel futurum, quo voluerit, velit aut voliturus sit Deus singulorum misereri, Beza par: 2. Resp. ad colloq. p. 194. Isti, qui Deum omnium misereri, & singulos saluari velle sibi imaginantur, toto coelo errant, & magnum peccatum admittunt, Rennech. de praedest. p. 114. Deus absolutè itidem vult electos saluos fieri, & absolutè itidem vult reprobos non seruari, Zanchius in Miscell. p. 302.

II. Nos verò credimus, docemus & profitemur, quòd Deus magno desiderio totum genus humanum serio & ardenter ita dilexerit, vt omnes & singulos, nullo excepto, velit & exoptet poenitentiam agere, aeternumque saluari; & quod nullum vnquam vel ab aeterno, vel in tempore occultum absolutumue decretum fecerit, quo vel multos, vel paucos, vel vnum duntaxat aut condiderit ad damnationem, aut conditos absque vllo incredulitatis respectu ex mero odio, aeterno exitio destinauerit. Quae hypothesis aduersus Caluinianos luculenter probanda, & probata firmiter tenenda est. Confirmabimus verò illam 1. Dictis Scriptura: 2. Rationibus. 3. Testimonijs.

III. DICTA SCRIPTVRAE. 1. Ex Ezech: 33. vers. 11. Vivo ego, dicit Dominus Deus, nolo mortem impij, sed vt conuertatur impius à via sua & viuat. Similia extant c. 18. v. 32. & 33. Quare moriemini domus Israel? Nolo mortem morientis, dicit Dominus Deus. Revertimini & vivite. Legimus autem Hebr. 6. 17. & seqq. quod homines per maiorem jus iurent, & omnis controversiae eorum finis ad confirmationem sit iuramentum. Deus ergo cùm eximiè nobis ostendere vellet firmitatem consilij & voluntatis suae interposuit hoc iusiurandum, vt per duas res immobiles (promissionem videlicet & iuramentum) in quibus fieri non possit, vt mentiretur Deus, validam consolationem haberemus. Hoc igitur religiosissimum Dei iuramentum merito finisse debebat omnis inter nos & Caluinianos controuersiae. Nam idcirco iurat, vt si non credimus promittenti Deo, credamus saltem pro salute iuranti, scribit Hieronymus tom. 2. epist. 46. Quid enim est Dei veri, veracisque iuratio, nisi promissi confirmatio, & infidelium quaedam increpatio? dicente Augustino lib. 16. de ciu. Dei cap. 32. O felices homines, exclamat quidam ex Patribus, quorum caussa Deus iurat, sed infeliciores, qui nec Deo iuranti fidem habent!

Verùm, etiamsi Deus sacrosanctissimo iureiurando obtestetur, se ex animo nolle mortem impij & morientis, nihilo minus tamen fidem derogant Caluiniani, excipientes 1. in Hebraeo non esse velle, sed delectari. 2. dictum istud loqui non de omnibus hominibus sed tantùm Iudaeis. 3. Sermonem esse non de omni impio, sed de eo duntaxat, qui conuertitur. 4. de morte temporali, non æterna accipiendum esse.

Resp. ad 1. habetur in textu Hebræo radix חפץ, quæ in genere significat, annotantibus Lexicographis, voluptatem habuit; volupe fuit; voluit, & legitur Psal. 5. v. 5. Deus non volens iniquitatem. Psalm. 113. vers. 3. quæ voluit, fecit, ex quo apparet vanitas obiectionis Caluinisticæ. Deinde quamuis Propheta posuisset hæc verba, Deus non delectatur morte impij; satis tamen fuisset ad retundendos Caluinianos. Nam delectatio eorum est, quæ vosumus, & contrà : Si igitur Deus non delectatur morte impij, vtique eam non vult, si enim vellet, certè istâ delectaretur.

Ad 2. Etiamsi concio ista Iudæis propriè & primò fuerit proposita, nihil tamen hoc facit pro sententia Caluinistica, quippe qui dicunt, Deum multorum ex Iudæis interitum & æternam damnationem voluisse: quod blasphemum dogma præsenti testimonio perspicuè refutatur.

Ad 3. Fit iniuria textui. Non enim dicitur: Deus non vult mortem impij, qui conuertitur, sed Deus non vult mortem impij, verùm (subintelligere vult) vt conuertatur. Deinde hæc exceptiuncula penitus profligatur ex c. 18. vbi Dominus inquit, Nolo mortem morientis.

Ad 4. Rursum textui vim inferunt. Quòd enim Propheta loquatur de morte & damnatione æternâ, patet, 1. quia mors ista opponitur vitæ æternæ. Nolo mortem impij, sed vt conuertatur & viuat, vbi vitam temporalem intelligere cùm sit absonum, vtique & huic vitæ opposita mors non temporalis, sed æterna erit. Licèt enim impius non conuerteretur, viuere tamen posset vitam temporalem. 2. quia mors corporis communis fuit Iudæis omnibus, resipiscentibus & impœnitentibus. Hic autem loquitur de tali morte, quâ soli impij moriuntur: in quem sensum ad Dauidem impœnitentem dicitur, 3. Sam. 12. vers. 13. Non morieris, id est, non damnaberis. 2. Et demus in meipoiar, loqui Deũ de morte temporali, nihil tamen inde præsidij accedet Caluinianis. Ita enim à minori ad maius argumentabimur: Si Deus nō vult mortem temporalē impij, multò minus volet mortem æternam. Si pater terrenus velle nequit, vt filius suus verberetur, multò minus velle poterit, vt capitis supplicio mulctetur.


### Question II. Sayings of Scripture: IV. 2. From 1 Tim. 2. v. 4. God wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth

IV. 2. From 1 Tim. 2. v. 4. God wills all men to be saved, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. Of this there are various interpretations. Augustine in Enchirid. c. 103. explains it thus: We must understand what is written, 'Who wills all men to be saved,' as if it were said, that no man is saved unless he whom He Himself willed to be saved: not that there is no man whom He does not will to be saved, but that no one is saved unless He wills it, and therefore He is to be entreated to will it, because it must happen if He wills it. For the Apostle was dealing with praying to God when he said this. For thus we understood that which is written in the Gospel: 'Who illuminates every man,' not because there is no man who is not illuminated, but because no one is illuminated except by Him. Or certainly it is said thus; 'who wills all men to be saved'; not that there was no man whom He did not will to be saved, He who did not will to perform the virtues of miracles among those whom He says would have done penance if He had done so; but that we may understand 'all men' as every human race, distributed through whatever differences, etc. This interpretation of Augustine flowed from the fact that he judged the Apostle to be speaking of the absolute will of God joined with efficacy: indeed, so that if God willed all to be saved, they would also be saved immediately. For thus he says at the end of that chapter: And in whatever other way it can be understood, provided we are not compelled to believe that God the Almighty willed something to be done, and it was not done, He who without any ambiguities is in heaven and on earth, just as the truth also sings: 'All things, whatsoever He willed, He did.' Certainly He did not will to do whatever He did not do. These things are there. From which it is clear that Augustine understood the present passage concerning a simple and always efficacious will, and for that reason brought forward these interpretations. But since many things happen which God nevertheless does not will to happen, and God wills many things which do not happen, for that reason, in question 2, we have rightly distinguished between an efficacious and an inefficacious will, a simple and a conditional one. Although, therefore, the present passage cannot be understood concerning the efficacious will of God (to which Augustine looked), it may nevertheless be very well expounded concerning the conditional one. For nothing is taken away from divine omnipotence in this way, since indeed He seriously wills all to be saved, but conditionally, if they accept the means of salvation. Since many neglect this, it does not follow from that, which God nevertheless wills to be done. And if this interpretation is held, there will be no need to invent foreign ones. Nor in this part do we do injury to Augustine, since he does not refuse that this passage be accepted however we might wish, provided that the omnipotence of God and His efficacious will is not denied.

Furthermore, Sedulius considers three expositions very briefly in these words: God wills all men to be saved, if they themselves, having been called, are willing to obey God: or all men, namely the predestined: or all men, that is, every sex, nation, and condition.

But our business is with the Calvinists, who agree in this, that by the universal particle are not understood individuals of kinds, but kinds of individuals, so that the sense is: God wills all, that is, some from all, to be saved. See Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard and Part 2 of the Response to the Acts, page 192. Hence, therefore, the state of the question arises: Is the universal particle in the present text to be taken universally, or indeed particularly? We here urge the theological rule: The literal sense always holds, when it does not clash with any article of faith, or with more manifest texts, nor produces any absurdities. Since, therefore, the present passage taken universally draws with it none of the stated inconveniences, for that reason we deservedly rest in the literal sense.

But the Calvinists object three things, on account of which they judge it impossible that it be understood according to the letter. 1. Because the particle 'all' often denotes kinds of individuals, not individuals of kinds, as Jer. 31 v. 34, Matt. 8 v. 26, c. 9 v. 36, Luke 6 v. 26, c. 11 v. 42, c. 21 v. 17, 1 Cor. 12 v. 6, Eph. 2 v. 3.

2. Because not all are saved: but whatever He has willed, He has done, Psalm 113 v. 3. 3. Because Paul speaks there of the various states and conditions of men.

Response to 1. That there is no consequence: Sometimes the particle 'all' is to be restricted. Therefore, also in this place. Furthermore, in the cited texts, the little word 'all' does not denote precisely the kinds of individuals, but is taken only synecdochically in the manner of Scripture for some, so that by synecdoche the whole is put for the part.

To 2. They confuse absolute and conditional will. Whatever God has absolutely willed to happen, happens, but those things which He wills conditionally do not always happen.

To 3. That it is against the text itself. For the Apostle speaks of all men in general, yet especially of the magistracy, because it can profit or harm the Church the most. Therefore our reason persists: Why is the particle (all) to be taken universally? Namely, because the literal sense does not clash with an article of faith, nor with other texts more manifest in the analogy of faith.

Now we shall add other reasons by which the universality of divine love can be demonstrated from the present passage.

1. God wills those to be saved for whom He commands prayer to be made: But He commands prayer to be made for all through the Apostle Paul v. 1. 'I exhort, therefore, that first of all, supplications, prayers, etc., be made for all men.' This very thing is also admitted by Calvin and Bullinger, whose words see in the one citing them, Schaff, lib. 1, de praedest. c. 2.

2. Those whom God wills to come to the knowledge of the truth, He also wills to be saved: for by the copulative particle these two cohere, to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. But He wills all to come to the knowledge of the truth. Because it is said even to the impenitent, and thus to all, 'Believe the Gospel.' Nor is there any reason why the Calvinists should resort here to the will of the sign: for it was proved above that it is nothing. 2. Because those heathen Kings and Princes, for whom Paul commands that prayers be made, and whom God wills to be saved, undoubtedly died in unbelief: for it is nowhere read that they were converted. 3. If the Apostle understood only kinds of individuals, he would not say in v. 2: Pray for Kings, and all who are set in high places: but according to the Calvinists he ought to have said, for only some placed in that order, because God does not will all: but only some from that order to be saved. 4. The Apostle renders reasons why one must pray for all men and why God wills all men to be saved, v. 5, 6, and 7: because 1. He is equally the God of all. 2. There is one Mediator of God and men. 3. Christ died for all, and 4. because he himself is an Apostle sent to preach to all. Since, therefore, these reasons concern all men, and not merely the kinds, but the individual persons, we rightly conclude from this that the preceding words, God wills all to be saved, must be taken universally of all and individual men.

V. 3. From 2 Pet. 3:9. The Lord does not delay his promise, as some think, but is patient toward us, while he does not wish any to perish, but all to return to repentance. Here, the coherence must be noted above all: God wishes that NONE should perish, but that ALL should return to repentance. For from this it clearly appears that the universal is not to be restricted, since not even one is excepted. The Calvinists, however, seek a defense in these words, God is patient toward us. They think, therefore, that only the reborn are meant, to whom that epistle was inscribed. But it can easily be proven that by the particle (us) the unbelieving and impenitent are denoted πρώτως & primarily. For although Paul seems to include himself, he does so in the manner of preachers through a certain συνκατάβασιν. For it is customary for the Apostles, themselves selves of the same crimes as the Gentiles; nay, to join them to the Gentiles, so that by this prudent submission they might both rebuke them more confidently and refute them more fruitfully, when nevertheless in reality they were most alien from those crimes. The reason, however, for our statement is this: The Apostle Peter is occupied there in the refutation of certain scoffers and impious men who are to be in the last times, and who will deny the final judgment. He proposes their objection in v. 4: Where is the promise or his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue thus from the beginning of the creation. He answers them in v. 9: God does not delay his promise, as some think: But he adds the reason why God defers his coming: Because he acts patiently for our sake, while he does not wish that any should perish; but that all should return to repentance, that is, God defers the coming to judgment for this reason, because he is mild and benevolent toward us men, and waits to see whether at long last they might wish to desist from malice, to believe in Christ, and to walk in newness of life. Now if he were speaking primarily of the faithful and the reborn, this reason would expire. For as for those who are already reborn and penitent, for their sake the delay of the final judgment is not necessary. Wherefore we argue from this as follows: He speaks of those for whose sake God is patient and defers his coming. But he is not patient for the sake of the reborn and the faithful, which is evident in the φαινομένω from Rom. 2. v. 4: Do you despise the riches of his goodness, and patience, and longsuffering, not knowing that the kindness of God invites you to repentance? But those who have already performed repentance, as the reborn and the faithful, these are not primarily invited to repentance through longsuffering. Therefore the Apostle is not speaking of the pious, but of the impious and the impenitent.

Finally, that we may answer to the oὐσίαν, even to the Calvinists, that Peter in the cited passage speaks only of those to whom he wrote this epistle; yet they will not thence prove that God wishes no one to be saved, unless who is actually saved. For in the first epistle, chapter 1, we read that Peter wrote his epistles to all in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia. However, in the visible Church there are always some putrid members, and in the field of the Lord the tares always grow together. It is not, therefore, probable that all living in those most extensive churches were saved. For if this were so, the field of the Lord would not have had tares mixed in, nor would a distinction remain between the visible and invisible Church. Since, therefore, without doubt, according to the parable in Luke 7, many have perished, and yet the Apostle affirms universally that God wills that not one should perish, it is undoubtedly concluded from this that many are damned whom God seriously willed to be saved and to arrive at the knowledge of the truth.

VI. 4. From Rom. 11, v. 32. God has concluded all under sin, that he might have mercy upon all. Where it is to be noted that God is said to conclude all under sin, not as if he forces men to sin, but because by his judicial sentence he declares men to be subject to sin. Thus Scripture is said in Gal. 3, v. 22, to conclude all under sin, because by the voice of the law it makes men guilty of sin. By equal reasoning, God is pronounced to conclude all men under unbelief by the voice of his word, not as the cause of unbelief, but as its judge. From this text, however, we draw this argument for the universality of the divine will: Those whom God has concluded under unbelief, he wills to have mercy on them all. But he has concluded all men whatsoever under unbelief. For all have turned aside. Rom. 3, v. 12. Therefore he wills to have mercy on all. But if this passage is explained particularly, this absurdity will follow, that only the elect are concluded under sin, since these things cohere: to conclude under sin, and to have mercy on those concluded.

Beza objects in part 2 of his Response to the Acts, page 223, that in the Greek there is the word ἀπειθείας, of contumacy, which includes preaching, which is resisted. Now, however, the Gospel is not announced to all; therefore not all are concluded under contumacy, but those to whom it is announced. For that ἀπείθειαν is the term from which men are called to faith.

Resp. If this ἀπείθεια is the term from which conversion begins, it follows that all whom God would have mercy upon must have contumaciously resisted the announced word, which is against Paul, Acts 13:46. It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you, but since you reject it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles. v. 48. And the Gentiles hearing this were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord. Did those Gentiles therefore resist the announced word? Or because they did not resist, did God not have mercy on them? Moreover, by ἀπείθειαν is understood ἁμαρτία and all disobedience against the law. For even those are called children of ἀπειθείας to whom the light of evangelical truth has never shone. Eph. 2:2 and 5:6. Col. 3:6. Indeed, the Apostle himself in Rom. 3:9 and Gal. 3:22 explains this ἀπείθειαν by ἁμαρτίαν.

Latin:

IV. 2. Ex 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire. huius variæ sunt interpretationes. Augustinus in Enchirid. c. 103. sic explicat: Ita intelligere debemus, quod scriptum est, Qui vult omnes homines saluos fieri, tanquam diceretur, nullum hominem fieri saluum, nisi quem saluum fieri ipse voluerit: non quod nullus sit hominum, nisi quem saluum fieri velis, sed quod nullus fiat, nisi quem velit, & ideò sit rogandus, vt velit, quia necesse est fieri, si voluerit. De orando quippe Deo agebat Apostolus, vt hoc diceret. Sic enim intelliximus id, quod in Euangelio scriptum est: Qui illuminat omnem hominem, non quia nullus est hominum, qui non illuminetur, sed quia nisi ab ipso nullus illuminatur. Aut certe sic dictum est; qui omnes homines vult saluos fieri; non quòd nullus hominum esset, quem saluum fieri nollet, qui virtutes miraculorum facere noluit apud eos, quos dicit acturos fuisse pænitentiam, si fecisset; sed vt omnes homines, omne genus humanum intelligamus, per quascunque differentias distributum, &c. Hæc autem interpretatio Augustini ex eo profluxit, quòd ipse censuit, loqui Apostolum de absoluta Dei voluntate cum efficacia coniuncta:ita quidem, vt si Deus omnes vellet saluari statim etiam saluarentur. Ita enim in fine eius capitis inquit: Et quocunque alio modo intelligi potest, dum tamen credere non cogamur, Deum omnipotentem aliquid voluisse fieri, factumque non esse, qui fine vllis ambiguitatibus sit in cælo & in terra, sicut & veritas cantat: Omnia, quæcunque voluit, fecit. Profectò facere noluit, quodcunque non fecit. Hæc ibi. Ex quibus patet, Augustinum præsentem locum de voluntate simplici & semper efficaci intellexisse, ac propterea interpretationes istas attulisse. Cùm verò multa fiant, quæ tamen Deus fieri non vult, & multa velit Deus, quæ non fiant, ob id merito, quæstione 2. distinximus inter voluntatem efficacem & inefficacem, simplicem & conditionatam. Licèt igitur præsens locus de efficaci voluntate Dei intelligi nequeat, (quò respexit Augustinus) optimè tamẽ de conditionata exponi potest. Nihil enim hoc pacto decedit omnipotentiae diuinae, siquidem omnes seriò vult saluos, sed conditionatè, si media salutis acceptent. Quod cùm multi negligant, inde non fit, quod tamen Deus vult fieri. Et haec interpretatio si teneatur, non opus erit alienas fingere. Neque hac in parte iniuriam facimus Augustino, quippe qui non renuit, hunc locum accipi qualitercunque voluerimus, modò non negetur omnipotentia Dei & eius voluntas efficax.

Porrò Sedulius tres expositiones breuissimè feecenset his verbis, Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri, si ipsi iam vocati Deo obedire voluerint: aut omnes homines, scilicet praedestinatos: siue omnes homines, hoc est, omnem sexum, gentem & conditionem.

Verùm res nobis est cum Caluinianis, qui consentiunt in eo quòd per particulam vniuersalem non intelligantur singuli generum, sed genera singulorum, ita vt sensus sit, Deus vult omnes, hoc est, ex omnibus aliquos fieri saluos. Videatur Beza in colloq. Mompelg. & Parte 2. Resp ad Acta pag. 192. Hinc ergo status quaestionis oritur: Num in praesenti textu particula vniuersalis vniuersaliter, an verò particulariter sit accipienda? Nos hic vrgemus regulam Theologicam: Semper obtinet sensus literalis, quando non impingit in aliquem fidei articulum, vel in textus manifestiores, neque aliqua parit absurda. Cùm igitur praesens locus vniuersaliter sumptus, nullum ex dictis incommodis secum trahat, ob id meritò in literali sensu acquiescimus.

Sed tria regerunt Caluiniani, propter quę fieri non posse censent, vt secundū literā intelligatur. 1. Quia particula omnis saepè notet genera singulorum, non singulos generum, vt Ierem. 31 v. 34. Matth. 8. v. 26. c. 9. v 36. Luc. 6. v. 26. c. 11. v. 42. c. 21. v. 17. 1. Cor. 12. v 6. Eph 2. v. 3.

2. Quia non omnes fiant salui: quaecunque autem voluit, fecit, Psal. 113. v. 3. 3. Quia Paulus ibi loquatur de variis hominum statibus & conditionibus.

Resp. ad 1. Nullam esse consequentiam: Quandoque particula omnis restringenda est. Ergo hac etiam in loco. Deinde in allegatis textibus vocula omnis non notat præcisè genera singulorum, sed duntaxat sinecdochicôs more Scripturæ accipitur pro aliquibus, ita vt per Synecdochen pro parte ponatur totum.

Ad. 2. Confundunt voluntatem absolutam & conditionatam. Quæcunque Deus absolutè voluit fieri, fiunt, sed non semper fiunt, quæ vult conditionatè.

Ad 3. Esse contra ipsum textum. Loquitur enim Apostolus de omnibus omninò hominibus in genere, maximè tamen de magistratu, quod is plurimum in Ecclesia prodesse vel obesse possit. Perstat igitur nostra ratio, Cur particula (omnis) vniuersaliter sit accipienda? nimirum, quòd literalis sensus nec in articulum fidei, nec in textus alios manifestiores in analogiam fidei impingat.

Nunc alias addemus rationes, quibus vniuersalitas dilectionis diuinæ ex præsenti loco demonstrari potest.

1. Eos vult Deus saluos, pro quibus orandum esse præcipit: Atqui pro omnibus orari præcipit per Apostolum Paulum v. 1. Adhortor, vt ante omnia fiaut deprecationes, obsecrationes &c. pro omnibus hominibus. Quod ipsum etiam fatetur Caluinus & Bullingerus, quorum verba vide apud citantem Schaff. l. 1. de prædest. c. 2.

2. Quos Deus vult ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire, eos etiam vult saluos fieri: per particulam enim copulatiuam cohærent hæc duo, saluos fieri & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire. Atqui vult omnes ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire. Quia impœnitentibus etiam, adeoque omnibus dicitur, Credite Euangelio. Nec est, vt hic ad voluntatem signi confugiant Caluiniani: eam enim nullam esse, supra probatum fuit. 2. Quia Reges illi & Principes Ethnici, proquibus Paulus orari mandat, quos Deus saluos fieri vult, proculdubio in incredulitate mortui sunt: nullibi enim legitur eos fuisse conuersos. 3. Si tantùm genera singulorum intelligeret Apostolus, non diceret v. 2. Orate pro Regibus, & omnibus, qui in sublimitate constituti sunt: sed debuisset secundùm Caluinianos dicere, pro aliquibus tantum in eo ordine positis, quia Deus non vult omnes: sed aliquos duntaxat ex illo ordine saluari. 4. Rationes reddit Apostolus, quare pro omnibus hominibus sit orandum & quare Deus omnes homines velit saluos fieri, v. 5. 6. & 7. quia 1. pariter omnium sit Deus. 2. vnus sit Mediator Dei & hominum. 3. Christus sit pro omnibus mortuus, & 4. quia ipse sit Apostolus missus ad prædicandum omnibus. Cùm igitur hæ rationes attineant omnes homines, & non duntaxat genera, sed singula indiuidua, rectè hinc concludimus, Verba præcedentia, Deus vult omnes fieri saluos, vniuersaliter de omnibus & singulis hominibus debere accipi.

V. 3. Ex 2. Pet 3. v. 9. Non tardat Dominus promissionem, sicut quidam existimant, sed patiens est erga nos, dum non vult vllos perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reuorti. Notanda hîc inprimis venit cohærentia: Deus vult, ne VLLVS pereat, sed vt OMNES ad pœnitentiam reuertantur. Nam ex eo luculenter apparet, vniuersalem non esse restringendam, si quidem nè vnus quidem excipitur. Caluiniani verò præsidium quærunt in his verbis, Deus patiens est erganos. Putant igitur solos renatos intelligi, quibus epistola ista sit inscripta. Sed per particulam (nos) πρώτως & primariò notari infideles & impœnitentes probare facile potest. Quamuis enim Paulus semet ipsum videatur includere, facit tamen id more concionatorű per quandam συνκατάβασιν. Nam vsitatum est Apostolis, semetipsos ijsdem cum Ethnicis criminibus insimulare; imò gentibus adiungere, vt hac prudenti submissione & confidentius illos increpare, & fructuosiùs refellere possint, cùm tamen reuera ab illis sceleribus alienissimi essent. Ratio verò nostri effati hæc est: Versatur ibi Apostolus Petrus in refutatione quorūdam scurrarum & empectarum qui futuri sint in ultimis temporibus, & negaturi extremum judicium. Obiectionem eorum proponit v. 4. Vbi est promissio aut aduentus eius? Ex quo enim patres dormierunt, omnia sic perseuerant ab initio creaturæ. His respondet. v. 9. Non tardat Deus promissionem suam, sicut quidam existimant: Addit verò rationem. cur Deus aduentum suum differat: Quia patienter agit propter nos, dum non vult, vt vllus pereat; sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reuertantur, hoc est, Ideò Deus differt aduentum ad judicium, quia mitis est & benevolus erga nos homines, & expectat, num tandem aliquando velint à malitia desistere, in Christum credere, & in nouitate vitæ ambulare. Iam si de fidelibus & renatis primò loqueretur, ratio hæc expiraret. Qui enim jam antè sunt renati & pœnitentes, propter eos nō est necessaria judicij extremi dilatio. Quare sic inde argumentamur: Propter quos Deus est patiens, & aduentum differt, de ijs loquitur. Atqui non propter renatos & fideles est patiens, quod in φαινομένω patent ex Rom. 2. v. 4. An diuitias bonitatis eius, & patientiæ, & longanimitatis contemnis, ignoras, quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te inuitat? Qui verò jam pœnitentiam egerunt, vt renati & fideles, hi non primùm per longanimitatem ad pœnitentiam invitantur. Ergo non de pijs, sed impijs & impœnitentibus loquitur Apostolus.

Tandem, vt in oὐσίαν respondeatur, demº Calvinianis, Petrum in loco allegato de ijs tantum loqui ad quos hanc epistolam scripsit; non tamen inde evincent, Deum neminem velle saluum, nisi qui actu saluatur. Nam in epistola 1. c. 1. legimus, quòd Petrus epistolas suas scripserit omnibus in Pon-to, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia & Bithynia. In visibili autem Ecclesia semper sunt aliqua membra putrida, & in agro Domini semper vnà crescunt zizania. Non ergo probabile est, omnes in amplissimis istis Ecclesiis viuentes, fuisse saluatos. Hoc enim si esset, ager Domini zizanium admixtum non habuisset, nec discrimen maneret inter Ecclesiam visibilem & inuisibilem. Cùm ergo procul dubio, iuxta parabolam Luc. 7. multi perierint, & tamen vniuersaliter adfirmet Apostolus, velle Deum, nè vnus pereat, indubitatò inde concluditur, multos damnari, quos Deus seriò voluit saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire.

VI. 4. Ex Rom 11. v. 32. Conclusit Deus omnia sub peccatum, vt omnibus misereatur. Vbi notādum, quod Deus dicatur omnia concludere sub peccatum, nõ ac si homines cogat ad peccandum, sed quoniam suâ judiciali sententia declarat homines peccato obnoxios. Sic Scriptura dicitur Gal 3. v. 22. omnia concludere sub peccatum, quia voce legis homines peccati reos agit. Pari ratione Deus non vt causa incredulitatis, sed vt eiusdem iudex, voce verbi sui omnes homines sub incredulitatem concludere pronunciatur. Ex hoc autem textu pro vniuersalitate voluntatis diuinæ rationem hāc depromimus: Quos Deus conclusit sub incredulitatem, eorum omnium vult misereri. Ast omnes omninò homines cōclusit sub incredulitatem. Omnes enim declinauerunt. Rom. 3: v. 12. Ergo omnium vult misereri. Quod si verò particulariter locus hic exponatur, absurdum hoc sequetur, tantùm electos sub peccatum esse conclusos, siquidem cohærent ista, concludere sub peccatum, & misereri conclusorum.

Excipit Beza part. 2. Resp. ad Acta pag. 223. in in græco esse vocem ἀπειθείας contumaciæ, quæ includat prædicationem, cui resistitur. Iam verò non omnibus annunciari Euangelium. Ergo non omnes sub contumaciam concludi, sed illos, quibus annunciatur. Nam ἀπείθειαν istam esse terminum, à quo homines ad fidem vocentur.

Resp. Si ἀπείθεια hæc est terminus à quo conversionis, sequitur, omnes, quorum misereretur Deus, oportuisse annunciato verbo contumaciter resistere, quod est contra Paulum Act. 13. v. 46. Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei, sed quoniam repellitis illud, ecce convertimur ad gentes. v. 48. Audientes vero gentes gavisi sunt, & glorificabant verbum Domini. Num igitur gentes istæ verbo annunciato restiterunt? Aut quia non restiterunt, num Deus eorum non est misertus? Cæterùm per ἀπείθειαν intelligitur ἁμαρτία & omnis inobedientia contra legem. Nam & ij vocantur filij ἀπειθείας, quibus lux Euangelicæ veritatis nunquam illuxit. Eph. 1. v. 2. & 5. v. 6. Col. 3. v. 6. Quin quod ipse Apostolus Rom. 3. v. 9. & Gal. 3. 22. hanc ἀπείθειαν per ἁμαρτίαν exponat.


### Question II. Sayings of Scripture: VII. 5. John 3:16 & 17. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish…

VII. 5. John 3:16 & 17. For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. For God sent not his Son into the world to judge the world; but that the world through him might be saved. Similar to this passage is that which is read in John 6:40. This is the will of the Father, that every one which seeth the Son, and believeth on him, may have everlasting life.

But the Calvinists object that by the world are not understood all men who are in the world, but only the elect from the world.

Resp. 1. It is a begging of the question: for whence will they prove this? There are two primary meanings of the word world: one, when it is taken for the impious and unbelievers, as John 17:9, I pray not for the world: the other, when it is taken for all men, believers and unbelievers. Nowhere, however, in the New Testament is the word world found used for the elect and believers alone. 2. He divides this very world in v. 18 into two classes, [he] saw of the faithful and the unfaithful, whence it appears that by the world are not understood the elect alone. 5. In the same v. 18 it is said: He who does not believe in him is already judged. Wherefore the Son of God was given also to the damned.
