For if they are damned for this reason, that they do not believe that the Son of God made satisfaction for them, then it must be that satisfaction was made for them: otherwise they would not be damned on account of unbelief: from which in turn it appears that the unfaithful are also understood by the world in the present passage. 4. To which world the Gospel is to be announced, to that world Christ was sent and given. For as widely as the Gospel extends, so widely extends the merit of Christ and the love of the Father. Otherwise the word would be mendacious, if it promised and offered more than Christ had acquired for us: But the Gospel concerning Christ is to be announced to the whole world Matt. 28. v. 19. Therefore God, by sending the Son, loved the whole world.

VIII. 6. From Matt. 11. v. 28. Come to me all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you: Hence we argue thus: Whosoever labor and are burdened, Christ wishes them to come to him, and consequently to be saved. But truly all men labor and are burdened. Therefore Christ wishes all men to come to him, and consequently to be saved. Although indeed not all come, yet Christ wishes those very ones not coming to come to him. Whence also Wisdom cries out Prov. 1. v. 24. & 25. I have called, but you refused: I have extended my hand and there was no one who would look: You have despised all my counsel. Thus Matt. 23. v. 37. Luke 13. v. 34. the Savior laments over Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often would I have gathered your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not? Luke 19. v. 41. he deplores the temporal destruction of the city of Jerusalem with profuse tears: how much more shall we believe that he himself grieved over the eternal destruction of the Jews? For tears are the ambassadors of grief, as Cyprian writes l. 2. epist.

7. Just as therefore Scripture by words, God by oaths, so Christ by tears made universal grace and love testified.

IX. 7. From 1 Thess. 5, v. 9. God has not appointed us to wrath, but to the acquisition of salvation. The Apostle, however, understands all Christians in the Church of Thessalonica, whom he addresses in ch. 1, v. 1, among whom without doubt there were many hypocrites, because the Church of Christ is never pure. Since, therefore, these are damned and yet no one is said to be appointed to wrath, it follows conversely that God does not delight in the destruction of those who perish. But that exception of Beza is frivolous: Some with whom Paul speaks are appointed to the acquisition of salvation. Therefore some are also appointed to wrath, namely those who are damned. For if God created no one for wrath, this will have been said in vain.

Resp. 1. We have just proved that, from those with whom Paul speaks, some were both thus appointed and created for salvation, and yet were damned.

2. N. C. Otherwise, one could similarly argue from ch. 1, v. 1 of the same Epistle: You were not redeemed with corruptible gold or silver. Therefore some are redeemed with corruptible gold and silver. And v. 23: You have been reborn not from mortal seed, but from immortal. Wherefore some are reborn from mortal seed. But the consequence does not hold, from the negation of one contrary to the position of the other.

X. REASONS. 1. From the end of man's creation. God created men for this end, that all might be saved. Therefore He wills all to be saved. I prove the antecedent. 1. Because in Adam we were all created to the image of God. But salvation and the divine image cohere in an individual bond. Whoever, therefore, is created to the image of God, he is created for salvation. 2. Because all were made guilty of damnation through the transgression of Adam, Rom. 5, v. 12. Wherefore all in Adam had salvation, which they lost by transgression. 3. Because no creature is for contrary ends: He, therefore, who is created so that he might be saved, is not created to fall, and vice versa. 4. Because the benevolence of God is greater than all human benevolence; Matt. 7, v. 11; Luke 11, v. 13: If you, who are evil, can give good gifts to your children, how much more the Heavenly Father? &c. 5. Because God is not the cause of sin. But He would be, if He had created anyone absolutely for destruction. For he who wills the end, also wills the means to the end.

XI. 2. From the propagation of man. God willed that those in whom the image of God was to be propagated should be saved. But it was to be propagated in all men: For God said to the πρωτοπλάσοις [first-formed] still established in the state of integrity, Gen. 1, v. 28: Increase and multiply. Since, however, like always produces like, it follows that God willed that Adam should procreate such as he himself was when he was blessed.

XII. 3. From the annexed condition, which is read in Gen. 2, v. 16: On the day that you eat of the fruit of the forbidden tree, you shall die the death. But every just condition must necessarily be possible: Therefore it was placed in Adam's power to eat and not to eat, which is itself evident from Ecclesiastes 7, v. 30, Eccles. 12, v. 16, in which places it is said that Adam was left to his own will. Therefore he was not created for the fall by an inevitable decree of God. For thus that condition would have been unjust, since it would have been impossible, nor would Adam have had free will. But if man was not created for the fall: Therefore [he was created] for life.

XIII. 4. From the universality of redemption and calling. God sent the Son to the whole world, that He might give Himself for all: at the same time He allows this word of grace to be preached everywhere, and seriously calls all to repentance, as will be proved in the following disputation. Therefore He also loves all from the heart, and wills them to be eternally saved, since these works of a beneficent will are undoubted τεκμήρια [proofs]. And thus the eternal Father makes His benevolent affection toward the whole human race attested by three principal deeds, namely 1. by creation to life, 2. by the Mission of the Son, and by universal calling.

XIV. 5. From the end of the law: The law by accident led to death. Therefore, of itself, it was given for life. Which the Apostle himself expressly confesses in Rom. 7, verse 10. But because the law was given to all, hence it follows that God willed that all should have life through the law.

XV. 6. From prayers: If God from eternity has decreed whom He wills to have mercy upon above others, certainly those prayers will be in vain by which we pray, whether for wicked Christians or for heretics or pagans, that God might have mercy on them as well. For it seems to be praying that God might change His absolute decrees, which are limited by no condition; if He were to do this, or could do it, He would not be God. Therefore, those prayers would not only be vain and useless, but even blasphemous.

XVI. 7. From the danger of despair: If God does not will the salvation of individuals, consolation cannot be instilled into anxious men, but mere despair will follow. For how will they be able to subsume, if this major premise is proposed to them: God wills to have mercy on some only, and wills that very few be saved? Can they conclude from this: Therefore He also wills to have mercy on me, and to confer salvation upon me as well? Zanchius indeed in Miscell. p. 322 prescribes this method: He who feels the effects of predestination, faith, hope, and the like, he ought to persuade himself that he is elect. But this is insufficient, because faith is often not felt, especially in temptation; where one concludes thus: I do not have faith. Therefore God did not will to give it, and therefore He has reprobated me. We, however, advise that one should think about election, both by reason of the causes and by reason of the signs. The causes are universal grace, universal merit. Therefore, no one is absolutely excluded. The signs are partly internal, 1. the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, 2. faith, 3. true invocation, 4. the pursuit of holiness: partly to the faithful, namely the cross, Rom. 8, v. 29. If anyone now doubts whether the grace of God and the merit of Christ pertains to him, we lead him to the calling and the universal promises of God. We say, therefore, that God seriously wills that he believe, and that He will give faith if he hears the word. But the Calvinists cannot console the tempted, as to have mercy on individuals. Thus, how will they recreate and raise up the tempted concerning perseverance? For they cannot flee to the sense of faith, because a certain faith is πρόσκαιρος (temporary). He will therefore doubt whether he has the true faith of the elect. We, however, send such a one to 1. the omnipotence of God, 2. His faithfulness or truth, 3. His good will. He can save us because He is omnipotent, 2 Tim. 1, v. 12; He wills it because He is good and truthful, 1 Cor. 1, v. 9; Philip. 2, v. 13. To this pertains that saying of Augustine, ext. l. Med. c. 14: I consider three things, in which my whole hope consists: The charity of adoption, the truth of the promise, the power of the restitution.

XVII. TESTIMONIES. 1. Irenaeus, l. 4, c. 76: Those who flee the eternal light of God, which contains in itself all good things, are themselves the cause that they inhabit eternal darkness. 2. Ambrose, l. 2, de Vocat. gent. c. 8: Whether we contemplate the latest ages, or the first, or the middle, it is reasonably and piously believed that God wills, and has always willed, all men to be saved. 3. Augustine, ad art. sibi falso impositos, art. 16: It is not the will of God that one should perish; but because they fail from piety, they do not fail from the work of God but from their own will. 4. Prosper, l. 2, de Vocat. gent. c. 28: It becomes manifest that God wills all men to be saved in diverse and innumerable ways, but those who come are directed by the help of God, those who do not come are retarded by their own stubbornness. 5. Primasius, super 1. Tim. 2: There is one God of all, and therefore He desires all to be saved whom He has made. 6. Bernard, Serm. 1, in Purif. Mariae. The mercy of God is placed in common: No one is devoid of it, unless he who refuses.

XIIX. We shall add, out of abundance, the confession of the adversaries themselves, who sometimes, as if forgetful of themselves, are compelled to give testimony to the truth. Thus, therefore, Bullinger on 1 Timothy ch. 2: God wills all men to be saved, He excludes no one from salvation. Hyperius, book 1, meth. p. 251: God wills all to be saved, from whom, however, because many perish, it is the merit of those perishing: because many are saved, it is the gift of the Savior. Pareus on ch. 2 to the Romans, dub. 4: God SERIOUSLY wills the conversion and salvation even of these (namely, the unconverted and reprobate), by a will of approbation, but not of effectuation.

XIX. And thus far we have produced the arguments confirming our thesis: Now the reasons of the Calvinistic party are to be discussed. But because they either beg the question with that fictitious will of sign and good pleasure, or can be easily refuted from the distinctions placed above, and most of the arguments pertain to the dispute concerning the absolute decree of Reprobation; for that reason we shall defer their λύσιν [solution] to that place, and therefore we conclude here, giving thanks to our God, who is rich in mercy, for His great love wherewith He loved us, Eph. 2, v. 4. To Him be honor and power and blessing for ever and ever, AMEN.

Latin:

VII. 5. Ioh. 3. v. 16. & 17. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut unigenitum suum Filium daret, ut omnis, qui credit in eum, non pereat, sed habeat vitam æternam. Non enim misit Deus filium suum in mundum, ut iudicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum. Cui loco consimilis est ille, qui legitur Ioh. 6. v. 39. Hæc est voluntas patris, ut omnis, qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam.

Excipiunt verò Galuiniani, per mundum non intelligi omnes homines, qui sunt in mundo, sed duntaxat electos ex mundo.

Resp. 1. esse petitionem principij: vnde enim hoc probabunt? Duæ sunt primariæ significationes vocabuli mundi, una, quando pro impijs & infidelibus sumitur, ut Ioh. 17. 9. non oro pro mundo: altera, quando pro omnibus hominibus fidelibus & infidelibus accipitur, Nuspiam verò in Nou. Test. vocabulum mundi pro electis & solis fidelibus usurpatum reperitur. 2. Hunc ipsum mundum v. 18. in duas classes dividit, vidit fidelium & infidelium, vnde apparet per mundum non intelligi solos electos. 5. Eodem v. 18. dicitur : Qui non credit in eum, iam iudicatus est. Quare damnatis quoque datus est Dei Filius. Si enim ideo damnantur, quia non credunt, quod Filius Dei pro ijs satisfecerit, vtique pro illis satisfactum sit oportet: alias propter incredulitatem non damnarentur: ex quo vicissim paret, infideles etiam per mundum in præsenti loco intelligi. 4. Cui mundo annunciandum est Euangelium, illi Christus missus & datus est. Quam late enim patet Euangelium, tam late patet Christi meritum & dilectio Patris. Alioqui mendax foret verbum, si promitteret & offerret plura, quam Christus nobis acquisiuisset: Atqui Euangelium de Christo annunciandum est toti mundo Matt. 28. v. 29. Ergo Deus Filium mittendo vniuersum mundum dilexit.

VIII. 6. Ex Matth. 11. v. 28. Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, ego reficiam vos: Hinc sic argumentamur: Quicunque laborant & onerati sunt, eos vult Christus ad se venire, & per consequens saluari. At vero omnes homines laborant & onerati sunt. Ergo Christus omnes homines vult ad se venire, & per consequens saluari. Licet vero non omnes veniant, eos ipsos tamen non venientes ad se venire vult Christus. Vnde & Sapientia clamat Prov. 1. v. 24. & 25. Vocaui, sed renuistis: extendi manum meam & non erat, qui aspiceret: Despexistis omne consilium meum. Sic Matth. 23. v. 37. Luc. 13. v. 34. conqueritur Saluator Ierusalem, Ierusalem, quoties volui congregare filios tuos, quemadmodum Gallina congregat pullos suos sub alas, & noluisti? Luc. 19. v. 41. temporale exitium vrbis Ierosolymæ profusis lacrymis deplorat: quanto magis ipsum doluisse credemus super æterno exitio Iudæorum? Lacrymæ enim sunt legati doloris, vti scribit Cyprianus l. 2. epist.

7. Siç ergo vt Scriptura dictis, Deus iuramentis, ita Christus lacrymis vniuersalem gratiam & dilectionem testatam fecit.

IX. 7. Ex 1. Thess. 5. v. 9. Deus non constituit nos ad iram, sed ad salutis acquisitionem. Intelligit autem Apostolus omnes Christianos in Ecclesia Thessalonicensi, quos alloquitur c. 1. v. 1. inter quos procul dubio multi fuerunt hyprocitae, quia Ecclesia Christi nunquam est pura. Cùm ergo hi damnentur & tamen nullus ad iram constitutus dicatur, vicissim sequitur, Deum exitio pereuntium non delectari. Friuola verò est ista Bezae exceptio: Aliqui cum quibus Paulus loquitur, ad salutis acquisitionem sunt constituti. Ergo aliqui etiam sunt constituti ad iram, nempe qui damnantur. Nam si nullos Deus ad iram condidit, frustrà hoc dictum erit.

Resp. 1. Modò probauimus, ex ijs, cum quibus loquitur Paulus, aliquos & sic ad salutem constitutos & creatos, fuisse damnatos.

2, N. C. Aliàs similiter ex c. 1. v. 1. eiusdem Epistolae argumentari quis posset: Non corruptibili auro vel argento redempti estis. Ergo aliqui sunt redempti corruptibili auro & argento. Et v. 23. Renati estis non ex semine mortali, sed ex immortali. Quare aliqui sunt renati ex semine mortali. Verum non valet consequentia, à negatione vnius contrarij ad positionem alterius,

X. RATIONES. 1. A fine conditi hominis. Deus hoc fine condidit homines, vt omnes saluarentur. Ergò vult omnes saluari. Antecedens probo. 1. Quia in Adamo omnes conditi sumus ad imaginem Dei Salus autem & imago diuina indiuiduo nexu cohærent. Quicunque igitur conditus est ad Dei imaginem, is conditus est ad salutem. 2. Quia omnes rei facti sunt damnationis per Adami transgressionem Rom. 5. vers. 12. Quare omnes in Adamo habuerunt salutem, quam transgressione perdiderunt. 3. Quia nullares creatura ad contrarios fines: Qui ergo conditus est, vt saluaretur, is non est conditus, vt laberetur, & contrà. 4. Quia benevolentia Dei maior est omni benevolentiá humana; Matth. 7. v. 11. Luc. 11. v. 13. Si vos qui mali estis, potestis pueris vestris bona dare, quantò magis Pater Cœlestis? &c. 5. Quia Deus non est causa peccati. Foret autem, si quenquam absolutè ad interitum creasset. Nam qui vult finem, vult etiam media ad finem.

XI. 2. A propagatione hominis. In quos propaganda erat imago Dei, eos voluit Deus saluari. Atqui in omnes homines erat propaganda: Dixit enim Deus adhuc in statu integro constitutis πρωτοπλάσοις Gen. 1. v. 28 Crescite & multiplicamini. Cùm autem simile semper producat simile, sequitur, Deũ voluisse, vt Adamus tales procrearet, qualis ipse erat, cùm benediceretur.

XII. 3. Ab annexa conditione, quæ legitur Gen. 2. v. 16. Quo die de fructu vetitæ arboris comederis, morte morieris. Omnis autem conditio justa, necesse est, vt sit possibilis: Fuit igitur in Adami potestate positum, comedere & non comedere, quod ipsum patet ex Ecclsiastæ, 7. v. 30. Eccles. 12. v. 16 in quibus locis dicitur, quòd Adąm suæ voluntati fuerit relictus. Ergò non ineuitabili decreto Dei ad lapsum conditus est. Sic enim conditio ista fuisset iniusta, quoniam impossibilis, nec habuisset Adam liberum arbitrium. Si verò ad lapsum non est conditus homo: Ergò ad vitam.

XIII. 4. Ab vniuersalitate redemtionis & vocationis. Deus misit Filium toti mundo, vt daret semetipsum pro omnibus: simul & hoc gratiæ verbum vbique prædicari sinit, omnesque seriò ad pœnitentiam vocat, vti disp. sequente probabitur. Ergò & omnes ex animo diligit, æternumque saluos vult, quoniam opera ista beneficæ voluntatis indubitata sunt τεκμήρια. Atque sic æternus Pater tribus potissimùm factis beneuolam affectionem suam erga totum genus humanum testatam facit, nempe 1. creatione ad vitam, 2. Missione Filij, & vocatione vniuersali.

XIV. 5. A fine legis: Lex per accidens cessit ad mortem. Per se igitur data fuit ad vitam. Quod ipsum expresse fatetur Apostolus Rom. 7. vers. 10. Quia vero lex omnibus data est, hinc sequitur, quod Deus voluerit, vt per legem omnes haberent vitam.

XV. 6. A precibus: Si Deus ab æterno decreuit, quorum præ aliis misereri velit, certe frustraneæ erunt preces, quibus vel pro Christianis improbis vel pro hæreticis aut paganis oramus, vt Deus eorum quoque misereatur. Videtur enim precari, vt Deus decreta sua absoluta, & nulla conditione limitata mutet; quod si faceret, vel facere posset, Deus non esset. Non igitur solum frustraneæ & inutiles, verum etiam blasphemæ forent preces istæ.

XVI. 7. A periculo desperationis: Si Deus singulorum salutem non vult, non potest anxiis hominibus instillari consolatio, sed sequetur mera desperatio. Quomodo enim poterunt subsumere; sillis hæc proponatur maior: Deus aliquorum duntaxat vult misereri, & paucissimos vult saluari? Num hinc poterunt concludere; Ergo mei etiam vult misereri, & mihi quoque salutem conferre? Zanchius quidem in Miscell. p. 322. hunc præscribit modum: Qui sentit prædestinationis effecta, fidem, spem & similia is debet sibi persuadere, se esse electum. Sed insufficiens hoc est, quia sæpe fides non sentitur, præsertim in tentatione; vbi quis ita colligit: Fidem non habeo. Ergo Deus dare noluit, ideoque me reprobauit. Nos autem monemus, de electione cogitandum esse, tum ratione causarum, tum ratione signorum. Causa sunt vniuersalis gratia, vniuersale meritum. Nemo igitur absolute excluditur. Signa sunt partim interna, 1. inhabitatio Spiritus sancti, 2. fides, 3. vera inuocatio, 4. studium sanctitatis: partim fidelibus nempe crux Rom. 8. v. 29. Si quis iam dubitet, an gratia Dei & meritum Christi ad se pertineat? illum deducimus ad vocationem & promissiones Dei vniuersales. Dicimus ergo, Deum serio velle, vt credat, & fidem daturum esse, si verbum audiat. Caluiniani vero tentatum solari nequeunt, quam diu statuunt, Deum nolle singulorum misereri. Sic tentatum de perseuerantia quo modo recreabunt & erigent? Ad fidei enim sensum confugere non possunt, quia quædam fides est πρόσκαιρος. Dubitabit ergo ille, an veram electorum habeat fidem? Nos autem talem ablegamus ad 1. Dei omnipotentiam, 2. fidelitatem vel veritatem, 3. bonam voluntatem. Potest nos seruare, quia omnipotens, 2. Tim. 1. v. 12. vult, quia bonus est & verax, 1. Cor. 1. v. 9. Philip. 2. v. 13. Huc pertinet illud Augustini ext. l. Med. c. 14. Tria considero, in quibus spes mea tota consistit: Charitatem adoptionis, veritatem promissionis, potestatem redditionis.

XVII. TESTIMONIA. 1. Irenæus l. 4. c. 76. Æternum Dei qui fugiunt lumen, quod continet in se omnia bona, Ipsi sibi causæ sunt, vt æternas inhabitent tenebras. 2. Ambrosius l. 2. de Vocat. gent. c. 8. Siue novissima contemplemur secula, seu prima, siue media, rationabiliter & pie creditur, omnes homines saluos fieri Deum velle, semperque voluisse. 3. Augustinus ad art. sibi falso impositos art. 16. Non est voluntas Dei, vt pereat vnus; Quia vero à pietate deficiunt, non ex Dei opéra sed ex sua voluntate deficiunt. 4. Prosper. l. 2. de Vocat. gent. c. 28. Fit manifestum, quòd diuersis & innumeris modis omnes homines vult Deus saluos fieri, sed qui veriunt, Dei auxilio diriguntur, qui non veniunt suâ pertinaciâ retardantur. 5. Primasius super 1. Tim. 2. Vnus est omnium Deus, & ideò cupit omnes saluari, quos fecit. 6. Bern. Serm. 1. in Purif. Mariæ. In communi posita est Dei misericordia: Nemo illius expers est, nisi qui renuit.

XIIX. Addemus ex abundanti confessionem ipsorum adversariorum, qui nonnunquam sui velut obliti testimonium veritati dare coguntur. Sic ergo Bullingerus in 1. ad Tim. c. 2. Vult Deus omnes homines salvos fieri, neminem excludit à salute. Hyperius l. 1. meth. p 251. Deus vult omnes salvos fieri, ex quibus tamen, quod multi pereunt, pereuntium est meritum: quod multi salvantur, servantis est donum. Pareus super c. 2. ad Rom. dub. 4. Etiam horum (videlicet non conversorum & reprobatorum) conversionem & salutem Deus SERIO vult, voluntate approbationis, non autem effectionis.

XIX. Et hactenus argumenta thesin nostram confirmantia produximus: Nunc rationes anticivs Caluinisticæ foret discutiendæ. Quia vero vel principium petūt fictâ illa signi & beneplaciti voluntate, vel ex supra positis distinctionibus refutari facilè queunt, & pleraque argumenta ad disputationem de absoluto Reprobationis decreto pertinent; propterea λύσιν illorum eò differemus, adeòque hîc concludimus gratias agentes Deo nostro, qui dives est in misericordia, propter nimiam charitatem suam, quâ dilexit nos, Eph. 2. v. 4. Ipsi sit honor & virtus & benedictio in sempiterna secula, AMEN.


### Question II. Sayings of Scripture: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 15 Disputation III. On the Universal Merit of Christ, and the Calling of Men to Salvation


### Thesis

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent, Friedrich Sengebähr, of Celle in Saxony.

Πρόδιοιον. I.

We have seen the first pillar of ordered election in the preceding συζητήσει: now we shall make an approach to the remaining two, namely the universal redemption of the whole human race through Christ, and the calling through the Word. For just as we demonstrated there that God the Father seriously loves and wishes to save all and everyone, with none excepted: so here we shall show that God the Son has died for all, and God the Holy Spirit seriously calls all to repentance through the preaching of the Word.

II. For all persons of the Trinity clearly declare their benevolent will. 1. The Father loves the fallen. 2. The Son redeems those loved. 3. The Holy Spirit calls and instructs those redeemed. That the love of the Father may not be in vain, the Son is sent, that He may suffer for all: that the passion of the Son may not become useless, the Holy Spirit calls all, and reveals the means of conversion. Salvation is prepared through the love of the Father, is procured through the death of the Son, and is announced through the Word of the Spirit. Therefore, just as we have established the amplitude of divine love, so now we shall prove the universality of merit and calling.

III. That this may be done distinctly, we shall present the whole matter enclosed in these three questions. 1. Whether Christ redeemed all men by his death? 2. Whether the merit of Christ, and salvation obtained by merit, is promised and offered to all? 3. Whether and how infidels constituted outside the Church are called to repentance? We shall therefore discuss each of these briefly, first confirming our own πρῶτον σφετέραν, and refuting the other ἕτερον σφέτερον, the Calvinistic one.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Friderico Sengebähr, Cellensi Saxone.

Πρόδιοιον. I.

PRimum electionis ordinatæ fulcrum præcedente συζητήσει vidimus: nunc accessum faciemus ad reliqua duo, nempè Vniuersalem totius generis humani redemtionem per Christum, & vocationem per verbum. Nam quemadmodum ibi demõstrauimus, Deum Patrem, vniuersos & singulos nullis exceptis, seriò diligere & saluos velle: Ita hic ostendemus, Deum Filium pro omnibus esse mortuum, & Deum Spiritum sanctum per prædicationem verbi omnes seriò vocare ad pœnitentiam.

II. Omnes enim Trinitatis personæ beneuolam voluntatem suam luculenter declarant. 1. Pater lapsos diligit. 2. Filius dilectos redimit. 3. Spiritus sanctus redemtos vocat & instruit. Dilectio Patris ne sit frustranea, mittitur Filius, vt patiatur pro omnibus: Passio filij ne inutilis fiat, Spiritus sanctus omnes vocat, & media conuersionis reuelat. Salus per amorem Patris præparatur, per mortem Filij comparatur per verbum Spiritus annunciatur. Vt ergò euicimus amplitudinem diuini amoris: ita jam probabimus vniuersalitatem meriti & vocationis.

III. Quod vt fiat distinctè, rem omnem tribus his quæstionibus inclusam dabimus. 1. Num Christus omnes homines morte sua redemerit? 2. Num meritum Christi, & parta merito salus omnibus promittatur & offeratur? 3. An & quomodo infideles extra Ecclesiam constituti vocentur ad pœnitentiam? De his ergò singulis disseremus paucis, πρῶτον σφετέραν nostram confirmando, & ἕτερον σφέτερον Caluinisticam refutando.


### Question I

I. The Calvinists maintain that Christ did not die for all men, believers and infidels, but only for the elect; for thus writes Beza in Antith. Colloq. Momp. p. 421: 'Certainly the statement that Christ died for the damned has seemed intolerable to us.' In resp. part 2 to the acts, page 221: 'I say again, and I profess before the whole Church of God, that it is false, blasphemous, and impious to say that Christ, whether regarding God's counsel or regarding the effect, suffered, was crucified, died, and made satisfaction no less for the sins of the damned than for the sins of Peter, Paul, and all the Saints.' Martyr, in c. 1 ad Rom., subscribes to this, saying: 'The Scriptures do not teach that God determined to free all from calamity and to bless them through Christ: wherefore we do not say without merit that he decreed to exempt certain ones.'

II. Since the Calvinists understand that this opinion is horrible even to hear, they strive to soften it somewhat by applying the plaster of a certain distinction between sufficiency and efficiency. They say, therefore, that Christ indeed redeemed all sufficiently, but not all efficiently. Which distinction they borrowed from the Scholastics, and indeed from book 3 of the Master of the Sentences, dist. 20, letter C, where these words are found: Christ is the priest, and the same is the victim and the price of our reconciliation, who offered himself on the altar of the cross not to the Devil, but to God the Trinity for all, as far as the sufficiency of the price is concerned: but for the elect only, as far as the efficacy is concerned, because he effected salvation only for the predestined.

III. But the Scholastics use these terms in one sense, and the Calvinists in another. By the sufficiency of merit, the Scholastics understand the very act of redemption and the acquisition of salvation; but by efficacy, they understand the application of merit and the bestowal of the acquired salvation; so that the sense is that Christ indeed redeemed all men, both collectively and individually, by that very act according to the counsel of God the Father, and restored life: but because most persist in impenitence, it happens from this that not all perceive the efficacy of the merit and are saved, but only the elect. Thus, therefore, they refer the cause of the inefficacy to the incredulity of men, not to some absolute good pleasure of God. The Calvinists, however, by the sufficiency of merit, do not wish the act of redemption itself to be noted, but only the power, writing that Christ indeed could have satisfied for the sins of the whole world, but did not satisfy by the act itself, because it so pleased God the Father from eternity. Therefore, that the merit of Christ is not efficacious among all, this does not happen because they do not apprehend the passion of Christ, since it was not made for them, but because they have been rejected and reprobated by an absolute decree. Thus, therefore, they change the actual sufficiency of the Lord's death into a potential or possible one, and they only play with this distinction so that they may cast a veil over the eyes of the simpler folk. Beza ingenuously confesses this in the Geneva Theses, fol. 129, while he argues thus: In that phrase, 'Christ died for all men sufficiently, but not efficiently' (as the Scholastics speak), there seems to be an ἀκυρολογία [improper use of terms]. For whether you look at the counsel of God, or the effect of the passion, or both, for the impious in no way is he dead: Otherwise we confess that this offering is of such value that it could have sufficed for infinite worlds (if there were so many), let alone for individual men, if God had willed to have mercy on them all, and had sent His Son for all. He has similar things in part 2, Resp. p. 217, where he says: That distinction between sufficiently and efficiently is a mere evasion. That the rest of the Calvinists also confess this same thing, they will easily be driven to it by this syllogism: Christ died for those whom God willed to have mercy upon: But God did not will to have mercy upon all (which is the common opinion of the Calvinists): Therefore Christ did not die for all.

IV. But we maintain that Christ died and made satisfaction for the sins of all and singular men, but because not all apply that satisfaction to themselves by faith, therefore not all become partakers of that saving fruit which Christ merited for men by His satisfaction.

V. Theologians illustrate this with a twofold similitude, the former of which is taken from the Babylonian captivity and the liberation from it. For just as King Cyrus, by public edicts, granted to all the Jews a return to their homeland, Ezra 1, v. 3 & 4, 2 Chronicles 36, v. 22, yet many who preferred to remain in the Babylonian captivity rather than enjoy that royal kindness were not actually or efficiently liberated from their servitude, for whom nevertheless the liberation itself had been sufficiently procured and acquired by the royal decree: So Christ merited righteousness for the whole human race, but because not all embrace that merit by faith, hence they do not actually and efficiently attain that righteousness sufficiently procured by the λύτρῳ of Christ.

VI. The latter is taken from the jubilee years in the O.T. For just as all slaves could reclaim their possessions in the jubilee years, by virtue of the divine command, and that liberty was sufficiently acquired for all, Leviticus 25, v. 40, yet those who were negligent were not liberated from servitude, although they could have been liberated so also it is compared with spiritual liberation, which has been provided for all, but not accepted by all.

VII. Hence, therefore, the state of the question arises between us and the Calvinists: Whether Christ truly died and made satisfaction for the sins of all and every human being, or indeed only for those of the elect? The Calvinists hold the negative, the Orthodox the affirmative, for the establishment of which we shall bring forward: 1. Sayings. 2. Reasons. 3. Testimonies.

Latin:

I. Caluiniani statuunt, Christum non esse pro omnibus hominibus, fidelibus & infidelibus mortuum, sed tantùm pro electis; ita enim scribit Beza in Antith. Colloq. Momp. m. p. 421. Certè nobis intolerabilis vox visa est, Christum esse mortuum pro damnatis. In resp. parte 2. ad acta pag. 221. Iterum dico, & coram tota Dei Ecclesia profiteor, falsum, blasphemum, imptum esse dicere, Christum, siue quoad Dei consilium, siue quoad effectum, non minùs pro damnandorum peccatis passum, crucifixum, mortuum esse & satisfecisse, quam pro peccatis Petri, Pauli & omnium Sanctorum. Martyr. in c. 1. ad Rom. subscribit, inquiens, Deum statuisse, omnes à calamitate liberare, ac per Christum beare, Scripturæ non docent: Quare non immeritò dicimus, ipsum decreuisse, quosdam eximere.

II. Quam opinionem cùm vel auditu horrendam esse intelligant Caluiniani, nonnihil eam emollire satagunt, adhibito distinctiunculæ cuiusdam emplastro inter sufficientiam & efficientiam. Dicunt ergò, Christum omnes quidẽ redemisse sufficienter, sed non omnes efficienter. Quã distinctionem mutuati sunt à Scholasticis, & quidem ex l. 3. Magistri sent. dist. 20. lit. C. vbi hæc verba: Christus est sacerdos, idemque hostia & pretium nostræ reconciliationis qui se in ara crucis non Diabolo, sed Deo Trinitati obtulit pro omnibus, quantum ad pretij sufficientiam: sed pro electis tantùm, quantum ad efficaciam, quia prædestinatis tantùm salutem effecit.

III. Verùm terminis istis sub sensu longè alio Scholastici, & alio Caluiniani vtuntur. Scholastici per sufficientiam meriti ipsum actum redemtionis, & acquisitionem salutis; per efficientiam verò applicationem meriti, & collationem salutis acquisitæ intelligunt; vt sensus sit, Christum quidem homines vniuersos & singulos actu ipso juxta consilium Dei Patris redemisse, & vitam reparâsse: quia verò plerique in impœnitentia perseuerant, hinc fieri, vt efficaciam meriti non omnes persentiscant, & saluentur, sed tantùm electi. Sic ergò causam inefficaciæ referunt in hominum incredulitatem; non in absolutum quoddam Dei beneplacitum. Caluiniani autem per sufficientiam meriti non ipsum redemtionis actum, sed potentiam tantùm notatam volunt, scribentes Christum quidem potuisse satisfacere pro peccatis totius mundi, sed non satisfecisse ipso actu, quia Deo Patri ab æterno ita placuerit. Quòd igitur Christi meritum non est efficax apud omnes, hoc non fieri, quia passionem Christi non apprehendant, cùm pro ijs facta non sit, sed quia per absolutum decretum rejecti & reprobati sint. Ita igitur actualem mortis Dominicæ sufficientiam in potentianalem vel possibilem commutant & distinctione istâ tantùm ludunt, vt simpliciorib. glaucoma objiciant. Ingenuè hoc fatetur Beza in thesib. Gen. fol. 129. dum ita differit: In illa phrasi, Christus mortuus est pro omnibus hominibus sufficienter, sed non efficienter (vt Scholastici loquuntur) ἀκυρολογία esse videtur. Siue enim consilium Dei, siue passionis effectum, siue vtrumque spectaueris, pro impiis NVLLO MODO est mortuus: Aliàs fatemur, tanti esse hanc oblationem, ut potuerit pro infinitis mundis (si tot essent) satisfacere, nedum pro singulis hominibus, si Deus eorum omnium voluerit miseri, & pro omnibus Filium misisset. Similia habet par. 2. Resp. p. 217. vbi dicit: Distinctio illa inter sufficienter & efficienter, mera est tergiuersatio. Quod ipsum vt fateantur reliqui quoque Caluiniani, hoc Syllogismo facilè adigentur: Pro iis Christus est mortuus, quorum voluit Deus misereri: Ast non omnium voluit misereri Deus, (quæ communis est sententia Caluinianorum) Ergo Christus pro omnibus non est mortuus.

IV. Nos verò statuimus, Christum fuisse mortuum & satis fecisse pro peccatis omnium & singulorum hominum, sed quia non omnes sibi fide applicant istam satisfactionem, ideò nec omnes fieri participes salutaris istius fructus, quem Christus satisfactione suâ hominibus promeruit.

V. Illustrant hoc Theologi geminâ similitudine, quarum prior desumitur à captiuitate Babylonicâ, & liberatione ex ea. Sicut enim Rex Cyrus publicis edictis, omnibus Iudæis indulsit reuersionem in patriam, Esdr. 1. v. 3. & 4. 2 Paralip. 36. v. 22. multi tamen, qui maluerunt in Babylonica captiuitate permanere, quâ regiâ benignitate frui, actu seu efficienter ex seruitute suâ liberati non sunt, quibus nihilominus regio diplomate ipsa liberatio sufficienter parta & acquisita erat: Ita Christus toti generi humano promeruit justitiam, quia vero nõ omnes meritum illud fide amplectuntur, hinc justitiam istam λύτρῳ Christi partam sufficienter, actu & efficienter non consequuntur.

VI. Posterior petita est ab annis iubilæis in. V. T. Sicut enim omnes serui poterant repetere possessiones suas in annis jubilæis, vi mandati diuini, & omnibus illa libertas erat sufficienter acquisita Leuit. 25. v. 40. qui vero negligentes erant, illi à seruitute non liberabantur, licet liberari potuisfent : ita quoque comparatum est cum liberatione spirituali , quæ omnibus parta, sed non omnibus accepta est .

VII. Hinc ergò status quæstionis exoritur inter nos & Caluinianos , Vtrum Christus reuerâ pro omnium & singulorum hominum peccatis, an verò tantùm pro electorum mortuus fuerit & satisfecerit? Negatiuam Caluiniani, affirmatiuam Orthodoxi tenent, in cujus stabilimentum proferemus. 1. Dicta. 2. Rationes, 3. Testimonia.


### Question I: Sayings of Scripture

SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE.

VIII. Since very many testimonies for universal merit are found in the sacred code, for the sake of distinction we shall divide them into three classes or theses.

IX. FIRST: Christ died for the whole world.

Which thesis is confirmed primarily by that classic passage from 1 John 2:2: He (Christ, of course) is the propitiation for our sins, and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. Where that distribution is to be noted primarily: not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. For by it, it is implied that Christ made satisfaction not only for the elect, but also for all others. For John wrote his Epistle to all believers, as is evident from chapter 5, verse 13: These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God. With these, therefore, he speaks when he says: Christ did not die only for our sins, that is, those of us who believe in the name of Christ, but truly also for the sins of the whole world. From which it appears how futile the Calvinistic objection is, when 1. they say that by 'world' only the elect and believers are understood. For it would be a ταυτολογία [tautology]: Christ died not only for the sins of believers, but also for the sins of non-believers. 2. When they say, in the former member, only believing Jews, in the latter, believing Gentiles. to be noted. For in the first member are understood those to whom the Apostle wrote his Epistle. But these are all who believe in the name of Christ, from ch. 5, v. 13. Whence the sense of the statement emerges as follows: Christ is the propitiation not only for the sins of the believers, and thus of all and singular men, even if they do not believe in the very act. For by the world John generally understands the assembly of the impious, as is evident from ch. 2, v. 15 & 16, ch. 3, v. 1, ch. 4, v. 5. Nor is there reason for Beza to take refuge in v. 7 of the same second chapter. For even if we grant that that verse pertains rather to the Jews and not to the Gentiles, can it truly be inferred immediately from that, that the whole epistle pertains only to the Jews? By no means: But because it is inscribed to both Jews and Gentiles, therefore it ought not to seem strange that some things pertain peculiarly to the Jews, and some things truly to the converted Gentiles. Thus Paul, ch. 3, v. 23, writing to the Galatians, says: Before faith came, we were kept under the law. But shall we conclude from that, that this epistle was written by Paul not to the Gentile Galatians, but to the Jews, to whom the law had been given? Wherefore let this Theological Canon be noted here: In the Pauline Epistles there are many things that pertain to the Jews, and many that pertain to the Gentiles, nor can it be inferred from those things which are said to the Jews that those epistles were not written to the Gentiles, and vice versa. Finally, ex abundanti, if it is even granted that by the little word (ours) the Jews are understood, yet it would still firmly follow that under the word world all Gentiles opposed to the Jews are noted, among whom there were many wicked and damnable, for whom, according to the Apostolic utterance, Christ no less died than for the Jews.

X. Furthermore, there are also other statements confirming the same thesis, as John 1, v. 29: Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world. John 3, ver. 16, 17: God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son. John 4, v. 42: We ourselves have heard and know that this is truly the Savior of the world, that is, not a particular, but a Catholic and universal. John 6, v. 51. The bread, which I will give you, is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world. John 12, v. 47. I came not to judge the world, but to save the world. 2 Corinthians 5, v. 19. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. 1 John 4, v. 14. We have seen and testify that the Father sent the Son as the Savior of the world. All these sayings are so clear that the Calvinists find nothing to oppose, except that old σοφισμον [sophism]; that by 'world' only the elect are denoted, not all men; from which defense, so that they may be cast down, we shall add a few things concerning the meaning of 'world'.

XI. 'World' has various meanings in the Scriptures. For it is taken 1. for the system of heaven and earth. 2. for the present age. 3. for the worldly condition and conversation, as 1 Corinthians 7, v. 33. 4. for men, and those 1. either all. 2. or all the called. 3. or only the reprobate. The Calvinists add, as we have said, a fourth meaning, which denotes only the elect, and thus they explain all the sayings in which God is said to have loved the world, and Christ is said to have died for the world. We, however, utterly deny that the word 'world' is ever taken in this sense, and we demand from our adversaries indubitable examples of this new acceptance, such as they have hitherto been unable to produce.

XII. They urge 1. the saying in Matthew 5, v. 14: 'You are the light of the world'; but here all men are understood to whom the Apostles were sent, and not only the elect.

2. Matthew 13, v. 38: 'The field is the world.' But not only the elect are understood, but also the reprobate, since only the fourth part of that field brings forth the due fruits.

3. John 6, v. 33: 'The true bread of God is that which descends from heaven and gives life to the world,' that is, to the elect. But 'world' here also signifies all men, as is evident from v. 51, and therefore by 'giving life' is understood not the actual bestowal of life, but only its acquisition, in which sense also Christ is said to illuminate every man, John 1. verse 9. 4. John 17. v. 21. That the world may believe, that thou hast sent me. But neither here is there any discourse about the elect alone, since God wills all to believe, and to come to the knowledge of the truth. 5. 1. Timothy 3 v. 6. Christ was believed in the world, that is, received by the elect alone. But it is not said that Christ was believed by the world, because the world did not know him, John 1. v. 10. but that ἐν κόσμῳ ἐπιστεύθη, that is, that he was received by the faithful living in the world, not otherwise than it is said in the preceding, that he was preached among the nations or among the Gentiles, although he was not apprehended by all Gentiles with true faith. Since therefore the Calvinistic exposition of the world concerning the elect alone can be demonstrated by no example, we conclude from this that it is fictitious and detracts nothing from the universal death of Christ.

Latin:

DICTA SCRIPTVRÆ.

IIX Cùm in sacro codice benè multa reperiantur pro vniuersali merito testimonia, distinctionis ergò in tres siue classes siue theses ea dispescemus.

IX. PRIMA: Christus pro toto mundo est mortuus.

Quam thesin inprimis confirmat locus ille classicus ex 1. Ioh. 2. v. 2. Ipse (Christus nimirum) est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, non pro nostris autem tantum sed etiam pro totius mundi. Vbi notanda inprimis venit illa distributio, non pro nostris tantùm , sed etiam pro totius mundi peccatis. Per eam enim innuitur, Christum non pro electis modò, sed pro alijs quoque omnibus satisfecisse. Nam Iohannes Epistolam suam scripsit ad cunctos credentes, sicuti patet ex c. 5. v. 13. Hæc scripsi vobis, qui creditis in nomine Filij Dei. Cum his ergò loquitur, quando ait; Christus non est mortuus pro peccatis tantùm nostris, hoc est qui credimus in nomen Christi , verum etiam pro peccatis totius mundi. Ex quo apparet, quàm futilis sit instantia Caluinistica, cùm 1. dicunt, per mundũ intelligi solos electos & credulos. Foret enim ταυτολογία Christus mortuus est:non tantum pro peccatis credentium, sed etiam pro peccatis non credentium. 2. Quando inquiunt , in priori membro, solos credulos Iudæos, in posteriori credulos gẽtiles notari. Nam in membro primo intelliguntur illi, quibus suam Epistolam scripsit Apostolus. Ast hi sunt omnes, qui credunt in nomen Christi ex. c. 5. v. 13. Vnde sensus dicti talis emergit: Christus est propitiatio non tantùm pro peccatis fidelium, adeoque omnium & singulorum hominum, licet actu ipso non credant. Per mundum enim Iohannes plerumque intelligit cœtum impiorum, vt patet ex c. 2. v. 15. & 16. c. 3. v. 1. c. 4. v. 5. Nec est, vt Beza confugiat ad v. 7. eiusdem capitis secundi. Etenim vt concedamus, versiculum illum attinere Iudæos potiùs & non gentiles, an verò statim inde potest colligi, quòd tota epistola solos attineat Iudæos? Neutiquam: Sed quia tùm Iudæis, tum gentilibus inscripta est, ideo mirum videri non debet, quædam peculiariter Iudæos, quædam vero conuersos Ethnicos spectare. Sic Paulus c. 3. v. 23. scribens ad Galatas inquit: Priusquam venisset fides, sub lege custodiebamur. Num verò inde concludemus, epistolam hanc non ad gentiles Galatas, sed Iudæos, quibus data erat lex, à Paulo fuisse scriptam? Quare notetur hic Canon Theologicus: In Paulinis Epistolis multa sunt, quæ Iudæos, & multa, quæ gentiles attinent, neque ab iis, quæ dicuntur Iudæis, potest colligi, quo ista epistola non sint scriptæ ad gentiles, & contrà. Tandem ex abundanti, si maximè ponatur, per voculam (nostris) intelligi Iudæos, tamen adhuc firmiter sequeretur, sub voce mundi gentes omnes Iudæis oppositas notari, quas inter multi fuerunt improbi & damnandi, pro quibus, juxta effatum Apostolicum, Christus non minùs est mortuus, quàm pro Iudæis.

X. Porrò sunt & alia dicta eandem thesin confirmantia, vt Ioh. 1. v. 29. Ecce agnus Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi. Ioh. 3. ver. 16. 17. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum vnigenitum daret. Ioh. 4. v. 23. Ipsi nos audiuimus & scimus, quòd hic est verè Seruator mundi, hoc est, non particularis, sed Catholicus & vniuersalis. Johan 6. v. 51. Panis, quem ego dabo vobis, caro mea est, quam dabo pro vita mundi. Ioh. 12. v. 47 Non veni, vt iudicem mundum, sed vt saluificem mundum, 2. Corinth. 5. vers. 19. Deus erat in Christo mundum reconcilians sibi. 1. Iohan. 4. vers. 14. Nos vidimus & testamur, quod Pater misit Filium Seruatorem mundi. Quæ dicta omnia tàm sunt perspicua, vt nihil inueniant Caluiniani, quod opponant, nisi veterẽ istum σοφισμον; per mundum notari tantùm electos, non vniuersos homines; à quo præsidio lo'vt dejiciantur, pauca de significatione mundi adiiciemus.

XI. Mundus in Scripturis varia habet significata. Sumitur enim 1. pro systemate cœli & terræ. 2. pro præsente seculo, 3. pro mundana conditione & conuersatione vt 1. Corinth. 7. v. 33. 4, pro hominibus ijsque 1. vel vniuersis. 2. vel omnibus vocatis. 3. vel duntaxat reprobis. Addunt Caluiniani, vt diximus, significatum quartum, quod solos electos denotet, atque ita exponunt omnia dicta, quibus Deus dilexisse mundum, & Christus pro mũdo mortuus dicitur. Nos autem omninò imus negatum, hoc sensu vocabulum mundi vnquam accipi, & requirimus ab adversariis huius nouę acceptionis indubitata exempla, qualia hactenus nulla proferre potuerunt.

XII. Vrgent 1. dictum Matth. 5. vers. 14. Vos estis lux mundi; sed hic omnes intelliguntur homines, ad quos missi sunt Apostoli, non autem soli electi.

2. Matth. 13. vers. 38. Ager est mundus. Verùm non soli electi intelliguntur, sed vna reprobi, quoniam quarta duntaxat illius agri pars fructus affert debitos.

3. Iohan. 6. vers. 33. Panis Dei verus est, quia de cœlo descendit, & dat vitam mundo, id est, electis. Mundus autem & hîc omnes homines significat, vti patet ex v. 51. ideoque per vitam dare non actualis vitæ collatio, sed eius duntaxat acquisitio intelligitur, quo etiam sensu Christus illuminare dicitur omnem hominem, Ioh. 1. vers. 9. 4. Ioh. 17. v. 21. Vt credat mundus, quia tu me misisti. Ast neque hic de solis electis est sermo, cum Deus velit omnes credere, & ad agnitionem veritatis pervenire. 5. 1. Timoth. 3 v. 6. Christus creditus est in mundo, id est, a solis electis receptus. Sed non dicitur, Christum a mundo creditum, quia mundus eum non cognovit, Ioh. 1. v. 10. sed quod ἐν κόσμῳ ἐπιστεύθη, hoc est, a fidelibus in mundo viventibus receptus sit, non secus atque in praecedentibus dicitur, quod sit praedicatus in gentibus vel inter gentes, licet ab omnibus gentilibus vera fide non fuerit apprehensus. Cum igitur nullo exemplo Calvinistica mundi expositio de solis electis demonstrari queat, hinc eam esse commentitiam nihilque vniversali morti Christi derogare concludimus.


### Question I: XIII. Second: Christ satisfied and died for all men

XIII. SECOND: Christ satisfied and died for all men:

The following testimonies of Scripture confirm this thesis. 1. Isaiah 53. v. 6. All we like sheep have gone astray, everyone has turned to his own way, and the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. From this we infer: The iniquities of those who have gone astray like sheep have been laid upon Christ. But all and every one have gone astray. Therefore the iniquities of all and every one have been laid upon Christ. If the Calvinists say that Isaiah is speaking only of his own hearers, we will immediately ask, Were all those faithful and elect? By no means, since in v. 1. he complains: Who has believed our report?

XIV. 2. From John 1. v. 9. He was the true light, which illuminates every man, coming into this world. Here, because Beza could not extinguish the universal particle on account of the added explanation, coming into this world (for not only the elect come into the world), he therefore sought in the word illuminating an escape, thinking the discourse is not about spiritual illumination, but about the light of nature or natural notions or the faculty of reasoning. But the text protests, since John there treats of the spiritual benefits of the Messiah, namely that he is the true light, and such that everyone who believes in him has eternal life. Therefore he argues thus: Such as the light is that Christ is, such is the illumination understood here. But Christ is a spiritual light. Therefore, a spiritual illumination is also understood here. Moreover, Christ illuminates every man, as much as in him lies, by reason of intention and acquired salvation, although not all are actually illuminated on account of their own unbelief, for the world loves darkness more than light.

XV. 3 Rom. 5. v. 18. & 19. As by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation; even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. For as by one man's disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. In which place the comparison must be well noted. For if the Calvinists introduce particularity in the ἀποδόσει, they will certainly be forced to admit the same in the προτάσει, from which will follow that, that not all were infected with original sin, but only those for whom Christ died.

XVI. 4. From 2. Cor. 5. v. 14. & 15. If one died for all, then were all dead: And Christ died for all. That indeed in this place not only the faithful but all and singular men are understood, is clear 1. From v. 10. We must all appear before the judgment seat. Because therefore the universal particle here is to be taken universally, certainly also in v. 14. For those whom he says here are to be presented before the tribunal, for them in v. 14. he says Christ died. 2. From v. 19. & 20. For whom Christ died, to them the Apostle uses the word of reconciliation, and performs the embassy for Christ, that they may be reconciled to the Lord. But Paul He also used the right of the word of reconciliation among the infidels and the reprobate, as in Acts 13 v. 46, and he performs the embassy for Christ among all. Rom. 1 v. 14. 3. From chapter 6 v. 1. Some of those for whom Christ died can perish. For that reason the Apostle exhorts them, c. 6 v. 1, not to receive the grace of God in vain. But the elect cannot receive it in vain. Therefore, he did not die for the elect alone. 4. Paul speaks with the whole Corinthian Church, as is clear from v. 12, for which he says Christ died. But in such populous assemblies not all are elect. Hence 1 Cor. 11 v. 18, 21, the Apostle himself complains that there are many impious people in the Church of the Corinthians, and yet he affirms that Christ died for them.

XVII. 5. Coloss. 1 v. 20. It pleased the Father, through Christ, to reconcile all things to himself, having made peace through the blood of his cross, whether they be things on earth, or things in heaven. A similar passage is Eph. 1 v. 10, that he might gather together in one all things, which are in heaven and on earth. But it is clear that this text is not to be understood as referring only to the elect. 1. From v. 21 and 22. Whoever were enemies of God, they are reconciled. But not only the elect were enemies of God. 2. From verse 23. To whomever this Gospel of reconciliation has been announced, they are reconciled. But it was not announced to the elect alone. 3. From the same verse: Some of those who are reconciled can fall from faith. For that reason the Apostle warns them to remain stable in the faith. But the elect cannot fall from faith, according to the Calvinists. 4. From v. 28, where in express words the benefit of reconciliation is said to be announced to all. 5. He speaks with the whole Colossian Church, which he says has been reconciled to God. But in it there were not only the elect, but also many reprobate together.

XVIII. 6. From 1 Tim. 2 v. 6. Christ gave himself a redemption for all. Where in turn only the elect can be understood, but all those whom God wills to be saved. And yet He wills not merely some, but absolutely all men to be saved, v. 4.

XIX. From 1 Tim. 4:10. 'For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.' This text is especially evident, and of the same sentiment as that Johannine one, 1 Epist. 2:2. 'He is the propitiation not only for our sins, but for the sins of the whole world.' For as John there proceeds συνθετικῶς from the elect to all in general, as from species to genus, so here Paul proceeds αναλυτικῶς from all in general back to the faithful and elect, as from genus to species, just as the excellent theologian Mr. Dr. Cramer, my honorable friend, speaks skillfully concerning predestination, ch. 4, p. 101. Beza, however, objects that the discourse is only about earthly and bodily salvation, and therefore rendered it: 'Who is the preserver of all.' But this exception is a vain begging of the question. For the whole text protests against that gloss, since in the preceding verses the Apostle always treats of spiritual benefits. Therefore, in the same sense that in John 4:42 Christ is called the Saviour of the world, He is here called the Saviour of all, on account of the acquisition of salvation, but especially of the faithful, on account of both the acquisition and the application.

XX. Finally, the following sayings, which we shall only recite, prove the same thing. 1. Luke 2:10. 'Behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people.' 2. John 12:32. 'And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me.' 3. Rom. 8:32. 'God spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all.' 4. Tit. 2:11. 'The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men.' 5. Heb. 2:9. 'Christ tasted death for every man.'

XXI. THIRD: Christ died for those who are damned by their own fault.

1. From Rom. 14:15. 'Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ has died.' A similar passage exists. 1 Cor. 8 v. 11. 'And the weak brother shall perish in your knowledge, for whom Christ has died.' From which we infer: If no one can perish for whom Christ has died, this Apostolic admonition will be null. Why does he not admonish us not to destroy the weak one, is true, and consequently many can be damned, indeed are even damned, for whom and on whose account Christ has died.

XXII. 2. Hebr. 6 v. 4, 5, & 6. It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, and have tasted of the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost, and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come, if they shall fall away, to renew them again unto repentance; seeing they crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh, &c. Here two things are said: 1. That some men fall into sins, and indeed so enormously, that for them there is no return open to repentance, since they crucify Christ. 2. What such persons were previously: 1. enlightened, 2. partakers of the Holy Spirit, 3. tasted the heavenly gift, 4. the good word of God, 5. the power of the world to come. Hence we argue thus: Whoever are enlightened and made partakers of the Holy Spirit, for them Christ truly died. For how could they have faith, how could they have the illumination of the Holy Spirit, if Christ had not died for them? For application and collation always presuppose acquisition. But indeed some who are damned were at one time enlightened and made partakers of the Holy Spirit. Therefore Christ has died for some who are damned, and therefore not for the elect alone. Furthermore, the word (crucify afresh, or re-crucify) has a peculiar emphasis. For how could they re-crucify Christ, if his crucifixion had concerned them not at all? And indeed, unless the Calvinists concede that for the most wicked sinners, namely those who against the Holy Spirit sin, then they will thoroughly deny that there is a sin against the Holy Spirit. For this is defined as the voluntary and malicious denial of the truth known, and in some cases graciously sealed. Therefore, of those who sin against the Holy Spirit, some were previously faithful and believed. But for him who truly believes, Christ has certainly died, unless you posit application without acquisition. For how can anyone believe that Christ died for him, if He did not die for him?

XXIII. 3. Heb. 10. v. 26. 27. 28. 29. Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God, and hath counted the blood of the covenant, wherewith he was sanctified, an unholy thing, and hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace? Hence we argue again. Sinners against the Holy Spirit tread under foot the Son of God, and the blood of the covenant, by which they were sanctified. Sinners against the Holy Spirit are damned. Therefore, some who are damned were sanctified by the blood of the covenant.

XXIV. 4. From 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. There shall be false teachers among you, who shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them. It is clear that the Apostle Peter is speaking about the impious and truly infidels. 1. because he calls them false prophets. 2. false teachers. 3. who bring in sects. 4. who deny the Lord. 5. who bring upon themselves swift destruction. 6. by whom the way of truth shall be blasphemed, v. 2: 7. to whom judgment now of a long time lingereth not; and whose damnation slumbereth not, v. 3. 8. who, with the devils, the impious Antediluvians, and the Sodomites, are to suffer just punishments, v. 4. 5. 6. And yet the Apostle affirms that these very people were bought or redeemed by the Lord. The Calvinists except; that those false prophets only said that they were bought by the Lord, and that the Apostles thought so. But this exception contains nothing in itself except a begging of the question. See v. 20. 21: and 22. where it is clearly said that they acknowledged the way of the Lord, that they denied the Lord, that they are again entangled in sins, etc. From which it follows that they were previously truly faithful and sanctified.

XXV. We add finally two more testimonies, 1. From John 15, v. 1 & 2. I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman: Every branch in Me that beareth not fruit, he taketh away. By which saying it is clearly hinted that some can be damned who were true and genuine branches, grafted into Christ himself. 2. From 2 Pet. 1, v. 9. He to whom these things (namely the true effects of faith) are not present, is blind, and groping his way with his hand, having forgotten that he was purged from his old sins. Therefore some can forget their purgation from sins and consequently be damned, from which it shines forth again that Christ did not make satisfaction for the elect alone.

Latin:

XIII. SECVNDA: Christus pro omnibus hominibus satisfecit & mortuus est:

Confirmant hanc thesin sequentia Scripturae testimonia. 1. Esai 53. v. 6. Omnes nos quasi oves erravimus, vnusquisque in viam suam declinavit & posuit Dominus in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Hinc inferimus: Qui erraverunt sicut oves, illorum iniquitates Christo sunt impositae. Atqui omnes & singuli erraverunt. Ergo omnium & singulorum iniquitates Christo sunt impositae. Si dixerint Calviniani, Esaiam loqui de suis tantum auditoribus, mox quaeremus, Num isti omnes fuerint fideles & electi? Neutiquam, cum v. 1. conqueratur: Quis credidit auditui nostro?

XIV. 2. Ex Ioh. 1. v 9. Erat lux vera, quae illuminat omnem hominem, venientem in hunc mundum. Hic quia Beza vniversalem particulam restinguere no potuit propter additam ἐξήγησιν, venientem in hunc mundum (non enim solum electi in mundum veniunt,) ideo in vocabulo illuminandi quaesivit effugium, sermonē esse putans non de illuminatione spirituali, sed delumine naturæ vel notitijs naturalibus aut facultate ratiocinandi. Verùm textus reclamat, siquidem Iohannes ibi de spiritualibus Messiæ beneficijs agit, quod videlicet sit verum lumen, & tale, vt omnis, qui credit in ipsum habeat vitam æternam. Proinde sic argumentatur: Qualis lux est Christus, talis illuminatio hic intelligitur. At Christus lux est spiritualis. Ergò & illuminatio spiritualis hic intelligitur. Illuminat autem Christus omnem hominem, quantum quidem in se est, ratione intentionis & acquisitæ salutis, licet non omnes actu illuminentur propter ipsorum incredulitatem, Mundus enim magis diligit tenebras quàm lucem.

XV. 3 Rom. 5. v. 18. & 19. Sicut per vnius delictum in omnes homines in condemnationem, sic & per vnius iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitæ. Sicut enim per nobedientiam vnius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita & per vnius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi. Quo in loco probè annotanda venit comparatio. Quòd si enim in ἀποδόσει particularitatem introducunt Caluiniani, vtique & eandem in προτάσει admittere cogētur, ex quo sequetur illud, non omnes peccato originali fuisse infectos, sed eos tantùm, pro quibus Christus est mortuus.

XVI. 4. Ex 2. Cor. 5. v. 14. & 15. Si vnus prò omnibus mortuus est, ergo omnes mortui sunt: Et pro omnibus mortuus est Christus. Quòd verò in hoc loco non soli fideles sed omnes & singuli homines intelligantur, patet 1. Ex v. 10. Omnes nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal. Quia igitur hic particula viuersalis vniuersaliter est accipienda, vtique & in v. 14. Quos enim hic ait sistendos ante tribunal, p illis v. 14. ait Christum esse mortuum 2. Ex v. 19. & 20. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus, ad eos Apostolus verbo recōciliationis vtitur, ac legatione p Christo fungitur, vt Domino recōciliētur. At PauIus verbo reconciliationis apud infideles & reprobos etiam vsus est, vt Act. 13 v. 46. & legatione pro Christo fungitur apud omnes. Rom. 1. v. 14, 3. Ex cap. 6. v. 1. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus eorum aliqui perire possunt. Ideò enim Apostolus hortatur eos, c. 6. v. 1. ne in vacuum accipiant gratiam Dei. Ast electi in vacuum accipere non possunt. Ergò pro solis electis non est mortuus. 4. Loquitur Paulus cum tota Ecclesia Corinthiaca, vt patet ex v. 12. pro qua Christum ait mortuum. In cœtibus verò tàm populosis non omnes sunt electi. Hinc 1. Cor. 11. v. 18. 21. conqueritur ipse Apostolus, quòd multi sint in Ecclesia Corinthiorum impij, & tamen pro ijs Christum esse mortuum affirmat.

XVII. 5. Coloss. 1. v. 20. Complacitum est Patri, per Christum omnia reconciliare erga se, pacificatis per sanguinem crucis eius, siue quæ in terra sunt, siue quæ in cælis. Similis locus est Eph. 1 v. 10. vt instauraret omnia, quæ in cœlo & in terris sunt. Non autem textum istum de solis electis accipiendum esse patet. 1. Ex v. 21. & 22. Quicunque fuerunt inimici Dei, illi sunt reconciliati. Atqui non soli electi fuerunt inimici Dei. 2. Ex vers. 23. Quibuscunque Euangelium hoc de reconciliatione est annunciatum, illi sunt reconciliati. Atqui non solis electis annunciatum est 3. Ex eodem versu: Eorum aliqui qui reconciliati sunt, possunt fide excidere. Ideò enim monet eos Apostolus, vt stabiles permaneant in fide, Atqui electi fide excidere nequeunt, juxta Caluinianos. 4, Ex v. 28. vbi disertis verbis beneficium reconciliationis omnibus annunciari dicitur. 5. Loquitur cum tota Ecclesia Colossensi, quam Deo ait reconciliatam esse. Ast in ea non fuerunt tantùm electi, sed vnà multi reprobi.

XVIII. 6. Ex 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Christus dedit redemtionem semetipsum pro omnibus. Vbi vicissim non intelligi possunt soli electi, sed omnes ij, quos Deus vult saluos fieri, Atqui non aliquos duntaxat, sed homines omninò omnes vult saluos fieri, v. 4.

XIX. Ex 1. Tim. 4. v. 10. In hoc laboramus & maledicimur, quòd sperauimus in Deum viuum, qui est saluator omnium hominum, maximè fidelium, Textus hic inprimis est euidens, eiusdemque sententiæ cum illo Iohannitico, 1. epist. 2. v. 2. Est propitiationon tantùm pro nostris, sed totius mundi peccatis. Nam vt ibi Iohannes συνθετικῶς procedit ab electis ad omnes in vniuersum, tanquam à specie ad genus, ita hic Paulus αναλυτικῶς ab omnibus in vniuersum retrogreditur ad fideles & electos tanquam à genere ad speciem, quemadmodum scite loquitur excellens Theologus Dn. D. Cramerus, amicus meus honorandus de prædest. cap. 4. p. 101. Excipit verò Beza, sermonem esse tantum de salute terrena & corporali, ideòque reddidit: Qui est conseruator omnium. Sed hæc exceptio inanis est principij petitio. Totus enim textus glossæ isti reclamat, cùm in præcedentibus versiculis semper de spiritualibus beneficijs agat Apostolus. Quo igitur sensu Ioh. 4. v. 43. Christus dicitur Saluator mundi, eodem hic vocatur Saluator omnium, propter acquisitionem salutis, maximè autem fidelium, propter acquisitionem & applicationem simul.

XX. Tandem idipsum comprobant & sequentia dicta, quæ solùm recitabimus. 1. Luc. 2. v. 10. Ecce annuncio vobis gaudium magnum, quod futurum est omni populo. 2. Ioh. 12. v. 32. Ego si exaltatus fuero à terra, omnes traham ad me ipsum. 3. Rom. 8. v. 32. Deus non pepercit proprio filio, sed tradidit ipsum in mortem pro omnibus. 4. Tit. 2. vers. 10. Gratia Dei saluifera apparuit omnibus hominibus. 5. Heb. 2. v. 9. Christus pro omnibus gustauit mortem.

XXI. TERTIA: Christus mortuus est pro his qui suâ culpâ damnantur.

1. Ex Rom. 14. v. 16. Noli cibo tuo illum perdere, pro quo Christus est mortuus. Similis locus extat. 1. Cor. 8. v. 11. Et peribit infirmus in tua scientia frater, propter quem Christus mortuus est. Ex quo inferimus: Si nemo potest perire, pro quo Christus est mortuus, admonitio haec Apostolica nulla erit. Cur non admoneret, ne perdamus infirmum, qui tamen perdi inquit? Consequens absurdum. Antecedens ergo verum & proinde damnari possunt, imo & damnantur multi, pro quibus & propter quos Christus est mortuus.

XXII. 2. Hebr. 6. v. 4. 5. & 6. Impossibile est eos, qui semel sunt illuminati, gustauerunt etiam donum caeleste, & participes facti sunt spiritus sancti, & gustauerunt bonum Dei verbum, virtutesque seculi venturi & prolapsi sunt, rursus renouari ad poenitentiam, rursum crucifigentes sibimetipsis Filium Dei, &c. Hic duo dicuntur 1. Quod aliqui homines prolabantur in peccata & quidem tam enormiter, vt ipsis non pateat reditus ad poenitentiam, quoniam crucifigunt Christum. 2. Quo tales prius fuerint 1. illuminati. 2. participes Spiritus sancti 3. gustauerint donum caeleste 4. bonum Dei verbum 5. virtute venturi seculi. Hinc ita argumentamur: Quicunque sunt illuminati & participes facti Spiritus sancti, pro ijs vere mortuus est Christus. Quomodo enim tidem, quomodo illuminationem Spiritus sancti habere possent, si Christus pro ijs non esset mortuus? Nam applicatio & collatio semper praesupponit acquisitionem. At vero nonnulli qui damnantur, fuerunt aliquando illuminati & participes facti Spiritus sancti. Ergo pro nonnullis, qui damnantur, ideoque non pro solis electis Christus est mortuus. Peculiarem insuper emphasin habet verbum (ab integro crucifigunt, vel recrucigunt,) Quomodo enim recrucifigere possent Christum, si crucifixio huius nihil eos attinuisset? Et sane nisi Caluiniani concesserint, pro scelestifsimis peccatoribus, ijs nempe, qui in Spiritum sanctum peccant, Christum fuisse mortuum, tum penitus negabunt, dari peccatum in Spiritum sanctum. Hoc enim definitur voluntaria & malitiosa veritatis cognitæ, & in nonnullis gratiosè obsignatæ abnegatio. Qui ergò peccant in Spiritum sanctum eorum aliqui prius fuerunt fideles & crediderunt. Qui autem verè credit pro eo sanè Christus est mortuus, nisi applicationem sine acquisitione statuas. Quomodo enim quis credere potest, pro se Christum esse mortuum, si pro ipso mortuus non sit?

XXIII. 3. Heb. 10. v. 26. 27. 28. 29. Quanto putatis acerbioresupplicio dignus censebitur, qui Filium Dei conculcarit & sanguinem fœderis, per quem fuerat sanctificatus, profanum duxerit, & Spiritum gratiæ contumeliâ affecerit? Hinc iterum argumentamur. Peccatores in Spiritum sanctum conculcant Filium Dei, & sanguinem fœderis, per quem fuerunt sanctificacati. Peccatores in Spiritum sanctum damnantur. Ergò quidam, qui damnantur, sanguine fœderis fuerunt sanctificati.

XXIV. 4. Ex 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. In vobis erunt magistri mendaces, qui introducent sectas perditionis, & eum, qui emit eos, Dominum negant. Loqui Apostolum Petrum de impijs & verè infidelibus patet. 1. quia vocat eos Pseudoprophetas. 2. magistros mendaces. 3. qui introducant sectas. 4. qui abnegent Dominum. 5. qui superinducant sibi celerem perditionem 6. per quos via veritatis blasphemetur, v. 2: 7. quibus iudicium iam olim non cesset; & quorum perditio non dormitet, v. 3. 8. qui cum Diabolis, impijs Antidiluvianis & Sodomitis iustas pœnas sint perpessuri, v. 4. 5. 6. Et tamen hos ipsos à Domino emtos vel redemtos esse affirmat Apostolus. Excipiunt Caluiniani; Pseudoprophetas illos tantùm dixisse, se à Domino emtos esse, & Apostolos ita sensisse. Verū nihil in se continet hæc exceptio præter petitionem principij. Videatur v. 20. 21: & 22. vbi clarè dicitur, quòd agnouerint viã Domini, quòd abnegauerint Dominum, quòd rursus implicantur peccatis &c. vnde sequitur, quòd prius verè fideles & sanctificati fuerint.

XXV. Addimus tandem duo adhuc testimonia, 1. Ex Ioh. 15. v. 1. & 2. Ego sum vitis vera, & Pater meus agricola est: Omnem palmitem in Me, non ferentem fructum, tollet eum. Quo dicto luculenter innuitur, posse aliquos damnari, qui fuerunt veri & genuini palmites, ipsi Christo insiti. 2. Ex 2. Pet. 1. v. 9. Cui haec (scilicet vera fidei effecta) non adsunt, caecus est, & manu viam tentans, oblitus se se à veteribus peccatis esse purgatum. Possunt ergò aliqui obliuisci purgationis suae à peccatis atque consequenter damnari, vnde rursus elucet, non pro solis electis Christum satisfecisse.


### Question I: Reasons

REASONS.

XXVI. 1. From the end of the incarnation of Christ. Whatever had perished, Christ came to save that, Matt. 18, v. 11, Luke 19, v. 10. But all had perished. Therefore Christ came for the sake of all, and made satisfaction for all.

XXVII. 2. From the destruction of the diabolical kingdom. Christ fully destroyed the kingdom of Satan. For in this the Son of God appeared, that he might dissolve the works of the Devil, 1 John 3, v. 5, Heb. 2, verse 14. But the sins not only of the elect, but of all and every single human being pertain to the kingdom of the Devil. Therefore Christ, by fully destroying the kingdom of the Devil, made satisfaction for the sins of all and every single one.

XXIIX. 3. From the affixing of the handwriting. Coloss. 2, v. 14. The handwriting of all sins was affixed to the cross. Therefore Christ died for all. Otherwise the handwriting of all sins would not have been affixed.

XXIX. 4. From the universal preaching of the Gospel. Bothis part of the Gospel is that Christ died for the sins of men: But this was to be announced to every creature, Mark 16, v. 15. Therefore the death and passion of Christ pertains to all, otherwise this Gospel ought not to have been announced to all.

XXX. 5. From exhortations to repentance. If the death of Christ does not pertain to all, certainly not all can be called to repentance. For the principal part of repentance is faith: but this presupposes the merit of Christ, which is to be apprehended. Therefore, those who ought to believe in Christ, to them certainly the merit to be apprehended must pertain. But all the impious ought to believe, because they are called to repentance, Ezek. 33, v. 11.

XXXI. From the reception of Baptism. Many who are baptized are damned. Because they were baptized into the death of Christ, they were baptized, Rom. 6, v. 3. But whoever is baptized into the death of Christ, for them certainly the death was performed.

XXXII. 7. From the reception of the Lord's Supper. Whoever receives the supper, they receive the body of Christ, which was delivered into death for them. For thus says Christ: This is my body which is delivered into death for you. Which words were said even to Judas, who was utterly reprobate. Therefore Christ also died for Judas, and therefore for all those who use the Supper unworthily.

XXXIII. 8. From the danger of diffidence and desperation. For with what hope and confidence can a weak mind raise itself, when it hears that Christ did not die for all.

XXXIV. 9. From the sin against the Holy Spirit. Ursinus, in part 1 of the explanation of the Catechism concerning sin, dist. p. 66, defines it thus: It is the denial of the acknowledged truth concerning God, and his will and works, of which minds have been thoroughly taught and convinced by the testimony of the Holy Spirit. And on page 67, he sets forth this canon: the sin against the Holy Spirit does not fall upon just any reprobates, but only upon those who have been illuminated by the Holy Spirit and convinced of the truth in their conscience. are, as Saul, Judas: Whoever, however, is illuminated and renewed by the Holy Spirit, he believes in Christ, apprehends his merit, and consequently ought not to be excluded from the number of those for whom Christ died. But since such persons are sinners in the Holy Spirit, as the Calvinists admit, a firm consequence is concluded from this, that Christ did not satisfy and pay a sufficient λύτρον for the elect alone, but also for the reprobate, and thus for all and individual men.

XXXV. 10. By the condemnation of the temporary (προσκαίρων), many are condemned who once believed, as is evident from the parable in Luke 8:13. They believe for a time, and in the time of temptation they fall away. Whoever, however, believes, for them Christ has died. Whence it follows that many are condemned for whom Christ suffered and died.

XXXVI. 11. From the condemnation of unbelievers. The world is condemned because it does not believe in Christ, John 3:18, 19, and 36. To believe in Christ, however, is nothing other than to establish with firm confidence that Christ was given for oneself and died for oneself. If, therefore, the impious are condemned because they did not believe that Christ died for them, they would certainly be condemned because they did not believe a lie. For according to the Calvinists, it is a lie that Christ died for the impious. But hence they heap error upon error, since Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 448, when Jacob Andreae had said, 'Men are condemned because they do not apply to themselves the benefit of the death of Christ through faith,' replied, 'This is entirely new to me, and previously unheard of.' Therefore, the Calvinists deny that men are condemned on account of unbelief alone. And this argument seems to favor their opinion.

If men are to be condemned and punished only on account of unbelief (ἀπιστίαν), there will certainly not be different degrees of punishments. For unbelief does not condemn insofar as it is a work and a quality, but insofar as it does not apprehend Christ: But in this sense unbelief is one and the same: For just as a small faith apprehends Christ just as much as a great one: so also a small unbelief does not apprehend Christ just as much as a great one. Therefore if all are punished on account of unbelief, all will be affected by the same punishment. Wherefore it will not be more tolerable for the Sodomites than for the Capernaites, which is against Christ, Matt. 11. v. 23. Resp. Just as those who are saved are saved on account of Christ alone apprehended, nevertheless, however, with respect to good works there will be distinct degrees of glory in eternal life: so those who are damned are indeed damned on account of unbelief alone; yet the degrees of punishments depend on evil works. For the more and the graver sins one has committed, the greater punishments he will also sustain. Glory therefore and eternal life depend on faith, eternal punishment on unbelief; but the degrees of life [depend] on good works, the degrees of punishment on evil works, with this distinction, that the former are rewarded out of grace, the latter are punished out of merit. And this is what some say, that unbelief damns formally, but not materially, by which last term they refer to the distinct degrees of damnation.

Latin:

RATIONES.

XXVI. 1. A fine incarnationis Christi. Quodcunque perierat, ad illud seruandum venit Christus Matt. 18. v. 11. Luc. 19. v. 10. Atqui omnes perierunt. Ergò propter omnes aduenit, & pro omnibus satisfecit Christus.

XXVII. 2. A destructione regni diabolici. Christus plenariè regnum Satanae destruxit. In hoc enim Filius Dei apparuit, vt solueret opera Diaboli 1. Ioh. 3. v. 5. Heb. 2. vers. 14. Ad regnum verò Diaboli non tantùm electorum, sed omnium & singuloru hominum peccata pertinent. Ergò Christus plenariè destruendo regnum Diaboli, pro omnium & singulorum peccatis satisfecit.
