XXIIX. 3. Ab affixione chirographi. Coloss. 2. v. 14. Omnium peccatorum chirographum cruci est affixum. Ergo pro omnibus Christus est mortuus. Aliàs non affixum fuisset chirographum peccatorum omnium.

XXIX. 4. Ab vniuersali praedicatione Euangelij. Bosta pars Euangelij est, Christum pro peccatis hominum fuisse mortuum: Hoc autem fuit annunciandum omni creaturæ, Marc. 16. v. 15. Ergò omnes attinet mors & passio Christi, aliàs Euangelium istud omnibus annunciari non debuisset.

XXX. 5. Ab adhortationibus ad pœnitentiam. Si non omnes atinet mors Christi, vtique non omnes ad pœnitentiam vocari possunt. Pœnitentiæ enim præcipua pars est fides: hæc autem præsupponit meritum Christi, quod apprehendendum. Qui ergo debent credere in Christum, illos sanè apprehendendum meritum attinere oportet. Omnes autem impij debent credere, quia vocantur ad pœnitentiam, Ezech. 33. v. 11.

XXXI. A perceptione Baptismi, Multi Baptizati damnantur. Quia baptizati sunt in mortem Christi Baptizati sunt, Rom. 6. v. 3. Quj verò in mortem Christi baptizatur, pro illis sanè mors est præstita.

XXXII. 7. A perceptione Cœnæ Dominicæ. Quicunque accipiunt cœnam, illi accipiunt corpus Christi, quod pro ipsis fuit traditum in mortem. Sic enim ait Christus. Hoc est corpus meum quod pro vobis traditur in mortem. Quæ verba dicebantur etiam ad Iudam summè reprobum. Ergò etiam pro Iuda Christus est mortuus, ideoque pro omnibus ijs, qui indigne vtuntur Cœna.

XXXIII. 8. A periculo diffidentiæ & desperationis. Quâ enim spe & fiduciâ infirmus animus sese erigere potest, quando audit Christum pro omnibus non esse mortuum.

XXXIV. 9. A peccato in Spiritum sanctum. Hoc Vrsinus parte 1. explic. Catech. de peccati dist. p. 66. sic definit: Est agnitæ veritatis de Deo, eiusque voluntate & operibus, de qua testimonio Spiritus sancti mentes eortò edoctæ & conuictæ sunt abnegatio. Et pag. 67. hunc ponit Canollem peccatum in Spiritum sanctum non in quosuis reprobos, sed in eos tantum cadit, qui à Spiritu sancto illuminati & de veritate in conscientiâ conuicti sunt, vt Saul, Iudas: Quicunque autem a Spiritu sancto illuminatur & renouatur, is in Christum credit, meritum eius apprehendit, ac per consequens e numero illorum, pro quibus Christus est mortuus, excludi non debet. Tales vero cum sint peccatores in Spiritu S. fatentibus Caluinianis, firma inde sequela concluditur, Christum non pro solis electis, sed reprobis etiam, adeoque vniuersis & singulis hominibus satisfecisse & sufficiens λύτρον persoluisse.

XXXV. 10. Adamnatione προσκαίρων, Multi damnantur, qui aliquando crediderunt, vt patet ex parabola Luc. 8. v. 13. Ad tempus credunt, & in tempore tentationis recedunt. Quicunque autem credunt, pro illis Christus est mortuus. Vnde sequitur, quod multi damnantur, pro quibus Christus passus fuit & mortuus.

XXXVI. 11. A condemnatione infidelium. Mundus condemnatur, quia non credit in Christum, Ioh. 3: v. 18. 19. & 36. Credere autem in Christum nihil est aliud, quam firma fiducia statuere, Christum sibi datum, & pro se esse mortuum. Si ergo impij damnantur, quia non crediderunt, Christum pro se esse mortuum, certe damnarentur, quia non crediderunt mendacio. Secundum Caluinianos enim mendacium est, Christum esse pro impijs mortuum. Atqui hinc errorem errore cumulant, siquidem Beza in Colloq. Mompelg. p. 448. cum Iacobus Andreæ dixisset, Homines ideo danantur, quoniam beneficium mortis Christi sibi per fidem non applicant, respondit, Hoc mihi plane nouum est, & prius inauditum: Negant ergo Caluiniani, homines propter solam incredulitatem damnari. Et videtur illorum sententiæ fauere hoc argumentum.

Si propter ἀπιστίαν tantum damnabuntur & punientur homines, vtique non erunt diuersi gradus pœnarū. Incredulitas enim non damnat, quatenus opus est & qualitas, sed quatenus no apprehendit Christum: Ast hoc sensu incredulitas vna est ac eadem: Sicut enim Fides parua tam apprehendit Christum quam magna: ita & incredulitas parua tam non apprehendit Christum, quam magna. Ergo si omnes propter incredulitate punientur, omnes eadem poena afficientur. Quare non tolerabilius erit Sodomitis quam Capernaunticis, quod est contra Christum, Matt. 11. v. 23. Resp. Quemadmodum qui saluantur, ob solum apprehensum Christum saluantur, nihilominus tamen respectu bonorum operum in vita aeterna distincti erunt gradus gloriae: ita qui damnantur, ob solam quidem incredulitatem damnantur; attamen gradus poenarum dependent a malis operibus. Quo quis enim plura commisit, & grauiora peccata, co etiam maiores poenas sustinebit. Gloria ergo & vita aeterna a fide, poena aeterna ab incredulitate dependet; gradus autem vitae a bonis, gradus poenae a malis operibus, cum hoc discrimine, quod illa ex gratia remunerentur, heec ex merito puniantur. Atque hoc est quod nonnulli dicunt, incredulitatem damnare formaliter, non autem materialiter, quo postremo vocabulo respiciunt ad distinctos damnationis gradus.


### Question I: Testimonies

TESTIMONIES.

XXXVII. Origen, book 1, on Job. Christ coming to the lands, in a human body sustained passions for the salvation of all men, so that through passion he might kill death: And through resurrection might show revived life to all. And book 2, on The only-begotten God descending from the heavens in the last time, clothing himself with the garment of an earthly body from a virgin, scraped and cleansed the health, uncleanness, and rottenness of the WHOLE world, by supporting the sins of ALL: by whose stripe ALL were also healed. Cyril, book 2, on John, chapter 1. The Father gave the Son for us for redemption, one for all. One died for all so that we may all live in him. For when death had swallowed the lamb slain for all, it could not retain him, but in him and with him it shall vomit forth all the others. Ambrose, sermon 8 on Psalm 118. The sun of righteousness has risen for all, came for all, suffered for all; and rose again for all. If, however, anyone does not believe in someone, with windows closed, should exclude the rays of the sun. And book 2 of the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 6. There is no reason to doubt that Jesus Christ our Lord died for the ungodly and for sinners.

Augustine, tractate 92 on John. Christ's blood was so shed for the remission of all sins, that it could even blot out the very sin by which it was shed. And in the book concerning the articles falsely attributed to him, he expressly rejects and condemns this article: That Christ did not suffer for the redemption of all men.

Basil, in the sermon on human nature: One price has been found worthy for all men together, the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ which he shed for us all.

Theophylact, on John 1. He wished to conglomerate and gather together all the sins of all men as if into one bundle and ball of sin.

CALVINISTIC OBJECTIONS.

38. Christ died for the elect, for his people, for his sheep, as is said everywhere in the Scriptures. Therefore not for the ungodly. Resp. I deny the consequence. For the elect only. By the same reasoning, the particular resurrection of the faithful could be proven. The faithful shall rise. The logician says: From an inclusive to an exclusive, the consequence is not valid. 39. 2. Christ died for many, Isaiah 53, v. 15. Therefore not for all.

Resp. It is a fallacy of equivocation, because the word for multitude often signifies all, as in Romans 5, v. 19. As by the disobedience of one, many were made sinners, that is, all. Compare verse 12 and 18. Thus Daniel 12, v. 2. Many of those sleeping in the ground shall awake, that is, all. Thus Gen. 17 v. 5 it is said: I have made you a father of many nations, which is explained thus in Gen. 22 v. 18: In your seed shall all nations be blessed. Hence theologians have constructed a rule: The word (many) is sometimes taken συμπληρωματικῶς for all, as: many shall rise again; sometimes Διαιρετικῶς for some, as: many shall inherit eternal life, many were baptized in the Jordan.

XL. 3. Matt. 16 v. 24. I am not come, but for the lost sheep of the house of Israel.

Resp. 1. If the Calvinists urge this passage strictly, certainly Christ did not come for them either, because they are not Jews by birth, but Gentiles. Nor can they except that they are spiritual Israelites. For the Canaanite woman was also such, yet nonetheless Christ denied that he was sent for her. 2. I distinguish between the prophetic and priestly office of Christ. This saying speaks of the prophetic, not the priestly: the latter concerned the whole world, the former concerned the Jews primarily. For Christ had to be a minister of the circumcision, Rom. 15 v. 18, Acts 13 v. 46.

XLI. 4. John 11 v. 52. Jesus was to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but that he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad.

Resp. From this passage, particularity of merit cannot be concluded. For although by the nation, for which Christ is said to have died, you understand only the Jews, or even only the elect, it matters nothing, since it is not added that Christ died only for the nation.

XLII. 5. For whom Christ did not pray, for them he did not suffer, because those two highest offices of the priest, to pray for the people and to offer for the people, were joined. But Christ, about to die, did not pray for the world or the unbelievers, John 17 v. 9.

Resp. 1. The prayer of Christ was twofold. The other general, as High Priest, in which way for all men he prayed, even for the impious and transgressors, according to the words of Isa. 53. v. 12. Luke 23. v. 34. The other is special, as a Pastor; in which sense he prayed only for his own hearers (not for obstinate sinners). Briefly, therefore, he prayed for all as High Priest; for some, as Pastor and Ecclesiastes, not otherwise than John 3. v. 16. says, that he was sent to the whole world, but by reason of his ministry and the performing of miracles he came only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Matt. 15. v. 24. Lyra interprets the cited text thus: Christ says that he does not pray for the world, because the efficacy of his prayer extends only to the elect. For although it is efficacious for all, yet the wicked place an impediment before themselves, so that they are not partakers of it.

XLIII, 6. John 9. v. 39. For judgment I am come into this world, that they which see not might see; and that they which see might be made blind.

Resp. The final words ought to be understood ἐκβατικῶς or eventually, not αἰτιολογικῶς or causally. For the sense is: Those who think they see well, by the just judgment of God will be made more blind. Christ indeed came so that all might see; but because they will not receive this saving light out of a persuasion of their own holiness, hence it will come to pass that they are rendered more and more blind.

XLIV. 7. Rev. 14. v. 3. & 4. These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men. But not all are immaculate, which is in the open, and is sufficiently indicated by the little word (from/out of). For just as by the force of this preposition, against Hubert, we infer particular election, so by the force of the same we ought to collect particular redemption. Let the passage Rev. 5. v. 9. be compared.

Resp. The Passion and redemption of Christ in Scripture is considered in two ways: 1. By reason of sufficiency, or the will and intention of God, and thus Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world. 2. By reason of efficacy, or application and saving fruit in men, which happens only to the faithful. When, therefore, Christ is said to sanctify a people for Himself by His passion, and to have redeemed some from among men, then it should be understood concerning redemption taken in the latter way. And in this sense the words of the Apostle are to be accepted: for they are from among men, namely, not only Apoc. 5. v. 9, where the elect, singing, say: You were slain and have redeemed us to God in your blood, out of every tribe, and have made us a kingdom and priests to our God; which latter words are exegetical of the former, whence it is evident that the discourse is concerning redemption, considered as to application and efficiency: In like manner also calling is taken in two ways, 1. for bare calling, in which sense it is universal, 2. for saving calling and that apprehended by faith, as Rom. 8. v. 30. Whom He called, them He also justified, in which sense it is particular. Thus also the manifestation of the divine name is accepted in a twofold way, 1. as it is alone, 2. as it is joined with fruit, in which manner Matth. 11. v. 25 it is said: You have hidden these things from the wise, and have revealed them to little ones.

XLV. 8. For whom Christ has died, him He draws to Himself, according to that Ioh. 12. v. 32. Therefore if I shall be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all to myself. But he who is drawn to Christ, he adheres to Christ. But he who adheres to the Lord, he is one Spirit with Him 1. Cor. 6. vers. 7. But only the faithful are one spirit with the Lord. Therefore these alone adhere to the Lord. Wherefore these alone are drawn by the Lord, and consequently for these alone the Lord has died.

Resp. That proposition is false: He whom Christ draws to Himself, he adheres to Christ. For Christ draws no one violently, but He draws all by reason of His will and intention, and of calling through the word. But those who do not wish to be drawn, as the impenitent, they also are not actually drawn to Christ, nor do they adhere to Him, although the Lord may wish to draw them and to Himself to adhere. Whence Antiquity said; Christ draws all, not by effect, but by affection and outpouring.

XLVI. 9. Christ distributes to the faithful alone the righteousness obtained by his death: but for the impious eternal fire is prepared: Therefore he died for the faithful alone, and not for the impious.

Resp. I deny the consequence, because the death of Christ and the fruit of his death are confused. The death is universal and provided for all; but the fruit belongs to the faithful alone. But what is this consequence: Not all obtain the fruit of the Lord's death. Therefore the death of Christ was not provided for all? Does the unbelief of men make void the faithfulness of God? Might one not argue in the same way: The Word is not salutary to all but to many is a savor of death unto death, Therefore it does not pertain to all: Wherefore it is not to be preached to every creature.

XLVII. 10. If Christ had reconciled the whole world to God the Father, the whole world would be saved.

Resp. There is no connection in the major premise in turn. For in order that the effect of salvation may emerge, there is required not only the acquisition of reconciliation, but furthermore its application through faith. Thus 2 Cor. 5, verse 19, it is said, God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, and yet immediately it is added in v. 20, Be ye reconciled to God. There seems to be an ἀντίφασις here, but the reconciliation is easy, but let it be said that the former member speaks of acquisition, but the latter of application and apprehension. Reconciliation has been made through Christ, as regards acquisition: it is to be made through repentance, as regards application. For example: If a physician has prepared a medicine for a sick person, and it is most effective for driving away the disease, the sick person will certainly not be healed unless he apprehends and takes the medicine. To this pertains that of Bernard, from sermon 32 on the Canticles: Each person possesses as much of these goods as he gathers with the vessel of trust. And rightly Augustine, on the article falsely attributed to him, art. 1: The

cup of immortality, which is prepared from our infirmity and divine power, indeed has in itself that it may benefit all, but if it is not drunk, it does not profit. XLIIX. 11. If Christ died for all men, therefore also for those actually damned, such as Cain, Pharaoh, whence it follows that the death of Christ in this respect was idle. Resp. It was not therefore void and superfluous. For just as Christ suffered for Abraham, who nevertheless was then actually saved, and had no need of the apprehension of merit: so although the damned cannot apprehend the satisfaction of Christ in hell, yet for that reason the passion was not idle. Why? Because in their own times they ought to have apprehended it. Therefore, if Christ had not willed to die for them, then they could not have believed in their own time, and thus could not have been damned on account of unbelief, but would be excusable: the judicial sentence holds thus: he who does not believe is already judged. Although therefore the satisfaction of Christ provided for the damned could not be apprehended by the damned in hell, because nevertheless at some time, namely when they lived, they could have apprehended it, and because all who are damned are to be condemned on account of unbelief, therefore that passion was not void and idle. XLIX. 12. For whom Christ died, to them the revelation of Christ is necessary, or to them it is necessarily revealed, but it is not revealed to all, nor has it been revealed. Resp. The major is not simply true. For application, indeed, revelation is always required: meanwhile, if you look at the acquisition itself, it is not necessary. For example: to Paul, when he was still Saul, Christ had not been revealed: and yet at that very time Christ had died for Paul. Thus someone can acquire freedom for a captive from a Prince by a petition: which if the Prince promises to the petitioner, then it is truly acquired for the captive, even if nothing of it has yet been has become known. But when one ought to become a participant in an acquired benefit, then there is need of revelation. But in Question 3 concerning this argument, it will be treated more fully when the calling of the infidels is disputed.

L. 13. Just as the Church is called and is Catholic and universal, so also the merit of Christ is catholic and universal. But the Church is called universal, not because individual and all men are members of the Church, but because it is gathered from the whole world, and is not bound to a certain place or people. Therefore, in this and no other sense is the merit of Christ universal.

Resp. The antecedent is false, as was proven above by the most evident testimonies of the Scriptures, all of which demonstrate that the merit of Christ is in many ways καθολικώτερον and universal, for the reason that that reconciliation was acquired not only for the Church, but for the whole world.

Latin:

TESTIMONIA.

XXXVII. Orig. l. 1. in Hiob. Christus ad terras veniens, in humano corpore passiones sustinuit pro omnium hominum salute, vt per passionem mortem interficeret: Et per resurrectionem redidiuam cunctis vitam ostenderet. Et l: 2. in Iob. Descendens de caelis vnigenitus Deus in nouissimo tempore, terreni corporis vestitu ex virgine se induens, TOTIVS Mundi saniem, immunditiem & putredinem rasit atque mundauit, OMNIVM peccata supportando: cuius liuore OMNES etiam sanati sunt, Cyrillus l. 2. in Ioh. cap. 1. Filium Pater in redemptionem pronobis dedit, vnum pro omnibus. Vnus pro omnibus mortuus vt omnes in ipso viuamus. Cùm enim pro omnibus occisum agnum mors inforbuerit, retinere non potuit, sed in ipso & cum ipso cæteros omnes euomet. Ambrosius sermone 8. in Psalm. 118. Sol iustitiæ omnibus ortus est, omnibus venit, omnibus passus est; & omnibus resurrexit. Si quis autem non credit in Christum; generali beneficio ipse se fraudat, vt si quis clausis fenestris, radios solis excludat. Et lib. 2. de voc. gent. cap. 6. Nulla ratio dubitandi est, Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum pro impijs & peccatoribus mortuum.

August. tract. 92. in Iohan. Christi sanguis sic in remissionem peccatorum omnium fusus est, vt ipsum etiam peccatum posset delere, quo fusus est. Et in l. de articulis sibi falsò impositis, expressè reijcit, & damnat hunc articulum: Quòd Christus non pro omnium hominum redemtione sit passus.

Basil. in serm. de hum. nat: Inuentum est vnum pro omnibus simul hominibus dignum pretium, sanguis Domini nostri Iesu Christi quem pro nobis omnibus effudit.

Theophyl. super Iohan. 1. Omnia omnium hominum peccata quasi in vnum fasciculum & globum peccati conglomerare & colligere voluit.

OBIECTIONES CALuinisticæ.

XXXIIX. Christus pro electis, pro suo populo, pro suis ouibus est mortuus, vti passim dicitur in Scripturis. Ergo non pro impijs. Resp. N. C. Pro electis tantùm. Pari ratione particularis fidelium resurrectio posset probari. Fideles resurgent. Logicus dicit: Ab inclusiua ad exclusiuam non valet consequentia. XXXIX. 2. Christus pro multis mortuus est, Esaia 53. v. 15. Ergo non pro omnibus.

Resp. Est fallacia æquiuocationis, quia vocabulum multitudinis, sæpè significat omnes, vt Rom. 5. v. 19. Sicut per vnius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, id est, omnes. Confer vers. 12. & 18. Sic Dan. 12. v. 2. Multi è dormientibus humi expergiscentur, h. e. omnes. Sic Gen. 17. v. 5. dicitur: Patrem multarum gentium posui te, quod ita exponitur Gen. 22. v. 18. In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes. Hinc Theologi extruxerunt regulam: Vox (multum) quandoque sumitur συμπληρωματικῶς pro omnibus, vt multi resurgent; quandoque Διαιρετικῶς pro aliquibus, vt: multi hæreditabunt vitam æternam, multi baptizabantur in Iordane.

XL. 3. Matt. 16. v. 24. Non veni, nisi propter perditas oues domus Israeltica.

Resp. 1. Si strictè hunc locum vrgent Caluiniani, certè nec propter ipsos venit Christus, quia non sunt natiuitate Iudæi, sed gentiles. Neque possunt excipere, se spirituales esse Israelitas. Nam & mulier Chananæa talis fuit, nihilo tamen minùs propter eam se missum esse Christus negauit. 2. Distinguo inter officium Christi Propheticum & Sacerdotale. Dictum hoc de Prophetico, non Sacerdotali loquitur: Hoc vniuersum mundum, illud Iudæos potissimùm attinebat. Christus enim minister esse debebat circumcisionis, Rom. 15. v. 18. Act. 13. v. 46.

XLI. 4. Ioh. 11. v. 52. Iesus moriturus erat pro gente, & non tantùm pro gente, sed vt filios Dei, qui erant dispersi, congregaret in vnum.

Resp. Ex hoc loco concludi nequit particularitas meriti. Nam licèt per gentem, pro qua Christus dicitur esse mortuus, intelligas solos Iudæos, vel etiam solos electos, nihil tamen refert, quoniam non additur, quòd Christus tantùm pro gente fuerit mortuus.

XLII. 5. Pro quibus Christus non orauit, pro iis non est passus, quia duo illa summa sacerdotis officia, pro populo orare, & pro populo offerre, erant coniuncta. Christus autem moriturus non orauit pro mundo seu infidelibus, Ioh. 17. v. 9.

Resp. 1. Duplex fuit oratio Christi. Altera generalis, vt Pontificis quo pacto pro omnibus hominibus orauit, etiam pro impijs & transgressoribus, iuxta dicta Esa. 53. v. 12. Luc. 23. v. 34. Altera specialis, vt Pastoris; quo sensu tantùm pro suis auditoribus (non præfractis peccatoribus) orauit. Breuiter ergò pro omnibus vt Pontifex; pro aliquibus, vt Pastor & Ecclesiastes rogauit, non secus atque Ioh. 3. v. 16. ait, se esse missum vniuerso mundo, ratione autem ministerij & edendorum miraculorum non nisi ad perditas oues dom^{9} Israeliticæ venit. Matth. 15. v. 24. Lyra textum allegatum sic interpretatur: Dicit Christus, se non rogare pro mundo, quia efficacia suæ orationis tantummodò se extendit ad electos. Quamuis enim sit efficax pro omnibus, tamen mali ponunt sibi impedimentum, ne sint participes eius.

XLIII, 6. Ioh. 9. v. 39. In hunc mundum veni, ut qui non vident, videant, & qui vident, cæci fiant.

Resp. ἐκβατικῶς vel euentualiter, non αἰτιολογικῶς vel causaliter intelligi debent verba vltima. Sensus enim est: Ii qui putant se probè videre, iusto Dei iudicio magis occæcabuntur. Christus quidem venit, vt omnes videant; quia verò ex persuasione propriæ sanctitatis salutare lumen istud non recipient, hinc fiet, vt magis magiśque cæci reddantur.

XLIV. 7. Apoc. 14. v. 3. & 4. Qui non sunt coinquinati cum mulieribus, qui virgines sunt, qui sequuntur agnum, quocunque ierit, hi sunt emti vel redempti ex hominibus. Atqui non omnes sunt immaculati, quod in aprico, & per voculam (ex) satis indicatur. Sicut enim vị huius præpositionis, contra Hubertum electionem particularem inferimus, ita vi eiusdem redemptionem particularem colligere debemus. Conferatur locus Apoc. 5. v. 9.

Resp. Passio & redemptio Christi in Scriptuconsideratur bifariam 1. Ratione sufficientiæ, vel voluntatis & intentionis Dei, & sic Christus est propitiatio pro peccatis totius mundi. 2. Ratione efficientiæ, vel applicationis atq; salutaris fructus in hominibus qui tantùm fidelibus cöntingit. Quando ergò Christus dicitur sanctificare sibi populum passione suâ, & redemisse aliquos ex hominibus, tum intelligatur de redemtione modo posteriori sumta. Et hoc sensu accipienda sunt verba Apostoli: H. sunt enim ex hominibus, scilicet non tantùm sufficienter, verùm etiam efficienter. Patet hoc ex Apoc. 5. v. 9. vbi electi cantantes ajunt: Occisus es & redemisti nos Deo in sanguine tuo, ex omni tribu, & fecisti nos Deo nostro regnum & sacerdotes; quæ posteriora verba exegetica sunt priorum, vnde patet, sermonem ipsis esse de redemtione, quoàd applicationem & efficientiam considerata: Pari modo & vocatio dupliciter sumitur, 1. pro nuda vocatione, quo sensu vniuersalis est, 2. pro vocatione salutari & fide apprehensa, vt Rom. 8. v. 30. Quos vocauit, hos & iustificauit, quo sensu particularis est. Sic & manifestatio nominis diuini duplici modo modo accipitur, 1. prout sola est, 2. prout cum fructu coniuncta est, quo pacto Matth. 11. v. 25. dicitur: Abscondisti hæc à sapientibus, & reuelasti paruulis.

XLV. 8. Pro quo Christus est mortuus, eum trahit ad se, juxta illud Ioh. 12. v. 32. Ergo si exaltatus fuero à terra, omnes traham ad meipsum Qui autem ad Christum trahitur, ille Christo adhæret. Qui verò adhæret Domino, is vnus est Spiritus cũ ipso 1. Cor. 6. vers. 7. Atqui soli fideles sunt vnus spiritus cum Domino. Ergò hi soli Domino adhærent. Quare hi soli à Domino trahuntur, & per consequens pro his solis Dominus est mortuus.

Resp. Illa propositio falsa est: Quem Christus ad se trahit, is Christo adhæret. Nam Christus neminem trahit violenter, sed omnes trahit ratione voluntatis & intentionis suæ, & vocationis per verbum. Qui vero se trahi nolunt, vt impœnitentes, illi quoque ad Christum actu non trahuntur, nec ipsi adhærent, quamvis eos attrahere & sibi ad hærere velit Dominus. Vnde dixit Antiquitas; Christus trahit omnes non effectu, sed affectu & affusu.

XLVI. 9. Christus solis fidelibus distribuit iustitiam morte sua partam : impiis verò æternus ignis est præparatus : Ergo pro solis fidelibus, non autem pro impiis est mortuus,

Resp. N. C. quia confunditur mors Christi, & mortis fructus. Mors vniuersalis est & p omnibus præstita; fructus autem solis fidelibus competit, Quæ verò consequentia: Non omnes consequuntur fructum mortis Dominicæ. Ergò mors Christi pro omnibus non est præstita? Num infidelitas hominum euacuat fidem Dei? Annòn liceret eodem modo argumentari : Verbum non omnibus est salutiferum sed multis sit odor mortis ad mortem, Ergò non omnes attinet : Quare non est prædicandum omni creaturæ,

XLVII. 10. Si Christus Deo Patri reconciliasset totum mundum, totus mundus saluaretur.

Resp. Nulla vicissim est connexio in maiore. Vtenim saluationis effectus emergat, requiritur non tantùm reconciliationis acquisitio, sed insuper eiusdem per fidem applicatio. Sic 2. Cor. 5. vers. 19. dicitur, Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, & mox tamen additur v. 20. Reconciliemini Deo. Videtur hic esse ἀντίφασις, sed facilis est conciliatio, sed dicatur quòd prius membrum de acquisitione, posterius verò de applicatione & apprehensione loquatur. Facta est reconciliatio per Christum, quoad acquisitionem: facienda est per pœnitentiam, quoad applicationem. Exempli gratiâ: Si medicus pharmacum parauerit pro ægroto, idque præsentissimum sit ad depellendum morbum, ægrotus sanè non sanabitur, nisi pharmacum apprehendat & assumat. Huc pertinet illud Bernh. de serm. 32. super Cantic. Tantum quisque de hisce bonis possidet quantum vase fiduciæ colligit. Et rectè August. ad artic. sibi falsò impos. art. 1. Fe-

culum immortalisatis, quod confectum est de infirmitate nostra, & virtute divina, habet equidem in se, vt omnibus prosit, sed si non bibitur, non proficit. XLIIX. 11. Si Christus pro omnibus hominibus est mortuus, Ergò etiam pro actu damnatis, vt Caino, Pharaone, vnde sequitur, mortem Christi hoc respectu fuissε otiosam. Resp. Non propterea fuit irrita & superuacanea. Sicut enim pro Abrahamo passus est Christus, qui tamen tum actu saluatus erat, nec opus habebat apprehensione meriti: ita licèt damnati satisfactionem Christi in inferno nequeant apprehendere, tamen ob id passio otiosa non fuit. Quare? quia temporibus suis debuerunt apprehendere. Proinde, si Christus pro ijs mori noluisset, tum suo tempore credere, atque sic propter incredulitatem damnari non potuissent, sed excusabiles forent: sententia judicialis sic habet: qui non credit iam judicatus est. Licet igitur satisfactio Christi pro damnatis praestita, non potuerit apprehendi à damnatis in inferno, quia tamen aliquando, cùm nempè vixerunt, eam apprehendere potuerunt, & quia omnes qui damnantur, propter incredulitatem sunt condemnandi, idcircò passio ista irrita & otiosa non fuit. XLIX. 12. Pro quibus Christus est mortuus, illis necessaria est Christi revelatio, seu illis necessariò revelatur, Atqui non omnibus revelatur, nec revelatus est. Resp. Major non est simpliciter vera. Ad applicationem quidem semper requiritur revelatio: Interim, si ipsam acquisitionem spectes, non est necessaria. Exempli gratiâ: Paulo, cùm adhuc Saulus esset non erat revelatus Christus: Et tamen eo ipso tempore pro Paulo Christus erat mortuus. Sic potest quis captiuo alicui per libellum supplicem à Principe liberatem acquirere: quam si Princeps supplicanti promittat, tùm captivo verè acquisita est, etiam si nondum aliquid de ea ipsi innotuerit. Quando verò beneficiij acquisiti debet fieri particeps, tùm opus est reuelatione. Sed questi. 3. de hoc argumento pluribus agetur, cùm de vocatione infidelium disputabitur.

L. 13. Sicut Ecclesia vocatur & est Catholica atque vniuersalis, ita & meritum Christi catholicum atque vniuersale est. Atqui Ecclesia dicitur vniuersalis, non quod singuli & vniuersi homines sint membra Ecclesiæ, sed quia ex toto mundo colligitur, neq; certo loco aut populo est alligata. Ergò hoc & non alio sensu meritum Christi est vniuersale.

Resp. Antecedens falsum est, vti suprà euidentissimis Scripturarum testimoniis probatum fuit, quæ omnia demonstrant meritum Christi multis modis esse καθολικώτερον & vniuersale, propterea, quod reconciliatio illa non Ecclesiæ tantùm, sed toti mundo fuit acquisita.


### Question II. Is the merit of Christ and the salvation acquired by that merit promised and offered by God to all?

I. The Calvinists, who imagine the decree of election to be absolute, from this opine that only the elect are loved by God, that the Son was sent to them alone, and consequently that the benefits obtained by the death of Christ according to the will of good pleasure, and in reality, are promised and offered only to the elect. They indeed confess that God calls all to faith, and promises salvation to all, but they say that this is done only by the will of sign. And hence it is that they establish a double calling, efficacious and inefficacious: where if they understood this, that not all obey the calling, and therefore that this κλῆσις does not attain the inefficacy which God intends, by accident, we would move no dispute with them on this name. For we ourselves confess that room is not left by all for the divine calling and invitation: on the part of the infidels, therefore, the calling becomes ineffi cacious. But because the Calvinists on one hand say that there is a certain ineffectual calling of God, in such a way that God never willed, by his secret will, that all should obey that calling, which they write comes about by the will of sign; this is that which the theologians of the Augustan Confession rightly criticize in them.

II. That this is indeed the opinion of the Calvinists is not difficult to prove: For thus he writes. 1. Calvin, Inst. 3, ch. 21, § 7. Just as the Lord marks the elect by calling and justification, so by excluding the reprobate either from the knowledge of his name or from the sanctification of the Holy Spirit, he reveals by these signs, as it were, what judgment awaits them. And ch. 24, § 12. Those whom he created for the reproach of life and the destruction of death, so that they might be instruments of his wrath and examples of severity, he, in order that they may arrive at their end, now deprives of the ability to hear his word, now blinds and stupefies them all the more by its preaching. 2. Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 385. Those whom the Lord has not chosen in this way, even if they were baptized a thousand times with the external baptism of water, yet faith or the Holy Spirit is never given to them. And p. 433. He either does not call the reprobate at all, or even if he calls them to the greatest extent, the calling is nevertheless entirely ineffectual. And shortly after. That the calling is not universal, so that all might be saved, is evident from the fact that there are many who have never heard the word of God, to whom it has also never been preached. Ursinus, part 2, Catechetical Explanations, p. 218. The promise is universal with respect to believers, that is, it pertains to all believers. For as God does not give grace to unbelievers, so he does not promise it; otherwise, if he were to promise and not give, he would not be truthful. 4. Perkins in the book on Predestination, p. 17. Joined with the promise is an exhortation or command to believe, which is more general than the promise, because the promise is only for believers, but the command is for both believers and non-believers: etc. 5. Zanchius on the Nature of God, book 3, q. 4. When I say that all men are called, I understand an external calling. But you say that the internal, which is done through the Holy Spirit and is therefore effectual, calls only the elect. 6. Whitaker on the question of the Church, book 1, ch. 7, p. 34. There is a twofold call ing, general and special. The former consists only in the external preaching of the word, by which all who are in the Church by external society are called. The latter, however, consists in a certain internal power of the Holy Spirit, working within the hearts, who draws those who are called to Christ. These only are of the Church, those sometimes are not. 7. Sibrandus Lubbertus, book 1, on the Church, chapter 4, page 7. Calling is twofold, one external, the other internal. The external is through the sensible voice of the herald of the Gospel: the internal, through the hidden operation of the Holy Spirit. These two sometimes concur, sometimes one is separated from the other. 9. Rennecherus in the golden chain of salvation, chapter 24, page 165. It must be known that one calling is external, and ineffectual for salvation, but another is internal, and effectual for salvation. The external is that which consists only in the external preaching of the Gospel; it reaches only to the surface of the intellect. This external [calling] indeed strikes the ears with sound, but does not penetrate into the heart itself, nor does it have a firm and fixed root in it. Conversely, page 166. From these it can be clearly gathered that the word of God is proposed to men not for one, but for diverse ends, and by the admirable judgment of God is so tempered and dispensed in both directions, that it is no less a savor of death unto death for the reprobate than it is a savor of life unto life for the elect. Thus, by one and the same word of God, the reprobate are killed unto damnation just as the elect are recreated unto salvation.

III. On the contrary, however, we believe, teach, and profess that God, just as He wills all men to be saved, and has sent His Son to all, so also promises eternal life to all and calls all by His word to embrace those benefits which Christ acquired by His death and passion. We distinguish, however, between the promise and the thing promised or the fruit of the promise. The promise itself is universal, and is offered to all: but the thing promised is given only to believers. All are invited through the promise: only believers obtain the fruit through faith. For in the reception of a gift, the hand of the one offering is not sufficient, but there is required also the hand of the recipient. For the confirmation of this opinion, in turn, we shall bring forward: 1. Sayings. 2. Reasons. 3. Testimonies.

Latin:

I. Caluiniani, qui decretum electionis fingunt absolutum, hinc opinantur, electos tantùm à Deo diligi, ijs solis missum esse Filium, & consequenter beneficia morte Christi parta secundum voluntatem beneplaciti, & reipsa non nisi electis promitti & obferri. Fatentur quidem, Deum omnes vocare ad fidem, omnibus salutem promittere, sed illud ajunt fieri duntaxat voluntate signi, Atque hinc est, quòd duplicem vocationem statuunt, efficacem & inefficacem: vbi si intelligerent hoc, quod vocationi non omnes obtemperent, ideoque κλῆσις ista inefficaciam, quam Deus intendit, per accidens non cõsequatur, litem hoc nomine eis nullam moueremus. Ipsi enim fatemur, vocationi & inuitationi diuinæ locum ab omnibus non relinqui: Ex parte igitur infidelium vocatio sit ineffigax. Verùm quia Caluiniani vna ex parte Dei quandam dicunt esse vocationem inefficacem, ita quidem, vt Deus nunquam voluerit, voluntate arcana, omnes vocationi isti, quam voluntate signi prouenire scriptitant, obedire; hoc illud est, quod Confess. Augustan. Theologi in ipsis meritò reprehendunt.

II. Esse verò hanc Caluinianorum sententiam, probatu non est difficile: Ita enim scribit. 1. Caluinus 3. Instit. c. 21. § 7. Quemadmodum autem vocatione & iustificatione electos Dominus signat, ita reprobos vel à notitia sui nominis, vel à Spiritus sancti sanctificatione excludendo, quale maneat eos iudicium, istis veluti notis aperit. Et c. 24. §. 12. Quos in vitæ contumeliam & mortis exitium creauit, vt iræ suæ organa forent & seueritatis exempla, eos, vt in finem suum perueniat, nunc audiendi verbi sui facultate priuat, nunc eius prædicatione magis excæcat & obstupefacit. 2. Beza in colloq. Momp. pag. 385. Quos Dominus hoc modo non elegit, etiamsi millies baptizarentur externo aquæ Baptismo, illis tamen nunquam fides, aut Spiritus sanctus donatur. Et pag. 433. Reprobatos vel prorsus non vocat, vel ut maximè vocet, vocatio tamen prorsus inefficax est. Et mox. Vocationem non esse vniuersalem, vt omnes saluantur, ex eo patet, quoniam multi sunt, qui nunquam verbum Dei audierunt, quibus etiam nunquam prædicatũ est. Vrsinus part. 2. Explic. Catechet. pag. 218. Promissio est vniuersalis, respectu credentium, id est, pertinet ad omnes credentes. Infidelibus enim Deus vt non dat, ita nec promittit gratiam, alioqui si promitteret, & non daret, non esset verax. 4. Perkinsius in l. de Prædest. p. 17. Cum promissione coniuncta est hortatio siue mandatum credendi, quod generalius est promissione, quia promissio tantùm credentium est mandatum, verò & credentium & non credentium: &c. 5. Zanchius de N Dei. l. 3. q. 4. Cũ dico, omnes homines vocari, intelligo externam vocationem. Cæterùm interna, quæ fit per S. S. & ideò efficaci, solos electos vocari ais. 6. Whitakerus de Eccles. quæstioni. 1. cap. 7. p. 34. Duplex est vocatio, generalis. & specialis. Illa in externa tantùm verbi predicatione consistit, quâ omnes, qui sunt in Ecclesia externa societate, vocantur, Hæc autem consistit in vi quadam interna Spiritus sancti, in cordibus intus operantis, qui attrahit eos, qui vocantur ad Christum. Hi tantùm sunt de Ecclesia, illi quandoque non. 7. Sibrandus Lubbertus l, 1. de Eccles. cap 4. p. 7. Vocatio sit duplex, vna externa, altera interna. Externa sit per sensibilem vocem præconis Euangelij: Interna, per occultam operationem Spiritus sancti. Hæ duæ quandoque concurrunt, quandoque vna ab altero separata est. 9. Rennecherus in aurea salutis catena, c. 24. p. 165. Sciendum est, quod vocatio alia sit externa, & ad salutem inefficax, alia vero interna, & ad salutem efficax. Externa est, quæ tantùm externâ Euangelij prædicatione constat, ea tantùm ad superficiem intellectus pertingit, Hæc externa sonitu aures quidem verberat, sed in ipsium cor non penetrat, nec in eo radicem firmam & defixam habet. Vicissim pag. 166. Ex his appertè colligi potest, verbum Dei hominibus non in vnum, sed in diuersos fines proponi, & admirando Dei iudicio sic in vtramque partem temperari & dispensari, vt non minùs reprobis odor mortis ad mortem, quàm electis odor vitæ ad vitam sit. Sic vno & eodem Dei verbo tam reprobi ad damnationem enecantur, quàm electi ad salutem recreantur.

III. Contrà verò, nos credimus, docemus & profitemur, quòd Deus, quemadmodum omnes homines vult saluos fieri, omnibusq́; misit Filium, ita & omnibus vitam æternam promittat & omnes verbo suo vocet ad amplectenda illa beneficia, quæ Christus morte & passione suâ acquisiuit. Distinguimus verò inter promissionem & rem promissam vel promissionis fructum. Ipsa promissio vniuersalis est, & offertur omnibus: Res autem promissa datur non nisi credentibus. Omnes inuitantur per promissionem: fructum adipiscuntur soli credentes per fidem. In doni enim receptione non sufficit manus porrigentis, sed requiritur vnà mafius accipientis. Pro huius autem sententiae confirmatione vicissim adducemus. 1: Dicta. 2. Rationis. 3. Testimonia.


### Question II. Is the merit of Christ and the salvation acquired by that merit…: Sayings of Scripture

SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE.

IV. Most of the sayings of the sacred book asserting the universality of the calling can be included in two classes or theses, of which this is the first.

FIRST. God truly and sincerely calls all men. To this pertain the following testimonies. Isa. 55:1. All you who thirst, come to the waters, and you who have no silver, hasten, buy and eat: come, buy without silver, and without any exchange, wine and milk. Matt. 11:28. Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Matt. 28:19. Go and teach all nations. Mark 16:15. Preach the Gospel to every creature: in which word lies an emphasis, as if Christ were saying: Whatever of the creatures can hear the Gospel, to them you ought to announce it. For thus it is explained in Matt. 28:19. Luke 24:27. Man is called, according to Gregory, a creature, on account of excellence and κατ' ἐξοχὴν [by way of eminence]. Luke 24:27. Thus it behooved Christ to suffer and to rise again from the dead the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins be preached in his name to all nations. Acts 17:30. The times of this ignorance God overlooked: but now he announces that all men everywhere should repent. Col. 1:28. We announce Christ, admonishing every man and teaching every man in all wisdom, that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus. All these sayings are so clear that anyone not completely blinded understands that God seriously calls all to repentance through his word, and therefore wills that not only the elect, but all who hear, should be converted through it, and be eternally saved.

V. SECOND: God truly and sincerely calls even the reprobate and those who are to perish. We confirm this thesis with these testimonies; Ps. 95. v. 8. Today if you will hear his voice, harden not your hearts. Prov. 1. v. 24. I have called, and you refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded, you have despised all my counsel. Isa. 1. v. 16. Wash you, make you clean, put away the evil of your doings from before mine eyes &c. Isa. 26. v. 10. Let grace be offered to the wicked, yet will he not learn righteousness. Isa. 55. v. 6. 7. Seek ye the Lord while he may be found, call ye upon him while he is near. Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts, and let him return unto the Lord, and he will have mercy upon him, and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon. Isa. 65. v. 2. I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people. And v. 12. I called, and ye did not answer, I spake, and ye did not hear, and did evil before mine eyes, and did choose that wherein I delighted not. Isa. 66. v. 4: I called, and there was none to answer: I spake, and they did not hear: but they did evil before mine eyes, and chose that wherein I delighted not. Hear the word of the Lord, ye that tremble at his word. Jer. 7. v. 13. I spake unto you, rising up early and speaking, but ye heard not. v. 14. And I called you, but ye answered not. v. 15. And I have sent unto you all my servants the prophets, daily rising up early and sending them. v. 26. And they hearkened not unto me, nor inclined their ear, but hardened their neck. Ezek. 33. v. 11. I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn ye, turn ye from your evil ways; for why will ye die, O house of Israel? Joel 2. v. 12. Turn ye even to me with all your heart. Zech. 1. v. 3. 4. Thus saith the Lord: Turn ye unto me, saith the Lord of hosts: and I will turn unto you, saith the Lord of hosts. Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried, saying: Thus saith the Lord of hosts: Turn ye now from your evil ways, and from your evil doings: but they did not hear, nor hearken unto me, saith the Lord. Matt. 3. v. 8: John addresses the wicked thus: Bring forth fruits meet for repentance. Matt. 23. v. 37. How often would I have gathered thy children together, and ye would not? Luke 7. v. 30: The Pharisees are said to have rejected the counsel of God, not having been baptized by John. But what indeed was that counsel? For both, this very thing, that God through the preaching and Baptism of John wished to call them to repentance, and to the kingdom of the Messiah, Luke 7, v. 16. They are also invited by those who do not wish to come, Apoc. 3, v. 20. Behold I stand at the door and voice and opens the door to me, I will enter to him, and will dine with him, and he with me. Since, therefore, it is evidently established from all that has been said that God seriously calls even the impious and all the unfaithful to repentance, the universality of the call certainly cannot be denied without manifest impiety.

Latin:

DICTA SCRIPTVRÆ.

IV. Pleráque sacri codicis dicta vniuersalitatem vocationis adstruentia duabus classibus aut thesibus includi possunt, quarum hæc est.

PRIMA. Deus verè & sincerè vocat omnes homines. Huc pertinent sequentia testimonia. Esa. 55. v. 1. Omnes sitientes venite ad aquas, & qui non habetis argentum, properate, emite & comedite: venite, emite absque argento, & absque vlla commutatione vinum & lac, Matt: 11. vers. 28. Venite ad me omnes, qui laboratis & onerati estis, & ego reficiam vos. Matt. 28: v. 19: Ite & docete omnes gentes. Marc. 16. v. 15. Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ : in qua voce latet emphasis, quasi dicat Christus: Quodcunque ex creaturis Euangelium audire potest, illi debetis annunciate. Sic enim explicatur Matth. 28. v. 19. Luc. 24. v. 27: Dicitur autem homo secundum Gregorium creatura, propter excellentiam & κατ' ἐξοχὴν Luc. 24. v. 27. Sic oportebat Christum pati & resurgere a mortuis tertio die, & prædicari in nomine eius pœnitentiam & remissionem peccatorum in omnes gentes Act. 17. v. 30. Tempora huius ignorantiæ dissimulauit Deus: nunc autem annunciat, vt omnes vbique homines resipiscant. Col. 1. v. 28. Annunciamus Christum, admonentes omnem hominem & docentes omnem hominem in omni sapientia, vt exhibeamus omnem hominem perfectum in Christo Iesu. Quæ dicta omnia tàm clara sunt, vt quiuis non plane occœcatus intelligat, Deum seriò per verbum suum omnes ad pœnitentiam vocare, adeóque velle, vt non tantum electi, sed omnes qui audiunt, per illud conuertantur, & æternum salui fiant.

V. SECVNDA: Deus verè & sincerè vocat etiam reprobos ac perituros. Quam thesin hisce testimonijs confirmamus; Psal. 95. v. 8. Hodie si audieritis vocem Domini, ne obduretis corda vestra. Prou. 1. v. 24. Vocavi & renuistis; extendi manum meam, & non erat, qui aspiceret, despexistis omne consilium meum Esai. 1. v. 16. Lauamini, mundi estote, aufertemalum cogitationum vestrarum ab oculis meis &c. Esai. 26. v. 10. Gratia offerretur impio, nec tamen discet iustitiam. Esai. 55. v. 6. 7. Quærite Dominum, dum inueniri potest, inuocate eum, dum prope est, Derelinquat impius viam suam, & vir iniquus cogi.ationes suas, reuertatur ad Dominum, & miserebitur eius, & ad Deum nostrum, quoniam multus est ad ignos-endum. Esai. 65. v. 2. Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum incredulum. Et v. 12. Vocaui, & non respond istis, locutus sum, & non audiuistis, & faciebatis malum in oculis meis, & quæ nolui elegistis. Esai. 66. v. 4: Vocaui, & non erat, qui responderet: Locutus sum, & non audierunt: feceruntque malum in oculis meis, & quæ nolui, elegerunt. Audite verbum Domini, qui tremitis ad verbum eius. Ierem: 7. v. 13. Locutus sum manè consurgens, & loquens ad eos, & non audistis. v. 14. Et vocaui vos, & non respondistis. v. 15. Et misi ad vos omnes seruos meos Prophetas, per diem, consurgens diluculo & mittens. v. 26. Et non audierunt me, nec inclinauerunt aurem suam, sed indurauerunt ceruicem suam. Ezech. 33. v. 11. Nolo mortem impij, sed vt conuertatur impius à via sua & viuat, Conuertimini, conuertimini à viis vestris pessimis: & quare moriemini domus Israel? Ioel. 2. v. 12. Conuertimini ad me in toto corde vestro. Zach. 1. v. 3. 4. Hæc dicit Dominus: Conuertimini ad me, ait Dominus exercituum: & conuertar ad vos, dicit Dominus exercituum. Ne sitis sicut patres vestri, ad quos clamabant Prophetæ priores, dicentes: Hæc dicit Dominus exercituum: Conuertimini de viis vestris malis, & de cogitationibus vestris pessimis: non audierunt, neque attenderunt ad me, dicit Dominus. Matth. 3. v. 8: Iohannes impios sic alloquitur Facite fructus dignos pœnitentiæ. Matt. 24. v. 37. Quoties volui filios tuos congregare, & noluisti? Luc. 7. v. 30: Pharisæi dicuntur sprevisse consilium Dei, non baptizati à Iohanne. Quod nam verò erat istud consilium? Vtrique hoc ipsun quòd Deus per concionem & Baptismum Iohannis voluit eos vocare ad pœnitentiam, & ad regnum Messiæ, Luc. 74. v. 16. Inuitantur etiam ijs, qui venire nolunt, Apoc. 3. v 20. Ecce sto ad ostium & pulso, si quis audierit vocem meam, & apperuerit mihi ianuam, intrabo ad illum, & cænabo cum illo, & ipse mecum. Cùm ergo ex dictis omnibus euidenter constet, Deum impios quoque & infideles omnes seriò vocare ad pœnitentiam, vtique vocationis vuiuersalitas citra manifestam impietatem negari non potest.


### Question II. Is the merit of Christ and the salvation acquired by that merit…: Reasons

REASONS.

VI. 1. From the truth and sincerity of God. God is not a hypocrite or a simulator: He would be such, if outwardly he offered grace to men, but inwardly decreed that he did not want those to whom he offers his grace to become participants of the same. Indeed, would he not be a deluder of men, calling all to embrace grace in his word, while excluding some from that grace by a secret decree? Not otherwise than if someone should draw up a Testament, and willingly exclude someone from the bequeathed goods by an inviolable decree, nevertheless offer those testamentary goods to him, pretending, nay swearing, that he does not desire him to be excluded, but included, when yet within the pages of the Testament he has sanctioned that this person is always to be excluded: would he not be held as a deluder, deservedly and by the best right? Ursinus in part 2 of the Catechetical Explanations is forced to admit this on page 226 in these words: He who calls all, and yet does not want all to come to him, or to save those coming to him, is to be called a simulator, a player, and a deceiver.

VII. 2. From the contempt of grace. Whomever the grace of God does not reach, they cannot despise it, and vice versa. But the unfaithful and those to be damned despise the grace of God, Prov. 1, v. 24. I have called, and you have refused.

Heb. 10:29. Of how much worse punishment do you suppose will he be thought worthy who has insulted the Spirit of grace? Rom. 2:8. To those who are self-seeking and do not obey the truth, but obey unrighteousness—indignation and wrath, etc. Therefore, the grace and promise of God pertain even to the unfaithful and those who are to be damned.

VIII. 3. From the danger of despair. If the promise of reconciliation pertains to a few, the consolation of sinners will be uncertain: for the mind will always remain in doubt whether the promise pertains to itself as well, since it is said to pertain to very few: which is certainly a step closest to despair.

IX. 4. From the perception of the Sacraments. By the Sacraments or through the Sacraments, the grace of God is offered. But not only the elect, but also many who are to be damned use the Sacraments. Therefore, it is offered not only to the elect, but also to many who are to be damned through the Sacraments; indeed, through Baptism, the grace of God is conferred upon every infant.

X. 5. From the damnation of the unfaithful. Whoever is damned is damned because of unbelief. This is the condemnation of the world, that light has come into the world, and the world loved darkness more than light, John 3:19. Unbelief, however, is nothing other than the refusal to believe that the grace which is offered to the world pertains to oneself. Therefore, those who are damned because of unbelief are damned for this reason: because they did not want to apprehend the grace of God, but despised it. Wherefore, this grace truly and in reality pertains to them; otherwise, they could not be damned for the reason that they did not want to apprehend it.

XI. 6. From the damnation of those who once had faith. To those who believe, the divine promises truly pertain. But many are damned who once believed. We prove this: 1. Sinners against the Holy Spirit perish. These, however, once believed, concerning which see chapters 6 and 10 of Hebrews. 2. Luke 8:13: They believe for a time, and in time of temptation fall away. Note the word 'fall away,' which indicates that the faith was true, not feigned, otherwise it could not be said that they withdrew. 3. Judas was condemned, Judas believed: Therefore someone who believed is condemned. I prove the minor premise from John 17, v. 12. Father, those whom you gave me, I have kept, and none of them perished, except the son of perdition. Judas, therefore, was given to Christ by the Father. If this is so, he was certainly pious and believing: And if he perished from the flock, certainly before he perished, he was numbered in the flock of Christ. For if he never believed, he certainly was never in the flock of the faithful: If this is so, how shall he be said to have perished from them? 4. Simon Magus, Acts 8, v. 13, is said to have believed in Christ, and yet afterwards he wanted to buy the gift of pouring out the Holy Spirit with money. 5. All infants are effectively called and regenerated by Baptism, yet many when they reach age, in turn fall back, and perish eternally. Therefore, an effective calling is not restricted to the elect and those to be saved alone.

Latin:

RATIONES.

VI. 1. A Dei veritate & sinceritate. Deus non est hypocrita aut simulator: Esset autem talis, si foris, hominib⁹ offerret gratiam, intus autem decerneret, se nolle illos, quibus gratiam suam offert, fieri eiusdem participes. Imò annòn foret delusor hominum, omnes ad amplectandam gratiam in verbo suo vocans, à gratiâ tamen illâ quosdam arcano decreto excludens. Non secus ac si quis Testamentum condat, & aliquem volenter per inviolabile decretum à bonis legatis excludat, nihilominùs tamen ipsi bona illa testamentaria offerat, simulans imò iurans, non se cupere eum exclusum, sed inclusum, cùm tamen intus in tabulis Testamenti sanxêrit, hunc semper excludendum: annòn hic pro delusore, merito atque optimo iure haberetur? Vrsinus parte 2. Explicat. Catechet. hoc fateri cogitur pag. 226. his verbis: Qui omnes vocat, nec tamen vult omnes ad se venire, aut ad se venientes seruare, is simulare, ludere & imponere dicendus est.

VII. 2. A comtemtu gratiæ. Quoscunque gratia Dei non attinet, illi nequeunt eam contemnere, & contrà. Atqui infideles & damnandi contemnunt gratiam Dei, Prou. 1. v. 24. Vocaui, & renuistis.

Hebr. 10. v. 29. Quanto magis putatis deteriora mereri supplicia, qui Spiritui gratiæ contumeliam fecerit? Rom. 2. v. 8. Hiis, qui veritati non obtemperant, sed injustitiæ, ventura est indignatio, &c. Ergò infideles etiam & damnandos attinet Dei gratia & promissio.

VIII. 3. A periculo desperationis. Si ad paucos reconciliationis promissio pertinet, consolatio peccatorum erit incerta: semper enim in ambiguo hærebit animus, vtrum ad se quoque promissio pertineat, siquidem paucissimos attinere dicitur: qui sanè proximus est ad desperationem gradus.

IX. 4. A perceptione Sacramentorum. Sacramentis vel per Sacramenta offertur gratia Dei. Atqui non soli electi, sed multi quoque damnandi vtuntur Sacramentis. Ergò non solis electis, sed multis quoque damnandis per Sacramenta offertur, imò per Baptismum infantibus singulis confertur gratia Dei.

X. 5. A damnatione infidelium. Quicunque damnantur: propter incredulitatem damnantur. Hæc estati est condemnatio mundi, quòd lux venit in mundum, & mundus pliùs dilexit tenebras, quàm lucem Ioh. 3. v. 19 Incredulitas autem nihil est aliud quàm nolle credere, ad se pertinere gratiam, quæ offertur mundo. Ergò qui damnantur propter incredulitatem, ideò damnantur, quia noluerunt gratiam Dei apprehendere, sed eam contempserunt. Quare ad illos verè & reipsa spectat hæc gratia, alias non ideò damnari possent, quia noluerint istam apprehendere.

XI. 6. A damnatione eorum, qui aliquando fidem habuerunt. Qui credunt, ad illos reuerâ pertinent promissiones diuinæ. At multi damnantur, qui aliquando crediderunt. Probamus 1. Peccatores in Spiritum sanctum pereunt. Hi verò aliquando crediderunt, de quo videatur c. 6. & 10. ad Hebr. 2. Luc. 8 v. 13: Ad tempus credunt, & in tempore tentationis recedunt. Nota vocabulum recedendi, quòd indicat veram fuisse fidem, non simulatam, alias dici non posset, quod recederent. 3. Iudas, damnatus est, Iudas credidit: Ergo aliquis, qui credidit, damnatur. Minorem probo ex Ioh. 17. v. 12. Pater quos dedisti mihi, custodiui, & nemo ex ijs perijt, nisi filius perditionis. Iudas igitur Christo fuit a Patre datus. Si hoc, vtique pius erat & credulus: Et si perijt ex grege, certe antequam periret, in grege Christi numerabatur. Si enim nunquam credidit, certe nunquam fuit in grege fidelium: Si hoc, quomodo ex eis perijsse dicetur? 4. Simon Magus Act. 8. v. 13. dicitur credidisse in Christum, & tamen postea volebat donum effundendi Spiritum sanctum pecunia emere. 5. Omnes infantes p Baptismum efficaciter vocantur & regenerantur, multi tamen cum ad ætatem perueniunt, vicissim resiliunt, & æternum pereunt. Vocatio ergo efficax ad solos electos & saluandos non est restricta.


### Question II. Is the merit of Christ and the salvation acquired by that merit…: Testimonies

TESTIMONIES.

XII. 1. Clement of Alexandria in his Exhortatory Oration to the Gentiles, past the middle: Hear, you who are far off, hear, you who are near, the Word is hidden from none, it is a common light, it shines upon all men, there is no Cimmerian in the Word.

2. Ambrose, book 2, on the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 10. No part of the world is void of the Gospel of Christ: And although that general calling does not cease, yet this special one also is now universal and has become common.

3. Eusebius, book 1, on the preparation for the Gospel. The Word, God sent by almighty God, announces to all the saving conversion of men to God and friendship. Not from here or elsewhere, but from all nations, he calls together Greeks and Barbarians, every sex, every age, rich and poor, the wise and the contrary, free and slaves, with a loud voice, and urges with all zeal that we should undertake this good.

OBJECTIONS of the Calvinists.

XIII 1. Psalm 147, v. 20. He announces his word to Jacob, and his justices to the people of Israel: he hath not done in like manner to every nation, and his judgments he hath not made manifest to them, etc.

Resp. He does not speak absolutely, but comparatively; 'He hath not done in like manner,' and therefore the nations were not simply excluded. They were indeed called, but not in like manner as the Jews. For the Psalmist speaks of the external ministry, namely, that to the nations in the Old Testament the word of God was not announced by Prophets, as it was to the Israelites. Meanwhile, they were not entirely excluded. For God revealed Himself to the Gentiles through created things in such a way that they are without excuse, Rom. 1, v. 19, in that, subsisting in their vanity, they did not inquire more studiously into the knowledge of the truth.

2. That God did not send forth Prophets, nor through them manifest His judgments to the nations, the cause is not some absolute decree by which He determined to pass over those nations, but vindictive justice, by which He punished the contempt of His word. For because He had once called the Gentiles through an external ministry, both in Adam and in the posterity of Noah, but they neglected this, and thus through carelessness lost it, therefore by this removal of His word He justly punished that ingratitude: although meanwhile they were not simply excluded from the Church. For those who wished could betake themselves to it, as examples testify. But how those nations were called, will be said more broadly in question 3.

3. That God chose the Israelite people above others as His own possession, the cause is not any dignity of that people, to which God could have looked, but His mere and gratuitous φιλανθρωπία [philanthropia]. For He wished always to cherish and preserve the Church in this world. Now if He had called it out from other peoples, a petulant reason would in turn ask, Why did He collect His Church from these, and not from others? Therefore, here we flee to the sole good pleasure of God, the cause of which can be hidden, but cannot be in that [good pleasure]. And here and in similar cases one must exclaim with the Apostle Rom. 11. v. 33. O the depth!

XIV. 2. Isaiah 55. v. 11. My word shall not return void; but it shall do whatsoever I have willed, it shall prosper in those things to which I sent it. But indeed, among the impenitent it produces no fruit. Therefore God did not will that it should do so, nor did He send it for this purpose.

Resp. 1. He speaks of the word, such as it is by itself and its own nature, but not such as it becomes by accident, on account of the unbelief of men. 2. It is not a discourse about individual hearers, but it is only noted that it never returns void, but always bears fruit, (as it is sent to bear fruit,) if not among all, yet among some.

XV. 3. Ezekiel 3. v. 6. If you were sent to them; they would listen. Therefore God, by denying the ministry, is the cause of their impenitence.

Resp. This discourse is not about ordinary conversion, but about the extraordinary mission of the Prophets, to which God is not obligated, which also detracts nothing from His beneficent will.

XVI. 4. Matthew 11. v. 21. If the mighty works had been done in Tyre and Sidon, which were done in you, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes. Therefore God did not offer the Tyrians and Sidonians such grace, by which they could have been moved to repentance.

Resp. N. C. For even if the Tyrians and Sidonians were not called in that extraordinary way through so many miracles, it does not follow that they were not called in any way at all, nor in an ordinary way. For just as the Sodomites had Lot, a preacher of righteousness: so the Tyrians and Sidonians were neighbors to the Israelite people, into whose worship they could have inquired as easily as Hiram, King of Tyre, once did, a friend of David and Solomon, whose mind was imbued with the true religion. Thus also an absolute hatred of God cannot be inferred, because He did not give that by which they would have been converted. For our question is about the ordinary mode of salvation, which is denied to no one, not the extraordinary and miraculous, as it applies to few. Therefore it does not follow: God did not perform miracles among the Tyrians. Therefore He did not wish them to be saved: Nay, He wished for their conversion, but an ordinary one. But for just reasons He did not wish to save them miraculously and immediately. We say, therefore, briefly, that one must not argue from the denial of an extraordinary will to the denial of an ordinary will.

Latin:

TESTIMONIA.

XII. 1. Clemens Alexandrinus in Orat. Exhortator. ad gentes vltra medium: Audite, qui estis longe, audite, qui prope, nullis celatum est verbum, lux est communis, omnibus illucescit hominibus, nullus est in verbo Cimmerius.

2. Ambros. l. 2. de voc. gen. c. 10. Nulla pars mundi ab Euang. vacat Christi: Et licet illa generalis vocatio non quiecat, tamen & ista specialis iam vniuersa est & facta communis.

3. Eusebius l. 1. de præparat. Ev. Salutarem hominum ad Deum conuersionem & amicitiam, ab omnipotenti Deo missus Deus verbum cunctis annunciat Non hinc aut aliunde, sed cunctis ex gentibus Græcos & Barbaros, omnem sexum, omnem ætatem diuites, & pauperes, sapientes & contrà, liberos & seruos, magna voce conuocat, hortaturq; omni studio, vt hoc bonum suscipiamus.

OBIECTIONES CALVInianorum.

XIII 1. Psal. 147. v. 20. Annunciat verbum suum Iacob, & justitias suas populo Israel: taliter non fecit omni nationi, & judicia sua non manifestavit eis, &c.

Resp. Non loquitur absolutè, sed comparatè, Non fecit taliter, ideoque gentes non erant simpliciter exclusae. Vocabantur quidem, sed non taliter, ut Judaei. Loquitur enim Psaltes de externo ministerio, nempè quod gentibus in veteri Testamento non fuerit per Prophetas annunciatum Dei verbum, sicut Israelitis. Interim ipsi non excludebantur penitùs. Nam Deus per creaturas Ethnicis ita se revelavit, vt sint inexcusabiles, Rom. 1. v. 19. eò quod in vanitate sua subsistentes in cognitionem veritatis studiosiùs non inquisierint.

2. Quòd Deus Prophetas non emisit, neque per hos judicia sua manifestavit gentibus, causa non est absolutum aliquod decretum, quo constitutit, gentes istas praeterire, sed vindex justitia, qua comtemtum verbi sui puniuit. Quia enim semel tum in Adamo tum in posteritate Noachi per externum ministerium Ethnicos vocauerat, ipsi verò hoc neglexerunt, & sic per incuriam amisitrunt, ideò hac verbi sui ablatione ingratitudinem illam iustè vindicauit: quamuis interea non essent simpliciter exclusi ab Ecclesia. Poterant enim ad eam se conferre, qui volebant, vti testantur Exempla. Sed quomodo gentes istae vocatæ sint, quæst. 3. dicetur latiùs.

3. Quòd populum Israeliticum Deus præ cęteris elegit in peculium, causa non est aliqua dignitas istius populi, ad quam Deus potuisset respicere, sed mera eius & gratuita φιλανθρωπία. Voluit enim in hoc mundo semper fouere & conseruare Ecclesiam. Iam si ex alijs istam euocasset populis, vicissim petulca ratio quæreret, Cur ex ijs, non alijs suam Ecclesiam collegisset? Proinde hic ad solum Dei beneplacitum confugimus, cuius causa occulta esse potest, in ista esse non potest. Atque hic & in similibus casibus exclamandum est cùm Apostolo Rom. 11. v. 33. O altitudo!

XIV. 2. Esai: 55. v. 11. Verbum meum non revertetur vacuum; sed faciet, quæcunque volui, prosperabitur in his, ad quæ misi illud. At verò apud impœnitentes fructum facit nullum. Ergo Deus non voluit, vt faceret, nec ad hoc misit.

Resp. 1. Loquitur de verbo, quale per se & naturam suam est, non autem, quale ex accidente fit, ob incredulitatem hominum. 2. Non est sermo de singulis auditoribus, sed notatur tantùm, quòd nunquam redeat vacuũ, sed semper fructificet, (vti ad fructificandũ mittitur,) sinon apud omnes, tamen apud aliquos.

VX. 3. Ezech. 3. v: 6. Si ad illos mittereris; ipsi audirent. Ergò Deus denegando ministerium, causa est impœnitentiæ eorum

Resp. Sermo hic est non de ordinaria conuersione, sed extraordinaria Prophetarum missione, ad quam Deus obligatus non est, quæ etiam ipsius beneficæ voluntati nihil derogat.

XVI, 4. Matth. 11. v. 21. Si in Tyro & Sidone factę essent virtutes, quæ facta sunt in vobis, olim in cilicio & cinere pœnitentiam egissent. Ergo Deus non obtulit Tyrijs & Sidonijs tantam gratiam, quâ potuissent ad pœnitentiam commoueri.

Resp. N. C. Etsi enim isto extraordinario modo per tot miracula non fuerint vocati Tyrij & Sidonij, non tamen sequitur, quòd nullo prorsus modo, neque ordinario vocati fuerint. Nam vti Sodomitæ habuerunt Lothum, iustitiæ præconem: ita Tyrij & Sidonij erant vicini populo Israelitico, in cuius cultum tàm facilè poterant inquirere, quàm facilè olim Hiram Rex Tyri, amicus Dauidis & Salomonis, cuius mens verâ religione fuit imbuta. Sic etiam nequit colligi absolutũ Dei odium, quia non dedit id, quo dato fuissent conversi. Nostra enim quæstio Est de modo salutis ordinario, qui nulli denegatur, non extaordinario & miraculoso quam paucis competit. Quare non sequitur: Deus miracula non edidit inter Tyrios. Ergò eos saluari noluit: Imò conuersionem ipsorum voluit, sed ordinariam. Miraculosè autem & immediatè eos saluare iustis de causis noluit. Dicimus ergò breuiter, quòd à negatione voluntatis extraordinariæ ad negationem voluntatis ordinariæ non sit argumentandum.


### Question II. Is the merit of Christ and the salvation acquired by that merit…: XVII. 5. Luke 8, v. 10. To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to others by parables, that seeing they may…

XVII. 5. Luke 8, v. 10. To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to others by parables, that seeing they may not see, etc.

Resp. 1. The purpose of the parables was not that the word should be obscured, but rather that it should be illustrated; Mark 4, v. 3. He spoke by parables; as they were able to hear. Hence Varinus: παραβολὴ παράθεσις ἐστιν ὁμοιωματικὴ ἐπὶ σαφηνείᾳ τῶν ὑποκειμένων.

2. The people, having heard that sermon about the fourfold seed, departed, nor did they seek an explanation from Christ. But the Apostles and certain other pious ones desired the ἐξήγησιν of that parabolic sermon. And for that reason Christ says, To you (namely, those seeking an explanation) it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven: to the rest (who value my sermons so little) let there be not the mystical understanding of the parable, but only the parable spoken according to the letter, without any understanding of it, so that they may pay the just penalties for their pernicious sloth. For not only the disciples asked, but also others, as Mark testifies in ch. 4, v. 10; otherwise only the disciples would have been converted and illuminated, which is false. Briefly, therefore, we distinguish between γραμματικὴν and πνευματικὴν knowledge of the mysteries: the former is not denied to others, but only the latter, because they placed an obstacle.

XVIII. 6. John 17, v. 6. I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. But not all are given to Christ. Therefore the name of the Father is not manifested to all. Therefore not all are called.

Resp. Just as the calling, so also the manifestation is twofold is: For it either denotes the announcement of the divine name or a saving announcement apprehended by faith, in which sense the Gospel is said to be manifested to little ones and hidden from the wise of this age, Matt. 11. v. 15. and 2. Cor. 2. v. 8. This one is particular, that one is universal. Therefore, just as this one does not take away that one, so neither will that one be able to abolish this one.

XIX. 7. Acts 16. v. 6. Paul and Silas are forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia, and when they attempted to go into Bithynia, the Spirit did not permit them. Thus Matt. 10. v. 5. Do not go into the way of the Gentiles and do not enter into the city of the Samaritans. Therefore God did not will, nor does He will, that all men be called.

Response: N. C. [Non Consequitur]. God at this time does not will the Gospel to be preached in these or those nations, therefore He does not will it simply. There is, I say, no consequence here. For history itself testifies to the contrary. For that the Gospel was later preached in Asia also and Bithynia is evident from 1 Pet. 1 verse 1 and Rev. 1 and 2. Thus the Gentiles and Samaritans were not simply deprived of the preaching of the Gospel. For those who dwelt in Judea and Galilee often heard the sermons of Christ. Thus John 4, the Messiah had a conversation with the Samaritan woman, from which many from that city were converted to Christ. But the fact that the Gospel was not announced to the Gentiles by the Apostles immediately at the first time, the reason is 1. because the promise concerning the Messiah was made peculiarly to the Jews, therefore it was necessary to speak the word of God to them first, Acts 13. v. 46. 2. because Christ had to be a minister of the circumcision, Rom. 15. v. 8. By reason, therefore, of the ministerial and pastoral office, Christ had to preach the Gospel primarily to the Jews (although His priestly office pertained to all men), from which it followed that at that time it was not permitted for the disciples, who had to adhere to their master, to preach ordinarily anywhere other than in Judea. Thus also for those who were in Asia & Bithynia, the Gospel was not preached at the very first moment, the cause was not an absolute rejection of any of those nations, but the foreknowledge of greater benefit in Macedonia. Hence Ambrose rightly: Grace was not denied to those peoples, but as much as appeared, it was delayed. For the Gospel was to be preached to every nation, but because that could not be done simultaneously and at once, therefore it was to be announced successively to one nation after another. But in whichever nation the Evangelical doctrine could obtain more benefit, in that it was to be preached first, an example of which thing is read in Acts 18, v. 10, where the Lord encouraged Paul through a vision to stay in Corinth and preach the word confidently, Because, he says, I have many people in this city. And if Paul, at the time when he was going not into Asia, but into Macedonia, had set out into Asia, the reason would in turn be sought, Why did God not send Paul into Macedonia, just as into Asia? We say, therefore, that this was done by the singular counsel of God. For since the Gospel could not be preached in the whole world at the same time, therefore God willed it to be announced first to those nations in which He foresaw He would accomplish more.

XX. 8. Acts 17. v. 30. The times of this ignorance God overlooked, but now He announces to all men, that all everywhere should repent.

Resp. Nothing else is proven in this place than that God did not manifest Himself to the nations in any particular way in the Old Testament, namely by sending Prophets, giving the law, performing miracles, etc. But it is not said that nothing at all was known to the nations about God. For He did not leave Himself without witness, Acts 14, v. 16,

XXI. 9. 1. Corinth. 1. v. 26. Consider your calling, brethren, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, but God chose the foolish things of the world. Therefore the calling is particular.

Resp. 1. This passage speaks of the calling, in so far as it is equivalent to election, and contains within it the acceptance and faith of men. For calling is sometimes taken for mere invitation, as far as it is on the part of God, and in this respect it is universal: sometimes for a calling that includes at the same time the obedience of men, as in Rom. 8:30, 'Whom he predestined, them he also called.' And in this sense it is particular. If the term 'called' also denotes: 1. All men who are invited to the heavenly wedding, and are called in Greek κεκλημένοι. 2. The visible assembly of the Church, in which there are many hypocrites; in which sense the Apostle Paul uses the term κλητῶν when he addresses his epistles to the called Christians. 3. Those who obey the call of God and apprehend it with firm faith, who are called κλητοὶ according to the πρόθεσιν, the counsel and decree of God.

XXII. 10. Scripture denies that Ishmael and Esau are children of the promise, Beza part 2, Response to the Acts, page 209.

Response. This is an ignorance of the refutation: We are inquiring about promises concerning eternal things: they bring forward examples of promises speaking of temporal things. Therefore, there is no connection in this argument. And however much those promises concerning the birthright are applied by Paul in Rom. 9 to the promises of eternal life, that is done only τυπικῶς and comparatively, nor are Ishmael and Esau excluded on that account from spiritual promises. For they are not brought forward by Paul as examples of spiritual reprobation, but only as types.

XXIII. 11. God is omniscient: Therefore He foresaw who would persist in sins, and who would not: If this is so, how can He seriously call to salvation those whom He foresaw would be stubborn and would remain in infidelity?

Response. This argument is opposed to Scripture itself. For we know from the revelation of the Word that God is able to do this, in which both things are stated, that God is omniscient, and of all things and events foreknowing of future things; at the same time also that all men wish to be saved, to send the Son to all, to offer His grace to all. There is, therefore, no consequence: God foresees that many will be resistant to the divine calling. Therefore He does not call them seriously: For someone could conclude in the same way: The magistrate knows that not all will obey the laws. Therefore he does not seriously promulgate his laws to all. The Prince, who seriously wishes to restore to liberty, through the intervention of a certain ransom, the Christians held captive in Turkey, and to adopt them as subjects, knows that not all will accept that grace, nor will all come to him. Must it therefore be said that he does not seriously desire the liberty of all the Christians who are held captive among the Turkish Tyrant?

XXIV. 12. All are deaf and blind: But why are some of these not healed, the cause certainly is not in them, but in God who heals. Resp. Nay, it is in them; for when they do not wish to use the means which the physician prescribes, then certainly they are not healed. Although, therefore, all are equal by reason of original blindness; they are nevertheless unequal by reason of actual blindness. For those who do not wish to use the means; they are not only originally, but also actually blind and deaf.

XXV. 13. If God were to call all seriously through His word, certainly all would conceive faith from the heard word. Resp. There is no connection in the major premise: because the cause, why some are not converted from the heard word, does not lie in some absolute and hidden decree of God, but rests with the hearing men themselves. This is taught by Christ through the Parable of the fourfold field, Matt. 13 v. 3, Luke 8 v. 5, in which parable it is shown that the cause, why the seed does not bear fruit in every field, is not situated in the seed, nor in the sower, but only in the field receiving the seed, that is, all the fault is situated in the hearers, who do not hear the word of God with equal zeal, and therefore do not bear fruit from it equally.
