For one has a hard heart that is, hearing the word negligently and sleepily, where the devil comes and takes that away. Another has a heart sown with rocks and stones, that is, he indeed receives the word with joy, but because it has no roots, therefore he believes for a time, and when temptation arises, he fails. Another has a heart wrapped in thorns and thickets, that is, he indeed hears the word, but in such a way that the thorns of pleasures and riches choke it, so that it cannot bear fruit. And what other many impediments there are, by which the power of the word is also retarded, see these in Hunnius on predestination, page 218. And it is notably said in that parable, not that he sowed his seed by the wayside, or upon the rock, but that the seed having fallen, it fell in such a way. For some of the hearers receive the word just as seed is received falling by the wayside or upon the rock.

Nor, however, can the Papistic merit of congruity or man's free will in spiritual matters be inferred from this.

Not that. 1. Because we do not say that hearing is a merit, but only a means. For just as we are not justified Διὰ τὴν πίσιν, because of faith, but Διὰ τῆς πίσεως, through faith, so we are not converted Διὰ τὴν ἀκρόασιν, because of hearing, but Διὰ τῆς ἀκροάσεως, through hearing: the former has the nature of merit, the latter of a means. For God does not convert men ἐνθυσιαστικῶς, by an immediate impulse, but ἀκροᾶτικῶς, through the preached word. 2. We do not establish that man by his hearing anticipates the grace of God; but rather this anticipates him. For God gave ears, the organs of hearing; He gave the word, the object of hearing; He gave ministers, announcing the word; and He implanted the efficacy of converting. For if a man were to hear the Gospel for a hundred continuous years, and God had not ordained to give faith through that listening, certainly not even the slightest bit of faith would ever be kindled in the hearts of the hearers. Therefore, our hearing is not an efficient cause, nor a merit of faith, but only a means. For God has so ordained, that through the preached and heard word faith might be engendered in hearts.

Not this, because we do not say that internal hearing, defined by the assent of the mind and the obedience of the will, is placed in human powers, but only external [hearing], consisting in the effort of knowing, learning, and in some way meditating: which can be proven to be situated in the power of man, both by the sayings of Scripture and by examples. The sayings are: Luke 13, verse 24. Many will seek to enter, and will not be able. Amos 8, v. 11, A famine, not a famine of hearing the word: that is, a notable desire. The examples are: Herod, who gladly heard John the Baptist preaching, Mark 6, v. 20. Sergius the Proconsul, who desired to hear the word of God from Paul and Barnabas, Acts 13, v. 7. The Athenians, who wish to hear Paul, Acts 17, v. 20. Felix, who heard Paul with interest, Acts 24, v. 14. Thus Acts 8, verse 6, the crowds προσέχον [gave heed] to those things which were said by Philip. Therefore, the reason that not all who hear the word are converted is that many place an obstacle before the Holy Spirit, nor do they remove the hindrances by which the power of the word is impeded. This is what is hinted at in Prov. 1, v. 24; Isaiah 65, v. 2; Matt. 23, v. 38; Luke 7, v. 30; Acts 7, v. 51.

Furthermore, it is asked, How can the unregenerate hear the word with interest, when this is foolishness to the natural man, 1 Cor. 2, v. 14.

Response: By this saying, it is not external hearing that is disparaged, but only internal. For the words sound thus: The natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God, for it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand. The sense is that the ψυχικὸς [natural man] cannot have a true understanding of the word from his own powers; but it is not said that he cannot hear the letters of the word with interest. For the examples and sayings brought forward above testify to the contrary. And although the word of God at first glance may seem foolishness to the unregenerate, nevertheless when he attends even slightly, it cannot be but that his mind is struck by a certain clearly singular force and power, just as the example of Felix testifies. Therefore, when the hearers do not place an obstacle to this motion, God without any doubt works faith in them.

Latin:

XVII. 5. Luc. 8. v. 10. Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni cælorum, cæteris autem per parabolas, vt videntes non videant, &c.

Resp. 1. Parabolarum finis erat, non vt obscuraretur verbum, sed potiús illustraretur; Marc. 4. v. 3. locutus est per parabolas; prout poterant audire Hinc Varinus: παραβολὴ παράθεσις ἐστιν ὁμοιωματικὴ ἐπὶ σαφηνείᾳ τῶν ὑποκειμένων.

2. Populus audita ista de quadruplici semine concione discedebat, nec à Christo petebat explicationem. Apostoli verò & alij quidam pij desiderabant ἐξήγησιν istius parabolicæ concionis. Atque eam ob causam Christus inquit, Vobis (scilicet petentibus explicationem) datum est nosse mysteria regni cælorum: reliquis, (qui tàm floccifaciunt conciones meas) non parabolæ intelligentia mystica, sed tantùm parabola secundum literam dicta esto, sine omni eius intellectu, vt perniciosæ suæ oscitantiæ justas pœnas luant. Non enim soli discipuli interrogarunt, sed etiam alij, teste Marco c. 14. v. 10. aliàs soli discipuli essent conuersi & illuminati, quod falsum. Breuiter ergo distinguimus inter γραμματικὴν & πνευματικὴν mysteriorum scientiam: illa non denegatur alijs, sed hac duntaxat, quia ponebant obicem.

XVIII. 6. Ioh. 17. v. 6. Manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi de mundo. At non omnes Christo sunt dati. Ergò non omnibus manifestatur nomen Patris. Quare nec omnes vocantur.

Resp. Sicuti vocatio, ita & manifestatio duplexest: Vel enim notat annunciationem nominis divini vel annunciationem salutarem & fide apprehensam, quo sensu Euangelium paruulis manifestari & sapientibus huius seculi abscondi dicitur, Matth. 11. v. 15. & 2. Cor. 2. v. 8. Hæc particularis est, illa vniuersalis. Sicut igitur hæc non tollit istam, ita nec ista hanc abolere poterit.

XIX. 7. Act. 16. v. 6. Paulus & Silas prohibentur à Spiritu sancto loqui sermonem in Asia, & cùm tentarent ire in Bithyniam, non permisit eis Spiritus. Sic Matth. 10. v. 5. In vias gentium ne abieritis & in ciuitatem Samaritanorum ne ingrediamini. Ergò Deus non voluit, neque vult omnes vocari homines.

Resp. N. C. Deus hoc tempore non vult Euangelium prædicari in his vel illis nationibus, Ergò simpliciter non vult. Nulla, inquam, hîc est consequentia. Contrarium enim testatur ipsa historia. Nam quòd Euangelium postea prædicatũ fuerit in Asia quoque & Bithynia, patet ex 1. Pet. 1 vers. 1. & Apoc. 1. & 2. Sic gentes & Samaritani non simpliciter erant orbati prædicatione Euangelij. Etenim, quæ habitabant in Iudæa & Galilæa, sæpè audiuerunt conciones Christi. Sic Ioh. 4. Messias habuit colloquium cum muliere Samaritanâ, vnde multi ex ciuitate ista ad Christum sunt conuersi. Quod vero non statim primo tempore gentibus annunciatum fuerit Euangelium per Apostolos, causa est 1. quia Iudæis peculiariter erat facta promissio de Messia, ideò oportebat ipsis primùm loqui verbum Dei, Act. 13. v 46. 2. quia Christus debebat esse minister circumcisionis, Rom. 15. v. 8. Ratione ergo ministerialis & pastoralis officij, Christus debebat inprimis prædicare Euangelium Iudæis, (quamuis eius officium Sacerdotale vniuersos homines attinuerit) vnde consequebatur, vt isto tempore discipulis quoque, qui suo magistro debebant adhærere, non licuerit ordinariè alibi quã in Iudæa prædicare. Sic & ijs, qui fuerunt in Asia & Bithynia, non primo statim tempore prædicabatur Euangelium, causa non fuit absoluta quapiam earum gentium rejectio, sed præuisio maioris emolumenti in Macedonia. Hinc rectè Ambrosius: Non fuit negata illis populis gratia, sed quantum apparuit, retardata. Omni n. genti erat prędicandum Euangelium, quia verò illud simul & semel fieri non poterat, ideo successiuè vni nationi post alteram erat annunciandum. In qua verò gente plus poterat emolumenti consequi doctrina Euangelica, in ea priùs erat prædicanda, cuius rei simile exemplum legitur Act. 18. v. 10. vbi per visionem Dominus Paulum hortabatur, vt subsisteret Corinthi, & prædicaret sermonem confidenter, Quoniam inquit, populus est mihi multus in hac ciuitate. Et si Paulus tum, quando non in Asiam, sed Macedoniam abibat, in Asiam profectus fuisset, vicissim quæreret ratio, Cur Deus non misisset Paulum in Macedoniam, sicut Asiam? Dicimus ergo, hoc factu esse singulari consilio Dei. Quoniam enim simul in omni terraru orbe prędicari Euang. non poterat, ideò Deus ijs nationib. prius voluit annunciari, in quibus se plus effecturum præuidit.

XX. 8. Act. 17. v. 30. Tempora huius ignorantiæ dissimulauit Deus, nunc autem annunciat omnibus hominibus, ut omnes vbiq; e agant pœnitentiam.

Resp. Nihil aliud hoc loco euincitur, quam quòd Deus non aliquo particulari modo sese manifestauit in veteri Testamento gentibus, nempè mittendo Prophetas, dando legem, edendo miracula &c. Non autem dicitur, quòd gentibus planè nihil innotuerit de Deo. Non enim sine testimonio reliquit semetipsum, Act. 14. v. 16,

XXI. 9. 1. Corinth. 1. v. 26. Videte vocationem vestram fratres, quia non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, sed quæ stulta sunt mundi, elegit Deus. Ergò vocatio est particularis.

Resp. 1. Loquitur hic locus de vocatione, quatetus æquipollet electioni, & acceptionem fidemque hominum inclusam habet. Etenim vocatio quandoque sumitur pro sola inuitatione, quantum est ex parte Dei, & hac ratione vniuersalis est: quandoque pro vocatione includente simul hominum obsequium, vt Rom. 8. v. 30. Quos prædestinauit, hos vocauit. Et hoc sensu particularis est. Si etiam vocabulum vocati notat. 1. Omnes homines, qui inuitantur ad cælestes nuptias, & Græcè dicuntur κεκλημένοι. 2. Cœtum visibilem Ecclesiæ, in quo multi sunt hypocritæ; quo sensu vocabulum κλητῶν sumit Apostolus Paulus, quando suas epistolas inscribit vocatis Christianis. 3. Eos, qui vocationi Dei obtemperant, eamque firmâ fide apprehendunt, qui dicuntur κλητοὶ iuxta πρόθεσιν consilium & decretum Dei.

XXII. 10. Scriptura Ismaelem & Esau filios promissionis esse negat, Beza part. 2 Respons. ad Acta pag. 209

Respond. Est ignoratio Elenchi: Quærimus nos de promissionibus concernentibus res sempiternas: proferunt illi exempla promissionum de rebus temporaribus loquentium. Nulla igitur huic argumento inest connexio. Et quantumuis istæ promissiones de primogenitura, â Paulo Rom. 9. accommodentur ad promissiones de vita æterna, id tamen fit tantùm τυπικῶς & comparatè, nec ob id, Ismael & Esau excluduntur à promissionibus spiritualibus. Non enim à Paulo adducuntur, velut exempla reprobationis spiritualis, sed duntaxat vttypi.

XXIII. 11. Deus est omniscius: Ergò præuidit, qui in peccatis sint præstituri, qui non: Si hoc, quomodo eos, qui contumaces, & in infidelitate permansuros præuidit, seriò potest salutis causa vocare?

Resp. Opponitur hoc argumentum ipsi Scripturæ. Deum enim istud posse, scimus ex reuelatione verbi, in quo vtrumque dicitur, Deum esse omnicium, cunctarumque rerum & euentuum futurorum praescium; simul & omnes homines velle saluos fieri, omnibus mittere Filium, omnibus gratiam suam offerre. Nulla proinde est consequentia: Deus praeuidit, multos vocationi diuinae fore resistentes. Ergo eos non seriò vocat: Posset enim quispiam eodem modo concludere: Scit magistratus non omnes obtemperaturos legibus. Ergo non ad omnes seriò promulgat leges suas. Scit Princeps, qui Christianos in Turcia captiuos, interuentu certi lytri, seriò vult libertati restituere, & in subditos adoptare, non omnes istam gratiam accepturos, nec omnes ad se venturos. Ergòne propterea dicendum, quòd non seriò velit omnium Christianorum, qui apud Tyrannum Turcicum captiui detinentur, libertatem?

XXIV. 12. Omnes sunt surdi & caeci: Cur autem quidam ex his non sanentur, causa certè est non in ipsis, sed in sanante Deo. Resp. Imò in ipsis est; quando enim nolunt vti medijs, quae medicus praescribit, tum certè non sanantur. Quamuis ergò omnes pares sint ratione caecitatis originalis; impares tamen sunt ratione caecitatis actualis. Qui enim medijs vti nolunt; ij non modò originaliter, sed & actualiter caeci atque surdi sunt.

XXV. 13. Si Deus omnes seriò per verbum suum vocaret, vtiq; omnes ex audito verbo fidem conciperent. Resp. Nulla est connexio in maiore: quia causa, cur quidam ex audito verbo non conuertantur, non haeret in absoluto quodam & abscondito Dei decreto, sed penes ipsos homines audientes. Docetur hoc à Christo per Parabolam de quadruplici agro, Matth. 13. v. 3 Luc. 8. v. 5. in qua parabola ostenditur, causam, cur semen non in omni agro fructificet, non esse sitam in semine, non in seminante, sed tantùm in agro semen recipiente, id est, omnis culpa sita est in auditoribus, qui no pari studio audiunt verbum Dei, atq; idcircò nec pariter inde fructum ferunt. Alius enim habet cor tes ugum, negligenter & somnolenter audiens verbum, vbi diabolus venit & tollit istud. Alius cor habet petris & saxis consitum, hoc est, cum gaudio quidem suscipit verbum, sed quia radices non habet, ideo ad tempus credit, & ingruente tentatione deficit. Alius cor habet spinis & dumetis inuolutum, hoc est, audit quidem verbum, sed ita, vt spinæ voluptatum ac diuitiarum illud suffocent, quò fructum ferre haut possit. Et quæ sunt alia plura impedimenta, quibus & potentia verbi retardatur, quæ vide apud Hunnium de prædestin. pag. 218. Et notanter dicitur in ista parabola, non quod seminauerit suum semen secus viam, aut super petram, sed quod semen prolapsum ita ceciderit. Auditorum enim aliqui verbum ita recipiunt, sicuti semen recipitur secus viam aut super petram cadens.

Neque tamen hinc inferri potest vel meritum congrui Papisticum, vel liberum hominis in spiritualibus arbitrium.

Non illud 1. Quia nos non dicimus, auditum esse meritum, sed duntaxat medium. Sicut enim non Διὰ τὴν πίσιν, propter fidem, sed Διὰ τῆς πίσεως, per fidem justificamur, ita non Διὰ τὴν ἀκρόασιν sed Διὰ τῆς ἀκροάσεως conuertimur: illud meriti, hoc medij rationem habet. Nam Deus homines non conuertit ἐνθυσιαστικῶς, per immediatum pulsum, sed ἀκροᾶτικῶς, per prædicatum verbum. 2. Non statuimus hominem suo auditu præuenire gratiam Dei; sed hæc potiùs illum præuenit. Deus enim dedit aures organa audiendi; dedit verbum, obiectum audiendi; dedit ministros, annunciantes verbum; & indidit efficaciam conuertendi. Si enim homo per centum côtinuos annos audiret Euangelium, nec constituisset Deus per istam auscultationem fidem dare, nunquam certè vel tantillum fidei in cordibus audientium accenderetur, Proinde auditus noster non est causa efficiens, nec meritum fidei, sed duntaxat medium. Deus enim sic ordinauit, vt per praedicatum & auditum verbum fides ingeneretur cordibus.

Non hoc, quia non dicimus, in humanis viribus positum esse auditum internum, assensu mentis, obsequio voluntatis definitum, sed tantum Extenum, consistentem in studio cognoscendi, discendi & aliquo modo meditandi: quem in potestate hominis situm esse probari potest, tum dictis scripturae, tum exemplis. Dicta sunt: Luc. 13.vers. 24. Multi quaerent intrare, & non poterunt. Amos. 8. v. 11, Famem non famem audiendi verbi: id est, insigne desiderium. Exempla sunt; Herodes, qui libenter audiuit Iohannem Baptistam concionantem Marc. 6. v. 20. Sergius Proconsul qui ex Paulo & Barnaba desiderauit audire verbum Dei, Act. 13. v. 7. Athenienses, qui volunt audire Paulum, Act. 17. v. 20. Felix, qui cum studio audiuit Paulum, Act. 24. v. 14. Sic Act. 8. vers. 6. turbae προσέχον intendebant illis quae dicebantur a Philippo. Quod igitur non omnes audientes verbum conuertuntur, causa est, quia multi obicem ponunt Spiritui sancto, nec remouent obstacula, quibus impeditur verbi potentia. Id quod innuitur Prov. 1. v. 24. Esai. 65. v. 2. Matth. 23. v. 38. Luc. 7. v. 30. Act. 7. v. 51.

Porro autem quaeritur, Quomodo non renatus cum studio audire possit verbum, cum hoc animali homini sit stultitia, 1. Cor. 2. v. 14.

Resp. hoc dicto detrahitur non auditus externus, sed tantum internus. Ita enim sonant verba: Animalis homo non percipit ea, quae sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia enim est illi, & non potest intelligere. Sensus est, quod ψυχικὸς veram intelligentiam verbi ex suis viribus habere nequeat; non autem dicitur, quod non possit literas verbi cum studio audire. Contrarium enim testantur exempla & dicta superius allata. Et licet verbum Dei primo intuitu stultitia videatur non renato, attamen quando vel leniter tantùm attendit, non potest fieri, quin planè singulari quâdam vi & potentiâ percellatur animus eius, sicuti testatur exemplum Felicis. Isti ergò motui cùm obicem non ponunt auditores, Deus absque omni dubio fidem in ijs operatur.


### Question III

I. For the particularity of the calling, the Calvinists have no argument more specious than this one, taken from experience: If the calling were universal, the word would certainly be preached to all, which however does not happen, nor was it done formerly in the Old Testament, as the histories of all times testify. For how many most populous regions have been and still are, which are completely destitute of the ministry and proclamation of the word? Who announced the Gospel to the Indians, who to the Americans, and to other barbarians? Are all therefore invited to repentance, and consequently is the calling particular, not universal?

II. However, two things must be explained for the full solution of this argument: 1. In what sense is the calling said and established by our people to be universal? 2. How are those to whom the Gospel was never preached, nor is it even now preached, called and able to be said to be called?

II. Regarding the FIRST, it must be known here that, just as universal love and redemption, so also universal calling is to be viewed in the merciful and antecedent will of God. Therefore, it is called universal primarily by reason of the intention of God. For because He wills His grace to be announced to all, therefore we establish the calling as catholic; for we oppose this universality to the Calvinistic particularity, which they define thus: That God not only does not call all, but does not even will to call them. For from the chain Of their absolute decree they weave this consequence: Because God from eternity decreed that the smallest part of men be saved, therefore He sent the Son only to them, and by the merit of the Son He willed that the grace obtained be offered only to them, and in act offers it. Hence the principal status in this question is this, Whether calling is universal from the intention of God, that is, Whether God has promised His grace to all, and has determined to offer it to all, and thus to call all:

IV. The affirmative of this question can easily be proved from the universality of the mercy of God's will and the Lord's passion. For since He wills all to be saved and has sent a Redeemer to all, He certainly wills that this grace be announced to all, lest these things be in vain. Added to this are the most clear promises, by which He calls all to Himself, and excludes no one. The same is proved by the serious command of Christ: Preach the Gospel to every creature, Matt. 28 v. 19, Mark 16 v. 15, which itself is preached in act not only to the elect, but to all established in the Church, although as to the greatest part they are reprobate: Nevertheless, however, they are called, and indeed as seriously as the elect, since the same proclamation of the word reaches all.

V. From these things, therefore, it appears that calling is and is rightly called universal, 1. By reason of the intention of God, because He wills that all, with no one excluded, come and hear the word. 2. By reason of the command; because He commanded that this be announced in the whole world. 3. By reason of the promises, because He promises favor and mercy to all. 4. By reason of the proclamation itself, in which not only the elect, but all established in the Church participate. Since God calls these seriously, no less than those, through the same word, the Calvinistic particularity concerning the κλήσει of the elect only falls, and we prove a universal calling on the part of God or as regards His intention.

VI. Meanwhile, however, we do not deny that in the event the calling becomes particular and inefficacious, not from the hatred of God, but only by the fault of men. It becomes particular by reason of the Gentiles, who are punished by the removal of the Word. It is ineffectual by reason of the baptized, who hear the Word negligently and persevere in impiety. But since both happen accidentally, it detracts nothing from the universality of the calling in itself and considered on the part of God.

VII. ON THE SECOND. Regarding the other question, whether God has actually called and calls all men? The answer to it is more difficult. Yet we hold the affirmative here as well. For God has called the whole world and all men, and thus the entire human race, by the voice of external ministry three times: 1. In the protoplasts. 2. In the family of Noah. 3. In the time of the Apostles, whose sound went out into all the earth, Mark 16 v. 20, Rom. 10 v. 18, so that even in the times of Paul the Gospel was preached to every creature which is under heaven and has borne fruit in the whole world, Coloss. 1 v. 6 and 23. From which it clearly appears that God has not reprobated anyone by some absolute decree in such a way that He would not even deign to honor him with the announcement of His Word, which is the blasphemous heresy of the Calvinists.

VIII. And from this we infer that the calling is and is called universal not only by reason of the divine will, but also by reason of act and execution; because God has called and calls all. But this latter seems to contradict experience. For the Gentiles in the Old Testament were not yet called by the external ministry of the Prophets. The Americans in the New [Testament] have not yet been called by the voice of pastors. How, therefore, are all invited by God to repentance by the act itself?

IX. Here, we call to our aid the distinction of antecedent and consequent will. God, indeed, by His antecedent will, which is of mercy, wishes to call all men, yet not absolutely, but conditionally, if indeed they have not despised the calling once offered, from which it is clear that the calling and the mission of the Son differ. For He is sent to all in act, whether they receive Him or otherwise: but not all are always called in act: for those who repel the word from themselves, to them it is not perpetually offered. When therefore the contempt and affected negligence of men intervenes, then God by a consequent will, which they call justice, does not call men: which very subtraction of the word does not indicate a certain absolute hatred of God, but rather a just punishment, with which He affects the contemners of His word. For when a loathing of the word is accustomed to arise in men, then God sends upon them a famine of it, Amos 8. v. 11. The Jews were called in act, but because they repelled the word; the Apostles were turned to the Gentiles; Acts 13. v. 46. If therefore you ask, Why are the Jews not called today? you hear the cause from the Apostle, namely that it happens because of a contumacious repulse, not the hatred of God. The calling, therefore, which by itself and from the intention of God would have always been universal, becomes particular by accident, on account of the carelessness of men, not indeed simply; but only at this or that time: For we do not concede that men living in the world were never all called, but we have named three times, namely of the protoplasts, of Noah, and of the Apostles, where all men who were living then were actually called by the voice of the word. That this does not always happen, let men impute to themselves, not to God.

X. Nor is this contrary to the antecedent will: For God never absolutely willed to call all men everywhere and always, whether they contemn the grace once offered or do not contemn it; but determinately: If they shall have refused to hear my word, I also, as a just judge of that ingratitude, will send upon men a famine of hearing the word. Just as therefore God loves all men by an antecedent will, yet by a consequent will He hates and punishes some on account of sins, and this hatred of the consequent will does not take away the universal love of the antecedent will: so according to the same antecedent will God wills all men to call, (conditionally, however), but by a consequent will He does not call all; nor can this judgment of the consequent will therefore take away the universal calling, which God antecedently willed.

XI. But they object: How in this way will that of Ezek. 18:20 be saved? The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father? Why is the word denied to descendants, which their ancestors justly despised? But the answer is ready, that this happens because the sons consented to the sins of their fathers. For, for example, first the whole family of the πρωτοπλάστων was called actually and indeed immediately by God. But because Cain spontaneously turned himself away from God and followed idolomania, therefore God took away His word from his family, which removal was a punishment for spurned grace, so that afterwards it was not offered again. But the descendants of Cain, because they consented to the sins of their father, following the same idolomania, hence were punished with equal punishments for the father's sins, and thus consequently. That, therefore, they were not actually called, depends on their own sins, not on any absolute decree or hatred.

XII. These things can be illustrated by the image of God, to which we were ALL created, but in Adam. To him God had given this gift under the condition that if he sinned, he would lose it both for himself and for his descendants, which the event, alas! has sufficiently taught. Therefore, just as we were all created for righteousness in Adam, but justly lost it when Adam sinned, on account of the conditional concession of that righteousness: So through the word, by which the image is repaired, all were called in their ancestors, who ought to be considered as parents of their descendants, not as private persons. But because they repelled the word of grace with the greatest ingratitude, hence God justly withdrew it, and therefore the descendants, just as by the loss of the image on account of the sin of Adam, so by the deprivation of the word on account of the contempt of their ancestors, are most justly punished, since of both Let the reasoning be the same, and let both be explained in this way in the Scriptures. Therefore, just as creation in the image of God is universal by the intention of God, although we have lost it on account of the transgression of Adam: so also the calling of men is rightly called universal on the part of God, who gave the word to the ancestors for this reason, that they might propagate it to their descendants; but because they reject that, hence from a just judgment follows the deprivation of grace, and thus the calling with respect to the descendants becomes particular by accident.

XIII. But since it seems too harsh that children should be deprived of the Gospel on account of the ἀπισίαν of their parents, we add two further causes for the denied proclamation, so that the justice of God may be the better defended.

1. It is the malice of the descendants, as we hinted in thesis 11. For the hardness and contumacy toward the word of God that parents have drawn upon themselves, they for the most part propagate into their children, both through birth and through education, so much so that they are polluted by the same offenses, and therefore are not undeservedly punished with the same punishments. This is to be seen in the Jews, in whose children is engendered, and as it were instilled with their mother's milk, the highest hatred toward Christ and any Christians whatsoever. Thus, therefore, the children do not bear the iniquity of their fathers, because they are punished with the deprivation of the word on account of the hardness which they have in common with their parents.

Latin:

I. Pro particularitate vocationis nõ habent Caluiniani argumentũ magis speciosum, quàm hoc, ab experientia desumtum: Si vocatio vniuersalis esset, certè omnibus prædicaretur verbum, quod tamen non fit, neque olim factum fuit in veteri Testamento, velut historiæ omnium temporum testantur. Quot enim populosissimæ regiones fuerunt & etiamnum sunt, quæ ministerio & præconio verbi penitus destituũtur? Quis Indis, quis Americanis, alijsque barbaris annunciauit Euangelium? Num igitur omnes inuitantur ad pœnitentiam, & per consequens vocatio particularis est, non vniuersalis.

II. Duo autem ad plenam huius argumenti solutionem explicanda sunt, 1. Quosensu à nostratibus vocatio dicatur & statuatur vniuersalis? 2. Quomodo illi, quibus nunquam prædicatum fuit Euangelium, nec etiamnum prædicatur, vocati sint & dici queant?

II. De PRIMO, Sciendum hîc, quòd sicut vniuersalis dilectio & redemptio, ita quoque vniuersalis vocatio in voluntate Dei misericordi & antecedente spectetur. Proinde vniuersalis dicitur potissimùm ratione intentionis Dei. Quia enim omnibus vult annunciari suam gratiam, ideò vocationem statuimus catholicam; Nam vniuersalitatem istam opponimus particularitati Caluinisticæ, quam sic definiunt. Quod Deus non solùm non vocet vniuersos, sed ne quidem vocare velit. Ex catenâ enim absoluti sui decreti hanc nectunt consequentiam: Quia Deus ab æterno decreuit, minimam hominum partem saluari, ideò & ijs tantùm misit Filium, meritoque Fuy partam gratiam iis tantùm voluit offerri, & actu offert. Proinde principalis status in quæstione hac est iste, Vtrum vocatio sit vniuersalis ex intentione Dei, hoc est, Vtrum Deus gratiam suam omnibus promiferit, eamque vniuersis offerre, adeoque omnes vocare constituerit:

IV. Cuius quæstionis affirmatiua ex vniuersalitate misericordiæ Dei voluntatis & Dominicæ passionis facilè potest probari. Cùm enim omnes velit saluos & omnibus Redemptorem miserit, vtique & omnibus gratiam istam vult annunciari nè ista sint frustranea. Accedunt elusissimæ promissiones, quibus ad se vocat vniuersos, & neminem excludit. Idem probat serium Christi mandatum: Prædicate Euangelium omni creaturæ, Matth. 28. v. 19. Marc. 16. v. 15. quod ipsum non modò electis, sed omnibus in Ecclesia constitutis actu prædicatur, licet quoad maximam partem sint reprobi: Nihilominus tamen vacantur, & quidem tàm seriò, vt electi, cùm idem verbi præconium ad omnes pertingat.

V. Ex his igitur apparet, quod vocatio sit & rectè dicatur vniuersalis, 1. Ratione intentionis Dei, quia vult, vt omnes, nullo excluso veniant & verbum audiant. 2. Ratione mandati; quia præcepit istud in toto orbe annunciari. 3. Ratione promissionum, quia omnibus, fauorem & misericordiam pollicetur. 4 Ratione ipsius præconij, quo participant non tantùm electi, sed omnes in Ecclesia constituti. Hos cùm seriò, non minus atque illos, per idem verbum vocet Deus, mox cadit particularitas Caluinistica de κλήσει electoru tantùm, & nos euicimus vocationem vniuersalem ex parte Dei siue quoad eius intentionem.

VI. Interim verò non negamus, in euentu particularem & inefficacem fieri vocationem, non ex odio Dei, sed tantùm culpâ hominum. Particularis fit, ratione gentilium; qui ablatione verbi puniuntur. Inefficax, ratione baptizatorum, qui verbum negligenter audiunt, & in impietate perseuerant. Vtrumque vero cùm per accidens contingat, vniuersalitati vocationis in se, & ex parte Dei consideratæ nihil derogat.

VII. DE SECVNDO. Quod alteram quæstionem spectat, Vtrum Deus actu omnes vocârit & vocet homines? Ad eam difficilior est responsio. Affirmatiuam tamen & hic tenemus. Nam tribus vicibus totum mundum & omnes homines, adeoque vniuersum genus humanum per vocem externi ministerij vocauit Deus. 1. In protoplastis. 2. in familia Noachi. 3. In Tempore Apostol. quorum sonus exiuit in omnem terram, Marc. 16 v. 20. Rom. 10. v. 18. adeò vt etiam Pauli temporibus prædicatū sit Euangelium apud omnem creaturam, quæ sub cælo & fructificârit in vniuerso mundo, Coloss. 1. v. 6. & 23. Ex quo sanè apparet, Deum neminem absoluto quodam decreto ita reprobasse, vt ne quidem illum annunciatione verbi sui dignari voluerit, quæ blasphema est Caluinianorum hæresis.

VIII. Atque hinc inferimus, vocationem vniuersalem esse & dici non modò ratione voluntatis diuinæ, sed vnà ratione actus & executionis; quia Deus omnes vocauit & vocat. Ast hoc posterius videtur reclamare experientiæ. Gentes enim in Veteri Testamento per externum ministeriū Prophetarum. Americani in Nouo, per vocem pastorum nondum vocati. Quomodo igitur omnes à Deo ad pœnitentiam ipso actu inuitantur?

IX. Hic, in subsidium vocamus distinctionem voluntatis antecedentis & consequentis. Deus voluntate quidem antecedente, quæ est misericordiæ, omnes homines vult vocare, non tamen absolutè, sed conditionatè, si nimirum semel oblatam vocationem non contempserint, vnde patet, quod vocatio & missio Filij differant. Hic enim omnibus actu missus, siue eum recipiant, vel secus: sed non omnes actu semper vocantur: qui enim verbū à se repellunt, ijs nō perpetuo offertur. Cùm ergò interuenit hominū contemptus & affectata negligentia, tum Deus voluntate consequente, quā iustitiā dicunt, non vocat homines: quę ipsa verbi subtractio non indicat absolutum quoddā Dei odium, sed iustum potius suppliciū, quo cōtemtores verbi sui afficit. Quando enim hominib^{9} fastidium verbi suboriri solet, tū Deus famē eius immittit, Amos 8. v. 11. A ctu vocabatur Iudęi, sed quia repellebant verbum; Apostoli conuertebātur ad gentes; Act. 13. v. 46. Si ergò, quæras, Cur hodiè nō vocentur Iudæi? causam audis ex Apostolo, fieri nempè ob contumacē repulsum, non Dei odium. Quæ igitur vocatio per se & ex intētione Dei semper fuisset vniuersalis, per accidens, ob incuriā hominū fit particularis, non quidem simpliciter; sed tātum hoc vel illo tempore: Non enim concedimus, homines in mūdo viuentes nunquā fuisse vocatos omnes, sed nominauimus tria tempora, videlicet protoplastorum, Noachi, & Apostol. vbi omnes homines, qui tum viuebant, per vocem verbi fuerunt actu vocati. Quòd cùm non semper fit, sibi homines imputent, non Deo.

X. Neque hoc est contrarium voluntati antecedenti: Nunquam enim Deus absolutè voluit omnes vbiq; & semper vocare homines, siue semel oblatam gratiā contemnant, siue non contemnart; verùm determinatè: Si meum verbum audire recusauerint, ego quoque tanquàm iustus iudex illius ingratitudinis, inmittam hominibus famem audiendi verbi. Sicut igitur Deus omnes homines voluntate antecedente diligit, voluntate tamen consequente quosdam ob peccata odit & punit, neque hoc voluntatis consequentis odium tollit vniuersalem voluntatis antecedentis dilectionem: ità secūdum eandem voluntatem antecedentem Deus vult omnes homines vocare, (condicionaliter tamen) voluntate autem confequente non omnes vocat; nec prop terea hoc voluntatis confequentis iudicium tollere poteft vniuerfalem vocationem, quam Deus antecedenter voluit.

XI. Verùm excipiunt: Quomodo hoc pacto saluabitur illud Ezech. 18; v. 20. Filius non portabit iniquitatem Patris? Cur posteris denegatur verbum, quod maiores iustè contempserunt? Sed parata est responsio, fieri istud, quia filij consenserunt in delicta patrum. Nam ex. gr. primùm tota familia πρωτοπλάστων actu & quidem immediatè à Deo vocabatur. Quia verò Cain spontè à Deo sese auertebat, & idolomaniam sectabatur, idcircò Deus auferebat ab eius familia verbum suum, quæ ablatio pœna fuit sprete gratiæ, ita vt postmodum non offerretur iterum. Posteri autem Caini, quia in delicta patris sui consenserunt, sectantes eandem idolomaniam, hinc ob patria delicta paribus pœnis sunt puniti, atque sic consequenter. Quod igitur illi actu non fuerunt vocati, dependet ab ipsorum peccatis, non absoluto aliquo decreto vel odio.

XII. Illustrari hæc possunt imagine Dei, ad quam OMNES sumus coditi, sed in Adamo. Huic dederat Deus donum istud sub conditione, vt si peccaret, & sibi & posteris amitteret, quod euétus, proh dolor! satis edocuit. Vt igitur in Adamo ad iustitiam omnes creati sumus, illam verò peccante Adamo iustè amisimus, ob concessionem istius iustitiæ conditionalem: Ita per verbum, quo reparatur imago, Omnes vocati sunt in maioribus suis, qui vt parentes posterorum, non vt priuatæ personæ considerari debent. Quoniam verò isti verbum gratię summa cum ingratitudine repulerunt, hinc Deus jure istud subtraxit, ideoque posteri, velut amissione imaginis ob peccatum Adæ, sic priuatione verbi ob contemptum maiorum iustissimè puniuntur, cùm vtriusque par sit ratio, & in Scripturis vtrumque hec modo explicatum habeatur. Vt ergò creatio ad imaginem Dei vniuersalis est ex intentione Dei, licet sitam ob præuaricationem Adæ amiserimus: sic & Vocatio hominum vniuersalis rectè dicitur ex parte Dei, qui verbum ideo dedit maioribus, vt ad posteros propagarent; quia verò istud abijciunt, hinc ex iusto iudicio sequitur priuatio gratiæ, atque sic vocatio respectu posteriorum per accidens fit particularis.

XIII. Verùm cùm nimis durum videatur ob parentum ἀπισίαν Euangelio priuari filios, duas insuper negati præconij causas addimus, vt iustitia Dei eò meliùs defendatur.

1. Est posteriorum malitia, vt th. 11. innuimus. Quam enim duritiem & contumaciam erga verbum Dei attraxere parentes, eam plerumq; propagant in filios, tum per natiuitatem, tum per educationem, adeò vt ijdem delictis polluantur, ideoque ijfdem supplicijs non immerito puniantur. Videre hoc est in Iudæis, quorum liberis ingeneratur, & quasi cum lacte materno instillatur summum odium erga Christum & Christianos quosuis. Ita ergo filij non portant iniquitatem patrum, quia ob duritiem, quam cum parentibus habent communem, priuatione verbi plectuntur.


### Question III: Perspicacious foreknowledge

2. Perspicacious foreknowledge. For since God is merciful, certainly if He foresaw that the word would be fruitful among the Gentiles, He would send His heralds there. But because He does not do this, we infer from the posterior that He Himself foresaw the contrary. And since He does not wish His word to return to Him empty, Isaiah 55, v. 11, hence He does not allow it to be preached in Gentilism. We have a most clear example of this in Acts 22, v. 18, where Paul is ordered to leave Jerusalem, lest he preach the Gospel, because it would bear no fruit. Make haste, says the Lord to Paul, and go out quickly ἐξ Jerusalem, because they will not receive your testimony concerning me.

In the same way, because God foresees that the Gentiles are not going to receive the Gospel, he does not send his ministers there. XIV. To speak summarily, therefore: either the question is about the withdrawal of the preached word, or about its repeated or new preaching. If about withdrawal, the cause is the contempt of the parents, in whom all descendants were called. For the word was given so that it might be propagated. If it is about a new preaching, this is interrupted, both because of their own malice and because of the foreknowledge of its inefficacy, and thus neither case implies an absolute decree or a particular calling on the part of God. XV. Furthermore, however much the heathens were not called through the preaching of the word, they were by no means lacking in all means of repentance. For God did not leave himself without witness, Acts 14:16. Therefore, we distinguish between calling and the mode of calling. All men everywhere and always are called, but not all by the same method. There is one calling, but a twofold mode of calling. The first we name special, open, direct, illustrious, and manifest, and we distinguish this in turn into extraordinary and ordinary. It is extraordinary when someone is converted to the light of the Gospel immediately either by the very voice of God or by some notable miracle: it is ordinary when men are called through the external and visible ministry of the word. The second mode of calling we call general, obscure, and implicit or indirect, to which belong the four universal heralds of repentance, by which the heathens are invited to the inquiry of truth. XVI. 1. It is the knowledge of God, proposed in the visible works of the world; concerning which the Apostle Paul discourses thus in Romans 1:19, 20, 21: τὸ γνωστὸν τῦ Θεῦ, is manifest in them: for God has manifested it to them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are seen by those things which have been made, so that they are without inexcusable: Because when they had known God, they did not glorify Him as God. Therefore, the first preacher of repentance and inviter of the Gentiles to the Church is the book of nature, or the visible things of this world. For these testify that God exists, and that He, on account of the production of such wonderful things, ought to be affected with a certain worship. But because they themselves were ignorant of the manner of worship, they were hence solicited to investigate it by silent and hidden stimuli through the sight of creatures. Since they neglected this, by that very fact they were made ἀναπολόγητοι.

XVII. 2. One's own conscience. For no nation, says Tully, was so barbarous and unbridled that it did not know that God exists. Paul mentions this preacher in turn in Rom. 2:15 and 16. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them, and their thoughts between themselves accusing or even defending them. It was therefore inscribed in their hearts that God exists, that God is to be glorified, that He is to be worshipped with a certain worship, and that God had revealed that worship to men. Therefore, they were in turn invited to the Church, in which that worship was proposed.

XVIII. 3. The celebrity of the Church. For in the Old Testament, God placed His Church in a celebrated place, in the center of the earth, or in the middle of the world, where Rabbi Abenezra writes on Ecclesiastes 1 that Jerusalem was situated, so that the fame of the God of the Israelites became known to all: how powerful He is in performing signs, how He submerged the king of Egypt in the Red Sea, how He led out His people, how He defeated those most populous nations, the Amorites, Philistines, etc. Yet this fame was nothing other than a universal herald of repentance, by which the Gentiles were likewise solicited to embrace the Israelite doctrine. To this point tends the fact that the Bible had also been translated into the Greek language, which was most well-known to all. Whence Cicero in his speech for Archias says: Greek, he says, is read among almost all nations. Therefore, they ought to have inquired, and not persisted so contumaciously in their idolomania.

XIX. 4. Examples of those who converted themselves from heathendom to the true Church. For we read in the Old Testament that many, having cast off the idolatry of the gentiles, professed their names to the true God, from which number were Job the Idumean, Jethro the Midianite, Uriah the Hittite, Rahab the Canaanite, Ruth the Moabitess, the Queen of Sheba, Naaman the Syrian, the Assyrians of Nineveh, Nebuchadnezzar, Darius, Cyrus, Ahasuerus, etc. Hence in Acts 2, v. 5, it is said that there were dwelling in Jerusalem devout men from every nation which is under heaven. All of which examples were nothing other than silent preachers, by whom other gentiles were truly invited to the true Church.

XX. From what has been said thus far, however, we infer two πορίσματα [corollaries]. 1. That those who are destitute of the visible ministry of the word are not absolutely rejected by God. For those who wished to convert themselves to the Church were not turned away, but a hearing was open to all. 2. That those who are destitute of the visible ministry of the word are nevertheless called by God, partly through the knowledge of God set forth in the invisible works of the world, partly through their own conscience, partly through the fame of the Church, and partly through the examples of those who associated themselves from heathendom with the true Church: all of which are evident testimonies that God never made such a decree whereby He absolutely ordained and predestined some to damnation. And although some might have been destitute of the latter two heralds, the fame of the Church and the examples of converts, as is reported concerning the Americans, that nothing was known to them about the true Church. Yet they always carried around with them the first heralds, the knowledge of God and the judgment of conscience, and since they do not follow their guidance, the fault is in them, not in God, and therefore they are rightly called inexcusable. Rom. 1, v. 20.

XXI. But what, you ask, must be said concerning the infants of the gentiles who died in infancy? Were they also called? But indeed they are not called by the illustrious mode of calling, through the Word and Sacraments; nor by an obscure mode of calling; because they are destitute of the use and judgment of reason, and therefore they cannot gather from the visible works of the world, from the celebrity of the Church, and from the examples of others, to which assembly they ought to associate themselves. Wherefore, either it must be said that they are plainly not called in act, or the mode of calling must be indicated. The former is joined with impossibility: the latter with the particularity of calling. Both, therefore, are absurd.

XXII. We answer 1. If, at most, nothing certain can be established concerning the infants of the Gentiles, for that reason, however, the certainty of divine promises ought not to be weakened. We have proven that God seriously wills the salvation of all, that in the Church He seriously calls all, not only the elect, and outside the Church invites all adults to repentance, which are certainly such that they powerfully destroy an absolute decree and clearly construct a universal calling. Although, therefore, we do not know the calling of infants, let us not for that reason impugn those things which have been certainly demonstrated, according to the admonition of Augustine, Tom. 10, serm. 147: If we solve arguments with difficulty, let us hold without difficulty of faith that which has been demonstrated in the Lord: let them chatter, we believe.

2. The Apostle went before us with his own example, while he did not wish to judge those who are outside. For thus he says, 1 Cor. 5:12, Τί γάρ μοι τῆς ἔξω κρίνειν; What have I to do with judging those who are outside? Since, therefore, the infants of the Gentiles are outside, we leave them to the judgment of God, and we affirm nothing rashly. For it does not follow: We know no mode of calling. Therefore they are plainly not called. Many things are done by the most wise God which escape human intellect. Wherefore, one must not argue from our ignorance to the negation of a thing: and consequently, since this case is in every way doubtful and uncertain, nothing can be concluded from it.

3. As the calling, so also the damnation of the infants of the Gentiles is uncertain. Although, indeed, in the Scriptures concerning this nothing has been revealed, and they are subject to eternal damnation according to the ordinary judgment, yet who will snatch from the Father of the τῶν ἀνειλήπτων [the unreceived/those not taken up] the right of doing good? Who indeed will demonstrate that God by an absolute decree has reprobated all the infants of the Gentiles? The Calvinistic objection therefore proceeds from a doubtful hypothesis and for that reason has no solidity. See what has been disputed in Dec. 1, disp. 7, quest. 2, concerning the infants of the Gentiles.

4. Christ instituted Baptism for all, and therefore excluded no one, by which pact He made His benevolent will sufficiently attested. That, however, not all are offered to the Church, this happens accidentally, not from God's hatred, but from the fault of the parents.

5. Although infants are not called outside the Church, this nevertheless happens in the Church, where the voice of the Savior sounds, Matt. 19:14, 'Suffer the little children to come unto me.' And Matt. 28:19, 'Teach all nations, baptize them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.' God therefore does not absolutely reprobate infants, but promises His grace to them also.

6. They were also called in their ancestors to whom the Sacraments were once granted. For just as they are rightly said to have been created in the image of God in Adam, so also they were called to salvation in their parents. And just as all infants are justly punished by the privation of the image of God on account of the transgression of Adam, so also [they are punished] by the privation of the means on account of the prevarications of their parents.

7. If anyone wishes to fly altogether into the rationale of divine judgment, and to know the cause why He snatches away the children of the Gentiles in infancy, before they can be converted, our theologians assume a double hypothesis: the one from the immense mercy of God, the other from His infinite omniscience. For first, God is supremely merciful, and does not wish that any should perish, but that all should come to the knowledge of the truth. Then, because God is omniscient, He therefore knows from eternity which ones are going to accept the means of salvation, and which ones are not. With these presupposed, we answer thus: If those infants had they become older, and been about to receive the means of salvation, and to aggregate themselves to the society of the Church, then God would certainly have foreknown that, and consequently, by the force of His mercy, would not have permitted them to perish in infidelity. But now, because God permitted such infants to perish both temporally and eternally, He certainly foresaw and foreknew that, even if they had reached a more adult age, they would nevertheless never have accepted the means of salvation, however much offered, but would rather have contumaciously neglected them. Therefore, although they could not inquire into the true worship in infancy, because God foresaw that they would not inquire even in adult age, He therefore justly punished them.

8. Finally, it must be known that many things lie hidden and unknown in the doctrine of predestination, the reason for which cannot be explained, and therefore one must say with the Apostle in Rom. 9:20: O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Therefore, revealed things ought not to be denied because hidden things are not known. Rightly Augustine, sermon 11 on the words of the Apostle: Do you wish to dispute with me? Marvel and exclaim, O the depth! Let us both agree in fear, lest we perish in error. Therefore, the question concerning the infants of the Gentiles should not disturb us, but let us acknowledge the grace of God, who calls all to the Church. From these abstruse things let us not weave cords of incredulity, but let them be stimuli of piety and of a more ardent desire, by which we may seek heavenly things more and hope for eternal things more fervently. For there, what is lacking here will be supplied; there our knowledge will be perfected; there that which is in part shall be done away, and then we shall see God face to face: then we shall know Him, even as we are known. 1 Cor. 13:11, 12. To Him alone be praise and everlasting blessing. Amen.

Latin:

2. Perspicax præscentia. Cùm enim Deus sit misericors, vtique si præuideret, verbum apud gentiles fore fructuosum, præcones suos còmisseret. Quia verò hoc non facit, à posteriori colligimus, ipsum præuidisse contrarium. Et cùm nolit verbum suum ad se redire vacuum, Esai. 55. v. 11. hinc in gentilismo istud prædicari non sinit. Huius rei exemplum habemus clariffimum Act. 22. v. 18. vbi Paulus iubetur Hierosolyma exire, ne prædicetur Euangelium, quia nihil sit fructificaturum. Festina, inquit Dominus ad Paulum, & exi velociter ἐξ Ierusalem, quoniam non recipient testimonium tuum de me.

Pari modo, quia præuidet Deus, gentiles non esse recepturos Euangelium, hinc ministros suos eò non ablegat. XIV. Summatim ergò dicendo, Aut quæritur de verbi prædicati subtractione, Aut de iterata nouaquè prædicatione. Si de subtractione, causa est Contemtus parentū, in quibus omnes posteri sunt vocati. Ideo enim datū fuit verbum vt propagaretur. Si de nonâ prædicatione hæc intermittitur, tum ob propriam malitiam, tum ob inefficaciæ præscientiam, adeoque neuter casus vel absolutum decretum vel particularem vocationem ex parte Dei innuit. XV. Porrò autem quantumuis Ethnici per prædicationem verbi non fuerint vocati, attamen omnibus pœnitentiæ medijs nequaquam caruerunt. Non enim sine testimonio reliquit Deus semetipsum, Act. 14. v. 16. Proinde distinguimus, inter vocationem & vocationis modum. Omnes homines vbique & semper vocantur, sed non omnes eâdem ratione. Vna est vocatio, sed duplex vocandi modus. Primum nominamus specialem, apertum, directum, illustrem & manifestum, eumque vicissim in extraordinarium & ordinarium distinguimus. Extraordinarius est, cùm quis immediatè vel per ipsam Dei vocem, vel per insigne quoddam miraculum ad lucem Euangelij conuertitur: Ordinarius, cùm homines per externum & visibile verbi ministerium vocantur. Secundum vocationis modum appellamus generalem, obscurum atque implicitum vel indirectum, ad quam spectant quatuor vniuersales pœnitentiæ præcones, quibus Ethnici ad inquisitionemm veritatis inuitantur. XVI. 1. Est notitia Dei, in visibilibus mundi operibus proposita; de qua ita disserit Apostolus Paulus Rom. 1. 19. 20. 21. τὸ γνωστὸν τῦ Θεῦ, manifestum est in illis: Deus enim illis manifestauit. Inuisibilia enim ipsius à creatura mundi per ea, quæ facta sunt, conspiciūtur, ita vt sint inexcusabiles: Quia cùm cognovissent Deum, non sicut Deum glorificaverunt. Primus ergò pœnitentiæ concionator, & gentilium ad Ecclesiam invitator est liber naturæ, seu visibilia huius mundi. Ista enim testantur, Deum esse, illumq́; ob productionem tàm mirabilium rerum cultu quodam afficiendum esse. Quia verò ipsi rationem cultus ignorabant, hinc ad eum indagandum tacitis occultisque stimulis per aspectum creaturarum solicitabantur. Quod cùm neglexerint, eo ipso facti sunt ἀναπολόγητοι

XVII. 2. Propria conscientia. Nulla enim gens, inquit Tullius, tàm barbara fuit & effrænis, quę non Deum esse cognoverit. Huius prædicatoris vicissim meminit Paulus Rom. 2. 15. & 16. Ostendunt opus legis scriptum in cordibus suis, testimoniū reddente illis conscientia ipsorum & inter se invicem cogitationum accusantium aut etiam defendentium. Cordibus igitur ipsorum inscriptum erat, Deum esse, Deum glorificandum, certoq́; cultu colendum esse, & Deum hominibus cultū istum patefecisse. Vicissim ergò invitabantur ad Ecclesiam, in qua iste cultus proponebatur.

XVIII. 3. Celebritas Ecclesiæ. In veteri enim Testamento Deus Ecclesiam suam in celebri loco collocavit, in meditullio terræ, vel in medio orbis, vbi Hierosolymam sitam fuisse scribit Rabbi Abenezra super 1. Eccles. ita vt omnibus innotuerit fama de Deo Israëlitarū, quàm potens sit in signis edendis, quomodo regem Ægypti mari rubro submerserit, quomodo populum suum eduxerit, quomodo illas populosissimas gētes, Amorrhæos, Philistæos, &c. deuicerit. Quæ tanē famà nil aliud erat, quam vniversalis præco pœnitētiæ, quo gentiles itidem ad amplectendam doctrinā Israëliticam solicitabantur. Huc spectat, quod & Biblia in Græcam linguam omnibus notissimam versa erant. Vnde Cic. pro Archia: Græca, inquit, in omnibus ferè gentibus leguntur. Inquirere ergò debuissent, & tam contumaciter in sua idolomania non persistere.

XIX. 4. Exempla eorum, qui se ex gentilitate ad veram Ecclesia conuerterunt. Legimus enim in Vet. Testam. multos abiecta gentiliū idololatria, nomina sua vero Deo professos fuisse, ex quorū numero fuerunt Iob Idumæus, Iethro Midianita, Vrias Hethita, Rachab Chananæa, Ruth Moabitis, Regina Sabæa, Naaman Syrus, Niniuitā Assyrij, Nabuchodonosor, Darius, Cyrus, Ahasverus, &c. Hinc Act. 1. v. 5. dicitur, quòd in Ierusalem fuerint habitantes viri turales ex omni natione, quæ sub cœlo est. Quæ exempla omnia nihil erant, aliud, quàm taciti concionatores, quibus ad Ecclesiam veramiterum inuitabantur gentiles alij.

XX. Ex hactenus verò dictis duo inferimus πορίσματα. 1. Eos qui destituuntur visibili verbi ministerio non esse à Deo absolutè reiectos. Qui enim sese volebāt ad Ecclesiam conuertere, illi non repudiabatur, sed omnibus patebat auditus. 2. Eos, qui destituuntur visibili verbi ministerio nihilominus vocari à Deo, partim per notitiam Dei inuisibilibus mundi operibus propositam, partim per propriam conscientiam, partim per celebritatem Ecclesiæ, partim per exempla eorum, qui se ex gentilitate veræ Ecclesiæ associauerunt: quæ omnia sunt euidentia testimonia, Deum nunquam tale decretum fecisse, quò aliquos absolutè ad damnationem ordinauerit & prædestinauerit. Et licèt nonnulli postremis duobus præconibus, celebritate Ecclessiæ & exemplis conuersorum destituti essent, vti de Americanis refertur, quòd nihil ipsis constiterit de Ecclesia vera. Primos tamen præcones, notitiam Dei & Iudicium conscientiæ semper secum circumportarunt, cuius ductum cùm non sequantur, culpa in ipsis est, non Deo, adeoquè rectè dicuntur inexcusabiles. Rom. 1. v. 20.

XXI. Quid verò inquis, de infantibus gentium in infantia mortuis dicendum? An & illi vocati sunt? At verò non vocatur, modo vocationis illustri, per verbum & Sacramenta; nec modo vocationis obscuro; quia destituuntur usu & iudicio rationis, ideoq; ex visibilib.mūdi operibus, ex celebritate Ecclesię, & aliorū exēplis colligere nequeūt, cuinam cœtui se associare debeāt. Quare aut dicendum est, illos planè nō vocari actu, aut indicetur modꝰ vocationis. Hęc coniunctū est cū impossibilitate: illud cum vocationis particularitate. Vtrumque igitur absurdum.

XXII. Respondemus 1. Si maximè de infantib. gentiliū nil certi queat statui, ob id tamen certitudo promissionum diuinarum nō debet infirmari. Probauimus, Deum seriò salutem omnium velle, in Ecclesia omnes, non tantùm electos seriò vocare, extra Ecclesiam omnes adultos ad pœnitentiam inuitare, quæ certè talia sunt, vt absolutum decretum potenter destruant, & vniuersalem vocationem luculenter adstruant. Licet ergò nesciamus vocationē infantum, ea tamen, quæ certò demonstrata sunt, propterea non impugnemus, iuxta monitum Augustini Tom. 10. serm. 147. Si argumenta difficile soluimus, illud quod demonstratum est in Domino, sine difficultate fidei teneamus: illi garriant, nos credimus.

2. Apostolus suo exemplo nobis præiuit, dum de ijs, qui foris sunt, iudicare noluit. Ita n. inquit 1. Cor. 5. 12. Τί γάρ μοι τῆς ἔξω κρίνειν; Quid mihi de ijs, qui foris sunt, iudicare? Cùm ergò infantes gentilium foris sint, iudicio Dei illos relinquimus, & nihil temerè adfirmamus. Neque n. sequitur: Nos modum vocationis nullum scimus. Ergò planè non vocantur. Multa fiunt à Deo sapientissimo, quæ humanum fugiunt intellectum. Quare à nostra ignorantia ad rei negationem non est argumentandum: & per consequens, cùm casus iste vndiquaque sit dubius & incertus nihil inde concludi poterit.

3. Vti vocatio, ita & damnatio infantum gentilium est incerta. Quamuis n. in Scripturis de hoc nihil reuelatum sit, & illi secundum ordinarium iudicium æternæ damnationi subiaceãt, quis tamen Patri τῶν ἀνειλήπτων ius benefaciendi eripiet? Quis vero demonstrabit Deum absoluto decreto omnes Ethnicorum paruulos reprobasse? Vicissim igitur ex dubia hypothesi procedit obiectio Caluinististica, ideóque nullam habet soliditatem. Vide quæ Dec. 1. disp 7. quæst. 2. de infantibus gentilium disputata sunt.

4. Christus Baptismum pro omnibus instituit, ideoque neminem exclusit, quo pacto beneuolam voluntatem suam satis testatam fecit. Quod a. non omnes offerantur Ecclesiæ, hoc fit per accidens, non ex Dei odio, sed parentum vitio.

5. Licet infantes non vocentur extra Ecclesiam, fit tamen hoc in Ecclesia, vbi sonat vox Saluatoris Matt. 19, 14. Sinite paruulos ad me venire. Et Matth. 28. 19 Docete omnes gentes baptizate eos in nomine Patris, & Filij, & Spir. S. Deus ergo infantes non absolutè reprobat, sed iis quoque suam gratiam promittit.

6. Vocati sunt etiam in maioribus quibus concessa olim fuerunt Sacramenta. Sicut enim rectè dicuntur creati ad imaginem Dei in Adamo, ita & vocati sunt ad salutem in parentibus. Et velut omnes infantes priuatione imaginis Dei ob transgression nem Adæ iustè puniuntur: ita & priuatione mediorum ob præuaricationes parentum.

7. Si quis omninò prouolare velit in rationale iudicij diuini, & causam scire, cur pueros gentilium in infantia abripiat, antequam conuerti queant, duplicem nostri Theologi assumunt hypothesin : Alteram ab immensa Dei misericordia, alteram ab infinita eiusdem omniscientia. Primò enim Deus est summè misericors, nec vult, vt vnus pergat, sed vt omnes ad agnitionem veritatis perueniant. Deinde, Deus quia est omnisciùs, ideò ab æterno nouit, quinam media salutis sint accepturi, qui verò non. His præsuppositis ita respondemus : Si infantes illi adultiores facti, media salutis accepturi, & ad Ecclesiæ societatem sese aggregaturi fuissent, tum Deus vtiq; illud præscivisset, & per consequens vi misericordiæ suæ, non in infidelitate ipsos interire permisisset. Iam verò, quia Deus tales infantes & temporaliter & æternùm perire permisit, vtique præuidit & præsciuit, ipsos si maximè ad ætate adultiorein peruenissent, nunquam tamen media salutis, quantumuis oblata accepturos, sed potiùs contumaciter neglecturos esse. Itaque licèt non potuerint in infantia inquirere in verum cultum, quia tamen Deus præuidit eos etiam in adulta ætate non inquisituros propterea justè puniuit.

8. Tandem sciendum, quòd in doctrina prædestinationis multa lateant abstrusa & incognita, quorum ratio exponi nequit, ideoq́ne dicendum cum Apostolo Rom. 9. 20. Tu quis es homo qui ex aduerso respondeas Deo? Non igitur negari debent reuelata, quia nesciuntur celata. Rectè August. serm. 11. de verbis Apostoli: Disputare vis mecum? Mirare & exclama, O altitudo! Ambo consentiamus in pauore ne pereamus in errore. Quæstio igitur de infantibus gentiliu non perturbet nos, sed agnoscamus Dei gratiam, qui omnes vocat ad Ecclesiam. Ex abstrusis istis nõ nectamus funiculos incredulitatis, sed sint stimuli pietatis, & desiderij ardentioris, quo magis quæramus cœlestia, & feruentius speramus æterna. Ibi enim quod hîc deest, supplebitur, ibi scientia nostra perficietur; Ibi euacuabitur, quod ex parte est, & tunc videbimus Deum a facie ad faciem: tunc cognoscemus eum, sicut & cogniti sumus. 1. Cor. 13. 11. 12. Ipsi soli sit laus & sempiterna benedictio. Amen.


### Question III: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA


## 16 Disputation IV. On the Eternal Predestination of Believers to Life

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Master Michael Hermann of Wrocław.

Proeisagoge. I.

After we have examined those sources of gratuitous election, namely the universal love of God and the offering of grace, we now descend in proper order to the mystery of Predestination itself.

II. But so that the knowledge of this mystery may be more expeditious, we shall discuss primarily six chapters: 1. Concerning the terms familiar in this article. 2. Concerning the various opinions. 3. Concerning the definition of election itself and its causes. 4. Concerning the book of life, in which the elect are inscribed. 5. Concerning the immutability of predestination, and 6. concerning the true use of this doctrine. We shall divide our labors, and in this disputation we shall treat of the first three chapters, deferring the remaining three to the following one, with the Most High consenting.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D.

Resp. M. Michaële Hermanno Vratislaviensi.

Προείσαγωγὴ. I.

POsteaquam istos electionis gratuitæ fontes inspeximus, nempè vniuersalem Dei dilectionem, & gratiæ oblationem, recto nunc ordine ad ipsum Prædestinationis arcanum descendimus.

II. Vt verò expeditior sit hujus mysterij cognitio, de sex potissimùm capitibus erit disserendum, 1. De terminis in articulo isto familiaribus. 2. De varijs opinionibus. 3. De ipsa electionis definitione & causis. 4. De libro vitæ, in quô electi sunt inscripti. 5. De immutabilitate prædestinationis, & 6. de verô huius doctrinæ usu. Partiemur autem operas, & de primis tribus capitibus hac disputatione agemus, cætera tria ad sequentem, annuente Altissimo, differentes.


### Question I. What is the genuine meaning of the terms occurring in the article of election?

I. There are four terms primarily, which frequently occur here: 1. Foreknowledge. 2. Will, to which we refer Purpose and Decree. 3. Election. 4. Predestination: concerning which we shall bring forward a few things.

II. 1. Concerning foreknowledge. Although Damascenus, in his dialogue on the Manichaean heresy, distinguishes between γνῶσιν, πρόγνωσιν καὶ ἐπίγνωσιν, of which the former is the knowledge of all things, both past and future, the latter [is the knowledge] only of future things, and the third [is the knowledge] only of past things—inasmuch as ἐπίγνωσις primarily denotes the diligent knowledge of a thing already done, and is attributed to judges who studiously know and inquire into a thing done, about which they must judge—nevertheless, all those things are one and the same in God. For with Him there is nothing past, which He might remember; nothing future, which He might foreknow, but all things are most present to Him. Whence theologians establish that God destines and knows believers unto salvation rather than predestining and foreknowing those who will believe. For things that are to be done stand in His sight just as much as those that are being done or have been done: for with one perpetual intuition He beholds at once things created and to be created, things arisen and to arise, things done and to be done. And to this point look the following testimonies of Scripture. Dan. 3, v. 42: O eternal God, who art the knower of hidden things, who knowest all things before they come to pass. Hosea 5, v. 3: I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me. Sirach 23, v. 29: To the Lord God, before they were created, all things were known: so also after they were perfected He looks upon all things. And the preceding verse, 17: He sees all things with His eyes. From age even unto age He looks upon them, and nothing is wonderful in His sight.

III. Although these things are so in God, nevertheless, according to anthropopathy and condescension, His knowledge is distinguished from foreknowledge by reason of the object, in such a way that we say the former is of all things, but the latter only of future things, And it is altogether fitting to say that future things are not known by God, but foreknown. For although they are most present to Him, just as if they had been done; yet because they have not yet been done in reality, therefore God is said to foreknow them.

IV. Moreover, by reason of its objects, the foreknowledge of God is threefold.

1. General, which extends itself to all creatures, good and bad alike, and likewise to all acts, however they may be compared.

2. Special, which respects only the faithful and the elect children of God, and is attended to primarily in this article. For as general foreknowledge pertains only to the intellect of God, so special foreknowledge includes, moreover, an approving will, and therefore the Scholastics call it the knowledge of approval and love. The Apostle Paul speaks of this in Rom. 8:29: 'Whom He foreknew, He also predestined.' Where it is proven that the word for foreknowing is taken ἰδιῶς (properly/specifically): 1. From the series of the Pauline chain. For it is such that the former members are determined and defined by the latter members, 'For whom He foreknew, He also predestined.' Whence we infer: If the foreknowledge of which Paul speaks here belongs to those whose predestination is also spoken of, and indeed this is not of all, then certainly this foreknowledge of which we speak here cannot be of all. 3. From the object of the πρόγνωσις (foreknowledge) or the thing foreknown. The object of this foreknowledge are the elect alone, namely those; who love God, to whom all things work together for good, who are called κατὰ πρόθεσιν (according to purpose), etc. Therefore, the foreknowledge of which there is discourse here will not be universal, extending itself to all men, but special and pertaining only to the elect. Thus in Amos 3:2 it is said: 'You only have I known of all the families of the earth': where everyone understands that the Prophet is speaking of a special προγνώσει (foreknowledge) because of the exclusive particle. John 10:14, 27: 'I know my sheep.' John 13:18: 'I know whom I have chosen.' Rom. 11:2: 'God has not rejected His people whom He foreknew.' 2 Tim. 2:19: 'The Lord knows' those who are His.' All these things which have been said speak of a certain special knowledge, by which God knows only the faithful and the elect, but not the infidels and the reprobate, to whom He will say at the final judgment, Matt. 7. v. 23: 'I never knew you.' And Luke 13. v. 27: 'I do not know you, where you are from.' For those whose names are not written in the book of life, God does not know them with this special προγνώσǫ. It is to be noted, however, that although this foreknowledge formally accepted differs from the ἐκλογῇ καὶ προθέσεως of God, (which is evident 1. From this: 'Whom He foreknew, He also predestined': where if to foreknow and to predestine were simply the same, a ταυτολογία would be committed; 2. Because we are said to be elect κατὰ πρόγνωσιν 1. Pet. 1. v. 1. & 2. But this expression would be inept if πρόγνωσις and ἐκλογὴ were the same). However, since by reason of their objects they extend equally widely, and when one is posited the other is immediately posited, (for those who are foreknown by this προγνώσǫ are the ἐκλεκτοὶ and vice versa), therefore in Scripture a permutation of these words occurs, so much so that the word for foreknowledge is put for election and vice versa.

3. Singular, which pertains to Christ, in which sense 1. Pet. 1. v. 20 He is called προεγνωσμένος, that is, foreknown before the foundation of the world.

V. 2 Concerning the will of God. Just as in man, who is the image of God, there is a twofold will: one ἐφετικὴ, which is the sole and bare appetite itself, by which someone simply wills and desires something; the other προβεβουλευμένη, a deliberate will, when someone does not simply desire a thing, but also proposes it to himself, and certainly decides that he will strive by all means to attain the thing which he seeks: so in God there is a certain simple will, and a certain one κατὰ πρόθεσιν, that is, will is one thing, purpose is another. For even in human affairs it is manifest that βόυλησιν, volition, and προαίρεσιν, election or purpose, differ. For we often will ἀδύνατα, which, however, we never propose to ourselves, unless we wish to be delirious. Thence Many things fall under the will, which are not performed by us, but by others, and therefore we never propose them to ourselves. Thus, all desire that the kingdom be well administered by the Emperor, yet no one thinks anxiously about the method of administering it well. In like manner, there is some distinction between the will of God, the purpose of God, and also the decree of God. Will is a more general term, and it includes even those things which do not happen. Thus, God wills all men to listen attentively to His word, which, however, never happens. But the purpose of God only embraces those things which certainly happen. For what God proposes, that happens without any exception. The decree of God is a still stricter degree, namely when God decrees that He will effect by certain means that which He has proposed within Himself. Thus, therefore, these things follow: God wills something, He proposes what is willed, He decrees what is proposed; and so these three things differ as broader and stricter, antecedents and consequents.

But that distinction of purpose and decree is to be noted especially against the Calvinists, who wish πρόθεσιν and ἐκλογὴν to denote scarcely the same thing, which is false. For the decree of election is to us nothing other than the very action of choosing or predestinating, but πρόθεσις or purpose is a degree higher than election; it is only βουλὴ τοῦ θελήματος Θεοῦ, Ephes. 1. v. 9. For if purpose and election were the same, would not Paul be speaking ineptly in Ephes. 1. v. 11, saying that we were predestinated κατὰ πρόθεσιν? And Rom. 8. verse 28, he establishes πρόθεσιν as the highest degree: Now if election and the purpose of choosing were the same, certainly the links in the Pauline chain would be confounded. Zanchius acknowledged this in book 5, de N. D., chapter 2, when he writes that predestination presupposes election, election love, love foreknowledge, and foreknowledge the good pleasure or purpose of the will.

But if it pleases to divide, we say that the will of God is either simple, in such a way that it is a bare denotation of his θελησιν; or it is the will of εὐδοκιας or of προθεσεως. When therefore we are said to be elected according to the will of God, you should understand this latter, not the former.

VI. 5. On Election. The noun of election, and the verb of choosing, has many meanings in the Scriptures, of which five are primary,

1. It is taken metonymically for the elect, as Rom. 11. v. 7. The election has obtained it, that is, the elect.

2. For the approval and love of an excellent thing, because we choose nothing except what we approve of and which excel others, as Isa. 58. v. 6. Is it such a fast that I have chosen? Hence, on account of the flower and vigor of age, excellent young men among the Hebrews are called בְּחוּרִים elect; And in daily speech we are accustomed to name an excellent thing elect, an elect gem, that is, precious; an elect horse, that is, excellent; elect children, that is, dear, upright, pious, auserwehlte liebe Kinder. Thus Gen. 23. v. 6. they are called elect sepulchers, that is, splendid. Exod. 15. v. 4. The election of princes, or the elect Princes of Pharaoh. Thus it seems to be taken in that Luke 23. verse 35. Let him save himself, if he is the Christ of God, the elect.

3. For the selection and separation of either men or other things for a certain use. Thus the city, in which is the house of the Lord, is called the place which the Lord chooses, Deut. 12. 15. 17. etc. Thus from three evils, war, famine, pestilence, David chose that which seemed to be the lesser evil, namely the pestilence. Thus the Apostles were selected by Christ from other men for the Apostleship: which election, for the sake of distinction, they call official, by which someone is chosen and destined for a certain office.

4. For the election of some people and the calling to the Church, in which sense it is said in Deut. 7. v. 6. The Lord your God has chosen you, that you may be a peculiar people to him. This election they name Provincial.

5. In the most special meaning for the eternal election of the faithful to eternal life, made before the foundations of the world were laid, which for that reason they designate as saving. And in this ultimate sense we take the word election, from which are properly and κατ' ἐξοχὴν named ἐκλεκτοὶ or ἐκλελεγμένοι, that is, chosen nominally and participially. For that there is no difference between these two words is evident from that passage in Mark 13, verse 20: Διὰ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς, οὓς ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεός.

From all these significations, however, it appears that the word to choose 1. Hints at a certain separation, by which a thing or person is set apart from others and selected for a certain purpose. Hence these terms are used interchangeably; as what Moses calls to choose in Deut. 7, v. 6, Solomon renders as to separate, 1 Kings 8, v. 53. Thus the election of the disciples in Luke 6, v. 13 is named a separation in Acts 13, v. 2. To have observed this will be of no small benefit for refuting the universal and indiscriminate Huberian election. 2. To presuppose gratuitous love from which it always proceeds. This is hinted at in Deut. 4, v. 37: Because Jehovah loved your fathers, he chose their seed after them, which is found in Deut. 7, v. 6, 7, 8. And the reason is at hand, since those things which are chosen must be pleasing and beloved to us above others: which ought to be noted against the champions of works and merits.

VII. 4 Concerning predestination. What the Latins call to predestine, whence predestination: the Greeks name προορίζειν, whence προορισμὸς. However, προορίζειν signifies to decree and predefine something before you do it. For ὅρος denotes a boundary, hence ὁρίζειν to bound, and προορίζειν to determine before or beforehand, as in 1 Cor. 2, verse 7: We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which προώρισεν ὁ θεὸς before the ages, that is, which he had decreed and preordained to reveal to us. Thus the chosen are called προορισμένοι, predestined, that is, destined to life before they existed. For the little word πρὸ in Greek, and præ in Latin, Latin, signifies that the election was made from eternity; and thus it looks to the decree of God, which He made concerning the ordaining and destining of the faithful to life, before they were created in time.

VIII. Here two things further come into controversy. 1. Does predestination signify the same thing as election?

The Calvinists think these two differ as genus and species: Predestination is for them the genus, Election and reprobation are the species. But this is said without testimonies of Scripture. For in Eph. 1:4, both terms of election and predestination are taken in the same sense: God chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, that we might be holy, when He had predestined us. Where the elect are called predestined, and conversely; the predestined are called elect. Moreover, in all places where mention is made of predestination, election to life is always understood: however, no text can be brought forward in which any are written as predestined to death and eternal damnation. For as regards that passage in Acts 4:28, The princes of the Jews gathered together to do what thy hand and thy counsel προώρισε γενέσθαι, predestined to be done: anyone surely sees that it does not deal with any reprobation of infidel men to eternal damnation, but only with the decree and preordination of the death and passion of Christ. If you except that passage, the Calvinists themselves admit that the term Predestination is taken only concerning the elect. For thus writes Ursinus, part 2, Explic. Catech., page 229: It is to be noted that in the Scriptures the name of Predestination is almost only taken concerning the elect; to which Zanchius subscribes, lib. 5, de N. D., cap. 2, quaest. 1, page 614: Scripture, he says, is accustomed to signify by this name properly the election of the saints, and the deputation to eternal life made before the foundation of the world. Keckermann agrees, lib. 3, Syst. Theol., c. 1, p. 296, who denies that predestination properly contains reprobation under itself, because predestination is the ordering of a thing to an end. But every end is either the perfection of a thing, but Damnation is not good, but the ultimate evil. Wherefore no one is preordained or predestined to it as to their end.
