Moreover, we cannot deny that the Fathers sometimes used the word 'predestination' generally for every decree by which God determined something certain concerning the salvation of the faithful and the damnation of the unfaithful, in which sense Isidore said in book 2 of 'De summo bono', ch. 5 and 6: 'Predestination is twofold, either of the elect to rest, or of the reprobate to death.' And Augustine, book 15 of 'De Civitate Dei', ch. 1: 'We mystically call them two cities, that is, societies of men, of which one is predestined to reign eternally with God, the other to undergo eternal judgment with the Devil.' And in 'Enchiridion', ch. 100, he teaches that God, as supremely good, makes good use of both good and evil, for the damnation of those whom He justly predestined to punishment, and for the salvation of those whom He benignly predestined to grace. Expressing this, Fulgentius, book 1 'ad Mon.', p. 8, says: 'I think nothing else is to be understood in that sermon of St. Augustine, in which he affirms that some are predestined to destruction;' except to the destruction of punishment, not of the offense; neither to the evil which they unjustly commit, but to the torment which they will most justly suffer: If, therefore, you take the word 'predestining' in a looser sense, for the constitution and ordination of any thing to a certain end, I say we do not write for that reason. Meanwhile, because we do not have Scripture shining before us, and indeed in this highest mystery one must speak cautiously and soberly, therefore we prefer to call only the faithful and the elect 'predestined', and the rest 'reprobate'. Hence Leo wrote in his Epistle to Peter of Antioch: 'I believe God only predestined good things: but foreknew both good and evil.' This very thing the Scholastics acknowledged: As is evident from Lombard, book 1, dist. 35, letter A, where a distinction is brought between knowledge, disposition, and predestination. 'Knowledge,' he says, 'is not only of future things, but of all things, namely good and evil. Disposition, however, is of things to be done:' predestination is of all those to be saved, and concerning all the good, who are both delivered here and will be crowned in the end. And letter B. Knowledge is of all things, foreknowledge of future things, disposition of things to be done, predestination of those to be saved. From which it becomes manifest that the Scholastics accepted the term predestination only in a good sense, namely for election to eternal life. Whence book 1, distinction 20, letter A, he expressly says: Predestination is concerning saving goods, and concerning men to be saved. Hence therefore let it be concluded that predestination and election do not differ as genus and species.

But those Calvinists are more absurd, who invent such a distinction, that election indeed was made from eternity, but predestination finally happens in time, which itself is against the clear pronouncement of Paul, Ephesians 1, verse 4: He chose in Christ, before the foundation of the world.

Although these terms are of equal scope and breadth, nevertheless some think that certain distinctions lie hidden: 1. By reason of order, because election is a higher degree of predestination. For first from the human race those who will persevere in believing are chosen, and afterwards they are preordained or predestined to eternal life. 2. By reason of the object, since election is concerned with men, while predestination is also concerned with the means of salvation. 3. By reason of the contrary. For election simultaneously includes a respect to the impious and the damned, because to choose is to take one and leave another, and therefore election denotes partly the purpose of God, partly the opposite member of the non-elect, from whom these are chosen, whence Bonaventure says: Election adds discretion or separation from its opposite; that which does not seem to be involved in the term predestination: which suggests to the mind the end and the goal more than the opposite of election. Moreover, there occur in the business of election three terms, or three goals, which the term predestination includes. 1. The term from which, the mercy and goodness of God. 2.

2. The term to which, eternal life. 3. The term for which or through which, the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. Hence Gesner warns in disp. 16 on the Formula of Concord that we ought not to say, if we wish to speak properly: That we are predestined either to the grace of God, or to redemption, but 1. From grace, 2. through the merit of redemption, 3. to life, since eternal salvation is properly ὄψ ἐστι προορισμὺς, just as runners are not said to run to the starting-gates, or to the stadium, but from the starting-gates through the intermediate stadium to the goal, 1 Cor. 9. verse 14.

But however these things may be, and although a certain distinction of reason may be granted; yet this remains certain and indubitable, that in Biblical usage election and predestination extend equally widely, and are synonyms, so that all and only the elect are predestined, and conversely; whence the Apostle in Rom. 8. v. 30 defines the elect, τοὺς πρόθεσιν, those whom God predestined to salvation.

Latin:

I. Quatuor præcipuè sunt termini, qui frequenter hîc occurrunt, 1. Præscientia. 2. Voluntas, quô referimus Propositum & Decretum. 3. Electio. 4. Prædestinatio: de quibus pauca in medium afferemus.

II. 1. De præscientia. Quantumuis Damascenus in dialogo de Manich. hæresi, distinguat inter γνῶσιν, πρόγνωσιν καὶ ἐπίγνωσιν, quarum illa rerum sit omnium, tàm præteritarum, quàm futurarum, ista tantùm futurarum, hæc tantùm præteritarum cognitio, siquidem ἐπίγνωσις potissimùm notat diligentem rei iam factæ cognitionem, & attribuitur iudicibus, qui studiosè cognoscunt & inquirunt in rem factam, de qua iudicare debent: attamen illa omnia in Deo vnum & idem sunt. Apud ipsum enim nihil est præteritum, cuius recordetur; nihil futurum, quod præcognoscat, sed omnia sunt ipsi præsentissima. Vnde statuunt Theologi, Deum potiùs ad salutem destinâre & cognoscere credentes, quàm prædestinâre & præcognoscere credituros. Tàm enim in conspectu eius astant eâ, quæ gerenda sunt, quàm illá, quæ aut geruntur, aut gesta sunt: vno namque perpetuoque intuitu creata & creanda, orta & oritura, acta & agenda simul aspicit. Atque huc spectant sequentia Scripturæ testimonia. Dan. 3. v. 42. Deus æterne, qui absconditorum es cognitor, qui nosti omnia, antequam fiant. Oseæ 5. v. 3. Ego scio Ephraim, & Israel non est absconditus à me, Sirac. 23. v. 29. Domino Deo, antequam crearentur omnia sunt agnita: sic & post perfectu respicit omnia. Et præc. vers. 17. Omnia videt oculis eius. A seculo vsque in seculum respicit, & nihil est mirabile in conspectu eius.

III. Quamuis verò hæc ita se habeant in Deo, attamen κατ' ἀνθρωποπάθειαν καὶ συγκατάβασιν vel cõndescensum, distinguitur eius scientia à præscientia, ratione obiecti, ita, vt illam dicamus rerum esse omnium, hanc verò tantùm futurarum, Et omninò conueniens est dicere, res futuras à Deo non sciri, sed præsciri. Quamuis enim ipsi sint præsentissimæ, non secus atque factæ essent; quia tamen nondum reipsâ factæ sunt, ideo Deus illas præscire dicitur.

IV. Est autem ratione obiectorum præscientia Dei triplex.

1. Generalis, quæ ad omnes creaturas, bonas pariter & malas, ad omnes itidém actus, qualitercunque sint comparati, se extendit.

2. Specialis, quæ tantum fideles ac electos Dei filios respicit, & in hoc articulo potissimùm attenditur. Vt enim præscientia generalis pertinet duntaxat ad intellectum Dei; sic specialis includit insuper voluntatem approbantem, ideoque Scholatici appellant scientiam approbationis & dilectionis. De ista loquitur Apostolus Paulus Rom. 8. v. 20. Quos præsciuit, hos & prædestinauit. Vbi verbum præsciendi ἰδιῶς accipi probatur, 1. Ex serie catenæ Paulinæ. Ea enim talis est, vt posterioribus membris priora determinentur & finiantur, Quos enim præsciuit, hos & prædestinauit. Vnde inferimus: Si præscientia, de quâ hic Paulus agit, eorum est, quorum prædestinatio, & verò hæc non est omnium, vtique nec ista præscientia, de quâ hic loquimur, poterit esse omnium. 3. Ex obiecto πρόγνωσεως vel præscito, Objectum huius præscientiæ sunt soli electi, ij nempè; qui diligunt Deum, quibus omnia cooperantur in bonum, qui sunt vocati κατὰ πρόθεσιν, &c. Ergò præscientia, de quâ hic sermo, non vniuersalis erit, extendens se ad omnes homines, verùm specialis & solos electos attinens, Sic Amos 3. v. 2. dicitur: Tantùm vos cognoui ex omnibus familijs terræ: vbi de speciali προγνώσει ob particulam exclusiuam loqui Prophetam nemo non intelligit. Ioh. 10. v. 14. 27. Cognosco meas oues Ioh. 13. v. 18. Ego scio quos elegerim, Rom. 11. v. 2. Non repulit Deus plebem suam quam præsciuit, 1. Tim. 2. v. 19. Nouit Dominus, qui fint sui Quæ dicta omnia de speciali quâdam scientiâ loquuntur, quâ Deus solos fideles & electos cognoscit, non autem infideles & reprobos, quibus dicet in extremo iudicio, Matt. 7. v. 23. Nunquam novi vos. Et Luc. 13. v. 27. Nescio vos, vnde sitis: Quorum enim nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitæ, eos Deus non nouit hac speciali προγνώσǫ. Est autem notandum quòd licèt hæc præscientia formaliter accepta differat ab ἐκλογῇ καὶ προθέσεως Dei, (quod patet 1. Ex isto: Quos præscivit, hos & prædestinavit: vbi si præscire & prædestinare simpliciter idem forent, ταυτολογία committeretur, 2. Quia dicimur electi κατὰ πρόγνωσιν 1. Pet. 1. v. 1. & 2. Inepta verò foret hæc locutio, si πρόγνωσις & ἐκλογὴ idem forent). attamen cùm ratione obiectorum æquè latè pateant, & vno posito statim ponatur alterum, (qui enim hac προγνώσǫ sunt præsciti, illi sunt ἐκλεκτοὶ & contrà) ideò in Scriptura permutatio fit horum vocabulorum, adeôvt pro electione ponatur vox præscientiæ & contrà.

3. Singularis, quæ ad Christum pertinet, quo sensu. 1. Pet 1. v. 20. dicitur προεγνωσμένος, hoc est, pręscitus ante constitutionem mundi.

V. 2 De voluntate Dei. Sicut in homine qui est imago Dei, duplex est voluntas, vna ἐφετικὴ, quæ est ipse solus & nudus appetitus, quo quis aliquid ἁπλῶς vult & appetit: altera προβεβουλευμένη, voluntas deliberata, quando aliquis rem non simpliciter cupit, sed sibi etiam proponit, & certò decernit se omnibus modis annixurum, vt rem, quam petit, assequatur: ita in Deo quædam voluntas simplex est, quædam verò κατὰ πρόθεσιν, hoc est, aliud voluntas, aliud est propositum. Nam & in humanis βόυλησιν volitionem, καὶ προαίρεσιν electionem seu propositum differre manifestum est. Sæpè enim volumus ἀδύνατα, quæ tamen nobis nunquam proponimus, nisi delirare velimus. Deinde multa cadunt sub voluntatem, quæ non à nobis, sed ab alijs perficiuntur, ideoque ea nobis nunquam proponimus. Sic omnes cupiunt, ab Imperatore benè administrari regnum, nemo tamen solicitè cogitat, de ratione benè administrandi. Pari modo datur aliquod discrìmen inter voluntatem Dei, propositum Dei, vt & decretum Dei. Voluntas terminus generalior est, & comprehendit eas etiam res, quæ non fiunt. Sic Deus vult omnes homines attentè audire verbũ suum, quod tamen nunquam fit. Propositum autem Dei tantùm complectitur ea, quæ certò fiunt. Quod enim Deus proponit, illud absque omni exceptione fit. Decretum Dei adhuc strictior gradus est, quãdo videlicet Deus decernit, se certis medijs effecturum id, quod apud se proposuit. Ita ergò hæc sequuntur; Deus aliquid vult, volitum proponit, propositum decernit; adeòque tria ista differunt, vt latiora & strictiora, antecedentia & consequentia.

Notandum verò est illud propositi & decreti discrimen præcipuè contra Caluinianos, qui πρόθεσιν & ἐκλογὴν vix idem notare volunt, quod falsum. Nam electionis decretum nobis nihil est aliud, quàm ipsa actio eligendi seu prædestinandi, πρόθεσις verò seu propositum est gradu superius electione; est tantùm βουλὴ τοῦ θελήματος Θεοῦ, Ephes. 1. v. 9. Si enim propositum & electio idem essent, annon inepte Paulus Ephes. 1. v. 11. dicens nos κατὰ πρόθεσιν prædestinatos esse? Et Rom. 8. vers. 28. Constituit supremum gradum πρόθεσιν : Iam si electio & propositum eligẽdi idem forent, certè confunderentur annuli in catena Paulina. Zanchius hoc agnouit l. 5. de N. D. cap. 2 quando scribit, quòd prædestinatio supponat electionem, electio dilectionem, dilectio præscientiam, præscientia beneplacitum vel propositum voluntatis.

Quod si autem διχοτομεῖν placuerit, dicimus, voluntatem Dei vel esse simplicem, ita, vt nudam eius denotet θελησιν; vel esse voluntatem εὐδοκιας vel προθεσεως. Quando ergo dicimur electi secundum voluntatem Dei, hanc posteriorem non priorem intelligas.

VI. 5. De Electione. Nomen electionis, & verbum eligendi multa habet in Scripturis significata quorum quinque sunt primaria,

1. Sumitur metonymicè pro electis, vt Rom. 11. v. 7. Electio consecuta est, id est, electi.

2. Pro approbatione & dilectione rei eximiae, quia non nisi quae probamus, caeterisque praestant, eligimus vt Esa. 58. v. 6. An tale est ieiunium, quod elegi? Hinc ob florem & vigorem aetatis iuuenes praestantes apud Hebraeos dicuntur בְּחוּרִים electi; Et in sermone quotidiano solemus rem praestantem nominare electam, Gemma electa, id est, pretiosa; Equus electus, id est, eximius; Liberi electi, id est, chari, probi, pij, auserwehlte liebe Kinder. Sic Genes. 23. v. 6. dicuntur electa sepulchra, id est splendida. Exod. 15. v. 4. Electio principum, seu electi Principes Pharaonis. Ita videtur sumi in isto Luc. 23. vers. 35. Se saluum faciat, si hic est Christus Dei electus.

3. Pro selectione & separatione vel hominum, vel aliarum rerum ad certum vsum. Ita ciuitas, in qua est domus Domini, dicitur locus, quem eligit Dominus, Deut. 12. 15. 17. &c. Sic ex tribus malis, bello, fame, peste, elegit Dauid id, quod minus videbatur esse malum, pestem nimirum. Sic Apostoli a Christo fuerunt ex alijs hominibus selecti ad Apostolatum: quam electionem distinctionis ergo vocant officialem, qua quis ad certum officium eligitur & destinatur.

4. Pro electione alicuius populi & vocatione ad Ecclesiam, quo sensu dicitur Deut. 7. v. 6. Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, vt sis ei populus peculiaris. Hanc electionem nominant Prouincialem.

5. In specialissima significatione pro el. Aeterna fidelium ad vitam æternam facta, priusquam iacerentur fundamenta mundi, quam propterea salutarem indigitant. Atque in hac significatione vltima sumimus vocabulum electionis, a qua denominatur propriè & κατ' ἐξοχὴν ἐκλεκτοὶ vel ἐκλελεγμένοι, hoc est, electi nominaliter & participialiter. Nam inter hæc duo vocabula nihil esse discriminis, patet ex illo Marc. 13. vers. 20. Διὰ τοὺς ἐκλεκτοὺς, οὓς ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεός.

Ex omnibus verò hic significationibus apparet, vocem eligendi 1. Innuere quandam separationem, quâ res vel persona ab aliis secernitur, & ad certum quid seligitur. Hinc isti termini permutantur inuicem; vt quod Moses vocat eligere Deut. 7. v. 6. Salomon reddit per separare, 1. Reg. 8. v. 53. Sic electio discipulorum Luc. 6. v. 13. nominatur separatio Act. 13. v. 2. Id quod obseruasse non parum proderit ad refutandam vniuersalem & indiscretam electionem Huberianam. 2. Præsupponere gratuitam dilectionem à qua semper procedit. Innuitur hoc Deut. 4. v. 37. Quoniam dilexit Iehouah patres tuos, elegit semen eorum post eos, quod reperitur Deut. 7. v. 6. 7. 8. Et ratio est in promptu, quoniam quæ eliguntur, præ alijs grata nobis & dilecta esse oportet: quod contra operum & meritorum propugnatores notari debet.

VII. 4 De prædestinatione. Quod Latini dicunt prædestinare, vnde prædestinatio: græci προορίζειν nominant, vnde προορισμὸς. Significat autem προορίζειν aliquid decernere & præfinire, antequam illud agas. ὅρος enim terminum notat, hinc ὁρίζειν terminare, & προορίζειν pro vel prius determinare, vt 1. Cor. 2. vers. 7. Loquimur Dei sapientiam in mysterio, quam προώρισεν ὁ θεὸς ante secula, id est, quam decreuerat & præordinaverat nobis reuelare. Sic electi dicuntur προορισμένοι, prædestinati hoc est, antequam existerent, ad vitam destinati. Vocula enim πρὸ Græca, & præ Latina, Latina, significat electionem ab æterno fuisse factam; atque ita respicit ad decretum Dei, quod fecit de fidelibus ad vitam ordinandis & destinandis, antequam in tempore crearentur.

VIII. Hic duo insuper in controuersiam veniunt. 1. An idem significet prædestinatio, quod electio?

Caluiniani hæc duo putant differre, vt genus & speciem: Prædestinatio ipsis genus est, Electio & reprobatio sunt species. Verum hoc sine testimonijs Scripturæ dicitur. Nam Ephes. 1. v. 4. vtrumq; vocabulum electionis & prædestinationis eodem sensu accipitur: Elegit nos Deus in Christo ante iacta fundamenta mundi, vt essemus sancti, cùm prædestinasset nos. Vbi electi dicuntur prædestinati, & contrà; prædestinati dicuntur Electi. Quin quòd in omnibus locis, vbi prædestinationis fit mentio, semper intelligatur electio ad vitam: nullus autem potest proferri textus, in quo aliqui ad mortem & æternam damnationem scribantur prædestinati. Nam quod attinet locum istum Act. 4. v. 28. Conuenerunt principes Iudæorum ad faciendam, quæ manus & consilium tuum προώρισε γενέσθαι, prædestinauit fieri: quiuis sanè videt, in eo non agi de aliqua hominum infidelium ad æternā damnationem reprobatione, sed tantùm de decreto & præordinatione mortis & passionis Christi. Quem locum si exceperis, fatentur ipsi Caluiniani, vocabulum Prædestinationis tantùm de electis accipi. Ita enim scribit Vrsinus par 2. Explic Catech. pag. 229. Notandum in Scripturis nomen Prædestinationis ferè de electis tantùm accipi; cui subscribit Zanchius lib. 5. de N. D. cap. 2. quæst. 1. pag. 614. Scriptura, inquit, hoc nomine propriè significare solet sanctorum electionem, & ad vitam æternam deputationem ante mundi constitutionem factam. Consentit Keckermannus lib. 3. Syst. Theol. c. 1. p. 296. qui prædestinationem propriè sub se continere reprobationem ideò negat, quia prædestinatio sit ordinatio rei ad finem. Omnis autem finis bonius est vel perfectio rei, Damnatio verò non est bona, sed ultimum malum. Quare ad illam tanquam ad finem suum nemo præordinatur vel prædestinatur.

Cæterùm negare non possumus. Patres nonnunquam voce prædestinationis generaliter usos pro omni decreto, quo Deus de hominum fidelium salute, & infidelium damnatione certi aliquid constituit, quo sensu dixit Isidorus l. 2. de summo bono, c. 5. & 6: Gemina est prædestinatio, siue electorum ad requiem, siue reproborum ad mortem. Et Aug. l. 15. de Civ. Dei c. 1. Mystice appellamus duas civitates, id est, hominum societates, quorum vna prædestinata est, æternum regnare cum Deo, altera æternum iudicium subire cum Diabolo. Et in Enchirid. c. 100. docet, Deum tanquam summe bonum benè vti & bonis & malis, ad eorum damnationem, quos iustè prædestinavit ad pœnam, & ad eorum salutem, quos benignè prædestinavit ad gratiam. Quod exprimens Fulgentius l. 1. ad Mon. p. 8. Nihil, inquit, aliud accipiendu existimo in illoS. Augustini sermone, quo ad interitū quosdam prædestinatos affirmat; nisi ad interitum supplicij, non delicti; neque ad malum, quod iniustè admittunt, sed ad cruciatum, quem iustissime patientur: Quòd si ergo in laxiore significatu sumas vocabulum prædestinandi, pro constitutione, ordinationeque alicuius rei ad certum finem, dicam ob id non scribimus. Interim, quia non habemus prælucentem Scripturam, & verò in hoc summo mysterio cautè sobrieque loquendum est, ideò malumus solos fideles & electos dicere prædestinatos, reliquos autem reprobos. Hinc Leo in Epistol. ad Petrum Antiochenum scripsit: Credo Deum tantùm prædestinasse bona: præscivisse autem bona & mala. Quod ipsum agnouêre Scholastici: Vt patet ex Lombardi lib. 1. dist 35. lit. A. vbi discrimen affertur inter sciētiam, dispositionem & prædestinationem. Scientia, inquit, est non de futuris tantùm, sed de omnibus, bonis scilicet & malis. Dispositio verò de faciendis: prædestinatio de omnibus saluandis, & de omnibus bonis, qui & hic liberantur, & in finem coronabuntur. Et lit. B. Scientia est omnium, praescientia futurorum, dispositio faciendorum, praedestinatio saluandorum. Ex quibus manifestum fit, Scholasticos vocabulum praedestinationis duntaxat in bonam partem accepisse, videlicet pro electione ad vitam aeternam Vnde l. 1. distinct. 20. lit. A. expresse ait: Praedestinatio de bonis salutaribus est, & de hominibus saluandis. Hinc igitur conclusum esto, Praedestinationem & electionem non differre, vt genus & speciem.

Absurdiores verò sunt isti Caluiniani, qui tale discrimen fingunt, quòd electio quidem sit facta ab aeterno, praedestinatio autem demum contingat in tempore, quod ipsum est contra clarum Pauli pronunciatum, Ephes. 1. vers. 4. Elegit in Christo, ante constitutionem mundi.

Licèt autem vocabula ista sint aequalis ambitus & latitudinis, tamen quaedam latere discrimina nonnulli existimant, 1. Ratione ordinis, quia electio Praedestinationis sit gradus superior. Primum enim ex genere humano eliguntur perseveranter credituri, & post ad vitam aeternam praeordinantur vel praedestinantur. 2. Ratione obiecti, quoniam electio circa homines, praedestinatio etiam circa media salutis versetur, 3. Ratione contrarij. Electio enim simul includit respectum ad impios & damnatos, quia eligere est vnum accipere, alterum relinquere, ideoque electio notat partim Dei propositum, partim oppositum non electorum membrum, ex quibus isti eliguntur, vnda Bonauentura ait: Electio adijcit discretionem siue separationem à suo opposito; id quod non inuul videtur vocabulo praedestinationis: quod magis finem & igon, quàm oppositum electionis animo suggerit. Occurrunt autem in electionis negotio tres termini, vel tres metae, quas praedestinationis vocabulum includit. 1. Terminus à quo, misericordia & ludonia Dei. 2.

2. Terminus ad quem, vita æterna 3. Terminus propter quem vel per quem, meritum Christi fide apprehensum. Hinc monet Gesnerus disp. 16. in Form. Conc. non debere dici, si propriè loqui velimus : Nos esse prædestinatos vel ad gratiam Dei, vel ad redemptionem, sed 1. Ex gratia, 2. per meritum redemptionis, 3. ad vitam, quoniam salus ęterna propriè ὄψ ἐστι προορισμὺς, non secus ac cursores non dicuntur currere ad carceres, vel ad stadium, sed à carceribus per intermedium stadium ad metam, 1 Cor. 9. vers. 14.

Vt autem ista sese habeant, & licet rationis discrimē quoddam concedi queat; attamen certum manet hoc & indubitatum, quòd acceptione Biblicâ electio & prædestinatio æquè latè pateant, & synonyma sint, ita vt omnes & soli electi sint prædestinati, & contrà; vnde Apostolus Rom. 8. v. 30. electos definit, τοὺς πρόθεσιν, quos Deus prædestinauit ad salutem.


### Question I. What is the genuine meaning of the terms occurring in the article…: IX. 2. Whether it should be said that God has predestined the faithful to life; or rather that God is still always predestining

IX. 2. Whether it should be said that God has predestined the faithful to life; or rather that God is still always predestining.

For there are found some who think it is not correctly said in the past tense, that God has predestined us, but that it should rather be said in the present, that God is predestining: And this is because God is not in time, but in eternity, in which there is neither past, nor future, but only present. But this subtlety is superfluous and useless. For why should we not say in the past tense that God has predestined, when the Holy Spirit has not blushed to speak thus in the Scriptures? John 13. v. 18 it is said: I know whom I have chosen. Eph. 1 v. 4. He chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world. And v. 5. He predestined us to the adoption of sons. 2 Tim. 2. v. 9. Grace was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal times. The reason, however, which they bring forward, has no weight. For although God acts without any vicissitude of times: yet the creature, because it is not coeval with God, can be predestined and foreknown before it exists; just as it is said of Jacob and Esau in Rom. 9. v. 11. that they were predestined to their end from eternity, before they were born. For predestination is from that kind of divine action which is πρός τι: for it has a relation to the chosen men. Although, therefore, God predestining is men whom He is said to have predestined are not coeternal with God, but are under time. And therefore, although with respect to God predestining, the action of predestining cannot properly be called past, yet with respect to the men whom He predestined in His eternity, it is past, that is, it was done before men were created, and so when we say in the past tense that God has predestined certain ones, we do not mean this as if there were some action in God which has now passed, but we only look to the predestined men, and we wish to imply that men are not predestined only when they are born and exist, but that they were predestined from all eternity before they were born. And thus that locution in the past tense does not denote any vicissitude of time in God, but indicates our predestination from eternity. If, therefore, you look at the predestined men, then indeed it cannot be said that they are being predestined now in the present (for this would signify and introduce a temporal election), but it must be said that they were chosen or predestined before the foundation of the world.

Latin:

IX. 2. An dicendum sit Deum prædestinâsse fideles ad vitam; an verò Deum adhuc semper prædestinare.

Reperiuntur enim aliqui, qui putant, non rectè dici in præterito, Deum nos prædestinâsse, sed dicendum potiùs in præsenti, Deum prædestinare: Et hoc ideò, quia Deus non sit in tempore, sed in æternitate, in qua nec præteritum, nec futurum, sed tantùm præsens. Verùm superuacanea & inutilis est hæc subtilitas. Cur enim non in præterito diceremus, Deum prædestinâsse, cùm ita loqui in Scripturis non erubuerit Spiritus sanctus? Ioh. 13. v. 18. dicitur: Scio, quos Elegerim. Eph. 1 v. 4. Elegit nos in Christo ante constitutionem mundi. Et v: 5. Prædestinauit nos in adoptionem filiorum. 2. Timoth. 2. v. 9. Gratia data est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia. Ratio verò, quam proferunt, momentum non habet. Etsi enim Deus sine vlla temporum vicissitudine agit: attamen creatura, quia Deo coætanea non est, prius prædestinari & præsciri potest antequam existat; sicuti de Iacobo & Esau dicitur Rom. 9. v. 11. quòd ad suum finem ab æterno prædestinati fuerint, antequam nati essent. Nam prædestinatio est ex illo diuinarum actionum genere, quæ sunt πρός τι: relationem enim habet ad homines electos. Quamuis igitur Deus prædestinans sit extra tempus, neque apud eum præteritum vel futurum, sed tantùm præsens inueniat locum; homines tamen, quos prædestinasse dicitur, Deo coæterni non sunt, sed sub tempore. Ac proinde licet respectu Dei prædestinantis, actio prædestinandi præterita dici propriè nequeat, respectu tamen hominum, quos in sua æternitate prædestinauit, præterita, hoc est, ante homines conditos facta est, adeóque cùm in præterito dicimus, Deum quosdam prædestinâsse, non hoc volumus, ac si quædam actio in Deo sit, quæ nunc præterierit, sed duntaxat respicimus, ad homines prædestinatos, & illud innuere volumus, quòd non tum demum prædestinentur homines, quando nascuntur & existunt, sed quòd prædestinati ab omni æternitate fuerint antequam nascerentur. Atque sic locutio illa in præterito non notat aliquam vicissitudinem temporis in Deo, sed indicat prædestinationem nostram ab æterno. Si ergò respicias homines prædestinatos, tum sanè dici nequit, quòd prædestinentur jam in præsenti, (hoc enim significaret & introduceret electionem temporalem) sed dicendum, quòd ante constitutionem mundi fuerint electi vel prædestinati.


### Question II. What indeed is the opinion of our adversaries, and what is ours, concerning predestination?

I. There are two main hosts of adversaries opposing us, the first of which is the Calvinian ists, it includes the Papists throughout. Therefore, we shall first review their opinions, and afterwards we shall append our orthodox confession: However, the dogma to be held regarding chapter 3, we shall defer concerning the elect.

I. THE OPINION OF THE CALVINISTS.

II. In order that it may be known more exactly what the opinion of the Calvinists is concerning Predestination, for that reason we shall note all those degrees of divine counsels and decrees made from eternity, about which one reads here and there in Calvinistic writings, especially in Calvin in the Instit., Beza in the Colloq. Mompelg. and Resp. ad Acta, Zanchius in book 5 de N. D. cap. 2, quaest. 1, Polanus in the Didascalia, Sturmius in the Diatribe de praedest. th. 6, 7, & 8, etc. These degrees, therefore, they establish.

III. 1. God from eternity decreed to create man to illustrate His own glory, especially indeed His mercy and justice. 2. But because there is no place for mercy where there is no misery, nor for justice where there is no guilt, therefore in turn He decreed from eternity that the first man should fall, and thus by that fall be cast down into a most sad and most miserable state. 3. From this human race, deeply immersed in sins, He decreed to adopt for Himself as sons only a very small part, out of the mere and absolute good pleasure of His will, preceding all causes. Indeed, there are those who say that God from eternity, before original sin was foreseen, out of the whole human race, still intact and not yet corrupted, chose some for life and destined others for death, without any fault of either the first parent or of themselves. 4. These, however, He foreknew from eternity, namely by a special and gracious foreknowledge. 5. 6. Those whom He thus foreknew and acknowledged as His own sons, He truly and sincerely loved from eternity above all others. 7. Those whom He thus loved, He also selected from the rest from all eternity.

These, however, he predestined, chosen and selected for eternal life.

IV. And Zanchius especially urges this gradation in book 5, chapter 2, question 1, while he says: Predestination presupposes Election, election love, love foreknowledge; and foreknowledge the good pleasure of the divine will. For predestination properly, as the word itself signifies, is to make a decree concerning those whom you have chosen for some end, to be led to that end through due means, before they are led to it. Thus predestination presupposes Election. Moreover, we choose those for some end from among others, whom we love above others. Thus election presupposes love: We love, however, after these very ones, those primarily whom we acknowledge as our own children. So also God, after himself and his Son, that is Christ, loved those primarily from eternity whom he acknowledged as his own children in Christ. Thus love presupposes foreknowledge. He foreknew, however, as his children in Christ, those whom he decreed and willed by the good pleasure of his will to adopt as children for himself in Christ. Thus foreknowledge presupposes the good pleasure of the divine will. Here, however, the step must be halted. For one cannot ascend above the good pleasure of the divine will; just as the Apostle does not ascend. Therefore, this free purpose or good pleasure of the divine will is the root of all those things which follow it concerning our salvation, namely first of foreknowledge, by which he acknowledged us from eternity as his own children: then of love, by which he loved us as children, in the beloved son Jesus Christ: thirdly of election, by which he chose us, as beloved, from the dregs of the rest of mankind for eternal life: fourthly of predestination, by which he prepared all the benefits by which he would lead us to the end, namely eternal life, etc. The summary is: God absolutely willed to adopt some as children: these he foreknew, having foreknown he loved, having loved he chose, he predestined to glory. Now follow the remaining steps.

V. 8. Since God predestined some to life, therefore from eternity he entered into counsel concerning the means by which they might be led to that end to which they were predestined. Therefore, those whom he decreed to predestine, to them he also decreed to bestow the means, of which Sturmius counts eleven in his Diatribe, thes. 8. Where note that the Calvinists do not agree among themselves. For some refer creation and the fall to the means of execution, as Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard and Tilenus, part 1 of the Syntagma, p. 144; but others refer them to the eligible object, and thus, just as those place predestination before the fall, so these place it after; concerning which more below. Now we shall add the common means according to the mind of the Calvinists.

VI. 9. Therefore, first, God sent His Son to the predestined, who by suffering and dying might make satisfaction for them. Christ therefore died for the elect alone. For means are ordained for those who are ordained to the end. But only the elect are such. Therefore, these means pertain only to the elect. 10. Then, those for whom Christ died, He called efficaciously in time. 11. To the called, He granted faith in Christ: for faith, since it is a gift of God, is given to no one except to whom He wills to give it. 12. God receives that faith paternally, and therefore absolves His faithful from sins. 13. In the justified, He kindles a serious love of justice and an ardent hatred of injustice, so that men begin to detest sins supremely, and on the contrary, to pursue justice with the greatest love. 14. Furthermore, He incites them by an internal force to the study of good works, so that they not only love good works, but also do them, and strive to do them ever more and more. 15. When, however, God tests their faith and sends many calamities upon them, then He kindles in them serious invocation, so that they may be able to call upon the Lord in truth and spirit. 16. But if they fall into sins against conscience, then God in turn invites them to repentance: for they never totally lose the grace of God and the Holy Spirit. 17. Besides, He stirs up in them a serious desire for the coming of Christ, so that they yearn for eternal life with their whole heart. 18. He also grants patience in the cross, in calamities; in persecutions. 19. And finally he confirms the good work which he has wrought in them, and grants them perseverance in the faith. 20. Which finally is followed by glorification in the other life, according to that of Paul, Rom. 8. v. 30. Whom he justified, them he also glorified. 21. From this glorification, however, arises the ultimate end, which is the glory of God, just as Paul speaks, Eph. 1. verses 5. 6. He predestined us, whom he would adopt as sons, according to the purpose of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace.

VII. And this is a brief synopsis of the Calvinistic opinion concerning the decree of election and the execution of the decree. If you wish to view it in a summary, have this: God willed to show his glory concerning man. Therefore, the human race necessarily fell. He willed, however, to adopt some men as sons. These he specially foreknew, having foreknown he loved, having loved he chose, having chosen he predestined, having predestined he gave to the Son, who redeemed them, having redeemed he calls, having called he grants faith, having granted faith he justifies, having justified he guards in faith, having guarded he glorifies, which glorification is the illustration of divine glory, which end God had proposed to himself from eternity. All of which, so that they may be the better held, can be included in this table or ladder of his.

Latin:

I. Duo sunt agmina aduersariorum præcipua nobis sese opponentium, quorum prius Caluinianos, passim Pontificios comprehendit. Primum igitur opiniones eorum recensebimus, & postea orthodoxam nostram confessionem subiungemus: Haberi autem dogma ad cap. 3. De electis differemus.

I. CALVINIANORVM OPINIO.

II. Quo exactiùs sciatur, quænam sit Caluinianoru de Prædestinatione opinio, eam ob causam annotabimus omnes illos gradus consiliorum diuinorum & ab æterno factorum decretorum, de quibus hinc inde in scriptis Caluinisticis legitur, præsertim apud Caluinum in Instit. Bezam in Colloq. Mompelg & Resp. ad Acta Zanchium lib. 5. de N. D. cap. 2. quæst. 1. Polanum in Didascalia, Sturmium in Diatribe de prędæst. th. 6, 7. & 8. &c. Hos igitur gradus constituunt.

III. 1. Deus ab æterno decreuit condere hominem ad suam gloriam illustrandam, præsertim verò misericordiam & iustitiam. 2. Quia verò misericordiæ non est locus, vbi nulla miseria, nec iustitiæ, vbi nulla culpa, ideò vicissim ab æterno decreuit, vt primus homo laberetur, & sic illo lapsu in tristissimum & miserrimum statum deiiceretur. 3. Ex hoc genere humano, peccatis altissimè immerso, minimam duntaxat partem, ex mero & absoluto voluntatis beneplacito, omnes causas antegrediente, decreuit sibi in filios adoptare. Iinò sunt, qui dicunt, Deum ab æterno ante præuisum peccatum originale, ex toto humano genere, adhuc integro & nondum corrupto, quosdam elegisse ad vitam, alios ad mortem destinâsse, sine vlla vel primi parentis, vel ipsorum culpa. 4. Hos verò ab æterno prænouit, speciali nempe & gratiosa præscientiâ. 5. Quos ita prænouit, & pro suis filijs agnouit, eos ab æterno verè & sincerè dilexit per cæteris omnib. 6. Quos ita dilexit, eos etiam ab omni æternitate è cæteris selegit. 7.

Hos verò electos & selectos ad vitam æternam prædestinauit.

IV. Et hanc gradationem præcipuè vrget Zanchius l. 5. c. 2. quæst: 1. dum ait: Prædestinatio supponit Electionem, electio dilectionem, dilectio præscientiam; & præscientia beneplacitum diuinæ voluntatis. Prædestinatio enim propriè, vt vox ipsa significat, est de iis, quos ad aliquem finem elegeris, per debita media ad eum finem deducendis; antèquam eo deducantur, decretum facere. Ita prædestinatio supponit Electionem. Illos autem ad finem aliquem è cæteris elegimus, quos præ cæteris amamus. Ita electio supponit dilectionem: Diligimus autem post hos ipsos, illos imprìmis, quos pro nostris agnoscimus filiis. Sic etiam Deus post se & Filium suum, id est Christum, illos imprimis amauit ab æterno, quos pro suis in Christo agnouit filiis. Ita dilectio supponit præscientiam. Prænouit autem pro filiis suis in Christo, quos pro beneplacito suæ voluntatis decreuit & voluit sibi in Christo in filios adoptare. Ita præscientia supponit beneplacitum voluntatis diuinæ. Hîc verò sistendus est gradus. Nam suprà beneplacitum voluntatis diuinæ adscendi non potest; quemadmodum nec adscendit Apostolus. Proinde liberum hoc voluntatis diuinæ propositum seu beneplacitum radix est eorum omnium, quæ de nostra salute illud consequuntur, nimirum præscientiæ primùm, quâ ab æterno pro suis nos agnouit filiis: dilectionis deinde, quâ vt filios dilexit, in dilecto filio Iesu Christo: tertiò electionis, qua nos, vt dilectos, ex reliquorum hominum fæce ad æternam elegit vitam: quartò prædestinationis, quâ præparauit omnia beneficia, quibus ad finem, æternam scilicet vitam nos deduceret, &c. Summá est: Deus absolutè aliquos voluit in filios adoptare:hos præsciuit, præscitos dilexit, dilectos elegit, prædestinauit ad gloriã. Nũc sequūtur reliqui gradus.

V. 8. Quoniam Deus ad vitam prædestinauit aliquos, ideò ab æterno de medijs consilium inijt, quibus ad finem illum, ad quem prędestinati sunt, deducerentur. Quos ergò decreuit prædestinate, ijs etiam decreuit media elargiri, quorum vndecim numerat Sturmius in sua Diatribe, thes. 8. Vbi nota, quòd Caluiniani secùm non consentiant. Quidam enim creationem & lapsum referunt ad media executionis, vt Beza in Colloquio Mompelg. & Tilenus par 1. Syntag. p. 144. quidam verò ad obiectum eligibile, adeoque vt illi prædestinationem lapsui anteponunt, ita hi postponunt; de quo infrà pluribus. Nunc communia media ex mente Caluinianorum addemus.

VI. 9. Primùm ergò Deus prædestinatis misit Filium suum, qui patiendo & moriendo pro ipsis satisfaceret. Pro solis igitur electis mortuus est Christus. Iis enim ordinantur media, qui sunt ordinati ad finem. Atqui soli electi sunt tales. Ergò etiam solos electos attinent ista media. 10 Deinde hos, pro quibus Christus est mortuus, efficaciter in tempore vocauit. 11. Vocatis fidem in Christum elargitus est: fides enim, cùm donum Dei sit, nemini datur, nisi cui ille dare vult. 12. Fidem verò istam Deus paternè accipit, ideoque fideles suos à peccatis absoluit. 13. In iustificatis accendit serium amorem iustitiæ, & odium ardens iniustitiæ, ità vt homines incipiant summè detestari peccata, econtra verò maximo amore prosequi iustitiam. 14. Eos porrò incitat interna vi ad studium bonorum operum, ita vt non modò diligant bona opera, sed etiam faciant, & semper magis magisque facere allaborent. 15. Quandò verò Deus eorum fidem tentat, iisque multas calamitates immittit, tum in iis accendit seriam inuocationem, ita vt in veritate & spiritu queant inuocare Dominum. 16. Quòd si prolabantur in peccata contra conscientiam, tunc Deus vicissim eos ad pœnitentiam inuitat: nunquam enim totaliter amittunt gratiam Dei & Spiritum sanctum. 17. Præterea suscitat in iis serium aduentus Christi desiderum, sic, vt toto pectore exoptent vitam æternam. 18. Elargitur quoque patientiam in cruce, in calamitatibus; in persecutionibus. 19. Et demum confirmat, quod in iis operatus est, opus bonum, ijsq; perseuerantiam infide donat. 20. Quam tandem subsequitur glorificatio in altera vita, iuxta illud Pauli Rom. 8. v. 30. Quos iustificauit, hos & glorificauit. 21. Ex hac autem glorificatione exoritur vltimus finis, qui est gloria Dei, quemadmodum loquitur Paulus Eph. 1. vers. 5. 6. Prædestinauit nos, quos adoptaret in filios, secundum propositum voluntatis suæ in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ suæ.

VII. Et hæc est breuis synopsis sententiæ Caluinisticæ de decreto electionis, decretique exsecutione. Si eam in compendio velis intueri, hoc habe: Deus circa hominem voluit ostendere suam gloriam. Igitur necessario lapsum est genus humanum. Voluit autem aliquos homines adoptare in filios. Hos specialiter præsciuit, præscitos dilexit, dilectos elegit, electos prædestinauit, prædestinatos donauit Filio, qui eos redemit, redemptos vocat, vocatos donat fide, fide donatos iustificat, iustificatos in fide custodit, custoditos glorificat, quæ glorificatio est illustratio gloriæ diuinæ, quem finem Deus sibi ab æterno proposuerat. Quæ omnia vt eò meliùs teneantur, huic siuę tabellæ siue scalæ includi poterunt.


### Question II. What indeed is the opinion of our adversaries, and what is ours…: The ladder of Calvinistic predestination with fifteen degrees

The ladder of Calvinistic predestination with fifteen degrees.

The purpose of manifesting glory in men. The absolute decree concerning certain ones to be glorified. The special foreknowledge of those to be glorified. The love of those foreknown. The election of those loved. The predestination of those elected. The creation of those predestined. The corruption of those created. The redemption of those corrupted. The calling of those redeemed. The faith of those called. The justification of the faithful. The preservation of those justified. The glorification of those preserved. From this glorification arises the manifestation of divine glory.

VIII. In this ladder, what is last in execution was first in intention: and these things are so connected that the later cannot exist without the former, nor the former without the later. For thus the Calvinists, descending from the prior, conclude: Whoever was not from eternity foreknown, loved, elected, predestined: for him the Son was not sent, he is not called, nor can he believe, much less be justified and glorified. But ascending from the posterior: He who is not glorified, nor justified, he is not called, for him Christ did not die, he is not predestined, elected, loved, foreknown, etc. This they call the analytical method, but that one the synthetic. If, therefore, you wish to consider predestination from the posterior, then one must ascend through this ladder; if from the prior, then descend. For the posterior the former presuppose the prior, and the latter follow from the former. And thus in one intuition you can comprehend the whole mystery of Calvinistic iniquity, which is included in this definition: Predestination is a decree of God, by which from eternity he chose certain and singular persons to life out of a mere and absolute decree, preceding all causes, with no respect to faith in Christ, so that it is most absolutely necessary that these be saved by virtue of this decree; the rest being reprobated without any consideration of impenitence, out of the same mere good pleasure, and destined to eternal damnation.

2. THE OPINION OF THE PAPISTS.

IX. All these serve in the camp of Pelagius, although not all wish to admit it. Now Pelagius taught that men were chosen on account of foreseen works and the good use of free will. For thus Augustine describes his opinion in the book On the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 18. God foreknew, says the Pelagian, who would be holy and immaculate through the choice of free will, and therefore he chose them before the foundation of the world in that very foreknowledge of his, by which he foreknew that they would be such.

X. The Scholastics are not far from this opinion of Pelagius. Lombard indeed, in Book 1 of the Sentences, dist. 41, letter A, affirms that the merit of hardening is found, but the merit of mercy is not found, and he rejects all foreknowledge of works from the business of election: yet the others who followed him approached more and more to the Pelagian errors. For although Thomas also, in Part 1 of the Summa, question 23, article 5, argues that predestination, since it is eternal on the part of the act of the one predestining, has no cause: yet soon contradicting himself, he wishes for a respect of merits to be included in the business of election, when he says: God preordained that he would give glory to someone out of merits. Bonaventure, in Book 1, distinction 41, art. 1, questions 1 and 2, indeed removes the meritorious cause, yet he concedes a motivating reason, and thus contends that election was made with respect to merits. For thus he says in the resolution of question 2: The cause of congruity in general is to be given, namely good or evil works. Gabriel Biel writes confidently, in book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 41, reason 2: 'There is some cause for any predestination, because some are predestined for this reason, because God foresees in them the good use of free will and merits.' This very opinion is defended by Albert Pighius in book 8 on the use of free will, chapter 2, expressly writing that GOD has regarded not persons, but MERITS.

XI. But the more recent Papists, especially the Jesuits, wish to depart from the Scholastics, yet they do not agree among themselves. Bellarmine is clearly unique regarding his words, whose opinion consists of three things: 1. In the exclusion of every cause. 2. In the description of the order of predestination. 3. In a certain distinction and limitation.

XII. 1. As regards the cause of predestination, he writes thus about it in book 2 on grace and free will, chapter 9: 'No reason for divine predestination can be assigned on our part.' By 'reason,' however, he says he excludes not only merits properly so called, but also the good use of free will or of grace, or of both together foreseen by God, even if it is not called merit except of congruity, and even if it is not called a true cause, but only a condition without which he who is predestined would not be predestined. How truly and seriously he wrote these things, will soon be evident.

XIII. 2. He depicts the order of predestination in the divine mind thus.

1. God foresaw, if He were to create man, that he would fall with all his posterity, and at the same time He saw that He could, according to His own will, liberate either all or some in various ways. We, however, although we do not set limits to divine wisdom, nevertheless know from Scripture that no other remedy could be found for fallen man than the passion of Christ.

2. He willed to create man, and to permit him to fall; and mercifully to liberate some from the number of the fallen, while others were justly left in the mass of perdition. But here, words should have been made not only about the permission of the fall, but rather concerning the first and highest decree of God, which was concerning the creation of all in Adam for eternal life.

3. He devised remedies, suitable for those to be saved, in which the incarnation and passion of the Savior held the first place. But he errs in two ways: 1. He disturbs the order of the decrees; because he postpones the counsel concerning the means of salvation to the purpose of election, when it ought to be placed before it. 2. He approves the Calvinistic particularity, because he implies that these means were devised for the elect alone. Therefore God does not love all, did not send the Son for all, and thus does not bestow sufficient aid upon all, which nevertheless Bellarmine himself asserted in book 2, chapter 5, and following.

4. He approved those remedies, and then chose Christ, and us in him before the foundation of the world. But why does he omit the respect of faith? We are indeed chosen in Christ, but not absolutely, but with respect to faith apprehending Christ.

5. He disposed, ordained, and in a certain way commanded, that it should be done so. But this step pertains to the counsel of the means rather than to the election of believers.

XIV. 3. He proposes a certain distinction and limitation in book 2, chapter 14, column 27, D, where he writes that election can be considered in two ways: In one way, as it is the intention of giving glory. In another way, as it is the disposition of execution, and as it were the execution in the divine mind. In the former way, election is merely gratuitous, and requires no foreknowledge of good works. In the latter way, it presupposes the foreknowledge of merits. For God did not dispose to give eternal life under the aspect of a reward, except to those whom he foresaw would act well. And a little later he adds: In the genus of the efficient cause, good works are prior to glory itself, since those are the causes, and it is the effect.

XV. From these words of Bellarmine, however, we gather two things against him. 1. That the little distinction begs the question. For nowhere in the Scriptures is a bare intention of giving glory accepted for election to salvation; nay, that intention or purpose is distinguished from election, while according to the former we are said to be predestined, Eph. 1. v. 5. 9. 11. Hence it is that election is described together through πρόγνωσιν, so that it may thus be shown that the τάξιν of the means and the foreknowledge of faith in Christ, and therefore the disposition of the execution, are always and essentially included in election itself, and consequently cannot be considered as a bare purpose of giving glory. 2. That he contradicts himself. He excludes it before any moving reason. Why then does he attack the Scholastics, and pretend to depart from them? For they are not so injurious to the grace of God as to maintain that this very grace, insofar as it is the beneficial and universal will of God, was excited by the foreseen merits of men: but they only seek the cause or moving reason of the electing will, why God chose these and not those, in the foreknowledge of works. Since he himself concedes this, he sticks in the same mire of the Pelagian heresy.

XVI. Nor can he determine otherwise, if he wishes his own hypotheses to be safe. There are three of these. 1. That men merit justification from congruity. 2. Glorification from condignity. 3. That the decree does not differ from the execution. For which causes, therefore, men are justified and saved in time, for the same causes God from eternity willed to save and chose them. But they are justified and saved on account of good merits. Therefore, God also from eternity decreed to save them on account of good merits, that is, chose them to life. Therefore, we propose this argument to Bellarmine and all Papists, from which they will never be able to extricate themselves: If election is gratuitous, and made without the foreknowledge of works, then we shall also be justified without works, on account of the most exact harmony of the decree and the execution. But because they are going to deny this, and attribute salvation to merits, hence it follows that gratuitous election is not to be, but to have flowed in equal measure from the foreknowledge of merits, which, however, they wish to appear foreign to heresy.

XVII. Gregorius de Valentia: Tom. 1. disput. 1. quaest. 23. punct. 5. §. 3. similarly wishes to appear foreign to the suspicion of Pelagianism. For he refutes both Pelagius, and the Semi-Pelagians, and all those who say that the cause of predestination is merits, whether antecedent or subsequent to grace. And §. 4. Col. 518. he posits this assertion: If predestination is referred to all its effects, there is no reason or cause of merit in any way in the predestined person himself, neither that for which, nor that without which not, but it ought to be referred solely to the gratuitous will of God. Soon, however, what he gave with one hand he takes away in turn with the other, while in col. 524 and following he defends at length that God predestines no one except with a certain respect to the cooperation of the will and good works. For hence against Calvin he wishes to demonstrate that election is not absolute, having proceeded from the bare and unlimited will of God, but rather ordered, and joined with the foreknowledge of works. Of the same opinion is Franciscus Suarez in part 1 of the Summa, tractate on predestination, book 2, where he discourses most extensively on the causes of election.

XVIII. Whatever therefore the Papists may say, and with whatever cloak they may veil their opinion, this axiom remains, according to them and their own hypotheses, perpetually certain: that the foreknowledge of merits is essentially included in election as a motivating reason and efficient cause, unless they say either that a man is saved without merits, or that there are other causes of election and salvation; both of which, however, they liberally concede elsewhere, indeed the former they urge against us, the latter against the Calvinists.

XIX. In place of a colophon I shall add the confession of Martinus Becanus, who in his disputation on Catholic predestination, chapter 3, expressly confesses that predestination has arisen from foreseen merits. For thus he speaks in thesis 5: The third question, whether election to glory was made from foreseen merits, also admits a double sense: one concerning the condign merits of free will, the other concerning the condign merits of grace. The former merit, which the Pelagians brought forward, has long since been exploded. Concerning the latter there is controversy. The Scholastics are divided; and on both sides they cite Augustine, concerning whose mind it is not sufficiently certain. If the rule given above be settled: For it is certain from the Scriptures that eternal life is given from merits, and therefore is called a reward, a prize, a stipend, a crown: therefore it cannot be doubted that it was prepared from eternity from the foreknowledge of merits, which is openly gathered from that passage in Matthew 25: Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: For I was hungry, and you gave me to eat. What is it for the kingdom to be prepared from the foundation of the world, if not that certain ones were elected from eternity to the celestial kingdom? And why were these elected from eternity and not those? He adds the cause, because these did good works, those did not do them; namely in the presence of God. And conversely, thesis 6: All obtain eternal life from merits, according to that saying of Paul, No one shall be crowned, unless he has contended lawfully: therefore according to the assigned rule, all are predestined to eternal life from foreseen merits.

XX. And thus from what has been said so far it is openly certain that the Papists in reality pelagianize, although they are unwilling to admit it. For they maintain that no one is elected, unless God foresaw that he would work well: And yet they do not concede that election was made from foreseen merits: Thus therefore they retain the mind of Pelagius, but change the language. Beccanus betrayed this same thing, while he begins thesis 7 thus: The matter is sufficiently explained. If it is asked concerning the name, whether it is permitted to say that predestination was made from foreseen [merits], that is simply to be denied, because neither the first effect, nor the whole complex of effects is from merits. This is surely to play in a serious matter, and to cast a veil over the eyes of the simpler ones: They admit that the Elect were therefore elected, because God foresaw their merits; And yet they simply deny that election was made from foreseen merits, which is gross and palpab le contradiction is worthy only of the Jesuit Wuicus's acumen.

Latin:

Scala prædestinationis Caluinisticæ cum quindecim gradibus.

Propositum de manifestanda gloria in hominibus. Absolutum decretum de quibusdam glori ficandis. Glorificandorum specialis præscientia. Præscitorum dilectio. Dilectorum electio. Electorum prædestinatio. Prædestinatorum creatio. Creatorum corruptio. Corruptorum redemptio. Redemptorum vocatio. Vocatorum fides. Fidelium iustificatio. Iustificatorum conseruatio. Conseruatorum glorificatio. Ex hac glorificatione orta gloriæ divinæ manifestatio.

IIX. In hac scala, quod vltimum est in exsecutione, primum fuit in intentione: suntque ista sic connexa, vt posteriora nequeant esse sine prioribus, nec priora sine posterioribus. Ita enim Caluiniani descendendo à priori colligunt: Quicunque ab æterno non fuit præscitus, dilectus, electus, prædestinatus: illi non est missus Filius, ille non vocatur, neque potest credere, multò minùs iustificari & glorificari, A posteriori verò ascendendo: Qui nõ glorificatur, nec iustificatur, ille non est vocatus, pro eo Christus non est mortuus, is non est prædestinatus, electus, dilectus, præscitus, &c. Hanc vocant methodum analyticam, illam verò syntheticam. Quòd si ergò à posteriori velis cõsiderare prædestinationẽ, tum per hãc scalam adscendendum est; sin à priori, tum descendendum. Posteriora ęnim praesupponunt priora, & ex prioribus consequuntur posteriora. Atque sic vno intuitu comprehendere potes totum mysterium iniquitatis Caluinisticae, quod huic definitioni inclusum: Praedestinatio est decretum Dei, quo ab aeterno quasdam certas & singulares personas ex mero & absoluto, omnesque causas antegrediente decreto, nullo fidei in Christum respectu ad vitam elegit, ita vt hos salvari vt istius decreti, absolutissimè sit necessum; reliquis sine ulla consideratione impoenitentiae, ex mero eodem beneplacito reprobatis, & ad aeternam damnationem destinatis.

2. PONTIFICIORVM OPINIO.

IX. Hi omnes in castris Pelagij militant, quamuis non omnes id fateri velint. Docebat autem Pelagius electos esse homines ob praeuisa opera, & bonum liberi arbitrij vsum. Ita enim sententiam eius describit August. l. de praedest. Sanct. c. 18. Praesciebat Deus, ait Pelagianus, qui futuri essent sancti & immaculati per liberae voluntatis arbitrium, & ideò eos ante mundi constitutionem in ipsa sua praescientia, quâ tales futuros esse praesciuit, elegit.

X. Ab hac Pelagij sententia non alieni sunt Scholastici. Lombardus quidem l. 1. sent. dist. 41. lit. A. affirmat, quòd obdurationis meritum inueniatur, misericordiae autem meritum non inueniatur, omnemque operum praeuisionem ex electionis negotio reÿcit: Caeteri tamen, qui ipsum secuti sunt, magis magisque ad Pelagianos errores accesserunt. Quamuis enim & Thomas part. 1. Summae quaest. 23. artic. 5. disputet, praedestinationem, cùm sit aeterna ex parte actus praedestinantis nullam habere causam: attamen mox sibi ipsi contradicens, respectum meritorum, negotio electionis inclusum vult, cùm ait: Deus praeordinauit se daturum alicui gloriam ex meritis. Bonaventura lib. 1. distinct. 41. art. 1. quaest. 1. & 2. remouet quidem causam meritoriam, concedit tamē rationem motiuam, adeoque electionem cum respectu meritorum factam esse contendit, Ita enim inquit in resolut. quaest. 2. Causam congruentiæ in generali dare est, bona scilicet vel mala opera. Gabriel Biel cõfidenter scribit, in l. 1. sent. dist. 41. rat. 2. Alicuius prædestinationis est aliqua causa, quia aliqui ideò prædestinantur, quia præuidet Deus in eis bonum vsum liberi arbitrij & merita. Quamipsam opinionem defendit Albertus Pighius l. 8. de vsu l. arbitrij c. 2. expressè scribens, DEVM non personas, sed MERITA respexisse.

XI. Recentiores autem Papicolæ, in primis Iesu Witæ, à Scholasticis volunt recedere, neque tamen secum ipsis consentiunt. Bellarminus planè singularis est quoad verba, cujus opinio consistit in tribus: 1. In exclusione omnis causæ. 2. In descriptione ordinis prædestinatorij. 3. In quadam distinctione & limitatione.

XII. 1. Quod causam prædestinationis spectat, de illa sic scribit l. 2. de grat. & lib. arbitrio, cap. 9. Prædestinationis diuinæ nulla ratio ex parte nostri assignari potest. Per rationem verò se excludere ait, non solùm merita propriè dicta, sed etiam bonum vsum liberi arbitrij aut gratiæ, aut vtriusque simul à Deo præuisum, etiamsi non dicatur meritum nisi de congruo, & etiamsi non dicatur vera causa, sed tantùm conditio, sine qua non prædestinaretur is, qui prædestinatur. Quam verè autem & seriò hæc scripserit, mox patebit.

XIII. 2. Ordinem prædestinationis in mente diuina sic depingit.

1. Præuidit Deus, si hominem conderet, eum lapsurum cum omni posteritate, & simul vidit, posse se varijs modis liberare vel omnes, vel aliquos, pro arbitratu suo. Nos verò, licèt sapientiæ diuinæ terminos haut ponamus, ex Scriptura tamen scimus, nullum aliud homini lapso remedium inueniri potuisse quàm passionem Christi.

2. Voluit hominem condere, ac vt laberetur permittere; & quosdam ex numero lapsorum misericorditer liberare, alijs in massa perditionis iustè relictis. At hîc non tantùm de permissione lapsus debebant verba fieri, sed potiùs de primo summoq; decreto Dei, quod fuit de omnibus in Adamo ad vitam æternam creandis.

3. Excogitavit remedia, salvandis electis idonea, in quibus primum locum habuit incarnatio & passio Salvatoris. Verùm dupliciter errat, 1. Ordinem decretorum turbat; quia consilium de mediis salutis postponit proposito electionis, cùm anteponi debeat. 2. Particularitatem Calvinisticam approbat, quia media ista pro solis electis excogitata esse innuit Non igitur Deus omnes diligit, non omnibus Filium misit, adeóque sufficiens auxilium non omnibus largitur, quod tamen Bellarm. ipse asseruit l. 2. c. 5. & seqq.

4. Approbavit ea remedia, & tunc elegit Christum, & nos in ipso antemundi constitutionem. Sed cur omittit respectum fidei? Sumus quidem in Christo electi, verùm non absolutè, sed cum respectu fidei Christum apprehendentis.

5. Disposuit, ordinavit, & quodammodo imperavit, ut ita fieret. Hic verò gradus ad consilium mediorum potiùs, quàm ad electionem credentium spectat.

XIV. 3. Distinctionem & limitationem quandam proponit l. 2. c. 14. col. 27. D. vbi Electionem scribit duobus modis considerari posse, Vno modo, vt est intentio dandi gloriam. Alio modo, vt est dispositio executionis, & quasi executio in mente diuinâ. Priore modo electio est merè gratuita, & nullam prærequirit præuisionem operum bonorum. Posteriore modo præexigit præuisionem meritorum. Non enim vitam æternam sub ratione præmij Deus dare disposuit, nisi ijs, quos benè operaturos esse præuidit. Et paulò post addit: In genere causæ efficientis priora esse opera bona, quam sit ipsa gloria, quoniam illa sunt causæ, ipsa est effectus.

XV. Ex his autem Bellarmini verbis duo adversus ipsum colligimus. 1. Quòd distinctiuncula tata petat principium. Nullibi enim in Scripturis nuda dandi gloriam intentio pro electione ad salutem accipitur; Imò ista intentio vel propositum ab electione distinguitur, dum secundum illud prædestinati dicimur, Eph. 1. v. 5. 9. 11. Hinc est, quòd electio describatur vnà per πρόγνωσιν, vt ita ostendatur, τάξιν mediorum & præuisionem fidei in Christum adeóq; dispositionem executionis ipsi electioni semper & essentialiter inclusam esse, & per consequens considerari non posse, vt nudum dandi gloriam propositum. 2. Quòd sibiipsi contradicat. Ante omnem rationem motiuam excludit. Cur igitur Scholasticos oppugnat, & ab ijs se discedere simulat? Non enim isti tam iniurij sunt in Dei gratiam, vt statuant, hanc ipsam, prout est benéfica & vniuersalis Dei voluntas, excitatam esse prævisis hominum meritis: sed tantùm causam vel rationem motiuam voluntatis eligentis, cur Deus hos, non illos elegerit, quærunt in præuisione operum. Quod cùm ipse concedat, in eodem Pelagianæ hæreseos luto hæret.

XVI. Neque aliter potest statuere, si proprias hypotheses velit saluas. Harũ tres sunt. 1 Homines ex congruo mereri iustificationem. 2. Ex condigno glorificationem. 3. Decretum ab executione non differre. Ob quas igitur causas homines in tempore iustificantur & saluantur, ob easdem Deus ab æterno illos saluare voluit & elegit. Iustificantur autem & saluantur propter bona merita. Ergò etiam Deus ab æterno propter bona merita eos saluare decreuit, hoc est, ad vitam elegit. Proinde hoc argumentum Bellarmino & omnibus Papicolis proponimus. ex quo se nunquam expedire poterunt: Si electio est gratuita, & sine operum præuisione facta, tum sine operibus etiam iustificabimur, ob exactissimam decreti & executionis consonantiam. Quia vero negaturum hoc eunt, & salutem meritis attribuunt, hinc sequitur, electionem gratuitam nonesse, sed pari modo ex praevisione meritorum profluxisse, quae tamen haeresi videri volunt alieni.

XVII. Gregorius de Valentia: Tom. 1. disput. 1. quaest. 23. punct. 5. §. 3. similiter alienus vult videri à Pelagianismi suspicione. Refutat enim & Pelagium, & Semi-pelagianos, & omnes eos, qui causam praedestinationis dicunt esse merita, sive antecedentia, sive subsequentia gratiam. Et §. 4. Col. 518. hanc ponit assertionem: Si praedestinatio referatur ad omnes ipsius effectus, nulla est ratio, seu causa ullo modo meriti in ipso praedestinato, neque propter quam, neque sine qua non, sed in solam gratuitam Dei voluntatem referri debet. Mox tamen, quod vnâ manu dedit alterâ vicissim adimit, dum col. 524. & seqq. prolixè defendit, Deum nemine praedestinare, nisi cum respectu quodam ad cooperationem arbitrij & bona opera. Hinc enim contra Caluinum vult demonstrare, electionem non esse absolutam, ex nuda & illimitata voluntate Dei profectam, sed potius ordinatam, & cum praevisione operum conjunctam. Eiusdem sententiae est Franciscus Suarez in par. 1. Summae tract. de praedest. l. 2. vbi fusissimè de causis electionis disserit.

XVIII. Quicquid ergò dicant, & quocunque pallio opinionem suam obuelent Papicolae, manet hoc secundum ipsos, ipsorumque hypotheses axioma perpetuò certum: Electioni praevisionem meritorum, vt rationem motiuam & causam efficientem, essentialiter inclusam esse, nisi dixerint, vel sine meritis hominem saluari, vel alias esse electionis & saluationis causas; quod vtrumque tamen alibi liberaliter concedunt, imò priùs contra nos vrgent, posterius contra Caluinianos.

XIX. Colophonis loco adscribam Martini Becani confessionem, qui in disp. de praedest. Cathol. c. 3. expressè fatetur, praedestinationem ex praeuisis meritis esse ortam. Ita enim loquitur thesis 5. Tertia quaestio, an electio ad gloriam facta sit ex preuisis meritis, patitur etiam duplicem sensum: Vnum de condignis meritis liberi arbitrij, alterum de condignis meritis gratiæ. Prius meritum, quod afferebant Pelagiani, iam pridem explosum est. De posteriori est controversia. Scholastici diuisi sunt; & in vtramque partem citant Augustinum, de cuius mente non satis constat. Si regula superiùs data teneatur, facilè negotium expedietur: Constat enim ex Scripturis, vitam æternam dari ex meritis, & ideo vocari mercedem, brauium, stipendium, coronam: ergò dubitari non potest, quin ab æterno præparata sit ex præuisione meritorum, quod apertè colligitur ex illo Matth. 25. Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum à constitutione mundi: Esuriui enim, & dedistis mihi manducare. Quid est paratum esse regnum à constitutione mundi, nisi quosdam ab æterno electos esse ad cæleste regnum? Et quare ab æterno hi electi sunt non illi? Causam addit, quia hi fecerunt bona opera, illi non fecerunt; scilicet in præsentia Dei. Et vicissim th. 6. Omnes ex meritis consequuntur vitam æternam, iuxta illud Pauli, Nemo coronabitur, nisi qui legitimè certauerit: ergò iuxta regulam assignatam, omnes ex præuisis meritis ad vitam æternam prædestinati sunt.

XX. Atque sic ex hactenus dictis apertè constat, Pontificios reipsâ pelagianízein, quamuis id fateri nolint. Statuunt enim neminem electum esse, nisi quem benè operaturum præuiderit Deus: Et tamen non concedunt, electionem factam esse ex præuisis meritis: Sic igitur mentem Pelagii retinent, sed linguam mutant. Prodidit hoc idem Beccanus, dum thesin 7. ita orditur: Res satis explicata est. Si de nomine quæratur, an liceat dicere, prædestinationem factam esse ex præuisis, id simpliciter est negandum, quia nec primus effectus; nec tota complexio effectuum ex meritis est. Huc nimirum est in re seria ludere, & simplicioribus glaucoma objicere: Fatentur Electos ideò electos esse, quia Deus præuidit illos rum merita; Et tamen simpliciter negant, electionem ex præuisis meritis factam esse, quæ crassa & palpabilis contradictio solo Iesu Wuico acumine digna est.


### Question II. What indeed is the opinion of our adversaries, and what is ours…: 3. Our and Orthodox opinion

3. OUR AND ORTHODOX opinion.

XXI. 1. After God had from eternity entered into a counsel concerning our πρωτογλωσίᾳ or first creation, by which He had determined to create man in His own image, that is, to instruct him with wisdom of mind, rectitude of will, and integrity of all powers; inasmuch as that God foresaw that man would not remain in that concreated wisdom and perfection, but would lose it through disobedience and sin.

2. Foreseeing, therefore, the most sad and miserable state of the human race, through His immense φιλανθρωπίαν and ineffable εὐσπλαγχνίαν, arising from the foreseen misery as a προκαταρκτικη̂ cause, He entered into a counsel concerning the παλιγγενεσίᾳ or regeneration and reparation of the human race. He willed, therefore, from all eternity that just as the whole race had fallen, so also the whole should emerge and be regenerated from that fall. And this is the antecedent will or that of mercy.

3. Hence He thought of certain means through which the fallen human race could in turn arrive at that lost justice. Because, indeed, He was most gravely offended by the sin of man, it was first necessary to satisfy His justice, and the Son interposed Himself as Mediator. Him, therefore, He decreed to send into the world, who by His passion and death would make satisfaction for the entire human race.

And this order of divine counsels is hinted at in Gen. 1, 2, and 3. For first, the decree concerning the creation of man is recounted there: Let us make man in our image and likeness, Gen. 1, v. 26. The next counsel of God from there is legal: Of every tree you shall eat, except for the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, Gen. 2, verse 16. The third counsel was concerning the punishment of man. Gen. 3. v. 8. From this finally follows the Evangelical decree concerning the seed of the woman, who will crush the head of the serpent, Genesis 3. v. 35. XXII. 4. But since men by their own powers could not rise to grasp that grace obtained by the death of Christ, for that reason God made a decree that He might redeem men; but also to promise and offer to all the grace obtained by redemption through the word. 5. At the same time He also decreed through the preaching of the Gospel to bestow faith as a means grasping grace, provided that men do not deny external hearing, or in other ways place an obstacle for themselves. 6. But since the omniscient God, who searches the reins and hearts, from eternity foresaw that many would remain in impenitence, and would not use those means, but that few would accept that grace with a willing mind, and would perseveringly believe in Christ the redeemer, therefore He willed these few to be saved by a special will and εὐδοκίᾳ (which is otherwise called πρόθεσις θεῦ) on account of the merit of Christ alone grasped by faith, according to that John 6. v. 40. This is the will of God the Father, that everyone who sees the Son, and believes in Him, may have eternal life. 7. But these very ones He specially foreknew, that is, He acknowledged them as His own children, just as He Himself says, John 10. v. 14: I know my sheep, And c. 13. verse 18. I know whom I have chosen. And this is that special πρόγνωσις according to which the Apostle says election has been made. 8. But these specially foreknown ones He in turn specially loved. For we love no one, unless he is first known to us. 9. And these beloved ones He chose for Himself as a peculiar possession out of the whole multitude of men, and finally ordained and predestined to eternal life, to the praise of his glorious grace.

XXIII. Formula of Concord, art. 11, m. p. 802, with all these things included in eight degrees, the first of which is the decree concerning universal redemption. 2. concerning the universal offering of the benefits of the merit of Christ. 3. concerning conversion through the Word. 4. concerning adoption and justification. 5. concerning renewal and sanctification. 6. concerning the protection and defense of believers. 7. concerning preservation to the end of life, and finally 8. concerning eternal glorification. XXIV: But just as God foresaw and decreed all these things from eternity, so they have come to pass and still come to pass in time. For 1. he created man in his own image, and gave him a commandment about not eating, which because he transgressed, therefore, having lost the image, he fell into a most sorrowful state of sin. 2. God, moved by this misery of man out of mere φιλανθρωπία, sent his Son into the world, who died for all, reconciled all to God the Father, and restored to all the lost righteousness. 3. That merit is announced and offered to the whole world: but most do not wish to receive it; but they resist with all their strength, and therefore few conceive faith from the preached word, and are regenerated through the faith conceived. 4. But these regenerated ones, if they persevere to the end of life, are certainly saved and finally glorified, to which salvation they were also predestined by God, under the condition of keeping this order. What therefore and how God decreed from eternity to be done, that also and in that same way is done in time, from which it appears how beautiful is the harmony between the eternal decree and the temporal execution of the decree. XXV. Therefore, to conclude, these were the degrees in the decree of election. 1. There was the decree of πρωτογενεσίας, 2. Foreknowledge of the fall. 3. Decree of παλιγγενεσίας. 4. Counsel concerning the means. 5. Foreknowledge of those who are to use the means or otherwise, a judgment of purpose concerning these few, who are to use the means, to be glorified. 7. Their special πρόγνωσις. 8. The love of those foreknown. 9. The election of those loved: And finally. 10. The predestination of those elected.

XXVI. And thus far we have reviewed the principal opinions concerning predestination. Now this remains, that orthodoxy may be confirmed and illustrated: but heterodoxy may be refuted, and contrary objections may be dissolved, which we shall provide expedited in the following problem.

Latin:

3. NOSTRA ET ORTHOdoxa sententia.

XXI. 1. Posteaquam Deus ab aeterno inierat consilium de πρωτογλωσίᾳ nostra vel prima creatione, quo constituerat, hominem ad imaginem suam creare, h. e. instruere sapientiâ mentis, rectitudine voluntatis, & integritate omnium virium; καθότι ille Deus praevidit, hominem in concreatâ illa sapientia & perfectione non permansurum, verùm inobedientiâ & peccato eam esse perditurum.

2. Praevidens ergò tristissimum & miserrimum humani generis statum, per immensam φιλανθρωπίαν suam & ineffabilem εὐσπλαγχνίαν, ex praevisâ miseriâ, tanquam causa προκαταρκτικη̂ subortum, iniit consilium de παλιγγενεσίᾳ seu regeneratione & reparatione humani generis. Voluit igitur ab omni aeternitate sicuti totum genus erat lapsum, ita & totum ex isto lapsu emergere & regenerari. Atque haec est voluntas antecedens seu misericordiae.

3. Proinde cogitavit, de certis mediis, per quae humanum genus lapsum vicissim posset ad perditam illam iustitiam devenire. Quia n. gravissimè offendebatur peccato hominis, prius erat satisfaciendum ipsius iustitiae, atq; sibi Mediatorem se interposuit Filius. Hunc igitur decrevit mittere in mundum, qui passione & morte suâ pro vninerso genere humano satisfaceret.

Et hic consiliorum diuinorum ordo innuitur Gen. 1. 2. & 3. Primum enim recensetur ibi decretum de creatione hominis: Faciamus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem nostram, Gen. 1. v. 26. Proximum inde consilium Dei est legale: De omni arbore comedes, praeterquam de arbore scientiae boni & mali, Gen. 2. vers. 16. Tertium consilium erat de puniẽdo homine. Gen. 3. v. 8. Hinc demum consequitur Euangelicum decretum de semine mulieris, contrituro caput serpentis, Genes. 3. v. 35. XXII. 4. Quoniam verò homines proprijs viribus non poterant assurgere ad capessendam illam gratiam morte Christi partam, ob id Deus fecit decretum de vniuersali vocatione: Se non tantùm velle mittere Filium in mundum, vt homines redimeret; verùm etiam partam redemptione gratiam omnibus promittere & offerre per verbum. 5. Simul etiam decreuit per Euangelij prædicationem elargiri fidem tanquam medium apprehendens gratiam, modò homines externum auditum non denegent, vel alijs modis sibi obicem ponant. 6. Quoniam verò omniscius Deus, qui scrutatur renes & corda, ab æterno præuidit, multos in impœnitentia mansuros, nec ijs medijs vsuros, paucos autem gratiam illam lubenti animo accepturos, atque in Christum redemptorem perseueranter credituros esse, idcircò hos paucos speciali voluntate & εὐδοκίᾳ (quæ aliàs vocatur πρόθεσις θεῦ) propter solum meritum Christi fide apprehensum, voluit saluos fieri, iuxta illud Ioh. 6. v. 40. Hæc est voluntas Dei Patris, vt omnis qui videt Filium, & credit in eum, habeat vitam æternam. 7. Hos ipsos verò specialiter præsciuit, hoc est, pro suis filijs agnouit, sicut ipse dicit, Ioh. 10. v. 14: Ego cognosco oues meas, Et c. 13. vers. 18. Scio quos elegerim. Atque hæc est illa πρόγνωσις specialis secundum quam factam esse electionem dicit Apostolus. 8. Hos autem specialiter præscitos rursus specialiter dilexit. Neminem enim diligimus, nisi qui priùs nobis sit cognitus. 9. Et hos dilectos sibi selegit in peculium ex omni hominum multitudine, & tandem ad vitam æternam ordinauit & prædestinauit, in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ suæ.

XXIII. Formula Concordiæ art. 11. m. p. 802. octo gradibus hæc omnia inclusis, quorum primus est decretum de vniuersali redemptione. 2. de vniuersali oblatione beneficiorum meriti Christi. 3. de conuersione per verbum. 4. de adoptione & iustificatione. 5. de renouatione & sanctificatione. 6. de tutela & defensione credentium. 7. de conseruatione ad finem vitę, & tandem 8. de ęternâ glorificatione. XXIV: Quemadmodum verò hæc omnia Deus ab æterno præuidit & decreuit, ita in tempore tum euenerunt, tum adhuc eueniunt. Nam 1. condidit hominem ad imaginem suam, ipsique præceptum dedit de non comedendo, quod quia transgrediebatur, idcircò, amissâ imagine, in tristiffimum peccati statum deueniebat. 2.
