Deus ista hominis miseriâ ex merâ φιλανθρωπία commotus, misit Filium suum in mũdum, qui pro omnibus mortuus, omnes Deo Patri reconciliauit, omnibusque amissam iustitiam reparauit. 3. Istud meritum toti mundo annunciatur & offertur: verùm plerique nolunt accipere: sed totis viribus reluctãtur, ideoque pauci fidem ex verbo prædicato concipiunt, & per conceptam fidem regenerãtur. 4. Hi autem regenerati, si perseuerent ad finem vitæ, certò saluantur & tandem glorificantur, ad quam salutem etiam erant à Deo prædestinati, sub conditione seruandi huius ordinis. Quod igitur & quomodo Deus ab æterno decreuit fieri, id etiam eoque modo fit in tempore, ex quo apparet, quàm pulchra sit harmonia inter decretum æternum, decretique executionem temporalem. XXV. Vt ergò concludamus, hi fuêre gradus in decreto electionis. 1. Fuit decretum πρωτογενεσίας, 2. Pręuisio lapsus. 3. Decretum παλιγγενεσίας. 4. Consilium de medijs. 5. Præuisio eorum, qui medijs sint vsuri vel secus, iudonia προθεσεως de istis paucis, qui sint medijs vsuri, glorificandis. 7. Eorum πρό- γνωσις specialis. 8. Præscitorum dilectio. 9. Dilectorum electio: Et tandem. 10. Electorum prædestinatio.

XXVI. Atque hactenus præcipuas de prædestinatione sententias recensuimus. Iam istud superest, vt ὀρθοδοξία confirmetur & illustretur : ἑτεροδοξία verò refutetur, & obiectiones contrariæ diluantur, id quod problemate sequenti expeditum dabimus.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?

I. Various definitions of predestination are found here and there both among the Fathers and among the Scholastics. Augustine says in book on the gift of perseverance, ch. 14: Predestination is the foreknowledge and preparation of the benefits of God, by which those who are delivered are most certainly delivered: Fulgentius in book 2 to Monimus: The predestination of God is nothing other than the preparation of his works, which in his eternal disposition he foreknew he would mercifully perform: Bernard in sermon 24 on the Song of Songs: Predestination is the heavenly generation by which God loved his elect, and graced them in his beloved Son before the foundation of the world, appearing thus holy to himself, that they might see his virtue and glory, so that they might be sharers of his inheritance, of which they would also appear conformed to his image:

II. The Scholastics in general describe it thus: Predestination is the preparation of grace in the present, and of glory in the future. Specifically, Thomas, part 1, question 24, article 1: Predestination is the plan of the transmission of a rational creature into eternal life. Durandus in 1, distinction 41, question 1: Predestination is the direction of a rational creature into eternal life. Scotus in 1, distinction 40, question 1: Predestination is the election of an intellectual or rational creature to grace and glory. Bellarm.

l. 2. de grat. & l. arbit. c. 9. Predestination is the providence of God, by which certain men from the mass of perdition are mercifully selected and directed through infallible means into eternal life. III. But since all these definitions are imperfect, we leave them in their place, and we choose and approve this one, which contains all causes, along with our own: Predestination is a consequent decree of the divine will, by which, before the foundations of the world were laid, not according to works, but out of mere grace and mercy in Christ, according to his purpose and foreknowledge, he ordained men to eternal life, who by the power of the Holy Spirit through the preaching of the Gospel would perseveringly believe, to the praise of his glorious grace. IV. That this definition may be explained and confirmed, four things are to be noted: 1. That predestination is a decree. 2. That this very thing is rightly placed in the position of genus. 3. That it is an eternal decree. And 4. that it is an ordered and mediated decree, not absolute, where it will be necessary to treat of the causes of gratuitous election.

I.

V. That Predestination is a decree of God does not require prolix proof. For this is hinted at by the Apostle in Eph. 1, verse 5, where he says that God predestined us according to the purpose or good pleasure of his will: κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ; 2 Tim. 1, v. 9, He called us with a holy calling, κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν, according to his own purpose. Rom. 9, v. 11, ἡ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τοῦ θεοῦ πρόθεσις: according to the purpose of God's election. Hence the orthodox Fathers referred election not to the absolute will of God, but to a determined and decretive one, the testimonies of whom see noted in Gesner, disp. 16, in Form. Concor. c. 3, quaest. 2, th. 4, 5, and following.

VI. From which we infer three corollaries (πορίσματα); the first against the Calvinists; the second against the Huberians; the third against the Papists. 1. Against the Calvinists: Because election is a decree of the divine will, revealed in Scripture, it ought not to be referred to the absolute, naked, hidden, and by no one explored or revealed will of God.

2. Against the Huberians: Because election is a decree of the consequent will, certainly not all can be elect. For the consequent will does not regard the whole human race indiscriminately, without any respect to faith or unbelief.

3. Against the Papists: Because election is a decree, it will not be formally and ultimately an act of the intellect, but of the will. This indeed Bellarmine defends in book 2 de grat. ch. 9, and Gregorius de Valentia in Vol. 1, disputation 1, question 23, point 2, but without reason. For Scripture always describes election through purpose and good pleasure. Wherefore formally it is an act of God, not insofar as He understands, but insofar as He decrees: It is properly the action of one willing well, not of one understanding. For we are not elected through the intellect, but through the benevolent will of God. Predestination was indeed made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, of the intellect, but it is not the πρόγνωσις itself nor does it formally consist in it, but rather in the decree of God choosing according to πρόγνωσις. Francisco Suarez saw this, and therefore in book 1 de prædest. ch. 17, p. 202, he concludes thus: By the name of predestination we always understand a decree of the divine will to give grace and glory, whether that word can also be adapted to the intellect or not,

VII. Regarding the genus of predestination, our people do not seem to agree in all things. For some define it by providence, others by action, some by decree.

Latin:

I. Variæ prædestinationis definitiones hinc inde tum apud Patres, tum apud Scholasticos reperiūtur Augustinus ait l. de bono perseuer. c. 14. Prædestinatio est præscientia & præparatio beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissimè liberantur, quicunque liberantur: Fulgentius l. 2. ad Monim. Prædestinatio Dei nihil aliud est, quàm præparatio operum eius, quæ in æterna suâ dispositione misericorditer se facturum præsciuit: Bernhardus serm. 24. in Canticum: Prædestinatio est cœlestis generatio quâ electos suos Deus dilexit, & gratificauit in dilecto Filio suo ante mundi constitutionem, sic in sancto apparentes sibi, vt viderent virtutem & gloriam suam, quò eius forent consortes hæreditatis, cuius & apparerent conformes imaginis:

II. Scholastici in genere ita describunt: Prædestinatio est præparatio gratiæ in præsenti, & gloriæ in futuro. In specie Thomas par. 1. quæst. 24. art. 1. Prædestinatio est ratio transmissionis creaturæ rationalis in vitam æternam. Durandus in 1. dist. 41. quæst. 1. Prædestinatio est directio creaturæ rationalis in vitā æternam. Scotus in 1. dist. 40. q. 1. Prædestinatio est electio creaturæ intellectiualis vel rationalis ad gratiā & gloriam. Bellarm.

l. 2. de grat. & l. arbit. c. 9. Prædestinatio est providentia Dei, quâ certi homines ex massa perditionis misericorditer selecti per infallibilia media in vitam diriguntur æternam. III. Verùm cùm definitiones istæ omnes sint imperfectæ, suo illas loco relinquimus, & hanc potiùs omnes causas continentem cum Nostris eligimus & adprobamus: Prædestinatio est decretum voluntatis divinæ consequens, quo ante iacta mundi fundamenta, non secundum opera, sed ex mera gratia & misericordia in Christo iuxta propositum & præscientiam ad salutem æternam ordinavit homines, virtute Spiritus sancti per Euangelij prædicationem perseverāter credituros in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ suæ. IV. Definitio hæc vt explicetur & confirmetur quatuor notanda veniunt 1. Quod prædestinatio sit decretum 2. Quod hoc ipsum loco generis rectè ponatur. 3. Quòd sit decretum æternum. Et 4. quòd sit decretum ordinatum & mediatum, non absolutum, vbi agendum erit de causis gratuitæ electionis.

I.

V. Quòd Prædestinatio sit decretum Dei, prolixâ probatione non indiget. Innuitur enim hoc ab Apostolo Eph. 1. vers. 5. vbi dicit, Deo nos prædestinâsse secundum propositum vel beneplacitum voluntatis suæ: κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ; 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. Vocavit nos vocatione sanctâ, κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν secundum suum propositum. Rom. 9. v. 11. ἡ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τοῦ θεοῦ πρόθεσις: secundum electionē Dei propositum. Hinc orthodoxi Patres electionem non ad voluntatem Dei absolutam, sed determinatam & decretiuam retulerunt, quorum testimonia vide annotata apud Gesnerum disp. 16. in Form. Concor. c. 3. quæst. 2. th. 4. 5. & seqq.

VI. Ex quibus tria inferimus πορίσματα; primum contra Caluinianos; secundum contra Huberianos; tertium contra Pontificios. 1. Contra Caluinianos: Quia electio est decretum voluntatis diuinæ, in Scriptura reuelatæ, non debet referri ad absolutam, nudam, occultam, nullique exploratam vel reuelatam Dei voluntatem.

2. Contra Huberianos: Quia electio est decretum voluntatis consequētis, vtique non omnes possunt esse electi. Consequens enim voluntas non spectat vniuersum genus humanum indiscretè, sine omni respectu fidei vel incredulitatis.

3. Contra Pontificios: Quia electio est decretum, non erit formaliter & vltimatè actus intelligentiæ, sed voluntatis. Istud quidem propugnat Bellarm. l. 2. de grat. c. 9. & Gregorius de Valentia Tom. 1. disput 1. quæst. 23. puncto 2. sed absque ratione. Scriptura enim semper electionem describit per propositum & beneplacitum. Quare formaliter est actus Dei, non quatenus intelligit, sed quatenus decernit: Est propriè beneuolentis, non intelligentis actio. Neque enim per intellectum, sed per beneuolam voluntatem Dei electi sumus. Facta quidem est prædestinatio κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, intellectus, sed non est ipsa πρόγνωσις nec in ea formaliter consistit, sed potiùs in decreto Dei secundum πρόγνωσιν eligentis. Vidit hoc Franciscus Suarez, ideoque l. 1 de prædest. cap. 17. p. 202. ita concludit: Nomine prædestinationis decretum voluntatis diuinæ dandi gratiam & gloriam semper intelligimus, siue illa vox etiam ad intellectum adaptari possit, siue non,

VII. Quoad genus prædestinationis, nostri non videntur per omnia conuenire. Quidam enim definiunt per prouidentiam, alii per actionem, nonnulli per decretum.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: II. Those who [define it] by providence are moved by the argument that…

II.

Those who [define it] by providence are moved by the argument that predestination is said to be a species of providence, for this in general embraces all the care of God concerning all and singular created things. But that is as it were a certain special providence, which is occupied not concerning universal things, but solely with the perpetual salvation of men.

Those who [define it] by action rely on these reasons. 1. Because election is described by the word action in Scripture. 2. Because synonyms imply the same, the inscription in the book of life, ordination to salvation, etc. 3. Because the purpose and decree of God, according to which we are chosen, is a certain rule of predestination, and therefore not the genus itself. 4. Because thus through a singular emphasis the power of God in saving us is expressed, so that nothing is ascribed to our works. 5. Because the Fathers described it through active words. Hence Augustine calls it the preparation of grace, Fulgentius a disposition, etc.

Those who [define it] by decree urge primarily the manifest texts of Scripture where we are said to be chosen according to the purpose of God, whence it follows that election is a purpose. Nor indeed do these things conflict with one another, since in like manner we can say that God provides for all things according to His purpose, nor is it permitted to conclude from that that providence is not a purpose. Moreover, this double mode of speaking arises from a double intuition of election: when it is not considered by reason of its essence, then it is certainly the eternal purpose of God; but when by reason of causes and origin, then it is said to be done according to the purpose of God.

VIII. We judge, however, that that disagreement is not real, but only verbal. For the special providence of God, the action of God choosing, and the decree of God do not differ in reality. For what is that providence if not the purpose of God or a provident decree? Thus the action of God choosing, since it does not denote a certain external or transient act, but an internal and perpetual one, is in turn nothing other than a decree. For internal actions are either personally divided, as to beget and to breathe; or essential and indivisible, which if they are acts of the intellect, are called knowledge or foreknowledge: if of the will, they are named decrees. Now since the action of choosing is an internal action of the divine will, hence it follows that nothing else is denoted by that than the purpose and decree of God. For what else does God do by choosing, than what a decree does concerning those who will persevere in believing who are to be saved? By acting, therefore, He decrees, and by decreeing He acts, and therefore the action of the divine will and the decree of God do not really differ. For which reason it will be the same, whether predestination is called a special providence, or a provident decree, or the action of God choosing. For it is one thing, but spoken of through different terms. We, however, have retained the name of decree or purpose, both because it is ἔγγραφον, and because it explains the mode of action in God choosing more clearly. For if it is named merely as an action, it is a genus too remote, since there are many species of divine acts. But when it is called a decree, the very reason of the action is expressed more specially: and at the same time the subject, namely that it is an action of the will, not of the intellect, is hinted at.

Latin:

II.

Qui per prouidentiam, illo mouentur argumento, quòd prædestinatio dicatur species prouidentiæ. Hæc enim in genere complectitur omnem curam Dei circa res creatas omnes & singulas. Illa verò est quasi specialis quædam prouidentia, quæ non circa res vniuersas, sed hominum perpetuam salutem vnicè occupata est.

Qui per actionem, his nituntur rationibus. 1. Quia electio vocabulo actionis in Scriptura describitur. 2. Quia idem innuunt Synonyma, inscriptio in librum vitæ, ordinatio ad salutem, &c. 3. Quia propositum & decretum Dei, secundum quod electi sumus, est regula quædam prædestinationis, ideoque non ipsum genus. 4. Quia sic per singularem emphasin exprimitur virtus Dei in saluandis nobis, vt nihil nostris operibus adscribatur. 5. Quia Patres per vocabula actiua descripserunt. Hinc Augustinus vocat præparationem gratiæ, Fulgentius dispositionem, &c.

Qui per decretum, vrgent inprimis manifestos Scripturæ textus vbi dicimur electi iuxta propositum Dei, vnde sequitur, electionem esse propositum. Neque enim ista inuicem pugnant, cùm pari modo queamus dicere, Deum omnibus rebus prouideré iuxta propositum suum, nec tamen inde licet concludere. Prouidentiam non esse propositum. Duplex autem iste loquendi modus oritur ex duplici electionis intuitu, Quando non consideratur ratione suæ essentiæ, tum vtique est æternum Dei propositum; quando autem ratione causarum & originis, tum facta dicitur iuxta propositum Dei.

IIX. Censemus autem dissensum illum non esse realem, sed tantùm verbalem. Non enim realiter differunt specialis prouidentia Dei, actio Dei eligentis, & decretum Dei. Nam illa prouidentia quid est nisi propositum Dei aut decretum prouidum? Sic actio eligentis Dei, cùm non denotet actum quendam externum vel transeuntem, sed internum & perpetuum, vicissim nihil est aliud, quàm decretum, Nam actiones internæ, vel sunt persomales divisa, vt gignere, & spirare; vel essentiales & indivisæ, quæ si sint actus intelligentiæ, vocantur scientia vel præscientia: si voluntatis nominantur decreta. Iam cùm actio eligendi sit interna voluntatis diuinæ actio, hinc sequitur, nil aliud per istam notari, quàm propositum & decretum Dei. Quid enim aliud agit Deus eligendo, quàm quod decretum facit de saluandis perseueranter credituris? Agendo igitur decernit, & decernendo agit, ideoque actio voluntatis diuinæ & decretum Dei realiter non differunt. Qua de causa perinde erit, siuè prædestinatio dicatur specialis prouidentia, siue prouidum decretum, siue actio Dei eligentis. Res enim vna dicitur, sed per diuersa vocabula. Nos autem retinuimus nomen decreti vel propositi, tum quia ἔγγραφον est, tum quia modum actionis in eligente Deo luculentiùs exponit. Nam si nudè nominatur actio, genus nimis remotum est, cùm actuum diuinorum multæ sint species. Quando autem decretum dicitur, ipsa ratio actionis specialiùs exprimitur: & simul subjectum, nempe quòd voluntatis, non intellectus sit actio, innuitur.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: III. IX. That predestination is an eternal decree can be proven to be given by the…

III.

IX. That predestination is an eternal decree can be proven to be given by the most manifest sayings of Scripture.

Eph. 1. v. 4. He chose us in Christ πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, before the foundations of the world were laid. Jerome abundantly warns about the force of the name καταβολὴ, that it signifies not so much the constitution of the work, as the foundations, which are laid in the deep: whence it follows that the Apostle here hints at the ultimate eternity, which itself also preceded the foundations of the world.

2. Tim. 1. vers. 9. He called us with a holy calling according to his purpose πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, before eternal times, by which words indeed the final eternity is noted in turn, or rather the Apostle says we were chosen as if before eternity itself. 2 Thess. 2, v. 13. God chose you ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς from the beginning, that is, as Micah interprets by another synonym in ch. 5, v. 2, from the days of eternity. Hence Augustine writes in his book on predestination and grace, ch. 5: Before He made us, He foreknew us, and in that very foreknowledge, when He had not yet made us, He chose us. And shortly after: We were made within the world, and we were chosen before the world.

X. Furthermore, two corollaries flow from this. 1. That the opinion of those is false who say that God indeed proposed from eternity to choose us, but does not choose us except in time: just as Beza, forcing the text, explains the Pauline passage in Eph. 1 not as the election itself but as the purpose of choosing. 2. That those slander who, hearing that perseverance is included in election, immediately infer that election is not eternal, but finally happens after death. For just as faith, so also perseverance in faith does not enter into the eternal decree of election as it is already in act (since before the world there was nothing besides God), but as it is foreseen by God.

IV.

XI. That election is a mediated and ordered decree, not absolute, as the Calvinists maintain, is the orthodox opinion of our Churches; for God chose us because He willed it. But He willed it because He saw the misery of man and foresaw the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. Therefore, the primary cause of predestination is the will of God: but this is not absolute, but was moved by the foresight of the fall and of faith. In order that this opinion may be better understood and more distinctly confirmed, we set forth the following assertions.

XII. 1. αἴτιον κύριον or the principal and primary cause of electio nis, not our cause, is the good and gratuitous will of God. This thesis is confirmed by the following testimonies. Luke 12:32. Fear not, little flock, for it has pleased the Father to give you the kingdom. Rom. 9:15. I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I have compassion. V. 16. So then it is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy. V. 18. He has mercy on whom He wills, and whom He wills, He hardens. Eph. 1:11. Predestined according to the purpose of Him who works all things according to the counsel of His will. To this, in a certain way, can also be referred the passage from Deut. 7 and 8. Not because you surpassed all nations in number did the Lord join Himself to you: and chose you, since you are fewer than all peoples, but because He loved you.

XIII. 2. The αἴτιον προκαταρκτικὸν of election, or the inciting cause and that which provides the occasion, is the misery of fallen men, or rather the foreknowledge and consideration of that misery. We oppose this thesis to the Calvinistic assertion, by which they establish that the decree of election is the first of all, and precedes all other causes, and is itself the πρωτογενεσίας and πανηγυρισίας, and therefore that God in election did not consider the misery of man, since the decree of election was prior to the decree of creation, and consequently to the consideration of misery. For the fall is to them the means by which God willed to execute His decree. But the means is subsequent to the end.

XIV. We refute this gross error, however, with the following arguments. 1. If election was made before the foreknowledge of the fall, it must have been made before the decreed incarnation of Christ: How then could it be founded on the merits of Christ? For Christ came into the world to save that which was lost. Wherefore the foreknowledge of the fall precedes the decree concerning the incarnation of the Son. Now if election was made before the foreknowledge of the fall, it was certainly also made before the decree of the incarnation, and thus we are not elected in Christ.

2. Mercy has no place in the one choosing, unless misery precedes it, as Beza himself testifies. But God chose us out of mercy. Therefore, when we were chosen, we were miserable. Wherefore the decree of election is not prior to, but posterior to, the foresight of sin. 3. To that which all possess, some from among all those cannot be chosen in preference to the others. In the state of integrity, all possessed life. Therefore, some from among them could not be selected or predestined to the same in preference to the others. 4. If election had been made from the integral state of man, neither could the elect be saved through mercy, nor the reprobate be damned through justice; and thus the former would not be vessels of mercy, nor the latter vessels of wrath. For where there is no guilt, there wrath and justice have no place; and where there is no misery, there mercy has no place. XV. From these arguments it is sufficiently clear how absurd is the opinion of Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, p. 428, and of Tilenus, part 1, Syntagma, page 144. when they depict such a diagram of God's counsels concerning man, that they assign the first and highest place to the decree of predestination, and finally place beneath this the counsel concerning creating mutable man, so that God might have those whom He might justly destroy and those whom He might mercifully save. This very opinion of Beza the Calvinist Sturm condemns in his diatribe, th. 2, p. 36, when he says: 'Those who undertake thoughts about Predestination without this consideration of the fall, act preposterously, and while they institute their thoughts contrary to the order preserved by God, they implicate themselves more thoughtlessly. For it must be firmly held and believed that we were all equally, in the sight of God, both impious and cursed in the choosing.' Sohnius also departs from Beza, vol. 2, pages 997, 999; Zanchius, book 5, de N. D., ch. 2, p. 672; and Perkins, book de Prædestinat., p. 16.

XVI. αἴτιον προηγούμενον, or impulsive cause, by which God was moved to choose men, is solely the merit of Christ apprehended by faith.

This thesis is the foundation upon which the whole doctrine of Predestination rests. And therefore, in this article, no question occurs that is more agitated back and forth by theologians than this present one, which asks about the cause by which God was impelled to make a decree concerning the choosing of certain men to eternal life. The Calvinists lead us to the simple and absolute εὐδοκίαν [good pleasure] or will of God, which precedes all causes, confusing κύριον αἴτιον [the principal cause] with προηγουμένῳ [that which precedes]. The Papists and Pelagians boast of their own works. The Orthodox or Lutherans acknowledge the merit of Christ apprehended by faith as the προηγουμένῃ [preceding] cause. For although God in election looks to no merit of ours, He does, however, look to our misery, by which His bowels are moved; He looks to the λύτρον [ransom] of His Son, by which satisfaction was made to Him for our sin; He looks to the faith by which we apprehend the merit of Christ and make it our own or apply it to ourselves. Therefore, it is not the merit of Christ considered in itself and without application that impelled God to choose (for thus all ought to have been chosen, or would have been elected, since by reason of acquisition it pertains to all and individual men), but rather as it is apprehended by faith. Whence it happens that because not all believe, a particular election emerges, which otherwise, if it were accomplished by the merit of Christ alone, would have been universal. Therefore, the merit of Christ and faith ought to be joined, so that neither merit alone, nor faith alone, but faith with merit, and merit with faith, or in one word, merit apprehended by faith, may be called the internal impulsive cause of election. For whomever God foresaw would perseveringly apprehend the merit of Christ by faith, all those, and those only, He chose to life.

XVII. This true, orthodox, and in the Scriptures founded doctrine of the primary cause of predestination, which we shall now undertake to establish. But that this confirmation may be joined with a clearer order, we shall proceed distinctly, and we shall demonstrate: 1. In general, of merit and faith. 2. In particular, of the merit of Christ. 3. That the consideration of faith is included in election. And 4. That every respect for merits and works, which the Papists invent, is excluded.

Latin:

III.

IX. Quòd Prædestinatio sit decretum æternum manifestissimis Scripturæ dictis comprobatum dari potest.

Eph. 1. v. 4. Elegit nos in Christo πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi. Hieronymus copiosè monet de vi nominis καταβολὴ, quòd non tàm constitutionem operis, quam fundamenta, quę in profundo iaciuntur significet: vnde sequitur; quòd Apostolus hîc vltimam æternitatem innuat, quæ ipsa quoque mundi fundamenta antecesserit.

2. Tim. 1. vers. 9. Vocauit nos vocatione sancta secundum propositum suum πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, ante tempora æterna quibus sandè verbis vicissim vltima notatur æternitas, imò quasi ante ipsam æternitatem nos electos dicit Apostolus. 2. Thess. 2. v. 13. Elegit vos Deus ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς ab initio, id est, vt Micheas per aliud Synonymum cap. 5. v. 2. interpretatur, à diebus æternitatis. Hinc Augustinus scribit l. de prædest. & gratia c. 5. Antequam faceret nos, præsciuit nos, & in ipsa nos præscientia, cùm nondum fecisset, elegit. Et mox, Intra mundum facti sumus, & ante mundum electi sumus.

X. Porrò autem duo hinc πορίσματα fluunt. 1. Quod falsa sit eorum sententia, qui dicunt, Deum ab æterno quidem proposuisse nos eligere, non autem nisi in tempore eligere: quemadmodum Beza locum Paulinum Eph. 1. non de ipsa electione sed de proposito eligendi, vim faciens textui, exponit. 2. Quod calumnientur ii, qui audientes perseuerantiam includi electioni, mox inferunt, quòd electio non sit æterna, sed post mortem demum fiat. Sicut enim fides, ita & perseuerantia in fide æternum electionis decretum non ingreditur, prout iam actu est, (cùm ante mundum præter Deum nihil fuerit) sed prout Deo præuisa est.

IV.

XI. Quòd electio sit decretum mediatum & ordinatum, non absolutum, vt Caluiniani statuunt, orthodoxa est nostrarum Ecclesiarum sententia, Deus enim nos elegit, quia voluit. Voluit autem, quia miseriam hominis vidit, & meritum Christi fide apprehensum præuidit. Prima ergò prædestinationis causa est voluntas Dei: sed hæc absoluta non est, verùm mouebatur lapsus & fidei prævisione. Quæ sententia vt eò meliùs intelligatur & distinctiùs confirmetur, sequentes ponimus assertiones.

XII. 1. αἴτιον κύριον vel princeps & primaria electionis nostra causa, est bona & gratuita Dei voluntas. Thesis hæc confirmatur sequentibus testimonijs. Luc. 12. v. 32. Ne time pusille grex, quia placuit Patri tibi dare regnum. Rom. 9. v. 15. Miserebor, cuius misereor, & misericordiam præstabo, cuius miserebor. V. 16. Igitur non volentis, nec currentis sed miserentis est Dei. Vers. 18 Cui vult miseretur & quem vult, indurat Eph. 1. v. 11. Prædestinati secundum propositum eius, qui operatur omnia secundum consilium voluntatis suæ. Huc & quodammodò referri potest locus ex Deut. 7. & 8. Non quia cunctas gentes numero vincebatis, vobis iunctus est Dominus: & elegit vos, cùm omnibus populis sitis pauciores, sed quia dilexit vos.

XIII. 2. Electionis αἴτιον προκαταρκτικὸν, vel causa irritans & occasionem præbens, est miseria lapsorum hominum, vel potiùs præuisio & consideratio miseriæ. Opponimus hanc thesin assertioni Caluinisticæ, quâ statuunt, electionis decretum esse omnium primum, & antecedere causas alias omnes, ipsumque decretum πρωτογενεσίας & πανηγυγυρισίας, ideoque Deum in electione non considerâsse hominis miseriam, quippe cùm decretum electionis priùs fuerit decreto creationis, & consequenter consideratione miseriæ. Lapsus enim est ipsis medium, quo Deus exequi voluerit suum decretum. Medium autem posterius est fine.

XIV. Refutamus autem hunc crassum errorem sequentibus argumentis. 1. Si electio facta est ante præuisionem lapsus, oportuit factam esse ante decretam Christi incarnationem: Quomodo ergò potuit in Christi meritis fundari? Nam Christus in mundum venit, vt saluaret id, quod perierat. Quare præuisio lapsus præcedit decretum de incarnatione Filij. Iam si electio facta est ante præuisionem lapsus, vtique & facta est ante decretū incarnationis, & sic in Christo electi non sumus.

2. Misericordia eligentis locum non habet, nisi præcedat miseria, testante ipso Beza. Atqui ex misericordia nos elegit Deus. Ergò cùm eligeremur, fuimus miseri. Quare decretum electionis non prius sed posterius est prævisione peccati. 3. Quod omnes habent, ad id aliqui ex iis omnibus, præ cæteris non possunt eligi. In statu integritatis vitam omnes habebant. Ergò aliqui ex iis præ cæteris ad eandem non poterant seligi, vel prædestinari. 4. Si ex statu hominis integro facta esset electio, neque electi per misericordiã servari, neque reprobi per iustitiam damnari potuissent; & sic illi non essent vasa misericordiæ, neque hi vasa iræ. Nam vbi nulla culpa, ibi locũ non habet ira & iustitia; & vbi nulla miseria, ibi locum non habet misericordia. XV. Ex his argumentis satis patet, quàm abfurda sit opinio Bezæ in Colloquio Mompelg. p. 428. & Tileni par. 1. Syntag. pag. 144. quando eiusmodi depingunt consiliorum Dei de homine diagramma, vt primum & summum locum tribuant decreto prædestinationis, atque huic demum substernant consilium de creando homine mutabili, vt Deus haberet quos iustè perderet & quos misericorditer seruaret. Quam ipsam Bezæ sententiam Caluinista Sturmius damnat in sua diatribe th. 2. p. 36. quando ait: Qui de Prædestinatione absq; hac consideratione lapsus cogitationes suscipiunt, præposterè agunt, & dum contra ordinem à Deo seruatum cogitationes suas instituunt, incogitantiùs se implicant. Omnes enim ex æquo nos in conspectu Dei & impios & maledictos fuisse in eligendo, firmiter tenendum, & credendum. Discedit etiam à Beza Sohnius tom. 2. pag. 997. 999. Zanchius l. 5. de N. D. c. 2. p. 672. & Perkinsus l. de Prædestinat. p. 16.

XVI. αἴτιον προηγούμενον, vel causa impulsiva, quâ mosus fuit Deus ad eligendum homines, est solum meritum Christi fide apprehensum.

Thesis hæc fundamentum est, cui tota de Prædestinatione doctrina innititur. Ideóque in hoc articulo nulla occurrit quæstio à Theologis vltrò citróque magis agitata, quàm hæc præsens, quæ de causa quærit, per quam Deus fuerit impulsus ad faciendum de quibusdam hominibus ad vitam æternam eligendis decretum. Calviniani nos ad simplicem & absolutam omnesque causas antegressam Dei εὐδοκίαν seu voluntatem deducunt confundentes κύριον αἴτιον προηγουμένῳ. Pontificij & Pelagiani opera sua iactitant. Orthodoxi seu Lutherani meritum Christi fide apprehensum pro causa προηγουμένῃ agnoscunt. Licèt enim Deus in electione nullum nostrum respiciat meritum, aspicit tamen nostram miseriam, qua viscera eius commouentur; aspicit Filij sui λύτρον, quo ipsi pro peccato nostro satisfactum est; aspicit fidem, quâ meritum Christi apprehendimus, nobísque id proprium facimus seu applicamus. Proinde non meritum Christi in se & sine applicatione consideratum, impulit Deum ad eligendum, (sic enim omnes debuissent eligi, vel fuissent electi, cùm ratione acquisitionis omnes & singulos homines illud attineat) sed potiùs vt est fide apprehensum. Vnde fit vt quia non omnes credunt, electio emergat particularis, quæ aliàs, si solo Christi merito absolueretur, vniuersalis fuisset. Coniungi ergo debent meritum Christi & fides, ita vt nec solum meritum, nec sola fides, sed cum merito fides, & cum fide meritum, seu vno verbo, meritum fide apprehensum, dicatur causa electionis impulsiua interna. Quoscunque n. Deus præuidit meritum Christi fide perseueranter apprehensuros, eos omnes, &c eos tantùm elegit ad vitam.

XVII. Hæc vera, orthodoxa & in Scripturis fundata est prædestinationis αἰτία προηγουμένη doctrina, quam nunc stabilire aggrediemur. Ea autem confirmatio vt euidentiori cum ordine coniuncta sit distinctè procedemus, & demonstrabimus. 1. in gener. meriti fideique. 2. In specie, meriti Christi. 3. Fidei intuitum electioni esse inclusum. Et 4. Omnem meritorum operumq́; respectum, quem fingunt Pontificii, esse exclusum.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: Member I. XIIX. That God, in choosing, had regard for both, both the merit of Christ and…

MEMBER I.

XIIX. That God, in choosing, had regard for both, both the merit of Christ and the faith that apprehends it, can be demonstrated by two general arguments.

1. From the harmony of the decree with the execution. God is immutable, and just as He does not change His essence, so He does not change His sentence. God is not as a man that He should lie, nor as the son of man that He should be changed. Hath He said, and shall He not do it? Or hath He spoken, and shall He not make it good? Num. 23 v. 19. Whatever, therefore, God has decreed from eternity, He executes in time, and in that way in which He decreed it, He executes it in time, and in that way in which He decreed it, and conversely. For if He were to execute it in another way and through other causes, this would be an indication of a changed sentence; as if some Prince were to decree that he would grant freedom to certain captives through a ransom interposed by another and not rashly neglected, and afterwards were to release them freely without any price; then certainly the former decree is annihilated, and the sentence is changed. In a similar way, God would be mutable if the execution differed from the decree. Sonius concedes this, who for this reason, in Vol. 2, art. on predestination, page 992, posits this maxim: Whatever God has decreed from eternity to do and execute in time, that He does and executes in time; and as He decreed, so He executes. And conversely, what He has not decreed to do, that He does not do, and as He did not decree to do it, so He does not do it. With this hypothesis presupposed, we weave a clearly invincible argument: For which causes God justifies and saves in time; because of these same causes He decreed from eternity to save men, that is, He elected them to life. Otherwise, the execution would differ from the decree, which is absurd. But God does not justify and save in time out of an absolute good pleasure, but because of Christ apprehended by faith, which the Calvinists themselves teach and confess. Therefore, God did not decree from eternity to save men out of an absolute good pleasure, but because of Christ apprehended by faith, that is, He elected them to life, which was to be demonstrated. XIX. Polanus objected in didasc. p. 23, that the decree of salvation and of election differ, since the former is broader, when we are said to be saved through the preaching and ministers of the word, but not to be predestined.

Resp. 1. He begs the question. For those decrees do not differ at all, since of both the 1. object, 2. end, [and] 3. act are the same.

2. God in electing had regard no less to the preaching and ministry of the word than to the merit of Christ. These, therefore, are not to be excluded from the business of election.

3. That we are said to be saved by ministers, but not predestined, the reason is that Predestination is the eternal decree of God, which He alone made; salvation is the execution of the decree, which happens through the mediation of ministers. God indeed alone decrees, but He does not alone execute. However, this very mode of executing is included in the decree. Although, therefore, we are not predestined by ministers, yet we are predestined because of the merit of Christ announced by ministers and apprehended by faith. You see, therefore, that this consistency remains intact: For just as in time we are saved through faith drawn from the preaching of ministers: so from eternity God decreed to save us through the same, that is, He elected [us]. And let this suffice for us; because we do not say that the decree and the execution are one and the same thing, but that they do not differ in their primary and impelling cause, which is in no way shaken by the brought-forward objection.

Latin:

MEMBRVM. I.

XIIX Deum in eligendo ad vtrumque respexisse, tum meritum Christi, tum fidem apprehendentem, duobus argumentis generalibus demonstrari potest.

1. A consonantia decreti cum executione. Deus est immutabilis, & quemadmodum non essentiam, ita nec mutat sententiam. Non est Deus quasi homo vt mentiatur, nec vt Filius hominis, vt mutetur. Dixit ergò & non faciet? Locutus est & non implebit? Num 23 v. 19. Quicquid igitur Deus ab æterno decreuit, hoc in tempore exequitur, eoque modo, quo decreuit, hoc in tempore exequitur, eoque modo, quo decreuit, & contrà. Sic enim alio modo, & per alias causas exequeretur, foret hoc indicium mutatæ sententiæ; vt, si Princeps aliquis decerneret, se interposito per alium λύτρῳ nec temerè neglecto, captiuos quosdam libertate donaturum esse, & postmodum eos gratis sine omni pretio dimitteret; tum sanè prius decretum annihilatur, & sententia mutatur. Pari modo mutabilis foret Deus, si à decreto differret executio. Concedit hoc Sonius, qui ob id Tom. 2. art. de prædest. pag. 992, hanc ponit maximam: Quæcunque Deus ab æterno decreuit in tempore facere & xequi, ea in tempore facit, & exequitur; & sicut decreuit ita exequitur. Et contrà, quæ non decreuit facere, ea non facit, & sicut non decreuit facere, ita non facit. Qua hypothesi præsuppositâ invictum planè argumentum nectimus: Propter quas causas Deus in tempore iustificat, saluat; propter easdem ab æterno homines saluare decreuit, hoc est, ad vitam elegit. Aliàs discreparct à decreto executio, quod absurdum. Atqui Deus in tempore non ex absoluto beneplacito, sed propter Christum fide apprehensum iustificat & saluat, quod docent & fatentur ipsi Calviniani. Ergò Deus ab æterno non ex absoluto beneplacito, sed propter Christum fide apprehensum homines saluare decreuit, hoc est, ad vitam elegit, quod fuit demonstrandum. XIX. Excepit Polanus in didasc. p. 23. decretum saluationis & electioms differre, siquidem illud sit latius, cùm per prædicationem & ministros verbi dicamur saluari, sed non prædestinari.

Resp. 1. Petit Principium. Nam decreta ista nequaquam differunt, cùm vtriusque idem sit 1. obiectum. 2. finis. 3. actus.

2. Deus in eligendo non minus ad prædicationem & ministerium verbi quàm meritum Christi respexit. Hæc igitur non sunt excludenda è negotio electionis.

3. Quod per ministros saluati, non prædestinati dicimur, causa ea est, quia Prædestinatio est æternum Dei decretum, quod solus fecit; saluatio est decreti executio, quæ sit mediantib. ministris. Deus quidem solus decernit, sed non solus exequitur. Hic ipse autem exequendi modus decreto est inclusus. Licèt ergò per ministros non simus prædestinati, non tamen propter meritum Christi per ministros annunciatum & fide apprehensum prædestinati sumus. Vides ergo, manere istam consonantiam saluam: Sicut enim in tépore per fidem ex prædicatione ministrorum haustam saluamur: ita ab æterno per eandem Deus nos saluare decreuit, hoc est, elegit. Atq; hoc nobis sufficiat; quia non dicimus, decretum & executionem vnum prorsus idemq; esse. sed causá primariâ & impellente non differre, id quod per allatam instantiam minimè labefactatur.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: XX. XX. From Foreknowledge

XX.

XX. From Foreknowledge. Predestination was made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν θε̃ [according to the foreknowledge of God], which the following prove. 1 Pet. 1:2, To the elect according to the πρόγνωσιν [foreknowledge] of God the Father. Rom. 8:29, Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated. Rom. 11:2, God has not cast away his people ὃν προέγνω [whom he foreknew], whom he foreknew. We ask, however, what God foreknew or foresaw and considered in choosing: Certainly nothing else than the merit of his Son apprehended by faith. For he did not regard our works, nor the dignity of our race: since all these things savor of Pelagianism, nor can anything else be named which he attended to in choosing, other than only the merit of Christ apprehended by faith: whence it follows that without the consideration of this, election was not made.

Piscator answers to this argument that this πρόγνωσιν [foreknowledge] is the same as the decree of election. But he is mistaken. 1. Because Paul in Rom. 8:29 separates πρόγνωσιν [foreknowledge] from προορισμῷ [predestination] by a gradation; if indeed they were the same, Paul's expression would be inept: Whom he foreknew, that is, predestinated, he also predestinated. 2. Because πρόγνωσις [foreknowledge] is of the intellect, 2 Tim. 2:19, [while] ἐκλογὴ [election] is an action of the will, Eph. 1:5.

MEMBER II.

XXI. That the merit of Christ is included in the decree of election can be proved specifically, both by sayings of Scripture and by reasons.

We shall allege only two sayings. The one is read in 2 Tim. 1:9, He called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus before the world began. That the Apostle here insinuates the business of eternal election is clear from the words πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων [before the world began]. Moreover, he clearly teaches that the grace of election was given in Christ. If, therefore, we are predestinated in Christ, then the decree of election is not absolute, but joined with respect to the Lord's merit, as an impelling cause. The other is primary, and is held in the proper seat of this article, Eph. 1. v. 3. & 4. The words are as follows: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, in Christ, just as He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame. From an accurate inspection of this saying, four arguments can be drawn against the Calvinists, which we shall briefly add.

XXII. 1. If we are chosen in Christ, certainly Christ will be the cause of our election, because the preposition in among the Hebrews mostly denotes the cause on account of which: as Gen. 29. verse 18. I will serve you for Rachel, in Hebrew it is בְּרָחֵל. Deuter. 24. verse 16. each one shall die in his own sins, that is, because of his sins. Thus Luke 22. verse 20. This is the New Testament in my blood, that is, ratified by and because of my blood. Similar phrases exist everywhere, such as: In Him we are, live, and move, that is, by Him. In my God I will leap over a wall. In God we shall do valiantly: This kind of demon is not cast out except in prayer and fasting. I can do all things in Him who strengthens me, &c. In a like manner, and in the same sense, it is said: God chose us in Christ, that is, by and because of Christ.

XXIII. The Calvinists object that the argument suffers from the vice of ψευδοερμηνείας [false interpretation], and that we do not correctly interpret the words, to be chosen in Christ, as, to be chosen because of Christ. They themselves, however, disagree among themselves in the explanation of this Pauline phrase.

Polanus in his didascalia, page 41, says: He chose us in Christ, as members in the head. Therefore, by these words Paul does not show the cause on account of which we were chosen, but the medium or subject in which we were chosen. And thus the order of election is shown; first the head was chosen, then the members in the head. For since the heavenly Father found nothing worthy of election in the whole seed of Adam, He turned His eyes to His Christ, so that as if from His body the members he might choose those whom he was about to take into the fellowship of life, etc. Thus Polanus. From which words it is certainly evident to the eye how great is the power of truth: for while he wishes to refute our opinion, he incautiously confirms it. For if to be chosen in Christ is the same as to be chosen in the head, then certainly this head was the moving cause that we should be chosen as members. God therefore chose us on account of the regard for the head, and therefore election is not entirely absolute. And those words of Polanus are to be noted: since God found nothing worthy of election in the whole seed of Adam, he therefore turned his eyes to Christ. But what need was there for God to look to dignity in election, if his εὐδοκία was the solitary and absolute cause of election? Likewise, if we are chosen because God found something in Christ worthy of election, then certainly Christ is the impulsive cause. For that dignity which the Father found in the Son moved the Father to choose us. Two things therefore are conceded here by Polanus. 1. That election is not absolute, because the Father, choosing, looked upon the merit of Christ. 2. That Christ is the impulsive cause of election, since God the Father chose us, in whom he discerned nothing worthy of election, because he attended to the merit of Christ.

Piscator explains the Pauline phrase thus: To be chosen in Christ is nothing other than to be chosen for this, that we, being chosen on account of Christ, might be sanctified, and thus be led to eternal life. Resp. This interpretation. 1. Is twisted, does violence to the text, and cannot be proven. 2. Makes Paul a ταυτολόγον, for this would be the paraphrase: He chose us for this, that we might be sanctified on account of Christ, that we might be holy. 3. It divides things that should be joined: For the sense of both phrases is the same: He blessed us with every spiritual blessing in Christ, just as he also chose in him. Now just as to bless in Christ does not signify to be blessed for this, that we might be sanctified on account of Christ, but rather we are blessed through and on account of Christ: so also that phrase

We are chosen in Christ, which is the same as being chosen through and because of Christ. 4. He overturns the elegance of the Pauline comparison. He compares blessing and election; he says that both were done in Christ. The Calvinist gloss disturbs this, and does not say: Just as we are blessed in Christ, so we are chosen in Christ: but it constructs it in this way: Just as we are blessed in Christ, so we are chosen to this end, that we might be sanctified because of Christ. Therefore, it refers those words (in Christ) not to both, but only to the first member of the comparison. 5. It fights against the time of the description. For Paul says that we were chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world, that is, from eternity. Sanctification, however, happens in time. Therefore, that which Paul says here was done in Christ is not sanctification, but election.

XXIV. 2. If we are thus chosen in Christ, just as we are blessed, we are certainly chosen through and because of Christ. Connection: the reason is that to be blessed in Christ is the same as to be blessed through and because of Christ. But the antecedent is true, Eph. 1. v. 3. & 4. ὁ εὐλογήσας ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ χριστῷ, καθὼς just as ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν αὐτῷ.

XXV. 3. From verse 5. Who predestined us unto the adoption of sons διὰ ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the good pleasure of his will. If we are predestined through Christ, then Christ is certainly included in the decree of election. Wherefore that is not absolute, but limited. Nor does the Apostle speak here of temporal execution, since he says that God predestined not into himself, εἰς αὐτὸν, through Christ, by which words indeed eternity itself is noted.

XXVI 4. From verses 6, 7, & 11. In whom we are made beloved, in whom we have redemption and the remission of sins, in whom we have been called by lot, in the same we are chosen. But in Christ, or through and because of Christ, we are made beloved, and have redemption, etc. Therefore, also in Christ, or through and because of Christ, we are chosen.

XXVII. After the things said from Scripture, we shall add Reasons, of which two are the principal ones. 1. Election was not made without regard for the benefits of Christ, such as redemption and remission. Therefore, not without Christ either. The antecedent is proven: if we had been predestined without regard for redemption and remission, 1. We would also be saved without redemption and remission, because we receive salvation in time just as we were predestined from eternity to receive it. 2. No grace would have been attributed to the elect in Christ from eternity, which is against Paul, 2 Tim. 1:9.

XXVIII. 2. If reconciliation made through Christ is the cause of the purpose of election, it will also be the cause of the decree of election. For the cause of a cause is the cause of the thing caused. The former is true, which I prove: God did not choose us while angry, because thus election would redound to our destruction, or God would have made this decree without judgment: Therefore, He was appeased. But He cannot be appeased except by the sole merit of Christ; wherefore the regard for the Lord's merit, by which God was appeased, preceded the purpose of choosing. 3. God was gravely offended by the fall of men. Therefore, He could not have mercy on them unless a sufficient reconciliation had first been decreed for the injured justice. Again, therefore, the respect for reconciliation preceded the decree of election.

XXIX. And these arguments are so strong that the Calvinists extorted this confession from Perkins, l. de prædest. p. 15: In Christ we are all chosen for grace and salvation, and to dream of any election outside of Christ is wonderfully absurd. You will find similar things in Zanchius, l. 5, d. N. D., c. 2, p. 676, b.

XXX. And thus far we have proven that the merit of Christ is included in the decree of election: now we shall briefly run through the objections of the Calvinists. The first is general, directed as much against faith as against the merit of Christ. It holds thus: An effect is not a cause. The merit of Christ and the faith of man are an effect of election, therefore not a cause.

Resp. 1. To the major premise, that it is not universally true, since one thing can sometimes be both cause and effect, as the Philosopher says in book 3 of the Physics, chapter 3, and book 2 of the Metaphysics, and as Goclenius admits in part 1 of the Logical problems, problem 23, Keckermann in book 1 of the System of Logic, chapter 18, and Timpler in book 3 of the Metaphysics, chapter 2, question 13. Nor are examples of this lacking. 1. A building is both the final cause and the effect of the architect. 2. Bodily exercise is the efficient cause of health, and that same health is the final cause of the exercise. 3. Happiness is defined by the Philosopher as ἐνέργεια ψυχῆς λογικῆς, in book 1 of the Ethics, chapter 6, which nevertheless is called the same end of man by the same author, book 1, chapter 1, and book 10, chapter 7. 4. For captives, released for a time through the intervention of sponsors, liberty is the cause of money being collected, and the money itself is the cause of liberty. 5. The celebration of the divine name is an action of man, and is rightly called its own end. 6. Faith is the effect of the word, Rom. 10, v. 17. & it is the cause, so that the word may exist as saving, Heb. 4, v. 2. 7. Thus the same faith is the effect of the Sacraments and at the same time the cause, so that they may be saving. And hence we conclude that the major premise is not universal, which we therefore limit thus: An effect is not a cause formally, yet it is a cause materially, and in a different respect; that is, the term of a cause either denotes an absolute being, and this under some aspect can be caused: or it denotes the relation itself, which is referred to the effect; and then the same thing cannot be cause and caused; because a relation always turns not between one, but two.

Latin:

XX.

XX. A Præscientia. Prædestinatio facta est κατὰ πρόγνωσιν θε̃ , quod probant sequentia. 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. Electis secundum πρόγνωσιν Dei Patris. Rom. 8. v. 29. Quos præsciuit, eos etiam prædestinauit. Rom. 11. v. 2. Non repulit Deus populum suum ὃν προέγνω, quem præsciuit. Quærimus autem, quid Deus pręscierit vel pręuiderit & eligendo considerauerit: Certè nil aliud, quàm meritum Filij sui fide apprehensum. Non enim opera nostra, non dignitatem generis respexit: siquidem hæc omnia Pelagianismum sapiunt, nec aliud quid nominari potest, quod in eligendo attenderit, quàm solum Christi meritum fide apprehensum: vnde sequitur, quòd sine huius insuitu electio non sit facta.

Piscator respondet ad hoc argumentum πρόγνωσιν istam esse idem, quod electionis decretum. Sed fallitur. 1. Quia Paulus Rom. 8. vers. 29. gradatione seiungit πρόγνωσιν à προορισμῷ, si verò idem essent, inepta foret locutio Pauli, Quos præsciuit, id est, prædestinauit eos etiam prædestinauit. 2. Quia πρόγνωσις intellectus 2. Tim 2. v. 9. ἐκλογὴ voluntatis, Ephes. 1. v. 5. actio est.

MEMBRVM II.

XXI. Quòd meritum Christi decreto electionis sit inclusum, in specie probari potest, tum dictis Scripturæ, tum rationibus.

Dicta tantùm duo allegabimus. Alterum legitur 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. Vocauit nos vocatione sanctâ, non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum propositum suum & gratiam, quæ data est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia. Apostolum hîc insinuare negotium electionis æternæ, patet ex verbis πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων. Electionis autem gratiam in Christo datam esse, luculenter docet. Quòd si igitur prædestinati sumus in Christo, vtique decretum electionis nõ est absolutum, sed cum respectu meriti Dominici, veluti causæ impellentis coniunctum. Alterum est primarium, & habetur in sede huius articuli propria, Eph. 1. v. 3. & 4. Verba sic habent: Benedictus Deus & Pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nos in omni benedictione spirituali, in cœlestibus, in Christo, sicut elegit nos in ipso ante mundi constitutionem, vt essemus sancti & immaculati. Ex huius dicti accurata inspectione quatuor argumenta depromi queunt contra Caluinianos, quæ breuiter addemus.

XXII. 1. Si eligimur in Christo, vtique Christus electionis nostræ causa erit, quia præpositio in apud Hebræos plerumque notat causam propter quam: vt Gen. 29. vers. 18. Seruiam tibi propter Rachel in Hebræo est בְּרָחֵל Deuter. 24. vers. 16. vnus quisque in peccatis suis, id est, propter peccata morietur. Sic Luc. 22. vers. 20. Hoc est Novum Testamentum in meo sanguine, id est, sancitum per & propter meum sanguinem. Similes phrases passim extant, vt: In ipso sumus, viuimus & mouemur, id est, per ipsum. In Deo meo transgrediar murum. In Deo faciemus virtutem: Hoc genus dæmoniorum non eiicitur nisi in oratione & ieiunio. Omnia possum in eo, qui me confortat, &c. Pari modo, eodemq; sensu dicitur; Elegit nos Deus in Christo, id est, per & propter Christum.

XXIII. Caluiniani excipiunt, argumentum laborare vitio ψευδοερμηνείας, & nos verba, eligi in Christo, non recte interpretari per hæc, eligi propter Christum. Ipsi autem inter se dissentiunt in explicatione phraseos huius Paulinæ.

Polanus in sua didascalia pag. 41. ait: Elegit nos in Christo, tanquam membra in capite. Ergo his verbis non ostendit Paulus causam, propter quam electi sumus, sed medium siue subiectum, in quo electi sumus. Atque sic ordo electionis monstratur; primò caput est electum, deinde in capite membra. Quoniam enim in vniuerso Adami semine nihil electione dignum reperiebat cœlestis Pater, in Christum suum oculos conuertit, vt tanquam ex eius corpore membra eligeret, quos in vitæ consortium assumpturus erat, &c. Hæc Polanus. Ex quibus certè verbis ad oculum patet, quanta sit vis veritatis: dum enim nostram sententiam refutare vult, incautus eam confirmat. Etenim si in Christo eligi est idem, quod in capite eligi, vtique caput hoc causa mouens fuit, vt nos eligeremur in membra. Deus ergò propter intuitum capitis nos elegit, ideoque electio non est penitus absoluta. Et notanda sunt illa Polani, verba: quoniam Deus nihil electione dignum reperiebat in vniuerso Adami semine, ideò oculos conuertit in Christum. Quid autem opus erat, vt Deus in electione ad dignitatem respiceret, si εὐδοκία ipsius solitaria & absoluta electionis causa fuit? Item, si electi sumus ideò, quia Deus in Christo reperit quiddam electione dignum, vtique Christus est causa impulsiua. Dignitas enim illa, quam Pater in Filio inuenit, mouit Patrem ad eligendum nos. Duo igitur à Polano hîc conceduntur. 1. electionem non esse absolutam, quia Pater eligens Christi meritum aspexit. 2. Christum electionis causam esse impulsiuam, quoniam Deus Pater nos, in quibus nihil electione dignum cernebat, ideò elegit, quia meritum Christi attendit.

Piscator phrasin Paulinam sic explicat: Eligi in Christo nihil aliud est, quam eligi ad hoc, vt electi propter Christum sanctificemur, atque ita ad vitam æternam perducamur. Resp. Hoc interpretamentum. 1. Est contortum, textui vim facit & probari nequit. 2. Facit Paulum ταυτολόγον, hæc enim foret paraphrasis: Elegit nos ad hoc, vt propter Christum sanctificemur, vt sancti essemus. 3. Diuidit componenda: Idem enim sensus est vtriusque phrasews: Benedixit nos in omni benedictione spirituali in Christo, sicut & elegit in ipso. Iam quemadmodum benedicere in Christo, non significat, benedici in hoc, vt propter Christum sanctificemur, sed potius benedicimur, per & propter Christum: ita etiam illa phrasis

Eligimur in Christo, idem est, ac eligi per & propter Christum. 4. intervertit concinnitatem Paulinae comparationis. Comparat ille benedictionem & electionem; vtramque in Christo ait esse factam. Caluiniana glossa hoc turbat, & non dicit: Sicut in Christo benedicimur, ita in Christo eligimur: sed hoc modo construit, Sicut in Christo benedicimur, ita eligimur ad hoc vt propter Christum sanctificemur. Refert ergò verba illa (in Christo) non ad vtrumque sed ad primum duntaxat comparationis membrum. 5. Pugnat cum descriptionis tempore. Paulus enim in Chri. sto nos ait esse electos ante constitutionem mundi, hoc est, ab aeterno. Sanctificatio autem fit in tempore. Ergò id, quod Paulus hic in Christo factum esse dicit, non est sanctificatio, sed electio.

XXIV. 2. Si ita in Christo eligimur, veluti benedicimur, vtiq; per & propter Christum eligimur. Conn: ratio est, quia benedici in Christo idem est, ac per & propter Christum benedici. Sed antecedens est verum, Eph. 1. v. 3. & 4. ὁ εὐλογήσας ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ χριστῷ, καθὼς quemadmodum ἐξελέξατο ἡμᾶς ἐν αὐτῷ.

XXV. 3. Ex. vers. 5. Qui praedestinauit nos in adoptionem filiorum διὰ ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ per Iesum Christum in sese, iuxta beneplacitum voluntatis suae. Si per Christum sumus praedestinati, vtique decreto electionis inclusus est Christus. Quare illa non est absoluta, sed limitata. Neque hic de temporali executione agit Apostolus, quoniam inquit, Deum non in se, εἰς αὐτὸν praedestinasse per Christum, quibus sanè verbis ipsa notatur aeternitas.

XXVI 4. Ex vers. 6. 7. & 11. In quo sumus chari redditi, in quo habemus redemtionem & remissionem peccatorum, in quo sorte vocati sumus, in eodem eligimur. Atqui in Christo seu per & propter Christum sumus chari redditi, & habemus redemptionem, &c. Ergo etiam in Christo seu per & propter Christum etigimur:

XXVII. Post dicta Scripturæ addemus Rationes, quarum duæ sunt præcipuæ 1. Electio non est facta sine intuitu beneficiorum Christi, puta redemtionis & remissionis. Ergò nec sine Christo. Antecedens probatur: si absque intuitu redemtionis & remissionis prædestinati essemus. 1. Etiam absque redēptione & remissione saluaremur, quia salutem ita accipimus in tempore, vti ad illam accipiendam ab æterno prædestinati sumus. 2. Nulla electis gratia in Christo ab æterno attributa fuiffet, quod est contra Paulum, 2. Tim 1. v. 9.

XXVIII. 2. Si reconciliatio per Christum facta, causa est propositi electionis, erit etiam causa decreti electionis. Nam causa causæ est causa causati. Prius verum, quod probo: Deus non elegit nos iratus, quia sic electio redundaret in perniciem nostram vel sine iudicio decretum hoc fecisset Deus: Ergò placatus. Placari autem nequit, nisi solo merito Christi; Quare intuitus meriti Dominici, quo placabatur Deus, præcessit propositum eligendi. 3. Deus erat grauiter hominum lapsu offensus. Ergò non potuit eorum misereri, nisi prius læsæ iustitiæ sufficiens decreta esset reconciliatio. Rursus igitur præcessit respectus reconciliationis decretum electionis.

XXIX. Et hæc argumenta tàm fortia sunt, vt Caluinistæ Perkinfo hanc confessionem extorserint l. de prædest. p. 15. In Christo omnes eligimur ad gratiam & salutem, & extra Christum electionem vllam vel somniare, mirè absurdum est. Similia inuenies apud Zanchium l. 5. d. N. D. c. 2. p. 676. b.

XXX. Atque hactenus meritum Christi decreto electionis inclusum esse probauimus: nunc obiectiones Caluinianorum breuiter percurremus. Prima generalis est, tam contra fidem, quàm meritum Christi directa. Sic autem habet: Effectum non est causa. Meritum Christi & fides hominis sunt effectum electionis, Non igitur causa.

Resp. 1. Ad Maiorem, quòd nón sit vniuersaliter vera, siquidem res vna quandoque causa & effectum esse potest, dicente Philosopho l. 3. Phys. cap. 3. l. Metaph. 2. & fatente Goclenio part. 1. problem. Log. problem 23. Keckermanno l. 1. syst. Log. cap. 18. Timplero, l. 3. Met c. 2. quæst 13. Neque desunt huius rei exempla. 1. Ædificium & causa finalis & effectum est architecti. 2. Exercitium corporis, est causa efficiens sanitatis, & eadem sanitas est causa finalis exercitij. 3. Felicitas definitur à Philosopho ἐνέργεια ψυχῆς λογικῆς, 1. Eth. cap. 6. quæ tamen eadem hominis finis ab eodem dicitur, lib 1. cap. 1. & l. 10. c. 7. 4 Captiuis, interuētu sponsorū ad tempus dimissis, libertas est causa pecuniæ colligendæ, & pecunia ipsa est causa libertatis. 5. Celebratio diuini nominis est actio hominis, & eiusdem finis rectè dicitur 6. Fides effectum est verbi, Rom. 10. v. 17. & causa est, vt verbum existat salutare, Heb. 4. v. 2. 7. Sic eadem fides, est effectus Sacramentorum & simul causa, vt illa sint salutaria. Atque hinc concludimus maiorem non esse vniuersalem, quam propterea sic limitamus: Effectum non est causa formaliter, est tamen causa materialiter, & diuerso respectu; hoc est, Terminus causæ vel notat ens absolutum, & hoc sub aliquo potest esse causatum: vel formaliter ipsum relatum, quod ad effectum refertur; & tunc idem non potest esse causa & causatum; quia relatio non inter vnum, sed duo semper vertitur.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: To the minor premise

2. To the minor premise. That it may be rightly understood how the merit of Christ and faith are both cause and effect of election, four things ought to be noted. 1. Both are considered in a twofold manner, either by reason of the divine intuition, which was from eternity: or by reason of the act itself, which follows in time. In that sense it is called the cause, in this the effect of election. For just as an end, when it is considered as preconceived and desired by the primary agent, has the force of a cause, as Zabarella explains in his commentary on the 52nd [question], 2nd part: the same thing is truly an effect, if it is considered as produced and existing: thus the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, insofar as it is conceived in the eternal divine foreknowledge, was the moving and impulsive cause which the benevolent Father attended to in choosing. But if it is considered by reason of the temporal act and execution, there it is rightly called an ἐντελῶς effect, because those whom He predestined, these God also called and justified, Rom. 8:30. And as many as were ordained believed, Acts 13:48. We shall declare these things with two examples, which the Calvinists will not be able to deny. The first is taken from the fall of the πρωτοπλάςων, to which all Calvinists admit God looked in the decree of reprobation. For it was from eternity a cause moving God to reprobate. And nevertheless they unanimously teach that the fall of Adam was the means and effect of that immutable decree. Thus, therefore, they themselves have one and the same sin of Adam, both as a moving cause, with respect to divine consideration, and as an effect, by reason of temporal execution. The second is sought from the decree of salvation, which the Calvinists distinguish (though falsely) from Election, pretending that the former is limited and the latter absolute. I ask, therefore, is not the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, the cause of the decree of salvation? They will not be able to deny it if they wish to defend their thesis. And yet faith, which follows in time and is given to man, is given because God decreed to give it. Therefore, they must necessarily admit that faith is both the cause of the decree of salvation, as it is foreseen, and the effect, as it is granted in time. Why, therefore, does this seem ἄτοπον and ἄλογον to them regarding election, which clearly is the same as and coincides with the decree of salvation?

2. Others advise that the eternal purpose of God regards two diverse objects, one of persons, the other of things. And according to these, two quasi-parts of the decree of election arise, of which the former In the case of persons, the election may be called the predestination or preordination of the means that follows. Both, although distinctly, yet not διηρημένως or separately, but ἡνωμένως and conjunctively concur to constitute one decree of election. And hence it now happens that the means of salvation, namely the merit of Christ and the faith that apprehends it, obtain a twofold respect: one of cause, the other of effect. For when related to the ἐκλογὴν of those to be saved, they obtain the status of cause; since without the merit of Christ apprehended by faith and foreseen, no one could have been elected to salvation. But again, these same things, when related to the ordination of the means, obtain the status of effect included in the election, since the merit of Christ and faith are conferred in time for the reason that God from eternity constituted and ordained that it should be so done.

3. Others also usefully add that a distinction must be made between popular and precise modes of speech. When election is called the cause of the merit of Christ and of faith, it is not an accurate but a popular formula of speaking, since the true cause of the merit is the gratuitous decree concerning the mission and passion, John 3. But the principal efficient cause of faith is the Holy Spirit, and the instrumental cause is the preaching and hearing of the word. It must therefore be known that the term cause is sometimes taken more broadly for any antecedent, and effect for a consequent, just as it is said that day begets day, or calamity begets calamity, between which, however, only a relation of certain sequence, not of true and properly called causation, intervenes. Thus also faith is named the effect of election, not as if election, speaking precisely, generated faith in the souls of men, but popularly, since faith always certainly and infallibly follows it, in which sense the Apostle says: Whom he predestined, these he also called, and justified. Rom. 8, verse 30, where not an accurate and proximate mode of causing, but only an invariable sequence of things cohering is implied. And thus that phrase, Faith which is given in time, the effect of election, we interpret and render in this way. Faith is a certain and infallible consequence of election.

4. Finally, theologians also wish for this to be observed, that some things are said of the whole, as it is a whole; others of the whole, because of some part of it. Thus children are a part of the family, and the effects of the same are rightly said to be so because of the parents who begat them. In like manner, since the decree of election enters as a principal cause, the grace and love of God; from which, as from a first fountain, emanates everything that is done for our salvation and is given in time, therefore the merit of Christ and faith are called the effect of election, not because of the election itself as a whole, but because of the love and grace of God, included in the election, so that this sense emerges: The mission and passion of the Son of God, and the faith of man, arise from the love of God, by which we were chosen from eternity. See all these things accurately explained by Mr. Menzer, vol. 1, Giessen disputations, p. 173.

XXXI. 2. A means is not prior to the end, nor the cause of the end, but the contrary. The merit of Christ is a means of election. Therefore it is neither prior, nor the cause of election. Resp. 1. The means of the decree of salvation as an end is the merit of Christ, according to the Calvinists. And yet this very merit was the cause of that decree. Therefore they are not ἐναντία (opposites), but ὑπάλληλα (subordinate).

2. The merit of Christ is not properly a means of election. For God did not first absolutely choose some and afterwards ordain the means; but the contrary. He first ordained the means for all, but because not all were going to accept, therefore He did not choose all. Thus, therefore, the decree of the means is in order prior to the decree of election, and therefore the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith and considered from eternity, is not a means of the decree, but a cause.

XXXII. 3. The cause of eternal election must have been from eternity. But the merit of Christ was not from eternity. Wherefore it is not the cause.

Response: A distinction must be made between the act of merit and the intention. The former was temporal, the latter eternal. For although Christ did not satisfy from eternity, God nevertheless viewed that future satisfaction as if it were present from eternity, and on account of it predestined believers.

XXXIII. 4. Christ himself was predestined, 1 Pet. 1:19 & 20. Therefore, he is not the cause of predestination.

Response: Distinguish between the predestination of Christ to merit salvation, and of men to obtain salvation. Although Christ was not the cause of his own predestination, he was nevertheless the cause of the predestination of men to obtain salvation.

XXXVI. 5. The good pleasure of God is the supreme and primary cause, one and eternal. Therefore, it has nothing superior to itself. Wherefore it cannot be caused by the merits of Christ. For thus merit would be superior to the good pleasure itself.

Response: The good pleasure of the divine will is the supreme cause in effecting salvation, and in that respect it has nothing superior: however, the merit of Christ is the supreme cause in meriting, which very meritorious cause can move and impel the supreme efficient cause by its own dignity to effect it. Note, therefore, that the exclusive (justice alone) is not opposed to other co-causes, just as it is not opposed in justification, but only to the merits of works.

XXXV. 6. The merit of Christ is indeed a cause of salvation, but not of election.

Response: 1. This distinction is futile. For if we are absolutely predestined to salvation, it is also absolutely conferred. For we receive salvation in time just as we were predestined from eternity to receive it. But we receive it in time on account of the merit of Christ. Therefore, we were also predestined to receive it on account of this.

2. Calvinists are forced to admit by the force of their own hypotheses, that the merit of Christ in many cases is not even the cause of salvation. For nothing profits without faith, nor is it applied except through faith. But they write that infants lack faith. Wherefore, either no infants dying in infancy are saved, or if they are saved, because they do not have faith, they will obtain salvation without the merit of Christ.

Latin:

2. Ad minorem. Vt rectè intelligatur quomodo meritum Christi & fides tum causa sint, tum effectum electionis, quatuor notari debent. 1. Vtrumque dupliciter consideratur, vel ratione diuini intuitus, qui fuit ab æterno: vel ratione ipsius actus, qui sequitur in tempore. Sensu illo causa, isto effectum electionis dicitur. Sicut enim finis; quando consideratur, vt à primario agente præconceptus & cupitus est, vim causæ habet, explicante Zab. ad cont. 52. 2. post. idem vero effectum est, si consideretur, vt productus & existens: ita meritum Christi fide apprehensum, quatenus in æterna præuisione diuina concipitur, causa fuit motrix, & impulsiua, quam in eligendo attendit beneuolus Pater. Sin verò ratione temporalis actus & executionis consideretur, ibi ἐντελῶς effectum rectè dicitur, quia quos prædestinauit, hos vocauit & iustificauit Deus, Rom. 8. v. 30. Et crediderunt, quotquot ordinati erant Act 13. vers. 48. Declarabimus hæc duobus exemplis, quæ Caluiniani negare non poterunt. Primum desumitur à lapsu πρωτοπλάςων ad quem Deum respexisse in decreto reprobationis, omnes fatentur Caluiniani. Fuit n. ab æterno causa mouens Deum ad reprobandum. Et nihilominùs vnanimiter docent, lapsum Adami fuisse medium & effectum istius decreti immutabilis. Sic ergò ipsi vnum idemq; peccatum Adæ, tum pro causa mouente habent, respectu diuinæ considerationis, tum pro effectu, ratione temporalis executionis. Secundum petitur à decreto saluationis quod ab Electione, (licèt falso) distinguunt Caluiniani, illud limitatum, hanc absolutam esse fingentes. Quæro igitur, An non meritum Christi fide apprehensum, sit causa decreti saluationis? Negare non poterunt, si thesin suam defendere voluerint. Et tamen fides, quæ in tempore sequitur, & homini datur, ideò datur, quia eam dare decreuit Deus. Ergò fateantur necesse est, fidem decreti saluationis & causam, vt præuidetur, & effectum esse, vt in tempore conceditur. Cur igitur hoc ijs ἄτοπον & ἄλογον videtur circa electionem, quæ cum saluationis decreto planè idem est & coincidit?

2. Monent alij, quòd æternum Dei propositum, duo respiciat diuersa obiecta, alterum personarum, alterum rerum. Et secundùm hæc duæ quasi partes decreti electionis oriuntur, quarum prior In specie personarum electio, posterior mediorum prædestinatio vel præordinatio dici possit. Vtraque licèt distinctè, non tamen διηρημένως vel sejunctim, sed ἡνωμένως & conjunctim ad vnum electionis decretum constituendum concurrit. Atque hinc jam sit, vt media salutis, nempè Christi meritum & fides apprehendens geminum sortiantur respectum, causæ alterum, alterum effectus. Relata enim ad ἐκλογὴν saluandorum, causæ rationem obtinent; siquidem sine merito Christi fide apprehenso & præviso nemo ad salutem potuisset eligi. Rursus vero hæc ipsa, relata ad ordinationem mediorum, electioni inclusam sortiuntur rationem effectus, quoniam ideò meritum Christi, & fides confertur in tempore, quia Deus ita fieri ab æterno constituit & ordinauit:

3. Vtiliter & hoc addunt alij, quòd distinguendum sit inter locutiones populares & exquisitas. Electio cùm dicitur causa meriti Christi, & fidei; non accurata, sed popularis est loquendi formula, cùm vera causa meriti sit gratuitum de missione & passione decretum, Ioh. 3. Fidei verò principalis efficiens sit Spirit. S. instrumentalis, verbi prædicatio & auditus. Sciendum ergò, quòd vocabulum causæ nonnunquam sumatur latiùs, pro omni antecedente: & effecti, pro consequente, sicuti dicitur dies diem, calamitas calamitatem parere, inter quæ tamen tantùm certæ consecutionis, non veræ & propriè dictæ causationis respectus intercedit. Ita quoque fides nominatur effectum electionis, non ac si electio exquisitè loquendo fidem in animis hominum gigneret, verùm populariter, quoniam illam certò semper & infallibiliter fides sequitur, quo sensu Apostolus dicit: Quos prædestinauit, hos vocauit, & iustificauit. Rom. 8. versu 30. vbi non accurata & proxima causandi ratio; sed invariabilis duntaxat cohærentium sequela innuitur. Et sic phrasin istam, Fides quæ datur in tempore, electionis effectum est, hoc modo interpretamur & reddimus. Fides certum & infallibile electionis consequens est.

4. Tandem & illud obseruatum volunt Theologi, quòd quædam dicantur de toto, quâ totum est; quædam de toto, propter aliquam ipsius partem. Sic pars familiæ sunt liberi, & eiusdem pariter effecta rectè dicuntur propter parentes, qui illos genuerunt. Pari modo, quoniam electionis decretum velut causa princeps ingreditur gratia & dilectio Dei; à qua ceu primo fonte, emanat omne id, quod nostram ob salutem fit, & in tempore donatur, ideò meritum Christi & fides, electionis effectum dicuntur, non ob ipsam electionem totam, sed ob amorem & gratiam Dei, electioni inclutam, ita, vt sensus emergat iste; Missionem & passionem Filij Dei, fidemǫ; hominis oriri à dilectione Dei, quâ ab æterno electi sumus. Vide hæc omnia accuratè explicantē Dn. Menzerū t. 1. disp. Giess. p. 173.

XXXI. 2, Medium non est prius fine neque causa finis, sed contrà. Meritum Christi est medium electionis. Ergo nec prius est, nec causa electionis. Resp. 1. Medium decreti saluationis tanquam finis, est Christi meritum, juxta Caluinianos. Et tamen hoc ipsum meritum causa fuit istius decreti. Non igitur sunt ἐναντία, sed ὑπάλληλα.

2. Meritum Christi non est propriè medium electionis. Non enim Deus primùm absolutè aliquos elegit & post media ordinauit; sed contrà. Primùm media ordinauit pro omnibus, quia verò non omnes accepturi erant, ideò non omnes elegit. Sic ergò decretum mediorum ordine prius est decreto electionis, ideoque meritum Christi fide apprehensum & ab æterno consideratum, non est medium decreti, sed causa.

XXXII. 3. Electionis æternæ causam ab æterno fuisse oportet. Meritum verò Christi non fuit ab æterno. Quare causa non est.
