Resp Distingui debet inter meriti actum & intentionem. Ille temporalis, hic æternus fuit. Quamvis enim Christus ab æterno non satisfecerit, Deus tamen futuram illam satisfactionem ceu præsentem ab æterno aspexit, & propter illam credentes prædestinauit.

XXXIII. 4. Christus ipse fuit prædestinatus, 1. Pet. 1. v. 19. & 20. Ergo non est causa prædestinationis.

Responde. Distingue inter prædestinationem Christi ad salutem promerendam, & hominum ad salutem consequendam. Licet Christus suæ prædestinationis causa non fuerit, causa tamen fuit prædestinationis hominum ad salutem consequendam.

XXXVI. 5. Beneplacitum Dei est summa & prima causa vna æterna. Ergo superiorem se non habet. Quare à meritis Christi causari nequit. Sic enim meritum superius esset ipso beneplacito.

Resp. Voluntatis diuinæ beneplacitum est summa causa in efficiendo salutem, atque eo respectu superiorem non habet : meritum Christi autem est summa causa in promerendo, quæ ipsa meritoria causa fummum efficientem sua dignitate mouere, & impellere potest ad efficiendum. Notes ergò, quòd Exclusiua (sola iustitia) non opponatur aliis concausis, sicut nec in iustificatione opponitur, sed duntaxat operum meritis.

XXXV. 6. Meritum Christi est quidem causa salutis, sed non electionis.

Resp. 1. Futile est hoc discretum. Si enim absolutè prædestinamur ad salutem, absolutè etiam eadem confertur. Ita enim salutem in tempore accipimus, vti ad illam accipiendam ab æterno prædestinati sumus. Accipimus autem in tempore propter meritum Christi. Ergò etiam propter hoc ad illam accipiendam prædestinati sumus.

2. Coguntur Caluinistæ fateri vi hypothesewn suarum, Christi meritum in multis nè quidem saluris causam esse. Nihil enim prodest sine fide, nec applicatur nisi per fidem. Ast infantes fide carere scribunt. Quare aut nulli infantes in infantia decedentes saluantur, aut si saluantur, quia fidem non habent, sine merito Christi salutem consequentur.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: Member III. XXXVI. After we have dealt with the merit of Christ, it remains to speak of…

MEMBER III.

XXXVI. After we have dealt with the merit of Christ, it remains to speak of faith. But when faith is called the cause of election, do not understand it as the principal, impelling, and meritorious cause, but only as the instrumental one, and indeed not of the whole decree, but rather of a part, namely the merit of Christ, which faith apprehends. For since it is the cause of a part of the decree, hence in a popular way of speaking it is called the cause of the decree itself. It is more convenient, however, to call faith either the condition of election, lest it be imagined to be absolute, or a part of the predestinarian order, as if God from eternity looked upon it no less than the merit of Christ. That seems most convenient, that faith not be considered separately, as a peculiar cause of election distinct from the merit of Christ, but conjointly, together with the merit itself as an apprehension, so that both joined together constitute one impelling cause of election. For neither did the merit without application, nor did faith by itself move God to elect, but both were joined in the divine foreknowledge, that is, the merit apprehending. But whatever may be the case regarding the appellations and the mode of speaking, it is enough if only this is held: that election was not made absolutely, but with respect to faith, by which the merit of Christ is apprehended, so that as in time we are saved because of the applied λύτρον of Christ, so we may believe that for the same reason we were predestined to life from eternity. We understand however, not a πρόσκαιρον or temporal faith, but a persevering and final one, in which a man departs and dies. As he who has persevered alone shall be saved, Matt. 10, verse 23; Mark 13, verse 13; 2 Tim. 4, verses 7, 8; Heb. 3, verse 14. Thus, no one is elected except him whom God foresaw would believe perseveringly

XXXVII. These are the principal sayings.

1. From 2 Thess. 2, v. 13. God chose you from the beginning for salvation in the sanctification of the Spirit and faith of the truth. If election was made in the faith of the truth and in the sanctification of the Spirit, it certainly was not made without any regard for faith. Piscator objects: 1. That Paul is not commemorating the causes of election, but of salvation. Response: This is false, because those words 'in the sanctification and faith of the truth' are not referred to the word 'salvation' but to 'election.' 2. That it follows that the holiness of life is no less a cause of election than faith. Response: By that ἁγιασμὸν is not understood the holiness of life—since salvation cannot be ascribed to these, namely, begun or good works—but rather the very sanctification of the Holy Spirit which purifies the hearts of men and sanctifies them in Christ. Therefore, one must distinguish between sanctification and holiness; the former is the cause of the latter, the latter is the effect of the former. Huberus says that Paul is speaking about those who, by the very effect, render election useful and efficacious to themselves. Response: On the contrary, Paul is dealing with election as it was made from the beginning, that is, from eternity, before it was brought into effect in time.

2. From Rom. 11, verse 20. Because of unbelief they were broken off, but you stand by faith; verse 22, 23. Behold therefore the goodness, etc. Here Paul, without any fear of Pelagianism, includes faith in the decree of the election of the Gentiles, and unbelief in the decree of the rejection of the Jews. The Calvinists object that Paul is not speaking about the causes of election, but of the ejection of the Jews from the Church, and reof the taking of the Gentiles into the same. Resp. Although it deals principally with temporal election, at the same time it sprinkles in certain things about eternal [election]. Furthermore, if God in the reception into the militant Church looks upon faith, much more will He look upon faith in the reception into the triumphant Church, or unto salvation. For if we are chosen unto grace through faith, we shall also be chosen unto glory through faith. The reason for the consequence is because grace and glory are conferred by the same means, and for the same reasons we are enrolled into the militant and triumphant Church.

3. From Ephes. 1. v. 12. Predestinated according to his purpose, who before hoped in Christ, that is, believed. For to hope and to believe are often put for the same thing in the Scriptures, as is evident from 1. Tim. 4. v. 10. 2. Thess. 2. verse 16. In the Psalms, to hope almost always signifies faith. And thus it is clearly evident that the elect are described by faith, and so the Apostle intimates that those are predestinated who have hoped or believed in Christ: which is also done in James 2. v. 5. Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith? For which reason faith is said to be of the elect of God. Tit. 1. v. 3. And the same is insinuated. 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. To the elect according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, through sanctification of the Spirit unto obedience and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ. Where by obedience we understand faith, following the guidance and nomenclature of Scripture, Acts 6. v. 7. Rom. 10. v. 16. 2. Thess. 1. v. 8. Rom. 1. v. 5. c. 16. v. 2. 2. Cor. 10. v. 5. Why therefore those are the elect, who before believed in the divine foreknowledge, from this we rightly conclude that election was made with a view to faith.

XXXIIX. Reasons 1. From the marks and titles by which the elect are described. Rom 8. v. 28 it is said that the decree of election comprehends those who love God. 1. Tim. 1. v. 16 they are called μελλοντες πιστευειν. Ephes. 1. v. 1 they are called ἁγιοι πιστοι etc. From which epithets we firmly gather that only those whom God he foresaw would believe, are the elect, from which it follows that the decree of election is not absolute, but mediate, and joined with the intuition of faith.

2. From the complacency of the elect. Whoever pleases God, they please through faith: for it is impossible to please God without faith. Heb. 11. v. 6. The elect please God. Therefore through faith. The minor premise is proven: because election presupposes love, not that indiscriminate and general one, but special and gracious: For God chose no one, unless whom He specially loved, which Zanchius himself concedes l. 5. de N. D. cap. 2. Now indeed God pursues no one with special love, unless those whom He sees believing. Wherefore since that precedes the decree of election, and indeed without the intuition of faith no one is specially loved by God, we conclude infallibly that election was not made without the aspect of faith.

3. From Christ, in whom we are chosen. No one is chosen outside of Christ, but all in Christ, Ephes. 1. v. 4. But sinners without faith are outside of Christ. For He does not dwell in us except through faith. Eph. 3. v. 17. Therefore sinners without faith, or the intuition of faith, are not chosen. Hence rightly Theophylactus in c. 1. ad Ephe. He chose us through Him, that is, through faith in Him. And Chrysostomus: What is it to be chosen in Him? Through faith, which would be in Him, Christ arranged this before we were born, indeed before the foundations of the world were laid.

4. From the grace of God. Without which grace was not given to us from eternity, without it we are not chosen: since for Paul, to be chosen from eternity, and to have grace given to oneself from eternity are synonyms. But without the intuition of faith grace was not given to us from eternity, as is manifest. Therefore neither were we chosen without the intuition of faith.

5. From ὑιοθεσίᾳ: We are predestined εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν Eph. 1. vers. 18. But there is no ὑιοθεσία without faith: For as many as received Him, to them He gave the power to become children of God, John 1. v. 12. And yet from eternity God gave the elect children

to be made of God, therefore without consideration of reception this ὑιοθεσία [adoption] does not happen to them. The syllogism is such: Whoever are made sons of God, they are made this through faith. John 1 v. 12. We were made sons of God from eternity in election. Therefore we were made [so] through faith.

6 From the inheritance of life, No one is assumed into the inheritance of eternal life without faith, because the just shall live by faith. Hab. 2 v. 4. But in election we were assumed into the inheritance of eternal life. For we who previously had no part in it, have obtained a part through election. Therefore we did not obtain it without faith, or the respect of faith.

7. From the purpose of God. If the purpose of the divine will concerning the salvation of men includes Christ and faith. Therefore also election, because it was made κατὰ πρόθεσιν [according to purpose] Rom. 8 v. 28. Eph. 1 v. 11. But the former is true, according to that John 6 v. 40. This is the will etc. Therefore also the latter.

8. From the merit of Christ. This enters into the decree of election. Therefore either simply, or relatively, or apprehended or rejected. Not simply, because 1. Christ would be profitable without faith. 2. All would be elected. Therefore relatively, insofar as it is apprehended by faith.

9. From the necessity of satisfaction. The grace of God has no place, unless satisfaction has first been made to justice injured by sin. But election presupposes the grace of God. Therefore we are not elected, unless satisfaction has first been made to divine justice. We have therefore made satisfaction either ourselves, or through another. Not ourselves. Therefore through another, but that satisfaction does not become ours except through faith. Wherefore no one is predestined to life, except with respect to the satisfaction of Christ imputed through faith.

10. From the intercession of Christ. No one is elected, except for whom Christ intercedes, that he may be elected. And Christ intercedes only for those who are to believe, as is evident from John 17 verse 20. I do not pray for them only, but also for those who are to believe in me through their word.

Therefore, faith is considered at the same time in election.

11. From God's foreknowledge. God from eternity foreknew who would believe and who would not. Therefore, He decreed something concerning both, or He did not. The latter is absurd and contrary to God's providence. Therefore, the former is true. He decreed, therefore, to save those who would believe and to condemn the unbelievers. And this is the decree of predestination, to which, for that reason, faith is rightly said to be included.

Finally, 12. From the particular grace of God. If the grace of God choosing is universal, but election is particular, it follows that election was made in faith in Christ. The consequent is proven. For either that universal grace is restricted to a particular effect through the faith of those to be chosen, or through works. But not through works, for these are not subordinated to, but opposed to, God's mercy, Rom 11. 6. Therefore, through faith.

Latin:

MEMBRVM III.

XXXVI. Postquam egimus de merito Christi, restat dicendum de fide. Cùm autem fides electionis causa dicitur, non intelligas principalem, impellentem ac meritoriam, sed tantùm instrumentalem, & quidem non totius decreti, sed potiùs partis, nempè meriti Christi, quod fides apprehendit. Cùm enim sit causa partis decreti, hinc populari modo loquendi causa dicitur ipsius decreti. Conuenientius tamen est, fidem nuncupare vel conditionem electionis, ne fingatur esse absoluta, vel partem ordinis prædestinatorij, quasi Deus ab æterno, non minùs vt Christi meritum aspexerit. Conuenientissimum illud videtur, fidem non considerari seorsum, vt causam electionis peculiarem à Christi merito distinctam, sed coniunctim, vnà cum ipso merito apprehensio, vt sic vtrumque copulatum vnam electionis causam impellentem constituat. Neque enim meritum sine applicatione, neque fides per se mouit Deum ad eligendum, sed vtrumque in præscientia diuina coniunctum, hoc est meritum apprehendens. Quicquid verò sit de appellationibus & modo loquendi, satis est si modò istud teneatur electionem non esse factam absolutè, sed cum respectu ad fidem, qua meritum Christi apprehenditur, vt in tempore saluamur ob applicatum Christi λύτρον, sic ob idem ab æterno ad vitam nos prædestinatos esse credamus. Intelligimus autem non fidem πρόσκαιρον vel temporalem, sed perseuerantem & finalem, in qua homo decedit & moritur. Vtn. is tantùm saluus erit qui perseuerauit, Matth. 10. versu 23. Marci 13. versu 13. 2. Timo: 4. versu 7. 8. Heb. 3. versu. 14. Ita nemo electus est, nisi quem perseueranter crediturũ præuidit Deus : id quod nunc vicissim probabimus, tum dictis, tum rationibus.

XXXVII. Dicta sunt hæc præcipua.

1. Ex 2. Thess. 2. v. 13. Elegit vos Deus ab initio ad salutem in sanctificatione Spiritus, & fide veritatis. Si electio facta est in fide veritatis, & in sanctificatione Spiritus, vtique non est facta absque omni intuitu fidei. Excipit Piscator. 1. Paulum non commemorare causas electionis, sed salutis. Respon. Falsum hoc est, quia verba illa in sanctificatione & fide veritatis non referuntur ad vocem (salutis) sed ad electionem. 2. Sequi, non minùs sanctitatem vitæ esse electionis causam, quàm fidem. Respon. Per illum ἁγιασμὸν non intelligitur sanctitas vitæ : inchoata seu bona opera cùm his non possit adscribi salus : sed potiùs ipsa Spiritus sanctificatio quæ corda hominum purificat, & in Christo sanctificat. Distinguendum est igitur inter sanctificationem & sanctitatem ; illa hujus causa, hæc illius effectum est. Huberus ait, loqui Paulum de ijs, qui ipso effectu sibi vtilem & efficacem reddant electionem. Respon. Imò Paulus agit de electione, vt ea facta ab initio, id est, ab æterno antequam in effectum traduceretur in tempore.

2. Ex Rom. 11. versu 20. Propter incredulitatem fracti sunt, tu autem fide stas versu 22. 23. Vide ergò bonitatem, &c. Hîc Paulus sine vllo Pelagianismi metu fidem decreto electionis gentium incredulitatem decreto rejectionis Iudæorum includit. Caluiniani excipiunt, Paulum non loqui de causis electionis, sed eiectionis Iudæorum ex Ecclesia, & recaptionis gentium in eandem. Resp. Licèt principaliter de temporali electione agat, simul tamen de æterna quædam inspergit. Deinde, si Deus in receptione ad Ecclesiam militantem intuetur fidem, multò magis fidem intuebitur in receptione ad Ecclesiam triumphantem, vel ad salutem. Nam si per fidem eligimur ad gratiam, per fidem quoque eligemur ad gloriam. Ratio consequentiæ est, quia iisdem medijs confertur gratia & gloria, easdemque ob causas in Ecclesiam militantem & triumphantem adscribimur.

3. Ex Ephes. 1. v. 12. Prædestinati secundum propositum ipsius, qui ante in Christo sperauimus, id est, credidimus. Sperare enim & credere in Scripturis sæpè pro eodem ponuntur, vt patet ex 1. Tim. 4. v. 10. 2. Thess. 2. vers 16. In Psalmis sperare fere semper fidem significat. Atque ita luculenter patet, quod à fide describantur electi, adeoque Apostolus innuat eos esse prædestinatos, qui sperauerunt vel crediderunt in Christum: quod fit etiam Iacobi 2. v. 5. Nonne Deus elegit pauperes huius mundi diuites in fide? Quâ de causa fides dicitur esse electorum Dei. Tit. 1. v. 3. Et idem insinuatur. 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. Dilectis iuxta præfinitionem Dei Patris, per sanctificationem Spiritus in obedientiam & aspersionem sanguinis Iesu Christi. Vbi per obedientiam intelligimus fidem, sequentes ductum & nomenclaturam Scripturæ, Act 6. v. 7. Rom. 10. v. 16. 2. Thess. 1. v. 8. Rom. 1. v. 5. c. 16. v. 2. 2. Cor. 10. v. 5. Cur igitur isti sint electi, qui in præscientia diuina ante crediderunt, hinc electionem cum fidei aspectu factam esse rectè concludimus.

XXXIIX. Rationes 1. A notis & titulis, quibus electi describuntur Rom 8. v. 28. dicitur, quòd decretum electionis comprehendat eos, qui diligunt Deum 1. Tim. 1. v. 16 dicuntur μελλοντες πιστευειν Epes. 1. v. 1. vocantur ἁγιοι πιστοι &c. Ex quibus sane epithetis firmiter colligimus, eos tantum, quos Deus credituros præuidit, electos esse, ex quo consequitur, decretum electionis non esse absolutum, sed mediatum, & cum intuitu fidei coniunctum.

2. A complacentia electorum. Quicunque Deo placent, ij per fidemplacent: impossibile enim est Deo absque fide placere. Heb. 11. v. 6. Electi placent Deo. Ergò per fidem. Minor probatur: quia electio præsupponit dilectionem, non illam indiscretam & generalem, sed specialem & gratiosam: Neminem enim Deus elegit, nisi quem specialiter dilexit, quod concedit ipse Zanchius l. 5. de N. D. cap. 2. Iam verò Deus neminem speciali dilectione prosequitur, nisi quos videt credentes. Quare cùm illa præcedat electionis decretum, & verò sine intuitu fidei nemo specialiter à Deo diligatur, concludimus infallibiliter, quòd electio sine fidei aspectu non sit facta.

3. A Christo, in quo eligimur. Nemo extra Christum eligitur, sed omnes in Christo, Ephes. 1. v. 4. Peccatores autem sine fide sunt extra Christum. Non enim nisi per fidem habitat in nobis. Eph. 3. v. 17. Ergo peccatores sine fide, vel fidei intuitu non eliguntur. Hinc rectè Theophylactus in c. 1. ad Ephe. Elegit nos per ipsum, id est, per fidem in ipsum Et Chrysostomus: Quid est eligi nos in ipso? Per fidem, quæ in ipsum esset istud Christus, antequam nasceremur, disposuit, imò prius quam orbis fundamenta iacerentur.

4 A gratia Dei. Sine quo gratia nobis ab æterno non fuit data, sine eo non sumus electi: cùm Paulo, ab æterno electum esse, & sibi ab æterno datam habere gratiam sint Synonyma. Ast sine fidei intuitu gratia nobis ab æterno data non fuit, vt est manifestum. Ergò nec sine fidei intuitu electi sumus.

5. Ab ὑιοθεσίᾳ: Prædestinati sumus εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν Eph. 1. vers. 18. Ast nulla est ὑιοθεσία sine fide: Nam quotquot eum receperunt, ijs dedit filios Dei fieri Ioh. 1. v. 12. Atqui ab æterno dedit Deus electis filios

Dei fieri, Ergò sine receptionis consideratione ista ὑιοθεσία ijs non obtigit. Syllogismus est talis; Quicunq; fiunt filij Dei, ij per fidem hoc fiunt. Ioh. 1 v. 12. Nos ab æterno sumus facti filij Dei in electione. Ergò per fidem facti sumus.

6 Ab hæreditate vitæ, Nemo sine fide assumitur in hæreditatem vitæ æternæ, quia iustus fide viuet. Hab. 2. v. 4. Ast in electione assumti sumus in hæreditatem vitæ æternæ. Qui enim antea non habueramus partem in ea, consecuti sumus partem per electionem. Ergò non sine fide, vel fidei respectu assecuti sumus.

7. A Proposito Dei. Si propositum diuinæ voluntatis de hominum saluatione includit Christum & fidem. Ergò & electio, quia facta est κατὰ πρόθεσιν Rom. 8. v. 28. Ephe 1. v. 11. Verum autem est prius, iuxta illud Ioh. 6. v. 40. Hæc est voluntas &c. Ergò & posterius.

8. A merito Christi. Hoc ingreditur decretum electionis. Ergò aut simpliciter, aut relatè, vel apprehensum vel spretum. Non simpliciter, quia 1. Christus sine fide prodesset. 2. omnes essent electi. Ergò relatè, quatenus fide apprehensum est.

9. A necessitate satisfactionis. Gratia Dei non habet locum, nisi prius satisfactum sit iustitiæ peccato læsæ. Electio autem præsupponit gratiam Dei. Ergò non sumus electi, nisi prius satisfactum fuerit diuinæ iustitiæ. Satis fecimus igitur vel ipsi, vel per alium. Non ipsi. Ergò per alium, Illa verò satisfactio non fit nostra nisi per fidem. Quare nemo ad vitam prædestinatur, nisi cum respectu per fidem imputatæ satisfactionis Christi.

10. Ab intercessione Christi. Nemo eligitur, nisi pro quo intercedit Christus, vt eligatur. Atque Christus pro credituris tantùm intercedit, vti patet ex Ioh. 17. vers. 20. Non oro pro eis tantum, sed & pro his, qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me.

Ergò fides simul in electione spectatur.

11. A Deipræscientia. Deus ab æterno præsciuit, præscienquinam essent credituri, qui non. Ergò de vtrisque aliquid decreuit, vel non. Posterius est absurdum, & contra Dei prouidentiam. Ergò prius verum. Decreuit igitur credituros saluare, incredulos damnare. Et hoc est decretum prædestinationis, cui propterea fides inclusa rectè dicitur.

Tandem 12. A gratia Dei particulari. Si gratia Dei eligentis est vniuersalis, electio verò particularis, sequitur electionem factam esse in fide Christi. Consequens probatur. Aut enim restringitur illa vniuersalis gratia ad particularem effectum per hominum eligendorum fidem, aut per opera.. Ast non per opera, hæc enim non subordinantur, sed opponuntur Dei misericordiæ, Rom 11. 7 5.6. Ergò per fidem.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: XXXIX. Having set forth our arguments, we shall see in a few words the stratagems of our adversaries

XXXIX. Having set forth our arguments, we shall see in a few words the stratagems of our adversaries.

1. John 10 verse 26. You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. Therefore, faith is given only to those who are elected into the number of the sheep by an absolute decree.

Resp. The particle (because) is not αἰτιολογικὴ or causal, but rather συλλογιστικὴ or ratiocinative, partly ἐκβατικὴ or indicating the outcome. It is not Christ's meaning that the Jews do not believe for the reason that they were reprobated from eternity, or because the Father did not wish them to be saved, since this is contrary to all Scripture, the office of Christ, and the whole analogy of faith: but He only argues from the antecedent to the consequent. You do not believe: How so? Because you are not of my sheep. As if He were to say: It is no wonder you do not believe, since my Father saw your unbelief from eternity and therefore could not co-opt you into the number of my sheep. Because, therefore, you are not my sheep, whose property it is to believe, for that reason you do not believe in me. Similar formulas of concluding are these: The sun has now risen, because it is day. Possess the kingdom of heaven, because you gave me to eat. Matt. 25 v. 35. But in the first place, this text can most conveniently be explained ἐκβατικῶς [ecbatically/as a result], so that the sense is: You do not believe, and hence it is evident that you are not of my sheep. The scope of Christ indicates this interpretation, and the antecedents and consequents confirm it. Nor is it new in the Scriptures for certain things to be said αἰτιολογικῶς [etiologically/as a cause], and to be understood ἐκβατικῶς [as a result]. We have examples: Psalm 51:6, John 12:39, Romans 11:32. See Damascene, book 4, On the Orthodox Faith, ch. 26.

XL. 2. John 15:16. You did not choose me, but I chose you. Therefore, faith is not the cause that impelled God to choose.

Response 1. We do not say that faith is the impulsive cause of election simply, insofar as it is a certain inherent quality on account of which God chose us, but rather we say that the impulsive cause is the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. For God chose those whom He foresaw would persevere in believing in Christ. Therefore, faith is included in the decree of election, not as an impulsive cause, but as an instrument receiving and apprehending the impulsive cause, which is the merit of Christ.

2. N. C. [Negatur Consequentia/The consequence is denied]. It is God who chose us. Therefore, God in His election did not look at our faith. For although we do not anticipate God, nor are we chosen on account of our works, nevertheless God has established this order, that He wills to save no one in time, and likewise has predestined no one from eternity to salvation, except the believer. Moreover, this faith itself is also a gift of God; it does not depend on our own powers.

XLI. Acts 13:48. As many as were ordained to eternal life believed. Wherefore faith is the effect of election, not the cause.

Response 1. We explained above in what sense faith is both an effect and a cause of election.

2. Here faith is said to be not so much an effect as a consequent of election. For the simplest sense is: Those elected from eternity believed in time. Election precedes, faith follows. There is, therefore, a description of the faithful from eternal election. The cause is not rendered why few have believed, but the execution is compared with the decree, and the faithful are described from their election. But what is this against the intuition of faith? Nothing at all. Not otherwise than if I were to conclude in this way: They believed, as many as God willed to justify, therefore we are not justified through faith.

3. The term of ordination ought to be observed, which hints that election was not made absolute, but with a certain order. The preceding words declare this very thing: 'And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord.' These, therefore, were ordained, who received the Gospel with joy; the rest, rejecting it, perished by their own fault. v. 46. For because they deemed themselves unworthy of eternal life, they were certainly reprobated by their own vice, not by an absolute hatred of God.

XLII. 4. Rom. 9 v. 16. It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. 1 John 4 v. 10. Herein is the love of God, not that we loved God, but that he first loved us.

Resp. 1. There is no consequence from the exclusion of works to the exclusion of faith. For although we are not elected on account of our works, it does not follow from this that God, in electing, had absolutely no respect to faith or the merit of Christ; because the principal cause does not remove the impulsive one. For just as we are freely justified and saved by the sole mercy of God, yet not without faith, so we were destined from eternity to salvation by sole mercy, but conversely not without faith: they are therefore ὑπάλληλα [subordinate/co-ordinate], not ἐναντία [contrary]: to be elected freely out of mercy, and with respect to faith, and these on account of the order constituted by God.

XLIII. 5. Augustine says: He chose us that we might believe, not because we believed. Otherwise, Pelagianism would follow.

Resp. Augustine does not simply exclude... not out of respect for faith, but by those phrases and similar ones, he excludes only two things. 1. Faith, as it is a quality, and is ascribed to free will. 2. Faith, insofar as it is called the meritorious cause of election. Pelagius affirmed both; Augustine rightly denied them, as do we. For faith does not enter into election as our quality, but ὀργανικῶς as an instrument apprehending, which is given by God alone, not had from the powers of the will. We are chosen not to faith, as a term, not because of faith, as a merit, but through faith, as a medium, or in faith, as a part of the predestinarian order. Therefore, just as it is not Pelagianism when we are said to be justified through faith, so it will not be Pelagianism when we describe election through the intuition of faith, excited in us by God alone, while we do not resist, without us cooperating. Whatever, therefore, is alleged from the Fathers, those things are opposed primarily to the Pelagians and to meritorious election, not to mediated election, as is evident from Augustine, book 1 de praedest. last chapter, book de dono persev. chapters 14 and 28, and book 1 Retr. 23. The other arguments impugning the foreknowledge of faith are easy to solve from what has been said, and if anyone desires a special λύσιν for them out of abundance, he will find it sufficiently clear in Mr. Dr. Cramer, book de praedest. chapter 8, question 6, and Mr. Dr. Gerhard, Volume 2, locus de elect. section 175, page 332.

Latin:

XXXIX. Expositis argumentis nostris, videbimus paucis aduersariorum strophas.

1. Ioh. 10 vers. 26. Vos non creditis, quia non estis ex ouibus meis. Ergò illis tantùm datur fides, qui ex absoluto decreto in numerum ouium sunt, electi.

Resp. Particula (quia) non est αἰτιολογικὴ vel causalis, sed parum συλλογιστικὴ seu ratiocinatiua, partim ἐκβατικὴ seu euentum indicans, Non p. Christi mens est, Iudæos non credere eam ob causam, quia ab æterno sint reprobati, aut quia Pater non illos saluos fieri, cùm hoc vniuersæ Scripturæ, officio Christi, & toti analogiæ fidei aduersetur: sed tantùm argumentatur ab antecedente ad consequens. Vos non creditis: Qui sic? Quia non estis ex ouibus meis. Aç si dicat: Non mirum est vos non credere, cum Pater meus ab æterno Infidelitatem vestram viderit, ideoque in ouium meorum numerum cooptare non potuerit. Quia igitur oues meæ non estis, quarum proprium est credere, propterea in me non creditis. Similes concludendi formulæ sunt hæ: Iam Sol ortus est, quia dies est. Possidete regnu cæli, quia dedistis mihi manducare. Ma. 254 v. 35. In primis verò ἐκβατικῶς commodissimè potest exponi hic textus, vt sit sensus: Vos non creditis, atque hinc patet, quòd ex ouibus meis non sitis. Quam interpretationem Christi scopus indicat, antecedentia & consrequentia confirmant. Neque nouum est, in Scripturis quædam dici αἰτιολογικῶς, & intelligi ἐκβατικῶς. Exempla habemus, Psal. 51. v. 6. Ioh. 12. v. 39. Rom. 11. vers. 32. Vide Damasc. lib. 4. de orthodox. fide, c. 26.

XL. 2. Ioh. 15. v. 16. Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos. Ergo fides non est causa, quæ Deum ad eligendum impulit.

Resp. 1. Non dicimus fidem esse causam electionis impulsiuam simpliciter, quatenus est qualitas quædam inhærens propter quam Deus nos elegerit, sed potiùs dicimus, causam impulsiuam esse meritum Christi fide apprehensum. Deus enim quos in Christum perseueranter credituros præuidit, eos elegit. Proindè fides includitur decreto electionis, non tanquam causa impulsiua, sed velut organum accipiens & apprehendens causam impulsiuam quod est meritum Christi.

2. N. C. Deus est qui elegit nos. Ergo Deus in electione sua non aspexit fidem nostram. Etsi enim nos non præuenimus Deum, nec propter opera nostra eligimur, attamen hunc Deus sanciuit ordinem, vt neminem in tempore saluare velit, neminem quoque ab æterno ad salutem prædestinauerit, nisi credentem. Fides autem hæc & ipsa Dei donum est, non ex viribus nostris dependet.

XLI. Act. 13. vers. 48. Crediderunt, quotquot erant ordinati ad vitam. Quare fides electionis effectum est, non causa.

Respond. 1. Quo sensu fides tùm effectum, tum causa sit electionis, suprà exposuimus.

2. Hic fides non tàm effectum quàm consequens electionis dicitur. Sensus enim simplicissimus est: Electi ab æterno crediderunt in tempore. Electio præcessit, fides sequitur. Est igitur descriptio fidelium ab æterna electione. Non redditur causa, cur pauci crediderint sed confertur executio cùm decreto, & describuntur fideles à sua electione, Quid autem hoc contra intuitum fidei ? Nihil omninò. Non secus, ac si hoc modo concluderem Crediderunt, quotquot Deus iustificare voluit, Ergò per fidem non iustificamur.

3. Vocabulum ordinationis obseruari debet, quod electionem non absolutam, sed certo cum ordine factam esse innuit. Declarant hoc ipsum verba antecedentia; Audientes autem gentes gauisæ sunt, & glorificauerunt verbum Domini. Hi ergo erant ordinati, qui Evangelium recipiebant cum gaudio, reliqui istud repellentes suâ culpâ perierunt. v. 46. Quia ehim seipsos reputârunt indignos vitâ æternâ, suo vtique vitio, non ex absoluto Dei odio sunt reprobati.

XLII. 4. Rom. 9 v. 16. Non est volentis, neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei. 1. Ioh. 4. v. 10. In hoc est charitas Dei, non quasi nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quoniam ipse prior dilexit nos

Resp. 1. Nulla est consequentia ab exclusione operum ad exclusionem fidei. Licèt enim propter opera nostra non simus electi, hinc tamen non sequitur, quòd Deus in eligendo nullum planè habuerit respectum ad fidem meritumue Christi; quia causa principalis non tollit impulsiuam. Nam vti gratis iustificamur & saluamur ex sola misericordia Dei, nec tamen sine fide, sic ab æterno ad salutem destinati sumus, ex sola misericordia, sed vicissim non sine fide: ὑπάλληλα igitur sunt, non ἐναντία: ex misericordia gratis eligi, & cum fidei respectu eisque propter ordinem a Deo constitutum.

XLIII. 5. Augustinus inquit : Elegit nos, vt credamus, non quia credidimus. Aliàs enim sequeretur Pelagianismus.

Resp. Augustinus non simpliciter excludit omnem fidei respectum, sed phrasibus istis; & similibus, duo tantum excludit. 1. Fidem, vt est qualitas, & libero arbitrio adscribitur. 2. Fidem, prout causa electionis meritoria dicitur. Vtrumque affumebat Pelagius, recte negabat Augustinus, cum quo & nos. Neque enim fides ingreditur electionem, vt qualitas nostra, sed ὀργανικῶς vt instrumentum apprehendens, quod a solo Deo datur, non ex viribus arbitrij habetur. Eligimur non ad fidem, vt terminum, non propter fidem, vt meritum, sed per fidem, tanquam medium, vel in fide, tanquam parte ordinis praedestinatorij. Vt ergo Pelagianismus non est, cum per fidem iustificari dicimur, ita nec Pelagianismus erit, cum electionem per intuitum fidei a solo Deo in nobis non repugnantibus, sine nobis cooperantibus excitatae describimus. Quaecunque igitur ex Patribus allegantur, ea sunt opposita Pelagianis potissimum & electioni meritoriae, non mediatae, vti patet ex Augustino l. 1. de praedest. c. ult. l. de dono persev. cap. 14. & 28. & lib. 1. Retr. 23. Caetera Argumenta fidei praeuisionem impugnantia ex dictis solutu sunt facilia, & si quis ex abundanti peculiarem eorum desiderat λύσιν, inueniet eam satis luculentam apud Dn. D. Cramerum. li. de praedest c. 8. quaest. 6. Dn. D. Gerhardum Tomo 2. loco de elect. sect. 175 p. 332.


### Question III. What is predestination, and what causes does it have?: Member IV. XLIII. Finally, that election is made without our merits and works and is…

MEMBER IV.

XLIII. Finally, that election is made without our merits and works and is entirely gratuitous is not difficult to prove. For the following sayings clearly confirm this very thing. Rom. 9:11-12: 'For when the children were not yet born, and had done neither good nor evil, etc.' v. 16: 'It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy.' Rom. 11:5-6: 'The remnant according to the election of grace have been saved. But if by grace, then it is no longer of works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.' 2 Tim. 1:9: 'He has called us with a holy calling, not according to our works' ours, but according to His own purpose and grace. Hence Augustine, book 3 against Julian the Pelagian, ch. 3, says: He chose no one who was worthy, but by choosing, He made them worthy. And Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, page 33: There is one God, who freely calls the predestined, and justifies the called, and glorifies the justified. The other Fathers also commonly maintain this against the Pelagians, that justification happens without works, whence it follows that election is also gratuitous, since the decree and the execution do not differ in their causes. Those things which are brought forward to the contrary by the Papists, we wish to defer their solution to the place concerning free will and justification, to which they principally pertain.

TO GOD ALONE BE GLORY

Latin:

MEMBRVM IV.

XLIII. Tandem quod electio, sine nostris meritis & operibus facta penitusque gratuita sit, probatu non est difficile. Hoc ipsum enim luculenter confirmant sequentia dicta. Rom. 9. v. 11. & 12. Cùm nondum nati essent pueri, nec quicquam fecissent boni vel mali, &c. v. 16. Non est volentis, non est currentis, sed miserentis Dei, Rom. 11. v. 5. 6. Reliquiae secundum electionem gratiae Dei saluae factae sunt. Si autem gratia, iam non ex operibus, alioquin gratia iam non esset gratia. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. Vocauit nos vocatione sancta non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum propositum suum & gratiam. Hinc Augustinus l. 3. contra Iulianum Pelag. c. 3. Nullum, inquit, elegit dignum, sed eligendo effecit dignum. Et Fulgent. l. 1. ad Monim. pag. 33. Vnus Deus est, qui gratis & vo at praedestinatos, & iustificat vocatos, & glorificat iustificatos. Patres etiam ceteri communiter vigent hoc contra Pelagianos, quod iustificatio sine operibus siat, vnde sequitur & electionem esse gratuitam, cum decretum & executio causis non differant. Quæ in contrarium proferuntur à Pontificijs, eorum solutionem ad locum de libero arbitrio & iustificatione, quo spectant principaliter, dilatam volumus.

SOLI DEO GLORIA


## 17 Disputation V. On the Book of Life

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Master Hieronymus Nymmanus of Wittenberg, Saxony:

Προόιμιον.

After enough has been said concerning the true nature and definition of eternal Predestination, the logic of our order demands that we add a few things concerning the BOOK OF LIFE and the inscription into it. For because Scripture describes the business of election with these phrases, it is altogether necessary that the true sense of them be clearly set forth, since, once these are explained, the doctrine of Predestination will be not a little illustrated. But since these things are less common and not obvious to everyone, we shall repeat the matter from a little higher up, and we shall discourse 1. concerning the Books of God in general, 2. concerning the Book of Life in particular, and We shall include everything in seven distinct questions.

Latin:

Præf. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. M. Hieronymo Nymmano Witteberga-Saxone:

Προόιμιον.

POsteaquàm de vera æternæ Prædestinationis natura & definitione dictum satis est, ordinis nostri ratio efflagitat, vt de LIBRO VITÆ; & inscriptione in vsum pauca quædam subiungamus. Quia enim Scriptura phrasibus hisce negotium electionis describit, necessarium omnino est, vt verus illarum sensus perspicuè proponatur, siquidem iis explicatis doctrina Prædestinationis non parùm illustrabitur. Cùm veró hæc minus trita, nec cuivis obvia sint, rem paulo altiùs repetemus, & 1 de Libris Dei in genere, 2. de Libro Vitæ in specie disseremus, & omnia septem distinctis quaestionibus includabimus.


### Question I. What does Scripture understand when it attributes a Book to God?

I. This expression is not literal, but metaphorical. For God does not need any material book in which He might record either His decrees or our deeds, or retrieve things recorded from it, since He is omniscient, and nothing at any time ever escapes His knowledge, Job 14:16, ch. 22:11, ch. 28:24, Ps. 90:8, Prov. 15:3, Dan. 2:22, Hos. 5:3, Sir. 23:27 & 29, ch. 39:24, 25.

II. Yet by metaphor a book is attributed to Him, just as other metaphorical attributes of God occur throughout the Scriptures, which are indeed proper to created things, but are predicated of God by a certain likeness, in order to outline actions to us in this way. For Scripture speaks most often according to our capacity and the mode of human cognition, whence the Fathers write that these things are enunciated not θεολογικῶς (theologically), but οἰκονομικῶς (economically) or by a certain dispensation, which others call ἀνθρωποπάθειαν (anthropopathy) or συγκaτάβασιν (condescension), when God condescends and accommodates Himself to our capacity. Ἀνθρώποις γαρ ὅσιν ἀνθρωπίνως ἡ γραφὴ διαλέγεται, Scripture speaks to us humans in a human manner, says Procopius in ch. 3 of Isaiah. Where, however, we must always be mindful of that ancient rule set down by Nazianzen: πολλὰ ἀνθρωποπαθῶς λέγονται, ἀλλὰ θεοπρεπῶς νοῦνται, Many things are said in a human manner, which are to be understood divinely.

III. The metaphor, however, is taken from wise men, who have been accustomed to diligently record in a certain book memorable things and acts which they wish to remember. Mention of such a book is made in Esther 6:1, where King Ahasuerus orders the histories and annals of former times to be brought to him, and it is called מזכרות ספר, a book of monuments or a memorial. Thus in Academies, when someone is received into the scholastic society, his name is inscribed in a particular book; which we are accustomed to call a Matricula; and through that inscription he becomes a participant in all Academic privileges, and is numbered among those whose studies are fostered and promoted with singular care.

IV. From this human custom it has flowed, that when God cares for creatures, or observes our deeds, or receives the faithful into favor, he is said to write a book; and in it to assign things or persons. In this sense our tears are said to be collected in the bottle of God, and recorded in his book, Psal. 56. v. 9. And in Malachi it is read c. 3. v. 16. The Lord attended and heard, and a book of remembrance was written before him for those who fear the Lord. In Hebrew it is ספר זכרון, among the LXX βιβλίον μνημοσύνου, in the Vulgate, a book of memory, such as men are accustomed to construct for themselves, so that it may suggest those things which they wish to remember faithfully, and to have diligent care for.

V. Therefore, when a book is attributed to God, nothing else is understood than his knowledge, and that either general, or special, and joined with singular care for things. But to be written into a book is to be diligently observed, or to be referred among those things which God powerfully preserves, or mercifully looks upon. For as a man's book is a written annotation: so the book of God is a living knowledge of a thing. And just as to write into a book is to record a thing, so that it may not fall from memory: so divine writing is a present inspection of things; a diligent observation; a singular love, care, and defense. Euthymius briefly comprehends these things, when he comments thus on Psal. 68 and 138: The book of God is his supreme knowledge: but the writing is a perpetual memory. For through books, divine letters figure and understand the varied and manifold knowledge of God.

Latin:

I. Locutio haec non est propria, sed metaphorica. Deus enim non indiget libro aliquo materiali, in quo vel decreta sua vel facta nostra annotet, aut annotata inde repetat, siquidem omniscius est, nec quicquam ullo nunquam tempore notitiam eius subterfugit, Iobi 14. v. 16. c. 22. v. 11. c. 28. v. 24. Ps. 90. v. 8. Prov. 15. v. 3. Dan. 2. v. 22. Ose 5. v. 3. Syr. 23. v. 27. & 29. c. 39. v. 24 24. 25.

II. Per metaphoram tamen liber ipsi tribuitur, sicut & alia in Scripturis passim occurrunt attributa Dei metaphorica, quae propria quidem sunt rerum creatarum, per similitudinem verò quandam praedicantur de Deo, actiones eis hoc pacto adumbrandas. Loquitur enim Scriptura saepiùs secundum captum nostrum & humanae cognitionis modum unde Patres ista enunciari scribunt non θελογικῶς, sed οἰκονομικῶς vel per quandam dispensationem, quam alij vocant ἀνθρωποπάθειαν vel συγκaτάβασιν, cùm Deus condescendit, & nostro se captui accommodat. Ἀνθρώποις γαρ ὅσιν ἀνθρωπίνως ἡ γραφὴ διαλέγεται, Scriptura nobis hominibus humano more loquitur, ait Procopius in cap. 3. Esa. Vbi tamen semper memores esse debemus antiquae illius regulae, à Nazianzeno positae, πολλὰ ἀνθρωποπαθῶς λέγονται, ἀλλὰ θεοπρεπῶς νοῦνται, Multa dicuntur humanitiùs, quae sunt intelligenda divinitiùs.

III. Metaphora verò desumta est à viris sapientibus, qui res & actus memorabiles, quorum meminisse volunt, in libro quodam diligenter annotare consueverunt. Talis libri mentio fit Esther. 6. v. 1. ubi Rex Ahasverus historias & annales priotemporum sibi iubet afferri, & appellatur מזכרות ספר liber monumentorum vel memorialis. Sic in Academiis, cùm quis in societatem scholasticam recipitur, nomen ipsius peculiari libro inscribitur; quem nuncupare solemus Matriculam; & per illam inscriptionem particeps fit omnium priuilegiorum Academicorum, illisque annumeratur, quorum studia singulari cura fouentur & promouentur.

IV. Ab hac consuetudine humana fluxit, vt cùm Deus creaturas curat, vel facta nostra obseruat, vel in gratiam recipit fideles, librum scribere; & in illo res aut personas adsignare dicatur. Hoc sensu lacrymę nostrę in vtre Dei collectæ, in libro ipsius consignatæ dicuntur, Psal. 56. v. 9. Et apud Malachiam legitur c. 3. v. 6. Attendit Dominus & audiuit, & scriptus est liber monumenti coram eo timentibus Dominum. In Hebræo est ספר זכרון apud LXX. βιβλίον μνημοσύνου, in Vulgata, liber memoriæ, quales sibi homines construere solent, vt illa suggerat, quorum fideliter meminisse, & curam diligenter habere volunt.

V. Proindè cùm Deo liber attribuitur, nihil aliud quàm eius notitia intelligitur, eaque vel generalis, vel specialis, & cum singulari rerum cura coniuncta. In librum verò scribi, est diligenter obseruari, vel inter illa referri, quæ Deus potenter conseruat, vel clementer adspicit. Vt enim liber hominis est scripta annotatio: sic liber Dei est viua rei cognitio. Et velut in librum scribere, est rem consignare, nè memoriâ excidat: Sic diuina scriptio est præsens rerum inspectio; diligens obseruatio; singularis dilectio, cura & defensio. Breuiter hæc comprehendit Euthymius, cùm in Psal. 68. & 138. ita commentatur: Liber Dei est summa eius scientia: scriptura verò perpetua memoria. Per libros enim variam & multiplicem Deicognitionem diuina literæ figuram & intelligunt:


### Question II. III. Others (whom Franc. Suarez seems to favor in 1

I. Since the Book of God is the knowledge of God, and indeed this is reciprocal with ἁγίᾳ [holy] divine [knowledge], and is therefore most simple and one in number, it follows that the book of God, considered in itself and essentially, is also necessarily one. But because the things or objects which are known by God and inscribed in the divine book are not of one but of a diverse kind, it happens from this that diverse books are also attributed to God, on account of the said variety of objects.

II. However, writers differ in enumerating the books of God. Polanus, in book 2 of his Syntagma Theologiae, chapter 35, column 1252, enumerates four βίβλους [books]. 1. The Book of Providence, which he in turn divides into the book of the World, in which the governance of all creatures stands recorded: and the book of the Church, which concerns the faithful and sacred events. 2. The Book of Scripture. 3. The Book of divine Judgment. 4. The Book of life. But he wrongly mixed in the book or sacred codex of Scripture. For although this can be called a book of God, and express mention of it is made in Isaiah 34:16, 'Seek in the Book of the Lord and read,' it is less correctly reckoned among the metaphorical books taken for the knowledge of God, about which Polanus discourses there. For the Biblical codex is a book properly, not by metaphor, and therefore it does not pertain to the present question.

III. Others (whom Franc. Suaretz seems to favor in his 1st tractate on Thomas, book 1, chapter 20) likewise mention 4 books, but in another way. He calls the first the book of Governance, the second of Judgment, the third of Life, and the fourth the book of death or damnation. But since we are to form a special question about this last one below, we wish our ἐπίνεψσιν [consideration] to be deferred until then.

IV. But briefly we answer the proposed ῥήτημα [proposition]: It is not asked how many books can be attributed to God, but how many Scripture attributes. For since various things fall under divine knowledge, various books of it can be marked, if we wish to distinguish all objects: But because in such abstruse questions it is safest to follow both the mind and the voice of Scripture, we count primarily three books of God, which are all expressly named in the sacred writings. The first we call the book of προνοίας or providence: The second of κρίσεως or judgment: The third of ζωῆς, or life.

V. Euthymius reviews this, although with the order slightly changed, upon Psalm 68 and 138, whose words, since they explain the matter quite clearly, we have thought should be added. There is, he says, a triple book of divine knowledge. And one indeed is more universal, in which all, as well the just as the sinners who are to come into this mortal life and afterwards die, are written. The other book of God's knowledge is more private, in which only the just are written, whom also alone God is said to know, namely by the knowledge of approbation. The third book is that in which sinners are written, concerning which book Daniel wrote in the seventh chapter, The judgment sat, and the books were opened. But thus Euthymius described the books of God, of which, so that the knowledge may be a little fuller, we shall add something concerning each one in particular.

VI. THE BOOK OF PROVIDENCE is universal, and contains all creatures inscribed, and so it is nothing other than the most present knowledge of created things, joined with the omnipotent conservation and governance of them. It is called by another name the Book of the governance of the World, the Book of all creatures, or the Book of universal governance. David treats of it in Psalm 139, verse 16, where he speaks thus concerning the providence of God: Your eyes saw my unformed substance, and in your book all shall be written; days shall be formed, and not one among them. Thus indeed the Vulgate edition has it, from the version of the LXX, Ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον σὲ πάντες γραφήσονται, etc. But from the Hebrew, Zanchius rendered the sense thus in book 5, de N.D. c. 3. q. 1. page 759: O God, my unformed mass (when, namely, I was not yet fully formed in my mother's womb) your eyes saw, and in your book (of eternal namely of foreknowledge and providence) all (that is to say, men) were written down, when the days were being formed; (or from the beginning of the World) and not even one was among them, that is, when as yet no one lived or existed. Arias Montanus, looking to the members of the body, translated it thus: In thy book were written, which were formed by days: Luther explains it concerning the days. All days were written in thy book, which were yet to be, and not one of them was there. However that may be, it is certain that the discourse there is concerning the providence of God; whence it follows that by that book nothing else is denoted than the universal knowledge of God, according to which he most certainly foreknows, forms, and directs all the members of all men and all days.

VII. But besides that passage of the Old Testament, some, for the sake of confirming the book of Providence, allege chapter 5 of the Apocalypse, whose first verse reads thus: And I saw in the right hand of him that sat upon the throne a Book written within and without, sealed with seven seals. A question arises here, whether by the βιβλίον seen in the right hand of God, the book of universal Government, or some other, is to be understood? Various opinions, however, are found among the Interpreters, which we shall note in a few words.

IIX. 1. The common exposition is that by this book the holy Scripture is denoted. For thus Augustine writes in Hom. 4. By the book written within and without, both Testaments are understood. From without, the old; from within, the new, which lay hidden within the old: Sealed, that is, obscured by the entire fullness of mysteries, which remained sealed until the passion and resurrection of Christ. Origen establishes the same in Hom. 12 on Exodus and Hom. 14 on Ezekiel; Hilary in the prologue on the Psalms; Eusebius of Caesarea in book 8 of the Evangelical Demonstration, chapter 2; Jerome in chapter 22 of Isaiah; whom Barradius follows in book 9 of the Concordance of the Gospels, p. 12. They say this book is in the right hand of God, because the spiritual good, which is contained in the sacred letters, is hidden from the evil, who are on the left; but is opened to the good, who are on the right. The writing within and without they explain, either concerning a double sense, literal and mystical: or concerning a double Testament, from which the old was written without, the new lay hidden within through mystery: or concerning a double instruction, both of the simpler, which is exterior and easy, and of the more perfect, which is recondite and difficult: or finally concerning a double respect of Scripture, which is either of external preaching, common to the pious and the impious, or of internal fructification and gracious sealing, which befalls only the pious and believers. But by the seven Seals, by which that book is said to be sealed, some think the principal mysteries concerning Christ, lying hidden in the Scriptures, are indicated, namely 1. Prophecies concerning the Messiah. 2. Types. 3. Promises. 4. The mystery of the Trinity. 5. The twofold advent of Christ. 6. The abrogation of the Priesthood. 7. The rejection of the Jews and the universal calling of the Gentiles. Others, among whom is Hugo the Cardinal, understand seven kinds of obscurities, and recount them thus: 1. The profundity of the sentences. 2. The multiplicity of the senses. 3. The variety of the figures. 4. The incomprehensibility of the things themselves. 5. The absurdity of the mysteries. 6. The sweetness of the tropologies. 7. The infallible truth, yet without the evidence of the sayings.

IX. But two things stand in the way, so that we cannot approve this opinion in all respects. 1. The scope of the Apostle, which is to announce the future state of the Church. For in chapter 4, verse 1, it is said to him, Come up hither, and I will show you what must happen after these things. And immediately in chapter 5 is the beginning of this revelation, while the sealed book is proposed, containing things done for the Church. Now how will it square with this scope, if that book is taken concerning the Old Testament? For its principal prophecies were fulfilled through the advent and passion of Christ, and the things predicted there were, in the time of John, not future, but rather past. Add that that book is shown to John as a thing entirely new, unknown, and not previously seen, which cannot be affirmed of the writings of the Prophets, since they are Apo stolic, as he knew very well. 2. The abuse of the Romanists. For by that interpretation they cloak the supreme obscurity of Scripture, which they always have in their mouths. From this, says Viega in c. 5 of the Apocalypse, sect. 1, p. 235, is sufficiently proven the incredible insanity of the heretics (he himself honors us with this title, the most heretical one), saying that Holy Scripture is most easy, and its own interpreter, and does not need a teacher, since no one was found, either in heaven or on earth, who could open this book sealed with seven seals. But he viciously cites our opinion. It is not that Scripture is in every part most easy, nor that it does not need a teacher, but we distinguish between dogmas of faith and prophecies about future events. These are for the most part obscure; those, if not in one place, are nevertheless clearly set forth in others, so that a devout and attentive reader may perceive the sense of the Holy Spirit, and does not need to rely on the judgment of the Pope or another. For to this end it was given, that the way of salvation might be learned from it. Either, therefore, God is frustrated of His end, or Scripture must be perspicuous, and easy to understand in matters of faith, to which point Lactantius looks in book 6 of the true worship of God, c. 21: 'Can God, the artificer of mind, voice, and tongue, not speak clearly?' Indeed, with supreme providence He wished that which is divine to be free from pretense, so that all might understand what He Himself spoke to all. Meanwhile, we do not deny that many things occur in the Scriptures that are δυσνόητα, and difficult to understand, such as Peter affirms are found even in the Pauline epistles, 2 epist. 3, verse 16. in respect of which Scripture is often compared by the Fathers to a sealed book: yet for those reasons, all perspicuity ought by no means to be denied. For it is not permitted to argue from one part to the whole. Some things are obscure, but not all. For the Holy Spirit so modified the Holy Scriptures that He might provide for hunger with more open passages, but wipe away disdain with more obscure ones, as Augustine says in book 2 of Christian Doctrine, c. 6.

Latin:

I. Cùm Liber Dei sit scientia Dei, & verò hæc cùm ἁγίᾳ diuinâ reciprocefur, adeóque simplicissima, & numero vna sit, vtique etiam librum Dei in se & essentialiter consideratum, non nisi vnum esse consequitur. Quia verò res vel obiecta, quæ à Deo cognoscuntur, & libro diuino inscribuntur, non vnius sed diuersi generis sunt, fit inde vt diuersi etiam libri Deo tribuantur, ob dictam obiectorum varietatem.

II. Discrepant autem Scriptores in recensendis Dei libris. Polanus lib. 2. Synt. Theol. c. 35. colomn. 1252. quatuor βίβλους enumerat. 1. Librum Prouidentiæ, quem vicissim diuidit in librum Mundi, in quo omnium creaturarum gubernatio annotata exstet: Et librum Ecclesiæ, qui fideles & euentus sacros attineat. 2. Librum Scripturæ, 3. Librum Iudicij diuini. 4. Librum vitæ. Sed malè immiscuit Scripturæ librum vel codicem sacrum. Hic enim quamuis Dei liber appellari queat, & eius expressa mentio fiat Esa. 34, v. 16. Quærite in Libro Dei & legite: libris tamen metaphoricis, pro notitia Dei sumptis, de quibus ibi Polanus disserit, minùs rectè accensetur. Nam codex Biblicus propriè liber est, non per metaphoram, ideóque ad præsentem quæstionem nou pertinet.

III. Alij (quibus fauere videtur Franc. Suaretz in 1. Thomæ tract. 2. li. 1. c. 20.) itidem 4. libros commemorant sed alio modo. Primùm Gubernationis, Secundum Iudicij, Tertium Vitæ, Quartum mortis vel damnationis librum nuncupat. Verùm de hoc vltimo cùm peculiarem infrà quæstionem formaturi simus, nostram eò ἐπίνεψσιν dilatam volumus.

IV. Breuiter autẽ ad ῥήτημα propositum respondemus: Non quæri quot libri Deo tribui queant, sed quot Scriptura tribuat. Nam cùm varia cadant sub diuinam notitiam, varij possunt codices ipsius signari, si obiecta omnia velimus distinguere: Quia verò in abstrusis huiusmodi quæstionibus, & menteni & vocem Scripturæ sequi tutissimum est, tres inprimis libros Dei numeramus, qui omnes expressè in sacris literis nominantur. Primum προνοίας seu prouidentiæ: Secundum κρίσεως vel iudicij: Tertium ζωῆς, vel vitæ librum dicimus.

V. Recenset hoc Euthymius, quamuis ordine paululum mutato, super Psal. 68. & 138. cuius verba, cùm rem satis luculenter explicent, adscribenda duximus. Est, inquit, triplex diuinæ scientiæ liber. Et vnus quidem magis est vniuersalis, in quo omnes tam iusti, quam peccatores in hanc mortalem vitam venturi, & postea morituri scribuntur. Alter liber scientiæ Dei est magis priuatus, in quo soli iusti scribuntur, quos etiam solos Deus nosse dicitur, scilicet cognitione approbationis. Tertius liber est, in quo peccatores scribuntur, de quo libro capite septimo scripsit Daniel, Iudicium sedit, & libri aperti sunt. At ita Euthymius libros Dei descripsit, quorum cognitio vt paulò sit plenior, de singulis aliquid in specie subiungemus.

VI I. LIBER PROVIDENTIÆ vniuersalis est, & omnes creaturas adscriptas continet adeòq; nihil est aliud, quam præsentissima rerum creatarum notitia, cùm omnipotenti earum conseruatione & gubernatione eon iuncta. Vocatur alio nomine L. regiminis Mundi, L. omnium creaturarum, vel L. vniuersalis gubernationis. Agit de illo Dauid Ps. 139. vers. 16. vbi de prouidentia Dei sic loquitur: Imperfectum meum viderunt oculi tui, & in l. tuo omnes scribentur; dies formabuntur, & nem in eis. Sic quidem vulgata editio habet, ex versione LXX. Ἐπὶ τὸ βιβλίον σὲ πάντες γραφήσονται, &c. Sed ex Hebræo sensum ita reddidit Zanchius lib. 5. de N.D. c. 3. q. 1. pag. 759. O Deus informem massam meam, (cùm scilicet in vtero matris nondum plenè formatus essem) viderunt oculi tui, & in libro tuo (· æternæ videlicet præscientiæ & prouidentiæ) omnes (nihirum homines) conscripti erant, cùm dies formarentur; (seu ab initio Mundi) & ne vnus quidem in eis esset, hoc est, cùm adhuc nemo viueret aut existeret. Ariamontanus ad mèbra corporis respiciens ita vertit: In libro tuo scripta erant, quæ per dies formata sunt: Lutherus de diebus exponit. Alle Tage waren auff dein Buch geschrieben / die noch werden solten/ vnnd derselbigen keiner da war. Vtut verò sit, certum est, de prouidentia Dei sermonem ibi fieri; vndè sequitur, per librum illum nil aliud denotari, quàm vniuersalem Dei notitiam, secundum quam omnia omnium hominum membra & dies omnes certissimè præscit, format & dirigit:

VII. Præter istum verò Testamenti veteris locum, nonnulli pro confirmando Prouidentiæ libro allegant cap. 5. Apocalypseos cuius primus vers. ita habet: Et vidi in dextera sedentis super thronum Librum intus & foris signatum sigillis septem. Oritur hîc quæstio, Num per βιβλίον in dextra Dei visum, Liber vniuersalis Gubernationis, vel alius quis intelligatur? Opiniones autem variæ apud Interpretes inueniuntur, quas paucis annotabimus.

IIX. 1. Vulgata expositio est, per librum istum Scripturam sacram denotari. Sic enim Augustinus scribit Hom. 4. Per librum intus & foris scriptum, vtrumque Testamentum intelligitur. A foris, vetus, ab intus, novum, quod intra vetus latebat: Signatum, id est, omni mysteriorum plenitudine obscuratum, quod vsque ad passionem & resurrectionē Christi mansit signatum, Idem statuunt Origenes Hom. 12. sup Exod. & Hom. 14. sup Ezech. Hilarius in prol. super Psalmos. Eusebius Cæsar. lib. 8. demonstr. Euang. cap. 2. Hieronymus in cap. 22. Esa. quos sequitur Barradius libr. Conc. Euang. cap. 9. p. 12. Librum hunc in dextera Dei dicunt esse, quia bonum spirituale, quod in sacris literis cōtinetur, malis, qui sunt ad sinistram, absconditur; bonis verò, qui sunt ad dextram aperitur. Scriptionem intus & foris exponunt, vel de duplici sensu, literali & mystico: vel de duplici Testamento, ex quibus antiquum foris scriptum fuit, novum intus per mysterium latuit: vel de duplici informatione, tum simpliciorum, quæ exterior & facilis, tùm perfectiorum, quæ recondita & difficilis: vel tandem de duplici Scripturæ respectu, qui est vel externæ prædicationis, pijs impijsque communis, vel internæ fructificationis & gratiosæ obsignationis, quæ solis pijs ac credentibus obtingit. Per septem verò Sigilla, quibus liber ille obsignatus dicitur, quidam præcipua de Christo mysteria, in Scripturis latentia, indicari putant, nempè 1. Vaticinia de Messia. 2. Typos 3. Promissiones. 4. Mysterium Trinitatis. 5. Geminum Christi aduentum. 6. Sacerdotij abrogationem. 7. Iudæorum reiectionem & vniversalem gentium vocationem. Alij, quos inter Hugo Cardinalis, septem obscuritatum genera intelligunt, & ita recensent. 1. Sententiarum profunditas. 2. Sensuum multiplicitas. 3. Figurarum varietas. 4. Rerum ipsarum incomprehensibilitas. 5. Mysteriorum abfurditas 6 Tropologiarum suauitas. 7. Infallibilis veritas, attamen absque dictorum euidentia.

IX. Verùm duo obstant, quò minus hanc per omnia sententiam adprobare possimus. 1. Apostoliscopus, qui est futurum Ecclesiæ statum prænunciare. Nam cap. 4. vers. 1. dicitur ipsi, Adscende huc, & ostendam tibi quæ oportet fieri post hæc Et statim cap. 5 sit initium huius reuelationis, dum liber signatus proponitur, Ecclesiæ facta continens. Iam quomodo quadrabit cum hoc scopo, si de Vet. Testamento liber ille accipiatur? Eius enim vaticinia præcipua per Christi aduentum & passionem impleta, & res ibi prædictæ Iohannis tempore non futuræ, sed potius præteritæ erant. Adde, quod liber ille Iohannis tanquam res planè noua, incognita, nec prius visa ostendatur, id quod de Prophetarum scriptis, quippè quæ Apostol. optimè noverat, affirmari nequit. 2. Romanensium abusus. Illâ enim interpretatione palliant summam, quâ semper in ore habẽt, Scripturæ obscuritatem, Ex hoc inq̃t Viega in c. 5. Apoc. sect. 1. p. 235. satis evincitur incredibilis hæreticorum (hoc titulo honorat nos ipse hæreticissimꝰ) insania, aientıũ, Scripturam sacram facilimã esse, ac sui ipsius interpretem, neque doctore indigere, cùm librum hunc septem signatum sigillis, nullus præter agnum inuentus fuerit, siue in cælo siue in terra, qui potuerit aperire. Sed vitiosè citat nostram sententiam. Non ea est, quòd Scriptura sit ex omni parte facillima, nec indigeat doctore, sed distinguimus inter dogmata fidei, & vaticinia de futuris. Hæc plerumque obscura sunt, illa, si maximè non in vno, in alijs tamen locis manifestè proponuntur, vt lector deuotus & attentus sensum Spiritus Sancti percipere possit, nec iudicio Papæ vel alterius stare necessum habeat. In hunc enim finem data est, vt salutis via inde addiscatur. Aut igitur fine suo frustratus est Deus, aut Scripturam oportet esse perspicuam, & in rebus fidei intellectu facilem, quò spectat istud Lactantij lib. 6. de vero Dei cultu, c. 21. Num Deus & mentis, & vocis, & linguæ artifex, disertè loqui non potest? Imò verò summâ prouidentia fuco carere voluit, quæ diuina sunt, vt omnes intelligerent quæ ipse omnibus loquebatur. Interim non diffitemur, multa in Scripturis occurrere dusnó- ητα, & intellectu difficilia, qualia in Paulinis etiam epistolis reperiri Petrus affirmat 2. epist. 3. vers. 16. quorum respectu à Patribus Scriptura sæpè libro signato comparatur: Ob ea tamen omnis perspicuitas negari minimè debet. Ab vna enim parte ad totum nõ licet argumentari. Quædam sunt obscura, sed non omnia. Spiritus enim sanctus ita Scripturas sacras modificauit, vt locis apertioribus fami occurreret, obscurioribus autẽ fastidia abstergeret, dicente Augustino lib. 2. de doct. Christ. c. 6.


### Question II. III. Others (whom Franc. Suarez seems to favor in 1: X. 2. Others interpret this book as being about…

X. 2. Others interpret this book as being about Christ, as Bernard does in his homily on the seven seals for the feast of Easter, where he wishes the seven seals to be the seven mysteries of our redemption, hidden in legal ceremonies and figures. The first for them is the Incarnation. 2. The Nativity. 3. The Passion. 4. The Resurrection. 5. The Ascension. 6. The Mission of the Holy Spirit. 7. The Advent to judgment. Bernard, however, understands by those seals the concealment of divinity made at the time of his vanishing, and refers to it: 1. The betrothal of Mary. 2. The infirmity of the body. 3. The Circumcision. 4. The flight into Egypt. 5. The temptation of Satan. 6. The Cross. 7. The Burial, through which he affirms the mystical book, namely Christ, to be entirely closed and hidden. Others say that this book was opened and extended on the cross, so that all might read in it the examples of the greatest virtues and understand the power of divine love. That it was written within and without: within indeed through love and sorrow, but without through the wounds and the opening of the side.

XI. But neither does this exposition seem sufficiently convenient. For 1. Christ opened this book, and loosened its seals, v. 5, 6. Who therefore can himself be understood by the book? For thus the book and the Lamb receiving the book would be confused. 2. The opening of the seals denotes future things, and the sad state of the Church. But indeed, the mysteries of redemption, just mentioned, were accomplished in the time of John. Therefore, those things are not prefigured by the seven seals.

XII. 3. Lyranus and others explain it concerning the book of divine providence, and they judge that by it are primarily denoted the secret counsels of God concerning the government and state of the Church. God has this book at his right hand, because the method of government is always at hand, and the right hand signifies strength, and is considered a symbol of better action, since movement is made from the right, and there is more strength in it than in the left. Furthermore, this book is said to be written within and without, either because it comprehends various and manifold things, and all things fall under the command of God; or because some things concerning the wonderful government of the world are known, while some are entirely secret, and these are said to be written inside, as those are outside. He is called signed, who contains the hidden judgments of God, transcending human reason. He is called sealed, because those things which ought to remain secret, or to have public authority, are accustomed to be fortified with a seal. There are, however, seven seals, a perfect number, to indicate the perfection of divine providence and the hidden reason of its governance.

XIII. This interpretation approaches the scope of the Apostle as closely as possible and responds sufficiently to the context. For because through the opening of this book and its seals, performed by the Lamb, the admirable judgments of God and the punishments of the impious were revealed to John, and it follows that these very things had been noted in that book, and thus it was nothing other than the sealing of divine counsels, which, like a book, were sealed and closed, but were shown and demonstrated to the Apostle when Christ opened them: the celebrated theologian Dn. D. Hoë approves this exposition in his most absolute commentary on the Apocalypse, Vol. 2, p. 140.

XIV. 4. There are finally others who interpret the book as the Apocalypse of John itself. For it is beyond controversy that the Apostle truly saw a certain book. But that imaginary book contained mysteries subsequently revealed, since the seven seals of the book are nothing other than the seven principal visions of the ἀποκαλύψεως. For as often as a new seal is opened, so often is a new mystery unfolded, and thus, what the Apostle wrote in his Apocalypse, he first learned and heard from that book, opened in heaven and shown through a vision.

XV. Therefore, to conclude, we judge that both of the latter expositions can be joined, in such a way that it is established that John truly saw some book in heaven, containing those Apocalypses which he subsequently wrote. It was, however, without doubt not some thick and material book, but an imaginary one, because a vision, not a history, is being narrated. That book itself was, as it were, a copy of the book of providence. For whatever God had established within in His secret counsel, and whatever He had decreed concerning the future state of the Church, all that the book shown in the vision contained, and it was revealed through Christ opening it. We say, therefore, most briefly, that the book seen by John was both an imaginary and prefigured ἀποκάλυψιν, and a copy and special expression of the book of providence.

XXI. II. The Book of Judgment, subordinate to the former and a little more restricted, which concerns not all creatures, but only men to be judged. This book is brought forth in two places of Scripture. The one exists in Dan. 7. v. 9. & 10. 'I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the judgment sat וספרין פתיחו καὶ βίβλοι ἀνεῴχθησαν, and the books were opened.' The other is a παράλληλος, and is read in Apoc. 20. v. 12. 'And I saw the dead, small and great, stand before God; καὶ βίβλια ἠνεῳχθήσαν, and the books were opened: and another book was opened, which is the book of life: and the dead were judged out of those things which were written in the books, according to their works.' But what is understood by these books of judgment is not the opinion of all; we shall touch upon the principal ones in the following.

XVII 1. Bede explains it concerning the book of Scripture, which he says will be opened at the final judgment, which will then be manifest, that the things which the sacred letter had taught us concerning that judgment were most true. But we know nothing about the reservation of any material book, since fire is to devour all things on the last day. Judgment will indeed be made according to the Scriptures, if indeed the Savior expressly says in John 12. verse 48, 'The word that I have spoken, the same shall judge him in the last day.' But that Christ will produce a certain Biblical codex, and from that opened book will pronounce sentence, cannot be proven, and it has more the appearance of an old woman's fable than of truth. But if it be said that the Biblical books are opened in judgment, not indeed visibly, but insofar as the sentence is passed from their meaning; yet it seems to stand in the way. 1. That the works of individuals are not annotated in the scriptures, which nevertheless is tacitly affirmed concerning those books of judgment. 2. That they are called books in that sense in which the book of life is spoken of. For the Apostle immediately subjoins a mention of this. But the book of life denotes not a Scripture outside of God, but something in God. Therefore also the books of judgment, especially since these are distinguished from the book of life, which could not happen if Scripture were denoted by them.

XVIII. 2. Augustine, in book 20 of The City of God, chapter 14, understands by the opened books the saints who are to come with Christ to judgment, whom he therefore thinks are called books because in them the will of God and the observance of the divine law will be known as expressed. They are to be understood, he says, as the saints, both of the old and new [covenants], so that in them it might be shown what God had commanded to be done through his mandates. He thinks that the dead are to be judged according to them, both because the saints will judge this world, 1 Cor. 6:2, and because the life of the saints will be as it were a judgment and condemnation of the wicked. But this interpretation seems too remote, less congruent with Scripture, and indeed more ingenious than probable.

For where are the saints called books of judgment, and indeed such books in which the works of others are described as existing? How will the saints be opened in judging, which is asserted of those books? And will not the saints themselves receive the testimony of their holiness and innocence from the books of judgment? If, therefore, by these βιβλία the ones to be saved are understood, then the books and those to be judged from the books are confounded, which two things, however, must necessarily be distinguished, as both the coherence of the text proves and right reason persuades.

XIX. 3. Jerome, in chapter 7 of Daniel, maintains that the consciences of men are denoted. The books, he says, are opened, and the consciences and works of individuals, whether good or evil, are revealed to all in both directions. That good book is the one which we often read, the book of the living. The bad book is the one which is held in the hand of the accuser, which is the enemy and avenger. Sebastian Barradius follows this opinion of Jerome. Vol. 3, Commentary on the Gospels, book 9, chapter 18, p. 694. But the book of conscience is rather of the consciences of men than of God. The book of life contains not so much our works as God's counsels concerning salvation. If a bad book is in the hand of an accuser, it ought to be called the book of the devil rather than of God. All of which moves us, so that we are not able to simply approve of that exposition of Jerome.

XX. 4. Maldonatus on chapter 7 of Daniel, p. 688, judges that neither the Scriptures nor the consciences of men are understood, but the objections of accusers and the responses of defending patrons. For he affirms that three kinds of books are given in the divine judgment. The first to him is that of the accusing angels or demons. The second, of the defending angels. The third, the book of life, from which the judge in a certain way brings forth the sentence. Therefore, he renders the sense of Daniel thus: The Prophet indicates that in the divine judgment, with the Angels standing by, there was a dispute concerning the fourth beast and its eleventh horn, that is, concerning the Human empire and the Antichrist, and that the books of both the accusers and the defenders were opened, that is, the reasons were set forth on both sides. This interpretation, although it may seem specious, will nevertheless hardly be able to be sufficiently proven. For by the customary phrase of Scripture, books are attributed not to good Angels or devils, but rather to God. Wherefore also those [words] 'were opened in the judgment of God' ought to be explained in such a way that they are understood of God, not of angels. Furthermore, those things which were brought forth from those books had already been noted before. For to open a book is to read through its contents. But shall we think that the reasons of the accusing and defending Angels were already recorded in a certain book before, and were not first proposed and ventilated in the judgment? Add that, while that ἐξηγήσει stands, the books of judgment from which men were judged cannot be spoken of. For reasons on both sides do not speak, but render the decision doubtful.

XXI. Thus, therefore, with foreign expositions removed, the opinion of those pleases us who interpret the books of judgment as concerning the divine knowledge and that of all words and human deeds. For God sees all thoughts and acts, and knows all our words; and since these are always most present to Him, hence He is said ἀνθρωποπαθῶς to have them recorded in a certain book. And since everyone will be judged according to his works, from this it came about that that deeds of men will be read out as if from a book, and will be recalled to our memory, so that the damned may understand that they have been consigned to eternal punishments by judgment.

XXII. Moreover, Scripture uses the plural number, and calls them not a book, but books, not with regard to the divine mind or knowledge, which is most simple, but with regard to the diversity of the objects and things in Scripture. For which reason Jerome rightly established a double book of judgment: one of the believers, the other of the impenitent. In the former, the good works of the pious are recorded; in the latter, the evil works of the impious exist. And from these two books the dead will be judged, so that the evil may be condemned on account of their sins; the good may be saved, not indeed on account of their works, but according to them, insofar as they are a testimony of true faith and sincere repentance.

XXIII. Franciscus Suarez in 1. Th. Tract. 2 lib. 1. c. 20. p. 209. l. A. likewise enumerates two books of judgment, but describes them differently.
