For he asserts that one contains deeds, the other law. God, he says, in His eternity first according to reason described the law, by assessing rewards and punishments for works. Then in another sign He had beforehand in His knowledge the future works and deeds of individuals. Therefore these two books are to be opened in judgment, so that the deed may be proven from one, and the law may be pronounced from the other. But Suarez deceives and is deceived, while he fabricates a peculiar code of written law. For the law is contained in no other book than the Biblical one. For what God decreed from eternity concerning the salvation and damnation of men, this He revealed in time through His word. That alone is the rule of law. divine; the sum of which is read in John 3, v. last: He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is incredulous to the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Therefore, there is no need for another book of law to be fabricated besides Scripture, but that one suffices for passing judgment upon men. For the entire judicial process will be completed by two syllogisms. The former will open the gate of heaven: Whoever has believed shall be saved; You standing on the right have believed; Therefore you shall be saved. The latter will open the prison of hell: Whoever has been unfaithful and impenitent shall be condemned; You on the left have been such; therefore you shall be condemned. In these syllogisms, the Biblical codex always provides the major premise. The minor premise, however, is derived and proven from the books of judgment, in which our deeds are recorded, whence it is clear that the book of divine law is not other than the Scriptures, and therefore if anyone claims that the whole process is denoted by the book of judgment, he can join both: the Biblical book, from which the major premise is formed, and the metaphorical books, written by God, and indices of the good and the bad, from which the minor premise is proven, since they convict the incredulous and hold them guilty of fault, and therefore they are usually called specifically βιβλία κρίματος.

Latin:

X. 2. Alij librum istum de Christo interpretantur, vt Bernhardus hom. de septem signaculis in festo Pasch. eiusq́; septem sigilla quidem esse volunt septem nostræ redemptionis mysteria, in ceremoniis & figuris legalibus abscondita. Primum ipsis est Incarnatio. 2. Natiuitas. 3. Passio. 4. Resurrectio. 5. Ascensio. 6 Missio Spiritus S. 7. Aduentus ad iudicium. Bernhardus vero per sigilla ista diuinitatis occultationē tempore euanitionis factā intelligit, eóq; refert 1. Mariæ desponsationem. 2. Corporis infirmitatem. 3. Circumcisionem, 4. Fugam in Ægyptum. 5. Tentationē Satanæ. 6. Crucem. 7. Sepulturam, per q̃ lib. mysticum, nempè Christum, prorsus clausum & occultatū esse affirmat. Alij eum librum in cruce apertū & extensum fuisse dicunt, vt omnes in eo maximarum virtutū exempla perlegerent & diuini amoris vim intelligerent. Scriptum esse intus & foris: intus quidē per amorem & dolorem, foris autem per vulnera & apertionē lateris.

XI. Sed neque hæc expositio satis videtur commoda. Nam 1. Christus aperuit librum istum, & sigilla eius soluit, v. 5. 6. Qui ergo ipse per librum potest intelligi? Ita enim confunderetur liber, & agnus librum accipiens, 2. Apertio sigillorum res futuras denotat, & tristem Ecclesiæ statum. At verò mysteria redemptionis, modò commemorata, Iohannis tempore peracta fuerunt. Ista ergo per sigilla septem non præfigurantur.

XII. 3. Lyranus & alij de libro prouidentiæ diuinæ exponunt, & per illum imprimis arcana Dei consilia de regimine & statu Ecclesiæ denotari censent. Addexteram Deus hunc librum habet, quia gubernationis ratio semper in promptu est, & dextra robur significat, ac melioris actionis symbolū putatur, cùm motus à dextris fiat, & in illa plus roboris sit, quàm in sinistra. Dicitur porrò hîc liber intus & foris scriptus, vel quia res varias & multiplices comprehendit, omniaq; sub imperium Dei cadunt; vel quia quædam de mirāda mundi gubernatione cognita, quædam prorsus arcana sunt, & hęc intus, vt illa foris, scripta dicuntur. Signatus est, qui occulta Dei judicia, hominis rationem transcendentia continet. Sigillatus dicitur, quia illa, quæ arcana manere, vel auctoritatem publicam habere debent, sigillo muniri solent. Septem autem sigilla sunt, numero perfecto, ad indicãdam diuinæ prouidentiæ perfectionem & gubernationis reconditam rationem.

XIII. Interpretatio hæc quàm proximè ad scopum Apostoli accedit & contextui satis respondet. Quia enim per apertionem libri huius & sigillorum eius ab agno factam, admiranda Dei judicia & impiorum supplicia Iohanni reuelata sunt, vtque hæc ipsa in libro illo annotata fuisse consequitur, adeoque nihil fuit aliud, quam consignatio diuinorum consiliorum, quæ libri instar obsignata & clausa, Apostolo autem Christo aperiente fuerunt ostensa & demonstrata: Expositionem hãc adprobat Theologus celeberrimˣ Dn. D. Hoë in absolutissimo suo super Apoc. cōment. T. 2. p. 140.

XIV. 4. Sunt tandem alij, qui librum de ipsâ Iohannis Apocalypsi interpretantur. Apostolum enim verè librum quendam vidisse extra controuersiam est. Liber a. iste imaginarius continuit mysteria postmodum patefacta, siquidem septem sigilla libri nihil sunt aliud, quàm septem præcipuæ visiones ἀποκαλύψεως. Quoties enim sigillum novum aperitur, toties mysterium novum panditur, atque sic, quæ Apostolus in sua Apocalypsi scripsit, ex libro isto, in cælis aperto ac per visionem ostento prius didicit & audiuit.

XV. Proinde vt concludamus, vtramque posterioriorum expositionem coniungi posse censemus, ita quidem vt statuatur, Iohannem verè aliquem librum in cœlis vidisse, Apocalypses istas, quas postmodum scripsit comprehendentem. Fuit autem procul dubio non crassus aliquis & materialis liber, sed imaginarius, quia visio, non historia narratur. Ille veto ipse liber una quasi exemplar fuit libri providentiae. Quod enim Deus in arcano consilio suo intus statuerat, & quod de futuro Ecclesiae statu decreverat, istud omne liber in visione ostensus continuit, & per Christum aperientem revelatum fuit. Brevissime ergo dicimus, Librum a Iohanne visum, fuisse tum imaginariam & praefiguratam ἀποκάλυψιν, tum exemplar & specialem Libri providentiae expressionem.

XXI. II. Liber Ivdicii Priori subordinatus & paulo restrictior, qui non creaturas omnes, sed tantum homines judicandos attinet. Proditur hic liber in duobus Scripturae locis. Alter exstat Dan. 7. v. 9. & 10. Adspiciebam donec throni positi sunt, & judicium sedit וספרין פתיחו καὶ βίβλοι ἀνεῴχθησαν, & libri aperti sunt. Alter est παράλληλος, & legitur Apoc. 10. v. 12. Et vidi mortuos magnos & pusillos stantes in conspectu throni, καὶ βίβλια ἠνεῳχθήσαν, & libri aperti sunt mortui ex his, quae scripta erant in libris secundum opera ipforum. Quid vero per hos judicij libb. intelligatur non eadem est omnium sententia: praecipuas sequentibus attingemus.

XVII 1. Beda exponit de libro Scripturae, quem in extremo judicio apertum iri ait, qui tunc patebit, verissima fuisse, qui nos de illo judicio sacra litera docuerat. Verum nihil scimus de reservatione alicujus libri materialis, cum ignis in die ultimo devoraturus sit omnia. Fiet quidem judiciu secundum Scripturas, si quidem Servator expresse ait Ioh. 12. vers. 48. Sermo, quem locutus sum, ille indicabit in novissimo die. Quod autem Christus codicem quendam Biblicum sit producturus, & ex illo aperto sententiam dicturus, probari nequit, & potius speciem habet anilis figmenti, quam veritatis. Quod si vero dicatur, libros Biblicos in judicio aperiri, non quidem visibiliter, sed quatenus ex illorum sensu fertur sententia; obstare tamen videtur. 1. Quod in scripturis singulorum opera non sint annotata, quod tamen de libris illis judicii tacite affirmatur. 2. Quòd illo sensu libri nuncupentur, quo liber vitæ dicitur. Huius enim mentionem subjicit statim Apostol. Atqui liber vitæ non Scripturam extra Deum, sed quiddam in Deo notat. Ergo & libri judicii, præsertim cùm hi à libro vitæ distinguantur, quod fieri non posset, si per illos Scriptura notaretur.

XIIX. 2. Augustinus lib. 20. de Civ. D. c. 14. per libros apertos intelligit sanctos, qui cum Christo venturi sunt ad judicium, quos propterea existimat appellari libros, quia in illis expressa cognoscetur Dei voluntas, & diuinæ legis obseruantia. Intelligendi sunt inquit, sancti & veteres & novi, ut in illis ostenderetur, quæ Deus fieri per sua mandata iussisset. Secundum eos autem judicandos esse mortuos existimat, tum quia sancti de hoc mundo judicabunt, 1. Cor. 6. v. 2. tum quia sanctorum vita quasi quoddam erit judicium & condemnatio improborum. Sed interpretatio hæc nimis remota, Scripturæ minus congrua, imo ingeniosa magis quàm verisimilis, videtur.

Ubi enim sancti dicuntur libri judicij, & quidem tales libri inquibus aliorum opera descripta extent? Quomodo in iudicando aperientur sancti, quo de libris istis asseritur? Et annon sancti ipsi ex libris judicij accipient suæ sanctitatis & innocētiæ testimonium? Si ergo per ista βιβλία intelligantur saluandi, tum confunduntur libri, & judicandi ex libris, quæ duo tamē necessario distinguenda esse, & textus cohærentia euincit, recta ratio persuadet.

XIX. 3. Hieronymus in cap. 7. Dan. conscientias hominum notari autumat. Libri inquit, aperti sunt conscientiæ & opera singulorum in vtramque partem vel bona vel mala omnibus reuelantur. Bonus liber ille est, quem sæpè legimus, liber viuentium. Malus liber, qui in accusatoris tenetur manu, qui est inimicus & vindex. Sequitur hanc opinionem Hieronymi Seb. Baradius. Tom. 3. conc. Euang. lib. 9. cap. 18. p. 694. Verùm liber conscientiæ potius hominũ est, quàm Dei. Vitæ liber non tàm opera nostra, quàm Dei consilia de salute continet. Malus liber si in manu accusatoris sit, diaboli potius, quàm Dei liber appellari debet. Quæ omnia nos mouent, vt istam Hieronymi expositionem simpliciter adprobare haut valeamus.

XX. 4. Maldonatus in cap. 7. Dan. p. 688. neque Scripturas, neque hominum conscientias intelligi censet, sed accusatorum obiectiones, & defendentium patronorum responsiones. Tria enim librorum genera in judicio diuino dari affirmat. Primus ipsi est angelorum aut dæmonum accusantium. Secundus angelorum defendentium. Tertius liber vitæ, ex quo judex profert quodammodo sententiam. Sensum proinde Danielis sic reddit: Indicat Propheta, in diuino iudicio, adstantibus Angelis, de quarta bestia, deque eius vndecimo cornu, hoc est, de Humano imperio & Antechristo disputatum esse, librosque & accusantium & defendentium apertos fuisse, id est expositas in vtramque partem rationes. Hæc. interpretatio quamuis speciosa videatur, vix tamen sufficiëter probari poterit. Nam vsitatâ Scripturæ phrasi non Angelis bonis aut diabolis, sed Deo potius libri attribuuntur. Quare & illi in Dei judicio aperti fuisset sic explicari debent, vt de Deo, non angelis accipiantur. Præterea, quæ ex libris istis prolatą sunt, jam antè annotata fuerunt. Librum enim aperire, est contenta eius prælegere. Num autem putabimus rationes Angelorum accusantium & defendentium jam antè in libro quodam consignatas, nec primùm in judicio fuisse propositas & ventitatas? Adde quòd stante illâ ἐξηγήσει haut dici queant libri iudicii ex quibus iudicati sint homines. Rationes enim in vtramq; partem non dicunt, sed decisionem redunt dubiam.

XXI. Sic igitur remotis expositionibus peregrinis, illorum nobis placet sententia, quilibros judicij de diuina eáque omnium dictorum & factorum humanorum notitia exponunt. Deus enim videt omnes cogitationes & actus, nouitque omnes sermones nostros; quæ cùm ipsi semper sint præsentissima, hinc ἀνθρωποπαθῶς in libro quodam annotata habere dicitur. Et quoniam secundum opera sua quisque iudicabitur, inde factum est. vt illa nostrarum actionum cognitio, iudicij liber appellatus sit. Nam in extremo die facta hominum quasi è libro prælegentur, & nobis in memoriam reuocabuntur, vt damnati æternis supplicijs iudicio addictos esse intelligant.

XXII. Vtitur autem Scriptura plurali numero, nec librum, sed libros appellat, non ad diuinæ mentis aut notitiæ, quæ simplicissima est, sed ad obiectorum, rerumque in Scripturam diuersitatem intuendam. Quam ob causam Hieronymus duplicem iudicij librum rectè constituit: Alterum credentium: Alterum impœnitentium. In illo bona piorum, in hoc mala impiorum opera consignata extstant. Atque ex his duobus libris iudicabuntur mortui, vt mali damnentur propter sua peccata; boni saluentur; non quidem propter opera, sed secundum illa, quatenus testimonium sunt veræ fidei & sinceræ pœnitentiæ.

XXIII. Franciscis Suareiz in 1. Th. Tract. 2 lib. 1. c. 20. p. 209. l. A. itidem duos iudicij libros recenset, sed aliter describit. Nam alterum facta, alterum ius continere asserit. Deus, inquit, in sua æternitate prius secundum rationem ius descripsit, præmia & pœnas operum taxando Deinde in alio signo singulorum opera & facta futura in notitia sua præhabuit. Hi ergo duo libri in iudicio aperiendi sunt, vt factum ex vno probetur, ex altero ius dicatur. Sed fallit & fallitur Suaretz, dum peculiarem scripti iuris codicem confingit. Ius enim in nullo alio libro continetur, quam in Biblico, Nam quod Deus ab æterno de hominum salute & damnatione statuit, hoc in tempore per verbum suum reuelauit. Illud solum est regula iuris divini ; cuius summa legitur Iohan. 3. v. ult. Qui credit in filium, habet vitam æternam; Qui autem incredulus est filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Proinde non opus est, ut præter Scripturam alius confingatur liber iuris, sed sufficit ille ad ferendam de hominibus sententiam. Nam totus processus iudicialis duobus syllogismis absoluetur. Prior cœli ianuam aperiet: Quicunque crediderit salvus sit, Vos ad dexteram stantes credidistis, Ergo salvi sitis. Posterior inferni carcerem pandet: Quisquis infidelis & impœnitens fuit, damnabitur: Vos ad sinistram tales fuistis, ergo damnabimini. In his syllogismis maiorem semper suppeditat codex Biblicus. Minor autem desumitur & probatur ex libris iudicij, in quibus facta nostra annotata sunt, vnde patet, librum divini iuris non esse à Scripturis alium, ideoque si per librum iudicij totum processum notari quis autumet, vtrumque coniungere potest, tum librum Biblicum, ex quo formatur maior, tum libros metaphoricos, à Deo scriptos, & Bonorum malorumq; indices, ex quibus probatur minor, siquidem illi incredulos convincunt & culpæ reos agunt, Ideoque specialiter βιβλία κρίματος nuncupari solent.


### Question II. III. Others (whom Franc. Suarez seems to favor in 1: XXIV. III. What the Book of Life is will become clear from the following. Here we shall only note the principal sayings that make mention…

XXIV. III. What the BOOK OF LIFE is will become clear from the following. Here we shall only note the principal sayings that make mention of it and respond to the question: Whether it exists. Scripture, however, does not always use the same manner of speaking.

For 1. sometimes without the added word 'life', it calls it 'the book' absolutely or as it were κατ' ἐξοχὴν, as in Dan. 12, v. 1: At that time your people shall be saved, everyone who shall be found written in the book. And some refer to this that passage in Exod. 32, v. 32: If you do not do so, blot me out of the book which you have written. 2. Sometimes the word 'life' or 'of the living' is expressly added, as in Psalm 69, v. 29: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living tium; and let us not be written with the just. Phil. 4. v. 3. Whose names are in the book of life. Apoc. 3. v. 5. He that shall overcome, I will not blot out his name out of the book of life. Apoc. 17. v. 8. Whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. Apoc. 20. v. 12. Another book was opened, which is the book of Life. V. 15. Whosoever was not found written in the book of life, was cast into the pool of fire. Apoc. 22. v. 19. If any man shall take away from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part out of the book of life.

3. Sometimes a double determination is added, as Apoc. 13. v. 8. Whose names are not written in the book of life of the lamb. And c. 21. v. last. There shall not enter into it any thing defiled, but they that are written in the book of life of the lamb.

XXV. All these sayings clearly bring forward that there is a certain book of life, in which the names of those to be saved are inscribed, so that no one may become a partaker of eternal beatitude unless he be inserted into that book.

By another name it is called the writing or catalog of the house of Israel. Ezech. 13. v. 9. in which are written those who pertain to the house of Israel, namely according to the spirit, not according to the flesh.

A similar phrase exists in Luke 10. v. 20. when the Savior says: Rejoice, that your names are written in heaven.

On which passage Theophylact says: Your names were written in heaven not with ink, but by the memory of God and by grace. But concerning the impenitent it is said that they are written in the earth; as a manifest passage is had, Jer. 17. v. 13. They that depart from thee shall be written in the earth; that is, they shall not arrive at heavenly beatitude, but all their happiness shall be only earthly, and shall be extinguished by death.

Hence some think that the names of the accusers of the adulteress were written by Christ on the ground with his finger, John 8. v. 6. to indicate their injustice and condemnation: as if Christ had represented this locution by gesture and in reality.

XXVI. Besides the sayings indeed alleged for confirming the book of life, the passage of Isaiah c. 4. verse 3. is usually brought forward in addition, whose words are thus: He that shall be left in Sion, and shall remain in Jerusalem, shall be called holy, everyone who is written in life, in Jerusalem. The Prophet is not speaking there of a bodily benefit, that some of the Jews were to remain in Jerusalem, as it seems to some. For the discourse is about the advent of Christ, who is called the branch v. 1. and this name is attributed to him also c. 11 v. 1. c. 53 v. 2. and at the same time to those who have been saved, whence it is clear that the Prophet is speaking of the time of the Messiah, of the new Jerusalem, that is, the Church of the New Testament, and therefore is describing spiritual goods, of which three in particular are enumerated in order. 1. Sanctification, v. 2. He who has been left, everyone shall be called holy. Where if a temporal remaining in the city of Jerusalem is understood, it follows that all its citizens were at some time holy, which kind of time can neither be said nor proved to have ever existed. The same benefit is hinted at v. 4. through the removal of filth and the washing away of blood. 2. Election, from which flows sanctification. He describes this with a peculiar phrase, namely through the writing כתוב לחיים in lives in Jerusalem. The LXX have ἐις ζωὴν into life, the Chaldean paraphrase, To eternal life. Luther. He who is written among the living. Therefore, nothing else is noted by these words than the predestination of those to be saved, who are said to be written to obtain life in the heavenly Jerusalem, which is said elsewhere, To be written in the book of life. 3. Defense v. 5. The Lord will create over every place of Mount Zion a cloud etc. v. 6. There will be a tabernacle for a shadow by day from the heat and for security, etc. From these, therefore, it is clearly evident that the whole context deals only with spiritual benefits, for which reason that very writing to life is rightly explained as predestination and the book of life specifically so called.

XXVII. And thus it has been demonstrated so far that there is a βιβλίον ζωῆς, distinct from the book of providence and judgment. It remains now to investigate in how many ways it is spoken of, what it properly is, how the inscription is made; then who can be erased from it, and what other things pertain to this, about which we shall add some things in order.

Latin:

XXIV. III. LIBER VITAE quid sit, ex sequentibus planum fiet. Hîc tantùm præcipua dicta annotabimus, quę mentionem eius faciunt, & quæstioni An sit, respondent. Non autem eodem loquendi modo Scriptura semper vtitur.

Nam 1. interdum sine addito vitæ vocabulo ἀθετως vel absolute & quasi κατ' ἐξοχὴν librum appellat, ut Dan. 12. v. 1. In tempore illo saluabitur populus tuus omnis, qui inuentus fuerit scriptus in libro. Et huc nonnulli referunt istud Exod. 32. v. 32. Sin on facis, dele me de libro, quem scripsisti. 2. Interdum vox vitæ aut viuentium expressè adiungitur, vt Psalm. 69. v. 29. Deleantur de libro viuentium; et cum iustis non scribamur. Phil. 4. v. 3. Quorum nomina sunt in libro vitae. Apoc. 3. v. 5. Qui vicerit non delebo nomen eius de libro vitae. Apoc. 17. v. 8. Quorum nomina non sunt scripta in libro vitae a constitutione mundi. Apoc. 20. v. 12. Alius liber apertus est, qui est Vitae. V. 15. Qui non inventus est in libro vitae scriptus, missus est in stagnum ignis. Apoc. 22. v. 19. Si quis diminuerit de verbis libri Prophetiae huius, auferet Deus partem eius de libro vitae.

3. Aliquando duplex determinatio additur, ut Apoc. 13. v. 8. Quorum non sunt scripta nomina in libro vitae agni. Et c. 21. v. ult. Non intrabit aliquid coinquinatum, nisi qui scripti sunt in libro vitae agni.

XXV. Omnia haec dicta luculenter afferunt, dati quendam vitae librum, in quo salvandorum nomina sint adscripta, sic ut nemo aeternae beatitudinis fiat particeps, nisi libro isti sit insertus.

Alio nomine vocatur scriptura vel catalogus domus Israelis. Ezech. 13. v. 9. in quo scripti sunt, qui ad domum Israel pertinent, nempe secundum spiritum, non secundum carnem.

Similis phrasis exstat Luc. 10. v. 20. cum Salvator ait: Gaudete, quod nomina vestra scripta sunt in caelis.

In quem locum Theophylactus ait: τὰ ὀνόματά ὑμῶν ἐγράφη ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς οὐ μέλανι, ἀλλὰ μνήμῃ τοῦ θεοῦ χάριτι. De impoenitentibus autem dicitur, quod in terra scribantur; sicut manifestus locus habetur, Ier. 17. v. 13. Recedentes a te in terra descibentur; h. e. non pervenient ad coelestem beatitudinem, sed omnis eorum felicitas terrestris tantum erit, et morte extinguetur.

Hinc nonnulli existimant, nomina accusatorum adulterae a Christo in terra fuisse scripta digito Ioh. 8. v. 6. ad indicandam eorum iniustitiam ac damnationem: veluti si Christus hanc locutionem gestu ac reipsa repraeflisset.

XXVI. Praeter allegata vero dicta ad confirmandum vitae librum, solet insuper adduci locus Esaiae c. 4. vers. 3. cuius verba sic habent: Qui relictus fuerit in Sion, et residuus in Ierusalem, sanctus vocabitur omnis omnis, qui scriptus est in vita, in Ierusalem. Loquitur ibi Propheta nō de beneficio corporali, ķ ex Iudæis quidã mansuri sint in Ierusalem reliqui, vt nonnullis videtur. Nam sermo est de aduentu Christi, qui germen dicitur v. 1. & hoc ipsi nomen tribuitur etiã c. 11 v. 1. ca. 53. v. 2. simulq; additur, germen istud fore in magnificentia & decorū his, qui saluati fuerint, vnde perspicuum sit, de Messiæ tempore, de noua Hierosolyma, hoc est, Ecclesia N. T. Prophetam loqui, adeoque spiritualia bona describere, quorū imprimis tria recensentur ordine. 1. Sanctificatio, v. 2. Qui relictus fuerit, sanctus vocabitur omnis. Vbi si remansio temporalis in vrbe Hierosolyma intelligatur, omnes eius ciues aliquãdo sanctos fuisse sequitur, quale tempus vnquã exstitisse dici probariue neqt. Idem beneficiū innuitur v. 4. per ablationē sordium & lotionem sanguinum. 2. Electio ex quæ fluit sanctificatio. Hanc describit peculiari phrasi, nempè per scriptionem כתוב לחיים in vitis in Ierusalem. LXX. habent ἐις ζωὴν in vitam, Chaldæa paraphrasis, Ad vitam æternam. Lutherus. Der geschrieben ist vnter die Lebendigen. Notatur ergo his verbis nihil aliud, quàm prædestinatio saluandorum, qui dicuntur scripti ad vitam consequêdam in cœlesti Hierosolyma, quod alibi dicitur, Scriptum esse in libro vitæ. 3. Defensio vers. 5. Creabit Dominus super omnem locum montis Sion nubem &c. v. 6. Tabernaculum erit in vnbraculum diei ab æstu & in securitatem, &c. Ex his ergo luculenter constat, totum contextum non nisi de spiritualibus beneficiis agere, quâ de caussa & illa ipsa ad vitam scriptio de prædestinatione, & libro vitæ specialiter sic dicto rectè exponitur.

XXVII. Atque ita demonstratum est hactenus dari βιβλίον ζωῆς, à libro prouidentiæ & judicij distinctum. Restat nunc indagandum, quot modis dicatur, quid propriè sit, quomodo fiat inscriptio; tum ex illo quis deleri possit, & quę alia sunt eò spectãtia, de quib. ordine quędã subiungemus.


### Question III. Whether there is one book of life, or several?

I. Thomas Aquinas in part 1 of the Summa Theologica, question 24, article 1, ad 1, and from him Pererius in book 8 of his commentary on Daniel, page 456, as also Becanus in part 1 of Thomas, treatise 1, chapter 14, question 8, page 167, commemorates three books of life; for just as a book of military service is taken in three ways: 1. In which those chosen for military service are written; 2. In which the military art is taught; 3. In which the deeds of the soldiers are contained: so they judge that the book of life is accepted in a threefold manner. 1. In which those chosen for life are written. 2. In which the manner of arriving at life is taught, and in this sense they claim that the Old and New Testament, or Scripture, is called the book of life: 3. In which the deeds and actions of those who strive for eternal life are written.

II. But that distinction is devised, and it has no foundation in the Scriptures, since in them there is mention of only one book of life, and that one is indeed described in such a way that the names of those to be saved are held to be recorded therein: But this cannot be affirmed of the Biblical codex. For although it contains the word of God, which is called the word of life, John 6, verse 69, and the power unto salvation, Rom. 1, v. 16, it is nevertheless never called the book of life. Greg. de Valent. T. 1, disp. 1, q. 24, punct. 1, col. 595, does indeed cite the saying of Sirach 24, v. 32: 'All these things are the book of life and the testament of the Most High': but besides the fact that Sirach is outside the canon, there is a fault in the Vulgate version. For in the Greek text the word 'life' is not held, but it is said in general: Ταῦτα πάντα βίβλος διαθήκης θεῦ, ὕψιστε: all these things are the book of the covenant made with the most high God: Furthermore, although in the Bibles the manner of arriving at life and salvation is taught, which Baruch hints at in chapter 4, verse 1, and the Savior in John 5, v. 39, nevertheless of all the names of those to be saved are by no means noted there, and therefore it cannot be called the book of life according to the phrase and acceptance of Scripture. III. But as regards the third book, namely of deeds, that is called the book of judgment, not of life. For the names of persons are one thing, and deeds are another; and therefore the books in which these are written are deservedly distinguished, which the Apostle explicitly hints at in Apoc. 20. v. 12, where he first writes that the books of judgment were opened, and immediately adds: And ANOTHER book was opened, which is of life. This, however, is said to be opened at the final judgment, insofar as God looks upon the inscribed names of those to be saved, and reads them out as if in the sight of the whole world, whence the Apostle generally affirms that the dead were judged from those things which were written in the books. Whence it follows that the book of life can also be called a book of judgment in a general sense, namely insofar as eternal life is adjudged to believers from its inspection. However, usage has prevailed in the Church that, for the sake of distinction only, the catalogs and indices of works are called Books of judgment.

IV. Sixtus Senensis, in book 2 of the Bibliotheca sancta, p. 126 et seqq., enumerates even more books of life, namely five. THE FIRST for him is the constant and perpetual knowledge of predestination in the mind of God, which alone we accept in that sense. THE SECOND is the Biblical codex, which it has just now been shown is by no means called the book of life in the sense and phrase of Scripture. THE THIRD he calls Christ the Savior, which opinion will be discussed in the following question.

V. He points out a FOURTH book of life of each one. He thinks that the discourse in Apoc. 20. ver. 12 is about this, where some read thus: καὶ βιβλίον ἄλλο ἠνεῴχθη, ὅ ἐστι τῆς ζωῆς ἑκάστῃ, Another book was opened, which is of the life OF EACH ONE. And indeed it is clear that Augustine read it so from book 20 of The City of God, chapter 14, who understands by that book of each one a certain wonderful power and potency of God in the final judgment which will bring back all deeds to man's memory, and will set them, as it were, in the sight of the mind to be recognized. For thus the words of Augustine hold: The opened book is a certain divine power of understanding: by which it comes to pass that all one's works, whether good or evil, are recalled to memory for each person, and are perceived by the intuition of the mind with wondrous speed, so that knowledge may excuse or accuse the conscience, and thus both all and individuals may be judged at once: Which divine power, indeed, has received the name of a book. For in it, in a certain way, is read whatever is recalled by the doer. Thomas follows this opinion in part 1, question 24, article 1, and Pererius in book 8 on Daniel, p. 456. And Sixtus, p. 150, says that the Roman Church looks to this when it chants these rhythms in the mysteries of the dead: The written book shall be brought forth, In which everything is contained, Whence the world shall be judged.

VI. But the following arguments move us to be less able to subscribe to this opinion. 1. In the authentic text, namely the Greek, the word βιβλίον is not had, as Ludovicus Vives also observes in his notes to chapter 14 of Augustine, p. 1223. D. Therefore, Augustine either added it of his own accord, or snatched it from a corrupt copy of the Vulgate version. 2. The book of life in the text of John is distinguished from the books of deeds. But now they would clearly coincide if by the book of life one also understands the knowledge of all the actions which men have performed throughout their entire life. 3. The book of life in the perpetual phrase of Scripture contains only the faithful and those to be saved, and therefore all who are not found written in the book of life are said to be cast into the lake of fire. Apoc. 20, last verse; 21, last verse. But the exposition of Augustine makes that book common to both the pious and the impious, so much so that not only good but also evil works are found recorded there. And those words are repugnant: The book of life is opened. For although by the power of God in the final judgment all things will be made manifest to all, nevertheless that will not so much be to open books already written, as to write them anew, or as it were to transcribe them into the notices of individuals, which method Suarez urges, contradicting other Romanists, Tr. 2. in 1. Thomae l. 1. c. 20. p. 207. D.

Finally, the fifth, the last verse, clearly proves that the discourse is not about the book of life of each and every one, but of eternal life, since in it it is openly said that he was cast into the lake of fire who was not found written in the book of life. Whence it is clear that βιβλίον ζωῆς ἑκάστ cannot be understood: for since this is common, and thus all are written in it, it would follow that all are saved, which is absurd. Therefore, it speaks not of a book common to the pious and the impious, but one pertaining only to those to be saved, which Scripture designates as the Book of eternal life.

VII. The fifth book of life, Senensis maintains, is the blessed and everlasting presence of Christ the Son of God according to his divinity, the contemplation of which is the reading of the book of life. He says Augustine speaks of this in his book on the triple habitation, ch. 4. Where these things are read: In that heavenly city, the food and drink of all will be the vision of Christ and the Holy Trinity, and the pure contemplation of the divinity itself by the eye of the heart, and the assiduous reading, so to speak, of the book of life, that is, of eternal truth, and of supreme wisdom, and of the Word of God, which is the vision of Christ Jesus. He adds in the same place that some understand by that last book of life a certain created light flowing from the uncreated, by whose splendor our soul, being suffused, lays aside its dullness and is raised to the sublimity of divine vision.

XIII. But these things are too forced and fetched from very far away. For where is eternal salvation called the book of life, or its enjoyment called the reading of the book of life? We do not indeed deny that the blessed will see Christ and be illuminated by heavenly light: but that either this vision or this light is conveniently called βιβλίον ζωῆς does not follow in the least. Augustine can easily be excused; because through speaks popularly, and calls not the presence of Christ, but Christ himself the book of life through a certain more remote metaphor.

IX. Thus, therefore, with the opinion of those rejected who count various books of life without foundation in Scripture; we stand with those who acknowledge only one βιβλίον ζωῆς, in which one the names of all who are to be saved, although various and most diverse, are contained and annotated: But what this book of life is, and how it ought to be defined, now remains to be explained.

Latin:

I. Thomas de Aquino parte 1. summæ Theol. qu. 24. art. 1. ad 1. & ex illo Pererius lib. 8. comm. in Dan. pag. 456. vt & Becanus in part. 1. Thomæ, tract. 1. c. 14. quæst. 8. pag. 167. tres vitæ libros commemorat, vt enim liber militiæ tribus modis sumitur, 1. in quo scribuntur electi ad militiam. 2. In quo traditur ars militaris: 3. In quo continentur militum res gestæ : sic vitæ librum tripliciter accipi arbitrantur. 1. In quo scribuntur electi ad vitam. 2. In quo traditur modus perueniendi ad vitam, & hoc sensu Vetus ac novum Test. vel Scripturam, vitæ librum nuncupari autumant: 3. In quo scribuntur facta & gesta eorum , qui tendunt ad vitam æternam.

II. Verùm excogitata est illa distinctio, neque in scripturis fundamentum habet, quippe in quibus tantùm vnius libri vitæ sit mentio, & ille quidem ita describitur, quod saluandorum nomina ibi consignata habeantur: Atqui hoc de codice Biblico affirmari nequit. Quamvis enim Dei verbum iste contineat, quod verbum vitæ dicitur, Ioh. 6. vers. 69. & potentia ad salutem, Rom. 1. v. 16. nunquam tamen liber vitæ appellatur. Citat quidem Greg: de Valent. T. 1. disp. 1. q: 24. punct: 1. col. 595. dictum Syrac. 24. v. 32. Hæc omnia liber vitæ & Testamentum Altissimi: sed præterquam, quod Siracides sit extra canonem, vitium est in vulgata versione. Nam in Græco textu vocabuluns vitæ non habetur, sed in genere dicitur. Ταῦτα πάντα βίβλος διαθήκης θεῦ, ὕψιστε: dis alles ist eben das Buch des Bundes mit dem höhesten Gott gemacht: Præterea licèt in Bibliis tradatur modus ad vitam & salutem perueniendi, quod Baruch innuit cap: 4. vers. 1. ac Saluator Ioh. 5. v. 39. omnium tamen saluandorum nomina ibi annotata minimè sunt, ideoque liber vitæ secundum Scripturæ phrasin & acceptionem vocari nequit. III. Quod autem tertium librum, nempè factorum, attinet, ille judicii, non vitæ liber dicitur. Aliud enim sunt personarum nomina, & aliud facta; ideoque libri in quibus ista sunt conscripta, meritò distinguuntur, id quòd Apostolus disertè innuit Apoc. 20. v. 12. vbi primùm libros judicij apertos esse scribit, statimque subijcit: Et ALIVS liber apertus est, qui est vitæ. Hic autem in extremo judicio aperiri dicitur, quatenus Deus nomina saluandorum inscripta aspicit, & velut in conspectu totius mundi prælegit, vnde Apostolus generatim affirmat, iudicatos esse mortuos ex his, quæ scripta erant in libris. Vnde sequitur & librum vitæ generali sensu judicij librum appellari posse, nimirum quatenus vita æterna ex eius inspectione adjudicatur credentibus. Vsus tamen in Ecclesia obtinuit, vt distinctionis ergò duntaxat operum catalogi & indices diuini nuncupentur Libri iudicij.

IV. Sixtus Senensis lib. 2. Bibliothecæ sanctæ, p. 126. seqq. adhuc plures vitæ libros, quinque nempe, recenset. PRIMVS ipsi est constans atque perpetua in mente Dei prædestinationis cognitio, quam solam acceptionē nos recipimus. SECVNDVS est codex Biblicus quem vitæ librum Scripturæ sensu & phrasi minimè dici, jam modò ostensum est. TERTIVM vocat Christum Seruatorem, quæ opinio seq. quæstione discutietur.

V. QVARTVM indigitat librum vitæ vnius cuiusque. De hoc putat sermonem esse Apoc. 20. ver. 12. vbi quidam sic legunt: καὶ βιβλίον ἄλλο ἠνεῴχθη, ὅ ἐστι τῆς ζωῆς ἑκάστῃ, Alius liber apertus est, qui est vitæ VNISCVIVSQVE. Et sanè Augustinum ità legisse patet ex libro 20. de Ciuitate Dei cap. 14. qui per librum illum vniuscuiusque intelligit miram quandam vim potentiam Dei in extremo iudicio quæ omnia facta hominibus in memoriam reducet, & quasi in conspectu mentis &- quislo recognoscenda constituet. Sic n. habent verba Augustini: Liber apertus quaedam vis est intelligendi divina: qua fiat, vt cuique opera sua, vel bona vel mala cuncta in memoriam reuocentur, & mentis intuitu mira celeritate cernantur, vt excuset vel accuset scientia conscientiam, atque ita simul & omnes & singuli iudicentur: Quae nimirum vis diuina libri nomen accepit. In eo quippe quodammodo legitur, quicquid a faciente recolitur. Opinionem hanc sequitur Thomas par 1. quaest. 24. art. 1. & Pererius l. 8. in Danielem. p. 456. eoq; Romanam Ecclesiam respicere ait Sixtus p. 150. cum in defunctorum mysterijs hos rythmos decantat: Liber scriptus proferetur, In quo totum continetur, Vnde mundus iudicetur.

VI. Quod autem minus sententiae huic queamus subscribere, argumenta nos mouent sequentia. 1. In textu authentico, videlicet graeco, vox inasu, non habetur, vt obseruat etia Ludovicus Vives in notis ad c. 14. August. p. 1223. D. Vel igitur de suo addidit, vel ex corrupto vulgatae versionis exemplari arripuit Augustinus. 2. Liber vitae in textu Iohannis distinguitur a libris factorum. Iam vero plane coincident, si etiam per vitae librum intelligatur notitia omnium actionum, quas per vniuersam vitam homines ediderunt. 3. Vitae liber perpetua Scrip. phrasi tantum fideles & saluandos continet, ideoq; coniecti dicuntur in stagnum ignis omnes, qui non inuenti sunt scripti in libro vitae. Apoc. 20. v. ult. c. 21. v. ult. Augustini vero expositio librum illum communem facit, & pijs & impijs, adeo vt non bona tantum, sed mala etiam opera ibi consignata inueniantur. 4. Repugnant & illa verba: Liber vitae apertus est. Quanquam enim virtute Dei in extremo iudicio facta omnia omnibus patebunt, illud tamen non tam erit aperire libros iam scriptos, quàm illos de novo scribere, vel quasi transcribere in notitiis singulorum, quam rationem vrget Suarez, alijs Romanensibus contradicens, Tr. 2. in 1. Thomae l. 1. c. 20. p. 207. D.

Tandem 5. versiculus vltimus luculenter evinacit, de libro vitæ non vniuscuiusque, sed æternæ sermonem fieri, quippe in quo apertè dicitur, quòd coiectus sit in stagnum ignis, qui non fuerit inventus in libro vitæ scriptus. Vnde perspicuum sit, βιβλίον ζωῆς ἑκάστ intelligi non posse: hic enim cùm communis sit, adeòque omnes in illo scripti, omnes saluari sequeretur, quod absurdum. Ergò loquitur non de libro piis impijsque communi, sed solos saluandos attinente, quem Librum vitæ æternæ Scriptura indigitat.

VII. QVINTVM vitę librum Senensis esse statuit, Beatā & sempiternam Christi Filij Dei secundum divinitatem presentiam, cuius contemplatio sit libri vitæ lectio. De hoc August. loqui ait l. de tripl. habitaculo c. 4. Vbi hæc leguntur: In illa cœlesti vrbe cibus & potus omnium erit visio Christi & sanctæ Trinitatis, & contemplatio pura cordis oculo ipsius diuinitatis, & assidua lectio, vt ita dicam, libri vitæ, id est æterna veritatis, & summæ sapientiæ & verbi Dei, quæ est Christi Iesu visio. Addit ibidem, quosdam per illum vltimum vitæ librum intelligere creatum quoddam lumen ab increato profluens, cuius splendore perfusus animus noster deponat hebetudinem, & ad sublimitatem diuinæ visionis extollatur.

XIII. Sed nimis hæc coacta, & quàm longissimè petita sunt, Vbi enim salus sempiterna vitæ liber, eius fruitio, liber vitæ lectio nuncupatur? Non quidem inficias imus, beatos esse Christum visuros, & cœlesti lumine collustrandos: Quòd autem vel visio, vel lumen istud conuenienter βιβλίον ζωῆς dicatur inde minimè sequitur. Augustinus excusari facilè potest; quia per pulariter loquitur, nec Christi præsentiam, sed Christum ipsum vitæ librum per remotiorem quandam metaphoram appellat.

IX. Sic ergò reiectâ illorum sententia, qui varios vitæ libros sine fundamento Scripturæ numerant; cum ijs statuimus, qui vnum duntaxat βιβλίον ζωῆς agnoscunt, in quo vno omnium saluandorum nomina, licèt varia & diuersissima continentur annotata: Quid autem sit hic vitæ liber, & quomodo definiri debeat, nunc explicandum restat.


### Question IV. What is the book of Life?

I. Some think that by this appellation Christ, the author of life, is denoted. Sixtus Senensis provides the reason for the name in lib. 2, Bibl. sanct. p. 129, because he himself is our life and resurrection from the death of sin; the life of present grace; and the happiness of eternal life. Especially because Christ, exalted on the wood of the cross, is as it were a certain famous and conspicuous book, not fitted with papyrus and membranes, but in his very flesh and members; not written with ink or red lead, but with precious blood; not with reeds and birds' feathers, but carved with thorns, nails, scourges, and a lance; and joined and enclosed by the double wood of the cross as if between two covers, from which book indeed any Christian can take the most perfect instruction of life. The same was established before Sixtus by Hugo Carenssis, for whom in chapter 13 of the Apocalypse the book of life is the Lamb himself, in whom all things were before they were made: For he himself is the mind of God: whence just as a house is in the mind of the craftsman before the action is performed: so all things were in him; who was the exemplar and idea of all things. Therefore, he is the book of life, insofar as he is God, insofar as he is man, because he gave us an example of living. And to this point look the allegorical meditations of the Fathers, which Mr. Dr. Pelargus recounts concerning the book of life, C. fasc. 1, in these words: Christ is a certain book, as it were, written on virgin parchment, and in the glorious chamber of the Virgin, dictated by the fingers of the Holy Spirit, composed in the Father's disposition, written in the mother's conception, exposed in the manifestation of the nativity, corrected in the passion, scraped in the scourging, punctuated in the piercing of the wounds, placed upon the pulpit in the crucifixion, illuminated in the shedding of blood, bound in the resurrection, disputed in the ascension, with the Angels asking, 'Whence is he who comes from Edom?', finally opened and unfolded in the promulgation of judgment. But if, furthermore, this book is looked upon only on the pulpit of the cross: the proud man will read humility in the inclination of the head; the avaricious man, liberality in the extension of the hands; the envious man, charity in the opening of the side; the rich man, spiritual poverty in the stripping of the whole body; the gluttonous man, abstinence in the bitter drinking of gall and vinegar; the voluptuous man, the harshness of penance in the imposition of the crown of thorns; the irascible man, finally, kindness in the reception of the crucified thief.

II. However much we may not deny that Christ can in a certain way and ἀλληγορικῶς (allegorically) be called the book of life, as our Megalander and truly Theander Luther called him, from whom the Formula of Concord repeated it, namely insofar as election to eternal life was made in him, and all the faithful, both collectively and individually, are grafted into him: yet it can be shown by the following arguments that Scripture, by βίβλιον ζωῆς (book of life), in which the names of the elect are inscribed, does not precisely and formally mean Christ himself, but something else.

III. 1. It is affirmed of the book of life that it is written. But it cannot be explained by any sufficiently convenient reason how Christ can be called a written book. For by what means, I ask, did the Father write the Son, if he himself is the written book?

IV. 2. It is an ancient rule of the Fathers concerning works ad extra (outwardly directed) that they are undivided and common to the individual persons. Now, the writing of the book of life is a work ad extra, since it concerns creatures, and in particular the saving of men as it pertains to them, therefore, the work is common, so much so that it can be affirmed no less of Christ than of the Father that He wrote the book of life. And some draw to this point that passage in Ezekiel 9:2 concerning the man having a writer's inkhorn at his loins, by whom they commonly understand Christ. Jerome, however, says in his Commentary on Ezekiel: 'He had a writer's inkhorn at his loins, with which he might describe the sins of all, and separate the number of the saints from the sinners.' If, therefore, Christ Himself wrote the book of life, these two will be distinct for both, so that Christ writing is one thing, and the book which He writes is another, unless we wish to assert, not without absurdity, that Christ wrote or writes Himself.

V. 3. The book of life must be opened at the final judgment, Revelation 20:12. 'And another book was opened, which is the book of life.' Now this book will be opened by Christ, since He is to be the universal judge of the world, and He will discern whose names are written in the book of life, so that they may be saved, and whose are not written, so that they may be cast into the lake of fire. Now if Christ were the book of life, how could it be said that it is opened at the final judgment? And would not the judge who opens it be confused in this way with the book which He opens, which two things, however, Scripture always distinguishes, and speaks of them as distinct?

VI. Since, therefore, the book of life cannot be explained as Christ Himself, it no longer requires divination as to what ought to be understood by it. For just as a book attributed to God in general denotes His knowledge and providence, so in particular the book of life or of the living will be nothing other than the singular knowledge of those to be saved, concerning which the Apostle says in 2 Timothy 2:19: 'The foundation of God stands sure, having this seal: The Lord knows those who are His.' The metaphor is taken from princes, who write down in a book those whom they choose for military service or some office, whence also the Fathers were once called 'conscripti' (conscript fathers) among the Romans.

Because therefore God chose those believing perseveringly unto eternal life, hence he is said by anthropopathy to have written their names in a certain book, which for that reason is designated βίβλος τῆς ζωῆς.

VII. If anyone therefore should request a brief and succinct description, we shall give this to him: The book of life, so called μεταφορικῶς, is a catalog of those to be saved, whom God out of grace, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by persevering faith, and foreseen from eternity, before the foundations of the world were laid, chose unto life, to the praise of his glorious grace.

VIII. I call it a catalog, so that the reason for the metaphor may be more expressed, since also elsewhere in the Scriptures a book is sometimes put for a catalog, as Flacius notes in part 1 of the Clavis, p. 567, as in Gen. 5:1, The book of the generations of Adam, that is, the series or recitation of the descendants of Adam. And Matt. 1:1, The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, that is, the catalog of the ancestors of Christ.

IX. Moreover, the whole sacrosanct Trinity wrote this book of life, while it chose those who would believe perseveringly, and as it were expressed and annotated their names in its own mind, and thus described those to be saved, what sort they would be before they were to be born: and what sort they would be judged before they were to be formed, and as it were by certain letters observed the works of individuals before the workers. But this book will be opened by Christ the judge on the day of universal judgment, while he will commend the faith of those to be saved, foreseen from eternity and performed in time, and will reveal that their names were always most known to God, and as it were inscribed in his memory as in a certain book, and thus will adjudge eternal salvation to them.

X. Augustine speaks of this book in book 20 of The City of God, ch. 15. That book, he says, does not remind God, lest he be deceived by forgetfulness: but it signifies the predestination of those to whom eternal life will be given. For God does not not know them and read them in this book, so that he may know: but rather his very foreknowledge of them, which cannot be deceived, is the book of life, in which they are written, that is, foreknown. Hence Augustine says the book of life is the knowledge of the elect, which does not conflict with our opinion, by which we said it is a catalog of those to be saved. For these agree as to the thing, they differ only in words. For if you call it the knowledge of God, it is a proper expression: if a catalog of the elect, it is a metaphorical expression: yet in both cases the same thing is expressed. For this catalog, as to the thing, is the very special knowledge of God, by which He knows His elect: And this knowledge, as to us, is called through ἀνθρωποπαθείαν a book or catalog of the living, written by God before the foundations of the world were laid. Anselm followed this same declaration of Augustine on Phil. 4. Tom. 2. p. 306, writing thus: Their names are written in the book of life, that is, they are held assigned to life, in the memory of divine predestination. For what is the book of life, if not the memory of God, in which are those who live forever.

XI. From what has been said thus far, three things can additionally be gathered and declared. 1. The reason for the denomination. For it is called the book of life, not by reason of the writer God, who is life, John 14. v. 6. 1. John 1. v. 2. not by reason of the matter insofar as it is written in God, essential life, since in this way even the reprobate would be consigned in the book of life, since their names and deeds are no less known to God than those of the pious, although in another way; but by reason of the object, since it contains only the living or heirs of eternal life, or because it is more clear, by reason of the term and end of the writing made, which is none other than salvation and everlasting life. Most briefly, therefore, it is called the book of life, because those written in it are elected to eternal life. But when it is called the book of life of the Lamb as in Apoc. 13. v. 8. c. 21. v. last, this does not rely on the fact that Christ the lamb is that book: but a reference is made. 1. To the writing, which is attributed to Christ together. 2. To the acquisition of life, the medium of which was the precious blood of the lamb 3. To the foundation of the written book, which

Christ is apprehended by faith; and finally 4. To the extreme judgment in which the Lamb of God will open the book of life, and will, as it were, read aloud and recite the names of those to be saved from it, in the sight of the whole world. For these four reasons it is most rightly called not only the book of life, but also the book of the life of the Lamb.

XII. 2. The difference from the remaining books of God. In this indeed they all agree. 1. That they are called μεταφορικῶς. 2. That they are written by God alone. 3. That they exist in and belong to God alone. 4. That they signify the knowledge and care of God. But they differ in turn in various ways. For, to speak first of the book of providence and of life, the former is universal, the latter special: the former contains all creatures, the latter only men to be saved: the end of the former is the preservation of creatures, of the latter the glorification of the elect: the foundation of the former is the infinite goodness of God, of the latter grace founded in the merit of Christ: the former will not be opened in the final judgment, but the latter will be opened, and whoever shall have been written in it will be saved. As for what concerns the book of judgment, it must similarly be distinguished from the book of life. For the former is twofold, and comprises partly the good, partly the evil works of men; but the latter is one and simple. In the former, deeds; in the latter, persons and their names are recorded. The former concerns all men; the latter only those who believe perseveringly. Finally, from the former, both life and death will be adjudged to men after the resurrection; but from the latter, nothing but life and eternal salvation.

XIII. Finally 3. The distinction from predestination. For however much inscription in the book of life and election may scarcely differ; yet it itself is distinguished from predestination by a certain liberation. For the latter is the action of God choosing; the former is a catalog of the elect. The latter is the decree of God; the former is the knowledge of the one decreeing. The latter pertains to the will, the former more to the intellect. The latter precedes in order, the former follows, since believers are chosen first, and afterwards the chosen are recorded. The latter embraces all causes and means of salvation, while the former formally contains only the names of those to be saved, signifying the constant knowledge and memory of God.

Latin:

I. Nonnulli hac appellatione Christum vitæ authorem denotari existimant. Causam nominis Sixtus Senensis affert l. 2. Bibl. sanct. p. 129. quia ipse sit nostra vita & resurrectio à morte peccati; vita præsentis gratiæ; & vitæ sempiternæ felicitatis. Imprimis quia Christus in ligno crucis exaltatus sit, veluti quidam celebris & conspicuus liber non, papyro ac membranis, verum in ipsa carne & membris aptatus; non atramento, miniove conscriptus, sed pretioso sanguine; non calamis & auium pennis; sed spinis, clauis, flagellis, & lancea exaratus; & gemino ligno crucis quasi intra duas tabellas compaginatus & conclusus, ex quo quidem libro possit quilibet Christianus sumere perfectissimam vitæ institutionem. Idem ante Sixtum statuit Hugo Carenssis, cui in 13. cap. Apoc. liber vitæ ipse est agnus, in quo omnia antequam fierent: Ipse enim est mens Dei: vnde sicut domus est in mente artificis, primquam fiat actio: sic omnia fuerunt in ipso; qui omnium erat exemplar & idéa. Sit ergò vitæ liber est, in quantum Deus, in quantum homo, quia dedit nobis exemplum viuendi. Et huc spectant Patrum meditationes allegoricæ, quas Dn. D. Pelargus de libro vitæ C. fasc. 1. his verbis recenset: Christum est quidam velut liber scriptus in pelle virginea, inque camera virginis gloriosa digitis Spiritus sancti, dictatus in Patris dispositione, scriptus in matris conceptione, expositus in natiuitatis manifestatione, correctus in passione, rasus in flagellatione, punctatus in vulnerum infixione, super pulpito positus in crucifixione, illuminatus in sanguinis effusione, colligatus in resurrectione, disputatus in ascensione, Angelis quærentibus, Vnde iste, qui venit de Edom? apertus tandem & explicatus in judicij promulgatione. Quòd si porrò liber hic in pulpito crucis tantùm aspiciatur: leget superbus humilitatem in capitis inclinatione: auarus liberalitatem in manuum extensione: inuidus caritatem in lateris apertione: diues paupertatem spiritualem in totius corporis denudatione: gulosus abstinentiam in amara fellis acetique potatione: delitiosus pœnitentiæ asperitatem in coronæ spineæ impositione: iracundus deniq; benignitatem in latronis crucifixi receptione.

II. Quantumuis autem non diffiteamur, Christum suo quodam modo & ἀλληγορικῶς librum vitæ nuncupari posse, vt eum nuncupauit Megalander noster & verè Theander Luther, ex quo ipsum repetiit Formula Concordiæ, nempe quatenus in ipso facta est ad vitam æternam electio, & fideles vniuersi atque singuli ipsi inseruntur: Scripturam tamē per βίβλιον ζωῆς, cui electorum nomina sunt inscripta, non præcisè & formaliter Christum ipsum, sed quiddam aliud inuertere sequentib. argumentis ostendi potest.

III. 1. De libro vitæ affirmatur, quod sit scriptus. Nullâ autem satis commoda ratione explicari potest, quomodo Christus liber scriptus appellari queat. Quo enim quæso pacto Pater scripsit Filium, si hic est ipse liber scriptus?

IV. 2. Antiqua Patrum est regula de operibus ad extra, quod sint indiuisa, & singulis personis communia. Iam verò scriptio libri vitæ, est opus ad extra, quoniam creaturas, & in specie homines saluandos attinet, Opus igitur commune est, adeò, venon minus de Christo, quàm de Patre affirmari queat, quod librum vitæ scripserit. Et huc trahunt nonnulli illud Ezech. 9. v. 2. de viro atramentarium scriptoris ad renes habente, per quem communiter Christum intelligunt, Habebat autem, inquit Hieronym. in Comment. super Ezech: atramentarium scriptoris ad renes suos, quo omnium peccata describeret, & sanctorum à peccatoribus numerum segregaret. Quòd si ergò Christus ipse librum vitæ scripsit, vtrique hæc duo distincta erunt vt aliud sit Christus scribens, aliud liber, quem scribit, nisi Christum scripsisse aut scribere seipsum non sine absurditate velimus asserere.

V. 3. Liber vitæ in extremo iudicio debet apeExiri Apoc. 20. v. 17. Et alius liber apertus est, qui est vitæ. Aperietur a. iste liber à Christo, quippe qui futurus est vniuersalis mundi iudex, & dignoscet, quorum nomina in libro vitæ scripta sint, vt saluentur, & quorum scripta non sint, vt in stagnum ignis mittantur. Iam si Christus liber vitæ foret, quomodo diceretur ille in extremo judicio aperiri? Et annon hoc pacto vicissim confundetur iudex aperiens, cum libro, quem aperit, quæ duo tamen Scriptura semper distinguit, deq; ijs tanquam de distinctis loquitur?

VI. Cùm igitur liber vitæ de Christo ipso exponi nequeat, diuinatione ampliùs non indiget, quid per illum intelligi debeat. Nam sicut in genere liber Deo tributus, notat eius scientiam & prouidentiam: sic in specie liber vitæ aut viuentium nihil erit aliud, quàm singularis saluandorum cognitio, de qua Apostolus 2. Tim. 2. v 9. Firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc: Nouit Dominus, qui sint sui. Desumta autem est metaphora à principibus, qui in libro conscribunt, quos ad militiam, vel munus aliquod eligunt, vnde & olim Patres conscripti apud Romanos nuncupati sunt.

Quia ergo Deus perseueranter credentes ad vitam æternam elegit, hinc illorum nomina in libro quodam, qui ob id βίβλος τῆς ζωῆς indigitatur, scripsisse per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν dicitur.

VII. Si quis igitur breuem succinctamque descriptionem postulet, hanc ipsi dabimus: Liber vitæ μεταφορικῶς ita dictus, est catalogus saluandorum, quos Deus ex gratia, propter meritum Christi, perseuerante fide apprehensum, & ab æterno præuisum, ante iacta mundi fundamenta, ad vitam elegit, in laudem gloriosæ gratiæ suæ.

VIII. Catalogum voco, vt metaphoræ ratio magis exprimatur, siquidem & aliàs in Scripturis liber pro catalogo nonnunquam ponitur, notante Flacio parte 1. Clau. p. 567. vt Gen. 5. v. 1. Liber generationum Adam, hoc est, series vel recitatio posterorum Adam. Et Matth. 1. v. 1. Liber generationis Iesu Christi, hoc est, catalogus majorum Christi.

IX. Istum autem librum vitæ conscripsit tota sacrosancta Trinitas, dum perseueranter credituros elegit, & ipsorum nomina in mente sua quasi expressit & annotauit, adeoque saluandos descripsit, quales futuri, priusquam nascituri: & quales iudicandi, priusquam formandi, & quasi literis quibusdam singulorum obseruauit opera, priusquam operatores. Aperietur autem liber hic à Christo iudice in die pantocritico, dum fidem saluandorum ab æterno præuisam, in tempore præstitam commendabit, & nomina ipsorum Deo semper notissima, inque memoria eius quasi libro quodam adscripta fuisse, patefaciet adeoque salutem ijs sempiternam adiudicabit.

X De hoc libro Augustinus verba facit li. 20. de Ciu. Dei. c. 15. Non Deum, inquit, liber iste conmemorat, ne obliuione fallatur: sed prædestinationem significat eorum, quibus æterna dabitur vita. Neq; enim nescit eos Deus & in hoc libro legit, vt sciat: sed potius eius ipsa præscientia de illis, quæ falli non potest liber est vitæ, in quo illi sunt scripti, id est, præcogniti. Hinc Augustinus librum vitæ dicit esse notitiam electorum, id quod non pugnat cum nostra sententia, quâ illum diximus esse catalogum saluandorum. Nam hæc quoad rem conueniunt, tantùm vocabulis differunt. Si enim notitiam Dei dicas, est locutio propria: si catalogum electorum, est locutio metaphorica: vtrobique tamen idem exprimitur. Nam iste catalogus, quoad rem est ipsa Dei notitia specialis, quâ nouit suos electos: Et hæc notitia, quoad nos, per ἀνθρωποπαθείαν vocatur liber vel catalogus viuentium, à Deo scriptus ante jacta fundamenta mundi, Eandem Augustini declarationem secutus est Anselmus super Phil. 4. Tom. 2. p. 306, ita scribens: Nomina eorum scripta sunt in libro vitæ, id est, adsignata tenentur ad vitam, in memoria diuinæ prædestinationis. Quid est enim liber vitæ, nisi memoria Dei, in qua sunt illi, qui viuunt in æternum.

XI. Ex hactenus vero dictis tria insuper possunt colligi & declarari. 1. Denominationis ratio. Liber enim vitæ dicitur, non ratione scribentis Dei, qui est vita, Ioh. 14. v. 6. 1. Ioh. 1. v. 2. non ratione materiæ quatenus in Deo, vita essentiali scriptus est, quoniam hoc pacto etiam reprobi forent in libro vitæ consignati, quandoquidem ipsorum nomina & facta non minus Deo nota sunt, quàm piorum, licèt alio modo sed ratione obiecti, quoniam viuentes tantùm seu æternæ vitæ hæredes continet, vel quòd magis perspicuum est, ratione termini & finis factæ scriptionis, qui nullus est alius quàm salvus & vita sempiterna. Breuissimè igitur vitæ liber nuncupatur, quia scripti in ipso, ad vitam æternam sunt electi. Cùm verò vitæ liber Agni dicitur vt Apoc. 13. v. 8. c. 21. v. vlt. non hoc innititur, quòd Christus agnus sit liber ille: sed fit respectus. 1. Ad scriptionem, quę Christo vnà tribuitur. 2. Ad vitæ acquisitionem, cuius medium fuit pretiosus sanguis agni 3. Ad libri scripti fundamentum, quod

Christus est fide apprehensus; & tandem 4. Ad iudicium extremum in quo agnus Dei librum vitæ aperiet, saluandorumq; nomina ex illo, in totius mundi conspectu, quasi præleget & recitabit. Ob has quatuor causas non vitæ duntaxat, sed etiam vitæ Agni liber rectissimè appellatur.

XII. 2. A reliquis Dei libris differentia. In eo quidem conueniunt omnes. 1. Quòd dicantur μεταφορικῶς 2. Quòd à solo Deo scribantur. 3. Quòd non nisi Deo insint & conueniant. 4. Quòd notitiam & curam Dei significent. Variis autẽ modis vicissim differunt. Nam vt primum de libro prouidentiæ & vitæ dicam, ille vniuersalis est, hic specialis: ille creaturas omnes, hic tantùm homines saluandos continet: illius finis est conseruatio creaturarum, huius glorificatio electorum: illius fundamentum est, infinita Dei bonitas, huius gratia in Christi merito fundata: ille non aperietur in extremo judicio, hic autem aperietur, quisquis in ipso scriptus fuerit, saluabitur. Librum vero iudicij quod spectat, similiter à vitæ libro distingui debet. Nam ille geminus est, & partim bona, partim mala hominum opera comprehendit; hic verò vnus & simplex est. In illo facta; in hoc personæ, earumque nomina consignantur. Ille homines omnes; hic tantùm perseueranter credentes attinet. Ex illo denique tùm vita, tùm mors; ex hoc autem non nisi vita & salus æterna hominibus post resurrectionem adiudicabitur.

XIII. Tandem 3. Discrimen à prædestinatione, Quantumvis enim inscriptio in librum vitæ & electio vix differant; ipse tamen liberatione quadam â prædestinatione distinguitur. Nam hæc est actio Dei eligentis; ille est catalogus electorum. Hæc decretum Dei est; ille decernentis notitia. Hæc ad voluntatem, ille magis ad intellectum spectat. Hæc præcedit ordine, ille sequitur, cùm credentes prius eligantur, & pòst electi consignentur. Hæc omnes salutis causas & media complectitur, ille nomina tantùm saluandorum formaliter continet, constantem notitiam ac memoriam Dei significat.


### Question V. What is the inscription into the book of life?

I. Since the book of life is a catalogue of the elect, it follows from this that the inscription in the book of life is, as regards the thing itself, nothing other than election, or when someone is referred among the elect and is numbered with them. Some concede a certain distinction of reason, so that election is prior in order, and the consignation of the elect follows; however, since this is very slight, and taken more from humans than it truly pertains to God—who indeed wrote by choosing believers, and chose by writing, and thus accomplished these things in a single act—it is rightly established that it is one and the same thing that is being noted.

II. But so that the nature of the inscription may be better perceived, three other special and subordinate questions must be examined: 1. Who are the inscribed? 2. What was the mode of inscription? And 3. Whether the inscription is twofold, one temporal, the other eternal? Therefore, we shall briefly open our mind concerning these.

III. 1. Who are inscribed in the book of life? Some think that not only humans, but also angels are predestined, and thus are inscribed in the book of life. For thus writes Franciscus Suarez, Tr. 2. in 1. Thomæ l. 1. c. 20 p. 280. c. b. C. 'I think that even the saved and predestined Angels are so through Christ, and therefore their names also are written in the book of life of the Lamb.' And Polanus in Didascalia de prædest. p. 9. and l. 4. syntag. c. 8. col. 1570. expressly establishes that election is of both angels and humans; we shall examine this opinion a little more fully in the following: here, for the negative, one or two arguments can be noted.

1. Inscription in the book of life is attributed only to men, and is never applied to angels in the Scriptures. Wherefore let us be mindful of the Apostolic Aphorism. 1 Cor. v. 6. μὴ φρονεῖν ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται Let us not be wise beyond that which is written.

2. The book of life presupposes the guilt of death, to which men, being liable, were inscribed, and by that very registration were translated from death to life. But the good angels never sinned, and therefore did not contract the guilt of death.

3. This book is called the book of life of the Lamb. Therefore, for those for whom Christ the Lamb of God did not satisfy, nor die, to them the book of life does not pertain. But Christ did not satisfy for the Angels. For He did not come for their sake, but to save that which was lost, Luke 19. v. 10. Wherefore the book of the Lamb does not pertain to the Angels.

4. Inscription in the book of life does not follow the actual possession of blessedness, but precedes it. For those who are always actually blessed, it is not necessary that their names be registered, so that they might one day become blessed. But now, the Angels have always been and are participants of blessedness and eternal life: who therefore could be inscribed in the book of life, for the fruition of heavenly joy that would one day follow?

Finally 5. The book of life will be opened on the last day, so that from it salvation may be adjudged to the elect. Apoc. 20. v. 12. If therefore the Angels are also included in this βιβλίῳ, it follows that they also must be judged on the last day, and must be introduced into the possession of eternal salvation for the first time, which is absurd.

IV. Having therefore proven that only men are inscribed in the book of life, it is further asked, whether a few or all? Where the answer is easy, if only the denomination itself is considered. For it is called the book of life. Wherefore it embraces only the heirs of eternal life, which Daniel affirms in express words c. 12 v. 1. At that time thy people shall be saved, every one that shall be found written in the book. Whoever therefore is not saved, he should not be thought to be inscribed in the book of life. But not all will be saved, but only those perseveringly believing. Therefore, these alone are inscribed in the book of life. Hence, Apoc. 17, verse 8, it is expressly asserted that those admiring the beast, many of whom were indeed baptized in infancy, and thus regenerated, had never been inscribed in the book of life κόσμου, from the very foundation of the world. It is therefore a gross error of those who affirm that all men without distinction are consigned to the book of the living, which opinion they can by no means defend, unless they simultaneously invent, most absurdly, a universal salvation. V. 2. What was the mode of inscription? The decision of this question is evident from the preceding disputation, where it was shown that the election of those to be saved is not absolute, but ordered, made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, according to Rom. 8, v. 29, c. 11, v. 2, 1 Petr. 1, v. 2. For fallen men are elected not from an absolute grace, but one founded on the merit of Christ. Those, therefore, whom God foresaw from eternity would perseveringly believe, these and no others He elected, and by electing, inscribed in the book of life. The Calvinists are therefore mistaken, who attribute to God I know not what fatal book, or rather Rhadamanthine tablets, as if from His sole and naked good pleasure, without any respect to Christ apprehended by faith, He had inscribed from eternity a very few certain ones in the book of life, while all others were neglected and rejected. This error attacks the beneficent will of God the Father, by which He loves all; the merit of Christ, by which He satisfied for all; and the Word of the Spirit, which is announced to all, concerning which, since it has been satisfied before, it is not necessary that we add more.

VI. 3. Whether there is a double inscription? So it seems to some, since all baptized infants are regenerated, and thus are inscribed into Christ, whom they call the book of life, yet not all persevere, but sometimes fall away through mortal sins from the grace which they once obtained. Hence it is said that there is one eternal inscription, which concerns the triumphant Church, is proper to the elect alone, and never becomes void: another temporal one, which pertains to the militant Church, comprehends all the reborn, and can be made void through impenitence on the part of men.

XII. Moreover, this question is not about the thing, but only about the manner of speaking, which if anyone wishes to retain, we do not indeed morosely oppose, nor do we tax anyone on this account: yet it seems to approach less to the language and sense of Scripture, as warned by Dn. D. Gerhard, Tom. 2, Loc. com., in the place concerning Election §. 40, p. 193:

For 1. Scripture never calls that mystical implantation, which occurs in Baptism, the book of life, or an inscription in it, but is entirely silent about this phrase, and therefore those who retain it do not speak with Scripture. But we are mindful of that Ambrosian warning, which is read in epistle 31, book 5: If the Holy Scriptures do not speak, who shall speak?

2. It is intimated that the inscription ἀπὸ βιβλίου τῆς ζωῆς (from the book of life) is only eternal in Apoc. 17, v. 8, while it is said to be omitted and thus made from the foundation of the world, which phrase denotes eternity.

3. If the inscription is doubled, the book of life itself must necessarily be doubled. For just as some are elect, others reborn, and just as the militant and triumphant Church differ: So if all the reborn, while they become members of the Church, are sealed by God and inscribed in some book, it must certainly be distinct from that which contains only the elect and those certainly to be saved.

4. The book of life is described in such a way that everyone inscribed is infallibly saved, which thesis our men have constantly defended against Huberus. If, therefore, all who are inscribed are saved, there will be only one inscription, namely the eternal one, and no temporal one ral, which can be made void. Finally 5. If the consignation be double, the common definition of the book of life falls, that it is a catalog of the elect or of those to be saved; our hypothesis, never hitherto restricted, that to be chosen and to be inscribed in the book of life are synonyms and are taken for the same things, will fall together with it. VIII. These are those things which render a temporal inscription somewhat improbable, whence it seems to follow that, just as there is one book of life, containing only the elect and those certainly to be saved, so there is only one inscription, namely the eternal one, which is convertible with predestination. But as for the reborn, that they are dear to God as such, and exist in His memory, there is no doubt. And indeed in this sense, insofar as every knowledge and memory of God is called a book in general, some could be said to be inscribed in a book. But that is not the book of eternal life, of which Scripture treats, but it ought to be designated by another name, namely the book of the Church or the book of grace: here is that other book of glory and salvation. But enough about this question, which we do not wish to be decided, but rather commit to be ventilated by the judgment and discretion of sounder others.

IV. Furthermore, what can be discussed here, such as, Whether anyone can certainly know his own inscription? and what depends on these: we wish all these things to be reserved for the following disputations, where it will be discussed professedly concerning the elect, who are no others than those inscribed in the book of life.

Latin:

I. Cùm liber vitæ sit catalogus electorum, sequitur inde, quòd inscriptio in librum vitæ, nihil, quoad rem, sit aliud, quàm electio, vel cùm quis inter electos refertur, iisque adnumeratur. Nonnulli rationis quoddam discrimen concedunt, ita yt prior ordine sit electio, & sequatur electorum consignatio, hoc tamen cùm perexiguum sit, & ab hominibus magis desumptum, quàm vt Deo verè competat, quippe qui credentes eligendo scripsit, scribendo elegit, adeoque vnico actu ista perfecit, propterea rem vnam, eandemque notari rectè statuitur.

II. Vt verò inscriptionis ratio melius percipiatur, aliæ tres speciales & subordinatæ quæstiones excutiendæ veniunt, 1. Quinam sint inscripti? 2. Quis fuerit inscriptionis modus? Et 3 Num duplex sit inscriptio, vna temporalis, æterna altera? De his ergo mentem nostram breuiter aperiemus.

III. 1. Quinam libro vitæ sint inscripti? Arbitrantur quidam non homines tantùm, sed angelos quoque prædestinatos, adeoque vitæ libro inscriptos esse. Ita enim scribit Franciscus Suarez, Tr. 2. in 1. Thomæ l. 1. c. 20 p. 280. c. b. C. Ego existimo, etiam Angelos saluos & prædestinatos esse per Christum, & ideò etiam illorum nomina scripta esse in libro vitæ agni. Et Polanus in didascalia de prædest. p. 9. ac l. 4. syntag. c. 8. col. 1570. expressè statuit, Electionem esse tùm angelorum, tùm hominum; Opinionem hanc in sequenti paulò fusius excutiemus: hic pro negatiua vnū duntaxat & alterum argumentū notari potest.

1. Inscriptio in librum vitæ tantùm hominibus tribuitur, nunquam ad angelos accommodatur in Scripturis. Quare memores simus Aphorismi Apostolici. 1. Cor. v. 6. μὴ φρονεῖν ὑπὲρ ὃ γέγραπται Ne sapiamus ultrà id, quod scriptum est.

2. Liber vitæ præsupponit reatum mortis, cui obnoxii homines inscripti, & illam ipsam consignationem à morte ad vitam translati sunt. Angeli autem boni nunquam peccarunt, ideoque nec reatum mortis contraxerunt.

3. Hic liber dicitur liber vitæ Agni. Pro quibus igitur Christus Dei agnus non satisfecit, nec mortuus est, ad illos liber vitę non pertinet. Atqui pro Angelis Christus non satisfecit. Nec enim propter illos venerat, sed salvare, quod perierat Luc. 19. v. 19. Quare ad Angelos liber Agni non pertinet.

4. Inscriptio in librum vitæ non sequitur actualem beatitudinis possessionem, sed præcedit. Qui enim actu semper beati sunt, illorum nomina consignari non oportet, vt aliquando beati fiant, Iam verò Angeli beatitudinis vitęque sempiternæ participes semper fuerunt & sunt: Qui ergò inscribi potuerunt libro vitæ, ad cœlestis gaudii fruitionem aliquando secuturam?

Tandem 5. Liber vitæ aperietur die vltimo, vt inde salus adjudicetur electis. Apoc. 20. v. 12. Si ergò & Angeli sunt isti βιβλίῳ inclusi, sequitur eos etiam die vltimo judicandos, & in salmis æternæ possessionem primùm intromittendos esse, quod absurdum.

IV. Euicto igitur, quòd soli homines libro vitæ inscripti sint, porrò quæritur, Num pauci vel omnes? Vbi responsio est facilis, si vel sola denominatio consideretur. Nam liber vitæ appellatur Quare tantùm hæredes vitæ æternæ complectitur, quod ipsum conceptis verbis affirmat Daniel c. 12 v. 1. In tempore illo saluabitur populus tuus omnis qui inuentus fuerit scriptus in libro. Quisquis ergò non saluatur, vitæ libro inscriptus non putetur. Atqui non saluabuntur omnes, sed tantùm perseueranter credentes. Ergò & hi soli libro vitæ sunt inscripti. Hinc Apoc. 17. vers. 8. expressè asseritur admirantes bestiam, quorum sanè multi in infantia sunt baptizati, adeoque regenerati, nunquam libro vitæ inscriptos fuisse ἀπὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, ab ipsius mundi constitutione. Crassus igitur error est eorum, qui homines indiscretè omnes libro viuentium consignatos esse affirmant, quam sanè opinionem defendere haut possunt, nisi vnà saluationem vniuersalem absurdissimè comminiscantur. V. 2. Quis fuerit inscriptionis modus? Patet hujus quæstionis decisio ex disputatione præcedenti, vbi ostensum fuit, electionem saluandorum non esse absolutam, sed ordinatam, κατὰ πρόγνωσιν factã, iuxta Rom. 8. v. 29. c. 11. v. 2. 1. Petr. 1. v. 2. Electi enim sunt homines lapsi ex gratiâ non absolutâ, sed in merito Christi fundata. Quos igitur Deus ab æterno perseueranter credituros præuidit, hos etiam non alios elegit, eligendoque libro vitæ inscripsit. Falluntur ergò Caluiniani, qui nescio quem fatalem librum, vel tabulas potiùs Rhadamanteas Deo affingunt, ac si ex solo nudoque beneplacito sine omni respectu Christi fide apprehensi, paucissimos quosdam, cæteris omnibus neglectis & reiectis, libro vitæ ab æterno inscripsisset. Error hic impugnat beneficam Dei Patris voluntatem, quâ omnes diligit; meritum Christi, quo pro omnib. satisfecit; Verbum Spiritus, quod omnibus annunciatur, de quibus cùm antè satisfactum sit, plura vt addamus necessarium non est.

VI. 3. Num duplex sit inscriptio? Ita nonnullis videtur, quoniam omnes baptizati infantes regenerantur, adeoque Christo, quem librum vitæ nuncupant, inscribuntur, nec tamen omnes perseuerant, sed quandoque gratiâ, quam semel adepti sunt, per lapsus mortales excidunt. Hinc disunt, aliam esse inscriptionem æternam, quæ Ecclesiam triumphantem spectet, solis electis sit propria, & nunquam fiat irrita: Temporalem aliam, quæ Ecclesiam militantem attineat, omnes renatos comprehendat, & per impœnitentiam ex parte hominum evacuati queat.

XII. Est autem hæc quæstio non de re, sed tantùm de modo loquendi, quem si quis retinere voluerit, non quidem morosius refragamur, nec quenquam hoc nomine taxamus: ad linguam tamen & sensum Scripturæ minus accedere videtur, monente Dn. D. Gerhardo Tomo 2. Loc. com. loco de Electione §. 40. p. 193:

Nam 1.
