Scriptura implantationem illam mysticam, quæ fit in Baptismo, nunquam vitæ librum, aut inscriptionem in illum appellat, sed de phrasi hac penitus tacet, ideòque non loquuntur cum Scriptura, qui illam retinent. Nos autem memores sumus moniti istius Ambrosiani, quod legitur epist. 31. lib. 5: Sanctis Scripturis non loquentibus, quis loquetur?

2. Inscriptionem ἀπὸ βιβλίου τῆς ζωῆς non nisi æternam esse innuitur Apoc. 17. v. 8. dum omissa adeoque & facta dicitur a constitutione mundi, quæ phrasis æternitatem denotat.

3. Si geminatur inscriptio, necessario & ipse liber vitæ duplicatur. Sicut enim alij sunt electi, alij renati, & quemadmodum Ecclesia militans & triumphans differunt: Ita si renati omnes dum membra Ecclesiæ fiunt, à Deo consignantur, & libro alicui inscribuntur, distinctus vtique sit oportet ab eo, qui solos electos & certò saluandos continet.

4. Vitæ liber sic describitur, quòd omnis adscriptus infallibiliter, quam ipsam thesin contra Huberum Nostri constanter defenderunt. Si ergo omnes inscripti saluantur, vnica tantùm erit inscriptio, æterna videlicet & nulla temporalis, quæ irrita posfit fieri. Tandem 5. Si gemina sit consignatio cadit vulgata libri vitæ definitio, quòd sit catalogus electorum vel saluandorum, cadet vnà hypothesis nostra nunquàm hactenus restricta, quòd eligi & in librum vitæ inscribi sint synonyma & pro ijsdem accipiantur. IIX. Hæc sunt illa, quæ inscriptionem temporalem nonnihil improbabilem reddunt, vnde sequi videtur, quòd sicut est vnus liber vitæ, tantùm electos continens & certò salvandos, sic vná tantùm sit inscriptio, nimirùm æterna, quæ cum prædestinatione conuertitur. Renatos verò quod attinet, illos, quà tales Deo charos esse, inque memoria eius existere, nullum est dubium. Et sanè hoc sensu, quatenus omnis Dei notitia & memoria liber vocatur in genere, dici possent libro quidam inscripti. Ast ille non est liber vitæ æternæ, de quo Scriptura agit, sed alio nomine indigitari debet, nempè liber Ecclesiæ vel liber gratiæ: heic alter ille est liber gloriæ & salutis. Verùm satis de hac quæstione, quam non decisam volumus, sed sanioris potius aliorū iudicio & discretioni ventilandam committimus.

IV. Quæ porrò hîč disceptari possunt, vt, Num quís inscriptionem suam certò possit scire? & quæ dependent: ista omnia reseruata volumus ad sequentes disputationes, vbi de electis, qui non sunt alij ab inscriptis in librum vitæ, ex professo dissputabitur.


### Question VI. Whether anyone inscribed in the book of life can be erased from it again?

I. Since the counsels and decrees of God are ἀμεταμέλητα,

Rom. 11. v. 29. Certainly, the inscription in the book of life will be immutable, since it differs in no way from election. Therefore, he whom God has once inscribed in the book of the living, he remains inscribed forever; whom He has predestined, him He will certainly glorify, according to that golden chain of the Apostle, Rom. 8. v. 30. And to this, in turn, looks that of the Prophet, Dan. 12. v. 1. Everyone written in the book of life shall be saved. And of the Apostle, Apoc. 20. v. 12. He who is not written is cast into the lake of fire. Therefore, by the contrary sense, all who are inscribed are saved; nor are they thrust into the lake of fire, from which it follows spontaneously that no one is erased from the book of life. For if erasure were possible, not all who are inscribed would be saved, and neither the election of God nor His decrees would be ἀμεταμέλητα, all of which are absurd and contrary to the Scriptures. Hence Cassiodorus rightly pronounced: The book of the knowledge of God is an inviolable and firm sentence: There, whatever is written cannot be erased, because the whole is solidified in predestination: nor can any event change what that supreme providence has decreed.

II. However, no light difficulty arises on account of certain Biblical texts which seem to abolish the stated opinion and to construct the possibility of erasure. Of these, there are primarily four which follow: Exod. 32. vers. 32, Psalm 69. v. 29, Apoc. 3. vers. 5, chap. 22. v. 19. Therefore, necessity itself demands of us that some things be added concerning the sense and true understanding of them.

III. THE FIRST PASSAGE Exod. 32. v. 32 has it thus: If you do not, blot me out of your book which you have written. To which the Lord responded, v. 33: Whoever has sinned against me, I will blot him out of my book. Now, the prayer of Moses is described there after the μοσχολατρείαν of the Jews. For God, on account of this great sin, had threatened the destruction and total erasure of the people, v. 10. Moses, about to pray against this punishment, breaks out into those words, verse 31: Either forgive them, or blot me out of your book. Now, indeed, if erasure were absolutely impossible, that certainly Moses would by no means have proposed the condition. And even if his speech is considered to be that of one unthinking, yet the same cannot be affirmed of the Lord's response without impiety, for He says, 'I will blot out him who has sinned.' Now, I ask, what kind of threat will that be, if no one can ever be blotted out, nor can be blotted out?

IV. Moreover, various interpretations of this text are circulated. 1. Rabbi Solomon Iarchi explains it as the book of the law, from which Moses asked that his name be blotted out, preferring that the memory of the deeds performed by him be removed by deletion, rather than the people be destroyed. But in truth, not God Himself, but Moses wrote the book of the law; although He inspired it: However, this discourse is about the book which God wrote, and indeed even before the law was committed to writing; and therefore Moses does not understand the book of the law to be written at that time, but another already written before.

V. 2. Augustine, in question 147 on Exodus, says that Moses, out of a certain immense security of divine familiarity, interpellated God with such reasoning: 'Either You forgive them this sin, or blot me out of Your book: but do not blot me out of Your book, in which You have inscribed me with an indelible character: therefore forgive them this sin.' This kind of argumentation is confirmed by Sixtus, book 3 of the Bibliotheca, p. 129, by that rule of the dialecticians: 'From a disjunctive whole, an argument holds affirmatively with the destruction of one part to the other part. Just as if we say, It is necessary that the soul be either mortal or immortal. But it is not mortal. Therefore it is immortal.' Although Moses' petition can be explained in such a way to some extent, a scruple nevertheless remains regarding the Lord's response, categorically saying: 'Whoever has sinned, him I will blot out.' It must therefore be explained how this threat has a place, if the writing of the book is indelible.

VI. 3. Bernard, in sermon 12 on the Song of Songs, writes that Moses, by that deletion, did not understand exclusion from glory, but rather asked that he not be introduced into the land alone without his people, just as if a poor woman, invited to the banquet of a rich man on the condition that she leave at home the little infant who is crying and troublesome, should give the answer that she would rather fast than, having abandoned a dear pledge, dine alone with the rich man. But, even if this were most certainly the intention of Moses: the possibility of deletion is nevertheless presupposed, which is established primarily by the response of God; so that in this way, through this ἐπίγνωσιν, the difficulty is increased rather than removed.

VII. 4. Rupert, in book 3 on Exodus, writes that Moses wished by these words to convince God to forgive the people, and that he used such an argument: If you do not forgive them this sin, blot me out of your book. The reason: because I too am a sinful man. If, therefore, you do not forgive sins to those who sin, but blot them out of the book of life, it follows that I, a sinner, should also be blotted out of your book. Since you will by no means do the latter, the former ought not to happen either. But besides the fact that the speech of Moses is not conditional, but disjunctive, the difficulty nevertheless remains concerning the possible deletion, especially because of the words of the Lord: He who has sinned, him I will blot out. For this proposition is categorical; and it seems to imply that just as it is possible for someone to sin, so also it is possible for him to be blotted out again from the book of life.

IIX. 5. Nicolaus Lyranus says that just as the Savior, according to the will of the sensitive part fearing death, asked that the cup of the passion be transferred from him, which the rational will most ardently desired: so Moses, according to the desire of the lower part of the soul, asked God to be blotted out of the book of life, which, however, according to the higher portion of the soul, he did not wish to happen, explaining by this prayer not what the mind itself, consenting to God, wanted, but what the will of the flesh itself, sympathizing with its own flesh, that is, the people, desired. But 1. The comparison is false, that the lower and higher power fought in Christ. For it is natural for the whole man, not only for the sense, to flee death. Wherefore the wills differed rather, in a certain respect, the divine and human will were in agreement, yet in such a way that the latter would willingly submit itself to the former. 2. If Moses, following the appetite of the flesh, sought deletion, shall we also think that God responded carnally, by saying: Whoever has sinned, him I will blot out.

IX. 6. Alphonsus, Bishop of Ávila, in his Commentary on Exodus, teaches that this statement is not to be understood according to the simple meaning of the word, but according to a hyperbolic trope by which we are accustomed to express the most ardent desire for a thing requested, saying: Either grant me this, or I shall die. This trope Rachel used when she said to her husband: Give me children, otherwise I shall die, Genesis 30, verse 1. But even if a hyperbole is placed in the speech of Moses, it does not have a place in the threat of the Lord. For a hyperbole says more than is in the reality, a thing which, regarding divine threats—which are always most certain and true in every respect—far be it from us to think, let alone affirm.

X. Thus, therefore, having set aside those expositions which do not have the appearance of truth, we shall now bring forward those which seem probable, and which neither do violence to the text nor impinge upon the analogy of faith. There are, however, two main categories of them. For some explain it concerning the book of life, others concerning another. And indeed, if we have a difficult adversary who wishes to conclude from this statement either mutability or the universality of Election, we shall not undeservedly urge him to demonstrate first that the passage cannot be understood as referring to any book other than the book of life, which will be most difficult for him to prove. For there is no addition or restriction in the text, but a simple and bare appellation of a book: Whence, therefore, will anyone provide proof that it must necessarily be taken concerning βιβλίῳ ζωῆς? Therefore, we are not moved by the consequences which are connected from it, since the passage is obscure and its interpretation doubtful, since also concerning another than the book of life it may be understood without absurdity.

* 1. Moreover, I find three expositions of those who interpret it as something other than the βιβλίῳ of life. 1. Some take it to be the book of temporal life, because Moses wished to die sooner than to behold the destruction of the Israelites before his eyes. This indeed displeases Chrysostom in his book On the Compunction of the Heart, and book 3 On Providence, and homily 16 on the Epistle to the Romans. It is approved, however, by Jerome, who in question 9 to Algasia writes expressly: that Moses, out of charity toward his people, did not wish to be blotted out of the book of life forever, but for the present, not in spirit, but in the flesh, that is, by bodily death. The same seems to be the opinion of Euthymius, in Psalms 68 and 138, while he considers that Moses spoke of the universal book of providence, and thus of a violent and accelerated removal from the land of the living. And this can in some way be established from the text. For God had threatened the sudden slaughter of the whole people, and He expresses this very thing through the word 'blot out,' verse 10: 'Let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation.' That by 'blotting out' here is primarily denoted a sudden and universal slaughter, hardly anyone would deny. Moses therefore retains this very phrase in his intercession, and as it were repeats it in this sense: Lord, You said that You would blot out or kill Your people, but forgive this sin, I pray, or if You will not, and desire to blot them out entirely, blot me out rather, or kill me suddenly. I know indeed that You have written a book, in which all my days are recorded, but blot me out from the number of the living, and break off all the remaining portion of my life this very day, only that Your people may live, and such a miserable slaughter may not occur. But there the Lord answers; Whosoever hath sinned against me, him will I blot out of my book, that is, him will I punish with a violent and swift death, not otherwise than in Ezekiel 18, verse 19, it is said: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father: The soul that sinneth, it shall die. Thus all things in the text cohere most excellently, nor

Latin:

I. Cùm consilia & decreta Dei sint ἀμεταμέλητα,

Rom. 11. v. 29. vtique & inscriptio in librum vitæ erit immutabilis, siquidem ab electione minimè differt. Quem igitur Deus viuentium libro semel adscripsit, is semper adscriptus manet; quem prædestinauit, hunc certo glorificabit, iuxta auream illam Apostoli catenam, Rom. 8. v. 30. Et huc vicissim spectat illud Prophetæ, Dan. 12. v. 1. Saluabitur omnis in vitæ libro scriptus. Et Apostoli Apoc. 20. v. 12 Qui non est scriptus, missus est in stagnum ignis. Ergò è contrario sensu adscripti omnes saluantur; nec in stagnum ignis detruduntur, ex quo sponte fluit illud quòd è libro vitę nemo deleatur. Nam si possibilis foret deletio, non saluarentur omnes inscripti, & neque electio Dei immutabilis, neque decreta eius essent ἀμεταμέλητα, quæ omnia sunt absurda: & Scripturis contraria. Hinc Cassiodorus rectè pronunciauit; Liber notitiæ Dei est inuiolabilis firmáque sententia: Ibi quot scribitur, deleri non potest, quod totum in prædestinatione solidatum: nec vllus euentus mutáre potest, quod illa suprema decreuit prouidentia.

II. Non autem leuis hic difficultas oritur, ob quosdam textus Biblicos, qui dictam sententiam tollere, & deletionis possibilitatem adstruere videntur. Horū imprimis sunt quatuor, qui sequuntur Exod. 32. vers. 32. Psalm. 69. v. 29. Apoc. 3. vers. 5. cap. 22. v. 19. De sensu igitur & vera illorum intelligentia vt quædam addantur, ipsa necessitas à nobis efflagitat.

III. PRIMVS LOCVS Exod. 32. v. 32. sic habet; Si non facis, dele me de libro tuo, quam scripsisti. Cui respondebat Dominus, v. 33. Qui peccauerit mihi, delebo eum de libro meo. Describitur autem ibi Mosis oratio post μοσχολατρείαν Iudæorum. Deus enim ob grande hoc peccatum minatus erat interitum & omnimodam populi deletionem v. 10. Hanc pœnam deprecaturus Moses in verba illa erupit vers. 31. Aut dimitte illis, aut dele me libro tuo. Iam verò si prorsus esset impossibilis litura, illam vtiq; conditionem Moses nequaquam proposuisset. Et si maximè locutio eius pro incogitanti habeatur; de responso tamen Domini sine impietate idem affirmari nequit, eum Delebo, inquit, qui peccaverit. Iam qualis quæso erit ista comminatio, si nullus vnquam vel deletus vel deleri potest?

IV. Variæ autem huius textus interpretationes circumferuntur, 1. Rabbi Salomon Iarchi de libro legis exponit, ex quo nomen suum deleri petierit Moses, malens memoriam rerum à se gestarum perpetuam deletione tolli, quàm populum perdi. At verò legis librum nõ Deus ipse, sed Moses scripsit; quanquam ille inspiravit: Hic autem sermo est de libro, quem Deus scripsit & quidem iam ante legem in literas relatam, ideoque Moses non intelligit librum legis tum temporis adhuc scribendum, sed alium iam antè scriptum.

V. 2. Augustinus quæstione 147. in Exodum ait, Mosen ex ingenti quadam divina familiaritatis securitate tali Deum ratiocinatione interpellasse: Aut dimittis eis hanc noxam, aut dele me de libro tuo: sed non deletis me de libro tuo, in quo me indelebili charactere conscripsisti: Duxit ergo ergo eis hanc noxam. Quod argumentationis genus confirmat Sixtus l. 3. Bibliothecæ p. 129. regulâ illâ dialecticorũ: A toto disiunctivo, affirmativè cum destructione unius partis ad alteram parte valet argumentum, Veluti si dicamus, Necesse est animã aut esse mortale aut immortalem. Atqui mortalis non est. Igitur immortalis. Licèt autẽ Mosis petitio sic exponi quodammodo possit, scrupulus tamen manet reliquus quoad Domini responsum categoricè dicentis: Qui peccaverit, eum delebo: Explicandum igitur est, quomodo hæc comminatio locum habeat, si scriptura libri sit indelebilis.

VI. 3. Bernhardus serm. 12. in Canticum scribit, Mosen per illam deletionem non intellexisse exclusionem à gloria, sed potius petiisse, ne solus absque gente sua introduceretur in terram, non secus acPaupercula mulier inuitata ad prandiũ diuitis sub hac conditione, vt infantulum, qui plorat & molestus est, relinquat domi, responsum det, malle se jejunare, quam exposito pignore charo, sola prandere cum diuite. Verùm, si maximè fuerit hæc Mosis intentio: præsupponitur tamen deletionis possibilitas, quæ imprimis responsione Dei stabilitur; vt ita per ἐπίγνωσιν istam difficultas magis augeatur, quam tollatur.

VII. 4. Rupertus l. 3. in Exod. scribit, Mosen voluisse his verbis conuincere Deum, vt ignosceret populo, eumque tali vsum fuisse argumento: Si non dimittis eis hanc noxam, dele me de libro tuo. Ratios quia & ego homo peccator sum. Si ergo peccantibus peccata non dimittis, sed eos deles de libro vitæ, consequens est, vt etiam ego peccator de libro tuo delear. Quod posterius cùm minimè fissurum sis, nec prius illud fieri debet. Sed præterquam quòd locutio Mosis non sit conditionalis, sed disjunctiua, manet nihilominus difficultas de possibili deletione præsertim ob verba Domini: Qui peccauerit eum delebo. Hæc enim propositio categorica est; & videtur innuere, quod sicut fieri potest, vt quis peccet, ita etiam fieri posse, vt ex libro vitæ iterum deleatur.

IIX. 5. Nicolaus Lyranus ait, quòd quemadmodum Seruator secundùm voluntatem partis sensitiuæ mortem reformidantis, petiit à se tranferri calicem passionis, quem voluntas rationalis ardentissimè appetebat: Sic Moses juxtá desiderium partis animæ inferioris petiit à Deo deleri de lib. vitæ, quod tamẽ secundùm portionem animæ superiorem fieri nolebat, explicans hac precatione, non quid ipsa mens Deo consentiens vellet, sed quid ipsa carnis voluntas, carni suæ, hoc est, populo compatiens desideraret. At. 1. Falsum est simile, potentiam inferiorem & superiorem in Christo pugnasse. Homini enim toti, non soli sensui naturale est, mortem fugere. Quare discrepabant potiùs certo respectu voluntas diuina & humana, ita tamen, vt hæc illi lubenter se subiiceret. 2. Si Moses carnis appetitum sequens deletionem petijt, num & Deum carnaliter respondisse putabimus, dicendo; Qui peccauerit eum delebo.

IX. 6. Alphonsus Episcopus Abulensis Comm. in Exod. docet, hoc dictum non esse intelligeudum iuxta simplicem vocis significationem, sed secundum hyperbolicum tropum quo ardentissimum efflagitatæ rei desiderium exprimere solemnus, dicentes: Aut hoc mihi concede, aut moriar. Quo tropo vsa est Rachel, cùm ad virum suum diceret: Da mihi liberos alioquin moriar, Genes. 30. vers. 1. Verùm si maximè in Mosis sermone ponatur hyperbole, non tamen locum illa habet in comminatione Domini. Nam hyperbole plus dicit, quàm in re est. id quod de minis diuinis semper certissimis: & vndiquaque verissimis absit vt cogitemus, nedum affirmemus.

X. Sic ergò sepositis expositionibus illis; quæ speciem non habent, istas nunc afferemus, quæ probabiles videntur, & neque textui vim faciunt, neque in analogiam fidei impingunt. Duo autem sunt illarum suinma genera. Quidam enim de libro vitæ, quidam de alio exponunt. Et sanè si morosum habeamus aduersarium, qui ex hoc dicto vel mutabilitatem, vel vniuersalitatem Electionis velit conclusam, non immerito ipsum vrgebimus, vt demonstret prius non posse locum illum de alio, quàm vitæ libro intelligi, quod ipsi erit probatu difficilimum. Nam nulla habetur in textu additio, aut restrictio, sed simplex & nuda libri appellatio: Vnde igitur quis fidem faciet, necessariò de βιβλίῳ ζωῆς accipiendum esse? Proinde non mouemur consequentijs, quæ nectuntur inde, cùm locus sit obscurus, eiusque interpretatio dubia, cùm & de alio quàm vitæ libro sine absurditate queat intelligi.

* 1. Tres autem expositiones inuenio illorum, qui de alio quàm vitæ βιβλίῳ interpretantur. 1. Quidam accipiunt de libro vitæ temporalis, quòd Moses mortem citiùs obire, quàm interitum Israëlitarum coràm intueri voluerit. Displicet quidem hoc Chrysostomo lib. de compunct. cordis, & lib. 3. de prouidentia, & hom. 16. in epist. ad Rom. Probatur tamen Hieronymo, qui quæst. 9. ad Algasiam expressè scribit: Mosen ex charitate erga populum suum noluisse deleri de libro vitæ in perpetuum, sed in præsentiarum, non in spiritu, sed in carne, hoc est, per mortem corpoream. Eadem videtur esse Euthymij sententia, in Psalm. 68. & 138. dum Mosen de vniuersali libro prouidentiæ, adeóque de violenta & accelerata è terris viuentium abreptione, locutum esse existimat. Et potest hoc quodammodo ex textu stabiliri. Nam Deus erat comminatus subitaneam totius populi interfectionem, & hanc ipsam per delendi verbum exprimit, vers. 10. Dimitte me, vt irascatur furor meus, & deleam eos, faciamque te in gentem magnam. Hîc per deletionem imprimis notari repentinam & vniuersalem stragem, vix quisquam negauerit. Moses igitur hanc ipsam phrasin in intercessione sua retinet, & q. repetit hoc sensu: Domine dixisti, te deleturũ vel interfecturum esse populum tuum sed dimitte precor hanc culpam, vel si nolis, & omninò delere cupias, me potiùs dêle, vel subitò interfice. Scio equidem te librum scripsisse, in quo consignati sunt omnes dies mei, sed dele me ex numero viuentium, & omnem vitæ meæ portionem reliquam, hoc ipso die abrumpe, tantùm vt viuat populus tuus, nec strages tàm miserabilis fiat. Ibi verò Dominus respondet; Qui peccauerit mihi, illum delebo de libro meo, hoc est, illum violentâ citâque morte puniam, non secus atque Ezech. 18. vers. 19. dicitur: Filius non portabit iniquitatem patris: Anima quæ peccauerit ipsa morietur. Sic omnia in textu optimè cohærent, nec


### Question VI. Whether anyone inscribed in the book of life can be erased from it…: I see no absurdity that could arise from this interpretation

I see no absurdity that could arise from this interpretation.

XII. 2. Others explain it as the book or catalog of heroes and illustrious men, which Cajetan in Exodus calls the book of leadership; Burgensis, the book of the just. For they write that it was established in the divine mind, and in it, as if most diligently inscribed in a book, who and how many or what kind of Princes, Leaders, and Kings there shall be among mortals in this life. Therefore, because God had said, v. 10, 'Let me alone, that I may blot them out, and I will make of thee a great nation,' Moses understood from this that God had written him in the book of leadership, indeed in such a way that even if the Jewish people were utterly destroyed, God would nevertheless establish him as prince over a great nation. Wherefore he asks that He either forgive the sin or blot him out of the book of leadership, signifying by this very thing that he does not wish to be the prince of another nation if this people is consumed. This interpretation is by no means absurd, although it does not seem to square so well with the response of God. For it does not sufficiently appear how one is blotted out from the book of leadership if he has sinned. Becanus, however, explains this in tract. 1. in 1. Thom. c. 14. q. 8. p. 168, and brings forward that sense: 'I do not wish to blot anyone out of the book of illustrious men, unless he has sinned.' Therefore, the sum of this ἐξηγήσεως is this: 'Lord, if You wish to utterly abolish the memory of this people, blot me rather out of the book and catalog of illustrious men, so that my name may no longer be celebrated among men.' But the Lord answers: 'Whoever has sinned, him I will blot out, his memory I will abolish, nor will I judge him worthy to be ascribed to the catalog of heroes, so that his name may be proclaimed among mortals.' And everyone understands that if this sense is held, no ἄτοπον follows from it in turn.

XIII. 3. Some distinguish between the book of present grace and future glory. The book of grace is the catalog of the reborn who are pleasing to God. The book of glory is the catalog of the elect and those certainly to be saved. They say, therefore, that those inscribed in the book of glory or life through eternal

Predestination cannot be blotted out. Those inscribed by the book of grace through justice are often blotted out through mortal sin, Lombard, book 3, dist. 31. Bonaventure in the said dist. dub. 2, fol. 401, face 1. Becanus, tract. 1, c. 14, qu. 8, p. 168. Suarez, tract. 2, book 1, c. 20, p. 210. Hugo Cardinalis on Ps. 138. And they draw here the distinction of Thomas from part 1, qu. 24, art. 3, between a simple inscription, which is for eternal life, and is immutable; and an inscription in a certain respect, when someone is referred to the catalog of the reborn, from which he is blotted out again through impenitence. Pererius, book 15, on Dan. p. 891, thinks that the figure of this thing was that book shown to Ezekiel, c. 2 v. 10, written within and without. He says the interior writing contains the elect, who are certainly saved; the exterior, the reborn, who for some time are in the grace of God, but through sin they fall out in turn. Some refer to this that of Durand, book 3, dist. 31, q. 1, p. 600, that the book of life is distinguished into two pages, of which one is called the page of present justice, but the other the page of eternal predestination. From the former someone can be blotted out, from the latter he cannot. But what Durand calls the pages of one book, he ought rather to have called two different books.

XIV. The aforesaid can indeed be applied quite conveniently to the Mosaic text. God threatens the subtraction of grace and the blotting out of the people; Moses, interceding, says: Either forgive, or blot me out, i.e., rather subtract your grace from me, expunge my name from the book of your love and favor in place of my brothers; I wish to be rejected and separated from your grace. Since this had proceeded from excessive affection, the Lord responded: Not so: I do not deny my grace to the innocent, but whoever has sinned, him I will blot out from my book, from the catalog of the just, to which I ascribed him on account of piety, but he is deservedly expunged on account of subsequent impiety and malice.

XV. These are those three expositions by which the book, from which Moses wishes to be blotted out, is understood not as the book of life, but as some other, all so compared so that they say nothing alien either to the text or to the analogy of faith, and therefore they are deservedly opposed to those who contend that the words of Moses concerning predestination and its mutability must necessarily be understood. XVI. Even if it is posited ex abundanti that the discourse there is specifically and properly about the book of life so-called, which some prove, partly from the phrase and manner of speaking, partly from the Lord's response, where respect is had to sin, the wages of which is death, the opposite of eternal life; it is nevertheless not necessary that we concede the possibility of deletion or the mutability of election. For Moses's locution is in a certain way hypothetical, while he does not seek deletion from the book of life absolutely, but with a condition understood, if indeed it pleases God, and if it is possible that one might be deleted again. Not otherwise than Paul says in Rom. 9. v. 2, I myself could wish to be anathema from Christ for my brethren, which word he certainly did not utter out of blind love, but deliberately, as is clear from v. 1. Nor did he understand by anathema temporal death, but rather eternal, and thus he noted perpetual rejection, but not except hypothetically, in this sense: If it were possible that the Jews might be saved through my perdition, I would not refuse this, but if the option were given, I would rather choose it; for exuberant charity desires even impossible things, as our Blessed Luther speaks. The same condition lies hidden in Moses's intercession, just as in all works of charity this condition underlies: if it so seems, if it is possible, etc. And Augustine looked to this in Psalm 77, writing: He intercedes, more prepared to be deleted for them than them, knowing that he is doing this before the merciful one: who, since he would in no way delete him, would also spare them on account of him. And again in Psalm 105. Secure in the justice of God, which could not delete him, Moses obtained mercy, that He might not delete those whom He could justly delete. XVII. But as far as the response of God pertains, the same hypothesis must be understood: just as Moses had requested, the Lord answered thus: I will blot out him who has sinned, namely, if it were possible that the inscribed or the elect should finally sin. Not otherwise than as it is read in Matthew 24, v. 24: False prophets will give great signs and wonders, so that even the elect might be led into error, but ei dunatòn, if it were possible. out the inscribed only if they sin, namely, if it is possible that they should sin and die in impenitence. This condition can also be expressed thus: If I were about to blot anyone out of my book, then I would blot out him who has sinned, not the innocent.

XVIII. Finally, we also add this, that it is a customary phrase of Scripture to explain a negation by way of an affirmation, whence the rule has drawn its origin: Sometimes affirmative words and nouns are put for their negated opposites. Thus God is said to hate him whom He does not love in a singular way, to harden when He does not soften, to blind when He does not enlighten. Thus we must hate our parents in comparison to Christ, that is, not love them more than is just, Luke 14, v. 26. In this way, therefore, the words of Moses can also be explained, namely, that by the affirmative verb 'to blot out,' he understands the negated opposite, 'not to write,' so that the sense is: If you do not forgive the fault, place me in their stead and never insert me into the catalog of the elect, which you have written from eternity. The Lord, however, answered, 'I will blot out him,' that is, I will never number him among the elect, who has sinned and by his final impenitence has rendered himself unworthy of life. These things can be illustrated from Ps. 69, v. 29. where 'to be blotted out' and 'not to be written' are joined as synonyms, concerning which more shortly in the following.

XIX. These responses, however, although they may seem somewhat violent and alien to the letter of the text, nevertheless declare the mind of Moses most excellently, and in more obscure passages interpretations ought to be conformed according to the analogy of faith, lest if we insist too much on the letter, it should suffer detriment.

XX. Therefore, to conclude, the sum of what has been said is: 1. That the Mosaic text is obscure and various

ἐξυγῆαί to admit, for which reason a doubtful question cannot be decided from it. 2. That it can be explained probably concerning something other than the book of life, if no determination is added, whether that be called the book of grace, or the book of illustrious men, or the book of temporal life, which last interpretation approaches most closely to the text and the mind of Moses, who wished to take upon himself the death threatened to the Jews. 3. Even if it be taken concerning the book of life, yet the mutability of inscription or predestination is not necessarily inferred from it, but the words ought to be understood either hypothetically or negatively.

XXI. THE SECOND PASSAGE exists in Psalm 69, v. 29. Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written with the righteous. A twofold exposition of this passage is usually brought forward: 1. That the latter words are ἐξήγητικά of the former; so that to be blotted out is the same as not to be written. And to this point tends the distinction of others between a privative deletion, which presupposes an inscription, and a negative one, which is nothing other than a denied inscription, or the negation of an inscription, Gesner in Psalm 69, p. 527. When, therefore, the wicked are said to be blotted out from the book of the living, it happens through negation, insofar as they are never written with the righteous, not through privation, as if they had been previously inscribed and afterwards erased.

XXII. 2. That inscription is considered in two ways, both κατ' ἀλήθειαν, according to the truth of the matter; and κατα δόξαν, or according to the opinion of men. Those who are truly inscribed in the book of life from eternity by predestination are never blotted out. But those who seem to themselves or others to be marked in that ὀρανογραφίᾳ, these are said to be blotted out when it is clearly shown that their hope, and the opinion of others, was vain and false. And in this sense the Psalmist says: Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, i.e., by the infliction of the punishments which they have deserved, let it be made known to all that they were never entered into the catalog of the elect, even though they may have boasted of this very thing, and others they have persuaded: not otherwise than as the Savior says, He who does not have, from him will be taken away even what he has, that is, what he thinks he has. Matt. 13, v 12. c. 25. v. 29.

XXIII. Augustine hands down this interpretation, Vol. 8, in Enarrations on the Psalm according to the Latin version 68, whose words are these: Brothers, we ought not to understand that God writes anyone in the book of life and afterwards deletes him. If a man said, What I have written, I have written, concerning the title in which it was written, King of the Jews: does God write anyone and delete him? He is foreknowing, He predestined all before the foundation of the world, who were to reign with His Son in eternal life, He wrote them down, the book of life contains them. And in the Apocalypse it is written: They will consent to him, that is, to the Antichrist, all who are not written in the book of life. Therefore, those who have been written in the book of life will not consent to him. How, therefore, are those deleted from the book of life who were never written in it? This was said according to their hope, because they thought themselves to be written there. What is it to be deleted from the book of life? Unless it also becomes clear to them that they are not in the book; just as the Jews, who hoped that they were written in the book of God as if by the merit of their own righteousness, to whom the Lord said: search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life: when their condemnation has been brought even to their own knowledge, they will be deleted from the book of the living, that is, they will acknowledge that they are not written there. For the following verse explains what was said: And let them not be written with the righteous. I said, therefore, let them be deleted, according to their hope. But according to your equity, what do I say? Let them not be written. Thus far Augustine.

XXIV. These things can be illustrated by similar phrases often occurring in Scripture, which not rarely speaks κατά τό ένδοξον, so that it says things or men are such as they seem to be, not such as they are in reality. Thus Christ says in Matt. 8. 12. that the children of the kingdom will be cast into outer darkness. He calls them children of the kingdom according to opinion, because they seemed to be such, but were not. Thus Matt. 9. v. 12. I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners. Here the Pharisees are named righteous κατά δόξαν, because they seemed such to themselves and others. The same happens in 1 Cor. 8. v. 5. and Gal. 4. v. 4.

XXV. Since, therefore, it is familiar to the Scriptures to speak παθολογούσης (in a way that attributes human passions to God), nothing prevents that deletion from the book of life from being explained in a similar way. Those, therefore, who seem to be inscribed in the βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς (book of life), while they conduct themselves as if they were inscribed, bearing before them an external appearance of holiness, just as the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees, of whom there is discourse primarily in the Psalm, and who were considered the chief members of the people, these very ones are said to be deleted when it becomes known from the outcome that they were never truly inscribed or included in the number of the predestined. For as the book and the writing, so also the deletion is spoken ἀνθρωποπαθῶς (in a way befitting human passions), but it ought to be understood θεοπρεπῶς (in a way befitting God). Human deletion indeed presupposes an inscription: but divine deletion denotes a simple negation, and therefore it is not permitted to argue from the former to the reason of the latter, since the former is spoken properly, the latter metaphorically, and it is necessarily explained according to the ἀναλογίαν (analogy) of faith. If, however, you maintain that those who were truly and really (ἀληθῶς καὶ ὄντως) inscribed are deleted in actual fact, that analogy is undermined, the immutability of election, which the Scriptures assert everywhere, is denied, and either the knowledge or the power of God is disparaged, as if He had either deserted His true citizens or could not have led them to the preordained end.

XXVI. In place of a colophon, the response of Mr. Dr. Gesner may be noted, who in his final disputation on Daniel, thesis 144 and 145, asserts that the impious are said to be inscribed in the book of life in a triple respect. 1. By reason of the means, insofar as not life itself, but the cause of life, pertains to them, which is the mercy of God, the merit of Christ, and the gratuitous calling. 2. By reason of their own persuasion and the estimation of men, of which we have just spoken. 3. By reason of their external conversation in the Church, because they are truly mixed with the faithful and the elect, so that they cannot easily be distinguished. They are therefore said to be deleted when it is manifest that they have despised the means of salvation, have falsely boasted of holiness, and have never been living members of the Church.

XXVII. Nor is the interpretation of those who understand it concerning the book of grace, in which all the reborn and just are recorded, entirely inappropriate. For the text seems to speak of those who are actually living, namely spiritually through grace, and not so much of those who are one day to live in heaven through glory. Whence they are called just, that is, justified and regenerated. The Psalmist therefore judges that the impious are to be blotted out from that number of the justified and from the book of grace, since by their impiety they have rendered themselves unworthy of divine love.

XIIX. THE THIRD PASSAGE exists in Apoc. 3 v. 5. He who overcomes, he shall be clothed in white garments, and I will not blot out his name from the book of life. From which some gather that those inscribed can be blotted out, otherwise this promise would be superfluous. But the argument lacks strength, since the sense of the Apostolic saying is very plain: He who overcomes, thus shall he certainly be saved. For this is hinted at by 'not being blotted out.' Nor is the promise superfluous, since for that very reason the Elect are not blotted out, because persevering faith and through this most certain salvation is promised to them. Nor do we deny that the Apostle simultaneously indicates the contrary, namely that everyone who has not overcome will be blotted out: But how this blotting out is to be understood, we have hitherto said abundantly enough, namely either concerning the book of grace or the book of glory, but not through privation, but through negation and the manifestation of a denied inscription.

XXIX. Finally, the FOURTH and last passage is had in Apoc. last v. 19. If anyone shall diminish from the words of the book of this prophecy, God shall take away his part from the book of life, and from the holy city, and from those things which are written in this book. Now if the blotting out were impossible, what kind of threat would this be? But this objection also has been satisfied in the preceding. For the same phrase recurs, which also obtains the same sense as the passages explained hitherto. For the Apostle speaks of heretics and false brothers, who corrupt the Scripture

Latin:

vllum video absurdum, quod ex interpretatione hac suboriri queat.

XII. 2. Alij exponunt de libro vel catalogo heroum & illustrium virorum, quem Caietanus in Exod. vocat librum principatus; Burgensis, librum iustorum. Scribunt enim, statutum esse in mente diuina, & in ipsa, tanquam in libro diligentissime exaratum, qui & quot vel quales, in hac vita futuri sint inter mortales Principes, Duces ac Reges. Quia ergo Deus dixerat, v. 10. Dimitte me, vt deleam eos, te autem faciam in gentem magnam, intellexit inde Moses, Deum scripsisse eum in libro principatus, ita quidem, vt si maxime destrueretur populus Iudaicus, Deus nihilominus ipsum sit constituturus principe super gentem magnam. Quocirca petit, vt vel condonet peccatum, vel deleat ipsum de libro principatus, significans hoc ipso, qd nolit esse princeps alterius gentis, si populus iste consumatur. Est q3 haec interpretatio minime absurda, quamuis ad responsionem Dei, non adeo quadrare videatur. Non n. satis apparet, quomodo e libro principatus quis deleatur, si peccauerit. Becanus tamen hoc explicat tract. 1. in 1. Thom. c. 14. q. 8. p. 168. & sensum illum affert; Non volo quenquam delere de lib. virorum illustrium, nisi qui peccauerit. Proinde summa istius ἐξηγήσεως haec est, Domine si prorsus abolere vis memoriam huius populi, me potius dele ex libro & catalogo virorum illustrium, ne nomen meum amplius celebretur inter homines. Sed respondet Dominus: Qui peccauerit, illum delebo, eius memoriam abolebo, nec dignum iudicabo, qui catalogo heroum adscribatur, vt eius nomen inter mortales praedicetur. Et hic sensus si teneatur nullum vicissim sequi inde ἄτοπον quiuis intelligit.

XIII. 3. Quidam distinguunt inter librum praesentis gratiae, & futurae gloriae. Liber gratiae est catalogus renatorum Deo placentium. Liber gloriae, est catalogus electorum & certo saluandorum. Dicunt ergo, libro gloriae vel vitae inscriptos per aeternam

Prædest. deleri non posse. Inscriptos a lib. gratiæ per iustitiam, sæpè deleri per pecc. mortale, Lombardus l. 3. dist. 31. Bonavent. in dictam dist. dub. 2. fol. 401. fac. 1. Becanus tract. 1. c 14. qu. 8. p. 168. Suarez tract. 2. l. 1. c. 20. p. 210. Hugo Cardinalis in Pf. 138. Et huc trahunt distinctionem Thomæ ex parte 1. qu. 24. art. 3. inter inscriptionem simplicem, quæ sit ad vitam æternam, estq́; immutabilis; & inter inscriptionem secundum quid, quando in catalogum renatorum quis refertur, ex quo per impœnitentiam iterum deletur. Pererius l. 15. in Dan. p. 891. huius rei figuram putat fuisse lib. illum Ezechieli ostensum, c. 2 v. 10. intus forisq́; scriptum. Interiorem scripturam ait continere electos, qui certò saluantur; Exteriorem renatos, qui ad aliquod tempus sunt in gratia Dei, per pecc. verò illa vicissim excidunt. Quidam huc referunt istud Durandi l. 3. dist. 31. q. 1. p. 600 librum vitæ distingui in duas paginas, quarum vna dicatur pagina præsentis iustitiæ, altera verò pagina prędestinationis æternę. Ex illa aliquem deleri posse, ex hac non posse. Sed quæ Durandus vnius libri paginas dicit, duos potiùs diuersos libros appellare debuisset.

XIV. Possunt v. prædicta satis commodè applicari ad textum Mosaicum. Deus subtractionē gratiæ & deletionem populi minatur, Moses intercedens ait: Aut dimitte, aut me dele, h. e. mihi potiùs gratiam tuā subtrahe, meum nomē ex lib. amoris & fauoris tui expūge fratrū meorū loco, ego reiectus & à gratia tua separatus esse volo. Quod cùm ex nimio affectu esset profectum respondit Dominus: Non ita: innocenti meam ego gratiam non denego, sed qui peccauerit, illum delebo ex libro meo, ex catalogo iustorum, cui eum adscripsi ob pietatem, sed meritò expungitur ob impietatem & malitiam subsequentem.

XV. Hæ sunt tres illæ expositiones, quibus liber, ex quo Moses deleri vult, non de vitæ libro, sed alio quodam accipitur, omnes ita comparatæ, vt nihil vel à textu, vel ab analogia fidei alienum dicant, ideoque meritò ijs opponuntur, qui verba Mosis de prædestinatione, eiusque mutabilitate necessariò intelligenda esse contendunt. XVI. Quòd si maximè ponatur ex abundanti de libro vitæ specialiter & propriè sic dicto sermonem ibi fieri, quod nonnulli probant, partim ex phrasi & modo loquendi, partim ex responsione Domini, vbi fit respectus ad peccatum, cuius stipendium est mors vitæ æternæ opposita; necesse tamen non est, vt deletionis possibilitatem aut electionis mutabilitatem concedamus. Mosis n. locutio quodammodo est hypothetica, dum non petit deletionem ex vitæ libro absolutè, sed cum conditione subintellecta, si nimirum Deo placeat, & si possibile sit, vt quis iterum deleatur. Non secus atque Paulus ait Rom. 9. v, 2, Optarim ego ipse anathema esse à Christo pro fratribus meis, quod sanè verbum non ex cæco amore protulit, sed consultò, vt patet ex v. 1. nec mortem temporalem, sed potius æternam per anathema intellexit, adeoque perpetuam reiectionem notauit, non a. nisi hypotheticè, hoc sensu, Si possibile esset, vt per meam perditionem Iudæi salui fierent, neque hoc detrectarem, sed si optio daretur, potiùs eligerem; Charitas n. exuberans optat etiam impossibilia, vti loquitur B. noster Lutherus. Eadem conditio in Mosis intercessione delitescit, sicut in omnibus charitatis operibus subest hæc conditio, si ita videatur, si sit possibile &c. Et huc respexit Augustinus in Psalm. 77. scribens: Ille intercedit, paratior deleri pro ipsis, quàm ipsos, sciens apud misericordem se id agere: qui quoniam nullo modo deleret ipsum, etiam illis parceret propter ipsum. Et rursus in Psalm. 105. Securus Moses de iustitia Dei, quæ eum delere non posset impetrauit misericordiam, ne illos, quos iustè posset, deleret. XVII. Quod verò responsionem Dei attinet, eandem hypothesin subintelligi oportet: Prout enim Moses petierat, ita respondit Dominus: Illum delebo, qui peccaverit, nempè si fieri possit, vt inscripti vel electi finaliter peccent. Non secus atque Matth. 24. v. 24 legitur: Pseudoprophetæ dabunt signa magna & prodigia, ita, vt in errorem inducantur etiam electi, sed ei dunatòn si fieri possit. Pari modo Deus dicit, deleturum inscriptos non nisi peccantes, nèpè si possibile sit, vt peccent, & in impenitentia decedant. Conditio ista sic etiam efferri potest, Siquem deleturus essem ex libro meo, tùm illum delerem, qui peccauerit non innocentem.

XIIX. Tandem & hoc addimus, consuetam scripturæ phrasin esse, negationem per modum affirmationis explicare, vnde ortum traxit regula: Quandoque verba & nomina affirmantia pro negatis contrariis ponuntur. Sic Deus dicitur odio habere, quem singulariter non diligit, indurare, cùm non emollit, excæcare, cùm non illuminat. Sic debemus parentes odisse præ Christo, hoc est, plus iusto non diligere, Luc 14. v. 26. Hoc igitur modo & Mosis verba exponi queunt, quòd nempè per verbum affirmativum delere, intelligat contrarium negatum, non scribere, vt sensus sit: Si non dimittis culpam, me illorum loco poni & nunquam catalogo electorum, quem scripsisti ab æterno, insere. Dominus a. respondit, Illum delebo h. e. illum inter electos nunquam numerabo, qui peccaverit, suaque impœnitentiâ finali se vitâ indignum reddiderit. Possunt hæc illustrari ex Ps. 69. v. 29. vbi tanquàm synonyma coniunguntur, deleri, & non scribi, de quo mox plura in sequentibus.

XIX. Hæ autem responsiones quamuis videantur nonnihil violentę, & à literæ textus alienę, mētem tamen Mosis optimè declarant, & in locis obscurioribus interpretationes secundum fidei analogiam conformari debent, ne si literæ nimium insistamus, illa detrimentum capiat,

XX. Vt ergo concludamus summa dictorum est, 1. Textum Mosaicum esse obscurum & varias

ἐξυγῆαί admittere, quâ de cauffa quæstio dubia ex illo decidi nequit. 2. Exponi probabiliter posse de alio quàm vitæ libro, non sit addita determinatio, siue iam ille dicatur liber gratiæ, siue liber virorum illustrium, siue liber vitæ temporalis, quæ vltima interpretatio ad textum & mentem Mofis mortem Iudæis intentatam in se suscipere volentis, quàm proximè accedit. 3. Si maximè de libro vitæ accipiatur, non tamen necessario inde inscriptionis vel prædestinationis mutabilitas infertur, sed verba debent intelligi vel hypotheticè, vel negatiuè.

XXI. SECVNDVS LOCVS exstat Psalm. 69. v. 29. Deleantur de libro viuentium, & cum iustis non scribantur. Huius loci duplex solet afferri expositio, 1. Quòd verba posteriora sint ἐξήγητικά priorum; adeò vt deleri sit idem, quod non scribi. Et huc spectat aliorum distinctio inter deletionem priuatiuam, quæ præsupponit inscriptionem negatiuam, quæ nihil est aliud, quam negata inscriptio, vel inscriptionis negatio, Gesnerus in Psalm. 69. p. 527. Cùm igitur impij è libro viuentium dicuntur deleri, fit illud per negationem, quatenus cū iustis nunquam scribuntur, non per priuationē ac si prius inscripti, post iterum expuncti fuissent.

XXII. 2. Quod inscriptio dupliciter consideretur, tum κατ' ἀλήθειαν, quoad rei veritatem: tùm κατα δόξαν, vel secundum opinionem hominum. Qui libro vitæ ab æterno per prædestinationem verè adscripti sunt, nunquam delentur. Qui autem sibi vel alijs signati videntur in ista ὀρανογραφίᾳ, hi deleri dicuntur, cum vanam falsamque fuisse illorum spem, aliorum opinionem, luculenter ostenditur. Et hoc sensu Psaltes inquit: Deleantur de libro viuentium, h. e. per pœnarum, quas meruerunt, irrogationem omnibus notum fiat, nunquam istos in catalogum electorum relatos fuisse, vt maximè hoc ipsum iactitauerint, alijsque persuaserint: non secus atque Saluator dicit, Qui non habet, ab eo auferetur etiam quod habet, id est, quod se habere putat. Matth. 13, v 12. c. 25. v. 29.

XXIII. Tradit hanc interpretationem Augustinus, Tom. 8. in Enarr. Psalmi iuxta vers. Lat. 68. cuius haec sunt verba, Fratres, non debemus intelligegere, quod Deus quenquam scribat in librum vitae, & postea deleat ipsum. Si homo dixit, Quod scripsi, scripsi, de titulo, in quo scriptum erat, Rex Iudaeorum: Deus quenquam scribit & delet? Praescius est, praedestinauit omnes ante constitutionem mundi, regnaturos cum filio suo in vita aeterna, Flos conscripsit, ipsos continet liber vitae. Et in Apocalypsi scriptum est: Consentient illi, id est, Antichristo omnes, qui non sunt scripti in libro vitae. Ergo non ei consentient, quicunque in libro vitae scripti fuerint. Quomodo igitur de libro vitae delentur, qui in eo nunquam scripti sunt? Hoc dictum est secundum spem ipsorum, quia ibi se scriptos putabant. Quid est deleantur de libro vitae? Nisi etiam ipsis constet, non se in libro esse; Sicut Iudaei, qui sperabant se tanquam merito iustitiae suae in libro Dei esse scriptos, quibus dixit Dominus: scrutamini Scripturas, in quibus putatis vos vitam aeternam habere: cùm perducta fuerit damnatio eorum ad ipsorum etiam cognitionem, delebuntur de libro viuentium, id est, non ibi se scriptos esse agnoscant. Nam versus sequens exponit, quod dictum est: Et cum iustis non scribantur. Dixi ergo, deleantur, secundum spem eorum, Secundum autem aequitatem tuam quid dico? Non scribantur. Hactenus Aug.

XXIV. Illustrari haec possunt similibus phrasibus in Scriptura saepè occurrentibus, quae haut rarò loquitur κατά τό ένδοξον, ita vt tales esse dicat res vel homines, quales videtur esse, non quales reuera sunt. Sic Christus ait Matth. 8. 12. Filios regni eiectum iri in tenebras exteriores. Filios regni vocat secundum opinionem, quia videbantur tales esse, sed no erant. Sic Matth. 9. v. 12. Non veni vocare iustos, sed peccatores. Hic Pharisaei nucupantur iusti κατά δόξαν, quia sibi & alijs tales videbantur. Idem fit. 1. Cor. 8. v. 5. & Gal. 4. v. 4.

XXV. Cùm igitur Scripturis familiare sit, παθολογούσης loqui, nihil obstat, quò minus illa è libro vitæ deletio similiter exponi possit. Qui ergo videntur adscripti βιβλίῳ τῆς ζωῆς, dum ita se gerunt, ac si inscripti essent, externam sanctitatis speciem præ se ferentes, quemadmodum Pontifices, Scribæ & Pharisæi, de quibus imprimis sermo sit in Psalmo, & qui pro præcipuis populi membris habebantur, hi ipsi dicuntur deleri, cùm ex euentu innotescit, nunquam eos verè inscriptos, numerouè prædestinatorum inclusos fuisse. Nam vt liber & scriptio, sic & deletio ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dicitur, θεοπρεπῶς autem debet intelligi. Humanum quidem delere præsupponit inscriptionem: sed diuinum notat simplicem negationem, ideoque ab illa ad huius rationem non licet argumentari, siquidem illud propriè, hoc metaphoricè dicitur, & iuxta fidei ἀναλογίαν necessariò exponitur. Si verò statuas, re ipsa deleri, qui ante ἀληθῶς καὶ ὄντως inscripti erant, labefactatur analogia illa, negatur electionis immutabilitas, quam Scripturæ passim asserunt, & vel scientiæ, vel potentiæ Dei derogatur, quasi aut deseruisset veros ciues suos, aut non potuisset ad finem præordinatum ipsos perducere.

XXVI. Colophonis loco notari potest Dn. D. Gesneri responsio, qui disputatione vltimâ in Danielem th. 144. & 145. triplici respectu impios libro vitæ adscriptos dici asserit. 1. Ratione mediorum, quatenus ad ipsos, non quidem ipsa vita, vitæ tameu causa spectat, quæ est misericordia Dei, Meritum Christi, & gratuita vocatio. 2. Ratione propriæ persuasionis, & existimationis hominum, de qua modo actum est. 3. Ratione externæ conuersationis in Ecclesia, quia verè fidelibus & electis immixti sunt, vt facilè discerni nequeant. Dicuntur ergo deleri, quando palam sit, ipsos media salutis contemsisse, sanctitatem falsò iactitasse, & viua Ecclesiæ membra nunquam fuisse.

XXVII. Nec prorsus inconueniens est illorum interpretatio, qui de libro gratiæ, in quo confignantur omnes renati & iusti, intelligunt. Videtur enim textus loqui de his, qui actu viuunt, nempè spiritualiter per gratiam, nec tam de illis, qui aliquando victuri sunt in cælis per gloriam. Vnde dicuntur iusti, hoc est, iustificati & regenerati. Impios igitur Psalmista ex isto iustificatorum numero, & gratiæ libro delendos esse iudicat, quoniam per impietatem suam seipsos amore diuino indignos reddiderunt.

XIIX. TERTIVS LOCVS existit Apoc. 5. v. 5. Qui vicerit, hic vestietur vestimentis albis, & non delebo nomen eius de libro vitæ. Ex quo nonnulli colligunt, inscriptos deleri posse, aliàs superuacanea foret hæc promissio. Sed argumētum neruis caret, cùm sensus dicti Apostolici sit planissimus, Qui vicerit,ita certò saluabitur. Hoc enim per non dēleri innuitur. Neque superuacanea est promissio, cùm ob illam ipsam caussam Electi non deleantur, quia fides perseuerans & per hanc certissima salus ipsis promissa est. Nec inficias imus, simul Apostolum indicare contrarium, nempè deletum iri omnem eum, qui non vicerit: Quomodo autem deletio ista intelligenda sit, hactenus abundè satis diximus, nempè vel de libro gratiæ, vel de libro gloriæ, verùm non per priuationem, sed negationem, & negatæ inscriptionis manifestationem.

XXIX. Tandem QVARTVS & vltimus locus habetur Apoc. ylt. v. 19. Si quis diminuerit de verbis libri Prophetiæ huius, auferet Deus partem eius de libro vitæ, & de ciuitate sancta, & de his, quæ scripta sunt in libro isto. Iam si impossibilis foret deletio, qualis esset ista comminatio? Verùm & huic obiectioni in præcedentibus satisfactum est. Recurrit enim eadem phrasis, quæ & eundem cum dictis hactenus explicatis sensum obtinet. Nam Apostolus loquitur de hæreticis falsisq; fratribus, qui Scripturā corrum-


### Question VII. and last. Does any book of death correspond to the book of life?

by adding or subtracting, or by changing; and nevertheless they will arise with the opinion of truth and holiness. To these, therefore, he denounces the severe judgment of God, that they shall have no part with the elect in heaven, and thus they are said metaphorically and by anthropopathy to be blotted out of the book, both negatively, insofar as they are never inscribed, and positively, insofar as their heresy is manifested, so that it may be gathered by all that they were never inserted into the catalog of the elect.

XXX. Thus, therefore, our thesis stands firm. That all who are written in the book of life are certainly saved and that this writing is by no means blotted out, since it is impossible for the foreknowledge of God to be deceived, and for the chosen sheep to be snatched from his hand. For, to conclude with the saying of Augustine: Believe most firmly and doubt in no way that all whom God predestined before the foundation of the world to the adoption of the sons of God cannot perish. lib. de fide ad Petrum. c. 35.

QUESTION VII. and last.

I. The opinions of authors are diverse. Jerome in the 7th chapter of Daniel establishes two books; one of the pious with good works; the other of the impious, with sins. He calls the former the book of life; he consequently indicates the latter to be the book of death. He adds, however, that the book of the good is in God; but that the book of death is in the Devil, as an accuser, which the latter can hardly be conceded. For although Satan may see the external deeds of men, yet because he does not know all their thoughts, he cannot record them. And since it is God's prerogative to elect or reprobate men, certainly if a book of death is given, as of life, it is fitting that it likewise be in God, and denote the knowledge of God.

II. Wherefore others simply confess that there is given in God a book of the evil, just as of the good, and of death, just as & of life. Which Basil seems to indicate on Isaiah 4, where, when he had said that there is a book of the elect in the heavenly Jerusalem, he adds, It is necessary to know whether there are some who are indeed written, but not likewise unto life, but according to the opinion of Jeremiah saying, they shall be written as deserters on the earth. According to this sense, therefore, two writings ought to be understood. One is of those who are written unto life, another is of those who are written unto perdition. Nazianzen also, in his ninth oration against Julian, commemorates βίβλον ζώντων, καὶ βίβλον ἀπολλυμένων, the book of the living and the book of the perishing.

III. But Thomas asserts the contrary in Part 1, Question 24, Article 1. It is not customary, he says, for those who are rejected to be written down, but those who are chosen. Whence a book of death does not correspond to reprobation, as a book of life does to predestination. Thomas is followed by Pererius on Daniel 6, book 8, page 45; Viega on chapter 20 of the Apocalypse, page 797; and Hieronymus Zanchius, book 5, de N. D., chapter 3, question 1, page 760, who relies on these reasons: 1. Scripture does not attribute such a book to God. 2. God would seem to be the author of eternal death, just as He is of life. 3. Those things which are rejected are not accustomed to be annotated in a book.

IV. We respond briefly, whether the question is about the thing itself, or about the designation of the writing. If about the thing, a book of death cannot be denied. For just as God from eternity foresaw all who would believe, and chose them: so He foreknew all the impenitent, and reprobated them. And just as the names of those to be saved are known to God, so also are those of the damned. Therefore, just as the catalog of the predestined is called the book of life, so since there is similarly in God a catalog of the reprobate, why could that not be called a book of death through the same metaphor? Nor does it follow that God is established as the author of damnation. For just as reprobation, so the inscription into the book of death is not absolute, but made on account of foreseen impenitence. To Thomas's argument, that those who are rejected are not written in any book, Becanus, himself a Papist and a disciple of Thomas, responds in tract 1, chapter 14, question 8, page 168.

q. 8. p. 168. Although soldiers who are rejected from the militia are not enrolled, those who are to be condemned to death are nevertheless accustomed to be enrolled. Since, therefore, God's reprobation is not a bare passing over, but a just sentence concerning future damnation, and since all who are to be damned are most well known to the omniscient God, what will prevent this knowledge of them and memory of God, through a customary metaphor, from being able to be called a book of damnation or of death?

V. Meanwhile, we willingly admit that an express mention of this book is not held in the Scriptures, unless someone might tacitly say it is implied by the contrary, and in the passage Apoc. 20. v. 12. If, therefore, in these abstruse questions we wish to employ only the language of the Holy Spirit, we can abstain from that phrase, especially since God is said to know the pious, Ps. 1. v. ult., 2. Tim 2. 19, but rather to not know and to be ignorant of the impious, Matth. 7. v. 23, Luc. 13. v. 27.

VI. And concerning the book of life, let these suffice, with which we may compare our books and all our deeds, so that we may rejoice in what is written in it. Christ is the tree of life, the giver of life, nay, he is life itself. Let us therefore believe in him, lest the book of Scripture be despised: let us give thanks to him, since the book of Nature also proclaims his goodness everywhere: let us conform our life to him, lest the book of conscience be stained; but so that when the term of life has elapsed, in the book of providence noted and the book of judgment opened, we may appear joyful, and be found written in the book of Life, and thus pass from the shadow of death into the region of the living, where we shall know perfectly without books the God whom we learned imperfectly from books, we shall triumph over death, we shall live without end, adhering to the lamb of God, who is the beginning and the end: to whom be praise and blessing, never to be ended at any time. AMEN.

SOLI DEO GLORIA.

Latin:

punt, vel addendo vel detrahendo, vel mutando; & nihilominus opinione veritatis & sanctitatis surgent. His igitur denunciat seuerum Dei iudidicium, quod nullam sint habituri partem cum electis in coelo, adeoque μεταφορικῶς & per ἀνθρωποπάθειαν dicuntur deleri e libro tum negatiuè, quatenus nunquam inscribuntur, tùm positiuè, quatenus ipsorum hæresis manifestatur, vt Electorum catalogo nunquam fuisse insertos inde ab omnibus colligatur.

XXX. Sic igitur firma perstat thesis nostra. Omnes in libro vitæ scriptos certò saluari eamque scripturã minimè deleri, cùm impossibile sit, præscientiã Dei falli, & electas oues ex manu eius eripi. Nam vt August. dicto concludam, Firmissimè crede & nullatenus dubites, omnes quos ante constitutionẽ mundi in adoptionem filiorum Dei, prædestinauit Deus, perire non posse. lib. de fide ad Petrum. c. 35.

QVÆSTIO VII. & vltima. Num libro vitæ respondeat aliquis liber mortis?

I. Diuersæ sunt auctorum sententiæ. Hieronymus in 7. Danielis duos libros constituit; vnum piorũ cum bonis operibus; alterum impiorum, cum peccatis. Priorem vitæ librum nuncupat; posteriorem consequenter indicat esse librum mortis. Addit autem librum bonorum esse in Deo; librum autem mortis esse in Diabolo, tanquam accusatore, quod posterius vix concedi potest. Satanas enim licèt externa facta hominum videat, cogitata tamen omnia quia nescit, annotare nequit. Et cùm Dei sit, homines eligere vel reprobare, vtique si datur liber mortis, vt vitæ, illum similiter in Deo esse, Deíque notitiam notare conuenit.

II. Quare alij simpliciter fatentur, dari in Deo librum malorum, sicut bonorum, & mortis, sicut & vitæ. Quod indicare videtur Bafilius Efai. 4. vbi cùm dixiset, ese in cœlesti Ierusalem librum electorum, subiungit, Necessarum ese scire, Vtrumnè sint quidam, qui scribantur quidem, non item ad vitam, sed iuxta sententiam Ieremiæ dicentis, desećtores in terra scribentur. Iuxta hunc igitur sensum duæ intelligi debent scriptiones. Vna eorum est, qui ad vitam, alia eorum est, qui scribuntur ad perditionem. Nazianzenus etiam oratione nonâ ad Iulian. βίβλον ζώντων, καὶ βίβλον ἀπολλυμένων, librum viuentium & librum pereuntium commemorat.

III. Contrarium verò Thomas asserit parte 1. qu. 24. art. 1. Non est, inquit, consuetum, conscribi eos, qui repudiantur, sed eos, qui eliguntur. Vnde reprobationi non respondet liber mortis, prædestinationi liber vitæ. Thomam sequitur Pererius in Daniel. 6. l. 8. pag. 45. Viega in cap. 20. Apoc. p. 797. & Hieron. Zanchius l. 5. de N. D. c. 3. q. 1. p. 760. qui rationib. his nititur. 1. Talem Deo librum Scriptura non attribuit. 2. Mortis æternæ auctor videretur esse Deus, atque etiam est vitæ. 3. Quæ reijciuntur, in libro non solent annotari.

IV. Nos breuiter respondemus, vel de re ipsa quæri, vel de appellatione scripturæ. Si de re, liber mortis negari nequit. Nam sicut Deus ab æterno præuidit omnes credituros, eosƊs elegit: Sic præsciuit omnes impœnitentes, eosque reprobauit. Et sicut Deo nota sunt omnia saluandorum, sic & damnatorum nomina. Velut ergo catalogus prædestinatorum vocatur liber vitæ, Ita cùm in Deo similiter sit catalogus reproborum, cur non ille per eandem metaphoram liber mortis nuncupari posset? Nec sequitur, Deum auctorem damnationis constitui. Nam vti reprobatio, sic inscriptio in librum mortis non est absoluta, sed ob præuisam impœnitentiã facta. Ad Thomæ argumentum, Non scribi in aliquo libro, qui reijciuntur, respondet Becanus, ipse Pontificius & Thomæ discipulus, tract. 1. cap. 14. q. 8. p. 168.

q. 8. p. 168. Quamvis non scribantur milites, qui rejiciuntur à militia, solent tamen scribi, qui morte damnandi sunt. Quia igitur Dei reprobatio non est nuda præteritio, sed justa de futurą damnatione sententia, adeoque damnandi omnes Deo omniscio sunt notissimi, quid obstabit, quò minus hæc illerum notitia & Dei memoria, per consuetam metaphoram, liber damnationis vel mortis appellari queat?

V. Interim lubenter fatemur, expressam huius libri mentionem in Scripturis non haberi, nisi qui tacitè dicat innui per contrarium, & in loco Apoc. 20. v. 12. Si ergò in abstrusis his quæst. solam Spiritus S. linguā adhibere velimus, à phrasi ista abstinere possumus, præsertim cùm Deus scire pios, Ps. 1. v. ult. 2. Tim 2. 19. sed impios nescire potius & ignorare dicatur, Matth. 7. v. 23. Luc. 13. v. 27.

VI. Et de libro vitæ sufficiant, cum quo libros nostros & omnia facta conferamus, vt in ipso scripti gaudeamus. Christus vitæ lignũ, vitæ dator, imò vită ipsa est. Huic ergò credamus, ne contemnatur liber Scripturæ: huic gratias agamus, cùm bonitatem eius vbique prædicet liber etiam Naturæ: huic vitam nostram conformemus, ne maculetur liber conscientiæ; verùm vt elapso vitæ termino, in libro prouidētiæ annotato & aperto libro iudicij, appareamus læti, & inueniamur in libro Vitæ scripti, adeoque ex vmbra mortis in regionem viuentium transeamus, vbi Deum, quem ex libris didicimus imperfectè sine libris cognoscemus perfectè, triumphabimus de morte, viuemus sine fine, adhærentes agno Dei, qui est principium & finis: cui sit laus & benedictio, nullo vnquam tempore finiendæ. AMEN.

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 18 Disputation VI. On the Immutability of Predestination, and the Use of the Whole Article

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Master Johannes Reiche of Lübeck.

Πρόθεσις.

Regarding the doctrine of predestination, two chapters still remain to be expounded, the former of which concerns the immutability of election; the latter concerns the utility of this article. We shall join both, and with this discussion with God, we shall provide an expedited account.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D.

Resp. M. Iohanne Reiche / Lubecensi.

Πρόθεσις.

CIrca doctrinam prædestinationis duo adhuc capita restant exponenda, quorum prius electionis immutabilitatem; posterius articuli huius vtilitatem concernit. Vtrumque coniungemus, & hac συζητήσει cum Deo, expeditum dabimus.


### Question I

I. So that the sense of the question may be correctly perceived, we shall briefly explain both its subject and its predicate. The word 'election' is ambiguous, and denotes either the love of a thing in general; as in Isaiah 58:6, Luke 23:35; or the calling of God in particular, which others call temporal love or [love] of grace, when either a whole people or individual persons are converted and inserted into the Catholic Church. In this sense, the Apostle writes concerning all those converted from paganism to the faith of Christ, 1 Thessalonians 1:2, 4: 'We give thanks to God always for you all, knowing, brethren beloved by God, your election.' Here it denotes the calling and conversion itself, 1. because he addresses all. 2. because the elect, properly so called, are known to God alone are. 3. because v. 5. he adds the reason why he names them the Elect, namely because the Gospel of Christ has borne fruit among them, that is, because they have received the faith, and therefore have been converted to the Church. Thus Col. 3, v. 12, the elect and the beloved are joined together as synonyms: Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies. Thus 2 Pet. 1, v. 10, calling and election are coupled: Strive, brethren, to make your calling and election sure through good works.

II. If election is taken in this somewhat more general sense, hardly anyone would deny that it is mutable. For it happens very often that those beloved by God sin mortally, and thus from sons of grace are rendered sons of wrath. Indeed, many fall away entirely from the faith and thus make their election, that is, their calling, void on their part. Hence the Apostle Peter says in 2 Epist. 2, v. 1, that there would come from among those whom he had previously called elect, false prophets, denying the Lord who bought them, and bringing upon themselves swift destruction.

III. Beyond this general meaning, however, election is taken specially and properly for the eternal decree of God, by which believers are destined for life; and according to which many are called, but few are said to be chosen in the Scriptures. We have hitherto explained this very thing abundantly enough, and it is concerning this that the question is further asked: Is it mutable?

IV. By mutability, however, nothing else is understood than the possibility of evacuation, when one can fall from election, and from an elect person can become a reprobate. For then, by reason of us, predestination is changed, so that he who was previously inscribed in the catalog of the elect through faith is erased from it on account of sins, but if he does penance, he is inscribed in turn, and thus by alternating turns, according to the measure of either faith or impenitence, he is now a reprobate, now elect. Whether such a reciprocal change should therefore be granted, or whether it has a place in the decree of election, is called into controversy.

V. But what must be answered will not be so obscure if the Formula of Concord is consulted. Thus, however, it is read in the Epitome, art. 11, p. 618, Leipzig edition, year 1606: Predestination or the eternal Election of God pertains only to the good and beloved children of God: and this is the cause of their salvation, it procures their salvation, and disposes those things which pertain to it. Upon this predestination of God our salvation is so founded that the gates of hell cannot overturn it. Again in the Solid Declaration, p. 799: The eternal election or predestination of God to salvation does not pertain at the same time to the good and to the bad, but only to the children of God, who have been chosen and ordained to obtain eternal life. A little later: In that divine eternal predestination our salvation is so founded that even the gates of hell cannot prevail against it, for it is written: No one shall snatch my sheep from my hand. And p. 803. He therefore in his eternal counsel decreed that those whom he chose, called, justified, he wills to make safe in that other eternal life, and to adorn with eternal glory. Soon below: He decreed that in that age (which we have mentioned) he wills to make them participants of eternal salvation, to help them, to promote their salvation, to preserve them and to keep them through his grace, gifts, and efficacy.

VI. From these words of the Concord we deduce the following aphorisms.

1. That election properly so-called pertains only to the faithful, not to all the called in general, much less to all men.

2. That all the elect are certainly saved, because it is said: 1. That election is the cause of salvation, and procures this very thing. 2. That the gates of hell cannot overturn it. 3. That it was made to obtain life. 4. So that the elect sheep cannot be snatched from the hand of God, that is, finally fall from grace and be damned. 5. Because God certainly wills to save his elect, and therefore to preserve them in faith until the end of life. Those therefore who are not preserved, do not persevere, and therefore are not saved, they truly and properly while the phraseology of Scripture and the explanation of the Concord cannot be called chosen.

3. That predestination is immutable, so that one who is chosen does not become a reprobate; or the reverse. Thus. All the predestined are preserved and are certainly saved; indeed, he who is damned was never predestined, even if he believed for a time and experienced the grace of God.

VII. The Wittenberg theologians hold the same opinion in the brief explanation against Huber, A. 3. page 2. B. 2: 1. B. 3. page 1. & 2. D. 3. page 2. E. 4. page 2. F. 1. 2. The Tübingen theologians, part 1, Acts of Huber, p. 3 & 182. 195. 266. 303. 304. Part 2, Acts, p. 33. 36. 107. 217. et seqq. Chemnitz in the Enchiridion p. 266. Hunnius on predestination p. 356. 357. et seqq. Frankfurt edition 1603. Vol. 1. disp. 10. Marburg thesis 88. Gesner, last disputation on Daniel, thesis 148. Gerlach, disputation on the eternal election of those to be saved, thesis 11. Rongius, disputation 10 on the Epistle to the Romans, page 179. Lord Dr. Hutter in the Formula of Concord p. 1121. 1163. 1124. 1177. & Lord Dr. Menzer, Vol. 1. Giessen disputation, disputation 14. thesis 10. 40 78. 109. 129. 131. 171. 192. et seqq.

VII. All these teach and confess: 1. That the decree of Election is as immutable and certain as it is eternal. For what God has once decreed to do, that He certainly executes; and if He did not do it, He would be frustrated of His end, and His truth, wisdom, and omnipotence would be detracted from: therefore, whom He has chosen, that is, decreed to save, Him He certainly saves, and the reverse. 2. Hence it follows that the chosen always remains chosen, and never becomes a reprobate, or the reverse, that is, that election cannot be rendered void or evacuated. 3. Although, therefore, some of the chosen may sin mortally, yet at that very time they truly are and can be called chosen on account of the divine decree and the certain number of the chosen, in which they always remain included in the eternal foreknowledge. 4. Likewise, although some truly believe for a time, yet they are not thus from eternity in the book of the living inscribed on account of foreseen final unbelief at that very time of faith, by virtue of a divine decree, truly are and can be called reprobated in divine foreknowledge. § There is therefore a great difference between the reborn and the elect, so much so that they cannot be held as synonyms, since they are distinguished as broader and narrower, if indeed at all times, yet at the time of death; but not conversely are all the reborn at the same time elect, namely those who lose faith and depart with final impenitence.

IX. That this opinion is most true, conformable to the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, and not destitute of the consensus of Antiquity, now further comes to be proved and illustrated by the solution of contrary objections. Wherefore we shall propose 1. The sayings of Scripture, 2. Arguments sought from the analogy of faith, 3. The testimonies of the Fathers, and 4. We shall subjoin a brief ἀνασκευὴν of the objections. For if this question shall have been sufficiently decided, now the way is open to the easiest refutation of Huberianism. For once it is evicted that only those are elect there who are certainly saved, it will follow that not indiscriminately all, but only those perseveringly believing were predestined from eternity. Therefore we shall be more accurate here, so that we may be able to proceed more happily in the following disputation.

Latin:

I. Vt sensus quæstionis rectè percipiatur, & subiectum & prædicatum eius breuiter explicabimus. Electionis vox est ambigua, & notat vel dilectionem rei in genere; vt Esai 58. v. 6. Luc. 23 v. 35. vel vocationem Dei in specie, quam alij dilectionẽ temporalem seu gratiæ, cùm aut totus populus aut singulares personæ conuertuntur, & Ecclesiæ Catholicæ inseruntur. Hoc sensu Apostolus scribit de omnibus ex gentilismo ad fidem Christi conuersis 1. Thess. 1. vers. 2. 4. Gratias agimus Deo semper de omnibus vobis, scientes fratres dilecti à Deo electionem vestram. Hic ipsam vocationem & conuersionem notat, 1. quia omnes alloquitur. 2. quia electi propriè sic dicti soli Deo noti sunt. 3. quia v. 5. rationem addit, cur ipsos nominet Electos, quoniam nempē Evangelium Christi apud ipsos fructum fecerit h. e. quia fidem receperunt, adeoque conuersi sunt ad Ecclesiam. Sic Col. 3. v. 12. coniunguntur electi & dilecti, tanquam Synonyma; Induite igitur, vt electi Dei, sancti & dilecti, viscera miserationum. Sic 2. Pet. 1. v. 10. vocatio & electio copulantur: Satagite fratres, vt per bona opera certam vestram vocationem & electionem faciatis.

II. Hoc igitur sensu paulò generaliori si accipiatur electio, illam esse mutabilem vix quisquam negauerit. Nam sæpissimè contingit, vt dilecti Deo peccent mortaliter, adeoque ex filiis gratiæ reddantur filij iræ. Imò multi prorsus à fide deficiunt atq; sic electionem, h. e. vocationem ex parte sua faciunt irritam. Hinc Apostolus Petrus ait 2. epist 2. v. 1. venturos ex illis, quos ante electos dixerat, Pseudo prophetas, negantes Dominum, à quo sunt emti, & celerem sibi perditionem superducentes.

III. Præter hanc verò generalem significatiō- nem specialiter & proprie accipitur electio, pro æterno Dei decreto, quo ad vitam destinantur credentes; & secundum quam multi vocati, pauci electi dicuntur in Scripturis. Hancipsam hactenus abundè satis explicuimus, & de hac porrò quæritur; Num sit mutabilis?

IV. Per mutabilitatem verò nil aliud intelligitur, quàm euacuationis possibilitas, cùm electione quis excidere, & ex electo potest fieri reprobus.
