Tum enim ratione nostri mutatur prædestinatio, sic vt qui antè per fidem catalogo electorum adscriptus fuit, ob peccata inde expungatur, si verò pœnitentiam agat, vicissim inscribatur, atque sic alternis vicibus pro ratione vel fidei vel impœnitentiæ, iam reprobus sit, iam electus. Talis igitur mutatio reciproca num cōcedi debeat, numuē in derceto electionis locum habeat? in controuersiam vocatur:

V. Quid verò respondendum sit, non adeò obscurum erit, si Concordiæ Formula consulatur. Sic autem in Epitome legitur art 11. p. 618. edit Lips. anno 1606. Prædestinatio seu æterna Dei Electio tantùm ad bonos & dilectos filios Dei pertinet: & hæc est causa ipsorum salutis, Eorum salutem procurat, & ea quæ ad ipsam pertinent, disponit. Super hanc Dei prædestinationem salus nostra ita fundata est, ut inferorum portæ eam euertere nequeant. Rursus in solida declaratione p. 799. Æterna electio seu prædestinatio Dei ad salutem, non simul ad bonos & ad malos pertinet, sed tantùm ad filios Dei, qui ad æternam vitam consequendam electi & ordinati sunt. Paulò pòst: In ea diuina prædestinatione æterna nostra salus ita fundata est, ut etiam inferorum portæ aduersus eam præualere nequeant, scriptum est enim: Oves meas nemo rapiet de manu mea. Et p. 803. Ille itaque in æterno consilio suo decreuit, quòd eos; quos elegit, vocauit, iustificauit, in altera æterna illa vita saluos facere, & æternâ gloria ornare velit. Mox infrà, Decreuit, quòd eam euo (quemiam retrauimus) ipsos per suam gratiam, dona atque efficaciam, salutis æternæ participes facere, iuuare, eorum salutem promouere, ipsos conseruare & conseruare velit.

VI. Ex istis Concordiæ verbis sequentes aphoristmos deducimus.

1. Quòd electio propriè dicta tantùm fideles attineat non omnes vocatos in genere, multò minùs omnes homines.

2. Quòd electi omnes certò saluantur, quia dicitur 1. electionem esse causam salutis, & hanc ipsam procurare. 2. Portas inferorum non posse euertere. 3. Factam esse ad vitam consequendam. 4. Sic ut oues electæ nequeant rapi è manu Dei, hoc est, gratia finaliter excidere & damnari. 5. Quia Deus electos suos certò vult saluare, & propterea in fide ad finem vitæ vsque conseruare. Qui ergò non conseruantur, non perseuerant, adeoque non saluantur, ij verè proprièque secundum Scripturae phrasin & Concordiae explicationem electi vocari nequeunt.

3. Quòd praedestinatio sit immutabilis, adeò ut ex electo non fiat reprobus; vel contra. Sic. Omnes praedestinati conseruantur & certò saluantur, vtique praedestinatus nunquam fuit, qui damnatur, licèt ad tempus crediderit, & gratiam Dei persenserit.

VII. Eandem sententiam tenent Theologi Wittebergenses in explic. breui contra Huberum A. 3. fac. 2. B. 2: 1. B. 3. fac. 1. & 2. D. 3. fac. 2. E. 4. fac. 2. F. 1. 2. Theologi Tubingenses par. 1. Act. Huber. p. 3 & 182. 195. 266. 303. 304. Par. 2. Act. p. 33. 36. 107. 217. seqq. Chemnitius in Enchiridio p. 266. Hunnius de praedestinat. p. 356. 357. seqq. edit. Francof. 1603. Tom. 1. disp. 10. Marp. th. 88. Gesnerus disp. vlt. in Dan. th. 148. Gerlachius disput. de aeterna saluandorum electione th. 11. Rongius disput. 10. in Epist. ad Rom. pag. 179. Dn. D. Hutterus in Form. Conc. p. 1121. 1163. 1124. 1177. & Dn. D. Menzerus Tom. 1. disp. Giess. disp. 14. th. 10. 40 78. 109. 129. 131. 171. 192. seqq.

VII. Hi omnes docent & fatentur. 1. Decretum Electionis vt aeternum, sic immutabile & certum esse. Quae enim Deus semel decreuit facere, ea certo exequitur; & nisi faceret, fine suo frustraretur, ejusque veritati, sapientiae, & omnipotentiae detraheretur: Quem igitur elegit, hoc est, saluare decreuit, illum certò saluat, & contra. 2. Hinc sequitur, quòd electus semper maneat electus, nec vnquam fiat reprobus, vel contrà, h. e. quod electio nequeat irrita reddi vel euacuari. 3. Licèt igitur electi quidam mortaliter peccent, eo tamen ipso tempore verè sunt & dici possunt electi ob decretum diuinum, & certum electorum numerum, cui in aeternâ praenotione semper manent inclusi. 4. Parimodo, quamuis nonnulli ad tempus verè credant, tamē sic ab aeterno viuentium librò non sunt inscripti ob præuisam incredulitatem finalem eò ipso fidei tempore, vi decreti diuini, verè sunt & dici possunt in diuina præscientia reprobati. § Magna proinde differentia est inter renatos & electos, adeò vt pro Synonymis haberi nequeant, cùm distinguantur tanquam latius & angustius, siquidem omnes electi sunt quidem renati, si non omni, tamen mortis tempore; sed non contrà omnes renati simul sunt electi, nempe ii, qui fidem amittunt, & cum finali impœnitentia decedunt.

IX. Hanc sententiam esse verissimam, Scripturis & analogiæ fidei conformem, nec Antiquitatis consensu destitutam, jam porrò probandum & contrariarum objectionum solutione illustrandum venit. Quocirca 1. Scripturæ dicta 2. Argumenta ab analogia fidei petita. 3. Patrum testimonia proponemus, & 4. breuem objectionum ἀνασκευὴν subjungemus. Si enim hæc quæstio sufficienter decisa fuerit, iam via est ad facillimam Huberianismi confutationem. Evicto enim quod ibi tantùm electi sint, qui certò saluantur, consequens erit, non promiscuè omnes, sed tantùm perseveratè credentes ab æterno fuisse prædestinatos. Proinde accuratiores hic erimus, vt in sequenti disputatione eò feliciùs progredi valeamus.


### Question I: I. Sayings of Scripture for the immutability of election

I. SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE FOR the immutability of election.

X. There are very many sayings establishing our thesis: but lest we be disturbed by the multitude, we shall include them all in distinct classes.

First class, containing sayings that every properly elect person is certainly saved.

XI. Let the argument be such: Every elect person will certainly be saved. Temporary (πρόσκαιροι) reborn persons will not be saved. Therefore, temporary (πρόσκαιροι) reborn persons are not Elect. In this syllogism the major comes into controversy, and therefore we give it proved by the following testimonies.

XII. 1. Dan. 12. v. 1. At that time your people shall be saved, everyone who shall be found written in the book. These words are so clear that they alone could suffice for the proof of the aforementioned θεσεως. We conclude from this, however, as follows: Everyone written in the book of life will certainly be saved, by the force of the cited saying: Every elect person is written in the book of life: Therefore, every elect person will certainly be saved.

XIII. 2. From John 10. v. 27. 28. 29. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, they follow me: And I will give them eternal life, they shall not perish forever: and no one shall snatch them from my hand. Here it must be known what Christ understands by sheep. Indeed, all believers, even πρόσκαιροι, are called sheep of the Lord in their own sense, insofar as they dwell in his fold, the Church, and hear the voice of the shepherd Christ: nevertheless, the discourse here is about peculiar sheep, namely those to whom eternal life is given. From which such was the argument: Christ speaks here of those to whom eternal life will certainly be given. But eternal life will not be given to all believers, namely the προσκαίροις. Therefore he is not speaking of them, and consequently, only of the elect. Furthermore, Christ's sheep will certainly have salvation, nor will they perish forever. But the elect are truly and properly those sheep of Christ. Therefore the elect will certainly have salvation, nor will they perish forever. Likewise: Those whom no one can snatch from the hand of Christ: they will be saved: No one can snatch the elect from the hand of Christ, therefore the elect will certainly be saved. But reborn πρόσκαιροι have often been snatched from the hand of the Lord by the Devil, by seducing men, and will still be able to be snatched, and therefore they cannot be numbered among the elect sheep of Christ.

XIV. 3. From John 17. v. 11. Keep them in your name, whom you have given me, that they may be with me. and v. 15. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil. v. 16. Sanctify them in your truth. v. 24. Father, those whom you have given me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory. Here two things are to be noted: 1. What. 2. For whom the Savior prays, the object and theme of the prayer was twofold, namely perseverance, and the end of perseverance, eternal life. For He asks the heavenly Father that He might be willing to save and keep His own from all evil, v. 15. He asks that He might be willing to sanctify or preserve them in the truth, v. 12. He asks that He might be willing to grant unity, so that no one might fall away, or finally lose the purity of faith, v. 24. Finally, He asks that, persevering in this unity and truth, He might at last be willing to glorify them, to render them partakers of eternal brightness. From which now the solution to the other doubt may also shine forth. For whom did Christ pray? Namely, for the elect alone. For these alone are saved from evil, persist in unity, and obtain the end of faith, eternal life. And these are called by a special name those given to Christ:

For there is a threefold mode of giving, or there are three orders of those given, according to some. For they are either given to Christ to be redeemed; or some are given to serve, of whom He seems to speak in verse 12; or finally, some are given to be certainly saved, of whom in verse 24. Those are all men, these are the Apostles alone, these are all and only the elect. For that Christ in this chapter prays for the elect is proved both from verse 6, where these given ones are said to have kept or preserved the word of the Father, and from verse 12, where no one is said to have perished from them; and especially because Christ prays that God might be willing to save them and, thus saved, to glorify them. Now, indeed, this petition of Christ was either heard or otherwise. The consequence is absurd, and contrary to all Christian consolation. Therefore, the former is true, and thus Christ was most certainly heard. Hence we now invincibly conclude: For whomever Christ prayed that they might be saved, so that they would not finally fall away, and thus might at last be glorified, all those will most truly be preserved by the heavenly Father, and will not finally fall away, but will at last be glorified in the final judgment, because this most ardent prayer of Christ was mercifully nevertheless heard. And yet he prayed for his elect, and asked for this, that they might be preserved and glorified. Therefore all the elect, by virtue of this prayer, do not finally fall away, but are preserved and certainly glorified, and therefore those who believe only for a time, but when temptation comes fall away, they are not truly elect, just as Scripture names and describes them.

XV. 4. From Rom. 8. verse 29. Whom he foreknew (namely, those who would finally believe) them he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son. v. 30. Whom he predestined, these he also called; whom he called, these he also justified; and whom he justified, them he also glorified. v. 33. Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he that condemns? It is Christ who died, yea rather who also is risen, who is also at the right hand of God, who also makes intercession for us. v. 38. I am certain that neither death, nor life, etc., shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus. From these Apostolic Aphorisms, we argue thus: Whoever must certainly be made conformed to the image of the Son of God, who are certainly glorified; whom no one can separate from the love of God; they cannot finally fall from grace and perish. But all the elect and predestined will finally be made conformed to the image of the Son of God, and will certainly be glorified, etc. Therefore, the truly elect cannot finally fall from grace and perish, and consequently those who believe for a time, and afterwards fail, are not truly and properly called elect.

XVI. 5. From 2 Tim. 2. verses 18 and 19. Hymenaeus and Philetus have fallen from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, but the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal: The LORD knows those who are his. In which statement, this ἀντίθεσις (antithesis) of those who fall away and the elect known by the Lord is most diligently to be observed. For because Hymenaeus and Philetus had indeed believed for a time, but afterwards had fallen from the faith, lest anyone should be offended, as if the elect also could finally fall away and perish, the Apostle immediately adds, but the firm foundation stands, as if to say: Do not be offended that these two, who at first became believers, afterwards became apostates; nor should you think that the elect can also perish, since those people, although they believed for a time, were nevertheless not truly elect, as the outcome shows, since the foundation of God stands firm, having this seal: The LORD knows those who are his. By the knowing of the Lord, however, is not understood bare knowledge, which they call theoretical or general in the schools; but rather the benefits of God to be conferred upon the elect, which they call practical or special knowledge. For theologians have a rule: Words of knowledge and knowing often denote not bare knowledge, but the effects following the knowledge. Thus it is taken in Psalm 1, last verse: The Lord knows the way of the righteous, where Bede writes that it is to be understood as knowledge: 1. of approval, 2. of promotion, 3. of remuneration. Thus it is taken in Matthew 7, verse 23: I never knew you. Luke 13, verse 27. You do not know whence you are, which things, explained only concerning general knowledge, produce a most false sense. Similarly in this saying, 2 Timothy 2, γνῶσις πρακτικὴ is understood, which consists primarily in three degrees: 1. In the love of the special. 2. In the consolation of the beloved, and 3. In the glorification of the preserved. Therefore, the sense here is: The Lord knows those who are his, i.e., the Lord specially loves his own who are chosen for himself, preserves them from every evil and final fall, and will finally glorify them, from which it is most evidently deduced that not every reborn person, who believes only for a time, is elect, because these are not known by God in this special way. But so that the nerve of the argument may be more apparent, we give it enclosed in this syllogism: The truly elect are always known to God by a knowledge 1. of love, 2. of preservation, 3. of glorification. Certain reborn and believing πρόσκαιροι [temporary ones] were never known to God in such a way, since they fall away finally and perish, nor are they glorified. Therefore, certain reborn and believing πρόσκαιροι are not truly elect. The minor premise is further proven by that saying in Matthew 7, verse 22, where the Lord says to the hypocrites and believing πρόσκαιροι: I never knew you, that is to say, by the knowledge of election; you were never inscribed in the book of the living. Also, you will not be able to be saved. Many certainly of them will be baptized, and yet it will be said to them: I never knew you, that is to say, by a special knowledge, pertaining only to the elect.

XVII. 6. From 1 Peter 1, to the elect strangers grace, v. 1, who are kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, v. 5, where the Apostle Peter clearly indicates that only those are true elect who are kept through faith, and are certainly saved by it. Whence now such an argument arises similar to the former: True elect are always kept by the power of God through faith unto salvation, i.e., they do not finally fall away, nor do they perish eternally, but πρόσκαιροι [temporary ones] are not kept because of their own malice, but finally fall away and perish. Therefore, πρόσκαιροι are not truly elect, which was to be demonstrated.

Latin:

I. DICTA SCRIPTVRÆ PRO electionis immutabilitate.

X. Plurima sunt dicta, thesin nostram stabilientia: verùm ne multitudine turbemur, omnia distinctis classibus includemus.

Classis prima, continens dicta, quòd omnis propriè electus certò saluetur.

XI. Argumentum sit tale: Omnis electus certò saluabitur. Renati πρόσκαιροι non saluabuntur. Ergo renati πρόσκαιροι non sunt Electi. In hoc Syllogismo maior venit in controuersiam, ideoque illam sequentibus testimoniis probatam damus.

XII. 1. Dan. 12. v. 1. In tempore illo saluabitur populus tuus omnis, qui inuentus fuerit scriptus in libro. Verba hæc tam clara sunt, vt vel sola ad prædictæ θεσεως probationem sufficere possint. Sic autem inde colligimus: Omnis libro vitæ inscriptus, vi allegati dicti certò saluabitur: Omnis electus libro vitæ inscriptus est: E. Omnis electus certò saluabitur.

XIII. 2. Ex Ioh. 10. v. 27. 28. 29. Oues meæ vocem meam audiunt, & ego cognosco eas, sequuntur me: Et ego vitam æternam dabo, non peribunt in æternum: non rapiet eas quisquam de manu mea. Hic sciendum est, quid per oues intelligat Christus. Omnes quidem credentes, etiam πρόσκαιροι, suo sensu vocantur oves Domini, quatenus in ovili eius, Ecclesia, degunt, & vocem pastoris Christi audiunt: attamen hic de ouibus peculiaribus sermo est, nempè iis, quibus datur æterna. Ex quo tale fuit argumentum: De iis Christus hic loquitur, quibus certò dabitur vita æterna. Atqui non omnibus credētibus, nempè προσκαίροις, vita æterna dabitur. Ergò de iis non loquitur, & per consequens, de solis electis. Porrò Christi oues habebunt certò salutem, nec peribunt in æternum. Ast electi vere & propriè sunt istæ oues Christi. Ergo Electi habebunt certò salutem, nec peribunt in æternum. Item: Quos nemo potest rapere de manu Christi: illi saluabuntur: Electos nemo potest rapere de manu Christi, electi igitur certò saluabuntur. Renati verò πρόσκαιροι è manu Domini à Diabolo, ab hominibus seducentibus sæpè rapti sunt, & adhuc poterunt rapi, ídeoque electis Christi ouibus annumerari nequeunt.

XIV. 3. Ex Ioh. 17. v. 11. Serua eos in nomine tuo, quos dedisti mihi, vt sint mecum. & v. 15. Non rogo, vt tollas eos de mundo, sed vt serues eos à malo. v. 16. Sanctifica eos in veritate tua. v. 24. Pater, quos dedisti mihi, volo, vt vbi ego sum, & illi sint mecum, vt videant claritatem meam. Hic duo sunt notanda: 1. Quid. 2. Pro quibus Saluator oret, Obiectum & thema orationis erat duplex nimirum perseuerantia, & perseuerantiæ finis, vita æterna. Rogat enim Patrem cœlestem, vt velit suos ab omni malo seruare & custodire, v. 15. Rogat, vt velit eos sanctificare vel conseruare in veritate, v. 12. Rogat, vt velit vnitatè concedere, ne quis excidat, vel fidei puritatem finaliter amittat, v. 24. Rogat denique, vt in hac vnitate & veritate perseuerantes tandem, velit glorificare, claritatis æternæ participes reddere. Ex quibus jam elucescat & alterius dubij solutio. Pro quibus Christus orauit? Nempe pro solis electis. Hi enim tantùm seruantur à malo, in vnitate persistunt, & finem fidei, vitam æternam reportant. Atque hi speciali nomine dicuntur Christo dati:

Triplex enim est dandi modus, siue tres sunt dato rum ordines, juxta nonnullos. Vel enim sunt Christo dati ad redimendum; vel quidam sunt dati ad inseruiendum, de quibus videtur loqui versu. 12. quidam denique dati sunt ad certò saluandum, de quibus versu 24. Illi sunt omnes homines, isti soli Apostoli, hi omnes & soli electi. Nam quòd Christus in hoc capite pro electis oret, hoc probatur tum ex versu. 6. vbi isti dati dicuntur seruâsse vel conseruasse sermonem Patris, tum ex, vers. 12. vbi nemo dicitur ex iis perijsse; tum potissimùm; quòd Christus orat, vt Deus velit eos seruare & sic seruatos glorificare. Iam verò hæc Christi petitio vel exaudita est, vel secus. Consequens abfurdum, & omni Christianæ consolationi contrarium. E. Prius verum, adeoque Christus certissimè exauditus est. Hinc jam inuictè concludimus: Pro quibuscunque Christus orauit, vt seruarentur, ne finaliter exciderent, adeoque glorificarentur tandem, illi omnes verissimè conseruabuntur à Patre cœlesti, neque finaliter excident, sed tandem in extremo iudicio glorificabuntur, quia ista Christi ardentissima oratio misericordistamò fuit exaudita. Atqui prae electis suis orauit, & hoc petiit, vt seruarentur & glorificarentur. Ergò omnes electi, vi huius precationis finaliter non excidunt, sed seruantur & certò glorificantur, ideoque qui ad tempus duntaxat credunt, veniente autem tentatione recedunt, ij non sunt verè electi, prout quidem Scriptura eos nuncupat & describit.

XV. 4. Ex Rom.8.vers. 29. Quos praesciuit (nempè finaliter credituros) eos & praedestinauit conformes fieri imaginis filij sui. v. 30. Quos praedestinauit, hos & vocauit, quos vocauit, hos & iustificauit, quos autem iustificauit, illos & glorificauit. v 33. Quis accusabit aduersus electos Dei? Deus est, qui iustificat. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus est, qui mortuus est, imo qui & resurrexit, qui & est ad dexteram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. v. 38. Certus sum, quòd neque mors, neque vita &c poterit nos separare à charitate Dei, qua est in Christo Iesu. Ex hisce Aphorismis Apostolicis, sic argumentamur: Quicunque certò debent fieri conformes imagini filij Dei, qui certò glorificantur; quos nemo potest separare à Dei dilectione; ij gratiâ finaliter excidere & perire nequeunt. Ast omnes electi & praedestinati fient tandem conformes imagini filij Dei, & certò glorificabuntur &c. Ergo verè electi gratiâ finaliter excidere & perire nequeunt, & per consequens illi, qui ad tempus credunt, post deficiunt, non sunt verè propriéque dicti electi.

XVI. 5. Ex 2. Tim. 2. vers. 18. & 19. Hymenaeus, & Philetus, à veritate exciderunt, dicentes resurrectionem esse iam factam, sed firmum fundamentum Dei stat, habens signaculum hoc: Nouit DOMINVS, qui sint sui. In quo dicto diligentissimè obseruanda est ista ἀντίθεσις excidentium, & electorum à Domino cognitorum. Quia enim Hymenaeus & Phyletus ad tempus quidem crediderant, post autem à fide defecerant, ne quis offenderetur, ac si electi etiam finaliter excidere & perire possent, statim subiungit Apostolus, sed firmum stat fundamentum q. d. Ne offendamini, quod isti duo, primùm fideles, pòst Apostatæ facti sint; nec putetis, electos etiam perire posse, quoniam isti, licèt crediderint ad tempus, non tamen fuerunt verò electi, quòd euentus decet, cùm firmum sit fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc, Nouit DOMINVS, qui sunt sui. Per nosse vero Domini non nuda intelligitur notitia, quam in scholis vocant Theoreticam vel generalem; sed potius Dei beneficia electis conferenda, quam vocant notitiam practicam vel specialem. Habent enim Theologi regulam: Verba scientiæ & notitiæ sæpè non notitiam nudam, sed effectus notitiam insequentes denotant. Ita sumitur Psal. 1. v. vlt. Nouit Dominus viam iustorum, vbi Beda intelligendum esse scribit notitiam. 1. approbationis, 2. promotionis, 3. remunerationis. Ita sumitur Matth. 7. v. 23. Nunquam noui vos. Luc. 13. v. 27. Nescitis vos, vndefitis, quæ dicta de generali tantum notitia explicata, sensum pariunt falsissimum. Similiter in hoc dicto. 2. Tim. 2. γνῶσις πρακτικὴ intelligitur, quæ consistit potissimum in tribus gradibus. 1. In specialis dilectione. 2. In dilectorum consolatione, & 3. In conseruatorum glorificatione. Hic ergò sensus est. Nouit Dominus, qui sunt sui. i. e. Dominus suos ergà se electos specialiter diligit, ab omni malo & finali lapsu conseruat, tandemque glorificabit, ex quo euidentissimè deducitur, non omnem renatum, qui ad tempus duntaxat credit, electum esse, quia isti hoc speciali modo nõ sunt Deo cogniti. Vt verò nervus argumenti magis pateat, huic Syllogismo eum inclusum damus: Verè electi Deo semper sunt noti notitia 1. dilectionis. 2. conseruationis. 3. glorificationis. Quidam renati & credentes πρόσκαιροι taliter Deo nunquam fuerunt noti, quoniam excidunt finaliter & pereunt, nec glorificantur. E. quidam renati & credentes πρόσκαιροι non sunt verè electi. Minor vlterius probatur illo dicto Matth. 7. vers. 22. vbi Dominus hypocritis & credentibus προσκαίροις dicit: Nunquam novi vos, nimirum notitia electionis, nunquam fuistis inscripti in librum viventium. Etiam non poteritis salvari. Multi certe ex ijs erunt baptizati, & tamen dicetur illis. Nunquam novi vos, nimirum notitia speciali, ad electos tantum pertinente.

XVII. 6. Ex 1. Petri 1, Electis advenis gratia, v. 1. qui in virtute Dei custodiuntur per fidem in salutem v. 5. vbi Apostolus Petrus clare indicat, eos tantum veros esse electos, qui custodiuntur per fidem, & per eam certo servantur. Vnde iam tale oritur prioribus simile argumentum: Veri electi semper custodiuntur virtute Dei per fidem in salutem, h. e. finaliter non excidunt, nec æternum pereunt, πρόσκαιροι autem non custodiuntur propter malitiam propriam, sed finaliter excidunt & pereunt. E. πρόσκαιροι non sunt vere electi, id quod erat demonstrandum,


### Question I: The second class, containing sayings concerning election made according to foreknowledge

The second class, containing sayings concerning election made according to foreknowledge.

XIIX. Such are 1 Peter 1, v. 2, To the elect according to the πρόγνωσιν [foreknowledge] of the Father. Romans 8, v. 26, Whom he foreknew, he also predestinated, etc. Romans 11, v. 2, God has not cast away his people ὃν προέγνω, whom he foreknew. From which sayings we deduce this corollary: There is no election other than that which is made according to the πρόγνωσιν and foreknowledge of God. Whoever wishes to consider election outside of this, it is necessary that he depart from Scripture.

XIX. This now being presupposed, we argue thus: God in electing looked either to all faith, and of all time, or only to persevering and final faith. Not to all faith, and of all time, 1. Because πρόσκαιροι [temporary ones] would be elect, and thus would be saved, the falsity of which we have just shown. 2. Someone would be many times elected and reprobated, that is to say, as often as he would rise again and fall, that which is absurd and cannot be proven. Whence it follows that God rather had regard for persevering and final faith, which is the very thesis unanimously defended by our people. For God chose to life or decreed to save, not because He saw that certain ones would believe for a time, but because He foresaw that they would persevere in faith He decreed to save from eternity and according to that He chose. But in time men are saved, not because they believed at some point, for thus all πρόσκαιροι would be saved, but because they persevered in faith and died. Wherefore God also had regard for this persevering faith in choosing from eternity, and thus election was made according to the foreknowledge of final and ultimate faith.

XX. With these things standing thus, we proceed by arguing: Whoever fails in time, and does not persevere in faith, in them God could not have foreseen persevering faith from eternity. For that which is not to be, that does not reach the foreknowledge of God. But πρόσκαιροι fail in time. Wherefore God could not have foreseen persevering faith in them, and therefore they are not elected from eternity, although they believe for a time, since predestination was made according to the foreknowledge of ultimate faith, as has been shown.

The third class proposing sayings that the number of the elect is certain and infallible.

XXI. The following pertain here: Luke 10:20, Your names are written in heaven. Luke 12:7, The hairs of your head are numbered. John 10:14, I know my sheep. John 15:18, I know whom I have chosen. 2 Tim. 2:14, I know my sheep. John 13:18, I know whom I have chosen. 2 Tim. 2:19, ἀμετακίνητον, the firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, The Lord knows who are His. From all of which it is deduced that the number of the elect is certain and altogether infallible, not not indeed on account of a certain absolute decree, but because of the most certain foreknowledge of God. Hence Augustine, in his book On Rebuke and Grace, chapters 12 and 13, writes: I speak these things concerning those who are predestined into the kingdom of God, whose number is so certain that no one is added to them, nor is anyone subtracted from them.

XXII. With this hypothesis presupposed, we conclude thus: If the number of the elect is infallible and immutable, it follows that a reprobate cannot be made from an elect person, or vice versa. But the former is true, therefore the latter is also. To prove the consequence of the major premise more strongly, I would like it to be noted that number is twofold: one is the numbering [number], which the Scholastics call formal; the other is the numbered [number], which they call material. When, therefore, theologians speak of the numbering and the numbered of the elect, that is, God has decreed from eternity and certainly known not only how many thousands of men (which is the formal number), but also which specific individuals (which is the material) He eternally wills to save and glorify. With this theological aphorism standing, the major premise of the proposed syllogism will be invincible. For if an elect person could become a reprobate, and a reprobate an elect person, the number would be diminished as often as some fall, and increased as often as they rise again.

How, therefore, would it be certain, not augmentable, not alterable? In what way would that purpose of God remain ἀμεταμέλητον [unregretted] and ἀμετακίνητον [unmovable]? The election would certainly be most uncertain if it were estimated not from persevering and final faith, but from any other. For God would have to change His decree and purpose as often as a man fell and as often as he returned in turn.

XXIII. In particular, however, let that passage of John 13, verse 18, be considered: I do not speak of you all; I know whom I have chosen: by which assertion it is most evidently clear that Judas was never chosen by Christ for eternal life, which [is a point] against Huber, the theologians of Wittenberg Burgensis in his brief explanation, p. 4, f. 1, expressly urges: That Judas never believed is entirely improbable. For if no other argument remained, this one would suffice, that Judas was circumcised in infancy, and thus regenerated through circumcision. From which it is now invincibly concluded: Judas was never elect; Judas was truly regenerated in circumcision. Therefore, some who are truly regenerated are not elect. The major premise, that Judas was never elect, is proved from the saying of Christ, where He makes a distinction between the elect Apostles and Judas who was not elect. For He says: I do not speak of you all; I know whom I have chosen. Therefore, of whom He does not speak, Him He did not choose. He does not speak of Judas, as the following verses teach. Therefore, He did not choose Judas, and consequently, not all who are circumcised and baptized, even if they are regenerated, ought immediately to be held as elect.

Latin:

Classis secunda, continens dicta, de electione secundum præscientiam facta.

XIIX. Talia sunt 1. Petr. 1. v. 2. Electis secundum πρόγνωσιν τοῦ πατρός. Rom. 8. v. 26. Quos præscivit hos prædestinavit, &c. Rom. 11. v. 2. Non repulit Deus populum suum ὃν προέγνω, quem præscivit. Ex quibus dictis deducimus hoc πόρισμα: Nulla est electio, quam ea quæ secundum Dei πρόγνωσιν & præscientiam facta est. Extra hanc, qui considerare vult electionem, a Scriptura discedat, necesse est.

XIX. Hoc iam præsupposito, sic argumentamur; Deus in eligendo respexit aut fidem omnem, omniśque temporis, aut fidem tantum perseverantem & finalem. Non fidem omnem, omnisq́; temporis, 1. Quoniam πρόσκαιροι forent electi, & sic salvarentur, cuius falsitatem modo ostendimus. 2. Aliquis multoties aligeretur & reprobaretur, nimirum quoties resurgeret & caderet, id quod absurdum & probari nequit. Vnde sequitur, Deum potius fidem perseuerantem & finalem respexisse, quæ ipsa thesis vnanimiter à nostris defenditur. Ideò enim elegit Deus ad vitam vel salvare decreuit, non quia vidit quosdam ad tempus esse credituros, sed quia præuidit, eos in fide esse perseueraturos. Nam quomodo homines in tempore saluantur, eo modo ab æterno saluare decreuit & secundum illum elegit. Ast in tempore homines saluantur, non quia aliquando crediderunt, sic enim omnes πρόσκαιροι saluarentur, sed quia in fide perseuerarunt & mortui sunt. Quare & Deus hanc perseuerantem fidem in eligendo ab æterno respexit, atque sic electio facta est secundum præscientiam fidei finalis & vltimæ.

XX. Quibus ita stantibus, argumentando pergimus: Quicunque in tempore deficiunt, nec in fide perseuerant, in ijs fidem perseuerantem, ab æterno Deus præuidere non potuit. Quod enim futurum non est, id Dei præscientiam non attingit. At πρόσκαιροι in tempore deficiunt. Quare in ijs fidem perseuerantem præuidere Deus haut potuit, & P. C. non sunt electi ab æterno, licèt ad tempus credant, quoniam prædestinatio facta est secundum fidei vltimæ præscientiam, vt ostensum.

Classis tertia proponens dicta quod certus & infallibilis sit electorum numerus.

XXI. Pertinent huc sequentia Luc. 10. v. 20 Nomina vestra sunt scripta in cœlis. Luc. 12. v. 7. Capilli capitis vestri sunt numerati. Ioh. 10. v. 14. Ego cognosco owes meas. Ioh. 15. v. 18. Scio, quos elegerim. 2. Tim. 2. v. 14. Ego cognosco oves meas. Ioh. 13. v. 18. Scio, quos elegerim. 2. Tim. 2. v. 19. ἀμετακίνητον firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc, Nouit Dominus, qui sunt sui. Ex quibus omnibus deducitur, quod certus sit & omninò infallibilis electorum numerus, non non quidem ob absolutum quoddam decretum, sed propter certissimam Dei praeuisionem. Hinc Aug. l. decorrupt. & gratia. c. 12. & 13. scribit: Haec de iis loquor qui praedestinati sunt in regno Dei quorum ita certa est numerus, vt nec addatur eis quisquam, nec minuatur ex eis.

XXII. Qua hypothesi praesupposita sic jam colligimus: Si infallibilis & immutabilis est electorum numerus, sequitur, quod ex electo non possit fieri reprobus, vel contra. Sed verum prius, Quare & posterius. Ad maioris consequentiam fortius probandam notari velim, quod numerus sit duplex, alius numerans, quem Scholastici vocat formalem; alius numeratus quem materiale indignant Quando igitur Theologi dicunt electorum numerantem & numeratum, h. e. Deus ab aeterno decreuit & certo sciuit, non tantum, quot millia hominum, (qui numerus formalis est) sed etiam quos nam in indiuiduo homines (qui materialis) aeternum velit saluare & glorificare. Stante hoc aphorismo Theologico, maior propositi Syllogismi erit inuicta. Si n. ex electo posset fieri reprobus, & ex reprobo electus, toties minueretur numerus, quo ties non nulli cadunt; toties augeretur quoties resurgunt.

Qui igitur certus, non augmentabilis non alterabilis esset? Quo modo istud Dei propositum ἀμεταμέλητον & ἀμετακίνητον maneret? Incertissima certe electio foret, sit non ex fide perseuerante, & finali, sed quauis aestimaretur. Toties enim mutandum foret Deo suum decretum & propositum, quoties homo caderet quoties vicissim rediret.

XXIII. In specie vero consideretur istud Iohan. 13. vers. 18. Non de omnibus vobis loquor; Scio quos elegerim: qua assertione patet euidentissime, quod Iudas a Christo nunqua fuerit elect ad vita aeternam, idquod contra Huberum Theologi Witteburgenfes in explicatione breui p. 4. f. 1. expressè vrgent. Iudam verò nunquam credidisse, prorfus improbabile est. Si enim nullum aliud superesset argumentum, hoc tamen sufficeret, quòd Iudas in infantia fuerit circumcisus, atque sic per circumcisionem regeneratus. Ex quibus iam inuictè concluditur, Iudas nunquam fuit electus: Iudas in circumcisione vere fuit regeneratus. E. quidam verè regenerati non sunt electi. Maior, quòd Iudas nunquã fuerit electus, probatur ex dicto Christi, vbi discrimen facit inter Apostolos electos, & Iudam non electum. Ait enim: Non de omnibus loquor, scio enim quos elegerim. Ergo de quo non loquitur, eum non elegit. De Iuda non loquitur, vt docent sequentia. E. Iudam non elegit, & P. C. non omnes circumcisi & baptizati, licèt regenerati sint, pro electis haberi protinus debent.


### Question I: The fourth class, comprising sayings speaking of the eternity of election and reprobation

The fourth class, comprising sayings speaking of the eternity of election and reprobation.

XXIV. To this I refer the following testimonies: Eph. 1, v. 4: He chose us in Christ πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, before the foundations of the world were laid. 2 Tim. 1, v. 9: He called us with a holy calling, according to His purpose, πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων. 2 Thess. 2, v. 13: God chose us ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς from the beginning, i.e., as Micah interprets by another synonym in 5, v. 2: from the days of eternity. Rom. 9, v. 11: When the children were not yet born, etc. Augustine, book on predestination and grace, ch. 5: Before He made us, He foreknew us, and in that very foreknowledge, when He had not yet made us, He chose us. And shortly after: We were made within the world, and we were chosen before the world.

XXV. With all these things standing thus, we infer as follows: If every believer becomes elect at the time when he is reborn, and if every unbeliever is reprobated, or becomes a reprobate, at the time when he sins mortally, then... it follows entirely that our election and reprobation were not made from eternity. The consequent is absurd. Therefore, the antecedent is as well. We prove the consequence, because those who dissent establish that one immediately becomes reprobate from being elect when he falls mortally, and elect from reprobate when he rises again. Since, therefore, he is reborn in time, and falls in time, certainly both the election which they place under renewal, and the reprobation which they place under impenitence, will be temporal and will happen in time. Whoever, therefore, calls the elect προκαταλήκτως [pre-emptively], this person departs from the language and mind of Scripture, since election, as it is described in the sacred writings, was made from eternity, [even if] that of the reborn is in time.

XXVI. And indeed from this confusion flowed the entire error concerning mutable predestination, because no distinction is made between the temporal election of grace and the eternal election of glory, which alone is truly and univocally, and is called in the Scriptures, election. Every reborn person can indeed be called elect in a certain way, insofar as the grace of the Holy Spirit happens to him above others; but the question here is concerning eternal election: Is every reborn person included in it? Has anyone who was not reborn at a certain time been excluded from it? Where certainly it has been sufficiently demonstrated thus far by our people that the negative must be defended.

XXVII. So that the whole matter may be illustrated, I will take the example of Paul. Concerning him at that time, when he was still persecuting the Church, I ask: Was he included in the eternal decree of election? If they deny it, it follows that Paul was not elected from eternity, but only in time, after he was converted. Wherefore not before the foundations of the world were laid, which is absurd. If they say that by reason of foreknowledge Paul can be called always elect, I will accept this, and they ought to remember that the whole of Scripture in its proper places speaks of no other election than this one, which is then placed under foreknowledge, and made according to πρόγνωσιν, then from all eternity was decreed. XXIIX. I urge therefore this dilemma: Paul in that eternity, which neither present nor future reaches, was by God either reprobated or elected. If they shall say reprobated, he would certainly be damned. For whom God from eternity has reprobated and decreed to damn, he is most certainly damned, unless you posit that God is deceived and changed in his decrees. Wherefore it is necessary that they say Paul was elected from eternity, or included in the decree of election and of those to be saved. If therefore he was elected from eternity, even then when he was born, he was elected; even then, when he was persecuting the Church, since those temporal things can change nothing in the eternal and immutable divine decrees. Otherwise certainly, if everyone not reborn is reprobated, this absurdity would follow, that Paul was at the same time both elected and reprobated, elected namely from eternity, insofar as he was inscribed in the book of those to be saved before the foundations of the world were laid, and reprobated according to them in time, insofar as he was unfaithful and not yet reborn, than which what is more absurd? Or if they shall deny this, this nevertheless will infallibly follow, that no one is elected from eternity before regeneration is made in time. For I take again the example of Paul, or of other Saints and those to be saved. Were all these in the womb still before circumcision or Baptism elected from eternity? He will answer negatively, because then they were children of wrath. Hence therefore it follows in turn, that no one was elected from eternity, but that anyone is only elected in time, when he is inserted into the Church, which is diametrically opposed to the holy Scriptures.

Latin:

Classis quarta, comprehendens dicta, de electionis & reprobationis æternitate loquentia.

XXIV. Huc refero sequentia testimonia Eph. 1. v. 4. Elegit nos in Christo πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου, antequam iacerentur fundamenta mundi. 2. Tim. 1 v. 9. Vocauit nos vocatione sancta, secundum propositum suum, πρὸ χρόνων αἰωνίων, 2. Thess. 2. v. 13. Elegit nos Deus ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς ab initio, i. e. vt Micheas per aliud συνώνυμον 3c 5. v. 2: interpretatur à diebus æternitatis. Rom. 9. v. 11. Cùm nondum nati essent pueri, &c. Au. l. de præ, & grat. c. 5. Antequam faceret nos, præsciuit nos, & in ipsa nos præscientia, cùm nondum fecisset, elegit. Et mox: Intra mundum facti sumus, & ante mundum electi sumus.

XXV. Quibus omnibus ita stantibus, sic inferimus: Si omnis credens tùm, quando renascitur, fit electus, & si omnis infidelis, tum quando mortaliter peccat, reprobatur, aut fit reprobus, sequitur omninò quòd electio nostra & reprobatio non sit facta ab æterno. Consequens absurdum est. E. & antecedens. Probamus consequentiam, quia dissentientes statuunt, ex electo statim fieri reprobum, quando cadit mortaliter, & ex reprobo electum, quando resurgit. Quoniam igitur in tempore renascitur, & in tempore cadit, vtique & electio quam renouationi, & reprobatio, quam impœnitentiæ substernunt, temporalis erit, & in tempore continget. Quisquis ergo προκαταλήκτως vocat electos, hic à Scripturæ lingua & mente discedit, quoniam electio, prout in sacris literis describitur, facta est ab æterno, illa renatorum sit in tempore.

XXVI. Et sanè ex hâc confusione profluxit totus error de prædestinatione mutabili, quod non distinguatur inter temporalem gratiæ & æternam gloriæ electionem, quæ sola verè & vniuocè est & in Scripturis dicitur electio. Omnis quidem renatus dici potest modo quodam electus, quatenus ipsi præ reliquis gratia Spiritus Sancti contingit; quæritur autem hic de æterna electione, An illi omnis renatus sit inclusus? Num ab ea quispiā quodam tempore non renatus sit exclusus? Vbi certè negatiuam defendendam esse satis hactenus à Nostris demonstratum fuit.

XXVII. Vt illustretur totum negotium, sumam exemplum Pauli. De hoc eo tempore, quo adhuc Ecclesiam persequebatur, quæro, Fueritnè æterno electionis decreto comprehensus? si negauerint, sequitur Paulum non ab æterno, sed demum in tempore, postquam conuerteretur, fuisse electum. Quare non ante iacta mundi fundamenta, quòd absurdum. Si dixerint, ratione præuisionis Paulum posse dici semper electum. Assumam hoc, & meminisse illi debent, Scripturam vniuersam in locis proprijs de nulla electione alia loqui, quàm de hâc, quæ tùm præuisioni substrata, & secundum πρόγνωσιν facta, tùm ab omni æternitate decreta fuit. XXIIX. Vrgeo igitur hoc dilemna: Paulus in æternitate illa, quàm nec præsens nec futurum attingit, à Deo fuit aut reprobatus, aut electus. Si dixerint reprobatum, vtique damnaretur. Quem enim Deus ab æterno reprobauit & damnare decreuit, ille certissimè damnatur, nisi Deum in decretis falli, mutarique statuas. Quare necessum est, vt Paulum ab æterno electum, vel decreto electionis & saluandorum inclusum dicant. Si igitur ab æterno fuit electus, etiam tum cùm nasceretur, fuit electus; etiam tum, cùm persequeretur Ecclesiam, quoniam ista temporalia in æternis, & immutabilibus decretis diuinis nihil immutare queunt. Aliàs certè, si omnis non renatus est reprobatus, sequeretur hoc absurdum, quòd Paulus simul fuerit & electus & reprobatus, electus nempè ab æterno, quatenus libro saluandorum ante iacta mundi fundamenta inscriptus fuit, & reprobatus secundum ipsos in tempore, quatenus infidelis & nondum renatus erat, quo quid absurdius? Vel si hoc negauerint, istud tamen infallibiliter sequetur, quòd nemo sit ab æterno electus ante factam in tempore regenerationem. Nam sumo iterum exemplum Pauli, vel aliorum Sanctorum & saluandorum. Hi omnes in vtero adhuc ante circumcisionem vel Baptismum erantne ab æterno electi? Negatiuè responderit, quia tum fuerint filij iræ. Hinc E. vicissim sequitur, nullum ab æterno fuisse electum, sed quemuis tantùm in tempore eligi, cùm Ecclesiæ inseritur, id quod Scripturis sanctis è diametro est oppositum.


### Question I: The fifth class, reviewing those sayings of Scripture which say that election is the purpose and decree of God

The fifth class, reviewing those sayings of Scripture which say that election is the purpose and decree of God.

XXIX. Such things are read in Eph. 1:5, where Paul affirms that God predestined us κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ, according to the purpose or good pleasure of His will. 2 Tim. 1:9: He called us with a holy calling κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν, according to His own purpose. Rom. 9:11: ἡ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τοῦ θεοῦ πρόθεσις, etc. From which sayings it is gathered that election is not of an antecedent and simple will, whose objects, as being dependent in part upon men, do not always come to pass; but of a consequent and decretory will, by which God does not merely wish that something be done from it, but by which He decrees that He will certainly do something.

For will, θέλημα, is one thing, and the decree of the will, θελήματος πρόθεσις, is another. For we often will those things which are not in our power, which nevertheless we never purpose or decree, unless we wish to be delirious. Thus, the pious wish to be freed from the body of sin, they wish to be immune from vicious intrusions; yet they cannot decree that they will do that very thing, since this is not in their power. Hence the Philosopher himself, in Ethics book 3, chapters 2, 3, and 4, lays the foundations of this distinction, that one will is ὀρεκτικὴ, which is the sole and naked appetite itself, by which someone simply wills and desires something; another is προβευλευτικὴ or deliberated, when someone does not simply desire a thing, but also proposes it to himself, and certainly decrees that he will labor by all means to attain the thing which he desires. In like manner, in God, simple will is one thing; decretory will, or will κατὰ πρόθεσιν, is another. Those things which fall under the former do not always come to pass, but those which fall under the latter most certainly happen. For He has done all things whatsoever He has willed, it is said in Psalm 115:3. ὃς ἂν θέλῃ γίνεται, says Damascenus in book 2 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 29. For unless those things which God decreed to do were to happen, happens, then it would either not want to do it, or would not be able to do it. The former cannot be said, since a decree is the highest and most efficacious degree of the will. The latter is blasphemous, and detracts much from the divine omnipotence. I conclude, therefore, that the decrees of God are infallible, and all those things which God does not merely wish, but proposes and decrees to do, most certainly and infallibly come to pass.

XXX. With this most firm ὑποθέσει (hypothesis) presupposed, we argue thus for the immutability of election: All decrees of God are infallible, and immutable, and unalterable. Election is a decree of God, or made κατὰ πρόθεσιν (according to purpose). Therefore, it is infallible, immutable, unalterable. Whoever, therefore, God has chosen from all eternity or decreed to save, he always remains chosen, and at every time before God is chosen, and finally will most certainly and infallibly be glorified. For if God had chosen someone from eternity, e.g., Paul, but he, while still existing as impious in time, were to be called not chosen but reprobate, would not the decree of God be changed? Since it is impious to say this, we conclude from this that, because God has decreed to save every chosen one, but not all who are reborn and baptized are actually saved, not all of them are truly and univocally chosen, or included in the decree of election.

Latin:

Classis quinta recensens ista Scripturæ dicta, quæ electionem dicunt esse propositum & decretum Dei.

XXIX. Talia leguntur Ephes. 1. v. 5. vbi Paulus affirmat, Deum nos prędestinasse κατὰ τὴν εὐδοκίαν τοῦ θελήματος αὐτοῦ. secundum propositum vel beneplacitum voluntatis suæ. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. Vocauit nos vocatione sancta κατ' ἰδίαν πρόθεσιν, secundum proprium propositum. Rom. 9. v. 11. ἡ κατ' ἐκλογὴν τοῦ θεοῦ πρόθεσις &c. Ex quibus dictis colligitur, electionem non esse voluntatis antecedentis & simplicis, cuius volita vt pote ab hominibus ex parte dependentia, non semper contingunt; sed voluntatis consequentis & decretoriæ, quam Deus non aliquid indè fieri vult, sed quam aliquid certò se facturum decernit.

Aliud enim est voluntas, θέλημα, & aliud est voluntatis decretum, θελήματος πρόθεσις. Nam sæpè volumus ea, quæ non sunt in nostra potestate, quæ tamen nunquam proponimus vel decernimus, nisi delirare velimus Sic pij volunt liberari à corpore peccati, volunt immunes esse à vitiosis subreptionibus: decernere tamen nequeunt, se idipsum facturos, quoniam in potestate eorum hoc non est. Hinc ipse Philosophus lib. 3. Eth. c. 2. 3. & 4. fundamenta ponit huius distinctionis, quòd voluntas alia sit ὀρεκτικὴ, quę est ipse solus & nudus appetitus, quo quis aliquid ἁπλῶς vult & appetit: alia προβευλευτικὴ vel deliberata, quando aliquis rẽ non simpliciter cupit, sed sibi etiam proponit, & certè decernit, se omnibus modis laboraturum, vt rem, quã appetit, assequatur. Pari modo in Deo aliud est voluntas, simplex; aliud volũtas decretoria, vel voluntas κατὰ πρόθεσιν. Quæ sub illam cadunt, non semper fiunt, quæ verò sub hanc certißimè contingunt. Omnia enim quę voluit, fecit, dicitur Psal. 115. v. 3. ὃς ἂν θέλῃ γίνεται, inquit Damascenus l. 2. Orth. fid. c. 29. Nisi enim fierent, quæ Deus facere decrefit, tum illa aut non facere vellet, aut non facere poffet. Prius dici nequit, quoniam decretum est summus & efficacissimus voluntatis gradus. Posterius blasphemum est, & omnipotentiæ diuinæ multum derogat, Concludo igitur, quod decreta Dei sint infallibilia, & omnia ea, quæ Deus non nudè vult tantùm, sed facere proponit & decernit, certissimè & infallibiliter fiant,

XXX. Hâc ὑποθέσει firmissimâ præsuppositâ, pro immutabilitate electionis sic argumentamur: Omnia decreta Dei sunt infallibilia, & immutabilia, & inalterabilia, Electio est decretum Dei, vel facta κατὰ πρόθεσιν. E. est infallibilis, immutabilis, inalterabilis. Quem igitur Deus ab omni æternitate elegit vel saluare decreuit is semper manet electus, & omni tempore coram Deo est electus, & tandem certissimè & infallibiliter glorificabitur. Nam si Deus quempiam ab æterno elegisset, v. e. g. Paulum, is autem in tempore adhuc impius existens, non electus sed reprobus dicendus sit, annon decretum Dei mutaretur? Quod cùm dicere sit impium, concludimus exinde, quia omnem electum Deus saluare decreuit, non autem omnes renati & baptizati actu saluantur, non omnes eos verè & vniuocè esse electos, vel decreto electionis inclusos.


### Question I: Sixth class, reviewing testimonies concerning the preparation of the heavenly kingdom from eternity

Sixth class, reviewing testimonies concerning the preparation of the heavenly kingdom from eternity,

XXXI. Matt. 25:34. Come, you blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom, which has been prepared for you from the foundation of the world. Mark 10:40. To sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to give, but to those for whom it has been prepared. And what other testimonies are similar to these: We indeed gather from this as follows: Whoever are the blessed of the Father, or chosen by the Father, they will possess the kingdom at the final judgment, and for them the heavenly life is prepared. But indeed, the reborn and baptized πρόσκαιροι (temporary ones) will not possess the kingdom, nor is it for them prepared. Therefore, the reborn and baptized πρόσκαιροι [temporary ones] were not, nor were they ever, elected by the Father.

XXXII. Or in this way: To whomever the kingdom is not prepared, they were never elected. But indeed it was never prepared for the πρόσκαιροι [temporary ones], but only for those who persevere. Therefore, the πρόσκαιροι were never truly elected. The major premise is proven by the saying of Matthew and the testimony of Fulgentius, which he has in book 1 to Monimus, p. 42, where he says: 'For there is no other predestination of his, except the eternal preparation of his future works.' However, a distinction must be made here between the promise of the kingdom and the preparation. It is indeed promised to all, but it is not prepared for all, only for those who persevere; since preparation is joined with the efficacious decree of admitting or receiving. The minor premise is likewise certain, that the kingdom is not prepared for the impious and the προσκαίροις [temporary ones]. For if this were the case, then they would certainly possess heaven. For Christ gives the reason why they ought to possess the kingdom: 1. Because they are the blessed of the Father or the elected. Therefore, those who ought not to possess, they were not elected. 2. Because for them it was thus prepared. Therefore, for those who do not possess, it was not prepared, unless it be impiously maintained that Christ proposed false causes of salvation.

The seventh class, containing sayings that election is firm and always attains its end.

XXXIII. 1. From 2 Tim. 2, v. 19: 'The foundation of God stands firm, the Lord knows who are his.' In this saying, there lie hidden almost as many arguments for the immutability of election as there are words. For 1. Election is called θεμέλιον [foundation], so that it may be indicated that election is most certain, just as a foundation is immovable and invariable: 2. It is called not of any man, who can be changed, but θεοῦ θεμέλιον [God's foundation], the foundation of God: Now indeed God is immutable, nor is he changed like a man from hour to hour. Mal. 3, v. 6. 3. It is said to stand: or by to stand, by which the eternal duration and invariable firmness of election is intimated, and finally 4. that nothing may be lacking, it is called εὐχερὲς, most certain, most firm, and adamantine; which can in no way be shaken, and by no reason be changed: whence it is concluded, that everyone who was included by God in this foundation and θεμελίῳ from eternity, always remains such, and can never fall away into eternity, so that thus only those who persevere are comprehended by this firm decree and foundation of election.

XXXIV. 2. From Rom. 11:7. What Israel was seeking, it has not obtained, but the rest were blinded. From which statement theologians unanimously gather that election is never frustrated of its end, but every elect person attains that to which he was elected, namely salvation and eternal life, which is the end of faith. 1 Pet. 1:9. For the words are most clear, 'But the election has obtained it.' Where, whether you understand the election itself in the abstract, or the elect in the concrete, it will be the same: since the sense remains the same in both cases. And let this ἀντίθεσις between the elect and the reprobate and the Jews be noted. For he says that the reprobate Jews were blinded, but the elect believed: Why? Because election is not frustrated of its end, but attains it. But certain Jews were elect, whence he concludes that these are to be saved.

XXXV. 7. Verse 1 and 2 of the same chapter 11 also pertain here, where Paul opposes himself. For because in the preceding he had said that the Jews were rejected by God on account of unbelief, he now proceeds by asking: Has God therefore rejected His people? That is, has God now rejected the people whom He once elected? Can one thus become a reprobate from being elect? Far be it, the Apostle answers. God has not rejected His people, whom He foreknew. Do not think at all that the election of God is mutable, but all those whom He foreknew or predestined from among the Jews, He has in no way rejected, but they attain their end, to which they are pre destined, even if the greatest part of the rest is blinded, and thus perishes eternally. Hence v. 5 he says: In this time a remnant according to the election of the grace of God have been saved. Which words certainly all tend to this, that it may be indicated that the elect do not finally fall away from grace and salvation, but although they may be ignored, although many others may fail, they themselves are nevertheless preserved by God, reserved from final unbelief, and thus according to election, by the force of an immutable decree, are saved.

Latin:

Classis sexta, recensens testimonia de præparatione regni cœlestis ab æterno,

XXXI. Matth. 25. v. 34. Venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete regnum, quod paratum est vobis à constitutione mundi. Marc. 10. v. 40. Sedere ad dextram meam & ad sinistram non est meum dare vobis, sed quibus paratum est. Et quæ sunt alia his similia testimonia: Nos vero inde sic colligimus: Quicunque sunt benedicti Patris, vel electi à Patre, illi in extremo iudicio possidebunt regnum, & iis vita cœlestis est præparata. At verò renati & baptizati πρόσκαιροι non possidebunt regnum, nec iis præparatum. E. renati & baptizati πρόσκαιροι non fuerũt nec fuerunt unquam electi à Patre.

XXXII. Vel hoc modo; Quibuscunque non est præparatum regnum, ij nunquam sunt electi. At verò nunquam πρόσκαιροις, sed solis perseuerantibus fuit præparatum. E. πρόσκαιροι nunquam fuerunt verè electi. Maior probatur dicto Matthæi, & Fulgentij testimonio, quod habet l. 1. ad Monim. p. 42. vbi inquit. Neque enim alia est eius prædestinatio, nisi futurorum operum eius æterna præparatio. Distinguendum verò hîc est inter regni promissionem & præparationem. Omnibus quidem est promissum, sed non omnibus, nisi solis perseuerantibus, præparatum; quoniam præparatio coniuncta est cum efficaci decreto intromittendi vel recipiendi: Minor similiter certa est, quòd impijs & προσκαίροις regnum non sit præparatum. Hoc enim si esset, tùm vtique cœlum possiderent. Reddit n. Christus caussam, cur possidere debeant regnum. 1. Quia sint benedicti Patris vel electi. E. qui non possidere debent, ij non fuerunt electi. 2. Quia ijs sic præparatum. E. qui non possident, ijs non fuit præparatum, nisi Christum falsas saluationis causas proposuisse impiè statuatur.

Classis septima, continens dicta, quod electio firma sit, & finem suum semper assequatur.

XXXIII. 1. Ex 2. Tim. 2. v. 19. Firmum stat fundamentum Dei, Nouit Dominus qui sint sui. In hoc dicto tot penè latent argumẽta pro immutabilitate electionis, quot sunt verba. Nam 1. Electio vocatur θεμέλιον fundamentum, vt indicetur electionem esse certissimam, sicut fundamentum est immotum & inuariabile: 2. Non hominis alicuius, qui mutari potest, sed θεõ θεμέλιον vocatur, Dei fundamentum: Iàm verò Deus est immutabilis, nec sicut homo mutatur in horas. Mal. 3. v. 6. 3. dicitur stare: vel perstare, quo æterna electionis duratio & inuariabilis firmitudo innuitur, & denique 4. nè quid desit, dicitur εὐχερὲς, certissimum, firmissimum & adamantinum; quod nullo modo labefactari, nulla ratione immutari queat: vnde concluditur, Omnem, qui huic fundamento & θεμελίῳ ab æternitate fuit inclusus à Deo, semper talem manere, & in æternum excidere non posse, vt ita soli perseuerantes firmo isto electionis decreto & fundamento sint comprehensi.

XXXIV. 2. Ex Rom. 11. v 7. Quod quærebat Israël, non est consecutus, cæteri verò excæcati sunt. Quo ex dicto Theologi vnanimiter colligunt, quòd electio suo fine nunquam frustretur, sed omnis electus assequatur id, ad quod electus est, nempè salutem & vitam æternam, quæ finis fidei. 1. Petr. 1. vers. 9. Sunt enim verba clarissima, Electio verò consecuta est. Vbi siue ipsam electionem in abstracto, siue electos in concreto intelligas, perinde erit: cùm sensus vtrobique idem maneat. Et notetur ἀντίθεσις ista inter electos & reprobatos & Iudæos. Dicit enim, Iudæos reprobos esse excæcatos, electos autem credidisse: Quare? Quia electio non frustratur fine suo, sed eum consequitur. Quidam autem Iudæi erant electi, vnde concludit, hos esse saluandos.

XXXV. 7 Pertinet huc etiam vers. 1. & 2. eiusdem capitis 11. vbi Paulus tibi ipsi opponit. Quia enim in præcedentibus dixerat, Iudæos à Deo ob infidelitatem esse reiectos, iam pergit quærendo; Numquid ergò Deus repulit populum suum? id est, Numne Deus populum, quem semel elegit, iam reiecit? Itanè ex electo reprobus fieri potest? Absit, respondit Apostolus. Non repulit Deus plebem suam, quam præsciuit. Minimè putetis electionem Dei esse mutabilem, sed omnes, quos præsciuit vel prædestinauit ex Iudæis, eos nullo modo repulit, sed assequuntur finem suum, ad quem sunt prædestinati, etiamsi maxima pars reliquorum excæcetur, atque sic æternùm pereat. Hinc v. 5. ait: In hoc tempore reliquiæ secundum electionem gratiæ Dei saluæ factæ sunt. Quæ certè verba omnia eò tendunt, vt indicetur, electos non excidere finaliter gratiâ & salute, sed licèt ignorentur, licet alij multi deficiant, ipsos tamen à Deo conseruari, à finali incredulitate reseruari, atque ita secūdum electionem, vi decreti immutabilis, saluari.


### Question I: The eighth class enumerating the sayings concerning those never written in the book of life

The eighth class enumerating the sayings concerning those never written in the book of life.

XXXVI. Apocal. 13. verse 8. All who inhabit the earth worshipped it, whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb. Apoc. 17. verse 8. Those who inhabit the earth will marvel, whose names are not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world. c. 20. v. last. Whoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire, etc. From these, but especially from c. 17, we argue thus: These admirers of the beast are either outside the Church or inside the Church: Not outside, since the Turks, Tartars, and other barbarians do not admire the primacy and glory of the Pope, but hold them in contempt. Wherefore these admirers are inside the Church, in the assembly of the called, and in infancy were truly regenerated through Baptism.

XXXVII. These things being posited, an invincible argument now arises. The admirers of the Roman beast were never written in this book of life, even from the first foundation of the world, according to the saying alleged. The admirers of the Roman beast in infancy were truly regenerated and sanctified through Baptism. Indeed, those truly regenerated on account of foreseen final impenitence were never holy in the book of life, that is, they were never chosen by God, so that from God's san-

The ninth and final class, containing sayings, that the elect cannot finally be seduced.

XXXIIX. Of these, the first is that of Matt. 24, v. 24, Mark 13, v. 22: 'False Christs and false prophets shall arise and shall give great signs and wonders, so that they might lead into error, εἰ δυνατὸν, if it were possible, or could be done, even the elect.' From this we infer: If it were possible for an elect person to become a reprobate, then at the same time it would be possible for the elect to be finally seduced. But according to Christ's assertion, it is not possible for the elect to be finally seduced. Therefore, it will not be possible for an elect person to become a reprobate.

XXXIX. Nor is the exception valid, that by impossibility one should understand difficulty, for the reason that 'impossible' is often the same as 'difficult.' For, to say nothing of the fact that this explanation is a begging of the question and proceeds from particulars alone, I would wish that this one thing be studiously considered: that Christ does not say it is impossible for the elect to be seduced, but He shapes the style thus: 'They will perform signs so great that even the elect would be led into error, if it were possible': by which words He certainly intends to be understood not merely a difficulty, but an altogether absolute impossibility of seduction. For even he who is seduced with difficulty is still seduced, but Christ altogether denies that any elect person will be seduced, because this is not possible. What kind of, and how absurd, a paraphrase would this be: 'Even the elect would be led into error on account of signs and wonders, if it were possible, that is, unless it were difficult.' Indeed, it could be inverted; although it is difficult, nevertheless they will be able to be led astray, since even those things which happen with difficulty, nevertheless sometimes happen, and can happen. Unless, therefore, it pleases one to completely invert the words of Christ, it is necessary that we confess that Christ spoke of the impossibility, rather than the difficulty, of seduction.

XL. Here, however, a question arises: whether by this means an absolute decree is established; or whether some other cause of impossibility can be assigned for these statements? We distinguish between absolute and ineffable, maintaining that the elect are not preserved and saved by an absolute and fatal necessity, as if it were simply impossible for them to perish, whatever they might do; but we mean only that they can sin and perish: yet this never happens, or can happen, because they are infallibly preserved. And thus we establish the cause of that weakness not as a fatal Calvinistic decree, not as the supreme perfection of the elect, but rather: 1. The power of God guarding the elect in faith unto salvation. 1 Pet. 1, verse 5. 2. The efficacious prayer of Christ for the perseverance and salvation of the elect, 1 John 17, 9. The power of Christ, by which no one can snatch the sheep from his hands, John 10, v. 28. 4. The firmness of the divine decree, 2 Tim. 2, v. 19. and finally 5. The infallibility of foreknowledge. XLI. Therefore we willingly concede this, that the elect, by reason of imperfect renewal, are so constituted that they could, as far as it lies in them, finally fall and perish; yet they by no means actually fall away or perish, not because of a fatal decree, not because of supreme perfection, but because God from eternity foresaw that they would persevere, because from eternity he decreed to preserve and save them; because in time he preserves them from final impenitence; because Christ prayed for all, and does not permit them to be snatched from his hand by the seducing Devil. Wherefore it is to be noted that the controversy is not so much about the power as about the act. For on the part of the elect I concede the power, that they could perish, unless they are preserved by God. But those who dissent maintain that many not only can perish, but have actually perished and are perishing, which they cannot prove from the present text. XLII. Some indeed object to verse 12. Ni si if those days had not been shortened, no flesh would be saved, but for the sake of the elect those days will be shortened. Whence they gather that even the elect can fall away from the grace of God both totally and finally. For if no flesh were saved, neither would the elect be saved, and P. C. would perish. I respond by an inversion of the argument. Unless the days were shortened, then not all flesh would be saved, and then the elect could perish. But now, since the text says, for the sake of the elect the days have been shortened. Therefore, by the shortening of the days having been made, in act they will no longer perish, nor will they be able to perish. And let this phrase be well considered. But for the sake of the elect they have been shortened. Why for the sake of the elect? For no other cause certainly than that which God from eternity has certainly decreed, to save all the elect in time. Before, therefore, He would change this decree, He prefers to shorten the days of this age, whence such a sense of this saying emerges. In the last times of the world there will be such perversity of heretics, such persecution of the pious and of the Church, that even the elect, on account of the annexed infirmity of the flesh and the weakness of the will and intellect, if they were considered from their own powers, could easily be seduced and thus perish, especially if God were to connive with heretics for longer and permit them to persecute the Church for more centuries. Since, however, He has decreed from eternity to save all the elect, therefore He is about to shorten the days of the age, lest the predestined be seduced or perish as they could perish, as far as it is in them; but so that all may be actually glorified, just as He decreed from eternity to glorify them.

XLIII. Therefore let our conclusion remain firm and immovable, that no one of the elect actually perishes, nor ever falls away from election, indeed in such a way that if God foresees the danger of the elect, He even wills to constitute the term and end of this age shorter than to permit that any of His elect be damned or perish. Nothing therefore can be proven by this saying other than this: That the elect are not of such strength of themselves that they can preserve themselves against all the snares of heretics and the machinations of persecutors, that which freely we grant. But since God has decreed that none of the predestined shall perish; hence, what they cannot perform by their own powers, God himself performs, and mercifully preserves all and each of the elect from final seduction, and for that very end shortens the days. What therefore was possible before the established abbreviation of days, this now after his decree has been made impossible, whence we conclude: From no elect person, by virtue of an immutable decree, can a reprobate be made; which was to be demonstrated.

Latin:

Classis octaua enumerans dicta, de nunquam inscriptis in librum vitæ.

XXXVI. Apocal. 13. vers. 8. Adorauerunt eam omnes qui inhabitant terram, quorum non sunt scripta nomina in libro vitæ agni. Apoc. 17. vers. 8. Mirabuntur inhabitantes terram, quorum non sunt scripta nomina in libro vitæ à constitutione mundi. c. 20. v. vlt. Qui non inuentus est in libro vitæ scriptus missus est in stagnum ignis, &c. Ex his, præsertim verò ex c. 17. sic argumentamur: Isti miratores bestiæ aut extrá Ecclesiam sunt aut intrá Ecclesiam: Non extra, quoniam Turcæ, Tartari, alijque barbari primatum & gloriam Papæ non mirantur, sed floccipendunt. Quare isti miratores sunt intra Ecclesiam, in cœtu vocatorum, & in infantia per Baptismum vere fuerunt regenerati.

XXXVII. Quibus positis, iam invictum oritur argumentum. Miratores bestiæ Romanæ nunquam fuerunt scripti in hoc libro vitæ, etiam à prima mundi constitutione, iuxta dictum allegatum. Miratores bestiæ Romanæ in infantia per Baptismum verè fuerunt regenerati & sanctificati. Equidem verè regenerati ob præuisam finalem impœnitentiam nunquam fuerunt sancti in libro vitæ, hoc est, nunquam fuerunt à Deo electi, ita quòd ex Dei san-

Classis nona & vltima, continens dicta, quod electi finaliter seduci nequeant

XXXIIX. Ex ijs primum est illud Matth. 24. v. 24. Marc. 13. v. 22. Surgent Pseudo Christi & Pseudo Prophetae & dabut signa magna & prodigia ita vt in errorem inducantur ei δυνατὸν, si possibile esset, vel fieri posset, etiam electi. Hinc inferimus: Si ex electo posset fieri reprobus, tum simul possibile foret, electos seduci finaliter. Atqui iuxta Christi assertionem, possibile non est, electos seduci finaliter. E. nec possibile erit, ex electo fieri reprobum.

XXXIX. Neque valet exceptio, per impossibilitatem esse intelligendam difficultatem, eo quod impossibile saepe idem sit, quod difficile. Etenim vt nihil, dicam, quod haec explicatio sit principij petitio, & ex solis particularibus procedat, vel illud solu studiose considerari velim, Christum non dicere, impossibile est electos seduci, sed ita informat stylum: Facient signa adeo magna: vt etiam in errorem inducerentur electi, si possibile esset: quibus certe verbis non modo difficultatem, sed omnimod prorsus impossibilitatem seductionis intellectam vult. Nam etiam seducitur qui difficulter seducitur, Christus autem omnino negat, seductum iri vllum electum, quia hoc non sit possibile. Qualis autem & quam absurda foret paraphrasis: In errorem propter signa & prodigia inducerentur etiam electi, si possibile foret, id est, nisi difficile foret. Imo inuerti posset; licet sit difficile, tamen induci poterunt, quoniam etiam ea, quae difficulter contingunt, tamen quandoque contingunt, & contingere possunt. Nisi ergo verba Christi omnino inuertere placeat, necesse est, vt fateamur, Christum potius de impossibilitate, quam difficultate seductionis locutum esse.

XL. Hic autem exoritur quaestio: Annon hoc pacto absolutum statuatur decretum; vel num alia dicta impossibilitatis caussa assignari queat? Nos distinguimus inter absolutum & ineffabile, statuentes non ex absoluta & fatali necessitate electos conseruari & saluari, quasi simpliciter impossibile sit, vt pereant, quicquid etiam agant; sed duntaxat infallibilitatem intellectam volumus. Ipsorum quidem conditio talis est, vt peccare & perire possint: nunquam tamen hoc contingit, aut contingere potest, quia infallibiliter conseruantur. Atque sic imbecillitatis istius causam constituimus non fatale decretum Caluinisticum, non perfectionem summam electorum, sed potius. 1. Virtutem Dei custodientis electos in fide ad salutem. 1. Pet. 1. vers. 5. 2. Precationem Christi efficacem pro perseverantia & & salute electorum, 1. Ioh. 17. 9. Potestatem Christi, qui nemo potest oves rapere ex manibus suis, Ioh. 10. v. 28. 4. Firmitatem decreti diuini, 2. Tim. 2. v. 19. & denique 5. Infallibilitatem præscientiæ. XLI. Proinde hoc lubenter concedimus, electos ratione imperfectæ renouationis taliter esse comparatos, vt possint, quantum in ipsis est, finaliter labi & perire; minimè tamen actu excidunt aut pereunt, nõ ob fatale decretum, non ob summam perfectionem, sed quia Devs ab æterno præuidit eos perseueraturos, quia ab æterno decreuit eos conseruare & saluare; quia in tempore præseruat eos à finali impœnitentia; quia Christus pro omnibus orauit, & de manu sua illos à Diabolo seducente rapi non permittit. Quare notandum est, quòd non tàm de potentia, quàm de actu sit controuersia. Etenim ex parte electorum concedo potentiam, quod possint perire, nisi conseruentur à Deo. Dissentientes verò statuunt, quòd multi non modo possint perire, sed etiam ipso actu perierint & pereant, id quod ex præsenti textu probare nequeunt. XLII. Objiciunt vero nonnulli versiculũ 12. Nisi breuiati fuissent dies illi, non fieret salua omnis caro, sed propter electos breuiabuntur dies illi. Vnde colligunt, Etiam electos gratia Dei & totaliter & finaliter excidere posse. Si enim nulla caro salua fieret, nec electi salui fierent, & P. C. perirent. Respon. per inuersionem argumenti. Nisi dies abbreuiarentur, tunc non salua fieret omnis caro, & tum electi possent perire. Iam verò dicente textu, propter electos abbreuiati sunt dies. E. facta dierum decurtatione, actu amplius nō peribunt, nec perire poterunt. Et benè consideretur phrasis ista. Sed propter electos abbreuiati sunt. Cur propter electos? Ob nullă certò causam aliam, quàm eam, quod Deus ab æternitate certò decreuit, omnes electos in tempore saluare. Priusquam igitur decretum hoc mutet, decurtare potius vult dies huius seculi, vnde talis dicti istius sensus emergit. Vltimis mundi temporibus tanta erit hæreticorum peruersitas, tanta piorum & Ecclesiæ persecutio, vt etiam electi propter annexam carnis infirmitatem, voluntatis & intellectus imbecillitatem, si ex suis considerentur viribus facilè possint seduci, & ita perire, præsertim si Deus hæreticis diutius conniueret, & ad plura secula Ecclesiam persequi permitteret. Quoniam autem ab æterno decreuit, omnes electos saluare; idcircò dies seculi abbreuiaturus est, ne prædestinati seducantur, aut pereant sicut perire possent, quantum in ipsis est; sed vt omnes actu glorificentur, sicut eos glorificare ab æterno decreuit.

XLIII. Firma igitur & immota persistat nostra conclusio, quòd nullus electorum actu pereat, nec vnquam electione excidat, ita quidem, vt si Deus præuideat periculum electorum, etiam velit terminum & finem huius seculi curtiorem constituere quàm permittere, vt nullus de suis electis damnetur vel pereat. Nihil proinde aliud probari potest isto dicto, quàm hoc; Quòd electi ex se tantarum virium non sint, vt semetipsos præseruare queant contra omnes hæreticorum insidias & persequentium machinas, id quod liberaliter concedimus. Quoniam verò Deus decreuit, nè vllus ex prædestinatis pereat; hinc quod ex proprijs viribus præstare nequeunt, Deus ipse præstat, & à finali seductione electos vniuersos & singulos clementer præseruat, & in eum etiam finem dies decurtat. Quod igitur ante constitutam dierum abbreuiationem erat possibile, hoc jam post ejus decretum factum est impossibile, vnde colligimus: Ex nullo electo, vi decreti immutabilis, fieri posse reprobum; id quod erat demonstrandum.


### Question I: II. Arguments from the Analogy of Faith

II. ARGUMENTS FROM the Analogy of Faith.

XLIV. 1. From the identity of the decree of those to be saved and the elect. Orthodox theologians commonly teach that the decree of election and that of salvation are one and the same. For the Calvinists indeed make a distinction, while they say that the decree of election and reprobation is absolute, but that of salvation and damnation is limited and joined with the intuition of faith and infidelity. To them we rightly oppose ourselves, with sincere theologians who militate sharply for the unity of the decrees, indeed so that they establish in express words that the decree concerning the elect is the decree concerning those to be saved, whence they often couple both, and call them the elect to be saved. Yet, so that no handle for excepting remains, we demonstrate this principle, otherwise most customary and undoubted in theological schools, as follows.

XLV. The defined and the definition do not differ really. But the decree of election and salvation stand as the defined and the definition. Therefore they do not differ really. The minor is proved, because both by the Formula of Concord and by all other theologians, election is commonly defined in this sense, that it is the eternal decree of God concerning those to be saved and glorified in Christ perseveringly to those who will believe. Whence it is evident that the decree of salvation, if not the entire definition of election, is nevertheless its greatest part, and therefore these do not really differ. This salvation indeed differs from predestination, as a temporal act from an eternal one, as the execution of a decree from the decree itself; nevertheless, the decree of election and of salvation do not really differ, but are one decree: which can be proven both from the argument set forth and from this theological στοιχεῖον besides. Election and salvation relate to each other as decree and the execution of a decree. Whence we conclude thus: Where the execution is one and the same in number, there the decree of which the execution is given is one and the same in number.
