But the execution of the decree of election and of salvation is one and the same, namely salvation and glorification. Therefore, the decree of election and of salvation are one decree in number, nor do they differ from each other really.

XLVI. With these things now standing most firmly, we form an invincible and completely insoluble argument: Those excluded from the decree of salvation are also excluded from the decree of election. The reason has already been given, because they are one and the same decree without any real difference. But many who are truly reborn and sanctified through Baptism, if they are πρόσκαιροι, are from all eternity and remain always excluded from the decree of salvation. Otherwise, they would eventually return to repentance and be saved. Therefore, many who are truly reborn and sanctified through Baptism, if they are πρόσκαιροι, are from all eternity and remain always excluded from the decree of election, that is, they never are or can be called elect.

XLVII. 3. From the immutability of God, God is immutable, Mal. 3, v. 6, Num. 23, v. 19. Moreover, a triple immutability is given in God. 1. Of essence. 2. Of attributes. 3. Of decrees. And concerning this the ancients said: God, as He does not change His essence, so He does not change His sentence. I subsume: Election is a decree of God concerning those to be saved. Therefore, it is immutable. Since, therefore, God has once decreed to save someone, and therefore has elected him, then if He does not save him, but condemns in time, he certainly changes his decree. Nor is it for them to say, God wills many things which do not come to pass. For we distinguish between a bare will and a decretory one. The former, since it depends on a condition, does not always attain its end, and to this belongs election,

XLIIX. 3. From the absurd. Either every elect person is to be saved, or a certain elect person can be called damnable. If the former, then no one of the elect will finally fall from election. If the latter, a certainly huge absurdity is established. For how, I ask, can we affirm without absurdity that a son of God who is elect, and inscribed in that book of life in which he who is found is said to be saved, how, I say, can we affirm that one predestined by God to eternal life and salvation is to be burned and damned by infernal flames? Nor can they weaken the cohesion of the major premise. For thus we conclude: God has decreed either something or nothing concerning all the baptized and regenerated and their salvation. The latter is absurd, and against divine providence. Therefore the former is true. Furthermore, he either decreed concerning all that he certainly wills to save them, or concerning some. Not concerning all, because not all persevere nor are all saved, and therefore they are not included in the most certain decree of salvation, whence the genuine decree follows immediately. The one, that God wills to save believers on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by persevering faith; the other, that he wills to condemn the unfaithful, on account of foreseen impenitence and incredulity. Now indeed, if it be said that all the reborn are truly elect, this absurdity arises from it, that God from eternity decreed to damn his own children who were truly elect and predestined to eternal life; and thus the elect is at the same time reprobate, which is a contradiction.

XLIX. I will illustrate this with a simile, taken from the Apostle Jude. This one from eternity was either elect or repro bate: either to be saved or to be damned. Not chosen or to be saved. And reprobated & to be damned. I ask further, whether this decree also endured in the time of the renewed and circumcised Judas? Certainly: For what God has once decreed, that he never changes. He decreed, however, from eternity, to damn Judas in time on account of his future desperation and impenitence. In God's foreknowledge, therefore, he was always to be damned. With this presupposed, there follows that huge absurdity, that one and the same Judas was at one and the same time reprobated and elected. Insofar as he was reprobated, God decreed to damn him; insofar as he was elected, God decreed to save him; which is ἀντιφατικὸν [contradictory].

I. From the τάξει [order] & order of election. The Formula of Concord, and with it the sounder theologians, instruct that in the decree of election, one must consider not merely God choosing, not only the persons chosen, but also the order and the means through which election ought to be ratified. For the eternal purpose of God regards two diverse objects, one of persons, the other of things; and according to these two objects there are two parts of the decree, of which the one is specially called election, which looks to the persons to be chosen: the other is predestination or preordination, which regards the means of salvation and election. Included in these means is this, that God from eternity decreed to preserve his elect, and to grant them perseverance, since he foresaw that they would not place an obstacle to the Holy Spirit. He indeed wills to give faith to all, yet he does not confer it upon all, but only upon the elect, since he foresaw that these alone would not resist, as he foresaw the others would; so that thus this distinction between simple and decretory will ought also to be referred here. From these theological hypotheses, however, it is inferred anew that whoever are not preserved in time, nor persevere, they are not included in the decree of election from eternity, since election with the preordination of preservation and perseverance has been made. And yet very many who are reborn fall away, and do not persevere, whence it is gathered that they were never truly elected.

LI. 5. From the consonance of the decree with the execution. I do not think there will be anyone who would deny that most celebrated element in theological schools, that salvation and election stand in relation to each other as a decree and the execution of a decree, and therefore they acknowledge exactly the same causes, and in this respect are in all things conformable. Whence such an argument arises: If salvation is the execution of the decree of election, then certainly if anyone is not saved, no decree was made concerning his being saved, that is, he was never elected, since to be saved and to be elected stand in relation to each other as execution and decree. Now, however, very many temporary believers (πρόσκαιροι) are not saved. Therefore, no decree was made concerning their being saved, and consequently they were not elected. Conversely, in whatever way God executes election in time, in that same way He elected from eternity, because of this conformity of decree and execution. And yet God in time does not save every baptized and regenerated person, but only the one who perseveres, and who is not finally impenitent. Therefore, God also from eternity elected not every baptized and regenerated person, but only the one who perseveres.

LII. 6. From the inconveniences. In all controversial questions we ought to consider and weigh that ancient formula: To what good? For a wise man does nothing in vain, or certainly ought to do nothing. For what is in vain, by this very fact is not: what is not, cannot move; says the most subtle Philosopher. Exerc. 161. sect. 1. There are, however, five general theological goods or benefits which are accustomed to arise from every dogma consonant with the Scriptures. 1. διδασκαλία (teaching). 2. ἔλεγχος (reproof). 3. παιδεία (instruction). 4. ἐπανόρθωσις (correction) & 5. παράκλησις (comfort) from 2 Tim. 3:16. Rom. 15:4. Others refer all these to two heads, namely πρὸς ἀλήθειαν καὶ ἐυσέβειαν (towards truth and godliness), from Tit. 1:1. For all Theology consists in these two, so that its perfect definition is delivered by the Apostle, when he defines the knowledge of the truth which is according to godliness. For not truth alone is godliness, but truth with godliness, and godliness with truth, and thus godly truth and true godliness complete the Theologian. Whatever therefore contributes not at all or but little compared to another to these, I do not think should be held as a Theological dogma to be preferred before others. Now therefore, that I may come to the present question, I certainly do not see what utility lies hidden in the opinion of others concerning the mutability of election: but I discover many inconveniences, which I shall deduce in order through these five uses.

LIII. 1. Inconveniences regarding doctrine. Many of these seem to exist, but I shall set down only the principal ones, also touched upon above. 1. It will no longer be possible to teach and urge that the number of the elect is infallible, so that it can neither be increased nor diminished. 2. That election was made from all eternity, but it must be taught that it is made in time. 3. How will the immutability and certainty of the divine decrees and their outcome be defended? 4. The identity of the decree of salvation and election will fall. 5. The indelibility of those inscribed in the book of life will collapse. 6. That order hitherto so often defended by our people will be removed from the decree of election; and finally 7. the harmony of the execution with the decree will be disturbed. All these are grave inconveniences in Theological schools, all of which are most happily avoided if we have received the opinion hitherto demonstrated.

LIV. 2. Inconveniences regarding refutation. It was truly said by Tertullian: The Church is always crucified in the middle between two heretics, just as Christ was between two thieves. We have an example in this sublime article of predestination also, which is attacked by a twin phalanx extremely opposed, namely by the Calvinists and the Huberians, of whom the former [defend] an absolute particular, the latter an absolute, universal election which they establish and defend. Both of these are to be refuted: yet they will not be able to be refuted easily if election is established as mutable. For as far as 1. the Calvinists are concerned, we urge nothing more against them than that election was made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, according to foreknowledge. Now, however, this very thing is consequently removed if every reborn person is said to be properly elected. Furthermore, up to this point we have also urged this against the Calvinists, that election is limited, including the order of all means to salvation, to which preservation and perseverance in faith are numbered. But if these are scraped away, that order will certainly be disturbed, and an opportunity for objecting will be provided to the Calvinists. For what will prevent election from being able to be said to be made without the intuition of all faith, if perseverance has been removed, since it is more necessary for obtaining salvation than temporary faith (πρόσκαιρος), inasmuch as he who has persevered, he at last will be saved. As regards the Huberians, they will certainly conclude their universal election quite probably if this is granted, that election can be made void. And although not of all indiscriminately, yet they could at least cloak the election of all the called.

IV. 3. Inconveniences regarding παιδείαν (instruction/discipline). This consists in the three Cardinal virtues: Faith, hope, and Charity, all of which, if the mutability of election is defended, we shall hinder, if not entirely, yet in part. For if men hear that the decrees of God are mutable, in such a way that God does not do in time what He certainly decreed from eternity that He would do, will not faith be shaken, so that men may think, If one decree of God is changed, another will be able to be as well, in which therefore is one to believe firmly? Hope will also collapse, since it does not rest on a firm foundation, when I cannot certainly persuade myself that God will not blot me out of the book of life, if we can fall from election. When, however, I hear of the immutability of predestination, then I firmly hope that God will not blot me out, that no one will snatch me from the hand of God, but that He will preserve me, and will certainly glorify me. Finally, charity toward God will in a certain way be endangered, since I will love more ardently Him whom I know will certainly save me, than one who has chosen mutably.

LVI. 4. Inconveniences regarding ἐπανόρθωσιν. The stubborn and contumacious must be terrified by the thunderbolt of reprobation and of the infallible threats of God. But they will immediately have an opportunity to retort if they hear that not all the decrees of God are fulfilled, but many are changed, and that God does not always execute in time what He has decreed and proposed from eternity.

LVII. 5. Inconveniences regarding παράκλησιν. Here we show two things: 1. That according to the opinion of others, we can no longer comfort the weak and the tempted. 2. That we can even do so less than according to our own opinion hitherto expounded.

1. Those who dissent always urge this, that they can most firmly uplift any believer if they proclaim to him this: that he is truly elect because he is reborn. But here he will be able to retort: Even if he is called elect, he nevertheless doubts about the end of his election, namely whether he is certainly going to attain the same, since he hears that not all the elect are saved? What will they answer here other than by bringing forward promises concerning perseverance, that God will not break the bruised reed, Isaiah 42:3, that God will not break the good work which He began, Phil. 1:6. And these very things we can also urge according to our own opinion. For that tempted person either believes or does not believe. If the latter, he will not be elect even according to the others; and such manifest sayings are to be proposed, and it is to be asked whether he has faith in these, so that he may be shown to believe in this way. But if he truly believes, yet doubts about his salvation; not certainly through that temporal election, which is often frustrated and vain, will he be able to be confirmed; but only through promises, that he who believes is chosen, and that the Lord will save him on the last day. If he should say that he hears that only those who persevere are chosen and saved, but that he himself doubts concerning his own perseverance, I will answer by asking, Does he himself have the purpose of avoiding mortal sins? If he denies it, he is already an unbeliever; but if he affirms it, I conclude that God is going to preserve him, and will most certainly glorify him in the end.

2 We maintain that someone can be less uplifted and confirmed concerning election if its mutability is defended. For if anyone believed himself to be chosen and yet doubted concerning his perseverance and salvation, because he heard that many of the chosen fall away and perish eternally, I do not know whether this scruple could be sufficiently removed from him, while the opinion of others stands: For he would urge thus, Not every chosen one perseveres and is saved, but many finally fall from election and are damned. Even if, therefore, I am now chosen, I cannot firmly conclude certainty of perseverance and salvation from this election for the stated reason. Conversely, however, if the αμεταμέλητον [irrevocability] of election is asserted, one can invincibly conclude: Every chosen one is preserved by God, and cannot be led into final error, but will certainly be saved and glorified. But I believe, and the Holy Spirit bears witness, that I am chosen. Wherefore I am certain, and I firmly believe, that God is going to preserve me, to keep me from all evil, and in the end infallibly to save and glorify me. Thus we see how great a πληροφορία [full assurance] and certainty of faith arises and is deduced from the immutability of election, which if it is denied, it is necessary that this [certainty], if not denied, is certainly at least in great part shaken.

Latin:

II. ARGVMENTA EX Analogia Fidei.

XLIV. 1. Ab identitate decreti saluandorum & electorum. Theologi Orthodoxi communiter docent, vnum & idem esse decretum electionis &c. saluationis. Nam Caluiniani quidem distinguunt, ea, dum electionis & reprobationis decretum dicunt esse absolutum, saluationis verò & damnationis limitatum & cum intuitu fidei atque infidelitatis conjunctum. Iis nos meritò opponimus cum Synceris Theologis pro vnitate decretorum, istorum acriter militantibus, ita quidem, vt disertis statuant verbis, decretum de electis esse decretum de Saluandis, vndè sæpè vtrumque copulant, & electorum saluandorum appellant. Ne tamen vlla excipiendi ansa maneat reliqua, principium istud in scholis Theologicis alias vsitatissimum & indubitatum, sic demonstramus.

XLV. Definitum & definitio non differunt realiter. Sed decretum electionis & saluationis habent se vt definitum & definitio. E non differunt realiter. Minor probatur, quia & à Formula Concordiæ, & ab alijs Theologis omnibus electio cõmuniter definitur hoc sensu, quod sit æternum Dei decretum de saluandis, glorificandis in Christum perseueranter credituris Vnde patet, quod saluationis decretum si non tota electionis definitio, tamen maxima ejus pars sit, ideoque realiter ista non differunt. Ista quidem saluatio differt a prædestinatione, tanquam actus temporalis ab æterno, tanquam executio decreti a decreto ipso; attamen decretum electionis & saluationis realiter non differunt, sed sunt vnum decretum: quod tum ex posita argumentatione, tum ex hoc insuper soixέιῳ Theologico probari potest. Electio & saluatio habent se vt decretum & decreti executio. Vnde sic colligimus: Vbi vna & eadem numero est executio, ibi vnum idemque numero est decretum, cuius datur executio. Atqui decreti electionis & saluationis vna & eadem est executio, nempe salus & glorificatio. E. decretum electionis & saluationis sunt vnum numero decretum, nec differunt inter se realiter.

XLVI. His jam firmissime stantibus, argumentum inuictum & penitus insolubile formamus: Exclusi e decreto saluationis, sunt etiam exclusi e decreto electionis. Ratio jam data fuit quia sunt vnum idemque decretum sine omni reali differentia. Sed multi vere renati & per Baptismum sanctificati, si sint πρόσκαιροι, ab omni æternitate sunt & manent semper exclusi e decreto saluationis. Alias tandem redirent ad pœnitentiam & saluarentur. E. multi vere renati & per Baptismum sanctificati, si sint πρόσκαιροι, ab omni æternitate sunt & manent semper exclusi e decreto electionis, id est, nunquam sunt aut dici possunt electi.

XLVII. 3. Ab immutabilitate Dei, Deus est imest immutabilis, Mal. 3. v. 6. Num 23. v. 19. Triplex autem in Deo immutabilitas datur. 1. Essentiæ. 2. Attributorum. 3. Decretorum. Et de hac antiqui dixerunt: Deus vt non essentiam ita nec sententiam mutat. Subsumo: Electio est decretum Dei de saluandis. E. est immutabilis. Cum igitur Deus semel aliquē decreuit saluare, ideoq; elegit, tum si eum non salnat, sed damnat in tempore, decretum vtiq; suum immutat. Neque est vt dicant, Multa Deum velle quæ non fiunt Nam distinguimus inter voluntatem nudam & decretoriam. Illa, quoniam à conditione dependet, finem suum non semper assequitur, & ad hanc pertinet electio,

XLIIX. 3. Ab absurdo. Aut omnis electus est salvandus, Aut quidam electus poterit dici damnandus. Si illud, tunc nemo electorum finaliter excidet electione. Si hoc, absurdum certè ingens statuitur. Quomodo enim electum Dei filium, & in eum vitæ librum inscriptum, in quo qui inuenitur saluari dicitur, quomodo inquam ad vitam & salutem æternam à Deo prædestinatum, flammis infernalibus comburendum & damnandum esse sinę absurditate adfirmare poterimus ? Neque maioris cohæsionem eneruare queunt. Sic enim colligimus : Deus de omnibus baptizatis & regeneratis eorumque salute, aut aliquid, aut nihil decreuit. Posterius est absurdum, & contra prouidentiam diuinam, Prius igitur verum. Porrò aut de omnibus decreuit, quòd certò eos velit saluare, aut de aliquibus. Non de omnibus, quia non omnes perseuerant nec omnes saluantur, ideoq; salutis decreto semper certissimo non sunt inclusi, Vnde mox sequitur decretum genuinum. Alterum, quòd Deus credentes velit saluare ob meritum Christi fide perseuerante apprehensum; Alterum, quòd velit infideles damnare, ob preuisam impœnitentiam & incredulitatem. Iam verò, si dicatur omnes renatos verè electos esse, oritur hinc absurdum istud, quòd Deus ab æterno filios suos verè electos & prædestinatos ad vitam æternam, decreuit damnare; atq; ita electus simul sit reprobatus, id quod contradictorium.

XLIX. Illustrabo hoc simili, ab Apostolo Iuda desumto. Hic ab æterno fuit vel electus vel reprobatus: aut saluandus aut damnandus. Non electus vel saluandus. Et reprobatus & damnandus. Vlterius quæro, An hoc decretum etiam durauerit tempore renouati & circumcisi Iudæ? Vtiquè: Quod n. Deus semel decreuit, id nunquam mutat, Decreuit autem ab æterno, Iudam ob futuram desperationẽ & impœnitentiam in tempore damnare, In Dei ergo præuisione semper damnandus fuit. Quo præsupposito, sequitur ingens illa absurditas, quod vnus idem Iudas vno eodéq; tempore fuerit reprobatus & electus. Quatenus reprobatus, decreuit Deus cum damnare: quatenus electus decreuit Deus eum saluare; id quod ἀντιφατικὸν.

I. A τάξει & ordine electionis. Formula Concordiæ, & cùm eâ Theologi saniores, in decreto electionis non nudè Deum eligentem, non solas personas electas, sed ordinem & media, per quæ ratificari debet electio, simul consideranda esse præcipiunt. Nam æternum Dei propositum duo respicit diuersa obiecta, alterum personarum, alterum rerum; & secundum hæc duo obiecta duæ sunt decreti partes, quarum altera specialiter vocatur electio, quæ spectat personas eligendas: altera prædestinatio vel præordinatio, quæ respicit media salutis & electionis. Istis medijs hoc inclusum est, quòd Deus ab æterno decreuit electos suos conseruare, ijsq́; perseuerantiam largiri, quoniam Spiritui sancto non esse posituros obicem præuidit. Vult quidem omnibus fidem dare, non tamen omnibus confert, sed tantum electis, quoniam hos solos non reluctaturos, vti cæteros præuidit; vt ita & huc debeat referri distinctio ista inter voluntatem simplicem & decretoriam. Ex ijs verò hypothesibus Theologicis denuò infertur, quòd quicunq́; non conseruantur in tempore, nec perseuerant, ij decreto electionis non sint inclusi ab æterno, quandoquidem electio cum præordinatione conseruationis & perseuerantiæ facta est. Atqui renati quàm plurimi excidunt, nec perseuerant, vnde colligitur, eos verè electos nunquam fuisse.

LI. 5. A consonantia decreti cum executione. Non puto quenquam fore, qui negauerit istud in scholis Theologicis decantatissimum σοιχᾶον, quod saluatio & electio habeant sese vt decretum & decreti executio, ideóque easdem prorsus agnoscant causas, & hoc respectu per omnia sint conformia. Vnde talis oritur argumentatio: Si saluatio est executio decreti electionis, tum vtique si quis non saluatur, de illo saluando decretum non est factum, hoc est, nunquam fuit electus, quoniam saluari & electum esse, habent sese vt executio & decretum. Iam verò plurimi πρόσκαιροι non saluantur. E. de ijs saluandis non fuit factum decretum, & P. C. non fuerunt electi. Vicissim, Qualiter Deus in tempore electionem exequitur, taliter ab æterno elegit, propter istam decreti & executionis conformitatem. Atqui Deus in tempore non quemuis baptizatum & regeneratum saluat, sed duntaxat perseuerantem, nec finaliter impœnitentem. E. Deus etiã ab æterno elegit non quemuis baptizatum & regeneratum, sed dūtaxat perseuerantem.

LII. 6. Ab incommodis. In omnibus controuersis quæstionibus considerare & perpendere debemus antiquam istam formulam: Cui bono? Sapiens enim frustrà nihil facit, nihil certè facere debet. Nam quod frustra hoc ipso non est: quod non est, non potest mouere; inquit subtilissimus Philosophus. Exerc. 161. sect. 1. Sunt autem quinque generalia bona vel commoda Theologica, quæ ex omni dogmate Scripturis consentaneo oriri consueuerunt. 1. διδασκαλία. 2. ἔλεγχος. 3. παιδεία. 4. ἐπανόρθωσις & 5. παράκλησις ex 2. Tim. 3. v. 19. Rom. 15. v. 4. Alij omnia ista ad duo capita referunt, nempè πρὸς ἀλήθειαν καὶ ἐυσέβειαν, ex Tit. 1, vers. 1. Tota enim Theologia in duobus his consistit, ita vt perfecta eius definitio sit ab Apostolo tradita, quando definit ἐπίγνωσις ἀληθείας τῆς κατ’ εὐσέβειαν. Non enim sola ἀλήθεια ἐυσέβεια, sed cum ἐυσεβείᾳ ἀλήθεια, & cum ἀληθείᾳ εὐσέβεια, adeoque εὐσεβής ἀλήθεια καὶ ἀληθὴς ἐυσέβεια absolvunt Theologum. Quicquid igitur ad hæc vel planè non vel parum præ alio conducit, id pro dogmate Theologico, alijsque anteponendo habendum esse haud existimo. Nunc igitur vt ad præsentem quæstionem deueniam, certè non video, quæ vtilitas in opinione aliorum de electionis mutabilitate lateat: multa autem deprehendo incommoda, quæ per quinque istos vsus ordine deducam.

LIII. 1. Incommoda quoad διδασκαλίαν. Eorum multa videntur esse, sed præcipua dūtaxat suprà etiam tacta apponam. 1. Doceri & vrgeri ampliùs non poterit quòd infallibilis sit electorum numerus, ita vt nec augeri, nec minui queat. 2. Quòd ab omni ęternitate sit facta electio, sed docendum, quòd in tempore fiat 3. Decretorum diuinorum immutabilitas & certitudo, euentus quomodo defendetur? 4. Identitas decreti saluationis & electionis cadet. 5. Indelebilitas inscriptorum in librum vitæ corruet. 6. τάξις ista hactenùs à nostris toties defensa è decreto electionis tolletur; & demque 7. consonantia executionis cum decreto turbabitur. Hæc omnia sunt grauia incommoda in scholis Theologicis, quæ omnia felicissimè declinantur, si demonstratam hactenus sententiam receperimus.

LIV. 2. Incommoda quoad ἔλεγχον. Verè dictum à Tertulliano: Ecclesia inter duos hæreticos semper media, sicut Christus inter duos latrones crucifigitur. Habemus exemplum in hoc quoque sublimi prædestinationis articulo, qui à gemina phalange extremè opposita impugnatur, à Caluinianis nimirum & Huberianis, quorum illi absolutam particularem, hi absolutam, vniuersalem electionem statuunt & defendunt. Vtrique hi consutandi sunt:consutari tamen facilè non poterunt, si electio mutabilis statuatur. Nam quod 1. Caluinianos attinet, nihil magis contra eos urgemus, quàm quòd electio sit facta κατὰ πρόγνωσιν, secundum præscientiam. Iam verò hoc ipsum consequenter remouetur si omnis renatus propriè electus dicatur. Porrò hactenus istud quoque aduersus Caluinianos vrsimus, quòd limitata sit electio, includens ordinem omnium mediorum ad salutem, quibus annumeratur conseruatio & perseuerātia in fide. Hæc verò si abradątur, ordo certè ille turbabitur, & Caluinianis excipiendi ansa præbebitur. Quid enim prohibebit, quò minus electio possit tacta dici sine intuitu omnis fidei, si perseuerantia fuerit remota, cùm ad salutem consequendam ea magis sit necessaria, quàm fides πρόσκαιρος, siquidem qui perseuerauerit, is demum saluus erit. Huberianos quod spectat, ii certè satis probabiliter concludent suam electionem vniuersalem, si hoc concedatur, quòd electio possit euacuari. Et licèt non omnium indiseretè, tamen omnium vocatorum electionem ad minimum possent palliare.

IV. 3. Incommoda quoad παιδείαν. Consistit hæc in tribus virtutibus Cardinalibus Fide, spe & Chartate,quas omnes,si mutabilitas electionis defenditur,quamuis nõ ex toto, ex parte tamen impediemus. Nam si audiuerint homines, Dei decreta esse mutabilia, ita quidem, vt Deus non faciat in tempore, quod ab æterno se facturum certo decreuit, annon labefactabitur fides, ita vt homines cogitare possint, Si Dei decretum vnum mutatur, poterit & alterum, quibus igitur firmiter credendum? Collabascet etiam spes, siquidem in moto fundamento non innititur, cùm certò mihi persuadere nequeam, quòd Deus me non sit deleturus è libro vitæ, si electione excidere possumus, Quando autem prædestinationis immutabilitatem audio, tunc firmiter spero, Deum me non deleturum, neminem me rapturum ex manu Dei, sed hunc me esse conseruaturum, & certò glorificaturum. Denique Charitas in Deum quodammodo periclitabitur, cùm ardentiùs diligam eum, quem me certò saluaturum scio, quàm illum qui mutabiliter elegit.

LVI. 4. Incommoda quoad ἐπανόρθωσιν. Terrendi sunt præfracti & contumaces fulmine reprobationis & minarum Dei infallibilium. Atqui statim regerendi ansam habebunt, si audierint, non omnia decreta Dei impleri, sed multa mutari, non semper in tempore Deum exequi, quod ab æterno decreuit & proposuit.

LVII. 5. Incommoda quoad παράκλησιν. Hic duo ostendimus: 1. Nos secundum opinionem aliorum infirmos & tentatos non plus solari posse. 2. Etiam minus posse, quàm secundum sententiam nostram hactenus expositam.

1. Dissentientes semper istud vrgent, se quemuis fidelem firmissimè erigere posse, si illi acclamauerint hoc, Eum verè esse electum, quia sit renatus. At hic regerere poterit; Etiam si electus dicatur, se tamen de electionis fine dubitare, an nimirum eundem certo sit consecuturus, quando quidem audiat, non omnes electos saluari? Quid hic respondebunt aliud, quàm proferendo promissiones de perseuerantia, quòd Deus non sit contriturus calamum quassatum, Esai 24. v. 3. quòd Deus non sit contriturus opus bonum, quod incepit, Phil. 1. versic. 6. Atque has ipsas ex nostra etiam opinione vrgere possumus. Iste enim tentatus aut credit aut non credit. Si hoc, nec secundum, alios erit electus; Et talia sunt proponenda dicta manifesta, & quætendum, Annon his fidem habeat, vt ita ipsum credere ostendatur. Quòd si verè credat, de salute tamen sua dubitet; non certè per illam electionem temporalem, quæ sæpè frustranea est, poterit confirmari; sed duntaxat per promissiones, quod qui credit, is sit electus, & eum sit saluaturus in extremo die Dominus. Si regere rat, Se audire, tantum perseuerantes esse electos & saluari, se autem de sua perseuerantia dubitare, respondebo quærendo, An habeat ipse propositum peccata mortalia vitandi? Si negat, iam incredulus est; Sin affirmat, concludo Deum ipsum esse conseruaturum, atque tandem certissime glorificaturum.

2 Statuimus aliquem minus posse erigi, & confirmari de electione, si huius mutabilitas defendatur. Nam si quis se electum crederet & tamen dubitaret de sua perseuerantia & salute, quia audiret, multos electos excidere & æternum perire, nescio, an satis posset hic scrupulus ipsi eximi, stante aliorum sententia: Ita enim instaret, Non omnis electus perseuerat & saluatur, sed multi finaliter excidunt electione & damnantur. Etiamsi igitur iam sim electus, non tamen ex hac electione certitudinem perseuerantiæ & salutis ob dictam causam firmiter concludere possum. Contra vero si to αμεταμέλητον electionis astruatur, inuicte quis concludere potest: Omnis electus a Deo præseruatur, & in errorem finalem induci nequit, sed certo saluabitur & glorificabitur. Atqui ego credo, & testimonium præbet Spiritus sanctus, quod sim electus. Quare certus sum, & credo firmiter, Deum me esse cõseruaturum, ab omni malo præseruaturum & tandem infallibiliter saluaturum, atque glorificaturum. Ita videmus quanta πληροφορία & certitudo fidei oriatur & deducatur ex immutabilitate electionis, quæ si negetur, & istam, si non negari, certe tamen magna ex parte labefactari necesse est.


### Question I: III. Testimonies of the Fathers

III. TESTIMONIES of the Fathers.

LVIII. We shall not heap up many things here, but we shall be content with one or two. Thus, however, he speaks

Augustine, book on Faith to Peter, chapter 35. Hold most firmly, and doubt in no way, that all whom God predestined before the foundation of the world to the adoption of sons, cannot perish. The same, Epistle 59. They are not in that calling who, in the faith which works through love, even if they walk for a little while, do not persevere to the end. Book 1 on the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 13. The gifts and the calling of God are without repentance: to which calling no man is to be said by men with certain assertion to belong, unless when he has departed from this world. And indeed the argument of that whole book is that perseverance is required for predestination. Book on Correction and Grace, chapter 13. I speak of these who are predestined to the kingdom of God, whose number is so certain that neither is anyone added to them nor is anyone subtracted from them. Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus, p. 51. God predestined to the kingdom those whom He foreknew would return by the aid of preceding mercy, and would remain by the aid of subsequent mercy. Page 21. All these things, that is, both the beginnings of our calling, and the increases of justification, and the rewards of glorification, God always had in predestination, etc. Let the whole passage be seen, where it is shown at length that God preserves the elect from every evil, and finally most certainly glorifies them. Add to these Ambrose, who in book 1 on the Calling of the Gentiles proves by the following sayings of Scripture that perseverance is required in election. 1 Cor. 15 v. 57. 1 Thess. 2 v. 1. 1 Thess. 5 v. 23. 2 Thess. 2 v. 16. 1 Pet. 1 v. 10. etc.

IV. OBJECTIONS of those who dissent.

LIX. Huberus in particular opposes himself sharply to the opinion demonstrated thus far. For he cannot maintain the universality of election unless he attacks the salvation of very many of the elect. For if he were to establish with us that any elect person is saved, he would not defend that all men are properly elected, since not all are saved. What, therefore, he himself may bring forward, or what may be brought forward for him, remains to be examined in a few words.

LX. The following sayings can be urged primarily: Coloss. 3. v. 12. Put on therefore as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies. 1. Thess. 1. v. 4. Knowing, brethren beloved of God, your election. 2. Pet. 1. v. 10. Wherefore, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure through good works. From which sayings it follows that all who are called, holy, and reborn are truly elect.

Resp. It is known, and has been said above, that the term election is ambiguous in the Scriptures and admits various meanings. For it denotes.

1. Generally, every excellent and approved thing, as Gen. 23. v. 6. Isa. 58. v. 6. Luke 23. 35. And this meaning can have a place in the saying at Coloss. 3. v. 12. For these three terms are synonymous, and one explains the other, so that to be elect is the same as to be holy, to be beloved, to be approved. Thus in sermons we adorn the whole assembly, to which many hypocrites are mixed in, with this eulogy and say, Geliebte vnd Auserwehlte im HERRN.

2. It is taken specially for the calling to the Church through the ministry of the word, in which sense all who are called, and especially those who are reborn, are called elect. Thus all the Jews in 1. Pet. 2. v. 9. are called a chosen generation. So Deut. 10. v. 15. it is said: The Lord was joined to your fathers, and loved them, and chose their seed. Here certainly all the Jews are implicitly called Elect. But shall we think that the election which was made from eternity is understood here? By no means, but only a temporal calling is denoted. Similar things are held in Deut. 4. v. 37. and 7. v. 6: The Lord your God chose you, that you might be a peculiar people to him, out of all peoples, And 14. 2. and 26. v. 18. Zech. 1. v. 17. and 2. v. 12. God chose our Jerusalem. Therefore, as it is necessary in these sayings that it be granted that everyone who is called, whether he believes or does not believe, is elect. But true and properly so-called election is not made without faith, whence I conclude. The word election often signifies only the calling, by which men are chosen to the Church. And the word election undoubtedly has this sense in 1 Thess. 1:4 and 2 Pet. 1:10. Especially when these two, calling and election, are joined ἐπισυλληπτικῶς. For thus we gather: To whomever the calling pertains, to them also pertains the election, of which there is speech in those sayings, because both are joined ἐπισυλληπτικῶς. But the calling pertains to all existing in the Church; wherefore also the election, of which the Apostle makes words there. Now, however, election properly so-called does not pertain to all the called. Therefore, here there is speech of another, namely of temporal election to the Church, which is convertible with calling. Hence, therefore, we form such a canon: From temporal election to eternal election the consequence is not firm. Paul and Peter speak of temporal election, insofar as the faithful were called through the word of the Gospel. But from this to wish to conclude that all were elected from eternity to life does not follow. The whole collection, therefore, begs the question, in that those sayings are explained concerning eternal election which speak only of calling or temporal election to the Church.

3. Election is taken most specially for the eternal decree concerning those to be saved who will persevere in faith. And concerning this the present controversy is chiefly instituted, by which not all the called, not all the reborn, but the holy and all who persevere are elected. That Paul and Peter do not speak of this is certain: 1. Because this title is applied to the whole Church, in which there are also hypocrites. 2. Because they explain themselves, that by election they understand calling. 3. They speak of such an election that is made in time through the word heard and received. 4. And otherwise this phrase is most customary in Scripture, that those called to the Church are said to be elect. Therefore, let the former to these rationes [reasons] answer, and let the dissenters firmly demonstrate their own opinion, from which they conclude the election of all the reborn, properly so called. But out of an abundance of caution, if it be posited in the highest degree that the discourse is about eternal election: it could nevertheless be answered that this is done through the customary κοινοποίησιν [common attribution], by which that which is proper to the invisible Church is attributed to the whole assembly of the called.

LXI. 2. To Rom. 8. ver. 13. If you live according to the flesh you shall die. From this they gather that it is possible for one of the elect to become a reprobate, namely if he lives according to the flesh.

Response. The very coherence of the text shows that this statement is to be understood concerning the reborn and their lapses, but not concerning the elect, as they are elect. For the Apostle addresses the Roman Church, already regenerated by the Word, and admonishes them to walk further in newness of life, lest they lose the grace once bestowed through the pursuits of this age, and thus perish eternally. Add that the Apostle speaks doubtfully about them in verse 6, when he says: You are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But those who are elect, concerning them one cannot doubt whether the Spirit of God dwells in them; whence it is concluded that the Apostle is not speaking of the elect, but of the reborn, and indeed of those whom he considers to be reborn out of Christian charity. Therefore, conversely, it is fallacious to argue from the lapse and final reprobation of the reborn to the lapse and reprobation of the elect.

Then I answer ὑποθετικῶς [hypothetically], that although he were speaking of the elect, it would not follow from this that they finally fall away from the grace of God, but only this follows: The elect, if they live according to the flesh, will die, namely spiritually by shaking off the Spirit, and indeed for a time, but afterwards they perform penance, and thus they are not blotted out from the Book of life, or reprobated: This therefore we liberally concede that the elect can both live according to the flesh and die spiritually, or the death of grace, but only for a time, so that before death they may still be converted, and thus by divine decree be saved. But what is the consequence? The elect can sin and die for a time: Therefore also finally; Christ teaches the contrary in Matt. 24, v. 24.

Others say that a conditional [statement] posits nothing, just as it does not follow from Isaiah 1, verse 19, 'If you are willing and obedient to me,' that they can by the powers of free will hear God or obey him: Similarly, here too, from the conditional power of dying and perishing, it is falsely concluded.

LXII. 3. To Eph. 1, verse 4. 'He chose us in him, that we should be holy and blameless.' But all the regenerate are, or ought to be, holy and blameless. Therefore all are elect.

Response. 1. Not only the regenerate, but also all the called, indeed all men in general, ought to be holy and blameless. 2. The syllogism is affirmative in the second figure. 3. There are four terms, because the major speaks of fact, the minor only of right. 4. One can distinguish between a common and a proper end, between an intermediate and an ultimate one. To be holy is a common and intermediate end of election, not a proper and ultimate one. But to wish to conclude from a common end to a proper act is vicious. 5. We invert the argument in this way: GOD chose us to eternal life. Therefore those who do not attain this are not elect. But many πρόσκοποι do not attain it. Therefore many πρόσκοποι are not elect. 6. We add this instance: God in time justifies us that we may be holy and blameless. But all in the Church and outside the Church ought to be holy. Therefore God justifies all. Whatever they may have answered here, let them consider it said to themselves. But in place of a colophon, let it be noted that by κατενώπιον Let the Apostle speak of the whole assembly, since those epithets befit only the elect, who exist within the assembly of the called.

LXIII. 4. From 1 Corinth. 9: v. 27. I chastise my body, lest I become a reprobate. Therefore, from an elect person, one can become a reprobate.

Response 1. This statement is directed solely against the absolute decree by which it is maintained that an elect person is certainly saved, whatever he may do. Paul refutes this opinion here, showing that election was made with the order of faith and perseverance preserved, in such a way indeed that one who sins mortally and finally is not elect, but reprobate. The sense is: Do not think that I am absolutely elect. By no means; for if I am an unbeliever, I shall be rejected. He does not say, however, that he will be an unbeliever finally; for thus God would be deceived in His foreknowledge and would be changed regarding His decrees.

2. The elect are considered either in relation to themselves, and thus they can finally fall; or in relation to the foreseen and decreed Divine preservation, and thus they cannot be seduced, Matt. 24: v. 24.

2. In the Greek there is the word ἀδόκιμος, which denotes not eternal reprobation, but often temporal uselessness, so that the sense is: I chastise my body, lest by living luxuriously I expel the Holy Spirit, and thus become useless to myself and others by a bad example. We grant this, that an elect person can for a time be useless and evil; but that an elect person is a reprobate, or that from an elect person one becomes a reprobate—that is, that he whom God has decreed from eternity to save is damned in time—cannot be proven from this passage.

LXIV. 5. From 1 Cor. 10: v. 12. Let him who stands take heed lest he fall. And Apoc. 3: v. 11. Hold fast what you have, that no one may take your crown.

Response. The former statement speaks of the mutability of regeneration, not of election: the latter speaks of the crown of ministry, not of heavenly joy. The former can be lost, the latter cannot.

LXV. 6. If election is immutable, every effort of acting well is taken away. Response. I deny the consequence. Because a cause does not take away an effect, but establishes it. Election, however, is the cause of good works, for we were chosen that we might be holy. Eph. 1. v. 4. Furthermore, we are predestined, not only to the end, but also to the means. Finally, those are chosen whom He foreknew would perseveringly believe and act well. Faith, therefore, working through love, is included in the decree of Election, not excluded.

LXVI. 7. A man sinning mortally, for example, the Prophet David, is either elect or reprobate. If you say he is elect, this can be objected: Every elect person pleases God. David, sinning mortally, at the very time of the sin, was elect. Therefore he pleased God, although no adulterer and murderer pleases Him. Response. 1. Some respond that a diversity of respect removes the φαινομένην ἀντίφασιν [apparent contradiction]. David the adulterer displeased God entirely, by reason of his present incredulity; he pleased Him by reason of his future repentance and faith, which was most present to God. 2. The grace of election is one thing, and the grace of renewal or sanctification is another. The elect fall totally from the grace of sanctification when they sin mortally, yet they do not fall from the grace of election; that is, they remain written in the book of life through future faith, although now, on account of present incredulity, they displease God in all things. 3. We give an example from Paul, not yet converted nor baptized, and yet chosen from all eternity, just as he, when he was not yet converted, was entirely a son of the Devil, under wrath, not under grace: And nevertheless, at that very time, he was elect through future faith foreseen: So also David, sinning mortally, remained elect; And conversely, another, although he may believe for a time, yet can be reprobate, by virtue of the eternal decree considering the end of the man.

4. I add finally an instance concerning being saved. Every man is either to be saved or to be damned, but Paul was to be saved; and such he could be called even at the very time of his persecution: Why then should he not also be truly named elect? Since everyone to be saved is at every time and can truly be called elect.

LXVII. Finally, 8. it would follow that no one can be called elect before death.

Resp. The judgment concerning the predestination of others is either simple, absolute, and most certain, such as is scarcely given, since we cannot look into the hearts of men to see whether they truly believe and will persevere in faith, or conditional, where someone is pronounced elect if he believes constantly. And in this sense it can be said of every believer that he is Elect, if indeed he perseveres in the faith. But this very thing is the question: Can the salvation or damnation of another be known before death? Where we answer not absolutely, but only under a condition: Those are to be saved who shall have believed and shall have persevered in the faith. In like manner, everyone who believes and is going to persevere can truly be called and named elect. But whether he truly believes, or whether he will certainly persevere, is not known to us, and therefore we can pronounce nothing simply and absolutely concerning the election and salvation of a man. We hope well of all, yet we affirm nothing certain, because the judgment of charity is one thing, and the judgment of truth is another.

Latin:

III. TESTIMONIA Patrum.

LVIII. Non hic multa glomerabimus, sed vno atque altero contenti erimus. Sic autem loquitur

Augustinus lib. de Fide ad Pet. cap. 35. Firmissimè tene, & nullatenus dubites, omnes, quos ante constitutisnem mundi ad adoptionem filiorum prædestinauit Deus, per rire non posse. Idem Epistola 59. Non sunt in ista vocatione, qui in fide, quæ per dilectionem operatur, & si aliquantulum ambulent, non perseueran. vsque in finem. Lib. 1. de Bono perseuerant. cap. 13. Sine pænitentia sunt dona & vocatio Dei: Ad quam vocationem pertinere nullus est homo ab hominibus certâ asseueratione dicendus, nisi cùm de seculo hoc exierit. Et sanè totius libri istius argumentum est, quod ad prædestinationem perseuerantia requiratur, Lib. de corrept. & grat. cap. 13. Hæc de ijs loquor, qui prædestinati sunt ad regnum Dei quorum ita certus est numerus, vt nec addatur eis quisquam nec minuatur ex eis. Fulgentius lib. 1. ad Mon. m. p. 51. Deus prædestinauit ad regnum, quos ad se præsciuit misericordiæ præuenientis auxilio redituros, & in semisericordiæ subsequentis auxilio esse mansuros. pag. 21. Hæc omnia, id est, & vocationis nostræ initia, & iustificationis augmenta, & glorificationis præmia, in prædestinatione Deus semper habuit, &c. videatur Locus integer, vbi fusè ostenditur, quòd Deus electos ab omni malo præseruet, & tandem certissimè glorificet. Adde his Ambrosium, qui lib. 1. de vocat. gent. sequentibus Scripturæ dictis euincit, perseuerantiam in electione requiri. 1. Cor. 15. v. 57. 1. Thess. 2. v. 1. 1. Thess. 5. v. 23. 2. Thess. 2. v. 16. 1. Pet. 1. v. 10. &c.

IV. OBIECTIONES DISsentientium.

LIX. Huberus inprimis acriter se opponit sententiæ hactenus demonstratæ. Electionis enim vniuersalitatem obtinere nequit, nisi salutem electorum plurimorum impugnet. Si enim electum quemuis saluari nobiscum statueret, omnes homines propriè electos esse non defenderet, siquidem omnes non saluantur. Quid ergò vel ipse proferat, vel pro ipso proferri queat, paucis dispiciendum restat.

LX. Vrgeri præcipuè posfunt sequentia dicta: Coloss. 3. v. 12. Induite vos ergò sicut electi Dei, sancti & dilecti viscera misericordiæ. 1. Thes. 1. v. 4. Scientes fratres dilecti à Deo electionem vestram 2. Pet. 1. v. 10. Quapropter fratres satagite, vt per bona opera certam vestram vocationem & electionem faciatis. Ex quibus dictis sequitur, Omnes vocatos sanctos & renatos, verè esse electos.

Resp. Notum, & suprà dictum est, quòd electionis vocabulum in Scripturis sit ambiguum, variasque significationes admittat. Denotat enim.

1. Generaliter omnem rem eximiam & probatam, vt Gen. 23. v. 6. Esai. 58. v. 6. Luc. 23. 35. Atq; hæc significatio potest locum habere in dicto ad Coloss. 3. v. 12. Tria enim ista vocabula sunt synonyma, & vnum explicat alterum, ita vt electum esse sit idem, quod sanctum, quod dilectum, quod probatum esse. Sic in concionibus totum cœtum, cui multi hypocritæ sunt admixti, hoc elogio ornamus & dicimus, Geliebte vnd Auserwehlte im HERRN.

2 Sumitur specialiter pro vocatione ad Ecclesiam per ministerium verbi, quo significatu omnes vocati, præsertim vero renati dicuntur electi. Ita Iudæi omnes 1. Pet. 2. vers. 9. vocantur genus electum. Sic Deut. 10. v. 15. dicitur: Patribus tuis conglutinatus est Dominus, & amauit eos, elegitq; semen eorum. Hic certè omnes Iudæi implicitè nuncupantur Electi. Num autem putabimus, eam hic electionem intelligi, quæ facta est ab æterno? Neutiquam, sed temporalis duntaxat denotatur vocatio. Similia habentur Deut. 4. vers. 37. & 7. vers. 6: Te elegit Dominus Deus tuus, vt sis eis populus peculiaris, de cunctis populis, Et 14. 2. & 26. v. 18. Zach. 1. vers. 17. & 2. vers. 12. Elegit Deus nostram Hierosolymam. Vtigitur horum dictorum necesse est, vt concedatur, omnem vocatum, sine credat credat, siue non credat, esse electum. Vera autem & proprie dicta electio nō est facta sine fide, vnde concludo. Electionis vocabulū sæpè vocationem duntaxat, quà ad Ecclesiam homines eliguntur, significare. Atque hunc sensum proculdubio habet vocabulum electionis in 1. Thess. 1. v. 4. & 2. Pet. 1. v. 10. Præsertim cùm ἐπισυλληπτικῶς coniungantur ista duo vocatio & electio. Sic enim colligimus: Quoscunque attinet vocatio, ad hos etiam spectat electio, de qua in istis dictis sermo est, quia vtrumque coniungitur ἐπισυλληπτικῶς. Sed vocatio attinet omnes in Ecclesia existentes; Quare & electio, de qua ibi verba facit Apostolus. Iam vero electio proprie dicta non attinet omnes vocatos. Ergo hic de alia est sermo, nempè de electione temporali ad Ecclefiam, quæ cùm vocatione conuertitur. Hinc igitur talem formamus canonem : Ab electione temporali ad electionem æternam firma non est consequentia. Loquitur Paulus & Petrus de electione temporali, quatenus fideles per verbum Euangelij erant vocati. Hinc autem velle concludere, omnes ab æterno ad vitam fuisse electos non sequitur. Tota igitur collectio petit principium, eò quod de electione æterna exponantur dicta, quæ tantùm de vocatione vel temporali ad Ecclesiam electione loquuntur.

3. Accipitur Electio specialissimè pro æterno decreto, de saluandis in fide perseueraturis. Et de hac potissimùm præsens controuersia instituitur, quâ non omnes vocati, non omnes renati, sed sancti & omnes perseuerantes electi sunt. De hac non loqui Paulum & Petrum certum est: 1. Quia titulus iste toti Ecclesiæ, in qua etiam hypocritæ, applicatur. 2. Quia semetipsos explicant, quod per electionem intelligant vocationem. 3. De tali loquuntur electione, quæ sit facta in tempore per verbum auditum & receptum. 4. Et aliàs hæc phrasis in Scriptura est vsitatissima, vt vocati ad Ecclesiam dicantur electi. Prius ergo ad has rationes respondeant, & suam opinionem firmiter demonstrent dissentientes, quam electionem omnium renatorum propriè dictam inde concludant. Ex abundanti verò, si maximè ponatur, de electione æterna sermonem esse: responderi tamen posset, quòd per usitatam κοινοποίησιν id fiat, qua toti vocatorum cœtui tribuitur, quod Ecclesiæ inuisibili est proprium.

LXI. 2. Ad Rom. 8. ver. 13. Si secundum carnem vixeritis moriemini. Hinc colligunt, ex electis posse fieri reprobum, nempe si secundum carnem viuat.

Respon. Ipsa textus cohærentia ostendit, quod de renatis & eorum lapsibus hoc dictum sit intelligendum, non autem de electis, quâ sunt electi. Alloquitur enim Apostolus Romanam Ecclesiam, per verbum jam regeneratam & admonet vt in nouitate vitæ porrò ambulent, nè gratiam semel collatam, per studia huius seculi amittant, atque ita æternùm pereant. Adde quòd dubitanter de ipsis loquatur Apostolus verf. 6. dum ait. Vos in carne non estis, sed Spiritu, si tamen Spiritus Dei habitat in vobis. Qui verò electi sunt, de iis dubitare non possunt, an Spiritus Dei in ipsis habitet; vnde concluditur, Apostolum non de electis, sed renatis loqui, & quidem iis quos ex charitate Christiana renatos esse existimat. Nihil ergò vicissim à renatorum lapsu & finali reprobatione ad lapsum & reprobationem electorum argumentari vitiosum est.

Deinde ὑποθετικῶς respondeo, quòd licèt de electis loqueretur, non tamen hinc probaretur, quòd finaliter excidant gratiâ Dei, sed hoc tantùm sequitur: Electi, si viuant secundum carnem, morientur, nempè spiritaliter excutiendo Spiritum, & quidem ad tempus, post autem pœnitentiam agunt, atque sic non delentur è Libro vitæ, aut reprobantur: Hoc ergò liberaliter concedimus, electos & secundum carnem viuere & mori posse spiritualiter, seu morte gratiæ, sed ad tempus duntaxat, ita vt ante obitum adhuc conuertantur, & sic ob decretum diuinum salui fiant. Quæ autem consequentia? Electis possunt ad tempus peccare, & mori: Ergò etiam finaliter; Contrarium docet Christus Matth. 24. v. 24.

Alij dicunt, conditionalem nihil ponere, sicutinon sequitur ex Esai. 1. versu 19. Si volueritis & audieritis me; quòd possint ex viribus arbitrii Deum audire, aut ipsi obtemperare: Similiter & hic ex conditionali potentia moriendi & pereundi falsò concluditur.

LXII. 3. Ad Ephes. 1. versu 4. Elegit nos in ipso, vt essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles. Atqui omnes renati sunt, vel esse debent sancti & irreprehensibiles. Ergò omnes sunt electi.

Respon. 1. Non soli renati, sed & omnes vocati, imò omnes in vniuersum homines debent esse sancti & immaculati. 2. Syllogismus in secunda figura est affirmativus. 3. Sunt quatuor termini, quia Maior de facto, Minor de jure tantùm loquitur. 4. Distingui potest inter finem communem & proprium, inter medium & vltimum. Esse sanctum, communis & intermedius, non proprius & vltimus electionis est finis. Velle autem concludere à fine communi ad actum proprium vitiosum est. 5. Inuertimus argumentum hoc pacto: DEVS nos elegit ad vitam æternam. Ergò qui hanc non consequuntur, non sunt electi Multi verò πρόσκοποι non consequuntur, Ergò multi πρόσκοποι non sunt electi. 6. Addimus hanc instanciam: Deus in tempore nos iustificat vt simus sancti & irreprehensibiles. Atqui omnes in Ecclesia & extra Ecclesiam sancti esse debent. Deus igitur omnes viuificat. Quicquid hic responderint, sibi dictum esse censeant. Colophonis autem loco notetur, quod per κατενώπιον de toto coetu loquatur Apostolus, cum Epitheta ista solis conueniant electis, in coetu vocatorum existentibus.

LXIII. 4. Ex Corinth. 9. v: 27. Castigo corpus meum, ne reprobus efficiar. Ergo ex electo potest fieri reprobus.

Respon 1. Hoc dictum duntaxat oppositum est absoluto decreto, quo statuitur, electum certe saluari, quicquid etiam agat: Hanc opinionem refutat hic Paulus, ostendens electionem factam esse seruato ordine fidei & perseuerantiae, Ita quidem vt mortaliter & finaliter peccans non sit electus, sed reprobus Sensus est: Ne putetis, me absolute esse electum. Minime; Nam si incredulus fuero, reprobatus ero. Non autem dicit, quod finaliter sit futurus incredulus: ita enim Deus in praescientia sua falleretur. & quoad decreta mutaretur.

2. Electi vel considerantur ratione sui atq; sic finaliter labi possunt; vel ratione praevisae & decretæ conseruationis Diuinae, atque sic seduci non possunt Matth. 24. v. 24.

2. In græco est vocabulum ἀδόκιμος quod non reprobationem æternam, sed sæpè inutilitatem temporalem notat, vt sit sensus: Ego castigo corpus meum, ne luxuriosè viuendo Spritum sanctum expellam, & sic inutilis mihi alijs q; malo exemplo fiam. Hoc autem concedimus, quod electus ab tempus possit esse inutilis & malus; Quod autem electus sit reprobus vel ex electo fiat reprobus, hoc est, quod ille, quem Deus ab æterno decreuit saluare, in tempore damnetur ex loco hoc probari nequit.

LXIV. 5. Ex 1. Cor 10. v. 12. Qui stat videat ne cadat. Et Apoc. 4. v. 11. Tene, quod habes ne alius accipiat coronam tuam.

Respon. Loquitur dictum prius de mutabilitate regenerationis non electionis: Posterius de corona ministerij, non cœlestis gaudij. Illa potest amitti, hac non potest.

LXV. 6. Si electio est immutabilis, tollitur omnis bene agendi conatus. Respon. N. C. Quia causa non tollit effectum, sed ponit. Electio autem est causa bonorum operum, Electi enim sumus, vt essemus sancti. Eph. 1. v. 4. Deinde sumus prædestinati, non ad finem tantum, sed etiam ad media. Denique ij sunt electi, quos præsciuit perseueranter credituros & bene acturos. Fides ergo per dilectionem operans inclusa est decreto Electionis, non exclusa.

LXVI. 7. Homo mortaliter peccans, Exempli gratia, Propheta Dauid, aut electus est, aut reprobus. Si dixeris eum electum, hoc objici potest: Omnis Electus Deo placet. Dauid mortaliter peccans, ipso peccati tempore, fuit electus. Ergo Deo placuit, cum tamen nullus adulter & homicida placeat. Respon. 1. Quidam respondent, quod diuerfitas respectus tollat φαινομένην ἀντίφασιν. Displicebat Dauid adulter Deo in totum, ratione præsentis incredulitatis, placebat ratione futura pœnitentiæ & fidei quæ Deo erat præsentissima. 2. Alia est gratia electionis, & alia renouationis vel sanctificationis. Electi totaliter excidunt gratia sanctificationis, quando mortaliter peccant, non tamen excidunt gratia electionis; hoc est, manent scripti in libro vitæ per futuram fidem, quamuis nunc ob præsentem incredulitatem Deo per omnia displiceant. 3. Exemplum damus a Paulo nondum conuerso nec baptizato & tamen ab omni æternitate electo, sicut hic cum nondum esset conuersus omnino erat filius Diaboli, sub ira non sub gratia: Et nihilominus eo ipso tempore erat electus per futuram fidem præuisam: Ita & Dauid mortaliter peccans manebat electus; Et contra, alius, licet ad tempus credat, tamen potest esse reprobatus, vi æterni decreti hominis finem considerantis.

4. Addo denique instantiam de saluando. Omnis homo est vel saluandus vel damnandus, Paulus autem erat saluandus; & talis dici poterat etiam ipso persecutionis tempore: Quid ni ergò electus etiam verè nominaretur? cùm omnis saluandus omni tempore sit veréque dici queat electus.

LXVII. Tandem 8. sequeretur neminem dici posse electum ante mortem.

Resp. Iudicium de aliorum prædestinatione, vel est simplex, absolutum & certissimum, quale vix datur, cùm introspicere nequeamus corda hominum, an verè credant, & in fide perseueraturi sint, vel conditionatum, vbi aliquis pronunciatur electus, si constanter credat. Et hoc sensu de omni credente dici potest, quòd sit Electus, si nimirum in fide perseueret. Hoc ipsum verò quæstio est: Nùm alterius salus aut damnatio sciri ante mortem queat? Vbi non absolutè, sed tantùm sub conditione respõdemus: Saluandi sunt, qui crediderint & in fide perseuerárint. Pari modo omnis qui credit & perseueraturus est, verè electus dici & nominari potest. An autem verè credat, an certò sit perseueraturus, nobis non constat, ideoq; simpliciter & absolutè de electione & salute hominis nihil pronunciare possumus. De omnibus benè speramus, nihil tamen certi affirmamus, quia aliud charitatis, aliud veritatis est iudicium.


### Question II. What is the use of the doctrine of Predestination explained thus far?

What is the use of the doctrine of Predestination explained thus far?

I. It was a proverb of the ancients that theology consists more in affection than in cognition. They hinted, however, that bare γνῶσις [knowledge] does not suffice, but that πράξις [practice] is primarily required, which they expressed by the word affection. The Philosopher says, book 8 of the Ethics, chapter 9: It is not concerning virtue enough to know, but one must strive to possess it and use it. The same can be affirmed concerning the articles of faith. To know them or to dispute about them is not enough: they must be transferred to use, and it must be shown how they are profitable, and how they can be applied in the exercises of repentance and obedience. It was the saying of Ignatius: ὁ ποιῇ χριστιανὸς. Not to say, but to be, makes a Christian: to which Justin Martyr agrees: The matters of our religion consist not in words, but in deeds. Thus, therefore, let it be disputed, lest that of Seneca be objected: Much knowledge, little conscience. The Apostle joins both, πίστιν καὶ ἀγαθὴν συνείδησιν, Faith and a good conscience, 1 Tim. 1 v. 19. Therefore, it must be discoursed about the articles of Faith in such a way that piety may be increased from it, and the holiness of life promoted, from which arises the tranquility of conscience.

II. After, therefore, the doctrine of Predestination itself has been explained thus far, it remains to be said how it can be accommodated to use: It has been disputed enough: It must be seen what use this disputation provides in Christianity: It is, moreover, manifold, and therefore can be expressed in many ways as well. We shall touch upon the principal ones in a few words.

III. Augustine warns that this article must be treated diligently for three reasons. 1. Lest exhortation grow lukewarm. 2. Lest prayer be extinguished. 3. Lest pride be kindled. Because, indeed, election was made so that we might be holy and blameless, Eph. 1 v. 4, everyone ought to be admonished of his duty from this. Because only those who persevere are elected. Therefore, God must be assiduously invoked, so that He may mercifully perfect the good work which He began in us. Because, finally, we are predestined out of the grace of God alone, not because of our merits, no one has an occasion for boasting or exalting himself. To which that Apostolic saying looks, Rom. 11 verse 20: Do not be high-minded, but fear.

IV. D. Gesnerus, Disp. 16 in For. Conc. c. 1, quest. 5, and Mr. D. Cramerus, my honorable friend, in his work on Predestination, ch. 10, p. 382, enumerate four uses common to all Scripture. 1 Tim. 3:6. For the sound doctrine of election is useful, πρὸς διδασκαλίαν or for teaching, because it shows the true dogma concerning God's will toward the human race regarding our redemption, vocation, and glorification. 2. πρὸς ἔλε their glosses miserably corrupt the truth of Scripture with subtleties. And to this point looks that statement of Augustine from book 2 de bono perseuerantiæ. The heretic does not keep silent, who speaks without Scripture, and shall we refuse to say what we can say with Scripture as our witness? For we fear, forsooth, that those who cannot or will not grasp the truth might be offended by our speaking; and do we not fear that those who can grasp the truth might be captured by falsehood if we remain silent? πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν or for correction, insofar as through this doctrine men are admonished to lay aside those things which are opposed to the divine will and the gratuitous decree of election, such as presumption, hypocrisy, diffidence, despair, and the like. 4. πρὸς παιδείαν or for training, insofar as it instigates toward piety and holiness of life, so that through good works we may make our election firm. 2. Pet. 1. ver. 10. so that we may work out our salvation with fear and trembling, Phil. 2. v. 12 with fear and reverence. Heb. 12. v. 19. Hence Augustine writes most gravely. l. 2. de bono perseuerant. cap. 17. Just as he whom God foreknew would be chaste, acts so that he may be chaste; so he whom He predestined would be chaste, does not for that reason not act so that he may be chaste, because by the gift of God he hears that he will be what he shall be: Nay, rather his charity rejoices, nor is he puffed up as if he had not received it. Not only is he not hindered from this work by predestination, but he is aided toward it, so that he who glories may glory in the Lord.

V. Lord D. Pelargus likewise establishes a fourfold use in his commonplaces, but in another way. For he says that the doctrine of election is conducive, 1. to exciting humility. 2. to acknowledging the sublimity of God.

3. For general confidence and for raising up spirits. 4. For kindling in us a zeal for piety.

VI. Lord D. Cramer, in his theses on Predestination, thesis 38, recounts a threefold use: παιδευτικὸν, by which pride is destroyed, humility is taught, and the handle for boasting is cut off. For since election is purely gratuitous, why do you exalt yourself, O clay? And what do you have that you did not receive? 1 Cor. 4:7. 2. παραμυθητικὸν, because the true πληροφορία of faith is kindled, and effective consolation is supplied, according to the sayings in Matt. 25:34, John 10:18, Rom. 8:17, 34, 2 Tim. 2:19. 3. παρακλητικὸν, while a true and serious zeal for piety is awakened, and threats against sins are sharpened. For he who by his impenitence makes it testified that he has not been enrolled among the elect, for him there remains a certain terrible expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire which is about to consume the adversaries, Heb. 10:27.

VII. Zanchius, book 1, On the Nature of God, ch. 745, posits two principal uses, but he cannot defend them from his own hypotheses; nevertheless, we shall briefly explain them. The course of human life is compared to a voyage. For the world in which we live is like a sea flowing and ebbing; the shore from which we set sail is birth itself; where we are heading is eternal happiness; the sailor whom we follow is Christ; the anchor upon which we rely is faith. In this sacred voyage, however, two reefs in particular are to be avoided, one to the left, the other to the right: the former we call despair or servile fear; the latter, boasting or Pharisaical swelling. There, men distrust God too much and become desperate; here, they trust themselves too much and become secure. Both reefs can be avoided if the doctrine of Predestination is rightly proposed. For no one has a cause for despair, since the will of God, and the passion of Christ, and the calling of the Holy Spirit are universal and exclude no one. Whence also the very [doctrine] of election... the decree is not absolute but joined with respect to faith. Whoever therefore believes in time and has the purpose of persevering, can most firmly at the same time believe that he was elected from eternity. If elected, therefore, he will not be snatched from the hand of the Lord, but will reach the harbor of heavenly joy. Now, as far as carnal security and confidence are concerned, we are led away from these rocks also by the doctrine of election. For there we hear that we are predestined out of mere grace, without merit, so that we may live piously. Let all boasting therefore cease; it is a gift of God, not from us. Let security cease, since if faith and the fruits of faith do not follow in time, election from eternity did not precede. Thus we see how the sound doctrine of predestination heals both despair and security, which is by no means the case if the hypotheses of Zanchius and other followers of Calvin are affirmed. For if by an absolute decree very few are elected and very many are reprobated, how shall I be able to console the doubter and persuade him of the certainty of his salvation? If the number of the elect is fatal, human reason will easily assume: I shall most certainly be saved, and I am a son of God, even if I indulge my genius for a time and gradually give myself over to the pleasures of the world. But more will be said about these things in the following.

VIII. Furthermore, that we may add something of our own, we can give five additional ways of discussing the uses of predestination. 1. A threefold γνῶθι must always be inculcated in man. 1. γνῶθι Θεὸν, Know God. 2. γνῶθι σεαυτὸν, Know yourself. 3. γνῶθι Διάβολον, Know your enemy the Devil. In God let us recognize mercy, that we may trust, and justice, that we may fear. In ourselves, infirmity, that we may repent: In the Devil, craftiness, that we may live circumspectly. The doctrine of predestination leads to all these things. For it supplies knowledge, 1. Of God, manifesting both the actions of the persons and two principal attributes. The actions are the universal love of the Father, the Redemption of the Son, and the calling of the Holy Spirit, from which, as from streams, the gratuitous decree of election has flowed forth. The attributes are God's Goodness and Severity, or Justice and Mercy. We learn the former from the election of believers; the latter from the reprobation of the impenitent. For the former let us give thanks, lest we be puffed up; for the latter let us fear, lest we be led astray. Augustine joins both when he writes in Psalm 100: God neither loses the severity of judgment in the goodness of mercy, nor does He lose the goodness of mercy when judging with severity.

2. Of ours, by calling to memory the state of human nature. For from this is evident the state of innocence, in which we were created before the decree of election was made: the state of misery, into which we have fallen by the fault of the πρωτοπλάστων [first-formed]: the state of grace, the beginning and foundation of which is gratuitous predestination: the state of glory to which the elect will be raised: the state of ignominy to which the reprobate will be subjected.

Finally 3. Of the devil, because he is the enemy of the whole human race, by tempting and persecuting the elect; but by binding the reprobate with his chains. Wherefore let us resist, strong in faith, and let us always implore the help of GOD, lest we be carried headlong into sins, but walking in the holiness of life, let us fight the good fight even to the end of life, so that we may be able to triumph eternally.

IX. There are two heads of heavenly doctrine, the Law and the Gospel. The former commands concerning works, the latter concerning faith. The former urges τὸ ἀκριβοδίκαιον [the exact justice], the latter applies ἐπιείκειαν [clemency]. The former shows the disease, the latter the remedy for the disease. Both are prefigured by two pastoral staves, by which Christ the ἀρχιποίμην [chief shepherd] rules the Church. Zech. 11. v. 7. The one staff is hard and troublesome, shadowing forth the law: the other is sweet and pleasant, denoting the Gospel. The sum of both is conspicuous from the article of election. is rendered, For predestination is an Evangelical act; Reprobation is a legal act. Predestination teaches that Christ made satisfaction for all, and that all who perseveringly apprehend his merit are inscribed in the book of life, and are no longer subject to the curse. Reprobation implies the supreme perfection of the law, requiring absolute obedience, which since the infidels neither have in themselves nor apprehend in Christ, therefore according to the infallible foreknowledge of ἀπτώσιας they are eternally reprobated by the just judgment of God, and separated from the elect sons of God. Thus, therefore, the locus on predestination can not undeservedly be called the Synopsis and compendium of the whole heavenly doctrine.

X. 3. There are three cardinal virtues of the Christian man, 1. Piety towards God, 2. Charity towards one's neighbor, 3. Sobriety towards oneself. The Apostle hints at these in Tit. 2. v. 12, where we are admonished that we should live ἐυσεβῶς or piously, δικαίως or justly, σωφρόνως or soberly. Opposed to these three virtues are three principal vices, namely ἀσέβεια or impiety, ἀδικία or iniquity, ἀκράτεια or luxury, intemperance, and the like. The doctrine of election, rightly explained, persuades those virtues but dissuades the vices. For behold! God has chosen you out of grace, and will you not worship Him, will you not fear, will you not love, will you not celebrate Him? You are inscribed in one book with other believers, and you will have them as partners of eternal joy, and will you not sincerely love them, will you not pursue them with brotherly benevolence? You are chosen so that you may live holily, and will you cling to the world, will you indulge your genius, and will you not fear to offend with sins your God, by whom you have been so dearly bought and so kindly assumed? Here, in particular, three other vices can be chastised, from 1 John 2. v. 16. Namely 1. Pleasure, 2. Avarice, 3. Pride. For these are the pursuits of the world, whence also the Philosopher recounts three kinds of men in 1 Eth. 3, of which the second is χρηματιστικὸν, occupied with riches, the third πολιτικὸν, contaminated by ambition. To these may we never be associated, election exhorts us again, For behold! You have been chosen for heavenly joy, not earthly: Why therefore do you seek the brief delights of the world and value eternal joy little? Why do you gape after the riches of this age, and meanwhile neglect heavenly things? Why do you collect treasures on earth, by defrauding your neighbor, and yourself? Why are you proud because of merits, when election has been made out of grace: Recognize rather your own infirmity: May you be delighted by humility, so that you may be glorified eternally with the elect:

XI. 4. There are three principal members of man, divinely granted. 1. The heart for thinking. 2. The tongue for speaking, and 3. The hand for working. The doctrine of election informs all these members. Because we are also freely predestined by God to life, Therefore let us love with the heart, let us firmly believe; let us celebrate with the mouth, and let us work well with the hands, and thus let us make our election firm and attested through our works.

XII. Finally 5. There are three proper and perpetual actions or affections of Christians. 1. To suffer. 2. To pray. 3. To praise and give thanks. For whom God loves, He chastises; and He scourges the son whom He receives, Hebr. 12. v. 6. Chastisement, however, excites prayer; Isa. 26. verse 16. which, when God hears, thanksgiving ought to follow, as is hinted in Psalm 50. v. 15. Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall honor me: For we ought to be patient in the cross, ardent in praying, diligent and indefatigable in praising, which the Germans express thus: A Christian must suffer patiently, pray devoutly, and give thanks fervently. The doctrine of election is useful for each in turn. For if GOD has decreed eternal life and salvation for you, why will you not patiently endure the cross for His favor and on account of His name, when you know that it will be compensated with eternal joy? Since the Son of God has been chosen, what will He deny to the bene gnignus Father? He urges therefore by praying; He himself coming will come, and he who chose you out of grace, will not desert you in distress. But when prayers have been heard, is it not right that such goodness be celebrated? For consider the mercy of God. Behold, from eternity He chose you, having chosen He created you in time, having created He redeemed you, having redeemed He justified you, having justified He preserved you, having preserved He glorified you, which is the end of gratuitous election. Rejoice on account of these benefits, O faithful soul, and offer to God a sacrifice of praise, singing with the Apostle from Eph. 1. v. 3. Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places, in Christ.

XIII. And these are the principal uses of the Article concerning predestination which we can combine thus; The doctrine of election leads partly to faith, partly to the Christian life. To faith, by showing the sum of the Law and the Gospel; by suggesting the knowledge of God; of ourselves; of the Devil: by refuting Pelagians, Calvinists, and other erroneous spirits. To life, both by strengthening the Heart, that it may love God, and believe Him equally on account of this; the Tongue, that it may celebrate Him; the Hands, that it may work well, and by persuading virtues, namely Piety toward God, charity toward one's neighbor, sobriety toward oneself; and again patience in adversities, ardor in prayers, tireless zeal in giving thanks; and by dissuading vices: which are opposed either to faith, such as despair and carnal confidence; or to the holiness of life, such as pleasure, avarice, and pride. May the Father of ages, who chose us in Christ through the faith of the Holy Spirit unto eternal salvation, grant that the doctrine explained thus far may bring forth these salutary uses in our hearts: to whom be praise and blessing never to be ended.

Latin:

Quis sit vsus doctrinæ de Prædestinatione hactenus explicatæ?

I. Antiquorum Prouerbiũ fuit, Theologia magis in adfectu consistit quàm in cognitione. Innuerunt a. non sufficere nudam γνώσιν, sed inprimis requiri πράξιν, quàm adfectus vocabulo expresserunt. Philosophus inquit, lib. 8. Ethic. cap. 9. Non de virtute scire satis est, sed enitendum, ipsam habere & vti. Idem de fidei articulis affirmari potest. Scire illos aut disputare de illis non satis est : Ad vsum transferri debent, & monstrandum quomodo conducant, qui applicari queant in exercitijs poenitentiæ & obedientiæ. Ignatij dictum fuit: ὁ λέγων μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐἶναι, ποιῇ χριστιανὸς. Non dicere, sed esse, Christianum facit: Cui Iustinus Martyr adstipulatur: Non in verbis, sed in factis res religionis nostra consistunt, Sic ergo disputetur, ne istud Senecæ obijciatur: Multum scientiæ, parum conscientiæ. Conjungit Apostolus vtrumque, πίστιν καὶ ἀγαθὴν συνείδησιν, Fidem & bonam conscientiam, 1. Tim. 1. v. 19. Proindè sic disserendum est de Fidei articulis; vt inde augeatur pietas, & promoueatur vitæ sanctitas, vnde oritur conscientiæ tranquillitas.

II. Postquam igitur ipsa Prædestinationis doctrina hactenus explicata est, ad vsum quomodo accommodari possit, dicendum superest: Satis disputatum fuit: Videndum, quem ista disputatio vsum præbeat in Christianismo: Est a. ille multiplex, ideoque multis etiam modis efferri potest. Præcipuos paucis attingemus.

III. Augustinus monet, articulum hunc diligenter tractandum esse tribus de causis. 1. Ne tepefcat hortatio. 2. Ne extinguatur oratio, 3. Ne accendatur elatio. Quia n. electio facta est, vt sancti essemus & irreprehensibiles. Ephes. 1. v. 4. quivis hinc sui admoneri debet officij. Quia electi sunt ij tantùm qui perseverant. Ergò Deus assiduè inuocandus est, vt opus bonum quod cœpit in nobis clementer perficiat.
