Quia denique ex sola Dei gratia, non propter nostra merita prædestinati sumus nemo gloriandi, vel sese efferendi occasionem habet. Quò spectat istud Apostolicum, Rom. 11. vers. 20. Noli altum sapere, sed time.

IV. D. Gesnerus Disp 16. in For. Conc. c. 1. quæst: & v. & Dn. D. Cramerus, Amicus meus honorandus l, de Prædest. c. 10. p 382. quatuor usus, omni Scripturæ communes. 1. Tim. 3. v. 6. enumerant. V tilis enim est sana electionis doctrina, πρὸς διδασκαλίαν vel ad docendum, quia ostendit verum dogma de Dei voluntate erga genus humanum de redemtione, vocatione & glorificatione nostra. 2. πρὸς ἔλεγχον vel ad arguendum, quia inferuit refutatione ἀγλωσσιῶν; qui suis glossis scripturam argutiis veritatem miserè corrumpunt, Et huc spectat istud Augustini ex libro 2. de bono perseuerantiæ. Hæreticus non tacet, qui loquitur absque Scriptura, Et nos nolumus dicere quod teste Scriptura possumus dicere? Timemus enim videlicet, ne loquentibus nobis offendatur, qui veritatem non potest aut non vult capere; & non timemus, ne tacentibus nobis qui veritatem potest capere, falsitate capiatur? πρὸς ἐπανόρθωσιν vel ad corrigendum quatenus per hanc doctrinam admonentur homines, vt de ponant illa, quæ voluntari diuinæ & gratuito electionis decreto aduersantur qualia sunt præsumtio, hypocrisis, diffidentia, desperatio, & similia. 4. πρὸς παιδείαν vel ad erudiendum, quatenus ad pietatem & vitæ sanctitatem instigat vt per bona opera firmam faciamus electionem. 2. Pet. 1. ver. 10. vt salutem operemur cum timore & tremore, Phil. 2. v. 12 cum metu & reuerentia. Heb. 12. v. 19. Hinc August. grauissime scribit. l. 2. de bono perseuerant. cap. 17. Sicut ille quem castum futurum Deus præsciuit, agit, vt castus sit; ita ille quem castum futurum prædestinauit, non ideo non agit vt castus sit, quoniam Dei dono audit se futurum esse, quod erit: Imo etiam gaudet eius charitas, nec inflatur tanquam non acceperit. Non solùm prædestinationis, ab hoc opere non impeditur, verù ad hoc adiuuatur, vt cum gloriatur in Domino glorietur,

V. Dominus D. Pelargus itidem vsum quadruplicem constituit in locis communibus, sed alio modo. Dicit enim doctrinam electionis conducere, 1. ad humilitatem excitandam. 2. sublimitatem Dei agnoscendam.

3. ad fiduciam generalem & animos erigendos. 4. ad accendendum in nobis pietatis studium.

VI. Dominus D. Cramerus in thesibus de Prædest. th. 38. triplicem vsum recenset, παιδευτικὸν quo destruitur superbia docetur humilitas, præciditur ansa gloriandi, Quia enim electio merè gratuita est, cur te extollis lutum? Et quid habes quod non acceperis? 1. Cor. 4. 17. 2. παραμυθητικὸν quia vera fidei πληροφορία accenditur, & efficax consolatio suppeditatur, secundum dicta Matth 25. v. 34. Ioh. 10. vers 18. Rom. 8. vers. 17. 34. 2. Tim. 2, vers. 19. 3, παρακλητικὸν, dum verum seriumque pietatis studium exsuscicatur, & comminationes aduersus peccata acuuntur. Qui enim impœnitentiâ suâ testatum facit, se electis adscriptum non esse, hunc manet terribilis quædam exspectatio iudicij & ignis æmulatio quæ consumptura est aduersarius, Hebr. 10. v. 27.

VII. Zanchius lib. 1. de Nat. D. c. 745. duos principales vsus ponit, sed ex hypothesibus suis defendere nequit, breuiter tamen eos explicabimus. Vitæ humanæ cursus comparatur nauigationi. Mundus enim in quo viuimus, est quasi mare fluens, & refluens; Litus vnde soluimus, natiuitas per se, quò tendimus æterna felicitas: Nauta quem sequimur Christus: Anchora, qua innitimur, fides est. In hac vero nauigatione sacra, duo inprimis scopuli vitandi sunt alter ad sinistram, alter ad dextram: Illum vocamus desperationem vel seruilem timorem; hunc gloriationem vel Pharisaicum tumorem. Ibi homines nimium diffidunt Deo, & fiunt desperabundi: hic nimium confidunt sibi & fiunt securi. Vterque scopulus vitari potest, si doctrina Prædestinationis ritè proponitur. Nam desperandi caussam nemo habet, quoniam voluntas Dei & passio Christi, & vocatio Spiritus Sancti vniuersalia sunt nec quenquam excludunt. Vnde & ipsum electionis denis decretum non est absolutum sed cum fidei respectu coniunctum. Qui igitur credit in tempore & perseuerandi habet propositum, firmissimè vnà potest credere se electum fuisse ab æterno. Si electus ergo non rapietur è manu Domini, sed attinget portum cœlestis gaudij. Iam verò securitatem & confidentiam carnalem quod attinet, his quoque scopulis per electionis doctrinam abducimur. Ibi n. audimus, quod prædestinati simus ex mera gratia, sine merito vt viuamus pie. Cesset igitur omnis gloriatio; Dei donum est, non ex nobis. Cesset securitas siquidem fides & fructus fidei nisi sequatur in tempore, non præcessit electio ab æterno, Ita videmus, quomodo tum desperationi, tum securitati medeatur sana de prædestinatione doctrina, id quod minimè fit, si affumantur hypotheses Zanchij & aliorum Caluinisequarum. Nam si ex absoluto decreto paucissimi electi & plurimi reprobati sunt quomodo dubitantem solari, & salutis certitudinem ipsi persuadere potero? si fatalis est electorum numerus, facilè subsumet humana ratio; certissime saluabor, & Dei Filius sum, si maximè ad tempus genio indulgeam, & voluptatibus mundi paulatim me dedam. Sed pluribus de his agetur in sequentibus.

IIX. Porrò, vt de nostro aliquid addamus, quinque prætereà modos de prædestinationis vsibus differendi dare possumus. 1. Triplex γνῶθι semper inculcandum est homini. 1. γνῶθι Θεὸν, Nosce Deum, 2. γνῶθι σεαυτὸν, Nosce teipsum. 3. γνῶθι Διάβολον, Nosce hostem tuum Diabolum. In Deo agnoscamus misericordiam, vt confidamus, & iustitiam, vt timeamus. In nobis infirmitatem, vt pœniteamus: In Diabolo calliditatem, vt circumspectè viuamus. Conducit ad hæc omnia prædestinationis doctrina. Suppeditat enim cognitionem, 1. Dei, manifestando tum personarum actiones, tum attributa duo principalia. Actiones sunt, vniuersalis dilectio Patris, Redemptio Filij, vocatio Spiritus S. ex quibus tanquam riuulis profluxit gratuitum electionis decretum. Attributa sunt Dei Bonitas & Seueritas, vel Iustitia & Misericordia. Illam discimus ex credentium electione; hanc ex impoenitentium reprobatione. Ob illam gratias agamus, ne efferamur; ob hanc timeamus, ne seducamur. Vtrumque coniungit August. cum scribit in Psal. 100. Deus nec in bonitate misericordiae perdit judicij seueritatem: nec in iudicando cum seueritate amittit misericordiae bonitatem.

2. Nostri, in memoriam reuocando status humanae naturae. Patet enim hinc status innocentiae, in qua creati sumus ante factum electionis decretum: status miseriae, in quam πρωτοπλάστων culpâ prolapsi sumus: Status gratiae, cuius initium & fundamentum est gratuita praedestinatio: Status gloriae ad quam euchentur electi: Status ignominiae cui subijcientur reprobati.

Tandem 3. Diaboli, quod sit hostis totius generis humani, electos tentando & persequendo: reprobos autem suis vinculis constringendo. Quare fortes in fide resistamus, & DEI auxilium semper imploremus, ne in peccata feramur praecipites, sed in sanctitate vitae ambulantes, bonum certamen vsque ad vitae terminum certemus, vt aeternùm triumphare valeamus.

IX. Duo sunt doctrinae coelestis capita, Lex & Euangelium. Illud de operibus, hoc de fide praecipit, Illud τὸ ἀκριβοδίκαιον vrget, hoc ἐπιείκειαν adhibet. Illud morbum, hoc morbi remedium ostendit. Vtrumque prefiguratum est per duos baculos pastorales, quibus Christus ἀρχιποίμην regit Ecclesiam. Zach. 11. v. 7. Alter baculus, est durus & molestus, adumbrans legem: alter suauis & amoenus, notans Euangelium. Vtriusque summa ex electionis articulo conspiredditur, Nam prædestinatio, actus Euangelicus; Reprobatio actus legalis est. Prædestinatio docet, quod Christus pro omnibus satis fecerit, & omnes meritum ejus perseueranter apprehendentes libro vitæ sint inscripti, nec maledictioni amplius subjaceant. Reprobatio subinnuit summam perfectionem legis, absolutam obedientiam requirentis, quàm cùm infideles nec in se habeant, nec in Christo apprehendant, ideo secundum infallibilem ἀπτώσιας præscientiam ex justo Dei judicio æternùm sunt reprobati, & ab electis Dei filijs separati. Sic ergo locus de prædestinatione Synopsis & compendium totius doctrinæ cœlestis non immeritò nuncupari potest.

X. 3. Tres sunt cardinales hominis Christiani virtutes, 1. Pietas erga Deum, 2. Charitas erga proximum. 3. Sobrietas erga seipsum. Innuit has Apost. Tit. 2. v. 12. vbi monemur, vt viuamus ἐυσεβῶς vel piè δικαίως vel justè σωφρόνως vel sobriè Tribus his virtutibus opposita sunt tria principalia vitia, nimirum ἀσέβεια vel impietas ἀδικία vel iniquitas ἀκράτεια vel luxus, intemperantia & similia. Virtutes illas suadet, sed vitia dissuadet doctrina electionis dextrè explicata. Nam ecce! Deus ex gratia Te elegit, & non coles ipsum, non timebis, non amabis, non celebrabis? Vni libro inscriptus es cum alijs fidelibus, eosque socios habebis æterni gaudij, Et tu illos non sincerè diliges, non fraterna benevolentia pro sequêris? Electus es vt sanctè viuas, & tu seculo adhærebis, genio indulgebis, & Deum tuum, à quo tàm carè emptus & tàm benignè assumtus es, peccatis offendere non vereberis? Possunt hic in specie & alia tria castigari vitia, ex Ioh. 2. v. 16. Nempè 1. voluptas 2. Avaritia. 3. Superbia. Hæc enim sunt studia mundi vnde & Philos. tria hominū genera enarrat 1. Eth. 3. quorū Secundum χρηματιστικὸν, circa diuitias occupatum, Tertium πολιτικὸν ambitione contaminatum. His ne vñquam associemúr, electio iterùm hortatur, Nam ecce! Ad cœleste gaudium electus es non terrestre: Cur igitur breues mundi delitias quæris & æternam lætitiam parui pendis? cur huius seculi opibus inhias, & interim cœlestia negligis? Cur thesauros colligis in terra, defraudando proxistrum, & amittis thesaurum cœli, perdendo teipsum? Quare superbis ob merita, cùm electio facta sit ex gratia: Agnosce potius tuam infirmitatem: Humilitate delecteris, vt cū electis æternùm glorificeris:

XI. 4.Tria sunt hominis membra principalia, diuinitus concessa. 1. Cor ad cogitandum. 2. Lingua ad loquendum, & 3. Manus ad operandum. Omnia hæc membrainformat electionis doctrina. Quia etiim à Deo gratis prædestinati sumus ad vitam, Ergo corde diligamus, firmiter credamus; ore celebremus, & manibus benè operemur, adeoque electionem per nostra opera firmam testatamque faciamus.

XII. Tandem 5. Tres sunt Christianorum siue actiones siue affectiones propriæ & perpetuæ. 1. Pati 2. Precari. 3. Laudare & gratias agere. Quem n. Deus diligit hunc castigat. & filium, quem recipit, flagellat Hebr. 12. v. 6. Castigatio autem excitat orationem; Esa. 26. vers. 16. quam cum Deus exaudit, sequi debet gratiarum actio, vt innuitur Psalm. 50. v. 15. Inuoca me in die tribulationis, & eruam te, & honorificabis me: Debemus enim esse in cruce patienter, in precando ardentes, in laudando diligentes & indefessi, quod Germáni ita efferunt. Ein Christ muß gedultig leiden/ andechtig betten/ inbrünstig Danck sagen. Ad singula vicissim conducit electionis doctrina. Nam si DEVS vitam & salutem sempiterna tibi decreuit, cur non in gratiam ipsius & propter nomen eius crucem patienter perferes, cùm illam æterno gaudio conspensatum iri scias? Cùm electus sit Dei Filius, quid denegabit benignus Pater? Instat igitur orando; Ipse veniens veniet, & qui te elegit ex gratia, non deferet in angustia. Cùm verò preces exauditæ sunt, annòn bonitatem tantam celebrari æquum est? Nam cogita Dei misericordiam. Ecce, ab æterno te elegit, electum in tempore creauit, creatum redemit, redemptum iustificauit, iustificatum conseruauit, conseruatum glorificauit, qui finis est electionis gratuitę. Gaude ob hæc beneficia, ô fidelis anima, & Deo sacrificium laudis immola, cum Apostolo canens ex Eph. 1. v. 3. Benedictus sit Deus & Pater Domini Iesu Christi, qui benedixit nos in omni benedictione spirituali in cœlestibus, in Christo.

XIII. Et hi sunt præcipui vsus Articuli de prædestinatione quos ita combinare possumus; Doctrina electionis conducit partim ad fidem partim ad vitam Christianam. Ad fidem, ostendendo summam legis & Euangelij; suggerendo cognitionem Dei; Nostri; Diaboli: arguendo Pelagianos, Caluinianos aliosque erroneos Spiritus. Ad vitam, tum infirmando Cor, vt Deum amet, & eum æquè propter credat; Linguam, vt celebret; Manus, vt bene operetur, tum suadendo virtutes, nempe Pietatem in Deum, charitate in proximum, sobrietatem erga seipsum; & iterum patientiam in aduersis, ardorem in precibus, indefessum studium in agendis gratiis; tum dissuadendo vitia: quæ sunt opposita vel fidei, vt desperatio & carnalis confidentia; vel sanctitati vitę, vt voluptas, auaritia & superbia. Hos igitur salutares vsus, vt in cordibus nostris pariat doctrina hactenus explicata, Faxit Pater seculorum qui elegit nos in Christo per fidem iancti Spiritus, ad salutem æternam: cui sit laus & benedictio nunquam finiênda.


### Question II. What is the use of the doctrine of Predestination explained thus…: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 19 Disputation VII. On the Universal Election Devised by Huber

Πρόπλασμα.

We distributed the whole ἐργασίαν [work] of the Article concerning predestination into four chapters in disputation 5, thesis 22. The first dealt with the three hypotheses. The second with election itself, its causes and immutability, all of which have been explained thus far. The third now follows, which is concerning the elect, where in the first place five questions come to be ventilated. 1. Whether all angels are elect? 2. Whether all men are elect? 3. Whether the number of the elect is certain? 4. Whether, and from where, election is certainly known? 5. Whether the Elect lose the grace of the Holy Spirit through sins? We shall discuss the first two at this time, and reserve the others for subsequent συζητήσεις [discussions].

Latin:

Πρόπλασμα.

TOtam ἐργασίαν Articuli de prædestinatione in quatuor capita distribuimus disput. 5. th. th. 22. Primum egit de tribus hypothesibus. Secundum de ipsa electione, eius causis & immutabilitate, quæ omnia hactenus sunt explicata. Tertium iam sequitur, quod est de electis, vbi quinque in primis quæstiones ventilandæ veniunt. 1. Num omnes angeli sint electi? 2. Num omnes homines sint electi? 3. An certus sit electorum numerus? 4. Num, & vnde certò constet electio? 5. Num Electi per peccata Spiritus S. gratiam amittant? Primas duas hâc vice discutiemus, & cæteras ad sequentes, συζητήσεις reseruabimus.


### Question I. Whether all angels are elect?

I. Since 'Angel' is a name of office, and 'Spirit' is a name of nature, and thus some angels are good and some are evil, the question here is instituted only concerning the good: The affirmative of which pleases both Papists and Calvinists. For thus writes Thomas, part 1, question 23, article 1, ad 3: It is fitting for angels to be predestined, just as it is for men, although they were never miserable:

Hence he defines predestination in general in this way in question 24, article 1: predestination is the plan of the transmission of a rational creature into eternal life. Following Thomas are Scotus in 1, distinction 40, question 1, and in 3, distinction 7, question 3; Bonaventure in 1, distinction 40, article 1, question 2; Durandus in 1, distinction 41, question 1; Bellarmine, Volume 5, book 2, on grace and free will, chapter 18, column 639, D; Becanus, Treatise 1, chapter 14, question 2, page 135, and question 5, page 162. Polanus allowed himself to be persuaded by these doctors to establish the same thing in his Didascalia on predestination, page 9. Election, he says, is of both the blessed angels and of men to be saved. He repeats this in book 4 of his Syntagma Theologiae, chapter 8, column 1760, and Bucanus agrees in place 36, question 6, page 420.

II. We, however, answer briefly that the term election or predestination is ambiguous. For it is taken either καταχρησικῶς (improperly) and in a certain breadth for every preordination and decree of glory, or strictly and properly according to the phrase and sense of Scripture, where it denotes the decree concerning those who are to be saved, having fallen and believing perseveringly. According to the first acceptance, indeed, it could be said that the angels, before they were created, were ordained by God from eternity to glory and the blessed life. For whatever He does in time, He decreed from eternity that He would do. Wherefore, as He proposed to Himself to create the angels, so also to confirm them in good and to make them eternally blessed. If this decree, therefore, is called predestination, let it be so in the broad, catachrestic sense; but according to the latter and proper acceptance, the angels are by no means elected, nor can they be called so, which is demonstrated by this most firm argument.

III. Election, of which Scripture speaks, 1. Concerns those who had fallen in Adam, as we showed in disputation 4, question 3, thesis 14. 2. Was made in Christ, Ephesians 1, verse 3-4, 2 Timothy 1, verse 9, as the foundation of election. 3. Through faith, 2 Thessalonians 2, verse 13, which is a part of the order of predestination. 4. And therefore those elected in time are called, believe, and are justified, Rom. 8. verse 30. Whence 5. many indeed are called, but few are said to be elected, Matth. 20. v. 16. c. 22. v. 14. who 6. in their own time obtain salvation Dan. 12. v. 1.

But no such thing can be affirmed concerning the blessed Angels. For 1. They never fell, how therefore could they have been elected to life after a fall? You except Thomas quest. 24. art. 1. to 3. that motion does not receive its species from the term from which, but from the term to which. Therefore it matters nothing to the reason of predestination, whether someone is predestined to eternal life from a state of misery, or not. I answer. These things are said without Scripture: For Scripture not only posits the term of election to which, namely glory, but also from which, namely misery. For God loved the world immersed in darkness, John 3. v. 16. 19. and to this he gave his son, in whom election was made: Wherefore when Scripture does not speak, he who considers predestination without this term from which.

2. In Christ the Angels could not be elected, because Christ is not their Redeemer. For he satisfied both for the ungodly and for sinners; Rom. 5. v. 6. Polanus insists in didascal. p. 10. that the Angels indeed did not have need of a Redeemer, yet [they did have need of] a preserver in good, and a head; through whose bond they might adhere to their God by covenant and without distinction. I answer. Election is said to be made in Christ not in any respect whatsoever, but insofar as he is Redeemer, and a victim for sins, as the Apostle explains Eph. 1. v. 6. 7. Those therefore whom Christ did not redeem, they are not elected in Christ according to the sense of Scripture. Furthermore, the necessity of the incarnation is feigned on the part of the Angels; as if they could neither be preserved in good, nor adhere to God, unless the λόγος had come into the flesh. Which assertion is partly rash, resting on no reasons; partly ἄγραφος, and in no way founded in the Scriptures: for Christ came for those whose seed he assumed. But this was of Abraham, Heb. 2. v. 16. And he came to save that which had perished, Luke 19. v. 10. that he might destroy the works of the Devil, 1 John 3, verse 8. But that He came on account of the Angels, so that they might be preserved in good and be able to cleave to God, is nowhere asserted, even indirectly. Indeed, it sets limits to divine power, as if He could not have immediately preserved and confirmed the Angels.

3. Faith does not belong to the Angels. For although they have knowledge of the articles and offer assent to the truth, yet justifying faith, which is the apprehension of the merit of the Redeemer, does not fall upon them. For since they are immune from sins, they need neither satisfaction nor the application of this through faith.

4. Whence it further follows that they are neither called through the Gospel to believe, nor are they justified through imputation, since they are most holy in their own nature and without sins to be remitted on account of Christ.

5. It cannot be said of the Angels that many of them are called, few are chosen, for all are righteous, all have persisted in good. Wherefore if they are chosen, not a few, but all are chosen. But indeed the predestination of Scripture is particular, in such a way that it includes a few, with the others, although they may have been called, excluded on account of their infidelity. Wherefore if the Angels are called predestined, it follows that this term is accepted in a sense other than that of Scripture.

Finally 6. Glory will not be conferred upon the blessed spirits at last in the final judgment, but they have possessed it from the beginning. But indeed predestination was made unto life to be obtained at some time, and its end is future, not present. How therefore can the Angels be said to be predestined to glory, which is present to them, not future.

IV. To the contrary they find nothing to oppose except a single passage from 1 Tim. 5, v. 2, which Polanus urges with Bellarmine in Didasc. page 10. The words, however, are as follows: I charge thee before God and Christ Jesus and ἐνώπιον τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων, and before the elect Angels, that thou keep these things, etc. Here they think their opinion is found according to the very letter. But we respond,

1. Scripture is opposed to Scripture. Therefore, a convenient διάνοια [meaning/interpretation] must be sought. 2. Some understand by Angels the ministers of the word, who on account of their office are called Angels. Mal. 2. v. 3. & c. 3. v. 1. For they are the legates of God, upon whom it is incumbent to ἀγγέλλειν [to announce] or to announce the law & knowledge. The Apostle therefore calls these to witness, who ought to revere one another, lest he commit such a thing that might need the correction of the others. According to this interpretation, therefore, this passage is impertinently alleged for establishing the election of Angels. For by ἐκλογὴν [election] is noted a temporal calling to the ministry, not an eternal predestination to glory. 3. Let us grant that by Angels are signified the blessed Spirits; yet the adversaries have not obtained what they want: for these are called elect in a general sense, insofar as they are loved by God and are acceptable to Him. For we do not deny that in this broad sense the title of elect is often taken. But our discourse is not about improper election, which denotes the excellence of a thing, but about special and proper election, which signifies the predestination of those to be saved unto life. Otherwise, they would say that not only Angels and men, but also other creatures are elected to life, since chariots are called elect, Ex. 14. v. 7, cedars elect, Jer. 22. v. 7, sepulchres elect, Gen. 23. v. 6. To avoid this absurdity, they find it necessary to admit that 'elect' is sometimes the same as dear, excellent, precious. And in this sense the blessed Angels are named elect: which if the adversaries deny, and take that word properly; 1. they beg the question, and cannot prove from the text what they say, 2. they oppose Scripture to itself, since it describes proper election to life in such a way that it in no way applies to Angels, as we have sufficiently shown hitherto, etc.

Latin:

I. Cùm Angelus sit nomen officij, & Spiritus nomen naturæ est, adeoque Angeli quidam boni, quidam mali sint, hîc de bonis tantum instituitur quæstio: Cuius affirmatina placet tùm Papicolis, tum Caluinisequis. Sic enim scribit Thomas part. 1. qu. 23. art. 1. ad. 3. Prædestinari conuenit Angelis, sicut & hominibus, licèt nunquã fuerint miseri:

Hinc prædestinationẽ in genere ita definit quæst. 24. art. 1. prædestinatio est ratio transmissionis creaturæ rationalis in vitam æternam. Thomam sequuntur, Scotus in 1. dist. 40. quæst. 1. & in 3. distinct. 7. quæst. 3. 3. Bonauentura in 1. distinct. 40. art. 1. quæst. 2. Durandusin 1. distinct. 41. quæst 1. Bellarminus Tom. 5. lib. 2. de grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 18. Col. 639. D. Becanus Tract. 1. cap. 14. quæst. 2. p. 135. & quæst. 5. q. 162. Ab his doctoribus persuaderi sibi passus est Polanus, vt idem statueret in didascalia de prædest. p. 9. Electio inquit est tum beatorum Angelorum, tum hominum saluandorum. Repetit hoc lib. 4. Syntag. Theolog. cap 8. col. 1760. & consentit Bucanus loco. 36, quæst. 6. p. 420.

II. Nos autem breuiter respondemus, quod Electionis siue prædestinationis vocabulum sit ambiguum. Vel enim sumitur καταχρησικῶς & in quadam latitudine pro omni præordinatione & decreto gloriæ: vel idius ac propriè secundum phrasin & sensum scripturæ, vbi notat decretum de saluandis lapsis & perseueranter credentibus. Iuxta primam quidem acceptionem dici posset; Angelos, antequam crearentur ab æterno ad gloriam & vitam beatam ordinatos esse à Deo. Hic enim quicquid in tempore agit, ab æterno re acturum decreuit. Quare vt sibi proposuit, Angelos creare; ita & in bono confirmare, & æternum beare. Hoc igitur decretum si dicatur prædestinatio, sit istud sensu lato catachristico: iuxta posteriorem verò & propriam acceptionem Angeli nequaquam electi sunt, aut dici possunt, id quod argumento hoc firmissimo demonstratum.

III. Electio, de qua Scriptura loquitur, 1. Concernit illos, qui fuere lapsi in Adamo, vt disput. 4. q. 3. the. 14. ostendimuus. 2. Facta est in Christo, Ephes. 1. v. 34 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. tanquam electionis fundamento. 3. per fidem 2. Thes. 2. Thes. 2. v. 13. quæ pars est ordinis prædestinatorij. 4. ideoque omstes electi in tempore vocantur, credunt, & iustificantur, Rom. 8. vers. 30. Vnde 5. multi quidem vocati, sed pauci electi dicuntur, Matth. 20. v. 16. c. 22. v. 14. qui 6. suo tempore salutem consequentur Dan. 12. v. 1.

Atqui nihil tale de beatis Angelis affirmari potest. Nam 1. Nunquam lapsi sunt, Quî ergo post lapsum ad vitam elegi potuerunt? Excipis Thomas quæst. 24. art. 1. ad 3. motum non accipere speciem à termino à quo, sed à termino ad quem. Nihil igitur referre ad rationem prædestinationis, vtrum aliquis prædestinetur in vitam æternam à statu miseriæ, vel non. Respon. Dicuntur hæc sine Scriptura : Nã Scriptura non modò ponit electionis terminum ad quem, nempè gloriam, sed etiam à quo, nempè miseriam. Deus enim dilexit mundum tenebris immersum, Ioh. 3. v. 16. 19. & huic dedit filiū, in quo facta est electio: Quare cum Scriptura non loquitur, qui prædestinationem absque hoc termino à quo considerat.

2. In Christo Angeli non potuerunt eligi, quia Chris stus ipsorū Redemtot non est. Hic enim satisfecit & impijs & peccatoribus; Rom. 5. v. 6. Instat Polanus in didascal. p. 10. Angelos non quidem opus habuisse Redemtore, attamen conservatore in bono, & capite; per cūius nexxum fœdere & indistinctè Deō suo cohærerēt. Resp. Electio facta dicitur in Christo non respectu quovis, sed quatenus Redemptor est, & victima pro peccatis, explicante Apostolo Eph. 1. v. 6. 7. Quos igitur Christus non redemit, illi in Christo juxtà Scripturæ sensum non sunt electi. Præterea fingitur incarnationis necessitas ex parte Angelorum; ac si in bono nec conservari, nec Deo cohærere potuissent, nisi λόγος in carnem venisset. Quæ assertio est partim temeraria, nullis rationibus nixa; partim ἄγραφος, & in Scripturis minimè fundata: Christus enim venit ob illos, quorum semen assumsit. Hoc autem Abrahæ fuit, Heb. 2. v. 16. Et venit salvare, quod perierat, Luc. 19. v. 10. vt destruerentur opera Diaboli, 1. Ioh. 3. vers. 8. Quod autem propter Angelos venerit, vt conseruarentur in bono, & cohærere possent Deo, nullibi vel per indirectum duntaxat asseritur. Imò limites figit potentiæ diuinæ, quasi Angelos immediatè conseruare ac confirmare non potuisset.

3. Fides Angelis non competit. Quamuis enim articulorum habent notitiam, & assensum præbeant veritati: non tamen in illos cadit fides iustificans, quæ est apprehensio meriti Redemptoris. Cùm enim à peccatis immunes sint, nec satisfactione, nec huius per fidem applicatione indigent.

4. Vnde porrò sequitur, quod neque per Evangelium vocentur, vt credant; neque per imputationẽ iustificentur, cum in sua natura sanctissimi & absq; peccatis sint propter Christū remittendis.

5. De Angelis dici nequit, Quod multi eorum sint vocati, pauci electi, omnes enim iusti sunt, omnes in bono perstiterunt. Quare si electi sunt, non pauci, sed omnes electi sunt. At verò scripturæ prædestinatio particularis est, ita quidem, vt paucos includat, cæteris, licet vocati sint, ob suam infidelitatem exclusis. Quare si Angeli dicuntur prædestinati, alio quam scripturæ sensu vocabulum istud accipi consequitur.

Tandem 6. Beatis spiritibus non conferetur demum gloria In extremo iudicio, sed illã possederunt ab initio. At verò prædestinatio facta est ad vitam, aliquādo consequendam, eiusq; terminus est futurus, non pręsens. Quî ergo Angeli dici queunt prædestinati ad gloriam, quæ ipsis præsens, non futura est.

IV. In contrarium nihil inueniunt quod opponant pręter vnicum locum ex 1. Tim. 5. v. 2. quem cum Bellarmino vrget Polanus in didasc. pag. 10. verba verò sic habent. Testor coram Deo & Christo Iesu atque ἐνώπιον τῶν ἐκλεκτῶν ἀγγέλων, & coram electis Angelis, vt hæc custodias &c. Hîc opinionem suam quod adipsam literam reperiri autumant. Sed respondemus,

1. Scriptura Scripturæ opponitur. Ergo commoda quæri debet διάνοια. 2. Quidam per Angelos intelligunt ministros verbi, qui propter officium suum dicuntur Angeli. Mal. 2. v. 3. & c. 3. v. 1. Sunt enim legati Dei, quibus incumbit ἀγγέλλειν vel annunciare legē & scientiam. Hos igitur in testimonium vocat Apostolus, qui alterum reuereri debet, nè tale quid committat, quod correctione cæterorum egeat. Secundum hanc igitur expositionē locus iste impertinenter allegatur pro stabilienda electione Angelorum. Notatur enim per ἐκλογὴν tēporalis vocatio ad ministerium, non æterna prædestinatio ad gloriam. 3. Demus, per Angelos significari beatos Spiritus, nondum tamen obtinuerunt aduersarij quod volunt: dicuntur enim isti electi in genere, quatenus à Deo sunt dilecti, ipsique accepti. Nā hoc sensu lato electoru titulu sæpius sumi non diffitemur. Nobis autē sermo est, non de electione impropria, quæ rei præstantiam denotat, sed speciali & propria, quæ saluandorum prædestinationē ad vitam significat. Alias non tantū Angelos & homines, Sed & alias creaturas ad vitam electos dicant, quonjā currus vocātur electi, Exo. 14. v. 7. cedri electæ, Ier. 22. v. 7. sepulchra electa, Gen. 23. v. 6. Quod absurdū vt deuitent, fateri necesse habēt, electum quandoq; idē esse, quod charū, execcellens, pretiosum. Et hoc sensu Angeli beati nominantur electi: Q ipsū si aduersarii negent, & vocem illam propriè accipiant; 1. principium petunt, & ex textu, quod dicunt, probare nequeunt, 2 scripturam sibi ipsi opponunt, quippe quæ electionem propriam ad vitam sic describit, vt Angelis nequaquā competat, sicut hactenus sufficienter ostendimus. &c.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?

I. An unhappy controversy was stirred up by Samuel Huber, a Swiss, who writes that all men for whom Christ died, whether they believe or do not believe, or are saved or are damned, are elected, predestined, and ordained in Christ unto salvation. For these are his very words in the book to which he gave the title: Bestendige entdeckung des Caluinischen geystes/ pag. 162. Die heylige Schrifft weyss von solchen (Caluinischen) Ausserwehlten nichts &c. Sondern das findet man wol/ dass Gott nenne ausserwehl- te/ welche er sonst nennet seine geliebten/ oder die er vom fall Adams durch seinen Sohn widerumb erlosset hatt. Vnnd da machet die heyl. Schriffte keinen vnterscheyd vnter den menschen : Where the apostles, and when the apostles preached of the Gospel of Christ (in which the redemption of the world stands), there they called all together and through one another the beloved of the heart, the sanctified, the redeemed, the elect. And in the writing to which the title is: Rettung meiner allezeyt bestendigen bekentnuss, etc., page 5, these things are read: Indeed, he (Huberus) says and confesses constantly that God made no separation in Christ, but elected and ordained one in Him just as the other to life: And confesses thereby that afterwards, when men should accept life in Christ, some become believers and some remain unbelievers, as they were prepared in Adam's fall, and there they still first push away from themselves all the power and effect of the death of Christ for their life.

II. But because Huberus mixes many things together and informs the state of the question in various ways, first of all the τὰ μὴ ζητούμενα [things not in question] must be removed, lest one fight in the manner of blindfolded gladiators. It must therefore be properly noted what is not being asked here. 1. Whether God seriously wills all men to be saved? For we ourselves acknowledge and believe that, according to the sayings 1 Tim. 2, verse 4, 2 Pet. 3, v. 9. 2. Whether Christ truly died for all and singular men? For this also is taught by us everywhere and sincerely believed.

3. Whether God calls all men to repentance? For that also is confessed on both sides.

4. Whether election was made from eternity? For this we very willingly concede to Huber. For when we include faith in the decree of election, we do not mean this, as if it precedes election in act, which is a malicious depravation of our opinion, but we consider faith only as it is foreseen by God. Therefore we distinguish between foreseen faith and actual faith: the latter follows, the former is included in the business of election; not otherwise than the death of Christ happens only in time, which nevertheless enters into the eternal decree of election. It is therefore a mere calumny which Huber attaches to our doctors, concerning faith having preceded election.

5. Whether we are elected on account of faith foreseen from eternity? For just as we are not justified and saved on account of faith, but through faith, or on account of Christ apprehended by faith, in time: so we are not elected from eternity on account of faith, but on account of Christ apprehended by faith. Therefore it is again a gross calumny by which we are burdened by Huber, as if we maintain that election is anticipated or preceded by our faith, whence we are also accused by him of the merit of Pelagianism.

6. Whether the number of the elect is certain by absolute necessity, so that God in Christ chose only a few men to life, who simply could not perish by any incredulity and fall from their salvation. For we acknowledge not unwillingly that the Calvinistic decree is established by this very thing, and therefore we by no means defend it.

7. Whether more could have been converted by the preached word, and therefore elected from eternity? Christ answers affirmatively, adducing the example of the Tyrians and Sidonians, Matt. 11. v. 21.

8. Does the cause of particularity depend upon a certain absolute and inevitable decree of God? We ourselves deny it, and we attribute this solely to the incredulity of men. 9. Whether the decree of election is absolute, or indeed ordered? We contend against the Calvinists for an ordered one, and that not mutilated, but entire: Huberus, however, admits only one part of the order, namely the merit of Christ, by which he thinks the universal decree of election is absolved. 10. Whether predestination is universal by reason of believers? We ourselves say with Scripture, that all who believe perseveringly in Christ are elect: but Huberus does not speak of this universality. 11. Whether the phrase that all are elect, with the word election taken improperly for the general love of God, can be conceded? If Huberus were to acknowledge a certain κατάχρησιν, I would say no one would write against him. And in this sense some of the Orthodox have said that election is universal, understanding this of the universal love of all men. For we often call him elect who is dear to us: just as any father calls all his children elect. Ihr seydt meine liebe ausserwehlte kinder, where the word of election does not have the force of separating, but only denotes the graciousness, love, and approval of some thing. But Huberus flatly refuses to acknowledge this κατάχρησιν, and maintains that all men are elect by election properly, nay, most properly so called. For he removes every aspect of faith from the decree of election, in which part he agrees with the Calvinists, from whom, however, he wishes to depart most of all in this controversy. But because not all are actually saved, he therefore distinguishes between the application and the constitution of election, between the decree itself and the event. For thus he writes in his confuted brief, page 30. As for what is objected regarding the things required for the act, it must be referred to the effect of the election, for the attaining of which all these things are required. But it is one thing concerning the act of God, and another

& to speak of the same effect. The act of election requires nothing for its own perfection beyond the mercy of God and the most holy merit of Christ. In the response to the Tubingen censure in the Tubingen acts, page 65, faith pertains to the application of election, but not to the constitution of election in God considered in Himself. Which distinction coincides with that by which Huberus distinguishes between general and special election. But the more sincere theologians insist on a middle way and establish that not all men indiscriminately, as Huberus, nor absolutely few, as Calvin, but some from all, namely those whom God foresaw would perseveringly believe in Christ, are elected and predestined. For the whole σύσημα of election cannot be terminated by the universal will of God and the merit of Christ, but the aspect of persevering faith must be added, which since it is not in all. is found, it happens that from there, not because of any absolute decree, but because of the unbelief of men, election turns out to be particular, which, however, we do not deny to be universally limited (if, of course, you understand all believers).

Therefore, from what has been said thus far, this state of the question emerges: Did God truly from eternity elect and preordain all men indiscriminately without any respect to faith unto eternal salvation? Huberus affirms it: We, with all the orthodox, deny it, which opinion, although he tears apart with many calumnies, calling it 'Eine verzweiffelte stümpelwal / Eine Götstlösterũg / Ein particulierisch / vnd Caluinisch Rauppenest / eine verzweiffelte lehr' etc., we shall now further demonstrate to the eye that it is most firmly founded in the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, and afterwards we shall append a brief λύσιν of the principal objections.

Latin:

I. Infelix certamen mouit Samuel huberus Helvetius, qui omnes homines, pro quibus Christus est mortuus, siue credant, siue non credant, vel saluentur vel damnantur, in Christo ad salutem electos, praedestinatos & ordinatos scribit. Haec enim ipsius verba sunt in libro, cui fecit titulum: Bestendige entdeckung des Caluinischen geystes/ pag. 162. Die heylige Schrifft weyss von solchen (Caluinischen) Ausserwehlten nichts &c. Sondern das findet man wol/ dass Gott nenne ausserwehlte/ welche er sonst nennet seine geliebten/ oder die er vom fall Adams durch seinen Sohn widerumb erlosset hatt. Vnnd da machet die heyl. Schriffte keinen vnterscheyd vnter den menschen : Wa die Apostel/ vnnd wann die Apostel vom Euangelio Christi/ (darinnen der welt erlosung stehet) geprediget haben/ da haben sie alle mit vnnd durch einander/ genennet die Geliebten des Herzen/ die Geheyligten/ die Erloseten/ die Ausserwehlten. Et in scripto, cui titulus est: Rettung meiner allezeyt bestendigen bekentnuss, &c. pag. 5. haec leguntur: Zwar das sagt Er (Huberus) wol/ vnnd bekennet immerzu / dass Gott in Christo keine sonderung gemacht/ sondern einen in Ihm/ sowol als den andern erwehlet vnnd verordnet habe zum Leben: Unnd bekennet dabey/ das hernach / da die menschen das Leben in Christo annehmen solten/ etliche Gleubige werden/ vnnd ettliche vngleubige bleyben/ wie sie in Adams fall zugerichtet waren/ vnd da sie noch erst darzu alle krafft vnnd wirckung des todtes Christi/ zu jhrem leben/ von sich stossen.

II. Quia vero Huberus multa commiscet, & statum varie informat, ante omnia remouenda sunt τὰ μὴ ζητούμενα, ne Andabatarum more pugnetur. Probe igitur notandum est, quod hic non quaratur. 1. An Deus serio velit omnes homines saluos? id enim nos ipsi fatemur & credimus, iuxta dicta 1. Tim. 2. vers. 4. 2. Pet. 3. v. 9. 2. An Christus verè sit mortuus pro omnibus & singulis hominibus? Nam & hoc à nobis passim docetur & sincerè creditur.

3. An Deus omnes homines vocet ad pœnitentiam? Nam istud etiam vtrinque in confesso est.

4. An electio facta sit ab æterno? Hoc enim Hubero perquã libenter cõcedimus. Nam cùm fidem electionis decreto includimus, nõ hoc volumus, ac si actu præcedat illa electionẽ, quæ est malitiosa nostræ sententiæ deprauatio, sed fidem duntaxat consideramus, prout á Deo præuisa est. Proindè distinguimus inter vian præuisam, & actualem: hæc sequitur, illa includitur negotio electionis; non secus atque mors Christi in tempore demum accidit, quæ tamen æternum electionis decretum ingreditur. Mera igitur est calumnia, quam Huberus nostris doctoribus affingit, de fide Electionem antegressa.

5. Nùm propter fidem ab æterno præcognitam simus electi? Sicut enim nõ propter fidem, verum p fidem, seu ppter Christũ fide apprehensum, in tempore iustificamur & saluamur: sic ab æterno non propter fidem, sed propter Christũ fide apprehensum sumus electi. Proinde crassa iterum est calumnia quâ ab Hubero grauamur, ac si statuamus, Electionem fide nostrâ præuerti, aut præueniri, vnde etiam præter meritum Pelagianismi ab ipso insimulamur.

6. An numerus electorum absolutâ necessitate sit certus, ita, vt Deus in Christo paucos tantũ homines elegerit ad vitã, qui simpliciter nullâ incredulitate perire & suâ salute excidere possint. Hoc ipso enim Caluinisticũ decretum stabiliri non inuiti agnoscimus & propterea minimè defendimus.

7. An plures potuerint per verbum prædicatum conuerti, ac proinde ab æterno eligi? Affirmatè respondet Christus, adducens exemplum Tyriorum & Sidoniorum Matth. 11. v. 21.

8. Num causa particularitatis dependeat ab absoluto & ineuitabili quoda decreto Dei? Negamus ipsi, soliq; hominum incredulitati istam acceptam ferimus. 9. An decretum electionis sit absolutum, an vero ordinatu? pugnamus contra Caluinianos pro ordinato, eoque non mutilo, sed integro: Huberus autem vnam duntaxat ordinis partem admittit, nempe Christi meritum, quo putat absolui vniuersum electionis decretum. 10. An praedestinatio sit vniuersalis ratione credentium? Nos ipsi dicimus cu scriptura, Omnes in Christum perseueranter credentes esse electos: sed de hac vniuersalitate non loquitur Huberus. 11. An phrasis omnes esse electos, vocabulo electionis improprie pro generali Dei dilectione accepto, possit cõcedi? Si Huberus agnosceret quandam κατάχρησιν, dicam ipsi nemo scriberet. Na & hoc sensu nõnulli ex Orthodoxis dixerunt electione esse vniuersalem, intelligentes istud de vniuersali omnium hominu dilectione. Electu enim saepe dicimus eu qui charus est nobis: sicut pater quisquam omnes liberos suos vocat electos. Ihr seydt meine liebe ausserwehlte kinder/ vbi vox electionis non habet vim separandi, sed duntaxat notat rei alicujus gratiositatem, dilectione, & ad probatione Sed Huberus hanc κατάχρησιν agnoscere plane renuit, omnesq; homines electione pprie, imo proprijssime dicta electos esse statuit. Omne enim fidei aspectu remouet ex decreto electionis, qua in parte consentit cu Caluinianis a quibus tame vel maxime discedere vult in hac controuersia. Quia vero non omnes actu saluatur, ideo distinguit inter applicationem & constitutionem electionis, inter ipsum decretum, & inter euentum. Ita enim scribit in confutata breui pag. 30. Quod vero obijcitur de actu requisitis, referendum est ad effectum electionis, pro quo consequendo omnia isthaec requiruntur. Aliud autem est de actu Dei, aliud

& eiuidem effectu loqui. Actus electionis ad sui perfectionem præter misericordiam Dei, & Sacrosanctum meritum Christi nihil requirit. In responso ad censur. Tubing. in actis Tubing. pag. 65. pertinet fides ad applicationem electionis, non aute ad cõstitutionem electionis in Deo in sese consideratæ. Quæ distinctio coincidit cū illa, qua Huberus distinguit inter electionẽ generalem & specialem. Theologi verò sinceriores media insistũt via & nec omnes indiscriminatim homines, vt Huberus, nec absolutè paucos, vt Caluinus, sed ex omnibus aliquos, eos nẽpe, quos perseueranter in Christum credituros præuidit Deus, electos & prædestinatos esse statuunt. Totũ enim electionis σύσημα vniuersali Dei voluntate & Christi merito terminari neqt, sed addẽdus. est fidei pseuerãtis adspectus, quę cū nõ in omnib. reperiatur, fit, vt indè non ex absoluto aliquo decreto, sed ob incredulitatem hominũ electio euadat particularis, quam tamen limitatè esse vniuersalem, (si nimirum omnes credentes intelligas) non imus inficias.

Proinde ex dictis hactenus iste status emergit: Verum Deus ab æterno omnes indiscretè homines sine vllo respectu fidei ad salutem æternã elegerit, ac præordinârit? Affirmat Huberus: Nos cū omnib. orthodoxis negamus, quã ille sententiam licet multis calumnijs proscindat, vocando, Eine verzweiffelte stümpelwal/ Eine Götstlösterũg/Ein particulierisch/vnd Caluinisch Rauppenest/eine verzweiffelte lehr &c. eã tamẽ in scripturis & analogia fidei fundatissimã esse, nũc porro ad oculũ demõstrabim?, & postea breuẽ præcipuarũ obiectionũ λύσιν subiungemus.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: I. Arguments from the Scriptures

I. Arguments from the Scriptures.

III. 1. From Matt. 20, v. 16 & ch. 22, v. 14. Many are called, few are chosen. By this brief aphorism, as if by some lightning bolt, that indiscriminate Huberian universality is relegated all the way to Orcus. For if only few are chosen, certainly all will not be chosen. Otherwise, calling and election would extend equally widely, so that as many as are called, so many would be chosen. The Savior, however, makes a clear distinction regarding the number between the called and the chosen, while He says that many indeed are called, but few are chosen. What does Huber say to these things? He brings forward two little responses, one of which he seeks from grammar, while he distinguishes between ἐκλελεγμένους and ἐκ few are ἐκλεκτοὺς, but all are ἐκλελεγμένους: which little distinction some declare with this analogy: in a school, all boys are 'learned' participially, because all are taught by the teacher; but they are not all 'learned' nominally, because they do not all grasp, nor fix in their memory those things which are said by the teacher: The other he takes from the distinction of Election into general and special, that the discourse here is about special, and not general election.

Response to 1. That distinction between ἐκλεκτοὺς and ἐκλελεγμένους is null. For it is destitute of all scriptural authority. For nowhere is it read that all men indiscriminately are ἐκλελεγμένοι, chosen participially, but few are ἐκλεκτοι or chosen nominally, but Scripture uses these words without any distinction: so that those who are ἐκλελεγμένοι, they are also ἐκλεκτοὶ and vice versa. Especially, however, let that of the Savior in Matthew 13:30 be referred to here, on account of ἐκλεκτοὺς οὓς ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεὸς &c., where indeed those whom God chose are called chosen, so that no distinction is left between ἐκλεκτοὺς and ἐκλελεγμένους, which the very sound of the words also argues. For the participle ἐκλελεγμένος is equally composed with a preposition having the force of separating or selecting, as is the verbal noun ἐκλεκτὸς. Therefore, those who are chosen by God, they are chosen: and he who is not chosen, him God did not choose, and therefore to say that God chose all, but that all are not chosen, is a hard saying. To 2. It is a begging of the question. For this is what is asked: Is there, besides that particular election which Scripture mentions, some other universal one? everywhere we read that many are called, few are chosen, and that God has not chosen all men absolutely, etc. But nowhere is it said that all are chosen without any distinction. Why, therefore, should we not believe Scripture more than the bare Huberist assertion?

IV. 2. From 1 Cor. 1, v. 26, 27, 28. 'Consider your calling, brethren, that not many wise according to the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, but God chose the foolish things of the world, that He might confound the wise, and God chose the weak things of the world, that He might confound the strong, and the base things of the world and the despised, God chose,' etc. We append this passage to the former so that that rancid little distinction between ἐκλεκτῶν and ἐκλελεγμένων may be refuted all the more strongly. For Huberus says, according to the saying of Mark ch. 13, that all the chosen are indeed ἐκλελεγμένους, but not the reverse, and therefore these two words (ἐκλεκτοὶ and ἐκλελεγμένοι) are indeed ἀναστρέφοντα, but not ἀντίστροφα. However, the present text most fully refutes this exception: for it is said there that not all are ἐκλελεγμένοι, or that God has not chosen all, but primarily the weak, the foolish, and the ignoble. Although there appears to be an ellipsis in the former member, yet because Paul institutes a removal, certainly an adversative cannot have a place unless you refer the word 'chose' simultaneously to the preceding things. Whence Luther supplied it thus: 'Not many wise' (i.e., are called), 'but what is foolish before the world, that God has chosen.' By 'calling,' however, Luther understands not a general one common to all, but one specifically spoken of, which simultaneously includes the faith and obedience of the called, in which special sense κλητοὶ and ἔκλεκτοὶ are convertible. Nor does the nominative case prejudice these things at all, because, clearly, it is not said: 'God did not choose many wise men.' For this permutation of cases is frequent, as in John 17, v. 2: 'You have given him power over all flesh, that all that you have given him, he may give them eternal life': where there is a double permutation.

Furthermore, it is evident from what has been said how foolish is that φρονήσις of Huber, who says that in that passage it is not a matter of the election of men, but the election of the Gospel, through which God converts men. For since in the former member men are understood, they must certainly be understood in the latter, if the adversative is to remain intact. For persons are compared with persons, namely that God chose not many wise and noble, but those things which are foolish before the world, that is, the ignoble, and before the world, the unwise. For what other coherence would there be? God chose not many nobles, but his word: here certainly there would be no antithesis, and thus there would be no need for an adversative. Since, therefore, the Apostle makes such a distinction between men, that not all, but few are elected by God, it is evident from this that not all are ἐκπεποιημένοι, or participially elected.

V. 3. From James 2. v. 5. Did not God choose the poor in this world, rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom, which God promised to those who love him? The sense of this saying is not that God chose only the poor, and none of the rich, but it ought to be understood comparatively, that most of the elect are poor, in which sense it is said 1 Cor. 1. verse 27: God chose not many nobles, but the things that are foolish. Therefore, the denomination is made here also from the more significant part. Thus, by the rich in faith, the ὀλιγόπιστοι are not excluded: for even those who are endowed with little faith are rich, insofar as they apprehend Christ, in whom lies hidden every treasure. However, with this sentence of James standing, the universality of election cannot stand. For if God chose the poor primarily, certainly not all could be called elect indiscriminately, which we think is clear to anyone.

VI. 4. From John 15. v. 19. I chose you out of the world. Whence it follows that not the whole world, or all men living in the world, are elected by God. But Christ is not speaking only of election to the Apostleship; because thus Judas would also be elected, whence it would follow that the world also hated Judas, because Judas was not of this world. For thus likewise are those selected from the world described. And because Christ, by saying, the world hates you, opposes the Apostles to the world, and the world to the Apostles, certainly, if this passage were to be understood concerning election to the Apostleship, it would follow that all men were enemies to Christ and to Christ's Apostles, which is utterly absurd. But because the Apostles were elected to life; not insofar as they were Apostles, but insofar as they were believers, it is evident from this that the remaining believers are not excluded, but included, as is manifest from John 17, v. 20. I do not pray for these only, but also for those who are to believe in me through their word.

VII. 5. From John 17, v. 6. I have manifested your name to the men whom you gave me out of the world. A manifest segregation of the worldly and the given is made here, from which it follows that not all were given. But by those given to Christ we understand all the elect, not only the Apostles, as such; for those for whom he prays here, they are those given to Christ by the Father: And yet he prays for all those who were to believe, v. 20. Therefore all who will perseveringly believe are said to be given to Christ. Furthermore, if the Apostles as such were noted, Judas also would have to be numbered among them. But how can he be, when it is said in John 6, v. 39, This is the will of the Father, that of all that he has given me, I should lose nothing.

Huberus objects to v. 12, chap. 17. Those whom you gave me, I have kept, and none of them perished except the son of perdition. Judas was therefore in the number of the given, otherwise it could not be said that he perished from among them.

Resp. Because in John 15, v. 19, those given to Christ are described in such a way that they are not of the world, that the world hates them, and v. 39, that they do not perish, it will certainly be absurd to number Judas (who was certainly so much of this world that Christ called him a Devil, John 6, v. 70, who also perished eternally) among those given. Therefore, a convenient explanation of this v. 12 must be sought, lest here something against let us speak of the analogy of faith. Schaffmann explains it regarding human judgment, and thinks that Christ is speaking according to the opinion of men, because most people thought that Judas was of the number of those given. But the interpretation of Hunnius seems more suitable, in my copy p. 341, when he says that the particle NISI [unless/except] is to be explained by the adversative SED [but]. He brings forward examples from 2 Kings 5:17: 'Your servant will not offer burnt offering and sacrifice to other gods, but [nisi] to the Lord alone'; Luke 4:27: 'There were many lepers in Israel, and none of them was cleansed, but [nisi] Naaman the Syrian'; John 5:19: 'The Son can do nothing of himself, but [nisi] what he sees the Father doing'; Galatians 2:16: 'We know that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but [nisi] through faith in Jesus Christ.' In all these sayings, the little word Nisi is taken adversatively for πλὴν [but/except]. I will not serve other gods, but the Lord: No leper in Israel under Elisha was cleansed, but Naaman, etc. In a similar way we can interpret the saying of John in this sense: Not one of the Apostles whom the Father gave to his Son perished, but Judas perished. But as concerns verse 2, 'you have given him power over all flesh,' the theologians understand it as the universal redemption of the human race; and therefore a distinction must be made between the general and the special mode of giving. For the sense is that Christ was sent as redeemer to the whole world, but that only those whom the Father specially gave to him are saved. These, however, who are given, are only the believers, v. 14. For 'All that the Father gives me will come to me,' says John 6:37. But not all come; therefore not all were given. We do not say that coming to Christ is the same thing as being given to the Son, or being elected: because not all who have once come persevere, but we say that the elect are those given, and that it is a requirement of those given that they come. Therefore all who are given come, but not all who come are given. See Hunnius p. 344 ff., who quite clearly hints at a threefold mode of giving: 1. General, by which all are given for redemption, John 17:2. 2. Special, by which the elect are given for salvation, v. 6, 23. 3. Most special, by which the Apostles were given to serve:

IIX. 6. From Acts 13, v. 48. 'As many as were ordained to eternal life believed.' But many were not ordained to life, that is, elected; that this verse speaks of the election of the faithful, besides the fact that the Formula of Concord explains it thus, the very sound of the words proves, ὅσοι τεταγμένοι ἦσαν πρὸς ζωὴν αἰώνιον. From which words it is clear that the discourse is made concerning the ordination or destination to everlasting life, which was made from eternity before the foundations of the world, and it can denote nothing else than the very election of the faithful:

IX. 7. From Rom. 8, v. 30. 'Whom he predestinated, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.' In this truly golden chain the links cohere in such a way that the prior members are always determined by the posterior ones, whence we gather thus: Not all are glorified, justified, called. Therefore, not all are predestinated by God. For the Apostle describes these predestinated, called, and glorified ones in such a way that the words cannot be understood concerning a universal calling and justification of men. For he says that through faith they are in Christ, that they are called κατὰ πρόθεσιν, etc.

But the fact that the Apostle does not speak in the future, 'he will justify, he will glorify,' but in the past, 'he justified, he glorified,' is no obstacle, since on account of the certainty of the matter something is often said to be done which is still future; to which point refers that statement of Fulgentius from book 1 to Monimus, p. 23: 'Paul saying that whom God justified, them he also glorified, does not assign both to the present life, but by that faith by which what is future is confirmed as if it were done, by which faith the Prophet says of God: Who made the things that are to be.' And page 24: 'Whatever he promised, we call already done, because we ought not to doubt concerning things to be done.'

X. 8. From Rom. 11, verse 7. 'Israel hath not obtained that which he seeketh for; but the election hath obtained it.' Whence flows such an argument: Whoever are elected to salvation, they also obtain salvation and eternal life: And yet not all obtain it. Therefore, not all are elect. Other sayings of Scripture can be added for the confirmation of the major premise, as Matt. 24, v. 24. False prophets will arise and will give great signs and wonders, so that, if it were possible, even the elect might be led into error. Rom. 8, v. 30. those predestined are glorified. John 10, v. 28. No one shall snatch my sheep from my hand. 1 John 2, v. 19. If they had been of us (the elect), they would surely have remained with us. And Dan. 12, v. 1, it is said that all inscribed in the book of life are saved: But all the elect are inscribed. Thus Apocal. 3, verse 5, God promises that He will not delete those inscribed from the βιβλίῳ ζωῆς, but this argument has been treated sufficiently at length in the preceding disputation.

XI. 9. From 2 Tim. 2, v. 19, 20. The firm foundation of God stands, having this seal, The Lord knows who are His. Whence we conclude thus: Those elected by God are υἱοὶ, for they are children of God who are led by the Spirit of God, Rom. 8, v. 14; they are Christ's who crucify their flesh with its vices and concupiscences, Gal. 5, v. 24, which is a property of believers alone. From which it follows that not all are elect.

A passage is objected from John 1, v. 11. His own did not receive Him. Resp. The Jews are said to have been Christ's, not by reason of grace and spiritual inheritance, but by reason of carnal kinship, as is evident from v. 13.

XII. We do not wish to heap up more sayings of Scripture, since these are sufficient, and are found explained more fully in the treatise of Dr. Hunnius on predestination, together with other testimonies. By way of a colophon, let this be noted, that certain classes of sayings can be established and opposed to the Huberians. For the sayings of Scripture are divided into peculiar classes. I. Some openly deny that all are elect, Matt. 20, v. 16, John 13, verse 18, 1 Cor. 1, verse 26. II. Some teach that only believers are elect, as John 6, v. 40, Acts 13, verse 48, Eph. 1, v. 3, seqq., 2 Thess. 2, v. 13.

III. Some passages oppose the elect to the world or to unbelievers, as John 15:19, 17:6. IV. Some passages assert that all the elect are saved, Rom. 8:30, 11:7, John 10:28. V. Some passages say that many were never written in the book of life, that is, were never elect, as Rev. 17:8, 20:15. VI. Some passages attribute such titles to the elect that they can by no means be affirmed of all, as Isa. 4:3, Eph. 1:1-2, Col. 3:12, etc.

Latin:

I. Argumenta ex Scripturis.

III. 1. Ex Matth. 20. v. 16. & c. 22. v, 14. Multi vocati, pauci electi. Hoc breui aphorismo, quasi fulmine quodam ad orcum vsque relegatur indiscreta illa vniuersalitas Huberiana. Si enim pauci tantum electi, vtique omnes non erunt electi. Aliàs vocatio & electio æquè latè paterent, ita, vt quot sunt vocati tot essent electi. Saluator autem euidens facit discrimen quoad numerum inter vocatos & electos, dum multos quidem vocatos, paucos vero dicit esse electos, Quid ad hec Huberus ? Duas affert responsiunculas, quarum vnam petit ex Grammatica, dum distinguit inter ἐκλελεγμένους & ἐκλεκτοὺς: se fateri paucos esse ἐκλεκτοὺς, omnes autem ἐκλελεγμένους: quam distincti-\unculam nonnulli hoc simili declarant: in ludo literario omnes pueri sunt docti participialiter, quia omnes docentur a præceptore; sed non sunt omnes docti nominaliter, quia non apprehēdunt omnes, nec memoria infigunt illa, quæ a præceptore dicuntur: Alteram desumit a distinctione Electionis in generalem & specialem, esse hic de speciali, non autem generali electione sermonem.

Resp. ad 1. Distinctio illa inter ἐκλεκτοὺς & ἐκλελεγμένους nulla est. Nam destituitur omni scripturaru authoritate. Nullibi enim legitur quod omnes indiscrete homines sint ἐκλελεγμένοι electi participialiter, pauci autem ἐκλεκτοι vel electi nominaliter, sed sine vllo discrimine his vocibus vtitur scriptura: ita, vt qui sint ἐκλελεγμένοι, illi sint etiam ἐκλεκτοὶ & contra. Præsertim vero huc referatur illud saluatoris Matth. 13. v. 30. propter ἐκλεκτοὺς οὓς ἐξελέξατο ὁ θεὸς &c. vbi sane illi, quos Deus elegit, dicuntur electi, ita vt nullum reliquatur discrimen inter ἐκλεκτοὺς καὶ ἐκλελεγμένους, quod ipsum etiam sonus vocabulorum arguit. Nam participium ἐκλελεγμένος æque componitur cum præpositione habente vim segregandi aut seligendi, atque nomen verbale ἐκλεκτὸς. Qui igitur a Deo eliguntur, illi sunt electi: & qui non est electus, illum Deus non elegit, ideoque dicere Deum omnes elegisse, non autem omnes esse electos σκληρόξυλον est. Ad 2. est petitio principij. Hoc enim quæritur, An sit preter illam electione particularem, cuius scriptura meminit, alia aliqua vniuersalis? passim quidem legimˣ, multos esse vocatos, paucos electos, Deum non elegisse omnes omninò homines &c. Nullibi vero dicitur, quod omnes sint electi sine vlla discretione. Cur non igitur plus crederemus Scripturæ, quam nudæ assertioni Huberianæ.

IV. 2. Ex 1. Cor. 1. v. 26. 27. 28. Videte vocationem vestram fratres, quia non multi sapientes secundum carnem, non multi potentes, non multi nobiles, sed quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus, vt confundat sapientes, & infirma mundi elegit Deus, vt confundat fortia, & ignobilia mundi & contemptibilia elegit Dᴇᴠꝰ &c. Hunc locum ideò subijcimus priori, vt eò fortiùs confutetur rancida illa ἐκλεκτῶν καὶ ἐκλελεγμένων distinctiuncula. Dicit enim Huberus iuxta dictum Marci cap. 13. omnes electos esse quidem ἐκλελεγμένους, sed non contra, ideoque ista duo vocabula (ἐκλεκτοὶ καὶ ἐκλελεγμένοι) esse quidem ἀναστρέφοντα, sed non ἀντίστροφα. Hanc autem exceptionem præsens textus plenissimè refutat: ibi .n. dicitur quod non omnes sint ἐκλελεγμένοι, seu quod Deus non omnes elegerit, sed in primis infirmos, stultos, ignobiles. Quamuis verò in priori membro videatur esse elipsis, attamen quia Paulus instituit remotionem, certè aduersatiua locum habere nequit, nisi verbum elegit simul ad præcedentia referas. Vnde Lutherus ita suppleuit; Nit viel weise sc. sind beruffen/ sondern was thöricht ist vor der welt / das hatt Gott erwehlet. Per vocationem verò Lutherus intelligit nō generalem omnibusq; communem, sed specialiter dictam, quæ simul vocatorū fidem & obedientiā includit, quo sensu speciali κλητοὶ καὶ ἔκλεκτοὶ conuertuntur. Neque verò his quicquam præiudicat casus nominatiuus, quia videlicet non dicitur: Non multos sapientes elegit Deus. Frequens n. est hæc permutatio casuum, vt Ioh. 17. v. 2. Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis, vt omne, quod dedisti ei, det eis vitam æternam: vbi gemina est permutatio.

Porrò autem ex dictis elucet, quàm stulta sit illa Huberi φρονήσις dicentis, in isto loco non agi de electione hominum, sed electione Euangelij, per quod Deus homines conuertit. Etenim cum in priori membro homines intelligantur, vtique ijs dem intelligentur in posteriori, si aduersatiua debeat manere salua. Conferuntur enim personæ cum personis, nempè quod Deus elegerit non multos sapientes & nobiles, sed quæ stulta sunt coram mundo, id est, ignobiles, & coram mundo, insipientes. Quæ enim alias foret cohæsio? Non multos nobiles, sed verbum suum elegit Deus: Hic sanè nulla foret antithesis, àdeoque aduersatiuâ opus non esset. Quoniam igitur Apostolus tale facit discrimen inter homines, quòd non omnes, sed pauci à Deo sint electi, patet hinc, quòd non omnes sint ἐκπεποιημένοι, vel participialiter electi.

V. 3. Ex Iacobi 2. v 5. Nonnè Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo, diuites in fide, & hæredes regni, quod repromisit Deus diligentibus se? Cuius dicti sensus non est iste, quod Deus solos pauperes, & nullum ex diuitibus elegerit, sed comparatè intelligi debet, quod plerique electorum sint pauperes, quo sensu dicitur. 1. Cor. 1. vers. 27. Non multos nobiles, sed quæ stulta sunt elegit Deus. A potiori ergò & hic fit denominatio. Sic per diuites in fide non excluduntur ὀλιγόπιστοι: Nam & ij qui pusilla fide sunt præditi, diuites sunt, quatenus apprehendunt Christum, in quo latet omnis thesaurus. Stante autem istâ Iacobi sententiâ, stare nequit vniuersalitas electionis. Nam si pauperes potissimum elegit Deus, vtique non indiscriminatim omnes dici potuerunt electi, id quod cuiuis arbitramur esse perspicuum.

VI. 4. Ex Ioh. 15. v. 19. Elegi vos de mundo. Vndè sequitur, non totum mundum, vel omnes homines in mūdo viuentes esse à Deo electos. Non autē de electione ad Apostolatū tantum Christus loquitur; quia sic & Iudas foret electus, vnde consequæreretur, quòd & mundus Iudam oderit, quod Iudas nõ fuerit de hoc mundo. Sic enim itidem describuntur isti è mundo selecti. Et quia Christus dicendo, vos odit mundus, Apostolos mũdo, mundumque Apostolis opponit, certè, si de electione ad Apostolatum intelligendus esset hic locus, sequeretur, omnes homines fuisse Christo Christíq; Apostolis, inimicos, quod oppidò absurdum. Quia verò Apostoli ad vitã electi sunt; non quatenus Apostoli, sed quatenus fideles, patet hinc, reliquos credentes nõ excludi, sed includi, vti manifestum ex Ioh. 17. v. 20. Non rogo pro his tantum, sed etiam pro iis, qui credituri sunt per verbum eorum in me.

VII. 5. Ex Ioh. 17. v. 6. Manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus, quos dedisti mihi de mundo. Fit hic manifesta segregatio mundanorum & datorum, vndè nõ omnes datos fuisse consequitur. Per datos au tem Christo intelligimus omnes electos, non solos Apostolos, quà tales; Pro quibus enim hîc orat, ij sunt Christo à patre dati: Atqui orat pro ijs omnibus qui erant credituri, v. 20. Ergo omnes perseuerãter credituri Christo dati dicũtur. Deinde, si notarentur Apostoli quâ tales, Iudas quoque ijs annumerandus esset. At quî potest, cum dicatur Ioh. 6. v. 39. Hæc est voluntas patris, vt omne, quod dedit mihi, non perdam.

Obiicit Huberus v. 12. cap. 17. Quos dedisti mihi, custodivi, & nemo ex ijs perijt nisi filius perditionis. Fuit ergo Iudas in numero datorum, aliàs non posset dici, quod ex ijs perierit.

Resp. Quia Ioh. 15. v. 19. ita describuntur Christo dati, quod non sint de mundo, quod mundus illos odio habeat, & v. 39. quòd non pereant, vtique absurdum erit, Iudam (qui certè adeò de hoc mundo fuit, vt Christus eum nominârit Diabolum Iohan. 6. v. 70. qui etiam in æternum perijt) istis datis annumerare. Commoda igitur huius v. 12. explicatio est quærenda, nè hic aliquid contra analogiam fidei dicamus. Schaffmannus exponit de iudicio humano, & putat Christum ex opinione hominū loqui, quia pleriq; opinabātur Iudam ex datorum numero esse. Sed conuenientior videtur interpretatio Hunnij, mihi pag. 341. cum ait, particulam NISI esse exponēdam per aduersatiuam SED. Profert exempla ex 2. Reg. 5. v. 17. Non faciet vltrà seruus tuus holocaustum, & victimam dijs alienis, nisi Domino soli, Luc. 4. v. 27. Multi erant leprosi in Israel, & nemo illorum mundatus est, nisi Naëman Syrus, Ioh. 5. v. 19. Nihil potest facere filius à semetipso, nisi quod viderit patrem facere. Gal. 2. v. 16. Scimus non iustificari hominem ex operibus legis, nisi per fidem Iesu Christi. In dictis his omnibus vocula Nisi sumitur aduersatiuè pro πλὴν pà. Non seruiam dijs, sed Domino: Nullus leprosus in Israel sub Elisæo mundatus est, sed Naëman &c. pari modo dictum Ioannis interpretari possumus hoc sensu: Non perijt quisquam ex Apostolis, quos filio suo dedit pater, sed Iudas perijt. Quod verò concernit versiculum 2. dedisti ei potestatē omnis carnis, intelligunt eū Theol. de vniuersali generis humani redemptione; ideoque distingui debet inter generalem & specialem dandi modum. Nam sensus est; Christum toti mundo redemptorem missum esse, saluari verò eos tantum, quos pater ipsi specialiter dedit. Hi verò dati, sunt soli credentes v. 14. Omne enim quod dat mihi pater, veniet ad me, inquit Iohan. 6. v. 37. Atqui non omnes veniunt; Ergò nec omnes dati sunt. Venire aut. ad Christum, non dicimus idem esse, quod dari filio, seu eligi: Quia non omnes perseuerant, qui semel venerunt, sed dicimus, datos esse electos, illorum vero datorum esse requisitum vt veniant. Omnes ergo dati veniunt, sed non omnes venientes dati sunt. Vide Hunnium p. 344. seqq. qui triplicem dandi modum haut obscurè innuit, 1. Generalem, quo dati sunt omnes ad redimendum, Ioh. 17. v. 2. 2. specialem, quo dati sunt electi ad saluandum v. 6. 23. 3. specialissimum, quodati sunt Apostoli ad inseruiendum:

IIX. 6. Ex Act. 13. v. 48. Crediderunt, quotquot ordinati erant ad vitam. Multi autem non fuerunt ad vitam ordinati, hoc est electi, istum v. locum de electione fidelium loqui, præterquam quòd Formula Cōcordiæ sic exponat, ipse sonus verborum euincit, ὅσοι τεταγμένοι ἦσαν πρὸς ζωὴν αἰώνιον. Ex quibus verbis patet, sermonem fieri de ordinatione vel destinatione ad vitam sempiternam, quæ ab æterno ante mundi fundamenta facta est, nec aliud denotare potest, quam ipsam fidelium electionem:

IX. 7. Ex Rom. 8. v. 30. Quos prædestinavit, hos & vocauit: & quos vocauit, hos & iustificauit: quos autem iustificauit, illos & glorificauit. In hac catena verè aureâ sic cohærent ansulæ, vt priora membra semper determinentur posterioribus, vndè ita colligimus. Non omnes glorificantur, iustificantur, vocantur. Ergo nec omnes à Deo prædestinantur; Ita enim describit Apostolus hos prædestinatos, vocatos & glorificatos, vt nequeant verba de vniuersali hominum vocatione, iustificatione intelligi. Nam dicit, quod per fidē sint in Christo, quod sint vocati κατὰ πρόθεσιν &c.

Quod autem Apostolus non loquitur in futuro, iustificabit, glorificabit, sed in præterito, iustificauit, glorificauit, nihil obstat, cum propter certitudinem rei sæpè aliquid dicatur factum, quod adhuc est futurum; quo spectat istud Fulgentij ex lib. 1. ad Mon. p. 23. Dicens Paulus, quia quos Deus iustificauit, illos & glorificauit, non vtrumque præsenti vitæ deputat, sed eâ fide, quod futurum est, velut factum firmat, quâ fide Propheta de Deo dicit: Qui fecit quæ futura sunt. Et pag. 24. Quæcunque promisit, iam facta dicimus, quia de faciendis dubitare non debemus

X. 8. Ex Rom. 11. vers. 7. Quod quærebat Israel, hoc non est consecutus, Electio autem consecuta est. Vnde fluit tale argumentum, Quicunque sunt electi ad salutem, illi etiam consequūtur salutem & vitam æternam : Atqui non omnes eam consequenturs Ergò nec omnes sunt electi. Addi possunt alia Scripturæ dicta pro confirmatione maioris, vt Matth. 24. v. 24. Surgent Pseudoprophetæ & dabunt signa & prodigia magna, ita vt, si fieri posset, in errorem etiam inducantur electi. Rom. 8. v. 30. prædestinati glorificantur. Ioh. 10. v. 28. Oues meas nemo rapiet de manu mea. 1. Ioh. 2. v. 19. Si fuissent ex nobis (electis) permansissent vtique nobiscum. Et Dan. 12. v. 1. dicitur quòd omnes inscripti in librum vitæ saluentur: Omnes autem electi sunt inscripti. Sic Apocal. 3. vers. 5. promittit Deus, se non deleturum esse inscriptos ex βιβλίῳ ζωῆς, sed de hoc argumento præcedenti disput. satis prolixè actum est.

XI. 9. Ex 2. Tim. 2 v. 19. 20. firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens sigillum hoc, Nouit Dominus qui sint sui. Vnde sic concludimus : Electi à Deo sunt υἱοὶ, illienim sunt filij Dei, qui spiritu Dei aguntur Rom. 8. v 14 illi sunt Christi qui carnem suam crucifigunt cum vitijs & concupiscentijs, Gal. 5. v. 24. id quod solis credentibus proprium est. Ex quo sequitur, non omnes esse electos.

Objicitur locus ex Iohan. 1, v. 11. Sui eum non receperunt. Resp. Iudæi dicuntur fuisse Christi, non ratione gratiæ & spiritualis hæreditatis, verùm ratione carnalis cognationis, vt patet ex v. 13.

XII. Plura Scripturæ dicta coaceruare nolumus, cum illa sufficiant, & in tractatu D. Hunnij de prædest. vnà cum alijs testimonijs fusius explicata reperiantur. Colophonis loco istud notetur, quòd certæ dictorum classes constitui, & Huberianis opponi possint. Nam dicta scripturæ in peculiares classes diuiduntur. I. Quædam apertè negant, omnes electos esse Matth. 20. v. 16. Ioh. 13. vers. 18. 1. Cor. 1 vers. 26. II. Quædam docent, tantum credentes electos esse, vt Iohan. 6. v. 40. Act. 13. vers. 48. Ephes. 1. v. 3. seqq. 2. Thess. 2. v. 13.

III. Quedam electos opponunt mundo vel incredulis, vt Iohan 15. v. 19. c. 17. v. 6. IV. Quædam afserunt Electos omnes saluari, Rom. 8. v. 30. 6. 11. v. 7. Iohan 10. v. 28. V. Quædam dicunt, multos libro vite nunquam inscriptos, h. e. nunquam electos fuisse, vt Apocal. 17. v. 8. c. 20 v. vlt. VI. Quædam electis tales titulos attribuunt, yt minimè de omnibus affirmari queant, vt, Esa. 4. v. 3. Ephes. 1. v. 1. 2. Col. 3. v. 12. &c.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: II. Arguments from the analogy of faith

II. Arguments from the analogy of faith.

XIII. 1. From the force of the word. The word election, when there is discourse about persons, always denotes separation, indeed in such a way that first some universality is implied, then the separation of some from it, which is called election. Now truly, if all men are said to be elected to life, that native meaning perishes. For how does separation have a place, if all are predestined? And how are men elected from the world, and some from among men, if all are included by the decree of ἐκλογῆς?

But they can object that 'elect' does not always denote the separation of one or some from many: as if a poor man is met, to whom alms are to be given, there is only one object, namely the alms, which if we do not give, we are said to have rejected; if we give, we are said to have chosen. Hence a twofold liberty of the will is established: one of contrariety, the other of contradiction: the former is when one is chosen out of many proposed; the latter is when, with a single proposal, that thing is either chosen or rejected. In a similar way it can be said that all fallen men, both collectively and individually, occurred to God in eternal foreknowledge, so that He might either reject them all on account of the fall, or receive them out of grace. And that God chose the latter, and thus loved the whole human race, and predestined them to life.

We answer briefly, however, that a distinction must be made between the election of a certain act and the election of persons. If the discussion is about an act, where one must choose either to will or not to will: there indeed only one object sometimes occurs, yet in such a way that in that election a certain separation intervenes; not indeed of objects, but of acts: For when something is ethically chosen, then the contrary, whether it be object or act, is rejected and excluded. But when the discussion is about the election of persons, there the separation of other persons is always involved at the same time. For while some are chosen, certainly the others are separated from the chosen. When someone is chosen as prince, consul, or pastor, by this very fact the others, from whom he is chosen, are deservedly considered as not chosen. Because, therefore, in this article the discussion is not about the election of an act in divine deliberation, but about the election of persons, and that very ἐκλογὴ is said to have been made out of the world, both everyone understands that that word has the force of separating; so much so that a universal election is nothing other than ἀσύστατον. For if the whole world and all men are chosen, what election is that which was made out of the world?

XIV. 2. From the inscription in the book of life. Whoever are chosen are inscribed in the book of life. But indeed not all are inscribed. Therefore, not all are chosen. The major premise cannot be denied, if one wishes to follow the Formula of Concord, which holds those phrases as synonyms. The minor is proven: Because Scripture proclaims as a singular benefit that the names of some are written in heaven, Luke 10:20, in the book of Daniel 12:1, in the book of life, Philippians 4:3, in the book of life of the Lamb, Revelation 21:last verse. Whence also all those are said to be perishing whose names have not been inscribed in the book of life, Revelation 13:8, ch. 17:8, ch. 20:last verse. I do not add the exceptions of Huber, since they are clearly futile, yet you can see them in Mr. Dr. Hunnius, page 394 and following, Frankfurt edition, year 1603, in octavo.

XV. 3. From the names by which the chosen are described. Vo cates are called πιστοὶ καὶ ἅγιοι [faithful and holy], to whom God has blessed with every blessing in the spirituals, Eph. 1. v. 1. & 3. holy & beloved, Coloss. 3. v. 12. firstfruits to God & the lamb; Apoc. 14. v. 4. bought from the earth from among men, verse 3. written in the book of life: Dan. 12. v. 1. Apoc. 17. v. 8 μέλλοντες πιστέ. [those who are to believe] in Christ, 1. Tim. 1. verse 16. a holy seed in Sion; the remnant in Jerusalem Eph. 4. v. 3.
