The remnant according to the election of grace Rom. 11. verse 5. &c. All these things oppose that indiscriminate & universal election, since they can be attributed not to all, but only to believers.

XVI. 4. From the antithesis, which is instituted between the elect & the non-elect. For Scripture makes a distinction between these, whence it follows that not all are elected indifferently: otherwise the distinction would be superfluous. It is truly proved from Matth. 24. v. 24. where a distinction is made between seducers, & the elect, who do not allow themselves to be seduced. Iohan. 10. v. 26. a distinction is made between the sheep of Christ; & the reprobate. Rom. 9. v. 22. 23. between vessels of wrath & of mercy Rom. 11. v. 7. between the elect and the blinded. 2. Thess. 2. v. 12, 13. between the elect & those who are perishing. 2. Tim. 2. v. 17, & 19. between the reprobate Hymenaeus & Philetus, & between those whom the Lord knows, 1. Pet. 2. v. 8. & 9. between the royal priesthood, the holy nation, & between those who stumble at the cornerstone. Thus the Apocalypse very often distinguishes between the sealed & the unsealed, the inscribed & the uninscribed.

XVII. 5. From reprobation. If many are reprobate, not all will be elect from eternity. But indeed many are reprobate, which, besides the testimonies of scripture Rom. 1. verse 28. 2. Tim. 3. verse 8. Tit. 1. verse 16. the very word of election itself argues. For if only certain ones are elected, it is necessary that the others be reprobate. And we ask here, Has not God decreed from eternity concerning the end of man, who are to be saved, and who are truly to be damned? If Huberus denies this, he will fashion God as idle, who has decreed nothing certain concerning the salvation or damnation of men. But if he affirms it, he will soon fall from the universal universality. For because God never decreed from eternity to actually save the impenitent in time, he certainly did not choose them from eternity, but reprobated them, since the decree of election and salvation did not differ either in causes or in objects. This argument concludes all the more strongly if the execution is attended to, according to which that which was decreed to be done from eternity comes to pass in time. Therefore, just as not all are saved, but many are damned, so God from eternity made a decree concerning those to be saved, not all, but only believers, and consequently he did not choose all, but only believers, with the others reprobated on account of foreseen impenitence. For such acts as God executes in time, such he decreed to execute, and therefore Huberus is forced to absurdly invent either an execution without a decree, or one alien to the decree, or contradictory decrees.

XVIII. 6. From Christ as the foundation. Election was made in Christ, Eph. 1:4; but we are not in him except through faith, since by it we are grafted into Christ as the vine and the true olive tree, John 15:4-5, Rom. 11:24, and are made partakers of him, Heb. 3:14, and remain founded in him through the same, Col. 1:23. For whoever are elected, they are elected not only in Christ as the author by reason of righteousness obtained, but also as the perfecter by reason of righteousness imputed. Since, therefore, election was made through faith, and indeed few believe, it follows that few are also elected.

XIX. 7. From special foreknowledge. God knew all the elect, 2 Tim. 2:19, but he never knew the unbelievers, Matt. 7:23. Therefore, the unbelievers were never elected. For the confirmation of the major premise, we add the sayings treating of divine προγνώσει (foreknowledge), according to which we are elected, as Rom. 8:30: Whom he foreknew, he also predestined; ch. 11:2: God has not rejected his people, ὃν προέγνω (whom he foreknew); 1 Pet. 1:2: Elect according to the πρόγνωσιν (foreknowledge) of God the Father. From these it becomes clear that all the elect were from eternity foreknown and specially known to God. Concerning the impenitent, it is said that they were never known. Who, therefore, are the elect, and indeed elected by a most proper election made according to πρόγνωσιν?

XX. 8. A Theological rule, which has been sung in the schools and always used: It is as follows: The elect are not to be sought outside the company of the called: The foundation of the rule is taken from the saying of Christ: Many are called, few are chosen. If, therefore, anyone is excluded from the number of the called, much more will he be excluded from the number of the elect. But Huberus clearly inverts the matter, and utterly destroys that rule, while he maintains that the most properly elect, and indeed none but the elect, are to be found not least outside the Church in Turkey and Tartary: whether this be absurd and scandalous, and provide an occasion for various calumnies, let all who think rightly judge.

XXI. To these arguments we finally add that the Huberine dogma is entirely unheard of, and is destitute of the testimonies of all antiquity: for the orthodox fathers clearly assert that election was made in Christ through faith, and therefore that it embraces none but believers and that they obtain salvation, all of which has been demonstrated in the preceding. In abundance we add these testimonies: Aug. Epist. 39 to Paulina: They are not in the just calling, who, even if they walk for a little while in the faith which works through love, do not persevere unto the end: Ambros. lib. 2 de vocat. gent. c. ult.: Just as no one of the infidels is numbered in this lot (he speaks of the elect), so no one of the pious is separated from this lot. Fulgent. lib. 1 Mon.: God has predestined to the kingdom those whom He foreknew would arrive to Him by the aid of preventing mercy, and would remain by the aid of subsequent mercy in Him.

XXII. The Book of Concord clearly asserts this Orthodox doctrine drawn from the Scriptures and the fathers, so that Huberus may boast ever so much of its consent. For the words are too clear to be eluded by that little distinction between the act and the effect: Thus it is read in the epitome, page 618, thesis 4: predestination or the eternal election of God, he says, pertains only to the good and beloved children of God.

& this is the cause of their salvation, Th 6. The Word of God leads us to Christ, he is that book of life, in which all are inscribed & elected, who attain eternal salvation. Pag. 619. th. 12. In Christ, the eternal election of God the Father is to be sought. He in his eternal decree, who wills to save no one except those who acknowledge his son Jesus Christ and truly believe in him. The same is repeated in the declaration pag 798.799. The eternal election or predestination of God to salvation does not pertain at the same time to the good and the bad, but only to the sons of God, who are elected and ordained to attain eternal life. pag. 808. It must by no means be thought that those are also to be held in the number of the elect who despise, repel, execrate, etc., the word of God, which passage is so clear that we may not undeservedly say that he who does not see it is blind in the midst of light.

Latin:

II. Argumenta ex analogia fidei.

XIII. 1. A vi vocabuli. Vox electionis, cùm de personis sermo est, separationem semper denotat, ita quidem, vt primum innuatur aliqua vniuersitas, deindè quorundam ex illa separatio, quæ vocatur electio. Iam vero, si omnes homines dicantur ad vitam electi, perit natiua illa significatio. Quî enim separatio locum habet, si omnes sunt prædestinati? Et quomodo ex mundo homines, ex hominibus aliqui sunt electi, si omnes decreto ἐκλογῆς sunt inclusi?

Objicere autem possunt, quod electi non semper notet vnius vel aliquorū è pluribus separationem: vt si pauper fiat obviam, cui danda est eleemosina, vnicum habetur obiectum, nempè eleemosina, quam si non damus, repudiasse; si damus, elegisse dicimur. Hinc duplex voluntatis libertas statuitur: Vna contrarietatis: Altera contradictionis: illa est, quando ex multis propositis vnum eligitur: hæc est, cum vnico proposito istud vel eligitur vel repudiatur, Pari modo dici potest, homines lapsos vniuersos & singulos Deo in præuisione æterna velut occurrisse, vt illos omnes vel reijceret ob lapsum, vel reciperet ex gratia. Deum verò elegisse posterius, adeoóque totum genus humanum dilexisse, ad vitam prædestinasse.

Respondemus autem breuiter, quod distinguendum sit inter electionem certi actus, & inter electionem personarum. Si de actu sit sermo, vbi eligi debet aut velle, aut nolle:ibi quidem vnum duntaxat obiectum aliquando occurrit, sic tamen, vt in illa electione quaedam separatio interueniat; non quidem obiectorum, sed actuum: Quando enim aliquid Ethice eligitur, tum contrarium, siue obiectu siue actus sit, reijcitur & secluditur. Cum vero de personarum electione sermo est, ibi simul aliarum personarum separatio semper inuoluitur. Dum enim aliqui eliguntur, vtique caeteri ab electis separantur. Cum quis princeps, consul, pastor eligitur, hoc ipso alij, ex quibus eligitur, pro non electis merito censentur. Quia ergo in hoc articulo non de electione actus in deliberatione diuina, sed de electione personarum sermo est, & illa ipsa ἐκλογὴ ex mundo facta esse dicitur, vtrq; separandi vim habere voce illam quiuis intelligit; adeo vt vniuersalis electio nil sit aliud, quam ἀσύστατον. Si enim totus mundus & omnes homines electi sunt, quj ex mundo facta est electio?

XIV. 2. Ab inscriptione in librum vitae. Quicunque sunt electi, lib. vitae sunt inscripti. At vero non omnes sunt inscripti. Ergo nec omnes electi. Maior negari nequit, si quis Formulae Concordiae sequi velit, quae phrases illas pro Synonymis habet, Minor probatur: Quia scriptura tanquam singulare beneficium praedicat, quod aliquorum nomina scripta sunt in coelis, Luc. 10. v. 20. in libro Dan. 12. v. 1. in libro vitae, Philip. 4. v. 3. in libro vitae agni, Apoc. 21. v. vlt. Vnde & perituri dicuntur omnes ij, quorum nomina non fuerint libro vitae adscripta, Apoc. 13. v. 8. c. 17. v. 8. c. 20. v. vlt. Exceptiones Huberi non addo, cum plane futiles sint, eas tamen videre poteris apud Dn. D. Hunnium pag. 394. & seqq. edit. Francof. Anno 1603. in octauo.

XV. 3. A nominibus, quibus electi describuntur. Vocantur πιστοὶ καὶ ἅγιοι, quibus Deus benedixit omni benedictione in spiritualibus, Eph. 1. v. 1. & 3. sancti & dilecti, Coloss. 3. v. 12. primitiae Deo & agno; Apoc. 14. v. 4. emti de terra ex hominibus, vers. 3. scripti in libro vitae: Dan. 12. v. 1. Apoc. 17. v. 8 μέλλοντες πιστέ. in Christum, 1. Tim. 1. vers. 16. semen sanctum in Sion; residui in Ierusalem Eph. 4. v. 3. Reliquiae secundum electionem gratiae Rom. 11. vers. 5. &c. Haec omnia electionem istam indiscretam & vniuersalem oppugnant, cum non vniuersis, sed tantum credentibus queant attribui.

XVI. 4. Ab antithesi, quae instituitur inter electos & non electos. Nam inter hos Scriptura discrimen facit, vnde sequitur, non omnes indifferenter electos esse: alias discretio superuacanea foret. Probatur vero ex Matth. 24. v. 24. vbi distinguitur inter seductores, & electos, qui seduci sese non patiuntur. Iohan. 10. v. 26. distinguitur inter oues Christi; & reprobos. Rom. 9. v. 22. 23. inter vasa irae & misericordiae Rom. 11. v. 7. inter electos exaecatos. 2. Thess. 2. v. 12, 13. inter electos & pereuntes. 2. Tim. 2. v. 17, & 19. inter reprobos Hymenaeum & Philetum, & inter eos, quos nouit Dominus, 1. Pet. 2. v. 8. & 9. inter regale sacerdotium, gentem sanctam, & inter eos qui impingunt in lapide angularem. Sic Apocalypsis saepissime distinguit inter signatos & non signatos, inscriptos & non inscriptos.

XVII. 5. A reprobatione. Si multi sunt reprobati, ab aeterno non omnes erunt electi. At vero multi sunt reprobati, quod praeter scripturae testimonia Rom. 1. vers. 28. 2. Tim. 3. vers. 8. Tit. 1. vers. 16. arguit vel ipsa vox electionis. Si enim quidam duntaxat sunt electi, oportet vtique caeteros esse reprobatos. Et quaerimus hic, Annon Deus ab aeterno decreverit severis de fine hominis, quinam saluandi sint, qui vero damnandi? Si neget Huberus, Deum effinget otiosum, qui nihil certi de salute vel damnatione hominum decreverit. Sin affirmet, mox cadet electionis vniuersalitas. Quia enim Deus impoenitentes actu saluare in tempore, nunquam decreuit ab æterno: vtique eosdem nec elegit ab æterno, sed reprobauit, cum decretum electionis & saluationis non different vel causis, vel obiectis. Quod argumentum eò fortius concludit, si executio attendatur, secundum quam id sit in tempore, quod fieri ab æterno decretum fuit. Sicut ergò non omnes saluantur; sed multi damnantur; Sic Deus ab æterno decretum fecit de saluandis non omnibus, sed tantum credentibus, & per consequens non elegit omnes, sed duntaxat credentes cæteris ob præuisam impœnitentiam reprobatis. Quales enim actus Deus in tempore exequitur, tales exequi decreuit, ideoque Huberus vel executionem sine decreto, vel alienam à decreto, vel contradictoria decreta absurdè comminisci cogitur.

XVIII. 6. A Christo ἐντογῆς fundamento. Facta est electio in Christo, Eph. 1. v. 4. in illo autem non sumus nisi per fidē, quippè p quam Christo tanquam viti & veræ oleæ inserimur. Ioh. 15, v. 4. 5. Rom. 11. v. 24. & ipsius participes reddimur, Heb. 3. v. 14 atq; in ipso per eandem fundati permanemus. Col. 1. v 11. Quicunq; enim electi sunt, ij non solū in Christo, vt authore ratione partæ iustitiæ, sed etiā vt consummatore ratione imputatæ iustitiæ sunt electi. Cum igitur facta sit electio per fidē, & verò pauci credant; paucos etiam electos esse consequitur.

XIX. 7. A speciali prænotione. Omnes electos nouit Deus. 2. Tim. 2. v. 19. incredulos vero nunquam nouit. Matth. 7. v. 23. Ergò increduli nunq̃ sunt electi. Pro Maioris confirmatione addimus dicta, de προγνώσει diuina, secundū quā electi sumus, agētia, vt Rom: 8. v. 30. Quos præsciuit, eos prædestinauit. c. 11. v. 2. Non repulit Deus populū, ὃν προέγνω. 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. Electis secundū πρόγνωσιν Dei patris. Ex hisce perspicuū fit, omnes electos ab æterno fuisse præscitos & specialiter notos Deo. De impœnitētibus verò dicitur quod nūquam noti fuerint. Qui ergò electi sunt, & quidem electione proprijssimâ secundum πρόγνωσιν facta?

XX. 8. Aregula Theologica, quæ in scholis decantata, & semper vsitata fuit: Ea vero sic habet: Extra cœtum vocato rū non sunt quærendi electi: Fundamētum regulæ desumitur ex dicto Christi: Multi vocati pauci electi. Si quis ergò exclusus sit è numero vocatorū, multò magis exclusus erit è numero electorū. Sed Huberus rē planè inuertit, regulaq; illam penitus tollit, dum non minᵉ extra Ecclesiam in Turcia & Tartaria proprijssimè electos, & quidem non nisi electos reperiri statuit: quod annòn absurdum & scandalosum sit, varijsq; calumnijs ansam suppeditet omnes rectè sentientes iudicent.

XXI. Hisce argumentis tandem addimús, quòd Huberianū dogma prórsus inauditū sit, & antiquitatis vniuersæ testimonijs destituatur: patres enim örthodoxi clarè asserunt, factam esse electionē in Christo per fidē, ideóq; nō nisi credentes cōplecti & eos salu ē consequi, quæ omnia in præcedētib. demonstrata sunt. Ex abundāti hẹc testimoniä adiungimus Aug Epist. 39. ad Paulinam. Non sunt inista vocatione, qui in fide, quæ per dilectione operatur, etiamsi aliquantulum ambulant, non perseuerant vsque in finem: Ambros. lib. 2. de vocat. gent. c. vlt. Sicut nullus infidelium in hac sorte (de electis loquitur) numeratur, ita nullus piorum ab hac sorte discretus est. Fulgent. lib. 1. Mon. Deus prædestinauit ad regnum, quos præsciuit ad se misericordiæ præuenientis auxilio peruenturos, & in se subsequentis misericordiæ auxilio mansuros.

XXII. Hanc Orthodoxam doctrinam ex Scripturis & patribus haustā liber concordiæ luculēter asserit, vt vel maximè de illius cōsensu Huberᵉ glorietur Verba enim clariora sunt, quà vt distinctiūcula illa inter actū & effectū eludi queant: Sic legitur in epitome mihi pag. 618. th. 4. prædestinatio seu æterna Dei electio, tantū ait bonos & dilectos filios Dei pertinet

& hæc est causa ipsorum salutis, Th 6. Verbum Dei deducit nos ad Christum, is est liber ille vitæ, in quo omnes inscripti& electi sunt, qui salutem æternam consequuntur. Pag. 619. th. 12. In Christo electio æterna Dei patris est quærenda. Is in æterno suo decreto, quod præter eos, qui filium eius Iesum Christum agnoscunt & in eum verè credunt, neminem saluum facere velit. Idem repetitur in declaratione pag 798.799. Æterna electio sive prædestinatio Dei ad salutem non simul ad bonos & malos pertinet, sed tantum ad filios Dei, qui ad æternam vitam consequendam electi & ordinati sunt. pag. 808. Nequaquam sentiendum est, eos etiam in electorum numero habendos, qui verbum Dei contemnunt, repellunt, execrantur &c. qui locus tam clarus est, vt qui nõ videat, eum in media luce cæcutire non immeritò dicamus.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: III. Huber's objections from the scriptures XXIII. 1 From Eph. 1. v. 4. He chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid,…

III. Huber's objections from the scriptures.

XXIII. 1 From Eph. 1. v. 4. He chose us in Christ before the foundations of the world were laid, that we might be holy and blameless. Those, therefore, whom Christ redeemed, they are the elect, since election was made in Christ. But he redeemed all, therefore all are elected.

Resp. The major premise is false, because Christ enters into the mystery of election, not only by reason of merit, but also by reason of application. For we are elected in Christ, but apprehended by faith. Otherwise, universal justification and salvation could similarly be concluded, because we are justified and saved in Christ. The words, therefore, of the cited text, 'He chose us,' do not pertain indifferently to all men but only to those who persevere in believing. For these he calls saints, faithful in Christ v. 1, blessed with every spiritual blessing v. 3, hoping in Christ v. 12, sealed with the holy spirit of promise v. 13, lovers of the saints v. 15. Nor let that indefinite particle 'He chose us' move anyone, since it is also said elsewhere, 'We are justified, we are saved in Christ' Acts 15. v. 10. Gal. 2. v. 16. Apoc. 1. v. 5. Shall we therefore on that account establish a universal justification and salvation of all men and although the Apostle speaks with the whole visible assembly of the called in the Ephesian Church, those epithets and praises nevertheless pertain primarily to the invisible. For it is familiar to the Scriptures that something is said about many which nevertheless does not apply to individuals: Thus Matt. 19, verse 28, Christ says to all his disciples, among whom Judas also was, 'Amen I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration when the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty, you also shall sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel': which itself, however, cannot be applied to the traitor Judas. Thus 1 Cor. 1, v. 23, the Apostle says of the visible assembly of the called Corinthians, that they are sanctified, called, saints, enriched through Christ in all speech, etc. And nevertheless he complains in the following chapters of many hypocrites in that Church. Such a synecdochical locution exists in the above. Gal. 3, v. 23. where Paul writes thus to the Galatians (which Church consisted mostly of Gentiles), 'before faith came, we were kept under the law': which itself can only be applied to the Jews.

The same answer is given to another passage from 2 Tim. 1, v. 9, 'he called us with a holy calling not according to our works, but according to his grace, which was given to us' (which particle Huberus urges) 'in Christ before the secular times.' The same synecdoche recurs here, which others call koinopoiēsin, when speech is directed to many, yet that which is said is not applied to all.

Objection: We were chosen to this end, that we might be holy and blameless: But God wills all men to be holy and blameless. Therefore he chose all.

Answer: The argument suffers from the ambiguity of terms. But if the major premise is formed thus: 'Whom God wills to be holy, all of them he chose,' we deny that, and it cannot be proven from the text, unless one also wishes to establish universal justification, because this also is done to the end that we might be holy and blameless.

XXIV. 2. From Eph. 1, v. 10, God in Christ made restoration of all things, which are in heaven and on earth. Tit. 2. vers. 11. The grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men. Luc. 7. v. 30. The Pharisees rejected the counsel of God against themselves. Since therefore God embraces all with his grace, so much so that the unbelieving are said to have rejected the counsel of God, the gratuitous decree of election will certainly be universal.

I answer. From the universality of redemption and the mercy of the will in God, there is no consequence to the universality of election. For many are called, but few are chosen. Furthermore, the counsel of God is viewed either in his antecedent will, and thus it is universal, and is rejected by the impenitent: or in his consequent will, insofar as it is joined with an infallible decree of salvation certainly to be conferred, and thus it is particular, not out of an absolute hatred of God toward some, but solely on account of the foreseen final impenitence of men. But because election pertains to the consequent will, where there is not one certain universal decree, but two particular ones, hence it follows that it itself is also particular.

XXV. 3. From Rom. 5. v. 18. As by the offence of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation: even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. Therefore, just as all men perished in the first Adam, so all are predestined to life in the second Adam.

I answer. There is more in the conclusion than follows from the premises. For the meaning of the Pauline antithesis is extended further by Huber than it ought to be extended. Paul compares the fault of Adam and the merit of Christ: namely, that the merit of the Savior extends as widely as the sin of Adam. Whoever gathers anything else from this antithesis does violence to the text and will conclude, most absurdly, a universal justification sooner than a universal election.

XXVI. Unbelievers fall from grace Gal. 3. v. 13. Therefore they are predestined to it.

I answer. Unbelievers are outside of grace, and therefore they cannot fall from it. For he who does not believe in the Son the wrath of God remains upon them, John 3:36. But this passage speaks of the Galatians, who were being solicited to defection by seducers. Therefore, the Apostle warns them not to obey them, otherwise it will come to pass that they fall from grace. From this, however, it by no means follows that predestination is universal. For the end of this is not grace, but glory and eternal salvation. We are speaking of election to life: Huber concludes concerning grace, and therefore commits the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi. It may be granted to him that election to grace, if anyone wishes to speak in that way, which is nothing other than calling, also includes those who believed for a time and afterwards fall away, so that that temporal ἐκλογὴ (election) may be mutable; but that the same ought to be affirmed of eternal election to salvation, and that properly so-called, is not proven by this nor by any other arguments.

Latin:

III. Obiectiones Huberi ex scripturis.

XXIII. 1 Ex Eph. 1. v. 4. Elegit nos in Christo ante iacta mundi fundamenta, vt essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles. Quos igitur Christus redemit, illi sunt electi, quoniam in Christo facta est electio. Atqui omnes redemit, omnes igitur electi sunt.

Resp. Maior falsa est, quia Christus ingreditur arkanum electionis, non tantum ratione meriti, sed etiam ratione applicationis. Electi enim sumus in Christo, sed fide apprehenso. Aliàs posset similiter concludi vniuersalis iustificatio & saluatio, quia in Christo iustificamur & saluamur. Verba igitur allegati textus, Elegit nos, nõ indifferẽter omnes homines sed duntaxat perseueranter credentes attinent. Hos enim vocat sanctos, fideles in Christo v. 1 benedictos in omni benedictione spirituali v. 3. sperantes in Christũ. v. 12. signatos spiritu promissionis sancto, v. 13. amatores sanctorum. v. 15. Nec quenq̃ moueat particula illa indefinita Elegit nos, siquidem & alibi dicitur, Nos iustificamur, nos saluamur in Christo Act. 15. v. 10. Gal. 2. v. 16. Apoc. 1. v. 5. Num ergo propterea vniuersalẽ omnium hominum iustificationem & saluationem statuemus ? Et quamuis cum toto visibili vocatorum cœtu in Ecclesia Ephesina loquatur Apostolus, illa tamen Epitheta & elogia inuisibili cum primis competunt. Scripturis enim familiare est, vt aliquid dicatur de multis, quod tamen non spectat ad singulos : Sic Matth. 19. vers. 28. dicit Christus ad omnes suos discipulos, inter quos & Iudas erat, Amen dico vobis, quod vos, qui secuti estis me, in generatione cum sederit filius hominis in sede maiestatis sua, sedebitis & vos super sedes duodecim, iudicantes duodecim tribus Israel : quod ipsum tamen ad proditorem Iudam accommodari nequit. Sic 1. Cor. 1. v. 23. ait Apostolus de cœtu visibili vocatorum Corinthiorum, quod sint sanctificati, vocati, sancti, ditati per Christum in omni sermone, &c. Et nihilominus conqueritur seqq. capp. de multis in ea Ecclesia hypocritis. Talis Synecdochica locutio extat in super. Gal. 3. v. 23. vbi Paulus ad Galatas (quæ Ecclesia potissimum constabat exgentilibus) ita scribit, antequam venisset fides, sub lege custodiebamur: quod ipsum Iudęis tantùm potest applicari.

Eadem responsio datur ad aliũ locũ ex 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. vocauit nos vocatione sancta nõ secũdum opera nostra, sed secundum gratiam, quæ data est nobis (quam particula vrget Huberus) in Christo ante tempora secularia, Recurrit hic eadẽ synecdoche, quam alij vocant κοινοπόιησιν cum ad multos sermo dirigitur, id tamen, quod dicitur, non omnibus accommodatur.

Inst. Electi sumus in hunc finem, vt essemus sancti & irreprehensibiles: Atqui Deus vult omnes homines esse sanEtos & irreprehensibiles. Ergò omnes elegit.

Resp. Argumentum laborat πλυνωφίᾳ terminorum. Quòd si verò maior ita informetur: Quos Deus vult esse sanctos, eos omnes elegit, negamus illam, & ex textu probari nequit, nisi quis vna velit statuere iustificationem vniuersalem, quia & hæc fit eum in finem, vt simus sancti & irreprehensibiles.

XXIV. 2. Ex Eph. 1. v. 10. Deus in Christo fecit restaurationem omnium, quæ in cælo & in terra sunt. Tit. 2. vers. 11. Apparuit gratia Dei salutifera omnibus hominibus Luc. 7. v. 30. Pharisæi consilium Dei aduersus semetipsos spreuerunt. Cum igitur Deus sua gratia omnes complectatur, adeò vt increduli dicantur spreuisse Dei consilium, vtiq; vniuersale erit gratuitum electionis decretum.

Respondeo. Ab vniuersalitate redemptionis & misericordiæ voluntatis in Deo, ad vniuersalitatem electionis nulla est consequentia. Multi enim sunt vocati, pauci verò electi. Deinde consilium Dei spectatur vel in voluntate antecedente, & sic vniuersale est, sperniturq; ab impoenitentibus: vel in voluntate consequente, quatenus cum infallibili salutis certò conferendæ decreto coniunctum, & sic particulare est, non ex absoluto Dei erga nonnullos odio, sed vnicè ob præuisam hominum impœnitētiam finalem. Quia verò electio ad voluntatem consequentem spectat, vbi non est vnum quoddam decretū vniuersale, sed duo particularia, hinc & ipsam particularem esse consequitur.

XXV. 3. Ex Rom. 5. v. 18. Sicut per vnius delictum in omnes homines in condemnationem: sic & per vnius iustitiā in omnes homines in iustificationē vitæ. Ergò sicut omnes homines in primo Adamo perierūt, ita om nes in secūdo Adamo ad vitam sunt prędestinati.

Resp. Plus est in conclusione, quam è præmissis sequitur. Longius enim ab Hubero extēditur sentētia Paulinæ antitheseos quā extēdi debet. Confert Paulus culpā Adæ, & meritum Christi: tam nimirūm latè se extēdere Saluatoris meritum, quam Adæ peccatum. Qui aliud ex ista antithesi colligit, vim infert textui & citius vniuersalē iustificationem, quàm electionem absurdissimè concludet.

XXVI. Increduli excidunt à gratia Gal. 3. v. 13. Ergo ad eam prædestinati sunt.

Resp. Increduli sunt extra gratiam, ideoq; illâ excidere nequeunt. Qui enim in filium non credunt super eos manet ira Dei, Iohan. 6. 36. locus autẽ iste loquitur de Galatis, qui ad defectionem solicitabãtur à seductoribus. Monet ergo Apostolus nè ijs obediat, alioqui futurum, vt excidant gratia. Hinc autem minimè sequitur quod vniuersalis sit prædestinatio. Huius n. terminus nõ est gratia, sed gloria, & salus sempiterna. Nos loquimur de electione ad vitam: Huberus concludit de gratia, ideoque committit ignorationẽ Elenchi. Potest hoc ipsi concedi quod electio ad gratiam, siquis ita loqui velit, quæ nihil est aliud quam vocatio, illos quoque comprehendat, qui ad tempus crediderũt & post excidunt, vt ita ἐκλογὴ illa temporalis sit mutabilis; q vera idẽ affirmari debeat de electione æterna ad salutẽ, eaq; propriè dicta, nec isto nec vllis alijs argumentis euincitur.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: XXVII. 5. From 1 Thess. 5, v. 9. God has not appointed us to wrath, but that we may obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.…

XXVII. 5. From 1 Thess. 5, v. 9. God has not appointed us to wrath, but that we may obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, all men are appointed or ordained by God to salvation.

Resp. By the pronoun (Us) all men are not understood, but the children of light, whom Paul distinguishes there, having made a separation from the children of darkness, as appears from a comparison of verses 7 and 8. Indeed, even if we were to grant as much as possible that all men are understood here, yet nothing else would be inferred than this: that God creates no one for wrath, that He appoints no one to destruction. But from the universal will of God to universal election, what is the consequence? Whatever interpretation, therefore, is assumed, nothing will be firmly inferred for Huber. If by appointment to salvation one understands the universal counsel of God, by which He wills all to be saved, then we willingly grant that the particle 'Us' is explained as the whole human race, but we deny the consequence from the universality of divine love to the universality of election. But if by that appointment both the acquisition and application of salvation are understood, then certainly the pronoun 'Us' must be restricted to the believers alone, since they alone actually achieve salvation. In brief: we are placed for salvation either through the counsel of Redemption: and this is universal, or through the decree of election and this is particular. Therefore, from the word 'position' alone, Huber can conclude nothing solid against us.

IV. Huber's objections from the analogy of faith.

XXIIX. 2. From the universal intention of God. It was the eternal counsel of God that the whole world should be chosen. Therefore, the whole world was chosen. Resp. The antecedent is not simply admitted. For because the election of God was made κατὰ πρόγνωσιν 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. and God truly foreknew in his eternal purpose that most would not believe, therefore the Book of Concord rightly established that it was rather the intention that the unbelieving, as despisers of grace, should be judged and condemned, and not be reckoned among the elect. Therefore, I will not concede this position: God proposed to himself to choose all: For what God proposes to himself, that comes to pass. But because he did not actually choose all, he certainly did not propose to choose all. Indeed, it does not even seem that this can be conceded, 'God willed to choose all,' since election always implies separation and segregation. For since the election of Scripture is said to be made from the world, what kind of phrase, I ask, would it be; God willed to select the whole world from the world? This, however, can be conceded in a certain way, that God by an antecedent will willed to destine all to life, if they should believe: for it is just as if I were to say: God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. But from this universal will, a universal election is wrongly inferred, just as it does not follow: God wills all men to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth: Therefore all are saved and arrive at the truth.

XXIX. From the generality of love. God loved all. Therefore he also chose all. Resp. N. C. [I do not concede]. For love is twofold, one general, the other special; the latter, not the former, extends as widely as election, John 3 deals with general [love]: Eph. 1 with special love, which is of the beloved in the beloved. He urges: The whole world could not be loved by God, unless the whole world were chosen and predestined to this love, and therefore election τάξει [in order] precedes the election of God. Resp. The order of the divine counsel is confused. For love is not the effect of election, but rather the cause, and therefore τάξει [in order] it is prior. For just as the supreme cause of justification is the grace of God, so also is it of election. Hence Scripture says that we, when we were enemies, were loved and reconciled, Rom. 5, v. 10. Furthermore, Huberus abuses the term of election. For this is never said to be made to the love of God, but from love to salvation. And if we wish to proceed in this way, as many predestinations will be invented as there are benefits of God. For in the same way I can say, if some benefit is conferred upon a man, it is necessary that he was previously predestined to this. Certainly, we do not deny that the will and decree of God always precede: but that this is election properly so called, whence will it be proved?

XXX. 3. From the mission of the Son into the flesh. Election is the cause of the mission of the Son. Therefore, those to whom the Son is sent, they are the elect. For to those to whom the means are supplied so that they may attain the end, the end pertains. But to all are given the means through which they attain the election to which they are destined. Therefore, consequently, all are elect. Resp. We do not simply concede the antecedent, because the order in the degrees of divine counsels is inverted. For the decree of election τάξει [in order] is posterior to the decree of the mission, and therefore the former cannot be the cause of the latter, since a cause is always prior, not posterior to its effect. For God first had mercy on the movement of the human race and thought of redeeming men: He decreed to give the means, to send the Son, to give the Word, to excite faith in all who do not place an obstacle: but because He foresaw that not all would remove the obstacles, therefore He chose in act, and ordained to life, only those who were going to believe perseveringly. Meanwhile, if the term 'cause' is taken generally for any antecedent; and the mission of the Son is considered in execution, not in decree, then indeed the election can in a certain way be called the cause of the mission, for that preceded from eternity: this followed in time. But then we deny the consequence of the argument, partly because a false hypothesis is presupposed, namely, that all are predestined, and therefore Christ was sent so that they might apprehend it: partly, because the connection is weak. If election precedes, and mission follows, all to whom the Son was sent will be elect. We see no solid reason for the consequence here, since Scripture itself so distinguishes between those elect from eternity and those redeemed in time, that the former are few, the latter are many.

XXXI. 4. From the universality of the calling. All are called, therefore all are elect. Resp. N. C. [Negatur Consequentia], because the calling does not yet complete the whole order which God looked to in the decree of election, but an application is required besides, which is made through faith. Hence many are indeed said to be called, yet few are elect. For the grace of God is as it were the term of election, from which the decree flows and arises. The term to which is salvation and eternal life, and therefore Huberus speaks incongruously when he asserts that we are elected to the grace and love of God, as also to faith. The term through which is, in one word, faith, for this includes the remaining means at the same time. These three terms must always be joined, otherwise we shall have an election not whole, but mutilated and truncated. XXXII. 5. From the universality of the promises. Divine promises are universal, pertaining to all men. E. Election also is universal. Resp. The antecedent requires explanation: For some Evangelical promises are simply universal, as, God wills all to be saved: But some are limitedly universal, under the condition of faith, as, everyone who believes has eternal life. The apprehend the universal promises by true faith. But the former kind of Evangelical promises does not absolve election, but the latter is required in the first place. And it is strange that Huberus dares to deny the particular decree of election, when nevertheless he receives special promises, which depend on nothing but a particular decree.

XXXIII. 6. From the passing over of no man: if God in choosing men passed over no one, he certainly chose all: but the former is true: Therefore also the latter.

Resp. The minor is false. God indeed by his antecedent will, which is of mercy, passed over no one, but desires all men to be saved. But by his consequent will, which regards the infidelity of men, he passes over those whom he sees will persevere in their incredulity, and for this very reason he does not choose them. Others form the argument thus: to pass over and to choose are immediately opposed: Therefore if God passed over no one, he chose all.

Resp. To pass over by consequent will and to choose are opposed, but not to pass over by antecedent will: For election is of the ἑπομένης [consequent] will: but to pass over is sometimes referred to the antecedent, so that the sense is, God simply excluded no one from his grace, but wills all to be saved. And thus they are not opposed, but ὑπάλληλα [subordinate]. Therefore it does not follow, God passed over no one by antecedent will: Therefore he chose all by consequent will. Nor can it be concluded: Therefore he chose all by antecedent will, because election is not of the antecedent will, but of the consequent.

If anyone requires brief terms of distinction, we say that preterition is twofold. 1. General, which is not opposed to election, but to the will of saving, according to which God passed over no one. 2. Special, which is opposed to election, in which way God passed over all whom he foresaw as impenitent, and therefore chose only those who would persevere in believing.

Latin:

XXVII. 5. Ex 1. Thess. 5. v. 9. Non posuit nos Deus ad iram sed vt salutem consequamur per Dominũ nostrum Iesum Christum. Ergò omnes homines sunt constituti à Deo vel ordinati ad salutem.

Resp. pronomen (Nos) non intelliguntur omnes homines, sed filij lucis, quos Paulus ibi distinguit, factâ segregatione à filijs tenebrarum, vt apparet ex collatione vers. 7. & 8. imò si maximè concederemus, hic intelligi omnes homines; nihil tamẽ inferretur aliud quã hoc, Deũ neminem creare ad iram, neminem ponere ad interitum. Ab vniuersali autem voluntate Dei ad vniuersalem electionem quæ consequentia? Quæcunque igitur interpretatio assumatur, nihil pro Hubero firmiter inferetur. Si per positionem ad salutem intelligatur vniuersale Dei consilium, quo omnes vult saluos fieri, tum particulam Nos de toto genere humano exponi lubenter concedimus, sed consequentiam ab vniuersalitate amoris diuini ad vniuersalitatem electionis negamus. Si verò per illam positionem & acquisitio & applicatio salutis intelligatur, vtiq; pronomen Nos ad solos credentes restringi oportet, quippe qui soli salutem actu consequuntur. Brevissime: positi sumus ad salutem vel per consilium Redemptionis: & hoc vniuersale est, vel per decretum electionis & hoc particulare est. Ex sola igitur positionis voce nihil solidi aduersus nos concludere potest Huberus.

IV. Obiectiones Huberi ex analogia fidei.

XXIIX. 2. Ab vniuersali intentione Dei. Aeternum Dei consilium fuit, vt totus eligeretur mundus. Ergo totus electus est. Resp. Antecedens non simpliciter admittitur. Quia enim electio Dei facta est κατὰ πρόγνωσιν 1. Pet.1.v.2. & vero præcognouit Deus in æterno suo proposito, plerosque non credituros esse, ideo liber Concordiæ rectè statuit illam potius fuisse intentionem, vt increduli, tanquam contemptores gratiæ iudicentur & damnentur, nec electis accenseantur. Propterea non concessero hanc positionem: Deus sibi proposuit omnes eligere: Quæ enim Deus sibi proponit, ea fiūt. Quia verò non omnes actu elegit, vtique nec omnes proposuit eligere. Imò nec videtur istæ concedi posse, Deus omnes voluit eligere, quoniã electio semper separationem importat & segregationem. Nam quia electio Scripturæ dicitur facta de mundo, qualis quæro phrasis esset; Deus totum mundum de mundo voluit seligere? Hoc verò quodammodo concedi potest, quod Deus voluntate antecedente voluerit omnes ad vitam destinare, si crederent: perinde enim est ac si dicerem: Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire. Ab hac autem voluntate vniuersali malè infertur vniuersalis electio, sicut non sequitur: Deus vult omnes homines saluos fieri & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire: Ergo omnes saluifiunt, & ad veritatem perueniunt.

XXIX. A generalitate dilectionis. Deus omnes dilexit. Ergo etiam omnes elegit. Resp. N. C. Est enim dilectio duplex, vna generalis altera, specialis; hec, non illa, tam late patet quam electio, Ioh. 3. agitur de generali: Eph. 1. de speciali dilectione, quæ est dilectorum in dilecto. Instat: Non potuit totus mundus à Deo diligi, nisi totus mundus ad hanc dilectionem esset e ctus & prædestinatus, ideoque electio τάξει præcedit elēctionem Dei. Resp. confunditur ordo consilij diuini. Nam dilectio non est effectus electionis, sed potius causa, ideoque τάξει prior. Sicut enim suprema iustificationis causa est gratia Dei, ita & electionis. Hinc scriptura dicit, nos cum inimici essemus, fuisse dilectos & reconciliatos, Rom. 5. v. 10. Deindè abutitur Huberus termino electionis. Hæc enim nunquam facta dicitur ad amorem Dei, sed ex amore ad salutem. Et si ita velimus procedere, tot fingentur prædestinationes, quot sunt Dei beneficia. Pari enim modo dicere possum, si aliquod beneficium confertur homini, oportet ipsum prius ad hoc fuisse prædestinatum. Sanè voluntatem & decretum Dei semper præcedere, non diffitemur: eam verò esse electionem propriè dictam vnde probabitur.

XXX. 3. A missione filij in carnem. Electio est causa missionis Filij. Ergo, quibus filius est missus, ij sunt electi. Quibus enim suppeditantur media, vt consequantur finem, eos attinet finis. Atqui omnibus dantur media, per quæ consequuntur electionem ad qua sunt destinati. E. per consequens omnes sunt electi. Resp. Antecedens non simpliciter concedimus, quia inuertitur ordo in gradibus diuinorum consiliorum. Nam decretum electionis τάξει posterius est decreto missionis, ideoque illud nequit esse causa huius, cùm causa semper sit prior, non po sterior suo effectu. Deus enim primùm misertà generis humani motus cogitavit de redimendis hominibus: decrevit dare media, mittere filium, dare verbum, excitare fidem in omnibus non ponentibus obicem: quia verò prævidit non omnes obstacula remoturos, ideò eos duntaxat actu elegit, & ad vitam ordinavit, qui perseveranter erant credituri. Interim, si vocabulum causæ sumatur generalitèr pro quovis antecedente; & missio filij consideretur in executione non in decreto, tum sanè electio missionis causa quodammodo dici potest, Illa enim præcessit ab æterno: Hæc secuta est in tempore. Tum verò negamus argumenti consequentiam, partim quia præsupponitur hypothesis falsa, nimirum, omnes esse prædestinatos, ideoq; Christum missum, vt illam apprehēdāt: partim, quia nexus infirmus est. Si electio præcedit, & missio insequitur, omnes erunt electi, quibus missus est filius. Nullam hic solidam consequentiæ rationem videmus, cum Scriptura ipsa inter electos ab æterno, & Redēptos in tempore ita distinguat, quod eorum pauci, horum multi sunt.

XXXI. 4. Ab vniuersalitate vocationis. Omnes sunt vocati Ergo omnes electi. Resp. N. C. quia vocatio nondum absoluit totum ordinem, quem Deus spectauit in decreto electionis, sed requiritur insuper applicatio, quæ fit per fidem. Hinc multi dicuntur quidem vocati, pauci tamen electi. Nam gratia Dei est veluti terminus electionis, à quo promanat & oritur decretum. Terminus ad quem, est salus & vita æterna, ideoquè incongruè Huberus loquitur, quando nos ad gratiam & amorem Dei, vt & ad fidem electos esse asserit. Terminus per quem, est vno verbo fides, hæc enim reliqua simul media includit. Tres hi termini semper sunt coniungendi, aliàs electionem non integram, sed mutilam & truncatam habebimus. XXXII. 5. Ab vniuersalitate promissionum. Diuinæ promissiones sunt vniuersales, pertinentes ad omnes homines. E. Electio quoq; vniuersalis est. Resp. Antecedens eget explicatione: Nam promissiones Evangelicę quædam sunt simpliciter vniuersales, vt, Deus vult omnes saluos fieri: Quædam verò sunt limitatè vniuersales, sub conditione fidei, vt, omnis, qui credit, habet vitam æternam. Illæ, non autem hæ ad omnes indiscretè homines pertinent, vnde fit, vt nec omnes vitam consequantur, quia non omnes verâ fide apprehendunt promissiones vniuersales. Prius autem genus promissionum Evangelicarum non absoluit electionem, sed requiritur in primis posterius. Et mirum est, quod Huberus audeat negare decretum electionis particulare, cum tamen promissiones speciales recipiat, quæ non nisi à decreto particulari dependent.

XXXIII. 6. A nullius hominis præteritione: si Deus eligendo homines neminem præterijt, vtique vniuersos elegit: sed verum est pmus: Ergo & posterius.

Resp. Minor falsa est. Deus quidem voluntate antecedēte, quę misericordię est, neminē pręteriit, sed omnes homines saluos cupit. Voluntate autem consequēte, quæ infidelitate hominum respicit, præterit eos, quos videt in incredulitate sua esse perseueraturos, eosq; ob hoc ipsum non elegit. Alij sic informant argumentum: præterire & eligere sunt immediatè opposita: Ergò si nullum præterijt Deus, omnes elegit.

Resp. præterire voluntate consequente & eligere, sunt opposita, sed non præterire voluntate antecedente: Electio enim est voluntatis ἑπομένης: præterire autem quandoque refertur ad antecedentem, ita, vt sit sensus, Deus neminem simpliciter exclusit â sua gratia, sed omnes vult fieri saluos. Atque sic non sunt opposita, sed ὑπάλληλα. Non ergò sequitur, Deus neminem præterijt voluntate antecedente: Ergò omnes elegit votuntate consequente. Neque concludi potest: Ergo omnes elegit voluntate antecedente, quia electio non est voluntatis antecedentis, sed consequētis.

Si quis breues distinctionis terminos requirat, dicimus præteritionem esse duplicem. 1. Generalem, quę non electioni opponitur, sed voluntati saluandi, Secundum quam Deus neminem præterijt. 2. specialem, quæ opponitur electioni, quo pacto præterijt Deus omnes quos præuidit impœnitentes, ideoq́; elegit tantum perseueranter credituros.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: XXXIV. 7. From the creation of man

XXXIV. 7. From the creation of man.

God in Adam created the whole human race to his own image and eternal life. Therefore: God destined and ordained the whole human race to eternal life.

Response. With Gesner from disp. 26 for the Formula of Concord, ch. 3, the. 45, the decree concerning creating man is wrongly confused with the decree of God concerning asserting man fallen into life. For election is in order posterior to the decree of creation, both because it is necessary that men be created first, who are chosen: and because election was made out of sinners. For if God by an absolute decree, and one preceding all causes and the order of means, decreed to choose all men and appoint them heirs of eternal life, then he either did not know that man had fallen and that most would perish by their own fault, which is against God's omniscience, or he knew, and then he made in vain an absolute decree which was intercepted by the malice of men. For since men do not sanction decrees rashly, shall we judge that the decrees of God can be made void? And because we are chosen in Christ; But the mission of Christ presupposes the fall, certainly the decree of election cannot precede the decree of creation and the intuition of the fall. Therefore, although God created man for life, let us grant he even ordained, nay and predestined, if anyone wishes to abuse this term, yet it does not follow that the whole human race having fallen, is simply destined by God for life after Adam's transgression, whether he believes or does not believe. For the entire Biblical codex testifies to the contrary.

XXXV. 8. Concerning the restitution made through Christ. Whatever was lost in Adam, that has been restored through Christ. But universal predestination to eternal life was lost in Adam. Therefore, it was restored through Christ. The minor premise is proven, because God had created all in Adam, and thus had destined them to salvation, which benefit if it was not repaired through Christ, it follows that the restoration was particular, which is ἄτοπον καὶ ἀντίγραφον.

Response 1. To the major premise. In the restitution made through Christ, either the gift itself is considered, or the subject to whom that gift is applied. If the gift itself, we concede the major premise, that Christ restored what Adam lost, namely justice and life. If the subject to whom the application is made is understood, in this sense, that to all those who lost the gifts in Adam, those lost things are actually restored through Christ, the major premise does not proceed absolutely, unless you wish to say that all are actually justified and saved, because all were created in Adam for justice and life. Therefore, by reason of the subject, there is a distinction between the first possession and Christ's restitution. We all had justice and life in Adam, which itself would have been propagated to all through generation. These gifts Christ fully repaired, yet so that a distinction must be made between the acquisition, which is universal, and the application, which is particular and proper only to believers. Although, therefore, all were created for life in Adam, and thus predestined in a general sense: it does not follow from this, however, that because of Christ's restitution all are properly elected to salvation, since the application, the consideration of which precedes the decree of election, as the execution teaches is not of all, but only of believers. As therefore Christ fully restored the salvation lost in Adam, although not all are saved; so destination to life, if anyone uses this word in a broad sense, he likewise fully restored, although not all are destined and elected to life.

2 To the minor: If εκλογὴ is taken properly, and according to the sense of Scripture, we deny the minor. For since election was made from the world, it certainly does not precede, but in order follows the fall. And since election was made in Christ, how in the state of integrity, before the decrees of the incarnation, could all be properly said to be elected to life in Christ? Thus therefore we see with what ambiguities Huber plays and how miserably he abuses the phrases of Scripture, who nevertheless falsely arrogates to himself the praise of the most proper locution.

Latin:

XXXIV. 7. A creatione hominis.

Deus in Adamo totum genus humanum condidit ad imaginem suam & vitam æternam. Er: Deus totum genus humanum destinauit & ordinauit ad vitam æternam.

Resp. Cum Gesnero ex disp. 26. pro form. concor: c. 3. the. 45. Decretum de creando homine, perperam confunditur cum decreto Dei de homine lapso in vitam asserendo. Electio enim ordine posterior est creationis decreto, tum quod prius conditos oportet esse homines, qui eliguntur: tum quòd ex peccatoribus facta est electio. Si enim Deus absoluto, omnesque causas & ordinem mediorum antegresso consulto decreuit, omnes homines eligere & vitæ æternæ hæredes cōstituere, tum aut ignorauit, hominem esse lapsum & plerosq́; sua culpâ perituros, quod est contra Dei omnisciētiam, aut sciuit, & tùm frustrà fecit absolutum decretum quod malitiâ hominum interceptum est. Cùm enim homines non temerè decreta sanciant, num Dei decreta irrita fieri posse cēsebimus. Et quia in Christo electi sumus; Christi autem missio præsupponit lapsum, vtique decretum electionis non potest præcedere decretum creationis & intuitum lapsus. Proinde quamuis Deus hominem ad vitam creauerit, demus etiam ordinauerit, imò & prædestinauerit, si quis termino hoc abuti velit, non tamē sequitur, quòd totum genus humanum lapsum, simpliciter sit à Deo post Adæ præuaricationem vicissim ad vitam destinatum, siuè credat, siuè non credat. Nam contrarium testatur vniuersus codex Biblicus.

XXXV. 8. A restitutione per Christum facta. Quodcunque in Adamo est perditum, illud per Christum est restitutum. Atqui vniuersalis prædestinatio ad vitam æternam deperdita est in Adamo. Quare restituta fuit per Christum. Minor probatur, quia Deus in Adamo omnes condiderat, adeoq; destinauerat ad salutem, quod beneficium si per Christum non est reparatum, particularem sequitur fuisse restaurationem, quod ἄτοπον καὶ ἀντίγραφον.

Resp. 1. Ad maiorem. In restitutione per Christum factâ, vel consideratur donum ipsum, vel subiectum, cui istud donum applicatur. Si donum ipsum, concedimus maiorem, quod Christus restituerit, quod Adamus perdidit, nempe iustitiam & vitam. Si subiectum, cui fit applicatio intelligatur, hoc sensu, Qui in Adamo dona amiserunt, illis omnibus amissa per Christum actu restituuntur, non procedit maior absolutè, nisi velis dicere, omnes actu iustificari & saluari, quia omnes in Adamo ad iustitiam & vitam fuerunt conditi. Quare subiecti ratione, discrimen est inter primā possessionem, & Christi restitutionem. Omnes in Adamo habuimus iustitiam & vitam, quæ ipsa in omnes per generationem fuisset propagata. Hæc dona Christus plenè reparauit, ita tamen, vt distingui debeat inter acquisitionem, quæ vniuersalis, & applicationem, quæ particularis solisque credentibus propria est. Licet ergo omnes ad vitam in Adamo sint conditi, adeoque generali sensu prædestinati: Non tamen hinc sequitur, quod propter Christi restitutionem omnes ad salutem propriè sint electi, quoniam applicatio, cuius intuitus decretum electionis præcedit, vti docet executio, non est omnium, sed duntaxat credentium. Vt igitur Christus, salutem in Adamo perditam plane restituit, licet non omnes saluentur. Sic destinationem ad vitam, si quis lato sensu hac voce vtatur. Pari modo plene restituit, licet no omnes sint ad vitam destinati & electi.

2 Ad minorem Si εκλογὴ sumatur proprie, & secundu scripturae sensu, negamus minorem, Quia enim electio facta est de mudo, vtiq; non praecedit, sed ordine sequitur lapsum. Et quia Electio facta est in Christo, quomodo in statu integritatis, ante decreta λογε in carnatione, omnes ad vita in Christo proprie electi dici potuerunt? Ita ergo videmus quantis ambiguitatibꝰ ludat & quam misere Scripturae phrasibus abutatur Huberus, qui tamen proprijssime locutionis laude, sed falso, sibi arrogat.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: XXXVI. 9. From the universal causes of election

XXXVI. 9. From the universal causes of election.

Whose all causes are universal, that same thing is also universal; since a determined effect presupposes determined causes, and conversely, if all causes of election are universal, namely the love of God and the merit of Christ, therefore the election itself will also be universal.

Response: To the minor, which we deny as nakedly accepted. For as to what first concerns the love of God, by which He embraces the elect and which is called the cause of election, that is not general, according to which God wills all to be saved, since that being posited, election is not yet posited; but it is special, restricted to believers alone, whom God pursues with a tighter love than the impenitent. Then, the merit of Christ is the cause of election, not absolutely, insofar as it is offered to all, but limitedly, insofar as it is apprehended through faith and considered with respect to application. From which it follows backwards that the causes of election are not universal, since special love and the merit of Christ imputed through faith do not pertain to all, but only to believers. If anyone with this response is unwilling to accept, to this we oppose an objection taken from the execution of the decree, in this way: That whose causes are universal, that same thing will be universal: the causes of justification and glorification are universal, namely the love of God and the merit of Christ: therefore justification and glorification themselves will also be universal. To this argument Huberus cannot respond unless he either limits the major premise, or in the minor distinguishes between the general and special love of God, and between the merit of Christ considered either by reason of offering or of imputation, which distinction, if it serves regarding the execution, why can it not also be applied regarding the decree itself.

XXXVII. 10. From the annihilation of exhortations.

If predestination is particular, all exhortations to repentance will be superfluous.

Resp. 1. N. C. [Negatur Consequentia]. For we do not defend the absolute Calvinistic decree, by which someone is so rejected that whatever he may do, he nevertheless cannot be saved. II. Huberus himself acknowledges a certain special election. Are exhortations therefore also superfluous for this reason? III. Justification and glorification are particular: Can men therefore not be admonished to repentance, so that they may be justified and glorified?

XXXIIX. 11. From the impediment of faith and repentance.

If election is particular, the reprobate will not be able to believe, because faith, according to them, belongs to the elect: Therefore all zeal for repentance will languish.

Resp. 1. By objection, because Huberus acknowledges that certain ones are specially elected, does he not oppose this argument to himself? For faith belongs to such specially elected ones. Can the rest, therefore, not elected in this way, not be admonished to repentance? II. The solution of this argument depends on the foreknowledge of God. He from eternity foresaw whether men would believe or not; and, because he foresaw that many would not believe, therefore he reprobated them; now indeed these reprobate cannot be made elect because of the infallibility of foreknowledge, yet it does not follow that they cannot, nor ought not, be admonished to repentance. For God wills this to be done, and this very admonition preceded in God's eternal foresight, and therefore it is deservedly applied in time. The whole error, therefore, arises from a confusion of order. It is not to be thought that absolute election preceded, and that the means were ordained afterwards, but the contrary. For as in time admonitions and promises precede, and afterwards either salvation or damnation follows: so also those things preceded in divine foresight, and afterwards the decree of election and reprobation was made. If, therefore, you ask, Can the reprobate believe and perform repentance? I answer: That this is not absolutely impossible, yet God foresaw that he would not believe, and therefore reprobated him. Meanwhile, before God reprobated, He decreed to offer all means of salvation to him, that He might testify to His beneficent will, for which reason they are deservedly offered in time according to the decree of God. Just as, therefore, the damned, after he has been damned, can no longer believe, though he could have before he was damned: so the reprobate, if he is considered after his foreseen impenitence, cannot believe, but if before, he could. Moreover, the heralds of the Word, since the judgments of God are unknown to them, deservedly persist by admonishing, rebuking, and soliciting.

XXXIX. 12. From the danger of desperation: if Election is particular, the foundation of consolation is removed and a window is opened to desperation. For under a particular [election] no one can firmly subsume. Resp. 1. This argument is rightly opposed to the Calvinistic decree, but not to us. For we do not establish that a few are absolutely elected, but orderly, and therefore we concede that election is in a certain way universal, indeed in such a way that everyone who perseveringly believes is elected. Whence one can easily subsume: I believe, and by the help of the Holy Spirit I will persevere, and therefore I am elected.

2. And justification and salvation are particular: But does it follow from this that no one can be raised up regarding the hope of eternal life? Or can no subsumption be made under the promises, which pertain only to believers? This is false, since the consequence is excellent and full of consolation; He who believes in Christ has eternal life (although I do not say, everyone will have life, whether he believes or does not believe) But indeed you have faith: Therefore you will also possess life. In a similar way I can prove the certainty of election, since the reason for it and for salvation is equal, on account of the agreement of the decree and the execution: As long, therefore, as Huber confesses with us a particular glorification, so long will he be able to obtain nothing against us by this and similar arguments. 3. From the doctrine of Huber no more effective consolation flows. For if one hears most of all that all are elected, at the same time he hears, however, that many perish eternally. Wherefore if anyone, being tempted, should fall into such thoughts, that he cannot be more certain of his salvation than an unbelieving man; what peculiar thing will Huberus be able to bring forth from his treasury? If he should urge the universality of election, the tempted man would retort, What does that election profit, in which all unbelievers, all who are to be eternally damned, are included? For since very many of the elect perish, whence shall I be certified of my salvation? This scruple Huberus cannot remove, unless he leads the tempted man to the special promises, concerning believers being certainly saved, concerning the sheep, which shall not be snatched from the hand of God, and the like. For in those certainty adheres, and by them a distinction is made between those to be saved and those to be damned: But when Huberus follows this method of consoling, he brings forward nothing peculiar, but speaks with us. There is therefore no cause that, under the pretext of a more efficacious solace, universal election should be established. For it is certain that that [thing], by itself and without the application which is made through faith, does not lift up tempted souls.

XL. 13. On the reprobation of demons. Universal election also denotes separation; for after the fallen Angels, men were elected to life. Resp. If one wishes to take the word election καταχρηστικῶς (improperly), one will indeed be able to affirm that all men were elected before the fallen Angels, that is, loved by God. We speak of election taken properly and according to the sense of Scripture, where Angels are not to be compared with men, but men with men, because Christ says, I have chosen you out of the world, whence it follows that the election was not made from the Angels, but from the world or from men. For the chosen must be of the same species as that from which it is chosen. Wherefore, although it may be said that men were elected before the Angels, it cannot be said that they were elected from the Angels. Nay, if even this were granted, it would not therefore immediately follow that the election was altogether unordered, and limited by no τάξει (order), so that whether one believes or does not believe, one nevertheless is and remains elected. XLI. And these were the principal σοφίσματα (sophisms) of Huber, the solution of which being known, the response to the remaining evasions will no longer be difficult, so that there is no evident cause why we should depart from the most clear sentence of Scripture: Many are called, but FEW are chosen. Wherefore let the absolute decree be refuted in such a way that an indiscriminate predestination is not established: let the truth be defended in such a way that falsehood is not assumed. For just as evils are not to be done so that goods may come, Rom. 3 v. 8, so falsehoods are not to be fashioned so that truths may be obtained. Truth does not need a lie, but is sufficient unto itself for its own defense, in which may the author of truth himself sanctify and confirm us, to whom be praise and eternal blessing, AMEN.

Latin:

XXXVI. 9. Ab electionis causis vniuersalibus.

Cuius omnes causae sunt vniuersales, id ipsum etiam est vniuersale; siquidem effectus determinatus praesupponit causas determinatas & contra sit omnes causae electionis sunt vniuersales, nempe dilectio Dei & meritum Christi. Ergo & ipsa electio vniuersalis erit.

Resp. Ad minorem, quam nude acceptam negamus. Nam quod primum dilectione Dei concernit, qua electos complectitur & quae electionis causa dicitur, ea non est generalis, secundum qua Deus vult omnes saluos fieri, siquidem illa posita nondum ponitur electio; sed est specialis, ad solos credentes restricta, quippe quos arctiori amore Deus prosequitur, qua impoenitentes. Deinde, meritu Christi electionis causa est, no absolute, quatenus omnibus offertur, sed limitate, quatenus per fide apprehenditur, & respectu applicationis consideratur. Ex quibꝰ retro sequitur, causas electionis vniuersales no esse, cum dilectio specialis, & meritum Christi p fidem imputatum no omnes, sed duntaxat credentes attineat. Quam responsione si quis acceptare nolit, huic instantiam ab executione decreti sumptam reponimus, hoc modo: Cuius causæ vniuersales sunt, id ipsum vniuersale erit: iustificationis & glorificationis causæ vniuersales sunt, nēpè dilectio Dei & meritū Christi: ergo ipsa etiam iustificatio & glorificatio vniuersalis erit. Ad hoc argumentum Huberus respondere nequit nisi vel majorem limitet, vel in minore distinguat inter dilectionem Dei generalem, & specialem, interque meritum Christi, vel oblationis vel imputationis ratione consideratum, quæ distinctio si circa executionem militat, cur non & citra decretum ipsum adhiberi possit.

XXXVII. 10. Ab annihilatione adhortationum.

Si particularis est prædestinatio, omnes adhortationes ad pœnitentiam erunt superuacaneæ.

Resp. 1. N. C. Non enim defendimus absolutum decretū Caluinisticū, quo quis ita sit rejectus vt quodcunq́; etiam agat, saluari tamē nequeat. II. Huberus ipse agnoscit electionem quandam specialem. Num igitur & hac ratione superuacaneæ sunt adhortationes? III. Iustificatio & glorificatio est particularis: An propterea non poterunt homines admoneri ad pœnitentiam, quo iustificentur & glorificentur.

XXXIIX. 11. Ab impedimento fidei & pœnitentiæ.

Si electio particularis est, reprobati non poterunt credere, quia fides, iuxta illos, electorum est: Omne igitur studium pœnitentiæ languescet.

Resp. 1. Per instantiam, quia Huberus agnoscit quosdam specialiter esse electos, annon hoc argumentū sibimetipsi opponit? Fides enim est talium specialiter electorum. An ergo reliqui hoc pacto non electi non poterunt ad pœnitentiā admoneri? II. Solutio huius argumenti dependet à præscientia Dei. Hic ab æterno præuidit, An homines credituri sint, nec nè; Et, quia multos præuidit non credituros, ideò reprobauit; jã verò hi reprobati non quidé possunt fieri electi propter infalibilitatem præscientiæ, attamen non sequitur, quod illi ad pœnitentiam moneri nequeant, nec debeant. Hoc enim Deus fieri vult, & hæc ipsa admonitio in Dei præuisione æterna præcessit, ideoque in tempore merito adhibetur. Totus igitur error ex confusione ordinis oritur. Nõ putandum est, electionem absolutam præcessisse, & post media ordinata esse, sed contrà. Vt enim in tempore præcedunt admonitiones & promissiones, & postea sequitur vel salus vel damnatio: Sic & illa in diuina præuisione antegressa sunt, pòst factum est electionis & reprobationis decretum. Si ergo quæras, An reprobatus possit credere & pœnitentiam agere? Resp. Non esse hoc absolutè impossibile, Deum tamen præuidisse, illum non crediturum, & propterea reprobasse. Interim priusquam Deus reprobaret, omnia salutis media ipsi offerre decreuit, vt suam beneficam voluntatem testaretur, quam ob causam meritò illa in tempore iuxta decretum Dei offeruntur. Sicut ergo damnatus, posteaquàm damnatus est, non potest amplius credere, potuit vero antequam damnaretur: Sic reprobatus, si consideretur post præuisam impœnitentiam, credere nequit, sin antè potuit. Verbi autem præcones, cum ipsis ignota sint Dei iudicia meritò instant, admonendo, increpando, solicitando.

XXXIX. 12. A periculo desperationis: si Electio particularis est, tollitur fundamẽtum consolationis & fenestra aperitur desperationi. Sub particulari enim nemo potest firmiter subsumere. Resp. 1. Decreto Caluinistico, non autem nobis argumentum hoc rectè opponitur. Non enim absolutè paucos statuimus electos, sed ordinatè, ac proindè concedimus electionem quodammodo vniuersalem, ita quidem, vt omnis perseueranter credens sit electus. vndè quis facilè potest subsumere: Ego credo, & auxilio Spiritus S. perseuerabo, ideoquè electus sum.

2. Et iustificatio & saluatio particularis est: Num autem hinc sequitur, quod nemo possit erigi quoad spem vitę æternæ? An nulla potest fieri subsumptio sub promissionibus, tantum credentes attinentibus? Falsum hoc cùm optima sit consequentia & consolationis plena; Qui credit in Christum, habet vitam æternam (licet no dicam, omnis vitam habebit, siuè credat, siue non credat) At vero tu fidem habes: Ergo & vitam possidebis. Pari modo electionis certitudinem probare possum, cum illius & salutis par sit ratio, ob decreti & executionis conuenientiam: Quamdiu ergo Huberus nobiscum fatetur particularem glorificationem, tamdiu & isto & similibus argumentis nihil contra nos obtinere poterit. 3. Ex doctrina Huberi nulla efficacior consolatio fluit. Nam si maximè quis audiat omnes esse electos, simul tamen audit, multos æternum perire. Quáre si quis tentatus in eas cogitationes deueniat, se non posse esse certiorem de salute sua, quam hominem incredulum; quid ex thesauro suo peculiare Huberus proferre poterit? si electionis vniuersalitatem vrgeat, tentatus regeret, Quid illa prodest electio, cui omnes increduli, omnes æternum damnandi sunt inclusi? Quia enim plurimi electorum pereunt, vnde ego de salute mea certificabor? Hunc scrupulum Huberus eximere nequit, nisi tentatum ad speciales promissiones deducat, de credentibus certò saluandis, de ouibus, quæ non rapientur è manu Dei, & similes. In illis enim hæret certitudo, & per illas inter saluandos & damnandos distinguitur: Hanc autem consolandi methodum Huberus cum sequitur, nihil peculiare affert, sed nobiscum loquitur. Nulla igitur causa est, vt sub prætextu efficacioris solatij vniuersalis electio statuatur. Nam certum est, istum per se & sine applicatione, quę fit per fidem, non erigere animos tentatos.

XL. 13. Areprobatione dæmonum. Electio vniuersalis etiam notat separationem; præ lapsis n. Angelis sunt electi ad vitam homines. Resp. Si vocem electionis καταχρηστικῶς quis accipere velit, omnes quidem homines esse electos præ Angelis lapsis, h. est a Deo dilectos, affirmare poterit. Nos a de propria & secundum Scripturæ sensum sumpta electione loquimur, vbi non sunt conferendi Angeli cum hominibus, sed homines cum hominibus, quia Christus ait, Elegi vos de mundo, vnde sequitur electionem factam non esse ex Angelis, sed ex mundo seu hominibus. Nam eiusdem specie esse debet electum, & id ex quo electum est. Quare licèt dici queat homines præ Angelis electos esse, dici tamen nequit, ex Angelis electos esse. Imò si & hoc daretur, non tamē protinus sequeretur, electionem prorsus fuisse inordinatam, nullaque τάξει limitatam, ita vt siuè quis credat, siuè non credat, tamen sit & maneat electus. XLI. Et hæc fuerunt præcipua Huberi σοφίσματα, quorum solutione cognitâ, non erit amplius difficilis & ad cæteras Euasiones responsio, vt nulla sit euidens causa, cur recedere debeamus à clarissima Scripturæ sententia: Multi sunt vocati, sed PAVCI ecti. Quare sic refutetur decretum absolutum, nè statuatur prædestinatio indiscreta: Sic defendatur veritas, nè assumatur falsitas. Vt enim non sunt facienda mala vt eueniāt bona, Rom. 3. v. 8. Sic non sunt effingenda falsa, vt obtineantur vera. Non eget mendacio veritas, sed ad sui defensionem sibi ipsi sufficiens est, in qua nos sanctificet & confirmet ipse veritatis author, cui sit laus & benedictio sempiterna, AMEN.


### Question II. Are all men indiscriminately properly elected unto salvation?: To God Alone Glory

TO GOD ALONE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 20 Disputation VIII. On the Number and Certainty of the Elect

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Heinrich Flugge of Lübeck.

Προοίμιον.

There will be two chapters of this disputation, the one of which will treat of the number of the elect: the other of the certainty, or certain knowledge, of election. Concerning both, special questions occur. For as regards the number of the elect, it is asked: 1. Whether it is infallible? 2. How many men are elected in comparison to the Angels? 3. Whether the number of the elect is smaller than that of the reprobate? Regarding the knowledge of election, two things especially come into controversy. 1. Whether anyone can be certain of his own election and how? 2. Whether the election of others can be known with certainty? We shall therefore briefly disclose our opinion on these five questions.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Henrico Flugge Lubecensi.

Προοίμιον.

DVo erunt huius disputationis capita, quorum alterum aget de electorum numero: alterum de certitudine, vel certa notitia electionis. Circa vtrumque speciales quæstiones occurrunt. Quod enim electorum numerum concernit, quæritur 1. Num ille sit infallibilis? 2. Quot homines in comparatione ad Angelos electi sint? 3. An numerus electorum minor sit, quam reprobatotorum? Quoad electionis notitiam, duo imprimis veniunt in controuersiam. 1. Num quis de sua electione possit certus esse & quomodo? 2. Num aliorum electio certò sciri possit? De his ergo quæstionibus quinque nostram breuiter sententiam aperiemus.


### Question I

I. When it is asked about the number of the elect, this can be understood either of the number itself, which they call the numbering, namely how great it is, or how many thousands of men have been elected; or of the numbered number, or the men numbered, namely who in particular have been elected, or which persons? The Scholastics call the former formal, the latter material. By the former it is asked, How many are elected? By the latter, however, Who are the elected? This distinction can be illustrated by a certain example. As if someone knows that a certain Prince maintains two hundred court ministers, but is ignorant as to who those might be? To him the number of courtiers is both certain and because he knows how many there are; uncertain materially, because he is ignorant of who they are. Whence it is clear that the distinction between the formal and material number is by no means to be rejected. II. Furthermore, when that number is said to be neither increased nor diminished, those two words refer to the numbering number itself, so that neither more nor fewer are saved than those who have been elected to salvation. When, however, it is added, that it cannot be altered, that pertains to the numbered number, or to the men themselves, so that the sense may be: Those who are once elected, always remain elected, and never become reprobate. For there are some of the opinion that the number of the elect, insofar as it is a number, is indeed most certain, since God from all eternity has determined how many thousands of men He wishes to be elected; but with respect to persons it is uncertain, since often he who was once elected loses the crown, and another, who was not previously elected, receives the lost crown, so that the numbered number is as it were altered, while the numbering number meanwhile remains certain and immutable. III. Furthermore, this also is to be noted, that the question here is not about human certainty, namely, whether men certainly know how many and who are the elect? (For to know this is impossible, to wish to investigate it is foolish, and impious, since it is the property of God alone) but about certainty with regard to God, so that the sense of the proposed question may emerge thus: Whether it is immutably certain before God how many men and who are elected? We hold the affirmative, for the following reasons. IV. The first is sought from the sayings of Scripture. 2 Tim. 2. v. 19. The foundation of God stands firm, having the seal of this, The Lord knows who are his, John 13, v. 18. I know whom I have chosen. John 10, v. 11. I know my sheep. Luke 10, v. 20. Your names are written in heaven, Luke 12, v. 7. The hairs of your head are numbered, Rom. 8. 28. Whom he foreknew, he also predestined. Wis. 11, v. 21. You have disposed all things by weight each of the elect, to the extent that he even has their names as if inscribed, the number of the elect must be certain and infallible with respect to God: But the antecedent is true, by virtue of the cited texts. Therefore, so is the consequent.

V. The second is derived from the analogy of faith, God is most wise and omniscient. Wherefore it is not hidden from him how many and who will persevere in believing until the end of life. Whence our thesis immediately follows, that with God the number, both formal and material, is most certain and infallible. For if the number of the elect could be increased or diminished, or altered, it would happen because one could become a reprobate from an elect, and an elect from a reprobate. But this is false, because thus God's foreknowledge and election would be mutable and uncertain, which is absurd.

VI. The third is drawn from the assertions of the Fathers. For thus Augustine writes in the book On Correction and Grace, ch. 12 & 13. He speaks these things concerning those who are predestined in the kingdom of God, whose number is so certain that no one is added to them nor is anyone diminished from them. L. 14, On the City of God, ch. 26. To the almighty God, supreme and supremely good, the creator of all natures, but the helper and rewarder of good wills, and the abandoner and punisher of evil ones, the ordainer of both, there was certainly no lack of counsel by which he might fill the number of the citizens of his city, predestined by his wisdom, even from the damned human race. Prosper, l. 2, On the Calling of the Gentiles, last ch. Concerning the fullness of the members of the body of Christ, the foreknowledge of God, which cannot be deceived, loses nothing: and the foreknown sum cannot be diminished by any detriment.
