The same is established in the Formula of Concord, whose words in article 11 of the declaration, page 812, are these: There is no doubt that God most exactly and most certainly foresaw before the times of the world, and even today knows, which of those who have been called are going to believe in Christ, or are not going to believe: who among the converted are going to persevere in the faith, who are not: and who, having fallen into grave sins, are going to return, and who are going to perish in their crimes. And without doubt also the number of those who will be saved, and of those to be damned, is well known to God.

VII. Furthermore, regarding this question, two things must be well noted. 1. Although the number of the elect is most certain on account of the infallible foreknowledge of God, it is not therefore fatal and absolutely necessary, as if those who are included in this number are absolutely and necessarily saved, while the rest are absolutely and necessarily damned. The absolute Calvinistic decree must here be removed from sight, and it should rather be held that God from eternity determined not only to save some thousands of men out of absolute love, but rather that He willed all to be saved through faith: therefore the others could also have been included in the number of those to be saved, provided they themselves did not despise the merit of Christ, as Christ Himself demonstrates from the examples of the Tyrians, Sidonians, and Sodomites, Matthew 11, verse 21. But since God from eternity infallibly foreknew how many and who would perseveringly believe in Christ, therefore He predestined only these to life and salvation. For if more were going to believe, God would certainly have foreseen these, and thus would have chosen them as well. Wherefore the certainty of the number of the elect does not depend on some absolute and fatal Calvinistic decree, but on the infallible foreknowledge of God, from which it further appears that the number can neither be increased nor diminished, not absolutely and simply, but only by hypothesis. The Lord Dr. Rungius in disputation 13 on the epistle to the Romans, p. 251, explains the whole matter with this example: They are certain, he says, if you look at the number of citizens of any Republic of Letters, inscribed in the register and actually residing in the Academy, as it is in act: but if you look at it as it could be, it is evident that it could be more or fewer: for more could have arrived, and likewise fewer could have departed.

VIII. Hieronymus Zanchius seems to establish this very thing in book 5, de N. D., chapter 2, question 5, page 628, column b, when he says: When we say that this number can neither be increased nor diminished, this can be understood in two ways. Either absolutely and simply, or by supposition. Simply, as if we were to say that in itself it is not possible, nor ever was possible, for more or others to be elected or reprobated. We do not accept those words in this sense, because that would conflict with the omnipotence of God. For could not God have elected both others and more from eternity than He did elect? For election and reprobation were made according to the purpose of His own will. Therefore, it must be said that He can do the same even now, if we look simply at His power. For the power of God always remains the same. It can be understood by supposition, what we have said, in this sense: if God has elected and reprobated so many and such, and neither more nor fewer, it cannot be but that the number of both the reprobate and the elect is so certain that it can neither be increased, nor diminished, nor altered. Thus he. But however much the alleged words of Zanchius may seem to smell of a certain orthodoxy, they include something fatalistic, since he estimates the certainty of the number from the simple good pleasure of God. We, however, do not establish that this certainty depends on a certain absolute decree, by which God willed to elect only these, but rather on foreknowledge. For if those who are not in the number of the elect had not placed an obstacle, nor despised Christ, they would certainly have been assumed into the catalog of the elect together with the others. But after God once decreed to elect only believers, and knows most certainly who are going to believe, He no longer changes His decree, but elects to life only those whom He foresaw would believe. And thus we neither receive a certain fatalistic decree, nor do we introduce uncertainty of the number: but we say that it is certain, but then not on account of some absolute decree, but on account of the infallible foreknowledge of God, from which, however, we do not wish the decree of God, if you understand it as ordered and limited, to be excluded.

IX. 2. There is only one certainty by which the number of the elect is certain, namely the certainty of foreknowledge, which is rightly called the foundation of the decree. Zanchius, however, in the cited place, adds yet another to this former one, namely the certainty of order, by which even if God (these are the words of Zanchius) did not foresee—which is ἀδύνατον—certainly how many and who were to be saved, yet such and so certain an order of means has been established and confirmed for saving so many and such men, that on account of this certain order of the benefits of God, by which whoever are saved are most certainly freed, such a number of such elect men is in itself most certain, so that it can neither be increased or diminished, nor varied. This is what he says. The certainty of this order is again founded on an absolute decree, and therefore it strikes 1. Against the universality of the calling, or of the means. For the Calvinists think that God ordained and prepared those means only for the elect, which we have proven above to be false. 2. Against the ordered election, since they think that God not only prepared for the elect those means which are required for acquiring salvation, but from an absolute and simple will most certainly applies them, from which infallible application of ὀργάνων, proceeding from the absolute εὐδοκία of God, they deduce that absolute certainty of order of theirs. But with the particularity of the calling destroyed, and the absolute election prostrated, which has been done thus far, this Calvinistic certainty of order collapses of its own accord.

Latin:

I. Cùm de electorum numero quæritur, intelligi hoc potest vel de numero ipso, quem numerantem vocant, quantus nimirum sit, siuè quot millia hominum sint electa? vel de numero numerato, seu hominibus numeratis, Quinam in specie electi sint, vel quæ personæ? Scholastici numerum illum formalem, hunc materialem appellant. Illo quæritur, Quot sint electi? Hoc autem, Qui sint electi? Distinctio hæc per exemplum quoddam illustrari potest. Vt si quis scit Principem quendam ducentos ministros aulicos alere, ignoret a. quinam illi sint? huic numerus aulicorum & certus est, & incertus: Certus formaliter, quia nouit quot sint, incertus materialiter, quia ignorat, qui sint. Vnde patet, quòd discrimen inter numerum formalem ac materialem minimè sit reijciendum. II. Porrò, cùm numerus iste nec augeri nec minui dicitur, duo illa verba referuntur ad ipsum numerantem numerum, ita vt nec plures nec pauciores saluentur, quàm qui ad salutem electi sunt. Cùm v. additur, nec alterari posse, id pertinet ad numerum numerátum, vel ad ipsos homines, vt sensus sit. Illos qui semel sunt electi, semper manere electos, nec vnquam fieri reprobos. Sunt enim aliqui in ea sententia, numerum electorum, in quantum est numerus, esse quidem certissimum, siquidem Deus ab omni æternitate constituerit, quot millia hominum velit electa; respectu autē personarum esse incertum, cùm sæpè is, qui semel fuit electus, amittat coronam, & alius, qui anteà electus non erat, amissam coronam accipiat, ita vt quasi alteretur numerus numeratus, certò interim & immutabiliter manente numero numerante. III. Præterea & istud notandum est, non quæri hîc de certitudine, humana, An nempè homines certò sciant, Quot & qui sint electi? (Hoc enim scire est impossibile, indagare velle stultum est, & impium, cùm solius Dei sit proprium) sed de certitudine quoad Deum, vt ita propositæ quæstionis sensus his emergat; Vtrum sit coram Deo immutabiliter certum, quot homines & quinam electi sint? Affirmatiuam tenemus, ob sequentes rationes. IV. Prima petitur ex dictis scripturæ. 2. Tim. 2. v. 19. Firmum stat fundamentum Dei, habens signaculum hoc, Nouit Dominus, qui sint sui, Ioh. 13. v. 18. Scio quos elegerim. Ioh. 10. v. 11. Ego cognosco oues meas. Luc. 10. vers. 20. Nomina vestra scripta sunt in cælis, Luc. 12. v. 7. Capilli capitis vestri numerati sunt, Rom. 8. 28. Quos præsciuit, hos prædestinauit. Sap. 11. v. 21. Omnia in pondere, numero & mensura disposuisti. Ex hisce testimonijs ita colligimus: Si Deus omnes & singulos electos nouit, adeò vt & nomina ipsorum velut adscripta habeat, certum oportet esse & infallibilem electorum numerum, respectu Dei: Sed antecedens verùm est, vi allegatorum textuum. Ergo & consequens.

V. Secunda desumitur ab analogia fidei, Deus est sapientissimus ac omnisciens. Quare ipsum non latet, quot & qui ad finem vsque vitæ perseueranter credituri sint. Vnde mox sequitur thesis nostra, quòd apud Deum numerus tàm formalis, quàm materialis sit certissimus & infallibilis. Si enim numerus electorum augeri minuiue, vel alterari posset, fieret id ideò, quia ex electo posset fieri reprobus, & ex reprobo electus. Hoc autem falsum est, quia sic Dei præuisio, & electio foret mutabilis & incerta, quod absurdum.

VI. Tertia depromitur ex Patrum assertionibus. Ita enim Augustinus scribit lib. de corrupt. & grat. c 12. & 13. Hæc de ijs loquitur, qui prædestinati sunt in regno Dei, quorum ita certus est numerus, vt nec addatur eis quisquam nec minuatur ex eis L. 14. de Civ. Dei. cap. 26. Omnipotenti Deo summo, ac summè bono, creatori omnium naturarum, voluntatum autem bonarum adiutori & remuneratori, malarũ autem relicsori & damnatori, vtrarumque ordinatori non defuit vtique consilium, quo certum numerum ciuium suâ sapientiâ prædestinatum, etiam ex damnato genere humano ciuitatis suæ impleret. Prosper l. 2. de Vocat. gent. cap. vlt. De plenitudine membrorum corporis Christi, præscientia Dei, quæ falli non potest, nihil perdit: & nullo detrimento minui potest summa præcognita. Idem statuitur in Formula Concor. cuius verba articulo 11. declar. pag. 812. hæc sunt: Dubium non est, quin Deus exactissimè & certissimè ante tempora mundi præuiderit, & hodiè etiam nôrit, quinam ex eorum numero, qui vocati sunt in Christum credituri, aut non credituri sint : qui ex conuersis in fide perseueraturi sint, qui non: & quin peccata grauia prolapsi, reuersuri sint, & in sceleribus perituri. Et haut dubiè etiam numerus eorum, qui saluabuntur, & damnandorum, Deo probè notus est.

VII. Vlterius autem circa quæstionem hanc duo probè notanda veniunt. 1. Licèt electorum numerus ob infallibilem Dei præscientiam sit certissimus, proptereà tamen fatalis & absolutè necessarius non est, ac si, qui numero huic sunt inserti, absolutè & necessario saluentur, reliqui verò absolutè & necessario damnentur. Removendum hîc est ex oculis absolutum decretum Caluinisticum, & ita potius habendum, Quòd Deus ab æterno constituerit, non aliquot tantùm millia hominum saluare ex absoluto amore, sed potiùs, quod voluerit omnes fieri saluos per fidem: Potuissent igitur & cęteri referri in numerum saluandorum, modò non ipsi meritum Christi contemnerent, vti Matth 11. v. 21. Christus ipse ab exemplis Tyriorum, Sidoniorum & Sodomitarum demonstrat. Quoniam verò Deus ab æterno infallibiliter præscivit, quot & qui perseueranter in Christum credituri essent, ideò hos tantum ad vitam & salutem prædestinauit. Si enim plures credituri fuissent, hos vtique Deus præuidisset, atque sic & istos elegisset. Quare certitudo numeri alectorum non ex absoluto quodam & fatali decreto Caluinistico, sed à præscientia Dei infallibili dependet, ex quo vlterius apparet, numerum nec augeri nec minui posse, non absolutè & simpliciter, sed tantùm ex hypothesi. Dominus D. Rungius in disput. 13 super epist. ad Rom. p. 251. rem omnem hoc exemplo declarat: Certi sunt, in quit, alicuius Reip: literariæ ciues, in album inscripti & actu in Academia versantes, si numerum spectes, vt actu est: Sin, vt esse poterat, patet, plures vel pauciores esse possit: poterant n. plures accedere, poterant item pauciores abire.

IIX. Hoc ipsum videtur statuere Hieronymus Zanchius l. 5. de N. D. c. 2. q. 5. p. 628. fac. b. dum ait: Cùm dicimus, numerum hunc nec augeri, nec minui posse, bifariam hoc potest intelligi. Aut absolutè & simpliciter, Aut ex suppositione. Simpliciter, vt si dicamus per se non posse, nec potuisse unquam, vel plures vel alios eligi aut reprobari. Hoc sensu non accipimus ea verba, quia id pugnaret cum omnipotentiâ Dei, Annon enim ab æterno potuisset & alios & plures eligere quàm elegit Deus? Est enim facta secundum propositum voluntatis ipsius electio & reprobatio. Ergò idem etiam nunc posse, si simpliciter eius potentiam spectemus, dicendum est. Manet enim eadem semper potentia Dei. Ex suppositione intelligi potest, quod diximus, hoc sensu: si Deus tot & tales elegit ac reprobauit, & nec plures, nec pauciores, fieri nequit, quin ita certus sit numerus tum reproborum, tum electorum, vt nec augeri, nec minui, nec alterari possit. Hæc ille. Vtut verò allegata Zanchij verba orthodoxiam quandam redolere videantur, auramẽ fatale quiddam includunt, quoniam certitudinẽ numeri à simplice beneplacito Dei æstimat. Nos autẽ non ab absoluto quodam decreto, quo hos tantùm voluerit eligere Deus, certitudinem istam dependere statuimus, sed potiùs à præscientia. Si enim ij, qui non sunt in numero electorum, obicem non posuissent, nec Christum contemsissent, vtique in catalogum electorum simul cum alijs assumpti fuissent. Postquam verò Deus semel decreuit, tantùm credentes eligere, nouit autem certissimè, qui sint credituri, jam non amplius mutat decretum suum, sed eos duntaxat, quos præuidit credituros, ad vitam elegit. Atque sic nec recipimus decretum quoddam fatale, nec incertitudinẽ numeri introducimus: sed eum esse certum dicimus, Certum autem non ob decretum aliquod absolutum sed ob infallibilem Dei praescientiam, a qua tamen decretum Dei, si ordinatum & limitatum intelligas, non seclusum volumus.

IX. 2. Vna tantum est certitudo, qua electorum numerus certus est, nimirum certitudo praescientiae, quae decreti fundametum recte dicitur. Zanchius autem dicto loco aliam adhuc priori isti adiungit, nempe certitudinem ordinis, qua etiamsi Deus (sunt verba Zanchij) quod ἀδύνατον non praeuideret certo, quot & qui seruandi essent, tamen talis & tam certus ordo mediorum ad tot & tales homines seruandos constitutus & firmatus est, vt propter ordinem hunc certum beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissime liberantur quicunque liberantur, talis & talium hominum electorum numerus per se certissimus sit, ita vt nec Augeri aut minui, nec variari possit. Haec ille. Ordinis huius certitudo iterum fundata est in absoluto decreto, ideoque impingit 1. In vniuersalitatem vocationis, vel mediorum. Putat enim Caluiniani, Deum media illa tantum ordinasse & praeparasse electis, quod falsum esse, supra probatum dedimus. 2. In electionem ordinatam, quoniam sensent, Deum illa media, quae ad acquirendam salutem requiruntur, non modo praeparasse electis, sed ex absoluta & simplici voluntate certissime applicare, ex qua infallibili ὀργάνων applicatione, ab absoluta Dei εὐδοκίᾳ proueniente, deducunt suam illam absolutam ordinis certitudinem. Sed destructa particularitate vocationis, & prostrata electione absoluta, quod hactenus factum, vltro corruit hec ordinis certitudo Caluinistica.


### Question II. How many men have been elected in comparison to the Angels?

I. We would not move this question, if others before us had not moved it, and dared to decide it. Reports that Thomas, part 1 of the Summa, question 24, article 3, says that some have said that as many men will be saved as there were angels who fell; others, as many as the angels who remained; and others, finally, as many as the angels who were created from the beginning. And indeed Gregory, in homily 35 on chapter 15 of Luke, according to the old calculation, expressly writes: That heavenly city consists of angels and men, to which we believe as many of the human race ascend as there happen to be angels who remained there. He presumes to prove this from the passage in Deut. 32, verse 8, which he rendered from the LXX version as follows: he set the boundaries of the peoples, according to the number of the angels of God. But in the Hebrew it is not 'angels of God,' but 'sons of Israel,' as the Vulgate correctly translates. Lombard follows Gregory in book 2 of the Sentences, dist. 9, letter H; he adds, however, that some have established that men are restored according to the number of the angels who fell.

II. We say, however, that all these things are uncertain and mere conjectures, destitute of solid reasons. For nothing at all has been revealed to us in the Scriptures concerning a certain and defined number of the elect, and therefore we ought not to be wise above what is written. God willed that the exact knowledge of His own be reserved for Himself alone; therefore, we must be silent and at rest, lest while we scrutinize hidden things, we be found illicitly curious.

III. Augustine taught us this in Enchiridion, chapter 29, where he says these words: 'Nor do we know the number either of the holy men or of the unclean demons, in whose place the sons of the holy mother Church, who appeared barren on earth, succeeding them, will remain in that peace from which they fell, without any end of time. But the number of those citizens, whether that which is or that which is to be, is in the contemplation of that Artificer who calls those things which are not as though they were, and disposes all things in measure and number and weight.' Thomas follows Augustine in the aforementioned place, at the end; he says, 'It is better said that the number of the elect to be placed in heavenly felicity is known to God alone.'

Latin:

I. Non moueremus hanc quaestionem, nisi alij ante nos mouissent, & decidere ausi fuissent. Refert enim Thomas par. 1. Summæ quæst. 24. art. 3. quosdam dixisse, tot ex hominibus saluos fore, quot Angeliceciderunt; quosdam, quot Angeli perstiterunt: quosdam denique, quot Angeli ab initio creati sunt. Et sanè Gregorius homil. 35. super cap. 150. Lucæ, juxta veterem supputationem, expressè scribit: Superna illa ciuitas ex Angelis & hominibus constat ad quam credimus tantos humani generis adscendere, quantos illic contingit Angelos remansisse. Probare hoc præsumit ex loco Deut. 32. versu 8. quem ex versione LXX. ita reddidit: statuit terminos populorum, iuxta numerum Angelorum Dei. Verum in Hebræo non est Angelorum Dei, sed Filiorum Israel, vti rectè vertit vulgata, Gregorium sequitur Lombardus lib. 2. sentent. dist. 9. lit. H. addit tamen, quosdam statuisse homines reparari juxta numerum Angelorum, qui ceciderunt.

II. Dicimus autem, hæc omnia esse incerta, merasque coniecturas, solidis rationibus destitutas. Nihil enim quicquam in Scripturis de certo definitoque electorum numero nobis revelatum est, ideoque supra illas sapere non debemus. Deus exactam suorum notitiam sibi soli reservatam voluit, nobis igitur tacendum & quiescendum nè dùm occulta scrutamur, illicitè curiosi deprehendamur.

III. Ita docuit nos Augustinus in Enchir. cap. 29. vbi hæc verba. Neque numerum aut sanctorum hominum, aut immundorum dæmonum nouimus, in quorum locum succedentes filij sanctæ matris Ecclesiæ, quæ sterilis apparebat in terris, in ea pace, de qua illi ceciderunt, sine vllo temporis termino permanebunt. Sed illorum ciuitum numerus siuè qui est, siuè qui futurus est in contemplatione est eius artificis, qui vocat ea, quæ non sunt, tanquam ea quæ sunt, atq; in mensura & numero & pondere cuncta disponit. Augustinum sequitur Thomas loco prædicto, in fine; Melius, inquit, dicitur, quod soli Deo est cognitus numerus electoru, in superna felicitate locãdus.


### Question III. Whether the number of the elect is smaller than that of the reprobate?

I. Although this question lacks difficulty, on account of the sufficiently clear assertion of Scripture, the diverse opinions of the Fathers and Doctors nevertheless cause it to be called into controversy. Wherefore we shall first recite those, and after the decision of the problem we shall subjoin them.

II. 1. This opinion is commonly attributed to Origen: that all rational creatures, both men and angels, will eventually be saved at some time; and that infernal punishments, although after many spaces of time, are to be ended; whence it would follow that all were predestined from eternity, and that our question is idle. And although some wish Origen to be freed from this error, as from the ancients Pamphilus the Martyr and Rufinus; and from the more recent ones Jacques Merlin and Pico della Mirandola: nevertheless his words are clear in Homily 8 on Joshua, Book 1 of περὶ ἀρχῶν ch. 6, and Book 3, last chapter; and the testimony of Jerome in his epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 2, is added, and of Augustine in Book 2 of De Civitate Dei, chapter 17, and of Epiphanius, who prohibited the reading of the books of Origen, as Socrates reports in Book 6, chapter 10.

III. However, this error does not require a prolix ἐλέγχῳ [refutation], since it is not only ἄγραφος [unscriptural], but manifestly ἀντίγραφος [contrary to Scripture]. For thus it is read in Isaiah 66, verse 24: Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched, which saying the Savior teaches is to be understood concerning the damned and the never-ending infernal fire in Mark 9, verse 44. Add to these the following testimonies: Daniel 12, verse 2: They who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to eternal life, others to eternal reproach. Matthew 25, verse 41: Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire. Apocalypse 20, verse 10: The devil who was seducing them was cast into the pool of fire and brimstone, where also the beast and the false prophet shall be tormented day and night, for ever and ever. Augustine urges these sayings primarily in Book 21 of De Civitate Dei, chapter 23. Sixtus of Siena, however, in his Bibliotheca... San. num. 290. brings forward these arguments from Jerome. 1. Because the opinion of Origen cannot be confirmed from the Scriptures. 2. Because in the Gospel the fire of hell is called eternal. 3. Because the fear of God is overturned, and an opportunity is provided for security. 4. Because in this way there would be no future distinction between a virgin and a prostitute; between the mother of the Lord and the victims of public lusts; between Gabriel and the Devil; between the Apostles and demons; between the Prophets and the false prophets; between the martyrs and the persecutors.

IV. 2. There were others who indeed established eternal punishments for demons, but promised salvation to all men on account of the intercessions of the saints. Augustine reports their opinion in book 21 of the City of God, chapter 18, in these words: They say that it was indeed truly predicted by God concerning evil and unfaithful men, that they are worthy of punishment. But when it comes to the judgment, mercy will prevail. For, they say, the merciful GOD will grant them [salvation] through the prayers and intercessions of His saints. But this opinion (which was in some way interpolated by Francesco Pucci in previous years) cannot be proven, and is opposed to the sayings just recited, and is refuted more extensively by Augustine in chapter 24, to which we wish to refer the benevolent reader, so that we do not have to dwell on it any longer.

V. 3. Some have said that the torments of all infidels, namely Turks, Jews, Pagans, and demons, will be perpetual, but that all the baptized, whether they be heretics or Catholics, or certainly all Catholics, whether living piously or impiously, will be saved and deservedly considered among the elect, as Augustine records in book 21 of the City of God, chapters 19 and 20. Some attribute this opinion to Jerome, because of the words which are read in book 1 of the Dialogue against the Pelagians, around title 72, but he is excused by Alfonso Mendoza in Theological Controversies, question 1, position, proposition 2, pages 84, 85.

VI. Conversely, however, this opinion is also entirely erroneous, since Scripture cries out everywhere that no one is justified or saved, unless he believes, but the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers, Rom. 16. v. 16. Ioh. 3. last verse, etc. Saving faith, however, is not bare knowledge and assent, since that falls even to the Devils, Iac. 2. v. 19, but a firm trust resting on the merit of Christ, which is always effective through charity, Gal. 5. v. 6, and without works is dead in itself, Iac. 2. v. 17. Because, therefore, they live and persevere in sins against conscience, these lack justifying faith, and therefore cannot be saved, according to the most certain pronouncement of the Apostle, Rom. 2. v. 9. Wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish, upon every soul of man that works evil. And 1. Cor. 6. v. 9, 10. Neither fornicators, nor adulterers, etc. shall possess the kingdom of God, which he repeats in Gal. 5. v. 21, Eph. 5. v. 5. This apostolic sentence is surely false, if such persons, after however much time, are liberated and will possess the kingdom of God. But since it is not false, surely they will not possess the kingdom of God. And if they will never be in the possession of the kingdom of God, they will be held in eternal punishment. Since there is no middle place, where he who has not been established in that kingdom is not in punishment.

VII. 4. Jerome in Nahum ch. 1 asserted that neither the men suffocated at the time of the flood, nor the Sodomites burned by heavenly fire, nor the Egyptians drowned in the sea were damned: But to all these (these are the words of Jerome) God rendered these punishments in this life, so that He might not punish them eternally. For the salvation of the antediluvians, some urge the passage from 1. Petr. 3. v. 19, 20, where it is said that Christ preached to the spirits in prison who were unbelieving at the time of Noah; whence they gather that they were liberated through Christ and transferred into heaven. But that passage is obscure, and its interpretation is uncertain, so that nothing certain can be inferred from it. Jerome's own opinion, however, is destitute of firm demonstrations, and contradicts the Scriptures diametrically, since in them the antediluvians, Sodomites, and Egyptians are described as having been most malicious, and with an obstinate heart in sins have persevered. And although it may be said that some have repented in the very punishment and agony, yet this cannot be proven, much less should it be affirmed of all.

VIII. Thus, therefore, with the false and doubtful opinions rejected, through which the number of those to be saved and the elect is constituted too large, we shall make plain in a few words what seems to us regarding the proposed question, and that through two distinct positions. IX. PRIOR: If the discourse is about the whole human race, the multitude of the reprobate is far greater and more numerous than that of the elect. This is asserted in set words in Matt. 7, verse 14: 'Narrow is the gate, and strait is the way, which leadeth unto life, and FEW there are who find it.' Now, indeed, a few is opposed to a multitude. If, therefore, few find the way of salvation, certainly many will wander from the straight path and perish eternally, which is clearly asserted in the preceding verse, 13. Whence Jerome says in epistle 14 to Celantia: 'How great is the separation between these ways, and how great the difference? That one tends to death, this one to life. That one is trodden by many, this one is scarcely found by a few.' Furthermore, this very thing is confirmed by that well-worn axiom: Outside the Church there is no salvation. For just as no one was freed from the flood except those who were in the ark of Noah, so no one will be saved unless he has been a member of the Church, as witnessed by Augustine, q. 65 to Orosius. 'Hold most firmly and doubt in no way that not only pagans, but also Jews, heretics, and schismatics, who end the present life outside the Catholic Church, are going to go into eternal fire,' says the same in 'On Faith to Peter,' chapter 38. Now, indeed, there are always more outside the Church than in the Church. For in the Old Testament, God's people were contained within the borders of Judea alone, Psalm 76, verse 1; Psalm 147, verse 10; Isaiah 3, last verse. In the New Testament, how many Gentiles are not inserted into the body of CHRIST? All Jews, all Turks, and pagans and the like remain outside. How many souls have perished in the vast regions of the New World, discovered a hundred years ago and more? How many children, how many adults, how many old men damned are condemned; If such a comparison is therefore instituted, few believe at all, few bring back the end of faith, the salvation of souls.

X. THE LATTER: Among Christians and those devoted to the true religion, there are more reprobates than elect. We shall say nothing of the various Heretics, with respect to whom the true Church, professing the true doctrine, is a little flock, Luke 12, v. 32. But let us look at the members of the holy religion themselves. Among these, there are by far more hypocrites and malicious persons than those endowed with true faith and devoted to good works. Christ taught this in the parable in Luke 8 concerning the seed scattered in the field, of which only a fourth part bears fruit, v. 15, while three parts of the hearers perish. Experience, alas, confirms this, while we see daily that the greatest part devotes itself to gluttony, avarice, ambition, and other vices. Charity is extinguished, faith has perished, simplicity is mocked, deceit reigns, and the needy is suppressed. The holy one has truly failed, and the faithful have been consumed from among the children of men, Psalm 11, v. 1. The holy one has perished from the earth, and there is no upright person among men, Micah. 7, v. 2. There is no truth, there is no mercy, there is no knowledge of God in the land. Cursing and lying and murder, and theft and adultery have overflowed, Hosea 4, v. 1, 2. Such persons, however, cannot possess the kingdom of God, and therefore, although many are called; many live in the Church, yet few are chosen, Matthew 20, v. 17. Few are they who are saved, Luke 13, v. 23, merely a remnant, Romans 11, v. 5, the residue in Jerusalem, Isaiah 4, v. 3, a few olives, Isaiah 24, v. 15, a few grapes, Micah 7, v. 1, redeemed from among men, Revelation 14, v. 4. The wicked, however, walk about in the circuit, or all around, Psalm 11, v. last. For the scope and center is reached with difficulty, but it is easy to wander from it; as the breadth of the circuit is manifold, but the center is simple and invisible: Thus very few attain the scope of faith and the center of blessedness; but very many dwell in the circuit of iniquity with the eternal destruction of their souls. From six hundred thousand men, only two arrived in the land of Canaan: thus, very rare are those who from among Christians arrive at the heavenly fatherland: most will remain exiles from it in the vast solitude of the Tartarean desert. All indeed run, but not all receive the βραβεῖον, 1 Cor. 9. v. 24. For more run to punishment than to glory; more are friendlier to vices that flatter badly than to the useful harshness of virtues, Aug. lib. 2. de C. D. c. 19. And for more, the goad of desires, the heap of miseries, and the sting of troubles are a hindrance, as Bernard speaks in his sentences. And to this point looks the complaint of Chrysost. homil. 40. ad Pop. Antioch. How many, he says, do you think there are in this city of ours who are saved? It is a hateful thing that I am about to say, yet I will say it. There cannot be found among so many thousands a hundred who are saved, and indeed I even doubt about these. For how great is the malice in the young? How great is the torpor in the old?

XI. Meanwhile, when there is talk of the paucity of the elect, all blame and cause should be transferred not to God or some absolute decree, but only to men. For God did not reprobate such a multitude of men out of hatred, but by just judgment, since He wills all to be saved, and would have predestined all to life, had they not themselves been unwilling, like the Jerusalemites, Matth. 23. v. 38. They spurned the counsel of God with the Pharisees, Luc. 7. v. 30. They resisted the Holy Spirit with the Jews, Act. 7. v. 51. and repelled the word of the Gospel, judging themselves unworthy of eternal life, Act. 13. v. 46. Thus, therefore, perdition is from men, salvation is from God alone, Ose. 13. v. 9. For that opinion is detestable and abominable which believes God to be the author of any evil will or action, as witnessed by August. ad art. 10. falsely imposed upon him.

XII. If, furthermore, we wish to know specifically why many are reprobated and follow the way of perdition, Christ hints that it is τὸ πλάτος, or breadth, Matth. 7. v. 13. Wide, he says, is the gate and spacious is the way that leads to perdition. That breadth consists for him in the fleshly inclination, the ease of erring, the variety of those who seduce, and the plurality of those who accompany, which a pagan man, Seneca, considering in Epistle 80, skillfully left written: We are easy toward worse things, because neither a leader nor a companion can be lacking: And the thing itself proceeds even without a companion, without a leader. The path is not only prone to vices, but precipitous.

XIII. If, however, it is asked why few persist on the way of salvation, the cause is rendered by Christ as τὸ ςενὸν or the narrowness itself, while He says, Narrow is the way which leads to life. Referred to this narrowness are the slipperiness of those going, the multiplicity of those failing, the rarity of those persisting, and the difficulty of the journey. Hugo brings these and other causes in chapter 7 of Matthew, when to the question of why few are chosen and saved, he responds thus: Because there is no diligence in seeking. Because in those seeking there is blindness of station, perversity of the concupiscible, the subtlety of the deceiving Devil, in us the proneness to falling, the difficulty of rising again, the weakness of resisting, and the multiplicity of those drawing us away from the way.

XIV. Therefore, let us beware of these causes and incitements to evils, rather than conceive a scruple from the fewness of those to be saved. If you desire to be of the number of the elect, strive to follow the examples of the pious. You hear that very many are damned, why therefore do you not think about your own salvation? Therefore, let us consider the fewness of the elect in such a way that we lay aside all security. Nor for that reason are you to despair, since you follow Christ as leader and you will easily enter. Few are of the number of the elect, but persevere in faith, and you will be of the number of the few. For no one is excluded by God through an absolute decree; but men destroy themselves through continued vice. And although they are few elect relatively, many nevertheless are elect in themselves and absolutely. Thus, therefore, fear, lest you despair: so trust, lest you become secure, but rather acknowledge the divine goodness regarding the elect, human depravity regarding the reprobate, and therefore flee the latter, proclaim the former, to which We are admonished by Augustine, book 2, On Grace and Free Will, chapter 8, with whose words we conclude: That grace is given to the few in comparison to those who perish, but in their own number they are delivered by many; it is given freely, thanks are to be given for grace.

Latin:

I. Quamvis hæc quæstio difficultate careat, ob claram satis Scripturæ assertionem, faciunt tamen diuersæ Patrum & Doctorum opiniones, vt sub controuersiam vocetur. Quare primùm istas recitabimus, post decisionem problematis subjungemus.

II. 1. Origeni vulgò tribuitur hæc opinio, Omnes creaturas rationales, & homines, & Angelos tandē aliquando saluatum iri; & pœnas infernales, licèt post multa temporum spacia, finiendas esse; vnde, tum omnes fuissse ab æterno prædestinatos, tum quæstionem nostram otiosam esse sequeretur. Et licèt nonnulli Origenem ab hoc errore liberatum velint, vt ex antiquis Pamphilus Martyr, & Ruffinus; ex recentioribus Iac. Merlinus, & Picus Mirandulanus: luculenta tamen ejus verba sunt homil. 8. in Iosu. lib. 1. περὶ ἀρχῶν c. 6. & 3. c. ult. & accedit testimonium Hieronymi in epist. ad Eph. cap. 2. 4. Augustini l. 2. de C. D. c. 17. & Epiphanij, qui lectionem librorū Origenis prohibuit, referente Socrate l. 6. c 10.

III. Prolixo autem ἐλέγχῳ error hic non indi get, cùm non modò sit ἄγραφος, sed manifestè ἀντίγραφος. Ita enim legitur Esa. 66. ver. 24. Vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis eorum non extinguetur, quod dictum de damnatis, & igne infernali nunquam finiendo, intelligendum esse Saluator docet Marc. 9. versu 44. Adde his sequentia testimonia Dan. 12. versu 2. Qui dormiunt in terræ puluere, euigilabunt, alij in vitam æternam, alij in opprobrium æternum Matth. 25. v. 41. Discedite à me maledicti in ignem æternum. Apoc. 20. versu 10. Diabolus qui seducebat eos, missus est in stagnum ignis & sulphuris, vbi & bestia & Pseudopropheta cruciabuntur die ac nocte, in secula seculorum. Vrget hæc dicta imprimis Aug. l. 21. de C. D. c. 23. Sixtus autem Senensis BibliothSan. num. 290. profert ex Hieronymo haec argumenta. 1. Quia opinio Origenis ex Scripturis confirmari nequeat, 2. Quia in Euangelio ignis inferni dicatur aeternus 3. Quia evertatur timor Dei, & praebeatur ansa securitati. 4. Quia hoc pacto nulla sit futura distantia inter virginem & proftibulum; inter matrem Domini, & victimas libidinum publicarum; inter Gabrielem & Diabolum; inter Apostolos & daemones; inter Prophetas, & Pseudoprophetas; inter martyres & persecutores.

IV. 2. Fuere alij, qui daemonum quidem poe nas aeternas statuerunt, omnibus v. hominibus ob sanctorum intercessiones salutem promiserunt. Refert eorum sententiam Aug. l. 21. de C. D. c. 18. his verbis: Dicunt de malis & infidelibus hominibus diuinitus quidem verum praedictum esse, quod digni sunt poena. Sed cùm ad iudicium ventum fuerit, misericordiam esse superaturam. Donabit enim eos, inquiunt, misericors DEVS precibus & intercessionibus sanctorum suorum. Verùm & haec opinio (quę à Franc. Puccio superioribus annis quodammodo interpolata est) probari nequit, & modò recitatis dictis aduersatur, & ab Aug. c. 24. fusiùs refutatur, quò benevolu Lectorem remissum volumus, ne diutius immorari necesse habeamus.

V. 3. Quidam dixerunt, omnium quidem infidelium, videlicet Turcarũ, Iudaeorum, Paganorum, & daemonum tormenta fore perpetua, omnes autem baptizatos, siue sint haeretici, siue Catholici, vel certè omnes Catholicos, piè aut impiè viuen tes saluatum iri, & pro electis meritò haberi, memorante Aug. l. 21. de C. D. c. 19. & 20. Nonnulli hanc opinionem tribuunt Hieronymo, ob verba quae leguntur l. 1. dial aduer. Pelag. circa. tit 72. sed excusatur ab Alphonso Mendoza in controv. Theol. quaest. 1. posit. propos. 2. pag. 84. 85.

VI. Vicissim autem & haec sententia prorsus est erronea, cùm Scriptura passim clamitet, neminem iustificari aut saluari, nisi credat, sed iram Dei manere super omnes incredulos, Rom. 16. v. 16. Ioh. 3. vers. ult. &c. Fides autem saluifica non est nuda notitia & assensus, quippè qui cadit etiam in Diabolos, Iac. 2. vers. 19. sed firma fiducia merito Christi nixa, quæ per charitatem semper est efficax, Gal, 5. vers. 6. & sine operibus mortua est in semetipsa, Iac. 2 vers. 7. Quia ergo in peccatis contra conscientiam vivunt & perseuerant, hi fide iustificante carent, ideoque saluari nequeunt, secundum certissimum Apostoli pronunciatum, Rom. 2. v. 9. Ira & indignatio, tribulatio & angustia, in omnem animam hominis operantis malum. Et 1. Cor. 6 v. 9. 10. Neƣ fornicarij, neƣ adulteri &c. possidebunt regnum Dei, quod repetit Gal. 5. v. 21. Eph. 5. v. 5. Hæc profectò apostolica falsa est sententia, si tales post quantalibet tempora liberati regnum Dei possidebunt. Sed quoniam falsa non est, profectò regnum Dei non possidebunt. Et si in regni Dei possessione nunquam erunt, æterno supplicio tenebuntur. Quoniam non est locus medius, vbi non sit in supplicio, qui illo non fuerit constitutus in regno.

VII. 4. Hieronymus in Nahum cap. 1. asseruit, nec homines tempore diluvij suffocatos, nec Sodomitas igne cœlesti combustos, nec Ægyptios in mari submersos fuisse damnatos: Sed his omnibus (sunt verba Hieronymi, ) hæc supplicia in hac vita reddidit Deus, ne in æternum puniret. Pro salute diluvianorum nonnulli vrgent locum ex. 1. Petr. 3. v. 19. 20. vbi dicitur Christus Spiritibus tempore Noëh incredulis prædicasse in custodia; vnde colligunt, illos per Christum liberatos, & in cœlum translatos esse. Sed locus ille obscurus, eiusque interpretatio incerta est, vt nihil inde certi inferri queat. Ipsa autem Hieronymi opinio firmis demonstrationibus destituitur, & Scripturis è diametro contradicit, quippe in quibus diluviani, Sodomitę & Ægyptij sic describuntur, quòd malitiosissimi fuerint, & obstinato corde in peccatis perseuerauerint. Et licèt dicatur quosdam in ipso supplicio & agone resipuisse, probari tamen hoc nequit, multo minus de omnibus affirmari debet

IIX. Sic igitur reiectis opinionibus falsis dubisque, per quas saluandorum & electorum numerus nimis magnus côstituitur, quid nobis de quaestione propositâ videatur, paucis planum faciemus, idéque per duas distinctas positiones. IX. PRIOR: Side vniuerso genere humano sermo sit, longè maior & numerosior est multitudo reproborum, quàm electorum. Conceptis verbis hoc asseritur Matth. 7. vers. 14 Angusta porta, & arcta via est, quæ ducit ad vitam, & PAVCI sunt qui inueniunt eam. Iam verò paucitas opponitur multitudini. Si ergò pauci salutis viam inueniunt, vtique multi à recto tramite aberrabunt, & æternùm peribunt, id quod clarè asseritur præced. vers. 13. vnde Hierony. ait epist. 14. ad Celan. Quanta inter has vias separatio sit, quantumque discrimen? Illa ad mortem, hæc tendit ad vitam. Illa teritur à multis, hæc vix inuenitur à paucis. Confirmatur insuper hoc ipsum pertritum illud ἀξίωμα: Extra Ecclesiam non est salus Sicut enim in arca Noah nemo, nisi qui in ea erat, à diluuio liberatus est: Ita nullus nisi Ecclesiæ membrum fuerit, saluabitur, teste Aug. q 65 ad Oros. Firmissimè tene & nullatenus dubites non solùm paganos, sed etiam Iudæos, hæreticos & Schismaticos, qui extra Ecclesiam Catholicam præsentem finiunt vitam in ignem æternum ituros, ait idem de fide ad Petrum cap. 38. Iam verò semper plures sunt extrà Ecclesiam, quàm in Ecclesia. In veteri enim Testamento solis Iudææ finibus continebatur Dei populus, Psal. 76. vers. 1. Psal. 147. vers. 10. Eja. 3. v. vlt. In Nouo Testamento quot gentilis CHRITI corpori non sunt inserti? Extra manent omnes Iudæi, omnes Turcæ, & pagani & similes. Quot animæ perierunt in vastissimis noui orbis regionibus, ab hinc annis centum, & quot excedit, adinuentis? Quot pueri, quod adulti, quot senes damnati damnati sunt; Talis igitur collatio si instituatur, pauci omninò credunt, pauci finem fidei, salutem animarum reportant.

X. POSTERIOR: Inter Christianos & veræ religioni addictos, plures sunt reprobati, quàm electi. Nihil dicemus de Hæreticis varijs, quorum respectu Ecclesia vera, veramque doctrinam profitens est pusillus grex, Luc. 12. v. 32. Sed ipsos sacræ religionis socios intueamur. Inter hos longè plures sunt hypocritæ & malitiosi, quàm verâ fide præditi, bonisque operibus dediti. Docuit hoc Christus in parabolâ Luc 8. de semine in agrum sparso, cuius quarta tantum pars fructificat v. 15. pereuntibus tribus auditorum partibus. Confirmat hoc, proh dolor! experientia, dum videmus quotidiè, ut maxima pars gulæ, avaritiæ, ambitioni cæterisque vitiis det operam. Extincta est charitas, periit fides, ridetur simplicitas, regnat dolus, & supprimitur egenus. Verè defecit sanctus, & consumti sunt fideles à filiis hominum Psal. 11. v. 1. Perijt sanctus de terra & rectus in hominibus non est. Mich. 7. v. 2. Non est veritas, non est misericordia, non est scientia Dei in terra. Maledictum & mendacium & homicidium, & furtum & adulterium inundaverunt, Ose. 4 v. 1.2 Tales autem regnum Dei possidere nequeunt, ideoque licet multi sint vocati; multi vivant in Ecclesia, pauci tamen sunt electi, Matth. 20. v. 17. Pauci sunt, qui salvantur, Luc. 13. v. 23. reliquiæ duntaxat, Rom. 11. v. 5. residui in Ierusalem. Esa 4. v. 3. paucæ olivæ Esa 24. v. 15. pauci racemi, Mich. 7. v. 1. emti ex hominibus, Apoc. 14. v. 4. Impij verò in circuitu, vel circumquaque obambulant, Psal. 11. v. ult. Vtonim scopus & centrum difficilè attingitur, sed facilè ab illo erratur; vt multiplex est latitudo circuitus, simplex verò & invisibile centrum: Sic paucisimi scopum fidei & centrum beatitudinis assequuntur; plurimi verò in circuitu iniquitatis cum æterno animarum exitio versantur. Ex sexcentishominum millibus duo tantùm pervenerunt in terrâ Canaan : Sic perrari sunt, qui ex Christianis ad cœlestem patriam perveniunt : plerique ab illa exules in deserti Tartarei vasta solitudine permanebunt. Omnes quidem currunt, sed non omnes βραβεῖον accipiunt, 1. Cor. 9. v. 24. Plures enim currunt ad pœnam, quam ad gloriam; plures vitijs malè blandientibus, quam vtili virtutum asperitati sunt amiciores, Aug. lib. 2. de C. D. c. 19. Et pluribus obest stimulus cupiditatum, cumulus ærumnarum, aculeus molestiarum, vti Bernardus loquitur in sententiis. Et huc spectat querela Chrysost. homil. 40. ad Pop. Antioch. Quot, inquit, putatis esse in hac civitate nostra, qui salvi fiant? Infestum est, quod dicturus sum, dicam tamen. Non possunt inveniri in tot millibus centum, qui salventur, quin & de his dubito. Quanta enim in iuvenibus malitia? Quantus in senibus torpor?

XI. Interim cùm de paucitate electorum sermo sit, non in Deum vel absolutum aliquod decretum, sed in homines tantùm culpa & caussa omnis transferri debet. Non enim Deus ex odio, sed iusto iudicio tantam multitudinem hominum reprobavit, siquidem omnes vult salvos fieri, & ad vitam prædestinasset omnes, nisi nollent ipsi cum Hierosolymitanis, Matth. 23. v. 38. Consilium Dei spernerent cum Pharisæis, Luc. 7. v. 30. Spiritui S. resisterent cum Iudæis, Act. 7. v. 51. & verbum Evangelij repellerent, indignos iudicantes seipsos æternâ vitâ. Act. 13. v. 46. Sic igitur ex hominibus est perditio, ex Deo tantùm salus Ose. 13. v. 9. Detestanda enim & abominanda opinio est, quæ Deum cuiusquam malæ voluntatis aut actionis authorem credit, teste August. ad art. 10. falsò sibi impositum.

XII. Si porrò scire volumus in specie, cur multi sint reprobati, & viam perditionis sectentur, Christus eam esse innuit τὸ πλάτος, vel latitudinem, Matth. 7. v. 13. Lata inquit, porta & spatiosa via est, quæ ducit ad perditionẽ. Cõsistit illi latitudo in carnis procliuitate, errandi facilitate, seducentium varietate, & comitantium pluralitate, quam considerans gentilis homo Seneca epist. 80. scitè scriptum reliquit: Ad deteriora faciles sumus, quia neque dux potest neque comes deesse: Et res etiam ipsa sine comite, sine duce procedit. Non pronum est iter tantùm ad vitia, sed præceps.

XIII. Si verò quæratur, cur pauci viam salutis insistant, causa redditur à Christo τὸ ςενὸν vel ipsa angustia, dum Arcta, inquit via est, quæ ducit ad vitam. Refertur ad istam angustiam lubricitas euntium, deficientium multiplicitas, persistentium raritas, itineris difficultas. Affert has & alias causas Hugo in cap. 7. Matth. dum ad quæstionem cur pauci electi sint & saluentur, ita respondet: Quia non est in quærendo sedulitas. Quia in quærentibus istationis cœcitas, concupiscibilis perversitas, Diaboli fallentis subtilitas, in nobis cadendi pronitas, resurgendi difficultas resistendi debilitas, retrahentium à via multiplicitas.

XIV. Ab his igitur caussis & malorum irritamentis potiùs caveamus, quàm vt scrupulum ex paucitate saluandorum concipiamus. Si cupis esse de numero electorum, studeas sequi exempla piorum. Plurimos damnari audis, cur ergò de salute tua non cogitas? Proindè sic consideremus electorum paucitatem, vt deponamus omnem securitatem. Nec tibi ob id est desperandum cùm Christum ducem sequaris & facilè intrabis. Pauci sunt de numero electorum, sed in fide perseueres, & eris de numero paucorum. Nullus enim à Deo excluditur per decretum absolutum; sed homines seipsos perdunt, per vitium continuatum. Et licèt pauci sint electi respectiuè, multi tamen sunt electi in se ac absolutè. Sic ergò timeas, ne desperes: ita confidas, nè securus fias, sed potius agnoscas bonitatem diuinam circà electos, pravitatem humanam circa reprobos, ideoque hanc fugias, illam prædices, ad quod monemur ab August. l. 2. de grat. & correp. c. 8. cuius verbis concludimus: Quod pauci in comparatione pereuntium, in suo autem numero liberantur multis, gratia fit, gratis fit, gratiæ agendæ sunt.


### Question IV

I. This whole question is practical, and has the greatest use in temptations, when a scruple pricks the conscience concerning the certainty of eternal election and future blessedness. But as it is commonly said that in the matter of salvation some doubt, some despair, some trust: so from the diverse opinions concerning the doctrine of election, an occasion is provided for either doubting, or despair, or faith. Doubt is generated by the hypotheses of the Papists; despair by those of the Calvinists. But those who teach that one ought to trust, in turn use diverse principles. Huber seeks certainty in the universality of election; Puccius promises salvation to all upright people, even those living outside the Church. But because all these are erroneous, therefore our people have hitherto usefully prescribed other means of certainty and consolation.

II. It is evident, however, from that divorce of opinions, that there are primarily five different practices concerning the business of our election, which Lord Doctor Cram. recounts in chapter 10, page 301. He calls the first Pyrrhonian or Academic, which is that of the doubting Papists. The second is called hypocritical or presumptuous, which is that of the Calvinists, who introduce either security or despair. The third is insufficient, namely that of Huber; the fourth indeed absurd, namely that of Puccius. The fifth finally is true and salutary, which is ours.

III. It will hardly be necessary for us to add much concerning the error of Huber and Puccius. For we refuted the former in the preceding disputation; the latter we judge unworthy of a lengthy refutation. Therefore, very few words can suffice for both.

IV. Huber's opinion is that, unless a universal election is established, the tempted person cannot be raised up, since under a particular one there is no firm subsumption. We, however, respond: As long as an indiscriminate and universal election is merely urged, no one is made certain of his own salvation. For if you conclude most strongly, 'Someone is elect because he is a man,' nevertheless no consolation comes to the tempted person from that, since he hears that most of the elect are damned. Wherefore that general election is insufficient for the certainty of salvation, and it is necessary that one should arrive at special promises, which, if they are not absolutely universal, are nevertheless universal in a limited way and with respect to believers, so that therefore the subsumption may not be doubtful or weak. From Huber's doctrine, however, such consolation cannot be sought, since he affirms that no one can be certain of his own perseverance in faith. If, therefore, any tempted person should urge this argument: 'He who shall have persevered will be saved; I, however,' do not know whether I am going to persevere; how, therefore, shall I be able to be confident about my salvation? Then Huber is able to answer nothing solid, and therefore he is deservedly exploded with his insufficient practice.

V. Francesco Pucci was a deceiver and a falsifier of the entire Christian religion. He issued a little book in the year 1592, which he entitled 'Catholic Assertion, agreeable to divine and human equity, proved by the consent of the entire Holy Scripture and the Holy Fathers, by the Spirit of discernment, by one hundred and twenty reasons, concerning the efficacy of Christ the Savior in all and singular men, insofar as they are men,' and he dedicated it to the Roman Pontiff, Clement VIII. He fashioned such a predestinarian practice, therefore, that every man, if he studies virtue—which he asserted he could do most easily by the power of free will—is certainly elect and will be saved. 'To us,' he says in the preface, 'has shone the Gospel, which declares and gives faith that all and singular men, by the benefit and universal grace of the supreme Father, are saved through CHRIST,' so that no one may perish eternally; except he who by his own perpetual ingratitude and malice in this life prepares for himself eternal punishments. Thus, therefore, through this most gross error, all foundations of the faith are torn up, and not a window, but a wide gate is opened to security and Epicureanism, and therefore it ought rather to be wrapped in perpetual silence than refuted at greater length: For how could or can the Gentiles be saved outside the Church, when the Gospel was hidden from them Rom. 16. v. 25. 26. 27. Coloss. 1. v. 26. 27. 1. Cor. 2. v. 7. 8. 9. Since they were ignorant of Christ the author of salvation, without the knowledge of whom no one is saved, Rom. 3. v. 25. Gal. 3. v. 7. 16. Hebr. 11. v. 6. But we shall add no more; if anyone, however, desires more, we wish him to be referred to the lengthy refutation of D. Lucas Osiander, opposed to this Puccian [error].

VI. And thus, having briefly discussed the absurd opinions of Huber and Pucci, it remains to treat of the threefold practice, namely, 1. of the Papistic, 2. of the Calvinistic, 3. of the true and Orthodox: That this may be done distinctly, we shall include the whole matter in three peculiar members.

Latin:

I. Quæstio hæc tota practica est, & in tentationibus vsum habet quàm maximum, quando conscientiam vellicat scrupulus de certitudine æternæ electionis, & futurę beatitudinis. Vti autem vulgò dicitur, quòd in re salutis quidam dubitent, quidam desperent, quidam confidant: Sic ex diuersis circà doctrinam electionis opinionibus, vel dubitationis vel desperationi, vel fidei occasio subministratur: Dubitatio per Pontificiorum; desperatio per Caluinianorum hypotheses gignitur. Qui verò confidendum esse docent, vicissim diuersis principiis vtuntur. Huberus in electionis vniuersalitate certitudinem quærit: Puccius, salutem probis omnibus, extra Ecclesiam quoq; viuentib. promittit. Quia verò erronea sut hęc omnia, idcircò alia certitudinis & solatij media Nostri hactenus vtiliter pręscripserunt.

II. Patet autem ex illo sententiarum diuortio, quinque imprimis diuersas dari praxes circa electionis nostræ negotium, quas: Dn. D. Cram. c. 10. p. 301. recenset. Primam appellat Pyrrhonicam vel Academicam, quæ est Pontificiorum dubitantium. Secunda dicitur hypocritica vel pręsumtuosa, quę est Caluinianorum, vel securitatem vel desperationem introducentium. Tertia est insufficiens, nimirum Huberi, Quarta verò absurda, nempè Puccij. Quinta denique vera & salutaris, quæ nostra est.

III. De Huberi & Puccij errore multa vt addamus necessarium vix erit. Illum n. disp. præced. refutauimus: hunc prolixo ἐλέγχῳ indignum iudicamus. Verba ergò paucissima vtrique sufficere possunt.

IV. Huberi mens est, Nisi statuatur vniuersalis electio, tentatum erigi non posse, quoniam sub particulari non datur firma subsumtio. Nos a. respondemus, Quamdiu electio indiscreta & vniuersalis tantùm vrgetur, de salute sua nemo certificatur. Si n. maximè concludas, Aliquē electum esse, quia sit homo: nihil tamen solatij tentato indè accedit, cùm plerosq; electorum damnari audiat. Quare insufficiens est illa electio generalis ad certitudinem salutis, & necesse est, vt deueniatur ad promissiones speciales, quę si maximè non absolutè, tamen limitatè & respectu credentium sunt vniuersales, vt proptereà subsumtio non sit dubia vel infirma. Ex Huberi v. doctrina talis consolatio peti nequit, quandoquidem de sua in fide perseuerantiâ neminem posse certum esse adfirmat. Si quis ergò tentatus hoc argumentum vrgeat; Qui perseuerauerit, salvus erit; Ego a. num perseueraturus sum, scire nequeo; De salute igitur mea quî confidere potero; Tum nihil solidi Huber. respondere potis est, ideoque cum insufficienti sua praxi meritò exploditur.

V. Franciscus Puccius illusor fuit & falsarius totius Christianæ religionis. Emisit hic libellum Anno 1592. quem inscripsit Assertioneã Catholicam, æquitati diuinæ & humanæ consentaneam, vniuersæ Sacræ scripturæ & S.S. Patrum consensu Spiritu discretionis, centum & viginti rationibus probatam, de Christi Servatoris efficacitate in omnibus & singulis hominibus, quatenus homines sunt, cumque dedicauit Romano Pontifici, Clementi IIX. Talem igitur praxin prædestinatoriam effinxit, quod omnis homo si virtuti studeat, id quod ipsum vi arbitrij facillimè posse asseruit, certò electus sit, & saluetur. Nobis, inquit in præfatione, affulsit Euangelium, quod declarat ac fidem facit omnes & singulos homines, beneficio & gratiâ vniuersali summi Patris esse per CHRISTVM saluatos, sta vt nullus in æternum pereat; nisi qui suā perpetua ingratitudine & malitia in hac vita sibi æternas pœnas parat. Sic ergò per hunc crassissimum errorem, omnia fidei fundamenta conuelluntur, securitati & Epicureismo non fenestra; sed lata porta panditur, ideoque silentio potiùs perpetuo inuolui; quam prolixiùs refutari debet: Qui enim gentiles extra Ecclesiam saluari potuerunt vel possunt, cum̄ Evangelium ijs fuerit absconditum Rom. 16. v. 25. 26. 27. Coloss. 1. v. 26. 27. 1. Cor. 2. v. 7. 8. 9. Cùm Christum salutis authorem ignorarint, sine cuius cognitione nemo saluatur, Rom. 3. v. 25. Gal. 3. v. 7. 16. Hebr. 11. v. 6. Sed plura non addemus, Si quis tamen plura desideret illum ad D. Lucæ Osiandri prolixam refutationem, de huic Pucciano oppositam, remissum volumus.

VI. Atque ita breuiter discussis Huberi & Puccij absurdis opinionibus; de triplici adhuc praxi agendum restat, nempè, 1. de Papistica. 2. de Caluinistica. 3. de vera & Orthodoxa: Quod vt distinctè fiat, tribus peculiaribus membris rem omnem includemus.


### Question IV: VII. Member I. concerning Papistic Practice

VII. MEMBER I. CONCERNING PAPISTIC PRACTICE.

This is rightly called Academic, since it approaches the opinion of the ancient philosophers, named from the Academy. They taught that all things are uncertain, and they were occupied in a perpetual τῆς ὑπολήψεως ἀπάτῃ, or fallacy of subsumption. They conceded the general thesis, as, that all snow is white; but in the subsumption they always doubted, whether this or that snow is white? Whence Aristotle writes in 2. Prior, cap. 21, in such examples that κατὰ τὴν ὑπόληψιν γίνεσθαι τὴν ἀπάτην, that is, that deception occurs by estimation or subsumption. The Papists stick in the same error of subsumption. For although they say that all believers and those who do good works are predestined: yet they judge that it must by no means be subsumed, nay, they pronounce anathema upon all who do subsume in the Council of Trent, Sess. 6, can. 15: No one, they say, as Paterculus says in ch. 12, as long as he lives in this mortality, ought to presume so far concerning the secret mystery of divine predestination, as to determine for certain that he is altogether in the number of the predestined. This opinion of the Council is defended by Gregorius de Valentia, T. 1, quæst. 23, pun. 6, ass. 4, and Becanus, Tr. 1, c. 14, quæst. 6, §. 6, and very many others, establishing that it can indeed be affirmed in general that those who believe perseveringly and work well are elect. But for you, whether you have been reckoned among the elect, you must always be in doubt, unless you wish to incur the Tridentine anathema.

VIII. This opinion of the Papists, in the place concerning justification, is accustomed to be refuted by various arguments, such as are taken from: 1. The firmness of divine promises. 2. The oath of God. 3. The efficacy of the Sacraments. 4. The testimony of the Holy Spirit in our hearts. 5. The certain hearing of prayers. 6. The true property of faith. 7. The deformity of doubt, while it is a torture of consciences, a workshop of desperation, takes away true solace, and renders all Christian doctrine suspect, as if it could not firmly guide the tempted and imbue them with efficacious consolation. To which arguments we add the testimonies of sounder Papists, such as are read in the Enchiridion Coloniense edited in the year 36, fol. 170. in the writings of Ambrosius Catharinus, in the treatise of Martin Eysengrein, in the book of Udalricus Pinder, and of Petrus de Ribadeneira, the Jesuit of Spain, which Ægidius Albertinus, Bavarian Secretary, translated into the German language, and published with the license of superiors at Munich, in the year 1600. I do not transcribe the words, since they can be read in the booklet of Mr. Dr. Cramer concerning predestination, ch. 10, p. 309, et seqq.

IX. The Papists, however, urge two sayings in particular, the solution of which we shall append, deferring the rest to the place concerning justification.

THE FIRST is taken from Prov. 20, verse 9: Who can say, My heart is clean, I am pure from sin less? Here they wish it to be noted that the style of Solomon is such that he did not say that no one is pure in heart, but that no one can say or know that his heart is pure. If, therefore, a man is ignorant of the purity of his own heart, who will be able to be certain of predestination?

Resp. 1. In Hebrew it is זכיתי I have cleansed & טהרתי I have purified. This, therefore, can be the first explanation, that this saying is opposed to hypocrites & Pharisees, who wished to be justified by their own powers, & to be immune from every sin. Solomon therefore censures the arrogance of these. And although Bellarmine objects that the opinion among the Jews was constant that the cleansing of the heart proceeds from God alone, it is nevertheless not to be doubted that there were many hypocrites & false prophets who attributed purity not to divine grace alone, but to the powers of nature, against whom King Solomon argues here.

2. Nothing is said here about the uncertainty of grace, but only the imperfection of our justice & holiness is hinted at, so that the sense is: No one in this life is entirely pure & immaculate. 1. because of the habitual corruption of nature. 2. because of the actual commission of venial sins, since all saints feel within themselves the struggle of the flesh & the Spirit. What, then, is the consequence? Our holiness here is not entirely & perfectly consummated, but only begun: Therefore, one ought to doubt about the remission of sins & salvation. If we were inherently just, then indeed the Papists would obtain something. But now we are rendered just by the alien & most perfect obedience of Christ. Therefore, we cannot doubt. Hence it is to be noted that the remission of sins is one thing, & renewal is another: The former is perfect & complete, because it rests upon a perfect foundation, namely the obedience of Christ: But this latter is begun & imperfect, because the subject in this life always remains liable to corruption. Let it therefore be held as a rule; From the imperfection of renewal, to the imperfection or uncertainty of justification and predestination there is no consequence. But when Bellarmine urges sayings in which it seems to be said that men in this life also are pure and immaculate, such as are Psal. 50 & 118, Matth. 5, Ephes. 1 & 2, Tit. 2, all those are to be understood either 1. of the holiness and purity of Christ imputed; or 2. of that which is begun, or 3. of that which is compared to the reason of others, especially hypocrites: But in no way of that which is inherent and consummated, since this is contrary to universal Scripture.

2. THE LATTER is read in Eccl. 9, verse 1. There are just and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God, and yet man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred, all things are kept uncertain for the future. Hence they conclude that the grace of God is uncertain in this life: but that on the last day finally everyone will know whether he is under grace or otherwise.

Resp. 1. By counter-argument: If this passage is understood absolutely, this absurdity would follow, that no one could know whether he is worthy of hatred. But if anyone believed in Christ, and exercised himself in the pursuit of good works, could such a one not know whether he is worthy of hatred or grace? Why therefore is it said in Rom. 8, verse 13, If you mortify the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, you shall live? Why is it said v. 16, The Spirit bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God? And 1 John 3, v. 14, We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers? And do not the Papists defend the merit of congruity and condignity? Do they not say, To a man doing what is in him, God cannot deny grace? Likewise, that the works of the reborn merit life by condignity? How therefore do they not know whether they are worthy of hatred or love? And how would the Martyrs suffer such torments, if they are ignorant whether they are worthy of hatred or love? Furthermore, since Ecclesiastes speaks universally, how will the Papistic exposition have a place regarding the impious and obstinate sinners? Do they also not know that they are worthy of hatred? Why then did Cain and Judas despair? Bellarmine excepts that Solomon is speaking only of the righteous. But the words are indefinite, which are equivalent to a universal. גם אהבה גם שנאה אין יודע האדם whence it is clear that the discourse is about the pious and the impious. That of the latter no one can know whether he is worthy of hatred is contrary to: 1. Scripture. 2. Experience and manifest examples. The Jesuit Salmeron saw this, and therefore on 1 Cor. 12, disp. 14, he writes thus: This passage by no means proves what some take from it, that a man does not know the love of God toward him, because it follows in the text: He does not know whether he is worthy of hatred. But the impious, on account of their greatest crimes, know that they are most worthy of the hatred of God.

2. There is a fault in the Vulgate version. For those words, 'All things are kept uncertain for the future,' which the Papists urge most strongly, are clearly not found in the Hebrew. Arias Montanus's version has it thus: 'The righteous and the wise are in the hand of God: also love, also hatred, man does not know, all is before their faces.' Therefore, from the faulty Vulgate version, the Papists weave a faulty argument, which, among others, Mercerus, a Parisian Professor, observed, discoursing on this passage thus: 'You must be careful, reader, not to err with the Vulgate interpreter, or to take an occasion for erring with the Sophists, who teach that we ought not to be certain in our conscience of the love of God.' This is openly against the Scriptures and the head of our faith concerning the remission of sins.

3. Either this passage is understood of different men, or of the same one. If of different ones, then the sense is that one man, however wise, yet cannot certainly know or pronounce concerning his neighbor whether he is in grace or hatred. And Luther seems to have indicated this sense in his German Bibles, which he translates thus: 'I have taken all this to heart to search out all this, that the righteous and the wise and their works are in God's hand; yet' no man knows either the love or the hatred of anyone which he has for himself. It happens to one as to the other. The reason is immediately added, because man sees only external things, and from them can judge. But all these things are equal, and common to the pious and the impious: Therefore no one can know who is truly pious and worthy of love, who impious and worthy of hatred. And because of this the human heart is wicked, as it is said in v. 3, while it sees its malice can be so dissimulated that no one knows whether it is pious. And to this seem to tend the words הכל לפניהם all that is before their faces: So that the sense may be, Man does not know how to judge even of him who daily moves before his face and eyes. Some render האדם as a genitive, in this way: Not knowing the love of man all before their faces. And this certainly seems a fitting interpretation, from which it sufficiently appears that no patronage for the Popish doubt accrues from this passage. For what is the consequence: One cannot be certain of another's piety and grace, since external judgments are fallible: Therefore, also no one can be certain of his own piety? This inference is weak, since from the uncertainty of another's state to the uncertainty of one's own righteousness there is no consequence. But if the words are understood of the same man, then they can be taken either absolutely or limitedly. The Papists take them absolutely, as if the sense were: Man is completely ignorant, and from no thing at all can he know, whether he is truly justified, or worthy of hatred or love. But this exposition has no place because of the stated objections. For how will a man, avoiding all mortal sins, be ignorant whether he is worthy of hatred? Therefore this passage ought to be taken limitedly, namely that a man does not know whether he is under grace, if he wishes to make a judgment from external events. For he himself immediately adds this reason, because the event of all is one. He does not therefore speak ἁπλῶς [simply], that a man is completely ignorant, but that from an external event, from his state and condition he cannot know that. Thus Caietanus himself expounded it, whose words are these: Solomon signifies that from external things we cannot discern good or evil. But what a consequence: Man does not know grace or hatred from external events. Ergo, he does not know it at all? From the negation of one to the negation of the other, the inference is not valid. We illustrate this response with a similar passage, which is read in Ecclesiastes 3, verse 21: Who knows whether the spirit of man ascends upward? Which words likewise are not understood absolutely but limitedly, regarding external events, namely that no one can know and recognize from external things whether the spirit of man is immortal, or indeed mortal like that of beasts? As therefore those words, so also these are to be accepted limitedly.

4. It is a doubt what ought to be understood by grace and hatred, whether divine hatred, or indeed that of men. The Papists understand it as divine, but it seems more convenient if human hatred is understood, so that the sense is: This is altogether to be pitied, that even the wisest of all do not sufficiently know men, whether they ought to love them and receive them into friendship as pious, or indeed hate them as impious? The reason is because from external events a judgment cannot be established, since all things happen alike. We prove this interpretation from verses 4 and 5, where it is said: that the living indeed are loved, but after death both love, and envy, and their hatred ceases. For a living dog is better than a dead lion. Therefore Solomon wishes to intimate this: This misery lasts only until death; but when men depart, then envy and hatred cease. But before they die, it is uncertain whether we ought to love or hate them. This interpretation, since it is both conformable to the text and to the analogy of faith; nothing stands in the way of it being retained.

Latin:

VII. MEMBRVM I. DE PRAXI PAPISTICA.

Recte vocatur hæc. Academica, quoniam accedit ad opinionem Philosophorum veterum, ab Academia denominatorum. Docebant hi, omnia incerta esse, & versabantur in perpetua τῆς ὑπολήψεως ἀπάτῃ, seu fallacia subsumtionis. Generalem thesin concedebant, vt, omnem niuem albam esse; sed in subsumtione semper dubitabant, num hæc vel illa nix alba sit? Vnde Aristoteles scribit 2. prior cap. 21. in exemplis talibus κατὰ τὴν ὑπόληψιν γίνεσθαι τὴν ἀπάτην, id est, existimatione vel subsumtione fieri deceptionem. In eodem subsumtionis errore hærent Papicolæ. Quāuis enim omnes credentes & benè operantes prædestinatos dicant: minimè tamen subsumendum esse iudicant, imò subsumentibus omnibus anathema denunciant, in Concilio Trid. Sess. 6. can. 15. Nemo, inquiunt Paterculi c. 12. quamdiu in hac mortalitate viuit, de arcano divinæ prædestinationis mysterio vsque adeò præsumere debet, vt certò statuat, se omninò esse in numero prædestinatorum. Hanc Concilij sententiam defendit Gregorius de Valentia T. 1. quæst. 23. pun. 6. ass. 4. & Becanus Tr. 1. c. 14. quæst. 6. §. 6. & plerique alij, statuentes, in genere quidem adfirmari posse, quòd perseveranter credentes, & benè operantes sint electi. Tibi verò, num inter electos relatus sis, semper dubitandum esse, nisi anathema Tridentinum velis incurrere.

IIX. Hæc Papicolarum sententia, in loco de iustificatione varijs argumentis refutari solet, qualia desumuntur. 1. A diuinarum promissionum firmitate. 2. A Dei iuramento. 3. A Sacramentorum efficacia. 4. A. Spiritus S. testimonio in cordibus nostris. 5. A certa precum exauditione. 6. A vera fidei proprietate. 7. A dubitationis deformitate, dum est carnificina conscientiarum, officina desperationis, verum solatium adimit, omnem doctrinam Christianam suspectam reddit, ac si tentatos firmiter regere & efficaci consolatione perfundere nequeat. Quibus argumentis addimus testimonia saniorum Papicolarum, qualia leguntur in Enchiridio Coloniensi edito Anno 36. fol. 170. in scriptis Ambrosij Catharini, in tractatu Martini Eysengrein, in libro Vdalrici Pinder, & Petri de Riebadeneyra Iesu Witæ Hispani, quem Ægidius Albertinus, Secretarius Bauaricus, in Germanicam linguam transtulit, & cum licentia superiorum Monachij edidit, Anno 1600. Verba non adscribo, cum illa legi possint, in libello Dn. D. Crameri de prædest. c. 10. p. 309. seqq.

IX. Vrgent autem Papicolæ duo imprimis dicta, quorum solutionem adponemus, cætera ad locum de iustificatione differentes.

PRIUS desumtum est ex Prov. 20; vers. 9. Quis potest dicere, Mundum est cor meum, purus sum à peccæ? Hic notari volunt stylum Salomonis, quòd non dixerit. Neminem esse purum corde, sed neminem posse dicere aut scire, cor suum esse purum. Si ergo ignorat homo puritatem cordis sui, qui certus esse poterit de prædestinatione?

Resp. 1. In Hebr. est זכיתי mundavi & טהרתי purificavi. Potest igitur hæc esse prima explicatio, quòd dictum istud sit oppositum hypocritis & Pharisæis, qui ex propriis viribus volebant iustificari, & ab omni peccato immunes esse. Horum ergò arrogantiam taxat Salomon. Et licèt Bellarminus excipiat, constantem fuisse apud Iudæos sententiam mundationem cordis à solo Deo prouenire, dubitandum tamen non est, multos fuisse hypocritas & Pseudoprophetas, qui munditiem non soli gratiæ diuinæ, sed naturę viribus acceptam tulerunt, contra quos hic disserit Rex Salomon.

2. Nihil hîc dicitur de incertitudine gratiæ, sed innuitur duntaxat imperfectio nostræ iustitiæ & sanctitatis, vt sit sensus. Neminem in hac vita vndiquaque esse purum & immaculatum. 1. ob corruptionem naturæ habitualem. 2. ob commissionem peccatorum venialium actualem, siquidem omnes sancti sentiunt in sese luctam carnis & Spiritus. Quæ v. consequentia? Sanctitas nostra hic non est vndiquaq; & perfectè consummata, sed tantùm inchoata: E. de remissione peccatorum & salute dubitari debet. Si inhærenter essemus iusti tum quidem aliquid obtinerent Pontificij. Iam v. alienâ perfectissimâque Christi obedientiâ reddimur iusti. Dubitare igitur non possumus. Proindè notandum, quòd aliud sit remissio peccatorū, & aliud renovatio: Illa perfecta est & completa, quia nititur fundamento perfecto, nempè obedientiâ Christi: Hæc autem inchoata est & imperfecta, quia subiectum in hac vita corruptioni semper manet obnoxium. Teneatur ergò regula; Ab imperfectione renovationis, ad imperfectionem vel incertitudinem iustificationis & praedestinationis nulla est consequentia. Cum verò Bellar vrget dicta in quibus dici videtur, quòd homines in hac etiam vita sint mundi & immaculati, qualia sunt, Psal. 50. & 118. Matth. 5. Ephes 1 & 2. Tit. 2. Illa omnia intelligenda sunt, vel 1. de sanctitate & mundicie Christi imputata; vel 2. de inchoata, vel 3. de comparata ratione aliorum, praesertim hypocritarum: Nullo autem modo de inhaerente consummataque quoniam hoc vniuersae Scripturae contrariatur.

2. POSTERIVS legitur Eccl. 9. versu 1. Sunt iusti atque sapientes, & opera eorum in manu Dei, & tamen nescit homo, vtrum amore an odio dignus sit, ambia in futurum seruantur incerta. Hinc concludunt incertam esse Dei gratiam in hac vita : vltimo autem die demum quemvis esse cogniturum, an sub gratia sit vel secus.

Resp. 1. Per instantiam: Si absolutè intelligatur hic locus, sequeretur absurdum hoc, neminem scire posse an odio sit dignus. Si quis autem crederet in Christum, inquè studio bonorum operum sese exerceret, num talis scire non posset, an odio vel gratiâ dignus sit? Cur ergò dicitur Rom. 8. versu 13. Si spiritu facta carnis mortificaueritis, viuetis? Cur dicitur v. 16. Spiritus reddit testimonium nostro spiritui quòd sumus filij Dei? & 1. Ioh. 3. v. 14. Scimus, quod translati sumus de morte in vitam, quia diligimus fratres? Et annon Pontificij meritum congrui & condigni defendunt? Annon dicunt, Homini facienti quod in se est, Deum non denegare posse gratiam? Item, opera renatorum ex condigno mereri vitam? Quomodo igitur nesciunt, an odio vel amore digni sint: Et quomodo Martyres tanta tormenta patientur, si ignorant, vtrum odio digni sint vel amore? Praeterea, cùm Ecclesiastes vniuersaliter loquatur, quomodo expositio Papistica locū habebit circa impios & obstinatos peccatores? An & hi nesciunt, se odio dignos esse? Cur ergò Cain & Iudas desperabant? Excipu Bellarminus Salomonem duntaxat loqui de iustis. Atqui verba sunt indefinita, quæ æquipollent vniuersali. גם אהבה גם שנאה אין יודע האדם vnde patet, sermonem fieri de piis & impijs. Horum v. neminem scire posse, an odio dignus sit, contrariatur. 1. Scripturæ. 2. Experientiæ & manifestis exēplis. Vidit hoc Iesussta Salmeron, ide ò- que super 1. Cor. 12. dif. 14. sic scribit: Hic locus nequaquam probat, quod aliqui inde accipiunt, hominem nescire amorem Dei erga se, quia sequitur in textu: Nescit an vel odio dignus sit. At impij propter maxima sua scalera nôrunt, se maximè dignos esse odio Dei.

2. Vitium est in vulgata versione. Verba euim ista, Omnia in futurum seruantur incerta, quæ Pontificij maximè vrgent, planè non reperiuntur in Hebræo. Ariæmontani versio ita habet: Iusti sunt & sapientes, seruitia eorum in manu Dei: Etiam amorem, etiam odium non sciens homo, omnis ante facies eorum. Ex vitiosa igitur vulgata versione vitiosum argumentum nectunt Papicolæ, quod inter cæteros obseruauit Mercerus, Professor Parisiensis, ita de hoc loco differens: Cauendum est, lector, ne cum vulgato interprete aut erres, vel cum Sophistis occasionem errandi sumas, qui docent, non debere nos esse certos in conscientia de amore Dei. Hoc est apertè contra Scripturas, & fidei nostræ caput de remissione peccatorum.

3.
