Vel intelligitur hic locus de diuersis hominibus, vel de eodem, Si de diuersis, tūc sensus est, quod vnus homo, quamuis sapientissimus, tamen certò scire aut pronunciare de proximo haut queat, an sit in gratia, vel odio. Et hunc sensum videtur indicâsse Lutherus in Biblijs Germanicis, qui sic vertit: Ich hab solches alles zu Hertzen genommen zu forschen das alles das Gerechte vnnd Weisen sind/vń ihre Vnterthane in Gottes hãd/doch keñet kein Mensch weder die Liebe noch den Hass irgend eines / den er für sich hat/Es begegnet einem wie dem andern. Ratio statim additur, quia homo tantùm externa videt, & ex ijs judicare potest. Ista a. omnia sunt paria, & pijs impijsœ; communia: Nemo igitur scire potest, quis sit verè pius & amore, quis impius & odio dignus. Et propter hoc pravum est cor humanum, vt i dicitur v. 3. dum videt malitiam suam ita posse dissimulari, vt nemo cognoscat, an sit pius. Atque huc videntur facere verba הכל לפניהם omnis qui ante facies eorum: Vt sit sensus, Homo nescit judicare etiam de eo, qui quotidiè ante faciem & oculos eius obuersatur. Quidam האדם per genitivum reddunt, hoc modo: Non sciens amorem hominis omnis ante faciem eorum. Et hæc certè videtur conueniens interpretatio, ex qua satis apparet, nihil ex hoc loco patrocinij accedere dubitationi Papisticæ. Quæ enim est consequentia: Non potest alter de alterius pietate & gratia certus esse, quoniam externa judicia sunt fallibilia: E. & nemo de sua pietate potest esse certus? Infirma est hæc illatio, quoniam ab incertitudine aliena subsiste ad incertitudinem propriæ iustitiæ nulla est consequentia. Quòd si autem de eodem homine intelligantur verba, tunc accipi possunt vel absolutè, vel limitatè. Absolutè accipiunt Pontificij, ac si sensus foret: Planè nescit homo, & ex nulla omninò re cognoscere potest, an verè sit justificatus, an odio vel amore dignus. Ast hæc expositio ob dictas instantias locum non habet. Quomodo enim homo, vitans omnia peccata mortalia ignorabit, nùm dignus sit odio? Proindè locus hic accipi debet limitatè, nempè hominem nescire, an sit sub gratia, si Iudicium velit facere ex eventibus externis. Ipse enim statim addit rationem hanc, quia omnium eventus vnus est. Non igitur ἁπλῶς loquitur, quòd homo planè desciat, sed quòd ex euentu externo, ex statu & conditione istud scire nequeat. Sic expopit Caietanus ipse, cuius hæc verba: Significat Salomon, ex rebus externis nos non posse discernere bonum aut malum. Quæ autem consequentia: Homo ex eventibus externis non cognoscit gratiam vel odium. E. planè non cognoscit? A negatione unius ad negationem alterius non valet collectio. Hanc responsionem illustramus simili loco, qui legitur Eccl. 3. versu 21. Quis novit, an spiritus hominum ascendat sursum? Quæ verba itidem non intelliguntur absolutè sed limitatè, quoad externos eventus, nempè neminem posse ex externis scire & cognoscere, an spiritus hominis sit immortalis, an verò mortalis sicut jumentorum? Vt igitur ista verba, ita & hæc limitatè sunt accipienda.

4. Dubium est, quid per gratiam & odium intelligi debeat, an odium divinum, an verò hominum. Pontificij intelligunt divinum, sed convenientius videtur esse, si intelligatur odium humanum, vt sensus sit? Hoc omninò miserandum est, quòd etiam sapientissimi quique non satis cognoscant homines, vtrum istos debeant diligere & in amicitiam recipere, tanquam pios, an verò odisse tanquam impios? Ratio est quia ex eventibus externis judicium nequit institui, cùm omnia pariter eveniant. Probamus hanc interpretationem ex vers. 4. & 5. vbi dicitur: quòd viventes quidem diligantur, sed post mortem cesset & amor, & invidia, & odium eorum. Canis enim vivus est melior Leone mortuo. Hoc ergò vult Salomon innuere: Durat hæc miseria tantùm vsque ad mortem; quando autem decedunt homines, tunc desinit invidia & odium. Antequam verò moriantur, incertum est, an eos debeamus diligere vel odisse. Hæc interpretatio, cum & textui conformis sit, & analogiæ fidei; nihil obstat, quò minus retineri queat.


### Question IV: XL Member II. on Calvinistic Practice

XL MEMBER II. ON CALVINISTIC PRACTICE.

Since the Calvinists know, Such premises suggest themselves, from which the way leads either to security or to doubt and despair; hence some wish the doctrine of predestination to be wrapped in silence rather than that words be spoken about it publicly: and therefore Beza in the Colloquy of Montbéliard did not wish to dispute about that matter. But we respond with Augustine, tract. 21 in John: Why were they said, unless to be known, unless to be heard? Why were they heard, unless to be understood? And for this reason, more recent Calvinists disapprove of Beza's timidity and do not blush to descend into the arena, yet they discourse in such a way that they are clearly stuck in practice, nor can they convert their theory into a salutary use.

XII. In order to demonstrate this, we premise this thesis: While the Calvinistic doctrine stands, no tempted person can be raised up, no one doubting about his election or salvation can be confirmed. We can establish this assertion with such an argument: He who ought to believe that God has chosen from the whole human race only some, and indeed the smallest part, out of an absolute and completely hidden εὐδοκίᾳ for eternal life, cannot firmly conclude that he himself is chosen and to be saved. But every Calvinist ought to believe that. Therefore, he cannot firmly conclude his own election and salvation. The major premise is certain, since under a particular, absolute, and entirely arcane decree, one cannot invincibly subsume. For what kind of argument would this be, and what consequence? God chose very few, whom He willed, without any regard for faith. Therefore, did He also number you among those chosen? Immediately the tempted person will object that he doubts this very thing, nor does he hear any argument by which he might be raised up.

XIII. For if you send him away to the revealed will of God, he will soon object, according to Calvinist hypotheses, that it is only the will of sign, but that he himself is in doubt about the will of good pleasure and the arcane will. For since these, when sometimes entirely contrary to that which is revealed, the tempted person will not be able to be persuaded from the Scriptures that God sincerely loves him and wishes him to be saved: But whatever is said, he will reply to that, that he hears the sign, but is ignorant of the good pleasure. If you press the merit of Christ, the response will be ready: that Christ died effectively not for all, but only for a very few. But how can he believe that he is included among those? If you urge universal promises, neither will those suffice, since they are restricted only to the kinds of individuals, not the individuals of the kinds. If you commend the use and efficacy of the sacraments, the tempted person will not acquiesce, but will reply that these pertain to the will of the sign, but do not show the secret good pleasure.

XIV. And thus nothing remains which can be solidly opposed to the temptation of Satan, and which can supply firm consolation to the mind of the doubter, from which we conclude that the Calvinistic dogma is not divine and Apostolic. For as all Scripture, so also all doctrine deduced from the Scriptures, makes for our consolation, Rom. 15 v. 4, and correction, 2 Tim. 3 v. 20. But indeed the Calvinistic dogma concerning the absolute decree neither raises up anxious minds with true παρακλήσει [consolation], nor secure ones with solid παιδεύσει [instruction], as has been shown thus far. Wherefore it is not a dogma founded in the Scriptures, or deduced from the sacred letters.

XV. But in order to free themselves from this difficulty, they prescribe different modes of consolation and certainty, which it will not be a waste of effort to run through in a few words. Zanchius, book 5 de N. Dei, ch. 2, p. 648, teaches first in general, that everyone is bound to believe that he is elected to eternal salvation in Christ; and he wishes no one to be excepted here, not even the reprobate. But this is a vain evasion, since it is evident from it that the Calvinists can console no one, unless they assume a falsehood. For that all are elected is false. And yet they say that everyone is bound to believe this. Are we therefore also obliged to believe false things are we bound? Then see book 5, De Natura Deorum, chapter 2, thesis 1, page 658, and following; he commemorates three primary modes of ratifying election.

XVI. He calls the internal testimony of the Spirit the FIRST. The Holy Spirit, he says, while He testifies internally to our spirit, that is, to our minds illuminated by His light, that we are children of God, most clearly reveals that we were predestined from eternity εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν. But besides the fact that this mode, as it is explained by Zanchius, seems to attribute much to Enthusiasm, we especially desire this, that it is not perpetual, but expires entirely during more serious temptations, when no sense of either faith or the testifying Spirit is perceived, when there are terrors within and fightings without, 2 Cor. 7:5, and our heart condemns us, 1 John 3:20, so that with David we think ourselves cast out from the face of God, Psalm 31:22. when mere lightnings and thunders are before our eyes, namely the immutable wrath and justice of God, the inflexible vigor of the law, the unbearable atrocity of sins, the intolerable torments of hell, the implacable mockery of the Devils, as Augustine speaks somewhere. Although, therefore, in a quiet time, when we are established outside of temptation, the Holy Spirit bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God, Rom. 8:16, yet when temptation encroaches, that ceases, and therefore it is not παιδεύειν. To which we also add this, that it is necessary for Calvinists always to remain in doubt whether that μαρτύριον proceeded from the Holy Spirit or rather from a certain carnal confidence, since they themselves teach, and everywhere inculcate, the absolute and thoroughly unknowable decree of God.

XVII. Zanchius takes the SECOND mode of confirming election from the Word or Gospel. It is manifest, he writes on page 659, that God, through the word of the Gospel, where He pronounces all the faithful to be elect, reveals His predestination to each faithful person. It is only required that the faithful person, having heard the universal propositions, assumes in his own mind: But I, by the grace and gift of God, am faithful, etc. But neither can it remove every scruple of doubt in this way. For 1. It is not perpetual, since it finds no place in the time of temptation. For how shall one who is tempted assume that he believes, when he doubts about this very thing, and feels no πληροφορίαν in his soul? 2. It is uncertain and weak. For while an absolute decree stands, the certainty of faith cannot stand. For whence shall anyone be confirmed that he can have and conceive faith? From the Word? But this contains only the will of the sign. From the promises? But these are particular. From the Sacraments? But these signify, they confer nothing. Wherefore this scruple will always remain, I do not know whether God seriously wishes to have mercy on me; because His will is hidden, nor is it revealed by any means. And even if I should wish most of all to believe, I am nevertheless ignorant whether this faith is temporary, whether it is living, since I have known many deceived in this persuasion, and I have no word, no promise, upon which I can firmly lean. Here, therefore, let the Calvinists exert themselves, and prescribe a method, how a man is to be raised up if he doubts whether God wishes to infuse faith into him, since He instills it into very few, and indeed out of an absolute good pleasure? They can bring forward nothing solid if they have denied the universality of the serious will, of the satisfaction of Christ, and of the divine promises.

XXIX. The THIRD method of making predestination known is sought from the effects. God, he says p. 660 a., seals us to Himself in Christ by the effects impressed upon our senses: and He seals us in such a way that, if we diligently turn our mind to it, we can recognize from it not obscurely that we have been selected from the rest of the crowd of men, and predestined to eternal life. He renders a double reason p. 661. both because causes are known through effects; and because they are expressly the forms of divine election. He enumerates, however, p. 661. three effects in particular. 1. Christ inhabiting. 2. Effectual calling. 3. Justification, to which he refers sanctification, a good conscience, unfeigned charity, patience in adversities, glorying in tribulations, etc. But, 1. We concede that these things testify to election, if one understands 'to believe' as an act: but what will happen in the time of temptation, when one doubts all these effects? Is he to be left as a reprobate without any consolation? 2. No one can be confirmed of the effect, unless he is first certain of the operation of the cause. But by what arguments will the Calvinists prove that GOD, the cause of these effects, wills to operate certainly in this or that individual? For with the universality of the will denied, and an absolute decree posited, no ὑπόληψις can be made. But as long as the doubter is not persuaded that God seriously wills to produce the said effects in him, so long can he not be confirmed of their presence and truth.

XIX. And thus, from what has been said so far, it may be clear that all the methods noted by Zanchius are both insufficient and uncertain, and in the time of temptation, about which there is the greatest dispute, can provide no effective consolation. Nor could Zanchius himself deny this, while he writes in his Miscellanea, fol. 302, that only a probable certainty of election flows from Scripture, where he uses these words: 'I have taught that this will, namely whom God has predestined to life or death, is not simply revealed in the Scriptures concerning individuals, but is only PROBABLY indicated from the effects.'

XX. Most Calvinists follow Zanchius, handing down the same methods, although in other words and a little more distinctly, just as a certain politician in a German book brings forward double signs of certainty: Internal and External. He says the internal ones are: 1. The testimony of the Holy Spirit. 2. The struggle of the Spirit against the flesh. 3. True faith in Christ. The external ones, however, are: 1. Repentance and amendment of life. 2. Serious study of hearing the word of God. 3. Salutary use of the Sacraments. 4. True and constant invocation of God in the name of Jesus Christ. 5. True confession of Christ. 6. Final perseverance and constancy. However much they do not Let us admit that these are signs of election and means of consolation, yet they cannot be used by Calvinists as long as they defend an absolute decree. For it can be certain to no one regarding the truth or the certainty of these effects, unless the beneficent will of God to give and communicate them is presupposed. But this cannot be presupposed and certainly apprehended unless it is established that it is universal. But if anyone imagines the grace of God for himself without the Word, it is mere presumption and hypocrisy. Furthermore, the elect of God often fall into mortal sins, as is evident from the example of David and Peter, where if the conscience awakens and exaggerates the crime committed, and no sense of those τεκμηρίων (proofs) is present, as is wont to happen in vehement temptations, from where then shall consolation and the certainty of election be sought?

XXI. Bucanus indeed in his Institutions, place 35, question 44, prescribes this counsel: Let him (namely, the tempted person) flee to the Word and the will of God revealed therein, so that by obeying it he may obtain salvation, nor should anyone despair of the mercy of God as long as he does not sin against the Holy Spirit. But this refuge is nothing if in the Word only the will of sign is expressed without an external good pleasure. And how can he hope for mercy, when he doubts vehemently about it because of sins and the absolute decree?

XXII. Therefore this remains certain and indubitable, that all Calvinists are burdensome comforters, lendige tröster, as Job calls his friends, chapter 16, verse 1. For the sum of all Calvinist παρακλήσεως (consolation), which it will suggest to the tempted, finally returns to this: God has elected some to life. Therefore perhaps He has elected you also, just as Piscator argues in his Disputation on Predestination, thesis 83; he could teach his disciples no other argument than this: Grace is offered to some with the intention of communicating it. Therefore it is possible that I also am elected. But all these things are uncertain and mere conjectures, since perhaps is refuted by not perhaps, and that (it is possible that I am) is infringed by (it is possible that I am not): from which nothing follows but ἀπορία and uncertainty, and therefore finally in practice the Romanists and Calvinists agree, although they differ in theory. For just as Bellarmine grants conjectural certainty to the pious, l. 3. de Iustif. c. 2. So Zanchius and his followers form nothing but a probable conclusion. Therefore, as much difference as there is between conjectural and probable, so much is there between the Papists and the Calvinists, that is, none. If, therefore, they wish to remove Papistic doubt, its foundations must be undermined. For the conclusion is wrongly denied if the premises have been posited. All roots must be dug up if the garden is to be purged of tares. One remains an incendiary if, even when the fire is blazing and overcoming, he carries water and strives to extinguish it. Either, therefore, let them admit with us an ordered election, or with the Papists [they must admit] the uncertainty of salvation, or it will follow that they teach one thing in words and express another in practice, and thus that Calvinistic practice does not at all agree with theory, and vice versa.

Latin:

XL MEMBRVM II. DE PRAXI CALVINISTICA.

Quandoquidem sciunt Calviniani, tales præmissas se suggerere, ex quibus via sit vel ad securitatem, vel ad dubitationem & desperationem, hinc nonnulli doctrinam prædestinationis silentio potius involutam volunt, quàm vt publicè de illa verba fiant: Ideoque Beza in Colloquio Momp. ea de re disputare nolebat. Sed respondemus nos cum Augustino, tract. 21. in Ioh. Quare dicta sunt, nisi vt sciantur, nisi vt audiantur? Quare audita sunt, nisi vt intelligantur? Et hanc ob causam Calviniani recentiores Bezæ timiditatem improbant, & in arenam descendere non erubescunt, ita verò disserunt, vt in praxi planè hæreant, nec in salutarem vsum theoriam suam conuertere queant.

XII. Quod vt demonstremus, hanc thesin præmittimus: Stante doctrina Caluinistica, nullus tentatus erigi, nullus dubitans de electione vel salute sua confirmari potest. Quam assertionem tali argumento stabilire possumus: Qui credere debet, Deum ex toto genere humano tantùm aliquos, & quidem minimam partem, ex absoluta planeque abscondita εὐδοκίᾳ ad vitam æternam elegisse, hic se electum & saluandum esse firmiter concludere nequit. At vero omnis Caluinianus istud credere debet. Ergo electionem & salutem suam firmiter concludere nequit. Maior certa est, cùm sub particulari, absoluto & prorsus arcano decreto, nequeat inuictè subsumere. Quale n. foret argumentum hoc, & quæ consequentia? Deus paucissimos, quos voluit, sine omni respectu fidei elegit. E. te quoque electis istis annumerauit? Statim excipiet tentatus, se de hoc ipso dubitare, nec vllum, quo erigi queat, argumentum audire.

XIII. Nam si ableges ipsum ad voluntatem Dei reuelatam, mox secundum hypotheses Calvinianas excipiet, eam esse tantùm signi volutatem, se autem ambigere de voluntate beneplaciti & arcana. Cùm enim hæc, quandoque prorsus contraria sit reuelatæ, nō poterit tentato ex Scripturis persuaderi, Deum sincerè ipsum diligere & saluum velle: Sed quicquid dicetur, ad istud regeret, se signum audire, sed beneplacitum ignorare. Si Christi meritum inculces, parata erit respōsio: Christum non pro omnibus, sed paucissimis tantùm efficaciter esse mortuum. Quî autem credere potest, se istis inclusum esse? Si promissiones vniuersales vrgeas, nec illæ suffifient, quoniam restringuntur tantùm ad genera singulorum, non singulos generum. Sacramentorum vsum & efficaciam commendes, non acquiescet tentatus, sed hæc ad signi voluntatem pertinere, non autem arcanum beneplacitum ostendere reponet.

XIV. Atque ita nihil manet reliquum, quod Satanæ tentationi solidè opponi, firmumque animo dubitantis solatium subministrare possit, vndè nos colligimus, dogma Caluinisticum non esse divinum & Apostolicum. Vt enim omnis Scriptura, sic & omnis doctrina ex Scripturis deducta, facit ad nostram consolationem, Rom. 15. v. 4. & correctionem, 2. Tim. 3. v. 20. At verò dogma Caluinisticum de absoluto decreto, nec anxias mentes verâ παρακλήσει, nec securas solidâ παιδεύσει erigit, vt ostensum hactenus fuit. Quare non est dogma in Scripturis fundatum, aut ex sacris literis deductum.

XV. Vt verò ab hac difficultate se liberent, diueros solatij & certitudinis modos præscribunt, quos paucis percurrere non erit operæ dispendium Zanchius l. 5. de N. Dei c. 2. p. 648. docet primùm in genere, quòd quisq; teneatur credere, se ad salutem æternam in Christo electum esse; & neminem hic excipi vult, nè reprobos quidem. Sed vanum h. e. effugium, quippe ex quo patet, Caluinianos neminem solari posse, nisi assumant falsum. Omnes n. electos esse, falsum est. Et tamen quemvis dicunt teneri, vt hoc credat. Num E. ad falsa etiam credēda obligati sumus? Deinde v. l. 5. de N. D. c. 2. 1. th. 2. p. 658. & seqq. tres imprimis modos ratificandæ electionis commemorat.

XVI. PRIMVM vocat testimonium Spiritus internum. Spiritus, inquit, Sanctus, dum testatur internè nostro Spiritui, hoc est, mentibus nostris lumine suo illustratis, nos esse filios Dei, apertissimè revelat, nos fuisse ab æterno prædestinatos εἰς ὑιοθεσίαν. Sed præterquā quod modus hic, prout à Zanchio explicatur, Enthusiasmis multum tribuere videtur, illud imprimis desideramus, quòd non sit perpetuus, sed ingravioribus tentationibus prorsus expiret, quando nullus vel fidei, vel testificantis Spiritus sensus deprehenditur, cum intus terrores sunt, & foris pugnæ, Cor. 7. v. 5. nostrumque cor nos condemnat 1. Ioh. 3. v. 20. adeò vt cum Dauide à facie Dei nos abiectos opinemur, Psal. 31. v. 23. quando ob oculos versantur mera fulgura & tonitrua, nempè ira ac iustitia Dei immutabilis, vigor legis inflexibilis, peccatorum atrocitas importabilis, inferni cruciatus intolerabilis, Diabolorum subsannatio implacabilis, vt August. alicubi loquitur. Quamuis ergo tempore quieto, cùm extra tentationem constituti sumus testimonium reddat Spiritus S. Spiritui nostro, quòd simus filij Dei Rom. 8 v. 16. ingruente tamē tentatione cessat istud, ideoq; παιδεύειν nõ est. Quibus & hoc ad dimus, quòd Caluinianos in dubio semper hærere oportat, nū μαρτύριον illud à Sp. S. vel potius carnali quādā confidētia profectum sit, cùm absolutum & penitus incognitum Dei decretum ipsi doceant, & nullibi non inculcent.

XVII. SECVNDVM confirmandæ electionis modum desumit Zanch. à verbo seu Evangelio. Manifestum est, scribit p. 659. Deum per verbum Evangelij, vbi omnes fideles pronunciat electos, suam cuique fideli revelare prædestinationem. Requiritur tantùm, vt fidelis auditis vniuersalibus propositionibus, in animo suo assumat: Atqui ego gratia & dono Dei fidelis sum, &c. Atneq; hoc modo omnem dubitationis scrupulum eximere potest. Nam 1. Non est perpetuus, siquidem tentationis tempore locum nullum inuenit. Quomodo n. tentatus subsumet, se credere, cùm de hoc ipso dubitet, & nullam in animo πληροφορίαν sentiat? 2. Incertus est & infirmus. Stante n. absoluto decreto, stare nequit fidei certitudo. Nam vndè quis confirmabitur, se fidem habere & concipere posse? Num ex verbo? Sed hoc voluntatem signi tantùm continet. Num ex promissionibus? Ast hæ particulares sunt. Num ex Sacramentis? Verùm hæc significant, nil conferunt. Quare semper manebit hic scrupulus, Nescio num Deus mei seriò velit misereri; quia voluntas eius arcana est, nec vllis mediis patefacta. Et si maximè velim credere, ignoro tamen an hæc fides sit temporaria, num viua, siquidem multos in hac persuasione deceptos noui, egóque nullum verbum, nullam promissionem habeo, cui firmiter inniti queam. Hic ergò Caluiniani se exerceant, modumque præscribant, Quomodo erigendus sit homo, si dubitet, nùm Deus fidem sibi velit infundere, siquidem paucissimis eam, & quidem ex absoluto beneplacito instillet? Nihil solidi proferre possunt, si vniuersalitatem voluntatis seriæ, satisfactionis Christi, & promissionum diuinarum negauerint.

XXIX. TERTIVM notificandæ prædestinationis modum petit ab effectis. Deus, ait p. 660 a. effectis sensusuis nobis impressis, nos sibi obsignat in Christo: atque ita obsignat, vt si diligenter animum aduertamus, agnoscere inde non obscurè possimus, nos à reliqua hominum turba selectos, & ad vitam æternam prædestinatos fuisse. Rationem reddit duplicem p. 661. tum quia per effecta cognoscantur causæ; tum quia expressè sint diuinæ electionis formæ. Recenset autem p. 661. tria imprimis effecta. 1. Christum inhabitantem. 2. Vocationem efficacem. 3. Iustificationem, ad quam refert sanctificationem, conscientiam bonam, charitatem non fictam, patientiam in aduersis, gloriationē in tribulationibus &c. Verùm, 1. Cõcedimus, hæc testari de electione, si quis actu credere sentiat: quid autem fiet tõpore tentationis, vbi quis de effectis his omnib. dubitat? Num ille tanquã reprobus absq; omni solatio relinquendus est? 2. De effectu nemo confirmari potest, nisi prius de causæ operatione certus sit. Quibus verò rationibus probabunt Caluiniani, DEVM, effectuum istorũ causam, in hoc vel illo indiuiduo certo operari velle? Negatâ enim voluntatis vniuersalitate, & posito decreto absoluto nullâ potest fieri ὑπόληψις. Quamdiu autem non persuadetur dubitanti, Deum seriò velle effectus dictos in isto producere, tamdiu de illorum præsentia & veritate confirmari nequit.

XIX. Atque sic ex hactenus dictis perspicuum sit, omnes à Zanchio annotatos modos, tum insufficientes, tum incertos esse, & tentationis tempore, de quo maximè disputatur, nullum efficax solatium suppeditare posse. Nec diffiteri hoc potuit ipse Zanchius, dum probabilem tãtum electionis certitudinem ex Scriptura fluere scribit in Miscella. fol. 302. vbi hæc verba; Docui voluntatem hanc, nimpe quosnam Deus ad vitam aut mortem prædestinarit, non esse in Scripturis simplicitèr de singulis revelatam, sed tantùm ab effectis PROBABILITER indicatam.

XX. Zanchium plerique ex Caluinianis sequuntur, eosdem modos tradentes, licèt aliis verbis, & paulò distinctius, sicut Politicus quidam in libro Germanico duplicia certitudinis signa adfert. Interna & Externa. Interna esse dicit 1. Testimoniũ Spiritus. S. 2. Luctam Spiritus aduersus carnem. 3. Veram in Christum fidem. Externam verò 1. Pænitentiam & vitæ emendationem. 2. Serium studiũ audiendi verbum Dei. 3. Salutarem vsum Sacramentorum. 4. Veram & constantem inuocationem Dei in nomine Iesu Christi. 5. Veram confessionem Christi. 6. Finalem perseverantiam & constantiam. Quantùmvis verò non diffiteamur, hæc electionis signa & consolationis media esse, à Caluinianis tamen vsurpari nequeunt, quamdiu decretum absolutum defendunt. Nec enim de veritate, nec de certitudine horum effectuum alicui constare potest, nisi benefica Dei voluntas ista dandi & communicandi præsupponatur. Hæc autem præsupponi & certò apprehendi nequit, nisi illam vniuersalem esse statuatur. Quod si verò gratiam Dei sine verbo sibi quis imaginetur, mera præsumptio est & hypocrisis. Accedit, quòd electi Dei sæpè ruant in peccata mortalia, vt exemplo Dauidis & Petri constat, vbi si conscientia euigilet, scelusq́; commissum exaggeret, nec vllus sensus illorū τεκμηρίων adsit, prout fieri solet in tentationibus vehementibus, vndè tunc consolatio & electionis certitudo petenda erit?

XXI. Bucanus quidem in Institutionibus loco 35. quæ: 44. hoc consilium præscribit: Ad verbum & voluntatem Dei in eo reuelatam confugiat (nempè tentatus) vt ei obediendo salutem consequatur, nec cuiquam desperandum est de misericordia Dei, quamdiu non peccat in Spiritum S. Sed refugium hoc nullum est, si in verbo non nisi voluntas signi sine beneplacito externo exprimitur. Et quomodo misericordiam sperare potest, cum de illa ob peccata & absolutum decretum vehementer dubitet?

XXII. Proindè certum hoc manet & indubitatum, Caluinistas omnes esse consolatores onerosos, lendige tröster, vti Iobus amicos suos nominat, cap. 16. vers. 1. Summa n̄. omnis παρακλήσεως Caluinianæ, quam tentato suggeret, huc tandem redit: Deus quosdam elegit ad vitam. Ergò te fortassis etiam elegit, sicuti Piscat. disputat. de prædestinat th. 83. non aliud, quàm hoc argumētum discipulos suos docere potuit: Gratia nonnullis offertur animo communicandi. Egò fieri potest, vt & ego sim electus. Ast omnia hæc incerta sunt & meræ cōiecturæ, siquidem fortasse refutatur, per non fortasse, & illud (fieri potest vt sim) infringitur per (per fieri potest vt non sim:) vnde nil sequitur quàm ἀπορία & incertitudo, adeoque tandeni in praxi Romanenses & Caluiniani conueniunt, quamuis in theoria discrepent. Nam sicut Bellarm. certitudinem coniecturalem concedit pijs, l. 3. de Iustif. c. 2. Sic Zanchius eiusque assectæ nõ nisi probabilem conclusionem formant. Quantum ergo discrimen est inter coniecturale & probabile, tantum inter Pontificios & Caluinianos hoc est, nullum. Quod si ergò dubitationem Papisticam locomouere velint, fundamenta eius subruenda sunt. Nam malè cõclusio negatur, si præmissæ sint positæ. Radices omnes eruendæ sunt, si hortus à lolio purgari debeat. Incendiarius quis manet, si maximè incendio gliscente & superante aquam portet, illudq; extinguere nitatur. Aut ergò nobiscum fateantur ordinatam electionem, aut cùm Pontificijs salutis incertitudinem, aut sequetur, ipsos aliud verbis docere, aliud vsu exprimere, adeoq; praxin Caluinisticam cùm theoria, & contrà minimè concordare.


### Question IV: XXIII. Member III. concerning True and Salutary Practice

XXIII. MEMBER III. CONCERNING TRUE AND SALUTARY PRACTICE.

This consists in the certainty of predestination and salvation, while one subsumes under universal promises, and firmly concludes from thence that he is elected. Two times, however, must be accurately distinguished here. 1. A tranquil time. 2. A time of a tempted and doubting conscience. When it is tranquil, and a man has a sense of faith, he can easily be confirmed concerning his election in this manner: Whoever believes and has a constant purpose of abstaining from mortal sins, he is truly elected from eternity. For ἐκλογὴ is not absolute, but made in Christ apprehended by faith, so that all who constantly believe are predestined, whence also it is called the faith of the elect, Tit. 1. v 1. But you believe, and you feel that you truly believe, and [have] a constant purpose from mortal sins you confess that you have the power of abstaining. Therefore, you are truly elected from eternity, nor ought you to doubt concerning your salvation; for God, who began the good work, will perfect it, nor does the Holy Spirit depart from anyone who has the purpose of persevering, nor does He willingly and knowingly expel Him through sins against conscience. For whom God predestined before the world, He called from the world, justified in the world, Him He will certainly glorify after the world, as Augustine intimates, c. 28, Soliloq.

XXIV. And thus far indeed the consolation has been set forth. But a great difficulty arises in the time of temptation, when the sense of faith is not present, and the conscience imagines God to be angry with itself on account of some transgression. For although you may form the most universal proposition, 'Every believer is elected,' the tempted person nevertheless sticks at the ὑποθέσει [hypothesis], and posits two things: 1. That he does not believe, because he feels God is angry, and lacks all consolation and testimony of the Holy Spirit. 2. That he is uncertain about perseverance: for if he even wished to believe now, he could nevertheless very easily fall away in turn. Now, just as no one is saved, so also no one is elected, unless he has persevered. Therefore, in order that these scruples may be removed, there is need of an accurate discourse, so that the doubting person may be fully informed: 1. concerning the subsumption of faith, 2. concerning the subsumption and certainty of perseverance. Concerning both, therefore, it will be necessary to treat in a few words.

XXV. 1. Concerning the subsumption of faith. Before one arrives at the direct proof of certainty itself, certain things, whether axioms or theological themes, can and ought to be premised, and demonstrated both through sayings and through examples, by which the tempted mind may be gradually led away from the reefs of doubt, and prepared for conceiving πληροφορíαν [full assurance]. Such are the following: 1. Election and eternal salvation do not rest upon our merits, but only upon divine promises. Wherefore our unworthiness and imperfection in no way stand in the way of certainty. Then, virtue and grace are effective in infirmity.

2. God is most kindly disposed toward all men, and seriously desires their salvation. He has made this will manifest by words, oaths, and examples, and therefore let us cast away every thought of an absolute decree.

3. Christ came into this world, that He might save that which was lost. Wherefore He made satisfaction for the sins not only of the elect, but of all mortals, and He waits daily that the burdened may come and receive refreshment.

4. The fruits of the Lord's Passion, and all benefits, such as the remission of sins, salvation, and election, are offered to all and singular in the Word and Sacraments, inasmuch as these are the hands of God, through which He extends His gifts to us.

5. Wherefore, that we may be made partakers of these benefits, nothing else is required than the use of the means. No meritorious disposition on our part is necessary here: Provided we conduct ourselves passively, and do not place an obstacle to the Spirit, we immediately receive from God what we ask.

6. If sins are even the most grievous, they are no obstacle. For this reason Christ came, that He might make satisfaction for them. Nor would there have been need of His passion, if men had been immune from sins.

7. God is indeed angry with transgressors, but He tempers anger with mercy, provided repentance is practiced. For He does not delight in the death of the dying, but that he may live. You are not yet Peter the denier, not yet Magdalene the harlot, or a thief, or an idolater, as the whole people in the desert. Since all these therefore have obtained pardon, and God has promised it to you in the Word; why will you doubt, and not have faith?

8. The cross and temptation are not signs of an angry God, but rather of a benevolent one: For He chastises whom He loves, and corrects His own in good time, lest they be condemned with the world. That very tribulation, therefore, which you now experience, testifies to the love of the Lord, and for the salvation of the soul and it will most certainly tend to your advantage.

XXVI. These things therefore having been premised by way of preparation, one may descend to the proof itself and demonstrate that no one has a reason to doubt concerning his own faith, but that it is done rashly, since anyone can know his own faith and be certain of it, both a priori, or by reason of causes, and a posteriori, or by reason of signs and effects: which is now to be deduced more broadly.

XXVII. 1. A PRIORI we can be certain when we consider the causes of faith, where such a collection ought to be instituted; the cause being placed in act, the effect certainly follows. But indeed the cause of your faith is already placed in act. Wherefore the effect certainly follows and is present. The minor is illustrated and proved, because the principal cause of faith is God's grace, and His benevolent will, according to which He wills to work faith in our hearts, without our merits and proper disposition: the instrumental is the Word of God with the Sacraments. Now indeed these are placed in act. For behold! God at this very time is prepared to give faith. The Son always waits for you to come, Matt. 11, v. 25; the Holy Spirit always knocks for you to open, Apoc. 3, v. 20. And lest you be able to doubt even this, He commands His Word, the instrument of faith and grace, to be announced to you, namely that Word which does not return empty, Isa. 55, v. 11. which is a hammer breaking in pieces, Jer. 23, v. 29, which is the power unto salvation, Rom. 1, v. 16, and from the hearing of which faith is begotten, Rom. 10, v. 18. Moreover, the Sacrament of the Supper has been instituted, in which Christ unites Himself with you, offering His body to be eaten and His blood to be drunk, lest you doubt in the least concerning His grace and presence. Therefore, since you now hear the Word of God and use the Sacraments, you know the cause of faith is placed in act. The effect therefore most certainly follows, nor do you have any further reason for doubting.

XXIIX. But the tempted are accustomed to object.

However, on the part of man, some preparation is required, a diligent listening. I do not know whether all these things are found in me in the due manner. Others also hear the word, they use many Sacraments, and yet not all draw saving faith from them. Perhaps the same will happen to me. To these it must be answered that faith and conversion are clearly not our works, but proceed solely from God. Nothing else is required of us than that we do not hinder, nor place an obstacle to the working Spirit. Whoever, therefore, conducts himself passively, who does not contumaciously resist, nor has the mind to resist, he neither can nor ought to doubt concerning the efficacious Spirit and the operation of the word. This can be illustrated by an example. 1. Solar illumination. The Sun is of such power that it illuminates all rooms, unless they are blocked or the windows are covered: Thus all hearers of the word are converted, provided they do not hinder the power of the divine light by spontaneous depravity 2. Of healing; If there were some medicine, concerning which it was indubitably certain that whoever used it would be healed, certainly no sick person using it would doubt concerning his health. Now, however, it is certain to all that the word of God is such an efficacious and salutary medicine of souls. If, therefore, you apply this, you will certainly be healed. Therefore, if anyone begins to doubt, immediately ask about the cause; why does he doubt? For he can allege no sufficiently pregnant reason. If he brings forward his sins, I will urge the promises, that God does not desire the death of the sinner, Ezek. 18 and 33; if he pretends his infirmity, I will advise that the power of God is perfected in infirmity, and that man himself ought to do absolutely nothing in effecting his own conversion. Let him only conduct himself passively, and not place an obstacle. Therefore, always ask, Do you wish to resist? If he denies it, the cause is placed in act, and it is not hindered; wherefore the effect infallibly follows. XXIX. Therefore, it must always be recalled to memory that God the Father spreads out His hands, God the Son waits, the Holy Spirit knocks, the Minister of grace announces it, and the Word and Sacraments offer it itself. Who therefore would not come? But if he should now answer that he wishes to come, and does not place an obstacle, he is undoubtedly converted. This can be declared by the example of David, 2 Sam. 12, of the Ninevites, Jonah 3, of the Jews, Acts 2. When all these heard, and did not resist, they were immediately converted. Thus, therefore, a priori and by the reason of causes, we can be certain of our faith and conversion.

XXX. 2. A POSTERIORI that certainty shines forth if the marks or signs, the effects or consequences of conversion, are attended to. For wherever the consequent is found, there the antecedent cannot be absent. Now you yourself may subsume: I discover in myself the consequent effect of conversion. Whence the conclusion will follow that faith and conversion are by no means absent. For the illustration and confirmation of the minor premise, the principal signs or effects of faith must be noted, of which we count four in particular.

XXXI. 1. Desire for divine grace. For whoever seeks the mercy of God with sincerity is led by the Holy Spirit; whence they are called blessed who hunger and thirst for righteousness, Matt. 5, v. 6. But if one who is tempted denies that he discovers such a desire in himself, the means by which it may be excited must be used, such as those sought from the dignity of salvation, from the gravity of infernal punishments, from the tranquility of conscience, from the vileness of worldly things, and similar things, all of which can excite a serious desire for conversion and repentance.

XXXII. 2. Renewal, which is known most especially from the struggle of the flesh and the spirit, from a serious displeasure with vices, and from a detestation of interior corruption, concerning which Rom. 6 and 7. For whenever someone feels such a struggle and displeasure, then he can be most certain of his renewal, since in the impenitent the flesh dominates, nor are they led by the Spirit, who would struggle against the flesh.

XXXIII. 3. The testimony of the moving Spirit. For when our hearts are pricked in sermons, when they as it were burn, as the Emmaus disciples confess of themselves, Luke 24:32, when we feel pious thoughts, are moved to the desertion of carnal things, are incited to spiritual things, sigh for heavenly things, and perceive comfort in distress, then all these things are works and motions of the Holy Spirit or effects of conversion: Since therefore we experience such things, it is most certain that we have the Spirit graciously inhabiting us, because these things by no means belong to the unregenerate.

XXXIV. 4. Studious observance of the law, or the exercise of good works. For whoever seriously loves God, who does good to his neighbor to the best of his ability, who patiently bears the cross, who courageously sustains all evils for Christ's sake, he in turn can gather from this that he is justified and regenerated. For these works can by no means proceed from an unregenerate and infidel person.

XXXV. If anyone should object: All these things can deceive, and therefore they are uncertain; any hypocrite can imagine the same for himself, as heretics, Papists, etc., do. Response: 1. The Holy Spirit cannot lie. He said, Where there is a struggle of the flesh, there is renewal. Therefore this cannot deceive. Do you feel such a struggle? You can therefore be certain of your conversion and the gracious καλοικήσει [indwelling] of the Spirit. 2. As for hypocrites and heretics, we do not care about them. Although they say and boast that they also feel the motions of the Spirit, yet from their works, from their contumacy, envy, infidelity, and the like, the contrary appears. Therefore, this hypocritical faith is not to be opposed to true faith. Anyone can certainly test himself, whether sins truly displease him, etc., although we know this about another only conjecturally. The saying from 2 Cor. 13:5 pertains to this. Test yourselves, whether you are in the faith. Do you not know yourselves, that Christ is in you, unless perhaps you are reprobate? This is diligently to be noted, that they are called reprobate who do not acknowledge, nor feel, that Christ dwells in them.

Latin:

XXIII. MEMBRVM III. DE PRAXI VERA ET SALVTARI.

Consistit hæc in certitudine prædestinationis & salutis, dùm quis sub promissionibus vniuersalib subsumit, & electum se esse firmiter indè concludit. Duo autem tempora hîc accuratè distinguenda sunt. 1. Tempus tranquillum. 2. Tempus tentatæ & dubitantis conscientiæ. Cùm tranquilla est, & homo fidei sensum habet, de electione sua facilè confirmari potest hoc pacto: Quicunque credit & constans propositum habet, à peccatis mortalibus abstinendi, hic verè ab æterno electus est. Nam ἐκλογὴ non est absoluta, sed in Christo fide apprehenso facta, sic, vt omnes constanter credentes, sint prædestinati, vndè & fides electorum esse dicitur Tit. 1. v 1. Atqui tu credis, & te verè credere sentis, & constans propositum à peccatis abstinendi te habere fateris. Ergo verò ab æterno electus es, nec de salute tua dubitare debes Deus n. qui inscepit, perficiet opus bonum, necă quoquam Spiritus S. recedit, qui propositum habet perseverandi, nec illum peccatis contra conscientiam volens sciensque expellit. Quem enim Deus prædestinavit antemundum, vocavit de mundo, justificavit in mundo, eum certò magnificabit, post mundum, innuente August. c. 28. Soliloq.

XXIV. Et hactenus quidem consolatio expedita est. Sed difficultas magna oritur tempore tentationis, quando fidei sensus non adest, & conscientia Deum sibi iratum ob transgressionem quandam imaginatur. Nam sitùm maximè vniversalem propositionem formes, Omnis credens est electus, hæret tamen tentatus in ὑποθέσει, & duo reponit. 1. Se non credere, quia sentiat Deum iratum, & careat omni Spiritus S. solatio & testimonio. 2. Se incertum esse de perseverantia: Si enim maximè iam vellet credere, tamen se vicissim labi facillimè posse. Iam vt nemo saluatur, sic & nemo electus est, nisi perseverauerit. Hi ergò scrupuli vt remoueantur, accurato discursu opùs est, quò dubitans plenè informetur. 1. de fidei, 2. de perseverantiæ subsumptione & certitudine. De vtroque igitur paucis agendum erit.

XXV. 1. De subsumptione fidei. Antequam ad ipsam certitudinis probationem directam perueniatur, præmitti possunt & debent quædam siue axiomata, siue themata Theologica, & tum per dicta, tum per exempla demonstrari, quo animus tentatus paulatim à scopulis dubitationum abducatur, & ad concipiendam πληροφορíαν præparetur. Talia sunt sequentia. 1. Electio & salus æterna non nititur nostris meritis, sed tantùm diuinis promissionibus. Quare indignitas nostra & imperfectio nequaquă obstat certitudini. Dein virtus & gratia in infirmitate est efficax.

2. Deus benignissimè erga omnes homines affectus est, illorúmq; salutem seriò desiderat. Testatam fecit hanc voluntatem dictis, iuramentis, exemplis, ideoq; omnê de absoluto decreto cogitationem abijciamus.

3. Christus in hunc mundũ venit, vt saluet quod perierat. Quare satisfecit pro peccatis nón electorum modò, sed cunctorum mortalium, & expectat quotidiè, vt onerati veniant & refrigerium accipiant.

4. Fructus Passionis Dominicæ, & omnia beneficia, vt remissio peccatorum, salus & electio, offeruntur omnibus & singulis in verbo & Sacramentis, quippe quæ sunt manus Dei, per quæ sua nobis dona porrigit.

5. Quare vt horum beneficiorum reddamur participes, nihil requiritur aliud, quàm vsurpatio mediorum. Nulla hîc dispositio meritoria ex partê nostri est necessaria: Modo nos habeamus passiuè, nec obicem ponamus Spiritui, statim accipimus à Deo, quod poscimus.

6. Peccata si vel grauissima sint, nihil obstant. Ideò enim venit Christus, vt pro ijs satisfaceret. Nec fuisset opus passione eius, si homines à peccatis immunes fuissent.

7. Deus quidem irascitur transgressoribus, sed iram tẽperat misericordia, modo agatur pœnitentia. Non enim delectatur morte morientis, sed vt viuat, Nondum es Petrus abnegator, nondum Magdelena meretrix, vel latro, vel idololatra, vt totus in deserto populus. Hi ergò omnes cùm veniam consecuti sint, & eam tibi, in verbo promiserit Deus; cur dubitabis, nec fidem habebis?

8. Crux & tentatio non sunt signa Dei irati, sed potius beneuoli: Castigat enim quem diligit, & suos maturè corripit, nè cum mundo damnentur. Illa ipsa ergò, quam nunc experiris tribulatio, de amore Domini testatur, & in salutem animæ tuumque commodum certissimè verget.

XXVI. His igitur præparationis loco præmissis ad ipsam probationem descendi potest & demonstrari, quod nemo de fide sua dubitandi caussam habeat, sed temerè id fiat, cum quiuis fidem suam scire, de que illa certus esse queat, tum à priori, vel ratione causarum, tum à posteriori, vel ratione notarum & effectuum: id quod nunc latius est deducendum.

XXVII. 1. A PRIORI possumus esse certi, quando consideramus caussas fidei, vbi talis collectio debet institui; Posita caussa in actu certò sequitur effectus. At verò fidei tuæ caussa iam in actu est posita. Quare affectus certò sequitur & præsens est. Minor illustratur & probatur, quia fidei caussa principalis est Dei gratia, & eius voluntas beneuola, secundum quam in cordib. nostris, sine meritis nostris ac dispositione propria fidem vult operari: Instrumentalis est verbum Dei cum Sacramentis. Iam verò hæc in actu sunt posita. Nam ecce! Deus hoc ipso tempore paratus est ad fidem dandum. Semper exspectat Filius, vt venias, Matth. 11. v. 25. semper pulsat S. S. vt aperias, Apoc. 3. v. 20. Et nè de hoc ipso dubitare possis, Verbum suum, fidei & gratiæ instrumentum tibi annunciari iubet, illud nempè verbum, quod non redit vacuum, Esa. 55, v. 11. quod est malleus conterens, Ier. 23. v. 29 quod est potentia ad salutem, Rom. 1. v. 16. & ex cuius auditu fides gignitur, Rom. 10. vers. 18. Institutum insuper est Sacramentum Cœnæ, in quo Christus tecum se vnit, corpus manducandum & sanguinem bibendum porrigit, nè in minimo ambigas de ipsius gratia & presentia. Proindè cùm iam verbum Dei audias, & Sacramenta vsurpes, nouisti caussam fidei in actu esse positam. Effectus igitur certissimè sequitur, nec vllam amplius dubitandi rationem habes.

XXIIX. Verùm tetati excipere solent.

tamen ex parte hominis aliqua preparatio, requiritur sedula auscultatio. Ignoro an hæc omnia debito modo in me reperiantur. Audiunt & alij verbum, vtuntur multis Sacramentis, nec tamen omnes fidem saluificam inde hauriunt. Fortassis & idem mihi eueniet. His respondendum est, quod fides & conuersio planè non sint opera nostra, sed vnicè à Deo proueniant. A nobis nihil aliud requiritur, quàm nè impediamus, nec obicem ponamus operanti Spiritui. Quicunque igitur se habet passiuè, qui contumaciter non resistit, nec resistendi animum habet, ille de efficaci Spiritu, & verbi operatione dubitare nec potest, nec debet. Illustrari hoc potest exemplo. 1. Illuminatio Solaris. Tantæ potentię Sol est, vt omnia illuminet conclauia, nisi obstruantur, vel fenestræ obvelentur: Sic omnes verbi auditores conuertuntur, modò non vim diuini luminis spontaneâ prauitate impediant 2. Sanationis; Si medicina quępiam foret, de qua indubitanter constaret, queuis illa vtentem sanari, nullus certè ægrotus vsurpans de sanitate sua dubitaret. Iam verò constat omnibus, Dei verbum tàm efficacem & salutarem animarum medicinam esse. Hanc igitur si adhibeas, vtiq; certò sanaberis. Proindè si quis dubitare incipiat, statim quære de caussa;ob quam dubitet? Nullam n. satis prægnantem allegare potest. Si peccata sua protulerit, vrgebo promissiones, quòd Deus nolit mortē peccatoris, Ezech. 18. & 33. si infirmitatem suam prætenderit, monebo, quòd Dei virtus in infirmitate perficiatur, & quòd homo ipse planè nihil debeat operari in efficienda sui conuersione. Tantùm se habeat passiuè, nec ponat obicem. Semper ergò quæras, Num velis resistere? Si neget, causa in actu est posita, nec impeditur; quare effectus infallibiliter sequitur. XXIX. Semper ergò in memoriam reuocandum est quòd Deus Pater expandat manus, Deus Filius exspectet, Spiritus S. pulset, Minister gratiam annunciet, verbum & Sacramenta eam ipsam offerant. Quis ergo non veniat? Quod si iam venire se velle respondeat, nec obicem ponat, indubitato conuertitur. Declarari potest exemplo Dauidis, 2. Sam. 12. Niniuittarum Ionae 3. Iudaeorum, Actor. 2. Hi omnes cum audirent, nec resisterent, statim conuertebantur. Ita igitur a priori, & ratione causarum certi esse possumus de nostra fide & conuersione.

XXX. 2. A POSTERIORI elucescit illa certitudo si attendantur notae vel signa, effectus vel consequentia conuersionis. Vbicunque enim consequens reperitur, ibi antecedens abesse nequit. Iam subsumas ipse: In me deprehendo consequentem conuersionis effectum. Vnde sequetur conclusio, fidem & conuersionem nequaquam abesse. Pro illustratione & confirmatione minoris notari debent praecipua signa vel effectus fidei, quorū imprimis quatuor numeramus.

XXXI. 1. Gratiae diuinae desiderium. Quicunque enim misericordiam Dei expetit sinceris is a Spiritu S. ducitur; vnde beati nominantur, qui esuriunt & sitiunt iustitiam, Matth. 5. v. 6. Quod si tentatus desiderium tale se deprehendere neget, usurpanda sunt media, quibus excitetur, qualia petuntur a salutis dignitate, a poenarum infernalium grauitate, a conscientiae tranquillitate a rerum mundanarum vilitate & similibus, quae omnia serium conuersionis & poenitentiae desiderium excitare, possunt.

XXXII. 2. Renouatio, quae cognoscitur potissimum ex lucta carnis & spiritus, ex seria vitiorum displicentia, & corruptionis interioris detestatione, de qua Rom 6. & 7. Quandocunque enim sentit aliquis talem luctam & displicentiam, tum certifsimus esse potest de sua renouatione, quoniam impoenitentibus caro dominatur, nec illi ducuntur a Spiritu, qui carni reluctetur.

XXXIII. 3. Spiritus mouentis testificatio. Quando enim in concionibus corda nostra compuguntur, cùm quasi ardent, sicuti de se fatentur Emauntici, Luc. 24. v. 32. quando sentimus pias cogitationes, mouemur ad desertionem rerum carnalium, incitamur ad spiritualia, suspiramus ad cœlestia, & solatium percipimus in angustia, tum hæc omnia sunt opera & motus Spiritus S. vel effectus conuersionis : Cùm igitur talia experimur, certissimum est, quòd Spiritum gratiosè inhabitantem habeamus, quoniam ista non renatis nequaquam comperunt.

XXXIV. 4. Studiosa legis obseruatio, vel bonorum operum exercitium. Quicunque enim seriò diligit Deum, qui proximo pro virili benefacit, qui crucem patienter perfert, qui animosè omnia mala propter Christum sustinet, is vicissim hinc colligere potest, se esse iustificatum & renatum. Opera enim ista à non renato & infideli nullo modo prouenire possunt.

XXXV. Si quis objecerit : Ista omnia queunt fallere, ideoque incerta sunt: potest eadem sibi imaginari quispiam hypocrita, vti faciunt hæretici, Pontificij &c. Respon. 1. Spiritus S. mentiri nequit. Ille dixit, Vbi est lucta carnis, ibi esse renouationem. Quare hoc fallere nequit. Sentis tu talem luctam? Certus igitur esse potes de tua conuersione & gratiosa καλοικήσει Spiritus. 2. Hypocritas & hæreticos quod attinet, illos non curamus Quamuis isti dicant & iactitent, se quoque sentire motus Spiritus, tamẽ ex operibus, ex cõtumacia, inuidia, infidelitate & similibus contrarium apparet. Fides igitur ista hypocritica nõ est opponẽda fidei veræ Quiuis certè semetipsum probare potest, an verè displiceant peccata &c. quamuis de alio coniecturaliter tantùm id sciamus. Huc pertinet dictum ex 2. Cor. 13. v. 5. Probate vos ipsos, an sitis in fide, Annõ cognoscitis vos ipsos, quòd Christus in vobis est, nisi forsan reprobi estis? Diligenter hoc notandum, quòd reprobi dicantur, qui non agnoscunt, nec sentiunt, Christum in se habitare.


### Question IV: XXXVI. Concerning the subsumption of perseverance

XXXVI. Concerning the subsumption of perseverance.

As regards this, we cannot indeed be absolutely certain, as if the contrary were plainly impossible; meanwhile, however, even here a certainty is given, although in a certain lower degree: Now these are the foundations of certainty.

1. The promise of God. He promised not only to begin, but also to perfect, Phil. 1. v. 6. and therefore He does not permit us to be tempted beyond our strength. I can therefore be certain because of this promise: that God will neither fail me, but will always preserve me in the faith. To this pertains the saying of Fulgentius, book 1, to Monimus: God prevents the impious, that he may become just: He follows the just, that he may not become impious. He prevents the blind, that He may bestow the light which he does not find: He follows the seeing, that He may preserve the light which He has bestowed. He prevents the fallen, that he may rise: He follows the raised, that he may not fall.

2. Earnest invocation. God promised without condition an answer to those asking, if they ask for those things which are necessary for salvation. Whatever you shall ask the Father in my name, this will be given to you. John 16. v. 23. But I, who now know myself to be converted, ask for perseverance out of true faith. I can therefore be certain that God will give it to me. There is no falsehood in His promises, because there is no difficulty for the Almighty in doing them, says Fulgentius, book 1.

3. Continued use of the means. For just as faith was conferred through the first application of the same: so if the use is continued, faith itself and conversion will be continued. Wherefore if I always hear the word, if I use the Sacraments, in turn I can be certain of perseverance. For although I may sometimes begin to doubt, nevertheless I immediately have a remedy, namely the Holy Supper, in which my faith is confirmed. Therefore, through the ordinary use of these, I can always persevere, and thus be certain.

4. A serious purpose of not resisting, nor of sinning mortally. Nothing can hinder perseverance and cast out the Holy Spirit like mortal sin. However, to avoid and flee this is in my power, especially if I am already converted. If, therefore, the resolution is fixed that I do not wish to sin mortally, I can certainly be sure of perseverance, since when the cause of loss is removed, the thing is not lost.

5. The absence of causes for doubting. For no argument can be brought forward for doubt to which an answer cannot most easily be made from Scripture. To the infirmity of the flesh I oppose the power of the Spirit dwelling in you. To temptation I oppose the grace of the Father, the promises, and the like. Just as he who does not place an obstacle is certainly converted, so he who does not maliciously sin, or presume to sin, without doubt perseveres and thus can be certain, nay, most certain, of his salvation and eternal election.

XXXVII. And to this point pertain those three foundations upon which Bernard was accustomed to raise himself, namely: 1. God's power, 2. Fidelity, 3. Good will. Now, what God can and wills to do, that He most certainly does. But indeed He can and wills to preserve you in good. Wherefore He will most certainly preserve you. It is not tedious to transcribe the words of Bernard, since they are full of Spirit and consolation. He speaks thus in Sermon 3 on the fragments of the 7 loaves: I consider three things, in which my whole hope consists: the charity of adoption, the truth of the promise, the power of the fulfillment. Let my foolish thought now murmur as much as it will, saying: For who are you? Or how great is that glory of yours, by what merits do you hope to obtain this? And I will confidently answer: I know whom I have believed, and I am certain, because in excessive charity He adopted me, because He is truthful in promise, because He is powerful in exhibition: for it is permitted to Him to do what He wills. This is the threefold cord which is not easily broken, which has been let down to us from our fatherland even into this prison, firm ly, I beseech you, let us hold fast, so that He himself may lift us up, He himself may draw and drag us, even to the sight of the glory of the great God, who is blessed for ever. To Bernard we join Augustine, who discourses elegantly on this question in Psalm 148. The words are as follows: Let human frailty raise itself up, let it not despair, let it not dash itself to pieces, let it not turn away, let it not say, 'I shall not be where He promised,' etc. He promised us that we shall be where He is; we shall be with Him. What has God promised you, O mortal man? That you shall live forever. Do you not believe? Believe, believe: what He has already done is greater than what He promised. What did He do? He died for you. What did He promise? That you shall live with Him. It is more incredible that the Eternal died than that a mortal should live forever. Now we hold that which is more incredible, etc.

XXXIIX. To all these things, if the Calvinists reply that a greater certainty flows from their own hypotheses, since they maintain that faith once received is not lost, nor is the Holy Spirit immediately expelled by mortal sins: we give this answer, that false things are not to be assumed so that good may come from them, or comfort be excited; indeed, even this will be nothing, since the tempted person can easily object and solidly demonstrate by both the sayings and examples of Scripture that the Spirit is entirely shaken off by mortal sins, and therefore whatever is said about faith never being lost is mere presumption. Add that he can also object thus: 'You say that the elect never lose faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit. But I have truly lost it, I have been cast out from the face of the Lord, I feel His wrath and avenging punishments. Therefore, what else can I conclude from this than that I am by no means elect?' If they say it is sufficient that he once felt a movement of faith. Nay, truly it is not sufficient, he will reply, because if the righteous man turns away and commits iniquity, all his righteousness that he had done shall not be remembered, Ezech. 18, v. 24. Here, therefore, since the afflicted person cannot be satisfied by Calvinist hypotheses, other foundations of consolation must be brought forward, which cannot immediately be argued of falsehood, and to which the tempted person can reply nothing solid, as if we were to address him thus: Why do you tremble? Why do you doubt about perseverance in faith and the grace of God? Is it because you have fallen into crimes? Do not think that on that account you are immediately reprobate; look at the examples of David and Peter, and raise yourself by them. Think of the benevolent will of God by which He seriously demands that all return to Him. Think of the passion of Christ, which He endured for your sins also. Think of the gratuitous election of God, in which all penitents and believers are included, etc. This consolation is far more effective than if many things were proposed about absolute perseverance and the secret decrees of God.

XXXIX. That we may finally conclude this question, we repeat this in place of a colophon, and we establish that it must always be urged in practice, that two rocks in particular are to be avoided: 1. Doubt, 2. Presumption. If you strike against the former, you follow the Papists, and finally you are tormented and despair: striking against the latter, you pass over to the Calvinists and fall into carnal security. Therefore, consider first the infallible promises of God, and thus you will be freed from doubt: afterwards the exhortations and threats, and thus you will be freed from security. Let there be here a mixture of hope and fear, not indeed servile, but filial. For thus the little ship of faith will hold the middle course between the Scylla of perpetual doubt and the Charybdis of absolute security, following the cynosure of the Word. Hugo writes elegantly about both in Psalm 115, from Gregory, with which words we wish this question to be concluded. They are as follows: Hope without fear luxuriates into presumption: And fear without hope degenerates into desperation. Therefore they must be held together, as David, joining them, adds: They that fear the Lord, have hoped in Him. These are the two millstones, between which the heart of man ought to be ground, so that from it bread may be made that is delightful to the Lord.

Latin:

XXXVI. De subsumsione perseuerantiæ.

Hanc quod attinet, non quidem absolutè possumus esse certi, ac si contrarium planè foret impossibile; interim tamen & hic datur certitudo, licèt quodam inferiori gradu: Fundamenta autem certitudinis hæc sunt.

1 Promissio Dei. Promisit non tantùm incipere, sed etiam perficere, Phil. 1. v. 6. & proptereà non permittit, nos tentari vltra vires. Certus E. esse possum ob hanc promissionem: Deum nec mihi defuturum, sed me semper in fide conseruaturum esse. Huc pertinet dictum Fulgentij l. 1. ad Monim. Deus præuenit impium, vt fiat iustus: subsequitur iustum, nè fiat impius. Præuenit cæcum vt lumen, quod non inuenit, donet: Subsequitur videntem, vt lumen, quod contulit, seruet. Præuenit elisum, vt surgat: Subsequitur eleuatum, nè cadat.

2. Seria inuocatio. Promisit Deus absque conditione petentibus exauditionem, si petunt ea, quæ ad salutem sunt necessaria. Quicquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, hoc dabitur vobis. Ioh. 16. v. 23. Ego autem, qui iam me conuersum scio, ex vera fide peto perseuerantiam. Certus E. esse possum, Deum mihi eam daturum. Nulla in promissis eius est falsitas, quia nulla in faciendis omnipotenti est difficultas, inquit Fulg. l. 1.

3. Continuata mediorum vsurpatio. Sicut enim per primam eorundem applicationem conferebatur fides: ita si continuetur vsurpatio, continuuabitur ipsa fides & conuersio. Quare si semper audiam verbum, si vsurpem Sacramenta, vicissim certus esse possum de perseuerantia. Licèt enim quandoque dubitare incipiam, attamen statim habeo remedium, nempe S S. Cœnam, in qua confirmatur fides mea. Per istorum E. medioriam vsurpationem semper perseuerare & sic certus esse possum.

4. Serium non resistendi, nec mortaliter pecandi propositum. Nihil impedire potest perseuerantiam & excutere Spiritum S. quam peccatum mortale. Hoc autem vitare & fugere in mea praesertim, si iam conuersus sum, potestate est. Quod si igitur fixa sit sententia, me nolle mortaliter peccare, de perse uerantia vtiq; certus esse possum, cum sublata amissionis causa res non amittatur.

5. Causarum dubitandi absentia. Nullum enim potest proferri argumentum pro dubitatione, ad quod non ex scriptura facillimè responderi queat. Carnis infirmitati oppono vim spiritus in te habitantis. Tentationi oppono gratiam Patris, promissiones & similia. Sicut E. qui non ponitobicem certǫ conuertitur : ita qui non malitiosè peccat, aut peccare praesumit, sine dubio perseuerat atque adeò de salute sua & aeterna electione certus esse potest, imò certissimus.

XXXVII. Et huc pertinent tria illa fundamenta, quibus se Bernhardus erigere fuit, solitus nimirum, 1. Dei potestas, 2. Fidelitas. 3. Bona voluntas. Iam quod Deus potest & vult facere, id certissimè facit. At vero potest & vult te in bono conseruare. Quare conseruabit certissimè. Verba Berhardi cùm plena sint Spiritus & solatij, non piget adscribere. Sic autem loquitur Serm. 3. de fragmentis 7. panum: Tria considero, in quibus tota spes mea consistit; charitatem adoptionis; veritatem promissionis, potestatem redditionis. Murmuret iam, quantum voluerit insipiens cogitatio mea, dicens: Quis enim es tu? aut quanta est illa gloria tua, quibus meritis hanc obtinere speras? Et ego fiducialiter respondebo: scio cui credidi, & certus sum, quia in charitate nimia adoptauit me, quia verax in promissione, quia potens in exhibitione: licet enim facere quod voluerit. Hic est funiculus triplex qui difficile rumpitur, quem nobis à patria nostra in hunc carcerem vsq; dimissum firmi, per obsecro teneamus, vt ipse nos subleuet, ipse trahat & pertrahat, usque ad conspectum gloriæ magni Dei, qui est benedictus in secula. Bernardo adiungimus Augustinum, qui eleganter de hac quæstione disserit in Psal. 148, Verba sic habent: Erigat se humana fragilitas, non desperet, non se collidat, non se auertat, non dicat, Non ero vbi promisit, &c. Promisit nobis, quòd ibi futuri simus, vbi ipse est, erimus cum illo. Quid tibi Deus promisit, ô homo mortalis? Quia victurus es in æternum. Non credis? Crede, crede: plus est iam quod fecit, quàm quod promisit. Quid fecit? Mortuus est pro te. Quid promisit? Vt viuas cum illo. Incredibilius est, quòd mortuus est æternus, quàm vt in æternum viuat mortalis. Iam quod incredibilius est, tenemus &c.

XXXIIX. Ad hæc omnia, si Caluiniani regerant, maiorem ex ipsorum hypothesibus fluere certitudinem, cum statuant, fidem semel haustam non amitti, neque per peccata mortalia Spiritum S. protinus expelli: responsum hoc damus, quòd non sint affumenda falsa, vt eueniat indè bonum, aut excitetur solatium, imò & hoc nullum erit, cum tentatus facilè sit excepturus, & solidè demonstraturus scripturę tum dictis, tum exemplis, quod omninò excutiatur Spiritus per peccata mortalia, ideoque meram præsumtionem esse, quicquid de fide nunquam amittenda dicatur. Adde, quòd & sic possit excipere: Dicitis, electos nunquam amittere fidem, & S. S. gratiam. At vero amisi ego, proiectus sum à facie Domini, sentio iram eius & vltrices pœnas. Quare quid aliud hinc concludere possum quàm mè minimè electum esse. Si dicant sufficere, quòd aliquando fidei motum senserit. Imo verò non sufficit, reponet ille, quia si auerterit se iustus & fecerit iniquitatem, omnes iustitiæ eius, quas fecerat, non commemorabuntur, Ezech. 18. v. 24. Hic igitur cùm afflicto per hypotheses Caluinianas satisfieri nequeat, alia consolationis fundamenta esunt proferenda, quę non statim falsitatis argui, & ad quæ tētatus nihil solidi reponere queat, vt si ipsum ita alloquamur, Cur trepidas? Cur de pseuerantia in fide & gratia Dei dubitas? An quia prolapsus es in scelera? Noli putare ob id te protinus reprobatū esse, Davidis & Petri exempla intuere, & ijs te erige. Cogita benevolā Dei voluntatē quâ omnes ad se redire seriò exposcit, Cogita Christi passionē, quam pro tuis quoq; peccatis sustinuit. Cogita gratuitam Dei electionem, cui omnes pœnitentes & credentes inclusi sunt &c. Hæc consolatio longè efficacior est, quàm si multa de absoluta perseuerantia, & arcanis Dei decretis proponantur.

XXXIX. Vt E. tandem hanc quæstionem concludamus, istud colophonis loco repetimus, & in praxi semper vrgendū statuim⁹, quòd duo imprimis scopuli vitandi sint, 1. Dubitatio, 2. Præsumtio. In illam si impingas, Pontificios sequeris, tandē angeris & desperas: In hanc impingens ad Caluinianos transis & in carnalem securitatē incidis. Quare cogites, Primum promissiones Dei infallibiles, & sic liberaberis à dubitatione: post exhortationes minasq́; & sic liberaberis à securitate. Sit hîc mixtura spei & timoris, non quidē servilis, sed filialis. Ita enim inter scyllā perpetuę dubitationis, & inter charybdin absolutæ securitatis medium tenebit navicula fidei, cynosurā verbi secuta. De viroq; eleganter scribit Hugo in Ps 115. ex Gregorio, quibus verbis conclusam hanc quæstionem volumus. Sic verò habent: Spes sine timore luxuriat in præsumptionem: Et timor sine spe degenerat in desperationem. Propterea simul habenda sunt, vt eas coniungens David subdit: Qui timent Dominum, sperauerunt in eum. Hæ sunt duæ Molæ, inter quas debet moli cor hominis, vt indè panis fiat delectabilis Domino.


### Question V

I. This question is not of such great moment. For what utility redounds to us, whether we know the election of others or do not know it? But rather let us live in such a way that each one may work out his own salvation with fear and trembling: concerning the rest, the Lord will judge. Wherefore let us be neither too curious in inquiring, nor too precipitate in judging, For who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Rom. 14. 4.

II. Meanwhile, however, since we are confirmed in good by the salvation of others, and terrified from evil by their reprobation, this question is not entirely idle or pernicious, to which, that it may be satisfied, one must distinguish above all between Pagans and Christians, of whom the former are outside the Church, the latter in the Church. As far as Pagans are concerned, just as also Jews, we should not consider them all simply and indiscriminately as reprobate. For God is accustomed to illuminate the hearts of some, and to call some to the Church, as it was predicted concerning the Jews, Isa. 10. v. 20. c. 65. verse 8. Zech. 8. 23. Rom. 6. 27.

III. As far as concerns Christians, these are either infants or adults. Infants, since they are regenerated through Baptism and adopted as children of God, if they depart immediately in infancy, before malice perverts their heart, without doubt they are saved, and are deservedly held as elect. Adults are addicted to either a false or a true faith. If a false one, and they err either from ignorance and simplicity, or they still retain the foundation safe, as many in the Papacy, we hope very well concerning their salvation and election. If they are confessors of the true faith, they either persist in mortal sins, or they exercise themselves in good The former, unless they return, and repent even in their death agony, the sentence stands that they shall not enter the kingdom of heaven. The latter are considered either before or after death. If they have died in the true faith and the invocation of the divine name, we can pronounce certainly concerning their salvation. If they are considered, when they are still among the living, in fallibly, concerning them it is not permitted to affirm anything, because we are ignorant, partly whether their works are hypocritical, partly, whether they will remain in faith and piety. Thus Jerome judged, book 2 against Pelagius: Do not call anyone blessed before death. For as long as we live, we are in a struggle: as long as we are in a struggle, there is no certain victory. And Prosper, book 2 on the calling of the Gentiles, last chapter: In a secret most remote from human knowledge, he says, the predefinition of this election is hidden. And concerning no one before his end can it be pronounced that he will be in the glory of the elect, so that useful fear may preserve persevering humility, and he who stands, let him see that he does not fall.

IV. Moreover, the decision of this question can be briefly comprehended by two distinctions.

1. One judgment is absolute, when we pronounce this one or that one as certainly elect as if a priori: another is hypothetical, when we respond under the condition of faith, and thus a posteriori, and we call someone elect, if he perseveres. The former is rash, the latter is permitted.

2. One judgment is of truth, another of charity. The former is entirely infallible, the latter is conjectural. The former belongs to God, the latter to us. For because charity hopes all things, 1 Cor 13 ver. 7, hence we should also always hope well concerning the election of others, especially those living piously, nor should we easily consider anyone a hypocrite. Meanwhile, this judgment is not entirely certain and apodictic, since it depends on opinion and good hope. Hence the Apostle Peter names Silvanus faithful not absolutely, but according to his opinion. By Silvanus, he says, a faithful brother, as I consider, I have written, 1 Pet. 5 v. 12.

And let these things suffice concerning this question also. May God grant that we may be included in the number of the elect, and that we may all live in such a way that we are able to believe in our own election and hope for that of others, to His glory and our salvation. Amen.

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

I. Quæstio hæc non est adeò magni momenti. Quid enim vtilitatis ad nos redundat, sivè aliorum electionem sciamus siuè nesciamus? Quin potius ita viuamus, vt suam quisque salutem cum timore & tremore operetur: de reliquis judicabit Dominus. Quare nec nimis curiosi simus in inquirendo, nec nimis præcipites in judicando, Tu enim quis es qui indicas servum alienum Domino suo stat aut cadit. Rom. 14. 4.

II. Interim tamen, cum aliorum salute confirmemur in bono, reprobatione terreamur à malo, non prorsus otiosa aut pernitiosa est hæc quæstio, cui, vt satisfiat distinguendum ante omnia est inter Paganos & Christianos, quorum illi sunt extra Ecclesiam, hi in Ecclesia Paganos quod attinet, sicut & Iudæos non simpliciter & indiscretè omnes pro reprobatis habeamus. Solet enim Deus quorundam corda illuminare, nonnullos ad Ecclesiam vocare, sicut de Iudæis prædictum est, Esa. 10. v. 20. c. 65. versu 8. Zach. 8. 23 Rom. 6. 27.

III. Christianos quod concernit, hi vel Infantes sunt, vel adulti. Infantes, quoniam per Baptismum regenerantur, & in filios Dei adoptantur, si statim infantia decedant, antequam malitia cor ipforum peruertat, sine dubio saluantur, & pro electis meritò habentur. Adulti vel falsa vel vera fidei sunt addicti. Si falsa, & vel ex imperitia & simplicitate errant, vel fundamentum adhuc salvum retinent, vt multi in Papatu, de ipsorum salute & electione optimè speramus. Si veræ fidei confessores sunt, vel in peccatis mortalibus hærent, vel in bonis operibus se exercent. Priores nisi redeant, & vel in agone resipiscant, stat sententia, quòd regnum cælorum non ingrediantur. Posteriores considerantur vel ante, vel post mortem. Si in vera fide & inuocatione diuini nominis fuerint mortui certò de ipsorum salute pronunciare possumus. Si considerantur, quando adhuc in viuis sunt, infallibiliter, de ipsis nihil affirmare licet, quia ignoramus, partim num opera ipsorum sint hypocritica, partim, num in fide & pietate permansuri sint. Ita censuit Hieronymus, l. 2. aduersus Pelag. Nè beatum quempiam dixeris ante mortem. Quamdiu enim viuimus, in certamine sumus: quam diu in certamine, nulla est certa victoria. Et Prosper. l. 2. de vocat. gent. c. ult. In remotissimo, inquit, ab humana cognitione secreto, præfinitio huius electionis abscondita est. Et de nullo ante ipsius finem pronunciari potest, quod in electorum gloria sit futurus, vt perseuerantem humilitatem vtilis metus seruet, & qui stat, videat nè cadat.

IV. Potest autem huius quæstionis decisio duabus distinctionibus breuiter comprehendi.

1. Iudicium aliud est absolutum, cùm velut à priori hunc vel illum certò electum pronunciamus: aliud hypotheticum, cùm sub conditione fidei, atque sic à posteriori respondemus, & aliquem electum dicimus, si perseueret. Prius illud temerarium, hoc posterius concessum est.

2. Iudicium aliud est veritatis, aliud Charitatis. Illud prorsus infallibile, hoc conjecturale est. Prius Deo, posterius nobis competit, Quia enim Charitas omnia sperat, 1. Cor 13 ver. 7. hinc etiam de aliorum, præsertim piè viuentium, electione semper benè speremus, nec facilè quempiam pro hypocrita habeamus. Interim judicium hoc certum prorsus & Apodicticum non est, cùm ab opinione & spe bona dependeat. Hinc Apostolus Petrus Siluanum nõ absolutè, sed secundum opinionem suam fidele nominat. Per Siluanum, inquit, fratrem, ut arbitror fidelem scripsi, 1. Petr. 5. v. 12.

Et hæc de ista etiam quæstione sufficiant. Faxit Deus, vt electorum numero inclusi simus, & omnes ita viuamus, quò electionem nostram credere, aliorum sperare valeamus, ad ipsius gloriam & nostram salutem. Amen.

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 21 Disputation IX. On the Fall of the Elect and the Casting Off of the Holy Spirit


### Single Question Πρόθεραπα

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Paul Rössel of Reichenbach-Varis.

Πρόθεραπα.

Regarding the third chapter of our treatise, which we have entitled 'On the Elect,' one question remains, namely concerning the perseverance or rather the temporal apostasy of the elect, or concerning the expulsion of the Holy Spirit. For it comes into controversy: Whether faith and the grace of the Holy Spirit are expelled through mortal sins? Since discrepant opinions are found concerning this problem, we shall consider them briefly, and with Scripture as our guide, we shall indicate how the true ought to be discerned from the false.

THE ONLY QUESTION. Whether faith and the grace of the indwelling Spirit are expelled from the elect through mortal sins?
