I. A twofold distinction must be noted beforehand for a better understanding of the question: The first is that some are reborn, others are elect. For although these two sometimes coincide in one subject, it does not always happen. There are those who are reborn, who nevertheless, on account of foreseen final impenitence, are reprobate. Thus, there are those who are elect, who nevertheless at some time are not reborn. The reason, indeed, is that the reborn are estimated by present faith, but the elect by final faith. Because, therefore, many believe for a time, and thus are reborn, but afterwards in turn fail, hence every regenerate person is immediately elect. And because some perform penance at the end, and are thus elect, hence not every elect person is always and at every time regenerate.

II. The latter: The casting off of faith and grace is twofold; the one is called total, when justifying faith and the gift of renewal are lost entirely, and thus one becomes a son of wrath from a son of grace: the other is final, when not only is faith lost, but it is also never recovered, but one departs from this life in infidelity. With this distinction presupposed, we say that the regenerate can cast off faith, or deflect from faith, both totally and finally, as the examples of Judas, Hymenaeus, and others who believed for a time testify. But as regards the elect, we willingly concede that they do not finally lose faith, but will certainly believe at the end of life, because God chose them from eternity through this foreseen final faith: meanwhile, however, if they sin mortally and indulge in grave crimes, we maintain that at that very time of sin they totally cast off the grace of sanctification, and thus saving faith.

III. However, the Calvinists vehemently attack this orthodox thesis of ours, who defend that faith is not lost, nor the Holy Spirit cast off, by any shameful acts. For thus Beza argues in the Colloquy of Montbéliard, page 380: Those who are once gifted by God with true faith can never lose it again. And a little later: I say that David, in committing adultery, retained faith and the Holy Spirit and did not lose them. Which I will declare with a simile: A drunkard does not lose his intellect or reason; although as long as drunkenness occupies his head, reason does not exert itself, but is like a brute animal. And just as fire covered by ashes is by no means extinguished, but lies hidden: so also grace, faith, and the Holy Spirit are covered for a time in the falls of the elect, so that they are not felt, until they return to themselves, and acknowledge their sin, and perform penance.

Which also happened in the adultery of David, in which the grace of God was covered for a time, but not lost. Zanchius writes similar things in part 1 of his Miscellanea, p. 119 and following. And Trelicatius, in book 3 of his Institutes, in the place concerning faith, says: Faith is firm in all to such an extent that it can never be lost either totally or finally at any time. According to some degree it is often diminished: but according to its form it can never perish. Bucanus, loc. 29, quest. 27: Faith can receive a decrease and suffer as it were an eclipse, so that sometimes it is shaken by the storms of various temptations, obscured, overwhelmed, and becomes languid: indeed, even in the saints, it may be lulled to sleep and buried, no differently than reason in drunkards and infants: As in David when he committed adultery and in Peter when he denied Christ three times: but yet it is never completely cast out, etc. Sturmius, in his diatribe on predestination, distinguishes between πῖπτειν or to fall and ἐκπῖπτειν or to fall away. For thus he writes on p. 150: It is one thing to fall (πίπτειν), another to fall away (ἐκπίπτειν). We grant the former, we deny the latter in the saints. Elsewhere he distinguishes between the habit and the act of faith, that the former remains, the latter is lost through mortal sins. And this opinion pleases most Calvinists, namely, that the elect, although they fall mortally and do not feel faith in act, nevertheless retain it as if covered in ashes. That this pernicious error may be fully refuted, we shall bring forward 1. Sayings of Scripture. 2. Examples. 3. Reasons. 4. Testimonies and 5. we shall respond to the contrary objections.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Paulo Rössel Reichenbachio-Varisco.

Πρόθεραπα.

CIrcà tertium tractationis nostræ caput, quod de Electis inscripsimus, restat vnica quæstio, nimirum de perseuerantia vel potiùs apostasiâ temporali electorum, vel de excussione Spiritus Sancti. Venit enim in controuersiam : Num per peccata mortalia fides & gratia Spiritus sancti excutiatur? De quo problemate cùm reperiantur discrepantes sententiæ, paucis illas considerabimus, & verum à falso, quî discerni debeat, Scripturâ duce, indicabimus.

QVÆSTIO VNICA. Num electis fidem & Spiritus inhabitantis gratiam per mortalia peccata excutiant?

I. Duplex distinctio prænotanda est, ad melio rem quæstionis intelligentiam: Prior, quòd alij sint renati, alij electi. Quamvis enim hæc duo quandoque conueniantin vno subjecto, non tamen semper id contingit. Dantur renati, qui tamen ob præuisam finalem impœnitentiam sunt reprobati. Sic dantur electi, qui tamen aliquo tempore non sunt renati. Causa verò est, quoniam renati æstimantur ex fide præsenti, sed electi ex fide finali. Quia ergò multi credunt ad tempus, adeoque renati sunt, pòst autem vicissim deficiunt, hinc omnis renatus statim est electus. Et quia nonnulli in fine agunt pœnitentiam, adeóq; electi sunt, hinc non omnis electus semper & omni tempore est renatus.

II. Posterior: Excussio fidei & gratiæ duplex est; Altera totalis vocatur, cùm fides iustificans & donum renouationis ex toto perditur, adeóq; ex filio gratiæ fit filius iræ: altera finalis, cùm non tantùm amittitur fides, sed etiam nunquam recuperatur, verùm in infidelitate ex hac vita migratur. Quâ distinctione præsuppositâ dicimus, Quod renati possint tum totaliter, tum finaliter fidem excutere, vel à fide deflectere, sicut Iudæ, Hymenæi, & aliorum ad tempus credentium exempla testantur. Quòd verò electos attinet, concedimus lubenter, quod illi finaliter non perdant fidem, sed in termino vitæ certo credituri sint, quia per hanc finalem fidem præuisam eos ab æterno elegit Deus: Interim tamen, si mortaliter peccent, grauibusque sceleribus indulgeant, tum illo ipso peccati tempore gratiam sanctificationis, adeóque fidem saluificam totaliter ipsos excutere statuimus.

III. Hanc autem thesin nostram orthodoxam vehementer impugnant Caluiniani qui nullis flagitiis fidem perdi, aut Spiritum sanctum excuti defendunt. Sic enim Beza disputat in colloq. Mompelg. pag. 380. Qui semel verâ fide à Deo donantur, eam nunquam ampliùs amittere possunt. Et paulò pòst: Ego dico, Dauidem in adulterio perpetrato retinuisse fidem & Spiritum S. neque eam amisisse. Quod similitudine declarabo: Ebrius non amittit intellectum seu rationem:etsi quamdiu ebrietas caput eius occupat, ratio sese non exerat, sed similis sit animali bruto. Et quemadmodum ignis cineribus tectus minimè extinctus est, sed latet: Ita etiam gratia, fides & Spiritus S. in lapsibus electorum ad tempus teguntur, vt non sentiantur, donec ad seipsos redeant, & peccatum suum agnoscant & pœnitentiam agant.

Quod in Davidis adulterio quoque factum est, in quo gratia Dei ad tempus tecta, sed non amissa fuit. Similia scribit Zanchius part. 1. Miscell. p. 119. & seqq. Et Trelicatius l. 3. instit, loco de fide ait: Eatenus firma est fides in omnibus, vt nec totaliter, nec finaliter vllo vnquam tempore amitti queas. Secundum gradum aliquem sæpe minuitur: perire autem secundum formam nunquam potest. Bucanus loc. 29. quæst. 27. Fides accipere potest decrementum & veluti deliquium pati, vt nonnunquam variarum tentationum procellis concutiatur, obscuretur, obruatur, languida fiat: imò etiam in sanctis haut aliter, quam in ebriis & infantibus ratio, sopiatur & sepeliatur: Sicut in Davide cùm admisit adulterium & in Petro, cùm ter negauit Christum: sed tamen Nunquam penitùs excutitur, &c. Sturmius in diatribe de prædest. distinguit inter πῖπτειν vel cadere & ἐκπῖπτειν vel excidere. Sic enim scribit p. 150. Aliud est πίπτειν, aliud ἐκπίπτειν. Illud damus, hoc negamus in sanctis. Alibi distinguit inter habitum & actum fidei, illum manere, hunc perdi per peccata mortalia. Et hæc opinio plerisq; Calvinianis arri det, videlicet, electos, licèt cadant mortaliter, fidemque actu non sentiant, attamen illam quasi cinerib. tectam retinere. Qui error perniciosus vt plenè refutetur, proferemus 1. Dicta Scripturæ. 2. Exempla. 3. Rationes. 4. Testimonia & 5. ad obiectiones contrarias respondebimus.


### Single Question: I. Sayings of Scripture, by which the casting out of faith and the Holy Spirit is proved

I. Sayings of Scripture, by which the casting out of faith and the Holy Spirit is proved.

IV. 1. Ezek. 18, v. 26. When the righteous man shall turn away from his righteousness and shall do iniquity, he shall die in them: In the iniquity that he has worked, he shall die. The same is found in ch. 33, v. 12, 13. Whence we argue thus: Whoever can turn himself away from his righteousness so that he may die, he totally loses the grace of God and faith, since that spiritual death is nothing other than the loss of grace. But the righteous man can so turn himself away from righteousness through iniquity that he may die, namely, spiritu ally. Therefore the righteous man, through iniquity, totally loses the grace of God and faith.

V. They object 1: That the Lord speaks under a condition which posits nothing.

Resp: 1. Although it is a condition, it is not however impossible, otherwise this threat would be a vain scarecrow. 2. Nor do we pronounce absolutely that the righteous man turns away from faith and dies, but truly ὑποθετικῶς (hypothetically), if he should sin mortally, which examples testify can happen, and sounder Calvinists do not deny. 3. In the text these two predications are opposed to one another; if the wicked man shall have done penance; And: if the righteous man shall have turned himself away. Since therefore the former is possible, why is the latter established as impossible? 4. Calvin himself admits that conditionals sometimes posit something, l. 3. Instit. c. 2. sect. 12. concerning the saying of John 8. v. 31, writing thus: Unless many were to fall away from common faith, Christ would not have said to the disciples: if you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, etc.

2. That the discourse is about hypocrites, not truly righteous men.

Resp. This clearly contradicts the text. For the description of the righteous man which exists in v. 6, 7, 8 does not befit hypocrites, especially because of the clause added in verse 9: This man is righteous, he shall live by life, says the Lord. But truly he who feigns himself righteous out of hypocrisy displeases God, and therefore shall not live by life. Add that the righteous and the unrighteous, the pious and the impious are here opposed. Just as therefore truly unrighteous men are understood, so also are truly pious and righteous men; concerning whose righteousnesses the Lord pronounces in verse 24 that He does not wish to remember them any longer, from which it follows that they were previously acceptable before God, and consequently by no means hypocritical.

3. That Jehovah speaks of temporal death and corporal punishments.

Resp. 1. The opposites are under the same genus. By the life of the righteous man, however, is not understood temporal life, but rather spiritual life, consisting in the gracious κατοικήσę (indwelling) of the Spirit, which a glorious exaltation in the heavens will follow. Therefore, by death also, not temporal death, but spiritual death is denoted.

2. It is familiar to the Scriptures that by the name of death is expressed the privation of grace and the guilt of damnation, as in Gen. 2, v. 17: in the day that you eat of it, you shall die the death. 2 Sam. 12, v. 14: You shall not die, that is, you shall not be stripped of the grace of God, nor shall you be damned. And it is known what is understood by death when it is announced as the wages of sin, namely, alienation from grace, exclusion from eternal life, or damnation, as is evident from the opposition in Rom. 6, v. last: The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life. 5. Temporal death is common to all men, since the just die no less than the impious. But the Lord speaks not of death common to the just and unjust, but of that proper to the unjust alone, and therefore it cannot be understood as temporal death by any sound mind.

VI. 2. From Matthew we see the following sayings. c. 18, v. 32: Wicked servant, did I not forgive you the whole debt? Should you not also have had mercy on your fellow servant? And his lord, being angry, delivered him to the torturers. So also will my heavenly Father do to you. Therefore, just as that servant fell from the grace of his master through the sin of unmercifulness, so the reborn fall from the grace of God if they are similarly unmerciful or pollute themselves with other sins.

Chap. 24, v. 12, 13: The charity of many will grow cold: But he who perseveres to the end will be saved. Here, by growing cold is understood the total extinction of charity, and consequently of faith; otherwise it could not be opposed to final perseverance. In those, however, in whom charity grows cold, it follows that it existed in them beforehand, otherwise it could not grow cold.

Chap. 15, v. 28: Take the talent from him, and give it to him who has ten talents; from this it appears in turn that the gifts of God once bestowed can be lost or diminished.

VII. 3. From Luke chap. 8, v. 13: They believe for a time, but in the time of temptation they fall away. Here the discourse is not about feigned faith, but true faith, since it is said: 1. They themselves receive the word with joy. 2. They believe for a time. 3. They are tempted or tested. But no one by God is tempted, unless he is a believer. 4. to fall away. But if they had never been endowed with true faith, they would not truly fall away. Therefore, the exception of Polanus is frivolous, who by τὸ credere understands not salvific faith, but only historical, or simple assent. For in the preceding verse 12, it appears sufficiently in what sense τὸ credere is taken here, when it is said, "Those by the way side are they that hear; then cometh the Devil, and taketh away the word out of their hearts, lest they should believe and be saved." Here certainly the discourse is about salvific faith, by which, namely, one is saved. But it is taken in the same sense in the following verse. For he compares those who are by the way side with those who are upon the rock; and he affirms that the former do not believe, but these believe for a time. By what faith, therefore, those are said not to believe, by the same these are said to believe for a time, if the comparison is to be legitimate. But those are said not to believe with salvific faith. Therefore, these will be said to believe with salvific faith. And if the Savior were speaking only of historical πίστει, could it not also be said of those who are by the way side, and who stand among thorns, that they believed, whom nevertheless Christ denies to believe? He speaks of those who are in the Church, but it is necessary that all members of the Church have historical faith, although not salvific. For he who does not even offer historical assent to the word of God, he is clearly ἄθεος, nor is he to be held as a member of the visible Church.

Chap. 11. v. 24. When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest; and finding none, he saith, I will return unto my house whence I came out. And when he cometh, he findeth it swept and garnished. Then goeth he, and taketh to him seven other spirits more wicked than himself; and they enter in, and dwell there: and the last state of that man is worse than the first. From these words our thesis flows openly, that the house garnished and purged, from which the unclean spirit was cast out, can again be defiled and occupied by Satan. For although Christ seems at first to speak of bodily obsession, yet that spiritual [obsession], which is denoted by the bodily, is at the same time included. is brought forward, it cannot be denied, since that house is said to be swept with brooms, and has been frequent with Christ, to accommodate the examples of those corporally obsessed to a corrupt nature.

VIII. 4. From John chap. 8, v. 34. Everyone who commits sin (namely against conscience) is a slave of sin. Whence we can gather thus: No one who retains faith and the Holy Spirit is a slave of sin. Everyone who sins against conscience is a slave of sin. Therefore, no one who sins against conscience retains faith. The proposition is true from Rom. 8, v. 2 and 1 John 5, v. 4. The minor is the Savior's. Wherefore the conclusion will be firm and immovable.

Chap. 15, v. 2. Every branch in me not bearing fruit, he will take it away. However, no branch is in Christ except through faith, Rom. 11, ver. 20. Hence we argue: Certain branches inserted into Christ are taken away and eradicated. All branches inserted into Christ are endowed with true faith. Therefore, certain ones who are endowed with true faith are taken away and eradicated. But it is false what Polanus says, that he who is called to the church by external vocation is called a branch here. For the words of Christ are clear; a branch in me κλῆμα ἐν ἐμοὶ. But no one is in Christ except through faith. Then it is said that if it does not bear fruit, the Father is about to take it away. He does not take it from the number of those externally called, but rather from the number of the reborn. Therefore, the former was truly reborn: which itself appears more evidently from v. 6; If anyone has not remained in me, he will be cast out, like a branch, and you will wither. Hence it is clear that he is a branch who is in Christ, and he bears fruit who remains in Christ, both of which can only be done through faith. Therefore, every branch that withers and is cast out is cast out for this reason, because it does not remain in Christ; but indeed it remains in the visible assembly of the called. Therefore, this ejection is to be understood as a spiritual deprivation of grace.

IX. 5. From the epistle to the Romans c. 8, v. 13. If you live according to the flesh, you shall die. Here the Apostle addresses those truly reborn, which is evident from v. 1, 9, & 11, and says, If they sin, and are about to live according to the flesh, they are immediately about to die. He speaks, however, not of bodily death, which is certain & inevitable, but of spiritual death, which consists in the casting out of grace & the Holy Spirit. Therefore, every reborn person who lives according to the flesh dies, that is, loses grace & the Holy Spirit.

Chap. 11. vers. 20. et seqq. Because of unbelief they were broken off. Wherefore they were previously in the tree of salvation, & fell away. But you stand by faith, and if you remain in goodness, otherwise you also shall be cut off. Whoever therefore does not remain in goodness, by this very fact is broken off, i.e., loses grace & the Holy Spirit. Reborn persons sinning mortally do not remain in goodness. Therefore, they are broken off, & lose grace.

X. 6. From the first to the Corinthians, chapter 6, last verse. I chastise my body, and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps when I have preached to others, I myself should become a castaway. From this statement it is elicited: 1. That election is not absolute, but made with the condition of perseverance. 2. That an elect person, even through mortal sins, if not finally, yet for a time, can become ἀδόκιμον or useless, that is, be deprived of the gracious presence of the Holy Spirit.

Chap. 10. vers. 12. Let him who thinks he stands, take heed lest he fall. Therefore, reborn persons who are standing can fall, and by falling lose the grace of God. They object that Paul is warning not the faithful but the δοκησισόφους [those who think themselves wise], who seem to stand and believe. But the preceding and subsequent verses protest; v. 11 it is said: These things were written for our admonition. v. 13. No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man. God is faithful, etc. All these things deal with truly faithful people: Why therefore should the intermediate words be understood as concerning hypocrites? By δοκεῖν, therefore, a false opinion is not denoted, but a true persuasion.

XI. 7. From the epistle to the Galatians c. 5. v. 4. You have been emptied of Christ, you who are justified by the law, you have fallen from grace. Paul speaks here of those who had truly been reborn, as is evident in verse 7: 'You were running well.' He says that these good runners are emptied of Christ and fall from grace if they wish to be justified by the law. But how can they be emptied of Christ if they were never in Him through faith? How will they fall from grace if they never came into the participation of it?

XII. 8. From the first to Timothy, ch. 1, v. 5 & 6: 'The goal of the commandment is love, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and a sincere faith, from which some, having wandered, have turned aside to empty talk.' The Apostle speaks of faith, not only historical, but justifying, which is joined 1. with love, 2. a pure heart, and 3. a good conscience. Since he says that some have wandered from this, it follows that the casting away of faith is certainly possible.

Ch. 1, v. 19: 'Wage the good warfare, having faith and a good conscience, which some having rejected have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith; of whom are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan.' Again the Apostle speaks of true, not hypocritical, of saving, not historical faith, because 1. he commends such to Timothy: but shall we think that a feigned faith is commended to be retained? 2. is the shipwreck of a hypocritical faith not dangerous? 3. hypocritical or historical. But the Apostle has a discourse concerning such.

The following sayings from ch. 4, v. 1 tend to the same goal: 'In the latter times some will depart from the faith.' Ch. 6, v. 10: 'The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, which some craving, have wandered from the faith.'

XIII. 9. From the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 3, v. 6: 'Whose house we are, if indeed we hold fast the confidence and the hope of which we boast, firm to the end.' Therefore the Spirit says: 'Today if you will hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.' From these words it is gathered thus: He who can harden his heart against himself, and is warned not to do so, is not finally deserted; justified believers can harden themselves and may be moved not to do so. Therefore, the just, the believers, can finally fall away.

Chap. 6 vers. 4. 5. 6. It is impossible for those who 1. were once enlightened. 2. and have tasted of the heavenly gift. 3. and were made partakers of the Holy Ghost. 4. and have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come; and have fallen away, to be renewed again unto repentance. Here it is said that those truly reborn, when they have once sinned, can never return to repentance, if indeed they have sinned against the Holy Ghost: which sin sometimes falls upon those who were truly reborn, and by sinning in such a way, they cast out the Holy Ghost. Two things, therefore, are observed in the text. 1. A description of the truly reborn. 2. A clear assertion that these reborn ones can sin, but after sinning cannot return to repentance. A similar passage exists, Hebr. 10. v. 26. & seqq.

XIV. 10. From the latter epistle of Peter, chap. 1. vers. 9. He to whom these things are not present is blind, and groping with his hand, receiving forgetfulness of the purging of his old sins. He, therefore, who has once been purged of his sins, can become blind, which is by the loss of grace and the Holy Ghost.

Chap. 2. vers. 20. 21. For if after they have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, they are again entangled therein, and overcome, the latter end is worse with them than the beginning. For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them. But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire. From this passage we conclude thus: Those who have been purged from the pollutions of the world, they are truly reborn: But indeed many such are again entangled. Therefore it is not impossible for the truly faithful to fall away, and to lose the grace of God. For this reason they are compared to a sow that was truly washed, but afterwards again defiled; likewise, to a dog, which had previously vomited, and had been purged, but afterwards but returns to his vomit.

XV. 11. From the first [epistle] of John, ch. 4, v. 20. If anyone says, I love God, and hates his brother, he is a liar. But indeed this will be false according to the Calvinists, who say that David nevertheless loved God, even though he had pursued his brother Uriah with such hatred that he gave him over to slaughter.

Ch. 2, v. 10, a similar passage is held: He who says he is in the light, and hates his brother, is in darkness even until now. And ch. 3, v. 15. Every murderer does not have life remaining in him. We urge the word μένουσαν, and we infer: Murder and other crimes cannot stand together with faith. Since, therefore, the reborn commit murder, it follows that they cast off faith.

XVI. 12. From the Apocalypse, ch. 2, v. 4, 5. You have left your first charity: remember therefore from where you have fallen, do penance, and do the first works. Ch. 3, v. 2. Hold what you have, so that no one may take your crown. These sayings are so manifest that there is no need for further proof and explanation. For to leave charity and to be able to be despoiled of the crown, do they not clearly indicate the possibility of ἀποστασίας?

Latin:

I. Dicta Scripturæ, quibus probatur excussio fidei & Spiritus sancti.

IV. 1. Ezech. 18. v. 26. Cùm auerserit se iustus à iustitia sua & fecerit iniquitatem, morietur in eis: In iniustitia, quam operatus est, morietur. Idem reperitur c. 33. v. 12. 13. Vnde sic argumentamur: Quicunq; à iustitia se sua potest auertere vt moriatur, is gratiam Dei & fidem totaliter perdit, quoniam mors illa spiritualis nihil est aliud, quàm gratiæ perditio. Atqui iustus per iniquitatem ita se potest auertere à iustitia, vt moriatur, nempè spiritualiter. Ergo iustus per iniquitatem, Dei gratiam & fidem totaliter perdit.

V. Excipiunt 1: Dominum loqui sub conditione, quæ nihil ponat.

Resp: 1. Quamuis sit conditio, non tamen est impossibilis, alias ista comminatio vanum esset terriculamentum. 2. Neque nos absolutè pronunciamus, justum deflectere à fide & mori verùm ὑποθετικῶς, si peccet mortaliter, id quod fieri posse exempla testantur, & saniores Calviniani non inficiantur. 3. In textu hæ duæ prædicationes sibi opponuntur; si impius pœnitentiam egerit; Et: si iustus se auerterit. Cùm igitur illa sit possibilis cur hæc statuitur impossibilis? 4. Calvinus ipse cõditionales quandoq; aliquid ponere fatetur l. 3. Instit. c. 2. sect. 12. de dicto Ioh. 8. v. 31. ita scribēs: Nisi à communi fide multi exciderent non dixisset Christus discipulis: si vos manseritis in sermone meo, verè discipuli mei estis, &c.

2. Sermonem esse de hypocritis, non verè iustis.

Resp. Hoc planè contrariatur textui. Nam descriptitio justi quæ extat v. 6. 7. 8. non competit hypocritis, pręsertim ob additā clausulam versu 9. Hic iustus est, vitâ vivet, ait Dominus. At verò qui iusstum se simulat ex hypocrisi, Deo displicet, ideoque vitâ non vivet. Adde, quòd iusti & iniusti, pij & impij hîc opponuntur. Sicut Ergò verè iniusti, sic etiam verè pij & iusti intelliguntur; de quorum iustitiis pronunciat Dominus vers. 24. quòd nolit earum ampliùs recordari, vnde sequitur, quòd antea fuerint coram Deo acceptæ, & per consequens nequaquam hypocriticæ.

3. Loqui Iehovam de morte temporali & pœnis corporalibus.

Resp. 1. Opposita sunt sub eodem genere. Per vitam verò iusti non intelligitur temporalis vita, sed potiùs spiritualis, consistens in gratiosa κατοικήσę Spiritus, quam sequetur gloriosa in cœlis exaltatio. E. & per mortem non temporalis mors, sed spiritualis denotatur.

2. Familiare est Scripturis, vt nomine mortis exprimatur priuatio gratiæ, & reatus damnationis, vt Gen. 2. v. 17. in die, qua comederis, moriendo morieris. 2 Sam. 12. vers. 14. Non morieris, id est non exueris gratiâ Dei, nec damnaberis. Et notum est, quid per mortem intelligatur, quando vt stipendium peccati annunciatur, nimirum alienatio à gratia, exclusio à vita æterna vel damnatio, vt patet ex oppositione Rom. 6. v. ult. Stipendium peccati mors, donum autem Dei est vita æterna. 5. Mors temporalis omnibus hominib. communis est, cùm iusti non minus moriantur, quàm impii Loquitur a. Dominus de morte non iustis & iniustis communi, sed solis iniustis propria, ideoq́; temporalis vix sani intelligi nequit.

VI. 2. Ex Matthæo sequentia dicta vigemus. c. 18. v. 32. Serue nequam, nonnè totum debitum remisi tibi? Nonne debuisti & tu misereri conservi tui? Et iratus Dominus tradidit eum tortoribus. Sic & Pater meus cælestis faciet vobis. Vt igitur servus ille per peccatum immisericordiæ excidit gratiâ heri: sic renati excidunt gratiâ Dei, si consimiliter immisericordes sint aut aliis peccatis se polluant.

Cap. 24. v. 12, 13. Refrigescet charitas multorum: Qui autem perseveraverit usque ad finem, salvus erit. Hic per refrigescere intelligitur omnimoda extinctio charitatis, & consequenter fidei; aliàs non posset opponi perseuerantiæ finali. In quibus autem refrigescit charitas, in ijs anteà extitisse sequitur, aliàs refrigerscere non posset.

Cap. 15. v. 28. Tollite ab eo talentum, & date ei, qui habet decem talenta; inde vicissim apparet, dona Dei semel tradita perdi posse aut deteri.

VII. 3. Ex Luca cap. 8. v. 13. Ad tempus credunt, tempore autem tentationis recedunt. Hic sermo est, non de fide ficta, sed vera, quoniam dicitur: 1. Ipsos verbum suscipere cum gaudio. 2 ad tempus credere. 3. tentari vel probari. Nemo autem à Deo centatur, nisi fidelis. 4. recedere. Sin autem verâ fide nunquàm præditi fuissent, verè non recedérent. Proindè frivola est exceptio Polani qui per τὸ credere intelligit non fidé salvificam, sed duntaxat historicam, seu simplicem assensum. Etenim versu præcedenti 12. satis apparet, quo τὸ credere hîc sumatur sensu, quando dicitur, Qui secus viam, hi sunt, qui audiunt, deinde Diabolus venit, & tollit verbum de corde eorum ne credentes salvi fiant. Hîc certè sermo est de fide saluifica, quâ nempè quis salvus fit. Eodem autem sensu accipitur v. sequenti. Cõfert enim eos, qui secus viam cum ijs, qui super petram sunt; Et eos non credere, hos autem ad tempus credere adfirmat. Quâ igitur fide illi non credére, eâdem hi ad tempus credere dicuntur, si comparatio legitima esse debeat. Ast illi dicuntur, non credere fide saluificâ. E. hi dicentur credere fide saluificâ. Et si de historica πίστει tantùm loqueretur salvator, annon & de ijs qui secus viam, & qui inter spinas consistunt, dici posset quod crederent, quos tamen credere Christus negat. Loquitur de iis, qui sunt in Ecclesia, omnia autem Ecclesiæ membra historicam vt habeant fidem necesse est, quamvis non salvificam. Nam qui ne quidem historicum præbet verbo Dei assensum, is planè ἄθεος, nec pro membro Ecclesiæ visibilis habendus est.

Cap. 11. v. 24. Cùm immundus spiritus exiverit de homine, ambulat per loca inaquosa, quærens requiem & non inueniens, dicit, Reuertar in domum meam unde exivi. Et cùm venerit, inuenit eam scopis mundatam & ornatam. Et tunc vadit, & assumit septem alios spiritus secum &c. Ex his verbis apertè fluit thesis nostra, quòd domus ornata & purgata, à quâ spiritus immundus ejectus fuit, iterùm à Satana possit conspurcari & occupari. Quamvis enim videatur Christus primò de corporali obsessiooe loqui, quin tamen spiritualis, quæ corporali denotatur simul inclulatur, negari nequit, cùm domus illa dicatur scopis mundata, Christoque frequens fuerit, exempla corporaliter obsessorum accomodare ad naturam corruptam.

IIX. 4. Ex Iohanne cap. 8. v. 34. Omnis qui peccatum committit, (videlicet contra conscientiam) peccati servus est. Vnde sic possumus colligere: Nullus, qui retinet fidem & Spiritum sanctum, est servus peccati. Omnis qui peccat contra conscientiam, est seruus peccati. Ergò nullus qui peccat contra conscientiam, retinet fidem, Propositio vera est ex Rom. 8. v. 2. & 1. Ioh. 5. v. 4. Minor est salvatoris Quare conclusio erit firma & immota.

Cap. 15. v. 2. Omnem palmitem in me, non ferentem fructum, tollet eum. Nullus autem palmes est in Christo nisi per fidem, Rom. 11. ver. 20. Hinc argumentamur Quidam palmites Christo inserti tolluntur & eradicantur. Omnes palmites Christo inserti verâ fide præditi sunt. E. quidam qui verâ fide sunt præditi, tolluntur & eradicantur. Falsum verò est, quod ait Polanus, palmitem hic vocari eum, qui externâ vocatione ad ecclesiam vocatus est. Nam verba Christi clara sunt; palmitem in me κλῆμα ἐν ἐμοὶ. In Christo vero nemo est nisi per fidem. Deindè dicitur, quòd si non ferat fructum, sublaturus sit eum Pater. Non autem tollit è numero externè vocatorum, sed potiùs numero renatorum. E. prius verè renatus fuit: quod ipsum ex v. 6. evidentius apparet; Si quis in me non manserit, mittetur foràs, sicut palmes & aresces. Hinc patet, quòd is sit palmes, qui in Christo est, & is ferat fructum, qui in Christo manet, quod vtrumque non nisi per fidem fieri potest. Omnis igitur palmes, qui arescit, & foràs ejicitur, ideò eijcitur, quia in Christo non manet; At verò in visibili vocatorum cœtu permanet. E. ista ejectio de spirituali priuatione gratiæ intelligenda est.

IX. 5. Ex epistola ad Romanos c. 8. v. 13. Si secundum carnem vixeritis, moriemini. Hic alloquitur Apostolus verè renatos quod patet ex v. 1. 9. & 11. & ait, Si peccent, & secundum carnem victuri sint, protinus eos esse morituros. Loquitur autem non de morte corporali, quæ certa & inevitabilis, sed de spirituali, quæ consistit in excussione gratiæ & S. S. Omnis ergò renatus, qui secundum carnem vivit, moritur, hoc est, amittit gratiam & Spiritum sanctum.

Cap. 11. vers. 20. seqq. Propter incredulitatem fracti sunt. Quare prius fuerunt in arbore salutis, & reciderunt. Tu autem fide stas, & si permanseris in bonitate, alioquin & tu excideris. Quisquis igitur non manet in bonitate, hoc ipso defringitur, h. e. amittit gratiam & Spiritum S. Renati mortaliter peccantes, non manent in bonitate. E. defringuntur, & gratiam amittunt.

X. 6. Ex priori ad Corinthios cap. 6. v. ult. Castigo corpus meum, & in servitutem redigo, nè fortè cum aliis prædicaverim, ipse reprobus efficiar. Ex hoc dicto elui cicit. 1. Electionem non absolutam, sed cum conditione perseverantiæ factam. 2. Electum etiam per peccata mortalia si non finaliter, ad tempus tamen posse fieri ἀδόκιμον vel inutilem, hoc est privari gratiosa Spiritus sancti præsentia.

Cap. 10. vers. 12. Qui sibi videtur stare, videat nè cadat. Possunt igitur renati stantes cadere, & cadendo gratiam Dei perdere. Excipiunt, Paulum monere non πίστους sed δοκησισόφους, qui videntur stare, & credere. Sed reclamant præcedentia & subsequentia, v. 11. dicitur: Hæc scripta sunt ad nostrâ admonitionem. v. 13. Tentatio vos non apprehendit, nisi humana. Fidelis Deus &c. Hæc omnia de verè fidelibus agunt: Cur ergò verba intermedia de hypocritis intelligenda essent? Per δοκεῖν igitur non denotatur fallax opinio, sed vera persuasio.

XI. 7. Ex epistola ad Galatas c. 5. v. 4. Evacuati estis à Christo, qui in lege iustificamini, à gratiâ excidistis. Paulas hic loquitur de ijs, qui verè fuerant renati, vt patet verf. 7. Currebatis benè. Hos bonos cursores ait à Christo euacuari, à gratia excidere, si per legem voluerint justificari. Quomodo autem euacuari possunt à Christo, si in ipso per fidem nunquam fuerunt? quomodo excident à gratia, si in huius participatum nunquam venerunt?

XII. 8. Ex priori ad Timoth. c. 1. v. 5. & 6. Finis præcepti est charitas, de corde puro, conscientia bonâ & fide non fictâ, à quibus quidam aberrantes, conuersi sunt in vaniloquium. Loquitur Apostolus de fide, non tantùm historicâ, sed justificante, quæ coniuncta est 1. cum charitate 2. corde puro 3. & bona conscientia. Ab hac cùm quosdam aberrasse dicat, vtique excussionem fidei possibilem esse sequitur.

Cap. 1. v. 19. Milites bonam militiam, habens fidem & bonam conscientiam, quam quidam repellentes circa fidem naufragauerunt; ex quibus est Hymenæus & Alexander, quos tradidi Satanæ. Iterum verba facit Apostolus de verâ, non hypocritica, de saluifica, non historica fide, quia 1. talem commendat Timotheo: num autem simulatam fidem ad retinendum commendari putabimus? 2. num hypocriticæ naufragium periculosum non est, 3. hypocritica vel historica. De tali autem sermonem habet Apostolus.

Ad eundem scopum tendunt sequentia dicta ex c. 4. v. 1. In nouissimis temporibus discedent quidam a fide C. 6. v. 10. Auaritia radix est omnium malorum quam quidam appetentes, errauerunt à fide.

XIII. 9. Ex epistola ad Hebræos c. 3. v 6. Cuius domus nos sumus, si modò fiduciam & spem illam, de qua gloriamur, ad finem vsque firmam retinuerimus. Quapropter dicit Spiritus: Hodiè si vocem eius audieritis, nolite indurare corda vestra. Ex his verbis ita colligitur : Qui potest sibi indurare cor, & monetur nè faciat, is non est finaliter deserto, Iustificati credentes possunt se bè tridicare tur, & moveantur ne id faciant. Ergò iusti, credentes possunt finaliter deficere.

Cap. 6 vers. 4. 5. 6. Impossibile est eos, qui 1 semel sunt illuminati. 2. gustaverunt etiam donum coeleste. 3. & participes facti sunt Spiritus sancti. 4. & gustaverunt bonum Dei verbum, virtutesque venturi seculi; & prolapsi sunt, rursus renovari ad poenitentiam. Hic dicitur, verè renatos quando semel peccârunt, nunquam redire posse ad poenitentiam, si videlicet in Spiritum sanctum peccârint: quod peccatum quandoque in illos cadit, qui verè fuerunt renati, & taliter peccando excutiunt Spiritum sanctum. Duo igitur in textu observantur. 1. Descriptio verè renatorum. 2. Clara assertio quod renati isti peccare queant, post peccatum autem ad poenitentiam redire nequeant. Similis locus extat, Hebr. 10. v. 26. & seqq.

XIV. 10. Ex posteriori Petri, cap. 1. vers. 9. Cui non praesto sunt haec, caecus est, & manu tentans, oblivionem accipiens purgationis veterum suorum delictorum. Ille igitur, qui semel purgatus est â dilectis suis, potest fieri caecus, quod sit amissione gratiae & Spiritus sancti.

Cap. 2. vers. 20. 21. Si refugientes coinquinationes mundi in cognitione Domini & Salvatoris Iesu Christi, his rursus implicati superantur, facta sunt eis posteriora deteriora prioribus. Melius enim erat illis non cognoscere viam iustitiae, quam post cognitionem retrorsum converti ab eo, quod illis traditum est, sancto mandato. Contigit enim illud veri Proverbij: Canis reversus ad suum vomitum, & sus lota in volutabro luti. Ex hoc loco ita colligimus: Qui ab inquinamentis mundi sunt purgati, ij sunt verè renati: At verò multi tales rursus implicantur. Ergo non impossibile est, verè fideles deficere, & gratiam Dei perdere. Ob hanc enim causam comparantur sui verè lotae, postmodum verò rursus conspurcatae; item, cani, qui prius vomuerat, & purgatus fuerat, postmodù autem ad vomitum reuertitur.

XV. 11. Ex priori Iohannis c. 4. 20. Si quis dixerit, diligo Deum, & fratrem suum oderit, mendax est. At verò falsum hoc erit iuxta Caluinianos, qui dicunt, Dauidem nihilominùs dilexisse Deum, etiamsi fratrem suum Vriam vsque adeò fuerit odio prosecutus, vt eum internecioni daret.

Cap. 2. v. 10 similis habetur locus: Qui dicit se in luce esse, & fratrem suum odio habet, in tenebris est vsque adhuc. Et c. 3. v. 15. Omnis homicida non habet vitam in se manentem. Vrgemus vocem μένουσαν, & inferimus: Homicidium & alia scelera non possunt simul stare cum fide, Cùm ergò renati homicidium committunt, fidem ipsos excutere consequens est.

XVI. 12. Ex Apocalypsi C. 2. v. 4. 5. Charitatem tuam primam reliquisti: memor esto itaq; vnde excideris, age pœnitentiam, & fac prima opera. C. 3. v. 2. Tene, quod habes, vt nemo accipiat coronam tuam. Dicta hæc adeò manifesta sunt, vt vlteriori probatione & explicatione opus non sit. Nam charitatem relinquere & coronâ spoliari posse, annon possibilitatem ἀποστασίας luculenter indicant?


### Single Question: II Examples

II EXAMPLES.

XVII. Although the question here is primarily about men after the state of the fall, two examples preceding that state are usually and can be set forth.

Of the angels, who were initially righteous, afterwards fell away out of pride, and were changed from angels of light into angels of darkness. To this point looks that [passage] of Jude 6: The angels who did not keep their origin, but left their dwelling, are reserved in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day. If, therefore, that concreated righteousness can be abandoned by angels, much more can the adventitious [righteousness] be abandoned by men. Thus the Apostle concludes in 2 Pet. 2, v. 4: God did not spare the sinning angels, but delivered them into Tartarus, dragged from the chains of night, and he will much less spare other sinners.

2. Of our first parents, who through the fall shook off the image of God, consisting in true righteousness Eph. 4. ver. 24, and lost the grace of God, as is evident from Gen. 3.

XIIX. But lest our adversaries complain that we have brought forward foreign examples alien to the state, many other examples can be added, which are recounted in the Scriptures after the fall.

We give therefore 1. The example of Aaron, who sinned most gravely by erecting the golden calf Exod. 32. v. 1. seqq. and most basely excluded the Holy Spirit through idolatry.

2: Of Saul, who previously had the Holy Spirit graciously dwelling within him 1. Sam. 9. v. 13, but afterwards he departed from him, as is evident from 1. Sam. 16, v. 14. The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul and an evil spirit agitated him. From which opposition of the evil and good spirit it appears that Saul had previously been truly reborn.

3. Of David, who was a murderer and an adulterer, and thus lived according to the flesh; but he who lives according to the flesh, dies, Rom. 8. ver. 13, and every murderer does not have eternal life remaining in him. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 15. Adulterers also do not have a part in the kingdom of GOD, Ephes. 5. ver. 5. Therefore David truly shook off the Holy Spirit through murder and adultery. Whence he had need of such serious repentance, which was nothing else than a return to the grace from which he had previously fallen. For whoever always retains grace has no need of repentance. Nor is it to be valued as of any trifle what the Calvinists say, that David did not lose the Holy Spirit because he prays that the Spirit not be taken away. For that prayer was made after repentance, where he in turn recovered the Holy Spirit previously shaken off. Hence Beza part. 2. Resp. ad colloq. Mompelg. p. 73. confesses that David would have perished, had he not repented. But in truth, no one can perish in whom even the smallest spark of faith is found, Matt. 12, v. 20; Isa. 42, v. 3.

4. Of Solomon, who was certainly loved singularly by God, as is evident in 1 Kings 3, v. 3 & ch. 8, v. 15; but afterwards, having become an idolater, he sinned horribly and cast off the Holy Spirit, 1 Kings 11, v. 15.

5. Of the Ninevites, whom the removal of the punishment and Jonah himself testify to have been truly, not hypocritically, converted, ch. 3, v. 10. These, however, in turn relapsed into impiety, as is evident from ch. 1 of Nahum, where he describes the burden of Nineveh.

XIX. We allege from the New Testament. 1. The example of Peter, denying Christ. Peter was reborn, as is evident from Matt. 16, v. 17: 'Blessed art thou, Bar-Jona, for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee.' Afterwards, however, he cast off the grace of God, because he who denies Christ will in turn be denied by Christ, Matt. 10, v. 21; and whoever is not of Christ does not have the Spirit of Christ, Rom. 8, v. 9. And how could Peter have faith in Christ, whom he denied? The form of faith is to apprehend Christ, John 1, v. 12. The opposite was present in Peter, namely, the denial of Christ, not the apprehension. Furthermore, where there is need for a new conversion, there a turning away has preceded. Peter had need of a new conversion, as is hinted at in Luke 22, v. 32: 'When thou art once converted, strengthen thy brethren.' Nor is it for the Calvinists to seek an escape in the prayer of Christ, by which He asked that the faith of Peter might not fail. For that prayer is not to be understood concerning a total, but a final, failure. Some declare this from that passage in Luke 8, v. 52: 'The maid is not dead, but sleepeth'; where death is not simply denied, but κατά τι [in a certain respect] on account of the subsequent resuscitation. Thus some say that the faith of Peter did not fail entirely in the denial, on account of the restoration and conversion that was to follow. Meanwhile, if we consider the act of faith itself and the time of the sin, it had totally failed, although Peter returned to it shortly.

2. Thomas, who truly believed in Christ as the Messiah of the world before the passion: but afterwards he was clearly incredulous, especially concerning the article about the resurrection of Christ, John 20, v. 25. Therefore, he did not have faith at that time, but cast it off.

3. Simon Magus, who truly believed and adhered to Philip, according to the statement in Acts 8, v. 13, but afterwards fell away most wickedly, and most miserably lost grace and the Holy Spirit.

4. Of the Galatians, who, as Paul says, were running well, but afterwards, when they wished to be justified by the law, were emptied of Christ and fell from grace, Gal. 5, verses 4, 6.

5. Of Alexander, 1 Tim. 1, v. 19. 6. Of Hymenaeus and Philetus, 2 Tim. 2, v. 17. 7. Of Demas, 2 Tim. 4, v. 10. To these may be added, by way of a conclusion, predictions concerning other apostates, such as are read in Acts 20, v. 30: 'From among yourselves men will arise, speaking perverse things.' 1 Tim. 4, v. 1: 'The Spirit says expressly that in the latter times some will depart from the faith.' 2 Pet. 2, v. 1: 'There were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you, who will introduce destructive sects, and deny the Lord who bought them.'

XX. From these examples and predictions, such an argument can be constructed: That which happened to the angels, to our first parents, to Saul, David, Solomon, Peter, and others endowed with true faith and holiness, and that which the Scriptures predict will happen to others, that can entirely come to pass. But indeed, it is read concerning the angels and our first parents that they fell from grace through sins and abandoned their original righteousness, and the same is foretold of others in the Scriptures. Therefore, this very thing can happen, and consequently, the Holy Spirit does not remain in the elect if they sin mortally.

Latin:

II EXEMPLA.

XVII. Quamuis de hominibus post statum lapsus potissimum hic quæratur, præmitti tamen solent & possunt duo exempla, istum statum præcedentia.

Angelorum, qui primitus iusti, postea ex superbia defecerunt, & ex angelis lucis in angelos tenebrarum mutati sunt. Quò spectat istud Iudæ 6. Angeli qui non seruauerunt suam originem, sed reliquerunt suum domicilium, in iudicium magni diei, vinculis æternis sub caligine reseruantur. Si ergò illa concreata iustitia ab angelis, multò magis aduentitia ab hominibus deseri potest. Ita concludit Apostolus 2. Pet. 2. v. 4. Deus Angelis peccantib. non pepercit, se & catenis noctis detractos in tartarum tradidit, multò minus alijs peccatoribus parcet.

2. Primorum parentum, qui per lapsum imaginem Dei, in iustitia vera consistentem Ephes. 4. vers. 24. excusserunt, & gratiam Dei perdiderunt vticonstat ex Gen. 3.

XIIX. Verùm nè conquerantur aduersarij, peregrina & à statu aliena exẽpla nos attulisse, subiungi queunt alia benè multa, quæ post lapsum in Scripturis recitantur.

Damus ergò 1. Exemplum Aaronis, qui erigendo vitulum aureum grauissimè peccauit Exod. 32. v. 1. seqq. & per idololatriam Spiritum sanctum turpissimè exclusit.

2: Saulis, qui prius habuit Spiritum sanctum gratiosè sibi inhabitantem 1, Sam. 9. v. 13. postea autem recessit ab eo, vti patet ex 1. Sam. 16, v. 14. Spiritus Domini recessit à Saul & exagilabat cum Spiritus nequam. Ex qua oppositione mali & boni Spiritus apparet Saulem prius verè fuisse renatum.

3. Dauidis, qui homicida fuit & adulter, atque sic secundum carnem vixit; qui autem secundum carnem vivit, moritur, Rom. 8. vers. 13. & omnis homicida non habet vitam æternam in se manentem. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 15. Adulteri etiam partem non habent in regno DEI, Ephes. 5. vers. 5. Ergo David verè per homicidium & adulterium excussit Spiritum sanctum. Vnde tàm seriâ opus habebet pœnitentiâ quæ nihil erat aliud, quàm reversio ad gratiam, quâ prius exciderat. Quisnim gratiam semper retinet, is pœnitentiâ opus non habet. Nec est vllius titiuilitij æstimandum, quod Caluiniani dicunt, Dauidem spiritum sanctum non amisisse ideò, quoniam petat, nè auferatur Spiritus. Nam ista precatio facta est post pœnitentiam, vbi vicissim Spiritum sanctum prius excussum recuperauit. Hinc Beza part. 2. Resp. ad colloq. Mompelg. p. 73. fatetur cogitur, Dauidem periturum fuisse, nisi resipisisset. At profectò nemo perire potest, in quo vel minima fidei scintillula reperitur, Matth. 12. v. 20. Esai. 42. v. 3.

4. Salomonis, qui certè singulariter à Deo dilectus fuit, vt patet 1. Reg. 3. v. 3. & c. 8. v. 15. postmodum autem idololatra factus horribiliter peccauit, & Spiritum sanctum excussit, 1. Reg. 11. v. 15.

5. Niniuatarum, quos verè, non hypocriticè conuersos fuisse ablatio pœnæ & ipse Ionas testatur c. 3. v. 10. Hi tamen vicissim fuerunt in impietatem relapsi, vt patet ex ca. 1. Nahum, vbi onus Niniuae describit.

X I X. Ex nouo Testamento allegamus. 1. Exemplum Petri, abnegantis Christum. Erat Petrus renatus, vti patet ex Matth. 16. v. 17 Beatus Bar Ionas, quia caro & sanguis non reuelauit tibi. Pòst autem gratiam Dei excussit, quia qui negat Christum, vicissim à Christo negabitur, Matth. 10. v. 21. & quicunque non est Christi, Spiritum Christi non habet Rom 8. v. 9. Et quomodo potuit Petrus fidem habere in Christum, quem abnegauit? Fidei forma est, Christum apprehendere Ioh. 1. vers. 12. Contrarium adfuit Petro, nempè Christi abnegatio, non apprehensio. Porrò vbi nouâ conuersione opus est, ibi præcessit auersio. Petro opus erat rouâ conuersione, vt innuitur Luc. 22. v. 32. Tualiquando conuersus confirma fratres tuos. Nec est, vt Caluiniani effugium quærant in precatione Christi, quâ petijt, nè fides Petri deficeret. Ea enim precatio non de totali, sed finali defectione est intelligenda. Nonnulli declarant hoc ex illo Luc. 8. vers. 52. Puella non est mortua, sed dormit: vbi non simpliciter mortua negatur, sed κατά τι propter secuturam resuscitationem: Ita quidam dicunt, fidem Petri in abnegatione non omnino defecisse, propter instaurationem & conuersionem secuturam. Interim si ipsum actum fidei & peccati tempus consideremus, totaliter illa defecerat, quamuis ad illam Petrus breui redierit.

2. Thoma, qui in Christum tanquam Messiam mundi verè credidit ante passionem: pòst autem planè incredulus fuit, præsertim circa articulum de resurrectione Christi, Ioh. 20. v. 25. Fidem ergò tum temporis non habuit, sed excussit.

3. Simonis Magi, qui verè credidit & Philippo adhæsit, iuxta dictum Actor. 8. v. 13. postmodum autem pessimè defecit, gratiamque & Spiritum sanctum miserrimè amisit.

4. Galatarum, qui dicente Paulo, currebant benè, posteà autem cùm per legem iustificari vellent, à Christo euacuabantur & gratia excidebant, Gal. 5. vers. 4. 6.

5. Alexandri, 1. Tim. 1. v. 19. 6. Hymenæi & Phileti, 2. Tim. 2. v. 17. 7. Demæ, 2. Tim. 4. v. 10. His addi possunt colophonis loco prædictiones de alijs Apostatis, quales leguntur Act. 20. v. 30. Ex vobis ipsis exurgent viri loquentes peruersa. 1. Tim. 4. v. 1. Spiritus manifestè dicit, quia in nouissimis temporibus discedent quidam à fide. 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. Fuerunt & Pseudeprophetæ in populo, sicut & in vobis erunt doctores mendaces, qui introducent sectas perditionis, & eum, qui emit eos, Dominum negans.

XX. Ex his verò exemplis & prædictionibus tale argumentum extrui potest: Quod angelis, quod primis parentibus, quod Sauli, Dauidi, Salomoni, Petro & alijs verâ fide & sanctitate præditis euenit, & quod Scripturæ in alijs futurum prædicunt, id omninò fieri potest. At verò de Angelis & primis parentibus legitur, quòd per peccata exciderint gratiâ, & deseruerint primam iustitiam, idemque de alijs prænunciatur in Scripturis. Ergò hoc ipsum fieri potest, & per consequens, Spiritus S. non manet in electis, si peccent mortaliter.


### Single Question: III. Reason III. Reasons

III. REASON

III. REASONS.

XXI. 1. From formulas of speaking. When Scripture speaks of the fall of the Saints, it uses such phrases and formulas as to openly imply that those, by sinning, at once lose and cast off true faith and the righteousness with which they were previously endowed. For it says that the Saints and those previously beloved by God alienate themselves backward and turn away. Isai. 1, v. 4; silver turned into dross, v. 22; the vineyard to degenerate, Isai. 5, v. 3; Jer. 11, v. 21; to turn away from righteousness, Ezech. 33, v. 18; charity to grow cold, Matth. 24, v. 12; salt to be rendered insipid, Marc. 9, v. 20; to begin in the spirit, to end in the flesh, Gal. 3, verse 3; to fall from grace, Gal. 5, v. 4; to extinguish the spirit, 1 Thess. 5, v. 19; to make shipwreck of the faith, 1 Tim. 1, verse 19; to fall away from the faith, 1 Tim. 4, verse 1; to fall away from the living God, Heb. 3, verse 12; to cast away confidence, Hebr. 10, verse 35; to withdraw oneself, Hebr. 10, v. 38; to turn away from God once known, Heb. 12, v. 25. to deny the Lord, 2 Pet. 2, v. 1; to fall from one's own steadfastness, 2 Pet. 3, v. 17; to recede and not remain in the doctrine of Christ, 2 Ioh. v. 9; to fall, Apoc. 2, v. 5. All these locutions must be corrupted and changed into a foreign and improper sense, if it is to be established that grace once bestowed cannot be lost through mortal sins.

XXII. 2. From the nature of the covenant and divine grace. If no one is received into the grace or covenant of God absolutely, but always with the condition, if he shall have remained in obedience, and shall not rebel, it follows that, this condition being posited, the grace of God is lost and cast off. The antecedent is true. Therefore, the consequent is also. The truth of the antecedent is proved from 2 Par. 15, verse 2: The Lord was with you, because you were with him. If you seek him, you will find him; if you forsake him, he will forsake you. Esa. 1, v. 19: If you are willing, you shall eat the good things of the land; if you are unwilling and rebellious, the sword shall devour you. Ezech. 17, v. 15: Shall he prosper or obtain salvation who has done these things? And he who has dissolved the covenant, shall he escape? Add Rom. 11, v. 7; 1 Cor. 15, v. 2; Hebr. 3, v. 7. To this also should be referred the punishments which God has threatened to the righteous departing from righteousness, which similarly prove that grace is conferred only under a condition. They are: the forgetting of former righteousness, Ezek. 33, v. 13; displeasure, Heb. 10, v. 38, Heb. 2, v. 4; denial, Luke 9, v. 26, 2 Tim. 2, v. 12; cutting off, John 15, v. 2; death, Heb. 6, v. 4.

XXIII. From admonitions. Admonitions are instituted everywhere so that the saints may not sin, or that by sinning they may not cast off the Holy Spirit, such as are read in Eph. 5, v. 14, 1 Cor. 6, v. 9, 10, ch. 10, v. 10, Gal. 5, v. 19, 20, 1 Pet. 2, v. 11, Rev. 3, v. 11. But to what purpose would these admonitions be necessary if the reborn could not desert the faith or in any way lose the grace of the Holy Spirit? They say that admonitions are instituted so that the reborn, sometimes becoming sluggish, may be aroused and run with greater alacrity. But in truth, they are not only premonitions that the reborn may proceed, but also that they may not fall, 1 Cor. 10, v. 12; that they may not be cut off, Rom. 11, v. 22; that they may not become reprobate, 1 Cor. 9, v. 27; or lose their crown, Rev. 3, v. 11.

XXIV. 4. From the fear of the faithful. Whoever are kept in their duty by the fear of rejection, these can fall from their state. But in truth, the saints keep themselves and others in their duty by the fear of rejection. Therefore, they can fall from their state. For otherwise, their fear in this matter would be clearly vain. The minor premise is proven by the examples of all the faithful and clear testimonies of Scripture, Matt. 5, v. 13, John 15, v. 5, 1 Cor. 9, v. 27, Phil. 2, v. 14, Heb. 4, v. 1. It was indeed an ancient error of the Jews, who thought that by the force of the covenant and the promises they were always in grace before God, even without the obedience of duty: but the Prophets refute this persuasion with many and long sermons. The same was the madness of the Corinthians, which the Apostle refutes in 1 Cor. 10, v. 1, et seqq.

XXV. 5. From the causes bringing about defection. Those upon whom the cause of defection can fall, they themselves can defect and fall away. But in truth, the causes of defection can fall upon the reborn, indeed they fall more often, and the reborn can fail and fall away. The minor is proved by an enumeration of causes and the application of the same. The causes are: untimely security, Apoc. 2. v. 5; contempt of the means, Luc. 13. v. 24, Ioh. 12. v. 35, 2 Cor. 6. v. 2, Heb. 3. v. 12; corrupt conversation, Psalm. 1. v. 1, 1 Cor. 15. v. 33, Gal. 1. v. 8; excessive credulity, Matt. 24. v. 24, 2 Cor. 11. v. 3, 2 Thess. 2. v. 10; sins against conscience, 1 Tim. 1. v. 19; love of pleasures, Ose. 4. v. 11, Luc. 21. v. 34, 2 Pet. 2. v. 18; horror of persecutions, Matth. 13. v. 20, 2 Tim. 4. v. 16; pursuit of riches, Matth. 13. v. 22, 1 Tim. 6. v. 10; pride and contempt of brothers, Rom. 11. v. 18; security and torpor, Matth. 12. v. 43, c. 13. v. 12; malignity of heart against divine threats, Deut. 29. v. 18; and finally, hardness and loss, Psal. 95. v. 8, Hebr. 3. v. 13, Act. 7. v. 51, Ephes. 4. v. 30, 1 Thess. 5. v. 19.

XXVI. 6. From the causes averting defection. If perseverance depends on certain causes, then the intermission of those will beget the shaking off of grace. But indeed, perseverance depends on certain causes. Wherefore, if these are omitted, a shaking off will immediately follow. The causes, however, of perseverance and conservation are: assiduous reading and meditation of Scripture, 1 Tim. 4. v. 13; attentive conservation of divine benefits, Ioh. 5. v. 18; continued faith, 1 Pet. 1. v. 5; prayers and vigils, Matth. 26. v. 41; pursuit of an integral conscience, 1 Tim. 1. v. 19; solicitous and holy fear, Rom. 11. v. 18, Phil. 2. v. 14; anxious examination of oneself, 2 Cor. 13. v. 5, etc. That these causes can sometimes be intermitted, indeed are intermitted in the very act, various examples prove, whence the possibility of defection is in turn clearly made known.

XXVII. 7. From regeneration made in Baptism. All infants are justified and renewed through Baptism. For it is the washing of regeneration, Tit. 3. v. 5, and as many as are baptized put on Christ, Gal. 3. v. 27. But many, having become adults, lose this gift of παλιγγενεσίας through mortal sins, since scarcely a fourth part of the baptized produce true fruits of faith, as is evident from the parable in Luke 8. Wherefore grace, which has once been bestowed, is not retained immutably.

XXIIX. 8. From the ἐνεργείᾳ [energy/activity] of faith. True and living faith is never silent or idle, but always efficacious, busy, and joined with good works. Whitaker confesses this in his last sermon, page 185, where he says these words: Those who think that true faith can be idle or dead, or void of good works, think contrary to the confession of our Church. Now, indeed, good works and mortal sins are opposites, since the one immediately expels the other. Whenever, therefore, a mortal sin is committed, then no place is given to good works. Wherefore faith is also immediately shaken off, since it is dead, or rather, it is nothing without good works.

XXIX. From contraries. These can never be together in one and the same subject. But mortal sin and faith are contraries. Therefore, they cannot exist together, but he who sins mortally loses faith immediately. The minor premise is proven, because as long as mortal sin has a place, it is not forgiven. But where sin is not forgiven, there faith finds no place, because faith apprehends the merit of Christ, by which all sins are covered. Therefore, when mortal sin is posited, guilt and the hatred of God are posited, and therefore faith is excluded.

XXX. 10. From repentance. Those who have need of new repentance are not in the grace of God. The regenerate who sin mortally have need of new repentance. Wherefore they are not in the grace of God. The major premise is proven, because repentance, new or as if snatched anew, is nothing other than a return to God and a conversion to Him. But he who is said to return and recover grace must surely have lost it first. For that which is always retained is not first recovered: And who can turn himself to grace who has never been turned away from it?

XXXI. 11. On the distinction between mortal and venial sins. This distinction cannot be denied, since it is most firmly grounded in the Scriptures. But this is the chief sign and foundation of this distinction, that mortal sins expel faith and the Holy Spirit, while venial ones do not. The Papists indeed wish for that distinction to be deduced from the nature of the thing and of the sin, but against them all the orthodox maintain that any sins whatsoever are by their own nature mortal, yet some are called venial insofar as they consist together with faith, by which they are covered and immediately remitted. Now, if you say that no sin at all expels faith in the elect, the given distinction of sins will collapse entirely; which is ἄτοπον καὶ ἀδιόλογον.

XXXII. 12. From Apostasy. If true justice and faith, once bestowed, are never shaken off, and indeed cannot be shaken off, it will follow that there is no ἀποστασίαν, which sin, however, is most frequently rebuked in the Scriptures. We prove the consequence, because the term from which the ἀποστασίας proceeds is not hypocritical faith and holiness (for he who deserts this is not to be blamed), but rather true, living, and saving faith. The possession of this, therefore, always precedes before a falling away occurs, whence it follows that either every ἀποστασίαν properly so-called must be denied, or someone can fall away from true faith who nevertheless never had it, and thus a privation can exist where a habit did not precede, both of which are most absurd and contrary to the Scriptures and the analogy of faith.

XXXIII. 13. From the sin against the Holy Spirit. Among the other properties of this sin, this one is also included, that an acknowledgment of the truth, and often a gracious sealing of the Holy Spirit's κατήχησιν, always precedes it, as is evident from Heb. 6:4, 5, 6. Ursinus seems to admit this in part 1 of his Catechetical explanations, p. 67, where he says these words: The sin against the Holy Spirit does not fall upon just any reprobates, but only upon those who have been illuminated by the Holy Spirit and in their consciences convinced of the truth, as Saul, Judas. But on the following page he immediately forgets himself, while he says: Who if they sin, have never been truly converted. Are they therefore enlightened by the Holy Spirit or as the epistle to the Hebrews describes, who have been made partakers of the Spirit, who have tasted the heavenly gift and the powers of the world to come, are they, This statement is ἄτοπον, and therefore our thesis stands, that there is a certain kind of sin against the Holy Spirit, which presupposes true faith and conversion, which malicious deniers of the truth lose, and thus cast off all grace, and despoil themselves of eternal salvation. Conversely, therefore, either the sin against the Holy Spirit must be denied in part, or the casting off of grace and faith must be conceded.

XXXIV. 14. From the absurd. If justice could not be abandoned, nor faith lost, it would be necessary for the just always to persevere; and consequently no one would deliberate about preserving justice and faith: for who undertakes deliberations about the impossible or the necessary? From which it would further follow that exhortations not to abandon it are void, counsels for perseverance are empty, and admonitions, reproofs, and other incitements to virtues and barriers against vices are conceived in vain, all of which are absurd. A not inelegant passage from 2. Nicomachean Ethics, ch. 4 & 5, can be referred to here.

Latin:

III. RATIO

III RATIONES.

XXI. 1. A formulis loquendi. Scriptura cùm de Sanctorum lapsu loquitur, tales phrases & formulas usurpat, vt apertè innuat, istos peccando vna perdere & excutere fidem veram & iustitiam, quâ anteà fuerunt præditi Dicit enim Sanctos & Deo priùs dilectos abalienare se retrorsum & apertere. Esai. 1. v. 4. argentum verti in scorias, v. 22. vineam degenerare, Esai. 5. v. 3. Ier. 11. v. 21. auertere se á iustitia, , Ezech. 33. v. 18. charitatem refrigescere, Matth. 24. v. 12. reddi sal insulsum, Marc. 9. v. 20. in spiritu incipere, in carne desinere, Gal. 3, vers. 3. à gratia excidere, Gal 5. v. 4. spiritum extinguere, 1. Thess. 5. v. 19. naufragium fidei facere, 1. Tim. 1, vers. 19 deficere à fide, 1 Tim. 4. vers. 1. deficere à Deo viuente, Herb. 3. vers. 12 fiduciam abijcere. Hebr. 10. vers. 35. se subducere. Hebr. 10. v. 38. auersari Deum ante cognitum, Heb. 12. v. 25. abnegare Dominum, 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. excidere à propria stabilitate, 2. Pet. 3. v. 17. recedere nec manere in doctrina Christi, Ioh. 2. v. 9. excidere, Apoc. 2. v. 5. Omnes, hæ locutiones deprauandæ & in alienum impropriumque sensu mutandæ sunt, si gratia semel collata per peccata mortalia perdi nō posse statuatur.

XXII. 2. A natura fœderis & gratię diuinæ. Si nemo in gratiam vel fœdus Dei recipitur absolutè, sed semper cum conditione, si manserit in obedientia, nec rebellet, sequitur, hac conditione positâ gratiam Dei perdi & excuti. Antecedens verum est. Ergò & consequens. Antecedentis veritas probatur ex 2. Par. 15. vers. 2. Dominus vobiscum fuit, quia fuistis cum eo. Si quæsieritis eum, inuenietis, si dereliqueritis eum, derelinquet vos. Esa. 1. v. 29. Si volueritis, bona terræ comedetis, si nolueritis & rebelles fueritis, gladius deuorabit vos, Ezech. 19, v. 15. Nunquid prosperabitur vel consequetur salutem, qui fecit hæc? & qui dissoluit pactum, nunquid effugit? Adde R. 11. v. 7. 4. C. 15. v. 2. Hebr. 3. v. 7. Huc etiam referri debent supplicia, quæ Deus minatus est justis à justitia discedentibus, quæ similiter evincunt, gratiam sub conditione tantùm conferri. Sunt illa, prioris justitiæ oblivio, Ezech. 33, v. 13. displicentia, Hebr. 10. v. 38. Heb. 2. v. 4. abnegatio, Luc. 9. v 26. 2. Tim. 2 v. 12. abscisio, Joh. 15. v. 2 mors, Ezech. 33. v. 18. Rom. 8. v. 12. & irreparabile exitium, Hebr. 6 v. 4.

XXIII. A commonefactionibus. Passim instituuntur admonitiones nè peccent sancti, neuè peccacando Spiritum sanctum excutiant, quales leguntur, Eph. 5. v. 14. 1. Cor. 6. v. 9. 10. c. 10. v. 10. Gal. 5. v. 19. 20. 1. Pet. 2. v. 11. Apoc. 3. v. 11. Ad quid autem opus foret his commonefactionibus, si renati fidem non deserere, aut gratiam Spiritus sancti nullo modo perdere possent? Dicunt, admonitiones institui, vt renati quandoque torpescentes excitentur, & eò majori alacritate currant. At verò non tantùm sunt præmonitiones, vt renati pergant, sed etiam, nè cadant, 1. Cor. 10. v. 12. nè excindantur, Rom. 11. vers. 22. nè reprobi fiant, 1. Cor. 9. v. 27. vel coronam suæ amittant, Apoc. 3. v. 11.

XXIV. 4. A metu fidelium, Quicunque metu rejectionis in officio continentur, hi de statu suo queunt excidere. At verò sancti metu rejectionis se aliosque in officio continent. Quare possunt de statu suo excidere. Alàs enim metus ipsorum hac de re planè foret irritus. Minorem probant exempla omnium fidelium & clara Scripturæ testimonia, Matth 5. vers. 13. Ioh. 15. v. 5 1. Cor. 9. v. 27. Phil 2. v. 14. Hebr. 4. v. 1. Antiquus quidem error fuit Judæorum, qui putabant vi fœderis & promissionum se coram Deo semper in gratia esse, etiam citra officij obsequium: Sed Prophetæ multis & prolixis concionibus hanc persuasionem reprehendunt. Eadem fuit Corinthiorum amentia, quam redarguit Apostolus 1. Cor. 10. v. 1. seqq.

XXV. 5. A caussis defectionem conciliantibus. In quos cadere potest causa defectionis, illi ipsi deficere & excidere possunt. At v. in renatos cadere possunt, imò & sæpiùs cadunt causæ defectionis, & renati deficere & excidere queunt. Minor probatur per causarum enumerationem, & earundem applicationem. Causæ a. sunt intempestiva securitas, Apoc. 2. v. 5. contemptus mediorum, Luc 13. v. 24. Ioh. 12. v. 35. 2 Cor. 6. v. 2. Heb. 3. v. 12 prava conversatio, Psalm. 1. v. 1. 1. Cor. 15. v. 33. Gal. 1. v. 8. nimia credulitas, Matt. 24. v. 24. 2. Cor. 11. v 3. 2. Thess. 2. v. 10. peccata contra conscientiam, 1. Tim. 1. v. 19. amor voluptatum, Ose. 4. v. 11. Luc. 21. v 34 2. Pet. 2. v. 18. horror persecutionum, Matth. 13. v. 20. 2. Tim. 4. v. 16 studium divitiarum, Matth. 13. v 22. 1. Tim. 6. v. 10. elatio & contemptus fratrum, Rom. 11. v. 18. securitas & torpor, Matth. 12. v 43. c. 13. v. 12 malignitas cordis adversus comminationes divinas, Deut. 29. v 18. & tandem industas & perdis, Psal. 95. v. 8 Hebr. 3. v 13. Act. 7. v. 51. Ephes. 4. v. 30. 1 Thess. 5. v. 19.

XXVI. 6 A causis defectionem avertentibus, Si perseverantia dependet a certis causis, cum illarum intermissio gignet excussionem gratiæ. At verò perseverantia dependet à causis certis. Quare si omittantur hæ, excussio protinus sequetur. Causæ autem perseverantiæ & conservationis sunt assidua Scripturæ lectio & meditatio, 1. Tim. 4. v. 13 attenta beneficiorum divinorum conservatio, Ioh. 5. v. 18 fides continuata, 1. Pet. 1. v. 5. preces & vigiliæ, Matth. 26. v. 41. studium integræ conscientiæ, 1. Tim 1. v. 19. sollicitus & sanctus timor, Rom. 11. v. 18 Phil. 2. v. 14. anxium sui examen, 2. Cor. 13. v. 5. &c. Has causas quandoque intermitti posse, imò actu ipso intermitti probant exempla varia, vnde possibilitas defectionis vicissim luculenter innotescit.

XXVII. 7. A regeneratione in Baptismo facta. Omnes infantes per Baptismum iustificantur & renovantur. Est enim lauacrum regenerationis Tit. 3. v. 5. & quotquot baptizantur, Christum induunt, Gal. 3. v. 27. Multi autem adultiores facti perdunt hoc donum παλιγγενεσίας per peccata mortalia, cùm vix quarta pars baptizatorum veros fidei fructus edat, vti constat ex parabola Luc. 8. quare non immutabiliter retinetur gratia, quæ semel est collata.

XXIIX. 8. Ab ἐνεργείᾳ fidei. Vera & viua fides nunquam est taciturna vel otiosa, sed semper efficax, negotiosa & cum bonis operibus coniuncta. Fatetur hoc Whitakerus in concione vltima pag. 185. vbi hæc verba: Qui veram fidem posse otiosam aut mortuam, aut bonorum operum inanem esse, arbitrantur, contra Ecclesiæ nostræ confessionem sentiunt. Iam verò bona opera & peccata mortalia sunt opposita, quoniam vnum statim expellit alterum Quandocunque igitur peccatum mortale committitur, tum bonis operibus locus non datur. Quocirca & fides protinus excutitur, quoniam illa mortua, imò nulla est absque bonis operibus.

XXIX. A contrarijs. Nunquam, hæc possunt esse simul in vno eodemque subiecto. Peccatum verò mortale & fides sunt contraria. E. simul consistere nequeunt, sed qui mortaliter peccat, ocyus fidem amittit. Minor probatur, quia peccatum mortale quamdiu locum habet, tamdiu non remittitur. Vbi verò peccatum nõ est remissum, ibi fides locum non inuenit, quia fides meritū Christi apprehendit, quo peccata omnia conteguntur. Posito igitur peccato mortali, ponitur reatus & Dei odiū, ideóque excluditur fides.

XXX. 10. A pœnitentiâ. Qui opus habent nouâ pœnitentiâ, illi non sunt in Dei gratiâ. Renati mortaliter peccantes, opus habent nouâ pœnitentiâ. Quare non sunt in Dei gratia. Maior probatur, quia pœnitentia nouavel de nouo quasi erepta nihil est aliud, quàm reditus ad Deum, & conuersio ad ipsum. Qui autem redire & gratiam recuperare dicitur, prius vtique illam perdidisse oportet. Quod enim semper retinetur, illud primùm non recuperatur: Et qui auersus nunquam fuit à gratiâ, qui ad eam se conuertere potest?

XXXI. 11. A discrimine peccatorum mortalium & venialium. Distinctio hæc negari nequit, cũm in scripturis sit fundatissima. Hoc autè præcipuum eius discriminis signum & fundamentum est, quòd peccata mortalia expellant fidem & Spiritum S. venialia non item. Pontificij quidem ex natura rei & peccati distinctionem illam deductam volunt, sed contra ipsos orthodoxi omnes statuunt, peccata quęuis ex natura sua esse mortalia, interim quædam dici venialia, quatenus vná cum fide consistunt, per quam teguntur, & protinùs remittuntur. Iam verò si dicas, nullum omninò peccatum fidem in electis pellere, prorsus concidet data peccatorum distinctio; quod ἄτοπον καὶ ἀδιόλογον.

XXXII. 12. Ab Apostasia. Si iustitia & fides vera semel collata nunquam excutitur, & nè quidem excuti potest, sequetur, nullã dari ἀποστασίαν, quod tamen peccatum in Scripturis sæpissimè reprehenditur. Probamus consequentiam, quia terminus à quo ἀποστασίας nõ est fides & sanctitas hypocritica, (hanc enim qui deserit, culpandus non est) sed potiùs vera, viua & salutaris. Huius igitur possessio semper præcedit, antequam fiat defectio, vndè sequitur, vel omnem ἀποστασίαν propriè dictam esse negandam, vel aliquem à verâ fide posse deficere, qui tamen illam nunquam habuit, adeoóque priuationem dari, vbi habitus non antecessit, quod vtrumque absurdissimum est, Scripturis & analogię fidei contrarium.

XXXIII. 13. A peccato in Spiritum S. Inter cæteras huius peccati proprietates & ista refertur, quòd semper veritatis agnitio, sæpè gratiosa pSpiritus S. κατήχησιν obsignatio præcedat, vti patet ex Heb. 6 v. 4 5. 6. Fateri hoc videtur Vrsinus part. 1. explic. Catechet. p. 67. vbi hæc verba: Peccatum in Spiritum S. nõ in quosvis reprobos, sed in eos tantùm cadit, qui à Spiritu S. illuminati & de veritate in conscientijs conuicti sunt, vt Saul, Iudas. Sed pag seq. sui statim obliuiscitur, dum ait: Qui si peccant, nunquam fuerunt verè conuersi. An ergò illuminati à Spiritu S. vel vt epistola ad Hebræos describit, qui participes facti sunt Spiritus, qui gustauerunt donum cœleste & virtutes venturi seculi, an, inquam illi non sunt verè conuersi? Dictum hoc ἄτοπον est, ideoque perstat thesis nostra, dari quandam peccati in Spiritum S. speciem, quæ præsupponit veram fidem & conuersionem, quam malitiosi veritatis abnegatores perdunt, adeoque omnem gratiam excutiunt, & semetipsos æterna salute spoliant. Vicissim ergò vel peccatum in Spiritum Sanctum ex parte est negandum, vel excussio gratiæ, fideique concedi debet.

XXXIV. 14. Ab absurdo. Si non posset deseri iustitia, nec perdi fides, necessarium esset, iustos semper perseuerare; ac proinde nemo de iustitia fideque conseruandæ deliberaret: quis enim deliberationes suscipit de impossibili aut necessario? Vnde porrò sequeretur, irritas esse adhortationes, de ea non deserenda, inania esse ad perseuerantiam consilia, frustrà concipi admonitiones, reprehensiones, aliaq; virtutum incitamenta, & vitiorum repagula, quæ omnia sunt absurda. Referri huc potest non inelegans locus ex 2. Ethic. Nicomach. c. 4. & 5.


### Single Question: I. Testimonies

I. TESTIMONIES.

XXXV. Clement of Alexandria, book 2, Stromata. Apostasy and excess are in our power. Tertullian, ch. 3, Prescription. Is it a wonder that someone approved before should fall away afterwards? Saul, good beyond the rest, is afterwards overturned by envy. Solomon, gifted by the Lord with all grace and wisdom, is led away to idolatry by women. Cyprian, epistle 7. Solomon, and Saul, and many others, as long as they walked in the ways of the Lord, were able to keep the grace given to them: when the Lord's discipline departed from them, grace also departed.

Athanasius, Oration 4 against the Arians: When someone falls away from that Spirit because of his own crimes, the grace indeed remains irrevocable in those who are willing: but if anyone falls away, he is no longer anything in God, because the Holy and Paraclete Spirit departs from him: But he is in him to whom the sinner has subjected himself. Basil to Chilo: The labor of the righteous is vain if a change follows. Chrysostom on 1 Corinthians: Charity never falls away of itself, but we sometimes fall away from it. Jerome on chapter 5 of Hosea: No one can be snatched from the hand of God. However, he who is held can fall away by his own will. Prosper of Aquitaine, response 7 to the Chapters: That some of those regenerated in Christ Jesus, having abandoned the faith and pious morals, apostatize from God and end an impious life in their turning away, is proven by many examples (which is to be lamented). Bernard, sermon 2 on the resurrection. of the Lord: When charity grows cold, faith dies, just as the body does when the soul departs. The testimonies of certain Calvinists can be added, such as Martyr on 1 Corinthians 13, Musculus in L. C. book 10 on the remission of sins, question 6, Hemmingius on chapter 14 to the Romans, and especially Petrus Berius, who published a special book against his Calvinist associates on this question, to which he gave the title, Hymenaeus the deserter, or on the apostasy of the saints. It was printed at Frankfurt in the year 1612 in quarto, to which they will be able to answer nothing solid,

Objections of the Calvinists.

XXXVI. 1. From Exodus 6, verse 7, Leviticus 11, verse 44, chapter 18, verse 2: I will be your God, and you shall be my people. Therefore, whom God once adopts as a son, he remains his Father perpetually.

Response: This promise and others like it are not absolute and simple, but conditional: joined with the condition of perseverance in the faith, as appears from Colossians 1, verse 21: God will present you holy and blameless in him, if indeed you remain founded and stable in the faith, and are not moved from the hope of the Gospel. Such was the promise made to Abraham, concerning his seed being blessed, that God wills to be their father, if indeed they observe his commandments, etc. Thus must that passage in Jeremiah 32, verses 39-40, be explained: 'I will give them one heart and one way, that they may fear me for all days, and it may be well with them, and with their children after them, and I will strike a perpetual covenant with them, and I will not cease to do them good, and I will put my fear in their hearts that they may not depart from me.' For if this promise is understood simply and absolutely, then it would follow that no one in the Church of the New Testament, indeed concerning which there is speech there, ever sins, or can sin, which the Calvinists themselves nevertheless concede. Therefore, this promise is limited, having the means included.
