For God does not give fear without means absolutely, but through means in an orderly fashion: He promised that He wills to give the Church of the New Testament a new heart, that they may fear Him for all days: how? not without means, but through means, which when they are neglected, the promised thing is not exhibited, although the promise itself remains firm and immovable. Such was also that promise in Genesis 17, verse 7: 'I will establish my covenant between me and thee, and between thy seed after thee in their generations by a perpetual covenant.' And yet this covenant was not perpetual, since on the part of the Israelites it was broken, whence the Jewish people were rejected, Romans 9, from which it is clear that even this promise, which seemed absolute, was only conditional, namely as long as the Israelites feared and worshipped God, just as the Lord Himself hints in chapter 17, verses 1 and 2: 'Walk before me and I will place my covenant between me and thee.' In a similar way, the remaining promises are to be explained: Psalm 103, Isaiah 49, Isaiah 59, 1 Corinthians 1, Hebrews 13.

Latin:

I. TESTIMONIA.

XXXV. Clemens Alexandr. l. 2. Strom. Apostasia & excessus sunt in nostra potestate. Tertull. c. 3. præscript. Est nè hoc mirum, vt probatus aliquis retrò posted excidat? Saul bonus præ cæteris, liuore posted euertitur. Salomon omni gratia & sapientiâ donatus à Domino ad idololatriam à mulieribus deducitur. Cyprianus epist. 7. Salomon, & Saul, & cæteri multi, quamdiu in vijs Domini ambulauerunt, datam sibi gratiam tenere potuerunt: recedente ab ijs disciplinâ dominica, recessit & gratia.

Athanasius orat. 4. contra Arrian., Cùm quis ob scedera sua ab isto Spiritu excidit, gratia quidem irreuocabilis manet in ijs, qui volunt: sed si quis excidat, non est ampliùs in Deo is quicquãs, quia recedit ab eo Sanctus & Paracletus Spiritus: Sed est in eo, cui semetipsum subiecit peccator. Basilius ad Chilonem: Inanis est iusti labor, si succedat immutatio. Chrysost. in 1. ad Cor. Charitas ex se nunquam excidit, sed nos ab illa interdum excidimus. Hieronymus in c. 5. Oseæ: Nullus potest rapi de manu Dei. Potest autem is, qui tenetur, propria voluntate excidere. Prosper. Aquitan. resp. 7. ad Capit. Ex regeneratis in Christo Iesu quosdam relicta fide, & pyjs moribus apostatare à Deo & impiam vitã in sua auersione finire, multis (quod dolendum est) probatur exemplis. Bernhardus serm. 2. de resurrect. Domini, Refrigescente charitate fides moritur, sicut corpus anima recedente. Addi possunt propria quorundam Caluinianorum testimonia, vt Martyris in 1. Cor. 13. Musculi in L. C. l. 10. de remissione peccat. quæst. 6. Hemmingij in cap. 14. ad Rom. in primis Petri Berij, qui peculiarem aduersus socios Caluinianos de hac quæstione librum edidit, cui titulum fecit, Hymenæus desertor, siue de sanctorum apostasia. Excusus est Francofurti anno 1612. in quarto ad quem nihil quicquã solide respondere poterunt,

Obiectiones Caluinianorum.

XXXVI. 1. Ex Exod. 6. v. 7. Leuit. 11. v. 44. cap. 18. v. 2. Ego ero Deus vester, & vos eritis mihi in populum. Quem ergò Deus semel in filium adoptat, illius Pater perpetuò manet.

Resp. Promissio hæc & aliæ similes, non sunt absolutæ & simplices, sed conditionales: coniunctæ cum conditione perseuerantiæ in fide, vti apparet ex Coloss. 1. v. 21. Deus exhibebit vos sanctos & irreprehensibiles in ipso, si tamen permaneat is in fide fundati, & stabiles, & non dimoueCc I mini à spe Euangelij. Talis erat promissio Abrahamo facta, de semine eius benedicendo, quòd Deus velit ipsorũ esse pater, si videlicet pręcepta ejus obseruauerint &c. Ita explicari debet locus iste Ierem. 32. versu 29. 40. Dabo eis cor vnum & viam vnam vt timeãt me vniuersis diebus, & bene sit eis, & filijs eorum post eos, & feriam eis pactum sempiternum, & non desinam eis benefacere & timorem meum dabo in corda eorum vt recedant à me. Etenim si hæc promissio simpliciter & absolutè intelligatur, tùm sequeretur, neminem vnquam in Ecclesia noui Testamenti, quippè de quâ ibi sermo est, peccare, vel peccare posse, qu. d ipsi tamen Caluiniani concedunt. Proinde hæc promissio limitata est, inclusa habens media. Non enim Deus dat timorem sine medijs absolutè, sed per media ordinatè : Promisit se velle Ecclesiæ N. T. dare cor novum, vt timeant ipsum vniversis diebus: quomodo? non sine medijs, sed per media, quæ cùm negliguntur, res promissa non exhibetur, licet ipsa promissio firma permaneat & immobilis. Talis fuit & illa pmissio Gen. 17. v. 7. statuam pactum meũ inter me & te, & inter semen tuum post te in generationibus suis foedere sempiterno. Et tamen foedus hoc sempiternum non fuit, quoniam ex parte Israëlicarum ruptum est, vnde populus Iudaicus rejectus Rom. 9. ex quo patet, & promissionem istam, quæ videbatur absoluta, tantùm conditionalem fuisse, quamdiu videlicet Deum Israëlitæ timerent & colerent, sicut ipse Dominus innuit cap. 17. v. 1. & 2. Ambula coram me & ponam fœdus meum inter me & te. Pari modo explicandæ sunt reliquæ promissiones, Psal. 103: Esai. 49. Esai. 59. 1. Cor. 1. Hebr. 13.


### Single Question: XXXVII. 2. From Psalm 1, verse 3: The leaf of the just shall never wither

XXXVII. 2. From Psalm 1, verse 3: The leaf of the just shall never wither.

Response 1. This saying of the Psalm seems to be contrary to the Calvinists, since according to their interpretation the sense is, the just man always continues to stand and to give fruit, that is, to make faith attested through good works. Wherefore where there are no good works, there neither faith nor true justice can exist.

2. From the comparison of the just and the impious, which David institutes in this Psalm, it sufficiently appears that the Psalmist speaks only of the happy state and condition, of the blessedness and prosperity of the just, namely that it is always well with the just (understanding true blessedness, not apparent and secular), and conversely ill with the impious.

3. This saying can be understood reduplicatively: It will always be well with the just and he will never wither; insofar, namely, as he is just and remains so.

XXXIIX. 3. Psalm 37, v. 24. When he shall fall, he shall not be bruised, because the Lord puts his hand under him.

Resp. 1. By 'fall' is understood either an external fall, or of fortune: or an internal fall, or of the soul, which is sin. If it is an external fall, the Calvinists have no support in this passage. For the elect and the faithful are not separated from their God by misfortunes, as the Apostle affirms in Rom. 8, verse 38, and Solomon in Cant. 8, verse 7. Many waters shall not be able to extinguish charity, namely the waters of tribulation. But what a consequence: The Holy Spirit is not shaken out of the reborn by external evils. Therefore, neither by mortal sins.

2. But if an internal fall is understood, or sin, because it is either venial or mortal, I say that this passage can conveniently be taken concerning venial sin: For even if the just man falls seven times in a day, the Lord nevertheless does not cast him off, but always in turn raises him up, so that he may rise again. However, there is no consequence: The Holy Spirit is not shaken out by venial sins: Wherefore neither by mortal ones.

3. Because in the Hebrew it is, 'He shall not be cast off,' which is understood of total and perpetual casting off: This passage can also be understood in a sound sense concerning mortal sin, namely thus: Even if the elect have fallen by sinning mortally, and by casting off faith totally, nevertheless shall not be cast away forever, because God places his hand underneath, which they can in turn grasp, and by which they are raised up.

XXXIX. 4. From Psalm 111, v. 3. The righteousness of the righteous remains for ever and ever. v. 6. He shall not be moved forever. v. 7. The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.

Resp. All these things are to be understood reduplicatively: the righteous, as righteous, shall be in everlasting remembrance, shall not be moved forever, shall not fear from evil report: thus righteousness, that is, righteous works, remain for ever and ever, as regards the memory of the Lord: for God will always remember his righteousness, and will render a reward in eternal life. He shall not be moved, that is, nothing shall move him, or separate him from God, just as Paul also asserts in Rom. 8, v. 35.

XL. 5. From Hosea 2, v. 19. I will betroth thee unto me forever.

Resp. The present passage is to be understood concerning the whole Church, which God has betrothed to himself forever: for he always has some mystical bride on this earth. But the consequence is null: God has betrothed the Church to himself, therefore no member of it can sin for a time, nor by sinning lose the Holy Spirit. It is not permitted to argue from the preservation of the Church to the salvation of individuals existing in the Church. An inference from the undistributed to the distributed is not valid.

XLI. 6. From Matt. 24, v. 24. It is impossible for the elect to be seduced. John 10, v. 28. No one shall snatch my sheep from my hands, etc.

These sayings speak only of final defection and impiety, namely that it is impossible that the elect should finally perish, and that they cannot be snatched from the hands of Christ by external force; nevertheless, they can for a time strip themselves of the grace of their shepherd, yet in such a way that they return in turn and finally believe. For if this saying had this sense, as if the elect could not even for a time be led into error it would certainly be most false. Did not David err in morals, when he committed homicide and adultery? Did not Augustine err in doctrine, when he was a Manichaean; Luther, when he was a Papist?

Latin:

XXXVII. 2. Ex Psal. 1. versu 3 Folium iusti nunquam arefcer.

Resp. 1. Dictum hoc Psalmi Caluinistis videtur contrariari, quoniam secundúm ipsorum interpretationem sensus est, iustum semper starere, & fructum dare, id est, fidem per bona opera testatam facere. Quare vbi non bona opera, ibi nec fides, nec justitia vera esse poterit.

2. Ex collatione justi & impij, quam in Psalamo isto instituit David, satis apparet, quod Psaltes tantum loquatur de felici statu & conditione, de beatitudine & prosperitate iusti, quod videlicet justo semper bene sit (beatitudinem veram, non apparentem & secularem intelligere) impijs contra male.

3. Reduplicative hoc dictum intelligi potest: Iusto semper erit bene & nunquam arescet; quatenus nempe justus est & permanet.

XXXIIX. 3. Psal. 37. v. 24. Dum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam.

Resp. 1. Per casum intelligitur vel casus externus, seu fortunæ: vel casus internus, seu animæ qui est peccatum. Si casus externus, Calviniani nihil habent in hoc loco præsidij. Nam electi & fideles per infortunia non separantur a Deo suo, sicut Apostolus affirmat Rom. 8. versu 38. & Salomon Cant. 8 versu. 7. Aquæ multæ non poterunt extinguere charitatem, aquæ nimirum tribulationis. Quæ vero consequentia, Per externa mala non excutitur Spiritus sanctus a renatis. Ergo nec per peccata mortalia.

2. Sin casus internus intelligitur, seu peccatum, quia id est vel veniale vel mortale, dico commode posse hunc locum de peccato veniali accipi: Etiamsi enim justus in die cadat septies, Dominus tamen non projicit, sed semper vicissim erigit, vt resurgat. Nulla autem est consequentia: Spiritus sanctus per peccata venialia non excutitur: Quare nec per mortalia.

3. Quia in Hebræo est, Non projicietur, quod de totali & perpetua proiectione intelligitur: Potest etiam hic locus sano sensu de peccato mortali intelligi, ita nimirum: Etiamsi ceciderint electi, peccando mortaliter, & excutiendo fidem totaliter, attamen non proijcientur in æternum, quia Deus supponit manum suam, quam vicissim apprehendere possunt, & quâ eriguntur.

XXXIX. 4. Ex Psalmo 111. v. 3. Iustitia iusti manet in seculum seculi. v. 6. in æternum non commovebitur. v. 7. in memoriâ æternâ erit iustus.

Resp. Hæc omnia reduplicativè sunt intelligenda, iustus, quà iustus, in æterna erit memoria, æternùm non commovebitur, ab auditione mala non timebit: sic iustitia, id est, iusta opera manent in seculum seculi, quoad memoriam Domini: Deus enim semper recordabitur eius iustitiæ, & reddet præmium in vita æterna. Non commovebitur, id est, nihil eum mouebit, vel separabit à Deo, sicut & Paulus asserit Rom. 8. v. 35.

XL. 5. Ex Osea 2. v. 19. Sponsabo te mihi in æternum.

Resp. Præsens locus intelligendus est de tota Ecclesia, quam Deus sibi in æternum sponsauit: Semper n. in his terris habet aliqua sponsam mysticam. Consequentia verò nulla est: Deus sibi sponsauit Ecclesiam, E. nullum eius membrum ad tempus potest peccare, nec peccando Spiritum sanctum perdere. Ab Ecclesiæ conseruatione ad singulorum in Ecclesia existentium salutem non licet argumentari. A non distributo ad distributum non valet collectio.

XLI. 6. Ex Matth. 24. v. 24. Impossibile est electos seduci. Iohan. 10. v. 28. Oves meas nemo rapiet è manibus meis &c.

Hæc dicta tantùm de finali defectione & impietate loquuntur, quòd videlicet impossibile sit, vt electi finaliter pereant, & quòd per externam vim rapi nequeant è manibus Christi; attamen pss ad tempus possunt se spoliare pastoris sui gratia, ita tamen vt vicissim redeant & finaliter credant. Si enim hunc haberet dictum istud sensum, ac si electi nè quidem ad tempus in errorem duci possent, falsissimum certè foret. Annòn errauit Dauid in moribus, cùm homicidium & adulterium committeret? Annòn errauit in doctrina Augustinus, cùm esset Manichæus; Lutherus, cùm esset Pontificius?


### Single Question: XLII. From John 4, v. 14. He who shall drink of the water that I shall give him, shall not thirst forever, but it shall become in him a…

XLII. From John 4, v. 14. He who shall drink of the water that I shall give him, shall not thirst forever, but it shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

Resp. Christ institutes here a comparison between earthly and heavenly, or spiritual, water, which is taken from the virtue of both. He who drinks earthly water thirsts again, for there is not such virtue in this worldly water that, once drunk, it should extinguish thirst perpetually: But the power and efficacy of spiritual water is such that, once drunk, it removes all thirst entirely, as far as it is in itself, and not only lasts in this life, but also recreates and refreshes man for the enjoyment of eternal life. Although indeed that water, as far as it is in itself, is the water of life, and totally extinguishes all thirst, it can nevertheless happen on the part of the drinker that its virtue sometimes ceases and is lost, if the mystical channel, which is the hearing of the word, by which grace is drawn and preserved, is voluntarily neglected, whence the Lord says in Jeremiah, They have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns that have no waters c. 2, v. 13. One must therefore distinguish here between the water itself and the one drinking the water. This is the virtue of the water itself, that it sufficiently removes thirst, nor does the drinker have need to recur repeatedly to the fountain, as happens in the drinking of earthly waters: but by the fault of the drinkers it happens that this vivid virtue of the water sometimes ceases, because they do not use the channel through which it is drawn and preserved, namely the word and the sacraments. But the mystical water is nothing other than the grace of God obtained by the merit of Christ. This is certainly so efficacious in itself that it drives away all thirst, provided that a man may drink that grace, and apply it to himself. Nor is that grace such in itself, that once bestowed it is ever lost: yet men themselves can lose it, when indeed the application ceases. For there is required not only the drinking of this water, but also the preservation of it once drunk. For if anyone drinking water were to spit it out immediately, it would be of little fruit to him, however much a certain potion might have the power of quenching thirst, or of driving away a certain disease, so that I may truly say, this potion most certainly cures this disease; yet if the sick person were to vomit it up immediately, the effect would by no means follow, not by the fault of the potion, but of the man drinking: in like manner the heavenly water is such in itself, that he who drinks it shall not thirst forever, yet under this proviso, that having once drunk it he does not immediately vomit and spit it out; but if that water once drunk is retained within, then it becomes actually and truly a fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

Latin:

XLII. Ex Ioh. 4. v. 14. Qui biberit ex aqua, quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum, sed fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam.

Resp. Instituit hîc Christus comparationem inter aquam terrenam & cœlestem, seu spiritualem, quæ desumitur ab vtriusque virtute. Aquam terrenam qui bibit, ille iterùm sitit, tanta enim virtus non est aquæ huius mundanæ, vt sitim perpetuò semel hausta restinguat: Ast aquæ spiritualis tanta vis est & efficacia, vt semel pota omnem prorsus sitim tollat, quantum in se est, & non solùm duret in hac vita, sed etiam recreet & reficiat hominem ad vitæ sempiternæ fruitionem. Licèt verò aqua ista, quantum in se est, aqua vitæ sit, omnemque sitim totaliter restinguat, potest tamen ex parte bibentis fieri, vt virtus eius quandoque cesset & amittatur, si canalis mysticus, qui est auditus verbi, quippè per quod hauritur gratia & conseruatur, spontè negligatur, vnde Dominus apud Ieremiam ait, Me fontem viuum dereliquerunt, & foderunt sibi cisternas non habentes aquas c 2. v. 13. Distinguendum igitur hîc est inter ipsam aquam, & bibentis aquam. Aquæ ipsius hæc est virtus, vt sufficienter sitim tollat, neque bibens opus habeat subinde ad fontem recurrere, sicut fit in potatione aquarum terrestrium: Bibentium verò culpâ contingit, vt quandoque ista viuida aquæ virtus desinat, quoniam non vtuntur canali, per quem hauritur & conseruatur, verbo nimirùm & sacramentis. Aqua verò mystica nihil est aliud quam gratia Dei merito Christi parta. Hæc certè in se adeò efficax est, vt omnem sitim depellat, modò gratiam istam homo hauriat, & sibi applicet. Neque gratia ista in se talis est, vt semel collata vnquam amittatur: Ipsi tamen homines possunt eam perdere, quando nimirum cessat applicatio. Requiritur enim aquæ istius non tantùm potatio, sed etiam semel haustæ conseruatio. Nam si quis aquam bibens, eam statim exspueret, parùm illi frugifera foret, Quantumumyis potio quædam haberet vim sedandi sitim, vel morbum quendam pellendi, ita vt verè possim dicere, hæc potio certissimè medetur huic morbo; attamen si ægrotus illam statim euomeret, effectus minimè sequeretur, non vitio potionis, sed potantis hominis: pari modo aqua cœlestis in se talis est, vt qui eam bibit, non sitiat in æternum, sub hac tamē cautione, vt eam semel potam non statim euomat & exspuat; sed si aqua ista pota intus retineatur, tum fit actu & reuerà fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam.


### Single Question: XLIII. 8. From John 14, v. 16. I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete, that He may remain with you forever

XLIII. 8. From John 14, v. 16. I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete, that He may remain with you forever.

Resp. This pertains especially to the disciples of Christ, who by a singular privilege above others always had the Holy Spirit most present to them. But let us grant that this is applied to other believers as well, yet the Calvinists will effect nothing from it. For with whom and among whom does the Holy Spirit remain? With you, says Christ, that is, with those who are true disciples, who know me, and indeed insofar as they are disciples, and as long as they know him.

XLIV. 9. From Rom. 11, v. 29. ἀμεταμέλητα [irrevocable] are the gifts of God and the calling, therefore God does not take away what is once granted.

Resp. God indeed does not deprive us of His gifts once granted, but we ourselves deprive ourselves of them through sins, with God bearing no blame for this matter. The gifts of God are ἀμεταμέλητα [irrevocable], but not absolute; just as He gives through the word, so He preserves through the word. And just as they are received through faith, so through in credulity they are lost. God does not repent of having given, but let us repent of having lost. They are ἀμεταμέλητα [irrevocable] in themselves and on the part of God: they become worthy of repentance accidentally, and on the part of us, who maliciously despise them, and by despising, neglect them.

XLV. 10. From 1 Cor. 13, v. 8. Charity never faileth. Resp. This is a manifest depravation of the Pauline text, the sense of which is that charity is not to cease in the other life. However, nothing is treated here concerning the perpetual or uninterrupted duration of charity in a regenerate person sinning mortally.

XLVI. 11. From 1 John 2, v. 19. If they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us. Therefore, those who are faithful, they always remain such.

Resp. 1. This argument does not conclude that the regenerate cannot cast off the Holy Spirit, but rather that they cannot err and fall away from the faith, which is, however, against experience itself. For how many have professed the true religion and deserted it?

2. The scope of John is that it is not to be imputed to the Gospel when heresies arise, but rather to the levity of men, who although they live in the midst of the bosom of the Church, and boast quite confidently that they are truly faithful and truly living members of the Church, are nevertheless nothing of the sort, which is evident from the effect, namely, the defection from the Evangelical doctrine. They went out from us, therefore, but they were not of us, that is, they were not true members of the true Church, they did not embrace the true doctrine. For if they had been of us, they would have remained with us, that is: If they had been truly faithful and genuine worshippers of the Evangelical doctrine, and still were, as they boast, certainly they would not have openly declared themselves enemies of the Gospel, but would have embraced that together with us. For whoever is truly faithful, he remains with us, that is, he embraces the Evangelical doctrine. From this act, therefore (namely, to defect from the Evangelical doctrine, nor to remain constantly in it) the Apostle indicates that those heresiarchs were never truly faithful, and therefore not that justifying faith, by which the doctrine of the Gospel is understood, from which because heretics fall away, the Apostle concludes that they are not truly faithful, nor ever were, even if they boast much about it. For he argues thus: Whoever is of us, he remains with us, or embraces our doctrine. Heretics do not remain with us, but follow a foreign doctrine. Therefore they are not, nor have they been, of us. 3. If absolutely no one could fall away from the faith, what need would there be for the serious admonition brought in, ver. 24, 27, 28, to what end that condition in ver. 24, to what end the threat in v. 28. Therefore the Apostle speaks not simply of any believers whatsoever, but of teachers, whom he calls Antichrists in v. 18 and Pseudoprophets in ch. 4, v. 1. For they had hitherto boasted themselves to be prophets, and endowed with an Apostolic spirit, that is, they had gloried that they were of the college of the Apostles. The Apostle refutes this vain boasting of theirs a posteriori, so that the sense here is: If they were such as we Apostles are, such as they wished to be seen by others, namely Prophets, colleagues of the Apostles, endowed with a Prophetic and Apostolic spirit, it was surely right that they should constantly maintain the same doctrine with us: but since they now not only openly profess a contrary doctrine, but have also made a departure from our very college and assembly, it is clear that their boasting was vain and their conversation feigned. Thus answers Mr. Dr. Eckhard, treatise on repentance, ch. 8, p. 292.

Latin:

XLIII. 8. Ex Ioh. 14. v. 16. Ego rogabo Patrem, & alium Paracletum dabit vobis, vt maneat vobiscum in æternum.

Resp. Hoc potissimùm attinet discipulos Christi, qui singulari priuilegio præ alijs semper sibi præsentissimum habuerunt Spiritum S. Sed demus, hoc & alijs applicari fidelibus, nihil tamen indè efficient Caluiniani. Apud quos enim & cum quib. manet Spiritus S? Vobiscum, inquit Christus, hoc est, cum ijs qui veri sunt discipuli, qui cognosunt me, & quidē quatenus sunt discipuli, & quàmdiu eum cognoscunt.

XLIV. 9. Ex Rom. 11. v. 29. ἀμεταμέλητα sunt dona Dei & vocatio, E. semel concessa non aufert Deus.

Resp. Deus quidem donis suis semel concessis non priuat nos, verùm ipsi per peccata priuamus nos ijsdem, Deo nullam huius rei culpam gerente. Sunt dona Dei ἀμεταμέλητα, sed non absoluta, sicuti per verbum dat, ita per verbum conservat. Et sicuti per fidem accipiuntur, ita per incredulitatem perduntur. Non pœnitet Deum dedisse, nos autem pœniteat perdidisse. Sunt ἀμεταμέλητα per se & ex parte Dei: fiunt pœnitentiâ digna per accidens, & ex parte nostri, qui malitiosè illa contemnimus, & contemnendo negligimus.

XLV. 10. Ex 1. Cor. 13. v. 8. Charitas nunquã excidit. Resp. Manifesta hæc est deprauatio textus Paulini, cuius sensus, quòd charitas non sit cessatura in altera vita. Nihil autem hîc agitur de perpetua nec interrupta charitatis duratione in renato mortaliter peccante.

XLVI. 11. Ex 1. Ioh. 2. v. 19. Si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent vtique nobiscum. Ergò qui sunt fideles, illi semper tales permanent.

Resp. 1. Hoc argumentum non concludit, renatos Spiritum sanctum excutere non posse, sed potiùs errare & à fide deficere non posse, quod tamen est contra ipsam experientiam. Quot enim veram religionem professi deseruerunt illam?

2. Scopus Iohannis est, quòd non sit imputandum Evangelio, quando hæreses exoriuntur, sed potiùs hominum leuitati, qui quamuis in medio Ecclesiæ gremio viuant, & satis confidenter glorientur, se esse verè fideles & viua verè Ecclesiæ membra, nihil tamen minus sunt, quod patet ex effectu, videlicet defectione à doctrina Euangelica. Prodierunt ergo ex nobis, sed nõ erant ex nobis, hoc est, nõ erãt vera veræ Ecclesiæ membra, non amplectebantur verã doctrinam. Si enim ex nobis fuissent, permãsissent nobiscum, hoc est. Si verè fideles & Euãgelicæ doctrinę cultores genuini fuissẽt, & adhuc essẽt, vt gloriatur, certè non apertè se hostes Euangelij declarâssent, sed istud vnà nobiscum amplexi fuissent. Quis enim verè fidelis est, is permanet nobiscum, hoc est, amplectitur doctrinam Euangelicam. Ab hoc igitur actu (nimirum deficere à doctrina Euangelica, nec in ea constanter permanere) indicat Apoftolus, illos hæresiarchas nunquam fuisse verè fideles, adeòque non eam fides iustificans, quam Ewangelij doctrina intelligitur, à qua quia deficiunt hæretici, colligit Apostolus, eos non esse verè fideles, nec fuisse vnquam, etiamsi de illo multum glorientur. Ita enim argumentatur: Quicunque est ex nobis ille permanet nobiscum, seu doctrinam nostram amplectitur. Hæretici non permanent nobiscum, sed alienam doctrinam sectantur. Ergo non sunt, nec fuerunt ex nobis. 3. Si absolutè nullus à fide posset deficere, quid opus foret illatam seriâ admonitione, vers. 24. 27. 28. quorsum conditio ista vers. 24. quorsum comminatio v. 28. Loquitur ergò Apostolus non simpliciter de quibusvis credentibus, sed de doctoribus, quosibi v. 28. Antichristos & c. 4. v. 1. Pseudoprophetas appellat. Prophetas enim sese hactenus iactitauerant, spirituquè Apostolico præditos, hoc est, ex Apostolorum collegio se esse gloriati fuerant. Hanc ipsorum vanam iactantiam Apostolus refutat à posteriori, vt hic sit sensus: Si tales erant, quales nos Apostoli sumus, quales ille ab alijs videri volebant, nimirum Prophetæ, Apostolorum collegæ, Prophetico & Apostolico spiritu præditi, æquum profecto erat, vt eandem doctrinam constanter nobiscum tuerentur: ast cùm iam non modo contrariam doctrinam apertè profiteantur; sed ab ipso quoque collegio & cætu nostro discessionem fecerint, patet, quod gloriatio ipsorum vana & conuersatio simulata fuerit. Ita respondet Dn. D. Eckerdus tract de pœnit: c. 8. p. 292.


### Single Question: XLVII. 12. From 1 John 3, v. 9, 10. Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because…

XLVII. 12. From 1 John 3, v. 9, 10. Whosoever is born of God doth not commit sin; for his seed remaineth in him: and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.

Resp. 1. The Calvinists cannot allege this passage for themselves against us. For the Apostle does not deny the casting away of grace, but rather every sin: He cannot sin. But indeed venial sins can be committed, the Calvinists themselves admit. For thus writes Whitaker in conc. Cygn. p. 20: We concede that men who are truly justified and regenerated can sin, and gravely offend God. Therefore, they themselves are also bound to respond to this Apostolic passage.

2. An explanation of this saying is brought forward in various ways by the doctors of the Church.

Ambrose refers it to the state of glory, not of grace, for there, in the second and plenary regeneration, we shall no longer be able to sin. But this ἑρμηνεία is foreign to the text, since John is dealing with the children of God and of the Devil, as they are distinguished in this life.

Bernard understands predestination by the seed of God, and says: Even if the elect sin, it is as if they did not sin, since they certainly attain salvation. This interpretation is also foreign to the text.

There are those who think that John is speaking not of fact, but of right, because the faithful and those born of God ought not to sin. But neither is this ἑρμηνεία altogether apt, especially because in this way there does not seem to be any distinction established between the children of God and of the Devil, which John is nevertheless striving to show here. For if this proposition, 'The regenerate do not sin,' is equivalent to this, 'The regenerate ought not to sin,' it can be attributed in the same sense to the unregenerate. For they, too, ought not to sin.

Therefore, the best interpretation of all seems to be that of those who understand this and other similar passages reduplicatively, namely, so that the sense is: He who is born of God does not sin, that is, as such, insofar as he is born of God. That the Calvinistic dogma concerning the invariable indwelling of the Holy Spirit is not proven by John is easily evident from v. 15, where he says, 'Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life remaining in him.' The question now is, can any regenerate person become a murderer? The example of David is at hand. Therefore, a fitting διάνοια of this passage must be sought, namely that which we have said, which is confirmed in verse 6: Everyone who abides in Him does not sin. If, therefore, anyone does not abide in Christ, he sins, and by sinning loses grace. These things can be illustrated from 1 John 5:18: Everyone who is born of God does not sin, but he who is born of God keeps himself. The Apostle clearly indicates a reduplicative sense with these words, that indeed the reborn person does not sin for the reason that he keeps himself, but he does this only as such: For it often happens out of human weakness that the reborn person does not keep himself, but willingly falls into sin, as the examples of the saints teach us.

And to this point also serves the response of those who say that John, by the word 'sinning,' does not understand any sin whatsoever, but rather malicious sin committed against conscience and with deliberate effort, so that the sense is: The reborn person does not sin, that is, he does not knowingly and willingly indulge in sins by habit and custom, but avoids them with all zeal and daily progresses in true piety. For John wishes to indicate what the pious are accustomed to do, and by what signs they can be distinguished from the impious, and therefore he says: The impious sin, this is their custom, that they pollute themselves with continuous crimes: But the pious do not sin, that is, as long as they are pious, they are not accustomed to loosen the reins on the flesh, they do not rush headlong into crimes, indeed they cannot even sin; as long as they are pious and retain the indwelling Holy Spirit. This is the simplest sense, which if the Calvinists deny, we will urge them to explain in what sense it is said by the Apostle that the reborn cannot sin at all. Where they will have to either depart from the text and invent foreign glosses, or approve and accept our interpretation.

Latin:

XLVII. 12. Ex. Ioh. 3. v. 9. 10. Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, peccatum non facit, quoniam semen ipsius in eo manet, & non potest peccare, quoniam ex Deo natus est.

Resp. 1. Locum hunc pro se aduersus nos allegare nequeunt Caluiniani. Apostolus enim non negat excussionem gratiæ, sed potiùs peccatum omne: Non potest peccare. Ast verò venastum labi posse fatentur ipsi Calviniani. Sic enim scribit Whitakerus in conc. Cygn. p. 20. Nos concedimus, homines verè iustificatos ac regeneratos posse peccare, Deumque graviter offendere. Tenentur ergò & ipsi ad hunc locum Apostolicum respondere.

2. Explicatio huius dicti à doctoribus Ecclesiæ varia adfertur.

Ambrosius refert ad statum gloriæ, non gratiæ, ibi enim in secunda & plenaria regeneratione non poterimus ampliùs peccare. Sed ἑρμηνεία isthæc à textu est aliena, cùm Iohannes agat de filiis Dei & Diaboli, prout in hac vita discernuntur.

Bernhardus per semen Dei intelligit prædestinationem, & ait: Etiamsi electi peccent, perindè esse, ac si non peccarent, cùm certò salutem consequantur. Aliena est à textu & hæc interpretatio.

Sunt, qui Iohannem loqui existimant, non de facto, sed de iure, quia fideles & ex Deo nati non debent peccare. Verùm neque hæc ἑρμηνεία vsque adeò concinna est, præsertim quòd sic non videatur constare aliquod discrimen inter filios Dei & Diaboli, quod tamen hîc ostendere satagit Iohannes. Etenim si hæc propositio: Renati non peccant, æquivalet huic: Renati non debent peccare; potest illa eodem sensu non renatis attribui. Nam & hi non debent peccare.

Proindè omnium optima videtur esse interpretatio illorum qui hunc & alios similes locos reduplicativè intelligunt, sic videlicet, vt sit sensus: Natus ex Deo non peccat, scilicet quà talis, quatenus ex Deo natus est. Quod enim Caluinisticum dogma de invariabili Spiritus sancti inhabitatione non probetur à Iohanne, facilè patet ex v. 15. vbi ait Omnis, qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est & scitis, quòd omnis homicida non habet vitam æternam in se manentem. Quæritur jam, An renatus aliquis possit fieri homicida? Exemplum Dauidis in promptu est. Proindè cõgrua loci huius quærēda est διάνοια, caninimirum quam diximus, quæ confirmatur ver. 6. Omnis, qui in eo manet, non peccat. Si quis igitur in Christo non manet, is peccat, & peccando gratiam perdit. Possunt hæc illustrari ex 1. Ioh. 5. v. 18. Omnis, qui natus est ex Deo, non peccat, sed qui natus est ex Deo, conservat seipsum. Reduplicativum sensum manifestè indicat his verbis Apostolus, ideò nimirùm renatum non peccare, qui seipsum conservat, hoc autem facit tantùm quà talis: Sæpè enim sit ex imbecillitate humana, vt renatus seipsum non conseruet, sed volens in peccatum prolabatur vt exempla sanctorum nos docent.

Atque huc facit & illorum responsio, qui dicunt, Iohannem per vocem peccandi non intelligere peccatum quodvis, sed potiùs peccatum malitiosum contra conscientiam & deditâ operâ perpetratum, vt sensus sit: Renatus non peccat, hoc est, Scienter & volenter, ex more & consuetudine peccatis non indulget, sed omni studio ista vitat, & in pietate vera quotidiè proficit. Indicare enim vult Iohannes, quid facere soleant pij, & quibus signis discerni queant ab impijs, ideoque ait, Impij peccant, hæc ipsorum consuetudo est, vt continuis sceleribus se polluant: Pij autem non peccant, hoc est, quàmdiu pij sunt, carni fræna laxare non solent, non in scelera præcipites ruunt, imò ne quidem peccare possunt; quàmdiu pij sunt, & Spiritum sanctum inhabitantē retinent. Hic est sensus simplicissimus, quem si Calviniani negaverint, ipsos vrgebimus, vt exponant, quo sensu renatos peccare prorsus non posse ab Apostolo dictum sit. Vbi ipsos vel à textu recedere & peregrinas glossas comminisci, vel nostram interpretationem adprobare & recipere oportebit.


### Single Question: XLIIX. 13. From the epistle of Jude, verse 3: The faith once delivered to the saints. Therefore, faith is given by God only once

XLIIX. 13. From the epistle of Jude, verse 3: The faith once delivered to the saints. Therefore, faith is given by God only once.

Response: Faith here does not mean trust, but the doctrine of faith, in which manner it is also taken in Gal. 1, verse 23, and chapter 3, verse 2; the sense is that the doctrine once delivered ought to be retained, and no other assumed.

XLIX. 14. It would follow that the faith of the elect is temporary, that the elect are προσκαίρους.

Resp. Temporary faith is opposed either to true faith or to perpetual faith. If to true, the faith of the elect who fall is not temporary; if to perpetual, we concede it to be temporary, regarding those who sin mortally. The Calvinists indeed say this is absurd, but they cannot prove it.

L. 15. Whoever is elect is pleasing to God. Certain ones sinning mortally are elect. Therefore they are pleasing to God, and consequently do not totally fall from the grace of God.

Resp. 1. A regenerate person sinning mortally is totally displeasing to God by reason of present unbelief, but pleasing by reason of future faith.

2. The grace of election is one thing, the grace of sanctification is another. The elect totally fall from the grace of sanctification while they sin mortally; however, they do not fall from the grace of predestination, because they remain written in the book of life through future faith, although now, on account of present unbelief, they are in all respects displeasing to God. We give an example from one not yet converted or baptized, and yet elect. Just as he who is not yet baptized is entirely a child of the Devil and under wrath, not under grace; nevertheless, he is elect on account of future faith: so also is it the case with the elect who sin mortally.

LI. 16. A drunkard possesses reason, even though he does not use it.

Resp. 1. Similar things illustrate a proven matter, but they do not prove a controversy.

2. There is a disparity in the example. Reason is the συνεκτικὸν of man and therefore inseparable, but faith is accidental, and likewise can be separated.

LII. 17. No one of the elect can be certain of his own salvation: For faith is a mark, by which those to be saved are distinguished from those to be damned.

Resp. The elect are certain not absolutely, but conditionally, if they have remained in the faith. Two things, however, must be avoided here: security and despair. Such a certainty is to be defended as is founded in the Scriptures and the analogy of faith, and is not contrary to good morals. Add that, through Calvinistic hypotheses, salvation and election are rendered more uncertain than firm, concerning which, since many things were well said in the preceding disputation, we add nothing further here, but we wish our disputation to be concluded and sealed with this vow: that God, the Father of mercy, may perfect in us the work which He began, and that we may run in such a way that we may attain, and that we may perpetually be such as we would wish to be seen on the last day. For as each one dies, so shall he be judged. Therefore, that we may live piously, die in the faith, and rise again with glory, may He grant it, who can do all things, God blessed and glorious forever. AMEN.

Latin:

XLIIX. 13. Ex epistola Iudæ versu 3. Fidei sanctis semel traditæ. Ergò fides semel duntaxat à Deo donatur.

Respon. Fides hîc non fiduciam, sed doctrinam fidei significat, quo etiam pacto sumitur Gal. 1. versu 23. & cap. 3. versu 2. sensus est quòd doctrina semel tradita debeat retineri , nec alia assumi.

XLIX. 14. Sequeretur fidem electorum esse temporariam, electos esse προσκαίρους.

Resp. Fides temporaria opponitur vel veræ, vel perpetuæ fidei. Si veræ, fides electorum labentium non est temporaria; Si perpetuæ, temporariam esse concedimus, quòad eos qui peccant mortaliter. Hoc autem absurdum esse Calviniani dicunt quidem, sed probare nequeunt.

L. 15. Quicunque electus est, Deo placet. Quidam mortaliter peccantes sunt electi. Ergò Deo placent, & per per consequens Dei gratiâ totaliter non excidunt.

Resp. 1. Renatus mortaliter peccans Deo in totum displicet ratione præsentis incredulitatis, placet ratione futuræ fidei.

2. Alia est gratia electionis, alia sanctificationis. Electi totaliter excidunt gratiâ sanctificationis, dum mortaliter peccant; non autem excidunt gratiâ prædestinationis, quia manent scripti in libro vitæ per futuram fidem, quamvis nunc ob præsentem incredulitatem Deo per omnia displiceant. Damus exemplum à nondum conuerso vel baptizato, & tamen electo. Sicut ille, qui nondum est baptizatus, omninò est filius Diaboli & sub ira, non sub gratia; nihilominùs tamen est electus ob futuram fidem: Ita quoque comparatum est cum electis mortaliter peccantibus.

LI. 16. Ebriosus rationem habet, quamvis eâ non utatur.

Resp. 1. Similia illustrant rem probatam, non autem probant controuersiam.

2. Disparitas est in exemplo. Ratio est συνεκτικὸν hominis & proindè inseparabilis, fides verò accidit, itemque separari potest.

LII. 17. Nemo electorum certus esse potest de salute sua: Fides enim nota est, quâ seruandi à damnandis discernuntur.

Resp. Certi sunt electi non absolutè, sed conditionaliter, si in fide permanserint. Duo autem hîc vitari debent, Securitas, & desperatio. Talis defendenda est certitudo, quæ in Scripturis fundetur & analogiæ fidei, bonísque moribus non contrarietur. Adde, quòd per hypotheses Caluinisticas magis incerta reddatur salus & electio, quàm firma, de quo cum præcedenti disputatione benè multa dicta sint, nihil ultrà hîc addimus, sed disputationem nostram voto hoc conclusam & obsignatam volumus, vt Deus, misericordiæ Pater, opus quod cœpit, in nobis perficiat, & nos ita currâmus, quò comprehendamus, vtque tales perpetuò simus, quales nos vltimo die conspici velimus. Nam qualis quisque moritur, talis iudicabitur. Vt igitur viuamus piè, moriamur in fide, & resurgamus cum gloria, faxit is, qui facere potest omnia, Deus benedictus & gloriosus in secula. AMEN.


### Single Question: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 22 Disputation X. On the Reprobation of Unbelievers

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Abraham Heinick of Wittenberg.

We have arrived, by the grace of God, at the final chapter in the doctrine of predestination, in which it is customary to dispute concerning its opposite, namely, Reprobation. However, this word is not found in the Scriptures. in the sense in which it is used by Ecclesiastical Writers. The name ἀδόκιμος appears in 1 Cor. 7. v. 29. & 2 Cor. 13. ver. 5, which the Vulgate interpreter translates as Reprobate. Some explain what a reprobate is by a similitude taken from Heb. 6. v. 8, where the land is called ἀδόκιμος, or reprobate, which brings forth thorns and thistles. Thus, the reprobate are those who spurn the saving seed of the word and hinder its fruit through the thorns of pleasure, whose τὸ τέλος, as also that of the land, is εἰς καῦσιν or burning. Gerhard vol. 2. page 197.

II. Hence it is easily understood what reprobation denotes. For because it is opposed to election, it can be nothing else than the eternal decree of God concerning the condemning of the impenitent. Therefore, as the end to which Election tends is salvation: so that of reprobation is eternal damnation. As one must judge concerning Election from the posterior, not the prior: so also concerning reprobation. As there, so also here, the execution manifests the decree; which therefore ought to be defined in such a way that it does not follow that God decreed one thing and executes another in time. Ambrose, book 2, on the calling of the Gentiles, chapter 8, calls reprobation an abdication. Fulgentius, book 1, to Monimus, calls it a destination to punishment.

III. Many questions are moved about this chapter by the scholastics, which can be seen in Thomas, Gregory of Valencia, Francis Suarez, and Becanus: One is the principal one, which inquires into the cause and manner of the reprobation that has been made: namely, whether it is absolute and founded solely in the good pleasure of God; or whether it is limited and restricted to the foreseen incredulity of men? We shall therefore consider this controversy in a few words, and by its treatment, we shall impose an end upon this second Decade.

THE ONLY QUESTION.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Abrahamo Heinick Witteb.

PErvenimus ex gratia Dei ad caput in doctrina de prædestinatione vltimum, in quo de ejus contrario, nimirum Reprobatione disputari solet. Non autem reperitur hæc vox in Scripturis eo sensu, quo a Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis usurpatur. Nomen ἀδόκιμος extat 1. Cor. 7. v. 29. & 2. Cor. 13. ver. 5. quod vulgatus interpres vertit Reprobum, Nonnulli quid sit reprobus, declarant per similitudinem ex Heb. 6. v. 8. desumptam, vbi terra ἀδόκιμος, vel reproba dicitur, quæ spinas profert, ac tribulos. Sic reprobi sunt, qui salutare verbi semen aspernantur eiusque fructum per spinas voluptatis impediunt, quorum τὸ τέλος, vt & terræ est εἰς καῦσιν vel combustionem, Gerhard tom 2. pag. 197.

II. Hinc quid reprobatio notet, facilè intelligitur. Quia enim electioni est opposita, nihil esse potest aliud, quàm decretum Dei æternum, de condemnandis impœnitentibus. Vt ergò terminus Electionis ad quem est salus: Sic reprobationis est damnatio æterna. Vt de Electione judicandum à posteriori non priori: Sic & de reprobatione. Vt ibi sic & hîc executio manifestat decretum; quod proptereà ita definiri debet, nè aliud Deum decrevisse, & aliud in tempore ipsum exequi sequatur. Ambrosius l. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. 8. reprobationem appellat abdicationem. Fulgentius lib. 1. ad Mon. destinationem ad supplicium.

III. Multæ autem circà hoc caput quæstiones moventur à scholasticis, quæ videri possunt apud Thomam, Gregorium de Valentia, Franciscum Suarez & Becanum: Vna est principalis, quæ causam & modum factæ reprobationis inquirit: videlicet. Num sit absoluta & in solo Dei beneplacito fundata; an verò limitata & ad prævisam hominum incredulitatem restricta? Hanc igitur controversiam paucis considerabimus & illius tractatione, finem huic Decadi secundæ imponemus.

QVAESTIO VNICA.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute; or rather limited, and conditional?

I. The Calvinists opine that God, without any regard for unbelief, has both predestined and created the greatest part of men for destruction, out of a simple and absolute good pleasure, preceding all other causes. For thus writes Calvin, l. 3. Inst. c. 22. §. 11: if we cannot assign a reason why He deems His own worthy of mercy, except because it so pleases Him; neither shall we have any other reason in reprobating others than His will. And c. 23. §. 1: It is by no means consistent to transfer the preparation for destruction anywhere else than to the secret counsel of God. Beza on c. 9 to the Romans: God hates the reprobate not yet born, and has destined them to destruction with no regard for unworthiness. Zanchius l. 5. de Nat. Dei cap. 7. t 3. 2. We contend with the Apostle that the whole of reprobation, that is, both rejection from grace and glory, and destination to disgrace and to the wrath of God, that is, that they might be vessels of wrath and vessels for dishonor, depends on the SOLE will of God, and not on foreseen works. Perkins, book on predestination, p. 26: God, by His supreme right, MAKES vessels for wrath, He does not find them. Sturmius in his diatribe on predestination, th. 14. p. 161: The efficient cause of reprobation is both sole and total and absolute, it is ONLY the eternal, most free, and most just good pleasure of God, COMPLETELY excluding the entire foreseen unworthiness of the reprobate. From this it is easily gathered what an absolute decree is for the Calvinists. For this embraces four other decrees. 1. It is about saving certain men and damning certain others. 2. About the fall of men, so that the first decree could be put into execution. 3. About choosing and redeeming certain ones from the fallen human race. 4. About the greatest part of men, to be consigned to eternal damnation out of absolute hatred.

II. To this horrendous error, full of desperation, the Orthodox rightly opposed themselves, with whom we establish that God is indeed the supreme and principal cause of all decrees, and thus also of reprobation: however, the subordinate and impelling cause ought not to be excluded, by which God, being moved, made the decree concerning the Reprobation of those to be damned; that moving cause is none other than the foreseen incredulity and impenitence of men. For just as God in time damns no one except on account of actual ἀπιστίαν (unbelief); so also from eternity He decreed to reprobate or damn no one, except on account of foreseen ἀπιστίαν (unbelief). Therefore, just as God alone condemns men, yet not out of absolute hatred; so also He alone reprobated, yet not except for those whom He foresaw would be finally impenitent. And for this reason it is rightly denied that the decree of reprobation is absolute; But rather it is limited and joined with respect to future incredulity, so that it is thus resolved by two causes, of which the one can be named the first, and is the will of God; the other, subordinate to the first or impelling, is the previous impenitence and ἀπιστία (unbelief) of men. In order that this orthodox thesis may be established, we will bring forward: 1. Sayings of Scripture. 2. Arguments from the analogy of faith. 3. Testimonies and 4. Responses, by which the sophisms of the Adversaries can easily be diluted and dispelled.

Latin:

I. Caluiniani opinantur, Deum sine vllo incredulitatis respectu, maximam hominũ partem ad interitum & prædestinasse, & creasse, ex simplici & absoluto beneplacito, omnes alias causas antegrediente. Ita enim scribit Caluinus l. 3. Inst. c. 22. §. 11. si non possumus rationem assignare, cur suos misericordia dignetur, nisi quoniam illi ita placet; neque etiam in aliis reprobandis aliud habebimus, quam eius voluntatem; Et c. 23. §. 1. Minimè consentaneum est, præparationem ad interitum aliò transferre, quàm ad arcanum consilium Dei. Beza super c. 9. ad Roman. Deus reprobos odio habet nondum natos, & nullo indignitatis respectu exitio destinauit. Zanchius l. 5. de Nat. Dei cap. 7. t 3. 2. Totius reprobationem hoc est tum reiectionem à gratia, & gloria, tum destinationem ad dedecus & ad iram Dei, hoc est, vt essent vasa iræ, & vasa in contumeliam, contendimus cum Apostolo ex SOLA Dei voluntate pendere, non autẽ ex præuisis operibus. Perkinsius lib. de prædest. p. 26. Deus pro summo iure suo vasa ad iram FACIT, non inuenit. Sturmius in diatribe de prædest. th. 14. p. 161. Causa reprobationis efficiens & sola & tota & absoluta est, SOLVM æternum, liberrimum atque iustissimum beneplacitum Dei uniuersam reprobatorum indignitatem præuisam PENETVS excludens. Hinc facilè colligitur, quid Caluinianis sit absolutum decretum. Hoc enim alia quatuor decreta complectitur. 1. Est de quibusdam hominibus saluandis, & de quibusdam damnandis. 2. De lapsu hominum, vt decretum primum dari posset executioni. 3. De quibusdam ex lapso genere humano eligendis & redimendis. 4. De maxima hominum parte, ex absoluto odio æternę damnationi addicendis.

II. Huic horrendo & desperationis pleno erroti meritò se opposuerunt Orthodoxi, cum quibus statuimus, Deum quidem, vt omnium decretorum, ita & reprobationis causam esse summam, & principem: non autem excludi debet causa subordinata, & impellens, quâ motus Deus decretum fecit de Reprobatione damnandorum, causa illa motrix non est alia, quam præuisa hominum incredulitas & impœnitentia. Sicut enim Deus in tempore neminem damnat, nisi propter ἀπιστίαν actualem; sic & ab æterno neminem reprobare vel damnare decreuit, nisi propter ἀπιστίαν præuisam. Vt igitur solus quidem Deus condemnat homines, non tamen ex absoluto odio; sic & solus reprobavit, non tamen nisi eos, quos finaliter impœnitentes fore præuidit. Et hanc ob causam rectè negatur, decretum reprobationis esse absolutum; Sed potius est limitatum & cum respectu futuræ incredulitatis coniunctum, vt ità duabus causis absoluatur, quarum altera nominari potest prima, & est voluntas Dei; altera primæ subordinata vel impellens, & est præuia hominum impœnitentia, & ἀπιστία. Thesis hæc orthodoxa vt stabiliatur, in medium afferemus, 1. Dicta Scripturæ. 2. Argumenta ex analogia fidei. 3. Testimonia & 4. Responsiones, quibus Aduersariorum sophismata facilè possunt dilui & dispelli.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: I. Sayings of Scripture

I. SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE.

II. Since those are not of one kind, we will divide them into certain classes or propositions for the sake of memory.

1. God created no one for damnation, but all for salvation and eternal blessedness Gen. 1. verse 27. God created man in His own image and likeness. Therefore the image consisted in righteousness and holiness Eph. 4. verse 24. which was implanted in Adam, to this end that, instructed by these safeguards, he might be able to obtain eternal life if he wished.

Nor is this to be understood only of the first parent, but also of his posterity, which was contained in him, as in a head and root. Therefore, the whole of Adam's posterity was destined by the Creator in their first origin to eternal happiness, which Calvin himself does not dare to deny in Inst. book 1, ch. 15, § 4, 5, 6, 8, and book 2, ch. 1, § 7, who in this part contradicts himself. We shall also add these sayings from 1 Thess. 5:19: 'He has not appointed us to wrath, but to the obtaining of salvation.' And 2 Pet. 3:9: 'God does not wish that any should perish.' Yet He would wish it if He had created some for damnation.

VI. 2. The beginning of human perdition is not from God. For He wishes all men to be saved, 1 Tim. 2:4. This would be false if reprobation proceeded simply from the will of God. The sayings from Ezek. 18:23 and ch. 33:11 pertain to this: 'I do not desire the death, etc.' From Psalm 5:5: 'God is not one who wills iniquity.' Hosea 13:9: 'Your perdition is from yourself, O Israel.' In the Hebrew it is שִׁחֶתְךָ, 'He has destroyed you'; others add 'your King,' as Tremellius; others 'the calf,' as Avenarius; others 'your fictitious consolation.' However that may be, the sense finally returns to this, that this perdition does not flow from God, but from the Israelites themselves, whether they were worshipping the calf, or obeying the King, or trusting too much in themselves. The sense of the Hebrew text is therefore best expressed by the Vulgate version. And although it speaks of temporal punishments, it can nevertheless be most correctly applied to eternal perdition; For if temporal punishments are not inflicted absolutely, much less are eternal ones. Add the saying from Wis. 1:12: 'God did not make death, nor does He rejoice in the destruction of the living.' Nor is there any reason for the Calvinists to object that these texts have nothing to do with reprobation, since they deal with perdition. For we prove that they do so thus: He who does not will the end, does not will the things ordered to the end. God does not will perdition, which is the proper end of reprobation. Therefore, He does not simply and absolutely will reprobation.

V. 3. In man himself is the beginning of perdition, not in the absolute will of God. Proverbs 1, verse 24: I have called and you have refused. Isaiah 65, verse 2: I have spread out my hands. Matthew 23, verse 37: I wanted to gather you, but you would not. Luke 14, verse 14: they themselves do not want to appear. Acts 13, verses 44 & 46: You yourselves reject the word. Romans 11, verse 20: unbelief stand by faith. Here the cause of damnation and destruction is transferred to the men themselves, not to some absolute, secret, and hidden will of God. The same is done in John 3, verse 19: This is the judgment, that the light has come into the world, and men loved darkness more than light. John 3, verse 36: He who is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him: Here unbelief is posited as the cause of both privative (not seeing life) and positive evils (the wrath of God remains upon him). Luke 7, verse 30: The Pharisees, while they did not want to be converted, are said to have rejected the counsel of God. E. God wanted them to be converted. Acts 7, verse 51: the Jews are said to have resisted the Holy Spirit. Here, therefore, He wanted to work faith in their hearts, and consequently, they are not absolutely reprobated by God.

VI. 4. The will of God concerning the salvation of man, the merit of Christ, and the offering of grace is universal, and embraces all mortals, not even one excepted. In demonstrating this assertion, all those sayings which we alleged in disputations 2 and 3 of this Decad 2, and defended at length against Calvinistic sophistries, are brought forward. From these, however, we reason thus: If God wills all men to be saved, and has sent His Son for all, that He might satisfy for their sins, and calls all, with none excluded, to Himself; it follows that no one is reprobated absolutely and out of mere good pleasure. For these are opposites, of which, one being demonstrated, the other cannot stand: which the Calvinists do not deny, and therefore, to maintain absolute reprobation, they have invented mere particularities. But we have given that antecedent as abundantly proven. E. And the consequent will stand as an immovable truth.

Latin:

I. DICTA SCRIPTVRÆ.

IIL Cùm illa non sint vnius generis, in certas siuè classes, siuè propositiones memoriæ causâ dispescemus.

1. Deus neminem ad damnationem creauit, sed omnes ad salutem & æternam beatitudinem Gen. 1. vers. 27. Creauit Deus hominem ad imaginem & similitudinem suam. Ergò imago consistebat in iustitia & sanctitate Eph. 4. vers. 24. quæ Adamo implantata fuit, hoc fine vt præsidiis istis instructus vitam æternam si vellet, adipisci posset.

Neque hoc de solo primo parente, sed & de eius posteritate, quæ in ipso, tanquam capite & radice continebatur, accipiendum est. Tota ergò Adami posteritas in prima sui origine ad æternam felicitatem à creatore fuit destinata, quod ipsum non negare audet Caluinus l. 1. Inst. c. 15. §. 4. 5. 6. 8. & l. 2. c. 1. §. 7. qui hac in parte sibi ipsi contradicit. Addemus & hæc dicta ex 1. Thes. 5. v. 19. Non posuit nos ad iram, sed ad salutis consecutionem. Et 2. Petr. 3. v. 9. Deus non vult, vt vnus pereat. Vellet autem si aliquos ad damnationem creasset.

VI. 2. Initium perditionis humanæ non est à Deo. Vult enim omnes homines saluos fieri, 1. Tim. 2. v. 4. Falsum hoc, si reprobatio simpliciter à Dei voluntate proueniret. Spectant huc dicta ex Ezech. 18. vers. 23. & cap. 33. vers. 11. Nolo mortem &c. Ex Psalmo. 5. v. 5. Non est Deus volens iniquitatem. Oseæ 13. 9 Perditio tua ex te Israel. In Hebræo est perdidit te שִׁחֶתְךָ alij addunt Rex tuus, vt Tremellius: alij vitulus, vt Auenarius; alij consolatio tua fictitia, Vtut autem sit, huc tandem redit sensus, quòd perditio ista non promanet ex Deo, sed ab ipsis Israëlitis, vel vitulum adorantibus, vel Regi obsequentibus, vel sibi nimium fidentibus. Sensus itaque Hebræi textus vulgatâ versione optimè exprimitur. Et quamuis loqueretur de pœnis temporalibus, rectissimè tamen applicari potest ad æternam perditionem; Si enim absolutè non infliguntur pœnæ temporales, multò minus æternæ. Adde dictum ex Sap. 1. v. 12. Deus mortem non fecit, neq; lætatur in perditione viuorum. Nec est vt Caluiniani excipiant, hos textus nihil facere ad reprobationem, cum agant de perditione. Facere enim sic euincimus: Qui non vult finem, is nec vult ordinata ad finem Deus non vult perditionem, quæ proprius reprobationis finis. E. nec simpliciter & absolutè vult reprobationem.

V. 3. In ipso homine initium est, perditionis, non in absoluta voluntate Dei. Prouerb. 1. vers 24. Vocaui & renuistis, Esa. 65.v. 2. Expandi manus meas. Matth. 23 v: 37. Ego volui vos congregare, sed sunt, noluistis. Luc. 14. v. 14. ipsi nolunt comparere, Act. 13. v. 44. & 46. Vos ipsi repellitis verbum. Rom. 11. vers. 20. incredulitate defracti sunt, tu verò fide stas. Hic damnationis & interitus causa in ipsos homines transfertur, non in absolutam, arcanam & absconditam quandam voluntatem Dei. Idem fit Ioh. 3.vers. 19. Hoc est iudicium, quia lux venit in Mundum, & dilexerunt homines magis tenebras, quam lucem. Iohan. 3. vers. 36. Qui incredulus est filio, non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum: Hic incredulitas ponitur ut causa tam priuatiuerum (non videre vitam) quam positiuorum malorum (ira Dei super ipsum manet) Luc. 7.v 30. Pharisaei, dum noluerunt conuerti, dicuntur sprevisse consilium Dei. E. voluit Deus ut conuerterentur. Act. 7.v. 51. dicuntur Iudaei resistete Spiritui Sancto. Hic igitur in ipsorum cordibus fidem operari voluit & per consequens, non sunt absolutè à Deo reprobati.

VI. 4. Dei voluntas de hominis salute, Christimeritum, & oblatio gratiae Vniuersalis est, omnesque mortales, nè vno quidem excepto, complectitur. In demostranda hac adfertione, faciut omnia illa dicta quae disp. 2. & 3. huius Dec. 2. allegauimus, & aduersus strophas Caluinisticas fusè defendimus. Ex ijs verò ita ratiocinamur: Si Deus omnes homines vult saluos, & omnibus misit filium, vt pro eorum peccatis satisfaceret, & omnes, nullo excluso, ad se vocat; Consequens est, quòd nemo absolutè, & ex mero beneplacito reprobetur. Sunt enim haec opposita, quorum vno demonstrato, alterum nequit consistere: quod Caluiniani non diffitentur, ideoq́ue ad obtinendam reprobationem absolutam, meras particularitates commenti sunt. Antecedens verò illud abundè probatum dedimus. E. & Consequens sua stabit immota veritas.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: Reasons

REASONS.

VII. We shall append only one or another; the rest can be repeated from the preceding ones.

1. From the justice of God. If God had decreed to damn anyone without regard to sins, he would certainly be unjust. For as it is unjust to afflict anyone with punishments without his own fault, so it is unjust to condemn anyone to punishments without his own fault. Hence Augustine says in book 3 against Julian, ch. 18: God is good, God is just; He can liberate without good merits because He is good; He cannot condemn without evil merits because He is just. Keckermann felt the force of this argument and therefore writes thus in book 3 of his System of Theology, ch. 1, p. 309: The absolute power of God is a virtue, but justice is a relative virtue, which necessarily includes either the innocence or the sin of the creature. Whence he constructs such an Axiom: Whatever is a work of justice punishing a man, that presupposes guilt. We subsume: Reprobation is a work of divine justice punishing a man: From which follows the Conclusion: Therefore, Reprobation presupposes guilt.

IIX. 2. From the goodness of God. In the Scriptures, the goodness and mercy of God are preached everywhere, as in Psalm 24, 32, 135, 144. And therefore in Luke 6, verse 36, we are admonished that we should be merciful, just as the heavenly Father is merciful. But what kind of goodness, what kind of mercy would this be, if God were to condemn a man to damnation from free will without any fault? He would certainly be most cruel, especially if it is established that the decree of reprobation was made before the foreseen fall, which the Calvinists are indeed forced to say, because according to them election also was made before the foreseen fall. But election and rejection are opposites: with some being elected, the rest were immediately rejected. In what state, therefore, they were to be elected, in that same state they were also established to be rejected. But according to them, they were to be elected in the state before the fall. Therefore, they were also to be rejected [in that state]. Wherefore they contradict themselves, when reprobation... they describe the [reprobation] in such a way that it is a decree about leaving some in sin, even though it was made before the foreseen sin.

IX. 3. From the perfection of the Gospel. The Gospel is manifestly argued to be imperfect if it does not explain the highest and principal cause of our salvation and damnation. I ask therefore: Are all things that pertain to our salvation revealed in the Gospel? If they affirm it, the decree of the secret will collapses: If they deny it, the Gospel will be imperfect.

X. 3. From the absurd. If reprobation were absolute, it would follow that there are more predestined than reprobated, which is άτοπον. The consequence is proven, since God is more inclined to show mercy than to punish, Psalm 145, v. 9. The Lord is sweet to all, and his mercies are over all his works, Isaiah 28, v. 21. To be angry is called God's strange and alien work, Ecclesiasticus 15, v. last. God does not desire a multitude of unfaithful and useless children.

XI. 5. From another absurdity. If the will of God alone is the cause of reprobation, and reprobation is the cause of sin, it follows that God is also the cause of sin: For the cause of a cause is also the cause of the caused: a principle which the Calvinists otherwise highly value. Nor does Hubertus Sturmius obscurely hint at this very thing when, in his diatribe on predestination, thesis 13, page 153, he discourses on reprobation thus: This word in this argument signifies three things: Rejection from the grace of election, its effects and ends: The ordination of the rejected to dishonest uses: and finally, the destination of these ordained ones to eternal death. By dishonest uses, however, he undoubtedly understands sins, and therefore it follows from this that God, out of mere good pleasure, ordains certain ones to sins, which is impious to say and blasphemous.

Latin:

RATIONES.

VII. Adponemus duntaxat vnam vel alteram, cæteræ ex præcedentibus possunt repeti.

1. A Dei iustitia. Si sine peccatorum intuitu Deus quempiam damnare decreuisset, vtique iniustus foret. Nam vt iniustum est, quemquam absque sua culpa pœnis afficere; ita iniustum est, quemquam absque suâ culpâ pœnis addicere. Hinc August. ait lib. 3. cont. Iulianum c. 18. Bonus est Deus, iustus est Deus; Potest sine bonis meritis liberare, quia bonus est; non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia iustus est. Vim huius argumenti sensit Keckermannus ideoq; l. 3. syst. Theol. cap. 1. p. 309. ita scribit, Potentia Dei absoluta virtus est, sed iustitia est virtus respectiua, quæ creaturæ vel innocentiam vel peccatum necessariò includit. Vnde tale Axioma extruit: Quodcunque est opus iustitiæ hominem punientis: id præsupponit culpam. Nos subsumimus: Reprobatio est opus iustitiæ diuinæ hominem punientis: Ex quo sequitur Conclusio: E. Reprobatio præsupponit culpam.

IIX. 2. A Dei bonitate. In Scripturis passim prædicatur bonitas & Misericordia Dei, vt Psal. 24. 32. 135. 144. Ideoque Luc. 6. vers. 36. admonemur, vt simus misericordes, sicut & pater cœlestis misericors est. Quæ verò hæc esset bonitas, quę misericordia, si Deus hominem absque vlla culpa damnationi ex libera voluntate addiceret? Crudelissimus sanè foret, pręsertim si statuatur reprobationis decretum factum fuisse ante præuisum lapsum, quod sanè dicere coguntur Caluiniani, quia secundum ipsos electio etiam facta fuit ante præuisum lapsum. Sunt verò opposita electio & reiectio: quibusdam electis, statim reliqui sunt reiecti. In quo igitur statu fuerunt eligendi, in eodem etiam constituti sunt reijciendi. At verò eligendi erant iuxta ipsos in statu antelapsum. E. & reijciendi. Quare contradicunt sibi, cùm reprobationem ita describūt, quòd sit decretum dè relinquendis nonnullis in peccato, cùm tamen facta sit ante praevisum peccatum.

IX. 3. Ab Euangelij perfectione. Evangelium manifestè arguitur imperfectionis, si non exponit causam summam & principem nostrae salutis, & damnationis. Quaero ergò: An omnia, quae ad salutem nostram pertinent, in Evangelio sint revelata? Si affirmant, concidit voluntatis arcanae decretum: Si negant, Evangelium erit imperfectum.

X. 3. Ab absurdo. Si absoluta esset reprobatio, sequeretur, plures esse praedestinatos, quàm reprobatos, quod άτοπον. Consequentia probatur, quoniam Deus propensior est ad miserendum, quàm ad puniēdum, Psal. 145. v. 9. Suavis Dominus universis, & miserationes eius super omnia opera ejus, Esa. 28. v. 21. Irasci vocatur opus Dei peregrinum & alienum Eccl. 15. v. vlt. Non concupiscit Deus multitudinem filiorum infidelium & inutilium.

XI. 5. Ab alio absurdo. Si sola Dei voluntas est causa reprobationis, & reprobatio est causa peccati, sequitur, Deum euàm esse causam peccati: Nam causa causae est etiam causa causati: quod principium aliàs magnifaciunt Caluiniani. Nec obscurè hoc ipsum innuit Hubertus Sturmius quandò diatribe de praedest. th. 13. p. 153. ità de probatione disserit: Vox haec isto argumento tria significat, Rejectionem à gratia electionis, effectis atque finibus: Reiectorum ad vsus non honestos ordinationem: denig; ordinatorum horum ad mortem aeternam destinationem. Per vsus autem non honestos procul dubio intelligit peccata, idèoque hinc sequitur, Deum ex mero beneplacito quosdā ad peccata ordinare, quod impium dictu & blasphemum.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: III. Testimonies

III. TESTIMONIES.

XII. Augustine, book on the articles falsely attributed to him, art. 2. God is indeed the creator of all men, but No one was created by Him for the purpose that he should perish, because the cause of being born is one thing, the cause of perishing is another. For that men are born is a benefit; but that they perish is the vice of transgression. Lib. de gratia & libero arbitrio c. 23. God renders evil for evil, because He is just; good for evil, because He is good; good for good, because He is good and just; only He does not render evil for good, because He is not unjust. But would He not render evil for good, if He were to absolutely reject and devote to death a man, whatever he might do, even if he were baptized a thousand times and diligently heard the Word? Lib. 1. ad Simplic. quæst. 2. God does not hate Esau the man, but Esau the sinner, idem epist 106: If God were to condemn anyone undeserving, He would not be believed to be free from iniquity. Fulgentius l. 1. ad Mon. p. 51. God, being about to show what He foreknew should be revealed and what should be granted, predestined those to punishment whom He foresaw would depart from Him by the evil vice of their own will. Here, the consideration of malice is manifestly included in the decree of reprobation. Prosper. ad Gallor. capitula: The grace of God does not desert them before it is deserted by them. We add to these the testimonies of those who otherwise follow Calvin, but in this dogma depart from him. Such are

Jacob Arminius, Petrus Bertius, Johannes Arnoldi Corvinus, who not long ago declared their agreement in public writings, and condemned Calvin's opinion as impious and false.

IV. OBJECTIONS OF THE CALVINISTS.

XIII. Before we make an approach to the objections of Calvin, we shall see in a few words the pretexts of the more recent ones, by which they are accustomed to cloak and varnish the absolute decree. There are three of them primarily, concerning which in order.

XIV. Trelcatius l. 2. Instit. m. p. 29. establishes two acts of reprobation: the one he calls preterition; by which God decreed that the greater part of men should be passed over, regarding the communion of grace and glory: the other pre-damnation, by which He proposed to devote men to eternal damnation. He establishes the object of preterition to be man considered generally, without any respect to any quality. But of pre-damnation, man as he is a sinner, or to be punished on account of sins, from the necessity of divine justice. Briefly, therefore, he wishes to intimate this, that preterition or non-election is absolute, but pre-damnation is conditional, and joined with the intuition of sins. Keckerman wishes the same, when in book 3, System of Theology, chapter 1, page 308, he distinguishes between the purpose of forsaking and of damning. He writes that the former is absolute, the latter is not absolute.

XV. This πρωτοφύγιον [first refuge] is indeed drawn from Scholastic and Papistic cisterns: For they distinguish between negative or passive reprobation, which is preterition, and affirmative or active reprobation, which is pre-damnation. The same is the mind of Bellarmine, who in book 1, On Grace and Free Will, chapter 16, acknowledges a double act of reprobation: One he calls negative, by which God does not have the will to save these: The other positive, by which God has the will to damn these: He writes that there is no cause given for the former on the part of men, but for the latter there is, namely, foreseen sins.

XVI. However much this opinion may seem milder, it is nevertheless no less erroneous, and this cloak will little help the Calvinists:

For 1. They depart from Calvin himself, whom they wish to follow and explain. For he thinks that the whole of reprobation is completed by the sole absolute and unconditioned decree of God.

2. They contradict their own principles. For they deny that the intuition of faith is included in election, because faith follows in time, and did not exist from eternity. But truly, the same must be confessed concerning sins. Why therefore do they call their το πρόγνωσιν [foreknowledge] the cause of pre-damnation? Furthermore, if reprobation is said to be made on account of sins, then it follows They shout that all ought to have been reprobated, because all have sinned. But see, they themselves now evacuate the force of this argument. If pre-damnation was made on account of sins, and yet not all are pre-damned, although all have been infected by sin, why could the same not be affirmed concerning preterition?

3. They double the one decree. For as there is a single election, consisting in the destination to salvation; so also there is one reprobation, consisting in pre-damnation. Why therefore do they double the former, and call one active, the other passive? This distinction must be proven, before that preconceived opinion is cloaked by it.

4. The arguments brought forward above militate no less against absolute preterition than against absolute pre-damnation. For if the beginning of perdition is not from God, but from man alone; if God seriously wills the salvation of all, and sent his son for all, and offers grace to all; how could he, out of absolute good pleasure, pass over the greatest part of mankind? For these are opposites, and express αντιφατικα (contradictories). Add that incredulity in the scriptures is said to be not only the cause of damnation, but also of exclusion from eternal life, and consequently of preterition. For thus it is read in John 3: He who is incredulous to the son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Here απιστια (unbelief) is called the cause both of the denied vision, which is to pass over, and of the future wrath, which is to pre-damn. Finally, we urge the Axiom of Keckermann: Whatever is a work of justice punishing man, that presupposes guilt. But negative reprobation, or its privative act, is a work of divine justice punishing man, since it is the first degree of punishment upon which the others depend. Therefore, negative reprobation also presupposes guilt, and consequently, it was not made without the intuition of sin.

XVII. And we wish these same reasons to be similarly opposed to the Bellarminian distinction. Where this can be noted in addition, the levity of the little brothers even if they in this forum vehemently disagree. For Bellarmine establishes the act of reprobation to be private and absolute, and to be absolved by the sole good pleasure of God, which he drew from Durandus in book 3 of the Sentences, dist. 40, q. 2, and Marsilius in 1, q. 4, c. 1, art. 2. But he is expressly refuted by Gregory of Valencia, Tom. 1, Com. in Thom. disp. 1, q. 23, part. post. punc. 3, col. 583. He took arguments from the writings of our countrymen, and primarily urges these. 1. God does not will the destruction of man, nor does He deprive anyone of His grace out of absolute hatred. 2. Rom. 9, Paul openly teaches that the sins of the reprobate are the cause for God why He absolutely reprobates him, that is, passes him over and predamns him. 3. The Fathers assert the same, for which end he cites primarily August. l. d. bono persev. c. 6. 8. 11. l. 2. ad Simpl. q. 2. & ep. 105. 4. The sins of the reprobate are the cause of all the effects of reprobation itself. Therefore, also of reprobation, as it regards those effects. Finally 5. there would be more predestined than reprobated, because God, by reason of His will, is more inclined to show mercy than to desert and destroy.

XIIX. II. Others distinguish between reprobation and damnation. They concede that the cause of the latter is incredulity, but they deny the same regarding the former, because they deem it to be absolute. And by this single little exception, they persuade themselves that all our arguments can be satisfied. For those [arguments] speak of damnation, and therefore conclude nothing against reprobation.

But we respond 1. For the same causes for which God in time does not save men, but damns them, for those same causes He decreed from eternity to damn, that is, He reprobated. For the decree of damnation is nothing other than reprobation. But in time He does this not out of absolute hatred, but on account of incredulity, and negatively, while He does not save; and positively, while He damns, Luke 14, v. 24, John 3, v. 36, Acts 13, v. 46. Therefore God decreed to damn men on account of the same incredulity, that is, He reprobated. The antecedent is proven, because the decree and the execution of the decree correspond most exactly to each other

2. The will of God would become mutable, if reprobation were absolute, [and] damnation conditional. For from eternity, according to the Calvinists, He willed to damn these very people absolutely; in time He wills to damn [them] on account of unbelief. Behold a mutable will in God! Or Reprobation is an absolute will concerning the perdition of men from eternity: Damnation is an absolute will of God in time concerning the perdition of men, but not absolute, but rather caused through anxiety. You see here again mutability.

3. God from eternity willed the salvation of all, [and] decreed to send the Son to all: Therefore, He reprobated no one from eternity by absolute hatred.

4. Beza concedes that God also predestined the causes of damnation. We ask, therefore: What is the cause, or why are men damned? They respond, because they remain in final impenitence. We continue by asking: Why do they remain in sins? They respond, Because God absolutely destined them to this. Hence we conclude thus: The cause of a cause is the cause of the thing caused. The absolute will of God is the cause of reprobation, Reprobation [is the cause] of final impenitence, this [is the cause] of damnation.
