Therefore, the absolute will is the cause of damnation: and consequently, regarding causes, they cannot distinguish between reprobation and damnation.

XIX. III. Pareus in this question is clearly doubtful: Now he speaks with us, soon with Calvin. For in chapter 9 to the Romans, doubt 8, column 908, he determines that a cause for negative reprobation must also be attributed on the part of men. Then, column 909, he strives to soften the crude dogma of Calvin with a certain small distinction. Scripture, he says, speaks of the judgments of God and of the cause of reprobation and damnation in two ways: Sometimes according to the absolute right of God over men and creatures. And thus he places the cause in the mere good pleasure of God. Sometimes according to the right of God ordained to the rule of distributive justice, revealed in the word of the Law and the Gospel. And thus he refers the cause partly to the will of God, and partly and proximately to the sins of men.

Latin:

III. TESTIMONIA.

XII. Augustinus l. de articulis sibi falsò impositis art. 2. Omnium quidem hominum Deus creator est, sed nemo ab eo ideo creatus est, vt pereat, quia alia causa est nascendi, alia pereundi. Vt enim nascantur homines est beneficium; vt autem pereant præuaricationis est vitium. Lib. de gratia & libero arbitrio c. 23. Deus reddit mala pro malis, quia iustus est; bona pro malis, quia bonus est; bona pro bonis quia bonus & iustus est; solùm non reddit mala pro bonis, quia iniustus non est. Annon autem redderet mala pro bonis, si hominem quodcunque etiã ageret, si vel millies baptizaretur, & verbum diligenter audiret, absolute rejiceret, mortique deuoueret? Lib. 1. ad Simplic. quæst. 2. Deus non odit Esau hominem, sed Esau peccatorem, idem epist 106: Si Deus quenquam immeritum damnaret, immunis ab iniquitate non crederetur. Fulgentius l. 1. ad Mon. p. 51. Ostensurus Deus, quid reuelandum præsciuerit, & quid donandum, prædestinauit illos ad supplicium, quos à se præsensis voluntatis malo vitio discessuros. Hîc decreto reprobationis manifestè includitur intuitus malitiæ. Prosper. ad Gallor. capitula: Gratia De. non prius eos deserit, quam ab eis deseratur. Addimus his testimonia eorum, qui aliàs Caluinum sequuntur, in hoc autem dogmate ab ipso recedunt. Tales sunt

Iacob. Arminius, Petrus Bertius, Iohannes Arnoldi Coruinus, qui consensum suum publicis scriptis haut ita pridem declarârunt, & Caluini sententiam velut impiam, & falsam condemnârunt.

IV. OBIECTIONES CALvinianorum.

XIII. Antequam ad obiectiones Caluini faciamus accessum paucis videbimus recentiorũ prætextus, quibus decretum absolutum palliare, & incrustare solent. Sunt eorum tres potissimum, de quibus ordiné.

XIV. Trelcatius l. 2. Instit. m. p. 29. duas reprobationis actus constituit: alterum vocat præteritionem; quo Deus decreuit maiorem hominum partem præterire, quoad gratiæ & gloriæ communionem: alterum prædamnationem, quo homines æternæ damnationi deuouere proposuit. Præteritionis obiectum statuit esse hominem communiter confideratum, absq; vllo qualitatis alicuius respectu. Prædamnationis verò, hominem qua peccator est, seu propter peccata puniendus, ex necessitate iustitiæ diuinæ. Breuiter ergò hoc vult innuere, quòd præteritio vel non electio sit absoluta, prædamnatio verò conditionata, & cum intuitu peccatorum coniuncta. Idem vult Keckerman, quando l. 3. Syst. Theol. c. 1. p. 308. inter propositum deserendi & damnandi distinguit. Illud absolutum, hoc non absolutum esse scribit.

XV. Haustum verò est hoc πρωτοφύγιον ex lacunis Scholasticis & Papisticis: Isti n. distinguunt inter reprobationē negatiuam vel passiuā, quę est pręteritio, & inter reprobationē affirmatiuā, vel actiuam, quæ est prædānatio. Eadē mens est Bellarmini qui lib. 1. de gra. & lib. arb. c. 16. duplicē repbationis actum agnoscit: Vnum appellat negatiuum, quo Deus non habet voluntatem hos saluandi: Alterum positiuum, quo Deus voluntatem habet hos damnandi: Illius scribit nullam dari causam ex parte hominum, huius autem dari, nimirum peccata præuisa.

XVI. Quantumuis a. sententia hæc videatur mollior, non minus tamen est erronea, & parum iuvabit Caluinianos hoc pallium:

Nam 1 A Caluino, quem sequi & explicare volunt, hoc ipso discedunt. Is n. reprobationem totam solo absoluto & inconditionato Dei decreto absolui existimat.

2. Suis principijs contradicunt. Nam fidei intuitum electioni inclusum esse ideò negant, quia fides sequatur in tempore, nec fuerit ab æterno. At v. idem de peccatis fatendum est. Cur ergo illorum το πρόγνωσιν prædamnationis causam dicunt? Deinde si reprobatio ob peccata dicatur facta, tum sequi clamitant, omnes fuisse reprobandos, quia omnes peccarunt. At v. jam ipsi huius argumenti vim evacuant. Sin. praedamnatio facta est ob peccata, nec tamen omnes sunt praedamnati, licet omnes fuerint peccato infecti, cur non idem de praeteritione affirmari posset?

3. Decretum vnum geminant. Nam vt vnica est electio, consistens in destinatione ad salutem; sic & vna est reprobatio, consistens in praedamnatione. Cur ergo illam duplicant, & altera activam, alteram passivam vocant? Probanda est haec distinctio, antequam illa pallietur praeconcepta opinio.

4. Argumenta superius prolata non minus contra absolutam praeteritionem, quam contra absolutam praedamnationem militant. Nam si perditionis initium non est a Deo, sed a solo homine; si Deus omnium vult salutem serio, & omnibus misit filium, omnibusque affert gratiam; quomodo ex absolute beneplacito maximam hominum partem potuit praeterire? sunt n. haec opposita, & expressae αντιφατικα. Adde, quod incredulitas in scripturis, non modo dicatur causa damnationis, sed & exclusionis a vita aeterna, & per consequens praeteritionis. Sic n. legitur Ioh. 3. v vult: Qui incredulus est filio non videbit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum, Hic απιστια causa dicitur tum negatae visionis, quod est praeterire, tum futurae irae, quod est praedamnare. Vrgemus tandem Axioma Keckermanni: Quodcunque est opus iustitiae hominem punientis, id praesupponit culpam. Atqui reprobatio negativa, vel actus ejus privativus est opus iustitiae divinae homine punietis, quippe cu sit primus supplicii gradus a quo caeteri dependent. Ergo & reprobatio negativa praesupponit culpam, & per consequens, sine intuitu peccati non est facta.

XVII. Et has ipsas rationes distinctioni Bellarminianae similiter volumus oppositas. vbi hoc insuper notari potest, levitas fraterculos etsi ea hoc forum vehementer diffentire. Nam Bellarminus reprobationis actum privatiunm statuit absolutum esse, & solo Dei beneplacito absolui, quòd hausit ex Durando in l. 3. sent. dist. 40. q. 2. Marsilio in 1. q. 4. c. 1. art. 2. Sed refutatur expressè à Gregorio de Valentia, Tomot. 1. Com. in Thom. disp. 1. q. 23. part. post. punc. 3. col. 583. Argumenta desumsit ex nostratium scriptis, & in primis hæc vrget. 1. Deus non vult hominis interitum, nec quemquam ex absoluto odio priuat suâ gratia. 2. Rom. 9. Paulus apertè docet, peccata reprobi esse Deo caussam, cur illum absolutè reprobet, h. e. prætereat, & prædamnet. 3. Patres idem asserunt, in quem finem citat in primis August. l. d. bono persev. c. 6. 8. 11. l. 2. ad Simpl. q. 2. & ep. 105. 4. Peccata reprobi sunt causa omnium effectuum reprobationis ipsius. E. & reprobationis, vt respicit illos effectus. Tandem 5. plures forent prædestinati quàm reprobati, quia Deus ratione voluntatis suæ propensior est ad miserendum, quàm ad deserendum, & perdendum.

XIIX. II. Distingunt alij inter reprobationem, & damnationē. Huius causam esse incredulitatem concedunt, sed de illa id ipsum negant, quia absolutam esse autumant. Et hac vnicâ exceptiunculâ omnibus argumentis nostris satisfieri posse sibi persuadent. Illa enim loqui de damnatione, ideoque nihil concludere aduersus reprobationem.

Sed respondemus 1. Ob quas causas Deus in tempore homines non saluat, sed damnat, ob easdem ab æterno damnare constituit, id est, reprobauit. Decretū enim damnationis nihil est aliud, quàm reprobatio. Ast in tempore id facit non ex absoluto odio, sed propter incredulitatem, & negatiuè, dum non saluat; & positiuè, dum damnat, Luc. 14. v. 24. Ioh. 3. v. 36. Actor. 13. v. 46. Ergò Deus propter eandem incredulitatem homines damnare constituit, h. e. reprobauit. Antecedens probatur, quia decretum & decreti executio sibi exactissimè ref-

2. Voluntas Dei fieret mutabilis, si reprobatio esset absoluta, damnatio conditionata. Nam ab aeterno juxta Calvinianos voluit hos ipsos damnare absolute, in tempore vult damnare ob incredulitatem. En mutabilem in Deo voluntatem! Vel Reprobatio est absoluta voluntas, de hominum perditione ab aeterno: Damnatio est absoluta voluntas Dei in tempore de hominum perditione, sed non absoluta, verum per anxiam causata. Vides hic iterum mutabilitatem.

3. Deus ab aeterno voluit omnium salutem, omnibus decrevit mittere filium: Ergo absoluto odio neminem ab aeterno reprobavit.

4. Concedit Beza, Deum ad causas damnationis quoque praedestinasse. Quaerimus igitur: Quae sit causa, vel quare damnentur homines? Respondent, quia in finali impoenitentia manent. Pergimus quaerendo: Cur in peccatis maneant. Respondent, Quia ad hoc absolute eos destinavit Deus. Hinc ita colligimus: Causa causae est causa causati. Absoluta voluntas Dei est causa reprobationis, Reprobatio finalis impoenitentiae, haec damnationis. E. absoluta voluntas est causa damnationis: & per consequens, quoad causas distinguere haut possunt inter reprobationem & damnationem.

XIX. III. Pareus in hac quaestione plane dubius est: Nunc nobiscum, mox cum Calvino loquitur. Nam in capite 9. ad Rom. dub. 8. Col. 908. reprobationi etiam negativae causam ex parte hominum attribuendam esse statuit. Deinde col. 909. distinctiuncula quadam crudum Calvini dogma emollire satagit. Scriptura, inquit, de Dei iudiciis deque causa reprobationis & damnationis loquitur dupliciter: Aliquando secundum absolutum ius Dei in homines & creaturas. Et sic causam in mero Dei beneplacito statuit. Aliquando secundum ius Dei ordinatum ad regulam iustitiae distributivae, in verbo Legis & Evangelij reuelatam. Et sic causam partim ad Dei voluntatem, partim & proxime ad hominum peccata refert.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: We answer briefly that Pareus wanders outside the scope of the question

We answer briefly that Pareus wanders outside the scope of the question. For the point in dispute is not, What can God do by His absolute right, by infinite power? But, What does He will in act, and what has He decreed concerning the salvation or damnation of men? Certainly, no one among us denies that God could have immediately cast away, annihilated, and thrust into the darkness of hell the whole human race after the fall, according to absolute right. But the question is about the fact itself and the decree; how was God in reality disposed toward fallen men? Did He destine the greatest part of them to eternal death from an unconditional good pleasure, with the denial of all means? Here Calvin holds the affirmative, which we have sufficiently demonstrated above to be both horrible to hear and diametrically contrary to the Scriptures. But if Pareus rejects that dogma of Calvin from his heart, and confesses that, according to ordained right, i.e. according to the word of God and His revealed will, the reprobation of men is not absolute regarding any act; we congratulate him on the acknowledgment of the truth, and at the same time we exhort him not to retain the language of Calvin, after he has departed from his mind. For in the following pages, at the cited place, he uses phrases that are very ambiguous and conceal something absolute, as he writes in col. 914: 'Why God has reprobated some, and not all, regarding both acts: the impulsive cause was not any foreseen sin, but the MERE ευδοκια of God.' I do not see how one can reconcile this thesis with the one immediately preceding, which holds as follows: 'Simple reprobation, considered definitely or indefinitely, is not to be called merely absolute regarding impulsive and final causes: because it is founded partly in the divine will, partly in the sins of men.' Thus, indeed, it usually happens that while pretexts and reconciliations are sought, nothing is brought forth but ἀντιλογίας and contradictions. They do not wish to yield the palm to us; and yet they see that Calvin's dogma cannot stand. Hence they prefer to speak ambiguously than to confess the truth openly. But truly, since you are sound in your senses, why do you rave with your voices? says Vigilius, book 2, p. 49. Do not fear to confess what it is not hard to feel in your heart. p. 50.

XX. Thus, therefore, having considered the pretexts and σοφοῖς φερχμάτοις of the moderns, we make an approach to the λύσιν of their objections. Indeed, those are taken primarily from chapter 9 of the epistle to the Romans, in which there are many things difficult to understand, which οἱ ἀμαθεῖς, καὶ ἀσήρικτοι τρεβλῶσιν, ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γρα- φὰς πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν ἀυτῶν ἀπώλειαν, the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do also the other scriptures, to their own destruction, 2 Peter 3, verse 16. Therefore, it is necessary that we institute a brief ἀνάλυσιν καὶ ἐξήγησιν of this chapter; in which we shall follow primarily Mr. Dr. Menzer and Mr. Schröder.

XXI. Above all, however, the intention and scope of the Apostle must be considered. Primarily and principally, he does not treat of the eternal reprobation of the Jews, or of gratuitous election to life, but rather of the temporal calling to the Church, which some call election to grace. Indeed, some things pertaining to the doctrine of predestination are occasionally intermingled, yet the principal scope is this: that the Jews were justly rejected, and in their place the Gentiles were assumed, to whom the Gospel is preached, and from whom the Church is gathered. For it did not seem possible that God would finally cast away the Israelite people, whom He had loved for so many years, and reveal His will to the Gentiles. Paul, therefore, wished to demonstrate in chapter 9 that this was done justly. So that this may become clearer, we shall briefly show the cohesion of the Pauline chapters. XX. After the Apostle had taught in chapters 4 and 5 that justification is gratuitous, in chapter 9 he describes the fruits of justification, namely, the tranquility of conscience and the firm hope of eternal life, which he wishes to show cannot or should not be disturbed. Therefore, in chapter 5, he shows that neither the cross nor sins can weaken the hope of the faithful. Whence he digresses to chapter 6. to the question: Whether it is lawful to persevere in sins, if they do no harm? And chapter 7. to the passage concerning the law, which is both abrogated to a certain extent, and yet ought to be the norm of works, and therefore he teaches that the cause of evils is to be referred not to the law, but to the concupiscence adhering to the regenerate. Chapter 7. he returns to the subject of hope not put to shame, and 1. he explodes the terrors of the law. 2. He removes the scruples of adversities, 3. he takes away the scruples of infirmities. Chapter 8. He casts away another certain scruple, which could shake the ship of hope, namely the rejection of the Israelitic people. He wishes therefore to demonstrate in chapters 9, 10, and 11 that the Israelitic people were justly rejected, on account of most grave causes, not indeed on account of an absolute decree of God. But 1. on account of security and carnal confidence, concerning which in chapter 9. 11. on account of trust in one's own righteousness, concerning which in chapter 10. 11. on account of horrible infidelity, concerning which in chapter 11. The scope therefore of Paul was 1. not to dispute about the predestination of the faithful, but about the rejection of the Israelites. 2. Not to establish an absolute decree, but to refute it, and to show that the causes of rejection are placed in man, not in God. Those, therefore, who drag the words of Paul elsewhere, they are injurious to him himself, and they altogether neglect his scope.

XXIII. Specifically, however, that the Apostle speaks about the temporal rejection of the Jews from grace, is evident clearly from this, because he leaves to the rejected a good hope of recovering salvation, when nevertheless the reprobate by no means attain salvation, and on account of the infallibility of foreknowledge they cannot even attain it, although by reason of causes and the divine will they could have been saved. This assertion, however, is proved. I. Because the Apostle prays for the salvation of the Jews, Rom. 10. verse 1. II. Because he trusts that the fallen Jews can be restored through his ministry. Rom. 11. verses 13 and 14. III. Because he judges that the Jews, like broken-off branches, can in turn be grafted into the olive tree, Rom. 11. v. 6, 23, 30, 31. IV. Because certain Jews by the very act at some time... He predicts that it will be turned, v. 25, 26, concerning which prophecy Augustine treats in book 20 of The City of God, chapters 29 & 30. From these, therefore, and similar arguments, it is rightly concluded that the whole nation of the Jews has not been absolutely reprobated, but only rejected from grace for a time.

XXIV. These things having therefore been premised concerning the scope of the Apostle, we shall subjoin the ἀνάλυσις of the chapter itself. It consists, moreover, of four parts primarily. The first is the Exordium, up to v. 6. The second treats of the rejection of the Jews, up to v. 24. The third of the calling of the Gentiles, up to v. 30. The fourth of the cause of the rejection of the Jews and the election of the Gentiles, up to the end.

XXV. PART ONE. Lest anyone think that this doctrine concerning the rejection of the Jews was proposed by the Apostle out of passion, or envy, or hatred, since he had suffered so many outrages from them and was also of a different religion; hence, from the beginning, he prefaces something about his most ardent love toward the Jews. Let this be the thesis: I, Paul, most ardently love the Jews, and I grieve exceedingly over their rejection. He confirms this thesis with a holy oath: I speak the truth in Christ Jesus, I do not lie, my conscience bearing me witness in the Holy Spirit. To this oath he now subjoins his love toward the Jews, which arose from serious grief over their rejection, v. 2, which he amplifies in such a way that he says he even wishes to be anathema, that is, to be separated from Christ, v. 3. He commemorates eight causes of this his grief: 1. Because they are his brethren, v. 3. 2. Because they are Israelites having many prerogatives, sprung from the most holy lineage of the Patriarchs. 3. Whose is the υἱοθεσία. 4. And the covenants. 5. Νομοθεσία. 6. The worship. 7. The promises. 8. The fathers, from whom is Christ according to the flesh, blessed forever.

XXVI. PART TWO. Now he approaches the question concerning the rejection of the Jews, which he proposes and explains in a disputatious manner, and as if under a dialogue and the person of an opponent and a respondent. Therefore, by three objections and their refutation the whole business is dispatched.

XXVII. First objection. If we Jews have been rejected from the kingdom of the Messiah, the promise of Jehovah made to us will be vain and void.

Paul responds in v. 6 by denying the consequence; The word of God has not failed. He adds the reason for the denial, taken from the distinction of the descendants of Abraham or the Israelites, For not all who are of the circumcision are true Israelites and children of God. But the promise was made only to the true Israelites. You, however, are not such (because you do not believe, but stumble against the cornerstone Rom. 9. v. 31.) Therefore, the promise does not pertain to you. Although, therefore, you are rejected on account of your unbelief, the promise nevertheless remains firm and valid.

XXIIX. Therefore it is to be noted here that there are two kinds of children of Abraham: some are children according to the flesh: others, however, are children of the promise, i.e., they have faith and embrace that promise with true faith, such as was Nathanael John 1. v. 47. Behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile. And this is what others say, that there is a twofold seed of Abraham: 1. σαρκικὸν, or seed of the flesh. 2. πνευματικὸν, or seed of the promise. Of the former, v. 7; of the latter, v. 8, the discourse is made. The Apostle illustrates these with a notable type in v. 7 and 9, taken from the children of Abraham according to the flesh, namely Ishmael and Isaac, in this manner: Just as both Ishmael and Isaac were truly children of Abraham according to the flesh, and yet Ishmael was cast out and not admitted into the fellowship of the inheritance of Abrahamic goods: but Isaac was made heir: So although you Jews descend from Abraham according to the flesh, this carnal prerogative helps you nothing, but because of your unbelief, by which it happens that you are not children of God and children of the promise, you are deservedly cast out from the kingdom of the Messiah,

XXIX. To this argument Paul adds two objections of the Jews, 1. They could have excepted that in the type there was a great disparity; because Ishmael was born of a handmaid; but they themselves were born of a free woman and mistress, from the very lineage of Israel.

Paul answers in verse 10. Even if you were entirely born of the holy family and lineage of Israel; nevertheless, you cannot claim this prerogative of carnal birth, which you cite from another type. Jacob and Esau were from one and the same parents, namely Isaac and Rebecca, and neither was born of a handmaid; furthermore, Esau was the firstborn and therefore still had a certain prerogative over Jacob, yet Esau was rejected from the right of primogeniture, and Jacob was assumed in his place: to whom even Esau, as the Lord willed, was compelled to serve, or rather the Esauitic progeny served the Israelitic stock. Thus (to refer this type to the antitype), even if you come from the most holy seed of Israel, and in this respect are nobler than the Gentiles, you are nevertheless deservedly expelled from the kingdom of the Messiah, just as Esau was rejected from the right of primogeniture.

Latin:

Nos respondemus breviter, Pareum vagari extra circum quæstionis. Non enim controuertitur, Quid Deus possit pro absoluto jure suo, potestate infinita? Sed, Quid velit actu, & quid de salute aut damnatione hominum decreverit? Sane ex nobis nemoinficiatur, Deum potuisse totum genus humanum post lapsum statim abijcere, annihilare, & in tenebras inferni detrudere, secundum jus absolutum. Quæritur a. de ipso facto & decreto; Qualiter Deus reipsa erga homines lapsos affectus fuerit? Num maximam illorum partem ex inconditionato beneplacito æternæ morti cum denegatione omnium mediorum destinârit? Hic Calvinus affirmativam tenet, quam & auditu horrendam & scripturis e diametro contrariam esse, supra satis demonstravimus. Quod si Pareus illud Calvini dogma rejicit ex animo, & fatetur, secundum ius ordinatum, h.e. secundum verbum Dei, & voluntatem eius revelatam, hominum reprobationem, quoad nullum actum absolutam esse; de agnitione veritatis ipsi gratulamur, & simul hortamur, ne linguam Calvini retineat, postquam a mente eius discessit. Nam in sequentibus paginis loco dicto, phrasibus utitur valde ambiguis, & absolutum quid occultantibus, vt scribit col. 914. Cur Deus aliquos reprobauerit, & non omnes quoad vtrumque actum: causa impulsiua non fuit peccatum aliquod præuisum, sed MERA Dei ευδοκια. Non video qui hanc thesin conciliare possit cum proxime præcedenti, quæ sic habet: Reprobatio simplex definitè vel indefinitè considerata, non est dicenda merè absoluta quoad causas impulsivas & finales: quia partim in diuina voluntate, partim in hominum peccatis fundatur. Ita nimirum fieri solet, vt dum prætextus & conciliationes quæruntur, nil nisi ἀντιλογίας & contradictiones afferantur. Nolunt nobis palmam dare; & tamen vident, Calvini dogma consistere non posse. Hinc malunt ambigue loqui, quam veritatem aperte fateri. At verò, Cùm sensu incolumes sitis, cur vocibus insanitis? ait Vigilius lib. 2. p. 49. Nolite metuere confiteri, quod non durum est corde sentire. p. 50.

XX. Sic ergo consideratis recentiorum prætextibus & σοφοῖς φερχμάτοις, ad ipsarum obiectionum λύσιν accessum facimus. Sunt verò illæ inprimis ex cap. 9. epistol. ad Romanos desumptæ, in quo sinè multa sunt intellectu difficilia, quæ οἱ ἀμαθεῖς, καὶ ἀσήρικτοι τρεβλῶσιν, ὡς καὶ τὰς λοιπὰς γραφὰς πρὸς τὴν ἰδίαν ἀυτῶν ἀπώλειαν, indocti & indociles deprauant ad suam ipsorum perditionem, 2. Petr. 3. vers. 16. Proindè necessarium est, vt breuem istius capitis ἀνάλυσιν καὶ ἐξήγησιν instituamus; in quo Dn. D. Menzerum, & Dn. Schröderum præcipuè sequemur.

XXI. Ante omnia v, considerari debet intentio & scopus Apostoli. Primariò & principaliter non agit de æterna vel Iudæorum reprobatione, vel gratuitâ electione ad vitam, sed potius de temporali vocatione ad Ecclesiam, quam nonnulli vocant electionem ad gratiam. Immiscentur quidem subinde aliqua ad doctrinam prædestinationis pertinentia, principalis tamen scopus hic est, quod Iudæis iustè sint reiecti, & in ipsorum locum gentiles assumpti, quibus prædicetur Euangelium, & ex quibus colligatur Ecclesia. Non enim videbatur fieri posse, vt Deus populum Israeliticum quem tot annis dilexerat, nunc demum abijceret, suamque voluntatem gentibus reuelaret. Iustè igitur hoc fieri Paulus c. 9. voluit demonstrare. Quod vt magis planū fiat, cohæsionem capitum Paulinorum breuiter ostendemus. XX. Postquam Apostolus cap. 5. & 4. docuerat, iustificationem esse gratuitam cap. 9. describit fructus iustificationis, videlicet trāquillitatem cōscientiæ, & spem firmam vitæ æternæ, quam non turbari posse, vel debere vult ostendere, Capite igitur 5. ostendit, quòd nec crux, nec peccata, fidelium spem possint infirmare. Vndè digreditur cap 6. ad quæstionem: An licitum sit in peccatis perseuerare, si ea nihil obsint? Et cap. 7. ad locum de lege, quæ & abrogata est quadantenus, & tamen operum norma esse debet, ideoque malorum causam non in legem, sed in concupiscētiam renatis adhærentem esse referendam docet. Cap. 7. redit ad institutum de spe non confusa, & 1. terriculamenta legis displodit. 2. aduersitatum scrupulos aufert, 3. infirmitatum scrupulos eximit Cap. 8. abijcit alium quendam scrupulum, qui spei nauim concutere possit, videlicet abiectionem populi Israelitici. Vult igitur demonstrare cap. 9. 10 & 11. iustè reiectum esse populum Israeliticum, ob grauissimas causas, non quidem ob absolutum Dei decretum. Sed 1. ob securitatem & confidentiam carnalem, de qua cap. 9. 11. ob iustitiæ propriæ fiduciam, de qua cap. 10. 11. ob horrendam infidelitatem, de qua cap. 11. Scopus igitur Pauli erat 1. non de prędestinatione fidelium, sed reiectione Israelitarum disputare. 2. absolutum decretum non stabilire, sed refutare, & ostendere causas rejectionis in homine, non in Deo positas esse. Qui igitur verba Pauli aliò trahūt, isti iniurij sunt in ipsum, eiusque scopum omninò negligunt.

XXIII. In specie v. quòd Apostolus loquatur de Iudæorum reiectione temporali à gratia, patet luculenter ex eo, quia reiectis spem bonam recuperandæ salutis relinquit, cùm tamen reprobati salutem minimè consequantur, & ob infallibilitatem præscientiæ ne quidem cōsequi possint, quamuis ratione causarum, & voluntatis diuinæ omninò potuerint saluari. Probatur v. isthæc assertio. I. Quia pro salute Iudæorum orat Apostolus Rom. 10. vers. 1. II. Quia per suum ministerium lapsos Iudæos restitui posse confidit. Rom. 11. vers. 13. & 14. III. Quia Iudæos tanquã ramos defractos vicissim in oleã inseri posse censet, Rom. 11. v. 6. 23. 30. 31. IV. Quia Iudęos quosdã ipso actu aliquando conversum iri prædicit v. 25. 26. de quo vaticinio agit Augustinus l. 20. de Civ. Dei c. 29. & 30. Ex his ergò & similibus argumentis, rectè concluditur. non totam Iudæorum gentem absolutè reprobatam esse, sed duntaxat ad tempus rejectam à gratia.

XXIV. His igitur de scopo Apostoli præmissi, ipsam ἀνάλυσιν capitis subiungemus. Constat a. partibus imprimis quatuor. Prima est Exordium, usque ad v. 6 Secunda agit de rejectione Iudæorum usque ad v. 24. Tertia de vocatione gentium, usque ad v. 30. Quarta de causa rejectionis Iudæorum, & electionis gentilium usque ad finem.

XXV. PARS PRIMA. Nè quis putet hanc de reiectione Iudæorum doctrinam, ab Apostolo ex affectu, vel inuidia, vel odio fuisse propositam, quippe cùm ab ijs tàm multa flagitia perpessus, tum etiam diuersæ fuerit religionis; hinc ab initio de ardentissimo suo erga Iudæos amore nonnihil præfatur. Thesis hæc esto: Ego Paulus ardentissimè diligo Iudæos, & summoperè doleo super eorum reiectione. Thesin hanc confirmat sancto iuramento: Veritatem dico in Christo Iesu, non mentior, testimonium mihi perhibente conscientiâ meâ in Spiritu sancto. Cui iuramento nunc subijcit suum amorem erga Iudæos, ex serio dolore super eorum reiectione ortum, v. 2. quem amplificat ita, vt dicat se etiam optare anathema, id est, separatum esse à Christo, v. 3. Huius sui doloris causas commemorat octo, 1. Quia sint fratres sui, v. 3. 2. Quia sint Israëlitæ multas habentes prærogatiuas, orti ex sanctissima Patriarcharum prosapia. 3. Quorum sit vioθeσία 4. & testamenta. 5. Νομοθεσία 6. Cultus. 7. Promissiones. 8. Patres, ex quib. Christus secundum carnem benedictus in secula.

XXVI. PARS SECVNDA. Nunc aggreditur quęstionem de rejectione Iudæorum, quam modo disputatorio, & quasi sub dialogo & persona opponentis ac respondentis proponit & explicat. Tribus igitur obiectionibus, earumque depulsionibus totum negotium expeditum dat.

XXVII. Obiectio prima. Si nos Iudæi reiecti sumus à regno Messiæ, vana erit & irrita promissio Iehouæ, nobis facta.

Respondet Paulus v. 6. negando consequentiam; Non excidit verbum Dei. Addit rationem negationis, desumptam à distinctione posteriorum Abrahæ seu Israëlitarum, Non enim omnes qui ex circumsione sunt, sunt Israëlitæ veri, & filij Dei. Atqui solis veris Israëlitis facta est promissio. Vos autem non estis tales (quia non creditis, sed in lapidem angularem impingitis Rom. 9. v. 31.) E. ad vos non pertinet promissio. Licèt igitur propter incredulitatem vestram reijciamini, nihilo minus firma & rata manet promissio.

XXIIX. Proindè notandum hic, quòd duplices sint filij Abrahæ: quidam sunt filij secundum carnem: quidam verò sunt filij promissionis, h. e. fidem habent, & verâ fide promissionem istam amplectuntur, qualis erat Nathanael Ioh. 1. v. 47. Ecce verè Israëlita, in quo dolus non est. Atque hoc est, quod alij dicunt, duplex esse semen Abrahæ 1. σαρκικὸν. vel semen carnis. 2. πνευματικὸν, vel semen promissionis. De illo v. 7. de hoc v, 8 sermo fit. Illustrat hæc Apostolus insigni typo v. 7. & 9. desumpto à filijs Abrahæ secundum carnem, Ismaele nimirum & Isaaco, hunc in modum: Quemadmodum vterq; tam Ismael, quàm Isaac verè fuit filius Abrahæ, secundum carnem, & tamen Ismael eiectus est, nec admissus intra consortium hæreditatis bonorum Abrahamiticorum: Isaac verò factus fuit hæres: Ita quamuis vos Iudæi secundum carnem ab Abrahamo descendatis, hæc tamen carnalis prærogatiua vos nihil iuuat, sed ob incredulitatem vestram, quâ sit, vt non sitis filij Dei & filij promissionis, merito ex regno Messiæ eijcimini,

XXIX. Huic argumento subiungit Paulus duas Iudæorum instantias, 1. Potuissent excipere; in typo proposito magnam esse disparitatem; quia Ismael fuerit prognatus ex ancilla; se verò ex libera & domina esse genitos, ex ipsissima Israelis prosapia.

Respondet Paulus ver. 10. Etiam si vos in totum ex familia & prosapia sancta Israelis geniti sitis; attamen hanc carnalis natiuitatis prærogativam non potestis prætendere, quod ex alio typo addicite. Iacob & Esau ex vnis ijsdemque parentibus Isaaco nim: & Rebecca, & neuter ex ancilla fuit prognatus, quin insuper Esau erat natu maiors ideoque quandam adhuc habebat præ Iacobo Prærogativam, attamen Esau à jure primogenituræ rejectus fuit, & in ejus locum assumptus Iacob: cui etiam Esau, sic volente Domino, inferuire coge batur, vel potius Esauitica progenies inseruiit stirpi Israeliticæ. Ita (vt hunc typum ad antitypum referamus) etiam si vos ex sanctissimo Israelis semine proveniatis, & hac in parte gentilibus nobiliores sitis, meritò tamen è regno Messiæ expellimini, non secus atque Esau à primogenituræ iure reiiciebatur.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: XXX. II. They could have objected; that Jacob was preferred to Esau on account of piety and probity

XXX. II. They could have objected; that Jacob was preferred to Esau on account of piety and probity.

Paul answers in verses 11, 12, 13. That the good works of Jacob were not the cause that he obtained the right of primogeniture and the blessing, because this election of Jacob was made 1. When they had not yet been born. 2. When they had done nothing good or evil. 3. Because it was not made from works. 4. But from Him who calls, so that the purpose of God might remain firm. Therefore, at the same time, he removes here the false cause of election, namely works; and external prerogatives, and substitutes the true one, namely the purpose τοῦ προθέσεως of Him who calls. Jacob was not chosen over Esau because he did good works, since God did not look to works in the election. Just as therefore Jacob was not assumed by God on account of works, so also we are not chosen on account of works. And this indeed is the secondary application, the primary is indeed this: Just as Jacob was chosen, Esau was rejected, and thus they clearly had an unequal lot, even though by reason of birth they were equal: so also you Jews cannot trust in your carnal prerogative, nor can it be proven from that, that you are the chosen peculiar people of God, because, as you see from the type, Esau no less than Jacob.

XXXI. Thus, therefore, this type can be applied to the business of eternal election: Just as Jacob was not chosen by God on account of works: so also those who are chosen, are not chosen on account of works. Likewise, just as Esau was rejected, even though he enjoyed a certain carnal prerogative; so many of the Jews are reprobated, even though they are the seed of Abraham according to the flesh. But if indeed anyone wished to extend this type more broadly, and to institute such a comparison: Just as Esau was not rejected on account of evil works; so also those who are reprobated, are not reprobated on account of evil works; then we say: 1. that this type is extended too broadly. 2. that it is done against the scope of Paul. 3. against the remaining scripture and the Analogy of faith. Let this therefore be held, that Paul wishes to inculcate this to us in this place, that election does not depend on works, or other external prerogatives, but from the sole mercy and love of God, and therefore the Jews cannot prove from their prerogative of carnal generation that they are the chosen peculiar people of God.

XXXII. These questions concerning election and rejection are indeed joined, so that Paul in this chapter does not treat of them separately: nevertheless, up to verse 17, in the type of Isaac and Jacob, he discourses chiefly concerning election, namely that neither was he chosen on account of carnal prerogative, but because he was the son of promise; so also that the Jews cannot prove from carnal prerogative that they are the chosen peculiar people of God.

Others say briefly, that Esau is indeed an example, that God is not bound by his own prerogatives which he bestows; but that it is not an example of reprobation, but a type. For there is a twofold exposition of words. 1. Literal. 2. Mystical. The literal [meaning] of this saying is that Esau was rejected from the right of primogeniture: the mystical, that he was a type of reprobation. Now, however, apodictic arguments are not drawn from a mystical sense, as Jerome holds in chapter 13 of Matthew.

Some add this, that it holds as a type regarding comparative election, and indeed regarding election to singular benefits, as that he called Abraham from Ur, but not the others. No cause for this thing is found, except for the sole εὐδοκία of God.

But the best exposition can be sought from the saying of Irenaeus, which is read in book 4, chapter 38. Esau was rejected from the primogeniture on account of foreseen impiety, even though he had not yet exercised the same. Therefore, we do not concede the πρότασιν in the comparison made, namely that Esau was not rejected on account of evil works: but we say that he was rejected on account of contempt and ingratitude toward the right of primogeniture. This was done, however, in the foreknowledge of God before he himself was born, or had actually done anything evil, although in the rejection God looked toward the future impiety and ingratitude of Esau. Therefore, those words only indicate that election was made from eternity, before those who are predestined exist and are born in time, or do anything good or evil. Otherwise, it would follow that men are predestined before they are known from eternity, according to the natural being by which men are. For similarly the Apostle says there, when they were not yet born.

XXXIII. Second objection v. 14. If we Jews, who are the seed of Abraham, who do good works, who observe the law, are therefore rejected by God, and on the contrary idolatrous nations become participants in the divine promise, God will be unjust and iniquitous.

Paul responds in v. 15 by denying the consequence: God forbid. He adds the reason, because elec tion is merely gratuitous, not done on account of works, not on account of faith or the running of men. For it is written: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, that is, on whom I have mercy, I have mercy out of grace alone, not on account of works. (For the repetition of the verb has this force and emphasis.) Even if you Jews therefore do good external works, by keeping the law, this external observance does not prove that you are still the chosen people of God, since election is not made from works, but from grace. Paul therefore shows the principal cause of election, namely Mercy, which however does not exclude other causes, the merit of Christ, and faith. For this is opposed only to external works, not to faith and the merit of Christ. For just as it does not follow: We are justified by grace alone, not from works. Therefore not on account of the merit of Christ, nor through faith: So it does not follow; Election is made from grace, therefore it excludes merit and faith, by which that is apprehended.

XXXIV. Furthermore, it must be observed here that Paul does not add whose he wishes to have mercy on, or whom he wishes to have mercy on, which nevertheless can be understood from other places of scripture, by which it is shown that God wishes to have mercy on all, although he could have mercy on no one; that he wishes to harden none but those who spurn the offered grace, although he could harden all. Therefore, those who wish to forge a certain absolute decree of Election from this place, as if God loved only some, with the rest being consigned to damnation out of simple hatred without any cause, these do most manifest violence to the text:

XXXV. Vers. 16. The Apostle infers a conclusion, or sets forth the sum of those things which have been said thus far: So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. You see here manifestly that Paul opposes the mercy of God not to the merit of Christ, not to faith, but to our will, to our running. To this end, therefore, we must uniquely refer those things which have been said by Paul, and thus more conveniently

XXXVI. And thus far the Apostle shows that not all Israelites are true Israelites, and therefore not all are dear to God, or the elect people of God, since election is not made from carnal prerogative, or from our works. But just as the first and principal cause of election is the merciful will of God: so now, on the contrary, Paul shows that the first and principal cause of hardening is also the just will of God, by the example of Pharaoh, v. 17. For the Scripture says, For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I may show in you, etc. It is not said, however: I raised you up so that you would be proud and stubborn, but the secondary end of divine μακροθυμίας is explained, for which God established Pharaoh, raised him to the kingdom, and sustained him until that point, as if it had been said, Even though I saw that you would be rebellious, nevertheless ἐξήγειρά σε. I raised you up (which word Paul uses) or העמד תיך (which word is in the Hebrew) I made you stand, or I made (according to Tremellius) that you should remain, or διετηρήθης ἕως τοῦ νῦν (according to the LXX) you were preserved, or I preserved you, as Munster interprets, that is, I allowed you to be born, and although you were rebellious, yet I did not immediately take you away, but I bore your tyranny with great patience, and I indulged you so that you might remain, and so that I might show my patience in your overthrow, through a most just judgment. Hence others say that that (That) is not ἀιτιολογικὸν, but ἐκϐατικὸν.

XXXVII. From these things Paul now concludes, v. 18. Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills, he hardens. But whom he wills to have mercy upon, and whom he wills to be hardened, he leaves to be learned from other Scriptures. The scope here is: That no injustice is found in God, even if he wills to have mercy on the children of the promise, and to harden the contumacious. For God is bound by no bond to have mercy on or to harden certain ones, he is tied by no merit, he is held by no obligation: but he has the most free, most entire, and absolute power of having mercy on whom he wills, and of hardening whom he wills. We understand these words, therefore, not concerning the action, but concerning the power of acting. He has mercy and hardens whom he wills, just as the Canonists teach: The Pope transfers kingdoms and deposes the Caesar, that is, he has the power. Thus John 10:17, 'I lay down my life,' which is explained not of the act, but of the power in verse 18. And that this is the sense of this passage appears from verse 21: 'Does not the potter have power,' etc.

XXXIIX. Third objection v. 19. If all things proceed from the will of God, and if he has mercy on whom he wills; he hardens whom he wills; why then does he complain about our obstinacy? It will not be our fault that we are not converted to Christ, for who will resist his will? Paul's response is twofold. The former is indirect, which is an ἐπιπληξις, a rebuke. For the Philosopher advises in 3 Top. 11 that those who dispute against sense and piety are in need of κολάσεως, of punishment, ἢ λόγου μᾶλλον ἢ αἰσθήσεως κολάσεως, rather of punishment of sense than of reason. Paul therefore refutes human rashness in verse 20: 'O man, who are you to answer back to God?' As if he were saying: The creature ought not to demand from the creator a reason for his deeds. He illustrates this from the lesser in verse 21: If the potter has power to make a vessel either for honor or for dishonor: much more does God have the power of having mercy on some, and of hardening others on account of sins. Or concerning the fact: just as the potter is not unjust, even if he makes some vessels for honor and some for dishonor out of the same lump: so God is not unjust, even if out of the same human race he has mercy on some, and does not have mercy on others—namely, sinners, who are vessels of wrath—but rather hardens them. Or: Even if out of the same human race he prepares vessels of mercy for glory, and bears with vessels of wrath with much patience, to show his wrath and his power, verses 22, 23. This, therefore, is the scope of the introduced similitude, that from the example of the potter men may be taught that God is not unjust, nor ought he to be blamed, although he prepares some men as vessels of mercy, but others as vessels he hardens. Otherwise there are many dissimilarities in this similarity: 1. The potter makes vessels of both kinds: God does not prepare vessels of wrath, but tolerates those that are prepared. 2. Clay is devoid of sense, nor does it resist the potter. But men resist God. 3. The potter does it for mere whim, but God for a grave reason. 4. The potter delights in vessels of both kinds: God does not likewise. 5. A potter's vessel made for ignominy always remains such. But a vessel of spiritual ignominy can, through repentance, become a vessel of mercy. 6. A potter's vessel is in itself indifferent: But the mass of man is by nature corrupted, from which nothing but sordid vessels can emerge, unless the mercy of God intervenes.

And this was an indirect response. Lest, however, foolish men think the Apostle failed in his response, he now adds in the second place, v. 22: 'What if God, willing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction,' supply: yet it cannot be said that he still finds fault, 'who will resist his will?' The argument is such: He who hardens whom he wills, yet in such a way that he is not the author of the hardness, does not unjustly accuse those who harden themselves: But such is God, which Mr. Schröder proves with four arguments, th. 194 & seq.

1. Because they are called vessels of wrath, or vessels with which God is angry in Himself. But He is angry with no one of whom He is the author, Wis. 11:25. He is, however, angry with the hardened: Therefore, either by reason of nature, or by reason of hardness. Not by reason of the former, therefore by reason of the latter. Hence Fulgentius rightly, l. 1 ad Mon.: 'I ask, dearest Monimus, that you diligently attend to this passage of the Apostle. For it is known that the wrath of God cannot be spoken of, unless it is believed that the iniquity of man has preceded it.' 2. Because God is said to have borne or tolerated them. But we do not tolerate things that please us, but those that displease us, and we are not the authors of them; for no one hates his own work. 3. Because it is said that He tolerated them in great μακροθυμίᾳ [long-suffering]. Of such evil, however, no one can be the author, both because the object of μακροθυμίας [long-suffering] is not pleasing, but displeasing, and because the end of μακροθυμίας is that that which is tolerated may become better. Rom. 2. verse 4. 2. Pet. 3. verse 9. Wisd. 11. v. 24. And before it was evil. Hence it appears that induration is not absolute, excluding every purpose of God concerning saving them, since He tolerates it to that end, that they may repent. This can be declared by a most elegant simile from the gardener, from Luke 13. v. 6. 7. 8. 9. which see in Schröd. th. 203. The ends, however, of this tolerance, if repentance does not follow, three secondary ones are indicated (for repentance is the primary one), namely the showing of wrath, the making known of power, the illustration of the riches of glory, toward the vessels of mercy. 4. Because He speaks in different ways about the vessels of wrath, and about the vessels of mercy. The latter He says God prepared, the former are said to have been fitted for destruction, which however He does not assert to proceed from God, but rather implies the contrary.

XXXIX. The third part is concerning the election, or calling of the Gentiles, to the Church, through the preaching of the Gospel, in which part there is nothing obscure.

XL. The fourth part deals with the causes of the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles. v. 30. & seq. What then shall we say? Why were the Gentiles taken up? Why were the Jews rejected? Is it because of some absolute decree? Not so: But the Gentiles, who were not following after righteousness, namely legal righteousness, apprehended righteousness, because they believed the Gospel. The Jews, however, He says were reprobated for a double cause. 1. Because of the pursuit of their own righteousness in the works of the law. 2. Because of the scandal taken from the servile form of Christ, v. 32. & 33. The sum therefore is: The Gentiles are taken into the kingdom of Christ because they hear the Gospel, and believe in Christ. The Jews are rejected, because trusting in their own righteousness they contemn Christ, and repel the Gospel. Refer here to Acts 13. verse 46. & Rom. 11. where this twin cause is indicated by the one name ἀπιστίας [unbelief] v. 20. Through unbelief they were broken off.

XLI. And this was a brief exposition of the ninth chapter of the Epistle to the Romans, from which it is very easy to respond to the Calvinistic objections. There is no need at all for them all to be examined separately: we shall set forth only two, which seem to be of some importance.

XLII. First: God loved Jacob, and hated Esau, without any regard for evil works, before they were born. Therefore, others who are chosen are chosen by the absolute will of God, and those who are reprobated are likewise reprobated by the absolute will of God.

Response: There is a manifold fallacy in this argument.

I. This passage does not deal with the election of Jacob to life nor the destination of Esau to eternal death, but only with the temporal prerogative of the younger brother, which is proven. 1. Because Isaac says to the troubled Esau that Jacob had taken away his blessing, which cannot be understood as a matter of eternal Election. 2. Because Isaac blessed Esau in part. He would therefore be, in part, elected, and in part, reprobated. 3. Because it is expressly said: The elder shall serve the younger. 4. Because the Apostle institutes the disputation here, not concerning eternal rejection, but temporal, which he wishes to declare by this type. Otherwise, it would follow that the whole posterity of Esau (for this is what is understood, which will be proven in the third member) is damned, and Jacob's saved, which is false. 2. That Esau was damned, which will be disproven and cannot be demonstrated. 3. That God adjudged Esau to eternal damnation without any merit, which is ἀσεβὲς καὶ ἀδιάλογον.

II. By hatred is not understood any absolute hatred, by which God would have so hated Esau that He did not wish him to be saved. For it is not improbable that Esau performed penance and was saved through faith in the Messiah, as Luther conjectures on chapter 20 of Genesis. For he cultivated concord with his brother Jacob, having returned from Mesopotamia, Gen. 33, by whom without doubt he was fraternally admonished concerning the cultivation of piety, especially around the burial of his father Isaac, where we read that they met. Gen. 33. v. ult. And indeed if Esau was reprobated 1. with what eyes could Rebecca, who understood the answer of God well, have looked upon this slave of Satan? 2. with what affection could Isaac have loved him so greatly? Genef. 25. v. 28. 3. How could he have conferred the sacrament of circumcision? Did God thus receive into His covenant one whom He would pursue with fatal hatred? Therefore, that hatred denotes nothing other than the passing over of Esau, while he was placed after Jacob by God. Scripture speaks similarly, Luke 14. v. 26. chap. 16. v. 13. Genesis 29. v. 31. Matthew 6. v. 24. chap. 10. v. 37. Psalm 78. v. 67. 68. Proverbs 13. v. 24. III. Persons are not understood, but the whole posterity, because 1. Gen. 25. v. 29. it is said: Two nations are in your womb, the greater shall serve the lesser. For it is familiar to the Hebrews to use the proper names of stocks for patronymics. Israel, that is, the Israelites: thus I hated Esau, i.e., the Edomites. 2. Gen. 27. v. 29. the same is indicated: Let peoples serve you, and tribes adore you. 3. The same is noted by the words of Malachi chap. 1. vers. 2. & seqq. 4. We never read that Esau in his own person served Jacob, but the descendants of Esau served the Jacobites, after David subdued the whole of Idumea, and the same threw off that yoke under King Joram. 2. Kings 8. v. 22 which was predicted, Gen. 27. v. 40. These nations, however, were not absolutely reprobated or damned, since it is certain from Isaiah 11. v. 14, Amos 9, 11. & 12, Mark 3. v. 7. & 8, that the Idumeans were called to the kingdom of God. Speaking summarily, therefore, Jacob and Esau are introduced τυπικῶς, not παραδειγματικῶς, as a type, not an example, the former of election, the latter of rejection. And the scope of Paul here is: just as the right of primogeniture and the blessing did not proceed from the carnal prerogative of birth, since by reason of that they were equals, but from the will of God: So also you Jews cannot prove that you are the chosen people of God, even if according to the flesh you are descended from the holy Father Abraham. Paul, therefore, in these words does not primarily deal with rejection, but only removes the false cause of election, which were external works. For he is engaged in the solution of the Jewish objection from birth: therefore, all things which are said here tend toward that goal, that the Apostle may show that carnal birth helps them nothing, which he wished to illustrate by this type. Let the whole of verses 11 and 12 be read through, and the scope of the Pauline sentence will appear, that he merely wished to exclude external works from the number of causes.

Latin:

XXX. II. Potuissent excipere; Iacobum Esao prælatum fuisse propter pietatem & probitatem

Respondet Paulus v. 11. 12. 13. Bona Iacobi opeta non fuisse in causa, vt ipse ius primogenituræ & benedictionem consequeretur, quia hæc Iacobi electio facta fuit 1. Cùm non dum nati fuissent. 2. cùm nihil boni vel mali egissent. 3. Quia non facta fuit ex operibus. 4. Sed ex vocante, vt propositum Dei firmum maneret. Simul ergo hic removet causam falsam electionis, videlicet opera; & extérnas prærogativas, & substituit verum, videlicet propositum τοῦ προθέσεων vocantis. Non electus est Iacob præ Efauo, quia bona opera fecit, cùm Deus non attenderit opera in electione. Sicut igitur Iacob non assumptus est à Deo, propter opera, ita & nos non eligimur propter opera. Et hæc quidem secundària est applicatio, primaria verò est illa : Sicut Iacob electus, Esau reiectus fuit, & sic planè inæqualem habuérunt sortem, etiamsi ratione nativitatis æquales essent : ita & vos Iudæi non potestis fidere carnali vestræ prærogativæ, nec indè probari potest, vos esse electum Dei peculium, quia, vtî videtis ex typo, Esau nihilominus reiectus fuit ; etiamsi carnaliter esset filius Isaac, non minùs quàm Iacob

XXXI. Ita ergo applicari potest typus hic ad negotium æternæ electionis: Quemadmodum Iacob non propter opera fuit à Deo electus : ita & qui eliguntur, non propter opera eliguntur. Item, Quemadmodum Esau reiectus fuit, etiamsi carnali quadam prærogativâ gauderet; ita multi ex Iudæis reprobantur, etiamsi semen Abrahæ sint secundum carnem. Quòd si verò quis typum hunc latiùs vellet extendere, & talem comparationem instituere : Sicut Esau non propter opera mala fuit reiectus ; sic etiam qui reprobantur, non propter opera mala reprobantur ; tum dicimus. 1. nimis latè extendi hunc typum. 2. fieri contra scopum Pauli. 3. contra scripturam reliquam & Analogiam fidei. Hoc igitur teneatur, quòd Paulus hoc in loco id nobis velit inculcatum, electionem non pendere ex operibus, vel aliis externis prærogativis, sed à sola misericordia & dilectione Dei, proinde Iudæos non posse ex sua prærogativa carnalis generationis probare, se electum esse Dei peculium.

XXXII. Sunt quidem coniunctæ hæ quæstiones de electione ac rejectione, ita vt Paulus in hoc capite seorsim de ijs non agat : attamen vsque ad v. 17. in typo Isaaci & Iacobi præcipuè disserit de electione, quòd videlicet nec hic sit electus propter carnalem prærogativam, sed quia fuit filius promissionis; sic etiam Iudæos ex carnali prærogatiua non posse probare, se esse electum Dei peculium.

Alii dicunt breuiter, quòd Esau sit quidem exemplum, Deum suis, quas elargitur, prærogatiuis non teneri; reprobationis autem non exemplum sed typum esse. Duplex enim est verborum expositio. 1. Literalis. 2. Mystica. Literalis huius dicti est, quòd Esau fuerit à iure primogenituræ reiectus : Mystica, quòd fuerit typus reprobationis. Iam autem à sensu mystico non ducuntur argumenta Apodictica, vti habet Hieronymus in cap. 13. Matthæi.

Nonnulli hoc addunt, de electione comparatâ typum valere, & quidem de electione ad beneficia singularia, vt quòd Abraham vocauit ex Vr, reliquos non item. Huius rei nulla inuenitur causa, præterquam sola Dei ἐυδοκία.

Verùm expositio peti potest optima ex dicto Irinæi, quod legitur l. 4. c. 38. Reiectus est Esau à primogenitura propter præuisam impietatem, etsi eandem nondum exercuerat. Πρότασιν igitur in facta comparatione non concedimus, nempè quòd propter mala opera non fuerit reiectus Esau: sed dicimus eum esse reiectum, propter contemptum & ingratitudinem ergà ius primogenituræ. Factum aute hoc fuit, in præuisione Dei antequam ipse natus esset, vel actu aliquid mali fecisset, quamuis in reiectione ad futuram Esaui impietatem & ingratitudinem Deus respexerit. Verba igitur, ista tantùm indicant, electionem factam esse ab æterno, priusquam sint & nescantur in tempore prædestinati, aut aliquid boni maliuè agant. Aliàs sequeretur, prædestinari homines, priusquam ab ęterno cogniti sint, secundum esse naturale, quo homines sunt. Nam similiter ibi dicit Apostolus, cùm nondum nati essent.

XXXIII. Obiectio secunda v. 14. Si nos Iudæi, qui sumus semen Abrahæ, qui facimus bona opera, qui obseruamus legem, ęo c. à Deo reijcimur, & contrà gentes Idololatricæ fiunt diuinæ promissionis participes, iniustus & iniquus erit Deus.

Respondet Paulus v: 15. negando consequentiam: Absit. Addit rationem, quia electio merè sit gratuita, non propter opera, non propter fidem vel cursum hominum facta. Scriptutum enim est: Misereor cuius misereor, id est cuius misereor, illius ex sola gratia, non propter opera misereor, (Hanc n. vim & emphasin habet verbi repetitio.) Etiamsi igitur vos Iudæi bona faciatis opera externa, seruando legem, hæc tamen externa vōs. obseruatio non probat, vos adhuc esse electum Dei populum, quoniam electio non fit ex operibus, sed ex gratia. Ostendit igitur Paulus principem electionis causam, videlicet Misericordiam, quæ tamē nō excludit alias causas, meritum Christi, & fidē. Opponitut enim hæc solùm externis operibˣ, nō a fidei & merito Christi. Sicut enim nō sequitur: Iustificamur sola gratia, nō ex operibus. Non ergo propter meritum Christi, nec per fidem: Ita non sequitur; Electio fit ex gratia, E. excludit meritum & fidem, quæ illud apprehenditur.

XXXIV. Porrò hic obseruandum est, Paulum non addere, quorum, vel cuius velit misereri, quod tamen ex alijs scripturæ locis potest intelligi, quibus ostenditur, quòd Deus velit misereri omnium, licèt possit nullius misereri; quòd velit indurare non nisi eos, qui gratiam oblatam aspernantur, licèt posset omnes indurare. Qui ergò ex hoc loco volunt absolutum quoddam Electionis decretum cudere, ac si Deus aliquos tantùm diligeret, reliquis simplici odio sine vlla causa damnationi addictis, ista vim faciunt textui manifestissimam:

XXXV. Vers. 16. infert Apostolus conclusionem, vel ponit summam eorum, quæ hacténus dicta sunt: Igitur non volentis, non currentis, sed miserantis est Dei. Vides hic manifestè, Paulum opponere misericordiam Dei non merito Christi, non fidei, sed nostræ voluntati, nostro cursui. Ad hunc igitur finem, quæ à Paulo dicta sunt, vnicè referre debemus, & ita conuenientius

XXXVI. Atque hactenus ostendit Apostolus, non omnes Israelitas, veros esse Israelitas, ideoque non omnes esse Deo charos, vel electum Dei populum, cùm electio non fiat ex carnali praerogatiua, vel ex operibus nostris. Quemadmodum verò prima & princeps causa electionis, est voluntas Dei misericors: ita nunc à contrario ostendit Paulus, etiam indurationis primam ac principem causam esse, iustam Dei voluntatem, exemplo Pharaonis v. 17. Dicit enim scriptura, In hoc ipsum te excitaui, vt ostendam in te, &c. Non autem dicitur: Excitaui te, vt superbus esses, & praefractus, sed exponitur finis secundarius μακροθυμίας diuinae, propter quem Deus Pharaonem condiderit, ad regnum euexerit, & eo vsque sustinuerit, Ac si dictum esset, Etiamsi videbam te rebellem futurum, nihilominus ἐξήγειρά σε. Excitaui te (qua voce vtitur Paulus) seu העמד תיך (quae vox est in Hebraeo) feci te stare, seu feci, (iuxta Tremellium) vt restares, seu διετηρήθης ἕως τοῦ νῦν (iuxta LXX.) conseruatus es seu conseruaui te, vt interpretatur Munsterus, id est passus sum te nasci, & licèt rebellis esses, tamen non te statim sustuli, sed tyrannidem tuam magnâ patientiâ tuli, indulsíq; vt maneres, adeoque; meam patientiam in tui euersione, per iustissimum iudicium ostenderem. Hinc alij dicunt illud (Vt) non esse ἀιτιολογικὸν, sed ἐκϐατικὸν.

XXXVII. Ex his nunc concludit Paulus v. 18. Itaque cuius vult miseretur, & quem vult, indurat. Quorum autem velit misereri, & quos velit induratos, ex alijs Scripturis ad discendum relinquit. Scopus hic est: Nihil inueniri apud Deum iniustitiae: etiamsi filiorum promissionis misereri, & contumaces indurare velit. Deus enim ad miserendum vel indurandum certos, nullo vinculo est obstrictus, nullo merito est deuinctus, nullâ obligatione tenetur: sed liberrimam, integerrimam & absolutam habet potestatem miserendi cuius velit, & indurandi quem velit. Non igitur de actione, sed de potestate agendi ista intelligimus verba. Miseretur & indurat quem vult, sicut Canonistae docent: Papa transfert regna & deponit Cæsarem, id est, potestatem habet. Sic Ioh. 10. 17. Ego pono animam meam, quod non de actu, sed potestate exponitur v. 18. Et hunc loci huius esse sensum apparet ex. v. 21. Annon figulus potesta em habet, &c.

XXXIIX. Obiectio tertia v. 19. Si omnia à voluntate Dei proueniunt, & si miseretur quorum vult; indurat quos vult; Cur igitur conqueritur de nostra obstinatione? Nostra non erit culpa, quòd non conuertamur ad Christum, voluntati enim eius quis resistet? Responsio Pauli duplex est. Prior indirecta, quæ est ἐπιπληξις obiurgatio. Monet enim Philosophus 3. Top. 11. quod κολάσεως indigeant contra sensum & pietatem disputantes ἢ λόγου μᾶλλον ἢ αἰσθήσεως κολάσεως. Redarguit ergò Paulus temeritatem humanã vers. 20. O homo tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Ac si diceret: Non debet creatura à creatore exposcere rationem factorum suorum. Illustrat hoc a minoribus v. 21. Si figulus potestatem habet, facere vas vel in honorem, vel in contumeliam: Multò magis Deus habet potestatem quorundam miserendi, quosdam ob peccata indurandi. Vel de facto: sicut figulus non est iniustus, etiamsi ex eadem massa quædam vasa in honorem, quædam in contumeliam faciat: ita Deus non est iniustus, etiamsi ex eodem genere humano, quorundam misereatur, quorundam v. peccatorum videlicet, qui sunt vasa iræ, non misereatur, sed illos poti⁹ induret Vel: Etiamsi ex eodẽ genere humano vasa Misericordiæ præparet in gloriam, & vasa irę perferat multâ lenitate, ad ostendendam iram & potentiam suam v. 22. 23. Hic igitur scopus est illatæ similitudinis, vt ab exemplo figuli doceantur homines, Deum non esse iniustum, nec debere reprehendi, quamuis quosdam homines præparet in vasa Misericordiæ, vasa vero induret. Aliàs multa sunt in hoc simili dissimilia: 1. Figulus vtriusque generis vasa facit : Deus vasa iræ non præparat, sed præparata tolerat. 2. Lutum est sensus expers, nec repugnat figulo. Homines a. repugnant Deo. 3. Figulus pro mero arbitrio id facit, Deus autem graui de causa. 4. Figulus vtriusque generis vasis delectatur: Deus non item. 5. Vas figulinum in Ignominiam factunt semper manet tale. Vas autem ignominisæ spiritualis, potest per pœnitentiam fieri vas Misericordiæ. 6. Vas figulinum perse est indifferens : Hominis autem massa naturâ est corrupta, è qua non nisi sordida vasa prodire queant, nisi interueniat misericordia Dei.

Et hęc fuit indirecta, responsio, Nè v. stulti putēt Apost. in responsione defecisse, iã secūdo loco subijcit v. 22. Quòd si Deus volēs ostendere ir,ā & notā facere potētiam suam, sustinuit in multâ patientia vasa iræ aptata in interitū, supple: tñ dici non poterit, quòd adhuc cqueritur, voluntati eius quis resistet? Argumentū est tale: Qui indurat quē vult, ita tamē, vt duriciei non sit author, is no immeritò accusat eos qui indurescunt : Talis verò est Deus, id quod argumentis quatuor probat Dn. Schröderus th. 194 & seq.

1. Quia dicuntur vasa iræ, vel vasa quibus Deus per se irascatur. Nulli autem irascitur, cuius author est, Sap. 11. v. 25. Irascitur verò induratis : E. vel ratione naturæ, vel ratione duriciei. Non ratione illius, E. ratione huius. Hinc Fulgentius rectè l. 1. ad Mon. Quæso Monime charissime vt hunc locum Apostoli diligenter attendas. Notum namque est, iram Dei dici non posse, nisi vbi creditur hominis iniquitas præcessisse. 2. Quia Deus dicitur illa tulisse, vel tolerasse. Non autem toleramus, quæ placent, sed quę displicent, eorum autores non sumus, Nemo enim odit opus suum. 3. Quia dicitur tolerâsse in magnâ μακροθυμίᾳ. Talis lium verò nemo potest esse autor, tum quia μακροθυμίας obiectum non est placens, sed displicens, tum quia μακροθυμίας finis est, vt id, quod toleratur, melius fiat. Rom. 2. vers. 4. 2. Petr. 3. vers. 9. Sap. 11. v. 24 E. anteà malum fuit. Hinc apparet, indurationem non esse absolutam, excludentem omne Dei propositum de salvandis ijs, cùm in eum finem toleret, vt resipiscant. Declarari hoc potest elegantissimo simili ab hortulano, ex Luc. 13. v. 6. 7. 8. 9. quod vide apud Schröd. th. 203. Fines a. huius tolerantiæ, si resipiscentia non sequatur, tres indicantur secundarij, (resipiscentia enim est primarius) videlicet ostensio iræ, patefactio potentiæ, illustratio diuitiarum glorię, erga vasa misericordię. 4. Quia diuersimodè loquitur de vasis iræ, & de vasis misericordiæ. Hæc dicit Deum præparâsse, illa in interitum apparata esse, quod tamen à Deo proficisci non asserit, sed contrarium potius innuit.

XXXIX. Pars tertia, est de electione, vel vocatione gentium, ad Ecclesiam, per prædicationem Evangelij, in qua parte nihil est obscuri.

XL. Quarta Pars agit de causis reiectionis Iudæorum & vocationis gentium. v. 30. & seq. Quid ergò dicemus? cur gentes sunt assumtæ? cur Iudæi sunt reiecti? Num propter absolutum quoddam decretum? Non ita: Sed gentes, quæ non sectabantur iustitiam, videlicet legalem, iustitiam apprehenderunt, quia crediderunt Evangelio. Iudæos a. duplici de causa dicit reprobatos. 1. Ob studium propriæ iustitiæ in operibus legis. 2. Ob scandalum acceptum ex Christi seruili forma, v. 32. & 33. Summa igitur est: Gentes assumuntur in regnum Christi quia Evangelium audiunt, & credunt in Christum. Iudæi reijciuntur, quia confisi propriæ iustitiæ contemnunt Christum, & repellunt Evangelium. Refer huc Act. 13. vers. 46. & Rom. 11. vbi hæc gemina causa, vno ἀπιστίας nomine indicatur v. 20. Per incredulitatem defracti sunt.

XLI. Et hæc fuit breuis expositio capitis noni Epist. ad Rom. vnde ad obiectiones Caluinisticas respondere est facillimum. Vt seorsim omnes excutiantur, minimè opus est: Duas duntaxat adponemus, quæ videntur esse alicuius momenti.

XLII. Prima: Deus Iacobum dilexit, Esavum odio habuit, sine vllo intuitu malorum operum, antequam nati essent. E. & alij qui eliguntur, absolutâ Dei voluntate eliguntur, & qui reprobantur, itidem absolutâ Dei voluntate reprobantur.

Resp. Multiplex inest huic argumento fallacia.

I. Locus iste non agit de electione Iacobi ad vitam nec destinatione Esaui ad mortem æternam, sed duntaxat de temporali prærogatiua fratris minoris, quod probatur. 1. Quia Isaac dicit turbato Esauo, Iacobum illi abstulisse benedictionem, quod de negotio æternæ Electionis accipi nequit. 2. Quia Isaac benedixit ex parte Esavo. Esset igitur, ex parte electus, ex parte reprobatus. 3. Quia expressè dicitur. Maior seruiet minori. 4. Quia Apostolus disputationem hic instituit, non de reiectione æternâ, sed temporali, quam hoc typo vult declarare. Aliàs sequeretur, totam Esavi posteritatem (hæc enim intelligitur, quod in tertio membro probabitur,) esse damnatam, Iacobi saluatam, quod falsum. 2. Esavum damnatum esse, quod improbabitur & demonstrari nequit. 3. Deum sine omni merito Esavum æternæ damnationi adiudicâsse, quod ἀσεβὲς καὶ ἀδιάλογον.

II. Per odium non intelligitur absolutum aliquod odium, quo Deus ita odisset Esavum, vt eum saluatum noluerit. Neque enim improbabile est, egisse Esavum pœnitentiam, & esse saluatum per fidem Messiæ, vti Lutherus conijcit super cap. 20. Gen. Coluit enim concordiam cum Iacobo fratre, reuerso ex Mesopotamia Gen. 33. à quo sine dubio fraternè fuit monitus de colēda piætate, inprimis circa sepulturam patris Isaaci, vbi eos conuenisse legimus. Gen. 33. v. ult. Et sanè si Esavus fuit reprobatus 1. quibus oculis Rebecca, quæ responsum Dei benè intelligebat, intueri poguisset hoc Satanæ mancipium? 2. quo affectu eum tantoperè amare potuisset Isaacus? Genef. 25. v. 28. 3. Quomodo circumcisionis sacramentum conferre potuit? Itanè Deus in fœdus suum recepit, quem fatali odio prosequatur? Proinde istud odium nihil notat aliud, quam præteritionem Esavi, dum à Deo fuit postpositus Iacobo. Similiter loquitur scriptura, Luc. 14. v. 26. cap. 16. v. 13. Genes. 29. v. 31. Matth. 6. v. 24. cap. 10. v. 37. Psal. 78. v. 67. 68. Prov. 13. v. 24. III. Non intelliguntur personæ, sed tota posteritas, quia 1. Gen. 25. v. 29. dicitur. Duæ gentes sunt in vtero tuo, Maior serviet minori. Familiare enim est Hebræis propria nomina stirpium, pro patronymicis vsurpare. Israel, id est, Israelitæ: sic Esau odio habui, i. e. Esauitas. 2. Gen. 27. v. 29. idem indicatur: Serviant tibi populi, & adorent te tribus. 3. Idem notant verba Malach. cap. 1. vers. 2. & seqq. 4. Nunquam legimus, Esavum in sua persona seruiisse Iacobo, sed posteri Esau seruierunt Iacobæis, postquam David vniuersam Idumæam subegit, & ijdem sub rege Ioram iugum illud excusserunt. 2. Reg. 8. v. 22 quod prædictum fuit, Gen. 27. v. 40. Hæ autem gentes non fuerunt absolutè reprobatæ, vel damnatæ, siquidem Idumæos vocatos esse ad regnum Dei, constat ex Ejai. 11. v. 14. Amos 9, 11. & 12. Marc. 3. v. 7. & 8. Summatim igitur loquendo introducitur Iacob ac Esau τυπικῶς, non παραδειγματικῶς, vt typus, non exemplum, ille electionis, hic reiectionis. Et scopus Pauli hic est: sicut ius primogenituræ & benedictio non proueniebant ex carnali natiuiuatis prærogatiuâ, quippe eius ratione pares erant, sed à voluntate Dei: Ita & vos Iudæi non potestis probare, vos esse electum Dei populum, etiamfi quoad carnem à sancto Patre Abrahamo dedaris. Paulus ergo in verbis istis primò non agit de reiectione, sed tantùm removet falsam causam electionis, quæ erant externa opera. Versatur enim in solutione obiectionis Iudaicæ à natiuitate: omnia ergò quæ hic dicuntur, ad eum tendunt scopum, vt ostendat Apostolus, carnalẽ natiuitatem eos nihil iuuare, quod typo hoc illustrare voluit. Perlegatur totus versus 11. & 12. atque apparebit scopus sententię Paulinæ, quòd duntaxat voluerit è numero causarum exclusa externa opera.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: XLIII. Second: God as a potter makes some vessels for honor, some for dishonor. Therefore, an absolute decree is given

XLIII. SECOND: God as a potter makes some vessels for honor, some for dishonor. Therefore, an absolute decree is given.

Response. God himself does not create or make vessels of wrath, nor does he prepare them. 1. Because God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good, Gen. 1. v. 3. 2. Because in Adam he created all in his own image. 3. He sent his Son to all. 4. He is supremely good. 5. He does not prepare, but finds them prepared. 6. But he tolerates them with great patience.

The word καταρτίζειν is often used for to join together, to repair, to adapt, to restore, as Matt. 4. v. 21, ch. 21. v. 16, Mark 1. v. 19, 2 Cor. 3. v. 11, Gal. 6. v. 1, Heb. 10. v. 5, ch. 13. 21, 1 Pet. 5. v. 10. It is taken from physicians, who call it καταρτισμὸν, when dislocated joints are composed and return to their natural junction and position. But vessels of wrath are joined together by the Devil and their own will, as the whole scripture testifies.

Then it could be answered: By denying the consequence. For it does not follow, The potter is the maker of the pot which is a vessel of dishonor. Therefore, God also makes man, as he is a vessel of wrath: since things which are similar in one respect are not immediately similar in all. They are compared 1. by reason of power. 2. By reason of the making in itself. 3. That the thing made ought not to ἀνταποκρίνεσθαι. If it is extended more broadly, then one errs, because of the arguments recited above.

XXIV. And these were the principal objections of the Calvinists, from the solution of which the rest can easily be dispelled. To these some add the authority of Luther, who in his book on the enslaved will seems similarly to establish an absolute decree. But Luther sufficiently explained himself in his commentary on chapter 26 of Genesis. He speaks sometimes of absolute right, what God can do not ordered, what He wills. And he opposes his entire disputation to the Pelagians, who assert free will: while he attacks this, he seems to ascribe all things to necessity and an absolute decree: but in other places he has declared his mind sufficiently clearly.

XLV. In place of a colophon for the explanation of our thesis, and for the dispelling of calumnies, it should be noted in what sense it was asserted by our side in the Colloquy of Montbéliard that unbelief alone condemns, not other sins. Our opinion is founded on that passage in John 3, v. 18: 'He who believes in him is not condemned; but he who does not believe is condemned already.' John 16, v. 9: 'The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in me.' Here the λόγος ἄμεσος (immediate reason) of condemnation is established as unbelief alone. Do other sins, therefore, not bring about the guilt of condemnation?

We answer that condemnation can be considered in two ways. 1. Formally in itself, as it is the sense of divine wrath and the most severe punishment. 2. Materially or by reason of the degrees, which in that condemnation will be unequal. For some will suffer more severe torments than others. We say, therefore, that the cause of condemnation, considered formally, is unbelief alone. But the degrees of punishments will be adjudged according to the quantity of sins, as they were either more severe or lighter.

Then the cause of condemnation can be considered either by reason of merit and guilt, or by reason of the judgment itself and its execution. Regarding merit, all sins condemn and are worthy of eternal death. Regarding the judgment and the execution, only unbelief condemns. For men will be consigned to the flames of hell for this reason, because they did not grasp with firm faith the merit of Christ, by which satisfaction was made for all their sins. Thus Judas will be condemned primarily, not because he betrayed Christ, but because he despaired, and did not apply to himself the passion of Christ, by which his betrayal was expiated. Meanwhile, we do not deny that Judas will suffer a greater punishment than others in hell, on account of the deformity of his crime and the nefarious betrayal of his Master.

XLVI. But we do not wish for more, since what has been said thus far suffices. Therefore, we fix our foot here, and we sing a hymn of glory to God the Father, who loved us from the heart; to God the Son, who redeemed those he loved; to God the Holy Spirit, who daily calls and regenerates the redeemed. O how much we owe for these benefits to the most holy and glorious Trinity! He gave not only being through creation: but after we perished in Adam, he gave well-being through love. No one is excluded here; the door is open to all who repent and believe. Therefore let there be praise, and blessing, and honor for such a gift. May the same most merciful Father grant that what has been begun in us may be perfected, that we may firmly believe, live piously, and in his own time bring back the end of faith, the salvation of souls, with all the elect, and thus that which we see here through a glass in a dark manner, we may know there clearly, adoring the Lamb who redeemed us all, celebrating God who predestined us out of grace, and singing with a full voice forever, from Apoc. 4, verse 8: Holy, Holy, Holy, Lord GOD Almighty, who was, and who is, and who is to come. May it so happen, good Jesus! May it so happen, on account of the most full and most holy merit of your passion. AMEN.

Latin:

XLIII. SECVNDA: Deus tanquam figulus facit quædam vasa in honorem, quædam in contumeliam, Datur ergo decretum absolutum.

Respon. Deus ipse non creat vel facit vasa iræ nec præparat. 1. Quia vidit Deus cuncta quæ fecerat, & erant valdè bona, Gen. 1. v. 3. 2. Quia in Adamo omnes creauit ad imaginem suam. 3. Omnibus misit filium. 4. Est summè bonus. 5. Non pręparat, sed pręparata inuenit. 6. Sed tolerat magnâ patientiâ.

Verbum καταρτίζειν sæpè vsurpatur pro coagmentare, refarcire, adaptare, instaurare, vt Matth. 4. v. 21. cap. 21. v. 16. Marc. 1. v. 19. 2; Cor. 3. v. 11. Gal. 6. v. 1. Hebr. 10. v. 5. c. 13. 21. Petr. 5. v. 10. Sumtum est à Medicis, qui καταρτισμὸν vocant, cùm luxari artus componendo redeunt ad naturalem iuncturam & positionem. Coagmentantur autẽ vasa iræ à Diabolo & propria voluntate, vt tota testatur scriptura.

Deindè responderi posset: Negãdo consequentiam. Non enim sequitur, Figulus est factor ollæ quâ est vas dedecoris. E. Deus hominem quoque facit, quâ est vas iræ: siquidem quæ similia sunt in vno, non statim sunt similia in omnibus. Conferuntur 1. ratione potestatis. 2. Ratione facturæ in se 3. q factura non debeat ἀνταποκρίνεσθαι. Latiùs si extendatur, tum erratur, ob argumẽta superius recitata.

XXIV. Et hæ fuerunt præcipuæ Calvinianorum obiectiones, ex quarum solutione & cætera facilè dispelli possunt. Istis nonnulli adiungunt authoritatem Lutheri, qui in l. de servo arbit. similiter decretum absolutum videtur statuere. Sed Lutherus semetipsum satis exposuit, in comment. super c. 26. Gen. Loquitur quandoque de iure absoluto, quid possit Deus non ordinato, quid velit. Et opponit totam suam disputationem Pelagianis, liberum arbitrium asserentibus: quod dum impugnat, videtur omnia necessitati & absoluto decreto ascribere: sed alijs in locis luculenter satis mentem suam declaravit.

XLV. Colophonis loco pro explicatione theseos nostræ, & pro dispulsione calumniarum notari debet, quo sensu in Colloq. Mompelg. à nostris assertum fuerit, solam incredulitatem damnare, non cætera peccata. Opinio nostra fundatur in illo Ioh. 3. v. 18. Qui credit in eum, non condemnatux. Qui autem non credit, iam condemnatus est. Ioh. 16. v. 9. Spiritus S. arguet mundum de peccato, quia non credunt in me. Hic λόγος ἄμεσος condemnationis statuitur sola incredulitas. Num E. cætera peccata reatum damnationis non inferunt?

Respondemus, damnationem posse considerari dupliciter. 1. Formaliter in se, prout est sensus iræ divinæ, & supplicium gravissimum. 2. Materialiter vel ratione graduum, qui in damnatione ista erunt inæquales. Graviora enim tormenta quidam patientur, quàm alij. Dicimus ergo causam damnationis formaliter consideratæ, solam esse incredulitatem. Gradus v. pœnarum adiudicabuntur secundum peccatorum quantitatem, prout illa fuerunt vel graviora, vel leuiora.

Deinde causa damnationis considerari potest, vel ratione meriti & reatus, vel ratione ipsius iudicij & executionis. Quoad meritum, omnia peccata damnant, & digna sunt æterna morte, Quoad ipsum iudicium & executionem, sola incredulitas damnat.
