Ideo enim homines flammis inferni addicentur, quia meritum Christi, quo pro peccatis ipsorum omnibus satis factum est, firma fide non apprehenderunt. Sic Iudas primò damnabitur, non quia Christum prodidit, sed quia desperauit, & Christi passionem, qua proditio eius expiata est, sibi non applicuit. Interim non diffitemur, Iudam maiorem prae alijs poenam in inferno passurum esse, ob deformitatem delicti, & nefandam Magistri sui proditionem,

XLVI. Sed nolumus plura, cùm sufficiant hactenus dicta Pedem ergò hic figimus, & hymnum glòriæ cantamus Deo patri, qui nos ex animo dilexit; Deo Filio, qui dilectos redemit : Deo Spiritui sancto, qui redemptos quotidiè vocat & regenerat. O quantum ob hæc beneficia debemus sacrosanctæ & gloriosæ Trinitati! Non tantum dedit esse per creationem: sed postquam in Adamo perijmus, dedit benè esse per dilectionem. Nemo hic excluditur; patet ianua omnibus resipiscentibus & credentibus. Laus igitur sit, & benedictio, & honos pro tanto munere. Faxit idem clementissimus Pater, vt quod cœptum est in nobis, perficiatur, vt firmiter credamus, piè vivamus, & suo tempore finem fidei, salutem animarum, cùm omnibus electis reportemus, adeóque quod hic videmus per speculum in ænigmate, ibi cognoscamus clarè, adorantes Agnum, qui nos omnes redemit, celebrantes Deum qui ex gratia prędestinauit & canentes plenâ voce in æternum, ex Apoc. 4. versu 8. Sanctus Sanctus Sanctus Dominus DEVS omnipotens qui erat, & qui est, & qui venturus est. Ita eueniat bone Iesu! Ita eveniat, ob meritũ tuę passionis plenissimum & sanctissimum. AMEN.


### Single Question whether the decree of eternal reprobation is absolute: The End of the Second Decade

THE END OF THE SECOND DECADE.

Latin:

FINIS DECADIS SECVNDÆ.


## 23 Preface to the Third Decade

MOST ILLUSTRIOUS COUNT AND Palatine, most clement Lord.

Augustine wrote most truly in his book On Original Sin, ch. 24: In the case of two men, through one of whom we were sold under sin, and through the other we are redeemed from sins, our faith properly consists. This sentence is taken from the Apostolic aphorism in Rom. 5, v. 19, which is as it were a certain compendium of the entire Christian faith, and it reads thus: As by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. He through whom we are made sinners is Adam; he through whom we are made righteous is Christ. From the former we draw the disease, from the latter we receive the remedy for the disease. Through the former, Nature is infected: through the latter, it is repaired by grace.

Preface.

Both are necessary to be known and well considered, both that vice of Nature, and that benefit of Grace. For in both cases the human mind, surrounded by various errors, is an impediment to itself for a saving conversion to God. There have been and are those who extenuate the vice of Nature, and thus do not acknowledge the benefit of Grace. For the patrons of nature become enemies of grace. By which means both free will, which is nevertheless asserted to be a slave in spiritual matters, and the righteousness of works, which is imperfect and insufficient, are established. Thus, indeed, it happens that if the corruption introduced through the first Adam is either denied or diminished, immediately true righteousness, acquired through Christ, the second Adam, is impugned. For as much as is ascribed to the powers of the will, so much is detracted from the merit of Christ. Let us therefore acknowledge the corruption of Nature, and let us rightly estimate the magnitude of Grace. Our powers are nothing in spiritual matters, even by the testimony of conscience itself: It is God alone who works in us, that we may will the good, and that we may be able to do what we will. Therefore our merits are nothing: No one perfectly observes the law, but every saint calls upon God for the remission of sins. Wherefore we are not justified by works, but by grace. We are righteous, not through the infusion of new

Preface.

qualities; but through the imputation of the obedience of Christ. He bore our infirmities, and by his stripes we are healed alone. All of which things are placed in such light that he who hears and reads the scripture can have no cause for doubting. And yet in the midst of the Church are found those who pertinaciously cherish and bitterly defend most grave errors concerning both articles. They wish to be called Catholics, and meanwhile they attack the Catholic faith. They wish to be seen as the gatekeepers of heaven, and nevertheless they either are ignorant themselves of the true way of arriving there, or refuse to acknowledge it when shown. I mean the Romanists, and especially their champions, the Jesuits. Who, although they may swell with the opinion of knowledge and truth, yet deceive and are miserably deceived. They do not succeed the Apostles, but the Pharisees, because they exaggerate the powers of nature, and everywhere inculcate the righteousness of works. This is evident from the leader of that sect, formerly a Father among them, now Cardinal Bellarmine: Who indeed in the last volume of his controversies seems to have aimed solely at this, that through the extenuation of sin and the assertion of free will, he might persuade the Christian people of an inherent and Philosophical righteousness, drawn from scholastic pits, and thus reintroduce that ancient butchery of consciences. To obtain which purpose, he scraped together various arguments from here and there, which at first appear specious, but when lightly touched, vanish into ashes and embers. Since, therefore, the controversy concerning sin, grace, and predestination having been concluded, there followed, according to the order of Bellarmine, whose thread it was proposed to follow, two most serious articles, concerning free will and justification before God; I wished to undertake an accurate analysis of them, and to propose them, comprised in theses, to the studious youth for disputation, so that they might maturely imbibe the truth of the faith and learn to avoid the precipices of errors. It was indeed my intention, when I finished the second decade, to remove my hand from the begun tablet henceforth, and to devote myself solely to the ordinary labors of my profession; however, my highest patrons, whom I ought to obey, and friends, whom I ought to gratify, wished that I should weave through the web once begun, and continue this Anthropological College. I did, therefore, what I was ordered to do, and included in ten disputations what I had to say concerning the will, free in moral matters, enslaved in spiritual matters, and concerning the true method of justification. So that this treatment might be complete, not so

Preface.

when I considered the Papist controversies, but I have also opposed some things from the most harmful sect of the Photinians. Indeed, I have often wished that it were permitted to wrap these things in silence rather than to expound upon them at such length. For is it not horrible to hear, and to be deplored with many tears, that matters in the Church, in such a great light of truth, have come to this point, that the most holy merit of Christ our only Redeemer, that merit indeed by which satisfaction was made for the sins of the whole world, the merit in whose confidence many thousands of Christians have fallen asleep, that I say that merit is not only diminished, but utterly impugned, and with more than giant-like audacity is completely denied? How often would Polycarp have exclaimed, if he had reached this age: O God, for what times have you reserved us! But these things must be deplored, they cannot be changed. Wherefore, one must stand against Satan, the Father of lies, lest the unwary be deceived and hold as solid and firm those things which are destitute of strength and are easily dissolved.

As for the controversy that remains in the state of restoration, concerning the distinction between the Law and the Gospel, and concerning good works, since it can scarcely constitute a separate Decade, I shall propose it either by public disputation or by some other method, so that in this way the Anthropological dissertations,

Preface.

be concluded here, and meet their end. This third and final Decade, most Illustrious Count and Palatine, most Clement Lord, I offer inscribed and most humbly dedicated to Your Highness. I shall not bring forward reasons at length, lest I seem to doubt anything regarding Your Clemency. Known to the Christian world, and especially to the kingdom of Hungary, is the singular zeal of Your Highness in asserting and propagating true piety toward God and the purity of the γνησίως Catholic religion. Who, therefore, would not readily offer to such a Hero, and defender of the faith, that which is written for the orthodox faith? The holy Cherubim covered with their wings the Ark of the Old Testament, placed in the innermost atrium of the temple. The Ark of Christ is the Church, which pious Princes protect, like heavenly Cherubim. That Your Highness has long since done this, and still does, the little flock of the Lord humbly acknowledges. You are truly a Cherub of the Hungarian Church, placed on the holy mountain, and protecting the shattered little ark. Who would not pray for the best things for such a Foster-father of the Church, and vow for him everlasting happiness? Added to this is the supreme clemency in that pinnacle of honor, which Your Highness has made manifest by frequent letters, and whose image daily

Preface.

Today it is permitted for me to discern, in the most illustrious and magnificent Count, Lord EMERIC THURZO of Bethlemfalva, Count of Arva, and hereditary Count of that same county, the only son of your Highness, the most magnificent Rector of this Academy, my clement and most benign Lord. In him, as if in a most clear mirror, I behold a living image of paternal virtue and heroic spirit, so that I cannot doubt the clemency of the most illustrious Parent, when I see it so clearly expressed in the illustrious Son. This Academy congratulates itself, not undeservedly, on such an illustrious and magnificent Guest, or rather Head, in whose breast, born and raised for any high purpose, both zeal for religion, sincere piety, and other heroic virtues have long since chosen a stable seat for themselves. May they live, I pray, may this most illustrious Pair live, Parent and Son, for the benefit of the struggling Church, for the patronage of oppressed truth, and for the far greatest increase of the whole Hungarian Kingdom. Thus I pray and vow most often, which same affection, as a sign of my humility and due gratitude, I wished to express in this public προσφωνήσει [address], asking most humbly that your most illustrious Highness most clemently receive this meager little work, and me, although undeserving

Preface

tem, may he not disdain to continue to pursue with his accustomed clemency. GOD, who defends the holy Cherubim, the defenders of his Church, may he preserve your most illustrious Highness with your entire magnificent Family, flourishing for a very long time, so that they may be confounded and put to shame together, who rejoice in evils: but let them exult and be glad, who seek justice, and let them say always: Let the LORD be magnified, who blesses his servant. Let it be done in the name of JESUS CHRIST, the Best and Greatest Protector; Let it be, Let it be! Given at Wittenberg, on the Sunday of Clemency, which is the 22nd after Trinity, in the year of the θεογονία 1615,

Most humbly honoring your most illustrious Highness

BALTHASAR MEISNERUS Doctor of Theology and Public Professor

Latin:

ILLVSTRISSIME COMES AC Palatine, Domine clementissime.

VErissimè scripsit Augustinus lib: de peccato originis c. 24. In causa duorum hominum, quorum per unum venundati sumus sub peccato, per alterum redimimur à peccatis, fides nostra propriè consistit. Desum ta est hæc sententia ex aphorismo Apostolico Rom. 5. v: 19. qui vniuersæ fidei Christianæ quasi compendiũ quoddam est, & sic habet: Sicut per inobediẽtiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita & per unius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi. Per quẽ verò peccatores cõstituimur, Adamus est; per quem iusti efficimur, Christus est. Ab illo haurimus morbum, ab hoc accipimus morbi remedium. Per illum infecta est Natura: per hunc reparata est gratia.

Præfatio.

Vtrumq; scitu necessarium & probè considerandum est, tùm illud Naturæ vitium, tùm istud Gratiæ beneficium. Nam vtrobiq; mens humana variis erroribus circumsepta, sibi ipsi impedimentum sit salutaris ad Deum conuersionis. Fuerunt & sunt, qui Naturæ vitium extenuant, atque ita beneficium Gratiæ non agnoscunt. Patroni enim naturæ, fiunt inimici gratiæ. Quo pacto tùm liberum arbitrium, quod tamen in spiritualibus servum, asseritur: tùm iustitia operum, quæ imperfecta & insufficiens, stabilitur. Ita nempè fit, vt si corruptio per primum Adamum invecta, vel negetur vel eleuetur: protinus vera iustitia, per Christum, Adamum alterum acquisita, impugnetur. Quantum enim arbitrii viribus adscribitur, tantum Christi merito detrahitur. Agnoscamus ergò corruptionem Naturæ, rectè æstimemus magnitudinem Gratiæ. Nullæ sunt vires nostræ in spiritualibus, vel ipsâ teste conscientiâ: Solus Deus est, qui operatur in nobis, vt bonum velimus, & quod volumus, facere valeamus. Nulla ergò sunt merita nostra: Nemo perfectè legem obseruat, sed pro remissione peccatorum omnis sanctus Deum inuocat. Quare ex operibus non iustificamur, sed ex gratia. Iusti sumus, non per infusionem nouarum

Praefatio.

qualitatum; sed per imputationem obedientiae Christi. Hic tulit languores nostros, & ipsius liuore sanati sumus vnicè. Quae omnia in tanta luce sunt posita, vt qui scripturam audit legitquè, nullam dubitandi caussam habere possit. Et tamen in media Ecclesia reperiuntur, qui errores circa vtrumque articulum grauissimos pertinaciter fouent, & acriter defendunt. Nuncupari volunt Catholici, & interim Catholicam fidem oppugnant. Videri volunt Ianitores coeli, & nihilominus veram eò perueniendi viam vel ignorant ipsi, vel monstratam nolunt agnoscere. Romanenses intelligo, & illorum praecipuè προμάχους Iesuwitas. Qui licèt turgeant opinione scientiae & veritatis, fallunt tamen & falluntur miserè. Non Apostolis, sed Pharisaeis succedunt, quia vires naturae exaggerant, & iustitiam operum nullibi non inculcant. Patet hoc ex sectae illius primipilo, quondam apud ipsos Patre, nunc Cardinale Bellarmino: Qui sanè in vltimo controuersiarum tomo ad id vnicè videtur collimâsse, vt per peccati extenuationem & liberi arbitrii assertionem, iustitiam inhaerentem & Philosophicam, è lacunis scholasticis haustam, populo Christiano persuaderet, atque sic antiquam conscientiarum carpificinam rursus inveheret. Pro quo instituto obtinendo varia hinc indè corrasit argumenta, quæ primùm apparent speciosa, sed leuiter tacta, in cineres abeunt & fauillas. Cùm ergò absolutâ controuersiâ de peccato, gratiâ & prædestinatione, sequerentur quoad ordinem Bellarmini, cuius filum sequi erat propositum, grauissimi duo articuli, de Liberi arbitrio, & de Iustificatione coram Deo; accuratam illorum anésin suscipere, thesibusq́; comprehensam ad disputandum studiosæ iuventuti proponere volui, vt veritatem fidei maturè imbiberent, & errorum præcipitia cauere discerent. Erat quidem mihi constitutum, cùm Decadem secundam finirem, imposterum amouere manum de cœpta tabula, & ordinariis meę professionis laboribus vnicè incumbere; Voluerunt tamen Patroni mei summi, quibus obtēperare, & Amici, quibus gratificari debeo; vt telam semel inchoatam pertexerem, & Collegium istud Anthropologicum continuarem. Feci ergò, quod facere iussus sum, decemque disputationibus inclusi, quæ de arbitrio in moralibus libero, in spiritualibus seruo, & de vera iustificandi ratione dicenda habui. Quæ tractatio vt completa esset, non tan-

Praefatio.

cum controuersias Papisticas spectaui, sed nonnulla insuper nocentissimae sectae Photinianorum opposui. Equidem optaui saepius, vt silentio ista liceret magis involuere, quàm prolixius exponere. Annon enim auditu horrendum, multis lachrymis deplorandum, rem eò devenisse in Ecclesia, in tanto veritatis lumine, vt Christi Redemptoris nostri vnici sanctissimum meritum, illud nempè meritum, quo pro peccatis totius mundi satisfactum, meritum, cuius fiducia multa Christianorum millia obdormiuerunt, vt illud inquam meritum, non minuatur tantùm, sed prorsus impugnetur, & plus quàm giganteâ audaciâ penitus negetur? Quoties exclamaret Polycarpus, si hoc seculum attigisset: O Deus, in quae tempora nos reseruâsti! Sed deplorari haec debent, mutari non possunt. Quare obviandum est Satanae, Patri mendaciorum, nè incauti decipiantur & pro solidis firmisquè habeantur, quae robore destituta & solutu sunt facilia.

Quae autem in statu reparationis restat controuersia, de discrimine legis & Evangelij, deque bonis operibus, illam, cum peculiarem Decadem vix constituere possit, vel disputatione publicâ, vel aliâ ratione proponam, vt ità dissertationes Anthropologicae,

Præfatio.

hîc concludantur, & finem suum sortiantur. Hanc verò Decadem tertiam vltimamq́; Illustrissime Comes ac Palatine, Domine Clementissime, Celsitudini Vestræ inscriptam humilimèq́ue dicatam offero. Caussas prolixè non adducam, nè de Vestra Clementia quicquam dubitare videar. Nota est orbi Christiano, & cum primis regno Hungariæ singularis Vestrę Celsitud. Zelus in vera pietate erga Deum ac puritate religionis γνησίως Catholicæ asserenda & propaganda. Quis igitur tanto Heroi, fideiq́; defensori, prõptus nõ offerret, quod pro fide orthodoxâ scriptum est? Arcam V. T. in intimo templi atrio repositam, alis suis tegebant sancti Cherubim. Arca Christi est Ecclesia, quam protegunt pii Principes, veluti cœlestes Che rubim. Hoc Celsitudinem Vestram iamdudum fecisse, & etiamnùm facere, humiliter agnoscit pusillus grex Domini. Verè Cherub es Ecclesiæ Hungaricæ, positus in sancto monte, & protegens quassatam arculam. Quis non tanto Ecclesiæ Nutritio precaretur optima, & perennem voueret felicitatem? Accedit summa in isto honoris fastigio clementia, quam Celsitudo Vestra crebris literis testatam fecit, & cuius Icona quoti-

Præfatio.

diè mihi cernere licet, in Perillustri & Magnifico Comite, Domino EMERICO THVRZO de Bethlemffalvva, Comite de Arvva, eiusq́; Comitatus perpetuo Comite , Celsitudinis vestræ filio vnico , Academiæ huius Rectore admodum Magnifico , Domino meo Clementi & perbenigno. In illo, veluti Clarisfimo speculo, paternæ virtutis & heroici animi viuam Ideam conspicor , vt de Parentis Illustrissimi Clementia nequeam dubitare, cum eam in Filio Illustri tàm luculenter expressam videam. Gratulator sibi non immeritò hæc Academia de Hospite, ìmò potius de Capite tàm Illustri & Magnifico, in cuius pectore ad quæuis alta nato & erecto , tùm Religionis Zelus, tùm sincera pietas aliæque virtutes heroicæ iamdudùm sedem sibi stabilem elegerunt. Viuat, opto , viuat hoc Par Illustrissimum, Parens & Filius, in laborantis Ecclesiæ commodum, in pressæ veritatis patrocinium , & totius Regni Hungarici incrementum longè maximum. Ita precor voueóque sæpius , quem ipsum affectum in humilitatis meæ & gratitudinis debitæ signum , hâc publicâ προσφωνήσει exprimere volui , rogans humillimè , vt Illustrissima Celsitudo vestra opusculum hoc exile, Clementissimè suscipere, & me, licèt immeren-

Præfatio

tem, solitâ clementiâ porrò profequi non dedignetur. DEVS, qui sanctos Cherubim, Ecclesiæ suæ defensores defendit, illustrissimam Celsitudinem Vestram cum Magnifica Familia vniuersa, diutissimè florentem conseruet, vt confundantur & erubescant simul, qui gaudent malis: exultent vero & lætentur, qui quærunt iustitiam, & dicant semper: Magnificetur DOMINVS, qui seruo suo benedicit. Fiat in nomine IESV CHRISTI, Protectoris Optimi Maximique; Fiat, Fiat! Dabam Wittebergæ, Dominicâ Clementiæ, Regiæ quæ est XXII post Trinitatis, Anno θεογονίας M, DC. XV,

Illustrissimam Celsitudinem Vestram humilimè colens

BALTHASAR MEISNERVS Th. D. & Prof. Pub.


## 24 Disputation I. On the Nature of Free Will and Its Powers in Civil Actions

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Aegidius Conradus Gualtperius of Marburg, Hessian.

Προοίμιον. I.

Having explained the sublime doctrine of our predestination, there follows the controversy concerning Free Will, which must be treated the more diligently the more weight is placed upon it. For if an error is made here, many articles collapse at once, and the very foundation of salvation, and the primary head concerning the gratuitous remission of sins, is torn away. For whatever is assigned to free will in the conversion of man, this is detracted from divine grace, according to that saying of the ancients: The patrons of nature are the enemies of grace. Looking to which, Augustine says in book 2 of On Original Sin, chapter 24: Grace, he says, is not grace in any way if it is not given freely in every way. To such an extent can grace and nature not stand together; that if we are justified by grace, nothing is to be attributed to the powers of nature, and conversely.

Grace and free will do not agree well, nor do they dwell in one seat: far, oh far away, be the followers of Pelagius. II. Our Luther knew this very well and often inculcated it, who, discussing Free Will in assertion 36, left it written thus: In other articles concerning the Papacy, Councils, indulgences, and other unnecessary trifles, the levity and folly of the Pope and his followers must be endured: but in this article, which is the best of all, and IS THE SUM OF OUR AFFAIRS; one must grieve and weep that the wretched are so insane. Since, therefore, in Luther's judgment the sum of our faith rests upon this head of doctrine, a more accurate consideration of it is not undeservedly to be instituted. While we are about to do this, we humbly invoke God, that He who by His prevenient grace has stirred up a good will, may by His subsequent mercy work in us the ability, so that we may be able to perform the good that we will, to the glory of the divine name, and to the well-pleasing and singular increase of the Church.

III. But that we may delineate the method of the future treatment in a few words, we shall have to deal chiefly with four heads. 1. Concerning the terms. 2. Concerning the nature of free will in general. 3. Concerning the liberty which is granted in civil actions. 4. Concerning the defect and nullity of liberty in spiritual matters or the conversion of man, which, since it is the principal theme, will come to be treated both κατασκευασικῶς (constructively) and ἀνασκευασικῶς (destructively). We shall deal with the first three heads in this disputation: where the following questions come to be resolved.

I. What is denoted by the terms free will?

II. Did Luther rightly call the will a slave?

III. Are Free and Slave rightly opposed?

IV. What distinctions of liberty commonly occur?

V. What is free will?

VI. Is the intellect radically free?

VII. Does the will in the use of its liberty depend upon the practical intellect, and is it determined by it to one side or the other through the final judgment?

VIII. What kind of liberty is required, so that something may be called free?

IX. What is the subject of liberty?

X. What is the object of liberty?

XI. Whether man is free, and what powers of will he possesses?

XII. What kind of liberty is granted regarding civil and moral actions?

XIII. What are the impediments to liberty?

XIV. What should be thought concerning the good works of the Gentiles?

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Aegidio Conrado Gualtperio Marpurg. Hasso.

Προοίμιον. I.

EXplicatâ sublimi praedestinationis nostrae doctrinâ, sequitur controuersia de Libero Arbitrio, quae tractanda est eò diligētius; quò plus illa in momēti positum. Hîc enim si erratum fuerit, multi vnà corruunt articuli, & ipsum salutis fundamentum, caputque primarium de gratuita remissione peccatorum, conuellitur. Nam quicquid in conuersione hominis libero arbitrio adsignatur, hoc diuinae gratiae detrahitur, iuxta illud veterum: Patroni naturae sunt inimici gratiae. Quò respiciens Augustinus lib. 2. de peccat. origin. cap. 24. Gratia, inquit, non est gratia vllo modo, si non gratis datur omni modo. Vsque adeò simul stare haud possunt gratia & natura; vt si iustificamur ex gratia, viribus naturae nihil tribuendum sit, & contrà.

Non benè conueniunt, nec in vnâ sede morantur Gratia & arbitrium: procul ô procul este Pelagi. II. Optimè hoc nouit & sæpius inculcauit Lutherus noster, qui de Libero Arbitrio disserens assert. 36. ita scriptum reliquit: In cæteris articulis de Papatu, de Concilijs, de indulgentijs, alijsque non necessarijs nugis ferenda est leuitas & stultitia Papæ & suorum: sed in hoc articulo, qui omnium optimus, & RERVM NOSTRARVM SVMMA EST; dolendum & flendum est, miseros sic insanire. Cùm igitur Lutheri iudicio summa nostræ fidei recumbat in hoc doctrinæ capite, non immeritò accuratior eius consideratio instituenda est. Quod dum facturi sumus, Deum humiliter inuocamus, vt qui gratiâ præueniente excitauit bonam voluntatem, misericordiâ subsequente operetur in nobis facultatem, vt quod volumus bonum, facere valeamus ad nominis diuini gloriam, & Ecclesiæ beneplacitum ac singulare incrementum.

III. Vt autem futuræ tractationis methodum paucis delineemus, de quatuor præcipuè capitibus agendum erit. 1. De vocabulis. 2. De natura liberi arbitrij in genere. 3. De Libertate, quæ in ciuilibus actionibus datur. 4. De libertatis defectu & nullitate in spiritualibus vel conuersione hominis, quod cùm sit thema præcipuum, tùm κατασκευασικῶς, tùm ἀνασκευασικῶς pertractandum veniet. De tribus primis capitibus hâc disputatione agemus: vbi Quæstiones sequentes enodandæ veniunt.

I. Quid per voces liberi arbitrij notetur?

II. An Lutherus arbitrium rectè appellauerit seruum?

III. An Liberum & Seruum rectè opponantur?

IV. Quæ libertatis distinctiones vulgò occurrant?

V. Quid sit liberum arbitrium?

VI. An intellectus radicaliter sit liber?

VII. An voluntas in vsu suæ libertatis dependeat ab intellectu practico, & ab eo in alteram partem per vltimum iudicium determinetur?

VIII. Qualis requiratur libertas, vt aliquid appelletur liberum?

IX. Quodnam libertatis subiectum sit?

X. Quodnam sit obiectum libertatis?

XI. An homo sit liber, & quas arbitrij vires habeat?

XII. Qualis detur libertas circa ciuiles & morales actiones?

XIII. Quæ sint impedimenta libertatis?

XIV. Quid de operibus bonis gentilium sentiendum sit?


### Question I

What is denoted by the terms free will?

IV. This title is more ecclesiastical than biblical, for those terms are not found joined together in the Scriptures. Only the name of will is read in Numbers 30, verse 14, which elsewhere is circumscribed by the word for choosing, Deuteronomy 30, verse 19, Joshua 24, verse 15, and is named ἐξουσία περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος, the power of the will, 1 Corinthians 7, verse 37, by which nothing else is understood than an election free both from necessity and from law or obligation.

V. These terms, however, derive their origin from Platonic philosophy, as Philippus notes in his Hypotyposis Theologica. For when the Stoics established a fatal necessity for all actions, the Platonists opposed them and extolled the liberty of the will too much. And since some of the Fathers were addicted to Platonic philosophy before their conversion, it happened that after their conversion they often retained philosophical terms and accommodated them to the dogmas of the faith, among which was also the title of free will, understood at first in a right sense concerning liberty in civil matters, but later wrongly accepted by Pelagius and badly twisted to assert liberty in spiritual matters. For which reason Philip wrote most truly in his book. Just as in these later times of the Church we have embraced Aristotle instead of Christ: so immediately after the beginnings of the Church the Christian doctrine was undermined by Platonic philosophy.

VI. Because, however, the use of a thing or a name ought not to be entirely abolished immediately on account of abuse, for that reason the Doctors of the Church, even after the Pelagian controversy, retained the term 'free will' as a customary term in the schools, though not always in the same sense, but in a different one. And indeed five acceptations in particular occur in the writings of the Fathers and Theologians, to review which individually will not be a waste of effort.

VII. 1. By free will is sometimes understood the mind and will itself, which are faculties of the rational soul, of which the former performs its duty by knowing and judging, the latter by choosing and rejecting. Augustine accepted it in this sense when he wrote in book 3 of the Hypognosticon: 'There is, therefore, free will, which whoever denies to exist is not a Catholic.'

IIX. 2. Sometimes by free will is denoted ἱκανότης or passive power, since the mind and will of man can be turned by the ordinary grace of God to receive the most holy gifts. For man is not a log or a stone, which cannot be turned; but some ἱκανότης is given, by which he cannot indeed turn himself, yet he can be turned by God, and therefore it is called a power not active, but passive; by which nothing else is implied than that man is not entirely incapable of conversion, if only he uses the means and does not place an obstacle before God. And the Fathers very often looked to this when they attributed free will to man in conversion.

IX. 3. This title is more often accepted not as a faculty which freely holds itself toward both opposites, good and evil, but only for that internal principle or inclination by which the will is led in desiring. And in this sense free will is attributed to the will, although it wills and desires nothing but evils. To this pertains that statement of Augustine, book 1 against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, chapter 2, volume 7: Free will has not so perished in the sinner that all who sin with delight do not sin through it, and by the love of sin that which pleases them is what they desire. And in the same place: This will, which is free in evils because it delights in evils, is therefore not free in goods because it has not been set free. Bernard writes similar things in his tract on grace and free will, where he says these words: Let no one think that free will is so called because it is exercised with equal power or faculty between good and evil, etc. And a little later: Now, therefore, it is called free will rather because it makes the will equally free whether in good or in evil, since no one ought to be called, nor can he be, either good or evil, unless he is willing.

X. 4. Nor is this acceptation infrequent, by which is understood through free will that power in the will of man by which he can choose either evil or good in external and civil matters, or even not choose the same good already chosen, but prefer and desire another which seemed better. We by no means deny this will to man after the fall, since he has been deprived of the soundness of the will, but not of the will itself, or of all manner of liberty.

XI. Finally 5. by free will some mean a certain power in man by which he can prepare himself for the grace of God, turn himself to God himself, and perform similar spiritual acts: such a will as the Pelagians established, but which the orthodox have always impugned: to which pertains that statement of Augustine, chapter 30 of the Enchiridion: Man, using free will badly, both lost himself and it. For when one sinned by free will, with sin as the victor, free will was also lost: for by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also enslaved.

XII. And these are the principal [meanings] of that term signified; which we can briefly combine thus: Free will either denotes a passive ἱκανότητα, or an active faculty. This in turn denotes either the powers of the will, or the will itself. If the powers, it is understood either as liberty in civil matters, or liberty in spiritual matters. If the will, then it denotes either its restricted inclination toward evil, or the faculty of choosing either opposite indifferently, which last acceptations are especially regarded in this disputation, when the nature of will in general is being disputed.

XIII. Furthermore, since there are two distinct terms by which that free faculty of choosing is expressed, the ancients noted that different faculties are referred to by them. For they say that the word 'will' [arbitrium] pertains to the mind, but 'free' [liberum] to the will, since it is the mind's role to arbitrate and judge, but the will's role to freely choose or reject what has been judged. And to this must be referred that statement of Augustine, lib. 3. Hypogno. t. 7: 'I think that will [arbitrium] received its name from arbitrating by rational consideration, or discerning what it chooses or what it refuses, or it is called free will because it is placed in its own power, having the possibility of doing what it wishes, which is a vital and rational motion of the soul.' Lombard expressed this more distinctly, l. 2. sentent. dist. 24. lit. E. It is called, he says, free, with regard to the will, which can be bent to either side: but will [arbitrium] with regard to reason; whose faculty or power that is, whose role it also is to discern between good and evil. We therefore retain this different respect of the terms, to indicate the distinct acts in free choice, although we are not ignorant that, if the discourse is about the thing itself, by free will is understood not the intellect and will together, but rather the will alone, as will become clear from what follows.

XIV. From what has been said, it is furthermore clear why it is called free will rather than free judgment. The cause they especially bring forward from the distinction between judges and arbitrators, the latter of whom are much freer than the former, since judges are bound to follow the laws, otherwise an appeal can be made from them: but arbitrators are unbound and free, and they pass sentence as they wish, nor is an appeal given from them: and therefore the free choice of the will is more correctly called arbitration than free judgment.

XV. By way of a colophon, let it be noted that the Greeks, in expressing the freedom of the will, use an overly arrogant term. For they say αυ̉τεξύσιον, α̉υτεξυσία, α̉υτεξυσιότης: which words signify τὸ α̉υτεδέσποτον, which is subject to no one's command, can be prohibited or hindered by no one, which is of its own proper power and right, such liberty as properly falls only to God, since no one can resist His will and power alone. Therefore, ἐκύσιον should rather be attributed to men, following the example of Scripture in the Epistle to Philemon, verse 14, Hebrews 10:26, 1 Peter 5:2, not α̉υτεξύσιον, a term which Justin and Damascenus used in book 2, de O. F. c. 25. For the latter joins three terms as synonyms: 1. α̉υτεξύσιον, 2. ἐλεύθερα προαίρεσις, 3. τὸ ἐφ̓ ήμι̃ν. Of which Damascenus was accustomed to use the first and the third.

Latin:

Quid per voces liberi arbitrij notetur?

IV. Titulus hic magis est Ecclesiasticus, quàm Biblicus, Neque enim voces illæ coniunctim reperiuntur in Scripturis. Solum arbitrij nomen legitur Numer. 30 vers. 14. quod alibi circumscribitur vocabulo eligendi, Deut. 30. v. 19. Ios. 24. v. 15. & nominatur ἐξουσία περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος, potestas voluntatis, 1. Cor. 7. v. 37. per quam nil aliud intelligitur quàm Electio libera tum à necessitate, tum à iure vel obligatione.

V. Trahunt autem ista vocabula ortum ex Philosophia Platonica, notante Philippo in Hypotypof. Theolog. Cùm enim Stoici fatalem omnium actionum necessitatem statuerent, Platonici sese opposuerunt, & libertatem arbitrij nimis extulerunt. Cùmque Patrum nonnulli ante conuersionem Platonicæ Philosophiæ addicti fuerint, inde factum vt post conuersionem terminos Philosophicos sæpe retinerent, & ad dogmata fidei accommodarent, inter quos etiam fuit titulus liberi arbitrij, primùm sensu dextro intellectus de libertate in ciuilibus, sed pòst à Pelagio sinistrè acceptus, & ad asserendam libertatem in spiritualibus malè detortus. Qua de caussa verissimè scripsit Philippus l. d. Porindè atque his posterioribus Ecclesiæ temporibus Aristotelem pro Christo sumus amplexi: itastatim post Ecclesiæ auspicia per Platonicam Philosophiam Christiana doctrina labefactata est.

VI. Quia tamen propter abusum non statim vel rei vel nominis vsus planè abrogari debet, propterea Doctores Ecclesiæ post certamen etiam Pelagianum, vocem Liberi arbitrij vt consuetum in scholis terminum retinuerunt, sensu tamen non semper eodem, sed diuerso. Et quidem acceptiones potissimum quinque in Patrum & Theologorum scriptis occurrunt, quas recensere singulas, non erit operæ dispendium.

VII. 1. Per liberum arbitrium nonnunquam intelligitur ipsa mens & voluntas, quæ sunt facultates animæ rationalis, quarum illa cognoscendo & iudicando, hæc eligendo & repudiando suum expedit officium. Hoc sensu accepit Augustinns, cùm l. 3, Hypogn. scripsit. Est igitur Liberum arbitrium, quod quisquis esse negauerit, Catholicus non est.

IIX. 2. Aliquando per Liberum arbitrium notatur ἱκανότης vel potentia passiua, quoniam mens & voluntas hominis per ordinariam Dei gratiam ad accipienda SS. dona conuerti potest. Nec enim homo vel truncus, vel lapis est, qui conuerti nequeat; sed datur aliqua ἱκανότης, quâ non quidem seipsum conuertere, à Deo tamen conuerti potest, ideoque potentia vocatur non actiua, sed passiua; quâ nihil aliud innuitur, quàm hominem conuersionis non esse prorsus incapacem, si modò medijs vtatur, nec Deo ponat obicem. Et huc sæpissimè respexerunt Patres, quando liberum in conuersione arbitrium homini attribuerunt.

IX. 3. Sæpius accipitur iste titulus non de facultate, quæ ad vtrumque oppositorum, bonum & malum, liberè se habeat, sed tantùm pro interno principio seu inclinatione ista, quâ voluntas in appetendo ducitur. Et hoc sensu liberum arbitrium voluntati tribuitur, quamuis nil nisi mala velit & appetat. Huc pertinet istud Augustini lib. 1. contra duas Epistolas Pelagij, cap. 2. t. 7. Liberum arbitrium vsque adeò in peccatore non perijt, vt per illud peccent maximè omnes, qui cum delectatione peccant, & amore peccati hoc eis placet, quod eis libet. Et ibidem: Hæc voluntas quæ libera est in malis, quia delectatur malis, ideò libera in bonis non est, quia liberata non est. Similia scribit Bernardus tract. de gratia & lib. arbit. vbi hæc verba: Nemo putet ideò dictum liberum arbitrium, quòd æquâ inter bonum & malum potestate aut facultate versetur, &c. Et paulò pòst: Nunc igitur potiùs ex eo liberum arbitrium dicitur, quòd siue in bono siue in malo, æquè liberam facit voluntatem, cùm nec bonus quispiam, nec item malus dici debeat aut esse valeat, nisi volens.

X. 4. Nec infrequens est hæc acceptio, quâ per liberum arbitrium intelligitur ista in voluntate hominis potentia, quâ in externis & ciuilibus rebus potest eligere vel malum vel bonum, vel etiam idem bonum iam non eligere, sed aliud, quod videbatur melius, præferre & appetere. Hoc arbitrium minimè denegamus homini post lapsum, quippe qui voluntatis sanitate, non autem ipsâ voluntate, vel omnimodâ libertate priuatus est.

XI. Tandem 5. per liberum arbitrium nonnulli volunt intellectum vim quandam in homine, quâ se possit ad gratiam Dei præparare, ad ipsum Deum conuertere, & similes actus spirituales edere: quale arbitrium Pelagiani statuerunt, sed orthodoxi semper impugnârunt: quò spectat illud Augustini capit. 30. Enchirid. Libero arbitrio malè vtens homo, & se perdidit, & ipsum. Cùm enim Libero peccaretur arbitrio, victore peccato amissum est & liberum arbitrium: à quo enim quis deuictus est, huic & seruus addictus est.

XII. Atque hæc sunt præcipua termini istius significatas; quæ breuiter ita combinare possumus: Liberum arbitrium vel notat ἱκανότητα passiuam, vel facultatem actiuam. Hæc vicissim aut vires voluntatis notat, aut ipsam voluntatem. Si vires, vel intelligitur libertas in ciuilibus, vel libertas in spiritualibus. Si voluntas, tum notatur aut eius restricta ad malum inclinatio, aut indifferens vtrumque oppositum eligendi facultas, quæ postremæ acceptiones in hæc potissimum disputatione spectantur, cùm de natura arbitrij in genere disputatur.

XIII. Porrò, cùm duo sint distincta vocabula, quibus illa eligendi facultas libera effertur, ad diuerfas per ea facultates respici veteres annotarunt. Arbitrij enim vocem dicunt ad mentem pertinere, Liberi verò ad voluntatem, quippe cùm mentis sit arbitrari & iudicare, voluntatis autem iudicata liberè vel eligere, vel reijcere. Atque huc referendum est illud Augustini lib. 3. Hypogno. t. 7. Arbitrium ab arbitrando rationali consideratione, vel discernendo, quid eligat quidue recuset, puto quòd nomen accepit, vel ideò liberum arbitrium dictum, quòd in sua positum sit potestate, habens agendi quod velit possibilitatem, quod est vitalis & rationalis animæ motus. Distinctius hoc expressit Lombardus l. 2. sentent. dist. 24. lit. E. Dicitur, ait, liberum, quantum ad voluntatem, quæ ad vtrumlibet flecti potest: arbitrium vero quantum ad rationem; cuius est facultas vel potentia illa, cuius etiam est discernere inter bonum & malum. Hunc igitur diuersum vocabulorum respectum retinemus, ad indicandos in electione libera distinctos actus, quamuis non ignoremus, si de re ipsa sermo sit, per liberum arbitrium non intellectum & voluntatem junctim sed solam potius voluntatem intelligi, vt ex sequentibus elucescet.

XIV. Ex dictis insuper patet, cur potius liberum arbitrium, quàm liberum judicium dicatur. Causam imprimis afferunt ex discrimine inter iudices & arbitros, quorum hi multò sunt liberiores quàm illi, siquidem iudices tenentur sequi leges, alias ab ijsappellari potest: Arbitri vero soluti sunt & liberi, feruntque sententiam prout volunt, nec ab cis datur appellatio: ac proinde libera voluntatis electio rectiùs arbitrium, quàm iudicium liberum nuncupatur.

XV. Colophonis loco notetur istud, quòd Graeci in exprimenda voluntatis libertate, nimis arroganti vocabulo vtantur. Dicunt enim αυ̉τεξύσιον, α̉υτεξυσία, α̉υτεξυσιότης: quæ vocabula significant τὸ α̉υτεδέσποτον, quod nullius imperio subest, à nemine prohiberi vel impediri potest, quòd suæ ipsius propriæque potestatis & iuris est, qualis libertas in solum Deum propriè cadit, quippe cuius vnius voluntati ac potestati nemo resistere potest. Proinde hominibus tribui potiùs debet ἐκύ- σιον exemplo Scripturæ in Epist. ad Philem. verf. 14. Hebr 10. 26. 1. Pet. 5 v. 2 non α̉υτεξύσιον quo tamen termino vsus est Iustinus & Damascenus lib. 2. de O. F. c. 25. Ille enim tria vocabula tanquam Synonyma coniungit, 1. α̉υτεξύσιον, 2. ἐλεύθερα προαίρεσις. 3. τὸ ἐφ̓ ήμι̃ν. Ex quibus primum & tertium Damascenus vsurpare consueuit.


### Question II. Whether Luther rightly calls the will 'servile'?

XVI. There are two hemispheres of things, according to Luther: the one lower, of civil matters; and the other higher, of spiritual matters. In the former, we do not maintain that the will is entirely enslaved, but we assert the contrary in Article 18 of the Augsburg Confession. But in the latter, since we have no strength, as will be proven in the following disputation, why should it not deservedly be called enslaved? We therefore briefly explain that free will is considered either in respect of its ἰσία or essence, insofar as it denotes the will as free in acting, or in respect of its ἐνεργεία or powers, which are estimated either with regard to civil actions or spiritual ones, that is, our conversion. We concede that the will is free both in respect of its ἰσία and in respect of its ἐνεργεία or powers in civil matters; but it is truly a slave, and is most rightly called a slave, with respect to conversion, since man can neither prepare himself for it by his own powers, nor efficiently concur in it.

XVII. The Papists therefore revile Luther without any cause on account of the change of name, who ought to remember that this name is partly founded in the Scriptures, and partly that Augustine long before Luther had already attributed the same appellation to the will. In the Scriptures it rests upon the saying of Christ in John 8, verse 34: 'Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin,' and of the Apostle in Romans 6, verse 20: 'When you were slaves of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.' Augustine, however, expressly writes in his book On Correction and Grace, chapter 13: 'Free will is free, but not freed; free from righteousness, a slave to sin.' In book 3 against the two epistles of the Pelagians, chapter 8: 'Free will, having been captivated, is of no avail except for sinning.' In Sermon 13 on the words of the Apostle: 'For doing evil you have a free will without the help of God, although it is not free; for by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also bound as a slave; and everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.' Book 2 against Julian: 'You wish man to be perfected, and would that it were by the gift of God, and not by free, or rather, slave will of his own volition.' In the Enchiridion, chapter 106: 'After that ruin, the mercy of God is greater, since free will itself must be freed from slavery.' To this also pertains that statement of Bernard, Sermon 81 on the Song of Songs: 'The soul under this voluntary and evil free necessity is held both as a handmaid and as free: a handmaid on account of necessity, free on account of the will.' From which

It is sufficiently apparent that the notable lie of Bellarmine in book 4, chapter 6, of On Free Choice, writing that the name of 'enslaved choice' had never been heard in the Catholic Church for a full fifteen hundred years, is a lie. Let it be noted finally that Bellarmine contradicts himself, while in book 6, chapter 15, he confesses that the freedom of choice is BOUND: but what is bound is nothing other than enslaved.

Latin:

XVI. Duo dantur rerum hemisphæria, iuxta Lutherum, Alterum inferius, rerum ciuilium: & alterum superius rerum spiritualium. In illo prorsus seruum esse arbitrium non statuimus, sed contrarium art. 18. A. C. afferimus. In hoc autem cum nullæ sint vires nostræ vt seq. disput. probabitur, cur non meritò seruum appelletur, Breuiter proinde nos explicamus, quod liberum arbitrium consideretur vel ratione ἰσίας seu essentiæ, prout notat voluntatem in agendo liberam, vel ratione ἐνεργείας seu virium, quæ vel respectu actionum ciuilium, vel spiritualium seu conuersionis nostræ æstimantur. Concedimus arbitrium esse liberum tum ratione ἰσίας, tum ratione ἐνεργείας vel virium in ciuilibus: seruum verò est & seruum optimo iure nuncupatur respectu conuersionis, quippe ad quam homo suis viribus neque se præparare, neque efficienter concurrere potest.

XVII. Lutherum igitur ob nominis mutationem sine omni caussa sugillant Papicolæ, qui recordari deberent, partim nomen istud in Scripturis fundari, partim Augustinum iam olim antè Lutherum eandem arbitrio appellationem tribuisse. In Scripturis innititur dicto Christi Iohan. 8. vers. 34. Qui facit peccatum, peccati seruus est, & Apostoli Rom. 6 vers. 20. Cùm serui essetis peccati, liberi fuistis iustitiæ; Augustinus verò expressè scribit lib. de corrept. & grat. cap. 13. Liberum arbitrium liberum est, sed non liberatum, liberum iustitiæ, seruum peccati, lib. 3. contra duas epistol. Pelagij cap. 8. liberum arbitrium captiuatum non nisi ad peccandum valet. Serm. 13. de verbis Apostoli; Ad malè agendum habes sine adiutorio DEI liberam voluntatem quanquam non est illa libera: A quo enim quis deuictus est, huic & seruus addictus est: & omnis qui facit peccatum, seruus est peccati. Lib. 2. cont. Iulian, Vultis hominem perfici, atque vtinam Dei d.no, & non libero, vel potiùs seruo propriæ voluntatis arbitrio. In Enchirid. c. 106. Post istam ruinam maior est miseri cordia Dei, quoniam & ipsum liberum arbitrium liberandum est à seruitute. Huc etiã spectat istud bernardi serm. 81. super Cantic. Anima sub hac voluntaria & malà libera necessitate & ancilla tenetur, & libera: ancilla propter necessitatem, libera propter voluntatem. Ex quib.

satis apparet insigne mendacium Bellarmini lib. 4. de lib. arb. capit. 6. scribentis, Nomen serui arbitrij in Ecclesia Catholica totos mille quingentos annos nunquam fuisse auditum. Notetur denique, Bellarminum sibiipsi contradicere, dum l. 6. c. 15. fatetur libertatem arbitrii esse LIGATAM: quod verò ligatum est, nil aliud quam servum est.


### Question III. Are free and servile truly opposed?

Are 'free' and 'enslaved' truly opposed?

XVIII. It seems that freedom can stand together with servitude. For the reborn are truly free, John 8:36. And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom, 2 Cor. 3:17. And yet with this freedom is joined servitude, which is evident from Rom. 6:18, where it is said: 'Having been set free from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness.' And Rom. 7:25: 'With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin.' Thus angels and the blessed serve God, and yet they perform all things freely. Why, therefore, did Luther hold these to be opposites, and instead of 'free,' say 'enslaved' choice?

XIX. We answer briefly that an ambiguity lies in the term 'slave' and 'servitude.' For it denotes 1. Right and obligation, in which sense the reborn are slaves of righteousness, that is, they are bound to live piously and justly. 2. Duty and ministry, which is performed for the Lord. And in this respect the angels serve God, and we are servants of God. 3. The captivity of the will and the total inability in spiritual matters, on account of which man serves sin only, nor can he turn himself to God by his own powers. For the sake of memory, we can call the first servitude that of right and obligation, the second of ministry, the third of sin.

XX. With this distinction presupposed, it will not be difficult to answer the objection. For we say that freedom consists well with the first two species of servitude, but not with the last. For the regenerate act freely in what they owe; and the angels, who serve, simultaneously perform their own tasks freely: but he who is a slave of sin, and whose will is thoroughly corrupted, he is not simultaneously free regarding spiritual acts. There is therefore an exact opposition between the freedom of the will and servitude, if by the latter an inability to act is understood. Since Luther attended to this sense, he rightly called the will not free, but enslaved.

Latin:

An liberum & servum verè opponantur?

XIIX. Videtur, quòd libertas simul stare possit cum seruitute. Nam renati sunt verè liberi, Ioh. 8. v. 36. Et vbi Spiritus Domini ibi libertas, 2. Cor. 3. v. 17. Et tamen cum hac libertate coniuncta est servitus, quod patet ex Rom. 6. v. 18. vbi dicitur: Liberati à peccato, serui facti estis iustitiae. Et Rom. 7, vers. 25. Mente seruio legi Dei, carne autem legi peccati. Sic angeli & beati Deo seruiunt, & tamen omnia liberè expediunt. Cur ergò Lutherus ista pro oppositis habuit, & loco liberi, arbitrium servum dixit?

XIX. Respondemus breuiter, quòd in vocabulo Servi & Servitutis lateat æquiuocatio. Notat enim 1. Ius & debitum, quo sensu renati servi sunt iustitiæ, hoc est, tenentur piè & iustè viuere. 2. Officium & ministerium, quod præstatur Domino. Et hoc respectu Angeli Dei seruiunt, nos que Dei servi sumus. 3. Captivationem voluntatis & summam in spiritualibus ἀδυναμίαν, ob quam homo seruit peccato tantùm, neque potest ex propriis viribus ad Deum se conuertere. Primam seruitutem memoriæ causâ nuncupare possumus iuris & debiti, secundam ministerij, tertiam peccati.

XX. Quâ distinctione præsuppositâ, non erit difficile ad objectionem respondere. Dicimus enim, quòd libertas cum primis duabus seruitu tis speciebus benè consistat, sed non cum ultima. Nam renati, quod debent, liberè agunt; & Angeli, qui seruiunt, simul liberè sua expediunt: Qui autem seruus est peccati, & cuius voluntas penitùs corrupta, is non simul liber est quoad actus spirituales. Exacta igitur oppositio est inter arbitrij libertatem & seruitutem, si per hanc agendi ἀδυναμία intelligatur. Quem sensum cùm Lutherus attenderit, rectè arbitrium non liberum, sed seruum nuncupauit.


### Question IV. What distinctions of liberty are commonly encountered?

XXI. Augustine complains everywhere of the remarkable difficulty that is wont to delay one discussing free will, Epist. 46 to Valentinus: he calls this question most difficult and intelligible to few. In his book On the Grace of Christ, chapter 47, he writes that the question is so difficult to discuss, when free will and grace are disputed, that when free will is defended, the grace of God seems to be denied: but when the grace of God is asserted, free will is thought to be taken away. Among other causes of the difficulty, not the least is the variety and ambiguity of the terms that occur in this doctrine, by which this article is very often obscured rather than explained. And indeed we would wish that it were permitted to us to use only the words of Scripture in true simplicity: yet the writings both of the Fathers and of our adversaries make it so that we cannot be occupied in the reading of the former, nor engage with the latter, unless we have acquired for ourselves some foreknowledge of the terms which they are accustomed to use, even if they are sometimes barbaric. Therefore, the principal distinctions of liberty, which are nothing other than different we shall touch upon the terms in a few words.

XXII. The first distinction. Freedom is threefold: one of nature, by which someone is free from coercion and violence, and in certain cases also from necessity, to which the passage of the Apostle refers, 1 Cor. 7, verse 37: He who stands firm in his heart, having no necessity, but having power over his own will. The second is the freedom of grace, through which someone is free from the slavery of sin, concerning which speech is made in Rom. chap. 6, verse 18: Having been set free from sin, you have become slaves of righteousness. The third is the freedom of glory, by which we shall be free from the misery of this life, and from every sense of sin, to which some refer that Pauline passage Rom. 8, verse 21: Then the creation itself also will be set free from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of GOD. This distinction is taken from the threefold state of man, namely: 1. Of sin. 2. Of renewal. 3. Of blessedness. For in the state of the fall, only the freedom of nature is granted: in the state of renewal, the freedom of grace is acquired: in the state of blessedness, the freedom of glory will be given. In the first we are more slaves than free: in the second we are set free: in the third we shall be most free. Indeed, the distinction is that posited by Lombard, who writes in book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 25, letter I: there is a threefold freedom, namely from necessity, from sin, from misery. He wished to call the first the freedom of nature, the second of grace, the third of glory. We, however, in the present disputation speak primarily of the freedom of nature, since it is common to both good and bad and is implanted by nature. The remaining freedoms do not pertain to free will absolutely, but to one considered in a certain state, and they are not so much freedoms of the will as of the whole man.

XXIII. The second distinction. There are others who recount not three, but rather five species of freedom. For there is given: 1. Freedom from coercion and violence, by which the violent impulse of an external principle and impediments opposing the will are removed. 2. Freedom from necessity, by which the will is not necessarily and intrinsically determined to choose one, nor does it even necessarily execute one,

3. Liberty from right or obligation, by which someone is released from laws, so that he may be ἀνυπεύθυνος & ἀνεξέταστος, which liberty is called by another name license, concerning which Paul 1 Cor. 6 verse 12, All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. But properly no creature is free from obligation, because all are subject to God, and especially man, who is bound to the divine law in all things. 4. Liberty from sin, when the flesh has been subdued and subjected to the Spirit, so that it can no longer rule, and man may serve righteousness rather than sin. 5. Liberty from misery, which Adam could in a certain way enjoy before the fall, but which Angels and the Blessed enjoy fully after the fall in heaven. But the last three distinctions of liberty do not enter into the state of our question, since we are not concerned with license, nor with the liberty of grace or glory, but with the powers of the will after the fall. However, the first two species, which pertain to the liberty of nature and belong to this place, must be explained a little more fully.

XXIV. That is therefore properly called liberty from coercion, when the will is indeed determined to choose one thing, yet it is not compelled, nor violently snatched by an external motion, but embraces or rejects something of its own accord or by an internal principle of motion. Thus God necessarily wills the good, yet at the same time freely, since He is not compelled to choose the good. Thus all things which we will, although we will them necessarily, we nevertheless will them freely, if you understand liberty from coercion, because our will cannot be compelled in acting. Some call this internal liberty, by which the will of man is moved ἑκουσίως, freely, spontaneously, without coercion, by a native power, through προαίρεσιν, and has an internal, not an external or violent, principle of its own motion.

XXV. Liberty from necessity, however, is that by which the will is not necessarily determined to one immutable act, but can at its own discretion will and not will, when it not only acts spontaneously, but so freely that, all things required for acting being posited, it can refrain from acting: Thus we are free regarding the external pursuit of virtue and the flight from pleasure, since we can choose either one, and we do not necessarily embrace either virtue or pleasure.

XXVI. These species of liberty differ primarily in two ways: 1. By reason of the subject. For liberty from coercion is common to man with beasts, since they do many things spontaneously, not under coercion. But liberty from necessity is common to man with God and the angels, since they act not only spontaneously, but furthermore freely, which does not apply to beasts. 2. By the mode of acting. For the will, insofar as it is free from coercion, is called a natural agent; insofar as it is free from necessity, it is then called a free agent in a special sense. Hence, actions that occur through liberty from coercion are named in general voluntary or spontaneous; but those that occur through liberty from necessity are named specifically free actions.

XXVII. Third distinction. Liberty of contrariety or of specification: another is of contradiction or of exercise. The Papists speak barbarously, yet so that we may understand them, these terms must be explained. Liberty of contrariety is when the will is not determined to a certain species, namely either to only good or to only evil, but can either choose or reject either one; it can will one and not will the other, and to will and not to will are contraries, whence it is called liberty of contrariety. Thus, with many means occurring, I have the liberty of contrariety, of selecting one from all these, whichever may please. Liberty of contradiction is concerned with the very exercise of the act, when someone with a single object proposed, one can act and not act, or will and not will. Now these two acts, to will and not to will, are contradictorily opposed, and therefore liberty itself is called liberty of contradiction. For example, when virtue and vice are proposed, and a conclusion is made in the choice: I will virtue; I do not will vice, then this is called liberty of contrariety: But when a single object is proposed which I can choose and not choose, will and not will, then it is accustomed to be named by the Scholastics liberty of contradiction. Both liberties are joined in Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14: GOD from the beginning created man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel: he added his commandments and precepts: If you will keep the commandments, they will preserve you: I have set before you water and fire, to which you will, stretch forth your hand. Before man is life and death, good and evil: that which shall please him, shall be given to him. Here an example of both liberties is had: For to keep and not to keep the precepts pertains to the liberty of contradiction; but to choose good or evil, water or fire, life or death, pertains to the liberty of contrariety.

XXIIX. And these have been the principal distinctions of liberty which the Romanists use in this matter, and for the sake of memory they can be combined thus: Liberty is either of nature, or of grace, or of glory; The liberty of nature is either from coaction, or from necessity. This in turn is either of contrariety, that is, regarding the species of the act; or of contradiction, that is, regarding the exercise of the act.

Latin:

XXI. Augustinus passim conqueritur de insigni difficultate quæ disserente de libero arbitrio retardare soleat, Epist. 46. ad Valentia: quæstionem hanc vocat difficillimam & paucis intelligibilem. L. de gratia Christi, cap. 47 scribit, Ita difficilem esse quæstionem ad dissernendum, vbi de libero arbitrio & gratia dissputatur, vt quando defenditur liberum arbitrium, negari DEI gratia videatur: Quando autem asseritur DEI gratia, liberum arbitrium putetur auferri. Inter cæteras verò difficultatis causas non postrema est terminorum, qui in hac doctrina occurrunt, varietas & ambiguitas, quibus sæpissimè hic articulus magis obscuratur, quàm explicatur. Et sanè optaremus, vt in vera simplicitate solis Scripturæ verbis vti nobis liceret: faciunt tamen tum Patrum tum adversariorum scripta, vt nec in lectione illorum versari, nec cum aduersariis congredi valeamus, nisi terminorum quos adhibere solent, licet nonnunquam barbarorum, πρόγνωσιν aliquam nobis comparaverimus. Præcipuas igitur libertatis distinctiones, quæ nihil sunt aliud quàm diversi termini paucis attingemus.

XXII. Prima distinctio. Triplex est libertas: vna naturæ, quâ quis liber est à coactione & violentia, in quibusdam etiam casibus à necessitate, quò spectat locus Apostoli, 1. Cor. 7. versu. 37. Qui statuit in corde suo firmus, non habens necessitatem, potestatem autem habens suæ voluntatis. Altera libertas gratiæ, per quam aliquis liber est à seruitute peccati, de qua sermo fit Rom. cap. 6. versu. 18. Liberati à peccato, serui facti estis iustitiæ. Tertia est libertas gloriæ, quâ liberi erimus à miseria huius vitæ, & ab omni sensu peccati, quò referunt nonnulli istud Paulinum Rom. 8. vers. 21. Tunc & ipsa creatura liberabitur à seruitute corruptionis in libertatem gloriæ filiorum DEI. Distinctio hæc petita est ex triplici statu hominis, nimirum. 1. Peccati. 2. Renouationis. 3. Beatitudinis. In statu enim lapsus non nisi libertas naturæ conceditur: In statu renouationis libertas gratiæ acquiritur: in statu beatitudinis libertas gloriæ donabitur. In primo magis servi sumus, quàm liberi: in secundo liberati: in tertio erimus liberrimi. Est verò distinctio posita Lombardi, qui l. 2. sentent. distinct. 25. lit. I. scribit: est libertas triplex, scilicet à necessitate, à peccato, à miseria. Primam naturæ, secundam gratiæ, tertiam gloriæ libertatem appellare voluit. Nos autem imprimis de libertate naturæ, quippe quæ tota bonis malisque communis & à natura insita est, in præsenti disputatione loquimur. Reliquæ libertates non pertinent ad liberum arbitrium absolutè sed in certo statu consideratum, nec tàm sunt libertates voluntatis, quàm totius hominis.

XXIII. Secunda distinctio. Sunt alij, qui non tres, sed potiùs quinque libertatis species recensent. Datur enim. 1. Libertas à coactione & violentia, quâ violentus externi principij impulsus & aduersantia voluntati impedimenta remouentur. 2. libertas à necessitate, quâ voluntas non necessariò & intrinsecè ad vnũ eligendum determinatur, nec etiā necessariò vnũ exequitur,

3. Libertas à iure vel obligatione, quâ quis legibus est solutus, vt sit ἀνυπεύθυνος & ἀνεξέταστος, quę libertas alio nomine vocatur licentia, de qua Paulus 1. Cor. 6. vers. 12. Omnia mihi licent, sed non omnia expediunt, Propriè verò nulla creatura ab obligatione est libera, quia omnes Deo subiectæ sunt, & in primis homo, qui ad legem diuinam in omnibus adstrictus est, 4. Libertas à peccato, quando subacta est earo & subiecta Spiritui, vt ipsa ampliùs dominari nequeat, & homo iustitiæ potiùs, quàm peccato seruiat. 5. Libertas à miseria, quâ quodammodò gaudere potuit Adam ante lapsum, plenariè verò gaudent post lapsum in cœlis Angeli & Beati. Verum vltimæ tres libertatis distinctiones nostrum quæstionis statum non ingrediuntur, quippè qui non de licentia, non de libertate gratiæ aut gloriæ, sed de viribus arbitrij post lapsum sumus solliciti. Duæ autem primæ species, quæ ad libertatem naturæ spectant, & huius loci sunt, paulò pleniùs explicandæ veniunt.

XXIV. Illa ergò propriè vocatur libertas à coactione, quando voluntas quidem ad vnum eligendum est determinata, non tamen cogitur, nec violenter externo motu rapitur, sed sponte suâ seu interno motus principio aliquid amplectitur vel rejicit Sic Deus necessariò vult bonum, simul tamen liberè, quoniam ad eligendum bonum non cogitur. Sic omnia quæ volumus, licet necessariò velimus, liberè tamen volumus, si libertatem à coactione intelligas, quia nostra voluntas cogi haut potest in agendo. Nonnulli vocant hanc libertatem interiorem, quâ voluntas hominis ἑκουσίως, liberè, sponte sine coactione, vi natiuâ, per προαίρεσιν mouetur, suique motus internum, non externum aut violentum habet principium.

XXV. Libertas verò à necessitate est, quâ voluntas non necessariò determinatur ad vnum actu immutabile, sed pro arbitrio potest velle & nolle, quando non solùm spontè agit, sed ita liberè, vt positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, possit non agere: Ita liberi sumus quoad externum studium virtutis & fugam voluptatis, siquidem alterutrum eligere possumus, neque necessariò vel virtutem vel voluptatem amplectimur.

XXVI. Istæ verò libertatis species dupliciter inprimis differunt, 1. Ratione subiecti. Libertas enim à coactione, homini communis est cum bestiis, quippe quæ multa spontè agunt, non coactè. Libertas verò à necessitate, homini communis est cum Deo & Angelis, quippe qui non tantùm spontè, sed insuper liberè agunt, quod non cadit in bestias. 2. Modo agendi. Nam voluntas quatenus est libera á coactione, dicitur agens naturale, quatenus est libera à necessitate, tum speciali sensu vocatur agens liberum. Hinc actiones quæ fiunt per libertatem à coactione, nominantur in genere voluntariæ vel spontaneæ; quæ autem fiunt per libertatem à necessitate, nominantur in specie actiones liberæ.

XXVII. Tertia distinctio. Libertas contrarietatis vel specificationis: alia est contradictionis seu exercitij. Ita barbarè loquuntur Pontificii, quos tamen vt intelligamus, termini isti explicari debent. Libertas contrarietatis est, quando voluntas non est determinata ad certam speciem, nempe vel ad solum bonum, vel ad solum malum, sed alterum potest vel eligere vel reijcere, potest vnum velle, alterum nolle, velle autem & nolle sunt contraria, vnde libertas contrarietatis vocatur. Sic multis mediis occurrentibus, libertatem contrarietatis habeo, existis omnibus vnum seligendi, quodcunque placuerit. Libertas contradictionis in ipso actus exercitio versatur, quando quis obiecto vnico proposito, agere & nón ágere, vel le & non velle potest. Duo autem isti actus Velle, Non velle, sunt contradictoriè oppositi, ideoqué libertas ipsa, contradictionis libertas nuncupatur. Exempli causâ, quando virtus & vitium proponuntur, & in electione fit conclusio: Volo virtutem; nolo vitium, tum hæc libertas contrarietatis dicitur: Quando autem obiectum vnicum próponitur quod possum eligere & non eligere, velle & non velle, tum libertas contradictionis nominari à Scholasticis consuevit. Vtraque libertas coniungitur Eccles. 15. vers. 14: DEVS ab initio constitit tuit hominem, & reliquit illum in manu consilij sui: adiecit mandata & præcepta sua: Si volueris mandata servare, conservabunt te: Apposui tibi aquam & ignem, ad quod volueris, porrige manum tuam. Ante hominem vita & mors, bonum & malum: quod placuerit ei, dabitur illi. Hic exemplum habetur vtriusque libertatis: Nam servare & non servare præcepta, ad libertatem contradictionis pertinet; eligere verò bonum aut malum, aquam aut ignem, vitam aut mortem, ad libertatem contrarietatis.

XXIIX. Ethæ fuerunt præcipuæ libertatis distinctiones, quas in hac materia Romanenses vsurpant, & memoriæ causâ ita combinari possunt: Libertas vel est naturæ, vel gratiæ, vel gloriæ; Libertas naturæ vel est à coactione, vel à necessitate. Hæc vicissim vel contrarietatis est, seu quoad speciem actus; vel contradictionis, seu quoad exercitium actus.


### Question V. What is free will?

XXIX. However much this question may be more scholastic than purely theological, since nevertheless its decision brings some light into rightly forming the state of the controversy, we did not wish to omit it entirely. Therefore, one must philosophize a little while, and briefly examine what the οὐσία of free will is.

XXX. But it is beyond doubt that liberty belongs only to an intelligent nature, from which it immediately follows that it is either a certain act passing from the soul, or some power remaining in the soul. Herveus assumed the first in Quodlibet 1, question 1, but he is refuted by Bellarmine himself, book 3, on free will, chapter 8. For free will is implanted in man by nature, which is never taken away. But acts are not present by nature, but are produced by us; and they are sometimes present, sometimes absent, from which it would follow that men sometimes lack free will, because they would not always be operating. Furthermore, that act in which liberty is said to consist is either elicited by a certain free power, or it is not elicited. If you assume the first, then liberty precedes that act, which for that reason cannot contain the ὐσία of liberty in itself. If you say the second, that act will be necessary. How, therefore, will liberty consist in it?

XXXI. Having therefore denied that liberty is an act, it follows spontaneously that it is some power remaining in the soul: for there are three things that occur in the soul, passions, powers, and habits, book 2, Nicomachean Ethics, chapter 4. Three things are present in the soul: affections, powers, and habits. But it would be absurd to count free will among the affections, which often creep in against one's will and do not make one choose, but rather hinder the one choosing. In like manner, it cannot be a habit. For it is not a διόοδος, since all natural habits incline toward only one thing, either good or evil. Nor is it ἔμφυτος, since men do not become, but are born free. With the other species therefore removed, it follows that liberty is a πλάτει or a power.

XXXII. It is further asked, whether it is a universal or a particular power? Some call it universal, containing under itself all the powers of the sentient and intelligent soul, in that in all these acts are found to be free. But they are free, not as from themselves, but insofar as they proceed from the will, by which they are commanded. For if all δυνάμεις were free of themselves, there would be as many free wills as there are powers, than which nothing can be said to be more absurd.

XXXIII. Since therefore it is a particular δύναμις, it will either be distinct from the intellect and will, or otherwise: Alexander of Hales argues for the first in part 2 of his Summa, question 72, member 1, article 3, but without reason: For where there is no distinct act, there is no distinct power. But no act can be named that is different from the operation of the intellect and will and proper to this third power. For will it be the motion of the will? But this is the intellect, which moves through proposed objects. Or will it be the first willing, as I will to choose, to deliberate? But this is of the will, which generally moves both itself and other powers, and applies them to acting: as Scaliger says in Exercise 207, section 25.

XXXIV. Finally, therefore, liberty will reside either in the intellect alone, or in the will alone, or in both: It cannot be located in the intellect, since it is not free; but is entangled in a double yoke of necessity: 1. Regarding the species of acts: For by its own nature it is so determined that it assents to the true and dissents from the false, and it cannot, if it has been exactly proposed, not assent to the true. The will, however, although it is restricted regarding the genus to the good, nevertheless regarding the species of the good, even when accurately proposed, is indifferent, so that it can most freely either choose or reject it. For the object of the will is τὰγαθὸν, which consists in suitability: and since the same thing can now be suitable, now unsuitable, hence the will has indifference regarding its object, so that it may either choose or repudiate it as it pleases.

XXXV. II. Regarding the exercise. For no action is understood except from an appetite for the good, which invites one to act. Whence it follows that the intellect is also inclined toward understanding by the rational appetite or will. For reason does not apply itself to acting, but its action or the cessation of action is persuaded by the appetite of the whole subject, or the will of man. The intellect indeed leans toward understanding, but that it undertakes to understand this and not another thing, that and not this, is to be referred not to the intellect, but solely to the will of the subject. Hence it is established by some that the will, because of its command, blinds the intellect, both στερητικῶς or privatively, insofar as it turns it away from correct consideration and does not permit it to remain long in the dictate of truth: and θετικῶς or positively, insofar as the will, eliciting for itself an evil end, commands the intellect to find means tending toward the attainment of that evil end.

XXVI. But it is objected that the intellect itself is indifferent in its acts and in the objects proposed, and therefore free. But here philosophers distinguish between objective and formal indifference. The former consists in judging in various ways and proposing various objects; the latter consists in freely choosing or neglecting what is proposed. The former is proper to the intellect, the latter to the will. The former is called by some judicial liberty, the latter elective. But judicial liberty and the motion of the intellect are not the primary cause of elective liberty, of which there is talk here, since it is often absent and, when present, the will does not always assent. Indeed, speaking accurately, the intellect is not even entirely indifferent in its acts, because the will of the subject always precedes, without which the intellect does not gird itself either to judge or to propose.

XXXVII. Having therefore proven that the intellect is not formally free, it follows spontaneously that liberty does not reside in the intellect and will combined. Where then, finally, shall it be placed? To express the whole matter in a few words: in the will of man alone, since it is a free and indifferent power, so that it can act and not act, choose good or evil. It is free 1. regarding the specific object, because two contraries are proposed to it, virtue and vice, to neither of which is it determined, but it can follow either at its own discretion. 2. regarding the acts themselves. For it is permitted to the will to pursue virtue or otherwise, it is permitted to flee or follow vice, since it indulges in neither necessarily. Hence even Scripture itself attributes freedom only to the will, as Deut. 30. v 19. Choose, whichever you wish, death or life. 1. Cor. 7. v. 37. Having his own will in his power. Gregory of Nyssa agrees, book 7 de Phil. Damascene, book 2 de O. F. c. 25. Ambrose, book 2 de fide c. 3. Augustine, book de grat. & lib. arb. c. 2. book 5 de C. Dei cap. 9. & the Council of Orange, can. 13, which Fathers, in order to show that freedom resides in the will alone, are accustomed to say, The free choice of the will.

XXXIIX. Furthermore, it is asked, is the choice of the will one thing and the freedom of the will another? We deny that they differ in reality, since the will formally is nothing other than a power free in acting. And if freedom were distinguished from the will, then an accident would reside in an accident, which is absurd. But if it is said that free choice resides in the soul itself, then it will not be proper to the will, but some third power, separated from the intellect and the will, which is likewise absurd. However much freedom may not differ from the will, yet by the operations of our mind they are distinguished in such a way that we conceive of the will as a kind of σύνολον, but freedom as its form. For the will is to us as a certain composite, consisting of its material, and likewise its formal. The former is the power, the latter the freedom of the power, whence if both are coupled, the will will be nothing other than a free power, which is mistress of its own act: and it can both produce that act at its discretion, and not produce it. And hence it happens that they are also distinguished by words, and it is not said, liberty is the will, or the contrary: But, liberty is of the will, or in the will, and again, the will has liberty, or is endowed with liberty.

XXXIX. A single doubt remains, why the will is called free choice, when nevertheless to judge or to discern is an act of the intellect, not of the will? But we respond. That name is rightly attributed to the will by reason of its act. For choice, which is an act of the free will, is as it were a certain judgment, by which the will freely embraces one thing over another. In which sense we commonly say: It is in my choice to do or omit this, that is, in my power and election. Thus Livy writes, To give someone free choice of his own affairs, that is, to submit oneself and one's own things to someone's will and power. From which it is gathered that the name of choice is accepted among the Latins in two ways. 1. For an act of the intellect, where it is the same as judgment or counsel. 2. For an act of the will, and thus it is the same as election. In this latter respect the will is called choice, so that by the name of the free act the free faculty itself may be denoted.

XL. And thus far we have philosophized enough about the nature of liberty, from which, however, the phrases of theologians sometimes seem to differ. But the reconciliation is easy, if a single distinction is held. Free choice is considered, 1. Philosophically, with respect to συζυγίας, insofar as it denotes an internal and free principle of acting. Where certainly it can be nothing else than the will, since it alone is an indifferent power, and that internal and free principle of actions. 2. Theologically, by reason of its ένερ- γείας, where it is not so much estimated What it is, as what it can do, or what powers it obtains in acting.
