In this respect free choice is not the will itself, because this remains the same in every state of man as regards its essence, but free choice is varied, indeed so much so, that it is said to be null or lost in the state of the fall, The will, however, is by no means lost, whence it follows that free choice, taken theologically, differs much from the will. It is, moreover, nothing other than a certain power superadded to the will, and perfecting it, through which it is promptly inclined toward the good, and easily executes what it chooses. I call it a power and faculty, not an act; because man's free choice is not the free action itself, but the principle of acting. Whence it is proven that Pareus speaks less conveniently when, in book 3 of De gratia et libero arbitrio, chapter 7, page 437, he maintains with Hervaeus that free choice is placed in the act of reason and will.

XLI. The arguments, however, which he brings forward are of little moment. 1. He says that in children and those sleeping, free choice is not given, because they do not exercise the act of reason and will. Resp. The point is begged. For although they do not act freely, they nevertheless have free choice or the power of acting freely. There is therefore no consequence, just as it also does not follow: They do not reason. Therefore, they lack reason. 2. A third faculty would be given in the rational soul, distinct from reason and will. Resp. If liberty is considered by reason of itself alone, then it is the will itself, not a third faculty. If by reason of ἐνεργείας and good operation, neither then is a third faculty given, since that power is not a peculiar δύναμις, but a perfection of a δυνάμιος, namely of the will, granted divinely. For when free choice is renewed in the regenerate, a new faculty properly so called, such as reason and will, does not arrive, but rather a perfection of the faculties, or some gift perfecting the faculty. 3. Free choice is not lost, in so far as it is a power. Resp. If natural power or will is understood, I concede it: But if the power of performing theological good, and of keeping the commandments of the Lord, then certainly that power or faculty was lost through the fall.

XLII. From these things, therefore, it is sufficiently evident that free will, speaking accurately and formally, is not an act; meanwhile we concede that sometimes, abusively, the act itself is denoted by the name of will: just as the term for will is ambiguous, which sometimes signifies τὴν θέλησιν and sometimes τὴν θελητικὴν δύναμιν, as Damascenus notes in book 2, de O. E., chapter 22. This of their own will, because they lack free will, that is, the free operation or exercise of will. It remains nonetheless that this popular and abusive acceptance prejudices nothing regarding the nature of the thing and its proper signification, according to which will, taken philosophically and with respect to οὐσίας, is the will itself; but theologically and with respect to ἐνεργείας in spiritual matters, it is an inclination toward the good and a certain power of operating well and easily, perfecting the will, first concreated, lost through the fall, somewhat restored in the reborn, and clearly consummated in the blessed.

Latin:

XXIX. Quantumvis hæc quęstio magis sit scholastica, quàm purè Theologica, cùm tamen eius decisio aliquam lucem importet in controversia statu ritè formando, illam prorsus omittere uoluimus. Philosophandum ergò par lisper erit, & quæ liberi ὐσία sit, paucis dispiciendum.

XXX. Extra dubium verò est, Libertatem non nisi naturæ intelligenti conuenire, vnde statim sequitur, vel esse actum quendam ab anima transeuntem, vel vim quampiam in anima permanentem, Primum assumsit Heruæus quodl 1.quæst. 1. sed refutatur ab ipso Bellarm. l. 3. de lib. arb: c. 8. Liberum enim arbitrium homini à natura est insitum, quod nunquam tollitur. Actus verò non insunt à natura, sed producuntur à nobis: & modò adsunt, modò absunt, vnde sequeretur, homines quandoque libero arbitrio carere, quia non semper operaretur. Præterea actus ille in quo libertas consistere dicitur, vel elicitus est à potentia quadam libera, vel non est elicitus. Si primum assumseris, iam libertas antecedit illum actum, quiob id libertatis ὐσίαν in se continere nequit. Si secundum dixeris, actus illi necessarius erit. Quomodo igitur libertas in eo consistet?

XXXI. Negato igitur, quòd libertas sit actus, vltrò sequitur, quòd sit vis quæpiam in anima permanens: τὰ γὰρ ἐν τῇ ψυχῇ γινόμενα τρία ἐστὶ, πάθη δυνάμεις ἕξεις, l. 2. Eth. Nic. c. 4. Tria insunt animæ, affectus, potentiæ, habitus. Sed absurdum foret liberum arbitrium affectibus accensere, qui sæpè inuitis obrepunt, nec eligere faciunt, verum eligentem potiùs impediunt. Pari modo nequit esse habitus, Nec enim est διόοδος, cùm toti habitus naturales ad vnum duntaxat vel bonum vel malum inclinent. Nec ἔμφυτος, cum non fiant, sed nascantur homines liberi. Remotis ergò speciebus cæteris, sequitur libertatem esse πλάτει vel potentiam.

XXXII. Vlterius quæritur, An potentia vniuersalis sis vel particularis? Quidam vocant vniuersalem, continentem sub se potentias omnes animæ sentientis & intelligētis, eo quòd in his omnibus actus inueniantur liberi. At vero liberi sunt, non vt ab ipsis, sed quatenus a voluntate procedunt, a qua imperantur. Si enim omnes δυνάμεις ex sese essent liberae, tot forent libera arbitria, quot sunt potentiae, quo nihil dici potest absurdius.

XXXIII. Cùm ergò particularis sit δύναμις, vel distincta erit ab intellectu & voluntate, vel secus: Pro primo pugnat Alexander Alensis 2. part. summae quaestio. 72. mem: 1. art. 3. sed absque ratione: Vbi enim distinctus actus non est, ibi nec distincta potentia. Atqui nullus actus nominari potest ab intellectus voluntatisque operatione diuersus & tertiae isti potentiae proprius. Num enim erit voluntatis motio? Ast intellectus hoc est, qui per objecta proposita mouet. An velle primum, vt volo eligere, deliberare? Sed voluntatis hoc est, quae & se, & alias potentias plerumque mouet, & ad agendum applicat: dicente Scaligero Exerc 207. sect. 25.

XXXIV. Tandem igitur aut in intellectu solo, aut in voluntate sola, aut in vtroque haerebit libertas: In intellectu locari nequit, quoniam ille liber non est; sed necessitatis jugo gemino implicatus: 1. Quoad speciem actuum: Ex natura enim sua sic est determinatus, vt assentietur vero, & dissentiat a falso, neque potest vero, si exacte fuerit propositum, non assentiri. Voluntas autem licet quoad genus ad bonum sit restricta, tamen quoad speciem boni accurate etiam propositi, est indifferens, ita vt illud vel eligere, vel reijcere queat liberrimè. Voluntatis enim objectum est τὰγαθὸν, quod consistit in conuenientia: & quoniam res eadem nunc conueniens, nunc esse potest inconueniens, hinc voluntas indifferentiam habet quoad objectum suum, vt illud vel eligat, vel repudiet prout placuerit.

XXXV. II. Quoad exercitium. Nulla enim actio scipitur nisi ex appetitu boni, qui inuitat ad agendum. Vnde sequitur, quòd intellectus etiam ad intelligendum ab appetitu rationali vel voluntate inclinetur. Nec enim seipsam ad operandum applicat ratio, sed eius actio vel actionis cessatio ab appetitu totius suppositi, vel voluntate hominis suadetur. Propendet quidem quoq́ ad intelligendum intellectus, sed quòd hoc & non alio tempore, illud & non istud intelligere aggrediatur, id non ad intellectum, sed suppositi voluntatem vnicè referendum est. Hinc a nonnullis statuitur, quòd voluntas ob imperium suum excæcet intellectum, tum στερητικῶς vel priuatiuè quatenus eum avertit à recta consideratione, nec permittit diu permanere in veri dictamine: tum θετικῶς vel positiuè, quatenus voluntas eliciens sibi malum finem, præcipit intellectui, inuenire medias ad mali illius finis consecutionem tendentia.

XXVI. Objicitur verò, quòd & ipse intellectus sit indifferens in suis actibus, & proponendis obiectis, ideoque liber. Verùm hic distinguunt Philosophi inter obiectiuam & formalem indifferentiam. Illa in diuersimodè judicando, & objecta varia proponendo, ista in propositis liberè eligendis vel negligendis consistit. Illa intellectus, ista voluntatis est propria. Illa vocatur à nonnullis libertas iudicatiua, hæc electiua. Libertas verò judicatiua & motio intellectus primá libertatis electiuæ, de quâ hic sermo, causa non est, cùm & sæpè desit & præsenti voluntas non semper assentiatur. Imò accuratè loquendo ne quidem in actibus suis planè indifferens est intellectus, quia semper præcedit suppositi, voluntas quâ demtam intellectus nec ad judicandum, nec ad proponendum accingit.

XXXVII. Evicto igitur, quòd intellectus formaliter nō sit liber, vltrò sequitur, quod in intellectu & voluntate con-ctis non hæreat libertas. Vbi ergo tandem collocabitur? Vt paucis rem omnem exprimam. In sola hominis voluntate, quippè quæ est potentia libera & indifferens, vt agere & non agere, bonum aut malum eligere possit. Libera est 1. quoad obiectum speciale, quia duo ipsi proponuntur contraria, virtus & vitium, ad quorum neutrum est determinata, sed potest vtrumque pro arbitratu sequi. 2. quoad actus ipsos. Licet enim voluntati virtutem sectari vel secus, licet vitium fugere vel sequi, quoniam neutri necessariò indulget. Hinc & ipsa Scriptura non nisi voluntati libertatem tribuit, vt Deut. 30. v 19. Eliges, vtrum volueris, mortem vel vitam. 1. Cor. 7. v. 37. In potestate habens propriam voluntatem. Consentiunt Gregorius Nyssenus lib. 7. de Phil. Damascenus l. 2. de O. F. c. 25. Ambrosius l. 2. de fide c. 3. Augustinus lib. de grat. & lib. arb. c. 2. l. 5. de C. Dei cap. 9. & concilium Arausicanum can. 13. qui Patres vt ostendant soli voluntati inesse libertatem, dicere solent, Liberum voluntatis arbitrium.

XXXIIX. Porrò autem quæritur, num aliud voluntatis arbitrium aliud voluntatis libertas? Nos realiter illa differre negamus, cùm voluntas formaliter nihil aliud sit, quàm potentia in agendo libera. Et si libertas distingueretur à voluntate, tum accidenti inesset accidens quod absurdum. Sin animæ ipsi dicatur inesse liberum arbitrium, tum non voluntatis erit propria, sed tertia quæpiam potestas, ab intellectu voluntateque sequestrata, quod itidem absurdum. Quantusuis autem non differat à voluntate libertas, mentis tamen nostræ opera sic distinguuntur, vt voluntatem quasi quoddam σύνολον, libertatem verò instar formæ concipiamus. Nam voluntas nobis est velut compositum quiddam, suo constans materiali, suo itidem formali. Illud est potentia, hoc potentiæ libertas, vnde si copuletur vtrumque voluntas nihil erit aliud, quàm potentia libera, quæ sui actus est domina: illumque pro arbitrio & producere potest, & nonproducere. Atque hinc fit, vt vocabulis etiam distinguantur, nec dicatur, libertas est voluntas, vel contrà: Sed, libertas est voluntatis, vel in voluntate, & rursus, volūtas habet libertatem, vel libertate prædita est.

XXXIX. Vnicus restat scrupulus, quare voluntas vocetur liberum arbitrium, cùm tamen arbitrari vel iudicare sit actus intellectus, non voluntatis? Sed respondemus. Nomen istud voluntati rectè tribui ratione sui actus. Nam electio, quæ est actus liberæ voluntatis, est quasi arbitrium quoddam, quo voluntas rem vnam præ alia liberè amplectitur. Quo sensu vulgò dicimus: In meo arbitrio est, hoc facere vel omittere, hoc est, in mea potestate & electione. Sic Levius scribit, Liberum suarum rerum arbitrium alicui facere, hoc est alicuius voluntati & potestati se suaque subijcere. Ex quo colligitur nomen arbitrij dupliciter apud Latinos accipi. 1. Pro actu intellectus, vbi idem est, quod iudicium seu consilium. 2. Pro actu voluntatis, & sic idem est, quod electio. Hoc posteriori respectu voluntas vocatur arbitrium, vt nomine actus liberi ipsa facultas libera denotetur.

XL. Atque hactenus satis Philosophati sumus de natura libertatis, à quibus tamē nonnunquam Theologorum phrases videntur discrepare. Sed conciliatio est facilis, si vnica distinctio teneatur. Liberum arbitrium consideratur, 1. Philosophicè, respectu συζυγίας, quatenus notat internum liberumque agendi principium. Vbi certè nihil esse potest aliud, quam voluntas, quippè quæ sola est potentia indifferens, & illud internum liberumq́ actionū principium. 2. Theologicè, ratione suæ ένεργείας, vbi non tàm æstimatur Quid sit, quàm, quid possit, vel quas in agēdo vires obtineat. Hoc respectu liberū arbitriū non est ipsa voluntas, quia hæq in omni statu hominis quoad essētiā manet eadē, liberū verò arbitriū variatur, adeò quidem, vt illud in statu lapsus nullū vel amissum esse dicatur, Voluntas verò minimè amissa est, vnde arbitrium Theologicè sumtum à voluntate multùm differre consequitur. Est autem nihil aliud, quàm vis quædam voluntati superaddita, eamque perficiens, per quam illa ad bonum promptè inclinatur, & quod elegit facilè exequitur. Vim & facultatem nomino, non actum; quia hominis arbitrium non est ipsa libera actio, sed agendi principium. Vnde minùs commodè Pareum loqui euincitur, quando lib: 3. de grat. & lib. arbit. cap. 7. pag. 437 Liberum arbitrium in actu rationis & voluntatis positum esse cum Hervæo statuit.

XLI. Rationes autem quas profert, parui momenti sunt 1. ait, In pueris & dormientibus non dari liberum arbitrium, quia rationis & voluntatis actum non exerceant. Resp. Principium petitur. Licèt enim liberè non agant, liberum tamen arbitrium vel potentiam liberè agendi habent. Nulla proinde sequela est, sicut quoque haud sequitur: Non ratiocinantur. E. ratione carent. 2. Daretur in anima rationali facultas tertia, à ratione & voluntate diversa. Resp. Si libertas consideratur ratione solius, tum est ipsa voluntas, non tertia facultas. Si ratione ἐνεργείας & bonæ operationis, neque tum datur facultas tertia, quoniam vis illa non est peculiaris δύναμις, sed δυνάμιος, videlicet voluntatis, perfectio diuinitùs concessa. Quando enim in renatis renouatur liberum arbitrium, non accedit noua facultas propriè dicta, qualis est ratio & voluntas, sed potius facultatum perfectio, vel donum aliquod facultatem perficiens. 3. Liberum arbitrium non est amissum, in quantum est potentia. Resp. Si naturalis potentia vel voluntas intelligatur, concedo: Sin autem vis operandi bonum Theologicum, & seruandi præcepta Domini, tum certè vis aut potentia illa per lapsum est amissa.

XLII. Ex his igitur satis euidenter patet, quòd liberum arbitrium accuratè loquendo & formaliter non sit actus; interim concedimus, nonunquam abusuè ipsum actum nomine arbitrij denotari: Sicut & voluntatis vocabulum est ambiguum, quod modò τὴν θέλησιν modò τὴν θελητικὴν δύναμιν significat, annotante Damasceno lib. 2. de O. E. cap. 22. Hoc sensu potest dici de pueris & dormientibus, quòd sui non sint arbitrij, quod careant libero arbitrio, hoc est, libera operatione seu exercitio arbitrij. Manet nihilominus, quòd isthæc popularis & abusiva acceptio nihil præiudicet naturæ rei & significationi propriæ, secundum quam arbitrium Philosophicè & respectu οὐσίας sumtum, est ipsa voluntas; Theologicè verò & respectu ἐνεργείας in spiritualibus est inclinatio ad bonum & vis quædam benè faciléque operandi, voluntatem perficiens, primùm concreata, per lapsum amifsa, in renatis nonnihil instaurata, in beatis planè consummata.


### Question VI. Whether the intellect is radically free?

XLIII. The affirmative pleases Bellarmino, while in book 3, chapter 8, proposition 7, he writes, 'Even if the will alone is formally free, the root of its liberty is nevertheless in the reason.' He proposes two arguments for his assertion: 1. The will is free because it is a rational appetite; just as, conversely, appetite in beasts is not free because it is not rational. Therefore, the cause of liberty is reason itself. 2. Appetite cannot be carried toward anything unless it is proposed to it by a cognitive power as good and convenient. Therefore, if the cognitive power is determined to one thing, the appetite will necessarily tend toward that. But because it is indeterminate and proposes various objects, hence the appetite is free and can be inclined toward various parts. The root of liberty, therefore, is in the intellect itself.

XLIV. But that this opinion is erroneous and the reasons weak, another Jesuit, Martin Becanus, saw, who in part 2 of his Theologia Scholastica, treatise 1, chapter 2, question 4, rightly assumed and defended the contrary. For the intellect is indeed a condition without which the will could not sometimes exercise its freedom, yet it is not the root, that is, the primary cause of freedom. For 1. Bellarmine asserts that the intellect is free in no degree of freedom, neither from coercion, nor from necessity, neither as regards specification nor as regards exercise. How then could it be the cause of freedom? For how will that which in no way participates in freedom exist as the parent of freedom? 2. If the intellect is the cause and root of free will, it will be the cause either as regards the first act or as regards the second act. But neither can be asserted: not the former, because freedom in the first act is the free will itself, of which the intellect is certainly not the cause. Not the latter, because the second act of freedom is the free volition or choice itself, to the eliciting of which the intellect does not concur as a cause, but only as a condition, insofar as the will would not act unless an object were proposed to it by the intellect.

XLV. The contrary arguments are easy to solve. To the first, we say that the will is free because God created it free, just as the appetite of brutes is not free because God did not will it to be free. That the will is called a rational appetite is not the cause, as if reason were the root of freedom, but because it is inherent in a rational nature and follows the dictate of reason, just as the appetite of brutes is called irrational because it is inherent in irrational beings and does not itself follow reason, but sense.

XLVI. To the second, Becanus replies that this only proves that unless the intellect were indeterminate and proposed various objects, the will could not choose one out of many, which we concede, because this is nothing other than that indetermination of the intellect is a condition, without which the will would not operate in this way, Bellarmine urges, book 3, chapter 9, column 673. An action never follows from a mere condition: but an appetite follows from the mere judgment of reason, by which a thing is proposed as good, even if by chance that thing is not good. Therefore, reason does not concur merely as a condition applying the object, but as a cause making the object, while it attributes a certain motive force to a good thing, and makes that thing to be actually desirable, which before was only desirable in potentiality. I reply: 1. An action is not always undertaken upon the judgment of reason, but the will sometimes chooses the contrary, when it sees better things proposed by the intellect, and yet follows worse ones. It is therefore a mere condition, but not the cause of a free action. 2. When the will chooses a proposed good, it does this from its own liberty, not from the determination of the intellect. 3. Reason can make something desirable through its judgment, but that it is actually desired does not originate from the intellect, which proposed the desirable thing, but from the liberty of the will alone.

Latin:

XLIII. Bellarmino placet affirmatiua, dum l. 3. cap. 8. propos. 7. scribit, Et si voluntas sola sit formaliter libera, radix tamen libertatis eius in ratione est. Argumenta suæ assertionis duo proponit 1. Voluntas ideo est libera quia est appetitus rationalis; sicut è contrario appetitus in bestijs idcò non est liber, quia non est rationalis. Igitur causa libertatis est ipsa ratio. 2. Appetitus non potest in aliquid ferri, nisi pponatur ei à potentia cognoscente tanquam bonum & conueniens. Igitur si potentia cognoscens sit determinata ad vnum, appetitus necessariò tendet in illud. Quia verò indeterminata est & proponit varia obiecta, hinc appetitus liber est, & inclinari potest in varias partes, Radix ergo libertatis est in ipso intellectu.

XLIV. Sed erroneam esse hanc opnionem & rationes infirmas, vidit alius Iesu Wita Martinus Becanus, qui parte 2. Theol. Scholast. tract. 1. c. 2. quæst. 4. contrarium rectè assumsit & defendit. Nam intellectus est quidem conditio sine qua voluntas aliquando non posset exercere suam libertatem, non tamen est radix, hoc est, causa prima libertatis. Nam 1. Bellarminus asserit, intellectum nullo gradu libertatis, neque à coactione, neq; à necessitate, ne que quoad specificationem neq; quoad exercitium esse liberum. Qui ergò libertatis causa esse poterit? Quod enim libertate nullo modo participat, libertatis parens quomodo existet? 2. Si intellectus est causa & radix liberi arbitrii vel erit causa quoad actum primum, vel quoad actum secundum. Sed neutrum asseri potest, Non prius, quia libertas actu primo est ipsa voluntas libera, cuius certè causa non est intellectus. Non posterius quia actus secundus libertatis est ipsa libera volitio vel electio, ad quam eliciendam non concurrit intellectus tanquam causa, sed solùm tanquam conditio quatenus voluntas non ageret, nisi obiectum illi ab intellectu proponeretur.

XLV. Argumenta contraria solutu sunt facilia. Ad 1. dicimus, quod voluntas ideo sit libera, quia Deus eam liberam creauit, sicut appetitus brutorum ideò non est liber, quia eum liberum esse DEVS non voluit. Quod autem voluntas vocatur appetitus rationalis, causa non est, ac si ratio libertatis radix foret, sed quia rationali naturæ inest, & rationis dictamen sequitur, velut appetitus brutorum dicitur irrationalis, quia inest irrationalibus, & ipse non sequitur rationem, sed sensum,

XLVI. Ad 2. Respondet Becanus, tantùm hoc probari, quòd nisi intellectus esset indeterminatus, & proponeret varia obiecta, voluntas non posset vnum ex multis eligere, quod concedimus, quia hoc nihil aliud est, quàm illam indeterminationem intellectus esse conditionem, sine qua voluntas hoc modo non operaretur, Instat Bellarm. l. 3. c. 9. Col. 673. Ad solam conditionem nunquam sequitur actio: At ad solum iudicium rationis, quo res proponitur, vt bona, sequitur appetitio, etiamsi fortè res illa non sit bona. Non igitur ratio concurrit solùm vt conditio applicans obiectum, sed vt causa faciens obiectum, dum rei bonæ tribuit vim quandam motiuam, & facit vt ea res sit actu expetibilis, quæ solùm antea erat expetibilis in potentia. Resp. 1. Ad iudicium rationis non semper suscipitnr actio, sed voluntas nonnũquam eligit contrarium, quando meliora ab intellectu proposita videt, & tamen deteriora sequitur. Est igitur mera conditio, non autem causa actionis liberæ. 2. Cum voluntas bonum propositum eligit, tum facit hoc ex libertate sua, non ex determinatione intellectus. 3. Potest ratio aliquid per iudicium suum facere appetibile, quod autem actu appetatur, non prouenit originaliter ab intellectu, qui proposuit appetibile, sed à sola voluntatis libertate.


### Question VII. Whether the will in the use of its liberty depends upon the practical intellect, and is determined by it to one side or the…

XLVII. The practical intellect or practical reason is called that which is concerned with τὰ πρακτά, and deliberates whether something is to be done or otherwise. Its final judgment is the conclusion judging what is to be undertaken, and it is usually expressed in these words: This now, all things considered, is to be chosen or done.

XLIIX. It is asked, therefore, whether the will always depends upon the intellect in its free actions, and whether it is determined by it to one side or the other through the final judgment? Bellarmine again chooses the affirmative, book 3, chapter 8. stating that the will depends on the judgment of the intellect, or that it can desire nothing unless the intellect practically judges that it ought to be desired: by which also the will is determined to follow necessarily the final judgment of the intellect. And indeed we do not deny that some difficulty lies hidden here: For if you affirm that the will depends on the intellect, its freedom will be endangered: If you allow it to be denied, that much-discussed saying will fall, the will is not carried except toward an object known and proposed by reason. But in order that we may in some way extricate ourselves from this Scholastic thicket, we shall bring forward two assertions.

XLIX. FIRST ASSERTION: The will in every action requires the prior cognition of the intellect, yet it does not always depend on the practical judgment of the intellect. The reason for the former is because the will desires nothing unless it is known and proposed. For it is moved by an object, not when it still lies hidden and is unknown, but when it is known and proposed. Hence philosophers say, Nothing is willed unless it is first known: And the poet sings: There is no desire for the unknown. The latter is proved because for the desire of some object a practical judgment of the intellect is not always required, but a bare apprehension under the aspect of good often suffices. Examples are the sudden movements of the will, which do not await the practical judgment of reason. Indeed, even in deliberate acts, although the intellect has sometimes judged that this ought to be desired, the will nevertheless chooses the contrary, following the example of Medea, as is testified by all those who commit sin against their conscience, which they know to be prohibited and in no way to be done. There, therefore, the will does not depend on the practical judgment of right reason, but rejects and despises it.

L. SECOND ASSERTION. The will in its free actions is not necessarily determined by the practical judgment of the intellect, whether regarding the exercise or regarding the species of the act. Not regarding the exercise, because although the judgment of reason may be posited, yet the will remains free, and can suspend the act of choosing, or at this time not choose what the intellect judges in practice ought to be chosen. Gregory of Valencia admits this in tom. 2 on Thomas, disputation 2, question 4, point 1, who nevertheless elsewhere keenly defends intellectual determination. Nor as regards the species of the act, because with a certain desirable object proposed which the intellect judges ought to be chosen, the will can choose the contrary, and very often does choose, as experience testifies.

LI. And indeed that the will is not necessarily determined to one side is evident from the very distinction between natural and free powers, of which the former, when all things required for acting are posited, are necessarily determined to act, so that they cannot not act: but the latter are not determined, but can act and not act. But the will is a free power, which is admitted. Therefore, when all things required are posited, among which is also apprehension and the judgment of the intellect, it can act and not act. If you maintain otherwise, two absurdities follow. 1. That the will cannot choose a lesser good while leaving a greater, because the intellect, unless it errs, always judges that the greater good is to be preferred to the lesser; yet the contrary happens, and often the lesser good is chosen, as experience is a witness. 2. That the will cannot choose either from two equal goods, because the right judgment of reason prefers neither to the other, and indeed cannot prefer it, since otherwise they would not be equal. Becanus himself urges these arguments against Bellarmine in part 2 of Scholastic Theology, tract 1, chapter 2, question 5, whence now again the vanity of the so often boasted Papist consensus shines forth.

LII. And thus far we have discoursed in general concerning the free actions of the will: It is pleasing to consider them in particular, and how the will conducts itself regarding them, how they are chosen, what the intellect contributes or does not contribute to volition, to explain in a few words. will be. For thus a fuller knowledge of the question will be had, and the reason for volition and every election will be better understood.

LIII. We say, therefore, that things which fall under free volition are sought either προαιρετικῶς or ἄνευ προαιρέσεως. In these, the will is often moved without a prior judgment of reason, from its own liberty alone. Such volitions are either ἐμμένουσαι, which have an internal object, such as the volition of understanding or of considering a certain thing at this time; which internal action is often undertaken without the persuasion of the intellect, from the good pleasure of the man acting freely alone, otherwise there would be a progression to infinity; or μεταβαίνουσαι, whose object is external, and is either an end or means. The ultimate and highest end the will seeks by its own φύσει, nor does it ask or wait for the counsel or judgment of the intellect as to whether it ought to seek it. Thus, when means are held to be entirely equal and equivalent, one is chosen not from a prior discourse of the mind, but more often from the mere good pleasure of the will.

LIV. Concerning those things which fall under προαίρεσιν properly so called, Bernard writes in his book on grace and free will: The will, whithersoever it turns itself, always has reason as a companion, not that it is always moved from reason, but that it is never moved without reason. For four acts concur, of which the first two are common to every volition along with the last, but the third remains proper to the διέξοδ of eligible things: of these we refer the last to the will, the preceding ones to the intellect. 1. There is the cognition of the object, because the will is not moved toward any thing unless it is previously known. 2. There is the proposition of the known, because when the intellect has known an object, it then proposes it to the will either to be chosen or to be neglected. 3. There is the persuasion or dissuasion of the proposal. For if the intellect thinks a certain thing convenient, then it persuades the will; but if it thinks it inconvenient, it dissuades. 4. Persuasion is choice, when that which has been judged eligible by the intellect, the will chooses and with every effort is uniquely borne toward it and strives for it.

LV. The will chooses, however, not impelled by some other principle, either external or internal, distinct from itself, but it moves itself immediately and applies itself to acting: otherwise the action of the will would not be free. Therefore, a persuasive judgment is indeed granted to the intellect, but command is denied. It judges what is eligible, yet it remains in the discretion of the will to freely obey or resist the judging intellect. Reason, says Bernard somewhere, is given to the will so that it may instruct it, not so that it may destroy it. But it would destroy it if it imposed any necessity, whereby it would be less able to turn itself according to its own discretion. And the commentator on Damascene in book 2, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 26, writes: The intellect is at least the directive principle of our actions, but the will is the imperative and primarily effective one.

LVI. In order that this very thing may be understood more distinctly, we say that eligible things are either evil or good by their own kind, or neither good nor evil, but indifferent. If they are good or evil, we choose them and pursue them either from habit or without habit. If from habit, the judgment and deliberation of the mind does not always precede the act, but the will is often borne most promptly toward the object through that habit, as the intemperate person is toward drinking and lusts, which actions are not simply free and contingent, except as to their principle, but in a certain way necessary, whence some call them virtually free, not formally. But if we act well or badly ἄνευ ἕξεως, there the judgment of reason always precedes, but it is twofold and mutually opposed. For there are two most diverse principles in man, ὀρθότης κακότης, rectitude depending on natural notions, and the depravity of reason, arisen from sin and mixed on all sides with the itching of various affections. Reason judges otherwise than we do. For thus a fuller knowledge of the question will be had, and the reason for every volition and choice will be better understood.

LIII. We say, therefore, that things which fall under free volition are sought either προαιρετικῶς or ἀπροαιρέτως. The will is often carried toward these without a prior judgment of reason, from its own liberty alone. Such volitions are either ἐμμένουσαι, which have an internal object, such as the volition of understanding or of considering a certain thing at this time; which internal action is often undertaken without the persuasion of the intellect, from the mere good pleasure of the man acting freely, otherwise there would be a progress to infinity; or μεταβαίνουσαι, whose object is external, and is either an end or means. The will seeks the ultimate and highest end by its own φύσει, nor does it ask or wait for the counsel or judgment of the intellect as to whether it ought to seek it. Thus, when means are held to be entirely equal and equivalent, one is taken not from a prior discourse of the mind, but more often from the mere good pleasure of the will.

LIV. Concerning those things which fall under προαίρεσιν properly so called, Bernard writes in his book on grace and free choice: The will, whithersoever it turns itself, always has reason as a companion, not that it is always moved from reason, but that it is never moved without reason. For four acts concur, the first two of which are common to every volition along with the last, but the third remains proper to the διεξόδῳ of eligible things: of these we refer the last to the will, and the preceding ones to the intellect. 1. There is the cognition of the object, because the will is carried toward no thing unless it is previously known. 2. There is the proposition of the known, because when the intellect has known an object, it then proposes it to the will either to choose or to neglect. 3. There is the persuasion or dissuasion of the proposition. For if the intellect thinks a certain thing is suitable, then it persuades the will; but if it thinks it unsuitable, it dissuades. dissuades. 4. It is the choice of the persuaded, when that which was judged eligible by the intellect, the will chooses and with every effort is borne solely toward it and strives.

LV. The will chooses, however, not impelled by some other principle, either external or internal, distinct from itself, but it moves itself immediately and applies itself to acting: otherwise the action of the will would not be free. Therefore, a persuasive judgment is indeed granted to the intellect, but command is denied. It judges what is eligible, yet it remains in the discretion of the will to obey or resist the judging intellect freely. Reason, says Bernard somewhere, is given to the will so that it may instruct it, not so that it may destroy it. But it would destroy it if it imposed any necessity, whereby it would be less able to turn itself according to its own discretion. And the commentator on Damascene in book 2, On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 26, writes: The intellect is at least the directive principle of our actions, but the will is the imperative and primarily the effective one.

LVI. In order that this very thing may be understood more distinctly, we say that eligible things are either evil or good by their own kind, or neither good nor evil, but indifferent. If they are good or evil, we choose them and pursue them either by habit or without habit. If by habit, judgment and deliberation of the mind do not always precede the act, but the will is often borne most promptly toward the object through that habit, as the intemperate person toward drinking and lusts, which actions are not simply free and contingent, except as to their principle, but in a certain way necessary, whence some call them virtually free, not formally. But if we act well or badly without habit (ἀνευ ἕξεως), there the judgment of reason always precedes, but a double one, and mutually opposed to itself. For there are two most diverse principles in man, rectitude (ὀρθότης) and depravity (κακότης), rectitude depending on natural notions, and the depravity of reason, arisen from sin, and mixed on every side with the itching of various affections. Reason judges otherwise when right, otherwise when depraved; or rather the man, who acting truly thinks otherwise according to right, and otherwise according to depraved reason. And hence the diversity of judgments, hence the struggle and fight often most grievous in man emerges.

LVII. To bring forward an example, when virtue is proposed, which is either to be followed or to be fled, then reason deliberates what is to be done, but quite unequally. In so far as it is right, and the light of innate knowledge is present, it determines that virtue is to be chosen and pleasures are to be avoided. It brings forward, moreover, a huge heap of arguments, by which it solicitously labors to persuade this: But this right judgment is soon contradicted by the corruption of the flesh introduced by perturbations, which inclines toward pleasure, and judges it far more useful and advisable if pleasure, not virtue, is chosen: What does the will or a man endowed with will do here? He sticks in doubt, and is uncertain to which he should assent. He considers the weight of the arguments, and often understands that right reason relies on better foundations. What happens? He gives assent to depraved reason and evil appetite, and chooses not virtue but pleasure, although he knows virtue to be more honorable, just as the Ovidian Medea confesses of herself in book 7 of the Metamorphoses: But a new force drags me, unwilling, and desire urges one thing, the mind another: I approve of the better things, I follow the worse.

LIIX And here the freedom of the will appears most of all. For it cannot be determined by the judgment of reason, since that is doubled and contrary, persuading now the true good, which is really good; now the apparent, which is apparently good. Nor is it always led to that by arguments, since it knows that more solid ones stand and exist on the side of reason, but from mere self-will, with the judgment of right reason spurned, the depraved one accepted, the sense irritating, the appetite soliciting, man chooses pleasure and turns away from virtue. For if this were not so, what cause could we name why, when two are equally affected in mind and body, and the same beauty is presented to them, one of them is moved to illicit enjoyment, while the other remains steadfast in a chaste will? In both, right reason dissuaded, equally to the sight of both, and both were free from the impulse of an external principle; yet the one declined toward an illicit deed, while the other recoiled from the same, where no one will be able to bring forward any other cause except the sole free power of the will.

LIX. But as regards indifferent things, which are in their own kind neither good nor evil, these are either external objects or internal acts, such as speculating, meditating, etc. The choice of both requires a prior judgment of reason, which is likewise either simple or doubled. For it happens more often that a double judgment precedes the volition of indifferent things, not indeed contrary, as in the case of good or evil things, but contradictory, when one object is held, and the intellect deems it to be chosen or not chosen, yet for different reasons. As if you are invited to a banquet, the mind judges that you ought to appear, by the right of friendship and humanity; soon it warns you to avoid drinking bouts, so that you may not be present. You see here two judgments, not contrary but contradictory, because one persuades the same thing, the other dissuades it. Where again there is the highest liberty of the will, since it is powerful to comply with either this or that judgment.

LX. But if the judgment of the intellect is simple, we grant it a motion that is not imperative, but only persuasive, which does not overturn the will. For although reason shows and warns what is to be done, and the will follows for a moment, it does not however follow by compulsion, or entirely necessarily, but most freely, since the persuasion of the intellect does not compel nor necessitate, but only invites in a friendly manner, and that the will does not resist this depends not on some necessary impulse, but on the free choice of the will.

LXI. If you object: The will cannot desire anything without the judgment of the intellect. Therefore, if the judgment is indeterminate, the will itself will also be indeterminate: If the judgment is determined, it too will be determined: But the final practical judgment is entirely determined. Therefore, the will will necessarily choose that which the final judgment determines is to be chosen. We respond by denying the consequence, because the liberty of the will consists in this, that even when the determined judgment of the intellect and all other things required for acting are posited, it itself still remains indeterminate and free. If you ask, by what is it finally determined? We say, by itself, because this is the nature of free power, that it moves itself immediately and applies itself to acting. The remaining objections of Bellarmine are solved in Becanus, vol. 1, ch. 2, quest. 5, p. 41 et seqq., and therefore we wish to add nothing, but rather to leave those brothers and associates to settle it.

LXII. Thus, therefore, it has been proven so far that the will is truly free and does not borrow its liberty from the intellect. Moreover, it is free not only internally and elicitiuè, as they call it, but also externally and imperatiuè, that is, it is not only the mistress of its own acts and produces and suspends them ἀντίρτως, but it also generally commands other powers, and applies them to acting or recalls them from acting according to its pleasure.

LXIII. From these things well considered, it is easy to answer that question: Whether the free will is a passive or active power? For although it could be named passive, insofar as it is moved by an object and receives its acts into itself, it is nevertheless properly active, since it is occupied in acting and effectively produces its own acts. Meanwhile, we do not judge it to be absolutely active as it pleases Bellarmine in book 3, chapter 10, since it is moved by its object, and the cognition of the intellect, in most cases, persuasion is required beforehand. But it may be a wonder by what reason Bellarmine can hold free will to be a simply active power, when in chapters 7, 8, and 9 he sharply defends that it is determined by the final judgment of practical reason. But indeed, to be determined by another is to behave passively toward another. And Thomas, in part 1, question 80, article 1, expressly calls the will or intellectual appetite a passive power, because it is moved by a known object, whence again the feigned and painted agreement of the Papists shines forth. Bellarmine is otherwise prolix in chapters 10 and 11 regarding this question, and he almost does not understand himself. The whole matter can be settled in a few words, if the will is said to be a passive power insofar as it is moved by an object, but active insofar as it produces its own acts freely and effectively.

Latin:

XLVII. Intellectus practicus vel practica ratio dicitur, quæ circa τὰ πρακτά versatur, & sit nè aliquid faciendum vel secus, deliberat. Vltimum vero eius iudicium est conclusio iudicans, quidnam sit suscipiendum, & exprimi solet his verbis: Hoc nunc omnibus consideratis eligendum aut faciendum est.

XLIIX. Quæritur ergo, An voluntas in suis liberis actionibus semper ab intellectu dependeat, & num ab eo per iudicium vltimum in alteram partem determinetur? Affirmatiuam rursus eligit Bellarminus l. 3. c. 8. statuens, quod voluntas ab intellectus iudicio pendeat, seu quod appetere nihil possit, nisi intellectus practice iudicet appetendum esse: a quo etiam voluntas determinetur ad sequendum necessario intellectus iudicium vltimum. Et sane non diffitemur aliquam hic difficultatem delitescere: Si enim affirmes, voluntatem ab intellectu pendere, periclitabitur eius libertas: Siniveris negatum, cadet illud πολυθρυλλητον, voluntas non fertur nisi in obiectum cognitum, & a ratione propositum. Vt autem ex hoc senticeto Scholastico nos quodammodo expediamus, duas assertiones in medium proferemus.

XLIX. PRIOR ASSERTIO: Voluntas in omni actione praerequirit intellectus cognitionem, non tamen dependet semper a practico iudicio Intellectus. Ratio prioris est, quia voluntas nihil appetit, nisi cognitum & propositum. Mouetur enim ab obiecto, non quando latet adhuc incognitumque est, sed quando cognoscitur & proponitur. Hinc Philosophi dicunt, Nihil esse volitum nisi prius sit cognitum: Et Poëta canit: Ignoti nulla cupido. Posterius probatur, quia ad obiecti alicuius appetitionem non semper requiritur iudicium practicum intellectus, sed sufficit saepe nuda apprehensio sub ratione boni. Exemplo sunt motus repentini voluntatis, qui iudicium rationis practicum non expectant. Imo etiam in actibus deliberatis, licet nonnunquam hoc appetendum esse intellectus iudicauerit, voluntas tamen exemplo Medeae contrarium eligit, vti testantur omnes ii, qui contra conscientiam peccatum committunt, quod sciunt esse prohibitum, & nullo modo faciendum. Ibi ergo voluntas non pendet a iudicio practico rectae rationis, sed illud respuit & contemnit.

L. POSTERIOR ASSERTIO. Voluntas in suis actionibus liberis non necessario determinatur a practico iudicio intellectus, siue quoad exercitium siue quoad speciem actus. Non quoad exercitium, quia licet ponatur rationis judicium, voluntas tamen manet libera, & potest actum eligendi suspendere, vel hoc tempore non eligere quod intellectus judicat in praxi eligendum esse. Fatetur hoc Gregorius de Valent. tom. 2. in Thomam disput. 2. quæst. 4. pun. 1. qui tamen aliàs intellectualem determinationem acriter propugnat. Nec quoad speciem actus, quia proposito certo appetibili quod intellectus eligendu judicat, volũtas contrariũ eligere potest, & sæpissimè eligit, vti testatur experientia.

LI. Et sanè quòd voluntas non necessario in alteram partem determinetur, patet ex ipso inter potentias naturales & liberas discrimine, quarum illæ positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, necessariò determinantur ad agendum, ita vt non possint non agere: hæc autem non determinantur sed agere & non agere possunt. Atqui voluntas est potentia libera, quod in confesso. E. Positis omnibus requisitis, ex quibus etiam est apprehensio & intellectus judicium, agere & non agere potest. Aliud si statuas, duo absurda consequuntur. 1. Voluntatem non posse eligere minus bonum relicto maiori, quia intellectus, nisi erret semperjudicat majus bonum minori esse præferendum, Contrarium v. fieri, & sæpè minus bonum eligi, testis est experientia, 2. Voluntatem ex duobus bonis æqualibus neutrum posse eligere, quia rectum judicium rationis neutrum alteri præponit, & quidem præponere nequit, cùm aliàs æqualia non essent, Argumenta hæc contra Bellarminum vrget Becanus ipse parte 2. Scholast. Theol. tract. 1. c. 2. quæst. 5. vnde nunc iterum consensus Papistici toties jactati vanitas elucescit.

LII. Et hactenus in genere de voluntatis actionibus liberis disseruimus: Placet in specie illas intueri, & quomodo circa istas se voluntas habeat, quomodo eligantur, quid intellectus ad volitionem conferat vel non conferat, paucis explicabimus. Ita enim plenior quæstionis cognitio habebitur, & volitionis omnisqúe electionis ratio melius intelligetur.

LIII. Dicimus ergo, quòd res, quæ sub volitionem liberam cadunt, vel προαιρετικῶς, vel ἄνευ προαιρέσεως expetantur. In his voluntas sæpè fertur absque præuio rationis iudicio, ex sola libertate sua. Tales volitiones vel sunt ἐμμένουσαι, quæ obiectum habent internum, qualis est volitio intelligendi vel rem quandam hoc tempore considerandi; quæ interna actio sæpè citra suasionem intellectus ex solo hominis liberè agentis beneplacito suscipitur, aliàs progressus daretur in infinitum; vel μεταβαίνουσαι, quarum obiectum est externum, & vel finis, vel media. Finem vltimum & summum, voluntas φύσει sua expetit, nec cōsilium aut iudicium intellectus, num eum expetere debeat poscit aut expectat. Sic quando media habentur prorsus paria & æqualia, non ex præuio quodam mentis discursu, sed sæpius ex solo voluntatis beneplacito alterum accipitur.

LIV. Quæ vero sub προαίρεσιν propriè dictam cadunt, de ijs Bernardus scribit lib. de grat. & libero arbitr. Voluntas, quocunque se volverit, semper comitem rationem habet, non quòd semper ex ratione, sed quòd nunquam absque ratione moneatur. Concurrunt enim actus quatuor, quorum priores duo cum postremo omni volitioni communes sunt, tertius autem proprius manet διέξοδ rerum eligibilium: ex ijs vltimum ad voluntatem, præcedentes ad intellectum referimus. 1. Est Obiecti cognitio, quia voluntas in nullam rem fertur, nisi quæ sit præcognita, 2. Est cogniti propositio, quia cum intellectus obiectum cognouit, tunc illud voluntati vel ad eligendum vel ad negligendum proponit. 3. Est Propositi persuasio vel dissuasio. Si enim intellectus rem quandam putet conuenientem, tum suadet voluntati; Sin verò inconuenientem, diffuadet. 4. Est persuasio electio, cum illud quod eligibile iudicatum fuit ab intellectu, voluntas eligit omniq; nisu in id vnice fertur & contendit.

LV. Eligit autem voluntas, non impulsa ab alio quodam principio vel externo, vel interno, a se diuerso sed ipsa seipsam immediate mouet, & ad agendum applicat: alioquin actio voluntatis non esset libera. Proinde intellectui conceditur quidem persuadens iudicium, sed denegatur imperium. Iudicat quid sit eligibile, in voluntatis tamen arbitrio manet, iudicanti intellectui libere obedire vel reluctari. Est ratio, inquit alicubi Bernardus, data voluntati, vt instruat illam, non vt destruat. Destrueret autem si necessitatem vllam imponeret, quo minus pro arbitrio suo sese volueret. Et commentator Damasceni in l. 2. de O.F. c. 26. scribit: Nostrarum actionum intellectus principium saltem directivum est, voluntas vero imperativum atque primario effectivum.

LVI. Quod ipsum vt distinctius intelligatur, dicimus, res eligibiles vel suo genere esse malas aut bonas, vel neque bonas neque malas, sed indifferentes. Si bonæ sunt malæue, eligimus eas & sectamur vel ex habitu, vel sine habitu, Si ex habitu, non semper actu præcedit iudicium & deliberatio mentis, sed voluntas sæpe per istum habitum promtissime fertur in obiectum, vt intemperans in potationes & libidines, quæ actiones non sunt simpliciter liberæ & contingentes, nisi quoad principium, sed quodammodo necessariæ, vnde nonnulli vocant eas virtualiter liberas, nonformaliter. Sin autem ἄνευ ἕξεως bene vel male agimus, ibi semper iudicium rationis præcedit, sed geminum, sibique inuicem oppositum. Duo enim in homine diuersissima sunt principia, ὀρθότης κακότης, rectitudo a notitijs naturalibus dependens, & depravatio rationis, ex peccato suborta, & prurigine variorum affectuum vndiquaque permixta. Aliter judicat ratio bimus. Ita enim plenior quæstionis cognitio habebitur, & volitionis omnisŃue electionis ratio melius intelligetur.

LIII. Dicimus ergo, quòd res, quæ sub volitionem liberam cadunt, vel προαιρετικῶς, vel ἀπροαιρέτως expetuntur. In has voluntas sæpè fertur absque præuio rationis iudicio, ex sola libertate sua. Tales volitiones vel sunt ἐμμένουσαι, quæ obiectum habent internum, qualis est volitio intelligendi vel rem quandam hoc tempore considerandi; quæ interna actio sæpè citra suasionem intellectus ex solo hominis liberè agentis beneplacito suscipitur, aliàs progressus daretur in infinitum; vel μεταβαίνουσαι, quarum obiectum est externum, & vel finis, vel media. Finem vltimum & summum, voluntas φύσει sua expetit, nec cōsilium aut iudicium intellectus, num eum expetere debeat poscit aut expectat. Sic quando media habentur prorsus paria & æqualia, non ex præuio quodam mentis discursu, sed sæpius ex solo voluntatis beneplacito alterum accipitur.

LIV. Quæ vero sub προαίρεσιν propriè dictam cadunt, de ijs Bernardus scribit lib. de grat. & libero arbitr. Voluntas, quocunque se volverit, semper comitem rationem habet, non quòd semper ex ratione, sed quòd nunquam absque ratione moueatur. Concurrunt enim actus quatuor, quorum priores duo cum postremo omni volitioni communes sunt, tertius autem proprius manet διεξόδῳ rerum eligibilium: ex ijs vltimum ad voluntatem, præcedentes ad intellectum referimus. 1. Est Obiecti cognitio, quia voluntas in nullam rem fertur, nisi quæ sit præcognita. 2. Est cogniti propositio, quia cum intellectus obiectum cognouit, tunc illud voluntati vel ad eligendum vel ad negligendum proponit. 3. Est Propositi persuasio vel dissuasio. Si enim intellectus rem quandam putet conuenientem, tum suadet voluntati; Sin verò inconuenientem, dissuadet. dissuadet. 4. Est persuasi electio, cum illud quod eligibile iudicatum fuit ab intellectu, voluntas eligit omniq; nisu in id vnicè fertur & contendit.

LV. Eligit autem voluntas, non impulsa ab alio quodam principio vel externo, vel interno, à se diuerso sed ipsa seipsam immediatè mouet, & ad agendum applicat: alioquin actio voluntatis non esset libera. Proinde intellectui conceditur quidem persuadens iudicium, sed denegatur imperium. Iudicat quid sit eligibile, in voluntatis tamen arbitrio manet, iudicanti intellectui liberè obedire vel reluctari. Est ratio, inquit alicubi Bernardus, data voluntati, vt instruat illam, non vt destruat. Destrueret autem si necessitatem vllam imponeret, quò minus pro arbitrio suo sese volveret. Et commentator Damasceni in l. 2. de O. F. c. 26. scribit: Nostrarum actionum intellectus principium saltem directivum est, voluntas verò imperativum atque primario effectivum.

LVI. Quod ipsum vt distinctiùs intelligatur, dicimus, res eligibiles vel suo genere esse malas aut bonas, vel neque bonas neque malas, sed indifferentes. Si bonæ sunt malave, eligimus eas & sectamur vel ex habitu, vel sine habitu, Si ex habitu, non semper actu præcedit iudicium & deliberatio mentis, sed voluntas sæpè per istum habitum promtissimè fertur in obiectum, vt intemperans in potationes & libidines, quæ actiones non sunt simpliciter liberæ & contingentes, nisi quoad principium, sed quodammodo necessariæ, vnde nonnulli vocant eas virtualiter liberas, non formaliter. Sin autem ἀνευ ἕξεως benè vel male agimus, ibi semper iudicium rationis præcedit, sed geminum, sibique inuicem oppositum. Duo enim in homine diuersissima sunt principia, ὀρθότης κακότης, rectitudo à notitijs naturalibus dependens, & depravatio rationis, ex peccato suborta, & prurigine variorum affectuum vndiquaque permixta. Aliter judicat ratio recta, aliter praua; vel homo potius, qui verum agens aliter sentit secundum rectam, & aliter secundum prauam rationem. Atque hinc judiciorum diuersitas, hinc lucta & pugna emergit in homine saepè grauissima.

LVII. Vt exemplum afferamus, cùm virtus proponitur, quæ vel sequenda vel fugienda, tum ratio deliberat quid faciendum sit, sed prorsus inæqualiter. In quantum recta est, & lumen notitiæ insitæ sequitur, virtutem eligendam, & voluptates vitandas statuit. Adfert insuper ingentem argumentorum struem, quibus hoc persuadere sollicitè allaborat: Sed recto huic judicio mox contradicitur per corruptionem carnis perturbationibus immissam, quæ ad voluptatem inclinat, & judicat longe vtiliùs ac consultiùs, si voluptas non virtus eligatur: Quid hic voluntas vel homo voluntate præditus agat? Hæret dubius, & cui assentiatur, ambigit. Considerat momenta argumentorum, & sæpè intelligit rationem rectam melioribus niti fundamentis. Quid fit; Assensum præbet rationi prauæ, & appetitui malo, nec virtutem sed voluptatem eligit, quamuis virtutem honestiorem esse cognoscat, sicuti, de se fatetur Medea Ouidiana lib. 7. Metamorph. Sed trahit inuitam noua vis, aliudque cupido. Mens aliud suadet: i’deo meliora proboque, Deteriora sequor.

LIIX Atque hic maximè apparet voluntatis libertas. Nec enim determinari potest à judicio rationis, cùm illud duplicatum sit & contrarium, suadens tum bonum ἀληθές, quod realiter; tum φαινόμενον, quod apparenter bonum est. Neque argumentis semper eò adducitur, cùm ex parte rationis stent & stare cognoscat solidiora, sed ex mera αὐδοκίᾳ, rationis rectæ judicio spreto, pravæ acceptato, sensu irritante, appetitu solicitante, voluptatem homo eligit, & virtutem auersatur. Hoc enim nisi foret, quam causam diceremus, cur duobus æqualiter animo & corpore affectis, obiecta eadem pulchritudine, vnus illorum ad illicitè perfruendum moueatur, alter in voluntate pudica stabilis perseueret? In vtroque recta ratio dissuafit, deprauata suasit impudicitiam, pulchritudo corporis vtriusque aspectui pariter obiecta est, vterque ab externi principij impulsu immunis fuit, ea tamen hic ad illicitum facinus declinauit, ille ab eodem abhorruit, vbi causam aliam nemo afferre poterit, nisi solam voluntatis potestatem liberam.

LIX. Quod vero attinet res indifferentes, & suo genere nec bonas, nec malas, eæ sunt vel obiecta externa vel actus interni, vtspeculari, meditari, &c. Vtrorumque electio prærequirit iudicium rationis, quod itidem vel simplex est, vel geminatum Fit enim sæpiùs, vt in volitione rerum indifferentium duplex præcedat iudicium, non quidem contrarium, sicut in bonis malisue, sed contradictorium, quando vnum habetur obiectum, idque intellectus eligendum vel non eligendum esse, respectibus tamen diuersis existimat. Vt si ad conuiuium voceris, mens iudicat, esse comparendum, iure amicitiæ & humanitatis; mox ad euitandas potationes, ne intersis admonet. Vides hîc duo iudicia, non contraria sed contradictoria, quia rem vnam alterum suadet, dissuadet alterum. Vbi summa iterum voluntatis est libertas, quippe potens vel isti vel illi iudicio obtemperare.

LX. Quod si verò simplex sit intellectus iudicium, motionem illi non imperatiuam, sed suasoriam tantum concedimus, quæ voluntatem non euertat, Licèt enim ratio, quid agendum sit, ostendat moneatque, & voluntas momenti obsequatur, non tamen coactè sequitur, vel prorsus necessariò, verùm liberrimè, quoniam suasio intellectus non cogit neque necessitat, sed solùm amicè inuitat, cui quod non reluctatur voluntas, id non ex inipulsu quodam necessario, sed ex libero voluntatis arbitrio dependet.

LXI. Si obijcias: Voluntas non potest aliquid velle sine iudicio intellectus. Ergo si iudicium est indeterminatum, & ipsa voluntas erit indeterminata: Si iudicium determinatum & ipsa erit determinata: Sed vltimum iudicium practicum est omnino determinatum. Ergo voluntas necessario eliget illud, quod vltimum iudicium determinat esse eligendum. Respondemus, negando consequentiam, quia in eo consistit libertas voluntatis, vt posito determinato intellectus iudicio omnibusque alijs ad agendum requisitis, ipsa adhuc maneat indeterminata & libera. Si quæras, à quo tandem determinetur? Dicimus, à seipsa, quia hæc liberæ potestatis natura est, vt seipsam immediatè moueat, & ad agendum applicet. Reliquæ obiectiones Bellarmini solutæ habentur apud Becanum tom. 1. c. 2. quæst. 5. p. 41. seqq. ideoq; nihil addere sed fratres potiùs sociosque illos committere volumus.

LXII. Ita ergo hactenus probatuum est, quòd voluntas verè sit libera, suamque ab intellectu libertatem non mutuetur. Est autem libera non internè tantùm & elicitiuè, vt vocant, sed externè etiam & imperatiuè, h. e. non solùm ipsa suorum actuú est Domina, & illos ἀντίρτως producit suspenditque sed & potentijs plerumque imperat alijs, easque pro lubitu vel ad agendum applicat, vel ab agendo reuocat.

LXIII. Ex quibus probè consideratis respondere facile est ad quæstionem illam: Num libera voluntas passiua vel actiua sit potētia? Quāuis enim passiua posset nominari, quatenº ab obiecto mouetur, & actus suos in se recepit, propriè tamen actiua est, quoniam in agēdo occupata, & suos ipsa actus effectiuè producit Interim non absolutè actiuam esse censemus, vt Bellarmino placet lib 3 ca. 10. cùm ab obiecto suo moueatur, & semper intellectus cognitio, in plerisque suasio prærequiratur. Mirum autem sit, quâ ratione Bellarminus liberum arbitrum pro potentia simpliciter actiua habere possit, cum cap. 7. 8. 9 acriter defendat, illud ab vltimo practicæ rationis judicio determinari. At verò determinari ab alio est passiuè se ad aliud habere. Et Thomas parte 1 quæst. 80. art. 1. voluntatem seu appetitum intellectiuum, expressè vocat potentiam passiuam, quia mouetur ab obiecto cognito, vnde iterum conficta & fucata Papicolarum consensio elucescit. Bellarminus alias prolixus est c. 10. & 11. circa hanc quæstionem, & fermè seipsum non intelligit. Res tota paucis cõponi potest, si voluntas dicatur potentia passiua, quatenus mouetur ab obiecto, sed actiua, quatenus suos ipsa actus liberè & effectiuè producit.


### Question VIII. What kind of liberty is required so that something may be called free?

LXIV. Bellarmine proposes this question in book 3, chapter 4, and establishes that for the constitution of free will, a twofold liberty is required, both from necessity and from coercion. He disputes so slippery, and makes a pretense with so many ambiguities, that it is difficult to perceive whether he understands himself, and whether he agrees with us or otherwise. For 1, he did not sufficiently explain which necessity he wishes to be excluded, since he could not have been ignorant of how ambiguous that term is.

LXV. It is commonly recounted in the schools. 1. Absolute necessity, which is of God. 2. Logical, or of demonstration. 3. Physical, or of causes. 4. Hypothetical, or of consequence. 5. Political, or of obligation. In Scripture, various species of necessity are read, as noted by Pareus in book 3 on free will, chapter 4, page 397. There is given a necessity of affliction and distress, Psalm 25, v. 17. The necessity of indigence: Rom. 13, v. 13. The necessity of obligation 1 Cor. 9, v. 16. Rom. 13, v. 5. The necessity of dependence, Psalm 104, 29. John 15, v. 15. The necessity of immutability, which is either absolute 2 Tim. 2, v. 13, or hypothetical Heb. 9, verse 16. He ought, therefore, to have explained in the first place which necessity he wishes to be understood, from which our free will ought to be free.

LXVI. For that not every necessity is repugnant to liberty, he has provided proof several times by his own testimony. In Book 5, On Justification, chapter 11, he distinguishes between internal necessity, which is the determination of natural power to one thing, and external, which arises from divine governance and the inclination of the will to choose the good. This necessity, he says, does not dissolve liberty, nor the reason of merit, and such was the case not only in Christ, but also in those who are said to be confirmed in grace. In Book 5, On Grace and Free Will, chapter 8, speaking of the state of sin, he writes thus: Now a certain necessity of sinning is present from vice, not from the condition of nature: From which necessity we ask to be delivered when we say, Deliver me from my necessities. Book 3, On Free Will, c. 3, he contends sharply that the will depends necessarily, is necessarily determined by the final judgment of reason; and necessarily chooses that which the final judgment of reason has determined is to be chosen. But if the matter is so, why then in chapter 5 does he write absolutely that liberty from necessity is entirely required for free will: and that elective power cannot be understood with determination to one thing and necessity: If the will, with liberty preserved, is determined by the judgment of reason, why could it not, with the same preserved, be determined to one thing either by the perfection of nature, as in God, only to the good: or by the perfection of grace, as in the Angels only to the good: or by the perfection of malice, as in the Demons immutably, in sinful men mutably, only to evil, as will be declared more fully a little later, Book 3, chapter 17, arguing that it is not of the reason and essence of free will to be able to will good and evil: or to be able now to will one thing and later to be unwilling: or not to be able to choose unless consultation in reality precedes: but that it is enough, if one has the option of different things and the choice is made with the full and perfect judgment of reason. Why therefore in ch. 5 and 6 does he judge that indifference and power toward opposites, without any necessity and determination toward one, pertain to the constitution of free will? In book 3, ch. 4, he writes that God's willing, with respect to an intrinsic object; when God wills his own essence, power, goodness, etc., to be necessary. In book 5, ch. 30, he says: Necessity is manifold, but not all of it is repugnant to the freedom of free will, to which he refers 1. the necessity of suffering the motions of concupiscence. 2. the necessity of sinning from ignorance. 3. the necessity of divine grace to avoid sins. 4. The necessity of having some venial sin. 5. The necessity of doing evil acts once an evil and efficacious will is posited. From all of which it is clear how many various species of necessity coexisting with freedom Bellarmine was driven by the force of truth to acknowledge. For besides the five species just enumerated, he concedes: 1. The necessity of divine government and ordination: 2. The necessity of sinning in the state of the fall: 3. The necessity of determination made by the intellect: 4. The necessity of the object or propensity toward one general object alone, all of which ought to have been expressed in the formation of the state; lest the reader be deceived by equivocation and the knowledge of the truth be rendered intricate. But the adversary wished to hide under an ambiguous term, so that it might not be clear to the reader whether he approves of our opinion or the Scholastic one, although elsewhere, when he is engaged outside the conflict of this question, he is compelled to speak and think with us.

LXVII. II. The distinction between coercion and necessity is not always observed in the writings of the Fathers, which, since the cunning Jesuit knew this, he has gathered various testimonies against us, where every necessity seems to be excluded from free will, and yet nothing else than coercion is understood, because if one is held, the whole Bellarminian demonstration falls, since it is built upon the sayings of the Fathers alone, with the exception of a single apocryphal passage of Scripture. We say, therefore, that the word necessity is sometimes taken for coercion and external violence, both in the Scriptures and in the commentaries of the Fathers. 1 Corinthians 8, verse 37: 'He is not compelled by necessity, but has it in his power.' 2 Corinthians 9, verse 7: 'Not out of sadness or necessity.' To Philemon, verse 16: 'That it might not be as if by necessity.' And the Greek to compel ἀναγκάζειν is to necessitate, to which the passage Luke 14, verse 23 refers: ἀνάγκασον compel, force, necessitate to enter. In the Fathers, almost innumerable sayings occur where necessity is taken for coercion, so that it seems superfluous to cite the passages. Coercion, therefore, is comprehended under necessity as a species under a genus, in which sense we also, with the Fathers, liberally concede that the will is free from necessity.

LXVIII. Thus, therefore, the frauds of Bellarmine, which he committed regarding the formation of the state, having been briefly exposed, it remains to declare what our opinion is. First, however, a twofold acceptation of liberty occurs, the one true and proper, the other too strict and short. This is when liberty is taken for the choice of means only, or for indifference both as to specification and as to exercise. In this sense, some distinguish liberty in reality from the will, as an inferior from a superior, and therefore they judge everything free to be voluntary, but not vice versa. Since, however, a power is not given, just as an accident of an accident is not, we do not separate liberty from the will by a real distinction, and thus every voluntary action is for us free, just as for them everything free is voluntary.

LXIX. We are not indeed ignorant that human actions are sometimes divided in the ethical schools so that some things are called free, others necessary? Yet all these have the same productive principle, namely the will. This, however, is nothing other than a free power, from which the individual and universal actions of an intelligent nature draw their origin. We do not therefore deny that some distinction is found in the acts of the will, while some include or presuppose indifference, others exclude it, and if the terms are taken strictly, these free acts can be pointed out as necessary: yet since, speaking precisely, the will and its liberty are one, therefore everything voluntary is likewise free. For they have one cause of their origin, nor do some actions proceed from a free power and others from a non-free one, but all are free daughters of one free mother, namely the will. And therefore true liberty for us is not that indifference, flexibility, and ambiguity, opposed to constancy, but the very free power of the will to will or not to will. Whatever therefore it wills, it wills this freely; what it does, it does freely; when it suspends an act, it suspends it freely, so indeed that if you have called anything voluntary and not at the same time free, you have immediately pronounced an opposite in the thing posited.

LXX. With these things thus presupposed, it will easily be evident that liberty and necessity do not conflict, but often concur in the same action, since many voluntary acts, which are free by that very fact, are at the same time necessary. Before we demonstrate this in particular, this must be noted beforehand, that there are two species of necessity, opposing the nature of liberty. The former is called physical necessity, which is the determination of a brute nature to always act in one and the same way, either from divine ordination, as the sun is moved; or from an occult instinct of nature, just as bees make honey. The latter is called coaction or coercive necessity, which is the determination of a rational nature to one, beyond or against the will by a violent external principle, as defined by Pareus in book 3, On Free Will, chapter 4. That free will cannot consist with such necessity, we willingly concede to him: but if other species are assumed, as is the necessity of immutability, hypothetical necessity, the necessity of sinning, of obligation, of object, of dependence, and the like, then we deny that the nature of liberty is immediately destroyed by them. A most clear example is held in the Scriptures concerning the passion of Christ, which he himself undertook for us with the highest will, and yet undertook necessarily or immutably, on account of the divine ordination, whence it is said, it behooved Christ to suffer, Luke 24, v. 26. Thus it must be done, Matt. 26, v. 54. The Son of Man must suffer, Mark 8, 31. If therefore Christ suffered voluntarily for us, and at the same time necessarily, it follows that some voluntary thing can be necessary, and some necessary thing can be voluntary. In order that this very thing may be better understood, we shall weigh the individual conditions of free substances, of which since there are four, God, Angels, Demons, man: something remains to be said about each one:

LXXI. I. God, although he is a most free agent; nevertheless wills and does very many things necessarily. And indeed a twofold necessity is found in his actions: The former is supreme and absolute with respect to internal actions; when God wills himself, his wisdom, and other attributes, which he cannot not will and approve. The latter is hypothetical with respect to external actions, which he produces and effects outside of himself. Moreover, regarding an action, there is usually considered both the genus itself, whether it be good or evil, and the species or individual, whether it be this or that. If the genus of divine actions is looked at, the necessity of immutability falls upon God. For from the perfection of his nature, which cannot deviate from the true good, he has immutably determined himself to one in genus, that is, to good only: For because he is essentially

Latin:

LXIV. Proponit hanc quæstionem Bellarminus l. 3. cap. 4. & statuit, Ad constitutionem liberi arbitrij duplicem requiri libertatem, tum à necessitate, tum à coa- &ione. Ita vero lubricè disputat, & tot ambiguitatibus fucum facit, vt num seipsum intelligat, & an nobiscum sentiat, vel secus, difficulter animaduerti queat. Nam 1. non satis explicuit, quam necessitatem exclusam velit, cum ignorare non potuerit, quam ambiguus sit iste terminus.

LXV. Vulgò in scholis recensetur. 1. Necessitas absoluta, quæ Dei. 2. Logica, vel demonstrationis, 3. Physica, vel causarum. 4. Hypothetica, seu consequentiæ. 5. Politica, seu obligationis. In Scriptura variæ necessitatis species leguntur, notante Pareo lib. 3. de lib. arb. cap. 4. p. 397. Datur necessitasafflictionis & angustiæ, Psalm. 25. v. 17. necessitas indigentiæ: Rom. 13. v. 13. necessitas obligationis 1. Cor. 9. v. 16. Rom 13. v. 5. necessitas dependentiæ, Psalm. 104. 29. Ioh. 15. v. 15. necessitas immutabilitatis, quę vel absoluta 2. Tim. 2. v. 13. vel hypothetica Heb. 9, vers. 16. Explicare ergo inprimis debuisset, quam necessitatem velit intellectam, à qua liberum esse debeat nostrum arbitrium.

LXVI. Quòd enim non omnis necessitas libertati repugnet, suo ipsius testimonio aliquoties comprobatum dedit. l. 5. de iustific. cap. 11. distinguit inter necessitatem internam, quæ est naturalis potentiæ determinatio ad vnum, & externam, quæ oritur à gubernatione diuina, & voluntatis ad bonum eligendum inclinatione. Hæc necessitas, ait, non solvit libertatem, nec meriti rationem, & talis fuit non solum in Christo, sed etiam in ijs, qui dicuntur confirmati in gratia. L. 5. de grat. & lib. arbitr. cap. 8. de peccati statu verba faciens ita scribit: Nunc quædam peccamdi necessitas adest ex vitio; non ex conditione naturæ: A qua necessitate liberari petimus, cùm dicimus, De necessitatibus meis erue me. L. 3. de lib. arbitr. c. 3. acriter contendit, voluntatem necessario pendere, necessario determinari ab vltimo iudicio rationis; & necessario eligere id, quod vltimum iudicium rationis determinauit esse eligendum. Quod si res ita se habet, cur igitur cap. 5. absolutè scribit, Libertatem à necessitate omninò requiri ad liberum arbitrium: & potestatem electiuam intelligi non posse cum determinatione ad vnum & necessitate: Si voluntas salua libertate determinatur à iudicio rationis, cur non eâdem saluâ determinari posset ad vnum vel à perfectione naturæ, vt in Deo, tantùm ad bonum: vel à perfectione gratiæ, vt in Angelis tantùm ad bonum: vel à perfectione malitiæ, vt in Dæmonibus immutabiliter, in hominibus peccatoribus mutabiliter, tantùm ad malum, vti paulò pòst fusius declarabitur, L. 3. cap. 17. disput. non esse de ratione & essentia liberi arbitrij, posse velle bonum & malum: aut posse nunc velle vnum postea nolle: aut non posse eligere nisi consultatio reipsa præcedat: sed satis esse, si quis habeat optionem diuersarum rerum & electio fiat cum pleno atque perfecto iudicio rationis. Cur igitur cap. 5. & 6. ad constitutionem arbitrij pertinere censet indifferentiam & potestatē ad opposita, sine omhi necessitate & determinatione ad vnum? L. 3. ca: d. scribit, Dei velle, respectu obiecti intrinseci; quando Deus suam vult essentiam, potentiam; bonitatem &c. esse necessariam L. 5. c. 30. ait: Multiplex est necessitas, sed non omnis repugnat arbitrij libertati, quò refert 1. necessitatem patiendi motus concupiscentiæ. 2. necessitatem peccandi ex ignorantia. 3. necessitatem diuinæ gratiæ ad vitanda peccata. 4. Necessitatem habendi aliquod peccatum veniale. 5. Necessitatem faciendi actus malos positâ malâ & efficaci voluntate. Ex quibus omnibus patet, quàm varias necessitatis species cum libertate concurrētes agnoscere vi veritatis adactus fuerit Bellarminus. Nam præter species quinque modò enumeratas concedit. 1. Necessitatem diuinæ gubernationis & ordinationis: 2. Necessitatem peccandi in statu lapsus: 3. Necessitatem determinationis ab intellectu factæ: 4. Necessitatem obiecti seu propensionem ad vnum duntaxat generale obiectum, quæ omnia in status formatione exprimi debuissent; ne lector æquiuocatione falleretur & veritatis cognitio intricata redderetur. Verùm latere voluit aduersarius sub ambiguo vocabulo, vt nostramnè an Scholasticam opinionem adprobet, lectori constare nequeat, alibi tamen extra conflictum huius quæstionis cùm versatur, nobiscum loqui & sentire cogitur.

LXVII. II. Distinctio coactionis & necessitâtis in Patrum scriptis nō semper obseruatur, quòd cùm nouisset Iesu vvita callidus testimonia contra nos varia congessit, vbi videtur excludi ab arbitrio omnis necessitas, & nil tamen aliud quam coactio intelligitur, quod vnum si tenetur, cadit omnis demonstratio Bellarminiana, quipe pe solis Patrum dictis, excepto vnico Scripturæ loco apocrypho superstructa. Dicimus ergo, necessitatis vocabulum nonnunquam pro coactione sumi, & externa violentia, tum in Scripturis, tum in Patrum commentarijs. In Scripturis, vt 1. Corinth. 8. vers. 37. Non adigitur necessitate, sed in potestate habet. 2. Corinth. 9. vers. 7. Non ex tristitia aut necessitate. Ad Philem. vers. 16. Vt ne velut ex necessitate. Et Græcis cogere ἀναγκάζειν necessitare, quo spectat locus Luc. 14. vers. 23. ἀνάγκασον coge, compelle necessita intrare. In Patribus innumera ferè dicta occurrunt, vbi necessitas pro coactione accipitur, vt loca allegare superuacaneum videatur. Coactio igitur sub necessitate tanquam species sub genere comprehenditur, quo sensu & nos cum Patribus arbitrium à necessitate liberum esse liberaliter concedimus.

LXVIII. Ita ergo fraudibus Bellarmini, quas circa status formationem commisit, breuiter expositis, quæ nostra sit sententia declarandum restat. Primum autem occurrit duplex libertatis acceptio, altera vera & propria: altera nimis stricta & curta. Hæc est, quando libertas sumitur pro electione mediorum tantùm, seu pro indifferentia tum quoad specificationem tum quoad exercitium. Hoc sensu libertatem nonnulli reipsâ distinguunt à voluntate, vt inferius à superiori, ideoque omne liberum arbitrantur esse voluntarium, sed non vice versa. Cum autem potentia non detur, sicut nec accidentis accidens, propterea libertatem à voluntate reali discrimine non seuingimus, adeoque omnis actio voluntaria nobis est libera, sicut ijs omne liberum est voluntarium.

LXIX. Non quidem ignoramus, actiones humanas quandoque ita diuidi in scholis Ethicis, vt quædam dicantur liberæ, quædam necessariæ? Idem tamen hæ omnes principium productiuum habent, videlicet voluntatem. Hæc autem nihil aliud est, quàm potentia libera, à qua ortum trahunt naturæ intelligentis actiones singulæ & vniuersæ. Non ergo diffitemur, in voluntatis actibus discrimen aliquod inueniri, dum quidam includunt, aut præsupponunt indifferentiam, alij excludunt illosque strictim si sumantur vocabula, liberos hos necessarios indigitari posse: attamen cum ἀκριβῶς loquendo voluntas eiusque libertas vnum sint, idcircò omne volūtarium pariter est liberum. Vnam enim originis suæ habent causam, neque actiones quædam à potentia libera, quædam à non libera proueniunt, sed omnes vnius liberæ matris, nempè voluntatis, liberæ sunt filiæ. Ac proinde libertas vera nobis non est indifferentia, flexibilitas & ambiguitas illa, constantiæ opposita, sed ipsa voluntatis volendi vel nolendi potestas libera.
