Quicquid ergo vult, hoc liberè vult, quæ agit, liberè agit; Cùm actum suspendit, liberè suspendit, ita quidem, vt si quidpiam voluntarium dixeris, nec vnà liberum, mox oppositum in apposito pronunciaueris.

LXX. Quibus ita præsuppositis, patebit facilè, libertatem & necessitatem non pugnare, sed in eadem sæpè actione concurrere, cùm multi actus voluntarij, qui eo ipso liberi simul sint necessarij. Quod antequam in specie demonstremus, prænotandum hoc occurrit, quòd duæ sint necessitatis species, libertatis naturæ aduersantes. Prior vocatur necessitas Physica, quæ est determinatio naturæ brutæ ad vnum semper eodem modo agendum, vel ex ordinatione diuina, vti Sol mouetur; vel ex occulto naturæ instinctu, velut apes mellificant. Posterior vocatur coactio vel coactiona necessitas, quæ est determinatio naturæ rationalis ad vnum, præter vel contra voluntatem à violento externo principio, definiente Pareo lib. 3. de lib. arb. cap. 4. Cum tali necessitate liberum arbitrium consistere non posse, lubenter ipsi concedimus: Sin vero aliæ species assumantur, vt est necessitas immutabilitatis, hypothetica, peccandi, obligationis, obiecti, dependentiæ & similes, tùm libertatis naturam per eas protinus tolli negatum imus. Clarissimum habetur exemplum in Scripturis de Christi passione, quam ipse summâ voluntate pro nobis suscepit, & tamen necessariò vel immutabiliter suscepit, ob diuinam ordinationem, vnde dicitur, oportuit Christu pati Luc. 24. v. 26. Ita oportet fieri Matt. 26. v. 54. oportet filium hominis pati, Marc. 8. 31. Si ergo Christus voluntariè pro nobis passus est, & simul necessariò, sequitur voluntarium aliquod necessarium, & necessarium aliquod voluntarium esse posse. Quod ipsum vt meliùs intelligatur, singulas liberarum substantiarum conditiones ponderabimus, quarum cùm sint, quatuor, Deus, Angeli, Dæmones, homo: de singulis aliquid dicendum superest:

LXXI. I. Deus, quamuis sit liberrimum agens; plurima tamen vult & facit necessariò. Et quidem duplex in actionibus eius reperitur necessitas: Prior est summa & absoluta respectu actionum internarum; quando Deus seipsum vult suam sapientiam & cætera attributa, quæ non potest non velle & adprobare. Posterior est hypothetica respectu actionum externarum, quas extra se producit & efficit. Solet autem circa actionem considerari tum genus ipsum, num bona vel mala sit, tum species vel indiuiduum, num hæc aut illa sit, Si genus actionum diuinarum aspiciatur, cadit in Deum necessitas immutabilitatis. Ex perfectione enim naturæ suæ, quæ à vero bono aberrare nequit, seipsum immutabiliter determinauit ad vnum genere, hoc est, ad bonum tantum: Nam quia essentialiter bo-


### Question VIII. What kind of liberty is required so that something may be called…: good, nay, He is goodness itself

good, nay, He is goodness itself. Hence it follows that God necessarily acts well when He acts, and cannot but work well. Nor indeed is this necessity contrary to liberty, which Augustine acknowledged in book 22 of The City of God, chapter 30, writing thus: As for God Himself, must we deny that He has free will because He cannot sin? And he argues to the same effect in book 5, chapter 10: If that necessity is defined according to which we say it is necessary that something be so, or be done so, I do not know why we should fear it, lest it take away from us the liberty of the will. For we do not place both the life of God and His foreknowledge under necessity (understand: of coercion, which takes away liberty) if we say it is necessary that God always sees and foreknows all things. Lombard agrees in book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 25, letters C and D, nor could Bellarmine clearly deny it in book 3, chapter 6.

LXXII. Furthermore, when divine action is considered in species or individual, a distinction must be made between His decree and its execution. The decree itself concerning external actions is not necessary, but so free that God could even decree the contrary: however, the execution, after the decree is made, is hypothetically necessary. For those things which God has once decreed, He necessarily executes, nor can He fail to execute them, since otherwise mutability and the fallibility of decrees would fall upon Him. Therefore, in the election, not the execution, the indeterminacy of divine liberty is chiefly to be observed. Thus, most freely, not necessarily, He decreed the creation of the world in time, and the redemption of the human race through the passion of the Son, etc. A twofold liberty, however, occurs in divine decrees: both of contrariety, by which He chooses one from several things proposed, and of contradiction, by which, one thing being proposed, He either chooses or rejects it, just as such examples of divine actions are everywhere obvious from the Scriptures.

LXXIII. Therefore, to summarize the nature of divine liberty, it should be noted, first, that that which God wills, either exists within Himself or outside of Himself. If within, and it is the same as Himself, He wills those things freely indeed and not under compulsion, yet necessarily, and indeed by absolute necessity. But if outside of Himself, then He either chooses or executes; the execution, on account of the infallibility of the decree, is necessary, and yet free, because it is not compelled. The choice has an attached necessity regarding the genus, or regarding the mode of action, because God necessarily chooses the good; but as regards the species or the individual action, the will of God is clearly free and indeterminate, even with the freedom of contrariety. For He can choose this or that out of many, He can, with one thing proposed, either embrace it or otherwise; so that freedom falls to God, both from necessity and from compulsion, regarding determined or singular external actions, which Bellarmine himself admits several times is sufficient for asserting free will.

LXXIV. II. As regards the angels, one can consider in turn either the genus of actions or a certain species. The genus is necessary and defined, because from the perfection of grace in which the good angels are confirmed, they immutably determine their good wills to one thing in genus, that is, to the good only, and thus they necessarily act well. In species, however, the actions of the angels are either commanded or elicited, as the ethicists say. Regarding actions commanded by God, the angels lack the freedom of contradiction: for they do not have the license to execute or not execute that which is commanded by God, but they necessarily carry out the commands of God, Psalm 103, v. 20, and yet they do it with the greatest will and pleasure. Where there is pleasure, there is freedom, says the Commentator on Damascene in book 2, de O. F., ch. 24. But the elicited actions of the angels can proceed from free will and the freedom of contrariety and contradiction, free from necessity and compulsion. For they can at this time converse and not converse, which is the freedom of contradiction: and they can, with various means proposed, a certain to choose something, which is the liberty of contrariety.

LXXV. III. Necessity of immutability likewise falls upon demons regarding the genus, because from the perfection of their malice they immutably determine their evil wills to one thing in genus, that is, to evil only: but contingently to one thing in species or individual, that is, to this or that, or to another evil, which however we wish to be understood only of elicited actions. But commanded actions are twofold; for they tend either to the benefit or to the punishment of man. If to the benefit of man and the own ruin of the demons, then they act not only necessarily, but moreover under compulsion, whence it is clear that the execution of diabolical actions commanded by God differs much from angelic. The latter is joined with the will and pleasure of those executing it; but the former is not, as when God commands the devil to go out from an obsessed man, the action is compelled, not free: But if it falls to the punishment of man, who ought to be afflicted and tormented, then indeed Satan does it necessarily, who is bound to obey the commands of the Lord always, which is a necessity of dependence and obligation, yet at the same time he is free and acts with the greatest pleasure, without any compulsion and violence.

LXXVI. IV. As regards man, we can discourse about him partly philosophically, with respect to moral actions, partly theologically, with respect to different states. In moral actions a twofold necessity is detected, one regarding the object, the other regarding the act itself.

The object of the free will is only one, not indeed in number, but in species, namely the good, whether true or apparent. For the will cannot desire evil, as evil. There is therefore no indifference here, but a termination to one thing in species; acts of the will regard either one object only, as the ultimate end; or several, as means. The act regarding the ultimate end is necessary (but I am speaking of specification not of exercise), namely its volition and desire, for all necessarily wish to be blessed, and not only do they not wish to be miserable, but they cannot even wish it. Therefore the ultimate end is necessarily desired, and yet freely. But where there are many means, there is given a preceding act, and there is also given a consequent one: The preceding is indifferent. For I can wish or not wish to choose or not choose one means. The consequent, however, is necessary, for when I have firmly pre-chosen this means, I cannot not neglect the others, and yet I neglect them freely. In those things also which cohere, if we wish for one, it is necessary that we wish for the other. Thus from the will to cross the sea arises a necessity in the will that it should wish for a ship: Thus, friendship being presupposed as indissoluble, I cannot not love a friend, and yet I love freely; whence Caelius Rhodiginus says, No necessity is considered more voluntary than that of love.

LXXVII. Just as some necessity is found in the actions of men, so also is indifference or mutability: For free will is, in respect of exercise, in acts both elicited and commanded: But especially in acts good or evil in their own kind is this indifference most observed, and it is twofold. I. Regarding the special object. For there are two contraries, virtue and vice: to neither is the will of man determined, but it is permitted to follow either at its own discretion. II. Regarding the acts themselves. For it is permitted to the will to follow or not to follow virtue, it is permitted to flee or to follow vice, nor does it necessarily indulge in virtues or vices. And this twofold indifference is rightly heeded by politicians and legislators, who decree punishments or rewards. For no one is worthy of praise or blame, punishment or reward, who is destitute of this indifference. Whence it also came about that afterwards, in common parlance, nothing other than this indetermination was understood by the name of liberty. But we rightly judge that a distinction must be made between the acceptance of the term Political, and accurately Philosophical. Politicians indeed, and even Ethicists, when speaking of virtues and vices, rightly accept liberty as indifference. But if we consider the matter accurately, the will itself is certainly denoted, inasmuch as it is free not through something superadded, but through itself, for which reason we pronounce even the actions of the will, as such, all to be free, even if they are necessary.

LXXIIX. Nor yet by this do we assert that any operations whatsoever, which are not forced, are free. Fire is not forced upward, water is not forced downward: yet they are not carried freely. Such effects are indeed free from force, but not simply free. Therefore we do not oppose the free to the necessary or the unforced, but primarily and per se to the involuntary. For just as the will, because it is the will and insofar as it is the will, and thus is free through itself, so also its actions, because they are actions of the will, and insofar as they are of the will, are free. Therefore also their opposite is nothing other than the involuntary. For every involuntary thing, because it is involuntary, and insofar as it is involuntary, is not free.

LXXIX. But when we consider man theologically, different states are to be attended to, namely: 1. Innocence. 2. Guilt. 3. Grace. 4. Glory. The liberty of men in the state of glory behaves in the same way as the liberty of the Angels, of which we spoke in thesis 74. Liberty in the state of innocence and grace agree almost entirely, and therefore only the state of integrity and the fall must be discussed, which can be dispatched in two assertions.

LXXX. 1. Man before the fall was free from necessity and force, as much regarding evil actions as good ones, with respect to both election and execution, and as much regarding specification as exercise. He was devoid of necessity before the fall, because God left him in the hand of his counsel, Ecclesiasticus 15. verse 14. freely therefore and contingently, not forcedly, not necessarily, he was then choosing and then pursuing good, he was now freely choosing and desiring evil, because he was not yet inclined to evil by an internal principle, and thus he was free from the servitude of sin, yet not from law or obligation, because it was only commanded to him that he should not sin. If therefore it is asked, Whether Adam before the fall had free power of choosing either good or evil, we answer, that he indeed had it, yet he ought not to have exercised the same. For God had commanded to choose and execute only good things. And hence appears the greatest difference between the liberty of God and of man, since God is most free from all law and obligation, for he has no superior, but man, since he is subject to God, was not endowed with that kind of liberty, yet he was free from coercion, from necessity, from sin and misery. Nor yet is it to be thought that man was more free than God, because his will was not determined to one thing, but indifferent: for this indetermination does not argue supreme liberty, but rather flexibility and ambiguity, opposed to constancy, and therefore, Luther in his book De servo arbitrio page 98 thinks that this will is more correctly named convertible and mutable than free. And the Commentator of Damascene says in book 2 de O. F. chapter 22. Convertibility is not required for the definition of liberty.

LXXXI. II. Man after the fall is free from coercion in all voluntary actions, since the will cannot be forced: he is free from necessity regarding the kind of actions considered theologically, which are evil and displeasing to God: for he has an internal principle of this necessity, namely original sin, by which the mind and will of man are so corrupted that nothing but evil things can proceed from them, for a bad tree is not productive of good fruits Matthew 7. verse 10. for which reason we are called by nature children of wrath Ephesians 2. verse 3.

& servants of sin Rom. 6. v. 17. But this necessity does not conflict with liberty, and therefore it could be called a voluntary necessity, and a necessary will, just as Bernard seems to hint in Sermon 81 on the Song of Songs: I know not by what perverse and wonderful way the will itself, having been changed for the worse by sin, makes a necessity for itself, so that necessity, when it is voluntary, cannot excuse the will, nor can the will, when it has been enticed, exclude necessity. And below: Thus the soul in a certain wonderful and evilly free way is held as a handmaid by necessity and is free, a handmaid on account of necessity, free on account of the will, and what is more wonderful and more miserable, it is guilty in that it is free, and a handmaid in that it is guilty, and by this it is a handmaid in that it is free.

LXXXII. But as regards the species of human actions, they are either commanded or elicited. As regards commanded actions, man is not free from law, although he is free from coercion and from necessity as regards execution and election, as when a magistrate commands that one must not steal, a man is indeed bound and held to obey, yet it is in the power of his judgment to choose to steal and to execute it or otherwise, which is the liberty of contradiction. He has furthermore the liberty of contrariety, as when an option is given to a delinquent by a magistrate to choose for a penalty either prison or a fine of money. As regards elicited actions, in turn, man is free from coercion and necessity both as regards election and execution. For he can freely and contingently, not necessarily, choose some morally good work, and after the election either execute it or not execute it, since election and execution differ much, nor do they necessarily cohere in human actions, as they do in divine ones. The reason for the diversity is easily given, because God is immutable, therefore what He has once decreed He will do, that He does immutably and necessarily: But man is mutable: whence it happens that he can now choose something, yet soon change his opinion, and not execute that which he chooses, although if the execution does not follow, let it be certain that the election also had been changed. For if the first election still held its place, without a doubt the execution would follow.

LXXXIII. And it is sufficiently apparent from this that liberty has been left to man in external actions, since he can do what he wills and not do what he does not will, although it sometimes happens in more specific actions that the human will is peculiarly inclined by God to do this and not that. We read an example of Cyrus, who in Isaiah ch. 45, verse 1, is called the Servant of the Lord; he conquered Babylon voluntarily, not under compulsion, yet his will was peculiarly directed and inclined to that by God: therefore that action was not contingent, but in a certain way necessary on account of the inclination of the will made divinely, which is commonly called the necessity of dependence. These, however, are extraordinary examples, which can prejudice ordinary ones in no way.

LXXXIV. Thus, therefore, through the individual species of free beings we have shown so far that liberty very often concurs with necessity and can consist with it most excellently, and that nothing is repugnant to free will other than the necessity of nature and of compulsion, which thing itself Bonaventure in book 2, dist. 25, q. 6, and Biel likewise in q. 1, taught before us, saying: Since there is a twofold necessity, of compulsion and of immutability, the necessity of compulsion is repugnant to the liberty of the will, but the necessity of immutability is not.

LXXXV. Regarding what Bellarmine might object to the contrary, he finds almost nothing. He alleges ch. 5, the saying of Ecclesiasticus 15, v. 14, which must be explained either concerning the state of integrity and grace, or if concerning the state of the fall, it notes only liberty in external matters and regarding exercise, where we do not deny that the will is indifferent and changeable. Thus the canons of councils and the sayings of the Fathers do not at all militate against us. For they either understand compulsion by necessity, or they speak of indifference regarding external actions, and as regards exercise. They do not, however, exclude all necessity in general and indistinctly from free will, just as Pareus shows in particular in book 3, chapter 5, page 415 and following. Afterwards he adds five reasons, but of little importance; nevertheless, in place of a conclusion, we shall briefly run through them. LXXXVI. 1. If freedom from coercion were sufficient for free will, it would follow that there is free will even in cattle. For they too are moved to fodder of their own accord without any coercion. Resp. Freedom from coercion alone is not sufficient, but freedom from physical necessity is required in addition, by which cattle are moved to fodder. Knowledge of the intellect and προαίρεσις of the agent are also required, both of which brutes lack. Since, therefore, man is free from both physical and coercive necessity, and acts by προαίρεσις, all of which are not found in brutes, it follows that man has free will, not cattle. 2. It would follow that in children, the insane, and those dreaming there is the use of free will, for they all act spontaneously. Resp. To act spontaneously is not to act by προαίρεσις, which is nevertheless required for the exercise of freedom. Because, therefore, that spontaneous motion in children and the insane arises not from the use of the rational, but of the sensitive appetite, for that reason they do not have the use of free will properly so called. 3. It would follow that God begat the Son through free will and by choice, since He did not beget Him under coercion. Resp. Although it may seem that it can be said in a certain way that the Father begat the Son freely, because not under coercion, we nevertheless judge it to be done more correctly if it is said simply that the Father begat the Son neither under coercion nor not under coercion; because He begat Him not by will, but by nature. 4. There would never have been any question about free will, nor would any controversy remain with heretics. For no one has ever denied that either God or men are free from coercion. Resp. Although there is consensus on this, disagreement nevertheless remains in many other matters. It must be disputed with the Stoics, Is God bound by the nexus of secondary causes? do all things happen by absolute necessity? with the Manichaeans, Does sin arise from a malignant nature rather than free will? with the Pelagians, Is the will sufficient unto itself without grace? With the Papists, Does the will of man concur efficiently to his own conversion? &c.

Finally 5. He seems to state contradictions who affirms that free will is freed from coercion, not from necessity, since it is an elective power, which cannot be understood with determination to one thing, and necessity. Resp. On the contrary, they are not contradictory. For the will remains an elective power, although it is involved in the necessity of immutability in certain respects, as we have shown by very many examples: it remains, moreover, free as to the exercise, although as to the species of acts it is determined to one kind.

Latin:

nus, imò ipsa bonitas est. hinc sequitur, Deum necessariò bene agere cum agit, & non posse non bene operari. Neque verò hæc necessitas libertati contraria est, quod agnouit Augustinus lib. 22. de Ciu. Dei cap. 30. ita scribens: Deus ipse, nunquid quoniam peccare non potest, ideò negandus est, habere liberum arbitrium? Et in eundem sensum lib 5. cap. 10. disputat. Si illa definitur necessitas secundum quam dicimus necesse esse, vt ita sit aliquid, vel ita fiat, nescio cur eam timeamus, ne nobis libertatem auferat voluntatis? Neque enim & vitam Dei & præscientiam sub necessitate ponimus (intellige coactionis, quæ tollit libertatem) Si dicamus necesse esse; Deum semper videre, & cuncta præscire. Consentit Lombardus l. 2. sent. dist. 25. lit. C. D. nec planè diffiteri potuit Bellarminus l. 3. c, 6.

LXXII. Porrò autem cum actio diuina consideratur in specie vel indiuiduo, distinguendum est inter eius decretum & executionem. Decretum ipsum de externis actionibus non est necessarium, sed ita liberum, vt possit Deus etiam contrarium decernere: Executio autem post factum decretum, hypotheticè est necessaria. Quæ enim Deus semel decreuit ea necessariò exequitur, nec potest non exequi, cum aliàs in ipsum caderet mutabilitas, & & decretorum fallibilitas. In electione igitur, non executione spectanda potissimum est libertatis diuinæ indeterminatio. Sic liberrimè, non necessariò decreuit creationem mundi in tempore, & redemptionem generis humani per passionem filij &c. Gemina verò libertas in decretis diuinis occurrit, tum contrarietatis quâ pluribus propositis vnum eligit, tum contradictionis, quâ vno propositoi istud vel eligit vel repudiat, quemadmodum talia diuinarum actionum exempla ex Scripturis passim sunt obuia.

LXXIII. Vt igitur in summam contrahamus libertatis diuinæ rationem, notari debet, Vti illud, quod Deus vult, vel esse intra ipsum, extra ipsum. Si intra, & idem est quod ipse, liberè quidem nec coactè illa vult, attamen necessariò, & quidem necessitate absolutâ. Sin extra ipsum tunc vel eligit vel exequitur, Executio ob infallibilitatem decreti est necessaria, & tamen libera, quia non coacta. Electio habet adiunctam necessitatem quoad genus, seu quoad modum actionis, quia Deus necessariò bonum eligit; quod ad speciem verò vel indiuiduum actionis, planè libera & indeterminata est Dei voluntas tùm libertate contrarietatis. Potest enim ex pluribus hoc aut illud eligere, potest vno proposito vel amplecti illud vel secus; vt ita in Deum cadat libertas, & à necessitate & à coactione, quoad determinatas vel singulares actiones externas, quod ad liberum arbitrium asserendum satis esse, Bellarminus ipse aliquoties fatetur.

LXXIV. II. Angelos quod spectat, vicissim considerari potest vel genus actionum, vel certa species. Genus est necessarium & definitum, quia ex perfectione gratiæ in qua confirmati sunt Angeli boni immutabiliter voluntates suas bonas determinant ad vnum genere, hoc est ad bonum tantùm, adeoque necessariò benè agunt. In specie autem actiones Angelorum vel sunt imperatæ, vel elicitæ, vt loquutur Ethici. Quoad actiones à Deo imperatas carent Angeli libertate contradictionis: nec n. habent licentiam id quod à Deo præcipitur exequendi vel non exequendi, verùm necessariò mandata Dei expediunt, Psalm. 103. v. 20. & tamen summa cum voluntate & voluptate id agunt. Vbi autem delectatio, ibi libertas, inquit Commentator Damasc. in l. 2. de O. F. c. 24. Actiones verò elicitæ Angelorum prouenire possunt ab arbitrio libero & libertate contrarietatis & contradictionis à necessitate & coactione. Possunt enim hoc tempore colloqui & non colloqui, quæ est libertas contradictionis: & possunt varijs medijs propositis, certum aliquod eligere, quæ est libertas contrarietatis.

LXXV. III. In dæmones similiter cadit necessitas immutabilitatis quoad genus, quia ex perfectione malitiæ immutabiliter voluntates suas malas determinant ad vnum genere h. e. ad malum tantùm: contingenter verò ad vnum specie vel indiuiduum h, e. ad hoc vel ad illud, vel ad aliud malum, quod tamen de actionibus elicitis tantùm intellectum volumus. Imperatæ verò sunt duplices, Vel enim tendunt in emolumentum, vel in supplicium hominis. Si in emolumentum hominis & propriam Dæmonum perniciem, tum non tantùm necessariò, sed insuper coactè operantur, vnde patet, quòd Diabolicæ actionum à Deo imperatarum executio multùm differat ab Angelica. Hæc n cum voluntate & voluptate exequentiũ est coniuncta; sed illa non item, vt quando Deus iubet Diabolum ex homine obsesso egredi, coacta est actio, non libera: Sin verò cadat in suppliciũ hominis, qui affligi & cruciari debet, tunc quidem necessariò id facit Satanas, qui mandatis Domini semper obedire tenetur, quę est necessitas dependentię & obligationis, simul tamen liber & cum summa voluptate, sine omni coactione & violẽtia.

LXXVI. IV. Hominem quod spectat, possumus de illo disserere partim Philosophicè, respectu actionum moralium, partim Theologicè, respectu diuersorũ statuum. In actionibus moralibus duplex deprehenditur necessitas, altera quoad obiectum, altera quoad actum ipsum.

Obiectum voluntatis liberæ tantum vnum est, non quidem numero, sed specie, bonum videlicet, siue ἀληθὲς, siue φαινόμενον Malum enim, quâ malum, voluntas velle nequit. Nulla igitur hîc indifferentia, sed terminatio ad vnum specie; Actus voluntatis vel vnum duntaxat objectum, vt finem vltimum; vel plura, vt media respiciunt. Actus quoad finem vltimum, est necessarius (loquor autẽ de specificationę non exercitio, ) nempè eius volitio & expetitio, Omnes enim beati esse necessariò volunt, & miseri esse non modò nolunt, sed nè velle quidem possunt. Necessariò ergo finis vltimus appetitur, & tamen liberè. Vbi verò multa sunt media, ibi datur actus præcedens, datur & consequens: Præcedens est indifferens. Possum enim medium vnum velle aut non velle eligere aut non eligere. Consequens autem necessarius est, Quando enim firmiter præelegi hoc medium, non possum non reliqua negligere & tamen liberè negligo. In ijs etiam quæ cohærent, si vnum volumus, necessum est vt velimus & alterum. Sic ex voluntate transeundi mare fit necessitas in voluntate, vt velit nauem: Sic præsuppositâ amicitiâ indissolubili, non possum non amicum diligere, & tamen liberè diligo; vnde Cælius Rhodiginus, Necessitas inquit, nulla magis censesur voluntaria, quàm amatoria.

LXXVII. Vti verò necessitas quæpiam in actionibus hominum inuenitur, ita & indifferentia seu vertibilitas: Libera enim voluntas est ratione exercitij in actibus tam elicitis quàm imperatis: Imprimis autem in actibus suo genere bonis vel malis hæc indifferentia maxime conspicitur, estque duplex. I. Quoad Obiectum speciale. Duo enim sunt contraria, virtus & vitium: ad neutrum voluntas hominis est determinata, sed licet illi vtrumque proarbitratu sequi, II. Quoad actus ipsos. Licet enim voluntati virtutem sectari vel non sectari, licet vitium fugere vel sequi, neque necessariò virtutibus aut vitiis indulget. Atque hæc indifferentia duplex jure attenditur à Politicis & legumlatoribus, pœnas aut præmia decernentibus. Nemo enim laude vel culpâ, pœnâ vel præmio dignus, hac qui indifferentia destituitur. Vnde & factum, vt postmodum vulgariter libertatis nomine nihil aliud quàm hæc indeterminatio fuerit intellecta. Sed nos meritò distinguendum esse censemus inter acceptionem vocis Politicam, & accuratè Philosophicam. Politici quidem, quin & Ethici, de virtutibus & vitiis verba facientes, libertatem pro indifferentia jure accipiunt. Sin autem ἀκριβῶς rem consideremus, ipsa certè notatur voluntas, quippè quᾳ non per superadditum aliquid, sed per seipsam libera est, qua de causa actiones etiam voluntatis, qua sic omnes liberas, etiamsi necessariæ sint, pronunciamus.

LXXIIX. Neque tamen hoc ipso asserimus, operationes quasvis, quæ coactæ non sunt, liberas esse. Ignis non coactè sursum, aqua non coacte deorsum fertur: haut tamen liberè. A coactione quidem liberæ sunt eiusmodi effectiones, sed non simpliciter liberæ. Igitur τὸ liberum non opponimus vel necessario vel non coacto, sed πρώτως & per se inuoluntario. Sicut enim voluntas quia voluntas & in quantum voluntas, adeoque per se ipsam est libera, ita & actiones ideò, quia sunt voluntatis actiones, & inquantum sunt voluntatis, liberæ sunt. Ergo & earum oppositum non est aliud, quàm inuoluntarium. Omne enim inuoluntarium, eò quòd involuntarium, & quatenus inuoluntarium, liberum non est.

LXXIX. Quando autem Theologicè consideramus hominem, diuersi status attendendi sunt, nimirum. 1. Innocentiæ. 2. Culpæ. 3. Gratiæ. 4. Gloriæ. Libertas hominum in statu gloriæ eodem modo se habet quo libertas Angelorum, de qua th. 74. verba fecimus. Libertas in statu innocentiæ & gratiæ conueniunt fermè, ideoque tantum de statu integritatis & lapsus dicendum est, id quod duabus assertionibus expedire potest.

LXXX. 1. Homo ante lapsum liber fuit à necessitate & coactione, tam quo ad actiones malas, quàm bonas, tam electionis quàm executionis respectu, tam quoad specificationem quàm exercitium. Expers necessitatis fuit ante lapsum, quia Deus reliquit eum in manu consilij suij, Ecclesiastici 15. ver. 14. liberè igitur & contingenter, non coactè, non necessariò bonum tùm eligebat & tùm prosequebatur, malum jam liberè eligebat & appetebat, quia nondum ab interno principio inclinabatur ad malum, atque sic à servitute peccati liber fuit, non tamen à jure seu obligatione, quia tantum ipsi erat præceptum, nepeccaret. Si ergo quæritur, An Adam ante lapsum habuerit liberam potestatem eligendi vel bonum vel malum, respondemus, quòd quidem eam habuerit, attamen eandem exerere non debuerit. Deus enim jusserat, bona duntaxat eligere & exequi. Atque hinc apparet maximum discrimē inter libertatem Dei & hominis, siquidem Deus ab omni jure & obligatione est liberrimus, superiorem enim se nõ habet, at homo quoniã Deo subjectus, istâ libertatis specie nõ fuit pręditus, Liber tamē erat a coactione, à necessitate, à peccato & miseria. Neq; tamen existimandum est, quod homo magis liber fuerit quàm Deus, quia eius arbitrium non erat ad vnum determinatum, sed indifferens: hæc enim indeterminatio non arguit summam libertatem, sed potius flexibilitatem & ambiguitatem, constantiæ oppositam, ideoque, Lutherus in libro de serv. arb. pag. 98 putat istud arbitrium rectius nominari vertibile & mutabile quam liberum. Et Commentator Damasceni ait in l. 2. de O. F. c. 22. Vertibilitas ad libertatis rationem non exigitur.

LXXXI. II. Homo post lapsum liber est à coactione in cunctis actionibus voluntarijs, siquidem voluntas cogi nequit: liber est à necessitate quoad genus actionũ Theologicè consideratarum, quæ malæ sunt & Deo displicent: habet enim internum huius necessitatis principium, videlicet peccatum originale, quo mens & voluntas hominis ita corrupta sunt, vt nihil nisi mala inde prouenire queant, arbor siquidem mala bonorum fructuum non est ferax Matth. 7. versu 10. qua de causa dicimur natura filij iræ Ephes. 2. ver. 3.

& ferui peccati Rom. 6. v. 17. Hæc autem necesfitas non repugnat libertati, ideoque dici posset voluntaria necessitas, & necessaria voluntas, sicut innuere videtur Bernhardus Sermo. 81. in Cantica: Nescio quo pravo & miro modo ipsa sibi voluntas peccato quidem in deterius mutata necessitatem faciat, vt necessitas cùm voluntaria sit, excusare non valeat voluntatem, nec voluntas, cum sit illecta excludere necessitatem. Et infra: Ita anima miro quodam modo ac malè libera necessitate ancilla tenetur & libera, ancilla propter necessitatem, libera propter voluntatem, & quod magis mirum, magisq; miserum est, eo rea, quo libera, eoq; ancilla, quo rea, ac per hoc eo ancilla, quo libera.

LXXXII. Quod verò attinet species actionum humanatum illæ sunt vel imperatæ vel elicitæ Quoad actiones imperatas non est liber à iure, quamuis liber sit â coactione & à necessitate quoad executionem & electionem, vt quando Magistratus iubet, non esse furandum, homo quidem obstrictus tenetur ad obediendum, in potestate tamen arbitrij est furtum eligere, & exequi vel secus, quę est libertas cōtradictionis. Habet insuper libertatem contrarietatis, vt quando delinqenti optio datur à Magistratu eligendi pro pœna vel carcerem vel mulctam pecuniarum. Quoad actiones elicitas vicissim homo liber est á coactione & necessitate tã quoad electionẽ quàm executionẽ. Potest enim liberè & contingēter, non necessariò opus aliquod moraliter bonum eligere, & post electionẽ vel exequi vel non exequi, cum electio & executio multùm differant, nec necessario cohæreant in actionibˡ humanis, sicut in divinis. Ratio diversitatis facilè datur, quia Deus est immutabilis, quod igitur semel decreuit se facturum, id immutabiliter & necessariò facit: Ast homo est mutabilis: vnde sit, vt possit iam aliquid eligere, mox tamen mutare sententiam, & id quod eligit, non exequi, quamvis si executio non accedit, certum sit, electionem quoque mutatam fuisse. Si enim prima electio adhuc locum haberet, procul dubio subsequeretur executio.

LXXXIII. Atque satis hinc apparet homini in externis actionibus relictam esse libertatem, cum agere possit quod vult & non agere quod non vult, quamvis nonnunquam fiat in specialioribus actionibus, vt voluntas humana peculiariter à Deo inclinetur ad hoc & non illud faciendum, Exemplum legimus de Cyro, qui apud Esaiam c. 45. vers. 1. vocatur Servus Domini; Is voluntariè, non coactè expugnabat Babylonem, attamen eius voluntas à Deo peculiariter ad id dirigebatur & inclinabatur: actio proinde ista non erat contingens, sed quodammodo necessaria ob voluntatis inclinationem diuinitus factam, quæ vulgo vocatur necessitas dependentia. Hęc verò sunt extraordinaria exempla, quæ ordinarijs nihil præjudicare possunt.

LXXXIV. Ita ergo per singulas liberorum entiũ species hactenus ostendimus, quod libertas cum necessitate sæpius concurrat optimeq; consistere possit, nec libero arbitrio alia repugnet, quam naturæ & coactionis necessitas, quod ipsum ante nos docuerunt Bonaventura in l. 2. dist. 25 q 6. & Biel itidem q. vn. dicẽtes: Cum duplex sit necessitas coactionis & immutabilitatis, necessitas coactionis repugnat libertati arbitrij, necessitas vero immutabilitatis non item.

LXXXV. In contrarium quod objiceret Bellarminus, ferè nihil inuenit. Allegat c. 5. dictum Ecclesiastici 15. v. 14. quod vel de statu integritatis & gratiæ exponi debet, vel si de statu lapsus, notatur tantum libertas in externis & quoad exercitium, vbi indifferens & vertibile esse arbitrium ipsi non diffitemur. Sic Canones conciliorum & dicta Patrum contra nos nequaquam militant. Vel enim per necessitatem intelligunt coactionem, vel loquuntur de indifferentia circa externas actiones, & quoad exercitium. Omnem autem in genere & indistincte necessitatem a libero arbitrio mihime excludunt, sicuti Pareus in specie ostendit lib. 3. c. 5. p. 415. seqq. Postmodo rationes quinque subiungit, sed exigui momenti, Colophonis tamen loco breuiter percurremus. LXXXVI. 1. Si ad liberum arbitrium sufficeret libertas a coactione, sequeretur etiam in pecoribus esse liberum arbitrium. Nam & illa sine coactione vlla sponte sua feruntur ad pabulum. Resp. Non sufficit sola libertas a coactione, sed requiritur insuper libertas a necessitate Physica, qua pecudes feruntur ad pabulum. Requiritur etiam cognitio intellectus & προαίρεσις agentis, qua vtraq; destituuntur bruta. Cum igitur homo a necessitate tam Physica quam coactiua liber sit, & προαίρεσει agat, quæ omnia in brutis non reperiuntur, sequitur hominem liberi arbitrij esse, non pecora. 2. Sequeretur in pueris, furiosis, somniantibus esse vsum liberi arbitrij, omnes enim sponte agunt. Resp. Sponte agere non est in προαίρεσει agere, quod tamen ad exercitium libertatis requiritur. Quia ergo motus ille spontaneus in pueris & furiosis non ex vsurationalis, sed sensitiui appetitus oritur, ob id vsum liberi arbitrij proprie dictum non habent. 3. Sequeretur Deum per liberum arbitrium & ex electione genuisse filium, quoniam non coactus genuit. Resp. Licet quodammodo dici posse videatur, quod Pater filium genuerit libere, quia non coacte, rectius tamen fieri censemus, si simpliciter dicatur, quod Pater filium neque coactus neque non coactus genuerit; quia non voluntate, sed natura genuit. 4. Nulla fuisset vnquam quæstio de libero arbitrio, neque vlla cum hæreticis controuersia remaneret. Nemo enim negauit vnquam vel Deum vel homines liberos esse a coactione. Resp. Licet in hoc sit consensus, manet tamen in alijs multis dissensus. Disputandum est cum Stoicis, An Deus causarum secundarum nexu teneatur? num omnia fiant ex absoluta necessitate? cum Manichæis, An peccatum ex natura maligna potius quam voluntate libera oriatur? cum Pelagianis, An arbitrium sibi sine gratia sufficiat? Cum Pontificijs Num voluntas hominis ad conuersionem sui efficienter concurrat? &c.

Tandem 5. Pugnantia videtur dicere, qui affirmat liberum arbitrium a coactione, non a necessitate solutum esse, cum sit potestas electiua, quæ non potest intelligi cum determinatione ad vnum, & necessitate. Resp. Imo vero non sunt pugnantia. Manet enim voluntas potentia electiua, licet necessitati immutabilitatis in quibusdam sit implicata, vti exemplis bene multis ostendimus: Manet insuper libera quoad exercitium, licet quoad speciem actuum ad vnum genere sit determinata.


### Question IX. What is the subject of liberty?

What is the subject of liberty?

LXXXVII. Since the cognition of the intellect is a prerequisite in a free action, it follows of its own accord that the first and immediate ὑποκείμενον (subject) of liberty is an intelligent nature, for this property always follows it, that it is free in its actions. In this subject, however, the efficient cause of liberty is simultaneously involved. For all ἐμμεινουσαι (immanent) effects, such as liberty is, are received first by their efficient causes, in such a way that from whom they received their essence, in the same they have their existence. Therefore, an intelligent nature is both the cause and the first subject of liberty.

LXXXIX. From what has been said, however, two πορίσματα (corollaries) flow. FIRST: παν λογικὸν καὶ ἀυτεξούσιον Every rational being is of free power and choice. Damasc. lib. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. & lib. 3. cap. 14. Since therefore Angels are intelligent substances, they will by no means lack freedom of choice, which the fall and the works of the Angels themselves sufficiently confirm, with the support of Irenaeus l. 4. cap. 71. Basil de Spir. S. cap. 16. Augustine de corrept. & grat. cap. 10. Gregory hom. 7. in Ezech. & Damascene lib. 2. de fide c. 3. 4.

LXXXIX. But since the intensification of a cause simultaneously intensifies the effect, that which is more rational will certainly be more self-determined. And since God is supremely intelligent, nay, is intelligence and Wisdom itself, he will certainly be also supremely free, or a most free agent, or rather freedom itself. All those sayings of Scripture testify to this, which teach that God works through knowledge and will, and that created things are such as God willed them to be, not such as necessity compelled, as Ps. 115. v. 3. Dan. 3. v. 18. 1. Cor. 11. v. 12. Eph. 1. v. 11. To this also pertain the miracles performed for the sake of the order of nature, such as that the Sun stood still at the prayers of Joshua, retreated at the prayers of Hezekiah, failed at the full moon at the death of the Savior: that a virgin conceived and gave birth, that sight was restored to the blind, hearing to the deaf, life to the dead, etc. For if God can now preserve the order of nature and now change it at his pleasure, it follows that he works not out of necessity, but freely.

XC. It is therefore a calumny when Bellarmine lib. 3. cap. 15. objects that Luther denied freedom of choice to God in assert. art. 36. inasmuch as he argues that all things happen by absolute necessity. But nothing of the sort is found in Luther, but he says this, that to those looking at things from above, all things are necessary, not indeed by necessity of nature, in the way that fire necessarily burns, but by the necessity of immutable foreknowledge and divine counsel, according to which, while the freedom and contingency of wills remain, it is necessary that scandals happen and it was necessary that Christ suffer. But it does not follow that God himself may be subject to necessity, although events are necessary with respect to divine foreknowledge.

XCI. It must be repeated, however, that no small distinction exists between the will of God and that of creatures. They do indeed have two things in common, namely 1. to act ἑκούσιως or spontaneously. 2. to act ἐκ προαιρέσεως with choice or deliberate counsel, yet they differ in turn in four ways. 1. With respect to the intellect; because God knows and understands all things most perfectly from himself; but creatures neither know all things, nor do they have from themselves what they do know, but rather most things from the divine Resolution, especially those which pertain to God and his will. 2. With respect to the will, for the divine will is ruled by or depends upon no superior: but the will of men is directed by God in good actions, and corrupted by the Devil in evil ones. 3. With respect to both, because both the knowledge and the preordination of God are immutable, but the notions and wills of men are ambulatory or mutable, so that they now want what they previously did not want and do not want what they previously wanted. 4. With respect to the manner of choosing, because God chooses without consultation properly so-called, which is a discourse of reason from the known to the unknown or from the notion of the end to the invention of means: but men cannot choose without prior consultation.

XCII. SECOND: τὰ ἄλογα οὐκ εἰσιν ἀυτεξόσια; Irrational beings lack free will, Damasc. bk. 2, ch. 27, and bk. 3, ch. 14. ἄγονται γὰρ μᾶλλον ὑπο τῆς φύσεως ἤπερ ἄγουσι. They are moved more by nature than they move themselves. Whence the Psalmist exhorts us not to be like the horse and the mule which have no understanding, Ps. 32, v. 9. But just as a certain shadow of reason is observed in brutes, so too is a shadow of liberty, while in the fields as it pleases them, they now stand, now lie down, now move forward, now feed on this grass, soon on that: which actions, however, we more correctly call spontaneous than free, since they are concerned only with the goods of the body and by natural instinct, and come from nothing but an inconsiderate appetite of the senses, so that Bellarmine is absurd in attributing natural judgment to beasts, book 3, chapter 15. And since liberty is nothing other than the will, certainly if you ascribe liberty properly so-called to brutes, you will not be able to deny them will. But the will is ἐν τῷ λογικῷ, which beasts lack, which are also not said to will, but to be instigated, Scal. Exerc. 307 sect. 4. ἡ γὰρ τῶν ἀλόγων ὄρεξις μὴ οὖσα λογικὴ, ὁ λέγεται θέλησις, as Damascene says in book 2 de O. F. cap. 22.

XCIII. And thus far we have considered the general subject of liberty, which is an intelligent nature: but specifically, as regards the liberty of the human will, the judgment concerning its subject is the same as that concerning the subject of other faculties. The matter is briefly thus: the subject of inhesion is either adequate or principal. The former we call man, consisting of soul and body, since both the δύναμις and ἐνέργεια belong to him. The latter, however, is the rational soul from which liberty or the free power of acting flows by immediate birth; indeed, since with respect to essence it is nothing other than the will: but when the powers of liberty are understood, then the will itself is often called the subject of free choice, because those powers are exerted not through the intellect, but through the will, meanwhile inhering not in the will itself, as it is an accident, but in the soul, yet through the mediation of the will.

Latin:

Quænam libertatis subiectum sit?

LXXXVII. Quandoquidem cognitio intellectus prærequiritur in actione libera, vltro sequitur, primum & immediatum libertatis ὑποκείμενον naturam esse intelligentem, quippe quam seimperinsequitur proprietas ista, vt in suis actionibus sit libera. In hoc autem subiecto simul implicata est libertatis causa efficiens. Omnes enim effectiones ἐμμεινουσαι, qualis est libertas, ab efficientibus suis primo recipiuntur, ita quidem, vt a quo acceperunt suam essentiam, in eodem suam habeant existentiam, Natura igitur intelligens & causa & subiectum primum libertatis est.

LXXXIX. Ex dictis autem duo fluunt πορίσματα. PRIMVM: παν λογικὸν καὶ ἀυτεξούσιον Omne ratiomale liberæ potestatis, & arbitrij est. Damasc. lib. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. & lib. 3. cap. 14. Cùm igitur Angeli substantiæ sint intelligentes, libertate arbitrij minimè carebunt, quam ipsam tùm lapsus tùm opera Angelorum satis confirmant, adstipulante Irenæo l. 4. cap. 71. Basilio de de Spir. S. cap. 16. Augustino de corrept. & grat. cap. 10. Gregorio. hom. 7. in Ezech. & Damasceno lib. 2. de fide c. 3. 4.

LXXXIX. Cùm autem causæ intensio simul intendat effectum, vtique magis ἀυτεξούσιον erit, quod magis λογικὸν. Et quoniam Deus summè intelligens, imò ipsa intelligentia & Sapientia est, vtique & summè liber, vel agens liberrimum, vel ipsa potius libertas erit. Hoc testantur omnia illa Scripturæ dicta, quæ docent, Deum operari per cognitionem & voluntatem, talesq; esse res creatas, quales Deum esse voluit, non quales necessitas coegit vt Psal 115. v. 3. Dan. 3. v. 18. 1. Cor. 11. v. 12. Eph. 1. v. 11. Hûc etiam spectant miracula propter ordinem naturæ facta, vt quòd Sol stetit ad preces Iosuæ, retrocessit ad preces Hiskiæ, Defecit in plenilunio sub mortem Saluatoris: quòd virgo concepit & peperit, quòd cæcis visus, surdis auditus, mortuis vita restituta est. &c. Si enim Deus ordinem naturæ nunc seruare nunc pro arbitratu mutare potest, vtiq; non ex necessitate, sed liberè operari ipsum consequitur.

XC. Calumnia igitur est, cùm Bellarminus lib. 3. cap. 15. objicit, Lutherum Deo libertatem arbitrij denegasse in assert. art. 36. siquidem disputet omnia ex necessitate absoluta euenire. Verum nihil tale in Luthero inuenitur, sed hoc dicit, superna spectantibus omnia esse necessaria, nimirum non necessitate naturæ, quomodo ignis necessariò vrit, sed necessitate immutabilis præscientiæ & consilij diuini, secundùm quæ saluâ voluntatum libertate & contingentiâ necesse est euenire scandala & Christum pati oportuit. Non autem sequitur, quòd Deus ipse necessitati subiaceat, licèt euentus respectu diuinae praescientiae sint necessarii.

XCI. Repetendum verò quòd inter Dei & creaturarum arbitrium non exiguum discrimen intercedat. Duo quidem habent communia, nempe 1. agere ἑκούσιως vel sponte. 2. agere ἐκ προαιρέσεως cum electione vel deliberato consilio, quatuor tamen modis vicissim differunt. 1 Respectu intellectus; quia Deus ex sese omnia perfectissimè scit & intelligit; creaturae verò nec omnia sciunt, nec quae sciunt, ex sese habent, sed pleraque ex diuina Resolutione, praesertim quae Deum eiusque voluntatem attinent. 2. Respectu voluntatis, Diuina enim voluntas à nulla superiori regitur aut dependet: Hominum autem voluntas in actionibus bonis à Deo dirigitur, in malis à Diabolo corrumpitur. 3. Respectu vtriusque quia Dei tùm scientia tùm praeordinatio immutabilis est, hominum verò & notitiae & voluntates sunt ambulatorię seu mutabiles, vt iam velint quod antea nolebant & nolint quod prius volebant. 4. Respectu modi etigendi, quia Deus eligit sine consultatione propriè dicta, quae est discursus rationis à noto ad ignotius seu à notione finis ad inuentionem mediorum: homines vero eligere nequeunt nisi consultatione praeuiâ.

XCII. SECVNDVM: τὰ ἄλογα οὐκ εἰσιν ἀυτεξόσια; Irrationalia carent libero arbitrio, Damasc. l. 2. cap. 27. & l. 3. cap. 14. ἄγονται γὰρ μᾶλλον ὑπο τῆς φύσεως ἤπερ ἄγουσι. Mouentur magis à natura, quam vt ipsa moueant. Vnde Psaltes hortatur, ne simus sicut equus & mulus quibus non est intellectus Psal. 32. v. 9. Quemadmodum verò vmbra quaedam rationis, ita & libertatis animaduertitur in brutis, dum in campis prout placuerit, nunc stant nunc iacent, nunc progrediuntur, iam hoc mox illo vescuntur gramine: quas tamen actiones rectiùs spontaneas quàm liberas appellamus, quoniam duntaxat circa corporis bona versantur atque naturali instinctu, & non nisi ex inconsiderato sensuum appetitu veniunt, vt absurdus sit Bellarminus bestijs naturale iudicium attribuens lib. 3. cap. 15. Cumque libertas, nihil sit aliud quàm voluntas; certè si brutis libertatem propriè dictam adscripseris, voluntatem denegare haut poteris. Voluntas autem est ἐν τῷ λογικῷ quo carent bestiæ quæ etiam non dicuntur velle, sed instigari, Scal. Exerc. 307 sect. 4. ἡ γὰρ τῶν ἀλόγων ὄρεξις μὴ οὖσα λογικὴ, ὁ λέγεται θέλησις dicente Damasceno libro 2. de O. F. cap. 22.

XCIII. Et hactenus generale libertatis subiectum, quod est natura intelligens, considerauimus: In specie autem quod libertatem voluntatis humanę attinet, de illius subiecto idem est iudicium, quod de subiecto aliarum facultatum. Res breuiter sic habet: subiectum inhæsionis vel est adæquatum vel principale. Illud hominem dicimus, animâ & corpore constantem, cùm eiusdem sit & δύναμις & ἐνέργεια. Hoc verò animam rationalem à qua libertas vel libera agendi potestas immediato partu profluit; quippe cum respectu essentiæ nihil aliud sit, quam voluntas: quando autem vires libertatis intelliguntur, tum sæpè ipsa voluntas liberi arbitrij subiectum dicitur, quia vires illæ non per intellectum, sed per voluntatem exeruntur, interim non voluntati ipsi, quippe accidenti, sed animæ, voluntate tamen mediante inhærent.


### Question X. What is the object of liberty?

XCIV. If what has been said thus far is repeated, the decision of this question will not be difficult. For presupposing that liberty, considered ὑποστάσει, is the very will, certainly the object of both will be the same. But indeed the will extends itself to all things which can be desired. Therefore also liberty. Whence it follows. 1. That free choice is of goods and evils, since very often the good being neglected, evil is chosen. Where however it must be known, that the object of liberty is considered either materially or formally. If materially, then good and evil fall under free choice. But if formally, only the good; not indeed that every desirable thing is truly good, but because it is not desired except under the aspect of good.

2. That free choice is of present and future things. For as we not only will in the present, but also choose in the future: so those things which we now choose, we likewise choose freely. Indeed, the free will desires many future things by the very act, as every end before we attain it. Nor indeed does it follow that the present act of the will is not free because it is necessary. For these two are subordinated, not contrary. The present act is free by reason of its principle, although it is necessary by reason of its existence.

3. That free choice is of means and the end. Concerning means there is no doubt, concerning the end Bellarmine is in doubt: lib. 3. c. 14. But without reason. For no one will deny that the end is the object of the will. But indeed liberty and will are the same, as Bellarmine admits: Wherefore the end will also be the object of liberty. The contrary arguments conclude nothing, because liberty is always confused with consultation and free election. This indeed is concerned only with means, but that with the end and means together, because all actions of man, whether they be natural or moral, are free, those extrinsically and imperatively, but these intrinsically and elicitively, as Damascene testifies in lib. 2. de O. F. chapter 22. See more concerning these in Bellarmine and Pareus in book 3. chapters 12, 13, 14, and Becanus part 2. tr. 1. c. 2. questions 7 and 8.

§. CV. And thus far the questions by Bellarmine

We briefly run through those proposed under 3, which we do not deny are more Scholastic and Philosophical than purely Theological. Let no one, however, infer from this that we wish to recall the thorns of the schools, long since happily extracted by Luther. Our intention is different, desiring nothing more than that we may be allowed to rest in the simplicity of the Apostolic faith. But the πανουργία of our adversaries, especially Bellarmine, makes it so that we cannot understand them, nor confer with them, unless those general questions, which they always interject and hold as the foundation of their opinion, have first been known and discussed. This one, and no other, end we have had, when we have hitherto followed Bellarmine and philosophized somewhat, which, although we did it even against our will, we clearly trust will be fruitful for younger students, and on this account we will the sooner obtain pardon from the fair reader. But now let us proceed to other matters.

Latin:

XCIV. Si hactenus dicta repetantur, non difficilis erit huius quæstionis decisio. Nam præsupposito, quòd libertas ὑποστάσει considerata, sit ipsa voluntas, vtique idem erit vtriusque objectum. At verò voluntas se extendit ad omnia, quæ appeti possunt. E. & libertas. Vnde sequitur. 1. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit bonorum & malorum, siquidem sæpissimè bono neglecto eligitur malum. Vbi tamen sciendum, quòd libertatis obiectum vel materialiter vel formaliter consideretur. Si materialiter, tum bonum malumque cadit sub electionem liberam. Sin formaliter, tantùm bonum; non quidem quòd omne Appetibile reuerà sit bonum, sed quia non appetitur nisi sub ratione boni.

2. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit præsentium & futurorum. Vt enim non tantum in præsenti volumus, sed etiam in futuro eligimus: sic quæ nunc eligimus, itidem liberè eligimus. Imò & multa futura ipso actu appetit voluntas libera, vt omnem finem antéquam eum consequamur. Neque verò sequitur, actum voluntatis præsentem non esse liberum, quia sit necessarius. Dúo n. hæc subordinata sunt, non contraria. Liber est actus præsens, ratione principij quamvis sit necessarius ratione existentiæ.

3. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit mediorum & finis. De medijs nullum est dubium, de fine ambigit Bellarm: lib. 3. c. 14. Sed absque ratione. Nam voluntatis obiectum esse finem, nemo ibit inficias. At verò libertas & voluntas idem sunt, fatente Bellarmino: Quare finis etiam libertatis obiectum erit. Argumenta contraria nihil concludunt, quia semper confunditur libertas cũ consultatione & electione libera, Hæc quidē versatur tantùm circa media, sed illa circa fidem & media simul, quia omnes actiones hominis siue fuerint naturales, siue morales, sunt liberæ, illæ extrinsecus & imperatiuè, hæ autem intrinsecus & elicitivè, teste Damasceno lib. 2. de O. F. capite 22. Plura de his vide apud Bellarminum & Pareum libro 3. cap. 12. 13. 14. & Becanum par. 2. tr. 1. c. 2. quæst. 7. & 8.

§. CV. Atque hactenus quæstiones à Bellarmino

sub 3. propositas breuiter percurrimus, quas magis esse Scholasticas & Philosophicas, quam pure Theologicas haut diffitemur. Nemo tamen inde inferat, quod spinas scholarum iamdiu per Lutherum feliciter extrusas iterum reuocaras velimus. Alius nobis est animus, qui nihil magis exoptat, quam vt in simplicitate fidei Apostolica nobis acquiescere liceat. Facit vero adversariorum imprimis Bellarmini πανουργία, vt illos intelligere, cumque illis conferre nequeamus, nisi quæstiones istæ generales, quas semper immiscent, & pro suæ opinionis fundamento habent, prius fuerint cognitæ & discussæ. Hunc vnum, nullum alium finem habuimus, quando hactenus Bellarminum secuti, nonnihil Philosophati sumus, quod licet vel inuiti fecerimus, iuniorib. tame studiosis fructuosum fore, & hoc nomine apud lectorem æquum nos veniam eo citius impetraturos esse plane confidimus. Sed nunc ad alia pergamus.


### Question XI. Whether man is free, and what powers of will he has

XCVI. Hitherto we have often warned that the liberty of man is considered either by reason of ὑπόστασις or by reason of ἐνεργεία, as to what it can do. As regards ὑπόστασις, liberty is the will itself, which, since it flows from the soul of man, is for that reason always and in every state present in man, and in that respect man is always free, and has the same essence of liberty, because the will itself, insofar as it is a free power, is not essentially changed, although it may be accidentally either depraved or perfected. Therefore, we do not so much deny the liberty of the will taken ὑποστατικῶς to man; that we rather assert that it perpetually accompanies him,

Bellarmino's accusation is therefore atrocious when in the preface to book 11 on free will he writes thus of our opinion: They have stripped us of the freedom of the will in all their opinions, and they have not hesitated to profess themselves not similar to beasts, but beasts clearly devoid of reason. That we determine something far different, he knows as well as his own fingers, indeed he himself even confessed it in book 3, chapter 15, arguing thus: It is certain that man, considered absolutely, has free will: for heretics do not contend about this matter, but only about man cast down from his state through the sin of the first parent. If, therefore, we do not contend about liberty taken absolutely and in general, why has he accused us of taking away all liberty and changing men into beasts?

XCVII. But if liberty is estimated by reason of ἐνεργείας, what it can do, it must be answered distinctly, for the states of man are diverse, for which reason the very powers of free will vary, nor do they always behave in the same way. Therefore we shall run through the individual states, and we shall indicate in a few words what powers the will either once had, or even now has, or will sometime have.

XCVIII. I. On the state of integrity. Our parents were free 1. from coercion, which is beyond doubt, because the will of man can never and in no state be coerced; 2. from necessity, since they were not bound by either an external or an internal principle to choose necessarily either only good or only evil, to which refers that passage in Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14. Man could sin and not sin, because his will was not yet so immutably determined to good that it could not turn itself away from good, but there was in it the δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως or power toward opposites, while he could will and not will good and evil, and therefore a commandment was given by God that he should not sin. 3. From the servitude of sin, since they were not ensnared by the necessity of sinning, but rather the will, on account of its concreated perfection, was inclined toward good, yet in such a way that at the same time he could, if he wished, choose evil.

XCIX. The powers of free will were therefore extraordinary in the state of innocence, since the first-formed could love God with their whole heart and fully observe his law. For their liberty was not a bare will, but rather a will with perfection, with rectitude and the powers of loving God and fulfilling the law. Hence it is named the liberty of rectitude, because the will could act rightly and obey the commands of God rightly and fully. Therefore, one must diligently distinguish here the ἰσία of liberty, which is the same in every state and is called by Bernard as something that can be lost, from the ἐνεργείᾳ of liberty, which was extraordinary in the first state, consisting in a prompt faculty by which man could easily produce not only moral but also supernatural good actions. This liberty of rectitude was not the will itself, but a perfection of the will, a certain separable accident, so constituted that it could be lost while the essence of the will remained intact, just as it was indeed lost. For Adam was indeed free from the servitude of sin and misery, yet he was not free from mutability, because his will could be changed and could freely choose evil.

C. Here, however, it is further asked, Why did God permit man to himself, and instruct him with free will? For it seems to follow from this as if he had preordained the fall of Adam, and for that end had created the first-formed as liable to fall. We are not, however, bound to answer this question, which is more curious than fruitful. The will of God suffices for us, whose decrees and the causes of whose decrees, although we may be ignorant of them, are always just. Basil answers in a few words, writing thus: He who blames that in our creator, that he did not create us so that we could not sin by nature, does nothing else than contend that it would have been better for God to have created us as irrational, or clearly as immobile, trunks. than rational men. If you ask for more, consult Damascenus, book 2 of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 12, and his commentator who discusses this problem at length.

CI. But so that we may gather the principal causes into a bundle for the sake of abundance, these are primarily brought forward by the Fathers. 1. The glory of God. For the power and wisdom of God the creator should shine forth from the excellence of the creature, endowed with reason and will. 2. The reason for worship: God demands spontaneous honor and voluntary obedience, not coerced or entirely necessary, since ἀβίαστον εἶναι πρέπει τὸ καλὸν, Damascenus, book 4 of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 20. But if man had lacked free will, how could he have exhibited free and contingent worship? The reward of man: for God wished to confer prizes upon man, for obeying out of free will. It was therefore given to Adam to be able to sin, not so that he would therefore sin, but so that he would appear more glorious if he did not sin, when he could have sinned, as Bernard testifies in his treatise on free will, book 4. The perfection and ornament of the universe. For since there is something that acts and is not acted upon, such as God; something that is acted upon and does not act, such as nature devoid of reason; it was fitting that there should also exist something that is acted upon and acts, namely man, who acts from liberty and is at the same time incited by God to choose the good. This reason is scholastic and probable, which Bellarmine urges among others in book 3 of On Free Will, chapter 18.

CII. II. On the state of corruption. As soon as man transgressed the commandment of the Lord, he immediately lost the concreated image, and consequently along with it the freedom of rectitude, that is, that faculty of loving God and fulfilling the law. For man, using free will badly, both lost himself and it. For since it was by free will that sin was committed, with sin as the victor, free will was also lost, "for by whom a man is overcome, to this he is enslaved," as Augustine says in Enchiridion, chapter 30. Nor indeed was man only despoiled of liberty, but there succeeded together an unbridled impulse toward evil, which always incites unregenerate men to evil, so that they can do nothing but sin. For just as during the state of innocence there flourished in the mind of man the knowledge of God, in the will, justice, holiness, and a zeal for obedience; in the appetite, ἁρμονία and conformity with reason; so, on the contrary, in the state of the fall, there succeeded in the mind ignorance and blindness, in the will aversion and an inclination toward evil, in the appetite contumacy and a zeal for resisting; whence it happens that man sins perpetually, and cannot convert himself to God.

CIII. Truly, therefore, Luther wrote in article 36 that free will is a title without a reality: he speaks, however, not of external actions, but of spiritual and theological ones. For although after the fall man is in a certain way free regarding the external pursuit of virtue, and conducts himself indifferently, nevertheless he is clearly a slave with respect to his conversion and the divine law, which he always transgresses and cannot observe. He has, therefore, free will not toward the good but only toward the evil: which is otherwise called freedom from righteousness, Rom. 6, verse 20, but is more correctly termed a miserable slavery to sin. For he who commits sin is a slave of sin, John 8, v. 34. And by whom anyone is overcome, his slave he is, 2 Pet. 2, v. 19.

CIV. III. Concerning the state of reparation. But when man is converted to God, and thus is transferred from the state of guilt into the state of grace, then at the same time the freedom of the will, i.e., the powers of loving God and observing the law, are in a certain way restored. For the dominion is taken away from sin, so that although it resists the Spirit with its affections, the Spirit nevertheless conquers and mortifies the flesh. The regenerate, therefore, have freedom from the slavery of sin, because they can perform good works that are pleasing to God, to which pertain the words of John 8, v. 36: If the Son shall make you free, you shall be truly free. Rom. 6, v. 18: Freed from sin you have been made servants of righteousness. 2 Cor. 3 v. 17. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. In that state of grace, therefore, we grant to the reborn συνεργέιαν [cooperation], because they have the powers of cooperating, not indeed sprouting from nature, but graciously infused and excited by the Holy Spirit through the word. Which powers of acting well, however, are not entirely perfected, but only begun, since as long as we live, the flesh remains in us, which resists the Spirit Gal. 5 v. 17 and fights against the law of the mind. Rom. 7 v. 23. Whence it happens that if a reborn person allows himself to be led away by the flesh, he can in turn return to his vomit and enslave himself again to the servitude of sin, and therefore so many exhortations are read, that we should stand in the faith, resist the Devil, and remain faithful even unto death.

CH. IV. Of the state of glorification. Just as in the other life the knowledge of the mind will be perfect, and that which is in part shall be abolished; so we shall also attain perfect freedom of the will, by which we shall be free both from the servitude of sin, and from misery and all the remnants of sin, and also from mutability itself, since we shall so love the good that we cannot will evil, since we shall be confirmed in grace, so that we can never fall from that happy state: For we shall be equal to the angels, Matt. 22 v. 30, who cannot but act well and enjoy eternal blessedness. There, therefore, free will shall be fully restored, nay, more shall be restored than was lost in Adam, for he was so free that he could sin and become miserable, but the blessed shall be so free that they cannot sin and become miserable. There, error shall be absent from reason, sorrow from the will, fear from memory, rancor from appetite: and on the contrary, there shall be present the serene light of the mind, joy and freedom of the will, where nothing sad shall be seen, where joy shall always be had, where no evil shall be feared; since there the highest good shall be possessed, which is to see always the face of the Lord of hosts, as Augustine says in his Soliloquies, chapter 35.

CVI. Thus, therefore, we have seen what powers human free will possesses in any state, all of which can be briefly expressed if we say: Man in the first state was free; in the second he is a slave, in the third liberated, in the fourth he will be most free. Free in the state of integrity, because he could sin and not sin. He is a slave in the state of the fall, because he cannot not sin. He is liberated in the state of grace, because he can again not sin, and do good. But he will be most free in the state of glory, because there he will no longer be able to sin or be made unhappy.

Latin:

XCVI. Hactenus sæpe monuimus, libertatem hominis considerari vel ratione ὑποστάσεως vel ratione ἐνεργείας, quid possit. Quoad ὑπόστασιν libertas est ipsa voluntas, quæ cum fluat ab anima hominis, ob id semper & in omni statu homini inest, istoqs respectu homo semp liber est, & eandẽ libertatis essentiā habet, quia volūtas ipsa, quatenus est potentia libera, essencialiter nō immutatur, licet accidẽtaliter vel deprauetur vel perficiatur. Arbitrij ergò libertatẽ ὑποστατικῶς sumtā adeò nō denegamus homini; vt potiùs perpetuò ipsum comitari asseramus,

Atrox igitur criminatio Bellarmini est cum in præfat. 11. de lib. arb. de nostra sententia ita scribit: Arbitrij libertatem nobis omnibus suis sententiis detraxerunt, séque ipsi non beluarum similes, sed Beluas planè rationis expertes profiteri non dubitarunt. Longè aliud nos statuere, tàm nouit quàm suos digitos, imò & ipse confessus est l. 3. c. 15. ita differens: Certum est, hominem absolutè consideratum esse liberi arbitrij: néq; enim hæretici de hac re contendunt, sed solum de homine per peccatum primi parentis de statu deiecto. Si ergo non contendimus de libertate absolutè & in genere sumta, cur omnem à nobis libertatem tolli & homines in beluas mutari criminatus est?

XCVII. Sin autem libertas æstimetur ratione ἐνεργείας, quid possit, distinctè respondendum est, Diuersi enim sunt status hominis, quam ob causam ipsæ liberi arbitrij vires variantur, nec eodem semper modo se habent. Proinde singulos status percurremus, & quasnam arbitrium vires vel olim habuerit, vel etiamnum habeat, vel aliquando habiturum sit, paucis indicabimus.

XCVIII. I. De statu integritatis. Fuerunt parentes nostri liberi 1. à coactione, quod extra dubium, quia voluntas hominis nunquam & in nullo statu cogi potest 2. à necessitate, quoniam nec per externum, nec per internum principium, vel ad solum bonum, vel ad solum malum necessariò eligendum astricti fuerunt, quò spectat istud Eccles. 15. vers. 14. Potuit homo peccare & non peccare, quia voluntas eius nondum erat ad bonum ita immutabiliter determinata, vt à bono se non posset auertere, verùm erat in ipsa δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως vel potentia ad opposita, dum bonum & malum, velle & nolle poterat, ideoque præceptum à Deo datum est ne peccaret. 3. A seruitute peccati quando quidem necessitate peccandi non fuerunt illaqueati sed potius voluntas ob perfectionem concreatam inclinabatur ad bonum, ita tamen vt simul malum, si vellet, eligere posset.

XCIX. Eximiae igitur fuerunt vires liberi arbitrij in statu innocentiae, siquidem Deum ex toto corde diligere, & eius legem plenè obseruare poterant protoplasti. Libertas enim ipsorum non fuit nuda voluntas, sed potius voluntas cum perfectione, cum rectitudine & viribus diligendi Deum, ac implendi legem. Hinc nominatur libertas rectitudinis, quia voluntas recte poterat agere, Deique mandatis rectè & plenè obtemperare. Diligenter ergò hic distingui debet libertatis ἰσία, quae in omni statu eadem est & amissibilis Bernardo dicitur, à libertatis ἐνεργείᾳ quae in primo statu eximia fuit, consistens in facultate promta, quâ non tantùm morales sed & supernaturales actiones bonas facilè potuit homo producere. Haec rectitudinis libertas non fuit ipsa voluntas, sed voluntatis perfectio, accidens quoddam separabile, ita comparatum, vt salua voluntatis essentiâ posset amitti, sicut etiam amissa est. Fuit enim Adamus liber quidem à servitute peccati & miseria, non tamen fuit liber à mutabilitate, quia voluntas eius mutari & malum liberè poterat eligere.

C. Hic autem porrò quaeritur, Cur Deus hominem sibiipsi permiserit, & libero arbitrio instruxerit? Videtur enim exinde sequi, ac si lapsum Adami praeordinâsse, & in eum finem protoplastos labiles condidisset. Non autem tenemur ad quaestionem hanc, curiosam magis quam fructuosam, respondere. Sufficit nobis voluntas Dei, cuius decreta & decretorum caussae licet nobis ignore, semper tamen iustae sunt. Basilius paucis respondit ita scribens: Qui illud reprehendit in creatore nostro, quòd nos non condiderit, vt naturâ peccare non possemus, is nihil facit aliud quam quod contendit melius fuisse, Deum nos creâsse irrationales, aut planè immobiles truncos quam homines rationales. Plura si poscis, Damascenum consule l. 2. de O. F. capite 12. & eius commentatorem prolixè de hoc problemate differentem.

CI. Vt verò ex abundanti in fasciculum colligamus præcipuas causas, hæ inprimis afferuntur à Patribus. 1. Dei gloria. Elucescat enim ex præstantia creaturæ, ratione & voluntate præditæ, Dei creatoris potentia & sapientia. 2. Cultus Ratio: Spontaneum honorem & voluntarium obsequium postulat Deus, non coactum, aut prorsus necessarium, siquidem ἀβίαστον εἶναι πρέπει τὸ καλὸν Damasc. l. 4. de O. F. cap. 20. Si autem libero arbitrio caruisset homo, quî exhibere potuisset cultum liberum & contingentem? Hominis præmium: volebat enim Deus βραβεῖα conferre homini, ex libera voluntate obsequenti. Datum igitur est Adamo posse peccare, non vt proinde peccaret, sed vt gloriosior appareret, si non peccaret, cùm pecare posset, teste Bernardo tr. de lib. arb. l. 4. Vniuersi perfectio & ornamentum. Cùm enim sit aliquid, quod agit & non agitur, vt Deus: aliquid quod agitur & non agit, vt natura rationis expers, æquum erat, vt etiam extaret aliquid quod ageretur & ageret, nimirum homo, qui agit ex libertate, & simul à Deo ad bonum eligēdum incitatur. Ratio hæc scholastica est & probabilis quam inter cæteras vrget Bellarminus l. 3. de lib, arb. c. 18.

CII. II. De statu corruptionis. Quam primum homo præceptum Domini transgressus est, statim imaginem concreatam amisit, & consequenter vnà rectitudinis libertatem, hoc est illam Deum diligendi & legem implendi facultatem. Homo enim malè vtens libero arbitrio, & se perdidit, & ipsum. Cum enim libero arbitrio peccaretur, victore peccato amissum est & liberum arbitrium, "à quo enim quis deuictus est, huic seruus addictus est, dicente Augustino in Enchirid. cap. 30. Neque verò tantum spoliatus est homo libertate, sed successit vnà effrenis ad malum impetus, qui homines non renatos semper incitat ad malum, vt nihil nisi peccare possint. Vti enim durante statu innocentiæ viguit in mente hominis cognitio Dei, in voluntate, iustitia, sanctitas & obediendi studium; in appetitu, ἁρμονία & cum ratione conformitas; sic contra in statu lapsus successit in mente ignorantia & cæcitas, in voluntate auersio & ad malum inclinatio, in appetitu contumacia & reluctandi studium; vnde fit, vt homo perpetuò peccet, seque ipsum ad Deum conuertere nequeat.

CIII. Verè igitur scripsit Lutherus art. 36. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit titulus sine re: loquitur autem non de actionibus externis, sed spiritualibus & Theologicis Quamuis enim post lapsum circa externum virtutis studium quodammodo liber sit homo, & indifferenter se habeat, attamen planè seruit respectu conuersionis suæ & legis diuinæ, quàm semper transgreditur & obseruare nequit. Habet igitur liberum arbitrium non ad bonum sed duntaxat ad malum: quæ alias vocatur libertas à iustitia Rom. 6. vers. 20. rectiùs autem miserabilis peccati seruitus nuncupatur. Qui enim facit peccatum, seruus est peccati. Ioh. 8. v. 34. Et à quo quis superatus eius & seruus est 2. Pet 2. v. 19.

CIV. III. De statu reparationis. Cum autem homo ad Deum conuertitur, adeoque ex statu culpæ in statum gratiæ transfertur, tum vnà libertas arbitrij h. e. vires diligendi Deum & obseruandi legem quodammodo restaurantur. Peccato enim dominium adimitur, vt quamuis Spiritui resistat suis affectibus, Spiritus tamen vincat & carnem mortificet. Habent igitur renati libertatem à seruitute peccati, quia possunt bona Deóque placentia opera exercere, quò pertinent dicta Joh. 8. v. 36. Si Filius vos liberauerit verè liberi eritis. Rom. 6. v. 18. Liberati à peccato serui facti estis iustitiæ. 2. Cor. 3. v. 17. Vbi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. In isto igitur gratiæ statu concedimus renatis συνεργέιαν, quia vires cooperandi non quidem ex natura pullulantes, sed à Spiritu sancto per verbum gratiosè infusas & excitatas habent. Quæ tamen benè agendi vires non sunt prorsus consummatæ, sed tantùm inchoatæ, quoniam quamdiu viuimus, caro in nobis remanet, quæ resistit Spiritui Gal. 5. ver. 17. & repugnat legi mentis. Rom. 7. v. 23. vnde fit, vt renatus si à carne se abduci patiatur, vicissim ad vomitum redire & peccati seruituti iterum se mancipare possit, ideoque tot adhortationes leguntur, vt stemus in fide, resistamus Diabolo, & fideles vsque ad mortem permaneamus.

CV. IV. De statu glorificationis. Quemadmodum in altera vita perfecta erit mentis cognitio, & abolebitur quod ex parte est; Ita perfectam quoque adipiscemur voluntatis libertatem, quâ liberi erimus tum à seruitute peccati, tum à miseria & omnibus reliquijs peccati, tum ab ipsa etiam mutabilitate, siquidem bonum ita amabimus, vt malum velle non possimus, siquidem confirmabimur in gratia, vt ex statu illo felici nunquam excidere valeamus: Erimus enim æquales angelis, Matth. 22. v. 30. qui non possunt non benè agere & æternâ beatitudine gaudere. Ibi ergò plenè restituetur liberum arbitrium, imò plus restituetur quàm amissum est in Adamo, quippe qui sic liber erat, vt peccare & miser fieri posset, beati verò ita erunt liberi, vt peccare miserique fieri non possint, Ibi aberit à ratione error, à voluntate dolor, à memoria timor, ab appetitu rancor: & contrà aderit serena lux mentis, gaudium & libertas voluntatis, vbi triste nihil videbitur, vbi lætitia semper habebitur, vbi malum nullum timebitur; quoniam ibi summum bonum possidebitur, quod est videre semper faciem Domini virtutum dicente Augustino in soliloquijs cap. 35.

CVI. Ita ergò vidimus, quas in quouis statu arbitrium humanum vires obtineat, quæ omnia breuiter efferri poterunt, si dicamus : Homo in primo statu fuit liber; in secundo est seruus, in tertio liberatus, in quarto erit liberrimus.
