Liber in statu integritatis, quia peccare & non peccare poterat. Seruus est in statu lapsus, quia non potest non peccare. Liberatus est est statu gratiæ, quia iterum potest non peccare, & bene agere. Liberrimus verò erit in statu glorię, quia ibi amplius peccare aut infelix effici non poterit.


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and moral actions?

CVII. The object of free will is either worldly and profane, which is subject to the senses and human reason, and thus is found outside the Church: or it is sacred and sublime, which surpasses the senses and is held only in the Church of Christ. From both arise diverse acts. For the worldly object comprises 1. Those things which pertain to animal life strictly accepted or to the vegetative, sentient, and locomotive power. 2. Civil conversation and all things which are required of a good citizen by the laws of the magistrate. 3. The external pursuit of virtue, about which instruction is given in Ethics; and 4. various arts, both liberal and illiberal. From this fourfold object arise four kinds of human acts. The first contains natural acts, which look to natural and animal life, as are eating, drinking, sleeping, and the like. The second, civil acts, such as waging war, paying tribute, and obeying prescribed laws. The third, moral acts, to which is referred in general the exercise of virtue or vices. The fourth, artificial arts, such as to speculate, to contemplate the nature of things, to till the earth, or to exercise other manual arts. In all these profane acts we grant man liberty and contingency, since he can act and not act, as experience testifies, so much so that Scotus rightly said that one should deal with those who deny this free will not so much by arguments as by torments. For they should be beaten with rods until they confessed that it is in our power not to beat them any longer. If they were to complain of the injury, it could be answered, Why do you complain of us, when you yourselves assert that it is not in our power to cease from beating?

CIIX. As for the sacred object of liberty, actions of a different kind arise from it as well. For they are either external, which concern the external exercise of religion, such as going to the temple, hearing the word of God, reading, etc. Or they are internal and spiritual, and singularly pleasing to God, such as truly knowing God, assenting to the Gospel, believing in Christ, and living according to the Spirit. By reason of these spiritual actions, the will of an unregenerate man is enslaved, not free, as will be demonstrated in the next disputation. But concerning external actions, just as in profane ones, we willingly grant man liberty, and we shall soon show this very thing.

CIX. No small difficulty lies hidden here, how the actions of men can be free and contingent, since all things depend upon the will and nod of God. For the ancient Stoics concluded thus: If all things are already defined and preordained from eternity by divine decree, it is certainly necessary that they …happen in time in that way. If it were otherwise, one thing would happen and another would have been sanctioned by God, and thus the will of God would either be deceived or changed. Since this is impious to say, it will follow that all things happen necessarily and indeed by the force of a divine, eternal, and immutable constitution. And from this they deduced that adamant and inex orabile, which was theirs, as defined by Chrysippus in Gellius, book 6, Attic Nights, chapter 2. A certain everlasting and unchangeable series of things, and a chain, rolling itself and entangling itself through eternal orders of consequence, from which it is fitted and connected. By this fate that thief excused his misdeeds, saying, 'I stole by fate,' but the other retorted: 'Therefore, by fate you shall be hanged.'

CX. However, we do not wish to deny that this argument is most difficult. For it can scarcely be perceived by reason how eternal preordination and infallible providence can stand together with the temporal and mutable contingency of things and the freedom of actions. For if you assume the one, you seem to have denied the other, and vice versa. Hence were born those two heretical enthymemes, the one Epicurean, the other Stoic. The Epicurean holds thus: 'Contingency is given; therefore, there is no providence, no eternal preordination.' The Stoic, however, concludes in the contrary manner: 'Providence is given; therefore, there is no contingency, and consequently all things happen by inevitable necessity.' These are those two most dangerous rocks upon which human reason most often strikes. But let us be mindful of that which is written by Augustine, book 5, On the City of God, chapter 9. However tortuous the contentions and disputations of the philosophers may be, a religious soul confesses both, and confirms both by the faith of piety. For what pagan superstition thought to be ἀνύφατα (inexplicable), the Christian religion teaches to be ὑπάλληλα (subordinate/interconnected). For neither does contingency abolish God's ordination or providence, nor does the latter abolish the former; and therefore we ought to teach, believe, and confess not contingency without providence, nor providence without contingency, but both together.

CXI. That providence exists is proved elsewhere against the Epicureans, who call it into doubt. Something must be added here concerning contingency and liberty, so that the Stoic objection may be sufficiently answered. Wherefore 1. The contingency of things and the liberty of actions we shall demonstrate, and we shall refute the necessity of events. 2 we shall set forth the boundaries of contingency & necessity. 3 In particular we shall respond to the argument itself.

CXII. I. Demonstration of liberty. That contingency exists and not all things happen necessarily, but many things freely, even if all things are predetermined from eternity, can be proven. 1. From the Scriptures. 2. By reasons. 3. By human testimonies. Scripture asserts contingency 1. By manifest sayings, such as are read in Gen. 4. v. 7. Its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it. Exod. 35. v. 5. Let everyone who is willing and of a ready mind offer offerings to the Lord. Num. 30. v. 14. It shall be in the man's discretion whether he does it or not. 1. Cor. 7. v. 36. we are said regarding marriage not to have necessity, but power of will. And in the Epistle to Philem. v. 14. Without your counsel I wanted to do nothing, so that your good might not be κατ' ἀνάγκην by necessity ἀλλὰ καθ' ἑκούσιον but voluntary.

2. By opinions, which it sometimes gives, as Deut. 30. v. 19. Choose life, &c. Jos. 24. verse 15. An option is given to you, choose today what pleases you, 2. Sam. 24 v. 12. An option of three is given to you, choose one that you wish. 1. Reg. 3. verse 5. Ask what you wish that I may give it to you. But if an option of choosing is given, absolute necessity finds no place. For if one thing is necessary, what can we choose?

3. By examples, as 1. Paral. 29. v. 9. the people rejoice, because they contributed willingly & liberally to the building of the temple. Thus Ananias freely, not necessarily, sold his field, for which reason Peter said to him in Acts 5. verse 4. While it remained, did it not remain your own? and after it was sold, was it in your own power? Thus the Apostle affirms 1. Cor. 9. verse 4. 5. 6. Do we not have power to eat and to drink and to lead about a wife? &c. And Ecclesiast. 31. verse 10. The rich man is commended, who could have transgressed and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it. To this also pertains the law concerning contingent or accidental homicides

Num. 5. v. 22. which nevertheless were not so fortuitous as to exclude divine ordination, since it is said in Exod. 21. v. 13. that he who was killed in this way was delivered by God himself into the hands of the slayer. Thus the Jews freely and deliberately adjudged Jesus to death, Matt. 27. and yet the Apostles affirm that they did that which the hand and counsel of the Lord had decreed to be done, Act. 2. v. 27. 28.

4. By the accusations of the impious and the unfaithful, to whose voluntary malice all punishment and penalty is ascribed, as in Num. 14. verse 43. You shall fall by the sword, because you would not acquiesce to the Lord. Isa. 65. v. 12. You have chosen the things that I did not want. If God did not want them, they were certainly not impelled by God to choose them. Jerem. 32. v. 23. Because you hardened your heart, and would not obey the Lord, all these evils have come upon you. Hosea 13. v. 9. Your destruction, O Israel. Matth. 23. v. 37. How often would I have gathered your children and you would not? Luke 7. v. 30. The Pharisees rejected the counsel of God against themselves. Act. 7. v. 52. You always resist the Holy Spirit: From which we conclude; He who sins either can not sin: If he can, contingency and liberty are granted; if he cannot, men are falsely accused, as if it depended on them that they acted less well. But since this is absurd and impious, the former will be true and must be asserted. To this also should be referred the rebukes, admonitions, and exhortations occurring most frequently in the Scriptures, which openly prove contingency and liberty.

CXIII. Reasons for contingency are derived, 1. from laws, which would be useless and vain in a state. 2. from sins, of which God would become the author if all things happened by the force of an eternal law, 3. from virtue, which must be χρῆμα ἀδέσποτον καὶ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον, a free and non-necessary thing, Damasc. lib. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. 4. from rewards and punishments, the former of which would be unmerited, the latter unjust, if actions were not in our power. 5. from deliberations, which would be taken away if nothing were in our power. 6. from prayers and supplications, which are various, if mere necessity reigns. 7. From the constitution of man, who consists of mind and reason, which is the perpetual parent of liberty. 8. from the perfection of the world. There are given servants, there are given things acting by necessity: therefore also things acting freely or contingently, lest any species be wanting to the world.ld.

CXIV. Very many testimonies could be alleged, but let three suffice here. 1. That of Augustine which is read in lib. 3. hypognost.: There is indeed free will, and if anyone denies that it exists, he is not a Catholic. And conversely in lib. de duabus animabus: Nor are obscure books to be searched by me here, from which I might learn that no one is worthy of blame or punishment who does not do what he cannot do. Do not both shepherds on the mountains, and poets in the theaters, and the unlearned in circles, and the learned in libraries, and masters in schools, and prelates in sacred places, and the human race throughout the world sing these things? 2. That of Damascenus in lib. 2. cap. 7: ἡμεῖς ἀυτεξούσιοι ὑπὸ τοῦ δημιοῦργοῦ γινόμενοι κύριοι τῶν ἡμε- τέρων ὑπαρχόμεν πράξεων. We, having been made by the Creator with free power, are masters of our own actions. 3. That of Lombard in lib. 1. sent. dist. 39. Those who deny all contingencies wish for everything to happen necessarily, and they ought to be exposed to the torments of four arguments and be tortured until they concede that it is possible for them not to be tortured. See more in Irenaeus, l. 4; Tertullian, lib. 2, contra Marcionem; Ambrose, lib. 2, de vocat. gent., cap. vlt.; Jerome, lib. 3, in Ierem., Hom. 50, in Matth.; and Fulgentius, lib. 1, ad Monicam.

Latin:

CVII. Objectum liberi arbitrij vel est mundanum & profanum quod subjacet sensibus & rationi humanæ, adeoque extra Ecclesiam reperitur: vel est sacrum & sublime, quod sensus superat & non nisi in Ecclesia Christi habetur. Ex utroque oriuntur diuersi actus. Obiectum enim mundanum comprehendit 1. Illa quæ ad vitam animalem strictè acceptam vel ad potentiam vegetatiuam, sentientem & locomouentem pertinent. 2. Ciuilem conuersationem & omnia, quæ à bono ciue per leges magistratus requiruntur. 3. Externum virtutis studium, de quo in Ethicis præcipitur; & 4. varias artes tam liberales quàm illiberales. Ex hoc quadruplici objecto exsurgunt quatuor genera actuum humanorum. Primum continet actus naturales, qui ad vitam naturalem & animalem spectant, vt sunt edere, bibere, dormire & similes. Secundum actus ciuiles, vt militiam gerere, tributum soluere, & legibus præscriptis obtemperare. Tertium actus morales, quò refertur in genere virtutis aut vitiorum exercitium. Quartum artes artificiales, vt speculari, naturam rerum consplerare, terrae colere, aliasue artes manuarias exercere. In his actibus profanis omnibus libertatem homini concedimus & contingentiam, quandoquidem agere & non agere potest, vti testatur experientia, adeo quidem vt recte dixerit Scotus, non tam rationibus quam cruciatibus esse agendum contra negantes hoc liberum arbitrium. Tamdiu enim verberibus pulfandi essent, donec confiterentur, in nostra potestate esse, eos non amplius pulfandi Si conquererentur de iniuria, responderi posset, Quid de nobis conquerimini, cum vos ipsi asseratis, non esse in nostra potestate cessare a verberando?

CIIX. Obiectum vero libertatis sacrum quod attinet, ex illo etiam diuersi generis actiones oriuntur. Vel enim externae sunt, quae circa religionis exercitium externum versantur, quales sunt templum accedere, verbum Dei audire, legere, &c. Vel internae & spirituales, Deoque singulariter placentes, vt sunt, Deum vere cognoscere, Euangelio assentiri, in Christum credere, & secundum Spiritum viuere. Ratione harum actionum spiritualium hominis non renati arbitrium seruum est, non liberum, vti proxima disputatione demonstrabitur. Sed circa actiones externas, sicut & in profanis, libertatem homini lubenter concedimus, & mox id ipsum ostensuri sumus.

CIX. Non exigua vero difficultas hic delitescit, quomodo liberæ & contingentes esse possint actiones hominum, cum omnia ex Dei arbitrio nutuque dependeant. Ita enim concluserunt antiqui Stoici: Si omnia iam ab æterno sunt definita & præordinata diuino decreto, vtique necesse est in tempore ita euenire. Secus si sit, aliud fieret & aliud a Deo sancitum esset, atque sic Dei voluntas aut falleretur aut mutaretur. Quod cum dictu sit impium, sequetur omnia fieri necessario & quidem vi constitutionis diuinæ, æternæ, immutabilis. Atque hinc deduxerunt fatum istud suum adamantinum & inexorabile, quod ipsis erat, definiente Chrysippo apud Gellium lib. 6. N. A. cap. 2. Sempiterna quædam & indeclinabilis series rerum, & catena, voluens semetipsa sese, & implicans per æternos consequentiæ ordines, ex quibus apta connexaque est. Hoc fato malefacta sua excusatus fur ille, dicebat, Fato furatus sum, sed regerebat alter: fato ergo suspenderis.

CX. Diffiteri autem nolumus, argumentum illud esse difficilimum. Vix enim percipi potest ratione, quomodo æterna præordinatio & infallibilis prouidentia simul stet cum temporali & mutabili rerum contingentia & actionum libertate. Nam si assumas illud, videris hoc negâsse, & contra. Vnde nata sunt duo illa enthymemata Hæretica, alterum Epicuræum, alterum Stoicum. Epicuræum sic habet, Datur contingêtia, Ergo, nulla providentia, nulla præordinatio æterna. Stoicum verò concludit modo contrario: Datur prouidentia: Ergo nulla contingêtia, ideoque ineuitabili necessitate omnia eveniunt. Hi sunt duo illi periculosissimi scopuli, in quos humana ratio sæpius impingit. Nos autê simus memores istius quod ab August. scribitur l. 5. de Ciu. Dei cap. 9. Quomodocunque se habeant tortuosissimæ concertationes & disputationes Philosophorum, religiosus animus vtrumque confitetur, & fide pietatis vtrumque confirmat. Nam quæ ἀνύφατα putauit Ethnica superstitio, ea ὑπάλληλα docet Christiana religio. Neque enim contingentia tollit Dei ordinationem aut prouidentiam, neque hæc illam; & propterea non solam sine prouidentia contingentiam, nec solam siue contingentia providentiam, sed vtramque simul docere, credere, & confiteri debemus.

CXI. Prouidentiam esse probatur alibi contra Epicuræos, istam in dubium vocantes. De contingentia & libertate hic aliquid addendum est, vt ad obiectionem Stoicam sufficienter respondeatur. Quapropter 1. Contingentiam rerum & libertatem actionum demonstrabimus, necessitatemque euentuum refutabimus. 2 terminos contingentiae & necessitatis exponemus. 3 In specie ad argumentum ipsum respondebimus.

CXII. I. Libertatis demonstratio. Dari contingentiam nec omnia fieri necessario, sed multa libere, etiamsi omnia ab aeterno sint praedefinita, probari potest. 1. Ex Scripturis. 2. Rationibus. 3. Humanis testimonijs. Scriptura contingentiam adstruit 1. Manifestis dictis, qualia leguntur Gen. 4. v. 7. Sub te erit appetitus ejus, & tu dominaberis illi. Exod. 35. v. 5. Omnis voluntarius & prono animo offerat oblationes Domino. Num. 30. v. 14. In arbitrio viri erit siue faciat siue non. 1. Cor. 7. v. 36. dicimur quoad conjugium non habere necessitatem, sed potestatem voluntatis. Et in Epistola ad Philem. v. 14. Sine tuo consilio nihil volui facere, vt bonum tuum non sit κατ' ἀνάγκην ex necessitate ἀλλὰ καθ' ἑκούσιον sed voluntarium.

2. Opinionibus, quas nonnunquam dat, vt Deut. 30. v. 19. Elige vitam, &c. Jos. 24. vers. 15. Optio vobis datur, eligite hodie quod placet, 2. Sam. 24 v. 12. Trium tibi datur optio, elige vnum quod volueris. 1. Reg. 3. vers. 5. Postula quod vis vt dem tibi. Si autem optio datur eligendi, necessitas absoluta locum non inuenit. Si enim vnum est necessarium, quid eligere possumus?

3. Exemplis, vt 1. Paral. 29. v. 9. laetatur populus, quod sponte & liberaliter contribuerent ad aedificationem templi. Sic Ananias libere non necessario vendidit agrum suum, qua de causa ad ipsum dixit A. Petrus Act. 5. vers. 4. Nonne manens tibi manebat, & venundatum in tua erat potestate? Sic Apostolus affirmat 1. Cor. 9. vers 4. 5. 6. An non habemus potestatem manducandi & bibendi & mulierem circumducendi? &c. Et Ecclesiast. 31. vers. 10. Commendatur diues, qui potuit transgredi & non est transgressus facere mala & non fecit. Huc etiam pertinet lex de homicidijs contingentibus vel fortuitis

Num. 5. v. 22. quæ tamen non ita fuêre fortuita, vt excluderent ordinationem diuinam, cum Exod. 21. v. 13. dicatur is, qui hoc modo occisus est, ab ipso Deo in manus interfectoris traditus. Sic Iudæi Iesum liberè & consultò morti adiudicârunt, Matt. 27. & tamen affirmant Apostoli, eos fecisse id, quod manus & consilium Domini decreuerat fieri, Act. 2. v. 27. 28.

4. Accusationibus impiorum & infidelium, quorum voluntariæ malitiæ pœna & supplicium omne asscribitur, vt Num. 14. vers. 43. Corruetis gladio, eo quod nolueritis acquiescere Domino. Efa: 65. v. 12. Quæ nolui elegistis. Si Deus noluit, à Deo vtique ad eligendum impulsi non sunt. Ierem. 32. v. 23. Quæ indurastis cor vestrum, & noluistis obedire Domino, hæc omnia mala euenerunt vobis. Oseæ 13. v. 9. Perditio tua Israël. Matth. 23. v. 37. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos & noluisti? Luc. 7. v. 30. Pharisæi spreuerunt consilium Dei aduersus semetipsos. Act. 7. v. 52. Semper Spiritui S. resistitis: Ex quibus concludimus; Is qui peccat vel potest non peccare: Si potest, datur contingentia & libertas, si non potest, falsò accusantur homines, quasi per ipsos steterit, quod minus benè agerent. Hoc autem cùm sit absurdum & impium, prius illud erit verum & asserendum. Huc quoque referantur increpationes, admonitiones & exhortationes in Scripturis sæpissimè occurrentes, quæ contingentiam & libertatem apertè comprobant.

CXIII. Rationes pro contingentia desumuntur, 1. à legibus, quæ essent inutiles & frustraneæ in po litia. 2. à peccatis, quorum author Deus fieret, si omnia vi legis sempiternæ euenirent, 3. à virtute, quæ debet esse χρῆμα ἀδέσποτον καὶ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον res libera & non necessaria Damasc. l. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. 4. à præmijs & supplicijs, quorum illa indebita, hæc iniusta forent, si actiones in potestate nostra non essent. 5. à deliberationibus, quæ tollerentur si nihil esset ipsius. 6. a precibus & supplicationibus, quae variae sunt, si mera regnet necessitas. 7. Ab hominis constitutione, qui mente constat & ratione, quae perpetua libertatis parens est. 8. a mundi perfectione. Dantur serva, dantur necessariò agentia: E. & libera vel contingenter operantia, ne mundo desit aliqua species.

CXIV. Testimonia benè multa possent allegari, sed sufficiant hîc tria. 1. Augustini quod legitur lib. 3. hypognost. Est utique liberum arbitrium, quod si quis esse negauerit, Catholicus non est. Et vicissim lib. de duabus animabus: Neque hîc libri obscuri mihi scrutandi, unde discam, neminem vituperatione suppliciove dignum, qui id non facit quod facere non potest. Nonne ista cantant & in montibus Pastores, & in theatris Poetae, & indocti in circulis, & docti in bibliothecis, & Magistri in scholis, & antistites in sacris locis, & in orbe terrarum genus humanum. 2. Damasceni lib. 2. cap. 7: ἡμεῖς ἀυτεξούσιοι ὑπὸ τοῦ δημιοῦργοῦ γινόμενοι κύριοι τῶν ἡμετέρων ὑπαρχόμεν πράξεων. Nos liberae potestatis à conditore facti, domini nostrarum actionum sumus. 3. Lombardi lib. 1. sent. dist. 39. Ii qui abnegant contingentia omnia volunt necessariò fieri, tormentis positis quatuor rationibus exponendi, & tandiu sunt cruciandi, donec concedant, possibile esse eos non torqueri. Plura vide apud Irenaeum l. 4. Tertull. lib. 2. contra Marcionem. Ambros. lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. vlt. Hieron. lib. 3. in Ierem. Hom. 50. in Matth. & Fulgent. lib. 1. ad Monicam.


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and…: CXV. II. Explanation of terms

CXV. II. Explanation of terms. The term for both contingency and necessity must be properly explained. 1. Contingency is derived from contingent, which in Greek is called ἐνδεχόμενον, and it is of such a nature that it can both be or not be, or be done or not be done, and whether it happens or does not happen, nothing absurd is committed, nor is there any contradiction, nor is it against the word of God. Contingency, therefore, is nothing other than δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως, or a propensity toward either side, to be and not to be, to be done and not to be done. Three degrees or species of this are recited by the Philosopher in the book On Interpretation, chapter 9, in the Posterior Analytics, chapter 12, and in the Topics, book 2, chapter 6. 1. is τὸ ὁπότερ ἔτυχεν, which can happen as well as not happen, such as winning at dice. 2. ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ, which for the most part and more often happen so: 3. ὡς ἐλάχισον, which do not happen except rarely and unusually. From this definition and division of the contingent, it clearly appears that the contingent is spoken of and considered only in relation to the future, and therefore that is contingent which is still in its causes, and can happen and not happen. Hence the Metaphysicians commonly say: A being and an effect is called contingent by reason of causes operating contingently: but not by reason of existence. From which follows the maxim, Whatever effect has not necessary but indifferent and contingently acting causes is called contingent, even if at the time when it is, it is necessarily and cannot be otherwise.

CXVI. 2. Necessity is derived from necessary, which is of such a kind that it is determined to one part only. And there is a twofold necessity, one is called of compulsion, the other of immutability. By necessity of compulsion are those things whose cause or active principle is outside us, so that we do not cooperate with that motion, but resist it, which kind of necessity some of the Stoics asserted. And such was that in Balaam, who was compelled to bless the Israelites, even though he resisted with his whole will. Necessity of immutability is when an agent is bound to one part only, yet without any compulsion and violence. And this in turn is either absolute or of the consequent, or hypothetical or of the consequence. The former consists in the essential cohesion of cause and effect, when indeed a thing follows from a necessary antecedent cause, so that the opposite is impossible: the latter consists in a connection with consequences by presupposition, when indeed the antecedent being posited, or not of exercise, namely its volition and seeking, for all necessarily wish to be blessed, and not only do they not wish to be miserable, but they cannot even wish it. Therefore the ultimate end is necessarily sought, and yet freely. But where there are many means, there is given a preceding act, and there is also given a consequent one: The preceding is indifferent. For I can wish or not wish to choose or not choose one means. The consequent, however, is necessary, for when I have firmly pre-chosen this means, I cannot not neglect the others, and yet I neglect them freely. In those things also which cohere, if we wish for one, it is necessary that we wish for the other. Thus from the will to cross the sea arises a necessity in the will that it should wish for a ship: Thus, with an indissoluble friendship presupposed, I cannot not love a friend, and yet I love freely; whence Caelius Rhodiginus says, No necessity is considered more voluntary than that of love.

LXXVII. But just as some necessity is found in the actions of men, so also is indifference or mutability: For free will is, by reason of exercise, in acts both elicited and commanded: But especially in acts good or evil in their own kind is this indifference most observed, and it is twofold. I. Regarding the special object. For there are two contraries, virtue and vice: to neither is the will of man determined, but it is permitted to follow either at its own discretion. II. Regarding the acts themselves. For it is permitted to the will to pursue or not to pursue virtue, it is permitted to flee or follow vice, nor does it necessarily indulge in virtues or vices. And this twofold indifference is rightly heeded by politicians and legislators, who decree punishments or rewards. For no one is worthy of praise or blame, punishment or reward, who is destitute of this indifference. Whence it also came about that afterwards, in common parlance, nothing other than this indetermination was understood by the name of liberty. But we must rightly distinguish between the acceptance of the term Political, and accurately Philosophical. Politicians indeed, and even Ethicists, when speaking of virtues and vices, rightly accept liberty as indifference. But if we consider the matter accurately, the will itself is certainly denoted, since it is free not through something superadded, but through itself, for which reason we pronounce the actions of the will also, as such, all free, even if they are necessary.

LXXIIX. Nor yet do we assert by this very fact that any operations whatsoever, which are not forced, are free. Fire is not carried upward by force, water is not carried downward by force: yet not freely. Such effects are indeed free from force, but not simply free. Therefore we do not oppose the free to the necessary or the unforced, but primarily and per se to the involuntary. For just as the will, because it is the will and insofar as it is the will, and thus is free through itself, so also actions, because they are actions of the will, and insofar as they are of the will, are free. Therefore also their opposite is nothing other than the involuntary. For everything involuntary, in that it is involuntary, and insofar as it is involuntary, is not free.

LXXIX. But when we consider man theologically, different states are to be attended to, namely: 1. Innocence. 2. Guilt. 3. Grace. 4. Glory. The liberty of men in the state of glory behaves in the same way as the liberty of the Angels, of which we spoke in thesis 74. Liberty in the state of innocence and grace agree almost entirely, and therefore only the state of integrity and the fall must be discussed, which can be dispatched in two assertions.

LXXX. 1. Man before the fall was free from necessity and force, as much regarding evil actions as good ones, as much in respect of election as of execution, as much regarding specification as exercise. He was devoid of necessity before the fall, because God left him in the hand of his counsel, Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14; therefore he was choosing and pursuing good freely and contingently, not forcedly, not necessarily, and he was choosing and desiring evil freely, because he was not yet inclined to evil by an internal principle, and thus he was free from the servitude of sin, yet not from law or obligation, because it was only commanded to him that he should not sin. If therefore it is asked, whether Adam before the fall had the free power of choosing either good or evil, we answer that he indeed had it, yet he ought not to have exercised the same. For God had commanded him to choose and execute only good things. And hence appears the greatest distinction between the liberty of God and of man, since God is most free from all law and obligation, for he has no superior, but man, since he is subject to God, was not endowed with that kind of liberty. He was, however, free from coercion, from necessity, from sin and misery. Nor, however, is it to be thought that man was more free than God, because his will was not determined to one thing, but indifferent: for this indetermination does not argue supreme liberty, but rather flexibility and ambiguity, opposed to constancy, and therefore Luther in his book De servo arbitrio, page 98, thinks that this will is more correctly named mutable and changeable than free. And the commentator of Damascene says in book 2, De Orthodoxa Fide, chapter 22: Mutability is not required for the definition of liberty.

LXXXI. II. Man after the fall is free from coercion in all voluntary actions, since the will cannot be forced: he is free from necessity regarding the kind of actions considered theologically, which are evil and displeasing to God: for he has an internal principle of this necessity, namely original sin, by which the mind and will of man are so corrupted that nothing but evil things can proceed from them, for a bad tree is not productive of good fruits, Matthew 7, verse 10, for which reason we are called by nature children of wrath, Ephesians 2, verse 3. & servants of sin Rom. 6. v. 17. However, this necessity does not conflict with liberty, and therefore it could be called a voluntary necessity, and a necessary will, just as Bernard seems to suggest in Sermon 81 on the Song of Songs: I know not by what perverse and wonderful way the will itself, having been changed for the worse by sin, makes a necessity for itself, so that the necessity, when it is voluntary, cannot excuse the will, nor can the will, when it has been enticed, exclude the necessity. And below: Thus the soul, in a certain wonderful and evilly free way, is held as a handmaid by necessity and is free, a handmaid on account of necessity, free on account of the will, and what is more wonderful and more miserable, it is guilty in that it is free, and therefore a handmaid in that it is guilty, and by this, a handmaid in that it is free.

LXXXII. But as regards the species of human actions, they are either commanded or elicited. Regarding commanded actions, man is not free from the law, although he is free from coercion and from necessity regarding execution and election, as when a magistrate commands that one must not steal, a man is indeed bound and held to obey, yet it is in the power of his will to choose to steal and to execute it or otherwise, which is the liberty of contradiction. He has, moreover, the liberty of contrariety, as when an option is given to a delinquent by a magistrate to choose for a penalty either prison or a fine of money. Regarding elicited actions, in turn, man is free from coercion and necessity both regarding election and execution. For he can freely and contingently, not necessarily, choose some morally good work, and after the election either execute it or not execute it, since election and execution differ much, nor do they necessarily cohere in human actions, as they do in divine ones. The reason for the diversity is easily given, because God is immutable, therefore what He has once decreed He will do, that He does immutably and necessarily: But man is mutable, whence it happens that he can now choose something, yet soon change his mind, and not execute that which he chooses, although thus the execution does not follow, even if it be certain that the election also had been changed. For if the first election still held its place, without a doubt the execution would follow.

LXXXIII. And it is sufficiently apparent from this that liberty has been left to man in external actions, since he can do what he wills and not do what he does not will, although it sometimes happens in more specific actions that the human will is peculiarly inclined by God to do this and not that. We read an example of Cyrus, who in Isaiah 45, verse 1, is called the Servant of the Lord; he was attacking Babylon voluntarily, not under compulsion, yet his will was peculiarly directed and inclined to that by God: that action, therefore, was not contingent, but in a certain way necessary on account of the inclination of the will brought about divinely, which is commonly called the necessity of dependence. These, however, are extraordinary examples, which can prejudice ordinary ones in no way.

LXXXIV. Thus, therefore, through the individual species of free beings we have shown so far that liberty very often concurs with necessity and can consist with it very well, and that nothing is repugnant to free will other than the necessity of nature and of compulsion, which very thing Bonaventure in book 2, distinction 25, question 6, and Biel likewise in question 1 taught before us, saying: Since there is a twofold necessity, of compulsion and of immutability, the necessity of compulsion is repugnant to the liberty of the will, but the necessity of immutability is not.

LXXXV. Against the contrary, what Bellarmine might object, he finds almost nothing. He alleges in chapter 5 the saying of Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14, which must be explained either concerning the state of integrity and grace, or if concerning the state of the fall, it notes only liberty in external matters and regarding exercise, where we do not deny that the will is indifferent and changeable. Thus the canons of the councils and the sayings of the Fathers do not at all militate against us. For they either understand compulsion by necessity, or they speak about indifference regarding external actions, and as regards exercise. They do not, however, exclude all necessity in general and indistinctly from free will, just as Pareus shows in particular in book 3, chapter 5, page 415 and following. Afterwards he adds five reasons, but of little importance; we shall, however, briefly run through them in place of a conclusion.

LXXXVI. 1. If freedom from coercion were sufficient for free will, it would follow that there is free will even in cattle. For they too are moved to fodder of their own accord without any coercion. Resp. Freedom from coercion alone is not sufficient, but freedom from physical necessity is required in addition, by which cattle are moved to fodder. Knowledge of the intellect and προαίρεσις of the agent are also required, both of which brutes lack. Since, therefore, man is free from both physical and coercive necessity, and acts προαιρετικῶς, all of which are not found in brutes, it follows that man has free will, not cattle.

2. It would follow that in children, the insane, and those dreaming there is the use of free will, for they all act of their own accord. Resp. To act of one's own accord is not to act in προαίρεσις, which is nevertheless required for the exercise of freedom. Because, therefore, that spontaneous motion in children and the insane arises not from the use of the rational, but of the sensitive appetite, for that reason they do not have the use of free will properly so called.

3. It would follow that God begat the Son through free will and by choice, since He did not beget Him under coercion. Resp. Although it may seem that it can be said in a certain way that the Father begat the Son freely, because not under coercion, we nevertheless judge it to be done more correctly if it is said simply that the Father begat the Son neither under coercion nor not under coercion, because He begat Him not by will, but by nature.

4. There would never have been any question about free will, nor would any controversy remain with heretics. For no one has ever denied that either God or men are free from coercion. Resp. Although there is consensus on this, disagreement nevertheless remains in many other matters. It must be disputed with the Stoics, whether God is bound by the nexus of secondary causes? whether all things happen from absolute necessity? with the Manichaeans, whether sin arises from a malignant nature rather than from free will? with the Pelagians, whether the will is sufficient for itself without grace? With the Papists, whether the will of man concurs efficiently to his own conversion? etc.

Finally 5. It seems to state a contradiction, for one who affirms that free will is freed from coercion, but not from necessity, since it is an elective power, which cannot be understood with determination to one thing, and necessity. Resp. On the contrary, they are not contradictory. For the will remains an elective power, although it is involved in the necessity of immutability in certain respects, as we have shown by very many examples: it remains, moreover, free as to the exercise, although as to the species of acts it is determined to one kind.

Latin:

CXV. II. Terminorum explicatio. Terminus tùm contingentiae tùm necessitatis probè explanandus est. 1. Contingentia deducitur à contingente, quod Graecis dicitur ἐνδεχόμενον, & est eiusmodi, vt & possit & non possit esse vel fieri, & sive fiat siue non fiat, nihil absurdi committitur, neque contrarietatem neque contra verbum Dei. Contingentia ergo nihil est aliud, quàm δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως seu vel ad vtrumlibet, esse & non esse fieri & non fieri propensio. Hujus tres recitantur sive gradus siue species à Philosopholib. de interpret. cap. 92. post. cap. 12. & 2. Top. cap. 6. 1. est τὸ ὁπότερ ἔτυχεν quæ fieri tam possunt, quam non possunt, vt ludentem alea vincere. 2. ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ, quæ plerunqve &, sæpiùs ita accidunt: 3. ὡς ἐλάχισον quæ non nisi rarò ac insolenter e-ueniunt. Ex ista vero contingentis & defini-tione & diuisione euidenter apparet quod con-tingens solùm ratione futuri dicatur & con-sideretur, adeoque contingens illud sit, quod in suis causis adhuc est, fieriqve & non fieri potest. Hinc communiter dicunt Methaphysici: Ens & effectum dicitur contingens ratione causarum contingenter operantium: non autem ratione existentiæ. Ex quo sequitur maxima, Quo unque effectus, non necessarias sed indifferentes & contingenter agentes causas habet, contingens dicitur, etiamsi tùm quando est, necessario sit & aliter esse non possit.

CXVI. 2. Necessitas dicitur a necessario, quod est eiusmodi vt ad vnam duntaxat partem sit determi-natum. Estque duplex necessitas, altera coactio-nis dicitur, altera immutabilitatis. Necessitate coactionis sunt ea, quorum causa vel principium actiuum est extra nos, ita vt ad motum illum non cooperemur, sed reluctemur, qualem ne-cessitatem nonnulli Stoicorum asseruerunt. Et talis fuit in Balaam, qui cogebatur Israelitis be-nedicere, etiamsi tota voluntate obluctaretur. Necessitas immutabilitatis est, quando agens ad vnam tantùm partem sine omni tamen coactione & violentia adstringitur. Et hæc vicissim vel est absoluta seu consequentis, vel hypothetica, seu con-sequentiæ. Illa consistit in essentiali causæ & effectus cohæsione, quando nimirum res se-quitur ex causa antecedente necessaria, sic vt oppositum sit impossibile: hæc consistit in præsuppositione cum consequentibus conne-xa, quando nimirum antecedente posito, vel non exercitio, ) nempè eius volitio & expetitio, Omnes enim beati esse necessariò volunt, & miseri esse non modò nolunt, sed nè velle quidem possunt. Necessariò ergo finis vltimus appetitur, & tamen liberè. Vbi verò multa sunt media, ibi datur actus præcedens, datur & consequens: Præcedens est indifferens. Possum enim medium vnum velle aut non velle eligere aut non eligere. Consequens autem necessarius est, Quando enim firmiter præelegi hoc medium, non possum non reliqua negligere & tamen liberè negligo. In ijs etiam quæ cohærent, si vnum volumus, necessum est vt velimus & alterum. Sic ex voluntate transeundi mare fit necessitas in voluntate, vt velit nauem: Sic præsuppositâ amicitiâ indissolubili, non possum non amicum diligere, & tamen libere diligo; vnde Cœlius Rhodiginus, Necessitas inquit, nulla magis censetur voluntaria, quàm amatoria.

LXXVII. Vti verò necessitas quæpiam in actionibus hominum inuenitur, ita & indifferentia seu vertibilitas: Libera enim voluntas est ratione exercitij in actibus tàm elicitis quàm imperatis: Imprimis autem in actibus suo genere bonis vel malis hæc indifferentia maxime conspicitur, estque duplex. I. Quoad Obiectum speciale. Duo enim sunt contraria, virtus & vitium: ad neutrum voluntas hominis est determinata, sed licet illi vtrumque pro arbitratu sequi, II. Quoad actus ipsos. Licet enim voluntati virtutem sectari vel non sectari, licet vitium fugere vel sequi, neque necessariò virtutibus aut vitiis indulget. Atque hæc indifferentia duplex jure attenditur à Politicis & legumlatoribus, pœnas aut præmia decernentibus. Nemo enim laude vel culpâ, pœnâ vel præmio dignus, hac qui indifferentia destituitur. Vnde & factum, vt postmodum vulgariter libertatis nomine nihil aliud quàm hæc indeterminatio fuerit intellecta. Sed nos meritò distinguendum esse censemus inter acceptionem vocis Politicam, & accuratè Philosophicam. Politici quidem, quin & Ethici, de virtutibus & vitiis verba facientes, libertatem pro indifferentia jure accipiunt. Sin autem ἀκριβῶς rem consideremus, ipsa certè notatur voluntas, quippè quę non per superadditum aliquid, sed per seipsam libera est, qua de causa actiones etiam voluntatis, qua sic omnes liberas, etiamsi necessariæ sint, pronunciamus.

LXXIIX. Neque tamen hoc ipso asserimus, operationes quasvis, quæ coactæ non sunt, liberas esse. Ignis non coactè sursum, aqua non coacte deorsum fertur: haut tamen liberè. A coactione quidem liberæ sunt eiusmodi effectiones, sed non simpliciter liberæ. Igitur τὸ liberum non opponimus vel necessario vel non coacto, sed πρώτως & per se involuntario. Sicut enim voluntas quia voluntas & in quantum voluntas, adeoque per se ipsam est libera, ita & actiones ideò, quia sunt voluntatis actiones, & inquantum sunt voluntatis, liberæ sunt. Ergo & earum oppositum non est aliud, quàm involuntarium. Omne enim involuntarium, eò quòd involuntarium, & quatenus involuntarium, liberum non est.

LXXIX. Quando autem Theologicè consideramus hominem, diversi status attendendi sunt, nimirum. 1. Innocentiæ. 2. Culpæ. 3. Gratiæ. 4. Gloriæ. Libertas hominum in statu gloriæ eodem modo se habet quo libertas Angelorum, de qua th. 74. verba fecimus. Libertas in statu innocentiæ & gratiæ conueniunt fermè, ideoque tantum de statu integritatis & lapsus dicendum est, id quod duabus assertionibus expedire potest.

LXXX. 1. Homo ante lapsum liber fuit à necessitate & coactione, tam quo ad actiones malas, quàm bonas, tam electionis quàm executionis respectu, tam quoad specificationem quàm exercitium. Expers necessitatis fuit ante lapsum, quia Deus reliquit eum in manu consilij suij, Ecclesiastici 15. ver. 14. liberè igitur & contingenter, non coactè, non necessariò bonum tùm eligebat & tùm prosequebatur, malum jam liberè eligebat & appetebat, quia nondum ab interno principio inclinabatur ad malum, atque sic à seruitute peccati liber fuit, non tamen à jure seu obligatione, quia tantum ipsi erat præceptum, ne peccaret. Si ergo quæritur, An Adam ante lapsum habuerit liberam potestatem eligendi vel bonum vel malum, respondemus, quòd quidem eam habuerit, attamen eandem exerere non debuerit. Deus enim jusserat, bona duntaxat eligere & exequi. Atque hinc apparet maximum discrimē inter libertatem Dei & hominis, siquidem Deus ab omni jure & obligatione est liberrimus, superiorem enim se nõ habet, at homo quoniã Deo subiectus, istâ libertatis specie nõ fuit pręditus, Liber tamē erat a coactione, à necessitate, à peccato & miseria. Neq; tamen existimandum est, quod homo magis liber fuerit quàm Deus, quia eius arbitrium non erat ad vnum determinatum, sed indifferens: hæc enim indeterminatio non arguit summam libertatem, sed potius flexibilitatem & ambiguitatem, constantiæ oppositam, ideòque, Lutherus in libro de serv. arb. pag. 98 putat istud arbitrium rectius nominari vertibile & mutabile quam liberum. Et Commentator Damasceni ait in l. 2. de O. F. c. 22. Vertibilitas ad libertatis rationem non exigitur.

LXXXI. II. Homo post lapsum liber est à coactione in cunctis actionibus voluntarijs, siquidem voluntas cogi nequit: liber est à necessitate quoad genus actionū theologicè consideratarum, quæ malæ sunt & Deo displicent: habet enim internum huius necessitatis principium, videlicet peccatum originale, quo mens & voluntas hominis ita corruptæ sunt, vt nihil nisi mala inde prouenire queant, arbor siquidem mala bonorum fructuum non est ferax Matth. 7. versu 10. qua de causa dicimur natura filij iræ Ephes. 2. ver. 3. & ferui peccati Rom. 6. v. 17. Hæc autem necessitas non repugnat libertati, ideoque dici posset voluntaria necessitas, & necessaria voluntas, sicut innuere videtur Bernhardus Sermo. 81. in Cantica: Nescio quo pravo & miro modo ipsa sibi voluntas peccato quidem in deterius mutata necessitatem faciat, vt necessitas cùm voluntaria sit, excusare non valeat voluntatem, nec voluntas, cum sit illecta excludere necessitatem. Et infra: Ita anima miro quodam modo ac malè libera necessitate ancilla tenetur & libera, ancilla propter necessitatem, libera propter voluntatem, & quod magis mirum, magisq́; miserum est, eo rea, quo libera, eoq́; ancilla, quo rea, ac per hoc eo ancilla, quo libera.

LXXXII. Quod verò attinet species actionum humanatum, illæ sunt vel imperatæ vel elicitæ. Quoad actiones imperatas non est liber à iure, quamuis liber sit à coactione & à necessitate quoad executionem & electionem, vt quando Magistratus iubet, non esse furandum, homo quidem obstrictus tenetur ad obediendum, in potestate tamen arbitrij est furtum eligere, & exequi vel secus, quę est libertas cōtradictionis. Habet insuper libertatem contrarietatis, vt quando delinquenti optio datur à Magistratu eligendi pro pœna vel carcerem vel mulctam pecuniarum. Quoad actiones elicitas vicissim homo liber est à coactione & necessitate tā quoad electionē quàm executionē. Potest enim liberè & contingēter, non necessariò opus aliquod moraliter bonum eligere, & post electionē vel exequi vel non exequi, cum electio & executio multùm differant, nec necessario cohæreant in actiōnib⁹ humanis, sicut in divinis. Ratio diversitatis facilè datur, quia Deus est immutabilis, quod igitur semel decreuit se facturum, id immutabiliter & necessariò facit: Ast homo est mutabilis, vnde fit, vt possit iam aliquid eligere, mox tamen mutare sententiam, & id quod eligit, non exequi, quamvis sic executio non accedat, certum sit, electionem quoque mutatam fuisse. Si enim prima electio adhuc locum haberet, procul dubio subsequeretur executio.

LXXXIII. Atque satis hinc apparet homini in externis actionibus relictam esse libertatem, cum agere possit quod vult & non agere quod non vult, quamvis nonnunquam fiat in specialioribus actionibus, vt voluntas humana peculiariter à Deo inclinetur ad hoc & non illud faciendum, Exemplum legimus de Cyro, qui apud Esaiam 6, 45. vers. 1. vocatur Servus Domini; Is voluntariè, non coactè expugnabat Babylonem, attamen eius voluntas à Deo peculiariter ad id dirigebatur & inclinabatur: actio proinde ista non erat contingens, sed quodammodo necessaria ob voluntatis inclinationem diuinitus factam, quæ vulgo vocatur necessitas dependentiæ. Hęc verò sunt extraordinaria exempla, quæ ordinarijs nihil præjudicare possunt.

LXXXIV. Ita ergo per singulas liberorum entiũ species hactenus ostendimus, quod libertas cum necessitate sæpius concurrat optimeq́; consistere possit, nec libero arbitrio alia repugnet, quam naturæ & coactionis necessitas, quod ipsum ante nos docuerunt Bonaventura in l. 2. dist. 25 q 6. & Biel itidem q. vn. dicẽtes: Cum duplex sit necessitas coactionis & immutabilitatis, necessitas coactionis repugnat libertati arbitrij, necessitas vero immutabilitatis non item.

LXXXV. In contrarium quod objiceret Bellarminus, ferè nihil inuenit. Allegat c. 5. dictum Ecclesiastici 15. v. 14. quod vel de statu integritatis & gratiæ exponi debet, vel si de statu lapsus, notatur tantum libertas in externis & quoad exercitium, vbi indifferens & vertibile esse arbitrium ipsi non diffitemur. Sic Canones conciliorum & dicta Patrum contra nos nequaquam militant. Vel enim per necessitatem intelligunt coactionem, vel loquuntur de indifferentia circa externas actiones, & quoad exercitium. Omnem aute in genere & indistincte necessitatem a libero arbitrio minime excludunt, ficuti Pareus in specie ostendit lib. 3. c. 5. p. 415. feqq. Postmodo rationes quinque fubiungit, sed exigui momenti, Colophonis tamen loco breuiter percurremus.

LXXXVI. 1. Si ad liberum arbitrium sufficeret libertas a coactione, sequeretur etiam in pecoribus esse liberum arbitrium. Nam & illa sine coactione vlla sponte sua feruntur ad pabulum. Resp. Non sufficit sola libertas a coactione, sed requiritur insuper libertas a necessitate Physica, qua pecudes feruntur ad pabulum. Requiritur etiam cognitio intellectus & προαίρεσις agentis, qua vtraq; destituuntur bruta. Cum igitur homo a necessitate tam Physica quam coactiua liber sit, & προαιρετικῶς agat, quæ omnia in brutis non reperiuntur, sequitur hominem liberi arbitrij esse, non pecora.

2. Sequeretur in pueris, furiosis, somniantibus esse vsum liberi arbitrij, omnes enim sponte agunt. Resp. Sponte agere non est in προαιρέσει agere, quod tamen ad exercitium libertatis requiritur. Quia ergo motus ille spontaneus in pueris & furiosis non ex vsu rationalis, sed sensitiui appetitus oritur, ob id vsum liberi arbitrij proprie dictum non habent.

3. Sequeretur Deum per liberum arbitrium & ex electione genuisse filium, quoniam non coactus genuit. Resp. Licet quodammodo dici posse videatur, quod Pater filium genuerit libere, quia non coacte, rectius tamen fieri censemus, si simpliciter dicatur, quod Pater filium neque coactus neque non coactus genuerit, quia non voluntate, sed natura genuit.

4. Nulla fuisset vnquam quæstio de libero arbitrio, neque vlla cum hæreticis controuersia remaneret. Nemo enim negauit vnquam vel Deum vel homines liberos esse a coactione. Resp. Licet in hoc sit consensus, manet tamen in alijs multis dissensus. Disputandum est cum Stoicis, An Deus causarum secundarum nexu teneatur? num omnia fiant ex absoluta necessitate? cum Manichæis, An peccatum ex natura maligna potius quàm voluntate libera oriatur? cum Pelagianis, An arbitrium sibi sine gratia sufficiat? Cum Pontificijs Num voluntas hominis ad conuersionem sui efficienter concurrat? &c.

Tandem 5. Pugnantia videtur dicere, qui affirmat liberum arbitrium à coactione, non à necessitate solutum esse, cum sit potestas electiua, quæ non potest intelligi cum determinatione ad vnum, & necessitate. Resp. Imo verò non sunt pugnantia. Manet enim voluntas potentia electiua, licèt necessitati immutabilitatis in quibusdam sit implicata, vti exemplis benè multis ostendimus: Manet insuper libera quoad exercitium, licèt quoad speciem actuum ad vnum genere sit determinata.


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and…: Question IX. What is the subject of liberty?

QUESTION IX. What is the subject of liberty?

LXXXVII. Since the cognition of the intellect is a prerequisite in a free action, it follows of its own accord that the first and immediate ὑποκείμενον (subject) of liberty is an intelligent nature, inasmuch as this property always follows it, so that it is free in its actions. In this subject, however, the efficient cause of liberty is simultaneously involved. For all immanent effects, such as liberty is, are primarily received from their efficient causes, in such a way that from whom they have received their essence, in the same they have their existence. Therefore, an intelligent nature is both the cause and the primary subject of liberty.

LXXXIIX. From what has been said, however, two corollaries flow. FIRST: πᾶν λογικὸν καὶ αὐτεξούσιον. Every rational being is of free power and choice. Damasc. lib. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. & lib. 3. cap. 14. Since therefore Angels are intelligent substances, they will by no means lack freedom of choice, which the fall as well as the works of the Angels sufficiently confirm, with the support of Irenaeus l. 4. cap. 71. Basil de Spir. S. cap. 16. Augustine de corrept. & grat. cap. 10. Gregory hom. 7. in Ezech. & Damascene lib. 2. de fide c. 3. 4.

LXXXIX. But since the intensification of a cause simultaneously intensifies the effect, that which is more rational will certainly be more self-determined. And since God is supremely intelligent, nay, is intelligence and Wisdom itself, he will certainly also be supremely free, either as the most free agent, or rather as liberty itself. All those sayings of Scripture testify to this, which teach that God works through knowledge and will, and that created things are such as God willed them to be, not such as necessity compelled, as Ps. 115. v. 3. Dan. 3. v. 18. 1. Cor. 11. v. 12. Eph. 1. v. 11. Miracles performed for the sake of the order of nature also look to this, such as that the Sun stood still at the prayers of Joshua, retreated at the prayers of Hezekiah, failed at the full moon at the death of the Savior: that a virgin conceived and gave birth, that sight was restored to the blind, hearing to the deaf, and life to the dead, etc. For if God can now preserve and now change the order of nature at his pleasure, it follows that he works not out of necessity, but freely.

XC. It is therefore a calumny when Bellarmine lib. 3. cap. 15. objects that Luther denied God freedom of choice in assert. art. 36. inasmuch as he argues that all things happen by absolute necessity. But nothing of the sort is found in Luther, but he says this, that to those looking at heavenly things all things are necessary, not indeed by necessity of nature, in the way that fire necessarily burns, but by the necessity of immutable foreknowledge and divine counsel, according to which, without prejudice to the freedom and contingency of wills, it is necessary that scandals happen and it was necessary for Christ to suffer. But it does not follow that God

God himself is subject to necessity, although events are necessary with respect to divine foreknowledge.

XCI. It must be repeated, however, that no small distinction exists between the will of God and that of creatures. They do indeed have two things in common, namely 1. to act ἑκουσίως or spontaneously. 2. to act ἐκ προαιρέσεως with choice or deliberate counsel, yet they differ in turn in four ways. 1. With respect to the intellect; because God knows and understands all things most perfectly from himself; but creatures neither know all things, nor do they have from themselves what they do know, but rather most things from the divine Resolution, especially those which pertain to God and his will. 2. With respect to the will, for the divine will is covered by or depends upon no superior: but the will of men is directed by God in good actions, and corrupted by the Devil in evil ones. 3. With respect to both, because both the knowledge and the preordination of God are immutable, but the notions and wills of men are ambulatory or mutable, so that they now want what they previously did not want and do not want what they previously wanted. 4. With respect to the mode of choosing, because God chooses without consultation properly so-called, which is a discourse of reason from the known to the more unknown or from the notion of the end to the invention of the means: but men cannot choose without prior consultation.

XCII. SECOND: τὰ ἄλογα οὐκ ἐστὶν αὐτεξούσια; Irrational beings lack free will, Damasc. b. 2. ch. 27. & b. 3. ch. 14. ἄγονται γὰρ μᾶλλον ὑπὸ τῆς φύσεως ἤπερ ἄγουσι. They are moved more by nature than they move themselves. Whence the Psalmist exhorts that we not be like the horse and the mule which have no understanding, Ps. 32. v. 9. But just as a certain shadow of reason is observed in brutes, so too is a shadow of liberty, while in the fields as it pleases them, they now stand, now lie down, now move forward, now feed on this grass, soon on that: which actions, however, we more correctly call spontaneous than free, since they are concerned only with the goods of the body and by the instinct of nature, and come only from an inconsiderate appetite of the senses, so that Bellarmine is absurd in attributing natural judgment to beasts, book 3, chapter 15. And since liberty is nothing other than the will, certainly if you ascribe liberty properly so-called to brutes, you will not be able to deny them a will. But the will is ἐν τῷ λογικῷ, which beasts lack, which are also not said to will, but to be instigated, Scal. Exerc. 307 sect. 4. For the appetite of the irrational is not rational, and is not called θέλησις, as Damascene says in book 2 de O. F. cap. 22.

XCIII. And thus far we have considered the general subject of liberty, which is an intelligent nature; but specifically, as regards the liberty of the human will, the judgment concerning its subject is the same as that concerning the subject of other faculties. The matter is briefly thus: the subject of inherence is either adequate or principal. The former we call man, consisting of soul and body, since both the δύναμις and ἐνέργεια belong to him. The latter, however, is the rational soul from which liberty or the free power of acting flows by immediate birth, since with respect to essence it is nothing other than the will: but when the powers of liberty are understood, then the will itself is often called the subject of free choice, because those powers are exerted not through the intellect, but through the will, meanwhile inhering not in the will itself, since it is an accident, but in the soul, yet through the mediation of the will.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO IX. Quædnam libertatis subiectum sit?

LXXXVII. Quandoquidem cognitio intellectus prærequiritur in actione libera, vltro sequitur, primum & immediatum libertatis ὑποκείμενον naturam esse intelligentem, quippè quam seimperinsequitur proprietas ista, vt in sui actionibus sit libera. In hoc autem subiecto simul implicata est libertatis causa efficiens. Omnes enim effectiones ἐμμινωσεις, qualis est libertas, ab efficientibus suis primò recipiuntur, ita quidem, vt à quo acceperunt suam essentiam, in eodem suam habeant existentiam, Natura igitur intelligens & causa & subiectum primum libertatis est.

LXXXIIX. Ex dictis autem duo fluunt πορίσματα. PRIMVM: πᾶν λογικὸν καὶ αὐτεξύσιον Omne ratiomale liberæ potestatis, & arbitrij est. Damasc. lib. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. & lib. 3. cap. 14. Cùm igitur Angeli substantiæ sint intelligentes, libertate arbitrij minimè carebunt, quam ipsam tùm lapsus tùm opera Angelorum satis confirmant, adstipulante Irenæo l. 4. cap. 71. Basilio de de Spir. S. cap. 16. Augustino de corrept. & grat. cap. 10. Gregorio. hom. 7. in Ezech. & Damasceno lib. 2. de fide c. 3. 4.

LXXXIX. Cum autem causæ intensio simul intendat effectum, vtique magis ἀυτεξούσιον erit, quod magis λογικὸν. Et quoniam Deus summè intelligens, imò ipsa intelligentia & Sapientia est, vtique & summè liber, vel agens liberrimum, vel ipsa potius libertas erit. Hoc testantur omnia illa Scripturæ dicta, quæ docent, Deum operari per cognitionem & voluntatem, talesq; esse res creatas, quales Deum esse voluit, non quales necessitas coegit vt Psal 115. v 3. Dan. 3. v. 18. 1. Cor. 11 v. 12. Eph. 1. v. 11. Hûc etiam spectant miracula propter ordinem naturæ facta, vt quòd Sol stetit ad preces Iosuæ, retrocessit ad preces Hiskiæ, Defecit in plenilunio sub mortem Saluatoris: quòd virgo concepit & peperit, quòd cæcis visus, surdis auditus, mortuis vita restituta est. &c. Si enim Deus ordinem naturæ nunc seruare nunc pro arbitratu mutare potest, vtiq; non ex necessitate, sed liberè operari ipsum consequitur.

XC. Calumnia igitur est, cùm Bellarminus lib. 3. cap. 15. obijcit, Lutherum Deo libertatem arbitrij denegasse in assert. art. 36. siquidem disputet omnia ex necessitate absoluta euenire. Verum nihil tale in Luthero inuenitur, sed hoc dicit, superna spectantibus omnia esse necessaria, nimirum non necessitate naturæ, quomodo ignis necessariò vrit, sed necessitate immutabilis præscientiæ & consilij diuini, secundùm quæ saluâ voluntatum libertate & contingentiâ necesse est euenire scandala & Christum pati oportuit. Non autem sequitur, quòd Deus

Deus ipse necessitati subiaceat, licèt euentus respectu diuinæ præscientiæ sint necessarii.

XCI. Repetendum verò quòd inter Dei & creaturarum arbitrium non exiguum discrimen intercedat. Duo quidem habent communia, nempe 1. agere ἑκουσίως vel sponte. 2. agere ἐκ προαιρέσεως cum electione vel deliberato consilio, quatuor tamen modis vicissim differunt. 1. Respectu intellectus; quia Deus ex sese omnia perfectissimè scit & intelligit; creaturæ verò nec omnia sciunt, nec quæ sciunt, ex sese habent, sed pleraque ex diuina Resolutione, præsertim quæ Deum eiusque voluntatem attinent. 2. Respectu voluntatis, Diuina enim voluntas à nulla superiori tegitur aut dependet: Hominum autem voluntas in actionibus bonis à Deo dirigitur, in malis à Diabolo corrumpitur. 3. Respectu vtriusque quia Dei tùm scientia tùm præordinatio inmutabilis est, hominum verò & notitiæ & voluntates sunt ambulatorię seu mutabiles, vt iam velint quod antea nolebant & nolint quod prius volebant. 4. Respectu modi eligendi, quia Deus eligit sine consultatione propriè dicta, quæ est discursus rationis à noto ad ignotius seu à notione finis ad inuentionem mediorum: homines vero eligere nequeunt nisi consultatione præuia.

XCII. SECVNDVM: τὰ ἄλογα οὐκ ἐστὶν αὐτεξούσια; Irrationalia carent libero arbitrio, Damasc. l. 2. cap. 27. & l. 3. cap. 14. ἄγονται γὰρ μᾶλλον ὑπὸ τῆς φύσεως ἤπερ ἄγουσι. Mouentur magis à natura, quam vt ipsa moueant. Vnde Psaltes hortatur, ne simus sicut equus & mulus quibus non est intellectus Psal. 32. v. 9. Quemadmodum verò vmbra quædam rationis, ita & libertatis animaduertitur in brutis, dum in campis prout placuerit, nunc stant nunc iacent, nunc progrediuntur, iam hoc mox illo vescuntur gramine: quas tamen actiones rectiùs spontaneas quàm liberas appellamus, quoniam duntaxat circa corporis bona versantur atque naturæ instinctu, & non nisi ex inconsiderato sensuum appetitu veniunt, vt absurdus sit Bellarminus bestijs naturale iudicium attribuens lib. 3. cap. 15. Cumque libertas, nihil sit aliud quàm voluntas; certè si brutis libertatem propriè dictam adscripseris, voluntatem denegare haut poteris. Voluntas autem est ἐν τῷ λογικῷ quo carent bestiæ quæ etiam non dicuntur velle, sed instigari, Scal. Exerc. 307 sect. 4. ἡ γὰρ τῶν ἀλόγων ὄρεξις μὴ ὄσα λογικη, & λέγεται θέλησις dicente Damasceno libro 2. de O. F. cap. 22.

XCIII. Et hactenus generale libertatis subiectum, quod est natura intelligens, considerauimus; In specie autem quod libertatem voluntatis humanę attinet, de illius subiecto idem est iudicium, quod de subiecto aliarum facultatum. Res breuiter sic habet: subiectum inhæsionis vel est adæquatum vel principale. Illud hominem dicimus, animâ & corpore constantem, cùm eiusdem sit & δύναμις & ἐνέργεια. Hoc verò animam rationalem à qua libertas vel libera agendi potestas immediato partu profluit, quippe cum respectu essentiæ nihil aliud sit, quam voluntas: quando autem vires libertatis intelliguntur, tùm sæpè ipsa voluntas liberi arbitrij subiectum dicitur, quia vires illæ non per intellectum, sed per voluntatem exeruntur, interim non voluntati ipsi, quippe accidenti, sed animæ, voluntate tamen mediante inhærent.


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and…: Question X. What is the object of liberty?

QUESTION X. What is the object of liberty?

XCIV. If what has been said thus far is repeated, the decision of this question will not be difficult. For presupposing that liberty, considered all day long, is the very will, certainly the object of both will be the same. But indeed the will extends to all things which can be desired. Therefore also liberty. Whence it follows. 1. That free choice is of goods and evils, since very often the good being neglected, evil is chosen. Where, however, it must be known that the object or matter of liberty fall into free choice. But if formally, only the good; not indeed that every desirable thing is truly good, but because it is not desired except under the aspect of good.

2. That free choice is of present and future things. For as we not only will in the present, but also choose in the future: so those things which we now choose, we likewise choose freely. Nay, the free will desires many future things by the very act, so that we may attain every end following it. Nor indeed does it follow that the present act of the will is not free because it is necessary. For these two are subordinate, not contrary. The present act is free by reason of its principle, although it is necessary by reason of its existence. 3. That free choice is of means and the end. Concerning means there is no doubt, concerning the end Bellarmine is in doubt, book 3, chapter 14. But without reason. For no one will deny that the end is the object of the will. But indeed liberty and will are the same, as Bellarmine admits: Wherefore the end will also be the object of liberty. The contrary arguments conclude nothing, because liberty is always confused with consultation and free election. This indeed is concerned only with means, but that with the end and means together, because all actions of man, whether they be natural or moral, are free, those extrinsically and imperatively, but these intrinsically and elicitively, as Damascene testifies in book 2 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 22. See more on these in Bellarmine and Pareus, book 3, chapters 12, 13, 14, and Becanus, part 2, treatise 1, chapter 2, questions 7 and 8.

§ CV. And thus far we have briefly run through the questions proposed by Bellarmine under 3, which we do not deny are more Scholastic and Philosophical than purely Theological. Let no one, however, infer from this that we wish to recall the thorns of the schools, long since happily extirpated by Luther. Our intention is different, desiring nothing more than that we may be allowed to rest in the simplicity of the Apostolic faith. But the πανουργία of our adversaries, especially Bellarmine, makes it so that we cannot understand them, nor confer with them, unless those general questions, which they always interject and hold as the foundation of their opinion, have first been known and discussed. This one, and no other, end we have had, when we have hitherto followed Bellarmine and philosophized somewhat; which, although we did it even against our will, we clearly trust will be fruitful for younger students, and that on this account we shall the more quickly obtain pardon from the fair reader. But now let us proceed to other matters.

Latin:

QVÆSTIO X. Quodnam sit obiectum libertatis?

XCIV. Si hactenus dicta repetantur, non difficilis erit huius quæstionis decisio. Nam præsupposito, quòd libertas totiusdie considerata, sit ipsa voluntas, vtique idem erit vtriusque objectum. At verò voluntas se extendit ad omnia, quæ appeti possunt. E. & libertas. Vnde sequitur. 1. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit bonorum & malorum, siquidem sæpissime bono neglecto eligitur malum. Vbi tamen sciendum, quòd libertatis obiectum vel materialiter vel formaliter consideretur. Si materialiter, tum bonum malumque cadit in electionem liberam. Sin formaliter, tantùm bonum; non quidem quòd omne Appetibile reuerà sit bonum, sed quia non appetitur nisi sub ratione boni.

2. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit præsentium & futurorum. Vt enim non tantum in præsenti volumus, sed etiam in futuro eligimus: sic quæ nunc eligimus, itidem liberè eligimus. Imò & multa futura ipso actu appetit voluntas libera, vt omnem finemansequam eum consequamur. Nequè verò sequitur, actum voluntatis præsentem non esse liberum, quia sit necessarius. Dúo n. hæc subordinata sunt, non contraria. Liber est actus præsens, ratione principij quamvis sit necessarius ratione existentiæ. 3. Quod liberum arbitrium sit mediorum & finis. De medijs nullum est dubium, de fine ambigit Bellarm. lib. 3. c. 14. Sed absque ratione. Nam voluntatis obiectum esse finem, nemo ibit inficias. At verò libertas & voluntas idem sunt, fatente Bellarmino: Quare finis etiam libertatis obiectum erit. Argumenta contraria nihil concludunt, quia semper confunditur libertas cű consultatione & electione libera, Hæc quidem versatur tantùm circa media, sed illa circa fidem & media simul, quia omnes actiones hominis siue fuerint naturales, siue morales, sunt liberæ, illæ extrinsecùs & imperatiuè, hæ autem intrinsecus & elicitivè, teste Damasceno lib. 2. de O. F. capite 22. Plura de his vide apud Bellarminum & Pareum libro 3. cap. 12. 13. 14. & Becanum par. 2. tr. 1. c. 2. quæst. 7. & 8.

§ C V. Atque hactenus quæstiones à Bellarmino sub 3. propositas breuiter percurrimus, quas magis esse Scholasticas & Philosophicas, quam pure Theologicas haut diffitemur. Nemo tamen inde inferat, quod spinas scholarum iamdiu per Lutherum feliciter extrusas iterum reuocatas velimus. Alius nobis est animus, qui nihil magis exoptat, quam vt in simplicitate fidei Apostolica nobis acquiescere liceat. Facit vero aduersariorum, imprimis Bellarmini πανουργία, vt illos intelligere, cumque illis conferre nequeamus, nisi quaestiones istae generales, quas semper immitcent, & pro suae opinionis fundamento habent, prius fuerint cognitae & discussae. Hunc vnum, nullum alium finem habuimus, quando hactenus Bellarminum secuti, nonnihil Philosophati sumus, quod licet vel inuiti fecerimus, iuniorib. tame studiosis fructuosum fore, & hoc nomine apud lectorem aequum nos veniam eo citius impetraturos esse plane confidimus. Sed nunc ad alia pergamus.


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and…: Question XI. Whether man is free, and what powers of will he possesses?

QUESTION XI. Whether man is free, and what powers of will he possesses?

XCVI. We have often warned hitherto that the liberty of man is considered either in respect of ἰδία or in respect of ἐνεργεία, as to what it can do. As regards ἰδία, liberty is the will itself, which, since it flows from the soul of man, is for that reason always and in every state present in man, and in that respect man is always free, and has the same essence of liberty, because the will itself, insofar as it is a free power, is not essentially changed, although it may be accidentally either depraved or perfected. Therefore, we do not so much deny to man the liberty of the will taken ἰσχυστῶς; rather, we assert that it perpetually accompanies him.

Bellarmino's accusation is therefore atrocious when in the preface to his book on free will he writes thus concerning our opinion: They have stripped us of freedom of will in all their opinions, and they have not hesitated to profess themselves not like beasts, but beasts plainly devoid of reason. That we maintain something far different, he knows as well as his own fingers; indeed, he himself confessed it in book 3, chapter 15, arguing thus: It is certain that man, considered absolutely, possesses free will; for heretics do not contend about this matter, but only about man cast down from his state through the sin of the first parent. If, therefore, we do not contend about liberty taken absolutely and in general, why has he accused us of taking away all liberty and changing men into beasts?

XCVII. But if liberty is estimated by reason of ἐνεργείας, what it can do, one must answer distinctly, for the states of man are diverse, for which reason the very powers of free will vary, nor do they always behave in the same way. Therefore, we shall run through the individual states; and we shall indicate in a few words what powers the will either formerly had, or even now has, or will sometime have.

XCVIII. I. On the state of integrity. Our parents were free 1. from coercion, which is beyond doubt, because the will of man can never and in no state be coerced; 2. from necessity, since they were not bound by either an external or an internal principle to choose necessarily either only good or only evil, to which refers that passage in Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14: Man could sin and not sin, because his will was not yet so immutably determined toward good that it could not turn itself away from good, but there was in it the δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως or power toward opposites, while he could will and not will good and evil, and therefore a commandment was given by God that he should not sin. 3. From the servitude of sin, since they were not ensnared by the necessity of sinning, but rather the will, on account of its concreated perfection, was inclined toward good, yet in such a way that at the same time he could, if he wished, choose evil.

XCIX. The powers of free will were therefore excellent in the state of innocence, since the first-formed could love God with their whole heart and fully observe his law. For their liberty was not a bare will, but rather a will with perfection, with rectitude and the powers of loving God and fulfilling the law. Hence it is named the liberty of rectitude, because the will could act rightly and could rightly and fully obey the commands of God. Therefore, a diligent distinction must be made here between the ἰσία of liberty, which in every state is the same and is called by Bernard unlosable, and the ἐνεργείᾳ of liberty, which in the first state was excellent, consisting in a prompt faculty by which man could easily produce not only moral but also supernatural good actions. This liberty of rectitude was not the will itself, but a perfection of the will, a certain separable accident, so constituted that, while the essence of the will remained, it could be lost, just as it was indeed lost. For Adam was indeed free from the servitude of sin and misery, yet he was not free from mutability, because his will could be changed and could freely choose evil.

C. Here, however, it is further asked, Why did God permit man to himself, and instruct him with free will? For it seems to follow from this as if he had preordained the fall of Adam, and for that end had created the first-formed capable of falling. We are not, however, bound to answer this question, which is more curious than fruitful. The will of God suffices for us, whose decrees and the causes of whose decrees, although unknown to us, are yet always just. Basil answers in a few words, writing thus: He who blames that in our creator, that he did not create us so that we could not sin by nature, does nothing else than contend that it would have been better for God to have created us irrational, or clearly immovable trunks rather than rational men. If you ask for more, consult Damascenus, book 2 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 12, and his commentator who discusses this problem at length. CI. But so that we may gather the principal causes into a bundle for good measure, these are primarily brought forward by the Fathers. 1. The glory of God. For the power and wisdom of God the Creator shine forth from the excellence of a creature endowed with reason and will. 2. The reason for worship: God demands spontaneous honor and voluntary obedience, not coerced or entirely necessary, since as Damascenus says in book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 20, the good must be ἀβίαστον (unforced). But if man had lacked free will, who could have exhibited free and contingent worship? The reward of man: for God wished to confer rewards upon man, who obeyed out of free will. Therefore, it was given to Adam to be able to sin, not so that he would consequently sin, but so that he would appear more glorious if he did not sin, when he could have sinned, as Bernard testifies in his treatise on free will, book 4. The perfection and ornament of the universe. For since there is something that acts and is not acted upon, such as God; and something that is acted upon and does not act, such as nature devoid of reason; it was fitting that there should also exist something that is acted upon and acts, namely man, who acts from freedom and is at the same time incited by God to choose the good. This scholastic and probable reason is one which, among others, Bellarmine urges in book 3 on free will, chapter 18.

CII. II. On the state of corruption. As soon as man transgressed the commandment of the Lord, he immediately lost the image created with him, and consequently along with it the freedom of rectitude, that is, that faculty of loving God and fulfilling the law. For man, using free will badly, destroyed both himself and it. For since it was by free will that sin was committed, with sin victorious, free will was also lost; for by whom a man is overcome, to him he is made a slave, as Augustine says in Enchiridion, chapter 30. Nor indeed was man only despoiled of freedom, but there succeeded together an unbridled impulse toward evil, which always incites unregenerate men to evil, so that they can do nothing but sin. For just as during the state of innocence there flourished in the mind of man the knowledge of God, in the will, justice, holiness & a zeal for obedience; in the appetite, ἁρμονία & conformity with reason; so on the contrary in the state of the fall there succeeded in the mind ignorance & blindness, in the will aversion & an inclination toward evil, in the appetite contumacy & a zeal for resisting; whence it happens that man sins perpetually, and is unable to turn himself to God.

CIII. Truly therefore Luther wrote in art. 36. That free will is a title without a reality: he speaks however not of external actions, but of spiritual & theological ones. For although after the fall man is in a certain way free regarding the external pursuit of virtue, and behaves indifferently, yet he is clearly a slave with respect to his conversion & the divine law, which he always transgresses and cannot observe. He has therefore free will not toward good but only toward evil: which is otherwise called liberty from righteousness Rom. 6. v. 20. but more correctly is termed a miserable slavery to sin. For he who commits sin, is a slave of sin. John 8. v. 34. And by whom anyone is overcome, his slave he is 2. Pet. 2. v. 19.

CIV. III. Concerning the state of restoration. But when man is turned to God, and thus is transferred from the state of guilt into the state of grace, then at the same time the liberty of the will, i.e., the powers of loving God & observing the law, are in a certain way restored. For dominion is taken away from sin, so that although it resists the Spirit with its affections, the Spirit nevertheless conquers and mortifies the flesh. The regenerate therefore have liberty from the slavery of sin, because they can perform good works that are pleasing to God, to which pertain the sayings John 8. v. 36. If the Son shall have made you free, you shall be truly free. Rom. 6. v. 18. Freed from sin you have been made servants of righteousness. 2 Cor. 3 v. 17. Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.
