In that state of grace, therefore, we grant to the reborn συνεργείαν, because they have the powers of cooperating, not indeed sprouting from nature, but graciously infused and excited by the Holy Spirit through the word. Which powers of acting well, however, are not but only begun, since as long as we live, the flesh remains in us, which resists the Spirit Gal. 5 v. 17 and fights against the law of the mind. Rom. 7 v. 23. Whence it is that if a reborn person allows himself to be led away by the flesh, he can in turn return to his vomit and again enslave himself to the servitude of sin, and therefore so many exhortations are read, that we should stand in the faith, resist the Devil, and remain faithful even unto death.

CH. IV. Of the state of glorification. Just as in the other life the knowledge of the mind will be perfect, and that which is in part shall be abolished; so we shall also attain perfect freedom of the will, by which we shall be free both from the servitude of sin, and from misery and all the remnants of sin, and also from mutability itself, since we shall so love the good that we cannot will the evil, since we shall be confirmed in grace, so that we shall never be able to fall from that happy state: For we shall be equal to the angels, Matt. 22 v. 30, who cannot but act well and enjoy eternal beatitude. There, therefore, free will shall be fully restored, indeed more shall be restored than was lost in Adam, for he was free in such a way that he could sin and become miserable, but the blessed will be free in such a way that they cannot sin and cannot become miserable. There, error will be absent from reason, pain from the will, fear from memory, rancor from appetite: and on the contrary, there will be present the serene light of the mind, joy and freedom of the will, where nothing sad will be seen, where joy will always be had, where no evil will be feared; since there the highest good will be possessed, which is to see always the face of the Lord of hosts, as Augustine says in his Soliloquies, chapter 35.

CVI. Thus therefore we have seen what powers human free will possesses in any state, all of which can be briefly expressed if we say: Man in the first state was free; in the second he is a slave, in the third liberated, in the fourth he will be most free. Free in the state of integrity, because he could sin and not sin. He is a slave in the state of the fall, because he cannot not sin. He is liberated in the state of grace, because he can again not sin, and do good. But he will be most free in the state of glory, because there he will no longer be able to sin or be made unhappy.

Latin:

QVAESTIO XI. Num homo sit liber, & quas arbitrij vires habeat?

XCVI. Hactenus saepe monuimus, libertatem hominis considerari vel ratione ἰδίας vel ratione ἐνεργείας quid possit. Quoad δ' ἰδίαν libertas est ipsa voluntas, quae cum fluat ab anima hominis, ob id semper & in omni statu homini inest, istoq; respectu homo semp liber est, & cande libertatis essentia habet, quia volutas ipsa, quatenus est potentia libera, essencialiter no immutatur, licet accidetaliter vel deprauetur vel perficiatur. Arbitrij ergo libertate ἰσχυστῶς sumta adeo no denegamus homini; vt potius perpetuo ipsum comitari asseramus.

Atrox igitur criminatio Bellarmini est cum in præfat. li. de lib. arb. de nostra sententia ita scribit: Arbitrij libertatem nobis omnibus suis sententijs detraxerunt, seque ipsi non beluarum similes, sed Beluas planè rationis expertes profiteri non dubitarunt. Longè aliud nos statuere, tàm nouit quàm suos digitos, imò & ipse confessus est l. 3. c. 15. ita differens: Certum est, hominem absolutè consideratum esse liberi arbitrij: neq; enim hæretici de hac re contendunt, sed solum de homine per peccatum primi parentis de statu deiecto. Si ergo non contendimus de libertate absolutè & in genere sumta, cur omnem à nobis libertatem tolli & homines in beluas mutari criminatus est?

XCVII. Sin autem libertas æstimetur ratione ἐνεργείας, quid possit, distinctè respondendum est, Diuersi enim sunt status hominis, quam ob causam ipsæ liberi arbitrij vires variantur, nec eodem semper modo se habent. Proinde singulos status percurremus; & quasnam arbitrium vires vel olim habuerit; vel etiamnum habeat, vel aliquando habiturum sit, paucis indicabimus.

XCVIII. I. De statu integritatis. Fuerunt parentes nostri liberi 1. à coactione, quod extra dubium, quia voluntas hominis nunquam & in nullo statu cogi potest 2. à necessitate, quoniam nec per externum, nec per internum principium, vel ad solum bonum, vel ad solum malum necessariò eligendum astricti fuerunt, quò spectat istud Eccles. 15. vers. 14. Potuit homo peccare & non peccare, quia voluntas eius nondum erat ad bonum itá immutabiliter determinata, vt à bono se non posset auertere, verùm erat in ipsa δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως vel potentia ad opposita, dum bonum & malum, velle & nolle poterat, ideoque præceptum à Deo datum est ne peccaret. 3. A seruitute peccati quado quidem necessitate peccandi non fuerunt illaqueati sed potius voluntas ob perfectionem concreatam inclinabatur ad bonum, ita tamen vt simul malum, si vellet, eligere posset.

XCIX. Eximiæ igitur fuerunt vires liberi arbitrij in statu innocentiæ, siquidem Deum ex toto corde diligere, & eius legem plenè obseruare poterant protoplasti. Libertas enim ipsorum non fuit nuda voluntas, sed potius voluntas cum perfectione, cum rectitudine & viribus diligendi Deum, ac implendi legem. Hinc nominatur libertas rectitudinis, quia voluntas recte poterat agere, Deíque mandatis rectè & plenè obtemperare. Diligenter ergò hic distingui debet libertatis ἰσία, quæ in omni statu eadem est & anamissibilis Bernhardo dicitur, à libertatis ἐνεργείᾳ quæ in primo statu eximia fuit, consistens in facultate promta, quâ non tantùm morales sed & supernaturales actiones bonas facilè potuit homo producere. Hæc rectitudinis libertas non fuit ipsa voluntas, sed voluntatis perfectio, accidens quoddam separabile, ita comparatum, vt salua voluntatis essentiâ posset amitti, sicut etiam amissa est. Fuit enim Adamus liber quidem à servitute peccati & miseria, non tamen fuit liber à mutabilitate, quia voluntas eius mutari & malum liberè poterat eligere.

C. Hîc autem porrò quæritur, Cur Deus hominem sibiipsi permiserit, & libero arbitrio instruxerit? Videtur enim exinde sequi, ac si lapsum Adami præordinâsse, & in eum finem protoplastos labiles condidisset. Non autem tenemur ad quæstionem hanc, curiosam magis quàm fructuosam, respondere. Sufficit nobis voluntas Dei, cuius decreta & decretorum caussæ licet nobis ignotę, semper tamen iustæ sunt. Basilius paucis respondit ita scribens: Qui illud reprehendit in creatore nostro, quòd nos non condiderit, vt naturâ peccare non possemus, is nihil facit aliud quam quod contendit melius fuisse, Deum nos creâsse irrationales, aut planè immobiles truncos quam homines rationales. Plura si poscis, Damascenum consule l. 2. de O. F. capite 12. & eius commentatorem prolixè de hoc problemate differentem. CI. Vt verò ex abundanti in fasciculum colligamus præcipuas causas, hæ inprimis afferuntur à Patribus. 1. Dei gloria. Elucescit enim ex præstantia creaturæ, ratione & voluntate præditæ, Dei creatoris potentia & sapientia. 2. Cultus Ratio: Spontaneum honorem & voluntarium obsequium postulat Deus, non coactum, aut prorsus necessarium, siquidem ἀβίαστον εἶναι πρέπει τὸ καλὸν Damasc. l. 4. de O. F. cap. 20. Si autem libero arbitrio caruisset homo, qui exhibere potuisset cultum liberum & contingentem? Hominis præmium: volebat enim Deus βραβεῖα conferre homini, ex libera voluntate obsequenti. Datum igitur est Adamo posse peccare, non vt proinde peccaret, sed vt gloriosior appareret, si non peccaret, cum peccare posset, teste Bernhardo tr. de lib. arb. l. 4. Vniuersi perfectio & ornamentum. Cùm enim sit aliquid, quod agit & non agitur, vt Deus: aliquid quod agitur & non agit, vt natura rationis expers, æquum erat, vt etiam extaret aliquid quod ageretur & ageret, nimirum homo, qui agit ex libertate, & simul à Deo ad bonum eligendum incitatur. Ratio hæc scholastica est & probabilis quam inter cæteras vrget Bellarminus l. 3. de lib. arb. c. 18.

CII. II. De statu corruptionis. Quam primum homo præceptum Domini transgressus est, statim imaginem concreatam amisit, & consequenter vnà rectitudinis libertatem, hoc est illam Deum diligendi & legem implendi facultatem. Homo enim malè vtens libero arbitrio, & se perdidit, & ipsum. Cùm enim libero arbitrio peccaretur, victore peccato amissum est & liberum arbitrium, à quo enim quis deuictus est, huic seruus addictus est, dicente Augustino in Enchirid. cap. 30. Neque verò tantum spoliatus est homo libertate, sed successit vnà effrenis ad malum impetus, qui homines non renatos semper incitat ad malum, vt nihil nisi peccare possint. Vti enim durante statu innocentiæ viguit in mente hominis cognitio Dei, in voluntate, iustitia, sanctitas & obediendi studium; in appetitu, ἁρμονία & cum ratione conformitas; sic contra in statu lapsus successit in mente ignorantia & cæcitas, in voluntate auersio & ad malum inclinatio, in appetitu contumacia & reluctandi studium; vnde fit, vt homo perpetuò peccet, séque ipsum ad Deum conuertere nequeat.

CIII. Verè igitur scripsit Lutherus art. 36. Quòd liberum arbitrium sit titulus sine re: loquitur autem non de actionibus externis, sed spiritualibus & Theologicis Quamuis enim post lapsum circa externum virtutis studium quodammodo liber sit homo, & indifferenter se habent, attamen planè seruit respectu conuersionis suæ & legis diuinæ, quàm semper transgreditur & obseruare nequit. Habet igitur liberum arbitrium non ad bonum sed duntaxat ad malum: quæ alias vocatur libertas à iustitia Rom. 6. vers. 20. rectiùs autem miserabilis peccati seruitus nuncupatur. Qui enim facit peccatum, seruus est peccati. Ioh. 8. v. 34. Et à quo quis superatus eius & seruus est 2. Pet 2. v. 19.

CIV. III. De statu reparationis. Cum autem homo ad Deum conuertitur, adeóque ex statu culpæ in statum gratiæ transfertur, tum vnà libertas arbitrij h. e. vires diligendi Deum & obseruandi legem quodammodo restaurantur. Peccato enim dominium adimitur, vt quamuis Spiritui resistat suis affectibus, Spiritus tamen vincat & carnem mortificet. Habent igitur renati libertatem à seruitute peccati, quia possunt bona Deóque placentia opera exercere, quò pertinent dicta Ioh. 8. v. 36. Si Filius vos liberauerit verè liberi eritis. Rom. 6. v. 18. Liberati à peccato serui facti estis iustitiae. 2. Cor. 3. v. 17. Vbi Spiritus Domini, ibi libertas. In isto igitur gratiae statu concedimus renatis συνεργείαν, quia vires cooperandi non quidem ex natura pullulantes, sed a Spiritu sancto per verbum gratiose infusas & excitatas habent. Quae tamen bene agendi vires non sunt prorsus consummatae, sed tantum inchoatae, quoniam quamdiu viuimus, caro in nobis remanet, quae resistit Spiritui Gal. 5. ver. 17 & repugnat legi mentis. Rom. 7. v. 23. vnde sit, vt renatus si a carne se abduci patiatur, vicissim ad vomitum redire & peccati seruituti iterum se mancipare possit, ideoque tot adhortationes leguntur, vt stemus in fide, resistamus Diabolo, & fideles vsque ad mortem permaneamus.

CV. IV. De statu glorificationis. Quemadmodum in altera vita perfecta erit mentis cognitio, & abolebitur quod ex parte est; Ita perfectam quoque adipiscemur voluntatis libertatem, qua liberi erimus tum a seruitute peccati, tum a miseria & omnibus reliquijs peccati, tum ab ipsa etiam mutabilitate, siquidem bonum ita amabimus, vt malum velle non possimus, siquidem confirmabimur in gratia, vt ex statu illo felici nunquam excidere valeamus: Erimus enim aequales angelis, Matth. 22. v. 30. qui non possunt non bene agere & aeterna beatitudine gaudere. Ibi ergo plene restituetur liberum arbitrium, imo plus restituetur quam amissum est in Adamo, quippe qui sic liber erat, vt peccare & miser fieri posset, beati vero ita erunt liberi, vt peccare miserique fieri non possint, Ibi aberit a ratione error, a voluntate dolor, a memoria timor, ab appetitu rancor: & contra aderit serena lux mentis, gaudium & libertas voluntatis, vbi triste nihil videbitur, vbi laetitia semper habebitur, vbi malum nullum timebitur; quoniam ibi summum bonum possidebitur, quod est videre semper faciem Domini virtutum dicente Augustino in soliloquijs cap. 35.

CVI. Ita ergò vidimus, quas in quouis statu arbitrium humanum vires obtineat, quæ omnia breuiter efferri poterunt, si dicamus : Homo in primo statu fuit liber; in secundo est seruus, in tertio liberatus, in quarto erit liberrimus. Liber in statu integritatis, quia peccare & non peccare poterat. Seruus est in statu lapsus, quia non potest non peccare. Liberatus est est statu gratiæ, quia iterum potest non peccare, & benè agere. Liberrimus verò erit in statu glorię, quia ibi amplius peccare aut infelix effici non poterit.


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and…: Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and moral actions?

QUESTION XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and moral actions?

CVII. The object of free will is either worldly and profane, which is subject to the senses and human reason, and thus is found outside the Church: or it is sacred and sublime, which surpasses the senses and is not had except in the Church of Christ. From both arise diverse acts. For the worldly object comprises 1. Those things which pertain to animal life strictly taken or to the vegetative, sentient, and locomotive power. 2. Civil conversation and all things which are required of a good citizen by the laws of the magistrate. 3. The external pursuit of virtue, about which instruction is given in Ethics; and 4. various arts, both liberal and illiberal. From this fourfold object arise four kinds of human acts. The first contains natural acts, which look to natural and animal life, as are eating, drinking, sleeping, and the like. The second are civil acts, such as waging war, paying tribute, and obeying prescribed laws. The third are moral acts, to which is referred in general the exercise of virtue or vices. The fourth are the artificial acts of the arts, such as to speculate, to contemplate the nature of things, to till the earth, or to practice other manual arts. In all these profane acts we grant to man liberty and contingency, since he is able to act and not to act, as experience testifies, so much so that Scotus rightly said that one should deal with those who deny this free will not so much by arguments as by torments. For they should be beaten with lashes until they confessed that it is in our power to stop beating them. If they were to complain of the injury, it could be answered, Why do you complain of us, when you yourselves assert that it is not in our power to cease from beating! CIIX. But as regards the sacred object of liberty, from it also arise actions of a different kind. For they are either external, which concern the external exercise of religion, such as going to church, hearing the word of God, reading, etc. Or they are internal and spiritual, and singularly pleasing to God, such as truly knowing God, assenting to the Gospel, believing in Christ, and living according to the Spirit. By reason of these spiritual actions, the will of an unregenerate man is enslaved, not free, as will be demonstrated in the next disputation. But concerning external actions, just as in profane ones, we willingly grant liberty to man, and we are about to show this very thing.

CIX. A not insignificant difficulty lies hidden here, how the actions of men can be free and contingent, when all things depend upon the will and nod of God. For thus the ancient Stoics concluded: If all things are already from eternity defined and preordained by divine decree, it is certainly necessary that they come to pass in time in that way. If it were otherwise, something else would happen and something else would have been ordained by God, and thus the will of God would either be deceived or changed. Since this is impious to say, it will follow that all things happen necessarily and indeed by the force of a divine, eternal, immutable constitution. And hence they deduced that adamant and inexorable fate of theirs. orabile, which was theirs, as defined by Chrysippus in Gellius, book 6, Attic Nights, chapter 2. A certain eternal and unchangeable series of things, and a chain, rolling itself and entangling itself through eternal orders of consequence, from which it is fitted and connected. By this fate that thief excused his misdeeds, saying, 'I stole by fate,' but the other retorted, 'Therefore, by fate you shall be hanged.'

CX. We do not wish to deny, however, that this argument is most difficult. For it can scarcely be grasped by reason how eternal preordination and infallible providence can stand together with the temporal and mutable contingency of things and the freedom of actions. For if you assume the one, you seem to have denied the other, and vice versa. Hence were born those two heretical enthymemes, the one Epicurean, the other Stoic. The Epicurean holds thus: 'Contingency is given, therefore, no providence, no eternal preordination.' The Stoic, however, concludes in the contrary manner: 'Providence is given: therefore, no contingency, and consequently all things happen by inevitable necessity.' These are those two most dangerous rocks upon which human reason most often strikes. But let us be mindful of that which is written by Augustine, book 5, On the City of God, chapter 9. However the most tortuous contentions and disputations of the philosophers may stand, a religious soul confesses both, and confirms both by the faith of piety. For those things which ethnic superstition thought to be ἀνύστακτα (unavoidable), the Christian religion teaches to be ὑπάλλακτα (interchangeable). For neither does contingency remove God's ordination or providence, nor does the latter remove the former; and therefore we ought to teach, believe, and confess not contingency alone without providence, nor providence alone without contingency, but both together.

CXI. That providence exists is proven elsewhere against the Epicureans, who call it into doubt. Something must be added here concerning contingency and liberty, so that the Stoic objection may be sufficiently answered. Wherefore 1. We shall demonstrate the contingency of things and the liberty of actions, and we shall refute the necessity of events. 2 We shall set forth the boundaries of contingency and necessity. 3 Specifically, we shall respond to the argument itself.

CXII. I. Demonstration of liberty. That contingency exists and not all things happen necessarily, but many things freely, even if all things are predetermined from eternity, can be proven. 1. From the Scriptures, 2. By reasons. 3. By human testimonies. Scripture asserts contingency 1. By manifest sayings, such as are read in Gen. 4. v. 7. Its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it. Exod. 35. v. 5. Let everyone who is willing and of a ready mind offer offerings to the Lord. Num. 30. v. 14. It shall be in the man's discretion whether he does it or not. 1 Cor. 7. v. 36. we are said regarding marriage not to have necessity, but power of will. And in the Epistle to Philemon v. 14. Without your counsel I wanted to do nothing, that your good might not be κατ' ἀνάγκην by necessity ἀλλὰ καθ' ἑκούσιον but voluntary.

2. By opinions, which it sometimes gives, as Deut. 30. v. 19. Choose life, etc. Josh. 24. v. 15. The choice is given to you, choose today what pleases you, 2 Sam. 24 v. 12. The choice of three is given to you, choose one that you wish. 1 Kings 3. v. 5. Ask what you wish that I may give it to you. But if the choice of choosing is given, absolute necessity finds no place. For if one thing is necessary, what can we choose?

3. By examples, as 1 Chron. 29. v. 9. the people rejoiced, because they contributed willingly and liberally to the building of the temple. Thus Ananias freely, not necessarily, sold his field, for which reason Peter said to him in Acts 5. v. 4. While it remained, did it not remain your own? and after it was sold, was it in your own power? Thus the Apostle affirms 1 Cor. 9. v. 4. 5. 6. Do we not have the power to eat and to drink and to lead about a wife? etc. And Ecclesiasticus 31. v. 10. The rich man is commended, who could have transgressed and did not transgress, to do evil and did not do it. To this also pertains the law concerning contingent or accidental homicides

Num. 5. v. 22. which nevertheless were not so fortuitous as to exclude divine ordination, since it is said in Exod. 21. v. 13. that he who was killed in this way was delivered by God himself into the hands of the slayer. Thus the Jews freely and deliberately adjudged Jesus to death, Matt. 27. and yet the Apostles affirm that they did that which the hand and counsel of the Lord had decreed to be done, Act. 2. v. 27. 28.

4. By the accusations of the impious and the unfaithful, to whose voluntary malice every penalty and punishment is ascribed, as in Num. 14. verse 43. You shall fall by the sword, because you would not acquiesce to the Lord. Isa. 65. v. 12. You chose what I did not want. If God did not want it, they were certainly not impelled by God to choose it. Jer. 32. v. 23. Because you hardened your heart, and would not obey the Lord, all these evils have come upon you. Hosea 13. v. 9. Your destruction, O Israel. Matt. 23. v. 37. How often would I have gathered your children and you would not? Luke 7. v. 30. The Pharisees rejected the counsel of God against themselves. Acts 7. v. 52. You always resist the Holy Spirit: From which we conclude; He who sins either can not sin: If he can, contingency and liberty are granted; if he cannot, men are falsely accused, as if it depended on them that they acted less well. But since this is absurd and impious, the former will be true and must be asserted. To this place also refer the rebukes, admonitions, and exhortations occurring most frequently in the Scriptures, which openly prove contingency and liberty.

CXIII. Reasons for contingency are derived, 1. from laws, which would be useless and vain in a polity. 2. from sins, of which God would become the author if all things happened by the force of an eternal law. 3. from virtue, which must be χρῆμα ἀδέσποτον περὶ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον, a free and non-necessary thing, Damasc. lib. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. 4. from rewards and punishments, the former of which would be unmerited, the latter unjust, if actions were not in our power. 5. from deliberations, which would be taken away if nothing were in our power. 6. from prayers and supplications, which are vain if mere necessity reigns. 7. From the constitution of man, who consists of mind and reason, which is the perpetual parent of liberty. 8. from the perfection of the world. There are given slaves, there are given things acting necessarily: therefore also things operating freely or contingently, lest any species be wanting to the world.

CXIV. Very many testimonies could be alleged, but let three suffice here. 1. That of Augustine which is read in book 3 of the Hypognosticon: There is indeed free will, and if anyone denies that it exists, he is not a Catholic. And conversely in the book On the Two Souls: Nor are obscure books to be searched by me here, from which I might learn that no one is worthy of blame or punishment who does not do what he cannot do. Do not shepherds in the mountains, and poets in the theaters, and the unlearned in circles, and the learned in libraries, and masters in schools, and bishops in sacred places, and the human race throughout the world sing these things? 2. That of Damascenus, book 2, chapter 7: ἡμεῖς ἀυτεξούσιοι ὑπὸ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ γινόμενοι κύριοι τῶν ἡμε- τέρων ὑπάρχομεν πράξεων. We, having been made by the Creator with free power, are masters of our own actions. 3. That of Lombard, book 1 of the Sentences, distinction 39. Those who deny all contingencies wish necessary things to be made, with torments applied for the sake of explaining any reasons, and they are to be tortured until they concede that it is possible for them not to be tortured. See more in Irenaeus, book 4; Tertullian, book 2 against Marcion; Ambrose, book 2 on the Calling of the Gentiles, last chapter; Jerome, book 3 on Jeremiah, Homily 20 on Matthew; and Fulgentius, book 1 to Monimus.

CXV. II. Explanation of terms. The term of both contingency and necessity must be properly explained. 1. Contingency is derived from contingent, which is called ἐνδεχόμενον by the Greeks, and is of such a kind that it can both be and not be, or be done and not be done, and whether it happens or does not happen, nothing absurd is committed, nor is there any contradiction, nor is it against the word of God.

Contingency therefore is nothing other than δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως or the propensity of a thing toward either side, to be and not to be, to be done and not to be done. Three of these are recited, or degrees or species, by the Philosopher in Lib. de interpret. cap. 9. post. cap. 12. & 2. Top. cap. 6. 1. is τὰ ὁπότερ᾿ ἔτυχεν which can as well happen as not happen, as winning at dice. 2. ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ, which for the most part and more often happen so: 3. ὡς ἐλάχισον which do not happen except rarely and unusually. From this definition and division of the contingent it evidently appears that the contingent is spoken of and considered only by reason of the future, and therefore that is contingent which is still in its causes, and can happen and not happen. Hence Metaphysicians commonly say: A being and an effect is called contingent by reason of causes operating contingently: but not by reason of existence. From which follows the maxim, Whatever effect has not necessary but indifferent and contingently acting causes, is called contingent, even if when it is, it is necessarily and cannot be otherwise.

CXVI. 2. Necessity is named from necessary, which is of such a kind that it is determined to one part only. And necessity is twofold, one is called of compulsion, the other of immutability. By necessity of compulsion those things happen, the cause or active principle of which is outside us, so that we do not cooperate with that motion, but resist it, which kind of necessity some of the Stoics asserted. And such was in Balaam, who was compelled to bless the Israelites, even though he resisted with his whole will. Necessity of immutability is when an agent is bound to one part only, yet without any compulsion and violence. And this in turn is either absolute or of the consequent, or hypothetical, or of the consequence. The former consists in the essential cohesion of cause and effect, when indeed a thing follows from a necessary antecedent cause, so that the opposite is impossible: the latter consists in a presupposition connected with consequences, when indeed the antecedent being posited, or the hypothesis being posited, the consequent necessarily follows or is included in the hypothesis. Thus, therefore, those things are hypothetically necessary which follow certainly and infallibly, yet the causes of them themselves could either not exist or change. And four degrees of this hypothetical necessity are commonly established. 1. It arises from the presupposition of the foreknowledge and decree of God. For these being posited, the thing itself necessarily follows. 2. From the presupposition of contingent causes, or those posited in act. Thus I say, calamities are necessary because men do not desist from sins (which, however, are contingent in themselves). Thus it is necessary that scandals come, on account of the cruelty of the Devil and the malice of men. 3. From the production and existence of a thing already made. For everything that is, insofar as it is, is necessary, although before it was, it could be and not be. 4. From the supposition of the end, which some call the necessity of expediency, or for well-being. Thus Philosophy is necessary for a student of Theology, since without it he cannot happily and well treat or complete the sacred study

Latin:

QVÆSTIO XII. An & qualis detur libertas circa ciuiles & morales actiones?

CVII. Objectum liberi arbitrij vel est mundanum & profanum quod subjacet sensibus & rationi humanæ, adeoque extra Ecclesiam reperitur: vel est sacrum & sublime, quod sensus superat & non nisi in Ecclesia Christi habetur. Ex utroque oriuntur diuersi actus. Obiectum enim mundanum comprehendit 1. Illa quæ ad vitam animalem strictè acceptam vel ad potentiam vegetatiuam, sentientem & locomouentem pertinent. 2. Ciuilem conuersationem & omnia, quæ à bono ciue per leges magistratus requiruntur. 3. Externum virtutis studium, de quo in Ethicis præcipitur; & 4. varias artes tam liberales quàm illiberales. Ex hoc quadruplici objecto exsurgunt quatuor genera actuum humanorum. Primum continet actus naturales, qui ad vitam naturalem & animalem spectant, vt sunt edere, bibere, dormire & similes. Secundum actus ciuiles, vt militiam gerere, tributum soluere, & legibus præscriptis obtemperare. Tertium actus morales, quò refertur in genere virtutis aut vitiorum exercitium. Quartum artium artificiales, vt speculari, naturam rerum consclerare, terræ colere, aliasuè artes manuarias exercere. In his actibus profanis omnibus libertatem homini concedimus & contingentiam, quandoquidem agere & non agere porest, vti testatur experientia, adeò quidem vt rectè dixerit Scotus, non tâm rationibus quàm cruciatibus esse agendum contra negantes hoc liberum arbitrium. Tamdiu enim verberibus pulsandi essent, donec confiterentur, in nostra potestate esse, eos non amplius pulsandi Si conquererentur de iniuria, responderi posset, Quid de nobis conquerimini, cùm vos ipsi asseratis, non esse in nostra potestate cessare à verberando! CIIX. Obiectum verò libertatis sacrum quod attinet, ex illo etiam diuersi generis actiones oriuntur. Vel enim externæ sunt, quæ circa religionis exercitium externum versantur, quales sunt templum accedere, verbum Dei audire, legere, &c. Vel internæ & spirituales, Deoque singulariter placentes, vt sunt, Deum verè cognoscere, Euangelio assentiri, in Christum credere, & secundum Spiritum viuere. Ratione harum actionum spiritualium hominis non renati arbitrium servum est, non liberum, vti proximâ disputatione demonstrabitur. Sed circa actiones externas, sicut & in profanis, libertatem homini lubenter concedimus, & mox idipsum ostensuri sumus.

CIX. Non exigua verò difficultas hîc delitescit, quomodo liberæ & contingentes esse possint actiones hominum, cum omnia ex Dei arbitrio nutuque dependeant, Ita enim concluserunt antiqui Stoici: Si omnia iam ab æterno sunt definita & præordinata diuino decreto, vtique necesse est in tempore ita euenire. Secus si sit, aliud fieret & aliud à Deo sancitum esset, atque sic Dei voluntas aut falleretur aut mutaretur. Quod cum dictu sit impium, sequetur omnia fieri necessariò & quidem vi constitutionis diuinæ, æternæ, immutabilis. Atque hinc deduxerūt fatum istud suum adamantinum & inexorabile, quod ipsis erat, definiente Chrysippo apud Gellium lib. 6. N. A. cap. 2. Sempiterna quædam & indeclinabilis series rerum, & catena, volvens semetipsa sese, & implicans per æternos consequentiæ ordines, ex quibus apta connexaque est. Hoc fato malefacta sua excusatus fur ille, dicebat, Fato furatus sum, sed regerebat alter; fato ergo suspenderis.

CX. Diffiteri autem nolumus, argumentum illud esse difficillimum. Vix enim percipi potest ratione, quomodo æterna præordinatio & infallibilis prouidentia simul stet cum temporali & mutabili rerum contingentia & actionum libertate. Nam si assumas illud, videris hoc negâsse, & contra. Vnde nata sunt duo illa enthymemata Hæretica, alterum Epicuræum, alterum Stoicum. Epicuræum sic habet, Datur contingẽtia, Ergo, nulla providentia, nulla præordinatio æterna. Stoicum verò concludit modo contrario: Datur prouidentia: Ergo nulla contingẽtia, ideoque ineuitabili necessitate omnia eveniunt. Hi sunt duo illi periculosissimi scopuli, in quos humana ratio sæpius impingit. Nos autẽ simus memores istius quod ab August. scribitur l. 5. de Ciu. Dei cap. 9. Quomodocunque se habeant tortuosissimæ concertationes & disputationes Philosophorum, religiosus animus vtrumque confitetur, & fide pietatis vtrumque confirmat. Nam quæ ἀνύστακτα putauit Ethnica superstitio, ea ὑπάλλακτα docet Christiana religio. Neque enim contingentia tollit Dei ordinationem aut prouidentiam, neque hæc illam; & propterea non solam sine prouidentia contingentiam, nec solam sine contingentia providentiam, sed vtramque simul docere, credere, & confiteri debemus.

CXI. Prouidentiam esse probatur alibi contra Epicuræos, istam in dubium vocantes. De contingentia & libertate hic aliquid addendum est, vt ad obiectionem Stoicam sufficienter respondeatur. Quapropter 1. Contingentiam rerum & libertatem actionum demonstrabimus, necessitatemque euentuum refutabimus. 2 terminos contingentiae & necessitatis exponemus. 3 In specie ad argumentum ipsum respondebimus.

CXII. I. Libertatis demonstratio. Dari contingentiam nec omnia fieri necessario, sed multa libere, etiamsi omnia ab aeterno sint praedefinita, probari potest. 1. Ex Scripturis, 2. Rationibus. 3. Humanis testimoniis. Scriptura contingentiam adstruit 1. Manifestis dictis, qualia leguntur Gen. 4. v. 7. Sub te erit appetitus eius, & tu dominaberis illi. Exod. 35. v. 5. Omnis voluntarius & prono animo offerat oblationes Domino. Num. 30. v. 14. In arbitrio viri erit siue faciat siue non. 1. Cor. 7. v. 36. dicimur quoad coniugium non habere necessitatem, sed potestatem voluntatis. Et in Epistola ad Philem. v. 14. Sine tuo consilio nihil volui facere, vt bonum tuum non sit κατ' ἀνάγκην ex necessitate ἀλλὰ καθ' ἑκούσιον sed voluntarium.

2. Opinionibus, quas nonnunquam dat, vt Deut. 30. v. 19. Elige vitam, &c. Ios. 24. vers. 15. Optio vobis datur, eligite hodie quod placet, 2. Sam. 24 v. 12. Trium tibi datur optio, elige vnum quod volueris. 1. Reg. 3. vers. 5. Postula quod vis vt dem tibi. Si autem optio datur eligendi, necessitas absoluta locum non inuenit. Si enim vnum est necessarium, quid eligere possumus?

3. Exemplis, vt 1. Paral. 29. v. 9. laetatur populus, quod sponte & liberaliter contribuerent ad aedificationem templi. Sic Ananias libere non necessario vendidit agrum suum, qua de causa ad ipsum dixit A. Petrus Act. 5. vers. 4. Nonne manens tibi manebat, & venundatum in tua erat potestate? Sic Apostolus affirmat 1. Cor. 9. vers 4. 5. 6. An non habemus potestatem manducandi & bibendi & mulierem circunducendi? &c. Et Ecclesiast. 31. vers. 10. Commendatur diues, qui potuit transgredi & non est transgressus facere mala & non fecit. Huc etiam pertinet lex de homicidijs contingentibus vel fortuitis

Num. 5. v. 22. quæ tamen non ita fuêre fortuita, vt excluderent ordinationem diuinam, cum Exod. 21. v. 13. dicatur is, qui hoc modo occisus est, ab ipso Deo in manus interfectoris traditus. Sic Iudæi Iesum liberè & consultò morti adiudicârunt, Matt. 27. & tamên affirmant Apostoli, eos fecisse id, quod manus & consilium Domini decreuerat fieri, Act. 2. v. 27. 28.

4. Accusationibus impiorum & infidelium, quorum voluntariæ malitiæ pœna & supplicium omne asscribitur, vt Num. 14. vers. 43. Corruetis gladio, eò quod nolueritis acquiescere Domino. Efa: 65. v. 12. Quæ nolui elegistis. Si Deus noluit, à Deo vtique ad eligendum impulsi non sunt. Ierem. 32. v. 23. Quia indurastis cor vestrum, & noluistis obedire Domino, hæc omnia mala euenerunt vobis. Oseæ 13. v. 9. Perditio tua Israel. Matth. 23. v. 37. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos & noluisti? Luc. 7. v. 30. Pharisæi spreuerunt consilium Dei aduersus semetipsos. Act. 7. v. 52. Semper Spiritui S. resistitis: Ex quibus concludimus; Is qui peccat vel potest non peccare: Si potest, datur contingentia & libertas, si non potest, falsò accusantur homines, quasi per ipsos steterit, quod minùs benè agerent. Hoc autem cùm sit absurdum & impium, prius illud erit verum & asserendum. Huc quòque referantur increpationes, admonitiones & exhortationes in Scripturis sæpissimè occurrentes, quæ contingentiam & libertatem apertè comprobant.

CXIII. Rationes pro contingentia desumuntur, 1. à legibus, quæ essent inutiles & frustraneæ in politia. 2. à peccatis, quorum author Deus fieret, si omnia vi legis sempiternæ euenirent, 3. à virtute, quæ debet esse χρῆμα ἀδέσποτον περὶ μὴ ἀναγκαῖον res libera & non necessaria Damasc. l. 2. de O. F. cap. 7. 4. à præmijs & supplicijs, quorum illa indebita, hæc injusta forent, si actiones in potestate nostra non essent. 5. à deliberationibus, quæ tollerentur si nihil esset ipsius. 6. a precibus & supplicationibus, quæ vanæ sunt, si mera regnet necessitas. 7. Ab hominis constitutione, qui mente constat & ratione, quæ perpetua libertatis parens est. 8. à mundi perfectione. Dantur servia, dantur necessariò agentia: E. & libera vel contingenter operantia, ne mundo desit aliqua species.

CXIV. Testimonia benè multa possent allegari, sed sufficiant hîc tria. 1. Augustini quod legitur lib. 3. hypognost. Est utique liberum arbitrium, quod si quis esse negaverit, Catholicus non est. Et vicissim lib. de duabus animabus: Neque hîc libri obscuri mihi scrutandi, unde discam, neminem vituperatione suppliciove dignum, qui id non facit quod facere non potest. Nonne ista cantant & in montibus Pastores, & in theatris Poetæ, & indocti in circulis, & docti in bibliothecis, & Magistri in scholis, & antistites in sacris locis, & in orbe terrarum genus humanum. 2. Damasceni lib. 2. cap. 7. ἡμεῖς ἀυτεξούσιοι ὑπὸ τοῦ δημιουργοῦ γινόμενοι κύριοι τῶν ἡμετέρων ὑπάρχομεν πράξεων. Nos liberæ potestatis à conditore facti, domini nostrarum actionum sumus. 3. Lombardi lib. 1. sent. dist. 39. Ii qui abnegant contingentia omnia volunt necessaria fieri, tormentis positis quavis ratione bus exponendis, & tandiu sunt cruciandi, donec concedant, possibile esse eos non torqueri. Plura vide apud Irenæum l. 4. Tertull. lib. 2. contra Marcionem. Ambros. lib. 2. de vocat. gent. cap. ult. Hieron. lib. 3. in Ierem. Hom. 20. in Matth. & Fulgent. lib. 1. ad Monicam.

CXV. II. Terminorum explicatio. Terminus tùm contingentiæ tùm necessitatis probè explanandus est. 1. Contingentia deducitur à contingente, quod Græcis dicitur ἐνδεχόμενον, & est eiusmodi, vt & possit & non possit esse vel fieri, & sive fiat sive non fiat, nihil absurdi committitur, neque contrariationem neque contra verbum Dei.

Contingentia ergo nihil est aliud, quàm δύναμις ἀντιφάσεως seu rei ad verumlibet, esse & non esse, fieri & non fieri propensio. Hujus tres recitantur sive gradus siue species à Philosopholib. de interpret. cap. 9. post. cap. 12. & 2. Top. cap. 6. 1. est τὰ ὁπότερ᾿ ἔτυχεν quæ fieri tàm possunt, quàm non possunt, vt ludentem aleâ vincere. 2. ὡς ἐπὶ πολύ, quæ pleruńque & sæpiùs ita accidunt: 3. ὡς ἐλάχισον quæ non nisi rarò ac insolenter eueniunt. Ex ista vero contingentis & definitione & diuisione euidenter apparet quòd contingens solùm ratione futuri dicatur & consideretur, adeoqué contingens illud sit, quod in suis causis adhuc est, fieriqué & non fieri potest. Hinc communiter dicunt Metaphysici: Ens & effectum dicitur contingens ratione causarum contingentèr operantium: non autem ratione existentiæ. Ex quo sequitur maxima, Quæ unque effectus, non necessarias sed indifferentes & contingenter agentes causas habet, contingens dicitur, etiamsi cùm quando est, necessariò sit & aliter esse non possit.

CXVI. 2. Necessitas dicitur à necessario, quod est eiusmodi vt ad vnam duntaxat partem sit determinatum. Est́que duplex necessitas, altera coactionis dicitur, altera immutabilitatis. Necessitate coactionis fiunt ea, quorum causa vel principium actiuum est extra nos, ita vt ad motum illum non cooperemur, sed reluctemur, qualem necessitatem nonnulli Stoicorum asseruerunt. Et talis fuit in Balaam, qui cogebatur Israelitis benedicere, etiamsi tota voluntate obluctaretur. Necessitas immutabilitatis est, quando agens ad vnam tantùm partem sine omni tamen coactione & violentia adstringitur. Et hæc vicissim vel est absoluta seu consequentis, vel hypothetica, seu consequentiæ. Illa consistit in essentiali causæ & effectus cohæsione, quando nimirum res sequitur ex causa antecedente necessaria, sic vt oppositum sit impossibile: hæc consistit in præsuppositione cum consequentibus connexâ, quando nimirum antecedente posito, vel hypothesi positâ, necessariò sequitur consequens vel hypothesi inclusum, Sic ergo hypothetice necessaria sunt, quæ certò quidem & in allibiliter sequuntur, ipsæ tamen causæ illarum vel non existere vel mutare poterant. Et huius hypotheticæ necessitatis quatuor vulgo constituuntur gradus. 1 oritur ex præsuppositione præscientiæ & decreti Dei. His enim positis ipsa necessariò sequitur. 2. ex præsuppositione causarum contingentium, sea in actu positarum. Sic dico, calamitates esse necessarias quia homines à peccatis (quæ tamen per se sunt contingentia) non desistunt. Sic necesse est venire scandala, ob Diaboli sæuitiæm & hominum malitiam. 3. Ex præsuppositæ rei factæ productione & existentiâ. Omne enim quod est, quatenus est, necessarium est, licèt ante quam esset, esse & non esse posset. 4. Ex finis suppositione, quam nonnulli vocant necessitatem expedientiæ, vel ad benè esse. Sic Philosophia necessaria est studioso Theologiæ, quoniam sine illa sacrum studium feliciter & benè tractare aut absoluere nequit


### Question XII. Whether and what kind of liberty is given regarding civil and…: CXVII. III. a direct response to the objection

CXVII. III. A direct response to the objection.

The terms having been explained, we shall briefly resolve the objection itself. It runs thus: If all things are preordained by God, they will happen necessarily, and thus contingency will be removed. Resp. 1. Every event is considered with respect to either God, or existence, or its causes. If with respect to God and actual existence, we concede that all things are done necessarily. For whatever is preordained by God and actually exists, insofar as it exists, is necessary, but only by a necessity of consequence, and not of the consequent or absolute. But if, however, events are estimated by reason of their causes, some are rightly called contingent, if, namely, their causes could act and not act. E.g., to enter a temple is contingent, because we can enter and not enter: yet it is rightly called necessary, insofar as it is foreseen and preordained by God, and we actually enter. Whence it appears that the same thing can be both necessary and contingent, necessary by hypothesis and by reason of the decrees, contingent by reason of its own principle. Wherefore if the necessity of the consequence is understood in the argument, we concede that, the eternal disposition being presupposed, all things happen necessarily, but we deny it if one wishes the necessity to be understood as absolute. And furthermore, there is no consequence. If all things happen necessarily by hypothesis, contingency is removed: Nay, in truth it is not removed, since contingency ought to be estimated only by reason of mutable and freely acting causes. Since therefore the divine disposition does not remove the very will of man, neither does it remove the contingency of acts, which cannot be denied as long as that is conceded.

CXIIX. 2. It is to be noted that God by his preordination does not destroy the natures of things; but as he created them, so he preserves them, and so he operates. Wherefore not only the acts, but also the mode of the acts is sanctioned by the eternal law, so that naturally operations are necessary, but moral and human ones are and remain free. Therefore, such as the nature of things is, the eternal law sanctions that it should be so, and that it should operate in such a way, namely that necessary things operate necessarily, contingent things contingently, free things freely, and so on. Whence it was aptly said by Mornæus in his book on the truth of religion, chapter 13: The prime mover moves inferior things according to the character of each; movable things according to motion; immovable things according to stability; natural things according to servitude, sensible things according to appetite, rational things according to will and liberty. Philosophers show and deduce these things more fully through four kinds of acting causes. For they teach that some things are ordained from eternity to come to pass through causes acting necessarily and not naturally impedible, such as the motions of the heavens and the eclipses of the sun and moon: some things through causes acting necessarily and impedible, but not hindered in acting, as the generation of man; others through causes acting necessarily, not only hinderable but also hindered, as the generation of a monster; which indeed is necessary by reason of the concurring causes, yet happens contingently with respect to the proximate cause, beside whose intention it is: others finally through c And hence it appears that contingency is so far from being taken away by God's providence, that it is rather established, since it is also decreed by it that some things should act not necessarily, but freely and contingently. And therefore it is truly said by Gregory, lib. 5. moral. cap. 18. at the end: Whatever is immutably established within is acted mutably without.

Latin:

CXVII. III. Directa ad obiectionem responsio.

Explicatis vocabulis, obiectionem ipsam breuiter absoluemus. Sic illa habet: Si omnia sunt à Deo præordinata, euenient necessariò, atque sic tolletur contingentia. Resp. 1. Omnis euentus consideratur respectu vel Dei vel existentiæ, vel causarum suarum. Si respectu Dei & actuaiis existentiæ, concedimus omnia geri necessariò. Quicquid enim à Deo præordinatum est & actu existit, quatenus existit, necessarium est, sed tantum necessitate consequentiæ, non autem consequentis vel absoluta. Quod si vero euentus æstimentur ratione causarum, rectè vocantur nonnulli contingentes, si nimirum causæ illorum agere & non agere poterant. E. g. ingredi templum est contingens, quia ingredi & non ingredi possumus: rectè tamen dicitur necessarium, quatenus à Deo præuisum & præordinatum est, actúque ipso ingredimur. Vnde apparet rem eandem posse esse & necessariam & contingentem, necessariam ex hypothesi & ratione decretis contingentem, ratione sui principij. Quocirca si intelligatur in argumento necessitas consequentiæ, concedimus, præsuppositâ dispositione æternâ, omnia fieri necessariò, negamus autem si necessitatem absolutam quis intellectam velit. Et sequela insuper nulla est. Si omnia fiunt necessariò per hypothesin, tollitur contingentia: Imò verò non tollitur, cùm contingentia tantùm ratione causarum mutabilium & liberè agentium æstimari debeat. Quoniam ergo diuina dispositio non tollit ipsum hominis arbitrium, neque tollit actuum contingentiam, quæ negari nequit, quamdiu illud conceditur.

CXIIX. 2. Notandum est, quòd Deus præordinatione suâ non destruat rerum naturas; sed prout creauit, ita eas conseruat, & ita operatur. Quocirca non tantùm actus, sed & actuum modus lege æternâ sancitus est, vt nimirum operationes naturales sint necessariæ, morales autem & humanæ sint maneantq́; liberæ. Qualis ergo est rerum natura, talis vt sit, & taliter vt operetur lex æterna sancit, nimirum vt necessaria necessariò, contingentia contingêter, libera liberè, & sic porrò. Vnde scitè dictum à Mornæo l. de verit. relig. ca. 13. Mouet motor primus inferiora secundum naturam cuiusq; indolem; mobiles secundum motum; immobiles secundum stabilitatem; naturales secundum seruitutem, sensibiles secundum appetitum, rationales secundum voluntatem & libertatem. Fusius hæc ostendunt & deducunt Philosophi per quatuor causarum agentium genera. Docent enim quòd quædam ab æterno ordinata sint, vt eueniant, per caussas necessariò agentes & non impedibiles naturaliter, vt motus cœlotum solisque ac Lunæ defectus: quædam per causas necessariò agentes & impedibiles, sed non impeditas in agendo, vt generatio hominis! alia per causas necessariò agentes, non solùm impedibiles sed etiam impeditas, vt generatio monstri; quæ quidem necessaria est ratione caurarum concurrentium, euenit tamen contingenter respectu proximæ causæ, præter cuius intentionem est: Alia denique per causas liberas, quæ nullâ necessitate eueniunt, vt externi actus humani. Atque hinc apparet contingentiam per Dei prouidentiam adeò non tolli, vt potiùs stabiliatur, siquidem & per illam decretum est, vt quædam agerent non necessariò, sed liberè & contingenter. Ideoque verè dictum à Gregorio lib. 5. moral. cap. 18. in fine: Quicquid intus immutabiliter constituitur foris mutabiliter agitur.


### Question XIII. What are the impediments to liberty?

CXIX. Thus far we have asserted the liberty of man in external actions: Now we add this: that this liberty is not absolute and perfect, but rather languid and entangled with many impediments. We languish toward the pursuit of virtue, and incline toward vices, so that we do not abstain from them except with great difficulty. In other affairs also we often do not attain the end, but many things are done beside our intention. Although the choice may be most free, yet the execution is not always in our power. Wherefore we shall briefly note here the principal impediments of liberty, which recent theologians have been accustomed to distinguish into External and Internal.

CXX. Of external ones, three are primarily numbered. 1. The disposition of God, since our will is in His hand, along with all actions. Which disposition indeed does not entirely take away liberty, but rather promotes it in good, while in evil it more often restrains it, and sets a limit to human fury, so that it cannot always reach where it wishes, by the example of Jeroboam: 1 Kings 13 verse 5, and of Sennacherib, Isaiah 37 verse 29. Thus the outcomes of actions are in the power of God, and therefore they more often fall out otherwise than we think and labor. For the way of man is not his own, Jer. 10 verse 23. See the explanation of this saying in Chemnitz in the place on free will, chapter 2, middle of folio 200 and following. 2. The seduction of the devil, who often carries the will astray, and when he sees it inclining toward good, he persuades it to evil, because he is accustomed to be effective in the children of disobedience, Eph. 2 verse 2. Thus the Apostle was hindered by Satan, 2 Tim. 4 verses 17, 18, and others experience the same. 3. The multitude of objects. For these things partly entice, if they are pleasant; partly they terrify and disturb the mind, if they are bitter and troublesome; for very often men are called away by the fear of danger from the good which they would otherwise have done.

CXXI. But the internal impediments are: 1. The defect of the divine image. 2. The blindness of the intellect, from which arise errors in counsels and deliberations, because we cannot foresee and guard against everything. 3. The infirmity of the will, which is languid in the choice of good and feeble in execution. 4. Natural impulse and propensity toward evil, which the flesh always seeks and prefers to good. 5. The vehemence of the affections, often so great that like a torrent they carry the will away with them and disturb the judgment of reason. All these things cause that whatever liberty is still remaining is often hindered and changed into servitude, which the Philosopher also acknowledged when he wrote in Alpha minor Metaphysics, chapter 2, πολλαχῆ ἡ φύσις δούλη τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶ, the nature or will of man is often a slave. Therefore let us acknowledge this weakness of nature, and let us not boast on account of any external discipline whatsoever, but rather let us deplore the imperfection of nature, and let us pray to God that He Himself may direct our steps, and remove the obstacles which can and are wont to call us back from the path of virtue and to cast us headlong into the pathless wilds of vices.

Latin:

CXIX. Hactenus libertatem hominis in externis actionibus asseruimus: Nunc illud addimus: quòd libertas ista non sit absoluta & perfecta, sed potiùs languida & multis impedimentis implicata. Languemus ad virtutis studium, & contra propendemus ad vitia, vt non nisi cum magna difficultate ab ijs abstineamus. In alijs quoque negotijs sæpè non assequimur finem, sed multa fiunt præter intentionem. Vt maximè libera sit electio, non tamen semper in potestate nostra est executio. Quare præcipua libertatis impedimenta breuiter hic annotabimus, quæ recentiores Theologi in Externa & Interna distinguere consueuerant.

CXX. Externorum tria imprimis numerantur. 1. Dei dispositio, quippe in cuius manu voluntas nostra est, cum actionibus vniuersis. Quæ quidem dispositio non planè tollit libertatem, sed potiùs promouet in bono, in malo autem sæpiùs cohibet, & modum statuit furori humano, vt quò: velit, peruenire semper non possit, exemplo Ieroboam: 1. Reg. 13 vers. 5. & Sennacheribi Esa. 37. v. 29. Sic euentus actionum in Dei potestate sunt, ideoque sæpiùs aliter cadunt atque cogitamus & laboramus. Nec enim hominis est via eius Ier. 10. v. 23. Cuius dicti explicationem vide apud Chemnitium loco de lib. arbitr. cap. 2 m. fol. 200. & seq. 2. Diaboli seductio, qui sæpè transuersam rapit voluntatem, & quando videt ad bonum inclinare, persuadet malum, quia efficax esse solet in filijs incredulitatis Eph. 2. v. 2. Sic à Satana impeditus est Apostolus 2. Tim. 4. vers. 17. 18. & idem experiuntur alij. 3. Obiectorum multitudo. Ista enim partim alliciunt, si sint iucunda; partim terrent & animū conturbant, si acerba sint & molesta; Sæpissimè enim metu periculi auocantur homines à bono, quod aliàs facturi fuissent.

C X X I. Interna verò impedimenta sunt. 1. Defectus imaginis diuinæ. 2. Cœcitas intellectus, vnde oriuntur errores in consilijs & deliberationibus, quia omnia prospicere & cauere non possumus. 3. Infirmitas voluntatis, quæ languida est in boni electione & imbecilla in executione. 4. Naturalis impetus & propensio ad malum, quod caro semper expetit & bono præponit. 5. Vehementia affectuum, sæpiùs tanta, vt instar torrentis voluntatem secum abripiant & rationis iudicium turbent. Hæc omnia faciunt, vt qualiscunque illa libertas adhuc reliqua sæpè impediatur, & in seruitutem mutetur, quod & Philosophus agnouit, cùm scripsit α. min. Metaph. cap. 2. πολλαχῆ ἡ φύσις δούλη τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἐστὶ, Natura vel voluntas hominis sæpiùs seruit. Proinde agnoscamus hanc naturæ imbecillitatem, nec gloriemur ob qualemcunque disciplinam externam, sed potiùs deploremus naturae imperfectionem, & oremus Deum, vtipse dirigat gressus nostros, & remoueat obstacula, quae nos à virtutis semitâ reuocare & in vitiorum auia praecipitare possunt & solent.


### Question XIV & last. What is to be thought concerning the good works of the Gentiles?

CXXII. Bellarmine treats this question at length in book 5, chapter 6 and following, and Becanus in part 2 of Scholastic Theology, treatise 1, chapter 2, question 10, where our people are accused because they have called all the good works and exercises of virtue of the Gentiles sins. We shall propose the sum of the matter in a few words, since otherwise these theses have grown beyond our intention.

CXXIII. The virtues of the Gentiles can be considered in two ways. 1. νομικῶς, or legally, by reason of their internal quiddity, insofar as they agree with the law. 2. συγκριτικῶς, and with respect to their external σχέσεως, insofar as they please or displease God. For in both ways the theologian considers works: in the former he says their form is ἐννομίαν or agreement with the law: in the latter πίστιν or justifying faith. This distinction being presupposed, we shall include the decision of the question in two theses.

CXXIV. I. The virtues of the Gentiles considered νομικῶς are not formally and per se sins. We add the reason, 1. From the efficient cause. The remote cause is God Himself, from whom is every gift, James 1, verse 17, and who is called the helper of all good wills, Aug. book 14 de Civ. D. ch. 26. But that which draws its origin from God is not essentially evil. The proximate cause is indeed not πνεῦμα or the Holy Spirit because the Gentiles are by no means reborn; nor is it σάρξ or corrupt flesh, because These virtues agree with the law, from which the flesh always deviates, but by the λόγῳ or right reason, endowed with the law of nature, from which it follows that those virtues are not formally sins. For a cause and its effect do not differ in their whole genus. Now the causes of these virtues are good, namely God and right reason: how therefore could the effect ὀσιώδως be evil? 2. From ἀνομίᾳ: Whatever is consonant with the divine law is not essentially a sin 1 Ioh. 3. v. 4. But the virtues of the Gentiles are consonant with the divine law. Therefore they are not essentially sins. I prove the minor, because the love of the Creator is conformable to the first table, and the love of the neighbor and an honest life to the second table. And whatever right reason prescribes, this depends on the law of nature, which does not differ essentially from the written moral law. 3. From remuneration, God compensated the virtues of the Gentiles with rewards, as is evident from the example of the Egyptian midwives. Therefore they were not intrinsically sins, since He is not accustomed to reward these.

CXXV. II. The virtues of the Gentiles considered ἐνσχετικῶς are not undeservedly called sins. For there it is not considered whether a work in some way agrees with the law, but whether it specifically pleases God and is accepted, which cannot be affirmed of the virtues of the Gentiles: for they displease God and are called sins. 1. By reason of the lacking faith, without which it is impossible to please God Hebr. 11. ver. 6. and what seem to be good works are turned into sins, as Augustine speaks in book 12 de Trin. cap 7. 2. By reason of the end, which among the Gentiles was illegitimate, since they sought not so much the glory of God as their own, for actions are judged by their ends. And virtues, unless they are referred to God, are not virtues, says Augustine in book 15 de Civ. Dei chapter 25. Whence the rule: Good works are to be judged not by nouns, but by adverbs, that is, those works are finally good which are also done well. 3. By reason of imperfection, which is always adjunct. For although the Gentiles did something conformable to the law, yet in that very action of virtue, insofar as it was imperfect, there lay hidden at the same time some deformity and ἀνομία, which, since it could not be covered by the merit of faith in Christ due to a defect of faith, defiled the whole work, which is therefore rightly designated a sin. a person not reborn and faithless, who, since he displeased God, it follows that the work itself also displeased.

CXXVI. Thus, therefore, we decide this question most briefly, that the virtues of the Gentiles, insofar as they were in part conformable to the divine law, were not sins formally and in themselves. Nevertheless, in the Evangelical sense and with respect to the external σχέσις, insofar as they did not please God, and thus accidentally, they are rightly called sins, on account of the defect of faith, on account of an illegitimate end, on account of the imperfection adjoined, on account of the person not being reborn. Which single thesis, if it be diligently weighed, it will be easy to answer all the arguments of Bellarmine, for which reason we stop here, praying to God that He may perfect the good work which He has begun, and confirm us daily in true liberty, through Christ Jesus, the author and sole perfecter of our reparation. AMEN.

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

CXXII. Prolixè tractat hanc quaestionem Bellarminus l. 5. c. 6. & seqq. & Becanus part. 2. Theolog. schol, tract. 1. cap. 2. qu. 10, vbi nostri accusantur, quòd omnia gentilium opera bona & virtutis exercitia nuncupârint peccata. Nos paucis summam rei proponemus, cùm aliàs praeter intentionem hae theses excreuerint.

CXXIII. Virtutes gentilium dupliciter considerari possunt. 1. νομικῶς, vel legaliter, ratione quidditatis suae internae, quatenus cùm lege conueniunt. 2. συγκριτικῶς, & respectu externae σχέσεως, quatenus Deo placent vel displicent. Vtroque enim modo Theologus considerat opera: priori formam illorum esse dicit ἐννομίαν vel cum lege conuenientiam : Posteriori πίστιν seu fidem iustificantem. Hâc distinctione praesuppositâ, quaestionis decisionem duabus thesibus includemus.

CXXIV. I. Virtutes gentilium νομικῶς consideratae formaliter & per se non sunt peccata. Rationem addimus, 1. A causa efficiente. Remota est Deus ipse, à quo omne donum Iac. 1. vers. 17. & qui adiutor dicitur omnium bonarum voluntatum, Aug. lib. 14. de Ciu. D. c. 26. Quod verò à Deo trahit ortum, essentialiter non est malum. Propinqua causa non quidem est πνεῦμα vel Spiritus Sanctus quia gentiles minimè sunt renati; neque σάρξ vel caro corrupta, quia virtutes istæ cum lege consentiunt, à qua caro semper exorbitat, sed λόγῳ vel recta ratio, lege naturæ prædita, vnde sequitur, virtutes illas formaliter peccata non esse. Causa enim & causatum toto genere non differunt. Iam causæ virtutum istarum bonæ sunt, videlicet Deus & recta ratio: qui ergò causatum ὀσιώδως esset malum? 2. Ab ἀνομίᾳ: Quicquid legi diuinæ est consonum, essentialiter non est peccatum 1. Ioh. 3. v. 4. Atqui virtutes gentilium legi diuinæ sunt consonæ. E. non sunt peccata essentialiter. Minorem probo, quia creatoris dilectio primæ, proximi amor & vita honesta secundæ tabulæ conformis est. Et quicquid præscribit recta ratio, hoc dependet à lege naturæ, quæ non differt essentialiter à lege morali scripta. 3. A remuneratione, Deus compensauit præmiis virtutes gentilium, vti constat exemplo obstetricum Ægyptiacarum. E. non fuerunt intrinsecus peccata, quoniam hæc remunerare non solet.

CXXV. II. Virtutes gentilium ἐνσχετικῶς consideratæ, non immerito nuncupantur peccata. Ibi enim non attenditur, an opus cum lege quodammodo conueniat, sed num Deo specialiter placeat & acceptum sit, id quod de virtutibus gentilium affirmari nequit: Displicent enim Deo & peccata vocantur. 1. Ratione fidei deficientis, sine qua Deo placere est impossibile Hebr. 11. verj. 6. & quæ videntur bona opera in peccata vertuntur, vt Augustinus l. 12. de Trin. cap 7. loquitur. 2. Ratione finis, qui apud gentiles fuit illegitimus, siquidem non tam Dei, quàm propriam gloriam quæsiuerunt, Finibus autem iudicantur actiones. Et virtutes nisi ad Deum referantur, non sunt virtutes, ait Augustinus lib. 15. de Civ. Dei capite 25. Vnde regula: Bona opera non nominibus, sed aduerbijs sunt iudicanda, hoc est, illa demum opera sunt bona, quæ etiam benè fiunt. 3. Ratione imperfectionis, quæ semper est adiuncta. Licet enim gentiles aliquid conforme legi fecerint, in illa ipsa tamen actione virtutis, quatenus imperfecta fuit, simul latuit aliqua difformitas & ἀνομία, quæ cum ob defectum fidei Christi merito tegi non potuerit, totum opus coinquinauit quod propterea recte peccatum indigitatur. 4. Ratione subiecti, quod fuit persona non renata & infidelis, quæ cum Deo displicuerit, & ipsum opus displicuisse sequitur.

CXXVI. Ita igitur breuissime hanc quæstionem decidimus, quod virtutes gentilium, quatenus ex parte erant conformes legi diuinæ, non fuerint peccata formaliter & per sese. Nihilominus sensu Euangelico & respectu externæ σχέσεως, quatenus non placuerunt Deo, adeoque per accidens, recte nuncupantur peccata, ob defectum fidei, ob finem illegitimum, ob imperfectionem adiunctam, ob personam non renatam. Quæ vnica thesis, si diligenter ponderetur, ad omnia Bellarmini argumenta respondere erit facile, qua de causa hic pedem sistimus, Deum orantes, vt quod cœpit opus bonum, perficiat, & in vera libertate nos indies confirmet, per Christum Iesum reparationis nostræ authorem & consummatorem vnicum. AMEN.

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 25 Disputation II. On the Servitude of the Will Concerning the Conversion of Man and Other Spiritual Acts

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Master Johannes Lucius of Dresden.

Thesis I.

In the previous disputation we saw both the οὐσίαν of the will, or what it is; and its ἐνέργειαν, or what it can do in external actions: Now we proceed to spiritual acts, among which the conversion of the sinner to God excels most of all; and we shall examine, whether any powers of the will are left to man after the fall, by which he might be able either to convert himself, or to prepare himself for conversion, or only, if he is helped, to cooperate with God? We Catholics and Orthodox choose and defend the affirmative, the Heretics the negative.

II. Moreover, this question is of the greatest importance, and is not to be relegated among useless and unnecessary problems, as Erasmus thought, but rather it must be considered to pertain to the foundation of our salvation, which Luther himself explained vigorously in his book On the Bondage of the Will, p. 22, small edition, Wittenberg, in 8vo, year 1526. If I am ignorant, he says, of what, to what extent, and how much I can do and perform toward God, it will be equally uncertain and unknown to me what, to what extent, and how much God can do and performs in me, since God works all things in all: But if the works and power of GOD are ignored, I am ignorant of GOD himself: If God is ignored, I cannot worship, praise, give thanks, or serve God, while I do not know how much I should attribute to myself, and how much I owe to God. It is necessary, therefore, to have a most certain distinction between the power of GOD and our own, if we wish to live thus. III. In this grave and vigorous judgment of Luther we entirely acquiesce, and therefore we determine that the present controversy concerning human powers must be treated all the more diligently: for which reason, in this disputation, we shall propose the κατασκευὴν (construction) of the true opinion concerning the enslaved will, intending to subjoin the ἀνασκευὴν (destruction) of the contrary and false one immediately after. Concerning the κατασκευὴν, however, six special questions in particular come to be ventilated. I. What is the opinion of the Papists concerning the powers of the will? II. Are the Papists rightly numbered among the Pelagians? III. What is our opinion concerning the will of unregenerate man? IV. What is the principal and true state of the controversy? V. By what arguments can the true opinion be defended? VI. What is the use of the doctrine concerning the servitude of the will?

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D.

Resp. M. Iohanne Lucio Dresdensi.

Thesis I.

SVperiori disputatione vidimus tum οὐσίαν arbitrij, vel quis sit; tum ἐνέργειαν eiusdem, vel quid possit in externis actionibus: Nunc pergimus ad actus spirituales, inter quos vel maximè excellit conuersio peccatoris ad Deum; & dispiciemus, Num aliquæ post lapsum vires arbitrij sint relictæ homini, quibus vel seipsum conuertere, vel ad conuersionem præparare, vel tantùm, si iuuetur, Deo cooperari valeat? Affirmatiuam nos Catholici & Orthodoxi, negatiuam Hæretici eligunt & propugnant.

II. Est autem quæstio hæc momenti maximi, nec referenda inter inutilia & non necessaria problemata, vti Erasmus censuit, sed potiùs salutis nostræ fundamentum attinere putandum est, quod ipsum Lutherus neruosè explicuit l. de seruo arbit. m. pag. 22. edit. min. Witt. in 8. anno 1526. Si ignorauero, ait, quid, quatenus & quantum ego possum, & faciam erga Deum, pariter incertum & ignotum mihi erit, quid, quatenus & quantum Deus in me potest & faciat, cùm Deus operetur omnia in omnibus: Ignoratis verò operibus & potentiâ DEI, DEVM ipsum ignoro: Ignorato Deô, colere, laudare, gratias agere, seruire Deo non possum, dum nescio, quantum mihi tribuere, quantum Deo debeo. Oportet igitur certissimam distinAionem habere inter virtutem DEI & nostram, si volumus sie viuere. III. In graui hoc & neruoso Lutheri iudicio toti acquiescimus, ideoque praesentem de viribus humanis controuersiam eo diligentiùs pertractandam esse statuimus: quam ob causam disputatione hac κατασκευὴν verae sententiae de seruo arbitrio proponemus, ἀνασκευὴν contrariae falsaeque subiuncturi proximè. Circa κατασκευὴν autem sex imprimis speciales quaestiones ventilandae veniunt. I. Quae Pontificiorum de viribus arbitrii sit opinio? II. Num Pelagianis rectè annumerantur Pontificii? III. Quae nostra de hominis non-renati arbitrio sit sententia? IV. Quis praecipuus & verus controuersię status? V. Quibus argumentis vera sententia propugnari queat? VI. Quis sit vsus doctrinę de seruitute arbitrii?


### Question I. What is the opinion of the Papists concerning the powers of the will?

IV. That which Luther complains of in his book On the Enslaved Will, page 4, that Erasmus his antagonist was slippery and double-tongued, while he wished to assert nothing, yet at the same time to appear an assertor: this very thing can most truly be said of modern Papists, especially the Jesuits, whose slippery and ambiguous locutions render this matter, otherwise difficult enough, even more difficult and intricate. For they are so two-headed and double-tongued that they belch forth now this and now that, and devise various things against Scripture. V. We shall not go far from here, nor shall we heap up many testimonies: one Bellarmine, who treated this controversy most extensively: and set before us the opinion of the whole Roman Church, which approved his books, yet so slippery and inconsistently, that he himself scarcely seems to understand what he finally determines. For now he disputes against us, now for us: now he asserts the servitude of the will, now he destroys it, and thus, like a serpent, he twists himself wonderfully and miserably into various parts.

VI. For 1. He seems to remove all freedom of the will regarding spiritual acts in the following places. Book 1, on grace and free will, chapter 12, he expressly denies that grace is rendered efficacious by free will, but that the acceptance of grace proceeds solely from God, so that no one may boast. Chapter 13, column 568 B. Truly, he says, a believer cannot boast or be puffed up against an unbeliever, because he who principally distinguishes him from the unbeliever is not he himself through free will, but God through efficacious grace, which He gave to him, and did not give to the other. Book 5, chapter 14, he responds to the error which Hesshusius noted: But here indeed a few Scholastics have written, but the opinion of a few ought not to be attributed to the Catholic Church, which more, and more serious [theologians] in the same Church refute, that Man from pure naturals can love God above all things. Book 6, chapter 9, he says: that it is taught by us that our will can effect nothing at all of spiritual and saving good without the help of grace. And in this matter, he says, they think correctly, but they do not correctly attribute the contrary opinion to Catholics. Book 6, chapter 13, column 910, he discourses thus: But this middle and natural way, when it is damaged by sin, so that it is called a heart of stone, does not have of itself the power by which it may turn itself to God and become flesh, but it receives it through the preventing grace of God. For free will, excited and prepared by preventing grace, can through the powers which it receives from God cooperate toward its own conversion. Nor does the similitude of the stone stand in the way; for similitudes ought not to agree in all things. The similitude has a place only in this, that just as a stone does not have of itself that it should cooperate, if by chance it should be turned into

flesh, so also free will does not have of itself that it should cooperate toward its own conversion; yet it can receive from God the power of operating through prevenient grace, which a stone cannot. And a little later: From which solution, the deception or fraud of Chemnitz is uncovered: For he writes that Catholics are of the opinion that free will, having been excited by grace, exerts the powers which it had even before it was excited, and through those powers of its own consents to the divine calling; so that prevenient grace does not bestow powers upon free will, but as it were excites them when they are dormant. But Catholics do not hold these views, but they do indeed acknowledge free will in man, even before divine grace prevents him, because free will is a natural thing, which is not lost through sin, but yet they do not say, nor do they think, that free will has of itself any power, at least proximate, for acts of piety, but that it receives it from God through prevenient grace. L. 5. cap. 10. col. 786. lit. C. he says: We willingly confess that all men are in a state of sin, and useless for performing works that please God, unless they are first reconciled through the grace of God. And yet in cap. 9. he argues at length that the unregenerate can perform a work that is morally good and pleasing to God. To Bellarmine we add Costerus, who likewise seems to speak orthodoxly in Enchirid. pag. 204. The sinner, he says, by his own powers is not only unable to be freed from sin, but he is also unable to rise from it, nor to conceive sorrow for sin, nor to dispose himself for grace or the remission of sins, nor to be piously affected toward God, or to speak with pious affection about Christ as his redeemer without divine motion and prevenient grace. And p. 205. In the sinful man there is such blindness of the intellect, and such hardness of the will and heart, that unless the merciful grace of God prevents him, and illuminates the mind, and moves the effect, he will never truly repent, or return to God. And again p. 206. They call this motion of God prevenient and operating grace, because God, out of his mercy, works it in us without us, while we do nothing and while we are resting securely in sin, with no merits of ours demanding it, moving the heart, and illuminating the mind. Thus also the Council of Trent, canon 3, session 6, seems to hold an orthodox view: If anyone shall say that man can believe, hope, love, or repent without the preceding inspiration of the Holy Spirit and His assistance, let him be anathema.

VII. 2. He asserts the freedom of the will in the following. Book 5, chapter 9, he affirms that a man can perform a morally good work by free will. Chapter 14, he defends that it was rightly said by the Scholastics that natural powers remained intact. Book 4, chapter 15, he proposes a simile of two men carrying one stone. Book 5, chapters 11 and 12, he argues that after the fall, free will remains in man for pious and salutary actions. Chapter 15, he proposes truly Pelagian axioms, such as: 1. Man, before any grace, has free will, not only for natural and moral works, but also for works of piety and supernatural ones. 2. Man has, before any grace, a remote and imperfect power to perform works of piety. 3. Neither exciting nor assisting grace imposes any necessity upon man, such that he cannot freely consent or dissent to God calling. 4. The conversion of man to God, as also any other pious work, insofar as it is a work, is from free will alone, yet not excluding general assistance; insofar as it is pious, it is from grace alone; insofar as it is a pious work, it is from free will and grace together. Book 1, chapter 13, at the end, he establishes a twofold cause why, of two equally excited, one is converted and the other is not; one primary, the operation of God; the other secondary, free will, because the former freely consented to the exciting grace, the latter did not: the contrary of which, however, he proposed a little before, in which he has Becanus as a dissenter, in his Disputations on the assistance of grace, part 2, chapter 7; Book 5, chapter 13, he contends that it was rightly said by Andradius that the freedom of the will is the efficient cause of the application of the will to grace, and by Ruard Tapper that the power of believing is in our own control, and that man after the fall has the right light of reason, and that the human mind understands many things by itself which pertain to the knowledge of divine matters.

IX. This, therefore, is Bellarmine's opinion, that free will regarding supernatural matters is not entirely lost, but only obscured and bound, so that it cannot be brought into secondary act unless it is released by prevenient grace. For this is evident from that simile which he proposes in these words, lib. 6, cap. 15, col. 918. B: We experience something similar in the power of seeing: for when the sensible species is absent, man has the power and freedom of seeing, for that species is not the cause of the freedom or power of seeing; nevertheless, the power is remote, and the freedom is bound, until, the species being received, the power is perfected and can proceed into act. From this we gather such an opinion: As there is in man a natural force and power of seeing, which is perfected by a visible object so that it may proceed into act, so in the will of man after the fall there remains a natural force and power for working well, or for conversion, which is perfected and proceeds into act when the motion and impulse of God, or internal grace, is aroused. He therefore establishes two partial causes of conversion, the grace of God and the will of man, which clearly shines forth from that simile of two men who together carry a huge stone, which one could not carry; where each freely applies his concurrence, and if the other is unwilling to concur, the work will not be done, lib. 4, cap. 15. Indeed, he makes the human will the first cause in conversion, as regards priority of order, while in the same chapter 15 he argues that the will by nature operates before God, and therefore that God operates because the will operates, not the contrary; whence this is the consequence, that God is said to cooperate with the will rather than the will with God.

IX. The same is the mind of Coster, who writes thus on page 203 of his Enchiridion: Free will can do much of itself and by its own nature, not only in indifferent things, which are not placed in vices and virtues, such as walking, sitting, buying, not buying, and things similar to these, but also in the moral works of virtues. For since the nature of the will is good, why should it not will and work the good, which indeed every good tree produces good fruits? Again p. 211. Is this grace in the choice of the will, so that it can use it, and not use it, retain it and cast it away; just as a staff in the hand of a convalescent, the help of which, if he wishes, he will use; but if not, he will be able to remove it. He adds a lengthy simile, p. 211, concerning a man falling among thieves, which he proposes thus: By the following similitude, which happens to be a parable of a man who had fallen among thieves, the whole matter seems to be able to be illustrated in some way. Let there be a man nearly finished by lethal wounds, who in the middle of winter in the darkness of night, destitute of all help, and stiff with cold, is almost failing. Let a friend approach with a light; who places the half-dead man, desiring help, and as much as is in him struggling, upon a beast of burden; brings him into a house; revives him with a bright fire, and treats his wounds with certain medicines, having treated him in some way; but, still languishing from the preceding disease, orders him to remain in a heated room; and so that he may walk, offers him a staff; and provides other aids for obtaining full and perfect health. By this similitude we understand first the misery of the sinful man; who, destitute of the warmth of the grace of God, is entirely cold, deprived of divine light, is situated in the densest darkness; and has his soul, and all his powers, gravely wounded by many sins, so that his every thought is prone to evil.
