Secondly, the manner by which he is led out of these calamities; with God preceding and accompanying with a certain light of grace, by which the intellect, beholding the foulness of sins and the kindness of God, begins to detest the former and aspire to the latter: the will also, aided in all ways, cooperates; so that he may be unburdened of such great evils, yet freely, because not unwillingly, but cooperating, that man was lifted onto the beast of burden. Then, that man having been brought into the house, let oil and wine be poured into the open wounds by the friend; certain most present remedies, namely the grace of justification; by which the wounds cease to be lethal, to the infusion of which the holy man does nothing further than to uncover the wounds and receive the ointment: because God alone works the remission of sins in us, with us only consenting, and receiving the infused grace and justice.

Thirdly, what grace effects in a justified man; namely, it frees him from the danger of eternal death: it illuminates the intellect with divine light: it kindles the will with the warmth of charity: it strengthens free will and the other powers of the soul: and it raises to his feet the whole man, who previously lay prostrate and in need of external help to rise again, and provides him with the strength and assistance to walk. Fourthly, we say in what manner the grace of God performs all these things in a justified man, namely, not by compelling, nor by imposing necessity, but by leaving his freedom to him. It will indeed affect the mind of man, so that he recognizes the good, and the will, so that the good pleases him, and it draws him sweetly, just as his own pleasure draws each person, just as a boy is drawn by an apple (says St. Augustine), and as a son is induced by a parent with little gifts and blandishments to learn his letters (as is in Methodius): meanwhile, free will remains, so that he may either follow or not follow the one persuading, affecting, and drawing him.

X. Furthermore, Costerus, against Bellarmine, book 6, chapter 15, maintains on page 206 that preventing grace is not an internal motion and inclination of the will, but merely an external impulse of the Spirit still dwelling outside, which a man can freely admit or reject. On pages 207 and 208 he says: The free will of man, by the help of God not yet dwelling within but moving and assisting, prepares itself for justification not only by suffering, but also by operating and acting. He brings forward a simile of one fallen into a pit, and concludes with these words: Thus free will, which by its own fault fell into sin, in order to be led out of the dark pit of sin, does not only receive, or suffer, or is agitated, but cooperates with the grace of God, prepares itself by believing, by assuming the duties of piety, until, ascending to the sun of justice, it is filled within with the divine light of grace. See more in the same place, all of which tends to the point that it is in the power of the will to prepare itself for grace, to accept or reject grace, to retain or dismiss it once accepted, all of which it denies from Canon 4 of the Council of Trent, which holds as follows: If anyone shall say that the free will of man, moved and excited by God, does nothing by cooperating by assenting to God who excites and calls, whereby he disposes and prepares himself to obtain the grace of justification, and that he cannot dissent if he wishes, but like some inanimate thing does nothing at all, and behaves himself merely passively, let him be anathema.

XI. Although this Council also makes mention of the help of the Holy Spirit and of prevenient grace: yet this is proposed by Andradius and his interpreters in such a way that free will indeed received a grievous wound through sin, but was not extinguished, and that although it cannot by its own strength and faculty raise itself; yet if it be moved by God from without through the word, it can assent and cooperate with God. Andradius uses this simile: Just as he who is bound with iron chains indeed has an innate δύναμιν or power of walking, but although he has it, he cannot nevertheless use it, so that it may proceed into act, unless the chains which repress and retard the motion are first broken: So free will is bound by the chains of sin, so that it cannot exert those powers which it has remaining for performing spiritual actions, unless it be moved and excited by God. But when the motion and impulse of the Holy Spirit has approached, by which the chains are broken and the wounds bound, then that δύναμιν exerts itself, and assents, and so cooperates with God in beginning and effecting spiritual motions. Furthermore, Andradius employs the simile of a sick man, whose powers have been broken, weakened, and attenuated by disease, when the physician confirms and strengthens the remaining powers, and restores those that were lost. Others delight in the simile of a little bird, which indeed retains the power of flying, but when it is tied by a little cord, it cannot exercise the use and motion of that faculty which is naturally implanted in it: if anyone breaks the cord, he does not insert into the little bird a new and peculiar δύναμιν of flying, which it did not have before, but only removes the impediment. but if you apply this to the business of conversion, it soon follows that divine grace is not the principal and primary efficient cause of conversion, but only effects conversion by way of removing an obstacle. For just as He is not called the efficient cause of flight who has removed an impediment: thus also it must be judged concerning the conversion of man according to the hypotheses of the Papists. Andradius has proposed yet another similitude taken from burning by fire: If I ask, he says, when you see wooden material burning, what is the efficient cause of that conflagration, it is necessary that you say fire, together with God the author and patron of nature, who supplies the fire with the power of burning, and conspires with it to work. Since therefore the motion of our free will does not depend more on the grace of God than the burning of stubble depends on divine power, why is it that you despoil free will of the dignity and name of an efficient cause? From which we infer: Just as the proximate and primary cause of burning is fire, but God is only the remote cause: so the principal efficient cause of conversion is free will, and the grace of God itself is only a remote and general cause; what could be said to be more Pelagian than this?

XII. The sum therefore of the Papistic opinion is this, that free will has not lost the faculty of converting itself to God, but that only the execution of that faculty has been lost; which is hindered by the bonds of sin. But when grace loosens that bond, and excites man, there then free will spontaneously converts itself to God. This opinion is that of the Council of Trent and of Andradius, and of the rest, from which it is clear that free will is solely the efficient cause of conversion, if we wish to speak properly, and that the grace of God does not immediately effect conversion, but does nothing else than remove the impediment from the true efficient cause, namely free will. For just as he who removes obstacles is not truly the efficient cause of motion, e.g., in a stone resting upon a statue, but the very form of the stone is the true principle of that downward motion; but he who has removed the impediment has only brought the efficient cause into act; but has not himself effected the motion: Thus since God, according to the opinion of the Papists does nothing else through His grace, than that He removes the impediment from the will, and it is situated in the will alone to turn itself to God or not to turn itself; it follows certainly; that God, speaking properly, is not the efficient cause of conversion, nor can or ought conversion to be named a work of God, since effects are primarily ascribed only to the proximate and immediate efficient cause, and not to the one removing the hindrance. Although therefore some part of efficiency in conversion can be ascribed to God, nevertheless far more will have to be assigned to the powers of the will, since they alone are the first and immediate principle of conversion: whence consequently Conversion will be a human work rather than a divine one, and the believer can ascribe far more to himself than to God, inasmuch as it was in his own faculty, after the impediment was removed, to turn himself to God or not to turn himself. And however much they often dissimulate this opinion; and wish to seem to establish something else; nevertheless if you examine all their principles, you will discover nothing other than the very Pelagianism itself hidden under these wrappings and pigments of words, which we now undertake to demonstrate in the second question.

Latin:

IV. Quod Lutherus l. de seruo arbitrio pag. 4. conqueritur, Erasmum antagonistam suum esse lubricum & flexiloquum, dum nihil voluit assertum, rursus tamen assertor videri: hoc ipsū de modernis Pontificijs, praecipuè IesuVVitis, verissimè dici potest, quorum lubricae & ambiguae locutiones materiam hanc aliàs difficilem satis, reddunt tamen difficiliorem magis que intricatam. Tam enim sunt bicipites & bilingues, vt modò hoc modò illud eructet, & aduersùs Scripturam varia cōminiscantur. V. Non longè hinc abibimus, nec multa testimonia coaceruabimus: sufficere potest vnus Bellarminus, qui hanc controuersiam fusissimè pertractauit: & totius Ecclesiae Romanae, quae libros eius adprobauit, sententiam nobis proposuit, tam lubricè autem & inconstanter, vt quid tandem statuat, vix ipse videatur intelligere. Modò enim contra nos, modò pro nobis disputat: Iam serui tutem arbitrii adstruit, nunc destruit, adeoque in partes varias, serpentis instar, mirè misereque se contorquet.

VI. Nam 1. Omnem arbitrij libertatem quoad actus spirituales, sequentibus locis tollere videtur. L. 1. de grat. & lib. arb. c. 12. disertè negat gratiam reddi efficacem per liberum arbitrium, sed acceptationem gratiae tantummodo à Deo prouenire, ne quis glorietur. C. 13. col. 568. B. Verò, inquit, non potest fidelis aduersus infidelem gloriari aut inflari, quia qui eum principaliter discernit ab infideli, non est ipse per liberum arbitrium, sed Deus per gratiam efficacem, quam ei dedit, & alteri non dedit. L. 5. cap. 14. ad errorem, quem Hesshusius annotauit, respondet: At hic scripserunt Scholastici quidem pauci, sed non debet Ecclesiae Catholicae tribui opinio paucorum, quam in eadem Ecclesia plures, & Homo ex puris naturalibus potest diligere Deum super omnia: grauiores refellunt. L. 6. c. 9. inquit; à nobis doceri, voluntatem nostram nihil omninò boni spiritualis & salutaris efficere posse, sine auxilio gratiae. Atque in hac re, ait, rectè sentiunt, sed non rectè contrariam sententiam Catholicis attribuunt. L. 6. cap. 13. col. 910. ita disserit: Haec autem via media & naturalis, quando per peccatum laesi est, vt dicatur cor lapideum, non habet ex se potestatem, quà se conuertat ad Deum, & fiat carneum, sed eam recipit per gratiam Dei praeuenientem, Liberum enim arbitrium per gratiam praeuenientem excitatum & praeparatum, potest per vires, quas à Deo recipit, cooperari ad suam ipsius conuersionem. Neque obstat similitudo lapidis; non enim similitudines conuenire debent in omnibus. In eo tantùm similitudo locum habet, quòd sicut lapis ex se non habet, vt cooperetur, si fortè conuertatur in car-

nem, sit etiam liberum arbitrium ex se non habet, vt conperetur ad suam ipsius, conuersionem; potest tamen a Deo recipere potestatem operandi per gratiam præuenientem, quod non potest lapis. Et paulo post: Ex qua solutione, detegitur deceptio vel fraus Kemnitij: Scribit enim, Catholicos in ea sententia esse, vt liberum arbitrium per gratiam excitatum, exerat vires, quas habebat etiam, antequam excitaretur, & per illas suas vires vocationi diuinæ consentiat; ita vt gratia præueniens, non tribuat vires libero arbitrio, sed quasi sopitas excitet. At non hæc sentiunt Catholici, sed agnoscunt quidem liberum arbitrium in homine, etiam antequam eum gratia diuina præueniat, quia liberum arbitrium est res naturalis, quæ per peccatum non amittitur, sed tamen non dicunt, nec sentiunt, liberum arbitrium habere ex se potentiam vllam, saltem proximam ad actus pietatis, sed eam accipere a Deo per gratiam præuenientem. L. 5. cap. 10. col. 786. lit. C. inquit: Libenter fatemur, omnes homines esse in statu peccati, & inutiles ad opera facienda, quæ Deo placeant, nisi prius per Dei gratiam reconcilientur. Atqui cap. 9. prolixe disputat, non renatos posse opus moraliter bonum & Deo placens præstare. Bellarmino adiungimus Costerum, qui itidem orthodoxe videtur loqui in Enchirid. pag. 204. Peccator, inquit, viribus suis non modo a peccato liberari non potest, sed neque ab illo potest resurgere, neque de peccato dolorem concipere, neque ad gratiam aut peccatorum remissionem se disponere, neque pie erga Deum affici, aut pio affectu de Christo vt redemtore suo, loqui sine diuina motione & gratia præueniente. Et p. 205. In homine peccatore tanta est intellectus cæcitas, tantaqs voluntatis & cordis duritia, vt nisi misericors gratia Dei præueniat, & mentem illustret, effectumq; moueat, nunquam ferio pœniteat, vel ad Deum reuertatur. Et iterum p. 206. Hanc Dei motionem appellant gratiam præuenientem & operantem, quod illam nullis meritis nostris exigentibus, nobisq; nihil agentibus, sed in peccato secure quiescentibus, Deus pro sua misericordia in nobis sine nobis operetur, cor moueat, & mentem illustet. Sic etiam orthodoxè videtur sentire Concil. Trident. can. 3. sess. 6. Si quis dixerit, sine præueniente Spiritus sancti inspiratione atque eius adiutorio hominem credere, sperare, diligere, aut pœnitere posse, anathema sit.

VII. 2. Libertatem arbitrii sequentibus adstruit. L. 5. c. 9. affirmat, posse hominem ex libero arbitrio opus moraliter bonum facere. C. 14. defendit, à quibus Scholasticis rectè esse dictum, quòd naturalia manserint integra. L. 4. c. 15. proponit simile de duobus vnum lapidem portantibus. L. 5. c. 11. & 12. disputat, homini post lapsum superesse liberum arbitrium in actionibus pijs & salutaribus. C 15. verè Pelagiana proponit axiomata, vt 1. Homo ante omnem gratiam liberum habet arbitrium, non solùm ad opera naturalia & moralia, sed etiam ad opera pietatis, & supernaturalia. 2. Habet homo ante omnem gratiam, potentiam remotam & imperfectam ad opera pietatis facienda. 3. Neque gratia excitans neque adiuvans, vllam imponit homini necessitatem, quò minus possit libere consentire aut dissentire Deo vocanti. 4. Conversio hominis ad Deum, vt etiam quodlibet aliud opus pium, quatenus opus, à libero arbitrio est tantùm, non tamen secluso auxilio generali; quatenus pium, à sola gratia est; quatenus opus pium, à libero arbitrio & gratia simul. L. 1. c. 13 in fine, constituit duplicem causam, cur duobus æqualiter excitatis vnus conuertatur, alter non item; vnam primam, Dei operationem; alteram secundariam, liberum arbitrium, quia hic libere consensit gratiæ excitanti, ille non item: cuius contrarium tamen paulò ante proposuit, in quo dissentientem habet Becanum disputat. de auxil. grat. par. 2. c. 7; L. 5. c. 13. contendit, rectè dictum esse ab Andradio, libertatem arbitrij esse causam efficientem applicationis voluntatis ad gratiam, & à Ruardo Tappero, arbitrium credendi esse in nostra potestate, & hominem post lapsum habere rectum lumen rationis, & mentem humanam multa per se intelligere, quæ ad cognitionem diuinarum rerum pertinent.

JIX. Haec igitur Bellarmini est sententia, quòd liberum arbitrium quoad supernaturalia non omninò sit amissum, sed duntaxat obfuscatum & alligatum, ita vt non possit in actum secundum deduci, nisi per praeuenientem gratiam soluatur. Hoc enim patet ex simili isto, quod his verbis proponit l. 6 c. 15. col. 918. B Simile aliquid experimur in potentia videndi : nam absente specie sensibili, habet homo potentiam & libertatem videndi, non enim ea species caussa est libertatis aut potentiae videndi, tamen potentia remota est, & libertas ligata, donec accepta specie potentia perficiatur, & in actum prodire possit. Hinc colligimus talem sententiam: Vt in homine est naturalis vis & potentia videndi, quæ perficitur objecto visibili, vt in actum prodeat: ita in arbitrio hominis post lapsum superest vis & potētia naturalis, ad benè operandum, siue ad conuersionem, quæ perficitur & in actum prodit, excitatâ motione & impulsu Dei, siue gratiâ internâ. Duas igitur partiales causas conuersionis constituit, gratiam Dei & voluntatem hominis, quòd apertè elucet ex illo simili à duobus viris, qui simul portant ingentem lapidem, quem vnus ferre non posset; vbi vterque concursum suum liberè adhibet, & si alter nolit concurrere, opus non fiet, l. 4. cap. 15. Imò primam, quoad prioritatem ordinis, causam in conuersione facit voluntatem humanam, dum eodem c. 15. difputat, voluntatem naturâ prius operari, quàm DEVM, ac proinde DEVM operari, quia voluntas operatur, non contrà; vnde hoc est consequens, vt Deus potiùs cooperari dicatur arbitrio, quàm arbitrium DEO.

IX. Eadem mens est Costeri, qui p. 203. Enchirid. ita scribit: Multa potest ex se naturáque suâ liberum arbitrium, non solùm ἀδιάφορα, quæ in vitijs & virtutibus non ponuntur, qualia sunt ambulare, sedere, emere, ninemere, hisque similia, sed moralia quoque virtutum opera. Nam cùm natura voluntatis bona sit, cur non velit, & operetur bonum, quàd-quidem omnis arbor bona fructus bonos facit? Rursus p. 211. Est hæc gratia in arbitrio voluntatis, vt ea vti possit, & non vti, retinere & abijcere; quemadmodum baculus in manu conualescēntis, cuius auxilio, si velit, vtetur; sin minus, poterit eum remouere. Addit prolixum simile, p. 211. de homine in latrones incidente, quod sic proponit: Sequenti similitudine, quæ ad parabolam accidit hominis, qui in latrones inciderat, res tota vtcunque illustrari posse videtur. Sit homo lethalibus vulneribus propè confectus, qui media hyeme in tenebris noctis, omni destitutus auxilio, & frigore rigidus ferè deficiat. Accedat amicus cum lumine; qui hominem semimortuum, desiderantem auxilium, & quantum in ipso est connitentem iumento imponat; in domum introducat; luculento igne refocillet, certisque medicamentis vulnera curet, curatum vtcunque; sed ex præcedenti morbo adhuc languentem, in calefacto cubiculo manere iubeat; atque vt incedat, scipionem porrigat; aliaque auxilia ad plenam perfectamque sanitatem consequendam præbeat. Hac similitudine intelligimus primò miseriam hominis peccatoris; qui destitutus calore gratiæ Dei totus alget, priuatus lumine diuino in densissimis versatur tenebris; multisque peccatis animam, omnesque potentias grauiter sauciatas habet, vt cuncta cogitatio eius prona sit ad malum. Secundò modum, quo ex his calamitatibus educitur; præueniente & accidente Deo cum lumine quodam gratiæ, quo intellectus fœditatem peccatorum, & Dei benignitatem aspiciens, illa detestare incipit, & ad hunc aspirare: voluntas etiam adiuta modis omnibus cooperatur; vt tantis exoneretur malis, libere tamen, quia non inuitus, sed cooperans sublatus est homo ille in iumentum. Adducto illo deinde in domum, apertis vulneribus infundatur ab amico oleum & vinum; præsentissima quædam pharmaca, nempè gratia iustificationis; quâ vulnera desinant esse lethalia, ad cuius infusionem nihil præterea agit homo sanctus, quàm vt vulnera detegat, & inguentum excipiat: quia remissionem peccatorum Deus solus in nobis operatur, nobis tantùm consentientibus, & gratiam atque iustitiam infusam excipientibus.

Tertiò quid gratia in homine iustificato efficiat ; nempe à periculo mortis æternæ liberat : intellectum lumine divino illustrat : calore charitatis voluntatem accendit : liberum arbitrium, cæterasque animæ potentias confirmat : totumque hominem prius iacentem, & externo ad resurgendum auxilio indigentem in pedes erigit, atq; ad ambulandum vires auxiliumque subministrat. Quarto dicimus , quonam modo præstet hæc omnia gratia Dei in homine iustificato , nempe non cogendo , nec imponendo necessitatem , sed suam ipsi relinquendo libertatem. Afficiet quipè hominis mentem , vt bonum agnoscat , & voluntatem vt bonum ei placeat, suauiter que trahit , sicut trahit sua quemque voluptas, sicut puer trahitur pomo (inquit D. Aug.) & (scut filius à parente munusculis & blandimentis ad literas discendas inducitur (vtest apud Methodium : ) liberum interim manet arbitrium , vt vel sequatur, vel non sequatur suadentem, afficientem , trahentem.

X. Porrò Costerus constra Bellarm: l. 6. c. 15. statuit p. 206. gratiam præuenientem non esse internam motionem & voluntatis inclinationem, sed duntaxat externum spiritus adhuc foris degentis impulsum, quem admittere vel reijcere homo liberè possit. Pag. 207. 208. ait : Liberum hominis arbitrium auxilio Dei necdum inhabitantis, sed mouentis & adiuuantis, se præparat ad iustificationem non solùm patiendo, sed etiam operando & agendo. Affert simile à lapso in foueam , & concludit his verbis. Ita liberum arbitrium, quod vitio suò in peccatum cecidit, vt de tenebricosâ foueâ peccati educatur , non suscipit tantùm, vel patitur, aut agitatur , sed cooperatur gratiæ Dei, præparat se credendo , pietatis officia assumendo , donec ad solem iustitiæ ascendentis diuino lumine gratiæ intùs repleatur. Vide ibidem plura , quæ omnia eò tendunt, quòd in potestate arbitrij sit ad gratiam se præparare, gratiam accipere vel reijcere, acceptam vel retinere vel dimittere , quæ vniuersa didicit ex Concilij Trident. can. 4. qui ita habet: Si quis dixerit liberum hominis arbitrium à Deo motum& excitatum, nihil cooperari assentiendo Deo excitanti atque vocatur, quo ad obtinendam iustificationis gratiam se disponat ac præparet, nec posse dissentire si velit, sed velut inanime quoddam nihil omnino agere, mereque passive se habere, anathema sit.

XI. Quamvis autem Concilium istud quoque mentionem faciat adjutorij Spiritus sancti & gratiæ præuenientis: hoc tamen ita poponitur ab Andradio & interpretibus, quod liberum arbitrium per peccatum quidem grave vulnus acceperit, verum non fct extinctum, & vt maximè non possit suâ vi & facultate sese erigere; tamen si à Deo moueatur extrinsecus per verbum posse illud assentiri & Deo cooperari. Vtitur autem Andradius hoc simili: Sicut ille, qui ferreis jo cis devinctus est habet quidem innatam incedendi δύναμιν seu potentiam, sed licet habeat illam, non tamen potest eâ vti, vt in actum prodeat, nisi priùs vincula rumpantur, quæ motum reprimunt & retardant: Ita peccati vinculis ligatum est liberum arbitrium, vt vires illas quas habet reliquas ad actiones spirituales efficiendas, non possit exerere, nisi à Deo moueatur & excitetur. Vbi verò accesserit motio & impulsus Spiritus sancti, quo vincula rumpantur & ligentur vulnera tùm δύναμιν illam sese exerere, & assentiri, adeoœ; cooperari Deo in inchoandis & efficiendis motibus spiritualibus. Adhibet porrò Andiadius similitudine ægroti, cuius vires morbo fractæ, debilitatę & attenuatæ sunt, vbi medicus vires reliquas confirmat roboratœ;, & amissas restituit. Alij gaudent similitudine auiculæ, quæ retinet quidē potentiã volandi, sed quando funiculo alligata est, nōpōtest vsum & motum illius facultatis, quæ naturaliter ipsi insita est, exercere: si quis aut rumpat funiculum, is non inserit aviculæ novam & peculiarem volandi δύναμιν, quam antea non habuerit, sed tant. impedimentum aufert. quod si ad negotium conuersionis accommodes, mox sequitur, gratiam diuinam non esse principem & primariam conuersionis causam efficientem, sed duntaxat conuersionem efficere per modum remouentis prohibens. Sicut.n. is non dicitur efficiens causa volatus, qui impedimentum remouit: ita & de conuersione hominis juxta Papistarum hypotheses judicari debet. Aliam adhuc similitudinem proposuit Andradius ab exustione igni sumtam: Si terogem inquit, cùm ligneam materiam conflagrare cernis, quæ sit conflagrationis illius efficiens causa, ignem dicas necesse est, vna cum Deo naturæ auctore & patrono, qui igni exurendi virtutem suppeditat, & ad operandum cum illo conspirat. Cùm igitur liberi nostri arbitrij motio, non magis a Dei gratia pendeat, quàm à diuina virtute stipulis exustio, quid est quòd liberum arbitrium efficientis causæ dignitate & nomine spolies? Ex quo inferimus: Sicut proxima & primaria exustionis causa ignis est, Deus verò nonnisi remota: ita conuersionis causam efficientem principalem esse arbitrium, non autem nisi remotam & generalem, ipsam Dei gratiam, quo quid magis Pelagianum dici posset?

XII. Summa igitur sententię Papisticæ hæc est, quòd liberum arbitrium non amiserit facultatem sese conuertendi ad Deum, sed quòd tantùm amissâ sit libera illius facultatis executio; quæ vinculis peccati impeditur. Quando autem gratia soluit istud vinculum, & hominem excitat, ibi tum liberum arbitrium spontè ad Deum se conuertere. Hæc sententia est Concilij Tridentini & Andradij, atque reliquorum, ex qua patet, liberum arbitrium vnicè causam conuersionis efficientem esse, si propriè loqui velimus, gratiamq; Dei non immediate efficere conuersionem, sed nihil aliud facere, quàm à vera causa efficiente, videlicet libero arbitrio impedimentum remouere. Quemadmodum enim qui tollit obstacula, non vere est causa efficiens motus, E. g. in lapide, super statua recumbente, sed ipsa lapidis forma est verum principium motus istius deorsum; qui verò impedimentum remouit, tantùm efficientem causam in actum produxit; non autem ipse motum effecit: Sic quoniam Deus ex sententia Pontificiorum nihil aliud per gratiam suam facit, quàm quòd à voluntate impedimentum remoueat, & in voluntate solâ situm ad Deum se conuertere vel non conuertere; sequitur certè; Deum proprie loquendo non esse causam conuersionis efficientem, nec conuersionem posse aut debere nominari opus Dei, cùm effectus tantùm efficienti proximæ & immediatæ, non autem remouenti prohibens primò ascribantur. Licèt igitur quædam pars efficientiæ in conuersione Deo possit ascribi, tamen longè plus viribus arbitrij erit assignandum, quippe quæ solæ sunt primum & immediatum conuersionis principium: vnde consequenter potiùs opus humanum, quam diuinum erit Conuersio, & longè plus sibi ipsi potest ascribere fidelis, quam Deo, siquidem in propriâ fuit facultate, post impedimentum remotum, sese ad Deum conuertere vel non conuertere. Et quantumuis hanc sententiam sæpè dissimulent; seŕ; aliud statuere velint videri; attamen si omnia ipsorum principia excusseris, nihil aliud quàm ipsissimum Pelagianismum sub istis verborum involucris & pigmentis occultatum fuisse deprehendes, id quod nunc secundâ quęstione demonstrare aggredimur.


### Question II

Are the Papists rightly numbered among the Pelagians?

XIII. The Romanists sometimes seem to fight and dispute quite sharply against the Pelagians, whose opinions, however, if you examine back and forth, you will find nothing other than the heresy of Pelagius beneath them, which, so that it may become more manifest, it pleases to note a certain collation of Papistic and Pelagian dogmas. But not at length shall I recount the history of the Pelagian controversy, which can be seen explained quite faithfully in the works of Mr. Chemnitz and Mr. Dr. Gerhard; but I wish to observe this one thing only, that a great distinction must be made between the earlier Pelagius, as some say, and the later.

XIV. For at the first time he was manifestly absurd and blasphemous, when he either simply denied that the grace of God and salvation were necessary, and on the contrary affirmed that the Gentiles were saved by the law of nature, or understood by grace nothing other than either the revelation of the divine will made manifest in the Word, or the very powers of the soul, freely given and granted. In all these things, however, he corrected his language, and began at the same time to defend the assistance of grace, and often spoke in such a way that Augustine said: It could be well understood, if it were not said by those whose meaning is known. For he began to speak thus: That grace assists the good purpose of man, yet does not instill the zeal for virtue into one who is unwilling and resisting; likewise, that the will is always assisted by grace in every work, concerning which see Augustine in his book De Haeresibus to Quodvultdeus, and in Enarrations on Psalm 107, book 1 of Retractations, chapters 9, 15, 23, and 42.

XV. Just as therefore Pelagius was as it were divided from himself, so also not undeservedly are two kinds of Pelagians established, some of whom imitate the earlier Pelagius, and can be called coarser, more open, and more stubborn Pelagians, such as were for the most part the Scholastics, among whom especially Biel, as also Andradius, both of whom granted such liberty to the will that they even assert that the Gentiles were saved by the law of nature: others imitate the later Pelagius, and can be named more cunning, more hidden, and more subtle Pelagians, by which epithets Augustine distinguished Caelestius from Pelagius in book 2 of De Gratia et Libero Arbitrio, chapter 12. And of the number of these are the modern Jesuits. Bellarmine, especially, and Costerus, who even if they very often have an orthodox tongue, always nevertheless retain a Pelagian and heterodox mind, so that it may truly be said of them what Irenaeus once said of the men of his own time, ὅμοια μὲν λαλοῦντες, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονοῦντες. Therefore, what was in use by almost all heretics, namely, to hold the same tongue with the orthodox but a mind entirely different, and conversely to hold the same mind with the heterodox but a different tongue, that is permitted to be observed even today among the Papists regarding this article. For I think it can be made clear from the following brief delineation and collation that they still retain the sinews of Pelagian doctrine.

XVI. 1. The Pelagians taught that free will is naturally in all men, and that it could not have perished through the sin of Adam. The Council of Trent defined the same in session 6, canon 5: If anyone shall say that the free will of man was lost and extinguished after the sin of Adam, etc., let him be anathema.

2. Pelagius taught, as witnessed by Augustine in the book on grace against Pelagius and Caelestius, chapter 18: We have the possibility of either part implanted by God, as a certain, if I may so say, fruitful and fecund root, which from the will of man may beget and bring forth diverse things, and which can, at the judgment of its own cultivator, either shine with the flower of virtues or bristle with the thorns of vices. Bellarmine holds the same opinion in book 5, chapter 9, where he asserts that it is situated in the power of man to perform some moral good: and all the remaining Jesuits think the same, who unanimously assert that a man can either receive or reject divine grace; and thus have the possibility of either part, just as Pelagius once spoke.

3. The Pelagians taught that exhortations would be useless if nothing had remained in man which correction could avail to excite: Hilary of Arles in his epistle to Augustine. Bellarmine uses the same argument against us in book 5, chapter 17: Clypeus, page 198.

4. The Pelagians taught that, once the doctrine of the Gospel is known, a man can complete the course by the powers of free will, Prosper on the ungrateful: Bellarmine holds the same opinion, book 6, chapter 15, Costerus, pages 210, 211.

5. The Pelagians taught that through the assertion of grace nothing is left to free will, but it is entirely destroyed, Prosper in his epistle to Ruffinus and on the ungrateful: All the Papists object the same, and Bellarmine especially, in the preface to his books on free will.

6. The Pelagians taught that free will can obey God when He calls. Prosper on the ungrateful. Bellarmine teaches the same, book 1, chapters 4 and 13, book 6, chapter 14, Costerus, 207, 208, and following.

7. The Pelagians taught: If nothing is attributed to free will in spiritual matters, the zeal and care for acting well is taken away. Bellarmine objects the same argument, book 5, chapters 15 and 17, Costerus, page 199.

8. The Pelagians taught that the commandments of God are easy and possible to be observed, Jerome in his epistle to Ctesiphon. Bellarmine teaches exactly the same, book 5, chapter 20.

9. The Pelagians taught that a threefold grace was given to man, of creation, of the preaching of the Gospel, and of regeneration, and that these graces always concur; but by the grace of creation they understood free will itself: Prosper in his epistle to Augustine on the remnants of the Pelagian heresy: The Papists teach the same, asserting that free will cooperates with God in regeneration or conversion. Bellarmine, book 6, chapters 13, 14, 15, Costerus, page 226.

10. The Pelagians taught that three causes concur in the conversion of man, namely the Word, the will, and the help of God, Prosper on the ungrateful: The Papists teach the same.

11. The Pelagians taught, especially Faustus, a Gallic Bishop in the year of Christ 500, that the aid of grace must be joined to human zeal and labor, which, being equally associated, might complete the remaining works; Maxentius against the epistle of Hormisdas. In the same way Bellarmine he says that the will cooperates with God, book 6, chapter 14, and book 4, chapter 15. And Costerus says: The will, assisted in all ways, cooperates.

12. The Pelagians placed the beginning of salvation in man, and preferred the human will to the divine, so that one is assisted because he willed, not that he wills because he is assisted. Prosper in his epistle to Augustine. Bellarmine approves this in book 4, chapter 15, where he says: From which it also follows that, although God and the will begin to work at the same moment of time and nature, nevertheless God works because the will works, not the contrary. And this is what others mean who say that the will works prior in nature to God, not by the property of the instant in which, but from which.

XVII. More points of comparison could be accumulated, but let these suffice, from which it is abundantly clear what a remarkable harmony and total agreement there is between the Pelagians and the Papists regarding the errors of free will, so much so that Pelagianism, long since dead and reduced to ashes, has in turn revived in the Papacy, and has recovered the obscene soul which it had breathed out in the time of Augustine and Prosper.

XIX. Nor is there any reason for you to object: Bellarmine and other Papists refute the Pelagians: how therefore can they be accused of Pelagianism? For the answer is at hand, that Bellarmine and the others do nothing else than refute the Pelagius of the first sort, as they call him, because he is too crude and open, and at first glance is an enemy of grace, but they greatly embrace the Pelagius of the second sort, because he is somewhat more subtle and hidden, while he does not at the very first sight profess himself an enemy of grace, but extols it with many words, meanwhile, however, ascribes such power to free will that there would be no efficacy of grace unless the will cooperated with it, that is, the Papists do not say that free will is sufficient to produce spiritual motions and actions, as the crasser Pelagians wished, yet they judge that to be necessary, and that no spiritual action can be perfected without the help of free will, which the more hidden and subtle Pelagians wished. What therefore those ascribed to free will alone, this the Papists assign not to free will alone, but together with divine grace, yet they attribute more to free will than to grace, which is evident from their comparisons; and from this maxim: That it is in the will of man either to accept or to reject offered grace. And because the acceptance of grace is nothing other than conversion, it follows that, because they accept grace solely from the powers of man left to him, the powers are the sole cause of conversion, which itself is the grossest Pelagianism.

Latin:

Num Pelagianis rectè annumerentur Pontificij?

XIII. COntra Pelagianos satis acriter pugnare & disputare aliquando videntur Romanenses, quorum tamen opiniones si vltrò citroŕue examinaueris, nihil aliud quam Pelagij hæresin sub illis inuenies, quod vt fiat manifestius, ideo quandam dogmatum Papisticorum & Pelagianorum collationem adnotare placet. Non autem prolixè certaminis Pelagiani historiam commemorabo, quæ videri potest apud Dn. Chemnitum & Dn. D. Gerhardum satis fideliter explicata; sed hoc vnicum duntaxat obseruari volo, quod maximè distingui debeat inter Pelagium priorem, vt nonnulli loquuntur, & posteriorem.

XIV. Primo enim tempore manifestè absurdus erat & blasphemus, quando aut simpliciter negabat, gratiam Dei ac salutem esse necessariam, & contra affirmabat, gentes per legem naturæ saluatas esse, aut per gratiam nihil aliud intelligebat, quàm vel reuelationem voluntatis diuinæ in verbo patefactæ, vel ipsas animæ potentias, gratis datas & concessas. In his autem omnibus correxit linguam, & cœpit simul gratiæ adiutorium defendere, & sæpè ita locutus est, vt Augustinus dixerit: Posset benè intelligi, si non ab istis, quorum sensus notus est, diceretur. Ita enim loqui cœpit, Gratiam adiuvare bonum hominis propositum, non tamen inuito & reluctandi studium virtutis immittere, item, voluntatem in omni opere à gratiâ semper adiuuari, de quo vide August. in lib. de hæres. ad Quod vult deum, & in Enarr. Ps. 107. libr. 1. Retractat. c. 9. 15. 23. & 42.

XV. Sicut igitur Pelagius fuit quasi à seipso divisus, ita quoque non immeritò duplices constituuntur Pelagiani, quorum aliqui Pelagium priorem imitantur, & dici possunt Pelagiani crassiores, apertiores, pertinaciores, quales ferè fuerunt Scholastici, ex quibus præsertim Biel, vt & Andradius, quorum vterque tantam voluntati concessit libertatem, vt etiam gentes lege naturæ saluatas fuisse asserant: alij, mirantur Pelagium posteriorem, & nominari queunt Pelagiani callidiores, occultiores subtiliores, quibus epithetis Augustinus Cælestium à Pelagio discernebat l. 2. de grat. & lib. arbitr. c. 12. Atqs ex horum numero sunt hodierni Iesu Witæ. Bellarminus præTertiim & Costerus, qui etiam si sæpissimè linguam habeant orthodoxam, semper tamen mentem retinent Pelagianam & heterodoxam, vt ita verè de ijs dici possit, quod Irenæus olim de sui temporis hominibus aiebat, ὅμοια μὲν λαλοῦντες, ἀνόμοια δὲ φρονοῦντες. Quod igitur penè omnibus hæreticis in vsu fuit, videlicet cùm orthodoxis eandem linguam, sed diuersam penitùs mentem & contra cùm heterodoxis eandem mentē, sed diuersam tenere linguam, id hodieque in Pontificijs quoad hunc articulum obseruare licet. Quod enim isti nervos doctrinæ Pelagianæ etiamnum retineant, ex subsequenti breui delineatione & collatione patere posse existimo.

XVI. 1. Pelagiani docebant, Omnibus hominibus liberum arbitrium naturaliter in esse, neque id per Adæ peccatum perire potuisse. Idem definiuit Concilium Tridentinum sess. 6. can. 5. Si quis liberum hominis arbitrium post Adæ peccatum amissum & extinctum esse dixerit, &c. anathema sit.

2. Pelagius docebat, teste Augustino l. de grat. contra Pelag. & Cælest. c. 18. Habemus possibilitatem vtriusque partis à Deo insitam, velut quandam, vt ita dicam radicem fructiferam atq; fœcundam, quæ ex voluntate hominis diuersa gignat & pariat, & quæ possit ad proprij cultoris arbitrium vel nitere flore virtutum vel sentibus horrere vitiorum Idem censet Bellarminus l. 5. cap. 9. vbi asserit, esse in potestate hominis situm, bonum aliquid morale perficere: & idem omnes reliqui sentiunt Iesu Witæ, qui vnanimiter asserunt, posse hominem gratiam diuinam vel accipere vel rejicere; & sic habere possibilitatem vtriusque partis, quemadmodum olim loquebatur Pelagius.

3. Pelagiani docebant, inutiles fore adhortationes; si nihil in homine remansisset, quod correctio valeat excitare: Hilarius Arelatensis in epist. ad August. Eodem argumento vtitur contra nos Bellarminus l. 5. c. 17: Clypeus p. 198.

4. Pelagiani docebant, cognita doctrina Euangelij, hominem liberi arbitrij viribus posse cursum perficere, Prosper de ingratis: Idem sentit Bellarminus l. 6. c. 15. Costerus p. 210. 211.

5. Pelagiani docebant, per gratiæ assertionem nihil relinqui libero arbitrio, sed prorsus deleri, Prosper in epist. ad Ruffinum & de ingratis: Idem omnes obijciunt Pontificij, & Bellarminus præsertim, in præfat. super libros de lib: arbitr.

6. Pelagiani docebant, liberum arbitrium posse obtemperare Deo vocanti. Prosper de ingratis. Idem docet Bellarminus l. 1. c. 4. & 13. l. 6. c. 14. Costerus 207. 208. seqq.

7. Pelagiani docebant: Si nihil tribuatur libero arbitrio in rebus spiritualibus, tollitur studium & cura bene agendi. Idem argumentum obijcit Bellarminus l. 5. c. 15. & 17. Costerus p. 199.

8. Pelagiani docebant, mandata Dei facilia, & obseruatu esse possibilia, Hieron. in epist. ad Ctesiphontem. Idem prorsus; docet Bellarminus l. 5. c. 20.

9. Pelagiani docebant, triplicem homini datam esse gratiam, creationis, prædicationis Euangelij & regenerationis, & has gratias semper concurrere? per creationis verò gratiam intelligebant ipsum liberum arbitrium: Prosper in epist. ad August. de reliquijs Pelagianæ hæresis: Idem docent Pontificij, asserentes liberum arbitrium in regeneratione seu conuersione cooperari Deo. Bellarm. l. 6. ca. 13. 14. 15. Costerus p. 226.

10. Pelagiani docebant, tres causas in conuersione hominis concurrere, nempe Verbum, voluntatem & auxilium Dei, Prosper de ingratis: Idem docent Pontificij.

11. Pelagiani docebant, Faustus præsertim, Episcopus Gallicus anno Christi 500. humano studio & labori adiungendum esse gratiæ adiutorium, quæ pariter sociata reliqua perficiant opera; Maxentius contra epist. Hormisdæ. Eodem modo Bellarminus ait, voluntatem cooperari Deo l. 6. cap. 14. & lib. 4. cap. 15. Et Costerus inquit: Voluntas adiuta modis omnibus cooperatur.

12. Pelagiani principium salutis in homine collocabant, diuinæque voluntati humanam præferebant, sic vt ideò quis adiuuetur, quia voluit, non ideò quia adiuuatur velit. Prosper in epist. ad August. Approbat hoc Bellarminus l. 4. c. 15. vbi ait: Ex quo etiam sequitur, vt licet in eodem momento temporis & naturæ Deus & voluntas operari incipiant, tamen Deus operatur, quia voluntas operatur, non contrà. Et hoc est quod alii qui dicunt, voluntatem prius naturâ operari quàm Deum, non proprietate instantis in quo sed à quo.

XVII. Plura possent membra collationis accumulari, sed hæc sufficiant, ex quibus abundè patet, quàm insignis harmonia, & omnimoda conuenientia sit inter Pelagianos & Papisticos de libero arbitrio errores, ita quidem, vt Pelagianismum dudum emortuum, & in cineres redactum, Papatu vicissim reuixisse, & animam obscenam, quam tempore Augustini & Prosperi efflauerat, recuperâsse.

XIX. Neque est, quod obijcias: Bellarminus & alij Pontificij refutant Pelagianos: quomodo igitur Pelagianismi accusari queunt? Responsio enim in promtu est, quòd Bellarminus & cæteri nihil aliud faciant, quàm quòd Pelagium prioristicum, quem vocant, quoniam nimis crassus & apertus, primâque fronte gratiæ inimicus est refutent, Pelagium vero posterioristicum maximè amplexantur, quoniam non nihil subtilior & occultior est, dum non primo statim aspectu se hostem gratiæ profitetur, sed eam verbis sat multis extollit, interim tamen tantam libero arbitrio vim asscribit, vt nulla foret gratiæ efficacia, nisi illi cooperaretur arbitrium, hoc est, Pontificij non dicunt liberum arbitrium sufficere ad motus & actiones spirituales efficiendas, quod volebant Pelagiani crassiores, attamen illud censent esse necessarium, & non posse vllam actionem spiritualem perfici sine ope liberi arbitrij, quod volebant Pelagiani occultiores & subtiliores, Quod igitur illi soli arbitrio libero asscrihebant, hoc Pontificij non soli arbitrio, sed vpâ gratiæ diuinæ assignant, plus tamen tribuunt arbitrio, quàm gratiæ, quod patet ex eorum similitudinibus; & hóc effato: In voluntate hominis esse, gratiam oblatam vel accipere vel reijcere. Et quia acceptatio gratiæ nihil est aliud, quàm conversio, sequitur, quia vnicè ex proprijs viribus accipiunt hominis gratiam vires relictas vnicam esse conuersionis causam, qui ipse est crassissimus Pelagianismus.


### Question III

XIX. Since it is primarily asked what free will can do in the conversion of man, it must be known above all what conversion is, and how it is taken. It is, however, nothing other than a certain spiritual motion, through which man is reborn and regenerated, and is turned to God, from whom he had been turned away. It is usually taken in 2 ways. 1. properly, for the spiritual change itself, by which man, because of sin entirely turned away from God, is turned to God through faith, apprehending the merit of Christ. 2. somewhat more broadly, for the continuation of conversion itself, and its daily increase: The subject of the former are sinful men, and children of wrath; but of the latter, regenerate men, yet stained by daily sins on account of the corruption of nature. For because even the righteous man sins often, therefore he always has need of resurrection, which occurs through conversion or repentance. This, however, is not properly a change of the man, because the reborn person is not turned away from God. When, therefore, he sins venially, he is not then converted anew, since he does not have an angry God, but merely perseveres in the conversion once made through the grace of God, and continues it, which continuation sometimes comes under the name of conversion itself. However, our discussion here is not primarily about conversion taken in such a way, since we willingly admit that in the daily repentance of the reborn, the will, because it has been liberated, can do much, not indeed of itself and its own nature, but because of the grace which it received in regeneration. For as Augustine speaks in book 3 of the Hypognosticon: The condition of a man not yet believing is one thing, and that of one already illuminated and repaired by grace is another.

XX. Therefore, the inquiry concerns that conversion which is the change of a man not yet reborn, while he turns himself from sin to God, from whom he is thus transferred from a state of wrath into a state of grace, which translation, as soon as it is made and as long as it lasts, the man is no longer called unconverted or to be converted, but already converted. This conversion is rightly named a change, since it contains all the requirements of a μεταβολῆς. For a subject is given, which is the man himself; a term from which is given, namely the slavery of sin and the state of wrath; a term to which is given, namely God and the state of grace. These terms are noted in Acts 14:15, where the Apostle says: We announce to you that you should turn from these vanities to the living God, who made heaven and earth: 1 Thess. 1:9. They report about you how you turned to God from idols. Acts 26:18. I send you to the Gentiles and peoples, that you may open their eyes, that they may be turned from darkness to light, and from the power of the Devil to God. 1 Pet. 2:25. You were like wandering sheep, but you have been turned to the Shepherd and guardian of your souls.

XXI. But a man is converted to God through consisting in true confidence of heart. For when he has acknowledged sins from the law, and in them does not despair, but seeks Christ the Physician, and apprehends him with true faith; then he is converted, and as it were born again. Here, however, it is soon disputed concerning the origin of these motions, and it is debated what is the efficient cause that a man may then will, and then be able to believe, to assent to the word, to love God, etc. For conversion is an illumination of the mind, a rectification of the will and heart, indeed in such a way that he whose intellect previously could not grasp divine mysteries, now grasps them, and not only grasps them, but also assents to them, when previously he had not even wished to assent, and much less had been able, so that the will which was turned away from God and Christ, may love him, and apprehend him with true confidence. It is asked, therefore, what is the cause, illuminating the mind of man, rectifying the will, renewing the heart and all the powers of the soul, and freeing it from the servitude of sin?

XXII. Here we answer that the one, solitary, and sufficient cause of all these things is the grace of God working, drawing, moving, illuminating, and rectifying through the word. For the mind does not illuminate itself, but is illuminated by God; the will does not rectify itself, but is rectified by God; the heart and the remaining powers do not renew themselves, but are renewed by God. The Papists, however, define conversion far otherwise, and therefore they also assign a far different cause of conversion.

XXIII. For to them conversion is not an illumination of the darkened mind, a rectification of the averted will, and a renewal of the depraved heart, but they think that a light naturally adheres in the mind, by which it can assent to the mysteries of faith, that in the will there is present δύναμιν, by which it can apprehend Christ with true confidence, and love God above all things, but that this light is merely eclipsed by sin, and that this δύναμιν is merely bound and hindered by the fall: when therefore by grace the density of sins is removed, which prevents [the light], into whose shadow the light of the intellect runs, and consequently was obscured, when likewise the bond of the fall is taken away, binding the will, there then the mind is able to believe from its own powers, the will is able to love God from its own powers, and to apprehend the merit of Christ, and therefore to cooperate strenuously with grace, which is added to the natural light of the mind and the innate δύναμις of the will.

XXIV. That this opinion is entirely erroneous, the Orthodox rightly assert: For through sin there was lost not only the second act of intellectual light, not only the second act of rectitude in the will, which the Papists say, but also the first act itself, that is, that very innate habit, that very δύναμις and power, innate in creation, by which man was always able to believe God, [to believe] in God, and to love Him, although the second act was not present: This, I say, power was also lost, and a contrary evil habit succeeded, that depraved and most tenaciously inherent concupiscence. For far greater is spiritual blindness and corruption than natural; for by the latter the power of seeing itself is not taken away, although the second act is taken away, but by the former, not only the second act, but the power and δύναμις itself was taken away at the same time, indeed in such a way that not only does man not see, but he cannot even actively see or wish regarding spiritual things. Therefore, through conversion and regeneration, no bond is loosened by which the power of believing and loving had been bound, so that it could not be brought into act, but both the act of believing itself, and the power of believing, is given and infused by God, with man contributing absolutely nothing from his own powers to his own conversion. Thus, therefore, we deny free will entirely, The Papists, however, take away only half, and ἡμίσει γὰρ ὅλων, from grace, and leave nothing but a μερικὸν, whence this συνέργεια arises.

XXV. Luther rightly opposed this Synergism, and correctly asserted that man in conversion behaves himself merely παθητικῶς or passively, not ἐνεργητικῶς or actively, that is, he is only the subject which is converted, not the efficient cause which converts itself. For the mind is blind, how then can it be the efficient cause of its own illumination? The will is turned away, how then can it convert itself? It is a slave, how then can it free itself? It is sick, how then can it heal itself? It is dead, how then can it quicken itself? Therefore, the will contributes nothing, absolutely nothing, and not even a little bit or a very small amount, for which Erasmus was fighting in his diatribe, to the effecting of its own regeneration, whence it follows that it behaves itself only passively and subjectively, but not operatively or cooperatively.

XXVI. Nor, however, can it be inferred from this by legitimate consequence that man is like an ἀψύχου, a log, who is converted as if unknowingly and violently, which calumny the Papists attribute to us, as is evident from Coster's Enchiridion, page 215, writing thus: The Lutherans teach that in the matter of justification the will of man is moved by God like a log, so that it only suffers, and does nothing at all, namely that the sinner is so converted by God to a sounder mind that he necessarily follows the divine motion, and cannot not follow, in almost the same way in which a sheep by natural instinct follows green turnip tops, and a dog is carried to bones. But let it be an injury to us, since we ourselves confess and teach that there is the greatest difference in this respect between a log and a man. For 1. a log, being irrational, lacking mind and will, is in no way a subject capable of conversion: but man by the yielding operation of the Holy Spirit can be converted and regenerated. For we do not hold the opinion of the Manichaeans, who imagined that certain men were generated from ὕλῃ, and were ἀλύτους and unredeemable, in such a way that even if the efficacy of the Spirit is present, they nevertheless cannot be converted on account of the magnitude of their corruptions, unless their nature is utterly destroyed: we do not, I say, hold this opinion, but rather assert the contrary, maintaining that man is a sufficiently suitable ὑποκείμενον for conversion, regarding which some Fathers seem to have asserted free will, when in fact they do nothing of the sort. In this sense Bernard said: Take away free will, there will be nothing to be saved; take away grace, there will be nothing from which it may be saved. For this is certain, that no one is saved unless he has free will, that is, mind and will, as Augustine truly wrote in book 3 against Julian, chapter 4. The grace of GOD through JESUS CHRIST our LORD is not offered to stones or wood or cattle; for they lack the subjects, namely mind and will, in which GOD is accustomed to act in the ordinary way through the Word and Sacraments, and in which it is necessary for conversion to take place. We therefore willingly grant that man, because he is a rational creature, can be converted, which they call a passive ἱκανότητα or power: but when he is actually converted, the cause is not within man, but outside of him, since he is utterly destitute of active power.

XXVII. 2. Moreover, a stone and a log lack this aptitude, by which it might be able to hear the word, the hearing of which is nevertheless most necessary for conversion. For God does not convert by a violent and Enthusiastic rapture, nor by such an impulse as was in Balaam, Num. 23, who against his will blessed the people of God, or such as was in Caiaphas, who prophesied while ignorant, John 11, v. 51, or such as in the ass of Balaam, which by a miracle rebuked its rider Num 22. v. 28. but God converts the hearts of men mediately through his word, which he wills to be read and heard. Such reading and ἀκρόασις, however, does not fall to a log, but is proper to man, and thus the log is destitute both of passive suitability, regarding the very reception of conversion, and of active suitability, regarding the χρῆσιν or employment of the means necessary for conversion. XXIIX. 3. Man has that δύναμιν, so that having heard the word he can resist, and struggle against the grace annexed to the word, as it is said in Matt. 23. 37. How often would I have gathered your children, and you would not. Such repugnance in no way falls to a lifeless and utterly inanimate log, whence it appears again that there is the greatest difference between man and a log. XXIX. 4. The will, moved and aided by the Holy Spirit, does not receive an impression, like a log or a stone, but begins to will and to work, so that immediately a difficult struggle arises between the flesh and the spirit, which is described in Rom. 7. v. 15. Gal. 5. v. 17. Such a struggle, however, is not, nor can it be, in a log. And it suffices to have proposed these things concerning our opinion: we proceed to the correct formulation of the state of the question itself.

Latin:

XIX. Cùm principaliter quæratur, quid possit arbitrium in conversione hominis, ante omnia sciendum, quid sit Conversio, & quomodo sumatur, Est autem nihil aliud, quàm motus quidam spiritualis, per quem homo renascitur & regeneratur, atque ad Deum, à quo auersus erat, convertitur. Solet autê 2. modis accipi. 1. propriè, pro ipsâ mutatione spirituali, quà homo propter peccatum omninò auersus à Deo, per fidem, Christi meritum apprehendentem ad Deum convertitur. 2. nonnihil latiùs, pro ipsâ simul conuersionis continuatione, & quotidiana adauctione: Illius subiectum sunt homines peccatores, filijque iræ; huius verò homines renati, quotidianis tamen peccatis, ob naturæ corruptionem, maculati, Quia enim & iustus peccat sæpiùs, proinde opus semper habet resurrectione, quæ fit per conversionem seu pœnitentiam. Hæc autem non est propriè mutatio hominis, quia renatus non est auersus à Deo. Cùm igitur peccat venialiter, tunc non de nouo conuertitur, siquidem non habet iratum Deum, sed duntaxat in conuersione, semel facta, per gratiam Dei perseuerat, eamque continuat, quæ continuatio quandoque ipsius conversionis nomine venit. Nobis autem de taliter sumtâ conuersione hîç primò non est sermo, cùm lubenter fateamur, quod in quotidiana renatorum pœnitentia arbitrium, quia liberatum est, multum possit, non quidem ex se & suâ naturâ, sed ob gratiam, quam in regeneratione accepit. Nam vt Augustinus lib. 3. hypognost. loquitur: Alia est ratio hominis nondum credentis, & alia iam illuminati & reparati per gratiam.

XX. De illa igitur conuersione quæritur, quæ est mutatio hominis non renati, dum à peccato se conuertit ad Deum, à quo ita è statu iræ transfertur in statum gratiæ, quæ translatio quamprimum facta est & quamdiu durat, non dicitur homo ampliùs non conuersus vel conuertendus, sed iam conuersus. Rectè autem ista conuersio nominatur mutatio, siquidem omnia μεταβολῆς requisita continet. Datur enim subiectum, quod est ipse homo; datur terminus à quo nempe seruitus peccati, & status iræ; datur terminus ad quem, nimirum Deus & status gratiæ. Termini hi notantur Act. 14. 14. vbi Apostolus inquit: Annunciamus vobis, vt ab istis vanis conuertamini ad Deum viuum, qui fecit cœlum & terram: 1. Thessal. 1. 9. Ipsi de vobis annunciant, quomodo conuersi fueritis ad Deum à simulacris. Act. 26. 18. Mittote in gentes & populos, vt aperias oculos eorum, vt conuertantur à tenebris ad lucem, & à potestate Diaboli ad Deum. 1. Petr. 2. 25. Eratis velut oues errantes, sed conuersi estis ad Pastorem, & curatorem animarum vestrarum.

XXI. Conuertitur autem homo ad Deum persdem in verâ cordis fiducia consistentem. Cùm enim ex lege agnouit peccata, in iiśque non desperat, sed quærit Medicum Christum, verâque fide apprehendit; tum conuertitur, & quasi de neuo generatur. Hîc autem mox controuertitur istorum motuů origine, & disceptatur, quæ sit causa efficiens, vt homo tùm velit, tùm possit credere, verbo assentire, Deum diligere &c. Conuersio enim est illuminatio mentis, rectificatio voluntatis & cordis, ita quidem, vt qui intellectus anteà non poterat capere mysteria diuina; ea iam capiat, & non solum capiat, sed etiam ijs assentiatur, cùm anteà ne quidem assentiri voluerit, & multò minus potuerit, vt voluntas quæ aversa erat à Deo & Christo, eum diligat, & verâ fiduciâ apprehendat. Quæritur ergò, quæ sit causa, mentem hominis illuminans, voluntatem rectificans, cor & omnes animæ potentias renouans, & à seruitute peccati liberans?

XXII. Hîc respondemus, vnicam, solitariam & sufficientem horum omnium causam esse gratiam Dei per verbum operantis, trahentis, mouentis, illuminantis & rectificantis. Non enim mens seipsam illuminat, sed illuminatur à Deo; voluntas non seipsam rectificat, sed rectificatur à Deo; cor & reliquæ potentiæ non semetipsas renouant, sed renouantur à Deo, Pontificij verò longe aliter & definiunt conuersionem, ideoque & longè aliam assignant conuersionis causam.

XXIII. Ipsis enim conuersio non est illuminatio mentis obtenebratæ, rectificatio voluntatis auersæ, & renouatio cordis deprauati, sed putant in mente naturaliter hærere lumen, quo possit mysterijs fidei assentiri, in voluntate adesse δύναμιν, quâ possit verâ fiduciâ Christum apprehendere, & Deum super omnia diligere, istud verò lumen per peccatum duntaxat esse eclipsatum, istam δύναμιν per lapsum duntaxat esse ligatam & impeditam: quando igitur per gratiam præuenientem remouetur densitas peccatorum, in quorum vmbram incurrit lumen intellectus, & consequenter obscurabatur, quando item tollitur vinculum lapsus, voluntatem ligans, ibi tùm mentem ex proprijs viribus posse credere, voluntatem ex proprijs viribus posse Deum diligere, & meritum Christi apprehendere, adeoque gratiæ, quæ accedit ad naturale mentis lumen & insitam voluntatis δύναμιν, strenuè cooperari.

XXIV. Hanc verò sententiam prorsus esse erroneam, rectè asserunt Orthodoxi: Per peccatum enim amissus est non solùm actus secundus luminis intellectualis, nòn solùm actus secundus rectitudinis in voluntate, quod dicunt Pontificij, sed etiam ipse actus primus, hoc est, Ille ipse ingenitus habitus, illa ipsa δύναμις & potentia, in creatione innata, quâ semper potis erat homo credere Deo, Deum, & in Deum, eumque diligere, quanquam actus secundus non aderat: Hæc, inquam, potentia etiam amissa est, & contrarius successit malus habitus, praua illa & tenacissimè inhærens concupiscentia. Longè enim maior est cæcitas & corruptio spiritualis, quàm naturalis; hâc enim non tollitur ipsa potentia videndi, licèt actus secundus tollatur, istâ verò, non solùm actus secundus, sed ipsa simul potentia & δύναμις sublata fuit, ita quidem, vt non solùm homo non videat, sed ne quidem actiuè videre possit aut velit quoad spiritualia. Per conuersionem igitur & regenerationem non soluitur vinculum aliquod, quo potentia credendi & diligendi reuincta fuerit, quò minùs in actum potuerit deduci, sed & ipse actus credendi, & potentia credendi à Deo datur & infunditur, homine nihil omninò ex proprijs viribus ad sui conuersionem conferente. Sic ergò nos ex asse negamus liberum arbitrium, Pontificii verò tantùm ex semisse, atque ἡμίσει γὰρ ὅλων adimunt gratiæ, & non nisi μερικὸν relinquunt, unde συνέργεια ista exoritur.

XXV. Huic Synergiæ meritò Lutherus se opposuit, & rectè asseruit, quòd homo in conuersione habeat se merè παθητικῶς vel passiuè, non ἐνεργητικῶς vel actiuè, hoc est, sit tantùmmodò subiectum, quod conuertitur, non causa efficiens, quæ seipsam conuertat. Cæca enim mens est, quomodo igitur suæ illuminationis causa efficiens esse possit? auersa est voluntas, quomodo igitur seipsam conuertat? serua est, quomodo seipsam liberet? ægrota est, quomodo seipsam sanet? mortua est, quomodo seipsam viuificet? Nihil proinde, nihil omnino, & ne modiculum quidem aut perpusillum, pro quo Erasmus pugnabat in suâ diatribe, confert voluntas ad sui regenerationem efficiendam, vnde sequitur, illam sese duntaxat habere passiuè & subiectiuè, non autem operatiuè, vel cooperatiuè.

XXVI. Neque tamen hinc legitimâ consequentiâ inferri potest, quòd homo instar ἀψύχου, trunci sit, qui quasi nesciens & violentè conuertatur, quam calumniam nobis affingunt Pontificii, vt patet ex Costeri Enchirid. pag. 215. ita scribentis: Lutherani docent in negotio iustificationis moueri voluntatem hominis à Deo instar stipitis, vt patiatur tantùm, & nihil quicquam agat, nimirùm peccatorem ita à Deo ad seniorem mentem conuerti, vt diuinam motionem necessariò sequatur, nec possit non sequi, ad eum ferè modum, quo ouis naturali instinctu rapusculum viridem sequitur, & canis fertur ad ossa. Verùm sit nobis iniuria, siquidem fatemur ipsi & docemus, maximam quoad truncum & hominem hac in parte differentiam esse. Nam 1. truncus, quippe irrationalis, carens mente & voluntate, nullo modo habile ad conuersionem subiectum: Homo verò accedente Spiritus Sancti operatione conuerti & regenerari potest. Nec enim sentimus cum Manichæis, qui quosdam homines ex ὕλῃ generatos, finxerunt ἀλύτους & irredemtibiles, ita quidem vt etiamsi efficacia Spiritus adsit, tamen ob summam corruptionum conuerti nequeant, nisi natura eorum penitùs destruatur: non, inquam, ita sentimus, sed contrarium potiùs asserimus, statuentes hominem satis idoneum conuersionis esse ὑποκείμενον, quò respicientes nonnulli Patres videntur liberum arbitrium asseruisse, cùm tamen nihil minus faciant. Hoc sensu dixit Bernhardus: Tolle liberum arbitrium, non erit, quod saluetur, tolle gratiam, non erit, vnde saluetur. Hoc enim certum est, neminem saluari, nisi qui habet liberum arbitrium, hoc est mentem & voluntatem, cùm verè scripserit Augustinus l. 3. contra Iulianum cap. 4. Gratia DEI per IESVM CHRISTVM DOMINVM nostrum non lapidibus aut lignis pecudibusque præstatur; carent enim subiectis, mente scilicet & voluntate in quibus DEVS ordinario modo per Verbum & Sacramenta agere solet, & in quibus necesse est fieri conuersionem. Damus ergò lubenter, hominem, quia rationalis creatura est, conuerti posse, quam ἱκανότητα vel potentiam vocant passiuam: cùm autem actu conuertitur, causa non est intra hominem, sed extra ipsum, quoniam actiuâ potentiâ prorsus destituitur.

XXVII. 2. Caret insuper lapis truncusque hâc aptitudine, quâ possit audire verbum, cuius tamen auditus ad conuersionem maximè est necessarius. Non enim raptu violento & Enthusiastico Deus conuertit, neque tali impulsu, qualis erat in Bileamo. Num. 23. qui inuitus benedicebat populo Dei, vel qualis erat in Caiphâ, qui ignorans prophetabat Ioh. 11. v. 51. vel qualis in asinâ Bileami, quæ per miraculū redarguebat sessorem suum Num 22. v. 28. sed conuertit Deus corda hominum mediatè per verbum suum, quod vult legi & audiri. Talis verò lectio & ἀκρόασις non cadit in truncum, sed homini propria est, atque ita destituitur truncus tùm idoneitate passiua, quoad ipsam conuersionis receptionem, tum idoneitate actiua, quoad mediorum ad conuersionem necessariorum χρῆσιν vel vsurpationem. XXIIX. 3. Habet homo δύναμιν istam, vt audito verbo possit resistere, & gratiæ verbo annexæ reluctari, sicut dicitur Matth. 23. 37. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, & vos noluistis. Talis repugnantia in ἄψυχον & prorsus inanimatum truncum nullo modo cadit, vnde rursus apparet, maximam inter hominem & truncum esse differentiam. XXIX. 4. Voluntas mota & adiuta à Spiritu sancto non recipit impressionem, sicuti truncus vel lapis, sed incipit velle, & operari, ita vt statim difficilis lucta inter carnem & spiritum oriatur, quæ describitur Rom. 7. v. 15. Gal. 5. v. 17. Talis verò lucta non est, nec esse potest in trunco, Atque hæc de nostra sententia proposuisse sufficit : ad ipsum statum rectè formandum pergimus.


### Question IV

XXX. Here the τὰ μὴ ζητούμενα must be removed, and then the true ζητόμενον must be annexed. Therefore it is not asked 1. concerning the power of the vegetative, sensitive, and locomotive soul, whether in these there is any liberty regarding natural actions, as Valla argues, whether it is in the power of man to move his foot, either the right or the left? In the Dialogues of Jerome, does the Pelagian say: If I wish to bend my finger, will special help from God always be necessary for me? In Augustine, On the perfection of justice, Caelestius objects to the passage of Paul 1 Cor. 7 concerning the freedom of marrying, Let him do what he wills. But Augustine rightly answers: As if it were to be held as a great thing, to wish to marry, when the help of divine mercy is being more laboriously disputed? For the present controversy is not about external acts, but about the conversion of man.

XXXI. 2. The question is not about the substance of the rational soul itself, whether it has some power of judgment in the mind, and of choice in the will, in which sense Augustine said in his book On Grace and Free Will, ch. 2: There is therefore free will, which whoever denies to exist, is not a Catholic.

XXXII. 3. The question is not, whether the mind and will are free to sin, that is, whether they sin freely, not forcedly, not by simple necessity. For no one has denied this, in which sense many sayings of the Fathers are alleged by Chemnitz, part 1, Examination, p. 114, side b. For man has free will in evil, as Augustine speaks in his book Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, ch. 2. And ch. 15 he says: There is always free will in us, but it is not always good; for it is either free from righteousness, when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin, when it serves righteousness, and then it is good.

XXXIII. 4. The question is not, whether man has freedom in external things, and in contracts; whether he can in some way act according to virtue? For this has been denied by no one, whence Prosper says in book 1 On the Calling of the Gentiles, ch. 3: The judgment of the will has been depraved, not taken away: And hence Justin, Apology 2, posits three kinds of those things which are moved: For some are moved without judgment, just as a stone is moved downwards; some are moved by judgment, but not free, as a sheep seeing a wolf judges that it must be fled from by natural instinct, not by deliberation, nor can it choose whether it wishes not to flee: but man through an intelligent power judges that something must be fled from or pursued: And because he chooses actions by a certain comparison of reason, not like a sheep, therefore he is called free will. This free will, however, does not extend further than to external works, which in a certain way are in agreement with the law by reason of themselves: for man can either perform or omit these according to his own judgment, as is evident from Rom. 2. v. 14, 15, & Philip. 3. v. 6, where Paul says that before his conversion, according to the righteousness which is in the law, he had been blameless in his conduct.

XXXIV. 5. The question is not concerning the state of integrity, since it is conceded that man was of free will in that state: nor concerning the state of reparation or restoration after conversion has taken place: that the will is free for all at that time, in so far as it has been liberated, no one denies, provided it be observed that that cooperation of the will proceeded not from nature, but from grace: Much less is there any discussion concerning liberty in the state of glorification; for then we shall truly be free, because perfectly liberated.

XXXV. 6. The question is not, Can a man freely hear the word of God, or not hear it; read it, or not read it? For that this is certain can be proved to many from examples in Scripture, whence Augustine says in his work on faith to Peter, chapter 32: Hold most firmly, and doubt in no way, that a man, whom neither ignorance of letters nor any weakness or adversity prevents, can indeed either read the words of the Law and the Gospel or hear them from the mouth of a preacher; but that he may also perceive with an attentive heart what he hears, and, with a good will received from God, may do and will and be able to do it, no one can, except him whom God has anticipated with His grace.

XXXVI. 7. The question is not, Can one who has been educated for a long time in the Church, and informed in it and by it, acquire for himself a certain theoretical and historical knowledge of the faith through the powers of the will? since the examples of heretics clearly prove that this can be done. But it is concerning the unbelieving man, and one situated outside the assembly of the Church, that the dispute is here primarily and chiefly held. For in such a person it is most conspicuous what free will is will is like, and what powers it possesses of itself after the fall.…

XXXVII: 8. It is not asked: Whether conversion happens without the motion of the mind and the action of the will? For we ourselves concede that no one can understand, think, or judge anything without mind and intellect, and without will no one can desire, seek, attempt, or struggle. For many things, says Augustine, men do unwillingly, but no one can believe unless he is willing. Therefore, in the very conversion itself, and in the beginning of conversion, the mind thinks; and by thinking it assents, the will desires, and by desiring it believes. However, the question is: what illuminates the intellect so that it may understand divine things? What rectifies the will so that it may believe piously and sincerely? The Papists answer: both nature and grace. Our side says: nature provides this in no way, but grace alone.

XXXIIX. Hence, therefore, this true and genuine state of the controversy emerges: Whether a man not yet reborn, when he is stirred by divine prevenient grace, has in himself any powers, or the faculty, of assenting to and cooperating with God in spiritual motions and actions? Or, which is the same thing: What is the cause, or what is it that makes the intellect, averted from God, assent to the word of God, and the will, resisting God, believe God and in God? The Papists assign two partial causes, free will and grace: Our side acknowledges only one, namely grace, since the mind and will of man after the fall have no powers to assent to God or to cooperate in spiritual matters, which we now undertake to demonstrate more fully.

Latin:

XXX. Remouenda hîc sunt τὰ μὴ ζητούμενα, & deinde annectendum erit verum ζητόμενον. Non ergo quæritur 1. de potentia animæ vegetatina, sensitiua, & locomotiua, an in ijs quoad actiones naturales sit aliqua libertas, sicut valla disputat, Num sit in hominis arbitrio mouere pedem, vel dextrum vel sinistrum? In Dialogis Hieronymi Pelagian? dicit: Si voluero curuare digitum, an semper mihi necessarium erit speciale Dei auxilium? Apud August. de perfect. iustitiæ, Cœlestinus obijcit locum Pauli 1. Cor. 7. de libertate nubendi, Faciat quod vult. Augustinus verò rectè respondet: Quasi pro magno habendum sit, velle nubere, vbi de adiutorio diuinæ misericordiæ operosiùs disputatur? Nec enim de externis actibus, sed de conuersione hominis præsens controuersia est.

XXXI. 2. Non quæritur de ipsâ animæ rationalis substantiâ, an habeat potestatem aliquam iudicij in mente, & electionis in voluntate, quo sensu Augustinus dixit l. de grat. & lib. arbit. c. 2. Est igitur liberum arbitrium, quod quisquis esse negauerit, Catholitus non est.

XXXII. 3. Non quæritur, An mens & voluntas liberæ sint ad peccandum, hoc est, liberè, non coactè, non simplici necessitate peccent. Nemo enim hoc negauit, quem in sensum multa allegantur dicta Patrum à Chemnitio part. 1. Exam. m. p. 114. fac. b. Habet enim homo in malo liberum arbitrium, vt loquitur Augustinus l. contra duas epist. Pelagian. cap. 2. Et c. 15. ait: Semper est in nobis voluntas libera, sed non semper est bona; Aut enim à iustitiâ libera est, quando seruit peccato, & tunc est mala; aut à peccato libera est, quando seruit iustitiæ, & tunc est bona.

XXXIII. 4. Non quæritur, An homo habeat libertatem in externis rebus, & in contractibus; An possit quodammodò secundùm virtutem agere? Hoc enim à nemine negatum fuit, vnde Prosper dicit l. 1. de vocat. gent. c. 3. Iudicium voluntatis deprauatum, non ablatum est: Atque hinc Iustinus apolog. 2. tria eorum, quæ mouentur, genera ponit: Quædam enim mouentur sine iudicio, sicut lapis mouetur deorsum; quædam mouentur iudicio, sed non libero, vt ouis videns lupum, iudicat eum fugiendum ex naturali instinctu, non ex deliberatione, nec potest eligere, an velit non fugere: homo verò per potentiam intelligentem iudicat aliquid fugiendum vel prosequendum: Et quia ex collatione quadam ratione eligit actiones, non vt ouis, ideò dicitur liberi arbitrij. Hoc autem liberum arbitrium latiùs non extenditur quàm ad externa opera, cum lege, ratione sui, quodammodo convenientia: hæc enim pro arbitratu suo potest homo vel efficere, vel omittere, vt patet ex Rom. 2. v. 14 15. & Philip. 3. v. 6. vbi Paulus inquit, se ante conversionem suam, secundum iustitiam, quæ in lege est, conversatione fuisse sine querela.

XXXIV. 5. Non quæritur de statu integritatis, quippe in quo fuisse hominem liberi arbitrij, conceditur: nec de statu reparationis vel restaurationis post factam conversionem : Liberam omni tunc esse voluntatem, in quantum liberata est, nemo inficiatur, modò observetur, illam voluntatis cooperationem non à natura, sed gratia provenisse: Multò minùs sermo est de libertate in statu glorificationis; tùm enim verè erimus liberi, quia perfectè liberati.

XXXV. 6. Non quæritur, An homo possit audire verbum Dei liberè, vel non audire; illud legere, vel non legere? Hoc enim certum esse multis probari potest è Scripturæ exemplis, vnde Augustinus inquit de fide ad Petrum cap. 32. Firmissimè tene, & nullatenus dubites, posse quidem hominem, quem nec ignorantia literarum, nec aliqua prohibet imbecillitas vel adversitas, verba Legis & Evangelij sive legere, sive ex prædicatoris ore audire; sed vt, quod audit, attento corde eiam percipiat, & accepta divinitus bona voluntate faciat & velit & possit, neminem posse, nisi quem Deus gratia sua prævenerit.

XXXVI. 7 Non quæritur, An qui diu in Ecclesia educatus, & in ea & ab ea informatus, theo-ricam quandam & historicam fidei cognitionem per vires arbitrij sibi possit comparare? cùm id fieri posse, exempla hæreticorum luculenter comprobent. De homine autem infideli & extra Ecclesiam cœtum constituto, hîc vnâ, & potissimùm disputatur. In tali enim maximè conspicuum est, quale sit liberum ararbitrium, & quasnam ex sese post lapsum vires obtineat.

XXXVII: 8. Non quæritur; An conuersio fiat sine motu mentis, & actione voluntatis? Ipsi enim concedimus, neminem sine mente & intellectu aliquid posse intelligere, cogitare aut iudicare, sine voluntate neminem desiderare, expetere, conari, luctari. Multa enim, inquit Augustinus, homines nolentes agunt, sed credere nisi volens nemo potest. Ergo in ipsâ simul conuersione, & conuersionis inchoatione mens cogitat; & cogitando assentitur, voluntas desiderat, desiderando credit. In quæstione autem est, quidnam illuminet intellectum, vt diuina intelligat? quidnam rectificet voluntatem, vt piè & sincerè credat? Pontificij respondent, & naturam & gratiam : Nostri dicunt, nullo modo id præstare naturam, sed vnicè gratiam.

XXXIIX. Hinc igitur verus & genuinus controuersiæ status emergit iste : An homo nondum renatus, quando excitatur gratiâ diuinâ præueniente habeat in se vires aliquas, siue facultatem Deo assentiendi & cooperandi in motibus & actionibus spiritualibus? Vel; quod idem est; Quænam sit causa, vel quidnam faciat, vt intellectus à Deo auersus assentiatnr verbo Dei, & voluntas Deo renitens, credat Deo & in Deum? Pontificij duas assignant causas partiales, arbitrium & gratiam: Nostri non nisi vnam agnoscunt, nimirum gratiam, siquidem mens & voluntas hominis post lapsum nullas habet vires Deo assentiendi, vel in spiritualibus cooperandi, quod nunc fusiùs demonstrare aggredimur.


### Question V. By what arguments can the true opinion concerning free will be defended?

XXXIX. The bondage of the will regarding the conversion of man and other spiritual acts can be proven, partly from Scripture; partly by reasons drawn from the analogy of faith; partly by the testimonies both of the Fathers and of the adversaries themselves. Many sayings can be drawn forth to this effect from the Scriptures, all of which, so that we may not be disturbed by confusion, we shall distribute into certain and specific classes.
