XL. SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE. The first class of sayings, in which are contained those passages which set before our eyes the corruption of man, introduced by sin, in a general way. We argue from thence in this manner: Whoever are thoroughly corrupted by sin, so that they are nothing but flesh; they do not have free will in spiritual matters. For flesh and spirit are opposites; where flesh reigns, there can be no spiritual works, but rather carnal ones; for such as the cause is, such is the effect: But unregenerate man is thoroughly corrupted by sin; so that he is nothing but flesh. Wherefore unregenerate man does not have free will in spiritual matters.

XLI. The minor premise is proven 1. John 3, v. 6. That which is born of the flesh is flesh, i.e., contaminated by sin, and savors of nothing but what is carnal. Whence Paul says, Rom. 8, v. 6. φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς θάνατος, and Gal. 5, v. 19. The works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication, uncleanness, etc. Bellarmine objects in book 5, ch. 10, col. 790, lit. B. and C. that the word flesh is indeed sometimes taken for a carnal man; but more often it is taken simply for man himself, and it is in such a way that it must be taken and understood in John 3. For the Lord, he says, in order to show that it is necessary for us to be born again if we wish to obtain the divine inheritance, said. That which is born of the flesh is flesh, i.e., it is not sufficient to have been born once from man, for man begets nothing other than man; but one must be born again, and that from God, so that we may be in a certain way Gods; and deserve to obtain the inheritance of the sons of God. But this Jesuitical interpretation is entirely new and com-

contrary to the opinion and the text itself. For Christ says in v. 5 that a man must be born again of water and the Spirit, and in v. 6 he adds the reason, because that which is born of the flesh is flesh. If here you understand by flesh the very substance of man, I ask, what kind of argument would this be: That which is born of man is man. Therefore man has need of Baptism? There would be no consequence here: For we do not have need of regeneration because we are men, that is, creatures of God; otherwise in the state of integrity before the fall there would also have been need of regeneration; but rather, because we are sinners. For we are cleansed in Baptism not from nature, but from the vice of nature: Therefore this is the reasoning of Christ, All are born sinners from sinners. Therefore they have need of Baptism, as a purgation of sin. And therefore by flesh is understood man, not as man, but as he is infected and corrupted by sin, which is evident from the antithesis: for he opposes flesh to spirit. Everything, he says, that is born of the flesh is flesh, but that which is born of the spirit is spirit: where by Spirit he understands nothing else than regeneration and renewal, or both the remission and the subjection of sin. Since therefore flesh is opposed to spirit, it certainly cannot be understood by flesh as human nature, since it is neither opposed to spirit, nor is it taken away by the Spirit. And a rule of Luther is worthy of note here, which he sets down in his book De servo arbitrio, page 235, which sounds as follows: You will observe this in the Scriptures, wherever flesh is treated by antithesis to spirit, there you should generally understand by flesh all things contrary to the Spirit: But where it is treated absolutely, there you should know it signifies the condition and bodily nature. But that is a manifest falsehood of Bellarmine, when he writes that in Rom. 8 by flesh nothing else is understood than concupiscibility, or the lower part of the soul, which they call the sensual. For the text expressly says, τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός. But shall we attribute τὸ φρόνημα, and τὸ φρονεῖν to the lower faculty of the soul, and not rather to the higher, namely to the mind and intellect itself?

2. Rom. 5. v. 19. By the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, that is, all, as the Papists themselves admit.

3. Job 14. v. 4. Who can make or give one clean from an unclean seed? Whence also David complains Psalm 51. v. 7. In sins did my mother conceive me.

4. Jer. 17. v. 9. The heart of man is perverse.

5. We were by nature children of wrath, even as others Ephes. 2. v. 3. Other Biblical texts can be referred here, which prove that man is corrupted by sin, for the explanation of which, and the demonstration derived thence, see Decad. 1 of our Anthropology, disputation 5, question 3.

XLII. The second class of sayings, in which are contained those passages which prove that man, after the fall, still constituted in a state of corruption, does nothing but act evilly, such as are, 1. Matth. 7. v. 18. Luke 6. v. 43. & 44. Every good tree brings forth good fruit: but a corrupt tree brings forth evil fruit: A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart brings forth good; And an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart brings forth evil, &c. Hence we conclude thus: An evil tree does not bring forth truly good and praiseworthy fruits. The will of man after the fall is nothing else than an evil tree, since it is most deeply infected with sin. Therefore it cannot bring forth truly good and praiseworthy fruits. The major premise is of Christ himself; the minor cannot be denied; the truth of the conclusion therefore stands.

XLIII. Bellarmine objects many things in book 5, ch. 10, col. 788 & 789. First, he says, that the sayings in Matthew and Luke are different. But they are not different as to sense, even if we grant that they were uttered at distinct times. For he who says today that the Jesuits are liars, impostors, and tomorrow repeats the same, he does not say something different and other, but the same.

although he says at different times. That, however, is manifestly false which he says, Matt. 7, that by bad and good trees nothing else is understood than false and true doctrines. For the sentiment of Christ is general; He wishes to prove that the doctrine of the false prophets is false, because its fruits are bad. Thus, therefore, he concludes: A good tree does not produce bad fruits; the doctrine of the false prophets produces bad fruits; therefore it is not a good tree. If here by a good tree the doctrine itself were understood, then Christ would have proved the same thing by the same thing, and consequently his argumentation would have been vain and of no consequence, which to say of Christ is impious and blasphemous. Rather, therefore, it must be established that this sentiment of Christ is general, equivalent to this one, which he sets down in verse 16: Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? That, however, is also most to be blamed in Jesu Wita, that he completely perverts the words of Christ, and makes a particular proposition out of a universal one, when he says that the Lord did not wish to signify that a good tree cannot produce any bad fruit, but that it cannot produce all or very many bad fruits; so also that a bad tree sometimes produces good fruit, for δένδρον σαπρὸν signifies not entirely corrupt, but an old and rotten tree. But the sentiment of CHRIST is manifest and clear: Every good tree produces good fruits. And although it sometimes happens that fruits are corrupted by worms, or are not brought to maturity on account of the inclemency of the air; nevertheless, the cause is not in the tree, but outside the tree. To such an extent is it universally true: A good tree cannot produce bad fruits: And where there are bad fruits, there is a bad tree, and vice versa. It is to be wondered at, however, that Jesu Wita here trusts so much in the Greek text, when nevertheless he should rather have stood by the Latin Vulgate version.

XLIV. Furthermore, he commits two petitions of the principle in the solution of this argument. The first is that, while he says that man, as he is a bad tree and acts out of desire, cannot indeed act well, yet if he acts out of the good of nature, he can produce a morally good work. For this is the question: is man after the fall partly good, partly bad, and thus as it were a mixture of goodness and malice? We say he is entirely corrupt, and therefore cannot act well. Nor is there indeed a certain middle ground between the flesh and the reigning Spirit, such as the Jesuit imagines, but man either obeys the flesh or the spirit; if the flesh, his works are carnal and impious; if the spirit, they are spiritual and good. For although it may be conceded that man, as regards external discipline, can produce some good work; yet that work is not spiritual, because it did not proceed from the spirit: Conversion, however, is a spiritual work. Therefore it cannot be caused by the natural or carnal will of man. He commits another begging of the question in that he contends that by good fruits are to be understood meritorious works of life, and that such cannot be performed by man. For Scripture is entirely silent about the merit of good works.

XLV. 2. Psalm 14, v. 1. Rom. 3, verses 9 and following. We have charged that Jews and Greeks are all under sin: as it is written, because there is no one righteous, there is no one understanding, there is no one seeking God, all have turned aside, together they have become useless, there is no one who does good, there is not even one. Here is described what the works of unregenerate men are like, namely, not to understand, not to seek God. How then, through the powers of the will, will they be able to assent to divine mysteries, to believe in Christ, and to love God? How will those who have become entirely useless be able to prepare themselves for conversion? 3. Gen. 6, v. 5 and ch. 8, v. 22. Every imagination of the human heart is only evil from his youth. 4. Matt. 15, v. 19. Out of the heart come evil thoughts, etc.

XLVI. The third class of sayings, in which are contained the

Latin:

XXXIX. Probari potest seruitus arbitrij circa conuersionem hominis, aliosque actus spirituales, partim ex Scriptura; partim rationibus ab analogia fidei desumtis; partim testimonijs tùm Patrum, tum ipsorum aduersariorum. Ex Scripturis multa in hunc sensum dicta depromi possunt, quæ omnia, ne turbemur confusione, in certas & peculiares classes distribuemus.

XL. DICTA SCRIPTVRAE. Prima classis dictorum, in qua continentur illa loca, quæ hominis corruptionem, peccato introductam, in genere ob oculos ponunt. Argumentamur inde hunc ad modum; Quicunque peccato penitus sunt corrupti, ita vt nil sint nisi caro; illi non habent liberum in spiritualibus arbitrium. Caro enim & spiritus sunt opposita; vbi caro regnat, ibi nulla possunt esse opera spiritualia, verùm potiùs carnalia; qualis enim causa, tale causatum: Atqui homo non renatus peccato penitus est corruptus; ita vt nil sit nisi caro. Quare homo non renatus non habet liberum in spiritualibus arbitrium.

XLI. Minor probatur 1. Ioh. 3. v. 6. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est, h. e. peccato contaminatum, & nil nisi carnale sapit. Vnde Paulus inquit, Rom. 8. v. 6. φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς θάνατος, & Gal. 5. v. 19. Manifesta sunt opera carnis, quæ sunt fornicatio, immunditia, &c. Excipit Bellarminus l. 5. c. 10. col. 790. lit. B. & C. accipi quidem vocabulum carnis quandoque pro homine carnali; sæpiùs autem simpliciter accipi pro ipso homine, & taliter sumendum esse ac intelligendum Iohan. 3. Dominus enim; inquit vt ostenderet oportere nos nasci denuò, si velimus hæreditatem diuinam consequi, dixit. Quod natum est ex carne, caro est, h. e. non sufficit natum esse semel ex homine, Nam homo nihil aliud quàm hominem gignit; Sed nascendum est iterum, idque ex Deo, vt simus quodammodo Dij; & hæreditatem filiorum Dei consequi mereamur, Verùm hæc interpretatio IesuWitica, noua prorsus est & com-

stentitiæ ipsique textui omnino contraria. Christus enim v. 5. inquit, oportere hominem renasci ex aqua & Spiritu, v. 6. addit rationem, quia quod natum est ex carne, caro est. Hic si per carnem intelligas ipsam hominis substantiam, quæso, quæ hæc foret argumentatio: Quod ex homine nascitur est homo. Ergo homo opus habet Baptismo? Nulla hic foret consequentia: Non enim ideo regeneratione nobis opus est, quia sumus homines, id est, creaturæ Dei; alioquin in statu integritatis ante lapsum regeneratione quoque fuisset opus; sed potiùs, quia sumus peccatores. Nam purgamur in Baptismo non à natura, sed naturæ vitio: Igitur hæc est ratio Christi, Omnes à peccatoribus nascuntur peccatores. Ergò opus habent Baptismo, tanquam purgamento peccati. Ac proinde per carnem intelligitur homo, non quâ homo, sed quâ peccato infectus & corruptus est, quod patet ex antithesi: opponit enim carnem spiritui. Omne, inquit, quod natum est ex carne, caro est, quod verò ex spiritu, spiritus est: vbi per Spiritum nihil aliud intelligit, quàm regenerationem & renouationem, seu peccati tùm remissionem tùm subactionem. Cùm igitur caro opponatur spiritui, nequit certè per carnem intelligi humana natura, quippe quæ nec spiritui opposita est, nec per Spiritũ tollitur. Et digna hîc notatu venit regula Lutheri, quam ponit in lib. de seruo arbitr. pag. 235. quæ ita sonat: Id obseruabis in Scripturis, vbicunque de carne agitur per antithesin ad spiritum, ibi fere per carnem intelligas omnia contraria Spiritui: Vbi verò absolutè tractatur, ibi conditionem naturamque corporalem significare scias. Illud verò manifestum ψεῦδος est Bellarmini, cùm scribit Rom. 8. per carnem nihil intelligi aliud, quàm concupiscibilitatem, seu partem animæ inferiorem, quam sensualem vocant. Expressè enim textus dicit, τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκός. An autem τὸ φρόνημα, & τὸ φρονεῖν inferiori animæ facultati, & non potiùs superiori, ipsi videlicet menti & intellectui affebemus?

2. Rom. 5. v. 19. Per inobedientiam unius hominis peccatores constituti sunt multi, id est, omnes, fatentibus ipsis Pontificijs.

3. Iob. 14. v. 4. Quis potest facere vel dare mundum de immund. conceptum semine? vnde & David conqueritur Psalm. 51. v. 7. In peccatis concepit me mater mea.

4. Ierem. 17. v 9. Pravum est cor hominis.

5. Eramus naturâ filij iræ, si ut & cæteri Ephes. 2. v. 3. Referri huc possunt alij textus Biblici, qui hominem peccato corruptum esse euincunt, quorum explicationem, & inde petitam demonstrationem vide Decad. 1. ἀνθρωπολογίας nostræ disputat. 5. quæst. 3.

XLII. Secunda classis dictorum, in quâ continentur ista loca, quæ hominem post lapsum, in statu corruptionis adhuc constitutum, non nisi malè agere euincunt qualia sunt, 1. Matth. 7. v. 18. Luc. 6. v. 43. & 44. Omnis arbor bona fructus bonos facit: putris autem arbor fructus malos facit: Non potest arbor bona fructus malos facere. Bonus homo ex bono thesauro cordis sui profert bonum; Et malus homo ex malo thesauro cordis sui profert malum, &c. Hinc ita concludimus: Mala arbor non profert verè bonos & laudabiles fructus. Arbitrium hominis post lapsum nil est aliud, quàm mala arbor, siquidem peccato penitissimè infectum est. Ergò nequit proferre fructus verè bonos & laudabiles. Maior est ipsius Christi; minor negari nequit; constat igitur sua conclusioni veritas.

XLIII. Multa excipit Bellarminus lib. 5 c. 10. col. 788. & 789. Primùm, inquit, esse diversa dicta apud Matthæum & Lucam. Sed non sunt diversa quoad sensum, licèt demus, distinctis ea fuisse prolata temporibus. Qui enim hodiè dicit, Iesu Witas esse mendaces, impostores, & cras idem repetit, is non diuersum & aliud dicit, sed idem.

quamuis diuersis dicat temporibus. Illud verò manifestè falsum est, quòd inquit, Matth. 7. per arbores malas & bonas nihil intelligi aliud, quam doctrinas falsas & veras. Sententia enim Christi generalis est; Vult probare, quòd doctrina Pseudoprophetarum sit falsa, quia fructus eius sunt mali. Sic ergò colligit, Arbor bona non profert fructus malos: doctrina Pseudoprophetarum profert fructus malos, Ergo non est arbor bona Si hic per arborem bonam intelligatur ipsa doctrina, tunc idem per idem probasset Christus, & per consequens eius argumentatio fuisset vana, & nullius sequelæ, quod de Christo dicere impium & blasphemum. Potius ergò statuendum, quòd ista Christi sententia generalis sit, æquipollens huic, quam ponit vers. 16 Numquid colligunt à spinis vuam, aut à tribulis ficus? Id verò etiam maximè culpandum in Iesu Wita, quòd verba Christi omninò peruertit, & ex vniuersali propositione particularem facit, quando inquit, Dominum non voluisse significare arborem bonam non posse facere vllum fructum malum, sed non posse facere omnes aut plurimos fructus malos; sic etiam arborem malam quandoque facere fructum bonum, δένδρον enim σαπρὸν significare non omnino corruptam, sed arborem antiquam & cariosam. Verùm CHRISTI sententia manifesta est perspicua : Omnis arbor bona, fructus bonos facit. Et licèt quandoque eueniat, vt fructus à vermibus corrumpantur, vel ob aëris intemperiem ad maturitatem non perducantur; tamen causa non est in arbore, sed extra arborem. Vsque adeò vniuersaliter verum est, Arbor bona non potest fructus malos facere : Et vbi sunt fructus mali, ibi arbor mala, & contra. Mirandum autem, quòd Iesu Wita hîc tantoperè Græco textui fidat, cùm tamen illi potiùs standum fuisset versione vulgatâ Latinâ.

XLIV. Porrò duas committit in solutione huius argumenti petitiones principii. Prima est, dum inquit, hominem, quà mala arbor est, & ex cupiditate agit, non posse quidem benè operari, attamen si agat ex bono naturæ, posse opus bonum morale producere. Hoc enim quæritur, an homo post lapsum partim sit bonus, partim malus, & sic quasi mixtura ex bonitate & malitiâ? Nos dicimus omninò esse corruptum, ideoque non posse benè operari. Neque verò medium quoddam est inter carnem & Spiritum regnantem, quale fingit IesuWita, sed homo aut obedit carni, aut spiritui; si carni, opera eius sunt carnalia & impia; si spiritui, spiritualia & bona. Quamuis enim concedi possit, hominem quoad externam disciplinam posse aliquod bonum opus producere; tamen id opus non est spirituale, quia non ex spiritu profectum: Conuersio verò opus est spirituale. Ergò non potest à naturali vel carnali arbitrio hominis causari. Alteram principii petitionem in eo committit, quòd per bonos fructus intelligi contendit opera vitæ meritoria, & talia ab homino præstari non posse. De merito enim bonorum operum vniuersa silet Scriptura.

XLV. 2. Psalm. 14. v. 1. Rom. 3. vers. 9. & seqq. Causati sumus, Iudæos & Græcos omnes sub peccato esse: sicut scriptum est, quia non est iustus quisquam, non est intelligens, non est requirens Deum, Omnes declinauerunt, simul inutiles facti sunt, non est qui facit bonum, non est vsque ad vnum. Hîc describitur, qualia sint opera hominum non renatorum, videlicet non intelligere, non requirere Deum. Quomodo ergò per vires arbitrij poterunt assentiri mysterijs diuinis, in Christum credere, & Deum diligere? Quomodo ij, qui prorsus inutiles facti sunt, poterunt sese ad conuersionem præparare? 3. Gen. 6. v. 5. & c. 8. v. 22. Omne figmentum cordis humani tantummodò malum est ab adolescentiâ suâ. 4. Matth. 15. v. 19. De corde exeunt cogitationes malæ &c.

XLVI. Tertia classis dictorum, in quâ continentur il-


### Question V. By what arguments can the true opinion concerning free will be…: & places, which show in particular both the blindness of the intellect and the aversion of the will in unregenerate man

& places, which show in particular both the blindness of the intellect and the aversion of the will in unregenerate man.

Hence we argue: He whose intellect is blind in spiritual matters does not understand spiritual things, much less assent to them; and he whose will is averse, stubborn, and refractory, does not wish, nor can he wish, to convert himself to God and believe in Christ. But the intellect of all unregenerate persons is blind, and their will is averse. Therefore, the unregenerate do not understand divine mysteries, nor can they perform spiritual actions.

XLVII. The minor premise is proven. I. That the intellect is blind in spiritual mysteries. 1 Cor. 2, verse 14: ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος, the natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned. It is to be observed in this place what the Apostle understands by ἄνθρωπον ψυχικὸν. Emser thought that the lower part of the soul was meant, which man has in common with brutes, in the sense in which motion is called animal, and spirits are called animal, whence he thought it should be rendered, 'the animal man.' But that this interpretation is entirely false is evident from the fact that he is speaking of such as he called in verse 6 the princes of this world, who excel in learning, prudence, eloquence, and other gifts of the mind, and therefore in verse 13 he attributes to them διδακτὸς τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγος. Such he calls ψυχικοὺς from the soul, because he does not wish to be understood as referring to the swine of Epicurus's herd, who in 2 Peter 2, verse 12 are called ἄλογα ζῶα, but those who cultivate the best part of themselves, namely the soul. Therefore, ἄνθρωποι ψυχικοὶ are opposed to πνευματικοῖς, that is, by the natural man is not understood he who is governed only by sense in the manner of brutes, but such a man as he is from his first origin and birth, polished with all the disciplines, arts, and virtues of human wisdom, who is governed by the leading of his soul, not by the Holy Spirit graciously indwelling him. For he who follows the guidance of reason is named ψυχικὸς; he who follows the Holy Spirit is called πνευματικὸς: this is evident from the epistle of Jude, verse 19, where it is said: These are they who separate themselves, ψυχικοὶ πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες: here it is explained who is a ψυχικὸς man, namely one who does not have the Holy Spirit; whence also human wisdom is called ψυχικὴ, James 3, v. 15. From all of which it appears sufficiently that by ἄνθρωπον ψυχικὸν is understood a man such as he is now constituted after the fall, and who follows nothing but the dictates of his own reason. Concerning such an animal man, however, the Apostle pronounces two things: that he can neither γνῶναι nor δέχεσθαι the mysteries of the Spirit: by γνῶναι he understands simple knowledge and understanding of spiritual things, but by δέχεσθαι, faithful assent. For in this way it is taken in Acts 8, verse 14: When the Apostles heard that Samaria δέδεκται, had received the word of God. Acts 17, verse 11, ἐδέξαντο τὸν λόγον, they received the word with all eagerness, 1 Thess. 2, verse 13, παραλαβόντες λόγον ἀκοῆς παρ' ἡμῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐδέξασθε ὦ λόγον ἀνθρώπων. Here a distinction is expressly made between παραλαμβάνειν τὸν λόγον and δέχεσθαι τὸν λόγον: the former pertains to external hearing, the latter to internal hearing, that is, faithful assent. Therefore Paul asserts two things: 1. that a man not reborn or ψυχικὸς cannot δέχεσθαι or receive with faithful assent the mysteries of the Spirit. 2. that of himself he cannot even have a bare γνῶσιν of them, which he asserted in the same chapter, verse 8, where he said that none of the princes of this world knew the wisdom of the Gospel; for it is ἀποκεκρυμμένη, hidden, verse 7, which flesh and blood do not reveal, Matt. 16, verse 17, but the Son alone, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared it to us, John 1, verse 18. The sum is: Even the wisest man cannot know by natural powers that God sent his Son to redeem the human race through death, and although it is revealed to him through the word, nevertheless he cannot δέχεσθαι [receive] it, nor believe, nor assent to it. He adds a double cause, the first of which is taken from the corruption of nature, which is so great that it mocks and cavils at heavenly mysteries as foolish fables and old wives' tales, μωρία αὐτῷ ἐςι [it is foolishness to him], as long, of course, as a man is ψυχικὸς [natural]. Hence we conclude: Whoever holds divine mysteries for foolishness and vanity, he cannot assent to them: The natural man, as long as he is such, holds divine mysteries for foolishness. Therefore he cannot assent. The second cause is taken from the condition of divine mysteries, which do not admit a ψυχικὸν [natural] and carnal judge, deeply immersed in philosophical and worldly opinions, but must be judged spiritually, i.e., according to the tenor of the divine word, which is spiritual, and according to the dictation of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of believers, Rom. 8. vers. 14. 15. Whence it is concluded: In whom there is not κρίσις πνευμα- τικὴ [spiritual judgment], in him does not fall the δοχὴ [reception] of divine mysteries. Into the natural man, as such, does not fall κρίσις πνευματικὴ [spiritual judgment], for the ψυχικὸς [natural man] πνεῦμα οὐκ ἔχει [does not have the Spirit], epist. Jude. vers. 19. Therefore neither does the δοχὴ [reception] of divine mysteries fall into him. The major premise is the Apostle's, the minor is of manifest truth, therefore its truth will also stand for the conclusion.

XLIIX. 2. 2 Cor. 3. v. 5. We are not sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as from ourselves. But if we cannot even think anything good from our own powers, much less shall we be able to fully assent to divine mysteries. Bellarmine, book 6, chapter 13, fol. 912, letter A, says that this passage favors him; since the Apostle does not deny that we are sufficient, but denies that we are sufficient from ourselves. And he adds, unless we were of free will, we would not rightly be said not to be sufficient from ourselves, just as someone would not rightly say that a beast of burden or a stone is not sufficient from itself to think anything about God. But this whole argument depends on the word of sufficiency, which is of the Latin version, not of the Greek text itself. For in this is found the word ἱκανὸὶ, from which comes ἱκανότης, by which they deny aptitude, suitability, not merely sufficiency. The sense therefore of the Pauline passage is that we are in no way apt or suitable, or accommodated to not only effecting or saying anything, but at least to thinking, but that all our ἱκανότητα is from God. And although Paul speaks principally of the ministers of God, nevertheless this sentence is general, applying to all men entirely, whence also Augustine says in the book on the Predestination of the Saints, ch. 2: As far as religion and piety are concerned, we are not sufficient to think anything as if from ourselves, and no one is sufficient for himself to begin or complete any good work whatsoever.

XLIX. 3. Rom. 8. verse 7. τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς is enmity against God. For it is not subject to the law of God; nor indeed can it be. But whatever is opposed to God, that as such does not turn itself to God. But the φρόνημα of an unregenerate man is opposed to God. Therefore it does not turn itself to God. 4. The intellect is often compared to darkness, Eph. 5. verse 6. You were sometimes darkness, but now light in the Lord. John 1. verse 5. Acts 26. v. 18. Luke 1. v. 79. Eph. 4. verses 18 & 19. And for this reason, 2. Corinth. 10. verse 5, we are warned that every reason and thought (πᾶν νόημα) must be taken captive into the obedience of Christ.

L. II. That the will is turned away from God is proved 1. from Gen. 6. verse 5. Every imagination of man, etc. 2. Job 14. verse 4. Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean seed conceived? 3. Eph. 2. v. 3. Doing the wills of the flesh and of the thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath. 4. John 3. v. 6. That which is born of the flesh is flesh. 5. Rom. 3. v. 11. There is none that seeketh after God, etc.

LI. The fourth class of sayings contains those passages by which it is intimated that a man cannot turn himself to God by his own powers, such as Matt. 12. verse 34. How can you speak good things when you are evil?

Jer. 13. v. 24. If the Ethiopian can change his skin, and the leopard his spots, then you also can do good, when you have learned to do evil. 1 Cor. 12. v. 3. No one can say that Jesus is Lord, except in the Holy Spirit. John 6. v. 44. No one comes to me, unless the Father draws him. John 15. v. 5. Without me you can do nothing: which statement is to be understood negatively, not privatively, exclusively, not conjunctively. Augustine says upon this passage: He does not say, without me you can do little, nor does he say, You cannot do anything arduous without me, or you will be able to do so with difficulty without me, but you can do nothing without me. Nor does he say, Without me you cannot perfect, but you can do nothing without me.

LII. The fifth class of statements contains passages in which our conversion and regeneration are attributed to God alone. Whence we argue thus: That which is proper to God alone cannot be attributed to other men. But to illuminate the mind, to renew the will, to convert hearts, are works proper to God alone. Therefore they cannot be attributed to man. The following passages prove the minor premise. 1. Ezek. 36. v. 26. I will give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit in the midst of you, and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh; and I will put my spirit in the midst of you, and I will make you walk in my statutes, etc. Similar passages are found in Ezek. 11. verse 19. Jer. 32. verse 39. From which we conclude thus: It belongs to God alone to give a new heart, and to change a stony one into one of flesh. Therefore it is not of free will, or of the heart itself. For just as that which is old does not renew itself, and a stone does not soften itself, so an unregenerate man does not convert himself. Bellarmino replies in chapter 13, book 6, that free will is not a stony heart, nor a heart of flesh, but a certain intermediate and natural power, which can receive the form of stone, that is, the hardness of sin, and the form of flesh, that is, the tenderness of grace. For he says that Augustine speaks thus in his book On the Letter and the Spirit, chapter 33, namely that free will is naturally attributed to every rational creature, and is that intermediate power which can be stretched toward faith and inclined toward infidelity.

Who, however, does not notice here that the Jesuit is playing with the word 'will,' which he takes for the very essence of the will, but we for the δύναμις [power] of choosing good and evil. This δύναμις, because it is most deeply corrupted by sin, is rightly called a stone, because sin hardens the heart of man, so that it does not care for supercelestial things, nor can it even care. But what he adds, that free will, when it is stony, does not have from itself the power by which it can turn itself to God, but when it has been both excited and prepared by grace, it can, through the powers which it receives from God, cooperate in its own conversion: in this he seems to contradict himself, since he takes away all δύναμις from the will of itself, yet our side also concedes that it can cooperate through powers that are not native, but θεοδότους [God-given]. Thus he seems to speak orthodoxly, explaining the similarity between a stone and the heart, when he writes: 'In this the similarity has a place, that just as a stone does not have from itself that it should cooperate, if by chance it were turned into flesh, so also free will does not have from itself that it should cooperate in its own conversion, yet it can receive from God the power of working through grace, which a stone cannot.' By which words he does nothing else than to approve and defend our opinion, whence it appears that the Jesuit, driven by the force of truth, contradicts himself and condemns his own opinion: which he does in more words in the following, when he writes that Catholics do not say, nor think, that free will has from itself any power, at least a proximate one, for acts of piety, but that it receives it from God through prevenient grace. And it is a wonder that Bellarmine, in this very chapter where he disputes against us, speaks for us against the remaining Papists.

LIII. 2. Deut. 29. verse 3. & 4. You have seen those signs, and great portents, and the Lord has not given you a heart to understand, nor eyes to see, even to this present day. Therefore it belongs to the Lord alone to give understanding of the heart, and to open the eyes. 3. That it belongs to the Lord to open the eyes, and to give the Spirit of understanding, is evident from the following sayings, Eph. 1. v. 17. 2. v. 5. 4. v. 7. Acts 26. v. 17. 2. Cor. 4. v. 6. Isa. 11. v. 2. Ps. 119. v. 34. 1 Kings 3. v. 9. & 8. v. 58. 4. Ps. 51. v. 12. the prayer of David, create in me a clean heart, O Lord. But just as creation is the work of God alone, so the generation of a clean heart is appropriate to none but God alone. 5. Phil. 1. v. 6. He who began a good work in you, will perfect it even unto the day of Jesus, etc. 2 v. 13. It is God who works in you both to will and to perform for his good pleasure.

LIV. The sixth class of sayings contains passages by which it is declared that conversion is not only the loosening of a bond by which the freedom of the will had been bound, but that it is a full change, renewal, and vivification of man. For thus we argue: If by conversion a dead man is vivified, a blind man is enlightened, the old is renewed, the hard is softened, the turned-away is converted; then it will follow that man can contribute nothing efficiently to his own conversion. The former is true, therefore the latter also. Many sayings prove the minor premise, such as that God is said in conversion to break hearts, 1 Sam. 10, v. 26, to incline hearts, 2 Sam. 19, v. 4, to change hearts, Job 12, v. 24, to soften hearts, 2 Chron. 34, v. 27, to open the heart, Acts 16, v. 14, to convert the heart, Luke 1, v. 17, Ezra 6, v. 22, to circumcise the heart, Deut. 30, v. 6, to crush the heart, Ezek. 6, v. 9, to create a new heart, Ps. 51, v. 19. Eph. 4. v. 24 to vivify the heart, Isa. 57, v. 15, to renew the heart, Eph. 4. v. 23 to take away the heart of stone, and to give a new heart: Ezek. 11. v. 19. & 36, v. 26. to purify the heart, Acts 15, v. 9, to awaken from the dead, Eph. 5, v. 14, to vivify, Eph. 2, v. 5, to regenerate 1 Pet. 1, v. 3, Tit. 3, v. 5. Hence it is necessary that the outward man be corrupted, 2 Cor. 4, v. 16, that the body of sin be destroyed, Rom. 6, v. 6, whence also the reborn are called his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus, Eph. 2, v. 10. From all of which it can be demonstrated to the eye that by grace in conversion not as it were some bond is removed, by the loosening of which man can believe and love God by his own powers, but that this is engendered in man anew and thus man is entirely changed.

LV. The seventh class of sayings can contain those passages in which the unregenerate man is called dead in spiritual matters. For where there is death, there no vital force or faculty remains, because death is the total privation of life. But the unregenerate man is spiritually dead. Therefore, in him no vital force remains; whence we further conclude: He in whom no vital force adheres can in no way concur in his own vivification; in the unregenerate man no vital force adheres. Therefore he can in no way concur in his own vivification. The minor premise of the former syllogism is proved from Ephesians 2, verse 1: And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins. A similar passage is read in Colossians 2, v. 13. Add John 5, v. 25 and Matthew 8, v. 22. Bellarmine objects, book 6, chapter 13, by distinguishing between that which is dead in all ways, and that which is dead in one way, but lives in another. That it is true of the first kind of dead that they cannot vivify themselves, but not of the second, to which he refers the unregenerate man: For he says that he is dead regarding spiritual life, but not dead but alive regarding natural life: therefore, that man, insofar as he lives naturally, can cooperate toward recovering spiritual life. Response: This is an entirely vain evasion: For just as natural life is truly distinct from spiritual life, so its actions contribute absolutely nothing to effecting the life of grace: For conversion is not a natural action, but a spiritual work: Therefore the natural man can contribute nothing to it.

LVI. The eighth class of sayings contains passages in which unregenerate men are called slaves of sin. But whoever is a slave to sin is not free to perform spiritual actions. And yet all unregenerate men are slaves to sin. Therefore they are not free to perform spiritual actions. The minor

The following sayings prove it. 1. John 8:24, Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin. 2. Rom 6:14. Do you not know that to whom you present yourselves as slaves to obey, you are slaves of the one whom you obey? & v. 19, You have presented your members to serve impurity. 3. 2 Pet 2:19. By whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also enslaved.

LVII. The ninth class of sayings contains passages which show that man cannot boast as if he were in some way the author of his own conversion. From this we conclude: If man were of free will, then he who uses his will rightly could boast against the unbeliever who uses his will wrongly. The consequent is false, as Bellarmine himself admits in book 1, chapter 13, according to the words of 1 Cor 1:31, He who boasts, let him boast in the Lord, and ch. 4:7, What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it? To this pertains that statement of Cyprian, book 3 to Quirinus, ch. 4: One must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own.

Latin:

& loca, quæ in specie tùm intellectus cæcitatem, tum voluntatis auersionem in homine non renato ostendunt.

Hinc argumentamur: Cuius intellectus cæcus est in spiritualibus, is non intelligit spiritualia, multò minùs ijs assentitur; & cuius voluntas auersa, contumax & refractaria est, is non vult, nec velle potest se ad Deum conuertere, & in Christum credere. Atqui intellectus omnium non renatorum cæcus, & voluntas auersa est. Ergo non renati non intelligunt diuina mysteria, nec possunt actiones spirituales edere.

XLVII. Minor probatur. I. Quòd intellectus cæcus sit in mysterijs spiritualibus. 1. Cor. 2. vers. 14. ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος, animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei, stultitia enim est illi, & non potest intelligere, quia spiritualiter examinantur, Obseruandum est hoc loco, quid intelligat Apostolus per ἄνθρωπον ψυχικὸν. Emserus putauit intelligi partem animæ inferiorem, quam homo cum brutis habet communem, eo sensu, quo motus dicitur animalis, & spiritus vocantur animales, vnde reddendum putauit, der Thierische Mensch. Sed prorsus falsam esse hanc interpretationem patet indè, quia de talibus loquitur, quos vers. 6. appellauit principes huius seculi, qui præstant doctrinâ, prudentiâ, eloquentiâ, & alijs animi dotibus, ideoque vers. 13. ijs attribuit διδακτὸς τῆς ἀνθρωπίνης σοφίας λόγος. Tales appellat ψυχικοὺς ab animâ, quia non vult intelligi Epicuri de grege porcos, qui 2. Pet. 2. vers. 12. vocantur ἄλογα ζῶα, sed qui potissimam sui partem animam scilicet, excolunt. Opponuntur ergò ἄνθρωποι ψυχικοὶ πνευματικοῖς, id est, per hominem animalem non intelligitur is, qui tantùm sensu regitur more brutorum, sed qualis homo est à primâ origine & natiuitate, expolitus omnibus humanæ sapientiæ disciplinis, artibus & virtutibus, qui animæ suæ ductu regitur, non à Spiritu sancto gratiosè inhabitante. Qui enim sequitur ductum rationis nominatur ψυχικὸς; qui sequitur Spiritum sanctum, vocatur πνευματικὸς: patet hoc ex epist. Iudæ vers. 19. vbi dicitur: Hi sunt, qui segregant semetipsos, ψυχικοὶ πνεῦμα μὴ ἔχοντες: hîc exponitur, quis sit homo ψυχικὸς, qui videlicet Spiritum sanctum non habet; Vnde & sapientia humana vocatur ψυχικὴ Iac. 3. v. 15. ex quibus omnibus satis apparet, per ἄνθρωπον ψυχικὸν intelligi hominem, qualis iam post lapsum est constitutus, & qui nil nisi suæ rationis dictamen sequitur. De tali autem homine animali duo pronunciat Apostolus, quòd mysteria Spiritus, nec possit γνῶναι, nec δέχεσθαι: Per γνῶναι intelligit simplicem notitiam & intelligentiam rerum spiritualium, per δέχεσθαι verò fidelem assensum. Hoc enim modo sumitur Actor. 8 vers. 14. Cùm audissent Apostoli, quòd δέδεκται, recepisset Samaria verbum Dei. Act. 17. vers. 11, ἐδέξαντο τὸν λόγον, receperunt verbum cum omni aviditate, 1. Thessal. 2. vers. 13. παραλαβόντες λόγον ἀκοῆς παρ' ἡμῶν τοῦ Θεοῦ, ἐδέξασθε ὦ λόγον ἀνθρώπων. Hîc distinguitur expressè inter παραλαμβάνειν τὸν λόγον, & inter δέχεσθαι τὸν λόγον: Illud ad auditum externum, hoc ad auditum internum, hoc est, fidelem assensum pertinet. Duo igitur Paulus asserit: 1. quòd homo non renatus seu ψυχικὸς non possit δέχεσθαι vel recipere fideli assensu mysteria Spiritus. 2. quòd ex sese non etiam possit nudam illorum γνῶσιν habere, quod asseruit eodem capite vers. 8. vbi dixit, quòd nemo principum hujus seculi sapientiam Euangelij cognovit; est enim ἀποκεκρυμμένη, abscondita vers. 7. quam caro & sanguis non reuelant, Matth. 16. vers. 17. sed solus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse nobis enarrauit, Iohan. 1. vers. 18. Summa est: Homo etiam sapientissimus nequit cognoscere ex naturalibus viribus, Deum misisse Filium ad redimendum per mortem genus humanum, & licet illi per verbum reveletur, tamen id non potest δέχεσθαι non credere, nec illi assentiri. Causam addit duplicem, quarum prima desumitur à corruptione naturæ, quæ tanta est, vt mysteria cœlestia tanquam stultas fabellas & aniles nugas irrideat & cauilletur μωρία αὐτῷ ἐςι, quamdiu nimirum homo est ψυχικὸς. Hinc colligimus: Quicunque mysteria diuina habet pro stultitiâ & vanitate, is non potest ijs assentiri: Homo animalis, quamdiu talis, habet mysteria diuina pro stultitiâ. Ergò assentiri nequit. Secunda causa desumitur à conditione mysteriorum diuinorum, quæ non admittunt iudicem ψυχικὸν & carnalem, opinionibus Philosophicis & mundanis penitùs immersum, sed spiritualiter dijudicanda sunt, h. e. secundùm tenorem verbi diuini, quod spirituale est, & secundum dictamen Spiritus sancti in cordibus credentium, Rom. 8. vers. 14. 15. Vnde concluditur: In quo non est κρίσις πνευματικὴ, in eum non cadit δοχὴ mysteriorum diuinorum. In hominem animalem, quà talis, non cadit κρίσις πνευματικὴ, ψυχικὸς enim πνεῦμα οὐκ ἔχει, epist. Judæ. vers. 19. Ergo nec in eum cadit δοχὴ mysteriorum diuinorum. Maior est Apostoli, minor manifestæ veritatis, sua igitur conclusioni quoque constabit veritas.

XLIIX. 2. 2. Cor. 3. v. 5. Non sufficientes sumus cogitare aliquid à nobis, tanquam ex nobis. Si verò ne quidem cogitare aliquid boni possumus ex proprijs viribus, multò minùs poterimus mysterijs diuinis plenè assentiri. Bellarminus lib. 6. cap. 13. fol. 912 lit. A. dicit, hunc locum sibi fauere; cùm non neget Apostolus, nos sufficientes esse, sed neget nos sufficientes esse ex nobis. Et addit, nisi liberi essemus arbitrij, non rectè diceremur non sufficere ex nobis, sicut non rectè diceret aliquis iumentum aut lapidem non sufficere ex se aliquid cogitare de Deo Verùm tota hæc argumentatio pendet ex vocabulo sufficientiæ, qꝫ versionis Latinæ est, non ipsius textus Græci. In hoc enim reperitur, vocabulum ἱκανὸὶ, vnde ἱκανότης, qua aptitudinem, idoneitatem, non solam sufficientiam negant. Sensus igitur loci Paulini est, quòd nullo modo apti vel idonei, vel accommodati simus ad aliquid non modò efficiendum, vel dicendum, sed ad cogitandum saltem, omnem verò ἱκανότητα ἡμῶν ἐκ τῶ Θεῶ esse. Et quamuis principaliter Paulus loquatur de ministris Dei, tamen sententia hæc generalis est, competens omnibus omninò hominibus, vnde & Augustinus inquit lib, de Prædest.sanctor c.2. Quod ad religionem & pietatem attinet, non sumus sufficientes cogitare aliquid, quasi ex nobis, & nemo sibi sufficit ad incipiendum vel perficiendum quodcunque opus bonum.

XLIX. 3. Rom. 8. vers. 7. τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς ἔχθρα εἰς Θεὸν. Legi enim Dei non subycitur; nec enim potest. Quodcunque autem Deo aduersatur, id quâ tale, ad Deum se non conuertit. Ast φρόνημα hominis non renati Deo aduersatur. Ergò seipsum ad Deum non conuertit. 4. Intellectus sæpè tenebris comparatur, Ephes.5.vers.6. Eratis aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino. Iohan. 1. vers.5. Actor. 26. v. 18. Luc. 1. v. 79. Ephes. 4. vers. 18. & 19. Et istam ob causam. 2. Corinth. 10. vers. 5. monemur, captiuandam esse omnem rationem & cogitationem (πᾶν νόημα) in obedientiam Christi.

L. II. Quod voluntas auersa sit à Deo, probatur 1. ex Genes. 6. vers. 5. Omne figmentum hominis, &c. 2. Iob. 14. vers. 4. Quis potest dare mundum de immundo conceptum semine? 3. Eph. 2. v. 3. Facientes voluntates carnis cogitationum, & eramus naturâ filij iræ, 4. Iohan. 3. v. 6. Quod ex carne natum est, caro est. 5. Rom. 3. v. 11. Non est requirens Deum, &c.

LI. Quarta classis dictorum continet illa loca, quibus innuitur, hominem non posse semetipsum ad Deum ex proprijs viribus conuertere, qualia sunt Matth. 12. vers. 34. Quomodo potestis bona loqui cùm sitis mali?

Ier. 13. v. 24. Si mutare potest Aethiops pellem suam, & pardus maculas suas, & vos poteritis benefacere, cùm didiceritis malè. 1. Cor. 12. v. 3. Nemo potest dicere Iesum Dominum, nisi in Spiritu sancto. Ioh. 6. v. 44. Nemo venit ad me, nisi Pater traxeris eum. Ioh. 15. v. 5. Sine me nihil potestis facere: quod dictum negatiuè, non priuatiuè, exclusiuè non coniunctiuè intelligendum est. Augustinus super hunc locum inquit: Non dicit, sine me parum potestis facere, nec dicit, Non potestis ardui aliquid sine me facere, vel difficulter sine me poteritis, sed nihil sine me potestis, Nec dicit, Sine me non potestis perficere sed nihil potestis facere sine me.

LII. Quinta classis dictorum continet loca, in quibus nostra conuersio, regeneratio soli Deo attribuitur. Vnde sic argumentamur: Quod soli Deo proprium, aliud hominibus attribui nequit. Atqui illuminare mentem, renouare voluntatem, corda conuertere, sunt opera soli Dei propria. Ergò homini attribui nequeunt. Minorem probant sequentia dicta. 1. Ezech. 36. v. 26. Dabo vobis cor novum, & Spiritum novum ponam in medio vestri, & auferam cor lapideum de carne vestrâ, & dabo vobis cor carneum; & spiritum meum ponam in medio vestri, & faciam, vt in præceptis meis ambuletis, &c. Similia loca habentur Ezech. 11. vers. 19. Ier. 32. vers. 39. Equibus ita concludimus: Solius Dei est dare cor novum, & lapideum mutare in carneum. Ergò non est liberi arbitrij, vel ipsius cordis. Sicut n. id, quòd vetus est, seipsum non renouat, & lapis seipsum non emollit, ita homo non renatus seipsum non conuertit. Respondet Bellarminus cap. 13. l. 6. arbitrium liberum non esse cor lapideum, neque carneum, sed vim quandam mediam & naturalem, quæ formam lapidis, id est, peccati duritiem, & formam carnis, id est, gratiæ teneritudinem recipere possit. Sic enim loqui Augustinum l. de lit. & spir. cap. 33. nempè liberum arbitrium naturaliter attribui omni rationali creaturæ, esse vim illam mediam, quæ prætendi ad fidem & inclinari ad infidelitatem potest.

Quis autem hic non animaduertit, ludere Iesuwitam vocabulo arbitrij, quod pro ipsa voluntatis essentia accipit, nos vero pro δυνάμει bonum malumque eligendi. Haec δύναμις, quia per peccatum altissime corrupta est, recte dicitur lapis dea, quia peccatum indurat cor hominis, vt non curet supercoelestia, nec etiam curare queat. Quod vero addit, liberum arbitrium, quando est lapideum, non habere ex se potestatem qua se possit ad Deum conuertere, sed quando per gratiam & excitatum & praeparatum est, posse per vires, quas a Deo recipit, cooperari ad suam ipsius conuersionem: in eo videtur sibi contradicere, siquidem omnem δύναμιν arbitrio ex se adimit, illud vero per vires non natiuas, sed θεοδότους cooperari posse, & Nostri concedunt. Sic videtur orthodoxe loqui, explicans similitudinem inter lapidem & cor, quando scribit: In eo similitudo locum habet, quod sicut lapis ex se non habet, vt cooperetur, si forte conuertatur in carnem, sic etiam liberum arbitrium ex se non habet, vt cooperetur ad suam ipsius conuersionem, potest tamen a Deo recipere potestatem operandi per gratiam, quod non potest lapis. Quibus verbis nil aliud agit, quam vt nostram adprobet & propugnet sententiam, vnde apparet, Iesu Witam vi veritatis adactum, sibiipsi contradicere, & propriam damnare sententiam: quod ipsum pluribus facit verbis in sequentibus, quando scribit, Catholicos non dicere, nec sentire, liberum arbitrium habere ex se potentiam vllam, saltem proximam ad actus pietatis, sed eam accipere a Deo per gratiam praeuenientem. Et mirum est, quod Bellarminus in hoc ipso capite, vbi contra nos disputat, pro nobis contra Pontificios reliquos loquatur.

LIII. 2. Deut. 29. versu 3. & 4. Vos vidistis signa illa, portentaque ingentia, & non dedit tibi Dominus cor ad intelligendum, nec oculos ac videndum usque in praesentem diem. Ergo Domini solius est dare intelligentiam cordis, & aperire oculos. 3. Domini esse aperire oculos, dare Spiritum intelligentiæ, patet ex fequentib. dictis, Eph. 1. v. 17. 2. v. 5. 4. v. 7. Act. 26. v. 17. 2. Cor. 4. v. 6. Esas. 11. v. 2. Psal. 119. v. 34. 3. Reg. 3. v. 9. & 8. v. 58. 4. Pf. 51. v. 12. orat Dauid, cor mundum crea in me Domine. Sicut autem creatio est opus solius Dei, ita cordis mundi ingeneratio non nisi soli Deo conuenit. 5. Philip. 1. v. 6. Qui cœpit in vobis opus bonum, perficiet vsq; ad diem Iesu, & c. 2 v. 13. Deus est, qui operatur in vobis velle & perficere pro bonâ voluntate suâ.

LIV. Sexta classis dictorum continet loca, quibus declaratur, quòd conuersio non sit solum solutio vinculi, quo libertas arbitrij ligata fuerit, sed quod sit plena hominis Immutatio, renouatio, viuificatio. Sic enim argumentamur, Si per conuersionem homo mortuus viuificatur, cæcus illuminatur, vetus renouatur, durus emollitur, auersus conuertitur; tum sequetur, quòd homo nihil possit ad sui conuersionem efficienter conferre. Verum est prius, Ergo & posterius. Minorem probant plurima dicta, vt quòd Deus dicitur in conuersione frangere corda, 1. Reg. 10, v. 26. inclinare corda, 2. Reg. 19. v. 4. immutare corda, Iob. 12. v. 24. emollire corda, 2. Paral. 34. vers. 27. aperire cor, Act. 16. vers. 14. convertere cor, Luc. 1. vers. 17. Esdræ 6. vers. 22. circumcidere cor, Deut 30. vers. 6. conterere cor, Ezech. 6. vers. 9. creare cor novum, Psal. 51. vers. 19. Ephes. 4. v. 24 viuificare cor, Esai. 57, vers. 15. renouare cor, Eph. 4. v. 23 auferre cor lapideum, & dare cor novum: Ezech. 11. v. 19. & 36, v. 26. purificare cor, Act. 15. v. 9. excitare à mortuis, Ephes. 5. v. 14. viuificare, Eph. 2. v. 5. regenerare 1. Pet. 1. v. 3. Tit. 3. v. 5. Hinc opus est, vt corrumpatur externus homo, 2. Cor. 4. v. 16. vt destruatur corpus peccati, Rom. 6. v. 6. vnde & renati ipsius factura dicuntur, creati in Christo Iesu, Ephes. 2. v. 10. Ex quibus omnibus ad oculum demonstrari potest, per gratiam in conuersione non tolli quasi vinculum aliquod, quo soluto possit homo ex propriis viribus credere, & Deum diligere, sed quòd ingeneretur homini ista duan-sus de nouo adeóque homo prorsus immutetur.

LV. Septima classis dictorum continere potest illa loca, in quibus homo non-renatus vocatur mortuus in spiritualibus. Vbi enim mors est, ibi nulla superest vis siue facultas vitalis, quia mors est totalis vitæ privatio. Homo autem non-renatus, mortuus est spiritualiter. Ergò in illo nulla superest vis vitalis; vnde porrò colligimus: In quo nulla hæret vis vitalis, is nullo modo ad viuificationem sui potest concurrere; In homine non-renato nulla hæret vis vitalis. Ergò nullo modo ad viuificationem sui potest concurrere. Minor prioris Syllogismi probatur ex Ephes. 2. vers. 1. Et vos conuiuificauit, cum essetis mortui delictis & peccatis vestris. Similis locus legitur Coloff. 2. v. 13. Adde Iohan. 5. v. 25. & Matth. 8. v. 22. Excipit Bellarmin. l. 6. 13. distinguendo inter id, quod omnibus modis est mortuum, & id quod vno modo est mortuum, altero viuit. De primo mortuorum genere verum esse, quòd seipsos viuificare nequeant, sed non de secundo, quò refert hominem non renatum: Dicit enim, ipsum mortuum esse quoad vitam spiritualem; non mortuum sed vivum quoad vitam naturalem: posse igitur hominem, quatenus naturaliter viuit, cooperari ad recuperandam vitam spiritualem. Resp. Vanum prorsus hoc est effugium: Vt enim vita naturalis verè distincta est à vita spirituali, ita illius actiones planè nihil conducunt ad vitam gratiæ efficiendam: Conuersio enim non est actio naturalis, sed opus spirituale: Homo igitur naturalis nihil potest ad eam conferre.

LVI. Octaua classis dictorum continet loca, in quibus homines non renati dicuntur serui peccati. Quicunque autem peccato seruit, is non liber est ad edendas actiones spirituales. Atqui omnes homines non-renati seruiunt peccato. Ergo non sunt liberi ad edendas actiones spirituales. Minorem

Probant sequentia dicta. 1. Ioh. 8. v. 24, Omnis qui committit peccatum, seruus est peccati. 2. Rom 6. v. 14. An nescitis, quod cui sistitis vos seruos ad obediendum, eius serui estis, cui obeditis? & v. 19, Statuistis membra vestra seruire impuritati. 3. 2. P. 2. v 19. A quo quis superatus est, huic etiam in seruitutem addictus est.

LVII. Nona classis dictorum continet loca, quæ ostendunt hominem non posse gloriari; ac si suæ conuersionis quodammodo autor fuerit. Hinc colligimus: Si homo liberi foret arbitrii, tùm posset is, qui suo arbitrio rectè vtitur, gloriari contra infidelem, qui arbitrio suo malè vtitur. Consequens falsum est, satente ipso Bellarmino l. 1. c. 13. iuxta dicta 1. Cor. 1. v. 31. Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, c. 4. v 7. Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Si autem accepisti, quid gloriaris, quasi non acceperis? Huc pertinet illud Cypriani l. 3. ad Quirinum c. 4. In nullo gloriandum, quando nostrum nihil est.


### Question V. By what arguments can the true opinion concerning free will be…: LVIII. Reasons from the Analogy of Faith

LVIII. REASONS FROM THE ANALOGY OF FAITH.

1. From the conversion to be sought. Whatever must be sought singularly from God is not in our power. Conversion must be sought singularly from God. Therefore, conversion is not in the free power of man. The major premise is manifest: for what I already have, or what is situated within me, I do not in the least demand from another through prayers, whence Augustine says in On Nature and Grace, chapter 18: What is more foolish than to pray that you may do what you have in your power? And epistle 107: We are not praying to God at all, but pretending to pray, if we think that we ourselves, not He, do the things for which we pray: we are not giving thanks to God at all, but pretending to give them, if we do not think that He does the things for which we give Him thanks. The minor premise is certain from those Scriptures in which the saints also prayed. Ps 119:34, 73, 125, 144, Give me understanding. Jer 17:14, Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed. Jer 31:18, Convert me, O Lord, and I shall be converted. Lam 5:21. Convert us, O Lord, to You, and we shall be converted.

LIX. II. From the imperfection of renewal. If men who are reborn complain that they cannot from their own powers perfect a good work, or remain in faith, but they ask that God may perfect what He began, and preserve them in faith; much less can the non-reborn convert themselves to God from their own powers. But the former is from Rom. 7. Therefore the latter also. Luther proposes this argument thus on page 329: If the nature of man is so evil that in those who are reborn by the Spirit, it not only does not strive toward good, but even fights against and is averse to good, how would it strive toward good in those who, not yet reborn, serve under Satan in the old man?

LX. III. From the appellation of conversion. Our conversion is called: 1. Regeneration. 2. Creation of a new heart. 3. Change. 4. Quickening. Hence we argue: 1. Generation and regeneration are the works of one agent. But man cannot generate himself. Therefore neither can he regenerate himself. But God, just as He alone created man in the beginning, so He alone recreates or regenerates; whence Bernard was accustomed to say: It is of no less wisdom and power to recreate than to create man. For κτίσιν and ἀνακτίσιν walk with equal step, as Athanasius speaks somewhere. 2. It is not for man to create, but for God alone: Conversion is a creation. Therefore conversion is in no way to be ascribed to man, but to God alone. 3. No one can change the natures of things except the creator of natures. Conversion is a change of human nature. Therefore it belongs to God alone. 4. He who does not have spiritual life cannot spiritually quicken himself. But man in no way has spiritual life. Therefore he cannot quicken himself. Luther looked to this when he wrote on page 270: Just as man, before he was created so that he might be a man, does nothing or strives for nothing by which he might become a creature. Then, having been made and created, he does nothing or strives for nothing by which he might persevere as a creature; but both come to pass by the sole will of the omnipotent power and goodness of God, who creates and preserves us without us, but does not work in us without us, as those whom He created and preserved for this, that He might work in us and we might cooperate with Him, whether this happens outside His kingdom by general omnipotence, or within His kingdom by the singular power of His Spirit. Thus we say thereafter: Man, before he is renewed into a new creature of the kingdom of the Spirit, does nothing, attempts nothing, whereby he may be prepared for that renewal and kingdom. Then, having been recreated, he does nothing, attempts nothing, whereby he may persevere in that kingdom, but the Spirit alone does both in us, recreating us without us and preserving us once recreated, as James also says, "Of His own will He begat us with the word of His power, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of His creatures," he speaks of the renewed creature. But He does not work without us, as those whom He has recreated and preserves for this very purpose, that He might work in us, and we might cooperate with Him. Thus through us He preaches, has mercy on the poor, and consoles the afflicted.

LVI. IV. From the opposition of flesh and spirit. Contraries do not have the same, but contrary effects. Flesh and Spirit, man reborn and not reborn, the new man and the old, are contraries. Therefore they do not have the same, but contrary effects. Man therefore not reborn or carnal, as such, cannot produce a spiritual action, and consequently cannot prepare himself for his own conversion, or effect the same, because conversion is a spiritual action. Just as therefore the flesh is not Spirit, so also the flesh cannot produce spiritual works.

LXII. V. From various comparison. Many similitudes and comparisons are read both in Scripture and in the orthodox Fathers, instituted between free will and other things. For it is compared 1. To darkness. Hence we gather: Darkness does not illuminate itself. Human will is compared to darkness. Therefore it cannot illuminate itself. 2. To a dead person: But a dead person cannot vivify himself. The will in spiritual matters is dead. Therefore it cannot vivify itself. 3. To a hard stone: But a stone cannot soften itself.

4. A trunk: this cannot turn itself either to this or that side. 5. Untamed beasts: this does not tame itself nor render itself tame. 6. A pillar of salt, which the Form. Conc. page 661 uses as a comparison. But a pillar of salt understands or perceives nothing. 7. Mud, which cannot purge or cleanse itself. 8. A sword, which does not actively concur in its own motion while it is moved by someone's hand, but only passively.

LXIII. VI. From the commendation of divine grace. I refer here to the rule of Luther, set forth in his book On the Bondage of the Will, p. 273. As many places as there are in the divine Scriptures which make mention of help, so many are they which abolish free will. For grace is needed for this reason, and for this reason the help of grace is conferred, because free will of itself can do nothing, and cannot even will the good.

LXIV. TESTIMONIES OF THE FATHERS AND OF ADVERSARIES. Irenaeus, book 3, chapter 65. Life is not from us, nor from our nature, but is given according to the grace of God. Cyprian, book 3, to Quirinus: We must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own. Ambrose, on chapter 1 of Luke: The will of men is prepared by God. For that God may be honored by a saint, it is the grace of God. Basil, on humility: We owe everything to the grace and gift of God. Augustine, in the Enchiridion to Laurentius, chapter 30: Man, using free will badly, destroyed both himself and it. For just as he who kills himself, certainly kills himself by living, but by killing himself he does not live, nor will he be able to raise himself up when he has killed himself. So, when sin was committed by free will, free will was lost by the victory of sin, for by whom anyone is overcome, to him he is also addicted as a slave. This is the opinion of the Apostle Peter, which, since it is true, what kind of liberty, I ask, can a slave who is addicted have, unless when it delights him to sin? For a slave is indeed free when he willingly does the will of his master; and by this, he who is a slave of sin is free to sin. Book 1, to Boniface, chapter 3. This will, which is free in evil things because it delights in evil things, is therefore not free in good things because it has not been set free. Book 1, Retractations, chapter 15. The will which is pious is free only in so far as it has been set free. Epist. 144. Without the grace of God the will cannot be free. L. 3. against the two letters of the Pelagians, c. 8. Free will, once captured, is of no avail except for sinning. L. de nat. & grat. c. 53. The possibility of nature has been wounded, injured, vexed, and lost. Epist. 107: We have lost free will for loving God through the magnitude of the first sin. Chrysostom homil. 30. on the Acts of the Apostles. Let us think that nothing is our own, since even faith itself is not our work: but that it is not ours, but rather God's, hear Paul saying, Even this is not of us; it is the gift of God. Likewise in the homily on Adam & Eve. Through whom it comes about that we are found both to will and to do something good, by which help and gift of God free will is not taken away but set free, so that from dark it becomes light, from crooked straight, from languid healthy, from imprudent prudent: For such is the goodness of God that He wishes those things to be our merits which are His own gifts: For He acts in us, so that we may will and do what He wills. Prosper c. 21. Infidelity snatched away faith, captivity took away liberty, nor could any portion of virtues reside there, when such a great crowd of vices had broken in. Fulgent. de incarn. & grat. ca. 13. Adam sins, who was created without the necessity of sinning; in that, by sinning, he lost the health of his soul, he immediately lost also the faculty of thinking about those things which pertain to God: He who desires more, let him consult the most learned commonplaces of Mr. Dr. Gerhard, our honorable friend, where he will find many testimonies of the Fathers, divided into five classes. For the Fathers 1: attribute everything to divine grace, nothing to human powers. 2. They say that free will with respect to spiritual things has been lost, and is of no avail except for sinning. 3. They assign the beginning of good motions also to divine grace. 4. They speak distinctly about the powers of free will in civil and spiritual matters. 5: And finally they teach that to will grace, and to assent to grace, is not of our powers, but of the human will, which hypotheses, confirmed by many testimonies, see T.

2. The aforementioned places of Gerhard, sect. 44. 45. 46. 47. 48. LXV. Furthermore, certain Scholastics, and they themselves adversaries, when they judge without prejudice, often approve our opinion, and thus we can oppose the testimonies of their own people to the Jesuits. σεμνὴ ἦ καὶ ἡ παρὰ τῶν ἐχθρῶν μαρτυρία, Grave and worthy of suspicion also is the testimony which proceeds from enemies, says Isidore of Pelusium, epistle 228. We wish therefore to note the following. 1. Lombard, book 2, sent. dist. 25, letter G. After sin, he says, before the restoration of grace, man is pressed by concupiscence and is overcome: and he has infirmity in evil; but he does not have grace in good; and therefore he can sin, and cannot not sin, even damnably. Again, letter H. through sin natural goods are corrupted, and gratuitous ones are withdrawn: For man incurs for sin the punishment in the corruption and depression of free will. 2. Gregory of Rimini, book 2, sent. dist. 26. 27. 28. accuses the remaining Scholastics that in the doctrine concerning the free will of man they are addicted to the Pelagian heresy, and he commends Thomas Bradwardine, who in the year of Christ 1330 had published a tripartite work on the grace of God against free will. 3. John Ferus the Minorite, on chapter 1 of John, verse 23, asserts that the old birth, and thus all the powers of nature which are transfused into offspring by natural propagation, are condemned in Scripture, whence the Spanish Expurgatory Index, fol. 123, orders these axioms to be expunged from the commentaries of Ferus: Nature produces no other than evil fruits: Our will is evil, and the root of all evils. 4. The judgment of Caesar on art. 18. The A. C. [Augsburg Confession] has it thus: In the eighteenth article they confess the power of free will, that it has liberty to effect civil righteousness, but does not have the power without the Holy Spirit to effect the righteousness of God, which Confession is accepted and approved. 5. John of Daventer commends the same article, as agreeing in all things with Papal doctrine. I shall discuss, quit, if more is attributed by our side to free will than these (Confessors) attribute. 6. Johannes Hoffmeister: Nothing, he says, does this article offend us, nor shall we interpret anything in a bad sense, since it seems to be taken from the monuments of the pious Fathers, nay, and from the holy Scriptures. 7. Georgius Cassander in Consultat. de Controuersi. fidei artic. 18. page 117. The sum of this controversy, which has existed both formerly and today concerning free will, consists in this: what is the value of free will or the will for obtaining righteousness before God? Truly the Orthodox have always contended against the Pelagians and Manichaeans that the righteousness by which we are justified before GOD is to be attributed not to the virtue of free will or of the will vitiated by sin, but to the singular grace of GOD, not that which we have from the nature in which we were created, which we have in common with the infidel and the impious, but that grace which is through faith in Jesus Christ, which belongs only to those whose faith itself is, by which grace a new will is not created, nor is an unwilling will forced, but the weak is healed, the depraved is corrected, and it is converted from bad to good, and is drawn by a certain interior motion, so that from unwilling one is made willing, and willingly consents to the divine calling, and afterwards obeys the same divine will as it cooperates, and by persevering in good works through the same grace, enters into the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom through the same grace, etc. He alleges furthermore. 119: this saying of Bonaventure: It is the mark of pious minds that they attribute nothing to themselves, but everything to the grace of God, whence however much one gives to the grace of God, one does not depart from piety, even if by attributing much to the grace of God, one subtracts something from the power of nature or free will. But when something is subtracted from the grace of God and attributed to nature, which belongs to grace, there danger can intervene. Let the Jesuits therefore consider these testimonies so clearly brought forth, and cease to accuse our doctrine of heresy, lest by proving the same dogma in Papistic writers as Catholic, and condemning it in ours as heretical, they betray their extreme malice and lust for slandering.

Latin:

LVIII. RATIONES AB ANALOGIA FIDEI.

1. A petenda conuersione. Quocunque à Deo singulariter petendum, id in nostra non est potestate. Conuersio singulariter à Deo petenda est. Ergò conuersio non est in libera hominis potestate. Maior est manifesta: quod enim iam habeo, vel in me situm est, id per preces ab alio minimè efflagito, vnde Augustinus inquit de nat. & grat cap. 18. Quid stultius, quam orare, vt facias, quod in potestate habes? & epist. 107. Prorsus non oramus Deum, sed orare nos fingimus, si nos ipsos, non ipsum putamus facere, quæ oramus: prorsus non gratias agimus Deo, sed agere nos fingimus, si vnde illi gratias agimus, ipsum facere non putamus. Minor certa est ex his Scripturis, in quibus sancti etiam orarunt. Ps. 119. v. 34. 73. 125. 144. Da mihi intellectum. Ierem. 17. v. 14. Sana me Domine, & sanabor. Ierem. 31. v. 18. Conuerte me Domine & conuertar. Thren. 5. v. 21. Conuerte nos Domine ad te, & conuertemur.

LIX. II. A renouationis imperfectione. Si homines renati conqueruntur, quòd ex proprijs viribus nequeant bonum opus perficere, vel in fide permanere, sed petunt, vt Deus perficiat quod cœpit, & illos in fide conseruet; multò minùs non-renati ex propriis viribus ad Deum se possunt conuertere. Verum prius ex Rom. 7. Ergò & posterius. Lutherus hoc argumentum ita proponit pag. 329. Si natura hominis adeò mala est, vt in ijs qui Spiritu renati sunt, non modò non conetur ad bonum, sed etiam pugnet & auersetur bonum, quomodo in illis, qui nondum renati in veteri homine sub Satana seruiunt, ad bonum conaretur?

LX. III. A conuersionis appellatione. Vocatur nostra conuersio. 1. Regeneratio. 2. Creatio cordis noui 3. Immutatio. 4. Viuificatio. Hinc argumentamur: 1. Generatio & regeneratio sunt vnius agentis opera. Atqui homo seipsum non potest generare. Ergò nec generare. DEVS autem sicuti solus hominem primitùs creauit, ita & solus recreat vel regenerat; vnde Bernhardus dicere est solitus: Non minoris est sapientiæ & virtutis recreare, quàm creave hominem. Pari enim passu ambulant κτίσιν & ἀνακτίσιν, vt Athanasius alicubi loquitur. 2. Hominis non est creare, sed solius Dei: Conuersio est creatio Ergò conuersio nullo modo adscribenda homini, sed soli Deo. 3. Naturas rerum mutare nemo potest, nisi creator naturarum. Conuersio est immutatio naturæ humanæ. Ergò soli Deo competit. 4. Qui vitam spiritualem non habet, is spiritualiter sefe viuificare nequit, Atqui homo vitam spiritualem nullo modo habet. Ergò seipsum viuificare nequit. Huc respexit Lutherus, cùm scripsit pag. 270: Sicut homo, antequam crearetur, vt sit homo, nihil facit aut conatur, quo fiat creatura. Deinde factus & creatus nihil facit aut conatur, quo perseueret creatura; sed vtrumque fit, solâ voluntate omnipotentis virtutis & bonitatis Dei, nos sine nobis creantis & conseruantis, sed non operaturnobis, fine nobis, vt quos ad hæc creauit & feruauit, vt innobis operaretur & nos ei cooperaremur, siue ho fiat extra regnum suum generali omnipotentia; siueintrar gnum suum singulari virtute Spiritus sui. Sic deinceps d.cimus Homo antequam renouetur in nouam creaturam regni spiritus, nihil facit, nihil conatur, quò paretur ad eam renouasionem & regnum. Deinde recreatus, nihil facit, nihil conatur, quò perseueret in eo regno, sed vtrumque f. cit solus spiritus in nobis, nos sine nobis re reans & conseruans recreatos, vt & Iacobus dicit, Voluntariè genuit nos verbo virtutis suæ, vt essemus initium creaturæ eius, loquitur de renouata creatura. Sed non operatur sine nobis, vt quos in hoc ipsum recreauit & conseruat, vt operaretur innobis, ei nos cooperaremur, Sic per nos prædicat, miseretur pauperibus, consolatur afflictos.

LVI. IV. A carnis & spiritus oppositione. Contraria non eosdem, sed contrarios habent effectus. Caro & Spritus, homo renatus & non-renatus, homo novus, & vetus, sunt contraria. Ergò non eosdem, sed contrarios habent effectus. Homo igitur non renatus seu carnalis, quà talis, non potest spiritualem producere actionem, & per consequens non potest se ad sui conuersionem præparare, vel eandem efficere, quia conuersio est actio spiritualis. Sicut igitur caro non est Spiritus, ita etiam caro spiritualia opera nequit producere.

LXII. V. A varia comparatione. Leguntur tùm in Scriptura tùm in Patribus orthodoxis multæ similitudines & comparationes, inter liberum arbitrium, & res alias institutæ. Comparatur enim 1. Tenebris. Hinc colligimus : Tenebræ seipsas non illuminant. Arbitrium humanum comparatur tenebris. Ergò seipsum illuminare nequit. 2. Mortuo : Mortuus autem seipsum viuificare nequit. Arbitrium in spiritualibus est mortuum. Ergò seipsum viuificare nequit. 3. Duro lapidi: Lapis autem seipsum emollire nequit.

4. Trunco: hic nequit se vel in hanc vel illam partem vertere. 5. Ferae indomitae: haec seipsam non domat nec cicurem reddit. 6. Statuae salis, quo simili vtitur Form. Conc. pag. 661. Statua salis autem nihil intelligit vel percipit. 7. Limo, qui se ipsum non poteit purgare aut mundare. 8. Gladio, qui ad motum suum non concurrit actiue, dum manu alicuius agitur, sed tantummodo passiue.

LXIII. VI. A gratia diuina commendatione. Refero huc regula Lutheri, positam in l. de seru. arb. p. 273. Quotquot sunt loca in Scripturis diuinis, qua meminerunt auxilij, tot sunt, quæ tollunt liberum arbitrium. Nam ideo gratia opus est, ideo auxilium gratia confertur, quod liberum arbitrium per se se nihil possit, & ne quidem velle bonum possit.

LXIV. TESTIMONIA PATRVM ET ADVERSARIORVM. Irenæus l. 3. c. 65. Non ex nobis, neque ex natura nostra est vita, sed secundum gratiam Dei datur. Cyprianus l. 3. ad Quirinum: In nullo gloriandum est, quando nihil est nostrum. Ambrosius in cap. 1. Luc. A Deo præparatur voluntas hominum. Vt enim Deus honorificetur à sancto; Dei gratia est. Basilius de humil. Totum Dei gratiæ & dono debemus. Augustinus in Enchir. ad Laureat. c. 30. Libero arbitrio malè vtens homo, & se perdidit & ipsum. Sicut enim qui occidit se, vtique viuendo occidit se, sed se occidendo non vivit, nec se ipsum poterit resuscitare, cùm occiderit. Ita cùm libero peccaretur arbitrio, victore peccato amissum est & liberum arbitrium, à quo enim quis deuictus est, huic & seruus addictus est. Petri Apostoli est ista sententia, quæ cùm vera sit, qualis quæso potest serui addicti esse libertas, nisi quando eum peccare delectat? liberè licet enim seruus, qui sui Domini voluntatem libenter facit: ac per hoc ad peccandum liber est, qui peccati seruus est. L. 1. ad Bonif. c. 3. Hæc voluntas quæ libera est in malis, quia delectatur malis, ideò libera in bonis non est, quia liberata non est. L. 1. Retract. cap. 15. Voluntas pia in tantum libera est, quia in tantum liberata est. Epist. 144. Sine gratia Dei non potest esse liberavoluntas. L. 3. contra duas Pelag. epist. c. 8. Liberum arbitrium captiuatum non nisi ad peccandum valet. L. de nat. & grat. c. 53. Naturæ possibilitas vulnerata, sauciata, vexata perdita est. Epist. 107: Liberum arbitrium ad diligendum Deum primi peccati granditate perdidimus. Chrysoftomus homil. 30. in Actor. Apostol. Nihil nostrum esse putemus, quandoquidem & ipsa fides non est nostrum opus: quòd autem non sit nostrum, sed magis Dei, audi Paulum dicentem, Etiam hoc non ex nobis; Dei donum est. Item in homil. de Adam & Eva. Per quem sit, vt aliquid boni & velle inueniamur, & facere, quo vtique auxilio & munere Dei non aufertur liberum arbitrium sed liberatur, vt de tenebroso lucidum, de pravo rectum; de de languido sanum, de imprudente prouidum fiat: Tanta enim est bonitas Dei, vt nostra esse velit merita, quæ ipsius sunt dona: Agit enim in nobis, vt quod vult, velimus & agamus. Prosper c. 21. Infidelitas rapuit fidem, captivitas abstulit libertatem, nec potuit illic vlla portio residere virtutum, cùm tanta irruperat turma vitiorum. Fulgent. de incarn. & grat. ca. 13. Peccant Adamus, qui sine peccandi necessitate creatus est; in eo, quòd animæ sanitatem delinquendo perdidit, etiam illa cogitandi, quæ ad Deum pertinent, amisit protinus facultatem: Plura qui desiderat, is doctissimos locos communes Dn. D. Gerhardi, Amici nostri honorandi; consulat, vbi multa Patrum testimonia, in quinque classes tributa inueniet. Nam Patres 1: omnia diuinæ gratiæ, viribus humanis nihil tribuunt. 2. Arbitrium respectu spiritualium dicunt amissum esse, ac nihil valere, nisi ad peccandum. Initium quoque bonorum motuum diuinæ gratiæ adsignant 4. De viribus arbitrij in ciuilibus & spiritualibus distinctè loquuntur. 5: Et denique docent, velle gratiam, & assentiri gratiæ, non esse virium nostrarum, sed voluntatis humanæ, quas hypotheses multis testimoniis firmatas vide T.

2. LL. CC. Gerhardi, sect. 44. 45. 46. 47. 48. LXV. Præterea Scholastici quidam, & ipsi adversarij, cùm absque præjudicio iudicant, sententiam nostram sæpè adprobant, adeoque propria suorum testimonia, Iesu Vitis opponere possumus. σεμνὴ ἦ καὶ ἡ παρὰ τῶν ἐχθρῶν μαρτυρία, Grave & suspiciendum etiam, quod ab hostibus proficiscitur testimonium, ait Isidorus Pelusiota epist. 228. Notarê ergò volumus sequentia. 1. Lombardus l. 2. sent. dist. 25. lit. G. Post peccatum, inquit, ante reparationem gratiæ premitur homo à concupiscentiâ, & vincitur: & habet infirmitatem in malo; sed non habet gratiam in bono; & ideò potest peccare, & non potest non peccare etiam damnabiliter. Rursus lit. H. per peccatum naturalia bona sunt corrupta, & gratuita detracta: Incurrit enim homo pro peccato pœnam in corruptione & depressione liberi arbitrij. 2. Gregorius Ariminensis l. 2. sent. dist. 26. 27. 28. accusat scholasticos reliquos, quòd in doctrinâ de libero hominis arbitrio hæresi Pelagianæ sint addicti, & commendat Thomam Bradvardinum, qui anno Christi 1330. opus tripartitum de gratiâ Dei contra liberum arbitrium ediderat. 3. Iohannes Ferus Minorita in cap. 1. Iohannis vers 23. veterem natiuitatem, atque adeò omnes vires naturæ, quæ naturali propagatione transfundūtur in sobolem, in Scriptura damnari asserit, vnde Index Expurgat. Hisp. fol. 123. ex commentariis Feri expungere iubet hæc axiomata: Non alios quàm molos fructus profert natura ex se: Voluntas nostra mala, & omnium malorum rad x. 4. Iudicium Cæsaris de art. 18. A. C. sic habet: In articulo decimo octauo confitentur liberi arbitrij virtutem, quod habeat libertatem ad efficiendam ciuilem iustitiam, sed non habeat vim sine Spiritu S. efficiendæ iustitiæ Dei, quæ Confessio acceptatur & approbatur. 5. Ioh. à Dauẽtriâ commendat eundum articulum, tanquam per omnia cum doctrina Pontificia consentientem. Disseram, inquit, si plus à nostris libero arbitrio attribution sit, quàm isti (Confessores) tribuunt. 6. Iohannes Hoffmeisterus: Nihil, inquit, offendi nos hic articulus, nec quicquam in malam partem interpretabimur, quoniam ex monumentis piorum Patrum, imò & ex sacris Scripturis videtur desumtus. 7. Georgius Cassander in Consultat. de Controuersi. fidei artic. 18. pag. 117. Summa huius controuersiæ, quæ & olim & hodie de libero arbitrio extitit, in eo consistit, quid valeat liberum arbitrium seu voluntas ad Iustitiam coram Deo consequendam?
