Sanè Orthodoxi semper contra Pelagianos & Manichæos contenderunt, iustitiam, quâ iustificamur coram DEO, artribuendam esse non virtuti liberi arbitrij seu voluntatis per peccatum vitiatæ, sed singulari gratiæ DEI, non quàm habemus ex naturâ, in quâ creati sumus, quæ nobis cum infidelibus & impijs communis sit, sed eâ gratiâ, quæ est per fidem Iesu Christi, quæ tantùmmodò eorum est quorum est ipsa fides, quâ gratiâ non noua voluntas creatur, neque invita voluntas cogitur, sed infirma sanatur, deprauata corrigitur, & ex malâ in bonam conuertitur, acinteriore quodam motu trahitur, vt ex nolente volens efficiatur, & diuiæ vocationi libenter consentiat, & postea eadem cooperanti diuinæ voluntati obediat, & in bonis operibus per eandem gratiam perseuerando, ex eadem gratia hæreditatem regni cœlestis adeat, &c. Allegat insuper. 119: hoc Bonauenturæ dictum: Hoc piarum mentium est, vt nil sibi tribuant, sed totum gratiæ Dei, vnde quantumcunque aliquis det gratiæ Dei, à pietate non recedit, etiamsi multà tribuendo gratiæ Dei, aliquid subtrahit potestati naturæ vel liberi arbitrij. Cùm verò aliquid gratiæ Dei subtrahitur, & naturæ tribuitur, quod gratiæ est, ibi potest periculum interuenire. Hæc igitur testimonia tàm perspicuè prolata Iesu Witæ considerent, & nostram doctrinam hæreseos accusare cessent, ne suam, idem dogma in Scriptoribus Papisticis vt Catholicum probando, in nostris vt hæreticum damnando, extremam pro dant malitiam, & calumniandi libidinem.


### Question VI. & Last. What is the use of the doctrine concerning the servitude of the will?

LXVI. As all Scripture is useful, so is every article of faith deduced from Scripture. The same can be affirmed of the present article, the use of which is given as manifold, and can be expressed in various ways. From it flows 1. The didactic use, by which we are taught concerning the sublimity of grace, and the greatness of the benefits of God. For He Himself is the one who works in us both to will and to perform. He Himself goes before the unwilling, that he may will; He follows the willing, that he may not will in vain: He goes before, that we may be healed; He follows, that we may be invigorated once healed; He goes before, that we may be called; He follows, that we may be glorified; He goes before, that we may live piously; He follows, that we may always remain with Him, just as Augustine speaks in the book on nature and grace, ch. 32. Therefore, let us humbly acknowledge such great grace of God, and always celebrate it with a grateful mind.

LXVII. 2. The refutatory use, since when this doctrine is rightly understood we are able to better resist adversaries and stop the mouths of heretics. Two precipices of errors in particular are to be avoided here. 1. The absolute necessity of the Manichaeans. 2. The freedom of the Pelagian will. From the former, despair can easily arise; from the latter, boasting. Both are guarded against while walking the middle path. We therefore assert freedom in civil matters against the Manichaeans; we deny freedom in spiritual matters against the Pelagians; by which agreement we can easily refute and convince any who speak against us on this article.

LXVIII. 2. The corrective use, because this article contributes much to shaking off the security by which some imagine to themselves that it is in their own powers to turn themselves to God and to persevere in faith. But in truth the matter stands far otherwise: faith is kindled by God alone; He is always to be invoked, that He may give us to will and to perform, that what is lacking to our powers, He Himself may bestow, and most clemently complete the work begun in us. Just as freedom of the will expels security, so too it expels sloth. Let no one think, I will wait with a secure and idle mind until the Holy Spirit converts me, because I can effect nothing in spiritual matters. This is an abuse, not a use of sound doctrine. For we are not converted ἐνθουσιαςικῶς, but ἀκητικῶς through the hearing of the word and the use of legitimate means, by which faith is begotten and preserved. If those are rashly neglected, no one ought to promise himself an extraordinary aid and arrival of the Holy Spirit.

LXIX. 4. The παιδευτικὸς use, because we are urged 1. to true humility. For when we acknowledge our corruption and the weakness of our powers, pride yields, and true humility of heart is born. Naturalists write of the peacock that, spreading its wings against the sun and gazing at itself, it grows proud, but when it turns its eyes to its feet, it lays aside its arrogance. Thus men are usually wont to be proud, contemplating their own gifts; but the elation of the mind will vanish if the servitude of our will is diligently considered, since through it the foulness and deformity of our nature is placed clearly enough before our eyes. Therefore, one must boast in nothing, because nothing is our own. Cyprian, book 3 to Quirinus: What do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you boast? 1 Cor. 4:7. That saying of Hugo is beautiful: My evils are purely evil, and they are mine; but my good things are neither purely good, nor are they mine.

2. To devout prayer. For he who knows his own sickness seeks the Physician all the more willingly. He who acknowledges his own weakness implores help all the more ardently. Prayers are never so devout if we flatter ourselves and attribute to ourselves the ability to do good. The heavenly Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask, Luke 11:13, where, however, the discourse is not so much about the first spark of faith as about its increase for neither do prayers themselves proceed from the will and natural powers, but are excited by the Holy Spirit in those who do not resist, inasmuch as He alone is the spirit of prayer, Zech. 12. v. 10. and teaches us to pray, Rom. 8 ver. 26. without whom no one can call Jesus Lord, 1. Cor. 12. ver 3. Moreover, we do not pray at all, but we pretend to pray, if we think that we ourselves, not He, do the things which we pray for, as August. epist. 107. speaks.

3. For due thanksgiving. For since we have everything that we are able to do from God, not from ourselves; we deservedly venerate and proclaim that kind Lord. But as much as is attributed to our own powers, so much is detracted from God and His proclamation. For we do not give thanks to God at all; but we pretend to give them, if we do not think that He does that for which we give Him thanks, according to the judgment of Augustine l. d.

4. For solicitous and indefatigable industry. For because we are renewed by grace; we certainly ought to be the more provident, lest we lose it, and by sinning again forfeit it. For if this happens, we do not so much do an injury to our nature, as we offend the Holy Spirit Himself, who works conversion in us, and bestows powers to that end, not that we should be idle, but that we should cooperate with Him, and be renewed from day to day.

XXL. 5. The consolatory use: For because we hear that salvation is not to be acquired by our own powers, but is to be conferred from the grace of God, we can conceive the greater hope, nor do we have any cause for doubting on account of the imperfection of our powers. If the flesh lusts, and struggles against the spirit, we ought not to despair, since God who gave the will, will also give the power to perform, Phil. 2. ver. 13. Hence Augustine l. de dogmat. Eccles. cap. 6. writes: We live more safely if we give everything to God, and not if we entrust ourselves partly to Him, and partly to ourselves.

LXXI. These are the principal uses of the sound doctrine concerning the servitude of the will, which can be expressed in other ways also, namely that it makes 1. πρὸς γνῶσιν Θεῶ, whose mercy we see in the converted, that we may trust; his justice in the unconverted, that we may fear. 2. πρὸς γνῶσιν ἑαυτῶ, while our infirmity is set forth, and all states of human nature are recalled to memory. 3. πρὸς γνῶσιν Διαβόλε, whose craftiness we observe, who both seduced our first parents and solicits us to place an obstacle to the converting Spirit. Thence the doctrine of both the Law and the Gospel becomes known: of the Law, while the disease and the punishment due to sin are indicated: of the Gospel, while the remedy, the grace and mercy of God, is shown. Finally, by this doctrine we are stimulated to the three cardinal Christian virtues, namely 1. to piety, that we may worship God who is so merciful. 2. to charity, that we may love our neighbor the more, the more we know his powers to be weaker. 3. to sobriety, that we may not lose again what we have received. May the Father of mercy, without whom we can do nothing, and through whom we can do all things, to whom be honor and thanksgiving forever, grant that the doctrine explained thus far may produce all these most wholesome uses in us: AMEN.

GLORY TO GOD ALONE.

Latin:

LXVI. Vt omnis Scriptura vtilis est, sic quiuis articulus fidei ex Scripturâ deductus. Idem affirmari potest de præsenti articulo, cuius vsus datur multiplex, modísque variis efferri potest. Fluit inde 1. Vsus διδασκαλικὸς, quo docemur de sublimitate gratiæ, & magnitudine beneficiorum Dei. Ipse enim est, qui & velle & perficere in nobis operatur. Ipse præuenit nolentem, vt velit; subsequitur volentem, nè frustrà velit: præuenit, vt sanemur; subsequitur, vt sanati vegetemur; præuenit, vt vocemur; subsequitur, vt glorificemur; præuenit, vt piè viuamus; subsequitur, vt cùm illo semper maneamus, quemadmodum Augustinus loquitur lib. de nat. & grat. c. 32. Tantam ergò Dei gratiam humiliter agnoscamus, & de voto semper animo celebremus.

LXVII. 2. Vsus ἐλεγκτικὸς, cùm rectè cognitâ hâc doctrinâ aduersariis meliùs resistere, & hæreticis ora obstruere valeamus. Duo imprimis errorum præcipitia hîc vitanda sunt. 1. Absoluta Manichæorum necessitas. 2. Pelagiani arbitrij libertas. Ex illa desperatio, ex hac gloriatio facilè oriri potest. Vtrumque præcauetur, dum mediâ viâ inceditur. Asserimus ergò libertatem in ciuilibus contra Manichæos; negamus libertatem in spiritualibus, cõtra Pelagianos; quo pacto ἀντιλέγοντας quosvis in hos articulo facilè redarguere possumus & conuincere.

LXVIII. 2. Vsus ἐπανορθωτικὸς, quia multùm conducit hic articulus ad excutiendam securitatem, quâ quidam sibi imaginantur, in suis esse viribus, ad Deum se conuertere, & in fide perseuerare. At verò res longè aliter se habet: à Deo solo fides accenditur, hic semper inuocandus est, vt det nobis velle & perficere, vt quod deest nostris viribus, ipse largiatur, & opus in nobis cœptum clementissimè consummet. Vti verò securitatem, ita & desidiam expellit libertas arbitrii. Nemo cogitet, secura & otiosa mente expectabo, donec Spiritus sanctus me conuertat, quia in spiritualibus nihil efficere valeo. Abusus hic est, non vsus doctrinæ sanæ. Nec enim ἐνθουσιαςικῶς conuertimur, sed ἀκητικῶς per auditum verbi & vsurpationem legitimorum mediorum, quibus fides gignitur & conseruatur. Illis temerè neglectis, nemo sibi extraordinarium Spiritus sancti adiutorium & aduentum polliceri debet.

LXIX. 4. Vsus παιδευτικὸς quia instigamur 1. ad veram humilitatem. Cùm enim nostram corruptionem & virium infirmitatem agnoscimus, cedet superbia, & vera cordis humilitas nascetur. De pauone scribunt Physici, quòd Sole aduerso alas suas expandens, seque ipsum intuens superbiat, ad pedes verò cùm oculos conuertit, fastum deponat. Ita plerumque superbire solent homines, dona sua contemplantes; sed euanescet animi elatio, si seruitus arbitrii nostri diligenter consideretur, quippè per quam fœditas & deformitas naturæ satis luculenter ante oculos nobis ponitur. In nullo igitur gloriandum, quia nihil nostrum est. Cyprianus l. 3. ad Quir. Quid habes, quod non accepisti? Si autem accepisti, quid gloriaris? 1. Cor. 4. v. 7. Pulchrum est illud Hugonis; Mala mea purè mala sunt, & mea sunt; bona autem mea nec purè bona sunt, nec mea sunt.

2. Ad deuotam orationem. Qui enim nouit suam ægritudinem, eò lubentiùs quærit Medicum. Qui agnoscit suam infirmitatem, eò ardentiùs implorat opem. Nunquam adeò deuotæ sunt preces, si nobis ipsis blandimur, & facultatem benè agendi attribuimus. Pater cœlestis dat Spiritum sanctum petentibus, Luc. 11. v. 13. vbi tamen non tàm de primâ fidei scintilla, quàm incremento sermo est: nec enim preces ipsæ ab arbitrio & viribus naturalibus proficiscuntur, sed à Spiritu sancto in non-resistentibus excitantur, quippe qui solus est precum spiritus, Zachar. 12. v. 10. & docet nos orare, Rom. 8 ver. 26. sine quo nemo Iesum potest vocare Dominum, 1. Cor. 10. ver 3. Prorsus autem non oramus, sed orare nos fingimus, si nos ipsos, non ipsum putamus facere, quæ oramus, vt August. epist. 107. loquitur.

3. Ad debitam gratiarum actionem. Cùm enim omne, quod possumus, à Deo habeamus, non ex nobis; meritò illum benignum Dominum veneramur & prædicamus. Quantum verò nostris viribus tribuitur, tantum Deo, ejusque præconio derogatur. Prorsus enim non gratias agimus Deo; sed agere nos fingimus, si unde illi gratias agimus, ipsum facere non putamus, juxtá Augustini judicium l. d.

4. Ad solicitam & indefessam industriam. Quia enim ex gratia renovamur; vtique eò magis esse debemus prouidi, ne illam perdamus, & iterum peccando amittamus. Hoc enim si fiat, non tàm naturę nostræ injuriam facimus, quàm ipsum lædimus Spiritum sanctum, qui conuersionem in nobis operatur, & vires eum in finem largitur, non vt otiosi simus, sed ipsi cooperemur, & de die in diem renouemur.

XXL. 5. Vsus παραμυθητικός: Quia enim non nostris viribus salutem acquirendam, sed ex gratiâ Dei conferendam esse audimus, eo maiorem spem concipere possumus, nec vllam dubitandi ob imperfectionem virium causam habemus. Si caro concupiscat, & reluctetur spiritui, desperare non debemus, quoniam Deus qui dedit velle, dabit etiam perficere, Phil. 2. ver. 13. Hinc Augustinus l. de dogmat. Eccles. cap. 6. scribit: Tutiores viuimus, si totum Deo damus, non autem si nos isti ex parte, & nobis ex parte committimus.

LXXI. Hi sunt præcipui vsus sanæ de seruitute arbitrij doctrinę, qui alijs etiam modis efferri possunt, nempe quod faciat 1. πρὸς γνῶσιν Θεῶ, cuius misericordiam videmus in conuersis, vt confidamus; iustitiam in non conuersis, vt timeamus. 2. πρὸς γνῶσιν ἑαυτῶ, dum infirmitas nostra proponitur, & omnes naturæ humanæ status in memoriam reuocantur. 3. πρὸς γνῶσιν Διαβόλε, cuius calliditatem animaduertimus, qui & parentes primos seduxit, & nos ad obicem Spiritui convertenti ponendum solicitat. Deinde innotescit hinc & legis & Euangelij doctrina: Legis dum indicatur morbus, & pœna peccato debita: Euangelij, dum monstratur remedium, Dei gratia & misericordia Tandem ad tres Cardinales Christiã nį virtutes hâc doctrinâ stimulamus. nempe 1. ad pietatem, vt colamus Deum tàm misericordem. 2. ad charitatem, vt eò magis diligamus proximum, quò vires eius debiliores nouimus. 3, ad sobrietatem, ne quod accepimus, iterum amittamus. Hosce vsvs saluberrimos omnes, vt doctrina hactenus explicata in nobis pariat, faxit Pater misericordię, sine quo nihil possumus, & per quem omnia possumus, cui sit honor & gratiarũ actio in æternum: AMEN.

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 26 Disputation III. On the Papist Arguments for Free Will

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent, Master Aegidius Hunnius of Wittenberg.

Thesis I.

After we have sufficiently corroborated the true opinion concerning the enslaved will with the sayings of Scripture and with reasons, nothing else remains than that the arguments of the adversaries be briefly discussed for the sake of confirming the truth. And since Bellarmine has diligently collected them, we shall primarily follow his footsteps and refute in few words the principal reasons proposed in books 5 and 6. Furthermore, since Luther's book on the Bondage of the Will offends many, it will not be without reason to explain, by way of a conclusion, what is to be determined concerning it. There will therefore be two principal questions of this discussion: I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections? II. What is to be determined concerning Luther's book, which has the title, On the Bondage of the Will?

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. M. Ægidio Hunnio Wittemberg.

Thesis I.

POsteaquã scripturæ dictis & rationib. verâ de seruo arbitrio sētentiâ satis corroboravimus, nihil aliud supersest, quam vt argumenta Aduersariorum veritatis confirmandae causa, breuiter discutiantur. Cumque illa Bellarminus diligenter collegerit; eius vestigia inprimis sequemur & praecipuas rationes l. 5. & 6. propositas paucis confutabimus Praeterea quoniam multos offendit Lutheri liber de Seruo arbitrio: non absq; re erit, quid de illo statuendum, colophonis loco exponere. Duae igitur huius disputationis quaestiones erunt principales: I. Quid ad Bellarmini obiectiones responderi possit & debeat? II. Quid de Lutheri libro, cui titulus, De Seruo arbitrio statuendum sit?


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?

II. The adversaries fight against us both with sayings of Scripture and with certain reasons. The sayings of Scripture are proposed in six distinct classes by Bellarmine in book 5, chapter 18 and following, to which he afterwards adds even more in book 6. We shall follow him κατα ποδα [step by step], and we shall examine each class to the best of our ability.

III. The First Class, containing sayings which command something to be done or not to be done. Bellarmine brings forward these precepts: Thou shalt have no other gods, Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain, Honour thy father and thy mother, and others which are enumerated in Exodus 20. Hence the Jesuit concludes thus: a precept is a rule of living well, but a rule is given in vain to him who cannot fail, or cannot not fail: it is only free will which, in the way of morals, can fail and not fail. Therefore, a precept is given to man by God in vain if he lacks free will, but God does nothing in vain. Therefore, man does not lack free will.

IV. We respond 1. Bellarmine is contrary to himself; for in book 2, chapter 16, to this argument of the Pelagians taken from precepts, he responds with these words: The Scriptures, while they exhort men to conversion, advise this, that when they are called and excited by God, they should not resist the Holy Spirit according to the Psalm: Today if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts. And in chapter 3, book 2, to the saying of Christ, Come, etc., he responds that Christ invites all to come, not because men can come by the powers of nature alone, since it is written in John 6: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him; but that he may admonish them to cooperate with the prevenient grace and not resist the Holy Spirit. Thus Bellarmine contradicts himself: For if a precept is given in vain if it is given to one who cannot keep it, these Bellarminian responses to the arguments of the Pelagians are worth nothing.

V. II. Theologians have a rule confirmed by many examples: The consequence from a precept to the ability does not hold. For in Isaiah 42, verse 18, it is said: Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see. But is it in the power of the blind to see, and of the deaf to hear? Genesis 15:5, God commands Abraham: Look up to heaven and count the stars. Matthew 9:25, it is said to the dead daughter of Jairus: Girl, arise. John 11:43, to the buried Lazarus: Lazarus, come out. Acts 9:40, to the deceased disciple: Tabitha, arise. On the last day, it is said to all the dead: Arise and come to judgment. All these precepts do not imply the power of acting, but rather indicate ἀδυναμίαν and impossibility, which same thing must be affirmed concerning the moral precepts of God made in the state of sin.

…VI. III. If a command always implied the power of effecting, then it would follow that man, by the powers of free will alone, could believe in God, could love God above all things, could perfectly fulfill the law, which even the Papists themselves do not concede. For precepts are read, Zechariah 1:3: Turn to me, Ezek. 18. verse 31. Make you a new heart, Matt. 11. verse 27. Come to me, etc. Hence for the same reason I could infer: A commandment is given in vain to him who cannot keep it: But it is commanded that men come to Christ, that they turn themselves to God. Therefore these things are situated in man's power: which is the very conclusion of Pelagius, which Bellarmine does not admit, since in this chapter he says: The law alone does not make men righteous, but on the contrary, those justified by grace fulfill the law. Whence I infer: If the law can be fulfilled only by the justified, it follows that it cannot be fulfilled by free will, which is common to all; likewise, that certain commandments are not given in vain, even if they have been given to those by whom they cannot be kept. For the commandment concerning fulfilling the law binds not only the justified, but all men whatsoever, even those placed outside of grace, nay, even outside the Church, whom—who but a Pelagian blasphemous against the merit of Christ would dare to say—could perfectly satisfy the law? Therefore, whether the Papists wish it or not, they must admit that the consequence from a commandment to the ability to perform it does not always hold.

VII. But Bellarmine objects that this response is clearly beside the point, since the dispute here is not whether the law can be fulfilled by the powers of nature alone (since he himself is not ignorant that the aid of grace is necessary in all ways), but the question is this: Whether, given the aid of grace, man is truly of free will, so that he can fulfill the law, or, if he prefers, transgress the same: We therefore say, he says, that given the necessary aid, whatever that may be, man is truly and properly free in moral matters. And we prove that, because otherwise all law would have been given in vain. But the words of Jesus are Jesuitical, that is, composed to deceive the simpler sort. For we are not now asking about the powers of grace or about the will after conversion, but about the freedom of the will in an unregenerate man before conversion. Bellarmine therefore commits an ignoratio elenchi. Then let him explain to us, whether the law was not given to every man whatsoever, not only to the regenerate? Nay, the law demands and seeks to extort obedience more from the unregenerate than from the regenerate, since νόμῳ δικαίῳ οὐ κεῖται. Let Bellarmine therefore answer explicitly. Can the unregenerate perform it or otherwise? If he denies that they can, he destroys his own argument by which he wishes to conclude that the law is given in vain unless obedience cannot be performed by men: But if he affirms it regarding the regenerate, he perverts the state of the question, since here the question is about the powers of the will not yet liberated. Therefore we argue thus: If the law given to all men, even the regenerate, can in no way be fulfilled by them, it follows that not everything which is commanded is in the power of him to whom it is commanded, or that the consequence from a precept to the ability to perform it is not valid. But the former is true, therefore the latter is also.

VIII. But it is soon objected: If the commandments of God are impossible, they will certainly be in vain and idle. For why is that required of man which cannot be done by him? But we deny the consequence, since the commandments of God, although they cannot be observed by us from our own powers, nevertheless contain many and very great uses. For 1. they admonish us of our debt and our infirmity. 2. They invite us to prayer. 3. They lead us to Christ. 4. They correct our disease, and 5. They restrain stubbornness, which uses, since I have explained them at greater length in part 2 of the Sobriety of Philosophy, section 2, question 3, I will not repeat, but I wish to refer the reader there.

IX. But the Papists insist: If God commands impossible things, that He is cruel, and by commanding does nothing other than insult human misery. They use for illustrating this argument certain similes, as if a servant with dislocated feet could not walk and his master were to command many things, Go there, do that, etc., threatening harsh things if he does not obey. Likewise if someone were to say to a blind man, open your eyes, you will find a treasure here; to a deaf man, listen, I will tell a story; to one bound by his right hand, I have placed wine for you on the right, poison on the left, reach out as you wish your hand. This was the simile of Erasmus: It would be ridiculously said to one standing at a crossroads, you see a double path, enter whichever you wish, when only one was open, as Luther recounts on page 15.

X. We respond, however: 1. Neither the cruelty of God nor a sarcastic mockery of men can or ought to be inferred from these impossible precepts. For if in Matthew 18:24 a creditor justly demands a debt from a debtor, for whom not even a deadline remained, why should God not most justly, without any cruelty, demand from men, His debtors, that which they owe? Thus there is no mockery, because these impossible precepts are not empty words, reproaching man for his misery, but rather they are remedies by which a way is opened to heal that misery. For they bring the knowledge of sin, incite to prayer, lead to Christ, and convert and renew man. Did Christ mock the dead girl by saying: Arise. Would he mock a sleeping person who would rouse him with this word, Awake; Therefore, impossible precepts argue for a healing God, not a mocking one: they are words not reproaching, but healing human misery, which is to be well noted against the Jesuits.

XI. 2. We do not concede that God in the law commands things that are simply and absolutely impossible. For the fulfillment of legal precepts is possible, both before the fall and after the fall. Before the fall indeed, because God had adorned Adam, and in Adam all of us, the descendants of Adam, with perfect knowledge of the mind and with righteousness and freedom of the will, so that we could have fulfilled the law of God in every way through the innate or concreated image of God. Wherefore it is not to be said that God absolutely commands impossible things to us in His law, because He commands such things as are congruent with, and therefore easy for, an integral nature, such as God created in the beginning. Which integrity, because we lost it through voluntary sin, not It is to be imputed to God if we are now unable to satisfy the law, nor is God bound to change his law: for that great theological maxim has a place here too: As God does not change his essence, so neither does he change his sentence, or his will, which is expressed by the law. Therefore, the will of God which existed before the fall is the same still after the fall: Hence, the same law which he originally enacted, he subsequently repeated on Mount Sinai, which, even if we cannot fulfill after the fall by our own powers, nevertheless God is not to be accused of any cruelty or injustice on that account, since we voluntarily lost that δύναμιν of fulfilling the law. Furthermore, even after the fall, the fulfillment of the law is not simply impossible for man, if we consult the Gospel. Man is indeed so corrupted that he cannot satisfy the law of himself, yet he satisfies it in Christ when apprehended by faith, for Christ has been made for us by God righteousness and redemption 1. Cor. 1. v. 30, which Paul also testifies in Rom. 10. 8. & 9. where he says that the fulfillment of the legal words is not only possible, but also easy through and because of Christ apprehended by faith. Therefore, the legal precepts are not simply impossible, but are partly impossible and partly possible: Impossible outside of Christ, possible and easy in Christ. To this can be referred that statement of Jerome in book 2 of his Dialogues. For when he had said that the commandments of God were impossible, he explains it in the said place thus: Impossible to nature, possible to grace. It is therefore an Ἀνακόλουθον, this Papistic argument: God does not command the impossible, but he does command the perfect fulfillment of the law. Therefore, the perfect fulfillment of the law is within our powers. For there is more in the conclusion than the premises allow: Since nothing else follows than that the fulfillment of the decalogue is possible, it does not follow that it is possible outside of Christ, but rather that it is possible in Christ, which the Gospel teaches. Therefore, the Law and the Gospel join their mutual efforts here. The Law requires perfect

Latin:

II. Et dictis Scripturae, & rationibus quibusdam, contra nos pugnant aduersarij. Dicta Scripturae distinctis sex classibus proponuntur a Bellarmino l. 5. c. 18. & seqqu. quibus postmodum lib. 6. adhuc plura subiungit. Nos κατα ποδα ipsum insequemur, singulasque classes pro virili examinabimus.

III. Classis Prima, continens dicta quae praecipiunt aliquid faciendum vel non faciendum. Profert Bellarminus haec praecepta. Non habebis Deos alienos, Non assumes nomen Domini Dei tui in vanum, Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam, & alia quae numerantur Exodi 20. Hinc ita concludit IesuWita; praeceptum est Regula bene viuendi, frustra autem datur Regula ei, qui non potest deficere, aut non potest non deficere: solum liberum arbitrium est, quod in via morum potest deficere: & non deficere. Igitur frustra homini praeceptum a Deo datur, si caret libero arbitrio, nihil autem Deus facit frustra. Igitur non caret homo libero arbitrio.

IV. Respondemus 1. Bellarminus subijpsi contrarius est, libro enim 2. C. 16. ad argumentum hoc Pelagianorum è præceptis sumptum, respondet his verbis: Scripturæ, dum hortantur homines ad conversionem id monent, vt cùm à Deo vocantur & excitantur, non resistant Spiritui sancto iuxta Psalmum: Hodiè si vocem eius audieritis, nolite obdurare corda vestra. Et c. 3. l. 2. ad dictum Christi, Venite, &c. respondet, Christum invitare omnes vt veniant, non quòd possint homines solis naturæ viribus venire, cùm scriptum sit Iohan. 6. Nemo potest ad me venire, nisi pater, qui misit me, traxerit eum; sed vt admoneat, vt gratiæ prævenienti cooperentur, & non resistant Spiritui sancto. Hæc Bellarminus sibi contradicens: Si enim Præceptum frustra datum est, si datum ei, qui servare non potest, responsiones hæ Bellarminianæ ad argumenta Pelagianorum nihil valent.

V. II. Habent Theologi Regulam multis exemplis confirmatam; A præcepto ad posse non valet consequentia. Nam Esa. 42. v. 18. dicitur, Surdi audite & cæci intuemini ad videndum, Nùm autem in viribus cæcorū est, vt videant, & surdorum, vt audiant; Gen. 15. 5. præcipit Deus Abrahamo: suspice cælu & numera stellas. Matt. 19. v. 5. dicitur filię Iairi mortuæ: Puella surge. Iohan. 11. vers. 47. Lazaro sepulto: Lazare veni foràs, Act. 9. 40. discipulæ defunctę: Tabitha surge. In extremo die cunctis mortuis dicitur: Surgite & venite ad iudicium. Hęc præcepta omnia non inferunt potestatem agendi, sed potius indicant ἀδυναμίαν & impossibilitatem, quod ipsum de præceptis Dei moralibus in statu peccati factis affirmandum est.

VI. III. Si mandatum vim efficiendi semper inferret, tum sequeretur, quod homo ex solis virib. liberi arbitrij possit in Deū credere, possit Deum super omnia diligere, possit legē perfectè implere, quòd tamen nec ipsi concedunt Pontificij. Leguntur enim præcepta, Zach. 1. v. 3. Convertimini ad me, Ezech. 18. vers. 31. Facite vobis cor novum, Matth. 11. vers. 27. Venite ad me, &c. Hinc eâdem ratione possem colligere: Præceptum frustra datur ei qui non potest servare: Atqui præcipitur, vt homines ad Christum veniant, ad Deum se conuertant. Ergo hæc sunt in hominis potestate sita: quæ est ipsa Pelagij conclusio, quam Bellarminus non admittit, siquidem hoc cap. inquit: Lex sola non facit iustos, sed contrà potius per gratiam iustificati faciunt legem. Vnde infero: Si tantum à iustificatis impleri lex potest, sequitur, quòd nequeat à libero arbitrio, omnibus communi impleri; item, quod quædam præcepta non frustra data sint, licèt data fuerint ijs, à quibus seruari nequeunt. Præceptum enim de implenda lege nõ solos iustificatos, sed omnes omninò homines obligat, etiam extra gratiam, imò extra Ecclesiam quoque constitutos, quos legi satisfacere perfectè posse, quis nisi Pelagianus in meritum Christi blasphemus, dicere auderet? Velint ergo, nolint Pontificij, fateantur oportet, à præcepto ad posse non semper valere consequentiam.

VII. Verùm excipit Bellarminus, hanc responsionem planè extra rem esse, siquidem hic non disputetur, possit nè lex solis naturæ viribus adimpleri (cum ipse non ignoret auxilium gratiæ esse modis omnibus necessarium) sed quæstio ea sit: Vtrum posito auxilio gratiæ, homo sit verè liberi arbitrij, ita ut possit legem implere, vel eandem, si maluerit, præuaricari: Nos igitur dicimus, inquit, posito auxilio necessario, quodcunque illud sit, hominem verè propriéque liberum esse in moralibus. Atque id probamus, quoniam alioquin lex omnis frustra data esset. Sed verba Iesu Witica sunt, hoc est, ad fallendum simpliciores composita. Non enim nunc quærimus de viribus gratiæ vel de arbitrio post conuersionem, sed de libertate arbitrij in homine non renato ante conuersionem. Committit ergo Bellarminus Ignorantiam ἐλέγχου. Deinde exponat nobis, Annon lex data sit omni omnino homini, non sobis venatis? Imò lex à non renatis obedientiam magis postulat & extorquere vult, quàm à renatis, siquidem νόμῳ δικαίῳ οὐ κεῖται. Disertè igitur respondeat Bellarmin. Possint ne illam non renati præstare vel secus? Si negat posse, destruit suum argumentum quo vult concludere, legem esse frustra latan nisi præstari nequeat ab hominibus obedientia: Sin affirmat quòad renatos, statum peruertit, quoniam hîc quæstio est de viribus arbitrij nondum liberati. Proinde sic argumentamur: Si lex omnibus hominibus etiam renatis data, ab ijs nullo modo impleri potest, sequitur quòd non omne id quod præcipitur, sit in potestate eius, cui præcipitur, seu quòd à præcepto ad posse non valeat consequentia. Verum autem est prius, Ergo etiam posterius.

IIX. Mox autem obijcitur: Si mandata Dei sunt impossibilia, erunt vtique frustranea & ociosa. Cur enim requiritur ab homine, quod ab ipso fieri non posses? Sed negamus consequentiam, siquidem præcepta Dei, licet à nobis ex proprijs viribus obseruari nequeant, multos tamen maximosque vsus continent. Nam 1. admonent nos debiti & infirmitatis nostræ. 2. Inuitant ad preces. 3. Adducunt ad Christũ. 4. Corrigunt morbum, & 5. Inhibent contumaciam, quos vsus singulos cùm prolixiùs explicuerim parte. 2. Phil. sobr. sect. 2. quęst. 3. actum non agam, sed Lectorem eò remissum volo.

IX. Ast instant Pontificij: Si Deus impossibilia præcipit, quòd sit crudelis, & præcipiendo nihil faciat aliud, quam quòd insultet miseriæ humanæ. Vtuntur ad hoc argumentum illustrandum quibusdam similitudinibus, vt si seruus luxatis pedibus ingredi non posset & herus multa præciperet, Abi illuc, fac istud, &c. dura minitans, nî pareat Item si quis ad cæcum diceret, aperi oculos, hîc thesaurum inuenies; ad surdum, audi, narrab. historiam: ad ligatum manu dexterâ, possui tibi vinum ad dexteram, ad læuam toxicum, vti velis porrige manum. Erasmi similitudo hæc fuit : Ridiculè diceretur in biuio consistenti, vides duplicem viam, vtram voles ingreditor, cùm altera tantùm pateret, prout Lutherus pagin 15. recenset.

X. Respondemus autem 1. Nulla præceptis istis impossibilibus colligi potest aut debet vel crudelitas Dei, vel sarcastica hominum illusio. Etenim si Matth. 18. v. 24. iustè exigit creditor debitum à debitore, cui nè terminus quidem supererat, quidni Deus iustissimè sine omni crudelitate ab hominibus, debitoribus suis, exigeret id quod debent? Sic nulla est illusio, quia præcepta ista impossibilia non sunt nuda verba, homini miseriam exprobrantia, sed potius sunt remedia, quibus ad sanandam miseriam via aperitur. Afferunt enim cognitionem peccati, incitant ad preces, ducunt ad Christum, conuertunt & renouant hominem. An illudebat Christus puellæ mortuæ dicens: Surge. An illuderet dormienti qui eum excitaret hoc vocabulo, Expergiscere; Præcepta igitur impossibilia Deum medētem, non illudentem arguunt: verba sunt non exprobrantia, sed sanantia miseriam humanam, quod benè contra Iesu Witas notandum.

XI. 2. Non concedimus, quòd Deus in lege præcipit simpliciter & absolutè ἀδύνατα. Etenim præceptorum legalium impletio possibilis est, tùm ante lapsum, tùm post lapsum, Ante lapsum quidem, quia Deus ornauerat Adamum & in Adamo nos omnes Adæ posteros perfectâ scientiâ mentis, & iustitiâ ac libertate voluntatis, vt legem Dei omnimodè per innatam vel concreatam Dei imaginem implere potuissemus. Quare non est dicendum, absolutè Deum nobis in sua lege præcipere impossibilia, quia talia præcipit, quæ congruunt, adeoque facilia sunt naturæ integræ, qualem Deus initio condidit. Quam integritatem quia per voluntarium peccatum perdidimus, non Deo imputandum est, si legi iam satisfacere non valemus, Neque tenetur Deus mutare suam legem: habet n. & hic locum illa maxima theologica: Deus vt non essetiam, ita nec mutat sententiam, seu voluntatem suam, quæ lege exprimitur. Quæ igitur Dei fuit voluntas ante lapsum, eadem adhuc est post lapsum: Proinde eandem legem, quam primitus tulit, postmodum in monte Sinai repetijt, quam etiamsi nos post lapsum implere ex proprijs viribus nequeamus, tamen exinde nullius crudelitatis vel iniustitiæ accusandus est Deus, siquidem spontè perdidimus δύναμιν istam implendi legem. Deinde v. etiam post lapsum impletio legis homini non est simpliciter impossibilis, si Euangelium consulamus. Homo quidem ita corruptus est, vt nequeat ex se satisfacere legis in Christo tamen fide apprehenso satisfacit, Christus n. nobis factus est à Deo iustitia ac redemtio 1. Cor. 1. v. 30 quòd etiam Paulus testatur Rom. 10. 8. & 9. vbi dicit, impletionem verborum legalium non modò possibilem, sed & facilem esse per & propter Christum fide apprehensum. Non igitur simpliciter impossibilia sunt præcepta legalia, sed sunt partim impossibilia partim possibilia: Impossibilia extra Christum, Possibilia ac facilia in Christo. Huc referri potest illud Hieronymi lib. 2. Dialog. Cùm enim dixisset mandata Dei esse impossibilia, id loco dicto sic explicat: Impossibilia naturæ, Possibilia gratiæ. Ἀνακόλουθον igitur est hoc argumentum Papisticum: Deus non præcipit impossibilia, præcipit autem perfectam legis impletionem. Ergo perfecta legis impletio in nostris est viribus. Plus enim in conclusione est, quàm præmissæ patiuntur: Cum nihil aliud sequatur, quam quòd impletio decalogi sit possibilis, non autem sequitur, quòd extra Christum, sed potiùs in Christo sit possibilis, quòd docet Euangelium. Coniungunt igitur hîc mutuas operas, Lex & Euãgelium. Lex requirit perfectam obe-


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?: obedience, which it indicates cannot be performed by us outside of Christ

obedience, which it indicates cannot be performed by us outside of Christ: the Gospel, however, shows how Christ has perfectly fulfilled the law, and that we, having apprehended Christ by faith, are able to fulfill the law and satisfy it.

XII. The second class, containing sayings by which something is promised to us by God under a condition, if we are willing: Bellarmine brings forward in Chapter 19, book 5, these sayings, Isaiah 1, verse 19: If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good of the land; if you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you. Amos 5, verse 14: Seek good and not evil, and you shall live. Matthew 19, verse 17: If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. From this he argues: Either it is in our power to perform the offered condition, or it is not. If the first is granted, free will is demonstrated; if the second, that is not truly a promise under a condition, but a manifest mockery. Not otherwise than if someone were to propose a prize, and order it to be proclaimed by the voice of a herald, that those who wish should run, for the prize is to be given to him who surpasses the others in running, and then he were to drag a few by force to the prize, and bind others with chains and fetters, so that they could not move themselves. Erasmus proposed the same argument, just as Luther recounts on page 117. Here the Diatribe argues: Ecclesiasticus, by saying 'if you will to keep,' signifies that there is in man a will to keep and not to keep; otherwise, what is the point of saying to one who has no will, 'if you will'? Is it not ridiculous if someone says to a blind man, 'if you will to see, you will find a treasure,' or to a deaf man, 'if you will to hear, I will tell you a good story'? This would be to mock their misery.

XIII. Luther indeed responds on page 117 that these are arguments of human reason, which is accustomed to pour forth such wisdom: and he urges that if 'if you will' is a verb of the subjunctive mood, it posits nothing, according to the rule of the dialecticians: a conditional brings nothing to the indicative, as, 'if the Devil is God, he is deservedly worshipped; if an ass flies, it has wings.' On page 121 he responds by an instance, because it would follow from that that man can keep all the commandments. But let it be, he says, that they do not prove that we leave here any zeal or attempt in man: but we shall attribute to him the whole fullness and abundance of keeping the commandments. For the words sound of keeping, not of attempting or studying. But if you deny to the Pelagians the consequence concerning keeping, they in turn will much more rightly deny the consequence concerning attempting they too will take away from you the little part of it that remains, so that you cannot assert of the part what you deny of the whole. Pag. 122 he concludes: That consequence is not therefore to be admitted, if you will, therefore you can. Thus it will be understood, that by that word and similar ones man is moved to his own impotence, which, ignorant and proud, he would not recognize nor feel without these divine admonitions. Pag. 123 he briefly comprehends these things: The sayings of Scripture if you will, if you hear, if you do, do not show what men can do, but what they ought to do. And thus Luther responded to this argument quite learnedly and vigorously.

XIV. We add this with other theologians, that the sayings of Scripture are of three kinds. 1. There are certain legal sayings, which promise external goods to those who render external obedience to the divine law. Such is that of Isaiah 1, verse 19. That man has free will regarding external actions has never been denied by us. 2. There are certain legal sayings, which demonstrate the corruption of human nature, so that sins may be made manifest, so far are they from proving free will. Such is Matthew 19, verse 17. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. For by this saying Christ wished to show the imperfection of nature rather than the freedom of the will. Otherwise Pelagianism would follow, as if it were in man's power to observe all the precepts of the Decalogue. And here that rule is especially valid, A conditional statement posits nothing. For it does not follow, if I should say to someone, If you wish to fly, having wings: Therefore you have them: in like manner it does not follow here, If you wish to be saved, keep the precepts: It is shown only how one might be able to [attain] life enter, but it is not indicated whether that manner is placed within the power of man. 3. There are certain evangelical sayings which show not what we can do of ourselves, but by what method we may arrive at Christ, so that we may enjoy his benefits; that is, they show the order of true conversion. For we are not converted immediately and as it were enthusiastically, but through faith kindled by the word. By those conditions, therefore, nothing else is denoted than that medium of both δόσεως and λήψεως, through which conversion happens. It is not indicated, however, whether it depends upon the choice of nature or upon the aid of grace; which is to be learned from other places of Scripture. From a condition, therefore, the consequence to the freedom of the will is not valid. From the negation of a condition to the removal of the conditioned, the argumentation is indeed firm; but not from a condition to the freedom of the will, since the fulfillment of the condition depends not upon nature, but rather upon grace.

XV. But Bellarmine’s little argument is empty: If GOD were to propose an impossible condition, that offering of a condition ought to be sought ironically, and it would be not a condition, but a mockery. For that condition is not simply impossible, but only to nature, yet possible to grace, as Jerome speaks in book 2 of his Dialogues. If it were simply impossible that anyone should perform them, hence it would also be a sarcastic mockery when GOD said, If you wish to be saved, believe. But it is not absolutely ἀδύνατον, but only to us corrupted by sin; it becomes, however, δυνατόν with the approach of grace, moving us through the word. Luther proposes the same on page 153: If such things, he says, were said about those things which are made altogether impossible, such as those which God would never do, now they would rightly be called either cold or ridiculous, as things which would be said in vain. But now they are said in such a way that not only is the impotence of free will shown, through which none of those things is done, but at the same time it is signified that all such things will sometime be and will be done, but by another’s power, namely divine, if at all we admit in such words a certain signification of things to be done and of possibilities.

XVI. By the annexed conditions, therefore, nothing else is denoted than the means of conversion, which is commanded and prescribed to man, for the reason that it is in man, not because it is from man. We have an example in Rom. 10. v. 9. If you shall believe in your heart that GOD raised the Lord Jesus from the dead, you shall be saved: Here salvation and the means of salvation, namely true faith, are joined together; but shall we conclude here, because of the added condition, that faith is a work of free will, and thus consequently conversion itself? By no means. For Bellarmine himself admits in book 6, chapter 5, that conversion to GOD is a work of GOD. Therefore, from a condition to free will there is no consequence. Luther, on page 155, learnedly replies: by what consequence, I ask, does it follow that will and power must be present as soon as it is said, if you will, if anyone wills, if you shall have willed? Do we not most frequently signify impotence and impossibility rather by such expressions, as if you wish to equal Virgil in singing, O Maevius, you must sing other things: If you wish to surpass Cicero, Scotus, you must have the highest eloquence for arguments: If you wish to be compared with David, it is necessary that you produce similar Psalms. Here are clearly signified things impossible by one's own powers, although by divine power all things can be done. Therefore, by similar sayings of Scripture it is only indicated what man ought to do, not what he can do, namely, that it is necessary for man to believe, but it is not hinted whence the believing comes to you, whether from our nature or from grace, which is explained elsewhere. And thus, speaking summarily, by conditional promises the means is indeed indicated, but not the principle of the means, and therefore from a condition to free will as the principle of the action required by the condition, no consequence is valid, no otherwise than if someone should say, if you wish to recover a copy and free yourself from debt, count out a thousand florins? Shall I therefore conclude that he possesses a thousand florins? If you wish to conquer the Turk, lead a numerous army against him. Does he therefore immediately have an army? The required action is shown, but not the power for the action.

XVII. Nor should that observation of the theologians be despised, that in many sayings of Scripture, which are either conditional or contain manifest precepts, demanding faith and repentance, regard is had only to the free use of the means established by God. For because God does not convert man immediately or ἐνθουσιαστικῶς (enthusiastically), but mediately and ἀκουστικῶς (audibly), hence phrases are often found in Scripture: Believe, Repent, Seek the Lord, If you shall believe, etc., by all of which sayings it is not implied that it is in man's power to believe himself, but this is required of man for this reason, because it is in his power to use those means by which he can obtain faith. Just as if I were to say to a sick person. Cure yourself; if you do not wish to heal yourself, no one will heal you; which things are said for this reason, not that the sick person can heal and cure himself, but that he has the power of using or not using the potions and other medicines prescribed by the physician. This is implied in Isaiah 1, verse 19: If you are willing and obedient. To listen, therefore, or not to listen, to harden the ears or to incline them, is placed in the power of man, and because faith is always kindled through the attentive hearing of the word, hence it is said to man, if you shall believe, as if it were in his power to believe, when nevertheless nothing is left to him but to listen.

XIIX. The third class, containing sayings which teach that it depended on man that he did not act well and avoid sins. Bellarmine brings forward these testimonies in chapter 20, book 5. Numbers 14, verse 43: You shall fall by the sword, because you would not acquiesce to the Lord. Deuteronomy 30, verse 11: The commandment which I command you today is not above you. Isaiah 5, verse 4: What could I have done for my vineyard, and did not do? Jeremiah 7, verse 28: This nation has not heard the

Latin:

dientiam, quam a nobis extra Christum praestari non posse indicat: Euangelium autem ostendit, quo modo Christus lege periectam impleuerit, adeoque & nos in Christo fide apprehenso legem implere ac illi satisfacere valeamus.

XII. Classis secunda, continens dicta quibus promittitur nobis aliquid a Deo sub conditione, si voluerimus: Profert Bellarminus C. 19. lib. 5. haec dicta, Esa. 1. vers. 19. Si volueritis & audieritis me, bona terrae comedetis, si nolueritis, gladius deuorabit vos. Amos 5. vers. 14. Quaerite bonitatem & non malitiam & viuetis, Matth. 19. v. 17. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata. Hinc argumentatur: Aut est in potestate nostra praestare conditionem oblatam, aut non est. Si datur primum, demonstratur liberum arbitrium; si secundum, illa non est vere sub conditione promissio, sed manifesta irrisio. Non secus ac si quis brauium proponeret, ac praeconis voce clamari iuberet, vt qui voluerint, currant, dandum enim brauium ei, qui caeteros currendo superauerit, deinde paucos quosdam vi traheret ad brauium, alios vinculis & catenis constringeret, ne se commouere possent. Idem argumentum proposuit Erasmus, sicuti recenset Lutherus pag. 117. Hic argutatur Diatribe, Ecclesiasticus dicendo si volueris seruare, significat inesse voluntatem homini ad seruandum & ad non seruandum, alioqui quid sonat dicere ad eum, qui voluntatem non habet, si volueris? Nonne ridiculum est si quis ad caecum dicat, si volueris videre, inuenies thesaurum, aut ad surdum, si volueris audire, narrabo tibi bona historiam? hoc esset miseriam illorum ridere.

XIII. Respondet vero Lutherus pagin. 117. esse haec argumenta rationis humanae, quae tales sapientias fundere soleat: & vrget, si volueris esse verbum coniunctiui modi, quod nihil ponat, iuxta regulam Dialecticorum: Conditionalis indicatiuo nihil affert, vt, si Diabolus est Deus; merito adoratur; si asinus volat, habet alas. Pagina 121. respondet per instantiam, quia sequatur inde hominem omnia mandata posse seruare. At sit, inquit, non probent tium studium vel conatulum aliquem hic reliquum faciemus in homine: sed totam plenitudinem & abundantiam seruandorũ mandatorum ei tribuemus. Nam verba sonãt de seruando, non de conando aut studendo. Quòd si Pelagianis negaueris sequelam de seruando, ipsi rursus multo rectiùs negabunt sequelam de conando: & si in illis totum liberum arbitrium abstuleris, auferent & ipsi tibi particulam eius reliquã, vt particulæ non possis asserere, quòd toti denegaris Pag. 122 concludit: Non igitur admittenda est illa sequela, si volueris, Ergo poteris. Sic intelligetur, eo verbo & similibus moueri hominem suæ impotentiæ, quam ignarus & superbus sine istis monitionibus diuinis non cognosceret nec sentiret. Pag. 123. breuiter ista comprehendit: Dicta Scripturæ si volueris, si audieris, si feceris, non oftendunt quid possint, sed quid debeant homines. Atque ita Lutherus satis doctè & neruosè ad hoc argumentum respondit.

XIV. Nos hoc addimus cum alijs Theologis, quòd dicta Scripturæ sint trium generum. 1. Sunt quædam dicta legalia, quæ promittunt externa bona ijs, qui externam legi diuinæ præstant obedientiam. Tale est illud Esa. 1. vers. 19. Habere verò hominem liberum arbitrium quo ad externas actiones, à nobis nunquam negatum fuit. 2. Sunt quædam dicta legalia, quæ demonstrant naturæ humanæ corruptionem, vt patefiant peccata, tantum abest, vt probent liberum arbitrium. Tale est Matth. 19. vers. 17. Si vis ad vitam ingredi, serua mandata. Hoc enim dicto Christus naturæ imperfectionem potiùs, quàm arbitrij libertatem ostendere volebat. Aliàs enim sequeretur Pelagianismus, ac si in hominis foret potestate, omnia Decalogi præcepta obseruare. Et hîc vel maximè valet illa regula, Conditionalis nihil ponit. Non enim sequitur, si alicui dixerem, Si volare vis, pennas habens: Ergo habes: pari modo hîc non sequitur, Si vis saluari, serua præcepta: Monstratur duntaxat quomodo quis posset vitam ingredi, non autem indicatur, an iste modus in hominis potestate situs sit. 3. Sunt quædam dictE- uangelica, quæ ostendunt non quid nos ex nobis ipsis possimus, sed qua ratione peruenire queamus ad Christum, vt eius beneficijs fruamur, hoc est, monstrant ordinem veræ conuersionis. Etenim non immediatè & quasi enthusiastice conuertimur, sed per fidem verbo accensam. Conditionibus igitur illis nihil aliud notatur, quam istud medium tum δόσεως, tum λήψεως, per quod fit conuersio. Non autem indicatur, an id à naturæ arbitrio, num à gratiæ adminiculo dependeat; quod ex alijs Scripturæ locis addiscendum est. A conditione igitur ad libertatem arbitrij non valet consequentia. A conditionis negatione ad conditionati sublationem firma quidem est argumentatio; non autem à conditione ad libertatem voluntatis, siquidem impletio conditionis non à natura, sed potiùs à gratia dependet.

XV. Inanis verò est ratiuncula Bellarmini: Si DEVS proponeret conditionem impossibilem, illa conditionis oblatio ironice expeti deberet, & esset non conditio, quàm irrisio. Nam conditio illa non simpliciter est impossibilis, sed tantùm naturæ, possibilis autem gratiæ, vti loquitur Hieronymus l. 2. Dialog. Si foret simpliciter impossibile, vt quis ea præstaret; hinc etiam foret sarcastica irrisio, cùm DEVS diceret, Si vis saluari crede. At vero non est absolutè ἀδύνατον, sed duntaxat nobis peccato corruptis; fit autem δυνατόν accedente gratia, per verbum nos mouente. Idem proponit Lutherus pag. 153: Si talia, inquit, dicerentur de ijs, quæ prorsus impossibilia sunt facta, vt quæ nec Deus vnquam esset facturus, nunc rectè dicerentur vel frigida vel ridicula, vt quæ frustrà dicerentur. Nunc verò sic dicuntur, vt non solum ostendatur impotentia liberi arbitrij, per quam nihil eorum fit, sed simul significatur, aliquando fore & factum iri omnia talia, verùm aliena virtute nempe diuina, si omnino admittamus in talibus verbis inesse quandam significationem faciendorum & possibilium.

XVI. Per annexas igitur conditiones nihil aliud denotatur, quàm conuersionis medium, quod homini præcipitur & præscribitur, ideò quia in homine non quia ab homine est. Exemplum habemus Rom. 10. v. 9. Si credideris in corde tuo quod DEVS Dominum Iesum excitauit à mortuis seruaberis: Hic salus & medium salutis vera nimirum fides, conjunguntur, an verò hic ob additam conditionem concludemus fidem esse opus liberi arbitrij, Et sic ipsam consequenter conuersionem? Neutis quam. Fatetur enim ipse Bell. l. 6. c. 5. conuersionem ad DEVM esse opus DEI. A conditione ergo ad liberum arbitrium nulla est consequentia. Lutherus pag 155. doctè respondet: quâ consequentia rogo fiat, vt mox voluntatem & potentiam adesse oporteat, quoties dicitur, si vis, si quis vult, si volueris? Nonne frequentissimè impotentiam potius & impossibilitatem significamus talibus sermonibus, vt si Virgilium voles æquare canendo, Mi Mœvi alia cantes oportet: Si Ciceronem superare veles, Scote pro argumentis summam eloquentiam habeas: Si cum Dauide comparari voles, similes Psalmos edas necesse est. Hic planè significantur impossibilia viribus proprijs, licet diuina virtute omnia fieri possint. Proinde similibus scripturæ dictis tantùm indicatur, quid homo facere debeat, non quid possit, nempè, hominem oportere credere, non autem innuitur, vnde te credete adueniat, an à nostra natura, an gratia, quod alibi explicatur. Et sic summatim dicendo, per conditionatas promissiones indicatur quidem medium, sed non medij principium, ideoque à conditione ad liberum arbitrium tanquam actionis per conditionem requisitæ principium, nulla valet consequentia, non secus ac si quis dicat si vis ἀντίγραφον repetere, & ære alieno te liberare, numera mille florenos? Ergone concludam quod is possideat mille florenos? Si vis Turcam vincere anmerosum contra illum duc exercitum. Ergonè statim habet exercitum. Ostenditur requisita actio, non autem actionis facultas.

XVII. Nec contemni debet illa Theologorum obseruatio, quòd in multis scripturæ dictis, quæ vel conditionata sunt, vel manifesta præcepta continent, fidem & pœnitentiam postulantia, duntaxat respiciatur ad liberam mediorum à Deo constitutorum vsurpationem. Quia enim DEVS non immediatè vel ἐνθουσιαστικῶς, sed mediatè & ἀκουστικῶς hominem conuertit hinc sæpè in scriptura reperiuntur phrases, Credite, Agite pœnitentiam, quærite Dominum, si credideris &c. quibus dictis omnibus non hoc innuitur, quòd in hominis potestate sit credere ipsum, sed propterea hoc de homine requiritur, quia in ipsius potestate est vti medijs ijs, quibus fidem potest consequi. Non secus ac si ægroto dicerem. Cura teipsum, si tibi ipsi non vis mederi, nemo medebitur; quæ ideò dicuntur, non quòd ægrotus seipsum sanare & curare queat, sed quòd habet potestatem potionibus & alijs pharmacis à medico præscriptis vtendi vel non vtendi. Innuitur hoc Esa. 1. vers. 19. Si volueritis, audieritis me. Audire igitur, vel non audire, aures obdurare vel inclinare in potestate hominis est positum, & quia per attentum auditum verbi semper accenditur fides, hinc dicitur homini, si credideris, ac si in ipsius potestate esset credere, cùm tamẽ nil nisi audire ipsi sit relictum.

XIIX. Classis tertia, continens dicta, quæ docent, per hominem stetisse, quo minùs benè ageret & peccata vitaret. Profert Bellarmin. cap. 20. lib. 5. hæc testimonia. Num. 14. vers. 43. Corruetis gladio, eò quod nolueritis acquiescere Domino, Deut. 30. vers. 11. Mandatum, quod ego præcipio tibi hodie, non supra te est. Esa: 5. vers. 4. Quid potui vineæ meæ facere, & non feci? Ier. 7: vers. 28. Hæc gens non audiuit vo-


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?: voice of the Lord their God, and you have not received discipline, therefore…

voice of the Lord their God, and you have not received discipline, therefore you have been cast off by the Lord. C. 32. vers. 23. Because you hardened your heart, and were unwilling to obey the Lord, all these evils have come upon you. Matth. 23. vers. 37. How often have I wished to gather your children, and you were unwilling? Act 7. v. 52. Uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit. Hence the Life of Jesus concludes thus; Either he who sins can not sin, or he can not: If he can, he therefore has free will; if he can not, then God complains in vain about man, as if it stood by him that he did not act well, when he himself could not have done otherwise.

XIX. We answer 1. If the argument concludes, gross Pelagianism is established. For God everywhere complains about men, that they were unwilling to believe, to repent. Therefore either they could believe, or they could not. If the former, one must pass over to Pelagius. But if the latter, the consequence lacks an argument. 2. From the freedom of the will toward evil, the freedom of the will toward good is not concluded. For man has free will in evil, but not in good: Whence Augustine rightly writes against the two Epistles of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 2. This will, which is free in evils, because it delights in evils, is therefore not free in goods because it has not been set free. We therefore deny this consequence: Man can place an obstacle to the Holy Spirit, resist and struggle against Him: Therefore he can also from his own powers turn himself to God and prepare himself for grace. For one can obstruct a window with linens or wood, so that a room is not illuminated, yet one can not illuminate the room: Thus man has free will, as it were, to close the window of his heart, and to weigh it down with a mass of sins, so that it is not illuminated by the Holy Spirit; nevertheless he does not have the power to illuminate that same thing. For it is the Holy Spirit alone who turns us to God, yet He does not turn those who are unwilling and actively resisting, but those who conduct themselves παθητικῶς, that is, neither ἀποίως, nor ἐνεσίως: for τὸ ἑκούσιον is introduced not into the ἀκούσιον, but into a man behaving merely passively. When therefore a man resists the Holy Spirit, then His operation is hindered, and therefore God can deservedly complain that man has been unwilling, that he has resisted Him. And thus we ascribe conversion to the Holy Spirit, and the hindering of conversion to man: but from the power of hindering, the power of acting is not to be concluded. A man can hinder the downward motion of a stone, yet he is not the cause of that motion: thus man can hinder the motion of the converting Spirit, yet he is not the cause of conversion.

XX. Specifically regarding the passage in Deuter. 30. verse 11. (for all other cited passages speak of liberty in evil,) we reply that Bellarmine contradicts himself. For in Chapter 6 of this book he brought forward a twofold explanation of this Mosaic text. First, that the Law of the Lord is not above the powers of men, not of just any men: but of those who have been healed by grace from self-love, and love God with their whole heart. Secondly, that Moses is not speaking of the ease of observing the Law, but of the ease of knowing it, which explanation seems to him most literal and proper, and he determines that it is confirmed in Rom. 10, while Paul, alluding to this place in Deut., says: The righteousness which is of faith speaks on this wise, Say not in thine heart, &c. He most openly contradicts these things in C. 20, when he writes: although Moses speaks of the ease of knowledge, as we showed above; yet from the ease of knowledge he wishes it to be gathered that it was in the power of the people to keep or not to keep the commandments; And he adds; that Calvin rightly wrote that this solution (that Moses speaks of the ease of knowledge, not of observation) is cavilling. Above he was denying altogether against the Pelagians that Moses speaks of the ease of observation, lest he be forced to concede that all moral precepts can be fulfilled by the powers of nature alone: Here, however, disputing against us, he recalls the very same thing and says that it can by no means be denied that Moses is also speaking about the keeping of the commandments, and is teaching that it is in the power of men to keep them or not to keep them, from which free will is demonstrated without any doubt. But is this not with full cheeks? For he who teaches that the observation of all legal commandments is situated in our powers of free will is a Pelagian. Nor is the exception valid that Moses, by preaching, did not cast the people into destruction; for Moses does not write that the commandments can be fulfilled by the powers of free will alone; but he also adds grace when he says: The Lord will circumcise your heart, that you may fear the Lord; Nothing, I say, is this exception worth, since it viciously perverts the state of the question, for here it is not asked what free will can do as it has been liberated, and thus from powers granted through grace, but what it can do from the powers left to nature? If, therefore, Bellarmine brings forward this Mosaic passage for free will, it is necessary that he say with Pelagius that it is in the power of man to keep or not to keep all the commandments of the law. For those words of Moses, 'it is not above you,' speak of man alone: for what kind of explanation would this be, 'it is not above you,' that is, it is not above divine grace and your free will? If, therefore, the Bellarminian exposition ought to have place, that Moses is speaking here about the observation of the commandments, it will have to be conceded that the observance of all the commandments is situated in the power of man using free will, since Moses does not say, 'the commandment which I command you is not above you and grace,' but only, 'it is not above you.'

XXI. 2. The interpreter of this passage who is greater than any exception is the Apostle, Rom. 10, verse 6 and following, who shows that this Mosaic text is not to be understood legally, but Evangelically. For thus he says: The righteousness which is of faith, speaks on this wise: Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven? that is, to bring Christ down from above. Or, Who shall descend into the deep? That is, to bring up Christ again from the dead. But what saith the Scripture? (he does not indeed understand any other Scripture than this text of Moses, for nowhere else are similar words read) The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: That is, the word of faith, which we preach. What could have been said more clearly, or what more manifestly? For does not Paul expressly affirm that those Mosaic words (it is nigh) are words of faith or Evangelical, and not legal words, whence the Jesuit is worthy of execration, who did not fear to write that clear Scripture ought not to be expounded by obscure, as if this Pauline passage were obscure, and did not manifestly interpret that Mosaic text.

XXII. In place of a colophon we append the words of Luther, with which he responds to this text. He discourses thus on page 145. If Moses so clearly pronounces that there is not only the ability in us, but also the facility of keeping all the commandments, why do we sweat so much? Why have we not immediately produced this passage? And asserted free will in an open field? What need is there now of Christ, what need of the Spirit? We have now found a passage which stops the mouth of all, and clearly asserts not only the freedom of the will, but also teaches the easy observance of the commandments, etc. Page 147. What therefore does Moses want with these most open and most clear words, unless that he has performed his duty as a faithful legislator excellently? So that it is not through him that they do not know and have the precepts placed before them, nor is any room left for them to excuse themselves, that they are ignorant or do not have the precepts, or that they must be sought from elsewhere, etc.

XXIII. The Fourth Class, containing those testimonies which teach that GOD as it were sits back and explores what men do, and to what end they turn their pursuits. To this Class Bellarmine refers in Chapter 21 the following sayings of Scripture. Deuteron. 8. verse 2. The Lord led you for forty years through the desert, that he might afflict you and test you, and that those things which were turning in your mind might become known, whether you would keep his commandments or not? And Chapter 13, verse 3: The Lord your God tests you, that he may see if you love him with all your heart. From this he gathers: God would explore in vain were able to do the same thing and not do it. For no prudent person explores the outcome of a thing determined to one. For who has ever explored whether fire is hot or cold? A hungry dog desires bread rather than a stone.

XXIV. We answer 1. These sayings speak not of free will, but of the end and utility of the cross. That it is a δοκιμασία of faith, and a testing of constancy. But what is the consequence? God sometimes afflicts the pious and faithful (for he speaks of those who are members of the Church), so that their faith and charity may become known. Therefore, before conversion, they can apprehend grace by the own powers of their will, or at least prepare themselves for it? There is no strength at all in this argument, since the end of calamities is not the demonstration of the will, which is none, but rather the acknowledgment of infirmity, true humiliation, ardent invocation, etc. For it is known that God is accustomed to chastise his children, Heb. 12, v. 6, so that they may learn to implore divine aid. According to Isa. 26, verse 16: Jehovah, in distress they visited you and poured out a prayer when your correction was upon them. For as it is in Isa. 28, verse 19. Vexation gives understanding, and Rom. 5, verse 3: Affliction produces patience. Wherefore that exploration and testing of God leads us to the acknowledgment of our misery and sins, so far is it from showing the freedom of the will.

XXV. But God is said to explore not for his own sake, so that he may know something new, since he is omniscient; but so that he may make us know what kind of people we are. Not so that he may know, from whom nothing is hidden, but so that he may make us know how much we have progressed in His love, God permits us to be tempted, says Augustine in De Genesi contra Manichaeos, book 1, chapter 22. Therefore, Bellarmine's insistence is empty: No prudent person explores the outcome of a thing determined to one. For this would be true if he who explores the outcome were exploring it for his own sake. intuition, most perfectly, and He is said to explore them, not so that He Himself may know, but so that He may make men know: This exploration, therefore, of a thing determined to one is not against the prudence of God. We read an example concerning the temptation of Abraham: God knew most certainly that Abraham would obey Him in sacrificing his son, and yet He is said to have explored whether Abraham would obey. That exploration, therefore, does not indicate an indetermination of the thing, but can consist with a thing certainly determined to one, so that the prudence of God is not undermined. And when He institutes this temptation for the sake of men, the reason is that faith lying hidden in the heart is not known to all: although, therefore, God knows that this one or that one certainly believes, yet not all men know it; but so that these also may know, He therefore sends calamities upon the pious, so that others also may recognize the faith of the pious through the patient reception of calamities. From this, however, it by no means follows that man has free will in spiritual matters even before conversion.

Latin:

bem Domini Dei sui, nec recepis disciplinam, ideò proiecta esft à Domino. C. 32. vers. 23. Quia indurastis cor vestrium, & noluistis obedire Domino, hæc omnia mala euenerunt vobis. Matth. 23. vers. 37. Quoties volui congregare filios tuos, & noluisti? Act 7. v. 52. Incircumcisi cordibus & auribus vos semper Spiritui Sancto resistıtis. Hinc ita colligit Iesu VVita; Vel potest is qui peccat non peccare, vel nõ potest: Si potest, habet igitur liberum arbitrium; si non potest, igitur Deus frustrà queritur de homine, quasi per illum steterit, quò minus benè ageret, cum ipse aliter facere non potuerit.

XIX. Respondemus 1. Si argumentum concludit, crassus Pelagianismus stabilictur Nam Deus passim queritur de hominibus, quòd noluerint credere, resipiscere. Ergo vel potuerunt credere, vel non potuerunt. Si illud ad Pelagium est transeundum. Sin hoc, consequentia caret argumento. 2. A libertate Arbitrij ad malum, non concluditur libertas arbitrij ad bonum. Habet enim homo liberum arbitrium in malo, sed non in bono: Vnde recte scribit Augustinus contra duas Epistolas Pelagian. lib. 2. cap. 2. Hæc voluntas, quæ libera est in malis, quia delectatur malis, ideò libera non est in bonis quia liberata non est. Negamus igitur istam consequentiam: Homo potest Spiritui Sancto obicem ponere, illi resistere & reluctari: Ergo ctiam ex proprijs viribus potest se ad Deum conuertere & ad gratiam præparare. Nam potest quis fenestram linteaminibus vel lignis obstruere, nè Museum illuminetur, non tamen potest Museum illuminare : Sic homo habet liberum arbitrium, fenestram cordis sui quasi concludendi, & mole peccatorum prægrauandi, ne à Spiritu Sancto illuminetur; attamen potestatem non habet, illud ipsum illuminandi. Solus enim Spiritus sanctus est, qui nos ad Deum convertit, non autem invitos & actu reluctantes conuertit, sed eos, qui sese παθητικῶς, hoc est, nec ἀποίως, nec ἐνεσίως habent: τὸ ἑκούσιον enim introducitur non in ἀκούσιον, sed in hominem merè se habentem passiuè. Quandò igitur homo reluctatur Spiritui sancto, tunc impeditur eius operatio, ideoque Deus meritò potest conqueri, quòd homo noluerit, quòd sibi restiterit. Atque ita Spiritui sancto adscribimus conuersionem, homini conuersionis impeditionem: à vi autem impediendi, non concludenda est vis agendi. Potest homo impedire motum lapidis deorsum, non tamen est causa illius motus: sic homo potest impedire motionem Spiritus conuertentis, non tamen est causa conuersionis.

XX. In specie quòd attinet locum Deuter. 30. vers. 11. (nam cætera dicta omnia loquuntur de libertate in malo,) Respondemus, Bellarminum sibi contradicere. Nam Cap. 6. huius libri duplicem istius textus Mosaici attulit explicationem. Primùm, Legem Domini non esse supra vires hominium, non quorumlibet: sed eorum, qui per gratiam sanati sunt ab amore proprio, Deumque toto corde diligunt. Deinde Mosen non loqui de facilitate obseruandæ legis, sed de facilitate cognoscendæ, quæ expositio ipsi maximè literalis, & propria videtur, eamque confirmari statuit Rom. 10. dum Paulus ad hunc locum Deut. alludens, inquit: Quæ ex fide est iustitia, sic dicit, Ne dixeris in corde suo, &c. Apertissimè his contradicit C. 20. quando scribit: licet Moyfes loquatur de facilitate cognitionis, vt suprà ostendimus; tamen ex facilitate cognitionis colligi vult, in potestate populi fuisse mandata seruare vel non seruare; Et addit; Caluinum meritò scripsisse, solutionem istam (Mosen loqui de facilitate cognitionis, non obseruationis) esse cauillatoriam. Suprà omnino negabat contra Pelagianos, loqui Mosen de facilitate obseruationis, nè concedere cogeretur, omnia præcepta moralia ex solis naturæ viribus posse impleri: Hîc verò contra nos disputans idipsum reuocat, & ait, nullà ratione negari posse, loqui Mosen etiam de præceptis seruandis, & docere, esse in potestate hominum illa seruare & non seruare, ex quo liberum sine vlla dubitatione demonstretur arbitrium. An non verò hoc est Pelagianismum plenis buccis incrustare? Qui enim docet, omnium præceptorum legalium obseruationem in nostris sitam esse viribus arbitrij, Pelagianus est. Neque valet Exceptio, Mosen prædicando, liberum arbitrium nō præcipitâsse populum in exitium; non enim scribere Mosen, solis viribus liberi arbitrij mandata posse compleri; sed adiungere etiam gratiam, cùm ait: Circumcidet Dominus cor tuum, vt timeas Dominum; Nihil, inquam, valet hæc exceptio, cùm vitiosè peruertat statum, siquidem hic non quæritur, quid possit arbitrium, quà liberatum est, atque sic ex viribus per gratiam concessis, sed quid possit ex viribus naturæ relictis? Quòd si igitur Bellarminus pro libero arbitrio hunc locum Mosaicum adducit, necesseum est, vt cum Pelagio dicat, in potestate hominis esse, omnia præcepta legis seruare vel non seruare. Verba enim ista Mosis, non supra te est, de solo homine loquuntur: quæ enim foret hæc explicatio, non supra te est, hoc est, non est supra diuinam gratiam & liberum tuum arbitrium? Si igitur expositio Bellarminiana locum habere debet, quòd Moses hic loquatur de obseruatione præceptorum, concedendum erit, omnium præceptorum obseruantiam in hominis, libero arbitrio vtentis, potestate sitam esse, cùm Moses non dicat, mandatum, quòd præcipio, non est supra te & gratiam, sed tantummodò, non est supra te.

XXI. 2. Interpres huius loci omni exceptione maior est Apostolus, Rom. 10. vers. 6. & seq. qui ostendit textum istum Mosaicum non intelligi degaliter, sed Euangelicè. Ita enim inquit: Quæ à fide est iustitia, sic dicit: Ne dixeris in corde tuo: quis ascendet in cœlum? id est Christum deducere. Aut quis descendet in abyssum? Hoc est Christum à mortuis reuocare. Sed quid dicit Scriptura? (non verò aliam Scripturam intelligit, quàm hunc textum Moysis, nullibi enim similia verba leguntur) Propè est verbum in ore tuo & in corde tuo, Hoc est, verbum fidei, quod prædicamus. Quid appertius, quidue manifestius dici potuisse? Annon enim Paulus disertè affirmat, verba illa Mosaica (prope est) esse verba fidei seu Euangelica, non autem verba legalia, vnde dignus execratione est IesuVVita, qui scribere non fuit veritus, non exponi debere Scripturam claram per obscuram, ac si locus hic Paulinus obscurus foret, & non manifestè interpretaretur textum istum Mosaicum.

XXII. Colophonis loco Lutheri verba adscribimus, quibus ad hunc textum respondit. Sic autem disserit pag. 145. Si Moses tam clarè pronunciat, non modò esse facultatem in nobis, sed etiam facilitatem seruandi omnia mandata, cur tantum sudamus? Cur non statim hunc locum produximus? Et liberum arbitrium asseruimus libero campo? Quid iam Christo, quid spiritu opus? Inuenimus iam locum, qui omnibus os obstruat, & clarè non modò libertatem arbitrij asserat, sed facilem quoque mandatorum obseruantiam doceat, &c. Pagina 147. Quid igitur Moses vult verbis istis apertissimis, & clarissimis, nisi seie suo officio ceu fidelem legislatorem esse perfunctum egregiè? vt per quem non stet, quo minus omnia sciant & coràm habeant posita præcepta, nec locum eis relictum excusandi, quod ignorent vel non habeat præcepta, aut aliunde petenda eis sint, &c.

XXIII. Quarta Classis, continens ea testimonia, quæ docent, DEVM quasi resedere & explorare, quid homines faciant, & quorsum studia sua conuertant. Ad hanc Classem refert Bellarminus Capit. 21. sequentia Scripturæ dicta. Deuteron. 8. vers. 2. Adduxit te Dominus quadraginta annis per desertum, ut affligeret te, atque tentaret, & nota fierent, quæ animo tuo versabantur vtrum custodires mandata illius annòn? Et Capit 13. versu 3. Tentat vos Dominus Deus vester, ut videat, si diligatis eum in toto corde. Hinc colligit: Frustrà exploraret Deus, quid homines facere velint, nisi possent eandem rem facere & non facere. Nemo enim prudens explorat euentum rei determinatæ ad vnum. Quis namque explorauit vnquam, calidusne sit ignis, an frigidus? appetit canis esuriens panem potius quam lapidem.

XXIV. Respondemus 1. Loquuntur ista dicta non de libero arbitrio, sed de fine & vtilitate crucis. Quòd sit δοκιμασία fidei, & probatio constantiæ. Quæ verò est consequentia. Deus quandoque pios & fideles (de ijs enim loquitur, qui sunt membra Ecclesiæ) affligit, vt eorum fides & charitas innotescat. Ergo ante conuersionem ex proprijs arbitrij viribus possunt gratiam apprehendere, vel saltem ad eam sese præparare?
