Nullus omnino nervus inest huic argumento, siquidem finis calamitatū non est ostensio arbitrij, quod nullum, sed potius agnitio infirmitatis, vera humiliatio, ardens invocatio, &c. Notum enim est consueuisse Deum castigare suos filios Heb. 12. v. 6. vt discant implorare diuinum auxilium. Iuxta Esa. 26. versu 6. Iehoua in angustia visitauerunt te & fuderunt orationem, cum correctio tua fuit eis. Nam vt est Esa. 28. versu. 19. Vexatio dat intellectum, & Rom. 5. versu 3. Afflictio efficit patientiam. Quare illa Dei exploratio & tentatio ducit nos ad miseriæ nostræ & peccatorum agnitionem, tantùm abest, vt ostendat arbitrij libertatem.

XXV. Dicitur autem Deus explorare non sui causâ, vt noui aliquid cognoscat, cùm sit omnisciùs; sed vt faciat nos cognoscere, quales simus. Non vt sciat, quem nihil latet, sed vt scire nos faciat, quantum in eius dilectione profecerimus, tentari Deus nos permittit, inquit Augustinus de Genes. contra Manich. l. 1. cap. 22. Inanis ergo est instantia Bellarmini: Nemo prudens explorat euentum rei determinatæ ad vnum. Nam verum hoc esset, si is, qui euentum explorat, eundem sui causâ exploraret. At verò Deus omnia vno intuitu, perfectisimè cognoscit, eaque explorare dicitur, non vt ipse sciat, sed vt scire homines faciat: Hæc igitur exploratio rei ad vnum determinatæ, non est contra prudentiam Dei. Exemplum legimus de tentatione Abrahæ: Nouerat Deus certissimè, Abrahamum sibi obtemperaturum in immolãdo filio, & tamen dicitur explorâsse, vtrum Abraham sit obtemperaturus. Ista igitur exploratio non indicat rei indeterminationem, sed potest consistere cum re ad vnum certò determinata, ita vt prudentia Dei non labefactetur. Et quando hoc tentamen instituit propter homines, causa est, quia fides in corde latens non omnibus est cognita: licèt igitur Deus sciat, hunc vel illum certò credere, non tamen omnes sciunt homines; Vt verò & hi nôrint, ideò pijs immittit calamitates, vt & alij per patiẽtem calamitatum susceptionem piorum fidem cognoscant. Hinc autem minimè sequitur, hominem esse liberi arbitrij in spiritualibus etiam ante conuersionem.


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?: XXVI. 2. Out of an abundance of caution we concede that by temptation free will…

XXVI. 2. Out of an abundance of caution we concede that by temptation free will is declared to some extent, but not regarding good, but only regarding evil. For we do not deny that men are of free will in external matters; they can, therefore, pretend as if they were true Christians, and as if they had faith, and loved God with their whole heart: to which can be referred that passage in 2 Corinthians 2:9: For to this end I wrote to you, that I might know your proof, whether you are obedient in all things. This hypocrisy, therefore, God manifests through the sending of calamities. No consequence, however, is: God confounds the boasting of men through the cross, and shows before all that those who had boasted so splendidly of their own integrity were mere hypocrites. Therefore they have free will in spiritual matters. This indeed follows, that they are free so that they can dissemble, and not dissemble, and thus are free in evil; yet it cannot be gathered from this that they are able, from the powers of their will, to believe, to be able to love God, and to fulfill the precepts of the law.

XXVII. The fifth class comprises two sayings from the Old Testament. Gen. 4, verse 7. Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14. Genesis 4, verse 7 is read thus: Why are you angry and why has your countenance fallen? If you do well, will you not be accepted, but if you do evil, sin will immediately be present at the door? But its desire will be under you, and you will rule over it. Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14 is written thus: God from the beginning created man, and left him in the hand of his own counsel. He added his commandments and precepts; if you will keep the commandments, they will preserve you. He has set fire and water before you; stretch forth your hand to whichever you will: Before man is life and death, good and evil, that which pleases him will be given to him.

XXIIX. From the former passage Bellarmine connects several arguments. 1. God says to Cain, why are you angry, and why has your countenance fallen? Here the interrogation indicates that Cain could have, if he had wished, not been angry, and not been sad. We answer by conceding the whole argument, namely that regarding the moderating of effects, man has some free will, but what does this have to do with freedom in spiritual matters?

XXIX. 2. If you do well, will you not be accepted? Do not that condition, if well, if evil, also show the free will of the volition? For why do we not say to a man, if you make the sun stand still, just as we say, if you do well, you will have this or that, unless because we are not ignorant that it is not in the power of man to make the sun stand still; but it is in his power to do well, if he wishes; or evil, if he does not wish. We answer. From the Hebrew these things are to be translated thus: If you do well, is there not

remission; if you do not do well, is not sin crouching at the door? The Chaldean Paraphrase confirms this interpretation, while it has it thus: Is it not that if you amend your works, they are forgiven you? But if you do not amend your works, your sin is kept until the day of judgment, at which it will come to pass that punishment is taken from you, if you do not perform penance: but if you perform penance, it will be forgiven you. The Jerusalem Targum rendered it thus: Is it not that if you amend your works in this world, it will be pardoned and forgiven you in the world to come? But if you do not amend your works in this world, your sin will be kept until the day of the great judgment, and it will rest at the door of the heart. The sense of those words is this: If you humbly perform penance, and believe in the future Messiah, you will be accepted by God; but if through impenitence you continue to act wickedly, you will at length feel the just punishment of your obstinacy. And Luther looked to this, translating thus: Is it not so? If you are pious, then you are acceptable; but if you are not pious, then sin rests before the door. For Cain was sad because God had not accepted his victim in the same way as Abel's: (but Abel's victim was accepted through faith, Heb. 11, verse 4.) To this now God responds, If you act well, that is, if you believe having performed serious penance, like Abel, you will be similarly accepted. Others explain it concerning the countenance or face, because the eyes are accustomed to be indicators of the mind, and the conscience itself seems to shine through the eyes. The sense therefore is: Your countenance betrays a bad conscience: but if you are well and sincerely affected toward your brother, your brow will be more cheerful and more open. Both interpretations, however, are of no value for free will. For by that condition, if you perform penance well, you will be accepted, it is not indicated that Cain is able from his own powers to believe in the Messiah, but it is only denoted what it is fitting for him to do, if his victim ought to be accepted, but not what he is able to do, or from where he might be able to do it, for if from the condition we should wish to argue for free will, it would follow that the whole of man's repentance is situated in his own powers, which would be manifest Pelagianism. Take the matter briefly, says Luther p. 124. By such sayings it is shown what man owes, not what he can do.

XXX. 3. Its desire shall be under you, and you shall rule over it. Here, indeed, free will is most openly proclaimed in the state of corrupt nature. For what is, its desire shall be under you, if not, the desire for sin shall be in your power? And what does it signify, you shall rule over it, if not, you will be able, if you wish, to resist desire, and thus bring it about that sin does not reign in your mortal body? Resp. There are those who translate it thus: Yet towards you is his desire, namely Abel's (for the suffix is masculine, but the noun which signifies sin is of the feminine gender) since you have power over him, namely Abel, to wit, because you are the firstborn, so that the sense is, Although you have sinned, yet Abel your brother will honor you, both by the law of nature, because he is younger than you, and by affection, because he is your brother, and you will always obtain the primacy and dominion and the birthright. This is the opinion of Calvin, Beza, Tremellius, and others. But there are not lacking examples, as Peter Martyr recounts in his Commentary on this passage, where the word חטאת which signifies sin is placed in the masculine gender. Therefore, that version is rather to be approved: Its desire shall be towards you, namely of sin, and you shall rule over it. For thus most all the ancient Doctors read, and Luther also understood it in such a way, whence he translated: Aber laß du ir nit jren willẽ/ sondern her- sche vber sie. For nothing is helped by this text for the Pelagian opinion of Bellarmine. For that speech of the Lord is either indicative or imperative, so that by it something is either indicated to Cain or commanded. If you call it indicative, it would have been a promise, says Luther p. 125. But it was not a promise, because the contrary happened and was done by Cain. For if he had indicated something, without doubt he would have indicated that Cain would be the Lord of desire and sin, which is contrary to experience. That speech, therefore, is rather imperative, which Bellarmine indeed denies, saying that God by these words neither promises nor commands, but signifies that sin is in the power of the sinner, and therefore warns Cain to consider that it is in his own will to assent or not to assent to perverse desire. But that this prayer was imperative is clear from this: for in the Hebrew text the future is placed ואתה תמשל בו and you shall rule over it. If the signification of the future had a place here, it would follow that Cain would certainly have ruled over sin, which the event itself refutes. Nor can the future be explained by the signification of the present, you rule over it, as Tremellius translates, because he thinks the discourse is about Abel, not sin. For sin was reigning in Cain, it was not being overcome: therefore it is necessary that we interpret that future by the signification of the imperative. For it is known, says Luther on page 124, that the Hebrews frequently use the indicative future for the imperative, as in Exodus 20: You shall have no other gods, you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, and infinite such things; otherwise, if they were taken indicatively (as they sound), they would be promises or certainly predictions of God, who, since He cannot lie, it would come to pass that no man would sin, and then they would be commanded without necessity. Here, therefore, is the true sense, that the Lord commands Cain not to loosen the rein to sin, but to repress and tame it, Las du Ihr nicht ihren willen/ sondern hersche vber sie. But that the consequence from a command to the ability to perform does not hold, was shown above. For just as it does not follow: The Baptist commands us to do penance; therefore conversion is a work of free will: so here it is not rightly concluded: God commands Cain to repress his desires and do penance; therefore he can do this by his own powers: otherwise Pelagianism would manifestly follow. Nor, however, by commanding penance, does God absolutely command impossibilities (ἀδύνατα). For what nature cannot do, divine grace can do, which is apprehended through faith in the word of the Gospel.

God therefore wished to lead him to repentance, whence Bernard, explaining this passage in Sermon 5 on Lent, piously and truly writes: This was certainly what the Lord was seeking, this was what He was striving to lead us to, that seeing our defect, and that there is no other help for us, we might run to His mercy with all humility.

XXXI. Finally, to answer specifically: Even if it is signified that it is in Cain's power to avoid sin, God nevertheless is not speaking of every sin, but of some certain one. For it is not even in the power of the reborn to avoid and tame every desire of sin, since the Apostle himself confesses: I am sold under sin. Rom. 7, verse 14. The evil which I do not want, I do, etc. The discourse, therefore, is not about the whole kind, but about a certain species of sin, namely, the monstrous hatred toward his brother. For after God looked upon the sacrifice of Abel, not Cain's, Cain's anger was kindled greatly, says the text, verse 5. To lay aside and omit this monstrous hatred, as also other gross external sins (which even the Gentiles could avoid), was in Cain's power, whence this sense emerges: If you continue to burn with hatred toward your brother, and have meditated upon fratricide, that sin will be manifest, and you will bear the due punishment: Wherefore, rule over that sin, lay aside that hatred, do not kill your brother, etc. But what is the consequence? A man not reborn can, without the help of special grace, lay aside monstrous hatred toward his brother, he can avoid gross sins. Therefore, he has free will in spiritual matters and can, by his own powers, perform repentance and avoid any sins whatsoever.

Latin:

XXVI. 2. Ex περισσοίἀ concedimus, per tenta tionem non nihil declarari liberum arbitrium, sed non quoad bonum, verùm duntaxat quoad malum. Homines enim in externis liberi esse arbitrij non inficiamur, possunt igitur simulalare, ac si veri essent Christiani, ac si fidem haberent, & Deum extoto corde diligerent: quò referri potest illud 2. Corinth. 2. v. 9. Ideo enim scripsi vobis, ut cognoscam experimentum vestrum, an in omnibus obedientes sitis. Hanc ergò hypocrisin Deus manifestat per immissionem calamitatum. Nulla verò Consequentia est: Deus iactantiam hominum per crucem confundit, & ostendit coram omnibus, meros fuisse hypocritas, qui ita splendidè de sua probitate gloriati fuerunt. Ergò habent liberum arbitrium in spiritualibus. Hoc quidem sequitur, illos liberos esse vt possint simulare, & non simulare, atque sic liberos in malo; non tamen hinc colligi potest, eos ex viribus arbitrij posse credere, posse Deum diligere, & præcepta legis implere.

XXVII. Quinta Classis complectitur duo dicta ex Veteri Testamento. Gen. 4. vers. 7. Ecclesiastici 15. vers. 14. Genes. 4. vers. 7. sic legitur: Quare iratus es & quare concidit vultus tuus? Nonne si benè egeris, recipies, sin autem malè, statim in foribus peccatum aderit? sed sub te erit appetitus, & tu dominaberis illi. Ecclesiastici 15. vers. 14. ita scriptum est; Deus ab initio constituit hominem, & reliquit illum in manu consilij sui. Adiecit mandata & præcepta sua, si volueris mandata seruare, conseruabunt te. Apposuit tibi ignem & aquam, ad quod volueris, porrige manum tuam: Ante hominem vita & mors, bonum & malum, quod placuerit ei, dabitur illi.

XXIIX. Ex priori loco Bellarminus aliquot nectit Argumenta. 1. Deus ad Cainum, quare iratus es, inquit, & cur concidit vultus tuus? Hic interrogatio indicat; potuisse Cainum, si voluisset, non irasci, & non tristari. Respondemus concedendo totum argumentum, nempè quoad effectus moderandos hominem esse arbitrij nonnihil liberi, quid verò hoc ad libertatem in spiritualibus?

XXIX. 2. Nonne si bene egeris, recipies? Illa conditio, si benè, si malè, nonne etiam liberum ostendunt voluntatis arbitrium? Cur enim non dicimus homini, si Solem stare feceris, sicut dicimus, si bene egeris, habebis hoc aut illud, nisi quia non ignoramus, non esse in potestate hominis, vt Solem stare faciat; esse autem, vt bene agat, si velit; vel malè, si nolit. Respond. Ex Hębręo ista sic vertenda sunt: Nonne si benè egeris re-

missio est; si non benè egeris, præ foribus est peccatum excubans? Paraphrasis Chaldaica confirmat hanc interpretationem, dum sic habet: Nunquid si emendaveris opera tua, remittuntur tibi? Quod si non emendaveris opera tua, ad diem iudicij peccatum tuum conservatur, quo futurum est, vt pœna sumatur à te, si non pœnitentiam egeris: quòd si pœnitentiam egeris, remittetur tibi. Targum Hierosolymitanum ita reddidit: Nonne si emendaveris opera tua in seculo isto, condonabitur & remittetur tibi in seculo futuro? Quòd si non emendaveris opera tua in seculo hoc, ad diem iudicij magni peccatum tuum conservabitur, & ad ostium cordis quiescet. Verborum illorum hic est sensus: Si humiliter egeris pœnitentiam, & credideris in futurum Messiam, acceptus eris Deo; sin per impœnitentiam malè agere pergas, tandem senties iustum pertinaciæ supplicium. Et huc respexit Lutherus ita vertens: Ists nicht also? Wenn du from bist / so bistu angenehm / bistu aber nicht from / so ruhet die Sünde vor der Thür. Nam Cain tristabatur, quod Deus non acceperit victimam ipsius similiter atque Abelis: (accepta verò erat Abelis victima per fidem, Hebr. 11. vers. 4.) huic iam respondet Deus, Si benè egeris, hoc est, si credideris actâ seria pœnitentia, sicut Abel, similiter acceptus eris. Alij exponunt de vultu seu facie quia oculi solent esse indices animi, & ipsa conscientia relucere videtur per oculos. Est ergo sensus: Vultus tuus prodit malam conscientiam: Si verò benè & sincere fueris erga fratrem tuum affectus, lætior tibi frons erit & explicatior. Vtraque autem interpretatio nihil valet pro libero arbitrio. Per conditionem enim istam, si bene egeris pœnitentiam, acceptus eris non indicatur, Cainum posse ex proprijs, virib. in Messia credere, sed duntaxat denotatur, quid ipsū facere conueniat, si victima ipsius accepta esse debeat, non autem quid possit, vel vnde id possit, Nam si à conditione vesimus argumentari ad liberum arbitrium, sequeretur totam hominis pœnitentiam in proprijs sitam esse viribus, qui apertus foret Pelagianismus. Rem breuiter accipe, inquit Lutherus p. 124. Talibus dictis ostenditur, homini quid debeat, non quid possit.

XXX. 3. Sub te erit appetitus eius, & tu dominaberis illius. Hic verò, apertissimè in statu naturæ corruptæ liberum prædicatur Arbitrium. Quid enim est, sub te erit appetitus eius, nisi in potestate tua erit peccati cupiditas? Et quid significat, tu dominaberis illius, nisi, poteris, si volueris, cupiditati resistere, & ita efficere, vt non regnet peccatum in mortali corpore? Resp. Sunt qui ita vertant: Tamen erga te est appetitus illius, scil. Abelis (nam affixum est masculinum, nomē autem quòd peccatum significat, est generis fœminini) cùm potestatem habes in illum, nempè Abelem, sc. quia es primogenitus, vt sit sensus, Quamuis peccaueris, tamen Abel frater tuus te colet, & naturæ lege, quia iunior te est, & affectu, quia frater est tuque primatum & dominium, & primogenituram semper obtinebis. Hæc est sententia Caluini, Bezæ Tremellij & aliorum. Sed non desunt exempla, recitante Petro Martyre in Commentario super hunc locum vbi masculino genere ponitur vox חטאת quæ peccatum significat. Potius igitur probanda est ista versio: Ad te erit appetitus illius, sc. peccati, & tu dominaberis illi. Sic enim pleriq; omnes veteres Doctores legunt, & taliter quoq; intellexit Lutherus, vnde vertit: Aber laß du ir nit jren willẽ/ sondern hersche vber sie. Nihil a. per hunc textum iuuatur Pelagiana Bellarmini opinio. Nam oratio ista Domini aut indicatiua est aut imperatiua, vt Caino per eam aut indicetur aliquid, aut imperetur. Si indicatiuam dicas, fuisset promissio, inquit Luth. p. 125. At promissio non fuit, quia contrarium euenit & factum est per Cainum. Si n. indicasset aliquid, procul dubio hoc indicasset Cainum fore Dominum cupiditatis & peccati, quod contra expétientiam. Oratio igitur ista potius imperatiua est, quod quidem Bellarminus negat, dicens, Deum istis verbis nec promittere, nec iubere, sed significare, peccatum esse in potestate peccantis, & proinde monere Cainum, vt cogitet, in suo arbitrio esse, cupiditati peruersæ assentiri, vel non assentiri. Sed imperatiuam fuisse orationem istam hinc patet. in Hebræo enim textu futurum ponitur ואתה תמשל בו & tu dominaberis illi. Si hic locum haberet significatio futuri, sequeretur, Cainum certò fuisse peccato dominaturum, quod euentus ipse redarguit, Nec etiam futurum exponi potest per significationem præsentis, tu dominaris illi, vt vertit Tremellius, quia de Abele, non peccato, sermonem esse, putat. Nam peccatum regnabat in Caino non vincebatur: Ergò necesse est, vt interpretemur illud futurum per significationem imperatiui. Notum enim est, inquit Lutherus pag. 124. Hebræos frequenter indicatiuo futuro vti pro imperatiuo vt Exod. 20. Non habebis Deos alienos, non occides, non fornicaberis, & talia infinita, alioqui si indicatiue (vt sonant) acciperentur, essent promissiones vel certè prædictiones Dei, qui cum mentiri nequeat, fieret, vt nullus homo peccaret, tum sine necessitate præciperentur. Hicigitur verus est sensus, quod Dominus præcipiat Caino, ne frænum laxet peccato, sed illud reprimat, & domet, Las du Ihr nicht ihren willen/ sondern hersche vber sie. A præcepto verò ad posse non valere consequentiam, supra fuit ostensum Sicut enim non sequitur Baptista iubet nos agere pœnitentiam: Ergo conuersio est opus liberi arbitrij: Ita hic non ritè concluditur, Deus iubet Cainum reprimere cupiditates, & agere pœnitentiam. Ergò hoc potest proprijs viribus: aliàs manifestus sequeretur Pelagianismus. Neque tamen præcipiendo pœnitentiam, Deus absolutè ἀδύνατα præcipit. Nam quod natura nequit, id potest diuina gratia, quę in verbo Euangelij per fidem apprehensa est.

Eum ergo Deus adducere voluit ad poenitentiam, vnde Bernhardus explicans hunc locuum Serm. 5. de Quad. piè & verè scribit: Hoc erat certè quod quærebat Dominus, hoc erat ad quod nos perducere satagebat, vt videntes defectum nostrum, & quod non est nobis auxilium aliud, ad eius misericordiam tota humilitate curramus.

XXXI. Tandem vt in specieias respondeamus; Si maximè significetur, in potestate Caini esse vitare peccatum, Deus tamen non de omni peccato loquitur, sed de aliquo certo. Nam ne quidem in renatorum potestate est, omnem vitare & domare peccati cupiditatem, siquidem ipse fatetur Apostolus: Venditus sum sub peccatum. Rom. 7. vers. 14. Malum, quod nolo, facio, &c. Sermo igitur est non de toto genere, sed de certa peccati specie, scilicet de immani odio ergà fratrem. Postquam enim Deus respexit ad sacrificium Abelis non Caini, accensa est ira Caini valde inquit textus vers. 5. Hoc immane odium, vt & alia externa crassa peccata, (quæ etiam Gentiles præcauere poterant) deponere & omittere, in potestate Caini erat, vnde sensus hic emergit: Si perrexeris flagrare odio erga fratrem tuum, & meditatus fueris fratricidium, manifestum erit istud peccatum, & debitum feres supplicium: Quare domineris illi peccato, deponas istud odium, noli fratrem tuum occidere, &c. Quę autem est consequentia? Potest homo non renatus sine gratiæ specialis adiutorio immane odium erga fratrem suum deponere, potest crassa peccata vitare. Ergo liberi est arbitrij in spiritualibus potestque ex propriis viribus pœnitentiam agere, & quæuis peccata vitare.


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?: XXXII. The latter passage, Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14, Bellarmine calls most…

XXXII. The latter passage, Ecclesiasticus 15, verse 14, Bellarmine calls most invincible, and so clear that it needs no explanation. It reads as follows according to the version of Tremellius: He from the beginning, when He made man, left him to his own counsel, saying, if you wish, you will keep the commandments and faith, by doing what is pleasing. He has set fire and water before you; stretch out your hand to whichever you wish. Before men are life and death, and whichever pleases him will be given to him. Luther responds on page 116. 1. That this passage of Ecclesiasticus is valid not for free will, but against free will, as that by which man is subjected to the precepts and will of God, and is exempted from his own will. But this objection does not seem sufficiently firm (unless it is opposed to those who fight for αὐτεξουσίῳ), since here the question is not about absolute liberty, even from law or precepts (for such falls only to God, and cannot be granted even to the blessed in the other life), but only about the liberty of observing precepts; that is, the question is not: whether man is entirely free, so that it is permitted to do what he wishes, but only, whether he can freely execute or not those things which are commanded and required of him? 2. That conditional, if you wish, asserts nothing. 3. It follows that all precepts, and thus the whole law, can be fulfilled from the powers of nature, because it is said, if you wish to observe the precepts. And thus we shall not make some small effort or endeavor remaining in man, but we shall attribute to him the whole fullness and abundance of the precepts to be kept.

XXXIII. The more recent ones respond briefly. 1. That the book of Ecclesiasticus is outside the Canon, and therefore irrelevant for primarily proving the dogmas of faith. 2. That Ecclesiasticus speaks of man before the fall, in instituted nature, but not of man after the fall, in destitute nature, which although Bellarmine presumes to deny, yet it becomes manifest from the fact that it is expressly said: From the beginning, when he made man, etc. Then the same appears from the scope of the author. For he deals with the cause of sin, which he denies is to be sought in God, and thus he argues: God from the beginning created man most free. Therefore God is not the author of sin, nor does he force anyone to sin, but man himself, having abused the freedom of his own will, was the cause of sin. 3. Manifest Pelagianism would follow, namely that it is in man's power to fulfill the whole law and to arrive at salvation. 4. Experience testifies to the contrary, which sufficiently proves that we, after the fall, are slaves of sin. Whence Augustine says in book 3 of the Hypognosticon: That saying of Ecclesiasticus 15 was spoken to Adam: If you will to keep the commandments, they will preserve you. But now they are slaves of sin, and what I do not want, this I do. And in the book On Grace and Free Will, against the Pelagians who urge that this saying must be understood of the present nature, he opposes that saying of Ecclesiasticus 22, verse 33: Who will set a guard over my mouth, etc. Therefore, just as these do not conflict, Gen. 1, verse 27: God created man to His own image, and Gen. 5, verse 3: He begot Adam to His own image, likewise, Gen. 1, verse 31: God saw that all things were very good, and Gen. 6, verse 5. God saw that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth, so these sayings of Ecclesiasticus 15, If you will, etc., and 2 Corinthians 3, verse 5, We are not sufficient to think anything good of ourselves, do not conflict. For the former speak of nature intact, the latter of nature corrupted, which is no longer free but a slave, whence also man, left to himself, does nothing but act evilly and sin, just as it is said in Psalm 81, verse 13: He gave them up to the hardness of their hearts, and they shall walk in their own counsels, that is, they sinned grievously. The sayings pertain here: Rom. 8, verse 6; Gen. 6, verse 5; and 8, verse 21; Matt. 15, verse 19. And it is to be noted that sin is described by the Apostle as doing those things which please the thoughts and the flesh, Eph. 2, verse 3. Hence the Gentiles became vain in their reasonings, Rom. 1, verse 21, and are occupied in the vanity of their mind, Eph. 4, verse 17.

XXXIV. The sixth class, containing five other passages, Deuteron. 30, Joshua 24, Ecclesiasticus 31, 2 Corinthians 7, 2 Corinthians 9. The first passage is Deuteron. 30, v. 15. Consider that today I have set before you life and good, and on the contrary death and evil v. 19. I call heaven and earth to witness, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing, choose therefore life, that both you and your seed may live. I do not see what can be answered to this passage, says Bellarmine, Chap. 23, book 5. But the answer is easy: 1. This whole passage is Evangelical. 2. The consequence from a precept to the ability to perform it is not valid, otherwise open Pelagianism would be concluded from this passage. 3. The Israelites could disobey or resist: in that, therefore, they had an option. 4. They were men in the Church, and already regenerate; they could obey the Lord, not by the powers of nature, but of grace. But from a liberated will to one not liberated, what is the consequence?

XXXV. The second passage stands in Josh. 24, ver. 15. Now, therefore, fear the Lord, and serve him with a perfect heart: but if it seems evil to you to serve the Lord, the option is given to you, choose today what pleases you. Bellarmine writes concerning this passage that not only is no true answer possible, but not even any likely one. We give, however, this most likely answer to Jesus Wita: 1. The consequence from a precept to the ability to perform it is not valid: otherwise it would follow that it is in the power of an unregenerate man to fear the Lord and serve him with a perfect heart. 2. This passage can be understood concerning external worship, that it is free for the Jews to associate themselves either with the assembly of the Gentiles or with the true Church, just as now it is in the power of anyone to join either the Popish assembly or the Calvinistic faction. 3. Joshua is speaking with the regenerate, and with men established in the Church of God, as appears from their own response v. 6. But to wish to argue from the will of the regenerate to the will of the unregenerate is sophistical.

XXXVI. The third passage is found in Ecclesiasticus 31, v. 10. Who could have transgressed, and has not transgressed, and done evil and has not done it. But the discourse there is about a rich man, who although he could abuse them, does not however abuse them, but rather uses his riches well; and Ecclesiasticus shows that such a one is very rarely found among men. But what is this to free will in spiritual matters?

XXXVII. The fourth and fifth passage speak of an external matter, such as marriage and munificence, which no one denies are placed in the liberty of an unregenerate man. Moreover, those things said about Christians and the regenerate speak rather than of the unregenerate, especially that 2 Cor. 9. Augustine responded to Caelestius, who brought forward the passage 1 Cor. 7:36: As if it were to be held as a great thing to wish to marry, where the assistance of divine mercy is more laboriously disputed.

XXXIIX. And thus far we have responded to those sayings which Bellarmine proposed in book 5, but in book 6, chapter 9, he forms as it were a new question: Is man after the fall truly of free will in those things which pertain to salvation? But this problem is not different from that which he treated in book 5, where he dealt with the moral obedience of the law. For this either pertains to salvation, and thus the same cabbage is repeated; or it does not pertain, whence it will follow that good moral works are not necessary for salvation, much less merit the same, which nevertheless in book 4 on Justification he keenly wishes to be defended. But let this idle ταυτολογία pass; let us see the arguments themselves which he brings forward.

XXXIX. He brings forward four orders of Testimonies in Chapter 10, but very weak and feeble ones: in the first order he includes those sayings where men are called workers, helpers, and co-workers in works of piety, as Matt. 20:16, 1 Cor. 3:6, Rom. 8:28. We respond: This argument is foreign to the question. We are debating about the powers of the unregenerate: Bellarmine brings forward sayings about the powers of the regenerate, since we willingly concede that they work together through a faculty granted by God. Then the saying Matthew 20 is parabolic. The statement in 1 Corinthians 3 does not speak of works of piety and salvation, but of the labors of the ministry. In Romans 8, it is not said that the Spirit cooperates with the pious, but πάντα συνεργεῖ, all things work together for good, that is, they are useful and result in salvation.

XL. The second order is taken from those passages which command or urge upon man works of piety and even conversion itself to God, as Zechariah 1, verse 3; Joel 2, verse 13; Jeremiah 3, verse 1; Ezekiel 18, verse 31; Isaiah 1, verse 16; John 6, verse 27; Colossians 3, verse 9; Philippians 2, verse 12. But it would be foolish to command or urge such works upon one who did not have freedom of will. We respond: 1. Precepts do not imply or presuppose a natural power to act; otherwise, gross Pelagianism would have to be approved. Therefore, let the rule be held: From a precept to the ability, from the will of God to the will of man, from duty to obedience, there is no firm consequence. 2. Free will is taken either for the will itself, or for the powers of converting oneself. It is foolish to urge good works upon one who lacks free will taken in the former respect, not the latter. Certain passages speak of the powers of the regenerate, not drawn from nature, but granted by grace, from which it is by no means permitted to argue to the powers of the unregenerate.

XLI. The third order is sought from those passages which teach that we are helped by God in works of piety, as in Psalm 27, verse 9; Psalm 60, verse 2; Romans 2, verse 26; 1 Corinthians 15, verse 10. But one who does nothing is not properly said to help, but rather one who labors by acting. I respond: 1. These passages speak of the converted, but we are inquiring about those to be converted. It is therefore an ignorance of the ἐλέγχου. 2. The word 'to help' alone concludes nothing. For the sick are helped by the physician, and infants by their mothers, who nevertheless do nothing, but only suffer. 3. The passages of the Psalms are not so much about the assistance of grace in works of piety as they are about the aid of...

Latin:

XXXII. Posteriorem locum, Ecclesiastici 15. vers. 14. vocat Bellarminus inuictissimum, & tam perspicuum, ut nulla declaratione indigeat. Is verò ita habet secundum versionem Tremellij: Ipse à principio cùm fœcit hominem, permisit ipsum consilio ipsius, dicens, si voles, custodies mandata & fidem, faciendo quod placet. Apposuit tibi ignem & aquam, ad vtrum volueris extende manum tuam; Coram hominibus est vita & mors & vtrumcunque placuerit dabitur ipsi Lutherus refpondet pag. 116. 1. Hunc locum Ecclesiastici non pro libero arbitrio, sed contra liberum arbitrium valere, vt quo subjicitur homo praeceptis & arbitrio Dei, & eximitur suo arbitrio. Verum non videtur haec instantia satis firma, (nisi opponatur ijs, qui pro αὐτεξουσίῳ pugnant) siquidem hic non est quaestio de absoluta libertate, etiam à jure vel praeceptis, (talis enim in solum Deum cadit, & nec in altera vita beatis coelitibus concedi potest) sed duntaxat de libertate praeceptorum obseruandorum; hoc est, non quaeritur: an homo omninò liber sit, ita vt agere liceat, quod velit, sed duntaxat, An ea quae praecipiuntur, & ab eo requiruntur, liberè possit exequi vel non? 2. Illam conditionalem, si volueris nihil asserere. 3. Sequi, omnia praecepta, adeoque totam legem posse ex viribus naturae impleri, quia dicatur, si volueris praecep. obseruare. Atque sic non modicum studium vel conatulum aliquem faciemus reliquum in homine, sed totam plenitudinem & abundantiam seruandorum praeceptorum ei tribuemus.

XXXIII. Recentiores breuiter respondent. 1. Librum Ecclesiastici esse extra Canonem, ideoque ad primò probanda fidei dogmata impertinentem 2. Loqui Ecclesiasticum de homine ante lapsum, in natura instituta, non autem de homine post lapsum, in natura destituta, quod licèt Bellarminus negare praesumat, tamen inde manifestum euadit, quòd expressè dicitur: A principio, cum fecit hominem, &c. Deinde idem apparet ex scopo authoris. Agit enim de causa peccati quam negat in Deo quaerendam esse, & sic arguit: Deus ab initio creauit hominem liberrimum. Ergo Deus non est peccati autor, nec quenquam cogit ad peccandum sed ipse homo arbitrij sui libertate abusus, peccati causa fuit. 3. Sequeretur manifestus Pelagianismus, videlicet in hominis potestate esse, totam legem implere, atque ad salutem peruenire. 4. Experientia contrarium testatur, quæ satis euincit, nos post lapsum esse seruos peccati. Vnde Augustinus inquit lib. 3. hypognoist Adamo dictum est illud Ecclesiastici 15. Si volueris mandata seruare conseruabunt te. Sed nunc sunt serui peccati, & quod nolo, hoc facio. Et libro de Gratia & libero a bitr. Pelagianis vrgentibus dictum hoc intelligendum esse de præsenti natura, opponit dictum illud Ecclesiastici. 22. versu 33. Quis dabit ori meo custodiam, &c. Sicut igitur non pugnant ista, Gen, 1. ver. 27. Creauit Deus hominem ad imaginem suam, & Gen. 5. versu 3. Genuit Adam ad imaginem suam, Item, Gen. 1. versu 31. Vidit Deus, quod omnia erant valde bona & Gen. 6. versu 5. Vidit Deus quod multa esset malitia hominum super terram, ita non pugnant hæc dicta Ecclesiastici 15. Si volueris, &c. & 2. ad Corinth. 3. versu 5. Non sumus idonei ex nobis ipsis aliquid boni cogitare. Illa enim de natura integra, hæc de corrupta loquuntur, quæ non amplius libera sed serua est, vnde etiam homo permissus sibi non nisi malè agit, & peccat, ficuti dicitur Psalmo 81. ver. 3. Permisit eos fortitudini cordis eorum, & ambulabunt in consilijs suis, id est, grauiter peccauerunt. Pertinent huc dicta, Rom. 8. versu. 6. Gen. 6. ver. 5. & 8. versu 21. Matth. 15. versu 19. Et notandum, ab Apostolo peccatum ita describi, quòd sit facere illa, quæ cogitationibus & carni libent Eph. 2. versu 3 Hinc gentiles, vani facti sunt in ratiocinationibus Rom. 1. versu 21. Et versantur in vanitate mentis suæ Eph. 4. ver. 17.

XXXIV. Classis sexta, continens alios quinque locos, Deuteron. 30. Iosuæ 24. Ecclesiastici 31. 2. ad Corinth 7. 2. Corinth. 9. Primus locus est Deuteron. 30. v. 15. Considera, quod hodie proposuerim in conspectu tuo vitam & bonum, & è contrario mortem & malum v. 19. Testes inuoco cælum & terram, quòd proposuerim vobis vitam & mortem, benedictionem & maledictionem, Elige ergo vitam, vt & tu viuas, semen tuum. Non video, quid ad hunc locum responderi possit, inquit Bellarminus Cap. 23. l. 5. Sed responsio est facilis, 1. locum hunc totum esse Euangelicum. 2. A præcepto ad posse non valere consequentiam, alias ex hoc loco concluderetur apertus Pelagianismus. 3. Poterant Israelitæ non obedire, vel repugnare: In eo igitur habebant optionem, 4. Erant homines in Ecclesia, & jam renati, illi poterant, non ex viribus naturæ, sed gratiæ obedire Domino. Ab arbitrio autem liberato, ad non liberatum, quæ consequentia?

XXXV. Secundus locus extat Ios. 24. ver. 15. Nunc, ergo timete Dominum, & seruite perfecto corde : sin autem malum vobis videtur, ut Domino seruiatis, optio vobis datur, eligite hodie, quod placet. Scribit Bellarminus, ad hunc locum, non solùm non veram, sed ne quidem verisimilem aliquam responsionem dari posse. Damus autem Iesu Witæ responsionem hanc verissimam, 1. A præcepto ad posse non valet consequentia: alias sequeretur, in hominis non renati potestate esse timere Dominum, & seruire ei perfecto corde. 2. De externo cultu potest hic locus intelligi, quòd Iudæis liberum sit, sese vel cætui gentilium, vel veræ Ecclesiæ associare, sicuti nunc in cuiusvis potestate est, sese vel cætui Papistico, vel factioni Caluinisticæ adjungere. 3. Loquitur Iosua cum renatis, & hominibus in Ecclesia Dei constitutis, vt apparet ex responsione ipsorum v. 6. Ab arbitrio autem Renatorum ad arbitrium non renatorum argumentari velle sophisticum est.

XXXVI. Tertius locus habetur Ecclesiastici 31. v. 10. Qui potuit transgredi, & non est transgressus, & facere mala & non fecit. Verùm sermo ibi est de homine diuite, qui cum abuti posset, non tamen abutitur, sed potius bene vtitur suis diuitijs; & ostendit Ecclesiasticus rarissimè talem inueniri inter homines. Quid autem hoc ad liberum arbitrium in rebus spiritualibus?

XXXVII. Locus quartus & quintus loquitur de re externa, quale est matrimonium & munificentia, quæ in hominis non renati libertate esse posita nemo negat. Ista insuper dicta de Christianis & renatis potius, quam nō renatis loquuntur, prēsertim illud 2. Cor. 9. Augustinus Cœlestio adducenti locum 1. Corinth. 7. v. 36. respondit: Quasi pro magno habendum sit velle nubere, vbi de adiutorio diuinæ misericordiæ operosius disputatur.

XXXIIX. Et hactenus ad illa dicta respondimus, quæ l. cis. Bell. 5. proposuit, libro autem 6. C. 9. quasi nouam quæstionem format; Sitnè homo post lapsum verè liberi arbitrij in ijs, quæ ad salutem pertinent? Sed hoc problema non est diuersum ab eo, quę tractauit lib. 5. vbi egit de morali obedientia legis. Hæc enim vel pertinet ad salutem, & sic eadem crambe repetitur; Vel non pertinet, vnde sequetur bona opera moralia non esseneceffaria ad salutem, multò minus eandem merere, quod tamen libro 4. de Iustificatione acriter vult propugnatum. Sed transeat ociosa hęc ταυτολογία, nos ipsa quæ profert, videamus argumenta.

XXXIX. Quatuor autem Testimoniorum ordines adducit Cap. 10. sed valde infirmos & debiles: Ordini primo includit ista dicta, vbi homines in operibus pietatis dicuntur operarij, adictores & cooperatores, vt Matth. 20. vers. 16. 1. Corinth. 3. vers. 6. Rom. 8. v. 28. Respondemus: Argumentum hoc à quæstione alienum est. Nos disceptamus de viribus non renatorum: Bellarminus affert dicta de viribus renatorum, quippe quos per facultatem diuinitus concessam vnà operari libenter concedimus. Deinde dictum Matthæi 20. est parabolicum. Dictum 1. Corintb. 3. non loquitur de operibus pietatis & salutis, sed de laboribus ministerij. Rom. 8. non dicitur, quòd spiritus cooperetur pijs, sed πάντα συνεργεῖ cuncta cooperantur in bonum, hoc est, sunt vtilia & cedunt in salutem.

XL. Secundus ordo desumitur ex illis locis, quæ imperant aut suadent homini opera pietatis & ipsam etiam conuersionem ad Deum, vt Zach. 1. vers. 3. Ioel. 2. vers. 13. Ier. 3. vers. 1. Ezech. 18. vers. 31. Esa. 1. vers. 16. Ioh. 6. v. 27. Col. 3. v 9. Phil. 2. v. 12. Stultum verò esse, imperare aut suadere eiusmodi opera ei, qui non haberet arbitrij libertatem. Respondemus 1. præcepta non inferunt aut præsupponunt naturalem vim agendi: aliàs crassus Pelagianismus foret adprobandus. Teneatur ergò Regula: A præcepto ad posse, à voluntate Dei ad voluntatem hominis, ab officio ad obedientiam, non est firma consequentia. 2. Liberum arbitrium vel sumitur pro voluntate ipsa, vel pro viribus sese conuertendi. Stultè suadenturbona opera illi qui caret libero arbitrio priori respectu sumto, non posteriori. 3. Quædam dicta loquuntur de viribus renatorum non ex natura haustis, sed ex gratia concessis à quibus ad vires non renatorum minimè licet argumentari.

XLI. Tertius ordo petitus est ex illis locis, quæ docent nos à Deo iuvari in operibus pietatis, vt Psalmo 27. vers. 9. Psal 60. vers. 2. Rom. 2. vers. 26. 1. Cor. 15. v. 10. Non autem propriè iuvare dicendus est, qui nihil agit, sed qui laborat agendo. Respondeo 1. Dicta hæc loquuntur de conuersis, non autem quęrimus de conuertendis, Est igitur ignoratio ἐλέγχε. 2. Solum iuvandi vocabulum nihil concludit. Nam & ægri iuuantur â medico, & infantes à matribus, qui tamen nihil agunt, sed tantùm patiuntur, 3. Loca Psalmorum non tam de adjucorio gratiæ in operibus pietatis, quàm de auxilio li-


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?: speak of deliverance from distresses

speak of deliverance from distresses. 4. God helps us by bestowing new powers of acting, not by exciting old ones, which are none. 5. Paul, 1 Cor. 15, attributes everything to divine grace, because he declares that by the grace of God he is what he is: the Greek text also has it thus: I labored more than all, yet not I, but the grace of God σὺν ἐμοὶ i.e. οὖσα, which is in me, or which is and was with me; which renders me fit; but not that which divided its works and the praise of the work with me, which that opposition between Paul and grace clearly indicates. Hence Erasmus in his annotations says: Paul corrects what he had just said, that he had labored more than all. Nay, he says, I am not the one who did this, but the grace of God which was present with me, so that we may understand that all this is to be attributed to God.

XLII. The last order contains sayings which teach that a man who is called can fail to come, as Prov. 1, verse 24, Matt. 23, verse 37, John 6, verse 67, Acts 7, verse 51, Rev. 3, verse 20. I answer: It is not permitted to argue from unwillingness to willingness, and from the power of rejecting grace to the power of embracing it in the state of sin. A man can resist by his own powers; but he cannot assent or turn himself to God by those same powers. Although it is in man to be unwilling for the good, yet unless it is given, he does not have the will for the good: nature contracted the former through guilt, nature receives the latter through grace, says Ambrose, lib. 2, de Vocat. gent. Cap. 9.

XLIII. And thus we have seen all the arguments which Bellarmine proposed from the Scriptures: Now we will run through others drawn from REASON and leading to the impossible. Four of them are primary, which he reviews in lib. 1, C. 14, and the following. We will briefly discuss each one.

XLIV. The first argument, From the voluntary which seems to be required in sin. Either sin is necessary or voluntary, if it is necessary, therefore it is not sin, and by this means sin It will not be a sin, which cannot be committed: if it is voluntary, therefore it can be avoided, and consequently man is of free will in moral matters, inasmuch as he can sin, and not sin.

XLV. I answer 1. This very argument was formerly objected to Augustine by the Pelagians, from which it appears that Bellarmine is fighting for Pelagius. He indeed tries to escape this suspicion, while he says that Pelagius maintained that man can avoid all and every sin: but that the Papists say that not all, but some can be avoided by man, rightly using free will: However, by saying this he contradicts himself. For is that sin which cannot be avoided truly a sin? This cannot be denied: and therefore we conclude that this consequence is null, If sin is necessary, it will not be sin.

XLVI. 2. Necessary is taken in two ways, for it either denotes the necessity of coercion, which cannot fall into sin, since the will cannot be compelled, not even by the Devil inciting it: Or the necessity of ὑποθέσεως (hypothesis), contracted from some preceding vice, which necessity we assert can consist together with voluntary sin: and therefore that disjunction of Bellarmine is not legitimate, when he writes: Sin is either necessary, or voluntary. For it can be both necessary and voluntary, Necessary, by hypothesis, and as to genus: Voluntary, on account of willingness or delight, and as to species. To this I refer that of Augustine in the Enchiridion, Chapter 30: the slave is free, who willingly does the will of his master, and through this he is free to sin, who is a slave of sin. And book 1 to Boniface, Chapter 3: The will is free in evils, because it delights in evils. Since therefore the unregenerate man sins willingly, and from the instinct of corrupt nature, and delights in sins, we conclude that he sins voluntarily. Furthermore, since he has the power now to do this, now that, we say. as regards the species of actions, they sin even more voluntarily, because there is no necessity there. Every action of an unregenerate man is indeed done badly on account of his innate or inherited corruption, and consequently is evil; nevertheless, his will is not determined to this evil action, but is entirely free: for an unregenerate man can serve his neighbor, or not. And hence it appears how both τὸ ἀναγκαῖον and τὸ ἑκόυσιον concur in the sins of unbelievers. They sin necessarily as regards the genus on account of original sin, and yet voluntarily, because they sin willingly, and likewise because they can choose this or that sin. There is therefore no consequence: Sin is necessary, therefore it is not voluntary. Other examples can be brought forward: 1. A slave, on account of the servitude once undertaken, necessarily serves his master, and yet at the same time serves willingly and voluntarily. Therefore, τὸ necessarium does not remove τὸ ἑκόυσιον, and τὸ ἑκόυσιον does not simply exclude the necessary. 2. Angels necessarily act well, demons necessarily act badly, and yet the good deeds of the former and the evil deeds of the latter are at the same time voluntary, a fact which not even Bellarmine could deny when he writes in book 9, chapter 14: That proposition of Calvin, 'Demons always necessarily act badly,' is in one sense false, in another true. For it is true in general that they cannot but act badly, yet it is false in particular that they necessarily do all the evils which they do, for they could not do many things which they do, and therefore they commit sins not by necessity, but by will. By this assertion he cuts his own throat, since our people, by saying that sin is necessary, mean nothing else than this, that unbelievers necessarily act badly, yet they do not deny that as regards certain special and particular actions, they are entirely free, even from necessity, just like the devils. For unbelievers do not necessarily steal, do not necessarily kill men, nor do they persecute the faithful, etc.

XLVII. 3. It has been stated ambiguously that there is no sin unless it is voluntary. For 1. do infants not have sin? Bellarmine indeed says that infants do not sin truly and properly. But is original sin not truly and properly sin? And yet, as regards the infants themselves, this sin is not voluntary, since no προαίρεσις or choice has preceded it. 2. It will be necessary that that most common division of sins be rejected: Sin is either voluntary or involuntary, which nevertheless is founded upon these sayings: Ps. 19, v. 13, Who can understand his errors? Cleanse me from my secret faults. Rom. 7, v. 19, For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do. Gal. 5, v. 17, The spirit lusteth against the flesh, so that ye cannot do the things that ye would.

XLIIX. Second argument: From punishments and rewards. If there is no freedom of will in man, there will be no place for punishment or reward; but that is refuted by the common consent and sense of the whole human race.

XLIX. I answer. 1. And this argument was originally devised by Pelagius against the Orthodox, which Bellarmine says, whom Jerome cannot excuse, for whom it is customary in his exhortations to piety to add the promise of rewards. For Jerome and Pelagius use this argument for a far different end and in a different way, although it may be conceded in the meantime that Jerome does not always appear sufficiently vigorous against the Pelagian heresy. But Pelagius himself, in his disputation concerning free will, clearly proposed that argument in the same way and for the same end as it was proposed by Bellarmine, namely, to assert the freedom of the will, whence I conclude that Bellarmine is here a Pelagian.

L. 2. External and political matters are confused with spiritual ones. For the assumption, namely that by the common consent and sense of the whole human race it is well established that there is no place for punishment or reward if there is no freedom of the will, speaks only of external virtues: For the whole human race left to itself knows nothing of spiritual matters. LI. If he speaks of rewards, not temporal but eternal, as he appears to speak, he commits the fallacy of ignoring the point at issue. For we are not inquiring about the will of the regenerate, whether it is free, but rather about the will of the unregenerate, who are still constituted outside of grace. Meanwhile, however, even if we concede the freedom of the will of the regenerate, in so far as it has been liberated, we nevertheless deny that such works can proceed from it as might of themselves merit eternal life (I say life, not rewards in life: for blessedness itself is one thing, the degree of blessedness is another; the former is conferred entirely freely, the latter, however, with respect to works.) Apply here the distinction of Luther, which he proposes against Erasmus. p. 157. In merit or reward, the question is either of dignity or of consequence. If you look at dignity, there is no merit, no reward. Whence Augustine rightly answered the Pelagians who were urging this very argument: Reward is not given on account of the merit or dignity of the work: And, God crowns nothing in us except his own gifts, for by grace we are saved. But if by grace, says Paul, Rom. 11:6, it is no longer of works, etc. To which point refers that statement of Augustine in the preface to Ps. 31: If that which is owed is rendered to you, you are now to be punished. What then happens? God did not render to you the punishment owed, but bestowed unowed grace. And below: If you wish to be a stranger to grace, boast of your merits. From the Sermons on the Words of the Apostle, 15: Do not think that you have received by meriting, you who would not have merited, unless you had received. Grace preceded your merit; grace is not from merit, but merit is from grace. While Bellarmine tries to twist these statements to works done without the aid of grace, he does violence both to the words themselves and to the meaning of Augustine. For he speaks of regenerate men, and his opinion agrees with that of David in Psalm 143:2: Enter not into judgment with thy servant, O Lord, for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. Psalm 130:3.

3. If you, O Lord, should mark iniquities, who shall stand? Whence Augustine in sermon 15 adds: You find nothing in these from which you may save, and yet you save: you give freely, you save freely. And again: Let it not be justice, but let it be grace; let it be from God to you, let it not be yours. And elsewhere he writes: God is our debtor, not from a commission, but from a promise. But if you look not at the dignity of the work, but at the consequence, there is nothing, says Luther on page 158, whether good or evil, which does not have its own reward. For hell and the judgment of God remain for the impious, a necessary consequence; they themselves neither desire nor think of such a reward for their sins; nay, they vehemently detest it, and as Peter says, execrate it; so the kingdom remains for the pious, even if they themselves neither seek nor think of it. And he adds on page 159: The kingdom is not prepared, but has been prepared, but the children of the kingdom are prepared, they do not prepare the kingdom, that is, the kingdom merits the children, not the children the kingdom. Page 160 Just as the words of the law are in place of instruction and illumination, to teach what we ought to do, and then what we cannot do, so the words of reward, while they signify what is to come, are in place of exhortation and threatening, by which the pious are excited, comforted, and raised up to proceed, to persevere, and to conquer, in doing good and bearing evil, lest they be wearied or broken, etc. And in this very way must that of Paul in 2 Timothy 4 be explained: There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord will render to me in that day, etc. For the Apostle speaks of the consequence, not of the dignity. Therefore, just as merit is not proved from reward, so free will is not proved from merit, says Luther on page 162. Otherwise it would follow that the will could do everything of itself alone. For if merit has a place only insofar as one has rightly used the will, it follows that the whole of eternal life, which is entirely called a prize and reward, depends not on grace (for thus far it is not merit) but solely on the true use of the will, which is manifest Pelagianism, which Bellarmine is not afraid to encrust here.

Latin:

berationis ex angustijs loquuntur 4. Adjuuat nos Deus, nouas agendi vires largiendo, non veteres, quæ nullæ sunt, excitando. 5. Paulus 1. Cor. 15. gratiæ diuinæ omnia tribuit, quia se gratiâ Dei esse quod est, pronunciat: Græcus etiam textus sic habet: Plus omnibus laboraui, non ego tamen, sed gratia Dei σὺν ἐμοὶ sc. οὖσα, quæ in me est, vel quæ mecum est & fuit; quæ me idoneum reddit; non verò, quæ mecum operas suas & operis laudem diuisit, quod ipsum oppositio illa inter Paulum & gratiam luculenter indicat. Hinc Erasmus in annotationibus ait: Corrigit Paulus, quod modò dixerat, se plus omnibus laborasse. Imò, inquit, non ego is sum, qui hoc feci, sed gratia possunt Dei, quæ mihi affuit, vt intelligamus, totum hoc Deo acceptum ferri.

XLII. Vltimus ordo continet dicta, quæ docent hominem vocatum posse non venire, vt Prouerb. 1. vers. 24. Matth. 23. vers. 37. Iohan. 6. vers. 67. Actor. 7. ver. 51. Apoc. 3. vers. 20. Respondeo: A noluntate ad voluntatem, & à potestate gratiam repudiandi, ad potestatem eam amplexandi in statu peccati non licet argumentari. Potest homo ex suis viribus resistere; non potest verò ex ijsdem assentiri vel ad Deum se conuertere. Licet homini insit nolle bonum, tamen nisi donatum non habet velle bonum: illud contraxit natura per culpam, hoc recipit natura per gratiam, inquit Ambrosius, lib. 2. de Vocat. gent. Cap. 9.

XLIII. Atque sic cuncta, quæ ex Scripturis Bellarminus proposuit, argumenta vidimus: Nunc alià è RATIONE petita & ad impossibile ducentia percurremus. Quatuor eorum sunt primaria, quæ recenset lib 1. C. 14. & sequentibus. Nos singula breuiter discutiemus.

XLIV. Primum argumentum, A voluntario quod requiri videtur in pecc. Aut pecc. est necessarium aut voluntarium, si est necessarium, igitur nō est pecc. ac per hoc peccatum non erit peccatum, quod fieri non potest: si est voluntarium, igitur vitari potest, & proinde homo est liberi arbitrij in moralibus, quippe qui potest peccare, & non peccare.

XLV. Respondeo 1. Hoc ipsum argumentum à Pelagianis olim objiciebatur Augustino, vnde apparet, pugnare pro Pelagio Bellarminum. Effugere quidem hanc suspicionem conatur, dum dicit, Pelagium statuisse, hominem omnia & singula peccata posse vitare: Pontificios autem dicere, non posse omnia, sed aliqua vitari ab homine, libero arbitrio rectè vtente: Attamen hoc dicendo sibi ipsi contradicit, Nam peccatum id quod vitari nequit, estne peccatum verè? Negari hoc nequit: ideoq; concludimus consequentiam istam esse nullam, Si peccatum necessarium est, peccatum non erit.

XLVI. 2. Necessarium dupliciter accipitur vel enim notat necessitatem coactionis, quæ non potest cadere in peccatum, cùm voluntas cogi non possit, nè quidem à Diabolo impellente: Vel necessitatem ὑποθέσεως, contractam à præcedente quodam vitio, quam necessitatem simul cum peccato voluntario consistere posse asserimus: itaque istud disjunctum Bellarmini non est legitimum, quando scribit: Peccatum aut est necessarium, aut voluntarium. Potest enim esse & necessarium & voluntarium, Necessarium, ex hypothesi, & quoad genus: Voluntarium, propter lubentiam seu delectationem, & quoad speciem. Huc refero istud Augustini in Enchiridio Cap. 30. liberaliter servus, qui sui domini voluntatem libenter facit, ac per hoc ad peccatdum liber est, qui peccati servus est. Et libr. 1. ad Bonifacium Cap. 3. Voluntas libera est in malis, quia delectatur malis. Quoniam igitur homo non renatus libenter, & ex instinctu naturæ corruptæ peccat, peccatisque delectatur, concludimus, illum voluntariè peccare. Præterea quoniam habet potestatem nunc hoc faciendi, nunc illud, dicimus. quoad speciem actionum adhuc magis voluntatariè peccare, quia ibi nulla est necessitas. Omnis quidem actio hominis non renati ob annatam vel innatam corruptionem malè fit, & per consequens mala est; attamen voluntas eius ad hanc actionem malam non est determinata, sed prorsus libera: Potest enim homo non renatus proximo seruire, vel non. Atque hinc apparet, quomodo in peccatis infideliũ & τὸ ἀναγκαῖον, & τὸ ἑκόυσιον concurrat. Necessariò peccant, quoad genus propter peccatum originis, & tamen voluntariè, quia libenter peccant, item, quia hoc vel illud peccatum eligere possunt. Nulla igitur est consequentia, Peccatum est necessarium, ergo non voluntarium. Possunt afferri exempla alia: 1. Servus, ob semel susceptam seruitutem necessariò seruit suo domino, & tamen simul libenter & voluntariè seruit. τὸ necessarium igitur non tollit τὸ ἑκόυσιον, & τὸ ἑκόυσιον non simpliciter excludit necessarium. 2. Angeli necessariò benè, Dæmones necessario malè agunt, & tamen illorum benefacta, horum malefacta simul sunt voluntaria, quod ipsum nè quidem Bellarminus negare potuit, quando scribit libr. 9. Cap. 14. Illa præpositio Caluini, Dæmones semper necessariò malè agunt, in aliquo sensu falsa est, in aliquo vera. Verum siquidem est in genere, eos non posse nisi male agere, falsum tamen est in particulari, omnia mala, quæ faciunt, illos necessario facere, possent enim multa non facere, quæ faciunt, & ideò non necessitate, sed voluntate peccata committunt. Quâ assertione proprium petit iugulum, siquidē nostrates dicendo peccatum esse necessarium, nihil aliud volunt, quam hoc, quòd infideles necessario malè agant, non tamen negant, quoad speciales & particulares quasdam actiones, omnino esse liberos, etiam à necessitate, non secus ac Diaboli. Infideles enim non necessariò furantur, non necessariò interficiunt homines, nec persequuntur fideles, &c,

XLVII. 3. Ambiguè dictum est, nullum esse peccatum nisi voluntarium. Nam 1. infantes annon peccatum habent? Dicit quidem Bellarminus, infantes non verè proprieque peccare. Sed an peccatum Originis non est verè proprieque peccatum? & tamen quoad infantes ipsos peccatum hoc non est voluntarium, cùm nulla praecesserit προαίρεσις vel electio. 2. Necessum erit, vt illa consuetissima peccatorum diuisio rejiciatur: Peccatum vel est voluntarium vel involuntarium, quae tamen fundata est in hisce dictis Psal. 19. v. 13. errores quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me. Rom. 7. vers. 19. Non quod volo, facio bonum, sed quod non volo malum, hoc ago. Gal. 5 v. 17. Spiritus concupiscit aduersus carnem, vt non quae vultis ea & faciatis.

XLIIX. Argumentum secundum: A poenis & praemijs. Si non sit in homine libertas arbitrij, nullus erit poenae aut praemij locus, id autem communi totius humani generis consensu, sensuq; refellitur.

XLIX. Respondeo. 1. & hoc argumentum à Pelagio primitùs fuit excogitatum contra Orthodoxos, quod nquit Bellarminus, quem non excusare potest Hieronimus, cui familiare est exhortationibus suis ad pietatem, addere promissionem praemiorum. Nam longè alio fine & modo vtitur hoc argumento Hieronymus & Pelagius, quanquam hoc interim concedi possit, Hieronymum non semper videri satis neruosum contra Pelagianam heresin. Ipse verò Pelagius in disputatione de libero arbitrio planè eodem modo, & fine proposuit istud argumentum, quo à Bellarmino propositum est, nempè ad asserendum arbitrij libertatem, vnde concludo Bellarminum hîc esse Pelagianum.

L. 2. Confunduntur res externae & politicae cum spiritualibus. Assumtio enim, quod videlicet totius humani generis consensu sensuq; constet nullum esse poenæ vel pręmij locum, si nulla sit arbitrij libertas, non nisi de virtutibus externis loquitur: De rebus enim spiritualibus nihil nouit vniuersum genus humanum sibi relictum. LI. Si de præmijs, non temporalibus, sed æternis loquitur, vti eum loqui apparet, committit ignorationem Elenchi. Non enim quærimus de arbitrio renatorum, an illud sit liberum, sed potius de arbitrio non renatorum, extra gratiam adhuc constitutorum. Interim verò etiamsi concedamus libertatem arbitrij renatorum, in quantum liberatum est, negamus tamen ab eo prouenire posse talia opera quæ per se vitam mereantur ęternam (vitam dico non præmia in vita: aliud enim est ipsa beatitudo, aliud beatitudinis gradus, illa omninò gratis, hic autem cum respectu ad opera conferetur.) Applice huc distinctionem Lutheri, quam contra Erasmum proponit. p. 157. In merito vel mercede agitur vel de dignitate, vel sequela. Si dignitatem spectes nullum est meritum, nulla merces. Vnde Aug. rectè respondit Pelagia. hoc ipsum argumentum vrgentib. Merces non datur propter meritum vel dignitatem operis: Et, nil Deus in nobis præter sua dona coronat, Gratiâ enim saluamur. Quod si per gratiam, inquit Paulus Rom. 11. v. 6. non iam ex operibus, &c. Quo spectat istud Aug. in præfatione super Ps. 31. Si redditur tibi, quod debetur iam puniendus es. Quid ergo fit? Non tibi reddidit Deus debitam pœnam, sed donauit indebitã gratiam, Et infra: Si vis alienus esse à gratia iacta merita tua. De verbis Apost. Serm. 15. Non putes te promerendo accepisse, qui nõ promereras, nisi accepisses. Gratia pręcessit meritũ tuum, non gratia ex merito est, sed meritum ex gratia. Quæ dicta dũ Bell. torquere conatur ad opera sine adiutorio gratię facta; vim facit & ipsis verbis & sẽtentiæ Aug. Loquitur enim de hominib. renatis & eius sententia conuenit cum illo Dauidis Psal. 134. v. 2. Ne venias in iudicium cum seruo tuo Domine, quia non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis viuens. Psal. 130. v.

3. Si iniquitates observaris Domine, quis stabit? Vnde Aug. sermone. 15. subijcit; Nihil in his inuenis, vnde salues, & tamen saluas: gratis das, gratis saluas: Et rursum: Non iustitia sit, sed gratia sit; a Deo tibi sit, non tua sit. Et alibi scribit: Deus debitor noster est, non ex commissa, sed promisso, Sin vero non operis dignitatem, sed sequelam spectes, nihil est, inquit Lutherus pag. 158. siue bonum, siue malum, quod non suam mercedem habeat, Manet enim impios infernus & iudicium Dei, necessaria sequela; ipsi salem mercedem pro suis peccatis, neque cupiant, neque cogitent; imo vehementer detestentur, & vt Petrus dicit, execrentur, ita manet pios regnum, etiamsi ipsi neque quærant, neque cogitent. Et addit pag. 159. Regnum non paratur, sed paratum est, filij vero regni parantur, non parant regnum, hoc est, regnum meretur filios, non filij regnum. Pag. 160 Sicut verba legis sunt vice instructionis & illuminationis, ad docendum quid debeamus, tum quid non possimus, ita verba mercedis dum significant, quid futurum sit, sunt vice exhortationis & comminationis, quibus pij excitantur, consolantur & eriguntur ad pergendum, perseuerandum, & vincendum, in bonis faciendis & malis ferendis, ne fatigentur, aut frangantur, &c. Et hoc ipso modo exponendum est illud Pauli 2. Timoth. 4. Reposita est mihi corona iustitiæ, quam reddet mihi in illo die, &c. De sequela enim loquitur Apostolus non de dignitate. Sicut igitur ex mercede non probatur meritum, ita ex merito non probatur liberum arbitrium, inquit Lutherus pagina 162. Alias sequeretur, quod arbitrium ex se solo possit omnia. Si enim meritum eactenus duntaxat habet locum, quatenus quis recte vsus est arbitrio, sequitur totam vitam æternam, quæ tota dicitur præmium & merces, dependere non ex gratia (hactenus enim non est meritum) sed vnice ex vero arbitrij vsu, qui manifestus est Pelagianismus, quem hic incrustare non veretur Bellarminus.


### Question I. What can and ought to be answered to Bellarmine's objections?: LIL. 4. He commits the fallacy of equals, when he writes

LIL. 4. He commits the fallacy of equals, when he writes: if there is no place for good merit without free will, by the same reasoning there will be no place for evil merit. For the same liberty is required for good and evil merit, and for punishment. For that a man can merit punishments, but cannot merit rewards, is evident from two things. 1. Because man, on account of original corruption, has free will in evil, but not in good: he can therefore act evilly, but not well. 2. Because evil actions contrary to the law of God are perfectly and absolutely evil, and therefore worthy of the most severe punishments in themselves: but the works of the unregenerate, which seem in some measure to be in accordance with the law of God, are not perfectly good, and indeed not even good, because they have arisen from a depraved principle; nor are they referred to their proper end, namely the glory of God. Therefore, such works are not in themselves worthy of rewards, just as evil works are in themselves worthy of punishments. This, therefore, we willingly concede, that there is no place for punishment where evil merits do not precede, and consequently free will in evil: from punishment, therefore, evil merit is gathered, and from evil merit free will is gathered, because the cause of sin is not GOD, but the own will of man: but for reward and the gift of life there is a place without any merit, and therefore from that source the liberty of the will cannot be concluded of itself, because God freely liberates the will, and endows the liberated one with eternal glory. I refer here to that statement of Augustine, book 3, against Julian, chapter 18: God is good, God is just; He can save without good merits, because He is good; He cannot condemn without evil merits, because He is just.

LIV. The sum, therefore, of our response to the Bellarminian argument is this: Either he speaks of temporal rewards, or of spiritual ones. If of temporal, he wanders off the track. But if of spiritual, that has no relevance to unregenerate men, but only to the faithful. And yet the whole question is concerning the powers of sinful man, and not yet regenerate, concerning spiritual actions. Therefore here too he craftily changes the state of the question, and deals sophistically with us.

LIV. The third argument, From the diversity of good and evil things. If there were no freedom of will in men, there would not be some good, others evil, but all would be evil; And if all were good, there would not be some better than others, but all would be equally good; And if all were evil, there would not be some worse than others, but all would be equally evil. But that this is false, experience teaches so openly that it can by no reasoning be denied.

LV. I answer. He speaks in turn either of ethical goodness or malice, or of theological goodness or malice. If of the former, he changes the state of the controversy: for we willingly concede that man, regarding ethical virtues, is of free will and therefore can apply himself either to virtue or to vices, and consequently that some are good, others truly are evil, and indeed some are better and worse than others. But if of the latter, the answer is manifest from the Scriptures, that theologically all are altogether evil and sinners, according to the sayings Gen. 6. v. 5. & 8. v. 21. Ex. 34. v. 7. Psal. 53 v. 3. Psal. 53. v. 3. Rom. 3. ver. 12. & 23. Hence by nature they are called children of wrath Eph. 2. v. 3. subject to eternal damnation, Rom. 5. ver. 12. & 18. And thus far there is no distinction between men, but all are evil and sinners before God, destitute of all free will regarding spiritual things

LVI. It must, however, be distinguished here also between original and actual malice: for all men are equal in original malice, for whatever is born of the flesh is flesh: but they are not all equal in actual malice; for Herod, Nero, Domitian and other tyrants were worse than other private men who, although otherwise evil, yet did not persecute the Church of Christ as those did. Therefore Bellarmine does not argue rightly: If all were evil, there would not be some worse than others: for all are equally evil originally, but some are actually worse than others, or with respect to actual sins, which differ by degrees: for some sins are graver than others, whence also such a gradual distinction arises among sinners, so that one is worse and more deteriorated than another, who, of course, has committed graver sins.…

LVII. But if you ask, whether none are good before God? The answer is ready, that none are good by merit: some are by grace, namely those who are converted from sins to God through the Gospel, and believing in Christ have been made free from sin, John 8, verse 36. But this goodness does not proceed from freedom of the will, which is non-existent among the infidels, but solely from the grace of God: for if theological goodness depended on the powers of nature, Pelagianism would certainly clearly follow. Thus, therefore, the matter stands: Man is endowed with free will regarding external things, since in him there still remains a distinction between honorable and base things. Some, therefore, are ethically good, some evil, and others better, others worse, but man is entirely destitute of free will in spiritual matters: Theologically, therefore, all are evil and slaves of sin, from which servitude they cannot free themselves, but the Holy Spirit alone accomplishes this, working through the word in the hearts of men. Wherefore that axiom of Jesu Wita, 'Divine election, in order to make men good, requires in them freedom of will,' unless it is understood concerning the very substance of the soul and will and thus physically, is false. For the Apostle, Rom. 8, verse 29 and 30, chapter 9, verse 11, Eph. 1, verse 4, expressly says that God chose us in Christ, not because we were holy, but that we might be holy and blameless before him through Charity. Indeed, Bellarmine contradicts himself, when in book 2 on grace, chapter 10, he writes that there is no cause of predestination in us, and that we were chosen not only freely, but also without any foresight of works.

LIIX. As for what Bellarmine adds: Why among good men some progress more daily, while others fail, and miserably fall and perish: no reason can be given, unless there be free will in man; this is simply false. For God alone is He who gives both the will and the performance, Phil. 2, v. 13. And just as man cannot of his own powers of will turn himself to God, so in conversion he cannot persevere by his own powers. For He who prevents the impious, that he may become just, follows the just, that he may not become impious, says Fulgentius, book to Monimus. A man can indeed lose the grace once received through voluntary sin, yet he cannot by his own powers persevere in the grace once received; hence we must pray daily: Confirm, O God, what You have wrought in us; the good work.

LIX. Fourth argument: From exhortations and rebukes. If free will is taken away from the human race in moral actions, it will also be necessary to take away exhortations, rebukes, praises, reproaches, precepts, counsels, admonitions, and other things of that kind. For why would you praise or blame, admonish, command, rebuke, or exhort, if men cannot do otherwise than they do?

LX. I answer 1. As regards exhortations, precepts, counsels, and admonitions, to all these it has been answered above, namely, that from a precept to the ability to perform it there is no consequence; otherwise it could be concluded from this that the entire conversion depends on the free will of man, because there is a precept: Turn, believe the Gospel. But is it to be concluded immediately from this that man has free will regarding conversion and faith? 2. Rebukes are not vain or mocking, since a man is deservedly rebuked because he resisted the Holy Spirit, when he could have not resisted. But that consequence is weak: Man can resist. Therefore he can also believe by his own powers. 3. If it concerns external things and actions, we willingly grant him free will. Hence Cicero says in book 5 of Divination; If there is no free faculty of human will, just and salutary laws will perish, no warnings or rebukes will be left, nor will there be any place for religion or prayers.

LXI. But these were Bellarmine's arguments, to which, by way of a finishing touch, we add this one: The natural man can understand the word and assent to it, as we see in the Papists, who acknowledge as true and hold sacred the sublime articles concerning the Trinity, the two natures of Christ, the resurrection, and the like. Therefore, the unregenerate have free will; because from those in whom a spiritual act falls, such as the understanding of Scripture, all liberty is not to be denied.

LXII. I answer 1. A distinction must be made between literal and spiritual knowledge. The former can fall to an unregenerate man, as the example of the Pharisees teaches: the latter does not. 2. We distinguish between knowledge that is proper and sprung from one's own powers, and knowledge acquired from the revelation of the word and the instruction of the Church. A man can know the mysteries of faith, but not from the light of nature, but rather from the revelation of the word. 3. We distinguish between those who are outside and those who are inside the Church. The former lack the word: the latter have the word, and can in a certain way assent. But as regards this assent, which they give to the word and the articles of faith, we say in turn that it is twofold, the one historical, the other salvific. The latter is not given except in the regenerate: where there is the special grace of the Spirit. But as for what concerns historical assent, I would like two things to be noted: 1. that it can fall to the unregenerate, nor does it presuppose the special grace of the Spirit. We prove this by the example of the devils, the Pharisees, John 3, verse 2, Saul, David, etc. 2. that some grace of the Spirit can fall to the unregenerate, although not that special one. I declare this by the example of Balaam, Numbers 22, and Caiaphas, John 11, who prophesied. It can therefore be said that partly from the light of nature, partly from the grace of the Spirit, let them read the word, and by the benefit of the Church let them understand and assent. Furthermore, we distinguish between the beginning of assent and its continuation. It begins in childhood, where they are reborn by the Spirit; when this is afterwards shaken off, the assent nevertheless remains and is continued, as examples teach. But why is it continued? Because they hold this principle, that the written word is the word of God, and therefore it must be believed. Whence this principle? I answer 1. from the preceding testimony of the Spirit, which convinces the conscience. 2. from the testimony of the Church. 3. and from internal τεκμηρίοις. For these arguments are so effective that they convince even a Gentile. Now, indeed, the intellect naturally apprehends, and cannot but apprehend, demonstrated truth. When, therefore, truth is proven by these apodictic arguments, the intellect of man cannot but assent. Thus, therefore, we see how this assent proceeds partly from nature, as regards the propensity of the intellect, and partly from the grace of the Spirit, as regards the information of the Church.

LXIII. After the reasons have been discussed, something should be added concerning the SAYINGS OF THE FATHERS, but since that would be too laborious and has been performed by others, we shall spare the effort and time. It can nevertheless be noted in general: 1. that the Fathers spoke more securely when the Pelagians were contending. 2. that in asserting free will they do not understand an active and natural faculty of converting oneself to God, but either the will itself, or freedom from coercion; or powers concerning external things, or a passive capacity by which a man can be converted by the Spirit, but not convert himself. You will find a special explanation of the individual testimonies in Chemnitz in his Examination, and in Pareus, books 5 and 6, on free will.

Latin:

LIL. 4. Committit Elenchum parium, quando scribit: Sinon est locus bono merito sine libero arbitrio, eadem ratione non erit locus malo merito, Eadem enim libertas ad bonum & malum meritum, ad pœnam requi ritur.
