Nam posse hominem mereri pœnas, sed non posse promereri præmia, patet ex duobus. 1. quia homo ob corruptionem originalem habet liberum arbitrium in malo, sed non in bono: potest igitur malè, sed non benè agere. 2. quia actiones malæ legi Dei contrariæ perfectè & absolutè sunt malæ, ideoque pœnis grauissimis per se dignæ: opera verò non renatorum, quæ legi Dei quadantenus videntur consentanea, non sunt perfectè bona, ac ne bona quidem, quia ex deprauato principio orta sunt; neque ad finem proprium, nempè gloriam Dei referuntur. Non igitur eiusmodi opera per se digna sunt pręmijs, si cuti mala per se digna sunt pœnis. Hoc igitur libenter concedimus, pœnę nullum esse locum, vbi non præcedunt mala merita, & per consequens liberum in malo arbitrium: ex pœna igitur malum meritum, ex malo merito colligitur liberum arbitrium, quia peccati causa non est DEVS, sed propria voluntas hominis: præmio autem & vitæ donationi locus est, sine vllo merito ideoque nec indè potest concludi libertas arbitrij ex se, quia Deus gratis arbitrium liberat, & liberatum gloriâ æternâ donat. Refero huc illud Augustini lib. 3. contra Iul. Cap. 18. Bonus est Deus, iustus est Deus; potest sine bonis meritis saluare, quia bonus est, non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia iustus est.

LIV. Summa igitur responsionis nostræ ad argumentum Bellarminianum hæc est: Aut de præmijs temporalibus loquitur, aut de spiritualibus. Si de temporalibus, currit extrà oleas. Sin de spiritualibus, nihil istud pertinet ad homines non renatos, sed ad solos fideles. Atqui tota quæstio est de viribus hominis peccatoris, & nondum renati, circa actiones spirituales. Ergo hic quoque statum veteratoriè mutat, & sophistice nobiscum agit.

LIV. Argumentum tertium, A diuersitate bonorum & malorum. Si non esset in hominibus libertas arbitrij, non essen: alij boni, alij mali, sed omnes mali; Et si essent omboni, non essent alij alijs meliores, sed omnes æquè boni; Et si essent omnes mali, non essent alij alijs peiores, sed omnes æquè mali. Id autem falsum esse tam aperiè experientia docet, vt nulla ratione negari possit.

LV. Respondeo. Vicissim aut loquitur de bonitate, malitiaue Ethica, aut de bonitate, maliciaue Theologica. Si de illa, mutat statum controversiæ: libenter enim concedimus, hominem quoad virtutes ethicas, liberi esse arbitrij ideoque posse vel virtuti, vel vitijs studere, ac proinde alios bonos, alios verò esse malos, quin & alios alijs meliores & pejores. Sin de hac manifestum est ex Scripturis responsum, Theologicè omnes omninò esse malos, & peccatores, juxta dicta Gen. 6. v. 5. & 8. v. 21. Ex. 34. v. 7. Psal. 53 v. 3. Psal. 53. v. 3. Rom. 3. ver. 12. & 23. Hinc naturâ dicuntur filij iræ Eph. 2. v. 3. obnoxij æternæ damnationi, Rom. 5. ver. 12. & 18. Atque hactenus nullum est discrimen inter homines, sed omnes sunt mali, & peccatores coram Deo, destituti omni libero arbitrio quoad spiritualia

LVI. Distinguendum tamen hic etiam est inter malitiam Originalem & actualem: Omnes enim homines in originali malitia pares sunt, nam quicquid de carne natum est, caro est: non autem omnes pares sunt in malitia actuali; Herodes enim, Nero, Domitianus & alij Tyrannipejores fuêre alijs priuatis hominibus qui etsi alias mali, tamen Ecclesiam Christi non fuerunt, vt illi, persecuti. Non igitur ritè argumentatur, Bellarminus: Si essent omnes mali, non essent alij alijs peiores: omnes enim sunt æquè mali originaliter, sunt verò alij aliis peiores actualiter, seu quoad peccata actualia, quæ gradibus differunt: nam peccata alia aliis sunt grauiora, vnde etiam inter peccatores tale discrimen graduale oritur, vt alius alio sit peior & deterior, qui nimirum graviora peccata commisit.

LVII. Si verò quæras, an nulli coram Deo sint boni? Parata est responsio, quod nulli sint boni ex merito: quidam ex gratia, nimirum qui à peccatis ad Deum per Evangelium conuertuntur, & in Christum credentes liberi facti sunt à peccato Iohan. 8. versu 36. Hæc verò bonitas non prouenit à libertate arbitrij, quod nullum est apud infideles, sed duntaxat à gratia Dei: si enim bonitas Theologica â viribus naturæ dependeret, manifestus certè sequeretur Pelagianisinus, Ita igitur se res habet: Homo præditus est libero arbitrio, quoad externa, quoniam in eo adhuc remansit discrimen honestorum & turpium. Quidam igitur Ethicè boni sunt, quidam mali, & alii meliores, alii pejores, homo autem omninò destituitur libero arbitrio in spiritualibus: Theologicè igitur omnes sunt mali & serui peccati, à qua servitute seipsos liberare nequeunt, sed solus id efficit Spiritus sanctus, per verbum in cordibus hominum operans. Quare axioma illud Iesu Witæ, Electio diuina, vt homines faciat bonos prærequirit in illis arbitrij libertatem; nisi de ipsa animæ voluntatisque substantia & sic physicè intelligatur, falsum est. Apostolus enim Rom. 8. versu 29. & 30. capite 9. versu 11. Ephes. 1. versu 4. disertè inquit, quod Deus nos elegerit in Christo, non quia eramus sancti, sed vt essemus sancti & inculpati coram ipso per Charitatem. Quin sibi ipsi contradicit Bellarminus, cùm l. 2. de gratia cap. 10. scribat, nullam esse in nobis prædestinationis causam, & electos nos esse non solùm gratis, sed etiam absque ulla præuisione operum.

LIIX. Quod verò addit Bellarminus : Cur inter bonos alij proficiant indies magis, alij deficiant, & miserè cadant ac perean: non potest reddi ratio, nisi sit in homine liberum arbitrium; simpliciter falsum est. Deus enim solus est, qui dat velle & perficere, Phil. 2. v. 13. Et sicut homo sese ex proprijs arbitrij viribus nequit ad Deum conuertere, ita in conuersione ex proprijs viribus non potest perseverare Qui enim praeuenit impium, vt fiat iustus, subsequitur iustum, ne fiat impius, inquit Fulgentius l. ad Monim. potest quidem homo gratiam semel acceptam perdere per voluntarium peccatum, non tamen potest ex proprijs viribus in semel accepta gratia perseuerare, proinde quotidiè orandum : Confirma Deus, quod in nobis operatus es; opus bonum.

LIX. Argumentum quartum: Ab exhortationibus & obiurgationibus. Si tollatur liberum arbitrium ab humano genere in actionibus morum, simul etiam tolli necesse erit exhortationes, obiurgationes, laudes, vituperationes, præcepta, consilia, monita & alia id genus. Quorsum enim laudes aut vituperes, admoneas, præcipias, reprehendas, hortaris, si non possunt homines aliud facere quàm faciunt?

LX. Respondeo 1. Quod attinet exhortationes, præceptiones, consilia & monita, ad ea omnia suprà est responsum, quòd videlicet, à præcepto ad posse nulla sit consequentia, aliàs hinc concludi posset totam conuersionem à libero hominis arbitrio dependere, quia præceptum est, Convertimini, credite Euangelio. An verò hinc protinus concludendum, hominem liberi esse arbitrij quoad conversionem & fidem ? 2. Objurgationes non sunt frustraneæ vel irrisoriæ, siquidem meritò obiurgatur homo, quòd restiterit Spiritui sancto, cùm nō resistere potuisset. Ista verò Consequentia infirma est : Potest homo resistere. Ergo etiam ex propriis viribus credere. 3. Si de rebus & actionibus externis agat, libenter ipsi liberum concedimus arbitrium. Hinc Cicero inquit l. 5. de Divinatione; Si non est humanæ voluntatis libera facultas, iustæ salutaresque leges peribunt, nullæ monitiones aut objurgationes relinquentur, neque religioni aut precibus locus esse poterit.

LXI. Atqui hæc fuerunt Bellarmini argumenta, quibus colophonis loco hoc vnicum adjungimus: Homo animalis potest intelligere verbum & illi assentiri, uti videmus in Pontificiis, qui sublimes articulos de Trinitate, de Christi duabus naturis, de resurrectione & similes, pro veris agnoscunt & sanctè credunt. Ergo non renati habent liberum arbitrium; quia in quos cadit spiritualis actus, qualis est scripturæ intelligentia, ijs non est abneganda omnis libertas.

LXII. Respondeo 1. Distinguendum est inter scientiam literalem & spiritualem. Illa cadere potest in hominem non renatum, vti docet exemplum Pharisæorum: Hæc non item. 2. Distinguimus inter scientiam propriam, proprijsque è viribus exortam, & inter scientiam ex revelatione verbi, & institutione Ecclesiæ acquisitam. Scire potest homo mysteria fidei, sed non ex lumine naturæ, verum ex reuelatione verbi. 3. Distinguimus inter eos, qui sunt extra, & qui intra Ecclesiam. Illi carent verbo: hi habent verbum, & assentiri quodammodo possunt, Quod vero attinet hunc assensum, quem dant verbo & articulis fidei, dicimus vicissim eum esse duplicem, alterum historicum, alterum saluificum. Hic non datur nisi in renatis: vbi est specialis gratia Spiritus. Quod autem spectat assensum historicum, duo notari velim, 1. quòd ille cadere possit in non renatis, nec præsupponat gratiam peculiarem Spiritus. Probamus exemplo Diabolorum, Pharisæorum, Iohan. 3. vers. 2. Saulis, Davidis, &c. 2. quòd in non renatos cadere possit aliqua gratia Spiritus, licet non illa specialis. Declaro exemplo Bileami, Numer. 22. & Caiphæ Ioh. 11. qui prophetârunt. Dici ergo potest, quòd partim ex naturæ lumine, partim ex gratia Spiritus verbum legant, beneficio Ecclesiæ intelligant & assentiantur. Prætereà distinguimus inter assensus inchoationem, & continuationem. Inchoatur in pueritia, vbi sunt renati à Spiritu; quo postmodum excusso, remanet tamen assensus, & continuatur, vti docent exempla. Quare autem continuatur? Quia isti tenent principium hoc, verbum scriptum esse Dei verbum, ideoque illi credendum. Vnde hoc principium? Respondeo 1. ex præcedenti testimonio Spiritus, qui conuincit conscientiam. 2. ex testimonio Ecclesiæ. 3. & ex internis τεκμηρίοις. Argumenta enim ista adeò sunt efficacia, vt etiam Ethnicum conuincant. Iam verò intellectus naturaliter apprehendit, & non potest non apprehendere veritatem demonstratam. Quando igitur veritas per ista argumenta apodictica euincitur, non potest non intellectus hominis assentiri. Ita ergo videmus, quomodo iste assensus proueniat partim ex natura, quoad propensionem intellectus partim ex gratia Spiritus, quoad informationem Ecclesiæ.

LXIII. Post discussas rationes, aliquid addendum esset de DICTIS PATRVM, sed cùm id nimis laboriosum sit futurum, & ab alijs præstitum, parcemus operæ & tempori. Potest nihilominus in genere notari. 1. quòd Patres Pelagianis litigantibus securiùs sint locuti. 2. quòd liberum arbitrium asserentes non intelligant facultatem actiuam & naturalem sese conuertendi ad Deum, sed vel ipsam voluntatem, vel libertatem à coactione; vel vires circa res externas, vel capacitatem passiuam, quâ homo conuerti á Spiritu, non autem seipsum conuertere potest. Specialem singulorum testimoniorum explicationem inuenies apud Chemnitium in Examine, & Paræum lib. 5. & 6. de lib. arbitrio.


### Question II. What is to be determined concerning Luther's book, which has the title, On the Bondage of the Will?

LXIV. We cannot deny that it contains very many harsh phrases, and ones inconvenient at first reading, which the Papists perpetually object to us, and which the Calvinists abuse most wickedly. For the former intend to render all of Luther's dogmas suspect on that account: the latter intend to cloak their own impious opinion concerning necessity and absolute predestination: and although they otherwise hold Luther's authority in low esteem, they are nevertheless accustomed to display this book of his as a kind of shield of Ajax, and to promise themselves certain victory over us from it. Therefore, in order to open our mind in a few words, we shall respond 1. in general, 2. in particular, and we shall briefly run through the principal, somewhat harsh expressions of Luther.

LXV. GENERAL RESPONSE 1. We are not bound by the authority of any man in matters of faith, because we know that Scripture alone is infallible, to which whatever is consonant must be judged truth: whatever is dissonant, falsehood. The writings of the holy Fathers themselves must be examined by that norm: whence Augustine, book 11 against Faustus the Manichaean, says: This kind of literature is to be read not with the necessity of believing, but with the liberty of judging. And Jerome in his Epistle to Theophilus: I know that I hold the Apostles differently, and other commentators differently. The former always speak the truth, the latter, as men, err in certain things. And yet Luther confessed this primarily about himself, whence in the preface to his works he diligently prays the reader to compare all things with the Scriptures, and to benevolently forgive him, as a man and formerly a seduced monk, if he has erred anywhere. But if, therefore, Luther has written certain things that are most absurd in that book, it does not shall the whole of religion be endangered for this reason, because we have not sworn to the words of Luther, but read his writings with the freedom of judgment? And whatever is brought forward from him without the Scriptures, all this is nothing but purely human testimony, which in divine matters has either no power of proof or certainly a foreign one. Let the Romanists therefore cease to cast this book in our teeth, because we do not deny that Luther, like all the Fathers, could have erred. Let the Calvinists cease to brandish him like some head of a Gorgon, since truth must be demonstrated from the Scriptures, not from human testimonies, which they themselves, especially Luther's, are otherwise accustomed to value little. If, therefore, we were not to undertake the defense of this book at all, nothing would follow other than 1. That Luther was a man, and could have erred. 2. That he also erred in some things, especially in the first time of the reformation. 3. And therefore that faith is to be resolved into the authority of no man, but of God alone or of holy Scripture. And indeed in this respect, before morose adversaries, it will be most safe. For just as they themselves merely laugh at the testimonies of Luther in other articles, so we can dispatch them in a few words if we recall them solely to Scripture, all human authority being set aside, which adds nothing to faith, nor takes anything away.

LXVI. 2. Luther composed this little book before the Calvinistic struggle, and therefore spoke somewhat more securely, not otherwise than other fathers, who wrote many things less cautiously before adversaries had arisen. Thus Augustine excused very many, while in book 1 against Julian, chapter 2, he says: Before the Pelagians were disputing, the Fathers spoke more securely. Before the Eutychian heresy, some said that the personal union was made κατὰ ἐπιμιξίαν, and that the Word was mixed with the flesh; Nyssen, as also Athanasius before Nestorius, called the flesh of Christ θεοφόρον θεοδόχον, which word was afterwards condemned in Nestorius. Justin first called a personal [union] συνάφειαν, as it were a soldering and joining: and likewise σύζευξιν, a copulation and connection, which terms Nestorius afterwards abused. The same happened to others, because they spoke more securely as long as they had no adversaries. Their mind indeed was orthodox, but their tongue was freer, so that it may be said of them what Scaliger said of the ancient philosophers: What they felt well, they expressed poorly. We discover that this very thing also happened to Luther. For because the dispute concerning the necessity of events and the reason for eternal predestination had not yet been stirred up by the Calvinists, he used in many places more secure phrases, which the faction of Calvin now abuses, just as before the Flacian controversy he wrote more harshly concerning sin, that it is the very nature of man, that he can do nothing else but sin, from which the Flacians afterwards sought patronage for their error, although Luther by no means abolished every distinction between substance and the sin inherent in the substance.

LXVII. 3. The Doctors of the Church, refuting a certain heretic and thinking nothing of the other extreme, often seem to incline toward that one, when nevertheless they do nothing of the sort. In which part the same happened to them as to peddlers, as Basil teaches in Epistle 41 to Maximus, when they strive to correct the crooked state of a tender tree, they sin by pulling too much to the other side. To this point also belongs that which Scaliger writes in Exercitation 307, section 28, concerning Averroes: It happens to him as to those who have both legs stuck in the mud. For the more strenuously they take care to extricate themselves with one or the other, the more firmly and deeply they fix the other. Of this matter not a few examples are obvious in the Fathers. Cyril, resisting Nestorius, in order to refute his dogma more strongly, said that the union of the two natures in Christ was φυσικήν κατὰ φύσιν, which Eutyches afterwards seized upon and pressed. Augustine and others disputing against Pelagius, who denied that the gift of renewal depends on grace, generally interpreted the term grace of infused gifts, which the scholastics later extending more broadly, intruded that meaning into the article of Justification, and thus contended that we are justified by an infused habit. Yet the very same thing clearly happened to our Luther, who while he was disputing sharply against the assertors of free will, seems to have lapsed into the other extreme, and to have removed all contingency, although elsewhere and outside of conflict he explained himself far otherwise.

LXIIX. 4. In the writings of Luther, this is to be observed, that he himself later limited and corrected some things published in earlier years. For he was at first stuck in thick darkness, and was progressing from day to day, so that he did not attain the truth in all things at one time. For which reason he himself in the preface to his Latin works warns the reader, and asks that he read those things with judgment, nay, with much compassion: Let him know, he says, that I was once a most insane Monk and Papist. And below: If you are going to read my little works, be mindful that I was one (as I said above) of those who (as Augustine writes of himself) have progressed by writing and teaching, not of those who from nothing suddenly become the highest, when they are nothing, having neither worked, nor felt, nor experienced, but at one glance of Scripture exhaust its whole Spirit. Therefore if anyone wishes for a compendium of Lutheran doctrine, and desires to be certain about his fixed and constant opinion, he will hardly attain his end better than if he runs through the articles of the Augsburg Confession, and compares them with the writings of Luther. For he subscribed to that with heart and pen; he inculcated that to all as the undoubted token of his confession. Whatever therefore is handed down in the Augsburg Confession, that Luther piously believed, and wished to be believed, even if in his earlier writings on the same subject he may have spoken somewhat more harshly. Now indeed the Augsburg Confession acknowledges the contingency of things, and grants to man freedom in external actions in Article 18. Therefore the same was the perpetual and constant opinion of Luther: For the sake of further illustration we append the very words of the Augsburg Confession, which are as follows: Concerning free will they teach that the human will has some freedom to effect civil righteousness and to choose things subject to reason: but it does not have the power without the Holy Spirit to effect the righteousness of God, or spiritual righteousness, because the natural man does not perceive the things which are of the Spirit of God, or this is done in hearts when the Holy Spirit is conceived through the word. Augustine says these same words in book 3 of the Hypognosticon. We confess that free will exists in all men, having indeed the judgment of reason, not by which it is fit in those things which pertain to God, without God either to begin or certainly to complete, but only in the works of the present life, both good and also evil: I say good, which arise from the good of nature, that is, to wish to labor in the field, to wish to eat and drink, to wish to have a friend, to wish to have clothing, to wish to build a house, to wish to take a wife, to feed cattle, to learn the art of various good things, to wish for whatever good pertains to the present life. All of which do not subsist without divine governance, nay, they are from Him and through Him, and began to be. But I say evil, as it is to wish to worship an idol, to wish for murder, etc. They condemn the Pelagians, and others who teach that without the Holy Spirit, by the powers of nature alone, we can love God above all things. Likewise to perform the precepts of God, as regards the substance of the acts. For although nature can in some way effect external works, for it can keep hands from theft, from murder, yet it cannot effect interior motions, such as fear of God, trust toward God, chastity, patience, etc. From these most clear words it shines forth sufficiently that an absolute necessity is not taught by Luther, that not all contingency is denied, and therefore whatever is written more harshly in the book concerning the enslaved will, that is not opposed to the public Confession always approved by Luther, but rather ought to be explained according to that, and mitigated by suitable limitations,

LXIX. 5. Luther himself in a certain way corrected what he had spoken more incautiously. For in his Commentary on Genesis chapter 26, he treats at length the topic of predestination, where we wish the following things in particular to be observed,

Latin:

LXIV. Diffiteri non possumus, in illo plurimas phrases duras, & prima lectione incōuenientes contineri, quas perpetuò nobis objiciunt Pontificij, & quibus pessimè abutuntur Caluiniani. Nam illi omnia Lutheri dogmata ob id suspecta reddere: hi opinionem suam impiam de necessitate, & prædestinatione absoluta palliare cogitant: cumque aliàs paruipendant Lutheri authoritatem, hunc tamen illius librum veluti quendam Ajacis clypeum nunquam non ostentare, & sibi exinde certam de nobis victoriam polliceri consueuerunt. Vt ergo paucis nostram aperiamus mentem, 1. in genere. 2. in specie respondebimus, & præcipuas locutiones Lutheri duriusculas paucis percurremus.

LXV. RESPONSIO GENERALIS 1. Nullius hominis authoritate tenemur in rebus fidei, quia novimus solam Scripturam esse infallibilem, cui quicquid consonum, veritas: quicquid dissonum, falsitas censeri debet. Ipsa sanctorum Patrum scripta ad normam illam examinanda sunt: vnde Augustinus lib. 11. contra Faustum Manichæum ait: Genus hoc literarum non cum credendi necessitate, sed cum iudicandi libertate legendum est. Et Hieronymus in Epistola ad Theophil. Scio me aliter habere Apostolos, aliter alios tractatores. Illos semper vero dicere, istos in quibusdam, ut homines, aberrare. Atqui hoc inprimis de seipso Lutherus fassus est, vnde in præfatione suorum operum lectorem diligenter orat, vt omnia cum Scripturis conferat, sibique tanquam homini, olim seducto Monacho, sicubi erratum, sit benevolè ignoscat. Quod si ergò maximè quædam Lutherus absurda scripserit in libro isto, non tamen ob id tota periclitabitur religio, quia in Lutheri verba non iurauimus, sed istius scripta cum libertate iudicandi legimus. Et quicquid ex illo profertur absque Scripturis, hoc omne nil nisi merè humanum testimonium est, quod in diuinis vel nullam vel certè peregrinam probandi vim habet. Desinant ergo Romanenses hunc librum nobis obijcere quia Lutherum, vti Patres omnes, errare potuisse non diffitemur. Cessent Caluiniani iactare istum veluti Gorgonis quoddam caput, cùm ex Scripturis demonstranda sit veritas, non ex humanis testimonijs, quæ ipsi, præsertim Lutheri, parùm aliàs æstimare solent. Si ergo maximè libri istius defensionem non susciperemus, nihil tamen sequeretur aliud, quàm 1. Lutherum fuisse hominem, & errare potuisse. 2. In quibus dam quoque præsertim primo reformationis tempore errâsse. 3. Ideoque fidem in nullius hominis, sed solius Dei vel sanctæ Scripturæ authoritatem esse resoluendam. Et sanè hoc respectu coram morosis aduersarijs tutissimum erit. Vt enim ipsi testimonia Lutheri tantùm rident in alijs articulis : sic paucis nos expedire possumus, si illos ad Scripturam, seposita omni authoritate humanâ, quæ fidei nihil addit, nec adimit, vnicè reuocemus.

LXVI. 2. Lutherus libellum istum confecit antę certamen Caluinisticum, ideoque nonnihil securius est locutus, non secus atque alij patres, qui aduersariis nondum exortis multa scripserunt incautius. Ita plurimos excusabat Augustinus, dum l. 1. contra Iulianum c. 2. inquit: Pelagianis nondum litigantibus, Patres securius locuti sunt. Ante hæresin Eutychianam dixêre quidam, Vnionem personalem esse factam κατὰ ἐπιμιξίαν, verbumque carni permixtum, Nyssenus, vt & Athanasius ánte Nestorium vocauit carnem Christi θεοφόρον θεόδοχον, quæ vox in Nestorio postmodum damnata est. Iustinus vnion nem personalem primùm vocauit συνάφειαν quasi ferruminationem & iuncturam: itemque σύζευξιν copulationem & connexionem, quibus vocibus postmodum abusus est Nestorius. Idem alijs contigit, quòd securius locuti fuerint, quamdiu nullos habuere aduersarios. Mens quidem orthodoxa fuit, sed lingua liberior, vt de illis dici possit, quod Scaliger de antiquis Philosophis: Quod benè senserunt, malè sunt elocuti. Hoc ipsum quoque Luthero euenisse deprehendimus. Quia enim lis de necessitate eventuum & ratione prædestinationis æternæ tum nondum mota fuit à Caluinianis, in multis securiores phrases adhibuit, quibus nunc factio Caluini abutitur, non secus atque ante certamen Flacianum durius scripsit de peccato, quod ipsa sit natura hominis, quod hic nihil aliud possit, quam peccare, vnde postmodum Flaciani erroris sui quæsiuerunt patrocinium, cùm tamen Lutherus omne inter substantiam & peccatum substantiæ inhærens discrimen minimè sustulerit.

LXVII. 3. Doctores Ecclesiæ, refutantes certum quendam hæreticum, nihilque cogitantes de altero extremo, sæpiùs videntur in istud inclinare, cùm tamen nihil minus faciant. Qua in parte idem ijs contigit, quod institoribus, quo docente Basilio, Epistola 41. ad Maximum, quando incurvam tenellæ arboris statum corrigere student, nimiâ attractione in alteram partem peccant. Facit huc & illud Scaligeri Exercit. 307. sect. 28. de Auerroe ita scribentis. Evenit ei, quod iis, qui in limo vtrumque crus impactum habent. Quò namque sese alterutro expedire enixius curant, eò fictius ac profundius alterum defigunt. Huius rei non pauca in Patribus exempla sunt obuia. Cyrillus Nestorio resistens, quò eius dogma fortiùs refutaret, vnionem duarum in Christo naturarum, dixit esse φυσικήν κατὰ φύσιν, quod postmodum arripuit & vrsit Eutyches. Augustinus & alij contra Pelagium diputantes, negantem, donum renouationis à gratia dependere, Vocabulum gratiae plerumque interpretati sunt de infusis donis, quod postea scholastici latius extendentes, significationem istam in articulum Iustificationis intruserunt, adeoque nos per infusum habitum iustificari contenderunt. Atqui idem planè Luthero nostro contigit, qui dùm acriter disputaret contra liberi arbitrij assertores, videtur in alterum extremum prolapsus, & omnem sustulisse contingentiam, cùm tamen alibi & extra conflictum longè aliter se explicuerit.

LXIIX. 4. In Lutheri scriptis hoc obseruandum, quòd nonnulla prioribus annis edita, ipse postmodum limitauerit & correxerit. Hærebat enim primùm in crassis tenebris, & proficiebat de die in diem, vt non vno tempore veritatem assecutus sit in omnibus. Quâ de causâ ipse in præfatione operum Latinorum lectorem monet, rogatque vt ista legat cum judicio, imò cum multa miseratione: Sciat, inquit, me fuisse aliquando Monachum & Papistam insanissimum. Et infra: Si facturus es opuscula mea, memor sis, me vnum fuisse (vt suprà dixi) ex illis, qui (vt Augustinus de se scribit) scribendo & docendo profecerunt, non ex illis qui de nihilo repentè fiunt summi, cùm nihil sint, neque operati, neque sentati, neque experti, sed ad vnum intuitum Scripturæ totum Spiritum eius exhauriunt. Proinde si compendium quis velit doctrinæ Lutheranæ, & de sententia eius immota constantique certus esse desideret, vix melius assequetur finem suum, quàm si articulos Augustanæ Confessionis percurrat, & cum scriptis Lutheri conferat. Illi enim corde & calamo subscripsit; illam omnibus tanquam indubitatam confessionis suæ tesseram inculcauit. Quicquid ergo in Augustana Confessione traditur, illud Lutherus sanctè credidit, credique voluit, si maximè in prioribus scriptis de eadem materia nonnihil durius fuerit lotutus. Iam verò Augustana Confessio agnoscit rerum contingentiam, & concedit homini libertatem in externis actionibus Articulo, 18. Ergo eadem fuit Lutheri perpetua constansque opinio: Pro minoris illustratione ipsa verba Augustanæ Confessionis adscribimus, quæ sic habent: De libero arbitrio docent, quòd humana voluntas habeat aliquam libertatem ad efficiendam civilem iustitiam, & diligendas res rationi subiectas: sed non habet vim sine Spiritu sancto efficiendæ iustitiæ Dei, seu iustitiæ spiritualis, quia animalis homo non percipit ea, quæ sunt Spiritus Dei seu hæc fit in cordibus, cùm per verbum Spiritus sanctus concipitur. Hæc totidem verbis dicit Augustin. libr. 3. Hypognosticon. Esse fatemur liberum arbitrium omnibus hominibus, habens quidem iudicium rationis, non per quod sit idoneum in iis, quæ ad Deum pertinent, sine Deo aut inchoare aut certè peragere, sed tantùm in operibus vitæ præsentis tam bonis quam etiam malis: Bonis dico, quæ de bono naturæ oriuntur, id est, velle Laborare in agro, velle manducare & bibere, velle habere amicum, velle habere indumenta, velle fabricare domum, uxorem velle ducere, pecora nutrire, artem discere diversarum rerum bonarum, velle quicquid bonũ ad præsentē pertinet vitam. Quæ omnia non sine divino gubernaculo subsistunt, imò ex ipso & per ipsum sunt, & esse cœperunt. Malis verò dico, vt est velle idolum colere, velle homicidium, &c. Damnant Pelagianos, & alios qui docent, quòd sine Spiritu sancto, solis naturæ viribus possumus Deum super omnia diligere. Item præcepta Dei facere, quoad substãtiam actuum. Quanquam enim externa opera aliquo modo efficere natura possit, potest enim continere manus à furto, à cæde, tamen interiores motus non potest efficere, vt timorem Dei, fiduciam erga Deum, castitatē, patientiam, &c. Ex hisce apertissimis verbis elucescit satis, q non doceatur à Luthero absoluta necessitas, nō negetur omnis Cōtingentia, ideoq; quicquid durius in libro de seruo arbitrio scriptum est, illud Confessioni publicæ à Luthero semper approbatæ, non opponi, sed potius fecundum illam exponi, & commodis limitationibus mitigari debet,

LXIX. 5. Lutherus ipse quodammodo correxit, quæ securius erat prolocutus, Nam in Commentario super Genesin cap. 26. prolixè tractat locum de prædestinatione, vbi sequentia inprimis obseruauari volumus,


### Question II. What is to be determined concerning Luther's book, which has the…: Fol. 384. A. He inveighs most gravely against the Epicureans who reason thus

1. Fol. 384. A. He inveighs most gravely against the Epicureans who reason thus: If I am predestined, whether I act well or ill, I shall be saved: If I am not predestined, I shall be damned, because what God has predetermined must come to pass. These, he says, are diabolical and poisonous darts, and original sin itself, by which the Devil seduced our first parents; from which it would follow that God sent his Son in vain, and in vain promulgated the Gospel and instituted the Sacraments. Luther therefore clearly rejects simple necessity, and considers it to be the illusions of the Devil; nor does he deduce predestination from an absolute decree, but wishes the respect of Christ and the means to be included, since he concludes that otherwise all things would be void if we were absolutely predestined.

2. On the same folio, page b, he distinguishes between the hidden God and the revealed God, and adds: Concerning God, insofar as he is not revealed, there is no faith, no knowledge, and no cognition. And there it must be held what is said, that things above us are nothing to us: for thoughts of this kind, which search for something more sublime above or outside the revelation of God, are utterly diabolical, by which nothing more is achieved than that we cast ourselves into destruction, because they present an uninvestigable object, namely God not revealed. But rather let God retain his decrees and mysteries in secret. There is no reason why we should labor so much that they be manifested to us. Luther, however, by the hidden God, wishes nothing else to be understood than certain secret counsels and particular judgments, which are sometimes hidden, but never unjust. By the revealed God he denotes the very word of God, or his will expressed by the word namely, where all are referred to Christ, and his gratuitous merit. He never therefore maintains that predestination is absolute, and to be sought in the hidden God: but only in the revealed God. Hence he always sends those who doubt to the universal will of God and the merit of Christ, while he writes on the same page: He who sees me, says CHRIST, sees the Father himself. If you hear him, and have been baptized in his name and love his word, then you are certainly predestined, and certain of your salvation. But if you curse or despise the word, then you are condemned, Because he who does not believe is condemned. And Folio 385. A. Hear the incarnate Son, and predestination will offer itself spontaneously. Look upon the wounds of CHRIST, and the blood shed for you: from these will shine forth predestination. Holy Neophytes are accustomed to think about GOD outside of CHRIST: these are they who attempt to ascend into heaven, and to plant both feet there: but suddenly they are plunged into the depths. Let the pious therefore beware and do this one thing, that they learn to adhere to the boy, and to the Son JESUS, who is your GOD, incarnate for your sake. Acknowledge and hear him, and take delight in him and give thanks. If you have him, then you also have the hidden GOD equally with the revealed one. And that is the only way, truth and life, outside of which you will find nothing except destruction and death. And a little below: These thoughts or doubts about predestination are therefore not free: But they are impious, wicked, diabolical. Therefore when the Devil attacks you with them, only say, I believe in our LORD JESUS CHRIST, concerning whom I have no doubt that he was incarnate, suffered, and died for me. Into whose death I have been baptized. With this response the temptation vanishes, and Satan turns his back. Thus therefore Luther most clearly teaches and defends that our predestination is not absolute, but limited, and restricted to the means, namely the merit of CHRIST and faith, and therefore is not to be sought in the hidden GOD.

8. Memorable are the words of Luther, which under it joins folio 383. B. I have wished to warn and teach thus studiously and accurately. Because after my death many will bring my books into the public eye, and from them will confirm errors of every kind and their own delusions. I wrote, however, among other things, that all things are absolute and necessary: but at the same time I added that GOD revealed must be looked upon, as we sing in the Psalm: He is Jesus Christ, the LORD of Hosts, and there is no other God; JESUS CHRIST is the Lord of Hosts, nor is there another GOD: and elsewhere very often. But they will pass over all these passages, and will seize only those concerning the hidden GOD. You, therefore, who now hear me, remember that I have taught this, that one must not inquire about the predestination of the hidden GOD. But one must rest in that which is revealed through the calling and through the ministry of the Word. For there you can be certain of your faith and salvation, and say: I believe in the Son of GOD, who said: He who believes in the Son has eternal life, therefore in him there is no condemnation, or wrath, but the good pleasure of GOD the Father. These same things, however, I have protested elsewhere also in my books, and now I also deliver them with a living voice, therefore I am excused. This prophecy of Luther is too true, and the Calvinists sufficiently prove its certainty by their own example. We, however, oppose to them the very explanation of Luther, by which he draws us back from speculations about the hidden God and secret particular counsels, about which he treated somewhat in 'On the Bondage of the Will', and warns that we should look upon the revealed GOD, and inquire for his will in the word, which leads us by the hand to CHRIST, outside of whom one must not think about predestination; if the Calvinists held this one thing in consideration, they would not defend that gross dogma of absolute Election, nor would they ignorantly and imprudently drag Luther's words about the particular and hidden judgments of GOD to describe the very nature of predestination in general.

LXX. Just as indeed in the Commentary on Genesis: So in Chapter 1 to the Galatians, he clearly explained his mind. For there too he warns that we should abstain from speculations of the divine majesty, and of the hidden GOD, what He wills, what pleases Him, but rather that eyes are to be turned to the revealed GOD, since no one knows the Father, except the Son, and he to whom the Son has willed to reveal Him. Besides this way, he says, you will simply find no other way to the Father; but error; not truth, but hypocrisy, and a lie: not life, but eternal death. And a little later: Christian and true Theology does not thrust GOD in Majesty, as Moses and other doctrines, does not command to search the nature of GOD, but to acknowledge His will proposed in CHRIST, whom He willed to assume flesh, to be born, to die, for our sins, and this to be preached to all nations.

LXXI. SPECIAL RESPONSE. There are many things which at first sight appear inconvenient in the said book of Luther: We, however, will touch upon only two in a few words, and at the same time we forewarn that we will use in the citation that edition which appeared separately in the year 1526 at Wittenberg in 8vo. He writes therefore on page 6. Free will is a mere lie, which by the example of that woman in the Gospel, the more she is treated by physicians, the worse she fares. But these words are not to be understood universally, as if all will were denied absolutely and in total, but rather according to the mind of the Augsburg Confession, concerning will in spiritual matters, where it is enslaved, nay, clearly nothing, and a mere lie.

LXXII. II. On page 26 he asserts: All things which we do, all things which happen, although they seem to us to happen mutably and contingently, in truth nevertheless happen necessarily and immutably, if you look at the will of GOD. For the will of GOD is efficacious, which cannot be hindered, since it is the very natural power of God: which same theme he treats at length in the following pages, but here we wish it to be considered.

1. That Luther in the Aug. Confession, to which he subscribed, expressly acknowledges contingency and liberty in external matters.

2. Nor does he deny this in the very booklet, if anyone [looks at] page 60, where he expressly writes: But if we are altogether unwilling to omit that word, which would be the safest and most religious course, let us nevertheless in good faith teach you to this extent, that free will is granted to man not with respect to a superior, but only to an inferior, that is, that he may know that he has the right in his own faculties and possessions to use, to do, and to omit according to his free will, although even that itself is governed by the free will of GOD alone, whatsoever it may please Him. Otherwise towards GOD, or in matters which pertain to salvation or damnation, he does not have free will, but is a captive, subject, and slave, either to the will of GOD or to the will of Satan. And page 115. he speaks even more clearly: From this place, he says, if you will, begins the question concerning free will, so that through Ecclesiasticus we may understand man to be distributed into two kingdoms, one in which he is carried by his own will and counsel, without the precepts and commands of GOD, for instance in matters inferior to himself: here he reigns and is Lord, left in these things to the hand of his own counsel: not that GOD so deserts him that He does not cooperate in all things, but that He has granted him the use of things freely according to his will, and has not inhibited him by any laws or prescriptions, etc.

3. If Luther is taken so crudely, that God wills all things, not even excepting sins, and works all things, so that all things thus happen necessarily, then it follows that GOD is the cause of sin, and concurs in all evil actions. This, however, is most clearly denied by the nineteenth article of the Augsburg Confession. Wherefore Luther's words are to be understood in a suitable manner.

4. A distinction must be made between human acts and the events themselves. As far as acts are concerned, Luther never denied that some are in our power: but with respect to events, all things happen necessarily. For GOD governs all things, and directs them to an end pleasing to Himself. Since, therefore, the outcome of things and acts is not in our power, in this respect it can certainly be said that all things which happen, happen necessarily. may not be done. And that Luther had regard to this, page 28 and following teach. 5. Actions are either good or evil. If good, God wills them, instigates man to them, and cooperates with man when they are done. With respect, therefore, to good actions, it is rightly said that all things depend upon the divine will, and this being presupposed, they are done necessarily. But God does not will evil actions, but hates them. Therefore, they can neither depend upon nor proceed from the will of God. Hence, those sayings of Luther are to be understood concerning good actions, lest the analogy of faith be disturbed, and God be blasphemously established as the cause of sin. 6. All actions, both good and evil, can be evaluated either with respect to God foreseeing, or with respect to us. If the former, then all things are done necessarily, because the foreknowledge of God is infallible. When, therefore, He foresaw what man was about to do, and preordained what he ought to do by reason of the good: then, on account of the immutability of the decree and preordination, all things are done necessarily, not indeed absolutely, but on account of the said hypothesis, which nevertheless, with respect to us and the acting cause, and thus in their principles, were free and contingent. 7. Finally, let us remember that Luther, by these phrases, wishes nothing other than that the business of salvation does not depend upon our powers, or upon our will, but that all things are carried out according to the will of God. We only suffer in conversion, God does everything: and thus with respect to Him, all things are done necessarily and immutably: He himself touches upon this on page 5, writing thus: Two things require such things to be preached. The first is the humiliation of our pride and the knowledge of grace: the other is the Christian faith itself. First, God has certainly promised His grace to the humbled, that is, to the deplored and the desperate. But man cannot be thoroughly humbled until he knows that his salvation depends entirely, outside of his own powers, counsels, endeavors, will, and works, altogether upon the will, counsel, volition, and work of another, namely of GOD alone, since, as long as he is persuaded that he can do even the slightest bit for his own salvation, he remains in self-confidence; nor does he despair of himself completely, therefore he is not humbled before GOD, but presumes or hopes for or at least desires some place, time, or work for himself, by which he may finally arrive at salvation. But he who doubts nothing, that everything depends on the will of GOD, he despairs completely of himself, chooses nothing, but awaits GOD working, he is nearest to grace, so that he may be saved. And again page 54. Active paradox; Let us briefly see that whatever is done by us is done not by free choice, but by mere necessity, lest we allow it to be called most pernicious. Here if I say: When it has been proven that, beyond our powers and counsels, our salvation depends on the work of GOD alone, which I hope I shall prove below in the body of the discussion, does it not clearly follow that, while GOD is at work in us, all things that we do are evil and we necessarily act, because they are of no value for salvation. For if not we, but GOD alone works salvation in us, we do nothing salutary before His work, whether we will it or not. You see therefore that Luther himself, in what he argues concerning the enslaved choice and the necessity of events, wishes them to be restricted to the business of our salvation, so that the meaning is: Concerning the business of salvation, man left to himself cannot but act evilly, and therefore when he acts, he necessarily acts evilly, on account of the corruption of nature, so that for Luther necessity is the same thing as the immutable slavery of sin outside the state of grace.

LXXIII. And thus we have vindicated two of Luther's assertions from a sinister and heterodox sense: We do not deny that more occur, but since those primarily look to the topic of predestination and its nature, we add nothing further here, but fixing our foot, we give thanks to GOD, that He has caused the liberty lost in Adam to be restored through CHRIST, and we pray Him that He may more and more illuminate our mind, and convert our will, so that we may walk in the path of His commandments, and thus always do things acceptable to Him and salutary to us. AMEN.

Latin:

1. Fol. 384. A. grauissimè inuehitur in Epicureos ita colligentes: Si sum prædestinatus, siue benè, siue malè egero, saluabor: Sinon sum prædestinatus, damnabor, quia oportet fieri, quod Deus præfiniuit. Hæc esse, dicit, diabolica & venenata tela, & ipsum peccatum originale, quo seduxit Diabolus primos parentes; vnde sequatur, frustrà Deum misisse filium, frustrà promulgâsse Evangelium ac instituisse Sacramenta. Lutherus ergo necessitatem simplicem clarè reijcit, & pro præstigiis Diaboli habet; nec prædestinationem ex absoluto decreto deducit, sed respectum Christi & mediorum vult inclusum, quippè quæ aliàs omnia fore irrita concludit, si absolutè essemus prædestinati.

2. Folio eodem fac. b. distinguit inter Deum absconditum & Deum reuelatum, & addit: De Deo, quatenus non est reuelatus, nulla est fides, nulla scientia & cognitio nulla. Atque ibi tenendum est, quod dicitur, quæ supra nos nihil ad nos : eiusmodi enim cogitationes, quæ supra aut extra reuelationem Dei, sublimius aliquid rimantur, prorsus diabolicæ sunt, quibus nihil amplius proficitur, quam vt nos ipsos in exitium præcipitemus, quia obijciunt obiectum imperuestigabile, videlicet Deum non reuelatum. Quin potius retineat Deus sua decreta & mysteria in abscondito Non est, cur ea manifestari nobis tantoperè laboremus. Lutherus verò per Deum absconditum, nihil vult aliud intellectum, quàm arcana quædam consilia, & particularia iudicia, quæ nonnunquam occulta, nunquam iniusta sunt. Per Deum reuelatum notat ipsum verbum Dei, vel voluntatem eius verbo expressam, vbi omnes remittuntur ad Christum, eiusque meritum gratuitum. Nunquam igitur statuit quòd prædestinatio sit absoluta, & in Deo abscondito quærenda: sed duntaxat in Deo reuelato. Hinc dubitantes semper ad voluntatem Dei vniversalem & meritum Christi ablegat, dum eâdem paginâ scribit: Qui videt me, inquit CHRISTVS, videt & patrem ipsum. Si hunc audieris, & in nomine eius baptisatus fueris & diligas verbum eius, tum certò es prædestinatus, & certus de tua salute. Si verò maledicis aut contemnis verbum, tum es damnatus, Quia qui non credit, condemnatur. Et Folio 385. A. Audi filium incarnatum, & spontè se offeret prædestinatio. Intuere vulnera CHRISTI, & sanguinem pro te fusum: ex istis fulgebit prædestinatio. Solent sancti Neophyti cogitare de DEO extra CHRISTVM: hi sunt, qui in cælum ascendere, & vtrumque pedem ibi figere conantur: sed subitò ad inferos demerguntur. Caueant igitur pij & id vnum agant, vt discant adhærere puero, & Filio IESV, qui est DEVS tuus, propter te incarnatus. Hunc agnosce & audi, ac delectare in eo & age gratias. Si hunc habes, tum etiam DEVM absconditum pariter cum reuelato habes. Et illa est vnica via, veritas & vita, extra quam nihil præter exitium & mortem inuenies. Et paulò infra: Non igitur liberæ sunt cogitationes istæ siue dubitationes de prædestinatione: Sed sunt impiæ sceleratæ, diabolicæ. Ideò quando Diabolus ijs te impugnat, tantum dicas, Credo in DOMINVM nostrum IESVM CHRISTVM, de quo mihi non est dubium quin sit incarnatus, passus, mortuus pro me. In cuius mortem ego sum baptisatus. Hoc responso euanescit tentatio, & tergum vertit Satan. Ita ergo Lutherus prædestinationem nostram non absolutam, sed limitatam, & ad media, nempe CHRISTI meritum ac fidem restrictam, ideóque in DEO abscondito non quærendam esse, clarissimè docet & propugnat.

8. Memorabilia sunt verba Lutheri, quæ subiungit folio 383. B. Hac studiosè & accuratè sic monere & tradere volui. Quia post meam mortem multi meos libros proferent in medium, & inde omnis generis errores, & deliria sua confirmabunt. Scripsi autem inter reliqua esse omnia absoluta & necessaria: sed simul addidi, quòd aspiciendus sit DEVS reuelatus, sicut in Psalmo canimus: Er heist JEsus Christ/ der HERR Zebaoth/ vnd ist kein ander GOtt/ IESVS CHRISTVS est Dominus Zebaoth, nec est alius DEVS:& alias sæpissimè. Sed istos locos omnes transibunt, & eos tantũ arripient, de DEO abscondito. Vos igitur, qui nunc me auditis, memineritis, me hoc docuisse, non esse inquirendum de prædestinatione DEI absconditi. Sed eâ acquiescendum esse, quæ reuelatur per vocationem & per ministerium Verbi. Ibi enim potes de fide & salute tua certus esse, ac dicere: Ego credo in Filium DEI, qui dixit: Qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam, Ergo in eo non est damnatio, aut ira, sed beneplacitum DEI Patris. Hæc eadem autem alibi quoque in libris meis protestatus sum, & nunc etiam viuâ voce trado, ideo sum excusatus. Nimis vera est hæc Lutheri Prophetia, eiusque certitudinem suo exemplo Caluiniani satis comprobant. Nos autem ijs ipsam Lutheri explicationem opponimus, quâ nos retrahit à speculationibus de Deo abscondito, & arcanis consilijs particularibus, de quibus egit nonnihil de seruo arbitrio, monetque, vt aspiciamus DEVM reuelatum, inquiramus eius voluntatem in verbo, quod nos manu ducit ad CHRISTVM, extra quem de præstinatione non sit cogitandum; quod vnum si pensi haberent Caluinicolæ, crassum istud de absoluta Electione dogma non defenderent, nec Lutheri verba de particularibus occultisque iudicijs DEI ad ipsam prædestinationis naturam in genere deseribendam, imperitè & imprudentertraherent.

LXX. Vti verò in Commentario super Genesin: Ita in Capit. 1. ad Galatas, suam mentem luculenter explicuit. Nam & ibi monet, vt abstineamus à speculationibus maiestatis divinæ, & DEI absconditi, quid ille velit, quid ipsi placeat, sed potius ad DEVM revelatum oculos esse flectendos, cùm nemo nouerit Patrem, nisi Filius, & cui Filius voluerit revelare. Præter hanc viam, inquit, simpliciter nullam inuenies aliam viam ad Patrem; sed errorem; non veritatem, sed hypocrisin, & mendacium: non vitam, sed æternam mortem. Et paulò pòst: Christiana & vera Theologia non ingerit DEVM in Majestate, vt Moses & alia doctrinæ, non iubet scrutari naturam DEI, sed agnoscere voluntatem eius propositam in CHRISTO, quem voluit assumere carnem, nasci, mori, propter peccata nostra, & hoc prædicari in omnes gentes.

LXXI. RESPONSIO SPECIALIS. Multa sunt, quæ primâ fronte in dicto Lutheri libello inconuenientia apparent: Nos autem duo tantum paucis attingemus, simulque hoc præmonemus, nos in citatione vsuros illa editione, quæ seorsum Anno 1526. Wittebergæ in 8. prodijt. Scribit igitur pagin. 6. Liberum arbitrium est merum mendacium, quod exemplo mulieris illius Euangelicæ, quò plus à medicis curatur, eo peius habet. Verùm hæc verba non sunt vniuersaliter intelligenda, ac si omne arbitrium prorsus & in totum negaretur, sed potius iuxta Confessionis Augustanæ mentem, de arbitrio in rebus spiritualibus, vbi illud servum est, imò planè nullum, & merum mendacium.

LXXII. II. Paginâ 26. asserit: Omnia, quæ facimus, omnia quæ fiunt, etsi nobis videntur mutabiliter & contingenter fieri, reverâ tamē fiunt necessariò & immutabiliter, si DEI voluntatem spectes. Voluntas enim DEI efficax est, quæ impediri non potest, cùm sit naturalis ipsa potentia Dei: quod ipsum Thema sequentibus paginis prolixè tractat, Hic autem considerari volumus.

1. Quòd Lutherus in Aug. Confessique, cui subscripsit, disertè agnoscat contingentiam & libertatem in externis.

2. Neque hanc diffitetur in ipso libello, siquis dem pagin. 60. expressè scribit: Quod si omnino vocem eam omittere nolumus, quod esset tutissimum & religiosissimum, bonâ fide tamen eatenus vos doceamus, vt homini arbitrium liberum non respectu superioris, sed tantum inferioris vel concedatur, hoc est, vt sciat, sese in suis facultatibus & possessionibus habere ius vtendi, faciendi, omittendi pro libero arbitrio, licet & id ipsum regatur solius DEI libero arbitrio, quæcunque illi placuerit. Ceterum erga DEVM, vel in rebus, quæ pertinent ad salutem vel damnationem, non habet liberum arbitrium, sed captivus, subiectus & seruus est, vel voluntatis DEI, vel voluntatis Satanæ. Et pagin. 115. clarius adhuc loquitur: Ab hoc loco, ait, si volueris incipit quæstio de libero arbitrio, vt per Ecclesiasticum intelligamus hominem in duo regna distribui, vno quo fertur suo arbitrio & consilio, absque præceptis & mandatis DEI, puta in rebus sese inferioribus: hic regnat & est Dominus, iis in manu consilij sui relictus: non quòd DEVS illum sic deserat, vt non in omnibus cooperetur, sed quod vsum rerum illi liberum pro arbitrio concesserit, nec ullis legibus aut præscriptis inhibuerit, &c.

3. Si Lutherus ita crassè accipiatur, quòd Deus Omnia, nè quidem peccatis exceptis, velit, & omnia operetur, vt ita cuncta eueniant necessariò, tùm sequitur, quod DEVS sit causa peccati, & concurrat ad omnes actiones malas. Hoc autem Articulo decimo nono Augustan. Confession. clarissimè negatur. Quare Lutheri verba commodè sunt intelligenda.

4. Distingui debet inter actus humanos & euentus ipsos. Quod actus attinet, quosdam in nostra esse potestate, Lutherus nusquam negauit: respectu verò euentuum omnia fiunt necessariò. DEVS enim gubernat omnia, & ad finem dirigit sibi placentem. Cùm igitur rerum actuumque euentus non sit in nostra potestate, hoc sanè respectu dici potest, quòd omnia quæ fiunt, necessariò fiant. nõ fiant. Et huc respexisse Lutherum, docet pagina 28. & seq. 5. Actiones vel bonæ sunt vel malæ. Si bonæ, Devs illas vult, ad illas hominem instigat, hominique; cum fiunt, cooperatur. Respectu ergò bomarum actionum rectè dicitur, quod omnia dependeant à voluntate diuina, & hac præsuppositâ, fiant necessariò. Malas verò actiones DEVS non vult, sed odit. Quia ergò à DEI voluntate vel pendere, vel prouenire possunt. Proinde ista Lutheri dicta de bonis actionibus sunt intelligenda, ne turbetur analogia fidei, & DEVS blasphemè statuatur causa peccati. 6. Omnes jactus, & boni & mali, possunt æstimari vel respectu DEI præuidentis, vel respectu nostri, Si illud, tum cuncta fiunt necessariò : quia DEI præscientia est infallibilis. Quando igitur præuidit quid homo acturus sit, & præordinauit, quid ratione boni agere debeat : tum ob immutabilitatem decreti & præordinationis cuncta fiunt necessariò, non quidem absolutè, sed ob dictam hypothesin, quæ tamen respectu nostri & causæ agentis, adeoque in suis principiis erant libera & contingentia. 7. Denique recordemur, Lutherum istis phrasibus nihil aliud velle quàm negotium salutis non pendere à nostris viribus, vel ab arbitrio nostro, sed omnia ad DEI voluntatem geri. Nos tantùm patimur in conuersione, DEVS agit omnia : atque sic respectu eius, cuncta fiunt necessariò & immutabiliter : Hoc tangit ipse pag. 5. ita scribens, Duæ res exigunt talia prædicari. Prima est humiliatio nostræ superbiæ & cognitio gratiæ : altera ipsa fides Christiana. Primum, DEVS certò promisit humiliatis, id est deploratis & desperatis gratiam suam. Humiliari verò penitus non potest homo, donec sciat, prorsus extra suas vires consilia, studia, voluntatem, opera omninò ex alterius arbitrio, consilio, voluntate, opere, suam pendere salutem, nempè DEI solius, siquidem, quam diu persuasus fuerit, sese vel tantulum posse pro salute sua, manet in fiducia sui; nec de se penitus desperat, ideò non humiliatur corã DEO, sed locum, tempus, opus aliquod sibi præsumit vel sperat vel optat saltem, quo tandem perveniat ad salutẽ. Qui verò nihil dubitat, totum in voluntate DEI pendere, is prorsus de se desperat, nihil eligit, sed expectat operantem DEVM, is proximus est gratiæ, ut salvus fiat. Et rursus pagin. 54. Activum paradoxon; Quicquid fit à nobis non arbitrio libero, sed merâ necessitate fieri, breviter videamus, ne perniciosissimum dici patiamur. Hic si dico: Vbi id probatum fuerit, extra vires & consilia nostra, in solius opere DEI pendere salutem nostram, quod infrà in corpore disputationis spero me evicturum, nonne clarè sequitur, dum DEVS opere suo in nobis est, omnia esse mala, quæ facimus & nos necessariò operari, quia nihil ad salutem valent. Si enim non nos, sed solus DEVS operatur salutem in nobis, nihil ante opus eius operamur salutare, velimus nolimus. Vides ergo Lutherum ipsum, quæ de arbitrio seruo, & necessitate euentuum disputat, ad negocium salutis nostræ restricta velle, vt sit sensus. Circa negotium salutis homo sibi relictus, non potest non malè agere, ideoque cum agit, necessariò malè agit, ob naturæ corruptionem, vt ita Luthero necessitas idem sit, quod immutabilis seruitus peccati extra statum gratiæ.

LXXIIL Atque sic duas Lutheri assertiones à sinistro & heterodoxo sensu vindicauimus: Plures occurrere non inficiamur, sed cum illæ primariò spectent ad locum de prędestinatione eiusque natura, nihil hîc vltra addimus, sed pedem figentes, DEO grates agimus, quòd libertatem in Adamo amissam per CHRISTVM reparari fecerit, eumque oramus, vt magis magisque mentem nostram illuminet, & voluntatem convertat, vt in semita mandatorum eius ambulemus, adeoque ipsi accepta, nobis salutaria semper faciamus. AMEN.


## 27 Disputation IV. On the Terms of the Article of Justification, and Its Efficient, Impelling and Meritorious Causes

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent, Master Johannes Rottlöben of Wittenberg.

Thesis I.

There is scarcely another article of the Christian faith that has been attacked by more adversaries and in more ways than this present one, which concerns the justification of man, or the gratuitous remission of sins. I will say nothing of the ancient heretics: the Papacy alone can provide clear testimony as to how hostile Satan is to this doctrine, while through his minions he has so miserably corrupted it in the Roman Church that the honor due to Christ the Redeemer has been diminished, the distinction between Law and Gospel has been removed, and firm comfort has been utterly denied to fearful consciences. Pighius himself was forced by the power of truth to confess this, writing as follows: We cannot hide the fact that this, the very first part of Christian doctrine, has been obscured rather than illustrated by our people through most of the thorny scholastic questions and definitions.

II. But God, at length taking pity on His Church, raised up the great man Luther, who faithfully pointed out the Papal corruptions and, with the Most High granting success, happily restored the doctrine of justification to its pristine and Apostolic purity. For in all his writings, nothing so gravely he urged, nothing so often he inculcated, as that man is justified by faith alone apprehending the merit of Christ, with all works of the law excluded. Hence in the preface to the epistle to the Galatians: In my heart, he says, this one article reigns, namely the faith of Christ. From whom, through whom, and in whom all my theological thoughts flow and reflow day and night. And yet I do not find that I have comprehended the height, breadth, and depth of such wisdom, except for certain weak and poor first fruits and as it were fragments. A little after these things he adds: It is necessary to treat this article as diligently as possible and to oppose it to Satan, whether we are infants, or eloquent, or learned, or unlearned. For it is necessary that this rock be cried out, if every man were silent, by the very rocks or stones. And again: This doctrine can never be sufficiently treated and inculcated. With it lying prostrate and perishing, the whole knowledge of truth lies prostrate and perishes at the same time; but with it flourishing, all good things flourish, religion, true worship, the glory of God, the certain knowledge of all states and things.

III. For this article is as it were the center of Theology, to which all things aim: it is a sacred ocean, into which all things flow; it is the ark of faith, which keeps all things safe and unharmed. If one errs here with the Papists, immediately the grace of GOD is changed into an infused habit, the merit of CHRIST is diminished, faith is held as a mere disposition, something inherent is substituted for Evangelical righteousness, the distinction between Law and Gospel is confounded, the πληροφορία of faith is taken away, the merit of works is established, satisfactions are urged, suffrages are sought, masses are celebrated, saints are invoked, purgatory is kindled, the monastic life is chosen, and many other elective forms of worship are introduced, as Luther most rightly pronounced in his narration of the argument on the Epistle to the Galatians: With the article of justification lost, the whole Christian doctrine is lost at the same time. But if the true opinion has been grasped in this head of doctrine, now almost the whole Papacy is conquered, and every business is accomplished, since the rest collapse of their own accord and cannot stand any longer. So very true is that proverb of Luther, which he used quite often: Justification is the article of the standing and falling Church.

IV. Therefore, the greater the dignity and utility of this article, the more diligent the effort that ought to be expended: that it may be purged of all corruptions and propagated uncorrupted to posterity, especially since our Luther predicted several times in his commentaries on Genesis and the Epistle to the Galatians that this doctrine of gratuitous Justification would be obscured again in our time, which prophecy experience testifies quite clearly has indeed been fulfilled. Therefore, just as we have hitherto considered the controversy concerning free will in thesis and antithesis, so now we shall treat with equal faithfulness the present doctrine of Justification, which Bellarmine immediately appended.

V. Moreover, the ὁμονοία of this article can be included in three principal chapters. In the first, certain terms must be explained. In the second, we shall have to discourse upon the individual causes of the nature of justification. In the third, the most salutary doctrine concerning the certainty of justification must be established and defended. We, about to make a beginning from the exposition of terms, premise this: that there are three kinds of words which we use in describing the dogmas of the Christian faith.

For 1. Some are only Biblical, which are found only in the sacred Scriptures, such as the word Jehovah, Messiah, CHRIST, etc. 2. Some are Ecclesiastical, which do not exist in the sacred code, but are nevertheless used by the Church to beat back heretics, such as Trinity, ὑπόστασις, Infant Baptism. 3. Some are common, which are not only held in the Scriptures, but are also heard quite often in daily conversation. These, however, are either common as to letter and sense alike, examples of which occur in great numbers: or they agree only as to the letters and differ in sense, which distinction must be most diligently observed, lest through foreign acceptations of words, a foreign doctrine contrary to the word of God be introduced. Such a common word, however, is justice, which both the Apostle and Aristotle use, but in a different sense: to the latter it is an inherent habit: to the former by no means, but rather the imputation of another's justice, and absolution from sins. While the scholastics did not consider this, they erred most gravely by defining theological justice through a habit, and thus perniciously changing that word into a philosophical sense. Wherefore it is worth the effort that we accustom ourselves to the language of the Holy Spirit, and diligently note what justice, just, to justify, what grace, freely, and the imputation of faith are to Him. Although, however, we have explained most of these terms elsewhere, it is nevertheless pleasing to repeat in a few words the principal points, the knowledge of which is prerequisite here, lest the treatment of this article be incomplete and half-full. But with these explained, we shall see the very nature of our justification, and we shall diligently explain the reason for each cause according to the powers which the Most High will supply.

OF THE WORDS USED IN THIS ARTICLE.

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. M. Iohanne Rottlöben Wittembergensi.

Thesis I.

VIx alius est articulus Christianae fidei, qui à pluribus aduersarijs, modisque pluribus fuerit oppugnatus, quàm hic praesens, qui est de Iustificatione hominis, seu gratuita remissione peccatorum. Nihil dicam de antiquis haereticis: vel solus Papatus luculentum praebere potest testimonium, quàm infensus huic doctrinae sit Satanas, dum per mancipia sua tam miserè illam corrupit in Ecclesia Romana, vt Christo Redemtori suus honor imminutus, discrimen Legis & Euangelij sublatum, pauidisque conscientijs firmum solatium prorsus denegatum fuerit. Quod ipsum vi veritatis fateri coactus est Pighius ita scribens: Dissimulare non possumus, à nostris hanc vel primam doctrinae Christiana partem, obscuratani quàm illustratam magis à scholasticis spinosis plerisque quaestionibus & definitionibus.

II. Deus verò Ecclesiae suae tandem misertus, excitauit Megalandrum Lutherum, qui corruptelas Papales fideliter monstrauit, & doctrinam de iustificatione puritati pristinae & Apostolicae, successum largiente Altissimo, feliciter restituit. In omnibus enim suis Scriptis nihil tàm grauitet graviter vrsit, nihil tàm sæpè inculcauit, quàm hominem iustificari sola fide meritum Christi apprehendente, omnibus legis operibus exclusis. Hinc in præfat. super epistolam ad Galatas: In corde meo, inquit, iste vnus regnat articulus, scilicet fides Christi. Ex quo, per quem, & in quem omnes meæ diu noctuque fluunt & refluunt Thealogicæ cogitationes. Nec tamen comprehendisse me experior detantæ altitudinis, latitudinis, profunditatis sapientiæ, nisi infirmas & pauperes quasdam primitias & velluti fragmenta. Paulò post hæc subjungit: Opus est hunc articulum quàm diligentissimè tractare & Satanæ opponere, siuè simus infantes, siuè eloquentes, siuè docti, siuè indocti. Oportet enim hanc petram clamari, si omnis homo taceret, ab ipsis petris seu lapidibus. Et rursus: Hæc doctrina nunquam satis tractari & inculcari potest Eà iacente & pereunte, iacet & perit simul tota cognitio veritatis; Eà verò florente, florent omnia bona, religio, verus cultus, gloria Dei, certa cognitio omnium statuum & rerum.

III. Nam articulus hic quasi centrum Theologiæ est, ad quod omnia collimant: Sacer oceanus est, in quem omnia confluunt; arca fidei est, quæ omnia seruat tuta & illibata. Hic si erretur cum Pontificiis, mox DEI gratia mutatur in habitum infusum, CHRISTI meritum extenuatur, fides pro sola dipositione habetur, justitiæ Euangelicæ quiddam inhærens substituitur, discrimen Legis & Evangelij confunditur, πληροφορία fidei tollitur, meritum operum stabilitur, satisfactiones vrgentur, suffragia conquiruntur, missæ celebrantur, sancti inuocantur, purgatorium succenditur, monastice eligitur, multiq; alij cultus electitij introducuntur, vt rectissimè pronunciârit Lutherus in enarratione argumenti super Epistolam ad Galatas: Amisso articulo iustificationis, amissa est simul tota doctrina Christiana. Quòd si verò in hoc doctrinæ capite vera sententia fuerit percepta, jam totus fermè Papatus expugnatus, & omne negotium confectum est, siquidem cætera vltrò ruunt, & diuitius consistere haut queunt. Adeò verissimum est illud Lutheri prouerbium, quo sæpius fuit vsus: Iustificatio est articulus stantis & cadetis Ecclesiæ.

IV. Quò igitur maior huius articuli & dignitas est & vtilitas, eò diligentior impendi debet opera: vt ab omnibus corruptelis purgetur, & incorruptus ad posteros propagetur, præsertim cùm Lutherus noster aliquoties in commentarijs suis super Genesin & Epistolam ad Galatas prædixerit, hanc de gratuita Iustificatione doctrinam, nostro tempore rursus obscuratam iri, quod sanè vaticinium reipsâ esse impletum, haut obscurè testatur experientia. Vt ergò hactenus controuersiam de libero arbitrio in thesi & autithesi considerauimus: ita nunc præsentem de Iustificatione doctrinam, quam Bellarminus immediatè subjunxit, pari fidelitate pertractabimus.

V. Potest autem ὁμονοία huius articuli tribus præcipuè capitibus includi. In primo vocabula quædam veniunt explicanda. In secundo de singulis causis naturæ justificationis disserendum erit. In tertio saluberima de certitudine iustificationis doctrina adstruenda & propugnanda est. Nos à terminorum expositione initium facturi, hoc præmonemus, quòd tria sint vocabulorum genera quibus vtimur circa dogmata Christianæ fidei describenda.

Nam 1. Quædam sunt tantùm Biblica, quæ non nisi in sacris reperiuntur Scripturis, vt vocabulum Iehouæ, Messiæ CHRRISTI, &c. 2. Quædam sunt Ecclesiastica, quæ non extant in sacro codice, ab Ecclesiatamen ad retundendos hæreticos vsurpantur, vt Trinitas, ὑγνοσία, Pædobaptismus. 3. Quædam sunt communia, quæ non tantùm in Scripturis habentur, sed in cotidiana etiã conuersatione sæpius audiuntur. Hæc autem vel sunt communia quoad literam & sensum simul, quorum exempla occurrunt plurima: vel tantùm quoad literas conueniunt & sensu differunt, quod discrimen diligentissimè obseruandum est, nè per peregrinas vocabulorum acceptiones, peregrina & verbo Dei contraria doctrina introducatur. Tale autem commune vocabulum est iustitia, quo vtitur & Apostolus & Aristoteles, sed diuerso sensu: Huic habitus inhærens est: Illi neutiquam, sed potius imputatio justitiæ alienæ, & absolutio à peccatis. Hoc dum non considerârunt scholastici, gravissimè errarunt, justitiam Theologicam per habitum definiendo, atque sic vocabulum istud in Philosophicum sensum perniciosè mutando. Quocirca operæ pretium est, vt linguæ Spiritus S. adsuescamus, & diligenter annotemus, quid ipsi sit iustitia, iustus, iustificare, quid gratia, gratis, fidei imputatio. Quamuis autem plerosque istos terminos alibi exposuerimus, placet tamen præcipua momenta, quorum cognitio hîc prærequiritur, paucis repetere, ne manca sit & semi plena huius articuli tractatio. Istis verò explicatis, ipsam iustificationis nostræ naturam videbimus, & singularum causarum rationem pro viribus, quas suppeditabit Altissimus, diligenter exponemus.

DE VOCABVLIS IN HOC ARticulo usitatis.


### Question I. What does the word justice denote?

What does the word justice denote?

VI. All terms in need of explanation can be comprehended by this one Aphorism: We are justified by the grace of God freely through faith, and the imputation of the justice of Christ. But because to justify descends from just and justice, for that reason we shall propose these words first, intending to proceed afterwards to the explanation of the rest.

VII. Justice has its name from right, which is from commanding. For whatever the Magistrate and the laws command, this is right, and he who obeys is considered endowed with justice. In Greek it is called δικαιοσύνη, from δίκαιον, which word Aristotle, 5 Eth. 7, derives from δίχα, bipartitely, because the just man divides a thing into two parts equal in their own way, so that δίκαιον is as it were διχαιον: and δικαστὴς as it were διχαστής, which etymology fits distributive justice well, by which to each is given his own. The Hebrews call justice צדק or צדקה from the root צדק which denotes to justify, to pronounce just, to absolve, to excuse, etc.

VIII. But as far as the meanings of this word are concerned, many of them are found here and there. The Philosopher inculcates universal and particular justice, which he divides into distributive and commutative. To the theologian, one justice is concreated, another simulated, another imputed, another begun, another consummated. Thus we commonly distinguish between Evangelical justice or that of faith, which is imputed; and legal, or that of works, which is either only external, or internal, and proper only to the reborn, and is begun in this life, and will be consummated in the other. Luther was accustomed to name Evangelical justice passive, because through it we are absolved by God, we working nothing, and legal active, because through this we strive to act well. He always, however, admonished that we should turn our eyes from active to passive justice. Bellarmine, book 1 on justification, chapter 1, recounts four meanings of justice, while he says he notes 1. Right. 2. Righteousness written in books. 3. Righteousness of external works. 4. Internal righteousness. But more occur here and there, which we will briefly enumerate.

IX. However, we will not be much concerned about the philosophical acceptations, where justice is taken

1. for the whole choir of virtues, which is called universal

2. for particular justice, divided into distributive and commutative.

3. For the obedience of an inferior towards the laws of his superior.

4. For faith and truth for

of missions, we shall see the Biblical and especially Theological meanings, where it is to be noted that Justice is attributed partly to God, partly to Christ, partly to men, and in each attribution different meanings occur.

X. 1. When it is attributed to God, it denotes 1. His essential rectitude and perfection, concerning which Deut. 32. v. 4. God is faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright: II. Judicial and vindicatory justice, which the modern Photinians deny. It is founded, however, on Rom. 1. v. 32, 2 Thess. 1. v. 5, 6, Ps. 9. v. 5, Ps. 119. v. 137, Ps. 145. v. 17. III. The truth of promises or faithfulness in keeping promises, Ps. 36. v. 7, Isa. 45. v. 19, 1 John 1. v. 9. IV. The will expressed by law or the commandments of God, which in the Psalms are frequently called justice, as Ps. 19. v. 9, Ps. 119. v. 12. V. Benefits proceeding mercifully from God, 1 Sam. 12. v. 7. VI. The very goodness and mercy of God, as Dan. 9. v. 16. According to all your justices turn away your wrath. Thus Ps. 51. v. 16, Ps. 69. v. 28, Ps. 71. v. 2, Ps. 143. v. 1, 2. Hence justice, truth, and mercy are interchanged, Ps. 40. v. 10, 12, which has also been done by interpreters Gen. 19. v. 19, ch. 20. v. 13, ch. 21. v. 23, ch. 32. v. 10, Ps. 103. v. 6. And thus this word is mostly taken when the discourse is about Justification. Nor was this acceptation entirely unknown to profane writers. For thus says Sostrata in Terence's Heautontimorumenos: Let there be some protection for my folly in your justice. VII. The justification of men or imputed justice. For this is often called by the Apostle the justice of God, as Rom. 3. v. 20, 21, 22, which happens 1. By reason of its arrival, because it pleases God, whence Luther significantly translates: The justice that is valid before God, to which Paul not obscurely refers in Rom. 4. v. 2, 2. By reason of the efficient cause, because it is from God, and is conferred upon us out of His grace, whence Phil. 3. v. 9.

is called righteousness from God or by God. 3. By reason of the meritorious cause, since it was performed in our place by Christ, the Son of God and true God, and then imputed to us. Furthermore, this also can be noted here: that the Greeks distinguish between δικαίωμα, between δικαίωσιν and δικαιοσύνην. By δικαίωμα is indicated the rule of divine righteousness revealed by the law, as in Rom. 1. v. last, ch. 2. v. 26, ch. 8. v. 4. δικαίωσις denotes the act of our justification, Rom. 5. v. 18. δικαιοσύνη is found taken partly for vindicatory righteousness, partly for the goodness and mercy of God.

XI. II. When it is attributed to CHRIST, then it signifies: 1. His habitual righteousness, which consists in plenary innocence and the absence of all sin. 2. His actual righteousness, which was perfect obedience and fulfillment of the law, which is commended in Rom. 5. v. 17, 18. 3. The righteousness acquired for us, which is called the righteousness of Christ, since it was obtained through him, whence he himself is also named our righteousness, Jer. 23. v. 6.

XII. III. When it is attributed to MEN, it denotes: I. Obedience toward the law of God, which he indeed demands to be perfect, Matt. 5. v. 20, but we are able to perform, and therefore sometimes external obedience of any kind is called righteousness, Phil. 3. v. 6: II. Any good works, Ps. 15. v. 6. III. Righteousness of a cause, Ps. 18. v. 21. IV. Beneficence, 2 Cor. 9. v. 10. V. Almsgiving, Dan. 4. v. 24. VI. The reward of a righteous life, Gen. 30. v. 33. VII. Evangelical righteousness or that of faith, by which we are righteous before God; and that consists in the gratuitous remission of sins on account of Christ apprehended by faith, who is the foundation of our righteousness; Rom. 3. v. 12, 22, 24, 1 Cor. 1. v. 30, Gal. 2. v. 16. But the Papists describe righteousness far differently, namely by an infused habit; or an internal rectitude, by which a man is rightly ordered toward God and neighbor, which alone is simply righteousness, and is called the righteousness of faith, because it begins from faith, and the righteousness of God, since it is given by him, which are the words of Bellarmine in book 1 of Justification, chapter 1. But since this figment is unknown to Scripture, and drawn from Aristotelian pits, it is deservedly rejected by us.

Latin:

Iustitiæ vocabulum quid notet?

VI. Omnes termini explicationis indigi possunt hoc vno Aphorismo comprehendi: Iustificamur ex gratia Dei gratis per fidem, & iustitiæ Christi imputationem. Quia vero justificare à justo & iustitia descendit, ob id vocabula isthæc prius proponemus, pòst ad reliquorum ἐξήγησιν accelluri.

VII. Iustitia nomen habet à jure, quod est à iubendo. Quicquid enim Magistratus & leges jubent hoc jus est, & qui obtemperat, justitiaque præditus censetur. Græcis δικαιοσύνη dicitur, a δικαιῷ, quam vocem Aristot. 5. Eth. 7. deriuat à δίχα bipartito, quòd justus in duas suo modo æquales partes rem diuidat, vt δίκαιον, sit quasi διχαιον: & δικαστὴς quasi διχαστής, quod ἔτυμον optin è conuenit justitiæ distributiuæ, quâ vnicuique suum datur. Hebræi iustitiam vocant צדק vel צדקה à rad. צדק quæ notat justificare, justum pronunciare, absoluere, excusare, &c

IIX. Quod verò significationes huius vocabuli attinet, multæ illarum passim reperiuntur. Philosophus inculcat iustitiam vniuersalem & particularem, quam in distributiuam & commutatiuam dispescit. Theologo alia est justitia concreata, alia simulata, alia imputata, alia inchoata, alia consummata. Sic vulgò distinguimus inter justitiam Euangelicam seu fidei, quæ imputata est; & legalem, seu operum, quæ vel externa tantùm, vel interna est, solisque renatis propria, & inchoatur in hac vita, consummabitur in altera.
