Lutherus iustitiam Euangelicam nominare solitus est passiuam, quia per eam absoluimur à Deo, nos nihil operantur, & legalem actiuam, quia per hanc benè agere studemus. Semper autem admonuit, vt ab actiua ad passiuam iustitiam oculos flectamus. Bellar. l. 1. de iustifi. c. 1. quatuor justitiæ significationes recenset, dum notare ait 1. Ius. 2. Rectitudinem scriptam in libris. 3. Rectitudinem operum externorum. 4. Rectitudinem internam. Verùm plures easque passim occurrūt, quas breuiter enumerabim⁹.

IX. Non autem multum soliciti erimus de acceptionibus Philosophicis, vbi iustitia sumitur.

1. pro toto virtutum choro, quæ vniuersalis dicitur

2. pro particulari iustitia, in distributivam & commutatiuam diuisa.

3. Pro obedientia inferioris erga leges sui superioris.

4. Pro fide & veritate pro

missionum, Biblicas potissimum & Theologicas fignificationes videbimus, vbi notandum, quòd Iustitia tribuatur partim Deo, partim Christo, partim hominibus, & in qualibet attributione diuersa significata occurrunt.

X. 1. Cùm Deo tribuitur, notat 1. Essentialem eius rectitudinem & perfectionem, de qua Deut. 32. v. 4. Deus fidelis & absque vlla iniquitate iustus & rectus: II. Iudiciariam & vindicatricem iustitiam, quam negant recentiores Photiniani. Fundatur autem Rom. 1. vers. 32. 3. Thess. 1. vers. 5. 6. Psal. 9. v. 5. Psal. 119. vers 137. Psal. 145. vers. 17. III. Veritatem promissionum vel fidelitatem in seruandis promissis, Ps. 36. v. 7. Esa. 45. vers. 19. 1. Ioh. 1. vers. 9. IV. Voluntatem lege expressam vel mandata Dei, quæ in Psalmis crebrò vocantur iustitia, vt Psal. 19. vers. 9. Psal. 119. vers. 12. V. Beneficia à Deo misericorditer profecta, 1. Sam. 12. vers. 7. VI. Ipsam bonitatem & misericordiam Dei, vt Dan. 9. vers. 16. Secundum omnes iustitias tuas auerte iram tuam. Sic Psal. 51. vers. 16. Psal. 69. vers. 28. Psal. 71. vers. 2. Psal. 143. vers. 1, 2. Hinc iustitia, veritas & misericordia permutantur, Psal. 40. vers. 10. 12. quod ab interpretibus quoque factum Gen. 19. vers. 19. cap. 20. vers. 13. cap. 21. vers. 23. cap. 32. vers. 10. Psal. 103. vers. 6. Et ita plerumque sumitur hoc vocabulum, cùm sermo est de Iustificatione. Neque profanis scriptoribus prorsus ignota fuit hæc acceptio. Sic enim apud Terentium ait Sostrata in Heaut. Mea stultitię in iustitia tua sit aliquid pręsidij. VII. Iustificationem hominum vel iustitiam imputatam. Hæc enim ab Apostolo sæpè vocatur iustitia Dei, vt Rom. 3. vers. 20. 21. 22. quod fit 1. Ratione aduentus, quia Deo placet, inde Lutherus significanter vertit. Die Gerechtigkeit die für Gott gilt/ quò Rom. 4. vers. 2. non obscurè Paulus respicit, 2. Ratione causæ efficientis, quia est à Deo, & nobis ex gratia ipsius confertur, vnde Phil. 3. vers 9.

vocatur iustitia ex Deo seu à Deo. 3. Ratione causæ meritoriæ, quoniam à Christo, Dei filio, veroque Deo nostri loco est præstita & deinde nobis imputata Porrò & illud hic notari potest;quod Græci distinguunt inter δικαίωμα diti:inter δικαίωσιν & δικαιοσύνην. Per δικαίωμα indicatur regula iustitiæ divinæ lege patefacta, vt Rom. 1. v. vlt cap. 2. v. 26. c. 8. vers. 4. δικαίωσις notat actum iustificationis nostræ Rom. 5. v. 18 δικαιοσύνη partim pro iustitia vindicatrice, partim pro bonitate & misericordia Dei sumta reperitur.

XI. II. Cùm CHRISTO tribuitur, tum signi ficat. 1. Iustitiam eius habitualem, quę consistit in plenaria innocentia, & omnis peccati absentia. 2. Iustitiam eius actualem, quæ fuit perfecta obedientia & impletio legis, quæ Rom. 5. vers. 17. 18. commendatur. 3. Iustitiam nobis acquisitam, quæ vocatur iustitia Christi, quoniam per illum parta est, vndè & ipse nostra iustitia nominatur, Ierem. 23. v. 6.

XII. III. Cum HOMINIBVS tribuitur, notat; 1 Obedientiam erga legem Dei, quam ipse quidem perfectam postulat, Matth. 5. v. 20. Nos autem præstare possumus, ideoque nonnunquam externa qualiscunque obedientia vocatur iustitia, Phil. 3. v. 6: 11. Quæuis bona opera. Psal. 15. vers. 6. III. Iustitiam causæ, Psal. 18. vers. 21. IV. Beneficentiam 2. Cor. 9. v. 10. V. Eleemosynam. Dan. 4. vers. 24 VI. Præmium instæ vitæ, Genes. 30. v. 33. VII. Iustitiam Euangelicam vel fidei, quâ iusti sumus coram Deo; & consistit illa in gratuita remissione peccatorum propter Christum fide apprehensum, qui est fundamentum nostræ iustitiæ; Rom. 3. vers. 12. 22. 24. 1. Corinth. 1. v. 30. Gal. 2. v. 16. Sed Pontificii longè aliter describunt iustitiam, nempe per infusum habitum; vel internã rectitudinem, quâ homo rectè ordinetur erga Deum & proximum quæ sola sit simpliciter iustitia, & dicatur iustitia fidei, quia à fide incipit, & iustitia Dei, quoniam ab illo donatur, quæ Bellarmini verba sunt l. 1. de Iustifi. cap. 1. Cùm verò figmentum hoc Scripturę sit ignotum, & ex lacunis Aristotelicis haustum, meritò à nobis reijcitur.


### Question II. In what ways is the term 'just' understood?

XIII. Some observe that someone can be just in three ways: 1. By nature. 2. By grace. 3. By voluntary and perfect obedience toward God and His law. Nature, in turn, is twofold, namely, either by one's own essence in and of itself, or because one is made or born just by the benefit of another. In the former way, God alone possesses justice, since He alone is essentially just. In the latter way, Adam was just at the beginning or in the state of integrity, because God created him just. By grace, however, all believers are just, whose justice is partly the imputed justice of Christ, by which they are just before God, and partly inherent and begun, by which they are called just before men. But by voluntary and perfect obedience, no man in this world after the fall of Adam is or can be just, on account of the excessive corruption of nature and the sin that perpetually adheres. Here we only begin obedience and the fulfillment of the law, but it will be consummated in the other life, where that which is in part will be abolished. Christ, however, possesses justice in all these ways, because He is just: 1. By nature, both by essence as He is God, and by birth, insofar as He is a man conceived of the Holy Spirit. 2. Graciously, on account of the personal union and in respect of habitual justice. 3. Voluntarily, on account of the most perfect obedience rendered to the heavenly Father.

XIV. But besides those meanings, there are far more, partly philosophical, partly theological that occur: philosophically, he is just: 1. Who is endowed with every virtue. 2. Who gives to each his own. 3. Who obeys the laws prescribed to him; & 4. who faithfully keeps what he has promised. Theologically, he is called just: I. God; 1. on account of His essential rectitude. 2. Insofar as He issues just precepts. 3. He judges justly. 4. & 6. He justifies believers. II. Christ: 1. Insofar as He is without sin. 2. Insofar as He fulfilled the law and acquired justice for us. III. Man: 1. Insofar as he obeys the law. 2. He acts well and justly. 3. He is beneficent, & 4. he has the justice of Christ imputed to him, which is the meaning of this passage, and holds the chief place among the others:

Latin:

XIII. Obseruant nonnulli, quòd trifariam aliquis esse possit iustus. 1. Naturâ. 2. Gratiâ. 3. Voluntariâ perfectâque erga Deum & legem eius obedientiâ. Natura rursus bifariam, nempè aut propriâ essentiâ per seipsum: aut quia iustus alterius beneficio factus vel natus est. Priori modo solus Deus iustitiam obtinet, quippe solus essentialiter iustus. Posteriori modo Adamus fuit iustus initiò vel in statu integritatis, quia Deus illum iustum condidit. Gratiâ verò iusti sunt omnes credentes, quorum iustitia partim est imputata Christi, quâ sunt iusti coram Deo, partim inhærens & inchoata, quâ dicuntur iusti coram hominibus. Sed voluntariâ perfectâque obedientiâ, nemo hominum in hoc mundo post lapsum Adami iustus est aut esse potest, ob nimiam naturæ corruptionem & perpetuò adhærens peccatum. Hîc duntaxat incipimus obedientiam & legis impletionem, sed consummabitur in altera vita, vbi abolebiturid, quod ex parte est. Christus autem his modis omnibus iustitiam possidet, quia iustus est. 1. Naturâ & tum per essentiam quâ Deus, tum per nativitatem, quatenus ex Spiritu sancto conceptus homo est. 2. Gratiosè ob vnionem personalem, & respectu habitualis iustitiæ. 3. voluntariâ propter perfectissimam obedientiam, Patri cœlesti præstitam.

XIV. Præter illas verò significationes longè plures partim Philosophicæ, partim Theologicæ occurrunt: Philosophicè justus est: 1. Qui omni virtute præditus. 2. Qui suum cuique tribuit. 3. Qui legibus sibi præscriptis obtemperat; & 4. quod promisit, fideliter seruat. Theologicè justus vocatur I. Deus; 1. ob essentialem rectitudinem. 2. quatenus justa præcepta fert. 3. justè judicat. 4. in seruandis promissionibus fidelis est. 5. Beneficia distribuit, & 6. credentes justificat. II. Christvs: 1. quatenus sine peccato est. 2. Quatenus legem impleuit & justitiam nobis acquisiuit. III. Homo: 1. quatenus legiobtemperat. 2. Benè justèque agit. 3. Beneficus est, & 4. Christi justitiam sibi habet imputatam, quæ significatio hujus loci est, & inter cæteras principatum obtinet:


### Question III. What does the word 'to justify' properly signify?

XV. The term to justify is not found among Latin writers: but the Greeks use the word δικαιόω, which is taken: 1. Neutrally, where it is the same as to deem, to consider just or equitable; thus it is read in Herodotus; δικαιοῦν Αἰγύπτιοι ἅγνον, the Egyptians consider it equitable to sacrifice. 2. Actively, and it is the same as to inflict punishment, to punish in reality. Hence δίκη sometimes signifies punishment, and among the Germans, einen armen Sünder rechtfertigen, is to exact punishment from him. 3. Passively, where δικαιοῦσθαι or to be justified is said of one to whom his right is given, who is acquitted; in which way the active δικαιόω would be to give one his right, or to declare someone just in court, and to acquit from a crime. More significations will hardly occur. Above all, the Popish interpretation of this word is clearly unknown to approved authors, when they explain to justify as to infuse a habit.

XVI. However much these acceptations may in some way be accommodated to the theological meaning of justifying, a great difference nevertheless intervenes at the same time. For one who is to be justified in the political forum must be inherently just, and have done nothing evil. But in the theological forum, he is justified who is inherently evil and contaminated by many sins, and therefore the genuine meaning of this word can and ought to be judged from the Scriptures alone.

XVII. It now remains to be seen, therefore, what meaning that word obtains in the sacred code, in the deciding of which question the Papists differ entirely from us. Bellarmine, lib. 1 de Iustificat. cap. 1, writes that the name of justification is taken in many ways in the sacred letters, and he recounts four principal acceptations: 1. For the law itself, which teaches justice, as Psalm 119, verses 8, 12; but it is a fault of the Vulgate version, which ought to have expounded the Hebrew חקים and the Greek δικαιώματα not as justifications, but as statutes or commandments. 2. For the acquisition of justice, which acquisition, however, is nothing else to him than infusion, and he cites the saying 1 Cor. 6, v. 11, Rom. 8, v. 30, chapter 4, verse 5, which testimonies the context itself and the analogy of faith prove to speak of imputed justice, not infused, of the absolution of sins, not of justification. 3. For the increase of justice, when from just one becomes more just, just as he is said to be warmed, not only he who becomes hot from cold, but also he who from hot becomes hotter. For this sense he alleges the saying Ecclesiast. 18, v. 22, James 2, verse 24, Apoc. …22, verse 11, to which it will be answered below. 4. For the declaration of justice, in a certain forensic manner, so that he is said to be justified who is declared just by a judge and is absolved, to which he applies the sayings Prov. 17, verse 15, Isa. 5, verse 13, Luke 7, verse 35, Luke 10, verse 29. From these meanings, however, he judges the second and third to pertain to the present article is, but rejects the fourth, as is evident from book 3, chapter 3. XIX. And hence it is that they distinguish between first and second justification. The first, says Becanus in his disputation on the justification of Catholics, chapter 1, consists in the acquisition of righteousness; the second in the increase of the same. The first is gratuitous, the second is from the merits of good works. Paul speaks of the first, James of the second. He explains the first more fully in chapter 2, and defines it as the translation from the state of sin into the state of grace, which happens in two ways: 1. By the remission or expulsion of sin. 2. By the infusion or acquisition of righteousness, not otherwise than as heating, by which someone becomes hot from being cold, contains two parts, the expulsion of cold and the acquisition of heat.

XIX. But we have a far different mind, since we say from Scripture that the term justifying is forensic, and denotes the gratuitous absolution of a sinful man about to be punished, on account of the merit of Christ, and his acceptance into grace, so that he is no longer pronounced and held as a guilty person, but as a just and absolved one. For that word comprises three things. 1. To absolve the accused, so that he may not be judicially condemned. 2. To judge and pronounce him just. 3. To grant to the one thus justified the testimony and rewards which are owed to the innocent.

XX. And indeed if we look at the force and use of the Hebrew root צדק, it is nowhere read to be used for the infusion of righteousness. For in Kal it denotes to have righteousness, or to be just positively, as Psalm 19, verse 10, Psalm 143, verse 2, Job 9, verse 20, sometimes also to act justly, Job 33, verses 9, 12. In Piel it denotes to attribute righteousness to oneself or another, Job 32, verse 2, Jeremiah 3, verse 11. In Hiphil, however, it obtains a forensic meaning, and is the same as to absolve someone in judgment and pronounce him just, whether it is done truly or falsely, and whether it is said of God or of creatures. In Hithpahel it signifies to justify oneself, and to prove the goodness of one's cause by arguments and testimonies to assert, as in Genesis 44, verse 16. And these meanings are found throughout the Scriptures: but concerning the Papist [meaning] taken as infusion, there is deep silence. XXI. For if we run through the principal texts of both Testaments, it will clearly appear that to justify primarily and chiefly signifies to absolve someone or to declare them just. From the Old Testament, let the passage be seen, Gen. 44, v. 16. Exod. 23, v. 7. Deut. 25, v. 1. 2 Sam. 15, verse 4. 1 Kings 8, verse 32. Job 27, verse 5. chap. 32, verse 2. chap. 33, verse 2. Psalm 51, verse 6. Psalm 82, verse 3. Psalm 145, verse 2. Prov. 17, verse 15. Isaiah 5, v. 23. chap. 50, v. 8. Jeremiah 3, v. 11. Sir. 1, v. 25, c. 7, v. 5. c. 19, v. 32. c. 26, v. 28.

XXII. Nor indeed does the statement from Psalm 73, verse 13 stand in the way: I have justified my heart in vain, that is, according to the Papists, I have rendered it just. For it is absurd that a man could render himself just before God, Psalm 143, verse 2. Furthermore, it is a fault of the Vulgate version, because in the Hebrew it is not 'I have justified,' but זכיתי 'I have cleansed,' and it denotes the pursuit of a blameless and innocent life. For David complains that it goes well for the wicked, but ill for the good and those following justice, and he adds, Have I therefore cleansed my heart in vain, have I labored in vain and without cause to lead a pure and innocent life?

XXIII. Thus that which is cited from Dan. 8, verse 14 is impertinent: The sanctuary shall be justified, that is, it shall be cleansed. For 1. that phrase does not denote the infusion of justice, but the restoration of worship. 2. We are inquiring about the justification of a man: they bring forward an example concerning the justification or purification of a sanctuary. 3. The Hebrew verb is not in Hiphil, of which alone we are speaking, but in Niphal ונצדק קדש. Wherefore again an Ignoratio Elenchi [ignorance of the refutation] is committed. And finally 4. that statement could be explained declaratively. It shall be sanctified, that is, it shall be declared to be holy and cleansed.

XXIV. But above all they urge the passage of Daniel

12, verse 3. Those who instruct many unto righteousness shall shine. In the Hebrew it is מצדיקים, that is, justifying, or those who justify, that is, according to Bellarmine, they make [men] righteous, because to instruct someone unto righteousness is in reality to make [them] righteous, book 2, chapter 3. But 1. It is false that one who instructs unto righteousness immediately makes the disciple righteous. For not even an ethicist teaching temperance or fortitude makes everyone strong and temperate by his footsteps. For the nature of theoretical habits, which are introduced little by little through information, is one thing; and that of moral virtues, which the teacher does not engender but merely shows the way of attaining them, is another. 2. It would be absurd to say that ministers, by justifying their hearers, infuse righteousness into them, since they themselves admit that this is the immediate action of God alone. 3. That statement is understood by reason of either theory or Christian practice. If by reason of theory, then ministers are said to justify insofar as they teach the true mode of justification and exhort men to repentance, whence the Vulgate rendered it: Those who instruct many unto righteousness. And Luther: Those who point many to righteousness. And even if such teachers are said to make [men] righteous, they do not do so by infusion, but by information and exhortation. If by reason of practice, then ministers justify insofar as they absolve from sins in the place of God and pronounce the penitent righteous. For that which is proper to God, namely to retain and remit sins, is often attributed to pastors as ministers and ambassadors of God, as Matthew 18, verse 18; John 20, verse 23; 2 Corinthians 5, verses 19, 20; for which reason Timothy is said to save both himself and his hearers, 1 Timothy 4, last verse. Thus, therefore, pastors justify their little sheep, not by infusing or really effecting righteousness in them, but 1. by informing. 2. By exhorting. 3. By absolving and pronouncing them righteous.

XXV. Furthermore, from the New Testament likewise many Passages can be produced in which 'to justify' is likewise taken in a forensic sense for 'to absolve' or 'to pronounce righteous.' See the sayings in Matt. 12:37, Luke 10:29, ch. 16:5, Acts 13:38, 39, Rom. 2:13, ch. 3:20, 26, 28, 30, ch. 4:5, ch. 5:1, 9, ch. 8:30, 33, 1 Cor. 4:4, Gal. 2:16, 17, ch. 3:8, 11, ch. 5:4, Tit. 3:7, Jas. 2:21, 24, 25. However, the passage in Matt. 11:19 and Luke 7:35, 'Wisdom is justified by her children,' is somewhat obscure, for it is accustomed to be explained in clearly different ways. To some, 'to be justified' is the same as 'to be condemned,' to which Luther seems to have referred: 'Wisdom must let itself be justified by its children.' But others explain the particle καὶ adversatively: 'But it is justified,' as it is also taken in Matt. 12:39, Acts 10:28. And thus, for them, 'to be justified' is the same as 'to obtain a testimony of righteousness and wisdom from one's children,' so that there is an opposition: 'The Pharisees rebuke me, but nevertheless I am absolved by my children.' Thus it is said in Luke 7:29, 'The publicans ἐδικαίωσαν, justified God,' that is, they pronounced Him just and good. Thus in Ps. 51:6, 'that you may be justified in your words,' that is, that you may be declared just and truthful. However, whichever explanation is held, nothing is said against the analogy of faith, nor do the Papists derive any support from it.

XXVI. And thus it has been demonstrated so far that the word 'to justify,' according to the usage of Scripture, primarily denotes 'to absolve' and 'to pronounce righteous'; against which thesis the Romanists find nothing solid to oppose. They urge the composition of the word and the grammatical analogy, because 'to justify' is the same as 'to make righteous,' just as 'to purify' denotes 'to make pure,' 'to sanctify' 'to make holy,' and 'to vivify' 'to make alive.' But 1. That analogy is not universal: we sanctify, glorify, and magnify God, not by making Him holy from profane, glorious from inglorious, or great from small, but by proclaiming Him as such.

& by celebrating: 2. One must judge the true meaning of that word not from the composition of the Latin term, but rather from the usage of the holy language. 3. A priest was said to sanctify a leper not by making him holy or cleansed, but by pronouncing him so. 4. Even if the sanctification of a man always denoted making him inherently holy, it would not follow from that that the same must be established regarding justification. 5. Hebrew verbs in Kal are neuter, in Hiphil they indeed become active and are explained by 'to make'; but it must be known that the quality of the first conjugation is attributed to another either in reality, or by permission, or by judgment, assertion, and declaration of another. Whence Flacius sets down this rule: Among the Hebrews, certain verbs which in the first conjugation signify being endowed with some quality or motion, in the third signify that that quality or motion is attributed to another by the judgment, words, and assertion of another. Thus רשע was impious; in Hiphil it denotes to condemn, or to pronounce as impious. So כזב to lie, in Hiphil is to convict of a lie. In a similar way, the Germans say: Einen fromb machen / Einen zum Dieb oder Lügener machen / not that one person makes another such in reality, but because he convicts him of theft and lying, and publicly proclaims him to be such. For the very same reason, צדק to be just, in Hiphil signifies to attribute justice to another by words, or to reckon him just and absolve him. Therefore, there is no consequence that הצדיק denotes to make just because of the mode of signifying in Hiphil. Wherefore it denotes to infuse justice. I say it does not follow, because someone can be made just also through the judgment, pronunciation, and declaration of another. Which very thing Bellarmine could not deny in book 2 of Justification, chapter 3, writing: that someone can be made just both intrinsically through the adoption of justice, and extrinsically through declaration.

Latin:

XV. Vocabulum justificandi apud scriptores Latinos non reperitur: Græci autem vsurpant verbum δικαιόω, quod sumitur. 1. Neutraliter, vbi idem est quod arbitrari, justum vel æquum censere; Sic legitur apud Herodotum; δικαιοῦν Αἰγύπτιοι ἅγνον, Ægyptij æquum censent sacrificare. 2. Actiuè, & idem est quod supplicio afficere, realiter punire. Hinc δίκη quandoque pœnam significat, & apud Germanos; einen armen Sünder rechtfertigen/ est supplicium de illo sumere, 3. Passivè, vbi δικαιοῦσθαι vel justificari dicitur, cui jus suum tribuitur, qui absoluitur; quo pacto activum δικαιόω foret, jus suum tribuere, vel in foro justum aliquem declarare, & à crimine absoluere. Plures significationes vix occurrent. Inprimis planè ignota est probatis authoribus Papistica huius vocis interpretatio, cum justificare per habitum infundere exponunt.

XVI. Quantumuis autem hæ acceptiones quodammodo accommodari possint ad Theologicam iustificãdi significationem, magnum tamen simul discrimen intercedit. Nam iustificandum in foro politico oportet inhærenter iustum esse, nihilque mali egisse. In foro autem Theologico iustificatur is, qui inhærenter malus, multisque peccatis contaminatus est, ideoq; de genuina vocis huius significatione ex solis Scripturis iudicari potest & debet.

XVII. Videndum iàm igitur restat, quamnàm in sacro codice significationem verbum illud obtineat, in qua quæstione decidenda, prorsus discrepant à nobis Pontificii, Bellarm. l. 1. de Iustificat. cap. 1. scribit, Iustificationis nomen in sacris literis multis modis accipi, & recenset quatuor potissimùm acceptiones: 1. Pro ipsa lege, quæ iustitiam docet, vt Psal. 119. vers. 8. 12. sed vitium est vulgatæ versionis, quæ Hebræum חקים & Græcum δικαιώματα non per iustificationes, sed statuta vel mandata debuit exponere. 2. Pro acquisitione iustitiæ, quæ tamen acquisitio ipsi nihil est aliud, quam infusio, citatq; dictum 1. Cor. 6. v. 11. Rom. 8. v. 30. cap. 4. vers. 5. quæ testimonia loqui de imputata iustitia, non infusa, de absolutione peccatorum, non de iustificatione contextus ipse induat & analogia fidei comprobat. 3. Pro incremento iustitiæ, cùm ex iusto fit iustior, sicut is dicitur calefieri, non solum qui fit calidus ex frigido, sed etiam qui ex calido fit calidior. Pro hoc sensu allegat dictum Ecclesiast. 18. v. 22. Iacob. 2. vers. 24. Apoc. 22. vers. 11. ad quæ infrà respondebitur. 4. Pro declaratione iustitiæ, modo quodam forensi, vt ille dicatur iustificari, qui è iudice iustus declaratur atque absoluitur, quò applicat dicta Prov. 17 vers. 15. Esa. 5. vers. 13. Luc. 7. vers. 35. Luc. 10. vers. 29. Ex his verò significationibus secundam & tertiam ad præsentem articulum pertinere arbitratur, quartam verò rejicit, vt patet ex l. 3 c. 3. X I I X. Atq; hinc est, quòd distinguūt inter iustificationem primam & secundam. Prima, inquit Becanus disputat. de iustificatione Catholicorum cap 1. constitit in acquisisione iustitiæ; secunda in augmento eiusdem. Prima est gratuita, secunda ex meritis bonorum operum. De prima loquitur Paulus, de secunda Iacobus. Primam cap. 2. fusiùs exponit, & definit translationem è statu peccati in statum gratiæ, quod fiat duobus modis: 1. Remissione seu expulsione peccati. 2. Infusione, seu acquisitione iustitiæ, non secus atque calefactio, quâ quis ex frigido fit calidus, continet duas partes, depulsionem frigoris & acquisitionem caloris.

X I X. Nobis verò longè alia mens est, quippe qui ex Scriptura dicimus, vocabulum iustificandi forense esse, & notare hominis peccatoris jamiam puniendi gratuitam ob Christi meritum absolutionem, & in gratiam acceptationem, vt non ampliùs pro reo, sed iusto absolutoque pronun cietur & habeatur. Tria enim vox illa complectitur. 1. Accusatum absoluere, nè iudicialiter condemnetur. 2. Pro iusto censere & pronunciare. 3. Ita iustificato tribuere testimonium & præmia, quæ innocentibus debentur.

X X. Et sanè si vim & vsum Hebrææ radicis צדק spectemus, nullibi pro iustitiæ infusione vsurpata legitur. Nam in kal notat iustitiam habere, vel iustum esse politiuè vt Psal. 19. vers. 10. Psal. 143. vers. 2. Iob. 9, vers. 20. quandoque etiam iustè agere, Iob. 33. vers 9. 12. In Piel notat tribuere sibi vel alteri iustitiam, Iob. 32. vers. 2. Ierem. 3. vers. 11. In Hiphil verò forensem significationem obtinet, idemque est, quod in Iudicio aliquem absoluere & iustum pronunciare, siue id verè fiat, siue falsò, & siue de Deo, siue de creaturis dicatur. In Hithpahel significat seipsum justificare, & bonitatem causæ suæ argumentis & testimoniis asserere, vt Genes. 44. vers. 16. Et hae significationes passim reperiuntur in Scripturis: de Papistica verò pro infusione sumta, altum est silentium. XXI. Si enim praecipuos vtriusque Testamenti textus percurramus, luculenter apparebit, quod justificare primariò & praecipuè significet aliquem absoluere vel justum declarare. Ex V. Testamento videatur locus, Gen. 44. v. 16. Exod. 23. v. 7. Deut. 25. v. 1. 2. Sam. 15. vers. 4. 1. Reg. 8. vers. 32. Iob. 27. vers. 5. cap. 32. vers. 2. cap. 33. vers. 2. Psal. 51. vers. 6. Psal. 82. vers. 3. Psal. 145. vers. 2. Prou. 17. vers. 15. Esai. 5. v. 23. cap. 50. v. 8. Ierem 3. v. 11. Sir. 1. v. 25, c. 7. v. 5. c. 19. v. 32. c. 26. v. 28.

XXII. Neque verò obstat dictum ex Psal 73. vers. 13. Sine causa justificavi cor meum, hoc est, juxta Pontificios, justum reddidi. Nam absurdum est quòd homo seipsum coram Deo possit justum reddere, Psal. 143. vers. 2. Deinde vitium est vulgatae versionis, quia in Hebraeo non est justificavi, sed זכיתי mundavi, notaturque studium inculpatae & innocentis vitae. Conqueritur enim David, quòd malis benè, bonis autem & justitiam sectantibus malè sit, & addit, Num igitur frustrà mundavi cor meum, num inaniter & sine causa vitam puram & innocentem ducere laboravi?

XXIII. Sic impertinens est illud, quod citatur ex Dan. 8. vers. 14. Iustificabitur sanctuarium, id est, mundabitur. Nam 1. phrasis illa non notat infusionem justitiae, sed restaurationem cultus. 2. Nos quaerimus de justificatione hominis: isti proferunt exemplum de justificatione vel purgatione sanctuarij. 3. Verbum Hebraeum non est in Hiphil, de quo solo nos loquimur, sed in Niphal ונצדק קדש. Quare rursus committitur Ignoratio Elenchi. Et tandem 4. dictum istud posset exponi declaratiuè. Sanctificabitur, id est, sanctum purgatumque esse declarabitur.

XXIV. Sed cumprimis vrgent locum Danielis

12. vers. 3. Qui ad iustitiam erudiunt multos, fulgebunt. In Hebræo est מצדיקים, id est, iustificantes, siue qui iustificant, hoc est, iuxta Bellarm. iustos faciunt, quia erudire aliquem ad iustitiam sit reipsa iustum facere l. 2. c. 3. Verùm 1. Falsum est, quòd erudiens ad iustitiam statim iustum faciat discipulum. Nec enim Ethicus docens temperantiam aut fortitudinem è vestigijs omnes facit fortes & temperantes. Nam alia est ratio habituum theoreticorum qui paulatim introducuntur perinformationem; & alia virtutū moralium quas præceptor non ingenerat, sed duntaxat modum illas consequendi monstrat. 2. Absurdum foret dicere, quod ministri iustificãdo auditores, iustitiam iis infundant cùm hancimmediatam solius Dei actionem esse ipsi fateantur 3. Dictum istud intelligitur ratione vel θεωρίας, vel πράξεως Christianæ. Si ratione θεωρίας, tum dicuntur ministri iustificare, quatenus verum iustificationis modum docent, & ad resipiscentiam homines hortantur, vndè vulgata reddidit: Qui ad iustitiam erudiunt multos. Et Luth. Die so viel zur Gerechtigkeit weisen. Et si maximè tales doctores dicãtur facere iustos, non tamẽ faciunt per infusionem, sed per informationem & adhortationem. Si ratione πράξεως, tum ministri iustificant, quatenus à peccatis loco Dei absolvunt, & pœnitentes iustos pronunciant. Quod enim Deo proprium est, vt retinere & remittere peccata, hoc pastoribus tanquam ministris & legatis Dei sæpè tribuitur, vt Matth. 18. vers. 18. Iohan. 20. vers. 23. 2. Cor. 5. vers. 19. 20. qua de causa Timotheus dicitur & se & suos auditores saluare. 1. Tim 4. vers vlt. Sic igitur pastores iustificant suas oviculas, non infundendo, aut realiter in ipsis efficiendo iustitiam, sed 1. informando. 2. Exhortando. 3. Absoluendo & iustos pronunciando.

XXV. Porrò ex Nouo Testamento similiter multa produci possunt loca, in quibus iustificare itidem forensi modo sumitur pro absoluere aut iustum pronunciare. Videantur dicta Matth. 12. v. 37. Luc. 10. vers. 29. cap. 16. vers. 5. Act. 13. vers. 38, 39. Rom. 2. vers. 13. cap. 3. vers. 20. 26. 28. 30. c. 4. vers. 5. cap. 5. vers. 1. 9. c. 8. vers. 30. 33. 1. Cor. 4. v. 4. Gal. 2. v. 16. 17. c. 3. v. 8. 11. c. 5. v. 4. Tit. 3. v. 7. Iac. 2. v. 21. 24. 25. Obscurus autem nonnihil est locus Matth. 11. v. 19. Luc. 7. v. 35. Iustificata est sapientia a filijs suis Nam diuersis plane modis solet exponi. Quibusdam iustificari est idem, quod condemnari, quo videtur respexisse Lutherus: Die Weisheit muss sich rechtfertigen lassen von ihren Kindern. Sed alii particulam καὶ exponunt aduersatiue: Sed iustificata est, vti quoque sumitur Matt. 12. vers. 39. Act 10. vers. 28. Atque sic iustificari ipsis idem est, quod iustitiae & sapientiae testimonium a filijs consequi, vt sit oppositio: Pharisaei me reprehendunt, sed tamen absoluor a filijs. Ita dicitur Luc. 7. vers. 29. Publicani ἐδικαίωσαν, Iustificauerunt Deum, id est, iustum & bonum pronuncia runt. Sic Psal. 51. vers. 6. vt iustificeris in sermonibus tuis, id est, vt justus & verax declareris. Quaecunque autem expositio teneatur, nihil contra analogiam fidei dicitur, nec quicquam patrocinij reportant inde Pontificii.

XXVI. Atque ita demonstratum est hactenus quod verbum iustificare, iuxta Scripturae vsum primario notet absoluere & iustum pronunciare: cotra quam thesin quod opponant Romanenses, nihil solidi inueniunt. Compositionem vocis vrgent & ἀναλογίαν Grammaticam, quia iustificare sit idem quod iustum facere, vti purificare notat purum, sanctificare sanctum, & viuificare viuum facere. Verum 1. Ista analogia non est vniuersalis: Sanctificamus, glorificamus, magnificamus Deum, non ex profano sanctum, non ex inglorio gloriosum, non ex paruo magnum faciendo, sed talem praedicando

& celebrando: 2. Non ex compositione vocis Latinæ, sed potius ex usu linguæ sanctæ de vero istius vocabuli sensu iudicandum est. 3. Sacerdos dicebatur sanctificare leprosum non faciendo, sed pronunciando sanctum vel purgatum. 4. Si maximè sanctificatio hominis semper notaret inhærenter sanctum facere, non tamen indè sequeretur, quòd idem de iustificatione statuendum sit. 5. Verba Hebræa in Kal neutra, in Hiphil quidem actiua fiunt, & per facere exponuntur; Sciendum verò, quòd qualitas primæ coniugationis tribuatur alteri vel reipsâ, vel permissione, vel iudicio, asseueratione & declaratione alterius. Vnde Flacius istam ponit regulam: Apud Hebræos verba quædam, quæ in prima coniugatione significant qualitate aliquâ vel motu præditum esse, in tertia significant, eam qualitatem vel motum alterius iudicio, verbis & asseueratione alteri tribui. Sic רשע impius fuit, in Hiphil notat condemnare, seu pro impio pronunciare. Ita כזב mentiri, in Hiphil est mendacij arguere. Pari modo Germani dicunt: Einen fromb machen / Einen zum Dieb oder Lügener machen / non quòd alter alterum reipsâ talem faciat, sed quia furti, mendaciique conuincit, & talem esse publicè proclamat. Eâdem prorsus ratione צדק iustum esse, in Hiphil significat, alteri verbis iustitiam tribuere seu iustum reputare & absoluere. Proinde nulla est sequela הצדיק notat iustum facere ob modum significandi in Hiphil. Quare notat iustitiam infundere. Non, inquam, sequitur, quia potest aliquis iustus fieri etiam per alterius iudicium, pronunciationem & declarationem. Quod ipsum non diffiteri potuit Bellarminus l. 2. de Iustificat. cap. 3. scribens: posse aliquem fieri iustum tum intrinsecè per adoptionem iustitiæ, tum extrinsecè per declarationem.


### Question III. What does the word 'to justify' properly signify?: XXVII. As we have hitherto discussed the principal signification in general

XXVII.

As we have hitherto discussed the principal signification in general: so now it must be demonstrated in particular, that this word, especially in the article of Justification, obtains a forensic signification, in such a way that to be justified before God is nothing else than for a sinner, constituted before the divine tribunal and fleeing to the throne of grace, to be absolved from guilt and punishment, and thus to be pronounced just. This very thing is usually proved by four principal arguments.

XXVIII. 1. From the Biblical description.

For thus our justification is described in the Scriptures as being a judicial act, in which there is a crime, and a defendant (the sinful man) and an accuser (the law) and a handwriting, and a witness (conscience) and a tribunal (of Christ) and an advocate (Christ) and a judge (the Lord) and grace, and absolution or the remission of sins, all of which clearly establish the forensic signification.

2. From the opposites, which are condemnation, the imputation of sin, and non-remission, all of which are forensic.

Whence it follows that the term 'to justify' is of the same nature, since opposites are always under the same genus.

3. From synonyms and equipollent phrases, which are all judicial, such as not to be called into judgment, not to be judged or condemned. to remit sins, to pardon, to loose or absolve, to cover and not to impute sins. to be reconciled, to be saved or to be made safe. where, however, it is to be noted It is to be noted that salvation denotes the enjoyment either of glory, and this is hoped for in the future; or of grace, and this can be had in the present life. Salvation taken in this latter respect does not differ from justification, since they are constituted by the same causes, and as ἰσοδύναμοι are used interchangeably in the Scriptures.

4. From absurdities. For it follows that the infusion of justice is the remission of sins, because justification is described by this, Rom. 3, verse 25, and that the form of justification is not single, but various, such as the remission of sins, the infusion of justice, and the production of good works, which stand in relation to one another as privation, habit, and act, and are therefore really distinct. Furthermore, testimonies could be added both of the Fathers and of the adversaries themselves: but we deliberately pass these over, since they have been copiously enumerated by Mr. Dr. Gerhard, Vol. 3, Loc. Com., page 990 and following. Let this one thing be noted, that the Holy Spirit did not without cause describe the doctrine of justification with a forensic term, namely to remove thoughts both Epicurean, when men are little solicitous about their salvation and consider justification a light matter; and Pharisaical, when they flatter themselves and boast too much of their own holiness: Both vices, however, both security and the persuasion of one's own justice, will easily vanish if you consider that justification is a judicial process, where we are set before the most severe tribunal of God, and are held bound to render an exact account of all our words and deeds.

XXIX. Now we shall see in a few words what the Romanists bring forward to the contrary. They allege 1. Isa. 53, verse 11. By his knowledge shall my servant justify many, that is, he shall make them just. Resp. 1. The point is begged when to justify is explained as to infuse justice. 2. It ought to be translated not 'by his knowledge', but 'of himself', so that it is understood as the knowledge of Christ, which ought not to be historical, but faithful, concerning which is the discourse in John 17, v. 3, so that this sense may emerge: Christ, in the knowledge of himself, durch sein Erkäntnuß, that is, through faith, by which Christ is acknowledged and apprehended, will justify many, that is, will pronounce them just, and will absolve them from punishment, which the Apostle himself repeats in Rom. 3, v. 26. Bellarmine therefore errs, who explains knowledge as the doctrine of Christ, when rather his faithful acknowledgment and apprehension is hinted at.

XXX. II. 1 Cor. 6: 11. Such indeed you were, but you have been washed, sanctified, and justified, which three words they have as synonyms. Resp. 1. The Apostle opposes the benefits by which the converted Corinthians were affected to the catalog of crimes. For washing is opposed to the filth of the former life, sanctification to contamination, justification to guilt and condemnation. Therefore, not exactly the same things are noted, but different benefits of God are indicated. 2. Sanctification consists in inherent justice or the renewal of man; but justification is situated in the remission of sins: therefore they ought not to be confused. 3. The Apostle notably adds: You have been justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, which is nothing other than to be absolved through faith in Christ, and to obtain the forgiveness of sins freely, according to the sayings in Acts 4, v. 12, and 10, v. 43, Tit. 3, v. 3.

XXXI. III. Apoc. 22, verse 11. He who is just, let him be justified still, that is, let him strive more and more that inherent justice may be increased. Respon. 1. Justification is distinguished from sanctification. Therefore they are not to be confused, lest an odious tautology emerge. 2. Many Papists explain this saying concerning second justification. This, however, is not defined by them through infusion, but through the exercise of good works. 3. The particle ἔτι is ambiguous. For it either denotes the increase of a thing, or its confirmation and perseverance. It cannot be taken here in the former way, since justification does not receive more and less because it is in relation, not in quality. And our righteousness is Christ, 1 Cor. 1, verse 30; Acts 10, v. 43. Yet He is apprehended wholly by as small as by great faith. Wherefore it ought to be taken in the latter sense, so that it is the same, which indicates παράρρησιν, and continuation in this sense: He who has obtained forgiveness of his sins, let him studiously see to it that he retains this benefit of imputed righteousness, and furthermore insists that daily debts be likewise remitted.

XXXII. Finally IV. Sirach 1, verse 18. Religion will guard and justify the heart. Chapter 18, verse 22. Do not fear to be justified even unto death. Response: 1. In the Greek text, the words cited from chapter 1 are not found at all; in verse 28 it is indeed said θυμώδης ἀνὴρ, an irascible man (Vulgate: He who is without fear) will not be able to be justified: But here the same thing is noted, namely, to be absolved from guilt. 2. In the other saying, likewise, the infusion of righteousness is not noted, but the whole work of our reconciliation and conversion, which Ecclesiasticus rightly warns should not be deferred until the day of death or late old age.

Latin:

XXVII.

XXVII. Vti vero hactenus de principali fignificatione differuimus in genere: Ita nunc in fpecie demonstrari debet, quod verbum istud cum primis in articulo Iustificationis forensem fignificationem obtineat, ita quidem, ut iustificari coram Deo nihil sit aliud, quam peccatorem coram tribunali divino constitutum, ad thronum gratiae confugientem a culpa & poena absolvi, adeoque iustum pronunciari. Hoc ipsum autem quatuor praecipue argumentis probari solet.

XXVIII. 1. A descriptione Biblica.

Sic enim iustificatio nostra describitur in Scripturis quod sit actus iudicialis, in quo est delictum, & reus (homo peccator) & accusator (lex) & Cheirographum, & testis (conscientia) & tribunal (Christi) & advocatus (Christus) & iudex (Dominus) & gratia, & absolutio seu peccatorum remissio, quæ omnia forensem fignificationem luculenter stabiliunt.

2. Ab oppositis, quæ sunt condemnatio, peccati imputatio, non dimissio, quæ omnia sunt forensia. Unde sequitur, & iustificandi vocabulum tale esse, cum opposita semper sint sub eodem genere.

3. A Synonymis & phrasibus æquipollentibus, quæ omnes sunt iudiciales, ut non vocari in iudicium, non iudicari aut condemnari. peccata remittere, condonare, solvere vel absolvere, tegere non imputare peccata. reconciliari, salvari aut salvum fieri. ubi tamen notandum quòd salus notet fruitionem vel gloriæ, & hæc speratur futura; vel gratiæ, & hæc haberi potest in præsenti vita. Hoc posteriori respectu sumta saluatio non differt à justificatione, siquidem iisdem causis constituuntur, & tanquam ἰσοδύναμοι [?] in Scripturis inuicem permutantur.

4. Ab absurdts. Sequitur enim, quòd infusio justitiæ sit remissio peccatorum, quia per hanc justificatio describitur, Rom. 3. versu 25. & quòd justificationis forma non sit vnica, sed varia, vt remissio peccatorum, infusio iustitiæ & productio bonorum operum, quæ se habent, vt priuatio, habitus, actus, adeóque realiter distincta sunt. Addi prætereà possent testimonia tùm Patrum, tùm ipsorum aduersariorum: sed ista consultò præterimus, cùm fusè sint enumerata à Dn. D. Gerharde T. 3. LL. CC. pag. 990. & seqq. Hoc vnum notetur, Spiritum sanctum non abfque causa doctrinam justificationis vocabulo forensi descripsisse nimirum ad tollendas cogitationes tum Epicureas, quando homines de sua salute parum sunt soliciti, & justificationem pro re leui habent: tùm pharisæicas, quando sibi blandiuntur, & propriam sanctitatem nimis prædicant: Vtrumque autem vitium, & securitas & justitiæ persuasio, evanescet facilè, sicogitaueris, justificationem esse processum judicialem, vbi coràm seuerissimo tribunali Dei sistimur, & exactam omnium dictorum factorumque rationem reddere tenemur.

XXIX. Nunc paucis videbimus, quid in contrarium proferant Romanenses. Allegant 1. Es. 53. versu 11. In scientia sua iustificabit ipse seruus meus multos, id est, iustos faciet. Resp. 1. Petitur principium, quando justificare per justitiam infundere explicatur 2. Verti debet non in scientia sua, sed Sui, vt intelligatur cognitio Christi, quę nõ debet esse historica, sed fidelis, de qua sermo Ioh. 17. v. 3. vt sensus iste emergat: Christus in cognitione sui, durch sein Erkäntnuß / h. e. per fidem, quâ Christus agnoscitur & apprehenditur, multos iustificabit, h. e. iustos pronunciabit, & à pœnia absoluet, quod ipsum repetit Apostolus Rom. 3. v. 26. Errat proinde Bellarminus qui scientiam exponit de doctrina Christi, cùm potius fidelis ejus agnitio & apprehensio innuatur.

XXX. II. 1. Cor. 6: 11. Hæc quidem fuistis, sed abluti, sanctificati & iustificati estis, quæ tria vocabula habent pro Synonymis. Resp. 1. Catalogo scelerum opponit Apostolus beneficia, quibus Corinthij conuersi fuerunt affecti. Nam sordibus prioris vitæ opponitur ablutio, contaminationi sanctificatio, reatui, condemnationi iustificatio. Non igitur eadem prorsus notantur, sed diuersa Dei beneficia subindicantur. 2. Sanctificatio consistit in iustitia inhærente vel renouatione hominis; Sed iustificatio sita est in remissione peccatorum: Non igitur debent confundi, 3. Notanter addit Apostolus: Iustificati estis in nomine Dn. nostri Iesu Christi, quod nihil aliud est, quam per fidem in Christum absolui, & veniam peccatorum, gratis consequi, iuxta dicta Act. 4. v. 12, & 10, v. 43., Tit. 3. v. 3.

XXXI. III. Apoc. 22. vers. 11. Qui iustus est, iustificetur adhuc, id est, magis magisque studeat, ut inhærens iustitia augeatur. Respon. 1. Distinguitur à sanctificatione iustificatio. Proindè non sunt confundenda, nè emergat odiosa ταυτολογία. 2. Multi Pontificij exponunt hoc dictum de iustificatione secunda, Hæc verò non definitur ab ipsis per infusionē, sed bonorum operum exercitium. 3. Particula ĕti est ambigua, Vel enim notat incrementum rei, vel eiusdem confirmationem & perseuerantiam. Priori modo hîc sumi nequit, cum iustificatio non recipiat magis & minus, quia in relatione est, non in qualitate. Et iustitia nostra Christus est, 1. Cor. 1. vers. 30. Act. 10. v. 43. Tàm autem à parua, quam magna fide totus apprehenditur. Quare posteriori sensu accipi debet, vt idem sit, quod παράρρησιν, & continuationem indicet hoc sensu: Qui peccatorum suorum veniam consecutus est, studiosè videat, vt hoc imputatæ iustitiæ beneficium retineat, & porrò instet, vt cotidiana debita similiter remittantur.

XXXII. Tandem IV. Syrac. 1. vers. 18. Religiositas custodias atque iustificabit cor. cap. 18. vers. 22. Non verearis usque ad mortem iustificari. Respond: 1. In græco textu verba ex cap. 1. citata prorsus non reperiuntur vers. 28. quidem dicitur θυμώδης ἀνὴρ iracundus vir (vulgata, Qui sine timore est) non poterit iustificari: Sed hic idem notatur, quòd à culpa absolui. 2. In altero dicto similiter non notatur infusio iustitiæ, sed totum reconciliationis & conuertionis nostræ opus, quod vsq; ad mortis diem vel seram senectam non esse differendum, rectè monet Ecclesiasticus.


### Question IV. What does Scripture understand by the word Grace?

XXXIII. It is accustomed to be taken in the Scriptures in three principal ways: 1. For the favor and mercy of God, by which He is affected toward us men; and some call this signification active, because it denotes the gratuitous action of God toward us. The Hebrews use the verb חָנַן, which is to affect with grace or to deem worthy of favor. The Septuagint for the most part translated it by 'to have mercy' and 'to spare.' Thus it is taken in Exodus 33, v. 19; Numbers 6, verse 25; Deuteronomy 28, verse 50; Judges 21, verse 22; Amos 5, verse 15. And this signification is the principal and most common one, upon which the others depend.

& to which it relates analogically.

XXXIV. II. For gifts bestowed freely or out of grace, by metonymy of the effect for the cause, because the principle of the donation, which is grace, is put for the gift. And this acceptation can be named passive, since it hints at the reception of a gift, which for philosophers is a passion. It is taken thus. Eph. 4, verse 7. 1 Pet. 4, v. 10. Nor is this signification unknown to the Greeks, since Suidas and Varinus note that χάριν signifies τὴν δωρεὰν καὶ ἀντίχαριν, and therefore they describe it thus: χάριν ἐστὶ πράγματος ὠφελίμου δόσις, grace is the donation of a fruitful thing.

XXXV. III. For graciousness, or for affability and gentleness, by which someone renders himself lovable and pleasing to all good people. Thus Luke 1, verse 26, Mary is called full of grace, Holdselig. And Christ, Luke 2, verse 52, was advancing in grace and wisdom before men. The sounder Papists do not deny these three acceptations, especially since Thomas 1. 2. quest. 110. art. 1. made express mention of them. According to the common, he says, way of speaking, grace is accustomed to be accepted in three ways. In one way for the love of someone: just as we are accustomed to say that this soldier has the grace of the King. Secondly, it is taken for some gift given freely: just as we are accustomed to say: I do this grace for you. In the third way, it is taken for the recompense of a benefit given freely, just as it is said that we are said to give thanks for benefits.

XXXVI. And thus the Papists can easily agree with us on the number of significations: but this is most controversial: What does the Grace of God, by which we are said to be justified everywhere, primarily denote? Where we understand the gratuitous favor of God, they understand infused gifts. For the confirmation of our opinion, we have brought forward many arguments in disp. 1. Decad. 2. quest. 2., to which we wish to refer the reader so that we do not do what is already done.

Latin:

XXXIII. Tribus præcipuè modis accipi solet in Scripturis 1. Pro fauore & misericordia Dei, quâ erga nos homines affectus est; & hanc significationem nonnulli vocant actiuam; quia gratuitam Dei circa nos actionem denotat. Hebræi vtuntur verbo חָנַן quod est Gratiâ afficere vel fauore dignari. Septuaginta plerumque verterunt per misereri & parcere. Ita sumitur Exod. 33. v. 19. Numer. 6. vers. 25. Deut. 28. vers. 50. Iud. 21. vers. 22. Amós. 5. vers. 15. Atque hæc significatio principalis & vsitatissima est, â qua reliquæ dependent

& ad quam se analogicè habent.

XXXIV. II. Pro donis gratuitis vel ex gratia collatis, per metonymiam effecti pro causa, quia pro dono ponitur principiū donationis, quod est gratia. Et hæc acceptio nominari potest passiva, quoniam doni receptionem, quæ philosophis est passio, subinnuit. Ita sumitur. Ephes. 4. versu 7. 1. Petr. 4. v. 10. Nec Græcis ignota est hæc significatio, cùm Suidas & Varinus annotent, χάριν significare τὴν δωρεὰν καὶ ἀντίχαριν, Ideóque sic describunt χάριν ἐστὶ πράγματος ὠφελίμου δόσις, Gratia est rei fructuosæ donatio.

XXXV. III. Pro gratiositate, seu pro comitate & mansuetudine, quâ quis se omnibus bonis amabilem reddit & gratum. Sic Luc. 1. versu 26. Maria dicitur gratiâ plena, Holdselig. Et Christus Luc. 2. versu 52. Proficiebat gratiâ & sapientiâ coram hominibus. Hasce tres acceptiones non inficiantur saniores Pontificij, præsertim cum Thomas 1. 2. quæst. 110. art. 1. expressam illarum mentionem fecerit. Secundum communem, inquit, modum loquendi, tripliciter gratia accipi consuevit. Vno modo pro dilectione alicuius: sicut consuevimus dicere, quòd iste miles habeas gratiam Regis. Secundo sumitur pro aliquo dono gratis dato: Sicut consuevimus dicere: Hanc gratiam facio tibi. Tertio modo sumitur pro recompensatione beneficij gratis dati, prout dicitur quod dicimur agere gratias beneficiorum.

XXXVI. Atque sic facilè nobiscum convenire possunt in numero significationum Pontificii: hoc autem maximè controversum est: Quid Gratia Dei, qua passim iustificari dicimur, primariò denotet? Vbi nos gratuitum Dei favorem, illi dona infusa intelligunt. Pro confirmatione nostræ sententiæ, benè multa argumenta protulimus disp. 1. Decad. 2. quæst. 2. quò nè actum agatur lectorem remissum volumus.


### Question V. How is the particle Gratis understood?

How is the particle GRATIS understood?

XXXVII. This word obtains four principal significations. 1. It is opposed to a hoped-for and intended outcome, and is the same as in vain, emptily, to no purpose. Galatians 2, last verse: If righteousness is through the law, Christ died gratis / So is Christ dead in vain. 2. It is opposed to the payment of a price, so that it is the same as gratuitously or without the intervention of money, for nothing and without money, Genesis 29, v. 15, Exodus 21, v. 22, 2 Kings 24, v. 24, etc. 3. It is opposed to a true and just cause, so that it means the same as rashly, unjustly, and without reason, Psalm 69, verse 5: They hated me gratis, without cause. 4. It is opposed to merit, whether for good or for evil. 1 Kings 19, verse 5: Slaying David gratis, that is, when he had deserved no such thing, without and against desert.

XXXVIII. The second and last signification especially has a place in the Pauline sayings, when we are said to be justified by grace, gratis. For the Apostle wishes to indicate by this that we have absolutely not merited righteousness, and indeed that no cause of any kind exists in us. For the word gratis is added as an explanation of grace. Because grace sometimes denotes gratuitous gifts and the benefit of renewal, someone could have estimated that this was hinted at by the justifying grace. Wherefore, so that no scruple might remain, the particle Gratis is added, so that thus everything inherent, every personal dignity, and payment is excluded, and our justification is attributed entirely to divine mercy alone.

XXXIX. Therefore, just as in that instance, when David complains, They hated me gratis, three things are noted. 1. That David had not merited that hatred. 2. That not only had he not merited it, but not even the slightest cause existed in him which could have moved others to hatred. 3. What is contrary rather, namely love and favor he has deserved. Thus Paul, asserting that we are justified freely, wished to indicate three things. 1. That in us there is no merit of justification and salvation. 2. That not even the smallest little reason is found in us, which moved God to impart justice. 3. That we have rather deserved punishments and eternal death, 1. That of Augustine, sermon 15, on the words of the Apostle: He gives entirely freely, he saves freely, who finds nothing from which he may save; and much, from which he may condemn

Latin:

Particula GRATIS quomodo accipiatur?

XXXVII. Vox hæc quatuor potissimum significationes obtinet. 1. Opponitur sperato & intento euentui, idemque est, quod frustrà, inaniter, incassum. Gal. 2. versu vlt. Si per legem iustitia, Christus gratis mortuus est / So ist Christus vergeblich gestorben. 2. Opponitur solutioni pretij, vt sit idem quod gratuitò vel sine interuentu pecuniæ, vmbsonst vnnd ohne Geld, Gen. 29. v. 15. Exod 21. v. 22. 2. Reg. 24. v. 24 &c. 3. Opponitur veræ & iustæ causæ vt valeat idem, quod temerè, iniquè & absque ratione Ps. 69. versu 5. Oderunt me gratis, ohne vrsach. 4 Opponitur merito siue ad bonum siue ad malum. 1. Reg. 19. ver. 5. Interficiens Dauid gratis, id est, cum nihil tale esset meritus, ohne vnd wider verdienst.

XXXVIII. Secunda & Vltima significatio inprimis locum habet in dictis Paulinis, cùm ju stificari dicimur ex gratia, gratis. Vult enim Apostolus hoc indicare, quòd iustitiam planè non simus promeriti, imò & nulla qualiscunque causa in nobis existat, Nam vocabulum gratis additur, gratiæ ἐξηγητικῶς. Quia enim gratia nonnunquam notat dona gratuita, & beneficium renouationis, potuisset quis æstimare, hoc per gratiâ justificantem innui. Quare nè vllus superesset scrupulus, adjuncta est particula Gratis, vt ita omne inhærens, omnis propria dignitas & solutio排除 exclutur, nostrisque justificatio soli misericordiæ divinæ in totum feratur accepta.

XXXIX. Proindè, sicut in isto, cùm Dauid conqueritur, Oderunt me gratis, tria notantur. 1. Quod Dauid non fuerit promeritus istud odium. 2. Quod non modò non fuerit promeritus, sed nè quidem leuissima in illo extiterit causa, quæ ad odium cõmouere alios potuisset. 3. Quid contrariù potius, videlicet amorem & fauorem promeruerit. Sic Paulus, nos gratis iustificari asserens, tria voluit indicare. 1. Quod in nobis nullum sit meritum iustificationis & salutis. 2. Quod nec minutissima quidē ratiūcula in nobis inveniatur, quæ Deum mouerit ad impertiendam iustitiam. 3. Quod pœnas potius & æternam mortem simus promeriti, 1. Illud Augustini serm. 15. de verbis Apostoli: Prorsus gratis dat, gratis saluat, qui nihil inuenit, vnde saluet; & multum, vnde damnet


### Question VI. What does faith signify?

XL. In Latin it generally denotes fidelity in one speaking, or truth in keeping promises. Whence Cicero thinks faith is so called, because that is done, which has been said or promised by someone, as if these two words Fiit dictum were mixed together. But it is more appropriate as an etymology if we derive faith from trusting. In Greek it is called πίστις from πείθω, which is I persuade or I teach by persuading, Acts 19:8, 28:23. As therefore πείθειν denotes to impress something and to persuade: So that which is effected in the human heart by persuading is designated as πίστις. The Hebrews commonly call faith אֱמוּנָה from the root אָמַן which in the passive signifies to be firm and stable, whence arises that seal and signet of prayer, Amen, that is, let it be ratified and firm. And hence אֱמוּנָה faith is nothing else than a certain and stable persuasion concerning the promises of God.

XLI. As regards the significations of faith, various ones are read, both in profane and in sacred authors. Among the profane it denotes 1. fidelity in keeping words 2. firm persuasion and assent 3. Certain and immovable confidence: 4. An argument worthy of belief. The Fathers distinguish between believing God, which is to believe that those things are true which he speaks; between believing God, or that there is a GOD, and between believing in GOD, which is to trust in Him. Hence Bernard says, that one faith is of the commandments, by which we believe God: another of the signs, by which we believe GOD, another of the promises, by which we believe in GOD:

XLII. In Scripture it is taken in various ways in turn, 1. for a bare profession of faith, Jas. 2 v. 14. 2. For the true doctrine of faith, Rom. 1 v. 5. Eph. 4 v. 5. 1 Tim. 1 v. 19. III. for assent, John 4 v. 50. Acts 13 v. 8. Eccl. 14 v. 22. IV. For πληροφορίᾳ or confidence, Matt. 8 v. 10 & c. 15 v. 28. Luke 17 v. 5. V. For constancy in religion, Rom. 1 v. 8. VI. for the whole course of life and piety, 2 Cor. 1 v. 24. VII. for conscience, Rom. 14 v. 23. VIII. For miraculous faith, Matt. 17 v. 20, 21. Mark 11 v. 12. 1 Cor. 13 v. 2. IX. For constancy in keeping promises, Ps. 23 v. 10. Ps. 86 v. 15. Rom. 3 v. 3. X. For fidelity in performing duty: Tit. 2 v. 10. XI. For justice, Ps. 119 v. 75. XII. For things believed or the fulfillment of promises, Gal. 4 v. 25.

XLIII. But from all these, four meanings in particular are most illustrious and should be well observed. For 1. Faith denotes the fidelity of the mind and constancy in keeping promises; which is commonly called active faith or faith of contracts, Isa. 11 v. 15. Jer. 7 v. 28. Rom. 3 v. 3. II. Assent and firm persuasion, which is passive faith, and has a relation to the active faith or truthfulness of the speaker, Exod. 14 v. 13. John 5 v. 46. Jas. 2 v. 19. III. The object to which we assent, or the heavenly doctrine itself divinely revealed, Gal. 1 v. 23. c. 6 v. 16. Tit. 1 v. 13. IV: The confidence of the mind or trust, where we assent to someone in such a way that we at the same time entrust our whole selves to him, and rely on him with all our thoughts: to assent, therefore, this fourth meaning adds πληροφορίαν and confidence of the mind, consisting in the particular apprehension of the promises: And in this sense it is taken in the present controversy and it is used everywhere by the Apostles, when they write that a man is justified by faith, a thing which has been demonstrated more fully elsewhere.

XLIV. The more recent authors refer all significations of faith to three classes, when they write that it signifies, First, truth and constancy in words and deeds, in which way it denotes, I. The faithfulness of God. Rom. 3. v. 3. II. The truthfulness of men. Jer. 7. v. 28. III. Constancy in retaining the truth of heavenly doctrine, Rom. 1. v. 8. IV. A covenant entered into with God in Baptism or a profession of faith. 1. Tim. 5. v. 12. Secondly, passive faith, by which we believe and assent to the word of God, by which reason it signifies, I. Historical faith. Exod. 14. v. 31. II. General assent. Jas. 2. v. 19. III. A naked profession and boasting of faith. Jas. 2. v. 14. IV. The faith of miracles. Matt. 17. v. 20. V. Justifying faith. Rom. 3. v. 26. Thirdly, the object of faith or heavenly doctrine divinely revealed, in which way it denotes, I. The whole doctrine in general. Gal. 6. v. 10. II. The doctrine of the Gospel in particular. Rom. 3. v. 27. III. The preaching of the coming of Christ. Gal. 3. v. 23. IV. The fundamental articles of heavenly doctrine. Rom. 12. v. 6.

Latin:

XL. Latinis plerumque notat fidelitatem in dicente, vel veritatem in seruandis promissis. Vnde Cicero fidem dictam putat, quia id fiat, quod ab aliquo dictum promissumve est, quasi isthæc duo verba Fiit dictum commixta sint. Sed conuenientius est έτυμον si fidem à fidendo deriuemus. Græcè πίστις dicitur à πείθω, quod est suadeo vel suadēdo doceo, Act. 19. v. 8. c. 28. v. 23. Vt igitur πείθειν notat inculcare aliquid & persuadere: Sic illud, quod suadendo in corde humano efficitur, πίστις indigitatur. Hebræi fidem communiter appellant אֱמוּנָה à rad. אָמַן quæ in passiuo significat firmum & stabiluum esse, vnde oritur illud precationis sigillum & obsignaculum Amen, id est, ratum firmumque sit. Atque hinc אֱמוּנָה fides nihil est aliud, quàm certa stabilisque persuasio de promissionibus Dei.

XLI. Significationes fidei quod spectat, variæ leguntur, tum in profanis, tum in sacris authoribus. Apud profanos denotat 1. fidelitatem in seruandis dictis 2. firmam persuasionem & assensum 3. Certam immotamque fiduciam: 4. Argumentum fide dignum Patres distinguunt inter credere Deo, quod est credere vera esse, quæ ille loquitur; Inter credere Deum, seu quod sit DEVS & inter credere in DEVM, quod est ipsi confidere. Hinc Bernhardus ait, fidem aliam esse præceptorum, quâ credimus Deo: aliam signorum, quâ credimus DEVM, aliam promissorum, quâ credimus in DEVM:

XLII. In Scriptura varijs vicissim modis accipitur, 1. pro nuda fidei professione Iac. 2. v. 14. 2. Pro vera de fide doctrina, Rom. 1. v. 5. Eph. 4. v. 5. 1. Tim. 1. v. 19. III. pro assensu. Ioh. 4. v. 50. Act. 13. v. 8. Ecc. 14. v. 22. IV. Pro πληροφορίᾳ vel fiducia Matt. 8. v. 10. & c. 15. v. 28. Luc. 17. v. 5. V. Pro constantia in religione, Rom. 1. v. 8. VI. pro toto cursu vitæ & pietatis. 2. Cor. 1. v. 24. VII. pro conscientia, Rom. 14. v. 23. VIII. Pro fide miraculosa. Matt. 17. v. 20. 21. Marc. 11. v. 12. 1. Cor. 13. v. 2. IX. Pro constantia in seruandis promissis, Ps. 23. v. 10. Ps. 86. v. 15. Rom. 3. v. 3. X. Pro fidelitate in faciendo officio: Tit. 2: v. 10. XI. Pro iustitia. Ps. 119 v. 75. XII. Pro rebus creditis seu impletione promissionum, Gal. 4. v. 25.

XLIII. Ex his verò omnibus quatuor inprimis significationes sunt maximè illustres, & probè obseruandæ. Nam 1. Fidei denotat fidelitatem animi & constantiam in seruandis promissis; quæ vocatur vulgò fides actiua vel contractuum Es. 11. v. 15. Ier. 7. vers. 28. Rom. 3. vers. 3. II. Assensum & persuasionem firmam quæ est fides passiua, & relationem habet ad dicentis fidem actiuam seu veracitatem. Exod. 14. v. 13 Ioh 5. v. 46. Iac. 2. v. 19 III. Obiectum, cui Assentimur, seu ipsam doctrinam cælestem diuinitus reuelatam. Gal. 1. v. 23. c. 6. vers. 16. Tit. 1. v. 13. IV: Fiduciam animi vel confidentiam, vbi sic alicui assentimur, vt simul nos totos ipsi credamus, & omnibus cogitationibus in eo confidamus: Ad assensum igitur hæc quarta significatio addit πληροφορίαν ac fiduciam animi, in particulari promissionum apprehensione consistentem: Atq; hoc sensu in præsenti controuersia accipitur & vfurpatur passim ab Apostolis, cùm hominem fide iustificari scribunt, id quod alibi fusiùs demonstratum est.

XLIV. Recentiores ad tres classes referunt omnes fidei significationes, quando scribunt illam significare, Primò veritatem & constantiam in dictis & factis, quo pacto notat, I. Dei fidelitatem. Rom. 3. vers. 3. II. Hominum veracitatem Ier. 7. v. 28. III. Constantiam in retinenda doctrina cœlestis veritate, Rom. 1. v. 8. IV. Pactum cum Deo initum in Baptismo vel professionem fidei. 1. Tim. 5. v. 12 Secundò fidem passivam, quâ credimus & assentimur Dei verbo, quâ ratione significat, I. Fidem historicam. Exod. 14. v. 31. II. Generalem assensum Iac. 2. v. 19. III. nudam fidei professionem & iactantiam Iac. 2. v. 14. IV. fidem miraculorum Matt. 17. v. 20. V. Fidem iustificantem. Rom. 3. v. 26. Tertiò obiectum fidei vel doctrinam cœlestem diuinitus reuelatam quo pacto denotat, I. totam doctrinam in genere Gal. 6. v. 10 II. doctrinam Evangelij in specie Rom. 3. v. 27. III. Prædicationem aduentus Christi. Gal. 3. v. 23. IV. fundamentales doctrinæ cœlestis articulos. Rom. 12. v. 6.


### Question VII. What significations does imputation have?

XLV. This word is often found in the Pauline epistles, as in Rom. 4. v. 3, 4, 5, etc., but it is explained in various ways. To the Osiandrists, to impute righteousness is the same as to implant and insert, just as to amputate is to take away. Bellarmine opposes this word to truth, and therefore frequently calls imputed righteousness putative and imaginary. Others explain faith being imputed for righteousness in this way, that faith is required beforehand as a necessary disposition for acquiring righteousness. There are, however, distinct phrases. 1. The righteousness of Christ being imputed. 2. Faith being imputed for righteousness. We shall treat of both in a few words.

XLVI. 2. Concerning the imputation of righteousness. The Papists, especially Costerus in Enchirid. m. p. 254 and Bellarmine in book 2, chapter 7, deny that this proposition, The righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, exists in the Scriptures, but without reason. For it exists expressly in Romans 4, verses 6 and 11, and those things which are understood from the Scriptures are equivalent to those which are written, according to the rule of Nazianzen. Indeed, that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us is easily understood from the fact that Christ is said to have been made righteousness for us by God, 1 Corinthians 1, verse 30.

XLVII. But that we may say something about the word itself, imputation in general signifies the transfer of some thing, when something is attributed to one by another, which happens in diverse ways, whence Flacius says that imputation is twofold. He calls the first essential, of which he recounts two modes. 1. When a thing that is true and existing is referred to accounts, as being of some moment and not to be neglected, as Psalm 144, verse 3: What is the son of man, that you impute or reckon him? 2. When its reward or price, good or evil, is assigned or ordained to a thing or deed; in this sense sin is said to be imputed or not imputed. To be imputed is the same as to be observed, noted, and adjudged to a certain punishment. It is not imputed, however, when it is covered by oblivion and buried, and no punishment is decreed for it. He calls the other species of imputation rational, which occurs by thought alone, and this he says is again: 1. Either of a thing or person, when a thing is transferred from one person to another by thought alone. Thus the righteousness of Christ is transferred from Him to us; and again our unrighteousness is transferred to Him by the will and decree of God and is imputed to Him. 2. Or of price or real, when the dignity, value, or preciousness of one thing is transcribed to another thing by thought. Thus nobility is for a courtier in place of virtue, and the beauty of a girl is for a King in place of a dowry, and vice versa. XLIIX. But the meanings of imputation can be more conveniently expressed if it is said that to impute is to ascribe to someone a thing or the cause of a thing, whether good or evil, which he has or does not have. The imputation of an evil thing happens in two ways; either by right and duly, when an evil thing or its cause truly resides in someone, as when guilt is imputed to a criminal and he is condemned on that account: Thus God rightfully imputes sins to the impenitent: or unduly and by injury, when the thing or the cause of the thing does not reside in him, as when guilt is imputed to an innocent person. Thus men unjustly impute the causes of punishments to the earth, to heaven, and the like. The imputation of a good thing happens in three ways. 1. By right and duly, when the thing which is imputed resides in him and is owed, and then it is improperly said to be imputed, or given, or attributed. Thus the Apostle says, it is imputed to the worker, that is, given as a debt. 2. By injury, when justice is imputed to an unjust person and the criminal is absolved against the laws. 3. By grace, when justice is imputed to an unjust person and the criminal is absolved, not as a debt, but by grace, yet having just causes. Thus faith is imputed for righteousness, or righteousness through faith.

XLIX. In the scriptures, however, only two species of imputation are recounted by Paul in Romans 4, verses 3, 4, 5. One according to debt, the other according to grace. The former regards works and the law, the latter faith and the Gospel: the former can be called real, the latter rational. Imputation according to debt is that whose foundation exists in the worker himself, to whom the imputation is made, which the Apostle expresses thus in Romans 4, v. 4: To him who works, the reward is imputed as a debt. This imputation is also spoken of in 2 Samuel 19, verse 19, Romans 4, verse 8, chapter 5, v. 13, 2 Timothy 4, verse 16. Imputation according to grace is that whose foundation is not held in him to whom the imputation is made, but in the grace and mercy of God, justifying the ungodly. Paul expresses it thus: But to him who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness. And by such gratuitous imputation the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, as the Pauline context clearly indicates.

L. And from this Chemnitz gathers: 1. That in believers there is not that foundation, by reason and respect of which righteousness is imputed for blessedness. 2. That the contrary foundation is found, if God were willing to enter into judgment, which must be covered so that it is not imputed, namely, sin. 3. That that imputation is a relation of the divine mind and will, while out of gratuitous mercy for Christ's sake He does not impute sins to believers, but rather imputes righteousness to them, that is, they are held before God in His judgment as if they had perfect inherent righteousness, and therefore salvation and eternal life are given to them as if they were righteous. From which it is clear that two modes of imputation concur in justification: one στερητικὸν (privative), which others call negative imputation, and it is the non-imputation of a thing which exists in man and ought to be imputed, and it consists both in the oblivion and non-annotation of sin, and in the dismissal of guilt: the other θετικὸν (positive), which they term affirmative imputation, when righteousness is imputed to us. This is the attribution of a thing which does not exist in us, and which we have in no way merited, as if it existed in us, namely when God holds us for truly righteous and holy men, when nevertheless we are not such through ourselves.

LI. But since a worldly judge, justifying the wicked without a foundation, is an abomination to the Lord, Ex. 23. ver. 1, Deut. 25. v. 1, 1 Kings 8. verse 32, Prov. 17. verse 15, Isa. 5. verse 23, much less will God justify anyone without a foundation and righteousness, i.e., unless the law has been satisfied for sin, and the law has been fulfilled by perfect obedience. Since this foundation of imputed righteousness does not reside in believers, it is necessary that it be outside them in another, who alone is Christ, who by God the Father was made for us a propitiator and Mediator, who, being made subject to the law for us, fulfilled it most perfectly, Gal. 4. v. 4. & 5. made by God for us righteousness, 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. 2. Cor. 5. v. last, Isa. 45. verse 24. & verse last. For by the obedience of one many are made righteous, Rom. 5. verse 19.

LII. And from this it is understood how these two are to be reconciled: He who justifies the wicked is an abomination before God, Prov. 17. verse 15. And to him who believes in him who justifies the wicked, Rom. 4. v. 5. For there is understood the wicked man for whom neither he himself nor another has made satisfaction: here, however, the wicked man who, though not himself, yet for whom another has made satisfaction. Therefore, when God in Rom. 4 is said to impute righteousness, it must be taken in two ways, as Flacius warns in his Clavis, page 422, namely, first by reason of the cause, then by reason of the effect. For 1. this expression indicates that the righteousness of Christ is transcribed onto the believer, just as conversely our unrighteousness was powerfully transcribed by God onto Christ; and this is properly the cause of our righteousness. 2. It also indicates the effect, namely, that someone is held to be righteous who is not such, which it further declares by the example of the contrary imputation, while our unrighteousness was imputed to Christ, and therefore he himself was held to be unrighteous. See the very words of Flacius, which are sufficiently emphatic and weighty.

LIII. II. Concerning the imputation of Faith. When faith is said to be imputed for righteousness, it is not taken absolutely, as it is a certain virtue and good work, but relatively, as it is an instrument and hand, receiving, apprehending, applying to itself, and appropriating the merit of Christ. The sense therefore of this phrase will be this: We are held and reputed righteous before God, because we apprehend through the payment and satisfaction made by Christ for us; whence it immediately appears that it is the same thing whether you say that faith is imputed to us for righteousness, or that righteousness is imputed to us through faith. In both cases nothing else is signified, than that we are just, and are reputed so before God, for no other cause, except for the satisfaction of Christ, which we apprehend by faith and make our own.

LIV. Costerus, page 254, brings forward such an interpretation: Faith formed by charity is the very justice inherent in us, by which we are just before God. But besides the fact that it is nothing but a mere begging of the question, it errs in many ways. 1. Because he speaks of the habit of faith as it is a virtue: but Scripture speaks of the act of faith, insofar as it is an apprehending instrument; the text says, Abraham believed, and this was imputed to him for justice. That act, not the habit, was imputed. 2. It is one thing to be justice, another to be imputed for justice. For just as a cause cannot be an effect, so faith, which is the cause of imputation for justice, cannot be justice itself, or the term itself. 3. Works are excluded from the circle of our justification. Therefore, faith, as a work, will not be our justice. Since we are to declare all these things more fully below, we add nothing further, but rather shall proceed to the explanation of the causes.

Latin:

XLV. Vocabulum hoc in epistolis Paulinis sæpè reperitur vt Rom. 4. v. 3. 4. 5. seqq. sed diuersimodè exponitur. Osiandristis imputare iustitiam idem est quod implantare & inserere, sicut amputare est auferre. Bellarminus veritati opponit vocem istam, ideoque iustitiam imputatam crebrò appellat putativam & imaginariam. Aliàs fidem imputari ad iustitiam sic exponût, quod ad iustitiam acquirendam fides tâquàm dispositio necessaria prærequiratur. Sunt autem distinctę phrases. 1. Christi iustitiam imputari. 2. fidem ad iustitiam imputari. De vtraq; paucis agemus.

XLVI. 2. De imputatione Iustitiae. Hanc propositionem, Iustitia Christi nobis imputatur, in Scripturis extare, negant Pontificij, praesertim Costerus in Enchirid. m. p. 254. & Bellarm. lib. 2. cap. 7 sed absque ratione. Nam disertè extat Rom. 4. v. 6. 11. & perinde sunt ea, quae ex Scripturis intelliguntur, at ea, quae scribuntur, iuxta regulam Nazianzeni. Iustitiam verò Christi nobis imputari, facilè intelligitur ex eo, quod Christus dicitur nobis factus à Deo iustitia 1. Cor. 1. v 30.

XLVII. Vt autem de ipso vocabulo aliquid dicamus, imputatio in genere significat translationem alicuius rei, cùm alteri ab altero aliquid attribuitur, quòd diuersis modis contingit, vndè Flacius imputationem dicit esse geminam. Primam vocat essentialem, cuius duos modos recenset. 1. Cùm res verâ & existens in rationes refertur, tanquam alicuius momenti & non negligenda, vt Pf. 144. vers. 3. Quid est filius hominis, quod imputas aut reputas eum? 2. Cùm rei aut facto suum praemium aut pretium, bonum aut malum deputatur ordinaturuè, hoc sensu peccatum imputari vel non imputari dicitur. Imputari est idem, quod obseruari, annotari, & certae poenae adiudicari. Non imputatur autem cùm obliuione contectum sepelitur & nulla ei poena decernitur. Alteram imputationis speciem vocat rationalem, quae fit solâ cogitatione, & hanc rursùs dicit esse. 1. vel rei seu personatam, cùm res ab alia persona ad aliam sola cogitatione transfertur. Sic iustitia Christi ab ipso ad nos; & rursùs nostra iniustitia ad ipsum voluntate & decreto Dei transfertur eique imputatur. 2. Vel pretij seu realem, cum dignitas, valor aut pretiositas alterius rei ad aliam rem cogitatione transcribitur. Sic aulico nobilitas pro virtute, apud Regem est forma puellae pro dote & contrâ. XLIIX. Sed conuenientius significata Imputationis exprimi possunt, si dicatur, quod imputare sit alicui rem vel rei causam, quam habet vel non habet bonam vel malam adjcribere. Imputatio rei male dupliciter fit; veliure & debitè, cùm res mala vel eius causa verè alicui inest, ut cùm reo imputatur culpa & proptereà damnatur: Sic Deus impœnitentibus peccata iure imputat: vel indebitè & iniuriâ, cùm res vel rei causa non inest, vt cùm culpa imputatur innocenti. Sic homines pœnarum causas injustè imputant terræ, cœlo, & similibus. Imputatio rei bonæ fit tripliciter. 1. iure & debitè, cùm res quæ imputatur, inest & debetur, & tunc impropriè dicitur imputari, seu dari, vel tribui. Sic Apostolus dicit, operanti imputari, id est dari ex debito. 2. Iniuriâ, cùm iniusto imputur iustitia & reus absoluitur contra leges. 3. Gratiâ, cùm iniusto imputatur iustitia & reus absolvitur, non ex debito, sed gratia, causas tamen iustas habente. Sic fides ad iustitiam, vel iustitia per fidem imputatur.

XLIX. In scripturis autem duæ tantùm imputationis species recensentur à Paulo Rom. 4. versu 34. 5. Vna secundum debitum, altera secundum gratiam. Illa respicit opera & legem, hæc fidem & Evangelium: Illa realis, hæc rationalis dici potest.
