Imputatio secundum debitum est, cujus fundamentum extat in ipso operante, cui fit imputatio, id quod Apostolus sic effatur Rom. 4. v. 4. Ei qui operatur, merces imputatur ex debito. De hac etiam imputatione sermo est 2. Sam 19 versu 19. Rom. 4. ver. 8. c. 5. v. 13. 2. Tim 4. versu 16. Imputatio secundum gratiam est, cujus fundamentum non habetur in eo, cui fit imputatio, sed in gratia & misericordia Dei, iustificantis impium. Paulus ita effert: Ei autem qui non operatur, credenti verò in eum qui iustificat impium, reputatur fides eius ad iustitiam. Atque tali gratuitâ imputatione justitia Christi nobis imputatur, vti contextus Paulinus luculenter indicat.

L. Atque hinc colligit Chemnitius 1. In credentibus non esse fundamentum illud, cuius ratione & respectu justitia ad beatitudinem imputetur. 2. Contrarium reperiri fundamentum, si Deus vellet in judicium intrare, quod tegendum est ne imputetur, nempe peccatum. 3. Esse illam imputationem relationem mentis & voluntatis divinae, dum ex gratuita misericordia propter Christum credentibus peccata non imputat, sed potius illis imputat iustitiam, id est habeantur coram Deo in iudicio ejus ac si perfectam haberent iustitiam inhaerentem, & ideo tanquam iustis datur eis salus & vita aeterna. Ex quo patet, duos in justificatione concurrere imputationis modos, vnum στερητικὸν privativum, quem alij vocant imputationem negatam, estque rei, quae in homine existit, & imputari deberet, non imputatio, & consistit, tum in oblivione & non annotatione peccati, tum in dimissione reatus: alterum θετικὸν positivum, quem nuncupant imputationem affirmatam, quando nobis iustitia imputatur. Est haec eius rei, quae in nobis non existit, & quam minimè promeruimus, ac si in nobis existeret attributio, quando videlicet Deus pro vere iustis, & sanctis hominibus nos habet, cùm tamen tales per nos ipsos non simus.

LI. Quoniam verò judex mundanus, sine fundamento justificans impium, abominatio est Domino, Ex. 23. ver. 1. Deut. 25. v. 1. 3. Reg. 8. versu 32. Prov. 17. vers. 15. Esa. 5. versu 23. multo minus Deus aliquem justificabit sine fundamento & justitia, h. e. nisi juxta legem satisfactum sit pro peccato, & lex perfecta obedientia fuerit impleta. Hoc fundamentum imputatae justitiae cùm in credentibus non haereat, necessum est, vt extra eos sit in alio, qui solus est Christus, qui a Deo Patre factus nobis est propiciator & Mediator, qui pro nobis legi subiectus eam perfectissimè impleuit, Gal. 4. v. 4. & 5. factus à Deo nobis justitia, 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. yt nos efficeremur Iustitia Dei in ipso. 2. Cor. 5. v. ult Esa. 45. vers 24. & versu. ult. Nam per vnius obedientiam justi constituuntur multi, Rom. 5. versu 19.

LII. Atque hinc intelligitur, quomodo concilianda sint hæc duo: Qui justificat impium, abominatio est coram Deo Prov. 17. versu 15. Et credenti in eum qui justificat impium, Rom 4. v. 5. Nam ibi intelligitur impius, qui nec ipse, pro quo nec alius satisfecit: hic autem impius, qui non ipse quidem, pro quo tamen satisfecit alius. Proinde cum Deus Rom. 4 dicitur imputare iustitiam, dupliciter id accipi debet, monente Flacio in clave, pagin. 422, nempè primum ratione causæ, deinde ratione effectus. Nam 1. indicat ista locutio, justitiam Christi in credentem transcribi, sicut contrà nostra iniustitia potenter à Deo in Christum transcripta est; atq; hæc est propriè causa nostræ justitiæ. 2. Indicat etiam effectum, nempè aliquem haberi pro justo, qui non talis sit, quod ipsum porrò declarat exemplo imputationis contrariæ, dum Christo nostra imputabatur injustitia, ideoque & ipse pro injusto habebatur. Vide ipsa Flacij verba satis emphatica & ponderosa.

LIII. II. De imputatione Fidei. Cùm fides imputari dicitur ad justitiam, non accipitur absolutè, prout virtus quædam & opus bonum est, sed relativè, prout instrumentum & manus est, meritum Christi recipiens, apprehendens, sibi applicans & adproprians. Sensus igitur phraseos huius erit iste: Habemur & reputamur justi coram Deo, quia apprehendimus per solutionem & satisfactionem à Christo pro nobis factam; vnde statim apparet, perindè esse, sive dicas fidem nobis imputari ad justitiam, sive justitiam nobis imputari per fidem. Vtrobique enim nihil aliud significatur, quàm quòd iusti simus, & reputemur coram Deo, nullam ob causam aliam, nisi ob satisfactionem Christi, quam fide apprehendimus & nobis propriam facimus.

LIV. Costerus pag 254. talem affert interpretationem: Fides charitate formata, est ipsa iustitia nobis inhaerens, quâ coram Deo iusti sumus. At præterquam quòd nil nisi mera sit principij petitio, multifariam errat. 1 Quia loquitur de habitu fidei prout virtus est: Scriptura verò de actu fidei, quatenus apprehendens instrumentum est, Credidit Abraham habet textus, & hoc imputatum est ei ad iustitiam. Actus ille, non habitus imputabatur. 2. Aliud est iustitiam esse, aliud ad iustitiam imputari. Sicut enim causa nequit esse effectus, ita fides, quæ causa est imputationis ad iustitiam, non potest esse ipsa justitia, vel ipse terminus. 3. Opera secluduntur è circulo justificationis nostræ. Ergò fides quâ opus non erit nostra justitia. Hæc autem omnia cùm infrà simus declaraturi fusius, vltrà nihil addimus, sed ad causarum potius explicationem accessum faciemus.


### Question VII. What significations does imputation have?: Concerning the Efficient Cause of Justification? The Only and Eighth Question. What is the true efficient cause of our Justification?

CONCERNING THE EFFICIENT CAUSE OF JUSTIFICATION?

THE ONLY AND EIGHTH QUESTION. What is the true efficient cause of our Justification?

LV. The Papists sometimes speak quite grossly concerning this. For in the Compendium of Theology, book 6, chapter 32, this stands: In the justification of the ungodly, there is something on the part of God, something on the part of the sinner, something on the part of the Church. On the part of God, two things: mercy, which is indulgent, and justice, which demands some small amends, either here or in the future purgatory. On the part of the sinner there are also two, namely the love of God and sorrow, and these are the two millstones by which sin is ground down. On the part of the Church there are likewise two, the first is the merit of Christ and the saints: the second is the indulgence through the Pope and the Bishops.

LVI. But the Jesuits know better how to hide their wolfish nature, and they seem to defend ὀρθοδοξίαν (orthodoxy). For thus writes Bellarmine, book 1, on Justification, chapter 2. The primary efficient cause is the goodness and mercy of God, the efficient cause by way of merit is the passion of Christ, the efficient cause by way of a conjoined instrument is the very humanity of CHRIST, by way of a separate instrument are the word and the Sacraments, and those who administer them in the name of CHRIST. Costerus in his Enchiridion, p. 236 in my edition, says: God alone is the efficient cause of justification, to whom alone it belongs to give grace, according to that saying, The Lord will give grace and glory. In the expression of this cause, therefore, the Papists seem to agree with us. For our opinion holds thus, that the primary and supreme efficient cause of justification is the gratuitous goodness of God the Best and Greatest, Tit. 3, v. 4, grace, Rom. 3, v. 24, mercy, Eph. 2, v. 4, 1. Pet. 1, v. 3, the good pleasure of his will, Eph. 1, v. 9, love and charity, John 4, v. 9 & 10, Rom. 5, v. 8, Ephes. 2, v. 4, Tit. 3, v. 4.

LVII. Nor indeed does Scripture commend this goodness of God to us only in general, but it declares the same even more specifically, namely that it consists both in the redemption of the human race and in the application of the redemption that was made. For when God had foreseen from eternity the misery of the human race, he made a decree concerning the sending of his son out of mere grace and mercy, Tit. 1, v. 2, 2 Tim. 1, v. 9, and he sent him in the fullness of time, and delivered him up for us all, Rom. 5, v. 8, 1 John 3, v. 9, Luke 1, v. 78 & 54, John 3, v. 16. And he not only took care for this redemption to be made, but also distributes and applies the same out of grace, while He sets forth His Son as a propitiation, Rom. 3 v. 25, before the face of all peoples, Luke 2 v. 32, instituting and preserving the ministry of reconciliation, 2 Cor. 5 v. 18, through which He calls us to His glory, 1 Pet. 5 v. 10, Gal. 1 v. 15, 2 Tim. 1 v. 9, nay, He even makes us fit for the participation of the lot of the saints, Col. 1 v. 12, gives repentance, Acts 5 v. 31, and faith, 1 Tim. 1 v. 14, and the remission of sins, Eph. 1 v. 7, 1 John 3 v. 1, and perseverance, Rom. 5 v. 2, 1 Pet. 5 v. 1, 1 Cor. 14 v. 26, 15 v. 40, 20 v. 32. These treasures and displays of divine mercy are indeed attributed to the whole Trinity, since works toward the outside are accustomed to be undivided; to the Father, who gave love to us, 1 John 3 v. 1; to the Son, who gave Himself for us, Gal. 2 v. 20, Eph. 5 v. 25, and became poor, 2 Cor. 8 v. 9. to the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies us, 1 Pet. 1 v. 2, Rom. 5 v. 5, 1 Cor. 6 v. 11.

LIIX. From the annotation of this cause, however, a most firm argument can be sought against the infused righteousness of the Papists. For if we are justified out of the sole grace and goodness of God, then certainly not out of works. For grace is not grace in any way, if it is not grace in every way, just as Augustine speaks somewhere, and Paul testifies, Rom. 11 v. 6. And we are justified by that sole grace of God. Therefore not out of works. Whence it further follows that the Papists harbor a ὑπολιν τι here. For they do indeed confess that God is the sole and principal cause of our justification, but they say and understand this in that sense, because He alone infuses the quality of love, by which we are afterwards righteous before God. Against them, therefore, let it be noted that justification is so ascribed to divine grace that at the same time everything that inheres in us is excluded, indeed so that it is that alone, and there is no infused virtue that justifies us. For thus the Scripture speaks, Isa. 43 v. 25 & 26: I, even I, am He who blots out your iniquities for My own sake: Declare, if you have anything; so that you may be justified. And Ezek. 36:25 & 32. You shall be cleansed from all your iniquities, I will not do this for your sake, let this be known to you, says the Lord, be ashamed and confounded for your ways. You may refer here all the sayings which contain an exclusive: And at the same time this of Augustine to the false article, response For it is worthy, says Gregory in the penitential Psalms, that remission should be made through him through whom creation was made; and he himself should be the bestower of grace, who was the author of nature to all.

Latin:

DE CAVSA IVSTIFICATIOnis Efficiente?

QVÆSTIO VNICA & IIX. Quænam sit vera causa efficiens nostræ Iustificationis?

LV. Satis crassè nonnunquam de hac loquuntur Pontificij. Nam in compendio Theologiç, l. 6. c. 32. hęc extat: In Iustificatione impij, est aliquid ex parte Dei, aliquid ex parte peccatoris, aliquid ex parte Ecclesiæ. Ex parte Dei duo; misericordia, quæ malum indulget, & iustitia, quæ emendam aliquantulam exigit, vel hic, vel in futuro purgatorio. Ex peccatoris parte sunt etiam duo, scilicet Dei amor & dolor & hæ sunt duæ molæ quibus peccatum conteritur. Ex parte Ecclesiæ similiter sunt duo, primum meritum Christi & sanctorum: secundum indulgentia per Papam & Episcopos.

LVI. Sed Iesu Witæ lupinam melius sciunt tegere, & ὀρθοδοξίαν videntur defendere. Ita enim scribit Bellar. lib. 1. de Iustifi. cap. 2. Causa efficiens primaria est bonitas & misericordia Dei, efficiens per modum meriti est Christi passio, efficiens per modum instrumenti coniuncti est ipsa CHRISTI humanitas, per modum instrumenti separati sunt verbum & Sacramenta, & qui illa nomine CHRISTI administrant. Costerus in Enchirid. mihi p. 236. inquit. Deus solus efficiens causa est iustificationis, cuius solius est dare gratiam, iuxta illud, Gratiam & gloriam dabit Dominus. In hujus igitur causæ expressione nobiscum consentire videntur pontificii. Nostra enim sententia sic habet, quod primaria & summa iustificationis causa efficiens sit Dei Opt. Max. gratuita bonitas, Tit. 3. v. 4. gratia, Rom. 3. v. 24. Misericordia Eph. 2. v. 4. 1. Pet. 1. v. 3. bene placitum voluntatis ipsius Eph 1. v. 9. dilectio & charitas, Iohan. 4. v. 9 & 10. Rom. 5. v. 8. Ephes. 2, v. 4. Tit. 3. v. 4.

LVII. Neque verò Scriptura in genere tantùm hanc bonitatem Dei nobis commendat, verùm eandem adhuc specialiùs declarat, quòd videlicet consistat, tùm in redemtione generis humani, tùm in applicatione factæ redemtionis. Cùm enim Deus ab æterno prævidisset miseriam generis humani, fecit decretum de mittendo filio suo ex mera gratia & misericordia, Tit. 1. v. 2. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. illumque in plenitudine temporis misit, & pro nobis omnibus tradidit, Rom. 5. v. 8. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 9. Luc. 1. v. 78 & 54. Ioh. 3. v. 16. Neque solùm hanc redemtionem fieri curauit, sed eandem etiam ex gratia distribuit & applicat, dùm Filium suum, tanquam propitiatorium proponit, Rom 3. v. 25. ante faciem omnium populorum, Luc. 2. v. 32.instituens & conseruans ministerium reconciliationis.2. Cor.5.v.18. per quod nos vocat ad suam gloriam, 1. Petr. 5. v. 10. Galat 1. v. 15. 2. Tim. 1. v. 9. quin & idoneos nos reddit ad participationem sortis sanctorum, Coloss. 1. v. 12. dat pœnitentiam Act. 5. v. 31 & fidem 1. Tim 1. v. 14. & remissionem peccatorum Eph. 1. v. 7. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 1 & perseuerantiam, Rom. 5. v. 2. 1. Petr. 5 v. 1. 1. Cor. 14. v. 26. 15. v. 40. 20. v. 32. His verò thesauri & ostentationes misericordiæ diuinæ tribuuntur toti Trinitati, cùm opera ad extra soleant esse indiuisa; Patri qui charitatem dedit nobis, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 1 Filio, qui semetipsum pro nobis tradidit, Gal: 2. v. 20. Eph. 5. v. 25. & pauper factus est, 2. Cor. 8. v. 9. Spiritui sancto, qui nos sanctificat, 1. Pet. 1. v. 2. Rom. 5. v. 5. 1. Cor. 6. v. 11.

LIIX. Ex huius verò causæ annotatione firmissimum potest argumentum peti contra Pontificiorum iustitiam infusam, Nam si ex sola Dei gratia & bonitate iustificamur, utique non ex operibus. Gratia enim non est gratia ullo modo, si non est gratia omni modo, quemadmodum Augustinus alicubi loquitur, & Paulus testatur, Rom. 11. v. 9 Atque eâ sola Dei gratiâ iustificamur. Ergò non ex operibus. Vnde porrò sequitur, quod hic ὑπολιν τι foveant Pontificij. Nam fatentur quidem, Deum esse vnicam & principem nostræ iustificationis causam, sed isto sensu dicunt hoc & intelligunt, quia solus infundat qualitatem dilectionis, quâ postea iusti simus coram Deo. Contra ipsos igitur notetur, quòd iustificatio ita diuinæ gratiæ adscribatur, vt simul excludatur omne id, quod in nobis hæret, ita quidem vt illa sola sit, & nulla virtus infusa, quæ nos iustificet. Ita enim Scriptura loquitur, Esa. 43. vers. 25. & 26. Ego ego ipse sum, qui deleo iniquitates tuas propter me: Narra, si quid habes; vt iustificeris. Et Ezech.36.v.25.& 32. Mundabimini ab omnibus iniquitatibus vestris, Non propter vos hoc ego faciam, notum sit vobis hoc, ait Dominus, confundimini, & erubescite super viis vestris. Potes huc referre omnia dicta, quæ exclusiuam continent: Simulque hoc Augustini ad artic.falsum respon, 2. Vt reus damnetur, inculpabilis est DEI gratia. Dignum enim est, inquit Gregor.in Psalm.pœnit. vt per eum fiat remissio, per quem facta est creatio; & ipse sit largitor gratiæ, qui omnibus fuit author naturæ.


### Question VII. What significations does imputation have?: Concerning the Impel- ling Cause. Single Question & IX. Whether and what is the impelling cause of Justification?

CONCERNING THE IMPEL- ling CAUSE. SINGLE QUESTION & IX. Whether and what is the impelling cause of Justification?

LIX. Although nothing can be given which properly moved God and effectively impelled Him to mercy, yet the orthodox Fathers are accustomed to allege the misery of the human race as the procatarctic cause. For mercy is an affection born from the depths of misery, whence it is said that God was moved by that extreme misery into which man had fallen through the seduction of the devil. And thus that calamity is not properly an impelling cause, but only in a certain way an inciting cause of divine mercy, whence the Church sings: Da iammerets Gott in Ewigkeit/Mein Elend vber die massen/ Er gedacht an seine Barmhertzigkeit / Er wolt mir helffen lassen. But this very thing is also sufficiently expressed in the scriptures. For thus St. Paul writes in Acts 13:38. Because you could not be justified by the law of Moses, And Acts 15:10 Because no one could bear the yoke of the law, therefore 1 John 3:8. The Son of God came, that he might destroy the works of the devil, which according to Rom. 8:3 was impossible for the law because of the flesh, that he might redeem those who were under the law, Gal. 4:5. Heb. 2:

And to this point also pertains that passage in Rom. 5. v. 8. God commends his love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. And John 3 v. 16. God so loved the world, etc.

LX. But the annotation of this cause likewise exhibits a certain use against the Papists, who assert that in the justifying of men there are certain qualities which God regards, and on account of which he accepts men into grace and to eternal life. For so Bellarmine thinks, book 1, chapter 2, that before justification there are certain necessary dispositions in man, which prepare the matter for receiving the form. Now, dispositions to justification are called (these are the words of Bellarmine) all those acts of grace and free will by which the gift of justification itself is acquired, such as are, according to the opinion of the Council of Trent, session 6, chapter 6, acts of faith, fear, hope, etc. Against this dogma, however, we argue thus: That alone is the true procatarctic cause of grace and divine love, which Scripture itself manifestly assigns. But it mentions only human misery, nowhere good works, nowhere any virtues, nowhere preceding dispositions. Therefore, these ought not to be peddled as a procatarctic cause.

LXI. Nor is there any reason for them to object that this is said of the grace of God and the love from which the Mediator was given to us, but not of the grace by which we are justified. For the grace and mercy of God is one and the same, from which flow absolutely all the spiritual benefits that are conferred upon us, James 1. v. 17. Thus, therefore, we argue, especially against Bellarmine: By the same grace of God by which we are chosen, we are justified. 1. On account of the harmony of the decree and the execution. 2. On account of the statements in Eph. 1. v. 4, 2 Tim. 1. v. 9 & 10: God saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was indeed given to us in Christ Jesus before the ages of time, but has now been manifested through that illustrious coming of our Savior. And yet the grace of God, by which we are chosen in Christ, in no way looks to the works, virtues, or dispositions of men, Rom. 9. v. 11, with Bellarmine agreeing against other Papists, book 2 on grace and free will, ch. 10, 11, 12. Therefore, the grace by which we are justified also looks to no works or virtues.

LXII. Furthermore, we can conclude thus: Where there is mercy, there no dignity of works has a place, but rather only misery. For, as has been said, mercy is an affection of the heart on account of misery. And yet God saves us by His mercy, Tit. 3. v. 5. Therefore, the misery of men, not the dignity of human works or virtues or dispositions, is the impulsive cause of the grace of God justifying us in Christ.

Latin:

DE CAVSA IMPELlente. QVÆSTIO VNICA & IX. An & quæ Iustificationis causa impellens sit?

LIX. Quantumuis nihil dari possit, quod propriè DEVM mouerit & ad misericordiam efficaciter impulerit, solent tamen orthodoxi Patres pro caussa προκαταρκτικῇ allegare miseriam generis humani. Est enim misericordia affectus ex intimis miseriæ prognatus, vnde dicitur quòd Deus commotus fuerit, per summam illam miseriam, in quam homo deuenerat per seductionem diaboli. Atque sic calamitas illa non est propriè impellens, sed duntaxat quodammodo irritans causa misericordiæ diuinæ, vnde canit Ecclesia; Da iammerets Gott in Ewigkeit/Mein Elend vber die massen/ Er gedacht an seine Barmhertzigkeit / Er wolt mir helffen lassen. Hoc ipsum verò in scripturis etiam satis expressum est. Ita enim scribit D. Paulus Act.13.v.38. Quia non potuistis lege Mosis iustificari, Et Actor.15.v.10 Quia iugum legis nemo potuit portare, ideò 1.Ioh.3.v.8. Filius Dei venit, vt destruat opera diaboli,quod iuxta Rom.8.v.3. impossibile erat legi ob carnem, vt eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret, Gal.4.v.5. Hebr.2.v.

35. Atque huc pertinet etiam illud Rom. 5. v. 8. Commendat Deus suam charitatem erga nos, quòd cum adhuc essemus peccatores, Christus pro nobis mortuus sit. Et Ioh. 3 v. 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum, &c.

LX. Huius verò causæ annotatio itidem vsum quendam exhibet contra Pontificios, asserentes in hominibus iustificandis esse quasdam qualitates, quas Deus respiciat, & propter quas acceptet homines in gratiam & ad vitam æternam. Ita enim sentit Bell. l. 1. cap. 2. nes. quod ante iustificationem in homine sint necessariæ quædam dispositiones, quæ materiam præparent ad recipiendam formam. Dicuntur autem dispositiones ad iustificationem (sunt verba Bellarmini) illi omnes actus gratiæ & liberi arbitrij, quibus donum ipsius iustificationis acquiritur, quales sunt, ex sententia Concilij Tridentini sessione. 6. cap. 6. actus fidei, Timoris Spei, &c. Contra hoc autem dogma sic argumentamur: Illa demum vera est causa προκαταρκτικὴ gratiæ & dilectionis diuinæ, quàm ipsa scriptura manifestè assignat. Sed solius meminit miseriæ humanæ, nusquam bonorum operum, nusquam aliquarum virtutum, nusquam præcedentium dispositionum. Ergò hæc pro causa προκαταρκτικῇ venditari non debent.

LXI. Neque est, vt excipiant, dici de gratia Dei, & dilectione ex qua nobis datus sit Mediator, non autem de gratia, quâ iustificemur. Nam vna est, eademque Dei gratia & misericordia, ex qua fluunt omnia omninò, quæ in nos conferuntur spiritualia beneficia, Iacob. 1. v. 17. Ita igitur, præsertim contra Bellarmin. argumentamur: Quâ Dei gratiâ eligimur, eâdem iustificamur. 1. Ob consonantiam decreti & executionis. 2. Ob dicta Ephes. 1. v. 4. Tim. 1. v. 9. & 10 Deus seruauit nos & vocauit vocatione sanctâ, non ex nostris operibus, sed ex proposito & gratia, quæ data quidem est nobis in Christo Iesu ante tempora secularia, sed patefacta est nunc per illustrem illum aduentum Seruatoris nostri. Atqui gratia Dei, quâ eligimur in Christo, nullo modo respicit opera, virtutes aut dispositiones hominum, Rom. 9. v. 11. adstipulante contra alios Pōtificios Bellarmino l. 2. de gratia & lib. arbitrio c. 10. 11. 12. Ergo & gratia, quâ iustificamur, nulla opera aut virtutes respicit.

LXII. Porrò ita concludere possumus : Vbi est misericordia, ibi locum nõ habet operum aliqua dignitas, sed sola potius miseria, Nam, vti dictum, misericordia est affectus cordis ob miseriam. Atqui Deus seruat nos suâ misericordiâ, Tit. 3. v. 5. Ergò miseria hominum, non operum aut virtutum aut dispositionum humanarum dignitas, causa impulsiua est gratiæ Dei in Christo nos iustificantis.


### Question VII. What significations does imputation have?: On the Meritorious Cause of our justification

ON THE MERITORIOUS CAUSE of our justification.

LXIII. We have said that the highest and primary cause of justification is the gratuitous mercy of God. But lest contrary wills be attributed to God, as if He pities sinners and the ungodly whom He nevertheless greatly abhors, therefore the doctrine concerning the merit of Christ must now be added immediately, so that it may be known that the grace of God is not to be considered except in Christ. Therefore, Chemnitius writes most correctly in my loci, p. 347: Outside of Christ, no grace or mercy of God toward sinners either should or can be rightly conceived, unless the law be dissolved, destroyed, and perish, which is impossible. And hence are those words of the Apostle: He loved us in the beloved; He chose us in Christ Jesus before the times of the ages. For God is so kind and merciful that He is at the same time also just. Lest, therefore, His justice should come into jeopardy, there was need of satisfaction for the sins of the world, without which it could not happen that one would be received into grace.

LXIV. Therefore, hold most firmly to this rule:

The mercy of God is to be maintained in such a way that his justice is not undermined, and justice in such a way that mercy is not destroyed. For we ought to acknowledge and teach in God not justice alone without mercy, nor mercy alone without justice, but justice in mercy and mercy in justice, and therefore a merciful justice and a just mercy.

LXV. And such an admirable and divine tempering of justice and kindness is seen in the redemption of the human race. Infinite justice is beheld there, punishing sins with most just judgment: yet this justice does not hinder the kindness that raises up and restores the human race, namely on account of the intercession and satisfaction of the Mediator, which brings it about that the justice of God is satisfied, and yet a place is also granted to divine kindness. Therefore God condemned the whole human race on account of sin, because he is just: the same he receives into grace on account of Christ, because he is also merciful. Outside of Christ, therefore, divine grace is not to be considered. For this is the only name in which we can please God and be saved, Acts 4:12, Ephesians 1:6.

LXVI. Nor indeed let it trouble anyone that Christ says in John 3:16, 'God so loved the world,' etc. Where love seems to precede the decree concerning the mission of the Mediator. For we do not deny that the Mediator is a gift of divine grace, but yet we firmly hold this at the same time, that the goodness of God is to be preached in such a way that his justice is not denied. Wherefore here shines forth that admirable tempering of divine justice and mercy. God loves the world contaminated by sins, but he ought to have hated and punished it according to the sentence passed in Genesis 2:17. For justice that loves sins and does not punish them is not justice, but an abomination, Proverbs 17:15, Isaiah 5:23. But God is essentially justice itself. Therefore he ought to have punished and avenged sins. In this sense must that saying be understood when we say: Outside of Christ there is no salvation, no grace, namely so that we may preserve unharmed the divine justice, without which, had it not been satisfied through Christ, the human race, as Scripture testifies, could not have been loved nor received into favor.

LXVII. And having premised these things by way of introduction concerning the meritorious cause, we approach the treatment itself, where various and diverse controversies occur, while some detract not a little from the merit of Christ, others impugn a part of it, and others the whole merit. For 1. The Papists weaken the λύτρον of Christ with many hypotheses. 2. Piscator with his followers excludes active obedience from merit. 3. The recent Photinians, having progressed further, utterly deny all merit and satisfaction of Christ. We shall deal with the first errors in this disputation; but we wish the Photinian controversy, since it requires a prolix explanation, to be reserved for the following disputations.

Latin:

DE CAVSA MERITORIA nostræ iustificationis.

LXIII. Diximus summam & primam Iustificationis causam esse gratuitam Dei misericordiam. Nè verò Deo contrariæ affingantur voluntates, ac si peccatorum & impiorum misereatur, quos tamen maximè auersatur: ideò nunc statim subiungenda est doctrina de merito Christi, vt sciatur, gratiam Dei non nisi in Christo esse cõsiderandam. Proindè rectissimè scribit Chemnitius in locis mihi p. 347. Extra Christum nulla aut gratia aut misericordia Dei erga peccatores, nec debet, nec potest rectè cogitari, nisi lex soluatur, destruatur & intereat, quod impossibile est. Et hinc sunt illæ voces Apostoli. Dilexit nos in dilecto: Elegit nos in Christo Iesu ante tempora seculoria. Nam Deus ita est benignus & misericors, vt simul etiam sit iustus. Nè itaque iustitia ipsius veniret in discrimen, opus erat satisfactione pro mundi peccatis, sine quâ fieri non poterat, vt in gratiam reciperetur.

LXIV. Firmissimè igitur teneas hanc regulam:

Ita est Dei misericordia adstruenda, ne eius labefactetur iustitia, & ita iustitia, ne destruatur misericordia. Non enim solam sine misericordia iustitiam, nec solam sine iustitia misericordiam, sed in misericordia iustitiam, & in iustitia misericordiam, adeoq; misericordem iustitiam & iustam misericordiam in Deo agnoscere & docere debemus.

LXV. Atq; tale admirandum & diuinū quodā dam iustitiæ ac benignitatis temperamentum cernitur in redemptione generis humani. Conspicitur ibi infinita iustitia, iustissimo iudicio puniens peccata: hæc tamen iustitia non impedit benignitatem, erigentem & restaurantem genus humanum, nimirum propter intercessionē & satisfactionem Mediatoris, quæ efficit, vt & iustitiæ Dei satis fiat, & tamen etiam locus concedatur benignitati diuinæ. Damnauit ergò Deus totum genus humanum propter peccatum, quia iustus est: Idem recipit in gratiam propter Christum, quia & misericors est. Extra Christum igitur non consideranda est gratia diuina. Hoc enim vnicum est nomen, in quo placere Deo & salui esse possumus, Act. 4. vers. 12. Ephes. 1. v. 6.

LXVI. Neque verò quemquam turbet, quod Christus inquit Ioh. 3. v. 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum &c. Vbi videtur dilectio præcedere decretum de missione Mediatoris. Non enim negamus, Mediatorem esse donum gratiæ diuinæ, sed tamen hoc simul firmiter tenemus, sic esse prædicandam Dei bonitatem, nè ipsius negetur iustitia. Quare hic elucet admiranda illa iustitiæ & misericordiæ diuinæ contemperatio. Deus diligit mundum peccatis contaminatum, ast odisse debuerat & punire iuxta sententiam latam Gen. 2. v. 17. Nam iustitia, quę peccata diligit, eaque non punit, iustitia nō est, sed abominatio, Prov. 17. v. 15. Esa. 5. v. 23. Atqui Deus est ipsa essentialiter iustitia. Ergò peccata punire & vlcisci debebat. Hoc igitur sensu intelligendum est illud, quando dicimus. Extra Christum nulla salus, nulla gratia, vtvidelicet illæsam seruēmus justitiam diuinam, cui nisi per Christum satisfactum fuisset, genus humanum teste Scripturâ non diligi nec in gratiam recipi potuisset.

LXVII. Atque his procœmij loco de causa meritoria præmissis, ad ipsam tractationem accedimus, vbi variæ diuersæque occurrant controversiæ, dum nonnulli merito Christi haud parum dêtrahunt, alij partem eius, alij totum meritum impugnant. Nam 1. Pontificij multis hypothese bus λύτρον Christi eneruant. 2. Piscator cum asseclis obedientiam actiuam à merito excludit. 3. Recentes Photiniani longiùs progressi, omne meritum & satisfactionem Christi penitùs inficiantur. De primis erroribus hac disputatione agemus: controuersiam verò Photinianam, cùm explicationem requirat prolixam, sequentibus disputationibus reseruatam volumus.


### Question I. & X

Who are the principal errors of the Papists concerning the merit of Christ?

LXIIX. The Romanists do not wish to appear to either weaken the merit of Christ or detract anything from it. For the Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 7, has it thus: The meritorious (cause) is the most beloved only-begotten of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, who, when we were enemies, through the exceeding charity with which He loved us, merited for us justification by His most holy passion on the wood of the cross. And Bellarmine, lib. 1 de justificat. c. 2, expressly says, The efficient cause of justification by way of merit is the passion of Christ. But these are cloaks with which they are accustomed to veil their errors, so that they may not be noticed by the simpler sort at the very first moment. For in Papistic writings its such assertions are found everywhere, so that if they stand, the merit of Christ cannot stand and remain safe and unimpaired. To touch upon only the principal errors, seven of them can be numbered.

LXIX. First error. They deny that Christ is Mediator according to both natures. Bellarmine, lib. 5 de Christo c. 1, writes indeed that the whole Christ is the principle of mediation; but that the principle by which is the humanity alone, which he undoubtedly drew from Lombard, l. 3 dist. 19 lit. 5. But in truth, neither nature ought to be excluded from the office of Mediation. Not the human, since the divinity could not suffer. Not the divine, since the suffering of the humanity alone cannot be of infinite merit. The humanity alone could suffer, but it could not suffer for the world. Thus the divinity could reconcile the world, but it could not do so by suffering, since it is impassible. Therefore, to suffer for the world belongs neither to the humanity alone, nor to the divinity alone, but to both natures. And this is what Augustine wrote somewhere: The humanity alone without the divinity is not Mediatrix, nor the divinity alone without the humanity; but between the humanity alone and the divinity alone, the human divinity and the divine humanity is the mediatrix.

LXX. Second error. They by no means concede that CHRIST felt the wrath of GOD in his passion and sustained infernal torments. It is a NEW and unheard-of impiety, writes Bellarmine, l. 4 de Christo c. 8, that Christ suffered the pains of hell. We, however, as willingly as we grant that Christ neither ever despaired, nor first felt the wrath of God in the descent into hell, which indeed happened after the resurrection: nevertheless, he sustained such great agonies in the garden that he emitted a bloody sweat, and cried out with a complaining voice: My soul is sorrowful even unto death, Matthew 26, verse 38; and then on the cross the wrath

of the Father he so felt, that he said, My GOD, my GOD, why hast thou forsaken me? The same is confirmed by the complaints of the Psalmist uttered in the person of Christ. Psalm 16. v. 10. Psalm 18. v. 6. Psalm 49. v. 6. Psalm 69. v. 15. 16. Psalm 86. v. 13. And indeed Christ would neither have satisfied perfectly for us, nor would he have been made a curse for us, unless he had felt the judgment of an angry God.

LXXI. The third error. Some have denied that Christ satisfied perfectly for the sins and punishments of our sins. Formerly it was disputed that Christ had satisfied only for original sin, and that for actual sins our own satisfaction is required. Catharinus maintained that the passion of Christ is indeed profitable for actual sins before Baptism, but that subsequent ones must be expiated by Masses and good works. More recent writers, although they say that Christ satisfied for all sins and eternal punishments, nevertheless write that a debt of temporal punishment remains: nay, that by the power of the keys the eternal punishment due to sins is changed into a temporal one, so that we may satisfy for it. But by these very assertions the merit of Christ is not a little weakened. For as much as is attributed to our works and satisfactions, so much is detracted from Christ, who nevertheless is said to have trodden the winepress alone, Isaiah 63. v. 3. Nor indeed is the customary exception of any value, that the satisfaction of Christ and our own are not to be opposed, since our works receive all their power of satisfying and meriting from the satisfaction of Christ. For 1. Scripture nowhere proposes this use and fruit of the merit of Christ; but rather: 2. It always opposes faith in the merit of Christ and our works. 3. It would also follow,

that the satisfaction of Christ was imperfect, since it has need of the addition of our works. 4. Nay, we would be Mediators in our own cause, if our works were satisfactory.

LXXII. The fourth error. They do not place the price and value of the satisfaction of Christ in the infinite efficacy of merit, but in the acceptance of divine mercy, by which God held the passion of Christ, proceeding from such great love, in the place of satisfaction. For thus writes Durandus in book 4 of the Sentences, distinction 19: Christ, according to strict rigor, could not make satisfaction, because whatever was in Christ according to human nature was obligated and owed to God: therefore it could not be satisfaction of condignity for any sin whatsoever, considering the nature of the work or thing, but it could only be satisfaction according to gratuitous acceptance. Bellarmine himself saw that this opinion was erroneous, and therefore he disapproves of it in book 2 of Justification, chapter 5.

LXXIII. The fifth error. They assert that the Virgin Mary was Christ's helper in the work of Redemption. For they attribute to her the crushing of the serpent's head in Genesis 3, and they place their own hope and trust in her as well. Indeed, they write expressly in the Mariale, published at Strasbourg, book 1, chapter 5: Finally, the Lord was with her (Mary) and she with the Lord in the same work of redemption. The Mother of mercies helped the Father of mercies in the work of our salvation, whence it was predicted concerning the first woman: We will make a helper for him. What is it, therefore, that the Lord says in Isaiah 63: I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me? It is true, Lord, that there was no man with you, but a woman is with you, who received in her heart all the wounds that you received in your body.

LXXIV. The sixth error. They join the merits of other saints partly, and partly our own works, with the merit of Christ, and thus they argue that it is imperfect. For they pray daily from the Hortulus Animae: May the Lord lead us to the kingdom of heaven through the prayers and merits of the Blessed Mary ever virgin and of all the saints. Biel teaches and inculcates this very thing in lecture 29 on the Canon of the Mass: We ought, he says, to flee to the holy Mediators and their aids; and we ought always to implore them with due veneration, so that we may be saved by their merits and vows. Besides the merits of the saints, they also require our own, as Peter de Palude contends in 4 Sentences, distinction 20, question 3. For little children the merit of Christ is sufficient; because they cannot merit, but the merit of Christ with Baptism is not yet sufficient, but they are bound to add their own merit. And hence it is that Biel denies, l. 3. sent. dist. 19. conclus. 8., that the Passion of Christ is the sole and total meritorious cause of our salvation. But Bernard rightly wrote, serm. 67. in Cant.: 'Whatever you attribute to merits, grace is lacking.'

LXXV. The seventh error. They do not hold the merit of Christ as the efficient cause of our justification, but only as an instrument. For Thomas Aquinas wrote that Christ is the cause of justification through ministry, and works human salvation only instrumentally. Bonaventure was crasser, who openly says: 'Causality of justification cannot properly be attributed to the Passion of Christ. For it belongs to no genus of causes. It has, however, some property of a cause by way of intervening merit, which has the nature of a disposition and is reduced to a material cause.' More recent writers indeed call Christ an efficient cause by way of merit, but they explain this falsely and viciously. For they understand it thus: that Christ by his passion merited that new qualities be infused into us, by which we are formally rendered just; or that the merit of Christ alone has procured for us the first grace, and before the remission of sins no man's work is meritorious, as Costerus explains in Enchirid. m. p. 260.

LXXVI. But the Orthodox rightly oppose this, with whom we also establish that Christ is less correctly excluded from the efficiency of justification, and falsely called merely an instrumental cause. Scripture indeed calls Christ a servant and minister, Matt. 20. v. 28, Heb. 5. v. 7, and specifically a minister of the circumcision or of the circumcised, Rom. 15. v. 8. But this ministry does not take away the proper efficiency of salvation. For Christ, by ministering and serving us, truly worked salvation: whence it is clear that through that ministry, not the manner of causing, but the end of the incarnation is denoted. For Christ came to minister to us, that is, to recover again the lost salvation.

LXXVII. Nor does it hinder that the Fathers sometimes called the humanity an instrument of the divinity. For we are not inquiring about the humanity of Christ, compared to the divinity, but about the whole Christ in the matter of justification, whether it is truly maintained that Christ is nothing but an instrument and a ministerial cause of our righteousness, and not properly an efficient one? This has not been affirmed by the Fathers; and if it were affirmed, it would be nonetheless most false, for Christ is the author of life, is the Lord of Christians, is Jehovah our righteousness: who therefore would be only an instrument of justification? He gave his own flesh for the life of the world, John 6, verse 51. His blood was shed for the remission of sins, Matthew 26, verse 28, and cleanses us from all sin, 1 John 1, verse 7. Nor is there any other name in which we can please God and be saved, Acts 4, verse 12. All of which provide clear testimony that CHRIST is the efficient cause of justification, properly so called.

LXXVIII. However, we cannot deny that different modes of speaking are employed by theologians. There are those who call the Father the commanding cause, and the Son the executing cause, because the Father sends, and the Son is sent. But in this way, a distinction of persons and operations is indeed hinted at, but the manner of causing itself is not expressed. Some call Christ an impelling cause rather than an efficient one. For the Father is impelled by the intuition of merit to receive us into grace and justify us. But we do not consider these to be contrary, since both can be affirmed of Christ. For he is considered in two ways: 1. In respect to the Father, whom he moves by his merit to justify; and in this sense he is rightly called impelling. 2. In relation to the righteousness which he has acquired and applies to us: and in this respect he can and ought to be called an efficient cause. For he who has restored righteousness and effectively confers it once restored, why should he not be called the efficient cause of righteousness? We distinguish, however, between the general or common cause of justification, and the special or proper one. The former is the grace of God, the latter is the obedience of Christ, inasmuch as he by his passion has expiated our sins and restored true righteousness.

LXXIX. That all these things may be better understood and more briefly proposed, it is to be noted that Christ is and can be called the cause of our justification in a threefold way. 1. By merit, because he merited the grace of the Father, reconciled us to him in turn, and took away all sins, according to the statements, Rom. 4. v. last, 1. Corinth. 15. v. 3. 2. By efficacy: For Christ's merit was not provided for this reason, that our satisfactions or those of others for us should become meritorious, since his obedience alone is a sufficient expiation for our sins, 1. John 1. v. 7. 1. John 2. v. 2. 1. Pet. 1. v. 19. needing no addition or appendix of our works, which are therefore entirely excluded from the business of salvation, Rom. 3. 4. 11. Gal. 3. Ephes. 2. 3. By application. For Christ not only acquired righteousness, but furthermore applies what has been acquired, so that we are righteous by no other thing than by his obedience alone imputed to us. Hence he is called our righteousness. Jerem. 23. v. 6. in whom are our righteousnesses, Isaiah 45. v. 24. made by God righteousness, 1. Corinth. 1. v. 30. that we might be made the righteousness of God in him, 2. Corinth. 5. v. last.

LXXX. From this triple respect a triple mode of causing flows, and therefore Christ can rightly be designated, 1. Impelling cause, on account of the merit by which the Father is moved. 2. Efficient cause, on account of the efficacy by which righteousness is acquired. 3. Formal cause, on account of the application, insofar as he himself applies his own merit to us, which application and imputation of merit is the formal cause. For on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, and imputed to us, we are formally righteous before God, so that there is no absurdity in referring Christ and his merit to different kinds of causes. This can be declared by a certain analogy, taken from the payment of another's debt. Insofar as it is estimated with respect to the payer, not the debtor, it is the efficient cause, on account of which the debtor is absolved and cannot be sued: but insofar as that payment of another is imputed to the debtor, as if it were his own, in this sense it is the formal cause, which bestows the τὸ ἄναι upon forensic justification and absolution.

Latin:

Quinam sint præcipui errores Pontificiorum circa meritum Christi?

LXIIX. Nolunt Romanenses videri, quòd meritum Christi vel eneruent vel illi aliquid detrahant. Ita enim habet Concilium Trident: sess. 6: c. 7. Meritoria (causa) est dilectissimus DEI unigenitus, Dominus noster Iesus Christus, qui cùm essemus inimici, per nimiam caritatem, quâ dilexit nos, suâ sanctissimâ passione in ligno crucis nobis iustificationem meruit. Et Bellarm. li 1. de justificat: c: 2. diserte ait, Efficiens iustificationis per modum meriti est Christi passio. Sed hæc pallia sunt, quibus errores suos obvelare solent, ne primo statim tempore à simplicioribus animaduertantur. Nam in scriptis Papisticis eius modi assertiones passim reperiuntur, vt iis stantibus, meritum Christi salvum illætumque stare ac permanere haut valeat. Vt præcipuos tantum errores attingamus, septem illorum numerari possunt.

LXIX. Primus error. Negant, Christum esse Mediatorem secundum vtramque naturam. Totum quidem Christum esse principium Quod mediationis scribit Bell. lib. 5. de Christo c. 1: Principium Quo autem solam esse humanitatem, quod ex Lombardo proculdubio hausit, l. 3. dist. 19. lit. 5. At verò neutra natura ab officio Mediationis excludi debet. Non humana, quoniam diuinitas pati non poterat. Non divina quoniam solius humanitatis passio nequit esse infiniti meriti. Pati poterat humanitas sola, sed pati pro mundo non poterat. Sic diuinitas mundum potuit reconciliare, sed pati pro mundo non poterat. Sic diuinitas mundum potuit reconciliare, sed patiendo non potuit cùm sit impassibilis. Pati igitur pro mundo, nec soli humanitati, nec soli diuinitati, sed vtrique naturæ competit. Atque hoc est, quod Augustinus alicubi scripsit: Sola humanitas sine diuinitate non est Mediatrix, nec sola divinitas sine humanitate; sed inter humanitatem solam, & inter diuinitatem solam mediatrix est humana divinitas & divina humanitas

LXX. Secundus error. Minimè concedunt, CHRISTVM in passione iram DEI sensisse & cruciatus infernales sustinuisse. NOVA, scribit Bellarm. l. 4. de Christo c. 8. & inaudita impietas est, quod Christus passus sit dolores inferni. Nos autem quantùmvis lubenter demus, Christum nec desperasse vnquam, nec in descensu ad inferos, quippe post resurrectionem facto, iram Dei primùm persentisse: nihilominus tamen tum in horto tantos sustinuit angores, vt sanguineum sudorem emitteret, & querula voce clamaret: Tristis est anima mea vsque ad mortem, Matth. 26. versu 38. tùm in cruce iram

Patris ita persensit, vt diceret, DEVS meus, DEVS meus, quare me dereliquisti? Idem confirmant querelæ Psaltis in persona Christi prolatæ. Psalm. 16. v. 10. Psal. 18. v. 6. Psalm. 49. v. 6. Psal. 69. v. 15. 16. Psal: 86. v. 13. Et sanè Christus nec perfectè pro nobis satisfecisset, nec maledictum pro nobis factus esset, nisi iudicium Dei irati persensisset.

LXXI. Tertius error. Negârunt nonnulli; Christum perfectè pro peccatis pœnísque peccatorum nostrorum satisfecisse. Quondam disputatum est, Christum duntaxat pro peccato originali fecisse satis, pro actualibus nostram requiri satisfactionem. Catharinus statuit, Christi passionem prodesse quidem pro actualibus peccatis ante Baptismum, sequentia vero esse Missis & bonis operibus expianda. Recentiores, quamuis dicant Christum pro peccatis omnibus & pœnis æternis satisfecisse, nihilo minus remanere scribunt debitum pœnæ temporalis : imo potestate clauium sempiternam & peccatis debitam pœnam mutari in temporalem, vt pro ea satisfacere possimus. His ipsis autem assertionibus non parum eneluatur meritum Christi. Quantum enim nostris operllis & satisfactionibus tribuitur, tantum Christo detrahitur, qui tamen solus torcular calcâsse dicitur, Esai. 63. v. 3. Neque verò quicquam valet consueta exceptio, satisfactionem Christi & nostram non esse opponendam, cùm nostra opera omnem vim satisfaciendi & merendi à Christi satisfactione accipiant, Nam 1. Scriptura hunc vsum fructúmque meriti Christi nuspiam proponit; sed potiùs: 2. Fidem in Christi meritum & opera nostra semper opponit. 3. Sequeretur etiam,

Christi satisfactionem fuisse imperfectam, cùm opus habeat adaliamento nostrorum operum. 4 Imo in propria causa essemus Mediatores, si opera nostra forent satisfactoria.

LXXII. Quartus error. Pretium & valorem satisfactionis Christi non in infinita meriti efficacia constituunt, sed in misericordiæ diuinæ acceptatione, quâ DEVS passionem Christi ex tanta caritate profectam, loco satisfactionis habuerit. Ita enim scribit Durandus in lib. 4 sent. dist. 19. Christus secundum strictum vigorem non potuit satisfacere, quia quicquid erat in Christo secundum humanam naturam, erat obligatum Deo et debitum: ideò non potuit esse satisfactio de condigno pro quocunque peccato, considerando naturam operis vel rei, sed solùm potuit esse satisfactio secundum acceptionem gratuitam. Opinionem hanc esse erroneam vidit ipse Bellarminus, ideoque illam improbat lib. 2. de Iustificat. c. 5.

LXXIII. Quintus error. Asserunt, Mariam virginem fuisse Christi adiutricem in opere Redemptionis. Nam contritionem capitis serpentini Genes. 3. ipsi attribuunt & suam unà spem ac fiduciam in illa ponunt. Imò expressè scribunt in Mariali, Argentinæ edito lib. 1. cap. 5. Ad ultimum fuit Dominus cum ea (Maria) & ipsa cum Domino in eodem opere redemptionis. Mater misericordiæ adiuvit Patrem misericordiarum in opere nostræ salutis, unde prædictum est de primamuliere; Faciemus ei adiutorium. Quid est ergò, quòd Dominus dicit, Esai. 63. Torcular calcavi solus, & de gentibus non fuit vir mecum ? Verum est Domine, quod non fuit vir tecum, sed mulier unà tecum est, quæ omnia vulnera, quæ tu suscepisti corpore, suscepit in corde.

LXXIV. Sextus error. Cum Christi merito partim aliorum sanctorum merita, partim nostra opera coniungunt, adeoque illud imperfectionis arguunt. Nam quotidiè orant ex hortulo animę: Precibus & meritis B. Mariæ semper virginis & omnium sanctorum, perducat nos Dominus ad regnum cælorum. Docet hoc ipsum inculcatque Biel lect. 29. in Canonem missæ: Nos, inquit, ad Mediatores sanctos, eorumque auxilia confugere debemus; ac debita veneratione eos semper implorare, vt saluemur eorum meritis ac votis. Præter sanctorum merita requirunt etiam propria, vti contendit Petrus de Palude in 4. sent. dist. 20. quæst. 3. Pro pattulis sufficit meritum Christi; quia non possunt mereri, sed adhuc non sufficit meritum Christi cum Baptismo, sed tenentur addere meritum proprium. Atque hinc est, quod Biel negat l. 3. sent. dist. 19. cōclus. 8. Passionem Christi esse solam & totalem causam salutis nostrae meritoriam. Recte autem Bernhardus scripsit serm. 67. in Cant. Deeft gratia, quicquid meritis deputas.

LXXV. Septimus error. Meritum Christi non habent pro causa efficiente nostrae iustificationis, sed tantùm pro instrumento. Thomas enim de Aquino scripsit, Christum esse causam iustificationis per ministerium, & instrumentaliter tantùm operari salutem humanam. Crassior fuit Bonaventura, qui apertè inquit : Passioni Christi propriè non potest tribui causalitas iustificationis. Ad nullum enim genus causarum pertinet. Habet tamen aliquam proprietatem causae per modum meriti interuenientis, quod habet rationem dispositionis & reducitur ad causam materialem. Recentiores Christum quidem causam vocant efficientem per modum meriti, sed falsò & vitiosè hoc exponunt. Sic enim intelligūt, quòd Christus passione sua promeruerit, vt nouae nobis infundantur qualitates, quibus formaliter iusti reddamur; vel quòd solum Christi meritum nobis comparauerit primam gratiam, & ante remissionem peccatorum nullius hominis opus sit meritorium, vti explicat Costerus in Enchirid. m. p. 260.

LXXVI. Sed meritò se opponunt Orthodoxi, cum quibus & nos statuimus, Christum minus rectè ab efficientia iustificationis excludi, & falsò instrumentalem duntaxat causam appellari. Scriptura quidem Christum vocat seruum & ministrum Matth. 20. v. 28. Hebr. 5. v. 7. & in specie ministrum circumcisionis vel circumcisorum, Rom. 15. v. 8. Hoc autem ministerium non tollit propriam salutis efficientiam. Christus enim ministrando & nobis inseruiendo salutem verè operatus est: vnde patet, quòd per illud ministerium, non modus causandi, sed finis incarnationis denotetur. Venit enim Christus ad ministrandum nobis, hoc est, ad salutem perditam iterum recuperandam.

LXXVII. Neque officit, quòd Patres humanitatem quandoq; instrumentum diuinitatis dixerunt. Non enim quærimus de humanitate Christi, ad diuinitatem collata, sed de toto Christo ratione justificationis, an verè statuatur, Christum nil nisi instrumentum esse & causam ministerialem nostræ justitiæ, non verò propriè efficientem? Hoc à Patribus affirmatum non est; Et si affirmavetur, foret nihilominus falsissimum, Christus enim est author vitæ, est Christianorum Dominus, est Iehoua iustificatio nostra: Qui ergò iustificationis tantùm esset instrumentum? Ipse carnem suam dedit pro mundi vita, Ioh. 6. vers. 51. Eius sanguis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. 26. vers. 28. & emundat nos ab omni peccato, 1. Iohan. 1. v. 7. Nec vllum est nomen aliud, in in quo Deo placere & salui esse possumus, Actor. 4. v. 12. Quæ omnia luculentum testimonium præbent, CHRISTVM iustificationis efficientem esse propriè dictam.

LXXVIII. Diffiteri autem non possumus, à Theologis diuersos adhiberi modos loquendi. Sunt, qui Patrem dicunt causam imperantem, Filium exequentem, quia Pater mittit, Filius mittitur. Verùm hoc pacto discrimen quidem personarum & operationum innuitur, sed non ipse causandi modus exprimitur. Quidam Christum impellentem potiùs, causam nominant, quàm efficientem. Pater enim per intuitum meriti impellitur, vt nos in gratiam recipiat & iustificet. At non censemus hæc esse contraria, cùm vtrumque de Christo affirmari queat. Nam consideratur dupliciter, 1. In respectu ad Patrem, quem suo merito mouet ad iustificandum; Et hoc sensu causa impellens rectè dicitur. 2. In relatione ad iustitiam, quam acquisiuit, nobisque applicat: & hoc respectu causa efficiens nuncupari tum potest tum debet. Qui enim iustitiam reparauit, & reparatam efficaciter confert, cur non iustitiæ causa efficiens diceretur? Distinguimus verò, inter causam iustificationis generalem vel communem, & specialem vel propriam. Illa est gratia Dei, hæc obedientia Christi, quippe qui passione suâ expiauit peccata nostra, & veram iustitiam reparauit.

LXXIX. Quæ omnia vt rectius intelligantur & breuius proponantur, notandum est, Christum tripliciter iustificationis nostræ causam esse & nuncupari posse. 1. Merito, quia gratiam Patris promeruit, illi nos vicissim reconciliauit, & peccata quæuis abstulit, iuxta dicta, Rom. 4. v. vlt. 1. Corinth. 15. vers. 3. 2. Efficaciâ: Non enim ob id præstitum est Christi meritum, vt nostræ vel aliorum pro nobis satisfactiones fiant meritoriæ, siquidem obedientia eius sola est & sufficiens expiatio pro peccatis nostris, 1. Ioh. 1. v. 7. 1. Ioh. 2. vers. 2. 1. Pet. 1. v. 19. nullo egens additamento vel appendice nostrorum operum, quæ proptereà è negotio salutis prorsus excluduntur, Rom. 3. 4. 11. Gal. 3. Ephes. 2. 3. Applicatione. Christus enim non modò iustitiam acquisiuit, sed insuper acquisitam applicat, vt nullâ re aliâ simus iusti, quàm solâ eius obedientiâ nobis imputata. Hinc dicitur iustitia nostra. Ierem. 23. v. 6. in quo sunt nostræ iustitiæ, Esai. 45. v. 24. factus à Deo iustitia, 1. Corinth. 1. v. 30. vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso, 2. Corinth. 5. v. vlt.

LXXX. Ex triplici hoc respectu triplex causandi modus profluit, ideoque Christus rectè indigitari potest, 1. Causa impellens, ob meritum, quo mouetur Pater. 2. Causa efficiens, ob efficaciam, quâ iustitia est acquisita. 3. Causa formalis, ob applicationem, quatenus meritum ipse suum nobis applicat, quæ meriti applicatio & imputatio causa formalis est. Nam propter Christi meritum fide apprehensum, nobisque imputatum, formaliter iusti sumus coram Deo, vt ita nullum sit absurdum, Christum eiusque meritum ad diuersa causarum genera reuocare. Declarari hoc potest similitudine quadam, à solutione alieni debiti petita. Quatenus ea respectu soluentis, non debitoris æstimatur, causa efficiens est, ob quam debitor absoluitur, & conueniri nequit: quatenus verò solutio ista aliena debitori, ac si esset propria, imputatur, hoc sensu causa formalis est, quæ ipsum τὸ ἄναι largitur iustificationi & absolutioni forensi.


### Question II. & XI

LXXXI. There were two evils; one of guilt, which man had unjustly committed; the other of punishment, which man was justly about to suffer. Each has its remedy in Christ; guilt was expiated through active obedience, punishment was removed through passive. Both therefore are necessary, both are meritorious, if only we wish to be freed from all evils through Christ. And as regards passive obedience, that it was meritorious and done for our sake is most manifest from the clearest testimonies of Scripture. For hence it is said 1 Pet. 1, verses 21 and 24, Christ suffered for sins. 1 Cor. 15, verse 3, Died for sins. Rom. 5, verse 6, Died for the ungodly. Rom. 4, last verse, Died for our sins, rose for our righteousness. 1 John 2, verse 2, and 4, verse 10, Christ is the propitiation for our sins, and also for the whole world, all of which will be proved more fully in the following disputation. But as regards active obedience, a controversy is raised by some, especially by Piscator of Herborn, when they dispute that it does not pertain to the merit and satisfaction of Christ for us, but is only required for the excellence and perfection of the person satisfying for us, which had to be most holy, so that it would be fit and suitable for undertaking such an office.

LXXXII. But this reasoning is entirely ineffective. It is indeed certain that the person of the Mediator had to be most holy. Heb. 7, verse 26. For nothing defiled can cleanse others from iniquity, Heb. 7, verse 27. But what this holiness of the person is, is expressed in Luke 1, verse 35: The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore that which will be born of you will be called holy, the Son of God. From this it is concluded that that mass of human nature in the Virgin Mary was purified and sanctified by the Holy Spirit, so that it could be hypostatically united to the Son of God, and be suitable for the office of redemption. But if, for the constitution of the person, besides this habitual holiness, an actual one were also required, which is the holy obedience to be rendered to the law, it would follow that more than thirty years were consumed in constituting the person of the Mediator; for that obedience lasted until the very death of the cross. From which it would further follow that Christ had performed the office of Mediator before his person was fully constituted, for in his very infancy he performed the parts of a Mediator.

LXXXIII. Therefore it should rather be established that in the one person of Christ there are two natures: Divine and human. The Divine is not only just and holy, but rather is itself essential holiness. The human, however, is just and holy because it was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born without any sin. This justice and this holiness are required for the ἱκανότητα [sufficiency] of the person of the Mediator, and the statement in Heb. 7, verse 26 speaks of this, and by that holiness Christ, our Mediator, is holy to himself. But there is still another justice of Christ, which is defined as the most perfect fulfillment of the divine law, and most absolute obedience, concerning which Rom. 5. v. 19. Galat. 4, verse 4. This very thing indeed concurs with the nature of merit, and can by no means be excluded from it. For we had committed sins, and therefore we ought to have suffered; moreover, we did not perform obedience, and therefore we still owed that to God. But both were required for our righteousness. For he is not righteous who pays the penalty of his injustice, but he who satisfies the law. Therefore, so that perfect righteousness might be acquired for us, it was necessary that Christ not only undergo the penalty for the evils which we had done, but also that by his obedience he satisfy for the good things which we had not done. For God requires both, not only the penalty for the evil act committed, but also the perfect fulfillment of his law. Christ therefore satisfied for our guilt by acting, and for the penalty by dying. And although Christ is said to have suffered and died even for our sins, this is not to be understood otherwise than concerning the guilt. For the things which have been done, Christ could not render undone, yet he could very well take away the penalty and the guilt. And this is to die for the sin of someone, when the penalty owed to the sin is expiated by death. But because the removal of the penalty does not yet make one righteous, but the perfect observance of the law is required besides, which is impossible for us, it is necessary that we say that Christ also accomplished this for our sake. Thus, therefore, by acting he took away the guilt, by suffering he took away the penalty.

Latin:

LXXXI. Duo erant mala; vnum culpæ, quod homo iniustè commiserat; alterum pœnæ, quod homo iustè perpessurus erat, Vtrumque suum in Christo habet remedium; Expiata fuit culpa per obedientiam actiuam, sublata pœna per passiuam. Vtraque ergò necessaria, vtraq; meritoria, si modò ab omnibus malis per Christum liberari voluerimus. Et quod attinet obedientiam passiuam, illam fuisse meritoriam & nostri causâ factam, manifestissimü est ex clarissimis Scripturæ testimonijs. Hinc enim dicitur 1. Pet. 1. vers. 21. & 24. Christus passus est pro peccatis. 1. Corinth. 15. vers. 3. Mortuus pro peccatis. Rom. 5. vers. 6. Mortuus pro impijs Rom. 4 vers. vlt. Mortuus propter peccata nostra, resurrexit propter iustitiam nostram. 1. Iohan. 2. vers. 2. & 4. vers. 10 Christus est propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, atiendq; totius mundi, quæ omnia sequenti disputatione probabuntur fusiùs. Quod verò actiuam spectat obedientiam, mouetur à nonnullis, Piscatore præsertim Herbornensi controuersia dum disputant, eam non pertinere ad Christi meritum & satisfactionem pro nobis, sed tantùm requiri ad personæ pro nobis satisfaciētis præstantiam & perfectionem, quam sanctissimam esse oportuit, vt apta & idonea esset ad subeundum tantum officium.

LXXXII. Verùm ratio hæc prorsus est inefficax. Id quidem certum, Mediatoris personam oportuisse esse sanctissimam. Hebr. 7. ver. 26 Nihil enim inquinatum potest alios ab iniquitate purgare, Heb. 7. ver. 27. Hæc verò personæ sanctitas qualis sit exprimitur Luc. 1. vers. 35. Spiritus sanctus superueniet in te, & virtus altissimi obumbrabit te, propterea id, quod nascetur ex te sanctum vocabitur Filius Dei. Vnde concluditur, massam illam humanæ naturæ in virgine Maria à Spiritu sancto purgatam & sanctificatam fuisse, vt vniri hypostaticè Filio Dei posset, & esset idonea ad officium redemtionis. Si verò ad personæ constitutionem, præter sanctitatem hanc habitualem requireretur etiam actualis, quæ est sancta obedientia legi præstanda, sequeretur, plures triginta annos in constituenda persona Mediatoris consumtos fuisse; ad ipsam enim mortem crucis obedientia illa durauit. Vndè porrò sequeretur, officio Mediatoris Christum esse perfunctum, antequam persona eius plenè constitueretur, in ipsa enim infantia Mediatoris partes peregit.

LXXXIII. Proinde sic potius statuendum, quòd in vna Christi persona duæ sint naturæ. Divina & humana. Divina non tantum iusta & sancta est, sed ipsa potius essentialis sanctitas. Humana verò iusta & sancta est, quia à Spiritu sancto concepta & absque omni peccato nata. Hæc iustitia & hæc sanctitas requiritur ad personæ Mediatoris ἱκανότητα, & de hac loquitur dictum Hebr. 7. ver. 26. eaque sanctitate sibi sanctus est Christus, Mediator noster. Est verò alia adhuc Christi justitia, quæ definitur perfectissima legis divinæ impletione, & obedientiâ absolutissimâ, de qua Rom. 5. v. 19. Galat. 4, versu 4. Hæc ipsa verò ad rationem meriti concurrit, & ab hoc secludi nequaquam potest. Nos enim peccata commiseramus, ideoque pati debebamus, nos insuper obedientiam non præstitimus, ideoque illam Deo adhuc debebamus. Vtrumque verò requirebatur ad nostram iustitiam, Nam iustus non est, qui luit pœnam suæ iniustitiæ, sed qui legi satisfacit. Igitur, vt perfecta nobis acquireretur justitia, opus erat, vt Christus non tantùm subiret pœnam pro malis quæ feceramus, sed etiam vt obedientiâ suâ satisfaceret probonis, quæ non feceramus. Vtrumque enim requirit Deus, non solùm pœnam pro commisso actu malo, sed etiam perfectam suæ legis adimpletionem. Satisfecit igitur Christus pro culpa nostra agendo, pro pœna moriendo. Et quamvis Christus pro peccatis etiam nostris dicatur passus & mortuus, non tamen id aliter, quàm de reatu est intelligendum. Quæ enim facta sunt, Christus infecta reddere non poterat, pœnam tamen & reatum optimè auferre poterat. Atque hoc est mori pro peccato alicuius, quando pœna peccato debita, morte expiatur. Quia vero sublatio pœnæ nondum facit iustum, sed requiritur præterea perfecta legis observatio, quæ nobis impossibilis, necesse est, vt dicamus, & hoc Christum nostri causâ expediisse. Ita igitur agendo culpam, patiendo pœnam sustulit.


### Question II. & XI: LXXIV. But in order that we may fortify our opinion with SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE, we wish…

LXXIV.

But in order that we may fortify our opinion with SAYINGS OF SCRIPTURE, we wish the following Sayings to be noted in the first place: 1. Romans 5, verses 18, 19. As by the offense of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation, even so by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification of life. For as by the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so also by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. But by the word obedience, the death and passion of Christ cannot be understood. 1. Because to obey properly denotes a certain action conformable to the law, 2. Because it is called the righteousness of Christ, but this cannot be said of the passion. For while that indeed becomes our righteousness, pro- of Christ. 3. The antithesis does not admit this. For just as by the disobedience of Adam is understood ἀνομία; so by the obedience of Christ nothing else can be understood than an action conformable to the law.

LXXXV. II. Matt. 5. v. 17, 18. I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill. The discourse is about the moral law, as the text indicates. Hence we gather: Christ came into the world that he might fulfill the moral law. But he did not come in vain, nor for his own sake, but for our sake, Heb. 10. v. 7, 10. Ps. 40. v. 10. Therefore he also fulfilled the law for our sake. For that he did not come to fulfill the law for himself is evident, 1. For he would become a servant and debtor of the law, who is the Lord of the same. 2. To obey the law and to fulfill it is a part of an office. But Christ neither undertook an office for himself, nor does he perform it for himself. 3. It would follow that the Word himself, who in human nature and through it rendered obedience to the law, also fulfilled the law for his own sake, and was subject to it by obligation. Furthermore, that is also false, that Christ by active obedience merited anything for himself. For 1. he himself was Lord of all. 2. The participation of majesty was a consequence of the union. But the particle in Philip. 2. v. 9, 'therefore,' is to be taken not in an etiological sense, but in an ecbatic sense.

LXXXVI. III. Galat. 4. v. 4 & 5. When the fullness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, to redeem them that were under the law. In whatever way, therefore, we were under the law, in that same way Christ also was made under the law. But we were under the law, not only by reason of the curse and of punishments, but also by reason of obedience. Therefore Christ also, that he might redeem us, was made under the law not only by reason of the curse and of punishments, but also by reason of obedience.

LXXXVII. IV. Romans 10, verse 4. CHRIST is the perfection of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. But Christ is called the end and perfection of the law, because he perfectly fulfilled it, which fulfillment is imputed for righteousness to every one that believeth. Nor can it be proved that the Apostle speaks only of the ceremonial law and its fulfillment. For the Apostle speaks chiefly of the moral law, from which the Jews sought the praise of righteousness, but in vain, because they spurned him who acquired for us the perfect righteousness by the fulfillment of the law.

LXXXVIII. V. Romans 8, verses 3, 4. For what was impossible to the law, in that it was weak through the flesh, GOD sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh, that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us. Whence we weave such an argument: the Son of GOD sent performed the το ἀδύνατον of the law. But the obedience of the law is that ἀδυνατον. Therefore Christ performed the obedience. Furthermore, what the Son of GOD sent performed, that was done for our sake. He performed the obedience of the law. Therefore for our sake: which was the thing to be proved.

LXXXIX. VI. 2 Corinthians 5, verse 21. Him, who knew no sin, he made sin, that we might be made the righteousness of GOD in him. In whatever way, therefore, Christ was made sin for us, in the same way we also are made righteousness in Christ: but Christ was made sin, because our sins were imputed to him. Therefore we also are made righteousness through the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. And because the sin which is imputed to Christ is the actual, total, and perfect transgression of the law, certainly by force of opposition, the righteousness of Christ, which is imputed to us, will be likewise the actual, total, and perfect fulfillment of the law. The same can be concluded from that 1 Corinthians 1, verse 30. CHRIST was made for us by GOD righteousness, holiness, and redemption.

XC. VII. Psalm 40, v. 10. Heb. 10, v. 7. 9. 10, Then I said: Behold I come (in the head of the book it is written of me) that I may do, O GOD, thy will, willing, and thy law in the midst of my heart. In which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once. In this saying the Apostle expressly joins the obedience of Christ according to the most holy law and will of the Father, with his offering for our sanctification, that is, justification.

XCI. Besides the sayings of Scripture, REASONS can be brought forward confirming the same, of which three are principal. 1. From the Absurdities: If the price of redemption is only the death of Christ, there will be excluded from the same, 1. The remaining sufferings; for he suffered thirst, hunger, insults, etc. 2. The resurrection, against the saying of Rom. 4, last verse. 3. The victory of Christ, which nevertheless likewise pertains to our total resurrection. For through it we have been freed from the power of hell and the devil. 4. The divine operations, from which nevertheless the sufferings have all their preciousness, power, and efficacy, which if you take away from the merit of Christ, you take away all merit. For human sufferings would not have been meritorious, unless aided by divine actions

XCII. From the perfection of righteousness. Perfect righteousness is not only to suffer punishments for sin, but also to satisfy the law by fulfilling it. For he is not just who pays the penalty of injustice, but he who either satisfies the law himself, or apprehends the satisfaction of another. But the righteousness of Christ, which he has procured for us, is indeed perfect righteousness. Therefore it includes the fulfillment of the law at the same time. And since GOD requires the most perfect obedience in his law from us, which we cannot perform on account of the flesh, Rom. 8, v. 3, from where does that come to us. For if from

if we do not have it in Christ, what is there in the whole universe that can give it to us? Likewise; how does it happen that the imperfect obedience of the pious is pleasing to God? Is it not for this reason, that our imperfections are governed by the supreme perfection of Christ's obedience?

XCIII. III. On the condition of active obedience. Whatever is truly and properly an effect of the person of the Mediator already constituted, that neither ought nor can be called a part constituting that person, or a quality pertaining to the constitution of his person. But the active obedience of Christ is truly an effect of the person of the Mediator already constituted, as is evident from Rom. 5:19, Gal. 4:4, Rom. 10:4. Therefore it ought not to be named a quality pertaining to the constitution of the person. Many testimonies of the Fathers could be added, but since Mr. Dr. Gerhard has reviewed them in Vol. 3, L.C.C., p. 1111, we wish to dispense with that labor.

XCIV. Nothing else now remains but that we should resolve one or another of Piscator's objections. Thus, therefore, he argues: 1. Every man is a debtor to the law, Christ is a man. Therefore, also by reason of his person, he was a debtor to the law. Resp. There are four terms in the argument, for the major speaks of a mere man, but the minor of the God-man, who for that reason is without controversy superior to every law. And because in performing this obedience, the human nature of Jesus does not act by itself, but the whole person, God and man; hence it cannot happen that you can place the humanity under the debt of the law, unless you also place God himself as subject to the law by debt, which is absurd. He insists: If Christ was not subject to the law, was it therefore lawful for him to resist the warnings of his parents against the fourth commandment, or to violate other mandates of the Decalogue? But our people respond; That Christ was subject to his parents according to the law, the whole order of nature is reversed in this matter, since it is against nature that the creator should obey his own creature, and that the Son of God should be subject to those whom he himself made and created. Therefore, if Christ had not submitted himself to this obedience of his parents, he would not have sinned, nor would he have done anything here against the law, but just as he was superior to the law; he would have acted above the law, which he also sometimes indicated not obscurely to his parents, as in Luke 2, v. 49 and John 2, v. 4. As for the other point, it does not follow from our assertion that it was lawful for Christ to swear falsely or to bear false witness, far be it; nor yet can or should it be concluded from that, that he was under the law for that reason, otherwise the same would have to be said of the Father and the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as the Father and the Holy Spirit abstain from sins not by any prescription of the law, but by the condition and perfection of their own nature, so it must be determined concerning Christ. And let it be noted here that there are two kinds of sins: some are evil in themselves, which always conflict with the nature of God, and these God does not admit, nor indeed can he admit, unless he were to deny himself; some are sins only by reason of an external command, such as the eating of swine's flesh, etc., which actions do not conflict with the nature or will of God simply, and therefore can be done rightly.

XCV. 2. If the active obedience of Christ's life is imputed to us for righteousness, there was no need for Christ to die for us.

Response. There is no consequence, for active obedience does not remove passive obedience, nor does the latter remove the former, but both are required; God must be perfectly satisfied. Both are perfect in their own kind, but neither one alone perfectly satisfies God, for God required not only the penalty from us, but also the perfect fulfillment of his law. He objects: if the law is fulfilled, no guilt remained. Therefore, neither did the penalty, and so there was no need for passive obedience. Response: distinguish between sins of commission and omission.

We were bound to undergo punishment on account of committed sins; Christ also underwent this while he was suffering: but the obedience which we had omitted; the law moreover demanded from us, and therefore there was need of the active obedience of Christ.

XCVI. 3. The law obliges either to punishment or to obedience, but not to both. If therefore Christ underwent punishment for us, there was no need to perform obedience in our place.

I answer: The antecedent is true concerning the state of integrity, false concerning the state of the fall and corruption. There, indeed, the law obliges only to obedience, not to punishment, because where there is no transgression, there punishment finds no place: here, however, it obliges to both: to obedience, by the right of creation; to punishment, on account of the fall and the transgression of the divine command.

XCVII. 4. Christ by one offering has perfected those who are being sanctified, Heb. 10. v. 14. Therefore the active obedience of Christ is not required.

I answer: 1. The Apostle does not tear apart, but joins both kinds of obedience, as is evident from verse 10. 2. He did not intend to describe every reason for merit, but only the completion and consummation, which we do not deny was accomplished in the death of Christ, according to John 19. verse 30. 3. The word μιᾶς is not opposed to the fulfillment of the law, but to the plurality and frequent repetition of the Levitical offerings, by which being excluded in the New Testament, we are said to be sanctified through the one and only immolation of Christ on the altar of the cross.

XCVIII. Whoever desires a specific answer to the remaining objections should consult and read the booklet of Mr. Dr. Eckard written specifically on this question. We break off here, and reserve what remains to be said about the merit of Christ for the following disputations, giving thanks to God the Father, that in the fullness of time He sent His Son, made under the law, that He might redeem those who were under the law, and that we might receive the adoption of sons; to Him alone and the merciful God be praise and thanksgiving everlasting, AMEN.

Latin:

LXXIV.

Vt autem sententiam nostram SCRIPTVRÆ DICTIS muniamus, sequentia Dicta cum primis notari volumus 1. Roman. 5. versu 18. 19. Sicut per vnius delictum in omnes homines in condemnationem, sic & per vnius iustitiam in omnes homines in iustificationem vitæ. Si ut enim per inobedientiam vnius hominis, peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita & per vnius obedientiam iusti constituentur multi.
