Vocabulo autem obedientiæ mors & passio Christi nequit intelligi. 1. Quia obedire propriè notat quandam actionem legi conformem, 2. Quia vocatur iustitia Christi, hoc autem de passione dici nequit. Nam illa quidem sit nostra iustitia, propriè tamen Christi iustitia dici nequit. 3. Antithesis hoc non admittit. Sicut enim per inobedientiam Adami intelligitur ἀνομία; ita per obedientiam Christi non potest aliud quàm actio legi conformis intelligi.

LXXXV. II. Matth. 5. v. 17 18. Non veni soluere legem, sed adimplere. De lege morali sermo est, vt textus indicat. Hinc colligimus : Venit Christus in mundum, vt impleret legem moralem. Non autem frustrà, nec sui, sed nostri causâ venit, Hebr. 10. vers. 7. 10. Psal. 40. vers. 10. Ergò etiam nostri causâ legem impleuit. Quod enim non venit legem implere pro se, patet, 1. Fieret enim seruus & debitor legis, qui est Dominus eiusdem. 2. Obedire legi eamque implere est pars officij. Pro se autem Christus officium neque suscepit, neque eo perfungitur. 3. Sequeretur, ipsum λόγον, qui in humana natura & per illam obsequium legi exsoluit, sui etiam causâ legem adimpleuisse, eique subiectum esse ex debito. Porrò & illud falsum est, quòd Christus obedientia actiuâ sibi ipsi aliquid promeruerit. Nam 1. ipse erat Dominus omniũ. 2. Participatio maiestatis erat consequens vnionis. Particula verò Philip 2. vers. 9. propterea non ἀιτιολογικῶς, sed ἐκβατικῶς accipienda est.

LXXXVI. III. Galat. 4. v. 4. & 5. Vbi venį splenitudo temporis, misit Devs Filium suum, factum ex muliere, factum sub lege, vt eos, qui sub lege erant redimeret. Quo igitur modo nos eramus ὑπονόμον, eo modo etiam Christus factus est ὑπο νόμον. Atqui nos eramus ὑπο νόμον, non tantùm maledictionis & poenarum, sed obedientiæ etiam ratione. Ergo etiam Christus, vt nos redimeret non tantùm maledictionis & pœnarum, sed obedientiæ etiam ratione factus est ὑπο νόμον.

LXXXVII. IV. Roman. 10. vers. 4. CHRISTVS est perfectio legis ad iustitiam omni credenti. Dicitur verò Christus finis & perfectio legis, quia illam perfectè impleuit, quæ impletio ad iustitiam imputatur omni credenti. Neque probari potest, quod Apostolus tantùm loquatur de lege ceremoniali & eius complemento. Nam Apostolus præcipuè loquitur de morali, ex qua Iudęi captabant laudem iustitię, sed frustrâ, quia spernebant eum, qui iustitiam perfectam legis impletione nobis acquisiuit.

LXXXVIII. V. Roman. 8. vers. 3. 4. Quod impossibile erat legi, in qua infirmabatur per carnem, DEVS mittens Filium suum in similitudine carnis peccati, de peccato damnavit peccatum in carne, vt iustificatio legis impleretur in nobis. Vnde argumentum tale nectimus: το ἀδύνατον legis præstitit missus DEI Filis. At verò obedientia legis est ἀδυνατον illud. Ergò Christus obedientiam pręstitit. Porrò, quod missus DEI Filius præstitit, id nostri causâ factum est. Obedientiam legis præstitit. Ergò nostri causâ: id quod erat probandum.

LXXXIX. VI. 2. Corinth. 5. vers. 21. Eum, qui non nouit peccatum, fecit peccatum, vt nos efficeremur iustitia DEI in ipso. Quo igitur modo Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum, eodem & nos in Christo efficimur iustitia: Christus autem factus est peccatum, quia illi peccata nostra imputabantur. Ergò & nos efficimur iustitia per imputationem iustitiæ Christi. Et quia peccatum, quod Christo imputatur, est actualis, totalis & perfecta transgressio legis, vtique vi oppositionis, iustitia Christi, quæ nobis imputatur, erit similiter actualis, totalis & perfecta impletio legis. Idem concludi potest ex illo 1. Corinth. 1, versu 30. CHRISTVS factus est nobis a DEO iustitia sanctitas & redemtio.

XC. VII. Psal. 40. v. 10. Heb. 10, v. 7. 9. 10, Tunc dixi: Ecce venio (in capite libri scriptum est de me) vt faciam DEVS voluntatem tuam volens & legem tuam in medio cordis mei, In qua voluntate sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel. In hoc dicto Apostolus expresse obedientiam Christi juxta legem & voluntatem Patris sanctissima, ejus oblatione conjungit ad nostri sanctificationem, id est, justificationem.

XCI. Præter dicta Scripturæ adduci possunt RATIONES idem confirmantes, quarum tres sunt præcipuæ. 1. ab Absurdis: Si pretium redemtionis est sola mors Christi, excludentur ab eodem, 1. Reliquæ passiones; passus enim est sitim, famem, conuitia, &c. 2. Resurrectio, contra dičtum Rom. 4. v. vltim. 3. Victoria Christi, quæ tamen itidem ad resurrectionem nostram totalem pertinet. Per eam enim liberati sumus à potestate inferni & diaboli. 4. Operationes diuinæ, à quibus tamen passiones omnem suam habent pretiositatem, virtutem & efficaciam, quas si sustuleris à merito Christi, omne meritum sustuleris. Passiones enim humanæ meritoriæ non fuissent, nisi actionibus diuinæ adiutæ

XCII. A perfectione iustitiæ. Iustitia perfecta est non tantùm pati pœnas propter peccatum, sed satis facere quoque legi eam implendo. Non eiam iustus est, qui iniustitiæ pœnam soluit sed qui legi vel ipse satisfacit, vel alterius satisfactionem apprehendit. Atqui Christi iustitia, quam nobis peperit, est sane iustitia perfecta. Ergò legis impletione simul includit. Et cùm perfectissimam obedientiam in lege sua à nobis requirat DEVS, quam nos ob carnem pręstare non possumus. Rom. 8. v, 3. vndenam nobis illa obvenit. Nam si ex

Christo eam non habemus, quid est in tota rerum vniuersitate, quod dare eam nobis possit? Item; quî fit, vt inchoata piorum obedientia D E o placeat? Annòn ideò, quia imperfectiones nostræ summâ Christi obedientiæ perfectione reguntur?

XCIII. III. A conditione actiua obedientia. Quicquid est verè & propriè effectum personæ Mediatoris iam constitutæ, illud non debet nec potest appellari pars eam personam constituens, siuè qualitas ad eius personæ constitutionem pertinens. Atqui actiua obedientia Christi est verè effectum personæ Mediatoris iam constitutæ, vt patet ex Rom. 5. v. 19. Galat. 4. v. 4 Rom. 10 v. 4. Ergò non debet nuncupari qualitas ad constitutionem personæ pertinens. Addi possent multa Patrum testimonia, sed cum illa Dn. D. Gerhardus recensuerit T. 3 LL. C C. p. 1111. operâ illâ supersedere volumus.

XCIV. Nihil verò iam aliud restat, quàm vt vnam alteramvè Piscatoris obiectionem diluamus. Sic ergò colligit: 1. Omnis homo est debitor legis, Christus est homo. Ergò etiam ratione personæ suæ fuit debitor legis. Resp. sunt quatuor termini in argumento, Maior enim loquitur de ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ minor autem de θεανθρώπῳ, qui ob id omni lege sine controuersia est superior, Et quia in ista obedientia præstanda, non natura Iesu humana per se agit, sed tota persona, Deus & homo; hinc fieri nequit, vt humanitatem, sub debito legis possis statuere, nisi & Deum ipsum legi ex debito subiectum statuas, quod absurdum. Instat: Si Christus legi non fuit subiectus, annè ergò licuit ipsi contra quartum Præceptum monitis parentum refragari, vel alia mandata Decalogi violare? Respondent verò nostri; Quod Christus secundum legem subditus fuit parentibus, inversus est hac in retotus naturæ ordo, siquidem contra naturam est, vt creator propriæ suæ creaturæ obtemperet, & vt Dei Filius ijs sit subditus, quos ipsemet fecit ac condidit. Itaque si huic obsequio, parentum Christus non se submisisset, non peccasset, neque hic fecisset aliquid contra legem, sed quemadmodum superior lege erat; fecisset supra legem, quod etiam nonunquam haud obscure parentibus suis subindicauit, vt Luc. 2, v. 49 Iohan. 2 ver. 4. Alterum quod attinet, non sequitur ex affirmato nostro, Christo licuisse peierare, falsum dicere testimonium, absit hoc; neque tamen inde concludi potest aut debet, quod ob id sub lege fuerit, alioquin idem de Patre & Spiritu sancto dicendum foret. Sicut ergo Pater & Spiritus sanctus a peccatis abstinent non ex quadam legis praescriptione, sed ex naturae suae conditione & perfectione, ita de Christo erit statuendum. Et notetur hic, quod duplicia sint peccata, quaedam per se mala, quae semper pugnant cum natura Dei, & haec Deus non admittit, nec admittere quidem potest, nisi seipsum negare voluerit; quaedam sint peccata ratione externi mandati duntaxat, vt comestio carnis suillae &c. quales actiones non pugnant cum Dei natura vel voluntate simpliciter, ideoque fieri recte possunt.

XCV. 2. Si obedientia vitae Christi actiua nobis imputatur ad iustitiam, non opus fuit Christum pro nobis mori.

Respond. Nulla est consequentia, non enim actiua tollit passivam obedientiam, nec haec illam, sed vtraque requiritur, Deo perfecte debet satisfieri. Vtraque in suo genere perfecta est, sed non alterutra perfecte Deo satisfacit, requirebat enim non solum poenam a nobis Deus, sed & perfectam suae legis adimpletionem. Excipit, si lex est impleta, nulla restabat culpa. Ergo nec poena, ideoq; non opus erat passiva obedientia. Resp. distingue inter peccata commissionis & omissionis.

Poenam debebamus suscipere propter commissa peccata, hanc etiam Christus suscepit dum pateretur: Obedientiam vero quam omiseramus; exigebat insuper à nobis lex, ideoque opus erat actiua Christi obedientia.

XCVI. 3. Lex obligat vel ad pœnam vel ad obedientiam, non autem ad vtrumque. Si igitur Christus pro nobis suscepit pœnam, non opus fuit nostri loco præstare obedientiam.

Respondeo Antecedens verum est de statu integritatis, falsum de statu lapsus & corruptionis. Ibi quidem obligat lex tantùm ad obedientiam, non ad pœnam, quia vbi nulla est transgressio, ibi pœna locum non inuenit: hic autem ad vtrumque obligat ad obedientiam, iure creationis; ad pœnam ob lapsum & mandati diuini transgressionem.

XCVII. 4. Christus vnicâ oblatione consummauit sanctificandos, Heb. 10. v. 14. Ergò obedientia Christi actiua non requiritur.

Resp. 1. Apostolus non discerpit, sed conjungit vtramque obedientiam, vt patet ex vers. 10. 2. Non voluit describere omnem meriti rationem, sed tantùm complementum & consummationem, quam in morte Christi peractam esse, iuxta Iohan. 19. vers. 30. non inficiamur. 3. Vocabulum μιᾶς non opponitur impletioni legis, sed pluralitati & crebræ repetioni Leuiticarum oblationum, quibus in Nouo Testamento exclusis per vnicam solamque Christi in ara crucis immolationem sanctificari dicimur.

XCVIII. Ad reliquas obiectiones peculiare qui desiderat responsum, Dn. D Eckardi libellum de hac quæstione singulariter scriptum consulat & euoluat. Nos hîc abrumpimus, & quæ de Christi merito dicenda restant, disputationibus secuturis reseruamus, gratias agentes Deo Patri, quod in plenitudine temporis misit Filium suum, factum sub lege, vt eos, qui sub lege erant, redimeret, nosque adoptionem filiorum reciperemus; ipsi soli & misericordi Deo sit laus & gratiarum actio sempiterna, AMEN.


## 28 Disputation V. On the Merit and Satisfaction of Christ, Opposed to the Photinians

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Michael Soporinus, a Hungarian.

Thesis I.

The scope of Scripture, of our faith, and of our life is Christ. Whoever therefore teaches falsely concerning Christ and His office, by that same act contemns the authority of Scripture, corrupts the purity of faith, and hinders the holiness of life; and therefore he is a falsifier in the interpretation of the Word, a deceiver in the dissemination of doctrine, and a seducer in the conduct of life. The recent Photinians prove this by their own example, whose doctrine is the sink of all heresies, who with ungrateful and blasphemous mouth utterly enervate the merit of Christ, and simply deny that He has made satisfaction for the sins of the human race.

II. They follow in this, 1. Photinus from the older heretics. He was a native of Lesser Galatia, Bishop of the Church of Sirmium around the year of Christ 345, and because he possessed a certain natural eloquence and power of persuasion, he drew to his opinion, as witnessed by Sozomen, book 4, Ecclesiastical History, chapter 6. He maintained, however, that Christ was a bare and mere man, and consequently did not make satisfaction to God the Father. The Socinians therefore confess that they follow this champion, and when they are numbered with the Arians, they clamor that an injustice is being done to them. Faustus Socinus certainly, in his final response to Andreas Volanus, p. 264, expressly writes that he adheres to the opinion of Paul of Samosata and Photinus concerning the existence of the Son of God. Ostorodus, in the German preface to his Institutes, page 3, when he wished to free his doctrine from the suspicion of Arianism, says: That our doctrine concerning Christ is not Arian can be easily understood from the fact that the Arians at the Council of Sirmium condemned Photinus along with his dogma, whose doctrine regarding Christ, as is clear from the histories, is plainly the same as ours is today. Thus, therefore, that heresiarch Photinus, whom Epiphanius, book 3, volume 1, heresy 71, calls a tiny insect and an earthworm, or an intestine of the earth, trampled underfoot by the authority of Scripture and the truth of the Word of God, was the predecessor and leader of the modern Photinians, to whom someone might not undeservedly shout that saying of Athanasius, Oration 4 against the Arians: ἡ ἀσέβεια ἐκείντινος (φωτίνε) σὺν ὑμῖν ἐςὶν ὥς ἀπόλεσαν.

III. 2. Master Peter Abelard among the more recent ones, or as some call him, Baleardus, who lived around the year of Christ 1140 and completely emptied the price of our redemption, contending: that Christ did not assume flesh in order to free us from the yoke of the Devil. And that the passion of Christ is of no benefit other than as an example of virtues. That Arnold of Brescia and Gilbert, Bishop of Poitiers, agreed with him is witnessed by the Magdeburg Centuries, 12, chapter 5, page 848.

IV. These are those distinguished Fathers of the Socinians, who paved the way for attacking the satisfaction of Christ, and again introduced this diabolical error into the Church. There followed them in our time Michael Servetus, Gentilis, and others whom it is superfluous to mention. Since, however, this error strikes at the throat of all Christianity, and utterly ruins the salutary doctrine of justification, we shall on this occasion, with God, undertake an accurate refutation of it, and we shall defend to the best of our ability the satisfaction and most holy merit of our Savior against the sophistries of our adversaries, intending to treat in this disputation of three questions.

1. On what occasion and for what causes this error of the Photinians began to be interpolated into the Churches? 2. What is the opinion of the Photinians concerning the merit of Christ: and what horrible corruptions in almost all articles follow from this one falsehood. 3. By what principal sayings and testimonies of Scripture the satisfaction of Christ for our sins may be established.

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D.

Resp. Michaële Soporino Hungaro.

Thesis I.

SCopus Scripturae, fidei & vitae nostrae Christus est. Qui igitur falsa docet de Christo, ejusque officio, is vna opera Scripturae authoritatem contemnit, fidei puritatem corrumpit, vitae sanctitatem impedit, ideoque Falsator est in interpretatione verbi, deceptor in disseminatione doctrinae, seductor in conuersatione vitae. Suo hoc exemplo comprobant recentes Photiniani, quorum doctrina omnium haereseon sentina est, qui ingrato & blasphemo ore, meritu Christi prorsus enervant, eumque pro peccatis humani generis satisfecisse simpliciter negant.

II. Sequuntur in hoc, 1. Photinum ex vetustioribus haereticis. Fuit is ex minori Galatia oriundus, Sirmiensis Ecclesiae Episcopus circa annum Christi 345. & quia naturali quadam facundia & persuadendi facultate pollebat, multos ad opinionem suam attraxit, teste Sozomeno. lib. 4. Hist. Eccles. cap. 6 Statuit autem, Christum fuisse nudum merumque hominem, & per consequens Dei Patri non satisfecisse. Hunc ergo πρόμαχον sequi se fatentur Sociniani, & cùm Arianis annumerantur, iniuriam sibi fieri clamitant. Faustus certè Socinus in Responsione ultima ad Andream Volanum p. 264. expressè scribit, se sententiæ Pauli Samosateni & Photini de Filij Dei existentia adhærere, Ostorodus in præfatione Germanica Instit. pag. 3. cum doctrinam suam ab Arianismi suspicione liberare vellet? Quod doctrina nostra, inquit, de Christo non sit Ariana, ex eo facilè intelligi potest, quod Ariani Concilio Sirmiensi Photinum cum suo dogmate damnarunt cuius doctrina quoad Christum, vt ex historiis liquet plane eadem est, quæ hodiè nostra. Sic igitur hæresiarcha iste Photinus, quem Epiphanius lib. 3. tom. 1. hæres. 71. vocat animaculum insectum ac lumbricum, seu terræ intestinum, pede Scripturæ, & Dei verbi veritate conculcatum, antecessor fuit, primipilus recentium Photinianorum, quibus non immeritò acclamet aliquis illud Athanas. Orat. 4. contra Arianos: ἡ ἀσέβεια ἐκείντινος (φωτίνε) σὺν ὑμῖν ἐςὶν ὥς ἀπόλεσαν.

III. 2. Magistrum Petrum Abelardum ex recentioribus, seu vt aliqui eum nuncupant Baleardum, qui vixit circa annum Christi 1140 & pretium redemptionis nostræ prorsus euacuauit, contendens: Christum non assumpsisse carnem, vt nos à iugo Diaboli liberaret. Et passionem Christi nihil prodesse, quam ad exemplum virtutum. Cui adstipulatum fuisse Arnoldum de Brixia, Gilbertum Pictauiensem Episcopum, testatur Centur. Magd. 12. cap. 5. pag. 848.

IV. Hi sunt illi egregij Patres Socinianorum, qui ad oppugnandam Christi satisfactionem straverunt viam, & errorem hunc Diabolicum itetum in Ecclesiam inuexerunt. Secuti sunt eos nostro tempore Michael Seruetus, Gentilis, & alijs quos commemorare superuacaneum est. Cùm verò hic error totius Christianismi iugulum petat, & salutarem de iustificatione doctrinam penitus corruatpat, accuratam illius refutationem hac occasione cū Deo suscipiemus, & Salvatoris nostri satisfactionem, meritumq; sanctissimum contra strophas aduersariorum pro virili vindicabimus, acturi hac disputatione de tribus quæstionibus.

1. Quâ occasione & quib. ex causis error iste Photinianorum in Ecclesijs interpolari cœperit? 2. Quæ sit Photinianorum sententia de Christi merito: & quàm horrendæ corruptelæ in omnibus ferè articulis hanc vnam falsitatem consequantur. 3. Quibus præcipuè dictis & testimonijs Scripturæ satisfactio Christi pro peccatis nostris stabiliri queat.


### Question I. By what occasion the error of the Photinians, denying the satisfaction of Christ, began to be interpolated into the Church

On what occasion the error of the Photinians, who deny the satisfaction of Christ, began to be interpolated into the Church.

V. Besides the occasion which they took from the ancient heretics Photinus and Abelard, six others can be enumerated.

1. The absurd pronouncements of the Scholastics, who gave no small handle for weakening the merit of Christ and denying his satisfaction. Thomas writes in part 3, question 46, article 2: That God can remit sins to man without satisfaction, since He has no superior. Durandus in 4, distinction 15: That Christ, according to the strict rigor of divine justice, could not make satisfaction. Biel in 3, sententiarum, distinction 20, question eleven, writes: The arguments of Anselm in the books, Why God became man, prove nothing, unless they proceed from the divine ordination presupposed, because God could not have created man, could have remitted sin by mere non-imputation, could have been satisfied by another, anyone could have made satisfaction for himself, if the first grace had been given without merit. Thus Tataretus in 4. sent. dist. 15. I say that any sinner whatsoever can make satisfaction for a sin committed, excluding the merit of the Passion of Christ by the absolute power of God, but not by his ordained power; except by the merit of the passion of Christ: These and similar pronouncements the Photinians now urge, and they have nothing more often in their mouths than this, that satisfaction was not necessary, that God remits and does not impute sins out of grace alone. Who therefore does not see from this that those Scholastics were the precursors of the Photinians with their absurd hypotheses?

VI: 2. Certain impious dogmas of the Calvinists. Of this kind are: 1. The absolute decree of predestination. For if men are elected to eternal life by the sole and absolute will of God, there was no need for the merit and satisfaction of Christ. Calvin defends the former in lib. 3. Instit. cap. 22. sect. 11. cap. 23. sect. 1. 5. 7. Beza in the preface to part 2 of the acts, p. 9. Kennecherus in the chain, p. 126. 127. Zanchius lib. 5. de natura Dei cap: 2. p. 739. Wherefore the latter cannot be denied: The consequence is certain, since the causes of election and salvation are the same. If therefore God from eternity elected certain ones out of his will alone, without any regard for apprehended merit, then certainly he will save, or at least will be able to save, those same ones in time, out of his benevolent will alone, without merit. 2. Nestorian locutions concerning the humanity having suffered alone. For the Calvinists write and teach that God has by no means suffered, and if this is said, it must be understood through anti-theosis, that there is given no true and real communication of properties, but that only the human nature of Christ underwent death for us. But if this is so, it follows that the passion of Christ was not satisfactory. For how could the death of mere humanity have been a sufficient ransom for the sins of the whole of the world, by which infinite wrath has been drawn down? 3, The Piscatorian dogma, that Christ performed obedience to the law for himself. If therefore he was a debtor to the Law, how could he merit anything for us? How was his obedience satisfactory? 4. The dogma concerning particular merit. For they maintain that Christ suffered and died for a few elect, not for the sins of the whole human race. Who does not see how much this detracts from the merit of Christ? For in this way all the sayings of Scripture concerning Christ as the Mediator of the world, concerning the propitiation for all sins, etc., are corrupted. Whence afterwards the Photinians take a handle to deny the satisfaction of Christ entirely, which the Calvinists restrict to such a small number. 5. Absurd phrases concerning the remission of sins, that it happens out of a certain absolute goodness and free will of God. For so Calvin, book 2 of the Institutes, chapter 17, section 1. Indeed I confess, if anyone wished to oppose Christ simply and by himself to the judgment of GOD, there would be no place for merit, because there would not be found in man a dignity which could merit GOD. Musculus in his Commonplaces, chapter 3, on justification, p. 267, writes that GOD can forgive sins without satisfaction out of his mere good pleasure. Faustus Socinus urges this concerning Christ, page 224, and there he attacks Calvin from his own principles. These, therefore, are the fruits of the Calvinist dogmas, so that what Neuser the Mahometan said about Arianism, we can very well pronounce about the new Photinianism: He who wishes to avoid Photinianism, let him avoid Calvinism. Certainly experience confirms that most of the Photinians were previously addicted to Calvinism. And since the Calvinists attribute much to the stars, let them consider what Leovitius the mathematician observed, namely, that Calvinism began in Germany under the same constellation as Arianism once did in the time of Constantine the Great. We must therefore be vigilant, lest in a short time this poison spread and the world, with head as it were raised, may marvel that it has so suddenly become Photinian, just as it once quickly degenerated into Arianism.

VII. 3. The denial of the divinity of Christ. Michael Servetus the Spaniard began to attack it even in the time of Luther, in the year of Christ 1532. Valentinus Gentilis, Blandrata, Alciatus, Ochinus, Franciscus Davidis, all of whom labored strenuously in overturning the deity of Christ. From this, what else can follow but the denial of satisfaction? For a mere man cannot pay an ἰσόῤῥοπον λύτρον for sins. Thus, therefore, because the Photinians could not comprehend the mystery of the Trinity and the personal union by their own reason, they therefore refused to believe it. For this is their principle, common with Zwingli, that things incomprehensible are not proposed by God to be believed. But with the divinity of Christ denied, on account of absurd speculations of reason, it follows spontaneously that the satisfaction of Christ must be denied at the same time. Error therefore has brought forth error, and with the person of Christ attacked, his office also began to be undermined.

IIX. 4. The preconceived opinion concerning the righteousness of works. For unless it is established that man is justified and saved by obedience to the Law, they think that all zeal for good works will soon become worthless. Wherefore, so that men may be kept in their duty and be the more stimulated to act well, they judge that the very hope of salvation must be placed in these. This is truly to do evil and to teach falsehood, so that good may come of it. This very thing was once objected to the Apostle, that the law is made void and an opportunity is given for evil actions if we are justified by the merit of Christ alone. But these are carnal thoughts. For both can stand, both the merit of Christ and the zeal for holiness. Since the Photinians do not sufficiently understand this, they therefore deny the latter so that they may obtain the former.

IX. 5. The pretext of divine grace and mercy: For when they read in the Scriptures that God forgives sins freely out of mere mercy, they conclude from this that no satisfaction or payment can be found. For it seems to them contradictory that sins are forgiven freely, and yet forgiven on account of a preceding λύτρον (ransom). Wherefore, in order to defend the grace of God, they denied the merit of Christ, although these things are ὑπάλληλα (subordinate/complementary), not ἐναντία (contrary), and by them the mercy of God is undermined rather than asserted. For in order to obtain the righteousness of works, they extol the powers of free will, and as much as they ascribe to these, they detract from the grace of God. For Augustine said most truly: The patrons of nature become the enemies of grace.

X. 6. Speculations of reason concerning the manner of human intercession and satisfaction. When a man pays in the place of another man, he is bound to pay everything. And yet the judge acquits, not out of grace, but by right. They think, therefore, that the reason for the Lord's λύτρον (ransom) must be similar. But because He did not endure eternal death, since the acquittal is said to be done freely, and thus the requirements of human satisfaction are lacking, they therefore deny it entirely, and thus in this article the Photinian dogma is resolved into no other principle than the judgment of blind reason. For because it does not sufficiently grasp how we are justified by the imputation of another's merit, and yet at the same time freely, for that reason it immediately accuses this orthodox doctrine, which is most firmly founded in the Scriptures, of falsehood.

XI. And these are those pestilential sources of the new Photinianism, from which it easily appears what is to be judged concerning it. It flows, of course, from errors, false opinions, and the dark dictates of reason, whence we conclude that it itself is erroneous and entirely contrary to the Apostolic faith.

Latin:

Quâ occasione error Photinianorum, Christi satisfactionem negantium, in Ecclesia interpolari cœperit.

V. Præter occasionem, quam ex antiquis hæreticis Photino & Abelardo sumpserunt, sex aliæ recenseri possunt.

1. Absurda Scholasticorum pronunciata, qui ad Christi meritum eneruandum, & satisfactionem eius negandum dederunt ansam non exiguam. Thomas scribit parte. 3. quæst. 46. art: 2. Quod Deus possit sine satisfactione homini remittere peccata, cum non habeat aliquem superiorem. Durandus in 4 dict. 15. Quod Christus secundum strictum rigorem iustitiæ diuinæ non potuerit satisfacere. Biel in 3. sentent. distinct. 20. quæst. vndec. scribit. Rationes Anselmi in libris, cur DEVS homo, nihil probant, nisi procedant ex ordinatione diuina præsuppositâ, quia posset Deus hominem nõ condere, posset remittere peccatum per solam nõ imputationem, posset per alium satisfieri, potuisset quislibet pro se satisfacere, si data fuisset prima gratia sine merito. Sic Tataretus in 4. sent. dist. 15. Dico, quòd quis cunque peccator potest satisfacere de peccato commisso, secluso merito Passionis Christi de potentia Dei absoluta, sed non de potentia ordinata; nisi merito passionis Christi: Hæc & similia effata nunc urgent Photiniani, nihilq; sæpius in ore habent, quàm istud, satisfactionem nõ fuisse necessariam, Deum ex sola gratia remittere, & non imputare peccata. Quis ergò hinc non videt Scholasticos istos absurdis suis hypothesibus Photinianorum præcursores fuisse?

VI: 2. Impia quædam Caluinianorum dogmata. Hujusmodi sunt. 1. Absolutum prædestinationis decretum. Si enim solâ & absolutâ Dei voluntate homines sunt electi ad vitam æternam, non opus fuit merito & satisfactione Christi. Prius autem defendit Caluinus li. 3. Instit. cap. 22. sect. 11. cap. 23. sect. 1. 5. 7. Beza in præfat: part 2. ad acta. p. 9. Kennecherus in cathena, p. 126. 127. Zanchius lib. 5. de natura Dei cap: 2. p. 739. Quare posterius negari nequit: Consequentia certa est, quoniam eædem sunt causæ electionis & saluationis. Si ergò Deus ex sola voluntate quosdam ab æterno elegit, omni intuitu meriti apprehensi, vtique & illos in tempore, ex sola voluntate benevolâ, sine merito saluabit vel certè saluare poterit. 2. Nestoriana locutiones de humanitate tantum passa. Scribunt enim Caluiniani & docent, quòd Deus nequaquam sit passus, & si hoc dicatur, per anthiœosin intelligendum esse, nullam dari veram & realem proprietatum xonariar, sed humanam duntaxat natu ram Christi mortem pro nobis subijsse. Quod si ita sits thox sequitur passionem Christi non fuisse satisfactoriam. Qui enim nudæ humanitatis mors sufficiens xúrgov esse potuisset pro peccatis totius mundi, quibus infinita ira est attracta? 3, Dogma Piscatorianum, quod Christus pro seipso legi obedientiam præstiterit. Si ergo Legis debitor fuit, quî aliquid nobis mereri potuit? Quomodo ipsius obedientia fuit satisfactoria? 4. Dogma de particulari merito. Statuunt enim Christum pro paucis electis non pro peccatis totius humani generis passum & mortuum esse. Quo pacto quantum decedat merito Christi quis non videt? Corrumpuntur enim hoc modo omnia Scripturæ dicta de Christo Mediatore mundi, de propitiatione pro peccatis omnibus & c. Vnde postmodum ansam capiunt Photiniani, in totum negandi satisfactionem Christi, quam ad tantam paucitatem restringunt Caluiniani, 5. Absurdæ phrases de remissione peccatorum, quod illa ex absoluta quadam Dei bonitate & libera voluntate contingat. Sic enim Caluinus l. 2. Instit. cap. 17. sect. 1. Equidem fateor, si quis simpliciter & per se Christum opponere vellet iudicio DEI, non fore merito locum, quia non reperiretur in homine dignitas, quæ possit DEVM promereri. Musculus in Locis communibus cap. 3. de iustificatione p. 267. scribit, DEVM sine satisfactione pro nudo beneplacito suo peccata condonare posse. Vrget hoc Faustus Socinus de Christo pag. 224. ibiq́; Caluinum ex pprsiis principijs oppugnat. Hi ergo sunt fructus Caluinianorū dogmatum, vt quod Neuserus Mahumetanus de Arianismo, id nos de nouo Photinianismo optimè pronunciare valeamus: Qui vult vitare Photinianismum, vitet Caluinianismum. Sanè experientia confirmat quòd plerique Photinianorum, prius Caluinisino fuerint addicti. Et quoniam Caluiniani multum tribuunt astris, cogitent quid Leouitius Mathematicus obseruauerit, nimirum, eâdem constellatione Caluinismum in Germania cœpisse, quali Aianismum olim tempore Constantini Magni. Vigilandum igitur, nè breui tempore venenum hoc ferpat, & mundus erecto quasi capite miretur, se tam subitò Photinianum factum esse, vti quondam ad Arianismum celeriter degenerauit.

VII. 3. Diuinitatis Christi abnegatio. Cœpit illam impugnare Michael Seruetus Hispanus adhuc tempore Lutheri, Anno Christi 1532. Valentinus Gentilis, Blandrata, Alciatus, Ochinus, Franciscus Dauidis, qui omnes in euertenda Christi Deitate strenuè laborârunt. Vnde quid aliud sequi potest, quàm abnegatio satisfactionis? Nudus enim homo ἰσόῤῥοπον pro peccatis λύτρον persoluere nequit. Sic ergo quia mysterium Trinitatis & personalis vnionis ratione sua Photiniani comprehendere haud potuerunt, ideò & credere noluerunt. Hoc enim ipsorum principium est, cum Zvinglio commune, à Deo credenda non proponi incomprehensibilia. Negatâ verò diuinitate Christi, ob absurdas rationis speculationes, satisfactionem Christi vnâ negandam esse, vltrò sequitur. Error igitur errorem peperit, & impugnata Christi persona, vnâ & officium eius labefactari cœpit.

IIX. 4. Præconcepta opinio de operum iustitia. Nisi enim statuatur, hominem iustificari & saluari per obedientiam Legis, mox omne bonorum operum studium vilescere existimant. Quocirca, vt homines in officio contineantur, & ad benè agendum eò magis extimulentur, hinc ipfam salutis spem in ijs collocandam esse censent. Hoc verè est malum facere, & falsum docere, vt eveniat bonum. Hoc ipsum & Apostolo olim obiectum fuit legem euacuari, malis actionibus ansam dari, si per solum Christi meritum iustificemur. Sed carnales hæ sunt cogitationes. Vtrumque enim stare potest, & Christi meritum, & sanctitatis studium. Quod cum non satis intelligant Photiniani, idcircò negant istud, vt hoc obtineant.

IX. 5. Prætextus divinæ gratiæ & misericordiæ: Quando enim in Scripturis legunt, Deum peccata condonare gratis ex merâ misericordia, indè colligunt satis factionem & persolutionem nullam invenire posse. Contraria enim ipsis videntur, gratis remitti peccata, & ob præcedens λύτρον remitti. Quare vt defenderent Dei gratiam, negârūt Christi meritum, cum tamen hæc ὑπάλληλα sint, non ἐναντία, & ab ijs misericordia Dei magis labefactetur, quàm asseratur. Vt enim iustitiam operum obtineant, vires liberi arbitrij extollunt, quibus quantum adscribunt, tantùm gratiæ Dei derogant. Verissimè enim dixit Augustinus: Patroni naturæ, fiunt inimici gratiæ.

X. 6. Speculationes rationis de humanæ intercessionis & satisfactionis modo. Homo hominis loco cum soluit, omnia persoluere tenetur. Et tamen iudex absoluit, non ex gratia, sed iure. Putant igitur, similem oportere rationem esse λύτρε Domini. Quia verò mortem æternam non sustinuit, cum absolutio gratis fieri dicatur, adeoque requisita humanę satisfactionis desint, idcircò ipsam prorsus inficiantur, adeoque & in hoc articulo Photinianum dogma in nullum prius principium, quam in cæcę rationis iudicium resoluitur. Quia enim illa non satis capit, quomodo per imputationem alieni meriti, & tamen vnà gratis iustificemur, ob id mox falsitatis arguit orthodoxam hanc, & in Scripturis fundatissimam doctrinam.

XI. Atque hij sunt illi pestilentes fontes noui Photinianismi, vndè quid de ipso judicandum sit, facilè apparet. Nimirum ex erroribus, falsis opinionibus & tenebricoso rationis dictamine fluit, vnde & ipsum erroneum, fideique Apostolicæ prorsus contrarium esse concludimus.


### Question II. What is the opinion of the Phountani [Socinians] concerning the merit of Christ, and how horribly do corruptions in almost all…

XII. Socinus proposes his opinion in part 1 of De Christo Servatore, chapter 1, in these words: I confess, and I consider it to be the orthodox opinion, that Jesus Christ is our Savior for this reason, because he announced to us the way of eternal salvation, confirmed it, and in his own person manifestly showed it both by the example of his life and by rising from the dead. But I affirm that he neither satisfied divine justice, through which we deserve to be condemned for our sins, nor was there any need for satisfaction to be made. He divides this opinion of his in the cited book into certain aphorisms, and attempts to defend them at length, such as: 1. That wrath does not fall upon God, but only goodness and mercy. 2. That God was never angry at the human race, nor alienated from men, even though men had become enemies of God through sin. 3. That for this reason no satisfaction for sins is necessary, since God has decreed to forgive them out of mercy alone without the intervention of merit. 4. That Christ by no means satisfied for us, indeed, he was not even sent to satisfy. 5. That Christ was not God, but only a man and a Prophet; sent to teach the true method of salvation, for which he was afflicted with martyrdom by the Jews just as other Prophets were. 6. That the phrases, that Christ redeemed us and makes us safe, ought to be understood only by reason of his doctrine, example, and the power handed down by God. For because he showed the way of salvation and expressed it by his own example, he is therefore called our Redeemer and Savior.

XIII. Ostorodus has similar things in his German Institution, chapter 36, page 298. So now the question is, whether in justification through Christ, our sins are taken away and abolished through recompense and satisfaction, or rather through forgiveness and pardon? The greatest part holds that this does not happen without recompense and satisfaction: We, however, believe simply through forgiveness or pardon. Catechismus Racouiensis c. 8. p. 254. Why is it necessary that Christ the Savior of his believers should take upon himself such tribulation and death, as they also do? There are two primary reasons for this, just as the LORD Christ is in a special way the Savior of his believers in two ways. FIRST, that he moves them by his example to hold fast to the way of salvation upon which they have stepped. AFTERWARDS, that He is the one who sustains them in all danger and temptation, and finally rescues them from eternal death. Rursus p 261. Is there not another reason why the LORD Jesus died? No, there is no other, even though it is currently believed for the most part in Christendom as if the LORD Christ had earned eternal salvation for us through his death, and had made complete satisfaction for our sins: which understanding is erroneous, full of seduction, and very harmful. From these words it is clear that they utterly deny the merit and satisfaction of Christ, and affirm that it is contrary to the scriptures and right reason; just as Gittichius also writes expressly in the defense of the 4th argument, page 101: That dogma concerning satisfaction, as is clear to anyone looking at the matter seriously, is nothing other than a horrible blasphemy against God.

XIV. Furthermore, the corruptions flowing from this doctrine are very many. For when one absurdity is granted, others follow, says the Philosopher. Thus, because the Photinian dogma concerning the forgiveness of sins without an intervening ransom is absurd, and tears down the very foundation of the faith, therefore the principal articles are together corrupted. For 1. A clearly new method of justification is devised, namely that a man is absolved not on account of the imputed merit of Christ, but out of grace alone, provided, however, that he works well and obeys the commandments of God. 2. Since no one can obey without the faculty of obeying, free will is feigned in man. 3. Since this cannot stand with the corruption of nature, original sin is utterly denied; 4. Because this cannot be done if righteousness and holiness are said to have been concreated in Adam and to be propagated to his descendants, the definition of the divine image, consisting chiefly in righteousness and the holiness of truth, is removed, it is established that man was created mortal, and the likeness of God is placed only in dominion over living creatures. 5. If Baptism is urged as a means of purification and a sign of corruption, they soon begin to doubt, Can water Baptism be proven from the scriptures? For they say that repentance is also called Baptism. Wherefore they deny that infants must necessarily be baptized, and if it be used at all, they claim it is nevertheless merely a ceremony and an external mark distinguishing a Christian from Pagans, instituted especially for those who are converted from Gentilism to Christianity: but not for those who live and are born in the Church. 6. With the efficacy of Baptism enervated, the fruit and salutary effect of the Lord’s Supper falls away at the same time. They do not wish it to be an ὄργανον effectively working and confirming faith in us, but only a memorial of the death and passion of Christ. And these are the principal consequences, to say nothing of very many others, one of which begets another, just as wave pushes wave. But who, hearing and considering these things, would not be struck with amazement? For what can be more monstrous and heretical than to infringe upon the Apostolic mode of justification, to extol the powers of nature with the denial of grace, to deny sin innate in all, [and] to deprave the image of God, and to despoil the most wholesome Sacrament of Baptism and the Supper of all its virtue and efficacy? Other heresies corrupt certain articles, but through this sect the entire faith is attacked, all its foundations are torn up with an utterly impious daring.

XV. Just as they are laborious in depraving the articles of faith, so in defending their own opinion they act as mere Sophists. They employ four stratagems in particular, from which it clearly appears that the Photinian mode of disputing is utterly Sophistical and ἀδιόλογον [non-dialogical]. For 1. They mostly only destroy, rarely do they build up. They indeed make exceptions to our statements, but they cannot establish their own faith. Hence, an argument that is κατασκευαστικόν [constructive] is very rarely heard; only evasions and diabolical perversions of the sayings of Scripture are brought forward. From which follows mere uncertainty and perpetual hesitation. For because they call the clearest testimonies into doubt with various glosses, and cannot evidently confirm them against their own dogmas, from that the mind begins to fluctuate, and knows not what is to be established. Therefore, the end of Photinianism intended by Satan is none other than Epicureanism and the confusion of religions. But we firmly establish that that mode of disputing, from which no certainty, no πληροφορία [full assurance] of mind follows, is Sophistical, not Theological.

XVI. 2. In making exceptions, they examine secondary sayings at length, [and] lightly touch upon the primary ones. For since there is not such force in them to be inserted, (since they are often cited not in the literal sense, but only by application, which was most customary to the Apostles themselves,) and sometimes they rely on the Vulgate version, (from which we rightly argue against the Papists, inasmuch as they solemnly approved it in the Council of Trent,) hence they easily find what to except against. And then they wonderfully agitate our exegeses with doctrine, and cast a cataract before the eyes of the simpler sort, as if all our arguments for proving were ineffective, while meanwhile they themselves know that far different ones are deployed by us in the battle line, to which they cannot even open their mouths, and when they attempt to respond, the fallacy is soon exposed and the Diabolical zeal for perverting is betrayed.

XVII. 3. Most of their instances do not teach what the sense is, but what it could be. For because they do not admit our interpretation due to a preconceived opinion, hence they wish to elicit another sense; which, in order to obtain, 1. they conglomerate innumerable sayings, partly for the sake of ostentation, partly so that the respondent may be led away from the goal and confused, partly so that the simpler-minded may suppose that something of truth underlies it. 2. They seize upon a certain word, which if it has a peculiar sense in another text of Scripture by reason of the adjuncts, they immediately conclude it is similarly used in the saying about which there is controversy. And this fallacy from the particular is most frequent for them: this little word is taken thus in that saying: Wherefore similarly also in the present. We know sophists to argue thus, not sincere and candid theologians. 3. If the words are too clear, they transpose the clauses, they distinguish the text in a new way, they imply certain words, and in other ways they corrupt Scripture, so that they may finally elicit another sense, which no one could dream of even in a fever. This could be demonstrated by various arguments, if reason admitted it at all. But who does not perceive from this that the author of this sect is Satan? If it is permitted to transpose words and change clauses, who could not most easily devise a new heresy and a strange interpretation of any saying? But when these σοφὰ φάρμακα are altogether applied, namely the conglomeration of sayings, the collation of little words, the transposition of clauses and the like, does the sense of Scripture become certainly known from them? Nothing less. Only this sometimes follows after long declamations, that some saying can be otherwise understood: but what the genuine sense is, remains in doubt. The hearer understands that our exegesis is in conformity with the letter of the text; afterwards he hears that, through glosses sought out here and there, it can be explained otherwise, and thus he is dismissed with a scruple and in suspense. This is that artifice of Satan, which he seeks through his Photinian satellites, namely that all authority of Scripture should collapse as if it were ambiguous, so that security may be introduced, and to everyone may be permitted the liberty of believing anything.

XVIII. 4. Finally, if they must come to their own construction, they produce nothing other than certain feeble consequences of reason, for the first and highest principle from which Photinianism arises, and into which it is resolved, is none other than human reason with its rules and speculations. Hence they expressly write that nothing is proposed by God to be believed which cannot be grasped by reason, or which cannot be argued by it to be false. This is that root and origin of all errors. From this maxim they began to deny the principal article of our faith, namely the mystery of the most holy Trinity. For no reason grasps, no mind understands, how one in number can subsist in three really distinct persons, without division or multiplication of essence. Because they could not reach this mystery by reason, they therefore refused to believe it. Having laid this unhappy foundation, soon followed corruptions in other articles as well. For because there are not multiple persons of the Godhead, hence they conclude that Christ was a mere man, not God, nor does he consist of two natures. If he is not God, he could not make satisfaction for us. Wherefore he was sent only to announce the way of salvation and to fulfill the precepts of the law, not to expiate the sins of the world. If no satisfaction was performed for us, certainly we shall not be justified through the imputation of another's merit. Wherefore the justification of man will be nothing other than a gratuitous remission of sins without an intervening ransom. Hence also faith, by which we are justified, according to them is not the apprehension of merit, but a general confidence, by which we believe that God wishes us well, and we obey His precepts. Therefore, whoever has lived piously will obtain salvation; unless he has done so, he will be condemned. But since no one can be justly punished unless that which he ought to have done was in his power, hence they conclude that faith and the fulfillment of the law are placed in our own powers, and that therefore we are endowed with free will. Wherefore there is no original sin, no corruption of nature. Adam, therefore, did not lose the primary gifts through the fall, but only lost dominion over living creatures, in which the reason for the divine image was placed, and introduced the necessity of dying. Wherefore, as he himself afterwards used his free will well, and being obedient to the precepts of God, obtained salvation: so also we, if we do what God wishes to be done by us, and what has been announced through Christ His Prophet, will in like manner be saved. They say that two Sacraments pertain to those precepts, Baptism and the Supper, which are not means conferring faith or grace, but only external ceremonies, by the observation of which we are distinguished from other assemblies, and declare our obedience to God. And this is the sum of the principal chapters of the doctrine which Socinus in his booklets, Ostorod in his institutions, and Smalcius in his Catechism have proposed. Since this doctrine relies on reason alone, and contains nothing that cannot be easily grasped, it is sufficiently clear even from this single fact that it is a human invention, contrary to Scripture and the whole analogy of faith, and built upon uncertain glosses, which is defended by sophistic means, and by which the πληροφωρία of doctrine is changed into mere doubts.

XIX. These things, therefore, having been premised in general concerning the corruptions and sophistry of the Photinians, now in particular to the ve-

Now we make an approach to asserting the doctrine concerning the merit of Christ. Our churches believe, teach, and confess that the eternal God, on account of the fall of the πρωτοπλάστων [first-formed], was indignant at the human race and condemned it to eternal death by the tenor of his threat and the force of justice. But out of grace, in the fullness of time, he sent his only-begotten and co-eternal Son into the world, that he might assume our flesh, and in it satisfy for our sins by acting and suffering. This very thing he also faithfully performed, having been made obedient to the Father even unto the death of the cross: which payment of his, made in our place, is imputed to individual believers, and therefore through that very imputed righteousness of Christ they are justified and obtain forgiveness of sins. The Augsburg Confession briefly sets forth this opinion in article. 3. where these words: Our churches teach that the Word, that is, the Son of God, assumed human nature in the womb of the blessed Virgin Mary, so that there are two natures, divine and human, inseparably joined in the unity of the person, one Christ, truly God and truly man, born of the Virgin Mary, truly suffered, was crucified, died, and was buried: that he might reconcile the Father to us and be a sacrifice, not only for original guilt, but also for all actual sins. And again in the fourth article: They teach that men cannot be justified before God by their own powers or works: but are justified freely on account of Christ through faith, when they believe that they are received into grace and that sins are remitted on account of Christ, who by his death satisfied for our sins. This faith God imputes for righteousness before himself. Rom. 3 & 4. We shall provide proof in the following question that this opinion is indeed conformable to the sacred scriptures and agreeable to Apostolic truth.

Latin:

XII. Socinus opinionem suam parte 1. de Chri sto Seruatore cap. 1. his verbis proponit: Ego confeor, & orthodoxam sententiam esse arbitror, Iesum Christum ideò Seruatorem nostrum esse, quia salutis æternæ viam nobis annunciauit, confirmâvit, & in sua ipsius persona tùm vitæ exemplo, tùm ex mortuis resurgendo manifestè ostenderit. Diuinæ autem iustitiæ per quam peccatores damnari meremur pro peccatis nostris, neque illum satisfecisse, neque vt satis fieret opus fuisse affirmo. Hanc suam sententiam libro allegato in certos aphorismos diuidit, eosque prolixè defendere tentat, quales sunt; 1. Quòd in Deum non cadat ira, sed tantùm bonitas & misericordia. 2. Quòd Deus nunquam fuerit iratus generi humano, nec abalienatus ab hominibus, etsi homines, hostes Dei per peccatum facti fuerint. 3. Quòd propterea nulla satisfactio pro peccatis sit necessaria, quoniam Deus illa, ex sola misericordia sinè interuentu meriti condonare decreuit. 4. Quòd Christus ob id pro nobis minimè satisfecerit, imò nec emissus sit, vt satisfaceret. 5. Quòd Christus non Deus, sed tantùm homo fuerit & Prophetæ; missus vt veram salutis rationem doceret, ob quod martyrjo fuerit affectus à Iudæis sicut & alij Prophetæ. 6. Quòd phrases. Christum nos redemisse, & saluos facere, non nisi ratione doctrinæ, exempli, & traditæ à Deo potestatis intelli gi debeant. Quia enim modum salutis monstrauit, ac suo exemplo expressit, hinc nostrum Redem ptorem, & Saluatorem appellari.

XIII. Similia habet Ostorodus in institutione Germ. c 36. p. 298. So ist nun die Frag/ ob in der Rechtfertigung durch Christum/ vnsere Sünde durch ein vergeltung vnnd gnugthuung/ oder aber durch die vergebung vnd verzeyhung weggethan vund auffgehoben werden? Der meiste theil helt es dafür / dass solches nicht geschehe ohne vergeltung vnd genugthuung: Wir aber gleubẽ schlecht/ durch die vergebung oder verzeyhung. Catechismus Racouiensis c. 8. p. 254. Warumb wie noͤtig/ dass Christus der Seligmacher seiner glaubigen solche Truͤbsal vnd den Todt auff sich nehme / wie auch sie? dessen sind zwo fuͤrnehme Vrsachen / wie auch der HERR Christus seiner glaubigen Seligmacher sonderlich auff zweyerley weise ist. ERSTLICH / dass er sie mit seinem Exempel beweget sich an den Weg der Seligkeit / auff welchen sie getretten / fest zu halten. DARNACH / dass Er der ist / der sie in aller Gefahr vnd versuchung erhelt / vnd endlich von dem ewigen Todt errettet. Rursus p 261. Ist nicht noch eine andere Vrsach / warumb der HERR Jesus gestorben ist? Nein es ist keine andere / ob man gleich ietzt in der Christenheit zum meistentheil meinet / als solt vns der HERR Christus durch seinen Todt die ewige Seligkeit verdienet / vnnd fuͤr vnsere Suͤnde volkomenen genug gethan haben: welcher Verstand irrig voll verfuͤhrung vnd sehr schaͤdlich ist. Ex hisce verbis liquet, quòd meritum & satisfactionem Christi prorsus negent, eamque scripturis & rectæ rationi contrariam esse affirment; Sicut & Gittichius in defensione 4. argumenti pag. 101. expressè scribit: Illud de satisfactione dogma, vt liquet ciuus rem serio intuenti, nihil aliud est, quàm horrenda in Deum blasphemia.

XIV. Cæterùm corruptelæ ex hac doctrina fluentes sunt quàm plurimæ. Nam ἐνὸς ἀτόπω δοθέντος τ᾿ ἄλλα συμβαίνει, vno inconueniente dato, infinita sequuntur, inquit Philosophus. Sic quia Photinianum dogma, de peccatorum venia, sine interueniente λύτρῳ absurdum est, & ipsum fidei fundamentum conuellit, propterea præcipui articuli vnà corrumpuntur. Nam 1. Planè nova iustificationis ratio excogitatur, nempè absolvi hominem non ob imputatum Christi meritum, sed ex sola gratia, si tamen benè operetur, & præceptis Dei obediat. 2. Quoniam nemo obedire potest sine obediendi facultate, liberum in homine arbitrium fingitur. 3. Hoc quoniam stare nequit cum corruptione naturæ, peccatum originis prorsus negatur; 4. Quod cùm fieri nequeat, si Adamo iustitia & sanctitas concreata inque posteros propaganda dicatur, ratio imaginis divinæ præcipuè in iustitia & sanctitate veritatis consistens, tollitur, hominem mortalem fuisse conditum statuitur, & similitudo DEI tantùm in domino super animantia ponitur. 5. Si Baptismus tanquam purgationis medium, & corruptionis signum vigetur, mox dubitare incipiunt, Num ex scripturis aquæ Baptismus probari queat? Nam & pœnitentiam nominari Baptismum. Quare infantes necessariò abluendos esse negant, & si omnino adhibeatur, esse tamen dūtaxat ceremoniā & externam notā Christiano à Paganis distinguentem, pro ijs præcipuè institutam, qui ex Gentilismo ad Christianismū convertūtur: non autem pro illis qui in Ecclesia vivant & nascuntur. 6. Enervatâ Baptismi efficaciâ, simul fructus & salutaris effectus Cœnæ Dominicæ concidit. Non illam esse volunt ὄργανον efficaciter operans & fidem in nobis confirmans, sed tantum memoriale mortis & passionis Christi. Et hæc sunt præcipua consectaria, vt taceam alia quàm plurima quorum alterum gignit alterum, non secus ac vnda trudit vndam. Quis verò hæc audiens & considerans non obstupescat? Quid enim monstrosum & hæreticum magis esse potest, quam Apostolicum justificationis modum infringere, vires naturæ cum abnegatione gratiæ extollere, peccatū omnib⁹ connatū inficiari, imaginē Dei depravare, saluberrimū Baptismi & cœnæ Sacramentum omni virtute suâque efficacia spoliare? Hæreses aliæ quodâ articulos corrūpunt, sed per hanc sectam fides vniuersa petitur, omnia eius fundamenta impio prorsus ausu convelluntur.

XV. Vti verò in depravandis fidei articulis laboriosi sunt, ita in defendenda opinione sua meros Sophistas agunt. Quatuor imprimis adhibent stratagemata, ex quibus luculenter apparet modum disputandi Photinianum prorsus esse Sophisticum & ἀδιόλογον. Nam. 1. Plerumque tantum destruunt, raro extruunt. Ad nostra quidem dicta excipiunt, suam verò fidem stabilire haut queunt. Hinc rarissimè auditur argumentum aliquod xaτασκευαστικόν; proferuntur tantùm elusiones & Diabolicæ perversiones dictorum scripturæ. Ex quo sequitur mera incertitudo & perpetua hæ sitatio. Quia enim clarissima testimonia, variis glossis in dubium vocant, & contra sua dogmata evidenter confirmare nequeunt, inde animus fluctuare incipit, & quid statuendum sit ignorat. Photinianismi igitur finis à Sathana intentus, nullus est alius, quàm Epicureismus & religionum confusio. Nos a. firmiter statuimus, eum disputandi modum, ex quo nulla certitudo, nulla πληροφωρία mentis sequitur, Sophisticum esse, non Theologicum.

XVI. 2. In excipiendo, dicta secundariâ fusè examinant, primaria leuiter tangunt. Quoniam enim illis tantus inserendi nervus non inest, (tùm sæpè non in sensu literali, sed per applicationem tantùm, ipsis Apostolis usitatissimam citentur,) & quandoque versione vulgatâ nituntur, (ex quâ contra Pontificios rectè argumentamur, quippe qui illam solenniter in Concilio Tridentino approbarunt) hinc quod excipiant facilè inveniunt. Atq; tum ἐξηγήσεις nostras cum doctrinâ mirè exagitant, & simplicioribus glaucoma obijciunt, ac si omnia nostra argumenta ad probandum sint inefficacia, cùm interim sciant ipsi, longè alia collocari à nobis in acie, ad quæ nè hiscere quidem possunt, & cùm respondere tentant, mòx patet fallacia & proditur Diabolicum pervertendi studium.

XVII. 3. Pleræque ipsorum instantiæ non docent quis sensus sit, sed quis esse possit. Quia enim nostram interpretationem ex præconceptâ opinione non admittunt, hinc alium sensum elicere volunt; Quod vt obtineant 1. innumerata dicta conglommerant, partim ostentationis ergò, partim vt à scopo abducatur & confundatur respondens, partim vt simpliciores aliquid veri subesse autument. 2. Vocabulum quoddam captant, quod si in alio scripturæ textu pro ratione adiunctorum peculiarem sensum habeat, mox in dicto de quo controvertitur, similiter vsurpari colligunt. Et hic Elenchus à particulari ipsis est frequentissimus: vocula hæc sic accipitur in isto dicto: Quare similiter & in præsenti. Sophistas ita argumentari scimus, non sinceros candidosque Theologos. 3. Si verba sint nimis clara transponunt commata, textum novo modo distinguunt, quasdam voces subintelligunt, aliisque modis scripturam corrumpunt, vt alium tandem sensum, quem quis nè per febrim quidem somniare possit, eliciant. Variis hoc argumentis demonstrari posset, si ratio ὅλως admitteret. Quis verò indè non authorem huius sectæ animaduertit Sathanam? Si verba transponere, commata mutare liceat, quis non hæresin novam, & peregrinam alicuius dicti interpretationem excogitare quàm facillimè posset? Quando verò omnino hæc σοφὰ φάρμακα sunt adhibita, nempè conglomeratio dictorum, collatio vocularum transpositio commatum & similia, num inde Scripturæ sensus certò innotescit? Nihil minus. Tantùm hoc quandoque sequitur post longas declamationes, posse aliquod dictum aliter intelligi: qui verò genuinus sensus sit, in dubio manet. Auditor intelligit nostram ἐξήγησιν literæ textus conformem esse; post audit, per glossemata hinc inde conquisita, aliter exponi posse, atque sic cum scrupulo & suspensus dimittitur. Hoc illud Satanæ artificium est, quod quærit per suos satellites Photinianos, nempè vt omnis authoritas Scripturæ tanquam ambiguæ concidat, vt introducatur securitas, & cuivis credendi quidvis permittatur libertas.

XVIII. 4. Tandem si ad κατασκευὴν ipsis deveniendum est, nihil aliud producunt, quam elumbes quasdam rationis consequentias, principium enim primum summumque ex quo oritur, & in quod resolvitur Photinianismus, nullum est aliud quam humana ratio cum suis regulis & speculationibus, Hinc expressè scribunt, nihil credendum proponi à Deo quod ratione capi nequeat, aut falsitatis ab ipsa argui possit. Hæc illa radix & origo est omnium errorum. Ex hac maximâ cœperunt negare principalem fidei nostrę articulum, nempè mysterium sacro sanctæ Trinitatis. Nulla enim ratio capit, nulla mens intelligit, qui numero vnum, in tribus realiter distinctis personis, sine essentiæ vel divisione, vel multiplicatione subsistat. Hoc igitur arcanum quia ratione attingere haud potuerunt, hinc credere noluerunt. Iacto hoc infelici fundamento, mox secutæ sunt corruptelæ in aliis etiam articulis. Quia enim plures personæ Deitatis non sunt, hinc Christum fuisse merum hominem non Deum, nec duabus constare naturis colligunt. Si Deus non est, satisfacere pro nobis haut potuit. Quare missus est, tantum ad annunciandam salutis viam, & perficienda legis præcepta, non ad expianda mundi peccata. Si satis factio pro nobis nulla est præstita, vtique per imputationem alieni meriti non justificabimur. Quare justificatio hominis nihil erit aliud, quam gratuita sine interveniente λύτρῳ peccatorum remissio. Hinc & fides, perquam iustificamur, juxta ipsos non est apprehensio meriti, sed fiducia generalis, quâ credimus, Deum nobis benè velle, & præceptis ipsius obedimus. Qui ergò piè vixerit, salutem consequetur, nisi fecerit, dānabitur. Quoniam verò iustè puniri nemo potest, nisi in potestate eius fuerit id, quod facere debuit: hinc concludunt, fidem & legis impletionem in nostris viribus sitam, adeoque nos libero præditos esse arbitrio, Quare nullum est peccatum originis, nulla corruptio naturæ. Adamus igitur dona prima per lapsum non perdidit, sed tantum dominium super animantia, in quo ratio imaginis diuinæ fuit posita, amisit, & necessitatem moriendi invexit. Quapropter vt ipse postmodum arbitrio benè vsus est, Deique præceptis obediens, salutem adeptus: Ita & nos si fecerimus, quod Deus à nobis fieri vult, & quod per Christum Prophetam eius annunciatum est, pari modo saluabimur. Ad illa pæcepta pertinere dicunt duo Sacramenta, Baptismum & Cœnam, quę non sint media fidem aut gratiam conferentia, sed tantum externæ Ceremoniæ, quarum observatione ab aliis cœtibus distinguimur, & nostram Deo obedientiam declaramus. Atque hæc summa est præcipuorū capitum doctrinæ quam Socinus in suis libellis, Ostorodus in institutionibus, Smalcius in Catechismo proposuerunt. Quæ doctrina cùm solâ ratione nitatur, & nihil contineat quod non facilè capi possit, vel ex hoc vnico perspicuum satis est, illam humanum inventum esse, Scripturæ & toti analogiæ fidei contrarium, incertisque glossis superstructum, quod Sophisticis mediis propugnatur, & quo doctrinæ πληροφωρία in meras dubitationes commutatur.

XIX. His igitur in genere de Photinianorū corruptelis & Sophistica præmissis, iam in specie ad ve-

Iam de Christi merito doctrinam asserendam accessum facimus. Credunt autem, docent, & confitentur nostræ Ecclesiæ, quod æternus Deus ob lapsum πρωτοπλάστων generi humano indignatus fuerit illudque tenore comminationis & vi iustitiæ ad æternam mortem condemnauerit. Ex gratia verò in plenitudine temporis vnigenitum & coæternum suum Filium misit in mundum, vt carnem nostram assumeret, & in illa pro peccatis nostris agendo & patiendo satisfaceret. Hoc ipsum quoque fideliter præstitit, factus Patri obediens vique ad mortem crucis: quæ ipsius nostri loco facta persolutio singulis credentibus imputatur, adeoquè per illam ipsam Christi iustitiam imputatam iustificantur, & peccatorum veniam consequuntur, Hanc sententiam Augustana Confessio breuiter exponit articulo. 3. vbi hæc verba: Docent nostræ Ecclesiæ, quod verbum, hoc est, Filius Dei assumpferit humanam naturam in vtero B. Mariæ virginis, vt sint duæ naturæ diuina & humana in vnitate personæ inseparabiliter coniunctæ, vnus Christus verè Deus & verè homo, natus ex virgine Maria, verè passus, crucifixus, mortuus & sepultus: vt reconciliaret nobis Patrem & hostia esset, non tantùm pro culpa Originis, sed etiam pro omnibus actualibus peccatis. Et rursus articulo quarto: Docent quòd homines, non possint iustificari coram Deo propriis viribus aut operibus: sed gratis iustificentur propter Christum per fidem, cùm credunt se in gratiam recipi, & peccata remitti propter Christum, qui suâ morte pro peccatis nostris satisfecit. Hanc fidem imputat Deus pro iustitia coram ipso. Rom. 3. & 4. Hanc verò sententiã sacris literis conformem, & veritati Apostolicæ consentaneam esse, sequẽti quæstione probatum dabimus.


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of Christ for our sins be established?

merit and satisfaction of Christ, either openly teaches, or obliquely insinuates. Wherefore if all the sayings pertaining to this were to be brought forward, not a disputation, but an entire treatise would be produced. Therefore we shall not propose all the testimonies separately, but we shall distribute them into certain classes of arguments, and at the same time we shall briefly refute the exceptions of the Photinians:

Latin:

meritum & satisfactionem Christi, vel apertè adceat, vel obliquè insinuet. Quare si dicta omnia huc facientia forent adducenda, non disputatio, sed tractatus integer prodiret. Non igitur cuncta testimonia seorsim proponemus, sed illa in certas argumentorum classes dispescemus, & vnà Photinianorum exceptiones breuiter refutabimus:


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: Argument I. From the redemption accomplished through Christ

XXI. The Apostle speaks emphatically concerning this in Rom. 3. v. 24. Δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτῇ Χάριτι Διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησῦ. We are justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ: And v. 25. Whom God hath set forth ἱλαστήριον a propitiation in his blood for the demonstration of his justice, through the remission of past sins. This passage is most worthy of note here, inasmuch as in it all the causes of justification are elegantly connected. 1. The efficient, which is the grace of God freely justifying us. 2. The meritorious, which is the ἀπολύτρωσις of Christ. And lest the redemption be understood metaphorically, it is added that Christ was set forth as ἱλαστήριον or a placation, and indeed in his blood, because the shedding of this yields to us a placation before God for the demonstration of justice, since through that shedding of blood, the divine wrath and justice have been satisfied. 3. The instrumental, which is faith. 4. The formal, which is the remission of sins. 5. The final, which is ἔνδειξις τῆς δικαιοσύνης and the manifestation of divine glory. The same is found 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. Christ is made unto us by God justice and sanctification and redemption. 1. Cor. 6. v. 20. ἠγοράσθητε τιμῆς, Ye were bought with a great price, Eph. 1. v. 8. Col. 1. v. 24. In Christ we have redemption through his blood, 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Christ gave himself a redemption for all, in the Greek is ἀντίλυτρον. Heb. 9. v. 12. Neither by the blood of goats and calves, Διὰ δὲ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος, but by his own blood he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption. And v. 15 Therefore he is the Mediator of the New Testament, that by means of death for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first Testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance, 1. Pet. 1. vers. 18. 19. You were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation, but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish, 2. Pet. 1. vers. 1. τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτοὺς. Him that bought them, denying the Lord, Apoc. 5. v. 9. You were slain and have redeemed us to God by your blood. Similar passages are found in Luke 1. v. 68. c. 2. v. 38. Gal. 3. v. 13. Tit. 2. v. 14.

XXIII. From these things said, however, we weave such an argument; Whoever are redeemed and justified by the intervention of death, and through or on account of shed blood, they are not redeemed without any price, but satisfaction has been made for them: But indeed faithful Christians are redeemed and justified by the intervention of the death of Christ, and through or on account of his shed blood. Therefore they are not redeemed without any price: but satisfaction has been made for them by Christ. The major premise is evident in itself, because the shedding of blood is the very price of redemption, and therefore those who are redeemed on account of shed blood, these are certainly redeemed by the intervention of a price. The minor premise is confirmed by the passages alleged above, in which let it be noted especially 1. That Christ is said to have bought us 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. Apoc. 5. v. 9. For the Apostles do not only use the word λυτρōv but also ἀγοράζειν. Buying, however, presupposes a true price, by the intervention of which something is bought. 2. That he is said to have redeemed us in such a way that he has become for us ἱλασμὸς or a propitiation. Therefore the wrath and indignation of God the Father preceded, inasmuch as he had to be appeased by the death of Christ. 3. That he is said to have redeemed us by his own blood, by which phrase nothing else can be meant than the very price of redemption, which is evident from the double opposition, both of the blood of goats and calves, Heb. 9. v. 12. and of corruptible gold and silver 1. Pet. 1, v. 18. For as this is the price of purchase, so it follows that the blood of Christ was the price of our ἀπολυτρώσεως (redemption), whence he himself is called ἀντίλυτρον (ransom) given for us, 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. And finally 4. That we are expressly said to be, Bought with a great price 1. Cor. 6. v. 20.

XXIII. But Socinus and his followers make various objections to this argument, which must be met in good time.

1. They say that the word to redeem often and almost always obtains a metaphorical meaning, so that to redeem is nothing else than to liberate or to claim for oneself, even though no true payment of a real price has intervened: as Exod. 15. v. 19. God is said to have redeemed the people from Egyptian servitude, that is, to have liberated them with no price paid. In like manner it is used, Deut. 9. v. 26. c. 13. v. 5. c. 21. v. 8. 2. Sam. 7. ver. 23. Nehem. 1. v. 10. Ps. 77. v. 16. Heb. 11. v. 35. They think, therefore, that this word is taken in the same meaning when Christ is said to have redeemed us.

Resp. 1 We are said to be redeemed with a great price through the blood of Christ and his intervening death. Therefore, the word to redeem cannot be taken metaphorically in such sayings. For if no price intervened, why are we said to be redeemed with a great price, and through the blood of Christ? If Christ is our redeemer for no other reason than that he showed the way of salvation by preaching, why is redemption said to be made through blood? Certainly some power of ἀπολυτρώσεως (redemption) is ascribed to the blood: but it would have none, unless it were a satisfying price: And the death of Christ ought to be called μάρτύριον (testimony) rather than λύτρον (ransom).

2. It is a common rule of interpreters that one should not depart from the literal sense, unless the evidence of the text or the analogy of faith commands us to take refuge in figures. But what necessity is there, what compelling reason, that all texts speaking of our redemption we should understand figuratively? 3. It would follow that the business of our ἀπολυτρώσεως [redemption] is proposed in mere wrappings of metaphors and figures, which is contrary to the intention and custom of the Holy Spirit, who is accustomed to express the principal articles of faith in Scripture in proper words. Although figurative locutions sometimes occur, they are nevertheless few, and are clearly explained by other, more manifest passages.

4. The argument proceeds from mere particulars: Sometimes the word 'to redeem' is taken metaphorically. Therefore, also in those places where it treats of our redemption made through the blood of Christ. Anyone can easily perceive that there is no consequence here. We indeed admit that there is a twofold acceptance of ἀπολυτρώσεως: one improper, which lacks a price; the other proper, which is the claiming of an alienated, occupied, or captured person or thing through an intervening price. Now the question is, what kind of ἀπολύτρωσις is to be understood when Christ is said to have redeemed the human race? Socinus argues for the improper, but he argues from particulars. We assert the proper, and we have demonstrated this very thing from the evidence of the texts above.

5. A distinction must be made between bodily redemption, by which one is redeemed ἀπὸ τῶν πρὸς θεοῦ συνισταμένων, from tribulation and distress, and spiritual redemption, by which we are redeemed ἀπὸ τῶ φθορᾶ κακῶν, as Damascene speaks in book 4 of the Orthodox Faith, chapter 20, that is, from sin and the captivity of Satan. Bodily [redemption] can be absolute and happen without a price, and denotes a merely gratuitous liberation; of which the sayings alleged in the objection speak. Spiritual redemption from sins, however, can never be absolute and without a λύτρῳ [ransom], 1. because of the holiness of the divine nature. 2. Because of the immutability of justice. 3. Because of incorrupt truthfulness. 4. Because of the inviolate authority of the law, which wills that those who sin should die, Rom 1 v. 32. For if God without a λύτρῳ

…XX. There is almost no book of Scripture that does not redeem and justify the sinner, then the holiness of nature would be endangered, because it would not have hated the sinner; and justice, because it would dismiss the guilty: and truth, because it would not inflict the punishment which it threatens; and the authority of the law, because its curse would be nothing.

6. Some distinguish between judicial and extrajudicial redemption. The latter can sometimes be absolute: the former cannot exist without a λύτρον (ransom); especially when the judge is angry; and has threatened the transgressor with punishment. Now, the redemption of man is judicial, because man was guilty, was accused by the Devil, God sat to judge, and the sentence of the law was present; You shall die the death. Now, however, a judge does not absolve the guilty; nor can he absolve while maintaining justice; especially 1. from all punishment and wrath, 2. so that he may furthermore bestow gifts; primarily 3. if he has previously threatened death; and 4. is angry with the transgressor: and 5. the guilty party is a captive and is actually undergoing punishment. But because it was so arranged with us, it was certainly necessary that a sufficient price should intervene to effect redemption.

7. Socinus recounts these obstacles to true and proper redemption, namely that there are required 1. A captive: 2. One holding the captive. 3. A redeemer; 4. A λύτρον (ransom). We accept this; and we say that all these things are found in the business of our ἀπολυτρώσεως (redemption). There are there 1. captives, namely the whole human race. 2. There is one holding the captive, namely the justice and law of God, as well as the Devil, hell, death, and sin: 3. The redeemer is Christ 4. The λύτρον (ransom) is the blood and death of Christ. From which we conclude: that the redemption by which Christ freed us is proper, and founded upon a satisfying λύτρον (ransom).

XXIV. Exception II: Stephen, Acts 7, v. 36, calls Moses a λυτρωτὴν (redeemer). But he redeemed without any price being given; Therefore, so also did Christ.

Resp. From Moses to Christ the consequence does not hold, since there is a dissimilarity in the examples. Moses was a Redeemer only from Pharaonic tyranny: but Christ redeemed us from the wrath of God, Rom. 5, verse 9, and the power of darkness, Col. 1, v. 13, and that through his own blood. Therefore, the redemption of Moses was corporal and without λύτρον [ransom], but the redemption of Christ was spiritual, proceeding from the price of his passion. If it be urged that Moses was a type of Christ, and the redemption of Moses was a type of the salvation obtained through Christ, and therefore that a metaphorical redemption is to be understood in both cases, we answer: 1. That there is often more in the antitype than was figured by the type. Moses was a mere man, Christ is the only-begotten Son of God: Moses was a corporal Mediator, Christ is an eternal Mediator: Moses delivered the Jews from Egypt, Christ delivers all men from the wrath of God and death. Moses was a Redeemer without death and his own blood, but Christ was through death. Moses led them to the land of Canaan, Christ gives the inheritance and heavenly life. Therefore, the redemption of Moses and Christ is far different. 2. Not only Moses, but many others were types of the Redeemer Christ, which if you join together, his office will be clearly adumbrated. Moses prefigured the office of preaching, and liberation in general: the mode of liberation, consisting in the appeasement of divine wrath and satisfaction for sins, was indicated by sacrifices, to which the scapegoat especially points, Lev. 16, v. 20, et seqq. 3. Moses was a type of our redemption as to the thing, but not as to the mode of the thing, which is expressed in the N.T. And Chrysostom wrote most truly in homily 61 on Genesis: It is necessary for the figure to have less than the truth, because otherwise it would not have been a figure of things to come. The corporal redemption effected through Moses could therefore prefigure the spiritual one to be effected through Christ, yet in such a way that by reason of the mode they remain distinct species, and the former excludes a price, while

Latin:

XXI. De hâc emphaticè loquitur Apostolus Rom. 3. v. 24. Δικαιούμενοι δωρεὰν τῇ αὐτῇ Χάριτι Διὰ τῆς ἀπολυτρώσεως τῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησῦ. Iustificamur gratis per gratiam ipsius, per redemptionem, quæ est in Christo: Et v. 25. Quem proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον propitiatorium in sanguine ipsius ad ostensionem iustitiæ suæ, per remissionem præteritorum peccatorum. Dignissimus notatu hîc locus est, quippè in quo omnes iustificationis causæ eleganter connectuntur. 1. efficiens, quæ est gratia Dei gratis nos iustificantis. 2. Meritoria quæ est ἀπολύτρωσις Christi. Et nè metaphorica intelligatur redemptio, additur, quòd Christus sit propositus ἱλαστήριον vel placamentum, & quidem in sanguine suo, quòd huius effusio nobis cedat in placationem coram Deo ad ostensionem iustitiæ, siquidem per illam sanguinis effusionem, iræ, iustitiæque diuinæ satisfactum est. 3. Instrumentalis, quæ est fides. 4. Formalis, quæ est remissio peccatorum. 5. Finalis quæ est ἔνδειξις τῆς δικαιοσύνης & diuinæ gloriæ manifestatio. Idem reperitur. 1. Cor. 1. v. 30. Christus factus nobis à Deo iustitia & sanctificatio & redemptio. 1. Cor. 6. v. 20. ἠγοράσθητε τιμῆς, Emi estis pretio magno, Eph. 1. v. 8. Col. 1. v. 24. In Christo habemus redemptionem per sanguinem eius, 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Christus dedit semesipsum redemptionem pro omnibus, in græco est ἀντίλυτρον. Heb. 9. v. 12. Neque per sanguinem hircorum ac vitulorum, Διὰ δὲ τοῦ ἰδίου αἵματος, sed per proprium sanguinem introivit semel in sancta, aeterna redemptione inventa.
