Et v. 15 Ideò Novi Testamenti Mediator est, ut morte intercedente in redemptionem earum praevaricationum, quae erant sub priori Testamento, repromissionem accipiant, qui vocati sunt ad aeternam haereditatem, 1. Pet. 1. vers. 18. 19. Non corruptibilibus auro vel argento redempti estis, de vana vestrâ conversatione, sed pretioso sanguine agni immaculati Christi, 2. Pet. 1. vers. 1. τὸν ἀγοράσαντα αὐτοὺς. Illum, qui emit eos, Dominum negantes, Apoc. 5. v. 9. Occisus es & redemisti nos in sanguine tuo. Similia loca habentur Luc. 1. v. 68. c. 2. v. 38. Gal. 3. v. 13. Tit. 2. v. 14.

XXIII. Ex hisce autem dictis tale argumentum nectimus; Quicunque intercedente morte, & per vel propter sanguinem effusum redimuntur ac justificantur, illi non sine omni pretio redimuntur, sed pro ijs satisfactum est: At verò Christiani fideles intercedente morte Christi, & per vel propter ejus sanguinem effusum redimuntur ac justificantur. Ergò non sine omni pretio redimuntur: sed pro ijs à Christo satisfactum est. Major per se patet, quia sanguinis effusio ipsum est redemptionis pretium, ideoque qui redimuntur ob effusum sanguinem, hivtique certo pretii interventu redimuntur. Minorem confirmant dicta superius allegata, in quibus notetur praecipuè 1. Quòd Christus dicatur nos emisse 2. Pet. 2. v. 1. Apoc. 5. v. 9. Nec enim Apostoli duntaxat verbum λυτρōv sed etiam ἀγοράζειν adhibent. Emtio autem praesupponit verum pretium, cujus interventu aliquid emitur. 2. Quod dicatur ita redemisse ut nobis factus sit ἱλασμὸς vel placamentum. Ergo ira & indignatio Dei Patris praecessit, quippe qui Christi morte placari debuit. 3. Quod dicatur nos redemisse per proprium sanguinem, quâ phrasi nihil potest aliud, quàm ipsum redemptionis pretium notari, quod patet ex oppositione gemina, tùm sanguinis hircorum & vitulorum, Hebr. 9. v. 12. tùm corruptibilis auri & argenti 1. Pet. 1, v. 18. Vt enim hoc est precium emptionis. Ita & Christi sanguinem nostræ ἀπολυτρώσεως pretiũ fuisse sequitur, vnde ipse vǒcatur ἀντίλυτρον pro nobis datum, 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. Et tandem 4. Quòd expressè dicamur, Emti magno pretio 1. Cor. 6. v. 20.

XXIII. Verùm Socinus & eius asseciæ ad hōc argumentũ varia excipiunt, quibus maturè obuiandum est.

1. Dicunt, Redimendi verbum sæpè & fermè semper metaphoricam significationem obtinere, vt nihil sit aliud redimere, quàm liberare aut sibi asserere, quamuis veri pretij solutio vera aliqua nō interuenerit: vt Exod. 15. v. 19. Dicitur Deus redemisse populũ ex seruitute Ægyptiaca, idest, liberasse nullo soluto pretio. Pari modo sumitur, Deut. 9. v. 26. c. 13. v. 5. c. 21. v. 8. 2. Sam. 7. ver. 23. Nehem. 1. v. 10. Ps. 77. v. 16. Heb. 11. v. 35. Eadẽ igitur significatione verbũ istud accipi arbitrātur, cùm Christus nos redemisse dicitur.

Resp. 1 Nos magno pretio per sanguinem Christi & mortem eius intercedentem dicimur redemptj. Ergo verbum redimendi in talibus dictis metaphoricè accipi nequit. Si enim nullum pretium interuenit, cur pretio magno, & per Christi Sanguinem redempti dicimur? Si Christus nullâ aliâ ratione noster est redemptor, quàm quia prędicando salutis viam mostrauit, cur redemptio per sanguinem facta dicitur? Virtus certè ἀπολυτρώσεως aliqua adscribitur sanguini: Nullam verò haberet; nisi pretium satisfaciens esset: Et mors Christi μάρτύριον potiùs, quàm λύτρον nuncupari deberet.

2. Communis interpretum est regula, quòd à literali sententia non sit recedendum, nisi textus euidentia, vel fidei analogia ad figuras nos confugere iubeat. Quæ autem necessitas est, quæ cogẽs ratio, vt omnes textus de redemptione nostra loquentes intelligamus figuratè? 3. Sequeretur ἀπολυτρώσεως nostrę negotium meris metaphorarum & figurarum involucris essé propositum, quod contra intentionem & consuetudinem Spiritus S. est, qui præcipuos fidei articulos proprijs verbis in scriptura solet exprimere. Etsi nonnunquâm occurrant locutiones figuratęs sunt tamen paucæ, & per alios locos manifestiores luculenter declaratæ.

4. Argumentum procedit ex meris particularibus: Nonnunquam redimendi verbum sumitur metaphoricè. Ergò etiam in illis locis, vbi de nostra per Christi sanguinem facta redemptione agitur. Nullam hîc consequentiam esse, quiuis facilè animaduertit. Fatemur quidem, quòd duplex ἀπολυτρώσεως sit acceptio: altera impropria, quæ pretio caret; altera propria, quæ est personæ aut rei alienatæ, occupatæ vel captæ vindicatio per interueniens pretium. Iam quæritur, Qualis sit intelligenda ἀπολύτρωσις, cum Christus humanum genus redemisse dicitur? Pro impropria pugnat Socinus, sed argumentatur ex particularibus. Propriam nos asserimus, & hoc ipsum ex euidentia textuum suprà demonstrauimus.

5. Distinguendum est inter redemptionem corporalem, qua ἀπὸ τῶν πρὸς θεοῦ συνισταμένων, à tribulatione & angustia quis redimitur, & inter spiritualem, quâ ἀπὸ τῶ φθορᾶ κακῶν, vti loquitur Damascenus l. 4. Orthodoxæ Fid. cap. 20. hoc est, à peccato & captiuitate Satanę redimimur. Corporalis potest absoluta esse & fieri sine pretio, notatque liberationem merè gratuitam; de qua loquuntur dicta in obiectione allegata. Spiritualis autem redemptio à peccatis nunquam potest esse absoluta & sine λύτρῳ, 1. ob naturæ diuinæ sanctitatem. 2. ob iustitiæ immutabilitatem. 3. ob incorruptam veracitatem. 4. ob intemeratam legis authoritatem, quę vult vt qui peccant, moriantur Rom 1. v. 32. Si enim Deus absque λύτρῳ

XX. Nullus fermè liber Scripturæ est, qui non peccatorem redimeret & iustificaret, tum periclitaretur natura sanctitas, quia non odisset peccatotem; & iustitia, quia dimitteret reos: & veritas, quia pœnam, quam minatur, non infligeret; & legis authoritas, quia nulla foret eius maledictio.

6. Aliqui distinguunt inter redemptionem iudicialem & extra iudicialem. Hæc quandoque absoluta esse potest: illa sine λύτρῳ esse non potest; præsertim cùm iudex iratus; & pœnam transgressori minatus est. Iam verò hominis redemptio est iudicialis, quia homo erat reus, accusabatur à Diabolo, Deus sedebat ad iudicandum, & aderat legis sententia; Morte morieris. Iam autem iudex non absoluit reum; nec saluâ iustitiâ potest absoluere; præsertim 1. ab omni pœna, & ira, 2. vt muneribus insuper afficiat; inprimis 3. se mortem antè interminârit; & 4. transgressori irascatur: 5. reusque captiuus sit & actu pœnam sustineat. Quia verò nobiscum ita comparatum fuit, necessarium erat vtique, vt ad faciendam redemptionem sufficiens pretium interveniret.

7. Socinus hæc veræ propriæque redemptionis προσκόμυθα recenset, quòd videlicet requiratur 1. Captiuus: 2. Captiuum detinens. 3. Redemptor; 4. λύτρον. Assumimus hoc; & dicimus, quòd isthæc omnia in negotio nostræ ἀπολυτρώσεως reperiantur. Sunt ibi 1. captiui, nempè totum genus humanum. 2. Est captiuum detinens, nimirum iustitia & lex Dei, tum Diabolus, infernus, mors & peccatum: 3. Redemptor est Christus 4. λύτρον est sanguis & mors Christi. Ex quo concludimus; Redemptionem, quâ nos Christus liberauit, esse propriam, & in λύτρῳ satisfaciente fundatam.

XXIV. Exceptio II: Stephanus Actor. 7. v. 36. Mosen vocat λυτρωτὴν redemptorem. At is redemit nullo pretio dato; Ergo sic & Christus.

Resp. A Mose ad Christum non valet consequentia, quoniam dissimilitudo est in exemplis. Moises fuit Redemptor tantum a tyrannide Pharaonica: Christus vero redemit nos ab ira Dei Rom. 5. vers. 9. & potestate tenebrarum Col. 1. v. 13. idque per sanguinem suum proprium, Redemptio igitur Mosis fuit corporalis & absque λύτρῳ, sed Christi redemptio fuit spiritualis, a pretio passionis profecta. Si urgeatur hoc quod Moses fuerit typus Christi, & redemptio Mosis fuerit typus salutis per Christum partae, adeoque metaphoricam redemptionem utrobique intelligendam esse, Respondemus 1. Quod saepe plus sit in antitypo, quam figuratum est per typum. Moses fuit merus homo, Christus est Dei Filius unigenitus: Moses fuit Mediator corporalis, Christus est Mediator aeternus: Moses liberavit Iudaeos ex Aegypto. Christus omnes homines ab ira Dei & morte. Moses fuit Redemptor absque morte & sanguine proprio, Christus vero per mortem. Moses deduxit ad terram Chanaan, Christus dat haereditatem & vitam caelestem. Longe igitur alia est Mosis & Christi redemptio 2. Non solus Moses, sed plures alij fuerunt typi Redemptoris Christi, quos si coniungas, officium eius plane adumbrabitur, Moses praefiguravit officium praedicandi, & liberationem in genere: modum liberationis, consistente in placatione irae diuinae & satisfactione pro peccatis, innuerunt sacrificia, quo imprimis spectat hircus emissarius Lev. 16, v. 20. seqq. 3. Moses fuit typus nostrae redemptionis quoad rem, sed non quoad modum rei, qui exprimitur in N T. Et verissime scripsit Chrysostomus homil. 61. in Gen. Oportet figuram minus habere, quam veritatem, quia alioquin non fuisset figura fututorum. Potuit ergo redemptio corporalis per Mosen facta praefigurare spiritualem, per Christum faciendam, ita tamen, ut ratione modi distinctae maneant species, & illa pretium excludat,


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: the latter includes it

the latter includes it. 4. Add that Moses reconciled God to the people when He was most angry, Exod. 32, v. 34. Wherefore, concerning Christ the Redeemer as the antitype, this ought to be affirmed much more; whence it follows that our Redemption includes the propitiation of an angry God, made by the intervention of a certain price by Christ.

XXV. Exception III. Christ Himself is said to be redeemed by God in Psalm 31, v. 6: Thou hast redeemed me, O Lord, God of truth. But He was not redeemed by a price. Therefore, to redeem signifies to liberate without any price.

Response. Some understand these words as referring to David, the type of Christ, and then it would denote a proper redemption, since David also was justified through the merit and satisfaction of Christ the Redeemer. But let it be that the Psalmist speaks only of Christ; nevertheless, nothing can be concluded against us from that. For we willingly concede that in certain texts of Scripture, to be redeemed is the same as to be liberated. And this word obtains this sense also in Psalm 31, v. 6, where Christ is said to be redeemed by God the Father, namely, when He was raised from the dead. But the Photinians are foolish when they infer from a particular case in this way: To redeem in Psalm 31 is taken metaphorically, therefore always, and even in those places where Christ is said to have redeemed us by His own blood. Who is there who does not understand that this argument has no strength?

XXVI. Exception IV: Redemption is properly said to be made by him who detains captives; but we are said to be redeemed either from our iniquities, Tit. 2, v. 14, or from our vain conversation, 1 Pet. 1, v. 18, or from the curse of the law, Gal. 3, v. 13, by which we were not held captive, and never indeed from GOD, or from divine justice, on account of which we deserved to be condemned as sinners. Wherefore, we are said to be redeemed by Christ improperly.

Response. 1. To the major premise; this is a particular case, 1. because redemption is properly said to be made not only by him who primarily detains captives; but also from the detainer less principally, likewise from captivity itself, and all its adjuncts and effects, from prison, from the filth and squalor of prison, from servitude, from chains, torture, fear of death, and finally from death itself, which often awaits captives, unless redemption is made. The major premise is true only concerning extrajudicial and civil redemption, and not concerning every kind, but only that which is a vindication from the power of one who possesses unjustly, by which a price is given so that the captive may be withdrawn from him who detains him unjustly and violently. But the major premise is false concerning judicial and spiritual redemption, in which a λύτρον is given to God, not as to an enemy possessing unjustly, but as to a judge who had justly consigned us to captivity on account of sin, and that not so that we may be withdrawn from his power, but so that we may be reconciled to him and joined with him. For our captivity is not as when someone is held captive in war by an enemy, from whose power he is alienated when redeemed through redemption, but as when a subject guilty of high treason is handed over by the King to a lictor to be imprisoned or punished with death, unless redemption is made through satisfaction, which when it is done, the subject's liberation is his reconciliation with the King. Indeed, this redemption has this peculiar feature, that another King hands over rebellious subjects to an attendant minister, not to his own enemy and that of his subjects: But God did not hand over the captives to attendants, who were indeed ministers, but also to his enemies and ours, to the Devil, to hell, to death, etc. Therefore, so that our redemption might be proper, we did not have to be redeemed from God, that is, withdrawn or alienated, but on the contrary, reconciled to God.

XXVII. To number 1. It is false that we were not held captive by iniquities, by vain conversation, etc. For captives are held not only by the judge who is offended, or by the lictor or torturer who awaits the judge's sentence, but also by the prison, by chains, by the judge's sentence and wrath. But our sins, what are they if not chains and snares,

8. 2 Tim. 2. ver. 6? execration, what is it but the wrath and sentence of God pronounced against us? 2. We are said to be delivered not only from sins, but also from the wrath of God, from the judgment and the avenging justice of God: For Rom. 5. ver. 9. and 1 Thess. 1. ver. 10, 11, we are said to be saved from the wrath of God. Therefore also from the avenging justice of God, because, as Socinus admits, this is called the wrath of God in the scriptures. Thus we are said to be delivered from the fear of death Heb. 2. ver. 15, from death itself Hosea 13. ver. 14, and therefore from the avenging justice itself, through which we were worthy of death Rom. 1. ver. 32. Again, we are said to be redeemed from the execration of the law Gal. 3. ver. 13, but this is nothing else than the sentence of condemnation pronounced by God in the law. We are said not to come into judgment John 5. ver. 24. Wherefore we are delivered from judgment, and consequently it is false, what Socinus writes, that we are never said to be redeemed from the judgment, wrath, and justice of God. Pareus responds at greater length in c. 3 ad Rom. dub. 10. col. 307, from which we have briefly excerpted these things.

XXVIII. But Socinus insists, 1. The execration of the law does not signify the justice of God, to which satisfaction must be made, but the penalty of execration established by the law, from which penalty we have been redeemed, not because any price was paid, but because we have been exempted from it.

Response. The execration of the law is taken in two ways: 1. Passively, and then it signifies the penalty of execration. 2. Actively, and then it denotes the voice or sentence of the law condemning with execration, or the law itself execrating those who sin. But what is the voice of the law if not the voice of God? And the law execrating, if not God execrating? And God execrating, if not God angry and the wrath of God? And the wrath of God, if not the justice of God? Therefore the execration of the law actively signifies the justice of God. And although the Apostle says in Gal. 3 that we are redeemed from the execration in both senses, yet he speaks primarily of the active execration, as is evident from ver. 10, As many as are under the works of the law are under the execration, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who does not continue, etc. Whence it follows that we also are redeemed from the wrath and avenging justice of God.

XXIX. He urges, 2. We are improperly said to be redeemed by one to whom the price has not been paid. The price has not been paid to the curse of the law. Therefore, we are improperly said to be redeemed from the curse of the law.

Resp. 1. The major premise is particular. For we are either redeemed from an iniquitous person holding us captive. Or we are redeemed from things afflicting us, such as from prison, from chains, etc. And in this latter way we are said to be redeemed from the curse of the law, not as from a person to whom satisfaction is made, but as from a thing which troubles us. 2. The minor premise is false. For to the curse actively, which is nothing other than God himself promulgating the sentence of the cursing law, the price has been paid. The Apostolic sense therefore is this: Christ redeems us from the curse of the law, that is, from the condemnatory sentence of the law, and consequently from the wrath and justice of God, while he was made a curse for us, that is, while sustaining for us the punishment of the curse, namely the execrable death of the cross, he satisfied the curse of the law and the wrath of God in our place.

XXX. Exception V. In true redemption, he who holds the captive receives the price. In Christ's redemption, the Devil, who held man, did not receive the price. Therefore it was not a true redemption.

Resp. 1. Even if the whole argument were granted, nothing else could be inferred than that our spiritual redemption and external bodily redemption differ in certain respects, which we by no means deny. 2. A false hypothesis lies hidden in the minor premise, as if the Devil alone held us captive, when yet this belongs primarily to God, who by his own right thrust us into the prison of damnation. For 1. God alone is the judge and Monarch of men, having the power to cast into hell. 2. We have sinned against him alone. 3. From him we seek to have our chains loosened and our sins dismissed. 4. He himself has concluded all under sin, Rom. 11, verse 32; Gal. 3, verse.

2. and the devils themselves he bound with eternal chains, 2 Pet. 2 v. 4. And 5. the same is confirmed by the parable of the angry King, delivering the wicked servant to the tormentors, Matt. 18 v. 34. From which it certainly follows that we are held captive through sin by God, as a just and offended judge, primarily and by right of supreme power: and secondarily by the devil, death, and the like, insofar as we have been delivered to them by the just judgment of God. For the devil is as it were the executioner, sins are the snares, the world and death are the prison and the torments. Since therefore God holds us primarily, the price was deservedly paid to him by Christ, which is expressly stated, Heb. 9 v. 14.

XXXI. Objection VI. In a proper redemption, the price is given for the sake of the captive so that he may be released, but not to him who procures the redemption. God the Father, however, procured the redemption of the Son. Therefore, the price was not given to him.

Resp. The major premise is false. For the price is given also to that end, that satisfaction may be made to the detaining judge; furthermore, the price can also be given to the one procuring the redemption, namely in such a species of redemption where a judge, loving the captive who is not himself solvent, procures that another may satisfy for him, indeed that the son of the judge may satisfy from the treasury of the judge his Father. And in this way all things which Socinus urges concur. For the price is given for the sake of the captive, that he may be freed; it is given for the sake of the judge, who himself procures the redemption, so that his justice may be satisfied: the judge is moved by the price to release the captive: he himself gives the price, because the son pays from his own treasury: and the price produces the liberation of the captive in his will and decree, because he willed and decreed that the captive should not be released unless satisfaction intervened. And thus the redemption made through Christ is exactly so. If he objects: that nothing accrues to the judge through the payment of such a price, we respond that it is enough that justice remains safe and the laws inviolate. Thus Zaleucus, King of the Locrians, having passed a law concerning the plucking out of both

Latin:

hæc includat. 4. Adde, quòd Deum, cùm maximè in l gnaretur; populo reconciliavit Moses, Exod; 32. v. 34. Quare de Christo Redemptore velut antitypo, id multò magis affirmari debet; vnde sequitur, Redemptionem nostram irati Dei placationem, interuētu certi pretij à Christo factam includere.

XXV. Exceptio III. Ipse Christus dicitur redemptus à Deo Psal. 31. v. 6. Redemisti me Domine; Deus veritatis: At non est redemptus pretio. Ergo redimere significat liberare sine omni pretio.

Resp. Quidam verba ista intelligunt de Dauide, Christi typo, & tum notaretur redemptio propria, quoniam & Dauid per Christi Redemptoris meritum & satisfactionem est iustificatus: Sed esto, Psaltem de Christo duntaxat loqui, nihil tamen contra nos indè poterit concludi, Nam libenter concedimus, in quibusdam scripturæ textibus, redimi esse idem quod liberari. Atq; hunc etiam sensum obtinet verbum istud Psal. 31. vers. 6. vbi Christus à Deo Patre redemptus dicitur, nempè cùm à mortuis excitatus est. Inepti verò sunt Photiniani, dum à particulari sic colligunt: Redimere Psal. 31. sumitur metaphoricè, Ergo semper & in illis etiam locis, vbi Christus per proprium sanguinem nos redemisse dicitur. Nullum huius argumēti neruum esse, quis est qui non intelligit.

XXVI. Exceptio IV: Redemptio propriè dicitur fieri ab eo, qui detinet captiuos; At nos dicimur redempti, vel ab iniquitatibus nostris, Tit. 2. v. 14. vel ex vana conuersatione nostra, 1. Pet. 1. v. 18. vel ab execratione legis, Gal. 3. v. 13. à quibus non detinebamur captiui, nusquam verò à DEO, vel à iustitia diuina, propter quà peccatores damnari merebamur, Quare per Christum impropriè redempti dicimur.

Resp. 1, Ad maiorem; Hæc particularis est. 1. quià redemptio proprià dicitur fieri non tantùm à detente captiuos principaliter; sed etiam à detinente minus principaliter, item à captiuitate ipsa, omnibusque eius adiunctis & effectis, à carcere, à sordibꝰ & squalore carceris, à seruitute, à vinculis, torturâ, metu mortis, & à morte denique ipsâ, quæ sæpè manet captiuos, nisi fiat redemptio. Maior vera est duntaxat de redemptione extraiudiciali & ciuili, nec de omni, sed tantum de eâ, quæ est à potestate iniquè possidentis vindicatio, quâ datur pretium, vt captiuus abstrahatur ab eo, qui eum iniquè ac violenter detinet. Falsa autem est Maior de redemptione iudiciali & spirituali, in quâ datur λύτρον Deo, non vt hosti iniquè possidenti, sed vt iudici, qui nos captiuitati iustè mancipauerat propter peccatum, idque non vt ab eius potestate abstrahamur, sed vt ei reconciliemur, & cum eo coniungamur. Habet enim se nostra captiuitas, nō vt cùm quis bello detinetur captus ab hoste à cuius potestate redemptus, per redemptionem alienatur, sed vt cùm subditus reus læsæ Maiestatis, traditur à Rege lictori incarcerandus, aut morte mulctandus, nisi per satisfactionem fiat redemptio, quæ cum fit, subditi liberatio est eius cum Rege reconciliatio. Quin hoc etiam peculiare habet hæc redemptio, quòd Rex alius subditos rebelles tradit apparitori ministro, non hosti suo & subditorum: At Deus non tradidit captiuos apparitoribus, ministris quidem, sed & hostibus suis & nostris, Diabolo, inferno, morti &c. Non igitur, vt propria esset nostra redemptio, debuimus redimi à Deo, hoc est, abstrahi, aut alienari, sed contra, Deo reconciliari.

XXVII. Ad numerum 1. Falsum est, quòd non fuerimus detenti captiui ab iniquitatibus, à conuersatione vanâ &c. Nam captiui detinentur non solùm à iudice, qui est læsus, vel à lictore vel tortore, qui iudicis sententiam expectat, sed etiam à carcere, à vinculis, à iudicis sententia & ira. At peccata nostra, quid sunt nisi vincula & laquei,

8. Tim. 2. verf. 6? execratio, quid nisi ira & sententia Dei in nos pronunciata? 2. Non dicimur tantum liberati a peccatis, verum etiam ab ira Dei, a iudicio & iustitia Dei vindicatrice: Nam Rom. 5. vers. 9. & 1. Thess. 1. vers. 18, 19. dicimur saluati ab ira Dei. Ergo etiam a iustitia Dei vindicatrice, quia fatente Socino, hæc vocatur ira Dei in scripturis. Sic dicimur liberati a metu mortis Heb. 2 v. 12. a morte ipsa Osea. 13. v. 14. ideoque ab ipsa iustitia vindicatrice, per quam digni eramus morte Rom. 1. v. 32. Rursus redemti dicimur ab execratione legis Gal 3. v. 13. hæc autem nihil est aliud, quam sententia damnationis, a Deo in lege pronunciata. Dicimur non venturi in iudicium Ioh: 5. vers. 24. Quare liberati sumus a judicio, & per consequens fallum est, quod Socinus scribit, nos nunquam redemtos dici a iudicio, ira & iustitia Dei. Pluribus respondet Pareus in c. 3. ad Rom. dub. 10. col. 307. ex quo ista breuiter excerpsimus.

XXIIX. Instat autem Socinus, 1. Execratio legis non significat iustitiam Dei, cui satisfaciendum esset, sed execrationis pœnam a lege statutam a qua pœna redemti sumus, non quia ulla aliquod pretium solutum fuerit, sed quia ab ea sumus exemti.

Respon. Execratio legis sumitur dupliciter: 1. Passivè, & tunc significat pœnam execrationis. 2. Activè, & tunc denotat vocem seu sententiam legis cum execratione damnantis, seu ipsam legem execrantem peccantes. Quid autem est vox legis nisi vox Dei? & lex execrans, nisi Deus execrans? & Deus execrans, nisi Deus iratus & ira Dei? & ira Dei, nisi iustitia Dei? Execratio igitur legis activè significat iustitiam Dei. Et si autem vtroque sensu ab execratione nos redemptos dicit Apostolus Gal. 3. tamen primariò loquitur de execratione actiua, vt patet ex v. 10. Quotquot sub operibus legis sunt, sub execratione sunt, scriptum enim, Execrabilis omnis, qui non manserit &c. Vndè consequitur, nos quoque esse redemptos ab irâ & iustitia Dei vindicatrice.

XXIX. Instat, 2. Cui non est persolutum pretium, ab eo impropriè dicimur redempti. Execrationi legis non est persolutum pretium. Ergo ab execratione legis impropriè dicimur redempti.

Resp. 1. Maior particularis est. Vel enim redimimur à persona iniquâ captiuante nos. Vel redimimur à rebus nos affligentibus, vt à carcere, à vinculis &c. Atque hoc posteriori modo redempti dicimur ab execratione legis, non tanquam à personâ cui satisfiat, sed tanquam à re, quæ nos molestat. 2. Minor falsa est. Execrationi enim actiue, quæ nihil aliud, quàm ipse Deus, legis execrantis sententiam promulgans, pretium est persolutum. Sensus igitur Apostolicus hic est: Christus nos redemit ab execratione legis, id est, à sententia damnatoria legis, & consequenter ab irâ & iustitia Dei, dum pro nobis factus est execratio, id est, dum pœnam execrationis, mortem nempè crucis execrabilem, pro nobis sustinens, execrationi legis & iræ Dei nostro loco satisfecit.

XXX. Exceptio V. In verâ redemptione pretium accipit is, qui captium detinet. In Christi redemptione pretium non accepit Diabolus, qui hominem detinebat. Non igitur fuit vera redemptione conuenit.

Respon. 1 Si maximè totum argumētum concederetur, nihil tamen inferri posset aliud, quam redemptionem nostram spiritualem, & externam corporalem in quibusdam discrepare, id quod nos minimè inficiamur. 2. In minori latet falsa hypothesis, ac si solus Diabolus nos detinuerit captiuos, cùm tamen hoc Deo πρώτως conueniat, qui suo iure nos in carcerem damnationis detrusit. Nam 1. solus Deus est iudex & Monarcha hominum habēs potestatem abiiciendi in gehennam. 2. Ipsi soli peccauimus. 3. Ab ipso petimus laxari vincula & dimitti peccata. 4. Ipse conclusit omnia sub peccatum Rom, 11. vers. 32. Gal. 3. vers.

&2. secut & ipse Diabolos æternis catenis alligauit, 2. Petr. 2. v. 4. Et 5. idem confirmat parabola Regis irati, tradentis servum nequam tortoribus Matth. 18. vers. 34. Ex quibus certò consequitur, nos per peccatum à Deo, tanquam iudice iusto & offenso, captiuos detineri primò & iure summæ potestatis: Adiabolo autem, morte, & similibus, secundariò, quatenus ijs iusto Dei iudicio sumus traditi. Diabolus enim quasi lictor est, peccatum sunt laquei, mundus & mors sut carcer & tormenta. Cùm igitur Deus nos primò detineat, meritò illi pretium à Christo est solutum id quòd expressè dicitur, Hebr. 9. v. 14.

XXXI. Exceptio VI. In redemtione propriâ pretium datur captivi causâ vt is soluatur, nō autem illi qui redemtionem procurat. Deus Pater autem procurauit redemtionem filij. Ergo illi non datum est pretium.

Resp. Maior est falsa. Datur enim pretium & illum in finem, vt satisfiat detinenti iudici; Deindè potest quoq; pretium dari redemtionem procuranti, nempè in tali redemtionis specie quâ iudex amans captivum, qui ipse non est soluendo, procurat, vt pro eo alius satisfaciat, imò vt filius iudicis ex Patris iudicis thesauro satisfaciat. AtŅ; hoc modo concurrunt omnia, quæ vrget Socin. Nam pretiū datur captiui causâ, veliberetur, datur iudicis causâ, qui ipse redēptionem procurat, vt suæ iustitiæ satisfiat: iudex movetur pretio, vt captivum dimittat: dat ipse pretiū, quia filius ex ipsius thesauro soluit: Et pretium gignit in eius voluntate atque decreto liberationem captiui, quia voluit atque decreuit, vt non nisi interueniente satisfactione dimitteretur captivus. Sic autem prorsus se habet redemtio per Christum facta. Si excipiat: iudici per talis pretij solutionem nihil accedere, respondemus, satis esse, quòd iustitia salua, & leges inuiolatæ maneant. Sic Zeleucus Locrensium Rex latâ lege de spoliandis vtroœus o-


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: eyes of adulterers, when his son had sinned, that he himself might be held just…

eyes of adulterers, when his son had sinned, that he himself might be held just and truthful, he deprived his son of one eye and himself of the other: by which satisfaction, certainly, nothing accrued to the judge beyond the praise of justice and constancy. Thus God, by the λύτρον, acquired no profit for himself, yet nonetheless by that his justice was fulfilled and his truth declared.

XXXII. And thus far we have seen the exceptions of Socinus. For the conclusion of this argument we shall add a few things concerning the passage in Job, chapter 19, verse 25, in which he makes mention of his Redeemer, by which name we judge that Christ, who alone redeems us through his blood, is denoted, but it pleases the Photinians otherwise. For they contend that Job is speaking not of the resurrection of the body, but of the restoration of health, not of eternal glory in the heavens, but of temporal happiness on earth, namely that, although he is now afflicted, God the Father will nevertheless, at the last time of his life, restore not only firm bodily health, but moreover more goods and greater glory than he ever had; that it is therefore a prophecy concerning future prosperity, the fulfillment of which is described in the last chapter, verse 12. We do not wish, however, in this place to institute a full analysis of that text, but we shall only consider the Redeemer of Job, namely what he understands when he says, 'I know that my גאלי Redeemer lives'? We infer from this as follows: If by the name of Redeemer Christ is understood in particular, and his resurrection is simultaneously looked to, then this passage is not to be explained in general concerning God restoring health, but rather concerning the benefit of Christ, who resurrects men, which consequence the adversaries do not attack. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also. The minor premise contains the κρινόμενον, and is called into doubt by the Photinians. Therefore it must be confirmed by some arguments.

XXXIII. Some lay down this rule: as often as the verb or a noun derived from it is attributed to God himself, then it is to be understood immediately concerning the second person of the Trinity, namely concerning the Son, who was therefore made man, that he might [redeem] us under he might redeem those sold into the power of Satan, and claim them for his own kingdom. And so all such passages of the O.T. confirmed the faith concerning the Son of God who was to be incarnate, and concerning the redemption of the human race in the flesh through his blood. This can be proven by an induction of passages, as Gen. 48, verse 16, the Angel הַגֹּאֵל who redeemed me from all evil, etc., which can be understood only of the Son of God, the uncreated Angel. Thus Exod. 6, verse 6, I will redeem you with an outstretched arm. Ex. chap. 15, verse 13, Thou hast led forth the people, whom thou hast claimed. But that leading forth is not obscurely ascribed to Christ, 1 Cor. 10, verses 3 and 9, inasmuch as he accompanied them, and whom they are said to have tempted. Thus Psalm 74, verse 2, Thou hast claimed the tribe of thine inheritance. Isa. 44, verse 22, Jehovah hath claimed Jacob. Especially does the passage from Isaiah 63, v. 9, look to this, where the Church of the Old Testament, by a Eucharistic proclamation, acknowledged and celebrated Christ as Redeemer. For he names the Angel of the face, who is none other than the Son of God, and to him is attributed the redemption, He himself redeemed them. Since, therefore, Job was also placed in straits here, he certainly fled to no other redeemer than Christ. Add Jer. 31, verse 11, Jehovah will redeem Jacob. Mic. 4, v. 10, God will redeem thee. Hosea 13, v. 14, I will redeem them from the hand of hell, which is expounded concerning the victory of Christ, 1 Cor. 15, v. 55. Since, therefore, the faithful in the Old Testament, by calling God Redeemer, always looked to Christ, as the future Messiah and Redeemer specifically so called, hence we conclude that Job did the same, being placed in those extreme miseries. For it cannot be denied that he is addressing God, as verse 26 clearly indicates. By the force, therefore, of the aforesaid rule, Christ must be immediately understood by the Redeemer.

XXXIV. 2. The same can be proven from the fact that the name of Redeemer properly belongs to Christ alone. For it denotes such a vindicator, who is both joined by consanguinity to those to be redeemed, and provides the price for redemption. Hence Forster, page 124, prescribes this rule: When Scripture calls God thus (that is, Redeemer), it simultaneously insinuates that the Son of God must assume our flesh, and become our kinsman, so that he may redeem us by right of kinship, as Isa. 59. v. 20 v. last, Ps. 72. v. 14, Ps. 74. v. 2, Ps. 78. v. 35. Since, therefore, the name of Redeemer properly belongs to Christ alone, inasmuch as he alone is our kinsman, and he has claimed us, devolved elsewhere or from God, into his kingdom by right of brotherhood through his blood, John 8. v. 3, certainly Job also, in placing hope in his Redeemer, understands none but Christ. Pineda enumerates five requirements of a true Redeemer for this passage: 1. Be a kinsman. 2. Redeem by right of consanguinity. 3. Snatch the prey from the unjust possessor. 4. Pay no price to him. 5. Offer blood as the price of redemption to the true Lord. These five requirements of a Redeemer (which can be proven from the Scriptures and the analogy of faith) do not belong to the Father, but to Christ alone, and therefore he alone is properly our Redeemer and is so called. XXX. 3. The whole Scripture testifies that the work of our redemption belongs to none but Christ. For whoever redeemed us with his own blood and satisfied God the Father for our sins, he alone is our Redeemer: But Christ redeemed us with his blood. Therefore Christ alone is our Redeemer. The minor premise is proven, because we are redeemed by the blood of Christ, not by gold, 1 Pet. 1. v. 18, 19. He gave himself for us, Tit. 2. 14. He is the living Redeemer. Gal. 3. v. 13. Rom. 6. v. 9. Heb. 7. 25. Add. Luke 21. v. 28. Rom. 3. v. 24. Eph. 1. v. 7. Col. 1. v. 14. Matt. 20. v. 28. Mark 10. v. 45. 1 Tim. 2. v. 6. Rev. 5. 7, 9. Now, whoever is our Redeemer specially so called, in him Job placed his hope, and of him he speaks v. 25. For no reason can be brought forward why he should not be speaking of this one. But Christ is the Redeemer specially so called. Therefore in him Job placed his hope, and of him he speaks in v. 25.

XXXVI. 4. By the Redeemer, Job understands him who will resurrect us. But the Son of Man, that is Christ, will resurrect us. Therefore Job understands the Son of Man, that is Christ, by the Redeemer. The major premise is proved from this, that Job places the hope of resurrection in this Redeemer, so that just as he rose, so he believes that he himself will also rise. The minor premise is demonstrated most clearly from John 5. v. 25, 28, 29. John 6. v. 40. Phil. 3. v. 20. Matt. 24. v. 30, 31.

XXXVII. 5. There is no doubt that this whole confession of Job proceeded from true faith and πληροφορίᾳ of heart. Indeed, Job's very knowing is nothing other than believing, since words of knowledge among the Hebrews denote not only γνῶσιν, but more often affection and the consequent effects. Whence faith itself is called knowledge, Isa. 53. v. 11, John 17. v. 4. With this hypothesis presupposed, we conclude thus. Whatever is the true object of saving faith, that is understood by the Redeemer. But Christ the Messiah of the world is the true object of saving faith. Therefore Christ the Messiah of the world is understood by the Redeemer. The major premise is certain from the hypothesis proved. For if by 'knowing' Job's faith is denoted, then certainly by 'Redeemer' the object of faith is denoted, so that the sense is, 'I believe that my Redeemer lives.' The minor premise is likewise firm, since saving faith does not apprehend God absolutely and in general, but rather Christ, as is hinted at in John 1. v. 12. Whence the Scripture of the New Testament always inculcates believing in Christ, faith in Christ, trust in Christ, etc., so that it may be shown that there is no other direct and immediate object of true saving faith than Christ, the Son of God and Mary,

XXXVIII. 6. Job describes his Redeemer thus, That he lives. But lest anyone object that God in general is also frequently named as living in the Scriptures, Job soon adds that he understands a natural life, into which his Redeemer is to be recalled, for he says, In the last day you shall stand upon the dust. From this we most firmly conclude that by living, the life of God is not understood: 1. because this is eternal, not to be in the future only in the last times, as Job here describes the life of the Redeemer. 2. because it cannot be said of God the Father that he is to stand upon the dust or be raised from the dust. For upon him into whom death does not fall, standing upon the dust does not fall, that is, a resurrection to natural life. But if the words, to stand upon the dust, are unwilling to be explained as ἀναστάσει, they will always beg the question, pervert the text, and invent glosses which can never be proven in eternity. Let us therefore remain in the simplicity of the letter, and by עפר we understand dust or earth, and by standing itself, the resurrection, by which one coming forth from the sepulchre in turn stands alive upon the earth. Therefore, the resurrection of Christ is noted most briefly, and that which depends upon it, our resurrection, which is to be in the last day, whence for this very reason it is called life, John 14, verse 6, 1 John 1, verse 1, 2. We, however, gather from what has been said thus: He to whom bodily life and resurrection does not belong, he is not understood by Job as the Redeemer: But to God considered absolutely, bodily life and resurrection does not belong; but only to the incarnate Son of God, Therefore, God considered absolutely is not understood by Job as the Redeemer, but only the incarnate Son of God.

XXXIX. 7. At the end of this confession Job speaks of a bodily vision, for he says that he will see God from his flesh, and with his own bodily eyes. But indeed God the Father cannot be seen with bodily eyes, since the divine essence is invisible, but Christ

The incarnate Son of God can be looked upon corporally, inasmuch as he has a true body, and he will be looked upon also on the last day, not only by the pious, but also by the impious, Zech. 11. verse 10. Whence it follows in turn, that by the Redeemer, whom Job believes he will see, none other than Christ is denoted. If they object, That God can also be seen, if not in his own essence, yet in an assumed form, Ezek. 1. Dan. 7. (Whence they think that by this vision of God, that apparition of God which is described in the last chapters of Job is noted,) I answer: That this is said, not proven, nay rather it is false, 1. because this apparition was unknown and unexpected to Job, as the context indicates. But the vision of which he speaks in chapter 19, verse 26, was promised to him, known, and certainly hoped for. 2. It is not read in the last chapter that GOD appeared to Job in some visible form, but it is only reported in chapter 38, verse 1, that he answered Job from the whirlwind, that is, with a certain huge storm having been sent before. And although in the last chapter, verse 5, it is said, My eye has seen you, it can nevertheless be taken concerning the knowledge of the mind, because the word ראה is general. Nay, if it be granted in the highest degree that God appeared to Job in a visible form, yet this apparition is not that vision of which Job speaks in chapter 19, as has been shown. Nor can it be evidently proven that God stood on the earth when he appeared to Job in chapter 42, as it is said in chapter 19, He shall stand upon the earth. For it is more consistent that, if God appeared, he was then seen higher than the earth, namely in that place from which he was previously speaking from the cloud and darkness, so that even then, with the whirlwind subsiding and the mist dissipating, the majesty of God might exhibit itself to be looked upon in some wonderful and illustrious form.

X L. The Photinians can reply nothing else than that our exposition is too arbitrary, inasmuch as the name of Redeemer is also attributed to the Father himself in the sacred writings, as 2 Sam. 7, verse 23, Isa. 50, verse 16. Resp. 1. There is no necessity in the argument. The name of Redeemer is attributed elsewhere to God in a general sense. Therefore, here also. For Moses is also called Redeemer, God, in verse 35 of chapter 7. Can it be immediately inferred from that, that Job also understands Moses by the name of Redeemer? The method of gathering is almost the same as that by which the Photinians argue; namely, from a particular; which proves nothing. 2: The cited passages are correctly explained as referring to the Son of God, so that the universality of the rule indicated above may remain. For Christ was the head of the Church even in the Old Testament, and therefore he deservedly redeemed it from temporal as well as spiritual enemies and dangers. 2 Sam. 7, the discourse is about the liberation and reduction of the Israelites from Egypt. But the Angel who appeared to Moses in the bush, Ex. 3, verse 26, who was seen by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire, Ex. 13, v. 21, Num. 9, v. 18, led that people out. But this one was none other than Christ. 1. Cor. 10, v. 4, 9. Isa. 36, v. 7, following. In like manner, Isa. 60, verse 16, Christ is hinted at, not excluded. It indeed seems from the preceding context as if the Father alone were speaking and attributing the name of Redeemer to himself: yet because the discourse is about salvation itself, and redemption, which was accomplished only through Christ, why should we not understand that 16th verse as referring to the second person of the Trinity? Similar texts are read, Isa. 43, verse 1, ch. 48, v. 17, 20, ch. 49, v. 7, 26, ch. 50, v. 2, ch. 64, v. 2, in all of which places Christ is included, because they are parts of Evangelical sermons, the fulcrum of which is Christ, with his merit.

Latin:

culo adulteris, cùm filius peccasset, vt ipse justus & verax haberetur, filium vno, seipsum altero priuauit oculo: quâ satisfactione iudici certè præter laudem iustitiæ atq; constantiæ nihil accessit. Ita Deus ex λύτρῳ sibi nullum quidem lucrum acquisiuit, nihilo minus per istud iustitia eius expleta, & veritas declarata fuit.

XXXII. Atque hactenus Socini exceptiones vidimus. Pro coronide huius argumenti pauca de loco Iobi cap. 19. vers. 25. addemus, in quo ille Redemtoris sui mentionem facit, quo nomine Christum, qui solus nos per sanguinem suum redemit, notari arbitramur, sed Photinianis placet contrarium. Contendunt enim, Iobum verba facere, non de resurrectione corporis, sed restitutione sanitatis, non de gloria sempiterna in cælis, sed de felicitate temporali in terris, fore nimirùm, vt licet nùnc affligatur, Deus tamen Pater vltimo vitæ tempore, non modo firmam corporis valetudinem, sed insuper plura bona & maiorem gloriam, quam habuerit vnquam, sit restituturus, Esse igitur vaticinium de futurâ prosperitate, cuius complementum describatur cap. vlt v. 12. Nolumus autem hoc loco plenam istius textus analysin instituere, sed tantùm Redemtorem Iobi considerabimus, quid nempe intelligat, cùm inquit, Noui גאלי Redemtorem meum viuere? Nos indè sic inferimus: Si per nomen Redemptoris in specie Christus intelligitur, & ad eius resurrectione simul respicitur, tùm exponi neq; hic sextus in genere de Deo, sanitatem restituēte, sed potiùs de beneficio Christi, homines resuscitantis, quam consequentiam non impugnant aduersarij. Sed verum est prius. Ergò & posterius Minor continet κρινόμενον, & in dubium vocatur à Photinianis. Proindè argumentis aliquot erit confirmanda.

XXXIII. Ponunt nonnulli hanc regulam: quoties verbum vel nomen indè deductum, ipsi Deo tribuitur, tum immediatè de secunda Trinitatis persona intelligendum est, nempè de Filio, qui ideò homo est factus, vt nos sub potestatem Satanæ venundatos redimeret, suoque regno vindicaret. Itaque eiusmodi omnes loci V. T. confirmarunt fidem de incarnando Filio DEI, & in carne redemptione humani generis per sanguinem ipsius. Potest hoc probari per inductionem locorum vt Genes. 48. vers. 16. Angelus הַגֹּאֵל qui redemit me ab omni malo &c. id quod non nisi de Filio Dei, Angelo increato, potest intelligi. Sic Exod. 6. vers. 6. Redemto. Redimam vos in brachio extento. Ex: cap. 15. vers. 13. Duxisti populum, quem vendicasti. Ista verò eductio non obscurè Christo adscribitur, 1. Cor. 10. vers. 3. & 9. quippè qui illos comitatus, & quem ipsi tentâsse dicuntur. Sic Psal. 74. vers. 2. Vendicasti tribum hæreditatis tuæ Efa. 44. vers. 22. Vendicauit Iehouah Iacob. In primis huc spectat locus ex Esaia 63. v. 9. vbi Ecclesia veteris Testamenti præconio Eucharistico Christum agnouit & celebrauit Redemptorem. Nominat enim Angelum faciei, qui non est nisi Filius Dei, & huic attribuitur redemptio, Ipse redemit eos. Quia ergò & hic in angustijs erat constitutus Iobus, vtique ad nullum redemptorem alium confugit, nisi ad Christum. Adde Ierem. 31. vers. 11, Redimet Iehouah Iacob. Mich. 4. v. 10. Redimet te Deus, Oseæ 13. v. 14. De manu inferni redimam eos, quod de victoria Christi exponitur. 1. Cor. 15. v. 15. Quia ergò fideles in veteri Testamento Deum vocando Redemptorem semper respexerunt ad Christum, tanquam Messiam futurum & Redemptorem in specie sic dictum, hinc concludimus, idem fecisse Iobum in summis istis miserijs constitutum. Nec enim negari potest quòd Deum alloquatur, vti clarè indicat v. 26. Vi ergo prædictæ regulæ, Christus per Redemptorem immediatè debet intelligi.

XXXIV. 2. Idem probari potest exindè, quia nomen Redemptoris soli Christo propriè competit. Notat verò talem vindicem, qui tùm redimendis consanguinitate iunctus est, tùm pretium quoddam pro redemtione interponit Hinc Forsterus pag, 124. hanc regulam præscribit : Quando Scriptura Deum sic vocat (id est Redemptorem) simul insinuat, quòd Filius Dei debeat assumere carnem nostram , & noster fieri consanguineus , vt possit nos iure propinquitatis redimere , vt Efa. 59. v. 20. E: veniet ad Sion Redemtor hoc est, Christus homo , & propinquus noster factus. Similes textus habentur, Psal. 19. v. ult. Psal. 72. v. 14 Psal. 74. v. 2. Psal. 78. v. 35. Cùm ergò nomen Redemptoris soli Christo propriè, conueniat, quippè qui solus est noster consanguineus, & nos aliò seu à Deo deuulutos iure fraternitatis per sanguinem suũ regno suo asseruit, Ioh. 8. v. 3. vtique & Iobus; spem ponendo in suum Redemptorem non nisi Christum intelligit. Pineda in hunc locum quinque Redemptioris veri legis enumerat : 1. Propinquus esto. 2. Consanguinitatis iure redimito. 3. Iniusto possessori prædam eripito. 4. Huic pretium nullum solvito. 5. Sanguinem pro redẽrtionis pretio verò Domino offerto. Hæc quinque Redemptoris requisita, (quæ ex Scripturis, & analogia fidei probari possunt, ) non Patri, sed soli Christo conueniunt, ideoq; is solus propriè Redemptor noster est & vocatur. XXX. 3. Vniuersa Scriptura testatur, opus redemtionis nostræ non nisi Christo competere. Quicunque enim suo nos sanguine redemit, & Deo Patri pro peccatis nostris satisfecit, is solus est noster Redemptor: Sed Christus suo nos sanguine redemit. Ergo solus Christus est noster Redemptor. Minor probatur, quia sanguine Christi sumus redemti, non auro, 1. Par. 1. v. 18. 19. dedit semetipsum pro nobis, Tit. 2. 16. Ipse est Redemptor vivus. Gal. 3. v. 13. Rom. 6. v. 9 Hebr. 7. 25. Adde. Luc. 21. v. 28. Rom. 3. v. 24. Ephes. 1. v. 7. Col. 1. v. 14. Matth. 20. v. 28. Marc. 10. v. 45 1. Timoth. 2. v. 6. Apoc. 5. 7. 9. Iam, Quicunque est Redemptor noster specialiter sic dictus, in illo spem suam posuit Iobus, & de illo loquitur v. 25. Nulla enim potest proferri ratio, cur de hoc non loquatur. Sed Christus est Redemptor specialiter dict9. Ergo in illo spem posuit Iobus, & de illo v. 25. loquitur.

XXXVI. 4. Qui nos resuscitabit, eum Iobus per Redemtorem intelligit. Sed Filius hominis, hoc est Christus nos resuscitabit. E. Iobus Filium hominis, hoc est Christum, per Redemtorem intelligit. Maior probatur exindè, quia spem resurrectionis collocat Iobus in isto Redemtore, vt sicut hic surrexit, ita & se resurrecturum credat. Minor demōstratur clarissimè ex Ioh. 5. v. 25 28. 29. Ioh. 6. v. 40. Phil. 3. v. 20. Matth. 24. v. 30. 31.

XXXVII. 5. Nullum est dubium, quin tota hæc confessio Iobi ex verâ fide & πληροφορίᾳ cordis sit profecta. Imò ipsum scire Iobi nihil est aliud quàm credere, siquidem verba notitiæ apud Hebræos non solam γνῶσιν denotant, sed sæpius affectum, effectusque consequentes. Vndè ipsa fides vocatur notitia Esa. 53. v. 11. Ioh. 17. v. 4. Quâ hypothesi presuppositâ, sic concludimus. Quicquid est verum fidei saluificæ obiectum, id per redemtorem intelligitur. Sed Christus Messias mundi est verum fidei saluificæ obiectum. Ergò Christus Messias mundi per Redemptorem intelligitur. Maior certa est ex hypothesi probata. Si enim per scire, Iobi fides notatur, vtique per Redemtorem fidei obiectum, vt sensus sit, Credo Redemptorem meum viuere. Minor pariter firma est, siquidem fides saluifica non apprehendit Deum absolutè & in genere, sed potius Christū, vt innuitur Ioh. 1. v. 12. Vndè Scriptura Noui T. semper inculcat credere in Christum, fidem Christo, fiduciam in Christo, &c. vt ostendatur, nullum aliud esse fidei salvantis veræque obiectum directum & immediatum, quàm Christum Dei & Mariæ Filium,

XXXVIII. 6. Iobus Redemptorem suum ita describit, Quòd vivat. Nè quis autem excipiat, etiam Deum in genere sæpiùs nominari viventem in Scripturis, mox addit Iobus, se vitam naturalem intelligere, in quam Redemptor suus sit revocandus, ait enim, Novissimè super pulverem stabis. Hinc firmissimè concludimus, quod per vivere non intelligatur vita Dei: 1. quia isthæc est æterna, non postremis demùm temporibus futura, prout Iobus Redemptoris vitam hîc describit. 2. quia de Deo Patre dici nequit, quòd is super pulverem sit staturus vel à pulvere excitandus. In quem enim non cadit mors, in eum non cadit statio super pulverem, hoc est, resurrectio ad vitam naturalem. Quòd si verba, super pulverem stare, nolint exponi de ἀναστάσει, semper petent principium, pervertent textum, confingent glossas, quæ in æternum probari nequeunt. Maneamus ergò in simplicitate literæ, & per עפר nos pulverem seu terram intelligimus, per ipsum verò stare, resurrectionem, quâ quis sepulchro prodiens vicissim vivus stat super terram, Brevissimis ergò, notatur resurrectio Christi, & quæ inde pendet, resurrectio nostra, in extremo die futura, vnde ob hoc ipsum vita vocatur Ioh. 14. versu. 6. 1. Ioh. 1. versu 1. 2. Nos autem ex dictis ita colligimus; Cui non competit vita & resurrectio corporalis, is per Redemptorem à Iobo non intelligitur: Sed Deo absolutè considerato, non competit vita & resurrectio corporalis; sed tantùm Dei Filio incarnato, E. Deus absolutè per Redemptorem à Iobo non intelligitur, sed tantùm Dei Filius incarnatus.

XXXIX. 7. In huius confessionis fine loquitur Iobus de visione corporali, Dicit enim, se de carne sua visurum Deum, suisque oculis corporeis. At verò Deus Pater oculis corporeis videri nequit cùm essentia divina sit invisibilis, Christus autem

Dei Filius incarnatus aspici potest corporaliter, siquidem verum corpus habet, & aspicietur etiam in extremo die, non tantum à piis, sed etiam impiis, Zach. 11. vers. 10. Vndè vicissim sequitur, per Redemptorem, quem se Iobus visurum credit, non nisi Christum denotari. Si excipiant, Etiam Deum videri posse, si non in suâ essentiâ, tamen in specie assumpta, Ezech. 1. Dan. 7. (Vnde putant, notari per hanc Dei visionem, illam Dei apparitionem quæ in vltimis Iobi capitibus describitur,) Resp. Id dici, non probari, imò falsum esse, 1. quia isthæc apparitio fuit Iobo ignota & inexpectata, vt contextus indicat. Visio autem de qua cap. 19. versu. 26. ipsi fuit promissa, cognita & certò sperata 2. Non legitur cap. ult. quòd DEVS visibili quadam specie apparuit Iobo, sed tantum refertur cap. 38. vers. 1. quod de turbine, h. e. præmissâ ingenti quâdam tempestate Iobo responderit. Et licet cap. ult. vers. 5. dicatur, Oculus meus vidit te, potest tamen id de cognitione mentis accipi, quia verbum ראה est generale. Imò si maximè concedatur, Deum visibili formâ Iobo apparuisse, non tamen hæc apparitio est illa visio, de qua Iobus caput 19. loquitur vt ostensum. Neque potest evidenter probari Deum in terra stetisse cum appareret Iobo cap. 42. sicut dicitur capite 19. Super terram stabit. Nam magis consentaneum est, si apparuit Deus, tum sublimiorem à terrâ visum esse, in eo videlicet loco, vndè prius de nube & caligine loquebatur, vt jam tunc quiescente turbine & dissipatâ nebulâ, Dei majestas mirabili aliquâ & illustri specie sese exhiberet conspiciendam.

X L. Photiniani nihil aliud reponere possunt, quam expositionem nostram nimis esse arbitrariam, quippè cùm nomen Redemptoris ipsi quoque Patri tribuatur in sacris, vt 2. Sam. 7. versu 23. Isai 50. vers. 16. Resp. 1. Nulla argumento inest necessitas Nomen Redemtoris alibi tribuitur Deo in genere. Ergo etiam hic. Nam & Moses vocatur Redemptor Deus 7. versu 35. Num inde statim inferri potest, quod & Iobus intelligat Mosen per nomen Redemptoris; Eadem ferme est colligendi ratio, vt Photiniani argumentantur; nempe a particulari; quod nihil probat. 2: Dicta allegata recte exponuntur de Filio Dei, vt maneat vniuersalitas regulae supra indicatae, Nam Christus & in Veteri etiam Testamento caput fuit Ecclesiae, ideoque eam merito redemit tam a temporalibus; quam a spiritualibus inimicis & periculis. 2. Sam 7. sermo est de liberatione & reductione Israelitarum ex Aegypto. Eduxit autem populum istum Angelus, qui Mosi apparuit in rubo Ex. 3: versu 26. qui visus est interdiu in columna nubis; noctu in columna ignis; Ex. 13. v. 21. Num. 9. v. 18. Hic autem non fuit alius, quam Christus. 1. Cor. 10. v. 4. 9. Esa. 36. v. 7. seqq. Pari modo Esa. 60. vers. 16. Christus innuitur, non excluditur. Videtur quidem ex antecedentibus, ac si solus Pater loqueretur, sibique nomen Redemptoris attribueret: quia tamen de ipsa saluatione est sermo, & redemptione, quae non nisi per Christum facta, cur non versum illum 16. de secunda Trinitatis persona intelligeremus? Similes textus leguntur, Esa. 43. versu. 1. cap. 48. v. 17. 20. c. 49. v. 7. 26. c. 50. v. 2. c. 64. v. 2. in quibus locis omnibus Christus includitur, quia sunt partes cõcionum Evangelicarum, quarum fulcrum est Christus, cum suo merito.


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: Argument II: From the office of Mediator

ARGUMENT II: From the office of Mediator

XLI. That Christ is our only Mediator, the following passages confirm: 1 Tim. 2, v. 5.

There is one God εἰς καὶ μεσίτης, one Mediator also of God and men, the man Christ Jesus. Heb. 8. ver. 6. But now he hath obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the Mediator of a better Testament. Chap. 9. vers: 15. He is the Mediator of the New Testament, that by means of death, for the redemption of the transgressions that were under the first Testament, they which are called might receive the promise of eternal inheritance, chap. 12. ver. 24. Ye are come to Jesus the Mediator of the New Testament and to the blood of sprinkling that speaketh better things than that of Abel. Three things indeed are especially intimated in sayings of this kind. 1. That God and men were equally at variance, in that God was alienated from men, and men indeed from God, rebellious, and enemies. 2. That Christ the Mediator therefore came, that he might reconcile those parties at variance, by appeasing God who was angry, and by converting rebellious men. 3. The means of this reconciliation was the sprinkling of blood, and intervening death. For he did not appease the wrath of the Father with bare words, but by the obedience of death, which was that means by which satisfaction was made to God, and grace was acquired for the human race.

XLII. These things being thus declared, we weave such an argument: Whoever is a Mediator between parties extremely at variance, in such a way indeed that for this he sheds his blood and undergoes death, he performs the office of Mediator by the intervention of a certain price, and thus by satisfying. But Christ is the Mediator between parties extremely at variance, namely between God angry on account of sins, and men turned away from God, and therefore he shed his precious blood, and underwent the death of the cross. Wherefore Christ performed the office of Mediator by the intervention of a certain price, and thus by satisfying. No one will deny the major premise, if he considers that we are not speaking of a bare Mediation, but of such a one as is founded in the shedding of blood and death. Where it is immediately asked. What did the blood contribute to the Mediation? It was certainly not a bare sign, but rather a means, since it is said to have been poured out for the redemption of sins, Heb. 9, verse 15, and therefore elsewhere called λύτρον or a price: And indeed the epistle to the Hebrews, l. d., expressly asserts that Christ is our Mediator for this reason, because he offered himself to God on the altar of the cross to cleanse our conscience 14: If the blood of goats and bulls, and the ashes of a heifer sprinkling the defiled, sanctifies for the cleansing of the flesh: How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, cleanse our conscience from dead works, to serve the living God. To which words he soon adds, ver. 15, καὶ διὰ τῦτο Διαθήκης καινῆς μεσίτης ἐστιν. And therefore he is the Mediator of the New Testament. You see from this that the foundation of the Mediation is established as the shedding of blood, and therefore Christ reconciled God and men, not by mere preaching, but rather by passion and death, which for that reason is most truly called either the means or the price of the mediation performed, since Christ is our Mediator for this reason, because he shed his blood, cleansing our consciences, and therefore turning them to God.

XLIII. From which it further becomes clear how inept is the gloss of the Photinians, who teach that Christ is our Mediator in no other way than that God used him as an intermediary and interpreter to establish and sanction his covenant with men, and through whom they can approach him, instructed by the knowledge of his will, but not that by having rendered satisfaction for our sins, he appeased God, who was angry with men, which is the exception of Socinus in book 1 de Servatore, ch. 7, and the Racovian Catechism, ch. 8.

8. For we have just shown that the foundation of the Mediation performed is placed not in preaching alone, but especially in the shedding of blood. For he was made Mediator of the N. T. for this reason, because he offered himself to God the Father on the altar of the cross, undergoing an ignominious death; Heb. 9, verse 14, 15. This very thing is also hinted at 1 Tim. 2 ver. 6. For when the Apostle had said in verse 5, That there is one mediator of God and men, the man Christ Jesus, he immediately adds in verse 6 the manner by which Christ is our Mediator, namely because he gave himself as ἀντίλυτρον and a price of redemption for all. But he who is a Mediator the will of God:

XLIV. But they urge that Moses also (a type of Christ) is called a Mediator, yet for no other reason than that he was a messenger between God and men in the work of legislation, Ex. 19 verse 3, Deut. 5 ver. 5, Gal. 3 v. 19. But we have said above that the consequence does not hold from Moses to Christ, since they are compared only by reason of the thing, not the manner, because there is more in the antitype than there was in the type. Moses is called a Mediator on account of the office of interpreting; but Christ primarily on account of the benefit of satisfying. He performed his duty merely by informing: but Christ, by giving himself as a price of redemption, and offering himself to God the Father: He therefore is called a Mediator because he was a messenger, but this one, not only because he acted as an interpreter, but because he shed his blood for us for the remission of sins. Nor was Moses only a type of Christ, but also the scapegoat Lev. 16 ver. 14. and the red heifer Num. 19 verse 4, upon which the sins of the people were laid, so that they might be purged from their guilt by the virtue of the antitype. If therefore the blood of goats sanctified the defiled, how much more shall the blood of Christ cleanse our conscience, as the Apostle concludes Heb. 9 verse 14.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM II: Ab officio Mediatoris

XLI. Christum esse Mediatorem nostrum vnicum, sequentia dicta confirmant 1. Tim. 2. v. 5.

Vnus est Deus εἰς καὶ μεσίτης, vnus & Mediator Dei & hominum homo christus Iesus. Heb. 8. ver. 6. Nunc autem melius sortitus est ministerium, quant. & melioris Testamenti Mediator est. Cap. 9. vers: 15. Noui Testamenti Mediator est, ut morte intercedente in redemptionem earum præuaricationum, quæ erant sub priori Testamento repromissionem accipiant, qui vocati sunt, æternam hereditatem, cap. 12. ver. 24. Accessistis ad Testamenti Noui Mediatorem Iesum & sanguinis aspersionem melius loquentem quàm Abel. Tria verò cumprimis innuuntur huiusmodi dictis. 1. Deum & homines fuisse pariter dissidentes, eò quod Deus ab hominibus, homines verò à Deo abalienati, rebelles, & inimici erant. 2. Mediatorem Christum ideo venisse, vt dissidentes illas partes reconciliaret, Deum iratum placando, & homines rebelles convertendo. 3. Medium huius reconciliationis fuit sanguinis aspersio, & mors intercedens. Nec enim nudis verbis placavit iram Patris, sed obedientiâ mortis, quæ fuit istud medium, quo satisfactum Deo, & gratia acquisita est humano generi.

XLII. Quibus ita declaratis, tale argumentum nectimus: Quicunque Mediator est inter partes extremè dissidentes, ita quidem vt propter hoc sanguinem suum effundat & mortem subeat, ille certi pretij interventu, adeoque satisfaciendo officium Mediatoris exequitur. Christus autem Mediator est inter partes extremè dissidentes, nempè inter Deum ob peccata iratum, & homines à Deo aversos, ideoque pretiosum sanguinem suum effudit, & mortem crucis subiit. Quarè Christus certi pretij interventu, adeoque satis faciendo officium Mediatoris executus est. Majorem nemo negabit, si cogitauerit, nos non de Mediatione nudâ, sed de tali, quæ in sanguinis effusione & morte fundata est, verba facere. Vbi statim quæritur. Quid sanguis ad Mediationem contulerit? Nudum sanè non fuit fignum sed potiùs medium, cùm in redemptionem peccatorum dicatur effusus Hebr. 9. versu 15. ideoque alibi λύτρον vel pretium nuncupatus: Et sanè epistola ad Hebr. l. d. expressè asserit, Christum ideò nostrum esse Mediatorem, quia semetipsum in arâ crucis obtulit Deo, ad emundandam nostram conscientiam. Ita enim c. 9. v. 13. 14. author differit: Si sanguis hircorum & taurorum, & cinis vitulae adsperjus, inquinatos sanctificat ad emundationem carnis: Quantò magis sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum sanctum semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo, emundabit conscientiam nostram ab operibus mortuis, ad serviendum Deo viventi. Quibus verbis mox subiungit, ver. 15. καὶ διὰ τῦτο Διαθήκης καινῆς μεσίτης ἐστιν. Et ideò Novi Testamenti Mediator est. Vides hinc, quòd fundamentum Mediationis constituatur effusio sanguinis, ideoque Christus Deum & homines reconciliauit, non nudâ prædicatione, sed potiùs passione & morte, quæ ob id verissimè vel medium vel pretium factæ mediationis vocatur, cùm Christus ideò sit noster Mediator, quia sanguinem effudit, nostras conscientias purgantem, adeoque ad Deum convertentem.

XLIII. Vndè porrò elucescit, quàm inepta sit glossa Photinianorum docentium, Christum esse Mediatorem nostrum non alio modo, quàm quòd Deus illo internuntio & interprete ad fœdus suum cum hominibus pangendum & sanciendum usus est, & per quem illi ad ipsum eius voluntatis cognitione instructi accedere possunt, non autem quòd satisfactione pro peccatis nostris præstitâ, Deum iratum hominibus placauerit, quæ Socini est exceptio lib. 1. de Seruatore c. 7. & Cath. Racov c.

8. Nam modò ostendimus, quòd fundamentum factæ Mediationis non in prædicatione solâ, sed potissimùm in sanguinis effusione collocetur. Ideò enim factus est Mediator N. T. quia in arâ crucis Deo Patri se obtulit, ignominiosam mortem subeundo; Hebr. 9. versu 14. 15. Hoc ipsum quoque innuitur 1. Tim. 2. ver. 6. Cùm enim Apostolus dixisset versu 5. Vnum esse mediatorem Dei & hominum, hominem Christum Iesum, mox versu 6. modum adjungit, quo Christus, noster Mediator sit, nempè quia semetipsum dederit ἀντίλυτρον & redemptionis pretium pro omnibus. Qui autem Mediator est moriendo, is non tantùm Mediator dici debet docendo, aut Dei voluntatem interpretando:

XLIV. Sed instant, Mosen quoque (Christi typum,) vocari Mediatorem, nullâ tamē ratione aliâ, quàm quia fuit internuncius Dei & hominum in opere legislationis, Ex. 19. versu 3. Deut 5. ver. 5. Gal. 3. v. 19 Verùm à Mose ad Christum non valere consequentiam, suprà diximus, cùm conferantur tantùm ratione rei, non modi, quia plus est in antitypo, quàm fuit in typo. Moses Mediator dicitur ob interpretandi officium; sed Christus imprimis ob satisfaciendi beneficium. Ille munere suo perfunctus est, duntaxat informando: Christus verò, semetipsum redemtionis pretium dando, ac Deo Patri offerendo: Ille igitur Mediator dicitur, quia fuit internuncius, hic autem, non tantùm quia interpretem egit, sed quia sanguinem pro nobis in remissionem peccatorum effudit. Neque Moses tantùm Christi typus fuit, sed & hircus emissarius Lev. 16. vers. 14. & juvenca rufa Num. 19. versu 4. quibus populi peccata fuerunt imposita, vt ab eorum reatu, virtute antitypi, purgarentur. Si ergo hircorum sanguis inquinatos sanctificavit, quantò magis sanguis Christi nostram conscientiam emundabit, vti concludit Apostolus Hebr. 9. versu 14.


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: Argument III. From ἱλασμός or propitiation and reconciliation

ARGUMENT III. From ἱλασμός or propitiation and reconciliation.

XLV. Two things come into consideration here:

1. That God was angry with us on account of sins.

2. That Christ appeased the angry God, and to us

that he reconciled, and thus was our propitiator. First, it is strengthened by these words of Psalm 5, verse 7: You hate all who work iniquity. Wherefore we also were subject to the hatred of God on account of sins. For these things divide between us and God, Isaiah 59, verse 2; whence by nature we are called children of wrath, Ephesians 2, verse 3, which remains upon all unbelievers, John 3, verse last. We are no less under the curse of the law, because cursed is everyone who has not remained in the words of the law, Deuteronomy 27, verse last, Galatians 3, verses 10, 13; under the slavery of sin, John 8, verse 34, Romans 6, verse 20; sold under sin, Romans 7, verse 14; and overcome by it, 2 Peter 2, verse 9; under the power of Satan, who had the empire of death over those who, through fear of death, were subject to slavery throughout their whole life, Hebrews 2, verses 14, 15; and under the guilt of eternal death, because it was said, You shall die the death, Genesis 2, verse 17; And the soul that has sinned, it shall die. Ezekiel 18, verse 20; whence death is called the wages of sin, Romans 6, verse last. From those, however, from whom God is divided, whom he holds in hatred, who are by nature children of wrath, subject to the curse of the law, to the slavery of sins, to Satan, to the power of death, it follows spontaneously that God was certainly hostile to these.

XLVI. All those sayings which announce the grace of the heavenly Father and promise the forgiveness of sins prove the latter part. For if God was previously angry, and yet receives us anew, and indeed forgives sins on account of the blood of Christ, it is rightly concluded that he is this Propitiator and Reconciler of ours, and that by the power of his passion and shed blood. It is pleasing, however, to note in particular certain sayings pertaining to this: 1. These speak concerning propitiation, Romans 3, verse 25: God set forth Christ as ἱλαστήριον, a propitiation or appeasement, through faith in his blood. Reference is made, however, to the propitiatory of the Old Testament placed upon the ark of the covenant, Exodus 25, verse 17, and so called because it was the place where God, speaking with Moses, was appeased and was propitious to the people Num 7. verse 89. Otherwise it is also called an oracle because sacred responses were given there, and a work of worship, because it covered the ark, in which the tables of the law were stored. It was, however, a type of Christ; who is compared to the propitiatory, both by reason of preaching, insofar as through him the Father gave responses and revealed his will, and by reason of our crimes, which Christ covered with his passion, just as the lid covered the ark, and by reason of appeasement, insofar as through his blood the Father was reconciled and appeased toward us, which reason the Apostle especially attends to, because he affirms that Christ is our propitiatory through faith in his blood. John teaches the same in his 1st Epistle, chapter 2, verse 2. Christ himself ἱλασμός ἐξτι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ὑμῶν; is the propitiation, the atonement / for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. Note here that the cause for making the ἱλασμόν is set as the sins of the world, for which satisfaction had to be made, which is itself repeated in 1 John 4, verse 10. God sent his son as ἱλασμόν, a propitiation for our sins. Thus, therefore, by the single word of propitiation are insinuated: 1. The indignation of God on account of sins. 2. His appeasement and reconciliation. 3. Accomplished through Christ. 4. By the shedding of his precious blood. For to propitiate is nothing other than to appease or to render propitious him who was previously offended and angry. Since, therefore, God had to be propitiated, it is certain that he was indeed angry with us.

XLVII. From this, however, flows such an argument: Whoever is appeased only through blood and death; he undoubtedly was vehemently angry with those to whom he is rendered propitious. But God is appeased only through the blood and death of Christ. Therefore, toward us, to whom he has been rendered propitious, he was previously vehemently angry. Furthermore: He who before

For an angry God, there is a propitiation for sins through blood shed; he, by the intervention of a true and certain price, satisfies God for sins. For what else is it to satisfy, than to appease the anger conceived on account of sins and offenses by the intervention of a certain λύτρῳ (ransom)? But Christ was before God a propitiation for our sins, through his shed blood, by the force of the words set down above. Therefore, Christ truly and by the intervention of a certain price satisfied God for our sins.

XLIIX. But Socinus objects in part 2, chapter, page 81, that Christ is called ἱλαστήριον (propitiation) in the same sense as the ark was formerly, which did not appease God, yet was called a placamentum (propitiatory), because God, showing himself propitious and appeased in it to the people, gave his responses. Thus, Christ is called a placamentum, not because he himself appeased God for us, but because not only does God show himself most appeased to us in him, but he also revealed whatever he wished us to know through him. But, I respond: 1. This gloss can never be proven, since it is contrary to the express letters of the divine word. For he who is a propitiation for sins certainly renders him appeased whom sins had offended. For what else is it to propitiate, than to appease one who is angry? And if God the Father shows himself most appeased in Christ, why was there need for death to intervene, and why could that propitiation not be accomplished except through the shedding of blood? 2. The heretic therefore wrongly opposes things that are subordinate. Christ is compared to the ancient propitiatory, not only by reason of the will manifested, but especially on account of the anger of God appeased, which, although the ancient ἱλαστήριον did not settle it, it was nevertheless a type of Christ, who was bound to appease it, and by whose intuition God was reconciled to the Israelite people in the Old Testament; for since without the shedding of blood, as there is no remission, so there is no appeasement, it is rightly asked, Why did God show himself appeased in the ark, and give responses? The ark certainly shed no blood, nor could it shed any. It is therefore necessary, at last to come to Christ, whom it prefigured, and who is called ἱλαστήριον in his blood, and ἱλασμὸς for the sins of the world. As therefore the ark made propitiation typically, so Christ does really and truly. As the ark prefigured propitiation: so it had to be fulfilled and consummated through Christ. There is therefore a great difference between the ark and Christ: the former was the type, the latter the antitype: the former the shadow, the latter the body: the former the figure, the latter the ἀλήθεια: the former a brute thing, the latter a living victim, offered to make true propitiation.

XLIX. They have, however, still another προσφύγιον, objecting that that propitiation is made not through true satisfaction, but through the bare purging of sins and the gratuitous removal of guilt. But this is again to put forward a gloss without any reason, and to contradict the Scriptures. 1. For every propitiation presupposes indignation in him who must be rendered propitious. Wherefore also God, whom Christ wished to render propitious, was angry on account of sins. These certainly cannot be taken away and merely purged unless God, having been moved, is first appeased and reconciled to us. 2. If Christ took away sins merely and out of grace alone without a λύτρῳ, what need was there for him to sustain such great torments for us and for our sins, and to undergo a most ignominious death? Indeed, why does the Apostle say, without the shedding of blood there is no remission of sins, Heb. 9. verse 25. Why is Christ said to be our propitiatory in his blood, Rom. 3. verse 25. Is it not noted by this very thing that the purging of crimes and the removal of guilt was not simple and absolute, but founded upon the death of Christ as an intervening λύτρῳ, and that ἱλασμὸς properly has a relation not so much to the offenses which are remitted, as to the offended person whose anger must be appeased? For after this person has been rendered propitious, then he the more willingly pardons the fault. But if anyone should remit an offense of his own accord, then this remission cannot be called propitiation, made through some Mediator. For this, by the force of its native meaning, always presupposes indignation in the offended person, who if they forgive immediately, then this is said to be done, not on account of the preceding propitiation of some Mediator, but through a spontaneous offering of grace and favor. There are therefore three things in true propitiation: 1. The indignation of the offended person. 2. The appeasement, made through a Mediator, and 3. the forgiveness of the fault after the appeasement. The Photinians, however, deny the first two, and by propitiation they understand nothing but a plainly gratuitous offering of sin, which is to establish ἀκύρωσον ἐν προσχηματίῳ. For propitiation without presupposed indignation and intervening appeasement is not propitiation; that is, the thing itself is not the thing itself.

L. But they still have something to grumble about, namely that Christ is called ἱλασμὸν, as were the old sacrifices: In those, however, there was no satisfaction or appeasement, but a simple offering of guilt. Therefore, neither in Christ does such a thing as ἱλασμὸς occur. But both propositions are false; for propitiation is attributed to the victims of animals in one way, and to the victim of Christ in another way in Scripture. Those were only a type and shadow: Christ, however, is the antitype, and therefore having entered into the holy of holies with his own blood, he found eternal redemption. Furthermore, it is false that in the sacrifices no appeasement was made, and no satisfaction existed. For God was truly appeased, not indeed through the blood of goats, but through the regard for the blood of Christ, which the victims foreshadowed. However much, therefore, they did not satisfy God of themselves, because they were types of true satisfaction, which God looked upon in those types, hence the victims themselves are said to appease God.

LI. And thus far we have dealt with propitiation: It remains that we add a few things II. concerning reconciliation. Let these testimonies of Scripture be noted concerning it: Rom. 5. ver. 10. When we were enemies we were reconciled (καταλλάγημεν) to God through the death of his Son. ver. 11. Through Christ we have received the reconciliation (καταλλαγὴν). Eph. 2. ver. 16. Christ reconciled both (Jews and Gentiles) in one body to God, through the cross, killing the enmity thereby. Col. 1. ver. 20. It pleased the Father, through Christ to reconcile all things to himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether they be things in earth, or things in heaven. ver. 21. & 22. He has reconciled you in the body of his cross through death. Now indeed to reconcile is nothing else than to bring back into favor, or to restore lost grace, which since it could be done in no other way than through the cross and the blood of Christ, a firm argument in turn arises from thence for our opinion. For that reconciliation implies.

1. Our sin, by which we offend God.

2. The indignation of God proceeding from the offense.

3. The loss of grace, inflicted in place of punishment.

4. The placation of God, and the restoration of grace.

5. The meritorious means of placation, which the Apostle calls the blood of the cross Col. 1, v. 20. and death Rom. 5, v. 10.

LII.
