Therefore we argue now as follows: In every true reconciliation, the indignation and alienation of the injured party from the offender precedes, on account of which reconciliation (καταλλαγὴ) is necessary. But the reconciliation made through Christ is a true reconciliation, unless you think the Apostle wrote falsehoods. Therefore, the indignation and alienation of the injured party, namely God, from the offender, which was the human race, preceded. Furthermore: He to whom the offending party is reconciled after indignation and alienation, is by this very fact placated, since to placate is nothing else than to render one who is angry and alienated propitious and clement. But the offending human race was reconciled through Christ to God who was angry and alienated. Therefore GOD is by this very fact placated. Furthermore, every placation, which is certainly made by the intervention of a price, is not bare, but satisfactory. Moreover, the appeasement of God was made by the intervention of a certain price, namely through the blood and death of Christ, as if by a λύτρον for our sins. Therefore, the appeasement of God through Christ, made by the power of reconciliation, was not bare, but satisfactory, which was what had to be concluded.

LIII. But these things having been diligently observed, whatever the Photinians object against this vanishes into smoke. For 1. They say that the reconciliation of men is not with God, but among themselves, that is, the concord produced between Gentiles and Jews, and between men and Angels. Response: The consequence from the inclusive to the exclusive is not valid; nor are those things to be mutually opposed to one another which the Apostles join together as subordinate. For a triple dissension is hinted at in the Scriptures, which was removed through the reconciliation of Christ. I. Dissension between Gentiles and Jews, who were burning with the greatest hatred toward one another, Eph. 2, ver. 16. II. Dissension between men and angels, inasmuch as they are enemies of the enemies of God, Col. 1, v. 20. III. Dissension between men and God, who, having been offended by them, was on account of this alienated, so that we had need to be reconciled to him again, Rom. 5, ver. 10. Just as, therefore, the former two dissensions include and presuppose the alienation of both parties, so also it must be judged concerning the dissension between God and men. Let it be noted, however, that the alienation of God was the first and greatest of all, upon which the remaining dissensions depend. For because God was offended, hence the Angels also were indignant at us, and from there followed the mutual discord between Jews and Gentiles. As, therefore, the alienation of God, so also the reconciliation is the first and greatest. For God having been appeased, the remaining dissensions ceased of their own accord. And since the appeasement of God was made through the shedding of blood, hence also Angels and men, Jews and Gentiles, are said to be reconciled through the cross of Christ, not because satisfaction was made by Christ to either the Angels or the Jews, but because that salutary concord is the fruit and effect following the reconciliation of God (to whom alone satisfaction was made) founded in the blood and death of Christ. For just as we did not sin against angels, nor against men, but against God alone, and nevertheless from the sin by which we offended God and caused him to be at variance, there arose remaining enmities between angels and men: so satisfaction was made to God alone through the blood of Christ, and nevertheless, from the death of Christ as the primary cause of all benefits, the reconciliation or mutual concord of angels and men is rightly said to have flowed.

LIV. They object. 2. That we indeed are reconciled to God through a simple reception into favor; but that God, as an enemy, is not reconciled to us. But although this is not expressly stated, it is nevertheless insinuated. For we were the injuring and offending party, God was the injured and offended party: and therefore we were divided, and alienated on both sides. Christ, however, intervened; he reconciled God to us by dying; he reconciles us to God by converting us through the power of his death. Therefore, just as the alienation was mutual, so also is the reconciliation. And just as in every καταλλαγῇ the injured party is said to be reconciled first, and to that party alone must satisfaction be made; so also God was to be reconciled first, and to him alone was satisfaction to be made. Hence we are said to be reconciled to himself through Christ, 2 Cor. 5, verse 18, and the manner of reconciliation is subjoined in verse 21, namely, while he made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. Nor does it stand in the way that God himself is said to have reconciled us to himself. For by this arrangement, the satisfaction and propitiation made through Christ is not excluded, but regard is had to the gratuitous love and counsel of God, by which he himself decreed to send his Son into the world, so that by dying for us he might make satisfaction, and thus reconcile us to God and God to us. Furthermore, this also is to be observed, that the word reconciliation signifies two things 1. The placation of the offended party, and thus Christ alone reconciled God by dying, that is, he made him placated from being angry. 2. Reception into grace, and the oblivion of the old offense, and thus God reconciled us to himself, that is, on account of the preceding placation of Christ, he received us into grace anew. Therefore these two things do not conflict, but cohere excellently, as antecedent and consequent, as cause and effect. More will be said about reconciliation next, when the eleventh objection of the Photinians is answered.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM. III. Ab ἱλασμῷ vel propitiatione & reconciliatione.

XLV. Duo hîcein considerationem veniunt:

1. Quòd Deus nobis ob peccata infensus fuerit.

2. Quòd Christus Deum iratum placaverit, nobisq;

que reconciliauerit, atque sic propitiator noster fuerit. Privs roboratur his dictis Psal. 5. vers. 7. Odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem. Quare & nos odio Dei ob peccata subiecti fuimus. Haec enim diuidunt inter nos & Deum Esa. 59. v. 2. vnde natura dicimur filij irae Eph. 2. vers. 3. quae manet super omnes incredulos Ioh. 3. v. ult. Non minùs sumus sub maledictione legis, quia maledictus omnis, qui non permanserit in sermonibus legis Deut. 27. v. ult. Gal. 3. v. 10. 13. sub seruitute peccati, Iohan. 8. vers. 34. Rom. 6. v. 20. venundati sub peccatum, Rom. 7. v. 14. & superati ab illo, 2. Petr. 2. vers. 9. sub potestate Sathanae, qui habebat mortis imperium in eos, qui timore mortis, per totam vitam, obnoxij erant seruituti, Hebr. 2. vers. 14. 15. & sub reatu mortis aeternae, quia dictum, Morte morieris, Gen. 2. v. 17. Et anima quae peccauerit ipsa morietur. Ezech. 18. v. 20. vnde mors peccati stipendium dicitur Rom. 6. v. ult. A quibus verò Deus divisus est, quos odio habet, qui naturâ sunt filij irae, subiecti legis maledictioni, peccatorum servituti, Satanae, mortis potestati, his certè Deum fuisse infensum, vltrò consequitur.

XLVI. Posterivs membrum probant omnia ista dicta, quae gratiam Patris coelestis annunciant, & peccatorum veniam promittunt. Si enim Deus antè iratus fuit, & verò nos denuò recipit, atqui ob Christi sanguinem peccata condonat, vtique hunc Propitiatorium & Reconciliatorem nostrum esse, idque vi passionis & sanguinis effusi, rectè concluditur. Placet tamen in specie quaedam dicta huc facientia annotare, 1. De propitiatione haec loquuntur Rom. 3. v. 25. Christum proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον propitiationem vel placamentum Ju emem Guadenstul/ per fidem in sanguine eius. Respicitur verò ad propitiatorium Veteris Testamenti in arca foederis collocatum Exod. 25. vers. 17. & ita dictum, quia locus erat, quo Deus cum Mose loquens placabatur & propitiabatur populo Num 7. vers. 89. Aliàs oraculum quoque nominatum est quòd ibi responsa redderentur sacra, & ope cultum, quia tegebat arcam, in quâ repositæ erant legis tabulæ. Fuit autem typus Christi; qui propitiatorio comparatur, tùm ratione prædicationis, quatenus per illum Pater responsa dedit, & voluntatem suam reuelauit, tùm ratione nostrorum criminum, quæ Christus suâ passione operuit, sicut arcam tegebat operculum, tùm ratione placationis, quatenus per eius sanguinem Pater nobis, reconciliatus & placatus est, quam rationem Apostolus cumprimis attendit, quia Christum per fidem in sanguine eius, nostrum esse propitiatorium affirmat. Idem docet Iohannes 1. Epistolæ 2. vers. 2. Ipse christus ἱλασμός ἐξτι περὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν ὑμῶν; propitiatio est die Versöhnung / propitiatis nostris; non pro nostris autem tantum, sed etiam pro totius mundi. Nota hîc, quòd causa faciendi ἱλασμόν ponantur peccata mundi, pro quibus erat satisfaciendum, quod ipsum repetitur 1. Iohannis 4. vers. 10. Deus misit filium suum ἱλασμόν propitiationem pro peccatis nostris. Sic igitur vnice propitiationis vocabulo insinuantur. 1. Indignatio Dei ob peccata. 2. Eius placatio & reconciliatio. 3. Facta per Christum. 4. Effusione pretiosi sanguinis. Nam propitiare nihil est aliud, quàm placare vel propitium reddere illum, qui ante fuit offensus & iratus. Cùm ergò Deus propitiari debuerit, vtique illum nobis succensuisse certum est.

XLVII. Fluit verò hinc tale argumentum: Quicunque placatur non nisi per sanguinem & mortem; ille proculdubio vehementer succensuit iis, quibus redditur propitius. Atqui Deus placatur non nisi per sanguinem & mortem Christi. Ergò nobis, quibus redditus est propitius, anteà vehementer succensuit. Porrò: Qui coram

Deo irato est propitiatio pro peccatis per sanguinem effusum, is verè certique pretij interuentu peccatis Deo satisfacit. Quid enim aliud est satisfacere, quàm iram ob peccata & offensas conceptam, certo λύτρῳ intercedete placare? Atqui Christus coram Deo fuit propitiatio pro peccatis nostris, per effusum sanguinem, vi dictorum suprà positorum. Ergò Christus verè certíq; pretij interuentu pro peccatis nostris Deo satisfecit.

XLIIX. Sed excipit Socinus part. 2. cap. pag. 81. Christum eodem sensu dici ἱλαστήριον, quo olim arca, quae Deum non placauit, placamentum tamen dicebatur, quia Deus in eâ se propitium & placatum praebens populo sua responsa dabat. Ita Christum dici placamentum, non quòd Deum ipse nobis placauerit, sed quia non modò Deus in ipso se nobis placatissimum ostendit, sed & quicquid nos scire voluit, per ipsum patefecit. Verùm, Respond. 1. Haec glossa in aeternum probari nequit, quoniam expressae verbi diuini literae adversatur. Qui enim pro peccatis est propitiatio, is certè illum reddit placatum, quem peccata offenderant. Quid enim aliud est propitiare, quàm iratum placare? Et si Deus Pater in Christo se placatissimum ostendit, cur opus erat mortem interueuenire, propitiatio ista non nisi per sanguinis effusionem expediri potuit? 2. Malè igitur opponit haereticus, quae subordinata sunt. Propitiatorio veteri Christus comparatur, non tantum ratione voluntatis manifestatae, sed cumprimis ob iram Dei placatam, quam licet non sedârit antiquum ἱλαστήριον, tamen typus Christi, qui placare illam debuit, & cuius intuitu Deus in V. T. populo Israelitico reconciliatus fuit; Cùm enim absque sanguinis effusione, vt nulla sit remissio, ita & nulla sit placatio, meritò queritur, Cur Deus in arca se placatum ostenderit, & responsa dederit? Arca sanè sanguinem nullum effudit, nec effundere potuit. Necesse igitur est, tandem venire ad Christum, quem figuravit, quique ἱλαστήριον in sanguine, & ἱλασμὸς dicitur pro peccatis mundi. Vt ergò arca placavit typicè, ita Christus realiter & verè. Vt arca placationem figuravit: ita per Christum impleri & consummari debuit. Magnum igitur discrimen est inter arcam & Christum: Illa typus fuit, hic antitypus: illa vmbra, hic corpus: Illa figura, hic ἀλήθεια: illa res bruta, hic viva victima, ad veram propitiationem faciendam oblata.

XLIX. Habent verò adhuc aliud προσφύγιον, excipientes, illam propitiationem fieri non per satisfactionem veram, sed per nudam peccatorum purgationem, & gratuitam reatus ablationem. Sed hoc iterùm est glossam absque omni ratione proferre, & Scripturis contradicere, 1. Omnis enim propitiatio præsupponit indignationem in illo, qui propitius reddi debet. Quare & Deus, quem Christus volebat propitiare, iratus fuit ob peccata. Hæc sanè auferri, nudéque purgari non possunt, nisi Deus commotus prius placetur & nobis reconcilietur. 2. Si nudè & ex sola gratia absque λύτρῳ Christus abstulit peccata, quid opus erat tantos ipsum pro nobis & pro peccatis nostris cruciatus sustinere, mortemque ignominiosissimam subire? Imò cur Apostolus inquit, sine sanguinis effusione nullam fieri peccatorum remissionem Hebr. 9. vers. 25. Cur nostrum dicitur Christus propitiatorium in suo sanguine, Rom. 3. vers. 25. Annon hoc ipso notatur, purgationem scelerum & ablationem reatus non fuisse simplicem & absolutam, sed in Christi morte, tanquam intercedente λύτρῳ fundatam, & ἱλασμὸς relationem propriè habet, non tam ad offensas, quæ remittuntur, quam ad offensam personam, cujus ira placanda est? Hæc enim postquam reddita est propitia, tum culpam eò libentiùs condonat. Quod si quis autem ultrò remittat offensam, tùm hæc remissio nequit vocari propitiatio, per Mediatorem aliquem facta. Hæc enim vi nativæ significationis semper præsupponit indignationem in personâ læsâ, quæ si statim condonat, tùm hoc fieri dicitur, non ob præcedentem propitiationem alicuius Mediatoris, sed per spontaneam gratiæ & fauoris oblationem. Tria igitur sunt in vera propitiatione, 1. Indignatio personæ læsæ. 2. Placatio, per Mediatorem facta, & 3. culpæ post placationem condonatio. Priora verò duo Photiniani negant, & per propitiationem nil nisi planè gratuitam peccati oblationem intelligunt, id quod est ἀκύρωσον ἐν προσχηματίῳ statuere. Propitiatio enim sine præsupposita indignatione, & interveniente placatione, non est propitiatio, hoc est ipsum non ipsum.

L. Sed etiamnum habent, quod ogganniant, nempè Christum dici ἱλασμὸν, vt vetera sacrificia: In istis autem nulla fuit satisfactio, vel placatio, sed simplex reatus oblatio. Ergo nec in Christo ἱλασμὸς tale quid occurrit. Verùm vtraque propositio fallit; Aliter enim victimis pecudum, & aliter victimæ Christi tribuitur propitiatio in Scriptura. Illa fuerunt tantùm typus & vmbra: Christus autem est antitypus, ideoque sanguine suo ingressus in sanctum sanctorum, veram & æternam redemptionem inuenit. Deinde falsum est, quòd in sacrificiis nulla facta sit placatio, nulla fuerit satisfactio. Verè enim placatus est Deus, non quidem per sanguinem hircorum, sed per intuitum sanguinis Christi, quem victimæ adumbrârunt. Quantumvis igitur ex sese non satisfecerint Deo, quia tamen typi fuerunt veræ satisfactionis, quam Deus in istis typis respexit, hinc ipsæ victimæ Deum placâre dicuntur.

LI. Et hactenus de propitiatione egimus: Restat vt II. de reconciliatione pauca subiungamus. De illa notētur hæc Scripturæ testimonia: Rom. 5. vers. 10. Cum inimici essemus καταλλάγημεν reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filij eius vers. 11. Per Christum καταλλαγὴν reconciliationem accepimus Eph. 2. vers. 16. Christus reconciliauit ambos (Iudæos & gentes) in vno corpore Deo, per crucem, interficiens inimicitiam per eam. Col: 1. vers. 20. Complacuit Patri, per Christum reconciliare omnia in ipsum pacificans per sanguinem crucis eius, siue quæ in terra sunt, siue quæ in cœlis. vers. 21. & 22. Reconciliauit vos in corpore crucis eius per mortem. Iam verò reconciliare nihil est aliud, quàm in gratiam reducere, vel amissam gratiam restituere, quod cum nullo alio modo quam per crucem, & Christi sanguinem fieri potuerit, firmum vicissim argumentum pro nostrâ sententiâ inde exoritur. Ista enim reconciliatio innuit.

1. Peccatum nostrum, quo Deum offendimus.

2. Indignationem Dei ex offensa profectam.

3. Amissionem gratiæ, loco pœnæ inslictam.

4. Placationem Dei, & restitutionem gratiæ.

5. Placationis medium meritorium, quod Apostolus vocat sanguinem crucis Col. 1, v. 20. & mortem Rom. 5. v. 10.

LII. Proinde ita nunc argumentamur: In omni vera reconciliatione præcedit partis læsæ indignatio, & abalienatio à lædente, ob quam καταλλαγὴ est necessaria, Sed reconciliatio per Christum facta est vera reconciliatio, nisi putes Apostolum falsa scripsisse. Præcessit igitur partis læsæ, videlicet Dei, indignatio, & abalienatio à lædente, quod fuit genus humanum, VIterius: Cui pars lædens post indignationem & abalienationem reconciliatur, ille hoc ipso placatur, quippe cùm placare nihil sit aliud, quam ex irato & abalienato propitium & clementem reddere. Atqui genus humanum lædens, Deo irato & abalienato per Christum est reconciliatum. Ergo DEVS hoc ipso est placatus. Porrò, Omnis placatio, quę fit certè pretij interventu, non est nuda, sed satisfactoria. Dei autem placatio facta est certi pretij interventu, nempè per sanguinem & mortem Christi, tanquam per λύτρον pro peccatis nostris, Ergo placatio Dei per Christum, vi reconciliationis facta, non fuit nuda, sed satisfactoria, id quod erat concludendum.

LIII. His autem diligenter observatis in fumum abeunt quaecunque Photiniani contrà obijciunt. Nam 1. Dicunt reconciliationem hominum, non esse cum Deo, sed secum ipsis, hoc est gentium cum Iudaeis, & hominum cum Angelis partam concordiam. Resp.. Ab inclusiva ad exclusivàm non valet consequentia; nec sibi sunt mutuò opponenda, quae Apostoli coniungunt, tanquam subordinata. Triplex enim dissidium innuitur in Scripturis, quod per Christi reconciliationem sublatum. I. Diffidium inter gentes & Iudaeos, qui summo erga se invicem odio flagrabant Eph. 2. ver. 16. II. Diffidium inter homines & angelos, quippè qui hostes sunt hostium Dei, Col. 1. v. 20. III. Dissidium inter homines & Deum, qui ab illis offensus, & propter hoc abalienatus fuit, vt illi rursum reconciliari opus habuerimus Rom. 5. ver. 10. Sicut ergò priora duo dissidia includunt & praesupponunt vtriusque partis abalienationem, ita quoque de dissidio inter Deum & homines censeri debet. Notetur autem, quod Dei abalienatio fuerit omnium prima & summa, à qua dependent reliqua dissidia. Quia enim Deus erat offensus, hinc Angeli quoque nobis indignabantur, & indè secuta est mutua inter Iudaeos & gentes discordia. Vt ergò Dei abalienatio, ita & reconciliatio prima & summa est. Placato enim Deo, spontè desierunt dissidia reliqua. Et quoniam Dei placatio per sanguinis effusionem facta est, hinc etiam Angeli hominesque Iudaei & gentiles per crucem Christi dicuntur reconciliati, non quod vel Angelis vel Iudaeis à Christo fuerit satis factum, sed qua salutaris illa concordia, fructus & effectus est consequens reconciliationem Dei. (cui soli satisfactu) in sanguine & morte Christi fundatam, Vtenim no Angelis, non hominibus peccavimus, sed soli Deo, & nihilominus ex peccato, quo Deum offendimus & dissidere fecimus, exortae sunt reliquae inter Angelos & homines inimicitiae: Sic soli Deo per Christi sanguinem satisfactum est, & nihilominus ex Christi morte tanquam prima omnium beneficiorum causa reconciliatio vel concordia mutua Angelorum & hominum profluxisse recte dicitur.

LIV. Excipiunt. 2. Nos quidem Deo reconciliatos esse per simplicem in gratiam receptionem; non vero Deum tanquam inimicum nobis esse reconciliatum. Sed licet hoc expresse non dicatur, attamen subinnuitur. Nos enim eramus pars laedens & offendens, Deus erat pars laesa & offensa: ideoque fuimus divisi, & vtrinque abalienati. Christus vero intervenit, Deum nobis reconciliavit moriendo; nos Deo reconciliat, vi mortis convertendo. Sicut igitur abalienatio fuit mutua: Sic & reconciliatio. Et sicut in omni καταλλαγῇ pars laesa primo dicitur reconciliari, illique soli satisfaciendum est; ita & Deus primo reconciliandus, eique soli satisfaciendum fuit. Hinc nos sibi reconciliari dicimur per Christum 2. Cor. 5. versu 18. & subjungitur reconciliationis modus versu 21. nempe, dum Deum, quinon nouerat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos effi ceremur iustitia in ipso. Neque obstat, quod Deus ipse nos sibi reconciliasse dicitur. Hoc enim pacto non excluditur satisfactio & placatio per Christum facta, sed respicitur ad gratuitum Dei amorem & consilium, quo ipse Filium suum in mundum mittere decreuit, vt moriendo pro nobis fatisfaceret, adeoque nos Deo & Deum nobis reconciliaret. Deinde & hoc obseruandum, quod vox reconciliationis duo significet. 1. Placationem partis offensæ, & sic solus Christus Deum moriendo reconciliavit, hoc est ex irato placatum effecit. 2. Receptionem in gratiam, veterisque offensæ oblivionem, & sic Deus nos sibi reconciliavit, hoc est, ob præcedentem Christi placationem nos in gratiam denuò recepit. Proindè duo isthæc non pugnant, sed optimè, velut antecedens & consequens, vt causa & effectus cohærent. Plura dereconciliationedicentur proximè, cùm ad objectionem Photinianorum vndecimam respondebitur.


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: Argument IV. From the shedding of blood and the immolation of Christ

ARGUMENT IV. From the shedding of blood and the immolation of Christ.

LV. A most worthy passage to be noted stands explained in Heb. 9, ver. 22. Almost all things are purged by blood according to the law: καὶ χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας οὐ γίνεται ἄφεσις: without shedding of blood there is no remission, ver. 23. It is necessary therefore that the patterns of things in the heavens should be purified with these; but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. Here the Apostle says that all things are purified by blood σχεδὸν, almost or nearly, because certain purifications were made, not by blood, but by lustral water and other washings, which nevertheless themselves drew the power of purifying from the sacrifices. Thence therefore the Apostle concludes that without the shedding of blood there is no remission, by which he looks to the type of the sacrificial blood, whose shedding and sprinkling was so necessary under the law that without it no ἄφεσις was made. For no one was absolved from impurity or guilt unless he had been ceremonially sprinkled with sacrificial blood. But what else was signified by these victims than that there is no remission of sins from God without of the blood of Christ, which that sacrificial victim prefigured, he could obtain, naturally because the justice of God stood in the way, to which satisfaction could not be made except by the death of the Mediator. And the Apostle infers this very thing from there in v. 22. It is necessary therefore that the patterns of heavenly things indeed be cleansed with these: but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices. By ὑποδείγματα or patterns he understands the Old Testament and the sanctuary, which had to be sprinkled with blood and similar things, which were a shadow of things to come; by τὰ ἐπουράνια or heavenly things is indicated the New Testament, etc., or heaven itself, represented by the sanctuary, since with spiritual goods, which were prefigured by Levitical rites, as therefore the high priest about to enter the sanctuary sprinkled blood: So Christ through his own blood entered once into the holy places εἰς τὰ ἐπουράνια, having found eternal redemption. And these are those better sacrifices, or this is that more excellent victim (for the plural is put for the singular, by an enallage of numbers, on account of the antithesis) by which eternal redemption was found for us.

LV I. Thus therefore from this text of the Apostle two things shine forth. 1. That the shedding of blood to be performed by Christ the mediator was necessary. 2. That this necessity depends upon the remission of sins, since those cannot be pardoned unless blood is shed. And Christ clearly protested this very thing at the last supper, when in Matthew 26, verse 28, he says, This is my blood which is shed for the remission of sins. You have here the end of the shed blood, clearly expressed, which is not either a mere signification, or a naked confirmation and sealing, but the very remission of sins. Christ therefore died, and his blood was shed, so that we might be cleansed through that blood, and thus sins might be remitted. From which we conclude thus: Whatever is shed for the remission of sins, this is the cause of remission, not a naked sign or seal, But the blood of Christ is shed is poured out for the remission of sins. Therefore the blood of Christ was poured out as the cause of remission, not a mere sign or seal. But immediately a question arises: What kind of cause is the blood of Christ, whether efficient or meritorious? The principal efficient cause is GOD, who out of grace forgives sins. Therefore it follows that the blood of Christ is the meritorious cause, and the particles 'by' and 'on account of' hint at this very thing, when God is said to justify us by the blood of Christ, in or on account of the blood, since these are marks of a moving, impelling, and meriting cause.

For whatever an offense is remitted on account of, that is certainly the cause impelling and moving the offended person to remit it. But God, offended by sins, remits these to us on account of the blood of Christ. Therefore the blood of Christ is the cause moving and impelling God to remit sins to us. It is false, therefore, what the Socinians say, that God forgives our debts to us merely and out of free will or without merit.

LVII. It must be noted, moreover, that the blood of Christ poured out for us was sacrificial, and Christ on the altar of the cross offered himself to God the Father as a victim for our sins. For he was the antitype foreshadowed by the sacrifices of the Old Testament, and so, in order that the type might be fulfilled, it was necessary that he himself be immolated through death and offered to God. The Apostle expressly hints at this in Eph. 5:2: Christ delivered himself for us προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν τῷ Θεῷ, an oblation and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor. The Epistle to the Hebrews confirms the same several times, which is almost entirely occupied with this, to show that the old types were fulfilled in Christ, and that our sins were expiated through the sacrifice of Christ. For so it is said in chapter 5:7. Christ in the days of his flesh, offering up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears unto him that was able to save him from death, was heard in that he feared, c. 7. v. 27. Christ has no need daily, as the Priests [did] to offer sacrifices first for their own sins, then for the people's. For this he did once by offering himself, chap. 9. v. 25. Christ does not offer himself often, just as the High Priest enters into the holy places every year with the blood of others v. 26. Otherwise he would have had to suffer frequently from the foundation of the world: but now once at the consummation of the ages he has appeared for the destruction of sin, by his own sacrifice, vers. 27. And just as it is appointed for men to die once, but after this the judgment, v. 28. So also Christ was offered once, to bear the sins of many, c. 10. v. 10. We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once, v. 11. And every Priest indeed stands, daily ministering, and often offering the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. v. 12. But this one, having offered one sacrifice for sins, sits forever at the right hand of God, v. 14. For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified.

LVIII. In these things said, however, it must be diligently observed, 1. That Christ's death and the shedding of his blood is called προσφορὰ an offering, and θυσία a victim, so that a bloody and proper sacrifice may be understood. 2. That this offering was made in the days of his flesh, that is, before Christ's glorious resurrection, namely when Christ shed his blood; whence Heb. 10. v. 10. the offering of the body of Christ is called. 3. That that bloody sacrifice was offered to God, whence his preceding indignation is gathered, since expiatory sacrifices are offered to God, so that from being angry he may be made appeased. 4. That this bloody offering of the body of Christ was made for the destruction of sin, Hebr. 9. v. 26. to bear sins, v. 28. for sins, c. 10. v. 12. for our sanctification, c. 10. v. 10. 12. Hence the very blood of Jesus Christ offered on the cross is said to cleanse us from all sin, 1. John 1. v. 10. and to purge our conscience, Hebr. 9. v. 14. Finally 5. That on account of this there is the greatest difference between the ancient Priests and Christ. For 1. They offered various kinds of offerings, Heb. 10. v. 11. But this one offered nothing but one or one kind of sacrifice. 2. They, through their sacrifices, by their own virtue, could not take away sins, Heb. 10. verses 11. 12. But this one offered himself for sins, to exhaust them, and to sanctify us. 3. They offered for the people's and for their own sins, Heb. 9. verse 7. This one made an offering only for our sins, since he himself was immaculate, Heb. 9. verse 14. innocent and undefiled, c. 7. v. 26. and 4. They offered the same sacrifices πολλάκις often, Heb. 10. v. 11. This one offered one ἐφάπαξ only once. 5. They stood daily and ministered: But this one sat down at the right hand of God, Heb. 10. verse 12. But to minister is for servants, to sit is for masters. 6. They could perfect nothing by their repeated sacrifices, this one by a single offering perfected all as many as are sanctified.

LIX. These things being thus declared, we connect the following arguments: 1. Every offering for sins presupposes the offense and indignation of God; since indeed a victim is offered to that end, that God who is angry may be appeased again. But the death of Christ and the shedding of blood was an offering for our sins, as the alleged texts show. Therefore the death of Christ and the shedding of blood presupposes the offense and indignation of God. 2. Whoever, being offended and angry on account of sins, justifies the offenders through and on account of the shed blood of the victim, and forgives sins, he is truly appeased, and does not remit guilt absolutely, but through the intervention of a certain means and satisfying price. But God, offended and angry on account of sins, justifies us who had offended him, and forgives our sins, through and on account of the shed blood of Christ, the immaculate victim. Therefore God is truly appeased, and not absolutely, but by a certain means and satisfying price remits the guilt through his intercession. 3. If the blood of calves expiated sins, much more must that be attributed to the blood of Christ. For that was only a type, but this is the antitype. But the true comes first, therefore the latter also, as the Apostle concludes in Heb. 9. v. 13. 14. Whatever, however, cleanses from sins is certainly not a bare sign or seal, but rather is the cause of purgation, the price of redemption, merit: and consequently satisfaction. But the blood of Christ offered on the altar of the cross cleanses us from sins. Therefore it is not a bare sign or seal, but rather the cause of our purgation, and because it cannot properly be the efficient cause, it is rightly termed meritorious, or the price of redemption, merit, and consequently satisfaction. For that by which cleansing, or the remission of sins, has been acquired, is rightly called merit. But by the blood of Christ offered, cleansing or the remission of sins has been acquired for us. Therefore, the blood of Christ offered is rightly called the merit of cleansing.

LX. But let us now hear how the Photinians strive to corrupt these most clear testimonies of Scripture. 1. They object thus: If Christ shed His blood to the end that He might make satisfaction for our sins, how could He have said that His blood was to be shed for the remission of sins? Forasmuch as the remission or pardon of sins and satisfaction are so much at odds that, if the one is posited, the other is taken away. Resp. This is the perpetual fallacy of our adversaries, that they oppose things which are subordinate and tear apart things which ought to be joined. It is not for us to invent ἀντιφάσεις and to hold as opposites those things which Scripture everywhere joins together. Now, in truth, the remission of sins and the shedding of blood to be performed for this cause are most frequently joined, as in Matt. 26:28, Rom. 3:24-25, Heb. 9:13-14, and following. Therefore, from the positing of remission, it will by no means be permissible to argue for the exclusion of satisfaction. Nay, the contrary

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM IV. A sanguinis effusione & Christi immolatione.

LV. Dignissimus notatu loçus extat Hebr. 9. vers. 22. explicatus. Omnia penè in sanguine secundum legem mundantur : καὶ χωρὶς αἱματεκχυσίας ὐ γίνεται ἄφεσις: sine sanguinis effusione non fit remissio, ver. 23. Necesse est ergo exemplaria quidem cælestium his mundari: ipsa autem cælestia melioribus hostiis, quàm istis. Hic Apostolus ait, omnia mundari sanguine σχεδὸν ferè vel propemodùm, quia purgationes quædam fiebant, non sanguine, sed aquâ lustrali, & lotionibus aliis, quæ tamen & ipsæ mundandi vim ex sacrificiis trahebant. Indè igitur concludit Apostolus, quòd absque sanguinis effusione nulla fiat remissio, quo respicit ad typum sanguinis victimalis, cuius fusio & sparsio fuit adeò necessaria sub lege, vt absque ea nulla fieret ἄφεσις. Nemo enim ab impuritate vel culpa absolvebatur, nisi sanguine victimali, ceremonialiter esset aspersus. Quid verò aliud istis victimis notabatur quàm nullam peccatorum remissionem, à Deo absque sanguinis Christi, quem ille victimalis figuravit effusione obtinere posse, nimirum obstante iustitia Dei, cui non nisi morte Mediatoris satis fieri potuit. Atque hoc ipsum inde infert Apost. v. 22. Necesse est ergo exemplaria quidem cælestium his mundari: ipsa autem cælestia melioribus hostiis. Per ὑποδείγματα vel exemplaria intelligit Testamentum vetus & sanctuarium, quod sanguine aspergendum fuit & similia, quæ vmbra fuerunt futurorum, per τὰ ἐπουράνια vel cælestia innuitur Novum Testamentum, &c vel cælum ipsum, sanctuario repræsentatum, cùm bonis spiritualibus, quæ Leuiticis cultibus sunt præfigurata, vt ergo Sacerdos summus sanctuarium ingressurus, sanguinem aspersit : Sic Christus per proprium sanguinem intrauit semel in sancta εἰς τὰ ἐπουράνια, æterna redemtione inventâ, Et hæ sunt illæ victimæ meliores, vel hæc est illa præstantior hostia (pluralis enim pro singulari ponitur, per enallagen numerorum, propter ἀντίθεσιν) quâ æterna nobis redemtio fuit inuenta.

LV I. Sic igitur ex hoc Apostoli textu duo elucescunt. 1. Quod effusio sanguinis à Christo mediatore facienda, fuerit necessaria. 2. Quod hæc necessitas à peccatorum remissione dependeat, siquidem illa condonari nequeunt, nisi sanguis effundatur. Et hoc ipsum Christus clarè protestus est in vltima cœna, cùm Matthei 26, versu 18. inquit, Hic est sanguis meus qui effunditur in remissionem peccatorum. Habes hîc finem effusi sanguinis, luculenter expressum, qui non est vel mera significatio, vel nuda confirmatio & obsignatio, sed ipsa peccatorum remissio. Christus ergò mortuus, & sanguis ejus effusus est, vt nos per illum sanguinem mundaremur, adeoque peccata remitterentur. Ex quo sic concludimus: Quicquid effunditur in remissionem peccatorum, hoc est causa remissionis, non nudum signum vel sigillum, Sed sanguis Christi effufus est in remissionem peccatorum. Ergò sanguis Christi effusus est causa remissionis, non nudum signum aut sigillum. Statim verò exoritur quæstio; Qualis causa sit sanguis Christi, nùm efficiens, vel meritoria? Efficiens principalis DEUS est, qui ex gratia condonat peccata. Ergò sequitur, quòd sanguis Christi sit causa meritoria, & & hoc ipsum innuunt particulæ per & propter, cùm Deus dicitur nos justificare per sanguinem Christi, in vel propter sanguinem, quippe quæ sunt notæ causæ mouentis, impellentis, promerentis.

Nam propter quodcunque offensa remittitur, illud sanè est causa impellens & mouens personam læsam, vt remittat. Sed Deus per peccata læsus propter sanguinem Christi nobis ista remittit. Ergò sanguis Christi est causa mouens & impellens Deum, vt peccata nobis remittat. Falsum igitur est, quod Sociniani dicunt, Deum nudè & ex liberâ voluntate vel promerente nobis debita nostra condonare.

LVII. Notandum verò est prætereà, quòd sanguis Christi pro nobis effusus fuerit victimalis, & Christus in ara crucis semetipsum Deo Patri tanquã victimam pro peccatis nostris obtulerit. Fuit enim antitypus per sacrificia Veteris Testamenti adumbra tus, adeóque vt compleretur typus, necesse erat, ipsum per mortē inmolari Deoque offerri. Hoc Apostolus expressè innuit Eph. 5. v. 2. Christus tradidit semetipsum pro nobis προσφορὰν καὶ θυσίαν τῷ Θεῷ oblationem & hosti am Deo in od rem suauitatis. Idem aliquoties confirmat epistola ad Hebræos, quæ tota ferè in hoc occupata est, vt ostendat veteres typos in Christo impletos, & peccata nostra per Christi sacrificium expiata esse. Itâ enim dicitur cap 5. v. 7. Christus in diebus carnis suæ preces supplicationesque ad eum, qui posset illum saluum facere à morte, cum clamore valido & lacrymis offerens, exauditus est pro sua reuerentia, c. 7. v. 27. Christus non habet necessitatem quotidie, quemadmodum Sacerdotes priùs pro suis delictis hostias offerre, deinde pro populi. Hoc enim fecit semel seipsum offerendo, cap. 9. v. 25. Christus non sæpè offert semeipsum, quemadmodum Pontifex intrat in sancta per singulos annos in sanguine alieno v. 26. Alioquin oportebat eum frequenter pati ab origine mundi: nunc autem semel in consummatione seculorum ad destructionem peccati, per hostiam suam apparuit, vers. 27. Et quemadmodum statutum est hominibus semel mori, post hoc autem iudicium, v. 28. Sic & Christus semel oblatus est, ad multorum exhaurienda peccata, c. 10. v. 10. Sanctificati sumus per oblationem corporis Iesu Christi semel, v. 11. Et omnis quidem Sacerdos præstò est, quotidie ministrans, & easdem sæpè offerens hostias, quæ nunquam possunt auferre peccata. v. 12. Hic autem vnam pro peccatis offerens hostiam, in sempiternum sedet in dextris Dei, v. 14. Vnâ enim oblatione consummauit in sempiternum sanctificatos.

LVIII. In hisce autem dictis diligenter obseruandum est, 1. Quòd Christi mors & effusio sanguinis vocetur προσφορὰ oblatio, & θυσία victima, vt cruentum propriumque sacrificium intelligatur. 2. Quòd hæc oblatio facta sit in diebus carnis, hoc est, ante gloriosam Christi resurrectionem, nempè cùm Christus sanguinem effunderet; vndè Heb. 1. v. 10. oblatio corporis Christi vocatur. 3. Quòd cruenta illa hostia sit oblata Deo, vndè præcedens eius indignatio colligitur, siquidē hostiæ expiatoriæ offeruntur Deo, vt ex irato placatus efficiatur. 4. Quòd cruenta ista corporis Christi oblatio sit facta ad destructio nem peccati, Hebr. 9. v. 26. ad exhaurienda peccata, v. 28. pro peccatis, c. 10. v. 12. propter nostram sanctificationem, c. 10. v. 10. 12. Hinc ipse sanguis Iesu Christi in cruce oblatus, dicitur nos emundare ab omni peccato, 1. Iohan. 1. v. 10. & purgare conscientiā nostram, Hebr. 9. v. 14. Tandem 5. Quòd propterea inter Sacerdotes veteres, & Christum maxima sit differentia. Nam 1. Illi varia oblationum genera offerebant, Hebr. 10. v. 11. Hic verò non nisi vnam vel vnius generis θυσίαν obtulit. 2. Illi per suas hostias, ex virtute propria, peccata auferre non potuerunt, Heb. 10. vers. 11. 12. Hic verò pro peccatis seipsum obtulit, ad illa exhaurienda, & nos sanctificandos. 3. Illi pro populi & pro suis peccatis obtulerunt, Heb. 9. vers. 7. Hic pro nostris tantùm peccatis oblationem fecit, cùm ipse fuerit immaculatus, Heb. 9. vers. 14. innocens & impollutus, c. 7. v. 26. & 4. Illi easdem hostias πολλάκις saepè obtulerunt, Hebr. 10. v. 11. Hic vnam ἐφάπαξ semel tantùm. 5. Illi quotidiè stabant & ministrabant: Hic autem consedit in dextram Dei, Hebr. 10. vers. 12. Ministrare autem famulorum est, sedere dominorum. 6. Illi nihil poterant perficere suis iteratis hostijs, hic vnicâ oblatione perfecit omnes quotquot sanctificantur.

LIX. Quibus ità declaratis, sequentia argumenta nectimus: 1. Omnis oblatio pro peccatis praesupponit offensionem & indignationem Dei; quippe cùm eum in finem offeratur victima, vt Deus irascens iterum placetur. Sed mors Christi & sanguinis effusio, fuit oblatio pro peccatis nostris, vt allegatorum textuum. Ergo mors Christi & sanguinis effusio praesupponit offensionem & indignationem Dei. 2. Quicunque offensus & iratus ob peccata, offendentes per ac propter effusum victimae sanguinem iustificat, & peccata condonat, is verè placatur, nec absolutè, sed certi medij, pretijque satisfacientis interuentu culpam remittit. Atqui Deus offensus & iratus ob peccata, nos qui ipsum offenderamus, per & propter effusum Christi, immaculatae victimae sanguinem, iustificat & peccata nobis condonat. Ergo Deus verè placatus est, nec absolutè, sed certi medij pretijque satisfacientisinteruentu culpam remittit. 3. Si sanguis vitulorum expiauit peccata, multò magis id Christi sanguini erit attribuendum. Ille enim typus tantùm fuit, hic autem antitypus est. Sed verum prius, Ergo & posterius, ita concludente Apostolo Ebr. 9. v. 13. 14. Quicquid autem emundat à peccatis hoc certè non nudum signum aut sigillum, sed potiùs causa est purgationis, pretium redemptiuum, meritum: & per consequens satisfactio. Atqui sanguis Christi in ara crucis oblatus nos emundat à peccatis. Ergo non nudum signum aut sigillum, sed potiùs causa est nostræ purgationis, & quia propriè efficiens esse nequit, meritoria rectè nuncupatur, vel pretium redemptiuum, meritum, & per consequens satisfactio. Per quod enim mundatio, vel peccatorum remissio acquisita est, meritum iure appellatur. Sed per sanguinem Christi oblatum mundatio vel peccatorum remissio nobis acquisita est. Ergo sanguis Christi oblatus meritum mundationis iure appellatur.

LX. Sed audiamus iam, quomodo hæc clarissima Scripturæ testimonia corrumpere nitantur Photiniani, 1. Sic excipiunt, Si Christus eo fine fudiffet sanguinem, vt pro nostris peccatis satisfaceret, quomodo dicere potuisset, sanguinem suum fundendum esse in remissionem peccatorum? Siquidem remissio seu condonatio peccatorum, & satisfactio ita pugnant, vt posito vno, tollatur alterum. Resp. Hic perpetuus aduersariorum Elenchus est, vt opponant subordinata, & diuellant coniungenda. Nostrum non est ἀντιφάσεις fingere, & pro oppositis habere, quæ Scriptura passim copulat. Iam verò remissio peccatorum, & huius causâ facienda sanguinis effusio, sæpissimè coniunguntur, vt Matth. 26. v. 28. Rom. 3. vers. 24. 25. Hebr. 9. v. 13. 14. & seq. A positione igitur remissionis ad exclusionem satisfactionis minimè licebit argumentari. Imò contrarium po-


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: rather must be inferred

rather must be inferred. For if there is no remission without the shedding of blood, and Christ therefore offered himself on the altar of the cross, that he might appease God, and so our sins might be remitted to us, certainly the forgiveness of them will not be bare and absolute, but will be founded in the blood of Christ as an expiatory sacrifice and meritorious cause.

LXI. II. They say that the blood of Christ is shed for the remission of sins, not because the blood moved God to forgive us our sins, or because there is a peculiar power in the blood of Christ to purge sins; but that Christ willed to die in order to acquire and perfect those things without which sins could not be remitted to us, such as faith on our part, and on Christ's part, that he might become Lord over all.

Resp. 1. This is a bare fiction proposed without any reason: and if such glosses were to be admitted, there will be nothing in the Scriptures so clear that it cannot be corrupted. 2. Let a single passage be brought forward, that the immediate and proximate end of the shed blood of Christ was the acquisition of either our faith or the lordship of Christ. We do not indeed deny that faith is conferred upon us by the power of the Lord's death, which is the source of all benefits, nor do we deny that the exaltation of Christ followed the preceding death, as is said in Phil. 2, verse 9. But that Christ died primarily to the end that he might acquire either faith for us or lordship for himself, where, I pray, is it ever noted in the Scriptures? But I read this, that the blood of Christ was shed for the remission of sins, Matt. 26, verse 28; that it was necessary for Christ to die for the remission of sins, Heb. 9:22, 23; that he was offered for the destruction of sin, ver. 26; to exhaust sins, v. last, and to take them away, c. 10, v. 11, 12. For the sake of sanctifying us in this way, v. 14. Is it not therefore diabolical audacity, to deny and take away this end of the Lord's death, so clearly expressed and so often

repeated? Wherefore we conclude thus: The end of the shed blood of Christ which Scripture establishes; that, and no other, we also ought to acknowledge: But Scripture says that Christ's blood is shed for the remission of sins, not for the confirmation of a covenant or for the acquisition of those things without which sins cannot be remitted; and thus it establishes the immediate end as the very ablation or destruction of sins acquired by the bloody sacrifice. Wherefore this end, and no other, we also ought to acknowledge. 3. If to be shed for the remission of sins is therefore to be shed, so that those things may be acquired without which the remission of sins cannot happen, it follows from this inept ἀδολεσχία that the blood of Christ was shed so that blood might be shed: For without that which we do not obtain the remission of sins, for that reason Christ shed his blood; as the Photinians teach. But without the shedding of blood we do not obtain the remission of sins. Hebr. 9. verse 22. Therefore Christ shed his blood so that blood might be shed, which is inept and ridiculous. 4. He who remits sins through and on account of shed blood, indeed in such a way that without shedding he is unwilling to forgive anything, he is certainly moved to remit by that very thing. But God remits sins through and on account of the shed blood of Christ, Rom. 3. verse 25. indeed in such a way that without shedding he is unwilling to forgive anything, Hebr. 9. verse 22. Therefore God is moved to remit by that very blood of Christ. 5. It is impious and unheard of that there is no power in the blood of Christ to purge sins. We, on the contrary, argue thus: Whatever cleanses the conscience from sins, this must certainly have the power of cleansing. For the second act infallibly presupposes the first, and operation presupposes the δύναμιν of operating itself. But the blood of Christ Jesus cleanses from sins; 1. John 1. verse 7. and our conscience Hebr. 9. verse 14. Therefore, it is necessary that the blood of Christ have the power of cleansing. Therefore, they brazenly contradict the Holy Spirit himself to his face, because they take away from the blood of Christ the power of purging. For if it lacks this, the utterance of the Holy Spirit immediately collapses and must be judged as false, namely this: The blood of Jesus Christ cleanses us from all sin, in the devout and pious meditation of which saying, however, countless believers have most peacefully fallen asleep in the Lord. Add the passage of the Apostle, that Christ entered into the holy places through his own blood, and found eternal redemption, Hebr. 9. v. 12. That if the blood of calves cleansed, how much more shall the blood of Christ cleanse. v. 12. 14. that the Son of God acquired the Church for himself with his own blood, Act. 20. v. 28. that we have redemption through his blood. Ephes. 1. v. 7. that we are reconciled through his blood, Coloss. 1. vers. 20. that we have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ. 1. Pet. 1. vers. 19. and therefore it is rightly called the price of redemption, that we have been washed from sins through the blood of Christ, Apoc. 1. v. 5. And you will see clearly how great a power is attributed to the blood of Christ, which, however, the Photinians attempt to detract from it entirely, not without signal sacrilege.

LXII. III. They imagine that Christ offered himself to God for our sins not on earth, when he was dying, but in heaven, when he ascended there. For the offering, of which the Apostle speaks, was not the victim on the cross, but rather the presentation of Christ in heaven before God.

Response. Not even in a dream could this gloss and interpretation have come into anyone's mind, which is surely a most certain indication that it is fabricated, forced, and by no means flowing from the letter of the text. We do not indeed deny that Christ in his own way offered himself to the Father in heaven through his appearance, that is, presented himself as our avτoυργητὴν and advocate; but that this presentation is that offering made for our sins, we shall easily prove to be most false. For 1.

Then the offering was made, when the blood of Christ was poured out, as is hinted several times in Heb. 9. But indeed it was poured out not in heaven, but on the altar of the cross, therefore the offering of Christ was made there too. 2. Furthermore, this is unique and made once. But the presentation of Christ in heaven is continuous and will last forever; therefore they will not be synonyms, but rather most distinct. The Apostle insinuates this in Heb. 9, verse 25. Nor that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters into the holy places every year, with the blood of others. Otherwise he would have had to suffer frequently. You see here expressly what it is for the Apostle to offer himself, namely to suffer frequently. For he brings forward this reason why Christ does not offer himself often, but has perfected all things by a single offering, namely because otherwise it would follow that he must suffer frequently. Moreover, this reason would be nothing if to offer were to present himself in heaven, and not rather to pour out his blood as a victim on earth. 3. The offering of Christ is said to have been made for sins, and it is placed before the exaltation, Heb. 10, verse 12. This man, having offered one sacrifice for our sins, sits forever at the right hand of God. But the presentation of Christ himself in heaven is nowhere said to be made for our sins (intercession indeed is made for them, but not presentation) nor does that precede the exaltation, but follows it, or at least is joined with it. 4. Where there is no altar, there is no victim and no offering properly so called can be made. But in heaven there is no altar. Therefore no offering of a victim can be made there. But the offering of Christ is described in such a way that it is a θυσίαν, or an offering of a victim, Eph. 2, verse 5; Heb. 10, verse 12. Wherefore it was made nowhere except on the altar of the cross. But how can the presentation of Christ in heaven be called the offering of a victim without absurdity? For Christ, by presenting himself, was no longer suffering, much less dying. But what tricks has he devised here

Socinus to examine them one by one, the reason of δυσωπία [shame/deference] does not allow. Let the solution of the principal ones be seen in Pareus's Commentary on the Epistle to the Hebrews, ch. 9, col. 472, and following.

LXIII. IV. They say that Christ offered himself for himself, and therefore his oblation was not satisfactory. They prove the antecedent from Heb. 7 v. 27: Christ does not have necessity daily, as the Priests, first to offer sacrifices for his own sins, then for the people's; for this he did once, by offering himself. Therefore, they infer, both preceding members ought to be referred to Christ because he is said to have done that same thing which other Priests did, namely, to have offered for himself and the people.

Resp. The Apostle does not say that the Priests offered for themselves, but for their own sins. But truly Christ did not have his own sins, as the Photinians admit. How therefore can both members be referred to Christ? 2. In the preceding verse 26, Christ is called a High Priest holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners. Why therefore should he have had to offer a victim for sins for his own sake? We invert, therefore, that this particle, 'this he did once,' is only to be referred to the latter member, speaking of the sins of the people, because, if referred to the former, it begets a sense simply false and blasphemous.

Latin:

tiùs inferendum est. Si enim nulla fit remissio sine sanguinis effusione, & Christus ideò seipsum in ara crucis obtulit, vt Deum placaret, adeoque nostra nobis remitti possent peccata, vtique condonatio illorum non erit nuda & absoluta, sed in sanguine Christi tanquam hostiâ expiatoriâ, causáque meritoria fundabitur.

LXI. II. Dicunt, Christi sanguinem effundi in remissionem peccatorum non quòd sanguis Deum permoverit, vt nobis peccata condonaret, aut quod in sanguine Christi peculiaris vis sit purgandi peccata; sed Christum ideo voluisse mori, vt ea acquireret & perficeret, sine quibus peccata nobis remitti non possent, qualia sunt ex parte nostra fides, ex Christi parte, vt fieret Dominus super omnia.

Resp. 1. Nudum hoc commentum est absque omni ratione propositum : Et si talia glossemata deberent admitti, nihil in Scripturis tàm clarum erit, quod deprauari nequeat. 2. Proferatur vnicus locus, quòd immediatus proximusq; finis effusi sanguinis Christi fuerit acquisitio vel fidei nostræ, vel dominij Christi. Non quidem negamus, fidem vi mortis Dominicæ, quæ fons est omnium beneficiorum, nobis conferri, nec imus inficias, Christi exaltatione secutam esse mortem præcedentem, vt dicitur Phil. 2. versu 9. Quòd autem Christus primò in eum finem sit mortuus, vt vel nobis fide, vel sibi dominium acquireret, vbi quæso vnquam in Scripturis annotatum est? Hoc autem lego, quòd sanguis Christi sit effusus in remissionem peccatorum, Matth. 26. versu 28; quòd necesse fuerit Christum mori ob remissionem peccatorum Hebr. 9 22. 23. quòd oblatus sit ad destructionem peccati ver. 26. ad exhaurienda peccata v. vltimo, & auferenda, c. 10. v. 11. 12. Propter nos hoc pacto sanctificandos, v. 14. An non igitur Diabolica est audacia, hunc mortis Dominicæ finem tàm clarè expressum, toties que re-

petitum negare & tollere? Quapropter ita concludimus: Quem effusi sanguinis Christi finem Scriptura statuit; illum, non alium & nos agnoscere debemus: Sed Scriptura dicit, Christi sanguinem effundi in remissionem peccatorum, non in confirmationem fœderis aut in acquisitionem eorum, sine quibuis peccata remitti non possint; adeoque finem proximum statuit ipsam peccatorum ablationem vel destructionem cruenta hostia acquisitam. Quare hunc finem, non alium & nos agnoscere debemus. 3. Si sanguinem effundi, in remissionem peccatorum est ideò effundi, vt acquirantur ea, sine quibus fieri nequit remissio peccatorum, sequitur hęc inepta ἀδολεσχία sanguinem Christi effusum esse, vt sanguis effunderetur: Nam sine quo non consequimur remissionem peccatorum, propter id Christus effudit sanguinem suum; docentibus Photinianis. At sine sanguinis effusione non consequimur remissionem peccatorum. Hebr. 9. versu 22. Ergo Christus effudit sanguinem suum, vt effunderetur sanguis quod ineptum & ridiculum. 4 Qui peccata remittit per & propter sanguinem effusum, ita quidem vt sine effusione nihil condonare velit, is sanè illo ipso ad remittendum permouetur. Sed Deus peccata remittit per & propter sanguinem Christi effusum, Rom. 3. versu 25. ita quidem, vt sine effusione nihil condonare velit Hebr. 9. versu 22. Ergo Deus illo ipso sanguine Christi ad remittendum permovetur. 5. Impium & inauditum est, nullam esse in Christi sanguine vim purgandi peccata. Nos contrà sic argumentamur: Quicquid emundat conscientiam à peccatis, hoc vtique vim mundandi habeat necesse est. Actus enim secundus primum, & operatio ipsam operandi δύναμιν inesse infallibiliter præsupponit. Sed sanguis Christi Iesu emundat à peccatis; 1. Iohan. 1. versu 7. &c conscientiam nostram Hebr. 9. versu 14. Ergo sanguis Christi vim mundandi vt habeat, necesse est. In os proinde ipsi Spiritui sancto proteruè contradicunt, quia sanguini Christi vim purgandi adimunt. Hac enim si caret, statim concidit & pro falso censeri debet affatum Spiritus sancti, nempè istud: Sanguis Iesu Christi emundat nos ab omni peccato, in cuius tamen dicti devotâ piâque meditatione innumeri fideles placidissimè obdormierunt in Domino. Adde locum Apostoli, quod Christus per proprium sanguinem introiuerit in sancta, & æternam redemtionem inuenerit, Hebr. 9. v. 12. Quòd si sanguis vitulorum mundauit, multò magis emundet sanguis Christi. v. 12. 14. quod Filius Dei Ecclesiam acquisiuerit sibi proprio sanguine, Act. 20. v. 28. quòd habeamus redemtionem per sanguinem. Ephes. 1. v. 7. quod simus reconciliati per sanguinem, Coloss. 1. vers. 20. quod pretioso Christi sanguine redemti simus. 1. Pet. 1. vers. 19. ideoque pretium redemtionis rectè appellatur, quòd abluti simus à peccatis per sanguinem Christi, Apoc. 1. v. 5. Et videbis luculenter, quanta vis Christi sanguini attribuatur, quam tamen omnem non sine insigni sacrilegio illi derogare conantur Photiniani.

LXII. III. Fingunt, Christum se obtulisse Deo pro peccatis nostris non in terris, cùm moreretur, sed in cœlis, cùm eò ascenderet. Oblationem enim, de quâ Apostolus loquitur, non fuisse victimam in cruce, sed potiùs præsentationem Christi in cælo coram Deo.

Respon. Nè quidem per somnium hæc glossa & interpretatio potuisset alicui venire in mentem, quod sanè indicium est certissimum, illam esse confictam, violentam, & ex litera textus minimè fluentem. Non quidem negamus Christum suo modo per apparitionem se Patri obtulisse in cœlo, hoc est, præsentâsse, vt αυτηγητὴν & aduocatum nostrum; quòd autem hæc præsentatio sit illa pro peccatis nostris facta oblatio, falsissimum esse facilè evincemus. Nam 1.

Tùm facta est oblatio, cùm effusus est sanguis Christi, vt Hebr. 9. aliquoties innuitur. At verò non in cœlis, sed in ara crucis effusus fuit, Ergo & ibi facta est Christi oblatio. 2. Hæc porrò vnica est & semel facta. Sed Christi in cœlis præsentatio, est continua & æternùm duratura; Ergo non erunt Synonyma, sed potiùs distinctissima. Insinuat hoc Apostolus Hebr. 9. vers. 25. Neque vt sæpè offerat semetipsum, quemadmodum Pontifex intrat in sancta per singulos annos, in sanguine alieno. Alioquin oportebat eum frequenter pati Vides hîc expressè, quid Apostolo sit semetipsum offerre, nimirùm frequenter pati. Hanc enim rationem affert, cur Christus seipsum non sæpè offerat, sed vnicâ oblatione omnia consummâuerit, nempè quia alias sequeretur, quòd frequenter pati debeat. Nulla autem foret hæc ratio, si offerre, esset sese præsentare in cœlo, & non potiùs sanguinem suum tanquam victimalem, in terris effundere. 3. Oblatio Christi dicitur facta esse pro peccatis, & præmittitur exaltationi, Hebr. 10. vers. 12. Hic vnam pro peccatis nostris offerens hostiam, in sempiternum sedet in dextera Dei. Sed ipsa Christi in cœlis præsentatio nullibi dicitur fieri pro peccatis nostris (intercessio quidem fit pro ijs, sed non præsentatio) nec illa præcedit exaltationem, sed sequitur, aut certè cum ipsa coniuncta est. 4. Vbi non habetur altare, ibi nulla est victima & nulla fieri potest oblatio propriè dicta. Sed in cœlo nullum est altare Ergò nulla ibi fieri potest oblatio victimæ. Christi autem oblatio ita describitur, quòd θυσίαν, vel hostiæ sit oblatio, Eph. 2. vers. 5. Hebr. 10. vers 12. Quare nullibi nisi in arâ crucis facta. Quomodo autem Christi præsentatio in cœlis, sine absurditate nominari potest victimæ oblatio? Christus enim se præsentando non ampliùs patiebatur, multò minùs moriebatur. Quas verò strophas hic confinxit

Socinus eas singulás examinare, δυσωπία ratio non admittit. Videatur præcipuarum solutio in Commentario Parei super Epistolam ad Heb. c. 9. col. 472. & seqq.

LXIII. IV. Aiunt Christum seipsum pro seipso obtulisse, ideóq́ oblationem eius satisfactoriā non fuisse. Anteçedés pbant ex Heb. 7 v. 27. Christus no h.. bet necessatè quôtidiè quēadmodu Sacerdotes, priùs pro suis deustis hostias offerre, deindè pro populi, Hoc enim fecit semel, seipsum offerendo. Ergó, inferunt, vtrumque præcedens membrum referri debet ad Christū quia illud spsum fecisse dicitur; quòd alij Sacerdotes, nempè pro se & populo obtulisse.

Resp. Apostolus non ait, Sacerdotes pro se, sed pro suis proprijs peccatis obtulisse. At verò Christus peccata propria non habuit, vufatentur Photiniani Qui ergo vtrumque membrum referri potest ad Christum? 2. Versu præcedente 26. Christus dicitur Pontifex sanctus, innocens, impollutus, segregatus a peccatoribus. Cur ergò victimā pro peccatis expiatoriam suâ causâ offerre debuisset? Inuertimus ergo quòd particula ista, hoc fecit semel, tantùm ad posterius membrum, de peccatis populi loquens sit referenda, quia relata ad prius, gignit sensum simpliciter falsum & blasphemum.


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: Argument V Concerning the assumption of our guilt and punishment

From the taking upon himself of our guilt and punishment.

LXIV. Three things especially said pertain to this, namely, Isaiah 53, 2 Cor. 5 v. 21, Gal. 3 v. 13. From which, taken together, we argue thus: If Christ received our sins into himself, and at the same time the punishments of sins, then it follows that he offered himself in our place, and thus satisfied God the Father for us. But the antecedent is true. Wherefore the consequent ought not to be denied. We shall provide the minor, proven by clear sayings.

LXV. ON THE TESTIMONY OF ISAIAH. CH. 53.

That the Prophet speaks of Christ in that chapter, the Photinians cannot deny, because the Evangelists and Apostles themselves interpreted it of Christ, Mark 8:17, Acts 8:32, 1 Pet. 2:24. What, therefore, the Prophet notes concerning him, let us hear. The fourth verse is as follows: Surely he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows, and we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and humbled. Two roots are found in the Hebrew text, נשא and סבל. Both denote to lift or to raise up, or to take upon oneself a certain burden to carry, to bear, and to carry. Thus נשא is used in Exod. 19:4, ואשא And I bore you on eagles' wings. Exod. 28:29, ונשא And Aaron shall bear or carry the names of the children of Israel in the breastplate. Josh. 3:3, The priests the Levites נשאים carrying it.

And from that is the noun משא a burden, which is carried, or a weight. But especially, when the discourse is about sins, then it signifies to pay, to give satisfaction, or to take the punishments of sins upon oneself, as Exod. 28:last verse, And they shall not ישאו bear the sin, that is, the punishment of the sin. Lev. 6:1, ונשא And he shall bear his sin. Targum ויקבל and he shall receive. Ezek. 18:19, Why does not נשא the son bear, because of the sin of the father? Targum by the latter. And verse 20, The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, and the father shall not bear the iniquity of the son.

The other root סבל is more significant and perpetually denotes to carry, to bear, to shoulder upon the shoulders, Gen. 49:15, He bowed his shoulder לסבל to bear. Isa. 46:4, even to old age I אסבל will carry you. Psalm 144:14, Our oxen מסבלים burdened. Thence is the noun, סבל a porter, by which something is carried or borne on the shoulder, as 1 Kings 5:15, And Solomon had seventy thousand, carrying סבל the burden. Targum בכתפא that is, they were porters, who carried on their shoulders stones to the place to which the wagons came, which could not ascend the mountain.

also from thence the name סבל or סבל, a burden or a load, or that which is carried on the shoulders, as Psalm 81, v. 7: I removed his shoulder from the burden [מסבל]. Nor can any passage be brought to the contrary where סבל, and those words which descend from it, does not denote the taking up of a weight or an onerous carrying, from which we conclude that this root is to be explained in the present text of Isaiah in the same and no other sense.

LXVI. Now, furthermore, it is asked: What did Christ take upon himself and carry as a burden? And the Prophet answers חלינו ומכאבינו, our infirmities and our sorrows. Now, infirmities are twofold: some of the body, some of the mind. The words of the Prophet cannot be taken concerning diseases of the body: for Christ did not receive those into himself, since it is never read that he was infirm in body and exposed to all diseases. Wherefore internal sorrows and agonies of the soul are chiefly understood, for which reason he himself is also said to have been scourged, humbled, and stricken by God. Now, since this burden of sorrows was imposed by God, it was imposed either justly or unjustly. No pious person would affirm the latter. But if the former is assumed, it follows that Christ was stricken on account of some fault, since every just affliction presupposes a fault. Therefore he was stricken either for his own or for another's. Not for his own, because he had none. Therefore for another's, or ours, and consequently our sins were imputed to him, and the punishments of our sins were imposed upon him to bear, so that by our infirmities nothing else can be understood than the sense of divine wrath, sorrow of soul, and death itself, which punishments Christ sustained in our place. The LXX notice this sense, and therefore translated it in this way: ὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται. He bears our sins and suffers for us. Now, to bear sins is the punishment to take up theirs, to carry as a burden, and patiently to sustain, the Chaldean looked to the same when he translated, He himself shall pray for our sins, and our offenses shall be forgiven on account of him. Which things being thus declared, we now conclude in this way: Whoever thus carries the sorrows of others, so that he himself is struck and humbled, he truly and really takes upon himself the punishments of others. But Christ so carried our sorrows and languors of soul, that he himself was struck and humbled. Therefore Christ truly and really took upon himself the punishments to be inflicted upon us.

LXVII. But the Prophet himself declares these things more clearly in v. 5, which reads thus: But he himself was wounded on account of our iniquities, he was bruised on account of our crimes, the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his stripe we are healed. Two things are touched upon in this verse: 1. What is derived from us onto Christ. 2. What is derived from Christ onto us. From us is derived the wounding and bruising, and imposed upon Christ. For for what cause was he himself wounded? On account of our iniquities, says the Prophet. In the Hebrew it is מִפְּשָׁעֵינוּ from our transgressions, and מֵעֲוֺנֹתֵינוּ from our iniquities, as if these very things had driven him and so pressed him, that he was necessarily wounded. The same is repeated in v. 8. On account of the transgression of my people a blow to him, or he was cut off from the land of the living on account of the transgression of the people, to whom the blow was otherwise owed. But to what end was he himself, innocent, bruised on account of our crimes? Namely, that we might have peace, lest we ourselves be forced to sustain those wounds. Hence in the Hebrew it is, The chastisement of our pacifications was upon him, that is, he was chastised for our peace, And in his stripe there is healing for us, that is; through and on account of his passion and death we have been freed from the punishments otherwise to be undergone, because he in our place took them up and thus satisfied the divine wrath.

LXIIX. But from these most clear words these arguments flow. 1. Whoever, being innocent, is struck by a just judge on account of the iniquities of others, that person suffers in the place of others, and by suffering satisfies the judge. But Christ, being innocent, was struck by God, a just judge, on account of our iniquities. Therefore, Christ suffered and died in our place, and by suffering satisfied God the judge. 2. Whatever passion and death yields to the pacification, liberation, and salvation of those who otherwise themselves ought to have suffered and died, that is meritorious and satisfactory. But the passion and death of Christ yields to the pacification, liberation, and salvation of all of us, who otherwise ourselves ought to have suffered and died. Therefore, the passion and death of Christ was meritorious and satisfactory. 3. Whatever impelling and final cause of the passion of Christ Scripture teaches, that and no other ought we to profess. But Scripture teaches that the impelling cause of the passion of Christ was our iniquities, which God laid upon Christ; but the final cause was our pacification and liberation, which Christ merited by his death. Therefore, we ought to profess these only, and not invent other causes. 4. Whatever heals us from the diseases of the soul, it is necessary that it have a singular power of healing. But the bruise, that is, the passion and death of Christ, heals us from the diseases of the soul. Therefore, the bruise, that is, the passion and death of Christ, must necessarily have a singular power of healing.

XIX. Moreover, so that no handle for doubting may remain concerning these things, the Prophet significantly adds in verse 6: The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all. Der HERR warff vnser aller Sünd auff jhn. Here is noted 1. The indignation of God. For he who casts various punishments and afflictions due to sins upon someone, must certainly be angry and alienated on account of sins. 2. The imputation of our crimes. For in no other way could our crimes be cast upon Christ, than insofar as they were imputed by God himself, whose wrath was to be appeased, and whose justice was to be satisfied. 3. The imposition of punishments. For this follows the imputation of sins. And that casting of iniquities was not bare, but burdensome, joined with the crushing of Christ. Wherefore both are understood by the word עון, both the sin itself, and the punishment due to the sin. 4. Our liberation. For while our transgressions were cast upon Christ, and he himself was crushed because of our iniquities, then we were liberated and reconciled with God, since through that passion of the innocent Christ, undertaken in our place, divine justice was satisfied. In the Hebrew text there is an elegant metaphor: God caused the iniquity or punishment of us all to meet upon him. The human race is introduced as a sheepfold dispersed and abandoned, and God as an angry judge, and alienated from us. Christ intervenes, and willed to act as Mediator. But because it was first necessary to satisfy God: Behold! upon Christ who placed himself as a mediator, God caused our sins to meet and rush, so that he might undergo the punishment due to us, and be crushed in our place. Thus therefore Christ the unique Mediator took away sins from us, by taking them upon himself: he appeased the wrath in God, by undergoing the punishments of sin: but to us he brings grace from the appeased God, by applying his precious λύτρον, and by imputing his own justice.

LXX. But so that the force of the saying may become more manifest, we include it in these Syllogisms 1. Whoever places or casts sins and the punishment of sins upon someone, he is angry and indignant because of the sins. But God the Father cast our sins and the punishment of our sins upon Christ. Therefore God the Father was angry and indignant because of the sins. 2. Upon whom the punishment of another is cast, he is necessarily compelled to bear it. But our punishment was cast upon Christ. Therefore he necessarily bore it, because the carrying follows immediately upon the casting or the imposition of a burden. 3. He who by suffering carries another's iniquity cast upon himself, he is punished and suffers in the place of others. But Christ by suffering carried the iniquities of us all, cast upon him by God the Father. Therefore, Christ was punished and suffered in the place of us all. 4. Whoever, being innocent, suffers in the place of the guilty, so that they might not suffer, he makes satisfaction by suffering for the guilty. But Christ, being innocent, suffered in the place of guilty men, so that they might not suffer. Therefore, Christ, being innocent, made satisfaction for guilty men. And this is what is said in verse 10, that Christ laid down his soul as אשם, a trespass, or a sacrifice for sin, zum Schuldtopffer; that is, he himself willed to suffer so that we might be freed, he himself to die so that we might live; he himself to offer his soul so that the wrath of the heavenly Father might be appeased, and he himself might be reconciled to us. The same is confirmed by the sayings in Isaiah 43, verse 24, John 1, verse 29, 1. Pet. 2, verse 24, the explanation of which is to be sought elsewhere.

Latin:

A susceptione culpæ & pœnæ nostræ.

LXIV. Tria cum primis dicta huc pertinent, nempè Esai. 53. seqq. 2. Cor. 5. v. 21. Gal. 3. v. 13. Ex quibus iunctim ita argumentamur: Si Christus peccata nostra in se recepit, & vnâ peccatorum pœnas, tùm sequitur, quòd nostri loco se obtulerit, adeoque Deo Patri pro nobis satisfecerit. Sed antecedens verum est. Quare consequens negari non debet. Minorem verò dictis luculentis probatam dabimus.

LXV. DE TESTIMONIO ESAIAS. C. 53.

DE Christo Prophetam loqui in isto capite, inficiari haut possunt Photiniani, quia ipsi Euangelistæ & Apostoli de Christo interpretati sunt, Marc. 8. v. 17. Act. 8. v. 32. 1. Pet. 2. v. 24. Quid igitur Propheta de ipso annotet, audiamus. Versus quartus sic habet: Verè languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portauit, & nos reputauimus eum flagellatum, percussum à Deo, & humiliatum. Duæ radices habentur in textu Hebraico נשא & סבל. Vtraque notat leuare vel eleuare, aut onus quoddam ad portandum assumere, gestare & portare. Ita sumitur נשא Exod. 19. vers. 4. ואשא Et portaui vos super alas aquilarum. Exod. 28. vers. 29. ונשא & portabit vel gestabit Aaron nomina filiorum Israel in pectorali. Ios. 3. v. 3. Sacerdotes Leuitæ נשאים portantes eam.

Et inde est nomen משא onus, quod portatur vel pondus. Imprimis vero, cùm sermo est de peccatis, tùm significat luere, pœnas dare, vel peccatorum pœnas in se recipere, vt Exod. 28. vers. vlt. Et non ישאו portabunt peccatum, id est, pœnam peccati. Leuit. 6. vers. 1. ונשא Et portabit peccatum suum. Targum ויקבל & accipiet. Ezech. 18. v. 19. Quare non נשא portat filius, ob peccatum patris? Targum per vltim. Et vers. 20. Filius non portabit iniquitatem Patris, & Pater non portabit iniquitatem filij.

Altera radix סבל significantior est & perpetuò notat gestare, portare, baiulare super humeris Gen. 49. v. 15. Inclinauit humerum suum לסבל ad portandum. Esa. 46. v. 4. hucusque ad senium ego אסבל ortabo vos. Psalm. 144. v. 14. Boues nostri מסבלים onusti. Inde est nomen, סבל baiulus, quo aliquid portatur aut gestatur humero, vt 1. Reg. 5. v. 15. Et erat Salomoni seu tuaginta millia, portant סבל cainlu. Targum בכתפא hoc est, erant baiuli, qui humeris suis deferebant lapides ad locum, in quem veniebant currus, qui non poterant montem afcendere.

etiam inde nomen סבל vel סבל Onus aut gestamen, vel id, quod humeris gestatur vt Psalm. 81. v. 7. Remoui מסבל ab onere humerum eius, Neque potest vllus in contrarium adferri locus, vbi סבל, & quæ descendunt indè, non denotet susceptionem ponderis, vel onerosam portationem, ex quo colligimus, eodem nec alio sensu sensu radicem istam in præsenti Esaiæ textu exponendam esse.

LXVI. Iam verò vlterius quæritur, Quidnam Christus in se susceperit & tanquam onus gestauerit? Et respondet Propheta חלינו ומכאבינו Languores nostros & dolores nostros. Sunt autem languores duplices, quidam corporis quidam animi. De morbis corporis verba Prophetæ nequeunt accipi: Nam illos Christus in se non recepit, siquidem corpore infirmatus & omnibus morbis expositus fuisse nunquam legitur. Quare dolores interni, & angores animæ potissimum intelliguntur, ob quam causam & ipse flagellatus, humiliatus, percussusq́; à Deo dicitur. Iam cùm à Deo fuerit impositum hoc onus dolorum, vel iustè est impositum vel iniustè. Hoc nemo pius affirmauerit. Illud verò si assumitur, ob culpam aliquam Christum fuisse percussum sequitur, cùm omnis afflictio iusta præsupponat culpam. Ergo percussus est vel ob suam, vel alienam. Non ob suam, quia nullam habuit. Ergo ob alienam seu nostram, & per consequens, nostra ipsi peccata imputata, & nostrorum peccatorum pœnæ ad portandum ipsi sunt impositæ, vt ita per languores nostros nihil possit intelligi aliud, quàm sensus iræ diuinæ, mœror animi & mors ipsa, quas pœnas Christus nostri loco sustinuit. Animaduertunt hunc sensum LXX. ideoque hoc modo verterunt, ὗτος τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν φέρει καὶ περὶ ἡμῶν ὀδυνᾶται. Iste peccata nostra portat & pro nobis dolet, Portare autem peccata, est pœnam eorum suscipere, gestare velut onus, & patienter sustinere, Chaldæus eodem respexit cùm vertit, Ipse deprecabitur pro peccatis nostris, & delicta nostra propter eum dimittentur. Quibus ita declaratis iam hoc modo colligimus: Quicunque sic portat alienos dolores, vt ipse percutiatur & humilietur, is verè & realiter pœnas aliorum in se suscipit. Sed Christus nostros dolores & languores animi sic portauit, vt ipse fuerit percussus & humiliatus. Ergo Christus verè & realiter pœnas nobis infligendas in sese suscepit.

LXVII. Sed ipse Propheta hæc luculentiùs declarat v. 5. qui sic habet: Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra, disciplina pacis nostræ super eum, & livore eius sanati sumus. Duo tanguntur hoc versiculo: 1. Quid à nobis in Christum deriuatum. 2. Quid à Christo in nos deriuatum sit. A nobis deriuata est vulneratio & attritio, Christóque imposita. Quam enim ob causam ipse vulneratus fuit? Propter iniquitates nostras, inquit Propheta. In Hebræo est מִפְּשָׁעֵינוּ à præuaricationibus nostris, & מֵעֲוֺנֹתֵינוּ ab iniquitatibus nostris, quasi hæ ipsæ illum adegerint & ita presserint, vt necessariò vulneraretur. Idem repetitur v. 8. Propter præuaricationem populi mei plaga ei, vel abscissus est de terrâ viuentium ob præuaricationem populi, cui plaga aliàs debebatur. Sed quem in finem ipse innocens ob scelera nostra est attritus? Nempè vt nos pacem haberemus, nè nos ipsi vulnera illa sustinere cogeremur. Hinc in Hebræo est, Castigatio pacificationum nostrarum super eum, id est, castigatus est pro pace nostra, Et in liuore eius medicatum est nobis, hoc est; per & propter eius passionem mortemque nos liberati sumus à pœnis, aliàs subeundis, quia ipse loco nostri eas suscepit adeóque iræ diuinæ satisfecit.

LXIIX. Ex istis verò clarissimis verbis hæc fluunt argumenta. 1. Quicunque innocens propter iniquitates alienas à iusto iudice percutitur, is loco aliorum patitur, patiendo iudici satisfacit. Sed Christus innocens, propter iniquitates nostras, à iusto iudice Deo percussus est. Ergo Christus loco nostri passus mortuusque est, & patiendo iudici Deo satisfecit, 2. Quaecunque passio & mors cedit in pacificationem, liberationem & salutem eorum, qui aliàs ipsi debebant pati & mori, ista est meritoria & satisfactoria. Sed Christi passio & mors cedit in pacificationem, liberationem & salutem nostrûm omnium, qui aliàs ipsi debebamus pati & mori. Ergo Christi passio & mors fuit meritoria & satisfactoria. 3. Quam passionis Christi causam impellentem & finalem Scriptura docet, illam non aliam nos profiteri debemus. Sed Scriptura docet, causam passionis Christi impellentem fuisse iniquitates nostras, quas Deus Christo imposuit; finalem verò pacificationem & liberationem nostram, quam Chri stus morte sua promeruit.
