Ergo has tantùm profiteri, non alias causas comminisci debemus. 4. Quicquid nos à morbis animae sanat, id vim sanandi singularem vt habeat necesse est. Sed liuor, hoc est, passio & mors Christi nos à morbis animae sanat. Ergo liuor, hoc est, passio & mors Christi vim sanandi singularem, vt habeat necesse est.

XIX. De his autem nè vlla dubitandi ansa remaneat, Propheta vers. 6. significanter addit: Dominus posuit in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrûm. Der HERR warff vnser aller Sünd auff jhn. Notatur hîc 1. Indignatio Dei. Qui enim varias poenas & afflictiones peccatis debitas in aliquem conjicit, eum sanè ob peccatis iratum & abalienatum esse oportet. 2. Imputatio nostrorum scelerum. Nullo enim alio modo nostra in Christum scelera conjici potuerunt, quàm in quantum imputata sunt ab ipso Deo, cuius ira placanda, & cuius iustitiæ satisfaciendum erat. 3. Impositio pœnarum. Hæc enim sequitur imputationem peccatorum. Et fuit coniectio illa iniquitatum non nuda, sed onerosa, cum attritione Christi coniuncta. Quare vtrumque intelligitur per vocem עון, tum peccatum ipsum, tùm pœna peccato debita. 4. Liberatio nostra. Dum enim in Christum prævaricationes nostræ sunt coniectæ, & attritus ipse fuit ob iniquitates nostras, tùm nos liberati sumus & cum Deo reconciliati, quoniam per illam innocentis Christi passionem, nostri loco susceptam, iustitiæ diuinæ satisfactum est. In textu Hebræo elegans est metaphora: Deus fecit occurrere in eum iniquitatem vel pœnam omnium nostrum. Introducitur genus humanum velut ouile dispersum & derelictum, Deusque vt iratus iudex, & abalienatus à nobis. Interuenit Christus, & Mediatorem agere voluit. Quia verò prius erat satisfaciendum Deo: Ecce! in Christum qui se medium ponebat, fecit Deus occurrere & irruere nostra peccata, vt pœnam nobis debitam subiret, & nostri loco attereretur. Ita igitur Christus Mediator vnicus à nobis abstulit peccata, in se suscipiendo: in Deo placauit iram, pœnas peccati subeundo: nobis verò affert à Deo placato gratiam, pretiosum λύτρον suum applicando, suamque iustitiam imputando.

LXX. Verum vt vis dicti evadat manifestior, his eam Syllogismis includimus 1. Quicunque peccata & pœnam peccatorum ponit vel conijcit in aliquem, ille succenset & indignatus ob peccata. Sed Deus Pater peccata & pœnam peccatorum nostrorum coniecit in Christum. Ergo Deus Pater succensuit & indignatus est ob peccata. 2. In quem conijcitur pœna aliena, ille necessario eam gestare cogitur. Sed in Christum pœna nostra est coniecta. Ergo illam necessario gestauit, quia coniectionem vel impositionem oneris statim sequitur gestatio. 3. Qui patiendo gestat alienam iniquitatem in se coniectam, is loco aliorum punitur & patitur. Sed Christus patiendo gestavit iniquitates omnium nostrûm, in se à Deo Patre coniectas. Ergò, Christus loco nostrûm omnium punitus & passus est. 4. Quicunque innocens loco reorum patitur, nè illi patiantur, hic pro reis patiendo satisfacit. Sed Christus innocens, loco reorum hominum passus est, nè illi paterentur, Ergò Christus innocens pro reis hominibus satisfecit. Atque hoc est, quod dicitur versu 10. Christum posuisse animam suam אשם delictum, seu hostiam pro delicto zum Schuldtopffer / hoc est ipse pati voluit vt nos liberaremur, ipse mori, vt nos viueremus; Ipse animam suam offerre vt ira cœlestis Patris placaretur, & ipse nobis reconciliaretur. Idem confirmant dicta Esa. 43. versu 24. Iohan. 1. v. 29. 1. Pet. 2. vir. 24 quorum explicatio aliundè est petanda.


### Question III. By what principal sayings of Scripture can the satisfaction of…: LXXI. concerning the Saying 2 Cor. 5, verse 21. Him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God…

LXXI. CONCERNING THE SAYING 2 Cor. 5, verse 21. Him who knew no sin he made to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him.

Here, in turn, it is hinted what loss Christ received from us, and what benefit we received from him: for he himself was made 1. sin, not by a change of essence, but by the imputation of our sin. For by this phrase, 'God made Christ sin,' the Apostle wishes nothing else to be understood than what Isaiah said, that God cast our iniquities upon Christ. And it is known that אשם or sin in the Old Testament is often taken for a sacrifice expiating sin; the Apostle wished to retain the Hebraism and to indicate that Christ was a victim offered to God the Father for the expiation of our iniquities, as is clearly asserted in Ephesians 5, verse 2, Hebrews 9, verse 26, chapter 10, verse 12. 2. For us, ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, that is, in our place. For because our sins were imputed to Christ, if he was indeed a victim for them, it follows that he suffered and died in our place, 3. To this end, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. For as our iniquity is imputed to Christ, so Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, by which agreement we are justified and obtain forgiveness of sins. From that statement, therefore, we conclude thus: for the sake of expiation, he suffers in the place of others, and by suffering satisfies for them. But Christ was made sin or a victim for the sin of other men, for the sake of expiation, Therefore Christ suffered in the place of men, and by suffering satisfied for them.

LXXII. ON THE STATEMENT Gal. 4. verse 13. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. Now the curse of the law is nothing other than a condemnatory sentence concerning the undergoing of punishments owed to sin. Christ did not fall into this curse by chance, but was made a curse by the Father who cast iniquities upon him, who willed him to be crushed and chastised, not indeed for his own sake, since he was innocent, but in our place, so that we would not be compelled to experience that curse of the law or sustain the punishments themselves. Whence an argument arises of this kind: Whoever, being innocent, undertakes the punishments expressed by the law for others, and thus becomes a curse, so that he may free the guilty from the guilt of the curse, he suffers in the place of others. But indeed Christ, being innocent, undertook the punishments expressed by the law for us who were guilty, and thus was made a curse, so that he might free us from the guilt of the curse. Therefore he suffered in our place, and satisfied for us who were guilty.

LXXIII. Now the exceptions of Socinus ought to be subjoined, as also other reasons for the merit of Christ, such as can be taken from the blotting out of the handwriting Col. 3. v. 14. from the crushing of the serpent Gen. 3. v. 15. from the making of peace Eph. 1. verse 14. Col. 1. v. 20. from the sacrifices which were types of Christ, from the scapegoat Lev. 16. v. 14.

from the red heifer. Num. 19. verses 4. 5. from the bronze serpent Num. 21. and similar things. But because this disputation has otherwise grown sufficiently, we reserve those arguments for another time and occasion, and thus we make an end here, devoutly invoking Christ the Mediator, that He may confound the enemies of His most holy merit, and may always preserve the truth of this article pure and unblemished against any insults of Satan, to the glory of His name, and the edification of the whole Church. AMEN.

Latin:

LXXI. DE DICTO 2. Cor. 5. versu 21. Eum qui non nouerat peccatum pro nobis peccatum fecit, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso.

Hic vicissim innuitur, quid Christus à nobis damni, quid nos ab ipso commodi accepèrimus: Ipse enim factus est. 1. peccatum non per mutationem essentiæ, sed per imputationem peccati nostri. Nam hâc phrasi, Deus fecit Christum peccatum, Apostolus nil aliud vult intellectum, quàm quod Esaias dixit, Deum coniecisse iniquitates nostras in Christum. Et notum est quod אשם vel peccatum in Veteri Testamēto sæpè sumitur pro hostiâ peccatũ expiante, Hebraismum Apostolus retinere voluit, & indicare, Christum fuisse victimam; Deo Patri pro expiandis nostris iniquitatibus oblatum, vti Ephes. 5. versu 2. Hebr. 9. versu 26. cap. 10. versu 12. clarè. asseritur. 2. Pronobis ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν, id est nostri loco. Quia enim Christo peccata nostra imputata funt, verò iis esset victima, vtique nostri loco eum passum mortuumque fuisse consequitur, 3. In hunc finem, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso. Vt enim Christo nostra iniquitas, sic nobis Christi iustitia imputatur, quo pacto iustificamur & peccatorum veniam consequimur. Ex isto igitur dicto sic concludimus: Quisunque sit peccatum, seu victima pro alieno peccato, expiationis causâ, is loco aliorum patitur, & patiendo pro ijs satisfacit. Sed Christus factus est peccatum seu victima pro alieno hominum peccato, expiationis causâ, Ergò Christus loco hominum passus est, & patiendo pro ijs satisfecit.

LXXII. DE DICTO Gal. 4. vers. 13. Christus nos redemit de maledictione legis, factus pro nobis maledictum. Est autem legis maledictio nihil aliud, quàm damnatoria sententia de subeundis pœnis peccato debitis. In hanc maledictionem non fortè fortunâ Christus incidit, sed factus est à Patre maledictum qui coniecit in ipsum iniquitates, qui voluit ipsum atteri & castigari, non quidem causa sui, cùm fuerit innocês, sed nostri loco, nè illam legis maledictionē experiri vel pœnas ipsas sustinere cogeremur. Vnde argumentum exurgit huiusmodi, Quicunque innocens pœnas lege expressas pro alijs suscipit, atque sic maledictum sit, vt nocentes à reatu maledictionis liberet, is loco aliorum patitur. At verò Christus innocens pœnas lege expressas pro nobis reis suscepit, atq; sic maledictum factus est, vt nos à reatu maledictionis liberaret. Ergo nostri loco passus est, & pro nobis reis satisfecit.

LXXIII. Subiungendæ nunc esset Socini exceptiones, yt & aliæ pro Christi merito rationes, quales desumi possunt à deletione chirographi Col. 3. v. 14. à contritione serpētis Gen. 3. v. 15. à pacificatione Eph. 1. vers. 14. Col. 1. v. 20. à sacrificijs quæ fuerunt typi Christi, ab hirco emissario Lev, 16. v. 14.

à rufa iuvenca. Num. 19. versu 4. 5. à serpente æneo Num. 21. & similibus. Quia verò hæc disputatio aliàs satis excrevit, nos argumenta ista alteri tempori & occasioni reservamus, adeoque hic finem facimus, Christum Mediatorem devotè invocantes, vt hostes meriti sui sanctissimi confundat, & veritatem huius articuli contra quosvis Satanæ insultus semper puram & illibatam conseruet, ad nominis sui gloriam, & totius Ecclesiæ ædificationem. AMEN.


## 29 Disputation VI. On the Photinian Arguments against the Merit and Satisfaction of Christ

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Salomon Lenz.

Thesis I.

After we have given in the preceding disputation the true and orthodox opinion concerning the merit of Christ, confirmed by many sayings of Scripture, it is furthermore necessary that we dissolve the principal objections of our adversaries. Socinus recounted them at length in his book on the Savior, but Ostorodus more succinctly in his Institution, chapters 36, 37, and part 5 of the disputation opposed to Ger. Tradelio. Likewise Smalcius in his Catechism, chapter 8, and G. Stuhl in the letters sent to Ludovicus Lucius, and printed at Basel in the year 1613. From these authors, therefore, we shall extract the principal arguments, and we shall consider in a few words, with God graciously helping us, what can and ought to be answered.

ARGUMENT I. From the name of satisfaction, because it does not exist in the Scriptures:

II. Whatever doctrine is proposed in unusual words and words that clearly do not exist in Scripture, that ought deservedly to be suspect: But such is the doctrine concerning the satisfaction of Christ, because that term exists nowhere in the Scriptures, which Ostorodus urges strongly in the aforementioned book, page 208. Therefore this doctrine ought deservedly to be suspect.

III. We answer. 1. By counter-example: If all phrases and terms by which the articles of faith are explained must exist κατὰ ῥητὸν (literally) in the Scriptures, many articles of the Photinian religion also fall. I will note a few examples: 1. They retain the distinction between Canonical and Apocryphal books. 2. They employ the terms of free will, des freyen Willens. 3. They use the word Sacrament and Lord's Supper, to pass over many other things in silence: Now let them show me these terms from the Scriptures; where is anything written about Canonical books, about free will, or about Sacraments? Either, therefore, all their doctrine concerning the alleged articles is suspect, or there is no consequence in this first argument.

VI. 2. We urge the example of the Fathers, who in disputation with adversaries assumed peculiar terms, partly for the sake of explanation, partly of distinction, partly of better refutation. For such is the perversity of heretics, that they retain and allege the phrases of Scripture, but in a foreign sense, so that they speak in our language, but under another understanding. Wherefore it is altogether necessary that such phrases be employed by which our mind may be clearly expounded nature, under which heretics may not so much lie hidden, but be more easily refuted. This was observed in the struggle with the Nestorians and Eutychians. Against the former it was concluded, ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν ἀδιαλύτως, ἀδι- αιρέτως, καὶ ἀδιασπάστως: against the latter ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως καὶ ἀναλλοιώτως. But where are these terms found in the Scriptures? And yet the thing itself ought not to be denied.

V. 3 Hence flowed that distinction, that in the Scriptures some things both are and are said, but some things are, but are not said. This we commonly express thus: In the sacred writings something is held either explicitly αὐτολεξεὶ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν and according to the letter; or implicitly κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν and according to the matter or sense. What exists in the Scriptures in neither way, ought deservedly to be considered suspect, nay, false. But what is not held as to the letter, and yet is found as to the sense, is not to be argued as false. And so it is with our doctrine concerning the satisfaction of Christ; which word, although it is not read in the sacred Code, yet the thing itself and equivalent phrases are contained therein. It suffices therefore that the sense is held; we do not care for the tips of the letters, otherwise it would be permitted to suspect similarly ill of the articles alleged above, which the Photinians themselves acknowledge, by which pact they would cut their own vineyards. Wherefore let them note this rule confirmed by many examples: From the negation of the letters or the literal expression, to the negation of the matter or the thing itself, it is not permitted to argue.

VI. 4. Even if the word satisfaction were read, the adversaries would nevertheless scarcely depart from their preconceived opinion, but would undoubtedly elude even that with some gloss. For they use this stratagem, that they render all things doubtful and involve them in their own glosses. If this diabolical study of perverting is brought forward, no words can be proposed so clear, but that Satan through his ministers might

corrupt them. And this very thing with the best of right renders suspicious to us all the doctrine of the Photinians, because they so corrupt the language of the Holy Spirit and the Apostolic faith, that if their glosses were to prevail, no limit could be given or perhaps even exist, which could not in like manner be corrupted, as they pervert phrases of Scripture similar to them. They urge primarily the term Satisfaction, because it is not found. But I will assume their hypotheses, and from them I will likewise dispute against you, even if these very words were read in the Scriptures: Christ Jesus by suffering satisfied for us to God the Father. For let it be so, and I will concede that these words exist in the sacred Code, yet I reply that the satisfaction of Christ is not yet proven according to the Photinian mode of disputing. For thus I object according to their sophistications: The term of satisfying is ambiguous, because it does not always denote an intervening and equivalent price for a fault or punishment, but 1. In general the fulfillment of a will or the observance of a precept: Now indeed it was the will of God that Christ should suffer and die, since He had sent Him into the world for this purpose. Rightly therefore is it said that He satisfied by suffering, since it was done as God willed it to be done. I allege these examples: 2 Sam. 19. verse 7. Joab says to David: Satisfy thy servants: In the Hebrew it is: Speak to the heart of thy servants. Luth. Speak kindly to your servants. Here therefore to satisfy is the same as to speak and act in a pleasing manner, so Mark 15. v. 15. Pilate wishing to satisfy the people, that is, to fulfill their will. In the Greek it is τό ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι. Luth. Pilate thought to do enough for the people. 2. To satisfy sometimes denotes to render an account or to defend. Thus it is taken in Levit. 10 v. 20. Which when Moses heard he received satisfaction: Luth. When Moses heard that, he was pleased with it, in the Hebrew it is, וייטב בעיניו it was good in his eyes Acts 24. v. 10. With good courage I will make my defense for myself. In Greek, ἐνθυμότερον τὰ περὶ ἐμαυτῦ ἀπολο- γῆσας Luth. I will fearlessly defend myself. And 1 Pet. 3 v. 15. Always ready for a defense to everyone who asks. In Greek πρὸς ἀπολογίαν παντὶ τῷ αἰτῦντι. Luther: Ready for a defense to everyone: We have another example in Acts 17 v. 9 where it is said of the people of Thessalonica that they received satisfaction from Jason, Λάβοντες τὸ ἱκανὸν, Luth. rendered it, When they received a defense from Jason. It can therefore also be said in this sense that Christ made satisfaction to God, namely by defending us, interceding for us, and repelling the accusations of the Devil. For just as Paul made satisfaction for himself when he warded off a charge: so Christ made satisfaction for us when he repels Satan and excuses us before the Father: 3. Finally, that also is called satisfaction, when someone is afflicted or received with blows: Thus the Fathers imposed satisfactions upon the sinner after repentance, that is, certain penalties by which he satisfied the Church, which he had scandalized. Since therefore the death of Christ was a most grievous affliction, imposed by God the Father, it can rightly be called satisfaction under a general sense. Now prove from the context and the Scriptures that the word satisfaction denotes a price of payment and not rather 1. the fulfillment of a will, or 2. our defense, or finally 3. in general an affliction. As regards the words for us, or for our sins, I similarly except, as they do, that they only denote benefit and utility, as if it were said, for our sake, so that our sins might be forgiven, but without a λύτρῳ. Indeed, even if it should be said most strongly that Christ made satisfaction in our place, it could still be excepted that it is the same as for our sake. Indeed, he also properly makes satisfaction in our place, that is, he answers when we are accused by the Devil. You see, therefore, that by equal reasoning it could be eluded by Photinian hypotheses and glosses, even if the most open statement about satisfaction were held.

VII. From these, however, I deduce two corollaries; 1. That it is mere play and trifling when the Photinians pretend that they would willingly concede to our side if only the word 'satisfaction' were read and a clear testimony concerning it were had. For as long as they retain their zeal for glossing and their preconceived opinion, for so long will they evade even the most manifest sayings of Scripture; there will be nothing so clear to which human reason cannot raise an objection, if all the thoughts of the mind are directed toward that end. 2. That one must not depart from the letter for any cleverly devised gloss. What can be said more clearly than this: Christ by dying satisfied the Father for us? Nevertheless, it can be corrupted and called into doubt according to the Photinian mode of disputing. And indeed, the cunning of the Devil in perverting the merit of Christ is to be wondered at. For if it must be proposed dogmatically without precision and the removal of glosses, there can hardly be any affirmative term given to express that which cannot be depraved through Photinian sophistries. For whether you say He satisfied, or paid a ransom, or died for sins, or for us, they immediately have something at hand to object. Thus, indeed, it happens when one departs from the clear letter, that all certainty is taken away, and only human glosses are heard: Wherefore I conclude that this heresy is truly pestilent and the final attempt of Satan: But let us learn from this to adhere all the more strongly to the words of God, so that we may not be carried about by any interpretation, but may constantly defend the literal sense: Otherwise we shall always be learning, never arriving at certainty, from which in the end will follow Atheism and Epicurean security. For this I am most persuaded of, that either Photinianism with its glosses must be abandoned, or it will shortly deflect to Atheism: For when all sayings, even the clearest, are obscured by human glosses, then the authority of Scripture collapses, together with the faith built upon it; from which what else can arise but barbarism and Epicureanism?

VIII. But they object, 1. That all doctrines which concern our salvation are contained literally in the word of God.

Resp. By the letter, either proper words are understood, which produce a literal sense, or all the terms used in a certain article: if the former, we concede it, and we affirm this very thing concerning the satisfaction of Christ, since it is described in the most proper and significant words, and therefore literally. But if the latter, we deny it, nor can it be proven. For how many phrases and forms of speech, not existing in Scripture, did the orthodox fathers assume for the sake of declaration, and because of the malice of adversaries? Nor was it said that this was written by them, except by heretics. And if beyond the letter, that is, beyond the words of Scripture, no terms are to be assumed, why do they call them Canonical books, why do they retain free will, why sacrament, and similar terms? Nay, where is this letter found; that Christ is Savior by announcing and confirming, as Socinus speaks; that his redemption is metaphorical, made for us, that is, for our sake? If this is their exposition of the letter of the article, where, I ask, is it found recorded in the Scriptures? They surely think it permitted to them, without any suspicion of novelty or falsehood, to explain their heresy with peculiar words and phrases: when we do the same, and use the term satisfaction, they immediately accuse us, and clamor that our doctrine is suspect because it is declared by words nowhere used in the Scriptures. Hypocrite, first cast the beam out of your own eye, Matt. 7. v. 5. And indeed if only the phrases of Scripture were to be used in explaining the articles of faith, mere confusion would follow and a mixture of religions. The reason is that both heretics admit Scripture and retain its words, but under a different sense. If this is only to be cherished in the heart and not expressed in significant terms, how will the false be distinguished from the true? For example, the Photinians confess with us that Christ is the Redeemer of the world and our Savior and mediator, that he died for us, and gave a λύτρον, and they admit all the locutions of Scripture. If, therefore, this article must be expressed by no other words than those enumerated, by which our interpretation of the Photinians might be declared; what will be the distinction of religion, whence will you distinguish a Photinian and a Lutheran? For each uses the same words, but hides the sense, which is different, and does not use significant phrases or circumlocution. Therefore, this exception of the Photinians reveals a double vice 1. Iniquity, while they snatch for themselves the right of using peculiar phrases, but are unwilling to grant the same to us: 2. Malice, while they urge such a thing from which a mixture of heresies and a confusion of religions would follow, so that no one could know who is addicted to this or that sect; since all seek a hiding place under the phrases of Scripture.

IX. They object II. that phrases equivalent to Satisfaction do not exist in the Scriptures: because it is nowhere said 1. that Christ by his death has appeased God. 2. or has paid every penalty of the justice of God 3. or has shed his blood as a payment. 4. or has compensated for our disobedience with his obedience; Or 5. that he has merited this, that God should forgive sins, or 6. that he has appeased the wrath of God for us.

Resp. 1. Even if all these things were read, they could nevertheless be no less evaded by those glosses which they apply to other sayings, if these had any validity: For Christ appeased God metaphorically, insofar as he satisfied his will and his passion had him appeased, so that sins might be forgiven us by grace. For just as he is said to have reconciled us, so he is said to have appeased God. He paid the penalty, in the sense in which the Apostle reports that he gave an ἀντίλυτρον, 1 Tim. 2, verse 6. Thus also the rest can easily be explained away through metaphors and other figures. Wherefore let them admit either that their glosses are vain, or that no phrase can be given that is immune from the corruption of reason; since the latter is absurd and impious, it follows that the former must be acknowledged. Nullibi & tamen ob id doctrinam suam suspectam fieri inficiantur. Nulla proindè argumento inerit consequentia. 3. Phrases æquipollentes considerantur vel ratione verborum, vel ratione sensus: Si verba respiciunt, suum sophisma de litera repetunt, principium petunt, propria vineta cædunt, sibi ipsis opponunt. Monstrent enim in Scripturis phrases & verba, quibus suam hæresin declarare solent. Si posterius, falsum est, quod æquipollentes phrases & huic, Christus satisfecit, & illis, quas ipsi recensent, in Scripturis non inueniantur. Multas istarum disputatione proximâ enumeravimus. Hic pauca sufficiant Eph. 5. vers. 5. Christus dedit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem & hostiam Deo in odorem suauitatis. Hostias autem, quarum sanguis effunditur, ad satisfactionem ac peccatorum expiationem offerri testatur totus Leuiticus, & cap. 10. Nowhere, and yet they deny that their doctrine is rendered suspect on that account. Consequently, there will be no logical force in the argument. 3. Equivalent phrases are considered either by reason of the words or by reason of the sense: If they look to the words, they repeat their sophism concerning the letter, they beg the question, they prune their own vineyards, they oppose themselves. For let them show in the Scriptures the phrases and words by which they are accustomed to declare their heresy. If the latter, it is false that equivalent phrases both to this, "Christ made satisfaction," and to those which they themselves recount, are not found in the Scriptures. We enumerated many of these in the previous disputation. Here let a few suffice: Eph. 5. vers. 5. "Christ gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savour." Now, the whole of Leviticus testifies that sacrifices, the blood of which is poured out, are offered for satisfaction and for the expiation of sins, and chapter 10. Heb. where it is said that the old sacrifices could by no means take away sins, but Christ came to do the will of God. ver. 7. and so

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Salomone Lenzio.

Thesis. I.

POsteaquam præcedenti disputatione veram ac orthodoxam de merito Christi sententiam multis scripturæ dictis confirmatam dedimus, necessarium porrò est, vt præcipuas aduersariorum obiectiones diluamus. Prolixè illas recensuit Socinus in lib. de Seruat. magis autem succinctè Ostorodus in instit cap. 36. 37. & part. 5. dissputationis Ger. Tradelio oppositæ. Itemque Smalcius in Catech. cap. 8. & G. stuhl. in Epistolis ad Ludovicum Lucium datis, & Basilææ anno 1613. impressis. Ex his igitur authoribus argumenta præcipua excerpemus, & quid responderi possit ac debeat paucis, Deo nos clementer adjuvante, considerabimus.

ARGVMENTVM I. A nomine satisfactiōnīs, quòd illud non extet in Scripturis:

II. Quæcunque doctrina verbis inusitatis & in Scriptura planè non extantibus proponitur, illa meritò suspecta esse debet: Sed talis est doctrina de satisfactione Christi, quia vocabulum illud nuslibi extat in Scripturis, quod valdè vrget Ostorodus lib. prædict. pag. 208. Ergò doctrina hæc meritò suspecta esse debet.

III. Respondemus. 1. Per instantiam Si omnes phrases & terminos, quibus articuli fidei explicantur in Scripturis, κατὰ ῥητὸν extare oportet, cadent etiam multi articuli religionis Photinianæ. Exempli loc. aliquot annotabo 1. Retinent illi distinctionem inter libros Canonicos & Apocryphos 2. adhibent terminos Liberi arbitrij, des freyen Willens. 3. vtuntur voce Sacramenti & Cœnæ Dominicæ, vt alia quam plurima silentio involuam: Iàm ex Scripturis hos mihi terminos ostendant; Vbi aliquid scriptum est de libris Canonicis, de de libero arbitrio, aut Sacramentis? Aut nulla igitur omnis ipsorum doctrina de allegatis articulis suspecta aut nulla in hoc argumento primo consequentia est.

VI. 2. Vrgemus exemplum Patrum, qui in disputatione cum adversariis peculiares terminos assumserunt, partim explicationis, partim distinctionis, artim melioris refutationis gratiâ Nam ea est hæreticorum peruersitas, vt phrases Scripturæ retineant & allegent, sed alieno sensu, vt nostrâ linguâ loquantur, sed sub alio intellectu. Quare omnino necessarium est, vt adhibeantur tales phrases, quibus mens nostra perspicuè exponatur, sub quibus hæretici non ita latere, sed faciliùs refutari queant. Obseruatum hoc est in certamine cum Nestorianis & Eutychianis. Contrà illos conclusum fuit, ἕνωσιν ὑποστατικὴν ἀδιαλύτως, ἀδιαιρέτως, καὶ ἀδιασπάστως: contra hos ἀσυγχύτως, ἀτρέπτως καὶ ἀναλλοιώτως. Vbi verò hi termini in Scripturis inueniuntur? nec tamen res ipsa negari debet.

V. 3 Fluxit hinc illa distinctio, quòd in Scripturis quædam & sint & dicantur, quædam verò sint, sed non dicantur. Hoc vulgò ita efferimus: In sacris literis aliquid habetur vel explicitè αὐτολεξεὶ κατὰ τὸ ῥητὸν & secundum literam; vel implicitè κατὰ τὴν διάνοιαν & secundum rem vel sensum. Quod neutro modo in Scripturis extat, meritò suspectum, imò falsum censeri debet. Quod autem non habetur quoad literam, & tamen inuenitur quoad sensum, falsitatis nõ est arguendum. Ita verò comparatum est cum doctrina nostra de satisfactione Christi; quæ vox, quamuis non legatur in sacro Codice, res tamen ipsa & phrases æquipollentes continentur. Sufficit proindè, quod sensus habeatur, literarum apices non curamus, aliàs de articulis suprà allegatis, quos Photiniani agnoscunt ipsi, similiter malè suspicari liceret, Quo pacto propria vineta cæderent. Quare notent regulam hanc multis exemplis confirmatam: A negatione τῶ γραμμάτων seu ῥητῶ, ad negationem τῶ πράγματος vel ipsius rei non licet argumentari

VI. 4. Si maximè satisfactionis vocabulum legeretur, aduersarij tamen à præconceptâ opinione suâ vix discederent, sed proculdubio & illud glossamate quodam eluderent. Hoc enim stratagemate vtuntur, vt omnia reddant dubia & suis glossis inuoluant. Quod diabolicum studiũ peruertendi si afferatur, nulla tàm clara possunt proponi verba, quin Satanas per ministros suos illa-

deprauet. Atque hoc ipsum iure optimo suspectam nobis reddit omnem doctrinam Photinianorum, quòd linguam Spiritus sancti & fidem Apostolicam sic corrumpunt, vt si ipsorum glossæ obtinere debeant, nullus vel detur vel dari fortè queat terminus, qui non pari modo depravari queat, vt illi similes Scripturæ phrases pervertunt. Vrgent imprimis Satisfactionis terminum, quòd non reperiatur. Ast assumam ego ipsorum hypotheses, & ex iis pariter contra te disputabo, si maximè hæc ipsa verba in Scripturis legantur: Christus Iesvs patiendo satisfecit pronobis Deo Patri. Nam sit ita, & concedam, hæc verba extare in sacro Codice, nondum tamen probatam esse Christi satisfactionem ad modum disputandi Photinianum regero. Sic enim iuxta ipsorum sophisticationes excipio: Vocabulum satisfaciendi est ambiguum, quia non semper denotat interueniens & æquiualens pro culpa aut pœna pretium, sed 1. In genere voluntatis impletionem aut præcepti obseruationem: Iam verò voluntas Dei fuit, vt Christus pateretur & moreretur, siquidem ip sum ad hoc in mundum miserat. Rectè igitur dicitur satisfecisse patiendo, quoniam ita factum est, quòd Devs fieri voluit. Exempla hæc allego: 2. Sam. 19. vers. 7. dicit Ioabus ad Dauidem: Satisfac servis tuis: In Hebræo est: Loquere ad cor servorum tuorum. Luth. Rede mit deinen Knechten freundlich. Hîce ergò satisfacere idem est, quod placentia loqui & agere, sic Marc. 15. v. 15. Pilatus volens populo satisfacere, hoc est, voluntatē ipsorum adimplere. In Gręco est τό ἱκανὸν ποιῆσαι. Luth. Pilatus gedachte dē Volck gnug zu thun. 2. Satisfacere nonnunquam notat rationem reddere aut defendere. Ita sumitur Leuit. 10 v. 20. Quod cùm audisset Moyses recepit satisfactionem: Luth. Da das Moses höret/ ließ ers jhm gefallen in Hebræo est, וייטב בעיניו num/fuit in oculis eius Act. 24. v. 10. Bono animo pro me satis faciam. In Graeco, ἐνθυμότερον τὰ περὶ ἐμαυτῦ ἀπολογῆσας Luth. Ich wil vnerschrocken mich verant= worten. Et 1. Pet. 3. v. 15. Parati semper ad fatisfa= ctionem omni petenti. In Graeco πρὸς ἀπολογίαν παντὶ τῷ αἰτῦντι. Lutherus: Bereit zur Verantwortung jederman: Exemplum aliud habemus Actor. 17. v. 9. vbì de populo Thessalonicensi dicitur, quòd satisfactionem acceperint ab Iasone, Λάβοντες τὸ ἱκανὸν, Luth. reddidit, Da sie Verantwortung von Jason empfangen. Potest igitur & hoc sensu dici, quòd Christus satis fecerit Deo, nimirum nos detendendo, intercedendo pro nobis, accusationes Diaboli repellendo. Sicut enim Paulus pro se satisfecit, quando crimen amolitus est: Sic Christus pro nobis satisfecit, cùm Satanam repellit, & nos apud Patrem excusat: 3. Tandem & illud vocatur satisfactio, cum aliquis affligitur, aut verberibus excipitur: Sic Patres imposuerunt peccatori post poenitentiam satisfactiones, id est, poenas aliquas, quibus Ecclesiae satisfecit, quam scandalizauit. Quoniam igitur mors Christi grauissima fuit afflictio, à Deo Patre imposita, rectè sub generali sensu satisfactio appellari poterit. Iam probes ex contextu & Scripturis, quòd vox satisfactionis notet pretium solutivum & non potiùs 1. impletionem voluntatis, aut 2. nostram defensionem, aut denique 3. in genere afflictionem. Quod spectat verba pro nobis, aut noftris peccatis, similiter excipio, vt illi, tantùm notare commodum & vtilitatem, ac si diceretur, nostri causâ, vt nobis dimittantur peccata, sed sine λύτρῳ. Imò si maximè dicatur, Nostri loco Christum satisfecisse, posset tamen excipi, idem esse ac nostri causâ. Imò & propriè nostri loco satisfacit, id est, respondet, cum à Diabolo accusamur. Vides igitur, pari ratione ex hypothesibus & glossis Photinianis eludi posse, si maximè apertissimum de satisfactione dictum haberetur.

VII. Ex his autem duo deduco corollaria; 1. Quòd merus lusus fususque sit, quando Photiniani prætendunt, se lubenter ad nostras partes concessuros esse, si modò satisfactionis vox legeretur, & clarum de illa testimonium haberetur. Nam quamdiu suum glossandi studium & præconceptam opinionem retinent, tàm diu apertissima etiam Scripturæ dicta eludent: nil tàm luculentum erit, ad quod humana ratio excipere nequeat, si omnes animi cogitationes eò dirigantur. 2. Quòd è literahon recedendum sit, quodvis argutè excogitatum glossema. Quid clariùs dici potest, quam istud: Christus moriendo pro nobis satisfecit Patri? Nihilominus corrumpi & in dubium potest vocari, juxta modum disputandi Photinianum. Et sanè admiranda est Diaboli astutia in peruertendo Christi merito. Si enim theticè proponi debeat sine ἀκλιβείᾳ & glossarum remotione, non potest vllus ferè terminus affirmativus dari, ad illud exprimendum, qui non per sophisticationes Photinianas depravari queat. Siuè enim dicas satisfecisse, siue λύτρον persoluisse, sivè pro peccatis, sivè pro nobis mortuum esse, mox in promptu habent, quod excipiant. Ita nimirum contingit, quum à clara litera receditur, vt omnis certitudo tollatur, & humana tantum gloffemata audiantur: Quare hæresin istam verè pestilentem & vltimum Satanæ conatum esse concludo: Nos autem indè discamus, eò fortius adhærere verbis Dei, nè quavis interpretatione circumferamur, sed literalem sensum constanter tueamur: Aliàs semper discemus, nunquam ad certitudinem peruenientes, vndè tandem sequetur Atheismus & Epicurea securitas. Hoc enim mihi persuasissimum est, aut Photinianismum cum suis glossis esse deserendum esse, aut breui ad Atheismum deflectetur: Quando enim omnia dicta, etiam clasissima; humanis glossis obnubilantur, tum concidit Scripturę authoritas, vnà cum fide illi superstructa; vnde quid aliud oriri potest, quàm barbaries & Epicureismus?

IIX. Verùm excipiunt, 1. Omnes doctrinas, quæ salutem nostram concernunt, ad literam in verbo Dei scriptas contineri.

Resp. Per literam vel intelliguntur verba propria, quæ pariunt literalem sensum, vel omnes termini in quodam articulo vsitati: si prius, Concedimus, & hoc ipsum de Christi satisfactione affirmamus, quippe, quæ verbis maximè propriis & significantibus, ideoque ad literam descripta est. Sin posterius, negatum imus, nec probari potest. Quot enim phrases & loquendi formulas, in Scriptura non extantes, assumserunt orthodoxi patres, declarationis ergò, & propter malitiam aduersariorum? Nec dica ab hoc ipsis scriptafuit, nisi ab hæreticis, Et si præter literam, hoc est, præter verba Scripturæ nulli sunt affumendi termini, cur libros Canonicos vocant, cur liberum arbitrium, cur Sacramentum & similes voces retinent? Imò, vbi hæc habetur litera; Christum esse Seruatorem annunciando & confirmando, vt Socinus loquitur; eius redemptionem esse metaphoricam, factam pro nobis, id est, nostrâ causâ? Si hæc ipsorum expositio est articuli litera, vbinam quæso ea in Scripturis consignata reperitur? Nimirum sibi licere putant, sine omni nouitatis aut falsitatis suspicione, peculiaribus verbis & phrasibus hæresin suam explicare: Nos, cùm idem facimus, & satisfactionis terminum adhibemus, mox accusant, nostramque doctrinam suspectam esse clamitant, quia verbis in Scripturis nullibi vsurpatis declaretur. Hypocrita ejice primùm trabem ex oculo tuo, Matth. 7. v. 5. Et sanè si tantùm Scripturæ phrases adhibendæ essent, in exponendis fidei articulis, sequeretur mera confusio & mixturâ religionum. Ratio est illa, quoniam & hæretici Scripturam admittunt, & eius verba tetinent, sed sub alio sensu. Qui si tantùm in corde foueri, nec terminis significantibus exprimi debeat, qui falsum à vero discernetur? Exempli gratiâ, Christum esse mundi Redemptorem & Seruatorem nostrumque mediatorem, pro nobis mortuum, & dedisse λύτρον, fatentur nobiscum Photiniani, omnesque Scripturæ locutiones admittunt. Si ergò hic articulus nullis alijs præter enumeratas vocibus efferri debeat, quibus nostra Photinianorum interpretatio declaretur; quæ erit religionis distinctio, vndè dignosces Photinianum & Lutheranum? Vterque enim eadem verba vsurpat, sensum vero, qui diuersus est, occultat, neque significantibus phrasibus deserchit aut circumloquitur. Proindè ista Photinianorum exceptio geminum vitium prodit 1. Iniquitatem, dum sibi rapiunt ius peculiares phrases adhibendi, nostris verò idem concedere nolunt: 2. Malitiam, dum tale quid vrgent ex quo hæreseōn permixtio & religionum confusio sequeretur, vt nemo scire posset, quis huic vel illi Sectæ addictus sit; siquidem omnes sub Scripturæ phrasibus latibulum quærunt.

IX. Excipiunt II. quòd phrases Satisfactioni æquipollentes non extent in Scripturis: quia nullibi dicatur 1. quòd Christus suâ morte Deum placauerit. 2. vel omnem pœnam iustitiæ Dei persoluerit 3. aut sanguinem suum tanquàm solutionem effuderit. 4. aut nostram inobedientiam suâ obedientiâ compensauerit; Vel 5. quòd hoc meritus sit, vt Deus peccata condonet, vel 6. quòd iram Dei pro nobis placauerit.

Resp. 1. Si maximè hæc omnia legerentur, non minus tamen eludi possent glossis istis, quas ad alia dicta reponunt, si hæ aliquid valerent: Nam Christus Deum placauit metaphoricè, quatenus voluntati eius satisfecit & passio illum rasum habuit, vt nobis ex gratiâ dimittatur peccata. Sicut enim nos reconciliâsse, ita Deum placasse dicitur. Pœnam persoluit, eo sensu quo ἀντίλυτρον dedisse refert Apostolus 1. Tim. 2. vers. 6. Sic & reliqua per metaphoras & alias figuras eludi facilè possunt. Quare fateantur, aut glossas suas vanas esse, aut nullã phrasin dari posse, à corruptela rationis immunẽ, posterius cü absurdum & impium sit, prius esse agnoscendum, sequitur. 2. Præscribam & ipsis quasdam æquipollentes phrases, vel ipsorum doctrinæ correspondentes; & vrgebo, vt literam ex Scripturis demonstrent; vt quòd Christus sit Saluator, quia in eius concionibus salutis ratio ostenditur, vel quia suo exemplo salutis modum docuit, vel quia non satisfaciendo nos redemit. Hæc omnia sunt phrases æquipollentes, quibus mentem suam exprimunt, aut certè exprimere possunt. Vbi nam verò extant aut leguntur? Nullibi & tamen ob id doctrinam suam suspectam fieri inficiantur. Nulla proindè argumento inerit consequentia. 3. Phrases æquipollentes considerantur vel ratione verborum, vel ratione sensus: Si verba respiciunt, suum sophisma de litera repetunt, principium petunt, propria vineta cædunt, sibi Ipsis opponunt. Monstrent enim in Scripturis phrases & verba, quibus suam hæresin declarare solent. Si posterius, falsum est, quod æquipollentes phrases & huic, Christus satisfecit, & illis, quas ipsi recensent, in Scripturis non inueniantur. Multas istarum disputatione proximâ enumeravimus. Hic pauca sufficiant Eph. 5. vers. 5. Christus dedit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem & hostiam Deo in odorem suauitatis. Hostias autem, quarum sanguis effunditur, ad satisfactionem ac peccatorum expiationem offerri testatur totus Leuiticus, & cap. 10. Heb. vbi dicitur, quòd victimæ veteres peccata auferre haud potuerint, Christus autem venit ad voluntatem Dei faciendam. vers. 7. adeoque


### Argument I

they are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all, verse 10. And thus through the act of offering, not of preaching, or through another respect. Add Heb. 9. verses 7, 11, and especially verse 22, and at the same time the word λύτρον Matth. 20 v. 28, ἀντίλυτρον, 1 Tim. 2 v. 5, λυτρώσεως Luke 1 v. 68, ἀντιλυτρώσεως Col. 1 v. 14, cursed Gal. 3 v. 13, 14, redemption from the law Gal. 4 v. 4, 5. We have just seen the force and emphasis of these and similar sayings, and we have shown their equivalence with satisfaction.

ARGUMENT II. From the hindrance of good works.

X. If Christ made satisfaction for us to the divine law, we shall not be bound to observe his commandment. For he for whom the price is once paid is not bound to pay again. And Socinus says, p. 105: From the fact that someone pays another's debts, it does not follow that he now contracts no new debt from him. Wherefore the doctrine of satisfaction provides a handle for wickedness, or at the very least renders men weak in piety. See Catech. Rac. p. 264.

XI. Response 1. This is an old song, objected to the Apostles themselves, as is evident from Rom. 6 verse 1. What shall we say? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. For we who are dead to sin, how shall we live any longer therein? As therefore the pseudo-Apostles once concluded (whom the Papists also imitate), if we are saved by the merit of Christ alone, freely and without works, the zeal for holiness will grow cold, and sin will abound; in like manner do the modern Photinians now argue; from which very fact we are the more confirmed, and thence we infer that our faith is Apostolic, and theirs is heretical, since they condemn in our doctrine the same thing which the false brethren once desired in the faith of the Apostles.

XII. 2. The same can be objected to the Photinians. For just as we found the remission of sins in the merit of Christ, so they found it in the mercy of God alone they say. Hence, therefore, one will conclude much more thus: If I shall be saved by the mercy of God alone, and indeed that which abounds as sin abounds, what need will there be for a rigorous and difficult flight from sins? The Socinians themselves deny this consequence. Whatever, therefore, they will answer on behalf of the mercy of God, the same the reason for both in this case is equal.

XIII. A distinction must be made between that which happens per se and that which happens per accidens. If security and perversity of life flowed from the satisfaction of Christ per se, then the argument would obtain some force. But in truth that does not happen at all, since Scripture itself concludes the contrary from it. Rom. 6. v. 11. Reckon yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body. 2 Cor. 5. v. 15. Christ died for all, that they who live should henceforth not live to themselves, but to Him who died for them and rose again. Gal. 5. v. 13. You have been called to liberty, brethren, (namely through the merit and satisfaction of Christ) only do not give liberty as an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another. Tit. 2. ver. 14. Christ gave Himself for us, that He might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify to Himself an acceptable people, zealous of good works. Heb. 9. ver. 14. The blood of Christ, who through the Holy Spirit offered Himself without spot to God, shall purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God. You see from this that the Apostles do not separate them as causes, but join them as συναιτια (co-causes), partly the satisfaction of Christ, partly the pursuit of holiness, so much so that they constitute the former as the cause of the latter. Who, therefore, would say that impiety and negligence in good works would follow per se from this doctrine? The Apostles conclude one thing from the merit of Christ, and the Photinians another, from which it is clear in turn that their religion is not Apostolic. Meanwhile, we do not deny that per accidens malicious men, by their own fault, [pervert] that saving doctrine can be turned into abuse, and under the hope of pardon, on account of Christ's satisfaction, persist in sins. But what is this against us? If we wished to judge from that which happens by accident and by the malice of men, not even the faith of Christ could be considered true. For how many have been offended by it, and in how many ways have they abused it? Where is a gathering found in which three parts of the word do not become unfruitful through the fault of men, Luke 8. 12. seqq. And does not one, from the mere preaching of grace, which the Socinians urge, likewise take an opportunity to continue in sins? Wherefore let them be mindful of the logical precept: from that which happens by accident to that which is by itself, it is not permitted to argue.

XIV. 4. The reason for the consequence which they bring forward is null. For they say: He for whom the price has been paid is not bound to pay it again. We admit it: And indeed we cannot pay, since our obedience is too imperfect. Therefore Christ alone has fully kept the law, and this is imputed to us for righteousness. Meanwhile, it does not follow that obedience and holiness of life are entirely free or unnecessary. For although we neither satisfy God through it, nor ought to satisfy Him, nor are able to, there are nevertheless other causes which demand this zeal from us. The removal of false causes does not take away the true and legitimate ones. Although a son does not merit his inheritance by acting well, he still owes obedience and reverence to his parents. Thus GOD requires good works from us, not that we may satisfy Him, but that we may declare our due thanks for them.

XV. And indeed there are various incentives to piety. But to pass over others, the very satisfaction of Christ adds many spurs to acting well.

1. From the end of the Lord's death. This is twofold here: The one principal, that by dying for us He might make satisfaction. The other subordinate, that He might sanctify a people for Himself, Him-

establisher of good works. Unless, therefore, you wish Christ to have died in vain, and to be frustrated of another end, it will be necessary that you strive for holiness. For he did not die for you so that you might continue in sins, but rather that you might send a message of dismissal to them? He redeemed you from sins, therefore you should no longer serve sin. Whence furthermore it shines forth that the similar falsehood of Socinus is [false]. For he who pays the debts of another, if he is otherwise a sincere friend, seriously desires that he contract no further debt. So also it is the will of Christ our liberator, that since he once satisfied for us, we should not contract a new debt, and be rendered guilty of fault again through gross and voluntary sins.

2. From the right of redemption. By whomever we are redeemed, to him we are bound by the right of redemption to serve and obey. But we have been redeemed by Christ. Therefore, we are likewise bound to obedience and service. Zacharias touches upon this reason in Luke 1, verse 74: That being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life. This can be declared by the example of bodily redemption. For he who frees others from captivity certainly has them bound to serve him, nor can they take an opportunity from that to revile their liberator or to persecute him. For they are bound by right to the contrary.

3. From the benefit of gratuitous remission. On account of the merit of Christ, our sins are freely forgiven us, without our own satisfaction. Therefore, it is fair and necessary that we, in turn, be grateful, that we love Christ the more ardently, and that we do not injure him again with sins. For the more benefits are received, the greater gratitude is owed. Thus David concludes in Psalm 130, verse 4: There is plenteous forgiveness with thee, that thou mayest be feared. And Christ himself in Luke 7, verse 42: Her sins are forgiven, for she loved much. But to whom less is forgiven, the same loveth less.

1. On the gravity of punishments. The payment of our debts cost Christ dearly. He endured various wounds and a most ignominious death. Wherefore do not sin any more, lest you heap up those punishments and afflict Christ anew. For to sin voluntarily after the law has been set forth is to trample underfoot the Son of God, and to count the blood of the covenant as polluted, Heb. 10, verse 29.

XVI. From the immensity of divine wrath. The passion of Christ, although he was most innocent, was a mirror of this. For when he felt the wrath of God in the garden, he even shed drops of blood. And so great was the indignation of the Father that it could be appeased by nothing other than the death of his only-begotten Son. Shall we not therefore revere this wrath? Shall we dare to kindle it anew by voluntary sins? For although satisfaction has been made, yet unless we are thankful for the satisfaction and live piously, the wrath of the Lord is doubled.

XVII. And thus we see that the doctrine of satisfaction does not weaken the pursuit of holiness, but that in it almost no more effective incentive, no sharper spurs to piety are to be found. Wherefore the merit of Christ and the pursuit of holiness do not conflict at all: they posit one another, they do not abolish one another. Christ died so that we might live piously. From this, however, it does not follow that he did not die to make satisfaction, or vice versa. Both ends are expressed in Scripture, and therefore one ought not to be opposed to the other. The death of Christ remains a medicine for spiritual diseases, both an alexipharmic, through which our sins are cured and taken away, and a prophylactic, through which future sins are prevented and hindered. Therefore, it is a calumny when the Photinians shout that the pursuit of good works is weakened by Christ's satisfaction. For they know that we join both together and seriously exhort our hearers to piety.

1. On account of God, who commanded and to whom gratitude is to be declared.

2, On account of Christ, who redeemed,

as has been said thus far. 3. on account of the Angels, who rejoice in probity, and are repelled by impiety 4. on account of our neighbor, that he may not be scandalized, but invited by our example to good works. 5. on account of ourselves, that we may show our faith, exercise it, avoid punishments, and obtain rewards. 6. on account of the Devils, that we may not fall into his snares; All these things are proposed in the Scriptures together with the doctrine of satisfaction, and are often repeated from the Scriptures; so that in this way, partly an injury is done to us by our adversaries, and partly those things which are nevertheless subordinate and most closely connected are opposed and torn apart by remarkable sophistication.

XVIII. We add that between Christ's satisfaction apprehended and the holiness of life there is not only a moral connection, insofar as men can be admonished and excited by the one to the other, but also, if I may so speak, a causal one, insofar as the one being posited, the other is necessarily posited and produced because of their cohesion. For where Christ's satisfaction is apprehended, there 1. the Holy Spirit dwells in the heart. 2. Justifying faith is present. Both are the efficient cause of good works, and these being posited, the pursuit of holiness cannot but be posited at the same time, just as the effect necessarily follows when the cause is posited in act and not hindered. For it is written concerning the Holy Spirit that He restrains the flesh, lest it luxuriate, and generates various fruits of good works in a pious heart. For if it is said in Galatians 5, verse 22. The fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, continence, chastity. Nor do the Photinians deny this, since they wish the Holy Spirit to be nothing other than a various singular gift. Wherever, therefore, the Holy Spirit is, there vices find no place, since He does not enter a soul unclean with virtues. Wisdom 1, verse 4. But indeed in any believer, apprehending the satisfaction of Christ, the Holy Spirit dwells, since it is from him that this faith proceeds. Therefore, as long as one remains faithful, sins do not find a place, and thus it is impossible that anyone should truly believe and live impiously: But as holiness is the fruit of the Spirit, so it is also the consequence of faith, since this is always effective through love Galat. 5. verse 6. Wherefore, just as solar rays always illuminate the air, so living faith always excites the ardor of piety. These are the two moments of Christianity, Faith and love, one of which perpetually includes and draws with itself the other, just as proper affections never fail to bubble up from the forms of things.

Latin:

sanctificati sunt per oblationem corporis Iesv Christi semel vers. 10. atque sic per actum oblationis, non praedicationis, aut per alium respectum. Adde Hebr. 9. vers. 7. 11. & inprimis vers. 22. simulq; vocabulum λύτρε Matth. 20 v. 28 ἀντιλύτρε, 1. Tim. 2. v. 5. λυτρώσεως Luc. 1. v. 60 ἀντιλυτρώσεως Col. 1. v. 14. maledicti Gal. 3. v. 13. 14. redemptionis à lege Gal. 4. v. 4. 5. Horum & similium dictorum vim & emphasin proximè vidimus, & aequipollentiam cum satisfactione ostendimus.

ARGVMENTVM II. Ab impedimento bonorum operum.

X. Si Christus pro nobis satisfecit legi divinae, nos non tenebimur mandatum eius observare. Nam pro quo precium semel est solutum, is non tenetur denuo solvere. Et Socinus inquit. p. 105. Ex eo quod quis alterius debita solvit, non sequitur jam vt ille nullum aes alienum iam ab ipso contrahi. Quare doctrina de satisfactione ansam praebet flagitijs, vel ad minimum homines in pietate debiles reddit. Vide Catech. Rac. p. 264.

XI. Respond 1. Antiqua haec cantilena est, ipsis Apostolis obiecta, vti constat ex Rom. 6. vers. 1. Quid dicemus? Manebimus in peccato, vt gratia abundet; absit. Qui enim mortui sumus peccato, quomodo adhuc vivemus in illo? vt igitur olim pseudo Apostoli colligebant, (quos imitantur etiam Pontificij) si ex solo Christi merito, gratis & sine operibus salvamur, frigebit sanctitatis studium, & abundabit peccatum pari modo nunc recentes Photiniani argumentantur; ex quo ipso nos magis confirmamur, & indè inferimus, si fidem nostram Apostolicam, ipsorum haereticam esse, cum idem in nostra doctrina damnent, quo olim in Apostolorum fide fratres falsi desiderarunt.

XII. 2. Idem Photinianis obijci potest. Vtenim nos remissionem peccatorum in Christi merito: sic illi in sola misericordia Dei fundatam dicunt. Hinc igitur multò magis quis ita colliget, Si ex sola Dei misericordia saluabor, & quidem illa abundat vti superabundat peccatum, quid opus erit rigorosâ & vitæ & tàm difficili peccatorum fugâ? Hanc cõsequentiam ipsi negant Sociniani. Quicquid ergò pro Dei misericordia respondebunt, idem nos pro Christi merito reponemus, cùm vtriusq́; in hoc casu par sit ratio.

XIII. Distinguendum est inter id, quod fit per se, & id, quod fit per accidens, Si per se ex satisfactione Christi flueret securitas & vitæ perversitas, tum aliquid obtineret argumentum. At verò istud minimè fit, siquidem Scriptura ipsa contrarium indè colligit. Rom. 6. v. 11. Existimate vos mortuos quidem esse peccato, viuentes autem Deo in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Non ergo regnet peccatum in mortali vestro corpore, 2. Cor. 5. v. 15 Pro omnibus mortuus est Christus, vt, qui viuunt, posthac nõ sibi viuant, sed ei, qui pro ipsis mortuus est & resurrexit. Gal: 5: v. 13. Vos in libertatem vocati estis fratres, (nempe per meritum & satisfactionem Christi) tantùm nè libertatem in occasionem detis carni, sed per charitatem seruite vobis inuicem. Tit. 2. vers. 14. Christus dedit semetipsum pro nobis, vt nos redimeret ab omni iniquitate, & mundaret sibi populum acceptabilem, sectatorem bonorum operum. Hebr. 9. ver: 14. Sanguis Christi, qui per Spiritum Sanctũ semetipsum obtulit immaculatum Deo emundabit conscientiam vestram ab operibus mortuis ad seruiendum Deo viuenti. Vides hinc, Apostolos non ut vasin disiungere, sed tanquam συναιτια coniungere partim satisfactionem Christi, partim sanctitatis studium, adeò vt illam huius causam constituant. Qui Ergò per se ex hac doctrina sequeretur impietas & negligentia in bonis operibus? Aliud ex Christi merito Apostoli, & aliud Photiniani colligunt, vnde vicissim liquet, ipsorum religionem non esse Apostolicam. Interim non diffitemur: per accidens malitiosos homines propriâ culpâ salutarem illam do&rinam in abusum posse couertere, & sub spe veniæ, ob Christi satis factionem, in peccatis perscuerare. Quid autem hoc contra nos? Si ab eo quod fit per accidens, & malitiâ hominum, judicare vellemus, nec Christi fides pro vera censeri posset, Quot enim illa offensi, quàm variis modis abusi sunt? Vbi reperitur cœtus, inquo non tres verbi partes infrugiferæ fiunt vitio hominum, Luc. 8. 12. seqq. Et annon ex sola gratiæ prædicatione, quam vrgent Sociniani, pariter quis ansam capere potest, peccata continuandi? Quare memores sint præcepti Logici: ab eo quod fit per accidens ad id, quod est per se, non licet argumentari.

XIV. 4. Ratio consequentiæ, quam afferunt, nulla est. Dicunt enim: Pro quo solutum est precium, is non tenetur denuò soluere, Fatemur: Et nè quidem soluere possumus, quoniam obedientia nostra nimis est imperfecta. Solus proindè Christus legem planè servauit, & hoc nobis imputatur ad justitiam. Interim non sequitur, liberam planè, nec necessariam esse obedientiam & vitæ sanctitatem. Licèt enim Deo per illam nec satisfaciamus, nec satisfacere debeamus, aut valeamus, aliæ tamen causæ sunt, quæ studium istud à nobis exigunt. Remotio falsarum causarum, non tollit veras & legitimas. Filius licet bene agendo non mereatur patrimonium, debet tamen obedientiam parentibus & reuerentiam. Sic DEVS requirit à nobis bona opera, non vt satisfaciamus, sed vt iis debitam gratitudinem declaremus.

XV. Et sanè varia sunt pietatis incentiva, Sed vt alia taceam, ipsa Christi satisfactio multos ad bene agendum stimulos addit.

1. A fine mortis Dominicæ. Duplex hîce est: Alter principalis, vt moriendo pro nobis satisfaceret. Alter subordinatus, vt sibi populum sanctificaret, se-

stator bonorum operum. Nisi ergo Christū velis frustrā mortuū esse, & altero fine frustrari, op' erit, ut sanctitati studeas. Non enim mortuus est p te, ut in peccatis pergas, sed ut illis potius nuncium mittas? Redemit te a peccatis, E. nō amplis? seruias peccato. Vnde porrò elucescit, Socini simile falsum esse. Omninò enim is qui alterius debita soluit, seriò vult, si alias sincerus est amicus, ut nullum deinceps æs alienum contrahat. Sic etiam Christi liberatoris nostri voluntas est, ut quoniam semel pro nobis satisfecit, nè nouum debitum contrahamus, & denuò culpæ rei reddamur per crassa &e voluntaria peccata.

2. Aiure redemptionis. A quocunque redimimur; illi redemptionis iure ad seruiendum & obsequendum obstricti sumus. Atqui à Christo sumus redempti. E. simul obstricti sumus ad obsequia & seruitia. Tangit hanc rationem Zacharias Luc 1. v. 74. V’t sine timore, de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati seruiamus illi in sanctitate & iustitia coram ipso, omnibus diebus vitæ nostræ. Declarari hoc potest exemplo redemptionis corporalis. Qui enim alios ex captiuitaté liberat, sibi certè ad seruiendum obstrictos habet, nec illi ansam indè capere possunt, liberatorem suum conuitijs proscindendi, aut illum persequendi. Ad contrarium enim iure obligati sunt.

3. A Beneficio gratuitæ remissionis. Ob Christi meritum gratis condonantur nobis peccata, sine satisfactione propria. E. æquum & necessarium est, ut vicissim grati simus, Christum eò ardentius diligamus, nec peccatis iterum lædamus. Quo enim plura beneficia accipiuntur, eò maior gratitudo debetur. Ita Dauid colligit Psalm. 130. vers. 4. Copiosa est apud te remissio, ut timearis. Et Christus ipse Luc. 7. vers, 42. Remittuntur ei peccata multa, hinc dilexit multum. Cui autem minus dimittitur, minus diligit.

1. Agravitate pœnarum. Christo carè constitit debitorum nostrorum solutio Varias plagas & ignominiosissimam mortem sustinuit. Quare non amplius pecces, nè pœnas illas cumules & Christum denuò affligas. Voluntariè enim peccare post νόμον præstitum est Filium Dei conculcare, & sanguinem testamenti pollutum ducere, Hebr. 10, vers. 29.

XVI. Ab iræ divinæ immensitate. Speculum istius fuit passio Christi, licèt innocentissimi. Iram enim Dei cùm sentiret in horto, sanguineas etiam guttas emisit. Et tanta fuit Patris indignatio, vt nullâ re aliâ quàm morte Filij vnigeniti placari potuerit. Ergòne non reuerebimur hanc iram? Num audebimus eam denuò peccatis voluntarijs accendere: Licet enim satisfactum sit, tamen nisi pro satisfactione grati simus, & piè viuamus, duplicatur ira Domini.

XVII. Atque sic videmus, doctrinâ de satisfactione non labefactari sanctitatis studium, sed illâ nullum ferè efficacius ὁρμητήριον, nullos acriores ad pietatem stimulos reperiri. Quare nequaquam pugnant Christi meritum, & sanctitatis studium: Ponunt se, non tollunt. Mortuus est Christus, vt nos piè viueremus, Hinc autem non sequitur, non esse mortuum, vt satisfaceret aut contrà. Vterque finis in Scriptura exprimitur, ideoque alter alteri, non debet opponi. Manet mors Christi medicina spiritualium morborum, tum alexicaca, per quam peccata nostra curantur & auferuntur tum Prophylactica, per quam futura peccata præcauentur & impediuntur. Proindè calumnia est, cùm per Christi satisfactionem bonorum operum studium eneruari Photiniani clamitant. Sciunt enim, quòd vtrumque coniungamus & seriò ad pietatem auditores nostros hortemur.

1. Propter Deum, qui mandauit & cui gratitudo declaranda est.

2, Propter Christum, qui redemit,

ut hactenus dictum. 3. propter Angelos, qui gaudent probitate, repelluntur impietate 4. propter proximum, nè scandalisetur, sed nostro exemplo ad bona opera invitetur. 5. propter nos ipsos, ut fidem ostendamus, exerceamus, poenas vitemus, praemia impetremus. 6. propter Diabolos, nè in ipsius casses incidamus; Haec omnia in Scripturis vna cum doctrina de satisfactione proponuntur, & ex Scripturis saepè repetuntur; vt ita partim nobis iniuria fiat ab adversariis, partim per insignem sophisticationem opponantur & divellantur ea, quae tamen subordinata & coniunctissima.

XIIX. Addimus, quòd inter Christi satisfactionem apprehensam, & vitae sanctimoniam non tantùm sit connexio moralis, quatenus homines per vnum admoneri & excitari possunt ad alterum, sed etiam, vt sic loquar, causalis, quatenus vno posito, necessario ob cohaesionem, ponitur & producitur alterum. Nam vbi Christi satisfactio apprehenditur ibi 1 Spiritus sanctus in corde habitat. 2. Fides iustificans adest. Vtrumque est causa efficiens bonorum operum & ijs positis non potest non simul poni sanctitatis studium, non secus atque causâ in actu positâ & non impeditâ necessario sequitur effectus. Nam de Spiritu sancto scriptum est, quod carnem compescat, nè luxuriet, variosque fructus bonorum operum in corde pio generet. Si enim dicitur Gala. 5. versu 22. Fructus spiritus est charitas, gaudium, pax, patientia, benignitas, bonitas, longanimitas, mansuetudo, fides, modestia, continentia, Castitas. Nec diffitẽtur hoc Photiniani, cum Spiritum sanctum nihil velint esse aliud, quàm donũ singulare varium. Vbicunque igitur est Spiritus sanctus ibi flagitia locum non inveniunt, siquidem animam virtutum immundam nõ ingreditur. Sapiens. 1. versu 4. At verò in quovis fideli, satisfactionem Christi apprehendente, Spiritus sanctus habitat, quippe à quo ista fides proficiscitur. Ergò quam diu fidelis manet, flagitia nõ inueniant locum, adeoque impossibile est vt quis verè credat & impiè viuat : Vt autem sanctitas est fructus Spiritus, ita & consequens fidei, quoniam hæc per charitatem semper efficax Galat. 5. versu 6. Quare vtrarij solares semper illuminant aerem, ita fides viva semper excitat pietatis ardorem. Sunt hæc duo momenta Christianismi, Fides & charitas, quorum vnum perpetuò includit & secum trahit alterum, non secus, ac è formis rerum nunquam non ebulliunt affectiones propriæ.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all

XIX. If Christ made satisfaction for all, all, even the manifestly impious, will be saved. For those for whom the λύτρον (ransom) has been paid are unjustly consigned to the prison of eternal damnation.

XX. Response 1. This argument is directly opposed to the Scriptures. For in them both things are said, that Christ is the propitiation for the sins of the whole world 1 John 2. verse 2, and that many perish, even those for whom Christ died and made satisfaction 2 Peter 2. verse 1, Hebrews 6. verses 4, 5, 6, Chapter 10. verse 26, Romans 14. verse 16, 1 Corinthians 8. verse 11. Wherefore, unless we wish to concede manifest ἀντιλογίας (contradictions) in the word of God, we must admit that there is no consequence in the argument.

XXI. 2. We distinguish between the acquisition of the benefit and the application of what has been acquired. The former is general, since Christ by his death merited the salvation of the whole world. The latter, however, is special, since only Believers and those receiving the Gospel with true faith become partakers of that benefit. But those who, in the manner of the stubborn Jews, the word they reject the instrument of faith, and with the Pharisees they spurn the Sacraments and the Counsels of God concerning their own salvation; they are deprived by their own fault of the benefits acquired by the death of Christ. The Apostle hints at this in 2 Cor. 5, verse 18: God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, and yet immediately it is added in verse 20: Be reconciled to God. There seems to be an ἀντίφασις here, but the reconciliation is easy if it be said that the former member treats of acquisition, the latter of application; reconciliation has been made through Christ, as regards attainment; it must be made through repentance and faith, as regards apprehension.

XXII. 3. All these things can be declared by certain similitudes. 1. From the liberation and the Babylonian Captivity. King Cyrus by public edicts granted to all the Jews a return to their homeland, Ezra 1, verses 3, 4; 2 Chron. 36, verse 22; yet many remained under servitude, not because of a defect in the liberty obtained, but by their own will, since they did not wish to accept the royal benefit, but loved the goods of Babylon more than the land of Canaan. Thus Christ by his death brought forth liberation for all: but not all individuals receive this gift, but rather they love the goods of the earth more than those of heaven and the divine word. 2. From the Jubilee years. When these arose, all slaves in the O.T. could reclaim their possessions, since by virtue of the command, Levit. 25, verse 40, that liberty was actually acquired for all. And nevertheless many remained under perpetual servitude, on account of their own negligence and neglect of their privileges. In like manner it is arranged with spiritual liberation, which is indeed acquired for all but not accepted by all. 3. From the Liberality of a Prince. If someone should count out a certain sum of money to the Turkish Emperor for the redemption of certain captives, liberty is sufficiently acquired for them by this pact. But let us suppose that some remain captives in Turkey, and are not actually liberated; what indeed is the cause? Certainly not a defect, for it was perfectly paid, no less for them than for others who have been liberated, but only their own will, since they despised the benefit of the Prince, and chose captivity over liberty. Thus all men are held captive in the kingdom of sin and Satan: yet for all Christ gave his precious blood as ἀντίλυτρον. If, however, some do not receive this out of their own malice: this itself detracts nothing from the merit or the universality of it. Thus Christ taught, John 3, v. 19, giving the reason why not all are saved, when nevertheless he himself came as a heavenly light to illuminate all: this is, he says, the judgment, The light came into the world, but men loved darkness more than light. The same is held in John 1, v. 11, and following. 4. From the acceptance of alms. If a gift or alms is offered to someone, no one becomes a participant in it if he spurns it, nor receives that gift by extending his hand: For both are required, both the hand offering, and the hand receiving what is offered. Thus the benefits obtained by the death of Christ are offered in the word to all, but they are not conferred except to believers: For faith is the hand on our part, receiving the gift offered. To which point refers that of Bernard, sermon 32 on the Song of Songs, and sermon 3 in the Annunciation: Each person possesses as much of these goods as he gathers with the vessel of trust. 5. From medicine. If some physician should bring a precious medicine of health to a city infected with plague, then salvation is by this very fact obtained for all: If, however, some spurn the physician and the physician's remedy and refuse to apply it, they are not healed, not because of a defect in the remedy, but because of the neglect of it. Thus the blood of Christ is a medicine for sins, most effective for the diseases of the soul; but that the effect does not follow in all, happens because of their own vice and contempt, just as all things were prepared at the Lord's Supper, Luke 14, and at the wedding, Matthew 22, yet, those who did not come, tasted nothing of the Lord's dishes. I conclude therefore with the saying of Augustine, which is read in l. art. sibi falsò impos. artic. 1. The cup of immortality, which is prepared from our infirmity and divine power, has indeed in itself that it may profit all, but if it is not drunk, it does not profit.

Latin:

XIX. Si Christus pro omnibus satisfecit, omnes, etiam manifestè impij saluabuntur. Nam pro quibus solutum est λύτρον, illi iniustè æternæ damnationis carcere mancipantur.

XX. Respond. 1. Argumentum hoc directè Scripturis est oppositum. In ijs enim vtrumque dicitur, tum Christum esse propitiationem pro peccatis totius mundi 1. Iohan. 2. versu 2. tum multos perire, etiam eos, pro quibus Christus est mortuus & satisfecit 2. Petr. 2. versu 1. Hebræor. 6. versu 4. 5. 6. Capit 10. versu 26. Romanor. 14. versu 16. 1. Corinth. 8. versu 11. Quare nisi ἀντιλογίας manifestas in Dei verbo concedere velimus, consequentiam in argumento nullam esse, fatendum est.

XXI. 2. Distinguimus inter beneficij acqui sitionem & acquisiti applicationem. Illa generalis est, quoniam Christus morte suâ totius mundi salutem promeruit. Hæc verò specialis est, quoniam soli Credentes & Euangelium verâ fide recipientes beneficij illius fiunt participes. Qui autem more Iudæorum pertinacium, verbum fidei organon repellunt, Sacramenta & Consilia Dei de salute sua cum Pharisaeis spernunt, illi propria culpa priuantur beneficijs, Christi morte acquisitis. Innuit hoc Apost. 2. Cor. 5. versu 18. Deus erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, & mox tamen additur versu 20. Reconciliemini Deo. Videtur hic esse ἀντίφασις, sed conciliatio est facilis, si dicatur prius membrum de acquisitione, posterius de applicatione agere; Facta est reconciliatio per Christum, quoad adeptionem; facienda est per poenitentiam & fidem, quoad aprehensionem.

XXII. 3. Declarari haec omnia possunt quibusdam similitudinibus. 1. A liberatione & Captiuitate Babylonica. Rex Cyrus publicis edictis omnibus Iudaeis reuersionem in patriam concessit Esdrae 1. versu. 3. 4. 2. Paral. 36. versu 22. multi tamen manserunt sub seruitute, non ob defectum libertatis partae, sed propria voluntate, quoniam regium beneficium acceptare noluerunt, sed bona Babylonis prae terra Chanaan dilexerunt. Sic Christus morte sua liberationem peperit vniuersis: Sed non singuli hoc donum accipiunt, verum magis bona terrae, quam coeli & verbi diuini diligunt. 2. Ab annis Iubilaeis. His exortis, poterant omnes serui in V. T. possessiones suas repetere, quoniam vi mandati, Leuit. 25. versu 40. omnibus libertas illa fuit actu acquisita. Et nihilominus multi manserunt sub perpetuis seruitijs, ob propriam negligentiam & neglectum priuilegiorum. Pari modo comparatum est cum liberatione spirituali, quae omnibus quidem acquisita At non omnibus accepta est. 3. A Liberalitate Principis. Si quis Imperatori Tucico pro redemtione quorundam captivorum certam pecuniae summam numeret, libertas ipsis sufficienter hoc pacto acquiritur. Sed ponamus, nonnullos in Turcia manere captivos, nec actu liberari, Quid vero causae? defectus certe non quippè quod perfectè solutum, non minus pro ipsîs quàm pro álijs qui liberati sunt, sed tantùm propria voluntas, quoniam contempserunt beneficium Principis, & captiuitatem præ libertate elegerunt. Sic omnes homines in regno peccati & Satanæ detinentur captiui: pro omnibus verò Christus pretiosum suum sanguinem dedit ἀντίλυτρον. Si verò hoc non accipiant quidam ex malitia propria: nihil hoc ipsùm merito aut vniuersalitati eius derogat. Ita Christus docuit, Iohan. 3. v. 19 reddens causam, cur non omnes saluentur, cùm tamen ipse tanquam lux cælica ad omnes illuminandum venerit: hoc est, inquit, iudicium, Lux venit in mundum, sed dilexerunt homines magis tenebras, quàm lucem. Idem habetur Iohan. 1. v. 11. & seqq. 4. Ab Eleemosinæ acceptatione. Si alicui donum vel eleemosyna porrigatur, nemo fit eius particeps, si spernat, nec manum extrudendo munus illud recipiat: Requiritur enim vtrumque, & manus offerens, & manus oblata accipiens. Sic beneficia morte Christi parta offeruntur in verbo omnibus, non autèm conferuntur nisi credentibus: Fides enim est manus altera ex parte nostri, donum porrectum accipiēs. Quò spectat istud Bernhard. serm. 32. super Cant. & serm. 3. in Annot: Tantum quisque de hisce bonis possidet, quantum vase fiduciæ colligit. 5. A medicamento. Si medicus aliquis ad vrbem peste infectam afferat pretiosam sanitatis medicinam, tum salus omnibus hoc ipso parta est: Si qui verò medicum mediciq́; pharmacum spernant & adhibere recusent, illi non sanantur, non ob defectum remedij, sed eius neglectum. Sic Christi sanguis medicamen est pro peccatis, animæ morbis efficacissimum; quòd verò effectus non sequitur in omnibus, fit ob ipsorum vitium & contemptum, sicut omnia parata erant in Cœna Domini, Luc. 14. & in nuptijs, Matth. 22 attamē, qui non veniebant, de ferculis Domini nihil gustâbant. Concludo igitur dicto Augustini, quod legitur l. art. sibi falsò impos. artic. 1. Poculum immortalitatis, quod confectum est de infirmitate nostra & virtute divina, habet quidem in se, vt omnibus profit, sed si non bibitur, non proficit.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: Argument IV. From the love of God

ARGUMENT IV. From the love of GOD.

XXIII. Concerning the dogma of Christ's satisfaction, they are openly at variance with the word of GOD, since it follows from that, that GOD did not love us before the death of Christ, which is against John ch. 3 v. 16. So GOD loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, and against Paul Rom. 5 v. 8. While we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.

XXIV. Response. It does not follow from our opinion, as the Photinians think it follows, nor do I remember that it has been said or written by any orthodox person. For we distinguish between the general and the special love of GOD. The former concerns the whole human race; the latter, the faithful alone; of the former, the discourse is in John 3 and Rom. 5; of the latter, Eph. 1 v. 6, he loved us in the beloved. The former precedes in order the death and merit of Christ, since it was done out of the singular love of God that He sent His Son to redeem the human race. But the latter follows His death and the apprehension of it: for GOD pursues no one with His special love (by which we are adopted into sons and are written as heirs of eternal life), unless through that which Christ satisfied, and those who appropriate this very thing to themselves by faith; those therefore who taught that Christ by His death obtained for us the grace and love of the Father, this is to be understood of special love, and of the grace of reconciliation itself. Otherwise we do not deny that God loved us in general before Christ died, when we were yet sinners. Chemnitius indeed in Tom. 2 of the Common Places, page 347, writes: Outside of Christ no grace or mercy of God toward sinners ought to be or can be rightly conceived, unless the Law is dissolved, destroyed, and perishes, which is impossible. But he himself also understands first and foremost special grace as consisting in benevolent acceptance and the forgiveness of sins.

XXV. Some object: If GOD loved us before the death of the Son, and the reconciliation was made, He was unjust, since sinners, who have deserved punishment, ought to be punished, not loved.

1. But I respond: 1. That Scripture joins all these things together, namely that God is just; that He loved us while we were still sinners and enemies, Rom. 5. v. 18. 19. and that we are not reconciled except through Christ. Wherefore these things will not conflict, but will stand together.

2. The affection of pitying is one thing, absolution is another. A judge can pity a sinner, but he cannot absolve him without satisfaction.
