Thus God first pitied us, since we fell into such great calamities through the seduction of Satan: and thus general mercy preceded in God. Because, however, He had threatened punishments, and justice demanded them, He did not wish to absolve fallen men, unless the merit was first paid through Christ. Therefore, general mercy is one thing, the grace of reconciliation is another. The former preceded merit, the latter followed the consideration of merit: the former commends the kindness of God, the latter His justice, which is a perpetual and admirable balance in our redemption.

3. Others distinguish between simple or internal mercy, and efficacious or external mercy, joined with the actual absolution of the sinner and his reception into grace. A judge can pity a sinner without injustice, according to the circumstances, and wish him well, and even think of means of redeeming him: meanwhile, if he dismisses the due punishments, which the laws require, which he himself seriously proclaimed and threatened, without any λύτρῳ, and thus includes him in efficacious mercy, this brands the judge with the mark of iniquity and falsehood,

of iniquity, since he himself transgresses his own laws. Of falsehood, because what he said and threatened, he does not keep.

XXVI. Now that this may be applied, we say that the mercy of God toward the human race, the first, by which He thought of the means, was simple and internal, which could have had a place without any injustice before the satisfaction. But because He had most certainly threatened death, Genesis 2, verse 17, and on that account was angry with the human race, and the law demanded punishment; hence He willed that the satisfaction of the Son should intervene before He received the fallen into grace and embraced them with efficacious mercy. If you say that anger and love cannot exist together, and therefore God, if He loved us, was not angry with us, and conversely: I respond by distinguishing between highest anger and tempered anger. The former excludes love, the latter includes it. However, the anger of God was not the highest; otherwise He would have immediately damned men, as He did Lucifer: But it was tempered and mixed with love, not otherwise than in even the most severe punishments, a certain little spark of God's love is accustomed to shine forth, whence Chrysostom said: God anointed the sword of justice with the oil of mercy. Therefore, the sign of an angry God was the removal of the concreated image, the corruption of nature, death, and similar punishments: but the sign of a merciful God was that love by which He so loved the world that He gave His Son for our sins unto death. This is that admirable tempering, for which a similar example is not found in the whole world.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM. IV. A dilectione DEI.

XXIII. Dogmade Christi satisfactione apertè diuersi satur DEI verbo, quoniam indè sequitur, DEVM ante mortem Christi nos non dilexisse, id quod est contra Iohannem c. 3. v. 16. Sic DEVS dilexit mundum, vt Filium suum vnigenitum daret, & contrà Paulum. Rom. 5. v. 8. Cùm adhuc peccatores essemus, Christus pro nobis mortuus est.

XXIV. Respond. Non sequitur ex nostra opinione, quod sequi putant Photiniani, nec à quovis orthodoxo id dictum scriptúmue memini. Distinguimus enim inter dilectionem DEI generalem & specialem. Illa concernit totum genus humanum; haec solos fideles, de illa sermo est Ioh. 3. & Rom 5. de hac Eph. 1. v. 6. dilexit nos in dilecto. Illa ordine praecellit mortem, meritúmque Christi, quoniam ex singulari amore Dei factum est, vt Filium suum mitteret ad redimendum genus humanum. Haec autē mortem eiusq; apprehensionem sequitur: DEVS enim neminem speciali amore suo (quo in filios adoptamur, & vitae aeternae scribimur haeredes) prosequitur, nisi p̃ quò Christus satisfecit, & qui hoc ipsum fide sibi appropriatis; qui ergò docuerunt, Christum morte sua, Patris gratiam & amorem nobis impetrasse, intelligendum hoc erit dilectione speciali, & ipsa reconciliationis gratia. Aliàs non negamus, Deum nos in genere dilexisse, antequam Christus moreretur, cùm adhuc peccatores essemus. Chemnitius quidē Tom. 2. locorum CC. pag. 347. scribit: Extrà Christum nulla gratia aut misericordia Dei erga peccatores, nec debet nec potest rectè cogitari, nisi Lex soluatur, destruatur, & intereat, quod impossibile est. Verùm & ipse cum primis intelligit gratiam specialem in acceptione beneuola & peccatorum veniâ consistentem.

XXV. Excipiunt quidam: Si DEVS nos dilexit ante mortem Filij, & factam reconciliationem, fuit iniustus, quoniam peccatores, qui pœnam promeruerunt, puniri, non diligi debent.

1. Sed Respond. 1. Scripturam hæc omnia coniungere, nempè Deum iustum esse; nos dilexisse adhuc peccatores & inimicos Rom. 5. v. 18. 19. & non nisi per Christum reconciliari. Quare non pugnabunt ista, sed simul consistent.

2. Aliud est affectus miserendi, aliud absolutio. Potest iudex misereri peccatoris, sed absoluere non potest sine satisfactione. Sic Deus primùm misertus est nostri, quoniam per seductionem Satanæ in tantas calamitates incidimus: atque sic præcessit in Deo generalis misericordia. Quia tamen pœnas minatus erat, & iustitia eas postulabat, hinc lapsos homines absoluere noluit, nisi soluto prius per Christum merito. Aliud ergò est generalis misericordia, aliud reconciliationis gratia. Illa præcessit meritum, hæc secuta est intuitum meriti: Illa Dei benignitatem: hæc iustitiam commendat, quod temperamentum in redemptione nostra perpetuum & admirandum est.

3. Alij distinguunt inter misericordiam simplicem vel internam, & efficacem vel externam, cum ipsa actuali peccatoris absolutione & in gratiam receptione coniunctum. Potest iudex peccatoris sine iniustitia misereri, pro ratione circumstantiarum & benè illi cupere, adeoque de medijs redimendi cogitare: Interim si pœnas debitas, quas leges requirunt, quas ipse seriò indixit & minatus est, sine omni λύτρῳ dimittat, adeoque efficaci misericordiâ comprehendat, hoc iudici iniquitatis & falsitatis notam inurit,

iniquitatis, quoniam leges suas ipse transilit. Falsitatis, quia quod dixit & minatus est, non seruat.

XXVI. Iam vt hoc applicetur, dicimus misericordiam Dei erga genus humanum primam, qua de medijs cogitauit, fuisse simplicem & internam, quæ sine omni iniustitia locum habere potuit ante satisfactionem. Quia verò mortem certissimè minatus fuerat. Genej 2. v. 17. & proptereà irascebatur humano generi, & lex supplicium exigebat; hinc satisfactionem filij interuenire voluit, antequam in gratiam lapsos reciperet & efficaci misericordia complecteretur. Si dicas, iram & amorem simul consistere non posse, ideóque Deum, si nos dilexit, iratum nobis non fuisse & contrà: Respond. Distinguendo inter inter iram summam & temperatam. Illa dilectionem excludit, hæc includit. Fuit autem ira Dei nõ summa; quidem protinus aliàs damnâsset homines, vti Luciferum: Sed temperata & amore mixta, non secus atque in grauissimis etiam pœnis, Dei quædam amoris scintillula emicare solet, vnde Chrysostomus dixit; Deus gladium iustitiæ oleo misericordiæ inunxit. Signum igitur irati Dei fuit, ablatio concreatæ imaginis, corruptio naturæ mors, & pœnæ similes: sed signum misericordis, fuit amor ille, quo sic dilexit mundum, vt daret Filium pro peccatis nostris in mortem. Hæc illa est admirabilis temperatura, cui simile exemplum non reperitur in orbe vniuerso.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: Argument V From the mercy of God, by which alone we are said to be saved

ARGUMENT V.

From the mercy of God, by which alone we are said to be saved.

XXVII. If we are saved on account of the payment rendered by Christ, we shall not be saved freely, and out of mercy alone, which is nevertheless asserted everywhere in the Scriptures. For freely and a price, whether paid by the debtor or by another, always conflict. The Turkish Emperor is not said to have released a captive freely, if a λύτρον is paid by another; and it would follow that salvation is gratuitous on the part of CHRIST, not on the part of GOD THE FATHER, who is the one to whom a sufficient price has been presented. This argument is urged by the Racovian Catechism, page 262, Osterodus page 211, and Gittichius page 90, who writes openly: that we make the Best and Greatest GOD out to be a Caracalla or some most vehement Nero, instead of a most clement Father.

XXIIX. Resp 1. This little argument is in turn directly opposed to the most clear word of God. For this happens everywhere, that what the Photinians separate, it teaches to be subordinate, which they hold to be repugnant. For both are asserted: that Christ gave himself as a price of redemption for all, 1 Tim. 2:6, and that we are saved freely by grace alone, Rom. 3:24. Therefore, since there is no falsehood in the words of Scripture, both will be true, without any ἀντιφάσει or contradiction.

XXIX. 2. We do not oppose the merit of Christ to the mercy of God, but to justice, which alone demanded it. But just as justice does not take away mercy, so neither does merit, by which justice was satisfied, exclude it: For in a fourfold respect we are said to be saved freely and by mercy alone: 1. In respect of the decreed satisfaction; for that God undertook the counsel of our liberation, that he found the means of the mission of his son, and thus he himself procured salvation and the instruments of salvation, without any merit or purchase price of ours, indeed even while we were ignorant; this is certainly a great argument of love, as it is said in John 3:16. So God loved the world that he gave his only begotten Son. Rom. 5:8. GOD commends his love, in that Christ died for us, when we were still sinners and enemies. 1 John 4:9. In this the love of God appeared in us, because GOD sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. And verse 10. In this is love, not that we loved GOD, but because he (first) loved us, and sent his Son as a propitiation for our sins.

2. With respect to gratuitous acceptance. If GOD had wished to deal with us according to the rigor of justice, He could have rejected another's satisfaction, as is hinted at in Ezekiel 18:20: The soul that sinneth, it shall die. As if another were willing to die for another, a son for a father or vice versa, in tyranny or persecution, or victory, then the victor does not immediately accept this condition, but it is a matter of clemency if he consents. Since, therefore, God undertook another's merit, and imputed it to us, and held it as our own, by this very fact He clearly declared His mercy.

3. With respect to the exclusion of legal justice. This is that principal opposition which the Apostle Paul always urges: for he perpetually opposes grace and works, If by grace, then it is no more of works, and conversely, Romans 11:6. Whoever, therefore, are saved without their own works, these are saved freely out of mercy alone, according to the perpetual inference of the Apostle. But indeed, those who are saved through faith in the merit of Christ are saved without their own works; therefore it remains firm and established that all believers are saved freely and out of mercy alone, although they are not saved without the merit of Christ. For those particles, freely, by grace, are never opposed to the merit and satisfaction of Christ, but only to the law and our works. They therefore pervert the Apostolic doctrine who argue from the position of grace to the exclusion of merit, since all grace is founded in merit, and salvation happens only through Christ as the cause, not merely as the herald of the cause.

4. With respect to gratuitous imputation and infused faith. For God not only sent His Son out of grace, and accepted His merit, but also [imputed] it it is imputed out of grace, and it generates faith in us without us, which is an argument of the greatest mercy and kindness, of which the Psalmist sings, Ps 32. v. 1. and the Apostle Rom. 4. v. 9. The Photinians remove this respect through their principles, who establish that faith is not a special gift of God; but they assert with the Pelagians that it proceeds from free will.

XXX. 3. While the Photinians wish to defend the mercy of God, they utterly remove and deny it. For they place their hope in works, and contend that salvation is given only through works, and indeed by merit, as Ostorodus teaches in his Institutiones, page 261. But now, what is more contrary to gratuitous salvation and the mercy of God than the merit of works? And is there not a perpetual opposition in the Apostle between grace and merit, faith and works, the Gospel and the Law? What is clearer than these words in Romans 4, verse 4: To him who works, the reward is not imputed according to grace, but according to debt. And Romans 11, verse 6: If it is by works, it is no longer by grace. Therefore it stands firm: He who constitutes works as the cause of salvation removes the grace and mercy of God. The Photinians assume the antecedent, and therefore they can by no reasoning remove the consequent from themselves. And indeed the impudence of Satan is to be wondered at here, in that he tries to persuade men that the most holy merit of Christ conflicts, but that the little works and merits of men do not conflict with the mercy of God, when the Apostle completely inverts the matter and defends the contrary everywhere, by including the blood of Christ and excluding any works whatsoever from the act of salvation.

XXXI. 4. The comparison regarding the Turkish Emperor is foreign, and does not fit. So that this may be understood, it must be known that there is a twofold payment of λύτρον as it is captivity; for some are held in prison by force by an enemy, without their own fault, which captivity here can be called [the captivity of] sons: Some are held by law by a judge on account of preceding sins; and this we call judicial captivity: He who is held by an enemy is not released for free, if a price is paid for them. For the Tyrant is satisfied in full, as much as he demands, and therefore no grace concurs. But those who are held captive by the force of laws by a judge on account of their own crimes, deserving a heavy penalty, to them is certainly shown great grace, if the judge accepts another's satisfaction. For thus he remits from the rigor, since he imposes part of the penalty on the delinquent himself, but part on another interceding: Although strict law demands that he who alone sinned should undergo the whole penalty. For example: Let there be a Law passed concerning the gouging out of both eyes for one who has committed adultery; Now if another should intercede for the adulterer, and wish to lose his eye in his place, then indeed the Law is satisfied, but yet not without the judge's grace, while he divides the penalty between the delinquent and his friend: That we may therefore apply these things, we are all captives, but not without our own fault; but on account of our sins. Although Christ satisfied for these, yet it is an indication of mercy that God the judge accepted another's λύτρον. Indeed there are also other members of dissimilarity, which we all join together in this way: 1. The Turkish Emperor is an enemy who gapes for money, God is a judge who wishes his justice to be satisfied. 2. Those captured by the Turk are without fault: but we are in fault, and we owe penalties to God the judge, which are not bare and common debts, depending solely on the will of the creditor, but have respect to the natural and immutable justice of God declared in the law. 3. Those captured by the Turk are held by force: we remain in captivity through the curse of the law and according to the tenor of justice. 4. The Turk demands only money: God threatens penalties to the offenders themselves, which if he remits, by accepting another's satisfaction, he makes his grace manifest by this very act.

5. The Turk does not initiate a plan concerning another's payment, nor does grace move the satisfier from that: but God consulted about redeeming the human race, and out of mere love sent his son into the world, and therefore grace concurs here, although it finds no place there. From all of which it becomes manifest that the Turkish remission and our justification are poorly compared in this case.

XXXII. 6. If we wish to argue from men to GOD, from human to divine forgiveness, then it will follow that GOD, without any repentance and faith, by his bare will, just as any other secular creditor, can remit sins, which however is contrary to the whole of Scripture. For however much a man may be able to forgive a fault to a man without any satisfaction, three things nevertheless stand in the way of this being done by God.

1. The immutability of justice. For GOD is a severe judge, who does not let the delinquent go unpunished. For punishment always follows fault, which the delinquent himself ought to undergo, by the rigor of justice, but GOD imposed it upon his son, through the greatness of mercy.

2. The incorrupt truth of GOD. GOD said, In whatever day you eat, you shall die the death. Here what is to be after the fault is indicated and predicted. Now if GOD had immediately remitted the sin, without the guilt of death and satisfaction, he would certainly have predicted a falsehood, and his truth would not stand.

3. The inviolate authority of the law. The sum of this is, Do and you shall live; If you do not do it, you shall be cursed. Now as the essence of GOD, so also the sentence, revealed by the law, is immutable. Wherefore when man sins, by this very act he immediately incurs the curse of the law. Whoever therefore he says, that GOD remits sins out of mere will without any satisfaction, by this very fact he abolishes the law of GOD, and enervates all its authority. And these are those reasons why GOD does not grant pardon without a preceding λύτρῳ, which nevertheless can be done by common debt, and sometimes happens; and therefore all the inferences of the Photinians sought from the likeness of human remission or dismissal lack strength, and conclude nothing.

XXXIII. 6. For a better understanding of the argument and our response, it is to be noted that the word grace is taken: 1. ἁπλῶς or absolutely, in respect of its being, in which way it is nothing else than an essential property of GOD. With the remaining attributes it is a most simple thing ταυτὸ, and therefore the same as God's omnipotence and justice, namely as regards ὑπόςασιν or essence, although by reason of κατηγορίας or predication it does not admit that identity. 2. σχετικῶς relatively, insofar as it proceeds outwardly, in which way that word is πολύσημος, and signifies 1. The grace of creation, by which GOD created us humans endowed with a rational soul: which acceptance, however, is catachrestic and improper. 2. The grace of conservation, by which things created by GOD are mercifully sustained, and therefore it is nothing else than universal providence, of which Paul speaks in Acts 17, verses 25, 28. 3. The grace of revelation, by which GOD manifested His will partly in the law, partly in the Gospel, which revelation happened primarily through Christ, as is taught in John 1, verses 16, 18. The law was given through Moses, Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; the only begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him. 4. The grace of vocation, through which the revealed word is preached in the whole world, announced to all nations, and most strongly sealed by the Sacraments as if by certain seals.

5. The grace of renewal, which comprises the illustrious gifts of piety, by which the body of sin is destroyed, the flesh is restrained, so that having cast aside worldly pursuits we may walk in holiness. Of these, discourse is made in Rom. 12, verse 6: Having gifts according to the grace that is given to us, etc. 1 Cor. 15, verse 10: His grace in me was not void. 6. The grace of salvation, or which is the same thing, of justification and election, since all these have the same causes. And this is that grace which we understand here, which by no means excludes satisfaction. For it is indeed gratuitous, yet not absolute, but founded in the merit of Christ. Hence we are said to be chosen in Christ, Eph. 1, verse 4, in whom we are also blessed, verse 5, and are rendered accepted, verse 6. In whom we have redemption through his blood, v. 7, in whom we are righteous, 2 Cor. 5, v. 21. and are saved, Acts 4, verse 12, to which add Romans 9, verse 24, chapter 4, verse 16, 1 Cor. 1, verses 4, 5, Galat. 2, verse 21, Eph. 2, v. 5, 8, 9. And this grace is the same as mercy, as is evident from Eph. 2, verses 4, 5, 6, 7, compared with 8. That is always opposed to our merits and works, but not to the blood and satisfaction of Christ, whence it follows that we are saved freely, and by grace, with regard to our merits, but not absolutely with regard to the merit of Christ. They therefore confuse contraries with relatives. They think the grace of God and the satisfaction of Christ are contrary to each other, when nevertheless they are most closely joined, which is evident even from a single aphorism of the Apostle, Rom. 3, v. 24. This would never happen if they were contrary. For these destroy each other, but when one of the relatives is posited, the other is immediately posited as well; wherefore, since the grace of God and the merit of Christ mutually regard each other, and are thus relatives, the argument of the Photinians must be vicious when they conclude from the position of grace to the exclusion of merit.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM V.

A misericordia Dei, quâ solâ seruari dicimur.

XXVII. Si saluamur ob persolutionem à Christo præstitam, non saluabimur gratis, & ex solâ misericordia, quod tamen passim in Scripturis asseritur. Gratuà enim & pretium, siue à debitore, siuè ab alio solutum, semper pugnant. Turcicus Imperator non dicitur gratis dimisisse captiuum, st ab alio λύτρον est persolutum; & sequeretur, saluationem esse gratuitam ex parte CHRISTI, non ex parte DEI PATRIS, quip, e, cui sufficiens pretium est exhibitum. Vrget hoc argumentum Ca-eches. Rackov: pag. 262. Osterodus pag. 211. & Gittichius pag. 90. qui apertè scribit: nos pro Patre clementissimo DEVM Optimum Maximum Caracallam aut Neronem aliquem vehementissimum efficere.

XXIIX. Resp 1. Ratiuncula hæc vicissim directè opponitur clarissimo Dei verbo. Hoc enim passim contingit, quæ Photiniani disiungunt, subordinata esse docet, quæ illi pro repugnantibus habent. Nam vtrumque asseritur, tum Christum semetipsum dedisse pretium redemptionis pro omnibus, 1. Tim. 5. v. 6. tum nos gratis ex sola gratia saluari, Rom. 3. v. 24. Proindè, cum in Scripturæ verbis nulla sit falsitas, verum erit vtrumque, sine omni ἀντιφάσει vel contradictione.

XXIX. 2. Meritum Christi non opponimus misericordiæ Dei, sed iustitiæ, quæ sola illud exigebat. Sicut autem iustitia non tollit misericordiam, ita nec meritum, quo iustitiæ satisfactum, eandem excludit: Nam quadruplici respectu alio dicimur gratis, & ex sola misericordia saluari: 1. Respectu decretæ satisfactionis; Quòd enim Deus consilium suscepit de nostra liberatione, quòd medium inuenit de missione filij, adeòque ipse saluteni & salutis organa procurauit, sine omni nostro vel merito vel emptionis pretio, imò & nobis ignorantibus; hoc vtique magnum dilectionis argumentum est, vt dicitur Iohan. 3. v. 16. Sic Deus dilexit mundum vt Filium suum vnigenitum daret. Rom. 5. v. 8. Commendat DEVS charitatem suam, quòd Christus pro nobis mortuus, cùm adhuc peccatores & inimici essemus. 1. Ioh. 4. ver. 9. In hoc apparuit charitas Dei in nobis, quoniam Filium suū vnigenitum misit DEVS in mundum, vt viuamus per eum. Et vers. 10. In hoc est charitas, non quòd nos dileximus DEVM, sed quoniam ipse (prior) dilexit nos, & misit Filium suum propitiationem pro peccatis nostris.

2. Respectu gratuita acceptationis. Si pro rigore iustitiæ nobiscum agere voluisset DEVS, repudiare potuisset alienam satisfactionem, sicut innuitur Ezech. 18. v. 20. Anima quæ peccaverit, ipsa morietur. Vt si alius pro alio filius pro patre vel contrà, mori vellet, in Tyrannide aut persecutione, vel victoria, tum victor hac conditionem non statim accipit, sed clementiæ est, si consentiat. Quoniam ergò Deus suscepit alienum meritum, & illud nobis imputavit, proque nostro habuit, hoc ipso misericordiam suam luculenter declaravit.

3. Respectu exclusæ iustitiæ legalis. Hoc illud principale est oppositum, quod Apostolus Paulus semper vrget : Gratiam enim & opera perpetuò opponit, Si ex gratia, iam non ex operibus, & contrà, Rom. 11. vers. 6. Quicunque igitur sine operibus proprijs salvantur, hi gratis ex solâ misericordiâ salvantur, secundùm perpetuam illationem Apostoli. At verò, qui per fidem in Christi meritum salvantur, illi sine suis operibus salvantur, Ergò manet firmum ratumque quòd gratis & ex sola misericordia salui fiant omnes credentes, licèt non sine Christi merito salventur. Illæ enim particulæ, gratis, ex gratia, nunquam opponuntur merito & satisfactioni Christi, sed tantùm legi & nostris operibus. Doctrinam igitur Apostolicam pervertunt, qui à positione gratiæ ad exclusionem meriti argumentantur, Cùm omnis gratia in merito fundetur, & salus non nisi per Christum tanquam causam non tanquam causæ præconem tantùm contingat.

4. Respectu gratuitæ imputationis & infusæ fidei. Deus enim non modò Filium ex gratiâ misit, eiusque meritum acceptavit, sed illud etiam ipsum ex gratia imputatur, & fidem sine nobis, in nobis generat, id quod maximæ misericordiæ & benignitatis argumentum est, de quo Psalmista canit, Ps 32. v. 1. & Apost. Rom. 4. v. 9. Huc respectum Photiniani tollunt per sua principia, qui fidem non Dei donum speciale esse statuunt; sed ex libero arbitrio proficiscicum Pelagianis antumant.

XXX. 3. Photiniani dum misericordiam Dei defendere volunt, prorsus illam tollunt & abnegant. In operibus enim spem collocant, & non nisi per opera salutem dari contendunt, & quidem ex merito, vt Ostorodus docet in instit. pag. 261. Iam verò quid saluti gratuitæ, & Dei miserirordiæ magis est contrarium, quàm meritum operum? & non perpetua apud Apostolum est oppositio inter gratiam & meritum, fidem & opera, Evangelium & Legem? Quid clarius his verbis Roman. 4. vers. 4. Ei qui operatur merces non imputatur secundum gratiam, sed secundum debitum. Et Roman. 11. vers. 6: Si ex operibus, iam non ex gratia. Stat ergò firmum: Qui opera salutis causam constituit, Dei gratiam & misericordiam tollit. Antecedens Photiniani assumunt, ideoque consequens à se nullâ ratione amoliri queunt. Et sanè miranda est hîc Satanæ impudentia, quòd hominibus persuadere conatur, meritum Christi sanctissimum pugnare, sed opellas & merita hominum non pugnare cum Dei misericordia, Cùm Apostolus rem planè inuertat, & contrarium vbique defendat, sanguinem Christi includendo, & opera quæuis ex actu saluationis excludendo.

XXXI. 4. Similitudo de Imperatore Turcico aliena est, nec quadrat. Quod vt intelligatur sciendum, quod duplex sit persolutio λύτρο vt est captiuitas; Quidam enim in carcere tenentur per vim ab hoste, sine sua culpa, quæ captiuitas heic filiis vocari potest: Quidam tenentur per ius à iudice ob peccata præcedentia; & hanc captiuitatem iudicialem nuncupamus : Qui ab hoste tenetur, non dimittitur gratis, si pro ijs soluatur pretium. Nam in totum satisfit Tyranno, quantum exigit, ideoque nihil gratiæ concurrit. Qui autem vigore legum captiui tenentur à iudice ob sua delicta, grauem pœnam promerentia, illis exhibetur vtique magna gratia, si iudex alienam satisfactionem recipiat. Sic enim remittit de rigore, siquidem partem pœnæ imponit delinquenti ipsi, partem verò alij intercedenti : Cùm tamen strictum ius postulet, vt totam pœnam subeat is, qui solus peccauit. Exempli gratiâ: Sit Lex lata de effodiendo vtroque oculo, qui commiserit adulterium; Iam si alius pro adultero intercedat, & oculum illius loco amittere velit, tunc quidem satisfit Legi, sed tamen non sine Iudicis gratia, dum pœnam partitur inter delinquentem & eius amicum : Vt igitur hæc applicemus, captiui nos omnes sumus, sed non absque propria culpa; verùm ob peccata nostra. Pro his licèt Christus satisfecerit, tamen misericordiæ indicium est, quod Deus iudex alienum λύτρον acceptauerit. Imò & alia sunt dissimilitudinis membra, quæ omnia hoc pacto copulamus: 1. Imperator Turcicus hostis est, qui pecuniæ inhiat, Deus iudex, qui suæ satisfactum vult iustitiæ. 2. Capti à Turca carent culpa: sed nos in culpa sumus, & Deo iudici pœnas debemus, quæ non sunt nuda & communia debita, ex sola creditoris voluntate pendentia, sed ad naturalem & immutabilem Dei iustitiam in lege declaratam respectum habent. 3. A Turca capti tenentur per vim: nos in captiuitate hæremus per maledictionem legis & secundum tenorem iustitiæ. 4. Turca postulat tantùm pecuniam: Deus minatur pœnas ipsis delinquentibus, quas si remittit, alienam satisfactionem accipiendo, gratiam suam hoc ipso luculentam facit.

5. Turca consilium de aliena persolutione non init, nec ex eo gratia satisfactorem excitat: Deus autem de redimendo genere humano consultauit, & ex mera dilectione filium misit in mundum, ideoque gratia hic concurrit, quamuis ibi locum non inueniat. Ex quibus omnibus manifestum euadit, male in hoc casu comparari dimissionem Turcicam & iustificationem nostram.

XXXII. 6. Si ab hominibus ad DEVM, ab humana ad diuinam condonationem argumentari velimus, tum sequetur, DEVM absque omni poenitentia & fide, pro nuda sua voluntate vt alius quispiam creditor secularis peccata posse remittere, quod tamen toti Scripturae est contrarium. Quantumuis enim homo homini sine omni satisfactione culpam queat dimittere, quo minus tamen a Deo id fiat, tria obstant.

1. Iustitiae immutabilitas. DEVS enim seuerus iudex est, qui delinquentes non dimittit impunitos. Nam culpam poena semper sequitur, quam delinquens ipse subire debet, pro rigore iustitiae, sed DEVS eam filio suo imposuit, per magnitudinem misericordiae.

2. Incorrupta DEI veritas. Dixit DEVS, Quacunque die comederis, morte morieris. Hic quid post culpa futuru sit, indicitur & praedicitur. Iam si DEVS peccatum protinus remisisset, absque reatu mortis & satisfactione, falsum vtique praedixisset, & veritas eius haud consisteret.

3. Intemerata legis authoritas. Huius summa est, Fac & viues; Ni feceris, maledictus eris. Iam vt DEI essentia, sic & sententia, lege patefacta, est immutabilis. Quare cum homo peccat, hoc ipso legis maledictionem protinus incurrit. Quisquis ergo dicit, DEVM ex nuda voluntate peccata remittere sine omni fatis factione, hoc ipso legem DEI tollit, omnemque eius authoritatem enervat. Et hæ sunt illæ causæ, cur DEYS non largiatur veniam sine prævio λύτρῳ, quod tamen vulgari debito fieri potest, & nonnunquam contingit; ideoque omnes Photinianorum illationes à similitudine humanæ remissionis aut dimissionis petitæ neruis çarent, & nihil concludunt.

XXXIII. 6. Pro meliori intelligentia argumenti, & responsionis nostræ notandum est, quod vox gratiæ sumatur. 1. ἁπλῶς vel absolutè, respectu sui esse, quo pacto nihil est aliud, quàm essentialis DEI proprietas. Cum reliquis attributis simplicissimum quiddam ταυτὸ, adeoque idem cum Dei omnipotentiâ, justitiâ, nempè quoad ὑπόςασιν vel essentiam, quamvis ratione κατηγορίας vel prædicationis identitatem istam non admittat. 2. σχετικῶς relatiuè, quatenus ad extra progreditur, quo pacto vox illa est πολύσημος, & significat 1. Gratiam creationis, qua DEVS nos homines condidit rationali anima præditos: quæ tamen acceptio catachrestica & impropria est. 2. Gratiam conservationis, quares creatæ a DEO clementer sustentantur, adeoque nihil est aliud, quàm vniuersalis prouidentia, de qua Act. 17. versu 25. 28. Paulus loquitur. 3. Gratiam revelationis, quâ DEVS voluntatem suam partim in lege; partim in Evangelio manifestavit, quæ revelatio inprimis per Christum contigit, vti docetur Iohan. 1. versu 16. 18. Lex per Mosen data est, Gratia & veritas per Iesum Christum facta est. Deum nemo vidit vnquam, Vnigenitus filius, qui est in sinu Patris ipsc enarrauit. 4. Gratiam vocationis, per quam revelatum verbum in vniverso mundo prædicatur, omnibus gentibus annunciatur, & Sacramentis ceu quibus dam sigillis, fortissimè obsignatur.

5. Gratiam renovationis, quæ complectitur illustria pietatis dona, quibus peccati corpus destruitur, caro compescitur, vt abiectis secularibus studijs in sanctitate ambulemus. De his sermo fit Rom. 12. vers. 6. Habentes donationes secundum gratiam, quæ data est nobis &c. 1. Cor. 15. vers. 10. Gratia eius in me vacua non fuit. 6. Gratiam Saluationis, vel quòd idem est, iustificationis & electionis, 'quoniam hæc omnia easdem causas habent. Et hæc est illa gratia, quam hic intelligimus, quæ satisfactionem minimè excludit. Nam gratuita quidem est, non tamen absoluta, sed in merito Christi fundata. Hinc dicimur electi in Christo, Eph. 1. vers. 4. in quo & benedicimur, vers. 5. & accepti reddimur. vers. 6. In quo habemus redemptionẽ per sanguinem eius, v. 7. in quo iusti sumus, 2. Cor. 5. v. 21. & saluamur Act. 4. vers. 12. quibus adde Roman. 9. vers. 24. cap. 4. vers. 16. 1. Cor. 1. vers. 4. 5. Galat. 2. vers. 21. Eph. 2. v. 5. 8. 9. Atque hæc gratia idem est, quod misericordia, vt patet ex Eph. 2. versiculis 4. 5. 6. 7. cum 8. collatis. Illa Meritis & operibus nostris semper opponitur, non autem sanguini & satisfactioni Christi, vnde sequitur, quòd gratis saluemur, & ex gratia, quoad nostra merita, sed non absolutè quoad meritum Christi. Confundunt igitur contraria cum relatis. Putant Dei gratiam & Christi satisfactionem sibi contrariari inuicem, cum tamen arctissimè coniuncta sint, quod patet vel ex vnico Apostoli aphorismo Rom. 3. v. 24. Nunquam hoc fieret, si contraria essent. Hæc enim se tollunt, sed relatorum vno posito, statim ponitur & alterum, quare cum gratia Dei & meritum Christi se mutuò respiciant, adeoque relata sint, vitiosum sit oportet Photinianorum argumentum, quando à positione gratiæ ad exclusionem meriti con, cludunt.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: XXXIV. But they object; Whatever may be said

XXXIV. But they object; Whatever may be said,

This flows from the fact that, if the principal end of the death of Christ had been to satisfy divine justice, God would have given Christ to death not so much for our sake as for His own, in order, forsooth, to receive a just debt. But where then is the munificence? Where is that supreme love of GOD for us? There is no regard here for those bound by debt, unless one yields from his own right and abandons the compulsion of satisfaction, from wheresoever it may proceed. Gittich. p. 5. Socinus par. 3. c. 2. pag. 237. 241.

Response 1. Nay, we shall invert the argument. For that on account of which each thing is such, that thing is more such. If, therefore, God gave Christ to death so that He might satisfy His own justice: but He willed this satisfaction so that, with justice preserved, He might be reconciled to us, then certainly He gave Christ to death more for our sake than for His own. For from the ultimate end, or from that which comes closest to the ultimate (because the ultimate of all is the glory of God, Prov. 16, verse 4), rather than from the intermediate, is the denomination made and actions judged. Certainly nothing accrued to God, nor did He demand satisfaction for His own sake, but solely for our sake. For because we were cursed by the sentence of the law, that curse had to be expiated first through the death of the Son, so that we might be saved eternally. 2. What he adds concerning a creditor, that is true of a private and pecuniary one, but not likewise of a public and judicial one, if I may so speak, that is, of the avenger of the law, the exactor and [guardian] of justice by his office. For if this one is not indignant at sinners, nor imposes a penalty, by this very fact he is unjust, not munificent. Meanwhile, if for the sake of the public good he partly shows a way by which the laws may be satisfied and the salvation of the debtor may be consulted, and partly provides from his own the price of redemption and satisfaction, then he is deservedly called both just and munificent and merciful at once; which can be most conveniently applied to our question in such a way that praise is attributed to God for both justice and mercy, namely that because he was indignant at us out of justice, out of mercy he thought about redeeming us, and so that the redemption might take place, he did not even spare his own son.

XXXV. Gittichius objects on page 91. Sordidness is joined with the greatest stupidity, not munificence, to give something to someone, which you immediately receive back from him. Who would not call me delirious and most alien to all reason, if, with my purse open, I were to order a debtor to pay me with my own money? Would it not be better, without the charge of stupidity, to immediately forgive the debt itself, rather than doing what I do through these delirious circumlocutions?

Resp. 1. It was a saying of Chrysostom, It is a great danger to entrust the matters of faith to human reasoning. Therefore, we do not care about this objection, since it has no strength beyond the figments and phantasies of blind reason. The thoughts of God are not as those of men, Isa. 55, v. 8.

2. They are delirious who call it delirium if someone shows a debtor another person who is willing and able to pay for him that which he himself is not equal to paying, and who cannot be dismissed without payment while maintaining the laws. But thus Christ was given to us by God, so that in our place he might give the ἀντίλυτρον of redemption, 1 Tim. 2, v. 6, and be the propitiation for our sins, 1 John 4, v. 10. This saving counsel of God and the admirable tempering of justice and love, which is inculcated everywhere in the scriptures, the Photinians call delirium with a wicked mouth, but may God rebuke you, Satan. It is one thing to pay for another out of one's own purse and immediately receive the same back to oneself; it is another thing for a judge, out of grace, to advise and move another to pay for the debtor. This is not the act of a delirious person, but of one who is merciful and benevolent.

…3. It would not be foolish or sordid if a prince, moved by clemency, were to give money from his own treasury to a criminal so that he might pay the fine owed to the public. He therefore who is said to be foolish, when God is determined to do the same; namely because the wisdom of God is foolishness to the world.

Latin:

XXXIV. Verùm excipiunt; Quicquid dicatur,

manat hoc, quòd, si principalis finis mortis Christi fuisset, diuinæ satisfaceret iustitiæ, non tam nostri, quàm suæ causa Christum Deus in mortem dederit, vt nimirum iustum debitum reciperet. Vbi verò munificentia? vbi summus ille amor DEI in nos? Nullus hic est respectus ære alieno obstrictis, nisi quis de suo iure cedat, & coactionem satisfactionis, à quocunq́; illa proficiscatur, relinquat. Gittich. p. 5. Socinus par. 3. c. 2. pag. 237. 241.

Respon. 1. Imò inuertemus argumentum. Nam propter quod vnumquoquetale est, illud magis est tale. Si ergo Deus Christum in mortem dedit, vt suæ iustitiæ satisfaceret: Hanc verò satisfactionem voluit, vt saluâ iustitiâ nobis possit reconciliari, vtique Christum magis nostri, quàm sui causâ in mortem dedit. Ab vltimo etim fine vel ad vltimum proximè accedente (quia omnium vltimus est gloria Dei, Prouer. 16. vers. 4.) magis quàm ab intermedio fit denominatio & diudicantur actiones. Deo certè nihil accessit, nec sui causa satisfactionem postulauit, sed vnicè propter nos. Quia enim maledicti eramus per legis sententiam, erat illa maledictio per mortem filij prius expianda, vt æternùm saluaremur. 2. Quod de Creditore addit, verum illud de priuato & pecuniario, non item de publico & judiciario, vt ita loquar, hoc est, de vindice legis, exactore & justitiæ ex officio suo. Hic enim si peccatoribus non indignetur, nec pœnam imponat, hoc ipso iniquus est, non munificus. Interim si boni publici causâ partim rationem monstret, quâ legibus satis fiat: & saluti debitoris consuli queat, partim de suo redemptionis pretium & satisfactionem præstet, tunc & justus & munificus vnà ac misericors meritò nuncupatur; id quod ad nostram quæstionem commodissimè sic applicari potest, vt & Iustitiæ & misericordiæ Laus Deo tribuatur, pempè quod ex iustitia nobis indignatus fuerit, ex misericordiâ de redimēdis nobis cogitauerit, îcò vt redemptio fieret, nè quidem proprio filio pepercerit.

XXXV. Instat Gittichius pagin. 91. Sordes cum maxima stultitia coniunctae sunt, non munificentia, donare alicui quidpiam, quod statim ab ipso recipias. Quis me non delirum ac ab omni ratione alienissimum diceret, si aperta crumena mea iuberem debitorem meâ pecuniâ mihi soluere? Annon praestaret, sine crimine stultitiae, quod per istas deliras ambages facio, statim ipsi debitum condonare?

Resp. 1. Chrysostomi dictum fuit, Magnum est periculum, res fidei humanis committere rationibus. Nihil ergò curamus hanc instantiam, cùm præter rationis cæcæ figmenta, & phantasias nihil neruorum habeat. Non sunt cogitationes Dei vt hominum Esa. 55. v. 8.

2. Delirant, qui delirium appellant, si quis debitori monstret alium, qui velit, possit pro ipso soluere id, cui soluendo ipse par non est, & qui absque solutione saluis legibus dimitti nequit. Ita verò Christus à Deo nobis datus est, vt nostri loco daret redemptionis ἀντίλυτρον 1. Timoth. 2. vers. 6. & propitiator esset pro peccatis nostris 1. Iohan. 4. vers. 10. Salutare hoc Dei consilium & admirandum iustitiæ amorisque temperamentum, quod in scripturis passim inculcatur, Photiniani scelesto ore nuncupant delirium, sed increpet te Deus Sathan. Aliud est ex propriâ crumenâ pro alio soluere, & statim ad se idem recipere, aliud est iudicem ex gratiâ monere & mouere alium, vt pro debitore soluat. Hoc delirantis non est, sed miserentis & beneuoli.

3. Stultum sordidumvè non foret, si princeps clementiâ impulsus ex suo ærario daret pecuniam reo, vt mulctam debitam solueret bong publico. Qui ergo stultum esse dicitur, cùm Deus idem facere statuitur; Nempè quia sapientia Dei stultitia est mundo.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: Argument VI. From the author of the reconciliation

ARGUMENT VI. From the author of the reconciliation.

XXXVI. God himself is the author of the reconciliation made through Christ, nay, he has reconciled us to himself 2 Cor. 5 v. 19. Col. 1 v. 20. Therefore it is absurd to say that Christ appeased the wrath of God for us, and by his own satisfaction rendered God propitious to us. Ostorodus in Institut. page 212.

XXXVII. Resp. 1. Some invert the argument in this way: If GOD reconciled us to himself, then it follows that Christ also reconciled us to himself and to the Father; because whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise John 5 v. 19. And Christ says, All thine are mine, John 17 v. 10.

XXXVII. 2. Conversely, those things which Scripture joins are separated, namely that GOD reconciled us to himself through the blood of Christ. For this is said in Rom. 5 v. 10. We were reconciled to God through the death of his son, verse 11. Through Christ we have received reconciliation, Ephes. 2 v. 4. GOD, when we were dead in sins, made us alive together in Christ. v. 15. Christ reconciles both to GOD, through the cross, killing the enmities in himself. In these sayings our reconciliation is expressly attributed partly to the love of GOD, partly to the merit of Christ, and therefore those things are not to be opposed, but held as subordinate. These are related, not contrary. Wherefore, one of these related things being posited, the other also ought to be posited, not removed as if it were contrary. And indeed from these and similar arguments of the Photinians we most firmly conclude that their doctrine is absolutely not Apostolic and divine, in that they always invert the Biblical method of inferring, and when Scripture proceeds from the positing of one thing to the positing of another also, they in a contrary manner infer removal and negation. For when they read that God has loved us and reconciled us to Himself, they immediately think all merit of Christ is excluded, although Scripture includes it and teaches everywhere that both the love of God and our reconciliation are founded in Christ.

XXXIX. 3. Our reconciliation can be considered in two ways: 1. By reason of the counsel or primary cause. 2. By reason of the execution or meritorious cause. As regards the counsel for bringing about reconciliation, the Father entered into this out of mere mercy, who also for our sake sent the Son, so that the beginning of our redemption is deservedly attributed to God the Father as the primary cause of all. Rightly, therefore, is He said to have reconciled us to Himself, since He procured our reconciliation and found the means for it. But as regards the execution and the meritorious cause, Christ ought not to be excluded here. For He was sent by the Father for this end, and no other, than that His counsel for bringing about reconciliation might be executed, both by acting and by suffering, which He performed most promptly and most fully: which in the meritorious respect the Father did not do for Himself, but the Son reconciled us to the Father: these are two subordinate causes, which if they are torn apart, reconciliation is destroyed. For the Father reconciled us to Himself, not by a mere acceptance, but by sending the Son; the Son, however, reconciled us to the Father by suffering, through the cross and blood, which should be well noted. For thus the merit itself is clearly expressed; that Christ is the reconciler not only by announcing the way of salvation, but by dying for us, and so by interposing His own blood as an ἀντίλυτρον of redemption. And thus our reconciliation is assigned to both persons, both to the Father and to the Son: to the Father as the primary and remote cause, to the Son as the meritorious and proximate cause; to the Father as regards the counsel, to the Son as regards the execution.

To the Father, because He gave the means of reconciliation; to the Son, because He Himself was the means; to the Father, as the first source and author; to the Son, as the mediator and redeemer Himself; to the Father, primarily or originally; to the Son, by way of atonement or meritoriously. This is indicated in those very testimonies of Scripture which Osterodus cites for himself in 2 Cor. 5, after the Apostle said in verse 19 that God had reconciled the world to Himself, he adds at the same time: in Christ. And afterwards he adds in the last verse: Him, who knew no sin, He made sin for us, that we might be made the righteousness of God in Him. You hear the Apostle clearly indicating that God indeed reconciled the world as the primary cause, but through Christ, not as a prophet and legate through mere preaching, but insofar as He made Him sin, that is, He laid all our sins upon Him as if He were a propitiatory victim, and thus He had to suffer and die in our place. The same is taught in Col. 1, where our redemption is in turn ascribed to the Father as the primary cause in verses 12 and 13, but the meritorious cause is soon added in verse 14. He transferred us into the kingdom of His Son, in whom we have redemption; in what manner and by what means? Διὰ τῶ αἷματος αὐτῶ. Through His blood; in turn, it is said in verse 20: It pleased God the Father through Christ to reconcile all things to Himself, through the blood of His cross, in verse 22, through death. You see here a perpetual subordination of causes, and the coupling of divine grace with the merit and blood of Christ, so that it is a most gross fallacy to wish to argue from the position of one relative to the exclusion of the other. We say most briefly: the efficient cause does not remove the meritorious and final cause. God, out of mercy, as the primary cause, sent His Son, yet to this end, that He might appease His wrath against our sins.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM VI. Ab autore reconciliationis.

XXXVI. Deus ipse autor est reconciliationis per Christum factæ, imò nos sibi ipsi reconciliauit 2. Cor. 5. v. 19. Col. 1. v. 20. Ergo absonum est dicere, Christum nobis placasse iram Dei, suáq; satisfactione Deum nobis propitium reddidisse Ostorodus in Institut. pag. 212.

XXXVII. Resp. 1. Nonnulli inuertunt argumentum hoc modo: Si DEVS nos sibi ipsi reconciliauit, tunc & Christum nos sibi, Patriq; reconciliâsse sequitur; Quia quæcunq; facit Pater, filius pariter facit Iohan. 5. v. 19. & Christus inquit, Omnia tua mea sunt, Ioh, 17. v. 10.

XXXVII. 2. Vicissim disiunguntur, quæ scriptura copulat, videlicet DEVM nos sibi reconciliâsse, per sanguinem Christi. Hoc enim dicitur Rom. 5. v. 10. Reconciliati sumus Deoper mortem filij eius vers. 11. Per Christum reconciliationem accepmus, Ephes 2. v. 4. DEVS cùm essemus mortui in peccatis convivificauit nos in Christo. v. 15. Christus reconciliat ambos DEO, per crucem, interficiens inimicitias in semetipso. In hisce dictis nostra reconciliatio expressè partim dilectioni DEI, partim merito Christi accepta fertur, Ideoq; illa non sunt opponenda, sed pro subordinatis habenda. Sunt hæc relata non contraria. Quare vno istorum relatorum posito, etiam alterum poni, non tanquam contrarium remoueri debet. Et sanè ex hisce & similibus Photinianorum argumentis nos firmissimè concludimus, ipsorum doctrinam prorsus non esse Apostolicam & diuinam, eò quòd modum inferendi Biblicum semper inuertunt, & cùm Scriptura ab vnius processione ad alterius quoque positionem progreditur, illi contrario modo remotionem & negationem colligunt, Cum enim legunt Deum nos dilexisse, & sibi reconciliasse, mox Christi meritum omne putant exclusum, Cum tamen Scriptura includat Deiq́; dilectionem & nostram reconciliationem in Christo fundatam esse passim doceat.

XXXIX. 3. Reconciliatio nostra dupliciter considerari potest, 1. Ratione Consilij vel causæ primæ. 2. Ratione executionis vel causæ meritoriæ. Quod spectat Consilium de facienda reconciliatione, istud pater ex merâ misericordia iniit, qui etiam nostri causâ Filium misit, vt ita redemptionis nostræ initium Deo Patri, tanquam causæ omnium primę meritò acceptum feratur, Rectè igitur nos sibi reconciliâsse dicitur, quoniam reconciliationem nostram procurauit, & media eius inuenit. Quod verò spectat executionem & causam meritoriam, hîc Christus excludi non debet. Nam eo fine missus est à Patre, & non alio, quàm vt consilium ipsius de facienda reconciliatione exequeretur, tum agendo, tum patiendo, quòd ipsum promptissimè & plenissimè præstitit: Quod respectu meritorio non Pater sibi, sed Patri Filius nos reconciliauit: Hæ sunt duæ causæ subordinatæ, quæ si diuellantur, reconciliatio tollitur, Pater enim nos sibi reconciliauit, non per nudam acceptionem, sed mittendo Filium; Filius autem nos Patri reconciliauit patiendo, per crucem & sanguinem, quod probè notetur. Sic enim ipsum meritum luculenter exprimitur; quòd reconciliator sit Christus non tantùm salutis modum annunciando, sed pro nobis moriendo, adeoquè sanguinem suum redemptionis ἀντίλυτρον interponendo. Atque sic vtrique personæ tum Patri tum Filio, nostra reconciliatio assignatur, Patri vt causæ primæ & remotæ: Filio vt causæ meritoriæ & propinquæ, Patri quoad consilium; Filio quoad executionem,

Patri quia medium reconciliationis dedit, Filio, quia ipse medium fuit; Patri vt primo fonti & autori, Filio, vt ipsi mediatori & redemptori; Patri πρώτως vel originaliter, Filio, obινασμῶν vel meritoriè. Indicatur hoc in illis ipsis Scripturæ testimonijs, quæ pro se citat Osterodus in 2. Cor. 5. postquam Apostolus dixit versu 19. Deum reconciliasse sibi mundum simul addit, in Christo: Et postmodum subijcit v. vlt. Eum, qui non nouerat peccatum pronobis peccatum fecit, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso. Audis, Apostolum manifestè indicare Deum reconciliâsse quidem mundum vt causam primam, sed per Christum, non vt prophetam & legatum per nudam prędicationem, sed quatenus ipsum fecit peccatum, hoc est, omnia nostra ipsi velut victimæ propitiatoriæ peccata imposuit, adeoque nostro loco pati & mori debuit. Idem docetur Col. 1. vbi Patri vicissim vt causæ primæ nostra redemptio adscribitur ver. 12, 13. sed mox additur causa meritoria v. 14. Transtulit nos in regnum Filij sui, in quo habemus Redemtionem; quo modo & medio? Διὰ τῶ αἷματος αὐτῶ. Per sanguinem ipsius, vicissim versu 20. dicitur; Placuit Deo Patri per Christum reconciliare omnia in ipso, per sanguinem crucis eius versu 22. per mortem. Vides hic perpetuam causarum subordinationem, & gratiæ diuinæ cum Christi merito & sanguine copulationem, vt ita crassissimus sit Elenchus, & ab vnius relati positione ab alterius exclusione m argumentari velle. Nos brevissimè dicimus Causa efficiens non tollit meritoriam & finalem. Deus ex misericordia, tanquàm causa prima misit Filium suum in hunc tamen finem, vt iram eius adversus peccata nostra placaret.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: Argument VII From the human remission of debts

ARGUMENT VII.

From the human remission of debts, XL. If God has not forgiven us our sins except through the intercession of satisfaction: it will be right for us also to do the same, especially because we are commanded to imitate God in forgiving the sins of our neighbor, Matt. 18. 27. Wherefore, unless satisfaction is first made to us, we should not forgive our neighbor, which is nevertheless against the Apostolic admonitions concerning kindness and mercy. Ephes. 4. last verse, Chap. 5. verse 1. Socinus uses this argument part 3. c. 2. p. 242. 243. Ostorodus against Tradel p. 212. & pag. 213. Gittichius in Epist. discept. p. 7.

XLI. Response 1. Again the fallacy of opposites is committed, since things that should be joined are torn apart, and things that are subordinate are opposed. For both are said in the Scriptures; both that Christ paid the price for us, and that sins are forgiven freely; and that in this free forgiveness we ought to imitate God. Therefore, the forgiveness is free κατὰ τὶ with respect to us, not absolutely with respect to Christ.

XLII. 2. Human forgiveness is free in such a way that it nevertheless includes something similar to satisfaction: this is the entreaty and request for pardon on the part of the offender. For just as the offended party in forgiving, so the offender in entreating ought to be easy and ready: Thus the Savior warns Matt. 5. verses 23. & 24. Leave your gift before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother: And Matt. 18. verse 16. If your brother has sinned against you, go and rebuke him. Therefore, just as men ought to forgive an offense after rebuke and entreaty have been made, which is in the place of satisfaction, if this word is taken generally for any just cause of reconciliation, or manner; so also God forgives our debts, since the intercession and satisfaction of Christ have preceded. Free pardon, therefore, does not exclude every condition, and every respect of intercession and satisfaction.

XLIII. 3. The argument lacks strength on account of the greatest disparity between God and men. God in forgiving sins does not have the regard of a mere creditor, but rather of a most just judge. For it is not to be thought that God does not abhor sins, does not punish them, but is equally disposed toward sins and non-sins. Far be this from the most just God, whose nature is justice itself; whose Law is immovable and invariable; whose threats are truthful and immutable. When, therefore, a man sins against God, then he offends his justice, violates his laws, incurs his threats, and is brought before his tribunal. Where God certainly, as a just judge, cannot forgive the debt without any satisfaction and dismiss the sinner unpunished; unless he wishes to deny himself, to abolish his own law, and indeed to accuse his own threats and word of lying. All these things cease as far as men are concerned, nor do they find a place. For man is not the primary rule of justice, he does not sin principally against him, but rather against God, who commands the love of neighbor; he does not have the status of a public person or Magistrate, but of a private one; there does not exist a Law or command about exacting satisfaction, but rather the contrary. Men are of equal condition, and one offends the other more often, and therefore he can, and indeed ought, to remit without satisfaction, on account of the Lord's command. God, however, owes us nothing, and has pregnant reasons why he both does not wish and cannot dismiss the debt without λύτρω. These things can be explained by the likeness of a judge; here, as a private person, he can remit injuries, but as a judge, he cannot absolve the guilty without satisfaction. How so? Because thus he would violate justice, would transgress the laws, and would be a liar in his threats. Now indeed God in the Scriptures professes himself a judge, who calls all delinquents to his tribunal, and punishes them by the force of his law, nor does he dismiss them before satisfaction has been made to justice and the law. Wherefore from this it becomes clear, that either the penalty must be inbinds, or that satisfaction must be interposed. For he would be an unjust judge if he were to absolve a defendant brought to the tribunal and dictate no punishment. You ask: How then can we imitate God in the forgiveness of sins, if he urges satisfaction, but we ought not to urge it? The fourth member of the response, which we now add, will satisfy this question.

XLIV. 4. A distinction must be made between mercy itself and the manner of mercy. God is merciful in the remission of sins in this way, while he accepts another's satisfaction, because he himself procured it and demands nothing from us. We therefore ought to imitate God in this, as is commanded, Luke 6, verse 36: Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. Here we are admonished toward the virtue itself, but not toward the manner of the virtue; God is merciful toward men, yet in another manner than men. Otherwise, if that likeness were extended beyond the thing to the manner of the thing, then it would follow that men also ought to hand over their sons to death for others, which however is prohibited. Besides this, we ought also to imitate God in that, that we remit a debt freely, on the part of the debtor. For just as our sins are forgiven us freely, without any merit of our own, without any satisfaction of our own, so also we ought to be disposed toward our neighbor. Therefore that conformity with God consists in three things. 1. In the thing, namely that we be merciful and prompt to forgive, just as God is merciful. 2. In this condition of the thing, that the remission be free on the part of the debtor, that we demand no λύτρον or price from him, just as we are justified by God without works. 3. In the sincerity of the remission, that it ought not to be feigned, but to have proceeded from a sincere and ingenuous affection of the mind, as Christ teaches in express words in the ἀπόδοσις of the parable in Matthew 18, verse 35: So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if you do not forgive each his brother ἀπὸ τῶν καρδιῶν, from your hearts, that is, sincerely and without guile. But he who extends that conformity more broadly to exclude all satisfaction, whether it be one's own or another's, he, 1. ἄτερ γραφῶν, speaks without the Scriptures, nay, against Scripture. 2. He begs the question. 3. He confuses the thing with the manner of the thing; and 4. He removes every distinction between human and divine forgiveness of debt, which is absurd: We sufficiently imitate God if we remit freely and promptly: but let this difference remain, that since God is judge, He may rightly urge another's satisfaction, but we, because we are private individuals, can demand nothing at all, nay, we even ought not to, because of the express command of God. Those things are similar in part, not in whole; in half-measure, not in full; as to the thing, not as to every manner: in a certain respect, not as to all things and absolutely.

XLV. But Gittichius, p. 49, objects thus from the mind of Socinus: If we follow your opinion, could not that debtor have objected against the King? Lord, you indeed remitted, but only then, when another satisfied you for me. I also have found a fellow servant who may satisfy me for him, and I will remit everything to him: Do you see what monsters your opinion brings forth for us?

XLVI. Resp. 1. The canons concerning parables are well known. 1. Parabolic theology is not argumentative. If, therefore, the Photinians have no firmer reasons for their faith than the applications of parables, and those quite violent ones, certainly they are leaning upon light and ruinous foundations: 2. Parables are not to be extended beyond their principal scope. Chrysostom teaches this in his Commentary on chapter 9 of the Epistle to the Romans. This, he says, ought to be observed everywhere in the examples brought forward; that we should not take them to prove just anything, but choose those things for which they were applied to use, and for which they were employed; let us leave all the rest. And upon the parable of the denarius in Matthew 20, It is not fitting in parables that excessive care in individual words be taken; but when we have learned what is intended by a parable, from that point nothing further is to be investigated with anxious effort from the things collected. If Socinus had been mindful of this rule, he would undoubtedly have noticed the vanity of his own little inference himself. For if it were permitted to collect anything from anything, we might conclude in the same way that all criminals should be dismissed unpunished. For just as that servant in the parable had his entire debt forgiven, only because he asked his Lord; so if a defendant should seek pardon before a judge, he ought immediately to be dismissed without punishment by the force of this parable. Many such consequences could be woven, which nevertheless do not flow from the text, and are devised only beyond the scope of Christ; who is so stupid as not to see it?

XLVII. Therefore, that we may add something concerning the genuine scope of that parable, it must be known: That Christ's purpose there was not to explain the mystery of Redemption, but he only wished to remind us of our duty: Peter provided the occasion, by asking in verse 21: Lord, how often shall my brother sin against me and I forgive him? Christ answers: always and as often as he prays for pardon, which he declares by the parable of the king, who forgave his servant a great debt: Where he employs three primary motives for gratuitous forgiveness. 1. That we may fear God, the king of the heavens, our Father. 2. That we may observe the law of nature, according to which we ought to do to others what we wish to be done to ourselves, which Christ regarded in verse 33: Ought you not to have had mercy on your fellow servant; just as I also had mercy on you? 3: That we may avoid the most grave punishment, for otherwise it will come to pass that not even God will forgive our sins, just as he did not hold valid the promise made to the servant concerning the forgiven debt, on account of his lack of mercy, which is clear from verse 34, where it is said: And his Lord being angry, delivered him to the torturers, until he should pay the whole debt.

Whence it is clear that, since in verse 32 the king is said to have forgiven the whole debt, this is to be understood not of the act itself, but of the hope of remission made through the promise. If all these things are applied to the purpose of Christ, nothing else follows than that it is our duty to forgive our neighbor, if we wish to have the hope of pardon made in Christ ratified, in order to escape punishment. Thus, therefore, Christ admonishes us regarding the matter itself, but He by no means expresses the manner of the matter on the part of God, whether, namely, God forgives the debt through or without satisfaction, but this is to be learned from other Scriptures, where that is most clearly asserted. Wherefore that parable ought to be expounded in such a way that other testimonies of Scripture, which establish the satisfaction of Christ, are not impugned. For the inference from silence to negation is not firm. Although in that parable there is silence concerning the merit of Christ, it ought not, however, to be denied on that account. Otherwise it would follow that remission is made without Christ, without any regard to His blood; since there is not even a word of mention made of either Christ or His blood; but it is said only that the King immediately forgave the debt at the servant's petition. But that consequence is against the whole of Scripture: Therefore the antecedent, from which that follows, is also [false].

XLVIII. 3: If that servant had been a Photinian, he could have eluded his King by that agreement: But at that time the new fraud and sophistication of Socinus had not yet become known: Meanwhile, that this exception is clearly frivolous is evident from the fact that it is not permitted for a man to call into doubt the deeds of the King toward the servant, or the judgments of God, or to expostulate about them; O man, who art thou that repliest against God, says the Apostle, Rom. 9, verse 20. If, therefore, anyone presumes to enter into judgment with God, he will deservedly be condemned and will receive this answer: Was it not commanded to you that you should grant pardon to your neighbor who asks? Am I not God and Creator, to whom you owe obedience? Are you ignorant of the lightning of my law, which I brandish against obstinate sinners? I am God, who do not deny myself, nor do I violate my justice, and therefore I demand satisfaction by right. You, however, are a servant and you yourself offend in many things; therefore, you ought to forgive your neighbor without satisfaction, as I have commanded. But if you do not do this, I will hand you over to the tormentors of eternity to be tortured. of the Socinian exception.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM. VII.

Ab humana debitorum dimissione, XL. Si Deus non nisi intercedente satis factione remisit nobis peccata nostra: nobis quoque idem facere erit integrum, præsertim quia iubemur Deum imitari in condonandis proximo peccatis Matth. 18. 27. Quare nisi prius nobis satisfiat, non remittamus proximo, id quod tamen est contra admonitiones Apostolicas de benignitate & misericordia. Ephes. 4. versu vltimo, Cap. 5. versu 1. Vtitur hoc argumento Socinus part. 3. c. 2. p. 242. 243. Ostorodus contra Tradel p. 212. & pag. 213. Gittichius in Epist. discept. p. 7.

XLI. Respond. 1. Iterum committitur Elenchus oppositorum, siquidem divelluntur conjungenda, & opponuntur subordinata. Vtrumqueq; enim in Scripturis dicitur; tum Christu pro nobis pretium persolvisse, tum peccata gratis remitti; in hac gratuita condonatione nos Deum imitari debere. Est igitur remissio gratuita κατὰ τὶ respectu nostri, non absolutè respectu Christi.

XLII. 2. Dimissio humana sic est gratuita, vt tamen quiddam satisfactioni simile includat: Est hæc deprecatio & veniæ petitio ex parte offendentis. Vt enim offensus in remittendo: Sic offendens in deprecando debet esse facilis & paratus: Ita monet Saluator Matth. 5. versu 23. & 24. Relinque munus tuum ante altare, & vade prius reconciliare fratrituo: Et Matth. 18. versu 16. Si peccauerit in te frater tuus, vade & corripe eum, Vt igitur offensam remittere debent homines, post factam correptionem & deprecationem, quæ est satisfactionis loco, si vox hæc sumatur generatim pro qualibet iusta reconciliationis causa, modouè; ita & Deus condonat nostra debita, quoniam præcessit intercessio & satisfactio Christi. Gratuita igitur venia non excludit omnem conditionem, omnemque intercessionis & satisfactionis respectum.

XLIII. 3. Argumentum nervis caret ob maximam Dei, hominumque disparitatem Deus in remittendis peccatis non habet respectum nudi creditoris, sed potius iustissimi judicis. Neque enim putandum est, Deum peccata non aversaris, non punire, sed aeque affectum esse erga peccata & non peccata. Absit hoc a Deo iustissimo, cuius natura est ipsa justitia; cuius Lex est immota & invariabilis; cuius comminationes sunt veraces & immutabiles. Quando igitur homo peccat in Deum, tum offendit eius justitiam, violat leges, ingurrit minas, & ante tribunal sistitur. Vbi Deus certe tanquam iustus iudex sine omni satisfactione debitum condonare, & peccatorem impunitum dimittere nequit; nisi seipsum negate, legem suam ipse tollere, imo minas verbumque suum mendacij arguere velit. Omnia haec quoad homines cessant, nec locum inveniunt. Nam homo non est prima justitiae regula, non principaliter contra ipsum, sed potius in Deum, dilectionem proximi praecipientem delinquitur, non habet rationem personae publicae aut Magistratus, sed privati; non extat Lex aut mandatum de exigenda satisfactione, sed potius contrarium. Homines aequalis sunt conditionis, & alter alterum saepius offendit, ideoque sine satisfactione remittere potest imo & debet, ob praeceptum Domini. Deus autem nihil nobis debet, & causas praegnantes habet, cur debitum absque λύτρω dimittere tum nolit, tum nequeat. Declarari haec possunt similitudine judicis; hic qua privatus, injurias remittere potest, sed qua judex, nocentem sine satisfactione absolvere non potest. Qui ita? quoniam sic violaret justitiam, transgrederetur leges, & mendax foret in comminationibus. Iam vero Deus in Scripturis se judicem profitetur, qui ad tribunal vocet omnes delinquentes, eosque vi legis suae puniat, nec antequam satisfactum sit justitiae & legi, dimittat. Quare hinc luculentum fit, aut poenam debere inligit, aut satisfactionem interponendam esse. Iniquus enim foret judex, si reum ad tribunal delatum absolueret; nullumque supplicium dictaret. Quæris: Qui ergo Deum imitari possumus in condonatione delictorum, si ille satisfactionem urget, nos autem non urgere debemus? Huic quæstioni satisfaciet quartum responsionis membrum, quod nunc addimus.

XLIV. 4. Distinguendum est in inter misericordiam ipsam & misericordiæ modum. Deus in remissione peccatorum misericors est hoc modo dum alienam satisfactionem recipit, quia eam ipse procurauit & a nobis nihil exigit, Nos ergo debemus in hoc Deum imitari, vti præcipitur, Luc. 6. versu 36. Estote misericordes, sicut & Pater vester misericors est. Hic ad virtutem ipsam admonemur, sed non ad virtutis modum; Est Deum misericors erga homines, alio tamen modo, quam homines. Aliàs si similitudo illa præter rein ad modum rei extendatur, tùm sequeretur & homines debere filios suos pro aliis in mortem tradere, quod tamen est prohibitum. Præter hoc & in illo Deum imitari debemus, vt debitum gratis remittamus, ex parte debitoris, Vt enim nobis condonantur peccata gratis, sine omni nostro merito, sine omni satisfactione propria, sic & nos affecti esse debemus erga proximum. Proindè illa conformitas cum Deo in tribus consistit. 1. In re, vt nempè misericordes simus & prompti ad remittendum, sicut & Deus misericors est. 2. In rei conditione hac, vt remissio gratuita ex parte debitoris, vt ab ipso nullum λύτρον vel pretium exigamus, sicut & nos sine operibus à Deo iustificamur, 3. In sinceritate remissionis quod non debeat esse simulata, sed ex sincero, ingenuoque animi adfectu profecta, vti Christus disertis verbis docet in ἀποδόσει parabolæ Math. 18. ver. 35. Sic & Pater meus cœlestis faciet vobis, si non remiseritis vnusquisque fratri suo ἀπὸ τῶν καρδιῶν, de cordibus vestris, hac est, sincerè & sine fuco. Qui verò istam conformitatẽ latius extendit ad excludendam satisfactionem omnem, siue propria sit, siue aliena, is, 1. ἄτερ γραφῶν, imò contra Scripturam loquitur. 2. Principium petit. 3. Rem cum rei modo confundit; & 4. Omne discrimen inter humanam & diuinam debiti condonationem tollit, quod absurdum: Satis imitamur Deum, si gratis & promptè remittamus: maneat verò ista differentia, quòd cùm Deus judex sit, alienam satisfactionem iure vrgeat, nos autem, quia priuati sumus, nihil quicquam postulare possumus, imò nec debemus ob expressum Dei mandatum. Sunt ista similia in tantum, non in totum, ex semisses non ex asse; quoad rem, non quoad omnem modum: Certo respectu, non quoad omnia & simpliciter.

XLV. Sed ex mente Socini sic excipit Gittichius, p. 49. Annon si vestram sententiam sequamur, potuisset debitor ille contra Regem excipere? Domine tu quidem remisisti, sed tum demum, cùm alter tibi pro me satisfecit. Inueni at quoq; iste conseruus mette qui pro illo mihi satisfaciat, & omnia ipsi remittam: Vides quæ monstra vestra sententia nobis pariat?

XLVI. Resp. 1. Noti sunt Canônes de parabolis. 1. Theologia parabolica non est argumentatiua. Si ergo fidei suæ Photiniani nullas habent firmiores rationes, quàm parabolarum applicationes, easque satis violentas, certè fundamentis leuibus & ruinosis innituûtur: 2. Parabolæ extra scopum principalem non sunt extendendæ. Docet hoc Chrysostomus in Commentario super caput 9. Epistol. ad Roman. Istud, inquit, vbique in adductis exemplis seruari oportet; nè illa ad quæuis probanda sumamus, sed electio ea quo daddicta sunt vsui, & ob quod vsurpata sunt; reliqua omnia sinamus. Et super parabolam de denario Matth. 20, Non oportet in parabolis nimia in singulis verbis cura perangi; sed cùm quid per parabulam intendatur, didicerimus, inde ynutare collectis nihil vlterius anxiori conatu investigandum. Cujus regulæ si memor fuisset Socinus, vanitatem suæ consequentunculæ procul dubio ipse animadvertisset. Nam si ex quovis quidvis liceat colligere, pari modo concludamus omnes facinorosos esse impunitos dimittendos. Vt enim illi servo in parabolâ omne debitum dimissum est, tantùm quia rogabat Dominum; ita si reus coram iudice veniam petat, mox sine supplicio dimitti deberet vi hujus parabolæ. Tales consequentiæ plures necti possent, quas tamen ex textu non fluere, & præter scopum Christi tantùm excogitari, tam stupidus quis est, quin videat?

XLVII. Proindè vt de genuino parabolæ istius scopo aliquid addamus, sciendum est: Quod Christi propositum ibi non fuerit Redemtionis mysterium exponere, sed tantùm nos officij nostri commonefacere voluit: Occasionem præbuit Petrus; quærendo versu 21: Domine quoties in me peccabit frater meus & dimittam ei? Respondet Christus: semper & quoties precatur veniam, id quod per parabolam declarat à rege, servo suo magnum debitum condonante: Vbi tria inprimis gratuitæ dimissionis motiua adhibet. 1. Vtimitemur Deum, regem cœlorum, Patrem nostrum. 2. Vt legem naturæ servemus, secundum quam alijs facere debemus; quod nobis fieri volumus, quod respexit Christus versu 33: Nonne oportuit te te misereri conservi tui; sicut & ego tui misertus sum? 3: Vt gravissimum supliciùm evitemus, aliàs enim futurum est, vt nè Deus quidem peccata nobis dimittat, sicut & promissionem; servo factam, de remisso debito, ob immisericordiam eius ratam non habuit, quod patet ex versu 34. vbi dicitur: Et iratus Dominus eius, tradit eum tortoribus, quousque redderet vniuersum debitum.

Vnde liquidum sit, quod cum ver. 32. rex dicitur totum debitum dimisisse, id non de facto ipso, sed de spe remissionis per promissionem facta intelligendum sit. Haec omnia si ad Christi scopum applicentur, nihil sequitur aliud, quàm nostri esse officij condonare proximo, si spem veniæ in Christo factam velimus habere ratam, ad effugiendum supplicium. Sic ergo Christus ad rem ipsam nos admonet, rei modum verò ex parte Dei nequaquam exprimit, an nimirum Deus per vel citrà satisfactionem remittat debitum, sed hoc aliis ex Scripturis addiscendum, vbi clarissimè illud asseritur. Quare sic exponi debet illa parabola, nè impugnentur alia Scripturæ testimonia, Christi satis factionem astruentia. Nec enim sequela firma est â silentio ad negationem. Quamvis in ista parabola sileatur de Christi merito, non tamen ob id negari debet. Aliàs sequeretur, sine Christo, sine omni ad sanguinem eius respectu fieri remissionem; quoniam nè quidem verbulo vel Christi vel sanguinis fit mentio; sed dicitur tantum Regem ad serui petitionem statim dimisisse debitum. Illud verò consequens est contra vniversam Scripturam: Ergò & antecedens, ex quo istud sequitur.

XLVIII. 3: Si servus ille Photinianus fuisset, Regem suum isto pacto eludere potuisset: Sed tum nondum innotuerat noua fraus & sophisticatio Socini: Interim istam exceptionem planè frivolam esse, inde patet, quòd seruo facta Regis, homini judicia Dei non liceat in dubium vocare, aut ob illa expostulare, ô Homo tu quis es qui respondeas Deo, inquit Apostolus, Rom. 9. ver: 20. si quis ergo præsumat cum Deo in judicium intrare, meritò damnabitur & responsum hoc accipiet: Annon tibi mandatum est, vt proximo petenti des veniam? Annon ego Deus & Creator sum, cui debes obedientiam? An ignoras legis meæ fulmen, quod vibrô in stanes præfractos peccatores? Deus ego sum, qui me ipsum non nego, nec iustitiam meam violo, ideoque satisfactionem iure exigo. Tu autem servus es & ipse in multis offendis, proinde sine satisfactione proximo, ut mandavi, condonare debes. Quod si non feceris tortoribus æternitati te cruciandus tradam. Hic finis & fructus est exceptionis Socinianæ.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: Argument VIII From the rule of Divine justice, Ezek. 18. v. 4. 20

ARGUMENT VIII.

From the rule of Divine justice, Ezek. 18. v. 4. 20.

XLIX. It holds thus: The soul that has sinned, it shall die. Now, if the dogma concerning satisfaction prevails, then it follows that delinquent men are released, and the innocent Christ is punished, which openly fights against the rule of justice.

Ostorod p. 213. Socinus. 3. p. 258. Gittichius page 1. & 2.

L. I respond. 1. Again, Scripture is opposed to Scripture. For in it both are asserted, that the sinning soul is punished, and that the innocent Christ died for us. Wherefore these will be parallels, not opposites, and therefore they ought to be reconciled, not set against each other.

LI. 2. There is no lack of examples where not only the soul itself that sinned, and others touching the author of the guilt by proximity, though not participants in it themselves, were punished according to the secret judgments of God. Thus the whole family and all the possessions of Achan were burned with flames, Josh. 7. v. 24. and because of his sin the whole Israelite people were punished, of which they complain in Josh. 22. v. 20. The abyss swallows all the substance of Korah and whatever belonged to them, not even excepting little children and infants, Num. 16. v. 32. To this point looks the passage in Is. 14. verse 21. Prepare his children for slaughter in the iniquity of their fathers. Add the infants extinguished through the cruelty of Herod and in both destructions of Jerusalem; the little son of David conceived from Bathsheba, and deprived of life because of the father's adultery, 2. Sam. 12. v. 14. as also the sons of Saul, who because of the tyranny of their parent or grandfather exercised against the Gibeonites were hanged, 2 Sam. 21. v. 1. 5. 6. & 9. And by that very thing the Lord was appeased in verse 14. Although indeed they were not simply innocent, nevertheless they were not participants in the guilt of Saul, namely the tyranny for which they were hanged. See furthermore Deut. 13. v. 15. where whole cities are consecrated to the sword on account of the crime of some. To these and similar examples even the Photinians themselves are compelled to respond, and let it be manifest from this that the rule of Ezekiel suffers a certain exception, nor is it to be understood so strictly. Some refer the example of original sin to this.
