For if the fall of Adam could be imputed to all his descendants without injury to justice, however much they did not commit it themselves, nor did they sin after the likeness of the transgression of Adam, Rom. 5. v. 14. then certainly GOD could also lay our iniquities upon Christ without any diminution of justice, especially since He willingly received them upon Himself.

LII. 3. Roman histories confirm that some have met death both in the place and for the cause of others, that is, by their own death they have forestalled the death of others and saved their lives, as reported by Pareus in his Epistle to the Romans, page 529. When the army was in danger, the consul Decius, by the warning of an oracle, threw himself into the enemy to save the army, which otherwise would have had to perish. Curtius, when his country was in danger because of a plague, threw himself headlong into a chasm for its sake and in its place, so that he might avert the evil. The three Curii and the two Horatii fell in duel for the liberty of their country. Nisus, in Virgil, wished to be killed by Volscens for his companion Euryalus. Codrus, King of the Athenians, voluntarily exposed himself to the swords of the enemy for his kingdom. Menoeceus, so that he might provide for the safety of his country Thebes, stabbed himself and, having been stabbed, threw himself down toward the enemies. And indeed in Rom. 5. verse 3 [sic], it is expressly said that someone can die for another. Although indeed in these examples 1. one is not punished for another, 2. nor does he make satisfaction, yet we say from this, 1. that it does not simply deviate from the rule of justice if someone dies for another; 2. that in these examples the particle PRO denotes not benefit, but substitution.

LIII. 4. We distinguish between strict law and equity. That rule is of strict law which detracts nothing from the equity and moderation of leniency revealed in the Gospel. If a judge applies the rigor of justice, he then drags the delinquent himself to punishment, nor does he accept another’s satisfaction: meanwhile, without injustice, he can remit something, so that severity is changed into equity, when he either accepts another’s payment in full, or divides the punishment between the delinquent and the intercessor. Now, that this may be applied, we say that that aphorism of the Prophet is legal and of strict law, where it always holds: The soul that hath sinned, it shall die: But as the Law does not abolish the Gospel, so legal sentences are not to be opposed to Evangelical ones. From which we learn that God the Father, out of His goodness, sent the Son, that He might give the price of redemption for us. To speak briefly and summarily: The sinning soul itself dies, by the judgment of strict law, in the human forum and the divine according to the law; for the sinning soul Christ dies by the judgment of equity and the benevolent counsel of the Trinity according to the επιείκειαν of the Gospel. The former shows the rigor, the latter the love of the judge, which Dn. D. Hunnius of blessed memory embraced in a few words in his tract on justification, Tom. 1, col. 557: This rule is of divine justice, if it is estimated from its ultimate rigor, when it is weighed without the addition of mercy, as is to be seen in the fallen angels, but in the mystery of our redemption this justice is tempered by the goodness of God, etc. Wherefore, as the mercy of GOD does not abolish His justice, so this work of mercy, by which the Son satisfied for us, is not opposed to justice, but manifests an admirable tempering of clemency, applied in our redemption.

LIIII. 5. We distinguish between a mere man and the God-man. The dictum speaks of mere men, of whom one does not bear the punishment of another: for the Son did not bear the punishment of the Father, since he himself walks in the piety of life. But the case of the God-man is different, on account of the special counsel of God. For although the Word was most innocent, and no guile was found in his mouth, and thus he deserved no punishment in respect to himself; it pleased God the Father, nevertheless, to lay upon him the iniquities of us all, and to wound him for our sins, Isa. 53. If the Photinians would consider this one text, they would be ashamed of such a putrid little argument. For there it is expressly said v. 5. he was wounded for our iniquities. v. 6. The Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. Which words will have to be entirely rescinded, if the rule of Ezekiel is urged without any exception. But because a Prophet does not contradict a Prophet, we conclude from this that Ezekiel speaks of mere men, and Isaiah of the Messiah of the world and the God-man Christ: that the former laid down the rule, and the latter showed an exception to the rule.

LV. 6. We distinguish between the voluntary acceptance of punishment and violent imposition. If anyone offers himself spontaneously and of his own accord to make satisfaction for another, no injury is done to him if the punishment is imposed, as when the Law demands the gouging out of both eyes; but the punishment will be divided between the delinquent and his friend, who offered himself of his own free will, then the judge by this very act is not unjust and severe, but mild and equitable, because he accepts the condition and remits from strict law. For he pities the delinquent and satisfies the will of the interceding friend. But to one who is willing, no injury is done. When, however, punishment is imposed upon an unwilling person, who has both lived rightly and refuses it in every way, then the judge would be unjust who would compel and drag the reluctant one to punishment, and punish him in the place of the criminal. For then that rule of justice is valid: The soul that has sinned, it shall die, and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father. This is evident from the whole context and scope of the Lord. The Jews were using this proverb: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge. verse 2. The sense was: Our fathers have sinned, we pay the penalty, although we diligently obey the commandments of God. God declares this to be false, and therefore in verse 4 he answers: The soul that has sinned, it shall die. The sense is, if anyone lives piously and serves me, he shall not be punished against his will for the sin of his father, he shall not be dragged to punishment, as is clearly taught in verses 17, 18, and 19. From which it is clear that that sentence treats only of punishment against one's will, such as the Jews thought had been imposed upon them without merit, which detracts nothing from a voluntary payment or the undertaking of a penalty, since anyone endowed with right reason and taught by frequent examples understands that it is done without injury to the one paying, and implies the leniency of the judge rather than severity. Now if we consider the death and passion of Christ, it was certainly voluntary and spontaneous; not violent or forced: Although therefore he did not deserve the penalty because he was devoid of all sin: Nevertheless no injury was done to him, when God the Father laid our transgressions upon him, since he bore them willingly, and promptly gave himself as the price of redemption, and paid it in our place. Therefore the inference from the violent imposition of punishment, which is unjust, to voluntary undertaking, which commends the equity of the judge and the love of the one undertaking it, is faulty.

LVI. 7. We distinguish between personal sin or that of one man or a people, and original or that of the whole world. The statement of Ezekiel speaks of personal sins, which are not imputed to other men, or of the individual sin of a father, whose the son does not pay the penalty, as is expressly indicated in verse 17. For it is true concerning these individual offenses that the soul that sins shall itself die, but the case of Christ's passion was truly far different. In it, the sins of the whole world were imputed, since he is the lamb, αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τῶ κόσμω: John 1, verse 29. Which was clearly unique and extraordinary. Although, therefore, a man is not punished for a man because of a personal offense; which is what the sentence of Ezekiel means, nevertheless the Son of God, by the decree of the Father according to the scriptures, died for the universal sin and that of the whole world, so that he might free us from eternal damnation and sanctify us to himself. This was a special case, not to be judged according to common rules. For that most sorrowful canon is known: From the ordinary to the extraordinary, the consequence does not hold. Just as it does not follow: GOD prohibited homicide and theft. Therefore he could not command Abraham the immolation of his son, Gen. 22, or the despoiling of the Egyptians by the Israelites, Exod. 11. For all these are unique examples and exceptions to the common rule; which same thing must also be thought concerning the passion of Christ, undertaken in our place.

LVII. Gittichius objects, p. 65, that the Jews complain not of the sin of one man but of the whole people of their ancestors. Resp. And these are called personal or singular, because they were not common to the whole human race, but only to a certain people, to certain individuals.

2. Pag. 67. That Christ could not have died for personal sins, but only for original sin. Resp. From an inclusive to an exclusive, the consequence does not hold. Christ died for universal sin in such a way that through his merit other sins flowing from original sin were at the same time expiated, and whatever is said here is taken from the judgment of blind reason against the express Scriptures. For they cry out everywhere, That Christ died for us and for our sins.

LVII. But Gitichius constantly urges this: To punish one for another is unjust; but it is much more unjust to punish an innocent person for a guilty one; and by far the most unjust to punish the most innocent for the most wicked. Socinus inculcates the same in part 3, chapter 3, pages 251 and 309.

Resp. 1. It is a mere repetition of the previous cuckoo-song, wherefore we repeat our answers, that this is indeed true: 1. concerning strict law; 2. concerning a ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ (mere man); 3. concerning singular and human judgment; 4. concerning the violent imposition of punishment; and 5. concerning personal sin. But it is false if it is applied to the temperament of God and the salvation of man, if it is understood concerning the θεανθρώπῳ (God-man), the singular and extraordinary counsel of God, concerning the voluntary undertaking of punishment, and universal sin. Others limit it thus: It is not cruel, 1. if the innocent is of the same nature as the guilty; 2. if he offers himself spontaneously to pay the penalty; 3. if he can emerge from the penalty by his own strength; 4. if he can liberate others by this agreement; 4. if he promotes the glory of God and the salvation of men, all of which concur in the satisfaction of Christ. That is absurd according to reason, which is blind in this mystery, but not according to the Gospel, whose judgment must be accurately distinguished here from the judgment 1. of reason, and 2. of the law. If you ask whence we prove this restriction. The answer is ready, and from manifest Scriptures, which say that Christ was struck for iniquities, made a curse, Galat. 3, and sin, 2 Cor. 5. Indeed, that the just died for the unjust, 1 Pet. 3, verse 18. Add moreover the manifest passage, Rom. 5, verse 6: Christ, when we were yet weak according to the time, died for the ungodly. For scarcely for a just man will one die. Yet perhaps for a good man one would dare to die. But Christ, when we were yet sinners, died for us. Just as here to die for a just man is to die in the place of a just man, (perhaps in tyranny and some persecution, where an option is given: either you or he must die. Or one chooses to die for another: so also when Christ is said to have died for us the ungodly, it is the same as to have died in our place.

Gstichius objects on p. 18: 1. That Christ indeed died for us, but was not punished, nor is it the same thing to die for someone and to die in the place or stead of someone. 2. That the same is evident from the opposite: to die for a pious person, for such a death can in no way be undertaken to provide satisfaction for a just person, since he is held guilty of no crime.

Response to 1. He who died for us sustained the punishment of sins for us, because death is the punishment of sin, and Christ is said to have died for us; therefore, He sustained the punishment of sins for us. Hence, Isaiah 53, verse 5, expressly says: 'He was chastised for our iniquities.' Furthermore, although 'to die for someone' and 'to die in the stead of someone' sometimes differ as general and special, here they coincide according to the clear testimonies of Scripture and the nature of the subject matter. And who would understand anything else, if he hears that one dies for an ungodly person, than that he undertakes that death in the place of the ungodly?

To 2. Although when someone undergoes death for a pious person, he does not provide satisfaction for sins, since he is just; nevertheless, this remains, that it is to die for him in his place, namely so that he may escape safely and be freed from the danger of life in which he was otherwise involved. Since all these things are manifest, we firmly adhere to them, although blind reason feigns for itself mere contradictions and political absurdities: the clear voice of Scripture suffices for us, which we care for more than the infinite inventions and colorings of contradicting reason. For indeed this mystery, silent for ages, was revealed in its own time, which we ought to believe religiously, not maliciously despise, nor evade with little reasons sought out here and there.

…LIIX. 2. In a pecuniary matter, when one for another has pledged, then if the debtor cannot pay, the sponsor, although he did not contract the debt, nor did he himself receive the money on loan, is deservedly pressed to pay, or if he refuses to pay, because of his pledge he is imprisoned without injustice or cruelty. And if he does not have the money from which to pay, he pays with his body; not only for the cause, but also in the place and stead of him for whom he pledged. If these things happen with justice preserved in a human court, why for that reason shall we accuse God of cruelty or injustice, especially when this satisfaction of the Son redounds to our use in a far greater way? If a sponsor can be punished for another, why could not Christ our mediator also have been crucified for us or in our place; as Scripture asserts throughout.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM IIX.

Ex regula iustitiæ Divinæ, Ezech. 18. v. 4. 20.

XLIX. Hæc ita habet: Anima, quæ peccaverit, ipsa morietur. Iam verò si dogma de satisfactione obtineat, tum sequitur, homines delinquentes dimitti, & Christum innocentem puniri, quod apertè pugnat cum regula iustitiæ.

Ostorod p. 213. Socinus. 3. p. 258. Gittichius pagina 1. & 2.

L. Respond. 1. Rursus Scriptura Scripturæ opponitur. Nam in illa utrumque asseritur, tum animam peccantem puniri, tum Christum innocentem pro nobis esse mortuum. Quare hæc παράλληλα erunt, non ἐναντία, ideoque conciliari debent non inter se committi.

LI. 2. Non desunt exempla, ubi non tantùm anima ipsa, quæ peccavit, & alij, culpæ autorem propinquitate attingentes, per se tamen eius non participes, secundum arcana Dei judicia puniti sunt. Sic tota familia & omnis supellex Achan flammis exusta est, Ios. 7. v. 24. & ob eius peccatum totus populus Israëliticus punitus, de quo conqueruntur Ios. 22. v 20. Omnem substantiam Core & quicquid ad eos pertinebat, nè quidem puerulis & infantibus exceptis, absorbet vorago, Num. 16. v. 32. Huc spectat locus Es. 14. versu 21. Præparate filios occisioni in iniquitate patrum suorum. Adde infantes per sævitiam Herodis & in utroque excidio Hierosolymitano extinctos; filiolum Dauidis ex Bethseba susceptum, & ob patris adulterium vita privatu 2. Sam. 12. v. 14. ut & filios Saulis, qui propter parentis vel avi Tyrannide adversus Gibeonitas exercitum suspensi sunt 2. Sam, 21. v. 1. 5. 6. & 9. Eoque ipso placatus est Dominus versu 14. Licet vero non fuerint simpliciter innocentes, attamen culpae Saulis, nimirum Tyrannidis ob quam suspendebantur, non erant participes, Vide insuper Deut. 13. v. 15. vbi totae civitates ob delectum quorundam gladio consecrantur. Ad haec & similia exempla respondere coguntur ipsi etiam Photiniani, & sit inde manifestum, quod Ezechielis regula, quandam patiatur exceptionem, nec stricte adeo intelligenda sit. Nonnulli huc referunt exemplum vitij originalis. Si enim Adae lapsus potuit imputari omnibus posteris citra laesionem iustitiae, quantumvis cum non ipsi commiserint, nec ad similitudinem praevaricationis, Adae peccaverint, Rom. 5. v. 14. tum vtique DEVS etiam iniquitates nostras absque iustitiae diminutione Christo imponere potuit, imprimis cum in se illas volens receperit.

LII. 3. Historiae Romanae confirmant, quosdam & vice & causa aliorum mortem oppetiisse, hoc est, morte sua mortem aliorum praevertisse, & vitam servasse, referente Pareo in Epist. ad Rom. pag. 529. Exercitu periclitante Decius consul oraculi monitu in hostes sese coniecit, pro exercitu salvando, Cui alioqui pereundum fuerat. Curtius periclitante patria ob pestem, eius causa & loco in specum se praecipitem dedit, vt malum averteret. Tres Curij & duo Horatij pro patriae libertate duello occubuerunt. Nisus apud Virgililium pro Euryalo socio Volscente interfici voluit. Codrus Atheniensium Rex hostium gladiis vltro sese objecit pro regno. Menecaeus vt Thebarum patriae saluti consuleret, seipsum confodit, confossum ad hostes deturbauit. Et sane Rom. 5. versu 3. expresse dicitur, aliquem pro altero mori posse. Quamvis vero in his exemplis 1. alter pro altero non puniatur, 2. nec satisfaciat, attamen hinc dicimus, 1. non simpliciter a regula iustitiae deviare, siquis pro alio moriatur. 2. in his exemplis particulam PRO non commodum, sed vicem notare.

LIII. 4. Distinguimus inter strictum ius & aequitatem. Est illa regula stricti iuris, quae nihil derogat aequitati & moderamini lenitatis, in Evangelio patefactae. Iudex si rigorem iustitiae adhibeat, tum delinquentem ipsum ad poenas rapit, nec alienam satisfactionem accipit: Interim sine iniustitia quidpiam remittere potest, vt severitas mutetur in aequitatem, quando vel in totum recipit solutionem alienam, vel poenam partitur inter delinquentem & intercedentem. Iam vt hoc applicetur, dicimus illum Prophetae aphorismum esse legalem & stricti juris, vbi semper valet: Anima quae peccaverit, ipsa morietur: Vt vero Lex non tollit Evangelium, sic legales sententiae, non sunt opponendae Euangelicis. Ex quibus discimus, Deum patrem ex sua bonitate misisse Filium, vt pro nobis daret pretium redemtionis. Breviter ergo & summatim dicendo; Anima peccans ipsa moritur, ex iudicio stricti iuris, in foro humano, & diuino secundum legem; pro anima peccante Christus moritur ex iudicio aequitatis, & benevolo consilio Trinitatis secundum επιείκειαν Evangelij. Illud rigorem, hoc amorem iudicis ostendit, quod ipsum paucis complexus est Dn. D. Hunnius p. m. tract. de iustif. Tom. 1. colum 557. Regula haec est iustitiae diuinae, si illa aestimetur ex vltimo rigore suo, quando sine misericordiae adiunctione pensitatur, vt videre est in lapsis Angelis, at in mysterio redemptionis nostrae haec iustitia temperatur bonitate Dei. &c. Quare vt misericordia DEI non tollit eius iustitiam, ita hoc opus misericordiae, quo Filius pro nobis satisfecit, iustitiae non aduersatur, sed admirandum clementiae temperamentum, in redemptione nostra adhibitum manifestat.

LIIII. 5. Distinguimus inter ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον & θεάνθρωπον. Loquitur dictum de hominibus meris, quorum alter alterius poenam non portat: Filius enim Patris supplicium non tulit, cum ipse in pietate vitae ambulat. Alia autem ratio est θεανθρώπου, ob speciale consilium Dei. Quamvis enim Λόγος innocentissimus extiterit, nec dolus in ore eius fuerit inuentus, adeoque nullum meruerit respectu sui supplicium; placuit nihilominus Deo Patri, omnium nostrum iniquitates super ipsum ponere, & propter peccata nostra vulnerare, Efa. 53. Quem vnicum textum si considerarent Photiniani, puderet ipsos tam putidae ratiunculae. Ibi enim expresse dicitur v. 5. ipse vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras. v. 6. Posuit Dominus in eum iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Quae verba prorsus resciscenda erunt, si regula Ezechielis sine omni exceptione vrgeatur. Quia vero Propheta Prophetae non contradicit, nos inde colligimus. Ezechielem de hominibus meris, Esaiam de Messia mundi & Christo θεανθρώπῳ loqui: Illum regulam posuisse, hunc exceptionem a regula ostendisse.

LV. 6. Distinguimus inter poenae susceptionem voluntariam & impositionem violentam. Si quis sponte & vltro se offerat ad satisfaciendum pro alio, illi non fit iniuria, si imponatur poena, vt cum Lex vtriusque oculi effossionem poscit; sed supplicium diuidetur inter delinquentem & eius amicum, qui se ex libera voluntate obtulit, tum judex hoc ipso non iniustus & seuerus, sed mitis & aequus est, quod conditionem accipit & a stricto iure remittit. Nam delinquentis miseretur & amici intercedentis voluntati satisfacit. Volenti autem non fit iniuria. Cum vero supplicium imponitur inuito, qui & recte vixit, & illud modis omnibus recusat, tum iniquus foret judex, qui ad poenam cogeret & traheret reluctantem, locóque facinorosi plecteret. Tunc enim valet illa iustitiæ regula: Quæ peccauit anima, morietur, & filius non portabit iniquitatem patris, Patet hoc ex toto contextu & scopo Domini. Iudæi vtebantur hoc prouerbio. Patres comederunt vuam acerbam & dentes filiorum obstupuerunt. vers. 2 Sensus erat; Patres nostri peccauerunt, nos pœnam luimus, quamuis præceptis Dei diligenter obediamus. Falsum hoc esse Deus pronunciat, ideoque vers. 4. respondet: Anima quæ peccauerit, ipsa morietur. Sensus est, si quis piè viuat, mihique seruiat, ille ob peccatum patris sui non punietur inuitus, non trahetur ad supplicium, vti clarè docetur, v. 17. 18. & 19. Ex quibus liquet, illam sententiam tantùm agere de supplicio inuito, quale præter meritum Iudæi opinabantur, sibi esse impositum, id quod voluntariæ solutioni aut pœnæ susceptioni nihil derogat, quippè, quam sine iniuriâ soluentis fieri, & iudicis lenitatem potius quàm seueritatem innuere, quiuis rectâ ratione præditus & frequentibus exemplis edoctus intelligit. Iam si consideremus mortem & passionem Christi, fuit vtique illa voluntaria, & spontanea; non violēta aut coacta: Licet ergo pœnam non meruerit quia omni peccato caruit: Attamen nulla ipsi facta est iniuria, Cum Deus Pater super eum præuaricationes nostras posuit, quoniam illas lubenter tulit, & semetipsum redemptionis pretium promptè dedit, nostriq́; loco persoluit. Vitiosa igitur est collectio à violenta supplicij impositione, quæ iniqua ad voluntariam susceptionem, quę judicis æquitatem & suscipientis amorem commendat.

LVI. 7. Distinguimus inter peccatum personale vel vnius hominis aut populi, & originale vel totius mundi. Dictum Ezechielis loquitur de peccatis personalibus, quæ non imputantur alijs hominibus, vel de peccato indiuiduali patris, cuius supplicium non luit filius, vti vers. 17, expresse indicatur. De his enim singularibus delictis verum est, quod anima peccans ipsa morietur, iam vero longe alia ratio fuit passionis Christi. In illa totius mundi peccata sunt imputata, siquidem agnus est, αἴρων τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τῶ κόσμω: Ioh. 1. vers. 29. Quod plane singulare fuit & extraordinarium. Quamuis igitur homo pro homine non puniatur ob delictum personale; quod vult sententia Ezechielis, Dei tamen filius ex decreto Patris secundum scripturas pro peccato vniuersali & totius mundi est mortuus, vt nos ab æterna damnatione liberaret, & sibi sanctificaret. Hoc speciale fuit, secundum communes regulas minime æstimandum. Notus enim est Canon ille tristissimus: Ab ordinario ad Extraordinarium non valet consequentia. Sicut non sequitur: DEVS prohibuit homicidium & furtum. Ergo non potuit Abrahamo imperare immolationem filij Gen. 22. Israelitis spoliationem Ægyptiorum Exod 11. Nam hæc omnia sunt exempla singularia & exceptiones a communi regula; quod ipsum etiam de Christi passione, nostri loco suscepta, cogitandum est.

LVII. Excipit Gittichius 1. p. 65. Iudæos conqueri non de peccato vnius hominis sed vniuersi populi maierum. Resp. Et hæc vocantur personalia vel singularia, quia non toti generi humano, sed tantum certo populo, certis indiuiduis fuerunt communia.

2. Pag. 67. Christum non potuisse mori pro personalibus, sed tantum pro originali. Resp. ab inclusiua ad Exclusiuam non valet consequentia. Christus sic mortuus est pro peccato vniuersali, vt per meritum eius expiata sint simul alia ex originali profluentia peccata, Et quicquid hic dicitur ex cœcæ rationis iudicio contra expressas Scripturas desumptum est. Illæ enim vbique clamant, Christum pro nobis & propter nostra peccata esse mortuum.

LVII. Verùm perpetuò vrget hoc Gitichius, Alterum pro altero punire est iniustum; multò verò iniustius, innocentem pro nocente: at longè iniustissimum, innocentissimum pro improbissimis. Eadem inculcat Socinus parte 3. c. 3. p. 251. & 309.

Resp. 1. Est nuda repetitio coccysmi prioris, quare repetimus nostras responsiones, quod istud quidem verum sit, 1. de stricto iure. 2. de ψιλῷ ἀνθρώπῳ, 3. de iudicio singulari & humano. 4. de pœnæ impositione violenta, & 5. de peccato personali. Falsum autem est, si applicetur ad temperamentum Dei & salutem hominis, si intelligatur de θεανθρώπῳ, singulari & extraordinario Dei consilio, de pœnæ susceptione voluntaria & peccato vniuersali. Alij sic limitant: Non est crudele, 1. si innocens cum nocentibus sit eiusdem naturæ. 2. si spontè ad pœnam luendam se offerat. 3. si possit suis viribus è pœna emergere. 4. alios isto pacto liberare. 4. Dei gloriam & salutem hominum promouere, quæ omnia in satisfactione Christi concurrunt. Absurdum id est quoad rationem, quæ in hoc mysterio cæca, sed non quoad Evangelium, cuius iudicium à iudicio 1. rationis, & 2. legis accuratè hic discernendum est. Si quæras, Vnde hanc restrictionem probemus. Parata est responsio, & manifestis Scripturis, quæ dicunt Christum ob iniquitates esse percussum, factum execrationem, Galat. 3. & peccatum, 2. Cor. 5. Imò iustum esse mortuum pro iniustis, 1. Pet. 3. vers. 18. Adde insuper manifestum locum, Rom. 5. vers. 6. Christus cum adhuc infirmi essemus secundum tempus, pro impijs mortuus est. Vix autem pro iusto quis moritur. Nam pro bono forsitan, quis audeat mori. Christus autem cùm adhuc peccatores essemus pro nobis mortuus est. Sicut hic mori pro iusto, est loco iusti mori, (fortè in Tyranide & persecutione aliqua, vbi optio datur, Aut tu, aut ille moriatur. Vel alter pro altero mori eligit :) sic etiam cum Christus pro nobis impjis dicitur mortuus, idem est ac loco nostri esse mortuum.

Excipit G stichius p. 18. 1. Christum pro nobis quidem esse mortuum, sed non punitum, no idem esse pro aliquo mori & vice seu loco alicuius mori. 2. patere idem ex opposito: mori pro pio, talis enim mors nullo modo ad satisfactionem pro iusto præstandam suscipi potest, cum ille nullius criminis reus teneatur.

Resp. ad 1. Qui pro nobis mortuns est, is pro nobis poenam peccatorum sustinuit, quia mors est pœna peccati, Christus autem pro nobis mortuus esse dicitur, Quare poenam peccatorum pro nobis sustinuit; Hinc Esai. 53., vers. 5. expresse dicitur, Castigatus propter iniquitates nostras; Deinde licet pro aliquo & vice alicuius mori nonnunqua differant vt generale & speciale, hic tamen ad aperta Scripturæ testimonia & materiæ subjectæ naturam coincidut Et quis aliud intelligat, si pro impio quem mori audiat, quam loco impij eam mortem suscipere.

Ad 2. Licet cum aliquis necem subit pro pio, non satisfaciat pro peccatis, cum iustus sit: attamem manet hoc, quod pro ipso sit loco ipsius mori, nempe vt salvus euadat, & ex vitæ periculo liberetur, in quo alioqui versabatur. Hæc omnia cum manifesta sint, firmiter illis inhęremus, quam uis cæca ratio meras sibi contradictiones & absurditates politicas fingat: Sufficit nobis Scripturæ vox aperta, quam plus curamus, quam infinita rationis obloquentis figmenta & pigmenta. Et enim hoc mysterium a seculis tacitum, suo tempore patefactum, quod religiosè credere, non malitiosè contemnere, nec hinc inde conqvisitis ratiunculis eludere debemus.

LIIX. 2. In re pecuniaria, quando alter pro altero spopondit, tum si debitor soluere nequeat, sponsor licet debitum non contraxerit, nec ipse pecuniam mutuò acceperit, meritò ad soluendum vrgetur, aut si recuset soluere, propter sponsionem suam carceri sine iniuriâ aut crudelitate includitur. Et si non habeat in ære, vndè soluat, luit in corpore; non solùm causâ, sed etiam loco & vice illius, pro quo spopondit. Si hæc saluâ iustitia in humano fore contingunt, cur ob id Deũ crudelitatis aut iniustitiæ accusabimus, præsertim cùm ista filij satisfactio in nostrum vsum longè maximum cedat? Si sponsor pro alio puniri potest, cur non etiam Christus mediator noster pro nobis seu nostri loco crucifigi potuisset; vtì Scriptura passim asserit.


### Argument III From the indiscriminate salvation of all: Argument IX From an absurd consequence

ARGUMENT IX.

From an absurd consequence.

LIX. If Christ made satisfaction for us, his mercy toward the human race was greater than the Father's. For Christ demanded nothing from anyone, but furthermore moved the Father to have mercy on us and to be reconciled to us. But the mover is more principal than the moved. Whence it follows that men owe more gratitude to Christ than to God the Father: Indeed, they owe nothing to the latter, since the price has been paid to him. Ostorod. p. 213. Catech. Racov. p. 263.

LX R. 1. A hostile dissension is feigned here between the persons of the Trinity, and the Son is wrongly opposed to the Father, since of both there is one essence, one mercy, one justice, and one will. If therefore the mercy of the Son toward the human race is great, certainly that of the Father is also: If satisfaction has been made to the justice of the Father, certainly it has been made to that of the Son, since that satisfaction does not regard the Father alone, but the divine justice, which is common to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Which admirable work, we freely admit is less agreeable to blind reason; and therefore it weaves various subtleties and consequences against the clearest testimonies of Scripture, when nevertheless that Economy of our salvation is to be proclaimed with a grateful heart rather than to be inquired into too curiously, much less to be involved in subtleties or deformed by diabolical calumnies.

LXI. 2. Although the Son alone suffered for us in the assumed humanity, the work of reconciliation itself is nevertheless common to the whole Trinity, since it proceeded from their counsel, Lombard. lib. 3. dist. 19. lit. F. He says, the whole Trinity reconciled us by a unitive way, namely, while it blots out sins; but the Son alone by the fulfillment of obedience. The assumption of humanity itself, although it is terminated in the Son, nevertheless draws its origin from the whole Trinity, which the ancients declared by the simile of three maidens, who all clothe one person with a certain tunic.

LXII. 3. Our theologians, when they speak accurately, do not maintain: that Christ by his satisfaction moved the Father, so that He might simply wish to have mercy on us. For justice, not mercy, demanded satisfaction, which itself did not effect, but followed, the love of God, which is rightly called the foundation and origin of our salvation, upon which the very satisfaction of Christ also depends, which God freely imputes to us through faith.

LXIII. 4. That it may be shown in particular how great is the mercy of the Father, and how much He excels in our salvation, we wish to be considered, 1. The mission of the Son, This proceeded from the highest love, and the secret counsel of the Father, John 3. Through which our redemption was decreed, so that thus there is no other prince and first cause of salvation than the benevolent will of the Father, sending the Son. For unless the Father had sent Him into the flesh, no redemption would have followed, so that the first place in the business of salvation must deservedly be ascribed to God the Father, 2. The closest conjunction of the Father and the Son

stem. Hence it happens that whatever the Son has done, consequently and in his own way is reckoned as accepted by the Father, since they are one. Christ himself testifies concerning this in John 14, v. 10: Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I speak to you, I do not speak from myself, but the Father remaining in me, he does the works. And v. 31, he says that he acts in the work of redemption just as it was commanded to him by the Father. The Apostle notably expresses this very thing in 2 Cor. 5, v. 18: GOD reconciled us to himself through Christ; and v. 19: For GOD was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not imputing their trespasses to them, etc. 3. By the acceptance of another's merit. If the Father had wished to deal with us by strict law, he would not have permitted the punishments to be diverted from us onto another. But mindful of his mercy, he held the obedience of the Son, our Redeemer, as valid and pleasing, and accepted the sacrifice of his death as a sweet-smelling savor, Eph. 5, v. 2. For which reason he says that Christ is his beloved Son, in whom he is well pleased, Matt. 3, v. 17. 4. The omitted exaction of further satisfaction. For God the Father does not demand from us works or full obedience to the law, if we wish to be justified, but without works, without our own merits, out of grace alone founded in Christ, he justifies us, which is an argument of the greatest kindness. 5. The concession of the Word and Sacraments. What would the merit of Christ profit, unless it were offered to us through certain instruments? But those, not the Son alone, but the whole Trinity provides. 6. The infusion of faith. It is not in our power to believe and to apprehend merit; God alone grants this gift to us, and in turn makes his mercy …testified. Eph. 2, v. 8: By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast. 7. Gratuitous imputation. This is ascribed to the Father and comprises the very essence of justification. Satisfaction would profit nothing, unless the Father imputed it to us and held it as valid, for in this consists the blessedness of ness, that God imputes righteousness without works, Rom. 4. v. 6. Finally 3. Consummation up to the end of life, and the soon-following glorification. This again is a benefit not of the Son alone, but of the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the good work, which he began in us, he perfects until the day of Jesus Christ, Philip. 1. v. 6. and whom he justifies, them he also glorifies, Rom. 8. v. 30. From these things, therefore, it is more than sufficiently evident how great is the mercy of God the Father, nay, of all the persons of the Trinity, which they employ in the business of our salvation: so that deservedly the same honor and worship should be rendered.

LXIV. If you ask: Whether the love of the Son is not greater than that of the Father, since he died for us, but the latter did not; since he made satisfaction for both? Resp. 1. That which is said concerning satisfaction cannot be simply approved. For satisfaction was made to divine justice, which is common to the whole Trinity, and therefore the Son ought not to be excluded from satisfaction at all. 2. Speculation about degrees of mercy is superfluous, proceeding from the curiosity of reason, nowhere founded in the Scriptures: We know that the whole Trinity has loved us intensely and still loves us. What need is there to discuss scrupulously about degrees of love? 3. Nay, no degrees are given here, since the love of both the Father and the Son is supreme. But in what is supreme, more and less have no place. Not more, because above the supreme would be given something higher, which is absurd. Not less, because then the supreme would not be supreme. For that above which a higher degree is given is by no means supreme. But indeed the love of the Father and of the Son toward us is in both cases supreme and in the highest degree, although in a different respect. The love of the Father is supreme, because he did not spare his Son, Rom. 8. v. 32. The love of the Son is supreme, because he did not refuse to die for us, even when we were enemies, Rom. 5. v. 6. 7. 8. Therefore, whatever Phrygian [notions] are figments of reason and mockeries of Satan nor do they dispute about an unequal love of the Father and the Son, since both are supreme; but in the highest degree inequality has no place. With this standing, that also immediately falls, that more is to be attributed to the Son, less to the Father. For if both loved us equally, they equally procure salvation, since the love and care for salvation of both is supreme; why should we pursue the Father and the Son with unequal honor? Christ denies this in John 5, v. 23, where he confirms the equality of worship with these words: The Father has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son even as they honor the Father.

LXV. Ostorodus objects: Either satisfaction has been made to Christ by another, in which case it is asked who that is? or satisfaction has not been made, and it still follows that greater mercy is found in Christ than in God the Father?

R. Satisfaction has been made through Christ to divine justice, which is one and common to all three Persons, and therefore there was no need for satisfaction to be made by another, but Christ made satisfaction to himself, while he made satisfaction to God, because he himself is God. You ask, Why did the Father not also make satisfaction to himself? Resp. 1. The order of the persons and the counsel of the Trinity, which is not to be examined according to the rules of reason, stands in the way. 2. And the Father in a certain way made satisfaction to himself, not indeed by suffering in his own person, but by sending the Son to suffer. Hence both is asserted in the Scriptures; both that Christ has reconciled us to God, Romans 5, verse 10, and that God has reconciled us to himself in Christ, 2 Cor. 5, v. 18, 19. You say: It is absurd for someone offended to make satisfaction to himself? Resp. However absurd it may be before reason, it is nonetheless written, and therefore true. The ways of God are not the ways of men, and the thoughts of God are not the thoughts of men: Isaiah 55, verse 8. We willingly confess that a great mystery and secret lies hidden here, but for that reason it ought not to be denied because it cannot be grasped, for the authority of Scripture is greater than all the capacity of human intellect. Augustine has encompassed this whole mystery briefly and acutely in the book On Faith to Peter, chapter 22, writing thus: One Christ the Priest, through whom we are reconciled: Then, line 18, in whom reconciled; God, to whom reconciled; Some explain the matter with the analogy of a judge passing a law concerning an adulterer, to be punished by the gouging out of both eyes. When his son was accused of this crime, he gouged out one eye for his son and the other for himself, and thus satisfied the law and himself.

LXXI. They continue by objecting: Either the Son was angry with us, and thus he himself needed satisfaction; or he was not angry; and thus he disagreed with the Father; by which the unity of will, and consequently of the divine essence, is destroyed:

Resp. The justice of the Father and the Son is one; and therefore he was no less angry with us than the former. Meanwhile, since that anger was tempered by kindness, and God was taking pity on the human race deceived by the serpent, and was thinking about redeeming it, the Son willingly obeyed the Father, and thus satisfied that justice and consequently himself, which, although the human mind does not grasp it, we nevertheless have revealed in the sacred Code. And this is an indication not of hostile discord but rather of obedience. For the Son undertook death, not because he disagreed with the Father and favored men more than was just, but so that the justice of God might be satisfied, to which that of the Psalmist refers, Ps. 40, v. 9: Behold I come, in the volume of the book it is written of me, that I should do thy will, O my God. And thus at once collapses that Satanic sarcasm of Ostorodius, p. 214: Did the Holy Spirit in the reconciliation differ on the part of the Father or the Son? This calumny flowed from the fact that he thinks the persons of the Trinity disagreed hostilely in the work of redemption, when nevertheless there was an identity of will and an excellent agreement.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM IX.

Ab absurdo consequente.

LIX. Si Christus pro nobis satisfecit, maior eius fuit misericordia in genus humanum, quam Patris. Christus enim à nemine quicquā postulauit, sed Patrem insuper mouerit, vt nostri misereretur, & nobis reconciliaretur. Mouens autem principale fortius est moto. Vndè sequitur, Homines plus gratitudinis debere Christo, quàm Deo Patri: Imò huic nihil debere, cùm ipsi pretium sit persolutum. Ostorod. p. 213. Catech. Racov. p. 263.

LX R. 1. Fingitur hic hostilis dissensio inter personas Trinitatis, & malè opponitur Patri Filius, cum vtriusque sit vna essentia, vna misericordia, vna justitia, & voluntas. Si ergò Filij magna est Misericordia ergà genus humanum, vtique & Patris: Si satisfactum est Iustitiæ Patris, vtique & Filij, quoniam satisfactio illa non respicit solum Patrem, sed diuinam iustitiam, quæ Patri, Filio, & Spiritui sancto communis est. Quod ad mirandum opus, caecae quidem rationi minus consentaneum esse libenter fatemur; Ideoque illa varias nectit argutias & consequentias aduersus clarissima Scripturae testimonia, cùm tamen illa salutis nostrae Oeconomia planè singularis & incomprehensibilis grato potiùs corde sit praedicanda, quàm curiosiùs inquirenda, multò minus argutijs inuoluenda, vel calumnijs diabolicis deformanda.

LXI. 2. Quamuis Filius sola in assumpta humanitate pro nobis passus sit, ipsum tamen reconciliationis opus toti Trinitati, quippè ex cuius consilio prodijt, commune est, Lombard. lib. 3. dist. 19. lit. F. Reconciliauit nos, inquit, tota Trinitas vnitiua via, scil. dum peccata delet; sed Filius solus impletione obedientiae. Ipsa humanitatis assumptio licèt terminetur in filio, ortum tamen trahit à tota Trinitate, quod veteres declarârunt similitudine trium puellarum, quae omnes vni quandam tunicam induunt.

LXII. 3. Nostri, cùm accuratè loquuntur, non statuunt: Christum satisfactione sua patrem mouisse, vt simpliciter vellet nostri misereri. Nam iustitia non misericordia flagitabat satisfactionem, quae ipsa non effecit, sed secuta est Dei amorem, qui rectè dicitur fundamentum & origo salutis nostrae, à quo ipsa etiam satisfactio Christi dependet, quam Deus gratis per fidem nobis imputat.

LXIII. 4. Vt in specie ostendatur, quanta sit Patris misericordia, & quantum praestet in saluatione nostra, considerari volumus, 1. Missionem Filij, Prodijt haec ex summa dilectione, & arcano Patris consilio, Ioh. 3. Per quod decreta est redēptio nostra, vt ità princeps & prima salutis causa nulla sit alia, quàm beneuola voluntas Patris, Filium mittentis. Nisi enim Pater ipsum in carnem misisset, redemptio nulla secuta fuisset, vt primae in salutis negotio Deo Patri meritò adscribi debeant, 2. Arctissimam Patris & Filij coniunctio-

stem. Hinc fit, vt quicquid filius egerit, consequenter & suo modo Patri acceptum feratur, quoniam vnum sunt. Testatur de hoc Christus ipse Ioh. 14. v. 10. Non creditis, quia ego in patre & pater in me est? Verba quæ loquor vobis, a meipso non loquor, Pater autem in me manens ipse facit opera. Et vers. 31. ait, se in redemptionis opere sic agere, sicut mandatum sibi fuerit a patre. Notanter hoc ipsum exprimit Apostolus 2. Tim. 5. v. 18. DEVS nos reconciliawit sibi ipsi per Christum; & v. 19. Quoniam DEVS erat in Christo, mundum reconcilians sibi, non imputans illis delicta eorum, &c. 3. Alieni meriti acceptatione. Stricto iure si nobiscum agere voluisset Pater, pœnas a nobis in alium deriuari non permisisset. Verum memor misericordiæ suæ obedientiam Filij Redemptoris nostri ratam & gratam habuit, ac sacrificium mortis eius in odorem suauitatis suscepit, Ephes. 5. vers. 2. Qua de causa dicit Christum esse suum filium dilectum, in quo beneplacitum habeat, Matth. 3. v. 17. 4. Vlterioris satisfactionis intermissam exactionem. Non enim Deus Pater a nobis postulat opera vel plenam legis obedientiam, si iustificari velimus, sed absque operibus, absque proprijs meritis, ex sola gratia in Christo fundata, nos iustificat, quod maximæ benignitatis argumentum est. 5. Verbi & Sacramentorum concessionem. Quid prodesset Christi meritum, nisi illud per certa nobis organa offerretur? Illa vero non solus filius, sed tota Trinitas procurat. 6. Fidei infusionem. Non est in potestate nostra credere & meritum apprehendere; solus Deus hoc nobis donum concedit, suamque vicissim testatam facit misericordiam. Ephes. 2 vers. 8. Gratia estis seruati per fidem, & hoc non ex vobis, Dei donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur 7. Gratuitam imputationem. Hæc Patri adscribitur & ipsam iustificationis essentiam complectitur. Nihil satisfactio prodesset, nisi pater eam nobis imputaret & pro rata haberet, Nam in hoc consistit beatitudo hominis, quòd Deus imputat iustitiam sine operibus, Rom. 4. v. 6. Tandem 3. Consummationem vsque ad finem vitæ, & mox subsequentem glorificationem. Hoc iterum est beneficium non solius Filij, sed Patris & Spiritus sancti, quia opus bonum, quod in nobis cœpit, perficit vsque in diem Iesu Christi, Philip. 1. v. 6. & quos iustificat, illos & glorificat, Rom. 8. v. 30. Ex hisce igitur satis superque patet, quanta sit Dei Patris, imò omnium Trinitatis personarum misericordia, quam in salutis nostræ negotio adhibent: vt ita meritò idem honos & cultus exhibendus sit.

LXIV. Si quæras: An non Filij maior sit amor, quam Patris, cùm ille pro nobis mortuus sit, hic non item; ille satisfactionem vtriusque fecerit? Resp. 1. Quòd de satisfactione dicitur, non potest simpliciter approbari. Satisfactum enim est iustitiæ diuinæ, quæ communis toti Trinitati, ideoque filius à satisfactione excludi planè non debet. 2. Speculatio de gradibus misericordiæ superuacanea est, ex rationis curiositate profecta, in Scripturis nullibi fundata: Scimus, quòd tota Trinitas nos impensè dilexerit & etiamnum diligat. Quid opus est de gradibus dilectionis scrupulosè disserere? 3. Imò gradus hîc nulli dantur, quoniam amor & Patris & Filij summus est. In summitate autem magis, & minus, locum non habet. Non magis, quia supra summum daretur superius, quod absurdum. Non minus, quia tum summum non foret summum. Supra quod enim datur gradus superior, id summum minimè est. At verò dilectio Patris & Filij erga nos vtrobique summa & in gradu summo est, quamuis diuerso respectu. Summa est charitas Patris, quia non pepercit filio, Rom. 8. v. 32. Summa est charitas Filij, quia non repugnauit pro nobis etiam inimicis mori, Rom. 5. v. 6. 7. 8. Figmenta igitur rationis & ludibria Satanæ sunt, quæcunque Phrygiani ni de inæquali Patris & Filij dilectione disputant, cùm vtraq; summa sit; in summo auté gradu inæqualitas locum nō habeat. Quo stante mox cadit & istud, Filio plus, Patri minus tribuendum. Si enim vterque ex æquo nos dilexit, ex æquo salutē procurat, quoniam vtriusque dilectio & salutis cura est summa; cur inæquali Patrem & Filium honore prosequeremur? Negat hæc Christus Iohan. 5. v. 23. vbi cultus æqualitatem his verbis confirmat. Pater omne iudicium dedit Filio, vt omnes honorificent Filium sicut & honorificent Patrem.

LXV. Excipit Ostorodus; Aut Christo satisfactum est ab alio, vbi quæritur quis ille sit? aut satisfactum non est, & adhuc sequitur, inuensiorem in Christo, quam in Deo Patre misericordiam inueniri?

R. Satisfactum est per Christum iustitiæ diuinæ, quæ vna est communis omnibus tribus Personis, ideoq; non opus fuit, vt ab alio satisfieret, sed sibiipsi satisfecit Christus, dum Deo satis, quia ipsa est Deus. Quæris, Cur non & Pater sibi ipsi satisfecit. Resp. 1. Obstat ordo personarum & Trinitatis consilium, quod secundum rationis regulas non est examinandum. 2. Et Pater quodammodo sibiipsi satisfecit, non quidem patiendo in sua persona, sed Filium ad patiendum mittendo. Hinc vtrumque asseritur in Scripturis; tum quòd Christus nos reconciliauerit Deo, Roman. 5. vers. 10. tùm quòd Deus nos sibiipsi reconciliauerit in Christo, 2. Cor. 5. v. 18. 19. Inquis; Absurdum est, aliquem offensum sibiipsi satisfacere? Resp Vtut sit absurdū corã ratione, nihilominus scriptum, ideoq; verum est. Viæ Dei non sunt viæ hominium, & cogitationes Dei non sunt cogitationes hominum: Esai. 55. vers. 8. Fatemur lubenter magnum hîc mysterium & arcanum latere, sed ob id negari non debet, quia capi nō potest, maior enim est Scripturæ authoritas quàm omnis ingenij humani capacitas. Complexus est totū hoc mysteriū Augustinus breuiter & argutè in lib. de fide ad Petrum cap. 22 sic scribens: Vnus Christus Sacerdos , per quem sumus reconciliati: Tum, l. 18, in quo reconciliati; Deus, cui reconciliati; Nonnulli declarant rem similitudine Iudecis legem ferentis de adultero, per effossionē vtriusque oculi puniendo. Cuius delicti cùm filius argueretur reus, filio vnum, sibi alterum oculum effodit, adeoque legi & sibiipsi satisfecit.

LXXI. Pergunt excipiendo: Filius aut nobis iratus fuit, & sic satisfactione ipse indiguit; aut non iratus; & sic à Patre dissensit; per quod tollitur vnitas voluntatis, & per consequens essentiae diuinae:

Resp. Vna est Patris & Filij iustitia; ideoq; hic non minus quàm ille nobis iratus fuit. Interim quoniam illa ira fuit benignitate tēperata, Deusque generis humani per serpentem decepti miserebatur, & de redimendo illo cogitabat, Filius Patri lubens obedijt, adeoque iustitiae illius & per consequens sibiipsi satisfecit, quod licèt humana mens non capiat, in sacro tamen Codice reuelatum habemus. Et hoc est Indicium non hostilis discordię sed potius obedientiae. Filius enim mortem suscepit, non quòd dissideret à Patre, & homnibus plus iusto faueret, sed vt iustitiae Dei satisfieret, quò spectat istud Psalmistae Psal. 40. v. 9. Ecce venio, in volumine libri scriptum est de me, vt facerem voluntatem tuam, Deus meus. Atque sic vnà concidit Satanicus ille sarcasmus Ostorodi p. 214. An Spiritus S. in reconciliatione Desiuerit à parte Patris vel Filij? Profluxit haec calumnia ex eo, quòd personas Trinitatis in opere redemptionis putet hostiliter dissensisse, cùm tamen identitas fuerit voluntatis & optima consensio.


### Argument X. from eternal death and damnation

LXVII. Whoever did not undergo eternal death, but only temporal, he by no means satisfied for us, nor did he sustain our punishments, indeed; the greatest part of which is eternal damnation. And yet Christ underwent only temporal, not eternal death. Therefore he by no means satisfied for us, nor did he sustain our punishments. Ostorod. p. 214. Catech. Rac. p. 263.

LXIIX. Resp. The conclusion is contrary to the Scriptures, especially chapter 53 of Isaiah, and therefore there will be a flaw in the argument. We say therefore 1. That in the major premise there is an insufficient enumeration; which defect ought to be completed thus: He who did not undergo eternal death, nor a punishment equivalent to it, he by no means satisfied for us. But indeed Christ, although he did not undergo eternal death, nevertheless suffered a punishment equivalent to it, namely the highest pains, which although temporal and finite, nevertheless have infinite weight on account of the dignity of his person and thus are equivalent to eternal death. For the passion was not of a mere man but of a God-man! Not of a mere man, but of the true God, who acquired the Church with his own blood, Acts 20, verse 28, and thus what is lacking in finite time is completed by the infinite person, who adds infinite weight to the temporal passion: For just as the sin of Adam was not in itself eternal and infinite; meanwhile, however, it had the force of infinite guilt subjecting the whole human race to damnation, because it offended the eternal and infinite God: So also the death of Christ is finite by reason of time, but infinite by reason of value, because it is the death of the infinite God. Thus, therefore, to infinite sin and infinite punishments contracted through sins is opposed the infinite merit of CHRIST, or his infinite satisfaction. The reason for the infinity in both cases is taken from the infinite God who is offended by sin and satisfies for sin.

LXIX. Socinus p. 267 objects: If this were true, some very light punishment taken from Christ could have satisfied the justice of God; and there would have been no need for him to be tortured with such dire afflictions. For even the lightest punishment could have been added to this weight by the eternal Deity.

Resp. The consequence from possibility to actuality is not valid. Nor must we consider here what could have been done, but what God willed to be done. For it pleased Him that the Son should be struck in various ways on account of our iniquities, to show the gravity of His wrath, the abomination of sins, and the certainty of satisfaction.

LXX. Gittichius, page 5, insists similarly: If one drop of blood was sufficient, or what are those shed in vain, and God was most cruel, who required more.

Respon. What theologians say about one sufficient drop is not to be understood absolutely concerning the consummation of merit and the counsel of God, but relatively regarding the dignity of the person. For the blood of this one was the blood of God Himself, Matt. 26 v. 18, 1 John 1 v. 7, Acts 20 verse 28, and therefore in itself worthy and sufficiently suitable, of which even a single drop would be an ἀντίλυτρον for the sins of the world. Meanwhile, it pleased God, and could please Him without cruelty, that the Son be most grievously struck and wounded, Isaiah 53, and therefore one drop was not sufficient by reason of the whole merit and divine counsel, since God willed the New Testament to be sanctioned by the shedding of much blood, to demonstrate more openly the glory of His justice and truthfulness. Nor was this a sign of cruelty or injustice, unless you blasphemously maintain that Scripture itself, which affirms these things about God, imputes such crimes to Him.

LXXI. Gittichius continues insisting, page 86. That the purpose and counsel of God cannot evade these absurdities. For if, on account of the dignity of the Person, one drop could satisfy, God ought to have decreed only one for Himself for satisfaction from eternity, unless He wished to become an unjust exactor of debt. Furthermore: Even if Christ had wished to pay more than He owed, the justice of God nevertheless ought not to have accepted more be. For it is of the same justice to beware of too much and too little.

Resp: 1. That phrase, that one drop sufficed, is of the Fathers, not of Scripture: it is a pious thought, not a foundation of our faith: Wherefore, if certain absurdities follow from it, we shall not defend it tooth and nail. This is certain from the Word of God, that one drop did not complete the whole merit and sacrifice to be offered for us, otherwise Christ would not have needed to die and suffer after the circumcision. Meanwhile, since the person is infinite, we say that in this respect any little drop was of infinite value, and by reason of itself, yet not sufficient for God, who alone knows best how much is required for full satisfaction, and why He willed His Son to suffer precisely so many wounds, neither fewer nor more. We know all His works are just, therefore also the crucifixion of the Son, although it may seem to us, because of the infinity of the person, that one drop sufficed. Meanwhile it is certain from Heb. 9. verse 15. that not one drop, but death itself was needed for satisfaction, the causes of which the Apostle commemorates there as sufficiently grave: 2. From the opinion of the Photinians it follows rather that God is a cruel Tyrant, inasmuch as He so tortured and struck Christ even unto death, neither for His own sins, which were none, nor for our sins, for unjust is every death and punishment which is not inflicted on account of guilt and sin.

LXXII. 2. Others respond to the minor premise, and concede that Christ in His own way underwent eternal death. But it must be known that this does not denote the perpetual separation of soul and body, since in this way, not even the damned would undergo eternal death, but 1. the immensity of infernal pains. 2. the eternal continuation of such pains. The former is essential to eternal death, the latter is accidental. The Savior underwent the former, as is clear from the most grave in his agony and by the statement of Psalm 18:6, 'The pains of hell compassed me about.' Hence he poured out such ardent prayers to God, Matthew 26:39 and 40, and was sorrowful even unto death, verse 37, because he felt that the wrath of God, from which he saved us, Romans 5:9, was poured out upon him, and that a horrible judgment against sin was laid upon him 5:21; Galatians 3:13. Otherwise, let them tell me how it happened that Christ so shuddered at death and even emitted drops of blood, Luke 22:44, unless he had felt the Father's wrath. The other martyrs underwent death joyfully, and yet they were not without sins. But why did Christ, who was most innocent, shudder so much? Why did he wish the cup to pass from him, if not because of the sense of wrath and the severity of the pain? This is taught by that cry in Matthew 27:46 and Psalm 22:1 and 2, 'My God, why hast thou forsaken me?' By this agreement, therefore, Christ endured the penalty of eternal death considered essentially in our place; indeed, he bore greater torments than all men could sustain. As concerns the latter, that is foreign to Christ, for neither the infinity of time nor the perpetual duration of pain could or should have had a place in Christ's passion. It should not have, since death, because of his infinite person, was even then of infinite value.

It could not, 1. because of the indissolubility of the personal union, because of which it was necessary for the body of Christ to rise again, and not be dissolved into ashes, because what the λόγος assumed, he never lays aside. 2. Because of the infallibility of the divine promises. For he had to crush the head of the serpent, Genesis 3:15, not see corruption, Psalm 16:10, and serve as a priest forever, Psalm 110:4, and ascend as a breaker-through, Micah 2:13. Finally, 3. because of the holiness of his body. Our bodies are resolved into ashes because they are subject to sin, Romans 6:6; but Christ's body was holy and undefiled, and therefore it could not see corruption, Psalm 16:10. Although, however, Christ did not suffer death eternal in respect of time; yet in respect of ἰσίας and infernal pains he did sustain it, in which the very essence of death consists, and thus nothing is detracted from the infinity of the punishment and the price, concerning which see the more extensive discussion by Mr. Dr. Gerhard, Vol. 3, Loci Communes, p. 1080.

LXXIII. 3, Lucius p. 15, answers that eternal is said equivocally, either by potentiality or by act: By potentiality and in itself every death is eternal, that is, it lasts forever, whether it be of the body, which is the separation of the soul, as in beasts; or of the soul, which is the desertion of God, as in the damned: But by act and accidentally not every death is eternal, neither of the body, as in those to be resurrected, nor of the soul, as in the elect; having presupposed these things, he says on p. 16 that Christ underwent death eternal not indeed by act, that is, that which would last forever, because of the office of mediator, because he had to overcome death: yet he did undergo death eternal by potentiality, that is, perpetually durable, which is hinted at in Heb. 2, v. 9 and 14.

Latin:

LXVII. Quicunque non subijt aeternam mortem, sed tantùm temporalem, is pro nobis nequaquā satisfecit, nec nostras pœnas sustinuit, quippe; quarum maxima pars est æterna damnatio. Atqui Christus tantum temporalem, no æternam mortem subyt. Ergo pro nobis nequaquam satisfecit, nec nostras pœnas sustinuit. Ostorod. pag. 214. Catech. Rac. p. 263.

LXIIX. Resp. Conclusio contrariatur Scripturis, præsertim c. 53. Esaiæ, ideoque vitium erit in argumento. Dicimus ergo 1. In maiori esse insufficientem enumerationem; qui defectus sic compleri debet: Qui non subiit mortem æternam, nec pœnam illi æquipollentem, is pro nobis minimè satisfecit. At verò Christus, licèt mortem æternam non subierit, tamen pœnam æquipollentem, summos nimirum dolores perpessus est, qui temporales quidem finiti fuerunt, nihilominus habent infinitum pondus ob dignitatem personæ atque sic morti æternæ æquipollent. Non enim fuit passio ψιλὂ ἀνθρώπὂ sed θεανθρώπὂ! Non meri hominis, sed veri Dei, qui suo sibi sanguine acquisiuit Ecclesiam, Actor. 20. vers. 28. adeoque quod deest finito tempori, hoc completur per personam infinitam, quæ temporali passioni pondus infinitum addit: Sicut enim peccatum Adæ in se quidem non fuit æternum & infinitum; interim tamen habuit vim culpæ infinitæ totum genus humanum damnationi subijcientis, quia æternum & infinitum Deum læsit: Sic & mors Christi ratione temporis finita, ratione valoris infinita est, quia Dei infiniti mors est. Sic igitur infinito peccato & infinitis pœnis, per peccata contractis opponitur infinitum CHRISTI meritum, vel infinita eius satisfactio. Ratio infinitatis vtrobique sumitur à Deo infinito qui per peccatum læditur & pro peccato satisfacit.

LXIX. Socinus pag. 267. excipit: Si verum hoc esset, leuissima aliqua pœna de Christo sumpta, iustitiæ Dei satisfieri potuisset; et non opus fuerit tàm diris eum cruciari tibus affligi. Nam & leuissima pœna hoc pondus ab æterna Deitate addi poterat.

Resp. A posse ad esse non valet consequentia. Nec hic respiciendum est quid fieri potuerit, sed quid Deus fieri voluerit. Ipsi enim placuit, vt Filius propter iniquitates nostras varijs modis percuteretur ad ostendendam iræ suæ grauitatem, peccatorum abominationem, & satisfactionis certitudinem.

LXX. Gittichius pag. 5. instat similiter: Si vna gutta sanguinis fuit sufficiens vel quæ sunt frustrà effusa, & Deus fuit crudelissimus, qui plus requisiuit.

Respon. Quod de vna guttâ sufficiente dicant Theologi, non est intelligendū absolutè de consummatione meriti & consilio Dei, sed respectiuè quoad dignitatem personæ. Huius enim sanguis fuit ipsius Dei sanguis, Matth. 26. v. 18. 1. Ioh. 1. v. 7. Actor. 20. versu 28. ideoque ex se dignus & idoneus satis, cuius vel vnica gutta esset ἀντίλυτρον pro peccatis mundi. Interim Deo placuit & placere sine crudelitate potuit, Filium grauissimè percuti & vulnerari, Esai. 53. ideoque vna gutta non fuit sufficiens ratione totius meriti, & consilij diuini, siquidem Deus multâ sanguinis effusione Testamentum nouum sanciri voluit, ad apertius demonstrandam iustitiæ & veracitatis gloriam. Neque fuit hoc crudelitatis, aut iniustitiæ signum, nisi Scripturam ipsam quæ de Deo isthæc affirmat, tanta illi crimina impingere, blasphemè statuas.

LXXI. Pergit instando Gittichius pag. 86. Propositum & consilium Dei absurda ista eludere non posse. Si enim propter Personæ dignitatem vna gutta satisfacere poterat, vnam tantùm decernere sibi pro satisfactione ab æterno Deus debuit, nisi iniquus coactor debiti fieri voluisset. Præterea: Etiamsi Christus plus voluisset soluere, quàm debebat, iusticia tamen Dei plus accipere non debebat. Eiusdem enim iustitiae est, cauere nimium & paucum.

Resp: 1. Phrasis ista, vnam guttarn suffecisse, Patrum est, non Scripturae: Pia cogitatio est, non fundamentum nostrae fidei: Quare, si quaedam inde sequantur absurda, mordicus eam non defendemus. Hoc certum est ex Verbo Dei, guttam vnam non absoluisse totum meritum & sacrificium pro nobis offerendum, alias post circumcisionem mori & pati Christus non debuisset. Interim cum persona sit infinita, dicimus hoc respectu quamuis guttulam fuisse infiniti valoris, & ratione sui, non tamen Dei sufficientem, qui optime solus nouit, quantum requiratur ad plenam satisfactionem, & cur Filium suum praecise tot plagas, nec pauciores nec plures pati voluerit. Scimus omnia opera eius esse iusta, ergo & filij crucifixio, licet videatur nobis ob infinitatem personae vnam guttulam suffecisse. Interim certum est ex Heb. 9. vers. 15. non vna gutta, sed morte ipsa ad satisfactionem opus fuisse, cuius causas satis graues ibi Apostolus commemorat: 2. Ex sententia Photinianorum potius consequitur, Deum esse Tyrannum crudelem, quippe, qui Christum nec propter sua, quae nulla erant, nec propter nostra peccata sic excruciavit & percusserit vsque ad mortem, iniusta enim est mors & poena omnis, quae non propter culpam & peccatum infligitur.

LXXII. 2. Alij ad minorem respondent, & Christum suo modo aeternam mortem subijsse concedunt, Sciendum vero, quod illa non denotet perpetua animae, corporisq; divulsionem, siquidem hoc pacto, ne damnati quide mortem aeterna subirent, sed 1. immensitatem doloru infernaliu. 2. aeternam talium doloru continuationem, Prius aeternae morti essentiale est, posterius accidentale, Prius Saluator subijt, vt liquet ex grauissima eius agone & dicto Psalm. 18. 6. Dolores inferni me circumdederunt. Hinc tam ardētes ad Deum preces effudit, Matth. 26. vers. 39. & 40. & tristis fuit vsque ad mortem. vers. 37. quia iram Dei, à quâ nos seruauit Rom. 5. v. 9. in se effusam, & horrendum iudicium aduersus peccatum sibi impositum esse sentiebat, Es. 53. v. 5. 6. 8. 9. Rom. 8. v. 3. 2. Cor. 3. ver. 21. Gal. 3. v. 13. Aliâs dicant mihi, quî factum, vt Christus ad mortem adeò exhorruerit & guttas etiam sanguineas emiserit Luc. 22. vers. 44. nisi Patris iram sensisset. Martyres reliqui mortem læti subiêre, & tamen peccatis non caruerunt. Christus autem innocentissimus cur adeò exhorruit? cur calicem à se transire voluit, nisi ob sensum iræ & grauitatem doloris? Docet hoc clamor iste Matth. 27. v. 46. & Psal. 22. v. 2. & 3. Deus quare me dereliquisti. Hoc igitur pacto æternæ mortis pœnam essentialiter consideratam, nostri loco Christus sustinuit, imò maiores cruciatus pertulit, quàm vniuersi homines sustinere possint. Posterius quod concernit, illud à Christo alienum est, nec enim infinitas temporis vel perpetua doloris duratio in Christi passione locum habere vel debuit vel potuit. Non debuit, quoniam mors ob infinitam personam iam tum erat infiniti valoris.

Non potuit 1. ob vnionis personalis indissolubilitatem, ob quam necessarium fuit, corpus Christi resurgere, nec in cineres dissolui, quia quæ λόγος assumpsit, nunquam deponit. 2. Ob diuinarum promissionum infallibilitatem. Debebat enim caput serpentis conterere Gen. 3. v. 15. corruptionem non videre Psalm. 16. v. 10. in æternum sacerdotio fungi. Ps. 110. v. 4. & tanquam perruptor ascendere; Micheæ 2. vers. 13. tandem 3. ob corporis sanctitatem. Nostra corpora in cineres resoluuntur, quia peccato sunt obnoxia, Rom 6. vers. 6. Christi autem corpus sanctum fuit & incontaminatum; ideoque corruptionem videre haud potuit, Ps. 16. v. 10. Licèt autem Christus mortem ratione temporis æternam non pertulerit; attamen ratione ἰσίας & dolorum infernalium sustinuit, in quibus ipsa mortis essentia consistit, adeoque hinc infinitati supplicij & pretij nil quicquam decedit, de quibus fusiùs disserentem vide Dn. Doct. Gerhardum Tom. 3. LL. C C.p. 1080.

LXXIII. 3, Lucius pag. 15. respondet, æternum æquivocè dici, vel potentiâ, vel actu: Potentiâ & per se omnis mors est æterna, hoc est, in æternum durat, siue corporis sit, quæ separatio animæ, vt in brutis; siue animæ, quæ desertio Dei, vt in damnatis: Actu verò & per accidens non omnis mors est æterna, nec corporis, vt in resuscitandis, nec animæ, vt in electis; quibus præsuppositis ait p. 16. Christum subijsse mortem æternam non quidem actu, hoc est, semper duraturam, propter officium mediatoris, quia mortem superare debebat: attamen subijsse mortem potentiâ æternam, hoc est, perpetuò durabilem quod innuitur Heb. 2, v. 9. & 14.


### Argument X. from eternal death and damnation: Argument XI. From the lack of wrath in God

ARGUMENT XI. From the lack of wrath in God.

LXXIV. Christ indeed reconciled us to God, but not conversely God to us, since Scripture nowhere asserts that God was hostile to us, but rather that He loved us seriously; and thus could not be angry. Ostorod p. 239, 242.

LXXV. R. This is a gross lie, which can be refuted from God's 1. Threats. 2. Deeds. 3. Sayings. 4. Reasons.

1. THREATS. Gen. 2, verse 17. In the day that you eat of it, you shall die the death. What kind of utterance is this, of a merciful God, or indeed of an indignant one? He who would say the former would be most absurd: For to announce punishments and to threaten death is the act of a severe judge, who is angry on account of sins, not of one who is propitious or who forgives guilt. Unless, therefore, to remove all threats, and to make them less if you should wish to affirm that they are serious, but only playful and not without blasphemy, it will be necessary that you confess that God is angry on account of sins, and with an alienated mind threatens and inflicts punishments. To that first threatening, which is the greatest of all, let others be added here and there, such as those which are read, Levit. 26. verse 14. whoever weighs that chapter, and does not understand that God is alienated on account of sins, I will pronounce him either extremely blind, or maliciously incredulous. Add Psalm 11. vers. 6. He who loves iniquity, the soul of the Lord hates him. He himself shall rain snares upon sinners, fire and brimstone, and the spirit of storms is the portion of their cup, because the Lord is just. Prov. 1. v. 14. Because I have called and you have refused etc. Is. 1. v. 20. If you are unwilling, the sword shall devour you. Is. 3. v. 11. Woe to the wicked for evil. Is. 5. v. 25. The fury of the Lord is kindled against the people. Is. 33. v. 1. Woe to you who plunder: shall you not also be plundered? Is. 65. v. 5. these shall be smoke in my fury. Jer. 14. 13. I will consume them with the sword, famine, and pestilence. Add Matth. 11. 21. C. 23. 37. Rom 2. 9. Wrath and indignation, and tribulation and anguish upon the soul of man working evil. Weighing these and similar things, one cannot but gather from them that God is seriously angry at sins, and is alienated from sinners, as they are such, since all threats of this kind breathe this, and the very sound also terrifies; in place of a finishing stroke and as a summary of all threats I subjoin that tremendous sentence of the law: which exists in Deut. 27. 26. and is repeated, Gal. 3. 10. Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all things which are written in the book of the law, to do them. Hence I conclude thus, He who curses sinners is not benevolently affected towards them, as they are such, but rather alienated. But God through the law curses all sinners. Therefore he is not benevolently affected, but rather alienated. Since our first parents transgressed the law of God, they certainly also subjected themselves to the curse, and thus drew the wrath of God upon themselves, and the whole human race.

Latin:

ARGVMENTVM XI. Ab iræ in Deo carentia.

LXXIV. Christus quidem nos reconciliavit Deo, sed non vice versâ Deum nobis, quoniam Scriptura nuspiam asserit, Deum nobis infensum fuisse, sed potius seriò dilexisse; adeoque irasci non potuisse. Ostorod p. 239 242.

LXXV. R. Spissum hoc est mendacium, quod refutari potest ex Dei 1. Minis. 2. Factis. 3. Dictis. 4. Rationibus.

1. MINAE. Gen. 2. vers. 17. Quocunque die comederis, morte morieris. Quale hoc effatum est, num misericordis, an verò indignantis Dei? Prius qui diceret, absurdissimus foret: Pœnas enim indicere, & mortem minari, iudicis seueri est, ob peccata irascentis, non propitij aut culpam dimittentis. Nisi ergò omnes minas tollere, easque minùs serias esse, sed tantùm ludicras non sine blasphemia affirmare velis, necesse erit, vt Deum ob peccata irasci, & abalienato animo poenas minari & infligere, fatearis. Ad primam illam comminationem, quæ summa est omnium, accedant passim aliæ, quales leguntur, Leuit. 26. versu 14. quod caput qui perpendit, nec Deum ob peccata abalienari intelligit, illum ego vel extremè cæcum, vel malitiosè incredulum pronunciavero. Adde Psalm. 11. vers. 6. Qui diligit iniquitatem, eum odit anima Domini. Pluet ipse super peccatores laqueos, ignem & sulphur, & Spiritus procellarum pars calicis eorum, quoniam iustus est Dominus. Prov. 1. v. 14. Quia vocavi & renuistis &c. Es. 1. v. 20. Si nolueritis, gladius deuorabit vos. Es. 3. v. 11. Væ impio in malum Es. 5. v. 25. Furor Domini iratus est in populum. Es. 33. v. 1. Væ qui prædaris: Nonnè & ipse prædaberis? Es. 65. v. 5. isti fumus erunt in furore meo. Ier. 14. 13. Gladio, fame, & peste consumam eos. Adde Matth. 11. 21. C. 23. 37. Rom 2. 9. Ira & indignatio, & tribulatio & angustia in animam hominis operantis malum. Hæc & similia perpendens, non potest non indè colligere, Deum seriò irasci peccatis, & alienari à peccatoribus, quà tales sunt, cùm omnes eiusmodi minziram spirent, & ipse sonus etiam terreat, Colophonis loco & velut compendium omnium minarum subijcio legis istam sententiam tremendam: quæ extat Deut. 27. 26. & repetitur, Gal. 3. 10. Maledictus omnis, qui non permanserit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro legis, vt faciat ea. Hinc ita concludo, Qui maledicit peccatoribus, non est benevolè affectus erga ipsos, quà tales, sed potius alienatus. Atqui Deus per legē maledicit omnib. peccatorib. E. non est benevolè affectus, sed potius abalienatus. Quoniam v parētes primilegem Dei sunt transgressi, vtiq; & subiecerunt maledictioni, adeoq; iram Dei attraxerūt super se, & vniuersum genus humanum.


### Argument X. from eternal death and damnation: LXXVI. 2. Deeds. Experience itself cries out

LXXVI. 2. DEEDS. Experience itself cries out On the indignation and alienation of God because of sins. As could be proven by innumerable examples: But let one or two suffice. 1. The punishment of the πρωτοπλάςων. If God had not been alienated from them, why would he have punished them so severely? 1. He took away the concreated image, which was followed by blindness, ignorance, malice. 2. He cursed the serpent and the earth. 3. He subjected them to various miseries, diseases, and death. 4. He expelled them from Paradise. 5. He exposed them to the snares and enmities of Satan. 6. And thus he pursues that fall not only in Adam, but in all his posterity, (for death reigns even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam's transgression Rom. 5. v. 14) 7. So that all are born children of wrath Eph. 2. v. 3. and guilty of eternal damnation. Are not all these by far the most grievous punishments signs of a mind greatly angered and alienated? For would anyone endowed with a sound mind affirm that such great miseries, such a mass of penalties, proceed from a benevolent God? The fear of the πρωτοπλάςων themselves argues the contrary. For as soon as they had violated the law, they immediately fled and trembled. Whence this, unless because their own conscience kept telling them that God was alienated? Add that discord and hostility of the creatures towards us, of which Eph. 1. v. 21. and Col. 1. v. 20. Whence this, unless because their creator had become an enemy and foe to us? II. The Universal Flood. By this one example alone the Lord sufficiently declared how alienated he is from sinners. For it repented God that he had made man on the earth, Genesis 6. v. 6. I will blot out, he says, man, whom I have created, from the face of the earth, from man even to beasts, and creeping things, even to the birds of the heavens. For it repenteth me that I have made them, v. 7. But Noah found grace. v. 8. Here both the word for repenting, and the purpose of blotting out, and the opposition of wrath and grace clearly teach the supreme indignation and alienation of God from the whole human race, which is also evident from the execution Gen. 7. 23. and following. Add the conflagration of Sodom Gen. 19. the drowning of Pharaoh Ex. 14. the expulsion of the Canaanites. Jos. 6. & seq. The crucifixion of the most innocent Christ upon whom God cast the sins of all: and therefore struck him most grievously. Isa. 53. & it will become clear that God is most severely angry with sinners, and was so offended with the whole human race, that by no other reason than through the death of the Only-begotten could reconciliation be made.

LXXVII. 3. Sayings.

1. Isa. 59. v. 2. Your iniquities have separated between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, that he might not hear. Now wherever there is a division of minds, there certainly is alienation on both sides; and when the face is turned away and hidden, it certainly follows that the mind is angry and resentful. But sins divide, and cause the face of God to be turned away. Therefore he is angry with the man of sin, and has his mind alienated from him. 2. Ps. 31. v. 7. You have hated those who observe lying vanities. Ps. 44. v. 8. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity. Zech. 8. v. 17. Let none of you think evil in your heart against his friend, etc. for all these are things that I hate, says the Lord. Wisd. 10. Similarly, the ungodly and his ungodliness are hateful to God. Which very thing is expressed by the canonical decree of the Psalmist. Ps. 11. v. 6. He who loves iniquity, him the soul of the Lord hates. From these sayings I argue thus; Wherever there is hatred, there is no benevolent affection, without any indignation and alienation. But in God there is hatred towards all sinners, and thus towards the whole human race, on account of the transgression of Adam; wherefore there is not in God a benevolent affection only towards the human race or sinners. 3. John 3. last verse. He who is unbelieving towards the Son, shall not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him. Here both the wrath of God is expressly named, and the cause is added, namely sin, and finally it is said that the wrath does not come after impenitence, but remains, to indicate that the wrath of God is upon every sinner from their first birth, but does not remain, except upon the unbelieving and impenitent. Now let the Photinians reconcile these two; that the wrath of GOD remains upon the unbelieving, which the Apostle says, and that GOD is not alienated from sinners before impenitence, which they themselves assert. To this we further refer that of the Apostle Rom. 1. verse 18. The wrath of GOD is revealed from heaven, against that God is angry, and has been angry, with the whole human race on account of sins, just as he shows more fully in chapter 3, but that few have believed in this wrath and indignation, and therefore it is now revealed and announced to all, lest they deceive themselves with a false persuasion concerning the love of God. Since, therefore, the Photinians remain in the same fantasy, we deservedly oppose them with this Apostolic statement as a kind of engine: The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. 4.
