Eph. 2. verse 3. We were by nature children of wrath, Therefore God is angry with the whole human race. For how can he be called a child of wrath from whom He is not alienated? 5. Rom. 4 v. 15. The law works wrath. But whose? Certainly that of GOD himself, since it is His Law, or whose will is expressed by the law. Therefore, whoever violates the law incurs the wrath of God, because it is universally true that the Law works wrath, which wrath of God comprises three things primarily: 1. aversion to sin: 2. displeasure with the person: 3. the will to take vengeance.

LXXVIII. 4. REASONS I. From the Law. This is the rule of the divine will, and therefore to depart from it is to be opposed to the will of God. But all sinners depart from it. Wherefore all are opposed to the divine will. But God hates him who opposes Him, and makes light of His will. For the cause of hatred is contumacy: when subjects do not do what the prince wants them to do, he begins to be angry with them, which ought not to be denied of GOD, the King of Kings. Now indeed these things cancel each other out, not to be ill-affected and yet to hate. Since therefore this latter is true, on account of the transgression of the law, how will the Photinians be able to affirm the former without ἀντιφάσει?

2. From the judgment of conscience. If God were not alienated from sinners, or angry, whence, I ask, the goads of conscience, whence that fear and trembling which is seen in transgressors? Why did Cain shudder so at fratricide? Is it not because God himself indicated his alienation in manifest words, Gen. 4, verse 10: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the ground: Now therefore you shall be cursed upon the earth. We reason from this as follows. The judgment of conscience is the judgment of GOD, inasmuch as he is the one who implanted this distinction between honorable and base things in our souls. Therefore, we ought not in the least to doubt that the sentence of conscience concerning a committed sin is true and divine. But indeed, conscience immediately accuses after the fault, proclaims that God is angry and alienated, and announces mere punishments and blows, whence arise pains and horrors in the mind of the sinner. Wherefore this very judgment will be true, as having proceeded from God himself accusing through conscience.

3. From the Nature of God. Whatever is contrary to the nature of God, from that God himself and his benevolent will is turned away. But every sin is contrary to the nature of God, which is most holy, and on account of this, the sinner himself, who commits it. Therefore, God and his benevolent affection are turned away from sin and on account of this from the sinner.

4. From the absurd. If the mind of God is not alienated from sinners, then this ἄτοπον follows: that in the sight of God the sinner and the non-sinner are of equal value: that God does not abominate or detest sins: that God loves men, however they may conduct themselves, whether they sin or abstain from sins, etc. That God is equally affected toward justice and injustice; not to hate that which is hostile to his nature is; that the sentence of the cursing law is a thunderbolt and an empty scarecrow, if indeed God never seriously becomes angry with sinners, nor bears an averted mind from them. But who that is pious, nay, who that is endowed with a sound mind, would admit these portents and monsters, by which the name of God is taken away, the law is mocked, and the force and entire value of threats is undermined? 5. From reconciliation, Christ reconciled us to God. But indeed to reconcile is nothing other than to bring back into favor. Since therefore Christ, by reconciling us to God, brought us back into favor, or restored grace, certainly that was previously lost, and thus God was alienated from us. For that which is never lost, there is no need for its restitution. Wherefore if God was never hostile to us, there was no need for reconciliation or reduction into favor. In vain therefore did Christ die. Or certainly that reconciliation must be described in such a way that it is not a reconciliation. 6. Eph. 1. v. 6. it is said ἐχαρίτωσεν, he rendered us grateful or accepted to himself in the beloved. Before therefore this beloved had made satisfaction for us, we were not accepted and grateful. If not accepted, certainly God had an alienated mind from us. 7. Roman. 8. cap. v. 32. GOD did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all. Not to spare, and not even one's own son, is [the act] of an indignant mind, and one that avenges sins. For he who is so angered that he urges satisfaction, he is said not to spare: but he who is always benevolently disposed, the same cannot be affirmed of him without absurdity, for he is spared who ought to sustain some punishment, whether for himself or for another. Because therefore God did not spare the Son. Therefore he was angry, and so he had to sustain the punishment in our place.

Latin:

LXXVI. 2. FACTA. Clamat ipsa experientia de indignatione & abalienatione Dei ob peccata. Vt innumeris exēplis probari posset: Sed vnum atque alterum sufficiat. 1. πρωτοπλάςων punitio. Si Deus ab ijs abalienatus haud fuisset, cur tam seuerè punijsset? 1. Imaginē concreatam abstulit, quam secuta est cæcitas, ignorantia, malitia. 2. Serpenti & terræ maledixit. 3. Varijs ærumnis, morbis & morti subiecit. 4. Paradyso expulit. 5. Insidijs & inimicitijs Satanæ exposuit. 6. Adeoque lapsum illum non in solo Adamo, sed in totâ posteritate persequitur, (regnat enim mors etiam in eos qui non peccauerunt in similitudine præuaricationis Adæ Rom. 5. v. 14) 7. Vt omnes nascantur filij iræ Eph. 2. vers 3. & æternæ damnationis rei. Hæc omnia longè grauissima supplicia annòn signa sunt animi valdè irati & abalienati? Tantas enim miserias, tantam pœnarum molem à beneuolo Deo proficisci, sanâ mente præditus affirmaret? Contrarium arguit ipse timor πρωτοπλάςων. Quam primum n. legem violauerant, mox fugie bant & trepidabant. Vnde hoc, nisi quia Deum esse abalienatum, ipsa conscientia dictitabat? Adde dissidium illud & hostilitatem creaturarum erga nos, de qua Eph. 1. v. 21. & Col. 1. v. 20. Vnde hoc nisi quod earum creator, nobis factus fuerat hostis & inimicus? II. Vniuersale Diluuium, Satis vel hoc vnico exemplo declarauit Dominus, quàm sit alienatus à peccatoribus. Nam pœnituit Deum, quòd fecisset hominem in terra, Genes. 6. v. 6. Delebo, inquit, hominem, quem creaui, à facie terræ, ab homine vsq; ad animantia, & reptilia, vsq; ad volucres cæli. Pœnitet n. me fecisse eos, v. 2. Noë a. inuenit gratiam. v. 8. Hic & pœnitendi vocabulu, & delendi ppositū, & iræ gratiæq; oppositio luculēter edocēt summam Dei indignationē & ab alienationem ab vniuerso genere humano, qꝫ ipsum liquet etiā ex executione Gen. 7. 23. & seq. Adde deslagrationē Sodomæ Gen. 19. submersionē Pharaonis Ex 14. Expulsionē Cananæorum. Ios. 6. & seq. Crucifixionem Christi innocentissimi super quem Devs omnium peccata coniecit: ádeoque percussit grauissimè. Esa 53. & liquidum fiet, Devm seuerissimè peccatoribus irasci, totique humano generi sic offensum fuisse, vt nullâ ratione aliâ, quam per mortem Vnigeniti reconciliatio fieri potuerit.

LXXVII. 3. Dicta.

1. Esa. 59. v. 2. iniquitates vestræ diuiserunt inter vos, & Deum vestrum, & peccata vestra absconderunt faciem eius à vobis, ne exaudiret. Iam vbicunq; sit diuisio animorum ibi certè ex vtraq; parte est abalienatio; & quandò facies auertitur & absconditur, animum iratum & insensum esse, certò sequitur. Atqui peccata diuidunt, & faciem Dei auerti faciunt. Homini ergo peccāti succenset, & animum ab ipso alienatum habet. 2. Psal. 31. v. 7. Odisti obseruantes vanitates superuacaneas. Psal. 44, v. 8. Dilexisti iustitiam & odisti iniquitatem. Zach. 8. v. 17. Vnusquisq; malū cōtra amicum suum nè cogitetis &c. omnia enim hæc sunt, quæ odi, dicit Dominus. Sap. 10. Similiter, odio sunt Deo impius & impietas eius. Quod ipsum canonico Psaltis edicto exprimitur. Psal. 11. v 6. Qui diligit iniquitatem, illum odit anima Domini. Ex hisce dictis ita argumentor; Vbicunque est odium, ibi non est affectus benevolus, sine omni indignatione & abalienatione. Atqui in Deo est odium erga omnes peccatores, atque sic erga totum genus humanum, ob Adæ præuaricationem; quare non est in Deo affectus beneuolus tantùm erga Genus humanum vel peccatores. 3. Iohan. 3. vers. vlt. Qui incredulus est filio, non habebit vitam, sed ira Dei manet super eum. Hîc & ira Dei expresse nominatur, & causa additur, nempè peccatum, nec demum post impœnitentiā ira venire, sed manere dicitur, ad indicandum, iram Dei esse super omnem peccatorem à prima natiuitate, non autem manere, nisi super incredulos & impoenitentes, Iam concilient Photiniani haec duo; Iram DEI manere super incredulos, quod dicit Apostolus, & DEVM ante impoenitentiam non esse abalienatum a peccatoribus, quod ipsi afferunt. Huc insuper referimus illud Apostoli Rom. 1. vers. 18. Reuelatur ira DEI de caelo, super omnem iniquitatem. Dicto hoc Paulus innuit, Deum vniuerso generi humano irasci, & iratum fuisse ob peccata, sicut cap. 3 ostendit fusius, istam vero iram & indignationem paucos credidisse ideoque nunc reuelari & omnibus anunciari, ne falsa persuasione de amore Dei seipsos decipiant Cùm igitur in eadem phantasia haereant Photiniani, meritò ipsis tanquam machinam quandam opponimus hoc Apostolicum: Reuelata est ira Dei de caelo super omnem iniquitatem & iniustitiam hominum. 4. Eph. 2. versu 3. Eramus natura filij irae, Ergo Deus toti humano generi succenset. Quomodo enim filius irae dici potest à quo abalienatus non est? 5. Rom. 4 v. 15. Lex iram operatur. Cuius verò? Certe ipsius DEI, quippe cuius est Lex, vel cuius voluntas lege expressa est, Proinde quisquis legem violat, iram Dei incurrit, quia vniuersaliter verum est Lex iram operatur, quae ira Dei tria in primis complectitur. 1. auersionem peccati: 2. displicentiam personae. 3. Vlciscendi voluntatem.

LXXVIII. 4. RATIONES I. A Lege. Est haec regula voluntatis diuinae, ideoque ab illa recedere, est voluntati Dei aduersari. Omnes autem peccatores ab illa recedunt. Quare omnes voluntati diuinae aduersantur. Deus verò illum odit, qui aduersatur sibi, & voluntatem suam floccifacit. Nam causa odij est contumacia: cum subditi non faciunt, quod ipsos facere vult princeps, succensere illis incipit, quod ipsum de DEO Regum Rege negari haut debet. Iam verò haec se tollunt, non malè affectum esse & tamẽ odisse. Cùm igitur hoc posterius verum sit, ob præuaricationem legis prius istud sine ἀντιφάσει quî affirmare poterunt Photiniani?

2. A iudicio conscientiæ. Si Deus non esset abalienatus à peccatoribus, aut iratus, vnde quæso stimuli conscientiæ, vnde timor ille & tremor, qui videtur in transgressoribus? Cur Cain ob fratricidium ita exhorruit? Annon, quia Deus ipse abalienationem suam manifestis verbis indicauit Gen. 4. vers. 10. Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me de terra: Nunc igitur maledictus eris super terram. Nos inde sic ratiocinamur. Iudicium conscientiæ est iudicium DEI, quippè, qui discrimen istud honestorum & turpium animis nostris implantauit. Quæ igitur est sententia conscientiæ de peccato commisso eam veram esse & diuinam dubitare minimè debemus. At verò conscientia statim accusat post culpam, Deum iratum abalienatᾶ esse prædicat, meras pœnas & plagis annunciat, vnde oriuntur dolores & horrores in animo peccatoris. Quare hoc ipsumiudiciũ verum erit, tanquam ab ipso Deo per consciẽtiąm accusante, profectum.

3. A Natura Dei. Quicquid aduersum est naturæ Dei, ab illo auersus est ipse Deus & beneuola ejus voluntas. Atqui naturæ Dei, quæ sanctissima, aduersatur peccatum omne, & propter hoc ipse peccator, illud perpetrans. Ergo, & Deus eiusœ; benevolus affectus à peccato & propter hoc à peccatore aversus est.

4. Ab absurdo. Si Dei animus non est abalienatus à peccatoribus, tum sequitur hoc ἄτοπον, in conspectu Dei idem valere peccantem & non peccanttem: Deum peccata non abominari aut detestari: Deum homines amare, quomodocumque se habeant, siue peccent, siue à peccatis abstineant. &c. Deum pariter affectum esse erga iustitiam & injustitiam; non odisse id, quod naturę eius inimieum est ; sententiam legis maledicentis fulmen epelui & inane terriculamentum esse, siquidem Deus seriò nunquam succenseat peccatoribus, nec ab ipsis auersum animum gerat Quis verò pius, imò quis sanâ mente præditus admitteret hęc portenta & monstra, quibus nomen Dei tollitur, lex irridetur, minarum vis & valor omnis labefactatur? 5. A reconciliatione, Christus nos Deo reconciliauit. At verò reconciliare nihil est , quàm in gratiam reducere. Cùm ergo Christus Deo nos reconciliando in gratiam reduxerit , vel gratiam restituerit, vtique illa prius amissa, & sic Deus à nobis abalienatus fuit. Quod enim nunquã est amissum, illius restitutione opus non est. Quare si Devs nunquam infensus nobis fuit reconciliatione vel reductione in gratiam opus non fuit. Frustra igitur Christus est mortuus. Aut certè illa reconciliatio sic describetur, vt non sit reconciliatio. 6. Eph. 1. v. 6. dicitur ἐχαρίτωσεν, gratos seu acceptos nos sibi reddidit in dilecto. Antequam igitur hic dilectus pro nobis satisfecisset, accepti gratique non fuimus. Si non accepti, vtiq; à nobis abalienatum animum Deus habuit. 7. Roman. 8. cap. v. 32. DEVS proprio Filio non pepercit , sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit. Non parcere & nè quidem proprio filio , animi indignantis, & peccata vindicantis est, Qui enim sic irascitur, vt satisfactionem vrgeat, ille dicitur non parcere : Qui autem benevolè semper affectus , de illo idem affirmari sine absurditate nequit, illi enim parcitur, qui pœnam quandam sustinere debet , siuè pro se, siuè pro alio. Quia igitur Devs Filio non pepercit. Ergo iratus ruit, adeoq; ille pœnam nostri loco sustinere debuit.


### Argument X. from eternal death and damnation: LXXI. But some exceptions are proposed

LXXI. But some exceptions are proposed

which it will not be a waste of effort to examine. 1. It is never said in the Scriptures that God is reconciled to us, but always that we are reconciled to God.

Resp. 1. However much you may dislike these words, the sense of the words nevertheless exists in the Scriptures. For 1. if God was angry with us and alienated from us, as we have just proved he was, and indeed through Christ all things have been reconciled in heaven and on earth, which is stated in Colossians 1, verse 20, and Ephesians 1:10, then certainly GOD himself has in turn been reconciled to us through the death of Christ. Otherwise, not all things would have been pacified. Although, therefore, the Apostle in Colossians 1 deals with the discord between Jews and Gentiles, and in Ephesians 2 between men and angels, nevertheless one must not immediately argue from an inclusive to an exclusive, or to a denial of the discord between God and men, especially since a universal term is used, for which no reason of necessity can be brought from the text why it should be restricted. 1. Paul expressly writes in Ephesians 2, v. 16, that Christ reconciled both (Jews and Gentiles) to God in one body through the cross, having put to death the enmities by it. We are said here to be reconciled to God himself and indeed through the blood of Christ, the shedding of which was not required primarily for this end, that the enmity between Jews and Gentiles might be removed, but that, with sin removed—which divides between us and God, Isaiah 59, v. 2—men might be reconciled to God and God to men. For these are relatives, and one does not remove, but posits the other. If we are reconciled to GOD, then certainly GOD is reconciled to us. For every reconciliation is between two parties, of whom one is the offender, the other the offended. We had offended God, he was the offended party, and therefore the reconciliation must be reciprocal. 3. All those texts should be referred here which speak of the imputation of sin, that our iniquities were laid upon Christ, Isaiah 53, that he was made a curse for us, Galatians 3, sin, 2 Corinthians 5. And the price of redemption he gave, 1 Tim. 2, and by his intervening death he expiated us, Heb. 9. For all these things indicate that God was angry and was not reconciled to us except through the death of his Son. For to whom the redemptive price is paid, who strikes someone on account of the sins of others and subjects him to the curse of the law, so that others may be freed, he certainly by this very act is truly reconciled to those for whom the price is given, who are redeemed through that λύτρον. Especially to this point must be referred that classic passage Rom. 3, ver. 24, 25, justified freely by his grace through the redemption made in Christ, whom God set forth as ἱλαστήριον, a propitiation through faith in his blood. I ask here, what did Christ appease? Certainly not us ourselves, since we were the offending party, nor was Christ sent for that reason, that he might reconcile our grace to God, which he in no way lacked. Now because between us and God there is no third party, it follows certainly that Christ is called a propitiation with respect to God, and thus by suffering his wrath he appeased him, and so reconciled him to us.

LII. That Scripture more often says that we are reconciled to God, not God to us, this happens because we were the offending and injuring party, but God was the offended and injured party. We were in fault, God was without fault. Something was added to us, nothing to God. We were in need of reconciliation, not God. Because therefore the passion of Christ tended to our benefit, and satisfaction was made in our place, hence Scripture for the most part shapes its style so that it says we are reconciled to God, to intimate the fruit and saving benefit of the passion. 2. Add that the offending party must first and indeed primarily be reconciled to the injured party, who afterwards more easily forgives the offense. 3. Others add this reason, that we are admonished of our duty, that we may not continue to hate God, but live as those truly reconciled to God, not still alienated by sin. In the mean time, however, it is at the same time hinted that God is also reconciled to us, since every true reconciliation is reciprocal between dissenting and divided parties, who in turn enter into a covenant and mutually assure one another, just as it is also expressly said in the Prophet Isaiah 59, verse 2, that sin divides between us and God, that is, makes both parties dissenting and different from one another. Since, therefore, reconciliation is indeed that reciprocal thing; so that God, divided from us by the divided ones themselves, and conversely, may be reconciled. For all relatives are convertible, and every such thing is reciprocal. Now, reconciliation is a relation. Wherefore it has a mutual respect to both parties that are reconciled: for it does not only respect the reconciling and the one reconciled party, but also the other, which stand as the offender and the offended. For every reconciliation presupposes an offense, where this is required. Since, therefore, men were in need of reconciliation, an offense certainly preceded, and consequently God himself, who had been offended, was reconciled to us through Christ; the Greek word καταλλαγὴ in 2 Corinthians 5, verse 18, and the verb καταλλάττω in Romans 5, verse 10, and 2 Corinthians 5, verse 19, confirm this reciprocation. For καταλλαγὴ signifies such a reconciliation, which is as it were a certain exchange, by which someone is as it were another (whence it is also derived from ἄλλος), not in respect of himself but of another, as Mr. Dr. Gravverus speaks in his disputation on the merit of Christ, page 183. In like manner, in our reconciliation a certain change occurred, by which we, from being children of wrath, have been made children of grace, and God, previously angry with us, has been made a God appeased and propitious through Christ, who for that reason is called the propitiation for our sins, 1 John 2, verse 2.

LXXX. 11. God himself reconciled us to himself through Christ, for which reason he was not angry with us, but loved us all the more. For to be an enemy and to love or to be reconciled to oneself

contrary evasion, Ostor. page 239. 240. 242. Catech. Racov. p. 274.

R. 1. N. C. For although God did not reconcile [the world] to Himself, yet this was done through the death of Christ, as the price of redemption. The former indicates the mercy, the latter the justice of GOD; both are hinted at in 2 Cor. 5. For after the Apostle had said in verse 18 that God reconciled us to Himself through Christ, he immediately adds in verse 21: Him who knew no sin, He made to be sin for us, where the manner of our reconciliation is shown not obscurely, namely that God cast all our sins upon Christ, and by this reason was appeased again. Therefore, both concur in this work of redemption. 1. Charity, which God commended in Rom. 5, verse 8, while He did not spare His own Son, Rom. 8, verse 32, and through Him reconciled us to Himself, 2 Cor. 5, verse 18. 2. Justice, insofar as it was necessary that the Son of God be delivered to an execrable death for us, so that He might thus pay our penalties and reconcile us with God.

2. Whence also it is soon clear that it is not contradictory for someone to hate and love [the same person], if indeed it is done in a different respect. God loved us: 1. as His creatures; 2. miserably deceived; 3. concerning whose reconciliation He entered into counsel. God hates us: 1. as sinners and transgressors of His law; 2. on account of the infallibility of His threats; 3. for which cause He made His Son an execration and sin. The former was of mercy, the latter of justice; He loved as a benevolent Creator, He hates as a just judge. For in man, two things are to be considered: 1. substance, and 2. the corruption of the substance. As to substance, man is the work of God, and thus is loved through mercy, for God hates nothing of those things which He has made, Wis. 11:25. As to corruption, he is a servant of the Devil, and thus is held in hatred through justice. Now indeed, just as God's justice does not remove mercy, and vice versa. Thus, hatred toward us as sinners, proceeding from justice, does not remove love toward us as men, which depends on mercy, especially since Scripture affirms both: that God is divided and alienated from us because of sins, Isa. 59, verse 2, and that He so loved the whole world that He gave His Son, John 3. These things can be explained by the example of David, who loved Absalom as a son, but pursued him with hatred as an enemy. Thus, a father offended by his son's petulance loves the son as a son, but is angry at the same one and inflicts the rod as a petulant one. Similarly, God as a just judge is angry with us as sinners, and meanwhile as a merciful father, He loves us generally, as His creatures, created in His own image. Therefore, in order that the love with which He might love us specially as pleasing and acceptable to Himself might be perfect, there was need of reconciliation, so that justice might thus be satisfied, and the truth of God not be shaken. When, therefore, it is said of Christ that He reconciled us to God, this is not to be understood as if God began to love us entirely anew, as if He had not loved us in any respect before, but because through the passion of Christ the cause of hatred was removed.

LXXXI. 3. God is said to be slow to anger. Therefore, He was not immediately angry with the human race because of the fall of Adam.

Response. 1. That slowness does not denote an entire lack of anger, but a slow infliction of punishment. For the anger of God itself, which denotes an alienation of mind, is one thing; and the punishment, which God imposes at His own discretion, now sooner, now later, is another. 2. Others distinguish between the sentence and the execution. The sentence of God is certain, that He holds sinners in hatred and subjects them to a curse. But the execution is sometimes protracted, so that either they may be invited to repentance, or if they neglect this, they may be affected by greater punishments. Wherefore, although God does not punish sins immediately, it does not follow from this in the least that that he may not be angry: The magistrate can also defer punishment and execution, meanwhile nothing is taken away from his anger and just indignation 3. Some say there is a fallacy of homonymy in the word anger. For it either denotes the vengeance and punishment itself, which is actually inflicted, as in Matt. 3, verse 7: Who has warned you to flee from the wrath to come? So it is also taken in Rom. 2, verse 5; 1 Thess. 1, verse 10; or it denotes the just indignation of God against sins and sinners, which punishment eventually follows, as in John 3, last verse: He who does not believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him; Ps. 6, verse 2: O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chasten me in your anger. In which very sense we are also called children of wrath, Eph. 2, verse 3, that is, such as those with whom God is actually angry, just as they are named children of grace, who are actually pleasing and acceptable to God. Now, that this may be applied to the argument, when God is said to be slow to anger, this word is taken in the former, not the latter, meaning. But it does not follow from this that God does not hate sins or is not indignant at sinners. For one meaning does not remove the other: although He is slow to punishment, He nevertheless always holds the wicked and impiety in hatred. Although the effect does not follow immediately, the affection is nonetheless present, which, however, we attribute to God only anthropopathically.

LXXXII. IV. If to reconcile is the same as to bring back into favor, and we who have been reconciled have been brought back into the favor of God, it follows conversely, since all reconciliation is established as reciprocal, that God has also been brought back into our favor, which is absurd.

Resp. 1. Reconciliation is indeed a bringing back into favor, but not of both, but truly only with respect to the offended party. For although reconciliation pertains to and regards both related parties as the dissenting sides, nevertheless only the one who causes the injury is properly said to be brought back into the favor of the one who is injured or offended. For reconciliation itself is indeed reciprocal, but not the offense, and therefore not the restoration of grace; and consequently the one offended alone, having forgiven the injuries, promises his benevolence again to the one who caused the harm. Now, that this may be applied to our reconciliation with God, it is beyond doubt that God, who had done us good, was gravely offended by our sins. might be appeased, Christ reconciled us to the offended God. Rom. 5. verse 10. with sins blotted out Dan. 9. v. 2. and expiated Heb. 2. 13. 1. Ioh. 2. Whence it follows of its own accord that only the grace of God has been restored to us, not the contrary. Meanwhile, the reciprocity of reconciliation remains intact. For Christ, reconciling us to God, insofar as he brought us back into the grace of God with the cause of the offense removed. And conversely, he reconciled God to us, insofar as he restored and recovered for us the special benevolence of God, which had been lost through sins, by his own blood.

LXXXIII. V. The reconciliation made through Christ is not the appeasement of God toward us, but our conversion toward him, because Christ was sent from God, already appeased, to us, who were still enemies to him, to reconcile us to himself. Socinus p. 55. 57.

Resp. 1. I hear a gloss without reason, without Scripture, which this exception directly contradicts, as was shown above. 2. If Christ announced that God was appeased, who appeased him? For every appeasement presupposes indignation. Wherefore if God is truly appeased, it must be that he was previously hostile to us. If therefore he is appeased, he was certainly appeased either through our satisfaction or another's. Let the Photinians choose and answer clearly. 3. The mode of appeasement is falsely imagined, namely that satisfaction was not made for sins, but that God freely forgives sins, just as the foolish Socinus thinks 2. Cor. 5. v. 19. Not imputing their sins to them. But I ask, why does he not impute them, when a judge who is often hostile ought to impute them? No other cause can be named here than that Christ expiated them with his own blood, Matth. 20. v. 28. his own soul offered for them, 1 Tim. 2:6, and thus made satisfaction; whence also Christ is said to have been made sin in our place, that we might be made the righteousness of God in him, 2 Cor. 5:21. Where Socinus's exception is vain, that Christ is called sin because he was held as a sinner. For 1. if it be permitted to feign thus, I shall elude all the sayings of Scripture concerning the humanity of Christ, namely that whatever is said, all this is said putatively and κατὰ δόξαν, not truly and κατ' ἀλήθειαν, by which instance I wish it to be well noted. 2. Paul explains himself, that Christ is called sin because he is a sacrifice or expiation for sins. Eph. 5:2, Heb. 9:26, 10:12, although Socinus denies this. 3. Why was Christ held for a sinner? Is it not because our sins were imputed to him, and were cast upon him by God the Father? Isaiah 53:8, no otherwise than as the faults of the people were laid upon the Mosaic sacrifices. Now what was prefigured in the types, this must needs be fulfilled in the antitype Christ.

LXXXIV. VI. The Apostles are called ministers of reconciliation, 2 Cor. 5:19. How can this be if that merit of Christ resides entirely? Nay, if we have been reconciled through Christ, why does the Apostle say: We beseech you: be reconciled to God? Socinus in the same place

Response. A distinction must be made between the acquisition of reconciliation and the application of what has been acquired. Christ indeed reconciled us to the Father by acquiring grace, yet we must furthermore be reconciled by apprehending the acquired grace through faith, and since heralds announce the word of this faith, they are hence rightly called ministers of reconciliation, namely not by effecting it but by preaching it to us. Unless a gift is offered, it does not become mine unless I extend my hand: And he who exhorts me to extend it can be called a minister of acceptance. Let the impiety and blasphemy of Socinus be noted here, while he did not shudder to write that the Apostles and other ministers were of reconciliation, as was Christ. Why then did he die here? Why is he called our reconciler, our peacemaker, and mediator? Why does the Apostle to the Hebrews pronounce that he alone is the high priest, who by the offering of his own blood made has redeemed us from sins and damnation? It is clear from this that Socinus and his followers do not think more highly of Christ than of the Prophets and Apostles, although they concede a difference according to more and less. Indeed, let all pious and sensible people judge whether this is blasphemous and extremely contrary to the whole of Scripture.

Latin:

LXXI. Verùm exceptiones aliquot proponun-

tur, quas examinare non erit operæ dispendium 1. Nunquam in Scripturis dicitur, Deum nobis, sed semper nos Deo reconciliatos esse.

Resp. 1. Quantum vis non hæc verba, verborum tamen sensus in Scripturis extat. Nam 1. si Deus nobis iratus & à nobis abalienatus fuit, vti fuisse modò probauimus, & verò per Christum omnia reconciliata sunt in cælis & terris, quod dicitur Coloss 1. versu 20. Eph. 1. 10. Vtique & DEVS ipse nobis per mortem Christi vicissim reconciliatus est. Aliàs non omnia forent pacificata. Quamvis igitur Apostolus Col. 1. agat de dissidio inter Iudæos & gentes Ephe. 2. inter homines & angelos, tamen ab inclusiva non est protinus argumentandum ad exclusivam, vel negationem dissidij inter Deum & homines, præsertim cum habeatur terminus vniuersalis, qui cur restringatur, nulla ex textu necessitatis ratio afferri potest. 1. Paulus diserte scribit Eph. 2. v. 16. Christum vtrosque (Iudæos & gentes) in vno corpore reconciliasse per omnia Deo peremtis inimicitijs per eum. Dicimur hîc reconciliari ipsi Deo & quidem per sanguinem Christi, cuius effusio non requirebatur principaliter hoc fine, vt inimicitia inter Iudæos & gentes tolleretur, sed vt sublato peccato, quod inter nos & Deum dividit Esa. 59. v. 2. homines Deo reconciliarentur & Deus hominibus. Hæc enim relata sunt, & vnum non tollit, sed ponit alterum. Si nos DEO, vtique & DEVS nobis reconciliatus est. Omnis enim reconciliatio est inter duos, quorum alter lædens, alter læsus est. Nos Deum læseramus, ipse pars læsa fuit, ideoque reconciliationem reciprocam esse oportet. 3. Referri huc debent omnes illi textus, qui loquuntur de imputatione peccati, quod in Christum iniquitates nostræ conjectæ sint Esa. 53 quòd factus fuerit maledictum pro nobis Gal. 3. peccatum 2. Cor. 5. Et precium redemtionis dederit, 1. Tim. 2. & intercedente morte nos expiaverit Heb. 9. Hæc enim omnia Deum iratum & non nisi per mortem Filij sui nobis reconciliatum fuisse indicant. Cui enim solvitur præcium redemtivum, qui propter aliena peccata aliquem percutit & legis maledictioni subiicit, vt alij liberentur, illé certè hoc ipso reverà reconciliatur iis, propter quos precium datur, qui per illud λύτρον redimuntur. Imprimis huc referri debet classicus iste locus Rom. 3. ver. 24. 25. iustificati gratis ipsius gratia per redemptionem factam in Christo, quem proposuit Deus ἱλαστήριον placamentum per fidem in sanguine ipsius. Quæro hic, quid Christus placauerit? non certè nos ipsos quoniam eramus pars lædens, nec Christus ideo missus, vt nostram Deo gratiam, quâ minimè eguit, conciliatet. Iam quia inter nos & Deum non datur tertium, sequitur vtique, quod Christus respectu Dei placamentum dicatur, adeoque patiendo iram eius placauerit, & sic ipsum nobis reconciliaverit.

LII. Quòd Scriptura sæpius nos Deo reconciliatos dicit, non Deum nobis, hoc ideò fit, quòd nos eramus pars offendens & lædens, Deus autem pars offensa & læsa. Nos in culpa, Deus extra culpam erat. Nobis aliquid, Deo nihil accessit. Nos reconciliatione indigebamus, non Deus. Quia igitur passio Christi in nostrum vergebat commodum, & nostri loco satisfactum fuit, hinc Scriptura stylum ita plerunque informat, vt nos Deo reconciliatos dicat, ad innuendum passionis fructum & salutare commodum. 2. Adde quòd pars lædens prius & quidem potissimùm reconciliari debet parti læsæ, quæ postmodum offensa facilius condonat. 3. Alij hanc addunt causam, nos admoneri nostri officij, nè pergamus odisse Deum, sed vivamus tanquam verè Deo reconciliati nõ per peccatum etiamnum abalienati. Interim tamen simul innuitur, Deum etiam nobis reconciliatum esse, cùm omnis vera reconciliatio sit reciproca inter partes dissidentes & diuisas, quæ vicissim fœdus ineunt & invicem se accertant, sicut etiam expressè dicitur apud Prophetam Esa. 59. ver. 2. peccatum diuidere inter nos & Deum, h. e. vtramque partem facere dissidentem & alteram ab altera diversam. Cum igitur reconciliatio, est vtique illa reciproca; vt Deus divisus nobis ab ipsos divisis, & contrâ reconcilietur. Nam omnia relata convertuntur, & sint quævis est reciproca. Iam verò reconciliatio est relatio. Quare mutuum respectum habet ad vtramque partem, quæ reconciliatur: Nec enim tantùm respicit reconciliantem & reconciliatam partem vnam, sed etiam alteram, quæ se habent vt lædens & læsus. Nam omnis reconciliatio præsupponit offensionē, Vbi hæc ista requiritur. Quoniã ergo homines indigebant recõciliatione, præcedebat vtique offensio, & per consequens Deus ipse, qui offensus erat nobis per Christum reconciliatus est; Confirmat hanc reciprocationem vox græca καταλλαγὴ 2. Corinth: 5: versu 18. & verbum καταλλάττω Rom. 5. versu. 10. 2. Cor: 5. versu. 19. καταλλαγὴ enim significat eiusmodi reconciliationem, quæ est quasi commutatio quædam, quâ quis quasi alius sit (vndè & ab ἄλλος derivatur) non sui sed alterius respectu, vti loquitur Dn. D. Gravverus in disp. de merito Christi. pag. 183. Pari modo in nostra reconciliatione quædam commutatio contigit, quâ nos ex filiis iræ facti sumus filij gratiæ, & DEVS antè nobis iratus, factus est Deus placatus & propitius per Christum, qui ob id propitiatio pro peccatis nostris dicitur. 1. Iohan. 2. versu 2.

LXXX. 11. Deus ipse nos per Christum reconciliavit sibi, quapropter nobis non fuit censens, sed multò magis dilexit. Hostem enim esse & diligere vel sibi reconcilia-

vafione contraria, Ostor. pagina 239. 240. 242. Catech. Racov. p. 274.

R. 1. N. C. Licèt enim Deus non sibi ipsi reconciliarit, factum tamen hoc est per mortem Christi, tanquam precium redemptionis. Illud prius misericordiam, hoc posterius iustitiam DEI indicat, vtrumque innuitur 2. Cor. 5. Postquam enim Apostolus dixerat versu 18. Deum nos sibi reconciliasse per Christum, mox subjungit versu. 21. Eum qui non nouerat peccatum, pro nobis fecit peccatum, vbi modus nostræ reconciliationis haud obscurè ostenditur, nimirum quòd Deus omnia peccata nostra in Christum conjecerit, & hac ratione iterum placatus sit. Proinde concurrit in hoc redemptionis opere vtrumque. 1. Charitas, quam commendauit Deus Rom. 5. versu 8. dum proprio filio non pepercit Rom. 8. versu. 32. & per illum nos sibiīpsi reconciliavit, 2. Cor. 5. versu 18. 2. Iustitia quatenus Filium Dei pro nobis in mortem execrabilem tradi necessarium fuit, vt ita pœnas nostras lueret & cum Deo reconciliaret.

2. Vnde mox & illud sit liquidum, contraria non esse, aliquem odisse & diligere, si nimirum diuerso id respectu fiat Dilexit nos Deus. 1. vt creaturas suias 2. Miserè deceptas. 3. de quarum reconciliatione inijt consilium, Odit nos Deus, 1. vt peccatores & legis suæ transgressores. 2. ob minarum infallibilitatem 3. qua de causa Filium suum execrationem & peccatum fecit. Prius misericordiæ, posterius iustitiæ fuit; dilexit vt beneuolus Creator, odit vt iustus iudex. Nam in homine, duo consideranda sunt, 1. substātia & 2. substantię corruptio. Quoad substantiā homo est opus Dei, & sic diligitur per misericordiam, nihil enim Deus odit eorum, quæ fecit Sap. 11. 25. Quoad corruptionem est servus Diaboli, & sic odio habetur per iustitiā, Iam verò sicut Dei iustitia non tollit misericordiam, & vicissim. Sic odium erga nos, vt peccatores, ex iustitia profectum, non tollit amorem erga nos, vt homines, â misericordia dependentem, præsertim cum Scriptura vtrumque affirmet, tum Deum ob peccata à nobis divisum & abalienatum esse, Esa. 59. versu 2. tum totum mundum dilexisse, vt daret Filium Iohan. 3. Declarari hæc possunt exemplo Davidis, qui Absolonem diligebat vt Filium, odio prosequebatur, vt hostem. Sic pater offensus filij petulantiâ, diligit filium vt filium, eisdem irascitur & ferulam infligit vt petulanti. Similiter Deus vt iustus iudex succenset nobis vt peccatoribus, & interim vt misericors pater, diligit nos generaliter, tanquam creaturas suas, ad imaginem ipsius creatas. Proindè vt perfecta esset dilectio, quâ nos diligeret specialiter tanquam sibi gratos & acceptos, reconciliatione opus fuit, vt ita iustitiæ satisfieret, nec veritas Dei labefactaretur. Cùm igitur de Christo dicitur, quòd Deo nos reconciliaverit, non ita hoc accipiendum est, quod Deus de novo prorsus nos amare inceperit, quasi antea nullo respectu amaverit, sed, quia per passionem Christi sublata est odii causa.

LXXXI. 3. Deus ad iram tardus esse dicitur, Ergo non statim succensuit generi humano ob lapsum Adæ.

Respon. 1, Tarditas illa non denotat omnimodam iræ carentiam, sed lentam pœnæ immissionem. Aliud autem est ipsa ira Dei, quæ notat abalienationem animi: & aliud est pœna, quam Deus pro arbitratu, nunc citius nunc tardius imponit. 2. Alij distinguunt inter sententiam & executionem. Sententia Dei certa est, quòd peccatores habeat odio & maledictioni subijciat. Sed executio nonnunquam protrahitur, vt vel illi ad pœnitentiam invitentur, vel si hoc negligant, maioribus supplicijs afficiantur. Quare licèt Deus peccata non statim puniat, hinc tamen minimè sequitur, quòd quòd non fuccenfeat: Magistratûs etiam differre potest supplicium & executionem, interim nil decedit iræ eius & iustæ indignationi 3. Nonnulli dicunt esse fallaciam ὁμωνυμίας in vocabulo iræ. Nam vel notat ipsam vltionem & pœnam, quæ actu infligitur, vt Matth. 3. vers. 7. Quis vobis monstravit, vt fugeretis à ventura ira: Sic etiam sumitur Rom. 2. vers 5. 1. Thess. 1. vers. 10. vel iustam Dei indignationem aduersus peccata & peccatores, quam pœna tandem insequitur vt Ioh. 3. vers. vlt. Qui non credit filio, super ipsum manet ira Dei: Pf. 6. vers. 2. Domine ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me. Quo ipso etiam sensu dicimur iræ filij Eph. 2. vers. 3. hoc est, tales, quibus Deus actu ipso irascitur, non secus ac gratiæ filij nominantur, qui actu ipso Deo sunt grati & accepti. Iam vt hoc applicetur ad argumentum cùm Deus ad iram tardus dicitur, vox hæc in priori, non posteriori significatu accipitur. Non autem indè sequitur, Deum peccata non odisse, aut peccatoribus non indignari. Significatio enim vna non tollit alteram : Licèt tardus sit ad pœnam, semper tamen odio habet impium & impietatem. Licèt non statim sequatur effectus, adest nihilominus affectus, quam tamen Deo non nisi ἀνθρωποπαθῶς tribuimus.

LXXXII. IV. Si reconciliare idem est, quod in gratiam reducere, & nos qui reconciliati, in gratiam Dei reducti sumus, sequitur vicissim, cùm reconciliatio omnis statuatur reciproca, & Deum in nostram gratiam redactum esse, quod absurdum.

Resp. 1. Reconciliatio est quidem gratiæ reductio, sed non vtriusque, verùm offensæ partis tantum respectu. Quamuis enim vtrumque relatum attineat, & respiciat reconciliatio, tanquam partes dissidentes, attamen lædens duntaxat propriè dicitur reduci in gratiam læsi seu offensi. Nam ipsa reconciliatio est quidem reciproca, sed non offensio, ideoque nec gratiae reductio; & per consequens solus offensus, condonatis injurijs, suam iterum beneuolentiam pollicetur laedenti. Iam vt hoc ad nostram cum Deo reconciliationem applicetur, extra dubium est, per peccata grauiter offensum fuisse Deum, qui nobis benefecerat, nulloque pacto nos laeserat. Vt autem offensa illa placaretur, Christus nos Deo offenso reconciliauit. Rom. 5. vers 10. peccatis deletis Dan. 9. v. 2. & expiatis Heb. 2. 13. 1. Ioh. 2. Vnde vltro sequitur, Dei tantùm gratiam nobis reductam esse, non contrà. Interim manet reconciliationis reciprocatio salua. Nam Christus nos Deo Reconcilians, quatenus remotâ offensionis causâ in gratiam Dei nos reduxit. Et vicissim, Deum nobis reconciliauit, quatenus Dei beneuolentiam specialem, per peccata amissam, sanguine suo restituit & recuperauit.

LXXXIII. V. Reconciliatio per Christum facta non est Dei erga nos placatio, sed nostri erga illum conuersio, quia Christus à Deo iam placato ad nos, qui adhuc illi inimici ci eramus, sibi reconciliandos missus est. Socinus p. 55. 57.

Resp. 1. Glossam audio sine ratione, sine Scriptura, cui haec exceptio directè contradicit, vt suprà ostensum. 2. Si Christus Deum placatum annunciauit, quis eum placauit? Nam omnis placatio praesupponit indignationem. Quare si Deus verè placatus est; prius infensum nobis fuisse oportet. Si ergò placatus est, vtiq; vel per nostram, vel alienam satisfactionem placatus fuit. Eligant Photiniani & disertè respondeant. 3. Modus placationis falsus fingitur, nempè quòd pro peccatis non satisfactum sit, sed Deus peccata largiter condonet, sicut insulsi Socinus putat 2. Cor. 5. v. 19. Non imputans eis peccata. Sed quaero, cur non imputet, cùm saepeaminfens judex imputare debeat? Nulla hîc alia nominari potest causa, quàm quia Christus suo sanguine illa expiauit, Matth. 20. v. 28. suam animam pro ijs obtulit, 1. Tim. 2. v. 6. & sic satisfecit; vnde & Christus nostri loco dicitur peccatum factus, vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso 2. Cor. 5. 21. Vbi vana est Socini exceptio, Christum dici peccatum, quia pro peccatore sis habitus. Nam 1. si ita fingere liceat, omnia Scripturae dicta de humanitate Christi eludam, nempe quicquid dicitur, hoc omne putatiue & κατὰ δόξαν non vere & κατ' ἀλήθειαν dici, qua instantiam probe notari velim. 2. Paulus seipsum explicat, Christu peccatum dici quia sit hostia vel piaculu pro peccatis. Eph. 5. versu 2. Heb. 9. versic. 26. 10. versu 12. licet id neget Socinus. 3. Cur Christus habebatur pro peccatore? Annon quia nostra ipsi peccata imputabantur, & a Deo Patre in ipsum conijciebantur. Esai 53. versu 8. non secus atque sacrificijs Mosaicis delicta populi imponebantur. Iam quod in typis praefiguratum, hoc in antitypo Christo implerunt sit oportet.

LXXXIV. VI. Apostoli dicuntur ministri reconciliationis, 2. Cor. 5. versu 19. Qui hoc fieri potest si illa Christi merito tota residet? Imo si per Christum reconciliati sumus, cur Apostolus inquit: Rogamus: reconciliemini Deo? Socinus ibidem

Respon. Distinguendum est inter reconciliationis acquisitionem & acquisitae applicationem. Christus quidem nos Patri reconciliauit, acquirendo gratiam, nos tamen insuper reconciliari debemus, acquisitam gratiam per fidem apprehendendo, cuius fidei verbum cum annuncient praecones, hinc recte dicuntur ministri reconciliationis, nempe non eam efficiendo sed nobis praedicando. Nisi donum porrigitur, non fit meum, nisi manum extedam: Et qui ad extendendum me hortatur, ille minister acceptionis nuncupari potest. Notetur autem hic impietas & blasphemia Socini, dum scribere non exhorruit, Apostolos aliosque ministros fuisse reconciliationis, ut Christum. Cur ergo hic est mortuus? cur noster reconciliator, noster pacificator & mediator dicitur? cur Apostolus ad Heb. pronunciat, ipsum solum esse summum Pontificem, qui oblatione sui sanguinis facta nos a peccatis & damnatione redemerit? Liquet hinc, Socinum & asseclas non altius de Christo sentire, quam de Prophetis & Apostolis, quamuis discrimen secundum magis & minus concedant. Annon vero hoc blasphemum & vniversae Scripturae sit extreme contrarium, omnes pij & cordati iudicent?


### Argument XII. On the glory and omnipotence of God

LXXXV. Whatever dogma obscures the glory and omnipotence of God is impious and blasphemous to say. But the dogma of satisfaction obscures the glory and omnipotence of God. Therefore, it is impious and blasphemous to say. The minor premise is proven, because God either would not forgive our sins without satisfaction, which is against the glory of mercy; or he could not, which is against the glory of omnipotence. Ostorod. c. 36. par. 3. p. 300. Socinus par. 3. c. 1. p. 221. & 399. Giesebus proposes this argument thus on p. 3. Our sins are nothing other than an offense against the divine majesty. But even the vilest little man can forgive his own offenses to another, not only without violation of justice, but even with the greatest praise of patience, mercy, goodness, etc. Therefore also, much more, God could forgive us our sins without any satisfaction: or, if he could not because of an imaginary justice, to which the patrons of this dogma bind him, he is less able than even the vilest little man.

LXXXVI. Response 1. By inversion. The glory of God is much more obscured if the dogma of satisfaction is denied. For to bear transgressions, to connive at them, to be in no way alienated by them is a sign of a judge who is either negligent, if he permits it out of injury, or unjust, if he winks at it willingly. But indeed God is not a God who wills iniquity, Ps. 5, verse 5; he hates those who work iniquity and destroys those who speak lies, verse 7. His wrath is so great that no man can endure it, Psalm 39, verse 1, seq. Wherefore the Son of God, having pitied our misery, came to us for help from Zion, Mich. 4. 7, and gave himself as a price of redemption, 1. Tim. 2, verse 6, having been made sin, that we might be made the righteousness in him, 2. Cor. 5, v. last. By which covenant the glory of God is not obscured, but is raised higher, while his majesty is so great that none but the only-begotten son could appease it when offended.

LXXVII. 2. By objection. If it be permitted to argue from private men to God the judge of the world, I shall infer in the same way that God is either unmerciful or impotent if he does not save all sinners and men eternally. For I ask, Why does God condemn impenitent sinners and not endow them with eternal beatitude? Either he cannot dismiss the guilt, and thus he is more impotent than a little man. For any man can dismiss the guilt to another who offends him, even if he is most unwilling to be reconciled here, and can show benefits to him. Indeed, we are commanded by God to do this, that we should do good even to our enemies and our foes, Matth. 5. 44, Rom. 12, verses 20, 21. If therefore a man can remit guilt to everyone who harms him, even to the stubborn, and as much as is in his power, do good, certainly if God cannot do this, he will be more impotent than the vilest little man. Indeed, since God is proposed to us as an example in this very case, Matth. 5, verses 44, 45, that method of imitating falls if it is established that we ought to and can love our enemies, and yet it is denied that God can love his enemies, namely the impenitent, and do them eternal good. Therefore I shall always urge this: If God cannot save the contumacious, he will be impotent, and we are poorly admonished by God's example to do good to all enemies. But if they say that God can indeed save all men, even the impenitent, but does not will to. R. 1. This is directly opposed by the Apostle, who in chapter 6 to the Hebrews, verse 4, says: It is impossible for those who were once enlightened, etc., to be renewed again to repentance, and chapter 10, 26: if we sin willfully after having received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain terrible expectation of judgment, etc. 2. That other absurdity will follow, that God is not merciful, nor supremely good or benevolent: for if He can save all men, and this is omitted solely out of the good pleasure of His will, then certainly He is malevolent, not mercifully disposed toward the human race. Therefore I press the Photinians with this dilemma, that they may answer directly: God either cannot save all men, and thus the glory of omnipotence is taken away: or He does not will to, and the glory of mercy is taken away. Whatever they may say, let them have it in turn as a response for themselves.

XXCVX. 3. By reduction to absurdity. If God ought to dismiss guilt without any satisfaction, His power indeed seems to be asserted, but His justice is denied, which is ἄτοπον. For it is by no means the act of a just judge, if, when by his own power he could dismiss a criminal who ought to be capitally punished, he immediately dismisses him unpunished. This act is not proclaimed as excellent, but is blamed as iniquitous and contrary to the rules of justice. The Photinians inflict this same crime upon God by their hypotheses: who therefore ought to have known that God is not only omnipotent, but also just. Whatever, therefore, so asserts God's power that it destroys His justice, this very thing tends not to the glory, but rather to the ignominy of God. Indeed, not only His justice, but also His truth and zeal against sins by punishments are denied. For those threats will be of no value

Cursed is he who does not abide in the words of this law, Deut. 27. last verse. Vengeance is mine, I will repay, Rom. 12. verse 19. Deut. 32. verse 35. Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord deceitfully, Jer. 48. v. 9. 10.

LXXIX. 4. This argument, drawn from the judgment of blind reason, is contrary to the revealed word. For it is said there that God is omnipotent, yet he does not remit guilt to all, or without a λύτρῳ. For we have the remission of sins only through the blood of Christ, who offered himself as a sacrifice for our sins. Wherefore a theological canon is to be noted here: What God does concerning our salvation is not to be gathered from arguments about the possible, but is to be learned from the Scriptures alone. In them I find both, that God is omnipotent, and that he is hostile to us and not appeased except through Christ. Therefore, subordinate things are wrongly opposed; since the merit of Christ does not take away the glory and power of God, but rather illustrates and amplifies it.

XC. 5. Through the denial of the Minor premise, that the dogma of satisfaction impugns the glory of God. But as for the probative dilemma: Either he could not, or he would not dismiss guilt without satisfaction, I answer. Both can be conceded in a sound sense. 1. He could not with respect to 1. his nature. 2. his justice. 3. his truth. 1. The nature of God is most upright, to which every sin is diametrically opposed. If, therefore, he were not angry with the sinner, but loved him no less after the fault than before the fault, then he would certainly destroy his own nature and contradict himself. 2. The justice of God is immutable, which demands penalties from every transgressor of the law, by virtue of which sinners are to be punished, not dismissed with impunity. Therefore, just as God cannot deny his own justice, so he cannot pardon guilt to delinquents without appeasement and satisfaction. The sayings in Rom. 1: v. 32 pertain to this: The judgment of God, light

It is of God that sinners are worthy of death. 2 Thess. 1 v. 6, that it is just ἀνταποδῶναι to render evil for evil. 3. God is truthful, nay, He is truth itself. But He said in Gen. 2 verse 17, In whatever day you eat, you shall die the death, and Deut. 27 last verse, Cursed is he who does not remain, etc. As soon, therefore, as men sin, they become infallibly guilty of death through sin, and are subject to the curse of the law, and consequently have God angry with them, whom it is altogether necessary to appease and reconcile if they wish to be saved and to enjoy His grace. But if God were not angry with sinners, then they would not be cursed, nor guilty of death. Therefore the sentence of the law would perish, and all God's truth would collapse. These are those foundations why God, being omnipotent, cannot forgive guilt without appeasement. From which nothing is taken away from His omnipotence; just as it is not by that, when it is said that He cannot die or sin. For the object of divine omnipotence is not just any thing, but only that which is not contrary to God's nature and will. All other things argue impotence rather than δύναμιν. Wherefore, since it would be taken away from God's nature if He were to dismiss sins immediately without any indignation, therefore the dogma concerning satisfaction declares God's omnipotence rather than arguing for impotence. God could not save without satisfaction, not because of a defect of power, but because of the perfection of His nature. For if it were done otherwise, God could not preserve His own nature, which is the greatest argument of one who is impotent. I confirm this response with an express aphorism of the Apostle, which is read in Heb. 9 verse 23. Without the shedding of blood there is no remission. Ἀνάγκη οὖν. It is necessary, therefore, that the copies of the heavenly things be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. But if God, out of grace alone, by His absolute right, can remit sins, let the Photinians give a reason why without the shedding of blood it cannot be that the remission of sins takes place; The saying of Athanasius looks to this, which is read in his oration on the incarnation of the Word, volume 1, page 42. Who, I ask, was it fitting should be done, or whose work was required for the recovering of that grace, if not the Word of God alone, who from the beginning had created all things out of nothing? For it was his to bring back that which was corruptible to incorruptibility, and to present that which was just and agreeable to reason to the Father. For since he is the Word of the Father and above all, he alone could deservedly recover all things and was fit to suffer for all, and to intercede with the Father.

And thus it has been shown so far why God could not, without detriment to his omnipotence, embrace sinners with a merely benevolent affection without indignation, or immediately dismiss guilt without any satisfaction. To enter into which dispute with adversaries is not so necessary: because inquiry is being made into the reasons of the divine counsel, which ought not to be done. It suffices for us that the revelation of the divine will, made in the Word, where he has declared himself in such a way, that he is unwilling to dismiss sin without a price and the intervening merit of the Son, since he holds that in hatred, and on account of that is angry with sinners. Let us believe, therefore, that the matter is so, and that nothing is taken away from the praise of divine omnipotence, since the Scriptures affirm both, although we cannot render the causes of all the counsels of God. These things are rather to be proclaimed with a grateful mind than to be examined too scrupulously or discussed too curiously,

As for what now concerns the other member of the dilemma, we willingly concede that God was unwilling to dismiss sins without a preceding reconciliation. And this is the fourth respect why he cannot. For because God does not wish to receive delinquents into grace, hence consequently he cannot do this, unless he acts against his will, and goes against his own will and truth, which is impious to say and to think. But that God does not will it, is proved by all the Scriptures that speak of satisfaction and the curse of the law. For since he wills that all transgressors be actually cursed after sin, he cannot but be indignant at them: And since this wrath must be appeased before the remission of guilt, and it could not be appeased by man, hence he did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us Rom. 8. vers. 32. so that divine justice might be satisfied. Another saying of Athanasius on p. 54 ought to be referred here. It is absurd, he says, for God to lie in his own words, if (when he had established by law that man would die the death whenever he transgressed the commandment) he should nevertheless escape death after the transgression, and not be bound by his word to them. For he would not have been the true God if (when he had said by law that we would not perish) we had not perished. Psalm 42. For it was absurd, for the sake of our utility and endurance, for God, the father of truth, to appear a liar. Add Augustine in his book on the struggle of Christ: God could do all things, if he had willed: But he did not will, and that for a just cause, even if it is unknown and incomprehensible to us. But even if he did otherwise, it would still equally displease your folly. Conversely, in sermon 3 on the Annunciation of the Lord: He thus willed to reform the ruin of the fragile vessel, so that he would neither leave the sin of man unpunished, because he is just: nor incurable, because he is merciful. It could have been done otherwise, as far as the power of the Physician is concerned (which ought to be understood concerning another mode of satisfaction, not concerning satisfaction being entirely excluded) but it could not have been prepared more conveniently or more skillfully, so that it might be medicine for the sick man and as far as the justice of God is concerned.

XCI. As concerns the likeness of an offended man who forgives without satisfaction, I say it is not to be extended too far; God also forgives freely κατὰ τι with respect to us, from whom he demands nothing further, not ἁπλῶς with respect to Christ, whom he would not spare as was shown more fully above in the solution to argument 7: Otherwise, if you press the example of men, it would follow that God is either impotent and unmerciful or that He can and ought to forgive the fault of all, even the impenitent, just as men ought to forgive and do good to any enemy, whether he seeks reconciliation or not. Since this is false and impious to say of God, let the Photinians acknowledge here the dissimilarity, that what a man can do regarding the forgiveness of an offense, God cannot. Nor does it follow from this, however, that He is impotent, or less able than men: because to do that in respect to God is a sign of impotence, not δυνάμεως, since then He would destroy, and could not preserve, His own nature; as He has revealed it in the Word. Just as therefore from other things which GOD cannot do, if those things are hostile to the nature of God, not any ἀδυναμία of His, but rather on the contrary His power and glory ought to be inferred: So also concerning our case, and the business of salvation, necessarily including satisfaction, one must think.

XCII. 7. Finally, it is not even universally true with respect to men that they can or ought to forgive every fault and offense without any punishment for the guilty party: For a distinction must be made between a private person and a public one or magistrate. A private person ought not to avenge himself, because he himself slips in many things; and he is bound to obey God. A magistrate, however, who is the minister of God for vengeance, cannot, with justice and the will of God preserved, dismiss a guilty person without punishment and satisfaction. For he is a judge ordained in the place of God to administer justice. Wherefore if he dismisses guilty persons unpunished, this act is blamed as iniquitous, Proverbs 17, verse 15; so far is he from deserving the praise of patience, goodness, or clemency. Now, however, since GOD is not equal to us or similar to any private person, but rather a most public person, indeed the judge of the whole world, hence He Himself, with justice preserved, does not wish, and cannot, to sinners, as long as they remain such, without any indignation favor, or dismiss them unpunished without satisfaction. For what one does not wish to be done in lower human courts, how could one wish it to be done in His supreme court, when if justice and the law of God are violated there, it follows that they are much more impugned here? Therefore, we invert the argument in turn in this way: If no judge can dismiss a guilty person with impunity, while maintaining justice, without injury to the divine will, certainly neither will nor can God, the judge of the whole world, dismiss him, unless one wishes to affirm with signal blasphemy that He contradicts Himself and His own will and nature, which is convertible with His will.

XCIII. But the exception of Gittichius on page 75 is feeble, that all our sins are against God as against a private person, according to that Psalm 51, verse 3: Against Thee only have I sinned and done evil before Thee. For it is one thing to commit a sin against God alone, and another thing for God to be a private person. This latter does not follow from the former, unless you wish to deny that God is the judge of the whole world, which is not the role of a private person, but of a Lord and supreme magistrate. What he adds about the distinction between God and a prince, who is bound by laws, is nothing to us. For although God has no superior who prescribes laws to Him, He is nevertheless a law unto Himself, which He can no more violate than He can His own nature, nor can earthly princes violate the law prescribed to them.

XCIV. Finally, if anyone stubbornly persists in asking, Could God not have found another bloodless way of salvation?

Resp. 1 Such questions are an indication of a curious reason, which must be restrained, not permitted to itself. 2 To what good is this asked? What will it add to our edification? Let us acknowledge and proclaim the redemption that has been made, let us not dispute about another one to be made, and the manner of making it. 3. Augustine, book 13 de Trin. ch. 20, answers that there was no more suitable way. For thus God declared His love, John 3. 1 John.

3.1. 1 John 3:4 and righteousness Rom. 3:25. Scripture testifies that God looked to these causes. Meanwhile, that counsel was free, not proceeding from absolute necessity. Hence, therefore, we say that God, on account of His absolute power, could certainly have found another way; yet by no means with satisfaction excluded. Another way perhaps could have been given, but to save without any satisfaction and propitiation of wrath is impossible, because the nature, justice, and truth of God would perish, and God would become not God.

Latin:

LXXXV. Quodcunque dogma gloriam & omnipotentiam Dei obscurat, dictu impium & blasphemum est. Sed dogma de satisfactione Dei gloriam & omnipotentiam obscurat. E. dictu impium & blasphemum est. Minor probatur, quia Deus peccata nostra sine satisfactione remittere vel noluit, quod contra gloriam misericordiae; vel non potuit; quod contra gloriam omnipotentiae. Ostodor. c. 36. par. 3. p. 300. Socinus par. 3. . 1. p. 221. & 399. Argumentum hoc Giesebus ita proponit p. 3. Peccata nostra nihil aliud sunt, quam offensa maiestatis diuinae. Offensas autem suas vel vilissimus quisq; homuncio non modo sine violatione iustitiae, sed etiam cum maxima laude patientiae, misericordiae, bonitatis, &c. alteri condonare potest. Ergo etiam taq; multo magis, Deus sine vlla satisfactione nobis remittere peccata nostra poterat: aut, si non poterat propter imaginariam iustitiam, ad quam ipsum patroni huius dogmatis adstringunt, minus potest, quam vel vilissimus homuncio.

LXXXVI. Respon. 1. Per inversionem. Dei gloria multo magis obscuratur, si dogma satisfactionis negatur. Nam transgressiones ferre, ad eas connivere, per eas nullo modo abalienari, indicium est iudicis vel negligentis, si ex iniuria permittat, vel iniqui si volens conniueat. At verò Deus non est Deus volens iniquitatem Ps. 5. verj. 5. odit operantes iniquitatem & perdit loquentes mendacium vers. 7. Ira eius tanta est vt nemo hominuin eam perferre possit Psal. 39. vers. 1. seq. Quare Filius Dei nostram miseratus miseriam è Sion nobis venit auxilium Mich. 4. 7. & seipsum dedit redemtionis precium 1. Tim. 2. vers. 6. factus peccatum, vt nos efficeremur iustitia in ipso 2. Cor. 5. v. ult. Quo pacto Dei gloria non obfuscatur, sed altius euehitur, dum tanta eius est maiestas, vt eam læsam non nisi vnigenitus filius placare potuerit.

LXXVII. 2. Per Instantiam. Si ab hominibus priuatis ad Deum mundi iudicem argumentari liceat, eodem modo inferam, Deum, aut immisericordem, aut impotentem esse, si non quosuis peccatores & homines æternùm saluet. Quæro enim, Cur Deus peccatores impoenitentes damnat, nec æternâ beatitudine donat? Aut non potest culpam dimittere, & sic humuncione est impotentior. Quivis enim homo offensas alteri offendenti, vt maximè hic reconciliari nolit, culpam tamen dimittere & illi beneficia exhibere potest. Imò hoc à Deo iussi sumus facere, vt inimicis etiam & nostris hostibus benefaciamus, Matth. 5. 44. Rom. 12. vers. 20. 21. Si igitur homo potest culpam lædenti omni, etiam præfracto remittere, & quantum in viribus eius est, benefacere, vtique si Deus hoc non poterit, vilissimo homuncione impotentior erit. Imò cùm Deus ad exemplum nobis hoc in ipso casu proponatur Matth. 5. vers. 44. 45. cadet illa imitandi ratio, si statuatur, nos debere & posse inimicos diligere, & tamen negetur, Deum posse inimicos suos nimirum impoenitentes diligere, ijsque æternum benefacere. Semper igitur hoc vrgebo: Si Deus contumaces saluare non potest, impotens erit, & nos malè à Dei exemplo ad benefaciendum inimicis omnibus admonemur. Quòd si dicant, Deum posse quidem omnes homines, etiam impœnitentes salvare, sed non velle. R. 1. hoc Apostolo directè opponi, qui cap. 6. ad Hebr. vers. 4. inquit: Impossibile est eos, qui semel sunt illuminati &c. rursus renovari ad pœnitentiam, & cap. 10. 26. voluntariè peccantibus nobis post acceptam iustitiam veritatis, iam non relinquitur pro peccatis hostia, sed terribilis quædam expectatio iudicij, &c. 2. Sequetur absurdum istud alterum, Deum non esse misericordem, nec summè bonum aut benevolum: Si enim potest omnes homines salvare, & ex solo voluntatis beneplacito hoc omittitur, tum certè maleuolus est, nõ misericorditer affectus erga genus humanum. Proindè vrgebo Photinianos hoc dilemmate, vt directè respondeant: Deus omnes homines salvare aut non potest, & sic tollitur gloria omnipotentiæ: aut non vult, & tollitur gloria misericordiæ. Quicquid dixerint, sibi vicissim responsionis loco habeant.

XXCVX. 3. Per deductionem ad absurdum. Si Deus sine omni satisfactione culpam dimittere debent, tam potentia eius quidem adstrui videtur, sed iustitia negatur, quod ἄτοπον. Iudicis enim iusti nequaquam est, si cùm pro sua potestate facinorosum & capitaliter puniendum dimittere possit, statim impunitum dimittat. Non prædicatur hoc factum tanquam eximium, sed vituperatur vt iniquum, & regulis iustitiæ contrarium. Idem crimen suis hypothesibus Deo impingunt Photiniani: qui proptereà nosse debebant, Deum non tantùm omnipotentem, sed etiam iustum esse. Quicquid ergo Dei potentiam sic adstruit, vt eius iustitiam destruat, hoc ipsum non ad gloriam: sed potiùs ad ignominiam Dei vergit. Imò non tantùm eius iustitia, sed & veritas & zelus ob peccata pœnis negantur. Nihil enim valebunt istæ minæ

Maledictus, qui non permanet in sermonibus legis huius, Deut. 27. versu vlt. Mihi vindictam ego retribuam, Rom. 12. versu 19. Deut. 32. versu 35. Maledictus, qui facit opus Domini fraudulenter Ier. 48. v. 9. 10.

LXXIX. 4. Argumentum hoc ex cæcæ rationis judicio depromptum, & revelato verbo contrarium est. Ibi enim dicitur quòd Deus sit omnipotens, nec tamen culpam omnibus, aut sine λύτρῳ remittat. Habemus enim remissionem peccatorum, non nisi per sanguinem Christi, qui se obtulit hostiam pro peccatis nostris. Quare notandus hîc est canon Theologicus: Quid Deus circa salutem nostram faciat non ex rationibus de possibili colligendum, sed ex solis Scripturis addiscendum est. In illis reperio vtrumque, tum Deum omnipotentem, tum nobis infensum & non nisi per Christum placatum esse. Malè igitur opponuntur subordinata; cùm Christi meritum Dei gloriam & potentiam nontollat, sed potius illustret atque amplificet.

XC. 5. Per inficiationem Minoris, quòd dogma satisfactionis impugnet gloriam Dei. Quod verò concernit dilemma probatorium: Aut non potuit, aut non voluit sine satisfactione culpam dimittere, Respondeo. Vtrumque sano sensu concedi potest. 1. Non potuit respectu. 1. suæ naturæ. 2. suæ justitiæ. 3. suæ veritatis. 1. Natura Dei est rectissima, cui peccatum omne diametraliter adversatur. Si ergo peccatori nonsuccenseret, sed illum post culpam non minus diligeret ac ante culpam, tum vtique naturam suam tolleret, sibique ipsi contradiceret. 2. Iustitia Dei est immutabilis, quæ pœnas postulat ab omni legis prævaricatore, vi cujus peccatores puniendi sunt, non impunè dimittendi. Vt ergo suam Deus justitiam negare, ita sine placatione & satisfactione culpam delinquentibus condonare non potest. Huc pertinent dicta Rom. 1: v. 32. Iudicium Dei, lux

Dei esse quod peccatores digni sint morte. 2. Thess. 1. v. 6. iustum esse ἀνταποδῶναι retribuere mala malis. 3. Deus verax, imò ipsa est veritas. Dixit autem Gen. 2. versu 17. Quacunque die comederis, morte morieris, & Deut. 27. versu vlt. Maledictus, qui non permanserit, &c. Quamprimum igitur homines delinquunt, per peccatum infallibiliter mortis rei fiunt, & maledictioni legis subiacent, ac proindè Deum habent sibi iratum, quem placari & reconciliari omninò opus est, si saluari & gratia eius frui voluerint. Quòd si verò Deus non irasceretur peccatoribus, tum isti non forent maledicti, non mortis rei. Periret ergo legis sententia, & concideret omnis Dei veritas. Hæc sunt illa fundamenta, cur Deus, omnipotens sine placatione culpam condonare nequeat. Quo ipso nihil decedit eius omnipotentiæ; sicut nec per illud, quando dicitur, ipsum mori aut peccare non posse. Nam omnipotentiæ divinæ obiectum non est res quævis, sed illa tantùm, quæ Dei naturæ & voluntati non contrariatur. Cætera omnia impotentiam magis arguunt, quàm δύναμιν. Quare cùm Dei naturæ tollatur, si peccata sine indignatione omni mox dimittat, idcircò dogma de satisfactione Dei potiùs omnipotentiam declarat, quàm vt impotentiam arguat. Non potuit Deus absque satisfactione saluare, non propter defectum potentiæ, sed propter perfectionem naturæ. Secus enim si fieret, Deus suam naturam conseruare non posset, quod maximè impotentis argumentum est. Respõsionem hanc confirmo expresso Apostoli aphorismo, qui legitur Heb. 9. versu. 23. Sine sanguinis effusione non fit remissio. Ἀνάγκη œν. Necesse est ergo exemplaria quidem cœlestium his mundari, ipsa autem cælestia melioribus hostiis quàm istis. Si verò Deus ex sola gratia, pro iure suo absoluto, potest remittere peccata, dent Photiniani rationem, cur absque sanguinis effusione non possit fieri peccatorum remissio; Spectat huc dictum Athanasij, quod legitur in orat. de incarnat. verbi, tom. 1. pagina 42. Quis quæso aliud decuit fieri, aut cuius opera ad recuperandam istam gratiam requirebatur, nisi solius Dei verbi quod ab initio omnia ex nihilo condiderat? Eius enim fuit id quod corruptibile erat iterum ad incorruptibilitatem reducere, & id quod æquum rationique consentaneum erat, Patre præstare. Cùm enim Patris sit verbum & supra, omnes, meritò etiam solus omnia recuperare potuit & idoneus fuit, qui pro omnibus pateretur, & apud Patrem intercederet.

Atque sic ostensum hactenus, cur Deum non potuerit sine detrimento suæ omnipotentiæ peccatores benevolo tantum sine indignatione affectu complecti, aut culpam protinus sine omni satisfactione dimittere. In quam quidem disputationem vt cum aduersariis descendamus, non adeò necessarium est: quia inquiritur in rationes consilij diuini quod fieri non debebat. Sufficit nobis divinæ voluntatis reuelatio, in verbo facta, vbi se ita declarauit, absque precio & intercedente Filij merito se nolle peccatū dimittere, quoniam istud odio habeat, & propter istud peccatoribus succenseat. Credamus igitur, rem ita se habere, nec quicquam laudi omnipotentiæ divinæ decedere, quoniam vtrumque Scripturæ affirmant, licet nos omnium consiliorum Dei causas reddere nequeamus. Miranda potius & grato animo hæc prædicanda sunt, quàm scrupulosiùs, rimanda, aut curiosius discutienda,

Quod iam alterum dilemmatis membrum concernit, lubenter concedimus, Deum sine præcedente reconciliatione peccata dimittere noluisse. Et hic est quartus respectus, cur non possit. Quia enim Deus non vult delinquentes in gratiam recipere, hinc ex consequenti hoc non potest, nisi invitus agat, suæque voluntati & veritati contrà eat, quod dictu & cogitatu est impium. Non autem velle Deum, probant omnes Scripturae, de satisfactione & legis maledictione loquentes. Quia n. omnes praeuaricatores vult actu post peccatum maledictos esse, vtique ijs non potest non indignari: Et quoniam haec ira placanda est ante culpae dimissionem, ab homine verò placari non potuit, hinc proprio filio suo non pepercit, sed eum pro nobis tradidit Rom. 8. vers. 32. vt diuinae iustitiae satisfieret. Referri huc debet aliud Athanasij dictum p. 54. Absurdum, inquit, Deum in suis verbis mentiri, si (cùm lege statuisset, morte moriturum hominem, quandocunque mandatum praeuaricaretur,) mortem tamen post praeuaricationem effugeret, nec verbo illis adstringeretur. Non enim verus Deus fuisset si(cùm legedixisset nor perituros) non perissemus. Psalm. 42. Absurdum quippè erat, ob nostram vtilitatem perdurationémque, Deum veritatis patrem mendacem videri. Adde Augustinum lib. de agone Christi: Omnia Deus poterat, si voluisset: Noluit autem, idque iusta de causa, etiamsi nobis ignota est & incomprehensibilis. Sed etsi aliter faceret, aequè tamen stultitiae vestrae displiceret. Vicissim sermon. 3. de Annunc. Dom. Sic voluit ruinam fragilis vasis reformare, vt nec peccatum hominis dimitteret impunitum, quia iustus est: nec insanabile, quia est misericors. Potuit aliter fieri, quantùm ad potentiam Medici(quod intelligi debet de alio satisfactionis modo, non de exclusa penitus satisfactione)sed non potuit commodiùs aut doctiùs praeparari, vt esset medicina aegroti & quantum ad iustitiam Dei.

XCI. Quod concernit similitudinem hominis offensi & sine satisfactione ignoscentis, dico non nimieam esse extendēdam, Deus etiam gratis dimittit κατὰ τι respectu nostri, à quibus nil vltrà exigit, non ἁπλῶς respectu Christi, cui parcere noluit vti supra in solut. argum 7. fusiùs ostensum est: Aliàs si hominum exemplum vrgeas, sequeretur Deum aut impotentem & immisericordem effe, aut omnibus etiam impoenitentibus culpam dimittere posse & debere, sicut homines cuivis inimico; sive reconciliationem petat, sive non, ignoscere & benefacere debent. Quod cùm sit falsum & dictu de Deo impium, agnoscant hic Photiniani dissimilitudinem, vt quod circa offensæ dimissionem homo potest istud, Deus non possit. Nec tamen hinc sequitur, impotentem illum esse, aut minus posse, quam homines: quia istud facere Dei respectu impotentiæ est non δυνάμεως, siquidem tùm destrueret, nec conseruare posset naturam suam; prout eam in verbo revelavit. Sicut ergo ex alijs, quæ DEVS non potest, si ista Dei naturæ inimica sint, non aliqua eius ἀδυναμία, sed potius contrà potestas & gloria colligi debet: Ita quoque de nostro casu, & salutis negotio, satisfactionem necessariò includente, cogitandum est.

XCII. 7. Tandem nè quidem respectu hominum vniversaliter verum est; quòd culpam offensamque omnem sine omni pœna reo dimittere possint aut debeant: Nam distinguendū est inter personam privatam & publicam seu magistratum. Privatus nō debet semetipsum vlcisci, quia ipse in multis labitur; & Deo obedire tenetur. Magistratus autem, qui Dei minister est ad vindictam, non potest salvâ justitiâ & Dei voluntate; reum absque pœna & satisfactione dimittere. Est enim judex loco Dei ordinatus, vt justitiam administret. Quare si impunitos dimittat reos, factum hoc culpatur vt iniquum Proverb. 17. versu 15. tantum abest, vt patientiæ, bonitatis aut clementiæ laudem mereatur. Iam verò quoniam DEVS non est nobis æqualis aut privato alicui similis, sed potius persona maximè publica, quippe judex vniversi terrarum orbis hinc & ipse justitiâ salvá non vult, nō potest peccatoribus, qua tales manēt, sine omni indignatione fauere, aut ipsos impunitos sine satisfactione dimittere. Quod enim fieri non vult, in iudicijs humanis inferioribus, quì fieri veller in iudicio suo summo, cùm si ibi violatur iustitia & lex Dei, multò magis hìc impugnari consequatur? Proindè vicissim inuertimus argumentum hoc modo: Si nullus iudex reum impunè potest dimittere, saluâ iustitiâ, sine laesione voluntatis diuinae, vtique nec Deus vniuersi mundi iudex, vel volet vel poterit dimittere, nisi ipsum sibi suæque voluntati & naturae, quæ cum voluntate conuertitur, contrariari, cum insigni blasphemia affirmare quis voluerit.

XCIII. Elumbis verò est exceptio Gittichij pag. 75. omnia peccata nostra esse contra Deum tanquam contra priuatum iuxta illud Psalm. 51. v. 3. Tibi soli peccaui & malum coram te feci. Aliud enim est in DEVM duntaxat peccatum committere, & aliud Deum priuatum esse. Hoc posterius ex priori non sequitur, nisi negare velis, Deum esse iudicem totius mundi, id quod non priuati est, sed Domini & magistratus summi. Quod addit de discrimine inter Deum & principem, qui ad leges sit adstrictus, nihil ad nos. Quamuis enim Deus non habeat se superiorem, qui leges præcribat, sibiipsi tamen est lex, quam violare tam non potest, vt nec naturam suam, nec terreni principes legem præscriptam.

XCIV. Tandem, si aliquis morosè pergat, quærendo, Annon potuerit Deus aliam salutis viam incruentam inuenire?

Resp. 1 Tales quæstiones sunt indicium curiosæ rationis, quæ compescenda, non sibi permittenda est, 2 Cui bono hoc quæritur? Quid accedet nostræ ædificationi?
