Agnoscamus & prædicemus factam redemptionem, non disputemus de facienda alia, & faciendi modo. 3. August. l. 13. de Trin. c. 20. respondet, nullum conuenientiorem modum fuisse. Ita enim Deus declarauit charitatem Iohan. 3. 1. Ioh.

3.1. Ioh. 3. 4. & iustitiam Rom. 3. v. 25. Has causas spectasse Deum, Scriptura testatur. Interim fuit istud consilium liberum, non ex necessitate absoluta profectum. Hinc ergo dicimus, Deum ob absolutam suam potestatem potuisse vtique alium modum inuenire; nequaquam tamen exclusa satisfactione. Alius modus fortè dari potuisset, sed saluare absque omni satisfactione & irae placatione impossibile est, quia perirent Dei natura, iustitia, veritas, fieretque ex Deo non Deus.


### Argument XIII. & last. On the justice of God

From the justice of God.

XCV. If there is no such justice in God that is opposed to His mercy, and to which it was necessary that satisfaction be made through Christ, then the dogma of satisfaction cannot be approved. But the former is true. Therefore, the latter. Socinus p. 8. Osterod. p. 212.

XCVI. But before this argument is answered, we shall premise a few things concerning the justice of God. There are various meanings of justice when attributed to God. It denotes 1. Essential justice and rectitude, Psalm 11:7, 'The Lord is righteous and loves righteousness.' 2. The truth of promises; so that justice is the same as faithfulness in keeping, and therefore it is joined, 1 John 1:9, 'He is faithful and just,' that is, truthful; add Psalm 36:6, Isaiah 49:9, etc. 3. The will of God expressed by law, Psalm 119:12, 'Teach me your statutes'; Psalm 19:9, 'the righteousnesses,' that is, the right precepts of the Lord. 4. The goodness of God, Rom. 3:21, 'Apart from the law the righteousness of God has been manifested.' If you understand the righteousness of works, do you think that was revealed apart from the law? Rom. 1:17, 'The righteousness of God is revealed in the Gospel.' But this only announces goodness. Add Dan. 9:16, Psalm 51:14, Psalm 69:27, Psalm 71:2. Psalm 143:1, 2, etc. 5. Benefits of mercy.

1. Sam. 12. vers. 7. Stand, that I may plead with you concerning all the righteousness of Jehovah, which he did with us,

§. The judicial and vindicatory justice of God, which is a just will in God, by which, doing well to the good and evil to the evil, he renders to each according to his works, by a just judgment. For thus God has revealed himself, that by nature he is averse to and punishes iniquity: but loves and compensates obedience with rewards. Therefore, this natural will of God concerning punishing evil and compensating the good is rightly called Justice.

XCVII. The Photinians indeed deny this, but against Scripture, which makes mention of it several times, as Job 8. v. 3. Doth God pervert judgment, or doth the Almighty pervert what is just? Psalm 9. v. 5. Thou hast maintained my judgment and my cause, thou satest on the throne judging right. Psalm 50. v. 6. The heavens declared his righteousness, for God is judge. Psalm 119. v. 137. Righteous art thou, O Lord, and upright is thy judgment. Psalm 145. v. 17. The Lord is righteous in all his works. Ezra 9. v. 4. 15. O Lord God of Israel, thou art righteous, for we are left escaped, as it is this day: Behold, we are before thee in our trespass, for we cannot stand before thee because of this. Rom. 1. ver. 32. Who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them. 2. Thes. 1. v. 5. 6. You endure tribulations ἐνδειγμα τῆς δικαίας κρίσεως τῦ θεῦ as a token of the righteous judgment of God, that you may be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you also suffer. If indeed it is just with God to recompense tribulation to those who trouble you: and to you who are troubled, rest with us.

XCVIII. But especially concerning the natural justice of God, his law testifies, partly inscribed upon our minds, partly promulgated through Moses. For this is the rule of things to be done and the clearest sign of the divine will, and therefore God is to be thought to feel in such a way, as his will is expressed by the law, namely, that he wishes to love the obedient and to curse the disobedient. For such as is the relation between the sign and the thing signified, such is it between the law and the will of God. The sign is false unless it expresses the thing signified as it is. Nor is the thing signified called a sign, which is observed to differ from the sign. Wherefore, since the law is a sign that law announces a curse to all transgressors, nay, by the very act immediately subjects them to a curse, it follows that such a will exists in God, provided you wish the due equality and relation of the sign and the thing signified to be preserved. Wherefore, as long as the Photinians concede the law of God, as they are altogether compelled to concede, so long they will not be able to deny the justice of God, since that is nothing other than the just will of God expressed by the law, to curse the transgressors by the very act, and to do good to the observers.

XCIX. Whence it appears that there are two different acts or effects of divine justice, according to the diversity of the objects. 1. To love obedience and to do good to the obedient. 2. To hate iniquity and to curse the disobedient. The former effect is expressed by the promises, the latter by the threatenings of the law. The promises are Leviticus 18, verse 5: Keep my laws, the man who does them shall live in them; Luke 10, verse 28: Do this and you shall live; Romans 10, verse 5: The man who shall have done the commandments of the law shall live in them; Galatians 3, verse 12: The law is not of faith, but he who shall have done them shall live by them. The Psalmist joins both, the justice of God and the act of justice. Psalm 11, verse 7: The Lord is just and has loved justices. The threatenings are read everywhere. Genesis 2, verse 17: On whatever day you shall eat, you shall die the death; Deuteronomy 27, last verse: Cursed is he who does not remain in the words of this law; Galatians 3, verse 10: Whoever are of the works of the law are under a curse. Hence it is said of God that he holds in hatred those who work iniquity, Psalm 5, verse 7, and turns away from all injustice injustice. Deut. 25. v. 16. The way of the wicked is an abomination before him, Prov. 8. v. 7. ch. 15. v. 9. His wrath shall be revealed upon impiety, Rom. 1. v. 18. From which latter act or effect we conclude thus: Whoever by nature turns away from iniquity, he is by nature just, since justice is nothing else than a just will abominating sin and punishing the sinner: But God by nature, that is, because of his essential righteousness and perfection, turns away from iniquity. Therefore GOD is by nature just. Furthermore, he who by nature is angry and indignant at sinners, he is again by nature just, since the second act always presupposes the first, and a constant just operation infallibly argues that justice exists and is found in the operator. For just as the existence of other divine virtues and properties is judged only from second acts, in such a way that from these the former are without any doubt inferred: So also from continued works of justice we invincibly conclude that someone is just. Now indeed God is angry and indignant at sinners, as the law and Scripture testify throughout. Wherefore it follows again that GOD is by nature or essentially just.

C. Socinus objects on pp. 7, 8, 9 that that action, abomination and punishment, is to be ascribed not to justice, but to the wrath of God. Indeed, that punishment is not called justice but fury, and also indignation.

Resp. 1. Subordinate things do not conflict. To punish is ascribed to both an angry and a just God. To the angry one, Rom. 1. v. 18. To the just one, Rom. 1. v. 32, 2 Thess. 1. v. 6. For every judge, by executing justice, punishes the wicked, and at the same time is indignant and angry at them. 2. The argument can be inverted. If God is angry because of sins, he is certainly just; since the effect testifies of the cause, and the sign of the thing signified. Now indeed, to be angry at sinners, which pertains to God, is a sign of justice: therefore God will be just even in this very thing. For the wrath and vengeance of God, do not proceed from a bare and absolute will, but from a just will expressed through the law, by which He turns away from sinners and immediately subjects them to a curse. For as every law proceeds not from the bare whim of the legislator, but from his just will which has regard for justice: so the divine law is not a sign and expression of a bare will, but of a will that is just and endowed with justice. Unless the law of God is denied by a wicked audacity, essential justice cannot be taken away from God. And how shall it be taken away, when it is immutable, no less than the law itself, concerning which Scripture speaks in Matthew 5, verse 18. Truly I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one iota or one dot will pass from the law until all is accomplished, and Luke 16, verse 17: it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one dot of the law to fall. Since, therefore, the law curses every transgressor, such will certainly be the will in God, and that will is entirely immutable, unless one absurdly posits two contrary acts; namely, that God wills to punish sins by the force of law and justice, and at the same time, out of an absolute and bare good pleasure, wills not to punish sins. But since two contraries cannot exist at the same time and in the same respect, hence, when it has been proven that God wills to punish sins, that absolute 'will not' or good pleasure of willing not is immediately excluded. Indeed, just as the justice of God cannot but love and reward obedience by the force of truthful promises, so the same justice cannot but turn away from and actually subject disobedience to a curse, since it is the act of one and the same justice to affect evil with punishments and good with rewards. From all of which this corollary flows spontaneously: that our first parents, and all of us, as transgressors of the law, according to the justice of God, were to be immutably punished with eternal death, according to the most certain threat, or that satisfaction had to be made to divine justice in another way; not otherwise than in human judgment, which itself is vicarious of divine justice, the defendant cannot justly be dismissed before due satisfaction,

CI. With these things thus presupposed, it is very easy to respond to the argument. For we deny what the adversaries assume as certain, namely that no essential justice is found in God, since the contrary has been established thus far by well-founded reasons. But because they have devised many exceptions and petty arguments against the justice of God, we shall now discuss them in order to further strengthen our thesis.

CII. Exception 1. God has absolute authority and is supremely free. Wherefore He consigned men to death by His free will, and conversely, by His free will, He can pardon that punishment without any satisfaction. Ostorod. p. 215. Socinus against Couetus. p. 9. 10. 11.

Resp. This is a bare assertion, no proof: wherefore a simple denial suffices. Yet that every mouth may be stopped against the adversaries, we shall subjoin the distinct members of our response and the infallible causes of our denial. 1. The whole argument is built upon the fantasy of reason, which cannot understand how God is free in acting, just, and merciful at the same time. But in these mysteries, reason is not to be consulted, but Scripture alone is to be looked to. For the Apostle teaches, Rom. 5:7, that there is no example given of our redemption. Although, therefore, such a thing does not happen in the world, nothing is lost to the Scriptures on that account; Christ does not say: I am the world or custom, but I am the way, the truth, and the life, says Cyprian. Nor is the question here about the absolute power of God, which reason acknowledges to be infinite and we willingly confess, but about His ordered power revealed in the Word of God, and therefore not what God could have done absolutely, but what He willed, and how He has revealed Himself. Wherefore, since we read that God did not spare His own Son, Rom. 8:32, but laid upon Him, though innocent, all our iniquities

Latin:

A Dei iustitia.

XC V. Si nulla est in Deo iustitia talis, quae misericordiae eius opponatur, & cui per Christum satisfieri necessum fuerit, tum dogma de satisfactione adprobari nequit. Sed prius est verum. E. & posterius. Socinus p. 8. Osterod. pag: 212.

XCVI. Antequam verò ad hoc argumentum respondeatur, pauca quaedam de iustitia Dei praemittemus. Varia iustitiae cùm Deo attributae, significata sunt. Notat 1. Iustitiam & rectitudinem essentialem, Psalm. 11. vers. 7. Iustus Iehouah & diligit iustitias. 2. Veritatem promissionum; vt iustitia idem sit, quod fidelitas in seruando, ideoque coniungitur, 1. Ioh. 1. v. 9. fidelis est & iustus, h. e. verax, adde Psalm. 36. v. 7. Esa 49. v. 9. &c. 3. Voluntatem Dei lege expressam, Psal. 119. v. 12. Doce me iustitias tuas Psal. 19. v. 9. iustitiae, id est, praeceptiones Domini rectae. 4. Bonitatem Dei, Rom. 3. v. 20. Absque lege iustitia Dei manifestata est. Operum iustitiam si intelligas, num illam absque lege reuelatam putas? Rom. 1. v. 17. Iustitia Dei reuelatur in Evangelio. Ast hoc tantùm bonitatem annunciat. Adde Dan. 9. v. 16. Psalm. 51. v. 6. Psalm. 69. v. 28. Psalm. 71. v. 2. Psalm. 143, vers. 1. 2, &c. 5. Beneficia misericordiae.

1. Sam. 12. vers. 7. state, vt disceptem vobiscum de omnibus iustitiis Iehouæh, quas fecit nobiscum,

§. Iudiciariam & vindicatricem Dei iustitiam, quæ est iusta in Deo voluntas, quâ bonis benè & malis malè faciens, vnicuique reddit secundum opera sua, iusto iudicio. Ita enim Deus se reuelauit quòd per naturam auersetur & puniat iniquitatem: amet autem præmijsque compenset obedientiam. Ista ergo naturalis Dei voluntas de malo puniendo & hunc compensando rectè vocatur Iustitia.

XCVII. Negant quidem hanc Photiniani, sed contra Scripturam, quæ illius mentionem facit aliquotjes, vt Iob. 8. v. 3. Numquid Deus corrumpit iudicium, aut omnipotens subuertit, quod iustum est. Psal. 9. v. 5. Fecisti iudicium meum & causam meam, sedisti super thronum qui iudicas iustitiam Psalm. 50. v. 6. Annuntiabant cœli iustitiam eius, quia Deus iudex est. Psalm. 119. v. 137. Iustus es Domine & rectum iudicium tuum. Psalm. 145. v. 17. Iustus Dominus in omnibus operibus suis. Esdræ 9. v. 4. 15. Domine Deus Israel iustus es tu, quoniam derelicti sumus, qui saluamur die hac: Ecce coram te sumus in delicto nostro, Non enim stari potest coram te super hoc. Rom. 1. ver. 32. Qui cum iustitiam Dei cognoscerent, quoniam qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte: non solum; qui ea faciunt, sed etiam, qui fauentibus consentiunt. 2. Thes. 1. v. 5. 6. Sustinetis tribulationes ἐνδειγμα τῆς δικαίας κρίσεως τῦ θεῦ in exemplum iusti iudicij Dei, ut digni habeamini regno Dei, pro quo & patimini. Si tamen iustum est apud Deum, retribuere tribulationem iis, qui vos tribulant: & vobis, qui tribulamini, requiem nobiscum.

XCVIII. Imprimis verò de naturali iustitia Dei testatur lex ipsius, partim mentib. nostris insculpta, partim per Mosen promulgata. Hæc n. est regula faciendorum & signum clarissimum voluntatis diuinæ, ideoque Deum ita sentire putandũ est, prout volut̄as ipsius lege exprimitur, nempè quòd obedientes amare, inobedietibus maledicere velit. Nam qualis est relatio inter signum & signatum : talis est inter legem, & Dei voluntatem. Falsum est signum, nisi exprimat signatū, prout est. Nec signo signatum dicitur, quod à signo discrepare animaduertitur. Quocirca cùm lex signum sit diuinæ voluntatis, & verò illa maledictionem annunciet omnibus præuaricatoribus, imò actu ipso statim maledictioni subijciat, vtique in Deo talem voluntatem esse sequitur, simodo debitum signi signatique ἴσον & relationem saluam velis. Quocirca quamdiu Photiniani legem Dei concedunt, vti concedere omninò coguntur, tamdiu iustitiam Dei negare haut poterunt, siquidem illa nihil est aliud, quàm iusta Dei voluntas lege expressa, transgressoribus actu ipso maledicendi, obseruatoribus benefaciendi.

XCIX. Vndè apparet duos iustitiæ diuinæ diuersos siuè actus siuè effectus esse, pro diuersitate obiectorū. 1. Obedientiam amare & obedienti benefacere. 2. Iniquitatem odisse & inobedieti maledicere. Prior effectus promissionibus, posterior comminationibus legis exprimitur. Promissiones sunt Leuit. 18. vers. 5. Custodite leges meas, Faciens homo viuet in eis, Luc. 10. vers. 28. Fac hoc & vives. Rom. 10. vers 5. Qui fecerit homo mandata legis, vivet in eis, Gal. 3. ver. 12. Lex nõ est ex fide, sed qui fecerit ea, viuet per illa. Psaltes vtrumque coniungit, Dei iustitiam & iustitiæ actum. Psalm. 11. v. 7. Iustus Dominus & iustitias dilexit. Comminationes passim leguntur. Gen. 2. vers. 17. Quacunque die comederis, morte morieris, Deut. 27 vers. vltim. Maledictus, qui non permanet in sermonibus legis huius Gal. 3. vers. 10. Quicunque ex operibus legis sunt, sub execratione sunt. Hinc de Deo dicitur, quòd odio habeat operantes iniquitatem, Psalm. 5. vers. 7. auersetur omnem inustitiam injustitiam. Deut. 25. v. 16. abominatio sit corã ipso via impij, Prov. 8. v. 7. c. 15. v. 9 Ira eius super impietatẽ reueletur, Rom. 1. v. 18. Ex quo posteriore actu vel effectu sic colligimus: Quicunque per naturam auersatur iniquitatem, is per naturam iustus est, cum iustitia nihil sit aliud, quam iusta voluntas peccatum abominans & peccatorem puniens: Atqui Deus per naturam, hoc est, ob essentialem suam rectitudinem & perfectionem, auersatur iniquitatem. Ergo D E V S per naturam iuamisstus est. Porrò, qui per naturam peccatoribus succenset & indignatur, is per naturam iterum iustus est, cum actus secundus semper praesupponat primum, & constans operatio iusta infallibiliter arguat, in operante ipsam esse & reperiri iustitiam. Sicut enim de aliarum virtutum & proprietatum diuinarum existentia non nisi ex actibus secundis iudicatur, ita quidem, vt ex his illae sine omni dubio colligantur: Ita etiam ex continuatis iustitiae operibus aliquem iustum esse inuictè concludimus. Iam verò Deus per iram peccatoribus succenset & indignatur, testante lege & Scripturâ passim. Quare iterum sequitur, D E V M per naturam vel essentialiter iustum esse.

C. Socinus excipit p. 7. 8. 9. Actionem illum, abominationem & punitionem, non iustitiae, sed irae Dei adscribi. Imo punitionem non dici iustitiam sed furorem, vnâ etiam, indignationem.

Resp. 1. Subordinata non pugnant. Punire & irato & iusto Deo adscribitur. Irato Rom. 1. ver. 18. Iusto Rom. 1. v. 32. 2. Thess. 1. v. 6. Omnis enim iudex iustitiam exequendo ẽigat acinorosos, simulque ijs indignatur, & succenset. 2. Argumentum inuerti potest. Si Deus irascitur ob peccata, vtique iustus est; quoniam effectus de causa, & signum de signato testatur. Iam verò irasci peccatoribus, quod Deo competit est signum iustitiae: Deus igitur & hoc ipsum iustus erit. Nam ira & vindictaDei, non proveniunt à nuda, absolutaque, sed à iustâ & per legem expressa voluntate, quâ peccatores aversatur, & maledictioni statim subijcit. Nam vt omnis lex non ab arbitrio nudo legislatoris, sed ab eius voluntate iusta & iustitiam respiciente prosiciscitur: Sic lex diuina nõ est signum & expressio voluntatis nudæ, sed iustæ & iustitia præditæ. Nisi lex Dei scelerato ausu negetur, essentialis iustitia Deo adimi non poterit. Et quî adimetur; cùm illa sit immutabilis, non minus atque lex ipsa, de qua scriptura Matth. 5. vers. 18. Amen dico vobis, donec transeat cælum & terra, iota vnum, aut apex vnus non præteribit à lege, donec omnia fiant, & Luc. 16. vers. 17. facilius est cælum & terram interire; quam de lege vnum apicem excidere: Cum igitur lex maledicat omni transgressori; vtique & in Deo voluntas talis erit; eaque prorsus immutabilis, nisi quis duos contrarios actus absurdè statuat; nimirum velle Deum vigore legis & iustitiæ peccata punire, & simul ex absoluto nudoque beneplacito nolle peccata punire. Quoniam verò duo contraria simul & eiusdem respectu locum non habent; hinc cùm probatum sit, Deum peccata punire velle, mox excluditur absolutum illud nolle, vel nolendi beneplacitum. Imò sicut iustitia Dei non potest non amare & remunerare vi promissionum veracium, obedientiam: Sic eadem iustitia non potest non aversari, & maledictioni actu subijcere inobedientiam, cùm vnius iustitiæ actus sint, malum pœnis, & bonum præmijs afficere. Ex quibus omnibus sponte fluit hoc πόρισμα, primos parentes, & nos omnes, tanquam transgressores legis, secundum iustitiam Dei, æterna morte; iuxta comminationem certissimam, immutabiliter puniendos fuisse, aut alio modo iustitiæ diuinæ satisfieri debuisse; non secus ac in iudicio humano, quod ipsum diuinæ iustitiæ est vicarium, reus aute debitam satisfactionem juste dimitti nequit,

CI. Quibus ita praesuppositis, ad argumentum respondere est quàm facillimum. Negamus enim quod aduersarij tanquam certum assumunt, nempè nullam in Deo essentiale iustitiam reperiri, cum contrarium rationibus benè firmis hactenus stabilitū sit. Quia vero multas exceptiones & ratiunculas contra iustitiam Dei effinxère, nunc illas pro magis reboranda thesi nostra ordine discutiemus.

CII. Exceptio. 1. Deus absolutum habet imperium & summe liber est. Quare homines libera ex voluntate morti mancipavit, & vicissim ex libera voluntate pœnam illam absque omni satisfactione condonare potest. Ostorod. p. 215. Socinus contra Couetum. p. 9. 10. 11.

Resp. Nuda haec assertio, nulla probatio: Quocirca sufficit simplex inficiatio. Vt tamen omne os obstruatur aduersarijs, distincta responsionis membra & infallibiles negationis nostrae causas subiungemus. 1. Totum argumentum rationis phantasiae superstructum est, quae intelligere nequit, quomodo Deus sit liber in agendo, iustus & simul misericors. At verò in his mysterijs non ratio consulenda, sed Scriptura vnicè adspicienda est. Nostrae enim redemtionis exemplum simile nullum dari, docet Apostolus Rom. 5. v. 7. Licèt igitur in mundo tale quid non contingat, nil tamen ob id Scripturis decedit, Christus non dicit: Ego sum mundus vel consuetudo, sed ego sum via veritas & vita, inquit Cyprianus. Neque hic quaeritur de absoluta Dei potentia, quam infinitam esse ratio agnoscit & nos lubenter fatemur, sed de ordinata & in verbo Dei reuelata, adeoque non quid Deus absolutè potuerit, sed quid voluerit, & quomodo sese reuelauerit. Quocirca cum legamus, Deum Filio suo non pepercisse Roman. 8. vers. 32 sed super ipsum licèt innocentem, omnes iniquitates nostras conjecisse


### Argument XIII. & last. On the justice of God: Isa. 53. vers. 7. 8. we rightly believe this, nor do we allow ourselves to be…

Isa. 53. vers. 7. 8. we rightly believe this, nor do we allow ourselves to be moved from that doctrine of Scripture by any petty arguments sought from the absolute sovereignty of God & free will: For if both are written, they will be subordinate to both, not contrary. Wherefore let them first prove from the Scriptures that God willed to forgive us our guilt without any satisfaction, before they flee to the κρησφύγετον concerning the absolute power of God, since here the question is not so much what God could have done regarding the salvation of the human race, but what He does, and what He wills to do, according to the revelation of Himself long since comprised in the Word.

2. God indeed has absolute sovereignty, because He is subject to no superior: Meanwhile, however, He cannot deny Himself, and therefore what is a prescribed law to others, this is nature to God; against which He does not act: Whatever is adverse and hostile to this, that does not fall under the power and will of God; since otherwise God would be contrary to Himself. Now, however, sin is adverse to the nature of God: Therefore He cannot but hate it, He cannot but curse the sinner on account of it. For otherwise He would not be a just judge, as nevertheless He ought to be. Psalm 7. verse 18. For it is not His to dismiss the wicked at His good pleasure. For as justice immutably demands that obedience be affected with rewards, so it demands that disobedience be affected with punishments. Unless God does this, distributive justice is taken away from Him.

And above we have brought forward sufficiently pregnant reasons from the nature, law, and truth of God, by which, while they remain intact, God cannot dismiss a guilty sinner unpunished without satisfaction: Wherefore the liberty of God must be defended in such a way that His justice, goodness, and truth are not taken away: For just as God, although He is free, nevertheless cannot sin, because He is good: so He cannot but hate and punish sins, because He is just by nature: For such as we are by nature, such things we will by nature. But God by nature is averse to impiety. Prov 8.

v, 7. 8. Therefore nature wills that it be removed, or if it be present, punished. For unless He were to punish, He would regard sin as not sin, and would sit by not as judge of the world, but as an idle spectator of iniquity, which however is foreign to the office of an earthly judge, who is a minister of God and an image of divine judgment. Wherefore as fire naturally cannot but burn, when material is brought to it: So God, who is a consuming fire Deut. 4. v. 24. because of His natural justice cannot but be indignant, when iniquity and disobedience are present.

3. If the consignment to death flows from the sole and bare will of God, very gross absurdities immediately follow therefrom. 1. That before God sin and not-sin are the same, since He is by nature equally affected toward both; 2. That sin is in itself nothing, but rather an opinion, to be estimated according to the diverse arbitration of the divine will. But where then remains that of the Apostle 1. Cor. 15. v. 56. The strength of sin is the law, i.e. justice expressed by law, not the bare will of God. 3. That God's love toward the pious, and hatred toward the impious, depend not on natural rectitude, but on some arbitrary choice. 4. That sin never opposes the nature of God. Otherwise indeed He would abhor and punish it, nor could He fail to consign the sinner to death for sin, which however the Photinians assert. 5. That idolatry, blasphemy, perjury are not sins, if God were to will them, since they are estimated from bare will. If they say that God does not will such things, I ask for the cause. If He is free, and can do all things, why can He not will these things? They will say nothing, unless they confess with us that these things are ἐναντίως evil, and contrary to God's nature and natural justice, and therefore do not fall under the will of God, who does not deny Himself: From which it is clear, in the question concerning sins and the punishment of sins, that not a bare will but a just one, or one modified by justice, is to be considered, just as an earthly judge is a minister of God Rom. 13. v.

he hates sins, and punishes the sinner, not because he himself merely wills it, but because he wills it justly, or because he is just himself, and it is just in itself that these things be done.

4. If the absolute command and liberty of God extends so widely, I shall similarly conclude from that, that he can, nay, ought to save all men, if he wishes to obtain the praise of infinite goodness and mercy. For who has laid down a law for him, that he should not do this? Does God lie subject to any superior? Let the Photinians therefore bring forward an express reason why they should maintain with us that only the penitent and faithful can be saved by God? They cannot take refuge in the decree: since his will is free: he can change, when he wills. Why therefore can God not even will that the stubborn and impenitent be saved? Unless they confess here with us that the natural justice of God stands in the way, they will be able to bring forward nothing solid. For it is for this reason that God does not save stubborn sinners, because the justice of God, and the law (its expression), hates sinners and requires that they be subjected to punishments. Unless therefore satisfaction is first made to justice, or the satisfaction of Christ is apprehended by faith, they cannot be saved. If they still say that God can save all men (as also the devils) by absolute power without any satisfaction: 1. They beg the question, 2. They contradict the Scriptures. 3. They establish many absurdities, that God does not hate the sinner, that his sin is not contrary to his nature, that he is not a just judge, and similar things. Since these are ἀτοπώτατα (most absurd), we maintain that God, with his nature safe, with his justice safe, with his truth and the sentence of the law safe, cannot love sin, or love the sinner, as such, unless he is first reconciled, and his wrath kindled on account of sin is appeased.

5. If the guilt of death on account of sin does not have its origin from the justice of God, it will follow that it flows from injustice. For no third thing can be given here, nor can it be excepted that act can be unjust, having proceeded from free will. For here there is a capable subject, in whom either a habit or a privation occurs by infallible necessity. And every act, by which punishments or rewards are distributed, is necessarily either just or unjust, since such is the object with which justice is occupied. Now, truly, the enslavement to death was a punishment, for it was done on account of sin. But guilt and punishment are always related. Whatever, therefore, is inflicted on account of sin has the nature of punishment, and consequently also the liability to death. This punishment, therefore, was either just or unjust; if you deny that it arose from justice, it follows that the other, that it flowed from injustice, is true. If you deny this also, it will follow 1. either that it was not a punishment. 2. or that a capable subject is given, in whom there is neither a habit nor a privation. 3. and that a punishment is distributed, and thus a judicial act is given, which nevertheless is neither just nor unjust, all of which are most absurd. Whatever, therefore, they may say about the will, I will always urge, whether it was just or unjust. Since the latter is false, the former will be true. Or let them provide a third option in a capable subject between two immediate contraries in a determined act, which is the same as providing a man who is neither blind nor sees; or an animal that is neither alive nor dead; or an act of judgment and a punishment that is neither just nor unjust. Since all these suffer from manifest absurdity, we conclude from this that the human race, because of the most just justice of God, violated by the fall, and therefore inflicting punishment rightly and according to law, and thus not from the bare will of God, was consigned to eternal death, which was what had to be concluded.

6 I ask, does God justly or unjustly consign men to eternal damnation on account of sin? If they assume the latter, they are more blasphemous than the Devil, and they will make God not God. If the former, it will be false: God that sinful men could not have been consigned to eternal death. For thus He would have acted unjustly, unmindful of His own law and justice. For if it was just to condemn sinners, certainly the contrary was unjust, and p.c. impossible for God, who could not act unjustly. A notable passage of Scaliger looks to this: Ex 249. sect. 3. the sum of which is this: that God, being most good and most perfect, is a law unto Himself. Therefore, what He determines, He determines rightly, and He cannot determine the contrary. For whatever is besides that is right, is not of God, but is not-God. Wherefore if God justly and rightly consigns sinful men to death on account of sin, then it is not right and just if they are not consigned: and therefore God cannot do this, because He can act only rightly and justly. And thus, when the Photinians wish to go about defending the power of God and His glory most of all, by that very act they attack it, and make a non-God out of God, because they determine that He can also act not rightly, than which impiety and blasphemy none greater can be conceived. Moreover, it follows from what has been said, furthermore, that if God has justly consigned men to death on account of sin, they cannot be exempted from the dominion of death by His mere will. For otherwise He would not have condemned them justly. Since this is an impious thing to say, either justice must be satisfied, or they cannot be exempted from the dominion of death, or justice must be abolished or completely changed, i.e., a non-God must be made out of God. The latter is blasphemous and heretical. The former, therefore, will be true and orthodox. Magistrates declare this with a similar example, who, if they have justly sentenced a parricide to death, cannot justly release him without satisfaction.

7. If condemnation is a work of justice, it follows that the destruction of man depends efficiently not from sin alone, but at the same time from the will of God, which, however, they blame in the Calvinists as heretical. For it is against that Hosea 13:9, 'destruction is from yourself.' The reason for the consequence is: because they say, that God, if he had willed, could easily have forgiven all guilt to men. Hence therefore it follows, 1. That God is malevolent. 2. That the cause of damnation is His will. For if He had willed to forgive the guilt, He could have, since there is no justice in Him which has been harmed by sin. But if sin is the sole cause of damnation, God could not have failed to condemn; since the cause being placed in act, the effect certainly follows. That therefore men are subject to death, that did not flow so much from sin as from the will of God: Why therefore is it written? God does not will the death of the dying; Ezek. 18. verse 33. This can be declared by the likeness of a naked debtor. When a debtor is thrown into prison on account of debt, the debt is indeed in a certain way the cause of this captivity, yet principally it flows from the will of the creditor, who if he had forgiven the debt, as he could easily have done, he would not have been thrown into prison; and thus that captivity proceeds entirely from the inclemency and hardness of the creditor. In like manner, if the guilt of death depends not on justice, but on the naked will of God, by this very fact God is accused of inclemency, and the primary cause of damnation is attributed to His will, which is contrary to the own hypotheses of the Photinians.

Latin:

Ifa. 53. vers. 7. 8. meritò id credimus, nec vllis ratiunculis ab absoluto Dei imperio & libero arbitrio petitis; ab illa Scripturæ doctrina nos dimoveri patimur: Si enim vtrumque scriptum est, vtrique subordinata erunt, non contraria. Quare prius ex Scripturis probent Deum voluisse, absque omni satisfactione culpam nobis condonare, quàm ad κρησφύγετον de absoluta Dei potentia confugiant, cùm hic quæstio sit, non tam quid Deus circa salutem generis humani facere potuerit, sed quid faciat, & quid facere velit, juxta patefactionem sui diutius & verbo comprehensam.

2. Deus absolutum quidem habet imperium, quia superiori nulli subjacet: Interim tamen seipsum negare nequit, Ideoque quod aliis est lex præscripta, hoc Deo est natura; contra quam non agit: Hic quicquid est adversum & inimicum, id sub Dei potestatem & voluntatem non cadit; cùm aliàs Deus sibi ipsi contrarius foret. Jam verò peccatum est naturæ Dei adversum: Ergo non potest non illud odisse, non potest non propter illud peccatori maledicere. Nam aliàs justus judex non esset, vt tamen esse debet. Psalm. 7. versu 18. Ejus enim non est facinorofos pro beneplacito dimittere. Nam vt justitia obedientiam præmiis, sic inobedientiam pœnis afficere immutabiliter postulat. Hoc nisi Deus faciat, justitia distributiva ipsi adimitur.

Et suprà rationes satis prægnantes à Dei natura, lege & veritate attulimus, quibus salvis non potest Deus peccatorem reum absque satisfactione impunitum dimittere: Quocirca sic defensenda est Dei libertas, ne tollatur ejus justitia, bonitas & veritas: Sicut enim Deus licèt liber sit, peccare tamen nequit, quia bonus est: ita peccata non potest non odisse & punire, quia naturâ justus est: Quales enim naturâ sumus, tales res naturâ volumus. Sed Deus naturâ impietatem aversatur. Prov 8.

v, 7. 8. Ergò natura vult illam sublatam, aut si adsit, punitam. Nisi enim puniret, peccatum pro non peccato reputaret, & non tanquam mundi iudex, sed velut ociosus iniquitatis spectator assideret, quod tamen à terreni iudicis officio, qui Dei minister, & iudicij diuini imago, alienum est. Quare vt ignis naturaliter non potest non vrere, admotâ materiâ: Sic Deus, qui ignis consumens est Deut. 4. v. 24. ob naturalem suam iustitiam non potest non indignari, præsente iniquitate & inobedientia.

3. Si ex sola & nuda Dei voluntate fluit mancipatio mortis, mox crassissima indè absurda consequuntur. 1. coram Deo idem esse peccatum & non peccatum, cùm erga vtrunque naturâ pariter sit affectus; 2. Peccatum per se nihil esse, sed potius opinionem, pro diuerso voluntatis diuinæ arbitrio æstimandam. Vbi verò manet illud Apostoli 1. Cor. 15. v. 56. Peccati vis est lex, h. e. justitia lege expressa, non nuda Dei voluntas. 3. Dei amorem erga pios, & odium erga impios non ex naturali rectitudine, sed qualicunque arbitrio dependere. 4. Peccatum naturæ Dei nunquam adversari. Aliàs n. abominaretur & puniret, neque posset peccatorem morte ob peccatum non mancipare, quod tamen Photiniani afferunt. 5. Idololatriam, blasphemiam, periurium non esse peccata, si Deus illa vellet, cum ex nuda voluntate illa æstimentur. Si dicant, Deum talia non velle, quæro de causa. Si liber est, & omnia potest, cur ista velle non potest? Nil dicent, nisi nobiscum fateantur, ista ἐναντίως mala, Deique naturæ & naturali iustitiæ contraria esse, ac proindè sub Dei, qui seipsum non negat, voluntatem haut cadere: Ex quo liquet, in quæstione de peccatis & peccatorum pœnâ, non voluntatem nudam sed iustam, vel iustitiâ modificatam esse considerandam, sicut iudex terrenus Dei minister Rom. 13. v.

peccata odit, & peccatorem punit, nō quia ipse nudè vult, sed quia iustè vult, seu quia iustus ipse, & per se iustum est, ista fieri.

4. Si absolutum Dei imperium & libertas eius tàm latè extenditur, ego similiter indè colligam, quòd possit, imò debeat omnes homines saluare, si laudem bonitatis & misericordiæ infinitæ consequi velit. Quis enim ipsi legem tulit, nè hoc faceret? Num Deus alicui superiori subiacet? Expressam igitur rationem Photiniani afferant, cur nobiscum statuant, solos pœnitentes & fideles à Deo saluari posse? Ad decretum confugere nequeunt: quoniam voluntas eius est libera: potest mutare, quando vult. Cur igitur, Dʎvs nē quidem velle potest, vt præfracti & impœnitentes saluentur. Nisi hîc iustitiam Dei naturalem obstare nobiscum fateantur, nihil solidi proferre poterunt. Ideo enim Dʎvs peccatores præfractos non saluat, quoniam iustitia Dei, & lex (eius expressio) peccatores odio habet, & pœnis subijci requirit. Nisi ergo prius iustitiæ satisfiat, aut satisfactio Christi fide apprehendatur, illi saluari nequeunt. Si adhuc dicant, Dʎvm homines omnes (vt & Diabolos) pro absoluta potestate sine omni satisfactione saluare posse. 1. Principium petunt, 2. Scripturis contradicunt. 3. Absurda multa statuunt, Deum non odisse peccatorem, peccatum eius naturæ non aduersari, iustum iudicem haut esse, & similia. Quæ cum sint ἀτοπώτατα, statuimus, Deum saluâ naturâ suâ, saluâ iustitiâ, saluâ veritate & legis sententiâ non posse peccatum amare, aut peccatorem, quâ sic, diligere, nisi prius reconcilietur, & ira eius ob peccatum succensa placetur.

5. Si reatus mortis ob peccatum, non ex iustitiâ Dei ortum habet, ex iniustitiâ fluere consequetur. Nullum enim tertium hîc dari, nec excipi potest esse actum illum non iustum, ex libera voluntate profectum. Nam adest hic subiectum habile, in quo vel habitus vel priuatio ex infallibili necessitate occurrit. Et omnis actus, quo poena vel præmia distribuuntur, necessario vel justus, vel iniustus est, cùm tale sit obiectum, circa quod iustitia occupatur. Iam verò mancipatio mortis fuit poena, facta enim est ob peccatum. Culpa verò & poena semper relata sunt. Quicquid igitur ob peccatum infligitur, poenæ rationem habet, & per consequens etiam reatus mortis. Hæc igitur poena aut iusta fuit, aut iniusta, si ex iustitia ortam negas, sequitur alterum, ex iniustitia profluxisse. Si & hoc negas, sequetur 1. aut poenam non fuisse. 2 aut subiectum habile dari, in quo nec sit habitus, nec priuatio. 3. & supplicium distribui, atque sic actum iudicialem dari, qui tamen nec sit iustus, nec iniustus, quæ omnia sunt absurdissima. Quicquid proinde de voluntate dixerint, semper vrgebo, num iusta vel iniusta fuerit, Posteriùs cùm falsum, prius erit verum. Aut tertium dent in subiecto habili inter duo contraria immediata in actu determinato, id quod est hominem dare, qui nec cæcus sit, nec videat; aut animal quod nec viuum, nec mortuum sit; actu in iudicij & poenam, quæ nec iusta, nec iniusta sit. Quæ omnia cùm manifesta absurditate laborent nos indè colligimus genus humanum ex iustissima Dei iustitia, per lapsum violata, ideoque poenam iure & secundum legem infligente atque sic non ex nuda Dei voluntate morti æternæ mancipatum esse, id quod concludendum fuit.

6 Quæro, Num Deus iustè vel iniustè homines propter peccatum æternæ damnationi mancipet? Si posterius assumunt, Diabolo magis blasphemi sunt, & ex Deo non Deum facient. Si prius, falsum erit: Deum homines peccantes potuisse non mancipare æternæ morti. Sic enim iniuste egisset, iuris iustitiæq́; suæ immemor. Nam si iustum fuit, peccatores damnare, vtique contrarium iniustum fuit, & p c. Deo, qui iniuste agere non potuit, impossibile. Spectat huc insignis locus Scaliger: Ex 249. sect. 3. cuius hæc summa: Deum esse optimum, perfectissimum sibiipsi legem. Quod ergò statuit, id rectè statuit, & contrarium statuere nequit. Nam quodcunque præter illud rectum est, non est Dei, sed non Dei. Quare si Deus homines peccantes iure & rectè propter peccatum morti mancipat, tum rectum iustumq́; non est, si non mancipentur: ideoque Deus hoc facere non potest, quia non nisi rectè & iustè agere potest. Atque sic, cum Photiniani potentiam Dei, eiusque gloriam maximè defensum ire volunt, eo ipso impugnant, & ex Deo non Deum faciunt, quia illum etiam non rectè operari posse statuunt, quâ impietate & blasphemia nulla maior cogitari potest. Sequitur verò ex dictis hoc insuper, si Deus homines ob peccatum morti iustè mancipauit, ex mortis imperio per nudam eius voluntatem eximi non posse. Aliàs enim non condemnasset iustè. Quod cum sit impium dictu, aut iustitiæ satisfieri debet, aut ex mortis imperio eximi nequeunt, aut iustitia tollenda, vel penitus immutanda, h. e. ex Deo non Deus faciendus erit. Vltimum est blasphemum & hæreticum, Priora igitur vera erunt & orthodoxa. Declarant hoc simili Magistratus, qui si parricidam iustè morti addixit, sine satisfactione iustè dimittere nequit.

7. Si damnatio est opus iustitiæ, sequitur interitum hominis non à solo peccato, sed simul à voluntate Dei efficienter pendere, quod tamen in Caluinianis ipsi tanquam hæreticum vituperant. Est enim contra istud Ose. 13. v 9 perditio ex te. Ratio consequentiæ est: quia dicunt, Deum, si voluisset, facilè potuisse hominibus omnem culpam condonare. Hinc ergo sequitur, 1. Deum esse malevolum. 2. causam damnationis esse eius voluntatem. Si enim voluisset culpam condonare potuisset, cum nulla sit in ipso iustitia, quæ per peccatum sit læsa. Si verò peccatum sit solitaria damnationis causa, Deus non potuisset non damnare; quoniam causâ in actu positâ, certo sequitur effectus. Quòd igitur homines morti sunt subiecti, id non tamen â peccato, quàm voluntate Dei promanavit: Cur ergo scriptum? Deus non vult mortem morientis; Ezech. 18. versu 33. Similitudine nudi debitoris declarari hæc potest. Cùm debitor in carcerem ob æs alienum conjicitur, debitum quidem huius captivitatis quodammodo causa est, principaliter tamen id promanat à creditoris voluntate, qui si debitum condonâsset, vt facilè potuisset, in carcerem coniectus non fuisset; adeoque illa captivitas prósus ab inclementia & duritie creditoris proficiscitur. Pari modo si reatus mortis non à iustitiâ, sed nudâ Dei voluntate pendet, hoc ipso Deus inclementiæ accusatur, & prima damnationis causa voluntati eius accepta fertur, quod contra proprias Photinianorum est hypotheses.


### Argument XIII. & last. On the justice of God: If the enslavement to death proceeds from the naked will of God, by what could…

8. If the enslavement to death proceeds from the naked will of God, by what could sin merit punishment? For what is the foundation of this merit? Nothing else can be said than the violation of the law. But why does the transgression of the law merit punishment? It cannot be answered otherwise than because justice demands it so. Therefore, let them either deny the merit of sin, or acknowledge justice in God. For these things are relative: one being posited, the other is posited; one being denied, the other is also denied. If therefore they maintain, as must be maintained, that sin justly merits punishment before God, they must confess that there is justice in God, since it is that alone which causes guilt to merit punishment. But if they deny justice in God, they will not give a sufficient reason why every sin must justly be punished for the violated law.

CIII. From ch. 2 God punishes only those sins which are joined with impenitence, but the rest, if repentance is added, he passes over unpunished, or remits. Wherefore there is no vindicatory justice in him, severely punishing every transgression.

Response. 1. But why does he not remit impenitence and contumacy? Is it because he cannot? Therefore he does not have absolute power, he is not of his own right, and he is more impotent than man, and a cause for this thing must be brought forward. Is it because he does not want to? Therefore he is unmerciful, nor is he absolutely good, and the clemency of certain men, even those forgiving and doing good to enemies, will be greater than the mercy of God. Whatever they answer here, we will twist back into their own throats. 2. The justice of God and the condonation of certain sins do not fight, but the latter illustrates the former. For sins are dismissed to the penitent for this reason, because the satisfaction of Christ performed for them is imputed through faith. Therefore satisfaction always precedes forgiveness, not indeed our own, but Christ's, whose merit when the impenitent spurn, they are justly condemned, and remain liable to the curse of the law. 3. When the adversaries say that only sins joined with impenitence are punished: they confuse sin itself with perseverance in sin. Sin is ἀνομία in general 1 John 3, verse 4, nor is it defined by impenitence. This, however, is an accident of sin. Wherefore let it not be thought that God punishes only this accident, not the sin itself. Indeed, rather, ἀνομία and even a single act, as is clear from the example of Adam, makes one guilty of eternal death at that very time in which it is committed, before anything is known of whether the sinner has persevered or otherwise. This passage of James 2, verse 10, looks to this.

Whoever shall have observed the whole law, but shall have stumbled in one point, has become guilty of all. For God is a most just judge, punishing both great and small sins. If it was against the law, by this very fact the justice of God is violated and a curse is incurred, whether it be a solitary or a continued act.

CIV. 1. The threats of the Law are determined by repentance. Wherefore, to those who perform it, sins are forgiven, not because of any satisfaction required by the justice of God, but on account of the sole merciful will of God.

I answer, 1. He separates things that should be joined. For repentance does not exclude, but includes the satisfaction of Christ, to be apprehended by faith. For thus Scripture everywhere describes the repentance of man, in whose place the Photinians substitute a thing clearly new. 2. The Law does not promise salvation and life under the condition of repentance, but of perfect fulfillment. Therefore, he who violates the Law and does not fully observe it, is always subject to its curse. Now Adam violated it, and with him all of us. Wherefore we were subject to the curse by the very act, not merely to be subjected if we should be impenitent. Hence Christ was made a curse in our place, Galat. 3, and subject to the Law, that He might redeem us who were under the Law and its curse. Galat. 4. The Photinians therefore confuse the Law and the Gospel. The Law promises life to those who fulfill it: the Gospel promises it only to the penitent and the faithful. 3. If by repentance alone, that is, the pursuit of virtue, the legal threat can be changed and removed, what need was there for the blessed seed? Or was it to announce the way of salvation? But this reasoning expires regarding the fathers of the Old Testament. Another prophet could have performed the same, and Scripture expresses a far different end for the incarnation and sending of the Son, namely to crush the head of the serpent, Gen. 3, verse 15, to give a price of redemption, 1 Timoth. 2, v. 6, and to take away sins, Hebr. 9, v. 28, etc.

CV. 4. If justice and mercy are simultaneously in God, it is possible for contraries to fall upon God, with respect to the same object.

Response. 1. Scripture affirms both of God. How, therefore, could these be either contrary or ἀνυπόστατα (unsubstantial)? We ought not to depart from the clear letter on account of certain futile little consequences of delirious reason. 2. Justice and mercy are not properties contrary in themselves and through themselves, since they are the very essence of God, which is most simple and devoid of all contrariety. Meanwhile, we acknowledge that they exert themselves through diverse acts, where that remark of Scaliger in Exercitation 312 is to be noted: It is not necessary that, if actions are contrary, the essential principles are also. Especially regarding the sins of men, these properties seemed in a certain way dissociated and opposed to one another. For mercy, according to its nature, wished to spare the fallen human race: Justice and the truth of God, according to the law, demanded punishment. And since neither of these could exert its nature, Christ intervened, who through his satisfaction joined both, so that an admirable tempering of justice and mercy arose from it. For the justice and mercy of God cannot be exerted simultaneously in act upon one and the same object, unless they are in some way reconciled by a medium. For justice demands perfect obedience to be rendered to the law, which, since it is found in no man, immediately condemns and actually subjects him to a curse. If the mercy of God were to liberate from this punishment simply, without any intervening medium, then it would decree the contrary of justice according to the same thing, toward the same thing, and at the same time. Therefore, so that this contrariety might be removed, the satisfaction of Christ intervened by the singular counsel of the Trinity. For he himself perfectly fulfilled the law in our place and suffered for us, from which work of redemption a wondrous consensus of divine justice and mercy shines forth. For through Christ, by grace, the punishments for sins due were transferred, so that thus, with His truth and justice preserved, God might receive us into favor. And these were the pious thoughts of the Fathers concerning this mystery, why God could not adopt us before satisfaction was rendered. Meanwhile, let us not easily allow ourselves to be driven into these straits: But let us hold the will and ordinance of GOD as the first and principal cause. For many things can be speciously objected concerning the disagreement of these properties: Has GOD disagreed with Himself? How can this be reconciled with His simplicity? Was there any conflict between the Father and the Son? And what other questions curious reason invents for itself. Wherefore if you ask, why does God not forgive sins out of mercy alone without justice? It is safest to answer: Because it is so written, and the will of God has not been revealed otherwise. In this simplicity I acquiesce, and I satisfy my conscience most excellently. After the truth has been demonstrated from the Scriptures, for the sake of declaration, and so that every mouth may be stopped against adversaries, that answer of the Fathers can be assumed, that it could not even have been done otherwise on account of God's justice, which had been injured because of sin, and therefore demanded a penalty, which was to be transferred from us through the satisfaction of Christ.

CVI. 5. The remission of sins is attributed to the justice of God, Rom. 3 verse 25, 1 John 3 v. 9. Therefore divine justice will not be the property of punishing sins. Ostor. p. 212. Catech. Racov. p. 267.

Resp. Neither passage concludes that for which it is brought forward to conclude. For 1. Rom. 3 it is not said that sins are remitted through justice, but that justice is declared in the remission, which happens insofar as the merit of Christ is apprehended in it, by which justice has been satisfied. So far, therefore, is it from the case that the justice of God is impugned by this statement, that it is rather confirmed and illustrated by it. Add that it is not absurd to understand by justice in that passage either the truth or the mercy of God, since the word δικαιοσύνης is not rarely taken in both senses in the Scriptures, as was said at the beginning of this argument. 2. 1. Iohan. 3. anyone sees that justice is placed in the stead of truth and faithfulness. For if we confess our sins, God is just, that is, truthful and faithful, who forgives those things.

CVII. 6. If justice were natural to God, he could save no one; if mercy, he could punish no one. For no one can act against his own nature.

Respond. 1. Attributes are one thing, the use and exercise of attributes are another. The former are natural, the exercise is free, yet ordered, not absolute; 2. I deny the consequence. For although God's justice is natural to him, yet he can save the faithful, since through Christ justice has been satisfied. Thus, although he is merciful, yet if his grace is stubbornly neglected, he is gravely angry and punishes. Both stand together, both justice and mercy. By the former the contumacious are condemned: by the latter the faithful are saved, as Scripture inculcates everywhere.

CXIIX. And these were the principal arguments of the Photinians, which we wished to set forth somewhat more lengthily and to refute more fully, since that sect begins to sing a triumph before victory and to boast everywhere of the invincible strength of its reasons, when nevertheless they are nothing other than mere sophistications and crafty depravations of the Scriptures, which to the minds of some, desirous of novelties and studious of singularities, and not yet confirmed in orthodox doctrine, seem very specious; but when examined more deeply, like the apples of Sodom, they will vanish into ashes and embers. CHRIST JESUS, the only Redeemer and Mediator, confirm us in the acknowledged truth, and seal the most holy merit of his passion in our hearts, so that it may be and remain our comfort in adversity, an asylum in dangers, a support in temptations, and finally a most sweet and most sought-after refreshment in the agonies of death. AMEN.

Latin:

8. Si mancipatio mortis à nuda Dei voluntate provenit, quâ peccatum mereri potuit pœnam. Quod enim est fundamentum huius meriti? Aliud dici nequit, quàm legis violatio. Cur autem prævaricatio legis meretur pœnam? Aliter responderi nequit, quàm quia iustitia ita flagitat. Aut ergo meritum peccati negent, aut iustitiam in Deo agnoscant. Sunt enim isthæc relata: Vno posito, ponitur; negato, negatur & alterum. Si ergo statuunt, vti statuendum est, peccatum pœnam iure promereri coram Deo, fateantur oportet, in Deo iustitiam esse, quippè quæ sola facit, vt culpa pœnam mereatur. Si verò iustitiam in Deo negant, rationem sufficientem non dabunt, cur omne peccatum jure ob violatam legem puniendum sit.

CIII. Ex c. 2 Deus non nisi peccata, quæ cum impœnitentiâ sunt conjuncta, punit, reliqua vero si pœnitentia accedat, impunita prætermittit, vel remittit. Quare nulla est in ipso justitia vindicatrix, omnes transgressione severè puniens.

Respon. 1. Cur autem impœnitentiam & contumaciam non remittit? Num quia non potest? Ergo absolutum imperium non habet, sui juris non est & homine impotentior est, & causa huius rei afferri debet. An quia non vult? Ergo immisericors, nec absolutè bonus est, & clementia quorundam hominum, etiam hostibus ignoscentium & benefacientium, erit maior misericordiâ Dei. Quicquid hic responderint, in ipsorum iugulum retorquebimus. 2. Non pugnat Dei justitia & quorundam peccatorum condonatio, sed hæc illam illustrat. Ideò enim pœnitentibus peccata dimittuntur, quoniam satisfactio Christi pro ipsis præstita per fidem imputatur. Semper ergo veniam præcedit satisfactio, non quidem nostra, sed Christi, cuius meritum cùm impœnitentes spernunt, jure damnantur, & legis maledictioni obnoxij manent. 3. Quando adversarij dicunt, non nisi peccata cum impœnitentiâ conjuncta puniri: confundunt peccatum ipsum, cum perseverantia in peccato. Peccatum est ἀνομία in genere 1. Ioh. 3. versu 4. nec definitur per impœnitentiam. Hæc autem peccati est accidens. Quare non putetur, Deum hoc duntaxat accidens punire, non peccatum ipsum. Imò verò ἀνομία & vel unicus actus, ut exemplo Adæ patet, æternæ mortis actureum facit illo ipso tempore, quo committitur, antequam, num perseverauerit peccator, vel secus, aliquid sciatur. Spectat huc istud Iacob. 2. versu 10.

Quisquis totam legem observaverit, impegerit autem in uno, reus factus est omnium. Est enim Deus justissimus iudex, & magna & parva peccata puniens. Si contrà legem fuit, violatur hoc ipso Dei justitia & incurritur maledictio, siue sit solitarius, siue continuatus actus.

CIV. 1. Legis comminationes sunt poenitentiâ determinatæ. Quapropter qui illam agunt, ijs peccata dimittuntur, non b aliquam satisfactionem, à iustitia Dei requisitam, sed ob solam misericordem Dei voluntatem.

Respondeo, 1. Disiungit conjungenda. Nam poenitentia non excludit, sed includit Christi satisfactionem, fide apprehendendam. Sic enim Scriptura passim describit hominis poenitentiam, in cuius locum Photiniani rem planè novam substituunt. 2. Lex non promittit salutem & vitam sub conditione pœnitentiæ, sed perfectæ impletionis. Legem igitur qui violat, nec plenè obfervat, maledictioni eius semper subjacet. Violavit autem Adam, & cum ipso nos omnes. Quare maledictioni actu ipso subiecti fuimus, non demùm subjiciendi, si impœnitentes simus. Hinc Christus nostri loco factus est maledictum, Galat. 3. & subiectus Legi, vt nos, qui sub lege, & ejus maledictione eramus, redimeret. Galat. 4. Confundunt igitur Photiniani Legem & Evangelium. Lex vitam implentibus: Evangelium duntaxat pœnitentibus, & fidelibus promittit. 3. Si per solam pœnitentiam, hoc est, virtutis studium, comminatio legalis potest mutari & tolli, quid opus erat semine benedicto? An vt viam salutis annunciaret? Sed hæc ratio expirat, quoad patres Veteris Testamenti. Alius Propheta idem præstare potuit, & Scriptura longè alium finem incarnationis & missi Filij exprimit, nempè caput serpentis conterere, Gen. 3. versu 15. redemptionis pretium dare, 1, Timoth. 2. v. 6. & peccata auferre, Hebr. 9, v. 28. &c.

CV. 4. Si in Deo simul est iustitia & misericordia, posse in Deum cadere contraria, respectu eiusdem obiecti.

Respond. 1. Scriptura de Deo vtrumque affirmat. Qui ergò ista vel contraria vel ἀνυπόστατα essent? Non debemus à clarâ literâ recedere ob futiles quasdam deliræ rationis consequentianculas. 2. Iustitia & misericordia non sunt proprietates in se ac per se contrariæ, cùm sint ipsa Dei essentia, quæ simplicissima & omnis cōtarietatis expers. Interim fatemur, ver diuersos actus se exerere, vbi notandum istud Scaligeri Exerc. 312. Non est necessarium, vt si actiones sint contrariæ, etiam essentialia principia. Imprimis circ̄a hominum peccata proprietates istæ quodammodò dissociatæ & sibi adversæ videbantur. Nam misericordia, juxta naturam suam volebat parcere lapso generi humano: Iustitia & Dei veritas secundum legem postulabat pœnam. Cumque neutra istarum suam exerere poterat naturam, interuenit Christus, qui per satisfactionem suam vtramque conjunxit vt admirandum iustitiæ & misericordiæ temperamentum inde ortum sit. Iustitia enim & misericordia Dei simul actu in vno eodemque objecto exerceri nequeunt, nisi medio aliquomodo reconcilientur. Nam justitia flagitat perfectam, legi præstandam obedientiam, quæ cùm in nullo hominum reperiatur, mox damnat & maledictioni actu subjicit. Ab hac pœna si Dei misericordia simpliciter absque vllo medio interueniente liberaret, tum secundum idem, ad idem, & eodem tempore contrarium iustitiæ decerneret. Hæc ergò contrarietas vt tolleretur, Christi satisfactio ex singulari Trinitatis consilio interuenit. Ipse enim legem nostri loco perfectè implevit & pro nobis passus est, ex quo redemtionis opere mirus iustitiæ & misericordiæ divinæ consensus elucescit. Per Christum enim, ex gratia, pœnæ pro peccatis debitæ facta est translatio, vt ita saluâ veritate & iustitia suâ, Deus in gratiam nos reciperet Et hæ fuerunt Patrum de hoc mysterio pię cogitationes, cur Deus non potuerit nos adoptare ante satisfactionem præstitam. Interim non facilè in has angustias nos depelli patiamur: Sed pro prima & principali causa habeamus DEI voluntatem & ordination. Multa enim speciose opponi possunt de diffidio istarum proprietatum, Num DEVS à seipso dissenserit? Quomodo hoc cum ipsius simplicitate conciliari queat? Num inter Patrem & Filium aliqua fuerit pugna? & quas sibi quæstiones alias curiosa ratio fingit. Quare si quæras, cur Deus non ex sola misericordia absque iusto peccata dimittat? Tutissimum est respondere; Quia sic scriptum, & voluntas Dei non aliter reuelata est. In hac simplicitate acquiesco, & conscientiæ meæ optimè satisfacio. Post demonstratam ex Scripturis veritatem, declarationis ergò, & vt omne os obstruatur aduersariis, assumi potest illa Patrum responsio, quòd ne quidem aliter fieri potuerit ob Dei iustitiam, quæ erat propter peccatum læsa, ideoque poscebat pœnam, quæ per Christi satisfactionem à nobis fuit transferenda.

CVI. 5. Iustitiæ Dei tribuitur remissio peccatorum, Rom. 3 vers. 25. 1. Johan. 3. v. 9. Ergò iustitia diuina non erit proprium peccata punire. Ostor. p. 212. Catech. Racov. p 267.

Resp. Neuter locus concludit id, ad quod concludendum affertur. Nam 1. Rom. 5. non dicitur, per iustitiam peccata remitti, sed in remissione iustitiam declarari, quod fit, quatenus in illa Christi meritum apprehenditur, quo iustitię satisfactum est. Tantum igitur abest, vt hoc dicto Dei iustitia impugnetur, vt magis per illud confirmetur & illustretur. Adde, quod non absurdum sit; in isto loco per iustitiam intelligere Dei vel veritatem vel misericordiam, cùm vox δικαιοσύνης vtroque sensu in Scripturis haut raro accipiatur, vt initio huius augumenti dictum est. 2. 1. Iohan. 3. quiuis videt, iustitiam loco veritatis & fidelitatis esse positam. Si enim confitemur peccata, Deus est iustus, hoc est, verax & fidelis, qui ista condonat.

CVII. 6. Si iustitia Deo foret naturalis neminem saluare, si misericordia; neminem punire posset. Contra naturam enim suam nemo quicquam agere potest.

Respond. 1. Aliud sunt attributa, aliud attributorum vsus & exercitium. Illa sunt naturalia, exercitium est liberum, ordinatum tamen, non absolutum; 2. Nego consequentiam. Quamuis enim Dei iustitia sit ipsi naturalis, attamen saluare potest fideles, quoniam per Christum iustitiæ satisfactum est. Sic licèt sit misericors, attamen si gratia eius præfractè negligatur, grauiter succenset & punit. Vtrumque stat simul & iustitia & misericordia. Per illam damnantur contumaces: Per hanc saluantur fideles, vti Scriptura passim inculcat.

CXIIX. Atque hæc fuerunt præcipua Photinianorum argumenta, quæ nonnihil prolixiùs proponere, & pleniùs refutare voluimus, quoniam Secta ista triumphum ante victoriam canere, & de inuincibili rationum suarum robore passim gloriari incipit, cùm tamen nihil aliud sint, quam meræ Sophisticationes & veteratoriæ Scripturarum deprauationes, quæ quorundam ingenijs, nouitatum cupidis; & singularitatum studiosis, inque orthodoxa doctrina nondum confirmatis perquàm speciolæ videntur; sed penitiùs discussæ instar pomorum Sodomiticorum in cineres abibunt & fauillas. CHRISTVS IESVS, Redemtor & Mediator vnicus, in veritate agnita nos confirmet, & sactosanctum passionis suæ meritum in cordibus nostris obsignet, quò sit & maneat nostrum in adversis solatium, in periculis asylum, in tentationibus sustentaculum, & denique in mortis angoribus refrigerium suavissimum & expetatissimum. AMEN.


## 30 Disputation VII. On the Formal Cause of Our Justification, against the Papists

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent, Heinrich Glambeck of Lübeck.

Thesis: I.

Hitherto the meritorious cause has been discussed sufficiently at length; now the approach should be made to the instrumental cause, which is faith, apprehending the merit of Christ. But because the subject of faith has been partly dealt with in a public dissertation, and partly remains to be dealt with, we have not wished to repeat the same doctrine here, but will proceed directly to the exposition of the remaining causes.

II. Three, however, remain: 1. Material: 2. Formal. 3. Final. There is the greatest controversy concerning the formal cause, and therefore a lengthy ἐξήγησις is required: but the material and final can be explained briefly, which we shall provide here, dispatched as if in the place of an introduction.

III. 1 On the material cause. Justification is an action, and therefore it has no matter from which it is made: but the matter about which, or the object, is the sinful man to be justified, according to that passage in Rom. 4, verse 5: You believe in him who justifies the ungodly; verse 7: Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven; verse 8: Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin. And hence against the Pontificians we argue thus: An impious man and sinner can in no way merit anything by his works, or apply himself to the grace of God, or anticipate the same, since all his works are evil. But indeed those who are justified are impious men and sinners; therefore they can in no way merit anything by their works or apply themselves to the grace of God.

IV. Bellarmine philosophizes here not very correctly, whose words are these in book 1 on justification, chapter 2: 'The material cause can be said to be the mind of man, or his very will, in which justice dwells as in its proper subject and seat. Dispositions, which prepare the matter to receive the form, also pertain to the material cause.' In which words some errors lie hidden. For 1, he constitutes one part of the name, namely the mind, as the object of justification, when nevertheless the whole man is to be justified, since he exists as a whole sinner. 2. He wishes the will to be the subject or matter to which justice adheres as a form. But justice is one thing, and justification, which is the subject of inquiry here, is another. For it is an action of God, of which there can be no subject in which it exists, since actions pass away and do not remain, except by reason of firmness and efficacy. He begs the question, moreover, in that we are just by inherent justice, concerning which more fully below. 3. He refers dispositions to the material cause, which Costerus, however, refers to the form in Enchiridion, page 261; others reduce them to the efficient cause. But we infer thus: Matter only suffers, it does not act. Therefore, whatever is an act is not matter. But those dispositions are acts, as Bellarmine admits and confirms from the Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 6. Therefore those dispositions are not matter, or anything material.

V. 2. Concerning the final cause. This is considered with respect to either God or ourselves. With respect to GOD, the final end is His own glory, which in the business of justification He manifests, uniquely declaring justice and mercy, as the Apostle intimates, Rom. 3:24, 25. With respect to us, the end in this life indeed is peace and tranquility of conscience, Rom. 5, verse 1: Being justified by faith we have peace with God: In the other life, salvation and eternal blessedness, according to that in Rom. 1, verse 16: The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth. 1 Pet. 1, verse 9: Receiving the fruit of your faith, the salvation of your souls.

V. 1. In the expression of this cause, the Papists agree with us. For thus writes Bellarmine, lib. 1 de Iustific. cap. 2: The end of the justification of the ungodly is the glory of God and of Christ, and the salvation of those who are justified. And Costerus in Enchirid: The end or final cause, the last, is the glory of GOD, because the Lord hath wrought all things for himself. Prov. 16, verse 4. The proximate [end] is the salvation of men, because God wills all men to be saved, 1 Tim. 2, ver. 4. Where, however, it is to be noted:

1. That these testimonies can indeed be accommodated here in a certain way, but yet it seems the Jesuit intends something else, namely that he may be able to abuse these most general sayings to cloak the opinion of certain Scholastics, by which they say that many are justified even outside of Christ, by the law of nature alone.

2. If the end of justification is the glory of God alone, we ask of the Jesuits, how can our works be introduced into the circle of justification? For whatever justifies, to that the glory of justification is attributed. Our good works justify, according to the mind of the Papists: Therefore, to our good works is attributed the glory of justification, and consequently, the end of justification is not the glory of God alone, but also the glory of good works: And here must be considered the corruption of hearts, which they establish beyond and against Scripture. Nor will they be able to extricate themselves from this, even if they say that this glory is owed to Christ, because by his death he conferred this dignity upon our works; so that to be justified

may be able to know: For from that this indeed follows, that the end of justification is the glory of Christ, but nevertheless that other thing remains, that the end of justification is also the glory of good works. And in whatever way they may finally differ, this is always most truly affirmed according to their opinion, that the end of justification is the glory of Christ, namely primarily, then also the glory of good works, namely secondarily: Which all who have learned from the Gospel that the glory of justification is to be ascribed entirely to Christ will confess to be blasphemous. Wherefore these testimonies of Scripture properly pertain here, Eph. 1. Verse 5. To the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he has justified us. Likewise Rom. 9. verse 25. 1. Cor. v. last. Rom. 5. 27. 1. Pet. 2. v. 9. From all of which it is evident that the glory of God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit alone is the end of justification.

VII. These things therefore having been declared in place of a preface, we approach the most serious controversy concerning the Formal cause, where the Romanists fight for inherent righteousness, but we for imputative. It pleases us, however, to propose that orthodox [view] in this disputation, and to relegate the ἀντίθεσιν to the following: Concerning that, two questions come to be discussed, about which there will be discourse in this συζητήσει:

I. What is the opinion both of us and of the Papists concerning the formal cause? whence the true state of the controversy emerges.

II. By what arguments principally the orthodox opinion concerning imputative righteousness may be confirmed.

Latin:

Praes. Balth: Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Henrico Glambecio Lubecensi.

Thesis: I.

HActenus prolixè satis causa meritoria disputatum est, nunc accessus foret faciendus ad causam instrumentalem, quae est fides, meritum Christi apprehendens. Quia verò de fide publica dissertatione partim actum est, partim agendum restat, eandem doctrinam hic repetere noluimus, sed recta ad reliquarum causarum expositionem pergemus.

II. Tres autem supersunt: 1. Materialis: 2. Formalis. 3. Finalis. De formali causa summè controvertitur, ideoque prolixa requiritur ἐξήγησις: Materialis verò & Finalis breviter explicari possunt, quod ipsum hic quasi prooemij loco expeditum dabimus.

III. 1 De Causa materiali. Iustificatio est actio, ideoque materiam, ex quâ nullam habet: materia verò circa quam seu obiectum est homo peccator iustificandus, juxta illud Rom. 4. vers. 5. Credis in eum, qui iustificat impium vers. 7. Beati quorum remissae sunt iniquitates. v. 8. Beatus vir, cui non imputavit Dominus peccatum. Atque hinc contra Pontificiós sic argumentamur : Homo impius & peccator suis operibus aliquid promereri aut se ad gratiam Dei applicare, aut eandem præuenire nullatenus potest, quoniam opera eius omnia mala sunt. At verò ij, qui iustificantur, sunt homines impij & peccatores, Ergò suis operibus aliquid promereri, aut se ad gratiam Dei applicare nullatenus possunt.

IV. Bellarminus parùm rectè hîc philosophætur, cuius hæc sunt verba l. 1. de iustific. cap. 2. Causa materialis dici potest animus hominis; siuè ipsa eius voluntas, in qua iustitia, tanquam in subiecto & sede propriá commoratur. Pertinent quoque ad materialem causam dispositiones, quæ materiam præparant ad recipiendam formam. In quibus verbis aliquot errores latent abditi. Nam 1 partem vnam nominis, nempè animum iustificationis obiectum constituit, cùm tamen totus homo sit iustificandus, quippe totus existens peccator, 2. Voluntatem vult esse subiectum siue materiam, cui inhæreat iustitia, tanquam forma. Verùm aliud est Iustitia, aliud Iustificatio, de qua hîc quæritur. Est enim actio Dei, cuius subiectum in quo nullum potest esse, cùm actiones transeant, non permaneant, nisi ratione firmitudinis & efficaciæ. Petit insuper principium in hoc, quòd iusti simus iustitiâ inhærente, de quo infrà fusiùs. 3. Dispositiones refert ad causam materialem, quas tamen ad formam refert Costerus in Enchirid. m. pag. 261, Alij ad causam efficientem reducunt. Sic autem inferimus : Materia tantùm patitur non agit. Quicquid ergò actus est materia nõ est Dispositiones verò illæ sunt actus, fatente Bellarm. Et confirmante ex Concil. Trident. Sess. 6. c. 6. Ergò dispositiones illæ non sunt materia, aut aliquid materiale.

V. 2. De causa finali. Hæc respectu vel Dei vel nostri consideratur. Respectu DEI finis finalis est ipsius gloria, quam in negotio Iustificationis manifestat, singulariter declarando iustitiam & misericordiam, innuente Apostolo Rom 3. v. 24. 25. Respectu nostri finis est in hac quidem vita pax & tranquillitas conscientiæ, Rom 5. verf. 1: Iustificati fide pacem habemus apud Deum: In altera vita salus & beatitudo æterna, iuxta illud Rom. 1: verf. 16. Evangelium est potentia Dei ad salutem omni credenti. 1. Petr. 1. verf. 9. Reportantes fructum fidei vestræ salutem animarum.

V. 1. In hujus causæ expressione nobiscum consentiunt Pontificij. Sic enim scribit Bellarminus lib. 1. de Iustific. cap. 2. Finis iustificationis impij est gloria Dei & Christi, & salus eorum, qui iustificantur. Et Costerus in Enchirid: Finis seu causa finalis postrema est DEI gloria, quia universa propter semetipsum operatus est Dominus. Prov. 16. verf. 4. Proxima est salus hominum, quia Deus omnes homines vult salvos fieri, 1. Tim. 2. ver. 4. Vbi tamen notandum:

1. Ista testimonia posse quidem certâ ratione huc accommodari, sed tamen videri Iesuitam aliud intendere, nimirum vt generalissimis istis dictis possit abuti, ad quorundam Scholasticorum opinionem palliandam, quâ multos dicunt extra Christum etiam justificari, solâ lege naturæ.

2. Si Iustificationis finis est gloria solius Dei quærimus ex Iesu Witis, quomodo intromitti possint nostra opera in circulum iustificationis? Quicquid enim iustificat, illi gloria iustificationis tribuitur. Bona nostra opera iustificant, ex mente Pontificiorum: Ergò bonis nostris operibus tribuitur gloria iustificationis, & per consequens, finis iustificationis non est gloria solius Dei, sed etiam gloria bonorum operum: Atque hic considerari debet mendum cordium, quod illi præter & contra Scripturam statuunt. Neque hinc se se extricare poterunt, si maximè dicunt, istam gloriam deberi Christo, quia morte suâ hanc dignitatem nostris operibus contulerit; vt iustificari

stire valeant: Nam inde hoc consequitur quidem, finem iustificationis esse gloriam Christi sed tamen alterum illud nihilominus manet, finem iustificationis etiam esse gloriam bonorum operum. Et quocunque tandem modo differant, semper hoc verissime affirmatur ex illorum opinione, finem iustificationis esse gloriam Christi, nempe primariò, deinde etiam gloriam bonorum operum, nempe secundariò: Quod blasphemum esse fatebuntur vniuersi, qui Christo in solidum ascribendam iustificationis gloriam ex Evangelio didicerunt. Quare hæc Scripturæ testimonia propriè huc pertinent, Eph. 1. Vers. 5. Ad laudem gloriæ gratiæ suæ, qua Iustificauit nos. Item Rom. 9. vers. 25. 1. Cor. v. ult. Rom. 5. 27. 1. Pet. 2. v. 9. Ex quib. omnibus patet, solius Dei Patris, Filij & Spiritus sancti gloriam esse iustificationis finem.

VII. His igitur Proœmij loco ita declaratis, ad grauissimam de causa Formali controuersiam accedimus, vbi Romanenses pugnant, pro iustitia inhærente, nos autem pro imputatiua. Placet autem illam orthodoxam hac disputatione proponere, & ἀντίθεσιν in sequentem reijcere: Circa illam duæ quæstiones discutiendæ veniunt, de quibus hac συζητήσει erit disserendum:

I. Quæ tum nostra, tum Pontificiorum de causa formali sit opinio? vndè verus emergit status controuersiæ.

II. Quibus præcipuè Argumentis orthodoxa sententia de imputatiua iustitia confirmari queat.


### Quaestio I: What is the opinion of the Pontificians & of Ours concerning the formal cause of justification

I. That which Athanasius once said, that the way of truth is always simple, but that there are many byways of unbelief is made sufficiently clear also from this controversy with the Papists. For they have not all always been, and are not, of one and the same opinion, but have proposed and cloaked their errors now in this way, now in another. We shall therefore first review their various opinions concerning formal justification, then we shall note what is for the most part taught today by the Jesuits.

IX. Peter Lombard, in order to be able to establish charity as the form of justification, argues in Book 3 of the Sentences, distinction 27, letter C, that it is not some quality in us, because all our qualities are imperfect, but that it is the Holy Spirit Himself. And from this seems to have flowed the argument of Johannes Cochlaeus: It is certain that God justifies us. But God is charity, not faith. Therefore charity, not faith, justifies. Which conclusion, as far as it pertains to faith, contradicts the Apostolic assertion, Rom. 3:28: We conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the law.
