Such also seems to have been the speculation of Osiander. For since he wished righteousness before God to be something inherent in us, and considered the pollution and imperfection of inherent newness, he fled to the essential righteousness of God.

X. Others, among whom is Gropper, say that the works of charity justify, not because they are ours, but because they have proceeded from the Holy Spirit or because they are stained with the blood of Christ. But Bellarmine expressly refutes this opinion concerning actual or active righteousness in Book 2 of Justification, chapter 16.

Hosius says that the works of charity are indeed imperfect, but that the habit of charity in believers is perfect and is also the form of our righteousness. But this is manifestly false. For the habit of charity looks to the renewal of the will, which is changed from day to day, and the oldness of the flesh remains to be mortified throughout the whole life, and therefore the habit of charity is not perfect; otherwise the commandment, 'You shall love your Lord God with all your heart,' could be fulfilled, which Lombard himself denies in Book 3, distinction 27.

XI. To Albert Pighius and the authors of the Cologne dogma, Bellarmine in book 3 of Justification, chapter 2, attributes this opinion, that they taught that the formal cause of justification is twofold: our inherent righteousness and the imputed righteousness of Christ; or the remission of sin and the infusion of grace. George Cassander also seems to have been of this opinion in his Consultation, where he writes that justification does not consist in the remission of sin alone, but at the same time also in renewal. But Bellarmine asserts that an anathema was pronounced by the Tridentine fathers against those who maintain that we are formally righteous through the righteousness of Christ. And he urges this argument: The formal cause of justification is single according to the decree of the Council of Trent. Therefore, it cannot be twofold.

XII. We also oppose this very thing to Johannes Pistorius, whose opinion on justification is as follows in thesis 65: It is true once, he says, that justification brings the remission of all preceding sins, as Paul says in Romans 3, verse 21. But this is not enough, nor is it fitting that because of the declaration of one part the other should be omitted, thesis 66. That the term justification signifies not only the remission of sins, but also the renewal of the mind and the vivification of the whole inner man, we shall show by several sayings of Scripture, and thesis 88: These two operations, namely the remission of sins and the infusion of grace, which are opposed as privation and form, or corruption and grace, produce one effect, which in Scripture is called justification: by which a man obtains not only the remission of sins, but also the power to resist sins, and by which he is formally righteous in himself.

XIII. However, we do not wish to examine more fully in this place this monstrous notion of Pistorius concerning privation and form concurring to constitute justification: The remission of sins is certainly not a privation or corruption, as Pistorius dreams, but sin itself is a privation of righteousness. Whence the remission of sin is not a privation, but the removal of a privation is, nor is it corruption, but it is true regeneration. And who has ever heard it said that one effect is produced from privation and form joined together? Indeed, how can it be that privation and form are joined, since they are opposites, of which, when one is posited, the other must necessarily be removed?

XIV. Becanus seems to agree with Pistorius in his disputation on the Justification of Catholics, chapter 2, thesis 2, where he says that justification consists of two things: first, in the remission or expulsion of sin; second, in the infusion and acquisition of righteousness. Just as heating, he says, by which someone becomes hot from being cold, contains two parts, the driving out of cold and the acquisition of heat. And in this it differs from the justification of our first parents and the angels, which consisted solely in the infusion of grace, but not in the remission of sin.

But Costerus disagrees with this on page 261, and Bellarmine in book 2, chapter 20, although this disagreement does not seem to be so great. For Bellarmine himself admits in the said place that there are two terms of that motion which is called justification, or two effects of the same cause. For justification, as the Council defines it, is the translation of a man from that state in which he is born a son of the first Adam into the state of adoption as sons of God. However, according to him, this translation cannot happen unless a man ceases to be ungodly through the remission of sin, and begins to be godly through the infusion of righteousness. But they differ only in this, that Bellarmine thinks inherent righteousness alone is the formal cause of justification, by which both sins are remitted and we are righteous; but Becanus and others maintain that the formal cause is twofold, and that for one reason sins are remitted, namely on account of the imputed merit of Christ, and for another reason we are righteous, namely on account of inherent righteousness. Bellarmine argues thus: Just as air, when it is illuminated by the sun, by the same light which it receives, ceases to be dark and begins to be bright, so also a man, through the same righteousness given and infused by the Sun of righteousness, ceases to be unrighteous, the light of grace evidently deleting the darkness of sins, and begins to be righteous, with the light of righteousness itself surely succeeding the darkness of sins. Hence therefore it seems to follow that they differ not so much in the thing itself as in the formal term,

XV. But that it may appear that these are not bare and mere logomachies, we shall consider the opinion of the Papists more accurately, as the Council of Trent, Bellarmine, Costerus, and Becanus have proposed it. The opinion of the Council of Trent stands thus, as is evident from the Examination of the same instituted by Chemnitz. In all natural changes, certain things precede which prepare the subject to receive the form: So also in this spiritual change of a sinful man, certain dispositions precede, by which a man is prepared to receive the new form of righteousness. For thus Canon 9, Session 6, states: If anyone shall say that the ungodly is justified by faith alone, in such wise that he does not cooperate to obtain the grace of justification, and that it is not necessary that he be prepared and disposed by the motion of his own will, let him be anathema. But by these dispositions and preparations the Tridentine Fathers do not understand that manner and order which is necessary in the repentance of a sinful man. For it is necessary that contrition precede justification, that is, a serious acknowledgment of sins, terrors of conscience, and a purpose to cast off crimes: it is necessary that faith be added, which by true confidence apprehends Christ and determines that sins are forgiven to it by his merit. If they understood this order by preparations, we would not disagree with them so much. For Luther also says in the 3rd chapter to the Galatians: That the Law in its true office is a minister and preparer for grace, because it is useful for this, that grace may have access to us. Hosius, however, explains what the Tridentines understood by preparations, namely, nothing else than what the Scholastics noted by merit of congruity, just as Chemnitz demonstrates this in Exam. Conc. Trid. pages 156, 157. Therefore they think those preparations are meritorious, because God infuses grace into anyone doing what is in him, and who is thereby sufficiently disposed for the reception of grace, on account of the merit of congruity. For it seems congruous to them that God should bestow His grace upon a man doing what is in him. And in this way they determine that faith justifies, namely, not in the capacity of an instrument apprehending the merit of Christ, but rather in the capacity of a disposition and preparation. For Andradius expressly writes that the power of justifying is attributed to faith in the Holy Scriptures, because it prepares, fortifies, and supports the mind for receiving righteousness. For just as in philosophy, the action of virtue is born in προαιρέσει [moral choice], but this arises from knowledge: so they say that righteousness is a habit of the will, but the will is not carried toward the unknown, but is moved by the knowing faculty; therefore they think faith is required for justification as something directing the will, so that it may elicit the motions of hope and love, by which it may be so prepared and disposed that it may merit the infusion of justification by congruity. By faith, therefore, they understand only historical knowledge and bare assent, by which we know in general and determine that those things which have been revealed concerning God and His will are true, not only in Scripture, but also through the unwritten traditions of the Roman Church.

XVI. But that we may know how many and what kind of acts of preparation are established, Gabriel Biel enumerates them thus in lib. 1, distinct. 14, quaest. 2. The will, he says, presupposes acts of the intellect in its own acts. 1. It is therefore necessary that an act of faith precede, by which the abomination of sin is apprehended, and that it is the wages of sin. 2. Thence follows fear of the wrath of God and the fire of hell. 3. Thence sins begin to displease with a certain detestation. And this

Latin:

I. Quod Athanasius olim dicebat, Veritatis viam semper simplicem, incredulitatis autem multa esse diverticula da, illud etiam ex hac cum Pontificijs controversia satis perspicuum evadit. Non enim omnes unius & eiusdem semper fuerunt, & sunt sententiæ sed errores suos nunc hoc, nunc alio modo proposuêre & palliauêre. Recensebimus ergo primùm varias eorú de Iustificatione formali opiniones, deinde, quid à Iesu Vvitis hodie plerumque docetur, adnotabimus.

IX. Petrus Lombardus vt charitatem posset constituere formam iustificationis, disputat l. 3. sen. dist. 27. lit. C. Eam non esse qualitatem aliquam in nobis, quia omnia nostra imperfecta sint, sed esse ipsum Spiritum sanctum. Atque hinc videtur promanasse Iohannis Cochlæi argumentum; Certum est, Deum nos iustificare. Sed Deus est charitas, non fides. Ergo charitas, non fides, iustificat. Quæ conclusio, quantum ad fidem attinet, contradicit assertioni Apostolicæ. Rom. 3. v. 28. Colligimus fide iustificari hominem absq; operibus.

Talis etiam videtur fuisse speculatio Osiandri. Cùm enim vellet iustitiam coram Deo esse aliquid nobis inhærens, & consideraret pollutionem & imperfectionem inhærentis novitatis, confugit ad iustitiam Dei essentialem.

X. Alij, inter quos est Gropperus, dicunt, opera charitatis iustificare, non, quia nostra sunt, sed quia profecta sunt à S. S. vel quia tincta sanguine Christi. Verùm hanc sententiam de actuali seu actiua iustitia ex professo refutat Bellarm. l. 2. de iust. c. 16.

Hosius dicit, opera charitatis esse quidem imperfecta, sed habitum charitatis in credentibus esse perfectum & illam etiam formam iustitiæ nostræ. Sed hoc manifestè falsum est. Habitus enim charitatis spectat ad renovationem voluntatis, quæ de die in diem mutatur, & manet vetustas carnis mortificandæ per totam vitam, ideoq́; charitatis habitus non est perfectus, aliàs posset impleri mandatum, Diliges Deum tuum ex toto corde, quod ipsum tamen negat Lomb. l. 3. dist. 27.

XI. Alberto Pighio & Auctoribus antetitdogmatis Colonienfis Bellarminus l. 3. de iustific. cap. 2. hanc tribuit sententiam, quod docuerint, formalem causam Iustificationis duplicem esse, iustitiam nostram inhærentem, & iustitiam Christi imputatam; seu remissionem peccati, & infusionem gratiæ. In hac quoque sententia videtur fuisse Georgius Cassander in Consultat. sua, vbi scribit iustificationem non consistere in sola peccati remissione, sed simul etiam in renouatione. Verùm Bellarminus asserit, anathema à Tridentinis dictum esse ijs, qui statuunt nos per Christi iustitiã esse iustos formaliter. Et vrget hoc argumentum, Formalis causa iustificationis est vnica secundum decretum Conci-lij Tridentini. Ergò non potest esse duplex.

XII. Hoc ipsum opponimus nos quoque Iohanni Pistorio, cuius hæc est sententia de Iust. th. germ. 65. Semel verum est, inquit ille, iustificationem afferre remissionem omnium antegressorum peccatorum, sicut Paulus ait Rom. 3. ver. 21. Sed hoc non sufficit, nec oportet propter declarationem vnicæ partis alterum omitti, th. 66. Quod autem vocabulum iustificationis non tantùm remissionem peccatorum significet, sed etiam renouationem mentis & viuificationem interioris totius hominis, aliquot dictis Scripturæ ostendemus & th. 88. Hæ duæ operationes sc. remissio peccatorum & infusio gratiæ, quæ vt priuatio & forma, siue corruptio & gratia opponuntur, producunt vnum effectum, qui in Scriptura dicitur iustificatio: quâ homo non tantùm remissionem peccatorum, sed etiam virtutem impetret peccatis resistendi, & qua formaliter in ipso an vnd in ihm selbst iustus sit.

XIII. Non autem hoc loco portentum istud Pistorianum fusiùs examinare volumus de priuatione & forma concurrentibus, ad constituendam iustificationem: Remissio sanè peccatorum non est priuatio seu corruptio, vt somniat Pistorius, sed ipsum peccatũ priuatio est iustitię. Vnde peccati remissio nõ priuatio, sed priuationis sublatio est, neq; corruptio, sed vera est regeneratio. Et quis vnquam fando audiuit, ex priuatione & forma conjunctis vnum produci effectum? Imo, qui fieri potest, vt priuatio & forma coniungantur, cùm sint opposita, quorum posito vno, alterum tolli necessum est?

XIV. Pistorio videtur assentire Becanus, in disputatione de Iustific. Catholicorum cap. 2. th. 2. vbi ait, iustificationem consistere in duobus, primò in remissione seu expulsione peccati? Secundò in infusione & acquisitione iustitiae. Sicut calefactio, inquit, qua quis ex frigido fit calidus, continet duas partes, depulsionem frigoris & acquisitionem caloris. Et in hoc differt à iustificatione primorum Parentum & Angelorum, quae constabat solâ infusione gratiae, non autem peccati remissione.

Sed ab hoc dissentit Costerus p. 261. Et Bellarm. lib. 2. cap. 20. quamuis haec dissensio non adeò magna esse videatur. Nam fatetur ipse Bellarminus d. l. duos esse terminos eius motus, qui dicitur iustificatio, siue duos effectus eiusdem causae. Iustificatio enim definiente Concilio, est translatio hominis ab eo statu, in quo nascitur filius primi Adami in statum adoptionis filiorum Dei. Non potest autem iuxta ipsum, haec translatio fieri; nisi homo per remissionem peccati desinat esse impius, & per infusionem iustitiae incipiat esse pius. In hoc verò solùm dissentiunt, quod Bellarminus putat, iustitiam inhaerentem solam esse formalem causam iustificationis, quâ & peccata remittantur, & nos iusti simus: Becanus verò & alij statuunt, formalem causam esse duplicem, &amp; propter aliud remitti peccata, videlicet propter Christi meritum imputatum, propter aliud nos esse iustos, videlicet propter iustitiam inhaerentem. Bellarminus ita disferit: Sicut aër cùm illustratur à Sole, per idem lumen, quod recipit, desinit esse tenebrosus, & incipit esse lucidus, sic etiam homo per eandem iustitiam, à Sole iustitiae donatam atque infusam, desinit esse iniustus, delente videlicet lumine gratiæ tenebras peccatorum, & incipit esse justus, succedente nimirum tenebris peccatorum ipsâ luce justitiæ. Hinc igitur sequi videtur, non tàm in re, quàm in termino formali ipsos dissentire,

XV. Verùm vt appareat, non nudas & meras esse λογομαχίας, sententiam Pontificiorum accuratius considerabimus, prout eam proposuit Concilium Tridentinum, Bellarminus, Costerus & Becanus. Sententia Concilij Tridentini ita habet, quemadmodum patet ex ejusdem Examine à Chemnitio instituto. In omnibus mutationibus naturalibus, antecedunt quædam, quæ subjectum præparant ad suscipiendam formam: Ita etiam in mutatione hac spirituali hominis peccatoris præcedunt quædam dispositiones, quibus homo præparatur ad suscipiendam nouam justitiæ formam. Ita enim habet Canon 9. Sess. 6. Si quis dixerit, solâ fide impium justificari, quod ad justificationis gratiam consequendam non cooperetur, & nullâ ex parte necesse esse, eum suæ voluntatis motu præparari atque disponi, anathema sit. Per has verò dispositiones & præparationes Tridentini Paterculi non intelligunt istum modum & ordinem, qui in pœnitentiâ hominis peccatoris necessarius est. Oportet enim ante justificationem præcedere contritionem, hoc est, seriam agnitionem peccatorum, pavores conscientiæ, propositum abjiciendi scelera: oportet accedere fidem, quæ verâ fiduciâ Christum apprehendat, & sibi peccata ejus merito condonari statuat. Si hunc ordinem per præparationes intelligerent, non vsque adeo ab ijs dissentiremus. Nam & Lutherus inquit in. 3. c. ad Galatas: Legem in vero suo officio esse ministram, & præparatricem ad gratiam, quia ad hoc prosit, vt gratia possit aditum ad nos habere. Hosius verò explicat, quid Tridentini per præparationes intellexerint, nempè nil aliud, quàm quod Scholastici per meritum congrui notârunt, quemadmodum hoc deducit Chemnitius in Exam. m. pag. 156. 157. Illas ergò præparationes putant esse meritorias, quia Deus cuilibet facienti, quod in se est, & per hoc sufficienter disposito ad susceptionem gratiæ, infundit gratiam propter meritum congrui. Congruum enim ipsis videtur vt homini facienti quod in se est, Deus suam largiatur gratiam. Atque hoc modo fidem iustificare statuunt, videlicet non sub ratione instrumenti apprehendentis meritum Christi, sed potiùs sub ratione dispositionis & præparationis. Expressè enim scribit Andradius, iustificando vim in sacris literis, fidei tribui, quia animum ad excipiendam iustitiam præparet, præmuniat & præfulciat. Sicut enim in Philosophia, actio virtutis nascitur in προαιρέσει, hæc verò oritur ex scientia: Ita dicunt, quòd iustitia sit habitus voluntatis, voluntas verò non fertur in incognitum, sed mouetur à potentia cognoscente, ideò fidem putant requiri, ad iustificationem, tanquam quoddam dirigens voluntatem, vt eliciat motus spei & dilectionis, quibus ita præparetur & disponatur, vt de congruo mereatur infusionem iustificationis. Per fidem igitur intelligunt historicam tantum notitiam & nudum assensum, quo in genere cognoscimus, & statuimus vera esse, quæ de Deo & voluntate eius reuelata sunt, non tantùm in Scriptura, verùm etiam per Traditiones non scriptas Ecclesiæ Romanæ.

XVI. Vt verò sciamus, quot & quales actus præparationis constituantur, sic illas enumerat Gabriel Biel lib. 1. distinct. 14. quæst. 2. Voluntas, inquit, in actibus suis præsupponit actus intellectus, 1. Oportet igitur actum fidei præcedere, quo apprehendatur peccati abominatio, & quòd sit stipendium peccati 2. Inde sequitur timor iræ Dei & gehennæ incendij, 3. Inde peccata incipiunt displicere cum quadam detestatione. Et hæc dispo-


### Quaestio I: disposition is of congruity, not immediate, nor sufficient, but very remote

disposition is of congruity, not immediate, nor sufficient, but very remote. 4. Faith turns itself to the consideration of divine mercy, and establishes that God is ready to remit debts, through the infusion of charity, to those who are sufficiently prepared and disposed. 5. From that consideration follows an act of hope, through which he begins to desire GOD, as the highest good. 6. From that act of hope one ascends to loving GOD above all things from natural powers, 7. From that love is elicited another displeasure and detestation of sin, not on account of the fear of damnation: but on account of GOD finally loved above all things. 8. These acts are followed by a purpose of amendment. And this at length is the merit of congruity sufficient, or the immediate sufficient and final disposition for the infusion of grace.

XVII. Hence therefore it appears what the Council seeks by those preparations of its, namely that some merit of ours should be established, as if that were required for obtaining justification. For they say that this so leans upon the mercy of God, that nevertheless divine justice must be preserved, nor should salvation be conferred without some merit of ours, or without our own dignity. For although in chapter 8 it is said that none of those things which precede justification, whether it be faith or works, merit the grace of justification itself, nevertheless they understand this only of the merit of condignity, but not of congruity, as is evident from the explanation of Andradius noted by Chemnitz, page 158. And just as dispositions are absolutely necessary for the bringing forth of a form, so because the Tridentine Fathers call the works of the faithful preparations, it would follow that our little works are altogether necessary and most useful for justification. Let this therefore be held first, that the Tridentines establish meritorious dispositions.

XVIII. But after a man has sufficiently disposed and prepared himself for future justification, there then God, according to the Papists, sends in and infuses into the human heart a habit of justice, by which sins are thoroughly washed away and extinguished, and man is rendered formally just, and is accepted for eternal life. For they decree that justification is not merely the imputation of the justice of Christ, or merely the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inner man. For in canon 7 they decree thus: The sole formal cause is the justice of God, not that by which He Himself is just, but that by which He makes us just, by which, namely, being gifted by Him, we are renewed in the spirit of our mind, and are not only reputed, but are truly named and are just, receiving justice in ourselves, which the Holy Spirit distributes to each as He wills, and according to the proper disposition and preparation of each. This very thing they soon explain more fully, when they say that charity is inherent justice. And that this is that white and immaculate robe which the reborn must wear before the tribunal of Christ in order to have eternal life. Without dissimulation, therefore, they take away from Christ, and attribute to our charity this, that we are justified by it.

XIX. They say furthermore in canon 7 that Christ by His most holy passion did not merit this, that the mercy of God, on account of that satisfaction and obedience of Christ, should absolve us from the sentence of damnation, receive us into grace, and adopt us as sons, but they say this is the whole merit of Christ, that on account of it the mercy of God infuses into us a new quality of inherent justice, that is, charity. They think, therefore, that we are immediately absolved from sins not on account of the obedience of Christ, but on account of our charity, and are accepted for eternal life. But as for what Paul says, that we are justified by grace, they interpret this in such a way that not on account of our preceding merits from worthiness, but on account of Christ, that habit of charity is freely given and infused into us, on account of which we are pronounced just before the tribunal of God for eternal life.

XX. That, moreover, is to be noted, how they consider justification to consist simultaneously in the remission of sins. Andradius explains this in truth as follows: Because he cannot be called just who is entirely defiled by the stains of sins, therefore God infuses charity into man, by the force and power of which all crimes are washed away, etc. This is the very thing which the Sententiaries say, that for the remission of guilt the infusion of grace is required, that is, of charity through which sin is expelled, just as for the expulsion of darkness the illumination of the air is required. Whoever therefore wishes to receive the remission of sins, he, according to the opinion of the Council, must interpose between his sins and the offense of God not the satisfaction of Christ, but his own inherent charity, and only then believe that God, having remitted the offense, is certainly appeased and propitious to him, when charity has so expelled sin that every trace of it has been abolished in man. Therefore, the remission of sin is not for them the removal of guilt, but the extinction and expulsion of the very ἀνομία (lawlessness) and deformity itself, which is not done immediately on account of the merit and satisfaction of Christ, but on account of infused charity. For Christ, according to them, did not merit for us the grace and mercy of God so that He might immediately forgive sins to those who believe, but rather so that charity might be infused, by which we are formally just, sins are remitted, and are utterly extinguished. But where is this founded in the Scriptures? Is it not said that Christ Himself bore our sins and satisfied for them by His death? Is not the supreme power of the merit of Christ thus taken away and ascribed to our works?

XXI. Nevertheless, Bellarmine fiercely defends this very opinion of the Council. In Book 2, chapter 2, he writes that we are justified formally on account of the newness inherent in us, not on account of the merit of CHRIST, which cannot be inherent. He also adds that by this same infused justice we are both freed from sins and formally constituted righteous, just as one and the same light both drives the darkness from the air and truly makes the air bright at the same time, he argues in chapter 15, that it is habitual righteousness alone through which we are named and are formally righteous, but that actual righteousness, that is, works, do indeed justify as St. James justified by works, but meritoriously, not formally.

XXII. Therefore, briefly, this is the opinion of the Council of Trent and Bellarmine, that the proximate, complete, and immediate cause of justification, by which both sins are remitted and we are constituted righteous, is the infused habit of charity, but the merit of Christ is the remote cause, on account of which sins are not directly remitted and we are righteous, but on account of which the habit of charity is infused, which both takes away sins and makes us truly righteous. Costerus determines the same, whose opinion concerning the twofold mode of preparation, concerning faith not justifying alone, and concerning the infusion of righteousness, see from page 261 to 271. For there is no need that we transcribe his individual words here.

XXIII. Becanus proposes the Papist doctrine thus, chapter 1, thesis 3; he makes a twofold justification: the first, which consists in the acquisition of righteousness; and the second, which consists in the increase of the same; the first is gratuitous, the second is from the merits of good works; that Paul speaks of the first, and James of the second. The first justification itself is in turn twofold, chapter 2, thesis 1. The one, by which someone is made righteous from not righteous, in which way the first parents in Paradise and the angels in their creation were justified. The other, by which someone is made righteous from unrighteous, in which way sinners are justified. Alphonsus Salmeron, in volume 13, page 243, adds a third species of justification, namely, when someone is absolved by the sentence of a Judge and pronounced righteous, which does not happen to the righteous until after this life, and that Paul looked to that, Romans 2, verse 13, when he speaks in the future tense: The doers of the law shall be justified. But Becanus says that the second justification is the translation from the state of sin into the state of grace, and consists both in the expulsion of sin and in the infusion of justice. For this, he teaches that certain dispositions are required in chapter 3, among which he numbers general faith, fear of divine judgment, hope of divine mercy, love toward God, and detestation of sin, with the annexed purpose of a better life and the observance of the commandments of God. When these dispositions are present, he says that habitual justice is immediately infused, which is nothing else than justifying grace, or grace making one pleasing, and he thinks it matters little whether one makes it distinct from charity or not: but that this very thing removes, abolishes, and extinguishes sin: and therefore he judges that for the true remission of sin, an extrinsic, as he calls it, condonation of God is not sufficient, but that there is need of some change which by its own nature is repugnant to sin and cannot consist with it, chapter 5, thesis 5. Furthermore, in thesis 9, he affirms that that very grace or habitual justice is not created, nor infused by creating, but rather is drawn out from the potentiality of the soul, as from matter, not indeed by natural potentiality but by obediential.

XXIV. And this is the opinion of the Papists concerning the justification of a sinful man, the sum and as it were a certain compendium of which we propose thus: For justification three things are required: disposition, infusion of justice, and expulsion of sin. The disposition is meritorious according to congruity, as it pleases some, or at least is entirely necessary. In infused justice consists the very form of justification: for because of that, both sins are expelled and we are constituted just: but the merit of Christ is not the proximate cause of the remission that has been made, but only justifies meritoriously, because he merited charity, by which we are justified: Faith also does not justify by way of an instrument, but only as a disposition, and preparatorily,

Latin:

ficio de congruo, non immediata, nec sufficiens, sed valdè remota 4. Fides conuertit se ad confiderationem diuinæ misericordiæ, & statuit Deum paratum remittere debita, per infusionem charitatis, illis qui sufficienter sunt præparati & dispositi. 5. Ex illa consideratione sequitur actus spei, per quem incipit DEVM concupiscere, vt summum bonum. 6. Ex illo actu spei adscenditur ad diligendum DEVM super omnia ex naturalibus, 7. Ex illa dilectione elicitur alia displicentia & detestatio peccati, non ob timorem damnationis: sed propter DEVM finaliter super omnia dilectum. 8. Istos actus sequitur propositum emendationis Et hoc tandem est meritum congrui sufficiens, seu immediata sufficiens & vltima dispositio ad infusionem gratiæ.

XVII. Hinc igitur apparet, quid Concilium suis illis præparationibus quærat, nempè vt stabiliatur meritum aliquod nostrum, ac si illud requireretur ad consequendam iustificationem. Dicunt enim hanc ita inniti misericordiæ Dei, vt tamen salva esse debeat iustitia divina, nec conferatur salus sine nostro aliquo merito, vel sine dignitate propriâ. Nam quamvis cap. 8. dicatur, nihil eorum, quæ iustificationem præcedunt, siue fides sit, siue opera, ipsam iustificationis gratiam promereri, attamen hoc tantum de merito condigni, non autem congrui intelligunt, vt patet ex Andradij explicatione à Chemnitio annotata, pagina 158. Et quemadmodum dispositiones prorsus necessariæ sunt ad eductionem formæ, sic quia Tridentini Patres opera fidelium vocant præparationes, sequeretur nostras opellas omninò necessarias & maxime vtiles esse ad iustificationem. Hoc igitur primum teneatur, Tridentinos statuere dispositiones meritorias.

XVIII. Postquam autem sufficienter homo sese disposuit & præparavit ad futuram iustificatione, ibi tum Devs, juxta Pontificios, immittit & infundit humano cordi justitiae habitum, quo peccata penitùs eluantur & extinguantur, homoque formaliter justus reddatur, & ad vitam æternam acceptetur. Statuunt enim, justificationem non esse solam imputationem justitiæ Christi, vel solam peccatorum remissionem, sed & sanctificationem & renovationem interioris hominis. Nam cano: 7. ita decernunt. Vnica formalis causa est justitia DEI, non quâ ipse justus est, sed quâ nos justos facit, quâ videlicet ab eo donati, renouamur spiritu mentis nostræ, & non modò reputamur, sed verè justi nominamur & sumus, justitiam in nobis recipientes, quam Spiritus sanctus partitur singulis prout vult, & secundum propriam cujusque dispositionem & præparationem. Hoc ipsum mox pleniùs explicant, cùm dicunt, charitatem esse justitiam inhærentem. Et hanc esse candidam & immaculatam illam stolam, quam renati perferre debeant ante tribunal Christi ut habeant vitam æternam. Sine dissimulatione igitur Christo adimunt, & nostræ charitati hoc tribuunt, quod eâ justificemur.

XIX. Dicunt insuper cano: 7. Christum sua sanctissima passione meruisse non hoc, ut misericordia Dei propter illam Christi satisfactionẽ & obedientiam nos à sententia damnationis absolvat, recipiat in gra iam adoptet in filios, sed hoc dicunt totum esse meritum Christi, quòd propter illud misericordia Dei infundat nobis nouam qualitatem justitiæ inhærentis, hæc est, charitatem. Putant ergò nos non propter Christi obedientiam, sed propter nostram charitatem à peccatis proximè absolui, & ad vitam æternam acceptari. Quòd verò Paulus dicit, gratia nos justificari, hoc ita interpretantur, quòd non propter nostra præcedentia merita ex condigno; sed propter Christum gratis nobis donetur & infundatur habitus ille charitatis, propter quam coram tribunali Dei justi pronunciemur ad vitam æternam.

XX. Illud verò insuper notandum quomodò exæstiment iustificationē simul cōnsistere in remissione peccatorum. Ita vero hoc explicat Andradius: Quia iustus is dici non potest, qui totum peccatorum maculis est inquinatus, ideò Deum infundere homini charitatem, cuius vi & potentia crimina omnia eluantur &c. Hoc ipsum est quod Sententiarij dicunt, ad remifsionem culpæ requiri infusionem gratiæ, hoc est, charitatis per quam peccatum expellatur, sicut ad expulsionem tenebrarum requiritur illuminatio aërisi Qui igitur vult remissionem peccatorum accipere, is juxta Concilii sententiam, interponere debet inter peccata sua & offensam Dei non satisfactionē Christi, sed inhærentē suam charitatem, & tum demum credat, Deum remissâ offensâ sibi certò placatum & propitium esse, quando charitas peccatum ita expulit, vt omne eius vestigium in homine abolitum sit. Peccati proindè remissio non est ipsis sublatio reatus, sed extinctio & expulsio ipsius etiam ἀνομίας & deformitatis, quæ proximè non fiat propter Christi meritum & satisfactionem, sed propter charitatem intusam. Non enim Christus juxta ipsos meruit nobis gratiam & misericordiã Dei, vt immediatè credentibus dimitat peccata, sed potius, vt charitas infundatur, quâ formaliter iusti simus, peccata remittantur, & prorsus extinguantur. Vbinam verò hoc in Scripturis fundatum? Annon Christus ipse peccata nostra sustulisse, & pro ijs morte suâ satisfećisse dicitur? Annon ita summa vis merito Christi adimitur, & nostris operlis asscribitur?

XXI. Hanc ipsam nihilominus Concilii sententiam acriter propugnat Bellarminus. Lib. 2. cap. 2. scribit, nos iustificari formaliter propter novitatem nobis inhærentem, non propter meritum CHRISTI, quod inhærere non potest. Addit etiam, quòd câdem iustitiâ infusâ & liberemur à peccatis, & constituamur formaliter iusti, sicut vnum & idem lumen, tum tenebras ex aère pellit, tum verò lucidum simul aerem efficit, capite 15. disputat, solam esse habitualem iustitiam, per quam formaliter iusti nominentur & simus, iustitiam verò actualem, hoc est, opera verè iustificare quidem vt A. Iacobus loquitur, cùm ait capite 2. Ex operibus hominem iustificari, sed meritoriè, non formaliter.

XXII. Proinde breuiter Concilij Tridentini & Bellarmini hæc est opinio, quod proxima, completa & immediata causa iustificationis, quâ & peccataremittuntur, & nos justi constituimur, sit infusus charitatis habitus, meritum Christi autem sit causa remota, ob quam non peccata prórsus remittantur, & nos iusti simus, sed ob quam charitatis habitus infundatur, qui & peccata tollat, & nos verè iustos faciat. Idem statuit Costerus, cuius sententiam de modo præparationis duplici, de fide non sola iustificante,de infusione Iustitiæ vide à pagina 261. vsque ad 271. Nec enim opus est, vt hìc singula ipsius verba asscribamus.

XXIII. Becanus doctrinam Pontificiam itą proponit, capite. 1. the. 3. facit duplicem iustificationem, primam, quæ consistat in acquisitione iustitiæ; & secundam, quæ consistat in augmento eiusdem; primam esse gratuitam, secundam ex meritis bonorum operum; de prima Paulum, de secunda loqui Iacobum. Prima iustificatio ipsi vicissim duplex est, cap. 2. thes. 1. Altera, quâ quis ex non justo fiat iustus, quo pacto primi parentes in Paradiso & Angeli in sua creatione iustificati sint. Altera, quâ quis ex iniusto fit iustus, quo pacto peccatores iustificantur. Alphonsus Salmeron tomo 13. pagina 243. tertiam iustificationis speciem adijcit, eam nempè, cùm quis sententiâ Iudicis absoluitur & pronunciatur iustus, quæ non nisi post hanc vitam iustis contingat, & ad illam respexisse Paulum, Rom, 2. versu 13. quansto inquit de futuro: Factores legis iustificabuntur. Iustificationem verò secundam dicit Becanus esse translationem à statu peccati in statum gratiæ, & consisteretum in expulsione peccati, tum in infusione iustitiæ. Ad hanc certas docet requiri dispositiones capite 3. inter quas numerat fidem generalem, timorem iudicij diuini, spem diuinæ misericordiæ, amorem erga Deum, & detestationem peccati, cum annexo proposito vitæ melioris & obseruationis mandatorum Dei. Quibus dispositionibus præsentibus, statim infundi ait iustitiam habitualem, quæ nihil sit aliud, quàm gratia iustificans, seu gratia gratum faciens, quam à charitate distinctam facere vel non, parum referre putat: hanc ipsam autem peccatum tollere, abolere & extinguere: ideoque censet ad veram peccati remissionem, non sufficere extrinsecam, vt vocat, Dei condonationem, sed opus esse aliquâ mutatione, quæ ex natura sua repugnet peccato, & cum illo consistere non possit, capite 5. thesi 5. Porrò thesi. 9. affirmat, illam ipsam gratiam vel iustitiam habitualem, non creari, nec creando infundi, sed potjùs educi è potentia animi, tanquam materia, non quidem potentiâ naturali sed obedientialli.

XXIV. Atque hæc est Pontificiorum de Iustificatione hominis peccatoris sententia, cuius summam & quasi quoddam compendium ita proponimus: Ad iustificationem tria requiruntur, dispositio, iustitiæ infusio, & peccati expulsio. Dispositio est meritoria secundum congruum, vt nonnullis placet, vel saltem omninò necessaria, In iustitia infusa consistit ipsa iustificationis forma: ob istam enim & peccata expelluntur, & nos iusti constituimur: Meritum Christi autem non est causa factæ remissionis proxima, sed solùm meritoriè iustificat, quia promeruit charitatem, quâ iustificamur: Fides etiam non iustificat per modum instrumenti, sed duntaxat dispositi, uè & præparatoriè,


### Quaestio I: XXV. Whence furthermore it appears that there is not a mere λογομαχία (war of words)…

XXV.

Whence furthermore it appears that there is not a mere λογομαχία (war of words) between us and the Papists, but that many and most serious errors are cherished by them. For 1. they establish that dispositions are meritorious, and thus they attribute not a little to works, contrary to Scripture. 2. They deny that faith alone justifies, and they think that it justifies only by way of disposition, but not by way of an instrument. 3. They define faith by mere knowledge without filial trust. 4. They make a twofold justification, first and second, which distinction, however, has no foundation in the Scriptures, and produces the greatest confusion, mixing justification with sanctification, and the latter with the former. 5. They clearly evacuate the merit of Christ, inasmuch as they do not think it removes sins, but only that it has procured this for us, that God infuses righteousness, which removes sin, which however is contrary to the whole of Scripture. 6. Of imputation, of which the sacred writings speak everywhere, they do not make even a mention by a word. 8. They say we are formally and solely righteous by renewal and infused holiness, when nevertheless all these things are imperfect and only begun, and when likewise good works follow the justified, and do not precede the one to be justified. 8. They think that sins are entirely removed, and so extinguished, that man after justification is free from sin, (since remission for them is not only absolution from punishment, but also the eradication and annihilation of the guilt itself,) when nevertheless the whole of Scripture, and the examples of all the saints, say exactly the contrary. And these are indeed most serious errors, from which it appears how the Papists dissent from us; and that this controversy is not a mere λογομαχία (war of words), but concerns the very foundation of our faith, which being shaken, we can in no way be saved.

XXVI. Re-

XXVI. It now remains that we recite the orthodox opinion of our Churches, opposed to the opinion of the Papists, and likewise explain it somewhat more fully. But before this is done, we shall remove two most common calumnies, with which the Romanists are accustomed to burden our doctrine concerning the gratuitous justification of a sinful man. The one is that we teach a merely putative righteousness, where we are indeed reputed as righteous, but are not righteous. Andradius certainly calls imputed righteousness a most senseless madness. Stapleton, in his Apostolic Antidotes, calls it a phantom of the Lutheran brain. To Bellarmine, it is imaginary, putative, fictitious righteousness. But this is a most manifest calumny, since imputed righteousness is true righteousness, although it does not inhere. For just as we believe that we have most truly satisfied for sins, because Christ satisfied for us: so we are most truly righteous, because the righteousness of CHRIST is imputed to us. Therefore these differ most greatly, to be imputatively and putatively righteous. These do not substitute for one another, but rather exclude and remove each other. The other is that we teach that sins are indeed forgiven to believers, but that they are not renewed, not changed. But we teach both, namely that Christ by his passion merited for us not only the remission of sins, but also this, that on account of his merit the Holy Spirit is given to us, that we may be renewed in the spirit of our mind. We say indeed that these benefits of the Son of God are joined, so that when we are reconciled, the Spirit of renewal is also given at the same time; but for that reason we do not confuse them, but distinguish them, indeed in such a way that we assign to each its own place, order, and property, as we have learned from Scripture, namely that reconciliation or remission of sins precedes, and renewal follows thereafter; on account of which certainly sins cannot be forgiven to us, 1. Since it follows the remission of sins. 2. Since on account of its own imperfection it cannot stand in the judgment of God. Meanwhile, we willingly confess that every justified person is at the same time renewed and, as it were, changed, but he is not absolved from punishment on account of this newness, nor is he pronounced righteous, but rather on account of the Mediator apprehended by faith.

XXVII. We therefore expressly condemn the blasphemy of Simon Magus, who feigned that it is free for men saved by faith to do whatever they wish: We condemn Basilides, who feigned that we are so saved by grace alone, through faith, that all actions of whatever kind, and indeed every lust, can be practiced indifferently. We condemn the Gnostics, who said that they are saved by knowledge alone, and that on account of the excellence of their faith they become so spiritual that they cannot fall from grace, whatever they may perpetrate. We condemn Aetius and Eunomius, whom Augustine in heresy 54 writes were so hostile to good morals that they asserted that the perpetration and perseverance in any sins whatsoever would harm no one, provided only that he was a participant in this faith which was taught by them.

For we know well that two extremes in this business of justification must be studiously avoided: Epicureanism and Pharisaism. For justification must be so ascribed to faith that we do not introduce Epicureanism and entirely abolish good works. So, in turn, good works must be defended, so that we do not introduce Pharisaism and ascribe justification itself to good works. Therefore, we do not deny the pursuit of good works at all, we do not abolish and deny the renewal of man, but we deny that our [salvation] consists in them.

XXIIX. These calumnies therefore being dispelled, we subjoin our opinion, which is this: Man is born entirely in sins, so that by nature he is a child of wrath, an enemy to God, and guilty of eternal damnation. these punishments, namely the wrath of God and eternal damnation, Christ has freed us by acting and suffering. But since no gift is both fruitful and salutary unless it is received, therefore faith is necessary if we wish to accept this grace. When, therefore, a man wishes to be justified, that is, to be absolved from the wrath of God and eternal damnation, and to be accepted into grace and to eternal life, it is asked what he ought to interpose between the wrath of God and his own sins: For he has not earned life, but death; it is asked, therefore, by what means he can be absolved from the punishment of death and thus be justified? Here, certainly, he cannot interpose novelty and good works, since he has none, and even if he had them, they would nonetheless be imperfect, and otherwise owed. The whole Scripture, therefore, cries out that man himself cannot make satisfaction for his sins, cannot stand in the judgment of God; but it is necessary that he apprehend that infinite and ἰσόῤῥοπον (equivalent) ransom of Christ the Mediator; on account of which apprehension it is imputed, just as if he himself had made satisfaction; on account of this satisfaction, he is absolved from punishment, and thus is justified, is accepted to eternal life, and is held as a Son of God. For justification comprises two things, absolution from punishment, and acceptance into grace: We are absolved from punishment because the satisfaction of Christ is imputed to us through faith: We are accepted into grace to eternal life because the obedience of Christ is imputed to us through faith. This is the very thing which others say, that a double imputation concurs in justification; not indeed differing in reality, but only distinguishing one act of justifying with respect to different terms; 1. affirmative, by which the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us, and negative, by which our unrighteousness is not imputed to us. Others express it thus; the mode of imputation is twofold, one στερητικὸς (privative), by which that which is present, or inherent, is not imputed; the other θετικὸς (positive), by which that which is not present, is imputed as if it were present. For God had threatened death to those who transgress, and had promised life to those who obey. But we all, who wish to be justified, are infected with sins and have deserved death, from which if we are to be absolved, it is necessary that either we ourselves, or another for us, make satisfaction. We ourselves cannot, and therefore Christ has made satisfaction for us, which satisfaction, in order that it may become ours, requires faith. Again, if we wish to be heirs of eternal life, it is required that we fulfill the law, either we ourselves, or another for us. Christ, however, fulfilled it, which fulfillment, if it is to be ours, in turn requires faith: Since therefore no other means is given by which we may apprehend the active and passive merit of Christ, hence it comes about that we are said to be justified by faith alone, and indeed not by way of any meritorious disposition, but rather by way of an instrument: For it is faith alone that apprehends and makes Christ's merit its own, through which apprehension our sins are remitted to us, yet in such a way that this remission is not an absolute deletion of sin (for if it is actual, it cannot be rendered undone from the fact, if it is original, it cannot be eradicated unless you destroy the nature), but a removal of the guilt, or a lifting of the penalty owed to sins.

XXIX. And from this it will be easy to judge what is the cause of justification: which, before it is explained, this distinction must first be noted: The formal cause either denotes the whole quiddity of a thing itself, or the cause of the quiddity, that by which a thing is what it is. For one is called a Metaphysical form, which implies the whole quiddity, such as humanity; another is a Logical form, which precisely posits the cause of the quiddity, such as rationality. If it denotes the whole quiddity, then we say the form of justification is the remission of sin, or absolution from the penalty of sin, and acceptance into grace for eternal life, on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. For in these consists our entire justifica-

know, according to that passage in Rom. 3:25, for the demonstration of his righteousness, Διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων, that he offers righteousness / in that / he forgives sin. Here our δικαίωσις is expressly said to be placed in the remission of sins. If by form you understand precisely not the whole quiddity, but only that by which a thing is what it is, I say this is nothing other than the merit of Christ imputed through faith, or the imputation of merit apprehended by faith. For if you ask, why are we absolved from the penalty of sin? And accepted into grace? The whole Scripture answers, because the passion and obedience of Christ is imputed through faith, as if we ourselves had satisfied for our sins.

Latin:

XXV.

Vnde porrò apparet, non meram esse λογομαχίαν inter nos & Pontificios, sed multos eosque grauissimos ab ijs foueri errores. Nam 1. statuunt dispositiones esse meritorias, atque sic operibus contra Scripturam haut parum affcribunt. 2 Fidem solam iustificare negant, eamque tantùm per dispositionis modum, non autem per rationem instrumenti iustificare arbitrantur. 3. Fidem definiunt per nudam sine filiali fiducia notitiam 4. Duplicem faciunt iustificationem, primam & secundam, quæ tamen distinctio in Scripturis nullum habet fundamentum, & maximam parit confusionem, iustificationem cum sanctificatione, & hanc cum illa permiscens. 5. Meritum Christi planè euacuant, quippè quod non arbitrantur peccata tollere, sed duntaxat nobis hoc conciliâsse, vt Deus infundat iustitiam, peccatum tollentem, quod tamen contra vniuersam est Scripturam. 6. Imputationis, de qua sacræ literæ passim loquuntur, nè verbo quidem mentionem faciunt. 8. Formaliter & vnicè nos iustos dicunt renouatione & infusâ sanctitate, cùm tamen hæc omnia sint imperfecta & nõ nisi inchoata, cùm itidem opera bona sequantur iustificatum, non præcedant iustificandum. 8. Arbitrantur peccata prorsus tolli, & ita extingui, vt homo post iustificationem liber sit à peccato, (siquidem remissio ipsis non tantum est absolutio à pœna, sed etiam eradicatio & annihilatio ipsius culpæ,) cùm tamen tota Scriptura, & omnium sanctorum exempla prorsus dicant contrarium. Et hæc sanè sunt errata grauissima, ex quibus apparet quomodo à nobis dissentiant Pontificij; & quod hæc controuersia non sit mera λογομαχία, sed concernat ipsum fidei nostræ fundamentum, quo labefactato saluari nullo modo possumus.

XXVI. Re-

XXVI. Restat iam, vt orthodoxam nostrarum Ecclesiarum sententiam, Pontificiorum opinioni oppositam, recitemus, & similiter nonnihil fusiùs explicemus. Antequam verò hoc fiat, duas vsitatissimas remouebimus calumnias, quibus Romanenses doctrinam nostram, de gratuita hominis peccatoris iustificatione pregrauare solent. Altera est, quòd putatiuam duntaxat doceamus iustitiam, vbi pro iustis quidem reputemur, sed iusti non simus. Andradius certè imputatã iustitiam vocat amentissimam insaniam. Stapletonius in Antidotis Apostolicis, spectrum nominat cerebri Lutherani. Bellarmino est iustitia imaginaria, putatiua, ficta. Verùm apertissima hæc est calũnia, quoniã imputatiua vera est iustitia, licèt non inhæreat. Sicut enim nos verissimè satisfecisse pro peccatis credimus, quia Christus pro nobis satisfecit: ita verissimè iusti sumus, quia iustitia CHRISTI nobis imputatur. Maximè ergò hęc differũt, esse imputatiuè & putatiuè iustum. Non hæc se inuicẽ ponũt, sed potiùs tollunt & remouẽt. Altera est, quòd doceamus, credentibus quidem remitti peccata, sed illos non renouari, non mutari. Verùm vtrumque docemus, nempè quòd Christus suâ passione meruerit nobis, non tantùm remissionem peccatorum, sed etiam hæc, quòd propter ipsius meritum detur nobis Spiritus S. vt renouemur Spiritu mentis nostræ. Hæc beneficia Filij Dei dicimüs quidem esse coniuncta, ita, vt quando reconciliamur, simul etiam detur Spiritus renouationis; ast propterea non confundimus illa, sed distinguimus, ita quidem, vt cuique suum locum, ordinem & suam proprietatem tribuamus, sicut ex Scriptura didicimus, nimirum vt reconciliatio seu remissio peccatorum præcedat, & sequatur deindè renouatio; ob quam certè peccata nobis remitti haud possunt, 1. Cùm peccatorum remissionem sequatur. 2. Cùm ob imperfectionent suam in iudicio Dei consistere nequeat. Interim libenter fatemur, omnem iustificatum simul renouari & quasi mutari, ob hanc verò nouitatem non absoluitur à poena, non iustus pronuntiatur, sed potiùs propter Mediatorem fide apprehensum.

XXVII. Damnamus igitur expressè Simonis Magi blasphemiam, qui finxit hominibus, fide saluatis, liberum esse, vt agant quæcunque velint: Damnamus Basilidem, qui finxit, ita nos solâ gratiâ, ex fide saluari, vt omnes qualecunque actiones, & quidem vniuersa libido indifferenter vsurpari possit. Damnamus Gnosticos, qui dixerunt, se saluari ex sola cognitione, & propter fidei excellentiam se adeo spirituales fieri, vt non possint gratiâ excidere, quicquid etiam perpetrent. Damnamus Aëtium & Eunomium, quos Augustinus hæresi 54. bonis moribus adeò inimicos fuisse scribit, vt asseuerarent, quòd nihil cuiquam obesset, quorumlibet perpetratio & perseuerantia peccatorum, si modò huius, quæ ab ipsis docebatur, fidei particeps esset.

Nos enim benè nouimus, duo extrema in hoc iustificationis negotio studiosè esse deuitanda, Epicureismum & Pharisæismum. Ita enim iustificatio adscribenda est fidei, nè Epicureismum introducamus, & bona opera prorsus tollamus. Ita vicissim defendenda sunt bona opera, nè Pharisæismum inuehamus, & bonis operibus ipsam adscribamus iustificationem. Non igitur studium bonorum operum omninò negamus, non tollimus & inficiamur renouationem hominis, sed in ijs nostram consistere damnatio[nem] imus inficias.

XXIIX. Calumnijs ergò istis dispulsis, nostram sententiam subiungimus, quæ hæc est: Nascitur homo totus in peccatis, ita, vt naturâ sit filius iræ, inimicus Deo, æternæ damnationis reus. Ab his pœnis, nimirum ira Dei & damnatione æterna, agendo & patiendo liberauit nos Christus. Quoniam verò nullum munus & frugiferum & salutare, nisi accipiatur, idcircò fide opus est, si hanc gratiam acceptare volumus. Quando igitur homo vult iustificari, hoc est, absolui ab ira Dei & damnatione æterna, atque in gratiam & ad vitam æternam acceptari, quæritur, quid interponere debeat inter iram Dei, & inter peccata sua: Non enim vitam meruit, sed mortem; quæritur proindè quâ ratione possit à pœnâ mortis absolui atque ita iustificari? Hic certè nouitatem & bona opera interponere nequit, cùm nulla habeat, & tametsi haberet, imperfecta nihilo minus forent, & aliàs debita. Vniuersa igitur clamat Scriptura, quòd homo ipse non possit satisfacere pro peccatis suis, non possit consistere in iudicio Dei; sed necesse sit, vt λύτρον illud infinitum & ἰσόῤῥοπον Christi Mediatoris apprehendat; ob quam apprehensionem imputatur, non secus ac si ipse satisfecisset; ob hanc satisfactionem, absoluitur à pœna, adeóque iustificatur, ad vitam æternam acceptatur, & pro Filio Dei habetur. Iustificatio enim duo complectitur, absolutionem à pœna, & acceptationem in gratiam: A pœna absoluimur, quia imputatur nobis per fidem Christi satisfactio: In gratiam ad vitam æternam acceptamur, quia imputatur nobis per fidem Christi obedientia. Hoc ipsum est, quod alij dicunt, in iustificatione concurrere duplicem imputationem; non quidem reipsâ differentem, sed tantùm distinguentem vnum iustificandi actum diuersorum terminorum respectu; 1. affirmatam, quâ Christi iustitia nobis imputatur, & negatam, quâ nostra iniustitia nobis non imputatur. Alij sic efferunt; Imputationis geminus est modus, vnus στερητικὸς, quo id quod adest, vel inest, non imputatur; alter θετικὸς, quo id, quod non inest, imputatur ac si adesset. Minatus enim erat Devs mortem delinquentibus, & promisserat vitam obedientibus. Nos verò omnes, qui iustificari volumus, peccatis infecti sumus & mortem promeruimus, à qua si absolui debeamus, necesse est, vt vel ipsi, vel pro nobis satisfaciat alius. Ipsi non possumus, ideoque pro nobis satisfecit Christus, quæ satisfactio, vt nostra fiat, fide opus est. Rursus si vitæ æternæ hæredes esse volumus, requiritur, vt legem impleamus, vel ipsi, vel pro nobis alius. Implevit autem Christus, quæ impletio si nostra esse debet, vicissim fide opus est: Quoniam igitur nullum aliud datur medium, quo Christi meritum activum & passivum apprehendamus, hinc fit, vt solâ fide iustificari dicamur, & quidem non per modum dispositionis alicuius meritoriæ, sed potiùs per modum instrumenti: Sola enim fides est, quæ apprehendit, & sibi propriam facit Christi meritum, per quam apprehensionem nobis remittuntur peccata, ita tamen, vt hæc remissio non sit peccati omnimoda deletio, (si enim actuale est, ex facto infectum reddi nequit, si originale, eradicari nequit, nisi naturam destruas) sed reatus ablatio, vel pœnæ peccatis debitæ sublatio.

XXIX. Atque hinc facilè erit iudicare, quæ sit causa iustificationis: quod antequam exponatur, hæc prius notanda est distinctio: Causa formalis vel notat ipsam totam rei quidditatem, vel causam quidditatis cam, per quam res est, id quod est. Nam alia dicitur, esse forma Metaphysica, quæ totam innuit quidditatem, vt humanitas; alia Logica, quæ præcisè ponit causam quidditatis, vt rationalitas. Si totam quidditatem notat, tunc dicimus iustificationis formam esse remissionem peccati, seu absolutionem à pœna peccati, & acceptionem in gratiam ad vitam æternam, propter Christi meritum fide apprehensum. In his enim consistit omnis nostra iustifica-

stio, iuxta illud Rom. 3. v. 25. ad ostensionem iustitiae, Διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων, dass er die Gerechtigkeit darbiete / in dem / dass er die Sůnde vergibt. Hic expressè δικαίωσις nostra in remissione peccatorum posita esse dicitur. Si per formam intelligis praecisè non totam quidditatem, sed id duntaxat, per quod res est, id quod est, dico hoc nihil aliud esse, quàm meritum Christi per fidem imputatum, vel meriti, fide apprehensi imputationem. Si enim quaeras, cur à paenà peccati absoluimur? & in gratiam acceptamur? Respondet vniuersa Scriptura, quia passio & obedientia Christi per fidem imputatur, ac si ipsi pro nos peccatis satisfecissemus.


### Quaestio I: XXX. And if this distinction is rightly held, our people can easily be…

XXX. And if this distinction is rightly held, our people can easily be reconciled, to whom otherwise a perpetual disagreement with the Papists is objected. Salmeron, vol. 15, p. 25, says: The Lutherans have arrived at nearly twenty-two opinions among themselves concerning justification. Bellarmine writes in book 2 on justification, ch. 1, that the errors of the Evangelicals concerning justification can be counted as five. One is that the formal cause of justification is faith, which he attributes to Luther and the Augsburg Confession. A second, that the formal cause is the obedience of Christ and his righteousness imputed to us, which Illyricus taught. A third, that the formal cause is the essential righteousness of God inhabiting us, which pleased Osiander. A fourth, that the formal cause is properly the remission of sin, which he assigns to Calvin. A fifth, that the formal cause of justification is twofold, our inherent righteousness and the imputed righteousness of Christ. For Pighius and certain others taught that. But he cannot object the error of Osiander to us, since we ourselves refute the same. We also have nothing in common with Pighius: Let him see, however, how he reconciles these clearest words of the Council of Trent, sess. 6, ch. 7, where it is decreed that justification is not only the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the inner man. The Tridentine Fathers themselves, therefore, maintain that justification consists in two things they assert. Nor will Bellarmine escape, if he says, in the place where the Council speaks, that you should note two terms of justification, or two effects of the same cause, book 2, chapter 2. For renewal is certainly not an effect, but the form of justification, according to him: And the Council there does not speak of terms or effects of justification, but rather defines it expressly, and says that it consists both of the remission of sins and of renewal. The remaining opinions, however, brought forth concerning the formal cause do not conflict. For when the remission of sins or acceptance into grace is called the formal cause of justification, by formal is understood the whole essence. But if indeed either faith, or the grace of God, or the obedience of Christ are named as the formal cause, then the cause of the essence is precisely understood. And these three should always be taken not separately, but conjointly, and when taken, should be understood in such a way that when one is named, the others are immediately included. Whence this axiom ought to be observed: Exclusive particles in the doctrine of justification do not exclude subordinate or connected causes, but only opposite and foreign ones. Thus it is rightly said: The righteousness and obedience of Christ alone justifies, namely, apprehended by faith and imputed by a merciful God; faith alone justifies, namely, apprehending the mercy of God and the righteousness of Christ; the grace of God alone justifies, namely, acquired for us through the obedience of Christ and apprehended by true faith. For without faith no justification can take place, as the Council of Trent admits, chapter 8.

XXXI. And from this it appears by how tight a bond the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and faith are linked together, indeed so that when one is named, the others must not be excluded, but comprehended at the same time, whence it happened that the Apostle Paul says indiscriminately that we are justified now by the grace of God, now by the merit of Christ, now by faith, since one includes the others. Wherefore we argue against the Papists thus: Those things which the Apostle Paul always joins together in the business of justification, as they themselves almost are of the same value, they cannot constitute different or contrary forms of justification. And yet Paul joins the grace of God, the merit of Christ, and faith, so that they are almost equivalent. Therefore, they cannot constitute different or contrary forms of justification. I prove the minor premise from Rom. 3. The righteousness of God has been manifested, v. 22. The righteousness of God through faith, v. 24. We are justified through the redemption made through Christ, ver. 23. God will justify, who is of the faith of Jesus v. 8. We conclude that a man is justified by faith, v. 30. God justifies the circumcision by faith, and the uncircumcision through faith, c. 4. v. 3. Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, v. 4. but not of grace, v. 5. who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness, v. 6. Faith is reckoned to Abraham for righteousness, v. 11. & 13. It is called the righteousness of faith, v. 6. the inheritance is of faith. v. 24. it is to be, that it might be reckoned to us, who have believed in him, Gal. 2. v. 16. Knowing that a man is justified by the faith of Jesus Christ, and we believe in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, ver. 17. We are justified through Christ, cap. 3. v. 9. They who are of faith are blessed, ver. 12. the just shall live by faith, v. 18. the inheritance is of promise, v. 22. the promise is given by the faith of Jesus Christ to those who believe. v. 24. we are justified by faith, v. 26. You are sons of God through faith etc. From all of which it is clear that it is the same to Paul as if he were to say that we are justified by God, through Christ, through the blood of Christ, through his redemption, by the grace of God, through the imputation of faith, by faith, of faith, through faith, by the righteousness of faith. Nor will you conclude from this that Paul has confused all these things, but rather that he wished to demonstrate the very close coherence of them. Whence we infer, whether you say, by the grace of God, or the merit of Christ apprehended by faith, or faith itself apprehending, that the formal cause of justification is not different, but that one only and proper form is expressed. If you object: The efficient cannot be the form: The grace of God and the merit of Christ are the efficient cause of our justification. Therefore, not the form: We answer that the grace of God and the merit of Christ are either considered absolutely, and thus they are the efficient cause and they concern all men, or relatively, insofar as they are apprehended by faith, and then they are the formal cause, and they concern none but believers.

XXXII. And thus far I have reviewed and in some way explained both opinions with such brevity and clarity as I could. Now it will be easy to discern what is the false and what is the true state of the controversy: It is not asked whether we are justified putatively, that is, only κατά δόξαν, which the Papists falsely attribute to us. It is not asked whether believers, after they have received the remission of sins by faith on account of Christ, are also renewed by the Spirit of their mind? For no one of our side would deny this. It is not asked: Whether it is necessary that contrition, repentance, a good purpose, and the beginning of love exist in man, and that good works follow? For we confess all these things plainly and clearly: But this is the state, and this

κρινόμενον is, as Chemnitius proposes in Exam. page 129. What that is, on account of which God receives a sinful man into grace, what ought to be and can be opposed to the judgment of God, so that we may not be condemned according to the rigid sentence of the law; what faith ought to apprehend and bring forward, upon what it ought to rely, when it wishes to deal with God; so that it may receive the remission of sins, what intervenes on account of which God is rendered appeased and propitious to a sinner who has deserved wrath and eternal condemnation, what the conscience ought to determine that thing to be, on account of which adoption is given to us, in which confidence can be safely placed, so that we may be accepted to eternal life? Whether that is the satisfaction, obedience, and merit of the Son of God the Mediator, or rather the newness of the beginning in us, love, and the remaining virtues? For since our righteousness and justification consist in nothing but the remission of sin, or absolution from the punishment of sin and adoption as sons, and acceptance to eternal life; it is necessary, if we wish to inquire into the formal cause of this justification, that the question be framed thus. By what or on account of what are we absolved from the punishments of sins in the most severe judgment of God, especially since we have deserved eternal damnation; whether on account of some infused novelty, or on account of the merit of Christ, which both regenerates us, and finally renews us after regeneration?

XXXIII. But Bellarmine criticizes Chemnitz for this formulation of the status, book 2, chapter 2. First, he says that he speaks improperly, so that you might confuse the formal cause with the meritorious one. For the little word per properly denotes the formal cause, but propter the final or meritorious cause. I reply 1. The Jesuit contradicts himself; for he himself uses the word propter to designate the formal cause, chapter 1, book 2, immediately from the beginning, when he says: Having finished those things which precede justification, we must discuss justification itself, that is, the formal cause on account of which a man is called righteous before GOD. 2. Justification is a certain action; therefore, no physical and substantial form is to be conceived here, just as the soul is the form of man, but by the form of justification must be understood that, on account of which, or through which, (if it pleases to speak so) we are absolved from sins. For just as in forensic actions the formal cause of absolution is denoted by the term propter, so that we say, on account of this or that he is justified and absolved; so also here the same term is not inconveniently applied. Nor do we deny that propter denotes the meritorious cause at the same time, but not absolutely, rather relatively, as it is applied to us. For the cause of justification is the same, both meritorious and formal: meritorious, insofar as it is viewed absolutely, formal, insofar as it is viewed relatively. Whence it happens that by the same word propter both the meritorious and formal cause are denoted, yet in a different respect. Indeed, this Jesuitical subtlety should rather be inverted, in such a way that we indicate the meritorious cause with the little word per, and the formal cause with the little word propter. For we say, through the merit of Christ, not on account of the merit, righteousness and the kingdom of heaven have been acquired for us. On account of this virtue [of] merit, those believing are justified. From which expressions it appears that the little word per denotes acquisition, but propter denotes application. 3. If the little word per is the mark of the formal cause, therefore faith will be the form of justification, because Scripture testifies everywhere that we are justified by faith, Galatians 2, verse nowhere says that we are justified by works or by inherent righteousness.

XXXIV. Next, the Jesuit accuses Chemnitz of having acted fraudulently by opposing the begun renewal to the merit of the Son of God. But I answer, that opposition of the merit of Christ and our virtues in the matter of justification was not invented by Chemnitz, but diligently handed down by the Apostle Paul, Romans 3, verse 28, and chapter 11, verse 6, Galatians 2, verse 16, and chapter 3, verses 2, 12, 13, Ephesians 2, verse 8. Where grace, Christ, faith, and works, or men, are clearly and expressly opposed; Not of ourselves, he says, it is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast.

XXXV. Bellarmine, however, further shapes the state of the question in chapter 2, book 2: Whether the formal cause of absolute justification is righteousness inherent in us or not? Note here that the word 'absolute' justification is insidiously added by Bellarmine. For Scripture acknowledges only one, and that a perfect, justification. And if the form of justification is unique, as the Council of Trent confirms, it will necessarily follow that justification itself is also only unique. Wherefore there is not one 'begun' and another 'absolute': nor does it befit justification to have its own degrees, so that one is lesser and another greater; for as there is one Christ, one merit of Christ, one mercy of God, so there is one perfect justification: an act, I say, one and individual, namely the remission of sins and the imputation of Christ's righteousness acquired through death. But is this not manifest blasphemy, that the righteousness of faith, which Scripture also calls the justice of God, should be called only begun and imperfect, while our own justice, inherent in us, is called absolute, complete, and perfect?

XXXVI. With the undergrowth therefore removed, the state of the question between us and the Papists can most conveniently be formed in this way.

Whether we are absolved from the punishments of our sins and accepted into grace for eternal life, or, in one word, justified, on account of the merit of Christ, apprehended by faith, or indeed on account of virtues infused and inherent in us in the most severe judgment of God? For in these two consists our justification.

The Papists assume the latter, who deny that we are formally justified on account of Christ's merit, and rather assert that we are just before God only on account of infused virtues. For thus Canon 10 of the Council of Trent holds: If anyone says that men are formally just through the justice of Christ, let him be anathema. And Bellarmine says, book 2, chapter 2: If that 'on account of' signifies the formal cause, we answer that we are justified on account of the newness inherent in us, not on account of the merit of Christ, which cannot be inherent, and therefore that we are justified on account of the merit of the Son only meritoriously, but on account of newness formally. Costerus repeats the same, p. 261: The formal cause is the quality which is received in justification, namely justice itself and grace: for thus by eternal justice a man is just, just as by wisdom he is wise, by whiteness white, by heat hot, by cleanliness clean. On the contrary, however, we, with the Orthodox, maintain that a sinner is justified and absolved from sins not on account of newness, not on account of infused virtues (for such are none in a man not yet reconciled: and, if they were, they would be imperfect, and therefore could not stand in the judgment of God) but solely and only on account of the merit of Christ apprehended by faith. Because, therefore, here a mutual affirmation and negation of the same thing is given, it appears from that the state of the controversy has been set by us, inasmuch as it always arises from the affirmation and negation of one and the same thing. For we affirm that the merit of Christ, imputed to us by faith, is the form of justification: The Papists deny this and affirm that newness and inherent virtues are the form of justification, which we Orthodox deny, and we impugn it with the firmest reasons, now to be enumerated,

Latin:

XXX. Atque haec distinctio si ritè teneatur, facilè conciliari nostrates poterunt, quibus aliàs perpetua obijcitur dissensio à Pontificijs Salmeron. tom. 15. pag. 25. inquit: Lutherani propè ad viginti duas opiniones de iustificatione inter se peruenerunt. Bellarminus scribit lib. 2. de iustific. c. 1. errores Evangelicorum de iustificatione quinque numerari possè videtur. Vnus est, formalem causam iustificationis esse fidem, quod Luthero & Augustanae Confessioni tribuit. Alter, formalem causam esse Christi obedientiam, & iustitiam nobis imputatam, quod Illyricus docuit. Tertius, formalem causam esse iustitiam Dei essentialem nobis inhabitantem, quod Osiandro placuit. Quartus, formalem causam propriè esse remissionem peccati, quod Caluino assignat. Quintus, formalem causam iustificationis duplicem esse, iustitiam nostram inhaerentem, & iustitiam Christi imputatam. Id enim Pighius, & quidam alij docuerunt. Sed errorem Osiandri nobis obijcere nequit, cùm ipsi eundem refutemus. Cum Pighio etiam nihil commune habemus: Viderit autē, quomodo conciliet haec verba clarissima Cōcilij Trident. sess. 6. c. 7. vbi decernitur, quòd iustificatio nō sit sola peccatorum remissio, sed & sanctificatio, & renouatio interioris hominis. Ipsi igitur Tridentini Patres in duobus iustificationem consistere asserunt. Neque effugiet Bellarminus, si dicat, in loquo Concilium, vt notes duos terminos iustificationis, siue duos effectus eiusdem causæ, lib. 2. c. 2. Nam renouatio profecto nõ est effectus, sed forma iustificationis, iuxta ipsum: Et Concilium ibi non loquitur de terminis, aut effectibus Iustificationis, sicu potius eam ex professo definit, dicitque constare & remissione peccatorum, & renouatione. Reliquæ vero sententiæ, de causa formali prolatæ non pugnant. Nam quando iustificationis formale dicitur remissio peccatorũ, vel acceptatio in gratiam, ibi per formale tota intelligitur quidditas. Quod si verò vel fides, vel gratia Dei, vel obedientia Christi formale nominantur, tum causa quidditatis præcisè intelligitur. Atque hæc tria non separatim, sed coniunctim semper sumantur, & sumpta intelligantur, ita vt vno nominato, statim includantur reliqua. Vndè obseruari debet hoc axioma: Particulæ exclusiuæ in doctrina iustificationis non excludunt causas subordinatas, siuè connexas, sed tantùm oppositas & alienas. Sic rectè dicitur; Sola Christi iustitia & obedientia iustificat, nimirum fide apprehensa, & à misericorde Deo imputata: Sola fides iustificat, nimirum Dei misericordiam, & Christi iustitiam apprehendens; Sola gratia Dei iustificat, scilicet p Christi obedientiam nobis acquisita, & verâ fide apprehensa. Absque fide enim nulla fieri potest iustificatio, fatente Concilio Tridens. c. 8.

XXXI. Atque hinc apparet, quàm arcto vinculo inter se colligatæ sint gratia Dei, meritum Christi & fides, ita quidem, vt vno nominato, reliqua non excludi, sed simul comprehendi oporreat, undè factum, vt Apostolus Paulus promiscuè nos dicat nunc gratiâ Dei, nunc merito Christi, nunc fide iustificari, quoniam vnum includit cætera. Quare contra Pontificios sic argumentamur: Quæ Apostolus Paulus in negotio iustificationis semper coniungit, vtipfi ferè idem valeant, eas non possunt constituere diuersas, aut contrarias formas iustificationis. Atqui gratiam Dei, meritum Christi, & fidem Paulus coniungit, vt ferè idem valeant. Ergò non possunt constituere diuersas, aut contrarias formas iustificationis. Minorem probo ex Rom. 3. Iustitia Dei manifestata est, v. 22. Iustitia Dei per fidem, v: 24. Iustificamur per redemptionem factam per Christum, ver. 23. Deum iustificaturum, qui est ex fide Iesu v. 8. Colligimus fide iustificari hominem, v. 30. Deus iustificat circumcisionem ex fide, & præputium per fidem, c. 4. v. 3. Credidit Abraham Deo, & imputatum est ei ad iustitiam, v. 4. sed nec ex gratia, v. 5. qui credit in eum, qui iustificat impium, imputatur fides sua pro iustitia, v. 6. Fides est Abrahæ imputata pro iustitia, v. 11. & 13. Appellatur iustitia fidei, v. 6. ex fide est hæreditas. v. 24. futurū est, vt imputetur nobis, qui crediderimus in eum, Gal. 2. v. 16. Scientes hominem iustificari per fidem Iesu Christi, & nos in Christum Iesum credimus, vt iustificaremur ex fide Christi, ver. 17. Iustificamur per Christum, cap. 3. v. 9. Qui ex fide sunt, benedicuntur, ver. 12. iustus ex fide viuit, v. 18. hæreditas est ex promissione, v. 22. promissio ex fide Iesu Christi datur credentibus. v. 24. ex fide iustificamur, v. 26. Filij Dei estis per fidem &c. Ex quib. omnib. patet, Paulo perindè esse, ac si dicat nos iustificari à Deo, per Christū, per Christi sanguinē, per redemptionē eius, gratiâ Dei, per imputationem fidei, fide, ex fide, per fidē, iustitiâ fidei. Neq; hinc colliges, Paulum ista omnia confudisse, sed potiùs, arctissimā horum cohærentiă demonstrare voluisse. Vnde inferimus, siuè dicas, gratiâ Dei, siuè meritū Christi fide apprehensum, siuè ipsam fidem apprehendentem, formálem iustificationis causam non diuersas, sed vnam duntaxat, & propriam formam exprimi. Si obijcis; Efficiens nequit esse forma: Gratia Dei & meritum Christi, sunt causa efficiēs nostræ iustificationis. E. non forma: Respondemus Gratia Dei, & meritū Christi, vel considerantur absolutè, & sic sunt causa efficiens atque omnes attinent homines, vel relatè, quatenus fide apprehenduntur, & tunc sunt causa formalis, atque non nisi credentes attinent.
