XXXII. Atque hactenus vtramque sententiam ea, qua potui, breuitate, & perspicuitate recensui, & qualitercunque explicui. Nunc qui falsi, quis verus sit controuersiæ status facilè deprehendi poterit: Non quæritur, an putatiuè, hoc est, κατά δόξαν solùm iustificemur, quod nobis falsò affingunt Pontificij. Non quæritur, an credentes, postquam remissionem peccatorum fide propter Christum acceperunt, renouentur etiam Spiritu mentis suæ? Hoc enim nostrarium nemo negauerit. Non quæritur: An oporteat existere in homine contritionem, pœnitentiam, bonum propositum, ac inchoari dilectionem, & sequi bona opera? Hæc enim omnia planè, & clarè confitemur: Hic verò status, & hoc

κρινόμενον est, vt proponit Chemnisius in Exam. pag. 129. Quidnam id sit, propter quod Deus hominem peccatorem in gratiam recipiat, quid iudicio Dei opponi debeat, & possit, nè iuxta rigidam legis sententiam damnemur; quid fides apprehendere, & adferre, quo niti debeat, quando vult cum Deo agere; vt accipiat remissionem peccatorum, quid interueniat propter quod Deus peccatori, qui commeritus est iram, & æternam damnationem, reddatur, placatus, & propitius, quid conscientia statuere debeat illud esse, propter, quod donetur nobis adoptio, in quo tutò collocari possit fiducia, vt acceptemur ad vitam æternam? An illud sit satisfactio, obedientia, & meritum Filij Dei Mediatoris, an verò inchoationis in nobis nouitas, dilectio, & reliquæ virtutes? Cùm enim nostra iustitia, & iustificatio consistat non nisi in remissione peccati, seu absolutione à pœna peccati & adoptione in filios, atque acceptatione ad vitam æternam; necesse est, si formale huius iustificationis inquirere volumus, vt quæstio ita informetur. Per quod vel propter quod à pœnis peccatorum in seuerissimo Dei iudicio absolvamur, præsertim cùm æternam simus promeriti damnationem; an propter novitatem aliquam infusam, an propter meritum Christi, quod nos & regenerat, & post regenerationem demum renovat?

XXXIII. Sed Bellarminus taxat Chemnitium ob hanc status formationem, lib: 2. cap. 2. Primùm ait, loqui illum impropriè, vt confundere possis causam formalem cùm meritoria. Nam voculam per notare causam formalem propriè, τὸ propter autem causam finalem vel meritoriam. Respondeo 1. IesuWitam sibi contradicere; Nam vocabulo propter vtitur ipse ad designandam causam formalem, cap. 1. lib. 2. statim ab initio, quando inquit: Expeditiys, quæ iustificationem præcedunt, de ipsa iustificatione, hoc est, de causa formali propter quam homo dicitur iustus coram DEO, disserendum est. 2. Iustificatio est quædam actio; non igitur forma aliqua Physica & substantialis hîc concipienda, sicut anima est forma hominis, sed per formam iustificationis intelligi debet illud, propter quod, vel per quod, (si ita loqui placeat) absolvimur à peccatis. Sicut enim in actionibus forensibus causa formalis absolutionis termino propter notatur, vt dicamus, propter hoc vel illud iustificatus & absolutus est; Ita & hic idem terminus non incommodè adhibetur. Neque negamus, τὸ propter notare simul causam meritoriam, verùm non absolutè, sed relatè, prout nobis applicatur. Eadem enim est iustificationis causa & meritoria, & formalis: Meritoria, quatenus absolutè, formalis quatenus relatè spectatur. Vnde fit, vt per idem vocabulum τὸ propter causa notetur & meritoria, & formalis, diuerso tamen respectu. Imò potiùs invertenda est subtilitas ista IesuWitica, ita quidem, vt potiùs meritoriam causam voculâ per, formalem voculâ propter indicemus. Nam dicimus, per meritum Christi, non propter meritum acquisita nobis est iustitia & regnum cælorum. Propter hoc tutem meritum credentes iustificantur. Ex quibus locutionibus apparet, voculam per propriè acquisitionem, propter verò applicationem notare. 3. Si vocula per est nota causæ formalis. Ergò fides erit forma justificationis, quia passim Scriptura testificatur, iustificari nos per fidem, Galat. 2. vers. fu 16. Rom. 3. versu 30. Nunquam autem & nusquam dicit, iustificari nos per opera seu per iustitiam inhærentem.

XXXIV. Deinde, accusat IesuWita Chemnitium, quòd fraudulenter egerit, opponendo merito Filii Dei inchoatam renovationem. Sed respondeo, oppositio illa meriti Christi & virtutum nostrarum in negotio iustificationis, non à Chemnitio conficta, sed ab Apostolo Paulo diligenter tradita est Roman. 3. versu 28. Et cap, 11. versu. 6. Galat. 2. versu 16. Et cap. 3. versu 2. 12. 13. Ephes. 2 versu 8. Vbi disertè & expressè opponuntur gratia, Christus, fides & opera, siuè homines, Non ex nobis, inquit, Dei donum est, non ex operibus, nequis glorietur.

XXXV. Bellarminus autem porrò statum quæstionis ita informat cap. 2. lib. 2. Sitne formalis causa absolutæ iustificationis, iustitia in nobis inhærens annou? Nota hic, Bellarmino insidiosè addi, vocem absolutæ iustificationis. Non enim nisi vnam eamque perfectam justificationem Scriptura agnosci. Et si iustificationis forma vnica est, confirmante Concilio Tridentino, ipsam etiam iustificationem non nisi vnicam esse, necesse erit. Quare non est alia inchoata, alia absoluta: nec deces, iustificationem habere suos gradus, vt sit alia minor, alia maior; Nam vt vnus est Christus, vnum Christi meritum, vna Dei misericordia, ita vnica est perfecta justificatio: actus inquam, vnus individuus, nempè remissio peccatorum. Et Christi justitiæ per mortem acquisitæ imputatio. Annon verò manifesta blasphemia hæc est, justitiam fidei, quam Scriptura etiam vocat iustitiam Dei, appellare inchoatam tantum imperfectam, nostram verò iustitiam, nobis inharentem vocare absolutam completam & perfectam?

XXXVI. Remotis igitur sub suriculis, omnium commodissimè status quæstionis inter nos & Pontificios ita formari poterit.

An propter meritum Christi, fide apprehensum, num verò propter virtutes nobis infusas & inhærentes in severissimo Dei iudicio, à pænis peccatorum nostrorum absolvamur, & in gratiam ad vitam æternam acceptemur, seu,uno verbo iustificemur? In his enim duobus consistit nostra iustificatio.

Posterius assumunt Pontificij, qui negant, nos propter Christi meritum formaliter iustificari, & potiùs asserunt, nos tantùm propter virtutes infusas coram Deo iustos esse Sic enim habet Canon. 10. Concil. Trid. Si quis dicat homines per Christi iustitiam formaliter iustos esse, anathema sit. Et Bellarminus inquit, l. 2. cap. 2 Si illud propter significat causam formalem, respondemus, nos iustificari propter novitatem nobis inhærentem, non propter meritum Christi, quod inhærere non potest, ideoque nos propter meritum Filij non nisi meritoriè, propter novitatem autem formaliter iustificari. Costerus idem repetit. p. 261. Causa formalis est qualitas, quæ iustificatione accipitur, nempè iustitia ipsa & gratia: Sic enim per iustitiam æternam homo est iustus, sicut per sapientiam, sapiens, per albedinem albus, per calorem, calidus, per munditiem, mundus. Contrà verò nos, cum Orthodoxis statuimus, peccatorem justificari, & à peccatis absolui non propter novitatem, non propter infusas virtutes, (tales enim nullæ sunt in homine nondum reconciliato: Et, si essent, imperfectæ essent. ideoq; in iudicio Dei consistere non possent) sed vnicè & tantùm, propter meritum Christi fide apprehensum. Quia igitur hic mutua datur eiusdem affirmatio & negatio, apparet inde verum a nobis controuersiae statum esse positum, quippe qui semper ex vnius & eiusdem affirmatione & negatione enascitur. Nos enim affirmamus, Christi meritum fide nobis imputatum, esse iustificationis formam: Negant hoc Pontificii & affirmant, nouitatem & virtutes inhaerentes esse iustificationis formam id quod nos Orthodoxi negamus, & rationibus firmissimis, jam enumerandis impugnamus,


### Quaestio I: Question II. By what arguments especially can the Orthodox opinion concerning imputed righteousness be confirmed against the defenders of…

QUESTION II. By what arguments especially can the Orthodox opinion concerning imputed righteousness be confirmed against the defenders of inherent [righteousness]?

XXXVII. Very many arguments can be produced for the confirmation of this opinion, which, however, according to the customary manner, we divide: 1. Into sayings of Scripture 2. Into reasons from the analogy of faith 3. And testimonies of the Fathers: Moreover, there occur very many sayings of Scripture which, so that they may be proposed distinctly, we shall include in peculiar and certain classes.

Latin:

QVAESTIO II. Quibus praecipue argumentis Orthodoxa sententia de imputatiua iustitia contra inhaerentis propugnatores confirmari queat?

XXXVII. Plurima pro confirmatione hujus sententiae produci possunt argumenta, quae tamen consueto more, 1. In dicta Scripturae 2. In rationes ab analogia fidei 3. Et testimonia Patrum dispesci: Occurrunt autem Scripturae dicta bene multa quae vt distincte proponantur, peculiaribus certisque classibus illa includemus.


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without works

XXXVIII. Such are read in Rom. 3, verse 20, and following, up to 31. Roman. 4, verse 2. Galat. 2, verse 16. Ephes. 2, verse 8. Tit. 3, v. 5. Philip. 3, v. 9. From which we argue thus. If the righteousness of GOD, by which a sinner is absolved from sins before GOD, is manifested without the Law, and it cannot be that any flesh is justified by the works of the Law in the sight of the Lord, but righteousness is given through faith in JESUS CHRIST to those who believe, then it follows that not works, not our virtues, but the sole righteousness of Christ applied through faith, justifies, and it is prior true, according to the cited statements. Therefore also the latter.

XXXIX. The consequence of the major premise is clear: 1 For whatever is from the Law, that does not justify, Rom. 3 v. 21. And Rom. 4 v. 13. Galat. 2 v. 21. All works and all mighty works are from the Law, or pertain to the Law, whence they are called works of the Law, because the Law is the doctrine of works, v. 20. Wherefore works and mighty works do not justify. The Apostle himself proves the major premise in v. 19 and 20, and Rom. 4 v. 14. Galat. 3 verse 10, for the Law condemns, and from the Law is the knowledge of sin, whence the Law cannot justify and cover sin. 2. Whatever pertains to the Gospel, that alone justifies, v. 21, 22. Rom. 4 v. 12. Faith, not works, pertains to the Gospel. Therefore faith, not works, justifies. 3. Whatever can produce glory, that whole thing is excluded from Justification, Rom. 3 v. 27. Eph. 2 v. 8. But inherent righteousness and works can produce glory, Rom. 4 v. 2. Therefore they do not justify. 4. Whatever did not justify Abraham, that does not justify even now. But inherent righteousness and works did not justify Abraham. Rom. 4 v. 3. Therefore they cannot justify anyone even now. 5 The effects of contraries are contrary; Faith and works, to believe and to do, in the article of justification are contrary, Rom. 4 v. 4 and 5. Therefore if faith justifies, works do not justify. Or: if works justify, then faith does not justify. But Paul expressly denies that we are justified by works of the law, and expressly affirms that we are justified by faith Rom. 3 verse 28. λογιζώμεδα πίσει δικαιῦσθαι ἄνθρωπον χωρὶς ἔργων νόμε. The righteousness of faith is true righteousness, valid before God. Philip. 3 v. 9. Rom. 3 v. 21 and 22. But mighty works and works do not produce the righteousness of faith but of the law, Philip. 3 v. 9. Therefore they are not righteousness valid before God.

XL. However, as much as the truth of these statements is so manifest that the Papists can find nothing solid to answer, they have nevertheless devised various evasions and cavils. For they say that by the works of the law they understand only those works which are extorted by fear of punishment, without the consent of internal motions. Others, works preceding justification, but not following it: Others, the works of unbelievers: Others, the works of the ceremonial law: Others, the works of the law, not of faith. Others interpret it thus, that Paul speaks of primary justification, which they admit happens without any works. For they think a man, who was justified by faith without works in primary justification, is afterwards righteous before God, and is saved by both faith and works. But Costerus and Bellarmine make no mention of this explanation, which silence is an evident indication that they do not approve of it. Nor can they do otherwise, since even the form of primary justification according to them is placed in inherent works and virtues. How, therefore, Bellarmine especially, whom most follow today, responds to the argument, we shall observe in a few words.

XLI. Therefore, in the first book, chapter 19, for the discussion of this argument, he premises three things; let us see them one by one. The first evasion contains the question, what is the Law of works and the Law of faith according to the Apostle? For because these are opposed to each other in Romans 3, verse 27, therefore they must be accurately distinguished, lest they be confused. Bellarmine proposes his opinion thus: The law of works according to the Apostle is that which commands what is to be done; the law of faith is faith itself, which obtains the grace of doing what the law of works commands. And so both laws require works, but the law of works contains the precept, the law of faith the aid. Briefly, therefore, this is his meaning, that the Law of works and the Law of faith are not distinguished in that the former requires works and the latter does not, but that these two Laws agree in this, that both require works, but are distinguished solely in this, that the former requires works from natural powers, these works, however, are to be performed with the help of the Spirit and the grace of God. Our opinion, indeed, is that in this Pauline opposition, by the law of works is understood every Law which requires works, whether natural, or supernatural, or of the regenerate. For whatever work there is, we refer it to the Law of works and deeds, and we say it is excluded by Paul from the circle of justification; since the law of faith is nothing else than the Gospel. The law of deeds, however, is that which we otherwise properly call the Law. Just as therefore the Gospel does not require works, and is not a sermon of repentance, so also the law of faith requires absolutely no works. Which opinion we provide proven by the following far most firm arguments.

XLII. I. Whatever of opposites is attributed to one in an opposition, that cannot be attributed to the other. The law of deeds and the law of faith, or, the Law and the Gospel, in the doctrine of justification are opposites, and in that opposition works and the act of working are attributed to the Law, Romans 3, verse 27, Galatians 2 and 3. Therefore works and the act of working cannot be attributed to the Gospel. 2. Whatever law accuses sins and condemns, that whole law is excluded from justification, Romans 3, verses 19 and 20. But every Law which requires works condemns and accuses sins. Therefore every Law requiring works is excluded. 3. That law of which it is said, he who shall have done them shall live in them, and Cursed is he who shall not have remained in all things which are written in the book of the Law, that law is excluded from justification, Galatians 3, verses 10 and 12. But every law requiring works is such. Wherefore it is excluded from justification. 4. Whatever Law commands to do something, which requires works, and in the doctrine of justification is opposed to faith and grace, that is excluded from justification, Romans 4, verses 2, 4, 5. But the moral Law, (not only the ceremonial;) commands to do something, and demands works, Luke 10. verses 25. 26. 28. And in the doctrine of justification it is opposed to faith, Romans 3. verse 24. & 4. verse 4. 5. Galatians 3. verse 12. Therefore the moral law will also have to be excluded; which very thing the Jesuit is forced to admit in chapter 19. And he adds this reason, because the Apostle simply excludes works, with no mention made of the Mosaic Law. 5. That Law from whose curse Christ has freed us, that Law is excluded from justification, Galatians 3. verses 12 & 13. But Christ has freed us especially from the curse of the moral Law. Wherefore the moral Law must again be excluded. 6. That Law which convicts all men whatsoever, and binds both Gentiles and Jews, that is excluded from justification, Rom. 3. verses 9. 10. 29. 30. But such was not the ceremonial, but especially the moral Law; and therefore it must again be excluded. 7. Paul speaks of that Law which is inscribed on the minds of men, Rom. 2. verse 15. Which shows sin, chapter 3. verse 20. Which condemns the whole world, verse 19. Which pertains to Jews and Gentiles, verses 6. & 29. Which curses all because of disobedience, Galatians 3. verse 10. Which was given because of transgressions, verse 19. Which is opposed to the promise, verse 18. From which Christ redeemed us, verse 13. Which is our tutor unto Christ, verse 24. Which shows that concupiscence is sin. Rom. 7. verse 7. Through which the flesh was weakened, Rom. 8. verse 3. But such is especially the moral Law. Therefore it is excluded.

XLIII. But Bellarmine will object that he willingly concedes that the moral Law is excluded, but not on that account the Law of faith, which similarly requires virtues and works. I answer, No work can be shown which is a work of faith and not of law. The Papists especially call hope, love, and contrition works of faith. But these very things are works of the moral Law. Therefore they also pertain to the moral Law. For whatever is commanded by the Mosaic moral Law pertains to the same law, and with it has been excluded by the Apostle Paul from the circle of justification. But hope, love, fear, and all other virtues are commanded by the moral Law. Therefore they pertain to the moral law, and consequently, together with that law, they are excluded from the business of justification. The minor premise is evident, because all things that follow faith (such as the charity, justice, and good works of the reborn) are of the Law, are legal charity and legal works. For the law is for the reborn also a norm of good works, Deut. 12. verse 8. and 32. The faithful also, following piety, are engaged and occupied with good works in the law and concerning the law of the Lord, as their object. Psalm 119. v. 1. Blessed are those who walk in the law of the Lord. Nor do any other works please God than those which are done according to the law, 1 John 3. v. 22.

XLIV. Nor is there any reason for the Jesuit to insist: that Paul removed those works insofar as they are of the Law, but not insofar as they are of faith, since the Law indeed commands, but does not bestow the faculty of doing, which is the property of the law of faith. For by this reasoning the Apostle would be very absurd, who had been so anxious that no one should think himself justified by the works of the moral law, which nevertheless are impossible. For if no one can do any work of the moral law, it would certainly not have been necessary to remove the suspicion of being justified. For of that which does not exist, there are no attributes. But according to the Jesuit, there are no, nor can there be, works of the moral law in man. Therefore justification cannot be ascribed to them either. Did the Apostle therefore forbid that to be done, which is otherwise impossible to be done? Not otherwise than if someone were to say, you ought not to boast of manly deeds, by which you killed so many thousands of enemies, when nevertheless there are no such deeds. In like manner the Jesuits imagine Paul to argue: You cannot be justified by your hope and charity, when nevertheless upon the unregenerate such

Latin:

XXXVIII. Talia leguntur Rom. 3. ver. 20, & sequentibus, vsque ad 31. Roman. 4. ver. 2. Galat. 2. ver. 16. Ephes. 2. ver. 8. Tit. 3. v. 5. Philip. 3. v. 9. Ex quibus ita argumentamur. Si iustitia DEI, qua peccator coram DEO a peccatis absolvitur, manifesta est absque Lege, & fieri non potest, vt ex operibus Legis vlla caro iustificetur in conspectu Domini, sed iustitia datur per fidem IESV CHRISTI, ijs, qui credunt, tunc sequitur, quod non opera, non virtutes nostrae, sed sola iustitia Christi per fidem applicata, iustificet, atque prius est verum, secundum dicta allegata. Ergò & posterius.

XXXIX. Consecutio Maioris patet: 1 Quicquid enim ex Lege est, id non justificat Rom 3. v. 21. Et Rom. 4. ver. 13. Galat. 2. v. 21. Omnia opera omneśque virtutes sunt ex Lege, vel pertinent ad Legem, vndè dicuntur opera Legis, quia Lex est doctrina operum, v. 20. Quare opera & virtutes non iustificant. Maiorem probat ipse Apostolus v. 19. & 20. & Rom. 4. v. 14. Galat. 3. versu 10 qui Lex damnat, & ex Lege est cognitio peccati, vndè Lex iustificare, & peccatum tegere haud potest. 2. Quicquid pertinet ad Evangelium, illud tantùm justificat, v. 21. 22. Rom. 4. ver. 12. Fides, non opera pertinent ad Evangelium. Ergò fides non opera justificant. 3. Quodcunque gloriam potest parere id omne exclusum est à Iustificatione, Rom. 3. v. 27. Eph. 2. v. 8. Atqui iustitia inhærens, & opera possunt parere gloriã, Rom. 4. v. 2 Ergò non iustificãt. 4. Quodcunq; Abrahamum non iustificauit, id neq; adhuc iustificat. Atqui iustitia inhærens & opera non iustificârunt Abrahamũ. Rom. 4. v. 3. Ergò nec adhuc aliquem iustificare possunt. 5 Contrariorum effecta sunt contraria; Fides & opera, credere & facere, in articulo iustificationis sunt contraria, Rom. 4. v. 4. & 5. Ergò si fides iustificat, opera non justificant. Aut: si opera iustificant, tum non iustificat fides. Atqui Paulus disertè negat, justificari nos ex operibus legis, & disertè affirmat iustificari nos fide Rom. 3. versu 28. λογιζώμεδα πίσει δικαιῦσθαι ἄνθρωπον χωρὶς ἔργων νόμε. Iustitia fidei est vera justitia, coram Deo valens. Philip. 3. ver. 9. Rom. 3. v. 21. & 22. Atqui virtutes & opera non pariunt iustitiam fidei sed legis, Philip. 3. v. 9. Ergò non sunt iustitia coram Deo valens.

XL. Quantum autem veritas horum dictodum adeò manifesta sit, vt nil solidi quod respondeant, invenire possint Pontificij, varias tamen elusiones & cavillationes confinxerunt. Aij enim per opera legis intelligunt tantùm ea opera, quæ extorquentur metu pœnæ, fine motuum interiorum consensione. Alij operaiustificationem præcedentia, non autem consequentia : Alij opera infidelium: Alij opera legis ceremonialis : Alij opera legis, non fidei. Alij sic interpretantur, quòd Paulus loquatur de justificatione prima, quam isti fatentur fieri sine vllis operibus. Putant enim hominem, qui fide sine operibus justificatus fuit in justificatione prima, postea justum esse coram Deo, salvarique & fide & operibus. Verùm Costerus & Bellarminus huius explicationis non neminerunt, quod silentium est evidens indicium, quod illam non adprobent. Neque aliter possunt facere, siquidem etiam primæ justificationis forma secundum ipsos posita est in operibus & virtutibus inhærentibus. Quomodo igitur Bellarminus potissimùm, quem hodiè sequuntur plerique, ad argumentum respondeat, paucis attendemus.

XLI. Libro igitur primo cap 19. ad discussionem huius argumenti, tria præmittit, nos singula videamus. Primum effugium continet quæstionem, quid sit apud Apostolum Lex factorum, & Lex fidei? Quia enim hæc invicem opponuntur Romam. 3. versu 27. Ideò accuratè pistinguenda sunt, ne confundantur. Ita autem suam Bellarminus proponit sententiam : Lex factorum apud Apostolum est ea, quæ iubet quid sit faciendum; Lex fidei est ipsa fides, quæ impetrat gratiam faciendi, quod lex factorum iubet. Itaque vtraque lex requirit opera, sed lex factorum continet præceptum, lex fidei auxilium. Breviter ergò hæc ipsius mens est, quòd Lex factorum & Lex fidei, non in eo distinguantur quòd illa requirat opera, hæc non requirat, sed duas istas Leges in hoc convenire, quòd vtraque requirat opera, in eo autem vnicè distingui, quòd illa requirat opera à viribus naturalibus, hæc autem opera, adjuvante Spiritu & gratia Dei præstanda. Nostra verò sententia est, quòd in ista oppositione Paulina per legem operum intelligatur omnis Lex, quæ requirit opera sive naturalia, sive supernaturalia, sive renatorum. Quodcunque enim opus est, id ad Legem operum & factorum referimus, atque à Paulo è circulo justificationis exclusum dicimus; siquidem Lex fidei nihil est aliud, quàm Evangelium. Lex factorum verò id, quod propriè alias Legem dicimus. Sicut igitur Evangelium non requirit opera, non est concio pœnitentiæ, ita etiam Lex fidei nulla planè opera exigit. Quam sententiam sequentibus argumentis longè firmissimis probatam damus.

XLII. I. Quicquid oppositorum vni tribuitur in oppositione, id alteri tribui nequit. Lex factorum & Lex fidei, seu, Lex & Evangelium, in doctrina justificationis sunt opposita, & in illa oppositione Legi tribuuntur opera & τό operari, Roman. 3, versu 27. Galat. 2, & 3. Ergò opera & τό operari Evangelio tribui non possunt. 2. Quæ lex accusat peccata & damnat, ea omnis excluditur à justificatione, Roman 3. vers. 19. & 20, Atqui omnis Lex, quæ requirit opera, damnat & accusat peccata. Ergò Omnis Lex requirens opera, excluditur. 3, De qua lege dicitur qui fecerit ea, vivet in eis, Et Maledictus qui non permanferit in omnibus, quæ scripta sunt in libro Legis, ea lex excluditur à justificatione, Galat. 3. versu 10. & 12. Atqui omnis lex requirens opera, talis est. Quare excluditur à justificatione. 4, Quæ Lex jubet facere aliquid, quæ exigit opera, & in doctrina justificationis opponitur fidei & gratiæ, illa excluditur à justificatione Roman. 4. versu 2. 4. 5. Atqui Lex moralis, (non tantùm ceremonialis;) jubet facere aliquid, & exigit opera, Luc. 10. vers. 25. 26. 28. Et in doctrina iustificationis opponitur fidei, Roman. 3. vers. 24. & 4. vers. 4. 5. Galat. 3. vers. 12. Ergò lex moralis etiam excludenda erit; quod ipsum fateri coactus est Iesuita cap. 19. Et addit hanc rationem, quia Apostolus simpliciter excludat opera, nullâ factâ mentione Legis Mosaicae. 5. A cuius Legis execratione Christus nos liberauit, ea Lex à iustificatione excluditur, Galat. 3. vers. 12 & 13. Atqui à Legis potissimùm moralis execratione Christus nos liberauit. Quare Lex moralis iterum debet excludi. 6. Quæ Lex omnes omninò arguit homines, & constringit tàm gentiles, quàm Iudæos, ea excluditur à iustificatione, Rom. 3. vers. 9. 10. 29. 30. Talis verò erat non ceremonialis, sed Lex potissimùm moralis; ideoque rursus excludi debet. 7. De ea Lege loquitur Paulus, quæ hominum animis est inscripta, Rom. 2. vers. 15. Quæ ostendit peccatum, cap. 3. vers. 20. Quæ damnat vniuersum mundum, vers. 19. Quæ pertinet ad Iudæos & Gentes, vers. 6. & 29. Quæ omnes execratur propter inobedientiam, Galat. 3. vers. 10. Quæ data est propter transgressiones, vers. 19. Quæ opponitur promissioni, vers. 18. A qua nos Christus redemit, vers. 13. Quæ pædagogus noster est in Christum, vers, 24. Quæ ostendit concupiscentiam esse peccatum. Rom. 7. vers. 7. Per quam infirmabatur caro, Rom. 8. vers. 13. Talis verò præcipuè est Lex moralis. Ergò exclusa.

XLIII. Sed excipiet Bellarminus, se lubenter concedere, Legem moralem exclusam esse, non autem ob id Legem fidei, quæ similiter requirat virtutes & opera. Respondeo, Nullum potest opus monstrari, quod sit opus fidei non legis. Fidei opera potissimùm dicunt Pontificij spem, dilectionem, contritionem. Atqui hæc ipsa sunt opera Legis moralis. Ergò etiam ad Legem moralem pertinent. Quodcunque enim à Lege morali Mosaica præcipitur; id pertinet ad eandem legem, & cum eadem ab Apostolo Paulo e circulo iustificationis exclusum est, At vero spes, dilectio, timor & aliae virtutes omnes a Lege morali praecipiuntur. Ergo ad legem moralem pertinent, & per consequens una cum lege illa sunt exclusa e negotio iustificationis. Minor patet, quia omnia, quae fidem consequuntur (ut renatorum charitas, iustitia & bona opera) Legis sunt, legalis charitas & legalia opera sunt. Est enim lex renatis etiam norma bonorum operum, Deut. 12. vers. 8. &. 32. Fideles quoque pietatem sectantes, bonis operibus in lege & circa legem Domini, velut objectum suum versantur & occupantur. Psal. 119. v. 1. Beati qui ambulant in lege Domini. Nec ulla alia opera Deo placent, quam quae secundum legem fiunt, 1. Ioh. 3. v. 22.

XLIV. Neque est ut instet IesuWita: Remouisse Paulum ista opera, in quantum sunt Legis, non autem in quantum fidei, quoniam Lex quidem praecipiat, sed faciendi facultatem non largiatur, quod sit proprium Legis fidei. Nam hac ratione valde absurdus esset Apostolus, qui tam anxius fuisset, ne quis putaret se justificari operibus legis moralis, que tamen sunt impossibilia. Si enim nemo potest aliquod opus legis moralis facere, non sane fuisset necessarium remouere suspicionem iustificandi. Quod enim non est, eius nullae sunt affectiones. Atqui secundum IesuWitam, nulla sunt vel esse possunt opera legis moralis in homine. Ergo nec illis potest adscribi iustificatio. Hoccine ergo prohibuit fieri Apostolus, quod fieri alias impossibile? non secus ac si quis diceret, tu non debes ob virilia facta, quibus tot mille hostes occidisti, gloriari, cum tamen nulla sint talia. Pari modo Paulum argumentari fingunt IesuWitae: Vos ex spe & charitate vestra non potestis iustificari, cum tamen in non renatos ta-


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: virtues do not fall at all

virtues do not fall at all.

XLV. This must be diligently considered, and always opposed to the Papists, who maintain that hope, faith, and love justify antecedently or dispositively, and that these works are not excluded from justification by the exclusion of the law of works, because they do not pertain to the law of works, but to the law of faith, inasmuch as it alone makes us fit for righteous virtues, whereas the moral law indeed commands them, but does not bestow the power of performing them, and therefore no one adhering merely to the moral law can love God, believe in God, or hope in God. Now, indeed, we conclude thus: If no one can do these things, no one can also ascribe justification to them. If this is so, why is Paul so solicitous that no one should attribute justification to them? Did he therefore not know this? Impious. Was he so foolish and absurd that he would solicitously forbid things that can in no way be done, lest they be done? ἄτοπον. Therefore it must be maintained, lest we impiously attribute any ignorance or absurdity to Paul and to the Holy Spirit himself. The Holy Spirit knew well that things which cannot otherwise be done are not to be forbidden (for who would forbid someone from placing this globe of the earth upon their shoulders and carrying it elsewhere, when this is simply impossible?). Since, therefore, he forbade something here, it is necessary that that which he forbade could be done. He forbade, however, that anyone should attribute justification to moral works, such as hope, love, and fear. Wherefore these things can be done: but not without the grace of the Holy Spirit and faith. The Apostle therefore included this very thing, and consequently did not mean the works of the unregenerate, since there are no such things, but rather those of the regenerate: And thus all those things which Bellarmine refers to the law of faith reach to the law of works, which Paul excluded.

XLVI. Furthermore, it is not without reason asked, from where this distinction between the law of works and the law of faith is drawn? And by what foundations it is proven? He brings Bell. bk. 1, ch. 16, proposes a certain little argument, why not all works whatsoever can be excluded by the law of works, as follows: If all works and every law are excluded, faith will also be excluded. For the act of faith is a certain work, as it is called in John 6:29: This is the work, that you believe in him whom he has sent. Therefore, either we shall be justified by this work; if faith without works excludes all works; and by this, to be justified by faith will be nothing else than to be justified without faith. There is also a certain law of faith, of which Rom. 3 speaks. But if justifying faith without the works of the law excludes every law, it will also exclude the law of faith: and since the law of faith is faith itself, faith excludes faith, and to be justified by faith will be to be justified without faith. Resp. 1. That there is an equivocation in the term work. For either by work is understood any action whatsoever, of whatever kind it may be, absolute or relative, and in this sense faith can be called a work, because it is an apprehension and application, and thus faith and work are not opposed: or properly and strictly it is understood as some action or some moral work, arising and proceeding from faith, where they differ as cause and effect. In this sense faith and works are opposed: And such are always excluded from the business of justification. 2. There is a homonymy in the term law. For it is either taken generally and broadly for every doctrine, and thus it is called the law of Christ, Galat. 6:2, and the law of faith, Rom. 3:27, or specifically and more strictly, for the Decalogue and the Mosaic law, in which latter signification only it is opposed to the Gospel and to faith. The Apostle therefore excludes from justification every law, namely that properly so called, that is, which demands works from men, and accuses and condemns the disobedient, so that the Apostolic opposition may remain perpetual: Gospel, not law; faith, not works; to believe, not to do, justifies. And thus our argument, placed above, stands firm: Whatever pertains to the law, that does not justify; but virtues and all works properly so called, of whatever kind they may be, pertain to the law

The Mosaic [law] excluded from justification. Therefore mighty works and works do not justify.

XLVII. The second evasion is that Bellarmine distinguishes between the righteousness of the law, and righteousness in the law, or from the law: that the righteousness of the law is just works, which the law prescribes to be done, and that this is true righteousness: but that righteousness from the law is those works which men do without the grace of faith, aided only by the knowledge of the law, and that this righteousness is useless, and these works do not justify before God, but only before men, who consider only external things. But by what testimonies will this distinction be proven, and where is it founded in the Scriptures? To us, the righteousness of the law and righteousness from the law are one and the same, and that is noted: when anyone wishes to be justified from the works of the law, whether external or internal; natural or supernatural. And because Paul opposes the righteousness of the law, in the absolution of a sinful man, to the righteousness of faith, rejecting the former and receiving the latter; we conclude from this that we can in no way be absolved from our sins by good works. For all works pertain to the righteousness of the law, to the standard of which they were done. Whatever, however, is such, that together with the righteousness of the law has been excluded by the Apostle Paul.

XLIIX. The third evasion contains this problem. What works does Paul understand, without which he asserts we are justified? Our people say that all works whatsoever are excluded, whether done before faith or after faith, which opinion Bellarmine calls most absurd, proceeding from an ignorance of Scripture, which he shows by the testimony of Augustine. But that does not militate against us, since it must be opposed to those who establish that works not only do not justify, but are not even required from the justified, so that they think faith suffices, even if one lives wickedly; which is not our opinion, as indicated above. Furthermore, in chapter 16, book 1, he says that not all works are excluded, but a certain kind of works, that is, works done by the powers alone of stature, or from the sole knowledge of the Mosaic law, or if in some other way the works of the law are to be understood in this place. Whence it appears that he himself, while he was writing these things, was not yet certain which works were excused by the Apostle: But in chapter 19 he reviews the opinion of those Catholics who think that by works, without which Paul says we are justified, nothing but the observations of legal ceremonies are to be understood, in which opinion, however, he himself does not acquiesce, but says that it is most true without ambiguity that by works are understood those things which precede faith and which are done by the sole powers of free will: He uses, however, a reason taken from Rom. 4, where it is read: To him who works, the reward is imputed according to debt; whence he gathers that those works are excluded by which that which is rendered is a reward, not grace; such as are only those which are done by free will: for that which is rendered to the rest is not simply a reward, but also grace, nay, more grace than reward. But we answer that this is not the purpose of Paul in that statement, but rather he argues from the genus to the species; To everyone working, the reward is imputed according to debt: Therefore also to the working person, whether regenerate or not regenerate. Furthermore, it is not said that to the worker alone the reward is imputed, but certainly to the one working and believing, the reward is said to be imputed, to the former according to debt, to the latter according to grace. For the justification of works is done according to debt, not indeed simple, but from a promise: That, therefore, he excludes, since he wishes our dikaiōsin to be purely gratuitous. Finally, Bellarmine is deceived when he writes that that which is rendered to works which are done from grace is partly reward, partly grace. For thus could contrary things consist together in a mediate way, which is against the Apostle, Rom. 11, verse 6, thus concluding: But if by grace, it is no longer from works, that is, from the merits of works, otherwise grace is no longer grace, etc.

XLIX. But that the adversary may be the more strongly repelled, and it may be proved that all works whatsoever are excluded from the circle of justification, certain reasons and examples must be diligently noted. REASONS: 1. If the whole law and all works of the law whatsoever are opposed to the promise and to faith, in the negation of justification before God, the distinction of works which precede or follow justification is vain in this argument. But the former is true from Rom. 3. v. 20. 21. c. 4 v. 14 Galat. 2. v, 16. 17. c. 3. v. 18. Therefore the latter will also be true. 2. If the Apostle Paul says indistinctly and generally, By the works of the law no flesh is justified, that distinction is vain. The antecedent is true, therefore the consequent also. 3. Whatsoever works can produce boasting, those are here excluded. But absolutely all works can produce boasting, Rom. 4. v. 2. If Abraham was justified by works, he has whereof to glory. Bellarmine excepts in c. 19. This boasting is done in the Lord, because He supplied the strength to do good works, and it is not a prohibition, according to that 1. Cor. 1. He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. I answer: this very thing could have been said also of Abraham, that he performed good works not by his own strength, but by the strength of the Holy Spirit; and yet Paul says: If Abraham was justified by works, he has whereof to glory, because the saints cooperate with God in good works. 1. Cor. 3. v. 19. Wherefore, it being posited that good works are done partly by the strength of the will, partly by the strength of grace, boasting cannot be excluded. For in as much as they are done by the strength of the will, in so much can one boast. 4. Paul argues against the false apostles. These, however, although they defined the just and the unjust differently than Scripture defines them, yet they were not so stupid as to indicate that the works of men who were still impious had the power of justifying. Therefore if the Apostle were taking away the efficacy of justification only from the works of the impious, would he not be straying from the scope of the disputation? If works, which Bellarmine does not wish to be excluded here, follow faith, they certainly do not justify, but

Latin:

les virtutes omninò non cadant.

XLV. Diligenter hoc est considerandum, & Pontificijs semper opponendum, qui statuunt, spem, fidem & dilectionem iustificare præcedenter vel dispositivè, & hæc opera à iustificatione non esse exclusa, per exclusionem legis factorum, quia non pertineant ad legem factorum, sed ad legem fidei, quippe quæ sola faciat nos idoneos ad virtutes iustas, lex verò moralis eas præcipiat quidem, sed non largiatur vim faciendi, ideoque neminem legi morali duntaxat adhærentem posse Deum diligere, Deo credere aut in Deum sperare. Iam verò ita colligimus; Si nemo potest hæc facere; nemo potest etiam ijs iustificationem ascribere. Si hoc, cur Paulus adeò solicitus est, ne aliquis iustificationem ijs acceptam ferat? Num igitur hoc ignorauit? impium. Num adeò insulsus & abiurdus fuit, vt ea quæ fieri nullo modo possunt, solicitè prohiberet, nè fierent? ἄτοπον. Proinde ita statuendum, nè Paulo & ipsi Spiritui sancto aliquam ignorantiam aut absurditatem impiè tribuamus. Benè nouerat Spiritus sanctus non prohibenda esse, quæ fieri aliàs nequeunt:(quis enim prohiberet, nè quis hunc globum terræ humeris imponat & aliò transferat, cùm hoc simpliciter sit impossibile?) Quoniam igitur, hic aliquid prohibuit, necesse est, vtid, quod prohibuit, fieri potuerit, Interdixit autem, nè quis operibus moralibus tribueret iustificationem, qualia sunt spes, dilectio, timor. Quare hæc fieri possunt: Non autem sine gratia Spiritus sancti & fide. Hoc ipsum igitur inclusit Apostolus, & per consequens non intellexit opera non renatorum, cùm talia nulla sint, sed potiùs renatorum: Atq; sic ad legem factorum, quam exclusit Paulus, pertingt illa omnia, quæ Bellar. ad legem fidei refert.

XLVI. Porrò non immeritò quæritur, Vndènam hæc distinctio inter legem factorum & legem fidei hausta sit? & quibus fundamentis probetur? Affert Bell. l. 1. c. 16. aliquam ratiunculam, cur per legem factorum non omnia omninò opera possint esse exclusa, quam sic, proponit: Si excluduntur omnia opera & omnis lex, excludetur etiam fides. Nam actus fidei est quoddam opus, vti vocatur Ioh. 6. 29. Hoc est opus, vt credatis in eum, quem misit ille. Sive hoc opere igitur iustificabimur; si fides sine operibus omnia opera excludit; ac per hoc iustificari, ex fide, nihil aliud erit, quàm iustificari sine fide. Est etiam quædam lex fidei, de qua Rom. 3. Quod si fides iustificans sine operibus legis, excludit omnem legem, excludet etiam legem fidei: & quoniam lex fidei est ipsa fides, fides excludit fidem, & ex fide iustificari erit sine fide iustificari. Resp. 1. Quòd sit æquivocatio in vocabulo operis. Vel enim per opus intelligitur quævis actio, qualiscunque ista sit, absoluta vel relata, & hoc sensu fides vocari potest opus, quia est apprehensio, & applicatio, atque sic non opponitur fides & opus: vel proprie & strictè intelligitur actio aliqua vel opus aliquod morale, ex fide ortum & profectu, vbi differunt tanquam causa & effectum. Hoc sensu fides & opera sunt opposita: Et talia semper excluduntur è negotio Iustificationis. 2. Est Homonymia in vocabulo legis. Vel enim generatim & latè accipitur pro omni doctrina, & sic dicitur lex Christi, Galat. 6. v. 2. Et lex fidei, Rom. 3. v. 27. vel speciatim & pressiùs, pro Decalogo, & lege Mosaica, quà posteriore tantùm significatione opponitur Evangelio, & fidei. Excludit igitur Apostolus à iustificatione omnem legem, videlicet propriè dictam, hæc est, quæ opera exigit ab hominibus, & accusat, damnatque inobedientes, vt ita perpetua maneat oppositio Apostolica: Evangelium, non lex, fides non opera; credere, non facere, iustificat. Atque sic firmum perstat nostrum argumentum, suprà positum: Quodcunque ad legem pertinet, id non iustificat, Atqui virtutes, & omnia opera propriè dicta, qualiacunque sint, pertinent ad legem

Mosaïcam à iustificatione exclusam. Ergò virtutes & opera non iustificant.

XLVII. Secundum effugium est, quòd Bellarminus distinguit inter iustitiam legis, & iustitiam in lege, vel ex lege: iustitiam legis esse opera iusta, quæ lex facienda præscribat, & hanc veram esse iustitiam: Ex lege verò iustitiam ea esse opera, quæ homines faciunt sine gratia fidei, solâ cognitione legis adiuti, & hanc iustitiam esse inutilem, & hac opera non iustificare coram Deo, sed solùm coram hominibus, qui tantùm externa considerant. Verùm, quibus testimoniis probabitur hæc distinctio, & vbinam in Scripturis fundata est? Nobis potiùs iustitia legis, iustitia ex lege vnum sunt, & notatur illud; quando quis ex operibus legis, siue externis, siue internis; naturalibus siue supernaturalibus vult iustificari. Et quia Paulus iustitiam legis, in absolutione hominis peccatoris, iustitiæ fidei opponit, illam reijciens, hanc recipiens; concludimus indè, bonis nos operibus à peccatis nostris absolui minimè posse. Omnia enim opera pertinent ad iustitiam legis, ad cuius normam facta sunt. Quodcunq; autem tale est, id vnà cùm iustitia legis ab Apostolo Paulo exclusum est.

XLIIX. Tertium effugium hoc problema continet. Quænam opera Paulus intelligat, sine quibus nos iustificari asserit? Nostri dicunt, omnia omninò excludi opera, siue ante fidem, siue post fidem facta, quam sententiam vocat Bellarminus absurdissimam, ab ignoratione Scripturæ profectam, quod ostendit testimonio August. Sed illud contrà nos non militat, siquidem ijs opponendum, qui non solùm opera non iustificare, sed à iustificatis etiam non requiri, statuunt, ita vt fidem putent sufficere, etiamsi quis malè viuat; quæ sententia nostra non est, vt suprà indicatum. Cæterùm cap. 16. l. 1. ait, non omnia opera excludi, sed certum genus operum, id est, opera facta solis viribus staturam, vel ex sola cognitione legis Mosaicae, vel si quo alio modo opera legis hoc loco intelligenda sunt. Vnde apparet, ipsum, dum haec scriberet, nondum certum fuisse, quaenam ab Apostolo excusa sint opera: Sed cap. 19. recenset illorum Catholicorum sententiam, qui putant, per opera, sine quibus nos justificari dicit Paulus, non nisi observationes legalium ceremoniarum intelligendas esse, in qua tamen sententia ipse non acquiescit, sed dicit, sine ambigatione verissimum esse, per opera intelligi ea, quae fidem praecedunt, quaeque solis viribus liberi arbitrij fiunt: Vtitur autem ratione, ex Rom. 4. petita, vbi legitur: Ei, qui operatur, merces imputatur propter debitum; vnde colligit, ea excludi opera, quibus id quod redditur, merces est non gratia; qualia sint solùm ea, quae fiant vili beri arbitrij: quod enim reliquis redditur, non esse simpliciter mercedem, sed etiam gratiam, imò magis gratiam, quàm mercedem. Verum respondemus, hoc non esse propositum Pauli in isto dicto, sed potiùs argumentatur à genere ad speciem; Omni operanti merces imputatur secundùm debitum: Ergò etiam operanti renato, vel non renato. Deindè non dicitur, quòd operanti soli merces imputetur, sed vtique operanti & credenti, merces imputari dicitur, illi secundum debitum, huic secundum gratiam. Iustificatio enim operum fit secundum debitum, non quidem simplex, sed ex promisso: Illam igitur excludit, siquidem vult nostram dikaíwsin merè gratuitam esse. Tandem fallitur Bellarminus, cum scribit, id quòd redditur operibus, quae ex gratia fiunt, esse partim mercede, partim gratiam. Ita enim consistere simul possent contraria in mediata, quod est contra Apostolum, Rom. 11. vers. 6. ita concludentem: Quod si per gratiam, non iam ex operibus, hoc est, ex meritis operum, alioquin gratia iam non est gratia. &c.

XLIX. Vt autem eò fortiùs retundatur aduersarius, & probetur, omnia prorsus opera ex circulo Iustificationis excludi, quædam & rationes & exempla diligenter annotanda sunt. RATIONES: 1. Si tota lex & omnia omninò opera legis opponuntur promissioni & fidei, in negatione iustificationis coram Deo, vana est in hoc argumento distinctio operum, quæ antecedunt, vel consequuntur iustificationem. Prius autem est verum ex Rom. 3. v. 20. 21. c. 4 v. 14 Galat. 2. v, 16. 17. c. 3. v. 18. Ergo verum etiam erit posterius. 2. Si Apostolus Paulus indistincte & generaliter ait, Ex operibus legis non iustificari carnem, vana est ista distinctio. Verum antecedens, Ergo & consequens. 3. Quæcunque opera parere possunt gloriationem, illa hîcc sunt exclusa. Atqui opera absolutè omnia parere possunt gloriationem, Rom. 4. v. 2. Si Abraham ex operibus iustificatus fuit, habet quo glorietur. Excipit Bell. c. 19. Hanc gloriatione fieri in Domino, quò suppeditauit vires bona opera faciendi, & non esse se prohibitionem, iuxta illud 1. Cor. 1. Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur. Resp. hoc ipsum etiam de Abrahamo dici potuisset, quòd non suis, sed Spir. sancti viribus bona opera ediderit; & tamen Paulus inquit: Si Abraham ex operibus iustificatus fuit, habet quo glorietur, quia sancti cooperantur Deo in bonis operibus. 1. Cor. 3. v. 19 Quare posito: quòd bona opera fiant, partim viribus arbitrij, partim viribus gratiæ, excludi nequit gloriatio. In quantum enim fiunt viribus arbitrij, in tantum gloriari quis potest. 4. Paulus disputat contra Pseudoapostolos. Hi autem quamvis justos & injustos aliter definiebant, quàm Scriptura definit: tamen non erant adeò stupidi, vt hominum adhuc impiorum opera vim iustificandi habere indicarent. Itaque si Apostolus impiorum tantùm operibus iustificationis efficaciam detraheret, nonnè à scopo disputationis aberraret? Siopera, quæ hîc non excludi vult Bellarminus, consequuntur fidem, vtique non iustificant, sed


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: follow justification

follow justification. For faith, as the Apostle says, justifies, but works, which the Papists wish to be understood here, follow faith. Therefore also justification. Wherefore they do not justify, nor can they be the form of justification. 6. If all those works are excluded which are done without the special grace of the Spirit, faith also will be excluded, because for that general knowledge, which… they think is faith, there is no need for the grace of the Holy Spirit, since that faith is found even among those who have cast off the Holy Spirit by mortal sins. For the Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 5, acknowledges faithful fornicators, faithful adulterers, etc. Whence we infer thus: Whatever good work is found in a man not reborn and sinning mortally, that is to be thought to be done not by the aid of the Spirit, but by the powers of free will alone. But Papistic faith is found in the not reborn, as in adulterers. Therefore it is a work of free will, and consequently excluded from justification: because they say that all those things which are done by the powers of free will are excluded.

D. EXAMPLES, 1. Of Abraham. Here in Rom. 4 he is introduced as a universal example of justification: Wherefore if even good works proceeding from faith are excluded from the justification of Abraham, it follows that they are also excluded from our justification. But the former is true, therefore also the latter. I prove the minor, because Abraham is set forth as an example not in his first conversion, but after his conversion, when he had already sufficiently proven his faith and had done many good works. In that middle, as it were, course of good works, the question is raised by Moses in the Old Testament and Paul in the New Testament: What now was his …justification before God? And Paul certainly applies these sentences to that Abraham, already reborn and adorned with many works: Rom. 4, v. 2, If from works; he has glory: v. 5, To him who does not work: v. 6, David says that the blessedness is of him to whom God imputes righteousness without works. For that he speaks of the reborn Abraham is easily evident from a comparison with Genesis 15, verse 6, & Rom. 4. v. 3. For when Moses said, c. 15. Abraham believed God, he was already long since converted, as is evident from Gen. 11. And when Paul repeats this statement from Moses, it is certain that he looked, together with Moses, to those times of Abraham in which he was already converted. See more in Chemnitz, part 2, L. L. C C. p. 232, and in Exam. p. 134. LI. But Bellarmine replies to this argument thus, l. 1. cap. 19: Abraham at that time, of which the Apostle speaks, was indeed reborn, and was doing many good works from faith: yet the Apostle, when he says he was justified by faith, not by works, does not reject works done from faith, but affirms that they were not done without faith; because, if they had been such, they would never have justified him. And so he excludes works which Abraham could have done, not from faith. But this is a mere cavil, by which the light of truth can in no way be obscured. For whence will the Jesuit prove that the Apostle is speaking of works, not which Abraham did, but which he could have done? The words are certainly most manifest: If Abraham was justified by works, he had glory. How could he have had glory from works which he had not done? The Apostle therefore speaks of the justification of Abraham, not which could have been done, but which was in act. Because therefore the matter was present and actual, namely the justification of Abraham, the form also of that matter must be actual and present. But a twofold matter is proposed, the faith and the works of Abraham, and it is asked, whether works or faith justified Abraham? The Apostle answers, he was justified by faith without works; here certainly you cannot understand potential works, but actual ones: since it is not asked by what Abraham could have been justified, but by what he was actually justified? Now therefore we conclude thus: All works which accompany the reborn Abraham are excluded from justification. Therefore also works proceeding from faith. This argument can rightly be opposed to those who ascribe secondary justification to works.

For Abraham had already been reborn, as Bellarmine admits. Wherefore the Apostle is not speaking of primary justification simply, which is what Becanus wants. Therefore I cannot say that works are excluded from the first, but included in the second justification. For Abraham had already been justified at that time, and yet concerning his justification, which was being continued, and therefore by reason of its continuation could be called second, it is expressly said that it was done by faith without works.

LII. Furthermore, the Jesuit objects that the Apostle is speaking with a condition: But what of that? Nothing certainly is added to him, nor is anything taken away from us, since otherwise all hypothetical syllogisms would have to be rejected as inept and concluding little. But he continues: that Abraham had glory before God, and therefore was justified by works. But this is against the Apostle, and requires great proof. For Paul reasons thus: Whoever is justified by works, of whatever kind they may be, he has glory before men, but not before God, because even the best works do not stand in the divine judgment. But Abraham was before God, he had glory, therefore he was justified by works, even the best ones, in no way.

LIII. 2 The example of David. Here, after he had said, Ps. 143, v. 2, Hear me in thy righteousness, he immediately adds, Enter not into judgment. But David does not fear some tyrannical cruelty. Whence it follows that God is said to enter into judgment when he demands the nature, life, actions, and works of men according to the norm of his righteousness. Why therefore does David pray against this judgment? Did he perhaps have no good works? But this is not credible concerning that Prophet, through whom the Holy Spirit spoke: especially since he calls himself the servant of God: Enter not into judgment with thy servant. Who, moreover, is the servant of God, he himself explains in Psalm 18. Thy servant keeps thy commandments. Therefore, when he was the servant of God, he does not wish to be judged according to the righteousness of inherent novelty, because he says: There shall not be justified in thy sight every living thing. And Psalm 32 says concerning all the saints, that righteousness is imputed to them without works. David therefore excluded the works of the saints and the regenerate from justification.

LIV. 3. The example of the Apostles Galatians 2, v. 16. The Apostle says: We have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the Law. Now if the holy Apostles of Jesus Christ were justified without their works (which without doubt were good) by faith alone, it follows that all works are absolutely excluded from justification. But first from that Gal. 2. E. and afterwards,

LV. 4. Of Paul in particular, who in Phil. 3, v. 8 says, that his, I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Jesus Christ, that I may be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. Here he speaks not only in the past but also in the present of his own works, done after conversion, which if they are held as the form of justification, he pronounces to be dung and loss, and therefore says that he does not have the righteousness which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ. Bellarmine says that the Apostle is speaking of works done without faith, because works done from faith cannot be called dung, and in Gal. 5 they are called fruits of the Spirit. But the answer is easy: works are condemned if they are said to justify, they are praised if they are not said to justify, but to follow the justified. In the former sense, if indeed they are assumed into the circle of justification, they can be called dung without blasphemy. And that the matter may be more manifest, if Paul wishes works to be excluded, let that which he writes in 1 Cor. 4, v. 4 be considered: I know nothing by myself, yet am I not hereby justified. For he says the same thing that he says in Acts 23: I have lived in all good conscience before God until this day of mine, and Acts 24: I exercise myself to have always a conscience void of offence toward God. But hear what the regenerate Paul pronounces concerning that righteousness of his of a good conscience, which he attributes to the grace of God, 1 Cor. 15: In this, he says, I am not justified.

LVI. These testimonies will be more evident and all examples, if the Pauline reasons are noted, for which he removed justification even from the good works of the reborn. 1. It is the Exclusion of the Law: Whatever pertains to the law, that is removed from justification, which is not from the Law, but from the Gospel. But all works whatsoever, even those of the reborn, pertain to the law, for they are commanded by God in the law. Therefore they are removed from justification. For if they justified, justification would certainly be in some measure from the law, which is against Paul Gal. 3. v. 2. Phil. 3. v. 9. And note, that Paul does not say that faith justifies in this sense, that it prepares or helps us to accept the righteousness of works, as the Papists wish, but rather that works are entirely excluded: Whence it is said Rom. 1. v. 17. In the Gospel the righteousness of God is revealed, not from faith into works, but from faith into faith. And Galat. 2. v. 16. We have believed in Christ, not that by faith we might attain the righteousness of works, but that we might be justified by faith, not by works. And that Apostolic distinction must be studiously observed, from faith not from works, nor is that Papistic conjunction to be admitted, that we are justified by faith and works together. For thus much would be detracted from the merit of Christ, as if that could not have justified us without us. Therefore, by virtue of this distinction and disjunction, those words of Paul conclude most truly, If from works, not from faith. If the inheritance is from the law, faith is made void and the promise is abolished, Rom. 4. v. 14. Gal. 3. v. 18. If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing. Galat. 2. These disjunctions are perpetual: Nor is it to be allowed that they be explained by the Papists thus, If we are justified from the law, Christ died for nothing, that is, if we are justified by our own powers. For generally and always these are opposed, Law and Gospel, to do and to believe, faith and works: which since the Papists conjoin, they certainly contradict the Apostles as it were to their faces. For these are Apostolic. 1 We are justified by faith, Rom. 3. v. 28. 2 Without works, ibid. 3. By not working, but by believing c. 4. v. 5 4. By imputation according to grace, in the same place. 5. By grace. chapter 3, verse 24. 6. Because of Christ, in the same place, 7. Without the law, chapter 3, verse 21. 8. Not except through faith, Galatians 2, verse 16. The Romanists, however, contradict these entirely. For these are their assertions: 1. That a man is justified by faith, hope, and charity together. 2. By the works of the Gospel. 3. By working evangelically. 4. According to debt and justice. 5. By meriting. 6. Through good works. 7. Not without works. 8. Through faith and works. For what the Apostles said generally concerning all works, these men interpret specifically concerning works done without faith: what they perpetually separated and opposed, these men join together and consider consistent, which is by no means to be conceded to them.

LVII. 2. The exclusion of boasting. For if we are justified without any boasting of our own, we certainly cannot be justified by works. But the former is true. Therefore the latter is also. For he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord, 1 Corinthians 1, verse 31. But boasting is not excluded by the law of works (that is, when someone receives the inheritance of eternal life because he has done those things which are written in the law), but by the law of faith, that is, because Christ is the perfection of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, etc.

LIIX. 3. The imperfection of works. Because all our works are imperfect, they cannot justify or stand in the judgment of the Lord: For they themselves have need of some pardon on account of the infirmity adhering to them, Psalm 32, verse 6. Matthew 6, verse 12. One must use with David from Psalm 143, verse 2: Enter not into judgment with thy servant. See Chemnitz pursuing these reasons more broadly in Exam. pages 136, 137, and in Locis page 334.

Latin:

sequuntur iustificationem. Fides enim dicente Apostolo iustificat, opera autem, quæ hîc volunt intelligi Pontificij, consequuntur fidem. Ergò & iustificationem. Quare non iustificant, neque forma iustificationis esse possunt. 6. Si illa opera excluduntur omnia, quæ sine speciali Spiritus fiunt gratia, etiam fides excludetur, quia ad notitiam illam generalem, quam isti fidem putant, non opus est gratiâ S.S. quippe cùm illa fides reperiatur etiam apud eos, qui mortalibus peccatis excusserunt, S.S. Concil. enim Trid. agnoscit, sess. 6. c. 5. fideles fornicarios, fideles adulteros, &c. Vnde sic inferimus, Quodcunq; opus bonum reperitur in homine nõ renato, & mortaliter peccante, id non adiuuãte Spiritu, sed solis arbitrij virib. fieri putandũ est. Atqui fides Papistica reperitur in nõ renatis, vt in adulteris. Ergò est opus a.bitrij, & p consequens exclusa à iustificatione: quia dicunt ea omnia, quæ fiunt viribus arbitrij, exclusa esse.

D. EXEMPLA, 1. Abrahami. Hic Rom. 4. introducitur tanquam vniuersale exemplum iustificationis: Quare si opera etiam bona & ex fide profecta excluduntur à iustificatione Abrahami, sequitur, quòd etiam è nostra iustificatione excludantur. Sed verum prius, Ergo & posterius. Minorem probo, Quia ponitur Abraham pro exemplo non in prima conuersione, sed post conuersionem, cùm iam fidem satis probâsset, & multa bona opera egisset. In illo igitur medio quasi cursu bonorum operum mouetur à Mose in V. & Paulo in N. T. quæstio, Quanam nunc fuerit iusstificatio coram Deo? Et Paulus sanè ad illum Abrahamum, iam renatum, & multis operibus ornatum accommodat has sententias Rom 4. vers. 2. Si ex operibus; habet gloriam: v. 5. Non operanti v. 6. David dicit, beatitudinem esse illius, cui Deus non imputat peccata sine operibus. Quod enim de Abrahamo renato loquatur, facilè patet ex collatione Genes. 15 ver. 6, & Rom. 4. v. 3. Cùm enim Moses diceret, c. 15. Credidit Abraham Deo, tum erat iam dudum conuersus, vt patet ex Genes. 11. Et quando Paulus hoc dictum ex Mose repetit, certum est, illum respexisse vnà cum Mose ad illa Abrahę tempora, quibus iam tum conuersus erat. Vide plura apud Chemnitium part. 2. L. L. C C. p. 232. & in Exam. p. 134. LI. Ad hoc autem argumentum ita respondet Bellarminus, l. 1. cap. 19 Abraham eo tempore, de quo loquitur Apostolus, renatus quidem erat, & ex fide multa bona opera faciebat: tamen Apostolus cùm dicit eum iustificatum esse ex fide, non ex operibus, non reyecit opera facta ex fide, sed affirmat, illa non esse facta sine fide; quia, si talia fuissent, nunquam eum iustificassent. Itaque excludit opera, quæ Abraham facere potuisset, non ex fide. Sed mera hæc est cauillatio, qua lux veritatis nullo modo obfuscaripotest. Vnde enim probabit Iesu Wita, loqui Apostolum de operibus, non quæ faciebat, sed quæ facere poterat Abrahamus? Verba certè sunt manifestissima: Si Abraham ex operibus iustificatus est, habuit gloriam. Quomodo gloriam habere potuisset, ab operibus, quæ non fecisset? Loquitur proindè Apostolus de iustificatione Abrahami, non quæ fieri poterat, sed quæ actu erat. Quia igitur res erat præsens & actualis, videl. iustificatio Abrahami, formam quoq; ejus rei oportet actualem esse & præsentem. Proponitur autem res duplex, fides & opera Abra hami, & quæritur, an opera, an fides Abrahamum iustificauerint? Respondet Apostolus, fide iustificatus est sine operibus; hic certè non potes intelligere opera potentialia, sed actualia: quandoquidem non quęritur, per quid iustificari potuerit Abrahamus, sed per quid iustificatus actu fuerit? Nunc igitur ita colligimus: Omnia opera, quæ comitantur Abrahamum renatum excluduntur à iustificatione. Ergò etiam opera ex fide profecta. Potest hoc argumentum rectè ijs opponi, qui iustificationem secundam operibus ascribunt.

Jam enim renatus erat Abraham, fatente Bellarmino. Quare non loquitur Apostolus de iustificatione prima simpliciter, quod vult Becanus. Non igitur possum dicere, quod opera excludantur a prima, includantur in secunda iustificatione. Nam Abraham iam tum iustificatus erat, & tamen de ipsius iustificatione, quæ continuabatur, ideoque ratione continuationis secunda nuncupari posset, expresse dicitur, quod facta fuerit fide sine operibus.

LII. Excipit porro Jesu Wita, loqui Apostolum cum coditione: Sed quid inde? Nihil sane ipsi accedit, nec nobis decedit, cum alias omnes syllogismi hypothetici forent rejiciendi, tanquam inepti, & paru concludentes. Sed pergit ille: Abrahamum habuisse gloriam apud Deum, ideoq̃ ex operibus iustificatum fuisse. Verum hoc est contra Apostolum, & magnâ eget probatione. Ita enim ratiocinatur Paulus: Quicunque iustificatur ex operibus, qualiacunq̃ sint, ille habet gloriam coram hominibus, sed non apud Deum, quia opera etiam optima in iudicio diuino non consistunt. Atqui Abraham apud Deum fuit, habuit gloriam, Ergo ex operibus etiam optimis iustificatus, nullo modo.

LIII. 2 Exemplum Dauidis. Hic postquam dixiffet, Pf. 143. v. 2. Exaudi me in iustitia tua, mox addit. Ne intres in iudicium. Non autem timet Dauid tyrannicam quandam crudelitatem. Vnde sequitur, quod Deus tum dicatur intrare in iudiciũ, quando hominum naturam, vitam, actiones, & opera exigit ad norman iustitię suæ Quare ergo hoc iudicium deprecatur Dauid? An forsan nulla habuit bona opera? Ast hoc de Propheta illo, per quem S.S. loquebatur, non est credibile: præsertim cum se vocet servum Dei: Ne intres in iudicium cum seruo tuo. Quis a. sit servus Dei, ipse explicat Psal. 18. Servus tuus custodit mandata tua. Tunc igitur cum esset servus Dei, non vult iuxta inhærentis nouitatis iustitiam iudicari, quia inquit: Non iustificabitur, in conspectu tuo omnis viuens. Et Psal. 32. de omnibus sanctis dicit, quod ipsis imputetur iustitia sine operibus. Dauid igitur à iustificatione exclusit etiam sanctorum, & renatorum opera.

LIV. 3. Exemplum Apostolorum Galat. 2, v. 16. dicit Apostolus: Nos in Iesum Christum credidimus, vt iustificaremur ex fide Christi, non ex operibus Legis. Iam verò si S. Iesu Christi Apost. sine suis operib (quæ procul dubio fuêre bona) ex sola fide iustificati sunt, seqtur, q ex iustificatione omnia absolutè sint exclusa opera. Verù pri9 ex illo Gal. 2. E. & postenus,

LV. 4. Pauli in specie, qui Phil. 3. v. 8. ait, q, suam, Existimo, omnia detrimentum esse propter eminentem, scientiam Iesu Christi, vt & inueniar in illo, non habens meam iustitiam, quæ ex lege est, sed illam, quæ ex fide est Christi, quæ ex Deo est iustitia in fide. Hic non solum in preterito sed in præsenti etiam de suis operibus, post conuersionem factis, loquitur, quę si pro forma iustificationis habeantur, pronunciat esse stercora, & detrimenta, ideoque dicit, se non habere iustitiam, quæ ex lege est, sed illam, quę ex fide est Christi, Bellar inquit, loqui Apostolum de operibus factis sine fide, quia facta ex fide nequeant nominari stercora, & Gal. 5. nominentur fructus Spiritus. Verùm responsio est facilis: opera damnantur, si iustificare, laudantur si non iustificare, sed iustificatum sequi dicantur. Priori sensu, si nimirum in circulum iustificationis assumantur, sine blasphemia nominari possunt stercora. Et vt res manifestior sit, si opera Paulus exclusa velit, consideretur id, quod scribit 1. Cor. 4. v. 4. Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non sum iustificatus. Idem enim dicit, quod Act. 23. Ego omni conscientia bona conuersatus sum ante Deum vsq; in hanc vsq; meum diem, & Actor. 24. Studeo sine offendiculo conscientiam habere ad Deum. Sed audi, quid Paulus renatus de sua illa iustitia bonæ conscientiæ, quam gratiæ Dei tribuit, cor. 15. pronunciat: In hoc inquit, iustificatus non sum.

LVI. Euidentiora v. eruut hæc testimonia & exempla omnia, si annotentur rationes Paulinæ, ob quas etiam bonis renatorum operibus iustificationem ademit. 1. est Exclusio Legis : Quodcunque ad legem pertinet, id remouetur a iustificatione, quæ no est ex Lege, sed Evangelio. Atqui omnia omnino etiam renatorum opera ad legem pertinent, sunt enim a Deo in lege præcepta. Ergo remouentur a iustificatione. Si enim iustificarent, profecto iustificatio quodamtenus ex lege esset, quod est contra Paulum Galat. 3. vers. 2. Phil. 3. vers. 9. Et nota, Paulum non dicere, fidem iustificare hoc sensu, quod præparet vel adiuuet nos ad acceptandam iusticiam operum, vti volunt Pontificij, sed potius omnino excludi opera: Vnde dicitur Rom. 1. ver. 17. In Evangelio reuelatur iustitia Dei, non ex fide in opera, sed ex fide in fidem. Et Galat. 2. v. 16. Nos credidimus in Christum, non vt fide assequeremur iustitiam operum, sed vt iustificemur fide non operibus. Et studiose obseruanda est illa distinctio Apostolica, ex fide non ex operibus, neque admittenda illa coniunctio Papistica, ex fide simul & operibus nos iustificari. Sic enim merito Christi multum detraheretur, ac si illud non potuisset nos sine nobis iustificare. Vi ergo huius distinctionis, & disiunctionis verissime concludunt illa Pauli, Si ex operibus, non ex fide. Si ex lege hæreditas, exinanita est fides & abolita est promissio, Rom. 4. v. 14. Gal. 3. v. 18. Si per legem iustitia, ergo Christus gratis mortuus est. Galat. 2. Perpetuæ sunt hæ disiunctiones: Neq; committendum, vt a Papistis ita explicentur, Si ex lege iustificamur, Christus gratis est mortuus, hoc est si proprijs viribus iustificamur. Nam generaliter & semp hæc opponntur, Lex & Evangelium credere facere, fides opera: quæ quoniam coniungunt Pontificij, certe Apostolis in os quasi contradicut. Hæc enim sunt Apostolica. 1 Nos fide iustificari, Rom. 3. v 28. 2 Sine operibus, ibidem. 3. Non operando, sed credendo c. 4. v. 5 4. Imputatione secundùm gratiam, ibidem. 5. Ex gratia. cap. 3. versu 24. 6. Propter Christum, ibidem, 7. Sine lege, cap. 3. versu 21. 8. Non nisi per fidem, Gala. 2. versu 16. Romanenses verò his prorsus contradicunt. Hæ enim illorum sunt assertiones: 1. Iustificari hominem fide, spe, & charitate simul. 2. Operibus Euangelii. 3. Operando Evangelicè. 4. Secundum debitum & iustitiam 5. Merendo. 6. Per bona opera. 7. Non sine operibus, 8. Per fidem & opera. Quæ enim Apostoli generaliter dixerunt, de omnibus operibus, hæc ipsi specialiter interpretantur de operibus factis sine fide: quæ illi perpetuò disiunxerunt & opposuerunt, hęc ipsi coniugunt, & pro consentaneis habent, quod minimè ipsis concedendum.

LVII. 2. Exclusio gloriationis. Si enim iustificamur sine omni nostrâ gloriatione, ex operibus certè iustificari non poterimus. Verum prius. Ergò & posterius. Qui enim gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, 1. Cor. 1. versu 31. Non autem excluditur gloriatio per legem factorum (hoc est, quando quis vitæ æternæ hæreditatem ideò accipit, quòd ea, quæ in lege scripta sunt, fecerit, ) sed per legem fidei, hoc est, quia Christus est perfectio legis ad iustitiam omni credenti, &c.

LIIX. 3. Imperfectio operum. Quia omnia nostra opera sunt imperfecta, ideò iustificare nequeunt, aut in judicio Domini consistere: Nam & ipsa opus habent aliquâ venia propter adhærescentem infirmitatem, Psalm. 32 versu 6. Matth. 6. versu 12. Vterandum sit cum Davide ex Psalmo 143. v. 2. Ne intres in iudicium cum servo tuo. Vide has rationes latiùs persequentem Chemnitium in Exam. pag. 136. 137. & in Locis pag. 334.


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: Second Class. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified freely or by grace

SECOND CLASS. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified freely or by grace.

LIX. Such things are read in Rom. 3, ver. 24; Acts 15, ver. 10; Rom. 4, v. 16; Rom. 5, v. 15, 17, 21; Rom. 11, ver. 5, 6; Gal. 2, v. 2; Gal. 5, ver. 4; Eph. 1, ver. 5, 6, 7; chap. 2, verse 8; Tit. 3, ver. 7. From which we argue thus: Whoever are justified freely by grace, they are not justified by their own virtues or works. But those who are justified, they are all justified freely, and by the grace of God. Therefore they are not justified by their own virtues. The major premise is most firm, on account of the perpetual antithesis between being given freely and being given on account of works, between grace and works. Therefore, one of the contraries being posited, the other is removed, and consequently, we shall not be justified freely by grace and at the same time by works, but rather it must be concluded, with the Apostle, if by works, not by grace, otherwise works are not works; if by grace, not by works, otherwise grace is not grace. For grace is not grace in any way, if it is not grace in every way, just as Augustine writes. And it is to be noted that the Apostle speaks, not specifically about these or those, but generally about all works. For the indefinite [proposition], which he uses, is equivalent to a universal. Certainly there would be no cause for doubting, he adds the word δωρεὰν, freely, lest anyone think that that grace happens because of our virtues and works. For whatever is given entirely freely, there can be no foundation for that thing in the recipient. But we are said to be justified freely. Therefore, not even the smallest cause of justification, much less the formal one, can inhere in us.

LX. Nor is it the case, as the Papists object, that we are justified freely by grace for the reason that a habit of justice is freely infused into us. For this objection would have a certain appearance, if the Apostle had not always opposed these two, grace and works, in such a way that in this matter they cannot stand together, which antithesis is certainly entirely removed if the interpretation of the Papists were to have a place. For Paul says: we are justified freely, without works, by faith, by grace alone; the Papists say thus: we are righteous freely by grace, and freely through an infused habit of righteousness, not without works. Is this not a most manifest contradiction, and a most open depravation of Paul's words? It must be observed here, and repeated, that the Papists take the word 'to justify' in one way, and our people in another. For they understand it actively, we passively: they take it ethically, we theologically. To them, to be justified is to be made inherently righteous, but to us it is to be absolved from punishments, which forensic interpretation, if we always urge it, will produce from their own glosses most absurd paraphrases of Pauline expressions.

LXI. Now we shall attend to what Bellarmino, in book 1, chapter 21, answers regarding the particle 'freely'. The sum of the response is this. The 'freely' of justification is opposed either to works done from nature, or to works done from grace. It is opposed to the former for this reason, because all such works do not lead to justification, nor are they meritorious by congruity or by condignity. It is opposed to the latter, in so far as they are considered meritorious by condignity. Therefore, the justification of man is called free, 1. because works done from faith do not merit the habit of righteousness by condignity, although they do by congruity. 2. because works done without faith in no way merit, neither by condignity nor by congruity. Therefore, by grace, the merit of condignity of works done without faith is properly excluded. This is Bellarmino's opinion.

LXII. But 1. the antithesis of the Apostle stands in the way, who always opposes the 'freely' to works, and indeed indefinitely, that is, to all. 2. The 'freely', properly spoken, excludes every cause in him to whom anything is given freely. If, therefore, our justification must truly be free, nothing will inhere in us that could be able to merit justification, whether that merit be by congruity or by condignity. 3. As much as to us and our merits is ascribed, so much is taken away from the most sufficient merit of Christ, which is impious. 4. How will the Jesuit prove that distinction from the Apostle Paul? Where indeed is there a distinction between the merit of congruity and condignity? 5. If they say that this redounds to CHRIST himself, because those works are not performed out of the powers of nature but of grace freely given, we immediately ask, what do they understand by that grace, which they call the efficient cause of these works? For it is either general or special. If the latter, they are entirely mistaken, because this falls to no one unless he is reconciled. For when a man is still a child of wrath, he cannot be a participant in the special grace of God, with which He pursues us as those pleasing to Him and beloved sons. Now whoever is outside the love or special grace of God, his works cannot be said to have proceeded from the special grace of God, for who is not yet, how can he have the power to act or work? But all who are not justified are outside the special grace and love of God, as was just concluded. Therefore, their works cannot have proceeded from the special grace of God, which was to be concluded. But if the Papists understand general grace, they are entirely selling smoke and substituting words for the thing, that is, sonorous lies. For that general grace is nothing other than the universal concurrence of the first cause, which is necessary in all actions, both moral and natural. Because of this concurrence, actions are not called theological or spiritual, even though they are not done without the aid of general divine grace.
