For in all actions there must be three principles: the universal, which is God; the common, which is nature; the particular or special, which is always the proximate agent. And from this the denomination is made. If the proximate principle is a natural agent, the action is called natural; if

Latin:

SECVNDA CLASSIS. Continens dicta, quæ docent hominem gratis vel ex gratia iustificari.

LIX. Talia leguntur Rom. 3. ver. 24. Actor. 15. ver. 10. Rom. 4. v. 16. Rom. 5. v. 15. 17. 21. Rom. 11. ver. 5. 6. Galat. 2. v. 2. Galat. 5 ver. 4. Ephes. 1. ver. 5. 6 7. cap. 2. versu 8. Tit. 3. ver. 7. Ex quibus ita argumentamur: Quicunque justificantur gratis ex gratia, illi non justificantur suis virtutibus vel operibus. Sed qui justificantur, illi omnes justificantur gratis, & per gratiam Dei. Ergò non iustificantur suis virtutibus. Maior est firmissima, ob perpetuam ἀντίθεσιν inter gratis dari, & propter opera dari, inter gratiam & opera. Vno igitur contrariorum posito, tollitur alterum, & per consequens, non justificabimur gratis ex gratia, & simul ex operibus, sed potiùs concludendum est, cum Apostolo, si ex operibus non ex gratia, alioquin opera non sunt opera; si ex gratia, non ex operibus, alioquin gratia non est gratia. Gratia enim non est gratia ullo modo, si non est gratia omni modo, quemadmodum scribit Augustinus. Et notandum quòd Apostolus loquatur, non in specie de his vel illis, sed in genere de omnibus operibus. Indefinita enim, quâ utitur, æquipollet universali. Vtique plane nulla esset dubitandi causa, addit vocabulum δωρεὰν gratis, ne quis putet illam gratiam ex nostris contingere virtutibus & operibus. Quodcunque enim omninò gratis datur, eius rei fundamentum nullum esse potest in accipiente. Atqui nos gratis iustificari dicimur. Ergò Iustificationis causa nè quidem minima, multò minus formalis, nobis inhærere potest.

LX. Neque est, ut excipiant Pontificij, nos gratis ex gratia iustificari ideò, quia habitus iustitiæ gratis nobis infundatur. Speciem enim quandam haberet hæc exceptio, nisi Apostolus hæc duo semper opposuisset, gratiam & opera, ita ut in hoc negotio simul stare nequeant, quæ profectò ἀντίθεσις omninò tollitur, si Pontificiorum interpretatio locum habere debeat. NamPaulus dicit: iustificamur gratis, sine operibus, fide, ex sola gratia, Pontificij ita dicunt: iusti sumus gratis ex gratia, & gratis per infusum iustitiæ habitum, non sine peribus. Nonne hæc est manifestissima cotradictio, & verborum Pauli apertissima deprauatio? Obseruandum verò hîc, & repetendum, aliter Pontificios, aliter nostros verbum iustificandi accipere. Illi enim actiuè, nos passiuè intelligimus: Illi sumunt Ethicè: nos Theologicè. Illis iustificari est inhærenter iustum fieri, nobis verò est à pœnis absolui, quam forensem interpretationem si semper vrgeamus, prodibunt ex ipsorum glossis paraphrases locutionum Paulinarum absurdissimæ.

LXI. Nunc quid Bellarminus lib. 1. cap. 21. ad particulam gratis respondeat, attendemus. Summa responsionis hæc est. τὸ gratuitum Iustificationis vel opponitur operibus factis ex natura, vel operibus factis ex gratia. Istis opponitur hac ratione, quia talia opera omnia non conducunt ad iustificationem, nec de congruo, nec de condigno sunt meritoria. His opponitur, in quantum meritoria censentur de condigno. Iustificatio igitur hominis dicitur gratuita, 1. quia opera facta ex fide non de condigno, licèt de congruo, habitum iustitiæ promerentur. 2. quia opera facta sine fide nullo modo, neque de condigno neque de congruo merentur. Per gratiam igitur propriè excludi meritum condigni operum sine fide factorum. Hæc Bellarmini est sententia.

LXII. Verùm 1. obstat ἀντίθεσις Apostoli, qui τὸ gratuitum semper opponit operibus, & quidem indefinitè, hoc est, omnibus. 2. τὸ gratuitum propriè dictum, excludit omnem causam, in eo, cui quid gratuitò donatur. Quòd si ergò iustificatio nostri verè debet esse gratuita, nihil in nobis hærebit, quod iustificationem promereri valeat, siuè meritum illud sit de congruo siuè de condigno. 3. Quantum nobis & nostris meritis adscribitur, tantum sufficientissimo Christi merito adimitur, quod impium. 4. Quomodo distinctionem illam ex Apostolo Paulo probabit IesuWita? Vbi nam distinguitur inter meritum congrui & condigni? 5. Si dicant, redundare hoc in ipsum CHRISTVM, quia illa opera non sint ex viribus naturæ sed gratiæ gratis datæ præstita, statim quærimus, quid intelligant per istam gratiam, quam horum operum causam efficientem appellant? Aut enim generalem, aut specialem. Sihanc, prorsus errant, quia hæc nemini contingit, nisi reconciliato. Cùm enim homo adhuc est filius iræ, tum nequit esse particeps gratiæ Dei specialis, quâ prosequitur nos, tanquam sibi placentes & dilectos filios. Iam quicunque est extra dilectionem vel gratiam Dei specialem, illius opera non possunt dici profecta ex gratia Dei speciali, quod enim nondum est, qui agere aut operari valeat? Atqui omnes non iustificati sunt extra gratiam ac dilectionem Dei specialem, quod modò conclusum, Ergò illorum opera ex gratia Dei speciali profecta esse nequeunt, quod erat concludendum. Sin autem Pontificij gratiam intelgant generalem, omninò fumos vendunt & pro re substituunt verba, hoc est, sonora mendacia, Nam generalis illa gratia nihil est aliud, quàm vniuersalis concursus primæ causæ, qui in omnibus actionibus & moralibus & naturalibus est necessarius. Ob istum concursum actiones non dicuntur Theologicæ aut spirituales, quamuis non sint absque generalis gratiæ diuinæ adiumento factæ. Nam in omnibus actionibus tria sint oportet principia, vniuersale, quod Deus est: commune, quod natura: particulare vel speciale, quod semper agens est proximum. Atque ab hoc fit denominatio. Si principium proximum est agens naturale, actio dicitur naturalis. si


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: Classis tertia

the agent is free, the action is called moral, but if the agent is [moved] by the peculiar grace of the Holy Spirit, then the action is called spiritual. Just as therefore eating is not called a Theological action, even though without the general grace of God a man cannot eat, so works done before justification cannot be called Theological works reason is this, because the denomination and distinction of actions is derived not from a general, but from a special and particular principle. Therefore, the Papists betray themselves in this place, because they openly Pelagianize. For Pelagius himself also explained himself in this way, that the works of free will are called works of grace, because a man without grace (he understood, however, general [grace]) can do nothing. But it was rightly answered to them, that the works of nature and grace cannot be distinguished in this way, because the grace of God concurs with every action. Therefore the Papists say nothing when they think that works of nature are excluded, but not those of grace. For what they themselves call works of grace are not such, but rather works of nature, because the ultimate and proximate principle is the powers of nature, not special grace, which has no place in those not yet justified. Whence it is manifestly gathered that it is a mere cataract [of the eyes] when they distinguish between works of nature and grace, [saying] that these are in no way meritorious, and thus all praise redounds to GOD.

The third class.

Containing those sayings in which faith alone is named, with the remaining works omitted.

LXIII. Such [passages] are read, Rom. 3, 4, 5, Galat. 2, Luke 7, etc., whence we argue thus. If virtues or works justified, our justification would certainly not be ascribed to faith alone, which nevertheless is done in the sayings just alleged. But Bellarmine replies in ch. 20 that it is often accustomed to happen that when many causes concur, the effect is ascribed now to this cause, now to that. Thus justification is now ascribed to faith, now to love, now to hope. But the Apostle Paul in Rom. 3 and Gal. 2 wishes to describe our justification accurately according to its causes; and there is no doubt that he also accomplished that. Whatever, therefore, the Apostle, while dealing expressly with justification, did not name, the very form and quiddity of our justification does not consist in that. And yet he did not name love, hope, and other virtues. Therefore, the very form of our justification does not consist in these. The major premise is proven, because it is not likely that the Apostle wrote superficially here about justification, but rather he expounded this matter most accurately, since he spent several chapters on its treatment. Who, therefore, could not be accused of either lazy negligence or some gross ignorance, if he had not expressed the formal cause of justification? We have elsewhere named there the primary efficient cause, namely the favor and grace of God; we have the secondary and meritorious efficient cause, namely the satisfaction of Christ; we have the instrumental cause, namely faith, apprehending the grace of God and the merit of Christ; we have the form and quiddity, namely the remission of sins, made on account of the imputed merit of Christ apprehended by faith; we have finally the end, namely the declaration of divine justice. But where are works, where are infused habits, where are inherent virtues? There is deep silence about these in the doctrine of justification. Costerus indeed writes on page 271 that remaining works are included under faith. But 1. he begs the question. 2. The Apostolic antithesis teaches the contrary: 3. He refers works to faith, which nevertheless formally pertain to the law. 4. Hope and other virtues would precede justification, which is most absurd.

Latin:

agens est liberum, actio dicitur moralis, si agens autem sit peculiaris Spiritus sancti gratia, tu actio vocatur spiritualis. Sicut igitur comestio non vocatur actio Theologica, etiamsi absque gratia Dei generali homo non possit comedere, sic opera ante iustificatione facta dici nequeunt opera Theologica vel opera gratiæ, licèt Deus generaliter concurrat. Ratio est hæc, quia denominatio & distinctio actionum desumitur non à generali, sed speciali & particulari principio. Produnt igitur hoc in loco sese Pontificij, quòd apertè pelagianizent. Nam & ipse Pelagius ita se explicabat, quòd opera liberi arbitrij vocentur opera gratiæ, quia homo sine gratia, (intelligebat vero generalem) nihil possit. Verum rectè ipsi respōsum, quòd opa naturę & gratię ita distingui nequeāt, quia ad omnem actionem gratia Dei concurrat. Nihil igitur dicunt Pōtificij, quando cesent, excludi opera naturæ, non verò gratiæ. Quæ enim ipsi vocant opera gratiæ, non sunt talia sed potiùs opera naturæ, quia vltimum & proximúm principium sunt vires naturæ, non specialis gratia, quæ in nondum iustificatis locum non habet. Vndè manifestè colligitur, merum esse glaucoma, quādo distinguunt inter opera naturæ & gratiæ, hæc, in, nulla esse meritoria, & sic omnem laudem ad DEVM redundare.

Classis tertia.

Continens ista dicta, in quibus sola fides, omissis operibus reliquis nominatur.

LXIII. Huiusmodi leguntur, Rom. 3. 4 5. Galat. 2. Luc 7. &c. vnde sic argumentamur. Si virtutes vel opera iustificarent, vtique iustificatio nostra non soli adscribere…ur fides, quod tamen fit in dictis modo allegatis. Sed respōdet Bellar. c. 20. quòd sępè soleat fieri, vt quando multæ cōcurrunt causæ, effectus nunc huic, nũc illi causæ ascribatur. Sic iustificationem nunc fidei ascribi, nunc dilectioni, nunc spei. Verùm Apostolus Paulus Rom. 3. & Gal. 2. nostram accurate vult describere iustificationem secundùm causas suas; & nullum est dubium, quòd etiam illud præstiterit. Quicquid igitur Apostolus de iustificatione ex professo agens non nominauit, in eo non consistet ipsa forma & quidditas iustificationis nostræ. Atqui dilectionem, spem, & alias virtutes non nominauit. E. in his non consistit ipsa iustificationis nostræ forma. Maior pbatur, quia verisimile nõ est, Apostolũ superficialiter hîc de iustificatione scripsifse, sed potiùs accuratissimè hoc negotium exposuit, cùm aliquot capita tractatione illius insumpserit. Qui ergò non accusari posset vel supinæ negligentiæ, vel crassæ alicuius inscitiæ, si formalem iustificationis causam non expressisset? Habemus aliàs ibi nominatam causam efficientem primam, videlicet Dei fauorem & gratiã, habemus causam efficientem secundam & meritoriam, videlicet Christi satisfactionem; habemus causam instrumentalem, videlicet fidem, Dei gratiam & meritum Christi apprehendentem; habemus formam & quidditatem, nempè remissionem peccatorum, factam ob imputatum, & fide apprehensum meritum Christi; habemus denique finem, nimirum declarationem iustitiæ diuinæ. Vbi verò opera, vbi habitus infusi, vbi virtutes inhærentes? Altum de his in doctrina iustificationis silentium. Costerus quidem scribit pag. 271. reliqua opera sub fide comprehendi. Sed 1. petit principium. 2. ἀντίθεσις Apostolica contratium docet: 3. Opera refert ad fidem, quæ tamen formaliter pertinent ad legem. 4. Spes & aliæ virtutes præcederent iustificationem, quod absurdissimum.


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: Fourth Class. Containing sayings which teach that our justification consists in the remission of sins and the imputation of faith

Fourth Class. Containing sayings which teach that our justification consists in the remission of sins and the imputation of faith.

LXIV. To this pertains the saying in Rom. 3:25, Rom. 4:5, 6, and following, 2 Cor. 5:19, Acts 13:38 and 39, Luke 18:13 and 14. From which we weave such an argument. If the whole justification of man consists in the imputation of faith, in the remission of iniquities, in the non-imputation of sin, in the promise of inheritance, then not works or inherent virtues, but the imputation of the righteousness of Christ or faith will be the form of justification. But the former is true. Therefore also the latter. That the minor premise may become more manifest, we shall prove it from the individual sayings.

LXV. In Rom. 3:25, justification is expressly said to consist in the remission of sins. For the words have it thus: GOD set forth Christ as a propitiator through faith in his blood, for the demonstration of his righteousness (now he recounts in what this righteousness consists) Διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων, on account of the remission of preceding offenses. Luther translates: Whom GOD has set forth as a mercy-seat, whereby he offers the righteousness which is valid before him, in that he forgives sins. Here certainly it is taught in the most open words that our righteousness and justification is situated in the remission of sins. Thus in Rom. 4:5, faith is said to be reckoned for righteousness, namely by reason of Christ apprehended, the sense of which phrase was explained and demonstrated in disputation 4 under the word imputation. In verse 6. from Psalm 32, our blessedness or justification is defined by the remission of sins, by the imputation of righteousness, by the covering of iniquities, by the non-imputation of offenses. Where it is to be observed that for David and Paul it amounts to the same thing, whether it is said that sins are forgiven or covered, just as scars, wounds, and filth on the body are covered by a garment: so the sins of believers are covered by the blood of Christ as if by a cloak, so that they may not come into the sight and judgment of God. Indeed, all things are obvious to the eyes of God, and nothing can be hidden from them, Eccl. 17. verses 16 & 23 v. 28. Psalm 139. verse 12. Nevertheless, the sins of believers are said to be covered κατὰ ἀνθρωποπάθειαν (according to human manner of speaking) in such a way that God does not wish to look upon them, nor to remember them, concerning which matter Ezekiel speaks thus in ch. 33. v. 16: All his sins (namely, of the repenting man) which he has committed shall not be remembered. And the opposition must be considered, because in v. 13 it is said of a just man falling into sins, All his righteousnesses shall not be remembered. But no one will affirm that all the works of the just, which they did before they fell into sin, are actually taken away and blotted out: The same must be said concerning crimes, whence it follows that the Papists err vehemently, arguing that in the justification of a man, all sins are plainly taken away and exterminated, so that nothing of them remains. If this were so, you could not rightly call David an adulterer and murderer, Paul a blasphemer and persecutor, Peter a denier of Christ, when these have repented and been justified.

LXVI. Furthermore, in 2 Corinth. 5. v. 19 it is said: Reconciling the world to himself, λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα not imputing to them their trespasses. You see here that reconciliation or justification is defined by the fact that sins are not imputed. Bellarmine objects, lib. 2. c. 10, that non-imputation denotes both the remission of sin and the infusion of righteousness, and to prove this he produces certain testimonies of Scripture, but they do not prove what he intends, IesuVVita, although some show that we are therefore reconciled to God through Christ, that He might present us holy and unblemished and irreproachable before Him, Col. 1. v. 22. Which final cause of reconciliation is ignorantly confounded by Bellarmine with the formal cause. Nor is it denied by us that both are a benefit of Christ, namely both the remission of sins and the newness of life: but nevertheless they must be distinguished according to the tenor of the Apostle, so that reconciliation indeed consists in the remission of sins, as a form; but internal renewal follows reconciliation, as an effect or fruit. LXVII. Further. 13. v. 38. it is read, Be it known unto you, that through this crucified Christ remission of sins is announced to you and that by him everyone who believes is justified, that is, is absolved, from all things from which you could not be justified by the law of Moses, that is, be absolved. In this saying many arguments lie hidden; which, although they do not all pertain to this order, we shall nevertheless recount together. We are justified through Christ, therefore not through our own virtues or works. 2. Justification is the announcement of the remission of sins through Christ, wherefore the remission of sins is the form of justification. 3. It is expressly said, From which you could not be justified, where nothing but a forensic signification obtains, so that it is the same as not to be absolved. Otherwise, indeed, the interpretation of this passage would be strange. 4. Through the law no one can be justified. Therefore virtues and works, because they are from the law and pertain to it, do not justify. 5. Everyone who believes is justified on account of Christ, but not through the law. Faith therefore (not works) is the form of justification. Bellarm. l. 2. c. 12. To these he objects; that we are indeed justified through Christ, but it does not follow from that that virtue and quality infused by God are excluded. For we are justified through Christ as the efficient cause, through infused virtue and quality as through the formal cause. Resp. The opposition in the words of Paul is too clear, where the Gospel and the Law, faith and works, Christ or the grace of God, and the yoke of the law are opposed, and there is no mention there of an infused quality, as if we were justified through it. Nor is it to be endured that the Jesuit should say that the Apostles, in setting forth the summary of the doctrine of justification, omitted the formal cause. And indeed Bellarmine's little argument is of no moment; Christ is the efficient cause of our justification. Therefore not the formal, for it can be both, but in a different respect, the former regarding acquisition, the latter regarding application: Thus when the Papists speak of dispositions, then it is not absurd to them to refer them now… to the efficient, now to the formal cause. But when they dispute about the merit of Christ, then this seems to them clearly absurd.

LXIIX: Furthermore, Bellarmine attaches a new meaning to the words of faith and believing. By them, he says, the remission of sins is announced to those who believe in Christ, as is fitting, namely by doing whatever He commanded to be done, etc. But one would like to ask Bellarmine, what Prophet, what Apostle, what Evangelist ever taught such a meaning of faith formally justifying? He has said more often that the form of faith is to believe; he also wrote that faith receives Christ by believing, book 2 on grace, chapter 3, and book 1 on justification, chapter 15. How therefore is faith concerned with doing, with fulfilling? For to Paul these are opposites, to believe and to work; Rom. 4, verse 5. While the Jesuit attributes these to faith at the same time in the argument of justification, does he not propose a new, absurd, and inept opinion? Does he not confound the Gospel and the Law? Does he not contradict Apostolic doctrine? He disagrees, moreover, with himself, because above he was arguing that faith is only in the intellect, not also in the will. But to work (which he here wishes to be proper to faith) out of charity, is surely of the will. He was also arguing in book 1, passim, that faith justifies meritoriously, namely of congruity, and has the efficiency of justifying: What therefore is the difference between Christ and faith, if both he and it are the meritorious efficient cause of justification? Thus he argued above, Christ is the efficient cause, therefore he cannot be its form. But in book 1, chapter 17, he joins both in faith, to which he attributes efficiency and merit of justification, and at the same time he writes that faith is the beginning of righteousness, and through this is the formal cause of justification begun, etc. 20. He establishes that faith, both dispositively and formally justifying, is the same faith. For he says that such is the beginning, which, when righteousness comes, does not yield and recede, but which remains and is perfected. In the way that the roots of trees do not wither, but grow and are strengthened as the tree grows. From which analogy it is gathered that for him it is the same faith which both begins and perfects justification, which is both the meritorious efficient and the formal cause. For if it were different, it would not be perfected. Therefore, for Bellarmine, faith can indeed be the efficient and formal cause of justification: but Christ cannot be both.

LXIX. But he objects again that when the remission of sins is named, the infusion of righteousness is understood at the same time, and he proves it from there, because in other places of Scripture there is mention of sanctification, cleansing, and offering, which show the other part of justification. We respond: It is not the case, because the form of justification is confused with its effect. We ourselves admit that in the justified there is required and exists a renewal and newness of life, but this is a consequence of justification, not its form, as the Apostle testifies. We also grant this, that in the form of justification, righteousness is joined with the remission of sins, but not our own, rather Christ's. Wherefore Bellarmine would rightly conclude thus: Justification requires righteousness. Therefore it does not consist solely in the remission of sins, to which no righteousness at all is joined, but rather in such a remission which has the righteousness of Christ coupled to itself in an indivisible bond. But that gloss, that by the law of Moses are understood works done by our own powers, we have refuted above.

LXX. Finally, our opinion is confirmed from Luke 18, v. 13 and 14. Where the publican is said to be justified, when he had only requested the remission of sins, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 12, objects that he had at the same time requested the infusion of righteousness.

For he did not merely ask for the forgiveness of the debt, as if he wished to be unjust, but that he might not be held by God, nor punished. Resp. This is a calumny, by which he mixes in the matter of putative justification. Furthermore, from where will he prove that the publican simultaneously sought the habit of justice, so that he might be justified? He errs, however, in that he says that he sought not only the remission of sins, but complete reconciliation; as if the remission of sins were not complete, but only a half-reconciliation, when nevertheless it is said in 2 Cor. 5, v. 19: reconciling the world, not imputing their sins to them.

Latin:

Classis quarta. Continens dicta, quæ docent nostram iustificationem consistere in remißione peccatorum & impu tatione fidei.

LXIV, Huc pertinet dictum Rom. 3. v. 25. Rom. 4. v. 5. 6. & seqq. 1. Cor. 5. v 19. Act. 13. v. 38. & 39. Luc. 28. v. 13. & 14. Ex quibus tale nectimus argumentum. Si tota hominis iustificatio consistit in imputatione fidei, in remissione iniquitatum, in non imputatione peccati, in promissione hæreditatis, tùm non opera aut virtutes inhærentes, sed imputatio iustitiæ Christi vel fides erit forma iustificationis, Atqui prius verum est. Ergo & posterius. Vt minor euadat manifestior, probabimus eam ex singulis dictis.

LXV. Rom. 3. v. 25. iustificatio disertè dicitur consistere in remissione peccatorum, Ita enim habent verba: DEVS Christum proposuit propitiatorem per fidem in sanguine ipsius, ad ostensionem iustitiæ suæ (nunc recenset, in quo consistat hæc iustitia) Διὰ τὴν πάρεσιν τῶν προγεγονότων ἁμαρτημάτων, propter remissionem præcedentium delictorum. Lutherus vertit: Welchen GOtt hat fürgestellet zu einem Gna= denstuel/darmit er die Gerechtigkeit die für ihm gilt/darbiete / indem daß er die Sünde vergibt. Hic certè verbis apertissimis docetur, in remissione peccatorum sitam esse nostram iustitiam & iustificationem. Sic Rom. 4. vers. 5. fides dicitur reputari ad iustitiam, videlicet ratione Christi apprehensi, cuius phraseos sensus disput. 4. in voce imputationis explicatus fuit & demonstratus. Versu 6.. ex Psalm. 32. beatitudo vel iustificatio nostra per remissionem peccatorum, per imputationem iustitiæ, per occultationem iniquitatum, per non imputationem delictorum definitur. Vbi obseruandum est, Dauidi & Paulo idem valere, siue dicatur, peccata remissa sine tegi. Nimiùm sicut veste conteguntur cicatrices, vulnera & sordes in corpore: Ita sanguine Christi tanquam pallio quodam conteguntur peccata credentium, ne veniant in conspectum Dei & iudicium. Sunt quidem omnia oculis Dei obuia, & occultari ab ijs nihil potest, Eccl. 17. vers. 16 & 23 v. 28. Psalm. 139. vers. 12. Credentium tamen peccata κατὰ ἀνθρωποπάθειαν sic dicuntur contecta, vt Deus ea intueri nolit, neque eorum meminisse, de qua re ita loquitur Ezechiel c. 33. v. 16. Omnia peccata eius (scilicet hominis resipiscentis) quæ peccauit non commemorabuntur. Et considerãda est oppositio, quia v. 13. dicitur de homine iusto in peccata ruẽte, Omnes iustitiæ eius non memorabuntur. Nemo autẽ affirmabit actu tolli & deleri opera iustorum omnia, quę fecerunt, antequam in peccatũ ruerent: idem dicendum de sceleribus, vndè sequitur, Pontificios vehementer errare, disputantes in iustificatione hominis, peccata vniuersa planè tolli, & exterminari, vt nihil de ijs permaneatreliquum. Quod si ita sit, non rectè iam dixeris, Davidem adulterum & homicidam, Paulum blasphemum & persecutorem, Petrum abnegatorem Christi, cùm isti resipuerint & iustificati sint.

LXVI. Porrò 2. Corinth. 5. v. 19. dicitur: Reconcilians sibi mundum, λογιζόμενος αὐτοῖς τὰ παραπτώματα non imputans illis delicta ipsorum. Vides hîc reconcitiationem seu iustificationẽ definiri ex eo, quòd peccata non imputentur. Excipit Bell. lib. 2. c. 10.. Non imputationem notare & remissionem peccati, & infusionem iustitiæ, quod vt probet producit quædam Scripturæ testimonia, sed ea non probant, quod intendit IesuVVita, quamuis nonnulla ostendant nos ideò esse Deo reconciliatos per Christum, vt sisteret nos sanctos & immaculatos & irreprehensibiles coràm se, Col. 1. v. 22. Quæ causa finalis reconciliationis inscitè cõfunditur à Bellar. cum causa formali. Neq; à nobis negatur, vtrumque effe Christi beneficium, scilicet & remissionem peccatorum, & vitæ nouitatem:sed tamen distinguenda sunt illa secundum tenorem Apostoli, vt reconciliatio quidem consistat in remissione peccatorum, tanquam forina ; interna autem renouatio sequatur reconciliationem,tanquam effectus siuè fructus. LXVII. Vlterius . 18. 13. v. 38. legitur, Notum sit vobis , quòd per hunc Christum crucifixum vobis remissio peccatorum annunciatur & quòd ab omnibus, à quibus non potuistis per legem Mofis iustificari, hoc est, abfolui, per hunc omnis, qui credit, iustificatur, hoc est, abfoluitur. In dicto hoc multa latent argumenta; quæ quamuis non omnia ad hunc pertineant ordinem, tamen simul recensebimus. Iustificamur per Christum, Ergò non per virtutes aut opera propria. 2. Iustificatio est annunciatio remissionis peccatorum per Christum, Quare remissio peccatorum, est forma iustificationis. 3. Expressè dicitur, A quibus non potuistis iustificari, vbi non nisi forensis significatio obtinet, vt sit idem, quod non absolui. Aliàs profectò mira foret huius loci interpretatio. 4. Per legem nemo potest iustificari. Ergò virtutes & opera, quia ex lege sunt, & ad eam pertinent, nõ iustificant. 5. Omnis qui credit, propter Christum iustificatur, non autem per legem. Fides igitur (non opera) est forma iustificationis. Bellarm. l. 2. c. 12. Ad hæc excipit; per Christum quidem nos iustificari, ast indè non sequi quod excludatur virtus & qualitas à Deo infusa. Nam per Christum nos iustificari, vt causam efficientem per virtutem & qualitatem infusam, vt per causam formalem. Resp. Oppositio in verbis Pauli nimis clara est, Vbi Evangelium & Lex, fides & opera, Christus seu Dei gratia, & iugum legis opponuntur, & nulla ibi sit mentio infusæ qualitatis, quasi per eam iustificemur Neque ferendum est, vt dicat Iesusita, Apostolos in summa doctrinæ de Iustificatione proponenda omisisse causam formalem. Et sanè nullius momenti est ratiuncula Bellarmini; Christus est efficiens causa nostræ iustificationis. Ergò non form ális, Potest enim vtrumque esse, sed diuerso respectu, illud quoad acquisitionem, hoc quoad applicationem: Sic quando de dispositionibus loquuntur Pontificij, tunc ijs absurdum non est, nunc ad efficientem nunc ad causam formalem illas refert. Cùm verò de merito Christi disputant, tunc ipsis hoc planè videtur absurdum.

LXIIX: Porrò vocabulis fidei & credendi nouam affingit Bellarminus significationem. Iis, inquit, annunciatur remissio peccatorum, qui credunt in Christum, vt oportet, scilicet faciendo quicquid ille fieri iussit &c. Sed quærere lubet ex Bellarmino, quis Propheta, quis Apostolus, quis Euangelista talem fidei formaliter iustificantis significationem vnquam docuerit? Dixit sæpiùs, fidei formam esse credere;scripsit etiam, fidem credendo recipere Christum, lib. 2. de gratia, capite 3. & lib. 1. de iustificat capite 15. Quomodo ergò fides versatur in faciendo, implendo? Nam Paulo hæc sunt opposita credere, & operari; Rom. 4. vers. 5. Quæ dum fidei simul tribuit Iesuwita in argumento iustificationis, annon proponit opinionem nouam, absurdam & ineptam? Annon confundit Euangelium & Legem? Annon contradicit doctrinæ Apostolicæ? Dissidet præterea à seipso, quià suprà disputabat, fidem esse tantùm in intellectu, non etiam in voluntate. Operari autem (quod hîc fidei proprium vult esse) ex charitate, sanè voluntatis est. Disserebat etiam l. 1. passim, fidem meritoriè, videlicet de congruo, iustificare & habere iustificandi efficientiam: Quæ ergò est differentia inter Christum & fidem, si & ille & ista est causa efficiens iustificationis meritoria? Sic arguebat suprà, Christus est causa efficiens, Ergò nequit esse eius forma. At l. 1. ca. 17. vtrumque coniungit, in fide, cui tribuit efficientiam & meritum iustificationis, simulque scribit, fidem esse initium iustitiae, ac per hoc causam esse formalem inchoatam iustificationis, & c. 20. fidem, tum dispositiue, tum formaliter iustificantem, eandem statuit esse fidem. Dicit enim tale esse initium, quod veniente iustitia non cedat & recedat, sed quod maneat & perficiatur. quo modo arborum radices non arescunt, sed crescunt & roborantur, crescente arbore. Ex quo simili colligitur, ipsi eandem esse fidem, quae & inchoat & perficit iustificationem, quae est & efficiens meritoria & causa formalis. Si n. diuersa foret, no perficeretur. Bellarmino igitur fides potest quide esse causa efficiens & formalis iustificationis: Christus autem vtrumque esse nequit.

LXIX. Sed rursus excipit, quod remissione peccatoru nominata, simul intelligatur infusio iustitiae, & probat inde, quia in alijs Scripturae locis sit mentio sanctificationis, mundationis, oblationis, quae alteram partem iustificationis ostendant. R. N. C. quia confunditur forma iustificationis cum eiusdem effectu. Fatemur ipsi, in iustificatis requiri & esse renouationem vitaeque nouitate, sed hoc est iustificationis consequens, no forma, teste Apostolo. Damus etiam hoc, coniungi in iusticationis forma, cu remissione peccatorum iustitiam, sed no nostram, verum Christi. Quare sic recte concluderet Bellarminus: Iustificatio requirit iustitiam. Ergo non constat sola peccatoru remissione, cui nulla plane sit coniuncta iustitia, sed potius tali remissione, quae indiuiso nexu copulatam sibi habeat iustitiam Christi. Istam vero glossam, quod per legem Mosis intelligantur opera viribus nostris facta, supra refutauimus.

LXX. Tandem confirmatur nostra sententia ex Luc. 18 v. 13. & 14. Vbi publicanus dicitur iustificatus, cum solum postulasset remissione peccatorum, dices, Deus esto propitius mihi peccatori, Bell. c. 12. l. 2. excipit, simul ipsum petijsse infusionem iustitiae.

Non enim postulâsse solùm debiti condonationem, quasi vellet iniquus esse, sed non haberi à Deo, neq; puniri. Resp. Calumnia est, quâ admiscet de putativa iustificatione. Deinde publicanũ simul petiisse iustitię habitum, vt iustificaretur, vndè probabit? Errat autem in eo, quod ait, ipsum nō solam peecatorum remissionem, sed integram petiisse reconciliationem; quasi peccatorum remissio non sit integra, sed tantùm dimidia reconciliatio, cum tamen dicatur 2. Cor. 5, v. 19. recōcilians mundum, nō imputans ipsis peccata.


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: Classis quinta. Enumerating the sayings which teach that Christ is our justice

LXXI. To this we refer the sayings: Jer. 23, v. 6; 1 Cor. 1, v. 30; 2 Cor. 5, v. ult.; Rom. 5, v. 19; 10, v. 3 & 4; Acts 15, v. 10; ch. 19, v. 38. And thus we conclude: Whatever justice is given to us by God himself, so that through it we may be justified, that is the formal cause of justification. But the justice of Christ, which he acquired for us by his own obedience and passion, is given to us by God himself, so that through it we may be justified, by virtue of the cited texts of Scripture. Therefore, the justice of Christ is the formal cause of justification.

LXXII. Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 10, objects to the saying of Jeremiah and 1 Corinthians 1, that Christ is called our justice not through the imputation of faith, but 1. because he is the efficient cause of our justification. 2. because he is our justice in the same way that he is our wisdom and redemption. 3. because he satisfied the Father for us, and bestows and communicates that satisfaction to us when he justifies us, so that it can be called our satisfaction and justice. Response: Bellarmine seems to be orthodox here. For we also concede to him that Christ is called our justice: 1. on account of the acquisition, and thus far he is the efficient cause. 2. on account of the imputation and application, and thus he is the formal cause. Wherefore, let these words of Bellarmine be noted most diligently, which the force of truth extorted from him even against his will. For, he says, by infusing into us that which is inherent, we are truly named and are righteous: Yet we do not through it satisfy God for our faults and eternal punishment, but that inherent righteousness, with the remission of fault and everlasting punishment, is the effect of the satisfaction of Christ, which (as the Council of Trent says, session 6, chapter 7) is conferred and applied to us in justification: And in this way it would not be absurd if someone were to say that the righteousness and merit of Christ are imputed to us, since they are given and applied to us, as if we ourselves had satisfied God, provided it is not denied that there is besides in us an inherent righteousness, and that it is a true and absolute righteousness, to which by the just judgment of God punishment is not due, but glory. This is Bellarmine, the first part of whose opinion is Evangelical and Apostolic, and therefore let this confession be noted as a place of perpetual instance, and always be opposed to the Papists, who deny imputed righteousness, and calumniously call it putative, fictitious, imaginary, fantastic righteousness, a thing of minimal entity, πανσπερμίαν, madness: But the latter part can neither consist with it, and is heterodox. For if the righteousness of Christ is ours by imputation, why is inherent righteousness thrust upon us? For there is one form of justification, according to the Council of Trent, and if indeed there is some righteousness of works inherent in us, yet that is not the form of justification, but its effect or consequence, nor can it bear the rigor of divine judgment on account of the manifold imperfection and infirmity adhering to it. But the contradiction of Bellarmine will be objected. He concedes from the passage of Jeremiah 23 that it follows that Christ is our righteousness by imputation, or that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us. But in book 2, chapter 7, he writes: that no place could hitherto be found where it might be read that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us for righteousness. And a little later: It cannot be that the righteousness of Christ is imputed to us; which is certainly a palpable contradiction.

LXXIII. But now we shall consider the text of 2 Cor. 5, last verse: Him, who knew no sin, for us he made sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. How therefore Christ was made sin for us, so we in him or through him are made the righteousness of God, that is, valid before God. But Christ was made sin for us by imputation. The minor premise is proved from 2 Cor. 5, last verse. God made Christ sin for us, that is, he esteemed him a criminal, and guilty of all the sins of the whole world, and willed him to be offered as an expiatory sacrifice and victim for sin. Both things therefore are noted by the word sin, which Christ is said to have been made, namely both the imputation of sin and the satisfaction for sin: Whence they do not attain the Apostolic emphasis, who take sin only for a sacrificial victim, but Paul rather means this: 1. That God cast all our sins upon Christ as if they were his own. 2. That Christ in his own body bore our sins upon the tree, 1. Pet. 2. v. 24. 3. That Christ as a victim on the cross expiated our sins, so that they might not be imputed to us, and thus we might be reconciled to God. For the Apostle opposes ἁμαρτίαν to δικαιοσύνην. He says we are made δικαιοσύνην, just as Christ was made ἁμαρτία. Therefore, just as by δικαιοσύνην righteousness properly so called is understood, not some victim, so also by ἁμαρτίαν sin not properly so called, but not solely a victim for sin, can be understood.

LXXIV. But Bellarmine, book 2, chapter 10, objects that Christ is not called sin or a sinner, nor are our sins imputed to him as if he himself had committed them, and he could be considered unrighteous, but they are imputed to him only as to the debt of satisfying. But we have just now proven the contrary from that antithesis which the Apostle institutes between δικαιοσύνην and ἁμαρτίαν. We do not indeed affirm that Christ himself committed sins, since no guile was found in his mouth, 1 Pet. 2, verse 22. But nevertheless

Our sins were imputed to Christ, so that because of our sins, not his own, he might be called a sinner, and indeed even be made sin, as the Apostle speaks here. For just as on account of imputation we are not only called righteous, but are also abstractly called righteousness: so Christ is named in this place not only a sinner, but also abstractly sin on account of imputation. So that this may become manifest, we shall also note other places of Scripture which prove the same.

LXXV. Isaiah 53, verse 6. It is said that God cast all our sins upon him. Whence John 1, verse 29, he is called the Lamb of God, who bears the sins of the world. Luke 22, verse 37, He was numbered with the iniquitous. Isaiah 63, verse 3, I have defiled my garments. And the following arguments also confirm this very thing. 1. Whoever pays for the sins of others, and makes satisfaction for them; to him those sins are imputed as if they were his own. But Christ paid for the sins of others, and made satisfaction for the debts of others, Isaiah 53, verse 6; Psalm 69, verse 5, Things which I did not steal, I then restored. Therefore, the sins of others were imputed to him. 2. Whoever calls sins his own, which however he himself did not commit, to him the sins of others are again imputed. But Christ calls sins his own, which however he himself did not commit, but others did. Therefore, conversely, the sins of others are imputed to him. The minor premise is evident from Psalm 69, verse 6, O God, you know my foolishness, and my faults are not hidden from you. Which words are Christ's, just as that whole Psalm deals with the passion of Christ, as witnessed by John chapter 19, verses 28 and 29, and Paul in Romans 10, verse 3. 3. He who truly undergoes and tastes death owed for sins, either he himself has sinned, or the sins of others are imputed to him. But Christ truly underwent and tasted death owed for sins, and yet he himself did not sin. Therefore, the sins of others are imputed to Christ. 4. To whom the punishment of another is imputed, to him also the guilt is imputed, because this is the cause of that. But the punishment of our sins was imputed to Christ, as the Papists themselves admit. Therefore, also the guilt. To this also pertains

The words of Bernard from Epistle 109 to Innocent: If one died for all, then all died, so that the satisfaction of one might be imputed to all, just as that one bore the sins of all. Hence Luther most correctly on chapter 3 of Galatians: Christ is indeed innocent because he is the immaculate, uncontaminated Lamb of God, but because he bears the sins of the world, his innocence is pressed by the sins and filth of the whole world. Whatever sins I, you, and we all have committed and will commit in the future are as much Christ's own as if he himself had committed them. In sum, our sin must become Christ's own sin, or we shall perish eternally.

LXXVI. From these arguments and testimonies, therefore, it is abundantly clear that it is not an impious or absurd dogma if it is said that the sins of the world are imputed to Christ, which the Apostle expresses thus: God made Christ sin. And lest the Papists object that the word 'sin' is only taken for a sacrifice for sin, we propose to them the Apostolic opposition of sin and righteousness, 2 Cor. 5, last verse; and the synonymy of sin, Gal. 3, verse 13. For just as Christ is said to be not only cursed but a curse itself, because he received our curse upon himself: so he is said to be not only a sinner, but sin itself, because he received our sins upon himself. 3. The Apostolic argumentation: God does not impute sins to the reconciled, because he made Christ sin for them. 4. The prophetic reason for the appellation. Why is Christ called sin? Isaiah answers: because God cast all our sins upon him, ch. 53, v. 6. Because he bears the sins of the world, John 1, verse 29; 1 Peter 2, verse 24. And finally the type of the scapegoat, Leviticus 16, verse 21, upon which the High Priest confessed all the sins of the people and placed them upon its head and thus sent it into the desert, by which it was prefigured that Christ, the antitype, would receive the sins of the whole world upon himself and would satisfy God the Father for them.

LXXVII. More classes of testimonies could now be added, confirming our θέσιν [thesis] concerning imputed, not inherent, righteousness. But because the things proposed thus far are sufficient and the rest have been explained at length and solidly by Mr. Dr. Gerhard in Volume 3 of his Loci Communes, we will not be more prolix here, but will briefly add other reasons drawn from the analogy of faith.

Latin:

LXXI. Huc referimus dicta: Ier. 23. v. 6. 1. Cor. 5. v. 30. 2. Cor. 5. v. vlt. Rom. 5. v. 19. 10. v. 3. & 4. Act. 15. v. 10. c. 19. v. 38. Et ita concludimus: Quæ iustitia à Deo ipso nobis datur, vt per eam iustificemur, illa est formalis causa iustificationis. Atqui iustitia Christi, quã suâ obedientiâ & passione nobis acquisiuit, ab ipso Deo nobis datur, vt per eã iustificemur, vi allegatorum Scripturæ textuum. E. iustia Christi, formalis causa est iustificationis.

LXXII. Bell. l. 2. c. 10. ad dictum Ieremiæ & 1. Corinth. 1. excipit, Christum dici nostram iustitiam non per imputatione fidei, sed 1. quia est causa efficiens nostræ iustificationis. 2. quia sic est nostra iustitia, sicut est nostra sapientia & redemptio. 3. quia satisfecit Patri pro nobis, & istam satisfactionem nobis donat & communicat, cùm nos iustificat, vt nostra satisfactio & iustitia dici possit. Respond. videtur Bellarm. hic orthodoxus esse. Nam & ipsi concedimus, Christum dici nostram iustitiam, 1. ob acquisitionem, & hactenus est causa efficiens. 2. ob imputationem & applicationem, & sic est causa formalis: Quocirca diligentissimè notentur verba isthæc Bellarmini, quæ vel ipsi invito vis veritatis extorsit. Eua, ait, per insluam nobi inhærentem verè iusti nominemur & simus: Tamen non per eam satisfacimus Deo pro culpis nostris & pœna æterna, sed est illa iustitia inhærens cum remissione culpæ & sempiternæ pœnæ, effectus satisfactionis Christi, quæ (vt dicit Cõcil. Trid. sess. 6. capite 7.) nobis in iustificatione confertur & applicatur: Et hoc modo non esset absurdum si quis diceret, nobis imputari Christi iustitiam & merirum, cùm nobis donentur & applicentur, ac si nos ipsi Deo satisfecissemus, modo non negetur esse præterea in nobis iustitiam inhærentem, eamque veram & absolutam esse iustitiam, cui iusto Dei iudicio non debeatur pœna sed gloria. Hęc Bellarminus, cuius sententiæ prior pars est Euangelica & Apostolica, ideoque hæc confessio instãtiæ perpetuæ loco notetur, semperque opponatur Pontificijs, imputatã iustitiam negantibus, & illa calumniosè vocantibus, iustitiam putativam, fictitiam, imaginariam, phantasticam, rem minimæ Entitatis, πανσπερμίαν, insaniam: Posterior verò pars neque cum ea potest consistere, & est heterodoxa. Si enim Christi iustitia est nostra per imputationem; cur nobis obtruditur, iustitia inhærens? Vnica enim est forma iustificationis, iuxta Concilium Tridentinum, Et si verò est aliqua iustitia operum, nobis inhærens tamen illa non est forma iustificationis, sed effectum eius siuè consequens, neque potest illa ferre rigorem diuini iudicij propter multiplicem imperfectionem & infirmitatem adhærentem. Obiicuetur autem contradictio Bellarmini. Concedit ex loco Ierem. 23. sequi, Christum esse nostram iustitiam per imputationem, vel iustitiam Christi nobis imputari. At lib. 2. capite 7. scribit: nullum potuisse hactenus inueniri locum, vbi legeretur Christi iustitiam nobis imputari ad iustitiam. Et Paulo pòst: Fieri non potest, vt Christi iustitia nobis imputetur; quæ certè palpabilis est ἀντίφασις.

LXXIII. Sed nunc considerabimus textum 2. Cor. 5. v. vlt: Eum, qui non nouerat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum peccatum fecit; vt nos efficeremur iustitia Dei in ipso. Quomodo ergô Christus factus est peccatum pro nobis, ita nos in ipso vel per ipsum efficimur iustitia Dei, hoc est, coram Deo valens. Atqui Christus factus est pro nobis peccatum per imputationem. Minor probatur ex 2. Cor. 5. vers. vlt. Deus fecit Christum pro nobis peccatum, hoc est, æstimauit eum sceleratum, atque omnium peccatorum totius mundi reum, & tanquam piacualrem hostiam ac victimam pro peccato offerri voluit. Vtrunque igitur vocabulo peccati, quod Christus dicitur factus, notatur, videlicet & imputatio peccati ac satisfactio pro peccato: Vnde non assequuntur emphasin Apostolicam, peccatum accipiunt tantùm pro hostia victimali, sed hoc potiùs vult Paulus 1. Deum omnia peccata nostra coniecisse in Christum ac si eius essent propria. 2. Christum in proprio corpore suo pertulisse peccata uostra super lignum, 1. Pet. 2. v. 24. 3. Christum tanquàm hostiam in cruce expiasse peccata nostra, vt eà non nobis imputentur, atque sic Deo reconciliemur. Opponit enim Apostolus ἁμαρτίαν πρὸς δικαιοσύνην. Dicit nos fieri δικαιοσύνην, sicut Christus factus est ἁμαρτία. Quemadmodum igitur per δικαιοσύνην iustitia propriè dicta, non aliqua hostia, intelligitur, ita étiam per ἁμαρτίαν peccatum non propriè dictum, non autem vnicè hostia pro peccato intelligi potest.

LXXIV. Verùm Bellarm. lib. 2. cap. 10. excipit, Christum non dici peccatum vel peccatorem, neq; ipsi peccata nostra imputari, quasi ipse illa fecerit, & iniquus haberi possit, sed solum imputantur illi quò ad debitum satisfaciendi. Ast cōtrarium iam modò euicimus ex illa ἀντιθέσει quam Apostolus instituit inter δικαιοσύνην & ἁμαρτίαν. Non quidem affirmamus, Christum ipsum peccata fecisse, cùm non sit in ore ipsius inuentus dolus 1. Pet. 2. vers. 22. Sed tamen

Christo imputata sunt nostra peccata, vt propter nostra, non sua peccata, diceretur peccator imo & fieret peccatum, vt hic Apostolus loquitur. Sicut enim ob imputationem non solum dicimur iusti, sed etiam abstracte dicimur iustitia: ita Christus non solum peccator, sed etiam abstracte peccatum propter imputationem hoc in loco nominatur. Quod vt manifestum fiat, alia etiam Scripturae loca, idem evincentią adnotabimus.

LXXV. Esa. 53. versu 6. dicitur Deus in eum coniecisse omnia peccata nostra. Vnde Ioan. 1. versu 29. Agnus Dei vocatur, qui portat peccata mundi. Luc. 22. versu 37 Numeratus est cum iniquis Esa. 63. versu 3. Indumenta mea inquinavi. Et hoc ipsum confirmant etiam sequentia argumenta. 1. Quicunque luit aliena peccata, & pro iis satisfacit; illi peccata ista imputantur, tanquam propria. Atqui Christus luit aliena peccata, & satisfecit pro alienis debitis Esa. 53. versu 6. Ps. 69. v. 5. Quae non rapui, tunc reddidi, E. aliena peccata ipsi sunt imputata, 2. Quicunque vocat sua peccata, que tamen ipse non commisit illi aliena peccata rursus imputantur. Atqui Christus vocat sua peccata, quae tamen ipse non commisit, sed alij. Vicissim igitur aliena peccata ipsi imputantur. Minor patet ex Psalm. 69, versu 6. Deus tu nosti stultitiam meam, & delicta mea a te non sunt abscondita. Quae verba sunt Christi, sicuti totus ille Psalmus agit de Christi passione, teste Iohan. cap. 19. ver. 28 & 29 Et Paulo Rom. 10. versu 3. Poro. 3. qui reuera mortem peccatis debitam subit & gustat, is aut ipse peccavit, aut imputantur ei peccata aliena Christus autem mortem peccatis debita reuera subiit & gustauit, nec tamē ipse peccavit. Ergo Christo imputatur peccata alie na. 4. Cui imputatur alterius poena, illi etiā imputatur culpa, quia haec est causa illius. Atqui Christo imputabatur poena peccatorum nostrorum, fatentibus ipsis Pontificijs. E. & culpa. Huc spectat etiā

Verba Bernh. Ex epift. 109. ad Innoc. Si vnus pro omnibus mortuus est, E. omnes mortui sunt, vt videlicet satisfactio vnius omnibus imputetur, sicut omnium peccata vnus ille portauit. Hinc Lutherus rectissimè super 3. c. ad Gal. Christus est quidem immotēs quia est immaculatus, incontaminatus Dei agnus, sed quia portat peccata mundi, premitur eius innocentia peccatis & scatu totius mundi. Quæcunque peccata ego, tu & nos omnes fecimus & insuturum faciemus, tam propria sunt Christi, quam si ipse esfecisset. In summa oportet nostrum peccatum fieri Christi peccatum proprium, aut in æternum peribimus.

LXXVI. Ex his igitur argumētis & testimoniis abundè patet, non esse dogma impium vel absurdum, si Christo peccata mundi imputari dicantur, quod Apostolus sic effert; Deus Christum fecit peccatum. Et nè Pontificij excipiant, peccati vocabulum tantum accipi pro victima pro peccato, proponimus illis oppositionem Apostolicam peccati & iustitiæ. 2. Synonymiam peccati. 2. Cor. 5. v. vlt. Et maledicti; Gal. it. v. 13. 2 Sicut enim Christus non solum maledictus sed ipsum dicitur maledictum, quia nostram in se recepit maledictionem: ita non solum peccator, sed ipsum dicitur peccatum, quia nostra in se recepit peccata. 3. Argumentationem Apostolicam, Deus non imputat peccata reconciliatis, quia Christum pro illis fecit peccatum. 4. Rationem appellationis propheticam. Quare Christus dicitur peccatum? Respondet Esaias, quia Deus in eum coniecit omnia nostrorum peccata c. 53. v. 6. Quia portat peccata mundi Ioh. 1. vers. 29. 1. Petr. 2. vers. 24. Et tandem typum hirci emissarij Leuit. 16. vers. 21. super quo confitebatur Pontifex omnia populi peccata, & ponebat ea super illius caput & sic emittebat in desertum, quo ipso præfiguratum est, Christum antitypum, totius mundi peccata in se esse recepturum; & pro ipsis Deo Patri satisfacturum.

LXXVII. Plures nunc addi possent testimoniorum classes, nostram θέσιν de iustitia imputata, non inhærente confirmantes. Sed quia sufficere queunt hactenus proposita & reliqua fusè & solidè explicata sunt, â Dn. D. GERHARDO Tomo. 3. L L. Commun. prolixores hîc non erimus, sed alias ab analogia fidei petitas rationes breuiter subiungemus.


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: LXXVIII. Arguments from the Analogy of Faith. I. From the imperfection of works

LXXVIII. ARGUMENTS FROM THE ANALOGY OF FAITH. I. From the imperfection of works,

the imperfect does not justify, because our righteousness standing in the judgment of God must be perfect: but works are imperfect. Isa. 64. All our righteousnesses are as a menstruous cloth. Dan. 9. Nor in our righteousnesses. Psalm 130. If thou, Lord, shouldest mark iniquities, who shall stand? Psalm 143. In thy sight shall no man living be justified. Luke 17. When you have done all, etc. 1 John 1. v. 8 & 10. If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. Hence the regenerate themselves carry about the remnants of the flesh in this life, and feel that they cannot satisfy the law of God, whence the Apostle says Rom. 7. ver. 14. The law is spiritual, but I am carnal. The same struggle is inculcated in Gal. 5. ver. 17. on account of which there is need for the petition for remission Matt. 6. verse 12. Psalm 31. verse 5. Psalm 19 verse 13. Bellarmino, chapter 14, book 6, distinguishes between actual and habitual righteousness; he concedes that the former is in a way imperfect, but not indeed the habitual, and that this, not that, formally justifies. But they urge this principle: such as the effect is, such is the cause; and in Book 2 of the Eudemian Ethics, chapter 13, the philosopher says τῆς βελτίσης ἕξεως ἡ βελτίση ἐνέργεια [the best activity belongs to the best state]. But works, which are the effects of habitual righteousness, are imperfect. Therefore, all inherent righteousness will be imperfect. For whatever is mixed with the remnants of sin cannot be perfect; that habitual righteousness is mixed with the remnants of sin. Wherefore it cannot be, nor be called, perfect.

LXXIX. II. FROM THE PERFECTION OF THE MERIT OF THE LORD

DOMINIC. The merit of Christ is sufficient for the remission of sins. Wherefore there is no need for our little works, or if there is need for them, the merit of Christ will be insufficient, imperfect, and much will be detracted from it, namely as much as is ascribed to our works. And how insulting the Papists are to the most sacred λύτρον of Christ, is easily evident from the fact that they do not call it the cause of remission, but only of habitual justice, on account of which sins are remitted.

LXXX. III. From the EXCLUSION OF BOASTING. The Papists indeed write that, according to their dogma, no handle for boasting is provided, yet this is false, since they make any dispositions whatsoever meritorious. But in truth those are nothing but works of nature, as was shown above. For the grace from which they wish these to be done is only general. Is not therefore a great handle for boasting provided, if anyone knows that by his own proper works he has merited justifying grace by congruity? Therefore we weave such an argument: Whatever doctrine opens a window to boasting is not Apostolic. But the doctrine of the Romanists concerning inherent justice opens a window to boasting. Therefore it is not Apostolic.

LXXXI. IV. FROM RECONCILIATION. Into a man not yet reconciled no virtues are infused, because these proceed from the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, which is only in those who are reconciled. Wherefore reconciliation itself precedes the infusion of virtues, but we are reconciled to God through justification, whence it follows that this also precedes it. Virtues therefore cannot be the form of justification, because a consequent can never be the form of an antecedent, since every form is prior to that which is formed.

LXXXII. V. From experience and the testimony of conscience. Every pious and devout Christian, when he considers that he must render an account before the tribunal of Christ, soon trembles, even if he has lived most holily. This testimony of conscience indicates that our works are imperfect and cannot stand before God. And indeed, if anyone in the fear of the Lord compares his good works with his evils and daily sins, he will clearly discover that no certain hope remains in his own virtues or works, but rather that this must be placed solely in the merit of Christ.

LXXIII. VI. From the remission of sins. In the same way that we obtain the remission of sins, by that same way we are justified: because to obtain the remission of sins is to be justified, Rom. 4, verse 7. But we obtain the remission of sins by faith in Christ alone, not on account of love or works. Therefore, in the same way we shall be justified. For the proof of the minor premise, we construct such an argument: in the same way that we apprehend Christ the Mediator, in that same way we obtain the remission of sins. For it is certain that sins are remitted on account of Christ the Mediator and propitiator, Rom. 3, ver. 25. But we do not apprehend Christ the Mediator except by faith, Heb. 4, verses 15, 16. Where the Apostle commands us to approach God, not with confidence in our own merits, but with confidence in the High Priest Christ, and therefore he demands nothing from us but faith.

LXXXIV. VII. On the fluctuation of conscience. If we were justified by works, or partly by faith and partly by works, consciences would perpetually fluctuate and would never find rest, since they would be leaning upon an infirm foundation, which is imperfect righteousness. But consciences ought not to fluctuate, as it is said in Rom. 4, verse 16: therefore it is of faith, that the promise might be sure. And in Rom. 5, verse 1: Being justified by faith, we have peace with God.

LXXXV. TESTIMONIES OF THE FATHERS. Of these, Chemnitz collects very many in his *Examen* and *Loci*, the Protestants in the causes for the retracted Council, and Gerhard Vol. 3, and others. Wherefore it will suffice here to add one or two things, which we place here by way of a colophon. 1. Justin Martyr in his epistle to Diognetus. What else could cover our sins, than the righteousness of Christ? In whom else could we, wicked and ungodly, be accounted righteous, except in the Son of God alone? O sweet exchange, O unsearchable artifice, and benefits exceeding all expectation, that the iniquity of many should be hidden in one righteous man, and the righteousness of one should cause that many unrighteous should be justified. 2. It is a saying of Jerome: our righteousness consists not of our own merit, but of the mercy of God.

3. Augustine, book 19, On the City of God, ch. 25. Our righteousness consists in the remission of sins, not in the perfection of virtues. And in Psalm 31. I shall only have believed in God, it will be reckoned to me for righteousness. 4. Bernard, Sermon 23 on the Song of Songs. Not to sin is the righteousness of God, the righteousness of man is the indulgence of God. The same, Sermon 51. My merit is the compassion of the Lord. And elsewhere; This suffices to know for merit, that merit does not suffice. 5. Anselm on chapter 6 of Romans, last verse. Whatever you attribute to merits is surely lacking to grace: nor is there room for grace to enter, where merit has already taken possession.

LXXXVII. There should now be subjoined a resolution of the contrary arguments: But because there are very many of them, and this discussion has already grown sufficiently long, we shall reserve them for the next disputation, here giving thanks to God, who adopted us by nature children of wrath into children of grace, by sending his only-begotten Son and bestowing faith in him, which may he mercifully confirm in us; so that we may attain the end of it, the salvation of souls, most desired with all the blessed in heaven. Amen.

Latin:

LXXVIII. ARGVMENTA AB ANALOGIA FIDEI. I. Ab imperfectione operum,

imperfectum non iustificat, quia iustitiam nostram in judicio Dei consistentem oportet esse perfectam: Opera verò sunt imperfecta. Esa. 64. Omnes nostræ justitiæ sunt instar panni mulieris menstruatæ. Dan. 9. Nec in institiis nostris, Psalm. 130. Si iniquitates obseruaueris Domine, quis sustinebit Psalm. 143. Non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis viuens. Luc. 17. Cùm feceritis omnia &c. 1. Ioh. 1. v. 8. & 10. Si dixerimus, quoniam peccatum non habemus, ipsinos seducimus, & veritas in nobis non est. Hinc ipsi renati carnis reliquias circumferunt in hac vita, ac sentiunt : se non posse legi Dei satisfacere, vnde Apostolus ait Rom 7. ver. 14. Lex spiritualis est, ego autem sum carnalis. Eadem lucta inculcatur Gal. 5. ver. 17. ob quam opus est petitione remissionis Matth. 6. versic 12. Psalm. 31. versic 5. Psalm. 19 versic 13. Bellarminus cap. 14. l 6. distinquit inter iustitiam actualem, & habitualem, illam quodammodo esse imperfectam concedit, non verò habitualem, hanc non illam formaliter iustifi are. Verùm ipsi vrgent hoc principium : qualis effectus, talis causa & L. 2. Eth. ad Eudem. cap. 13 ait Philosophus τῆς βελτίσης ἕξεως ἡ βελτίση ἐνέργεια. Opera verò quæ sunt effectus institiæ habitualis, sunt imperfecta. Ergò omnis justitia inhærens erit imperfecta. Quodcunque enim permixtum est reliquiis peccati, id perfectum esse nequit ; Iustitia illa habitualis permixta est reliquijs peccati. Quare perfecta esse, dicive haut poterit.

LXXIX. II. A PERFECTIONE MERITI DOMINICI

DOMINIC. Sufficiens est Christi meritum ad remittenda peccata. Quare non opus est nostris opesculis, aut si iis opus, Christi meritū erit insufficiens, imperfectū illiq; multum detrahetur, tantùm nimirum, quantū nostris operib. adscribitur. Et quàm contumeliosi sint Pontificij in sacratissimum Christi λύτρον, facilè patet inde quòd istud non dicant causam remissionis, sed duntaxat iustitiæ habitualis, ob quam peccata remittantur.

LXXX. III. Ab EXCLVSIONE GLORIATIONIS. Scribunt quidem Pontificii, ex suo dogmate non præberi ansam gloriandi, hoc tamen falsum est, quoniam dispositiones quasuis faciunt meritorias. At verò illæ nil sunt, quam opera naturæ, vti supra ostensum. Gratia enim, ex qua ista fieri volunt, tantum generalis est. Annon igitur magna gloriandi ansa suppeditatur, si quis sciat, suis se operibus propriis de congruo fuisse promeritum gratiam justificantem; Tale igitur argumentum nectimus: Quæcunque doctrina gloriationi fenestram aperit non est Apostolica. Sed doctrina Romanensium de justitia inhærente, fenestram aperit gloriationi. Ergo non est Apostolica.

LXXXI. IV A RECONCILIATIONE. Homini nondum reconciliato nullę infunduntur virtutes, quia hæ proueniunt à gratiosa Spiritus sancti inhabitatione, quæ non est nisi in reconciliatis. Quare ipsa reconciliatio pręcedit infusionem virtutum, reconciliamur autem Deoper iustificationem, vnde & hanc præcedere consequitur. Virtutes igitur nequeunt esse forma iustificationis, quia consequens nunquam potest forma esse antecedentis, cum omnis forma prior sit formato.

LXXXII. V. Ab experientia & testimonio conscien tiæ. Quiuis Christianus pius & deuotus, cùm cogitat, sibi esse reddendam rationem coram tribunali Christi, mox contremiscit, etiam si sanctissimè vixerit. Quod testimonium conscientiae indicat, nostra opera esse imperfecta, & consistere non posse coram Deo. Et sane si quis in timore Domini conferat bona opera sua cum malis, & peccatis quotidianis, deprehendet luculenter, nullam in propriis virtutibus, aut operibus spem certam esse reliquam, sed hanc in solo potius Christi merito collocandam.

LXXIII. VI. A remissione peccatorum. Quo modo consequimur remissionem peccatorum, eodem justificamur: quia consequi remissionem peccatorum est justificari Rom. 4. versu 7. At solâ fide in Christum, non propter dilectionem aut opera consequimur remissionem peccatorum. Ergo eodem modo iustificabimur. Pro minoris probatione tale argumentum nectimus: quo modo Christum Mediatorem apprehendimus, eodem modo consequimur remissionem peccatorum. Nam certum est, peccata remitti propter Christum Mediatorem & propitiatorem Rom. 3. ver. 25. At Christum Mediatorem non apprehendimus, nisi fide, Hebr. 4 versu 15. 16. Vbi Apostolus jubet accedere ad Deum, non fiducia nostrorum meritorum, sed fiducia Pontificis Christi, ideoque nihil nisi fidem à nobis postulat.

LXXXIV. VII. A fluctuatione conscientiae. Si operibus, aut partim fide partim operibus justificaremur, perpetuò fluctuarent, nunquam verò quiescerent conscientiae, quippe infirmo fundamento, quod est imperfecta iustitia, innitentes. At non debent fluctuare conscientiae sicut dicitur Rom. 4. ver. 16. ideò ex fide, vt firma sit promissio. Et Rom. 5. versu 1 Iustificati fide pacem habemus cum Deo.

LXXXV. TESTIMONIA PATRVM Horum plurima colligit Chemnitius in Examine & locis, Protestantes in causis retractati Concilij, & Gerberdus Tom. 3. & alij. Quare sufficiet hîc vnum atque alterum, quod Colophonis loco adponemus. 1. Iustinus Martyr epistola ad Diognetum. Quid aliud peccata nostra tegere potuit, quam christiiustitia? In quo alio nos iniqui & impij pro iustis haberi possumus, nisi in solo Dei Filio? O dulcem permutationem, ō imperscrutabile artificium, & beneficia expectationem omnem superantia, vt iniquitas quidem multorum in iusto vno abscondatur, iustitia autem vnius faciat, vt multi iniusti iustificentur. 2. Hieronymi dictum est: iustitia nostra non ex proprio merito, sed ex Dei misericordia consistit.

3. August. l. 19. de C. D. c. 25. Iustitia nostra, peccatorum constat remissione non perfectione virtutum. Et in Psal. 31. Tantùm credidero in Deum, deputabitur mihi ad iustitiam. 4. Bernhardus Serm. 23. super canticum. Non peccare Dei iustitia est, hominis iustitia indulgentia Dei est. Idem Serm. 51. Meritum meum miseratio Domini. Et alibi; Haec sufficit scire ad meritum, quòd non sufficiat meritum. 5. Anshelmus super c. Rom. 6. v. vlt. deest profectò gratiae quicquid meritis deputas: nec est, quò gratia intret, vbi iam meritum occupavit.

LXXXVII. Subjungenda nunc esset διάλυσις rationum contrariarum: Quia verò illarum plurimae sunt, & haec συζήτησις iam antè satis excrevit, proximae illas disputationi reservabimus, hîc Deo agentes gratias, qui nos naturâ filios irae adoptavit in filios gratiae, mittendo Filium vnigenitum & largiendo fidem in ipsum, quam confirmet in nobis clementer; vt finem eius salutem animarum, desideratissimam cum omnibus beatis in caelo consequamur. Amen.


### Question II. Containing sayings which teach that a man is justified without…: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 31 Disputation VIII. On the Papist Arguments against Justification by Faith Alone

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Theodor von Essen, of Greifswald, Pomeranian.

Thesis I.

Since the article concerning justification is cardinal, upon which many others depend, for that reason the Romanists oppose us by all means, and by various kinds of arguments they strive to invade and storm the imputed righteousness of Christ, the citadel of true religion. Those, therefore, must come to be examined, and what strength they contain must be seen and diligently considered. We shall view them divided into classes, since certain arguments prove the necessity of dispositions, certain ones [prove] the righteousness of works, [and] certain ones are accustomed to be opposed to imputed righteousness and to faith which alone justifies, διακενῦν. Therefore, lest confusion disturb the memory and weariness be created for the reader, it is our intention to both propose and refute the Papistic objections distinctly.

The first class containing sayings by which justification is ascribed to fear.

II. Bellarmine, book 1, on justification, chapter 13, enumerates seven dispositions, to all of which he strives to prove that justification is attributed in the Scriptures as to preparing dispositions. They are indeed

1. Faith. 2. Fear. 3. Hope. 4. Love. 5. Sorrow or contrition. 6. The intention of receiving the Sacrament in reality. 7. The intention of a new life. That faith justifies is confessed on both sides: it remains, therefore, to treat only of the remaining dispositions, and so we shall begin from Fear, to which, because justification is assigned, Bellarmine wishes to establish by the following sayings. Ecclesiasticus 1, v. 27: The fear of the Lord expels sin, for he who is without fear will not be able to be justified. Similar passages exist in Psalm 110, verse 10. Proverbs 1, v. 7. ch. 9, v. 10. Ecclesiasticus 1, v. 16. Isaiah 26, etc. He adds, moreover, this reason, that it is the nature of fear that it flees evils and seeks remedies by which it can escape them. To this some also refer that passage in Philippians 2, verse 12: Work out your salvation with fear and trembling.

III. Response 1. GENERALLY: The fear of God in the Scriptures and among the Fathers is taken equivocally. For it denotes either that which precedes faith, or faith itself, or that which follows faith. It denotes that which precedes when it is taken for servile fear, such as Bellarmine understands here, and which falls even upon infidels, who feel the sting of conscience, from which fear arises. It denotes faith itself when it is taken for the whole of divine worship, or for piety, and thus it involves the knowledge of the articles and at the same time trust. It signifies that which follows faith; when it is taken for filial fear, which is the zeal for avoiding sins and performing justice, and therefore follows faith, as fruit follows a good tree: However, whatever is attributed to the fear of God in the cited sayings, those things are not attributed to fear in the first signification, as Bellarmine wishes, but either in the second by synecdoche, or in the third by metonymy of the effect: For that servile fear is found even in infidels, the despairing, and the damned. Must it therefore be said that their fear expels sins, that it is in them the beginning of wisdom, that is, of perfect justification, as Bellarmine explains; that it is in them the fountain of life, that they have conceived and brought forth through it the Spirit of salvation? Since all these things are discordant, therefore these statements about servile fear can in no way be understood:

IV. 2. SPECIFICALLY to the statement of Ecclesiasticus 1, v. 27 and Psalm 110, v. 10, we respond that by fear nothing else is understood than the whole of divine worship, which we otherwise call piety, Gottes furcht. For that reason Tremellius translates it, reverence of the Lord. And because faith is the chief part of piety, by synecdoche the driving away of sin is attributed to the whole, which properly belongs to the part: But those words: without fear no one can be justified, are not found in the text, indeed which reads thus: ὐ δυνήσεται θυμὼς ἄνηρ δικαιωθῆναι, ἡ γὰρ ῥοπὴ τῶ θυμῶ αὐτῶ πτῶσις αὐτῷ, That is, an irascible man cannot be justified, etc. which can either be understood of justification before a political judge, so that the sense is that those who indulge their anger eventually commit those crimes on account of which they are dragged into court and cannot be justified, that is, acquitted: Or of justification before God, so that the sense is that he who is irascible and does not willingly forgive his brother is not justified. And thus it would agree with that: Forgive, and it will be forgiven you. Superfluously we respond concerning the Vulgate version, that it is not said that fear justifies, but that no one who is without fear is justified, which we ourselves concede. For this order is observed in conversion, that fear, sorrow, and contrition precede, but these do not justify, nor do they merit justification, which the Papists maintain. The statement of Isaiah clearly deals with nothing concerning the justification and salvation of man, as is evident to anyone inspecting the text. The same is answered to the others. For it is not proven that fear justifies, but that it always precedes justification, which we do not deny. For to him who is converted or justified, the curse of the law and the wrath of God which he has deserved are set forth, whence arises fear, which was present even in Cain and Judas. But this fear does not justify, nor does it merit justification, as a disposithe fiction of congruity, otherwise Judas also would have been justified, Phil 2. v. 12 salvation is not ascribed to fear and trembling, but is prohibited, for that trembling and fear, which is also commanded in Psalm 2. v. 11, is nothing other than filial reverence toward God, vigilance toward the Devil, prudence and constancy toward the world and one's own flesh: and the simplest sense is that we ought so to believe in Christ and expect eternal life, that we are not puffed up in spirit and rendered secure.

Latin:

Præs. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp. Theodoro von Essen / GripsWaldensi Pomerano.

Thesis. I.

CVm articulus de iustificatione cardinalis sit, à quo multi dependent alij, propterea Romanenses modis omnibus sese opponunt nobis, & varijs argumentorum generibus iustitiam Christi imputatam, veræ religionis arcem, inuadere & expugnare moliuntur. Illa igitur examinanda veniant, & quid roboris contineant, videndum ac diligenter considerandum. Nos in classes distinctis illa spescemus, quoniam quædam argumenta probant dispositionum necessitatem, quædam operum iustitia, quædam diffusum iustitiæ habitum Aste imputatę διακενῦν, & fidei q sola iustificet, opponi consueverunt, Ne igitur confusio turbet memoriam, & Lectori creetur tædium, distinctè obiectiones Papisticas tum proponere, tum eneruare nobis est animus.

Classis prima continens dicta, quibus timori iustificatio adscribitur.

II. Bellarm. l. 1. de iustifi. c. 13. septem enumerat dispositiones, quibus omnibus iustificationem in Scripturis attribui. tanquam dispositionibus præparantibus, probare annititur. Sunt verò

1. Fides. 2. Timor. 3. Spes. 4. Dilectio. 5. Dolor seu contritio. 6. Propositum Sacramenti reipsa percipiendi, 7. Propositum novæ vitæ. Fidem iustificare vtrinq; in confessio est : De reliquis ergo dispositionibus tantùm agendum restat, ideoque ordiemur à Timore, cui quod iustificatio adsignetur, sequentibus dictis stabilire vult Bellarminus. Ecclesiast. 1. v. 27: Timor Domini expellit peccatum, Nam qui sine timore est, non poterit iustificari. Similia extant Psal. 110, ver. 10. Prov. 1. v. 7. c. 9. v. 10. Ecclesiaft. 1. v. 16. Esa. 26. &c. Addit insuper rationem hanc, quòd natura timoris sit, vt fugiat mala, & quærat remedia, quibus illa possit evadere. Huc referunt nonnulli & istud Philip. 2. vers. 12. Operamini salutem vestram cum timore & tremore.

III. Resp. 1. GENERALITER: Timor Dei in Scripturis & apud Patres sumitur æquivocè, Vel enim notat fidei antecedentis, vel fidem ipsam, vel consequens fidei, Antecedens notat, quando pro timore servili accipitur, qualem hic intelligit Bellarminus, & cadit etiam in infideles, conscientiæ morsum sentientes, vnde timor exoritur. Fidem ipsam notat, cùm pro toto cultu diuino, seu pro pietate accipitur, & sic cognitionem articulorum simulque fiduciam involuit. Fidei consequens significat; quando pro timore filiali sumitur, qui est studium vitandi peccata, & præstandi iustitiam, ideoquè fidem, tanquam fructus bonam arbore consequitur: Quæcunque autem dictis allegatis timori Dei tribuuntur; ea non tribuuntur timori in prima significatione, vt vult Bellarminus, sed vel in secunda per Synecdochen, vel in tertiâ per Metonymiam effecti: Nam timor ille servilis reperitur etiam in infidelibus, desperantibus & damnatis. Ergonè dicendum, quòd timor ipsorum peccata expellat, quod sit in ijs sapientiæ, id est, perfectæ iustificationis, vt Bellarminus exponit, initium; quòd sit in ijs fons vitæ, quòd conceperint & pererint per eum Spiritum salutis? Quae omnia cùm sint absona, idcircò de timore seruili dicta ista, intelligi minimè possunt:

IV. 2. SPECIALITER ad dictum Ecclesiastici 1. v. 27. & Psal. 110. v. 10. respondemus, per timorem intelligi nihil aliud, quàm totam cultum diuinum, quem nos aliàs vocamus pietatem, Gottes furcht/ Ea propter Tremellius vertit, reverentia Domini. Et quia pietatis princeps pars est Fides, per Synecdochen toti attribuitur depulsio peccati, quae ppriè est partis: Ista verò verba: sine timore nemo potest iustificari, nõ reperiūtur in textu, quippè qui sic habet: ὐ δυνήσεται θυμὼς ἄνηρ δικαιωθῆναι, ἡ γὰρ ῥοπὴ τῶ θυμῶ αὐτῶ πτῶσις αὐτῷ, Id est, non potest iracundus vir iustificari, &c. quod vel intelligi potest de iustificatione coram politico iudice, vt sit sensus, eos qui iracundiae suae indulgent, committere tandem ea flagitia, propter quae in iudicium tracti, non possunt iustificari, id est, absolui: Vel de iustificatione coram Deo, vt sit sensus, eum, qui iracundus est, nec fratri suo libenter ignoscit, non iustificari. Atque sic congrueret cum illo: Remittite, & remittetur vobis. Ἐκ περισσίας respondemus de vulgata versione, non dici timorem iustificare, sed neminem, qui sine timore est, iustificari, quod ipsi concedimus. Hic enim ordo in conuersione obseruatur, vt praecedat timor, dolor, contritio, sed haec non iustificant, nec iustificationem merentur, quod volunt Pontificij. Dictum Esaiae planè nihil agit de iustificatione & salute hominis, vt patet cuiuis textum inspicienti. Idem respondetur ad alia. Nec enim probatur timore iustificare, sed illum semper praecedere iustificationem, quod non negamus. Qui enim conuertitur vel iustificatur, illi proponitur legis maledictio & ira Dei, quam promeruit, vnde oritur Timor, qui etiam in Caino & Iuda aderat. Hic verò timor non iustificat, nec iustificationem meretur, tanquam dispofictio de congruo, alias & Iudas fuisset iustificatus, Phil 2. v. 12 salus non adscribitur timori & tremori, sed prohibetur, ille enim tremor & timor, qui etiam Psal. 2. v 11 præcipitur, nihil est aliud quàm filialis reuerentia, quo ad DeVM, vigilantia quoad Diabolum, prudentia & constantia quoad mundum & propriam carnem: sentusque simplicissimus est, quod ita debeamus credere Christum & expectate vitam æternam, ne efferamur animo & reddamur securi.


### Second class. Containing sayings to which hope of justification is attributed
