Second class. Containing sayings to which hope of justification is attributed.

V. Bellarmine brings forward these sayings, Prov. 28. v. 25. He who hopes in the Lord shall be saved. Psalm 37. v. 40. He will save them, because they have hoped in him. Psalm 91. v. 14. Because he has hoped in me, I will deliver him, Matt. 9. v. 2. Take heart, son, your sins are forgiven you.

VI. Response 1. GENERALLY. The word hope is sometimes taken for trust itself, just as the verb to hope sometimes signifies to trust, sometimes to expect something: Sometimes it is taken in opposition, so that faith is of past and present things, hope only of future things. It is taken in the former, not the latter way, in the cited sayings. For it is most frequent in the Psalms that to hope is used for to trust.

2. SPECIFICALLY, the sayings cited from the Proverbs and Psalms do not speak of the attainment of the remission of sins, but of external happiness and liberation from external dangers. Nor in that saying of Prov. 28. v. 25 is the word 'shall be saved' found, but the root דשן 'shall be made fat'. In Psalm 91. v. 16 it is not found, 'because he has hoped in me', but 'because he clings to me in love'. The saying in Matt. 9 does not speak of hope, but of true and constant trust and confidence. We willingly concede to Bellarmine, however, that trust is prior in the order of nature to the remission of sins itself; for the former is the cause of the latter: But this does not follow, because it is prior in time. Wherefore this is the sense of the Evangelical saying, take heart son, that is, conceive confidence and believe most firmly, for thus your sins will be forgiven you. Here the remission of sins, and consequently justification, is not ascribed to fear, nor to any other disposition, but to faith alone. For it is most certain that Christ fully taught the Paralytic how he might obtain the remission of sins; yet he mentions no disposition, but names only confidence.

VII. That passage from Romans 8: verse 24 could also be referred here, τῇ ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν, we are saved by hope. Therefore not by faith alone. Response: This passage is understood in two ways. 1. Either concerning the reconciliation of man or justification, which is done through faith, as when it is said, your faith has made you safe; likewise, by grace you are saved through faith. And then by ἐλπίδα nothing else is understood than πίστις itself. 2. Or concerning the glory of the future life, or concerning final liberation and glorification after this life, which we still hope for and expect. When therefore the Apostle says, We are saved by hope, glorification can be understood, that is, the Apostle signifies not that we are justified by hope, but that by hope, not in reality, we are glorified and freed from all miseries, of which he had spoken in the preceding verses. The sense therefore is: We possess eternal life not in reality, but in hope in this life. For now we are children of God, but it does not yet appear what we shall be, 1 John 3, verse 2.

Latin:

Classis secunda. Continens dicta, quibus spes iustificatio tribuitur.

V. Profert Bellarm. hec dicta, Prov. 28. v. 25. Qui sperat in Domino, saluabitur. Psal. 37. v. 40. Saluabit eos, quia sperauerunt in eo. Psal 91 v. 14. Quoniam in me sperauit, liberabo eum, Matth. 9. v. 2. Confide fili, remittuntur tibi peccata tua.

VI. Resp. 1. GENERALITER. Spei vocabulum aliquando sumitur pro ipsâ fiduciâ, sicut & verbum sperare modò fidere, modò aliquid expectare significat: Aliquando sumitur oppositè, vt fides sit de rebus preteritis & præsentibus, spes tantùm de futuris. Priori non posteriori modo, accipitur in dictis allegatis. Frequentissimum enim hoc est in Psalmis, vt sperare ponatur pro confidere.

2. SPECIALITER, dicta ex Prouerbijs & Psalmis citata, non loquuntur de adeptione remifsionis peccatorum, sed de felicitate externâ & liberatione à periculis externis. Nec in dicto illo Prou. 28. v. 25. habetur verbum sanabitur, sed rad. דשן pinguis efficietur. Psal. 91. v. 16. non habetur, quia in me sperauit, sed quia in me amore propendet. Dictum Matth. 9. non de spe, sed vera & constanti fiduciâ & confidentiâ loquitur. Lubenter autem Bellarmino concedimus, fiduciâ ordine naturæ priorem esse ipsâ peccatorum remissione; illa enim huius causa est: Hoc verò non sequitur, quod sit prior tempore. Quare hic est sensus dicti Evangelici, confide fili, id est, fiduciam concipe & firmissimè crede, sic enim tua tibi peccata remittentur. Hic remissio peccatorum, & consequenter iustificatio nō timori, non etiam alij alicui dispositioni adscribitur, sed soli fidei. Certissimum enim est Christū plenariè docuisse Paralyticū, quomodo consequi posset peccatorum remissionem; nullius autem meminit dispositionis, sed solam nominat fiduciam.

VII. Referri huc etiam posset illud Roman. 8: vers. 24. τῇ ἐλπίδι ἐσώθημεν spe salui facti sumus. Ergò non sola fide. Resp. Dupliciter hic locus intelligitur. 1. Vel de reconciliatione hominis seu iustificatione, quæ fit per fidem, vt cum dicitur, fides tua te saluum fecit; Item gratia estis saluati per fidem. Et tunc per ἐλπίδα nihil intelligitur aliud quàm ipsa πίστις. 2. Vel de gloria futuræ vitæ, seu de finali liberatione & glorificatione post hanc vitam, quam adhuc speramus & expectamus. Cùm igitur dicit Apostolus, Spe saluati sumus, intelligi potest glorificatio, hoc est, Apostolus significat non quòd spe simus iustificati, sed quod spe, non re simus glorificati & liberati ab omnibus miserijs, de quibus in præcedentibus dixerat. Sensus ergò est; Vitam æternam non re, sed spe possidemus in hac vitâ, Nunc enim Dei filij sumus, sed nondum apparet quod erimus, 1. Iohan. 3. versu 2.


### Third class, containing sayings by which justification is attributed to love

Third class, containing sayings by which justification is attributed to love.

IIX. Ecclesiasticus 2. v. 10. You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts will be enlightened, Luke 7. ver: 47. Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much, Galatians 5. v. 6. Neither circumcision avails anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith, which works through love, 1 John 3. v. 14:

16. v. 14. We have been translated from death to life; because we love the brethren: Others add the following 1 Cor. 13: v. 2. If I should have all faith, but have not charity, I am nothing: Likewise: Now there remain faith, hope, charity, but the greatest of these is charity: Therefore equally or certainly more than faith it will justify: Proverbs 10. v. 12. Charity covereth a multitude of sins. 1 John 4. v. 12. If we love one another, charity abideth in us, Colossians 3. v. 14. Charity is the bond of perfection. John 14: v. 21. He that loveth me, shall be loved by my Father. 1 John 4. v. 7. He that loveth, is born of God: Romans 13. v. 8. He that loveth his neighbor, hath fulfilled the law. James 2. v. 5. God hath promised the kingdom to those by whom he shall have been loved.

IX. Response 1. GENERALLY. True love, which in this world can never be perfect, is prior to justification neither in time nor in nature, inasmuch as it follows faith, as its cause, as if it were an effect; not indeed immediately, but mediately, and in this order, that by faith first the righteousness of Christ is received Col. 2. v. 6. and which we have in him; the remission of sins, Eph. 1. v. 7. Acts 26. v. 18. Hence furthermore by faith also the Holy Spirit is received Gal. 3. v. 14. promised to those believing in Christ. John 7: v. 39. and thus to those already justified by faith and children of God, Gal. 4. v. 6. which Spirit begins to effect and work the renewal, charity, and the remaining new obedience in the justified, Tit. 3. v. 5. 2 Cor. 3. v. 18. Gal. 5. 22. Eze. 36. v. 25. 26. 27. where this order is exquisitely expressed. It may be noted here as if incidentally and in passing, that there is a twofold energy of faith: One primary and immediate, which is the apprehension of Christ, and is not exercised through charity: The other secondary and mediate, by which faith, through the intervening and in order prior gratuitous justification of man, adoption, and the gift of the Holy Spirit, produces the works of charity. In no respect, therefore, is charity prior to true faith, but always posterior. For no one loves God, unless he has the Holy Spirit dwelling within according to Rom. 8. v. 5. Charity is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us. But no one has this Spirit in himself unless he is justified, which Bellarmine himself easily concedes. There is, however, one distinction of his, by which he makes a difference between incipient and perfect love: that the latter is not without the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, but the former is without this, although not without the special help of God. For, 1. Love in this life is not given as perfect, but is and remains, even in the most holy, only incipient. 2. No one can love God by his own powers. Wherefore the operation of the Holy Spirit must necessarily be added. But He does not work good works except in the reconciled, because He is given to no one unless he is justified. 3. The passages alleged above conclude nothing, because they do not speak of the love of the unregenerate, but of the justified and those actually converted. This having therefore been proven, we conclude that love follows justification, because love does not justify formally or justificatorily, but only συμπτωματικῶς, argumentatively or significantly, and is rather a mark of justification than a cause, and justification itself is attributed to it as to a fruit and effect, testifying of its cause a posteriori, not a priori. And consequently, the Pontificians argue viciously from the mark to the cause.

X. 2. SPECIALLY, regarding the passage of Ecclesiasticus 2, we say that it speaks of the regenerate and those who fear the Lord. Wherefore it does nothing for that love which Bellarmine establishes as preparatory. Moreover, in the Greek text nothing of the sort is read, but verses 8 and 9 read thus, as Tremellius translates: You who fear the Lord, have hope of good things and of the joy of eternity and of mercy; you who fear the Lord, expect His mercy, and do not turn aside, that you may not fall. But what patronage comes to the Pontificians from this?

VI. To Luke 7. verse 47, we respond that the love of the woman cannot there be constituted as the cause of remission. For Christ Himself says: Your faith has made you safe. He was arguing therefore not from the cause, but from the effect. For he wished to confound the thoughts of Simon, who thought the deed unjust because Christ was speaking and associating so familiarly with a sinner. And so he desired to show him that she was no longer a sinner, but that her sins had been forgiven her, which he shows from the fruit or effect, namely love. And he illustrates this with a simile taken from two debtors, where he makes the forgiveness of a greater debt the cause of greater love, not the contrary. And he adds, Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much: but to whom less is forgiven, he loves less. In which latter words the forgiveness of a smaller debt is established as the cause of smaller love. Such also is the sense of the former words, namely that that great love is the effect of a great forgiveness, and therefore that she no longer remains in sins. As regards the particle ὅτι, it does not always signify the cause of a thing but often an effect conjoined with the cause, as The sun has risen, because it is day; You live, because you walk; You are a man, because you laugh. The particle ὅτι therefore remains causal here, but it does not denote the cause of the thing, but rather of the conclusion; it is syllogistic, not aetiological. For the middle term, which is the cause of the conclusion, is not always taken from the cause of the thing, but more often also from the effect, which makes it known. Let this logical canon therefore be noted: Not everything that is the cause of the consequence is also the cause of the consequent, as it does not follow; The sun has risen, because it is day, Therefore day is the cause of the sun's rising. Likewise; You live because you walk, Therefore your walking is the cause of your life. In the same way it does not follow: That woman's many sins are forgiven, because she loved much, Therefore love is the cause of the forgiveness of sins. For love is not alleged as the cause and merit, but as the fruit and effect of forgiveness, and the argument is not a priori to posterior, not from cause to effect, but a posteriori to prior from the effect or sign to the cause, which is most clearly established by that analogy, and from the words of Christ, 'He to whom less is forgiven, the same loves less.' But the true cause of remission is shown in the following, where He says to Christ, 'Your faith has made you safe, go in peace.' Philippus responds by a distinction that there is a twofold absolution: one private, of the conscience struggling with the wrath of God; this is not on account of Christ apprehended by faith, whence it is said: 'Your faith has made you safe': The other is public before the Church; this is on account of good works, which are testimonies of conversion, as Christ here declares to the Pharisee why He receives the harlot woman, namely because she loved much, and the testimonies of conversion are present.

XII. Galatians 5, verse 6, it is not said of charity that it justifies; but faith is described by its sign and effect, or by its mediate and secondary ένεργείᾳ, namely that it works through love. To 1 John 3, verse 14, we respond that the translation from death into life cannot be ascribed to love as a cause; for this is proper to faith, John 5, verse 24, 'He who believes has passed from death into life.' Wherefore that rule of Damascenus, book 4, chapter 20, applies here: ἔθος τῇ γραφῇ τινὰ ἐκβατικῶς ὀφείλοντα λέγεσθαι, αἰτιολογικῶς λέγειν: It is the custom of Scripture to speak causally of certain things which ought to be understood eventually, as Psalm 51, verse 6, 'Against You only have I sinned, that You might be justified,' where the prophet does not note the αἴτιον, but the ἔκβασιν. However, sin is not the cause of divine justice and truth, but when he had sinned; thence GOD shows His justice. Romans 11, verse 32. GOD has concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy on all. Thus John 12, verse 39, 'Therefore they could not believe, that the word of Isaiah might be fulfilled.' On which passage Theophylact writes thus, ὀὐκ ἔστιν αἰτιολογίας, ἀλλ̓ ἐκβάσεως. Thus when Christ, John 9, verse 39, says that He came into the world for this reason, that those who see might become blind, according to the Greek Isagoge of Adrian, the non-causal is put for the causal, or the event for the cause. In like manner we can interpret this passage: We have been translated from death into life, because we love the brethren, so that the particle ὅτι denotes the outcome, not the cause, and the sense may be: Because we have been translated from death into life, hence we love the brethren. The Apostle therefore does not argue from cause to effect, but conversely. We know, he says, that we have been translated from death into life. He does not say simply, we have been translated, but, we know that we have been translated. Whence do we know this? From the effect, Because we love the brethren. The particle ὅτι therefore denotes the cause of the consequence, not of the consequent.

XIII. To 1 Corinthians 13, verse 2, we respond: 1. If we take this passage concerning justifying faith, the Apostle argues from an impossible hypothesis: If it were possible that I should have all faith, that I should spend all my goods in feeding the poor, that I should speak with the tongues of angels, but have not charity, I am nothing. From this impossible hypothetical, against all the canons of the logicians, the Papists make a categorical. And Bellarmine, book 1, chapter 15, concedes that this expression of the Apostle is hyperbolic, because he saw the impossibility of the thing.

2. Others respond that the discourse is about the faith of signs or miracles, because it is expressly added, that I should remove mountains. That this can be separated from charity, we willingly concede. Here the Papists object that faith is but one, Ephesians 4, and that the faith of signs is nothing other than true Christian faith, but an excellent one, as Bellarmine says, or as Stapleton speaks, an argument, magnitude, force, and intensity of integral or full faith. But Bellarmine, book 1, chapter 15, contradicts himself; for in column 981, letter B, he concedes that the faith of miracles can in reality be separated from charity, and proves it from that Matthew 7, verse 22: Many will say to me in that day, have we not prophesied in thy name? He writes the same in book 1 on grace, chapter 10. And indeed Balaam was

Latin:

Classis tertia, continens dicta, quibus dilectioni iustificatio attribuitur.

IIX. Ecclesiast: 2. v. 10. Qui timetis Dominum, diligite illum, & illuminabuntur corda vestra, Luc. 7. ver: 47. Remissa sunt ei peccata multa, quoniam dilexit multum Galat. 5. v 6. Neque circumcisio aliquid valet, neque præputium, sed fides, quæ per dilectionem operatur, 1. Ioh: 3. v. 14:

16. v. 14. Translati sumus de morte ad vitam; quoniam diligimus fratres: Addunt alij sequentia 1. Cor. 13: v. 2. Si habuero omnem fidem, charitatem autem non habuero, nihil sum: Item: Nunc manet fides, spes, charitas, sed maxima in his charitas: Ergò æquè aut certè magis quàm fides iustificabit: Proverb. 10. v. 12. Charitas operit multitudinem peccatorum. 1. Iohan. 4. v. 12. Si diligimus nos inuicem, charitas in nobis manet, Coloss. 3. v. 14. Charitas est vinculum perfectionis. Ioh 14: v. 21. Qui diligit me, diligetur à Patre meo. 1. Ioh 4. v. 7. Qui diligit, ex Deo natus est: Rom. 13. v. 8. Qui diligit proximum, legem impleuit. Iacob 2. v. 5. Deus promisit regnum iis à quibus dilectus fuerit.

IX. Resp. 1. GENERALITER. Dilectio vera, quæ in hoc mundo nunquam perfecta esse potest, nec tempore, nec naturâ iustificatione prior est, vt potè quæ velut effectus; fidem, tanquam causam suam consequitur; non quidem ἀμέσως, sed ἐμμέσως, & hoc ordine, quòd fide primùm accipitur iustitia Christi Col. 2. v. 6. & quam in ipso habemus; remissio peccatorum, Eph. 1. v. 7. Act. 26. v. 18. Hinc porrò fide quoq; accipitur Spiritus S. Gal. 3. v. 14. promissus credentibus in Christum. Ioh. 7: v. 39. atque sic fide iam iustificatis & filijs Dei, Gal. 4. v. 6. qui Spiritus renouationem, charitatem & reliquam nouam obedientiam, in iustificatis efficere, & operari incipit, Tit. 3. v. 5. 2. Cor. 3. v. 18. Gal. 5. 22. Eze. 36. v. 25. 26. 27. vbi ordo hic exquisitè expressus. Notari v. hic potest velut obiter & in transcursu, quòd fidei duplex sit ἐνέργεια: Vna primaria & immediata, quæ est apprehensio Christi, & non exeritur per charitatem: Altera secundaria & mediata, quâ fides, mediante & ordine prius interueniente gratuitâ hominis iustificatione, adoptione & donatione Spiritus sancti, charitatis opera pducit. Nullo igitur respectu charitas verâ fide prior est, sed semper posterior. Nemo enim diligit Deum, nisi S. S. habeat inhabitantem, iuxta Rom. 8. v. 5. Charitas diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis. At nemo hunc Spiritum habet in se, nisi iustificatus, quod ipse Bellarminus facilè concedit. Vna autem est distinctió eius, quâ discrimen facit inter dilectionem inchoatam & perfectam, Hanc esse non absque inhabitatione Spiritus sancti, Illam autem absque hac esse, licet non sinè auxilio Dei speciali. Nam, 1 Dilectio in hac vita non datur perfecta, sed est & manet in sanctissimis etiam, duntaxat inchoata. 2. Nemo potest diligere Deum ex proprijs viribus. Quare accedat necesse est operatio Spiritus sancti. Hic autem non operatur bona opera, nisi in reconciliatis, quia nemini datur, nisi iustificato. 3. Dicta superius allegata nihil concludunt, quia non loquuntur de dilectione non renatorum, sed iustificatorum & actu conuersorum. Hoc igitur euicto dilectionem sequi iustificationem concludimus, quòd dilectio non iustificet formaliter aut iustificè, sed duntaxat συμπτωματικῶς arguitiue vel significatiuè, Et iustificationis potiùs nota sit, quàm causa, ipsáque iustificatio attribuatur tanquam fructui & effectui, de causa sua testificanti à posteriori, non priori. Et per consequens, à notâ ad causam vitiosè argumentantur Pontificij.

X. 2. SPECIALITER, ad locum Ecclesiastici 2. dicimus, quòd de renatis & Dominum timentibus loquatur, Quare nihil facit ad dilectionem eam, quam Bellarminus statuit præparatoriam. In textu insuper Græco tale nihil legitur, sed versus 8. & 9. ita habet, vt vertit Tremellius: Qui reueremini Dominum, spem habetote de bonis & de lætitia æternitatis ac misericordiæ, qui reueremini Dominum, expectate misericordiam eius, neq; declinate, vt non decidatis. Quid verò hinc patrocisij accedit Pontificijs.

VI. Ad Lucæ. 7. vers. 47. respondemus, dilectionem mulieris ibi non posse constitui causam remissionis. Nam Christus ipse inquit: Fides tua te salvum fecit. Argumentabatur ergo non à causa, sed ab effectu. Volebat enim cogitationes Simonis confundere, qui iniquum putabat factum quòd Christus ita familiariter cum peccatrice colloqueretur & conversaretur. Itaque ostendere ipsi cupiebat, eam non amplius esse peccatricem, verùm remissa ipsi esse peccata, id quod ostendit à fructu vel effectu, nimirum dilectione. Atque hoc illustrat simili à duobus debitoribus sumpto, ubi condonationem maioris debiti facit causam maioris dilectionis, non contrà. Et addit, Remissa sunt ei peccata multa, quia dilexit multùm: Cui autem minus remittitur, is minus diligit. In quibus posterioribus verbis remissio minoris debiti, causà constituitur minoris dilectionis. Talis etiam sensus est priorum verborum quòd videlicet ista dilectio magna, sit effectus magnæ remissionis, ideoqué illam non amplius hærere in peccatis. Quod particulam ὅτι attinet, non semper ea significat causam rei sed sæpè effectum cum causà coniunctum, ut Sol ortus, quia dies est; Tu vivis, quia ambulas; Tu homo es, quia rides. Causalis igitur ac huc manet particula ὅτι, sed non notat causam rei, verùm conclusionis, est συλλογιστικὴ non ἀιτιολογικὴ. Medius enim terminus, qui causa est conclusionis, non semper desumitur à causa rei, sed sæpiùs etiam ab effectu, qui illum notificat. Notetur proindè canon hic logicus: Non quicquid est causa consequentià, est etiam causa consequentis, ut non sequitur; Sol ortus est, quia dies est, Ergo dies est causà orti Solis. Item; Tu vivis quia ambulas, Ergo ambulatio tua est causa vitæ tuæ. Eodem modo non sequitur: Illi mulieri remissa sunt peccata multa, quia dilexit multùm, Ergò dilectio est causa remissionis peccatorum. Nâm dilectio non allegatur ut causa & meritũ, sed fructus & effectus remissionis, argumentumq́; nõ à priori ad posterius, nõ à causa ad effectum, sed à posteriori ad prius ab effectu seu signo ad causam ducitur, quod constat apertissime illo simili, & ex verbis Christi, Cui minis remittitur, is minus diligit, Vera autē remissionis causa ostenditur in sequētibus, vbi Christᵘ̄ dicit, Fides tua te saluam fecit, abi in pace. Philippᵘ̄ respondet, per distinctionem quòd duplex sit absolutio: alia priuata conscientiae luctantis cum ira Dei; haec sit non ppter Christum fide apprehēsum, vnde dicitur: Fides tua te saluam fecit: Alia est publica coram Ecclesia; haec sit propter bonā opera, quae sunt testimonia conversionis, vt hîc Christus Pharisaeo declarat, cur mulierem meretriciam recipiat, nempè quia dilexerit multum, & extent testimonia conversionis.

XII. Galat. 5. vers. 6. non dicitur de charitate, quòd iustificet; sed fides describitur à signo & effectu, vel ένεργείᾳ ipsius mediatà & secundaria, quòd videlicet per dilectionem operetur. Ad 1. Iohan. 3. vers. 14. respondemus, quòd dilectioni tanquam causae adscribi nequeat translatio è morte in vitam; Hoc enim fidei proprium, Iohan. 5. vers. 15. qui credit, transiit à morte in vitam. Quare huc spectat illá regulá Damasceni lib. 4. cap. 20. ἔθος τῇ γραφῇ τινὰ ἐκβατικῶς ὀφείλοντα λέγεσθαι, αἰτιολογικῶς λέγειν: Mos est Scripturae, quaedam quae eventualiter debent intelligi, causaliter dicere, vt Psal. 51. vers: 6. Tibi soli peccavi, vt iustificeris, vbi propheta non αἴτιον notat, sed ἔκβασιν. Non autem peccatum est causa iustitiae & veritatis diuinae, sed cùm ille peccasset; inde DEVS suam ostendit iustitiam. Rom. 11. vers. 32. DEVS conclusit omnes sub peccatum, vt omnium misereatur. Sic Iohan. 12. vers. 39. Propterea non poterant credere, vt impleretur verbum Esaiae. In quem locum ita scribit Theophylactus, ὀὐκ ἔστιν αἰτιολογίας, ἀλλ̓ ἐκβάσεως. Sic cùm Christus Iohan. 9. vers. 29. in mundum propterea se venisse ait, vt qui vident caeci fiant, iuxta Graecam Adriani Isagogen, τὸ ἀπαίτιον ὡς αἴτιον ponitur, siue euentus pro causâ. Pari modo interpretari possumus hunc locum: Translati sumus de forte in vitam, quia diligimus fratres, vt particula ὅτι ἔκβασιν notet, non αἰτίαν, & sit sensus: Quia translati sumus è morte in vitam, hinc diligimus fratres. Non igitur à causâ ad effectum, sed contra argumentatur Apostolus, Nos scimus, inquit, quòd translati sumus de morte in vitam. Non dicit simpliciter, translati sumus, sed, scimus quòd translati sumus. Vnde hoc scimus? Ex effectu, Quia diligimus fratres. Particula igitur ὅτι notat causam consequentię, non consequentis.

XIII. Ad. 1. Corinth. 13. v. 2. respondemus 1. Si de fide iustificante accipimus hunc locum, argumentatur Apostolus ab hypothesi impossibili, Si fieri posset, vt omnem fidem habeam, ut omnia bona insumam alendis pauperibus, ut loquar linguis Angelorum, charitatem vero non habeam, nihil sum. Ex hac hypothetica impossibili, contra omnes Logicorum Canones, Pontificij faciunt categoricam. Et Bellarm. lib. 1. c. 15. concedit hanc locutionem Apostolis esse hyperbolicam, quia vidit rei impossibilitatem.

2. Alij respondent, sermonem esse de fide signorum aut miraculorum, quia expressè additur, vt montes transferam. Hanc verò à charitate separari posse, lubenter concedimus. Hîc excipiunt Pontificij, fidem non nisi vnam esse, Ephes. 4 & fidem signorum esse nihil aliud, nisi veram fidem Christianam, sed excellentem, vt ait Bellarminus, vel vt Stapletonus loquitur, fidei integræ aut plenæ argumentum, magnitudinem, vim & intensionem. Sed Bellarminus lib. 1. cap. 15. sibijpsi contradicit, Nam colomn. 981. lit. B. concedit, fidem miraculorum separatam esse posse reipsâ à charitate, & probat ex illo Matth. 7. vers. 12. Multi mihi dicent in illo die, nonne in nomine tuo prophetavimus? Idem scribit lib. 1. de gratiâ cap. 10. Et sanè Bileam erat


### endowed with the gift of prophesying, but on account of that he did not have…

endowed with the gift of prophesying, but on account of that he did not have true faith, nor was he justified. But soon Bellarmine, forgetting himself, col. d. lit. D., writes that the faith of miracles is nothing else than true and excellent faith; from which we infer thus: True and excellent faith is never without charity. The faith of miracles is such. Therefore it is never without charity, which conclusion contradicts Bellarmine's first assertion. Furthermore, we conclude thus: True and justifying faith is never without charity, which they themselves concede, and it is easily proved from that Gal. 5, verse 6: Faith works through charity. But the faith of which the Apostle speaks in 1 Cor. 13 is and was without charity, as Bellarmine admits. Therefore the faith of which the Apostle speaks here is not justifying faith. Note here in passing the unheard-of absurdity of Stapleton, who in Antidotes to Apostolic Faith, page 680, writes thus: that those who have faith without charity indeed comprehend the whole Christ, but comprehend him badly. On the contrary, every apprehension of Christ which occurs through faith is salutary and good. For as many as received him, to them he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, John 1, verse 12. Therefore it is impossible that there should be given a faith which is a bad apprehension of Christ.

Finally 3. Others understand historical and hypocritical faith, and even that of miracles, and all that which is without justifying faith: for the Apostle censures those who boasted of faith and meanwhile lived badly. To these that saying is opposed: if I have all faith, that is, if I have professed faith, and even confirmed it with miracles, but have not charity, it is a most certain indication that true faith is not present, not because charity informs faith and renders it apt for justifying, as Bellarmine wishes, but because the absence of charity shows likewise the absence of true and saving faith, since it always is effective through charity: Even if therefore I have all faith, namely that which is separated or can be separated from charity, such as 1. historical faith, 2. hypocritical faith, or 3. the faith of miracles, I am not yet righteous before God, or elect. For if charity is absent, we are nothing, because it is an indication that true faith is not present. It does not follow, however, Charity must be present, therefore it also justifies. For it must be present, not as a cause, but as a fruit and effect. The cause of justification is one thing, a necessary consequence is another. Just as the cause of life is one thing, the effect following life is another, as is the motion which necessarily exists in a man or any living thing, not as a cause of life, but as an effect following it.

XIV. From 1 Cor. 13, last verse, where charity is called the greatest virtue, they argue thus: The greatest virtue justifies the most. Stapleton in his Antidotes calls this argument good and invincible. But I reply 1. That both premises are legal, whereas justification is not from the law, but from the Gospel, Rom. 3, v. 21. Wherefore this legal conclusion does not hinder our opinion at all. For we admit that if anyone perfectly loves God and his neighbor, that is, keeps the entire law completely, he is justified. But this perfection falls to no man, wherefore no one can be justified by that love. 2. The major premise is false, because neither the greatest, nor the least, nor an intermediate virtue, as a virtue, justifies, but only that which, by a certain relation, looks upon and embraces Christ and his most holy merit, such as faith alone, Rom. 3 and 4, Gal. 2. and 3. not charity, since it follows justification, as Christ testifies in Luke 7, verse 47, where he affirms that he to whom many sins have been forgiven, loves much. And Bellarmine concedes in book 2 of Justification, ch. 15, that Augustine teaches in very many places that works are the effects of justification. Whence we conclude against Stapleton, that good or just works do not justify formally, but are effects of justification: Against Bellarmine, that Charity does not justify dispositively, because the disposition precedes, but charity, as also the virtues and other good works, follow justification. Stapleton objects that he is speaking of the habit, not the act of love: To which I reply, that the passage of Paul, which is brought forward for the sake of proof, speaks of love as a work, as is evident from the entire context. 3. Love is called the greatest, not ἁπλῶς but κατὰ τί. The Apostle speaks of the gifts used in the Church of the Corinthians, among all of which love stands out. 1. As to breadth, because it benefits not only the one loving, but also the neighbor of the one loving, and extends to him. 2. As to duration: The rest will eventually be abolished and will cease, but love is to remain forever. For faith also will be abolished, insofar as it is defined as the ὑπόστασις of things hoped for and the ἔλεγχος of things invisible. For in eternal life there will no longer be things to be hoped for and invisible goods. And only thus far is charity greater, but that it is absolutely the greatest, and therefore simply greater than faith itself, is most false. For faith is called the base and mother and foundation of all the remaining virtues, as the Council of Trent and Bellarmine admit. But a cause is always nobler than its effect. I add this syllogism besides. Whatever apprehends Christ, and applies justice to us, and overcomes the world, and therefore can do all things and is the foundation and root of all Christian virtues, without which it is impossible for anyone to please God and obtain eternal life; that is without doubt by far the greatest and most excellent. But faith apprehends Christ, John 1, verse 12, and applies justice to us, Rom. 3, 4, Gal. 2, 3. & overcomes the world, 1 John 5, verse 4, and therefore can do all things, Mark 9, verse 23. And it is the foundation and root of all Christian virtues. of Christian [virtues] also of Charity Heb. 11: verse 1, Gal. 5, verse 6. And without it, it is impossible that anyone should please GOD, Heb. 11. verse 6. and obtain eternal life John 3. verse 11. Mark 16. verse 16, Therefore faith is without any doubt the greatest and most excellent virtue. Stapleton shouts that in this way Paul is accused of lying, inasmuch as he pronounces love to be greater than faith. But he commits the fallacy of shifting from a statement in a certain respect to a statement in an unqualified sense. For the whole matter stands thus: For Love is the greatest virtue on account of the edification of the Church, and the utility of the neighbor, and perpetual duration. Faith is the greatest on account of Christ, whom the faithful man apprehends in the promise of the Gospel, and in whom, and through whom he receives righteousness and eternal salvation! Love has the greatest excellence, but nevertheless it receives it from faith. Love is the greatest with respect to the neighbor, whom it serves and whom it edifies: Faith is the greatest with respect to Him whom it apprehends. And thus these things are not opposed, but can exist together. But we ask of the Papists: If charity is absolutely the greatest and justifies most, how does it happen that in evangelical sermons faith is always required, for the most part without any mention of charity? For this is the sum of the Gospel: Believe in Christ, or he who believes in Christ will be saved. And Paul, expressly treating the entire doctrine of justification, makes mention of faith alone, and not only does he not name charity among the causes of justification, but he also explicitly excludes all works of the law. Where the Papists profit nothing by denying that charity is a work of the law. For is not the sum of the whole law, Love GOD and your neighbor, Matt. 22, v. 37. Rom. 13. verse 9.

XV. To Prov. 10. v. 12. We answer that the words according to the sources sound thus: Hatred stirs up contentions, but love covers all transgressions. Whence it becomes manifest that this does not treat of justification, but rather that the duty and nature of charity is described, namely that it knows the faults of a neighbor, but does not hate them, does not reveal them, but covers and conceals them, according to the commandment of the Lord in Leviticus 19, verse 17. This is apparent from the preceding words, Hatred stirs up strife, that is, when a neighbor hates a neighbor, then one reproaches the other with his faults, from which contentions arise: But he who loves another, he covers and conceals the failings and errors of the ἀδελφότητα with the cloak of charity. Therefore, the covering of sins is twofold: ONE which is done before GOD, of this there is no discussion at present: THE OTHER, which is done before man, and covers not one's own sins, but those of a neighbor, and of this the present text speaks only.

XVI. To 1 John 4, verse 16, we respond that it is taught there, not how we are grafted into GOD and justified, but what kind of people the justified are, or how it is known that we are justified and grafted into GOD. The condition of the person is indicated, not the cause of righteousness: For brotherly love is an argument and evidence that we are in GOD, and GOD in us, according to that in John 15, verse 5. He who abides in me, and I in him, bears much fruit. For no one can have sincere love and produce the works of faith, unless he is in Him, and has Him remaining in himself, John 15, verse 5, John 6, verse 56. He who eats my flesh, abides in me and I in him. The same response is to be given to that in John 14, 1 John 4, Romans 13.

XVII. To Colossians 3, verse 14, charity is called the bond of perfection, because by the bond of charity all Christians are bound together into one certain whole and perfect body as if by a certain bond; when this bond is broken, with dissensions stirred up, that body does not remain whole, but becomes gaping, torn, mutilated, and maimed. Therefore, perfection is twofold; One Ecclesiastical or public, which consists in true concord and mutual society, the bond of which is charity. The other purely theological or private, which consists in true justice, which we obtain only through faith.

Latin:

indutus dono prophetandi, sed ob id veram fidem non habuit, nec justificatus fuit. Mox autem sibi oblitus Bellarminus col. d. lit. D. scribit, fidem miraculorum nihil esse aliud, quàm veram & excellentem fidem; ex quo sic inferimus: Vera & excellens fides nunquam est sine charitate. Fides miraculorum est talis. Ergò nunquàm sine charitate, quæ conclusio contradicit primæ Bellarmini assertioni. Ulterius ita concludimus: Fides vera & justifica nunquam est sine charitate, quod & ipsi concedunt, & facilè probatur ex illo Gal 5. versu 6. Fides per charitatem operatur. Atqui fides, de qua 1. Cor. 13. loquitur Apostolus, est & fuit absque charitate, fatente Bellarmino. Ergo fides, de qua hic loquitur Apostolus, non est fides iustificans. Notes hic obiter inauditam absurditatem Stapletoni, qui in Antidotis fidei Apostolicæ pag. 680, ita scribit, eos qui habent fidem sine charitate, totum quidem Christum comprehendere, sed malè comprehendere. Contrà Omnis Christi apprehensio, quæ fit per fidem, est salutaris & bona. Quotquot enim receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri, his qui credunt in nomen eius Iohan 1. versu 12. Ergo impossibile est, vt detur fides, quæ sit mala comprehensio Christi.

Tandem 3. Alij fidem intelligunt historicam & hypocriticam, quin & miraculorum, omnemque eam quæ est sine fide iustificante: Taxat enim Apostolus eos, qui fidem iactabant, & interim malè viuebant. His dictum illud opponitur: si habuero omnem fidem, id est, si diuictavero fidem, quin & illam miraculis confirmaverò, Charitatem autem non habeam, certissimum indicium est non ad esse veram fidem, non quòd charitatis informet fidem & eam ad justificandam aptam reddat, quemadmodum vult Bellarminus, sed quia charitatis absentia oftendit itidem absentiam veræ & saluificæ fidei, quippe quæ semper per charitate est efficax: Etiam si ergo habeam omnem fidem, videlicet quæ seiuncta est aut esse potest à charitate, qualis est 1. fides historica. 2. hy pocritica, aut 3. miraculorum, non tamen sum justus coram Deo, aut electus. Si enim charitas absit, nihil sumus, quia est indicium, quòd non adsit vera fides. Non autem sequitur, Charitas adesse debet, Ergò etiam justificat. Nam adesse debet, non ut causa, sed ut fructus & effectus. Aliud est causa iustificationis, aliud consequens necessarium. Sicut aliud est causa vitæ, aliud effectus consequens vitam, Vt motus qui in homine vel viuente quouis necessariò inest, non vt causa vitæ, sed vt effectus sequens.

XIV. Ex 1. Cor. 13. ver. ult Vbi charitas vocatur virtus maxima, sic argumentantur: Maxima virmaximè justificat. Argumentum hoc Stapletonus in Antidotis vocat bonum & inuictum. Sed respondeo 1. Vtramque præmissarum esse legalem, justificatio autem non ex lege est, sed Evangelio Rom. 3. v. 21. Quare conclusio ista legalis nihil officit nostræ sententiæ. Fatemur enim, si quis perfectè Deum & proximum diligat, hoc est vniversam legem integrè servet, eum iustificari. Hæc autem perfectio in nullum cadit hominem, quare ex eâ dilectione iustificari nemo potest. 2. Maior falsa est, quia nec maxima nec minima, nec intermedia virtus, vt virtus, justificat, sed eâ tantum, quæ relatione quadam Christum eiusque sacrosanctum meritum intuetur & amplectitur, qualis est sola fides Rom. 3. & 4. Gal 2. & 3. non charitas, quippe quæ justificationem sequitur, sicuti Christus testatur Luc 7. versu 47. vbi affirmat, eum, cui multa peccata remissa sunt, multa diligere. Et Bellarminus concedit lib. 2. de iustificat. c. 15. quod Augustinus plurimis in locis doceat, opera iustifiesse effectus iustificationis. Vnde concludimus aduers Stapletonum, opera bona seu iusta non iustificare formaliter, sed effecta esse iustificationis: Contra Bellarminum, Charitatem non iustificare dispositiuè, quia dispositio præcedit, charitas verò, vt & virtutes, atque opera bona alia sequuntur iustificationem. Excipit Stapletonus, se loqui de habitu, non actu dilectionis: Cui respondeo, Pauli locum, qui probationis ergò adducitur, loqui de dilectione, tanquam opere, vt ex integro contextu patet. 3. Dilectio, vocatur maxima, non ἁπλῶς κατὰ τί. Loquitur Apostolus de donis in Ecclesia Corinthiorum vsitatis, inter quæ omnia dilectio eminet. 1. Quoad latitudinem, quia illa non solùm diligenti, sed etiam proximo diligentis prodest, & ad illum extenditur. 2. Quo ad durationem: Reliqua tandem abolebuntur & cessabunt, dilectio autem perpetuo mansura est. Nam & fides abolebitur, quatenus ea definitur Sperandarum rerum ὑπόστασις & inuisibilium ἔλεγχος. In vitâ enim æterna non amplius erunt res sperandæ & bona inuisibilia. Et hactenus duntaxat charitas maior est, absolutè autem esse maximam, adeoque ipsâ fide simpliciter maiorem, falsissimum est. Nam fides & basis & mater & fundamentum dicitur omnium virtutum reliquarum, fatente Concilio Tridentino & Bellarmino. Causa autē suo effectu semper nobilior est. Addo hunc præterea Syllogismum. Quicquid apprehendit Christum, & nobis applicat iustitiam & vincit mundum, adeoque omnia potest & est fundamentum & radix omnium virtutum Christianarum, sine qua fieri non potest, vt quisquam placeat Deo, & æternam vitam consequatur; illud sine dubitatione longè maximum est & præstantissimum. Atqui fides apprehendit Christum Iohan 1. ver. 12. & nobis applicat iustitiam Rom. 3. 4. Gal. 2. 3. & vincit mundum, 1. Iohan 5. ver. 4. adeoque omnia potest, Marc. 9. versu 23. Estque fundamentum & radix omnium virtutum Christianarum stianarum etiam Charitatis Ebr. 11: versu 1, Gal. 5, versu 6. & sine eâ fieri non potest, vt quisquam placeat DEO, Hebr. 11. versu 6. & æternam vitam consequatur Iohan. 3. versu 11. Marc 16. versu 16, Ergò fides sine omni dubitatione virtus maxima, & præstantissima. Vociferatur Stapletonus, hoc pacto Paulum argui mendacij, quippe qui dilectionem maiorem esse fide pronunciat. Sed committit elenchum à dicto secundum quid, ad dictum simpliciter. Res enim tota sic habet: Nam Dilectio est virtus maxima propter ædificationem Ecclesiæ, & vtilitatem proximi, & perpetuam durationem. Fides est maxima Propter Christum, quem in Evangelij promissione fidelis homo apprehendit, & in quo, & per quem accipit iustitiam, & salutem æternam! Dilectio præstantiam habet maximam, sed tamen eam à fide accipit. Dilectio est maxima respectu proximi, cui inseruit & quem ædificat: Fides est maxima respectu eius quem apprehendit. Et sic ista non sunt opposita, sed simul queunt consistere. Quærimus autem ex Pontificijs: Si charitas absolutè est maxima & maximè iustificat, qui fit, vt in Evangelicis concionibus semper requiratur fides, plerumque sine aliquâ mentione charitatis? Hæc enim summa est Evangelij: Credite in Christum, vel qui credit in Christum, salvus erit. Et Paulus ex professo pertractans integram doctrinam justificationis, solius fidei meminit, & non tantùm charitatem non nominat inter causas iustificationis, sed etiam disertè excludit omnia opera legis. Vbi nihil proficiunt Pontificij, negando charitatem esse opus legis. Annon enim totius legis summa est, Dilige DEVM & proximum, Math. 22, v. 37. Rom. 13. versu. 9.

XV. Ad Proverb. 10. v. 12. Respondemus, verba juxta fontes ita sonare: Odium excitat contentiones, omnes verò defectiones obtegit charitas. Vnde manifestum evadit, hic de justificatione non agi, sed potius charitatis officium, & indolem describi, quòd videlicet proximi vitia nouerit, sed non oderit, non reuelet, sed obtegat & dissimulet, iuxta præceptum Domini Leuitici 19. vers. 7. Apparet hœc ex præcedentibus verbis, Odium excitat contentiones, hoc est, cùm proximus proximum odit, tum alter alteri sua delicta exprobrat, vnde oriuntur contentiones: Sed qui alterum diligit, ille pallio charitatis defectiones & errata ἀδελφότητα contegit ac dissimulat. Opertio igitur delictorum duplex? VNA quæ fit coram DEO, de hac in præsenti non est sermo: ALTERA, quæ fit coram homine, & tegit non peccata propria, sed proximi, & de hac præsens textus tantùmmodò loquitur.

XVI. Ad 1. Iohan. 4. versu 16. respondemus quòd docetur ibi, non quomodo DEO inseramur & iustificemur, sed quales sint iustificati, seu quomodo nos iustificatos & DEO insitos esse cognoscatur, Conditio personæ, non causa iustitiæ innuitur: Nam charitas fraterna argumentum & indicium est, nos esse in DEO, & DEVM in nobis iuxta illud Iohan. 15. versu 5. Qui manet in me, & ego in illo, fert fructum multum. Dilectionem enim sinceram habere, & fidei opera edere nemo potest, nisi sit in ipso, ipsumque in se manentem habeat, Iohan 15. versu 15. Iohan. 6 versu. 56. Qui odit carnem meam, in me manet & ego in illo. Eadem responsio danda est ad illud Iohan. 14. 1. Iohan. 4. Rom. 13.

XVII. Ad Coloss. 3. versu 14. charitas dicitur vinculum perfectionis, quia nexu charitatis Christiani simul omnes in vnum quoddam integrum perfectumque corpus ceu vinculo quodam colligantur; quo vinculo rupto, excitatis dissensionibus, corpus illud non manet integrum, sed fit hiulcum, lacerum, mutilum atque mancum. Duplex igitur perfectio; Vna Ecclesiastica seu publica, quæ consistit in verâ concordiâ & mutuâ mutuâ societate, cuius vinculum est charitas. Altera purè Theologica seu priuata, quæ consistit in iustitiâ verâ, quam non nisi fide obtinemus.


### Fourth class. Containing sayings to which justification is attributed for repentance, contrition, and confession

Fourth class. Containing sayings to which justification is attributed for repentance, contrition, and confession.

XVIII. These are brought forward by Bellarmine. Acts 11, verse 18: Therefore God has granted repentance unto life even to the Gentiles. 2 Corinthians 7, verse 10: For godly sorrow works repentance unto salvation not to be repented of. Ezekiel 18, verse 27: When the wicked man turns away from his wickedness, he shall save his soul alive. To these could be added those from Matthew 5, verse 3: Blessed are the poor in spirit, blessed are they that mourn. 1 John 1, verse 9: If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins. Matthew 10, verse 32: Whoever shall confess me before men, I will confess him before my Father. Romans 10, verse 10: With the mouth confession is made unto salvation. Leviticus 5, verse 5: Let him repent for his sin. 2 Chronicles 7, verse 14: If my people shall turn, and pray, etc. 1 Kings 21, verse 28: Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me? Ezekiel 33, verses 14, 19. When the wicked man has turned away from his wickedness, and has done judgment and justice, he shall live because of it; which is also said in Jeremiah 8, verse 7.

XIX. We answer 1. GENERALLY, repentance is proposed in the Scriptures as twofold: True and Hypocritical. Faith defines and circumscribes the true, the absence of faith the hypocritical. Wherefore, those things which are attributed to true repentance in the Scriptures are attributed not simply in respect of itself, but in respect of faith, as the principal part, in a certain sense. Add that, by a metonymy most customary in the Scriptures, that which belongs to the cause is attributed to the effect. Finally, temporal contrition and repentance can indeed avert or interrupt temporal punishment, but not eternal, because for this an infinite merit is required, such as is found in no man, but in the God-man Christ alone.

XX. 2. SPECIFICALLY, Regarding the passages, Acts 11, verse 18. Ezekiel 18, verse 27. Leviticus 5, verse 5. 2 Chronicles 7, verse 14. Ezekiel 33, verses 14, 19. Jeremiah 8, verse 7. Let the given response suffice, that reconciliation and justification are ascribed to repentance on account of faith. To 2 Corinthians 7, v. 10, we respond that it is not said that godly sorrow merits salvation, but that from it arises true repentance, which through faith, its principal part, works out salvation not to be repented of. And the passage speaks of that order which God has established, namely that no one is converted unless he has first conceived sorrow for sins; but these are not meritorious. They have the nature of a means, not of a merit, and that sorrow is said to produce true repentance insofar as it is the first way to conversion. Matthew 5, verse 3. Mourning is established as a sign, not a cause, of blessedness. 1. 1 John 1, verse 9, confession is introduced, not as the total cause of pardon, but only as a necessary condition, without which remission does not occur in adults. Or it must be said that by confession is understood the whole of a man's repentance. To Matthew 10, verse 32, we respond that the confession of God is not the cause of salvation, but either a sign or some kind of condition, without which salvation comes to no one. For he who denies Him will be denied by Him, where denial is indeed the cause of perdition, but confession is not the cause of salvation, because the reason for good and evil works is different here. To Romans 10, verse 10, confession unto salvation is the same as confession of salvation, whence this sense emerges, that faith does not lie hidden in the heart alone, but also breaks forth outwardly and exerts itself by saving confession. Salvation, therefore, is attributed to confession as a condition without which it does not happen. But how will Bellarmine prove from this that confession justifies dispositively, when the

Classis quarta. Continens dicta, quibus pœnitentiæ, contritioni & confessioni iustificatio attribuitur.

XIIX. Proferuntur hæc à Bellarmino. Actor, 11. vers. 18. Ergo & gentibus pœnitentiam dedit DEVS ad vitam. 2. Corinth. 7. vers. 10. Quæ secundum DEVM tristitia est, pœnitentiam in salutem stabilem operatur. Ezech. 18. vers. 27. Cùm auerterit se impius ab impietate sua, ipse animam suam viuificabit. His addi possent illa Matth. 5. v. 3. Beati pauperes spiritu, beati qui lugent. 1. Iohan. 1: v. 9. Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est & iustus, vt remittat nobis peccata nostra. Matth. 10. v 32. Qui me cõfessus fuerit corã hominibus, confitebor illum coram Patre meo. Roman. 10. vers 10. Ore fit confessio ad salutem. Leuit. 5. v. 5. Agat pœnitentiam pro peccato. 2. Paral. 7. v. 14. Si conuersus populus meus, deprecatus fuerit, &c. 1. Reg. 21. v. 28. Nunquid vidisti, quòd humilis sit factus Achab coram me? Ezech. 33. v. 14. 19. Cùm auersus fuerit impius ab impietate sua, & fecerit iudicium & iustitiam, propter ipsam viuet; Quòd etiam dicitur Ierem. 8. v. 7.

XIX. Respondemus 1. GENERALITER, Pœnitentia in Scripturis duplex proponitur: Vera & Hypocritica. Veram definit ac circumscribit fides, Hypocriticam fidei absentia. Quocirca, quæ veræ pœnitentiæ tribuuntur in Scripturis, ea non respectu sui simpliciter, sed respectu fidei, tanquam partis principalis, secũdum quid attribuuntur. Adde, quòd per Metonymiam Scripturis vsitatissimam effectui tribuitur, quod causæ est. Denique temporalis contritio & pœnitentia, temporalem quidem pœnam potest auertere, vel interuertere, non autem æternam, quia ad hoc infinitum requiritur meritum, quale in nullo inuenitur homine, sed in solo θεανθρώπῳ Christo.

XX. 2. SPECIALITER, Ad dicta, Actor. 11. vers. 18. Ezechiel. 18. versu 27. Leuit. 5. versu 5. 2. Paral. 7. versu 14. Ezech. 33. versu 14. 19. Ierem. 8. vers 7. Sufficiat data responsio, quod poenitentiæ propter fidem adscribatur reconciliatio & iustificatio. Ad 2. Corinth. 7. v. 10. respondemus, non dici, quod κατὰ τὸν θεὸν λύπη mereatur vel salutem, sed quod ex illâ oriatur vera pœnitentia, quæ per fidem, partem eius principalem σωτηρίαν ἀμεταμέλητον κατεργάζεται. Et loquitur dictum de illo ordine, quem Deus sanciuit, quòd videlicet nemo conuertatur, nisi qui prius concepit dolorem de peccatis; sed hæc non sunt meritoria. Habent rationem medij non meriti, & dolor ille dicitur parere veram pœnitentiam, quatenus est via prima ad conuersionem. Matth. 5. versu 3. Luctus constituitur nota non causa beatitudinis. 1. Iohan. 1. versu 9. confessio, non tanquam totalis causa veniæ, sed duntaxat velut necessaria conditio, sine quâ non fit remissio in adultis, introducitur. Vel dicendum, quòd per Confessionem intelligatur tota hominis pœnitentia. Ad Matth. 10. versu 32. respondemus; quòd confessio Dei non sit causa salutis, sed vel nota, vel aliqualis conditio, sine qua nemini obuigit salus. Qui enim illum negauerit, negabitur ab illo, ubi abnegatio est quidem causa perditionis, sed non confessio est causa saluationis, quia dispar hîc est ratio operum bonorum & malorum. Ad Rom. 10. versu 10. Confessio ad salutem idem est, quod confessio salutis, vnde hic emergit sensus, quòd fides non in solo lateat corde, sed foras etiam prorumpat & confessione salutari se exerat. Salus ergo tribuitur confessioni, tanquam conditioni sine qua non. Quomodo autem probabit hinc Bellarminus, confessionem dispositiuè iustificare, cùm il-


### Classis quinta

latter follows faith and justification, according to the saying of David: I believed, therefore have I spoken. 1 Kings 21, verse 28. God willed to reward the temporal repentance of Ahab with some temporal benefit.

XXI. To this order can also be referred those sayings in which the remission of sins, and thus justification, is ascribed to our reconciliation with our neighbor, which precedes repentance, such as Luke 6, verse 37: Forgive and it shall be forgiven you; Matthew 6: If you forgive men, etc. But all these do not denote a cause, but only a certain condition necessarily preceding by Divine ordinance; they contain the removal of obstacles, not the promotion or causation of justification itself. For if those are absent, they can hinder; but if they are present, they do not cause; but they merely prepare the way, that is, they are conditions without which the effect does not follow. For if our remission, by which we pardon offenses to our neighbor, is the cause of the remission of sins before God, it will be either meritorious, or instrumental, or formal; it is not meritorious, because only the obedience of Christ reconciles us to God: nor is it instrumental; which is evident: nor is it formal, because it is a good work; but good works are not the form, but the effect of justification, as Bellarmine admits in book 2, chapters 15 and 16.

Fifth class. Containing sayings to which the proposition of receiving the Sacraments and the justification of a new life is ascribed:

XXII: John 3, verse 5: Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven. John 20, verse 23: Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them. Acts 2, verse 38: Repent, and let every one of you be baptized for the remission of sins. Ezekiel 18, verse 31: Cast away from you all your iniquities, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new Spirit? To this place also can be referred that passage in Tit. 3. v. 5. He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal.

XXIII. I respond. The desire of actually receiving the Sacrament, and at the same time the purpose of a new life and obedience, are excluded from justification, but not from the justified person. For one thing is the cause of justification, and another is the condition of the person. Neither are effects to be confounded with causes, nor causes with effects. But as for the Sacraments themselves, we do not exclude them from the forum of justification, but include them as προσφορητικα organs offering grace to us, without which also no one is justified: But what kind of consequence is this, Sacraments are necessary for justification, in so far as they are means: Therefore good works justify? Nor is the exclusive particle, when we are said to be justified by faith alone, to be opposed to the Sacraments, or to the grace of God, or to the merit of Christ, but rather to our works, as the Apostle clearly hints.

Latin:

la sequatur fidem & iustificationem, iuxta dictum Dauidis: Credidi, propter quod locutus sum. 3. Regum 21. versu 28. temporalem pœnitentiam Achabi. voluit Deus temporali aliquo beneficio remunerare.

XXI. Ad hunc ordinem referri etiam possunt illa dicta, in quibus nostræ cum proximo reconciliationi, quæ pœnitentiam antecedit, remissio peccatorum & sic iustificatio adscribitur, qualia sunt Luc. 6. vers. 37. Remittite & Remittetur vobis; Matth. 6. Si remiseritis hominibus &c. Sed hæc omnia non notant causam, sed tātum conditionē quandā ex ordinatione Diuina necessariò pręcedētem; Continent remotionem obstaculorum, non promotionem aut causationem ipsius iustificationis. Illa n. si absunt, impedire possūt; sed si adsunt, non causant; sed duntaxat viā parant, id est, sunt conditiones, sine quib. nō sequitur effectus. Si enim: nostra remissio, quâ proximo condonamus offensas, est causa remissionis peccatorum apud Deum, aut erit meritoria, aut instrumentalis, aut formalis; Meritoria non est, quia solius Christi obedientia Deo nos reconciliat: Nec est instrumentalis; quod patet: Nec est formalis, quia est opus bonum; opera autem bona non sunt forma, sed effectus iustificationis, fatente Bellarmino lib. 2. c. 15. & 16.

Classis quinta. Continens dicta; quibus propositio percipiendi Sacramenta & nouæ vitæ iustificatio adscribitur:

XXII: Iohan. 3. v, 5. Nisi quis renatus fuerit ex aqua & Spiritu; non poterit introire in regnum cælorum. Ioh. 20. v. 23. Quorum remiseritis peccata remittuntur eis, Actor. 2. & 38. Pœnitentiam agite, & vnusquisque vestrum baptizetur in remissionem peccatorum Ezech. 18. v. 31; Projicite à vobis omnes iniquitates vestras, & facite dabis cor nouum & Spiritum nouum? Huc etiam referri potest illud Tit. 3. v. 5. Saluos nos fecit per lauacrum regenerationis & renouationis.

XXIII. Respond. Desiderium reipsa percipiendi Sacramentum, simulque propositum nouae vitae & obedientiae a iustificatione excluduntur, non autem a iustificato. Aliud enim est causa iustificationis, & aliud conditio personae. Nec effectus cum causis, nec causae cum effectis confundendae sunt. Quod vero ipsa attinet Sacramenta, ea non excludimus a foro iustificationis, sed includimus, tanquam organa προσφορητικα offerentia nobis gratiam, sine quibus etiam nemo iustificatur: Quae vero consequentia est, Sacramenta sunt ad iustificationem necessaria, in quantum sunt media: Ergo bona opera iustificant? Neque particula exclusiua, cum sola fide iustificari dicimur, opponenda est Sacramentis, vel gratiae Dei, vel merito Christi, sed potius nostris operibus, vt Apostolus luculenter innuit.


### Classis quinta: Sixth class. Containing passages by which we are said to be justified by works

Sixth class. Containing passages by which we are said to be justified by works.

To prove this they produce chapter 2 of the epistle of James, who in v. 14 says, What will it profit, my brothers, if someone says he has faith, but does not have works? Can faith save him? verse 24. You see that a man is justified by works, ouk ek pisteos monon etc. See that by good works you make your calling firm 2. Petr. 1. v. 10.

XXIV. I respond. 1. The proper place for the doctrine concerning the justification of man is the epistle to the Romans and Galatians. From there, therefore, the method of justifying ought to be sought, and other passages are to be explained according to that one. For it is a saying of Tertullian: It is necessary that the fewer be understood according to the more, and that one statement may not overturn others, it should be accepted according to all rather than against all.

will be the action; 2. A double homonymy is to be noted, namely in the word faith and in the word justification. Both are taken in a different sense by blessed Paul and by James. To Paul, faith is true confidence; to James, it is either mere knowledge of the articles and profession of the Christian faith, or a hypocritical boasting of justifying faith, as is evident from verse 14. To Paul, justification is the same as being absolved from sins. To James, it is the same as being declared righteous, as is evident from verses 18 and 21. Show me your faith: For then also something is said to be done, Matt. 12, verse 37. By your words you will be justified. Add Rom. 3, verses 4 and 20. 1 Tim. 1, verse 6. The sense of James, therefore, is not so obscure or intricate. He says that faith without works is dead, that is. to be understood as such: that faith is perfected by works, that is, it is declared to be perfect, living, true, and sincere, just as the goodness of a tree is understood to be perfect when it brings forth good fruit in great abundance: that Abraham was justified by works, namely declaratively: that a man is justified by works and not by faith only, that is, that an external profession of faith is not enough to indicate true justification; but that truly Christian works are required. For from these alone can a most conspicuous and manifest judgment be made concerning justification. The sum, therefore, of the Jacobean proposition is that we do not obtain salvation by a bare knowledge of God, nor is that true faith which is without works, nor are we justified before God by such faith. He proves this 1. from a likeness, v. 15, 16, 17. For he does not have true faith who does not assist a needy brother. 2. Because that external profession of faith is often found in the impious and unmerciful, v. 15, 16. 3. Because faith, if it does not have works, is dead by itself, ver. 17, that is, it is argued to be dead, v. 26. For a cause perishes when the effect is lacking. 4. Because faith is shown by works, v. 18, and is perfected, that is, it is declared perfect, v. 22. For men cannot look into hearts (which belongs to God alone, 1 Kings 8, v. 30) but judge of faith from works. 5. Because the devils also believe and shudder, v. 9. for Satan has often professed that Christ is the Son of God, Matt. 8. v. 29. Mark 1. v. 24. & c. 3. v. 11. & c. 5. v. 7. Luke 4. v. 34. & c. 4. v. 41. Luke 8. v. 28. Acts 19. v. 15. Costerus indeed in his Enchiridion and others deny that the devil has faith. Bellarmine however in book 5, v. 15, affirms it, and proves it by the testimony of Augustine. 6. Because Abraham was justified, that is, declared righteous, by works, verse 21, which is shown by the testimony of Scripture Gen. 22. v. 12. & 15. v. 6. And finally the Apostle concludes thus v. 24. You see therefore that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only; as if he were to say, if you wish to be held for a truly Christian and righteous man, do not merely profess with an external voice that you have been baptized and that you believe in Christ; (for that can be common even to the wicked,) but it is necessary that you show, exert, declare, make manifest, and prove this faith of yours by good works, as by certain effects. For just as breathing and motion (which two things are understood by πνεῦμα) are the most certain sign of bodily life, so that without these the body is dead v. 26, that is, it is evident that in their absence life is absent, so good works are the signs of true faith, and therefore without them faith is dead, that is, it is discovered to be false and feigned. 7. The example of Rahab is also brought forward, who also herself by her works showed and proved that she had a faith far different from a dead one: and therefore she was justified by a true and living faith, whence Heb. 11. v. 31 it is said: By faith Rahab received the spies. That this is the genuine meaning of James is easily demonstrated from the primary scope of the whole epistle, from the entire context, from the phraseology itself, from the application of the individual arguments, from the cited testimonies of Scripture concerning Abraham and Rahab, from the brought-forward examples, similitudes, and the analogy of faith. Moreover, one may add a certain testimony of Bellarmine, who in book 2 de Iustif. c. 16. where he responds to the statement of 1 John 3, 'he who does righteousness is righteous,' he writes thus: This testimony does not teach what makes a man formally righteous, but from where it may be known whether someone is righteous. For he is righteous who does righteousness, just as he is living who moves, and that tree is good which produces good fruits; nor does someone live because he moves, but on the contrary, he moves because he lives; and he produces fruits because he is a good tree. Thus, therefore, he who does righteousness is righteous, but he is not righteous because he does righteousness, but he does righteousness because he is righteous. I apply this opinion to the present passage of James, and I willingly concede that good works justify, that is, as an effect, they show a man to be justified, just as movement proves life, and fruits prove the tree.

XXV. Furthermore, the contradictions of the Papists ought to be noted. For most of them strive to confirm their opinion concerning justification from this. Bellarmine argues to the contrary in book 2, chapter 16, that this passage is not to be understood concerning the form of justification, because he establishes in chapter 15 that the righteousness by which we are formally justified is habitual, not actual, and he brings forward there a triple response concerning the word 'to justify.' 1. To be justified is to merit an increase of righteousness. 2. To devote effort so that you may be justified. 3. In divine judgment, to be judged righteous, and to justly obtain the crown of righteousness. In book 4 of justification, chapter 18, he explains this text concerning secondary, not primary, justification, which opinion other Papists also accept, who therefore contradict those who prove from James the primary justification of works.

XXVI. But the Jesuit sweats vehemently in book 4, chapter 18, to reconcile the passage of Genesis 15, verse 6, 'Abraham believed God,' and Paul in Romans 4, verse 3, Galatians 3, verse 6, and James chapter 2, verse 23. But his interpretation is so twisted and forced that it is immediately rendered suspect to anyone reading it. They commonly say that Paul speaks of the first, James of the second justification. Now primary justification is for them the infusion of charity, formally justifying before God: Secondary is the performance of works justifying before God meritoriously, the former habitual and formal; the latter actual and material: the former gratuitous; the latter they call meritorious. But this fiction, I. Is new, and is required neither in the Scriptures nor among the Fathers. Indeed, not even in Lombard, who in book 3, distinction 19, brings forward four meanings, but makes no mention of this distinction. Nor will it be easily found in Thomas or Scotus. It was therefore devised to corrupt the Scriptures. II. It is false, 1. because there is one justification just as there is one God, Rom. 3, v. 30. 2. Either the first is perfect or it is not; if perfect, then the second is useless and unnecessary. If imperfect, how will it stand in the judgment of God? 3. They confuse renewal with justification, the effect with the cause. 4. To works that are due and imperfect they assign merit. 5. Faith in the Scriptures is not said to dispose toward justification, but to justify and to be imputed for righteousness. 6. God justifies the ungodly, therefore no dispositions precede in them. 7. Scripture defines justification not by infusion, but by the remission of sins. III. It is impious 1. because it pretends that the first justification is empty and null without the second, and leaves to faith nothing but the beginning of a dispositive righteousness. 2. Because it pretends that that which reconciles man is a habit in man, which is blasphemy against the death of the Son of God, by which alone we are said to be reconciled to God, Romans 5, v. 10. 3. Because it pretends that the second justification is meritorious by condignity.

XXVII. The false reconciliation being therefore removed, we establish that Moses speaks of true justifying faith, and of the justification of faith, and that it is cited by Paul in the very same sense, Rom. 4, v. 3, Gal. 3, v. 8. James, however, to confirm his own opinion, cites not simply the very words of Moses, but the fulfillment of them, arguing a posteriori; The scripture was fulfilled, he says v. 23. Abraham believed God, &c. as if he were to say, when Abraham was about to offer Isaac by the command of God Gen. 22. then from that most illustrious work it was most manifestly evident that it was true what Moses had said in chap. 15. v. 6: Abraham believed God and it was reckoned to him for righteousness. And thus also the Angel of Jehovah speaks in chap. 22. verse 12. Now I have known that you are fearing God. For it is evident from the history of Moses, and the Pauline disputation in Rom. 4. that Abraham had been justified by faith before he offered Isaac. Wherefore it is absurd to conclude thus: Abraham was justified, that is, declared himself to be righteous, by works, when he had offered Isaac his son. Therefore works justify, that is, make men righteous. For not even the Papists themselves will deny that Abraham was justified by faith in Gen. 15. and therefore at that time, when he was called by faith he obeyed God, so that he might go out into the place which he was about to receive for an inheritance, Heb. 11. verse 8. Gen. 12. verse 4. But the history of the immolation of Isaac followed long after the calling of Abraham. How can it be that he was finally justified before God by that work, that is, reputed righteous? Unless you invert the order of nature and the series of the sacred history itself, and call the cause posterior to the effect, you cannot answer otherwise than that the word justifying in James is accepted for the declaration, showing, and manifestation of righteousness. But as regards those expressions, when James says that faith cooperates with works and is perfected by works, we answer that they do not denote the formal perfection of faith, which consists entirely in the apprehension of Christ the Redeemer; but that they refer only to declaration and manifestation, as if he were to say, that the cause is perfected by the effect, in so far as it is argued and shown through it. Otherwise no learned man will deny, whatever perfection there is in the effect, that the whole of it is from causes. Faith, however, is the cause of good works, even by the admission of the Papists. Wherefore, when it is said to cooperate with works, it is to be understood only by way of declaration. For just as works alone, although specious, do not prove one a Christian (for even the Gentiles are often adorned with notable mighty works and deeds), nor does the mere profession of faith (which is not rarely found in the wicked and perverse) indicate Christianity without good works: So if anyone professes in words that he is a Christian and confirms that profession with works worthy of a Christian, of this person James pronounces that faith cooperates with works, in that effect of declaration,

XXIIX. To 2 Pet. 1. v. 10. Study, brothers, to make your calling firm through good works. We answer 1, That in the Greek copies διὰ τῶν ἔργων is not read. 2. We ourselves concede that this is a fruit of good works, that they confirm us concerning our calling and election, namely as regards knowledge a posteriori, just as Christ says: The tree is known by its fruits. But it is another thing to speak of the foundation and cause of calling and election. Peter therefore urges that we should study good works, for thus we shall be confirmed more and more, because through this the children of God and the children of the Devil are manifest, that whoever does not practice righteousness is not of God, 1 John 3. verse 10.

XXIX. These sayings could also be referred to this order: Lev. 18. v. 5. He who does my laws shall live in them, Deut. 6. It shall be righteousness for us, if we have done them. Matt. 19. v. 17. If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments. Luke 10. v. 15. Do this and you shall live: But we answer 1. That these sayings are legal, and preach concerning perfect obedience which is impossible for us, as is taught in Rom. 8. v. 3. Gal. 3. v. 11. 12. 13. 2. The laws, judgments, and commandments of God can be taken generally for the word of God or doctrine divinely revealed, to which even the Gospel

Latin:

Classis sexta. Continens dicta, quibus ex operibus iustificari dicimur.

Ad hoc probandum producunt e. 2. epist. Iacobi, qui v. 14. dicit, Quid proderit, fratres mei, si fidem quis dicat se habere, opera autem non habeat? Nunquid poterit fides saluare eum? vers. 24. Videtis quoniam ex operibus iustificatur homo, ouk ek pisteos monon &c. Videte ut per bona opera firmam faciatis vocationem vestram 2. Petr. 1. v. 10.

XXIV. Respond. 1. Proprius locus doctrinae de iustificatione hominis, est epistola ad Romanos & Galatas, Inde igitur peti debet ratio iustificandi, & alia loca secundum istam sunt explicanda, Tertulliani enim dictum est: Oportet secundum plura intelligi pauciora, & ne vnus sermo alia euertat, secundum omnia potius, quam aduersus omnia accipien-

ctio erit; 2. Duplex notanda est Homonymia, nempe in vocabulo fides & in vocabulò iustificationis, Vtrumque alio sensu à B. Paulo, & à Iacobo accipitur. Paulo fides est vera fiducia: Iacobo vel sola notitia articulorum, & professio fidei Christianæ, vel hypocritica fidei iustificantis iactantia, vt patet ex vers. 14. Paulo iustificatio idem est, quod à peccatis absolui. Iacobo idem est, quod iustum declarari, vt patet ex versu 18. & 21. Ostende mihi fidem tuam: Nam & tunc aliquid fieri dicitur, Matth. 12. vers. 37. Ex sermonibus tuis iustificaberis. Adde Rom. 3. vers. 4. & 20. 1. Tim. 1. versu 6. Sensus igitur Iacobi non est adeò obscurus vel intricatus. Dicit; fidem sine operibus esse mortuam, hoc est. Talem intelligi: fidem ex operibus perfici, h. e. perfectam, viuam veram & sinceram esse declarari, sicut arboris bonitas tunc perfecta esse intelligitur cum fructus bonos magnâ copiâ profert: Abrahamum ex operibus iustificatum esse, videlicet declaratiuè: Hominem iustificari ex operibus & non ex fide tantùm, h. e. Non satis esse ad indicadam veram iustificationem, externam fidei professionem; sed requiri opera verè Christiana. Ex his enim solis maximè conspicuum & manifestum potest fieri iudicium de iustificatione. Summa igitur propositionis Iacobææ est, Nos nuda Dei notitia salutem non consequi, neque veram fidem esse, quæ sit absque operibus, neque nos tali fide coram Deo iustificari. Hoc probat 1. à simili v. 15. 16. 17. Non enim illum habere veram fidem, qui fratri indigenti non subuenit. 2. Quia illa externa fidei professio sæpè reperitur in impijs & immisericordibus v. 15. 16 3. Quia fides, si opera non habeat, mortua sit per se, ver. 17. id est mortua esse arguitur, v. 26. Nam causa, effectu deficiente perit, 4. Quia ex operibus fides ostenditur v. 18. & perficitur, id est, perfecta declaratur v. 22. Homines enim nequeunt intueri corda (quod solius Dei est, 1. Reg. 8. v. 30.) sed exoperibus judicant de fide. 5. Quia Diaboli etiam credunt & cohorrescunt, v. 9. saepè enim professus est Satan Christum, esse Filium Dei, Matth. 8. v. 29. Marc. 1. v. 24. & c. 3. v. 11. & c. 5. v. 7. Luc. 4. v. 34. & 4. c. 14. Luc. 8. v. 28 Actor. 19. v. 15. Costerus quidem in Enchirid. & alii negant, Diabolum habere fidem. Bellarminus autem lib. 5. v. 15. affirmat, & Augustini testimonio probat. 6. Quia Abraham justificatus sid est, justus declaratus est ex operibus, versu. 21. id quod ostenditur ex Scripturae testimonio Gen: 22. v. 12. & 15. v. 6. Et tandem ita concludit Apostolus v. 24. Videtis igitur quòd ex operibus justificetur homo, & non ex fide tantum; quasi dicat, si velis haberi pro homine verè Christiano & justo, non tantùm externâ voce profitearis te baptizatum esse, & in Christum credere; (id enim impiis etiam commune esse potest,) sed opus est, ut hanc fidem tuam ostendas, exeras, declares, manifestam facias & probes bonis operibus, tanquam certis effectis. Vt enint spiratio & motus (quae duo per πνεῦμα intelliguntur) certissimum signum sunt vitae corporalis, adeò ut sine his corpus sit mortuum v. 26. hoc est, illis absentibus vitam abesse constet, sic bona opera sunt signa verae fidei, adeoque sine illis fides est mortua, id est, falsa & ficta esse deprehenditur. 7. Adducitur etiam exemplum Rachab, quae & ipsa operibus suis ostendit & probavit se longè aliam fidem habuisse, quàm mortuam: ideoque verâ & vivâ fide iustificata est, Vnde Hebr. 11. v. 31 dicitur: Per fidem suscepit Rachab exploratores. Hanc genuinam esse Iacobi sententiam, facilè demonstratur ex primario totius epistolae scopo, ex integro comtextu, ex ipsa phrasi, ex applicatione singulorum argumentorum, ex citatis de Abrahame & Rachab Scripturae testimoniis, ex allatis exemplis, similitudinibus, & analogia fidei. Potest insuper addi testimonium quoddam Bellarmini, qui lib. 2. de Iustif. c. 16. vbi respondet ad dictum 1. Iohan. 3. qui facit iustitiam iustus est, ita scribit: Hoc testimonium non docet, quid faciat hominem formaliter iustum, sed vnde possit cognosci, an aliquis sit iustus. Ille enim iustus est, qui iustitiam facit, sicut ille viuens est, qui mouetur & illa arbor bona, quæ fructus facit bonos, nec ideò viuit aliquis, quia mouetur, sed contrà, ideò mouetur, quia viuit; & ideò facit fructus, quia est arbor bona, Sic igitur qui facit iustitiam iustus est, sed non ideò iustus, quia facit iustitiam, sed ideò iustitiam facit, quia iustus est. Hanc sententiam applico ad præsentem Iacobi locum, & lubenter concedo, bona opera iustificare, hoc est, tanquam effectum ostendere hominem esse iustificatum, sicut motus arguit vitam, & fructus arborem.

XXV. Notari porrò debent contradictiones Pontificiorum. Plerique enim hinc confirmare satagunt suam de iustificatione sententiam. Contrà disputat Bellarminus lib. 2. ca. 16. hunc locum non esse intelligendum de formâ iustificationis, quia statuit cap. 15. iustitiam, quâ formaliter iustificamur, habitualem esse non actualem, & affert ibi triplicem responsionem de verbo iustificandi. 1. Iustificari est mereri augmentum iustitiæ. 2. Dare operam vt iustificeris. 3. In diuino iudicio, iustum iudicari, & iustitiæ coronam iustè consequi. Lib. 4. de iustif. cap. 18. exponit hunc textum de iustificatione secundâ non primâ, quam etiam sententiam alii acceptant Pontificij, qui propterea contradicunt ijs, qui ex Iacobo primam operum iustificationem probant.

XXVI. Vehementer autem sudat Iesuwi ta lib. 4. capite 18. vt conciliet locum Genes. 15. vers. 6. Credidit Abraham Deo, & Paulum Roman. 4. vers. 3. Gal. 3. v. 6. & Iacobum cap 2. v. 23. Sed eius interpretatio tam est contorta & coacta vt cuiuis legenti statim suspecta reddatur. Vulgò dicunt, Paulum loqui de prima, Iacobum de secundâ iustificatione. Est autem iustificatio prima ipsis infusio charitatis, formaliter iustificantis coram Deo: Secunda est praestatio operum iustificantium coram Deo meritoriè, Illam habitualem & formalem; Hanc actualem materialem: Illam gratuitam; Hanc vocant meritoriam.
