Verùm hoc commentum, I. Novum est, nec in Scripturis nec apud Patres requiritur. Imò nec apud Lombardum qui lib. 3. distinct. 19. significata quatuor affert, sed huius distinctionis mentionem non facit. Neque apud Thomam nec Scotum facilè reperietur. Excogitata igitur est ad deprauandas Scripturas. II. Falsum, 1. quia vna est iustificatio sicut vnus Deus Rom. 3. v. 30. 2. Vel prima perfecta est vel non, si perfecta, ergo secunda inutilis, nec neceffaria. Si imperfecta, quomodo consistet in iudicio Dei. 3. Confundunt renovationem cum iustificatione, effectum cum causâ. 4. Operibus debitis & imperfectis meritum assignant. 5. Fides in Scripturis non dicitur disponere ad iustificationem, sed iustificare & ad iustitiam imputari. 6. Deus iustificat impios, Ergò in ijs nullæ præcedunt dispositiones. 7. Scriptura iustificationem non infusione, sed remissione peccatorum definit. III. Impium 1. quia primam iustificationem fingit inanem & nullam absque secundâ, & fidei nil nisi initium iustitiæ dispositiuum relinquit. 2. Quia fingit id, quod hominem reconciliat, esse habitum in homine, quæ est blasphemia in mortem Filij Dei, quâ solâ dicimur reconciliari Deo, Roman. 5. v. 10. 3. Quia secundam iustificationem fingit meritoriam ex condigno.

XXVII. Remotâ igitur falsâ conciliatione, ita statuimus, quòd Moses loquitur de verâ fide iustificante, & de fidei iustificatione, eodemque planè sensu à Paulo allegetur Rom. 4. v. 3. Gal. 3. v. 8. Iacobus autem pro suâ sententiâ confirmandâ citat non simpliciter ipsa verba Mosis, sed complementum istorum, arguens à posteriori; Impleta est scriptura, inquit v. 23. Credidit Abraham Deo, &c. quasi dicat, cùm Isaacum esset Abraham oblaturus ex Dei mandato Genes. 22. tum ex illo tam præclaro opere patuit manifestissimè, verum esse quod cap. 15. v 6. dixerat Moses: Credidit Abraham Deo & imputatum est illi ad iustitiam, Atque sic etiam Angelus Iehovæ loquitur cap. 22. versu 12. Nunc cognovi, quod timens Deies. Nam constat ex historiâ Mosis, & disputatione Paulinâ Rom 4. iustificatum fuisse Abrahamum per fidem, antequam offerret Isaacum. Quare absurdum est ita concludere: Abraham iustificatus est, hoc est, iustum se esse declaravit, ex operibus, cùm obtulisset Isaacum filium suum. Ergo opera iustificant, hoc est, iustos efficiunt. Nam nec ipsi quidem Pontificij negabunt, Abrahamum fuisse per fidem iustificatum Genes. 15. adeóque tum, cùm per fidem vocatus auscultaret Deo, ut abiret in locum quem accepturus erat pro hæreditate, Ebr. 11. vers. 8. Genes. 12. vers. 4. Historia verò immolationis Isaaci longe pòst secuta est vocationem Abrahami. Quomodo fieri potest, ut illo opere demum fuerit coram Deo iustificatus, hoc est, iustus reputatus? Nisi naturæ ordinem, & seriem ipsius sacræ historiæ inuertas, & causam dicas effectu posteriorem, aliter non potes respondere, quàm iustificandi verbum apud Iacobum accipi pro declaratione, ostensione & manifestatione iustitiæ. Locutiones verò istas quod attinet, cùm Iacobus dicit, fidem cooperari operibus & ex operibus perfici, respondemus, Notare eas non perfectionem fidei formalem, quæ tota consistit in Christi Redemptoris apprehensione; sed referri tantùm ad declarationem & manifestationem, ac si dicat, ex effectu perfici causam, quatenus per illum arguitur & ostenditur. Alioquin nemo eruditus negabit, quicquid est perfectionis in effectu, id totum esse ex causis. Fides autem est bonorum operum causa, fatentibus etiam Pontificijs. Quare cùm cooperari dicitur operibus non nisi ratione declarationis, hoc intelligendum est. Vt enim sola opera, quanquam speciosa, sine fide non arguunt Christianum, (nam & Ethnici sæpè insignibus virtutibus & factis ornantur, ) nec sola fidei professio (quæ haut rarò reperitur in sceleratis & peruersis) sine bonis operibus Christianismum indicat: Ita si quis verbis profiteatur se Christianum & operibus Christiano dignis illam professionem confirmet, de hoc pronunciat Iacobus, fidem cooperari operibus, in illo effectu declarationis,

XXIIX. Ad 2. Pet. 1. v. 10. Studete fratres vocationem vestram firmam reddere per bona opera. Respondemus 1, In Græcis exemplaribus non legi διὰ τῶν ἔργων. 2. Ipsi concedimus, quòd hic sit fructus bonorum operum, vt nos confirment de vocatione & electione nostra, videlicet quoad cognitionem à posteriori, sicut Christus dicit: Ex fructibus agnoscitur arbor. Aliud verò est de fundamento & causa vocationis atque electionis loqui. Suadet igitur Petrus, vt bonis operibus studeamus, sic enim magis magisque confirmabimur, quia per hoc manifesti sunt filij Dei & filij Diaboli, quòd quisquis non exercet iustitiam, non est ex Deo, 1. Ioh. 3. vers. 10.

XXIX. Possent ad hunc ordinem ista etiam dicta referri Leuit. 18. v. 5. Faciens leges meas, viuet in eis, Deut. 6. Erit nobis iustitia, si fecerimus. Matth. 19. v. 17. Si vis vitam ingredi, serua mandata. Luc. 10. v. 15. Fac hoc & viues: Sed respondemus 1. Dicta ista esse legalia, & concionari de perfecta obedientia quæ nobis est impossibilis vt docetur Rom. 8. v. 3. Gal. 3. v. 11. 12. 13. 2. Leges, iudicia & mandata Dei, generatim accipi possunt, pro verbo Dei seu doctrina diuinitus patefacta, cui etiam Euangelium


### Classis septima. Containing the sayings by which our justification is attributed to mercy and beneficence

is included. Thus, therefore, righteousness is to do the commandments of God, that is, to do penance and to believe the Gospel, or to acknowledge that righteousness is not from the law of Moses, and to seek and find it in Christ alone, the unique Mediator.

Seventh class, containing sayings to which the justification of our mercy and beneficence is attributed.

XXX. These are the principal sayings: Psalm 41:1, Blessed is he who considers the needy and the poor; Psalm 112:5, Blessed is he who shows mercy and lends; Proverbs 16:5, By beneficence and faith iniquity is expiated; Isaiah 1:17, Learn to do good, judge the orphan, seek justice: If your sins have been as scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; Daniel 4:24, Redeem your sins with righteousness and alms, and there shall be a healing of your offenses; Tobit 4:11, Alms delivers from all sin and death; Ecclesiasticus 3:33, Water quenches a flaming fire, and alms expiates sin; Ecclesiasticus 16:15, Every mercy makes a place for each one according to the merit of his works; Matthew 5:7, Blessed are the merciful; Matthew 25:34, Come, you blessed of my Father, for I was hungry, etc.; Luke 11:41, Give alms, and behold, all things will be clean to you; Luke 16:9. Make for yourselves friends of unrighteous Mammon, so that when you fail, they may receive you. Acts 10:4, Your prayers and alms have ascended into the sight of God. 1 Timothy 6:17, Charge those who are rich in this world that they do good to others, etc. Hebrews 13:16, Do not forget beneficence and communication, for with such sacrifices God is pleased. 1 Timothy 4:8, Piety has a promise. James 2:13, Judgment without mercy to him who has not shown mercy. Hebrews 10:35, You have had compassion on those in bonds, therefore do not lose your confidence. Matthew 10:41, He who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man shall receive the reward of a righteous man. Luke 19:8, When Zacchaeus had said, Behold, I give half of my goods to the poor, the Lord added, Today salvation has come to this house. Prov. 19. verse 17. He who has pity on the poor lends to the Lord. Prov. 28. v. 27. He who gives to the poor will never lack.

XXXI. Resp. 1. GENERALLY. Some sayings speak of alms insofar as they are signs, not insofar as they are causes of blessedness and eternal happiness, such as Psalm 41. verse 1. Matt. 5. verse 7. Some speak of the temporal retribution of alms, such as Prov. 19. v. 17. Prov. 28. v. 27. To which also pertains the opinion of Jerome: I do not remember having read that anyone died a bad death who had led a merciful life.

XXXII. Respond. 2. SPECIFICALLY. The words of Prov. 16. verse 6 sound thus: By mercy and truth iniquity is purged; but Tremellius adds that it is to be understood not of the mercy of man, but of God, as it is explained in v. 7: When Jehovah favors the ways of anyone, he will turn even his enemies to peace, which explains the meaning of the preceding verse. Luther rendered it, durch Güte vnd Trewe wird Missetbat versühnet. Others explain it thus, that by exercising mercy toward the miserable, many temporal punishments are averted, which men have deserved by their iniquities. For if a certain saying clashes with a manifest article, then a solution is to be sought, so that Scripture may be treated according to the analogy of faith. These heads, however, are firm, certain, and clear. 1. To redeem from sins, to free from death, to merit eternal life are the duties proper to Christ alone, the Mediator and High Priest. 2. These benefits are offered through the Gospel. 3. They are to be received by faith, not by works. Others respond that it is not the effect that is noted, but a necessary concomitant or consequence of alms. For he who bestows alms from a faithful soul, his sins are purged. For a thing is then said to be done when it is manifested and rendered conspicuous. Just as therefore James says that we are justified by works, that is, declared to be justified, so alms expiate sins, that is, show them to be expiated.

XXXIII. To Isaiah 1, v. 17, we respond that the Lord requires entire repentance and conversion, the parts of which are contrition and faith; the fruits, new obedience, among which is also alms.

To Daniel 4, verse 24. The letter strikes against the analogy of faith, for Christ alone redeemed us from sins. Therefore the διάνοια must be sought. Tremellius urges the Hebrew text, which has 'break off your sins by righteousness,' that is, because you have lived badly up to now, and have treated your subjects cruelly; therefore perform true repentance, and see that you are justified, and thus by righteousness make an end to sins. Luther rendered it: 'Mache dich loß von deinen Sünden durch Gerechtigkeit/ vnnd ledig von deiner Missethat durch Wolthat an den Armen.' For in Hebrew it is, 'redeem your sins' בצדקת 'by righteousness.' The Septuagint rendered it poorly as 'alms.' Then there is the word חסד which signifies piety, mercy, the affection of charity, from the root חסד 'he consecrated,' whence חסידה 'stork.' The sense therefore is: Perform true repentance for committed sins, and expiate them by mercy, that is, show them to be expiated. For because your greatest sin was cruelty and inhumanity: Therefore, if you wish to be justified before men, that is, to show that you have performed true repentance, be liberal and beneficent toward the afflicted. Therefore Daniel persuades nothing else here than true repentance, by which righteousness is acquired, and the fruit of repentance, namely new obedience. Brentius urges such an ἀναλογίαν. Because alms is not the merit of remission and eternal life, nor is it an instrument of application, but a fruit of repentance, it is said to redeem from death, and to free from sin σημαντικῶς or μετωνυμικῶς, because it testifies concerning faith, concerning the remission of sins, as fruit concerning the goodness of a tree. Others interpret it concerning the mitigation or removal of temporal punishments, which interpretation is also not foreign to the text. For what is said in the Vulgate version, behold there shall be a healing of thy sins, that according to the Hebrew sources stands thus: Behold there shall be a prolongation of thy peace, from which it appears that Daniel had spoken concerning the removal of temporal punishments. For the Lord had threatened Nebuchadnezzar with expulsion from the kingdom: if he wishes this punishment to be removed, the Prophet Daniel urges that he study justice and mercy. For by good works a temporal calamity can often be averted. In which sense it is said in Psalm 41, verse 1: Blessed is he who is beneficent to the poor, in the evil day the Lord will deliver him. Although the text has, redeem thy sin, nevertheless it is familiar in the Scriptures that sin is spoken of for the punishment of sin, as in Leviticus 20, verse 19, Numbers 9, verse 13. The sense therefore is: If you wish to remove from yourself this bodily punishment of sin, you should study beneficence and mercy. Others bring forward such an explanation, that almsgiving and other good works are said to free from sins, but that sins are to be understood not as past, but as future. For when good works are exercised, then evils are avoided, and God preserves pious and holy men, so that they do not fall into tragic sins. Hence it is that some say that not so much the redemption of sins is understood by Daniel, as a cessation from sins, as if he were saying, cease from sins, or free yourself from sins, take away your sins through almsgiving, cease to sin and exercise justice and mercy, that is, do penance and declare faith by good works, as by fruits. For the word פְּרַק which Daniel uses here, properly signifies to the Chaldeans to break off, and to take away.

XXXIV. On Tobit 4, verse 11, and chapter 12, verse 9. Besides the fact that the book is Apocryphal, we add this, that the letter is against the ἀναλογίαν fidei (analogy of faith), since Christ alone purges sins and has acquired eternal life for us. Wherefore the διάνοια (meaning) must be sought again. Therefore this passage can be explained in such a way that almsgiving frees from every sin, that is, from the temporal punishment of sin, namely from premature death: for God has promised long life to the pious, and will not suffer the soul to go into darkness, namely of temporal calamities: for often by darkness are signified calamities of every kind, 2 Sam. 22, verse 12, Micah 7, Psalm 112, verse 4. The word death also often denotes the dangers of the present life, as 2 Cor. 11:23. Or it can be said that almsgiving purges sins μετωνυμικῶς (metonymically), that is, shows them to be purged, just as James says that works justify, that is, indicate justification. Osiander and Tremellius urge the former explanation, namely that these sayings are to be understood only concerning the averting of temporal punishments: Hunnius urges the latter: others urge both. The same answer is given to Ecclesiasticus 3, verse 33. Bellarmine, book 3 on good works in particular, chapter 3, explains it thus, that alms are said to free from sin 1. dispositively, while they obtain the grace of justification, by which guilt is removed: 2. effectively, while they make satisfaction for temporal punishment. This latter interpretation, if merit is removed, can be tolerated, but the former cannot.

XXXV. On Ecclesiasticus 16, verse 14, we say that there is a fault in the Vulgate version: According to the Greek text it sounds thus: To every merciful deed a place shall be given, for everyone shall be found according to his works: πάσῃ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ποιήσει τόπον, ἕκαστος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἑαυτοῦ εὕρησει, Luther rendered it, All good deeds will find their place, and to each one it will happen as he has deserved. From this, however, no support comes to the Papists.

XXXVI. To Matt. 25, verses 34 & 35, Dr. Hunnius, of blessed memory, responds that from this very passage three arguments can be formed by which it is proved that eternal life is gratuitous. 1. Because they are named blessed, namely with a spiritual blessing, which is apprehended by faith, not by works, Gal. 3, verse 8. 2. Because it is said κληρονομήσατε, by inheritance. But an inheritance falls to no one by merit, but by grace. For we were by nature children of wrath. 3. Because that kingdom is said to have been prepared from the beginning. Therefore we cannot earn it by works. The particle γὰρ, therefore, is not causal, but ratiocinative, and Christ argues from the effect to the cause. For because faith is hidden, therefore it produces the fruits of faith, by which the pious abundantly rendered their faith, the instrument of receiving the heavenly inheritance, attested. The sum is this: I pronounce these to be heirs of the eternal kingdom. Do you want the proof? For when I was hungry, you fed me, and they proved the truth of their faith to the eye by these witnesses. Hence, therefore, it is clear that the particle γὰρ is a mark not of efficiency, but of order and consequence; and that it is not taught by what causes the kingdom is acquired, but by what signs the heirs of that kingdom are recognized.

XXXVII. The same response is given to that saying of Rom. 2, v. 6. God will render to everyone according to his works, to those indeed who persevere, the glory of a good work. For the Apostle does not say that glory is to be rendered to us on account of works, as if they were merits, but according to works, namely as fruits of faith and testimonies by which it is manifestly declared that we are endowed with true faith: But the Lord is said to be about to judge not according to faith, but according to works, because works are manifest, but faith is hidden.

XXXVIII. To Luke 11, v. 41, some respond that it is an irony, by which Christ taxes the hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who thought that their sins, even the most grave, were nothing to them, provided that they bestow

alms abundantly upon the poor. Bellarmine, book 3 on good works, part, chapter 3, recounts four expositions of that saying. 1. It is that of those who, as we have said, maintain that this text is to be understood ironically; or they explain 'give' as 'you give', so that the sense is, you give alms, and you think that thus all things are clean for you. 2. It is that of Augustine, who extends alms broadly, and understands it also as that which one does for his own soul, by purging it from vices through conversion and repentance, in Enchiridion, chapter 76. 3. It is that of Basil, who understands not all sins, but only those which arise from avarice, such as thefts and rapine, for these have no place where generous alms are given. 4. It is that of Theophylact, which Bellarmine approves. The Pharisees were suffering from avarice; the Lord wished this to be rooted out; therefore he commends alms to them. For just as a physician, seeing that the cause of the disease in a sick person is repletion, can say, 'Apply the remedy, and you will be completely restored,' because, clearly, with the principal root of the disease removed, the other diseases can easily be taken away: so the Lord also says to the Pharisees, 'Give,' etc., since, when avarice was the root of all evils, if it had been overturned by the contrary virtue, they would easily have arrived at faith and repentance. Let this explanation of Bellarmine be noted and opposed to other Papists: for thus nothing can be concluded from this passage for the justification of works. Others explain it thus, that the Lord is instructing the Pharisees as to what are true and God-pleasing alms, namely those which are given from what is at hand, that is, from goods legitimately acquired, and not from those which have been scraped together by wickedness and rapine. Philippus replies that this is a fallacy of division. For CHRIST, reproving the superstition of the Pharisees in the external washing of cups, dishes, etc., opposes to them a twofold cleanness, internal and external, warning that the heart must be purged within, and that one must serve one's neighbor outwardly out of charity. He speaks of internal purity, saying: That which is within you is rapine: He makes a discourse on external purity, immediately adding: Yea, those things which are present; give, and behold all things will be clean to you, as if he were saying, then all things will be clean to you, internally and externally, if you have purged yourselves within, that is, have believed, and outwardly have given alms. For hearts are purified by faith. The adversaries, however, sophistically restrict that universal particle, All things will be clean to you, to the external kind of purity only, which should not have been done. Finally, some establish that here is not signified the cause of internal purity, but a declaration, so that the sense may be: Give alms, and all things will be clean to you, that is, then it will appear that you are clean on every side. For from those works of charity, and not from external washings, one can judge concerning faith and internal purity. And these latter two interpretations seem the best and most appropriate of all.

XXXIX To Luke 16, verse 9, we respond that two things must be explained: 1. What is the Mammon of iniquity? 2. How do friends receive us into eternal tabernacles? By the Mammon of iniquity are understood riches, which are so called because they are often acquired unjustly and iniquitously, and because the greatest part of men abuse riches for injustice, luxury, and pride. Our friends, that is, pious and holy men, receive us into the society of eternal life, not as authors and givers of the same (for this is against all Scripture) but as witnesses of our works, and especially of the beneficence applied by us in this age. They receive us, therefore, while they provide testimony of faith, so that through faith we may be rendered heirs of the kingdom. Others add that the needy are said to receive their benefactors into eternal tabernacles in this way also, because they

They assiduously commend them to God with pious prayers, and pray that He may mercifully have pity on them, and when they must depart from this world, He may deign to receive them into the heavenly kingdom.

XL. Regarding Acts 10:4, we say that it is not taught there that the prayers and alms of Cornelius merited the grace of God, but it is only signified that those prayers and alms pleased God in such a way that He gave Cornelius a fuller knowledge of Christ. Hebrews 13:16. In the Greek it is read εὐαρεστεῖται, which word does not signify to merit or to be appeased by meriting, but to be made pleasing. The sense is: By such sacrifices as fruits of faith, the duty is made pleasing to God, or GOD is delighted by such sacrifices; or such sacrifices please and are acceptable to God. To the remaining passages that follow, the answer is easy, so that it is not necessary to dwell on them longer.

Latin:

includitur. Sic igitur iustitia est, facere præcepta Dei, hoc est agere pœnitentiam, & credere Evangelio, vel agnoscere, quòd ex lege Mosis non sit iustitia, & quærere atque inuenire eam in solo Christo Mediatore vnico.

Classis septima, Continens dicta, quibus misericordiæ & beneficentiæ nostræ iustificatio attribuitur.

XXX. Dicta potissimum sunt ista Psalm. 41. v. 1. Beatus qui intelligit super egenum & pauperem, Psalm. 112. vers. 5. Beatus qui miseretur & mutuò dat. Proverb. 16. v. 5. Beneficentiâ & fide expiatur iniquitas. Es. 1. vers. 17. Discite benefacere, iudicate pupillum, quærite iustitiam: Si fuerint peccata vestra, tanquam coccinum, velut nix dealbabuntur, Dan. 4. v. 24. Redime peccata tua iustitiâ & eleemosina, & erit sanatio delictorum tuorum. Tob. 4. v. 11. Eleemosina ab omni peccato & morte liberat. Ecclesiastici 3. v. 33. Ignem ardentem extinguit aqua, & Eleemosina expiat peccatum. Ecclesiastici 16. vers: 15 Omnis misericordia facit locum vnicuique secundum meritum operum suorum. Matth. 5. vers 7. Beati misericordes. Matth. 25. vers: 34. Venite benedicti Patris mei, esuriui enim, &c, Luc. 11. vers, 41. Date Eleemosynam, & ecce omnia vobis erunt munda, Luc. 16. v. 9. Facite vobis amicos de Mammone iniusto, vt cùm defeceritis, recipiant vos. Actor. 10. v. 4. Preces tuæ & Eleemosynæ ascenderunt in conspectum Dei. 1. Timoth. 6. v. 17. His, qui diuites sunt in hoc seculo, denunciatione esserantur, vt alijs benefaciant, &c. Ebr. 13. v. 16. Beneficentiæ & communicationis nè obliuiscimini, talibus enim hostijs promeretur Deus 1. Timoth. 4. v. 8. Pietas promissionem habet. Iacob. 2. versu 13. Iudicium sine misericordiâ ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam. Heb. 10. v. 35. Vinclis compassi estis, nolite itaque amittere confidentiam vestram. Matth. 10. versu 41. Qui recipit iustum in nomine iusti, mercedem iusti accipiet. Luc. 19. v. 8. Cùm dixiffet Zachæus, Ecce dimidium bonorum meorum do pauperibus, adiunxit Dominus, Hodiè salus huic domui facta est. Proverb. 19. vers. 17. Fœneratur Domino, qui miseretur pauperis. Prov. 28. v. 27. Qui dat pauperibus, nunquam egebit.

XXXI. Resp. 1. GENERALITER. Quædam dicta loquuntur de Eleemosynis, in quantû sunt notæ, non in quantum causæ beatitudinis & æternæ felicitatis, qualia sunt Psalm. 41. vers. 1. Matth. 5. vers. 7. Quædam loquuntur de temporali Eleemosynarum retributione, qualia sunt Prov. 19. v. 17. Prov 28. v. 27. Quò etiam pertinet Hieronymi sententia. Nõ memini me mala morte legisse mortuum, qui misericordem duxerit vitam.

XXXII. Respond. 2. SPECIALITER. Prov. 16. vers. 6 verba ita sonant: Benignitate & veritate expiatur iniquitas; Addit verò Tremellius, intelligi non benignitatē hominis, sed Dei, sicut exponitur, v. 7. Cùm benevolentiâ prosequitur Iehova vias alicuius, inimicos quoque eius convertet ad pacem, qui versus præcedentis sententiam exponit. Lutherus reddidit, durch Güte vnd Trewe wird Missetbat versühnet. Alij sic exponunt, quod exercendo misericordiam erga miseros, auertantur multæ pœnæ temporales, quas homines suis iniquitatibus sint promeriti Si enim dictum quoddam impingit in articulum manifestum, tunc διάλυσις quærenda est, vt Scriptura tractetur secundum ἀναλογίαν fidei. Hæc autem capita firma sunt, certa & perspicua. 1. Redimere à peccatis, liberare à morte, mereri vitam æternam esse officia solius Christi Mediatoris & Pontificis propria. 2. Hæc beneficia offerri per Evangelium. 3. Accipienda esse fide, non operibus. Alij respondent, notari non effectum, sed necessarium cohærens vel consequens Eleemosynæ. Qui enim ex fideli anima Eleemosynam erogat, illius peccata expiata sunt. Res enim quando tum dicitur fieri, cùm manifestatur & conspicua redditur. Sicut igitur Iacobus dicit, nos operibus iustificari, id est iustificatos declarari, sic Eleemosynæ expiant peccata, id est, expiata esse ostendunt.

XXXIII. Ad Esai. 1. v. 17. respondemus, quòd Dominus requirat integram pœnitentiam & conuersionem, cuius partes sunt, contritio & fides; fructus, noua obedientia, inter quæ etiam Eleemosyna.

Ad Dan. 4. vers. 24. Litera impingit in analogiam fidei, solus enim Christus redemit nos à peccatis. Ergo quærenda διάνοια. Tremellius vrget Hebræum textum, qui habet peccata tua iustitia abrumpe, hoc est, quia hactenus malè vixisti, subditos crudeliter tractasti; idcircò veram agas pœnitentiam, & videas vt iustificeris, atque ita iustitiâ peccatis finem facias. Lutherus reddidit: Mache dich loß von deinen Sünden durch Gerechtigkeit/ vnnd ledig von deiner Missethat durch Wolthat an den Armen. Nam in Hebręo est, redime peccata tua בצדקת in iustitia. Septuaginta malè reddiderunt Eleemosynam. Deinde habetur vocabulum חסד quod significat pietatem, misericordiam, affectum charitatis, à radice חסד sacrauit, vndè חסידה Ciconia. Sensus igitur est: Veram age pœnitentiam ob commissa peccata, eáque expia misericordia, id est, ostende expiata esse. Quia enim maximum tuum peccatum fuit crudelitas & inhumanitas: Quare, si vis coram hominibus iustificari, hoc est, te veram egisse pœnitentiam ostendere, esto liberalis & beneficus erga afflictos. Nihil proindè aliud hîc suadet Daniel, quam veram pœnitentiam, quâ acquiritur iustitia, & pœnitentiæ fructum, videlicet nouam obedientiam. Brentius talem vrget ἀναλογίαν. Quia Eleemosyna non est meritum remissionis & vitæ æternæ, nec est organũ applicationis, sed fructus pœnitentiæ, igitur dicitur redimere à morte, & liberare à peccato σημαντικῶς vel μετωνυμικῶς, quia testificatur de fide, de remissione peccatorum, tanquam fructus de bonitate arboris. Alij interpretantur de mitigatione vel ablatione temporalium pœnarum, Quæ interpretatio à textu etiam non est aliena. Quod enim in vulgatâ versione dicitur, ecce erit sanatio peccatorum tuorum, id secundum fontes Hebræos sic habet: Ecce erit prolongatio pacis tuæ, vnde apparet, Danielem de ablatione pœnarum temporalium locutum fuisse. Minatus enim fuerat Dominus Nebucadnezari, depulsionem ex regno: Hanc pœnam si sublatam velit, suadet Propheta Daniel, vt iustitiæ & misericordiæ studeat. Bonis enim operibus calamitas temporalis sæpè potest auerti. Quo sensu dicitur Psal. 41. vers. 1. Beatus qui beneficus est pauperi, in die malà liberabit eum Dominus. Licèt autem textus habeat, redime peccatum tuum, tamen in Scripturis familiare est, vt peccatum pro pœnâ peccati dicatur, vt Leuit. 20. vers. 19. Num. 9. ver. 13. Sensus igitur est: Si corporalem istam peccati pœnam vis à te amoliri, beneficentiæ & misericordiæ studeas. Alij talem afferunt explicationem, quòd Eleemosyna & alia bona opera dicantur liberare à peccatis, sed intelligenda esse peccata non prȩterita, sed futura. Cùm enim bona opera exercentur, tum mala cauentur, & Deus pios sanctosque homines conseruat, nè in tragica peccata incidant. Hinc est, quòd nonnulli dicunt, non tàm intelligi à Daniele peccatorum redemptionem, quàm cessationem à peccatis, quasi dicat, cessa à peccatis, seu libera te à peccatis, aufer peccata tua per Eleemosynas, desine peccare & exerce iustitiam atque misericordiam, hoc est, pœnitentiam age & fidem declara bonis operibus, tanquam fructibus. Nam verbum פְּרַק quo hic vtitur Daniel, Chaldæis propriè significat abrumpere, & auferre.

XXXIV. Ad Tob. 4. vers. 11. & cap. 12. v. 9. Præterquàm quòd liber sit Apocryphus, hoc addimus, literam esse contra ἀναλογίαν fidei, cùm solus Christus purget peccata, & vitani acquisirit nobis æternam. Quare iterum quærenda est διάνοια. Ergò ita potest hic locus exponi, quòd Eleemosyna liberet ab omni peccato, id est, peccati pœnâ temporali, à morte videlicet immaturâ: Deus enim pijs longæuam promisit vitam, & non patietur animam ire in tenebras, videlicet calamitatum temporalium: Sæpè enim tenebris significantur omnis generis calamitates 2. Sam. 22. vers. 12. Micheæ 7. Psal. 112. vers. 4. Mortis etiam vocabulum sæpè notat vitæ præsentis pericula, vt 2. Cor. 11. 23. Vel dici potest, quòd Eleemosyna purget peccata μετωνυμικῶς, id est, purgata esse ostendat, sicuti Iacobus dicit, opera iustificare, id est, iustificationem indicare. Priorem explicationem, quòd videlicet hæc dicta non nisi de auersione pœnarum temporalium intelligenda sint, vrget Osiander & Tremellius: posteriorem Hunnius: vtramque alij. Eadem responsio datur ad Eccl. 3. v. 33. Bell. l. 3. de bon oper. in partic. c. 3. ita exponit, quòd Eleemosynæ dicantur a peccato liberare 1. dispositiuè, dum gratiam iustificationis, quâ culpa tollitur, impetrant: 2. effectiuè, dum pro pœna temporali satisfaciunt. Hæc posterior interpretatio si meritum tollatur, tolerari potest, ista verò non potest,

XXXV. Ad Eccles. 16. v. 14. dicimus, quòd sit vitium in vulgata versione: Secundum textum Græcum ita sonat: Omni misericordi beneficentiá dabitur, nam quisq; secundum opera sua inueniurus est: πάσῃ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ποιήσᾳ τόπον, ἕκαστος κατὰ τὰ ἔργα ἑαυτοῦ εὕρησει, Lutherus reddidit, Alle Wolthat wird ihre stäte finden/ vnd einem ieglichen wird widerfahren wie er verdienet hat. Hinc verò patrocinij nihil accedit Pontificijs.

XXXVI. Ad Matth. 25. verf. 34 & 35. refpondet D. Hunnius, p. m. quod ex hoc ipso loco tria possint argumenta formari, quibus probetur vitam æternam gratuitam esse. 1. Quia nominantur benedicti, benedictione videlicet spirituali, quæ fide non operibus apprehenditur, Gal. 3. vers. 8. 2. Quia dicitur κληρονομήσατε hæreditate. Hæreditas autem nemini obtingit ex merito, sed ex gratia. Eramus enim filij iræ naturâ. 3. Quia regnum illud ab initio paratum esse dicitur. Ergo non possumus promereri operibus. Particula igitur γὰρ non est causalis, sed ratiocinativa, & argumentatur Christus ab effectu ad causam. Quia enim fides occulta est, ideo fidei fructus producit, quibus pij abundè fidem suam, cœlestis hæreditatis accipiendæ ὄργανον testatam reddiderunt. Summa hæc est: Pronuncio istos æterni regni hæredes, Vis probationem? Qui cùm esurirem, pavistis me, & fidei suæ veritatem his testibus ad oculum comprobarunt. Hinc ergo constat Particulam γὰρ non efficientiæ, sed ordinis & consequentiæ notam existere; nec doceri, quibus causis regnum acquiratur, sed quibus signis regni eius hæredes cognoscantur.

XXXVII. Eadem responsio datur ad istud dictum Rom. 2. v. 6. Reddet Deus unicuique secundum opera ipsius, ijs quidem qui perstant, boni operis gloriam. Non enim dicit Apostolus, nobis reddendam esse gloriam, propter opera, tanquam merita, sed secundum opera, videlicet tà quam fructus fidei & testimonia, quibus manifestò declaratur, nos verâ fide præditos esse: Non autem secundum fidem. sed secundum opera dicitur iudicaturus Dominus, quia opera sunt manifesta, fides autem occulta.

XXXVIII. Ad Luc. 11. v. 41. respondent nonnulli, quòd ironia sit, quâ Christus Pharisæorum hypocrisin taxet, putantium, sibi nihilobesse peccata, etiam gravissima, modò Elee-

mosynas in pauperes cumulatè erogent. Bellarm. lib 3. de bonis operibus. partic. c. 3 quatuor istius dicti expositionis recenset. 1. Est eorum, qui, vt diximus ironicè hunc textum esse intelligendum autumant; vel dóte pro datis exponunt, vt sit sensus, vos datis Eleemosynam, & putatis, ita vobis omnia esse munda. 2. Est Augustini, qui eleemosynam latè extendit, eamque etiam intelligit, quâ quis animæ suæ eleemosynam facit, eam purgando à vitijs, per conuersionem & pœnitentiam, in Enchirid. c. 76. 3. Est Basilij, qui non omnia peccata, sed ea duntaxat intelligit, quæ nascuntur ex avaritiâ, vt furta, rapinæ, hæc enim locum non habent, vbi largæ dantur eleemosynæ. 4. Est Theophylacti, quam Bellarminus approbat. Laborabant Pharisæi auaritiâ, hanc Dominus volebat evulsam; ideo commendat ipsis eleemosynam. Sicut enim Medicus, videns causam morbi in ægroto esse repletionem, dicere potest, Adhibe medelam, & integrè conualesces, quia videlicet, radice principali morbi sublatą, cæteri morbi facilè tolli possunt: Sic Dominus etiam diçit Pharisæis, Date, &c. quoniam cùm radix omnium malorum avaritia esset, si ea per virtutem contrariam eversa fuiffet, facilè illi ad fidem & pœnitentiam pervenissent. Hæc Bellarmini explicatio notetur & alijs Pontificijs opponatur: Sic enim nihil ex hoc loco concludi poterit pro iustificatione operum. Alij sic exponunt, quòd Dominus Pharisæos instruat, quænam sint veræ & Deo placentes eleemosynæ, nimirum illæ, quæ dentur de ijs, quæ adsunt, hoc est, de bonis legitimè partis, non autem de ijs, quæ scelere & rapinâ sunt corrasa. Philippus respondet, esse fallaciam diuisionis. Nam CHRISTVS reprehendens Pharisæorum superstitionem in externa lotione poculorum, patinarum &c. opponit eis duplicem munditiem internam & externam, monens cor intus purgandum, & foris proximo ex charitate subseruiendum esse. De interna loquitur dicens: Quod intra vos est rapina: De externa sermonem facit, mox subijciens: Imo ea, quæ adsunt; date, & ecce omnia erut vobis munda, quasi dicat, tunc omnia erunt vobis mūda, interne & externe, si intus vos purgaueritis id est, credideritis & foris eleemosynam dederitis. Nam fide purificantur corda Aduersarii autem particulam illam vniuersalem, Omnia vobis erunt munda, sophistice restringunt ad externum munditiei genus tantum, quod non erat faciendum. Tandem nonnulli statuunt, hic non significari causam internæ munditiei, sed declarationem, vt sit sensus: Date eleemosynam, & omnia vobis erunt munda, hoc est, tum apparebit, vos vndiquaque mundos esse. Nam ex illis operibus charitatis, non autem ex lotionibus externis, de fide & interna munditie judicari potest. Atque hæ posteriores duæ interpretationes videntur omnium optimæ & appositissimæ.

XXXIX Ad Luc. 16. versu 9. respondemus, quod duo veniant explicanda, 1. Quid sit Mammon iniquitatis? 2. Quomodo amici nos recipiant in æterna tabernacula? Per Mammona iniquitatis intelliguntur divitiæ, quæ sic dicuntur, quia sæpè iniustè & iniquè acquiruntur, & quia maxima hominum pars divitiis ad iniustitiam, luxum & superbiam abutitur. Amici nostri, hoc est, pii & sancti homines recipiunt nos ad societatem vitæ æternæ, non vt authores & datores eiusdem (hoc enim contra omnem scripturam) sed vt testes operum nostrorum, inprimis verò beneficentiæ, a nobis in hoc seculo adhibitæ. Nos ergo recipiunt, dum testimonium fidei præbent, vt ita per fidem hæredes regni reddamur. Addunt alij, q egeni suos benefactores in æterna tabernacula dicantur recipere hoc etiam modo, quia illos

Deo piis precibus assiduè commendant, & precantur, vt illorum clementer misereari, & cùm ex hoc seculo migrandum fuerit, recipere eos dignetur in regnum coeleste.

XL. Ad Actor. 10. v. 4. dicimus, non doceri ibi, preces & eleemosynas Cornelij promeruisse gratiam Dei, sed significari tantùm, preces illas & eleemosynas Deo placuisse ita, vt pleniorem Christi notitiam daret Cornelio Hebr. 13. v. 16. In Gręco legitur εὐαρεστεῖται, quæ vox non significat promereri aut promerendo placari, sed gratum fieri. Sensus est: Talibus hostijs tanquam fidei fructibus, gratum fieri Deo officium, vel talibus hostijs oblectari DEVM; vel tales hostias placere & acceptas esse Deo. Ad reliqua, quæ supersunt, dicta, facilis est responsio, vt diutius immorari non sit necesse.


### Classis octaua. Containing sayings in which eternal life is called the wages or reward of good works

XLI. The Papists allege these passages: Genesis 15:1, 'I am your protector, and your reward exceeding great.' Jeremiah 31:16, 'Restrain your voice from weeping, because there is a reward for your work.' Matthew 5:7, 'Your reward will be abundant in heaven.' Matthew 10:42, and chapter 19:29, and chapter 20:8, 9. 1 Corinthians 3:8, 14, 'Each one will receive his own reward according to his labor.' 1 Corinthians 9:17, 'If I do it willingly, I have a reward.' Colossians 3:24. 2 Timothy 4:7, 'There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness.' 2 John 8, 'That we may not lose what we have worked for, but that we may receive a full reward.' Revelation 11:18, 'You may give the reward, etc.' And chapter 22:12, 'I am coming quickly and my reward is with me.' Bellarmine cites these passages in book 5 on justification, chapter 2.

XLII. Response. There is an equivocation in the word reward. For there is a twofold reward, as is evident from Romans 4:4 and chapter 11:6. I. A reward that is owed, which is opposed to what is gratuitous, and denotes the due price, or the compensation due for a service or labor. The Apostle speaks of this kind of reward in Romans 4, verse 4: To him who works, the reward is given as a debt. Such a reward and compensation exists in human contracts. II. An undue reward, which is opposed to what is empty, fruitless, and vain, which is followed by no utility, and denotes not a due, but a gratuitous premium for a service or labor otherwise due. For often in Scripture reward signifies the fruit which follows, even an undue one, as in Proverbs 23, verse 18: because it is a reward or end; in Hebrew it is אחרית. The Old Interpreter rendered it: you will have hope in the end, and your expectation will not be taken away. Thus in Jeremiah 31, verse 17. There is also hope for your end, which is expressed in verse 16 with these words: because there is a reward for your work. Thus, if a parent promises something to a son, so that he may be more diligent in his studies, and says, If you learn this, or if you can perform that, this will be your reward, nothing but a gratuitous premium is denoted, because diligence in studies is otherwise due. Of this reward it is said in Romans 4, verse 4: To him who does not work, the reward is imputed according to grace. And Ambrose indicated this distinction of reward in book 1, epistle 1, where he says: One is the reward of liberality and grace: another is the stipend of virtue, and the remuneration of labor. The former is a legal reward, the latter is Evangelical. The former includes the merit of works, the latter excludes it. Therefore, that Papist axiom is not universal: Where there is reward, there is merit, but it is true only concerning a reward that is due.

XLIII. But when eternal life is called the reward of our works (although this phrase is never found in the Scriptures), then it cannot be understood as a due reward with the Papists. 1. Because of the lack of proportion between our works (which are finite and imperfect) and eternal life, which is an infinite and supremely perfect good. 2. Because otherwise we would owe more than we are able to perform. But by duties no one can earn anything. 3. Eternal life is elsewhere called the gift of God, Rom. 6 v. 23. If it is a gift, it is certainly not a due reward, and if it is given out of grace, it is certainly not out of works, Rom. 11 v. 6. It is signified, therefore, that it is not owed to us on account of our duties, but is given as to sons and heirs. 4 Good 1 Corinthians 4 verse 7. Which if God crowns, He does not crown our merits, but His own gifts, according to that saying of Augustine: God crowns nothing in us except His own gifts. And Bernard says: All our merits are gifts of God, so that man is more a debtor to God on account of them than God is to man. 5. Paul expressly excludes works or merits from our justification and salvation, Rom. 4 verse 5 and Tit. 3 verse 5. Not out of righteous works which we had done, but out of His mercy He saved us. Where is the Papist relation here between reward and merit or works? Once a reward is posited, says Bellarmine, works or merits are necessarily posited also. But Paul expressly removes and takes away works; to him who does not work, he says, but believes, faith is imputed as righteousness. 6. Synonomously, reward and grace and inheritance are sometimes accepted, Psalm 127 verse 3. Behold, the inheritance of Jehovah is faith, the reward is the fruit of the womb; and what is called μισθòς in Matthew 6 verse 1, is named χάρις in Luke 6 verse 32. I conclude, therefore, with this syllogism: If eternal life must be called a reward, it must be done in such a way that it is also truly called and is a gratuitous gift of God. But this cannot be done if you interpret reward as compensation, owed to works, according to an adequate proportion. For thus a contradiction would be implied, since a due reward is opposed to a gratuitous gift. Wherefore, when eternal life is called a reward, it is understood as nothing other than an undue reward.

XLIV. The reasons, however, for which the gratuitous gift of eternal life is sometimes called a reward in the Scriptures are these: 1. On account of the attainment.

For just as every reward which follows some labor, even if it is unmerited, is called wages, as in Genesis 15:1, Psalm 127:3, so eternal life, because it follows our works as some fruit and utility, is not inappropriately termed wages. For thus Christians are stirred to the pursuit of good works, while they know that they do not labor in vain, but that, even if by grace, a great utility is prepared for them. Thus an inheritance is given to a son, not because of his services (otherwise servants, who labor more, ought to inherit more), but because of his sonship, according to that saying: 'When a son is born, a portion is born,' and yet at the same time in compensation for obedience, though a gratuitous one: in a similar way it is arranged with our salvation, whence in Colossians 3:24 it is called the reward of the inheritance, to indicate that the reward is not owed, but unmerited and gratuitous; for those things which come to us by inheritance are not assigned to us because of works.

XLV. II. Because of the promise. For since God promised that He would give eternal life to those working well, hence it is as it were a debt (for every promise falls into a debt), which nevertheless does not take away the gratuitous nature, nor build up the merit of works, but rather destroys it. For if life is given to us because of the promise, certainly it will not be given because of good works. Therefore God owes eternal life, not by reason of our debt, but by reason of His promise, whence Augustine elegantly said: God is our debtor, not from what He has committed, but from what He has promised. And in Psalm 32 he says: The Lord is faithful, who made Himself a debtor to us, not by receiving anything from us, but by promising everything. And in sermon 31 on Luke: Not by owing, but by promising, God made Himself a debtor. Which itself is so true that Stapleton was forced to admit this, who in Antidot. Evangelical on Matthew chapter 5, page 45, writes thus: The promise of God is indeed gratuitous, but the promise having once been made, the retribution is not gratuitous, but owed, not because GOD owes us anything, but because he has become a debtor of that which he promised gratuitously, and he cannot deny himself. From which words it follows openly that Bellarmine wrote falsely in book 5 of Justification, chapter 3, when he says that Scripture says in express words that this reward is given to works, not to the promise alone. Those things have a manifest contradiction: that GOD owes us nothing, as Stapleton truly writes: And that GOD gives a reward owed to our works, which Bellarmine affirms.

XLVI. Toward the end of this response, let it be noted that eternal life itself must be accurately distinguished from the rewards in eternal life. Concerning the rewards, it is indeed true that the good works of the pious are adorned and crowned by them, but nevertheless out of grace; even though we do not deny that those degrees of glory in eternal life have some respect to the works of the saints. Therefore we willingly use those phrases of Scripture: Great is your reward in heaven, Matt. 5, verse 12; it is not said, Heaven will be the reward. Thus Matt. 19, v. 21: Sell what you have, and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Luke 14, verse 14: It will be repaid to you at the resurrection of the just. In these and similar sayings is contained a description of rewards or compensation, but such as always requires before it the possession of eternal life itself. Whence from them it is rightly shown that there will be a compensation for good works in eternal life. namely gratuitous, the foundation of which is the gratuitous divine promise, but it does not follow from that that eternal life itself is a reward properly so called, as the Papists contend.

XLVII. To the saying of Paul in 2 Tim. 4, v. 7-8, we respond specifically that eternal life is called a crown because it is given to one struggling and winning, 2 Tim. 2, v. 5. It is called a crown of righteousness (not of our works, as the Papists explain against manifest sayings, Ps. 143, v. 2, Rom. 3, v. 20, 1 Cor. 4, v. 4, Tit. 3, v. 5) and indeed of the righteousness of God, Rom. 3, v. 25, 2 Corinth. 5, v. last, Philip. 3, v. 9, both because Christ acquired it for us, 1. Corinth. 1. v. 30, 2. Cor. 5. v. last, and because that which God promises freely, He keeps for the sake of His justice, Hebr. 6. v. 10. And God is called here a just judge, not legally, but evangelically, just as the judgment of God, by which He saves the nations, is called just. 'Just' can also be explained as faithful and truthful. Or, God, as a just judge, will justly render to us what He will render; not because He owes us anything, but because He promised it and because truth, which is a part of His justice, demands that He perform that which He even voluntarily and freely promised. God is therefore just, because He pays, not what He owes to our works, but what He promised, and He pays it because He promised it, and because He forgives our works, nay, because He does not look upon our works, but upon His grace in them. To this also can be referred the passage in Apocal. 4. verse 10, where the twenty-four elders cast their crowns before the throne, saying: Thou art worthy, O Lord, to receive glory. By this very act showing that they obtain these crowns not by their own merit, but by the grace of the Lamb, that is, of Christ the Lord.

Latin:

XLI. Dicta hæc allegant Pontificij Genes. 15. v. 1. Ego protector tuus sum, & merces magna nimis. Ierem. 31. vers. 16. Prohibe vocem tuam à fletu, quia merces est operi tuo. Matth. 5. v. 7. Merces vestra copiosa erit in cælo. Matth. 10. v. 42. & c. 19. v. 29. & c. 20. ver. 8. 9. 1. Corinth. 3. v. 8. 14. Vnusquisque suam mercedem accipiet secundum laborem suū. 1. Cor. 9. v. 17. Si volens faciam, mercedem habeo. Coloss. 3. v. 24. 2. Tim. 4. v. 7. Reposita est mihi corona iustitiæ. 2. Ioh. v. 8. Ne perdamus, quæ operati sumus, sed vt mercedē plenam recipiamus. Apoc. 11. v. 18. Des præmiū &c. Et c. 22. v. 12. Venio citò & merces mea mecum est. Dicta hæc citat Bell. l. 5. de iustific. c. 2.

XLII. Resp. Est æquiuocatio in vocabulo mercedis. Duplex enim merces est, vt patet ex Rom. 4. vers. 4. & c. 11. vers. 6. I. Merces debita, quæ opponitur gratuito, & notat precium debitum, seu compensatiouem officij aut laboris debitam. De hoc genere mercedis loquitur Apostolus Rom. 4. vers. 4. Ei qui operatur, merces datur ex debito. Talis merces & compensatio est in contractibus humanis. II. Merces indebita, quæ opponitur inani, frustraneo & vano, quod nulla insequitur vtilitas, notatque non debitum, sed gratuitum officij aut laboris aliàs debiti præmium. Sæpè enim in Scriptura merces significat fructum, qui sequitur, etiam indebitum, vt Proverb. 23. vers. 18. quia est merces seu finis; In Hebræo est אחרית Vetus interpres reddidit, habebis spem in novissimo & præstolatio tua non auferetur. Sic Ieremiæ 31. vers. 17. Est quoque spes novissimo tuo, quod vers. 16. his verbis enunciatur, quia est merces operi tuo, Ita si parens filio aliquid promittat, quò diligentior sit in studiis, & dicat, Si hoc edidiceris, vel si illud præstare potueris, hæc erit merces tua, non nisi gratuitum præmium notatur, quia diligentia in studiis aliàs est debita. De hâc mercede dicitur Roman. 4. vers. 4. Ei, qui non operatur, imputatur merces secundùm gratiam. Atque hanc distinctionem mercedis indicauit Ambrosius lib 1. epist. 1. vbi inquit: Alia est merces liberalitatis & gratiæ: Aliud virtutis stipendium est, & laboris remuneratio. Prior merces legalis est, posterior Euangelica. Prior meritum operũ includit, posterior excludit, Nō igitur vniuersale est axioma istud Pontificium: Vbi merces, ibi meritum, sed de mercede duntaxat debita verū est.

XLIII. Quando autem vita æterna dicitur merces operum nostrorum (quanquam phrasis hæc nunquam in Scripturis reperiatur) tum nequis merces debita intelligi cum Pontificiis. 1. Ob carentiam proportionis inter nostra opera, (quę sunt finita & imperfecta) atq; inter vitam æternam, quæ est bonum infinitum & summè perfectum. 2. Quia aliàs debemus plus, quàm præstare possumus. Debitis auté officijs nemo potest aliquid promereri. 3. Vita æterna alibi vocatur donum Dei, Rom. 6 v. 23. Si donum, certè merces debita nõ est, & si ex gratia datur vtique non ex operibᵉ, Rom. 11. v. 6. Significatur igitur non deberi nobis propter officia nostra sed tanquã filiis & hæredibus darı, 4 Bona opera non sunt nostra, sed sunt dona Dei, 1. Corinth. 4 versu 7. quæ si coronat Devs, non merita nostra. sed dona sua coronat, juxta illud Augustini: Nihil Devs in nobis præter sua dona coronat. Et Bernhardus dicit. Omnia merita nostra esse dona Dei, itavt homo propter ipsa magis debitor sit Deo, quàm Devs homini. 5. Paulus disertè à Iustificatione & saluatione nostra excludit opera seu merita Rom. 4. versu 5. & Tit. 3. ver. 5. Non ex operibus iustis, quæ feceramus nos, sed ex suamisericordia eruasit. Vbi hîc est relatio Pontificia inter mercedem & meritum sive opera? Positâ mercede, inquit Bellarminus, necessariò etiam ponuntur opera seu merita At Paulus disertè opera removet & tollit, Non operanti, sed credenti, inquit, fides imputatur, ac iustitiam. 6. συνωνύμως nonnunquam aecipiuntur merces & gratia atque hæreditas, Psal. 127. versu 3. Ecce hæreditas Iehovæ fides merces fructus ventris; Et quod Matth. 6. versu 1. dicitur μισθòς, id Luc 6. versu 32. nominatur χάρις. Concludo igitur hoc Syllogismo: Si vita æterna merces dicenda est, illud ita fieri oportet, vt verè etiam dicatur & sit donum Dei gratuitum. Atqui hoc fieri nequit, si mercedem exponas de compensatione, debita operibus, secundum adæquatam proportionem. Sic enim implicaretur contradictio, cum merces debita opposita sit dono gratuito. Quare cùm vita æterna merces dicitur, non nisi indebita merces intelligitur.

XLIV. Causæ autem, ob quas gratuitum vitæ æternæ donum nonnunquam merces in Scripturis dicatur, hæ sunt, 1. Propter consecutionem.

Sicut enim omne præmium, quod laborem aliquem consequitur, etiamsi sit indebitum, merces vocatur, vt Genes. 15. vers. 1. Psal. 127. vers. 3. Ita vita æterna, quia consequitur nostra opera, tanquam fructus aliquis & vtilitas, non incommodè merces nuncupatur. Sic enim Christiani excitantur ad studia bonorum operum, dum sciunt, se non frustrà laborare, sed sibi, etiamsi ex gratiâ, magnam esse paratam vtilitatem. Sic hæreditas datur filio, non propter officia sua (aliàs serui, qui plus laborant, plus hæreditare deberent,) sed ob filiationem iuxta illud; Nato filio, nata portio: & tamen simul in compensationem obedientiæ, gratuitam tamen: Pari modo cum salute nostra comparatum est, vnde Coloss. 3. vers. 24. merces hæreditatis appellatur, ad indicandum, mercedem esse non debitam, sed indebitam & gratuitam; Quæ enim hæreditariò ad nos deveniunt, illa non propter opera nobis assignantur.

XLV. II. Propter promissionem. Quoniam enim Deus promisit, se benè operantibus vitam æternam daturum, hinc quasi debitum est, (Omne enim promissum cadit in debitum) quod tamen non tollit gratuitum, nec extruit meritum operum, sed potiùs destruit. Si enim propter promissionem vita nobis datur, vtique non propter bona opera dabitur. Debet igitur DEVS vitam æternam, non ratione debiti nostri, sed ratione promissionis suæ, vnde Augustinus eleganter dixit: DEVS debitor noster est, non ex commisso sed promisso. Et in Psalmo 32. ait: Fidelis Dominus, qui se nobis fecit debitorem, non aliquid à nobis accipiendo, sed omnia promittendo. Et serm. 31. in Lucam. Non debendo, sed promittendo DEVS se fecit debitorem. Quod ipsum adeò verum est, vt hoc fateri coactus fuerit Stapletonus, qui in Antidot. Evang. super Matth. cap. 5. pag. 45. ita scribit: Est quidem promissio DEI gratuita, promissione autem semel factâ, retributio non est gratuita, sed debita, non quia DEVS nobis aliquid debet, sed quia eius, quod gratuitò promisit, debitor factus est, & se ipsum negare non potest. Ex quibus verbis aperte sequitur, falsum scripsisse Bellarminum lib. 5. de iustificat. cap. 3. dum inquit, Scripturam disertis verbis dicere, hanc mercedem dari operibus, non soli promissioni. Contradictionem illa habent manifestam: DEVM nobis nihil debere, vt verè scribit Stapletonus: Et DEVM dare mercedem debitam operibus nostris, quòd affirmat Bellarminus.

XLVI. Sub finem responsionis huius illud notetur, quòd accuratè distinguenda sit ipsa vita æterna, à præmijs in vitâ æternâ. De præmijs quidem verum est, ornari ijs & coronari bona piotum opera, sed tamen ex gratiâ; etiamsi non inficiemur, gradus istos gloriæ in vitâ æternâ habere aliquem respectum ad opera sanctorum. Ideò libenter vsurpamur istas Scripturæ phrases, Merces erit in cœlo, Matth. 5. vers. 12. non dicitur, Cælum erit merces. Sic Matth. 19. v. 21. Vende quæ habes, & da pauperibus, & habebis thesaurum in cælo. Luc. 14. vers. 13. Retribuetur tibi iis resurrectione iustorum. In his & similibus dictis continetur descriptio præmiorum siue compensationis, sed talis, quæ semper ante se requirit ipsam vitæ æternæ possessionem. Vnde ex illis rectè ostenditur, fore compensationem bonorum operum in vita æternâ. nempe gratuitam, cuius fundamentum est promissio gratuita diuina, non autem inde sequitur, ipsam vitam æternam esse mercedem propriè sic dictam vt Pontificij contendunt.

XLVII. Ad dictum Pauli 2. Tim. 4. v. 7. 8 in specie respondemus, quòd vita æterna vocetur corona, quia datur certanti & vincenti, 2. Timoth. 2. v. 5. Corona iustitiæ dicitur, (non nostrorum operum, vt Pontificij exponunt contra manifesta dicta, Pf. 143, v. 2. Rom. 3. v. 20. 1. Cor. 4. v. 4. Tit. 3. v. 5.) & quidem iustitiæ Dei Rom. 3. v. 25. 2. Corinth. 5. v. ult. Phillip. 3. v. 9. tum quia Christus nobis eam acquisiuit, 1. Corinth. 1. v. 30. 2. Cor. 5. v. ult. tum quia illud, quod Deus gratis promittit, pro sua iustitia seruat, Hebr. 6. v. 10. Et vocatur Deus hic iustus iudex, non Legaliter, sed Evangelicè, sicut iudicium Dei, quo gentes saluat, iustum dicitur. Potest etiam iustus exponi, pro fideli & veraci. Vel, Deus, vt iustus iudex, iustè nobis reddet, quod reddet; non quòd nobis quicquam debeat, sed quia promisit & quia veritas, quæ est pars iustitiæ eius, postulat, vt id, quod etiam vltrò & gratis promisit, præstet. Iustus igitur Deus est, quia soluit, non quod nostris operibus debet, sed quod promisit, & ideò soluit, quia promisit, & quia nostris operibus ignoscit, imò quia non opera nostra, sed suam in eis intuetur gratiam. Huc etiam referri potest locus Apocal. 4. versu 10. vbi viginti quatuor seniores abijciunt coronas suas ante thronum, dicentes: Dignus es Domine, qui accipias gloriam. Hoc ipso facto ostendentes, se non suo merito, sed gratiâ agni, hoc est, Christi Domini coronas istas obtinere.


### Classis octaua. Containing sayings in which eternal life is called the wages or…: Ninth class

Ninth class.

Latin:

Classis nona.


### Classis nona. Containing the sayings which Bellarmine alleged for inherent justice

XLVIII. He takes the first from Rom. 5, where a comparison is instituted between Adam and Christ. From this passage we have, says Bellarmine, that to be justified through Christ is not to be held or pronounced just, but to be truly made and constituted just; through the adoption of inherent justice, which he proves, both from those words, 'many shall be constituted just,' and from the opposition of Christ and Adam: For just as through Adam we are inherently unjust, so through Christ we are inherently just.

Response to 1. That it is nothing but a mere begging of the question. For the use of the word 'to be constituted' extends very widely.

Someone can be made and constituted righteous, either through the infusion of righteousness, or through imputation, or through declaration. Therefore, nothing can be firmly concluded from that word: Bellarmine himself, in Colossians 10, verse 4, letter D, concedes that someone can be made righteous both intrinsically through the attainment of righteousness, and extrinsically through declaration. How, therefore, can he prove infused righteousness from the word 'to be made' or 'to be constituted,' when, by his own admission, it signifies both, namely, the imputative and the infused, at different times?

To the second, we respond that this comparison is not to be extended more broadly than the Apostle intended it to be extended. He wishes here to show the lot and the extent of both extremes, righteousness and unrighteousness, of which the latter draws its origin from Adam, the former from Christ. He therefore compares thing with thing, but not mode with mode. And the Apostle speaks of the acquisition, but not of the application of righteousness: otherwise the πρότασις and ἀπόδοσις would not agree. For whether by the word 'many' you understand 'all' or 'few,' you are always absurd. If 'all,' the ἀπόδοσις is false, for not all are actually righteous: if 'few,' the πρότασις is false, for not few are sinners. Therefore, if we wish to avoid these absurdities, it must be said that these things are compared only by reason of extent, so that Paul teaches that just as the fall involved all in sins, so also the righteousness of Christ can evolve all out of the same; just as that one was effective for condemnation, so this one is effective for salvation. This Apostolic comparison can neither be extended more broadly, nor ought it to be, otherwise many absurdities would follow, namely: 1. Just as all are naturally and are born sinners, so all are truly and inherently righteous. 2. Just as unrighteousness is derived into us through carnal generation, so also righteousness is propagated into us through carnal generation. I add that that actual disobedience

of Adam, by which we are all constituted sinners, does not inhere in us, but is only imputed. Therefore, granted that a mode is also conferred, yet justice infused would not be established by this, but rather imputed. For just as the actual disobedience of Adam is ours, not by inherence, but by imputation only, even the Papists themselves admitting this: So the justice of Christ, by which we are just, becomes ours not by infusion or inherence, but by true and real imputation. Finally, we can concede that inherent justice is perfectly restored through Christ, but that is not infused into us in this life, but is expected in the future.

XLIX. The second [argument] is sought from Romans chapter 3: Justified freely, by his grace. In which passage he thinks that by grace is denoted infused, grace-making justice. But we have sufficiently refuted this error in decade 2, disputation 1. The third is from 1 Corinthians 6, verse 11: And such were some of you, but you are washed. Which statement we explained in disputation 4 of this decade.

L. The fourth [argument] is from Titus 3, verse 5: He saved us by the washing of regeneration and renewal. Whence Bellarmine concludes that justification consists in regeneration and renewal. But Paul in those words does not describe the parts of justification, but the double effect of Baptism: We willingly concede, however, that renewal implies some change, but that our justification formally consists in this, that cannot be proven from this passage. From elsewhere, however, we learn that justification is the remission of sins, of which renewal, with various good works, is an effect or consequent.

LI. The fifth [argument] is from Hebrews 11, where Abel, Noah, and others are called just, which he thinks must be understood of inherent justice. He also alleges that [passage] from Genesis 6, verse 9: Noah is called a just and perfect man. And Luke 1, verse 6, where Zechariah and Elizabeth are called just, walking in all the commandments and justifications of the Lord,

Resp. 1. Bellarmine cannot from this seek any support for his cause, since just works, about which there is discussion in the cited sayings, are not the form, but the effects of just men, which he himself proves in chapters 15 and 16. Therefore, they are impertinently cited by him to prove the formal cause of justification. 2. Justice is twofold, imputative and inherent; by both we are called just, truly indeed, but in different ways, the former relatively and perfectly. These two species of justice are not to be confounded, but accurately distinguished. 3. Bellarmine cites the passage about Abel in a mutilated fashion. For thus says the Apostle: By faith Abel offered a sacrifice of greater value than Cain, through which he obtained testimony that he was just. Where it is manifest that faith is established as the cause, both of the preciousness of Abel's sacrifice and also of his justice. Wherefore it is clear that the discussion here is about the justice of faith, which is even more evident from the other testimony, namely that Noah was constituted an heir of the justice which is through faith. But that Noah is called a just man; add also perfect, that is to be understood primarily of the justice of faith, because he found grace before God, Genesis 6, verse 8. Note besides that, that the perfection which is attributed to the faithful in Scripture has a twofold respect, namely of the foundation apprehended by faith in Christ, then either of comparison or opposition to the injustice or hypocritical justice of others, or of the goal of perfection toward which one tends. Outside of these respects there is no perfection of the faithful in this world: For they themselves confess that they cannot perform the good; and they feel the stings of the flesh, etc. But that Zacharias and Elisabeth are called irreprehensible and just, that is not to be taken simply (for Zacharias was blameworthy, because he did not believe the Angel, on account of which incredulity he was also punished by God) but either of the justice of faith, or of new obedience, according to human judgment, (or as Augustine writes in book 1 on grace, chapter 48) according to a certain praiseworthy and approved conduct among men, which no man could justly call into a complaint of accusation and crimination, and which therefore they are reported to have had in the sight of God, because in it men deceived with no dissimulation, but as they appeared, so they were known to the eyes of God. But if these things are to be understood not only according to the judgment of men, but also of God, because they are said to be righteous before God; the judgment of God can again be understood in this place, not severe and exact according to the law, but clement and benign according to the Gospel. For even if those works could not have stood in His judgment, yet they were pleasing and acceptable to God, since they proceeded from faithful persons; and the infirmities that were present were covered by the merit of Christ. Their works were therefore irreprehensible, not simply, but in a certain respect; since that which was reprehensible was covered by the cloak of Christ.

LII. The sixth is sought from Romans 8, verse 29, and 1 Corinthians 15, verse 49, where the righteous are said to be conformed to the image of Christ, and to bear His image. And yet Christ was not putatively righteous, but truly and properly. Therefore the same must be affirmed of us: Otherwise it would follow that we are more conformed to the image of the Devil than of Christ if our sins were not blotted out by an infused habit of righteousness, etc.

Response 1. The Jesuit mixes in a calumny about putative righteousness. For it is not taught by us that we are righteous putatively, according to opinion, but imputatively and at the same time most truly, namely by the righteousness and satisfaction of Christ, apprehended through faith. 2. Our conformity with the image of Christ is threefold; one to the image of glory, opposed to that which is to the image of the afflicted Christ: And it is of this that we are chiefly treating in the cited passages, which for the opposition is instituted between the image of the first Adam and the second, it looks in both places from the sense of the Apostle to mortality and immortality, to earthly and heavenly qualities of the body, not properly to sin or the imputed righteousness of CHRIST. The other [looks] to the image of the obedience of CHRIST, which indeed we perform imperfectly in this world, but having been perfectly performed by Christ, is applied to us. For there is a twofold use of the righteousness of Christ: One primary, of satisfaction and merit, which is imputed to us. The other secondary, of example and instruction, according to which his righteousness is the rule of our inherent righteousness, which we also express to a certain extent, though not totally, according to which we are deservedly called conformed to him. The third and final conformity is of the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ. But the cited passages speak either of the conformity of glory, which is finally to be; or of the conformity of righteousness, which is in a certain way unconformed, since no man is able to equal the righteousness of Christ.

LIII. Seventhly, from Romans 6, where it is said that by justification, by which we die to sin and rise again to righteousness, the death and resurrection of Christ are represented, but CHRIST died not putatively, but truly.

Resp. The Apostle does not say that we represent the death of Christ by justification: nor is the subject there justification, but its fruits. But as for what Paul writes in verse 7, 'He who has died is justified from sin,' it must be known that in that place 'to be justified' is taken for 'to be freed,' according to the idiom of the Hebrews, who join the consequent with the antecedent. For thus it is explained in verse 18, 'having been freed from sin, you have been enslaved to righteousness.' This argument of Bellarmine is also foreign to the question. For we do not deny that a man dies through Baptism sin, and to rise again to righteousness, yet in the meantime we distinguish the distinct benefits of Christ; for justification, which is brought about through faith and is conferred in Baptism, is one thing, and new obedience or sanctification is another, being indeed its effect and consequence, which does not justify, but proceeds from the justified, and is a fruit of faith.

LIV. The eighth is sought from Rom. 8, v. 10, which saying is so mutilated and corrupted by Bellarmine that the mere reading of the Apostle's text abundantly refutes the Jesuitical frauds. For what Paul calls the body (that is, the unregenerate man) and the Spirit (that is, the regenerate man), the Jesuit takes as the two parts of man, namely body and soul, and where the Apostle says, the body is dead, the Jesuit corrupts it thus, the body is still mortal, and for these words of Paul, the Spirit is life, he substitutes those, the soul, which lives. Since this corruption is most gross, we shall not dwell on it, but rather proceed to other things.

Latin:

XLVIII. Primum sumit ex Rom. 5. vbi collatio instituitur inter Adamum & Christum. Ex hoc loco habemus, inquit Bellarminus, iustificari per Christum, non esse haberi aut pronunciari iustos, sed verè fieri atque constitui iustos; per adoptionem inhærentis iustitiæ, quod probat, tum ex illis verbis, iusti constituentur multi, tum ex oppositione Christi & Adami: Sicut enim per Adamum inhærenter sumus iniusti, ita per Christium inhærenter iusti.

Resp. ad 1. Quòd nihil sit nisi mera petitio principii. Latissimè enim patet vocis constituendi vsus.

Potest aliquis fieri & constitui iustus, vel per iustitiæ infusionem, vel per imputationem, vel per declarationem. Nihil igitur firmiter ex eâ voce concludi potest: Bellarminus ipse Coium. 10. vers. 4. lit. D. concedit, quòd aliquis fieri possit iustus tum intrinsecus per adeptionem iustitiæ, tum extrinsecùs per declarationem. Quomodo ergò ex voce, fieri vel constitui, iustitiam infusam probare potest, cùm vtramque ipso fatente, nimirum imputativam & infusam quandoque significet?

Ad 2. respondemus, quòd comparatio ista non sit latiùs extendenda, quàm extendi voluit Apostolus. Vult hic monstrare sortem & amplitudinem vtriusque extremi, iustitiæ & iniustitiæ, quarum hæc ab Adamo, illa à Christo originem trahit. Confert igitur rem cum re, non autem modum cum modo. Et loquitur Apostolus de acquisitione, non autem de applicatione iustitiæ: alias πρότασις & ἀπόδοσις non conuenirent. Siuè enim per vocem, multi intelligas omnes, siue paucos, semper absurdus es, Si omnes, ἀπόδοσις est falsa, non enim omnes actu sunt iusti: Sin paucos, πρότασις est falsa, non enim pauci sunt peccatores. Ergò, si has absurditates euitare voluerimus, dicendum, quòd hæc conferantur duntaxat ratione amplitudinis, sic vt doceat Paulus, quemadmodum lapsus omnes peccatis involuit, sic & Christi iustitiam posse omnes ex ijsdem evoluere; sicut ille efficax fuit ad condemnationem, sic hanc efficacem esse ad salvationem. Latiùs hęc comparatio Apostolica extendi nec potest, nec debet, aliàs multa sequerentur absurda, videlicet 1. Sicut omnes naturaliter sunt & nascuntur peccatores, ita omnes verè & inhærenter iustos esse. 2. Sicut per carnalem generationem iniustitia in nos deriuatur, ita & iustitiam per carnalem generationem in nos propagari. Addo, quòd inobedientia illa actualis

Adami, per quæ omnes sumus constituti peccatores, nobis nõ inhæreat, sed duntaxat imputata sit. Ergò dato, quòd & modus conferatur, non tamen hinc stabiliretur iustitia infusa, sed potiùs imputata. Sicut enim actualis Adæ inobedientia nostra est, non per inhæsionem, sed imputationem duntaxat, fatentibus hæc ipsis etiam Pontificijs: Ita iustitia Christi, quâ nos iusti sumus, uostra fit non per infusionem aut inhætionem, sed per veram & realē imputationem. Deniq; concedere possumus iustitiam inhærentem perfectam esse reparatam per Christum, sed illa nobis in hac vita non infunditur, verum in futura expectatur.

XLIX. Secundum petit ex c. 3 Rom. Iustificati gratis, per gratiam ipsius. Quo in loco putat per gratiã notari iusticiam infusam, gratum facientem. Sed hunc errorem decad. 2. disp. 1. satis refutauimus. Tertium est ex 1. Cor. 6. v. 11. Et hæc quidem fuistis, sed abluti estis. Quod dictum disp. 4. huius decadis explicuimus.

L. Quartum ex Tit. 3. v. 5. Saluos nos fecit per lavacrum regenerationis & renouationis. Vnde concludit Bellarminus, iustificationem consistere in regeneratione & renouatione. Atqui Paulus ijs verbis non partes iustificationis, sed duplicem Baptismi effectum describit: Lubenter autem concedimus, quod renouatio aliquam importat mutationem, quòd autem formaliter in hac consistat nostra iustificatio, illud ex hoc loco probari nequit. Aliundè verò discimˣ, quàd iustificatio sit remissio peccatorum cuius effectus vel consequens sit renouatio, cum varijs bonis operibus.

LI. Quintum ex Hebr. 11. vbi Abel, Noah & alij dicuntur iusti, quod de inhærente iustitiâ accipiendū esse censet. Allegat etiam illud Gen. 6. v. 9. Noah dicitur vir iustˣ & perfectus. Et Luc. 1. v. 6 vbi Zacharias & Elisabetha dicuntur iusti, ambulantes in omnibus mandatis & iustificationibus Domini,

Resp. 1. Bellarminus hinc non potest aliquod causæ suæ petere patrocinium, cum opera iusta, de quibus in allegatis dictis sermo est, non sint forma, sed effecta iustorum hominum, quod insi à probat ipse cap. 15. & 16. Impertinenter igitur ab ipso ad probandum formale Iustificationis allegantur 2. Iustitia duplex est imputatina & inhærens; vtrâque dicimur iusti, verè quidem, sed variè, illa relatiuè & perfectè. Duæ hæ species iustitiæ non sunt confundendæ, sed accuratè distinguendæ. 3. Locum de Abele mutilatè citat Bellarminus. Sic enim ait Apostolus: Abel per fidem maioris pretij sacrificium obtulit, quàm Cain, per quam testimonium obtinuit, quòd esset iustus. Vbi manifestum est fidem statui causam, tùm pretiositatis sacrificij Abelis, tum etiam iustitiæ ipsius, Quare patet sermonem hîc esse de iustitia fidei, quod ipsum magis liquet ex altero testimonio, nempe quòd Noah iustitiæ, quæ per fidem est, hæres sit constitutus. Quòd verò Noah dicitur vir iustus; adde & perfectus, id potissimùm de iustitiâ fidei intelligendum est, quia inuenit gratiam coram Deo, Genes. 6. versu 8. Notes prætereà illud, quòd perfectio, quæ fidelibus in Scripturâ tribuitur, duplicem habeat respectum, videlicet fundamenti in Christo fide apprehensos deinde vel comparationis, vel oppositionis ad iniustitiam, aut iustitiam hypocriticam aliorum, vel termini perfectionis, ad quem tendit. Extra hos respectus nulla est fidelium perfectio in hoc mundo: Ipsi enim fatentur, quòd bonum non possint perficere; & sentiant stimulos carnis, &c. Quòd verò Zacharias & Elisabetha irreprehensibiles & iusti dicuntur, id non simpliciter accipiendum, (erat enim Zacharias vituperabilis, quòd Angelo non credebat, ob quam etiam incredulitatem à Deo puniebatur) sed vel de iustitiâ fidei, vel de nouâ obedientia, secundum iudicium humanum, (vel vt Augustinus scribit lib. 1. de gratia cap. 48.) secundum quandam inter homines conuersationem laudabilem atque probatam, quam nullus hominum posset iustè in accusationis & criminationis querelam vocare, & quam proterea in Dei conspectu habuisse referuntur, quia in ea homines nulla dissimulatione fallebant, sed vt apparebant, ita noti erant oculis DEI. Quòd si non tantùm secundum hominum, sed & Dei iudicium videntur haec intelligenda, quia coram DEO iusti esse dicuntur; iudicium Dei iterum hoc loco intelligi potest, non seuerum & exactum secundum legem, sed clemens & benignum secundum Evangelium. Etiamsi enim opera illa in judicio ipsius consistere non potuerint, tamen D E O grata erant & accepta, quoniam proficiscebantur à personis fidelibus; & infirmitates, que aderāt, merito Christi tegebantur. Erant igitur opera illorum irreprehensibilia, non simpliciter, sed κατά τι; quoniam id, quod reprehensibile erat, Christi pallio tegebatur.

LII. Sextum petitur ex Rom. 8. v. 29. & 1. Corinth. 15. v. 49. vbi dicuntur iusti conformes esse imagini Christi, & portare imaginem eius. Atqui CHRISTVS non fuit putatiuè iustus, sed verè & propriè. Ergò idem de nobis affirmandum: Alias sequeretur, nos magis esse conformes imagini Diaboli, quàm Christi si peccata nostra non delerentur infuso iustitiae habitu, &c.

Resp. 1. Calumniam admiscet IesuWita de iustitia putatiuâ. Non enim à nobis docetur, quod putatiuè κατά δόξαν, iusti simus, sed imputatiuè & simul verissimè, nempè iustitiâ & satisfactione Christi, per fidem apprehensâ. 2. Conformitas nostra cum imagine Christi triplex est; Vna ad imaginem gloriae, opposita ei, quæ est ad imaginem afflictorum Christi: Et de hac potissimùm agitur in citatis locis. Quæ enim oppositio instituitur inter imaginem primi Adami & secundi, ea ex sensu Apostoli, in vtroque loco mortalitatem & immortalitatem, terrenas & cœlestes corporis qualitates spectat, non peccatum propriè aut CHRISTI iustitiam imputatam. Altera ad imaginem obedientiæ CHRISTI, quam quidem imperfectè præstamus in hoc mundo, perfectè autem præstita â Chri sto, nobis applicatur. Est enim duplex vsus iustitiæ Christi : Vnus primarius, satisfactionis & meriti, quod nobis imputatur. Alter secundarius, exemplaris ac documenti, secundum quem iustitia eius, nostræ inhærentis iustitiæ regula est, quem etiam quadantenus, licèt non totaliter, exprimimus, secundum quam meritò ipsi conformes dicimur. Tertia & postrema conformitas est mortis, sepulturæ & resurrectionis Christi. Dicta verò allegata loquuntur vel de conformitate gloriæ, quæ demum futura est; vel de conformitate iustitiæ, quæ quodammodò inconformis est, cùm nemo hominum iustitiam Christi adæquare valeat.

LIII. Septimò ex Roman 6. vbi dicitur, per iustificationem, quâ morimur peccato, & resurgimus iustitiæ; repræsentari Christi mortem & resurrectionem, CHRISTVS autem non putatiuè, sed verè mortuus est.

Resp. Non dicit Apostolus, nos per iustificationem repræsentare Christi mortem: neque agitur ibi de iustificatione, sed de illius fructibus. Quòd autem scribit Paulus vers. 7. Qui mortuus est, iustificatus est à peccato; sciendum, quòd eo in loco iustificari accipiatur pro liberari, ex Hebræorum idiotismo, qui cum antecedente consequens coniungat. Ita enim hoc exponitur v. 18 deliberati à peccato, mancipati estis iustitiæ. Alienum etiam est à quæstione hoc argumentum Bellarmini. Nos enim non negamus, hominem per Baptismum mori peccato, & resurgere ad iustitiam, interim tamen distinguimus distincta Christi beneficia; Aliud enim est iustificatio, quæ fit per fidem, & confertur in Baptismo, aliud est noua obedientia siue sanctificatio, quippe illius effectum & consequens, quod non iustificat, sed à iustificato proficiscitur, & fructus est fidei.

LIV. Octavum petitur ex Rom. 8. v. 10, quod dictum à Bellarmino ita mutilatè & deprauatè citatur, vt sola lectio textus Apostoli, fraudes IesuWiticas abundè refutet. Nam quod Paulus vocat corpus, (id est, hominem non regeneratum,) & Spiritum, (id est hominem regeneratum,) id accipit IesuWita de partibus hominis duabus, corpo re nimirum & animâ, & vbi Apostolus dicit, corpus mortuum est, IesuWita sic deprauat, corpus adhuc mortale est & pro his Pauli verbis; Spiritus vita est, substituit illa, Anima, quæ viuit. Quæ deprauatio cũ sit crassifsima, non immorabimur, sed potius ad alia pergemus.


### Classis nona. Containing the sayings which Bellarmine alleged for inherent…: The tenth class Containing the arguments of Bellarmine, by which he denies that faith alone justifies
