The tenth class,

Containing the arguments of Bellarmine, by which he denies that faith alone justifies.

LV. The Jesuit argues in book 1 on justification, in the entire last thirteen chapters, against this proposition: Faith alone justifies. But most of the arguments are such that they can be very easily dissolved, and therefore we shall not devote much effort to their examination.

LVI. In chapter 12 he proposes a triple state: Does faith alone justify formally, does it alone justify dispositively, or does it alone justify conservatively? That is, is faith sufficient for preserving righteousness? He adds that the most important matter for him will be concerning dispositions: Does faith alone dispose one toward justification? To which we reply that this state is clearly alien For, if we teach that this phrase, 'Faith alone justifies,' is not to be taken dispositively; but we ask, Is there any other instrument or medium by which the righteousness of Christ is apprehended and applied to us than faith? The dissensions of our theologians, which Bellarmine objects, are not of great moment. For it is often wont to happen that at the beginnings of any controversy not all think the same, especially in such matters as do not concern the foundation itself.

LVII. Chapter 13 attempts to demonstrate that fear, love, and hope are also said in the Scriptures to justify, most of which arguments were discussed above. Chapter 14 proposes such a little argument: If faith is separated from hope and love and other virtues, without doubt it will not be able to justify. Wherefore hope and love justify together. Response: There is an homonymy in the words 'by faith alone,' which Bellarmine takes for solitary or separated faith, which we by no means teach. For true faith cannot be alone, that is, actually separated from love and hope. Faith indeed alone has this property peculiar to itself, not common with other virtues, that it apprehends in the promise of the Gospel the merit and obedience of Christ, and thus justifies. This, I say, belongs to faith alone, not to love, not to hope, or to other virtues. But it does not immediately follow that other virtues are entirely separated from faith; we teach a distinction, not a removal. Let there be a distinction between the essence or the essential properties of faith, and its existence. Faith does not exist alone without other virtues (for it is never idle), but for that reason it does not follow that by reason of its essence and essential attributes it cannot operate alone. Many things exist together which nevertheless are most distinct in their essences and essential properties. A man never exists without color; yet he reasons without the benefit of color. A man never exists without feet, yet he sees without the benefit of feet. Therefore, not all things that are joined together act jointly. For what reason? Because the unity of existence does not imply the unity of essence and essential properties, from which actions flow. Although, therefore, many things exist together, so that they cannot be separated from one another, yet because they still retain diverse essences and essential properties in this one existence, it happens that, just as one does not constitute the other, so neither does one perform and carry out the same duties entirely as the other. Thus, the hand in man is not alone, that is, without the other members of the body, and yet it alone receives what is given. The eyes are not alone without the other members; and yet they alone see. The mouth is not alone without the other members, and yet it alone eats. The splendor of the sun is never without heat, and yet it shines without heat. The gravity of the earth is not without dryness, and yet the earth is not carried downward by dryness. Thus, faith is never alone, that is, it does not exist alone without other virtues; yet it performs its essential duty, which is to justify, without them, and therefore, so that the cause may not be confused with the effect, faith must be distinguished from the virtues, both by reason of essence, and by reason of essential properties, and by reason of its duty and peculiar action, namely justification, since the essence of faith is not the essence of charity, although they exist together. Let this, therefore, be the conclusion: Justifying faith does not exist alone without works, but it justifies alone without the work and assistance of the virtues. And to this I refer the words of Luther in chapter 15 of Genesis: I know these virtues are distinguished gifts of God, I know faith does not exist without these gifts. But now the question for us is, what is the property of each? You hold various seeds in your hand; I do not ask which are joined to which, but what is the proper virtue of each. Here I say openly, what faith alone does, not with which virtues it is joined, etc.

LVIII. But the Jesuit urges that faith precedes love by nature, and therefore if it is said to justify alone, he immediately infers that it exists alone without love when it justifies. I respond. Priority of nature proceeds from essence, priority of time regards existence. I willingly concede, therefore, that faith, as it is prior to love by nature, can also perform its own office; but it does not follow that one can exist without the other. Furthermore, speaking properly, that phrase is awkward: Faith justifies before love; just as it is said awkwardly that the Sun shines before the ray, although the Sun is prior to the ray by nature. Thus, the effect of reason is to speak and to see, to which reason is prior by nature, and yet no time can be conceived in which reason exists and the property of speaking and seeing does not yet exist. Thus, justifying faith apprehends Christ first in the order of nature, and love follows; but in time they are simultaneous and cannot be separated. For this axiom is most true: The form of a thing is prior by nature to the properties which flow from it, even if they are simultaneous in time.

LIX. In chapter 15, he intends to prove that faith can in reality be separated from love and other virtues, and he does this with seven arguments. I. From John 12, verse 42. I respond. That statement speaks of dogmatic faith and historical assent only. II. From 1 Corinthians 13, v. 2. I respond. It speaks not of justifying faith, but either of historical or miraculous faith. III. From James 2, ver. 14. I respond. It speaks of hypocritical faith, or of a naked profession and boasting of faith. IV. From the similitudes which show that there are good and bad together in the Church, Matthew 3, 13, 22, 25. I respond. These statements speak only of the external profession of faith, on account of which we are called faithful, because we are in the visible assembly of the Church. V. He denies that love arises from faith as a proper effect from a proper cause, affirming that faith only disposes and inclines toward loving, for which thing we require a clear and evident reason. VI. From the absurd, because if love is necessarily joined with faith, it will follow from that that justification also depends upon works and love, and by this means no one can be certain of his own justification faith is not without works, therefore justification will depend upon works, since these are two different statements: to be without works, and to justify without works. justify. Nor does love perfect the form of faith, so that through love faith is true faith; but it is a property of faith that, with Christ apprehended in the promise of the Gospel, it exerts and exercises itself through love, from which love as an effect it is recognized and indicated that faith is true and living; just as a good tree is proven by good fruits, nor can it be gathered from this that the goodness of the tree depends upon the fruits, even if judgment is made about it from these. VII. From the consensus of the Fathers, whose testimonies speak of the profession of faith, which they deny is sufficient for salvation, since it can be separated from love: which we also publicly and privately constantly teach.

LX. Chapter 16. He argues from the removal of causes which could be given as to why faith justifies. The first is the authority of the word, since holy Scripture teaches thus: To which he himself responds negatively: But the affirmative has just now been proven. 2. It is the will of God: who wishes to justify us with the condition of faith alone. Bellarmine responds that Scripture says the contrary, which also posits the condition of repentance. Response. It is known to what things the exclusive is opposed, namely not to the word and Sacraments, not to the grace and merit of Christ, but to other apprehending instruments and good works. Therefore these can well stand together. We are justified by faith alone, and: We are not justified without the word and Sacraments. The

reconciliation is easy, and known to everyone. 3. It is the nature of faith, which alone apprehends righteousness, and by so apprehending justifies. Bellarmine objects, 1. that faith does not properly apprehend, for this belongs neither to knowledge nor to trust. 2. If it be said to apprehend in a certain way, this same thing can equally be said of love and the Sacraments. I answer: Apprehension is twofold: One is corporal, which is done with the hands: The other is spiritual, which is done with the mind. And this again is either an apprehension of the intellect, and is nothing else than the knowledge of a thing: for by apprehending a thing, we know it; Or it is an apprehension of the will, denoting desire and approach to Christ and the trustful application of his most sufficient merit. Both apprehensions concur in justifying faith, indeed in such a way that the apprehension of faith is nothing else than a trustful persuasion, by which a penitent sinner believes that Christ died for him also, and has made satisfaction for his sins, on account of which apprehension of righteousness God absolves man from the punishment of sin, and pronounces him righteous. Therefore, apprehension belongs to faith most truly; Inasmuch as it is knowledge, it apprehends by knowing; Inasmuch as it is trust, it apprehends by trusting. Join both, and you will have the true and justifying apprehension of faith. For it is not to be thought that faith justifies, insofar as it is mere knowledge and apprehension of the mind, that is, insofar as a man believes in general that Christ died for sins, but rather, insofar as it is trust and apprehension of the will, that is, insofar as a man not only holds for certain that Christ died, but also trusts that, through this very death of Christ, satisfaction has been made for his own sins also, and therefore that he will be absolved from the punishments of sins before the judgment of God. But this belongs neither to charity, nor to the Sacraments. For, as has been said, to apprehend the merit of Christ is to believe most firmly; and to judge most truly (which is the intellect's part) that Christ has satisfied for all his own sins also, and at the same time to place all confidence in this, (which belongs to the will.) And yet love performs neither. For while I love, by loving I do not confidently persuade myself that Christ has satisfied for me; for this act is not proper to love; but rather, because I know, believe, and trust that Christ has paid the λύτρον for me, therefore I love him, that is, nothing pleases me out of all things as much as Christ; I incline toward no thing more than toward Christ, which inclination is certainly not a fiducial persuasion, although they are mutually connected and joined. For there are three acts of charity: the first is seen in the affection by which we wish well to another: the second in the desire by which we wish to be united with the beloved object: the third in the joy by which, having become possessors of this union, we enjoy it. But none of these acts contains the act of apprehending. For although Bellarmine may think that the desire for union, or rather the union itself of the lover and the beloved, can be called an apprehension, and in his own sense this may be conceded; yet this is not an apprehension of the Lord's merit, which alone justifies; it is not a fiducial persuasion that CHRIST has satisfied. Wherefore the apprehension of faith is far different from that of charity: the former apprehends the merit of CHRIST, while a man persuades himself that CHRIST died for him, and places his confidence in this, and is thus justified: the latter apprehends not the action or passion of CHRIST (and thus these apprehensions differ in their objects), but CHRIST himself, or rather the whole TRINITY, while a man thinks of it more often, desires it, and delights himself uniquely in it. From which it follows that we are justified by faith alone, not by charity, as the apprehending instrument. But as regards the sacraments, the power of justifying apprehension cannot be attributed to them. For they are instruments and means not apprehending, but offering and exhibiting: but only Faith is an instrument apprehending, or receiving.

LXI. In chapter 17, he intends to prove that faith justifies by way of dignity and merit, and that there are many works which merit faith. Whence he concludes that faith does not justify alone. He proves this from testimonies which teach that faith is the cause of justification. I respond: It is one thing to say διὰ τὴν πίστιν, another to say διὰ τῆς πίστεως: The former is of cause and merit, such as are read in Romans 3 and 5, and Ephesians 1. The latter is of instrument and medium. We are said, however, to be justified not διὰ τὴν πίστιν, but διὰ τῆς πίστεως. Nor is the reason for works and faith the same in opposition; because works have the nature of inherent righteousness, but faith has the nature of righteousness imputed to us. The sense, therefore, of the Pauline assertion is this: We are justified not by works, namely as merits, but by faith, namely by reason of the apprehended merit. Therefore, when works are removed, they are removed then not only under the aspect of a false instrument, but also under the aspect of a false merit. And consequently, faith cannot have a meritorious aspect, otherwise that exclusion would be null. For, as may be noted in this concluding point, the exclusive particles in this article have a triple use.

1. They are opposed to other instruments, and it is noted that faith alone is the apprehensive medium.

2. They are opposed to works and merits, so that it may be indicated that we are not justified by any inherent dignity, but only by the righteousness of Christ imputed through faith:

3. They are opposed to the general objects of faith, such as Biblical histories and all the articles of the Christian religion, to which to assent is not to be righteous, but only faith in Christ, or faith apprehending the merit of Christ, is imputed for righteousness.

Latin:

Classis decima,

Continens argumenta Bellarmini, quibus negat fidem solam iustificare.

LV. Disputat IesuWita lib. 1. de iustificatione, totis tredecim capitibus vltimis, cōtra hanc propositionem Sola fides iustificat. Argumenta verò pleraque talia sunt, vt facilimè dissolui possint ideoque non multum operæ in eorum examinatione ponemus.

LVI. C. 12. proponit statum triplicem, An fides sola iustificet formaliter, An sola dispositiuè, an sola conseruatiuè? hoc est, num sufficiat fides ad conseruandam iustitiam? Addit qs; sibi rem potissimam fore de dispositionibus, Annè fides sola disponat ad iustificationem? Cui respondemˣ, hūc statum planè esse alienum, siquidem non dispositiuè accipiendam docemus hanc phrasin, Sola fides iustificat; sed quærimus, Annè aliud sit instrumentum vel medium, quo iusticia Christi apprehendatur, & nobis applicetur, quàm fides? De dissensionibus nostratiũ Theologorum, quæ obijcit Bellarminus, non magni sunt momenti. Sæpiùs enim solet fieri, vt sub initijs alicujus controuersiæ non omnes vnum sentiant, præsertim in talibus, quæ non concernunt ipsum fundamentum.

LVII. Cap. 13. demonstrare conatur, quòd etiam timor, dilectio & spes in Scripturis dicantur justificare, quæ argumenta pleraque suprà sunt discusssa. Cap. 14. talem proponit ratiunculam: Si fides à spe & dilectione alijsque virtutibus separetur, sine dubio iustificare non poterit. Quare spes & dilectio vnà iustificant. Respon. Est ὁμωνυμία in verbis Sola fide, quæ accipit Iesussita pro solitaria vel separata fide, quod nos minimè docemus. Nam fides vera nequit esse sola, hoc est, actu separata à dilectione & spe. Fides quidem sola habet hanc proprietatem sibi peculiarem, non cum virtutibus alijs communem, vt apprehendat in Euangelij promissione Christi meritum & obedientiam, atque ita iustificet, Hoc inquam, solius est fidei, non dilectionis, non spei, vel aliarum virtutum. Non autem statim sequitur, quòd virtutes aliæ à fide prorsus sint separatæ; Διαίρεσιν docemus, non ἀφαίρεσιν. Distinguatur inter essentiam vel essentialia fidei propria, & inter eius existentiam. Fides non existit sola sine aljjs virtutibus, (nunquam enim est otiosa) sed ob id non sequitur, quòd ratione suæ essentiæ & essentialium attributorum non sola possit operari. Multa simul existunt, quæ tamen suis essentijs & essentialibus proprietatibus maximè sunt distincta. Nunquam existit homo sine colore; attamen ratiocinatur sine beneficio coloris. Nunquam existit homo sine pedibus, attamen videt sine beneficio pedum. Non igitur omnia, quæ coniuncta sunt, coniunctim agunt. Quam ob causam? Quia vnitas existentiæ non importat vnitatem essentiæ & essentialium proprietatum, à quibus actiones profluunt. Licèt igitur multa existant vnà, vt inuicem separari nequeant, attamen quia diuersas adhuç in istâ vnâ existentiâ retinent essentias & essentiales proprietates, hinc fit, vt sicut vnum non constituit alterum, ita neque vnum eadem omninò cum altero efficiat & præstet officia. Sic manus in homine non est sola, hoc est, sine alijs membris corporis, & tamen sola accipit, quod datur. Oculi non sunt soli sine alijs membris; & tamen soli vident, . Os non est solum sine alijs membris, & tamen solum manducat. Solis splendor nunquam est sine calore, & tamen absque calore splendet Terræ gravitas non est absque siccitate, & tamen terra nõ fertur deorsum per siccitatem. Ita fides nunquam est sola, hoc est, non existit sola sine alijs virtutibus; attamen suum essentiale officium, quod est iustificare, sine ijs expedit, ideoque nè causa cum effectu confundatur, distinguenda est fides à virtutibus, tùm ratione essentiæ, tùm ratione proprietatum essentialium, tùm ratione officij & actionis peculiaris, videlicet iustificationis, quoniam essentia fidei non est essentia charitatis, licèt simul existant. Sit igitur hæc conclusio: Fides iustificans sine operibus sola non existit, sola autem sine ope & adiumento virtutum iustificat. Atque huc refero verba Lutheri in capite 15. Genes. Scio has virtutes esse insignia Dei dona, scio fidem sine his donis non existere. Sed nunc nobis quæstio est, quid cuiusque proprium sit? Tenes manu varia semina, non quæro ego, quæ quibus coniuncta sint, sed quæ cuiusque propria virtus sit. Hic apertè dico, quod fides solafaciat, non cum quibus virtutibus coniuncta sit, &c.

LVIII. Sed vrget IesuWita, quòd fides naturâ præcedat dilectionem, ideoque si sola iustificare dicatur, mox infert, quòd sola existat sine dilectione, cùm iustificat. Respond. Prioritas naturæ prouenit ab essentia, prioritas temporis spectat existentiam. Libenter igitur concedo fidem, vt naturâ prior est dilectione, sic suum etiam posse exequi officium; sed non sequitur, quòd vnum possit existere sine altero. Deindè propriè loquendo incommoda est phrasis ista: Fides ante dilectionem iustificat; non secus atque incommodè dicitur, Solem lucere ante radium, licèt Sol naturâ prior sit radio. Sic rationis effectus est loqui & videre, quibus naturâ prior est ratio, & tamen tempus nullum cogitari potest, quo existat ratio, & nondum existat proprietas loquendi & videndi. Ita fides iustificans naturæ ordine prius apprehendit Christum, & sequitur dilectio; tempore autem illa sunt simul & separari nequeunt, Nam verissimum est axioma istud: Forma rei natura prior est proprietatibus, quæ ex ea promanant, etiamsi tempore sint simul.

LIX. Capite 15. probare intendit, fidem posse re ipsâ à dilectione alijsque virtutib. separari, idque facit argumentis septem. I. Ex Iohan. 12. versu 42. Resp. dictum istud loquitur de fide dogmaticâ, & assensu historico tantùm. II. Ex 1. Corinth. 13. v. 2. Resp. Loquitur non de fide iustificâ, sed vel historicâ, vel miraculosâ. III. Ex Iacob. 2. ver. 14. Resp. Loquitur de fide hypocritica, seu de nudâ fidei professione & iactantiâ. IV. Ex similitudinibus, quæ ostēdunt in Ecclesiâ esse bonos & malos simul, Matth. 3. 13. 22. 25. Respond. Loquuntur ista dicta de externâ tantùm fidei professione, ob quam fideles dicimur, quiâ sumus in visibili cœtu Ecclesiæ. V. Negat dilectionem oriri ex fide, tanquam proprium effectum ex propriâ causâ, affirmans fidem tantùm disponere & inclinare ad diligendum, cuius rei nos requirimus perspicuam & euidentem rationem. VI. Ab absurdo, quia si necessariò cum fide coniuncta sit dilectio, inde sequetur iustificationem etiam pendere ab operibus & dilectione, ac per hoc neminem de suâ iustificatione posse esse certum. Resp. est ἀναντίποδον. Nec enim quia fides sine operib. non est, idcircò iustificatio ab operibus pendebit, cùm duo sint diuersa enunciata, esse absque operibus, & absque operib. iustificare Neqs dilectio perficit formam fidei, vt per dilectionē fides sit vera fides; verùm ea est fidei proprietas, vt Christo in Euangelij promissione apprehenso, sese exerat & exerceat per dilectionem, ex quâ dilectione tanquam effectu agnoscitur & indicatur, fidem esse veram & viuam; sicut arbor bona arguitur ex fructibus bonis, neque hinc colligi potest, bonitatem arboris pendere à fructibus, etiamsi ex his de eâ fiat iudicium. VII. Ex consensu Patrum, quorum testimonia loquuntur de fidei professione, quam illi negant sufficere ad salutem, cùm possit separi à dilectione: quod & nos publicè priuatimque constanter docemus.

LX. Cap. 16. argumentatur à remotione causarum, quæ possent reddi, cur fides iustificet. Prima est authoritas verbi, quoniam sacra Scriptura ita docet: Ad quod respondet ipse negatiuè: Affirmatiua autem iam modò probata fuit. 2. Est voluntas Dei: qui nos cum sola fidei conditione vult iustificare. Respondet Bellarminus contrarium dicere Scripturam, quæ ponat etiam conditionem pœnitentiæ. Respond. Notum est, quibus rebus opponatur exclusiua, videlicet non verbo & Sacramentis, non gratiæ & merito Christi, sed instrumentis apprehendentibus alijs & bonis operibus. Possunt igitur hæc benè stare. Sola fide iustificamur, &: Non sine verbo & Sacramentis iustificamur. Concilia-

tio est facilis, & cuiuis nota, 3. Est natura fidei, quæ sola apprehendit iustitiam, & sic apprehendendo iustificat. Excipit Bellarminus, 1. fidem propriè non apprehendere, hoc enim neque notitiæ neque fiduciæ connenire. 2. Si quodam modo apprehendere dicatur, pariter hoc ipsum posse dici de dilectione & Sacramentis. Resp. Apprehensio duplex est : Vna corporalis, quæ fit manibus: Altera Spiritualis, quæ fit animo. Et hæc rursum vel est appprehensio intellectus, & nihil est aliud, quam cognitio rei : apprehendendo enim rem, cognoscimus eam; Vel est apprehensio voluntatis, notans desiderium & accessum ad Christum eiusque meriti sufficientissimi applicationem fiducialem. Vtraque apprehensio concurrit in fide iustificante, ita quidem, vt apprehensio fidei nihil sit aliud, quàm fiducialis persuasio, quà peccator pœnitens Christum pro se quoque mortuum esse, & pro suis peccatis satisfecisse credit, ob quam iustitiæ apprehensionem Deus hominem à pœnâ peccati absoluit, & iustum pronunciat. Competit igitur fidei apprehensio verissimè; In quantum est notitia apprehendit cognoscendo; In quantum est fiducia, apprehendit confidendo. Coniunge vtrumque, & habebis veram ac iustificantem fidei apprehensionem. Non enim putandum, quòd fides iustificet, quatenus mera est notitia & apprehensio mentis, hoc est, quatenus in genere credit homo, Christum pro peccatis esse mortuum, sed potius, quatenus est fiducia & apprehensio voluntatis, hoc est, quatenus homo nō solùm pro certo habet, Christum esse mortuum, sed etiam confidit, per hanc ipsam Christi mortem, pro suis quoque peccatis satisfactum esse, ideoque se coram iudicio Dei à pœnis peccatorum absolutum iri. Hoc autem neque charitati, neque Sacramentis competit Nam, vti dixtum, apprehendere meritum Christi, est firmissimè credere; & verissimum iudicare (quod intellectus est,) Christum pro suis quoque peccatis omnibus satisfecisse, simulque in hoc fiduciam omnem collocare, (quod est voluntatis.) Atqui dilectio neutrum præstat. Dum enim diligo, diligendo non fiducialiter mihi persuadeo, Christum pro me satisfecisse; Nam hic actus non est dilectioni proprius; sed potiùs, quia scio, credo & confido, Christum pro me solvisse λύτρον, ideo ipsum diligo, hoc est, nihil mihi placet ex rebus omnibus, quàm Christus; ad nullam rem magis propendeo, quàm ad Christum, quæ propensio certè no est fiducialis persuasio, licèt sint invicem connexa & conjuncta. Actus enim charitatis tres sunt, Primus spectatur in affectu, quo alteri benè volumus: Secundus in desiderio, quo cum re amata vniri cupimus: Tertius in gaudio, quo vnionis huius compotes facti perfruimur. Nullus verò ex his actibus continet actum apprehendendi. Quamvis enim Bellarminus putet, vnionis desiderium, vel ipsam potiùs vnione amantis & amati, apprehensionem dici posse, suoq; sensu id concedi queat; attamē hæc non est apprehensio meriti Dominici, quæ sola iustificat; non est fiducialis persuasio, CHRISTVM satisfecisse. Quare longè alia est apprehensio fidei, & alia charitatis: Illa apprehendit meritum CHRISTI, dum homo sibi persuadet, CHRISTVM pro se esse mortuum, & in hoc fiduciam collocat, atque ita iustificatur: Hæc apprehendit non actionem vel passionem CHRISTI (& sic obiectis differunt hæ apprehensiones,) sed ipsum CHRISTVM, vel potiùs totam TRINITATEM, dum homo sæpiùs de illa cogitat, illam desiderat, & in eâ vnice seie oblectat. Ex quo fide solâ, non charitate, tanquam instrumento apprehendente nos iustificari. Sacramenta verò quod attinet, illis nequit vis apprehensionis iustificantis tribui. Sunt enim instrumenta & media non apprehendentia, sed offerentia, & exhibentia: Sola autem fides est instrumentum apprehendens, siue recipiens.

LXI. Capite 17. intendit probare, quòd fides iustificet per modum dignitatis & meriti, plura verò esse opera, quæ fidem merentur. Vnde concludit, fidem non iustificare solùm. Probat id ex testimonijs, quæ docent, fidei esse caussam iustificationis. Respond. Aliud est διὰ τὴν πίστιν, aliud διὰ τῆς πίστεως: Illud caussæ est & meriti, qualia leguntur Roman. 3. & 5. Ephes. 1. Hoc instrumenti & medij. Dicimur autem iustificari non διὰ τὴν πίστιν, sed διὰ τῆς πίστεως. Nec eadem est ratio operum, & fidei in oppositione; quia opera rationem habent iustitiæ inhærentis, fides autem rationem habet iustitiæ, nobis imputatæ. Sensus igitur assertionis Paulinæ hic est: Iustificamur non ex operibus, videlicet tanquam meritis, sed ex fide videlicet ratione apprehensi meriti. Proindè quando remouentur opera, tunc non solùm sub ratione falsi instrumenti, verùm etiam sub ratione falsi meriti remouentur. Et per consequens fides nequit habere rationem meritoriam, aliàs ista exclusio nulla foret. Nam vt hoc Colophonis loco notetur, particulæ exclusiuæ in hoc articulo triplicem habent vsum.

1. Opponuntur instrumentis alijs, & notatur, quòd sola fides sit medium apprehensiuum.

2. Opponuntur operibus & meritis, vt indicetur, nos non per dignitatem aliquam inhærentem, sed tantùm per Christi iustitiam fide imputatam iustificari:

3. Opponuntur obiectis fidei generalibus, qualia sunt historiæ Biblicæ & omnes articuli religionis Christianæ, quibus assentiri non est iustum esse, sed sola fides in Christum, vel Christi meritum apprehendens imputatur ad iustitiam.


### Classis nona. Containing the sayings which Bellarmine alleged for inherent…: Eleventh Class. Containing the arguments of Bellarmine, opposed specifically to the imputed righteousness of Christ

Eleventh Class. Containing the arguments of Bellarmine, opposed specifically to the imputed righteousness of Christ.

LXII. V. In Book 2 on Justification, chapter 7, Bellarmine proposes ten arguments that justification does not consist in the imputation of the righteousness of CHRIST, which we shall examine in order, yet briefly. First: Nowhere in Scripture is it read that Christ's righteousness is imputed to us for righteousness, or that we are righteous through Christ's righteousness imputed to us. Response. 1. This doctrine is held expressly, Rom. 4. v. 6. Ὧ χαρίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρίς ἔργων, 1. Corinth. 1. verse 30. Christ is made unto us of God wisdom and righteousness. 2. It is deduced from the Scriptures by good consequence, because the remission of sins is expressed by the name of non-imputation, Rom. 4. v. 7. & 8. because the Apostle denies his own or inherent righteousness, lest he should establish that which is by imputation through faith, Phil. 4. v. 8. & finally, what is the account of our sin in Christ, the same is said to be of the righteousness of Christ in us, 2. Cor. 5. v. 21.

LXIII. Second: No necessity for such an imputation can be brought forward. Response. Does not the sacrosanct authority of the divine word import a sufficiently great necessity that we should embrace this doctrine concerning imputed righteousness? For what the word of God teaches, that must necessarily be received and believed, if only one desires to be saved. Furthermore, there are also other causes for this necessity. 1. We were subject to a double evil, namely, of penalty and of guilt. To this, two benefits also had to be opposed, namely, to the penalty, the remission of sins; to the guilt, the imputation of righteousness. Two things are necessary so that the law may be satisfied: 1. that we be freed from the penalty which the law threatens: 2. that we fulfill the precepts of the law. The former is done by the imputation of the passion, the latter by the imputation of the righteousness of Christ.

LXIV. Third: If inherent righteousness is perfect and absolute, there is no need for the imputation of the righteousness of Christ. But the former, which he proves with some sayings. Therefore the latter. But to those sayings most of them were answered above. For they either speak of imputed righteousness, which we do not deny to be perfect; or they must be explained comparatively, by comparing such works with the deeds of hypocrites.

LXV. Fourth. When two contrary forms are present, one is denominated from that which is more proper. Wherefore since a twofold righteousness is present, inherent and imputed; man will be more rightly denominated just from the inherent, than from the imputed. Resp. Inherent righteousness is imperfect. Therefore it renders no one perfectly just. But he who wishes to be absolved from punishment in the judgment of God, he must be perfectly just, which cannot be done otherwise, except through the imputation of the righteousness of CHRIST.

LXVI. Fifth. It would follow that we could be called Redeemers and Mediators. Resp. The name of Redeemer and Mediator is a name of office: But the office of Christ is not imputed, nor does it become ours, but the righteousness acquired by the office. For that reason we are indeed called just, but not redeemers. The office is one thing, the fruit of the office is another; this is imputed, not that. Furthermore, in order for someone to be a Mediator, there is required a universality of the subject, so that he may have satisfied for the whole world, and an ability of person, which must be God and man, which conditions are clearly lacking in the reborn.

LXVII. Sixth: Christ restored those things which we lost in Adam: But we had lost not imputative, but inherent righteousness. Resp. There are two parts to the restoration of the Divine image: The one, the abolition of the depraved image: The other, the repair of the original one. Christ acquired and merited both: but he does not apply them at once, but gradually. In this life he begins the repair, in the other he will consummate it.

LXVIII. Seventh: If the sins of the world were imputed to Christ, it follows that he can also truly be called unjust, and a sinner, and the son of the Devil. Resp. Christ is considered in two ways, 1. In respect of himself: 2. In respect of us, insofar as he sustained our person. In respect of himself he is called just, holy, and immaculate: in respect of us he was made sin, 2 Cor. 5 v. 21, and even a curse, Gal. 3 v. 13. But he cannot be called the son of the Devil without blasphemy, because he was not inherently unjust.

LXIX. Eighth. The Church in the Canticle is called the Spouse of Christ; but it is necessary for the Spouse to be inherently beautiful. Resp. The Spouse of Christ in the Canticle confesses that she is black, and meanwhile affirms that she is comely, chap. 1 v. 5. By that confession she acknowledges her native and inherent deformity. By that affirmation she proclaims the beauty received from the Spouse, which is either imputed, or inherent, but begun. Nor do the beauty of Christ and the Church differ, but only in their subjects and the mode of property. For one and the same is the beauty of the Spousegroom and the Spouse; but it belongs to Christ by the mode of inherence; to the Church, by the mode of imputation, who is called beautiful among women, not in opposition to Christ, but to other women.

LXX. Ninth. In justification we are prepared for the vision of God, but for this, imputed purity does not suffice, but inherent is required. Resp. The purity by which we are prepared for the vision of God is as much that which we have by imputation, as that which subjectively exists in us in this life. Nor is imputation an empty thing, which is only seen or thought to be, but rather it is a most certain and most powerful thing, resting upon a most immovable foundation.

LXXI. Tenth, Christ suffered, that he might sanctify the Church, Heb. 13. Eph. 5. Tit. 2. John 17. Therefore it is inherently holy. Resp. Sanctification either signifies justification itself, consisting in the imputation of holiness; or the effect of justification, consisting in the inherence of holiness. That

Latin:

Classis vndecima. Continens argumenta Bellarmini, iustitiae Christi imputatae in specie opposita.

LXII. V. Lib. 2. de Iustificat. cap. 7. proponit Bellarminus decem argumenta, iustificationem non consistere in imputatione iustitiae CHRISTI, quae ordine, attamen breuiter, examinabimus. Primùm: Nullobi in Scriptura legitur, Christi iustitia imputari nobis ad iustitiam, vel nos iustos esse per Christi iustitia nobis imputatam. Respond. 1. Habetur haec doctrina expressa, Rom. 4. v. 6. Ὧ χαρίζεται δικαιοσύνην χωρίς ἔργων, 1. Corinth. 1. vers. 30. Christus factus est nobis à Deo sapientia & iustitia. 2. Per bonam consequentiam è Scripturis deducitur, quia remissio peccatorum non imputationis nomine exprimitur, Rom. 4. v. 7. & 8. quia propriam seu inhaerentem iustitiam negat Apostolus, nè stabiliat eam, quae ex imputatione est per fidem, Phil. 4. v. 8. & tandem quae est ratio peccati nostri in Christo, eadem esse dicitur iustitiae Christi in nobis, 2. Cor. 5. v. 21..

LXIII. Secundum: Nulla necessitas talis imputationis afferri potest. Resp. Sacrosancta verbi diuini authoritas, annòn necessitatem satis magnam importat, vt hâc doctrinam de imputatâ iustitiâ amplectamur? Quod enim verbum Dei docet, illud necessariò est recipiendum & credendum, si modò saluari quis cupiat. Deinde sunt & aliae necessitatis huius causae. 1. Duplici malo subiecti eramus, poenae nimirum & culpae. Huic duo etiam beneficia opponi oportuit, videlicet poenae, remissionem peccatorum; Culpae imputationem iustitiae, Duo sunt necessaria vt legi satis fiat, 1. vt liberemur à poenâ, quâ lex minatur: 2. vt praecepta legis impleamus. Illud fit imputatione passionis, hoc imputatione iustitiae Christi.

LXIV. Tertium: Si iustitia inhaerens perfecta est & absoluta, non opus est imputatione iustitiæ Christi. Verùm prius, quod probat nonnullis dictis. Ergò posterius. Sed ad dicta ista pleraque supra fuit responsum. Vel enim loquuntur de iustitiâ imputata, quam perfectam esse non negamus; vel explicanda sunt comparatè, conferendo talia opera cum factis hypocritarum.

LXV. Quartum. Duabus formis contrarijs præsentibus, is denominatur ab eo, quod magis est propriũ. Quare cùm adsit duplex Iustitia, inhærens & imputata; homo ab inhærente potiùs, quàm ab imputata iustus erit denominandus. Resp. Inhærens iustitia imperfecta est. Ergo neminem reddit perfectè iustum. Qui autem vult à pœna absolui in iudicio Dei, illum oportet perfectè iustum esse, quod aliter fieri nequit, nisi per imputationem iustitiæ CHRISTI.

LXVI. Quintum. Sequeretur, nos dici posse Redemptores & Mediatores. Resp. Nomen Redemptoris & Mediatoris est nomen officij: Non autem imputatur, nec nostrum fit Christi officium, sed officio acquisita iustitia. Ob id iusti quidem, sed non redemptores dicimur. Aliud est officium, Aliud est officij fructus, Hic, non illud imputatur. Deinde vt aliquis sit Mediator, requiritur vniuersalitas subiecti, vt pro toto mundo satisfecerit, & habilitas personæ, quam oportet esse Deum & hominem, quæ conditiones in renatis planè deficiunt.

LXVII. Sextum: Christus restituit ea, quæ in Adamo perdidimus: Non autem imputatiuam, sed inhærentem iustitiam perdideramus. Resp. Restitutionis ima ginis Diuinæ duæ sunt partes, Altera, deprauatæ imaginis abolitio: Altera, pristinæ reparatio. Vtrumque Christus acquisiuit & promeruit: verùm non statim, sed paulatim applicat. In hac vita reparationem inchoat, in altera consummabit.

LXVIII. Septimum: Si Christo imputata sunt peccata mundi, sequitur quòd & verè iniustus, & peccator, & filius Diaboli dici queat. Resp. Christus consideratur dupliciter, 1. Respectu sui: 2. Respectu nostri, quatenus personam nostram sustinuit. Respectu sui dicitur justus, sanctus & immaculatus: respectu nostri factus est peccatum, 2. Corinth. 5. v. 21. imo & maledictum, Galat. 3. v. 13. Filius autem Diaboli sine blasphemia nuncupari nequit, quia inhærenter injustus non fuit.

LXIX. Octavum. Ecclesia in cantico vocatur Sponsa Christi; Sponsam autem inhærenter oportet pulchram esse. Respond. Sponsa Christi in cantico fatetur, se esse nigram, & interim affirmat se esse decoram, cap. 1. v. 5. Confessione illâ agnoscit deformitatem suam nativam & inhærentem. Affirmatione illâ prædicat pulchritudinem acceptam à Sponso, quæ vel imputata est, vel inhærens, sed inchoata. Neque pulchritudo Christi & Ecclesiæ differunt, sed subjectis duntaxat & modo proprietatis. Una enim & eadem est pulchritudo Sponsi & Sponsæ; sed Christo competit modo inhærentiæ; Ecclesiæ, modo imputationis, quæ pulchra dicitur inter mulieres, non opposita ad Christum, sed ad alias mulieres.

LXX. Nonum. In justificatione præparamur ad visionem Dei, ad hanc autem non sufficit mundities imputata, sed requiritur inhærens. Respon. Mundities, quâ præparamur ad visionem Dei, tàm ea est, quàm imputatione habemus, quàm quæ nobis subjectivè inest in hac vitâ. Neque imputatio est res inanis, quæ tantùm videatur aut putetur esse, sed potiùs res est certissima & potentissima, fundamento nitens immotissimo.

LXXI. Decimum, Christus passus est, ut sanctificaret Ecclesiam, Ebr. 13. Ephes. 5. Tit. 2. Iohan. 17. Ergo inhærenter sancta est. Resp. Sanctificatio vel significat ipsam justificationem, consistentem in sanctitatis imputatione; vel justificationis effectum, consistentem in sanctitatis inhæsione. Ista dictis


### Classis duodecima

is denoted; this is only begun in this age, and yet it must also be ascribed in full to the merit of Christ.

Twelfth Class. Containing arguments, taken from the analogy of faith and reason:

LXXII. 1. If the renewal of the mind is prior to faith, it will also be prior to justification; and consequently its cause, not its effect. The former is true. Therefore also the latter. The minor premise is proven: From natural powers no one can believe. Since therefore faith is partly knowledge, partly trust, it will be necessary that he who ought to believe should first have an enlightened intellect and a changed will, so that he may thus assent to the word of God, insofar as his mind is enlightened, and be able to place trust in Christ, insofar as his will is changed. Therefore renewal always precedes faith, and thus also justification itself. It will not, therefore, be its effect or its consequence.

Resp. It is false that no one can believe unless he is already totally renewed in act. For faith is twofold, Actual and Habitual: The latter indeed cannot have a place except in a man already renewed; but the reason for the former is different. For the cause of faith is the Holy Spirit, who works it either immediately without us; or mediately together with us, and through the gift of renewal, granted to justified men. The first faith of a sinful man who is to be justified (which is not habitual, since it is the first) proceeds and is excited without us immediately, and only by the Holy Spirit, who by his word causes us to assent and trust, and therefore this grace is called operating, not cooperating; because the gift of renewal has not yet been infused. And for this faith, renewal is not necessary; since the immediate, or rather the solitary, action of the Holy Spirit suffices. And thus stands the faith of those to be justified, but as for that which to the justified concerns, whose faith is as it were habitual, we willingly concede that they are renewed, and therefore the cause of that faith can be twofold; the Holy Spirit and the renewed mind, whence the grace of God, which produces this faith in the regenerate, is said not to be simply operating, but cooperating, so that by this very fact it may be indicated that it is not the solitary cause of habitual faith, but that there is present at the same time also that with which it may work, or with which the grace of the Holy Spirit may cooperate, namely that inherent and incipient holiness.

LXXIII. II. By faith we are righteous; faith is a work: Therefore by works we are righteous. Bellarmine inculcates this argument in book 1 of Justification, chapter 6, where he says: The act of faith is a certain work and indeed a notable one, and by this name it is called in the Gospel of John 6. The Lord saying, Work not for the food which perishes, but for that which remains unto eternal life, the Jews answered; What shall we do, that we may work the works of God? To whom the Lord says, This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.

Response. 1. That the Papists can infer nothing solid from this for obtaining their cause, since they think that justification consists not formally in works (which is what is concluded by this argument), but in an infused habit of righteousness. See Bellarmine, book 2 of Justification, chapter 14, where he says: We are not formally righteous by our work, but by the work of God. 2. As regards that passage in John 6:29, we say that the words of Christ are accommodated to the question of his hearers, which is contained in verse 28, What shall we do, that we may work the works of God, as if they were saying, it is already sufficiently clear to us from the divine law what works God requires, namely circumcision, sacrifices, etc. Why therefore do you command us to work for food? Are you about to prescribe other works for us than Moses prescribed? Here Christ answers: This is the work of God, etc. Whence it is clear that the designation of work in this place is broad and general, and denotes the worship of God. It is therefore the opinion of Christ: This is the one true and highest worship of God, to believe in the Messiah and Redeemer of the world. Faith is called the work of God, 1. Because it is commanded by God, Matt. 17, ver. 5. Hear him. 2. Because it is the most excellent worship, by which God is honored by us, and thus κατ’ ἐξοχὴν; 3. Because it is not of human powers, but a gift of God himself, 1 Cor. 12, ver. 3, 9. Phil. 1, ver. 29. 3. There are four terms: For faith in the major premise is taken relatively, in the minor absolutely, whence arises the πλεονεξία of terms. For if the major premise takes faith absolutely, it is false, for we do not say that faith justifies insofar as it is a work, but insofar as it is an instrument, apprehending the merit of Christ.

LXXIV. The Papists insist, The apprehension itself is a work. Therefore if faith justifies, as an apprehension, a work as a work will justify. For the very τὸ apprehendere is nothing else than to work. I respond, there is an ὁμωνυμία in the word work: For it is taken 1. γενικῶς, for every action, without the addition of any respect; and thus it cannot be denied that faith or the apprehension of merit is a certain work of the Lord. 2. ἐιδικῶς & ἰδίως for a work commanded in the law, following faith, with this addition, that it simultaneously includes the notion of merit. And such works are understood, and such actions, when our people say, we are not justified by works, that is, we are not justified on account of moral works. For they deny that we are justified by works for this reason, that no merit may be ascribed to them, but that justification may remain gratuitous, and be placed in the sole imputation of the righteousness of Christ. But if therefore these themes are granted; 1. That we are in no way justified and saved on account of works. 2. That we are in no other way righteous than by the imputation of the merit of Christ; then we will easily grant to the Papists, that a certain work or some action concurs in justification, just as in other acceptances of gifts, it is necessary that apprehension should concur, yet we are not made partakers of the gift on account of this apprehension, as if it were a merit: Thus it can be said that by apprehending the merit of the Lord we are justified, yet not on account of that apprehension; and therefore it still remains that we are not justified by works nothing other than to be justified on account of works. Therefore we do not exclude every work nor every action, but only the meritorious work and the meritorious action.

We are not justified by works, namely as by a meritorious cause; but we are justified by faith, which is a work, yet not as by a merit, but as by an instrument and means, which does not effect, but applies righteousness. And thus these things do not conflict: we are justified by faith, which is a work, and we are not justified by works. One could also distinguish between works and actions, so that some are receiving actions, which on account of the reception are more passions than actions, such as faith: some are producing something, and not receiving, but proceeding forth, and of these it is said that they do not justify.

LXXV. III. Evil works condemn, therefore good ones save, because the reason for contraries is the same, or because the consequences of contraries are contrary.

Response 1. To the antecedent, that is not simply granted. For evil works precisely will not condemn, but as was asserted in the Colloquy of Montbéliard by Jakob Andreae, unbelief will rather condemn, namely because men did not apprehend the merit of Christ, by which satisfaction was sufficiently made for their sins. Thus Judas will be condemned not so much because he betrayed Christ, as because he did not apprehend the merit of Christ, by which satisfaction was made for this betrayal, according to that passage in John 3, verse 18: He who believes in him will not be condemned; but he who does not believe is already condemned, John 16, verse 9. The Holy Spirit will convict the world of sin, because they do not believe in me. Where such an assertion is held: He who believes in Christ is justified or is not condemned: why? because he believes. But he who does not believe is condemned, why? because he does not believe. Thus the λόγος ἄμεσος of condemnation is unbelief. And although other sins are also said in the Scriptures to condemn, and those doing such things to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, on account of evil works as in Matthew 25, Galatians 5 verse 21, nevertheless this is to be reconciled in such a way that all sins condemn, namely efficiently, since they merit eternal damnation; but unbelief alone condemns, formally and actually; for on account of this the impenitent will actually be condemned. All sins are worthy of eternal death, and have guilt annexed to them; they can therefore condemn; but they do not actually condemn, but rather unbelief alone does this. Thus the reborn are not condemned on account of adhering sins, but the unfaithful are condemned by it. How so? Because the former believe, the latter do not believe. Therefore the cause of actual damnation is not the sins themselves, but rather unbelief. 2. We deny the consequence, and to the proof we say, that the reason for contraries is the same only then, if the contraries are equal, that is, if the contrariety is true. But the contraries in this place are not equal; therefore the contrariety is not true. For evil works are perfectly evil, and perfectly repugnant to the law of God: But good works are not perfectly good. For which reason in Romans 6, last verse, the Apostle did not wish to draw an argument from contraries; but when he had said, the wages of sin is death, and from the nature of contraries he should now say, the wages of righteousness and good works is eternal life, he says, The gift of God is eternal life. Indeed, even if our works were perfect, yet because they are otherwise owed, they cannot be meritorious, according to that, Luke 17, verse 10, Even if you have done all things, etc. Therefore those who are saved, are saved by grace: and therefore not from works. Those who are condemned, are justly condemned, and therefore on account of evil works, because justice is not just, if it does not find sufficient causes of condemnation in the accused. To this may be referred that of Augustine, book 3 against Julian, chapter 18. God is good, God is just: He can save without good merits, because He is good; He cannot condemn without evil merits, because He is just.

LXXVI. Finally IV. The fulfilling of the law is justice, Love is the fulfilling of the law, Rom. 13. v. 10. Therefore by love we are justified.

Resp. Concerning legal justice I concede the whole argument, namely that he who perfectly loves both God and neighbor is legally just. But the question is, Can anyone perfectly love God? Here Scripture instructs us that no one can do this, and therefore another means must be sought if we wish to be just, which the Gospel shows, where Christ comes to our aid with His merit, which when it is apprehended, then at last we are rendered truly just. Wherefore if the distinction between Legal and Evangelical justice is observed, we shall easily be able to respond to this and similar arguments.

Latin:

stis denotatur; hæc tantùm inchoatur in hoc seculo, & tamen Christi etiam merito in solidum adscribenda est.

Classis duodecima. Continens argumenta, ex analogia fidei & ratione desumpta:

LXXII. 1. Si renouatio mentis prior est fide, prior etiam erit iustificatione; & per consequens causa eius, non effectus. Verum est prius. Ergo & posterius. Minor probatur: Ex naturalibus viribus nemo potest credere. Cùm igitur fides partim sit notitia, partim fiducia, necessum erit, vt is qui debet credere, illuminatum prius habeat intellectum & immutatam voluntatem, vt sic verbo Dei assentiri, quatenus mens eius est illuminata, & in Christum fiduciam possit collocare, quatenus voluntas eius immutata. Ergò renouatio semper præcedit fidem, adeóque & ipsam iustificationem. Huius igitur vel effectus vel consequens non erit.

Resp. Falsum est, quòd nemo possit credere, nisi qui sit iam ipso actu totaliter renouatus. Nam fides duplex est, Actualis & Habitualis: Hæc quidem locum habere nequit nisi in homine iam renouato; sed illius alia est ratio. Nam fidei causa est Spiritus sanctus, qui operatur illam vel immediatè sine nobis; vel mediatè vnà cum nobis, & per donum renouationis, hominibus iustificatis concessum. Fides prima hominis peccatoris & iustificandi, (quæ habitualis nõ est, cùm prima sit) prouenit & excitatur sine nobis immediatè, & tantùm à Spiritu sancto, qui verbo suo facit, vt assentiamur & confidamus, ideoque gratia hæc vocatur operans, nõ cooperans; quia nondúm infusum est renouationis donum. Et ad hanc fidem non est necessaria renouatio; siquidem sufficit immediata Spiritus sancti, vel potiùs solitaria eius actio. Atque ita se habet fides iustificandorum, Quod autem iustificatoattinet, quorum fides quasi habitualis est, libenter concedimus, quòd illi sint renouati, ideoque fidei istius causa duplex esse potest; Spiritus sanctus & mens Renouata, vnde gratia Dei, quæ fidem hanc in renatis efficit, non simpliciter operans, sed cooperans dicitur, vt hoc ipso indicetur, illam non esse solitariam causam fidei habitualis, sed adesse simul etiam, cum quâ operetur, vel cui cooperetur gratia Spiritus sancti, videlicet inhærentem istam & inchoatam sanctitatem.

LXXIII. II. Fide sumus iusti; fides est opus: Ergò operibus sumus iusti. Argumentum hoc inculcat Bellarminus lib. 1. de iustificat. capite 6. vbi dicit: Actus fidei est quoddam opus & quidem insigne, & hoc nomine appellatur in Evangelio Iohan. 6. Dicente Domino, Operamini non cibum, qui perit, sed qui permanet in vitam æternam, responderunt Iudæi; Quid faciemus, vt operemur opera Dei? quibus Dominus ait, hoc est opus D E I, vt credatis in eum, quem misit ille.

Respond. 1. Quòd nihil indè solidi queant inferre Pontificij, pro obtinenda causa sua, siquidem iustificationem non formaliter in operibus (quod hoc argumento concluditur,) sed in habitu iustitiæ infuso consistere putant. Vid Bellarminum lib. 2. de iustificat. cap. 14. vbi inquit: Non formaliter iusti sumus opere nostro, sed opere Dei. 2. Quod attinet locum istum Ioh. 6. v. 29. dicimus, verba Christi esse accommodata ad quæstionem suorum auditorum, quæ continetur vers. 28. Quid faciemus, vt operemur opera Dei, quasi dicant, iam antè nobis satis constat, ex diuinâ lege, quæ opera D E V S requirat, nempè circumcisionem, sacrificia, &c. Quid ergo est, quòd nos iubes operari cibum? An alia opera nobis præcepturus es, quàm Moses præcepit? Hic Christus respondet: Hoc est opus D E I, &c. Undè constat appellationem operis hoc loco latam esse & generalem, Deique cultum notare. Est igitur Christi sententia: Unus hic verus & summus Dei cultus est, credere in Messiam & Redemptorem mundi. Dicitur autem fides Opus Dei, 1. Quia à Deo præcepta est, Matth. 17. ver. 5. Hunc audite. 2. Quia præstantissimus cultus est, quo Deus à nobis honoratur, & sic κατ’ ἐξοχὴν; 3. Quia non est virium humanarum, sed donum ipsius Dei, 1. Cor. 12. verf. 3. 9. Philip. 1. vers. 29. 3. Sunt quatuor termini: Fides enim in maiore accipitur relatiuè, in minore absolutè, vndè emergit πλεονεξία terminorum. Maior enim si fidem absolutè sumat, falsa est, nos enim non dicimus fidem iustificare in quantum opus est, sed quatenus instrumentum est, apprehendens meritum Christi.

LXXIV. Instant Pontificij, Ipsa apprehensio est opus. Ergo si fides iustificat, quà apprehensio, opus quà opus iustificabit. Ipsum enim τὸ apprehendere nihil est aliud, quàm operari. Respond. est ὁμωνυμία in vocabulo operis: Accipitur enim 1. γενικῶς, pro omni actione, sine additamento alicuius respectus; & sic fidem vel apprehensionem meriti, Domini opus quoddam esse negari haut potest. 2. ἐιδικῶς & ἰδίως pro opere in lege præcepto, fidem consequente, cum additione hac, vt simul includat rationem meriti. Atque talia opera intelliguntur, & tales actiones, quando nostri dicunt, operibus non iustificamur, hoc est, propter opera moralia non iustificamur. Idcò enim negant, operibus nos iustificari, nè ijs aliquod adscribatur meritum, sed vt gratuita maneat iustificatio, & ponatur in solâ imputatione justitiæ Christi. Quòd si ergo hæc themata concedantur; 1. Nos nullo modo propter opera iustificari & saluari. 2. Nos non alio modo iustos esse, quàm imputatione meriti Christi; tunc facilè dabimus Pontificijs, in iustificatione concurrere opus quoddam vel actionem quampiam, sicut in aliis acceptationib. donorum, necesse est, vt concurrat apprehensio, non tamen propter hanc apprehensionem, tanquam meritum reddimur participes doni: Ita potest dici, quòd apprehendendo meritum Domini iustificemur, non tamen propter istam apprehensionem; Ideoque adhuc manet, quòd operibus non iustificemur, quia iustificari operibus, nihil est aliud, quàm propter opera iustificari. Proindè non omne opus nec omnem actionem excludimus, sed duntaxat opus meritorium, & actionem meritoriam.

Operibus non iustificamur, videlicet tanquam causâ meritoria; Fide autem, quæ opus est, iustificamur, verùm non tanquàm merito, sed velut instrumento & medio, quod non efficit, sed applicat iustitiam. Atque sic non pugnant ista, Fide, quæ opus est, iustificamur, & operibus non iustificamur. Distigui etiam posset inter opera & actiones, ita quod quædam sint actiones recipientes, quæ ob receptionem magis sunt passiones, quàm actiones, qualis fides: quædam producentes aliquid, & non recipientes, sed egredientes, & de his dicitur, quòd non iustificent.

LXXV. III. Mala opera damnant, E. bona saluant, quia contrariorum eadem est ratio, vel quia contraria contrariorum consequentia.

Respond. 1. Ad antecedens, illud simpliciter non concedi. Mala enim opera præcisè non damnabunt, sed sicut in Colloquio Mompelg. à Iacobo Andreæ assertum fuit, incredulitas potiùs damnabit, nempè quia homines non apprehenderunt meritum Christi, quo sufficienter pro ipsorum peccatis satisfactum est Sic Iudas damnabitur non tàm, quia Christum prodidit, quàm quia Christi meritum, quo pro istâ proditione satisfactum, non apprehendit, iuxta illud Iohan. 3. vers. 18. Qui credit in eum, non condemnabitur; qui verò non credit, iam condemnatus est, Ioh. 16. vers. 9. Spiritussanctum arguet mundum de peccato, quia non credunt in me. Vbi assertio habetur talis : Qui credit in Christum, iustificatur sivè non condemnatur: quare? quia credit. Qui verò non credit condemnatur, Quare? quia non credit. Sic λόγος ἄμεσος condemnationis est incredulitas. Et licèt quoque in Scripturis alia peccata dicantur damnare, & talia facientes à regno cœlorum excludi, propter mala opera ut Matth. 25. Galat. 5 versu 21. tamen hoc ita conciliandum est, quòd omnia peccata damnent, videlicet efficienter, quoniam merentur æternam damnationem; sola autem incredulitas damnat, formaliter & actualiter; ob hanc enim impœnitentes actu condemnabuntur. Omnia peccata digna sunt morte æternâ, & annexum habent reatum; Possunt ergò damnare; sed actu non damnant, verùm sola incredulitas hoc facit. Sic renati ob peccata adhærentia non damnantur, infideles autem damnantur ab ea. Quî sic? Quoniam illi credunt, hi non credunt. Ergo actualis damnationis causa non sunt ipsa peccata, sed potiùs incredulitas. 2. Negamus consequentiam, & ad probationem dicimus, tunc demum contrariorum eandem esse rationem, si contraria sint paria, hoc est, si vera sit contrarietas. At contraria hoc loco non sunt paria; proin dè non est vera contrarietas. Nam mala opera sunt perfectè mala, perfectèque repugnant legi Dei: At bona opera non sunt perfectè bona. Quam ob causam Rom. 6. v. vlt. Apostolus noluit argumentum ducere à contrarijs; sed cùm dixisset, stipendium peccati est mors, & ex naturâ contrariorum iam dicere deberet, stipendium iustitiæ & bonorum operum est vita æterna, dicit, Donum Dei vita æterna. Imò etiamsi perfecta forent opera nostra, tamen quia aliàs sunt debita, meritoria esse non possunt, iuxta illud, Luc. 10. v. 10. Etiamsi omnia feceritis, &c. Igitur qui saluantur, ex gratiâ saluantur: & proinde non ex operibus. Qui damnantur, juste damnantur, ideoque propter mala opera, quia justitia justa non est, si non causas damnationis sufficientes in reo inueniat. Potest huc referri illud Augustini lib. 3. contra Iulian, capite 18. Bonus est Deus, justus est Deus: potest sine bonis meritis saluare, quia bonus est; non potest sine malis meritis damnare, quia justus est.

LXXVI. Tandem IV. Impletio legis est justitia, Dilectio est impletio legis, Rom. 13. v. 10. Ergo per dilectionem justificamur.

Resp. De legali justitia concedo totum argumentum, quod videlicet is, qui perfecte & Deum & proximum diligit, legaliter justus sit. Quæritur autem, Num aliquis perfecte possit diligere Deum? Hic Scriptura nos erudit, quod hoc nemo possit, ideoque aliud medium sit quærendum, si justi esse velimus, quod monstrat Evangelium, ubi succurrit Christus cum suo merito, quod quando apprehenditur, tum demum vere justi reddimur. Quare si obseruetur distinctio inter justitiam Legalem & Evangelicam, facile ad hoc & similia argumenta respondere poterimus.


### Classis duodecima: To God Alone the Glory

TO GOD ALONE THE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 32 Disputation IX. On the Certainty of Justification, or of the Remission of Sins

Presiding: Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology.

Respondent: Bernhard Derschov from Königsberg, Prussia.

Thesis I.

We have divided the doctrine of justification into three principal chapters. The first dealt with the terms frequently occurring in this article. The second explained the individual causes in which the whole business of our dikaio- seos consists. The third chapter remains, where we must discourse on the Certainty of Justification, namely, whether a Christian can and ought to believe with certainty that his sins have been freely remitted to him on account of Christ? This question is grave and of the greatest importance, indeed so much so that if one errs regarding its decision, we are cast headlong into mere doubts, nay, into the very abyss of despair, with the eternal destruction of souls. Therefore, it must be diligently inquired what is to be established concerning this theme according to the guidance of Scripture? We, however, fight for the certainty of salvation, the Papists for doubt. Therefore, so that the true doctrine may be both known and asserted, we shall form two questions.

I. What is the true state of the controversy between us and the Papists concerning the certainty of grace.

II. By what arguments especially we may be able to impugn doubt and prove certainty?

Latin:

Praes. Balth. Meisnero, SS. Th. D.

Resp. Bernhardo Derschovy Regiomontano Borusso.

Thesis. I.

DOctrinam de iustificatione in tria praecipuè capita dispescuimus, Primum egit de terminis, in hoc articulo saepè occurrentibus. Secundum expoluit singulas causas, in quibus totum dikaioseos nostrae negotium consistit. Restat caput tertium, vbi de Certitudine Iustificationis disserendum, Num videlicet Christianus certò & possit & debeat credere, sibi propter Christum peccata gratuitò esse remissa? Grauis est maximique momenti haec quaestio, ita quidem, vt si circa illius decisionem erretur, in meras dubitationes, imò ipsius desperationis voraginem, cùm aeterno animarum exitio praecipitemur. Diligenter proindè inquirendum erit, quid secundum Scripturae ductum de hoc themate statuendum sit? Nos autem pugnamus pro certitudine salutis, Pontificij pro dubitatione. Vt igitur vera doctrina & cognoscatur & asseratur, duas quaestiones formabimus.

I. Quis inter nos & Pontificios de certitudine gratiae verus sit controuersiae status.

II. Quibus praecipuè argumentis dubitationem impugnare, certitudinem probare valeamus?


### Question I

II. Regarding the formation of the state [of the question], the following chapters may be observed. 1. The dissension of the Papists. 2. The tergiversation of the Council of Trent. 3. The opinion of Bellarmine. 4. Whether the Papists advocate doubt? 5. The origin and sources of this dogma. 6. The exposition of our opinion. 7. Τὰ μὲν ῥητά, 8. The true state of the controversy, concerning which members we shall treat in order.

III. 1. THE DISSENSION OF THE PAPISTS. Not even Bellarmine himself could disguise this, since in book 3 of Justification, chapter 11, he expressly confesses that three opinions are numbered among Catholics, of which one, he says, which is that of Ambrosius Catharinus, not only excludes all doubt, but also adds that the righteous can have the certainty of divine faith concerning their justification. The second opinion does not indeed teach the certainty of divine faith, yet it affirms that perfect men can, and indeed are even accustomed to, come to that security, so that they have no fear concerning their security. The third, he says, is more common in the Church, which does not remove all fear, and grants some certainty, but only moral and conjectural. Thus, therefore, in the Roman Church, some wish for certainty to be attributed to all the righteous, some only to the perfect, and some to no Christian at all.

And indeed, that huge disagreement between Ambrosius Catharinus, Archbishop of Minori, and Dominicus à Soto is well known, the former of whom defended the certainty of justification most gravely with many arguments, while the latter attacked it most fiercely, when he responded to Catharinus thus: The dissension, which you think exists between my mind and yours in nothing beyond words, is this in a matter of the greatest importance. Furthermore, that you think a man can be made certain of the certainty of his grace, which although it may not be equal to catholic faith, is nevertheless true faith, that is, excluding all doubt whatsoever, and that indeed by common law, namely by that common testimony, which, with Paul as the author, the Holy Spirit renders to our spirit, that we are children of God; but this, with all respect to his peace and authority, I believe to be entirely false. Nor, however, did Catharinus alone acknowledge the common error of the Roman Church, but besides him others also have not obscurely approved our doctrine concerning certainty. For in the Enchiridion of Cologne, published in the year '36, these most clear words are read on folio 170: We confess it to be true that for the justification of a man it is entirely required that a man believe not only generally that sins are remitted to those who are truly penitent on account of Christ, but also that they have been remitted to the believing man himself on account of Christ through faith. And this opinion of the Enchiridion is vehemently commended by Georgius Cassander in his consultation, article 4, page 11, and he adds that that book had been highly praised by all the more learned theologians even throughout Italy and France, as one which most beautifully presents the sum of the opinion of the ancients concerning the Christian religion (from whose writings it is as it were confirmed): but to Bellarmine that book seems worthy of ecclesiastical censure, book 3 de Iustific. chapter 3. The same Cassander mentions on page 12 that that very explanation (concerning the certainty of the remission of sins) had been placed in the book of the Imperial Majesty at Ratisbon, whose manner of speaking, inasmuch as it was not sufficiently scholastic, although Eck did not approve of it in all respects, he writes that he did not disapprove of the thing itself, to which his colleagues had consented. In that book, however, it is thus established: It is a firm and sacred doctrine that the sinner is justified through a living and efficacious faith. Moreover, we call living faith the motion of the Holy Spirit, by which those who are truly penitent for their old life are raised up to God, and truly apprehend the mercy promised in Christ, so that they now truly feel that they have received the remission of sins and reconciliation, on account of the merit of Christ, by the gratuitous goodness of God, and they cry out, Abba Father. Cassander adds on page 15: Certainly there is no one among the ecclesiastics, nor indeed among the Scholastics, who does not diligently urge, and deems it should be opposed to doubt and diffidence. And page 17. Furthermore, the doctors of this age say they do not teach a doubt, whereby one might doubt and be diffident concerning the mercy of GOD, but the fear of GOD, by which the solicitude of working well and of preserving the received glory might be excited and increased in us, concerning which the Apostle says: Work out your salvation with fear and trembling. This they call a chaste and filial fear, which perfect charity does not cast out, but revives and fosters, which fear always has confidence and hope of paternal benevolence joined to it. Cornelius Bitontinus wrote similar things in chapter 8 of Romans, where these words are: Those who are in Christ Jesus have nothing from which they ought to fear, since they are secure concerning their salvation. And it is reported of Antonio Marinario that in the assembly of the Fathers of the Council of Trent on the 4th Sunday in Lent, in the year 1546, he expressly refuted doubt, whose words, since they are prolix, I shall not transcribe, but they can be seen in Mr. Dr. Gerhard, Volume 3, Loci Communes, article on justification, § 93, page 1241. Hence Bellarmine himself admits in book 3 of Justification, chapter 1: That the uncertainty of justice and grace must be proven not only against heretics, but also against certain Catholics. Therefore, the so often boasted agreement and unity of the Romanists falls, nor is the Papal doctrine rendered little suspected, inasmuch as it is so uncertain that it is by no means approved even by the more learned Papistic theologians, who are exercised in Scripture.

Latin:

II. Circa formationem status observari possunt sequentia capita. 1. Dissensio Pontificiorum. 2. Tergiversatio Concilii Tridentini. 3. Opinio Bellarmini. 4. Num Pontificii propugnent dubitationem? 5. Origo & fontes huius dogmatis. 6. Expositio nostrae sententiae. 7. Τὰ μὲν ῥητά, 8. Verus controversiae status, de quibus membris ordine agemus.

III. 1. DISSENSIO PONTIFICIORVM. Hanc nè quidem Bellarminus ipse dissimulare potuit, siquidem l. 3. de Iustif. c. 11. expressè fatetur, tres numerari inter Catholicos sententias, quarum Vna inquit, quae est Ambrosii Catharini, non solùm dubitationem omnem excludit, sed etiam addit, posse iustos habere de sua iustificatione certitudinem fidei divinae. Altera sententia non docet quidem certitudinem fidei divinae, affirmat tamen, posse, imò etiam solere homines perfectos ad eam securitatem venire, vt nullam habeant de sua securitate formidinem. Tertiam ait, in Ecclesia communiorem esse, quae non tollatur omnis formido, & concedatur aliqua certitudo, sed moralis tantùm & coniecturalis Ita ergò in Ecclesia Romana quidam certitudinem omnibus iustis, quidam solis perfectis, quidam nulli prorsus Christiano tributam volunt.

Et sanè notum est ingens istud dissidium Ambrosii Catharini, Archiepiscopi Minoriensis, & Dominici à Soto, quorum ille iustificationis certitudinem multis argumentis gravissimè defendit, hic acerrimè impugnavit, dum Catharino sic respondit. Dissensio, quam inter meam, tuamq; mentem nullam extra verba esse existimas, haec est in re maxima. Porrò quod tu arbitraris posse fieri hominem certum de suae gratiae certitudine, quae licet non sit aequalis fidei catholicae, sit tamen vera fides, id est, omnem prorsus dubitationem excludens, atq; id quidem lege communi nempè testimonio illo, quod, Authore Paulo Spiritus sanctus reddit Spiritui nostro, quod sumus filij DEI; hoc ego verò falua pace & autoritate suâ, credo esse omninò falsum. Neque tamen solus ille Catharinus communem Ecclesiæ Romanæ errorem agnouit, sed præter ipsum & alij nostram de certitudine doctrinam haut obscurè adprobârunt. Nam in Enchiridio Coloniensi, anno 36. edito, hæc leguntur verba clarissima fol. 170. Fatemur verum esse, ad iustificationem hominis omninò requiri, vt homo credat non tantùm generalitèr, quòd propter Christum verè pœnitentibus remittantur peccata, sed & quòd ipsimet homini credenti remissa sint propter Christum per fidem, Et hanc Euchiridii sententiam vehementer commendat Georgius Cassander in sua consultatione artic. 4. pag. 11. additque, librum illum ab omnibus eruditioribus Theologis etiam per Italiam & Galliam summoperè fuisse collaudatum vt qui summam sententiæ veterum de Christiana religione (ex quorum scriptis quasi confirmatus sit) pulcherrimè referat: Bellarmino verò liber ille censurâ Ecclesiasticâ dignus videtur l. 3. de Iustific. c. 3. Idem Cassander commemorat pag. 12. quod illa ipsa explicatio (de certitudine remissionis peccatorum) posita fuerit in libro Cæsar Maiestat. Ratisbonensi, cuius formam loquendi, vtpote non satis scholasticam, quamuis Eccius per omnia non probarit, rem tamen ipsam, in quam Collegæ eius consenserant, non improbasse scribit. In eo autem libro ita statuiter: Firma & sacra doctrina est, per fidem viuam & efficacem iustificari peccatorem. Vocamus autem fidem viuam, motum Spiritus sancti, quo verè pœnitentes veteris vitæ, eriguntur ad DEVM, & verè apprehendunt misericordiam in Christo promissam, vt iam verè sentiant, quod remissionem peccatorum & reconciliationem, propter meritum Christi, gratuitâ Dei bonitate acceperunt, & clamant, Abba Pater. Addit Cassander pag. 15. Certè nemo est Ecclesiasticorum, nec è Scholasticis quidem, qui non hanc fiduciam & certitudinem de gratia & misericordia DEI, & glorificatione futura diligenter vrgeat, & dubitationi ac diffidentiae opponendam censeat. Et pag. 17. Adhaec doctores huius aetatis non se dubitationem docere dicunt, quà de misericordiâ DEI dubitetur & diffidatur, sed timorem DEI, quo solicitudo benè operandi, & acceptam gloriam conseruandi in nobis excitetur & augeatur, de quo Apostolus. Cum timore & tremore vestram salutem operamini. Hunc timorem castum & filialem appellant, quem perfestae charitas non pellit, sed reuiuet & fouet, qui timor semper fiduciam & spem paternae beneuolentiae adiunctam habet. Similia scripsit Cornelius Bitontinus in cap. 8 Rom. vbi haec verba: Qui in Christo Iesu sunt, nihil habent, vndè timere debeant, siquidem securi sunt de salute. Et refertur de Antonio Marinario, quòd in confessu Patrum Concilij Tridentini Dominica 4. in Quadragesima, anno 1546. dubitationem ex professo refutârit, cuius verba, cùm sint prolixa, non adscribam, videri autem possunt apud Dn. D. Gerhardum Tomo 3. L L. CC. art. de iustific. §. 93. pag. 1241. Hinc Bellarminus ipse fatetur l. 3. de Iustific. cap. 1. Incertitudinem iustitiae & gratiae non solùm contra haereticos, sed etiam contra Catholicos quosdam probandam esse. Cadit igitur toties iactata Romanensium consensio & vnitas, nec parum suspecta redditur doctrina Papalis, quippè quae tam incerta est, vt ab ipsis etiam eruditioribus, inque Scriptura exercitatis Theologis Papisticis minimè adprobetur.


### Question I: IV. II. Evasion of the Council of Trent

IV. II. EVASION OF THE COUNCIL OF TRENT.

Those Fathers seem not to have agreed concerning this highest article of the Christian religion, and therefore they fashioned their style in such a way that it cannot be sufficiently perceived which opinion they favor. Hence they made such a title for chapter 9, session 6: Against the vain confidence of heretics, implying that they only wish the rash boasting of faith to be condemned. For thus they decree in the said place: Although it is necessary to believe that sins are neither remitted, nor ever have been remitted, things except by the free divine mercy on account of Christ: yet it is not to be said that sins are forgiven or have been forgiven to anyone boasting of confidence and certainty of the remission of his sins, and resting in that alone: since among heretics and schismatics there can be, and indeed in our time is, and is preached with great contention against the Catholic Church, this one confidence, and one removed from all piety. Which words indeed exclude nothing other than the proud boasting of confidence. But soon they proceed more broadly, and establish the very dogma of doubt when they say: But neither is it to be asserted that those who are truly justified ought to determine within themselves, without any doubt at all, that they are justified, and that no one is absolved from sins and justified, unless he who certainly believes that he is absolved and justified: and that by this faith alone absolution and justification are perfected, as if he who does not believe this, doubts concerning the promises of God, and concerning the efficacy of the death and resurrection of Christ. By these words, indeed, a certain confidence of pardon and an infallible hope of grace seems to be excluded entirely, and therefore Bellarmine especially urges the authority of the Council against Catharinus, book 3 on Justification, chapter 3. But again they add signs of a wavering mind, and wish to exclude doubt with respect to divine promises, yet they reintroduce it with respect to our infirmity. For thus they conclude: For just as no pious person ought to doubt concerning the mercy of God, concerning the merit of Christ, and concerning the virtue and efficacy of the Sacraments: So anyone, while he looks at himself and his own proper infirmity and indisposition, can dread and fear concerning his grace: since no one is able to know with the certainty of faith, in which there cannot be falsehood, that he has obtained the grace of God. Who does not see that here various things are mixed, and that the Fathers are not at all consistent with themselves? It is not denied that if we look at our own infirmity, there is cause for dread: Meanwhile, since the divine promises are certain, since the grace of God and the merit of Christ are efficacious, since the Sacraments establish faith most firmly, the confidence will certainly not be empty, if anyone, fixed upon these most solid supports, believes without hesitation in the gratuitous forgiveness of sins.

V. The Papists themselves observed this ambiguous and evasive nature of the Council, among whose number is Catharinus, who, as Flacius reports in his book on the dissensions of the Papacy, p. 83, openly wrote: I deduce that the Synod of Trent pronounced nothing contrary to our opinion, which I uncovered in my first booklet, when I addressed the presidents of the council themselves (one of whom, by the grace of God, is the Supreme Pontiff, Julius III) and the most holy Synod itself, addressing them in these very words; I add that both presidents protested quite often, and especially in this controversy, both in the assembly of the Fathers and in the congregation of Theologians, and we heard both of them testifying that this question did not seem to them sufficiently discussed for a decision; indeed, the Holy Synod itself declared by these means that the definition of this matter should be omitted then and reserved for another time, as can appear in the acts. Finally, the very title of the new chapter manifests this abundantly, which reads thus: Against the empty confidence of the heretics. Similarly, Martin Eysengrein attacked the dogma of doubt in a special writing, and openly contended that the opinion of the Council of Trent was none other than that hypocrites, Epicureans, heretics, those destitute of true faith, those persisting in atrocious crimes against conscience, and the like, ought not to certainly establish that they are in grace. From these assertions of the Papists, therefore, it may be manifest how uncertain they themselves are about their doctrine of uncertainty, and how meticulous and trembling the Tridentine Fathers were concerning the decision of this problem, which again renders the Papistic opinion vehemently suspect to us.
