For although the Synod defends doubt more than confidence, and strikes with an anathema all who certainly believe in the forgiveness of sins: yet they do this in words so ambiguous that it is asserted by no ordinary Papists that they feared to decree anything concluded.

VI. III. Bellarmino's opinion proposes this in book 3 on Justification, chapter 2 and following, and says: That certainty is nothing other than a certain firmness and immutability of truth. For that is named certain which is explored and immovably true. We admit this general description of certainty, yet in such a way that its distinct degrees are not removed or denied. He adds, however, a distinction, that there is one certainty of the object, that is, of the thing known, and another of the subject, that is, of the man knowing. The former certainty, according to him, is the immobility of the thing, which in reality cannot be otherwise than it is believed or known: by which notion we say it is certain that God is good, that sin is evil. But this certainty is not of this place, since the question is not about the necessity or immutability of things, but about the knowledge and faith of the pious, whether they know and can believe that for Christ's sake their sins have been forgiven? Furthermore, it is an abusive way of speaking if anyone calls the necessity of an object certainty. For this term is not absolute, but rather relative, having a relation to a man's knowledge and assent, which is called either certain, if the thing is fully and plainly known, or uncertain, if the mind fluctuates and does not sufficiently perceive the truth. Certainty, therefore, is an affection not so much of things as of our knowledge, indeed in such a way that when it is said, it is certain that God is good, by certainty is understood not precisely the immutability of the object, but rather the firmness of our knowledge, and so the sense is: it is certain, that is, it is explored as true, and as if impressed upon all by nature, that God is good and sin is evil.

VII. The certainty of the object having therefore been exploded, there remains the certainty of the subject, or of the man knowing, which Bellarmino says is a certain firmness of our assent to the thing which is proposed to be known or believed; as when we say, this is certain to me, I am certain of this thing, that is, I adhere so firmly to this opinion that I do not doubt its truth at all. This certainty he divides again into two species: the first he calls evident certainty, which is of those things which are in some way seen; and again it is either of the intellect, or of science, or of experience. The former arises from first principles, the latter from conclusions deduced thence, the last from sensory perception. he says that evident certainty is of those things which are in some way seen. For either bodily or external seeing, or mental or internal, is denoted. If external, how will this square with the certainty of the intellect and of science? For are first principles and conclusions likewise seen? And why does he say that those things which are perceived by the senses of the body constitute a peculiar species of certainty, if all things that are evidently certain ought to be seen? But let this pass, since it is of little moment, and perhaps the Jesuit understands not immediate seeing, when we look at a thing face to face, as it is; but mediate, when we see something in examples and individuals.

VIII. He names the second species of certainty obscure, which is of those things which rely solely on faith or opinion. Of this, however, he establishes three degrees. He says that the first degree is held by those things which are certainly believed on account of divine authority; and that this is the certainty of Catholic and divine faith. We wonder, however, why he calls the most certain assent of faith an obscure certainty. Truly, the dogmas to be believed are proposed not obscurely but clearly, in and from the Scriptures. The certainty of them, therefore, ought to be named not obscure, but evident and bright. But if Bellarmine understands this, that the mysteries of our faith are obscure to reason, he is truly acting as a notable sophist. For 1. he confuses conclusions with things. The certainty of faith regards not so much the things themselves, as the assertions about the things. Those assertions, however, are not obscure, but most clear, as when I say; The Son assumed flesh into his own ἐνσωσασιν, the thing indeed is obscure to our mind itself, but that assertion or proposition is not obscure, but rather sufficiently evident and easy to understand. 2. He judges concerning matters of faith according to reason. It is indeed true that Christian dogmas are obscure with respect to reason, yet they are clear with respect to faith, by which we know and believe all those things perspicuously. Therefore, just as the condition of philosophical sciences is one thing, and that of theological is another, so the light of reason is one thing, and that of faith is another, and therefore the certainty of faith, because it cannot be comprehended by reason, ought not immediately to be called obscure. Here indeed we know as if through a mirror and our knowledge is enigmatic 1 Cor. 13:12, comparably, to be sure, with respect to the most full knowledge which we expect in heaven: yet for that reason neither faith nor the certainty of faith is absolutely obscure, as Bellarmine trifles; who, in his book on Justification, ch. 7, does not fear to write that faith is better defined by ignorance than by knowledge, which very error he wished to encrust here under the cloak of obscure certainty.

IX. But Bellarmine continues; and according to the degree of obscure certainty he mentions, in which he places those things which are believed on account of human authority, but so confirmed and celebrated that it excludes all fear entirely, such as these; that Cicero and Virgil were distinguished men, that Augustus ruled happily over a great part of the world, etc. And this he calls the certainty of human faith, or moral certainty, which although it is not so great that it is impossible for anything false to underlie it (for every man is a liar), yet he judges it to be so great that he who thinks or disputes against it is deservedly judged to be rash. We acknowledge this certainty to be by far inferior in degree with respect to the first, since it has no foundation other than human authority, which

Latin:

IV. II. TERGIVERSATIO CONCILII TRIDENTINI.

Videntur Patres isti non consensisse de summo hoc religionis Christianae articulo, ideoque stylum sic informârunt, vt cui sententiae faveant, haut satis animaduerti possit. Hinc talem fecêre titulum cap. 9. sess. 6. Contra inanem haereticorum fiduciam, innuentes, quòd temerariam fidei iactantiam tantùm velint damnatam. Ita enim decernunt l. d. Quamuis necessarium sit credere, neque remitti, neque remissa fuisse vnquam pecentea nisi gratis diuina misericordia propter Christum: neminitamen fiduciam & certitudinem remissionis peccatorum suorum iactanti, & in ea sola quiescenti, peccata dimitti vel dimissa esse dicendum est: cum apud haereticos & schismaticos possit esse, imo nostra tempestate sit, & magna contra Ecclesiam Catholicam contentione praedice tur vna haec, & ab omni pietate remota fiducia. Quae sane verba nihil aliud, quàm superbam fiduciae iactantiam excludunt. Mox verò latiùs progrediuntur, & ipsum dubitationis dogma stabiliunt cùm dicunt: Sed neque illud asserendum est, oportere eos qui verè iustificati sunt absque vlla omninò dubitatione, apud semetipsos statuere, se esse iustificatos neminemque a peccatis absolutum & iustificari, nisi eum, qui certò credat, se absolutum & iustificatum esse: atque hac sola fide absolutionem & iustificationem perfici quasi qui hoc non credit, de Dei promissis, déque mortis & resurrectionis Christi efficacia dubitet. His profectò verbis certa fiducia veniae, & infallibilis spes gratiae in totum videtur excludi, ideoque Concilij authoritatem cumprimis viget Bellarminus contra Catharinum l. 3. de Iustific. cap. 3. Sed rursus fluctuantis animi signa addunt, & dubitationem respectu promissionum diuinatum exculam volunt, respectu tamen infirmitatis nostrae iterum introducunt. Ita enim concludunt: Nam sicut nemo pius de DEI misericordia, de Christi merito, deque Sacramentorum virtute & efficacia dubitare debet: Sic quilibet dum seipsum, suamque propriam infirmitatem & indispositionem respicit, de sua gratia formidare ac timere potest: cùm nullus scire valeat certitudine fidei, cui non potest subesse falsum, se gratiam DEI esse consecutum. Quis non videt, hic varia misceri, & Patres sibiipsis minimè constare? Non negatur, quòd si propriam infirmitatem spectemus, formidandum sit: Interim cùm promissiones diuinae sint certae, cum gratia Dei & meritum Christi sit efficax, cùm Sacramenta fidem stabiliant firmissimè, non vtique inanis erit fiducia, si quis fia xus his fulcris solidissimis, gratuitam peccatorum veniam sine dubitatione credat.

V. Obseruârunt hanc Concilij ambiguitatem flexiloquam ipsi Pontificij, ex quorum numero est Catharinus, qui referente Flacio l. de dissent. Pontif. p. p. 83. apertè scripsit: Deduco, contrariam nostram sententiam nihil pronunciasse Synodum Tridentinam, quod ego in primo meo detexi libello, quùm ad præsidentes ipsi concilio (quorum alter Dei gratia summus est Pontifex, Iulius III.) & ad ipsam sacrosanctam Synodum destinaui, eos alloquens his planè verbis; Addo, quòd sæpius protestati sint ambo præsidentes, & specialiter in hac controuersia, tùm in conuentu Patrum, tum vero in congregatione Theologorum, & ambos audiuimus contestantes, non videri sibi quæstionem hanc satis discussam ad decisionem; Imo ipsamet S. S. Synodus his declarauit, huius rei definitionem tunc omittendam esse, & in aliud tempus seruandam, sicut in actis possit apparere. Denique ipse titulus noui capitis hoc manifestat abundè, qui sic habet: Contra inanem hæreticorũ fiduciam. Consimiliter Martinus Eysengrein peculiari scripto dogma dubitationis impugnauit, & apertè contendit Concil. Tridenti sententia non fuisse aliam, quàm ῗ hypocritæ, Epicurei, hęretici, destituti verâ fide, perseuerãtes in atrocibus delictis contra conscientiã & similes, non debeant certò statuere, quòd sint in gratia. Ex his ergo Papicolarum assertioribus manifestũ sit, quàm incerti sint ipsi de incertitudinis suæ doctrina, & quàm meticulosi trepidiq́; fuerint circa huius problematis decisionem Patres Tridentini, quod iterum opinionem Papisticam nobis vehementer suspectam reddit. Quamuis enim dubitationem magis propugnet Synodus, quàm fiduciam, & anathemate percutiat omnes certò credentes peccatorũ veniam:attamen verbis hoc faciũt adeò ambiguis, vt nihil cōclusum decriums metuisse à Pontificijs non vulgaribus asseratur.

VI. III. Opinio Bellarmini Proponit hanc l. 3. de Iustific. c. 2. & seqq. dicitque: Certitudinem nihil aliud esse, nisi firmitatem quandam, & immutabilitatem veritatis. Illud enim nominari certum, quod exploratè & immobiliter est verum. Admittimus hanc generalem certitudinis descriptionem, ita tamen nè distincti illius gradus tollantur aut negentur. Subiungit verò distinctionem, quòd alia sit certitudo obiecti, id est, rei cognitæ, Alia subiecti, id est, hominis cognoscentis. Prior certitudo iuxta ipsum est immobilitas rei, quæ reuerà aliter se habere non potest, quàm creditur vel cognoscitur: quâ notione dicimus, certum esse, Devm esse bonum, peccatum esse malum. Verùm hæc certitudo non est huius loci, quippe cùm non quæratur de rerum necessitate aut immutabilitate, sed de piorum cognitione & fide, Num sciunt & credere possint sibi, propter Christum peccata esse remissa? Deinde abusiua locutio est, si quis necessitatem obiecti appellet certitudinem. Nam hic terminus non est absolutus, sed magis respectivus χεσιν habens, ad hominis notitiam & assensum, qui vel certus vocatur, si res plenè planéq; sit cognita, vel incertus, si animus fluctuet, nec veritatem satis percipiat. Certitudo igitur est affectio non tàm rerum quàm cognitionis nostræ, ita quidem, vt cùm dicitur, certum est, Devm esse bonum, per certitudinem non præcisè immutabilitas obiecti, sed potiùs firmitas nostræ notitię intelligatur, adeóq; sensus sit: certum est, hoc est exploratè verum, omnibusque naturâ quasi impressum, quòd Devs sit bonus, & peccatum sit malum.

VII. Explosâ igitur certitudine obiecti, restat certitudo subiecti, vel hominis cognoscentis, quem Bellarminus dicit esse firmitatem quandam afsensus nostri ad rem quæ cognoscenda vel credenda proponitur; vt cùm dicimus, hoc mihi est certum, ego de hac re certus sum, id est, ita firmiter adhæreo huic sententiæ, vt prorsus de illius veritate non dubitem. Hanc verò certitudine rursus dispescit in duas species: Primam vocat certitudinem evidentem, quæ sit earum rerum, quæ aliquo modo videntur; & rursus esse vel intellectus, vel scientiæ, vel experientiæ certitudinem. Illam ex principijs primis, istam ex conclusionibus indè deductis, hanc ex sensualj præceptione oriri. Vbi hoc quæri posset, quid Bellarminus intelligat per videri, cùm ait certitudinem evidentem esse earum rerum, quæ aliquo modo videntur. Nam vel videre corporis seu externum, vel mentis seu internum denotatur. Si externum, quomodo hoc ad certitudinem intellectus & scientiæ quadrabit? Num enim principia prima & conclusiones itidem videntur? Et cur peculiarem certitudinis speciem dicit constituere illas res, quæ sensibus corporis percipiuntur, si omnia evidenter certa videri debent? Sed transeat hoc, cùm exigui momenti sit, & fortè IesuWita intelligat non videri immediatum, quandoreincoram, vt est, aspicimus; sed mediatum, cum aliquid videmus in exemplis & indiuiduis.

IIX. Secundam certitudinis speciem nominat obscuram, quæ sit earum rerum, quæ sola fide vel opinione nitantur. Huius verò tres gradus constituit. Primum gradum habere dicit, quæ propter diuinam authoritatem certò creduntur; & hanc esse certitudinem fidei Catholicæ & diuinæ. Miramur verò, cur certissimum fidei assensum vocet certudinem obscuram. Sanè dogmata credenda non obscurè sed perspicuè, in & ex Scripturis proponuntur. Certitudo igitur illorum non obscura, sed evidens & luculenta nominari debet. Si verò Bellarminus hoc intelligat, quòd mysteria fidei nostræ rationi sint obscura, insignem profectò Sophistam agit. Nam 1. confundit conclusiones cum rebus. Certitudo fidei non tàm ipsas res, quàm assertiones de rebus respiscit. Illæ verò assertiones non sunt obscuræ, sed clarissimæ, vt cùm dico; Filius assumsit carnem in suam ἐνσωσασιν, res quidem ipsi menti nostræ obscura est, sed assertio vel propositio ista non est obscura, verùm evidens satis & intellectu facilis. 2. De rebus fidei secundùm rationem iudicat. Verum quidem est, quòd Christiana dogmata sim obscura respectu rationis, sunt tamen clara respectu fidei, quâ illa omnia perspicuè scimus & credimus. Proinde vt alia scientiæ Philosophicæ, & alia Theologicæ est conditio, sic aliud rationis, & aliud fidei est lumen, ideoque certitudo fidei, quia ratione comprehendi nequit, non statim obscura nuncupari debet. Hic quidem cognoscimus quasi per speculum & scientia nostra est ænigmatica 1. Cor. 13. v. 12. comparatè nimirum respectu scientiæ plenissimæ, quàm expectamus in cœlo: ob id tamen non absolutè obscura est vel fides, vel certitudo fidei, vt Bellarminus nugatur; quippe qui l. de Iustificat. c. 7. scribere non veretur, fidem meliùs per ignorantiam, quam notitiam definiri, quem ipsum errorem sub pallio certitudinis obscuræ hîc incrustate voluit:

IX. Sed pergit Bellarminus; & secundùm obscuræ certitudinis gradum commemorat, in quo res illas collocat, quæ creduntur ob autoritatem humanam, sed ita confirmatam & celebrem, vt omnem formidinem prorsus excludat, qualia sint; Ciceronem & Virgilium fuisse insignes viros, Augustum magnâ parte orbis terrarum feliciter imperâsse, &c. Atque hanc vocat certitudinem fidei humanæ, siue certitudinem moralem, quæ tametsi non tanta sit, vt est, ei nullo modo falsum subesse possit, (omnis enim homo mēdax) tamen tantam esse iudicat, vt temerarius meritò iudicetur qui contra sentiat aut disputet. Agnoscimus hanc certitudinem gradu longè inferiorem esse respectu primæ, cùm nullum fundamentum habeat aliud, quàm authoritatem humanam, quæ opi-


### Question I: indeed produces opinion, but not faith or knowledge, since that which is false…

indeed produces opinion, but not faith or knowledge, since that which is false cannot underlie it, as it can the former. Meanwhile, if the consensus of all, or of most men, conspires in some matter, and is consistently affirmed by those who have seen it for themselves, or have gathered it from certain principles, then surely this is not an obscure certainty, but rather in its own way evident and clear. For as in certainty, so also in evidence, distinct degrees must be established. But there is no need for us to dwell long here, since our inquiry is primarily concerned with this moral certainty, which is built upon human testimony.

X. There remains, therefore, the third degree of certainty, to which Bellarmine refers those things which rely on signs and conjectures, so as to render a man secure, yet not to expel all fear, and this he calls conjectural certainty, which is rather of opinion than of faith. But this certainty is to me nothing other than a contradiction in terms and mere uncertainty. Above, Bellarmine defined certainty in general as a certain firmness and immutability of truth, since only that is said to be certain which is explored and immovably true. But indeed, conjectural certainty is not the firmness and immutability of truth, but a naked opinion, built upon conjectures alone, and those fallible ones. Therefore, conjectural certainty is not certainty; that is, the thing itself is not the thing itself. Again, everything certain is explored as true, according to Bellarmine's description. But those things which we opine from conjectures are not explored as true. Therefore, they are not certain, from which it follows again that conjectural certainty is no certainty at all. Finally, he who fears, and ought to fear, that perhaps the contrary is true, he cannot but fluctuate and be anxious. But indeed, he who has conjectural certainty always fears, and ought to fear, that perhaps the contrary is true. Therefore, he who has conjectural certainty cannot but fluctuate and be anxious. From which it follows in turn that Bellarmine involves a contradiction, when he writes that conjectural certainty indeed excludes anxiety, but not fear. For where fear is not excluded, there neither is anxiety excluded, since fear is nothing other than the anguish of a mind fearing that which can bring both pain and sorrow: It remains, therefore, that conjectural certainty is not able to render a man secure; but because it does not expel the fear of the contrary, it is mere doubt and uncertainty, from which it follows that he who is certain of his salvation only conjecturally, is always doubting, and therefore most uncertain: concerning which very thing more will be said in the 4th member.

XI. These distinctions of certainty having now been premised, Bellarmine proceeds to investigate the state of the controversy, and 1. denies that the Papists teach that justifying faith is doubt. But this very thing will be demonstrated to the eye in the following. II. He examines the state proposed by Chemnitz, which stands thus: Whether a sinner in serious repentance, from true faith in Christ, can with certain confidence determine that his sins have been forgiven him. He finds two things lacking here: 1, That the question is conditional. For that phrase, in serious repentance, signifies the same as if it were said, if the repentance be serious: which being presupposed, it is true that no Catholic answers that question negatively. Bellarmine acts sophistically, since he ought to have known that by those words no meritorious condition is proposed; but only the subject is described, which ought to believe in the forgiveness of sins. For neither can anyone be certain of the grace of God, since Epicureans and the impenitent draw wrath upon themselves, and cannot boast of forgiveness. We know that this is proper only to the penitent and the faithful, and we ourselves urge it. But that someone can be certain of his own repentance, no one will easily deny who has recognized that it is nothing other than contrition for sins, and faith in Christ, which whether it was present or otherwise, anyone can certainly know, and therefore can test himself, though Papists indeed must doubt about this, since for them penance is the highest contrition, a perfect enumeration of all sins, and an equivalent satisfaction for sins, which, since they do not fall to man, it follows of its own accord that he always remains in doubt. 2. That the dispute is not about confidence, but about the certainty of faith. For he does not say that Catholics deny that certain confidence is to be placed in God, and that one must certainly trust that, after penance has been legitimately performed and the Sacrament of Baptism or absolution has been duly received, sins are forgiven. But the adversaries, just as they confuse faith with confidence, so they confuse the certainty of faith with the certainty of confidence. But he wrongly separates faith from confidence, since faith is nothing but confidence. Furthermore, by the certainty of confidence he understands nothing other than conjectural. That this is mere doubt, we have both proved before, and will later clearly demonstrate. 3. He proposes the state of the question thus: Whether anyone ought and can, without special revelation, be certain with the certainty of divine faith, which can in no way be false, that his sins have been forgiven him? But he proposes the subject too generally and without limitation. For the question is not about any man, but about a penitent and one converted to God. It is disputed about such a one: Whether or not, relying on divine promises, which he apprehends with true faith, he can and ought to believe certainly without doubt that he has been received into grace, and that his sins have been forgiven him? The Papists choose the negative, we the affirmative, which will be more fully declared below.

XII. IV. Whether the Papists maintain that one must doubt about the remission of sins? The Jesuits strenuously deny this, inasmuch as Bellarmine, book 1, chapter 11, boldly asserts: There is no Catholic writer who teaches that men ought perpetually to doubt and hesitate about their reconciliation with God. And Reihing writes in Fundam. civit. sanctæ, p. 13: Neither do our people command, nor do they exhort, that one should doubt, but that one should fear and be in awe with a good conscience. But fear is either joined with confidence, and is celestial or separated from confidence, and is called servile. The former does not admit doubt, the latter always has it as a companion. Papists do not understand the former, they press the latter, and therefore they do not exclude doubt from fear: which itself is clearly evident partly from the words, partly from the hypotheses of the Papists. The Council of Trent, sess. 6, c. 9, decrees that it is not to be asserted that those who are truly justified ought to determine within themselves, without any doubt at all, that they are justified. If, therefore, this is not to be determined without doubt, then certainly some room for hesitation is left. Andradius, in his defense of the Council of Trent, intending to respond to that which the Jesuits wrote (The faithful one indeed firmly hopes for eternal life, and what is more, even trusts, yet does not certainly believe, but doubts, for hope can deceive), says that hope has some doubt joined and implicated with it. Petrus à Soto, in his Confessio, says: It is safe, it is most humble, to DOUBT concerning the grace and presence of God in me. Costerus teaches the same in Enchir. c. 4, on faith, on p. 187, concluding thus: Christ did not wish the certainty of faith to be in us without all doubt.

XIII. Now if we consider the hypotheses and practice of the Roman Church, it will appear most clearly that Papists are the patrons of doubt and uncertainty.

For 1. They prohibit certain confidence in divine grace: from which nothing else can follow than mere doubt: for with one of two contraries removed, the other must be posited. But confidence and hesitation or doubt are opposites, as is clear from that of the Apostle James 1, v. 6: Let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. Because, therefore, Papists wish certain confidence to be removed, by this very fact they establish doubt.

2. They decree that hope for pardon and salvation must be placed, if not entirely, yet in part, in one's own merits. For thus writes Gregorius de Val. tom. 3, disp. 1, quæst. 1, punct. 1: From which doctrine the error of the sectarians of this time can easily be refuted, who in no way think that a man ought to place the hope of his salvation in any of his own good works, but in the grace of God alone. But from these things which we have said, it is clear that good works also, as they proceed from grace, can and ought to be a support for our hope of salvation; by this very fact, that they contribute in their own way to salvation. Hence they perpetually urge their own dispositions, satisfactions, and little works. Hence they lead all who seek the forgiveness of sins not rightly to Christ, but rather away from Christ to Moses, from the Gospel to the law, and lead them around through works of penance, through masses, pilgrimages, Papal indulgences, and fabricated traditions, so that they may seek in them some hope of remission. But because our merits are nothing, our works imperfect, our dispositions insufficient, and many sins can lie hidden in secret for which satisfaction has not been made, hence nothing other than mere fluctuation and anxiety of conscience can arise. For such as the foundation is, such also is the superstructure. But the foundation of forgiveness and salvation in the Papacy is doubtful and uncertain, namely, one's own merits and satisfactions. Therefore, the very forgiveness and salvation of a man will also be doubtful and uncertain. To this point looks that statement of Bernard, sermon 5 on the vigil of the Nativity: To trust in oneself is not faith, but perfidy; and it is not confidence, but rather diffidence, to have trust in oneself.

8. They urge the fear of the contrary, namely that sins might be forgiven. But wherever anything is believed in such a way that the contrary must always be feared, there is mere doubt and anxiety. But Papists want the remission of sins to be believed in such a way that, nevertheless, on account of one's own infirmity and indisposition, it must always be feared that sins are perhaps not forgiven. Wherefore they inculcate mere doubt and anxiety. The major premise is certain, since doubt, as defined by Isidore, is nothing other than a mind indifferent toward both sides of a contradiction, or that it is the acceptance of both parts with

Latin:

nionem quidem parit, sed non fidem vel scientiam, quippe cui, vt illi, falsum subesse haut potest. Interim si consensus omnium, vel plerorumque hominum in aliqua re conspiret, & consentienter affirmetur ab ijs, qui coram viderunt, vel ex certis principijs collegerunt, tum sane non est haec obscura certitudo, sed potius suo modo evidens & luculenta. Vt enim in certitudine, sic & in evidentia distincti gradus debent constitui. Verum non op' est, vt diuhic immoremur, cu de hac morali, & humanis tatu testimonijs superstructa certitudine questio nostra maxime sit instituta.

X. Restat ergo tertius gradus objecta a certitudinis, ad quem Bellarminus illa refert, qua tus signis & coniecturis nituntur, vt securum hominem reddant, non tamen formidinem omnem expellant, atque hanc vocat certitudinem coniecturalem, qua opinionis potius sit, quam fidei. Verum haec certitudo mihi est aliud, quam contradictionis implicatio & mera incertitudo. Supra Bellarminus certitudinem in genere definiuit, quod sit firmitas quaedam & immutabilitas veritatis, siquidem non nisi illud dicatur certum, quod explorate & immobiliter sit verum. At vero certitudo coniecturalis, non est firmitas & inmutabilitas veritatis, sed nuda opinio, solis conjecturis, ijsque fallibilibus superstructa. Ergo certitudo coniecturalis non est certitudo, hoc est, ipsum non est ipsum. Rursus, Omne certum est explorate verum, iuxta Bellarmini descriptionem. Sed quae ex coniecturis opinamur, illa non sunt explorate vera. Ergo nec sunt certa, vnde iterum sequitur, quod certitudo coiecturalis nulla sit certitudo. Tandem, qui formidat & formidare debet, quod forte contrarium sit verum. ille non potest no fluctuare & anxius esse. At vero qui certitudinem habet coniecturalem, ille semper formidat & formidare debet, quod forte contrarium sit verum. Ergo qui certitudinem habet coniecturalem non potest non fluctuare & anxius esse. Vnde vicissim sequitur, Bellarminum implicare ἀντίφασιν, cùm scribit, certitudinem coniecturalem excludere quidē anxietatem, sed non formidinem. Vbi enim nō excluditur metus, ibi nec excluditur anxietas, cùm metus nihil sit aliud, quàm angor animi formidantis id, quod duplicet & dolorem afferre potest: Manet igitur, quòd certitudo coniecturalis, hominem securum reddere haut valeat; sed quia mętum contrarij non expellit, mera sit dubitatio & incertitudo, vnde sequitur, eum qui de salute sua non nisi coniecturaliter certus est, semper dubitare, adeoq́; incertissimum esse: de quo ipso plura membro 4. dicentur.

XI. Præmissis iam istis distinctionibus certitudinis, pergit Bellarminus ad indagandum controuersiæ statum, & 1. negat, quod Pontificij fidem iustificantem doceant esse dubitationem. Hoc ipsum verò in sequentibus ad oculum demonstrabitur. II. Statum à Chemnitio propositum examinat, qui sic habet: Vtrum peccator in seria pœnitentia, ex fide vera in Christum, possit certa fiducia statuere, sibi remissa esse peccata. Duo hîc desiderat: 1, Quod quæstio sit conditionalis. Nam illud, in seria pœnitentia, idem significare; ac si diceretur, si seria sit pœnitentia: qua præsuppositâ, neminem Catholicorū ad quæstionem istam negatiuè respondere, verum. Sophisticè agit Bellarminus, quippè qui nosse debebat, verbis illis non proponi conditionem aliquam meritoriam; sed duntaxat describi subiectum, quod veniam peccatorum debet credere. Nec n. quiuis de gratia Dei potest esse certus, cùm Epicurei & impœnitentes iram sibi attrahant, & de venia gloriari nequeant. Pœnitentib. tantùm & fidelib. hoc esse proprium nouimus, & ipsi vrgemus. Quòd autem aliquis de sua pœnitentia possit esse certus, nemo negabit facilè, qui cognouerit, eam nihil esse aliud, quàm contritionem ob peccata, & fidem in Christum, quæ num adfuit, vel secus, quiuis sanè cognoscere, ideóq; seipsum probare potest, Papicolas quidem de hoc dubitare oportet, cùm ijs pœnitentia sit summa contritio, perfecta omnium delictorum enumeratio, & æquiualens pro peccatis satisfactio, quæ cùm in hominem non cadant, dubius semper vt hæreat, vltrò consequitur. 2. Quòd non de fiducia, sed de fidei certitudine disputetur. Neque enim ait, Catholicos negare, certam fiduciam in Deo collocandam esse, & certò confidendum, post actam legitimè pœnitentiam & Sacramentum Baptismi, vel absolutionis ritè perceptum, remissa esse peccata. Sed aduersarij vt fidem cum fiducia, ità certitudinem fidei cùm certitudine fiduciæ confundunt. Verùm malè fidem à fiducia discerpit, cùm fides nihil sit nisi fiducia. Deindè per certitudinem fiduciæ non intelligit aliam, quàm coniecturalem. Hanc verò meram esse dubitationem, & antè probauimus, & postmodum luculenter evincemus. 3. Statum quæstionis sic proponit; Vtrum debeat ac possit aliquis, sine speciali reuelatione certus esse, certitudine fidei diuinæ, cui nullo modo potest subesse esse falsum sibi remissa peccata? Verùm nimis generaliter & illimitatè proponit subiectum. Non enim quæstio de quouis homine est, sed de pœnitente & ad Deum conuerso. De tali controuertitur, Annon innitens diuinis promissionibus, quas verâ fide apprehendit, certò sine dubitatione possit ac debeat credere, se in gratiam receptum, & sibi peccata esse remissa? Negatiuam eligunt Papicolæ, nos affirmatiuam, quæ infrà pleniùs declarabitur.

XII. IV. Num Pontificij statuant, de remissione peccatorum esse dubitandum? Strenuè hoc inficiantur Iesuitæ, siquidem Bellarminus l. 1. c. 11. audacter asserit: Nullum esse Catholicum scriptorem, qui doceat, ortere homines perpetuò dubitare & hæsitare de sua cum Deo reconciliatione. Et Reihing scribit Fundam.l.civit. sanctæ p. 13. Nec iubent nostri, nec hortantur, vt dubitet, sed vt formidet ac timeat bona conscientia. Verùm metus vel cum fiducia coniunctus est, & sebilis stialis, vel à fiducia separatus, & servilis nuncupatur. Ille dubitationem non admittit, hic semper comitem habet. Illum Papicolæ non intelligunt, hunc vrgent, ideoque dubitationem à metu non excludunt: quod ipsum partim ex verbis, partim hypothesibus Papicolarum luculenter patet. Concilium Tridentinum sess. 6. c. 9. decernit, non esse afferendũ, oportere eos, qui verè iustificati sunt, absq; vlla omninò dubitatione apud semetipsos statuere, se esse iustificatos. Si ergò non absq; dubitatione hoc statuendum est, vtique aliquis hæsitatiqni locus relinquitur. Andradius in defensione Concilii Trident. ad illud, quod Iesu Witæ scripserunt, (Fidelis quidem firmiter sperat vitam æternam, & quod magis est, confidit etiam, non tamen certò credit, sed dubitat, spes enim fallere potest) responsurus inquit, spem habere aliquam dubitationem coniunctam & implicatam. Petrus à Soto, in Confess. Tutum, ait, humillimum est, de Dei in me gratia atque præsentia DVBJTARE. Costerus idem tradit in Enchir. c. 4. de fide, in p. 187. sic concludens: Fidei certitudinem citra omnem dubitationem noluit Christus in nobis esse.

XIII. Iam si hypotheses & praxin Ecclesiæ Romanæ consideremus, clarissimè apparebit, Papicolas du bitationis & incertitudinis patronos esse.

Nam 1. Certam diuinæ gratiæ fiduciam prohibent: vndè nil sequi potest aliud, quàm mera dubitatio: Contrariorum enim vno remoto, ponendum est alterum. Fiducia verò & hæsitatio vel dubitatio, sunt opposita, vt liquet ex illo Apostoli Iac. 1. v. 6. Postulet in fide, nihil hæsitans. Quia ergò certam fiduciam Papicolæ volunt remotam, hoc ipso dubitationem stabiliunt.

2. Spem veniæ & salutis, si non in totum, tamen ex parte, in propriis meritis ponendam esse statuunt. Ita enim scribit Gregorius de Val. tom. 3. disp. 1. quæst. 1. punct. 1. Ex qua doctrina facilè confutari potest error huius temporis sectariorum, qui nullo modo pugant, hominem debere spem salutis collocare in ullis bonis operibus suis, sed in sola gratia Dei. Sed ex his, quae diximus, perspicuum est, operibus etiam bonis, vt a gratia procedunt, posse quoque ac debere piti nostrae salutis spem; huc ipso, quod ea conducunt suo modo ad salutem. Hinc perpetuo vrgent proprias dispositiones, satisfactiones, opellas. Hinc omnes, qui peccatorum veniam quaerunt, non recte ad Christum, sed potius a Christo ad Mosen, ab Evangelio ad legem deducunt & per opera poenitentiae, per missas, peregrinationes, indulgentias Papales, & confictas traditiones circunducunt, vt in illis aliquam remissionis spem quaerant. Quia vero merita nostra nulla, opera imperfecta, dispositiones insufficientes sunt, & multa peccata in occulto latere possunt, pro quibus non sit satisfactum, hinc aliud nihil, quam mera fluctuatio & conscientiae anxietas oriri potest. Quale enim est fundamentum, tale & superstructum. Sed fundamentum veniae & salutis in Papatu est dubium, incertumque, nempe propria merita & satisfactiones. Ergo etiam ipsa venia salusque hominis erit dubia & incerta. Huc spectat illud Bernardi serm. 5. in vigil. nativ. Sibi ipsi fidere, non fides, sed perfidia est; nec confidentia, sed diffidentia magis in semetipso habere fiduciam.

8. Vrgent formidinem contrarij, nempe quod peccata possint esse remissa. Vbicunque vero aliquid ita creditur; vt contrarium semper metuendum sit, ibi est mera dubitatio & anxietas. Sed Papicolae volunt remissionem peccatorum sic esse credendam, vt tamen ob infirmitatem & indispositionem propriam semper metuendum sit, peccata forte non esse remissa. Quare meram dubitationem & anxietatem inculcant. Maior certa est, cum dubitatio, definiente Isidoro, nihil sit aliud quam mens indifferens in vtramque partem contradictionis, vel quod sit acceptio vtriusque partis cum-


### Question I: fear, and a determination to neither side

fear, and a determination to neither side. Now such indifference and indetermination flows from Papistic hypotheses. For if I ought to hope for the grace of God in such a way that I must nevertheless fear lest I be outside of grace, I certainly cannot assent to any side. What kind of assent will this be, if I am ignorant of what is to be certainly established, and if I must believe that the contrary can also hold true? Therefore we conclude thus: Every indeterminate assent is mere doubt. But the Papistic assent concerning the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins is indeterminate, because they teach that neither is to be believed with certainty, but rather that it is to be feared and established that, on account of our own indisposition, we can lack the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins. Therefore, the Papistic assent is mere doubt.

4 They themselves call the conjectures from which the grace of God is to be gathered fallacious. For Bellarmine writes thus in book 3, chapter 9, testimony 6: This very thing, that it is the Holy Spirit who moves us when we say, Abba Father, is not certain to us by divine faith, but only from conjectures, which can be FALLACIOUS. But whatever rests upon fallacious conjectures produces no certainty, but mere doubt and anxiety of mind. And yet the opinion concerning the grace of God and the presence of the Holy Spirit rests, according to the Papists, upon fallacious conjectures. Therefore it produces no certainty, but mere doubt and anxiety of mind, unless perhaps the Papists can by some new artifice gather the certain from the uncertain. For fallacious conjectures are uncertain conjectures, from which alone, when the grace of God is to be estimated, what kind of certainty, I ask, can arise from thence? More arguments could be formed from Papistic hypotheses, by which one might easily prove that doubt is inculcated by them: but let those enumerated thus far suffice, lest we dwell too prolixly on a manifest matter.

XIV. The Papists do, however, have something to object, namely that they do not deny all certainty, but only some degree of it, that is, the certainty of faith: but that they willingly concede a conjectural one, which Bellarmine in book 3, chapter 11, attributes to the hope of Christians. But above in member 3, we showed that conjectural certainty is uncertainty itself, and therefore by what reason at length will it be able to render the mind certain and quiet? As often, therefore, as he rhetorizes about hope and conjectural certainty, let us think that he is casting glaucoma upon them themselves, and committing an arriqasw in adiecto.

XV. But let us see abundantly how Bellarmine in chapter 11 has described that certainty. A twofold certainty, he says, can be considered in hope. One on the part of the will, the other on the part of the intellect. On the part of the will, the certainty of hope is a firm adhesion of the will to the thing hoped for, and this can be greatest, even if on the part of the intellect a man is not certain that he will obtain that thing. Indeed, hope seems not only not to require, but not even to be able to bear absolute certainty on the part of the intellect. For what we know for certain that we shall have, we do not properly hope for, but simply expect.

Response 1. The Jesuit confuses distinct questions. It is one thing when the question is about the forgiveness of sins: and another when the question is about eternal salvation and the participation in it. There, the controversy is about a present good; here, about a future one. The former question is the one for this place, not the latter: and therefore the things he brings forward about the certainty of hope are irrelevant. For a penitent sinner ought not to hope that the remission of crimes will be lacking; but to believe it as having been done. For when we are absolved from sins, a future good is not promised, but a present one is conferred. The faithful indeed hope for eternal life, but they do not hope for the grace of God, but believe it.

2. If expectation presupposes certain knowledge, it follows that the faithful know for certain their future glorification. For they say that they not only hope for this. Rom. 5. v. 2 chapter 8. v. 24. but also expect it. 2. Pet. 3. v. 13. We expect new heavens and a new earth according to his promises.

3. The degrees of hope are distinct. For sometimes it is languid, sometimes firm. But if it is languid, and a man is uncertain whether he will obtain the thing hoped for, then certainly such hope does not involve the firm certainty which is required of the pious. Indeed, there is perpetual anxiety in the mind when hope and fear are mixed, so much so that there is almost no greater torture for a man than to be tossed between hope and fear, as we see in captives who hope for clemency and at the same time fear death. Now, the Papists leave no other hope for Christians. For we are guilty because of our sins, and we have deserved condemnation. They want us, however, to hope for forgiveness in a certain way, because of God's grace and the merit of Christ, but meanwhile to fear wrath and death at the same time, because of our own indisposition. Thus, therefore, one must remain in perpetual anxieties, while we remain doubtful between hope and fear, and we must not believe with certainty that we will obtain grace and life. Whatever, therefore, they prattle about the firmest hope and the greatest adhesion of the will to the thing hoped for, is mere pretense and a pretext devised to cloak the deformity of doubt. For he who is not certain that he will obtain some thing, but ought to hope in such a way that he simultaneously fears the contrary; he is destitute of all certainty that quiets the mind, and is forced to remain in perpetual solicitude and anxiety of mind.

4. We deny that hope excludes knowledge and the certainty of the intellect. For we hope for the return of Christ to judgment and the resurrection of our bodies: yet we know both most certainly and believe them with Catholic faith. Languid and doubtful hope indeed excludes knowledge, but not a firm and certain one, which does not disappoint. Rom. 5 v. 5. Indeed, this finds no place unless, when without doubt, we either know or believe that we shall obtain the thing. In which way that distinction between hoping and expecting collapses, namely that we hope for uncertain things and expect things that are explored and true. For what else is it to hope firmly than to expect with certainty a future good? And if hope, properly so called, is not expectation, why do all the Scholastics define it as being a certain expectation of a future good? Indeed, why does Bellarmine write in book 1, On Justification, chapter 6, near the end, that hope is placed in the intellect regarding certainty not essentially but causally, because, forsooth, hope is certain for this reason, because it presupposes the certainty of faith concerning the omnipotence and faithfulness of God? Does Bellarmine not expressly admit here that certain hope presupposes the certainty of faith, namely that by which one certainly believes that he will certainly obtain the good promised by Him on account of God's omnipotence and faithfulness?

5. The Papists do not even leave to Christians the certainty of hope regarding the business of salvation. For they do indeed concede this, that someone may hope for the possibility of salvation, but they do not concede that he may hope for salvation itself; that is, it is permitted to hope that we can be saved, but it is not permitted to hope that we shall certainly be saved. Thus thinks Gregorius de Valentia, volume 3, disputation 2, question 1, point 4, where he establishes the object of certain hope, not blessedness itself, but only the possibility of obtaining blessedness. For that, he says, by which anyone can think that he will in reality obtain blessedness, is by no means a judgment of faith, but is altogether uncertain.

XVI. But let us proceed to the other certainty of hope, which Bellarmine establishes as being on the part of the intellect, and that twofold. The first, he says, arises from the primary foundation of hope, which is the promise of God. For we know certainly that GOD cannot deceive. And if indeed nothing were required for justification or salvation, we would have an absolute and infallible certainty even concerning these matters: yet because other things are also required, about which we are not so certain, nay, hope does not expel all fear. Here lies the snake in the grass, and the adversary reveals his most gross error. For he confesses that if one must rely solely on the promises of God, an infallible certainty follows. But truly this is what we maintain, for no hope is to be placed in our merits or works, they are not required as causes of salvation: But justifying faith is founded only on the gratuitous promises of God concerning the forgiveness of sins on account of the merit of Christ, which when we apprehend with firm faith, we are made most certain with the Apostle Paul, that nothing can separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, Rom. 8. v. last. We therefore receive and always urge this certainty of faith, rather than of hope, built upon an infallible support, and making us most certain of the forgiveness of sins. To this point looks a notable passage of Luther, in chapter 4 to the Galatians, where he discourses thus: The Gospel commands us to look not at our good deeds and perfection, but at God Himself promising, at Christ Himself the Mediator. On the contrary, the Pope commands us to look not at God promising, not at Christ the High Priest, but at our works or merits; there doubt and despair necessarily follow, but there [in the Gospel] certainty and the joy of the Spirit. Because I cling to God, who cannot lie, for He says, Behold I deliver my Son to death, that He may redeem you by His blood from sins and death, there I cannot doubt, unless I wish to deny God entirely.

The other, says the Jesuit, the certainty of hope on the part of the intellect, arises from charity, and through this it is fitting only for righteous men. For a friend can hope for all good things from a friend, nor is there danger that he may be confounded. And if indeed this friendship with God could not be corrupted, those who are joined with God by charity would be infallibly and absolutely secure of salvation: yet because while we are pilgrims from the Lord it can happen that he who is a friend may immediately become an enemy, therefore even the righteous cannot live without some fear. But 1. he confuses the question concerning perseverance, with the question concerning pardon, which is proper to this place. 2. We do not wish for every fear to be removed from the righteous, but only servile fear, which produces doubt and anxiety of mind. Otherwise, we willingly concede that friendship with God can be corrupted, and his friend can become an enemy through mortal sins, and from this we deduce that we ought to work out our salvation with fear, Philip. 2. v. 12, always taking care that we do not cast off the grace of God, and turn ourselves from the path of righteousness. 3. If this certainty is true, then it follows that someone can know that he is a friend of God. For it is founded in charity; and presupposes this. It is required, therefore, that someone should know that he is dear to God, before he can certainly hope that he will receive all good things from God, as from a friend. Now if someone can know, and ought to certainly establish, that he is a friend of God; certainly he can also know that his sins have been forgiven him. For God loves no one to whom he still imputes sins, and does not forgive. If Iesu Wita has said that someone cannot certainly know whether he is dear to God, this second certainty of hope, which he builds upon charity, immediately perishes. We, however, affirm that former point, and from there infer that a man, just as he can be most certain concerning his friendship with God, so also can he be most certain concerning the pardon of his sins.

Latin:

formidine, & ad neutram partem determinatio. Iam talis indifferentia & indeterminatio fluit ex hypothesibus Papisticis. Si enim gratiam Dei sic sperare debeo, vt tamen timendum sit, ne sim extra gratiam, certè nulli parti assentiri queo, Qualis non hic erit assensus, si ignorem, quid sit certò statuendum, & si debeam credere, contrarium quoque locum habere posse? Proinde sic concludimus: Omnis assensus indeterminatus est mera dubitatio. Sed assensus Papisticus de gratia Dei & venia peccatorum est indeterminatus, quia neutrum certò credendum esse præcipiunt, sed potius formidandum & statuendum, quod ob propriam indispositionem carere possimus gratia Dei & venia peccatorum. Ergò assensus Papisticus est mera dubitatio.

4 Coniecturas, ex quibus colligenda est Dei gratia, ipsi fallaces nominant. Ita enim scribit Bellarminus l. 3. cap. 9. test. 6. Hoc ipsum quod Spiritus sanctus sit, qui nos mouet, cùm dicimus, Abba Pater, non constat nobis ex fide diuina, sed solùm ex coniecturis, quæ FALLACES esse possunt. Quicquid verò nititur coniecturis fallacibus, id nullam certitudinem, sed meram parit dubitationem & animi anxietatem. Atqui opinio de gratia Dei & præsentia Spiritus sancti nititur iuxta Pontificios coniecturis fallacibus. Ergo nullam parit certitudinem, sed meram dubitationem & animi anxietatem, nisi fortè Pontificij nouo artificio certum possint colligere ex incertis. Nam fallaces coniecturæ sunt incertæ coniecturæ, ex quibus solis cùm de gratia Dei sit æstimandum, qualis quæso oriri potest indè certitudo? Plura possent ex hypothesibus Papisticis argumenta formari, quibus dubitationem ab ipsis inculcari, facilè quis evincat: sed sufficiant hactenus enumerata, nè in re manifesta nimis prolixè immoremur.

XIV. Habent verò Papicolæ, quod obiiciant, nempe se non omnem certitudinem, sed duntaxat aliquam illius gradum, hoc est, fidei certitudinem negare: libenter autem se concedere coniecturalem, quam Bellarminus lib. 3. c. 11. spei Christianorum attribuit. Sed supra membro 3. ostendimus, quod certitudo coniecturalis sit ipsa incertitudo, adeoque adpheton. Cum enim fallacibus & incertis coniecturis superstruatur, qua tandem ratione animum poterit certum & quietum reddere? Quoties igitur de spe & coniecturali certitudine rhetoricatur, toties ipsos glaucoma objicere, & arriqasw in adiecto committere cogitemus.

XV. Sed videamus ex abundanti, quomodo Bellarminus cap. 11. certitudinem illam descripserit. Duplex, inquit, in spe certitudo considerari potest. Altera ex parte voluntatis, altera ex parte intellectus. Ex parte voluntatis, certitudo spei est firma adhæsio voluntatis ad rem speratam, & hæc maxima esse potest, etiamsi ex parte intellectus non sit homo certus, se rem illam consecuturum. Imo videtur spes non solum non exigere, sed nec ferre posse ex parte intellectus certitudinem absolutam. Nam quod certo scimus, nos habituros, non proprie speramus sed simpliciter expectamus.

Respon. 1. Confundit IesuWita quæstiones distinctas. Aliud est, cum quæritur de venia peccatorum: & aliud, cum quæritur de salute æterna & eius participatione. Ibi de præsenti, hic de futuro bono controuertitur. Prior quæstio est hujus loci, non posterior: ideoque aliena sunt, quæ de spei certitudine affert. Nam peccator pœnitens remissionem criminum no sperare debet defuturam; sed credere, vt factam. Cum enim absolvimur a peccatis, non bonum futurum promittur, sed præsens confertur. Vitam quidem æternam sperant fideles, Dei vero gratiam nonsperant, sed credunt.

2. Si expectatio præsupponit certam scientiam, sequitur quod fideles certo nouerint suam glorificationem futuram. Hanc enim non tantùm dicunt sperare. Rom. 5. v. 2 capite 8. v. 24. verùm etiam expectare. 2. Pet. 3. v. 13. Nouos cælos & nouam terram secundùm promissa ipsius expectamus.

3. Distincti sunt gradus spei. Quandoque enim languida est, nonnunquam firma. Quòd si sit languida, & homo incertus sit, se rem speratam consecuturum, tùm sanè spes talis firmam certitudinem, qualis requiritur à pijs, non inuoluit. Imò perpetua est in mente anxietas, quando spes metusque commiscentur, ita quidem, vt ferè nulla sit maior tortura hominis, quam inter spem metumque versari, vt videmus in captiuis, qui sperant clementiam, & vnà metuunt mortem. Iam verò non aliam Christianis spem faciunt reliquam Papicolę. Nos enim rei sumus ob peccata, & damnationem meruimus. Volunt autem vt quodammodò speremus quidem veniam, ob Dei gratiam & Christi meritum, sed vt interim vnà metuamus iram & mortem, ob propriam indispositionem. Ita ergò in perpetuis hærendum est anxietatibus, dum inter spem metumque dubij hæremus, & certò credere non debemus, nos gratiam & vitam consecuturos. Quicquid igitur de spe firmissima & adhæsione voluntatis maxima ad rem speratam blaterant, merus fucus est & prætextus ad palliandam dubitationis deformitatem excogitatus. Qui enim certus non est, se rem aliquam impetraturum, sed ita sperare debet, vt simul metuat contrarium; is omni certitudine animum quietante destituitur, & in perpetua solicitudine ac anxietate mentis hærere cogitur.

4. Negamus, quòd spes excludat scientiam & intellectus certitudinem. Reditum enim Christi ad iudicium & resurrectionem nostrorum corporum speramus : certissimè tamen vtrumque scimus & Catholicâ fide credimus. Spes quidem languida & dubia excludit scientiam, sed non firma certaque, quæ non confundit. Rom. 5 v. 5. siquidem hæc locum nõ inuenit, nisi cùm absq; dubitatione vel scimus vel credimus, nos rem consecuturos. Quo pacto vnà concidit discrimen illud inter sperare & expectare, quòd incerta speremus, & exploratè vera expectemus. Nam quid aliud est firmiter sperare, quàm certò expectare bonum futurum? Et si spes propriè dicta non est expectatio, cur omnes Scholastici eam definiunt, quòd sit certa expectatio boni futuri? Imò cur Bellarminus scribit l. 1. de Iustific. c. 6. sub finem, Poni spem in intellectu quoad certitudinem non essentialiter sed causaliter, quia videlicet idcò spes cera est, quia præsupponit certitudinem fidei de omnipotentia & fidelitate Dei? Annón Bellarminus hîc expressè fatetur, quòd spes certa præsupponat fidei certitudinem, nempè quâ quis certò credit, se ob Dei omnipotentiam & fidelitatem certò consecuturum esse bonum ab ipso promissum?

5. Pontificij nè quidem spei certitudinem circa salutis negotium relinquunt Christianis. Nam hoc quidem concedunt, vt aliquis speret possibilitatem salutis, non verò concedunt vt speret ipsam salutem, hoc est, sperare licet, nos posse saluos fieri, sed non licet sperare, nos certò saluos fore. Ita censet Gregorius de Valent. tom. 3 disput. 2. quæst. 1. punct. 4. vbi certæ spei obiectum constituit, non ipsam beatitudinem, sed tantùm possibilitatem consequendæ beatitudinis. Nam illud, inquit, quo quispiam cogitare potest, se reipsa consecuturum beatitudinem, nequaquam est iudicium fidei, sed omninò incertum.

XVI. Pergamus verò ad alteram spei certitudinem, quam Bellarminus ex parte intellectus esse statuit, eamque duplicem. Prima, inquit, oritur ex fundamento spei primario, quod est promissio Dei. Certo enim scimus, DEVM non posse fallere. Et si quidem nihil requiriretur ad iustificationem vel salutem, haberemus etiam de his rebus absolutam & infallibilem certitudinem: tamen quia requiruntur etiam alia, de quibus non sumus tam certi, imò spes non expellit omnem timorem. Hic latet anguis in herba, & prodit aduersarius errorem suum crassissimum. Fatetur enim, quòd si solis promissionibus Dei nitendum sit, infallibilis certitudo sequatur. At verò hoc est, quod nos vigemus, Non enim in nostris meritis vel operibus spes vlla ponenda est, non requiruntur ea, vt salutis causæ : Sed fides iustificans tantùm fundatur in gratuitis Dei promissis de venia peccatorum ob Christi meritum quæ cùm firmâ fide apprehendimus, cum Apostolo Paulo certissimi reddimur, quòd nihil nos separare possit à charitate Dei, quæ est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Rom. 8. v. vlt. Recipimus ergò & semper vrgemus hanc fidei potiùs, quàm spei certitudinem, infallibili fulcro superstructam, & de peccatorũ venia nos certissimos reddentem. Huc spectat insignis locus Lutheri, in ca. 4. ad Gal. vbi sic disserit: Evangelium iubet intueri nos, non benefacta & perfectionem nostram, sed ipsum DEVM promittentem, ipsum Christum Mediatorem. Econtra Papa iubet respicere non DEVM promittentem, non Christum Pontificem, sed nostra opera aut merita, ibi necessariò sequitur dubitatio & desperatio, illic verò certitudo & gaudium Spiritus. Quia in Deo hareo, qui mentiri non potest, dicit enim, Ecce trado Filium meum in mortem, vt te sanguine suo redimat à peccatis & morte, ibi non possum dubitare, nisi prorsus velim DEVM negare.

Altera, inquit Iesusita, certitudo spei ex parte intellectus, oritur ex charitate, ac per hoc conuenit nisi hominibus iustis. Amicus enim ab amico omnia bona sperare potest, neque periculum est, nè confundatur. Et siquidem amicitia ista cum DEO corrumpi non posset, infallibiliter & absolutè de salute securi essent, qui charitate cum DEO coniuncti sunt: tamẽ quia dum peregrinamur à Domino fieri potest, vt qui amicus est, statim fiat inimicus, idcircò non possunt etiam iusti sine timore aliquo viuere. Sed 1. confunditur quæstio de perseuerantia, cum quaestione de venia, quae huius loci est propria. 2. Non omnem a iustis timorem remotum volumus, sed tantum seruilem, qui parit dubitationem & anxietatem animi. Aliàs lubenter concedimus, quòd amicitia cum Deo corrumpi, & eius amicus, possit fieri inimicus per peccata mortalia, & hinc deducimus, quòd salutem nostram cum timore operari debeamus, Philip. 2. v. 12. semper curantes, ne gratiam Dei excutiamus, & a iustitiae semita nos auertamus. 3. Si haec certitudo vera est, tum sequitur, quòd aliquis scire possit, se Dei amicum esse. Fundatur enim in charitate; & hanc praesupponit. Requiritur ergò, vt aliquis nouerit, se Deo esse charum, antequam certò sperare possit, se a Deo, tanquam ab amico, omnia bona accepturum. Iam si quis scire potest, & certò statuere debet, se Dei esse amicum; vtique scire etiam potest, sibi remissa esse peccata. Neminem enim Deus diligit, cui peccata adhuc imputat, & non condonat. Si Iesu Wita dixerit, aliquem certò scire non posse num sit Deo charus, statim perit haec altera spei certitudo quam charitati superstruit. Nos autem illud prius affirmamus, & indè inferimus, hominem, vt de amicitia cum Deo, sic & de peccatorum venia posse esse certissimum.


### Question I: And thus it has been shown so far that the Papists teach doubt, and that that…

And thus it has been shown so far that the Papists teach doubt, and that that absurd προσφύγετον of Bellarmine concerning the certainty of hope, inasmuch as it is either uncertain or presupposes the certainty of faith, cannot be excused or avoided.

XVII. V. The origin and sources of this dogma. Chemnitz wrote that the doctrine which commands believers to doubt concerning the remission of sins arose from the schools of the Pharisees and the Novatians. But this, says Bellarmine, l. 3 c. 11. rat. 5, is not arguments, but impostures and lies.

For 1. The Gospel most openly testifies that the Pharisees did not murmur that Christ commanded that confidence be conceived in particular concerning the remission of sins, but that he seemed to make himself GOD, while he assumed to himself the power of relaxing sins, which is proper to GOD alone. Resp. These are not contrary, but subordinate, and therefore they do not fight against each other. For the Pharisees established both, that no man in particular ought to remit sins; and that Christ, because he did this, was a blasphemer. They denied, therefore, to every man the power of forgiving sins in particular; both ministerial and αὐτοκρατορικὴν or authentic. And because they sought righteousness in the law, which no one can perfectly fulfill, doubt certainly flowed from their hypotheses without a doubt. If some boasted of perfection, this was hypocritical presumption, not a true and faithful assertion.

2. Add that the Lord did not command men to believe with Catholic faith that their sins were remitted to them, but only to trust. Which very thing all Catholics teach, since they know that faith and trust are not the same, and that a man can trust that his sins are remitted to him, even if he does not have absolute certainty of that matter from the side of the intellect. Resp. The Jesuit dreams wonderful things when he distinguishes between faith and trust, when nevertheless justifying faith, and that which apprehends the benefits of Christ, is nothing other than trust, and conversely, which has been most clearly proved elsewhere. Furthermore, when Christ says, Trust, your sins are remitted to you, he generates not only some hope, but the very most certain faith in the mind of the paralytic. For the words were clear and the absolution manifest: Your sins are remitted to you, whence the Papists themselves elsewhere concede that Catholic faith is generated. And finally, that he says Catholics teach that a man can trust that his sins are remitted to him is mere pretense. For that which they teach, to trust, is nothing other than to doubt, as we have most clearly shown above:

3. Concerning the Novatians he writes that they only admonished those who had lapsed after baptism to deal with God, for in the Church there is no power of reconciling. Response. If they had taught nothing else at all, this would still suffice to prove our thesis, that the doubt took its origin from the school of the Novatians. For those who teach that there is no power in the Church to remit sins, they certainly introduce doubt and make consciences burdened with guilt fluctuate regarding pardon. Rightly, therefore, did Ambrose oppose them in book 1 of De poenitentia, chapter 2, writing thus: The Novatians say that they reserve the power of remitting crimes to God alone, but Christ commanded his disciples to loose sins.

XVIII. Having therefore proven that that Papistical error was born from the schools of heretics, one can note in addition the sources and Papistical hypotheses from which the dogma of doubt flows. Such are 1. that they hold faith only as assent, not as trust; 2. that they suspend the virtue of the Sacraments from the intention of the minister, which is doubtful; 3. that they do not believe sins are remitted unless each one is enumerated in the confessional, which is uncertain; 4. that they place hope in their own merits and works, which are imperfect; 5. that they consider only the doubts which sometimes come to the saints from the infirmity of the flesh; 6. that they distinguish between faith and trust. And Cassander himself notes this in Consult. p. 15. On account of this, he says, doubt, which is born from the consideration of one's own infirmity, always clings even in the most holy men: Likewise, because this persuasion could be false and empty in the impious, namely those destitute of the Spirit of God, some have felt that this certainty should be attributed not to faith properly so-called, in which doubt makes one a heretic, but rather to trust, which is born from a certain sense of divine benevolence, to which a certain hesitation, opposed to it, argues for an infirmity of faith, with which hesitation there is a struggle for the faithful. And he adds: The ancients certainly did not distinguish much between hope and faith in this passage, as is evident from Hilary.

XIX. Furthermore, the cause remains to be explained why the Papists so defend and urge doubt. He expresses it, Chemnitz, in his Examination of the Council of Trent, part 1, p. 165 in my copy, whose words, since they are notable, we shall recount. Nor, says he, are there no reasons why the Papists fight so fiercely to retain doubt. For they understand that the whole business of Papal trafficking rests upon this foundation that faith itself, even when it apprehends Christ the Mediator in the promise, must doubt concerning the remission of sins, thinks that it wishes to accumulate so many and so various works, so that, according to the poet, 'If individual ones do not avail, may more help.' Hence, beyond the works commanded by God, self-chosen acts of worship were devised without end or measure. Hence vows, pilgrimages, and invocations of saints, fraternities, undue works, works of supererogation, the trafficking of Masses; the negotiation of indulgences, and, in short, that whole Lernaean swamp of Papal superstitions. And since the conscience in its agony could not find certain and firm consolation in all those things, purgatory was finally devised, and redemptions by suffrages after death were proposed. The Papal publicans fear for these revenues of their kingdom. For they see that it will come to pass that they will be diminished and perish if men are taught from the Word of God that faith is a confidence which finds, receives, and possesses in the promise of the Gospel certain and firm consolation concerning reconciliation with God. Hence those tears, hence that struggle for establishing doubt. I wished to set these forth in the very words of Chemnitz, since they contain with rounded brevity all the causes by which Papists are privately moved to assert doubt: which having been thus declared, we proceed to the conformation of the state [of the question].

XX. VI. Exposition of our opinion. We know from the Scriptures that the heavenly doctrine was revealed to the human race so that believers and penitents might have firm consolation, in which they might safely rest against all temptations. Thus, therefore, are hearers to be instructed, lest the fountains of consolation be obstructed, and fearful consciences be cast into the abyss of despair. There are, however, distinct questions which can cause scruple to a penitent: For he is either anxious about his future repentance and salvation, or about the remission of sins in the present.

The former question is not proper to this place, since here it is primarily disputed concerning the certainty of justification, not of glorification. We say, however, that the certainty of perseverance is not absolute, but only hypothetical, insofar as the means of perseverance are not spurned, but always employed. For faith is not given in such a way as if it could never be lost again, but the Holy Spirit is cast out through mortal sins, and therefore one must always be vigilant, lest the flesh overcome the Spirit, and we return to our vomit, which is that fear and trembling with which we ought to work out our salvation, according to that of the Apostle Phil. 2, verse 12. Meanwhile, however, if I consider the promises, that God wills to perfect the work which He began and that Christ still intercedes for us: a firm faith can arise from thence concerning perseverance, since I know that nothing can move me from the state of grace, unless I maliciously wish to fail myself.

But as concerns the other question about the remission of sins, we say that any faithful person, and one who is truly penitent, can be most certain of it. It is to be noted, however, that 1. We do not wish by this very fact to establish a rash presumption, because we maintain that not just anyone, but only the faithful and truly penitent person can be certain. If you ask, whence does one know that he truly believes and repents? We say that anyone can test himself, and that there are given most certain κριτήρια (criteria) of faith, both present and absent. 2. That we do not place the foundation of certainty in the perfection of our works, but solely in the most absolute λύτρῳ (ransom) of Christ, and the gratuitous promises of God, which if anyone apprehends with true faith, he cannot but become certain of the grace of God, since he knows That God deceives no one, because He is truthful; and that He is willing to forgive sins to the penitent, because He is good; and that He is able, because He is omnipotent, and because Christ most perfectly made satisfaction for us. 3. That that certainty is not conjectural, and with implicit doubt; but most firm, and such entirely, that falsehood does not underlie it, nor can it underlie it. For when a believer is carried toward the promises of God, then he cannot but obtain pardon for his sins by the force of the divine promises which never deceive.

This, therefore, is our opinion in brief, that whoever is truly penitent and faithful (of which anyone can be certain, if he examines himself), on account of the imputed merit of Christ, and by the force of the divine promises, can, nay must, believe certainly and without any doubt, that all his sins are truly forgiven him through faith, by the grace of God, on account of Christ's satisfaction, so that nothing of condemnation remains in him any longer.

Bellarmino furthermore attributes this opinion to us in book 3 of Justification, chapter 5, that we maintain that men are justified by that faith alone by which we believe that sins have been forgiven. But he confuses the distinct objects of faith. We do indeed believe that our sins have been forgiven, but this faith does not formally justify, but rather follows justification. For the immediate object of justifying faith is nothing other than the merit of Christ. When this is apprehended by faith, it is immediately imputed, and thus sins are forgiven, and then we believe that they have been forgiven. Briefly, we declare this thus: The remission of sins is considered in two ways: 1. As it is being done, 2. As it has been done. In the first respect, it is simultaneous with justifying faith, which are related: In the second respect, it follows justifying faith, but in order it precedes that faith by which we believe that remission has already been made. Thus, therefore, justifying faith is directed primarily not to remission that has been made, but to remission that is future and promised, and so we are justified or obtain remission, not because we believe that we have already obtained tos, but because we believe that Christ has made satisfaction for us, and thus sins are forgiven or not imputed.

XXII. VII. Removal of false states of the question. From what has been said thus far, it is easily apparent what does not come into question. For 1. the inquiry is not about the faith of heretics, who defend erroneous and false opinions. For heresies are works of the flesh, Gal. 5, verse 20, which exclude from the kingdom of heaven, verse 21. Therefore, true faith or confidence does not fall upon them, and so they cannot be certain of the grace of God and their own salvation, but rather they should conclude that the wrath of God and eternal condemnation are prepared for them.

2. The inquiry is not about the falsely boasted faith of Epicureans and the impenitent, such as are many in the true Church, who, living most wickedly, nevertheless promise themselves the grace of God. But this faith is a phantom, not true faith, since it is always effective through love, Gal. 5, v. 6, and is dead without works, James 2, v. 26.

Thus 3. The inquiry is not about historical faith and general assent, which can fall upon hypocrites, and indeed even demons, but about special faith, which embraces the promise of grace, and in it Christ the Mediator, and applies his benefits to itself. Where it is to be noted that, among other things, this difference occurs between general and special faith: that the object of general faith always remains uniform and is never varied by reason of the person; for since what is once apprehended as true, and is proposed in the Scriptures as an article of faith and believed by us, remains perpetually true and its opposite can never obtain. But the matter stands otherwise regarding the object of special faith, which is the remission of sins. For this can again be shaken off and lost, and therefore can be varied with respect to the believing person, so that although it is impossible for a falsehood to underlie faith as long as we believe, yet a time can come when we both lose faith and can no longer boast of the object of special faith, or of the remission of sins. And hence it is that the certainty of faith does not beget security of the flesh, does not expel all fear, but together includes vigilance and circumspection, which, however, the Papists falsely allege against us that we abolish.

4. The question is not about the certainty of election and perseverance. For this controversy was treated in the second decade. And although these questions are joined, they are not, however, to be thoroughly confounded, lest confusion arise from that, and the true understanding of both be disturbed.

5. The question is not about great faith and confidence devoid of all doubt. For we ourselves admit that the faith of the regenerate often languishes and is shaken by various doubts, so that it is not always robust and excellent, especially in time of temptation; but we do not urge that doubt, nor do we inculcate it in the regenerate as necessary, as the Papists do; but rather we disapprove of it, as vicious and sprung from the weakness of the flesh, which must be diligently striven against by faith, prayer, and other means so that it may be overcome, that we may say with the father of the lunatic from Mark 9:24: I believe, Lord, but help my weakness.

6. Nor, finally, is the question, whether the foundation of that certainty and confidence is situated in our virtues or merits? For we presuppose that our works are imperfect and have many impurities mixed in, so that they cannot bear the severe examination of God. If anyone, therefore, places his confidence in them, we willingly admit that no certainty flows, or can flow, from that, but rather mere fluctuation and anxiety of mind.

XXIII. IIX. The true state of the controversy. Thus, therefore, with those things removed which do not come into question, the true ζητούμενον (point at issue) will not be able to be obscure. Namely, the controversy is about a penitent man, whether or not he can and ought to apply to himself the promises of grace concerning the remission of sins, on account of the imputed merit of Christ, and apprehend them with true faith in such a way, that he does not merely hope conjecturally; but rather believes with the certainty of faith that all his sins have been forgiven him and that he has returned into favor with God? Or, more briefly, this is the question: Can and ought faith not produce a firm and immovable confidence of divine grace in the hearts of the faithful? The Papists deny it, we affirm it, and we can demonstrate this very thing with very many arguments.

Latin:

Atque sic ostensum est hactenus, Pontificios dubitationem docere, nec absurdum illud Bellarmini προσφύγετον de spei certitudine, quippè quae vel incerta est, vel fidei certitudinem praesupponit, excusari aut declinari posse.

XVII. V. Origo & fontes huius dogmatis. Scripsit Chemnisius, doctrinam, quae iubet credentes dubitare de remissione peccatorum, ortam esse ex scholis Pharisaeorum & Niuataenorum. Haec verò inquit Bellarminus l. 3 c. 11. rat. 5. non argumenta, sed imposturae & mendacia sunt.

Nam 1. Evangelium apertissimè testatur, Pharisaeos non murmurasse, quòd Christus iuberet in particulari fiduciam concipi de remissione peccatorum, sed quòd se DEVM facere videretur, dum potestatem peccata relaxandi, Soli DEO propriam, sibi sumebat. Resp. Non sunt hæc contraria, sed subordinata, ideoque non pugnant inuicem. Nam Pharisæi statuerunt vtrumque, tum nullum hominem in particulari peccata debere remittere; tum Christum, quia id fecerit, blasphemum esse. Denegarunt ergò omni homini, potestatem peccata condonãdi in particulari; tum ministerialem, tum αὐτοκρατορικὴν vel authenticam. Et quia iustitiam quæsierunt in lege, quam nemo perfectè potest implere, vtique dubitatio ex illorum hypothesibus sine dubio profluxit. Si quidam de perfectione gloriati sunt, fuit hæc hypocritica præsumptio, non vera & fidelis assertio.

2. Addè quòd Dominus non iussit, homines credere fide Catholica, sibi peccata esse remissa, sed tantùm confidere. Quod ipsum Catholici omnes docent, quippè qui sciunt, fidem & fiduciam non esse idem, & posse hominem confidere sibi remissa esse peccata, etsi ex parte intellectus non habeat eius rei certitudinẽ absolutam. Resp. Mira somniat Iesuwita, quãdo inter fidem & fiduciam distinguit, cùm tamen fides iustificans, & beneficia Christi apprehendens nihil sit aliud, quàm fiducia, & contrà, quod clarissimè alibi probatum est. Deindè cùm Christus ait, Confide, remittuntur tibi peccata, non tantùm aliquam spem, sed ipsam fidem certissimam in animo paralytici gignit. Verba enim erant clara & absolutio manifesta: Remittuntur tibi peccata, vndè fidem Catholicam gigni, ipsi aliàs concedunt Papicolæ. Tandemque Catholicos docere ait, posse hominem confidere, sibi remissa esse peccata, merus fucus est. Istud enim quod docent, confidere, nihil est aliud, quàm dubitare, vti suprà clarissimè ostendimus:

3. De Nouatianis scribit, eos tantùm admonuisse lapsos post baptismum, vt cum Deo agerent, in Ecclesia enim non esse potestatem reconciliandi. Respond. Si maxime nihil aliud docuissent, tamen hoc sufficeret, ad probandam thesin nostram, quod dubitatio e schola Nouatianorum ortum traxerit. Nam qui docent, in Ecclesia non esse potestatem remittendi peccata, hi sane dubitationem inuehunt, & consciencias pressas de venia fluctuare faciunt. Recte igitur se ijs opposuit Ambrosius l. 1. de poenit. c. 2. ita scribens: Nouatiani dicunt, se soli Deo remittendorum criminum potestatem reseruare, sed Christus mandans discipulis suis soluere peccata.

XIIX. Euicto igitur, quod error ille Papisticus ex hæreticorum scholis prognatus sit, notari possunt insuper fontes & hypotheses Papisticæ, ex quibus fluit dubitationis dogma. Tales sunt 1. quod fidem habent tantum pro assensu, non pro fiducia 2. quod Sacramentorum virtutem ab intentione ministri suspendunt, quæ dubia. 3. quod remitti peccata non censent, nisi enumerata sine confessionario singula, quod incertum 4. quod spem ponunt in meritis & operibus proprijs, quæ imperfecta. 5. quod dubitationes, quę sanctis nonnunquam ex infirmitate carnis obueniunt, vnice considerant 6 quod inter fidem & fiduciam distinguunt. Et hoc ipse Cassander annotat in Consult. p. 15. Ob hanc, inquit, dubitationem, quæ ex consideratione propriæ infirmitatis nata, semper hæret etiam in sanctissimis viris: Item, quia persuasio hæc falsa & inanis esse possit, in impijs, videlicet Spiritu Dei destitutis, ideo nonnulli senserunt, hanc certitudinem non fidei proprie, in qua dubitatio hæreticum facit, sed fiduciæ potiùs, quæ ex sensu quodam diuinæ beneuolentiæ nascitur, esse tribuendam, cui opposita aliquata hæsitatio, infirmitatem fidei arguit, cum qua hæsitatione fidelibus anxietas est luctan lum. Et addit: Veteres sane in hoc loco inter spem & fidem non admodum distinxerunt, vt patet ex Hilario.

XIX. Porro exponenda restat causa, cur dubitationem adeo propugnent & vrgeant Pontificij, Exprimit illam Chemnitius in Exam. Concilij Tridentini p. 1. mihi p 165. cuius verba, cùm sint notabilia, recensebimus. Nec tanè, inquit, nullæ sunt causæ, quarè tam acriter Pontificij de retinenda dubitatione gladiaritur.
