Intelligunt enim totam negotiationem Pontificiæ nundinationis hoc fundamento niti. Conscientia enim quærens certam aliquam & firmam consolationem, quando audit, ipsam fidem, etiam quando in promissione Christum Mediatorem apprehendit, debere dubitare de remissione peccatorum, cogitat, se velle cumulare tam multa & tam varia opera, vt iuxta Poëtam, Si non prosint singula, plura iuuent. Hinc vltra opera diuinitùs mandata electitij cultus sine fine & modo excogitati fuerunt. Hinc vota, peregrinationes, & inuocationes sanctorum, fraternitates, opera indebita, opera supererogationis, nundinatio Missarum; negotiatio indulgentiarum, & breuiter, tota illa lerna superstitionum Pontificiarum. Cúmque in agone conscientia in illis omnibus non inueniret certam & firmam consolationem, excogitatum tandem est purgatorium, & propositæ redemptiones suffragiorum post mortem. His regni sui vectigalibus timent publicani Pontificij. Vident enim fore, vt minuantur & intercidant, si homines ex verbo Dei doceantur, fidem esse fiduciam, quæ in promissione Evangelij inueniat, accipiat & possideat certam & firmam consolationem de reconciliatione cum Deo. Hinc illæ lacrymæ, hinc certamen istud pro stabilienda dubitatione. Hæc ipsis Chemnitij verbis proponere volui, cùm rotunda breuitate omnes contineant causas, quibus Papicolæ ad asserendam dubitationem priuatim mouentur: quibus ita declaratis, ad status conformationem accedimus.

XX. VI. Nostræ sententiæ expositio. Scimus ex Scripturis, quòd doctrina cælestis ideò patefacta sit generi humano, vt credentes & pœnitentes firmam consolationem habeant, in qua contra omnes tentationes tutò acquiescere possint. Ita igitur informandi sunt auditores, nè obstruantur consolationum fontes, & pauidæ conscientiæ in desperationis barathrum præcipitentur. Sunt autem distinctæ quæstiones, quæ scrupulum mouere possunt pœnitenti: Vel enim solicitus est de sua pœnitentia & salute futura: vel de peccatorum remissione in præsenti.

Prior quæstio non est propria huius loci, quippè vbi de iustificationis, non glorificationis certitudine primò disputatur. Dicimus autem quòd perseuerantiæ certitudo non sit absoluta, sed tantùm hypothetica, quâtenus media perseuerantiæ non spernuntur, sed semper vsurpantur. Fides enim non datur hoc modo, ac si nunquam possit iterum amitti, sed excutitur Spiritus sanctus per peccata mortalia, ideoque semper vigilandum est, nè caro vincat Spiritum, & redeamus ad vomitum, qui est timor ille & tremor, cum quo salutem nostram operari debemus, iuxta illud Apostoli Phil. 2. ver. 12. Interim tamen si promissiones considera vero, Deum velle opus, quod incepit perficere & Christum pro nobis etiamnùm intercedere: firma inde fides oriri potest de perseuetantia, cùm sciam, nihil me posse è statu gratiæ dimouere, nisi mihi ipsi malitiosè velim deesse.

Quod autem concernit quæstionem alteram de remissione peccatorum, dicimus quemuis fidelem, & verè pœnitentem, de illa posse esse certissimum. Notandum verò est, quòd 1. Non stabilitam hoc ipso velimus temerariam præsumptionem, quia non quemuis, sed duntaxat fidelem & verè pœnitentē posse certum esse statuimus. Si quæras, vndè quis sciat, se verè credere & pœnitere? dicimus, quemuis seipsum probare posse, & dari certissima κριτήρια fidei & præsentis, & absentis 2. Quòd fundamentum certitudinis non ponamus in perfectione nostrorum operum, sed vnicè in absolutissimo Christi λύτρῳ, & gratuitis Dei promissionibus, quas si quis verâ fide apprehendat, non potest non de gratia Dei certus fieri, cùm sciat Deum neminem fallere, quia verax est; & pœnitentibus peccata velle dimittere, quia bonus est; posse, quia omnipotens est, & quia Christus pro nobis perfectissimè satisfecit. 3. Quòd illa certitudo non sit conjecturalis, & cum dubitatione implicita; sed firmissima, & talis omninò, cui nõ subsit, nec subesse possit falsum. Cùm enim fidelis in promissiones Dei fertur, tùm non potest non peccatorum suorum veniam impetrare vi promissionum diuinarum nunquam fallentium.

Hæc igitur paucis nostra est opinio, quòd quisuis verè pœnitens & fidelis (de quo cuiuis, si seipsum examinet, cõstare potest,) ob Christi meritum imputatum, & vi promissionum diuinarum, certò & sine omni dubitatione queat, imò debeat credere, sibi per fidem, ex Dei gratia, ob Christi satisfactionem, cuncta peccata verè esse remissa, vt nihil ampliùs in ipso damnationis sit reliquum.

Affingit prætereá Bellarminus hanc nobis sententiam librò 3. de Iustificat. capite 5. quòd statui mus, solâ illâ fide, quâ credimus peccata esse remissa, homines iustificari. Sed confundit distincta fidei obiecta. Credimus quidem, peccata nobis esse remifsa, sed hæc fides formaliter non iustificat verùm iustificationem sequitur. Nam immediatum iustificantis fidei obiectum non est aliud, quàm Christi meritum. Hoc cum fide apprehenditur, statim imputatur, & sic peccata remittuntur, atque tum illa remissa esse credimus. Breuiter hoc ita declaramus: Remissio peccatorũ dupliciter consideratur: 1. Vt fit, 2. vt facta est. Respectu primo simul est cum fide iustificante, quæ sunt relata: Respectu secũdo, sequitur fidẽ iustificantẽ, sed ordine præcedit fidem eam quâ credimus, remissionem iam factam esse. Ita igitur fides iustificans fertur primò non in factã, sed futuram & promissam remissionem, adeoque iustificamur vel remissionem consequimur, non quia credimus nos iam consecutos, sed quia credimus, Christum pro nobis satisfecisse, & ita peccata remitti vel non imputari.

XXII. VII. Remotio falsorum statuum. Ex hactenus dictis facilè apparet, quid in quæstionem non veniat. Nam 1. non quæritur de fide hæreticorum, qui erroneas falsásque opiniones propugnant. Hæreses enim sunt opera carnis, Galat. 5. versu 20. quæ excludunt è regno cœlorum, versu 21. In illos igitur vera fides aut fiducia non cadit, ideoą; certi esse nequeunt de Dei gratia & sua salute, sed potiùs Dei iram & æternam condemnationem sibi paratam esse statuant.

2. Non quæritur de falsò iactata fide Epicureorum & impœnitentium, quales sunt multi in vera Ecclesia, qui pessimè viuentes, gratiam Dei nihilominùs sibi pollicentur. Sed spectrum hoc fides, non fides vera, quippe quæ per charitatem semper efficax, Gal. 5. v. 6. & sine operibus mortua est, Iac. 2. v. 26.

Sic 3. Non quæritur de fide historica & assensu generali, qui cadere potest in hypocritas, imò & dæmones, sed de fide speciali, quæ promissionem gratiæ, & in ea Christum Mediatorem amplectitur eiusque beneficia sibi applicat. Vbi notandum, inter fidem generalem & specialem hoc inter cætera discrimen occurrere, quòd fidei generalis obiectum semper se habeat vniformiter, & nunquam ratione personæ varietur; siquidem quod semel vt verum apprehenditur, & tanquam articulus fidei in Scripturis proponitur & a nobis creditur, illud perpetuò verum manet, & nunquam eius contrarium obtinere potest. Secus autem se res habet, quoad obiectum fidei specialis, quod est remissio peccatorum. Hæc enim iterum excuti & amitti, ideoque respectu personæ credentis variari potest, vt licet fidei, quamdiu credimus, falsum subesse nõ possit, tempus tamen venire queat, quo & fidē perdamus, & de fidei specialis obiecto, seu de peccatorũ remissione nõ amplius glostari valeamus. Atque hinc sit vt certitudo fidei non gignat securitatem carnis, non expellat omnem timorem, sed vnà includat vigilãtiam & circumspectionem, quam tamen tolli falsò nobis affingunt Pontificij.

4. Non quæritur de certitudine electionis & perseuerantiæ. Hæc enim controuersia decade secundâ est pertractata. Et licet quæstiones istæ sint conjunctæ, non tamen penitùs sunt confundendæ, nē oriatur indè confusio, & turbetur vera vtriusque intelligentia.

5. Non quæritur de fide magna, & omnis dubitationis experte confidentia. Nam fatemur ipsi, renatorum fidem sæpiùs languescere, varijsque dubitationibus concuti, vt non semper sit robusta & excellens, præsertim tentationis tempore, verùmt non vrgemus dubitationem illam, nec inculcamus renatis, tanquam necessariam, vt faciunt Pontificij; sed potiùs improbamus; tanquam vitiosam & ex imbecillitate carnis ortam, quæ fide, precatione, álijsque medijs vt superetur, diligenter annitendum est, vt dicamus cum patre lunatici ex Marci 9. v. 24. Credo Domine, sed fer opem imbecillitati meæ.

6. Nec tandem quæritur, An certitudinis & fiduciæ illius fundamentum sit in nostris virtutibus meritisuè situm? Nam præsupponimus, opera nostra esse imperfecta, & multas impuritates habere admixtas, vt seuerum Dei examen ferre nequeant. Si quis ergò in ijs suam locet fiduciam, libenter fatemur, quòd indè nulla fluat, vel fluere possit certitudo, sed potiùs mera fluctuatio & anxietas animi.

XXIII. IIX. Verus controuersiæ status. Ita igitur remotis ijs, quæ in quæstionem non veniunt, nõ obscurum esse poterit verum ζητούμενον. Nempè controuersia est de homine pœnitente, Annon iste promissiones gratiæ de peccatorum remissione ne, ob imputatum Christi meritum, sibi cùm firmiter applicare, veráque fide sic apprehendere possit & debeat, vt non tantùm conjecturaliter speret; sed potiùs certitudine fidei credat, sibi peccata omnia esse remissa & se iterum cum Deo redijsse in gratiam? Vel bréuius hoc in quæstione est; Annon vera pœnitentia & fides justissima firmam immotamque diuinæ gratiæ fiduciam in cordibus fidelium parere possit ac debeat? Negant Pontificij, nos affirmamus, & hoc ipsum argumentis benè multis demonstrare possumus.


### Question II

XXIV. Dr. Sigfridus Saccus, one of our own, wrote a special treatise on this question, published at Magdeburg in the year '69, in which the arguments pertaining to this are recounted at length. Dr. Chemnitius, however, reduced them to a compendium in part 1 of his Examination, p. 168 et seqq., from which we shall repeat the principal ones and include them under certain titles or classes, not being so concerned about the evasions of Bellarmine in book 3, chapter 9, since he merely collected sayings that are almost ἀπροσδιόνυσα, so that he might answer more easily and be able to deceive the reader, as if our opinion did not rest upon firmer supports. Those absurdities therefore being dismissed, we shall bring forward the most solid reasons.

XXV. 1. From the nature of justifying faith. If faith is a firm and immovable confidence of the soul, apprehending the promises without hesitation, then every believer will be able to be certain with the certainty of faith concerning the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins. The reason for the consequence is firm, since confidence and hesitation or uncertainty exclude one another. But indeed, justifying faith is a firm and immovable confidence of the soul, apprehending the promises without apprehending with doubt: Wherefore every believer will be able to be certain with the certainty of faith concerning the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins. We have most clearly proved the minor premise elsewhere from the etymology of faith. 2. From synonymy. 3. From the testimony of interpreters. 4. From exegetical declaration. 5. From manifest sayings of Scripture. 6. From parallel passages. 7. From the proper object of faith. 8. From the form of justifying faith. 9. From the effects of faith. 10. From typical and metaphorical descriptions. 11. From examples. 12. From prayers. 13. From opposites. 14. From the authority of the Fathers. 15. From the confession of adversaries, all of which are indeed so great that they render the mind most firm and expel every doubt.

XXVI. II. From sayings of Scripture, clearly indicating certainty.

1. Romans 5, verse 1. Being justified by faith, we have peace with God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, verse 2. Through whom we have access by faith into this grace, in which we stand and glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God. But whoever has peace and tranquility of mind, to whom such access into grace is granted, so that they stand in it and glory on account of the hope of glory, they are most certain of the remission of sins. But all the just or justified have peace and tranquility of mind, etc. Wherefore all the just are most certain of the remission of sins. The major premise is beyond doubt, on account of the perpetual opposition of peace and anxiety, of certain access and the doubt of shame, and of uncertainty. The minor premise is in the text of the Apostle. Therefore, its truth shall not be denied to the conclusion.

If they should object, that faith can indeed establish in general that the promises of grace are most certain, but that the application is uncertain, since no one knows whether he is just on account of his own unworthiness and indisposition. We answer 1. that by this agreement the nature of justifying faith is utterly overturned. For it is not some universal idea, but a particular trust, by which not only we believe in general, but every penitent person applies the promises to himself in particular. For the devils also believe the truth of the promises in general, but they cannot accommodate them to themselves in particular. Therefore, while the Papists deny special application, they leave no distinction between the faith of demons and the faith of the justified is not doubtful, but certain. Just as all the justified have peace with God, I can certainly subsume also concerning myself in particular, that through the faith by which I apprehend the merit of Christ, I have peace with God. For that which is truly said of a universal or of a whole kind, this same thing is most rightly affirmed also of any particular and individual. 3. It is false that no one can know whether he has faith and is justified. For if anyone understands the nature of justifying faith, and knows what is required for it, or in what it consists; then he can certainly test himself and know whether justifying faith and true repentance are absent or present. Then indeed these things would be uncertain if proper dispositions, satisfactions, and the like were required: since we know that these little works are excluded from the circle of faith and justification, the faithful have no further cause for doubting.

II. Eph. 3, verse 12. In Christ we have τὴν παῤῥησίαν καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐν πεποιθήσει διὰ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ, boldness and access in confidence through faith in him. But where there is παῤῥησία and πεποίθησις, there every servile fear, every uncertainty and anxiety is banished. Bellarmine objects in book 3 de Iustific. c. 9, that by παῤῥησία is indeed understood boldness, arising from a certain supreme and infallible certainty, but that this certainty is not concerning our righteousness, but concerning the truth of the mysteries of faith. I respond: The principle is begged, and a gloss is invented without reason. For to approach God, and to have πεποίθησιν, does not denote a general assent, by which we believe the mysteries, but rather a special confidence, by which we believe in the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins. For those are acts not of the intellect, but of the will. And hence the Apostle deduces in verse 13 that we must not fail in tribulations, namely because we are certain through that πεποίθησιν [confidence] of God's mercy and help. Thus therefore we conclude: Every approach ἐν πεποιθήσει [in confidence] is joined with the highest certainty of faith. But the approach of the faithful to Christ and the throne of grace, when indeed they seek the remission of sins, is ἐν πεποιθήσει [in confidence]. Therefore it is joined with the highest certainty of faith.

III. James 1. v. 6. Let one ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he who wavers is like a wave of the sea, which is moved and tossed by the wind. But wherever wavering is excluded, there certainty is posited. But James wishes wavering to be excluded by every faithful person. Therefore he wishes certainty to be present in every faithful person. The major premise is evident, because every uncertainty brings with it at the same time fluctuation and hesitation of mind. For while I am uncertain, I always waver as to what should be determined.

IV. 1 John 3. v. 14. ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν, We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren, chapter 4, verse 13. ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν. In this we know that we abide in him, and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit. By these sayings not only some conjectural certainty is hinted at, but rather such a one as is coupled with certain knowledge and indubitable cognition, from which an argument of this kind flows: That which someone knows and recognizes well, of that he is certainly most sure. But the faithful know and recognize their justification and adoption as sons. Therefore the faithful are most sure of this very thing. Bellarmine objects in chapter 9: By the words We know and we recognize, the certainty of divine faith is not understood, but that which arises from signs and conjectures. But this is not to answer, but to beg the question,

And if such glosses ought to serve, every science can be called into doubt, and whatever is said about the certainty of knowledge, that could be explained by conjectures and signs. The Apostle certainly argues from love to knowledge. That, however, is not a conjectural, but a most firm argument. For whoever loves his brother, he is truly faithful and reborn. Now any penitent person subsumes: I love the brothers, which he knows most certainly in the examination of himself. Therefore he concludes, and thus knows, that he is truly faithful and reborn. The Apostle adds a most firm reason: Because he has given us of his Spirit, by which he refers to the internal testimony of the Spirit, while it testifies that we are children of GOD, which testimony is certainly not conjectural, but most certain and infallible. A similar passage exists in 1 John 5. v. 19. We know that we are from GOD. v. 20. We know that the Son of GOD has come and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God and be in his true Son, this is the true God and eternal life, where indeed to those believing in Christ is not attributed opinion, doubt, or conjectural certainty, but rather full knowledge and immovable cognition. To this also can be referred that passage of Job 19. v. 25. I know that my Redeemer lives.

Latin:

XXIV. Scripsit ex nostris D. Sigfridus Saccus peculiarem de hac quēstione tractatum; Magdeburgi anno 69. editum, in quo prolixè recensentur argumenta huc facientia. In compendium verò redegit illa D. Chemnitius par 1. Examinis m. p. 168. seqq. vndè præcipua repetemus, & certis siue titulis, siue classibus includemus, non adeò soliciti de elusionibus Bellarmini l. 3. c. 9. quippè qui dicta ferè ἀπροσδιόνυσα tantum collegit, vt responderet faciliùs, & lectori fucum facere posset, quasi nostra sententia firmiorib. fulcris non inniteretur. Istis ergò ineptijs missis, rationes maximè solidas in medium afferemus.

XXV. 1. A fidei iustificantis natura. Si fides est firma & immota animi fiducia, promissiones sine dubitatione apprehendens, tum omnis fidelis certitudine fidei certus esse poterit de gratia Dei & peccatorum venia. Ratio consequentiæ est firma, quoniam se inuicem excludunt fiducia & hæsitatio vel incertitudo. At verò iustificans fides est firma & immota animi fiducia, promissiones sine dubitatione apprehēdens: Quare omnis fidelis certitudine fidei certus esse poterit de gratia Dei & peccatorum venia. Minorem alibi clarissimè probauimus ab etymologia fidei. 2. A Synonymia. 3. A testimonio interpretum. 4. A declaratione exegetica. 5. A dictis Scripturæ manifestis 6. Ex locis parallelis. 7. A proprio fidei obiecto. 8. A forma fidei iustificantis. 9. Ab effectibus fidei. 10. A typicis & metaphoricis descriptionibus. 11. Ab exemplis. 12. A precationibus, 13. Ab oppositis. 14. Ab authoritate Patrum. 15. A confessione aduersariorum, quæ omnia sanè tanta sunt, vt animum reddant firmissimum, & omnem dubitationem expellant.

XXVI. II. A Dictis Scriptvrae, Certitvdinem Manifeste Innventibvs.

1. Roman. 5. v. 1. Iustificati ex fide, pacem habemus ad Deum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, v. 2. Per quem habemus accessum fide in gratiam istam, in qua stamus & gloriamur in spe gloriæ filiorum Dei. Quicunque verò habent pacem & tranquillitatē mentis, quibus conceditur talis accessus in gratiam, vt in illa stent & glorientur ob spem gloriæ, illi sunt certissimi de peccatorum remissione. Sed omnes iusti vel iustificati habent pacem & tranquillitatem mentis &c. Quare omnes iusti certissimi sunt de peccatorū remissione. Maior extra dubium est, ob perpetuam oppositionē pacis, & anxietatis, certi accessus & dubitationis καταισχύνης, & incertitudinis. Minor est in textu Apostoli. Sua igitur conclusioni non deneganda erit veritas.

Si exceperint, Exceptio fidem in genere quidem statuere posse, promissiones gratię esse certissimas, applicationem verò fidem in geincertam esse, cùm nemo sciat, an sit iustus ob indignitatem & indispositionē propriam. Respondemus 1. quòd hoc pacto fidei iustificantis natura prorsus euertatur. Non enim est vniuersalis quædam idea, sed particularis fiducia, quâ nō tantùm in genere credimus, sed quiuis poenitens sibi in specie promissiones applicat. Credunt enim alias & diaboli promissionum veritatem in genere, sed sibi accommodare nequeunt in specie. Dum ergo Pontificij specialem applicationem negant, nullum discrimen relinquunt inter fidem dæmonum & fidem iustificatorum. 2. Non dubia, sed certa est sub generali themate subsumptio. Sicut omne niusti pacem habent cum Deo, vtique de me etiam subsumere possum in specie, quòd per fidem quâ Christi meritum apprehendo, pacem habeam apud Deum. Quod enim verè dicitur de vniuersali vel de vniuerso genere, hoc ipsum de quouis etiam particulari & indiuiduo rectissimè affirmatur 3. Falsum est, quòd nemo scire possit, an fidem habeat & iustificatus sit. Si enim ratione fidei iustificantis quis intelligat, & quid ad ipsam requiratur, vel in quo consistat nouerit; tum sanè probare potest seipsum & cognoscere, an fides iustificans, & vera poenitentia desit vel adsit. Tum quidem hæc incerta forent, si requirerentur propriæ dispositiones, satisfactiones & similia: quas opellas cùm nos è fidei & iustificationis circulo exclusas sciamus, nullam ampliùs dubitandi causam habent fideles.

II. Ephes. 3. vers. 12. In christo habemus τὴν παῤῥησίαν καὶ τὴν προσαγωγὴν ἐν πεποιθήσει διὰ τῆς πίστεως αὐτοῦ, fiduciam & accessum in confidentia per fidem eius. Vbi verò est παῤῥησία καὶ πεποίθησις, ibi exulat omnis timor seruilis, omnis incertitudo & anxietas. Excipis Bellarminus lib. 3. de Iustific. c. 9. per παῤῥησίαν intelligi quidem audaciam, ortam ex quadam summa & infallibili certitudine, sed eam certitudinem non esse de iustitia nostra, sed de veritate mysteriorum fidei. Respond. Princicipium petitur, & glossa sine ratione fingitur. Nam accedere ad Deum, & habere πεποίθησιν, non notat assensum generalem, quo credimus mysteria, sed potiùs fiduciam specialem, quâ credimus Dei gratiam & peccatorum veniam. Sunt enim illi non intellectus, sed voluntatis actus. Et hinc deducit Apostolus ver. 13. non esse deficiendum in tribulationibus, nempè quoniam certi sumus per illam πεποίθησιν de Dei misericordia & auxilio. Sic igitur colligimus: Omnis accessus ἐν πεποιθήσει est cum summa certitudine fidei coniunctus. Sed accessus fidelium ad Christum thronumque gratiæ, cùm nempè petunt remissionem peccatorum, sit ἐν πεποιθήσει. Ergò cum summa certitudine fidei coniunctus est.

III. Iacobi 1. v. 6. Postulet quis in fide, nihil hæsitans, Qui enim hæsitat, similis est fluctui maris, qui à vento movetur & circumfertur. Vbicunque autem excluditur hæsitatio, ibi ponitur certitudo. Sed à quovis fideli Iacobus exclusam vult hæsitationem. Ergò in quovis fideli adesse vult certitudinem. Maior patet, quia omnis incertitudo vnà trahit secum fluctuationem & animi hæsitationem. Dum enim incertus sum, semper hæsito, quid statuendum sit.

IV. 1. Ioh. 3. v. 14. ἡμεῖς οἴδαμεν, Nos scimus, quoniam translati sumus de morte ad vitam, quoniam diligimus, fratres, capite 4. versu 13. ἐν τούτῳ γινώσκομεν. In hoc cognoscimus, quoniam in eo manemus, & ipse in nobis, quoniam de spiritu suo dedit nobis. His dictis non tantùm aliqua coniecturalis certitudo innuitur, sed talis potius, quæ cù certa scientia & indubitata cognitione copulata sit, vndè argumentū fluit eiusmodi: Quod aliquis benè scit & cognoscit, de illo vtiq; certissimus est. Sed fideles sciunt & agnoscunt suā iustificationē & adoptionem in filios. Ergò fideles de hoc ipso sunt certissimi. Excipit Bellarminus c. 9. Per vocabula Scimus & cognoscimus, nõ intelligi certitudinem fidei diuinæ, sed eam, quę ex signis & coniecturis oritur. Verùm hoc nõ est respōdere, sed principiū petere,

Et si tales glossæ militare debeant, omnis scientia vocari potest in dubium, & quicquid dicitur de certitudine notitiæ, id posset de cōiecturis signisque exponi. Apostolus sanè ex dilectione argumentatur ad cognitionem. Illud verò non est coniecturale, sed firmissimum argumentum. Quicunque enim fratrem diligit, is verè fidelis & renatus est. Iam quivis pœnitens subsumit: Ego diligo fratres, id quod in sui ipsius examine certissimè cognoscit. Ergò concludit, atque ita scit, se verè fidelem & renatum esse. Addit Apostolus rationem firmissimam: Quoniam de spiritu suo dedit nobis, quo ipso respicit internum spiritus testimonium, dum testatur, nos esse DEI filios, quod sanè testimonium coniecturale non est, sed certissimum & infallibile. Similis locus extat 1 Iohan. 5. v. 19. Scimus, quoniam ex DEO sumus. v. 20. Scimus, quoniam Filius DEI venit & dedit nobis sensum, vt cognoscamus verum Deum & simus in vero Filio eius, hic est verus Deus & vita æterna, vbi sanè credentibus in Christum non tribuitur opinio, dubitatio, coniecturalis certitudo, sed plena potiùs scientia, & immota cognitio. Huc etiam referri potest illud Iobi 19. v. 25. Scio, quòd Redemptor meus vivit.


### Question II: XXXVII. III. From the testimony of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the pious

XXXVII. III. From the testimony of the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the pious.

Whatever the Holy Spirit seals, and confirms in the hearts of the faithful by his testimony, that is most certain without any doubt, and ought to be most certainly believed by the pious. But the Holy Spirit seals the remission of sins and confirms it in the hearts of the faithful by his testimony. Therefore the remission of sins is most certain, and ought to be most certainly believed by the pious. The major premise is sufficiently manifest in itself, since the Holy Spirit, who is truth itself, is an infallible testimony and greater than any exception. The minor premise can be proven by very many passages, such as those read in Romans 8. verse 15. You have not received the Spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the Spirit of the adoption of the Sons of GOD; in whom we cry, Abba Father. And verse 16. The Spirit himself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of GOD. And if children, then heirs. 1 Cor. 2, verse 12. We have received the Spirit, which is of GOD, that we might know the things that are freely given to us of GOD. 2 Cor. 1, verses 21, 22, 23. Now he which stablisheth us with you in Christ, and hath anointed us, is GOD: Who hath also sealed us, and given τὸν ἀῥῥαβῶνα τῦ πνεύματος the earnest of the Spirit in our hearts. Eph. 1, verses 13, 14. Believing, έσφραγί- σθητε ye were sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, which is the earnest of our inheritance. So chapter 4, verse 30. Grieve not the holy Spirit, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. 1 John 5, verse 10. He that believeth on the Son of GOD hath the witness of GOD in himself. Verse 11. And this is the witness, that GOD hath given to us eternal life. Here both are joined, both the infallible witness and the object of the witness, which is the giving of eternal life, which is not believed in general, but is applied by each person to himself in particular, since the words are most clear: This is the witness, that GOD hath given to us eternal life. The Apostle declares this very thing more fully in the following verses, while in verse 13 he says, These things have I written unto you, that ye may know that ye have eternal life, ye that believe on the name of the Son of God. And hence he says that we have such confidence, by which we are certain of the hearing of our prayers, verses 14, 15.

XXXVIII. Bellarmine did not propose nor refute this entire argument, but wished to respond to only one or another passage, in book 3, chapter 9. Regarding the statement in Rom. 8, that the Holy Spirit beareth witness with our spirit, he objects thus, that there are two readings and expositions of this passage. One, he says, is the reading of the Latin codex, which holds that the Holy Spirit beareth witness with our spirit, but that this witness is not through any express word, that is, through revelation, but through the experience of a certain sweetness and internal peace, which does not beget certainty, except conjectural,

Reply. It is impious to hold the testimony of the Holy Spirit as a mere conjecture. For He neither deceives, nor is He deceived. Why, therefore, is His testimony called nothing but conjectural? As regards special revelation, that is necessary neither in respect of the Spirit, nor of us. Not by reason of the Holy Spirit, since all things are most known to Him by Himself, nor does He need any testimony by which He might learn first whether the man in whom He dwells truly believes or otherwise. Not by reason of us, because the internal testimony of the Spirit itself is divine, and is equivalent to revelation. But do the Jesu-Witae think that God testifying within is not to be believed, unless one confirms that same thing from without and extrinsically? Thus, therefore, we conclude against him: Whatever the Holy Spirit brings forth, this is the word of God, because the Holy Spirit is God. But the internal testimony that we are children of God is brought forth by the Holy Spirit. Therefore, the internal testimony is the word of God Himself, and consequently, we have no need of special revelation.

Furthermore, regarding the second exception, Bellarmine writes that there is another reading of the Greek codex, which has the Holy Spirit testifying together with our spirit: αὐτο τὸ πνευ̃μα συμμαρτυρει̃ τω̃ πνεύματι ἠμω̃ν. And that this testimony is nothing else but the prayer itself, by which we say: Abba Father.

Reply. 1. I do not see how these readings differ. For he who testifies with someone, he together with him renders testimony to this, that he testifies to the truth. It is therefore the same, whether the Holy Spirit is said to testify with our spirit, or to render testimony to our spirit, since by both phrases the consensus of the witnesses and the certainty of the testimony is denoted. 2. Bellarmine begs the question by asserting that the internal testimony of the Spirit is nothing else but prayer. For it is rather a confirmation of grace, and a sealing of forgiveness, made by the Holy Spirit dwelling within, of which the consequent is confident prayer. And one thing is the work of the Holy Spirit, both to seal and to intercede for us, and to stir us up to pray, which, since they are distinct, ought not to be confused without reason. 3. If by that testimony one understands the prayer of the faithful, it will nevertheless harm the Papist cause more than it will help it. For such a prayer presupposes the gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, and a certain sealing concerning the remission of sins. For no one can call upon the Lord, except in the Holy Spirit. 1 Cor. 12 v. 3. And such a one asks in faith, nothing wavering, James 1 v. 6, and therefore the prayer of a godly person is a certain sign of the sealing Spirit. From which it further follows that there is a twofold testimony of the Holy Spirit concerning the certainty of grace. The one is internal, which is the sealing and interior certification itself, from which arises peace and joy of conscience: the other is external, which is the fruit and consequence of the former, namely, an ardent and nothing-wavering prayer, together with other exercises of virtues. Thus, therefore, this external testimony does not remove, but rather presupposes, the internal.

XXXIX. But these things do not yet satisfy Bellarmine, because he further objects: This very thing, namely, that it is the Holy Spirit who moves us when we say, Abba Father, is not certain to us by divine faith, but only by conjectures, which can be fallacious. For many, not only sinners among Catholics, but also heretics, say to GOD, Our Father, who art in heaven, and yet they themselves are not truly children of GOD.

Resp. This is to introduce doubt with full sails, which, however, Bellarmine does not wish to appear to do. For whatever relies only on fallacious conjectures must be doubted; but the grace of the indwelling Spirit relies only on fallacious conjectures, according to Bellarmine. Therefore, the grace of the indwelling Spirit must be doubted. 2. This assertion both begs the question, and contradicts the Scriptures, and afflicts us all most miserably. It begs the question, because it is brought forward without a firm reason. For that which is said concerning heretics and Catholics praying is of no moment, since we are not speaking of presumption and false boasting, nor of hypocritical prayers, but of true and serious ones which only fall to the penitent and the faithful. Nor could the certainty of the entire Catholic faith be any less called into doubt, since heretics have also boasted of that. It contradicts the Scriptures, which expressly affirm that the pious feel the impulse of the Holy Spirit and know that they are born of God, 1 John 5, verses 10, 13. It makes us most miserable, because if the remission of sins is built upon nothing but fallacious conjectures, the pious must certainly remain in perpetual torments and anxieties of mind. For there can be no greater torture than to fluctuate perpetually and to be tossed about between hope and doubtful fear. Wherefore God gave us the earnest of the promise, the Holy Spirit, who renders us certain and seals the grace of God within us. The pious easily recognize Him and discern Him from the evil spirit. For just as when they believe, they know that they believe, so when they are led by the Holy Spirit, they understand that they are ruled and guided by Him, and not by another. To this point looks that passage of the Apostle, 2 Cor. 13, verse 5: Examine yourselves, whether you are in the faith; prove your own selves; do you not know your own selves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Where the Apostle is certainly not speaking of the general presence of Christ, which they call that of power and providence, but rather of the special presence, or that of grace, which arises from faith, which the Corinthians were bound to prove. For although some were perverse, many nevertheless in that Church were pious and truly faithful, whom the Apostle addresses in that text, and to whom he most openly assigns a sign for proving and certainly knowing the faith, and adds, unless perhaps you are reprobates, from which it follows that doubt is a sign of reprobation. For those fluctuate, those do not prove themselves, whether they are in the faith, who are reprobates, and by sins are given over against conscience.

XL. To the passage 1 Cor. 2. v. 12. he objects that it does not treat of the knowledge of the benefits of God which pertain in particular to this one or that one, but of the knowledge of the benefits of GOD which GOD has prepared for His elect.

Resp. Papists always oppose things that are subordinate. For Scripture joins both together, and attributes both to faith: both the general assent regarding the benefits of God, and the special confidence regarding the attainment of them. And the Apostle especially regards this latter. For he does not describe some Platonic idea fluttering in the air, but shows the consolation of every pious person, which he says consists in the reception of the Holy Spirit, who is given to that end that we may know: what indeed? Certainly not only the articles and mysteries of faith in general, but especially what things have been given to us, what benefits we have attained, and have obtained from God, such as reconciliation, remission, adoption, etc. These are those goods given to us, concerning which, that we may not have any handle for doubting, the Apostle writes that the Holy Spirit, certifying us, has been poured into our hearts.

XLI. IV. From the examples of the Saints, who are narrated to have been certain of their righteousness. Whatever very many saints have believed with the certainty of faith, and in which very thing they are proposed to you for imitation, concerning that one must not doubt, nor only hope well, but rather must most certainly trust. But very many saints believed the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins with the certainty of faith, and in this very thing they are proposed to us for imitation. Therefore, concerning the grace of God one must not doubt, nor only hope well, but must most certainly trust. For the proof of the minor, many examples could be produced, such as those of Abel, Enoch, Noah, and other believers who are recounted in Heb. 11, but lest we be too prolix, only three, and those most notable examples

Latin:

XXXVII. III. A Spiritus sancti in cordibus piorum testificatione.

Quicquid Spiritus sanctus obsignat, & in cordibus fidelium suo testimonio confirmat, id sine omni dubitatione certissimum est, & à pijs certissimè credi debet. Sed remissionem peccatorum Spiritus sanctus obsignat & in cordibus fidelium suo testimonio confirmat. Ergò remissio peccatorum certissima est, & à pijs certissimè credi debet. Maior per se est satis manifesta, cùm Spiritus sanctus, qui ipsa veritas, testimonium sit infallibile & omni exceptione maius. Minor dictis probari potest quam plurimis, qualia leguntur, Roman. 8. ver. 15. Non accepistis Spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis Spiritum adoptionis Filiorum DEI; in quo clamamus, Abba Pater. Et vers. 16. Ipse Spiritus testimonium reddit Spiritui nostro, quod simus filij DEI. Si autem filij, vtique & hæredes. 1. Cor. 2. vers. 12. Nos accepimus Spiritum, qui ex DEO est, vt sciamus quæ à DEO donata sint nobis. 2. Cor. 1, vers. 21. 22. 23. Qui confirmat nos vobiscum in Christum, & qui vnxit nos, DEVS: Qui & signauit nos, & dedit τὸν ἀῥῥαβῶνα τῦ πνεύματος pignus Spiritus in cordibus nostris. Eph. 1. vers. 13 14. Credentes έσφραγίσθητε signati estis Spiritu promissionis sancto, qui est pignus hæreditatis nostræ. Sic cap. 4. vers. 30. Nolite contristari Spiritum sanctum, in quo signati estis in diem Redemptionis. 1. Ioh. 5. vers. 10. Qui credit in Filium DEI habet testimonium DEI in se. vers. 11. Et hoc est testimonium, quoniam vitam æternam dedit nobis DEVS. Copulatur hic vtrumq;, tum testimonium infallibile, tum testimonij obiectum, quod est datio vitæ æternæ, quæ non creditur in genere, sed à quouis sibi applicatur in specie, cùm verba sint clarissima: Hoc est testimonium, quoniam vitam æternam dedit nobis DEVS. Hoc ipsum in sequentibus magis declarat Apostolus, dum vers. 13. inquit, Hæc scripsi vobis, vt sciatis, quoniam vitam habetis æternam, qui creditis in nomine Filij Dei. Et hinc ait, talem stuere fiduciam, quâ certi simus de exauditione precum, v. 14. 15.

XXXVIII. Argumentum hoc integrum non proposuit, nec refutauit Bellarminus, sed ad vnum duntaxat & alterum locum respondere voluit, l. 3. cap. 9. de dicto Rom. 8, quod Spiritus sanctus testimonium reddat spiritui nostro, sic excipit, quod duæ huius loci sint lectiones & expositiones, Vna, inquit, lectio est latini codicis, quæ habet, Spiritum sanctum testimonium reddere Spiritui nostro, sed hoc testimonium non esse per verbum aliquod expressum, id est per reuelationem, sed per experimentum cuiusdam sauitatis & pacis internæ, quæ non gignat certitudinem, nisi coniecturalem,

Respond. Impium est Spiritus sancti testimonium habere pro mera coniectura. Ipse enim nec fallit, nec fallitur. Cur eius ergo testimonium non nisi coniecturale dicitur? Quod reuelationem specialem spectat, illa nec Spiritus, nec nostri respectu necessaria est. Non ratione Spiritus sancti, quoniam illi cuncta per se sunt notissima, nec eget aliquo testimonio, per quod addiscat primum, hominem, in quo habitat, vere credat vel secus, Non ratione nostri, quia ipsum Spiritus testimonium internum est diuinum, & aequipollet revelationi. Num autem putant Iesu Witae, non esse credendum Deo intus testanti, nisi vna foris & extrinsecus illud ipsum confirmet? Sic ergo contra ipsum concludimus: Quicquid Spiritus sanctus profert, hoc est Dei verbum, quia Spiritus sanctus est Deus, Sed testimonium internum, quod simus filij Dei, profertur a S. S. E. testimoniū internum est ipsius Dei verbum, & per consequens, non opus habemus speciali reuelatione.

Vlterius, quod secundam exceptionem attinet, scribit Bellarminus, alteram lectionem esse codicis Graeci, qui habeat, Spiritum sanctum simul testari cum Spiritu nostro: αὐτο τὸ πνευ̃μα συμμαρτυρει̃ τω̃ πνεύματι ἠμω̃ν. Et hoc testimonium nihil esse aliud, nisi ipsam orationem, qua dicimus: Abba Pater.

Resp. 1. Non video, qui discrepent istae lectiones. Nam qui testatur cum aliquo, is vnà testimonium huic reddit, quod verum testetur. Perinde igitur est, siue Spiritus S. dicatur testari cum spiritu nostro, siue testimonium reddere spiritui nostro, siquidem vtraque phrasi consensus testium & certitudo testimonij denotatur. 2. Principium petit Bellarminus, asserendo, quod internum Spiritus testimonium nihil sit aliud, nisi i- ̄oratio. Nam est potius gratiae confirmatio, & v- ̄niae obsignatio, per ipsum inhabitantē S. S. facta, cuius consequens est fiducialis oratio. Vnumque enim opus est Spiritus S. tum obsignare, tum pro nobis intercedere, & nos ad precandum excitare, quæ cùm distincta sint, sine ratione confundi non debent. 3. Si maximè per illud testimonium intelligatur oratio fidelis, causæ tamen Papisticæ magis nocebit hoc, quàm proderit. Nam talis precatio præsupponit gratiosam inhabitationem Spiritus sancti, & certam obsignationem de remissione peccatorum. Nemo enim potest vocare Dominum, nisi in Spiritu sancto. 1. Cor. 12. v. 3. Et talis postulat in fide nihil hæsitans, Iac. 1. v. 6. ideoque precatio pij tum obsignantis Spiritus certum est indicium. Ex quo porrò consequitur, quòd duplex sit testimoniū Spiritus sancti de certitudine gratię, Alterum est internum, quod ipsa obsignatio & certificatio interior, vnde oritur pax & gaudium conscientiæ: Alterum verò est externum, quod prioris fructus & consequens est, nempè ardens nihilq́; hæsitans oratio, vnà cum alijs virtutum exercitijs. Ita ergò testimonium hoc externum non tollit, sed potiùs præsupponit internum.

XXXIX. Verùm hæc nondum satisfaciunt Bellarmino, quia porrò excipit: Hoc ipsum, quòd videlicet Spiritus sanctus sit, qui nos mouet, cùm dicimus, Abba Pater, non constat nobis ex fide diuina, sed solum ex coniecturis, quæ fallaces esse possunt. Multi enim non solùm peccatores inter Catholicos, sed etiam hæretici dicunt DEO, Pater noster, qui es in cælis, & tamen non sunt ipsi verè filij DEI.

Resp. Hoc est plenis velis inuehere dubitationem, quòd tamen videri non vult Bellarminus. Nam quicquid non nisi coniecturis fallacibus innititur, de illo dubitandum est, Sed gratia inhabitantis Spiritus non nisi coniecturis fallacibus innititur, iuxta Bellarminum. Ergò de gratia inhabitantis Spiritus dubitandum est. 2. Assertio ista & principium petit, & Scripturis contradicit, & nos omnes miserrimè afflicit, Principium petit, quia sine firma ratione profertur. Illud enim, quod de Hæreticis & Catholicis orantibus dicitur, nullius est momenti, quoniam non loquimur de præsumtione & gloriatione falsa, non de precibus hypocriticis, sed de veris serijsque quajestantùm cadunt in pœnitentes & fideles. Nec minus omnis fidei Catholicę certitudo in dubium vocari posset, cùm & de illa gloriati sint hæretici. Scripturæ contradicit, quippè quæ disertè affirmant, quòd pij sentiant impulsum S. S. & sciant, quòd ex Deo nati sint, 1. Ioh. 5. vers. 10. 13. Nos miserrimos efficit, quia si remissio peccatorum non nisi fallacibus coniecturis superstructa est, sanè pios in perpetuis animi cruciatibus & anxietatibus hærere oportet. Nulla enim maior esse potest carnificina, quàm perpetuò fluctuare & inter spem metumque dubium versari. Quocirca dedit nobis Deus arrham promissionis, Spiritum sanctum, qui nos certos reddet, & gratiam Dei in nobis obsignat. Hunc facilè agnoscunt, & à Spiritu malo discernunt pij. Vt enim cùm credunt, se credere sciunt, ita cùm aguntur Spiritu sancto, se ab illo, non alio regi flectique intelligunt. Hûc spectat illud Apostoli 2. Cor. 13, vers. 5. Vos ipsos tentate, an sitis in fide, ipsi vos probate; annon cognoscitis vosmetipsos, quia Christus Iesus in vobis est? Vbi sanè non loquitur Apostolus de præsentia Christi generali, quam vocant potentiæ & prouidentiæ, sed potius de speciali, seu gratiæ, quæ oritur ex fide, quam probare debebant Corinthij. Licèt enim quidam essent perversi, multi tamen in illa Ecclesia fuerunt pij & verè fideles, quos Apostolus in illo textu alloquitur, & quibus signum probandi ac certò cognoscendi fidem apertissimè adsignat, & addit, nisi fortè estis reprobi, vnde sequitur, quòd dubitatio sit signum reprobationis. Illi enim fluctuant, illi semetipsos non probant, num sint in fide, qui reprobi, & peccatis contra conscientiam sunt dediti.

XL. Ad dictum 1. Cor. 2. v. 12. excipit, non agi in eo de notitia beneficiorum Dei, quæ in particulari ad hunc aut illum pertinent, sed de notitia beneficiorum DEI, quæ DEVS præparauit electis suis.

Resp. Semper Papicolæ opponunt, quæ subordinata sunt. Vtrumque enim Scriptura coniungit, & vtrumque fidei attribuit, tum generalem assensum, quoad Dei beneficia; tum specialem fiduciam, quoad illorum adeptionem. Et hoc posterius cumprimis respicit Apostolus. Non enim aliquam ideam Platonicam, in aëre volitantem describit, sed consolationem cuiusvis pij ostendit, quam ait consistere in Spiritus sancti acceptatione, qui detur eo fine, vt sciamus: quidnam? Non sanè tantùm articulus & mysteria fidei: in genere, sed cumprimis. quæ donata sint nobis, quæ beneficia adepti sumus, & à Deo impetrauerimus, qualia sunt reconciliatio, remissio, adoptio &c. Hęc sunt illa bona nobis donata, de quibus nè vllam dubitandi ansam habeamus, Spiritu sanctum nos certificantem in corda nostra effusum esse scribit Apostolus.

XLI. IV. Ab exemplis Sanctorum, qui certi fuisse narrantur de sua iustitia. Quodcunque plurimi sancti certitudine fidei crediderunt, & in quo ipso ad imitandum uobis proponuntur, de illo non dubitandum, nec tantùm benè sperandum, sed potius certissimè confidendum est. Sed plurimi sancti gratiam Dei & peccatorum veniam certitudine fidei crediderunt, & in hoc ipso nobis ad imitandum proponuntur Ergò de gratia Dei non dubitandum, nec tantùm benè sperandum, sed certissimè confidendum est. Pro minoris probatione multa produci possent exempla, vt Abelis, Enochi, Noachi & aliorum fidelium, qui recensentur Hebr. 11. sed nè nimium simus prolixi, tria tantùm, eaque maximè insignia exempla in medium


### Question II: we shall adduce, namely 1

we shall adduce, namely 1. of Abraham, 2. of Job, 3. of Paul. XLII. Abraham. Rom. 4. vers. 12. & 16. is called the Father of all believers, not by reason of carnal generation, because not all are born from the seed of Abraham; nor by reason of spiritual regeneration; because not Abraham, but God regenerates us through the word & Sacraments: But by reason of his example and teaching, since in the Scriptures a father is often the same as a teacher, who instructs others either by precept or by his own example. In this sense Elisha cried out 2. Kings 2. vers. 22. My father, that is, master or preceptor: whence also disciples were formerly called sons of the Prophets. Hence therefore we deduce, that while Abraham was constituted the Father of believers, he was proposed to us all for an example & imitation: which is expressly hinted at Rom. 4. v. 23. 24. It is not written only for his sake, that it was reckoned to him for righteousness, but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned if we believe in him who raised up Jesus Christ. As therefore the faith of Abraham behaved itself, so also it behooves our faith to behave itself. But the faith of Abraham was a certain and immovable confidence, by which he firmly and without any hesitation apprehended the promises of God. Therefore it also behooves our faith to be a firm and immovable confidence: We prove the minor Rom. 4. v. 18. where the faith of Abraham is thus described, that against hope he believed in hope, that he might become the father of many nations v. 19. that he was not weakened in faith, nor did he consider his own body as dead. v. 20. that he did not waver in the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened by faith, giving glory to God. vers. 21. most fully knowing that whatever God promised, he is able also to do, vers. 22. Therefore it was also reckoned to him for righteousness. In these words two things are to be observed, 1. The nature & property of faith. 2. The object of faith. The nature is thus described, that the faith of Abraham was a firm and certain confidence, which is evident from the manner, because he believed against hope in hope; from the opposite, because he did not waver through distrust; from the adjunct, because he was strengthened by faith, knowing most fully that God was able to do what He promised. The object of faith is in general the promise of God, by which both corporal and spiritual goods were contained. The corporal benefit is the generation of a son and the multiplication of the seed, to which indeed reference is made in verse 19; at the same time, however, the Messiah is included, the blessed seed, along with spiritual benefits. For who would think that Abraham had been justified and had obtained the forgiveness of sins only because he believed the promise of God concerning the generation of Isaac? Nor does the faith of Abraham apprehend only one, but every promise of God. And even if Paul had looked only to the multiplication of the seed, we would nevertheless obtain from this that very thing which we desire. For such as was the faith of Abraham concerning the promise of the multiplication of the seed, such ought our faith to be concerning the promise of grace and forgiveness, by the force of the Apostolic text. But the faith of Abraham concerning the promise of the multiplication of the seed was a certain confidence, opposed to all hesitation, and joined with the most full knowledge of the promised good. Therefore our faith also ought to be such concerning the promise of grace and forgiveness. But that the object of Abrahamic faith was not solely the promise concerning the multiplication of the seed has been shown at length in the public disputation on faith, thesis 106.

XLIII. To this and other examples Bellarmine, book 3, chapter 11, makes two exceptions: 1. Those few men, and they very eminent, perhaps deserved to be made certain by a special revelation concerning the grace which they found before the Lord. Certainly we read that it was said manifestly to Abraham in Genesis 22: Now I have known that you fear the Lord, that is, I have made you known to be such, that you are a true worshiper and lover of God.

- Response 1. Bellarmine names a few, of whom there are very many, since all believers have imitated the faith of Abraham. 2. Bellarmine speaks doubtfully, 'perhaps'; which can be refuted by

Perhaps not. For in matters of faith, doubtful and uncertain glosses, which cannot be proven, are not to be fabricated, 3. The firmness of Abrahamic faith is nowhere said to have arisen from a special revelation, but from the consideration of divine power, truth, and promises. Abraham considered that God is omnipotent in doing and truthful in promising: hence, therefore, against hope he believed in hope, nor did he hesitate through unbelief. Now believers ought to consider the same foundations, and then they will similarly draw forth a certain and immovable confidence. 4. The exposition is foreign, 'Now I have known,' that is, 'I have made you know.' For He did not ignore this before Abraham, since long before the undertaking of the immolation of Isaac he had been justified, and had believed against hope in hope, hesitating at nothing, but knowing most fully. Therefore that word is to be understood not of Abraham, but rather of the knowledge of God, who is said ἀνθρωποπαθῶς to have known the piety of Abraham from his willingness to immolate, not because He did not know it before, but because that deed was an illustrious sign by which the interior piety, faith, and obedience of Abraham were manifested. 5. If Abraham infallibly knew his faith from that good work, then the grace of God, why could not other believers also know the same from their good works.

II. He objects that Scripture, while it commends the saints and praises their righteousness and virtues, intends to make us certain, for whom that was most useful, rather than them.

Resp. 1. The example of Abraham clearly refutes this Jesuit sophism. For Scripture intimates that he himself was certain of the grace of God, not indeed from a special revelation, but by the virtue of faith, which relied upon the promise and divine truthfulness. As therefore Abraham was certain for his own person: so it follows that any believer can, and ought to, be certain. 2. We accept that the examples of the faith of the saints were recorded for our sake so that we might be. To what end, however? Certainly not that we should waver, or live in perpetual anguish because of our own infirmity, but rather that, having imitated them, we might simply conceive a firm confidence, hesitating at nothing, but trusting in the promises of God without any doubt, so that we may thus be made certain of the gratuitous remission of sins, and be confirmed in the faith. That this, and no other, was the end of the cited examples, Paul shows most clearly in the place alleged.

XLIV. 2. We can likewise urge the example of Job, seeing that he was certain not only of the grace of God, but moreover of his own glorious resurrection, when in chapter 19, verse 25, he writes: I know that my Redeemer lives, and that in the last day I shall rise from the earth; and I shall be clothed again with my skin, and in my flesh I shall see God, whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold, and not another: This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom. That the blessed vision is noted here, there is no one among the Papists who will easily deny; but that Job was certain of this, the very words indicate, while he says, I know, ידעתי from the root ידע, which denotes full, certain, and indubitable knowledge of a thing, in which manner it is taken in Genesis 15:13, 48:19, 1 Samuel 24:11, Psalm 138:2, Psalm 143:3, Proverbs 27:5. The Jesuit Pineda saw this, who in his commentary on chapter 19 of Job, on verse 25, number 1, page 96, expressly writes: The knowledge of faith (of which he concedes Job is speaking) and this obscure knowledge of divine things is inferior to the blessed vision alone in clarity, equal in certainty, and far superior and more certain than all other sciences. Since Bellarmine has not taken up this example, nor answered anything, we have no need to dwell on it any longer.

XLV 3. The Apostle Paul, in Romans 8:38-39, shines before us with his own example, which is by far the clearest, for thus he writes: I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor Angels, nor Principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor strength, nor height, nor depth nor shall any other creature be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. By these words, indeed, the Apostle promises the grace of God most firmly both to himself and to all the faithful, and implies that he is most certain of it, inasmuch as it is so strengthened in Christ that nothing can avail to separate us from it. Nor does he report this boastfully of himself alone, but rather piously commends the grace of God, and humbly proposes his own example, so that we may imitate it and be strengthened in faith. For he does not recount any peculiar cause of this certainty, denied to us, namely a singular revelation, as the Papists think: but he narrates general foundations, common to all the faithful, and from them deduces that certainty. Such are 1. Mystical incorporation, by which we are inserted into Christ through faith, of which verse 1: There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus. 2. The removal of guilt, effected through the obedience of Christ. verses 3, 4. What was impossible for the law, in which it was weakened through the flesh, God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin condemned sin in the flesh, that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us. 3. The gracious indwelling of the Holy Spirit, of which verses 9, 10, 11, and especially verse 15, treat: You have not received the spirit of bondage, but of adoption. 4. The testimony of the Holy Spirit, verse 16, because he bears witness to our spirit that we are the children of God. 5. The firmness of hope, by which we certainly expect the redemption of our body, verse 23, and by which we have already been saved, verse 24. 6. The help of the Holy Spirit, who helps our infirmity, and intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be uttered, verse 26. But who would not believe that this Spirit is certainly heard? 7. The certainty of the divine decree, concerning those called and justified, to be glorified in his own time. v. 29. 30. 8. Divine protection, verse 31. If God is for us, who is against us? 9. The supreme love of God, with which he has so pursued us, that even his own

Latin:

adducemus, nempe 1. Abrahami. 1. Iobi, 3. Pauli. XLII. Abraham. Rom. 4. vers. 12. & 16. vocatur Pater omnium credentium, non ratione carnalis generationis, quia non omnes ex Abrahami semis ne nascuntur; nec ratione spiritualis regenerationis; quia non Abraham, sed Deus per verbum & Sacramenta nos regenerat: Verùm ratine exempli sui & documenti, siquidem in Scripturis pater saepè idem est, quod doctor, qui alios informat vel praecepto, vel exemplo suo. Hoc sensu clamauit Elisaeus 2. Reg. 2. vers. 22. Pater mi, id est, magister vel praeceptor: vndè & discipuli olim dicti sunt Prophetarum filij. Hinc ergò deducimus, quòd dum Abraham credentium Pater constitutus est, nobis omnibus ad exemplum & imitationem fuerit propositus: quod expressè innuitur Rom. 4. v. 23. 24. Non est scriptum tantum propter ipsum, quod reputatum sit illi ad iustitiam, sed & propter nos, quibus reputabitur credentibus in eum, qui suscitauit Iesum Christum. Prout igitur fides Abrahami se habuit, ita & nostra fides vt se habeat, oportet. Sed fides Abrahami fuit certa & immota fiducia, qua firmiter & sine omni haesitatione apprehendit promissiones Dei. Ergo & nostram fidem oportet esse firmam ac immotam fiduciam: Minorem probamus Rom. 4. v. 18. vbi fides Abrahae sic describitur, quòd contra spem in spem crediderit, vt fieret pater multarum gentium v. 19. quod non infirmatus fuerit in fide, nec considerauit corpus suum emortuum. v. 20. quòd in promissione Dei non haesitauerit diffidentia, sed confortatus sit fide, dans gloriam Deo. vers. 21. plenissimè sciens quia quaecunque promisit Deus, potens est & facere, vers. 22. Ideò & reputatum est illi ad iustitiam. In his verbis duo obseruanda sunt, 1. Natura & propietas fidei. 2. Obiectum fidei. Natura sic describitur, quòd fides Abrahae fuerit firma certaque fiducia, quod patet ex modo, quia credidit contra spem in spem; ex opposito, quia non haesitavit diffidentia; ex adiuncto, quia confortatus est fide plenissime sciens, Deum posse facere, quae promisit. Obiectum fidei est in genere promissio Dei, qua tum corporalia, tum spiritualia bona continebantur. Corporale beneficium est, generatio filij & multiplicatio seminis, quo quidem respicitur ver. 19. simul autem includitur Messias, semen benedictum, cum beneficijs spiritualibus. Quis enim putaret, Abrahamum fuisse iustificatum & impetrasse veniam peccatorumideo, quia credidit promissioni Dei de generatione Isaaci. Nec fides Abrahae vnam duntaxat, sed omnem Dei promissionem apprehendit. Et si maxime Paulus tantum ad multiplicationem seminis respexiffet; hinc tamen illud ipsum, quod volumus, obtineremus. Nam qualis fuit Abrahae fides circa promissionem de multiplicatione seminis, talis esse debet nostra fides, circa promissionem gratiae & veniae, vi textus Apostolici. Sed fides Abrahae circa promissionem de multiplicatione seminis fuit certa fiducia, omni hesitationi opposita, & cum plenissima scientia boni promissi coniuncta. Ergo & nostra fides talis esse debet circa promissionem gratiae & veniae. Quod autem Abrahamiticae fidei obiectum non fuerit sola promissio de seminis multiplicatione, fuse ostensum est disput. publ. de fide, thesi. 106.

XLIII. Ad hoc, & alia exempla Bellarminus l. 3. c. 11. duo excipit: 1. Pauci illi viri, & ij valde eximij, fortasse peculiari revelatione certi fieri meruerunt de gratia, quam apud Dominum inuenerunt. Certe ad Abraham manifeste dictum esse legimus Gen. 22. Nunc agnovi, quod timeas Dominum, id est, fic te agnoscere feci, quod verus sis cultor & amator Dei.

- Resp. 1. Paucos nominat Bellarminus, quorum sunt plurimi, quippe cum omnes credentes fidem Abrahae imitati fuerint. 2. Loquitur Bellarminus dubitative Fortasse; quod refutari potest per

Non fortassè. Nec enim in rebus fidei dubiæ incertæque glossæ, quæ probari nequeunt, consingendæ sunt, 3. Firmitudo fidei Abrahamiticæ nullibi orta dicitur ex peculiari reuelatione, sed ex consideratione diuinæ potentiæ, veritatis & promissionum. Cogitauit Abraham, quòd Deus sit omnipotens in faciendo, & verax in promittendo: Hinc igitur contra spem in spem credidit, nec hæsitauit dissidentia. Iam credentes eadem fundamenta considerare debent, & tum similiter certam immotamque fiduciam haurient. 4. Peregrina est expositio, Nunc cognoui, id est, cognoscere te feci. Non enim antè ignorauit hoc Abrahams cùm jamdudum ante susceptam Isaaci immolationem fuerit iustificatus, & contra spem in spem crediderit, nihil hæsitans, sed plenissimè sciens. Proinde verbum illud non de Abraham, sed Dei potiùs cognitione intelligendum est, qui pietatem Abrahæ ex voluntate immolandi ἀνθρωποπαθῶς dicitur cognouisse, non quòd priùs nescierit, sed quia factum istud illustre fuit signum, quo interior pietas, fides & obedientia Abrahæ fuit manifestata. 5. Si Abraham ex illo bono opere infallibiliter cognouit fidem suam, tum Dei gratiam, cur non & alij fideles ex bonis operibus suis idem possent cognoscere.

II. Excipit, Scripturam dum sanctos commendat, & eorum iustitiam & virtutes laudat, nos certos reddere, quibus id vtississimum erat potiùs quàm illos.

Resp. 1. Exemplum Abrahæ luculenter refutat hoc σόφισμα IesuWiticum. Scriptura enim innuit, illum ipsum fuisse certum de gratia Dei, non quidem ex peculiari reuelatione, sed virtute fidei, quæ nitebatur promissione & veracitate diuinâ. Vt igitur Abraham certus fuit pro sua persona: sic quemlibet fidelem, tum posse, tum dębere certum esse consequitur. 2. Accipimus, quòd exempla fidei sanctorum propter nos annotata sint. In quem verò finem? Non sanè vt fluctuemus, aut in perpetuo angore ob infirmitatem propriam versemur, sed potiùs, vt illos imitati, simpliciter firmam fiduciam concipiamus, nihil hæsitantes, sed Dei promissionibus sine omni dubitatione confidentes, vt ita de peccatorum remissione gratuita reddamur certi, & confirmemur i fide. Hunc, non alium finem annotatorum exemplorum fuisse, Paulus loco allegato clarissimè ostendit.

XLIV. 2. Iobi exemplum pariter vrgere possumus, quippe qui certus fuit non tantùm de gratia Dei, sed de gloriosa insuper resurrectione sua, cùm cap. 19. vers. 25. scribit: Ego scio, quod Redemptor meus viuit, & in nouissimo de terra surrecturus sum; & rursum circumdabor pelle mea, & in carne videbo Deum, quem visurus sum ego ipse, & oculi mei conspecturi sunt, & non alienus: Reposita est hæc spes mea in sinu meo. Beatam visionem hîc notari, nemo est ex Pontificiis, qui facilè negauerit; De hac autem Iobum fuisse certum, ipsa verba indicant, dum ait, Scio, ידעתי à Rad. ידע, quæ notat plenam, certam ac indubitatam rei scientiam, quo pacto sumitur Genes. 15. v. 13. c. 48. v. 19. 1. Sam. 24. v. 11. Ps. 138. v. 2. Ps. 143. v. 3. Prou. 27. v. 5. Vidit hoc Iesu Wita Pineda, qui in comment. super c. 19. Iobi, in vers. 25. num. 1. p. 96. expressè scribit: Fidei cognitio (de quâ Iobum loqui concedit) & obscura hæc scientia diuinorum, sola visione beatâ inferior est claritate, æqualis certitudine, reliquis omnibus alijs scientijs longè superior atque certior. Hoc autem exemplum cùm Bellarm. non assumserit, nec quicquam responderit diutius immorari non habemus necesse.

XLV 3. Apostolus Paulus. Rom. 8. v. 38. 39. suo nobis exemplo prælucet longè clarissimo, Sic enim scribit: Certus sum quia neque mors, neque vita neque Angeli, neque Principatus, neque virtutes, neque instantia, neq; futura, neq; fortitudo, neque altitudo, neq; profundum neque creatura alia poterit nos separare à charitate Dei, quae est in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. His sanè verbis Apostol. & sibi, & omnibus fidelibus gratiam Dei firmissimè promittit, & de illa se certissimum esse innuit, quippe quæ in Christo ita sit roborata, vt nihil ab illa nos separare valeat Neque hoc iactabundè de se solo refert, sed potiùs Dei gratiam piè commendat, suumque exemplum humiliter proponit, vt nos illud imitemur, & in fide confortemur. Nec enim istius certitudinis peculiarem aliquam, nobisque denegatam causam recenset, videlicet reuelationem singularem, vt putant Pontificij: sed generalia, omnibusque fidelibus communia fundamenta enarrat, & ex ijs certitudinem istam deducit. Talia sunt 1. Incorporatio mystica, quâ per fidem Christo inserimur, de qua vers. 1: Nihil ergò nunc damnationis est his, qui sunt in Christo Iesu. 2. Sublatio reatus, per Christi obedientiam facta. verf. 3. 4. Quod impossibile erat legi, in qua infirmabatur per carnem, Deus Filium suum mittens in similitudine carnis peccati, & de peccato damnauit peccatum in carne, vt iustificatio legis impleretur in nobis. 3. Gratiosa Spiritus sancti inhabitatio, de qua v. 9. 10. 11. & inprimis v. 15. agitur: Non accepistis Spiritum seruitutis, sed adoptionis 4. Spiritus sancti testificatio,, ver. 16. quia testimonium reddit Spiritui nostro, quòd simus filij Dei. 5. Spei firmitudo, quâ certò expectamus redemptionem corporis nostri. v. 23. & quâ iam salui facti sumus. v. 24. 6. Spiritus sancti auxilium. qui infirmitatem nostram adiuuat, & pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus intercedit. v. 26. Hunc autem Spiritum certò exaudiri, quis non crederet? 7. Certitudo decreti diuini, de vocatis & iustificatis, suo tempore glorificandis. v. 29. 30. 8. Diuina protectio, veri. 31. Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? 9. Summa Dei dilectio, qua nos ita prosecutus est, vt etiam proprio


### Question II: He did not spare His Son, but delivered Him up for us all, ver

He did not spare His Son, but delivered Him up for us all, ver. 32. How shall He not also with Him freely give us all things? 10. The gratuitous absolution of God, v. 33. Who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth. 11. The satisfaction of Christ, by which He liberated us, and His placement at the right hand of God, by the power of which He can apply His merit, and His intercession for us, by which He wills to apply it, v. 34. Who is he that condemneth? Christ Jesus is present, who died, yea rather who also is risen again, who is even at the right hand of God, who also maketh intercession for us. And from these now common foundations the Apostle deduces the sum of grace and the certainty of salvation, concluding thus: Who therefore shall separate us from the love of Christ? I am certain that nothing can separate us.

XLVI. Although these foundations of our certainty are by far the most solid; nevertheless, Bellarmine attempts to shake them in book 3, chapter 9, through a twofold exposition of the Apostolic text. His first is that the Apostle is speaking of the predestined in general, so that the sense is that it is certain that all the predestined will persevere in the love of God.

Resp. It is not permitted to argue from an inclusive to an exclusive. We acknowledge that the certainty of predestination is included, but it does not follow from this that a special certainty consisting in firm application is excluded. For all those foundations just enumerated confirm this; those applying pronouns demonstrate this: If GOD is for US, who is against US? Who shall separate US? Nothing shall be able to separate US. For by these particles is denoted not so much a general faith concerning the certainty that the elect will be saved, as a special confidence, by which every believer is certain of the grace of God and His love toward himself individually.

The other exposition of Bellarmine is that the Apostle is speaking of himself in particular and others similar to him, but that by that, I am certain, the certainty of faith is not understood divine, but a certain persuasion and confidence, for the generation of which a conjectural certainty is sufficient. And he proves this from the word πέπεισμαι, which properly signifies I am persuaded: or I am confident.

Resp. 1. Bellarmine departs from other Papists, who say that Paul is speaking only of himself, and that he was certain of his own predestination from a special revelation. Bellarmine saw that this gloss could not stand, since the Apostle is speaking not of himself alone, but of all the faithful, saying, I am certain that nothing can separate us. 2. He begs the question, while he says that a conjectural certainty is denoted, not one of faith. For he who knows and believes that there is no condemnation for those who are in the faith, who feels the testimony of the Holy Spirit that he is a Son of God; who believes that he is justified and absolved, that he will not be condemned, that he cannot be separated from the love of God (all of which Paul affirms), he is certainly not conjecturally, but infallibly certain of the grace of God: This very thing he explains elsewhere by the word to know, namely 2 Corinthians 4, verses 13, 14. Having the same Spirit of faith, we also believe, knowing that he who raised Jesus, will also raise us with Jesus (namely to eternal life) and will establish us with you. But if the Apostle Paul knew this, and by knowing believed it, certainly there was not in him only a conjectural certainty and no persuasion, but rather a firm and infallible confidence, joined with certain knowledge. Whence at once the little argument, taken from the word πέπεισμαι, collapses. For let it be that elsewhere it denotes persuasion, yet from the circumstances of this place it appears that a certain and indubitable confidence is indicated by it. It is therefore a general word, signifying persuasion, which whether it be certain or doubtful, must be inquired into from the circumstances of each text. For that by that very word not always a spiritual persuasion, but often an infallible certainty of faith is denoted, is evident from

Rom. 14. v. 14. ὄιδα καὶ πέπεισμαι, I know and am persuaded, (that is, I firmly believe) in the Lord Jesus, that nothing is common through him. And, 2. Tim. 1. v. 12. πέπεισμαι I am persuaded, that is, I most certainly believe, that GOD is able to keep that which I have committed unto him against that day. We conclude therefore this argument with the saying of Bernard, which is read in sermon 3. on Pentecost: Let us be certain, that neither death nor life, nor other things, which the Apostle enumerates as manifoldly as he does boldly, shall be able to separate us from the love of GOD, which is in Christ Jesus.

XLVII. V. FROM THE CERTAINTY OF BEING HEARD. Whoever praying is certainly heard, he can and ought to believe certainly in the attainment of the good which he has requested. But all who request spiritual goods are certainly heard. Therefore they can and ought to believe certainly in the attainment of the spiritual goods which they request. The major premise is beyond doubt: The minor is proved from Matt. 18. v. 19. If two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven. Matt. 21. verse 22. All things, whatsoever ye shall ask in prayer, believing, ye shall receive. Mark 11. verse 24. What things soever ye desire, when ye pray, believe that ye receive them, and ye shall have them. John 16. verse 23. Verily, verily I say unto you, whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, he will give it you. By these words indeed every doubt and servile fear is removed, namely that we who pray ought not to doubt concerning the attainment of the good requested, but rather to believe this most firmly, to which also that of James ch. 1. verse 6 pertains: If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not; and it shall be given him. But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. Whence we conclude thus: Whoever ought to believe without wavering that he will obtain some good, he ought to be certain of that with the certainty of faith. But all the pious, requesting spiritual benefits, to which primarily pertains the remission of sins, Matt. 6. v. 12. ought to believe that they will obtain those goods. Therefore, pious people seeking spiritual benefits ought to be certain of them with the certainty of faith. XLVIII. Bellarmine has nothing to object, except this one thing, that the promises of being heard are to be understood with this condition, if we ask well, and if it is expedient that that thing be given to us, lib. 1. de Iustificat. cap. 11. Resp. 1. As regards the latter condition, it is only to be applied concerning the petition for temporal goods. We, however, are speaking here of spiritual benefits, which it is always expedient for us to be given. 2. The former condition, if we ask well, we willingly admit, but in such a way that the manner of praying well and rightly is learned only from the Scriptures. These, however, intimate that we pray well if we believe that we shall obtain what we ask, and do not hesitate at all. Wherefore, confidence itself is required under that condition. For he who doubts obtains nothing: but he who firmly believes, and therefore puts faith in the promises, he is certainly heard, according to that 1 John 5:14. This is the confidence that we have in God, that whatsoever we ask according to his will, he hears us: And v. 15. We know that he hears us, whatsoever we ask, we know that we have the petitions that we requested of him. With such confidence, he who approaches the throne of grace prays in the best and most certain way. But he who doubts can neither call God his Father, nor add Amen; since that word is not only of one wishing, but also of one believing and confirming. And thus the Papists act with their hypotheses, so that we are unable to pronounce correctly either the first or the last word of the Lord's Prayer. For if I neither can nor ought to firmly believe ὑποδιστάς, with what conscience shall I be able to address God and say: Our Father, who art in heaven? If I doubt concerning my sonship, how shall I name him Father? Thus, if I cannot be certain of being heard, with what conscience shall I pronounce Amen, or Let it be, or, this will most certainly be true? For I ought not to pronounce as certainly future that which is uncertain to me.

XLIX. VI. Concerning the truth and immovable firmness of divine promises. Those who ought to believe divine promises must be certain of the promised goods with the certainty of faith. But all the pious and penitent ought to believe divine promises. Therefore, all both pious and penitent ought to be certain with the certainty of faith concerning the promised goods. Note here: that we are not speaking of Epicureans or the impious, but of the pious and penitent, since it is proper to them alone to believe. But whether anyone is pious and truly penitent, this is not uncertain or impossible to know, since anyone can prove and examine himself. 2. That we are not speaking of promises of temporal goods, which are conditional, but rather of spiritual ones, which are absolute and require nothing but faith. These things being presupposed, for the demonstration of the minor premise and the confirmation of the whole argument, those points must be well observed which Dr. Gerhard learnedly collected and reviewed in volume 3, § 83, on Justification.

The first is the end of the promises, which is none other than that we may be rendered certain of the grace and love of God. Therefore, the promise being placed as a foundation, trust can and ought to lean firmly upon it. 2. The distinction between legal and evangelical promises. The former render us doubtful on account of the added condition of perfect obedience, which is impossible: the latter lift us up, since they are gratuitous and not built upon our works. Hence we are said to be justified by faith, Rom. 4:16, so that the promise may be firm. 3. The truth of God. He has never deceived, nor can He deceive, because He is truthful, Rom. 3:4, and His faithfulness is not made void by the unbelief of men, verse 3, 2 Tim. 2:13. Let us therefore believe firmly, because there is no falsehood in the promises of God, since in doing them there is no difficulty for His omnipotent power, as Fulgentius says in book 1 to Monimus.

4. The property of divine promises. They are not ambiguous, like Delphic oracles, but open and certain: they are not doubtful and fallacious, but immovable and truthful, so that to be unwilling to trust in them is a most certain τεκμήριον of a desperate mind,

Latin:

Filio non pepercerit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradiderit illum, vers. 32. Quomodo non etiam cum illo omnia nobis donauit? 10. Gratuita Dei absolutio, v. 33. Quis accusabit electos Dei? Deus est, qui iustificat. 11. Christi satisfactio, quâ nos liberauit, & collocatio ad dextram Dei, cuius vi meritum suu applicare potest, & interpellatio pro nobis, quâ applicare vult, v. 34. Quis est, qui condemnet? Christus Iesus adest, qui mortuus est, imò qui & resurrexit, qui & est ad dexteram Dei, qui etiam interpellat pro nobis. Atque ex his iam communibus fundamentis summam gratiæ & salutis certitudinem deducit Apostolus, ita concludens: Quis ergò nos separabit a charitate Christi? Certus sum, quod nihil nos separare queat.

XLVI. Hæc certitudinis nostræ fundamenta licèt sint longè solidissima; Bellarminus tamen illa concutere tentat l. 3. cap. 9. per geminam textus Apostolici expositionem. Prima ipsi est, quod loquatur Apostolus de prædestinatis in genere, vt sensus sit, certum esse, omnes prædestinatos perseueraturos in charitate Dei.

Resp. Ab inclusiua ad exclusiuam non licet argumentari. Fatemur, quòd certitudo prædestinationis includatur, sed hinc non sequitur, quòd specialis certitudo in firma applicatione consistens excludatur. Hanc enim confirmant omnia illa fundamenta, modò enumerata: hanc demonstrant Pronomina illa applicantia, Si DEVS pro NOBIS, quis contra Nos? Quis Nos separabit? Nihil Nos separare poterit. His enim particulis nõ tam generalis fides de certò saluandis electis, quàm fiducia specialis, quâ quilibet fidelis certus est de gratia Dei & dilectione erga se in indiuiduo, denotatur.
