Altera expositio Bellarmini est, quod loquatur Apostolus de se in particulari & alijs similibus sibi, sed per illud, certus sum, non intelligi certitudinem fidei diuinæ, sed quandam persuasionem & confidentiam, ad quam gignendam satis sit certitudo coniecturalis. Et hoc probat ex verbo πέπεισμαι, quod significat propriè persuasus sum: sive confido.

Resp. 1. Discedit Bellarminus ab alijs Pontificijs, qui Paulum dicunt de se solo loqui, & eum certum fuisse de sua prædestinatione ex peculiari reuelatione. Quam glossam non consistere posse vidit Bellarminus, quippe cùm Apostolus non de se vno, sed de omnibus fidelibus loquatur, dicens, Certus sum, quòd nos nihil separare valeat. 2. Petit principium, dum ait, Notari certitudinem coniecturalem, non fidei. Qui enim scit & credit, nihil esse damnationis in fidelibus, qui sentit testimonium sancti Spiritus, quòd sit Filius Dei; qui credit se iustificari & absolui, se non condemnatum iri, se à dilectione Dei separari non posse, (quæ omnia Paulus affirmat) is sanè non coniecturaliter, sed infallibiliter certus est de gratia Dei: Hoc ipsum alibi per verbum scire explicat, nempè 2. Corinth. 4. vers. 13. 14. Habentes eundem Spiritum fidei, & nos credimus, scientes quoniam qui suscitauit Iesum, & nos cum Iesu suscitabit (nempe ad vitam æternam) & constituet vobiscum. Quod si Apostolus Paulus hoc sciuit, & sciendo credidit, vtique non fuit in ipso tantùm coniecturalis certitudo & nulla persuasio, sed potiùs firma & infallibilis fiducia, cum certa cognitione coniuncta. Vnde vnà concidit ratiuncula, ex verbo πέπεισμαι petita. Sit enim quod alibi persuasionem notet, ex circumstantijs tamen huius loci apparet, certam & indubitatam fiduciam per illud indicari. Est ergò verbum generale, persuasionem significans, quę num sit certa vel dubia, ex cuiuslibet textus circumstantiis inquirendum est. Nam per illud ipsum verbum non perpetuò persuasionem spiritualem, sed sæpè infallibilem fidei certitudinem inaui, patet ex

Rom. 14. v. 14. ὄιδα καὶ πέπεισμαι, Scio & persuasus sum, (id est, firmiter credo) in Domino Iesu, quia nihil commune per ipsum. Et, 2. Tim. 1. v. 12. πέπεισμαι persuasus sum, hoc est, certissimè credo, quia potens est DEVS depositum meum servare in diem illum. Concludimus ergò hoc argumentum dicto Bernhardi, quod legitur serm. 3. in Pentecosten: Simus certi, quia neq; mors neq; vita, neq; caetera alia, quæ Apostolus tam multipliciter quam audacter enumerat poterunt nos separare à charitate DE I, quæ est in Christo Iesu.

XLVII. V. AB EXAVDITIONIS CERTITVDINE. Quicunque supplicans certò exauditur, is boni, quod petiit, adeptionem certò potest & debet credere. Sed omnes bona spiritualia petentes, certò exaudiuntur. Ergò adeptionem bonorum spiritualium, quæ petunt, certò credere possunt & debent. Maior extra dubium est: Minor probatur ex Matth. 18. v. 19. Si duo ex vobis consenserint super terram, de omni re quamcunque petierint, fiet illis a Patre meo, qui in cœlis est. Matth. 21. vers. 22. Omnia, quæcunque petieritis in oratione, credentes accipietis. Marci 11. vers. 24. Omnia quæcunque orantes petitis, credite, quia accipietis, & evenient vobis. Iohan. 16. vers. 23. Amen, Amen dico vobis, si quid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, dabit vobis. His sanè dictis removetur omnis dubitatio & servilis formido, quòd nempè orantes non debeamus dubitare de boni petiti adeptione, sed hanc potiùs firmissimè credere, quò spectat etiam illud Iacobi c. 1. vers. 6. Siquis vestrum indiget Sapientiâ, postulet à Deo, qui dat omnibus affluenter, & non improperat, & dabitur ei. Postulet autem in fide, nihil hæsitans, Vnde sic colligimus: Quicunque debet credere sine hæsitatione, se aliquod bonum impetraturum, is certitudine fidei de illo certus esse debet. Sed omnes pii, petentes spiritualia beneficia, quò in primis spectat remissio peccatorum, Matth. 6. v. 12. debent credere, se illa bona impetraturos. Ergo pii petentes spiritualia beneficia, de illis certi esse debent certitudine fidei. XLVIII. Nihil habet Bellarminus, quod excipiat, nisi hoc unum, intelligendas esse promissiones exauditionis cum ista conditione, si benè petamus, & si expediat, illud nobis dari, lib. 1. de Iustificat. cap. 11. Resp. 1. Quod attinet posteriorem conditionem, illa tantùm adhibenda est circa petitionem bonorum temporalium. Nos autem loquimur hîc de beneficiis spiritualibus, quæ dari nobis semper expedit. 2. Priorem conditionem, si benè petamus, libenter admittimus, sed ita, ut non nisi ex Scripturis addiscatur modus benè rectéque orandi. Hæ autem innuunt, tum nos benè precari, si credamus, nos impetraturos, quæ petimus, nihilque hæsitemus. Quare ipsa fiducia sub conditione illa requiritur. Qui enim dubitat, nihil impetrat: qui autem firmiter credit, ideoque promissionibus fidem adhibet, is certò exauditur, iuxta illud 1. Ioh. 5. v. 14. Hæc est fiducia, quam habemus ad Deum, quia quodcunque petierimus, secundum voluntatem ipsius, audit nos: Et v. 15. Scimus, quia audit nos, quicquid petierimus, scimus, quia habemus petitiones, quas postulavimus ab eo. Tali fiduciâ, qui accedit ad thronum gratiæ, is optimè & certissimè precatur. Qui autem dubitat, is nec Deum Patrem suum appellare, nec Amen adiicere potest; cùm vox illa sit non tantùm optantis, sed credentis etiam ac confirmantis. Atque sic faciunt Papicolæ suis hypothesibus, ut nec primam nec ultimam orationis Dominicæ vocem rectè pronunciare valeamus. Si enim ὑποδιστάς firmiter credere nec possum, nec debeo, quâ conscientiâ Deum compellare potero & dicere: Pater noster, qui es in cælis? Si de filiatione dubito, quî Patrem nūcupabo? Ita si de exauditione certus esse nequeam, quâ conscientiâ pronunciabo Amen, vel Fiat, siuè, hoc certissimè verum erit? Quod enim mihi incertum, hoc tanquam certò futurum pronunciare non debeo.

XLIX. VI. A promissionum diuinarum veritate & immota firmitate. Qui credere debent promissionibus diuinis, illi debent esse certi de bonis promissis, certitudine fidei. Sed omnes pij & pœnitentes debent credere promissionibus diuinis.. Quare omnes & pij & pœnitentes debent certi esse certitudine fidei, de bonis promissis. Notes hic. Quod non loquamur de Epicureis vel impiis, sed de pijs & pœnitentibus, quippè quibus solis proprium est credere. Num verò aliquis sit pius & verè pœnitens, hoc non incertum est, vel scitu impossibile, cum quiuis seipsum probare & tentare valeat. 2. Quòd non loquamur de promissionibus bonorum temporalium, quæ conditionatæ sunt, sed potiùs spiritualium, quæ absolutæ, & nihil nisi fidem pręrequirunt. Quibus præsuppositis, pro demonstratione minoris & confirmatione totius argumenti probè obseruanda sunt polo illa membra, quæ Dn. D Gerhardus eruditè collegit & recensuit tom. 3. § 83. de Iustific.

Primum est Finis promissionum, qui non alius, quâm vt de gratia & charitate Dei reddamur certi. Positâ ergò promissione tanquain basi, firmiter inniti potest, debetq́; fiducia. 2. Discrimen legalium & Euangelicarum promissionum. Illæ reddunt nos dubios ob additam conditionem perfectæ obedientiæ, quæ impossibilis: hæ nos erigunt, cùm gratuitæ sint, nec nostris operibus superstructæ. Hinc ex fide dicimur iustificari, Rom. 4. v. 16. vt firma sit promissio. 2. Dei veritas. Nunquam fefellit, nec fallere potest, quia verax est, Rom. 3. vers. 4. eiusque fides per incredulitatem hominum non euacuatur. vers. 3, 2. Tim. 2. vers. 13. Credamus ergò firmiter, quia in promissis Dei nulla est falsitas, cùm in faciēdis omnipotennulla sit difficultas, vti Fulgentius loquitur l. 1. ad Monimum.

4. Divinarum promissionum proprietas. Non sunt ambiguæ, instar oraculorũ Delphicorum, sed apertæ, certæq;: non sunt dubiæ & fallaces, sed immotæ & veraces, vti ijs fidere nolle, desperati animi sit τεκμήριον certissimum,


### Question II: ὁμογένεια of the promises with the word

5. ὁμογένεια of the promises with the word. As this does not pass away forever, Luke 21 v. 33, so the promises of God are most certainly fulfilled.

6. Examples of kept promises. Almost innumerable ones of these exist in the Scriptures: however, none can be brought forward where God has not kept some promise.

7. Similar things by which the certainty of the promises is declared. For they are compared to immovable rocks, Matt. 7 v. 25, to firm anchors, Heb. 6 v. 19, and to an infallible covenant, Jer. 31 v. 33, 34, Hosea 2 v. 19.

Finally, the 8th distinction between human and divine promises. The former are slippery and fallible, because every man is a liar: the latter are indubitable and infallible, because God alone is truthful, nay, truth itself.

These things indeed all powerfully prove that we ought to believe the divine promises firmly, without any hesitation, and consequently be certain of the promised goods, especially of the remission of sins, with the certainty of faith. For thus we conclude: to whomever the remission of sins is most truly promised, he can and ought to be certain of it with the certainty of faith. But to every penitent (and let everyone examine himself whether he be such) the remission of sins is most truly promised. Wherefore every penitent can and ought to be certain of the remission of sins with the certainty of faith.

Bellarmine finds nothing to object, except this one thing, that the promises, when they are applied in particular, are conditional, not absolute. For he says in book 3, chapter 11, that the things promised to the Church apply to individual men, unless they begin through faith and charity to be living members of the body and of the Church.

Response. Who among us has ever even dreamed that the promises can be applied to individual men, even without faith? From this, however, it is by no means concluded that the promises of the Gospel are conditional and that the certainty of grace is undermined. They do not require our merits or works, in respect of which only is some promise called conditional. And as far as faith is concerned, it is itself kindled by the promises, since they are correlates. For while I hear the promise, I immediately conceive faith because of God's truth, and thus I apprehend the promised good. So far, therefore, is it from the case that certainty is removed by this, because faith is required, that it is rather established more and more. For because, with works excluded, faith alone, as an apprehending instrument, is demanded, and because this faith is excited in us by the promises themselves, hence certainly no cause is left any longer for the doubter. If you doubt concerning faith? Behold the promise, by which GOD has promised the infusion of faith. If you doubt concerning the remission of sins? Behold the faith kindled in you by the benefit of the promise, by which you will be able to apprehend the grace of GOD firmly, and be certain of it. And indeed, if this one thing is noted, the absurdity of the Papistic doctrine will soon shine forth. The question is asked, Can anyone believe in the remission of his sins with the certainty of faith? They affirm it, but under this condition, if he has faith. But we immediately retort that the promises were given for this very purpose, that you might have faith.

For everyone ought to believe that God is certainly propitious to him. Why? Because this is promised to all, with no one excluded, and therefore what concerns all, individuals ought to believe. Therefore we conclude thus: Whatever is an object of faith, expressed in the Scriptures themselves, this individuals are bound to believe, and there is no need to dispute at length whether it is permitted and required that it be believed. But that Christ has made satisfaction for our sins, and that GOD is willing to remit our debts to us when we ask, is the object of faith, expressed throughout the Scriptures themselves; therefore individuals are bound to believe this, and there is no need to dispute at length whether it is permitted and required to be believed: so that our Luther most rightly wrote, Such as is the union of husband and wife in lawful matrimony, namely indissoluble: such also is the connection of faith and promise.

LI. VII. From the most holy oath of God. Whatever God has not only promised simply, but has furthermore confirmed with an oath, of that we can and ought to be most certain. But he has not only promised the free remission of sins simply, but has furthermore confirmed it with an oath. Wherefore the pious can and ought to be most certain of the remission of sins. With the major premise placed beyond doubt, we prove the truth of the minor from Ezech. 33. verse 18. As I live, says the Lord, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he may be converted and live. And John 5. v. 24. Amen, Amen I say to you, he who hears my word, and believes him who sent me, has eternal life, and shall not come into condemnation, but has passed from death into life. This oath is most clear, which the Apostle affirms in Heb. 6. v. 16. 17. was brought forth for this purpose, that the τὸ ἀμετάθετον, the firmness and immobility of the divine counsel, might be shown, and that we might have strong consolation. O therefore blessed are we, for whose sake God swears! O most miserable, if we do not believe even GOD swearing, writes Tertullian, book on repentance. For what is the oath of the living and truthful God, if not a confirmation of the promise, and a certain rebuke of the faithless? as Augustine testifies, book 16 of the City of God, ch. 32.

LII. IIX. From the efficacy of the Sacraments. Whatever is confirmed and sealed by certain seals, of that we do not doubt, but rather are most certain. But indeed the remission of sins is confirmed and sealed by certain seals, namely the Sacraments. Therefore let us not doubt concerning the remission of sins, because we can be most certain. We prove and illustrate this from the end of the Sacraments, which among other causes were instituted also for this reason, that they might confirm adults as if with a divine seal, and make them certain of the grace of God and the forgiveness of sins. Hence circumcision is called σφραγὶς or a seal of the righteousness of faith, Romans 4, verse 11, because it designated gratuitous justification. And Baptism is the ἐπερώτημα of a good conscience toward God, 1 Peter 3, verse 21, because through Baptism we are rendered certain of the benevolent affection of God toward us. Thus in the supper we eat the very body of Christ delivered to death for us, and we drink that very blood which was shed for us on the altar of the cross. Who therefore can doubt concerning the grace of Christ, confirmed by such firm seals.

LIII. To this argument Bellarmine, book 3, chapter 11, objects in two ways.

1. That it is falsely assumed that the Sacraments were instituted principally to sustain faith and to render us certain of the will of God. But this is a most gross error, the contrary of which is easily proven from Romans 4 and 1 Peter 3, concerning which it is customary to treat more fully in the place concerning the Sacraments.

2. That the Sacraments are indeed signs of justification on their part, meanwhile the effect of them is hindered by the indisposition of the recipient, since faith and repentance are required for a salutary use. I reply: If the discourse is about infant baptism, faith is not pre-required, nor can it be present before baptism, since infants are by nature children of wrath, Ephesians 2, verse 3. If the Sacrament of the supper is understood, we confess that faith and repentance are required, but from this it by no means follows that the Sacraments cannot seal, and that no one can be certain of remission. For that faith is not our work, and repentance does not consist in satisfaction, or even in the enumeration of sins, from which we easily grant that doubt arises: but faith is The fiducial apprehension of the merit of Christ, and the principal part of repentance, which one can prove to himself whether it is present, and draw its confirmation from the Sacraments. For we do not extend that sealing of grace to anyone using the Sacrament, but only to those using it worthily or the penitent, who can examine and discern themselves. Therefore our argument stands firm: That which is sealed with a certain seal is not to be doubted. But the grace of God is sealed with a certain seal, namely the Sacrament. Therefore, the grace of God is not to be doubted. What Bellarmine sprinkles about the intention of the minister, since they are sought from Scholastic puddles and contain a mere begging of the question, we judge unworthy of a response.

LIV. IX. Concerning private and public absolution by ministers. He to whom, in the place of God, through the minister of Christ, all sins are remitted on earth, in such a way indeed that this remission is held valid in heaven, he will be able to be most certain of the grace of God. But to every penitent, in the place of God through the minister of Christ, his sins are remitted on earth, in such a way indeed that this remission is held valid in heaven, by virtue of the promise made. Matt. 18, verse 18, and John 20, verse 23. Wherefore the penitent sinner will be able to be most certain of the grace of God. I do not see what the Papists can solidly object. For when the minister in the name of Christ pronounces, I absolve you, it is either certain what he says, or uncertain. If it is certain, we have what we want, since by this agreement anyone receiving absolution can and ought to believe most certainly in the forgiveness of sins. But if it is uncertain, then the minister sins by boldly pronouncing in the name of Christ what is perhaps false. And it can be said to him, Lord, you are lying, as Luther rightly concluded.

LV. Bellarmine indeed proposed this argument in chapter 11, but he touches upon it lightly in his response, and mixes absolution with Baptism, writing thus: It cannot be said to a minister, Lord you are lying, if someone perhaps approaching with a feigned heart to a minister, who is ignorant of it, is simply baptized. For he, when he says, I baptize you, signifies nothing else, except I offer you the Sacrament, which has the power of blotting out all sins, or, (which is in me) I wash you, and cleanse you from the filth of sins. Resp. 1. The minister neither baptizes, nor washes in his own name, but in the place of God. Therefore let that gloss be valid: Which is in me. For there is nothing in the minister, considered by reason of himself, for which reason all virtue of the Sacraments would perish, if another respect did not approach. They ought therefore to be esteemed, as they are instruments divinely instituted for faith both to be infused, which happens in Infant baptism, and to be nourished and confirmed, which happens in the Sacrament of the supper. That effect always has a place in infants, this in penitent adults, nor does the intention of the minister either add or take away anything. 2. As regards absolution, we confess that it is not to be accepted so crudely, that sins are certainly remitted, whether repentance is present or absent, and whether it is serious or feigned and hypocritical. For true repentance is altogether required beforehand, which however itself does not have the nature of merit, nor does it consist in one's own works, but is founded in faith, which Christ kindles through promises, and whose presence is not hidden, but easily becomes known to anyone proving himself. When therefore I know that I am seriously repenting, desiring grace, and placing no obstacle to the Holy Spirit, and at the same time I hear, from the minister of Christ in the place of God, that all my sins are remitted to me; then indeed no cause for doubt remains, but rather I can be most certain of the grace of God, and the forgiveness of sins.

Latin:

5. ὁμογένεια promissionum cum verbo. Vt hoc in æternum non transit, Luc. 21. v. 33. ita promissiones Dej certissimè implentur.

6. Exempla servatarum promissionum. Horum fermè innumera extant in Scripturis: nullum autem proferri potest, quòd Deus promissionem aliquam non servauerit.

7. Similia, quibus certitudo promissionum declaratur. Comparantur enim petræ immotę Matth. 7. v. 25. terię firmæ, Heb. 6. v. 19. & pacto infallibili. Ier. 31. v. 33. 34. Oseæ 2. v. 19.

Tandem 8. discrimen humanarum ac divinarum promissionum. Illæ sunt lubricæ & fallibiles, quia omnis homo mendax: hæ sunt indubitatæ & infallibiles, quia solus DEVS verax, imo ipsa veritas.

Hæc sanè omnia potenter evincunt quòd firmiter, sine omni hæsitatione, promissionibus diuinis credere, & per consequens de bonis promissis, præsertim de remissione peccatorum, certitudine fidei certi esse debeamus. Sic enim colligimus, Cuicunq; peccatorum remissio verissimè est promissa, is certitudine fidei certus de illą esse potest & debet. Sed omni pœnitenti (num & quis autē talis sit, seipsum probet) peccatorum remissio verissimè est promissa. Quare omnis pœnitens de remissione peccatorum certitudine fidei certus esse potest & debet.

L. Bellarminus, quod excipiat, nihil inuenit, nisi hoc vnum, promissiones, cùm applycantur in particulari, esse conditionatas, non absolutas. Non enim ait l. 3. c. 11. quæ promittuntur Ecclesiæ conueniunt singulis hominibus, nisi illi per fidem & charitatem incipiant esse membra viua corporis & Ecclesiæ.

Resp. Quis ex nostris vnquam vel somniauit saltem, promissiones singulis hominibus, sine fide etiam applicari posse? Hinc tamen minimè conficitur, promissiones Euangelij esse conditionatas & certitudinem gratiæ labefactari. Non requirunt illæ nostra merita vel opera, quorum respectu tantùm promissio aliqua vocatur conditionata. Et fidem quod concernit, illa ipsa per promissiones accenditur, quoniam sunt correlata. Dum enim promissionem audio, statim fidem concipio ob Dei veritatem, & ita bonum promissum apprehendo. Tantum igitur abest, vt certitudo tollatur per hoc, quia fides requiritur, vt potius illa magis magisque stabiliatur. Quia enim exclusis operibus, sola fides, vt instrumentum apprehendens, postulatur, & quia hæc fides per ipsas promissiones in nobis excitatur, hinc vtique dubitanti nulla ampliùs causa relinquitur. Si ambigis de fide? En promissionem, quâ DEVS fidei infusionem est pollicitus. Si ambigis de remissione peccatorum? En fidem in te beneficio promissionis accensam, quâ DEI gratiam firmiter apprehendere, & de illa certus esse poteris. Et sanè hoc vnũ si notetur, absurditas doctrinæ Papisticæ mox elucescat. Quæritur, An possis aliquis certitudine fidei peccatorum suorum remissionem credere? Affirmant illi, sed sub hac conditione, si fidem habeat. Verùm nos statim regerimus, hoc ipso fine promissiones esse datas, vt fidem habeas.

Debet enim quivis credere, Deum certò sibi propitium esse. Cur? Quia hoc omnibus promissum est, nullo excluso, ideoque quod omnes concernit, singuli debent credere. Proindè sic concludimus: Quicquid est obiectum fidei, in ipsis Scripturis expressum, hoc tenentur singuli credere, nec disputandum est prolixè, num liceat debeatque illud credi. Sed Christum satisfecisse pro peccatis nostris, & velle DEVM nobis petentibus debita nostra remittere, est obiectum fidei, in Scripturis ipsis passim expressum, Ergô singuli tenentur hoc credere, nec disputandum est prolixè, num liceat debeatque credi: vt ita rectissimè Lutherus noster scripserit, Qualis est copulatio maris & fœminæ in legitimo matrimonio, videlicet indissolubilis: talis quoque fidei & promissionis connexio.

LI. VII. A sanctissimo Dei iuramento. Quicquid Deus non simpliciter promisit, sed insuper iuramento confirmauit, de illo possumus & debemus esse certissimi. Sed remissionem peccatorum gratuitam non tantùm simpliciter promisit, sed insuper iuramento confirmauit. Quare pij de remissione peccatorum possunt & debent esse certissimi. Majore extra dubium positâ, minoris veritatem euincimus ex Ezech. 33. vers. 18. Viuo ego, dicit Dominus, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed vt conuertatur & viuat. Et Ioh 5. v. 24. Amen, Amen dico vobis, qui sermonem meum audit, & credit ei, qui misit me, habet vitam æternam, & in condemnationem non veniet, sed à morte transiuit in vitam. Clarissimum est hoc iuramentum, quod eo fine prolatum esse affirmat Apostolus Hebr. 6. v. 16. 17. vt ostenderetur τὸ ἀμετάθετον firmitas atque immobilitas consilij diuini, & nos validam habere possimus consolationem. O igitur beatos nos, quorum causa iurat Deus! O miserrimos, si nec DEO iuranti credimus, scribit Tertull. l, de pœni. Quid enim est Dei viui veracisque iuratio, nisi promissio confirmatio, & infidelium quædam increpatio? teste Augustino l. 16. de ciuit. Dei c. 32.

LII. IIX. A Sacramentorum efficacia. Quicquid certis sigillis confirmatur & obsignatur, de illo non dubitamus, sed potius certissimi sumus. At verò remissio peccatorum certis sigillis nimirum Sacramentis, confirmatur & obsignatur. Ergô de remissione peccatorum non dubitemus, quia certissimi esse possumus. Minorem probamus & illustramus à Sacramentorum fine, quæ inter alias causas ideò quoque instituta sunt, vt adultos tanquam sigillo diuino confirment, certosque efficiant de gratia Dei & peccatorum venia. Hinc circumcisio vocatur σφραγὶς vel signaculum iustitiæ fidei, Roman. 4. versu 11. quoniam designabat gratuitam iustificationem. Et Baptismus est ἐπερώτημα bonæ conscientiæ ἐις θεὸν, 1. Petr. 3. ver. 21. quia per Baptismum de beneuolo Dei erga nos affectu certi reddimur. Sic in cœna manducamus ipsum Christi corpus pro nobis in mortem traditum, & bibimus illum ipsum sanguinem, qui pro nobis in ara crucis effusus est. Qui ergò de Christi gratia, tàm firmis sigillis confirmatâ, dubitare possumus.

LIII. Ad hanc rationem Bellarminus lib. 3. ca. 11. excipit dupliciter.

1. Falsò affumi, quòd Sacramenta instituta sint præcipuè ad fidem sustentandam, & nos certos de voluntate Dei reddendos. Sed crassissimus hic error est, cuius contrarium ex Rom. 4. & 1. Pet. 3. facilè evincitur, de quo in loco de Sacramentis fusiùs agi consueuit.

2. Sacramenta esse quidem signa iustificationis ex parte sua, interim effectum eorum impediri per indispositionem suscipientis, cùm ad salutarem vsum requiratur fides & pœnitentia. Resp. Si de Pædobaptismo sermo sit, fides non prærequiritur, nec antè baptismum adesse potest, cùm infantes naturâ sint filij iræ, Ephes. 2. versu 3. Si Sacramentum cœnæ intelligatur, fatemur, fidem & pœnitentiam requiri, sed hinc minimè sequitur, quòd Sacramenta obsignare nequeant, & nemo de remissione certus esse possit. Nam fides illa non est opus nostrum, & pœnitentia non consistit in satisfactione, aut etiam peccatorum enumeratione, vndè dubitationem oriri facilè largimur: sed fides est fiducialis apprehensio meriti Christi, & præcipua pars pœnitentiæ, quę num adsit probare seipsum quis potest, & eius confirmationem è Sacramentis haurire. Nec enim illam obsignationem gratiæ extendimus ad quemuis vtentem Sacramento, sed tantùm ad dignè vtentes seu pœnitentes, qui seipsos examinare, & discernere possunt. Firmum proindè stat argumentum nostrum: Quod sigillo certo obsignatur de illo dubitandum non est. Sed gratia Dei sigillo certo nempè Sacramento obsignatur. Ergo de gratia Dei dubitandum non est. Quæ Bellarminus aspergit de intentione ministri, cùm è lacunis Scholasticis petita sint, & meram principij petitionem contineant, responso indigna iudicamus.

LIV. IX. A privata publicáque ministrorum absolutione. Cui loco Dei, per ministrum Christi, peccata omnia remittuntur in terris, ita quidem, vt hæc remissio rata habeatur in cœlis, is de gratia Dei certissimus esse poterit. Sed omni pœnitenti, loco Dei per ministrum Christi peccata sua remittuntur in terris, ita quidem, vt hæc remissio rata habeatur in cœlis, vi factæ promissionis. Matth. 18. versu 18. & Iohan. 20. versu 23. Quare peccator pœnitens de gratia Dei certissimus esse poterit. Non video, quid solidè possint excipere Pontificij. Cùm enim minister in Christi nomine pronunciat, Ego te absolvo, vel est certum, quod dicit, vel incertum. Si certum est, habemus quod volumus, siquidem hoc pacto quiuis absolutionem accipiens, peccatorum veniam certissimè credere potest & debet. Sin incertum, tum peccat minister nomine Christi audacter pronuncians, quod fortassis est falsum. Et potest ei dici, Domine tu mentiris, vt rectè conclusit Lutherus.

LV. Argumentum hoc proposuit quidem Bellarminus c. 11. sed leuiter tangit in responsione, & miscet absolutionem cum Baptismo, ita scribens: Non potest dici ministro, Domine tu mentiris, si quis fortè ficto corde accedens à ministro, qui id ignorat, simpliciter baptizetur. Non enim ille, cùm dicit, ego te baptizo, aliud significat, nisi ego Sacramentum tibi præbeo, quod vim habet omnia peccata delendi, vel, (quod est in me) abluo te, & mundo a sordibus peccatorum. Resp. 1. Minister nec baptizat, nec abluit suo, sed Dei loco. Valeat ergò glossema istud: Quod est in me. Nihil enim est in ministro, ratione sui considerato, qua de causa periret omnis Sacramentorum virtus, si non alius respectus accederet. Debent igitur æstimari, vt sunt organa diuinitùs instituta pro fide tum infundenda, quod fit in Pædobaptismo, tum alenda & confirmanda, quod fit in Sacramento cœnæ. Effectus ille semper locum habet in infantibus, iste in adultis pœnitentibus, nec ministri intentio aliquid vel addit vel demit. 2. Absolutionem quod spectat, fatemur eam tàm crudè non esse accipiendam, quòd certò remittantur peccata, siuè pœnitentia adsit vel absit, & siuè seria sit vel ficta & hypocritica. Nam vera omninò prærequiritur, quæ tamen ipsa non habet rationem meriti, nec consistit in proprijs opellis, sed fundatur in fide, quam Christus accendit per promissiones, & cuius præsentia non est occulta, sed cuiuis semetipsum probanti facilè innotescit. Cùm igitur scio, me seriò pœnitere, gratiam optare nullumque Spiritui sancto obicem ponere, & simul audio, à Christi ministro loco Dei, peccata mihi omnia remitti; tùm sanè nulla dubitationis causa manet reliqua, sed potiùs de Dei gratia, & peccatorum venia possum esse certissimus.


### Question II: LVI. X. From pronouns denoting application

LVI. X. From pronouns denoting application. For when faith is described in its very exercise and act of justifying, pronouns such as our, to us, me etc. are often used in the Scriptures, to indicate that the nature of justifying faith is to be so occupied with the promises of salvation, that by thrusting itself into them, and subsuming itself under them, they are applied to each individual believer. To this point refer the sayings in Galatians 2, verse 3 [sic]: Christ gave himself for our sins, ch. 2, v. 20: Who loved me, and gave himself for me. ch. 3, v. 13: Christ was made a curse for us, etc. From these, however, we conclude thus: Whoever must apply to themselves individually the grace of God and the merit of Christ, they must at the same time most firmly believe in the forgiveness of sins, since it is always coupled with application, just as an effect is with its cause. But all believers must apply to themselves individually the grace of God and the merit of Christ, by virtue of the cited texts, and the example of Paul. Wherefore all believers must at the same time most firmly believe in the forgiveness of sins.

LVII. XI. From the removal of the causes of doubting. Where no causes of doubt are present, there it is rash to wish to doubt. But there are no causes present why the pious should doubt concerning the grace of God and the remission of sins. Therefore it is rash to wish to doubt. We prove the minor premise, because all those things which can render the mind doubtful are of no strength, and have already been removed in the Scriptures:

Of this kind are 1. One's own unworthiness and the imperfection of works. But we know that the business of salvation does not rest upon our merits, but solely upon divine promises. Therefore our unworthiness and imperfection by no means stand in the way of certainty, since the power of GOD is effective in weakness.

2. The suspicion of divine hatred. But God in Christ is most kindly disposed toward us, and seriously desires the salvation of all. He has made this will attested by sayings, oaths, and examples, and therefore let us cast away every thought of an absolute decree.

3. The particularity of the merit of Christ. But he came to save all that which had perished. Wherefore it is a propitiation, not only for our sins or those of the faithful, but also for the sins of the whole world, and he waits daily that the burdened may come and receive refreshment.

4. The particularity of the calling. But all who are baptized and live in the Church, (of whom alone we speak here,) are called at the same time, and divine benefits are offered to them in the Word and Sacraments, since these are the hands of God, through which he extends his gifts to us.

5. Our indisposition, on account of which we often think that we are unfit and unworthy to receive grace. But nothing is required of us other than the use of the means: No meritorious disposition on our part is necessary: Provided we conduct ourselves passively, and do not place an obstacle to the Holy Spirit, then we shall receive from God faith and the remaining spiritual gifts.

6. The consideration of sins. But Christ came for this reason, that he might make satisfaction for sins; if, therefore, we apprehend his merit, sins will not be able to harm us. God is indeed angry with transgressors, but he tempers his wrath with mercy, provided repentance is practiced. For he does not delight in the death of the one who dies, but that he may live. There have been many sinners polluted by the most heinous crimes, and yet they obtained remission. You are not yet Peter the denier, or the thief, or the harlot Magdalene. Since all these, however, obtained pardon, why do you doubt, and not apply faith to the promises of God?

7. The imposition of the cross and the multiplication of calamities. But these are signs of a benevolent God, not an angry one. For he chastises whom he loves, and corrects his own in good time, lest they be condemned with the world. If, therefore, you experience any tribulation, hold it for a sign of love, and believe most certainly that it tends to your benefit.

8. The presence of doubts arising from time to time. For we are very often troubled by them, so that God [is hidden] from us we should think it is turned away; but let us consider that this arises not from the nature of faith, not from the impossibility of certainty, but rather from the infirmity of the flesh, and is permitted by God, not so that we may indulge in doubts, but rather so that we may struggle against them and overcome them with true faith. Thus, therefore, since Scripture has removed the causes of doubting from every part, we ought deservedly to acquiesce and be most certain of the benevolent affection of God.

LVIII. XII. From the purpose of Scripture. It is given to us among other things, so that through repentance and consolation we may have hope, not indeed ambiguous and doubtful, but rather certain and immovable, Rom. 15. v. 4. Whatever dogma, therefore, takes away solid consolation and certain hope, that is not in agreement with the sacred writings. But the Papist dogma concerning the uncertainty of the remission of sins takes away solid consolation and certain hope. Wherefore it is not in agreement with the sacred writings. The minor premise does not need a lengthy proof, but is manifest in itself. For how will true παράκλησις, peace and rest of conscience, find a place if anyone cannot be certain of the favor of God and the forgiveness of sins? How will a troubled mind be raised up in temptation? For he will always object to the cited promises of God that they are merely conditional and require the perfect fulfillment of the law and plenary satisfaction beforehand; which fall to no mortal, and therefore no one who is a pure and simple Papist can have a tranquil and joyful conscience.

LIX. XIII. From the deformity of doubting. For this to be demonstrated, a lengthy proof is not required. For what is it to doubt, except to dwell in perpetual anguish of mind and to hang suspended between hope and fear? What can even be thought of that is sadder or more troublesome than this interior torture of the heart? Other inconveniences follow, since doubt 1. Takes away the nature of faith, which is trust. 2. Is opposed to the first table of the law, which requires that we [rely] upon God Let us trust in all things. 3. It accuses God of lying and perjury, according to that 1 John 5, verse 10: He who does not believe God, makes Him a liar. 4. It hinders effective prayer, since a man receives nothing if he wavers. 5. It takes away solid consolation in the cross and temptations. 6. It renders the conscience restless. 7. It weakens the internal testimony of the Holy Spirit. 8. It renders the efficacy of the Sacraments uncertain. 9. It attacks the firmness of absolution. 10. It arises from the corruption of the flesh. 11. It is a fiery dart of the devil. 12. A sign of reprobation. 13. And the mother of despair. Considering all these things, our blessed Luther wrote most correctly in chapter 41 of Genesis: Even if there had been nothing else in the Pontifical doctrine than what they taught, that we ought to wander and fluctuate, being uncertain and doubtful about the remission of sins, our grace and our salvation, we would nevertheless have just causes why we should separate ourselves from the unfaithful Church.

LX. XIV. From the testimony of the Fathers. Chemnitz has reviewed many of theirs on our part, Catharinus on the part of the Pontificians; we shall be content with a few. Thus indeed writes Tertullian, from the most ancient, in his book On the Resurrection of the Flesh, chapter 37: Be secure, flesh and blood: You have taken possession of both heaven and the kingdom of God in Christ. Or if they deny you are in Christ, let them also deny Christ is in heaven, who have denied heaven to you. Cyprian, in his book against Demetrianus: The strength of hope flourishes among us, and the firmness of faith, and a mind upright amidst the very ruins of the age, and an immovable virtue, and a soul always secure concerning its God. The same, sermon 4 on mortality: If you are righteous, if you truly believe in God, why do you not embrace the promise of the Lord, being secure that you will be with Christ? God promises you immortality as you depart from this world: And do you doubt and fluctuate? This is, not to know God at all, this is, to offend Christ, the teacher of believers, with the sin of unbelief, this is, being established in the Church, not to have faith in the house of faith. Augustine, sermon 28 on the words of the Lord: All your sins are forgiven standing. Therefore presume not of your own operation, but of the grace of Christ. Therefore it is not arrogance here, but faith, to preach what you have received; it is not pride but devotion. The same in Psalm 148. What did God promise you, not a mortal man? That you shall live forever. Do you not believe? Believe, believe; what He has already done is more than what He promised. What did He do? He died for you. What did He promise? That you shall live with Him. It is more incredible that the Eternal died, than that a mortal should live eternally: Now we hold that which is more incredible. Chrysostom homily 11 on Jeremiah. Whoever do not believe in Christ at all, condemn Him: But those who believe, and yet doubt, judge Him. He suffers two things therefore among men: He is condemned by the unbelieving, and He is judged by the doubting. Bernard on the fragments of the seven loaves, sermon 3. Consider three things, in which my whole hope consists: the Charity of adoption, the Truth of the promise, the Power of the fulfillment. If these three strengthen and confirm my heart, so that no lack of merits, no consideration of my own vileness, no estimation of heavenly blessedness can cast me down from the height of hope, firmly rooted in them. The same, sermon 61 on the Song of Songs. The world rages, the body presses, the devil lies in wait. I do not fall, for I am founded upon a firm rock; I have committed a great sin, my conscience is troubled, but it is not confounded, because I will remember the wounds of Christ. And Epistle 190 against Abailard: If faith wavers, is not our hope vain? Therefore our martyrs are fools, enduring such bitter things for uncertain things, and not doubting under the doubt of the reward of remuneration, to enter upon a long-lasting destruction, a long-lasting destruction.

LXI. XV. Finally, an argument may be sought from the testimonies and hypotheses of adversaries. We have spoken above concerning the consensus of the Enchiridion of Cologne, Cassander, Catharinus, and the like: now we shall bring forward the testimonies of others. Vincent reports, book 30, chapter 107, that Almericus the Gaul in the year of Christ 1210 taught publicly at Paris; that every Christian ought to believe firmly and indubitably that he is a member of the body of Christ, and that this is an article of the Christian faith, without which no one can attain salvation. Jacob Velsius, whom Aegidius Topiarius calls a man in theological matters in all respects most perfect, in the epilogue of his sermon on the Epistle for Ash Wednesday, establishes two parts of repentance, namely both contrition and confession of the internal Adam mourning and lamenting his sins, and a firm faith in God and a certain confidence in divine grace. Claudius Guilliandus of Belloy, formerly Provost of the Church of the Aedui, writes in chapter 6 of John: To believe in Christ is to attain righteousness and eternal life through Christ by a certain persuasion, and to adhere to him with all one's heart, with all one's soul, and with all one's strength. Whoever has done this will embrace all good things and will adhere to them from the heart. To this must be referred the notable testimony of Pedro de Ribadeneira, a Spaniard of the Society of Jesus, whom Aegidius Albertinus, Bavarian Secretary, translated into the German language and published with the permission of his superiors in Munich in the year 1600. I do not transcribe the words, since they are lengthy and can be read as cited in the booklet of Mr. Dr. Cramer on predestination, chapter 20, page 304 and following.

LXII. As for the hypotheses of the Papists, there are many of them with which the dogma of doubt can in no way be reconciled. For they write: 1. That the law can be perfectly fulfilled by a regenerate person in this life. 2. That original sin is completely removed and extirpated through Baptism. 3. That God necessarily gives grace to a man doing what is in him, namely by a necessity of immutability. 4. That every act of charity absolutely merits eternal life. 5. That monks have certain works of supererogation which can be communicated to others for the merit of eternal life. 6. That the monastic reception purges one from all sins. If these hypotheses are true, as the Papists wish them to be true, they certainly leave no doubt anymore, but rather beget an entirely immovable certainty. For if I have fulfilled the law, if original sin has been removed, if God necessarily gives grace, if every good work merits eternal life, if the works of Monks result in salvation, and the Monastic life purges from sins, how I pray shall I be able to doubt concerning grace, concerning the forgiveness of sins and concerning eternal salvation? Nay, and I would like to ask this by way of a finishing touch, why do Monks pledge their own souls for the salvation of those from whom they receive benefits? Why does the Pontiff promise the remission of sins to all who run to Rome and seek Papal indulgences? Why does he command the Angels, that if it happens that travelers, journeying to Rome for the sake of indulgences, die on the journey, they should immediately receive their souls and carry them straight to heaven? If they are so certain about the salvation of others, why do they doubt their own? These things can in no way be reconciled or palliated, but are an indication of a very bad cause, concerning which, when we have brought forward enough into the open, we wish to conclude here, with an ardent vow, that God may excite a firm confidence in our souls; preserve it once excited; and once preserved, seal it with the Spirit of adoption, to His own glory, and our everlasting salvation, Amen.

Latin:

LVI. X. A pronominibus applicationem notantibus. Quando enim fides in ipso exercitio & iustificandi actu describitur, sæpè pronomina nostris, nobis, me &c. adhibentur in Scripturis, ad indicandum, fidei iustificantis naturam esse, circa promissiones salutis ita versari, vt illis se ingerendo, & sub ijs subsumendo, vnicuique indiuiduo credenti applicentur. Quo spectant dicta Galat. 2. vers. 3. Christus dedit semetipsum pro peccatis nostris, c. 2. v. 20. Qui dilexit me, & tradit semetipsum pro me. c. 3. v. 13. Christus factus est pro nobis maledictum, &c. Ex his verò ita concludimus. Quicunque gratiam Dei & meritum Christi sibi in indiuiduo debent applicare, illi vnà firmissimè debent credere peccatorum veniam, quippè quae cum applicatione, velut effectus cum causa, semper est copulata. Sed omnes credentes gratiam Dei & meritum Christi, sibi in indiuiduo debent applicare, vi allegatorum textuum, & exemplo Pauli. Quare omnes credētes vnà firmissimè debent credere peccatorum veniam.

LVII. XI. A remotione causarum dubitandi. Vbi nullae adsunt dubitationis causae, ibi temerarium est dubitare velle. Sed nullae adsunt causae, an pij de gratia Dei & remissione peccatorum dubitare debeant. Ergò temerarium est, dubitare velle. Minorem probamus, quia omnia illa, quae animum reddere possunt dubium, nullius sunt roboris, & iam antè in Scripturis remota:

Huiusmodi sunt 1. Propria indignitas & operum imperfectio. At verò scimus, quòd salutis negotium non nitatur nostris meritis, sed vnicè diuinis promissionibus. Nostra igitur indignitas & imperfectio nequaquam obstat certitudini, cùm DEI virtus in infirmitate sit efficax.

2. Odij diuini suspicio. Atqui Deus in Christo benignissimè erga nos affectus est, & omnium salutem seriò desiderat. Testatam fecit hanc voluntatem dictis, iuramentis, exemplis, ideoq́ue omnem de absoluto decreto cogitationem abijciamus.

3. Particularitas meriti Christi. At venit saluare id omne, quod perierat. Quare propitiatio est, non tantùm pro nostris vel fideliũ, sed etiam p totius mundi peccatis, & expectat quotidiè vt onerati veniant, & refrigerium accipiant.

4. Particularitas vocationis. Sed omnes qui sunt baptizati & viuunt in Ecclesia, (de quibus solis hic loquimur,) sunt simul vocati, & illis diuina beneficia offeruntur in verbo & Sacramentis, quippè quæ sunt manus Dei, per quæ sua nobis dona porrigit.

5. Nostra indispositio, ob quam putamus sæpè, nos ad accipiendam gratiam esse ineptos & indignos. Verùm nihil requiritur à nobis, quàm vsurpatio mediorum: Nulla ex parte nostri dispositio meritoria est necessaria: Modò nos habeamus passiuè, nec obicem ponamus Spiritui sancto, tum accipiemus à Deo fidem, & reliqua dona spiritualia.

6. Peccatorum consideratio. Sed ideò venit Christus, vt pro peccatis satisfaceret, Eius ergò meritum si apprehendimus, peccata nobis nocere haud poterunt. Deus quidem irascitur transgressoribus, sed iram temperat misericordiâ, modò agatur pœnitentia, Non enim delectatur morte morientis, sed vt viuat. Multi fuêre peccatores trassissimis sceleribus polluti, & tamen remissionem impetrârunt. Nondum es Petrus abnegator, vel latro, vel Magdalena meretrix. Hi tamẽ omnes, cùm veniam consecuti sint, quare tu ambiges, nec fidem Dei promissionibus adhibebis?

7. Crucis impositio & calamitatum multiplicatio. Sed hæc signa sunt Dei beneuoli, non irati. Castigat enim quem diligit, & suos maturè corripit, nè cum mundo damnentur, Si quam ergò experieris tribulationem, habeas illam pro amoris signo, & in tuum vergere emolumentum, certissimè credas.

8. Dubitationum subindè assurgentium præsentia. Per illas enim sæpissimè turbamur, vt Deum à nobis aversum esse arbitremur; sed cogitemus, hoc non ex fidei natura, non ex certitudinis impossibilitate, sed potùs ex carnis infirmitate oriri, & à Deo permitti, non vt dubitationibus indulgeamus, sed potius vt ijs reluctemur, & verâ fide superemus. Ita ergò cùm Scriptura ex omni parte dubitandi causas remouerit, meritò acquiescere, & de beneuolo Dei affectu certissimi esse debemus.

LVIII. XII. A fine Scripturæ. Data nobis est inter cætera, vt per pœnitentiam & consolationem, spem habeamus, non sanè ambiguam, dubiamque, sed potiùs certam & immotam, Rom. 15. v. 4. Quodcunque igitur dogma consolationem solidam, & spem certam adimit, illud non est sacris literis consentaneum. Sed dogma Papisticum, de incertitudine remissionis peccatorum, consolationem solidam & spem certam adimit. Quare non est sacris literis consentaneum. Minor prolixâ probatione non indiget, sed per se manifesta est. Quomodo enim locum inueniet vera παράκλησις, pax & quies conscientiæ, si quis de favore Dei & peccatorũ veniâ certus esse nequeat? Quomodo erigetur turbatus animus in tentatione? Semper enim excipiet ad allegatas Dei promissiones, esse eas merè conditionales, & prærequirere perfectam legis impletionem, plenariamque satisfactionem; quæ in mortalium neminem cadant, ideò & nemo qui purus putus Pontificius est, tranquillam lætamque conscientiam habere potest.

LIX. XIII. A dubitationis deformitate. Hæc vt demonstretur, prolixa probatio non requiritur. Quid enim est dubitare, nisi in perpetuo mentis angore versari, & suspensum inter spem & metum hærere? Quâ interiori cordis carnificinâ quid tristius, quidvè molestius vel cogitari saltem potest? Accedunt alia incommoda, siquidem dubitatio 1. Tollit naturã fidei, quæ est fiducia. 2. Aduersatur primæ legis tabulæ, quę requirit, vt Deo super Omnia confidamus. 3. Arguit Deum mendacij & periurij, iuxta illud 1. Iohan. 5. versu 10. Qui non credit Deo, mendacem facit eum. 4. Impedit efficacem orationem, cùm nihil accipiat homo, si hæsitet. 5. Adimit consolationem solidam, in cruce & tentationibus. 6. Reddit conscientiam irrequietam. 7. Eneruat internam Spiritus sancti testificationem. 8. Incertam reddit Sacramentorum efficaciam. 9. Impugnat absolutionis firmitatem. 10 Oritur ex corruptione carnis. 11. Est ignitum telum dæmonis. 12. Signum reprobationis. 13. & Mater desperationis. Quæ omnia considerans B. Lutherus noster rectissimè scripsit in cap. 41. Gen: Etiamsi nihil præterea fuisset in doctrina Pontifificia, quàm quod docuerunt, nos debere vagari & fluctuare ambigentes & dubios de remissione peccatorum, gratia & salute nostra, iustas tamen haberemus causas, cur ab Ecclesia infideli nos seiungeremus.

LX. XIV. A testimonio Patrum. Multa illorum recensuit ex parte nostra Chemnitius, ex parte Pontificiorum Catharinus, nos paucis contenti erimus. Ita verò scribit ex antiquissimis Tertullianus lib. de resurrectione carnis capite 37. Securæ estote caro & sanguis: Vsurpastis & cælum & regnum Dei in Christo. Aut si negent vos in Christo, negent & in cælo Christum, qui vobis cælum negauerunt. Cyprianus lib. aduers. Demetrianum; Viget apud nos spei robur, & firmitas fidei, & inter ipsas seculi ruinas erecta mens, & immobilis virtus, & de Deo suo semper anima secura. Idem sermon. 4. de mortalitate: Si iustus es, si verè in Deum credis, cur non cum Christo futurus & pollicitationem Domini securus amplecteris? Deus tibi de hoc mundo recedenti immortalitatem pollicetur: Et tu dubitas & fluctuas? Hoc est, Deum omninò non nosse, hoc est, Christum, credentium magistrum, peccato incredulitatis offendere, hoc est, in Ecclesia constitutū, fidem in domo fidei non habere Augustinus serm. 28. de verbis Domini: Omnia tibi peccata dimissa stans. Ideò praesume non de operatione tua, sed de Christi gratia. Non ergò hic arrogantia est, sed fides, praedicare quod acceperis, non est superbia sed devotio. Idem in Psalm. 148. Quid tibi promisit Deus non homo mortalis? quia victurus es in aeternum. Non credis? crede, crede, plus est iam quod fecit, quàm quod promisit. Quid fecit? Mortuus est pro te. Quid promisit? Vt vivas cum illo. Incredibilius est, quòd mortuus est aeternus, quàm vt aeternum vivat mortalis: Iam quod incredibilius est, tenemus. Chrysostomus homil. 11. in Ierem. Quicunque penitus Christo non credunt, condemnant eum: Qui autem credunt, & adhuc ambigunt, dijudicant illum. Duo igitur apud homines perpessus: Ab incredulis condemnatur, ab ambigentibus discernitur. Bernhardus de fragmentis septem panum serm. 3. Tria considera, in quibus tota spes mea consistit, Charitate adoptionis, Veritate promissionis, Potestate redditionis. Haec tria si roborent & confirment cor meum, vt nulla me penuria meritorum, nulla consideratio propriae vilitatis, nulla aestimatio caelestis beatitudinis ab altitudine spei deijcere possit in ea firmiter radicata. Idem serm. 61. in Cant. Fremit mundus, premit corpus, diabolus insidiatur. Nō cado, fundatus enim sum super petram firmam; peccavi peccatum grande, turbatur conscientia, sed non perturbatur, quoniam vulnerum Christi recordabor. Et Epist. 190. contra Abailardum: Nonne si fluctuat fides, inanis est spes nostra? Stulti ergò martyres nostri, sustinentes tam acerba propter incerta, nec dubitantes sub dubio remunerationis praemio, diuturnum per exitium, diuturnum inire exitium.

LXI. XV. Tandem peti potest argumentum à testimonijs & hypothesibus adversariorum. De consensu Enchiridij Coloniensis, Cassandri, Catharini & similium suprà diximus: nunc aliorum testimonia in medium afferemus. Vincentius refert. l. 30. c. 107. Almericum Gallum anno Christi 1210. Parisiis publicè docuisse; quemlibet Christianum debere firmiter & indubitatò credere, se esse membrum ex Christi corpore, & hoc esse articulum Christiana fidei, sine quo salutem nemo consequi possit. Iacobus Veldius, quem Ægidius Topiarius virum in re Theologica omnibus numeris absolutissimum nominat, in Epilogo concionis, in Epistolam diei cinerum, partes poenitentiæ duas constituit, nempè tùm contritionem & confessionem Adami interni lugentis & plangentis peccata, tùm fidem in Deum firmam, & certam fiduciam gratiæ diuinæ. Claudius Guilliandus Bellioensis Eduorum Ecclesiæ quondam Præpositus scribit in c. 6 Iohannis: Credere in Christum, est certâ a uasestatione per Christum contingere iustitiam & vitam æternam, eíque toto corde, totâ anima, totis viribus inhærere. Hoc qui fecerit omnia bona complectetur, illisque ex animo adhærescet. Hùc referri debet insigne testimonium Petri de Ribadeneÿra, Iesu Witæ Hispani quem Ægidius Albertinus, Secretarius Bauaricus in Germanicam linguam transtulit, & cum licentia superiorum Monachij edidit, anno 1600. Verba non adscribo, cùm prolixa sint, & citata legi possint in libello Dn. D. Crameri de prædest. c. 20 p. 304. seqq.

LXII. Quod denique Papicolarum hypotheses attinet, multæ illarum sunt, cum quibus dogma dubitationis conciliari minimè potest. Scribunt enim 1. Legem à renato in hac vita perfectè impleri posse. 2. Peccatū originis per Baptismum penitùs tolli & extirpari. 3. Deum homini facienti quod in se est, dare gratiam necessariò, nempè necessitate immutabilitatis. 4. Omne actum caritatis absolute mereri vitam æternam. 5. Monachos habere opera quædam supererogationis, quæ alijs communicari queant in meritum vitæ æternæ 6. Susceptionem Monasticam purgare ab omnibus peccatis. Quæ hypothesies si veræ sunt, ut veras esse volunt Pontificij, nullam certè dubitationem relinquunt ampliùs, sed prorsus immotam certitudinem gignunt. Si enim legem impleuero, si peccatum originis sit sublatum, si Deus necessariò dat gratiam, si omne opus bonum meretur vitam æternam, si Monachorum opera cedunt in salutem, & Monastica vita purgat à peccatis, quî quæso de gratia, de peccatorum venia & de salute æterna dubitare potero? Imò & hoc colophonis loco quærere lubet, cur Monachi suas oppignerent animas pro salute eorum, à quibus accipiunt beneficia? Cur Pontifex promittat remissionem peccatorum omnibus, qui Romam excurrunt & Papales indulgentias quærunt? Cur Angelis præcipiat, vt viatorum, Romam indulgentiarum gratiâ peregrinantium, si illos in itinere mori contingat, animas protinus exceptas, in cœlum rectâ deportent? Si de aliorum salute tàm certi sunt, cur de sua dubitant? Conciliari hæc vel palliari nullo modo queunt, sed pessimæ causæ sunt indicium, de qua cùm satis multa in medium attulerimus, hîc conclusum volumus, cū ardenti voto, vt Deus firmam in animis nostris fiduciam excitet; exitatam conseruet; & conseruatam Spiritu adoptionis obsignet, ad ipsius gloriam, & salutem nostram sempiternam, Amen.


### Question II: To God Alone Glory

TO GOD ALONE GLORY.

Latin:

SOLI DEO GLORIA.


## 33 Disputation X. On Bellarmine's Arguments against the Certainty of Grace

Presided over by Balthasar Meisner, Doctor of Sacred Theology. Respondent: Crispin Flugge of Lübeck.

Thesis I.

After the orthodox thesis concerning the certainty of Justification, which we gave as proven in the previous discussion, follows the antithesis concerning ambiguity and uncertainty

grace, which Bellarmine in book 3 of Justification, chapters 4, 5, 6, 7, and 8, attempts to establish. He acts there as a skeptic or Academic, intending to prove that no one can certainly subsume concerning his own justification or the remission of his sins, just as the Academics formerly taught that all things are uncertain, and they were engaged in a perpetual τῆς ὑπολήψεως ἀπάτη or fallacy of subsumption. For they conceded the general θέσιν, as that all snow is white, but in the subsumption they always doubted whether this or that snow is white. The Papists are stuck in the same error of subsumption. For they decree that it must be believed in general that sins are freely remitted on account of the merit of Christ: but they judge that no one should subsume concerning himself individually, but rather they say anathema to all who faithfully subsume. It remains to be seen in order by what means Bellarmine labors to prove this most harsh opinion, which is full of despair.

II. IN CHAPTER IV he writes that the uncertainty of one's own grace and righteousness can be proven from the testimonies of Solomon, and he proposes three of them. THE FIRST is taken from Proverbs 20, v. 9: Who can say, my heart is clean, I am pure from sin. Here he wishes to note the style of Solomon, that he did not say that no one is pure in heart, but that no one can say or know that his heart is pure. If, therefore, a man is ignorant of the purity of his heart, how can he be certain of the grace of God and of the remission of sins?

Resp. 1. In the Hebrew it is 'I have cleansed' and 'I have purified,' from which it appears that that saying is opposed to hypocrites and Pharisees, who wished to be justified by their own powers and presumed immunity from all sins; although not all Jews were such, many nevertheless cherished this arrogant opinion.

2. Solomon is not dealing with the uncertainty of grace, but with the imperfection of our righteousness and inherent holiness. For the remission of sins is one thing, and another is renewal. That is perfect and complete, because it rests upon a perfect foundation, namely the obedience of Christ: But this is begun and imperfect, on account of the habitual corruption of nature, and the commission of actual sins, for which all saints have need to pray, Psalm 32. v. 6. But from the imperfection of

III. THE SECOND is read in Eccles. 9. v. 1. There are righteous and wise men, and their works are in the hand of God, and yet man knows not whether he is worthy of love or hatred, but all things are kept uncertain for the future. Hence he concludes, that the grace of God in this life is uncertain: But that on the last day at length everyone will know, whether he is under grace or otherwise.

Resp. 1. If this passage is understood absolutely, it will follow that neither can the righteous know that they are loved, nor the ungodly that they are worthy of hatred. Both are absurd. For the righteous can know that they are under grace, Rom. 8. v. 12. 1. John 3. v. 14. And the ungodly can know that they have God angry in the heavens, whence it happens that many despair. Nor can that saying be restricted to the righteous alone, since Solomon speaks of any man in general, which reason the Jesuit Salmeron attending to, denies in 1. Cor. 12. disput. 14. that the uncertainty of divine grace can be proved from this text.

2. There is a fault in the Vulgate version, which added these words, all things are kept uncertain for the future, when nevertheless they are not found in the Hebrew text, but it is read thus, as Pagninus translates: The righteous are, and the wise, and their services in the hand of God: Even love, the hatred itself man not knowing, all before their faces.

3. This passage can be understood, either of different men, or of the same one, if of different ones, the uncertainty of another's righteousness is noted: For no one can infallibly know, whether others truly believe or otherwise, since he is not a καρδιογνώστης, and external signs are fallible, and common to the pious and to hypocrites, which sense Luther expressed in the German version, But from the uncertainty of another's righteousness, to the uncertainty of one's own righteousness there is no consequence. If those words are understood of the same man, then they can be accepted, either absolutely, that no one, whoever he may be, is able to know whether he is worthy of love or hatred: but this contradicts the scriptures, examples, and theological hypotheses: or limitedly, namely that a man does not know whether he is under grace, if he wishes to make a judgment from external events, concerning which alone Solomon speaks there, with Cajetan not dissenting.

4, It is doubtful whether divine or human hatred ought to be understood. The Papists assume the former, the latter seems more convenient, so that the sense may be: This is altogether mystical, that even the wisest of all men do not know whether they ought to love these men, and receive them into friendship, or indeed hate them, as impious. The reason is added, because a judgment cannot be established from external events, since all things happen alike. But to this and the preceding statement I have replied at greater length in Decad. 2. disp. 8. Quæst. 4. thes. 9. & 10.

IV. The third statement is taken from an Apocryphal book, namely Ecclesiasticus, which the Papists falsely attribute to Solomon. But in chapter 5, v. 5, it reads thus: Concerning propitiated sin be not without fear, nor add sin upon sin, And do not say; The mercy of God is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins. This passage, says Bellarmine, wonderfully stings the heretics of this time, For they themselves are properly those who, when they have seemed to themselves by faith to have apprehended the righteousness of Christ, are touched by no fear thereafter.

Resp. 1, He slanders, when he writes that all fear is excluded by us. We remove servile fear, we urge filial fear, and we warn our hearers that they should work out their salvation with fear and trembling.

2. Nothing is contained in the cited text concerning doubting faith, nothing concerning the uncertain remission of sins, but Ecclesiasticus merely warns that no one should sin without hope of pardon, as the context clearly indicates. For there is a fault in the Vulgate version, because in the original text there is no mention of a propitiated sin, but the words sound thus: περὶ ἐξιλασμῦ μὴ ἄφοβος γίνο ἐν πολυ- φασμῷ προσθεῖναι ἁμαρτίας ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίαις: concerning propitiation be not without fear beyond measure, to add sins upon sins; that is, do not persuade yourself of propitiation while you are sinning, do not offend through hope of pardon and mercy, etc. The following words, which are explanatory of the former, immediately indicate this sense: For Ecclesiasticus continues thus: And do not say, the mercy of the Lord is great, He will have mercy on the multitude of my sins. But what is the consequence: Let no one sin through hope of pardon, and let no one presume upon mercy in his sins; therefore, must the faithful and penitent doubt and be uncertain of the grace of God and the pardon of their sins?

Bellarmino objects that Ecclesiasticus is speaking not of future propitiation, but of past, because we ought to fear especially in regard to this. But this gloss is opposed both to the scope of Ecclesiasticus and to the whole context, which Jansenius, Bishop of Ghent, acknowledged, who discourses on this passage as follows: It is read in Hebrew, concerning propitiation do not be without fear, and it is understood of obtaining the remission of a sin committed, against presumption; not of a propitiated sin, for one committed, as the Vulgate has it, which the text contradicts.

IN CHAPTER V. he wishes to prove his thesis by three examples of saints. The first is that of Job, from which he reasons thus: Job doubted of his grace and salvation, therefore no one will be able to be certain. He proves the antecedent from Job chapter nine, verses eleven and twelve: If he passes by me I will not see him, if he suddenly questions, who will answer him? Verse 20: If I wish to justify myself, my own mouth will condemn me; verse 21: Even if I were simple, my soul would not know this; verse 28: I feared all my works, knowing that you would not spare the offender. And chapter 31, verse 14: What would I do if God should arise, and if he should visit, what am I to answer him? From all these, Bellarmino concludes that Job doubted of his salvation, and was not certain of it by the certainty of faith.

R. N. C. because those sayings only prove the imperfection of works and the corruption of our nature; from which it follows that no one is righteous before God by their own righteousness. For if we wished to be justified by our works, and God were to contend with us in judgment, no one would be saved, because works are imperfect. And St. Job (who was otherwise most certain of his salvation, as is evident from chapter 19, verse 25) wished to indicate only this by those sayings, just as David pronounces in Psalm 143, verse 2: If you wish to enter into judgment, no living person will be justified before you. And yet it is said elsewhere that many are justified, for the reconciliation of which it is necessary that we distinguish between proper and alien righteousness: by the former, no one can be justified before God; but through the righteousness of Christ, everyone who believes is justified; and since this itself is perfect, a firm foundation of certainty can be sought from it. That Job is speaking about proper righteousness and its imperfection is indicated by 1. the words themselves, 2. the whole context, 3. the scope and intention of Job.

VI. But as regards verse 21 of chapter 9. There is a fault in the Vulgate; the words are thus: תָּם אָנִי לֹא אֵדַע נַפְשִׁי I am perfect, I will not know my soul. Luther rendered it thus: 'Bin ich fromb / so thut sichs meine Seele nicht annemen.' But the genuine sense appears from the previous verse. He speaks there hypothetically, 'if I justify myself,' and so here תם אני, that is, if I were seen as just and perfect, or if I seem perfect to myself, yet I will not know, that is, I am ignorant of my soul, or I am unable to justify myself, because perhaps there are hidden sins. He says, therefore, the same thing that Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4, verse 4: 'I am conscious of nothing, yet I am not justified by this.' Therefore, Job wished to indicate this: Even if I seem perfect, indeed even if nothing is known to me myself regarding some gross crime, yet I do not know my soul, whether it is exempt from every stain; indeed, I know it is not, and therefore no one can be justified by works.

Latin:

Præs. Balth: Meisnero, SS. Th. D. Resp: Crispino Flugge Lubecensi.

Thesis I.

POst orthodoxam θέσιν de certitudine Iustificationis, quam superiori συζητήσει probatam dedimus, sequitur ἀντίθεσις de ambiguitate & de incertitu-

stine gratia, quam Bellarminus lib. 3. de Iustificatione c. 4. 5. 6. 7. & 8. astruere conatur. Agit ibi scepticum vel Academicum probare intendens, neminem certò posse subsumere de sua iustificatione, vel suorum peccatorum remissione, non secus ac Academici olim docuerunt, omnia incerta esse, & versati sunt in perpetua τῆς ὑπολήψεως ἀπάτη vel subsumptionis fallacia. Generalem enim θέσιν concesserunt, vt, omnem nivem albam esse, sed in subsumptione semper dubitârunt, num haec vel illa nix alba sit? In eodem subsumptionis errore hærent Papicolæ. Statuunt enim, in genere credendum esse, peccata propter Christi meritum gratis remitti: Sed nemini de se in indiuiduo subsumendum esse iudicant, sed potius omnibus fideliter subsumentibus anathema dicunt. Quam durissimam & desperationis plenam opinionem, quâ Bellarminus euincere moliatur, ordine videndum restat.

II. CAPITE IV. scribit, ex testimoniis Salomonis probari posse incertitudinem propriæ gratiæ atque iustitiæ, & illorum tria proponit. PRIMVM est desumptum ex Prouerbiorum 20. v. 9. Quis potest dicere, mundum est cor meum, purus sum à Peccato. Hic notari vult stylum Salomonis, quòd non dixerit, nemi nem esse purum corde, sed neminem posse dicere aut scire, cor suum esse purum. Si ergo ignorat homo puritatem cordis sui, quî certus esse poterit de gratia Dei & de remissione peccatorum?

Resp. 1. In Hebræo est Mundaui & Purificaui, vndè apparet, quod dictum illud sit oppositum hypocritis & Pharisæis, qui ex proprijs viribus volebant iustificari, & immunitatem ab omnibus peccatis præsumebant, quales licèt non fuerint Iudæi omnes, multi tamen opinionem hanc arrogantem fouerunt.

2. Non agit Salomon de incertitudine gratiæ, sed de imperfectione nostræ iustitiæ & inhærentis sanctimoniæ. Aliud enim est remissio peccatorum, & aliud renouatio. Illa perfecta est & completa, quia nititur fundamento perfecto, nempè obedientiâ Christi: Hæc autem inchoata est & imperfecta, ob corruptionem naturæ habitualem, & commissionem peccatorum actualem, pro qua omnes sancti orari necessum habent, Psalm. 32. v. 6. Ab imperfectione autem renouationis, ad incertitudinem iustificationis nulla est consequentia,

III. SECVNDVM legitur Ecclef. 9. v. 1. Sunt iusti atque sapientes, & opera eorum in manu Dei, & tamen nescit homo vtrum amore an odio dignus sit, sed omnia in futurum seruantur incerta. Hinc concludit, Gratiam Dei in hac vita incertam esse: Vltimo autem die demum quemuis esse cogniturum, an sub gratia sit vel secus.

Resp. 1. Si absolutè intelligatur hic locus, sequetur, nec iustos scire posse, se amari, nec impios, se odio dignos esse. Vtrumque absurdum. Possunt enim scire iusti se esse sub gratia, Rom. 8. v. 12. 1. Iohan. 3. v. 14. Et possunt scire iniusti; se iratum in cœlis habere Deum, vndè fit vt multi desperent. Nec potest dictum illud ad solos iustos restringi, cùm Salomon loquatur de homine quouis in genere, quam rationem attendens Iesuita Salmeron negat in 1. Cor. 12. disput. 14. ex hoc textu probari posse incertitudinem diuinæ gratiæ.

2. Vitium est in vulgata versione, quæ addidit hæc verba, omnia in futurum seruantur incerta, cùm tamen in Hebræo textu non inueniantur, sed ita legatur, vt vertit Pagninus: Iusti sunt, & sapientes, & seruitia eorũ in manu Dei: Etiam amorem, ipsum odium non sciens homo, omnis ante facies eorum.

3. Locus hic intelligi potest, vel de diuersis hominibus, vel de eodem, si de diuersis, notatur incertitudo iustitiæ alienæ: Nemo enim infallibiliter scire potest, num alij verè credant vel secus, cùm non sit καρδιογνώστης, & signa externa sint fallibilia, pijsque ac hypocritis communia, quem sensum Lutherus in versione germanica expressit, Ab incertitudine autem aliena iustitiæ, ad incertitudinem propriæ iustitiæ nulla est consequentia. Si de eodem homine intelligantur verba ista, tum accipi possunt, vel absolutè, quòd nemo qualiscunque sit scire valeat, num amore sit dignus vel odio: sed hoc contradicit scripturis, exemplis, & hypothesibus theologicis: vel limitatè, nempè hominem nescire an sit sub gratia, si judicium velit facere ex eventibus externis, de quibus solis ibi sermonem facit Salomon, non dissentiente Cajetano.

4, Dubium est, num intelligi debeat odium divinum vel humanum Prius assumunt Pontificij, posterius videtur convenientius, vt sit sensus: Hoc omnino mysticum est, quòd etiam sapientissimi quique non cognoscant homines, vtrum istos debeant diligere, & in amicitiam recipere, an verò odisse, tanquam impios. Ratio additur, quia ex eventibus externis judicium nequit institui, cùm omnia pariter eveniant. Ad hoc autem & præcedens dictum prolixius respondi Decad. 2. disp. 8. Quæst. 4. thes. 9. & 10.

IV. Tertium dictum est petitum ex libro Apocrypho, nempè Ecclesiastico, quem falsò Salomoni tribuunt Papicolę. Capite autem 5. v. 5. sic legitur: De propitiato Peccato noli esse sine metu, neque adjicias peccatum super peccatum, Et nè dicas; Miseratio Dei magna est; multitudinis peccatorum meorum miserebitur. Hic locus, ait Bellarminus, mirificè pungit hæreticos hujus temporis, Ipsi enim propriè illi sunt qui vbi fide sibi visi sunt Christi iustitiam apprehendisse, nullo deinceps metu tanguntur.

Resp. 1, Calumniatur, cùm metum à nobis omnem excludi scribit. Servilem tollimus, filialem urgemus, & auditores monemus, vt salutem cum timore & tremore operentur.

2. Nihil in textu allegato habetur de fide dubitante, nihil de incerta remissione peccatorum, sed duntaxat monet Ecclesiasticus, nè quis pecset spe veniæ, vti contextus manifestè indicat. Vitium enim est in vulgata versione, quia in textu originali non habetur de propitiato peccato, sed verba ita sonant: περὶ ἐξιλασμῦ μὴ ἄφοβος γίνο ἐν πολυφασμῷ προσθεῖναι ἁμαρτίας ἐφ’ ἁμαρτίαις: de propitiatione non sis sine metu supra modum; id est, ne persuadeas tibi propitiationem, dum peccas, non spe veniæ & misericordiæ delinquas &c. Hunc sensum statim indicant verba sequentia, quæ sunt priorum ἐξηγητικὰ: Ita enim pergit Ecclesiasticus: Et nè dicas, miseratio Domini magna est, multitudini peccatorum meorum miserebitur. Quæ verò est consequentia: Nemo peccet spe veniæ, & nemo in peccatis præsumat misericordiam; Ergo fideles & pœnitentes dubitare debent incertiq́; suns de gratia Dei, & peccatorum venia?

Excipit Bellarminus, loqui Ecclesiasticum non de propitiatione futurá, sed de præteritá, quòd huius præcipuè respectu timere debeamus. Sed glossahæc, & scopo Ecclesiastici, & toti cōtextui aduersatur, quod agnouit Iansenius, Episcopus Gandauensis, qui in hunc locum ita disserit. Hebraicè legitur, de propitiatione noli esse sine metu, & intelligitur de obtinenda remissione peccati perpetrati, contra præsumptionē; non de propitiato, pro perpetrato, vt vulgata habet, cui textus repugnat.

V. CAPITE V. thesin suam vult euincere, per tria sanctorum exempla. Primum est Iobi, vndè sic ratiocinatur: Iob dubitabat de suâ gratiâ & salute, Ergo nemo certus esse poterit. Antecedens probat ex Iobi nono, versu vndecimo & duodecimo si præterierit me non videbo eum, repentè interroget, quis respondebit? versu 20. si iustificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me, versu 21. Etiamsi simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea, vers. 28. Verebar omnia opera mea, sciens, quòd non parceres delinquenti. Et capite 31. vers. 14. Quid facerem si Deus consurgeret, & si visitaret quid sum responsurus illi? Ex his omnibus concludit Bellarminus, Iobum dubitasse de suâ salute, nec certitudine fidei de illâ certum fuisse.

R. N. C. quia dicta ista duntaxat probant operum imperfectionem, & naturæ nostræ corruptionem; vnde sequitur, neminem propriâ iustitiâ coram Deo esse iustum. Si enim ex operibus nostris iustificari vellemus, & Deus iudicio contenderet nobiscum, nemo saluaretur, quia opera sunt imperfecta. Et hoc tantùm dictis istis indicare voluit S. Iobus, (qui aliàs de sua salute fuit certissimus, vt constat ex cap. 19: vers. 25.) non secus atque David pronunciat Psal. 143. vers. 2. Si intrare volueris in iudicium, non iustificabitur coram te omnis viuens. Et tamen alibi dicitur, quòd multi iustificentur, pro quorum conciliatione necessarium est, vt distinguamus inter iustitiam propriam & alienam: Illâ nemo iustificari potest coram Deo; per Christi autem iustitiam omnis qui credit, iustificatur; & cùm hæc ipsa sit perfecta: firmum inde certitudinis fundamentum peti potest. Loqui autem Iobum de iustitiâ propriâ & eius imperfectione, indicant 1. ipsa verba, 2. totus contextus, 3. scopus Iobi & intentio.

VI. Quod verò attinet ver. 21. cap. 9. Vitium est in vulgata, verba sic habent תָּם אָנִי לֹא אֵדַע נַפְשִׁי Perfectus ego, non noscam animam meam. Luth. ita reddidit, Bin ich fromb / so thut sichs meine Seele nicht annemen. Ex priori autem versiculo sensus genuinus apparet. Loquitur ibi hypotheticè, si iustificauero me, & ita hic תם אני id est, si iustus & perfectus fuero visus, vel si mihi perfectus videar, tamen nō noscam, hoc est, ignoro animam meam, vel nequeo meipsum iustificare, quia fortassis occulta sunt delicta. Idem igitur dicit, quod Paulus 1. Cor. 4. vers. 4. Nihil quidem mihi conscius sum, sed in hoc non iustificatus sum. Proindè Iobus hoc indicare voluit: Etiamsi perfectus videar, imo etiamsi mihi ipsi de scelere quodam crasso nil constet, tamen nescio animam meam, an sit omni labe exempta, imo scio non esse, ideoque ex operibus neminem posse iustificari.


### VII. The second example is that of David, whom he thinks to have doubted, as is…

VII. The second example is that of David, whom he thinks to have doubted, as is manifest in Psalm 19, where David says in v. 13: Who can understand his errors? Cleanse thou me from secret faults, O Lord, and spare thy servant from the faults of others.

Response. There is no consequence in this argument either. For it is not contradictory that we sin daily out of ignorance and yet be certain of salvation, since the foundation of certainty is placed not in us, but outside of us solely in the obedience of Christ. If we were to be justified by our works, then indeed we could not be certain, as long as we know that we sin. But now we are rendered saved through the righteousness of Christ, which, since it covers all sins, even secret ones, therefore they can do no harm, nor can they hinder the certainty of salvation. For that which is covered, that which is forgiven, and from which we are said to be cleansed, how can it generate doubt? David certainly declared his certainty in express words elsewhere: namely, Ps. 32 v. 5: I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord, and thou forgavest or tookest away the iniquity of my sin.

VIII. The third example is that of the Apostle Paul, who writes thus in 1 Cor. 4:4: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι, ὁ δὲ ἀνακρίνων με Κύριός ἐστιν, I am conscious of nothing in myself, yet I am not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord. Bellarmine says that this passage is opposed to rash judgments, both of others and of one's own self, and therefore Paul says, I do not even judge myself, that is, I do not dare to sit in my own judgment, because even if I am conscious of nothing in myself, yet I am not hereby justified, that is, I am not righteous for that reason, because I have a good conscience. For perhaps God sees in my conscience that which I do not see there.

Response 1. There are some who explain the apostolic statement thus: I am conscious of nothing in myself, that is, I indeed know that I am righteous and innocent: yet I am not hereby justified, that is, not on that account

I am righteous before men, who cannot see my internal righteousness. But he who judges me is the Lord, that is, God himself will declare me righteous before others in the final judgment. Therefore, they do not understand justification before God in the internal forum of conscience, but justification before men, in the external forum of holiness. And yet Catharinus explained it thus against Soto.
