But that interpretation does not seem entirely conformable to the text, since the Apostle does not speak of his righteousness limitedly before men, but absolutely about it. Moreover, the words, 'Neither do I judge myself,' would not sufficiently cohere with what follows.

Therefore we say that this 2nd passage ought to be understood either of fidelity in ministry, or of the zeal and exercise of good works in general. If of fidelity (as the second verse certainly hints, where it is said that this is required in a steward, that he be found faithful), then this sense emerges: I am indeed conscious of nothing against myself, as if I had been negligent in my office and ministry, yet I am not justified by that, that is, I cannot pronounce myself absolutely righteous, I cannot boast of an all-encompassing and in every way perfect fidelity, because I could have sinned even ignorantly and involuntarily. But the Lord judges me; he knows whether I have fully satisfied my office. But what does this do for Papist doubt? And what is the consequence: We do not know whether we have always been faithful in our office; therefore we also do not know whether our sins have been forgiven us? But if the words of Paul are understood concerning the exercise of works in general, again the Pontificians cannot gather from them an uncertainty of justification. For shall we think that he doubted his own salvation, who says in Romans 5, verse 1, 'Being justified by faith we have peace'; who in Romans 8, v. 38, says with such πληροφορίᾳ, 'I am certain'? Most absurd indeed are the Jesuits, while they propose the example of Paul, who was so far from doubting about his own salvation, that he was rather infallibly certain of it, even by their own admission, and by attributing this to a special revelation. Furthermore, St. Paul does not speak doubtfully; he does not say, 'I am conscious of nothing, but I do not know whether I am justified by this,' but he speaks assertively and plainly says, 'I am not justified in this.' He therefore denies all justification and power of justifying to his own works, so that this is the sense: 'Although I am conscious of nothing regarding grosser and mortal offenses, but I know that I have striven to the best of my ability for good works, and have exercised them in no way; yet, in turn, I know that I am not justified by those works of mine, because I can in no way have righteousness and salvation in them, since they are 1. due, 2. imperfect, and 3. mixed with many venial sins.' But what kind of consequence is it: 'No one is justified by works, nor can one be certain of the remission of sins from them: therefore, one cannot be certain at all'? Does it follow that because this means does not conclude it, other means bringing certainty cannot be given?

Bellarmino is mistaken, and is deceived, while he writes that this exposition is repugnant to the scope and purpose of the Apostle, who wishes to dissuade from rash judgment, and therefore says, 'neither do I judge myself.' For the individual parts cohere very well. 'I do not judge myself, I do not justify myself, I do not seek praise and glory in works.' For even if I am conscious of nothing, I am not therefore justified before God. For it is God alone who judges me. Therefore, human judgments are not to be greatly heeded. He demonstrates, therefore, the vanity of human judgments, 1. from the impossible, and from his own example, because he himself cannot judge and justify himself from external works: much less can others do this. 2. From the prerogative of God, that it is the right of God alone to judge, and to either absolve or condemn men. IX. Chap. VI. He produces various passages of the Prophets and Apostles, which can be divided into three classes. In the first he places those sayings which show that contrition, faith, repentance, and conversion are required if anyone is to be righteous or justified, such as are read in Deut. 4, 2 Paralip. 6, Ezd. 1, Ezech. 18, John 13, Luke 13, Acts 8, etc. But no one, he says, can be certain, especially with the certainty of faith, that he has been converted to the Lord with his whole heart, and possesses faith and repentance such as is required, since in no Scripture is such a testimony found concerning our faith and repentance in particular. And hence he concludes: That no one can be certain of the grace of God and the remission of sins.

Response. The minor premise is false. For although it does not exist in Scripture that this or that person believes, yet there exists a promise that GOD wills to work faith and repentance in men who do not place an obstacle: Furthermore, Sacraments have been instituted so that by them faith may be confirmed; a ministry has been ordained, by whose work sins are remitted and faith is kindled. For faith is from hearing. Wherefore he who hears, and does not place an obstacle, he receives faith.

Furthermore, I can be certain of my repentance.

1. On account of the certainty of the promises. 2. The efficacy of the Word and Sacraments. 3. The proclamation of the Ministry. 4. The power of prayers. 5. The sense of the indwelling Spirit. 6. The struggle of the flesh. 7. The pursuit of good works. For wherever there is displeasure at vices, there is the Spirit and renewal; or where there is the struggle of the flesh, there is a reborn man: where this is, there can be certainty of faith. Wherefore whoever feels that sins are displeasing to him, whoever seriously desires to be freed from the flesh of sin, who wills the good, although he does not find how to perform it, he is certainly reborn: if reborn, he certainly has faith, and thus can be certain of the remission of sins. Thus patience in the cross is an infallible sign of true conversion and repentance; therefore let these certainties always be considered foundations of certainty 1. The Father's promise. 2. Christ's satisfaction. 3. The Spirit's sealing. 4. The proclamation of the Word. 5. The apprehension of faith. 6. The confirmation of the sacraments. 7. The attestation of works (to which belong struggle, displeasure at evil, patience). 8. The testing of the cross. 9. The obtaining of prayers.

All these things will be revealed on the last day; whence the Germans say: 1. GOTT gibts. 2. Christus erwirbts. 3. Der Heilige Geist bekræfftigets 4. Das Wort verkündigets. 5. Der Glaub empfehets. 6. Die Sacramenta versiegelens. 7. Die Wercke bezeugens. 8. Das Creutz prüfets. 9. Der Jüngste Tag eröfsnets. In these consists our entire Christianity and certainty of salvation.

X. In the second class he places those sayings which speak doubtfully concerning the grace of GOD and the remission of sins. He mentions four of these principally. The first stands in Daniel 4. v. 24. Perhaps God will forgive your transgressions,

Response: it is a fault of the Vulgate version, because in the original text the dubitative particle is not present. The words sound thus: הֵן תֶּהֱוֵא אַרְכָא לִשְׁלֵוְתָךְ Behold, there shall be a prolonging of your peace. Luther: So will God have patience with your sins. Whence it appears that the words of the Prophet are by no means dubitative, but most highly assertive. They can, however, be understood either of the temporal peace and kingdom of Nebuchadnezzar, or of the spiritual remission of sins. Pagninus indeed translates, if perhaps, but no place will easily be shown where the particle הֵן is taken for a mark of doubt, but it is then for the most part employed when the Prophets are about to bring forth something certain and excellent, so that they may render the hearers attentive.

XI. The second stands in Joel 2. verse 14. Who knows, whether God will turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?

Response. The words are thus, מִי יוֹדֵעַ יָשׁוּב וְנִחָם

Who knows if he may turn and repent? Who knows/it may repent him again/and leave a blessing behind him: But from this a Popish doubt cannot be gathered. For the discourse is not about the remission of sins, but about the infliction of temporal punishments. For the Prophet has threatened in the preceding verses various punishments, overthrow, sterility, etc. Afterwards he adds consolation and an exhortation to repentance, with the reason added, because perhaps he will suffer, so that the Lord may change his decree concerning temporal punishments, and bestow a blessing. We grant willingly, however, that we are uncertain whether God will always avert punishments, because he chastises even the pious who are justified. But what is the consequence: We cannot know for certain whether God is going to avert temporal punishments: Therefore neither can we know whether he is going to remit sins? It is not permitted to argue from the infliction of punishment to the remission of guilt.

Latin:

VII. Secundum exemplum est Davidis, quem ipsum dubitâsse putat psal. 19 manifestum esse, vbi Dauid inquit v. 13. Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me Domine, & ab alienis parce servo tuo.

Respon. Nulla & huic argumento inest consequentia. Non enim sunt ἐναντία, nos quotidiè ex ignorantiâ peccare, & de salute certos esse, quandoquidem fundamentum certitudinis, non in nobis, sed extra nos in Christi obedientia vnicè positum est. Si nostris operibus iustificari debeamus, tum quidem certi esse non possumus, quàm diu nos peccare scimus. Iam verò per Christi iustitiam salui reddimur, quæ cùm tegat omnia delicta etiam occulta, idcircò nihil illa nocere, nec certitudinem salutis impedire possunt. Quod enim tectum, quod remissum est, & à quo mundati dicimur, quomodo dubitationem potest gignere? David sanè certitudinem suam expressis verbis declarauit alibi: nempè Ps. 32. v. 5. Dixi, confitebor Domino prævaricationes meas, & tu remisisti siue abstulisti iniquitatem peccati mei.

IIX. Tertium Exemplum est Apostoli Pauli, qui 1. Cor. 4. 4. ita scribit: οὐδὲν γὰρ ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα, ἀλλ᾽ οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ δεδικαίωμαι, ὁ δὲ ἀνακρίνων με Κύριός ἐστιν, Nihil mihi conscius sum, sed non in hoc iustificatus sum: qui autem iudicat me, Dominus est. Hunc locum dicit Bellarminus oppositum esse temerariis iudiciis, & alienis & propriis, ideoque dicere Paulum, Ego neque meipsum iudico, id est, nec meo iudicio sedere audeo, quoniam etiamsi nihil mihi conscius sum, tamen non in hoc iustificatus sum, id est, non ideò iustus sum, quia bonam conscientiam habeo. Fortasse enim Deus videt in conscientiâ mea id quod ego ibi non video.

Resp. 1. Sunt nonnulli, qui dictum Apostolicum sic exponunt: Nihil mihi conscius sum, id est, ego quidem scio, me iustum & innocentem esse: tamen non in hoc iustificatus sum, id est, non propterea

Iustus sum coram hominibus, qui iustitiam meam internam videre nequeunt. Qui autem iudicat me Dominus est, id est, Deus ipse in extremo iudicio me iustum esse coram alijs declarabit. Itagitur isti non intelligunt iustificationem coram Deo in foro conscientiæ interno, sed iustificationem coram hominibus, in foro sanctimoniæ externo. Atqui ita exposuit Catharinus contra Sotum. Verùm non videtur interpretatio illa textui per omnia conformis, quoniam Apostolus non limitatè de iustitiâ sua coram hominibus, sed absolutè de ista loquitur. Verba insuper, Neque meipsum iudico, non satis cohærerent cum sequentibus.

Proinde dicimus 2. locum istum intelligi debere, vel de fidelitate in ministerio, vel de studio & exercitio bonorum operum in genere, Si de fidelitate (vti certè versus secundus innuit, vbi dicitur, quòd hoc requiratur in dispensatore, vt fidelis inveniatur) tum sensus hic emergit: Nihil mihi quidem conscius sum, ac si negligens fuissem in officio & ministerio meo, attamen non propterea sum iustificatus, id est, non possum me absolutè iustum pronunciare, non possum gloriari de omnimoda & vndiquaque perfectâ fidelitate, quia ignoranter etiam & involuntariè peccare potui. Dominus autem iudicat me, ille novit, an meo officio plenè satisfecerim. Quid autem hoc pro dubitatione Papistica facit? Et quæ est consequentia: Ignoramus an semper fuerimus in officio fideles: quare ignoramus etiam num peccata nobis remissa sint? Sin verba Pauli de exercitio operum in genere intelliguntur, rursus nequeunt ex illis incertitudinem iustificationis colligere Pontificij. Num enim existimabimus, de salute suâ dubitâsse eum, qui dicit Rom 5. versu 1. Iustificati fide pacem habemus; qui Rom. 8. v. 38. tantâ πληροφορίᾳ ait, certus sum? Absurdissimi sanè funt IefuWitæ, dum Pauli exemplum proponunt, qui adeò non dubitabat de salute suâ, vt potius de illa infallibiliter fuerit certus, ipsis quoque fatentibus, & hoc speciali reuelationi ascribentibus, Prætereà D Paulus non loquitur dubitanter, non dicit, nihil quidem mihi sum conscius, sed nefscio, an hinc sim iustificatus, verùm asseueranter loquitur & planè dicit, Non sum in hoc iustificatus. Derogat igitur omnem iustificationem & iustificandi vim suis operibus, vt iste sit sensus: Ego quod grassiora & mortalia delicta nihil mihi sum conscius, sed scio me bonis operibus pro virili studuisse, & ea nullô inter exercuisse; attamen vicissim scio, quod per ista opera meo non sim iustificatus, quod in ijs iusticiam & salutem habere nequaquam, quoniam sunt 1. debita. 2. imperfecta, Et 3. multis venialibus peccatis permixta. Quæ autem consequentia est, ex operibus nemo iustificatur, nec de remissione peccatorum ex ijs potest esse certus: quare omnino nequit esse certus? Num quia hoc medium non concludit, non dari possunt alia, certitudinem inferentia.

Fallit autem Bellarminus, & fallitur, dum scribit, hanc expositionem repugnare scopo & proposito Apostoli, volentis dehortari à iudicio temerario, & ideo dicentis, neque memetipsum iudico. Singula enim cohærent optimè. Ego me ipsum non iudico, non me iustifico, non laudem & gloriam quæro in operibus. Etsi enim nihil mihi sim conscius, non tamen proptereà coram Deo sum iustificatus. Solus enim Deus est, qui me iudicat. Quare humana iudicia non sunt magnoperè attendenda. Demonstrat igitur vanitatem iudiciorum humanorum, 1. ab impossibili, & exemplo proprio, quia ipse seipsum ex externis operibus iudicare & iustificare nequeat: multò minus hoc alij facere poterunt. 2. à Proprio Dei, quòd solius Dei sit iudicare, & homines vel absoluere vel condemnare. IX. Cap. VI. Producit varia loca Prophetarum & Apostolorum, quæ in tres classes dispesci possunt. In prima collocat ista dicta, quæ ostendunt prærequiri contritionem, fidem, pœnitentiam & conuersionem, si aliquis debeat esse iustus vel iustificatus, qualia leguntur. Deut: 4. 2. Paralip. 6. Ejd 1. Ezech. 18. Iohan. 13. Luc. 13 Actor. 8. &c. At nemo, inquit, certu esse potest, præsertim certitudine fidei, se toto corde conuersum esse ad Dominum, & fidem ac pœnitentia habere qualis requiritur, cum in nulla Scriptura testimonium eiusmodi inueniatur de fide & pœnitentia nostra in particulari. Et hinc concludit. Neminem posse certum esse de gratia Dei & peccatorum remissione.

Respon. Minor falsa est. Quamuis enim in Scripturâ non extet, hunc vel illum credere, tamen extat promissio, quòd DEVS fidem & pœnitentiam operari velit in hominibus obice non ponentibus: Prætereà institutæ sunt Sacramenta, vt ijs fides confirmetur; ordinatum est ministerium, cuius opera peccata remittuntur, & fides accenditur. Ex auditu enim fides est. Quare qui audit, nec ponit obicem, is fidem accipit.

Deinde certus esse possum de mea pœnitentia.

1. ob promissionum certitudinem. 2. Verbi & Sacramentorum efficaciam. 3. Ministerij præconium. 4. Precum virtutem. 5. Sensum inhabitantis Spiritus. 6. Luctam carnis. 7. Studium bonorum operum. Vbicunque enim est displicentia vitiorum, ibi est Spiritus & renouatio; vel vbi est lucta carnis, ibi est homo renatus: vbi hic, ibi certitudo esse potest de fide. Quare quicunque sentit, sibi displicere peccata, quicunque seriò optat, vt à carne peccati liberetur, qui vult bonum, licèt perficere non inueniat, ille certò renatus est: si renatus, vtique fidem habet, & sic certus esse potest de remissione peccatorum. Sic patientia in cruce est infallibile signum veræ conuersionis & pœnitentiæ; semper ergo cogitentur hæc certitudinis fundamenta 1. Patris promissio. 2. Christi satisfactio. 3. Spiritus obsignatio. 4. Verbi annunciatio. 5. Fidei apprehensio. 6. Sacramentorum confirmatio. 7. Operum (quo pertinet lucta, displicentia mali, patientia) attestatio. 8. Crucis probatio. 9. Precum impetratio.

Hæc omnia in extremo die aperientur ; Vnde Germani dicunt. 1. GOTT gibts. 2. Christus erwirbts. 3. Der Heilige Geist bekræfftigets 4. Das Wort verkündigets. 5. Der Glaub empfehets. 6. Die Sacramenta versiegelens. 7. Die Wercke bezeugens. 8. Das Creutz prüfets. 9. Der Jüngste Tag eröfsnets. In his totus noster Christianismus & certitudo salutis consistit.

X. In secunda classe ponit ea dicta, quæ de gratia DEI & remissione peccatorum dubitanter loquuntur. Horum quatuor præcipuè commemorat. Primum extat Danielis 4. v. 24. Forsitan ignoscet Deus delictis tuis,

Responsio: est vitium vulgatæ versionis, quia in textu originali dubitativa particula non habetur. verba sic sonant: הֵן תֶּהֱוֵא אַרְכָא לִשְׁלֵוְתָךְ Ecce erit prolongatio paci tuæ. Luther. So wird Gott gedult haben mit deinen sünden. Vnde apparet, quòd verba Prophetæ minimè sint dubitativa, sed maximè asseueratiua. Possunt autem vel de temporali pace & regno Nebucadnezaris; vel de spirituali remissione peccatorum intelligi. Pagninus quidem vertit, sifortè, sed nullus facilè locus monstrabitur vbi particulari חֵן accipiatur pro dubitationis nota, sed tum plerumque adhibetur, cùm Prophetæ aliquid certi & eximij prolaturi sunt, vt auditores reddat attentos.

XI. Secundum extat Ioëlis 2. vers. 14. Quis scit, an conuertatur & ignoscat Deus, & relinquat post se benedictionem?

Respon. Verba sic habent, מִי יוֹדֵעַ יָשׁוּב וְנִחָם

Quis scit si conuertatur & pœniteat eum? Wer weis/es mag jn widerumb gerewen / vnd einen Segen hinder sich lassen : Non autem exindè colligi potest dubitatio Papistica. Sermo enim est non de remissione peccatorum , sed de immissione pœnarum temporalium. Minatus namque est in præcedentibus Propheta varia supplicia , euersionem , sterilitatem &c. pōst addit consolationem & adhortationem ad pœnitentiam, addita ratione, quia fortè passurum, vt Dominus mutet suum decretum de pœnis temporalibus, & largiatur benedictionem. Concedimus autem libenter, nos incertos esse, an Deus semper pœnas auertat, quia pios etiam iustificatos castigat. Quæ autem est consequentia: Certo scire non possumus, an Deus pœnas temporales sit auersurus: Ergo nec scire possumus, an peccata sit remissurus? Ab immissione pœnæ ad dimissionem culpæ argumentari non conceditur.


### XII. The third exists in Jonah 3

XII. The third exists in Jonah 3. v. 9. Who knows, if God may turn, and forgive.

I respond similarly, that it does not speak of the remission of guilt, but of the averting of temporal punishment. And we add, that that phrase, Who knows, is not so much of one doubting, as of one hoping well and desiring the help of God as appears from the sayings, 2. Sam. 12. v. 22. Joel 2. ver. 14.

XIII. The fourth testimony exists in Acts 8. v. 22. Repent of this thy wickedness, and pray God if perhaps the thought of thine heart may be forgiven thee.

I respond. The speech of the Apostle is conditional, presupposing true and serious repentance. But where this has a place, there remission follows not doubtfully and perhaps, but infallibly, just as the whole scripture cries out, if you shall have repented, you shall certainly live. Therefore the sense cannot be here, If you shall have performed serious repentance, then perhaps it will be remitted. For this is contrary to the whole Scripture, and the analogy of faith, and the assertions of the Papists themselves.

A safer and more convenient solution is to be sought. We therefore explain those words. 1. That the particle ἄρα is not always a mark of one doubting, signifying perhaps, but more often of one asserting, examples of which thing are read. Exod. 32. verse 30. Num. 20, verse 18. Joshua 14. v. 12. Jud. 15. v 12. 1. Sam. 14. v. 6. See the explanation of these in part. 2. Phil. sobr. sect. 1. c. 4. Quest. 11. page 680. & seq. It can therefore and ought, in that text of Acts 8 also, to have an assertive sense, Repent and it shall be forgiven. For otherwise, if you understand it doubtfully, this absurdity will follow, that with true repentance posited, the forgiveness of sins is nevertheless uncertain, which is contrary to the whole of Scripture, which testifies that God no longer remembers transgressions, if anyone seriously turns himself to Him, and performs true repentance. Wherefore we interpret it rather in an assertive sense, so that εἰ ἄρα may be the same as ὅπως δή so that indeed it may be forgiven you, not in a doubting manner but in a syllogistic manner. 2. If those words ought to obtain a doubting sense, then it can be said from an abundance that Peter doubted not concerning the indulgence of God, but concerning the repentance of Simon Magus, for the reason that he was entirely in the gall of bitterness verse 23. and there was little hope of true amendment remaining. Those words, therefore, if perhaps, are not referred to the condition of repentance and prayer, but to the future act of remission itself, which, viewed absolutely, was uncertain. For it is one thing to speak conditionally, another absolutely. In this way the justification of one's neighbor is uncertain, not in that. XIV. The third contains sayings speaking of fear such as exist in Proverbs 2. 2. Cor. 10. Philip 2. 1. Pet. 1. 2. Pet. 1. etc. Resp. 1. A distinction must be made between servile and filial fear. This (not that) can well consist with the certainty of grace and salvation. 2. Those sayings only prohibit carnal security, not they take away the believer's certainty of salvation.

XV. Chap. VII. Bellarmine produces some testimonies of the Fathers, but most are irrelevant, and do not directly touch the state of the question.

1. For some condemn carnal presumption and confidence in one's own powers, undertaken without true faith and repentance.

2. Some speak of the imperfection of the saints, that in this life they are not without sins, especially hidden ones.

3. Some deal with the impossibility of knowledge as limited, not absolute, that is, that from present things (prosperous or adverse) and external state we cannot conclude the grace of God, but they do not imply that it is absolutely uncertain.

4. Some distinguish between human and divine judgment. With respect to the former, something often appears clean which before God is filthy; by which method the perfection of inherent righteousness is indeed refuted, but not the certainty of grace.

5. Some concern the certainty of perseverance, about which our question is not instituted.

6. Some, finally, are opposed only to carnal security; when the ungodly presume certainty, and abuse divine promises for a license to sin, which security arises from the instinct of Satan, the corruption of nature, ignorance of the word, abuse of external happiness, and the opinion of one's own righteousness. We ourselves tax and disapprove of all these things, but meanwhile the Orthodox Fathers never taught that the certainty of faith should be weakened or denied because of the perversity of hypocrites.

XVI. Chap. VIII. He produces four reasons, which he himself calls excellent: The first is as follows: Nothing can be certain with the certainty of faith, unless it is either immediately contained in the word of God, or deduced from the word of God by evident consequence. For faith is nothing but if it rests upon divine authority. But that this or that person in particular is justified is neither contained immediately in the word of God, nor can it be deduced from it by good consequence: Wherefore this cannot be certain with the certainty of faith.

I respond. 1. We admit the major premise, and the Romanists ought to be mindful of that, in the place concerning traditions, which the Tridentine Fathers decree are to be regarded with equal affection of piety as the written word of God; yet they cannot be proved from the Scriptures either immediately or by consequence. 2. The minor premise is false, since that certainty can be very well deduced from the word of God and his promises. For where the genus is held, there also is held that which is contained under the genus, or is included in the genus. Now indeed the genus is held in the Scriptures, namely the universal promise: He who believes shall be saved, Mark 16:16. Under this universal, the subsumption is easy, since from genus to species, and from species to individual, the inference is always firm and indubitable.

XVII. The Papists object, however, that they willingly concede that sins are remitted to the believer and the penitent; but that it is uncertain whether anyone truly believes and performs serious repentance. To this πρωθύστερον I have responded in decad. 2, disputat. 8, qu. 4, thes. 26, and following, where I clearly showed that someone can be certain of his own faith and repentance, both a priori, or by reason of the causes, and a posteriori, or by reason of the signs.

A priori by concluding thus: the cause being placed in act, the effect follows certainly. But the cause of your faith is already placed in act, namely the grace of God, the merit of Christ, the word and the Sacraments, which are the most certain means of faith. You hear the word and you use the Sacraments. Wherefore the effect will most certainly be present, nor do you have any reason any longer to doubt concerning your faith. For the confirmation of the minor premise, it is to be noted that on our part nothing else is required than that we do not hinder, nor place an obstacle in the way of the working Holy Spirit. Whoever therefore conducts himself passively, and does not stubbornly resist, he neither can nor ought to doubt concerning the efficacious operation of the Spirit and the word; that which can be illustrated by the example of solar illumination and spiritual healing. Therefore, always ask the doubter: Do you wish to resist? If you affirm it, he is stubborn. If you deny it, the cause is placed in act, and it is not hindered: Wherefore the effect follows infallibly.

That certainty shines forth a posteriori, if the marks or effects of true faith and repentance are attended to, such as: 1. The desire for divine grace. 2. Renewal and interior struggle. 3. The testimony of the moving Spirit. 4. And the diligent observance of the law, or the exercise of good works. From there, indeed, such an argument can be formed: Wherever the consequent is found, there the antecedent cannot be absent: Now you yourself subsume: I perceive in myself the effects following true faith. And soon a firm conclusion will follow, that true faith and repentance are by no means absent.

XVIII But Bellarmine objects two things, since such a subsumption is not only false, but also impossible unless a special revelation is present.

1. He alleges the saying of Jeremiah 17:9: The heart of man is perverse and inscrutable: who shall know it? I respond: I do not see what kind of argument can be formed from this for the Popish opinion. The Prophet speaks of the natural corruption of the human heart, that it is perverse ואנש and supplanting, or anxious: From this, however, it does not follow that no certainty of grace is given. For the guilt of natural depravity is remitted through Christ, and this remission is graciously sealed in the hearts of the faithful, whence arises πληροφορία and certainty. Furthermore, although others cannot know or search out the heart of their neighbor, yet everyone can test himself, and know whether he is in a state of wrath or of grace.

3. We see, he says, in reality many are deceived, who think they have what they do not have, which he proves by the example of Peter wishing to die with Christ, and Paul persecuting the Church, and martyrs among heretics. Resp. 1. It is one thing to have confidence relying on promises, another to have a rash presumption of strength without a promise. The former was lacking in Peter, the latter was present, and therefore we ought not to wonder that he fell. 2. Paul was an unbeliever, and he erred in doctrine, and thus he was deceived by his own opinion: but we are speaking of the faithful, and those addicted to the true faith, who hear the word sincerely preached, and receive it with desire, and thus become certain of grace. We give the same answer to the examples of martyrs in false doctrine, since they are not true martyrs, because the cause, not the punishment, makes the martyr, and we are disputing about the faithful, not about heretics.

XIX. This is the second reason, that no one is bound to believe with the certainty of faith that his sins have been forgiven him. For such an article is contained in no creed of faith. And such a precept is found in no ecclesiastical canon.

I answer, it is enough that the genus and universal proposition is held: I believe in the forgiveness of sins. Under this genus anyone can, and ought to, subsume himself in the individual. Nor does that article signify only this: that in the Church baptism is given for the forgiveness of sins. For even the demons believe this, and yet they are not for that reason imbued with justifying faith. And therefore that historical assent does not suffice, but a special confidence must be applied in addition, by which the forgiveness of sins is certainly applied. He who does not do this is an unbeliever and impious, but not a heretic. For he who does not believe what he ought to believe, he is finally a heretic. But the impious as such are not bound to believe in pardon, but only then, when they do penance. Therefore as long as they remain in their sins, they are to be called unbelievers and impenitent, but not heretics.

XX. Third reason: It is not expedient that men should ordinarily have certainty of their own grace, because that begets pride, whereas ignorance of this secret preserves and increases humility.

Resp. 1. No Biblical dogma begets pride; but the dogma concerning the certainty of grace is Biblical, or deduced from the Scriptures. Wherefore it does not beget pride.

2. Certainty of remission and humility of mind are not contrary but subordinate. For we are so certain of salvation that we must nevertheless work it out with fear and trembling.

3. David, as also other saints, were most certain, and yet not proud on that account, but always humble, and adhering to God in intimate subjection.

4. Whatever dogma produces desperation and perpetual anxiety of mind, that is rather to be disapproved. But we have proven above that the Papistic dogma concerning the uncertainty of grace is such.

5. A distinction must be made between Legal and Evangelical righteousness; the former, since it relies on one's own merits, exalts; the latter, since it is founded outside of us in Christ, makes us humble and lowly in respect to ourselves, although it makes us confident and certain in respect to God, who does not impute sins.

6. The use of a thing is one thing, the abuse another. Certain confidence of grace is to be used for humility, not abused for elation. If it happens otherwise, that occurs not of itself, as if certainty begat pride, but accidentally, through the malice and abuse of men.

7. If certainty begets arrogance, why did God reveal their own justification to some?

But you object, Jesuit, that this was done because God foresaw that they were so rooted in charity and humility that there was no danger of elation.

Resp. 1. καθ' αὑτὸ presupposes κατὰ παντὸς. Wherefore if certainty produces pride of itself, then always it will bring forth, and no exception will have a place; therefore, the principle is begged while recourse is had to the foreknowledge of God.…

Those who are adorned with greater gifts are more prone to pride than others, 2 Cor. 12:7. Therefore, in them, the certainty of grace would more generate elation.

XXI. The fourth and final reason: In reality, such certainty is not present to the faithful, which it proves: 1. Because to some, by a singular benefit, the grace of God has been revealed; as to Anthony, Gallus, and Francis. Wherefore this knowledge is not common to the faithful.

Resp. 1. Concerning those saints and those revelations which the Jesuit commemorates, it is still possible to doubt greatly.

2. There is no consequence in the argument. For Christ also revealed faith singularly to Paul; therefore, because of that, is the knowledge of faith not common?

3. Wherefore a fallacy of cause is committed; for special revelations, of which Scripture makes mention, do not imply that the certainty of grace does not belong to others, but rather they were made, both for the sake of the saints themselves to whom this was revealed, so that they might resist the temptations of Satan more readily; and for the sake of others, so that by their example they might be uplifted in faith, which is expressly said of Peter, Luke 22:32, and of Paul, 2 Tim. 1:16, and of Abraham, Rom. 4:16.

XXII. II. It is no less certain that certain others, otherwise most perfect, trembled not moderately at their death because of this uncertainty.

Resp. The doubting of the saints is a mark of infirmity, not a foundation of uncertainty. It shows what more often happens in fact, not what ought to happen by right. We confess that many tremble on account of the weakness of the flesh: but they ought to believe and firmly trust on account of the goodness of God. Many doubt even in their death throes about the true religion, although they have lived for a very long time in the true Church; but must it be inferred from this that no one can be certain which religion is true, which is false? A distinction must be made between a question of law and of fact. It is the former, not the latter, that is being debated in the present place.

XXIII. III. The experience of the heretics of this time proves the same thing most clearly. For although they all without exception boast of this certainty, yet by their own opinion very many are deceived, whereas all of ours are not.

Resp: Rash presumption is one thing, fiducial certainty is another. Presumption is found in heretics; fiducial certainty in the orthodox alone. Therefore that example is irrelevant and foreign to the question. Nor does it follow that true confidence is given in all those who believe themselves to be righteous on account of the imputed merits of Christ. For true πληροφορία (full assurance) not only presupposes assent in this article, but also in others. Whoever errs in the foundation, they can indeed presume confidence, but they never truly obtain it.

XXIV. And thus we have run through all those arguments so far which Bellarmine brought forward for asserting the profane dogma of uncertainty, and these having been sufficiently refuted, we put an end both to this disputation and to the whole Anthropological college; giving thanks to the Most High for the assistance of the Holy Spirit, and supplicating the same, that He may preserve the deposit of sacred doctrine; that He may confirm us in it, and powerfully build us up against any machinations of adversaries; so that His name may be hallowed among us, His kingdom may come, and His will may be done, as in heaven by the Church triumphant, so by us in the Church militant; and so may we always remain most certain of the way of Scripture, through which we must go, of the way of faith, in which we must proceed, of the way of salvation, to which we must uniquely tend; and may we perpetually sigh for it. To Him alone, the blessed and wise God, be honor, and power, and glory, and blessing, to be ended by no ages, AMEN.

Latin:

XII. Tertium extat Ionæ 3. v. 9. Quis scit, si conuertatur Deus, & ignoscat.

Respon. similiter, quòd non loquatur de remissione culpæ, sed aversione pœnæ temporalis. Et addimus, quòd phrasis illa, Quis scit, non tàm dubitantis sit, quàm benè sperantis & opem Dei desiderantis vt apparet ex dictis, 2. Sam. 12. v. 22. Ioel 2. ver. 14.

XIII. Quartum testimonium extat Actor. 8. v. 22. Pœnitentiam age ab hac nequitia tua, & roga Deum si fortè remittatur tibi cogitatio cordis tui.

Resp. Conditionata est locutio Apostoli, præsupponens veram & seriam pœnitentiam. Hæc autem vbi locum habet, ibi non dubitatiuè & fortè sed infallibiliter sequitur remissio, quemadmodum vniuersa scriptura clamat, si egeritis pœnitentiam, viuetis certò. Nequit igitur hic esse sensus, Si seriam egeris pœnitentiam, tum fortè remittetur. Hoc enim toti Scripturæ, & analogiæ fidei, & ipsis Papicolarum assertionibus contraria-

tutior éaque commoda quaerenda est διέλυσις. Explicamus proindè verba illa. 1. Quod particula ἄρα non semper sit nota dubitantis, significans fortè, sed saepiùs asseuerantis, cuius rei exempla leguntur. Exod. 32. vers. 30. Num. 20, vers. 18. Iosuae 14. v. 12. Iud. 15. v 12. 1. Sam. 14. v. 6. Quorum explicationem vide parte. 2. Phil. sobr. sect. 1. c. 4. Quaest. 11. pag. 680. & seq. Potest igitur & debet, in isto etiam textu Act. 8. asseuerativum habere sensum, Age poenitentiam & remittetur. Aliàs enim, si dubitatiuè intelligas, sequetur hoc absurdum, quòd positâ verâ poenitentiâ, nihilominus incerta sit peccatorum venia, quod vniuersae Scripturae contrarium, quae testatur, Deum non ampliùs recordari delictorum, si quis ad ipsum seriò se conuertat, veramq; poenitentiam agat. Quare sensu potius assertiuo interpretamur, vt εἰ ἄρα sit idom quod ὅπως δή vt sanè dimittatur tibi, non ἀπορηματικῶς sed συλλογιστικῶς. 2. Si dubitativum sensum obtinere debeant verba ista, tunc ex abundanti dici poterit, quòd Petrus dubitauerit non de Dei indulgentia, sed de Simonis Magi resipiscentia, eò quòd in felle amaritudinis totus erat vers. 23. exigua verae emendationis spes fuerit reliqua. Verba igitur ista, si fortè, non referuntur ad conditionem poenitentiae & precationis, sed ad ipsum futurum actum remissionis, qui absolutè spectatus, erat incertus. Nam aliud est loqui conditionatè, aliud absolutè. Hoc modo incerta est proximi iustificatio, non isto. XIV. Tertia continet dicta de timore loquentia qualia extant Prouerb. 2. 2. Cor. 10. Philip 2. 1. Pet. 1. 2. Pet. 1. &c. Resp. 1. Distingui debet inter timorem seruitem & filialem. Hic, (non ille) cum certitudine gratiae & salutis benè consistere potest. 2. Dicta ista tantùm prohibent carnalem securitatem, non tollunt fidelem salutis certitudinem.

XV. Cap. VII. Producit Bellarminus aliquot Patrum testimonia, sed pleraq; sunt impertinentia, nec directè statum quæstionis attingunt.

1. Nam Quædam damnant carnalem præsumptionem, & propriarum virium confidentiam, sine verâ fide & pœnitentiâ susceptam.

2. Quædam loquuntur de sanctorum imperfectione, quòd in hac vitâ non sint absq; peccatis, præsertim occultis.

3. Quædam agunt de impossibilitate cognitionis limitatâ, non absolutâ, quòd nempè ex rebus præsentibus (prosperis vel aduersis) & statu externo nequeamus cõcludere gratiam Dei, non autem innuunt, quòd absolutè illa sit incerta.

4. Quædam distinguunt inter iudicium humanum & diuinum. Respectu illius sæpè apparet aliquid mundum, quod coram Deo est sordidum; quo pacto refellitur quidem perfectio inhærentis iustitiæ, sed non certitudo gratiæ.

5. Quædam concernunt certitudinem perseuerantiæ, de qua nostra non est instituta quæstio.

6. Quædam deniq; oppositâ sunt carnali tantùm securitati; cùm impij præsumunt certitudinem, & diuinis promissionibus abutuntur ad peccandi licentiam, quæ securitas oritur ex instinctu Satanæ, corruptione naturæ; ignorantiâ verbi, abusu felicitatis externæ, & opinione propriæ Iustitiæ. Hæc omnia nos ipsi taxamus & improbamus, interim verò certitudinem fidei ob hypocritarum peruersitatem, vel labefactandam, vel negandam esse nunquam docuerunt Patres Orthodoxi.

XVI. Cap. IIX. producit quatuor rationes, quas ipse vocat egregias: Prima sic habet: Non potest aliquid certum esse certitudine fidei, nisi aut immediatè contineatur in verbo Dei, aut ex verbo Dei per evidentem consequentiam deducatur. Fides enim non est, nisi verbi diuini authoritate nitatur. At hunc vel illum in particulari esse iustificatum, nec immediatè continetur in verbo Dei, nec ex illo per bonam consequentiam deduci potest: Quare hoc nequit esse certum certitudine fidei.

Respond. 1. Maiorem admittimus & debebant Romanenses illius memores esse, in loco de traditionibus, quas pari pietatis affectu cum scripto Dei verbo suspiciendas esse statuunt Patres Tridentini; ex Scripturis autem nec immediatè nec per consequentiam probari queunt. 2. Minor falsa est, quoniam illa certitudo ex Dei verbo & promissionibus optimè potest deduci. Vbi enim habetur genus, ibi & illud habetur, quod sub genere continetur, vel generi est inclusum. Iam verò genus habetur in Scripturis, nempè vniuersalis promissio: Qui crediderit saluus erit, Marci 16. v. 16. sub hac vniuersali facilis est subsumptio, siquidem à genere ad speciem, à specie ad indiuiduum firma semper & indubitata est collectio.

XVII. Excipiunt vero Pontificij, se lubenter concedere, credenti & pœnitenti peccata remitti; sed incertum esse, num quis verè credat & seriam pænitentiam agat. Ad hoc πρωθύστερον respondi decad. 2. disputat. 8. qu. 4. thes. 26. & seqq. vbi luculenter ostendi, quòd aliquis de fide & pœnitentia sua possit certus esse, tùm à priori vel ratione causarum, tùm à posteriori vel ratione notarum.

A priori sic colligendo: posita causâ in actu certò sequitur effectus. At fidei tuæ causa iam in actu est posita, videlicet gratia Dei, meritum Christi; verbum & Sacramenta, quæ sunt fidei media certissima. Audis autem verbum & vteris Sacramentis. Quare effectus certissimè aderit, nec vllam amplius de fide tua dubitandi rationem habes. Pro minoris confirmatione notandum, quòd ex parte nostri nihil aliud requiratur, quàm nè impediamus, nèque obicem ponamus operanti Spiritui sancto. Quicunque igitur se habet passiuè, nec resistit contumaciter, ille de efficaci Spiritus & verbi operatione dubitare nec potest, nec debet; id quod illustrari potest exemplo illuminationis solaris, & sanationis spiritualis. Semper ergo quæras dubitantem; Num velis resistere? Si affirmes, contumax est. Si neges causa in actu posita est, nec impeditur: Quare effectus infallibiliter sequitur.

A posteriori elucescit illa certitudo, si attendantur notæ vel effectus veræ fidei & pœnitentiæ, qualia sunt. 1. Gratiæ diuinæ desiderium. 2. Renouatio & lucta interior. 3. Spiritus moventis testificatio. 4. Et studiosą legis obseruatio, vel bonorum operum exercitium. Inde verò tale formari potest argumentum. Vbicunq; consequens reperitur, ibi antecedens abesse nequit: Iam subsumas ipse: in me deprehēdo effectus, veram fidem consequentes. Et mox sequetur firma conclusio, fidem veram & pœnitentiam nequaquam abesse.

XIIX Sed duo Bellarminus obuertit, cum talis subsumtio non tantùm falsa, sed etiam impossibilis sit nisi adsit specialis reuelatio.

1. Allegat dictum Ierem. 17. v. 9. Pravum est cor hominis & inscrutabile: quis cognoscet illud? Respon. Non video, quale hinc argumentum pro opinione Papistica formari possit. Loquitur Propheta de cordis humani corruptione naturali, quòd sit pravum ואנש & supplantativum, vel anxium: Hinc autem non sequitur, quòd nulla detur certitudo gratiæ. Nam reatus prauitatis naturalis remittitur per Christum, & hæc remissio in cordibus fidelium gratiosè obsignatur, vnde oritur πληροφορία & certitudo. Deinde licèt alij cor proximi cognoscere aut perscrutari nequeant, quiuis tamen seipsum probare, & nùm in statu iræ vel gratiæ sit cognoscere potest.

3. Videmus, inquit, reipsa multos falli, qui se putant habere, quod non habent, quod probat exemplo Petri volentis cum Christo mori, & Pauli persequentis Ecclesiam, & martyrum inter hæreticos. Resp. 1. Aliud est fiducia nitens promissionibus, aliud est temeraria virium præsumtio sine promissione. Illa Petro defuit, hæc adfuit, ideoque ipsum lapsum esse mirari non debemus. 2. Paulus erat infidelis, & errabat in doctrina, atq; sic opinione sua est deceptus: Nos autem loquimur de fidelibus, & veræ fidei addictis, qui verbum sincerè prædicatum audiunt, & cum desiderio recipiunt, atq; sic de gratia certi fiunt. Idem respondemus ad exempla martyrum in falsa doctrina, quippè qui non sunt veri martyres, cùm causa non pœna faciat martyrem, & nos de fidelibus, non autem hæreticis disputemus.

XIX. Secunda ratio hæc est, quòd nemo teneatur certò credere certitudine fidei, sibi remissa esse peccata. Nam eiusmodi articulus in nullo symbolo fidei continetur. Et eiusmodi præceptum in nullo canone Ecclesiastico reperitur.

Respondeo, satis est quòd habeatur genus & propositio vniuersalis: Credo remissionem peccatorum. Sub hoc genere quiuis de se in indiuiduo potest, & debet subsumere. Neque articulus ille tantùm hoc significat; In Ecclesia dari Baptismum in remissionem peccatorum. Hoc enim & Dæmones credunt, nec tamen ob id fide iustificante imbuti sunt. Ideoque non sufficit assensus ille historicus, sed adhibenda insuper est fiducia specialis, quâ remissio peccatorum certò applicetur. Quod qui non facit, infidelis est & impius, non verò hæreticus. Qui enim non credit, quod credere debet, is demum hæreticus est. Impij verò quâ tales, non tenentur credere veniam, sed tùm demum, quando agunt pœnitentiam. Ersio quamdiu manent in peccatis, infideles dicendi sunt & impœnitentes, non autem hæretici.

XX. Tertia ratio: Non expedit vt homines habeant ordinariè certitudinem de propria gratia, quia illa gignit superbiam, ignoratio autem huius secreti, conseruat & auget humilitatem.

Resp. 1. Nullum dogma Biblicum gignit superbiam; At verò dogma de certitudine gratię est Biblicũ, vel è Scripturis deductum. Quare superbiam non gignit.

2. Certitudo remissionis & humilitas mentis non sunt contraria sed subordinata. Sic enim certi sumus de salute, vt nihilominus illam operari debeamus cum timore & tremore.

3. David, vt & alij sancti fuere certissimi, nec tamen ob id superbi, sed humiles semper, & Deo intimâ subiectione adhærentes.

4. Quodcunq́; dogma parit desperationem, & perpetuam animi anxietatem, illud potius improbandũ est. Ita verò se habere dogma Papisticum de incertitudine gratiæ, suprà evicimus.

5. Distinguendum est inter iustitiam Legalem & Evangelicam; Illa, cum proprijs meritis nitatur, extollit; Hæc cùm extra nos in Christo fundetur, humiles & demissos facit ratione nostri, licèt confidentes certosq́; efficiat ratione Dei, non imputantis peccata.

6. Aliud est vsus, aliud abusus rei. Certâ gratiæ fiduciâ vtendum est ad humilitatem, non abutendum ad elationem. Aliter si eveniat, fit illud non per se, ac si certitudo pareret superbiam, sed per accidens, & hominum malitiam & abusum.

7. Si certitudo parit arrogantiam, cur Deus aliquibus Iustificationem propriam reuelauit?

Verùm excipis Iesuita, id factum, quia Deus præuiderit illos in charitate & humilitate ita radicatos esse, vt non sit vllum ab elatione periculum.

Resp. 1. καθ' αὑτὸ præsupponit κατὰ παντὸς. Quare si certitudo parit superbiam per se, tum semper pariet, nec ylla exceptio locu habebit, petitur ergo principiu, dum ad Dei præuisione confugitur.

2 Qui maioribus donis sunt ornati, hi pronrores sunt ad superbiam, quam alij, 2. Cor. 12. v. 7. Ergo in illis certitudo gratiæ magis elationem gigneret.

XXI. Quarta & postrema ratio: Reipsa fidelibus eiusmodi certitudo non adest, quod probat, 1. Quia nonnullis singulari beneficio reuelata est Dei gratia; vt Anthonio, Gallo & Francisco. Quare notitia hæc non est fidelibus communis.

Resp. 1. Quos Iesuwita sanctos, & quas reuelationes commemorat, de ijs adhuc plurimùm dubitari potest.

2. Nulla inest argumento consequentia. Nam & Christus Paulo singulariter reuelauit fidem, Ergóne ob id notitia fidei non est communis?

3. Quare committitur elenchus causæ; speciales enim reuelationes, quarum Scriptura meminit, nõ innuunt, quòd certitudo gratiæ alijs haut competat, sed potius factæ sunt, tum ob ipsos sanctos, quibus hoc reuelatum, vt in tentationibus Satanæ resisterent alacriùs; tum ob alios, vt illorum exemplo in fide erigerentur, quod de Petro expressè dicitur, Lu. 22. v. 32. & de Paulo 2. Tim. 1. v. 16 & de Abrahamo Rom. 4 v. 16.

XXII. II. Non minus constat, alios quosdam, alioqui perfectissimos, in obitu suo propter hoc incertum non mediocriter trepidasse.

Resp. Dubitatio sanctorum nota est infirmitatis, non firmamentum incertitudinis. Ostendit quid sæpiùs fiat de facto, non quid fieri debeat de iure. Fatemur multos trepidare, ob carnis inbecillitatē: deberent autē credere & firmiter confidere, ob Dei bonitatem. Multi ambigunt etiam in agone de vera religione, licèt diutissimè vixerint in vera Ecclesia; Num autē hinc inferri debet, quòd nemo possit certus esse, quę religio vera sit, quæ falsa? Distinguendum est inter quæstiohem iuris & facti De illâ non hâc, præsenti loco controuertitur.

XXIII. III. Idem apertissimè probat experientia hujus temporis hæreticorum. Nam cùm omnes omninò hanc certitudinem iactent, tamen ipsorum sententia falluntur plurimi, nostra autem omnes.

Resp: Aliud est temeraria præsumptio, aliud fiducialis certitudo. Præsumptio reperitur in hæreticis; fiducialis certitudo in solis orthodoxis. Est igitur exemplum illud impertinens, & à quæstine alienum. Nec sequitur quòd fiducia vera detur in omnibus ijs, qui credunt se iustos esse propter Christi merita imputata. Nam vera πληροφορία, non tantùm præsupponit assensum in hoc articulo, sed etiam in alijs. Quicunque errant in fundamento, illi fiduciam quidem præsumere possunt, sed verè nunquàm obtinent.

XXIV. Et ita percurrimus hactenus omnia illa Argumenta, quæ Bellarminus pro asserendo incertitudinis profano dogmate adduxit, quibus sufficienter solutis, finem tùm huic disputationi, tùm toti collegio Anthropologico imponimus; gratias agentes Altissimo procumini S. sancti adiutorio, & eundem Venerati supplices, vt sacrosanctæ doctrinæ depositum conseruet; in illa nos confirmet, & contrà quæsuis aduersariorum molitiones potenter adstruat; quo nomen eius inter nos sanctificetur, regnum adueniat, & voluntas fiat, vt in cælis ab Ecclesia triumphante, sic à nobis in Ecclesia militante; adeoque semper certissimos & maneamus de viâ scripturæ, per quam eundum, de viâ fidei, in qua pergendum, de viâ salutis, ad quam vnicè tendendum; & perpetuò suspiramus. Ipsi soli benedicto & sapienti Deo, sit honor, & virtus, & gloria, & benedictio, nullis seculis terminanda, AMEN.


### The End

THE END.

Latin:

FINIS.
